### What to ask in the first meeting
A real consultation leaves you calmer than you walked in. You should leave with straight answers to these:
How often do you handle cases like mine? Family petitions, naturalization, asylum and removal defense are different work. You want someone who does your kind every week.
What is your fee, and what are the government fees, separately and in writing? A real office hands you a written agreement.
Who will actually work on my file? And how will we talk - phone, email, in person?
What could go wrong? An honest lawyer talks about risk. Only USCIS decides the outcome, so a promise of approval is a reason to leave.
Cash only, no receipt, a push to sign today, or a suggestion to leave something off a form: any one of those ends the meeting.
The government’s share of the bill
### How much does an immigration lawyer normally cost?
Each office sets its own fee, which is why you get it in writing. The government’s share is fixed: for citizenship, USCIS charges $760 to file Form N-400 on paper or $710 online, or a reduced $380 for those who qualify, and these fees are set by USCIS and adjusted from time to time (check the official N-400 page). For low-income people who qualify, LSEM’s civil legal help is free.
### What kind of case is it?
Immigration law is several jobs wearing one name, and knowing roughly which one is yours makes the first phone call shorter. Petitioning for a husband, a mother or a child is family work. Becoming a citizen is naturalization, often the most paperwork-heavy and the least dramatic. A person who was hurt, threatened or forced to work may have humanitarian options, the kind LSEM describes for victims of violent crime. And anything with the word “hearing” or “court” on it is the highest-stakes category of all, because missed dates there do not wait for you.
You do not have to diagnose yourself. That is the lawyer’s job. But walking in able to say “this is about my wife’s green card” or “I got a letter about a hearing” gets you to the right person faster, and keeps the first meeting about your life instead of about sorting folders. A lawyer who lives in family petitions every day may send an asylum case to a colleague, and that is a good sign, not a brush-off.
### Getting ready for the first appointment
Lay everything out on the table the night before: every notice in its envelope, the receipt numbers, copies of anything you filed before, passports, and that list of dates in your own handwriting. Put it in one folder you can carry with one hand. Write your questions on the front so you do not forget them when your heart is pounding in the waiting room.
If English is your second language, plan for it before the day, not at the desk. LSEM asks for interpreter requests on the first call to intake, and a private office should be asked the same thing when you book. Then, in the meeting, slow is fine. Ask them to repeat. Ask them to write it down. A good lawyer would rather explain twice than have you guess once.
One last habit that saves real grief: never hand over an original document you cannot replace. Bring originals so the lawyer can see them, but leave with them, and let the office make the copies. Ask for a copy of anything filed in your name, every time, and keep it in that same folder at home.
### When money is the wall
Cost is exactly how people end up at the wrong storefront. If a private lawyer is out of reach, call LSEM first. Their help is free for those who qualify by income, and if your case is not one they take, ask them where to go next. USCIS also points to the Justice Department’s list of recognized organizations, where accredited representatives work. The choice is never an expensive lawyer or a dangerous notario. There is a third door, and it has a phone number.

### Q. How do I find a good immigration lawyer?
A.  Check the credential first: a lawyer in good standing with a U.S. state bar or a DOJ-accredited representative at a recognized organization. In Missouri, the Missouri Bar’s free LawyerSearch shows lawyers in good standing who are accepting new clients. Then ask how often they handle your exact kind of case, and get the fee in writing.
### Q. How much is U.S. citizenship now?
A.  USCIS lists the Form N-400 fee as $760 on paper or $710 online, with a reduced $380 fee for those who qualify. If you ask for a reduced fee or a fee waiver, you must file on paper. Fees are set by USCIS and adjusted from time to time, so check the official N-400 page first.
### Q. How can I get a free immigration lawyer in the US?
A.  Start with legal aid. In eastern Missouri that is Legal Services of Eastern Missouri’s Immigration Law Program, 314.256.8705, which serves low-income individuals and the elderly for free. ## Car Detailing in St. Louis: What It Is, and What It’s Worth
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-succeed-in-the-st-louis-auto-detailing-industry
You slide into the car on the first warm day of spring and really see it for the first time in months: the chalky film of road salt down the doors, the grit ground into the floor mats, a windshield haze no wiper will touch, and a dull grey cast where the paint used to shine. Winter did this. Whether you park in Affton, Florissant, or out in St. Charles, a St. Louis winter is hard on a car — and this is the moment a lot of people start wondering whether a real detail is worth it.
Here’s the honest answer, plus how detailing actually differs from a car wash, what the different service tiers include, when to DIY, roughly what it costs, and how to choose a detailer who’ll protect your investment rather than just make it shiny for a week.
### The honest case for a real detail
For most St. Louis drivers, yes — at least once a year, and ideally twice. The reason is local: our winters coat a car in road salt that drives rust and corrosion, and our summers bake interiors and clear coat under strong sun. A proper detail (especially a spring one that strips out the season’s salt) does real protective work under the shine, and it pays off again at resale, where a clean, well-kept car reliably earns a better, faster offer. If you plan to keep a car for years or sell it well, detailing is one of the higher-return things you can do for it.
### Detailing vs. a car wash
A car wash cleans the surface. Detailing is a deep, meticulous restoration inside and out: thorough interior cleaning (vacuum, shampoo, conditioning), exterior paint decontamination and polishing, and a protective finish — wax, a longer-lasting sealant, or a ceramic coating that shields the paint for years. It’s the difference between “clean for now” and “protected and preserved.”
Think of it as a spectrum. An automatic car wash is maintenance — good for knocking salt off between details, though the brush-style tunnels can add fine swirl marks over time. A hand wash is gentler. A full detail is a different category of work entirely: hours of labor, specialized products, and a finish designed to last months, not days. Knowing which one you actually need for the job in front of you is the first step to not overpaying — or underdoing it.
### What the service tiers usually include
“Detailing” means wildly different things at different shops, so it helps to know the rough ladder before you call. Most detailers offer some version of these:
Basic / maintenance detail. A thorough wash, interior vacuum and wipe-down, windows, and a spray wax or quick sealant. Great upkeep between bigger services; the least expensive tier.
Full interior detail. Deep extraction of carpets and upholstery, shampooing, leather cleaning and conditioning, vents and crevices, and odor treatment. This is the one to book after a winter of salt and slush tracked inside, or before selling.
Full exterior detail. A careful hand wash, clay-bar decontamination to pull embedded grime out of the paint, and a wax or sealant. Some add a light polish to knock back haze.
Paint correction. Machine polishing that actually removes swirl marks, light scratches, and oxidation to restore real depth and gloss. Skilled, time-intensive work — the biggest visual transformation, and priced accordingly.
Ceramic coating. A semi-permanent protective layer applied over corrected paint that repels water, salt, and UV and can last years. The premium tier, and the one where a detailer’s skill matters most.
The single most useful habit when comparing shops: ask exactly what each named package includes, in writing. Two detailers can both sell a “full detail” that differ by hours of labor and a hundred dollars — you want to compare the same thing, not the same word.

### Wax, sealant, or ceramic coating?
These three are the protection step, and they’re easy to confuse. In plain terms: wax is the traditional finish — a warm shine that’s inexpensive but only lasts weeks to a couple of months. A sealant is a synthetic step up that bonds better and lasts several months. A ceramic coating is the durable option: a hard, glass-like layer that chemically bonds to the paint, sheds water and road salt, resists UV fade, and can last years with care.
For a St. Louis daily driver you plan to keep, a sealant or ceramic coating makes the most sense — the longer protection is exactly what fights our salt-and-sun cycle. If you’re detailing a car you’ll sell soon, a good wax or sealant delivers the shine buyers respond to without the coating’s cost. Match the protection to how long you’ll own the car.
### Why it matters more here
Our climate makes the case. Every winter, road salt coats your paint and cakes the undercarriage — and salt is a leading cause of rust and corrosion, the kind of damage that quietly eats a car’s value from underneath. A spring detail with a good undercarriage wash to strip out the season’s salt earns its keep by stopping rust before it starts.
Then summer flips the problem: intense sun and heat fade interiors, dry out leather and dashboards, and stress the clear coat. That’s the case for two details a year — one in spring to undo winter’s salt, one heading into or out of summer to protect against the sun. And if you’re about to sell or trade in, a professional detail routinely returns more than it costs in a better offer and a faster sale; a buyer’s first impression is almost entirely about how the car looks and smells.
### DIY or pro?
Regular washing and vacuuming at home is great upkeep — do it, especially rinsing salt off through the winter. A weekly-ish rinse that includes the wheel wells and a spray under the car does real anti-rust work for the price of a hose. Keep a basic kit — a couple of microfiber wash mitts, two buckets, a pH-neutral car soap, glass cleaner, and a handful of microfiber towels — and you can handle maintenance yourself all season.
Where a pro earns the money is the stuff that’s genuinely hard to do well yourself: paint correction (removing swirls and oxidation without burning the clear coat), ceramic coating application, deep interior extraction, and pre-sale details. Those take skill, specialized tools, and time most of us don’t have — and a machine polisher in inexperienced hands can do more harm than good. A fair rule: do the maintenance yourself, and hire out the transformation and the protection.
### What detailing typically costs
Prices vary widely by vehicle size, condition, and the shop, so treat these as rough brackets rather than quotes. A basic maintenance detail commonly runs in the low hundreds; a full interior-and-exterior detail lands higher depending on how much work the car needs. Paint correction is priced by the hour or by the stage and can climb quickly on a neglected finish, and a full ceramic-coating package — which includes the correction first — is the biggest single spend, often several hundred to a few thousand dollars depending on the coating and the car.
The honest way to shop it: get itemized quotes from two or three detailers for the same defined service, and ask what’s included and how long it’ll take. A quote that’s dramatically cheaper usually means fewer steps or less labor, not a better deal. And a coating quoted without any paint-correction step first is a red flag — you’d be sealing the swirls in.

### How to choose a detailer
Once you know what you want, vetting the shop is straightforward:
Get the package in writing. Ask exactly what each tier includes so you’re comparing the same thing across shops.
Read reviews for specifics — consistent results, careful work, no missed spots, cars ready when promised. Look for photos of real jobs, since a five-star average tells you little on its own.
Ask about ceramic coating warranties if that’s what you’re after; a real coating comes with real terms, and a real installer will explain the prep and the maintenance the warranty requires.
Mobile or shop? Mobile detailers come to you and are perfect for maintenance and interior work; a fixed shop usually has more equipment, controlled lighting, and space for heavy correction and coatings. Pick what fits the job.
Ask to see before-and-afters of cars like yours. A detailer proud of their correction work will have plenty.
### Don’t forget the interior
It’s easy to fixate on the paint, but the inside of the car is where you actually spend your time — and where a St. Louis summer does quiet damage. Parked in the sun, a dashboard and door panels bake, leather dries and cracks, and that faint musty smell can set in after humid months and a few spilled coffees. A full interior detail resets all of it: extraction of the carpets and seats, a proper leather clean-and-condition, vents and cupholders and seat tracks, and an odor treatment that actually removes the source rather than masking it.
Between details, a few small habits go a long way — a windshield sunshade to cut the dashboard heat, a quick weekly vacuum, and wiping down surfaces with the right products rather than whatever’s under the sink. Harsh household cleaners can dull or crack interior plastics and leather over time, so it’s worth using something made for a car’s materials. Protect the interior and the car doesn’t just clean up nicer at trade-in time; it’s a more pleasant place to sit every single day.
### A simple year-round routine
You don’t need to overthink it. A realistic St. Louis schedule looks like this: through winter, rinse the car (undercarriage included) whenever the salt is heavy. In spring, book a full detail to strip the salt and, if you’re keeping the car, refresh the sealant or coating. Through summer, keep up the washes and park in shade when you can to spare the interior and clear coat. That rhythm — DIY maintenance plus one or two real details a year — keeps a car looking sharp and holding its value for the price of a little attention.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between a car wash and detailing?
A.  A car wash cleans the exterior surface. Detailing is a deep, meticulous restoration inside and out — interior extraction and conditioning, paint decontamination and often polishing, and a protective finish like wax, sealant, or a ceramic coating. A wash makes a car clean for now; a detail leaves it cleaned, corrected, and protected for months.
### Q. How often should I detail my car in St. Louis?
A.  Twice a year suits most St. Louis drivers: a spring detail to strip out winter road salt (a leading cause of rust), and one around summer to protect the interior and paint from strong sun. Keep up simple washes and salt rinses in between, and that rhythm protects both the look and the resale value of the car.
### Q. Is a ceramic coating worth it?
A.  For a car you plan to keep, often yes. A ceramic coating bonds to the paint and repels water, road salt, and UV for years, which directly fights St. Louis’s salt-and-sun cycle and cuts down maintenance. It’s the priciest option and must be applied over corrected paint, so it’s best value on a car you’ll own a while rather than one you’re about to sell.
### Q. Can I detail my car myself?
A.  You can handle the maintenance — washing, vacuuming, glass, and especially rinsing off winter salt — with a basic kit and some time. What’s worth hiring out is the skilled work: machine paint correction, ceramic coating application, deep interior extraction, and pre-sale details, where the right tools and experience make a real difference and mistakes are costly.

That’s the short answer. The longer one is about what you’re hungry for, because the place that nails a crisp-edged carnitas taco is rarely the same place that nails a lamb barbacoa you have to eat leaning over the plate.
### Cherokee Street is still the first stop
Walk this stretch of Cherokee on a warm evening and you smell it before you see it: griddle smoke, charred onion, the sweet, sticky note of something with sugar in it from the ice cream counter. You can make a whole taco night of it here without moving the car, and that’s the argument for coming.
Taqueria El Bronco, 2817 Cherokee. St. Louis Magazine’s own Cherokee guide puts it plainly: “This longtime Cherokee spot favors food over décor.” Believe it. You come here for a plate of small tacos, the corn tortillas soft and a little oily from the griddle, onion and cilantro piled on, lime on the side. Nobody’s here for the wallpaper.
La Vallesana, 2801 Cherokee. The same guide’s advice is the right order of operations: “Top off cheap tacos and spicy burritos with a stop at the ice cream parlor.” Eat the hot thing, then the cold thing. The chile heat sitting on your lips when the ice cream hits is half the reason to go.
El Torito, 2753 Cherokee. A grocery store with a taco stand. Per that guide, you can “Grab overflowing tacos from the Tacos El Torito stand outside, or dine inside for the full menu.” Overflowing is accurate. Eat them standing up and fold them hard, or wear them.
Small taquerias change hours without telling the internet. If you’re crossing the metro for one specific counter, call or check its socials first. If you’re just hungry, go to the block. Something will be open, and something will smell good.
### Al pastor off a spit: the trompo test
Real al pastor comes off a trompo, a vertical spit stacked with marinated pork, the outside crisping and caramelizing as it turns, shaved off in thin, red-edged ribbons. A lot of places sell “al pastor” that was chopped on a flat-top instead. It can still taste good. It’s just a different thing, and once you’ve had the spit version, the difference is in the first bite: the charred tips, the fat that’s rendered instead of fried.
Mestiza, 3279 Hampton Avenue, calls itself “The best tacos in Lindenwood Park,” and its own site points you to the right order: “Go for Del Trompo, Birria Fundida, Casi Alucinógenos, and churros when you want something smoky, crisp, rich, and just sweet enough to finish strong.” Order the Del Trompo first. Its posted hours run noon to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday and noon to 8 p.m. on Sunday, and Monday isn’t on that list, so don’t plan a Monday taco night here.
### Birria, and the woman who sold it off her porch
Birria is a taco you hear before you taste: the crackle of a shell that’s been dipped in red, fatty broth and crisped on the griddle, then the slurp when you dunk it in a cup of consommé. It’s on half the menus in town now. One place built its whole name on it.
Taco Drip STL opened a takeout-only storefront at 1920 Carr Street in the Carr Square neighborhood, as St. Louis Magazine reported. The story behind it is better than any tagline. Stephanie Boyd, known as “Chef Stef,” started by selling tacos off her front porch, and the brand still carries the line “off-the-porch original STL birria tacos.” The same reporting says the menu runs to birria tacos, loaded drippin’ nachos, birria fries and crispy “birri-tos.” Bring napkins. The name is a warning, not a joke. It’s takeout, so check its socials for the day’s hours before you head over.
### Vegan tacos that don’t apologize
Terror Tacos, 3191 S. Grand. A fully vegan taco shop on South Grand, built, as St. Louis Magazine put it, to reflect the owners’ love of hardcore and metal music. The same story called it “a bold, in-your-face vegan taco joint” when it was coming to that address. Bring the friend who swears they hate fake meat and don’t tell them until the plate is empty.
### The Grove and Botanical Heights
Chico Bueno, 4156 Manchester Ave in the Grove, calls itself a “TAQUERIA DE BARRIO,” and the posted menu is short in the way good taco menus are. Every taco is $5. The one to order is the lamb barbacoa, built with “guajillo, cinnamon & clove,” warm spice you smell when the plate lands. The site says it’s “OPEN DAILY 11:00AM - 9:00PM,” and there are no reservations; you just walk in.
Taco Buddha, 1634 Tower Grove Ave in Botanical Heights, with sister shops at 7405 Pershing Ave in University City and 11111 Manchester Rd in Kirkwood. This one isn’t trying to be a Cherokee taqueria; it calls its roots “New Mex Tex.” The weekend move is breakfast tacos, served 8:30 a.m. to noon on Saturday and Sunday, eaten on a covered patio with a dog under the table. Weekdays from 3 to 5 p.m., dine-in happy hour means half-off chips, dips and house margaritas.
### Mission Taco became Session Taco, and then it was gone
It started in the Delmar Loop in 2013 as Mission Taco Joint. According to Sauce Magazine, Gruma Corp., the parent company of Mission Foods, sued over the Mission name in 2023; the settlement required a new name, and the brand became Session Taco in September 2024.
Then it shrank. Sauce reports the group closed Town & Country and Kirkwood in late 2025 and early 2026. The St. Charles location was converted into Sobremesa, a broader Mexican concept, in June 2026, and Sobremesa closed in September. The last two Session Tacos, in the Delmar Loop and Soulard, closed on Saturday, Oct. 17. In the Central West End, LaPez Mod Mex, which used to be a Session Taco, is closing too.
So if a list, an app or a friend sends you to any of those names, it’s sending you to an empty room. The good news is the list above. Every one of those kitchens is a short drive from where a Session Taco used to be.
### The average cost of a taco, and why tacos feel so expensive now
Here’s a real number instead of a guess: Chico Bueno’s posted menu puts every taco at $5, so a three-taco plate there runs $15 before a drink. That’s the honest frame for the average cost of a taco at a sit-down taqueria in this city. You don’t pay for one. You pay for the three or four it takes to feel full.
Why are tacos so expensive now? A taco is small, but everything in it is a cost a kitchen can’t cut: meat, a griddle running all day, a person pressing or warming every tortilla, rent on the block. Slow food like birria or barbacoa ties up a pot for hours. The best defense is the one the good spots already use. Short menus, high volume, no wasted trays.
For your wallet, the trick is simple. Compare by the order, not by the taco. A cheap-looking taco that’s half the size isn’t cheaper.
Quick detour for the Creve Coeur shop owners reading over someone’s shoulder: here’s how locals find you.
### How to order like you’ve done this before
A traditional taqueria taco is small and usually sits on two stacked corn tortillas. That second tortilla isn’t filler. It’s structure. Juicy fillings soak straight through one, and the double layer is what keeps the whole thing from falling apart in your hand halfway through the second bite.
The classic dressing is onion, cilantro and a squeeze of lime, and that’s it. No lettuce, no shredded cheese, no sour cream. The raw onion gives you the crunch, the cilantro gives you the green, the lime cuts the fat. When it’s right, every bite tastes bright, hot and clean.
The words on the board, plainly. Asada is grilled beef. Carnitas is pork braised low and then crisped, soft in the middle and crackly at the edges. Al pastor is marinated pork, ideally off the spit. Barbacoa is slow-cooked meat, usually beef, sometimes lamb. Lengua is beef tongue, and it’s the most tender thing on most menus; the name scares people off and they miss out. Tripa is intestine, crisped hard, and it’s an acquired texture. Suadero is a thin beef cut cooked slow in fat, and when a place offers it, someone in that kitchen is serious.
Order three or four, all different. That’s how you learn what a kitchen does best, and it’s how regulars order anyway. Then go back for a second round of whichever one made you stop talking.
Hit the salsa first, carefully. The green one isn’t always the mild one. Taste a drop on a chip before you pour it over the whole plate, because the burn that sneaks up on you three bites later is real, and water won’t fix it. A bite of tortilla will.
### A taco night that doesn’t fall apart
Pick by craving, not by ranking. If someone in the car wants birria, someone wants vegan and someone just wants a plain asada taco with lime, you’re not going to make everyone happy at one counter. Cherokee covers the plain-and-perfect crowd. Mestiza covers the al pastor purist. Terror Tacos covers the vegan. Taco Drip covers the person who wants their hands red to the wrist.
Check the day. Mestiza’s posted hours skip Monday. Taco Buddha’s breakfast tacos are a weekend thing. Takeout spots move fast and close early when they sell out. A two-minute look at a restaurant’s own page saves you a twenty-minute drive to a dark window, and after what happened on Delmar, that’s a habit worth keeping.

### Frequently asked questions about tacos in St. Louis
### Q. What happened to Mission Taco Joint?
A.  It opened in the Delmar Loop in 2013 and became Session Taco in September 2024 after a settlement over the Mission name with Gruma Corp., the parent company of Mission Foods. The St. Charles location became Sobremesa in June 2026, which closed in September, and the last two Session Tacos, in the Delmar Loop and Soulard, closed on Saturday, Oct. 17.
### Q. How much is the average cost of a taco?
A.  At Chico Bueno in the Grove, every taco on the posted menu is $5, so three tacos come to $15 before a drink. Most people need three or four to feel full, so compare taquerias by the cost of a full order, not by the price of one taco.
### Q. Why are tacos so expensive now?
A.  The same pressures behind every menu: meat, labor, rent and the hours slow-cooked fillings like birria and barbacoa tie up a kitchen. The places that hold the line usually keep a short menu and move a lot of tacos, so less food goes to waste.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  Locals will name toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake and St. Louis-style pizza first. Add a plate of tacos on Cherokee Street to that list: a few small tacos from different counters on the same block, eaten with lime and onion, is about as St. Louis as an evening gets.
### Q. What areas to stay away from in St. Louis?
A.  We won’t rank neighborhoods by fear. Every place on this list sits in a neighborhood where people live, work and eat every night. Use the same sense you’d use anywhere: park where it’s lit, keep valuables out of sight in the car, and check a restaurant’s hours before you go so you’re not wandering a closed block.

## St. Louis City Home? Budget the 1% Earnings Tax, Then Pick a Lender
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-mortgage-lender-in-st-louis
Buying inside the city limits? Did anyone tell you your paycheck gets 1% lighter once you live there?
Probably not. It is 11 at night, the laptop fan is whirring, and there are fourteen tabs open, each one shouting a slightly different rate. One loan officer texted you a smiley face. Another sent a PDF you have not opened. Your coffee went cold two hours ago, and the brick two-bedroom you toured last weekend is still sitting in your head with its creaky stairs and the radiator that ticked when the heat came on. You want it. You want this part over.
Here is the number none of those online mortgage calculators knows about. The City of St. Louis Collector of Revenue says the earnings tax is a one percent tax on earned income, collected from all city residents regardless of where they work. So if you earn $70,000 and move into the city from the county, that is $700 a year, about $58 a month, gone before your mortgage payment is even counted. Same job. Same commute, maybe. Smaller check.
That is not a reason to skip the city. It is a reason to run your budget with the right number before a lender runs it for you. Say it out loud to the friend who is house hunting too: in St. Louis, the address on your deed can change your take-home pay.
And there is good news to balance it. Missouri has a law called the First-Time Home Buyer Savings Account Act. Under it, you can open an account with a financial institution and name it a first-time home buyer savings account, for buying a primary residence in Missouri. Put in up to $1,600 a year, or $3,200 for a married couple filing combined, and half of what you put in comes off your Missouri taxable income, up to $800 a person or $1,600 for a married couple filing combined.
Now, the lender.
### How do you choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis?
Get written Loan Estimates from at least three different kinds of lenders, a bank, a local credit union and a mortgage broker, then compare the APR and the total fees side by side, not the headline rate. Ask each one whether it is a Certified Lender for the Missouri Housing Development Commission’s First Place Program. Pick the one whose numbers are clear and who answers every question without rushing you.
### Three Loan Estimates on one kitchen table
Here is how this goes when it goes right. You apply with three lenders inside a short window. A few days later, three Loan Estimates land in your inbox. You print them, lay them on the kitchen table under the hanging light, and grab a highlighter. Same form, same boxes, three different stories.
The headline rate is the number every ad shouts, and it is the least useful number on the page. A lender can show you a low rate and quietly make it back in fees. The APR folds most of those costs into one yearly percentage, so it is the fairer number to line up. Then go straight to the closing costs section and run your highlighter down every fee. Origination charges. Points. Fees with names you have never heard. Circle anything you do not understand, and make the loan officer explain it in plain words.
That is the whole trick. The lender who explains the circled items patiently is usually the one you want on the phone when something goes sideways two days before closing. The one who sighs, or says “that’s standard,” just told you how the next six weeks will feel.
One more thing about that kitchen table. Do not let anybody hurry you off it. A good offer will still be a good offer tomorrow morning, after you have slept on it and read it with fresh coffee.
### What grants are available for first-time homebuyers in Missouri?
The word “grant” gets thrown around a lot. What Missouri actually runs is a little different, and better to know before you talk to anyone.
The Missouri Housing Development Commission sets the rates for the First Place Program. MHDC says it helps first-time homebuyers and qualified Veterans save money with mortgage financing at interest rates that are lower than regular market rates. For buyers with limited savings, the program offers the option of cash assistance for the down payment and closing costs. MHDC sets the interest rates and allowable closing costs itself, with no minimum down payment or minimum loan amount.
The catch is that you cannot walk into MHDC and get one. The loans come through Certified Lenders. So the single most useful question you can ask on your first call is, “Are you an MHDC Certified Lender?” If the answer is no, you have just learned that lender cannot offer you the state program at all. Check the current income and purchase price limits on MHDC’s First Place page before you get your heart set on a price.
Then there is the savings account from the top of this page. The law lets the person who opens it name the first-time buyer it is for, and that person can be the account holder. It also caps lifetime contributions at $20,000 and the total in the account at $30,000. Open it at your own bank or credit union, and keep the paperwork with your tax records.
Salary math and a tax break
### Can I afford a 300k house on a $70k salary?
Maybe. A $70,000 salary is about $5,833 a month before taxes, and a city address takes 1% of it, about $58 a month. Whether a $300,000 house fits depends on your rate, property taxes, insurance and other debts, so ask each lender to run that exact price on a Loan Estimate. While you save, a Missouri first-time home buyer savings account takes up to $1,600 a year ($3,200 married filing combined), and half of it is deductible, capped at $800 a person or $1,600 for a couple.
### Bank, credit union or broker?
There is no single best kind of lender. There is only the best total deal for you, from someone who treats you like a person instead of a file number.
A bank is easy if you already have your checking there. You walk past the same teller you have seen for years, and the paperwork feels familiar. The trade-off is that a big bank’s loan menu can be rigid if your situation is anything but textbook.
A local credit union is member-owned, and it often feels like it. The loan officer may live ten minutes from the house you want. Joining usually means opening a small savings account, which is also a fine place to start that first-time buyer savings account.
A mortgage broker does not lend the money. A broker shops your file across several lenders, which helps if you are self-employed, working two jobs or rebuilding credit. Ask exactly how the broker gets paid, and get the answer in writing.
An online lender can be quick and sharp on rate. You trade the local handshake for a call center, and that matters most on the one afternoon a closing goes wrong.
Whatever mix you choose, ask every one of them the same MHDC question. It is the fastest way to tell which lenders work with first-time buyers every day and which ones mostly refinance houses on the other side of the county.
Wondering why a starter home here still feels within reach? Here is why St. Louis real estate stays affordable.
### Pre-approved beats pre-qualified
These two sound alike and are not. A pre-qualification is a rough guess based on what you tell the lender over the phone. A pre-approval comes after the lender looks at your actual pay stubs, bank statements and credit, then puts a number in a letter.
Get the letter before you fall for a house. It tells you your real budget, and it tells a seller you are serious. Picture two offers on the same south city bungalow, and only one has a letter attached. You already know which one the seller reads first.
Pre-approval also pairs with the other early decision you have to make, picking an agent. Our guide on how to choose a real estate agent in St. Louis walks through what to ask now that the commission rules have changed.
### Questions to ask every lender
A good loan officer welcomes these. A pushy one dodges them.
What is the rate, the APR and the total estimated closing cost? Get it on the Loan Estimate, not in a text.
Are you an MHDC Certified Lender, and would I qualify for First Place?
What loan type do you recommend for me, and why that one?
What could change my rate or costs before closing, and when can I lock?
Who handles my file day to day, and how do I reach them?
### Know what you can actually afford
The lender will tell you the most you can borrow. That is not the same as the most you should borrow. Your monthly payment carries more than principal and interest. Property taxes, homeowner’s insurance and often mortgage insurance ride along in the same bill, every month, for years.
Build your own number first, and if the house is inside the city limits, start from your pay after the 1% earnings tax. Add up the car payment, the student loans, the daycare, the cash you want left for a night out. Then decide the payment you can live with on a bad month, not a good one. Borrowing a little less than the maximum leaves room for the furnace that dies in January and the gutter that pulls loose in the first big storm. That is what turns a house into a home instead of a stretch.
### Get your credit ready before you apply
Your credit score moves your rate, and a small bump can move it a lot over a long loan. Pull your reports, fix the errors, and pay credit card balances down. Then go boring. No new car, no new store card, no big furniture on credit between pre-approval and closing. Plenty of loans have wobbled at the last minute over a new couch.
If your score is not there yet, a HUD-approved housing counselor can map a realistic plan, and a good lender will tell you plainly what to fix instead of pushing you into a loan that does not fit.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How to pick the right mortgage broker?
A.  Ask how the broker is paid, get that answer in writing, and ask how many lenders they will shop your file with. Then compare the broker’s Loan Estimate against a bank and a credit union. A good broker earns the fee by finding a lender that fits your situation, especially if you are self-employed or rebuilding credit.
### Q. What is the easiest mortgage to get approved for?
A.  The easiest one is the one that fits your income, savings and credit, and a good lender will tell you which that is. First-time Missouri buyers should also ask about MHDC’s First Place Program, which MHDC says has no minimum down payment and offers cash assistance for the down payment and closing costs to buyers with limited savings.
### Q. What is the best option for a first-time home buyer?
A.  Compare at least three written Loan Estimates, and ask each lender about MHDC’s First Place Program, which offers rates lower than regular market rates through Certified Lenders. While you save, a Missouri first-time home buyer savings account lets you deduct half of what you put in from your Missouri taxable income, within the limits in the law.
### Q. What should you not tell a mortgage lender?
A.  Do not tell them anything untrue, and do not leave out a debt. Beyond that, skip the guesswork. Do not commit to a maximum loan amount before you have run your own budget, and do not promise to sign before you have seen the other Loan Estimates. Let them compete for you.
### Q. Are there first-time homebuyer programs in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The statewide MHDC First Place Program works for St. Louis buyers through Certified Lenders, with below-market rates and an option for cash assistance toward the down payment and closing costs. Check MHDC’s current income and purchase price limits, and ask your lender whether you qualify.

## Nail Salons in St. Louis: Where to Go, What It Costs, and What to Check
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/nail-salons-in-st-louis
Most guides to nail salons are a list of names and a star rating. That tells you where people liked the polish. It doesn’t tell you whether the tools touching your skin were disinfected properly, or that there’s a flyer Missouri legally requires every salon to post that almost nobody knows to look for.
This covers both. Where to go across the metro, what things cost, and — the part that actually matters — what you can check in the first thirty seconds of walking in.
### What are the best nail salons in St. Louis?
It depends what you want. For nail art, Polish Room Nail Bar in Richmond Heights does bespoke work and Nails By MIMI in Ballwin prices designs per nail. For Gel-X and soft gel, Jonails in Breckenridge Hills and Nails By Sofia in O’Fallon. For the cleanest setup in the metro, Sonder Lush downtown runs waterless manicures and jetless ceramic pedicure basins, and Frenchies in O’Fallon refuses acrylic, dip powder, drills and jetted tubs entirely. For all-inclusive pricing with no tipping, Tints Polish in Frontenac.
### By area
City. Sonder Lush Nail Studio, 2704 Locust St — a solo, appointment-only studio doing waterless manicures and jetless pedicures in ceramic basins. 314 Nails and Spa, 2329 N. Union Blvd, which also runs as a training academy and is one of the more affordable options in the city. Kary Beauty Salon, 5633 S. Kings Highway in St. Louis Hills, with a Spanish-language service menu.
Mid-county. Tints Polish, 10281 Clayton Rd — all-inclusive pricing, no tipping accepted, five-free polishes and LED lamps only. Frontenac Nail Lounge, 9838 Clayton Rd, for spa pedicures and rhinestone work. Polish Room Nail Bar at 18 The Boulevard in Richmond Heights for bespoke art. Olivia & Oliver, 8472 Eager Rd in Brentwood. Nail Doctor Unblemished, 7403 Manchester Ave in Maplewood, which does corrective and therapeutic pedicure work in long appointment slots, booked more like the metro’s top-rated Asian massage and bodywork spas than a walk-in polish change.
West County. Sweet Mia Nail Spa, 13275 Manchester Rd in Des Peres. The Pedicure Plus in Ellisville, a pedicure-only specialist. Nails By MIMI, 13949 Manchester Rd in Ballwin, pricing chrome and French tip and per-nail designs individually. Color Nails in Ellisville for acrylic. Lisa Amor Nails N Spa, 12528 Olive Blvd in Creve Coeur, with tiered spa pedicures.
North and northwest county. Janae Nail Co, 2055 Craigshire Rd in Maryland Heights. Lavish Lab Nails, 2278 McKelvey Rd. V Nail Lounge, 13933 New Halls Ferry Rd in Florissant, open until 8 most nights. Jonails, 9456 St. Charles Rock Rd in Breckenridge Hills, the best-verified Gel-X option out this way — and one of the few that offers Gel-X refills rather than a full new set every time.
South County. Gentle Nails, 9949 Lin Ferry Dr in Green Park, appointment-only and inexpensive. TD Nail & Bar, 9800 Watson Rd in Crestwood.
St. Charles County. Frenchies Modern Nail Care, 3027 Hwy K in O’Fallon. Nails By Sofia, 33 Coach Line Dr in O’Fallon, with the cheapest verified Gel-X in the metro. Sa’Chas Nailz & More in St. Charles for a long-format luxury combo.
Metro East. EXO Nail Bar in Edwardsville, inside a large med-spa complex of the kind covered in our guide to massage, medical spas and wellness retreats, and open until 10 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Nail Pro’s, 5800 W. Main St in Belleville — appointment only, explicitly no walk-ins. Mi Nail, 5725 Belleville Crossing St, which publishes its prices, and Kreative to the T on W. Main for colored acrylic.
### What things cost here
These are published prices from live booking pages, not estimates.
Manicure: $25 at Mi Nail in Belleville and Kary Beauty, up to $65 for a signature luxury manicure in St. Charles. Gel manicure: around $35 at Lavish Lab and Mi Nail, $45 and up at EXO. Pedicure: $25 at 314 Nails, $40 for a classic at Lisa Amor or a wellness pedi at The Pedicure Plus, $50 for tiered spa versions, and $85 and up at Nail Doctor Unblemished for corrective work in an 80-minute to two-hour slot. Acrylic full set: $55 at Color Nails, $60 at Kreative to the T, $65 for colored acrylic. Gel-X: $30 for a short set at Nails By Sofia, $75 to $82 at Jonails — where a refill runs $60, which is worth asking about since many technicians only do full new sets.
One pricing model worth knowing about: Tints Polish charges all-inclusive and does not accept tips, and sells a monthly membership for unlimited polish changes. Whether that suits you depends on how often you go, but it removes the arithmetic at the end.
### What Missouri actually requires
Missouri regulates nail work as its own license class. A manicurist is anyone doing this work for compensation, and they need a full manicurist license — not a lighter registration. This is a genuine difference from hair braiding, which Missouri moved to a simpler registration track in 2018. That change applied only to braiding. Nail technicians were never part of it.
Three specific rules in Missouri’s cosmetology sanitation regulations are worth knowing as a customer.
Tools must be immersed, not wiped. Implements that touch your skin must be completely immersed in an EPA-registered disinfectant — one labeled as bactericidal, virucidal and fungicidal — for at least five minutes. Afterward they’re either kept in the solution or stored in a covered container or drawer. A quick spray and wipe between clients does not meet that standard.
MMA is banned in Missouri, by name. The rule prohibits any liquid product containing methyl methacrylate, and puts the responsibility on the licensee to ensure their products don’t contain it. Ethyl and butyl methacrylate are permitted. Worth being precise here, because most articles get it wrong: there is no federal regulation specifically prohibiting MMA in nail products. The FDA considers it harmful in fingernail preparations and removed products from the market decades ago through court action rather than rulemaking. So MMA isn’t banned by the FDA — it’s banned in Missouri.
Callus razors are illegal to use or even possess. Missouri bars licensees from using or keeping a credo blade or any razor-type callus shaver on the premises — possession alone counts as rendering services in an unsafe and unsanitary manner. And every establishment is required to post a flyer about it in plain view of the public. That flyer is the single easiest compliance signal to check, and virtually no customer knows to look for it.
### The thing nobody tells you about inspections
You cannot look up a Missouri nail salon’s inspection results. The state doesn’t publish them and doesn’t require salons to post them, and complaint files are closed to the public.
Kansas City television station KSHB reported on this gap, noting that Kansas requires inspection results be posted publicly and makes complaint investigations public, and that Kansas inspects twice a year to Missouri’s annual schedule. A bill to open Missouri’s cosmetology investigations to the public was filed and never referred to committee.
What you can check is licensing. The Missouri Division of Professional Registration runs a public licensee search where you can verify an individual or establishment’s license status, number, expiration and any disciplinary action, at pr.mo.gov. It won’t show you inspection findings, but it will tell you whether the person doing your nails is licensed and in good standing.
### Pedicure tubs: the risk that's actually documented
This is the best-evidenced hygiene issue in the whole category, and it’s about plumbing.
In 2000, more than a hundred pedicure customers at a northern California salon developed persistent boils on their lower legs caused by Mycobacterium fortuitum, a bacterium that had colonized the footspas. Investigators found it behind the recirculation screens of all ten tubs, and matched the strains from the tubs to the strains from patients.
A follow-up study published by the CDC in 2005 sampled thirty whirlpool footbaths across eighteen salons. Twenty-nine of the thirty grew mycobacteria. Nearly half carried M. fortuitum specifically. Twenty-five of thirty had visible debris or slime behind the recirculation screen, and half of the operators said they had never cleaned behind that screen at all. The organisms turned up whether or not disinfectants were reportedly used.
The researchers were careful to add that while the bacteria are widespread in footspas, the actual risk of infection remains unclear — so this isn’t a reason to panic. But one detail is directly actionable: customers who had shaved their legs before the pedicure were at higher risk. Tiny nicks are the entry point.
The mechanism explains the fix. Bacteria colonize the internal piping and the debris trap behind the screen. Pipeless and jetless tubs have no internal plumbing to colonize. That’s why Sonder Lush’s ceramic basins and Frenchies’ refusal to use jetted tubs are substantive choices rather than marketing.
Wildly off-topic: polish dries in ten minutes, so go eat in Bunker Hill.
Worth noting plainly: Missouri’s sanitation rule for cosmetology establishments does not address pedicure footbaths at all. California adopted specific footspa cleaning regulations after the outbreak. Missouri’s rule, last amended in 2013, is silent on them — which means how a salon cleans its tubs is largely a matter of that salon’s own standards.
### Eleven things you can check yourself
All of these are observable in the first few minutes, and each maps to a rule or a documented risk rather than a hunch — the same walk-in read that separates the best tattoo studios in St. Louis from the rest.
1. Look for the posted callus-blade flyer. Missouri requires it in plain view. Its absence is a real signal. 2. Look for posted licenses, then verify the names at pr.mo.gov. 3. Ask what kind of pedicure tub it is — pipeless, jetless or ceramic basin, or a jetted whirlpool. If it’s jetted, ask whether they scrub behind the screen nightly. 4. Watch how tools are handled. Five minutes fully immersed in disinfectant is the standard; a wipe-down is not. 5. Tools should come out of a covered container or a sealed pouch, not a drawer of loose metal. 6. A UV box is storage, not disinfection. If that’s all they show you, ask what the tools were immersed in first. 7. Ask whether they use MMA. It’s banned here. A harsh sweet smell and a product that won’t soak off in acetone are the classic tells. 8. Notice the air. Heavy fumes mean poor ventilation, which is worse for the technician than for you. 9. Don’t shave your legs in the twenty-four hours before a pedicure. 10. Don’t let anyone cut your cuticles — push them back instead. 11. If you go often, consider bringing your own tools.
Points nine through eleven come from the American Academy of Dermatology.
### Gel, acrylic and your actual nails
A systematic review published in late 2025 looked at fifty-eight studies on nail cosmetics, and the pattern is consistent: acrylates are the main culprit in reactions. Allergic contact dermatitis showed up in roughly half the gel-manicure literature and around sixty percent of the acrylic literature.
One ingredient does most of the work — HEMA, found in about sixty percent of the nearly four hundred products reviewed. Nail technicians bear the heaviest burden: they made up eighty percent of occupational cases in one multi-year study, which is the strongest practical argument for choosing a well-ventilated salon.
On UV lamps, the same review found documented cases of skin reactions and, in one long-term immunosuppressed patient, skin cancers — but judged the overall carcinogenic potential low while advising caution. That’s the honest framing. If it concerns you, LED-only salons exist; Tints Polish is one.
The most encouraging finding: among patients with acrylate dermatitis, simply avoiding contact cleared it completely in eighty percent of cases.
### A note on what we couldn't verify
Every salon above was confirmed through its own website or a live booking calendar in July 2026. Several others that come up in local roundups were left out because we couldn’t confirm them — one salon’s domain now redirects to a parking page, another’s website has an expired security certificate.
Also worth flagging: Sonder Lush appears at an old Washington Avenue address on at least one major review site. Its own website gives 2704 Locust St. When a business’s own site and an aggregator disagree, trust the business.
And one genuine gap: we couldn’t verify a single St. Louis salon offering a Russian manicure from a source we’d stand behind, so we’re not naming one. If you find a good one, we’d like to know.
Two things are worth knowing before you sit down: how to tell if a nail salon is good from across the room, and what type of salon nails are least damaging to the nail you have to live with afterwards. Both are checkable in the first two minutes.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you look up nail salon inspection results in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri does not publish nail salon inspection results and does not require salons to post them, and complaint files are closed to the public. You can verify license status, expiration and disciplinary history for individuals and establishments through the Missouri Division of Professional Registration licensee search at pr.mo.gov — but not inspection findings.
### Q. Is MMA banned in nail salons?
A.  In Missouri, yes — state cosmetology rules prohibit any liquid product containing methyl methacrylate by name, and permit ethyl or butyl methacrylate instead. There is no federal regulation specifically prohibiting MMA; the FDA considers it harmful in nail products and acted through the courts rather than rulemaking. Telltale signs are a harsh sweet odor and a product that won’t soak off in acetone.
### Q. Are pedicure foot spas safe?
A.  Jetted whirlpool tubs carry a documented risk. A CDC study of thirty salon footbaths found mycobacteria in twenty-nine of them, with visible debris behind the recirculation screen in twenty-five and half of operators reporting they had never cleaned behind it. Researchers noted the actual infection risk remains unclear, but customers who shaved their legs beforehand were at higher risk. Pipeless and jetless tubs have no internal plumbing for bacteria to colonize.
### Q. Should you shave your legs before a pedicure?
A.  No — shave afterward, or at least twenty-four hours before. The American Academy of Dermatology advises against pre-pedicure shaving, and the CDC footbath outbreak investigation found that customers who had shaved beforehand were at higher risk of infection, because small nicks provide an entry point.
### Q. Is a UV sterilizer box enough to clean nail tools?
A.  Not on its own under Missouri’s rule. Implements must be completely immersed in an EPA-registered disinfectant for at least five minutes; the regulation describes cabinets only as storage for tools already disinfected. If a salon shows you a UV box, ask what the tools were immersed in first.
### Q. Do nail technicians need a license in Missouri?
A.  Yes, a full manicurist license — Missouri defines manicuring as its own regulated practice covering nail care, artificial nails, and hand and arm work for compensation. This differs from hair braiding, which Missouri moved to a lighter registration track in 2018; that change did not apply to nail technicians.
### Q. How much does a manicure cost in St. Louis?
A.  Published prices run from about $25 for a classic manicure at budget-friendly salons up to $65 for a signature luxury service. Gel manicures generally start around $35. Pedicures range from $25 to $85 or more for corrective and therapeutic work. Gel-X sets span $30 to $82 depending on length and salon.
### Q. How to tell if a nail salon is good?
A.  Watch the things that do not depend on taste: a current license posted where you can read it, tools that come out of sealed pouches, pedicure basins with disposable liners, and staff wearing masks when they file. A salon that is relaxed about being watched on those points is usually the one to book.
### Q. What type of salon nails are least damaging?
A.  A plain manicure on your own nail with regular polish does the least. Gel is gentler than acrylic on the nail plate, but only if it is soaked off rather than scraped or peeled — removal causes most of the damage people blame on the product. Give bare nails a break between sets.
### Q. How much do you tip for a $40.00 pedicure?
A.  The usual range people work from is eighteen to twenty percent, and more if the technician fixed something or ran long. Cash reaches the technician directly in a way a card line sometimes does not, and it matters most in salons where technicians rent their station.
### Q. How much does it cost to get nails done in Missouri?
A.  Booking lashes as well as nails? Read how long eyelash extensions really last before you pick a date.
Price tracks service and time: a basic manicure, a gel set, and a full acrylic set with art are three different numbers, and removal is often billed separately. Ask what the quote covers before you sit down — a set that arrives cheap and leaves expensive is almost always about add-ons.

## Free for 10 Days, $75 a Month, and One 7-Day Rule: Jiu-Jitsu in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/jiu-jitsu-and-bjj-in-st-louis
Your first jiu-jitsu class starts in bare feet. At Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis someone hands you a uniform, and an instructor gives you a focused introductory lesson before you join the group. The mat gives a little under your heels, a partner taps twice to say stop, and the whole room is built around honoring that tap. Nobody has asked you for money yet, and the gi you’re wearing is a loaner that weighs more than it looks.
Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis gives you 10 days. BJJ Lifestyle Academy gives a free week. Revive books a first class free, Onyx Grappling offers a free class, and Wise Warriors on Manchester Road gives a first workout free.
The 7-day rule: at Revive, to cancel future billing you must contact the gym at least 7 days before your next scheduled payment. Put the date in your calendar the day you sign up. Its code NEW100 takes $100 off the first month.
### How much does a BJJ gym cost per month?
Money comes up after the class, when you’re sweaty and flattered and ready to say yes. That’s the moment to slow down. Wise Warriors (7403 Manchester Road, #130; 314-630-7280) prints a full price list on its own site and sells its memberships by training hours: $75 a month for three hours a week, $99 for five, $150 for unlimited. The first workout is free, and the classes include jiu jitsu alongside MMA, kickboxing and wrestling, so the price buys more than one sport.
Maelstrom BJJ on Ohio Avenue lists a Monthly Unlimited membership and shows no dollar amount. At the others, the free class is how you learn what a month costs. Get three answers before you pay: the monthly price, any sign-up fee, and exactly how to cancel, in writing. A cancellation rule like Revive’s is fair, and it’s the kind of detail that costs you a month if you miss it.
### The honest downside
Your body keeps score the next morning, in places you didn’t know you had, and your knees will have opinions by noon. Jiu-jitsu hurts sometimes, and the research says so plainly. In a survey of 1,140 jiu-jitsu athletes from 62 countries, two out of three reported at least one injury in three years that kept them out of training for two weeks. The knee was the most common site, at 27.1% of injuries, and 77.6% of injuries happened during sparring. Competing regularly, older age and a higher belt rank were significant risk factors too.
None of that is a reason to stay home. It’s a reason to ask, on the free class, how beginners are introduced to sparring and how often the mats are cleaned.
### Where to take the free class
Bring a water bottle and your nerve; the rest is on loan. At Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis (314-659-8200) the trial runs 10 days, and when you arrive you’re given a uniform and walked through a focused introductory lesson before you join the group. The kids’ side starts at age 3 with Mat Munchkins, then Little Champs for ages 5 to 7 and Jr. Grapplers for ages 7 to 12.
At BJJ Lifestyle Academy (4274 Telegraph Road; 314-780-4222) the free week starts with a phone call or an email, because you must schedule your first visit. You sign a release on-site, and a guardian signs for a minor. Wear comfortable athletic gear without pockets or zippers. The head coach, Mike Rethmeyer, is a 4th degree black belt under Leo Peçanha and a 20-time IBJJF medalist.
Two academies sit on Jungermann Road in St. Peters. Revive (1278 Jungermann Rd., Suite A; 636-344-9334) books a first class free, with no commitment and no gear needed, and says everything will be ready when you arrive. Onyx Grappling (953 Jungermann Road; 636-339-4277) offers a free class and runs kids’ classes for ages 4 to 6 and 7 to 9, plus kids and teens classes for ages 10 to 12 and 13 to 15.
In Collinsville, Gracie Barra Collinsville (2539 Vandalia St.; 618-213-2422) books a free class. Fathom BJJ (618-979-8010) takes free-trial requests.
### What to ask before you sign
Take the free class with a short list. What is the monthly price, and does it cover every class or only some? Is there a sign-up fee? How long is the commitment, and how do you cancel? ### A five-minute hygiene check
The mat itself is worth a look before you commit. Stand at the edge and watch. Do people take their shoes off before they step on? Is there a place to put them? Does anyone wipe the mat down, and is a cleaner kept where you can see it? Do students arrive in a clean gi, and does the coach send someone with a visible rash or sore to the side? None of that takes a question. All of it takes a few minutes of looking.
Then do your part. Shower after class, wash your gi or training clothes every time, cover any cut before you step on, and tell the coach about anything that looks like ringworm or a sore that won’t heal. A good school wants to hear it.

## Eco-Friendly Cleaning Services: How to Tell Who Actually Means It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/eco-friendly-cleaning-services
You come home to a spotless house, and the first thing that hits you is not how clean it looks. It is the smell — that sharp chemical bite that makes your eyes water a little and hangs in the air for hours.
Then the baby crawls across the just-mopped floor. Or the dog stretches out on it and rolls. And a small thought nags at you: what exactly did they wipe all of this down with?
Whether your place is a bungalow in Affton, a rental in Belleville, a farmhouse outside Wentzville or a shared office suite in Maryland Heights, it is a fair question — and a surprisingly hard one to get a straight answer to.
### What does eco-friendly cleaning actually mean?
By itself, almost nothing. “Eco-friendly” and “green” are marketing words, not regulated terms — anybody can print them on a van.
What separates a real green cleaner from a claim is verifiable, and it comes down to two things:
EPA Safer Choice — certifies the products. Every ingredient is screened, including fragrance.
Green Seal GS-37 — certifies the service company, not just what is in the bottle.
Ask which of those a company can point to. That single question does more than an hour of reading reviews, because it is the one thing a business cannot answer with adjectives.
### Why the label alone tells you nothing
Search for a green cleaner and look at what comes back: cleaning companies. All of them. A map pack of three, then a page of firms with “eco” or “green” in the business name, then two booking aggregators.
Every result is a company applying the label to itself. Not one of them explains how you would check. That is not a conspiracy — it is just what happens when a term has commercial value and no definition behind it.
The practical consequence shows up in an unexpected place. Look at what people actually do when they need one of these services, and you find neighborhood groups full of posts like this, from the last few weeks alone: “I have searched and haven’t seen anyone advertising green, non-toxic products, and it’s very important to me.” “I searched the group with no luck.” “Looking for a house cleaner — need eco-friendly products.”
People who want this cannot find it by searching, so they fall back on asking a neighbor. That is a failure on both sides of the transaction: the customer cannot find the cleaner, and the cleaner — who may well be doing everything right — is invisible to the exact person looking for them.
### The two certifications that mean something
### EPA Safer Choice (the products)
This is the one worth knowing about, and it is stricter than most people assume. To carry the Safer Choice label, every single ingredient in a product is evaluated against the EPA’s Safer Chemical Ingredients List and rated on a traffic-light system — green for preferred, yellow for use with caution, red for not allowed. A product containing any red-rated ingredient cannot be certified. Nearly 2,000 products currently qualify.
Here is the detail that matters most in a house with a kid or an asthmatic in it: the screening includes fragrance components. Fragrance is normally exempt from ingredient disclosure — a manufacturer can list “fragrance” and stop there, covering dozens of compounds. Safer Choice does not permit that shortcut. Given that scent is what most people actually react to, this is the difference between a real standard and a nice-sounding one.
It is also not a boutique label. Under the fiscal year 2025 National Defense Authorization Act, the Department of Defense is required to purchase Safer Choice-certified products to the maximum extent possible — a procurement standard, not a marketing badge.
You can look products up yourself on the EPA’s searchable list, which is the fastest way to check whether the products your cleaner named are actually certified.
### Green Seal GS-37 (the company)
The distinction people miss: Safer Choice certifies bottles. Green Seal GS-37 certifies the cleaning service itself — how the company works, not only what it buys.
That matters because a crew can carry excellent products and still undo the benefit: over-applying, cross-contaminating cloths between the bathroom and the kitchen, running a vacuum that pushes fine dust straight back into the room. Products are the easy half. Practice is the half that shows up in your air.
### The questions to ask before you book
Five minutes on the phone settles it. Ask these in this order:
“What products do you actually use?” You want brand names, not categories. A company doing this properly answers immediately, because they chose those products on purpose.
“Are any of them Safer Choice certified?” Then look them up. It takes a minute and it is the whole ballgame.
“What do you use for disinfecting, specifically?” This is where honest companies get precise and vague ones get uncomfortable.
“How do you handle cloths between rooms?” Microfiber, color-coded or separated by area, laundered between homes. A shrug here tells you about the practice half.
“Do your vacuums have HEPA filtration?” For allergies this matters as much as anything in a bottle.
And say the specific thing out loud — a child with asthma, a chemical sensitivity, a new baby, a cat that licks the floor. A good company will adjust, tell you exactly what they will change, and sometimes tell you honestly that one particular job needs a product they would rather you were out of the house for. That last answer is the most reassuring one you can get.
### What green cleaning does not mean
This part gets skipped in the enthusiasm, and skipping it is how people end up worse off.
Green does not mean anything goes. Gentle plant-based products are excellent for routine cleaning — floors, counters, glass, dust, the ordinary weekly work that is most of what a cleaner does. They are not always the right tool when someone in the house has a stomach virus, or after a raw-chicken spill, or in a bathroom during a norovirus week. Real disinfection sometimes calls for a registered disinfectant used correctly, with the contact time the label specifies.
The good news is that Safer Choice includes disinfecting products, so this is rarely an either/or. But a company that claims it never needs anything stronger, in any circumstance, is telling you something about its willingness to say inconvenient things.
“Natural” does not automatically mean safe, either. Plenty of natural substances irritate lungs and skin. And two common household staples should never be combined — never mix bleach with ammonia, or bleach with vinegar. That is not a green-cleaning rule, it is a basic safety one, and it sends people to the emergency room every year.
Unrelated, and we know it: Hi Pointe, block by block.
### What you can handle yourself between visits
A professional cleaner is not an all-or-nothing decision, and a surprising share of routine work needs almost nothing.
White vinegar handles glass, hard water spots and a lot of kitchen surfaces. Baking soda handles scrubbing and odors. A good microfiber cloth, used dry, picks up more dust than any spray does — most dusting sprays exist to make dust stick to the cloth, which is a job the cloth already does. Between them, those three cover a large share of ordinary weekly cleaning without a cabinet full of sprays.
Two caveats worth carrying: vinegar should stay off natural stone, where the acid etches the surface, and it belongs nowhere near bleach. And ventilation is free — open a window while you clean and for half an hour after, whatever you are using. In this climate that is easy for a good part of the year and worth remembering in January anyway.
### For the businesses on the other side of this
If you run a cleaning company that genuinely uses non-toxic products, the neighborhood-group posts above are worth reading twice. Those are customers with money in hand, actively looking, who could not find you.
What fixes that is boring and specific: say the words they are typing. “Eco-friendly” in your business name is not enough. Name the certifications you actually hold, name the products, say plainly that you accommodate asthma, allergies, pets and infants, and list every town you cover. Those are the phrases people search and the phrases they ask their neighbors in — and if none of them appear anywhere you can be found, the search simply fails.
It is also worth remembering that this is a two-audience service. Offices, salons, daycares and clinics increasingly want the same thing for the people who spend forty hours a week in the building, and that is a different pitch to a different buyer.
### Finding one around here
The most efficient approach is to compare several local companies at once, then make the five-minute call to the two or three that look right.
For an office, salon, daycare or clinic, the commercial cleaning map covers janitorial services across the metro on both sides of the river. For your own home, search the directory for cleaning companies serving your area, shortlist two or three, and ask each one the five questions above. If a company has taken the trouble to list its certifications and the towns it covers, that is already a signal about how it runs.
A clean home and a healthy one should be the same thing. Ask what is in the bottle, look the products up, speak up about sensitivities, and you can have floors clean enough for the baby to crawl on without the chemical cloud that used to come with them.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is considered green cleaning?
A.  Cleaning that uses non-toxic, often plant-based products in place of harsh chemicals, combined with practices that keep dust and residue out of your air — microfiber instead of disposables, HEPA vacuums, sensible ventilation. The term itself is unregulated, so the meaningful markers are EPA Safer Choice for products and Green Seal GS-37 for the company.
### Q. Is green cleaning more expensive?
A.  Not inherently. Certified products cost a little more per bottle than commodity chemicals, but products are a small share of what you pay for — most of a cleaning bill is labor. Where you may see a difference is with companies that market green as a premium tier. Get two or three quotes and compare like for like.
### Q. How much do 2 hours of cleaning cost?
A.  It depends on the size of the home, how many bathrooms, whether it is a first deep clean or ongoing upkeep, and whether one cleaner comes or a team. Any number quoted online before someone has asked those questions is a guess. Ask for a written quote based on your actual home — reputable companies give one readily.
### Q. Is $50 an hour for cleaning good?
A.  Compare the total job, not the hourly figure. A team of two at a lower rate each can finish in half the time; an experienced solo cleaner may charge more per hour and need fewer of them. Ask what the whole job costs, how long it should take, and what is included — inside the oven, inside the fridge, and baseboards are the usual line items people assume and should not.
### Q. Do I tip a house cleaner?
A.  It is not required and it is genuinely appreciated. Common practice is to tip for one-off deep cleans or move-out jobs, and to give something at the holidays for a regular cleaner rather than every visit. If you use a company rather than an independent cleaner, ask whether tips reach the crew — sometimes they do not.
### Q. What is the 20 minute rule of cleaning?
A.  Setting a timer and cleaning for twenty focused minutes rather than waiting for a free afternoon that never arrives. It works because most household mess is accumulation, not catastrophe. It also reduces how often you need heavy products at all, which is the cheapest form of green cleaning there is.
