## DIY Interior Painting in St. Louis: Lead, Plaster, and What It Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/diy-interior-painting-in-st-louis
Federal lead-paint rules do not apply to you painting your own house.
That is the actual text of the EPA rule, and almost nobody says it plainly — the guidance you find is written for contractors, so homeowners come away thinking they need certification to paint a bedroom.
But before you reach for the sander: 87% of houses in the City of St. Louis were built in 1979 or earlier — before the 1978 lead-paint ban. The rule doesn’t bind you. The dust doesn’t care.
### Do I need to be certified to paint my own house?
No. EPA states that the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule “does not apply to homeowners doing RRP projects in their own home.” The rule governs anyone paid to disturb painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing. There are three exceptions that pull you back in: it does apply if you rent out all or part of your home, operate a childcare center in it, or buy and renovate homes to sell for profit. If any of those describe you, you are inside the rule and need a certified firm.
### The square-footage numbers are not your permission slip
You’ll see thresholds quoted everywhere: more than 6 square feet of paint disturbed inside a room, or more than 20 square feet outside, makes a job a regulated renovation. Below that it’s “minor repair and maintenance.”
Those numbers decide whether a paid contractor’s job is regulated. They are not a homeowner safety line. A homeowner painting their own primary residence is outside the rule at 6 square feet and at 600.
Two details worth knowing anyway, because they catch people hiring out small jobs: window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered regardless of square footage, and multiple jobs in the same room within 30 days count as one job for the threshold.
### Why 1978 matters so much here
Lead in consumer paint was banned effective February 1978. The ban stopped new sales; it did not require anyone to remove what was already on the walls.
Which is why the date lands so hard in this market. About 87% of St. Louis city housing units were built in 1979 or earlier, and the median city home dates to 1938 — forty years before the ban. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services designates the entire city a high-risk area for lead poisoning.
And this is not only a city story, which is where most coverage gets it wrong. St. Louis County’s median home was built in 1970 — also pre-1978 — and about 67% of county housing predates 1980. Florissant, Webster Groves, Kirkwood, Maplewood, Overland, Ferguson: all inside the frame.
### Before you sand anything, check this
Here is the most useful thing in this article, and it is buried on a page almost nobody reads.
The City of St. Louis offers free lead inspections on residential property where a child under six or a pregnant woman lives. Call the Building Division’s lead program at 622-4800. There is also remediation assistance, income- and occupancy-based.
If that describes your household and you are about to disturb paint in a pre-1978 house, make the call first. It costs nothing and it changes what you should do next.
### Test kits work in one direction only
EPA recognizes exactly three lead test kits: LeadCheck, D-Lead, and a Massachusetts state kit that works on drywall and plaster only. The first two work on wood, ferrous metal, drywall and plaster.
Now the part that changes how you should read your result. EPA says plainly that “to date no lead test kit has met both of the performance criteria outlined in the RRP rule.” The recognized kits satisfy only the negative-response criterion — a demonstrated false-negative rate of no more than 5% at 95% confidence.
In plain terms: a negative result is reasonably trustworthy. A positive result is not independently validated. A swab turning red is a signal to stop and get real testing — not a confirmed measurement.
Real testing means one of two things a homeowner can’t do at the kitchen table: XRF analysis, which reads lead concentration through multiple layers without damaging anything, or paint chips sent to an accredited lab.
And know which service you’re buying. An inspection tells you whether the building has lead-based paint and where it is. A risk assessment tells you whether there are actual hazards right now and what to do about them — usually the more useful product for someone deciding whether to start a project.
### How to work without making it worse
The rule doesn’t bind a homeowner, but EPA’s practices are the practices for a reason. The whole game is not turning paint into airborne dust.
Don’t dry sand and don’t dry scrape. Mist the surface first and use wet-dry sandpaper. Don’t use a heat gun above 1,100°F, and never open flame. Don’t use power tools without HEPA exhaust control — an ordinary shop vac spreads fine lead dust rather than capturing it.
Contain the room with plastic sheeting and an airlock at the door. Wear a respirator, coveralls, gloves and shoe covers. Clean at the end of every day rather than at the end of the project, because you are still living in the house while the work goes on — the same reason it’s worth knowing how long to wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room. Finish by HEPA-vacuuming and then wet-wiping until the cloths come away clean.
One more, which people get wrong constantly: painting over a lead hazard with ordinary paint is not abatement. It is a temporary encapsulation at best, and if the underlying surface is failing it will fail again through your new paint.
Nothing to do with paint — but Columbus Square is a neighborhood worth knowing.
### Plaster is not drywall, and it changes the job
A house built in 1938 almost certainly has lath-and-plaster walls, and if you have only ever painted drywall, some of what you know doesn’t transfer.
Here is how plaster actually holds on, which explains everything else. Thin wood lath was nailed across the studs with gaps between the strips. A rough basecoat about three-quarters of an inch thick was applied and squeezed into those gaps, forming “keys” behind the lath. Those keys are what hold the whole surface up, including on ceilings.
So there are two completely different problems that look similar from the front. Surface cracking is cosmetic. Plaster that has pulled loose from the lath is structural — the keys have broken — and the National Park Service describes that as requiring specialized restoration rather than patching. Press gently on a suspect area: if it moves or sounds hollow, you are looking at the second problem, and painting over it accomplishes nothing.
Before you decide to tear it out, know what you have. Multi-coat plaster is extremely durable, fire resistant, and it reduces sound transmission in ways drywall does not, and federal preservation standards strongly recommend repair over wholesale replacement. The instinct to strip to the studs and hang sheetrock produces a flatter wall and a worse house.
Two practical notes. Old plaster is rarely perfectly flat, so a flat or matte sheen hides what satin and eggshell reveal under raking light. And ask an experienced local plasterer which patching material suits your specific substrate — the compatible-compound question depends on what kind of plaster you have, and it’s worth a real answer rather than a guess from a blog.
### What it costs, honestly
There is no St. Louis-specific pricing source for painting from any government or research body. The best national figure we could verify directly puts professional interior painting at roughly $4.22 to $8.19 per square foot as of spring 2026 — a national marketplace estimate, not a St. Louis quote, and our market generally runs below national labor rates.
On the materials side, the math is simple. A gallon covers about 350 to 400 square feet in one coat on a smooth surface, less on texture. Most interiors need two coats, so plan on roughly 175 to 200 square feet of finished wall per gallon.
And on paint quality: Consumer Reports’ testing spans interior paints from about $17 to $105 a gallon, and their finding is worth internalizing — a higher price does not guarantee better paint. Mid-priced lines routinely score within a few points of flagship products. Buy on tested performance, not on the shelf position.
The honest structural point about DIY savings: on a small, simple room you save roughly half, because materials and labor run close to even. On a complicated room you save much less, because prep is the part that scales with difficulty and it’s the part you cannot skip. A pro is fast at prep. That’s most of what you’re paying for.
### When to hire it out
Genuinely call someone when you are disturbing lead paint at scale in a pre-1978 house — the homeowner exemption removes your legal duty, not your exposure. When you rent out part of the house, run a daycare in it, or are flipping it, in which case the exemption doesn’t apply at all. When plaster has pulled away from the lath or there’s long-term moisture damage. And when the work is high ceilings or a stairwell — that’s ladder work over a drop, and it is where DIY painting projects turn into emergency room visits.
Spraying deserves its own mention. In a pre-1978 house, spraying atomizes coating in a room where you may have just created lead dust. If you’ve never sprayed, an old house is the wrong place to learn — that is the point to start comparing painting contractors across the St. Louis metro.
### The question to ask any painter you hire
Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration lists no painting license — painters are not a licensed profession in this state. Missouri’s health department licenses lead abatement, and it says explicitly that incidental disturbance of lead paint during remodeling doesn’t meet its definition of abatement, so no state lead license is required for ordinary repainting.
But federal law fills that gap, and this is the one thing to remember:
Missouri does not license painters — but if someone takes your money to disturb paint in a pre-1978 St. Louis home, federal law requires their firm to be EPA Lead-Safe certified. And roughly 87% of city housing is pre-1978.
So the question is simply: “Are you EPA Lead-Safe certified, and can I see the certificate?” A legitimate firm answers instantly. EPA maintains a public list of certified firms you can check yourself.
Separately, the City of St. Louis requires contractors to hold a Construction Industry business license, which involves a clearance from the Collector of Revenue and proof of workers’ compensation coverage. The City’s page names general and sub-contractors without listing painting specifically, so call the License Collector at (314) 622-4528 to confirm how your trade is classified.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a lead certification to paint my own house?
A.  No. EPA states the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule does not apply to homeowners working on their own home. It does apply if you rent out all or part of the house, operate a childcare center in it, or buy and renovate homes to sell for profit — in those cases you are treated as a regulated renovator.
### Q. How do I know if my St. Louis house has lead paint?
A.  Assume it does if it was built before 1978, which covers roughly 87% of city housing and about two-thirds of the county. Confirm with an EPA-recognized test kit — LeadCheck or D-Lead — or with professional XRF testing or lab-analyzed paint chips. If a child under six or a pregnant woman lives there, the City offers a free lead inspection.
### Q. Are lead paint test kits accurate?
A.  Only in one direction. EPA states that no lead test kit has met both of its performance criteria; the recognized kits satisfy only the negative-response standard, meaning a false negative no more than 5% of the time. So a negative result is reasonably reliable, but a positive is not independently validated — treat it as a signal to get real testing.
### Q. What if I accidentally sanded lead paint?
A.  Stop, and do not dry-sweep or reach for a shop vac — both throw the dust back into the air. Keep children and pets out of the room. Clean with wet methods and a HEPA vacuum rather than a broom, wipe down horizontal surfaces and window wells, and bag the debris. If anyone, especially a child or someone pregnant, may have been exposed, that is a question for a doctor rather than a website. For anything beyond a small patch, bring in a certified firm.
### Q. Can I just paint over lead paint?
A.  Painting over a lead hazard with ordinary paint is not abatement, and EPA is explicit about that. Intact, undisturbed lead paint in good condition is generally lower risk than damaged paint, but if the surface underneath is failing, it will fail again through your new coat. The hazard is deteriorating paint and the dust from disturbing it.
One limit worth knowing: encapsulation works on surfaces that stay still. It is a poor answer for friction surfaces — window sashes that slide, doors that rub, stair treads — because those grind through any coating and start making dust again. Those are the components a certified firm will usually recommend replacing rather than sealing.
### Q. How do you paint plaster walls?
A.  First determine whether the problem is cosmetic cracking or structural. Plaster holds on via “keys” squeezed through gaps in wood lath; when plaster has pulled loose from the lath, that is a structural failure requiring specialized repair, not patching. Press gently — movement or a hollow sound means stop. Flat or matte sheens hide old plaster’s irregularity better than satin.
### Q. How much paint do I need for a room?
A.  A gallon covers roughly 350 to 400 square feet in one coat on a smooth surface, less on texture. Since most interiors need two coats, plan on about 175 to 200 square feet of finished wall per gallon. Measure wall length times height, subtract large openings, and buy one extra quart for touch-ups.
### Q. Is expensive paint worth it?
A.  Not automatically. Consumer Reports tests interior paints ranging from about $17 to $105 a gallon and has found that a higher price does not guarantee better performance — mid-priced lines often score within a few points of flagship products. Buy on tested hiding and durability rather than on price.
### Q. Does Missouri license painters?
A.  The Missouri Division of Professional Registration lists no painting license. However, any firm paid to disturb paint in a pre-1978 home must be EPA Lead-Safe certified under federal law — which covers most St. Louis housing. Ask any painter you hire for their certification, and check the City’s business license requirements at (314) 622-4528.

## How to Choose a Commercial Cleaner in St. Louis: Start With the $15.00 Wage
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-rated-commercial-cleaners-in-st-louis-your-ultimate-guide
$15.00 an hour. That is Missouri’s minimum wage, and it is the number hiding inside the bin that is still overflowing next to your desk in a Clayton office suite at 7 a.m. You step off the elevator with road salt still crunching on the lobby tile, unlock the door, flip on the lights and smell it before you see it: yesterday’s toasted ravioli boxes in the breakroom trash, a gray film on the glass door, a restroom that nobody touched overnight. You pay a cleaning company so this never happens. And somewhere in the bid you signed, somebody decided how many paid hours your office was worth.
Here is the St. Louis math nobody puts on a pricing page. A commercial cleaning bid is mostly labor. The Missouri Department of Labor lists the state minimum wage at $15.00 per hour. There is a catch most buyers never hear: the same Missouri page says retail or service businesses with annual gross income under $500,000 are not required to pay the state minimum wage rate. So two cleaning bids for the same Clayton suite can rest on very different paychecks, and you are allowed to ask every bidder one plain question: do you pay your crew at least the Missouri minimum wage? When one number comes in far below the rest, the gap did not vanish. Somebody absorbs it, usually the crew first and your office next.
The enemy here is not the cleaners pushing carts down a dark hallway after everyone else went home. It is the lowball bid built to win the contract, not to clean the building, and the long contract that locks you in before anyone has proved a thing. The fix is simple. Stop comparing prices. Start comparing the hours, the people and the paper behind each price.
### How much does commercial cleaning cost?
Commercial cleaning is priced per square foot or per hour after a walk-through, and the total depends on square footage, how often the crew comes, the layout and what is in scope. In Missouri, labor drives most of every bid, and the state minimum wage is $15.00 an hour for covered employers. Ask each company to show the labor hours behind its price, so you are comparing real work instead of a guess.
That one request changes the whole conversation. A company that can spell out its crew size, hours per visit and visits per week has actually thought about your building. If those numbers add up to 30 labor hours a week, then at $15.00 an hour that is $450 in wages before payroll taxes, insurance, supplies or profit. A company that cannot tell you the hours is guessing, and a guess is what you will get at 7 a.m.
### Why the cheapest bid gets expensive by the third week
The first week usually looks fine. The crew is fresh, the supervisor walks through, the carpet has those clean vacuum lines that make a lobby look cared for. By the third week the lines are gone. A trash liner did not get changed. The breakroom sink has a ring of coffee grounds that sits there all day, and your best client sees it on the way to the conference room.
That slide is predictable when a bid is too thin for the hours the building needs. The crew is not lazy. They are being asked to clean 10,000 square feet in the time it takes to clean 6,000, so they skip what nobody checks. Corners. Baseboards. The restroom partitions where the grime builds. You end up as the unpaid quality inspector, writing notes to a voicemail box, and the hours you lose doing that cost more than the gap between the cheapest bid and the honest one.
Layout matters as much as footage. An open office on one floor in Earth City cleans faster than the same footage chopped into private offices, exam rooms, closets and multiple restrooms. Frequency matters too: nightly service costs more each month than three visits a week, but it keeps restrooms and kitchens from turning sour. A walk-through and a written, itemized quote for your space will always beat a per-foot average pulled off a website.
### The Missouri paperwork that protects you
Every cleaner in your building after dark has your keys, your alarm code and a clear path to every desk. So the vetting has to go past a friendly phone call. Start with the one rule most buyers have never heard: in Missouri, an employer with five or more employees is required to carry workers’ compensation insurance, according to the state Division of Workers’ Compensation. If a cleaner slips on your wet tile, that coverage is what answers the injury. Ask for the certificate. The division’s employer page also links a tool to verify coverage, so you can check it yourself in a few minutes instead of taking anyone’s word.
Then ask for proof of general liability insurance, which covers accidental damage to your property, and a fidelity bond, which protects you if something walks out of the building. Get the certificate emailed straight from the insurance agent, not a scan from the salesperson. It takes one phone call, and it is the cheapest protection you will ever buy.
Start with the labor
### How much should I charge per square foot for commercial cleaning?
There is no honest per-square-foot average, because size, frequency, layout and scope swing it. Build the number from labor: at Missouri’s $15.00 minimum wage for covered employers, 30 crew hours a week is $450 in wages before payroll taxes, insurance, supplies or profit.
### Define the job before you take a single bid
“Commercial cleaning” can mean nightly trash and restrooms, or it can mean floor stripping, carpet extraction, window work and disinfection. Before anyone walks your space, write a one-page scope: what needs cleaning, how often and when. After-hours service is standard for offices. Give every company the same page, so their bids answer the same question.
That page becomes your checklist later. When the restrooms were in the deal and they were not cleaned, you point to the line. When the crew asks to add window work, you know whether it was included. It stops you from paying for services you do not need, and it stops the worst surprise of all: finding out after you signed that the restrooms were never in the price.
For a small office, the scope also lets you sanity-check the hours. A suite of a few thousand square feet with one restroom and a small kitchen is a short job, and a good company will tell you how many labor hours each visit takes before you ask. Multiply those hours by a fair wage, add supplies, insurance and a reasonable profit, and you can see in a minute whether a bid is honest or too thin to last past the first month. If the math only works when the crew rushes, the crew will rush, and you will see it in the corners first.
### Employees or subcontractors: ask it out loud
One question separates steady companies from chaotic ones: are the people cleaning your office the company’s own employees, or subcontractors? Employees typically come with background checks, training and a supervisor who answers for their work. Subcontracted labor can be fine, but it adds variables: who actually shows up, how they were screened and who is responsible when something goes missing.
It also decides whether you get the same crew. The same team, week after week, learns that the conference room needs extra attention before a big meeting and that the third-floor restroom runs out of paper towels first. A rotating cast of strangers never learns any of it. Ask directly, and write the answer into your notes.
### Contract terms: start on a short leash
A confident company will start you on a trial period or month-to-month terms, because it expects to earn the renewal. Be cautious of anyone who insists on a long, hard-to-exit contract before cleaning a single night. Read for automatic renewals and price-escalation clauses, so a fair starting rate does not quietly climb. The goal is a cleaner you keep because the work is good, not because the paperwork makes leaving painful.
Office smells like bleach and you need a real lunch? West County’s dinner and lunch lineup is one click away.
### Supplies, green products and quality control
Ask who supplies what. Some companies bring all equipment and restroom consumables, like paper towels, soap and liners. Others expect you to stock them. Unclear supply terms are one of the most common fights in a cleaning contract, so get them in writing. If your team is sensitive to harsh smells, ask about lower-VOC products, and read how to tell which cleaners are genuinely eco-friendly before you accept a green label at face value.
Then ask how they catch their own mistakes. Supervisor walk-throughs, a simple checklist the crew signs, a way for you to flag a miss and see it fixed the next night. A company with a system for its own misses is a company that takes the work seriously.
### Red flags when hiring a cleaning company
No certificate of insurance, or one sent as a scan instead of straight from the agent.
No written scope, or a scope that says “general cleaning” and nothing else.
Vague answers about who actually does the cleaning.
A bid far below the others with no labor hours to explain it.
Pressure to sign a long contract on the first visit.
No references from businesses like yours, and no named point of contact.
### Questions to ask before you hire
How many labor hours a week is this price built on?
Do you carry workers’ compensation and general liability insurance, and can your agent send the certificates?
Are your cleaners employees or subcontractors, and are they background-checked?
Will the same crew clean my space each visit?
Who supplies equipment and restroom consumables?
Is this month-to-month, and what are the cancellation terms?
How do you handle quality control and missed items?
The questions are a filter. Accountable companies expect them and answer fast. The ones to avoid get vague exactly where it matters.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the average cost for commercial cleaning?
A.  There is no honest single average, because square footage, frequency, layout and scope swing the price more than anything else. Labor is the biggest piece, and Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour for covered employers. Get a walk-through, an itemized written quote and the labor hours behind it from at least three companies.
### Q. What’s the difference between commercial cleaning and janitorial cleaning?
A.  Janitorial cleaning is the routine, recurring work: trash, restrooms, vacuuming, dusting and wiping surfaces, usually nightly or several times a week. Commercial cleaning is the broader term, and it also covers periodic deep cleaning, floor stripping and waxing, carpet extraction, window work and disinfection.
### Q. What qualifies as commercial cleaning?
A.  Cleaning done for a business space rather than a home: offices, storefronts, medical and dental suites, restaurants, warehouses and shared building areas. It is usually done after hours under a written scope and a service contract, and the company should carry business insurance for working inside your property.
### Q. What are the cleaning duties in an office?
A.  Emptying trash and recycling, cleaning and restocking restrooms, cleaning the breakroom and sink, vacuuming and mopping floors, dusting and wiping desks and high-touch surfaces like door handles and light switches, and spot-cleaning glass. Periodic duties include deep cleaning, floor care and windows.

## St. Louis Coffee Started With a Name Spelled Backwards
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-coffee-shops-in-st-louis-a-local-guide
A low rushing hiss comes from the back of the room on Hartford Street, steady as a box fan, under the clink of cups. It isn’t the espresso machine. It’s the roaster. Hartford Coffee roasts on-site, five pounds at a time, and the beans float on hot air instead of sitting against hot metal, so nothing scorches. You can smell the batch before you can see the counter.
That sound is the whole case for drinking coffee in this city. Here’s the part almost no coffee guide tells you: St. Louis was roasting before most of the country cared. The name you’ve seen on gas station cups and hotel urns your whole life, Ronnoco, is O’Connor spelled backwards. Two brothers, J.P. and James O’Connor, tasted imported beans roasted over a gas flame at the World’s Fair in St. Louis, started their own company, and delivered coffee beans to local hotels by horse-drawn buggy.
Say that one out loud at the next table and watch somebody turn their cup around to read it. Then go find the rooms that still roast within earshot.
### What’s the most popular coffee shop in St. Louis?
Nobody keeps an official count, so pick by the time you have. Fifteen minutes: Blueprint’s Watson Coffee Bar, 4206 Watson Rd, take-out 8a-4p. An hour with a laptop: Fiddlehead Fern Cafe, 4066 Russell Blvd, open 7am-4pm all seven days. A slow half-day with kids: Hartford Coffee in Tower Grove South, open every day, 7am to 6pm, with a train table in the back. Showing off for visitors: Shaw’s Coffee on The Hill, inside an old bank building.
Sit by the front window at 700 DeMun Ave on a cold morning and the street feels like a small town that forgot it’s next to a city. The Kaldi’s DeMun story starts in that building, once a travel agency and then a transcendental meditation center. Its founders went to a coffee show to learn roasting and ordered a machine from the man who built it.
### Pick the shop by the hour you have
Rankings are useless at 7:40 with a meeting at 8:15. What helps is matching the room to the errand, so here is the same city sorted by the clock, with the hours each shop posts on its own site.
Fifteen minutes, on the way somewhere: Blueprint, Watson Coffee Bar. 4206 Watson Rd, dine-in, take-out and patio, 8a-4p. You want a counter, not a couch. Order an Americano or a drip, keep your keys in your hand, and you are back in the car with the cup warming your palm before the next light changes. Heading the other way? Blueprint’s Delmar Coffee Bar at 6225 Delmar Blvd keeps the same 8a-4p.
A full hour with a laptop: Fiddlehead Fern Cafe. 4066 Russell Blvd, 7am-4pm all seven days. The cafe says it outright: whether you are working, studying or meeting neighbors, there is a place for you. Walk the wall, find the plug, then order. A table under a window beats a soft chair you will sink into and regret by the second email.
A slow half-day with kids in tow: Hartford Coffee. 3974 Hartford St in Tower Grove South, open every day, 7am to 6pm. There is a train table in the back, and the clack of a wooden engine over a bridge does more for a parent’s nerves than any latte. Bring a book for yourself anyway, and listen for the roaster. On the way out, turn a bag of beans over: every Hartford bag shows its roast date. Make that your rule at every roaster in town. If a bag will not tell you when it was roasted, put it back.
A warm afternoon outside: Blueprint’s High Low bar. 3301 Washington Blvd, patio, 8a-4p. Get there before the last hour, sit in the half-shade, and let the ice in the cold brew rattle while you decide nothing in particular.
A first date or a visitor from out of town: Shaw’s Coffee. 5147 Shaw Ave on The Hill, in the building once called “The Bank.” Order at the counter, then take the table farthest from the grinder, so the only thing you have to talk over is each other. Call ahead for the hours before you drive across town.
Bringing the dog. Blueprint lists patios at both the Watson and High Low bars, so sit outside, and ask before you walk a leash through the door. Bring your own water bowl. Nobody minds a quiet dog under the table; everybody minds the one that greets every stroller.
### The rooms that roast within earshot
At Hartford Coffee Company, 3974 Hartford St in Tower Grove South, that hiss you heard is Joe doing all the roasting on-site. Families know it for the train table in the back, where kids grew up and some are now old enough to order their own coffee.

On a warm afternoon the Watson patio smells of espresso and car exhaust in equal measure, which is about as South City as a coffee break gets.
### Where the building is half the reason
Shaw’s Coffee, 5147 Shaw Ave, works out of what was once “The Bank,” also called the Riggio Building, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Heavy old walls, a grinder going behind the counter, and the Italian streets of The Hill outside the door. Take someone from out of town here.
Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop in Webster Groves pairs coffee and plants. You drink your latte with damp potting soil and green leaves in the air, which does more for a gray Tuesday than any syrup.
Fiddlehead Fern Cafe, 4066 Russell Blvd, opened in a new building on the parking lot of a gas station. A corner made for fill-ups now smells like steamed milk.
### Is there a new coffee shop in St. Louis?
Yes, and it doubles as a warning about old lists. Shortwave Coffee opened in Quarrelsome’s previous space in the Central West End, at 33 N. Sarah St. Shortwave was founded in Columbia, Missouri. If an old list sends you to Quarrelsome, this is the door it means.
The same goes for every name here. Small shops change hours fast. If you are driving across town for one cup, call first.
### Which neighborhoods have the most coffee?
A mid-century corner shop on Watson Road in St. Louis, MO, photographed by Lane Forman for St Louis Near Me Directory
The good cups cluster. Tower Grove South, the Central West End, Maplewood and Webster Groves are the easiest places to walk from one shop to the next. Maplewood has enough of its own for a separate trip, so we wrote up coffee shops in Maplewood on their own.
Downtown and the Central West End get their own map in coffee shops in the Central West End and downtown. Out west, the good ones are spread thinner, and coffee shops in Chesterfield and West County covers that drive. Farther west, out past the Missouri River, see coffee shops in Wentzville. Crossing the river for the day instead? Start with a day trip on the Illinois side, and fill the thermos before the bridge.
Some afternoons call for a pot, not a pour-over: what to expect at a tea house in St. Louis.
### What to order when the menu looks like a test
Most of a coffee menu is one question: how much milk goes with the espresso. Espresso is a brewing method, not a special bean. Hot water is forced through finely ground coffee under pressure and comes out as a small, thick shot.
An Americano is espresso plus hot water, no cream unless you ask, and a safe order when the drip pot has been sitting. A cortado is close to equal parts espresso and steamed milk. A flat white has more milk and a thin, velvety foam. A latte has the most milk and tastes the mildest. A cappuccino wears a thick, airy cap of foam you can feel on your lip.
A macchiato at an independent shop is usually a shot of espresso marked with a spoonful of foam, small and strong, gone in three sips. The big sweet caramel drink with the same name at the chains is a different animal. A chai latte is spiced tea with steamed milk and no coffee at all, unless you order it “dirty,” which adds a shot.
At a shop that roasts its own, ask what they are proud of this week. People who roast love that question, and you will get a better cup than the one on the board.
### Coffee etiquette, the St. Louis way
Most of it is plain neighbor manners. Know your order by the time you reach the register, or step aside and let the person behind you go. Say thank you to whoever is steaming the milk, because they heard you even over the scream of the wand.
Take phone calls outside. A small room with hard floors carries every word, and nobody at the next table needs your quarterly numbers. Bus your own cup if there is a tub by the door, and wipe up the sugar you spilled. And if a place roasts its own, buy a bag of beans on your way out now and then. That bag is how a neighborhood shop pays the rent between the morning and lunch rushes.
Want the shop closest to where you’re standing right now? Browse coffee shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then choose by the hour you have: a quick counter on the way in, or a room you can sit in until the cup goes cold.
If you own the cafe with the hissing roaster or the good corner table, a Gold listing puts your room in front of the customers searching for a place to sit, and it is under a dollar a day. Or see every plan.

## Stop Flipping Your AC Off and On, St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/smart-ac-repair-your-eco-friendly-guide
“Please stop turning it off and on.”
The AC tech says it in the front hall of a brick two-story in south city, his bag still on his shoulder.
You’d told him on the phone, a little proudly, that you’d already shut it off and on. Twice. Like a router.
Four in the afternoon. July. The house is 84 degrees and climbing, and the vents push out air that feels like somebody breathing on you. Out by the alley, the condenser hums, clicks, and goes quiet again.
Here’s why he winced. That off-and-on trick can be the worst thing you do to an air conditioner. TCL, the air conditioner maker, puts it flatly: after the air conditioner is shut down, it should be at least three minutes before it can be turned on again. Otherwise, it warns, liquid hammer can show up in the compressor and damage parts. Trane’s own controls build the pause in, keeping a compressor off for at least 3 minutes once it shuts down. That’s the 3-minute rule for air conditioners.
Three minutes. Count them on the kitchen clock. Text that to whoever in your family flips the thermostat like a light switch.
When the three minutes don’t fix it, the next call costs real money, and your shirt is stuck to your back before you reach the car. Slow down first, and carry four St. Louis things into it.
The card. Ask the tech at the door for his EPA 608 card, because federal rules say anyone who services equipment that could release ozone-depleting refrigerants must be certified.
The permit. Live inside the city and the outdoor unit has to go? The City of St. Louis fee schedule lists residential condensing units at $40 each, plus a $25 application fee, and the city issues those mechanical permits to licensed contractors it certifies, so ask whether the permit is in the price.
The bill. Ameren Missouri’s FastTrack HVAC PAYS lets Ameren Missouri electric customers pay for new heating and cooling equipment monthly on the utility bill.
The fire department. In the city, the St. Louis Fire Department will help seniors and individuals with disabilities install window air conditioning units. The number is 314-533-3406.
### Is it better to run AC all day or just when home in St. Louis?
Run it on a schedule, so you walk in from a sticky St. Louis driveway to cool, dry air instead of a house that has been baking since noon. Ameren Missouri says smart or programmable thermostats that adjust settings when you’re away save the average household about $180 per year. Ameren Missouri also has two rates with a summer-only option, Smart Savers and Overnight Savers, so your schedule can follow your rate.
### When repair turns into replace: Ameren’s on-bill option
Sometimes the tech stands up from the condenser, wipes his hands on his jeans and says the words you were dreading: it’s done. You can hear it in his voice before he says it, and you can feel the house getting warmer while he talks. This is where Ameren Missouri customers have a tool worth knowing before anyone hands them a financing brochure. Picture the replacement not as one terrifying number on a clipboard but as a line on the electric bill you already open at the kitchen counter every month. That’s the idea behind FastTrack HVAC PAYS: Ameren says it offsets upfront costs and lets you pay for the equipment monthly on your utility bill.
It even shapes how you choose the pro. Ameren’s page says you select up to three contractors of your choice and schedule a visit, and the contractor then determines your eligibility and walks you through the offer. The charge on your bill includes the cost of the installation, 3% interest and a small program close-out fee. One catch for the folks across the river: Ameren says HVAC PAYS is not available for Illinois customers, so a Belleville address is out. Everyone else starts on Ameren Missouri’s HVAC PAYS page, by picking the contractors you want to see.
### How to pick the tech who walks up your driveway
You hear the truck door slam out front, then boots on the steps. Start with a card most homeowners never think to ask about. Federal rules under Section 608 of the Clean Air Act require that technicians who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of equipment that could release ozone-depleting refrigerants be certified, and the EPA even runs a process for replacing a lost Section 608 technician card. So ask, plainly, standing on the hot front step with the screen door propped on your hip: can I see your 608 card? A real pro has it in a wallet or on a phone and doesn’t blink. Anyone who gets defensive just answered a bigger question.
Then ask the money questions before anyone opens a panel. What’s the diagnostic fee? Does it go toward the repair if I say yes today? Will I get the quote itemized, in writing, before you start? Listen to how they answer, not just what. The tech who explains the problem in plain English, shows you the burnt capacitor or the iced-up line in your own hand, and texts you a photo of the failed part is showing you how the whole job will go.
And watch the pitch. If somebody looks at an air conditioner that is a few years old and goes straight to a full replacement before testing a single part, thank them, pay the diagnostic fee, and get a second opinion. Comparing two or three companies on the same problem is the cheapest insurance you’ll ever buy.
One more tell, and it’s about the truck. A company that shows up when it said it would, calls ahead, and puts on shoe covers before stepping onto your carpet is usually the same company that tightens every connection before it leaves. You can feel it in the first sixty seconds at the door. Trust that feeling, then check the card anyway.
### The first ten minutes after it quits
Before you call anyone, stand in the hallway and listen. Is the indoor blower running? Is the outdoor unit humming, or dead silent? Then check the three things you can fix in socks: the thermostat setting, the breaker panel in the basement, and the filter. Ameren Missouri says keeping your air filters clean helps your cooling system run efficiently. Pull it out and hold it up to the window. If it’s gray felt, swap it before the tech arrives, because you’re about to pay somebody to tell you the same thing.
If all three check out, leave it off. Give it the three minutes, try it once, and if it still blows warm, make the call. Don’t sit there toggling it while the compressor strains. The calm version of you saves money. The panicked version, standing over the thermostat with sweat running down the back of your neck, pays for parts.
### If it’s your mom’s house that’s too hot
Sometimes the dead air conditioner isn’t yours. It’s the one in your mother’s bedroom, where the window faces west and the afternoon sun bakes the bedspread, and she’s telling you on the phone she’s fine when you can hear the box fan rattling behind her.
Here’s who to call. In June, Ameren Missouri donated 950 ENERGY STAR certified window air conditioners to Cooldownstlouis.org and Cooldownmissouri.org for qualifying customers. Ameren says it and its volunteers have helped deliver more than 20,000 donated window units through the effort. Older adults and people with disabilities can also apply for energy assistance funds through Cooldownstlouis.org or by calling 314.241.0001 or 314.834.0034, the hotlines for seniors and people with disabilities. Write the number on the fridge before you leave her house.
Then the call most families never think to make. If she lives in the City of St. Louis, the St. Louis Fire Department will help seniors and individuals with disabilities install window air conditioning units if they need assistance, so nobody has to wrestle that heavy box up her stairs alone. Residents in need of installation assistance can call 314-533-3406. And if the bedroom is too hot to wait out the afternoon, the city says residents are welcome to cool down in public buildings, such as the City’s public libraries and community centers, during regular business hours. Call 2-1-1 for the full metro list, and call the library first, because hours can change.
Hot house, cold drink, somebody else cooking: people eat in Sauget, and they eat well.
### Window units: sizing the bedroom stopgap
Under the store lights every window-unit box looks the same. While you wait for a part, one of them can keep one room livable, and the most common mistake is grabbing whatever box is on the end cap. ENERGY STAR’s sizing chart puts 100 up to 150 square feet at 5,000 BTUs per hour, and 150 up to 250 square feet at 6,000. So the difference between a 5000 and 6000 BTU air conditioner is roughly the difference between a small bedroom and a bigger one.
ENERGY STAR adds a few adjustments worth knowing. If the room is very sunny, increase capacity by 10 percent. If it’s heavily shaded, reduce it by 10 percent. If the unit is going in a kitchen, increase capacity by 4,000 BTUs. That west-facing upstairs bedroom in an old brick house is the sunny one, every time.
Wondering what it costs to run that stopgap around the clock? Flip the box over and find the watts on the label. Multiply it by every hour in the month, convert the result to kilowatt-hours, and multiply by the price per kilowatt-hour on your electric bill. That’s the ceiling for a month of running a 5000 BTU air conditioner nonstop, and it’s a number worth knowing before you decide how long you can wait on a part.
Put the unit in the window, close the bedroom door, and set a fan by the doorway. On a 98-degree night that hum, and the cool spot on the pillow, is the difference between sleeping and lying there counting the hours until the tech shows up.

### Getting quotes without getting burned
Three quotes on the kitchen table, three different totals, a box fan rattling in the doorway. For a big repair, get it in writing and get it itemized: the part, the labor, the refrigerant if any, and the warranty on each. Be just as wary of a quote that comes in far below the others as one far above. Cheap often means something left out, and you find out what in August.
Then keep the good one. When you find a tech who showed you the part, answered the 608 question without flinching and called back when he said he would, save the number in your phone under “AC” and book the spring tune-up before the first 90-degree week. The people who stay cool in a St. Louis summer aren’t lucky. They made this call in April.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the 3-minute rule for air conditioners?
A.  Wait at least three minutes after the air conditioner shuts down before turning it back on. TCL warns that restarting sooner can cause liquid hammer in the compressor, damaging parts and shortening the compressor’s service life, and Trane’s controls hold a compressor off for at least 3 minutes after it stops.
### Q. Is there a big difference between a 5000 and 6000 BTU air conditioner?
A.  About one room size. ENERGY STAR’s chart matches 5,000 BTUs per hour to 100 up to 150 square feet and 6,000 BTUs to 150 up to 250 square feet. Bump it up 10 percent for a very sunny room, and down 10 percent for a heavily shaded one.
### Q. How much does it cost to run a 5000 BTU air conditioner 24 hours a day for 30 days?
A.  It depends on two numbers you can find tonight: the watts on the unit’s label and the price per kilowatt-hour on your electric bill. Multiply the watts by every hour in the month, convert that to kilowatt-hours, then multiply by your price per kilowatt-hour. That’s your nonstop worst case.

## DIY Lawn Care vs. Hiring a Pro in St. Louis: What the Science Says
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/diy-lawn-care-vs-hiring-a-pro-in-st-louis
University of Missouri Extension has a sentence about seeding a lawn in spring that ought to be printed on every bag of grass seed sold in this state:
“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”
That is a land-grant university telling you that the seed everyone buys in April is largely money in the trash. Timing, not effort and not equipment, is what separates a good St. Louis lawn from a bad one — and it’s also what decides whether you should be doing this yourself.
### Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis?
Mostly yes, with two exceptions. Missouri law lets you apply any general-use product to your own lawn with no license, and the highest-value task — seeding in the August 25 to October 10 window — requires timing rather than skill. Hire out core aeration, where renting the machine barely beats the roughly $107–$202 a service charges, and hire out anything on a neighbor’s property, because applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a certified commercial applicator’s license.
### Why nothing quite works here
St. Louis sits in what turf scientists call the Transition Zone — and MU Extension defines it exactly as bluntly as it deserves: an area “where neither warm- nor cool-season grass species are completely adapted.”
There is no perfect grass for this city. There are only trade-offs, and picking one means choosing which season you’re willing to lose.
Cool-season grasses grow best between 60 and 75 degrees — spring and fall — and struggle through a St. Louis August. Warm-season grasses want 80 to 95 degrees and go dormant in the cold.
MU’s recommendation for Missouri lawns has been the same for decades: turf-type tall fescue, ideally as a mix of 90% tall fescue and 10% Kentucky bluegrass. It has a deep root system and handles heat and drought better than other cool-season options. It is green in April and green in November and it suffers in high summer.
Zoysia is the other legitimate choice, adapted to the southern two-thirds of Missouri. It is genuinely tough — durable, weed-resistant, heat- and drought-tolerant, easy to mow. The price is that it goes straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring. Roughly half the year, your lawn is brown while your neighbor’s is green.
Neither is wrong. But bermudagrass is, at least here — MU says flatly that it is “not recommended for lawns in Transition Zone,” and is best adapted to the southern third of the state.
One number worth having if you pay a water bill: properly managed, tall fescue needs about 25% less water and zoysia about 50% less than Kentucky bluegrass to stay green and growing here.
### The three weeks that decide your year
If you take one thing from this article, take this. For cool-season grass in Missouri, the seeding window is August 25 to October 10, and lawns seeded around Labor Day outperform ones seeded in October.
Spring seeding fails because spring moisture feeds weeds that outcompete your seedlings, and then summer heat kills whatever survived. Fall works because the soil is still warm enough for fast germination while the air is cooling, rain is more regular, and weed pressure has dropped.
The seeding rates make the point by themselves. MU specifies 7 pounds of tall fescue per 1,000 square feet in fall — and 10 pounds in spring. Forty percent more seed, for a result the same publication says may fail completely.
And here is what makes that window so efficient: the three highest-value jobs of the entire lawn year all land in it. Aeration is best in early fall. Seeding runs August 25 to October 10. And September is, in MU’s words, the most important time to fertilize — 1 to 1½ pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet.
Done as one operation, the sequence is: mow low, aerate, seed, lightly rake in, fertilize, water. One weekend in early September does more for your lawn than everything you will do in April, May and June combined.
### The rest of the calendar
For tall fescue: half a pound to a pound of slow-release nitrogen in early-to-mid April, the big feeding in September, and a moderate application in late October or November once temperatures drop below 50 degrees to push root growth.
Mowing height matters more than people think. MU gives 2 to 3½ inches in spring, 3 to 4 inches in summer, and 2½ to 3½ in fall. Cutting tall fescue short in a St. Louis July is a self-inflicted wound — taller grass shades its own roots and holds soil moisture.
If you have zoysia, throw all of that out, because the calendar is nearly the mirror image. Fertilize from late May through mid-August only — MU is explicit: do not fertilize into September, because the plant is heading for dormancy. Plant it in mid-May to early June, not fall. Mow it short, 1½ to 2 inches.
Applying the fescue program to a zoysia lawn is actively harmful, and a lot of people do it without realizing they have zoysia at all. If your lawn browns out every October while the neighborhood stays green, that’s your answer.
### Clay, and what actually helps
Heavy clay compacts, restricts water and air movement, and produces shallow roots that stress fast in drought. Two things about it are worth knowing before you spend money.
Do not add sand. This is the single most common expensive mistake. MU is unambiguous: sand mixed into clay “can set up into a bricklike mixture,” and you need 75% or more sand by volume before you see any improvement in aeration, drainage or texture. Anything less makes it worse. A few bags of sand on a clay lawn is money spent making the problem harder.
What does work is organic matter — compost, peat or well-rotted manure, 1 to 3 inches worked into the top 6 inches, aiming for 2.5 to 3% organic matter. And note this carefully: MU says topdressing with topsoil “does not generally improve” heavy clay “unless it is done in combination with core aerification.” The aeration is what makes the amendment reach anything.
Test your drainage before you diagnose anything. Dig a hole and fill it with water. Gone within 18 to 24 hours is satisfactory. Two days or longer and you have a drainage problem that no fertilizer program will fix.
One thing in clay’s favor, since it gets a uniformly bad press: it holds water and nutrients well — ammonium, potassium, calcium, magnesium — which makes it naturally fertile. It’s a mixed blessing, not a curse.
### Aeration is the one to hire out
Core aeration — pulling plugs rather than poking holes — is the highest-value service on this list, and it’s the one where DIY math stops working.
Early fall is the best timing for cool-season lawns, which conveniently puts it in the same window as seeding. Coring also stresses the lawn less than dethatching with a power rake, and it reduces compaction at the same time.
A service runs roughly $107 to $202 nationally, with a second independent source putting it at $100 to $300 — those ranges corroborate each other, which is more than can be said for most home-services pricing. Against that: renting the machine, getting it home, running it, and returning it. The margin is thin and the machine is heavy. This is where hiring wins on the merits, and where it pays to compare the lawn and landscaping crews working your part of the metro before you book one.
Whoever does it, leave the plugs on the lawn to dry and crumble. Mowing them once dry redistributes the soil microbes that break down thatch. Raking them up throws away half the benefit.
Unrelated, and we know it — but Ellendale is worth a scroll.
### What you can legally do yourself
There is a clean legal line here, and almost no local lawn content states it correctly.
On your own lawn: MU Extension puts it plainly — general-use pesticides “may be used by anyone, so long as the pesticide is used only on lands owned or rented by that person,” and “homeowners do not need a private applicator license.” Anything you can buy off the shelf at a hardware store is general-use. Read the label, follow it, and you’re fine.
On anyone else’s lawn, for money: Missouri law states that no individual shall use any pesticide “on the lands of another at any time without a certified commercial applicator’s license.” That’s $65 a year, under Category 3, Ornamental and Turf Pest Control, plus proof of financial responsibility through bond or insurance.
Which means the mowing side-hustle is fine, and the moment it becomes a spraying side-hustle it isn’t — not even once, not even as a favor with twenty dollars attached.
It also gives you a way to vet a lawn company in one sentence: “What’s your Missouri commercial applicator license number and category?” A legitimate operator has it ready. Certified applicators also recertify on a three-year cycle and must keep application records for three years, so a company that treats your yard should be able to tell you exactly what went down and when.
### What hiring costs
There is no government or research source for lawn service pricing — not the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not the Department of Agriculture, not Extension. Every figure available comes from lawn-service marketplaces, which have an obvious interest in the framing. So treat these as national marketplace estimates, not St. Louis quotes:
Mowing: roughly $42 to $68 per visit. Core aeration: $107 to $202. Fertilization: $67 to $405 depending on program. Full-service monthly: $100 to $410.
Mowing is the biggest line item in any full-service quote, because it’s the highest-frequency task. It’s also the lowest-skill one. If you want to cut a lawn bill in half without learning anything, mow it yourself and buy the rest.
### The honest split
DIY genuinely wins on mowing, and on seeding and fertilizing your own lawn — where the law is entirely on your side and where timing beats technique. A homeowner who seeds on Labor Day weekend beats a professional who seeds in April, because MU says the April job risks complete failure regardless of who does it.
Hiring genuinely wins on core aeration, on anything touching a property you don’t own, on a lawn you suspect is zoysia and can’t confirm, and on a drainage failure — if water sits in that test hole past two days, you need grading and soil work, not a fertilizer program.
And if you do nothing else this year: put the seed and the fertilizer down in the first half of September. That single decision outweighs everything else on this page.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should I seed my lawn in St. Louis?
A.  Between August 25 and October 10, with Labor Day weekend the sweet spot — MU Extension finds Labor Day seedings outperform October ones. Spring seeding is far riskier; MU states that with spring seeding “in some cases, complete failure should be expected,” because weeds outcompete seedlings and summer heat finishes them.
### Q. What is the best grass for St. Louis?
A.  Turf-type tall fescue, ideally in a 90% fescue / 10% Kentucky bluegrass mix, is MU Extension’s long-standing recommendation for Missouri lawns. Zoysia is the warm-season alternative — tougher in summer but straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring. Bermudagrass is explicitly not recommended for our transition zone.
### Q. How much seed do I need per 1,000 square feet?
A.  For tall fescue, MU specifies 7 pounds per 1,000 square feet when seeding in fall, and 10 pounds in spring. That 40% increase for spring seeding — for a worse expected result — is itself the strongest argument for waiting until late August.
### Q. When should I fertilize my lawn in Missouri?
A.  For cool-season grass, September is the most important application at 1 to 1½ pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet, with a half to one pound of slow-release in early-to-mid April and a moderate rate in late fall once temperatures fall below 50 degrees. Zoysia is the opposite — feed late May through mid-August and never into September.
### Q. Should I add sand to clay soil?
A.  No. MU Extension warns that sand mixed with clay “can set up into a bricklike mixture,” and you would need 75% or more sand by volume before seeing any improvement. Use organic matter instead — 1 to 3 inches of compost worked into the top 6 inches — and note that topdressing generally does not help heavy clay unless combined with core aeration.
### Q. Do I need a license to spray my own lawn in Missouri?
A.  No. General-use pesticides may be used by anyone on land they own or rent, and MU Extension states plainly that homeowners do not need a private applicator license. But applying pesticide on someone else’s property for compensation requires a certified commercial applicator’s license — $65 a year, Category 3 Ornamental and Turf.
### Q. How much does lawn care cost per month?
A.  National marketplace estimates put full-service programs at roughly $100 to $410 a month, with mowing at $42 to $68 per visit and core aeration at $107 to $202. No government or research source publishes lawn service pricing, so treat all of these as national estimates rather than St. Louis quotes.

## The St. Louis Homeowner Starter Toolkit (and Knowing Your Limits)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/must-have-handyman-tools-for-st-louis-homeowners
There’s a small, specific pride in fixing something yourself. The picture finally hung straight. The kitchen drawer that glides again. The wobbly chair made solid. You don’t need to be handy by nature — you just need a handful of the right tools and the confidence to start. Whether you just bought your first bungalow in south city or you’ve rented the same place in Overland for years, a basic toolkit turns “I should call someone” into “I’ll just do it.”
Here’s the honest starter kit — what actually earns its place in a St. Louis home, a couple of things our older houses specifically demand, the first projects to cut your teeth on, and, just as importantly, where to put the tools down and call a pro.
### The starter kit at a glance
The honest starter kit is short: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set (or a multi-bit driver), a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, and a stud finder — plus one cordless drill/driver. That handful covers the overwhelming majority of everyday household fixes. What St. Louis adds to the standard list is proper wall anchors for plaster, because so much of our housing stock has plaster-and-lath walls rather than drywall. Buy quality on the few tools you’ll use most, and add the rest as real projects call for them.
### The core hand tools every homeowner should own
Claw hammer — comfortable grip, solid head. The workhorse; a 16-ounce is the do-everything size.
Screwdriver set — a range of flathead and Phillips sizes, or a good multi-bit driver that stores the tips in the handle.
Tape measure — retractable, with a lock. “Measure twice” is real, and a 25-foot tape reaches across a room.
Level — so shelves and pictures are actually straight, not just close. A torpedo level fits a drawer; a longer one is better for shelving.
Pliers — needle-nose for fiddly work, standard for gripping, and a pair of channel-locks once you start on plumbing fixtures.
Adjustable wrench — for the nut the pliers keep slipping off.
Utility knife — with spare blades; a sharp blade is safer than a dull one you have to force.
Stud finder — cheap, and it saves you from anchoring a heavy shelf into thin air.
Round it out with the small consumables that live in the same box: a tape measure’s useless without a pencil, and a starter assortment of screws, nails, and wall anchors, a roll of painter’s tape, and a tube of caulk will handle half the little jobs a house throws at you. None of it is expensive, and buying it once means you’re never stuck mid-project driving to the hardware store.
### The two power tools to add first
You don’t need a garage full of machines. Start with a cordless drill/driver and a set of bits — it drills holes and drives screws and will earn its keep the first weekend. Look for one with two batteries so you’re never waiting on a charge. When your projects grow, a circular or reciprocating saw covers most cutting and light demolition. Add tools as real projects call for them, not before — a tool you bought for one job and never touch again is just clutter with a cord.
When a project’s bigger than the toolbox, St Louis Near Me Directory is where you find the right person fast - browse local handymen and licensed trades across the metro, compare reviews, and reach out. Keeping the car in shape too? See our St. Louis car care guide.
