### What a St. Louis old house specifically demands
Here’s the local twist most tool lists miss. A huge share of our housing stock — the brick bungalows, two-families, and century homes — has plaster-and-lath walls, not modern drywall. Plaster is brittle and behaves differently: a standard drywall anchor can crack it, and screws don’t bite the same way. So stock proper wall anchors (toggle or molly bolts for heavy items), use that stud finder, and drill a pilot hole rather than muscling a screw in. Get that right and you’ll hang a heavy mirror on 1920s plaster with total confidence.
Two more worth having in our climate: a plunger and a basic drain auger for the inevitable clog, and, if you’ve got the kind of basement a lot of St. Louis homes have, a wet/dry shop vac is a genuine hero after a heavy rain. Older homes here also tend to have quirks worth a few dollars of prevention — painted-shut windows, settling that leaves nothing quite plumb, and galvanized or cast-iron plumbing that’s less forgiving than modern PVC. None of that changes the starter kit; it just means going gently and expecting a house with history to have opinions.
### Your first five projects
The fastest way to get comfortable is to actually use the kit on small, forgiving jobs. A good progression:
Hang a picture or a shelf — find the stud or set the right anchor, check it with the level, done. The confidence-builder.
Tighten everything loose — cabinet knobs, door hinges, a wobbly toilet-paper holder, the handrail. A ten-minute lap of the house with a screwdriver.
Fix a sticky drawer or door — a little sanding, a new glide, or a tightened hinge, and something that annoyed you daily just stops.
Re-caulk a tub or sink — peel the old bead, run a clean new one; it looks pro and it keeps water where it belongs.
Clear a slow drain — plunger first, then the auger. You’ll never dread a clog the same way again.
Each one teaches a tool and a little patience, and none risks much if it goes sideways. String a few of these together and the mental shift happens on its own — the house stops feeling like a series of things to call about and starts feeling like something you can actually take care of.
### A few safety basics
None of this kit is dangerous if you respect it, and a couple of cheap habits keep it that way. Grab a pair of safety glasses and wear them any time something might fly — drilling into masonry, cutting, or hammering. Keep blades sharp (a dull utility knife slips and cuts you, not the box), unplug or remove the battery before you change a drill bit or saw blade, point a fan out the window on any paint job and know how long to wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room, and before you put a screw or a nail into any wall, be sure there’s no electrical or plumbing line behind it — a basic wall scanner that flags wires and pipes is a few dollars well spent in an older home. Small stuff, but it’s the difference between a satisfying afternoon and a trip to urgent care.
### Buy once, cry once: quality over quantity
The temptation with a first toolkit is to grab the cheapest big-box “100-piece homeowner set” and call it done. Resist it a little. Those kits are mostly filler — a dozen sockets you’ll never use around a few tools that strip and bend the first time you lean on them. You’re better off spending the same money on fewer, better versions of the tools you’ll actually reach for: a solid hammer, a good driver, a tape that doesn’t rattle apart, and a drill from a name-brand line.
The old carpenter’s line — “buy once, cry once” — is exactly right for the handful of tools that get daily use. Where cheap is fine: consumables and the odd single-job specialty tool you might never touch again. Where it isn’t: anything with a moving part or a cutting edge you’re trusting with your knuckles. A quality core kit will outlast the house’s next three owners; a bargain-bin one lives in a landfill by spring.
Random, but: put the drill down and eat in Mt Olive instead.
### Where to buy it around St. Louis
You’ve got options at every price point. The big-box stores — Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Menards, scattered across the metro — carry everything on this list under one roof and are open early and late for the mid-project run. For advice with your purchase, the neighborhood hardware stores and local Ace and True Value shops are worth the slightly higher sticker: the person helping you has usually done the exact repair you’re describing and will steer you to the right anchor or bit in two minutes.
Don’t overlook the secondhand route, either. Estate sales, resale shops, pawn shops, and online marketplace listings around St. Louis are full of good old hand tools — a solid vintage hammer or wrench often outclasses a new budget one for a few dollars. For anything with a battery or a motor, though, buy new and stick to a major brand so batteries and parts stay easy to find down the road.
### The most important tool is knowing your limits
Confidence is great; overconfidence with the wrong job is expensive. Cosmetic and mechanical fixes — hanging, patching, assembling, tightening, unclogging — are exactly what this kit is for. But electrical work, plumbing beyond a simple fixture, anything with a gas line, and structural changes aren’t DIY territory here — those need the appropriate licensed St. Louis contractor and, often, a permit pulled with your municipality. Knowing which side of that line you’re on is the mark of a genuinely handy homeowner, not a limitation.
The stakes make the rule easy to remember. A botched shelf falls down; a botched electrical or gas job can burn a house down or void your insurance, and unpermitted work can come back to bite you at resale. When a job crosses into wiring, the main plumbing stack, gas, or the structure of the house, the smart, handy move is to hire the right licensed trade — and to know how to pick a home repair company in St. Louis well enough to tell a straight quote from a scary one.
### When a project’s bigger than the toolbox
Some jobs are a quick fix; others are a “call a pro” the moment you open the wall and see what’s really going on. When that happens, St Louis Near Me Directory is where you find the right person fast — browse the map of local handymen and licensed trades across the metro, compare reviews, and reach out. Start small, buy quality over quantity, respect the plaster and the licensed-trade line, and add tools as you grow. The toolkit is really just permission — permission to look at a small problem and think, “yeah, I’ve got this.”
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What tools should every homeowner have?
A.  The essential starter kit: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set or multi-bit driver, a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, a stud finder, and one cordless drill/driver. Add a plunger, a small drain auger, and — for St. Louis’s plaster walls — proper toggle or molly wall anchors. That handful handles most everyday household fixes.
### Q. How do I hang things on plaster walls?
A.  Many older St. Louis homes have plaster-and-lath walls, which are brittle. Use a stud finder to hit framing where you can, drill a pilot hole instead of forcing a screw, and for heavier items use toggle or molly bolts rated for the weight rather than standard drywall anchors. Go slowly — plaster can crack if you rush — and it’ll hold a heavy mirror with confidence.
### Q. What home repairs should I not do myself?
A.  Leave electrical work, plumbing beyond a simple fixture swap, anything involving a gas line, and structural changes to licensed professionals — these carry real safety, insurance, and permit consequences in St. Louis. Cosmetic and mechanical fixes like hanging, patching, assembling, tightening, and unclogging are exactly what a homeowner’s starter kit is for.
### Q. What’s the one power tool to buy first?
A.  A cordless drill/driver. It drills pilot holes and drives screws, which covers the majority of small projects, and it pays for itself the first weekend. Get one with two batteries so you’re never waiting on a charge, and add a circular or reciprocating saw only later, once real cutting or demolition projects call for it.

## 7 of 8 St. Louis Renovators the EPA Penalized Lacked Lead Certification - Ask Your Painter First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-smart-tips-for-choosing-the-best-interior-painting-company-in-st-louis
The sander whines against the old window trim, and a pale cloud drifts out across the room. It settles on the sill, on the radiator, on the floor where the kids were sprawled with a coloring book an hour ago. It smells like nothing. It looks like ordinary dust. In a St. Louis house built before 1978, it may not be ordinary at all, because sanding or scraping lead paint, even paint from many decades ago, can create hazardous lead dust.
That isn’t a scare line. According to the City of St. Louis health department, homes built before 1978 make up the majority of the housing stock in St. Louis. And in June 2024, the EPA announced that eight home renovation companies in the St. Louis area had agreed to pay over $65,000 in penalties for lead-based paint violations. The agency said seven of them had worked on pre-1978 properties without the renovator certification federal law requires.
Seven out of eight. So the first question to ask a St. Louis painter isn’t “How much?” It’s “Can I see your EPA lead-safe certification?” Ask it on the phone, before anybody walks your rooms with a tape measure and a clipboard. A real pro answers in one breath. Anyone who laughs it off has just saved you the trouble of comparing bids.
One more call costs you nothing. If you live in the city and a child under six or a pregnant woman lives in the house, the City of St. Louis inspects residential properties for lead-based paint hazards free of charge. Call the Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800 or request it online, and you’ll know what’s under the old color before anybody sands it.
Then talk money. Here’s what painters charge, what the price is really buying, and the small tells that separate a crew you’ll recommend to your sister from one you’ll be painting over yourself next spring.
### What do painters usually charge per room?
Nationally, Angi puts the average cost to paint a room at around $1,100, with most jobs between $200 and $2,000. Pros typically charge $2 to $6 per square foot, so a 12x12 room runs about $290 to $870. Tall ceilings, heavy patching and dark-to-light color changes push you toward the top. In a pre-1978 St. Louis home, add one non-negotiable: a certified lead-safe firm.
### You’re paying for hands, not paint
Pop the lid on a gallon and stir it. That gallon is the cheap part. Angi notes that most painting contractors quote by the square foot rather than by the hour, and that 60% to 90% of the total typically goes to labor. So when two bids for the same bedroom land hundreds of dollars apart, the paint isn’t the difference. The hours are. Somebody is either filling the nail holes, sanding the patches smooth and caulking the gap where the trim pulled away from the wall, or they aren’t.
In an old St. Louis house, those hours climb. Plaster that has settled for generations has hairline cracks, ridges from earlier patches and trim with a dozen coats on it. Expect a St. Louis quote for a plaster room to sit higher in the national range than the same size room in new drywall, and be suspicious of one that doesn’t.
You’ll find out which one you hired at about four in the afternoon, the first sunny day after the crew leaves. Low light rakes across a wall and shows everything: the roller lap marks, the patch that was painted over instead of sanded, the wobble where the cut line meets the ceiling. A good paint job looks the same in that light as it does at noon. That’s what the extra few hundred dollars buys.
### The six-square-foot line that decides who you can legally hire
Here’s the part most homeowners never hear. Under EPA rules, anyone paid to perform work that disturbs paint in housing built before 1978 must be certified. The exemption is narrow: minor repair and maintenance that disturbs six square feet or less of paint per room inside. That’s a patch smaller than a bath towel. Scrape and sand the window frames and baseboards of one old bedroom and a painter can pass that before lunch.
The certification rule cuts two ways, and you want both. EPA requires the firm itself to be EPA- or state-certified, and it requires the firm to use certified renovators who follow specific work practices to prevent lead contamination. In plain terms: plastic sheeting taped down over the floor, doors sealed, the hum of a HEPA vacuum instead of a broom at cleanup. If you don’t see the plastic go down before the scraper comes out, stop the job and ask why.
Don’t take a painter’s word for the certificate. EPA’s firm search lets you look up certified firms in your area, or you can call the National Lead Information Center at 1-800-424-LEAD (5323) for a list of contractors near you. It takes a few minutes at the kitchen table, coffee going cold beside the laptop, and it’s the cheapest insurance you’ll buy for this whole job.
Why it matters to the people inside your house: the EPA says lead-contaminated dust from disturbed paint in pre-1978 homes is one of the most common causes of elevated blood lead levels in children. That’s the sentence to keep in your head when a lower bid tempts you.
### What should the written quote say?
Everything you’d argue about later. The paint brand and line, the sheen, the number of coats, which surfaces are in (walls, ceilings, trim, doors), what prep is included, and how the crew cleans up. “Two coats over full prep” and “we’ll roll a coat on” can look like the same price on a napkin and feel like two different houses a year later. If your home is pre-1978, the quote should also name the certified renovator who’ll be on site.
Ask for proof of liability insurance, and workers’ compensation if they run a crew. If a ladder foot goes through the window over your kitchen sink, that certificate is the difference between their problem and yours. Then ask what the warranty covers and for how long, in writing. A painter who trusts their prep will put a date on it.
### What a good crew does on day one
You can judge a painter in the first hour they’re in your house. A good crew walks the rooms with you before a brush comes out. They ask which outlets stay live, where the pets will be and whether the piano can be moved or has to be wrapped where it stands. Furniture slides to the middle of the room and disappears under drop cloths. Outlet covers come off and go into a labeled bag. You hear tape tearing off the roll in long, steady strips, not short angry ones.
Then comes the part that never shows up in the before-and-after photos: the patching. A putty knife scraping across a nail hole. The faint chalk smell of joint compound drying. The soft rasp of a sanding sponge. On older St. Louis plaster, a careful painter taps along a crack with a knuckle, listening for the hollow sound that means the plaster has pulled loose from the lath behind it, because paint over loose plaster just cracks again. If your painter skips straight to the roller on the first morning, you already know how the job will look in a year.
At the end of each day, the room should be swept, the brushes cleaned and the ladders out of the way. At the end of the job, they should walk it with you in good light and touch up anything you point to while the paint and the crew are still there. Write down the color names and sheens before they go. Tape the list inside a closet door. Two years from now, when a chair back nicks the hallway, you’ll be glad you did.
### Does the season matter for interior painting?
Less than you’d think. Inside, the furnace or the air conditioner sets the conditions, so a pro can paint a bedroom in January as well as in May. What changes with the season is the airflow. In spring and fall you can crack the windows and let the smell of fresh latex drift out over the porch. In the dead of a St. Louis summer, when the air outside feels like a wet towel, painters lean on fans and the AC to keep things drying. In winter, keep the heat on and the room comfortable while the paint dries and cures.
Busy seasons matter more than weather. Many homeowners want everything fresh before the holidays or before a house goes on the market, so book early if your deadline is fixed, and ask any painter how long their wait is before you fall in love with their quote.
### How to read a painter’s reviews
Skip the five-star reviews that just say “great job.” Look for the ones with details: the crew showed up when they said they would, protected the hardwood, finished on the day promised, came back for a touch-up without an argument. Those details are what a good job actually feels like from the inside. One bad review in a long run of good ones means little. A pattern of “never came back to finish” means everything. Ask for two or three recent customers you can call, ideally with houses about as old as yours, and ask them one question: would you let this crew back in?
Whole-house math
### How much should it cost to paint the interior of a 2000 sq ft house?
Angi’s interior chart puts a 2,300-square-foot home at $4,600 to $13,800, so a 2,000-square-foot house lands just under that. Pros charge $2 to $6 per square foot. Walls-only jobs sit low; ceilings, trim and heavy patching in an old St. Louis house push you toward the top.
### Flat, eggshell or semi-gloss?
Run your palm across an old plaster wall and you’ll feel every ripple from a century of patches. Shine makes those ripples louder. Flat and matte hide flaws best but scuff and smudge easily, so they suit ceilings and formal rooms. Eggshell and satin are the everyday choice for living rooms, bedrooms and halls: a soft glow that wipes clean. Semi-gloss belongs on trim, doors, kitchens and baths, where you scrub. If a painter recommends a sheen, ask why for that room. The answer tells you whether they know their trade.
Moving the couch for the painters? That’s the moment you see the rug. Every metro carpet cleaner is mapped here.
### When to DIY and when to hire
One small room with sound drywall is a fair weekend project if you’re patient with the tape and the cut lines. Hire out the jobs where mistakes are expensive: stairwells and high ceilings, cracked plaster, a lot of trim, big dark-to-light color changes, and any pre-1978 room where the prep means sanding or scraping old paint. Whoever does the work, keep the windows cracked and the air moving while it dries, and read how long you should wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room. If you’re leaning DIY in an older house, DIY Interior Painting in St. Louis: Lead, Plaster, and What It Really Costs walks through what that really involves.
Ready to collect two or three bids this week? Start with the painters on the St. Louis Painters Map, compare service areas and reviews, and put the lead-safe question first on every call.
If you run a painting crew, one truck or five, the homeowners reading this are about to call somebody. Make sure your certification and your best rooms are where they’re looking, so you get more customers from the people already searching. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much would a painter charge to paint a 12x12 room?
A.  Angi puts a 12x12 room at about $290 to $870. Where you land depends on ceiling height, how much patching the walls need, whether trim and doors are included and how many coats a color change takes.
### Q. How much should it cost to paint the interior of a 2,000 sq ft house?
A.  Angi’s interior chart puts a 1,200-square-foot home at $2,400 to $7,200 and a 2,300-square-foot home at $4,600 to $13,800, so a house your size lands just under the second range. Walls-only jobs sit near the bottom; ceilings, trim and heavy prep throughout push toward the top.
### Q. How much should I pay a painter per day?
A.  Most painting contractors quote by the square foot, not by the hour or day. Angi puts house painters at $20 to $50 per hour, so multiply that by the hours your painter expects to put in. If you’re quoted a day rate, ask how many days the job should take and what happens if it runs over.
### Q. How much should I charge to paint a 20x20 room?
A.  At $2 to $6 per square foot, a 20x20 room comes to about $800 to $2,400. Angi adds $1 to $6 per square foot for ceilings, so quote those separately, and price old plaster and lots of trim toward the top.
### Q. Is 1 gallon of paint enough for a living room?
A.  Usually not. Angi says each gallon covers between 300 and 400 square feet, and a living room’s walls plus a second coat can easily pass that. Buy two, and box them together so the color matches from wall to wall.
### Q. Does my painter need EPA lead-safe certification?
A.  If your home was built before 1978 and the job disturbs more than six square feet of paint per room, yes. EPA rules require anyone paid to do that work to be certified, and the firm must use certified renovators who follow lead-safe work practices.

## Missouri Keeps a File on Your Dog's Kennel: St. Louis Boarding Costs and How to Get It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-boarding-and-daycare-in-st-louis
The leash goes slack the second the kennel tech takes it. Your dog looks back once through the glass door, the barking rolls off the concrete, and you walk to the car smelling faintly of bleach and wondering who will actually be in that building at 2 a.m.
Here’s the part almost no one does before that moment. Missouri inspects licensed boarding kennels at least once a year, unannounced, and the state keeps every inspection report on file for anyone who asks. Not a review. Not a star average. The file.
A five-star rating tells you how the lobby felt. The inspection report tells you what a state inspector found on a weekday nobody was warned about. This guide shows you how to get that file, what six St. Louis kennels really charge on their own websites, and the pickup-time fee that quietly turns a $53 night into more.
### How much should dog boarding cost per day in St. Louis?
Among St. Louis kennels that post rates on their own sites, a standard night for one dog runs about $43 to $60. Baronwood Kennels charges $43, Silver Maple in Des Peres $44 to $54.50 by size, Arch City Dog Boarding and The Watering Bowl $53, and Sled & Breakfast in Fenton $60. Suites run about $55 to $78. Add holiday surcharges, required fees and late-pickup charges before you compare.
### The kennel file you’re allowed to read
Under Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act, the rule is blunt: if animals are cared for overnight somewhere other than the owner’s home, for any kind of payment, that place must be licensed. That covers the big resort off the highway and the sitter who boards dogs in her spare bedroom. Every license expires January 31, so a certificate on the wall can be out of date by February.
The Missouri Department of Agriculture says routine inspections happen at least once yearly and are unannounced, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., Monday through Friday. When an inspector finds multiple, direct or repeat violations, a reinspection follows, and that one is unannounced too. Complaints, names and allegations included, are public records under the Missouri Sunshine Law.
You don’t need a lawyer to get any of it. Call the Animal Care Facilities program at (573) 751-3076, email acfa@mda.mo.gov, or use the department’s online open records request and ask for a facility’s recent inspection reports. It costs you a phone call. It tells you what no review can: whether an inspector had to come back.
And the inspections have teeth here at home. St. Louis County’s own animal shelter in Olivette failed three state inspections over its cleaning protocols and other deficiencies before it finally passed and got its license. Two more failures and the state could have shut it down. That’s a shelter, not a boarding kennel, but it’s the same state program, and it didn’t go easy on the county.
One more thing the license buys you. Every licensee must keep a program of veterinary care, a written agreement with an attending veterinarian, and that vet has to visit the premises at least once a year. So ask the kennel a simple question at the counter: who’s your vet? A good place answers before you finish the sentence.
### What six St. Louis kennels actually charge
You know the moment: three browser tabs open, a flight already booked, and every kennel’s price page written a little differently. Here are the rates each business publishes on its own website, side by side. Call to confirm before you book, because prices move.
Baronwood Kennels charges $43 for one dog in a regular kennel, $78 for two dogs together, and $55 for a penthouse suite. Silver Maple Pet Center, on two acres at 2014 N Ballas Rd in Des Peres, prices by size at $44 small, $49.50 medium and $54.50 large, with villas from $78, and every rate includes a private room with an adjoining outdoor run and a daily hands-on exam. On a hot July afternoon that means a dog that can step outside on its own instead of waiting for a turn in the yard.
Arch City Dog Boarding at 6256 Gravois Ave charges $53 for the first dog and $43 for each additional dog. The Watering Bowl, with three locations including Brentwood, charges $53 for a standard room and $59.50 for a suite, and the price is boarding plus a full day of daycare, so your dog spends the day playing instead of pacing. Sled & Breakfast at 1051 Old Gravois Rd in Fenton is $60 for a standard kennel and $70 for a luxury suite, and it says someone is on site 24/7.
Kennelwood Pet Resorts adds a line many owners miss: a required resort fee, per dog, per visit, for its Healthy Paws Program, which covers unexpected illness or injury during the stay up to $500. That’s a real benefit. It’s also money that isn’t in the nightly sticker, so put it in your math.
### The fee that bites isn’t the cancellation. It’s the pickup clock.
You land at Lambert, the carousel takes forever, and it’s 1:20 by the time you pull into the lot, and you can hear the barking before you open the car door. That relaxed afternoon pickup can cost you. Sled & Breakfast and The Watering Bowl both run the same clock: pick up before 10 a.m. and there’s no daycare charge, before 1 p.m. it’s a half day of daycare, and after 1 p.m. it’s a full day. Sled & Breakfast’s Sunday pickup window is 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., so ask how that clock applies before you plan a Sunday flight home.
Check the calendar too. Arch City Dog Boarding is closed on Saturdays and closes daily from noon to 3 p.m., so a Saturday homecoming means a wait. Its holidays carry an extra $5 charge, and a “holiday” can mean a whole week: its Independence Day period runs July 1 through July 7.
Deposits are where the cancellation risk lives. The Watering Bowl takes a $50 boarding deposit that becomes non-refundable once it’s fully booked for any night of your stay, which on a holiday weekend can happen fast. Ask every kennel the same three things before you pay: when does the deposit stop being refundable, which dates count as holidays, and what time is checkout?
People are asking
### How do you compare pet boarding facilities on price, safety ratings and cancellation policies?
On price, compare the whole bill for your real dates, not the nightly sticker: add holiday surcharges, required fees like Kennelwood’s resort fee, and late-pickup daycare charges. On safety, look past star ratings and ask the Missouri Department of Agriculture for the kennel’s inspection reports, which it keeps on file for the public; a trail of reinspections means an inspector found multiple, direct or repeat violations. On cancellation policies, ask when the deposit stops being refundable, since The Watering Bowl’s $50 deposit turns non-refundable once it’s fully booked for any night of your stay.
### How to check a kennel for safety, not stars
Walk in with your nose and your ears first. A clean kennel smells like disinfectant, not like a full litter box; the noise is loud but it settles. Then do the four checks that most owners skip.
Ask for the license, and look at the date. Missouri licenses expire January 31 every year. Confirm it with the program at (573) 751-3076.
Request the inspection reports. Start from the department’s Animal Care Facilities Act program page or go straight to its open records request form.
Read for patterns. One routine report is the baseline. Reinspections are the tell.
Ask who the vet is and where your dog goes in an emergency. Every licensee keeps a program of veterinary care with an attending veterinarian, who visits at least once a year.
Vaccines are the other gate. Baronwood requires rabies, bordetella and distemper for dogs. Silver Maple goes further and requires the H3N2 canine influenza vaccine on top of rabies, distemper and bordetella, which tells you how seriously a place takes a cough moving through a room.
### Who’s there at 2 a.m.?
This is the question that keeps owners awake in a hotel room three states away. Most kennel websites never answer it. Sled & Breakfast does, in plain words: someone is on site 24/7. If a kennel’s site is silent, that isn’t proof the dogs are alone overnight, but it does mean you have to ask, out loud, at the desk: is a person in this building all night?
Off topic, but if you’ve never spent an afternoon in Fairground, put it on the list for after the trip.
### Why the bill looks the way it does
Owners flinch at $53 a night until they see what’s in it. Run the numbers on a ten-day trip and it adds up, so it helps to know where the money goes before you start comparing.

### Why is dog boarding so expensive?
Because you’re paying for care, not just a bed. At Silver Maple in Des Peres the nightly rate includes a private room with an outdoor run, a daily hands-on exam and meals, and The Watering Bowl’s $53 rate includes a full day of daycare. Missouri also requires every licensee to keep a program of veterinary care with an attending veterinarian who visits at least once a year, and some kennels add required extras on top, like Kennelwood’s resort fee that covers up to $500 of vet care during a stay.

Run the dog tired on drop-off morning. A long walk or an hour at one of the dog-friendly places in St. Louis makes the first night in a strange room a lot easier. Pack a T-shirt you’ve slept in if the kennel allows it. Then ask the five questions that matter:

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the average cost to board a dog for 10 days?
A.  At the $43 to $60 standard nightly rates St. Louis kennels publish, ten nights for one dog comes to about $430 to $600 before extras. Some places package it: The Watering Bowl lists a 10-night standard package at $470, with a full day of daycare built into its boarding rate. Add any holiday surcharge and a late-pickup daycare charge on the last day.
### Q. Do dogs feel abandoned when boarded?
A.  Many dogs show stress at first: pacing, skipping a meal, clinging at pickup. Most settle as the routine takes over. You can help by keeping goodbyes short and calm, bringing food they know, and choosing a kennel that keeps them busy during the day, like one that folds daycare into the nightly rate.
### Q. Are dogs usually tired after being boarded?
A.  Yes, and a sleepy dog after a stay full of play and new noises is normal. What isn’t normal is a dog that won’t eat, stays lethargic for days, or has a honking cough. Silver Maple, for one, requires proof of the bordetella vaccine. Call your vet if you see any of those signs.
### Q. Is it better to leave a dog at home or board?
A.  It depends on the dog. A social, high-energy dog often does well with group play; an anxious or senior dog may do better at home with a sitter. One difference worth knowing: Missouri’s license rule covers overnight care at a place other than the owner’s home, so a kennel, or a sitter boarding dogs in her own house, has to be licensed.
### Q. What is day boarding for dogs?
A.  Day boarding is daycare: your dog spends the day at the facility and comes home at night. Some St. Louis kennels blend the two for overnight guests, so a boarded dog spends its days in play groups instead of a room. The Watering Bowl’s boarding rate includes a full day of daycare.
### Q. How long is too long to leave a dog at boarding?
A.  There’s no fixed limit, and The Watering Bowl sells a 10-night package for longer trips. What matters is how your dog handles it. Try one test night before a long trip, ask the kennel to call you if your dog stops eating, and favor a place with daily play and a vet it can reach quickly.
### Q. Is dog boarding worth it?
A.  For most trips, yes, if you pick a licensed kennel and check its file. You get staff, other dogs to play with and a vet relationship, at about $43 to $60 a night for a standard room here. It’s worth less for a dog that panics in noisy rooms; that dog may be happier with a sitter at home.

## Your Deductible Is the Tell: 10 St. Louis Roofers With the Receipts, and the Law That Protects You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-roofing-contractor-your-digital-edge
“We’re doing your neighbor’s roof. Want us to take a look at yours?” You hear it the morning after the hail, standing on the porch in your socks, the yard still glittering with shredded leaves and the air smelling like wet asphalt. Upstairs there’s a brown ring on the bedroom ceiling that wasn’t there yesterday. The roofer at the door is friendly, the truck in the street has fresh lettering, and they’re already pointing at your gutters.
Then comes the line that should end the conversation: don’t worry about the deductible, we’ll take care of it. In Missouri that offer isn’t a favor. It’s against the law. Under RSMo 407.725, a contractor shall not advertise or promise to pay or rebate any part of your insurance deductible to win the job, and that includes dressing it up as a discount or a gift. A roofer who offers to eat your deductible has just told you the most important thing about how they do business.
The same law hands you a second protection most homeowners never hear about. If you sign a contract for work your insurance is supposed to pay for, and the insurer then tells you in writing that all or part of the claim isn’t covered, you can cancel the contract up until midnight on the fifth business day after that notice. The contractor is required to attach a detachable form captioned NOTICE OF CANCELLATION to the contract before you sign. No form? Walk away. Leaving it off breaks state law. That one sheet of paper sorts the honest roofers from the ones chasing the storm.
Live on the Illinois side, in the Metro East? Illinois law bans the deductible offer too, and it gives you the same right to cancel, with two differences. The window closes on whichever comes first: the fifth business day after the insurer’s written denial, or the thirtieth business day after your insurer receives your signed proof of loss. And your cancellation has to include a copy of that denial letter.
### Who is the best roofing company in St. Louis, Missouri?
No single company is best for every roof, but on our October 12 snapshot of Google’s listings, Conner Roofing at 5.0 stars from 514 reviews, Andres Roofing at 5.0 from 285 and Guaranteed Roofing & Contracting at 5.0 from 280 rated highest when rating and review count are weighed together. The full shortlist is further down, with what each company says about itself and a link to call it directly.
The best roofer for your house, though, is the one that clears a handful of plain tests: a real local address and history, proof of insurance before anyone climbs a ladder, a detailed written estimate, and a contract with that cancellation notice stapled to it. Ratings get you a shortlist. Paperwork gets you a roof. Nobody paid to be on our list, and St Louis Near Me Directory doesn’t vouch for any company on it. Use it as a starting point, then run every name through the questions below.
Before anyone climbs a ladder, with the estimate still on the kitchen table, do two things. Ask for proof of insurance and check the paperwork yourself. Then call the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection hotline at 800-392-8222 and ask about complaints against the company; checking on complaints with the Better Business Bureau and the Attorney General’s Office is the office’s own storm-scam advice. It isn’t a formality. In May 2026 the Attorney General filed charges against a contractor accused of taking upfront payments from 16 Missourians to replace roofs, gutters and siding, then abandoning the projects. Most of those customers were St. Louis tornado victims. The charges are allegations, and the contractor is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Upfront money, then silence: that is the sound to listen for.
### The knock comes the morning after the hail
Ask anyone who lived through May 16, 2025. That afternoon an EF3 tornado tore through St. Louis County and the city, killed five people, and was later measured at 1.8 miles wide, the widest tornado in the region since reliable records began in 1950. A storm like that leaves a whole city of torn roofs at the same time, and that is exactly when a stranger with a clipboard looks most like a rescuer.
And the hail mornings come around a lot. Conner Roofing, which has worked out of an office on Watson Road since 1993, says the metro averages three to five significant hail events a year. Big storms bring crews from out of town, and they move fast because the next storm is somewhere else. You can usually hear them before you see them: the hollow thump of a ladder against the house next door, a pitch delivered through a screen door, a clipboard and a promise of a free inspection. Most are legitimate. Most local roofers run their own crews most of the year, and many bring in subcontracted crews after a big storm so they can get to more of their neighbors. If you’ve done your homework on the local company you hired, there’s likely no reason for alarm when its crew climbs out of a truck with Colorado or Texas plates. The local company vetted that crew, and it’s responsible for the workmanship and for any warranty you were given when you hired it.
The ones to watch for give themselves away the same few ways. A push to sign on the spot. No local office you could drive to. A demand for most of the money up front, or cash before a shingle is touched. A bid far below everyone else’s, which usually means corners or a bait-and-switch later. And the deductible offer, which in Missouri is your cue to close the door. Slow down. A real roof is worth a week of due diligence, and the honest companies will still be here next week. If a crew takes a deposit and vanishes anyway, the Missouri Attorney General takes fraud complaints at 800-392-8222.
### How do you pick a good roofer in St. Louis?
Start with track record. A company with a St. Louis address, years of work here and a trail of verifiable reviews has a reputation to protect, and it will still answer the phone if a flashing lifts five winters from now. Then check the paperwork: insurance for both liability and workers’ compensation, because if a worker gets hurt on your roof and the company isn’t covered, the bill can find its way to you. Ask to see the certificates, and notice whether they arrive in an hour or never.
Then get the estimate in writing, with materials, scope, timeline, cleanup and warranty spelled out, not a number scribbled on the back of a business card. If it’s an insurance job, ask to see the contract before anyone climbs up, and look for the NOTICE OF CANCELLATION form Missouri requires. Ask who will actually be on your roof, the company’s own crew or subcontractors. Ask how they’ll protect the landscaping and the driveway. If it’s a storm claim, ask how they work with adjusters. Listen to the tone as much as the answers. Calm and specific is what a good roofer sounds like. Irritation at being asked is an answer too.
Ask one more question: does this job need a city building permit, and who is pulling it? Permit rules change from one municipality to the next across the metro. In the City of St. Louis, the Building Division’s building permit is the formal, legal authorization to start construction inside city limits. The application needs the property address and a $25 application fee, plus a letter of authorization from the owner if someone else is filing it, and it can be filed online or in person at the Permit office in City Hall, where only check or cash is accepted. The permit fee itself is based on the job’s estimated cost and is paid once every reviewing agency has signed off, and the permit document then has to be displayed on site while the work goes on. If your roofer does need one and you never see it taped up at the house, that silence is an answer.

### Should you repair the roof or replace it?
Climb into the attic on a sunny afternoon and look up. Pinpricks of daylight, a soft spot in the decking, the smell of damp wood: those tell you more than any sales pitch. A repair usually makes sense when the roof is otherwise sound and the damage stays in one place, like a few lifted shingles, a leak around a vent or one patch of hail damage. Replacement starts to make sense when the problems are everywhere or the roof is simply old. Andres Roofing puts the typical life of a roof in our region at about 20 years before it deteriorates to the point of needing replacement, so a roof near that age with several problems is usually a replacement conversation.
An honest roofer tells you which camp you’re in, and shows you why. Be wary of anyone who jumps to a full tear-off without really looking. A second opinion costs you an afternoon. A roof you didn’t need costs you a car.

Roofers are busiest right after storm season and through the long, hot middle of the year, and a busy roofer has little reason to sharpen a bid. The quieter months, late winter into early spring before the storm rush, are when you have the most leverage and the most choice of crews. Line up quotes a few weeks before you actually need the work.

## How to Find a Good Handyman in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/choose-a-top-rated-handyman-essential-tips-for-st-louis
Every home has a running list of them: the leaky faucet, the door that won’t latch, the ceiling fan still in its box, the fence board that’s been loose since spring. Individually they’re small; together they’re the low hum of a to-do list that never ends — and none of them is big enough to justify calling a specialized contractor. What you need is a good handyman: a skilled, reliable jack-of-all-trades who can knock out a dozen small jobs in an afternoon and actually show up when they say they will.
The catch is that “handyman” covers everyone from a true craftsman to a guy with a truck and a Facebook post, and telling them apart before you hand over your list (and your key) isn’t easy. This guide walks through how to find a good handyman in St. Louis: the best way to find one, what they typically charge, the red flags to avoid, what they can and can’t legally do, and how to hire someone you’ll want to call again.
### What Is the Best Way to Find a Good Handyman?
Two things find you the best handyman: reputation and verification. Strong reviews or a personal referral get you a name; a quick check of their work and reliability confirms it. Start with recommendations. A neighbor’s trusted handyman or a well-reviewed local pro beats a random ad every time. Then verify: read recent reviews, ask for references, and have a plain conversation about your specific jobs. Skill matters, but consistency and communication matter just as much. You want someone who returns calls, shows up on time, quotes fairly, and does tidy work you don’t have to redo. And because a handyman often works inside your home with little oversight, trust counts for a lot. Favor an established local pro with a track record over the cheapest unknown quote.
### What Do Most Handymen Charge?
There’s no single magic rate. Handyman pricing shifts with region, experience, and the job itself, so pay attention to how someone charges. Many bill by the hour, usually with a minimum, a first hour or a service-call fee, because small jobs still take showing up and setting up. Others quote a flat rate per job when the task is well defined. Here’s the counterintuitive part: a more experienced handyman may charge more per hour, then work faster and better and cost you less overall. So describe your full list up front and get an estimate. Bundling several small jobs into one visit almost always drops the per-task cost versus calling again and again. Ask what’s included, whether materials are billed separately, and whether there’s a minimum. Then compare a couple of quotes on value, not the lowest hourly figure.
### What Is the Most Requested Handyman Service?
A handful of jobs come up over and over. They’re the everyday fixes and installs most homeowners can’t or would rather not do themselves: minor plumbing (leaky faucets, running toilets, new fixtures), drywall repair and painting (patching holes, touch-ups), furniture and fixture assembly and mounting (TVs, shelves, ceiling fans, blinds), door and window fixes (sticking doors, broken latches, weatherstripping), general carpentry (trim, decking boards, small repairs), and a long tail of odd jobs from caulking to gutter cleaning to hanging pictures. One person, the whole pile of small tasks that don’t each warrant a specialist. That’s why a reliable handyman on speed dial feels like such a find. Share the whole list when you call. You’ll often be surprised how much gets done in a single visit, and how much cheaper that is than tackling each job on its own.
### What Are Red Flags When Hiring a Handyman?
Handyman work is largely unregulated compared to the licensed trades, so the vetting is on you. The same warning signs that get homeowners burned hiring a home repair company apply just as much here. Watch for anyone who demands full payment upfront (a reasonable deposit for materials is fine; paying in full before the work is done is not), has no reviews or references you can check, won’t put the scope or price in writing, quotes far below everyone else, or gets vague about their experience with your kind of job. Poor communication is its own red flag. Missed calls and a no-show for the estimate only get worse once you’ve paid. And here’s the big one: a handyman willing to take on work that legally requires a licensed pro, major electrical, gas, or structural work, is telling you something about how they operate. A good one knows the limits of what they should touch and refers you out when a job needs a licensed electrician or plumber. Honesty about scope is the real tell.
### What a Handyman Can — and Can’t — Legally Do
Knowing where the line falls keeps you safe and keeps your work legal. A handyman is the right call for small, non-specialized repairs and installations, the kinds of jobs listed above. Some work, though, legally requires a licensed specialist, and a trustworthy handyman won’t cross that line. Significant electrical work (new circuits, panel work), gas line work, major plumbing, and structural changes usually need a licensed electrician, plumber, or contractor, both for safety and to keep the job insurable. Depending on local rules, there may also be a cap on the total dollar value of work a handyman can do without a contractor’s license. So use a handyman for the many small things they do well. When a job is big, specialized, or safety-critical, hire the licensed pro. A good handyman will tell you honestly which is which, and that honesty is exactly what you want to see.
### How to Get the Most From Your Handyman
A little prep makes a visit far more efficient, and cheaper. Because many handymen charge by the hour with a minimum, the smart move is to save up a list and clear several tasks in one visit instead of calling for each little thing. The second and third jobs cost far less per task once someone’s already standing in your kitchen. Before they arrive, write down every job clearly, gather any parts or fixtures you’ve already bought, and clear access to the work areas. If painting is on the list, plan around the fumes, since there’s a real wait before it’s safe to sleep in a freshly painted room. Be upfront about the full scope so the estimate is accurate and nobody’s caught off guard. Then, when you find a good one, keep them. A handyman who already knows your home and its quirks gets faster and more useful over time, and being an easy, organized, fair-paying customer keeps you near the top of their call-back list. Treat the relationship well and it pays off every time the to-do list grows again.
Total tangent — but The Ville’s business lineup is right here.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before handing over your list, ask: Do you have experience with jobs like these? Can I see reviews or references? Are you insured? How do you charge — hourly with a minimum, or flat per job — and what’s included? Will you put the scope and price in writing? Roughly how long will my list take? And the honesty test: Is there anything on my list you’d refer to a licensed specialist instead? A trustworthy handyman answers plainly, gives a fair estimate without pressure, and readily admits when a job is outside their lane. How they handle that last question in particular separates the reliable pros from the ones who’ll take on anything for a paycheck and leave you with a mess.
### St. Louis-Specific: Older Homes and a Long Punch List

In a metro this full of character homes, a reliable local handyman who knows the housing stock becomes one of the most useful contacts a homeowner has. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What do most handymen charge?
A.  It varies by region, experience, and job, so focus on how they charge. Many bill hourly with a minimum or service-call fee; others quote a flat rate per task. A more experienced handyman may cost more hourly but work faster and better. Describe your full list up front — bundling several small jobs into one visit almost always lowers the per-task cost — and compare a couple of quotes on value, not just the lowest rate.
### Q. What is the most requested handyman service?
A.  The everyday fixes and installs most homeowners can’t or won’t do themselves: minor plumbing (faucets, toilets, fixtures), drywall repair and painting, furniture and fixture assembly and mounting (TVs, shelves, fans), door and window fixes, general carpentry, and a long tail of odd jobs like caulking and gutter cleaning. A good handyman is a one-stop solution for the pile of small tasks that don’t each warrant a specialist.
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a handyman?
A.  Demands for full payment upfront, no checkable reviews or references, refusal to put scope and price in writing, a quote far below the others, vagueness about relevant experience, and poor communication from the start (missed calls, no-shows). Another: willingness to take on work that legally needs a licensed pro — major electrical, gas, or structural jobs — since a good handyman knows their limits and refers those out.
### Q. What can a handyman legally do?
A.  A handyman is ideal for small, non-specialized repairs and installations — minor plumbing, drywall, painting, assembly, mounting, carpentry, and odd jobs. But significant electrical, gas, major plumbing, and structural work legally require a licensed specialist for safety and insurance reasons, and some areas cap the dollar value of work a handyman can do without a contractor’s license. A trustworthy handyman won’t cross those lines and will refer you to the right licensed pro for the job.

### Q. How do you find a reliable handyman?
A.  Referrals from neighbors first, then a directory listing you can verify, then reviews read for patterns rather than star counts. Ask what they will not do — a handyman who is clear about where licensed trades take over is usually the one who does the rest properly.
### Q. What are some red flags when hiring a handyman?
A.  Cash only, a large deposit before any work, no written scope, and vagueness about insurance. Add anyone willing to do electrical or gas work that legally needs a licensed trade — that willingness tells you how they handle the rest.
### Q. How much should I pay my handyman per hour?
A.  Rates vary widely with skill and whether they carry insurance, so compare what is included rather than the number alone. Most quote a minimum call-out covering the first hour. For anything touching wiring, gas or structure, you want a licensed trade instead, at trade rates.

## No Flags, No Dig: How to Pick a St. Louis Landscaper
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/transform-your-space-top-landscaping-services-in-st-louis
A skid steer idles at the curb, shovels come off the trailer, and there isn’t a single paint flag in your lawn. Remember that bare grass. Clay grabs a spade like wet cement here. You push, it holds, and when it finally lets go it comes up in a gray-brown slab that keeps the exact shape of the blade. Anyone who has tried to plant one shrub in a St. Louis yard knows that feel in the shoulders. It is also the quickest way to sort the landscapers worth hiring from the ones who will hand you a pretty drawing and a dead hedge by August.
Here is the part nobody puts on a flyer: the good ones start talking about what is under your yard before they talk about what goes on top of it. The soil. The water. The lines buried in it. A crew that skips straight to plant names and patio colors is selling you the picture. A crew that kneels down, pushes a thumb into the dirt and asks where the downspouts drain is selling you a yard that is still alive in three summers.
### How to pick a good landscaper?
Start with one question at the first visit and listen to how the answer sounds: “Who calls 811, and when?” Missouri’s underground facility law, section 319.026, says notice goes in at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before the dig starts. That second number is the one almost nobody knows. If the crew can’t start within ten working days of the request, the law says they have to make a relocate request before they dig. So a landscaper who calls in your locate, then gets rained out for two weeks and shows up anyway, is digging on a stale ticket. A landscaper who answers right away, names who files the request and explains that window has done real installs here. One who shrugs, or says they “just dig around it,” has told you everything about how they treat the parts of the job you cannot see.
Better still, you get to check their work with your own eyes. The locate is free: request it by calling 811 or at missouri-811.org. A few days later little paint lines and flags appear across your grass, each color its own buried danger: red for electric, yellow for gas, blue for water, orange for communications, green for sewer. Those marks show the approximate location of the lines, which is why careful crews switch to hand tools near them. So here is the tell to text every neighbor who is about to hire someone: if the morning of the dig arrives and your lawn has no colored flags in it, nobody called. Stop the job right there, before the first machine bites into the clay.
After that, match the crew to the job (mowing, planting and hardscape are sorted out further down) and keep the checklist short; the full version sits at the bottom of this page. The question on it that matters most: what happens if a tree they planted is dead next spring, after its first St. Louis August in clay? A pause there is an answer too.
### Walk the Garden before you sign anything
Gravel crunches underfoot, the air smells like wet mulch, and for the first time you can see what a ten-year-old planting actually looks like instead of a nursery tag. That is the best hour you can spend before hiring a landscaper, and it starts with a parking spot on Tower Grove Avenue. The William T. Kemper Center for Home Gardening at the Missouri Botanical Garden spreads 23 demonstration gardens over 8.5 acres, planted for the same heat, the same humidity and the same clay you are fighting at home. Walk it slowly. Feel the shade drop ten degrees under a mature tree. Notice which plants look tired in late summer and which still look crisp. Take pictures of what you love, with the plant tags in the frame.
Stuck on a question before you even call anyone? The Garden runs a Horticulture Answer Service by phone, Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to noon, at (314) 577-5143, staffed by Garden staff and Master Gardeners. Ask them whether the plant a bidder suggested will handle your wet corner or your hot south wall. It is a neutral second opinion from people with nothing to sell you, and it takes one phone call. If you are buying some of the plants yourself, read what to know before you buy them in St. Louis first. Zone, frost dates and the clay underneath all decide what survives.
Now you are not walking into a sales conversation with a vague wish for “something nice.” You are walking in with a phone full of plants that already proved they survive here, at full size, so you can see exactly how big that “compact” shrub really gets. Show the photos to every landscaper who bids and ask which of those plants they would put in your yard, and why. The good ones dig into it with you, because you just did half their homework. The weak ones steer you back toward whatever they already had in mind.
### The quote that should make you nervous
Lay three written estimates on the kitchen table and one of them will be a lot lower than the others. It feels like relief for about a minute. Then read what is missing. Usually it is soil prep, grading, drainage, haul-away, or a plant list that just says “shrubs.” On clay those are not extras. Water that has nowhere to go sits around roots until they rot, or runs toward your foundation, and you only find out after the first hard rain when the bed looks like a bathtub.
So compare scope, not totals. Same plants, same sizes, same depth of new soil, same cleanup, same guarantee. Once the lines match, the price gap usually shrinks or disappears. If it does not, ask the high bidder what they are doing that the low bidder is not. Sometimes the answer is “nothing,” and you have saved real money. Often it is the drainage work that keeps the whole project alive.
A few other things should stop you cold: a big cash deposit before any materials show up, no address or insurance paperwork, pressure to sign today, and anyone who waves off your worry about water. Good crews are busy. They do not need to rush you.
### Go stand in the rain first
The next time a real storm rolls across the city, put on boots, grab an umbrella and walk your yard while it is still coming down. Listen to the gutters. Watch where the water sheets off the roof, where it pools against the foundation, where it cuts a little brown channel across the lawn toward the alley. Wait an hour after it stops and walk it again. The low spot that is still holding water, still squishing under your heel, is the spot that will drown whatever gets planted there.
Take photos and short videos of all of it. This is the most useful thing you can hand a landscaper, and almost nobody does it, because the bids happen on dry, sunny afternoons when every yard looks fine. A dry yard hides its problems. A wet one confesses them.
When the landscaper comes out, show them the videos before they show you their portfolio. A good one will want to see every clip, ask where the downspouts empty and start sketching how to move that water away from the house, whether that means regrading, a dry creek bed, a rain garden or simply extending a downspout ten feet. A weak one will glance at the phone, nod and go back to talking about mulch color. You have just learned which crew to hire, and it cost you a wet pair of socks.
If that brown channel runs toward the house, ask every bidder whether a rain garden makes sense. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District’s Project Clear Rainscaping pages explain how a rain garden gives runoff a safe place to go and keeps it away from your foundation, and the program also lists a Small Grants Program with a program area map. Check whether your address falls inside it before you sign, and ask whether the landscaper has built one before. Most homeowners never hear the word rainscaping until after the bed has already flooded.
Do the same with sun. Stand in the spot where you want the new bed at nine in the morning, at noon and at five, or just snap a photo at each time from the back door. Full sun, part shade and deep shade need completely different plants, and the honest answer to “how much sun does it get?” is almost never the one you guess.

### Can ChatGPT design my landscaping?
As an idea generator, yes; as a designer, no: it has never pushed a thumb into your clay or watched where your yard floods, and OpenAI’s own help page warns that ChatGPT can sound confident even when it’s wrong. Treat its plant list as a rough draft and check every name in the Missouri Botanical Garden’s Plant Finder, which covers more than 7,500 plants grown in the Kemper Center display gardens and lets you filter by sun, by plants that tolerate clay or wet soil, and by rain-garden use. Whatever survives that check goes on your phone next to the rain videos, ready for the landscaper’s first walk-through.
### Mowing crew, design crew, or both?
The Saturday you finally stop pushing a mower in July heat is a real kind of freedom, and a maintenance contract buys it. That is a different hire from the crew who rebuilds your front yard. For upkeep, you want consistency: the same people, the same day, a fair seasonal price, and someone who notices when a shrub starts browning. For a project, you want a portfolio and a designer who asks about how you actually use the yard, where the kids run, where the dog wears a path, where you want to sit with coffee in the morning.
Many homeowners end up wanting both, a one-time build and then steady care so it stays that way. Some full-service companies handle the whole thing. Others are honest that they only do one side, which is worth respecting. What you want to avoid is hiring a mow-and-go outfit to design a patio, or paying design-firm rates for someone to edge your sidewalk.
Match the kind of company to the job. Weekly mowing and cleanup, design-and-install work like new beds and plantings, and hardscape like patios, walkways and retaining walls are three different trades with three different sets of tools. Plenty of companies do two of them well. Very few do all three well. Ask which kind of job fills most of their calendar, and make sure it matches the thing you actually want built.

### What to ask at the first walk-through
Bring these questions on paper and write the answers down while the landscaper is still standing in your yard. The smell of cut grass and the friendly handshake fade fast. The notes do not.
Who files the Missouri 811 request, and how many working days does that add to the schedule?
Can I see a job you finished two or three years ago, and can I call that homeowner?
What will you do about drainage and soil before anything goes in the ground?
Which plants are you proposing, at what size, and how big will they be at maturity?
Do you guarantee plants, and for how long? What does the guarantee require of me?
Is it your own crew doing the work, and who do I call if something goes wrong?
Can I have a certificate of insurance and a written, itemized estimate?
A good landscaper answers every one of these without flinching and usually adds something you did not think to ask. That is the person you want leaning on the shovel.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the rule of 3 in landscaping?
A.  Plant in odd-numbered groups, threes, fives and sevens, because the eye reads them as natural and pairs as stiff. It also works for layers: something tall, something mid-height and something low in each bed, so the planting reads as one picture instead of a row of soldiers.
### Q. What are common landscaping mistakes to avoid?
A.  Putting sun plants in shade, ignoring how big plants get, skipping soil prep and drainage on heavy clay, and building more than you have time to maintain. The other classic is digging before the utilities have marked their buried lines. A good landscaper plans around all of it before the first shovel goes in.
### Q. What to look for when hiring a landscaper?
A.  Insurance, references you can call, finished work that is a few years old, and a written estimate with the plant list on it. Ask what they do about clay soil and drainage. The answer separates people who plant here from people who plant anywhere.
### Q. Is $100 an hour too much for landscape work?
A.  It depends on what that hour buys. For a crew with equipment, insurance and disposal, an hourly rate covers several people and a truck. For one person with a mower, the same number is a lot. Compare crew size and what is included, not the hourly number on its own.
### Q. How much tip should you give a landscaper?
A.  Tipping a company owner is not expected. Many homeowners thank a crew that did hard work in the heat with cold drinks, a cash thank-you split among the workers, or a strong review with the crew members named. On a big install, a referral to a neighbor is often worth more to the business than cash.

## How to Choose a Carpet Cleaner in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-carpet-cleaners-in-st-louis-for-a-spotless-home
The traffic path down the hallway has gone gray. A mystery stain sits by the couch, and a faint pet smell lingers no matter how often you vacuum. Carpet takes a beating in a busy St. Louis home — kids, pets, muddy shoes, a whole season tracked across the floor — and every so often it needs a real professional cleaning that a rented machine can’t match. So you start searching. Almost immediately you hit a wall of “$29 whole-house special!” ads that sound too good to be true. They usually are.
Choosing a good carpet cleaner is trickier than it looks. The industry runs on bargain-bait pricing, and the gap between a quality job and a cheap one shows up later: in whether your carpets actually come clean, dry right, and stay fresh. This guide covers how to choose a carpet cleaner in St. Louis: the cleaning methods and which to pick, what it really costs, how often to clean, the bait-and-switch to sidestep, and how to find a trustworthy pro near you.
### How Do You Choose a Good Carpet Cleaner?
Hire an experienced, well-reviewed, insured carpet cleaner who gives you an honest, upfront price and uses the right method for your carpet. Treat suspiciously cheap ads with real skepticism. The single biggest tell of a good carpet cleaner is transparent pricing: a reputable company quotes from the actual square footage and condition, explains what’s included, and doesn’t bait you with a rock-bottom number only to pile on charges once they’re inside your home. Beyond price, check the reviews, the years in business, and the insurance that covers you if something gets damaged. Ask how they clean, how long it dries, and whether the work is guaranteed. Heavy stains and pet odor need more than a quick surface pass, so a good cleaner tailors the approach to your carpet and your problem.
### Steam Cleaning vs. Dry Cleaning: Which Method?
Two methods cover almost every professional job. Hot water extraction — what most people call steam cleaning — sprays hot water and solution deep into the pile, then immediately pulls it back out along with the dirt. It’s the method most manufacturers recommend, and the most thorough for lifting stubborn dirt and allergens. The tradeoff is drying time, often several hours. Low-moisture or “dry” cleaning uses far less water with specialized compounds or pads, so carpets dry fast. That’s handy for quick turnarounds or moisture-sensitive rooms, but it doesn’t clean as deep. For a genuine deep clean, hot water extraction is the default. Low-moisture wins when speed matters most. A good cleaner picks the method that fits your carpet and explains why, instead of running the same process on every floor.
### What Does Carpet Cleaning Cost?
Price tracks the square footage, the number of rooms, the carpet’s condition, and any add-ons: heavy stain treatment, pet-odor removal, protectant. That’s exactly why the flashy flat-rate ads mean nothing. Get a real quote instead. Reputable cleaners price by the room or by the square foot and give an honest estimate up front, usually after asking about your space or seeing it. The classic warning sign is the absurdly low advertised price that exists only to get a technician in your door, where the “real” price for anything past a token surface pass suddenly appears. Do what you’d do for any home service: get two or three clear quotes for the same scope, ask exactly what’s included (pre-treatment, spot treatment, moving furniture, drying), and pick on value and trust, not the lowest headline number. A fair price for good work beats a bait price every time.
### How Often Should You Have Carpets Cleaned?
For most homes, plan on a professional cleaning about once a year. Bump that to every six months or so if you have pets, kids, allergies, or heavy foot traffic. The payoff goes past a fresher look. A deep clean pulls out the set-in dirt, allergens, and dust mites that vacuuming leaves behind, which helps indoor air quality, and it stretches the carpet’s lifespan by clearing the abrasive grit that grinds down the fibers. Many carpet warranties actually require periodic professional cleaning to stay valid, so skipping it can cost you the coverage too. Between visits, vacuum often and hit spills fast. The sooner you treat a spill, the less likely it sets into a permanent stain. Regular cleaning is maintenance that pays for itself in carpet that lasts longer and stays healthier.
### Red Flags: The Bait-and-Switch and Other Warning Signs
The carpet-cleaning industry has a well-known bad-actor problem, so vet carefully. The biggest red flag is the bait-and-switch: an unbelievably low advertised price (“3 rooms for $49!”) built to get a technician in your door. Once inside, he decides your carpets need “deep cleaning,” “pet treatment,” or “protectant” at several times the quoted price, and leans on you hard if you hesitate. Watch for the rest of the pattern too: no verifiable reviews or business history, no insurance (which matters the moment furniture or flooring gets damaged), vague answers about their method or what’s included, a demand for full payment upfront, and pressure to add services on the spot. A trustworthy cleaner does the opposite. Straight quote, clear process, no ambush charges, and a guarantee behind the work. If a price seems too good to be true, it is. Letting that operator into your home usually costs more in the end, not less.
### DIY Rental vs. Hiring a Pro
You’ve seen the rental machines parked by the grocery-store exit. For a light freshen-up, they earn their keep. They are not professional cleaning, though, and the difference is worth knowing. A rental unit has far less suction and heat than truck-mounted equipment, so it pulls out less dirt and leaves more water in the pile. Carpet that stays over-wet and dries slowly can turn mildewy or musty, and St. Louis humidity only makes that worse. A rental also can’t match a pro’s pre-treatment and stain know-how. Between professional visits, a rental or a decent spot cleaner handles routine touch-ups fine. For a real deep clean, set-in stains, pet odor, or a carpet warranty you need to protect, professional hot water extraction cleans far better and dries the way it should. DIY for touch-ups, a pro for the real thing. And whatever you use, never leave the carpet soaked.

### What to Do Before the Cleaner Arrives
A few minutes of prep makes the visit faster and cheaper, and the result better. Vacuum first if the company asks you to, and many do; it lifts the loose surface dirt so the crew can focus on the deep cleaning. Clear the floor. Pick up toys, cords, and small items, and move any small or fragile furniture you can, because some companies charge to move furniture and all of them work faster with open access. Point out problem areas and specific stains before they start, and say what caused them if you know (pet accidents, wine, grease), since different stains call for different treatment. Put pets somewhere safe and out of the way. Then plan for drying time: keep foot traffic off the fresh carpet for several hours, and run fans or the AC to speed things along. That small bit of prep helps the cleaner do their best work, and it protects you from surprise charges for extra labor.
### St. Louis-Specific: Allergens, Pets, and Older Homes
A few local realities make professional carpet cleaning especially worth it here. St. Louis’s humid climate and notorious allergy seasons — the region regularly ranks among the tougher places for seasonal allergies — leave carpets holding a lot of pollen, dust, and allergens. A deep clean noticeably helps indoor air quality in allergy-prone households. The area’s many pet-loving homes add dander and the occasional odor that only proper extraction and treatment fully clear. Then there are the metro’s countless older homes, where you find aging carpet, delicate fibers, or wall-to-wall laid straight over hardwood: the kind of floor a careless cleaner over-wets and ruins. That’s one more reason to hire an experienced pro who matches method to material. A cleaner who knows St. Louis homes, seasons, and allergy patterns leaves you with a healthier result than a bargain crew rushing through on a single setting.

### Q. Is it better to shampoo or steam clean carpets?
A.  Hot water extraction — what most people call steam cleaning — is the method most manufacturers specify, because it rinses rather than leaving detergent in the pile. Shampooing can look good immediately and re-soil quickly for exactly that reason.
### Q. What is the most recommended carpet cleaner?
