## How to Choose a Pest Control Company in St. Louis (Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-pest-control-options-in-st-louis-easy-guide
It usually starts small. A trail of ants across the kitchen counter, a single mouse dropping behind the pantry, a wasp nest tucked under the eaves. Then comes the one that makes every St. Louis homeowner tense up: the first sign of termites in a region where they thrive. The pest changes. The reaction doesn’t. You want it gone, gone safely, and gone for good. So you start searching, and within minutes you’re staring at a wall of companies all promising the same fix.
Which one you pick matters more than most people think. The gap between a good exterminator and a bad one is the gap between a solved problem and a recurring nightmare, plus a real question of what chemicals end up sprayed around your kids and pets. This guide walks through how to choose a pest control company in St. Louis: what to look for, the types of pest control, which pests are genuinely hard to beat, the red flags to avoid, and how to find a trustworthy local pro.
### What Should You Look for When Choosing a Pest Control Company?
The essentials come down to a short, non-negotiable list. Start with licensed and insured. Pest control means regulated chemicals, and a licensed operator is trained to apply them safely and legally, so ask to see proof. Next, look for experience with your specific pest; treating termites, bed bugs, and mice each calls for different expertise.
You also want a strong local reputation, the kind that shows up in recent reviews and references you can actually check. Insist on a clear plan and written estimate that explains what they’ll treat, how, what it costs, and what happens if the pests come back. Ask about safety, meaning the products they use and how they protect children and pets. And favor a company that offers a guarantee or warranty and stands behind its work. Check those boxes and you hire someone who solves the problem instead of spraying once and driving off.
### What Are the Types of Pest Control?
Knowing the main approaches helps you judge what a company is actually offering. There are four broad categories. Chemical control is the pesticides and baits most people picture. Biological control uses natural predators or organisms to manage pests, and it shows up more in gardens and on farms. Physical or mechanical control covers traps, barriers, and exclusion, sealing the gaps pests use to get in. Cultural or preventive control removes the food, water, and shelter that draw pests in to begin with.
The best modern companies practice Integrated Pest Management (IPM). They combine those methods on purpose: identify the pest, use the least-toxic effective treatment, seal entry points, and head off the next wave, instead of blasting everything with chemicals. So when a company leads with prevention and exclusion rather than a quick spray, take it as a sign you’ve found a real professional.
### What Is the Hardest Pest to Get Rid Of?
Some pests are simply tougher, and knowing which ones keeps your expectations honest. Bed bugs top the list. They hide in tiny cracks, shrug off many treatments, and usually take specialized, repeated effort. Termites are both hard to eliminate and genuinely destructive, which is why they demand a specialist and why prevention matters so much around St. Louis. Cockroaches, German cockroaches especially, breed fast and build resistance, so full eradication becomes a persistent job. Rodents keep coming back whenever the entry points stay open.
The lesson runs through all four: a cheap one-time spray rarely holds. You want specific expertise, a thorough plan, and a company willing to follow up. If someone promises to wipe out bed bugs or termites in a single quick visit for a bargain price, be skeptical.
### What Are the 3 C’s of Pest Control?
One useful frame is the “three C’s.” Control is dealing with the active infestation you have right now. Correction is fixing the underlying conditions, the gaps, moisture, and food sources, that let the pests in. Continuity is the ongoing monitoring and prevention that keeps them from coming back. A good company works all three.
Anyone can spray to knock down what you can see. The professionals also trace how the pests got in and make it harder for the next batch. So when you’re comparing companies, ask how they’ll keep pests out, not only how they’ll kill the ones you’ve got. A real answer to that question is the mark of a company worth hiring.
### Red Flags When Hiring a Pest Control Company
Watch for warning signs before you let anyone spray around your home. A company that’s not licensed or insured, or won’t show proof. One that pressures you to sign a long contract on the spot. A price far below everyone else, which often means a quick spray that never touches the real problem. Vague answers about what chemicals they use or how they’ll protect your family and pets. Guarantees that sound too good to be true, like “100% gone forever in one visit.” And door-to-door outfits that turn up out of nowhere with a high-pressure pitch.
A trustworthy pest professional is transparent about methods, honest about what the job takes, and easy to talk to about safety. Feel rushed, kept in the dark about the products going into your home, or pushed toward a big contract before anyone has diagnosed the problem? Keep looking.
### One-Time Treatment vs. an Ongoing Plan
People often ask whether they need recurring service or just a single visit. The honest answer depends on the pest and the situation. A one-time treatment can be plenty for a specific, contained problem, a single wasp nest or an occasional invader, especially when you also fix the conditions that caused it. An ongoing plan, quarterly or seasonal, earns its keep against steady pressure, tough recurring pests, or the plain peace of mind of regular monitoring. In a long-season, termite-prone metro like St. Louis, that preventive service genuinely pays off for a lot of homeowners.
The real test is whether a company recommends what your situation needs instead of defaulting to the priciest plan. Be wary of anyone pushing a costly long-term contract for a minor one-off. Be just as wary of a one-time spray sold as a permanent fix for something that clearly needs follow-up.
Random, but: Maryland Heights restaurants are better than the town gets credit for.
### What Does Pest Control Cost?
Costs swing widely with the pest, the severity, the size of your home, and whether you pick one-time or ongoing service. Rather than chase a single number, get clear itemized quotes. A simple one-time treatment for a common pest usually runs modest. Specialized work like termite treatment or bed-bug eradication costs considerably more, given the expertise and repeat visits it takes. Recurring plans tend to be priced per visit or as an annual agreement.
Get two or three detailed estimates for the same scope so the comparison is fair, and make sure each quote spells out what’s treated, how many visits are included, and what the guarantee covers. The cheapest bid isn’t automatically the best value. A slightly higher price from a company that actually solves the problem, and stands behind it, beats a bargain spray you end up redoing.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before you let anyone treat your home, run a short list out loud. Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof? Do you have experience with my specific pest? What products will you use, and how will you keep my kids and pets safe? What’s your plan — and how will you keep the pests from coming back? Is the estimate detailed and in writing? Do you offer a guarantee, and what does it cover? Is this a one-time treatment or an ongoing plan, and why? A professional answers every one clearly and without pressure. How a company handles the questions, patient and transparent versus vague and rushed, tells you most of what you need to know before they set foot inside.
### St. Louis-Specific: Termites, Humidity, and Old Homes
A few local realities make pest control here its own beast. The region’s humid summers and mild shoulder seasons stretch the pest calendar long and active. This is genuine termite country, where subterranean termites pose a real and costly threat to homes, so termite inspections and prevention deserve extra attention, and a termite specialist beats a generalist. The metro’s many older brick homes, deep basements, and mature trees hand pests plenty of entry points and harborage, everything from ants and spiders to mice and the occasional bat.
The calendar drives predictable invasions, too. Ants and wasps push in through the warm months; rodents come looking for heat as things cool. A local company that knows St. Louis’s specific pests and seasons sees problems coming that a generic outfit won’t. That’s a strong reason to hire a pro who actually knows the area.

### Q. What is the hardest pest to get rid of?

For these, a cheap one-time spray rarely works; hire a company with specific expertise, a thorough plan, and follow-up.
### Q. What are the 3 C’s of pest control?

Control (handling the active infestation), Correction (fixing the underlying conditions — gaps, moisture, food sources — that let pests in), and Continuity (ongoing monitoring and prevention so they stay out). A.  Commonly given as cleaning, closing and calling — remove what attracts them, seal what lets them in, and bring in a professional when the first two are not enough. Exclusion is the step people skip, which is why the same problem returns each season.
### Q. How much should you spend on pest control?
A.  For routine ant, spider and roach work in St. Louis, $85 to $189 a visit is normal, averaging near $133. Monthly plans run $40 to $70 and quarterly service $100 to $275 a visit here. Spending well past that usually means a specific problem priced separately.

## Your $28 Sewer Fee and the Best Plumbers in St. Louis, Ranked
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-top-plumbers-in-st-louis-now
If you own a home in the city of St. Louis with six or fewer units, there’s a $28 sewer lateral fee on your property tax bill every year, and almost nobody reads that line. Here’s what it buys: when your sewer line breaks under the public right of way, the street side of the pipe, the city repairs it at no fee, as long as your taxes are paid. You learn what that line is worth on the night the floor drain gurgles, the basement smells like the street, and cold water creeps across the concrete toward the furnace.
The catch is who you call. The city wants a report and video from a plumber licensed in the city of St. Louis before it will look at your claim. That $28 is the cheapest insurance in St. Louis, and it only pays off if the right plumber shows up with a camera. And the right plumber is not simply the one with the shiniest stars. A perfect score from a few dozen customers is a coin toss with good lighting. A 4.9 that has held steady across nearly 12,000 Google reviews is a track record, built one flooded basement at a time by people who had every reason to complain and mostly didn’t.
So we did the counting for you, in daylight, with dry feet. We pulled Google’s plumber listings across the St. Louis metro, set aside anyone we couldn’t verify, and ranked the rest on rating and review count together. ### What’s the best way to find a plumber in St. Louis?
Start with the plumbers thousands of St. Louis customers have already rated, not a perfect score from a handful, and then confirm the license before anyone opens a wall. On our October 12 snapshot of Google’s listings, Hoffmann Brothers led at 4.9 stars from 11,999 reviews, with Classic Aire Care at 4.9 from 5,615 and Grasser Electric & Home Services at 5.0 from 636 right behind.
The license is where St. Louis gets particular, and where most out-of-town advice goes quiet. Inside the city limits, plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors who are certified by the City of St. Louis, and a sewer lateral replacement is one of the jobs that needs a permit and an inspection. The city even publishes its plumbing permits on an open plumbing permit data dashboard, sorted by neighborhood, so you can see that the trade is being watched. Out in the county, ask which license they carry instead. Either way, ask for the license number on the first call and write it on the back of an envelope. A good plumber answers before you finish the question. A shaky one changes the subject.
If the job is in the city and you want a human on the phone about permits, the city’s permit section is at (314) 622-3313, in Room 425 at 1200 Market Street. That call costs you nothing, and it is the cheapest insurance in the whole process.
Back to that $28 sewer lateral fee. It funds the city’s Sewer Lateral Repair Program, and when your sewer line breaks under the public right of way, the street side of the line, there is no fee for the repair as long as your taxes are paid. The catch is the paperwork. The city wants a report and video from a plumber licensed in the city of St. Louis before it will look at your claim. Many of the city’s sewer lines are over 100 years old and made of clay, so this is not a rare situation. A plumber with a camera and a city license can save you the most expensive check you’ll ever write for a pipe you never see. The program doesn’t cover clogs, tree roots or the part of the line under your own yard.

Look for the words that matter at a kitchen table late at night: on time, explained it, price matched the quote, cleaned up after. That’s the stuff a star can’t hold.

### What should you ask before anyone goes down the basement stairs?
The plumber is in your driveway, the water is off, and your heart is finally slowing down. This is the moment that decides whether the bill is fair. Three questions, asked calmly, protect you better than any star rating.

That’s how you avoid being ripped off by a plumber: not by haggling, but by getting the number on paper while you still have the power to say no.

## 7 Up Was Born in St. Louis, and Its Famous First Name Never Existed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-where-flavor-tells-a-story
Crack open a cold 7 Up and the fizz prickles your nose before the lemon-lime lands on your tongue. That soda was born here: a St. Louis firm, the Howdy Co., applied for the SEVEN UP trademark on Oct. 4, 1928.
Now the part your trivia friend gets wrong. More than 150 websites say its first name was “Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda.” Bottle historians Bob Brown and Bill Lockhart dug through the trademarks, the ads and the old paper labels looking for it. They found bib-labels, all right: paper cards hung on a string over the bottles like bibs, one of them bright orange and promising to take the ‘ouch’ out of grouch. The long name, never. Their verdict, in their study of the company and its bottles: “The obvious answer is that it never existed.” The name was Seven-Up from the start; “Lithiated Lemon Soda” was only a descriptive second line on labels from about 1931 to 1935.
So the soda story everyone repeats is a myth. The best dare in town is real, and it’s printed on the menu. The line under the malts on Crown Candy Kitchen’s own menu calls it “our policy since 1913”: five malts lined up in front of you, cold enough to ache in your teeth, a 30-minute clock, and if every one is gone in time, they’re free. The house rules read like a referee wrote them: all five ordered at once, nobody helps, no bathroom trips, no stepping outside, and no attempts during the lunch rush or whenever the staff decide it’s too busy. At $5.75 a regular malt, that’s $28.75 of ice cream riding on a policy dated seven years before Prohibition began. Send this to the friend who still quotes the Bib-Label name.
Make a Saturday of it, four stops in this order.
11 a.m.: Balkan Treat Box, 8103 Big Bend in Webster Groves, open 11 to 8 every day, (314) 733-5700. Get the pide. It comes out of the wood-fired oven blistered at the edges, slicked with red-pepper ajvar and cool, tangy kajmak, and you’ll burn your fingers on the first piece because you can’t wait. The chef, Loryn Nalić, won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Midwest cooking there.
12:30 p.m.: Berix, 2201 Lemay Ferry Road, open 9 to 7 on Saturdays, (314) 845-3711. Bosnian coffee, dark and unfiltered, the grounds settling at the bottom of the cup.
2:30 p.m.: Crown Candy Kitchen, 1401 St. Louis Ave. in Old North, open 10:30 to 5 Monday through Saturday, (314) 621-9650. Call ahead and ask whether it’s a good hour for the dare. Two friends from Greece, Harry Karandzieff and Pete Jugaloff, opened the counter in 1913, and Harry’s grandsons Andy, Tommy and Mike run it now, the shop’s own history says.
5 p.m.: Charlie Gitto’s On the Hill, 5226 Shaw Ave., opens at 5 on Saturdays, (314) 772-8898. Order the toasted ravioli the house calls its signature, if the malts left you any room, and listen for the breading to crackle.
### Does St. Louis have a dining scene?
Yes, and the awards are the least of it. Nalić’s win was only the third Best Chef: Midwest for a St. Louis chef, after Gerard Craft of Niche and Kevin Nashan of Sidney Street Cafe, as FOX 2 reported, and it came on her fifth nomination, years after she started out running catering at Pappy’s Smokehouse.
Under the trophies sit the plates nobody else makes: toasted ravioli with the breading still crackling, Provel turning glossy on a cracker-thin crust cut into squares, pork steaks going sticky with sauce on a backyard grill. Then whole neighborhoods built by immigrant cooks: pho steam and torn injera on South Grand, a flat-top hissing on Cherokee Street, Bosnian coffee poured thick around Bevo Mill. A town that gave the world 7 Up, and still hands out free malts under a rule from 1913, doesn’t need a critic to settle the question. Is St. Louis a foodie city? Esquire once found a line down the block on Big Bend at 11 in the morning. That’s your answer.
### From meat-and-potatoes town to a Beard winner on Big Bend
St. Louis spent decades as a meat-and-potatoes town, and plenty of those plates are still worth ordering. What changed is the range. At Vicia, a James Beard finalist for Outstanding Restaurant, the menu turns with whatever the farms are pulling out of the ground that week. At Balkan Treat Box, the ćevapi come on wood-fired somun that soaks up the sausages’ peppery juices, and the restaurant now ships its pide across the country.
### Taquerias on Cherokee, Bosnian coffee near Bevo Mill
Walk Cherokee Street and the taquerias set the soundtrack: a flat-top hissing, a radio in Spanish, a stack of warm tortillas on every table. Head south to the Bevo Mill area, home to one of the largest Bosnian communities outside Bosnia, and the coffee at Berix Coffeehouse on Lemay Ferry Road comes thick and strong, the Bosnian way. Nearby, a Bosnian refugee family, the Grbićs, turned an old Gravois dive into Lemmons by Grbic, where the ćevapi come hot off the grill.
At Meskerem Restaurant on South Grand, you tear the injera with your fingers, sour and spongy, and scoop up the stews with it. Seoul Taco folds Korean barbecue into tortillas, and on The Hill, Zia’s still sends out the Italian-American plates the neighborhood was built on.
### Slow pour-overs and a cocktail called In A Pickle
At Sump Coffee and Blueprint Coffee, the pour-over drips slowly enough that you smell it long before the first sip, and the conversation at the next table is usually about the Cardinals. After dark, Planter’s House in Lafayette Square pours from a list of 350-plus spirits, 39 of them bottled just for the bar, and its house cocktail In A Pickle is exactly the conversation starter it sounds like.

### Institutions and immigrant kitchens worth the trip
Some of the best St. Louis food stories aren’t trends at all - they’re institutions that have fed the city for generations. In Old North, Crown Candy Kitchen has run since 1913, founded by Macedonian immigrant Harry Karandzieff and still family-owned four generations later; its malts, sundaes, and BLT are a genuine piece of living history. Just as important are the kitchens that arrived with newer waves of immigrants. Mai Lee in Brentwood opened in 1985 as St. Louis’s first Vietnamese restaurant - a refugee family’s enterprise that now runs a menu of two hundred-plus dishes - and it helped introduce a whole city to pho. For barbecue, Pappy’s Smokehouse in Midtown carries the Memphis-style-rib torch that made St. Louis a serious smoke town. And at the fine-dining end, chef Nick Bognar’s Indo in Botanical Heights blends his Thai heritage with sushi craft - work that has earned repeated James Beard recognition. Together they trace the whole arc: a century-old soda fountain, a pioneering immigrant kitchen, a smokehouse, and a nationally acclaimed fusion room, all in one metro. What ties them together is the thing this whole city does best with food: it holds onto its history while constantly making room for the next wave of cooks and cultures, so the story on the plate keeps getting richer without ever forgetting where it started.
### How restaurants helped bring South Grand back
The growth of the restaurant industry has a positive ripple effect on St. Louis’s economy. These establishments create jobs for chefs, servers, bartenders, and countless others, revitalizing the local workforce. The economic impact is substantial, with restaurants contributing significantly to the St Louis City GDP and tax revenue.
This growth also spurs ancillary industries, such as food suppliers, local farmers, and artisanal producers, creating a multiplier effect that benefits the entire regional economy. The continuous development and expansion of the culinary sector are crucial for St. Louis’s economic vitality, attracting investment and fostering a climate of entrepreneurship.
Additionally, successful restaurants often act as anchors for community renewal. Take, for example, the burgeoning South Grand district, where innovative restaurants have attracted residents and tourists, breathing new life into a previously neglected area.
The industry’s resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic further exemplifies the city’s spirit of innovation. Faced with unprecedented challenges, St. Louis restaurants embraced creative solutions like delivery and outdoor dining, ensuring the survival of their businesses and the continuation of their culinary stories.
Many pivoted to offering meal kits, virtual cooking classes, and expanded take-out services, demonstrating an adaptability that has become a hallmark of the St. Louis culinary community. This period highlighted the deep connection between residents and their local eateries, with many patrons actively supporting restaurants through various means, underscoring the integral role these establishments play in the city’s social fabric.
### Farmers markets, CSAs and the Soulard stalls
The future of St. Louis’s restaurant scene is brimming with promise. A focus on sustainability, community, and culinary exploration ensures a constant evolution. Chefs are increasingly partnering with local farmers, minimizing their environmental impact and highlighting the region’s fresh produce.
The farm-to-table movement is a fundamental shift towards a more responsible, ethical food system rather than a passing trend, and it benefits both the environment and the local economy. The emphasis on seasonality and local sourcing results in fresher, more flavorful dishes and supports the livelihoods of regional agricultural producers.
Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) programs and farmer’s markets are thriving, fostering a deep connection between diners and the source of their food. These initiatives provide consumers with direct access to high-quality, seasonal produce while offering farmers a stable market for their goods.
The transparency and traceability offered by these programs build trust and encourage a greater appreciation for the effort and dedication involved in food production. Whether you’re a seasoned gourmand with a discerning palate or a curious first-timer eager to embark on a global culinary adventure, St. Louis offers a unique and unforgettable dining experience that is constantly being redefined by its passionate culinary community.

## Your Plumber's Magnet Proves Nothing. The City's Permits Do
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/streamline-your-life-master-st-louis-services-in-one-place
The magnet on the fridge says LICENSED & INSURED in block capitals. It has pinned the same takeout menu to the door for years, it came from a plumber nobody in the house can quite picture anymore, and no one has ever asked it the obvious question. Licensed by whom?
If you live in the City of St. Louis, you can find out without making a single call. The City’s free Address & Property Search shows the Building Permit Records for any address: the permit type, the application, issue and completion dates, the estimated cost and a short line describing the work. Type your own address into the City’s Address & Property Search tonight and the screen tells you what was actually filed on your house. It also tells you, by its silence, what never was.
Here’s the part people screenshot. That estimated cost is the figure filed with the City for the job. Hold it next to the invoice in your kitchen drawer and read both numbers out loud.
That silence matters because of who the City lets pull a permit. Plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors certified by the City of St. Louis, and the City names the replacement of sewer laterals and water supply lines as plumbing work that needs a permit and an inspection. So the next time someone stands in your basement, flashlight on the old pipe, the cold smell of wet concrete coming up off the floor, and says this one doesn’t need paperwork, you’ll know exactly which question to ask next.
### How do I keep track of all my household services?
One page. A note on your phone or a sheet taped inside a kitchen cabinet, it doesn’t matter which, as long as everyone in the house knows where it lives. Each line gets the trade, the company, the date they last came out, the model number of whatever they touched and where the receipt went. The furnace filter size goes on it. So does the spot where the main water shutoff hides behind the paint cans. Before any new name earns a line, it passes the permit check above. The page holds your people. The check decides who gets to become one of them.
Most of us skip both steps until something is dripping. You know the night. The steady tick of water on the basement floor, socks soaked through, a phone glowing with twelve open tabs and three phone numbers that all claim to be the same company. Nobody vets a plumber well at that hour. You vet them on a quiet evening, with coffee, before you need them, and then the bad night turns into one phone call to a name you already trust.
### The St. Louis vetting routine, in the order that saves you the most
Start with your own address in the Address & Property Search. The property page shows the five most recent permits and a link to view all of them, so you can see whether the water heater swap or the new circuit the seller mentioned at closing was ever filed. Read the description line slowly. It’s the closest thing your house has to a medical chart.
Next, ask the contractor, out loud and before any money moves, whose name goes on the permit. For electrical work the City issues permits to licensed electrical contractors it has certified. A homeowner can get one too, for some jobs on an owner-occupied, single-family dwelling, after showing the City’s Electrical Section enough knowledge of the code, but the City says service changes, rehab and new construction need to be performed by a licensed contractor. If the answer to your question is a shrug, that’s your answer as well.
Not sure what you’re reading? The City’s Permit Section answers at (314) 622-3313, weekdays during business hours, and it’s in City Hall, 1200 Market, Room 425.
Hiring a general contractor for something bigger, a kitchen or a back porch rebuild? Ask for the list of subs. The City requires a Construction Industry Contractor Graduated Business License for construction contracting businesses, and it says all general contractors are required to furnish a list of the sub-contractors on any job to the License Collector. A contractor who works in the city should already have those names written down. Then ask for proof of workers’ compensation coverage, the same proof the City asks contractors to bring when they apply for that license. For a contractor who has it, that’s a quick call to their insurance agent. A long pause before they answer tells you something too.
Live past the city line? Call your own city hall and ask the same two questions: who issues permits for my street, and where can I see them? Every answer you get goes straight onto your one page.
### What the permit record can’t tell you
A permit proves work was filed and, once it shows a completion date, that it went through the process. It doesn’t prove the crew was pleasant, on time or careful with your carpet. For that you still need a short list and a phone. Pick two or three names, read their recent reviews and their own site, and then call. How a business handles that first call, whether someone picks up, whether they ask about the house before they quote, whether they mention the permit before you do, tells you plenty about the fifth visit.
A metro directory like St Louis Near Me Directory lets you browse local businesses by category and town, so your short list starts close to home. No listing anywhere, ours included, beats the permit check and a thirty-second phone call.
### A year of household services on one calendar
Once the people are on the page, the dates go on the calendar you already live by. Most of what a house here needs follows the seasons:
Spring: the air conditioning check before the first sticky week, when every HVAC phone line is busy. Gutters after the maple seeds come down. Storm season starts too; if your big trees haven’t been looked at in a while, our tree storm-proofing guide is the place to begin.
Summer: exterior work, painting, decks, concrete, roofing. Good crews book out, so summer jobs are really spring phone calls. If the AC is groaning by July, the AC repair guide covers repair or replace honestly.
Fall: the furnace check before the first cold snap, the gutters again once the leaves are down, and the chimney before the first fire if you burn wood.
Winter: planning season. Get estimates for next year’s project while contractors have time to talk, and watch the basement walls during a thaw; our waterproofing guide explains what’s normal and what isn’t.
For the full hiring walk-through, estimates and red flags included, our step-by-step guide to hiring home repair pros works for every trade on your page.
### The rest of life’s services fit on the same page
Dentist, doctor, barber, stylist, vet, groomer, mechanic. Nobody texts you that the dog is overdue for a trim, so give each one a row and a rough due date. The single best habit on this whole page: book the next visit before you walk out of the current one, while the receptionist is still looking at the calendar. Choosing well is its own skill, and our personal care guide covers picking salons and stylists you’ll keep. A mechanic found before the check-engine light comes on is the car version of the vetted plumber, and you’ll feel the relief the first time you skip the where-do-I-even-take-it search.
Wildly off-topic: St. Louis commercial cleaning crews, all on one map.
### The jobs people forget until they’re urgent
Dryer vent. If a load of towels takes two cycles and still comes out damp, the vent is the first place to look.
Water heater. Find the model number, write it on your page, and check the manual for how often the maker wants the tank flushed.
Sump pump. Pour a bucket of water into the pit before spring rain does it for you, and listen for the motor.
Sewer lateral. In the City, replacing one is plumbing work that needs a permit and an inspection, so if slow drains turn into a dig, the plumber’s license is the first thing to confirm.
Chimney. Have it looked at before the first fire of the season, not the week of the first freeze.
### The handoff test
Here’s how you know the page works: could someone else run the house from it? If your partner, a house-sitter or the neighbor feeding the cat can find the plumber’s number, the furnace filter size and the water shutoff without texting you, you’ve put the invisible clipboard down. If every answer still lives in your head, you’ve only given it a nicer cover. Add three lines for a passing grade: where the main water shutoff, the breaker panel and the gas valve are; which pro to call for which emergency; and where the spare key and the wifi password live. Ten minutes of writing turns the worst night of the year into a checklist, with the hiss of a broken pipe in the background and a calm voice reading the plumber’s number off the page.
### DIY or call someone?
A simple split works for most houses. Cosmetic, ground-level and reversible, paint, caulk, cabinet hardware, filters, is fair game for a Saturday. The electrical panel, gas, anything structural, the roof and plumbing past the trap belong to the person on your page. In the City the line is partly drawn for you: a homeowner can test for some electrical permits, but service changes have to be done by a licensed contractor. Your one page isn’t only who to call. It’s permission to stop pretending you were ever going to rewire the panel yourself.
Run the permit check, then fill in your one page. When a line on it is empty, browse local pros by category and town on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three, and ask each one whose name goes on the permit.
If you’re the plumber, the electrician or the one-truck crew whose magnet is on that fridge, make sure the customers holding it can find you again the next time something drips: see your listing options.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How do you know if you have a good contractor?
A.  Check the paper before the personality. In the City of St. Louis, look up the job address in the free Address & Property Search to see its building permit records, ask whose name goes on the permit, and ask for proof of workers’ compensation coverage. Plumbing and electrical permits are issued to contractors licensed and certified by the City. After that, a good contractor is the one who calls back, explains the work in plain words and puts the estimate in writing.
### Q. Is St. Louis a good place to move?
A.  That depends on what you’re moving for, and only a few visits will tell you. One thing is easy here, though: before you buy a house in the City, you can type the address into the City’s free Address & Property Search and read its year built, sale information, tax history and building permit records. That’s a lot of homework for the price of nothing.
### Q. What is the most common home service?
A.  No City office publishes a ranking, so treat any confident number with care. On a St. Louis house, the visits that come back every year are the spring cooling check and the fall furnace check. Both are predictable enough to live on a calendar instead of a crisis list.
### Q. What are some good apps to keep track of household items?
A.  Whichever one you will actually open twice a year. A plain phone note with the trade, the company, the date, the model number and the price beats a dedicated app you abandon by spring. The value is in having last time’s number when the same thing breaks again.
### Q. How do I keep track of all my expenses?
A.  Split recurring from one-off. Recurring household services, the lawn crew, the pest contract, the HVAC plan, go on the calendar with their renewal dates, because those are the ones that quietly renew. One-off repairs only need the receipt, the warranty term and a line on your one page.
### Q. How far back can I trace my house's history?
A.  Further than most people try. For a City of St. Louis address, the Address & Property Search shows the year built, sale information, real estate tax history and building permit records, with a link to view every permit filed for that address. Start there, then take what you find to the library or a local historical society for the older chapters.
### Q. How do I find service providers I can trust?
A.  Referrals from neighbors first, then the permit check, then the phone. Browse candidates by category and town on a local directory, shortlist two or three, ask each one whose name goes on the permit, and let the first call be part of the test.

## How to Check If a Contractor Is Licensed in Missouri (the Answer Surprises People)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-check-if-a-contractor-is-licensed-in-missouri
### How do you check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri?
Search that question and you will get a wall of official-looking answers, nearly all of them useless to you. We pulled the live results for this exact phrase from a Missouri location, and page one was nine different state license lookup portals — California, Washington, Florida, South Carolina, New Jersey, Tennessee, Virginia, Minnesota, North Carolina.
Missouri was not among them. Not lower down, not on page two. Missouri has no statewide licensing board for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors, so there is no state database to search. The advice everyone gives — “just check the state license board” — describes a thing that does not exist here.
That is not a loophole or an oversight anyone is hiding. Bills to create statewide contractor licensing have been introduced in Jefferson City repeatedly and have not passed. So the verification job falls to you, and it works differently than it does almost anywhere else.
### What Missouri does license, and what it doesn’t
The distinction matters, because “unlicensed” sounds alarming until you understand it is often just how the state is organized.
The state does license a long list of professions through its Division of Professional Registration — electricians in some contexts, elevator mechanics, engineers and architects, cosmetologists, and many health professions. If your project needs a licensed design professional, there is a state record to check.
The state does not license general contractors, remodelers, plumbers, HVAC contractors, roofers, painters, or handymen. There is no state exam, no state number, no state complaint history. Home inspectors are not licensed by the state either — a fact worth knowing before you rely on an inspection report.
So when a roofer tells you they are “fully licensed,” the honest follow-up is: licensed by whom? The answer should be a city. If they cannot name one, that is your first real signal.
### Where the license actually lives: your city hall
Missouri pushes this work down to local government, and in the St. Louis metro that means it is fragmented to an unusual degree.
The City of St. Louis licenses contractors directly through its License Collector, with its own application and its own requirements. If work is happening inside the city limits, that is where the record is.
St. Louis County is not one jurisdiction. It holds more than eighty separate incorporated municipalities — the published count runs 84 or 88 depending on whether villages are counted — plus unincorporated territory. Kirkwood, Clayton, Florissant, Webster Groves, Chesterfield and the rest each write their own contractor rules. Some require a bonded registration or a master’s card. Some require little.
The practical consequence: a contractor can be perfectly licensed for the job they did last week and not licensed for yours, purely because your house sits in a different municipality. This is not misconduct. It is the structure. It also means the only license that matters to you is the one valid where your address is.
### How to actually verify a contractor here
Since there is no portal, the sequence is manual. It takes about twenty minutes and it works.
1. Find out which city governs your address. Do not assume. A “St. Louis, MO” mailing address frequently sits in a county municipality with entirely separate rules. Get this right first or every other step points at the wrong office.
2. Call that city’s permit or building office and ask two questions. Does this trade require a license or registration here? And is this specific company current? Permit desks answer this routinely — it is not an unusual request, and they will tell you.
3. Ask who is pulling the permit. This is the highest-value question on this page. A licensed contractor pulls the permit in their own name. If they suggest you pull it as the homeowner, understand what that means: liability shifts to you, inspections become your responsibility, and the arrangement is frequently a sign the contractor cannot pull one. Occasionally there are legitimate reasons. Usually there are not.
4. Verify insurance directly with the insurer, not the contractor. Ask for the certificate, then call the number on it. A certificate is a PDF; anyone can edit a PDF. The insurer will confirm the policy is active in about a minute. Ask for general liability and, if they have employees, workers’ compensation — without the latter, an injury on your property can become your problem.
5. Check the paper trail that does exist. No state board does not mean no record. Look at Better Business Bureau complaint history, Missouri Attorney General consumer complaints, and county court records for judgments and mechanic’s liens. Court records are public and are far more revealing than reviews.
6. Ask for two recent local addresses. Not a reference list — specific jobs in your area within the last year. A contractor working steadily nearby can produce them without effort. One who hesitates is telling you something.
### What to weigh instead of a state license
Because the state signal is missing, other signals carry more weight here than they would in California or Florida:
Whether they pull permits as a matter of course. The single strongest indicator of a legitimate operation.
Insurance you confirmed yourself. Not a certificate you were handed.
How long they have worked in this metro. A contractor who has been doing this in the same municipalities for a decade has passed inspections there repeatedly.
Trade certifications the state doesn’t require. Manufacturer certifications, trade association membership, EPA certification for refrigerant work. Voluntary credentials mean more where mandatory ones are absent.
A written contract with a defined scope. Missouri does not hand you a licensing board to complain to, so your contract is your protection.
### The lien notice: a verification test almost nobody knows
This one is worth the whole page, and most homeowners have never heard of it.
Under Chapter 429 of the Missouri statutes, a general contractor is required to give the property owner a conspicuous written notice about mechanic’s liens — in at least 10-point type — at the front end of the project. Not at the end. Not buried in an invoice. Up front, as a matter of law.
Which hands you a clean test. A contractor who gives you that notice unprompted is running a real operation. One who has never heard of it is telling you how they work, without meaning to. You do not have to be confrontational about it — just notice whether it arrives.
And here is why it exists, which is the part that should get your attention: in Missouri, a subcontractor who does not get paid can place a lien on your house even if you already paid the general contractor in full. Your payment to the contractor only offsets the claim to the extent of what was actually paid through. If your GC pockets the money and stiffs the drywall crew, the drywall crew’s claim can land on your title. Subcontractors must give you ten days’ notice before filing, stating the amount and who owes it — so if a letter like that ever arrives, it is not junk mail.
The protection is straightforward and you should ask for it every time: lien waivers from every subcontractor and supplier, collected before you release final payment. A contractor who works this way already has a process for it. A contractor who reacts badly to the request has just answered a question you were going to have to ask eventually.
Nothing to do with permits — cross the river and eat in Collinsville.
In a state with a licensing board, some of this gets screened out before you ever meet the person. Missouri does not have that filter. Which is exactly why the paperwork habits — permits, notices, waivers — carry so much more signal here than a friendly estimate does.
### Red flags that matter more in a no-license state
Some warning signs are universal. These three are sharper here, precisely because there is no board doing any screening for you:
A large deposit up front. Materials deposits are normal. Half the job before anyone shows up is not. Without a licensing authority, there is no fast administrative remedy if the crew never returns — your recourse is civil court.
Storm-chasers after severe weather. Hail and wind events reliably bring out-of-state crews into the metro. They are often not licensed in your municipality, may not be insured locally, and are gone before problems surface. Ask where their office is and how long they have worked in your city.
Cash-only, no contract, no permit. Any one of these is a caution. All three together is not a discount — it is an operation with nothing to lose. If the work fails inspection later, or shows up as an unpermitted improvement when you sell, the cost lands on you.
### If you are the contractor reading this
The same gap cuts against you. Homeowners here have no state directory that proves you are legitimate, which means an established, insured, permit-pulling business looks identical online to someone who started last Tuesday. Nothing sorts you apart automatically.
So the sorting has to be something you do. Name the municipalities you are licensed in. Say plainly that you pull your own permits. Put your insurance status and your years in the metro where people can see them before they call. In a state with no license lookup, being easy to verify is the competitive advantage — and most of your competitors are not bothering.
Worth knowing what you owe on the paperwork side too: our guide to business licenses in St. Louis covers the city versus county split and what each actually costs.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri require a contractor license?
A.  Not at the state level. Missouri issues no statewide license for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors, and has no state board that maintains a lookup. Licensing is handled by individual cities and counties, so requirements change from one municipality to the next — and a contractor may hold several.
### Q. How do I verify a contractor in St. Louis?
A.  Identify the municipality your address falls in, then call that city’s permit or building office and ask whether the trade requires licensing there and whether the company is current. Confirm insurance by calling the insurer directly rather than trusting the certificate. Then check BBB history, Missouri Attorney General complaints, and county court records for liens or judgments.
### Q. Is it legal to hire an unlicensed contractor in Missouri?
A.  Because there is no statewide license, “unlicensed” usually means not registered with a specific city rather than breaking state law. The real risk is practical: work that never gets permitted or inspected can fail, may surface as an unpermitted improvement when you sell, and leaves you with civil court as your only recourse.
### Q. Should I pull the permit myself as the homeowner?
A.  Generally no. Homeowner-pulled permits shift responsibility for inspections and code compliance to you, and a contractor who asks for this is often unable to pull one themselves. There are occasional legitimate reasons, but treat the request as a question to be answered rather than a convenience.
### Q. What should I check if there is no state license to look up?
A.  Weight shifts to what you can verify yourself: whether they pull permits in their own name, insurance you confirmed with the insurer, how long they have worked in your specific municipalities, voluntary trade certifications, and a written contract with a defined scope. Court records and complaint history fill in the rest.
### Q. Can a subcontractor put a lien on my house if I already paid the contractor?
A.  Yes. Under Missouri's Chapter 429, payment to the general contractor only offsets a claim to the extent it was actually paid through. If your contractor doesn't pay a subcontractor or supplier, that party can pursue a lien against your property. Subcontractors must give you ten days' notice before filing. Collect signed lien waivers from every sub and supplier before releasing final payment.
### Q. Does Missouri license home inspectors?
A.  No. Home inspector does not appear among the state’s licensed professions, and bills to create licensing have not passed. Look for ASHI or InterNACHI certification instead, since those impose exams and continuing education that state law does not require.

## Master Home Repair in St. Louis: A Step-by-Step Guide to Hiring the Right Pro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/master-home-repair-your-step-by-step-guide-to-top-services
Updated June 21, 2026.
The water heater quits on a Sunday. Or a storm drops a branch through the gutter, or that “I’ll get to it” repair finally can’t wait another week. However it starts, you end up staring at your phone, about to hand a stranger your house, your money, and your trust, and hoping you pick a good one.
The steps below find you a home repair pro in St. Louis you can actually count on, and help you spot the ones you can’t. They work the same for a century-old brick two-family in the city and a newer build out in the county.
### 1. Get clear on what you need
Before you call anyone, name the job: plumbing, electrical, roofing, HVAC, drywall, general handyman work — and be honest about which of those needs a licensed pro and which you could handle yourself with a basic St. Louis homeowner toolkit. The clearer you are, the easier it is to find a specialist instead of a jack-of-all-trades who dabbles — and the more accurate your quotes will be.
### 2. Ask the people you trust
A neighbor who just had the same work done is worth more than any ad — they’ve seen the crew’s punctuality, the cleanup, and the final invoice. Ask friends, family, and your neighborhood Facebook group who they’d use again — and, just as useful, who they’d warn you away from.
### 3. Do a little homework online
Look the company up: their website, recent reviews across Google and other sites, and a local directory listing. You’re looking for a real, consistent track record — and recent reviews, since a company can change a lot in a year.
### 4. Check the credentials that protect you
This is the step that saves people thousands. Confirm the company is licensed for the work (and that any required St. Louis city or county permits will be pulled), and — this is the big one — that they carry liability insurance and workers’ compensation. Ask for a certificate of insurance. If an uninsured worker is hurt on your property, you don’t want to be the one holding that bill.
### 5. Get at least three written estimates
Don’t take the first number. Get three, in writing, and read them closely — the cheapest bid often leaves something out, while a higher one may include better materials or a step the others skipped. Price is one factor; understanding exactly what each includes is the real goal. Be especially wary of a quote that’s dramatically lower than the rest.
### 6. Test how they communicate
Call the office. Does a real person answer, or does it ring out? How quickly do they call back? The way a company communicates before they have your money is a pretty good preview of how they’ll treat you after. Prompt, clear, patient communication is a green flag.
### 7. Ask about warranties — and get it in writing
A confident pro stands behind their work with a warranty on parts and labor. Ask what’s covered and for how long, and make sure the scope, price, timeline, and warranty all land in a signed written agreement before work starts.
### 8. Trust your gut
You’ll know. The right pro listens, answers your questions in plain English without hiding behind jargon, doesn’t pressure you, and makes you feel like a customer rather than a transaction. If something feels off, keep looking — there are plenty of good ones in this town.
One quiet tell: look at how a company keeps its online presence and directory profile. A business that takes the time to maintain a complete, professional profile tends to bring that same care to the work itself.
### Reading three estimates side by side
Once the three written quotes are in hand, don’t just compare the bottom lines — compare what each one actually commits to:
Scope: Does each bid describe the same job? A cheaper bid that quietly omits haul-away, patching, or a code-required upgrade only looks cheaper. You pay the difference later.
Materials: Brand and grade matter. “Water heater” tells you nothing; a specific model with a specific warranty tells you plenty.
Allowances and exclusions: The fine print where surprises live. What happens if they open the wall and find rot, old wiring, or a surprise from a previous owner’s handiwork? A good estimate says how change orders get priced and approved.
Timeline and payment schedule: Start date, duration, and payments tied to completed milestones — not the calendar.
If a bid is dramatically lower than the other two, ask the contractor to walk you through it line by line. Sometimes there’s an honest reason — lighter overhead, a slower season, a simpler approach. Often, though, the walkthrough answers the question for you: something was missing, and you’d have paid for it later as a change order.
### The St. Louis homework: what makes repairs here different
Generic hiring advice misses the things this metro’s housing actually throws at you. A few local realities worth knowing before you talk to anyone:
Clay soil moves. The region’s expansive clay swells when wet and shrinks in drought, which is why foundation cracks, sticking doors, and bowing basement walls are such common calls here. For anything structural, you want a contractor who works with St. Louis soil for a living — and for water in the basement, start with our basement waterproofing guide.
This is a brick town. Much of the city’s housing stock is century-old brick, and old mortar joints eventually need tuckpointing. It’s a specialty trade — done badly, it’s ugly and traps moisture; done well, it buys your walls decades.
Old houses carry old systems. Knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and undersized panels still hide in older homes across the city and inner suburbs. If your house predates the 1950s, budget for surprises behind the walls — and hire accordingly (our electrician guide covers what to ask).
Storm season brings storm chasers. After every big hail or wind event, out-of-town crews sweep neighborhoods knocking on doors. Some are legitimate; plenty are not. The safest rule: never sign anything on your doorstep the day of the knock, and run any roofer through the checks above first — our roofing contractor guide goes deeper.
### Build your bench before you need it
The single best home-repair habit costs nothing: assemble your shortlist while nothing is broken. One plumber, one electrician, one HVAC company, one handyman pulled from the St. Louis handyman services map — each vetted with the steps above, on a calm afternoon, with time to check reviews and make an unhurried call. Save the numbers in your phone, and note who answered fast and who explained things clearly — that’s your tiebreaker later.
Then, when the sump pump quits during an April downpour or the furnace gives up on the coldest night of January, you’re not vetting strangers under pressure — you’re calling someone you already chose. Every step in this guide works twice as well when you run it before the emergency instead of during one — calm decisions are cheaper than panicked ones, in this trade more than most. (For the household-wide version of that habit — a seasonal calendar and one page for every service you use — see our streamline-your-services guide.)
### Emergency or can-it-wait? A quick triage
Half of hiring well is knowing how much time you actually have. A rough triage:
Call now, tonight if needed: active water leaks you can’t shut off, no heat in winter or no AC in a St. Louis heat wave, sparking outlets or burning smells, sewage backup. Pay the emergency rate — it’s cheaper than the damage. (Guides: plumbers, AC repair.)
This week: a roof leak you’ve bucketed, a water heater limping along, a tree limb resting where it shouldn’t. Urgent, but you still have time to get two or three quotes — use it.
This season: peeling paint, drafty windows, that gutter run that overflows. These reward patience: off-season scheduling often gets you better attention and sometimes better pricing. (Guides: interior painters, window companies, handymen.)
The emergencies are where bad decisions happen — which is exactly why it pays to keep a short list of vetted pros before the water heater dies on a Sunday.

### Storm damage and insurance: a St. Louis rite of passage
Sooner or later, hail or straight-line winds will find your roof — it’s practically a metro tradition, from Arnold to Alton and every zip code in between. When it happens, the order of operations matters: document the damage with photos before anything is touched, call your insurance company before signing with any contractor, and be careful with paperwork that assigns your insurance benefits to the contractor — read anything called an “assignment of benefits” closely, and ask your insurer about it before signing.
Legitimate local roofers work with insurance claims every week and will walk the adjuster’s report with you. The crews that pressure you to sign on the doorstep “so we can get you on the schedule” are the ones this guide exists to help you avoid. Slow down by one day; a real company will still be there tomorrow — and the good ones will respect you more for checking.
### Red flags that end the conversation
Any one of these is reason enough to keep looking:
Cash only, no paperwork. No written estimate, no contract, no receipt — no job.
A huge deposit up front. Materials deposits are normal; demanding most of the money before work starts is not. Be wary of anyone who needs the bulk of payment to begin.
Pressure to sign today. “This price is only good right now” is a sales tactic, not a deadline. Good contractors are busy, not desperate.
No local footprint. No verifiable local address, no local reviews, a magnetic sign on the truck door — especially after a storm, that pattern deserves extra scrutiny.
Vague about permits. “We don’t really need one” for electrical, plumbing, or structural work is a red flag; the permit protects you. Requirements vary by municipality, so a quick call to your city or county building department settles it.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do contractors need a license in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no statewide general-contractor license — licensing happens at the city and county level, and requirements differ between St. Louis city, St. Louis County, and each municipality. Electricians, plumbers, and mechanical contractors are typically licensed locally. The practical move: ask which license the work requires in your municipality and verify it with your local building department.
### Q. When does a home repair need a permit in St. Louis?
A.  Rules vary by municipality, but electrical, plumbing, structural, and most roofing or HVAC replacement work commonly require permits in both the city and county, while cosmetic work like painting generally doesn’t. A reputable contractor pulls the permit themselves and builds it into the quote — a contractor who asks you to pull the permit is shifting liability onto you, and that’s worth questioning.
### Q. How do I find a trustworthy contractor in St. Louis?
A.  Start with referrals, check recent online reviews, confirm the company is licensed and carries liability insurance and workers’ compensation, get at least three written estimates, and make sure everything — scope, price, timeline, and warranty — is in a signed agreement.
### Q. Why does insurance matter when hiring a home repair company?
A.  If a worker is injured on your property or your home is damaged and the company isn’t properly insured, you could be left responsible. Always ask for a certificate of liability insurance and workers’ compensation before work begins.
### Q. Should I always choose the lowest bid?
A.  No. Get three written estimates and compare what each actually includes. A very low bid may use lower-grade materials or skip a needed step, so weigh value and what’s covered, not just the price.

## Your St. Louis Home Inspector Isn't Required to Check for Radon or Lead
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/home-inspections-in-st-louis
“The inspector said it was fine.”
People say it standing on the basement steps after the first hard rain, the floor drain gurgling, a sour sewer smell coming up off the cold concrete. They said it at the closing table too, pen in hand, a forty-page report full of photos sitting in their inbox. Here is the part that stings: the inspector was probably telling the truth. The pipe under the yard was never on the list.
Start with the City’s own words. Every property in St. Louis sits in a Housing Conservation District, and a residential sale needs a City Certificate of Inspection before anyone moves in. Then the City’s permit page says, in plain print, that its inspection “does not imply a guarantee or warranty as to the overall condition of the building and/or its systems,” and that buyers may want a separate commercial grade building inspection. The private inspector you hire for that job? In Missouri, home inspectors do not need a license or training. And the InterNACHI standard of practice tells inspectors they are not required to determine radon or lead paint, or to inspect underground items.
So “it passed inspection” can mean two different inspections, and neither one promised to look at the line that carries your sewage to the street.
So do this before your inspection deadline runs out. Book a sewer scope and watch the camera crawl down your line to the street. Order the free state radon kit with the coupon code TESTING. If the house was built before 1978, use your 10-day window for a lead paint inspection instead of signing it away. Then get a contractor quote on every big finding, because the inspector is not required to price a single repair.
### What does a home inspection cover in St. Louis?
A home inspection is a non-invasive, visual examination of the accessible areas of a house. Under the InterNACHI standard it is not technically exhaustive, and the inspector is not required to check for radon, lead paint, asbestos, mold, pests or underground items, or to estimate repair costs. In the City of St. Louis, the separate $120 occupancy inspection is a basic code check, not a condition report.
Read that list again with an old St. Louis house in mind. The brick basement that smells like wet stone. The painted-over trim. The yard where the sewer line runs out toward the street, out of sight. The standard says an inspection “will not identify concealed or latent defects,” and that it does not estimate what any repair will cost. That is not an inspector cutting corners. That is the rulebook. A buyer who assumes the report covered those things finds out later, usually with a plumber’s invoice in one hand.
### The City’s inspection is a code check, and the City says so
The City visit feels official, and it is: a City inspector with a clipboard walking through your rooms and around the outside of the house. The City’s Housing Conservation District inspection is real, it is required on a sale, and it is cheap: the application is $120, and the certificate is good for 12 months. A City inspector walks the exterior and interior and sets the dwelling’s occupancy load. If the certificate comes back with violations, the owner has 30 days to fix them. You can read how St. Louis occupancy and code inspections actually work before your closing date.
But look at what the City says it is checking: minimal interior code violations and minimum exterior standards under the International Property Maintenance Code. Minimum. A furnace can rattle to life, pass a code walk-through and still be close to the end. Nobody on that visit is paid to tell you how many winters it has left.
So when a seller or a listing says the house “passed inspection,” ask one question: which one? The City’s certificate protects the City’s housing stock. The private inspection is the one meant to protect you, and it has its own blind spots.
### Nobody licensed the person with the flashlight
You will spend an afternoon following a stranger with a flashlight and a moisture meter through the biggest purchase of your life. In Missouri, that person does not need a state license or any training to do the job. Professional engineers are licensed by the state. Home inspectors are not.
And the seller’s agent? Missouri law is blunt about that too. Section 339.730 says a seller’s or landlord’s agent “owes no duty to conduct an independent inspection or discover any adverse material facts” for the buyer.
Line it up and it reads like a joke nobody laughs at. The City’s inspection guarantees nothing. The private inspector needs no license. The seller’s agent has no duty to go looking. That leaves you. Screenshot that and send it to anyone about to buy in this town.
### The pipe under the yard is yours
Flush the upstairs toilet and listen. If the basement floor drain answers with a slow gurgle, you are hearing the part of the house nobody inspected.
Here is the St. Louis fact that turns a house from a good deal into a bad week. The City’s Street Department says the entire sewer lateral line from your home to the MSD main is private property. Your pipe, all the way out.
There is a safety net, and it is smaller than people think. Owners of homes with 6 or fewer units pay a $28 fee on their real estate tax bill for the City’s Sewer Lateral Repair Program. It pays to repair broken lateral lines under the public right of way. It does not cover breaks in the part of the line under private property, and it does not cover clearing clogs or tree roots along any part of the line. To use it, you need a licensed plumber’s report and video of the problem.
That is why the add-on worth paying for on an older house is a sewer scope: a plumber or inspector feeds a camera down the line while you watch the screen, and you see roots fanning through the joints or a sag holding standing water before you own it, not after. A general inspection will not do it. The standard says the inspector is not required to inspect underground items.
Done reading about sewer lines for one sitting? Fair. Go get dinner in Cedar Hill and come back for the radon part.
### Radon is on the skip list, and the state will mail you a test
Radon has no smell, no color, no sound. You can stand in a finished basement with the dehumidifier humming and never know. The inspection standard lists airborne hazards, including radon, among the things the inspector is not required to determine.
The Missouri health department says data from its residential radon testing program shows that 1 in 3 homes tested were above the recommended action level of 4.0 pCi/L. It also offers free radon test kits to Missouri residents, limit one per household, sent to your home at no cost. Use the coupon code TESTING on the request form linked from the state’s radon page. A free envelope in your mailbox beats a guess.
### Lead paint, and the 10 days you can sign away
Run a thumbnail along the windowsill of an old house and the paint comes up in chips, layer under layer. The InterNACHI standard does not require the inspector to determine lead paint either. Federal law gives you a separate tool.
For most housing built before 1978, federal law requires sellers to provide homebuyers a 10-day period to conduct a paint inspection or risk assessment for lead-based paint hazards. The two sides can agree in writing to lengthen or shorten that window, and homebuyers may waive it. That waiver is one checkbox in a stack of paperwork. Decide on purpose whether you are giving it up.
Got a report full of red flags and need someone to fix them? Get quotes before your inspection window closes, and find local plumbers, electricians and contractors on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you run a home inspection, sewer scope or radon testing business in St. Louis, a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your name on the page buyers read before they hire, so see how to get more customers here.
### Inspection day: go, and bring a notebook
Ask when you book whether you can come along, and then show up in shoes you don’t mind getting dusty. Follow the flashlight into the basement. Stand next to the electrical panel when the cover comes off. Listen when the furnace kicks on: the click, the whoosh, any rattle the inspector stops to note. A photo in a PDF never lands the way that sound does in a cold basement.
Keep two columns in your notebook. One is what the inspector found. The other is what the inspector says is outside the job: the sewer line, radon, lead, pests, whatever sits behind a wall or under the ground. That second column is your shopping list for the week, and it is the one most buyers never write down.
Before you leave, ask three plain questions. Which of these findings would you fix first in your own house? What did you not look at today, and why? And when will the report land in my inbox? Then put your inspection deadline from the contract on the calendar in red, because every specialist you need has to fit inside it.
### What to order for an older St. Louis house
The general inspection is the starting point. For an older house here, add the pieces the standard leaves out:
A sewer scope of the lateral, because the whole line to the MSD main is yours.
A termite or pest inspection, since the standard does not require the inspector to determine pests.
The free state radon kit, if your timeline allows for it.
A deliberate choice on the 10-day lead window if the house predates 1978.
Contractor quotes for anything flagged, because the inspector is not required to estimate repair costs.
