### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth doing a sewer scope inspection?
A.  On an older St. Louis house, yes. The City says the entire sewer lateral from your home to the MSD main is private property, and its repair program covers only breaks under the public right of way, not breaks under your yard or clogs and tree roots. A general inspection is not required to inspect underground items, so the scope is the only way to see the line before you own it.
### Q. What is the biggest red flag in a home inspection?
A.  Often it is what the report leaves out. A standard inspection is not required to check radon, lead paint, pests or anything underground, and it will not identify concealed defects. If the report is thin and photo-free, or the inspector will not show you a sample report, treat that as the flag. Missouri does not require inspectors to be licensed, so vetting them is your job.
### Q. What is a deal breaker in a home inspection?
A.  That depends on your budget and the repair quotes, not on a fixed list. In St. Louis, some of the costliest surprises sit outside a general inspection entirely, like a broken sewer lateral under the yard that the City’s program will not pay for. Get a sewer scope and contractor quotes before your inspection window closes.
### Q. Do the seller have to fix everything on a home inspection?
A.  A private inspection report is information for you, not an order, so repairs are something you negotiate in the contract: a fix, a credit, a lower price, or nothing. The City’s occupancy inspection is different. If its certificate is issued with violations, the property owner has 30 days to make the repairs.
### Q. How much does a good house inspection cost?
A.  Prices vary from one inspector to the next, so call three inspectors, ask for a sample report and ask what add-ons like a sewer scope cost. The City of St. Louis does publish one fee: $120 for its occupancy inspection application, and that is a basic code check, not a condition inspection.
### Q. Do you lose earnest money if an inspection fails?
A.  Whether you can walk away and keep your earnest money depends on the inspection terms and deadlines written into your contract, so read them before inspection day and ask your agent which date matters.
### Q. Does Missouri license home inspectors?
A.  No. In Missouri, home inspectors do not need a license or training, while professional engineers are licensed by the state. Ask any inspector for a sample report and for the standard of practice they follow before you book.

## How to Choose a Home Repair Company in St. Louis: Ask Who Pulls the Permit
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/10-must-know-tips-for-finding-top-home-repair-services
The water heater is already on a dolly, half out the basement door, when the guy says it. “You’ll want to pull the permit yourself. It’s quicker that way.” He says it the way you’d say the Cardinals lost again, easy and a little bored, while the old tank drips a rusty line across the floor you mopped this morning. You nod. You almost say yes. Most of us do, because the shower has been cold for three days and the man with the truck is right here.
Here is what that sentence means inside the city limits. The City of St. Louis says plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors who are certified by the City of Saint Louis, and the city lists the replacement of water supply lines among the jobs that need a permit and an inspection. Electrical works the same way, with one narrow door for homeowners: you can get your own electrical permit if you pass a short test given by the Building Division Electrical Section and the work is on an owner-occupied, single-family dwelling. So when a contractor in the city asks you to pull the permit, he isn’t saving you time. He’s handing you his paperwork, his test and his inspection. Write that line on the fridge.
That one question, “Who pulls the permit?”, sorts more home-repair companies than any star rating ever will. The rest of this guide is how to ask it, and the handful of questions that go with it, before anybody touches your house.
### How do I choose a home repair company in St. Louis?
Pick a company that pulls its own permit, puts the price and the payment schedule in writing, and shows proof of insurance before anyone climbs a ladder. In the City of St. Louis, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are issued to contractors certified by the city, so ask which license they hold and check it. Get two or three itemized quotes, call recent local references, and pay as the work gets done, never most of it up front.
That’s the short version. The long version matters because the bad hires rarely look bad. They look friendly, and they look available.
### Why the permit question works better than reviews
Reviews tell you how a company made people feel. The permit tells you whether the city trusts them to do the work at all. Those are different things, and the second one is harder to fake.
Think about what the city actually checks. It says mechanical permits are issued to licensed mechanical contractors certified by the City of Saint Louis, and that those permits are required to install things like boilers, furnaces, exhaust fans and ventilation systems. That covers the furnace that wheezes every November in a brick two-family off Gravois, the bathroom fan that never quite cleared the steam, and the boiler that knocks like someone is trapped in the radiator. If a company wants to swap any of those and doesn’t want a permit in its own name, you’ve learned the one thing a glowing review can’t tell you.
And the homeowner door is narrower than people think. On an electrical job, the city says you may not apply for permits for service changes, rehab or new construction. Those need a licensed contractor. So the new panel your inspector flagged when you bought the place, the one with the scorch mark you try not to look at, is not a weekend project you can sign off on yourself, no matter how confident the guy on the porch sounds.
This isn’t about paperwork for its own sake. A permit means an inspector looks at the work before the drywall goes back up.
### The sentence at the door that should end the visit
When hail comes through St. Louis, the trucks follow it. You hear the ladders bang against gutters two streets over. Then the knock. A clipboard, a company shirt, a free roof inspection, and somewhere in the first five minutes, the offer: “Don’t worry about your deductible. We’ll take care of it.”
Missouri law forbids that offer. Under section 407.725 of the state statutes, a contractor who repairs or replaces roof systems or does other exterior work shall not advertise or promise to pay or rebate all or any portion of any insurance deductible as an inducement to the sale. A company willing to break that rule in your driveway is telling you how it will treat the rest of the contract.
The same law gives you an exit most homeowners never hear about. If you sign a written contract for work to be paid under your property insurance, you may cancel it before midnight on the fifth business day after you receive written notice from your insurer that all or part of the claim is not covered. You cancel by written notice to the contractor at the address stated in the contract. Keep that in your back pocket, because storm contracts get signed fast, with wet shoes in the front hall.
Above all of it sits section 407.020, which declares any deception, fraud, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation in connection with the sale of merchandise an unlawful practice. You don’t need to quote it to anyone. You only need to know that a promise made at your door counts.
People are asking
### How do I choose a home repair company in St. Louis?
Ask who pulls the permit before you ask the price. In the city, plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors certified by the City of Saint Louis, and mechanical permits for furnaces and boilers go to city-certified mechanical contractors, so the company you hire should pull them in its own name. For roof and other exterior work, Missouri law bars a contractor from promising to pay or rebate your insurance deductible, so walk away from anyone who offers.
### Start with what’s actually broken
Before you call anybody, stand where the problem is and write down what you see, hear and smell. The brown ring on the ceiling and when it showed up. The furnace that clicks three times and quits. The basement corner that smells like wet cardboard after every hard rain. Take photos on your phone. Then describe it the same way to every company you call, so the quotes you get back are for the same job.
That note also tells you which trade you need. A roofer for the roof. A licensed plumber for the water heater. An electrician for the panel. A specialist in the exact problem usually spots the cause a generalist misses, and in the city the permit rules above already sort the trades for you. If you can’t tell whether it’s a handyman job or a licensed trade, our home-services hiring guide breaks the trades down.
### Check the license where your house actually sits
St. Louis homeowners get tripped up here because the rules are local. The city issues electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits to contractors certified by the City of St. Louis, and the permit pages say so plainly. If your house is out in the county or in one of the many small municipalities around it, the rules are set closer to home, so call that city hall or building department and ask what a contractor needs for your job.
So “licensed” on a truck door means very little on its own. Ask which city or county issued the license, write the answer down, and check it with that office. A real pro answers in one breath. Hesitation, a change of subject, or “I’ll get that to you later” is your first real red flag.
Insurance comes next. Ask for a current certificate of liability insurance, and proof of workers’ comp if a crew is coming. Hold the paper in your hand and read the dates. If someone falls off a ladder in your side yard and there’s no coverage, you don’t want to learn on that day whose problem it is.
Building your shortlist tonight? Start with the map of St. Louis handyman and home-repair pros, then run every name through the permit question above before you book a single estimate.

### Reviews, references and work you can see
Reputation still matters. It just comes after the permit and the paper. Work it from three sides:
Read the bad reviews first. A calm, specific reply to an angry customer tells you more than forty five-star ratings. Check Google and directories that show real local businesses.
Call two recent local references. Ask the questions that matter: did the work hold up through a winter, did they stick to the quote, would you hire them again?
See a similar job. Photos are fine. A porch or a basement you can drive past is better.
Look for a real address and some history. Everyone starts somewhere, but a company with a shop you can find is easier to hold to its word than a name that showed up last month.
### Get written estimates and read what’s missing
Never hire off one quote. Get two or three, in writing and itemized, and spread them across the kitchen table side by side.
Be wary of the lowball. A number far under the others often means a missing step, a skipped permit, or labor you’ll pay for later.
Make the high bid explain itself. Sometimes it’s the only one that included the permit and the haul-away. Sometimes it’s padding.
Hunt for the blanks. Materials, cleanup, disposal, the permit and who pulls it. A vague quote is where surprises hide.
### Red flags worth walking away over
“You pull the permit.” In the city, the permit belongs with the licensed contractor. Being asked to carry it for a pro’s work is the clearest warning on this list.
“We’ll cover your deductible.” On roof and exterior work, Missouri law forbids that promise.
A big payment before any work, especially in cash. A modest deposit for materials is normal. Half or more up front, in cash, leaves you with nothing to hold.
“Today only” pressure. A good roofer will still be a good roofer on Thursday.
No written contract, or a vague one. Scope, price, timeline, payment schedule and warranty, on paper, before anyone starts.
Not sure if it’s a handyman job or a licensed trade? Sort the trades out first.
### Questions to ask at the estimate
The estimate visit is a job interview, and you’re the one hiring. Stand in the kitchen with a notepad and ask these, in this order:
“Who pulls the permit, and under whose license?” The answer you want is “we do, under ours.”
“Which city or county issued your license?” Then check it.
“Can I see a current insurance certificate?” The document, not a promise.
“Your crew or subcontractors?” If they sub it out, the subs need to be licensed and insured too.
“What does the warranty cover, and for how long?” In writing, labor and materials both.
“What’s the payment schedule?” Payments tied to finished stages, not one lump sum before the first nail.
One quiet tip: don’t open with your top budget. Describe the job and let them price it. Lead with your ceiling and the quote has a way of rising to meet it.
### Once the work starts
Vetting doesn’t end at the signature. Pay by check or card so there’s a record, and keep every receipt in one folder. Take photos before, during and after, especially of anything that’s about to be covered by drywall or shingles. Hold a real final payment until you’ve walked the finished job in daylight and the inspection has passed. On bigger jobs with subcontractors or suppliers, ask for lien waivers so nobody can come after your house later for a bill the contractor didn’t pay.
Good contractors expect this. The ones who bristle at a homeowner keeping clean records are telling you something, and it’s worth hearing before the money is gone.
### Where St. Louis homeowners can build a shortlist
A neighbor’s name, a few honest reviews and a local directory will get you three candidates in an evening. Browse by area, like all of Creve Coeur, if that’s your side of the county. Then run the checks: who pulls the permit, which license, what insurance, what’s in writing. Whether the house is a city brick two-family, a ranch in Florissant or a bungalow in Webster Groves, the company that makes those four answers easy is the one to hire. The one that rushes you past them is the one to send home.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a contractor?
A.  Asking you to pull the permit for their work, promising to cover your insurance deductible on a roof or exterior job, wanting a large cash payment before work starts, “today only” pressure, and no written contract. In Missouri the deductible promise is barred by state law, so treat it as a reason to end the visit.
### Q. Should I pay a contractor 50% upfront?
A.  Generally no. A modest deposit to cover materials is normal, but half or more before any work, especially in cash, leaves you with no leverage. Tie payments to finished stages and hold the final payment until the job is done and, where a permit was pulled, the inspection has passed.
### Q. What to check before hiring a contractor?
A.  Check who will pull the permit, which city or county issued the contractor’s license, and a current certificate of liability insurance. In the City of St. Louis, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are issued to contractors certified by the city. Then read two or three itemized written quotes and call recent local references.
### Q. How to protect yourself when hiring a contractor?
A.  Get scope, price, timeline and payment schedule in a signed contract, pay by check or card, and keep receipts and photos. If you sign a contract for work paid by your property insurance in Missouri, you can cancel it by written notice to the contractor before midnight on the fifth business day after you receive written notice from your insurer that all or part of the claim isn’t covered.
### Q. Is it cheaper to hire a handyman or contractor?
A.  For small fixes like a sticking door or a loose railing, a handyman often costs less. For permitted work, hire the licensed trade: in the city, plumbing and mechanical permits are issued to licensed contractors certified by the City of Saint Louis.
### Q. What is the safest way to find a handyman?
A.  Start with neighbors you trust and a local directory that shows real businesses and their service areas, then ask every candidate for proof of insurance and a written quote. If the job needs a permit, it isn’t a handyman job, so hire the licensed trade instead.

## Summer Jobs for St. Louis Students: The Form Most Teens Miss
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/summer-jobs-in-st-louis-for-students
What stands between a 14-year-old in St. Louis and a first paycheck? Usually not a boss who says no. A form. Eight hours is the most a 14- or 15-year-old in Missouri can legally work on a summer day, only between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m., and not one of those hours starts until a work certificate is on file. Plenty of families find out the hard way, after a week of online applications that vanish into a void, when a manager finally calls back and asks one question: “Do you have your work certificate?”
That piece of paper is the difference between a phone that stays silent and a first shift on a St. Louis pool deck, whistle on a cord, the concrete already hot under your feet by noon. The grind of applying is the enemy here, not you. You are not unemployable at 14 or 15. You are just missing a form, a plan and the one St. Louis program most families scroll right past. Here are all three, starting with the two St. Louis doors.
### Where can students find summer jobs in St. Louis?
Start with two City of St. Louis doors: the Recreation Division’s pool and recreation jobs, and the City Summer Jobs program for city residents ages 16 to 24. Then try day camps, grocery stores, restaurants and event crews. Students who are 14 or 15 need a Missouri work certificate, signed through their public school district, before the first shift. Campus career centers are the easiest first stop for college students.
Notice what is missing from that list: the job board where you send a stack of applications and hear back from none. The fastest summer jobs in this city still come from crossing a hot parking lot, pushing open the door into the air conditioning, asking for the manager, and having your paperwork ready before they ask.
### St. Louis has its own summer jobs program, and most families miss it
One word typed into a phone, sent to a city number, and the updates start landing in your texts. Here is the piece the national job sites will never tell you. The City of St. Louis runs a Summer Jobs program through its Agency on Training and Employment, for youth between the ages of 16 and 24. It is built around paid on-the-job training, the kind that teaches a teenager how to show up on time, take direction and handle a cranky customer without melting down.
Who qualifies: applicants must live in the City of St. Louis and be between 16 and 24. Eligible residents must live in a household with an income below $69,090 or in a Qualified Census Tract. Students under 17 need a parent or legal guardian signature on the eligibility form. You will need documents that show proof of age, St. Louis residency and household income, so dig out the birth certificate and proof of household income now, not the night before.
How to get in: the city’s page asks you to fill out an interest form, and staff review it to see whether you qualify. Bookmark the City of St. Louis Summer Jobs page and check it in late winter and again in spring. The page also says you can get updates by texting JOBS to 314-438-5432. That is a ten-second task that beats a pile of cold applications.
### The city pools will train a 15-year-old lifeguard
Chlorine in your hair on the ride home. A whistle on a cord. Pool concrete warm under bare feet. This is the St. Louis door almost nobody knocks on. The City of St. Louis Recreation Department offers the American Red Cross lifeguard course free of charge to candidates who are not yet certified, and helps them apply to guard with the City. Candidates must be at least 15 years of age on or before the final scheduled session of the course, and they need a City and County police record check. At 15, the city will train you to lifeguard for free.
The City Recreation Division has hired for hourly lifeguard and hourly recreation assistant jobs, and its posting lists duties that include checking the chemical balance of pool water, enforcing rules, giving swimming safety instruction and coaching swim teams. Watch the city’s Recreation Division lifeguard posting in late winter, so the course is done before summer.
### Can you legally work at 14 in Missouri?
A clipboard, a pen and a form with two signature lines. Yes, you can work at 14 in Missouri, with conditions, and the conditions are where most first job hunts stall. The Missouri Department of Labor says it straight: any person who is 14 or 15 years old must give an employer a completed Work Certificate before performing work. No certificate, no shift, no matter how badly the snow cone stand needs help on a hot weekend.
There are two versions of the form. During the school year it is the Certificate to Employ a Child 14 or 15 Years of Age During School Term. For summer, it is the Certificate to Employ a Child 14 or 15 Years of Age During Non-School Term. The student and a parent fill in the first section together, usually at the kitchen table, and the employer fills in the next.
Then comes the part that surprises families. Missouri law requires that work certificates are issued and signed by or under the direction of the superintendent of public schools in the district where the child lives. That is true even for private school and home-school students. So if your teen goes to a parish school in south city, the signature still comes from the public school district you live in. Call that district office early, before everyone else in the county remembers it exists.
### The hours rule, in plain numbers
Watch the clock on the snack bar wall, because the state already is. The state’s youth employment bulletin lays out two seasons. From Labor Day to June 1, while school is in session, 14- and 15-year-olds can work between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., no more than 3 hours on school days and no more than 8 hours on non-school days. From June 1 to Labor Day, the window stretches to 9 p.m., with no more than 8 hours on non-school days, no more than 6 days a week, and a 40-hour weekly cap.
Read that again if you are a parent. That is not a little pocket-money summer. Your 15-year-old can legally earn real money this summer, as long as the job ends by 9 p.m. and the certificate is on file. That one sentence is worth texting to the other parents in the group chat, because some of them may assume teens cannot work until 16.
There is a second rule worth knowing before you apply. The state lists prohibited occupations for 14- and 15-year-olds, which generally involve dangerous equipment like cookers and slicers. So the deli counter with the spinning blade is out. The front counter, the bagging station, the pool deck snack bar and the camp craft table are where a younger teen fits. Aim there and the yes comes faster.
### What is the best summer job for a teenager?
The best summer job is the one that teaches you something you can say out loud in your next interview. A pool job teaches you to stay calm with a whistle in your mouth and chlorine stinging your eyes. A grocery job teaches you to smile at the last customer of a long day while the scanner beeps in your ear. A day camp job teaches you patience, mostly with little kids who will not put their shoes back on. Each of those turns into a story an employer remembers.
College students have one more door that high schoolers do not: the campus career center. Career centers post openings from employers who already expect class schedules, and campus jobs like library desks, tutoring centers and research help are built around your timetable by design. Find yours on the campus website, and a short visit there can beat a weekend of cold applications.
### How to beat the application grind
The laptop fan hums, application number twelve goes out, and the inbox stays empty. The grind wins when you play its game: one more online form, one more silent inbox. Change the game instead:
Get the paperwork first. At 14 or 15, have the work certificate started before you apply. If you are older, have an ID ready. A manager who can hire you on the spot often will.
Walk in, mid-afternoon. Not at the lunch rush. Ask for the manager by title, hand over a one-page sheet with your name, phone and the days you can work, and say the hours out loud.
Use the people you know. The neighbor who runs a landscaping crew, the coach whose cousin manages the custard stand, the church that runs a summer camp. Most first jobs come through a person, not a portal.
Follow up once, in person. A week later, stop back in. It shows you are the kind of hire who comes back.
Stack two small jobs that do not fight. Camp mornings and pool evenings beat two jobs fighting over the same afternoon.
### Once you are over 16
The ache in your feet after a doubleheader shift is real. So is the first paycheck that is entirely yours. And once you are over 16, the rules loosen. The Missouri Department of Labor says individuals over 16 do not need a work certificate, but may have limitations by federal laws. That opens up later shifts at restaurants, more hours at grocery stores, and event crews that work nights at the ballpark and the arena. It is also when the City Summer Jobs program becomes an option for city residents.
Hunting for employers near home? Browse local businesses by category and town on St Louis Near Me Directory, then check our jobs board for openings posted by St. Louis employers.
If you run the pool, the snow cone stand or the day camp that needs teen hands by June, a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your business in front of the local families searching every week, so you fill shifts and get more customers from the same page.
### For parents: the first job, from your side of the table
You remember your first job. The polyester uniform, the boss who seemed a hundred years old, the first time you held a paycheck with your own name on it. Your teen is about to get that, and your job is mostly logistics. Start the work certificate early. Know the hours rule so nobody schedules your 15-year-old until close. Ask the manager who supervises the teens. Then step back. The rides home after a first shift, when they cannot stop talking, are the payoff.
One more thing parents can do that no job site will: open a door. Ask the owner of the shop you have bought from for years whether they need summer help. Ask the camp your kids aged out of. A parent’s quick word with a person who already knows the family turns a cold application into a warm one, and it costs nothing but a little pride. Your teen still has to show up, work hard and earn the second week. You just help them get the first.
Graduating soon? The summer job ends; the career starts. Our entry-level jobs guide picks up where this one stops.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can you legally work at 14 in Missouri?
A.  Yes. A 14- or 15-year-old must give the employer a completed Work Certificate before working, signed by or under the direction of the public school superintendent in the district where the child lives. In summer, the hours run from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., with no more than 8 hours a day, 6 days a week and 40 hours a week.
### Q. Who hires 14 year olds in St. Louis?
A.  At 15, the City of St. Louis pools are worth a call, because the Recreation Department offers its lifeguard course free to candidates at least 15. Otherwise, look for jobs that keep a younger teen away from dangerous equipment, since Missouri bars 14- and 15-year-olds from work with cookers and slicers. Pools, day camps, snack bars, front counters and family businesses run by neighbors are the usual first yes. Have the work certificate started before you ask.
### Q. What are some jobs available for 15-year-olds in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Camp helper, grocery bagger, snack bar or front counter worker, landscaping crew helper and office help at a family business are all common fits. A 15-year-old follows the same certificate and hours rules as a 14-year-old.
### Q. What is the best summer job for a teenager?
A.  The one that gives you a story for your next interview: a pool, a camp, a grocery store or a ballpark crew. Pick the job where you will learn to handle people, because that skill follows you into every job after it.
### Q. How to get a job this summer?
A.  Get your paperwork ready first, walk in mid-afternoon and ask for the manager, use the people you already know, and follow up once in person. City residents ages 16 to 24 should also check the City of St. Louis Summer Jobs page, and can text JOBS to 314-438-5432 for updates.
### Q. Is there anywhere that hires at 14?
A.  Yes. Missouri allows 14-year-olds to work with a Work Certificate and within the state’s hours limits. Small local businesses, camps and pools are often the most open to a first-time worker who shows up with the form already started.

### Your Story Sells Better Than Any List of Tasks
“I kept nine trucks moving in a snowstorm.” I adjusted routes in real time. We finished on schedule with zero incidents.
“I cut stockroom errors by half.” A simple bin system and a weekly 20-minute huddle changed everything.
“I trained two new hires who now train others.” We built a sturdy ladder together — both climbed.
“I turned a lobby from tense to calm.” A friendly check-in script and clear signage cut wait-time complaints by 60%.
### Set Expectations You’ll Feel Good About
Hours. Many part time jobs for retirees near me run 10–20 hours per week in 4–6 hour shifts; project roles come in bursts.
Flexibility. Set boundaries kindly. “I’m available Mon–Wed mornings,” “No nights,” or “I deliver milestones, not clock hours.”
Pay. Rates vary. Customer-facing roles often pay hourly; advisory and tax roles pay premium for short, focused spurts. If you improve outcomes, you can ask for fair compensation.
### Stay Sharp, Safe, and Satisfied
Pacing and ergonomics. Good shoes, breaks, smart lifting. Choose roles that respect your energy.
Simple tech. Calendar, messaging, basic POS/CRM. Would a one-hour tutorial remove any last hesitation?
Boundaries. Written scopes and schedules. Gracious “no’s” when scope creeps. Your clarity helps everyone.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best part-time job for a retired person?
A.  The best fits blend flexible hours with your experience: retail and customer service, tutoring or teaching, library and administrative work, bookkeeping or tax prep, consulting in a former field, driving or delivery, and caregiving. Pick one that matches your energy and pays for what you need — in St. Louis you can find part-time openings on the St. Louis Near Me jobs board.
### Q. What is the best side hustle for retirees?
A.  Flexible, low-overhead side hustles fit retirement best: tutoring or test prep, consulting in a former field, pet sitting and dog walking, bookkeeping or tax prep, driving or delivery, and selling crafts or expertise online. Many pay $20–$31 an hour and let you set your own schedule — the goal is supplemental income without a rigid commitment.
### Q. Where is a good place for seniors to work?
A.  Age-friendly employers span retail (customer service, greeting), healthcare and caregiving, schools and libraries, and administrative roles — big names like Home Depot and Verizon plus many local small businesses actively value older workers. In St. Louis, look for part-time openings on the jobs board and tap AARP’s free job resources.
### Q. What jobs are available for a 70 year old?
A.  Plenty — and flexibility matters most at 70. Common options include greeter or retail associate, tutor, library or administrative assistant, event attendant, driver, translator, and consulting or freelance work in a past field. Choose roles that match your energy and let you work the hours you want.
### Q. What is the $1000 a month rule for retirees?
A.  It’s a rough retirement-savings guideline: for every $1,000 a month of income you want, you need roughly $240,000 saved (assuming about a 5% withdrawal rate). Part-time work can bridge the gap — even $500–$1,000 a month of earned income eases the pressure on your savings.
### Q. How can I help a retired parent find part-time work?
A.  Match their interests and desired hours to flexible, age-friendly roles, then help them write a short, current resume and set up a couple of profiles. Point them to AARP’s free job resources and local workforce centers, and browse openings together on the St. Louis Near Me jobs board. A reminder that their experience is an asset goes a long way. ## Lost Money, Still on Top: St. Louis Companies Ranked by Revenue
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-company-st-louis-picks-for-2025
Three careers pages, three browser tabs, and a laptop fan whirring like it wants out of the room. Every page promises a “global leader.” None of them says how big the place really is. So you guess: the brewery, maybe, or the Edward Jones branch you pass on the way to the grocery store.
Guess again. The company at the top of this list is a health insurer most St. Louisans only ever meet as a plastic card in a wallet. Fortune lists Centene with its headquarters in St. Louis and revenues of $194,777 million. That’s about $194.8 billion. Then read the next line on the same profile: profits of negative $6,674 million. The company on top lost money.
Big in dollars, or big in people? Which ones are private, which one is owned by the people who work there, and which famous “St. Louis” name is legally Swiss? When you’re the one about to hit submit, those stop being trivia questions.
So here are the ten, ranked by the revenue on each company’s own Fortune profile, with the headcount, the headquarters town and one move to make on each before you apply.
### What companies are HQ in St. Louis?
The box above has the roll call. What it can’t show is how far apart the front doors are: Fortune files RGA under Chesterfield and World Wide Technology under Maryland Heights, and it puts Edward Jones in a third suburb. Same metro, very different drives.
### Before you apply: the three numbers to bring
A big name on the letterhead doesn’t pay your rent. Before you walk into any of these ten buildings, flip open the notepad in your bag and write down three numbers.
The first is your floor. MIT’s Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for one adult with no children at $20.04 an hour in St. Louis city and $22.11 in St. Louis County. Multiply an hourly offer by 2,080, the full-time hours MIT uses. Thumb on the phone calculator in the parking lot, you know in ten seconds whether the job clears the line, before anyone across a desk has finished the pitch.
The second is a phone number: (314) 589-8000, the SLATE job center at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor. SLATE says its training programs help St. Louisans who are minorities, women, and long-term unemployed enter careers in growing industries, and that it conducts frequent hiring events for jobseekers to meet and talk with prospective employers. Save it in your phone before you need it, then call and ask what’s coming up.
The third is the drive. Put each headquarters town into your map app on a weekday morning, with the coffee still too hot to drink, and watch what color the line turns.
### The ten biggest, by the money
### 1. Centene: about $194.8 billion
The phone line you call when a prescription gets denied. The enrollment letter on the kitchen table in November. The clinic waiting room with the TV on mute. That is the business. Fortune calls Centene the largest Medicaid managed-care organization in the U.S. as of 2026, counts 61,100 employees, and notes it also operates its own health care and dental clinics and pharmacies, so the jobs run well past insurance desks. Your move: open the careers section at centene.com and filter to Missouri first.
### 2. Bunge: about $70.3 billion
Start in a soybean field, the pods rattling dry on the stalk. Follow the beans and you end up in the oil that goes into food processing, the meal in a feed bin, even biofuels. That whole chain is Bunge’s business: it sources, processes and trades oilseeds and grains. Here’s the Swiss part. Fortune says Bunge Global is incorporated in Geneva, Switzerland, with its operational headquarters in St. Louis, Missouri, and lists revenues of $70,329 million and 34,000 employees. Your move: search the jobs at bunge.com for St. Louis, where the operational headquarters sits.
### 3. Reinsurance Group of America: about $23.7 billion
No storefront, no logo-wrapped truck, nothing you can hold in your hand. Reinsurance is insurance for insurers, as the American Council of Life Insurers puts it, and Fortune calls RGA one of the largest global providers of life and health-related reinsurance. It puts the headquarters in Chesterfield, Mo., with revenues of $23,698 million and 4,300 employees. Do the math: that’s a lot of revenue for 4,300 people, and it tells a job seeker what kind of seat this is. Analysts, underwriters, quiet floors and big spreadsheets. Your move: look for the Chesterfield openings at rgare.com.
### 4. World Wide Technology: about $20 billion
Even the address is a tagline: 1 World Wide Way. WWT lists its Americas global headquarters there, in Maryland Heights, and says that, headquartered in St. Louis, it has nearly 5 million square feet of warehousing, distribution and integration space around the world. That’s the part of “tech” people don’t picture: warehouse and integration floor. Fortune lists WWT as a private company with revenues of $20,000 million and 9,399 employees. WWT says its global headquarters is located in Maryland Heights’ Westport Plaza, seven stories tall and 208,000 square feet. For anyone in IT, that’s the reason “St. Louis tech job” is a real search. Your move: search Maryland Heights on the careers pages at wwt.com.
### 5. Emerson: about $18 billion
Somewhere right now a sensor is reading a pipe in a plant you will never walk through. That is Emerson’s side of the economy. Fortune lists Emerson with its headquarters in St. Louis, revenues of $18,016 million for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, 2025, and 71,000 employees. It makes automation systems, sensors and software for industries including energy, manufacturing and utilities, and Fortune says it was founded in 1890. You’ve probably never bought anything from Emerson, and that’s the point: it sells to the plants and utilities, not to you. Your move: on emerson.com, filter its careers listings to St. Louis.
### 6. Edward Jones: about $17.9 billion
Drive past the branch office on the way to the grocery store and you’ve met the whole business model. Fortune lists Edward Jones as a private partnership with revenues of $17,897 million and 55,000 employees. Its more than 19,000 financial advisors serve more than 8 million clients, according to Fortune, which counts nearly 16,000 branch locations throughout North America. Your move: before you open edwardjones.com, decide whether you want a seat at headquarters or a desk as one of those advisors.
### 7. Graybar: about $12.9 billion
The share-it-at-dinner fact on this list: Fortune says Graybar Electric is employee owned. It lists Graybar as private, headquartered in St. Louis, with revenues of $12,876 million and 10,000 employees. It distributes electrical, communications and data networking products, the wiring, lighting and networking gear that contractors load onto a truck. Founded in 1869, according to Fortune. Your move: check graybar.com for St. Louis openings, and ask in the interview what employee ownership means for your paycheck.
### 8. Ameren: about $8.5 billion
The furnace clicks on in February, the house ticks as it warms, and a few weeks later the bill on the counter is thicker. That’s the one you pay every month. Fortune lists Ameren with its headquarters in St. Louis, revenues of $8,470 million and 8,913 employees. It serves about 2.5 million electric customers and more than 900,000 natural gas customers across Illinois and Missouri. Your move: start at ameren.com and look for the careers link.
### 9. Post Holdings: about $8.2 billion
Open the pantry. Fortune says Post Holdings’ products include Honey Bunches of Oats cereal, Peter Pan peanut butter and Simply Potatoes potato products. It lists Post’s headquarters in St. Louis, revenues of $8,158 million for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, 2025, and 13,180 employees. Fortune also notes Post made the Fortune 500 for the first time in 2025. Your move: search St. Louis on the careers pages at postholdings.com.
### 10. Core & Main: about $7.6 billion
Think about what runs under the street and behind the drywall: the water line, the storm drain, the fire sprinkler pipe. Core & Main supplies water, wastewater, storm drainage and fire protection products to municipalities, private water companies and professional contractors. Fortune lists it in St. Louis with revenues of $7,647 million for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, and 5,600 employees, filed under diversified wholesalers. Just behind it on revenue: Olin in Clayton at $6,781 million and Stifel in St. Louis at $6,348 million. Your move: if you know water and wastewater work, coreandmain.com is the careers page to read first.
### Who is the biggest employer in St. Louis?
Look past revenue to people. BJC Health, which isn’t on the list above, says it includes more than 48,000 employees, 24 hospitals, and hundreds of clinics and service organizations across two brands: BJC HealthCare in the St. Louis region and Saint Luke’s in the Kansas City region. BJC Health says it expanded to include Saint Luke’s on Jan. 1, 2024, and you can read the hospital system’s own announcement of the BJC and Saint Luke’s combination.
Here’s the catch with every headcount on this page: the Fortune numbers count employees company-wide, not just in St. Louis. Fortune says Emerson operates in over 170 countries, so its 71,000 are not all sitting in St. Louis. We could not find a current official count of local-only jobs for each company, so treat the headcounts as a measure of size, not as a count of St. Louis openings. The careers page is where that answer lives.
Hunting a seat at one of these ten? Pick the two that match your field, bookmark their careers pages tonight, and check the St. Louis jobs board for the local companies that sell to them, because the suppliers hire too.
If you run the caterer, the cleaning crew or the IT shop that serves these campuses, list your business so more customers in Clayton, Chesterfield and Maryland Heights can pick you before they pick up the phone.
### How to use this list if you want a job here
Read it twice, once for money and once for people. Revenue tells you who can afford big projects. Headcount tells you who hires at volume. RGA brings in $23,698 million with 4,300 employees. Edward Jones brings in $17,897 million with 55,000. Those are two completely different job hunts.
Then match the company to your field instead of chasing the logo:
Health care and insurance: Centene for managed care, RGA for reinsurance, and BJC for hospital work.
Finance: Edward Jones and its more than 19,000 financial advisors, plus Stifel.
Technology: World Wide Technology in Maryland Heights, and the software side of Emerson.
Trades, logistics and distribution: Graybar and Core & Main, where the product moves on trucks.
Food and agriculture: Bunge and Post Holdings.
Utilities: Ameren, across Missouri and Illinois.
Our guide to the best jobs near St. Louis covers the career paths in more depth, and if you’re aiming at the corporate marketing seats inside these headquarters, start with the St. Louis marketing jobs guide.
And don’t skip the companies around the companies. Every headquarters on this list buys lunch, cleaning, wiring, printing and software from somebody local. Those smaller firms hire too, and the person who answers their phone is often the person who decides. The giant’s careers page is one door. The vendor parked out front is another.
### Why the list keeps surprising people
Because the famous names and the big names aren’t the same names. The one on top of the ranking lost money. The one with 71,000 employees makes things you’ll never see. Graybar is owned by its employees. Bunge is legally Swiss. And one of the largest employers in Missouri, by BJC’s own account, doesn’t sell a product at all. It runs hospitals.
Next time someone says St. Louis is a small market, you have the receipts: a $194.8 billion insurer, a $70.3 billion agribusiness and a $20 billion private tech company, all with St. Louis-area headquarters on Fortune’s own pages.

### A City with a Story: What St. Louis Has to Offer
St. Louis is one of the oldest major cities in the Midwest, founded in 1764 by French fur traders Pierre Laclède and Auguste Chouteau. Its location at the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers made it a vital hub for trade, exploration, and migration. This is why St. Louis became known as “the Gateway to the West”—it was the launching point for countless pioneers heading into the American frontier. Today, exploring St. Louis means discovering a metropolis where history, innovation, and community spirit come together.
Historic Landmarks: Stand in awe at the Gateway Arch, stroll through Soulard, Lafayette Square, and the lush Tower Grove Park, where 19th-century brick homes and gardens whisper stories of the past.
Modern Marvels: Marvel at the St. Louis Aquarium and ride the St. Louis Wheel for sweeping city views.
Neighborhood Vibes: Each area, from The Hill to The Delmar Loop, South City St. Louis, North St. Louis, Downtown St. Louis, and Forest Park, has its own flavor—literally and figuratively.
Fun for Kids: Discover family adventures with 25 Things Every St. Louis Kid Must Do.
Revitalization: See how the city is evolving at PlanSTL.
### Making a Living: Jobs and the Economy
What’s it like to build a life here? Look around and you’ll find a city with a resilient, diverse economy. From Fortune 500 giants like Anheuser-Busch and Emerson Electric to biotech startups and creative agencies, opportunity is everywhere.
Major Employers: Centene, Enterprise Holdings, World Wide Technology, and more.
City of St Louis: Explore career opportunities with the City of St. Louis—enjoy steady employment and excellent benefits.
Cost of Living: Your dollar stretches further here than in most big cities—think more home, more fun, more savings.
Entrepreneurial Spirit: The city’s startup scene is thriving, with resources like Cortex Innovation Community and T-REX fueling new ideas.
The economic landscape in the St Louis region is flourishing. St Louis and the entire area have a diverse mix of industries—from finance and healthcare to technology, manufacturing, and education. This variety has created a resilient foundation, allowing each company St Louis features to weather economic shifts while seizing new opportunities.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How many days do you need in St. Louis?
A.  A long weekend covers the icons — the Gateway Arch, City Museum, Forest Park’s museums, and a neighborhood food crawl. Give it four or five days and you can add the day trips: Missouri wine country in Augusta and Hermann, historic St. Charles, or Cahokia Mounds just across the river.
### Q. Is there anything fun to do in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty — climb through the City Museum, a playground for all ages built from salvaged architecture, ride the St. Louis Wheel, catch a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium, then pick a neighborhood: The Hill for Italian, the Delmar Loop for music, Soulard for its market and nightlife.
### Q. Is it safe to walk around downtown St. Louis?
A.  Downtown is generally fine in the daytime and around the event districts — the Arch grounds, Ballpark Village, and stadium crowds keep things lively. Like any big city, use common sense after dark: stay where the activity is, park in lit lots, and don’t wander somewhere unfamiliar alone.
### Q. What is a must do in St. Louis?
A.  The Gateway Arch for the view, then Forest Park for a whole day — the Zoo, the Art Museum and the History Museum are all free and all inside it. Add Soulard or Lafayette Square if you want the older architecture rather than the postcard.
### Q. Is it safe to ride the MetroLink in St. Louis?
A.  Generally yes, particularly during the day and on event trains, and it is the easiest way to reach downtown from the airport. Use ordinary city sense — stay on populated platforms, keep valuables put away late at night — the same as any transit system.
### Q. Why are so many people leaving St. Louis?
A.  The city proper has lost population for decades while the metro has broadly held, which is a suburbanisation story more than a decline story. Cost of living stays low and the metro spans two states, so much of the movement is people relocating within it.
### Q. What are the biggest issues in St. Louis?
A.  Population loss in the city core, uneven investment between neighborhoods, and the fragmentation of dozens of separate municipalities across the county. Founded in 1764, it carries a lot of history and a lot of inherited boundaries — the second is the harder problem.

## $200 in December, $100 in January: What a St. Louis Business Really Costs to Start
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cost-to-start-a-business-missouri-illinois
Two people carry the same folder into Room 104 of St. Louis City Hall, a week apart. Same one-person crew, same paperwork going soft at the corners from riding around on the passenger seat all week, same damp thumb on the edge of it while the line inches toward the counter. The one who walks in the last week of December pays $200.00 for a Graduated Business License. The one who walks in the first week of January pays $100.00. Both licenses expire on the same day, May 31. Nobody at the counter warned the first one.
That isn’t a loophole. It’s printed on the City’s own fee schedule: new businesses that start between June 1 and January 1 pay $200.00, and new businesses that start after January 1 and up to May 31 pay $100.00. No checkout page and no formation site puts that date in front of you. If your launch date can slide a few days, that’s a hundred dollars the process was never going to mention.
Most of us meet this process the same way: at the kitchen table at 11 p.m., still in the work shirt from a shift that ran long, the laptop fan whirring, a formation website’s checkout page glowing in the dark kitchen. A registered agent subscription. An “EIN package.” Rush processing. Each add-on worded like the State would turn you away without it. The page was built to sell add-ons, not to tell you about January.
Here’s what the State actually charges. The Missouri Secretary of State takes $50.00 to file an LLC’s articles of organization online, or $105.00 on paper, and its own FAQ asks, “Do limited liability companies have to file an annual report?” The answer is one word. No. And that EIN package? The IRS says it on its own application page, in a sentence worth taping to the fridge: “You never have to pay a fee for an EIN.”
### How much money does it cost to open a small business in St. Louis?
Less than the checkout pages suggest. A Missouri LLC costs $50 to file online and never needs an annual report, while an Illinois LLC costs $150 plus a $75 annual report every year. The IRS issues an EIN for free. Inside City of St. Louis limits, the business license starts at $200, or $100 if you start after January 1. Insurance and winning customers cost more than the paperwork.
The City adds two details the formation sites never mention. First, you must obtain a Graduated Business License before commencing business activity, and the City’s license page says, word for word, that registering for an LLC does not qualify as a business license in the City of St. Louis. The $50 receipt from Jefferson City doesn’t open the door at 1200 Market Street.
Second, renewals are priced by the number of St. Louis employees, and the fee schedule counts “owners, partners and officers” in that number. In the City’s eyes, you are an employee of your own business. At 0-2 employees the renewal is $200 a year, and it has to be paid before June 1 to avoid penalties. Write June 1 on the calendar the day the license arrives.
Where do you actually go? The Office of the License Collector is at 1200 Market Street, City Hall Room 102-104, and answers at (314) 622-4528, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Call before you go, because fee schedules get updated. The LLC itself is filed online with the Secretary of State, and online fees are paid by credit card.
### Across the river, the bill comes back every year
Drive east over the Mississippi, the bridge joints thumping under the tires, and the math changes. Under the Illinois Limited Liability Company Act, filing articles of organization costs $150. Then the annual report costs $75, every year the company exists. Miss it and the statute adds a penalty of $100, plus another $100 for each further year the company stays delinquent.
The timing is fussy, too. The Illinois act says the report is due within the 60 days before the first day of the company’s anniversary month. Put that month on the calendar the day you file, right next to the lease renewal.
Neither number will sink a business. But one state sends you a bill every year and the other never does, and that difference compounds quietly while you’re busy doing the work. If you live on one side and work on the other, ask an accountant once where your business really operates. Where you do the work drives what you owe, not where the filing is cheaper.
### What you do not have to buy
Most of what people spend forming a business is optional. The add-ons sell hard because the margins are good, and the checkout pages are built for the hour when anyone would be tired and nervous at the kitchen table.
A formation service. Filing directly with the Secretary of State is the same filing. A service is a convenience purchase, not a legal requirement.
A paid registered agent, maybe. Missouri’s FAQ says an agent may be an individual who is a resident of Missouri and whose business office is identical with the entity’s registered office. For a lot of one-person shops, that’s you. The honest reason to pay someone is privacy, because the agent’s address goes on the public record.
A “business license package.” The Secretary of State’s own FAQ explains that a business license comes from your city or county and is not the same as the certificate of organization it issues. Our guide to what licensing you actually need in St. Louis covers which office to visit.
A trademark on day one. Worth doing later if the brand takes off. Not a startup cost.
### The $7 filing almost nobody mentions
If you answer the phone with any name that isn’t your own legal name or your LLC’s exact registered name, Missouri wants a fictitious name registration, the thing everyone calls a DBA. The cost for registering a fictitious name is $7, and the registration is good for five years. It catches sole proprietors most often, because nothing in the process flags it: no formation filing, no reminder, no form that mentions it. The name on the side of the truck still counts.

### The costs that show up in month two
Formation is cheap. These are the bills that arrive after the excitement wears off.
Insurance. General liability is the real first bill for most service businesses, and premiums swing hard by trade. A bookkeeper and a roofer live in different worlds, which is worth weighing while you decide which services to build the business around. Get two or three real quotes.
A separate bank account. Once you have an LLC, mixing personal and business money can quietly undercut the protection the LLC is there to give.
Accounting help. Cheaper than the first sales tax mistake. An hour with a local bookkeeper before you open, with your receipts in a folder and your questions on one page, usually saves more than it costs. Ask about sales tax, estimated payments and how to pay yourself, and write the answers down.
Customers. The line nobody budgets. You can be filed, licensed, insured and squared away, right down to the legal pages your website is supposed to carry, and still sit next to a phone that doesn’t ring. None of that paperwork shows up when a neighbor searches for what you sell, or asks ChatGPT who to call. That isn’t a flaw in you. It’s the old idea that a website plus a Google listing means people will see you. You’re not broken. You’re invisible, and that part is fixable.
That’s where a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory earns its keep: up to 10 categories across up to 40 location tags, no public address required, so a kitchen-table or truck-based business can show up where neighbors look. It doesn’t replace the website or Google profile you already have. It points people to them.

### How much money does it cost to open a small business?
Less than the formation sites charge. A Missouri LLC is $50 to file online with no annual report, while an Illinois LLC is $150 plus a $75 report every year. The IRS hands out an EIN for free, and a City of St. Louis business license is $200, or $100 if you open after January 1.
### Can you skip the LLC altogether?
Often, yes, and the $50 isn’t the deciding factor. A sole proprietorship starts the moment you do business under your own name, which is where most people going solo as a freelancer in St. Louis begin. There’s no state formation filing for it. You still handle local licensing and taxes.
What the LLC buys is a line between business debts and personal property. That matters more when you work inside strangers’ homes, hire help, sign a lease or carry inventory. It matters less for a low-risk weekend side business. If you can’t tell which one you are, that’s a question for an attorney or accountant, asked once.
Before you spend a dollar on any of it, make sure somebody wants to buy. Our guide on testing a business idea before you spend money walks through it.
### A realistic first-year floor in the City
One person, a Missouri LLC filed online, acting as your own registered agent, working inside City of St. Louis limits:
LLC filing: $50
EIN: $0
Graduated Business License: $200, or $100 if you start after January 1
Missouri annual report: $0, because there isn’t one
Add the $50 filing to the $100 or $200 license and you’re legal, before insurance and before a single customer. In Illinois, swap the $50 for $150 and add $75 every year. The cheap part is becoming legal. The part that decides whether you last is being the name people see when they need you. Refuse to be invisible.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do you have to pay for your LLC every year in Missouri?
A.  Not to the State. The Missouri Secretary of State’s FAQ says limited liability companies do not have to file an annual report, so there is no yearly state fee for a Missouri LLC. Local business licenses are separate. In the City of St. Louis, the Graduated Business License renews every year.
### Q. How much does it cost to get a business license in Missouri?
A.  Missouri licenses businesses at the city or county level, so the price depends on where you operate. Inside the City of St. Louis, a new Graduated Business License costs $200.00, or $100.00 if you start after January 1 and up to May 31. Renewals are priced by your number of St. Louis employees, owners included.
### Q. What is needed for an LLC in Missouri?
A.  Articles of organization filed with the Secretary of State, $50.00 online or $105.00 on paper, and a registered agent. An agent may be an individual who is a Missouri resident and whose business office is identical with the registered office, and for a one-person shop that individual can be you. An EIN from the IRS is free.
### Q. Can I run my business without an LLC?
A.  Yes. A sole proprietorship needs no state formation filing, though a trade name needs a $7 fictitious name registration and a City business still needs its license. You can also list it on St Louis Near Me Directory without an LLC; a Gold listing needs no public address.
### Q. At what point would I need an LLC?
A.  When the risk grows: working inside customers’ homes, hiring help, signing a lease or holding inventory. An LLC puts a line between business debts and personal property. If you’re unsure, one conversation with an attorney or accountant settles it.
### Q. Is there any downside to having an LLC?
A.  Some paperwork and discipline. You keep business money separate, and in Illinois you pay a $75 annual report every year. In Missouri there is no annual report to file, so the main downside is the habit of keeping things separate.

## The Heart of Community: Why Local Matters
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-heart-of-community-why-local-matters
Sit with me for a moment. Picture lunchtime on a Saturday: the sun soft on the corner of Main Street, the warm smell of fresh barbecue drifting from a small café or food truck, and you hear the low, satisfied rumble of a lawn mower being tuned at a family-run garage down the block.
That feeling — of places that know your name, of streets threaded together by familiar faces and dependable services — is what the St. Louis Near Me spirit is about.
This is not a sales pitch; it's an invitation to hold a door open for neighbors and friends, to make daily life a little easier for the people who make our neighborhood, city, and region hum.
### Why Choosing Local Is an Act of Community
When you choose a local barbecue restaurant instead of a chain, you're doing more than buying a sandwich. You're making possible the sound of the smoker timer, the restaurant or food truck owner's family who remembers your order, and the teenager saving for college who works the register.
Have you patronized a business like this? That single, small act ripples: dollars that stay close by, jobs that support families, and the authentic character of neighborhoods from Warrenton to Highland and from Bonne Terre to Jerseyville. The human economy is woven from these small local choices we make to support our friends and neighbors.
Think about the sensory memory of a place you love: the softness of a storefront's worn wooden sign and the creak in the store's old wooden floors, the spicy tang of a food truck's simmering sauce that you remember from your last visit, the distant rhythm of a band tuning up at a town festival that you've been looking forward to for weeks.
Those layers — sight, smell, sound, texture, taste — are the town's real capital. It's where life is made and experiences are photographed, and those photos are sent to friends and remembered forever.
You're not just shopping or buying a barbecue sandwich; you're supporting local businesses, which keeps those delicate layers of interaction alive. Those businesses train the younger generation and teach the skills that are necessary to lead a long, productive, and happy life right here in our community.
Whether those businesses support a single mother, an older couple, or a larger business with many employees, you know that all of us are in this community together and that we need to continue to support each other. These small, human insights turn discovery into trust.

### How Supporting Local Businesses Strengthens Our Regional Fabric
Dollars spent locally recirculate. A resident or business that hires a gardener or landscaper from the neighborhood spends more locally on supplies; a plumber who hires an apprentice keeps wages within the community. It means the person who fixes your roof might also be the one coaching at the local youth league in the evening. Beyond economics, local businesses hold the civic memory of a place. ## The $25 Gig Paid Less Than the $15 Dock: Part-Time Jobs in St. Louis, With the Real Math
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/part-time-jobs-in-st-louis-a-local-guide
5:58 on a Saturday morning. The time clock beeps at a warehouse dock in the Hazelwood Logistics Center, and you’re in: cold concrete under your shoes, a box cutter in your back pocket, cardboard and diesel on the air. You drove up from your place in the city while it was still dark. Four hours on the line, then you’re due somewhere else.
A week later the stub lands. Twenty hours at Missouri’s $15.00 minimum is $300 on paper. Social Security and Medicare take $22.95. Because you live in the city, its 1% earnings tax takes $3.00 more, and that tax follows anyone who works a shift inside city limits, too. What reaches your account: $274.05, before any income-tax withholding. No job posting tells you that number.
So on Sunday you try the thing everyone mentions and open a delivery app. Take a four-hour block that really does pay $25 an hour and covers 60 miles. That’s $100 in. At the IRS business mileage rate, 76 cents a mile right now (the IRS adjusts it, sometimes mid-year), those miles use up about $45.60 of your car, and self-employment tax takes roughly another $7.70. You keep about $46. Saturday’s four hours on the dock kept about $55. The $25 job paid less.
The work usually isn’t the hard part. The grind of getting hired is: the same application retyped for the fifth time, a resume uploaded and then keyed in again box by box, then silence. Three moves shorten it. Filter Indeed or jobs.mo.gov to part-time and apply where the shift actually fits your week. Ask a small shop its hourly rate up front, because Missouri retail and service businesses grossing under $500,000 a year don’t have to pay the state minimum. And walk in on day one with your I-9 papers: a U.S. passport, or a driver’s license plus a Social Security card or birth certificate.
One thing you can do today, free: the SLATE Missouri Job Center at 1520 Market Street, Room 3050, downtown (314-589-8000; weekdays, opening at 9 on Wednesdays and closing at 4 on Thursdays and Fridays) does job referrals, resume and interview workshops and free computer time. It also handles federal bonding, the free bond an employer can get when hiring someone with a record.
### What does the job have to fit around?
Start from your own limits, not the biggest number on the posting. A student at UMSL, where MetroLink stops right on campus, wants hours that bend around class. A parent wants the shift over before the school pickup line forms. Retirees tend to want a few social mornings a week that use what they already know. Career-changers use a part-time role to test an industry before they jump. And plenty of people want a second income stacked on a full-time job, which means evenings and weekends. Hours, commute, energy. Settle those three first, then chase the pay.
### Where the part-time jobs actually are in St. Louis
A handful of categories drive most of the metro’s part-time hiring. Here’s where to apply today, and the catch in each:
Warehouse & delivery: Scanner beeps and the shriek of a tape gun. Amazon posts shifts for its Hazelwood sortation center and its St. Peters fulfillment center at hiring.amazon.com, and smaller logistics outfits hire for package handling and sorting, often with evening and weekend shifts. The catch: it’s on-your-feet work, and an open dock door in January lets the cold in.
Healthcare support: A hospital hallway at 11 p.m. is still bright and still busy. Barnes-Jewish posts part-time patient-services, transport and aide openings, steady W-2 work that can lead to full-time. The catch: hospital shifts run nights and weekends too.
Education: substitute teaching starts with a phone that buzzes before sunrise. Subbing with St. Louis Public Schools and area districts commonly pays in the mid-$100s a day. Missouri issues a substitute certificate if you have 36 college credit hours, or after a 20-hour state-approved online course from providers like Frontline Education or Kelly Education, plus a fingerprint background check. The catch: the calls come early and the days are unpredictable.
Seasonal & guest services: the Saint Louis Zoo, museums, stadiums and event venues staff up for their busy seasons, and summer is the big wave. Apply a few weeks before the season, while managers are still building the roster.
Food service: restaurants and coffee shops across the metro hire constantly, often with same-week starts. Missouri lets a tipped job pay a $7.50 base, but tips have to bring you to at least $15.00 an hour, and the employer owes the difference when they don’t.
Retail: the most flexible on-ramp. Hiring spikes from roughly October through the new year, so apply in September, a few weeks before the rush.
Gig & rideshare: the most schedule-in-your-own-hands option. Amazon Flex requires you to be 21 and pass a background check. The catch is the one from Sunday: you pay for the car.
### Seven part-time roles worth a look
These are real, currently-hiring kinds of part-time work in St. Louis, spanning gig, institutional, and seasonal:
Amazon Flex delivery - deliver packages on blocks you choose through the Amazon Flex app. You need to be 21+, have a reliable vehicle, and pass a background check. Pay is often quoted around the high-teens to mid-$20s an hour, but it’s 1099 contractor work: earnings vary and are before gas and vehicle wear, so treat any number as an estimate, not a promise.
Patient services at a hospital - front-desk and patient-support roles at systems like Barnes-Jewish are steady W-2 work with real advancement paths.
Substitute teacher - St. Louis Public Schools and area districts hire subs on flexible day-by-day schedules; daily pay commonly runs in the mid-$100s per day.
Instacart shopper - shop and deliver groceries on your own hours via Instacart. Like Flex, it’s contractor gig work - flexible, but earnings vary and come before expenses.
Zoo guest services - the Saint Louis Zoo hires seasonal and part-time guest-services staff; a great fit if you want a lively, people-facing shift.
Research or campus roles - universities like Washington University post part-time research and support jobs (some are best suited to enrolled students).
Retail or food service near you - the quiet workhorse of part-time work: a shop, cafe, or restaurant within a short commute, hiring year-round and hard around the holidays.
### What does a part-time job in St. Louis actually pay?
Right now, Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour (raised by Proposition A; it has changed almost every January, so check labor.mo.gov for the current rate), so any legitimate W-2 hourly job should start at or above that. Be skeptical of a posting advertising less. On a 20-hour week, a year of paychecks comes to $15,600, under the federal standard deduction for a single filer, so if it’s your only job, little or no federal income tax should come out. Two footnotes from the state: tipped workers can be paid a $7.50 base as long as tips bring them to at least $15.00 an hour, and retail or service businesses with less than $500,000 a year in gross sales don’t have to pay the state minimum, so at a small shop, ask the hourly rate before you say yes. The big exception is gig work - Amazon Flex, Instacart, rideshare and the like are independent-contractor roles, which means no hourly floor, no benefits, and pay that’s quoted before you subtract gas, vehicle wear, and self-employment taxes. Gig work can be genuinely flexible and worth it, but read those “$25/hour” claims as gross, best-case, and variable - not a guaranteed wage.
### Where to actually look
Skip the sketchy corners of the internet and start where the real listings are. On the big boards, use the part-time filter: Indeed and Snagajob both let you narrow to part-time, local roles. Go straight to employer career pages for the places you’d actually like to work - a nearby hospital, shop, or restaurant. And don’t overlook the free help: Missouri Job Centers (through jobs.mo.gov) offer no-cost job-search support, computers, and workshops across the metro. You can also browse current local openings right here on our St. Louis Jobs Board’s part-time listings - a directory of local roles, no national-board clutter. The advantage of a local board is exactly that focus: instead of scrolling past hundreds of listings two counties away, you’re seeing roles from St. Louis-area employers who actually want someone nearby.
