## Felony in Illinois, Small Claims in Missouri: When a Contractor Won't Finish the Job
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/contractor-wont-finish-the-job-missouri-illinois
The dumpster has been in the driveway so long the grass under it has gone yellow. Upstairs, the bathroom is studs and a bare subfloor, and the new vanity is still in its box in the hall, corners soft from being bumped every morning. The last text from the contractor said “back Monday.” That was three Mondays ago.
Here is what most people in that hallway don’t know. The answer to “what can I do about it” changes at the Mississippi. Same crew, same truck, same bridge, and a different set of laws waiting on each bank.
In Illinois, a contractor who takes deposits for work he never does can be charged with home repair fraud. When the Illinois Attorney General charged one fence company owner over work he allegedly never completed, the home repair fraud counts were Class 4 felonies, each punishable by up to three years in prison. In Missouri, the same walk-off usually lands in civil territory: a written demand, small claims court up to $5,000, and a complaint to the Attorney General under the Merchandising Practices Act.
A house in Belleville and a house in St. Louis County can have the same half-finished bathroom and two very different sets of tools to fix it. Know which side of the river your tools come from before you pick up the phone.
This is general information, not legal advice. When real money or a lien is on the line, an hour with a construction lawyer is cheap.
### What to do if a contractor does not finish the job?
Stop paying, and start a paper trail. Photograph the unfinished work, gather the contract, receipts and texts, then send a dated written demand by certified mail with a firm deadline. If nothing changes, file in small claims (Missouri caps it at $5,000) or talk to a lawyer, and file a consumer complaint with your state Attorney General.
### The first hour: build the record before you make the angry call
Your thumb is already over his name in your phone. Put it down for an hour. Everything that gets your money back later rests on what you write down now, and it only gets harder to rebuild.
Walk the job with your phone and take more pictures than feel reasonable: the open wall, the missing trim, the tile stacked in the garage, the date on the screen. Then sit at the kitchen table with the contract, every change order, every canceled check and card statement, and the whole text thread. Texts count. A timeline goes on one sheet of paper: what he promised and when, when the crew actually showed up, and the day the phone went quiet.
Call the permit office too. In the City of St. Louis that is the Permit Section at (314) 622-3313, 1200 Market, Room 425, open Monday - Friday 8:00 AM - 4:30 PM; in St. Louis County or on the Illinois side, call your own city or county building department. Ask whether a permit was pulled, in whose name, and whether any inspection passed. A contractor who never pulled one has left you unfinished work and unpermitted work, and the second problem shows up again the day you try to sell.
### The letter that changes the tone
A voicemail is easy to ignore. A certified letter that someone has to sign for at his front door is not, and the signed return-receipt card that comes back in your mailbox is proof he got it. Keep it short and flat: what you agreed to, what you paid, what is not done, what you want, and the date you want it by. No adjectives, no threats you won’t carry out. Dates, dollars, deliverables.
Some contractors come back the week that letter arrives. The ones who don’t have just handed you Exhibit A, because every next step goes better when you can show you asked plainly and gave him a fair chance.
If you also paid a deposit and he never showed up at all, that is a different story with its own playbook. Our guide on what to do when a contractor took your money and disappeared covers the vanished-deposit version. This page is about the job that was started and then abandoned.
### On the Missouri side: your levers
Missouri small claims is built for exactly this fight. Under RSMo 482.305, the small claims judge hears civil cases where the amount in controversy does not exceed five thousand dollars, and RSMo 482.310 says parties may bring their claims without the assistance of an attorney. You sit on a hard bench with a folder on your lap, photos in date order, the letter and the receipt card on top. When your case is called, you tell the story in plain words and the judge decides.
The Missouri Attorney General enforces the Merchandising Practices Act, RSMo 407.020, which makes it unlawful to use deception, fraud, false promise or misrepresentation in connection with a sale. The AG’s office takes consumer complaints and says it mediates disputes between businesses and consumers. Enclose copies of your contract, invoices and canceled checks, never the originals. The Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222. Be clear-eyed: the office acts for the state, not for you personally, and says it cannot give you legal advice.
Missouri’s Merchandising Practices Act also lets a consumer bring a private suit for actual damages under RSMo 407.025. That is lawyer territory. So is any claim large enough that you are tempted to skip small claims.
And watch the clock. RSMo 516.120 gives five years for actions upon contracts, except those covered by RSMo 516.110, which allows ten years for an action upon a writing for the payment of money. Which one fits your contract is a question for a lawyer, but neither is a reason to wait.
Need an afternoon away from the drywall dust? Walk Wydown Skinker and let somebody else’s finished porches remind you how this ends.
### The lien trap: paying in full doesn’t always protect you
This is the part that turns a bad month into a bad year. Missouri’s mechanic’s lien law requires a written warning to owners, in bold type: “FAILURE OF THIS CONTRACTOR TO PAY THOSE PERSONS SUPPLYING MATERIAL OR SERVICES TO COMPLETE THIS CONTRACT CAN RESULT IN THE FILING OF A MECHANIC’S LIEN ON THE PROPERTY.” The notice points to Chapter 429, the same chapter that spells out when a subcontractor has a lien.
Read that sentence again with the half-finished bathroom in mind. If the contractor took your money and never paid the tile supplier, the supplier may come after the house.
Two dates matter. A party who wants a lien has to give ten days’ notice before filing it, under RSMo 429.100, and the lien claim has to be filed within six months after the debt accrued, under RSMo 429.080. If an envelope from a supplier you have never heard of shows up, do not set it on the counter. That is your window to call a lawyer.
The same statute tells you the fix for next time: ask the contractor for “lien waivers” from everyone supplying material or services. Get them in hand before you write the last check.
### Across the river: Illinois puts more in your hands
If the house is in Belleville, Edwardsville, O’Fallon, Collinsville or Alton, open the contract and look at it again. Illinois wrote more of the rules down.
Under the Home Repair and Remodeling Act, before starting home repair or remodeling work for over $1,000, the contractor has to give you a written contract or work order for signature stating the total cost, including parts and materials. The contractor also has to hand you the state pamphlet “Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights” before the contract is signed, and you sign an acknowledgment that you got it.
No contract, or no pamphlet, and the contractor was out of compliance before the first wall came down. A person who suffers actual damage from a violation of that Act can sue under Section 10a of the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.
Then there is the criminal side. Illinois treats home repair fraud as a crime, and the Attorney General uses it. In one case the office charged the owner of a suburban fencing company after eight consumers made down payments totaling $20,449 and the fences were never installed. A charge is not a conviction. A contractor who simply ran out of money is not the same as one who never meant to do the work, and that line is for prosecutors and courts to draw.
Roofing is the trade where the gap is sharpest. Illinois issues a roofing contractor license, and before issuing or renewing one the state requires the licensee to file and maintain a bond. On the Illinois side, ask for that license number before anyone climbs a ladder.
To complain, use the Illinois Attorney General’s online consumer complaint, which the office calls the preferred method. Its Consumer Protection Division offers informal dispute resolution, but like Missouri’s office, it cannot represent you privately.
### Finding the crew that finishes it
Tell the next contractor the truth about what happened, and let them walk the job before they quote. Many crews won’t touch another crew’s half-done work, and the ones who will need to see the open wall with their own flashlight.
Then vet them properly before any money moves:
Check local licensing and permits with our guide on checking whether a contractor is licensed in Missouri.
In Illinois, insist on the written contract and the consumer rights pamphlet.
Pay by card where you can, tie payments to finished stages, and collect lien waivers before the last check.
Before you buy, know what home inspections miss.
Ready to hire the crew that actually finishes? Browse local pros on St Louis Near Me Directory, ask each for a written contract, and compare at least two quotes before anyone touches the open wall.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is contractor abandonment?
A.  It is the plain-English name for a contractor who starts a job and stops showing up without finishing it or ending the contract properly. Whether it counts as a breach of your contract depends on its terms and the facts, so write down the last day anyone worked and send a dated written demand before you hire someone else.
### Q. Is it worth suing a contractor?
A.  Often, for amounts that fit Missouri small claims, where the judge hears cases up to $5,000 and you can appear without a lawyer. Above that, weigh legal fees against what you can actually collect. A judgment against a business with nothing left is paper, so ask a lawyer about collection before you file.
### Q. Can a contractor go to jail for not finishing a job?
A.  It turns on intent and on the state. In Illinois, home repair fraud is a crime: the Attorney General has charged it as a Class 4 felony, punishable by up to three years in prison, against a contractor accused of taking down payments for work never done. In Missouri, report suspected fraud to the Attorney General and talk to police if there was clear deceit.
### Q. Can I do a civil suit without a lawyer?
A.  In Missouri small claims, yes. RSMo 482.310 says parties may prosecute their claims and defenses without the assistance of an attorney, and RSMo 482.305 covers civil cases up to $5,000. For anything bigger, a lawyer is usually worth the fee.
### Q. What is the statute of limitations for breach of contract in Missouri?
A.  RSMo 516.120 sets five years for actions upon contracts, except those under RSMo 516.110, which allows ten years for an action upon a writing for the payment of money. Which one applies depends on your contract and claim, so confirm it with a lawyer and don’t wait on either.
### Q. How can I file a complaint against a contractor in Illinois?
A.  File a consumer complaint with the Illinois Attorney General. The office says online submission is the preferred method, and its Consumer Protection Division offers informal dispute resolution. It cannot act as your personal lawyer, so pair the complaint with your own demand letter or small claims case.
### Q. Should I pay a contractor who did a bad job?
A.  Not before you document the problems and put your objections in writing. Hold back payment for work that is unfinished or defective, but read your contract first and get advice, because withholding the wrong amount can hand the contractor a claim of his own. In Missouri, also check for lien notices from his suppliers.

## Your St. Louis Business License Counts You as an Employee
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-license-st-louis-what-you-need
Headcount: one. The count starts on a thumb at the kitchen table, and the thumb is yours. City Hall counts it the same way. Its own Graduated Business License fee schedule says to “count the number of full time and full time equivalent employees (including owners, partners and officers)” who worked within the City of St. Louis the year before. Owners. Partners. Officers. The one-person company is a company of one employee.
That line sits on a city web page, under a fee table, and the closure rule sits under that. The state’s startup checklist sends owners to the “local city or county” and stops there. St. Louis County says it does not issue a business license per se. Three offices, three answers, and none of them hands the owner the one that applies to a kitchen table inside city limits.
### Do I need a business license in St. Louis?
Yes, if the work happens inside the City of St. Louis. The city’s rule is that a Graduated Business License comes “before commencing business activity,” and the License Collector counts the owner when it sets the price.
### Priced by people, not by sales
The folder rides on the passenger seat down Market Street toward City Hall, and the number it will cost was set by a headcount, not a sales total. On the city’s renewal fee schedule, a business with 0-2 St. Louis employees pays $200. Three to five people is $325. The side hustle, the one-person crew, the couple running a shop together: $200, and the number does not move with sales.
The work done out of a truck cab counts too. St. Louis City Ordinance 60643 puts the license tax “on all merchants, manufacturers, businesses, avocations, pursuits and callings that are not exempt from the payment of a license by law.” Avocations. Pursuits. Callings. The weekend thing counts.
What goes in that folder is short. The city’s application wants an EIN or Social Security number, a trade name and true name, a structure address (a P.O. box is not allowed), the number of employees, and the owner’s name, date of birth and driver’s license information. A business selling a product needs its state sales tax number first; the city wants it before it registers the license. The License Collector takes applications online or in person in Room 104 of City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM, and answers questions at (314) 622-4528.
Which leaves one honest question: is the business licensed in the city where it actually runs?
### Why June 15 matters more than the $200
June in St. Louis is a truck cab that turns into an oven by mid-morning and a phone that will not stop ringing. That is exactly when the license year turns over, and a renewal is easy to lose under a stack of mail on the counter. On the same city page, below the fee table, the License Collector states its policy plainly: “It is the policy of the License Collector to begin closure procedures on June 15th of any business operating without a valid business license.”
The license year runs June 1 through May 31, and the license tax has to be paid before June 1 to avoid penalties. June 15, closure procedures. Not a reminder letter. Closure procedures.
Then the penalty ladder, and it is built with a trap door. The city lists the combined late filing and payment rates month by month: 5% the first month, 10% the second, then a jump to 35% in the third, 40% in the fourth, and a total penalty of 45% from the fifth month on. The jump comes from a second rule stacked on the first: if payment is not made within sixty days of the due date, the city increases the tax twenty percent on top of the filing penalty. A $200 renewal that waited out the busy season is carrying a 45% penalty by the fifth month, and “no business license will be issued until all late filing and payment penalties are paid.”
That ladder does not ask why the payment was late. It just climbs. New businesses get one break on the front end: the city charges $200 for a start between June 1 and January 1, and $100 for a start after January 1 and up to May 31. Either way, the license comes before the first paid job, not after the first good month.
### Is a St. Louis County address the same thing?
No, and this is where most people living on the county side get turned around. A mailing address that says “St. Louis, MO” can sit in the City of St. Louis or out in the county, and the two run on different rules.
St. Louis County’s own answer is short. “The County does not issue a business license per se.” What it does require: “All businesses are required to register with the Assessor’s office for personal property taxes.” The Assessor’s office also issues Merchant’s Licenses for retail or wholesale sellers and Manufacturer’s Licenses for businesses that make products.
The license itself, if your town requires one, comes from the local city hall. The Missouri Secretary of State’s own startup checklist says it the same way in Step 8: register “for a business license and other necessary permits (if any) with local city or county.” Clayton, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Florissant, Chesterfield and Maplewood each answer that question for themselves. The city clerk where the address actually sits is the one who answers it, and the question is short: do I need a business license to operate here from my home?
There is a reason this page keeps coming back to the address. Two neighbors on either side of a city boundary can do the same work, at the same kitchen table, under different rules. One answers to the City License Collector. The other registers with the county Assessor. Neither one is doing it wrong. They just answer to different desks.
### Who has to pay St. Louis city taxes?
The license is one bill. The earnings tax is the other one new owners in the city miss, and it is the question that lands right after this one: do I need to file a St. Louis City tax return?
According to the City’s Collector of Revenue, “All businesses located in the City of St. Louis, except those exempted by law, are required to pay the earnings tax of 1% of the business’s earnings.” Live in the county and do the work in the city? “Non-resident businesses, except those exempted by law, who perform work, services or business activity in the City of St. Louis are also required to pay earnings tax.”
And the solo owner with a storefront and no staff does not get a pass: “A company that has a physical location in the City of St. Louis, but has no employees is still subject to earnings tax on the business and is required to file the E-234.” For a calendar-year business, the city lists the E-234 return as due April 15.
On the personal side, the one percent earnings tax is collected from city residents regardless of where their employer is, and from employees of businesses located or performing work in the city, regardless of where they live. The city says the earnings tax became law in 1954 and pays for general city services like the police and fire departments.
### What does the state of Missouri ask for?
Less than people expect, and none of it is called a general business license. Forming an LLC or a corporation starts with a creation filing at the Secretary of State, such as articles of organization or articles of incorporation. Selling products brings in the Department of Revenue: “A business must obtain a sales tax license by registering with the Department of Revenue if it’s making sales of tangible personal property and taxable services.” We walk through that one step by step in our guide to the Missouri sales tax license.
For a wider national summary, Wolters Kluwer’s Missouri licensing overview covers the state layer. For St. Louis, the city and county pages above are the ones that set your bill.
There is also an old state category worth knowing about: the merchant. Under Missouri’s merchant statute, a merchant is anyone who deals “in the selling of goods, wares and merchandise at any store, stand or place occupied for that purpose.” The word doing the work is goods. A bookkeeper, a dog walker or a mobile groomer sells time and skill, the way most freelancers going solo in St. Louis do, and that definition was not written for them. If you sell physical things from a stand or a shop, it was.
### The mistakes that cost St. Louis owners money
Thinking the LLC was the license. It is not. An LLC is an entity filed with the state. The Graduated Business License is the city’s permission and the city’s tax. Plenty of people finish the LLC paperwork, feel the relief of a stamped certificate, and are still unlicensed where they actually work. It is the same blind spot that leaves a new website without the legal pages a small business site is expected to carry.
Leaving yourself off the headcount. The fee schedule counts owners, partners and officers. Two partners and a part-timer is still in the $200 bracket. Five people, owners included, is the $325 bracket.
Trusting the mailing address. “St. Louis, MO” on an envelope does not tell you whether you answer to the City License Collector or a county municipality. Check before you file.
Letting June slide. Renewal is due before June 1. Closure procedures start June 15. Put both dates in your phone the day the license arrives.
If you work in the trades, the licensing question has another layer on top of this one. We cover it in our guide on how to check a contractor’s license in Missouri.
Different state, different desks: Troy, Illinois, business by business.

If you are starting fresh, still working out which services are worth building a business around, this sequence keeps you from backtracking:
Find out which desk you answer to. City of St. Louis, a county municipality, or unincorporated county. Everything after this depends on it.
Form the entity, if you want one, with the Missouri Secretary of State.
Register with the Department of Revenue if you sell tangible goods or taxable services.
Get the local license before your first paid job. In the city, that is the Graduated Business License: $200 for 0-2 people, owners included.
Put two dates in your phone: June 1 for the renewal, April 15 for the city E-234 if you have a city location.
In the county, register with the Assessor’s office for personal property taxes.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who needs a business license in Missouri?
A.  Look local first. The Missouri Secretary of State tells new owners to register for a business license with their local city or county. In the City of St. Louis, Ordinance 60643 covers nearly every business, avocation and calling that is not exempt by law, and the license must come before your first sale.
### Q. Do I need a local business license if I have an LLC?
A.  Yes, in the City of St. Louis. The LLC is a state filing that creates the company. The Graduated Business License is separate, and the city says you must obtain it before commencing business activity. The fee follows your headcount, owners included, so a one-member LLC with no staff pays $200 a year.
### Q. Do I need a business license to sell online in Missouri?
A.  If you run the shop from inside St. Louis city limits, the city license covers all merchants and businesses that are not exempt, so plan on it. Selling tangible goods also means a sales tax license from the Missouri Department of Revenue. In the county, all businesses register with the Assessor’s office.
### Q. Do I need to file a St. Louis City tax return?
A.  If your business is located in the city, yes. The city’s earnings tax is 1% of the business’s earnings, and a company with a physical location in the city but no employees still files the E-234. For a calendar-year business the city lists the E-234 as due April 15.
### Q. Who has to pay St. Louis city taxes?
A.  The one percent earnings tax is collected from city residents, wherever their employer is, and from employees of businesses located or working in the city, wherever they live. Businesses located in the city pay it on their earnings, and so do non-resident businesses that perform work, services or business activity in the City of St. Louis.
### Q. Does my side hustle need an LLC?
A.  The city license does not ask. Ordinance 60643 taxes businesses, avocations, pursuits and callings, so a side hustle inside city limits needs the Graduated Business License either way. An LLC is a separate choice, created with articles of organization filed with the Missouri Secretary of State. A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory works either way and needs no public address.
### Q. How much does it cost to get a business license in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the city. In the City of St. Louis, a new business pays $200 if it starts between June 1 and January 1, or $100 after January 1 and up to May 31. Renewals run $200 for 0-2 St. Louis employees, owners included, and $325 for three to five people.
### Q. What do I need to start a small business in Missouri?
A.  Know which city governs your address, file articles of organization with the Secretary of State if you want an LLC, register with the Department of Revenue if you sell taxable goods, and get the local license first. Then make sure customers can reach you. St Louis Near Me Directory’s Gold listing runs $357 a year, under a dollar a day.

## The Real Cost of Living in St. Louis (It's the Housing, Not Everything Else)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cost-of-living-in-st-louis
### What does it actually cost to live in St. Louis?
About 10% below the national average — and almost all of that discount is one category.
Missouri’s own state agency, the Missouri Economic Research and Information Center, puts the St. Louis MO-IL metro at a composite cost-of-living index of 89.8 for the first quarter of 2026, where 100 is the national average. Statewide, Missouri sits at 88.6, tied with Iowa for the seventh-lowest cost of living in the country.
But the composite hides the interesting part. Break it into components and St. Louis stops looking uniformly cheap:
Source: MERIC Cost of Living Data Series, Q1 2026.
So the honest summary is not “everything is cheap in the Midwest.” It is: your housing costs drop sharply, your grocery bill barely moves, and your health care costs go up.
### Why every website gives you a different number
If you have already searched this, you have noticed the answers do not agree. We pulled the current page one and counted:
Salary.com — about 2% below national
Payscale — 6% below
MERIC — 10.2% below
Apartments.com — 10.4% below
Google’s own summary panel currently repeats the 2% figure. That is a five-fold spread on the same question, and none of these sources is lying.
They differ because a cost-of-living index is a basket, and everyone builds the basket differently. How much weight goes on housing versus groceries? Is it the city or the whole metro? Renting or owning? Change those and the answer moves several points.
Which is why we lead with MERIC here: it is a state agency, it is dated to a specific quarter, and it publishes the components rather than one blended number. You can see which parts are cheap instead of taking a single percentage on faith.
The practical takeaway is not to trust any one figure — including ours. Look at the category that dominates your budget. If you rent modestly and have a chronic condition, the health line matters more to you than the housing line, and your personal index looks nothing like 89.8.
### What earning a living actually requires here
The MIT Living Wage Calculator estimates the living wage in the St. Louis metro at $21.79 an hour for one adult with no children. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 as of January 1, 2026.
That gap — roughly $6.79 an hour, or about $14,000 a year at full time — is the honest shape of affordability here. St. Louis is genuinely inexpensive compared with the coasts, and a full-time minimum-wage job still does not reach a single adult’s baseline. Both things are true, and most cost-of-living pages only tell you the first one.
### How St. Louis compares inside Missouri
Every participating Missouri city sat below the national average in Q1 2026:
Joplin — 83.7, the lowest in the state, with housing at 59.8
Springfield — 89.7
St. Louis MO-IL — 89.8
Columbia — 91.3
What driving school costs in St. Louis
St. Louis and Springfield are effectively tied, which surprises people who assume a large metro must cost more than a smaller city. It does not, here — because the housing stock is old, plentiful, and spread across a very large area.
That last point deserves its own note, because it is where the metro’s averages become almost meaningless in practice.
### The average is not a place you can live
A hillside block of brick homes in south St. Louis, MO, photographed by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026 for St Louis Near Me Directory.
“St. Louis” in these indexes means the whole MO-IL metro — the city, all of St. Louis County’s eighty-plus municipalities, St. Charles County, and the Illinois side. The spread inside that area is enormous.
Housing in Clayton and housing in Florissant are not the same market. A house in Belleville, Illinois and a house in Chesterfield are not the same purchase, and they are not even in the same state for tax purposes. The index averages all of it into one number that describes no actual neighborhood.
So use the index for the question it answers — is this metro cheaper than where I live now? — and then look at specific municipalities for the question you actually care about. Our guide to why St. Louis real estate is so affordable goes deeper on the housing side, which is where most of your savings live.
### How to actually use this if you are comparing a job offer
Here is where most people misuse a cost-of-living index, and it can cost them real money in a negotiation.
The instinct is to take the composite and apply it to the whole salary — “St. Louis is about 10% cheaper, so I can accept about 10% less.” That is the wrong calculation, and depending on your situation it is wrong in either direction.
The composite is a weighted blend of six categories, and your household does not spend like the blend. Do it this way instead:
Split your current spending into the same six buckets — housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health, everything else. Rough percentages are fine. Then apply each index to its own bucket rather than applying one number to everything.
Unrelated, and we know it — North Pointe, if you’re curious.
Two examples of how differently that lands, both clearly hypothetical:
Someone spending half their income on rent gets most of the benefit. Housing at 80.4 is doing the heavy lifting, and it is the biggest slice of their budget, so their personal saving lands well above the headline 10%.
Someone with modest housing costs and high medical spending gets almost none of it. Their largest categories are groceries at 98.7, utilities at 98.0, and health at 103.6 — that is roughly break-even or slightly worse. For that household, moving here on a 10% pay cut is a real pay cut.
Same city, same quarter, same official numbers, opposite conclusions. Which is why the component table above matters more than any single percentage anyone quotes at you.
Two practical notes if you are running this exercise. Renting and buying are not the same bet. The 80.4 housing index reflects both, and a renter feels it immediately while a buyer feels it over years — alongside the maintenance costs of older housing stock. And health care weighting rises with age and household size. A 103.6 index on a small share of a young single person’s budget is noise; on a retired couple’s budget it is the headline.
### Costs the index does not really capture
A few things surprise people who move here, none of which show up cleanly in a composite number.
Personal property tax on vehicles. Missouri counties assess an annual tax on cars, trucks and boats. Newcomers from states without it are reliably caught out by the first bill. Rates are set locally, so check with the assessor for the county you are moving to rather than assuming a figure.
Two states, two tax systems. The metro spans Missouri and Illinois, and where you live determines your income tax, your property tax, and your sales tax — while your commute may cross the river daily. If you are weighing sides, that comparison is worth doing properly rather than by rule of thumb.
Sales tax stacking. Missouri layers state, county, city and special district rates, so the rate at one shopping center differs from another a few blocks away. It is a small effect on a coffee and a real one on a car.
Older housing stock. The savings on the purchase price are real. So are the maintenance costs of a house built in the 1930s — sewer laterals, original wiring, foundations on clay soil. Budget for the house you are actually buying, not the index.
Utilities are an annual average hiding two extremes. The 98.0 index is a yearly figure, and St. Louis does not have a mild year. Summers are hot and genuinely humid, winters get cold, and the bills follow — so a household that budgets by the monthly average will be caught out twice a year. If you are moving from a temperate climate, ask a prospective landlord or seller for twelve months of actual utility bills rather than a typical month. In an older, poorly insulated house the gap between July and October is not small.
Car dependence outside the core. Transportation scores well at 88.8, but that assumes driving. Much of the metro has limited transit, so a household running two cars will not feel the transport discount the way the index implies.
### So is it affordable?
For most people moving from a larger or coastal metro, yes — and the reason is specific rather than general. You will spend meaningfully less on housing, slightly less on getting around, about the same on food and utilities, and somewhat more on health care.
If you are moving here from elsewhere in the Midwest, the difference narrows to very little. And if you are already here on a lower income, the state ranking is cold comfort: a low cost of living and a wage that does not reach the local living wage still leaves a gap.
Both of those are the honest answer, and it is a more useful one than a single percentage.
For the tax side of a St. Louis budget, see how the St. Louis sales tax rate changes by address, what the St. Louis County personal property tax adds every year, and the Missouri state income tax rate.
Turning these numbers into a plan? Start with how to budget on a St. Louis paycheck, and what causes inflation explains why the prices keep moving.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it expensive to live in St. Louis, MO?
A.  By the numbers, no — it is cheaper than most of the country. The metro sits at a cost-of-living index of 89.8 against a national average of 100, and Missouri as a whole is tied for the seventh-lowest in the country. But the discount is concentrated in housing, at 80.4. Groceries and utilities run close to national, and health care is above it at 103.6.
### Q. What salary do you need to live in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single honest figure, and published estimates vary widely because each uses a different basket. A useful floor: the MIT Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for one adult with no children in this metro at $21.79 an hour. Comfort above that depends most on whether you rent or own, and in which municipality.
### Q. What is middle class income in St. Louis?
A.  Definitions vary by source and none is authoritative, so treat any specific bracket cautiously. What is measurable is that local costs run roughly 10% below the national average overall, driven by housing, meaning a given income stretches further here than the same income in a coastal metro — but less far than the headline suggests once health care is included.
### Q. Is $40 an hour good in Missouri?
A.  It is well above both the state minimum wage of $15.00 and the MIT living-wage estimate of $21.79 an hour for a single adult in the St. Louis metro. Whether it is comfortable depends on household size and municipality — the same wage supports a very different life in Joplin, at an index of 83.7, than in a higher-cost pocket of St. Louis County.
### Q. Why do different websites give different costs of living for St. Louis?
A.  Because each builds a different basket and weights it differently. Current published estimates for St. Louis range from about 2% below national to about 10.4% below. MERIC, a Missouri state agency, is the one that publishes the underlying components by quarter, which is why its 89.8 composite is the most inspectable figure rather than simply the most favorable.
### Q. Is the cost of living the same across the St. Louis metro?
A.  No, and the average can be misleading. The index covers the whole MO-IL metro — the city, more than eighty municipalities in St. Louis County, St. Charles County and the Illinois side. Housing costs, property taxes and sales tax rates all vary considerably between them, and the Illinois side sits under a different state tax system entirely.

### Q. What is a livable salary in St. Louis?
A.  The MIT Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for one adult in the St. Louis metro at $21.79 an hour, against a Missouri minimum wage of $15.00. That is a floor for one person covering their own costs, not a comfortable salary and not a household figure - add children or a second earner and the number moves substantially.

A.  Housing is where nearly all of the savings live. ## Marketing Jobs in St. Louis: What They Pay and How to Land One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-8-marketing-job-st-louis-opportunities-for-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Imagine it’s a Tuesday night and you’re at a coffee shop in Maplewood with your laptop open, scrolling marketing listings. One says a “St. Louis” marketing director role pays $230,000. The next says a marketing assistant in Earth City pays $17 an hour. A third wants eight years of experience, four certifications, and calls itself entry-level. If you’ve been trying to make sense of the marketing job market here — from Florissant to Fenton, Edwardsville to O’Fallon — you already know the listings don’t add up.
Here’s the thing: they don’t add up because they’re not describing the same market. Some of those postings are real St. Louis jobs at real St. Louis companies. Others are national remote roles wearing a St. Louis costume, benchmarked to coastal salaries you will rarely see from a local employer.
This guide separates the two — with real government wage data for our metro, the honest gap between national medians and local offers, who actually hires marketers here, and the doors (some of them literal, with name tags and free appetizers) that get people hired.
### What Marketing Jobs in St. Louis Actually Pay
Start with the most reliable numbers available: the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics wage survey for the St. Louis metro area. In its most recent published metro table, the BLS counted about 6,960 marketing specialists and market research analysts working in greater St. Louis at a mean wage of $78,660, and about 2,330 marketing managers at a mean of $136,680. Public relations specialists — a close cousin — averaged $73,450 across roughly 3,780 jobs.
Marketing specialist / market research analyst: ~$78,660 mean (about 6,960 jobs in the metro)
Marketing manager: ~$136,680 mean (about 2,330 jobs)
Advertising & promotions manager: ~$81,930 mean (a small field — only about 170 jobs)
Public relations specialist: ~$73,450 mean (about 3,780 jobs)
Those are averages across all experience levels, pulled up by senior people — not starting offers. Look at what employers are actually posting and the picture gets more grounded: Indeed pegs the average St. Louis marketing manager posting around $81,000, and ZipRecruiter’s middle range for the same title runs roughly $58,000 to $95,000. For marketing specialists, current local postings commonly land in the $40,000–$69,000 band. (Sources: BLS OEWS, St. Louis MSA; Indeed; ZipRecruiter.)
One more number worth knowing: nationally, the median marketing manager earns about $161,030 per the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook. Which brings us to the trap.
### The Remote-Listing Trap
Search “marketing jobs St. Louis” on any national board and you’ll see six-figure director and VP roles that seem wildly out of step with the local numbers above. Most aren’t St. Louis jobs at all — they’re remote-national roles at companies headquartered in San Francisco, New York, or Denver, shown to you because remote listings render in every city’s search results. The pay is real, but you’re competing against the entire country for it, and the company has no St. Louis office, no local network, and no local ladder.
The remote market is also smaller than the listings make it feel. Staffing firm Robert Half analyzed 376,200 U.S. marketing and creative postings and found only about 21% advertised as hybrid — and across all occupations, only around 12% of new postings are fully remote (Robert Half research). Apply to remote roles if they fit — just don’t let a $230K remote listing convince you a $75K offer from a solid Clayton employer is an insult. In a metro where the cost of living sits well below the national average, that local offer often lives better.
### Who Actually Hires Marketers in St. Louis
The good news: this metro has an unusually deep bench of major employers with real, local marketing teams. Greater St. Louis is home to a long list of Fortune 1000 headquarters (Greater St. Louis, Inc.), and most of them market consumer or business brands at national scale from right here: (For the full tour of the metro’s corporate giants — who they are and where they sit — see our top companies in St. Louis guide.)
Consumer brands: Anheuser-Busch (Soulard), Nestlé Purina (downtown), Post Holdings, Energizer, Build-A-Bear (downtown)
Healthcare & insurance: Centene, BJC Health System — the largest private employer in Missouri — and Mercy
Finance & B2B: Edward Jones, Enterprise Mobility, Emerson (Clayton), RGA (Chesterfield), World Wide Technology (Maryland Heights), Graybar, Bunge
On the agency side, be honest with yourself about the landscape: the traditional ad-agency world here has consolidated hard. Rodgers Townsend — for years one of the city’s biggest shops — closed its doors in 2024. Independent shops like HLK (downtown, founded 1977) and Obata are still working, and healthcare-marketing specialists maintain a presence here, but agency seats are fewer than they were a decade ago. Brand-side and healthcare-side is where most of the local headcount lives now.
And demand is genuinely there: as of mid-2026, Indeed alone listed over 1,200 marketing jobs in the St. Louis area, with LinkedIn showing 400+ at the entry level.
### Where the Jobs Sit on the Map
Marketing work here clusters in a handful of corridors, and knowing them helps you target a commute you can live with. Downtown holds consumer-brand headquarters — Nestlé Purina on Chouteau, Build-A-Bear on 18th Street — with Anheuser-Busch just south in Soulard. Clayton is corporate territory, anchored by Emerson. West County stacks up quickly: Edward Jones’s sprawling campus, RGA out in Chesterfield, and World Wide Technology’s headquarters at Westport Plaza in Maryland Heights. Centene sits in Clayton and north county; BJC and the medical-center marketing teams concentrate in the Central West End. And the Metro East is not empty — regional healthcare systems, banks, and manufacturers across Edwardsville, Belleville, and O’Fallon, Illinois all staff their own marketing seats.
One underrated pocket: small business. Beyond the Fortune 1000 names, thousands of St. Louis-area small companies — contractors, medical practices, restaurants groups, professional firms — hire their first in-house marketer once word-of-mouth stops scaling. These jobs rarely make the national boards. They show up on company sites, in chamber newsletters, and through referrals, which is exactly why the networking rooms below punch above their weight.
### The Two-Rung Ladder: Specialist, Then Manager
Nationally, the BLS projects marketing manager roles to grow about 6% and market research/marketing specialist roles about 7% through 2034 — both faster than average, with a combined 120,000+ openings a year (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook). The practical read for St. Louis: the specialist tier is where the volume is — nearly 7,000 metro jobs versus 2,330 manager seats — so plan your first three to five years there, building a portfolio of measurable wins, then compete for the manager tier where the pay jumps sharply.
Skills that move you up the ladder here are the same ones employers list everywhere: analytics and reporting you can actually defend, hands-on experience with a major CRM or automation platform, and increasingly, fluency with AI tools as an accelerant rather than a novelty. Certifications in Google Analytics or HubSpot won’t land a job alone, but they get resumes past filters.
### How People Actually Get Hired Here
St. Louis is a warm-introduction town. Two organizations put working marketers in the same room regularly, and both are active right now:
AMA Saint Louis — the local American Marketing Association chapter runs regular networking events and an annual “Art & Science of Marketing” conference.
AAF-STL — the Advertising Club of Greater St. Louis, host of the annual American Advertising Awards show, where the region’s creative community gathers in one building.
Beyond the name-tag circuit: tailor every application to the posting, lead your resume with numbers (“grew email list 40%” beats “managed email marketing”), and build a portfolio even if your current title isn’t “marketing” — a campaign you ran for a family business or a nonprofit counts. If you’re starting from zero, our guide to St. Louis entry-level jobs covers adjacent first rungs, and the broader 9 best jobs near St. Louis shows how marketing pay compares to other local careers.
Random, but: Fairview Heights dinner options go well past the mall.
### Search Beyond the Word “Marketing”
A surprising share of St. Louis marketing work is posted under other names. Cast your alerts wider and you’ll surface roles the “marketing” keyword misses entirely:
Communications specialist / coordinator — common at hospitals, universities, and nonprofits, and often marketing in everything but name
Content strategist, copywriter, social media manager — the creative seats, frequently hired separately from the marketing team
Brand manager — the consumer-products ladder at places like Purina and Post
Demand generation, growth, lifecycle — the tech-company dialect for revenue-side marketing, common at WWT and the software firms
Development or membership coordinator — the nonprofit world’s version, and a genuine portfolio-builder
Recruiters filter by titles; job seekers who search by skills find the postings their competitors never see. Set one alert per title above and let the boards prove it to you within a week.
### A Week-One Search Plan
If you’re starting cold, here’s a first week that beats a hundred scattershot applications:
Day 1: Set alerts on Indeed, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, and Built In for “marketing specialist,” “marketing coordinator,” and “marketing manager” within 25 miles. Let the boards work for you overnight.
Day 2: Build a target list of ten local employers from the names above, and bookmark each careers page — many post there before (or instead of) the boards.
Day 3: Check the AMA Saint Louis and AAF-STL calendars and register for the next event on either one. A name tag beats a cover letter.
Day 4: Assemble a one-page portfolio — three campaigns or projects with a number attached to each. If you don’t have three, that’s this month’s assignment, not a disqualification.
Day 5: Send three informational-interview requests to St. Louis marketers on LinkedIn — alumni of your school first. Ask about their path, not for a job. The jobs follow.
Repeat the rhythm weekly: applications go out steadily, but the compounding returns come from the target list, the rooms, and the conversations. For the wider toolkit — workforce agencies, library job clubs, and every free metro resource — see our St. Louis local-jobs roadmap.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the average salary for a marketing specialist in St. Louis, MO?

A realistic read: entry offers commonly start around $40,000–$50,000, mid-career specialists cluster in the $60,000s–$70,000s.
### Q. Which marketing job pays the most?
A.  Management. Marketing managers in the St. Louis metro average about $136,680 per the BLS — roughly $58,000 more than the specialist tier — and director and VP roles at the region’s Fortune 1000 headquarters climb from there. The catch is scarcity: the metro has roughly one manager seat for every three specialist jobs.
### Q. Is it hard to get a marketing job right now?

What has changed is the skill mix — employers increasingly expect analytics fluency and comfort with AI-assisted tools alongside the creative fundamentals.
### Q. What is considered a good salary in St. Louis?
A.  Because the metro’s cost of living sits well below the national average, salaries stretch further here than the raw number suggests. A mid-career marketing specialist income in the $60,000s–$70,000s supports a comfortable life in most of the metro, and a marketing manager’s six-figure income here buys what considerably more would on either coast.

## A St. Louis Job Has to Pay $20.04 an Hour. Cross Into the County, $22.11.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/all-jobs-local-guide-your-roadmap-to-local-careers-2025
Fifteen dollars an hour. The offer sits in your inbox, the coffee has gone cold next to the laptop, and the phone calculator is already open on the table: 15 times 2,080 hours is $31,200 a year, before a single dollar comes out. It’s a real job. It’s a yes after weeks of silence. And there’s still a knot under your ribs, because you already know what the rent, the car payment and the Ameren bill add up to.
Here is the number that knot is trying to tell you. MIT’s Living Wage Calculator figures full time as 2,080 hours a year, and for one adult with no children in St. Louis city it lands on $20.04 an hour. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour. That gap, about five dollars an hour, is the quiet math under every St. Louis job search.
Add one kid and the line jumps. The same calculator puts a single parent with one child in St. Louis city at $35.49 an hour, or $73,823 a year before taxes. Two adults who both work and have no children each need $13.98. So the exact same $15 offer can be enough for one household and a slow leak for the family next door.
And here’s the part that only happens in St. Louis. Cross the city limits and the line moves. MIT puts one adult with no children in St. Louis County at $22.11 an hour, more than two dollars above the city. Same metro, same brake lights on the highway at rush hour, a different number depending on which side of the line your lease is on.
Blame a recount. The St. Louis County Library says voters decided in 1876 whether the City of St. Louis should separate from the county and become an independent city, and the first count showed separation failing by just over 100 votes. Supporters charged fraud, a recount was ordered, and it took four months to find that separation had passed.
So before you send the next fifty applications, flip the order. Don’t start with who’s hiring. Start with which kinds of work clear $20.04 in this town, then go find the employers who hire for them. The applications are the grind. The math is the shortcut, and it costs you one evening instead of one more month. And when the inbox goes quiet, the city’s own Missouri Job Center, run by SLATE at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor, answers at (314) 589-8000. More on that below.
Do this tonight, before the next application. Open MIT’s Living Wage Calculator at livingwage.mit.edu, choose Missouri, then your county or St. Louis city, and find the row for your household. Take any hourly offer and multiply it by 2,080 to see the yearly number. If it lands under your line, you haven’t failed. You’ve just found the question to ask in the interview, or the training to ask SLATE about when you call.
### What is a livable salary in St. Louis, MO?
For one adult with no children in St. Louis city, MIT’s Living Wage Calculator puts it at $20.04 an hour, or $41,687 a year before taxes. A single parent with one child needs $35.49 an hour. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00, so a full-time minimum-wage job falls about five dollars an hour short even for one adult living alone.
### Two Missouri wage rules that change the math
The first one lives on the tip line. Missouri’s Department of Labor says employers are required to pay tipped employees at least 50 percent of the minimum wage, $7.50 per hour, plus whatever it takes to bring total pay to at least $15.00 an hour. Think of the server at close on a slow weeknight, smoothing crumpled bills flat on the bar and counting them twice. If the tips don’t carry the shift to $15 an hour, the base isn’t the whole story: the employer owes the rest. Keep your own record of hours and tips, every shift, in the notes app on your phone.
The second one surprises people. The same state page says employers engaged in retail or service businesses whose annual gross income is less than $500,000 are not required to pay the state minimum wage rate. That can include small storefronts on any St. Louis main street. So an offer under $15 from a small retail or service shop isn’t automatically illegal under the state rule.
Neither rule makes a job good or bad. Both tell you the two questions to ask before you say yes: what is the base, and what is guaranteed?
### Which St. Louis jobs clear the $20.04 line?
MIT’s St. Louis city page also lists typical annual salaries by job family, drawn from Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data. Here they are next to $41,687, in three piles.
Under the line: food preparation and serving at $33,160, personal care and service at $36,140, healthcare support at $36,320, and building and grounds cleaning and maintenance at $36,820. The drive-thru headset crackling at 6 a.m. The first MetroLink train of the morning, half empty, carrying the people who open everything else. The fryer smell that follows you home in your hair. The floor buffer humming down an empty office hallway at midnight. Honest work, every bit of it. For one adult on one paycheck, the typical salary still lands under the line.
Just over it: transportation and material moving at $45,060, office and administrative support at $47,000, sales at $47,530, and production at $50,230. The warehouse dock door rattling up before sunrise. The front-desk phone that rings while you’re already on the other line. These clear a single adult’s line. They don’t clear a single parent’s.
Well over it: installation, maintenance and repair at $58,690, and construction and extraction at $65,000. A brick two-family in January with a furnace that just quit, and the one person on the block who knows how to fix it. And at the top of MIT’s table: legal at $118,150, management at $111,750, architecture and engineering at $91,900, healthcare practitioners and technical work at $91,660, and computer and mathematical work at $90,910.
Now read the two healthcare rows side by side. Healthcare support, $36,320. Healthcare practitioners and technical, $91,660. Same hallways, same badge readers, same sting of hand sanitizer at the door, and $55,340 a year apart on MIT’s table. If you’re already in scrubs, that gap is the ladder. If you’re not, it’s the reason to walk in the side door anyway.
### What are the major employers in St. Louis?
Start with the one most St. Louisans have been inside. BJC Health says it includes more than 48,000 employees and 24 hospitals across two brands: BJC HealthCare in the St. Louis region and Saint Luke’s in the Kansas City region. Hospitals need both healthcare rows above. Browse current healthcare openings on our board, then check the hospital’s own careers page for the same title.
Government is the other steady door. On its city jobs page, the City of St. Louis shows you how to apply for jobs with the city. Hold every listing up to $20.04 before you spend an hour on the application.
For the trades, the line is easier to clear than most people think, because the typical salaries in that pile start at $58,690. Look at who’s working in your own neighborhood: the plumbers, electricians and HVAC crews listed under home services are small employers, and small employers still hire the person who calls, shows up and asks.
And if you want the corporate side, the big headquarters names get their own breakdown in our guide to the largest companies in St. Louis.
Same math, other side of the counter: local SEO in Arnold, MO decides which shop gets the call.
### The free room on Market Street most job seekers skip
When the applications go quiet, there’s a place in the city that does this for a living. It’s the SLATE Missouri Job Center, and SLATE lists its address as 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor. One elevator ride, and a room built for exactly this.
SLATE says its Job Center is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Wednesdays, when it opens at 9 a.m. The number is (314) 589-8000. One small thing saves you a long wait: SLATE says registering with MoJobs and updating your profile before you visit will save you time at the Job Center, so do that from your couch first, at jobs.mo.gov. Then keep the local jobs board open in the next tab.
It isn’t just a computer lab. SLATE says its training programs help St. Louisans who are minorities, women, and long-term unemployed enter careers in growing industries, and its events calendar lists hiring events at the center, including one it calls Workforce Wednesday. If you’re sitting in the under-the-line pile and want to move up a pile, training is the cheapest elevator in town.
Bring what makes the visit count: a resume on paper and on your phone, your MoJobs login, the number on your sticky note, and one job family you want to move into. Then ask the plain question out loud. What would it take for me to get from this pile to that one? You don’t walk back down Market Street with a job in hand. You walk out with a next step that has a name and a date on it.
### Where the $41,687 actually goes
The living wage isn’t a wish list. MIT lists the cost of each basic need behind it, and for one adult with no children in St. Louis city they read like a kitchen-table budget: $10,312 a year for housing, $7,088 for transportation, $4,954 for food, $3,343 for medical, and $6,660 in annual taxes. Rent, the gas tank, the grocery cart, the copay. Nothing in there for a vacation.
Now add a child. MIT’s child care line for a single parent with one kid is $12,322 a year, and housing climbs to $13,152. That’s the daycare door at closing time, a small backpack already zipped and waiting on the hook, and it’s why the hourly line nearly doubles, from $20.04 to $35.49. If you’re a parent job hunting alone, the under-the-line pile is a bridge at best. Aim your applications at the piles above it, and use SLATE’s training to get there faster.
### A one-week plan built on the line
Day 1: Write your own line. Pull up MIT’s number for your household, one adult or a parent with kids, and write it on a sticky note on the laptop.
Day 2: Pick one job family from the pile above your line and browse it on the St. Louis jobs board, including entry-level and remote listings.
Day 3: Register on MoJobs, then call SLATE and ask what training or hiring events are coming up.
Day 4: Scout ten local employers in that field by category and check each one’s own careers page.
Day 5: Apply to the three that print a pay range at or above your line. Skip the ones that won’t say.
Your next move takes ten minutes. Open the St Louis Near Me Directory, find three local employers in a job family that clears your line, and save their careers pages before you close the tab.
If you run the shop, the clinic or the one-truck crew that’s hiring, list your business so more customers, and the neighbors who want to work for you, see your name first. Then pick a Gold listing and post your openings where St. Louis job seekers already look.

### Q. What does the Missouri job center do for a person?

SLATE calls MoJobs the first step for both job seekers and employers: a no-cost online system for job postings, hiring events, educational and skills learning programs, and labor market information. ### Q. Is $15 an hour a living wage in St. Louis?
A.  For one adult living alone, no. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour, and MIT puts the living wage for one adult with no children in St. Louis city at $20.04. For two adults who both work and have no children, MIT’s figure is $13.98 each, so $15 can clear it there.
### Q. What are the highest-paid jobs in Missouri?
A.  Pay runs by metro, so check the county you’ll actually work in. ## St. Louis Jobs: The City Can Help Pay Your New Boss to Train You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-jobs-near-me-your-local-career-roadmap-for-2025
Application forty-one goes out at 11:52 p.m. The laptop fan hums, the kitchen light buzzes over the sink, and the reply lands before you can stand up: Thank you for your interest. Somewhere inside that company, a hiring manager is doing quiet math on what it costs to train a stranger. Nobody told them you might come with help paying for it.
That help is real, and it is sitting in a city office downtown. SLATE, the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment, says its On-The-Job Training program offers financial reimbursement to employers that hire new, full-time employees in permanent positions. Federal workforce rules say employers may be reimbursed up to 50 percent of the wage rate of an OJT participant. Read that from the hiring manager’s side of the desk. You are not one more resume in the pile. You are a hire whose training can come partly paid for.
You do not get that by applying online at midnight. You get it by walking in. On the third floor of 1520 Market St., SLATE runs a job center where the employers come to you, and its own services page says that each week SLATE hosts Workforce Wednesdays, offering resume and application help, job search support, and walk-in interview opportunities with local employers. A person across a table, looking at you, not a filter scanning you for keywords. Ask there whether you qualify for on-the-job training before your next interview, so you can say it out loud when it counts.
You do not need a referral, a cousin who knows somebody, or a perfect resume. You need one morning, a clean shirt and a phone with your login saved. That is the one move on this page that beats the online pile, and almost everything else here is about making that morning count.
The rest of this guide is for the person who has already sent the forty-one applications. You are not lazy and you are not unemployable. You have been playing the hardest version of the game, alone, at night. There is an easier version, and it opens at 8 a.m.
### What companies are currently hiring in St. Louis?
The roster changes every week, so go where employers show up in person. The SLATE Missouri Job Center, 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor, hosts Workforce Wednesdays each week with walk-in interview opportunities with local employers. Register on Jobs.mo.gov first; SLATE advisors use your profile to match you to open positions. Call (314) 589-8000 to confirm this week’s schedule.
### Why a list of hiring companies goes stale by Friday
You have seen the lists: twenty logos, a cheerful headline, “hiring now.” You click three of them and hit two closed postings and a login wall. Every guide that names twenty companies “hiring now” was out of date the week it was printed. Postings open and close in days. A hiring manager who needed four warehouse leads on Monday has three of them by Thursday, and the posting you found on Saturday is a ghost.
That is why the useful question is not “who is hiring” but “where do the people who are hiring actually go to find workers.” In the City of St. Louis, one honest answer is SLATE. Its employer page says SLATE uses JobsMoGov, the State of Missouri’s online job-matching platform, to find qualified candidates, and that employers can post their job openings at no cost through it. Read that twice. The free state system you may have skipped is the same platform SLATE uses to find qualified candidates for employers.
So the job board you scroll and the profile you fill out are not the same thing. Scrolling is you hunting. A complete profile is you being found.
### The profile most people leave half-empty
You know the feeling of a form you are tired of filling out: the same work history, the same dates, the cursor blinking in a box that asks for a skill you already listed twice. Most people quit that profile halfway. Do not quit this one.
SLATE’s services page is plain about why. If you need help finding open positions that match your qualifications, you have to fully complete your registration on Jobs.Mo.Gov, because that helps its advisors understand your qualifications and the positions you are looking for. A half-finished profile gives an advisor nothing to match. A finished one gives them something to say yes to.
Make it count in one sitting. Use the job titles people actually search: “forklift operator,” not “material handling professional.” List every certification and license, even the small ones, because a food handler card or a forklift card is something an advisor can match. Fill the gaps honestly, whether it was caregiving, school, a side business or just a hard year; one plain line beats a blank. And upload a resume, even an ugly one.
Then walk in. The profile gets you into the system. The walk-in gets you a face and a name.
### Before you walk in on a Wednesday
Lay the shirt out the night before. Charge the phone. Put the folder by the door so you are not hunting for it with your keys in your teeth. SLATE lists the Job Center hours as Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Wednesdays, when it opens at 9 a.m. That Wednesday detail is the one people miss. Show up at 8 on interview day and you will spend an hour on the sidewalk getting nervous.
Bring a photo ID and a few printed copies of your resume if you have one. Dress for the interview you might get, because on Workforce Wednesdays the interviews are walk-in. If you do not have a resume yet, go anyway: SLATE’s services page offers resume and application help on those same Wednesdays.
Its home page says SLATE conducts frequent hiring events for jobseekers to meet and talk with prospective employers. Check the SLATE Missouri Job Center pages before you go, since dates move.
### Free workshops, by the clock
The worst part of a long search is the feeling that you are guessing. Workshops end the guessing. They run on a schedule, and somebody who reads resumes for a living looks at yours and tells you the truth.
SLATE’s workshop page lists these, and you must register in MoJobs at least one day before the workshop you want:
Resume Essentials: Tuesdays, 10 AM - 12 PM, and Thursdays, 2 PM - 4 PM, with personalized feedback.
Computer Basics: Wednesdays, 10 AM - 12 PM.
Ace The Interview: the first Wednesday of the month, 3 - 4:30 PM.
Career Exploration: the first Thursday of the month, 9:30 - 10:30 AM.
Network Like A Boss: the first Thursday of the month, 11 AM - 12:30 PM.
Job Search/Resume Support: Fridays, 11 AM - 1 PM, with one-on-one help.
If you have already registered, the page says you can sign up for a workshop up to one hour before it begins. That means a bad Tuesday morning can still turn into a better resume by lunch.
Nothing to do with job hunting - all of Maryland Heights, one page.
### Which jobs are in-demand here, and who keeps the real list
National “hottest jobs” lists are written for the whole country. The most in-demand jobs in St. Louis are a local question with a local answer, and it changes. SLATE’s Workforce Data page says the Missouri Economic Research and Information Center prepares a Real Time Labor Market Summary for the public workforce system, covering the state and each of its ten workforce development regions, including the City of St. Louis. The report is released every two months.
That is your list. Open the St. Louis Region report, look at which occupations had the most postings, and ask a SLATE advisor which of those fit what you already know how to do. It beats guessing from a headline written in another city.
For a wider view of where national growth is, the federal fastest-growing occupations table is useful background. Just remember that the St. Louis report is the one that tells you who is posting jobs here.
### Paid to learn: the no-degree routes
Maybe the posting you want says “degree required” and you feel the door close before you knock. Some doors in this city are built for people without one. They pay you, or train you for free, while you learn the job.
SLATE says it offers a wide variety of earn-while-you-learn apprenticeships for in-demand fields outside construction, and its home page describes registered apprenticeships where you receive paid training. For construction, its BUD program offers eight weeks of construction training for work-ready job seekers ages 18 and up, especially women and minorities. Its employer page also lists skills-training scholarships for job seekers, a line almost nobody reads. Its training programs are aimed at helping St. Louisans who are minorities, women and long-term unemployed enter careers in growing industries.
Younger job seekers have their own doors. SLATE’s home page features YouthBuild, a program for disadvantaged City of St. Louis youth ages 17-24 that lets them earn pay, help build affordable housing and learn leadership skills. The state’s Jobs League Program helps teens and young adults get paid on-the-job training, and you can take part for up to 320 hours. Here is the line worth forwarding to every 16-to-24-year-old you know: for employers who host a young worker in SLATE’s Summer Youth Employment Program, SLATE says it covers 100% of participants’ wages and insurance. To a business, that summer hire costs nothing in pay. No high school diploma yet? SLATE’s services page lists a 24-Hour Workforce High School for young adults ages 17-21 and HiSET testing.
None of this is a get-rich promise. Nobody honest can promise a no-degree path to big money a month in year one. What these programs do is put a paycheck and a skill in the same week, and that is how most real raises start.
### Coming back after time away
The gap on your resume feels like a spotlight. You were raising kids, caring for a parent, getting well, or just surviving a year that did not care about your career. When an interviewer asks about it, your throat tightens before you even answer.
Give it one sentence and move on. “I spent two years caring for my father full time, and I’m ready to come back.” That is complete. Then talk about what you did inside that gap: the budget you ran, the appointments you juggled, the insurance calls you won. Those are workplace skills wearing different clothes.
SLATE says job seekers who already have skills and experience but feel stuck, or who want to change careers, can sign up for its Advanced/Professional Series Workshops. Ask about them at the front desk.
### Veterans: translate before you apply
You can strip and reassemble a weapon in the dark, lead a team through a long night and keep a vehicle running on parts you scrounged. Then a civilian job posting asks for “stakeholder management” and you stare at it like it is written in another language. It sort of is.
Translate first. “Supervised a squad” becomes “led and trained a team of eight.” “Maintained readiness” becomes “kept equipment in service with scheduled maintenance.” My Next Move for Veterans shows which military jobs are similar to careers with a bright outlook, and CareerOneStop has a Veterans Job Matcher for putting your military experience to work in a civilian career. Then bring the translated version to a SLATE workshop and have someone read it out loud back to you.
You can also browse OneTen.
### Interviews: the ten minutes that matter
Your palms are damp, the lobby chair squeaks every time you shift, and the receptionist is typing something you are sure is about you. It is not. Breathe.
Most first interviews ask three things in different clothes: tell me about yourself, why this job, and tell me about a hard moment. Write one honest paragraph for each before you go. Say them out loud in the car until they stop sounding memorized. Then bring two questions of your own. “What does a great first month look like in this job?” works almost everywhere, and it tells you something real about the place.
Send a short thank-you note the same day. Mention one thing you talked about. It is a small thing, and people remember it.
### Resumes that get read by a human
A resume is not a list of duties. It is proof. “Responsible for customer service” says nothing. “Handled the returns counter alone on Saturdays” puts a picture in someone’s head.
Keep it to one page if you can. Put the job title you want at the top. Use the same words the posting uses, because whoever reads it, a person or a program, is looking for them. If you want a second opinion and can pay for it, private services like professional resume services exist. SLATE’s Resume Essentials workshop also gives personalized feedback on your resume.
### The first ninety days after yes
The offer call comes. Your face gets hot, you say yes too fast, and then you sit in the car for a minute doing nothing at all. Enjoy that minute.
Then get ready for the first three months. A probationary period usually lasts 90 days but can go up to six months, depending on the employer, so ask human resources in writing what your probation period is and what happens at the end of it. Keep notes on what the job really is. If it does not match what you were promised, those notes are what you bring to the conversation.
Before you accept, check the math. Our guide to what it actually costs to live here shows why one percentage applied to your whole salary gets it wrong.
