## The Best Free Local Business Listing Sites (and How to Use Them Right)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-free-local-listing-sites-to-boost-your-business-in-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Most “top 10” listing posts hand you a long checklist and call it a strategy. This one runs in the right order instead. First, the list you came for: the free listing sites that actually matter in 2026, and how to use each one. Then the part those roundups skip: why a short, consistent list beats a long one, which sites to ignore, and where all of this fits in a real St. Louis growth plan.
Short version: you don’t need to be on 50 directories. You need to be on a handful that actually feed the search-and-AI ecosystem — with identical information on every one. Ten accurate, consistent listings beat a hundred half-filled, contradictory ones every time. Below are the free sites worth your time, in rough order of impact. Get these right and stop chasing the rest.
### Why a Short, Consistent List Wins
The old advice was “submit your business to as many directories as possible.” That’s a relic. Citation volume barely moves the needle anymore — an analysis of thousands of sites found that appearing in hundreds of directories barely out-performed appearing in none (Near Media). What matters now is consistency: the same name, address, and phone (your “NAP”) on every platform that counts. Every extra no-name directory is one more place your information can drift out of date and start contradicting the others — which actively hurts you. So the goal isn’t a long list. It’s a right list, kept identical everywhere. Quick gut-check: if you searched your own business name right now, would every listing agree — or would the mismatches quietly tell Google you’re not quite who you claim to be?
### Watch: Dominate “Near Me” Search
### The Best Free Local Business Listing Sites in 2026
Here are the ones genuinely worth claiming, and what each one does for you:
Google Business Profile — start here, full stop. This is the single biggest lever in local search: it controls how you appear in Google Search, Google Maps, and the local “3-pack.” Claim it at google.com/business, verify, and fill in everything — categories, hours, service area, photos, and regular posts. If you do only one thing on this list, do this.
Bing Places for Business — free, and it feeds AI. Bing’s local data powers Microsoft Copilot, Edge’s AI answers, and DuckDuckGo — and Yahoo Search runs on Bing too. Claim it at bingplaces.com and, in two clicks, import it straight from your Google Business Profile. One of the highest-value ten minutes you can spend.
Apple Business — don’t forget the iPhone crowd. Every “near me” search on an iPhone runs through Apple Maps and Siri. Apple Business (formerly Apple Business; business.apple.com) is free and lets you control your Apple Maps place card — name, hours, photos, and offers. For a huge share of mobile customers, this is your storefront.
Yelp — still matters, and it feeds others. Beyond its own traffic, Yelp supplies business data and reviews to Yahoo and Apple Maps. Claim your page at biz.yelp.com, complete it, and never fake a review — but do make it easy for happy customers to leave real ones. A strong Yelp profile does quiet double duty across the web.
Facebook Business Page — free reach and social proof. A complete Facebook Page is a free listing that shows up in search, gives customers a familiar place to check you out, and collects recommendations. Keep the NAP identical to your other listings and post enough to look active.
Nextdoor Business Page — the hyper-local one. Nextdoor is where neighbors ask “who do you recommend for…” every single day. A free business page puts you in those neighborhood conversations — especially powerful for home services, and for anyone whose customers are literally down the street.
A strong local directory — the location-centric anchor. A well-run local directory (for St. Louis, that’s St Louis Near Me Directory) reinforces your NAP and puts you in front of people specifically searching your metro, not the whole country. More on why this one punches above its weight in a moment.
That’s the core. Notice what it is: the platforms that own the maps, the search engines, the AI assistants, the reviews, and the neighborhood — plus a local anchor. Cover those with identical information and you’ve done 95% of what listings can do for you. The other 5% is industry-specific — the two or three directories that matter for your trade.
### What to Skip
Just as useful as knowing where to list is knowing where not to spend your time. Skip pay-to-blast services that promise to “submit your business to 500 directories” — volume was never the point, and half those sites are ghost towns that only create more places for your info to go stale. Skip obscure, no-name directories with no real traffic and no data relationships; a listing there does nothing but add maintenance risk. The Better Business Bureau, Foursquare and Manta come up on almost every “best free listing sites” roundup, so they deserve a straight answer. Foursquare is the one worth ten minutes: its location data still feeds a long list of apps and devices that never ask you directly, so a correct record there quietly fixes your address in places you would never think to check. A BBB profile is free to claim and buys credibility with a certain kind of customer — but accreditation is a paid membership, and paying for it is a reputation decision, not an SEO one. Manta is a general B2B directory that costs nothing to claim and does very little; claim it for the citation, then forget it. None of the three belongs ahead of the core list above. General directories like EZlocal and Cylex are legitimate and free to claim, but treat them as minor extras, not a substitute for the core list — and the old print Yellow Pages is a legacy channel, not a strategy. And be wary of anyone selling a “Yahoo listing” or similar — you can usually get that coverage for free by claiming Yelp and Bing. If a site isn’t on the core list above and can’t explain what ecosystem it feeds, it’s probably not worth the ten minutes.
### The Honest Verdict, at a Glance
### What Actually Moves Your Ranking
Listings are table stakes, not the game. Rank the work honestly and it comes out like this: the Google Business Profile does the heavy lifting; real reviews, arriving steadily rather than in one old cluster, do the next most; and a name, address, and phone that agree across the places that count does the rest (a well-documented edge in the local pack, per Whitespark, 2026). The sites above serve all three — they are the raw material consistency gets built from. But it is the reviews and the Google profile that convert a listing into a ringing phone, and no amount of listing volume substitutes for either.
And here’s the math these roundups never show you: listings do not pay off evenly. The second one is worth a great deal — it’s the first time two independent sources agree on your name, address, and phone, and that agreement is the entire signal. The sixth still helps. The twenty-sixth is doing something close to nothing. The fiftieth is a login you’ll forget, on a site you’ll never revisit, holding a phone number that will eventually be wrong. The return curve flattens fast; the risk curve doesn’t, because every additional listing is one more place your information can quietly go stale while you assume it’s working for you. That’s why the list above is short on purpose. Six finished profiles beat thirty opened ones, and it isn’t close.
Total tangent — Maplewood’s food scene is worth a whole afternoon.
### The 3 Mistakes That Make Listings Backfire
None of this is difficult. It just rewards a little discipline, and punishes three habits in particular. One: opening accounts instead of finishing them. A profile with no hours, no categories, and no photos is a placeholder with your phone number on it, and it competes with your real presence in the results. Finish the sites above — every field, every hour, real photos — before you go looking for a seventh. Two: treating a listing as finished. Hours change at holidays. Suites get renumbered. Numbers get ported. A short list is only an advantage if you actually revisit it — and six sites is few enough that a twice-a-year pass over all of them takes one coffee. Three: chasing quantity over quality. Ten accurate, consistent listings on the sites that matter beat a hundred half-filled ones on sites nobody uses. Depth on the core list beats a scattershot blast every time.
### How to Keep It All Consistent (the Part Everyone Skips)
Claiming the listings is the easy afternoon; keeping them aligned is the quiet work that actually pays off. Start by writing down your business details once — the exact name, the exact address format (decide “Suite” vs. “Ste.” and never waver), the exact phone number, your hours, and your primary categories — and treat that as the master copy every listing must match. When anything changes — a new phone line, a move, new holiday hours — update the master copy first, then walk it across every platform the same day, because a half-updated set of listings is exactly the contradiction that confuses search engines. Set a reminder to spot-check your core listings a couple of times a year; five minutes of maintenance prevents the slow drift that quietly buries a business. And where a platform lets you sync — like importing Bing from Google — use it, so you’re maintaining one source of truth instead of six.
### The Smarter Play for a St. Louis Business
Work the short list — Google, Bing, Apple, Yelp, Facebook, Nextdoor — with identical information, then anchor it locally. A verified listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is the local anchor at the end of that short list — the one that ties the other five together by carrying the same name, address, and phone, and the one that puts you in front of a homeowner in Oakville looking for a handyman rather than a shopper three states away. It’s also what AI assistants reach for when the question is local. The national platforms make you findable. A local listing makes you the answer. You want both. And the highest-return move here isn’t adding a seventh site — it’s going back to the six and finishing every field on each one: hours, categories, real photos, a current phone number, and the same address characters throughout. Most businesses that feel invisible aren’t missing listings at all; they’re carrying six half-built ones.

## Your Old Half-Page Ad Is Propping Open a Garage Door in Mehlville
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-essential-free-business-listing-yellow-pages-for-2025-success
Your shop phone sits on the counter, quiet. Across town, a woman in the Schnucks parking lot, engine running, a dishwasher leaking onto her kitchen floor at home, says “plumber near me” to her phone. Whoever the map shows in the next four seconds gets the call.
Your old half-page ad? It’s propping open a garage door in Mehlville.
Remember the thud of that book on the front porch, the rubber band, the pages so thin they tore if you flipped too fast? Getting “in the book” was the whole marketing plan. A bold-print line if you felt flush. A half-page ad if you felt brave. Then you waited for the phone on the wall to ring.
Now even the Yellow Pages has given up on paper. The company that owns it agreed to sell the print book for $142 million and keep only the website.
Tonight, before you close the laptop: search your trade plus your suburb on your phone the way she would, say “roofer Kirkwood” or “florist Florissant,” and count the reviews and photos on the three businesses the map shows against yours. Then claim the free listings that feed most phones: your Google Business Profile first, then Bing Places, which can import your Google profile in a few clicks and also feeds Microsoft’s Copilot answers, then Apple Maps through Apple Business Connect. Two of the three take less time than this article.
Still paying for a print ad? Find one date this week. Open your print-directory contract and look for the words “Close Date.” In one major publisher’s current standard agreement, if the publisher doesn’t receive your written cancellation by that date, it may renew your ad for the next issue, which typically runs 18 to 24 months, at the then-current undiscounted rate. That same kind of clause makes finding the date your job. Call the customer-care number printed on your contract, ask for the Close Date on your directory, and circle it on the calendar.
St. Louis has lived through a split like this once. In 1897 the city got a second phone company, Kinloch, and for more than two decades its lines didn’t connect to Bell’s. A Kinloch customer couldn’t call a Bell subscriber.
So a shop that wanted every customer kept two phones on the counter, one of each, until Southwestern Bell bought Kinloch in 1923.
Today the networks are Google, Apple Maps, Bing and ChatGPT, and nobody sent a notice when the switch happened. When your next customer asks her phone, which phone is on your counter? The happy difference from 1923: joining every network is free.
Here’s the part the old ad reps never had a reason to tell you. Even the company that owns the Yellow Pages doesn’t want the book anymore, and almost every listing that matters now is free. The book charged you by the size of your ad. Google Business Profile, Apple Maps and Bing Places charge nothing. The only people still charging you for a spot in the new book are the ones selling ads around it.
The rule nobody mailed you: the old book rewarded bigger and bolder, so the habit makes sense. Google plays it the other way. Its own guidelines say extra words in the name field, like “Joe’s Plumbing, Best Plumber St. Louis,” can get a free profile suspended. The name painted on your truck is all it wants.
Then run the index-card test before that Close Date. For one month, tape a card by the phone, ask every new caller “how’d you hear about us?” and make a tick mark under the answer. If “the book” gets fewer ticks than Google, you have your answer, and your budget back.
### The new phone book lives in your customer’s pocket
The phone on the wall used to ring because she found you on page 412. The phone in your pocket rings because a map put your name under her thumb at a red light on Big Bend. No single product made that switch. Google and its map, Apple Maps, review sites, directories and AI assistants like ChatGPT split the job the book did alone, and most of them read from listings you can claim for free. Which one is your next customer asking today?
The most important single replacement is your Google Business Profile. Think of it as your old half-page ad, rebuilt and free: it’s what surfaces in the map pack, and instead of a clip-art logo it carries the photo of your storefront, your stars, your hours and a button that dials you from a stranger’s pocket. If the old goal was to be “in the book,” the new goal is to be complete and consistent across a handful of free platforms.

### The paper book is on its way out, and its owner knows it
Technically, yes - but their role has collapsed. Printed directories are still produced and distributed in some areas, and a small segment of the population, skewing older, still occasionally reaches for one. But for the overwhelming majority of customers, the search has moved to their phone and their browser, and paying for a prominent print Yellow Pages ad is, for most businesses, no longer money well spent. The Yellow Pages name lives on as an online directory, and a free, accurate listing there is a minor consistency signal worth claiming, but the print book is a legacy channel, not a growth strategy. If your marketing budget is going into a big print directory ad out of habit, that money almost certainly works harder on the free and low-cost digital foundations below.

### Why it matters more now that neighbors ask AI
AI is the reason to get this right in 2026. Customers increasingly skip searching entirely and ask an assistant: BrightLocal’s 2026 research found about 45% of consumers now use AI tools like ChatGPT for local recommendations, up from just 6% a year earlier. When an AI answers “who’s a good option near me?”, it builds that answer from the consistent, trustworthy local data it can find - exactly the data your listings provide. The humble business listing has quietly become one of your most important marketing assets: it’s how you stay visible in Google and in the AI answers that a growing share of your customers now trust. The Yellow Pages is gone, but being findable has never mattered more.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do physical Yellow Pages still exist?
A.  Technically yes - printed directories are still produced in some areas, and a small, older-skewing segment occasionally uses them - but their role has collapsed. Nearly all customers now search on their phones. The Yellow Pages name survives as an online directory, and a free accurate listing there is a minor consistency signal, but paying for a big print ad is, for most businesses, no longer money well spent.
### Q. What sites can I list my business for free?
A.  Google Business Profile, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places, Facebook, Yelp and your local Chamber - all free. St Louis Near Me Directory on top of those is about local relevance, not volume, and its basic listing is free too. The one principle that matters more than the list: identical name, address and phone everywhere.
### Q. What are some alternatives to Yellow Pages?
A.  The maps platforms took the demand, so the practical alternatives are Google, Apple and Bing, plus a category directory where your industry genuinely has one. What is not an alternative is a service submitting you to hundreds of junk sites - that multiplies inconsistency rather than reach.
### Q. Why are there no Yellow Pages anymore?
A.  Search moved the demand, and the advertising revenue followed it. Print directories still exist in some markets, but nobody reaches for one to find a plumber at nine at night. The behavior changed first and the book simply caught up.
### Q. Who owns Yellow Pages now?
A.  The company that publishes the print directories also runs the Yellow Pages website. It has agreed to sell its print Yellow and White Pages business in the U.S., Australia and New Zealand to the private equity firm Carolwood L.P. for $142 million, and it keeps the website, so the online listing you may already have stays where it is.
### Q. Do they still make phone books?
A.  Yes, a few are still printed in some markets, and you can generally opt out of delivery. The print business is changing hands rather than shutting down. Still, circulation and use have fallen far enough that no St. Louis business should count on one for calls. If you inherited a listing, leave it be; just do not pay to renew it.

## St. Louis Is Two Places. Your Listings Must Pick One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/local-seo-citations-guide-proven-citation-strategies
The phone on the counter stays quiet on a day that should have been busy. You check that it’s charged. You check that the ringer is on. Somewhere out there, the old number is still lettered on a listing you forgot existed, or one site shows your suite as #5, another says Ste 5, and a third still points to the place you moved out of. Each one looks harmless. Together they tell Google, Apple Maps and every assistant three slightly different stories about one business. You never hear the call you lost. It rings across town.
Here’s the part no national guide will tell you, because it only happens here. On paper, “St. Louis” is two different places. Since 1876, the City of St. Louis has been an independent city, not part of any county. It is the only city in Missouri that runs its own “county” offices, and St. Louis County is an entirely separate government wrapped around it. So every listing form you’ve ever filled in here quietly asked a question most owners never notice answering: which St. Louis?
Here are the two easiest ways to get it wrong. A barber in Tower Grove is in the city, full stop, and a listing that tags the shop “St. Louis County” is telling a story that isn’t true. A salon in Ladue that says “Ladue” on one site and plain “St. Louis” on the next has just split itself into two businesses as far as a machine can tell. Neither owner did anything careless. That’s the leftovers of a process: sites that scrape your details and never ask, a lead-farm that listed you years ago and moved on, a form rushed through late at night after a long shift. The fix isn’t another contract with someone promising page one. It’s one honest decision and an afternoon of your own time.
### What are local SEO citations and do they still matter?
A local citation is any place online that names your business with its address and phone number: your Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business, Yelp, Facebook, a chamber listing, a local directory. Yes, they still matter. Google’s own help page says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity, and it describes prominence as how well-known a business is, based partly on how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have. Citations are how the rest of the web vouches that you’re real and that you are where you say you are.
You can’t move closer to the person searching. You can make sure every place that mentions you tells the same story, word for word. That’s the part of local search that belongs to you, and it’s cheaper than anything anyone will try to sell you.
### Do this today, in this order
Start with a sticky note, not a website. Write your one true address line on it: the exact business name, the street, the suite written one way, the town, and the phone number a customer actually reaches you on. If you’re in the city, write “St. Louis, MO” and never let a site tack “County” onto it. If you’re in a county town, choose the town’s own name or plain “St. Louis” once, write it on the note, and use that exact word on every single listing. Same with the ZIP, the suite and the way you write the phone number. Stick the note to your monitor. Everything else gets matched to it, letter for letter.
Next, search your business name, then your phone number, and open every listing that comes up in its own tab. Some will surprise you. Then fix your Google Business Profile first, because it’s the listing most neighbors see before they ever call. After that, Bing Places, Apple Business, Yelp and Facebook, each one matched to the sticky note. Where you find a duplicate, or a listing still carrying your old number, claim it and correct it, or ask the site to take it down. That’s the whole first afternoon, and nobody needs your password to do it for you.
People ask whether doing local SEO is worth it, and whether you can do SEO yourself. For this piece of it, yes and yes. Getting your name, address and phone consistent is work only you can do well, because only you know which number is real and which suite is current. No agency knows that your landline died two winters ago. You do.
### Why one stray listing costs more than it looks
A wrong address doesn’t send an angry email. It just sits there. A customer taps the old number and hears a disconnect tone. Someone drives to the corner you left and finds a different sign over the door. An assistant on a phone, asked who to call, weighs your listings against a competitor whose details all agree, and names them. You don’t lose that job loudly. You lose it in silence, and you never even learn it existed.
That’s why consistency is one of the first things to rule out when your business isn’t showing up on Google at all. Keep it in proportion, though. Your Google Business Profile and your reviews do most of the heavy lifting. Citations are the foundation under them: not glamorous, not optional. A great profile with real reviews will usually beat a weak one padded with a hundred junk directory links, and a great profile with three conflicting addresses around the web is a great profile working with one hand tied.
### Make your Google Business Profile the strongest listing you own
Because it carries the most weight, build it out completely and keep it alive:
Claim and verify it, then fill in every field: name, address, phone, hours, website and the most accurate primary category you can choose.
Describe what you really do in the words a customer would type, with your services and attributes filled in. Write it for people, not robots.
Post real photos of your storefront, your crew and your finished work. Swap them out as the seasons change.
Use Google Posts for offers, events and news, so the profile looks like a business that is open and answering.
Earn and answer reviews. Ask happy customers, and reply to every review, good or bad, like a neighbor would.
Keep your hours right, especially around holidays. A customer who drives over on a holiday and finds a dark window and a locked door doesn’t blame the listing. They blame you.
### A simple citation workflow you can repeat
You don’t need hundreds of listings. You need the right ones, entered the same way every time.
Audit. Search your name and phone number and write down every place you appear, plus every mismatch: old addresses, dead numbers, duplicates.
Standardize. Match every listing to the sticky note, and make your website say exactly the same thing.
Prioritize. Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business, Yelp and Facebook first, then respected St. Louis and trade directories.
Recheck. Put a reminder on the calendar every few months. A new phone line or a move can quietly undo all of it.
Your next step: write your one true address line before you open a single website. Then fix Google first and work outward from there. If you’re still missing from the map after that, walk through why a business isn’t showing up on Google.
If you’re the plumber, the salon or the one-person crew whose address shows up three different ways online, this part is for you. A Gold listing in the St Louis Near Me Directory is one more clean, consistent citation built to bring you more customers, sitting beside your Google profile instead of competing with it. It’s $357 a year, under a dollar a day, and you get 7 days to look around: cancel before the trial ends and your card isn’t charged.
### Mistakes that quietly cost you calls
Most citation problems are small, and they pile up.
Duplicate listings. Two profiles for one business split your reviews and confuse the machines. Merge or remove the extra.
The old address or number left behind after a move. It’s worth a dedicated hunt.
Format drift. “Suite 5” here, “#5” there, “Ste 5” somewhere else. Pick one.
City and county mixed up. A city shop listed as if it sits in the county, or a county town name on one site and plain “St. Louis” on the next.
Chasing quantity. A dozen consistent listings on sites people actually use beat a hundred spammy ones.
Nothing to do with your NAP, but after an afternoon of fixing listings you’ve earned it - Ladue’s dinner options.
### Where St. Louis owners get the most for their afternoon
Lock down the big five first, then add the local layer the big platforms can’t give you: your chamber of commerce, the directories built for your trade, and a St. Louis directory that sorts you by the part of town you really serve. A Gold listing in the St Louis Near Me Directory lets you list in up to 10 categories with up to 40 location tags, so the electrician who works the whole metro can show up for the neighborhoods and towns where the trucks actually go. Same name, same address, same phone, everywhere.
Working out of your truck or your kitchen table instead of a storefront? That changes how you list, not whether you can. Google’s own help page says that if you don’t serve customers at your business address, you should remove your address from your Business Profile. On a Gold listing you can show a PO Box, a service area, or no address at all. The rule doesn’t change: whatever you choose, choose it once and repeat it. A side-hustle detailer who lists a home address on one site, a PO Box on another and nothing on a third has built three different businesses in the eyes of a machine, and none of them looks sure of itself.
Running more than one location? Give each spot its own verified Google Business Profile, its own phone number and its own set of matching listings. Don’t let two shops share one profile, and don’t let one shop claim a footprint it doesn’t really have. Honest and identical, location by location, is what holds up when a neighbor, a map or an assistant comes looking.

Watch the numbers in your Google Business Profile: calls, direction requests and website clicks. Line them up against what you did, a cleanup here, a run of new reviews there, so you learn what moves your phone instead of guessing. And ask every new customer one question: “How did you find us?” That answer, asked every time, beats any dashboard.
The businesses that keep winning local search aren’t the ones with the cleverest trick. They’re the ones whose name, address and phone are the same everywhere a neighbor or a machine looks, month after month. Write the sticky note. Fix the listings. Refuse to be invisible.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are citations in SEO?
A.  In local SEO, a citation is any online mention of your business’s name, address and phone number, on a directory, a review site, a social profile or a news story. Search engines compare those mentions to confirm you’re real and located where you say. The more of them agree, the more confidently you can be shown.
### Q. What does “local citation” mean?
A.  It means a mention of your business tied to a place: your name plus your local address and phone number. A complete, accurate listing in the St Louis Near Me Directory is one, and so is your chamber listing or your Yelp page. What makes them work is that they match each other exactly.
### Q. Is doing local SEO worth it?
A.  For a business that serves customers nearby, yes. The core work, a complete Google Business Profile, consistent listings and steady reviews, costs mostly time, and it keeps paying off long after the afternoon you spent on it. Skip anyone selling shortcuts or guaranteed rankings.
### Q. Can I do SEO myself?
A.  The local basics, yes. You know your real address, phone and hours better than anyone, and you can fix listings, ask for reviews and post updates yourself. If you’d rather have one clean, local listing that sends you more customers while you work, the St Louis Near Me Directory Gold plan is built for exactly that owner.
### Q. How can I get more reviews on Google?
A.  Ask, in person, right after a job goes well, while the customer is still smiling. Then make it easy: text or email them the review link from your Google Business Profile. Reply to every review you get, good or bad. People notice an owner who answers.
### Q. What is the difference between SEO and local SEO?
A.  SEO is about ranking a website for searches anywhere. Local SEO is about showing up for searches near you, in the map results and when someone asks an assistant who to call nearby. It leans on your Google Business Profile, your reviews and consistent citations, not just your website.

## Is Bing Telling St. Louis You Are Closed? Claim Your Listing
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/bing-local-business-listing-guide-boost-visibility-in-2025
Bing says your shop is closed. You are standing in it with the lights on. Check, because a listing you never wrote can do exactly that: search your own business name and “St. Louis” on your phone, then read the box out loud the way a stranger would from a truck idling on Gravois. The hours. The phone number. The little pin. If the pin sits a block off, or the number rings a line you cancelled two years ago, that driver is already dialing the next name down the list.
You did not write that box. Bing assembled it from whatever it could find. Microsoft’s own support page says as much, in a line that is easy to read past: business owners can “claim and verify existing listings.” Existing. Your listing was there before you were, and Bing Places for Business is the free tool that lets you take the pen back. Scroll to the bottom of that box and look for “Data from.” Microsoft says many of the sources Bing pulls from are publicly visible there. That short list is your to-do list.
How many people read that box? Statcounter’s September figures for the United States give Bing 9.89 percent of searches and Google 85.19. About one search in ten. Small next to Google, and still a real person with a question about someone who does what you do.
St. Louis makes that box harder to get right than most places. The City alone has 79 different neighborhoods, St. Louis County has 88 municipalities, and then come the names people swear by that are not cities at all. The Census Bureau lists Sappington, Concord and Glasgow Village as “census designated places,” communities known by name but “not legally incorporated.” Say a customer types “Sappington plumber.” Your invoice says Sappington, your Google profile says St. Louis, your Facebook page says Concord. Bing sees three towns for one door, and it has other people’s data to settle the argument.
### How do I list my business on Bing Places?
Start at bing.com/forbusiness. If a guide sent you to bingplaces.com, it was written before October 2025, when Microsoft announced that “the domain will change from www.bingplaces.com to www.bing.com/forbusiness.” Sign in with a Microsoft, Google or Facebook account, or a work account. Choose with care, because Microsoft says any listings you claim or create are “associated with the email credentials you’ve used to sign in.” Use a login the business owns, not the nephew’s or the freelancer’s. One owner on Microsoft’s own question forum wrote that they had old listings and “no longer have the login details for those accounts.”
Search before you create. Microsoft’s steps say: “First, search for your business on Bing to see if it is already listed. If so, claim it.” Pick the entry whose address matches yours. If two entries point at the same door, report the duplicate instead of making a third. If nothing comes up, choose to create a new business and fill in the name, address, phone, website, hours and category.
Then verify. Microsoft sends a PIN “via phone, mail, email, or text,” though some options will not be offered to everyone. Postcards, Microsoft says, “typically take 5-6 business days to arrive within the United States,” and it asks you to wait at least 12 days before contacting support. Tell whoever opens the mail at your shop that a postcard from Bing is coming, because a postcard that gets tossed with the coupon flyers costs you another week. Nothing you change goes live until the listing is verified. After that, the publish cycle runs 7-12 days in North America, and every edit you make resets the date. Change it once, correctly, and then go do something else.
Three numbers worth a screenshot: 7-12 days for a change to show up, 20 service areas, and no Google reviews carried over. The rest of this page explains why.
### Does Bing take your word for it?
No. Microsoft’s help page says Bing “verifies the details submitted by business owners by comparing them with information available across search engines, websites, and social media platforms.” Read that as a warning. The form is not a billboard you rent. It is an exam, and the answer key is everything else on the internet that mentions you.
Count where your phone number lives. The vinyl on the van door. The invoice pad. The Facebook page. The glass on the front door. A directory page somebody else started for you and never finished. Every one of those is a vote, and back at our Sappington plumber the van says one thing, the invoice another and the Facebook page a third. Now run the test the way St. Louis customers search: your name plus your neighborhood, your name plus “South City” or “West County,” your trade plus “near me,” and your phone number by itself. Each search shows you a different corner of what the web says about you.
Microsoft spells out what happens when the votes disagree. Your basic details go through automated validation, and “these changes are only applied if they align with trusted external data. If inconsistencies are detected, changes may not publish or may be overwritten.” Bing Places is “one of the primary sources” for a listing, not the only one, and Microsoft says other sources can take priority when their information is fresher, giving the example of Bing Places data that “hasn’t been updated for more than 6 months.”
So the old advice, fill out the form and you are done, loses twice. A tidy form can be outvoted by a messy web, and a form you stop touching can be outvoted by anyone who updated more recently. Bing bears no grudge against you. The enemy is a web full of unowned copies of your business, each one a little out of date. If you want the short list of places worth tidying, our guide to the free local listing sites that customers and AI assistants actually use is the place to start.

### Who still uses Bing, and does it matter in St. Louis?
Here is the whole United States picture from Statcounter for September: Google 85.19 percent, Bing 9.89, Yahoo 2.64, DuckDuckGo 1.75. Does anyone still use Bing? One search in ten says yes. Whether that matters to you depends on what you sell. A roofer, a dentist and a diner all get asked the same kind of question, “who is near me and open,” and the answer on Bing is the box you read at the top of this page.
Now the part most guides skip. Microsoft’s October 2025 announcement says only that it is investing in “deeper integrations with Bing Maps and Copilot.” That is a plan, not a feature. ### Is Bing worth the hour? The honest verdict
Yes, as a supporting move, and the hour pays off the same whether the search says “South City” or “West County.” Microsoft calls Bing Places for Business “a free online platform” for managing how you appear in Bing search results and Bing Maps, so the price is your afternoon and one postcard. The disadvantages are real, and they are small: a modest slice of searches, a publishing delay measured in days, and one more profile that goes stale if you ignore it. A stale listing can lose to fresher data, so claim it only if you will look at it again.
### The Google import: two clicks, four catches
If your Google Business Profile is already set up, Bing Places will pull it in. Microsoft’s steps are short: select “Import from your Google Business Profile,” choose whether to sync weekly, biweekly or monthly, sign in to Google, and import the listings it detects. In October 2025 Microsoft said the new import flow is “faster, more reliable, and better at preserving key attributes like business name, hours, and contact details.” If your business is already verified on Google, Bing “automatically verifies the imported listing.”
Now the catches, all from Microsoft’s own help pages. First, you cannot pick and choose: “You cannot manually select specific listings to import.” Second, “syncing may create duplicate listings, especially if a listing already exists on Bing.” Third, if Bing finds a match, “Bing will use Google data to overwrite the Bing Places for Business listing information,” so whatever is wrong on Google arrives intact. Fourth, you lose the edit button: “Direct editing isn’t currently available in the Bing Places for Business dashboard for listings linked to a Google Business Profile.” You fix the Google profile and wait for the next sync. Turning sync off, Microsoft adds, does not unlink the two.
So read your Google profile like a stranger before you press import. Hours, address, phone, primary category. Five minutes, and the mistake you were going to copy gets caught while it is still one mistake. Our guide to getting your Google Business Profile right covers that side.
### Do your Google reviews follow you to Bing?
Here is the surprise that stings. An owner with “over 90 customer reviews” on Google asked Microsoft’s question forum why only reviews from one other site showed up on the Bing listing. The answer on Microsoft’s forum: “Bing Places for Business does not pull reviews directly from your Google Business Profile (GBP), even if you have synced the two profiles.” Microsoft’s own ranking page explains the logic: listings with “more positive reviews and ratings on sites like Yelp and TripAdvisor” count as more popular. Years of five-star work on one platform do not travel on their own. Ask a few happy customers to leave an honest review where Bing looks, and do it without incentives.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is Bing Places for Business free?
A.  Yes. Microsoft describes Bing Places for Business as a free online platform for creating and managing listings that appear in Bing search results and Bing Maps. The cost is time: a verification PIN, a publish cycle of about 7-12 days, and a look at the listing whenever something about your business changes.
### Q. How can I verify my business on Bing Places?
A.  Claim or create the listing, then request a PIN. Microsoft says you can receive it by phone, mail, email or text, though not every option is offered for every listing. Postcards usually take 5-6 business days in the United States. If your Google profile is already verified and you import it, Bing automatically verifies the imported listing.
### Q. How do I edit business information on Bing?
A.  Sign in at bing.com/forbusiness, select your listing and choose Edit. Changes go live only after the listing has been successfully verified. Basic details are validated against trusted external data, so changes may not publish or may be overwritten. If the listing is linked to a Google Business Profile, update it in Google, then sync it with Bing Places.
### Q. Does anyone still use Bing?
A.  Yes. Statcounter’s September figures for the United States show Bing handling 9.89 percent of searches against Google’s 85.19. That is roughly one search in ten, which is small beside Google and large enough to be worth an hour of your time for a free listing.
### Q. Is Bing search engine any good?
A.  For finding a nearby business it does the job. Microsoft says Bing ranks local listings on relevance, distance and popularity, and that website SEO plays an important role. The practical lesson is the same as on Google: complete, accurate details and real reviews win. A local directory listing on St Louis Near Me Directory backs up the same facts.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of using Bing?
A.  For a business owner, the main disadvantage is reach. Bing handles about one US search in ten, so it will not carry your marketing alone. Listings can also take 7-12 days to publish, synced listings cannot be edited in Bing, and Google reviews do not follow you over. Treat it as a supporting listing, then anchor locally.
### Q. Can I sync Bing Places with my Google Business Profile?
A.  Yes. Select Import from your Google Business Profile, choose weekly, biweekly or monthly sync, sign in to your Google Business Profile, and import the detected listings. Microsoft warns that syncing may create duplicates if a listing already exists on Bing, so search for your business first and clean up Google before you import.

### The Directories That Matter for Your Industry
So where else can you list your business beyond the big six? That depends entirely on your trade — because niche directories only help when your customers actually use them to decide. Here are the ones that matter, by industry:
Home services & contractors (roofers, plumbers, HVAC, remodelers): Angi (formerly Angie’s List) and Thumbtack for lead generation, the Better Business Bureau (BBB) for trust, Houzz for remodeling and design portfolios, Porch, and Nextdoor for neighborhood word-of-mouth. For most trades, Angi, the BBB, and Nextdoor are the three that earn their keep.
Restaurants & food: Yelp (already in your core, but critical here), Tripadvisor, OpenTable or Resy for reservations, and the delivery platforms (DoorDash, Grubhub) that double as discovery. Reviews and photos carry more weight in food than almost anywhere else.
Medical & health (doctors, dentists, clinics): Healthgrades, Zocdoc, WebMD, and Vitals. Patients research providers on these before they ever call, so accurate profiles and reviews here directly shape who books.
Legal: Avvo, FindLaw, Justia, and Martindale-Hubbell. Legal directories with peer ratings and verified credentials are where prospective clients vet an attorney’s reputation.
Beauty & wellness (salons, spas, barbers): Vagaro, Booksy, and StyleSeat — booking-first platforms where clients discover, review, and schedule in one place.
Automotive: Cars.com, CarGurus, and RepairPal for repair shops. Buyers and drivers comparison-shop here before choosing.
Weddings & events: The Knot and WeddingWire — the two directories couples live in while planning.
Real estate & home: Zillow and Realtor.com for agents; Houzz for designers and remodelers.
Notice the pattern: two or three sites per industry, not twenty. Find the ones your customers actually open when they’re ready to buy, claim those, and skip the rest.
### How to Find the Right Directories for Your Trade
Not sure which niche sites matter for you? Three quick tests answer it. Search the way a customer would — type your service plus “near me” or “best [service] in St. Louis” into Google and see which directories keep showing up on page one; those are the ones with real authority in your field. Ask your own customers where they found you or how they usually pick a provider like you — their answer is your shortlist. And check a few successful competitors: the directories where your best-reviewed rivals appear are almost certainly the ones worth claiming. If a site fails all three tests — it doesn’t rank, no customer names it, and your competitors ignore it — it isn’t worth your ten minutes. Which is the filter most owners skip: not “is this directory real?” but “do my customers actually use it to choose?” So — do they?
### Are Business Directories Still Useful in 2026?
Yes — but not the way they were a decade ago. Directories didn’t disappear; their job changed. They no longer drive much direct browsing traffic, and citation volume barely moves rankings anymore (Near Media). What they still do is two things that matter: feed consistent, verifiable business data to the search engines and AI assistants that decide who to recommend, and give your customers a trusted place to vet you in the moment they’re choosing. A complete Healthgrades profile or a strong Angi rating isn’t traffic — it’s a trust signal exactly where a decision gets made. So the useful directories are the ones with real authority in your niche, kept accurate. The rest are noise.
### The Honest Verdict, at a Glance
### Are These Niche Directories Worth It?
Only the one or two your customers actually use — and then, yes, genuinely. The mistake is treating “get listed on more sites” as a strategy. A dentist gains nothing from Angi, and a roofer gains nothing from Zocdoc. But a roofer with a strong, accurate BBB and Angi presence, or a dentist with a complete Healthgrades and Zocdoc profile, is showing up exactly where a ready-to-buy customer is looking. Claim the two that fit your trade, fill them in completely, gather real reviews, and keep the details identical to your other listings. Skip anything that isn’t on your industry’s short list — a listing on an off-topic or no-name directory does nothing but add one more place for your information to drift out of date.
Random, but: if the dog needs a groomer, here’s the pet-services map.
### What Actually Moves Your Ranking
Industry directories are a multiplier on fundamentals, not a replacement for them, so it’s worth naming the fundamentals plainly. A complete, active Google Business Profile leads. Real reviews follow. Then a name, address, and phone that agree across every place they appear (a well-documented edge in the local pack, per Whitespark, 2026). Your trade’s directories amplify all three in front of a narrower, better-qualified audience — which is precisely why they’re worth doing, and precisely why they can’t carry a business on their own.
And here’s what a niche directory does that a general one structurally cannot: it narrows on a second axis. A local directory tells search engines where you work. An industry directory tells them what you do — to an audience that has already settled the question of whether they need it. Nobody browsing Healthgrades is deciding whether to see a doctor. Nobody on Avvo is deciding whether they need a lawyer. They are down to choosing one, and that proximity to the decision is the whole value. It’s also why an off-industry listing does nothing at all: a roofer on a wedding-vendor site has narrowed on neither axis, and volume can’t rescue that. Two directories that match your trade will out-earn twenty that don’t. The pair worth having is one that knows your city and one that knows your category.
### The 3 Mistakes That Make Directory Listings Backfire
Picking the right directories is half of it. The other half is not undoing the work. One: spreading thin instead of deep. Twenty half-filled listings on the wrong sites lose to three complete, accurate ones on the right sites. Pick your industry’s short list and finish those profiles. Two: ignoring the niche sites your customers live on. If patients vet doctors on Healthgrades and you have no profile, you’re invisible at the exact decision point — being on Google isn’t enough by itself. Three: letting the niche profile drift from the main one. Industry directories are the ones owners forget they joined, and they are often the oldest surviving record of a business anywhere online. If your Healthgrades or Avvo page still names the practice you left, that contradiction sits in front of exactly the readers who were closest to hiring you. Avoid those three and your listings quietly reinforce a business that’s already doing the fundamentals right.

Your trade directories say what you do. A local one says where. You want both. And the move here is narrow: name the two directories your trade actually uses — two, not ten — and go finish those profiles completely. If you can’t name them off the top of your head, your customers can, because those are the sites they check before they call. Ask the last three people who hired you where they looked.

## Your Business Is Probably on Yahoo Already. You Just Didn't Put It There.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-essential-yahoo-business-directories-for-2025-success
The bookmark still sits in your browser bar from the last time somebody told you to “get on Yahoo.” You click it at the kitchen table after the second shift, laptop fan whirring, coffee gone cold, ready to fill in a form. There is no form. Type local.yahoo.com/claim-business.html today and Yahoo drops you on the front page of Yahoo Local.
Meanwhile a homeowner in South City, water spotting the bedroom ceiling, taps a roofer’s number on Yahoo and hears the three-tone beep: the number you have dialed is not in service. She doesn’t leave a message. She taps the next name. St. Louis now has two area codes on the same streets, 314 and 557, and every local call takes ten digits, so the number Yahoo shows for you has to be the right ten, not one you gave up years ago. Open Yahoo’s roofing contractors page for St. Louis, MO and you can see how it happens. It runs at least nine pages deep, from Clayton Rd to Gravois Rd, and a roofer on Rosy Ln shows an address, a rating and a 314 number, and nothing else.
Here is the part nobody who charged you for “Yahoo submission” ever said out loud. Your business may already be on Yahoo. You just didn’t put it there. Yahoo Local builds its business pages out of other companies’ data, and the reviews on those pages come from Yelp. Somebody else’s record of your phone number, your hours and your old address can be sitting on Yahoo right now, and it never sends you a notification when it gets something wrong.
Yahoo works with The Real Yellow Pages on claims. It takes dictation from Yellow Pages and Yelp. Send that to the next owner who gets the “submit to Yahoo” call.
That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to stop paying anyone to “add” you to a site that already decides what it shows from feeds. The real job is smaller and it is free: find your page on Yahoo Local, click “Is this your business? Verify your listing,” claim the free profile at The Real Yellow Pages, and make the name, street and phone match everything else. One sitting, once. Then put your energy where customers actually decide who to call.
### How do I get my business listed on Yahoo?
Open any business page on Yahoo Local and two things sit right there: a link that asks “Is this your business? Verify your listing,” and a Reviews block labeled Yelp, with a “More reviews on Yelp” link at the bottom. The first is your door. The second is why a bad Yelp review follows you onto Yahoo.
So the doorway is not Yahoo at all. It is The Real Yellow Pages, whose sites are provided by Thryv. Its Yahoo claim page says Yahoo is working in collaboration with it so you can claim your business profile for free, and that your updates will be shared with Yahoo. Yahoo’s own partner list names Yellow Pages as the source of its local business listings.
Think about what that means for a roofer on Gravois, a one-chair salon on Cherokee Street, a guy in Dutchtown with a truck and a pressure washer. You never touched Yahoo. Your listing exists anyway, stitched together from a phone-book company’s file and a review site you may not check. If that file still has the number from your old shop, Yahoo shows the old number, and your phone sits silent on the dashboard while the job goes down the street. The name matters as much as the number. Missouri law calls any business name other than your own true name a fictitious name, and makes it unlawful to do business under one without first registering it with the Secretary of State. So before you claim anything, search your name at bsd.sos.mo.gov and copy the registered version exactly as filed. Registering costs $7.00 on the paper form and, the Secretary of State says, gives the name no protection, so your registered name, your street and your phone have to travel together on every record, Yahoo’s included.
Anyone charging you to “submit to Yahoo” is selling you a door that opens for free. Most of the internet now works this way. Directories, maps and AI assistants read each other’s data, and the business that keeps one clean, consistent record wins, while the business that keeps paying for submissions stays a stranger with three different phone numbers.
### What a stale Yahoo record quietly costs you
The old shop key is still on your ring, the one for a door you haven’t walked through in two years. Now think about the last time you moved, changed numbers or cut your Sunday hours. You updated Google. You told your regulars. You probably did not call a phone-book company. So the file Yahoo reads can still carry the old version of you, and the person who finds it has no way to know.
Here is how that plays out in St. Louis. Got a newer business line? It may start with 557, the area code the Missouri Public Service Commission layered over the 314 region. If an old file still carries the 314 number you gave up, that is the number a stranger can tap. The job pays someone else, and you never see the call that didn’t happen. No invoice, no complaint, no clue. Just a slow week you blame on the weather.
You’re not careless. You’re running a business, maybe two jobs at once, and nobody told you that listings got built for you by companies you never hired. The fix is not another subscription. It is knowing where the record lives and correcting it at the source, once, and then keeping one clean record of your own that everything else can point back to.
### Claim the Yahoo record in one sitting
Do it at the same table, same cold coffee. Have five things open before you start: your business name exactly as you registered it with the Missouri Secretary of State if you use a trade name, the street address you use today, written the way the post office writes it, your main phone with the right area code (Missouri’s area codes include 314, 557 and 636), your real hours and your main category. Then follow the path Yahoo’s own pages send you down.
First, search for yourself on Yahoo Local. Yahoo’s St. Louis directory lives at local.yahoo.com/mo/st-louis/, and each trade gets its own page under it, such as local.yahoo.com/consumer-services/home-and-garden-services/roofing-contractors/mo/st-louis/. Find your trade, find your name, and open your page if one exists. Second, click “Is this your business? Verify your listing.” It sits right on the business page and hands you to The Real Yellow Pages. Third, claim the free profile. The Real Yellow Pages page says the claim is free; you may see enhanced profile options pitched alongside it, and you don’t need them to fix your basics.
Fourth, copy your name, address and phone exactly as your Google Business Profile shows them. Same suite format, same abbreviations. Paste, don’t retype. Fifth, check the Yelp side: Yahoo Local shows Yelp reviews, so claim your Yelp page too and make it say the same thing. Last, save the login somewhere you will find it. A listing you can’t log into is a listing you can’t correct.
Not on Yahoo Local at all? The Real Yellow Pages claim page has a link for businesses it can’t find. Start there, not with anyone selling a Yahoo package.
### Bing is the other half of Yahoo
Keep the laptop open; the coffee is cold anyway. Yahoo’s search box has a partner too. Microsoft lists Yahoo among the exclusive search partnerships in its advertising network, alongside DuckDuckGo and Ecosia. That is one more reason a clean Bing Places for Business listing belongs on the same short list. Same name, same address, same phone. The machines read these sources together, and a mismatch you would never notice is one they do.

### Where “Yahoo Small Business” went
Maybe there’s still a renewal email in your inbox with a purple Yahoo logo on it, from a web store you set up years ago. If you remember Yahoo Small Business, the hosting and web store side, it is not where listings live either. Turbify sells Localworks, a dashboard it pitches for managing your listings across 70+ directories, Yahoo Local among them. That is a paid tool, and it is a different thing from claiming the Yahoo record for free.
So when an old guide tells you to “submit to seven Yahoo directories,” it is describing roads that were rerouted years ago. Yahoo Local’s pages lean on partners: Yellow Pages for listings and Yelp for reviews. You claim yours, you match it, you move on.
### Is Yahoo worth your time at all?
One sitting, yes. A budget line, no. Think of the salesman’s voice on the phone, warm and fast, promising first-page Yahoo. Hang up.
