## St. Louis Restaurant SEO: 30% to the App or 2.5% to You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/local-seo-for-restaurants-in-st-louis
Thirty percent. That is what the Uber Eats Premium delivery plan takes once its 30-day intro rate runs out, by the company’s own merchant pricing page. Here is the Friday version of that number: the ticket printer chattering through the dinner rush, a basket of toasted ravioli coming up golden, another bag sealed with somebody else’s sticker on it, a driver leaning on the host stand while the fries go soft under the heat lamp. On a $40 order, that one ticket just paid the app $12.
Scroll down the same page and there is a second number, for an online ordering site you control: “a 2.5% order processing fee + $0.29 per order.” On the same $40 order, that is $1.29. Same company. Same page. The only difference is whose front door the customer walked through. Whoever owns the link owns the customer, and the fee sheet is built around the app owning it. That is not a failure in your kitchen. It is a fee sheet doing what it was written to do.
St. Louis has been angry about this before. In July 2020 the Board of Aldermen passed Ordinance 71193, which capped what delivery apps could charge city restaurants at 20% of each online order. The cap was written to expire 60 days after the city lifted its pandemic limits on dine-in restaurants. Uber’s Premium plan sits ten points above it.
Here is the other public record nobody warns a restaurant about. Inspection reports issued after May 10, 2012 sit in the City of St. Louis’s Healthspace system at healthspace.com/Clients/Missouri/StLouis, linked from the Restaurant Health Ratings and Inspection Reports page. St. Louis County posts its own scores on its own website, so which system holds yours depends on which side of the city line your door is on. A stranger can read your last inspection before they read your menu. Shouldn’t you get to see what they see first?
### Can a beginner do SEO?
Yes. For a single restaurant, most local SEO is data entry and consistency, work you can finish at the bar after close. In St. Louis that includes reading the inspection report the city or county publishes under your name. Claim and complete your Google Business Profile, keep your hours right, add your menu in Google’s menu editor, set your own ordering links and a preferred provider, then ask for honest reviews and reply to them. What is still hard after that is the only part worth paying for.
### How do I do SEO for my restaurant?
Start where the work is free and the coffee is still hot. Sit in a parked car outside your own place and look yourself up the way a first-timer would, one thumb on a glowing screen. Whatever that screen shows is the job. To point the order button at your own link: Business Profile, Food ordering, pick the link, Set as preferred. And know the limit up front: Google states plainly that “there’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.” Which of those would you finish tonight?
### Who owes the sales tax on an app order?
At month end the app statements pile up next to the register tape, each one with a neat little tax line at the bottom. It looks finished. It looks handled. In Missouri, for a Missouri restaurant selling to Missouri diners, the Department of Revenue says the restaurant, not the app, is the seller with the primary reporting and remittance duty.
In Letter Ruling LR 8316 (August 30, 2024), the Department told an online ordering company that it is not required to collect and remit Missouri sales tax as a marketplace facilitator for a Missouri restaurant, because those restaurants “are the sellers with primary reporting and remittance obligations under Missouri sales tax law.” Its reading is plain: the restaurant’s responsibility to remit the tax is “a mandatory requirement.”
So the tax line on that receipt is a picture of the liability, not a transfer of it, and the “the app handles it” habit is baked into how these statements read. A short call settles it before an audit does: the Department’s sales tax line is (573) 751-2836, and its tax calendar lists your next due date. Which day this week has ten minutes for that call?
While we’re in the tax weeds: Missouri’s reduced state rate on food is 1.225%, down from 4.225%, but the Department excludes an establishment when food prepared for immediate consumption is more than 80% of its total gross receipts. Its own example is a restaurant over that line, charging the regular rate on all of its food sales.
### What do the apps charge, side by side?
This is the part with real money in it, and every number here comes from the platforms’ own published pricing pages, DoorDash’s and Uber’s.
DoorDash lists three marketplace plans: 15% Basic, 25% Plus and 30% Premier on delivery orders, with pickup at 6% on all three. No monthly fee, no signup cost, no cancellation penalty.
Uber Eats lists 20% Lite, 25% Plus and 30% Premium on delivery, with pickup at 7% when your in-app pickup prices match in-store, and 10% without. Self-delivery, where you use your own staff, is 15%.
Then the line on Uber’s own page that stops the conversation. Its Webshop product, a commission-free online ordering site you control, is 2.5% plus 29 cents per order. Same company. Same page. Between 2.5% and 30%, depending entirely on whose front door the customer walks through.
Nobody is telling you to drop the marketplaces. They bring discovery you don’t otherwise get, and for a new restaurant that matters. But St. Louis aldermen looked at this kind of fee sheet in 2020 and wrote 20% into law as the ceiling. What would a Friday night look like if the link on the ticket were yours?
### Whose link does your Google profile send people to?
Here is the free part that never shows up in an app’s sales pitch. Google’s Business Profile lets you add custom links that “direct customers to other web pages where they can place orders” from your business, your own site included. You can mark a preferred provider, with separate switches for pickup and for delivery. And when you want a third-party link gone, Google states that “providers must remove third-party links from a profile within 5 business days” of your request.
One trap, because it is an easy mistake with a real cost: Google says that if you turn off “Accept orders on your profile,” any third-party order options and links you add are hidden from your Business Profile. If the goal is to steer people to direct ordering, set a preferred provider instead of switching ordering off. When a hungry stranger taps the order button on that profile, whose link should they land on first?
Wildly off-topic - even restaurant owners get a night off, and Dardenne Prairie eats well.
### What does Google say about reviews?
Google’s published position on reviews and local ranking is a single sentence: “More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” On replying, it says that when you reply to customer reviews, “it shows that you value their feedback,” and that positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out. Nothing there promises you a rank. Reply because the next reader sees that somebody is home. What would your last three replies tell a stranger about the kitchen?
### What does a diner see before they walk in?
A couple stands on a Tower Grove sidewalk at seven in the evening, deciding between your door and the one across the street. Phones come out. They tap your profile: are the hours right, does the menu read like food, which button says order online and where does it go. If they are the careful sort, they open the city’s inspection page too. It takes a few taps, and none of it is the apps’ doing. It is the facts you left sitting out there for anyone to find, set next to the competitor’s facts, side by side on the same small screen. The apps will gladly show their version of your restaurant. What does yours say when nobody is guiding the tap?
### What’s actually worth doing?
Free, documented, and in rough order of return:
Fix your hours, and keep special hours current. Google lets you set special hours for holidays, special events and other exceptional circumstances. A closed door at a listed open time costs you the customer who already drove over.
Use the menu editor. Items with descriptions and prices, grouped into sections. Allow 24 to 48 hours for changes to appear on Search and Maps.
Set your ordering links and preferred provider. This is the free setting that decides whether an order is a 2.5% order or a 30% one.
Ask for honest reviews and reply to them all. The next reader is watching how you talk to the last one.
Read your own city inspection report. It is public and searchable online, and you will not be the only one reading it.
Put it on the calendar. Pick one slow evening before the month ends, write it on the prep list next to the order sheet, and work down this list with the laptop open and a coffee at your elbow. A job with a date on it gets done; a job that is only a good idea waits for next quarter.
None of that costs anything but an afternoon at the bar after close, laptop next to the register tape. And the restaurant a hungry stranger picks is very often just the one whose information is correct.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should I pay for local SEO?
A.  Quotes swing widely, so get any price in writing with exactly what you get each month. What you can do yourself for nothing: profile completion, menu, ordering links, hours, photos and review responses. Establish that before you evaluate any quote. For a yardstick, a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is $357 a year, paid annually.
### Q. Can ChatGPT do SEO?
A.  It can help draft descriptions and organize a menu, but it cannot verify your hours, claim your profile, or change your ranking, and it does not have access to your local data. A more useful question is whether your restaurant information is accurate enough for an assistant to describe you correctly.
### Q. What is the 30/30/30 rule for restaurants?
A.  That one is about your books, not about search, and versions get passed around. Ask your accountant which split they mean before you lean on it. Either way it has nothing to do with whether a hungry stranger finds you.
### Q. Does the delivery app handle my Missouri sales tax?
A.  Not necessarily. In a 2024 letter ruling (LR 8316) the Missouri Department of Revenue told an online ordering company it is not required to collect and remit Missouri sales tax as a marketplace facilitator for a Missouri restaurant, because the restaurants are the sellers with primary reporting and remittance obligations. Ask your accountant, or the Department, how your own app orders are treated.
### Q. Are St. Louis restaurant inspection scores public?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis publishes restaurant inspection reports online through a searchable system covering reports issued after May 2012, including restaurants, taverns, carry-outs, grocery stores, caterers and day cares. St. Louis County posts its own scores on its own website. Anyone comparing you to a competitor can look up both in about a minute.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for SEO?
A.  For a restaurant, read it as a short pile of unglamorous work that does most of the job: an accurate Google Business Profile, correct hours, a real menu, a way to order from you directly, and reviews you actually respond to. Do those before anything anyone sells you as advanced.
### Q. How much does SEO typically cost?
A.  Quotes swing widely. The fair test is simple: ask any vendor to list, in writing, the specific tasks they will do each month, then cross off everything on the free list above. Whatever is left is what you would actually be paying for.
### Q. What are the 3 C's of SEO?
A.  Versions differ, so ask whoever uses the phrase to name theirs. For a restaurant, the three that matter are on this page: facts that are correct everywhere, a way to order from you directly, and reviews you answer.
Tonight, after the last ticket clears, open your own Google Business Profile and check two things: your hours and your preferred ordering provider. Then keep going with optimizing your Business Profile and responding to reviews.
If you run the kitchen, the bar or the carry-out counter yourself, you already pay for a website, a Google listing and an app that takes its cut. A Gold listing is the piece that makes them work harder: up to 10 categories across 40 location tags, a page that can be indexed and cited by AI on its own, for under a dollar a day. That is how a restaurant gets more customers who order from you, not from the app. See the Gold plan or compare every option. Refuse to be invisible.

## Black-Owned Restaurants in St. Louis: What's Actually Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/black-owned-restaurants-in-st-louis
In September 2025, Lee Enterprises shut down Feast Magazine.
Feast maintained the guide — the one everybody linked to, the one that got updated when a place moved or closed. When it went dark, the maintenance stopped, and every list that had been quietly copying from it stopped being true at the same time.
That’s why the first page of results right now will send you to a restaurant that closed in 2022, one that closed this past May, one whose owners retired in 2024, and at least one that isn’t Black-owned at all. We checked every name against a source. Here’s what’s actually open.
### What are the best Black-owned restaurants in St. Louis?
For barbecue, C&K Barbecue (4390 Jennings Station Rd) has been serving snoots and rib tips since 1963. For West African, FUFU n’ Sauce (8100 Page Ave) is run by a winner of PBS’s The Great American Recipe. For Senegalese, Chez Ali at City Foundry. For soul food, Gourmet Soul (1620 Delmar Blvd), whose chef won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown. For pastry, La Pâtisserie Chouquette (1626 Tower Grove Ave). For coffee, Northwest Coffee Roasting (4251 Laclede Ave). And in Ferguson, Cathy’s Kitchen (250 S Florissant Rd), which stayed open through 2014 and never left.
### The sixty-year-old one
C&K Barbecue, 4390 Jennings Station Rd, is the deepest story on this list and the one most worth your afternoon.
It was founded in 1963 by Forris and Lucille King, who came to St. Louis from Mississippi during the Second World War — part of the same migration that built much of north city and north county. Daryle Brantley came into the business as a partner in 1982 and opened the Jennings Station Road location in 1983. It has been family-operated the whole time.
Order the snoots if you have never had them. They are pig snouts, fried crisp, and they are a genuinely St. Louis thing that barely exists anywhere else in America — a dish that came up out of making the whole animal worth eating and stayed on the menu because people love it. Rib tips are the other order.
### Where to eat, by what you’re after
Cathy’s Kitchen, 250 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson. Cathy and Jerome Jenkins opened it in 2013, which means it was one year old when Ferguson became a word the whole country knew. It stayed open. It is still there, and a second counter — Cathy’s Kitchen ToGo, 10198 W Florissant Ave in Dellwood — opened on Juneteenth 2024. Diner food, soul food and seafood. Their food later reached Schnucks shelves.
FUFU n’ Sauce, 8100 Page Ave, University City. Adjo Honsou started it as a food truck in May 2022 and opened her first storefront in August 2025. The food is Togolese — West African, built around fufu and the sauces that go with it. She won season three of PBS’s The Great American Recipe. If you have never eaten West African food, this is the easiest possible place to start.
Chez Ali, in the food hall at City Foundry. Alioun Thiam came to the United States in 1999 and to St. Louis in 2013 by way of New York. The food is Senegalese and Afro-Caribbean — yassa chicken, thieboudienne, which is essentially Senegal’s national dish. Sauce named it one of the year’s best new restaurants in 2021.
Gourmet Soul, 1620 Delmar Blvd, Downtown West. Chef Lavinia McCoy won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown, which is a national credential almost nobody in this market has. Elevated soul food — lamb chops, an Old Bay bowl. Their published hours are unusual, running Friday through Sunday, so check before you go.
Jerk Unlimited, 3108 Cherokee St. Jamaican, chef-owned by Trevoy Woods. This address previously held Jerk Soul, whose founder relocated to Ghana; Jerk Unlimited is the rebrand that continued in the space.
### Coffee, pastry and dessert
The most interesting part of this list isn’t restaurants at all.
Northwest Coffee Roasting Co., 4251 Laclede Ave in the Central West End, has been roasting since 2003. Jason Wilson acquired the company around 2012 and runs it now — a Black-owned roaster, not just a cafe, which is rare anywhere in the country. Open 7am to 6pm daily, with a second counter inside the Schnucks at 8650 Big Bend in Webster Groves that opened, pointedly, on the last day of Black History Month.
La Pâtisserie Chouquette, 1626 Tower Grove Ave, Botanical Heights. Simone Faure is a New Orleans native who trained in Ritz-Carlton kitchens and opened her own patisserie here in 2013. Macarons, cakes, French pastry done properly. Tuesday to Friday 9 to 2, Saturday 9 to 3.
SweetArt, 3701 Lindell Blvd. Chef Reine Keis has been at this since 2008, and the food is entirely plant-based — vegan soul food and baking, which is a harder trick than it sounds. There’s also a SweetArt stall at City Foundry, though the Lindell location is the one we could confirm operating.
### What closed, and what’s still being recommended anyway
This section exists so you don’t drive somewhere that isn’t there. Every one of these still appears on live pages as a going concern.
Sweetie Pie’s is the big one. The last location closed in 2022. A revival called Sweetie Pie’s 2nd Act has been announced for north city with a $1.5 million city grant and a banner on the building — but it is not open, and no opening date has been given. Do not plan a meal around it.
Turn, in Midtown, closed at the end of May; the chef and his wife relocated to Little Rock. Ms. Piggies’ Smokehouse on Page closed when the Matthews family retired around Thanksgiving 2024. Brother’s Diner on Whittier is permanently closed. Jerk Soul on Cherokee is gone, though its address lives on as Jerk Unlimited. Prime 55 shows one location closed and another permanently closed.
And the instructive one: Deli Divine on Delmar appears on Black-owned roundups constantly. It is not Black-owned. Its owner is Ben Poremba, an Israeli-born restaurateur. It ends up on those lists because it sits inside the Delmar DivINe building. Nobody did that maliciously — one list guessed from the address, and everyone downstream copied it. That is exactly how these lists decay.
### Two we won’t claim either way
If you search this term right now, Google’s own local results put Blazin Kitchen (3636 Page Blvd) and 4 Hens Creole Kitchen (City Foundry) at the top. Both are open — we verified that — and both look genuinely good.
We could not find a published source naming their ownership. Google’s ranking is an inference from how people search and tag, not a statement of fact. So we’re telling you they exist, that they’re open, and that we couldn’t confirm the one thing this list is about. That’s more useful to you than a confident guess, and it’s the same standard that kept Deli Divine off the list above.
### Where the map is thin
Honest geography, because padding this would be easy and useless.
The verified list concentrates in the city (Gourmet Soul, SweetArt, Chouquette, Northwest Coffee, Chez Ali, Jerk Unlimited) and north county (Cathy’s Kitchen and ToGo, C&K, plus FUFU n’ Sauce just over in University City). North county also holds the oldest and deepest roots on the list.
Hard left turn — Highland, Illinois is a short drive east and worth a Saturday.
South county, west county and the Metro East are effectively uncovered. We found no Black-owned restaurant in west county or Illinois that we could source ownership for — not because none exist, but because nobody has documented them. Several candidates appear on old lists with no owner named and no independent confirmation anywhere.
If you run one of those places, that gap is the whole point of the box at the bottom of this page.
### About the numbers you’ll see quoted
One more thing worth being straight about, because it gets repeated locally as though it were local.
The encouraging figures — Black-owned employer businesses up roughly 57 percent between 2017 and 2022, revenue up about two thirds — come from U.S. Census Bureau data and are national. They are real, and they are not a St. Louis statistic. We looked for a trustworthy metro-level number and could not confirm one we’d be willing to print, so we’re not printing one.
What we can tell you is what we found doing this: a short list of operators, several of them decades deep, working in a market where the publication that used to keep track of them no longer exists. Whether that’s a boom or a squeeze, the practical response is the same — go eat at them.
Two searches bring most people to this page: what are some black-owned businesses in St. Louis beyond the obvious, and what are some good black soul food restaurants in St. Louis, Missouri specifically. This guide answers the first through food and points the second at the dedicated soul food list.

## What a Complete Directory Profile Actually Does for Your Business (An Honest Anatomy)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-directory-goldmine-seo-backlinks-citations
Ask ten marketers what a directory listing does and you’ll get everything from “nothing, directories are dead” to “secret SEO goldmine.” Both answers are lazy. The truth is more useful: a complete profile on a quality local directory is a working asset with seven distinct parts — each doing a specific, explainable job — plus a few things it genuinely cannot do, which we’ll cover too, because you deserve the whole picture before you spend an evening building one. If you finish this piece and decide a profile isn’t for you, that’s a fine outcome too — at least the decision will be an informed one.
Here’s the honest anatomy.
### Part 1: The citation — your verifiable public record
At its base, your profile is a citation: a public, structured record of your name, address, phone, hours, and services. Search engines and AI assistants cross-check your details across sources before trusting them, and every consistent citation is a small vote of confidence in your legitimacy. One clean, maintained citation from a relevant regional directory is a solid brick in that foundation — our local citations guide explains the whole system, including why consistency beats volume.
### Part 2: The backlink — one honest signal, not a magic trick
Yes, your profile links to your website, and yes, a link from an established, geographically relevant directory is a legitimate signal — a St. Louis business linked from a St. Louis directory makes contextual sense to a search engine in a way a random link from nowhere doesn’t.
Now the honesty part, because this topic attracts nonsense: one link is one signal, not a rocket. Anyone selling you directory submissions in bulk as an SEO strategy — five hundred listings, guaranteed “link juice” — is selling you something search engines actively discount and sometimes penalize. The value here comes from the link being real, relevant, and singular: a directory your neighbors actually use, linking to a business that actually serves them. That’s the kind of link that ages well. Chase quantity and you’re buying yesterday’s spam tactic at today’s prices.
### Part 3: The independently-ranking page
This one surprises owners: your profile isn’t just an entry in a list — it’s its own full page that can appear in search results on its own merits. Say you’re a wedding photographer. Your website might rank for “St. Louis wedding photographer,” but searches like “affordable wedding photography St. Louis” or “event photographer near me” are separate contests — and a complete, well-written profile page can show up for long-tail searches your website misses. More lines in the water, each one honestly baited with real information about what you do.
### Part 4: More of the first page that’s about you
Search your business name and look at what comes up. Ideally the first results are all yours — website, Google Business Profile, directory profile, social pages. Every result you own is one a customer can trust and one a competitor’s ad isn’t occupying. A complete directory profile reliably becomes one of those owned results for your name searches — which matters most at the exact moment a referred customer is checking you out before calling. Referrals don’t convert on the recommendation alone; they convert after the quick search that confirms it.
### Part 5: The referral traffic — fewer visitors, better ones
Directories will never out-traffic Google, and anyone claiming otherwise is fibbing. But consider who visits a local directory: someone who came specifically to find a local business to hire. That’s as high-intent as traffic gets. A profile that answers their questions — services, photos, reviews, hours — converts that intent instead of bouncing it. Quality of visitor beats quantity of visitor for a business that needs customers, not pageviews — ten people actively hiring beat a thousand people idly scrolling.
### Part 6: Location and category reach — claimed honestly
A Gold profile can carry up to 40 location tags and 10 business categories, surfacing your business in searches across every community and service you cover — the full mechanics, with a worked example, live in the Up to 400 Keywords section of the Gold Plan page.
The rule that makes this work: claim what you genuinely serve. Most businesses under-claim — they tag three towns and stay invisible in the ten others they’d happily drive to. A metro-wide service company or a destination restaurant legitimately claims dozens of communities, because that’s the truth of its footprint. But padding your tags with towns you’d decline a job in just generates wrong-fit calls and clutter. Accuracy converts; padding doesn’t.
### Part 7: The working extras
The rest of a complete profile is practical machinery: photos that let customers judge your work before calling; reviews you can respond to (on the Gold plan) so your side of every story gets told; coupons and deals that give fence-sitters a reason to choose you today; event and job posts when you have them; and a complimentary QR code that puts your profile one phone-scan away on invoices, signage, and business cards — a genuinely underused bridge between your offline presence and your online one. None of these extras is revolutionary alone; together they turn a static listing into a page that gives customers reasons to choose you today.
### A tale of two profiles
Two electricians, both excellent, both on the directory. The first — call him the Skeleton — entered his name, one phone number, one town, one category, no photos. His profile sits there like an unplugged appliance — technically present, functionally useless. The second — call her the Builder — spent one Tuesday evening: every community from Affton to St. Peters she actually drives to, categories for panel upgrades and EV chargers alongside general electrical, twenty photos of tidy panel work, a description that mentions she answers her own phone.
Six months later the Builder’s profile shows up for her name, for “EV charger installation” searches her website never targeted, and in a dozen towns the Skeleton also serves but never claimed. Same platform, same price, same trade. The difference was one evening of honest completeness — which is the entire thesis of this article in two paragraphs. Platforms don’t pick winners; effort does. So be honest for a second: which one is your business right now — the Builder, or the appliance that’s technically plugged in but quietly doing nothing?
### What a profile honestly cannot do
Fair is fair — here’s the other side of the ledger:
It won’t rescue a bad reputation. A profile amplifies what’s true about your business. If the reviews are rough, fix the operations first.
It won’t replace your website or your Google profile. It’s a complement — one more strong, consistent surface — not a substitute for the others.
It won’t work empty. A name-and-phone-number skeleton produces skeleton results. The value scales with completeness, and completeness costs you an evening plus a couple of hours a month.
It won’t move rankings overnight. Citations and links age into trust. Expect compounding, not fireworks — and know that the compounding is real: reviews accumulate, content ages into authority, and a profile that’s been complete and active for two years carries weight a fresh one can’t fake.
### The compounding curve (and the first-mover truth)
The most under-appreciated property of a maintained profile is that its value curve bends upward. Reviews accumulate and age into credibility. Photos build a visual track record no new competitor can backfill. The citation itself gains historical weight the longer it stays accurate. And as the directory around it grows — more businesses, more visitors, more content — every established profile rides that rising tide.
That’s the honest version of “first-mover advantage”: not a gimmick, just arithmetic. A profile that’s been complete and active since this year will, two years from now, carry signals a brand-new profile simply cannot manufacture. The best time to start was a while ago; the practical time is this week.
Totally unrelated, but — Tower Grove’s food scene deserves your next Friday.
### Who gets the most out of it
Local businesses serving St. Louis-area customers get the full stack: citation, visibility across their real service area, referral traffic, and the owned name-search result. Multi-location businesses with a St. Louis-area presence get location-specific validation for that branch — a citation that confirms to search engines this location is real and open. And early, active members get compounding: profiles that age with the platform accumulate reviews, content, and trust signals that newer listings take time to match. What we’d honestly steer away from: joining a local directory purely as a link-building play with no intention of serving local customers. It’s against the spirit of the platform, and the SEO era that rewarded it is over.
### The fair question for your web developer
If you pay someone to manage your online presence, here’s a reasonable question: “Which local directories and citations have you set up for us, and are they complete and consistent?” A good local-SEO practitioner will have a ready answer — citations are foundational work. If the answer is a blank look, that’s worth a longer conversation about what else the checklist is missing. (Not a gotcha — just diligence. Plenty of excellent web developers focus on the website itself and assume someone else owns the visibility layer. Make sure someone actually does — because the visibility layer is where customers are actually deciding.)
### The one-evening build order
If you’re convinced, here’s the sequence that gets the most value per minute:
First 10 minutes: enter your NAP exactly as it appears on your Google profile and website — character for character. Consistency is the whole point; start there.
Next 15: tag every community you genuinely serve and every category you truly offer. Be honest in both directions.
Next 20: upload fifteen-plus real photos — finished work, your team, your space. Phone photos in daylight beat stock art every time.
Next 10: write the description a customer would want: what you do, where, what makes you different, how fast you respond.
Last 5: put the profile link in your email signature and text your three happiest recent customers a review request.
After that, the maintenance is a couple of hours a month: new photos as work happens, prompt replies, and a seasonal once-over to keep hours and services current.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do directory backlinks still help SEO?
A.  Quality ones do, modestly and honestly: a link from an established, relevant local directory is a legitimate trust and relevance signal, and one more consistent citation for search engines and AI assistants to verify you against. Bulk directory submissions do not help and can hurt — search engines have discounted mass low-quality directory links for years. One good beats fifty junk.
### Q. What makes a directory profile “complete”?
A.  Name, address, and phone exactly matching your other listings; every genuinely-served location and truly-offered category tagged; current hours; a description written for customers rather than keywords; fifteen-plus real photos; and a habit of answering reviews and inquiries quickly. Complete profiles consistently outperform skeletons — the gap is not subtle.
### Q. Can a directory profile really rank on Google by itself?
A.  Yes — a profile is a full page on an established domain, and complete, well-written profiles appear in search results for business-name searches and long-tail service searches, sometimes for phrases your own website doesn’t target. It’s a complement to your website’s rankings, not a replacement for them.
### Q. Is a directory listing worth it if I already have a website and Google profile?
A.  That’s exactly when it’s worth it: you’re adding a third consistent, owned surface — one more citation confirming your details, one more first-page result for your name, one more place high-intent local searchers and AI assistants can find and verify you. Discovery has fragmented; the businesses that win show up consistently in more of the places customers actually look.

## 75 Shops, 70 Searches a Month: Why SEO and Google Ads Fail in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-typical-seo-google-ads-fail
Seventy. That’s about how many times a month people around Florissant search for “hvac near me,” “ac repair near me” or “furnace repair near me,” going by Google Ads’ own 12-month average. Google Maps shows 75 heating and AC businesses within five miles of the town’s center. Roughly one search a month for every shop.
So when the first cold snap frosts the truck windshield before dawn and the phone on the seat beside you stays quiet, Florissant didn’t stop getting cold. The few people searching were split many ways, and they went to whoever Google judged closest and most relevant.
Now look at O’Fallon, Missouri. Same three searches, about 540 a month, with 80 heating and AC businesses within five miles. About the same number of shops; seventy searches in one town, 540 in the other. Those numbers come from St Louis Near Me Directory’s own count, built from Google Ads and Google Maps data pulled in October, and they explain more failed marketing than any agency report ever has.
Nobody on the sales call showed you that math. They sold “St. Louis SEO” and “St. Louis ads” as if St. Louis were one market. It isn’t. St. Louis County alone is cut into 88 municipalities, and Google ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and popularity, with distance meaning how far your business is from the customer who’s searching.
Then the ad defaults made it worse. Every keyword in a Google Ads account starts on broad match unless somebody changes it; Google calls it “the default match type that all your keywords are assigned,” and it lets an ad show on searches that don’t contain the direct meaning of your keywords. Add the location setting Google recommends, “Presence or Interest,” which also reaches people who have only shown an interest in your area, and a small local budget can drain on clicks that were never going to become a service call.
So no, you weren’t too small, too late or “not tech-savvy.” The defaults were set for reach, the promises were set for the sale, and the map was drawn for a market that doesn’t exist. Google’s own pages admit it. Three lines worth taping above the desk:
“No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google.” (Google Search Central)
“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.” (Google Business Profile Help)
Treat unsolicited email about search engines with the same skepticism you’d give “burn fat at night” diet pills. (Google’s own guide to hiring an SEO)
If someone sold you a guarantee, a shortcut onto the map, or page one by next month, you weren’t bad at marketing. You bought something Google says doesn’t exist.
### What “near me” means in a county with 88 towns
You can’t move your shop closer to every customer. Google says there’s no way to pay for a better local ranking, and distance is distance. What you can control is the rest, and it’s less glamorous than any pitch. Relevance is how well your Business Profile matches the search, and Google’s fix is complete, detailed business info. Prominence leans on how many websites link to you and how many reviews you have.
Reviews come with a clock, too. In BrightLocal’s consumer survey, 47% of consumers won’t use a business with fewer than 20 reviews, and 74% only care about reviews written in the last three months. Answer them, and not with a template: 42% are unlikely to use a business that never replies, and generic or templated replies put off 50%. That buzz in your pocket when a new review lands? It’s a stranger in Affton or Ballwin deciding, in public, whether you’re worth the call.
### Why aren’t my Google Ads working?
Start with what you can check tonight, coffee going cold next to the laptop. Open your Google Ads account, go to Keywords, and look at the match type column. If it says broad, your ad is eligible for searches merely related to your words. Then open the search terms report, which shows how your ads did when triggered by actual searches. That list is where the money went, line by line.
Two more settings deserve a hard look before you spend another dollar:
Who counts as local. “Presence or Interest” is Google’s recommended best practice on Search, but its own help page says to consider plain “Presence” when you only want people in specific locations. If your van only runs on this side of the river, that’s you.
What counts as a win. Conversions don’t pick themselves: you choose what you treat as valuable, like a purchase, a sign-up or a phone call. Phone call conversions show which ads are driving valuable phone leads. Skip that step and no report on earth can tell a booked job from a wasted click.
Then stop poking it. Google says Smart Bidding needs a 7-14 day learning phase, and frequent changes to budgets or targets reset the learning window. And when a budget is too small for your settings, Google shows your ads less often. So when an owner asks why are my Google Ads suddenly not working, the answer is usually a setting nobody explained, not a business that can’t be advertised.
Want the whole map, not just the ad settings? Read the St. Louis small-business growth playbook, for owners doing their own marketing.
If you’re the contractor, the salon or the one-truck crew who paid for clicks and heard nothing, run a cheaper test than another contract. Ask who AI recommends for what you do in your part of town, and see whether it’s you. Check who AI recommends near you.
### How long does SEO take, by Google’s own clock?
Most of the frustration lives in the gap between two calendars: the one on the sales call and the one Google publishes. You know the first one. It’s the renewal email that lands the same morning the phone stays quiet.
Google’s version is plainer than any pitch. Every change takes some time to be reflected on Google’s end: some take effect in a few hours, others take several months. Google suggests waiting a few weeks before you judge whether a change helped, and it warns that not every change produces a noticeable impact at all.
Read that twice and two common stories fall apart. The promise of page one in a hurry falls apart, because nobody controls that clock. So does the verdict that “SEO doesn’t work,” handed down after a few quiet weeks. Sometimes the work was wrong. Sometimes it simply hadn’t had time. The way to tell the difference isn’t a prettier chart. It’s the phone.
### The guarantee Google says nobody can make
Maybe it arrived at dinner, the pot still on the stove: a call from a number you didn’t recognize, or an email swearing your business could be on page one. Google’s own guide to hiring an SEO has a list of tells. Be wary of anyone who claims to guarantee rankings, claims a “special relationship” with Google, or advertises a “priority submit” to Google. If an audit promises their changes will put you in first place, Google’s advice is blunt: find someone else. A real audit, Google says, gives you realistic estimates of improvement and of the work involved. And if you let anyone look under the hood, give them read access to Search Console, not write access.
None of that makes the people who signed those contracts foolish. The pitch was built to sound exactly like help, and it was aimed at owners too busy doing the actual work to fact-check it.
### The customer who never opens a search bar
Your next customer may never type a search at all. She asks her phone, out loud, from the passenger seat on the way home: who fixes furnaces near Florissant? BrightLocal’s consumer survey found that use of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in a year, making AI the third most popular source of business recommendations.
That’s the door the old playbook never planned for. Ranking a blue link is one way in. Being the name an assistant repeats is another, and your best bet there is the same groundwork: accurate details everywhere you’re listed, real reviews, and pages that answer real questions. BrightLocal’s own advice to businesses is to keep listings accurate and check the sources AI tools reference.
And no, the fix isn’t a chatbot cranking out pages by the pile. Google says generative AI can help with research and with adding structure to original content, but using it to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate its spam policy on scaled content abuse.
Out in west county? Local SEO in Chesterfield runs on a map of its own.
### How to tell if it’s working, or just billing
Forget the glossy monthly PDF for a minute. Your Google Business Profile already counts the moments that pay rent:
Calls: how many times someone tapped the call button on your profile. Add your phone number, or Google can’t track it.
Directions: how many people asked how to get to you.
Website clicks: how many people clicked through to your site.
Bookings: completed bookings, if you take them through a booking provider.
On the ads side, set phone calls up as a conversion and read the search terms report once a week. Give any SEO change a few weeks before you judge it, as Google suggests. And if a report brags about impressions and rankings but can’t point to a single call, that’s your answer, whatever the arrows say.

Here’s the belief that cost the most money: that a website plus a Google listing equals customers. For years that was close enough. Then the search box turned into a conversation, and people started asking for answers instead of websites. A website is one thread. Winning now means showing up everywhere neighbors and machines look, with your details matching and your work described in plain words.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are common SEO mistakes?
A.  For local businesses, the costly ones are boring: a half-finished Business Profile, too few or stale reviews, replies that sound like templates, and judging results before Google says you should. Google suggests waiting a few weeks to assess a change. The most expensive mistake is paying anyone who guarantees a #1 ranking, because Google says no one can.
### Q. Is SEO dead now with AI?
A.  No, but the front door moved. BrightLocal found use of ChatGPT and other AI tools for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in a year, while Google still ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and popularity. Accurate details, real reviews and pages that answer real questions serve both. What died is the shortcut.
### Q. Can ChatGPT do SEO?
A.  It can help with parts of it. Google says generative AI can be useful for researching a topic and adding structure to original content. But using it to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate Google’s spam policy on scaled content abuse. It also can’t earn your reviews or answer your phone.
### Q. Is SEO paid or free?
A.  Ranking itself can’t be bought: Google says it doesn’t accept payment to rank pages higher, and there’s no way to pay for a better local ranking. What costs money is the work behind it, whether that’s your time or a hired pro’s. Ads are the paid placements, and Google shows them less often when the budget runs short.
### Q. What are the downsides of using SEO?
A.  Mostly time and uncertainty. Google says some changes take several months to be reflected, suggests waiting a few weeks before judging one, and admits not every change makes a noticeable difference. Nobody can guarantee where you’ll rank. The upside: Google doesn’t take payment to rank pages higher, so a bigger budget can’t simply buy your organic spot.
### Q. Why are my Google Ads eligible but not running?
A.  Eligible means the ad was reviewed and is able to run, not that it will win. Google lists the usual culprits: a budget too small for your settings, bids too low to win auctions, an audience too narrow or search volume too low, weak ad relevance, or a learning phase. New campaigns need 1-2 weeks to optimize.
### Q. How difficult is SEO?
A.  The basics aren’t hard; the patience is. Google’s starter guide walks through the most common and effective improvements, and admits not every change will make a noticeable difference. For a local business, most of the work is a complete Business Profile, recent reviews with real replies, and pages that answer what neighbors ask.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for SEO?
A.  It’s a rule of thumb, not a Google rule: a small share of the work drives most of the results. For a St. Louis business that share is usually the Business Profile, reviews and replies, and pages that answer real questions. Google says local results rest mainly on relevance, distance and popularity, so start there.

## 10 Questions Local Business Owners Ask About Online Visibility (Answered Honestly)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/10-questions-local-business-owners-ask-about-online-visibility-answered
Every week we hear the same questions from business owners across Missouri and Illinois — frustrated with ad budgets that evaporated, confused by SEO advice that contradicts itself, and suspicious of anyone promising page one by Friday. Fair enough. The suspicion is earned; this industry has done a lot of over-promising. So let’s do the opposite of over-promising and answer plainly — starting with the one every owner quietly wonders: why can the competitor down the street get found when you can’t?
So here are the ten questions owners actually ask us, answered the way we’d want them answered if we were on your side of the desk: straight, specific, and honest about both what works and what it costs you in effort. No fake ROI tables, no magic buttons.
### 1. “Why can’t potential customers find my business online?”
Short answer: you’re invisible in the searches that matter — and it’s almost never about the quality of your work.
When someone types “emergency plumber near me” or asks an AI assistant for a restaurant recommendation, they’re not browsing — they’re choosing. If you don’t appear, the choice happens without you. The usual culprits: your information doesn’t match across the web, you’re present on fewer surfaces than competitors, your reviews are stale or unanswered, your profiles are skeletons, and nothing you’ve published answers the questions customers actually ask. We wrote a full six-reason diagnostic with a self-scoring checklist — ten minutes there will tell you exactly which reasons apply to you.
### 2. “I spent $5,000 on Google Ads with terrible results. What went wrong?”
Short answer: probably nothing unusual — ads are an auction, and auctions are expensive for the unprepared.
Here’s the honest version, without the horror-story math some marketers use: Google Ads genuinely works for many businesses, but it’s a skill-intensive auction. Click prices in competitive local categories run high, budgets drain fast without careful keyword and negative-keyword management, and a slow website quietly wastes every click you buy. If nobody was actively managing your campaign, mediocre results are the expected outcome, not bad luck.
The structural thing to understand: ads rent visibility. The day you stop paying, it’s gone. That doesn’t make ads bad — it makes them a tool for moments when you need volume now and have someone skilled at the wheel. The complement is owned visibility: profiles, reviews, content, and citations that keep working after the spend stops. Most resilient local businesses eventually run on the owned foundation, with ads as an accelerant when it makes sense — not the other way around.
When do ads make sense? Honestly: when you’re new and need calls before organic visibility matures, when you’re filling a slow season, or when you’ve got a high-value service where one job covers a month of clicks — and in every case, only with someone competent watching the campaign weekly. If none of those describe you, fix the free foundation first. (For the full channel-by-channel map — including offline options and where the first 00 a month should go — see our local marketing strategies guide.)
### 3. “What about SEO? Everyone says I need SEO.”
Short answer: you need the fundamentals, which are free; whether you need an agency depends on your ambitions and your patience.
The honest timeline nobody advertises: meaningful SEO results typically build over months, not weeks, and no honest practitioner guarantees rankings — Google’s own updates reshuffle results regularly. Agency retainers commonly run from hundreds to thousands per month, and quality varies wildly.
The good news: the highest-return work is the unglamorous stuff you can do yourself — consistent business information everywhere (our citations guide is the one-afternoon version), complete profiles, real reviews, and a handful of pages that answer your most-asked customer questions. One legitimate shortcut: platforms that already carry authority. A complete profile on an established local directory gets indexed and surfaced far faster than a new website earns rankings on its own — it’s borrowing a running start rather than building alone in an empty field.
### 4. “How can one listing appear in multiple cities?”
Short answer: location tags and category tags — and the honest rule is to claim exactly what you genuinely serve.
On St Louis Near Me Directory, a Gold profile can carry up to 40 location tags and 10 business categories, which means your one profile can surface in searches across every community and every service you actually cover — the mechanics, with a worked example, are laid out in the Up to 400 Keywords section of the Gold Plan page.
The key word is genuinely. This cuts both ways:
Most businesses under-claim. A typical owner tags three or four towns and stops — then wonders why the next suburb over never calls. If you’d happily take the job in Fenton, Fenton should be able to find you.
A metro-wide business should claim metro-wide. An HVAC company that trucks to every corner of the region, or a destination restaurant that draws diners from across both states, is genuinely a 30-or-40-community business — claiming that footprint isn’t inflation, it’s accuracy.
Nobody should claim towns they wouldn’t serve. Tagging communities you’d decline a job in doesn’t bring customers; it brings wrong-fit calls, disappointed neighbors, and clutter. Accuracy converts; padding doesn’t.
Same with categories: list every service you truly offer — a remodeler legitimately spans kitchens, bathrooms, and basements — and skip the ones you’d subcontract away. (The full setup walkthrough — steps, mistakes, and honest economics — is in our complete guide to multi-location listings.)
### 5. “This sounds good. What’s the catch?”
Short answer: the catch is that you have to do the work.
A directory profile isn’t a customer machine you switch on. The businesses that get real results build a complete profile, upload real photos, actively request reviews, answer inquiries fast, and refresh things monthly. The ones that create a bare listing and vanish get bare-listing results. The platform provides reach and structure; the effort is yours. Anyone who tells you otherwise — about any marketing channel — is selling the dream instead of the tool.
### 6. “How do I know if this will work for MY business?”
Short answer: three yes/no questions settle it.
Do potential customers search online (or ask AI assistants) for businesses like yours? For nearly every home-service, professional, health, restaurant, retail, automotive, and personal-care business, yes.
Do you serve customers across multiple communities? Then multi-location visibility applies to you.
Can you invest a few hours up front and a couple of hours a month after? Then you can execute it.
Where it’s honestly a poor fit: pure e-commerce with no local component, ultra-niche B2B serving a handful of national clients, or any owner who truly won’t touch the profile after day one. Better to know that now.
### 7. “What results should I realistically expect?”
Short answer: we won’t hand you a fake ROI table — results vary too much by industry, competition, and effort to promise numbers.
What we can say honestly: businesses with complete profiles, steady reviews, and fast response times consistently outperform bare listings — not by a little — and visibility compounds, because reviews accumulate, content ages into authority, and familiarity breeds referrals. Early weeks are about being findable and trustworthy; the payoff curve builds over months.
The discipline that makes results visible: ask every new customer how they found you, and write it down. Attribution is the difference between knowing a channel works and guessing. If after a few months of genuine effort nothing is moving, diagnose before abandoning — usually one of the six reasons from question 1 is still unfixed — and it’s fixable this week.
Early signals it’s working, before the revenue shows: profile views trending up in your dashboard, calls that start with “I found you online,” review count climbing, and your business appearing when you run the logged-out self-search — and, increasingly, when you ask an AI assistant who it recommends in your category.
### 8. “How do I actually get started?”
Short answer: one focused first week.
Day 1: Create your profile — name, location, contact, logo, a two-sentence description. Live in minutes.
Day 2: Expand the description to a genuine 200–300 words, complete hours and service area, connect your socials.
Day 3: Tag every community you genuinely serve and every category you truly offer (see question 4 for the honest rule).
Day 4: Upload 15–25 real photos — your work, your team, your space. Phone photos in good light beat stock every time.
Day 5: Create one honest offer (a first-visit discount, a free consultation) and ask your three happiest recent customers for a review.
After that: a couple of hours a month keeping it current, answering inquiries fast, and adding photos as work happens. That cadence is the whole maintenance plan.
Random, but: here’s every business in Ballwin, all at once.
### 9. “What mistakes should I avoid?”
Short answer: the fatal one is the bare listing; the sneaky ones are below.
Claiming less than you serve — invisible in the suburbs that would happily hire you.
Claiming more than you serve — wrong-fit calls and clutter that helps nobody, starting with you.
Three dark, blurry photos — customers judge your work by your pictures long before they call.
A description that could be anyone’s — if a competitor could paste their name over yours, rewrite it.
No review habit — the competitor with thirty answered reviews wins the tie every time.
Set-it-and-forget-it — stale profiles fade; fifteen minutes a week keeps yours alive.
Never promoting your own profile — put the link in your email signature, your receipts, your counter QR code.
Slow replies — the customer who messaged three businesses hires the one who answered first.
Ignoring your analytics — the dashboard tells you which towns and categories pull; double down there.
No attribution question — “how’d you find us?” is four words that justify (or redirect) every marketing dollar you spend.
### 10. “How is this different from Yelp, Angi, or HomeAdvisor?”
Short answer: different models, honestly described — per-lead resale, ad-boosted review platforms, and owned profiles are three different deals.
Lead-resale platforms take a customer’s request and sell it to several businesses at once, charging each per lead — you pay whether or not the job closes, and you’re bidding against everyone who bought the same lead. That model suits businesses that want volume and can absorb the per-lead economics; it builds no lasting asset.
Review platforms with paid placement offer free listings, with paid tiers for prominence — and on many of them, competitors’ ads can appear on your own profile page. Useful reach, limited control.
An owned directory profile is a fixed, flat cost — the Gold plan runs $29.75/month paid annually — for a page you control completely: your locations, your categories, your photos, your content, no competitor ads on your page, no per-lead meter. Every review and photo you add builds an asset that keeps working.
None of these are scams and none are magic; they’re different economics. Our bias is obvious — we built the owned model because we think local businesses deserve an asset instead of a meter — but the honest advice is to know exactly which deal you’re accepting from each platform you use.
### The pattern across all ten
Read the answers back and one theme repeats: completeness, honesty, and consistency beat cleverness every single time. Complete information beats scattered brilliance. Honest claims — the towns you truly serve, the services you truly offer, the results you can truly expect — convert better than inflated ones and never blow up on you later. And consistent, boring maintenance outperforms heroic weekend sprints followed by silence.
That’s also why this work is genuinely available to every owner reading this: none of it requires a budget you don’t have or expertise you can’t learn in an afternoon. It requires deciding that being findable is part of running the business — the same way answering the phone is. The owners who internalize that stop chasing tricks — and quietly start winning the searches their competitors still think are luck.

### Q. How can I list multiple locations on my Google Business profile?
A.  Each staffed location needs its own profile, managed together under a business group. What you cannot do is make one profile appear across several cities — that is the distinction people miss, and attempting it is a common route to suspension.

### Q. How do I show multiple locations on maps?
A.  For a business, that means separate verified profiles per location rather than pins on one map. For a route or a service area, a custom map layer does it — but a custom map does not help you rank, which is usually the real question underneath.
### Q. How do I map a bunch of addresses at once?
A.  Bulk-import them into a custom map from a spreadsheet with one address per row. Useful for planning routes or visualising coverage. It is a private planning tool though — it does not create business listings or affect what customers find when they search.
### Q. How do I show two locations in a map?
A.  Add both as separate points on a custom map, or if they are business premises, hold two verified profiles. The second is what customers actually search; the first is for you. Do not substitute one for the other.

## Soul Food in St. Louis: Who's Still Open, and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/soul-food-in-st-louis
Every few months someone posts the same question to the St. Louis subreddit: where do you get good soul food here? The replies are always long, always contradictory, and always contain at least three places that have closed.
There’s a reason for the confusion. This city lost an unusual number of its best-known soul food restaurants in a short stretch — and the guides never caught up. One of the most-linked lists for this search was published in 2017.
So here is a current one. Every restaurant below was checked against its live business listing this week, and the ones that are gone are named so you don’t go looking.
### Where is the best soul food in St. Louis?
Gourmet Soul (1620 Delmar Blvd) is the most decorated — its chef won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown — though it keeps limited weekend hours. Diner’s Delight (1504 S Compton Ave) is the South City institution, with well over a thousand reviews. C&K Barbecue (4390 Jennings Station Rd) has been serving snoots and rib tips since 1963. Cathy’s Kitchen (250 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson) is the north county standard. For something different, SweetArt (3701 Lindell Blvd) does soul food entirely plant-based.
### The city
Diner’s Delight, 1504 S Compton Ave. If one place is the answer to the Reddit question, it’s probably this one — a South City fixture with more reviews than almost anything else in this category and a rating that has held up under all of them. Fried chicken, catfish, the sides, the desserts.
Gourmet Soul, 1620 Delmar Blvd, Downtown West. Chef Lavinia McCoy won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown, and the menu leans upscale — lamb chops, an Old Bay bowl — rather than traditional. The catch is the schedule: their published hours run Friday through Sunday only, so this is a weekend plan, not a Tuesday one.
Karsyn Soule’ 2.0, 635 Washington Ave. Downtown, newer, and worth knowing about precisely because it’s new enough that it hasn’t reached most lists yet.
Your Place Diner, 5510 Virginia Ave. A family-run South City spot that describes itself simply as a place to eat, drink and gather. High marks from the people who go.
Mom’s Soul Food Kitchen & Catering, 1507 Goodfellow Blvd. Close to twelve hundred reviews, which in this category means it has been feeding the same neighborhood for a long time.
SweetArt, 3701 Lindell Blvd, is the outlier and the one to try if you think you already know what soul food is. It’s entirely plant-based — the collards, the mac, the sweets, all of it, without the meat that traditionally carries the flavor. Doing that well is genuinely difficult, and the reviews suggest they manage it.
### North county
North county has the deepest bench in the metro for this food, and it is the part of the map most guides skip.
C&K Barbecue, 4390 Jennings Station Rd, opened in 1963 and has been family-operated ever since. Snoots — crisp-fried pig snouts — are the order here, and they are close to a St. Louis-only dish. Rib tips too. Sixteen hundred reviews and counting.
Cathy’s Kitchen, 250 S Florissant Rd in Ferguson, opened in 2013 and became something more than a restaurant in the years after. Diner food, soul food and seafood. There’s now a carryout counter as well, Cathy’s Kitchen ToGo at 10198 W Florissant Ave in Dellwood, which opened on Juneteenth 2024.
Son-Ja’s Soul Food, 9841 W Florissant Ave. Carryout-focused, and it now serves breakfast — chicken and waffles, shrimp and grits, salmon croquettes with buttered rice — which is a rarer thing here than you’d expect.
Ol’ Henry Restaurant, 8600 Airport Rd. Long-standing, and busy enough to have accumulated close to a thousand reviews.
Chef Daddy’s, 9617 St Charles Rock Rd in Breckenridge Hills, rounds out the northwest corner.
### What St. Louis lost
This is the part that explains the confusion, and it’s worth reading before you trust any other list.
Sweetie Pie’s is the obvious one. The restaurant that put St. Louis soul food on national television closed its last location in 2022. There is a revival in the works — Sweetie Pie’s 2nd Act, announced for north city with a $1.5 million city grant and a banner already up — but it has not opened and no date has been given.
Ms. Piggies’ Smokehouse on Page closed when the Matthews family retired around Thanksgiving 2024. Brother’s Diner on Whittier, which appears near the top of that widely-linked 2017 guide, is permanently closed. Turn in Midtown closed at the end of May when its chef relocated to Little Rock.
Four well-loved kitchens in roughly two years. That’s the honest shape of this scene right now — not thriving, not dead, but thinner than it was, with the survivors carrying more weight.
It’s also why the remaining ones are worth actually going to rather than bookmarking.
### Why this food is here at all
Soul food in St. Louis isn’t a transplant or a trend. It arrived the same way most of north St. Louis did — up the Mississippi.
During and after the Second World War, hundreds of thousands of Black families left the rural South for Northern cities with wartime factory work, part of the movement historians call the Great Migration. St. Louis sat at the top of the river, which made it a natural destination for people leaving Mississippi, Arkansas and Tennessee. The founders of C&K Barbecue, Forris and Lucille King, made exactly that trip from Mississippi during the war years and opened their restaurant in 1963.
That’s why the food here looks the way it does. The catfish is a river fish from the Delta. The greens and the cornbread are Southern farm cooking. And the snoots are what happens when a cuisine built on using every part of the animal meets a city with a working meatpacking trade — a genuinely local dish that exists because two histories overlapped in one place.
It also explains the geography of this list. The restaurants cluster in north city and north county because that is where those families settled, and the kitchens stayed where the neighborhoods were.
### Where you won’t find much
Worth saying plainly so you don’t drive in circles: south county, west county and the Metro East have very little.
A handful of names come up on the Illinois side and in the western suburbs, but we could not confirm enough about them this week to send you there. If you’re in Chesterfield or Belleville and you want this food, the realistic move is a drive into the city or up to north county — and it’s worth the drive rather than settling.
### What to order if you didn’t grow up on it
Soul food isn’t a single menu, and ordering badly is an easy way to decide you don’t like something you’d actually love.
The reliable first order almost anywhere is fried chicken with two sides — because the sides are where a kitchen shows what it can do. Collard greens tell you whether they cook with patience. Macaroni and cheese tells you whether they bake it or shortcut it. Cornbread tells you whether it’s a Southern kitchen or a Northern one; sweeter and cakier leans north, denser and less sweet leans south.
Wildly off-topic — Washington Park, Illinois has a lunch scene worth the bridge.
If you want the specifically St. Louis thing, order snoots at C&K. They’re pig snouts fried until they shatter, they came out of using every part of the animal, and they stayed on menus here because people genuinely love them. You will not find them in most American cities.
Catfish is the other regional marker — a Mississippi River staple that came upriver with the families who brought this food to St. Louis in the first place.
### If you’re feeding a crowd
A large share of what these kitchens actually do never shows up on a restaurant list, because it leaves through the back door.
Several here are catering operations as much as restaurants — it’s in the business name at both Gourmet Soul Restaurant and Catering and Mom’s Soul Food Kitchen & Catering. This is the food people in St. Louis order for repasts, church functions, graduations and holidays, and the kitchens are built for it.
If you’re planning something, call further ahead than you think you need to, particularly around Thanksgiving and the December holidays, when these places book out. And ask about trays rather than reading the dine-in menu — the catering side is frequently a different list at a different price.
### A note on hours
More than any other category we cover, soul food restaurants here keep hours that will catch you out. Several are carryout-first. At least one runs Friday to Sunday only. Some close in the late afternoon rather than the evening, because they cook until they sell out and then they’re done.
That is not disorganization — it’s a lot of these places being genuinely small operations. But it does mean a phone call before you drive is worth more here than almost anywhere else, particularly on Sundays and Mondays.
Two questions worth settling first: what is St. Louis style soul food, given the city has its own name attached to half the local menu, and what are the most common soul foods you should expect to see on a plate here. The answer to both is continuity, not invention.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Sweetie Pie's still open in St. Louis?
A.  No. Sweetie Pie’s closed its last St. Louis location in 2022. A revival called Sweetie Pie’s 2nd Act has been announced for north St. Louis with a $1.5 million city grant and signage on the building, but it is not open and no opening date has been announced.
### Q. What soul food restaurants in St. Louis have closed recently?
A.  Sweetie Pie’s closed in 2022, Ms. Piggies’ Smokehouse closed when its owners retired around Thanksgiving 2024, Turn in Midtown closed at the end of May 2026, and Brother’s Diner on Whittier Street is permanently closed. All four still appear on older guides.
### Q. What are snoots and where can I get them in St. Louis?
A.  Snoots are pig snouts fried until crisp — a St. Louis specialty that barely exists elsewhere in the country. C&K Barbecue at 4390 Jennings Station Rd, open since 1963, is the best-known place to order them, usually alongside rib tips.
### Q. Is there vegan or plant-based soul food in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. SweetArt at 3701 Lindell Blvd serves entirely plant-based soul food and baked goods, and has been operating since 2008. It is the only fully plant-based soul food kitchen we could verify in the metro.
### Q. Where can I get soul food in north St. Louis County?
A.  North county has the deepest selection: C&K Barbecue (4390 Jennings Station Rd), Cathy’s Kitchen in Ferguson plus its Dellwood carryout, Son-Ja’s Soul Food (9841 W Florissant Ave), Ol’ Henry (8600 Airport Rd) and Chef Daddy’s in Breckenridge Hills.
### Q. Where can I get soul food breakfast in St. Louis?
A.  Son-Ja’s Soul Food at 9841 W Florissant Ave now serves breakfast, including chicken and waffles, shrimp and grits, and salmon croquettes with buttered rice. Soul food breakfast is uncommon in the metro, so call to confirm the days before going.
### Q. What should I order at a soul food restaurant for the first time?
A.  Fried chicken with two sides is the reliable first order, because the sides show what a kitchen can do — collard greens reveal patience, macaroni and cheese reveals whether it’s baked or shortcut. Catfish is the regional marker, and snoots are the specifically St. Louis order.
### Q. What is St. Louis style soul food?
A.  There is no separate regional style the way there is with pizza or ribs. What you get here is the food that traveled up the Mississippi with the families who moved north, cooked close to how it was cooked further south, with local barbecue habits bleeding into it at the edges.
### Q. What are the most common soul foods?
A.  Fried chicken, smothered pork chops, oxtails, catfish, and greens cooked long with smoked meat. Sides carry as much weight as the entree — mac and cheese, candied yams, cornbread and dressing. A plate is usually one meat and two or three sides, and the sides are where kitchens separate themselves.
### Q. Where can I go to get some good soul food?
A.  The city and north county hold most of it, and this guide is organized that way rather than as a ranking. Check hours before you drive — several of these kitchens close when the food runs out, which is a good sign and an inconvenient one.
### Q. What food should I try in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  The standard list is toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, St. Louis-style pizza and ribs. Soul food belongs on it and rarely makes the tourist version, which is part of why this guide exists — a plate of greens and smothered chops tells you more about the city than a novelty slice does.
