## Your Card Won’t Open the MetroLink Gate: St. Louis Public Transit, the $1 Bus and the $5 Day
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-essential-guide-to-getting-around-st-louis-by-public-transit
Tap a credit card on a MetroLink validator and nothing happens. No green flash, no beep, no open gate. On the other side, the train you hurried for pulls away without you.
That’s the newest trap in St. Louis transit. Every MetroLink station now sits behind automated security gates that open only for a fare you’ve validated, and Metro’s validators don’t accept tap to pay from credit or debit cards. The gate doesn’t care that your card works everywhere else in town.
The bus has a surprise too, a kinder one. The whole cash fare on a MetroBus is $1.00. Smooth the bill flat on your knee, feed it into the farebox, and you’re riding. Have it exact, because operators can’t make change.
One move handles both, so do it before you leave the house: download the free Transit app, set up Tap & Ride, and let fare capping do the math. Metro caps what you pay at the price of a pass, so a day of riding never costs more than $5 and a month never more than $78. Two train rides at $2.50 each already reach that $5. Every ride after that, the same day, costs nothing.
The rest of this guide is the neighbor-to-neighbor version of Metro Transit: which train goes where, what each ride really costs, the stop for the Arch and the Zoo, the free parking most drivers never use, and the help that exists if a regular bus or train isn’t workable for you.
### Does St. Louis have light rail downtown?
Yes. When the windows go black for a stretch and the rumble gets louder, you’re in the Union Station Tunnel, which Metro says is more than 130 years old. That’s older than anyone you’ll sit next to.
MetroLink is the region’s light rail: 46 miles of track and 38 stations, 27 in Missouri and 11 in Illinois. Downtown you can board at Union Station, Civic Center, Stadium, 8th & Pine, Convention Center and Laclede’s Landing, then cross into Illinois at East Riverfront.
There are two lines, and the train tells you which is which. Look for the red or blue sign on the front and sides of the cars before you step on.
Red Line: Lambert Airport Terminal #1 in Missouri to Shiloh-Scott in Illinois. This is the airport train.
Blue Line: Shrewsbury-Lansdowne I-44 in Missouri to Fairview Heights in Illinois.
Shared track: both lines stop at every station between Forest Park-DeBaliviere and Fairview Heights. If you need to switch lines, Forest Park-DeBaliviere is where you change trains.
Trains run seven days a week from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m. Once you’re aboard, the operator announces each upcoming station and a route map hangs in every car, so nobody has to count stops with their nose against the window.
### What a ride costs, and the cap that stops the meter
A green flash and a short beep at the validator mean your fare worked. What that beep cost you depends on how you paid. Metro’s fare table is short enough to memorize on the walk to the stop:
MetroBus, cash: $1.00 (reduced fare $0.50)
MetroLink, cash: $2.50 (reduced fare $1.25)
One-Day Pass, bus and rail: $5.00
7-Day Pass: $27.00
30-Day Pass: $78.00 (reduced fare $39.00)
Metro Call-A-Ride: $2.00
Children 4 and younger ride free and kids 5 to 12 pay half, with no special pass needed, though someone may ask for proof of age. Riders 65 and older ride MetroBus and MetroLink for half price with a Senior Reduced Fare Permit, which you get through Metro’s ADA Services office at 314-982-1510.
Now the part the fare table doesn’t shout about. With Tap & Ride, you load money onto a balance in the Transit app or on a reloadable Ride On card, and each time you board, the validator draws the fare from it. Fare capping runs on top of that automatically: once what you’ve paid reaches the price of the pass that would have been your best deal, the charging stops. You never have to guess on Monday whether this week is a 7-Day Pass week. The system works it out for you, and you never have to front $78 at once to get the monthly price.
The one-day version is the one visitors feel. Ride the train downtown in the morning, out to the Delmar Loop for lunch, and back to your hotel at night. That’s three train rides, and with Tap & Ride the third one is free.
Bus fare, counted in coins
### How much does it cost to ride the MetroBus in St. Louis?
A MetroBus ride is $1.00 in cash, or $0.50 at the reduced fare with a Metro permit. What moves your total is how often you ride: with Tap & Ride, Metro stops charging at $5 for a day and $78 for a month, and children 4 and younger always ride free.
### How to pay for a St. Louis MetroBus?
You have three ways, and one of them needs no phone at all.
Exact cash. The farebox takes bills and coins. Operators can’t make change, so whatever bill goes in stays in.
The Transit app. Buy a ticket or set up Tap & Ride (look for “Pay with QR code”), then scan the QR code at the validator as you board. Metro charges no service fee for fares bought on your phone.
A Ride On card. Ticket vending machines at every MetroLink station and Metro transit center sell them. Load a Tap & Ride balance or a 7-Day or 30-Day Pass and tap the card on the validator.
If you qualify for a reduced fare, show your reduced-fare ID to the operator before you pay.
Can a single-ride ticket carry you onto a second bus? Don’t count on it. Metro’s own mobile-fare page says paper transfers are suspended, so there’s no transfer slip coming with your dollar. If your trip needs two buses, Tap & Ride is the cleaner answer, because the $5 daily cap means changing buses all afternoon can never cost more than a day pass.
Catching the bus itself has its own little rhythm. Get to the stop at least five minutes early. As the bus rolls up, check that the lighted sign above the windshield shows your route number, then stand or raise a hand so the operator knows you’re boarding. Operators call out major intersections along the way. When your stop is close, pull the cord that runs above the windows or press the strip between them, and you can step off through the front or rear door.
Fare sorted? Now pick somewhere worth riding to. Our season-by-season guide to St. Louis festivals and annual events lays out the big ones, so you can plan which train to catch.
If you’re the coffee counter, the bookshop or the lunch spot a few blocks from a MetroLink station, think about the rider stepping off the train and asking a phone where to eat nearby. Whose name does it say? If it isn’t yours, that rider walks past your door to someone else’s. See who AI names instead of you.
### Which stop for the Arch, the Zoo and the City Museum?
Metro’s own exploring guide matches the big attractions to a station or a bus route. Save this list to your phone:
Gateway Arch National Park and the riverboats: Laclede’s Landing MetroLink Station.
City Museum: Convention Center MetroLink Station, or the #97 Delmar bus.
Union Station, the aquarium and the St. Louis Wheel: Union Station MetroLink Station, or the #11 Chippewa.
Saint Louis Zoo, Saint Louis Art Museum and the Missouri History Museum: Forest Park-DeBaliviere, or the #90 Hampton. Metro calls the Zoo always-free, so the train fare can be the only ticket you buy that day.
Saint Louis Science Center: Central West End, or the #59 Oakland.
Delmar Loop: the Delmar Loop station, or buses #2, #16, #91 and #97.
The Fabulous Fox, South Grand and Tower Grove Park: the #70 Grand.
Missouri Botanical Garden: the #8 Shaw-Cherokee.
Soulard Farmers Market: the #30 Arsenal or #73 Carondelet.
### Your ticket doubles as a coupon
Here’s a perk worth knowing. Metro’s Destination Deals program partners with local merchants to give special discounts to Metro riders. Show a current pass or a same-day ticket when you visit. On the list today: 10% off tickets bought at the Aquarium or Wheel ticket office at Union Station, and 25% off scoops at Jeni’s Splendid Ice Creams. That’s a cold scoop dripping down the cone on the walk back to the station, at 25% less. Merchants change, so check the current list on Metro’s Destination Deals page before you go.
Every MetroBus, MetroLink train and Call-A-Ride van also carries free Wi-Fi. Join the network called “Metro Public Wi-Fi” and accept the terms. It’s a public, unencrypted network, so save the banking for later.
Off the Red Line entirely: Local SEO in Troy decides which Troy shops show first.
### The airport run, the free parking and this fall’s detours
Suitcase wheels clattering across a Park-Ride lot at dawn, a free parking space behind you: that’s how a flight from the Illinois side can start without a parking bill. The Red Line is how you fly out of Lambert from there. Metro runs free Park-Ride lots at 24 locations, and nine MetroLink stations hold free long-term spaces for up to 14 days, first come, first served: Shrewsbury-Lansdowne I-44, Brentwood I-64, Emerson Park, Washington Park, Fairview Heights, Swansea, Belleville, College and Shiloh-Scott. Leave the car at Shiloh-Scott, roll your suitcase onto a Red Line train, and the same line carries you to the airport.
Check the calendar before you try it this season, though. Metro has closed the Lambert Airport Terminal #1 station since October 12 for airport construction, with free shuttles running between Terminal #2 and Terminal #1 that add a few minutes to the trip. The Terminal #2 station closes November 2. Metro expects the Terminal #1 work to be finished in mid-December. The Terminal #2 work is also expected to wrap up in mid-December, and Metro says it will share how riders can connect closer to that closure.
The Blue Line changes the same day. From November 2 through December 23, Blue Line trains run only between Shrewsbury-Lansdowne I-44 and Forest Park-DeBaliviere while crews work in the Union Station Tunnel. Blue Line riders headed east switch to a Red Line train at Forest Park-DeBaliviere. Expect a train every 20 minutes and allow at least 5 extra minutes if you’re changing lines. Check Metro’s Rider Alerts page before you ride, or let the Transit app send rider alerts to your phone.
Coming in by train instead? Amtrak’s St. Louis stop is the Gateway Transportation Center at 430 S. 15th St., which Amtrak describes as an intermodal facility serving Amtrak, light rail, and intercity and local buses.
### Is it safe to take the MetroLink in St. Louis?
A late train, a quiet platform, your own footsteps a little too loud: that’s when the safety question stops being abstract. Nobody can promise you a perfect ride on any city’s transit, so here is what’s actually in place. Every MetroLink station now sits behind automated security gates that open only for a validated fare. Dispatchers watch every MetroLink platform on closed-circuit cameras around the clock and can call for security or police right away. Cameras also cover Park-Ride lots, stairwells, trains, buses and vans. Security guards and fare inspectors patrol trains, stations and transit centers, backed by officers from the St. Louis County Police Department, the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, the St. Louis City Sheriff’s Department and the St. Clair County Sheriff’s Department.
If something feels wrong, Metro Public Safety answers 24 hours a day: call 314-289-6873 or text 314-300-0188. And if your fare is good but the gate won’t budge, look for the nearby Passenger Assistance Telephone, a blue pillar with call buttons.
### When a regular bus or train isn’t the right fit
Coat on, keys in hand, watching the street through the front window for a van: that’s what a Call-A-Ride morning looks like, so here’s how to make the wait short and the ride sure.
Metro Call-A-Ride is the paratransit service for riders whose disabilities keep them off MetroBus and MetroLink. Its wheelchair-lift vans cover St. Louis City and St. Louis County, curb to curb. Book at 314-982-1505 (Relay Missouri at 711), any day including holidays, from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Have the rider’s full name, home address, phone number and the exact pickup and drop-off addresses ready. Metro may schedule your trip up to an hour before or after the time you asked for, and you get a 30-minute pickup window. Be at the door, coat on, at the start of that window. Cancel at least two hours ahead or it counts as a no-show. To check a van or cancel by text, use 314-742-3051. It’s a shared ride, so the van may stop for other passengers on the way.
On The Way With ADA is the money-saver most people miss. If you’re a qualified ADA paratransit rider, you can ride MetroBus and MetroLink for free with an On The Way With ADA card. Metro is phasing out the old red Gateway Cards, so if you still carry one, ask ADA Services at 314-982-1510 about the new card. Call the same number about Metro’s travel training, where trainers teach riders with disabilities to pay a fare, cross streets safely, spot landmarks, recognize bus numbers and handle an emergency, until riding alone feels normal.
Via Metro STL fills gaps in parts of North, South and West St. Louis County. You hail a shared van in the Via app, or by phone at 636-251-3328, and a ride is $2 with a seven-mile limit. If you need a ride to a doctor rather than a ballgame, our guide to free and low-cost rides to medical appointments covers the options built for that.
### Who to call, including the number that works at midnight
Midnight, a bus shelter, cold hands in your pockets, and no idea whether the next bus is two minutes out or forty. One of these numbers fixes that.
Transit Information (trip plans, schedules, transfers, walking directions): 314-231-2345 or 618-271-2345, text 314-207-9786, Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Next bus, any hour: call 314-231-2345, press 1, and enter the Stop ID printed at the top of every MetroBus stop sign. You’ll hear the next three arrival times for your route.
Customer Service and lost items: 314-982-1406 or 618-271-7879, text 314-669-8576.
Ride On card help: 314-982-1424, weekdays 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. and weekends 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Metro Public Safety, 24/7: 314-289-6873, text 314-300-0188.
Hearing impaired: Relay Missouri at 711.
Bringing a bike? Every MetroBus has a two-bike rack, first come, first served, and riders 13 and older can roll a bike onto MetroLink.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Does STL have public transportation?
A.  Yes. Metro Transit runs MetroLink light rail, two lines and 38 stations across Missouri and Illinois, plus 58 MetroBus routes and Metro Call-A-Ride paratransit vans. Via Metro STL adds $2 shared rides in parts of North, South and West St. Louis County. The Transit app plans trips across all of it.
### Q. Is MetroLink free in St. Louis?
A.  Not for most riders: a MetroLink ride is $2.50 in cash. It is free for children 4 and younger, and for qualified ADA paratransit riders through the On The Way With ADA program. With Tap & Ride, every ride after you reach $5 in a day costs nothing.
### Q. How much is MetroLink in St. Louis?
A.  A single MetroLink ride is $2.50, or $1.25 at the reduced fare with a Metro permit. A One-Day Pass is $5.00, a 7-Day Pass $27.00 and a 30-Day Pass $78.00, all good on buses too. Tap & Ride caps your spending at those pass prices automatically.
### Q. Is St. Louis MetroLink 24 hours?
A.  No. MetroLink runs seven days a week from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m., so plan a late return before the last train. For buses, the automated line at 314-231-2345 (press 1, then the Stop ID) reads out the next three arrivals at any hour.
### Q. Can I take a bus with a debit card?
A.  Not by tapping it. Metro’s validators don’t accept tap to pay with debit or credit cards. Pay exact cash in the farebox, buy a ticket or set up Tap & Ride in the Transit app, or load a Ride On card at a ticket vending machine before you board.
### Q. Is the transit app not free anymore?
A.  The Transit app Metro recommends is still a free download from the Apple App Store and Google Play. Metro says it charges no service fees for fares you buy through mobile, and the app also shows real-time bus locations, rider alerts and trip plans that mix MetroLink, MetroBus and Via.
### Q. How to ride the MetroLink in St. Louis?
A.  Buy your fare in the Transit app or at a station ticket machine. Scan your QR code or tap your card on the validator in front of the security gate, then walk through. Check the red or blue sign on the train, listen for station announcements, and change lines at Forest Park-DeBaliviere.
### Q. Can a single-ride MetroBus ticket be used to transfer to another bus?
A.  Don’t count on it. Metro’s mobile-fare page says paper transfers are suspended, so a $1.00 cash fare covers your ride, not a transfer slip. If you need two buses, Tap & Ride is cheaper insurance: Metro’s fare capping stops charging once you reach the $5.00 One-Day Pass price.

## Promised the Kids Garden Glow on Christmas Night? It's Closed. Here's What's Lit
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-ultimate-guide-to-christmas-events-in-st-louis-for-2025
Millions of lights, and your kid has gone completely quiet. Your breath hangs in the air, wood smoke drifts over from the s’mores pits, and the path through the Missouri Botanical Garden glows end to end. Somebody behind you says “oh” out loud, then laughs at themselves. That’s Garden Glow on a December night, and it’s the first thing to book, because the Garden says its tickets sell out well in advance, especially from mid-December through Jan. 1.
Now the part that wrecks Christmas plans every year: the Garden’s own visitor page lists Garden Glow as closed Dec. 24 and 25 this season, and Winterfest’s schedule skips Christmas Day too. The lights still burning that night are mostly the ones you watch through a windshield. WonderLight’s at World Wide Technology Raceway posts “open nightly, including holidays,” and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka lists Christmas Day hours of 5:30 to 10 p.m. Kids in pajamas in the back seat, the defroster roaring, the lights pulsing in time to your car radio. Christmas night rule of thumb: if you have to walk it, it’s probably closed; if you can stay in the car, it’s probably open.
The free one almost nobody mentions: from Dec. 27 to 30, Brewery Lights turns into a drive-thru, and Anheuser-Busch says the public is free to enter Pestalozzi Street at the brewery’s main gate from 5 to 10 p.m. For skating, head downtown to Winterfest in Kiener Plaza, in the shadow of the Arch. Winterfest is free to attend, and kids skate free on Fridays.
Dates, prices and closed nights re-checked against each organizer’s own page in late October
### Your December, in order
Book first: Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden, select nights Nov. 14 through Jan. 2, millions of lights on foot. The Garden says mid-December through Jan. 1 sells out first, so the easy nights are the earlier weeks. On its Family Nights (Nov. 23-24 and 30, Dec. 1-3) kids 3 to 12 get in for $6, and same-night adult tickets bought after 4:30 p.m. cost $2 more.
Saturday, Nov. 21: the 42nd Thanks-For-Giving Parade steps off downtown at 2 p.m., the same day Winterfest opens in Kiener Plaza. That evening the Salvation Army tree of lights goes on at 5:45, with a drone show at 6:30 and fireworks at 7.
Friday, Nov. 27, the day after Thanksgiving: Belleville’s Santa Parade rolls through downtown Belleville at 10 a.m., St. Charles Christmas Traditions® opens on Main Street, and Wild Lights opens at the Zoo.
Weekends to Christmas Eve: Santa and Mrs. Claus ride down Main Street in St. Charles in a horse-drawn carriage at the end of a noon parade every Saturday and Sunday of the festival.
Nov. 28 to Dec. 23: Saint Louis Ballet’s The Nutcracker at the Touhill, with a 70-minute Shorter Tale version for little kids on Dec. 1 and Dec. 18 at 11 a.m.
Christmas night: WonderLight’s drive-through ($35 a carload, up to eight people), or Santa’s Magical Kingdom (5:30 to 10 p.m.).
Dec. 27 to 30: Brewery Lights turns into a drive-thru, and the brewery says the public is free to drive Pestalozzi Street from 5 to 10 p.m. Most of the rest wraps up Jan. 2 or 3.
### Garden Glow, WonderLight’s and Brewery Lights
If you’re asking where to see Christmas lights in STL, start here. Dress warmer than you think you need to.
### Missouri Botanical Garden's Garden Glow
A small mitten tugs you toward the fire pits before you’re even past the entrance. Let it pull. The path runs about a mile through millions of lights and takes 45 minutes to an hour, and the warming fire pits at the Central Axis and Linnean Plaza throw off wood smoke and the smell of toasted marshmallow (s’mores kits are sold on the grounds), and the glow on the faces around the fire is half the show. Park free in the Garden’s two lots at Shaw and Vandeventer and ride the shuttle; skip the side streets, where private lots tow. Buy ahead, because tickets are good only for the date and time you pick, and admission varies by night. Santa poses for photos on Mondays and Tuesdays from Nov. 23 through Dec. 8, and if your kid is sensitive to flashing lights, Sensory Night is Monday, Nov. 30, with reduced sensory stimuli. Full details are on their website.
### WonderLight's Christmas Drive-Through
The car goes dark at the booth, the radio clicks over to 89.5 FM, and the windshield fills with color. WonderLight's Christmas fills World Wide Technology Raceway in Fairmont City, just across the river in Illinois, with more than a million LED lights synchronized to music. It runs Nov. 13 through Jan. 3, and $35 gets the whole car in, up to eight people, every night from 5 to 10, holidays included. You kill your headlights at the booth, then roll through at 2 to 5 miles an hour while about 45 minutes of Christmas music drives the lights and the kids press their noses to the glass. The parent move: hit the portable toilets by the entrance, because the next ones are at the exit. The dog can come if it stays in the car, and a two-hour time slot bought ahead keeps the wait short.
### Brewery Lights Spectacle
Cold air, old red brick, and the clop of Clydesdale hooves on the street: Brewery Lights at the Anheuser-Busch brewery is in its 41st year, on select nights from Nov. 21 through Dec. 26, and the date list skips straight from Dec. 23 to Dec. 26. A reservation gets you free parking, a complimentary beer if you’re 21 or older, brewery tours, a light tunnel, two 50-foot digital holiday trees and the nightly 7:30 parade, with floats, a trolley, a marching band and the Clydesdales (weather permitting). Kids get their own Winter Wonderland with two carnival rides and a light-up dance floor. Book the VIP Fire Pit package and the evening slows down: a heated tent, a buffet, s’mores kits and your own fire to hold your hands over while the brick glows behind you. Not sure which night? A $25 Flex Ticket gets you into any available night, even a sold-out one. Then, from Dec. 27 to 30, it becomes a drive-thru: the brewery says the public is free to enter Pestalozzi Street at the main gate at Busch Place and Arsenal from 5 to 10 p.m.
One planning note before you load up the car: Garden Glow sells dated, timed tickets, WonderLight’s sells two-hour time slots, and Brewery Lights requires reservations, so buy the slot first. Garden Glow charges $2 more for same-night adult tickets after 4:30, and Brewery Lights stops letting people in at 8. And if the drive-through format is your family’s favorite, our complete drive-through Christmas lights guide covers every display in the metro.
### With the kids: The Polar Express, a wagon through the lights, the zoo after dark
These are the nights kids still talk about in March. Book the ticketed ones early, because the good nights go first.
### The Polar Express Train Ride at Union Station
The train boards at Union Station and heads for the North Pole, which, according to the ride’s own FAQ, sits just north of the Arch grounds. It’s an immersive experience, start to finish. Families are encouraged to come in their warmest pajamas, characters from the story work the cars, and then Santa Claus and his elves show up, the moment the kids have been waiting for. The ride itself runs about 45 minutes, from Nov. 13 to Dec. 30. Get there 45 minutes before departure for check-in and the family photo, prepay $5 to park in the Union Station lot off 18th Street, and know that kids 2 and under ride free on a lap.
### Santa’s Magical Kingdom Wagon Ride
Santa's Magical Kingdom in Eureka spreads over 35 acres, from the elves’ village in the trees to a lighted Gateway Arch with a fireworks effect, and it has a slower way through: an open-air Old Fashioned Holiday Wagon, bundled up under the blankets they hand you at Kringle’s General Store. It costs $18 a person, and booking a wagon or train ride for two or more waives your car’s admission. Watch the calendar, though: shared wagon rides don’t run Dec. 5, 11, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 23 and 24, the Kingdom’s heaviest traffic nights. After the ride you can drive back through the newer section and drop the kids’ letters in Santa’s North Pole Mailbox. Santa himself is at Kringle’s nightly through Dec. 23, and if you only drive, it’s $35 a car Sunday through Friday and $40 on Saturday, cash at the exit. It’s more intimate than a drive-through, and you hear the kids instead of the radio.
### Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo
The Saint Louis Zoo after dark is a different place. Wild Lights strings over a million twinkling lights through the grounds, and you walk it with a cold nose and your hood up, a cup of specialty hot chocolate in your hand (the Zoo sells it in naughty or nice versions) and s’mores roasting over the firepits. It runs select nights Nov. 27 through Dec. 30, 5 to 8:30 p.m. with last entry at 8, and there’s no timed entry. Tickets are $19, or $16 for Zoo members, kids under 2 get in free, and parking on both Zoo lots is free while it lasts. Santa takes pictures every night through Dec. 23, and Sensory-Friendly Night is Dec. 7. Tickets do sell out, so the Zoo recommends buying in advance.
### City Museum's Weirdly Wonderful Holidays
City Museum is already a place of wonder, and from Nov. 19 through Jan. 3 its Weirdly Wonderful Holidays are included with general admission. Lights dance across the museum’s historic façade every day, Santa works in his fourth-floor workshop Fridays through Sundays, then every day from Dec. 18 to 24, and Mrs. Claus reads stories on the same dates. On select December evenings you can belt out a carol at holiday karaoke in front of the giant underwear on Beatnik Bob’s stage, and on New Year’s Eve the balloons drop at 8 p.m. It’s a great spot for families who love a bit of adventure mixed with their holiday spirit - and one of the standouts in our guide to indoor things to do in St. Louis when the weather turns.
Many of these events book up quickly, so lock in dates before the week you want to go.
Here's a quick look at what you can expect:
The Polar Express: A train ride to the North Pole with characters and Santa.
Santa's Magical Kingdom: Wagon rides through acres of holiday magic.
Wild Lights: A nighttime light display at the zoo.
City Museum: Holiday twists on their unique attractions, plus special events.

### The Nutcracker, the Symphony and TSO
A hundred pounds of snow drifting down onto the Touhill stage, a hall full of kids holding their breath. St. Louis does the big holiday shows well, and the best seats go early.
### Saint Louis Ballet Presents The Nutcracker
The Nutcracker is Saint Louis Ballet’s big holiday show, and the company’s own fun facts tell you what you’re in for: 100 pounds of snow and 10 pounds of confetti dropped, 500 pounds of dry ice, more than 170 costumes, and more than 440 cubes of cheese thrown throughout the production. Buy only through MetroTix; the Ballet calls it the only official ticket seller.
When: Nov. 28 through Dec. 23, matinees and evenings
Venue: Touhill Performing Arts Center, with free parking
Special Note: The Shorter Tale, cut to 1 hour and 10 minutes for the youngest and wiggliest, plays Dec. 1 and Dec. 18 at 11 a.m.
### The Symphony’s Mercy Holiday Celebration
Broadway star Norm Lewis joins the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra and the St. Louis Symphony Chorus at Powell Hall Dec. 18-20 for the orchestra’s annual holiday concert: fireside ballads, carols, the jingle of sleigh bells and, the Symphony hints, maybe a visit from Santa Claus. If your crew would rather laugh, the SLSO also plays The Muppet Christmas Carol live to the film at Powell Hall on Dec. 12 and 13.
### Trans-Siberian Orchestra's Holiday Show
The Trans-Siberian Orchestra brings its new production of The Ghosts of Christmas Eve: The Best of TSO and More to Enterprise Center on Wednesday, Dec. 30, the holiday rock opera plus the TSO classics, with tickets on the band’s tour page starting at $59 plus tax. It plays like a spectacle, not a straight concert, and it’s loud enough that you feel the bass in your ribs.
The Fox books its own holiday run each season. On the calendar this year:
Cirque Dreams Holidaze: Dec. 18-19 at the Fox.
NUTCRACKER! Magical Christmas Ballet: Dec. 20-21, with an international cast and whimsical puppetry.
### Skating under the Arch, LIT at Molly’s and cocoa on a rooftop
### Winterfest at Kiener Plaza
Downtown’s winter festival sets up in Kiener Plaza, in the shadow of the Arch, from Nov. 21 through Jan. 3. Winterfest is free to attend. Skate rentals run $15 for adults and $10 for kids 3 to 15 (bring your own skates and the ice is free, and kids skate free on Fridays), heated igloos for up to six start at $100 for 90 minutes, and an $18 s’mores kit makes four s’mores and gets you a spot at one of the marshmallow fire pits. The rink is open Thursdays and Fridays 4 to 8 p.m. and weekends noon to 8, then daily noon to 8 from Dec. 26 to Jan. 3. It’s closed on Christmas Day. Opening day, Nov. 21, ends with the Ameren Missouri Festival of Lights, and the year ends with a family-friendly New Year’s Eve party and fireworks at 8 p.m. Reserve skating time ahead on busy weekends.
### LIT at Molly's in Soulard
Looking for something a bit different? Molly's in Soulard runs a 21-and-over Christmas pop-up called LIT, with outrageous decor, a Christmas menu, costumes and timed reservation slots. When we checked, the LIT page on Molly’s site was still titled for last season’s pop-up. Watch that page before you promise anyone a seat.
### Up on the Housetop at City Museum
City Museum’s holiday lineup includes the Up On The Housetop Café, the rooftop café on the 11th floor: hot cocoa with chocolate chips, hot apple cider with cinnamon, and seasonal beers, with downtown spread out below you and the wind finding every gap in your scarf. Rooftop access isn’t automatically included with general admission and can cost extra, and the hours move with the weather. ### St. Louis Christmas Parades
Parade season starts before the turkey is even thawed. Downtown’s 42nd Thanks-For-Giving Parade steps off at 2 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21, with marching bands, festive floats and a special appearance by Santa Claus; Celebrate St. Louis puts it on with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, and Winterfest opens in Kiener Plaza the same day. The day after Thanksgiving, Friday, Nov. 27, Belleville’s Santa Parade, hosted by the Optimist Club of Belleville and billed by the city as the largest holiday parade in Southern Illinois, brings floats, marching bands and dance groups through downtown at 10 a.m. and welcomes Santa to his house on the Public Square. Stay for the open-air Christkindlmarkt on the square (Thursdays through Sundays, Nov. 27 to Dec. 23) and the free horse-drawn trolley rides on weekends through Dec. 20. Then, every Saturday and Sunday of St. Charles Christmas Traditions, a noon Santa parade marches down historic Main Street, the easiest one to catch if your weekend is already booked: carolers singing, an international delegation of gift-givers carrying their countries’ flags, and Santa and Mrs. Claus arriving last in a horse-drawn carriage. Bring a thermos and claim your curb early.
### Main Street chestnuts, Delmar makers and the Winter Market
Cold fingers, a paper bag of something warm, and a list that is still too long. These three beat another lap around a parking garage, and the gifts come from people who made them.
### St. Charles Christmas Traditions®
This is a big one, folks. From Nov. 27 to Dec. 24, historic Main Street in St. Charles turns into what the festival calls a Dickensian winter wonderland: gas lamps glowing, crisp pine greenery trimming the historic district, centuries-old bricks under your boots, and the smell of chestnuts roasting on an open fire (they cost a nominal fee and double as hand warmers). Nearly a dozen international Santas and global gift-givers wander the street, each Legend of Christmas you meet hands out a commemorative trading card, and on Friday nights Krampus takes over the KATY Depot with a carnival of the weirder holiday customs. The St. Charles visitors bureau calls it a free Christmas festival, NBC’s Today Show declared it the “Merriest Main Street in America,” and it draws a quarter of a million people a season. On Wednesday evenings, the “A Christmas Carol” Stroll turns Main Street into the foggy streets of 1840s London.
Hours: Opening day noon to 8:30 p.m., then Fridays 6 to 8:30 p.m., Saturdays noon to 8:30, Sundays noon to 5, and Christmas Eve 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Victorian Carolers: Enjoy live festive music.
Hot-Roasted Chestnuts: A classic holiday treat.
“A Christmas Carol” Stroll: Wednesdays, 6 to 8:30 p.m.
### Delmar Maker District Holiday Shopping
If you're into the artsy, crafty scene, the Delmar Maker District is your go-to: a handmade stretch of Delmar Boulevard between Union and Kingshighway with arts and craft studios, eclectic shops and restaurants. At Third Degree Glass there are glassblowing, kiln and flame studios, demos and a retail gallery of local art, so you can feel the furnace heat on your face before you browse the gallery. The Front Room, in the lobby of MADE Makerspace, sells work by MADE members and other local artists, and the district’s own site lists Craft Alliance, a nonprofit art center. Short on time? The district sells gift cards to its restaurants and one-of-a-kind shops. Plus, you're supporting local artists and entrepreneurs, which is always a good feeling.
### Winter Market at Gateway Convention Center
This market is a bit more of a traditional, large-scale holiday shopping event, and it lands late: the Gateway Winter Market is Dec. 19-20 at the Gateway Convention Center in Collinsville, the weekend you suddenly remember three people you forgot. It's a good spot if you're looking to get a lot of your holiday shopping done under one roof, with your coat off and your list in your hand.
Key Features:
Late on the calendar: The weekend before Christmas.
Under one roof: No standing in the cold between vendors.
Convenient Location: The Gateway Convention Center in Collinsville, Illinois.
Gift Variety: A good place to finish the list in one stop.
### The Sleigh Shed, a curling lane and The Lodge
Warm drinks, twinkling lights, good company
Somewhere around the second week of December, every parent needs one evening that isn’t about the kids. Here are the warm room, the cold lane and the one door you shouldn’t count on for that night.
### The Sleigh Shed Holiday Cocktails
Get ready for some serious sparkle at The Sleigh Shed. The Train Shed restaurant turns into a holiday pop-up from Nov. 7 through Dec. 31, decorated top to bottom in traditional Christmas colors, with dripping icicle lights and over-the-top table and bar decor. The menu runs to creative cocktails, mocktails, holiday appetizers and sweets, and it’s open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 11 on Fridays and Saturdays. It's the perfect spot to unwind after a day of holiday shopping or exploring the city's festive sights.
### Curling at the Winterfest Curling Cafe
For a unique twist on holiday fun, Winterfest added a Curling Cafe this season: two tented curling bays with seating around the lane and synthetic ice for “street curling,” an approachable take on the sport. A 90-minute session is $65 for up to four people per lane, and the Arch Park Foundation strongly suggests booking ahead. It's a fantastic way to have some laughs with friends, your breath fogging over the lane while somebody yells “sweep!”
### The Lodge at Winterfest
Don’t plan on wandering into The Lodge. This season the Winterfest page lists it under All Access Winterfest Private Events, as an add-on at $500 an hour with a two-hour minimum, on top of a rink buyout that closes the event to the public. If you’re booking the office party, that’s your warm room by the ice; if you’re a family of four, the heated igloos are the better bet.
Here's a quick look at what you might find:
Festive Drink Menus: Expect creative concoctions with holiday spices and flavors.
Cozy Ambiance: Think warm lighting, comfortable seating, and festive decor.
Unique Activities: From curling to simply enjoying the view, the draw goes beyond the drinks.
Great Company: Perfect for dates, friend gatherings, or family outings.
### What to book first
Start with whatever sells out. Garden Glow says its tickets go well in advance, especially mid-December through Jan. 1, so lock that in before the walk-up markets and pop-up bars you can catch on a whim. That’s the honest answer to what to do in St. Louis for Christmas: book the timed lights first, then fill the gaps with the free things, Winterfest, the St. Charles parades and the Brewery Lights drive-thru nights. And when the presents are wrapped and the lights come down, our guide to New Year’s Eve in St. Louis carries the celebration into the new year.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. When do the Christmas events in St. Louis usually start?
A.  Most open in mid-November. WonderLight’s drive-through and the Polar Express start Nov. 13, Garden Glow on Nov. 14, Winterfest and the Thanks-For-Giving Parade on Saturday, Nov. 21, and St. Charles Christmas Traditions and Wild Lights the day after Thanksgiving. Several run to Jan. 2 or 3.
### Q. Are there any Christmas concerts in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Symphony’s Mercy Holiday Celebration with Broadway star Norm Lewis fills Powell Hall Dec. 18-20, Saint Louis Ballet’s Nutcracker runs at the Touhill from Nov. 28 to Dec. 23, and the Trans-Siberian Orchestra closes the year at Enterprise Center on Dec. 30. The SLSO plays The Muppet Christmas Carol live to the film on Dec. 12 and 13.
### Q. What activities can I do on Christmas Day?
A.  Plan around closures: Garden Glow and Winterfest both close on Christmas Day. WonderLight’s drive-through stays open nightly, holidays included, and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka runs its lights from 5:30 to 10 p.m. A drive-through is the safest Christmas-night plan. If Santa is the point, go earlier: his last nights at the Zoo and the Kingdom are Dec. 23.
### Q. What are some free Christmas activities in Saint Louis?
A.  Winterfest in Kiener Plaza is free to attend, and kids skate free on Fridays. St. Charles Christmas Traditions is a free festival with noon Santa parades on weekends, Belleville runs free horse-drawn trolley rides on weekends through Dec. 20, and from Dec. 27 to 30 the public is free to enter Pestalozzi Street for the Brewery Lights drive-thru.
### Q. Where to see Christmas lights in STL?
A.  On foot: Garden Glow’s millions of lights at the Missouri Botanical Garden and Wild Lights’ more than a million at the Zoo. Brewery Lights adds the Budweiser Clydesdales and a nightly parade. From the car: WonderLight’s more than a million LEDs at World Wide Technology Raceway and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka. City Museum lights its historic facade every day of the season.
### Q. What is the most Christmassy town in Missouri?
A.  Around St. Louis, it’s St. Charles, which NBC’s Today Show named the “Merriest Main Street in America.” From Nov. 27 to Dec. 24, Christmas Traditions brings Victorian carolers, hot-roasted chestnuts, nearly a dozen international Santas, a Wednesday-night Christmas Carol stroll and noon Santa parades on weekends, and about a quarter of a million people come each season.
### Q. Where to go in Missouri for Christmas?
A.  Start in St. Louis: Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden, Wild Lights at the Zoo, the Polar Express at Union Station and skating under the Arch at Winterfest fill a long weekend. Add a Friday, Saturday or Sunday on Main Street in St. Charles for Christmas Traditions, or a night drive through Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka.

## Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill: He Peeled Potatoes Here at Nine, Then Bought the Place
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-charlie-gitto-s-on-the-hill-a-st-louis-italian-dining-gem
Peeling potatoes. Polishing the brass. Those were the jobs, and the boy doing them was nine years old.
His father worked the dining room at Angelo’s on The Hill as the maître d’hôtel, and young Charlie tagged along to help. According to the restaurant’s own history, nobody in that room could have imagined the kid would grow up to buy the place from Angelo himself. He did. Charlie Gitto Jr. opened it as Charlie Gitto’s in 1981, and it still sits at 5226 Shaw Avenue, in a neighborhood that got its name from sitting an eighth of a mile from the highest point in St. Louis.
Walk in tonight and it’s the room the restaurant describes: warm wood, soft lighting, classic Italian décor. Then a plate of toasted ravioli lands in front of you, golden-brown, the shell crisp enough to crackle when you bite, the inside soft and savory, a side of marinara waiting for the dunk. It’s $16, and the menu calls it “The Original.” Two restaurants on The Hill claim to have invented it. We’ll get to that fight.
First, three things that change the night:
No high chairs. Booster seats and high chairs are not provided. Bringing a toddler? Know that before you pick the date.
Six or more means one check and 20%. Parties of 6 or more are put on one check with a 20% automatic gratuity.
Your jersey is welcome on game day. The dress code is smart casual to business casual, but during home sporting events, tasteful sports attire is welcome.
To book, use the Make a Reservation button on the restaurant’s site or call (314) 772-8898. Regular hours are evenings only: Monday through Thursday 5 to 9 p.m., Friday and Saturday 5 to 10 p.m., and Sunday 4 to 9 p.m.
### “The Original,” as legend has it
Here’s the detail that makes St. Louisans grin. On the menu, Gitto’s calls its toasted ravioli “The Original.” On its own website, the restaurant tells the origin story and hedges it in the same breath. The story dates back to the 1940s, when an unnamed chef at Angelo’s on the Hill “accidentally dropped a ravioli in hot oil instead of water.” Then the hedge: “as legend has it.”
Then there’s Mama’s on the Hill, at 2132 Edwards Street. Its listing with The Hill Business Association calls Mama’s the “Home of the Toasted Ravioli” and tells nearly the same accident: the early 1940s, a chef named Fritz, an order of ravioli dropped into hot oil instead of hot water, and Mickey Garagiola, older brother of Hall of Famer Joe Garagiola, sitting at the bar and tasting the first one. Did it really start at Mama’s? Mickey’s answer in that listing: “I’ll bet my house on it.”
Now look at the calendar. Both stories land in the 1940s, and that was the decade The Hill was turning. The neighborhood’s own history says taverns once dotted most corners, and that restaurants only slowly took over after World War II. In Mama’s version, the first person to taste toasted ravioli was sitting at a bar. So did toasted ravioli originate in St. Louis? By both restaurants that claim it, yes: in the hiss of ravioli hitting hot oil, in a kitchen on The Hill. Who fried it first, we can’t settle. At Gitto’s, “The Original” is handmade, meat-filled ravioli with the house pomodoro sauce, $16.
### What to order, course by course, with the prices
The online dinner menu for the Hill location shows prices, so you can picture the check before you sit down. Here’s a meal, start to finish.
To start. The ravioli, obviously, $16. If the table wants a second starter, the arancini are risotto balls filled with fresh mozzarella, served with pomodoro and walnut pesto cream sauce, $15. The CG Signature Shrimp come extra large, roasted in garlic butter and seasoned breadcrumbs, $22.
The pasta. Fiore Borghese is small flower-shaped hollow noodles in a pink Cognac sauce with prosciutto, onions and parsley, $24, the kind of sauce you chase to the last noodle. The lasagna stacks six layers of meat-filled noodles with cheese, tomato and cream sauce, $25. For heat, the Seafood Pasta Suzanne tosses homemade tagliatelle with shrimp, scallops, clams, langostinos and mussels in a spicy three-pepper cream sauce, $38.
The main event. Veal Nunzio tops thinly sliced veal with jumbo lump crabmeat, finished with CG cheeses and lemon butter sauce, $49. Veal Parmigiano comes bone-in, breaded and baked with pomodoro sauce and CG cheeses, $55. The 14-ounce Ruth Family Farms Certified Prime NY Strip is $68.
The money math for two: ravioli to share plus the Fiore Borghese and the lasagna comes to $65 on the menu, before drinks, tax and tip. That’s three dollars less than the 14-ounce strip by itself. Screenshot that before your anniversary.
The finish. Every dessert is handmade, from the tiramisu of lady fingers, espresso and mascarpone ($12) to cannoli filled with sweetened ricotta and chocolate chips ($13). At the bar, the Sicilian Manhattan pairs your choice of whiskey, bourbon or rye with Blood Orange Amara, $15. The restaurant says its wine list, domestic and imported Italian, was recognized by Wine Spectator with the Award of Excellence.
### What is the dress code at Charlie Gitto’s on the Hill?
Dress for the room, not the parking lot: soft light on warm wood and a table you’ll want to linger at. The Hill location asks for smart casual to business casual, polished and well-kept. Take your hat off while you dine. The contact page spells out the rest: it asks gentlemen to skip ball caps, cut-offs and tank tops, asks for no holes in jeans or pants, and allows nothing with offensive language or pictures. Management can refuse service over attire. One exception St. Louis will appreciate: during home sporting events, tasteful sports attire is welcome. A tasteful jersey can come to dinner on a home game day.
Turning dinner into a whole night on The Hill? Our guide to where to eat on The Hill maps the neighborhood’s other Italian rooms, bakeries and markets, so the evening can start with a walk.
If you’re the family restaurant, the bakery or the deli that has been feeding this neighborhood for years, notice how the people reading this found Gitto’s story: in a search, not on a sidewalk. Own a spot with a story like this one? See what a Gold listing tells them about yours.
### Private rooms, and the other Gitto’s
A private room for the big birthday. The LaSorda Room on the Hill seats up to 12 and rents in 2-hour blocks for a $200 room fee. The Garden Room handles groups up to 100, and the Hill location’s full capacity is 180.
Check your GPS. There’s a second Charlie Gitto’s at Hollywood Casino, 777 Casino Center in Maryland Heights, opened in 2004 in what was then Harrah’s. The original is the one on Shaw.
### Which night it’s right for, and when to pick somewhere else
The anniversary or the first date. The restaurant calls itself the backdrop of family gatherings, first dates and large celebrations, and its press page lists OpenTable’s Top 100 Romantic Restaurants in America. Order the ravioli to share, let the second glass of wine happen, and don’t look at the time.
The rehearsal dinner or the retirement party. The private dining rooms are popular for retirements, wedding rehearsal dinners and family celebrations, and they take parties from 8 to 100. Start with the events coordinator at events@charliegittos.com.
The office lunch. Regular hours are evenings, but the restaurant says its dining rooms are also available for luncheon events, so a group lunch is an email away, not a walk-in.
The family with a toddler. Plan around the one hard limit: booster seats and high chairs are not provided. If the night has to revolve around a two-year-old, our guide to the best Italian food in St. Louis has other rooms to weigh.
The table of eight after the game. Remember the house math before anyone orders a round: six or more means one check and a 20% automatic gratuity. Tasteful jerseys are welcome on home game days, so nobody has to change.
### Is it the oldest Italian restaurant on The Hill?
It’s a fair question for a room with this much history, so here’s the straight answer. The Gitto name on Shaw Avenue dates to 1981. The room’s story runs further back, through Angelo’s and a toasted ravioli legend the restaurant places in the 1940s. And as the tavern history above shows, The Hill’s restaurant era itself only took hold after World War II. We could not find a primary source that names the oldest restaurant on The Hill still operating, so we won’t crown one.
### The neighborhood that built it
The Hill is a 52-square-block section of the city’s near south side. Italian immigrants first arrived in the 1880s to work the clay mines; then came the sons, brothers and cousins, then the grocers, bakers and barbers. Yogi Berra was born here, and so was his best friend, Joe Garagiola. Today the neighborhood counts more than 30 restaurants and four Italian grocery stores, and the fountain in Piazza Imo was imported from Italy.
Come early and walk it before dinner. St. Ambrose Church, dedicated in 1926, anchors the streets. Gitto’s says its focus since the beginning has been sharing the family’s Sicilian roots, and the family supports the Children’s Miracle Network and local Catholic Charities. Our Hill neighborhood guide has the rest of the map.
Kids along tomorrow instead? Here’s how to beat the clock at St. Louis Union Station.
### What the critics and lists have said
By the restaurant’s own count, it has been named one of the nation’s top 50 Italian restaurants by OpenTable, and its press page lists OpenTable’s Top 100 Romantic Restaurants in America and a DIRoNA Award of Excellence. Its own site says it has been featured in The New York Times, Feast, Tasting Table and Epicurious, among others. Lists are lists. The better proof is the one in the first paragraph: a kid who polished the brass in this room, and then bought it.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best dish at Charlie Gitto’s?
A.  The restaurant calls its toasted ravioli its signature, and the menu labels it “The Original”: handmade, meat-filled ravioli with the house pomodoro sauce for $16. For a main course, the Veal Nunzio tops thinly sliced veal with jumbo lump crabmeat, CG cheeses and lemon butter sauce, $49 on the Hill dinner menu.
### Q. What is the dress code for Charlie Gitto’s on the Hill in St. Louis?
A.  Smart casual to business casual. Hats come off while dining, the restaurant asks gentlemen not to wear ball caps, cut-offs or tank tops, and it asks for no holes in jeans or pants and nothing with offensive language or pictures. During home sporting events, tasteful sports attire is welcome. Management can refuse service over attire.
### Q. What is on the menu at Charlie Gitto’s ‘On the Hill’ in St. Louis?
A.  A Sicilian-inspired dinner menu: appetizers like toasted ravioli ($16) and arancini ($15), brick oven pizzas, handcrafted pastas from $24 to $25 plus seafood pastas, veal from $42 to $55, chicken, seafood and Prime steaks up to a $68 NY strip. Desserts are handmade, and the cocktail list runs from $11 to $15.
### Q. Did toasted ravioli originate in St. Louis?
A.  Both restaurants that claim it are on The Hill in St. Louis. Charlie Gitto’s traces it, “as legend has it,” to a 1940s kitchen accident at Angelo’s. Mama’s on the Hill tells of a chef named Fritz dropping ravioli into hot oil in the early 1940s. We can’t prove either story, but both put the dish on The Hill.
### Q. What is toasted ravioli?
A.  Ravioli that is breaded and deep-fried instead of boiled. At Charlie Gitto’s, plump handmade ravioli is breaded and fried into a golden-brown pocket of pasta, crispy outside with a soft, savory filling, and served with tangy marinara or a savory dipping sauce. On the Hill menu it’s meat-filled and $16.
### Q. What is a signature dish of St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli is a good first answer. Charlie Gitto’s calls it an icon of St. Louis cuisine and a dish locals proudly recommend to visitors, and two Hill restaurants claim to have invented it in the 1940s. Order it as an appetizer to share; at Gitto’s on the Hill it’s $16.
### Q. Do I need a reservation at Charlie Gitto’s?
A.  Book ahead to be safe. The restaurant’s website has a Make a Reservation button, and the phone number is (314) 772-8898. Regular hours start at 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 4 p.m. on Sunday. Parties of 6 or more go on one check with a 20% automatic gratuity.

## Thai Kitchen in O’Fallon, MO: Authentic Thai in St. Charles County
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-authentic-flavors-thai-kitchen-in-o-fallon-mo
Some nights only Thai food will do — that particular balance of sweet, sour, salty, and spicy that no other cuisine quite hits. Out in O’Fallon, Missouri, Thai Kitchen has become the go-to answer for exactly that craving. This is an honest look at what it is, what to order, and why it’s earned such a loyal following in St. Charles County.
The short version: it’s a genuinely good, family-run Thai restaurant that’s part of a beloved St. Louis-area brand with real staying power — and it brings authentic Thai cooking to a part of the metro that’s glad to have it. If you’ve been settling for chain takeout when the Thai craving hits, this is your upgrade — and if you’re already a devotee, it’s a reliable neighborhood option worth putting in the regular rotation.
### A local Thai family brand, in O’Fallon
Thai Kitchen O’Fallon sits at 8632 Mexico Road, O’Fallon, MO 63366 — that’s O’Fallon, Missouri, in St. Charles County, not the Illinois town of the same name — phone (636) 281-2389. It’s one location of a family-owned Thai restaurant brand that has been part of the St. Louis dining scene for more than two decades, tracing back to an original Thai Kitchen that opened in Maryland Heights in 1999.
A quick, honest clarification on the timeline, since it’s easy to muddle: the brand is 20-plus years old, but the O’Fallon location itself is newer — it opened in 2022. So you get the best of both: a kitchen backed by decades of experience and a proven recipe book, in a location that’s a relatively recent, welcome addition to St. Charles County. The family behind it has deep roots in St. Louis Thai cooking — the brand has been recognized in local restaurant coverage for its contribution to the metro’s dining scene — and that experience shows in the food. When a family has been cooking the same cuisine across the region for two decades, they’ve had time to get the details right, and a newer location gets to open with that whole track record behind it rather than starting from scratch.
### What to order
Thai Kitchen covers the classics and does them well. A few dishes to build an order around:
Pad Thai — billed as the best-selling entree, and the right starting point if you’re new to the cuisine: stir-fried rice noodles, sweet-savory sauce, peanuts, and lime.
The curries — massaman, yellow, green, and panang are all here, each with its own personality, from the mild, peanutty massaman to the herbaceous green. There’s even a pineapple duck curry for something a little special and a step beyond the usual chicken or beef.
Tom Yam Goong — the classic hot-and-sour shrimp soup, bright with lemongrass and lime, and a great way to wake up your palate before the main courses arrive.
Som Tam — green papaya salad, crunchy and punchy, for the table that wants something fresh and fiery.
Thai fried rice and Nam Tok — a comforting fried rice and a grilled-pork salad, rounding out a well-balanced order.
Start with chicken satay or crab rangoon to share, and don’t leave without mango and sweet sticky rice if it’s available — the perfect cooling, sweet finish to a spicy meal. Vegetarians are well looked after too, with tofu and vegetable versions of many dishes. Menus evolve, so if you have a specific dish in mind, glance at the current menu or ask when you order.

### Why Thai food hits different
If you’re new to Thai cuisine, here’s what makes it so addictive: it’s built on balancing four flavors at once — sweet, sour, salty, and spicy — often in a single bite. A good Thai kitchen plays those elements against each other so nothing dominates: the lime brightens the richness, the fish sauce deepens the sweetness, the chili lifts everything. It’s a cuisine of contrast and freshness, heavy on herbs like lemongrass, basil, cilantro, and galangal, and it tends to feel lighter and more vivid than the heavier comfort food many Americans default to.
That’s exactly why Thai food inspires the loyalty it does — once your palate learns to love that push-pull of flavors, an ordinary dinner can feel flat by comparison. A kitchen with real experience, like Thai Kitchen’s, is where you taste that balance done right rather than flattened into generic sweet-and-heavy takeout. The difference between competent Thai food and great Thai food is precisely this attention to balance, and it’s what a two-decade family brand has had time to master.
### On spice: order it your way
One of the pleasures of a real Thai kitchen is that heat is a dial, not a fixed setting. Thai Kitchen will cook to your preferred spice level, so don’t be shy about asking — whether you want it mild enough for a spice-averse dinner guest or hot enough to make your eyes water. A good rule for first-timers: order a notch below what you think you can handle, since authentic Thai heat runs hotter than the Americanized version many people are used to. You can always add chili; you can’t take it out.
That flexibility is part of what makes Thai food such a crowd-pleaser for mixed groups. The same table can have a fiery green curry, a mild massaman, and a kid-friendly pad thai, and everyone leaves happy. It’s a cuisine built for sharing and customizing, which suits a family restaurant perfectly. And because the heat is adjustable, Thai Kitchen works just as well for a cautious first date or a family with young kids as it does for a chili-head who wants their green curry to fight back. Few cuisines flex so gracefully across such different eaters at the same table.

From there, branch out with one curry to share — massaman is the gentlest, a mild, faintly sweet coconut-and-peanut braise that even the most spice-averse diners tend to enjoy — and maybe a tom yam goong for the adventurous, so the table gets a taste of Thai food’s brighter, bolder side. Don’t overthink it: this is welcoming, approachable food, and the staff are used to guiding newcomers, so lean on them if you’re unsure.
Order family-style and pass everything around; Thai food is made for sharing, and sampling several dishes is far more fun than everyone hiding behind a single plate. Steamed jasmine rice is the great equalizer — it cools the heat and stretches the meal — so get plenty. And save room for mango sticky rice: sweet coconut-soaked rice with ripe mango is the perfect, gentle finish, and it converts skeptics into regulars as reliably as anything on the menu — and if the sweet end of Thai cooking is what wins you over, Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe in Valley Park is named for the Thai dessert cups that are its calling card.

## $150,000 St. Louis Verdict: The Bad Review Wasn't a Customer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-remove-a-google-review
### Can you actually remove a Google review?
Only if it breaks a Google rule, or the person who wrote it deletes it. You can report any Google review, but only reviews that violate Google’s policies are eligible for removal. Flag it in the Reviews Management Tool, and if Google finds no violation you get one appeal. An unfair review that breaks no rule stays up, so your public reply becomes the part that matters.
The phone buzzes face-down on the counter after close, and the screen lights up the dark room: one star, from a name you’ve never heard. Your stomach drops before the second sentence. Your thumb is already hunting for a delete button.
“Dealing with these people was the single biggest mistake I have ever made in my whole life.”
That review went up on Google and Yahoo with a “Grade: F” and the name of a real former customer of The Fireworks Restoration Company, a property damage restoration company. It told readers that if the crew showed up in their front yard in the middle of the night after a house fire, they should run. No customer wrote it. According to the Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, the company’s own co-founder posted three fictitious, derogatory reviews after a bitter split, and the company had to file a “John Doe” lawsuit just to learn who he was. A St. Louis County jury awarded $1 in actual damages and $150,000 in punitive damages, and the appeals court affirmed.
That took a lawsuit and a jury, because the review system itself checks policy, not truth. Google won’t play judge, and its help center says so in a sentence the removal-for-hire outfits would rather you never read: “Google doesn’t get involved in conflict between businesses and customers.” Flagged reviews that break its content policies come down from Maps and Search. A review that is just wrong, unfair or written on someone’s rotten week stays. That gap is the whole business model for the outfits selling a delete button Google never built.
So which one is glowing on your screen? A broken rule, or somebody’s bad week? And if it is a broken rule, which one would you point to, knowing the appeal only comes once?
The process itself asks for five things, in order. First, a screenshot before anything else: the review, the date, the reviewer’s profile and how many other reviews that account has left, because reviews get edited and screenshots don’t. Second, the flag. Google’s own steps read: next to the review you’d like to flag, select Report, select the reason, then select Send report.
Third, one named policy in two sentences a stranger could check in a minute: fake engagement, conflict of interest or impersonation. “This reviewer is a former employee” does that. “This is unfair” doesn’t. Fourth, a few days of waiting; Google says evaluation typically takes several days, and the status shows in the Reviews Management Tool. Fifth, and only if the answer comes back “no policy violation,” the one-time appeal, carrying the evidence from that first screenshot.
The Fireworks reviews would have fit a rule on day one: Google’s policy counts current or former employment, or another professional or personal affiliation, as a conflict of interest.
None of that is a verdict on your work. A stranger can post about everything you’ve built, and the only exit is a rule they broke. Once you see that, the knot in your chest has somewhere to go: you stop arguing about fairness and start arguing about policy, which is the only argument Google listens to.
### Before anyone says “lawyer,” Missouri changed the rules
Here’s the part no national how-to will tell a St. Louis owner. Missouri repealed section 537.528 and enacted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, now section 537.529 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri. Under it, a person sued over speech on a matter of public concern can file a special motion to dismiss, and if they win, the court “shall award costs, reasonable attorney’s fees, and reasonable litigation expenses” to them.
Whether any single review counts as that kind of speech is a question for a Missouri attorney, not a web page. The Fireworks reviews were fabricated, posted under the names of prior customers; most one-stars are a real customer’s opinion. Hold that sentence next to the pitch some removal outfits make: “We’ll send the reviewer a letter.” The bluff can end with the business paying the reviewer’s lawyer.
Federal law points the same way. The FTC’s consumer review rule, in its review suppression section, makes it a violation for anyone to use “an unfounded or groundless legal threat, a physical threat, intimidation, or a public false accusation” in response to a consumer review. Say it out loud to the next person who offers to make a review disappear in a week: in a review fight, the scariest letter is often the one a removal seller sends in your name.
### Can you report a fake Google review?
Yes, and fakes are where reports actually win. Google’s contribution policy says contributions to Maps “should reflect a genuine experience at a place or business,” and that fake engagement “is not allowed and will be removed.” A review from someone who was never there is a policy argument, not a feelings argument.
The insider move most owners miss: Google’s policy names “current or former employment” as a conflict of interest. The ex-employee who left angry and posted as a “customer”? That review sits squarely inside a rule. So does a cluster of one-star ratings landing the same afternoon, because the policy also covers patterns “indicative of efforts to manipulate a place’s rating.”
“Same text, same afternoon, five accounts with no history” is a pattern, and patterns are what the policy was written for. A hurt feeling is not.
### The one appeal, and how not to burn it
Google says evaluation “typically takes several days,” and you can watch the status in the Reviews Management Tool. If the answer comes back that no violation was found, you can submit a one-time appeal. One. That is the number to remember, because most owners spend it angry, on the same words that just failed.
Spend it on evidence instead. Name the exact policy. Attach the pattern you documented. Keep it to facts a stranger could check in a minute. A cold, specific appeal reads like a case; a hot one reads like a business that can’t take criticism, and that is exactly what Google said it stays out of.
### When it’s not one review but twenty
Some owners wake up to a wall of it: six, ten, twenty one-star ratings stacked overnight, accounts with no photo and no history, sometimes the same name on several of them. Your chest goes tight and your thumbs want to answer every single one.
Don’t. Ten defensive replies in a row turn a profile into a shouting match and bury your real customers underneath it. A coordinated attack needs a different play than a single bad review.
Document the whole cluster first. Every review, every date, every reviewer profile, how many reviews each account has ever left, whether the wording repeats and how tightly the timestamps bunch. One of these looks like an opinion. Twenty together look like coordination, and Google’s policy is written for exactly that pattern.
Report them as one pattern, not twenty grievances. Point each report at the same policy and describe the cluster, so whoever reads it sees the shape. Then reply once, publicly, to the most visible review: you have no record of these visits, you’ve reported the activity, and here is how a real customer can reach you. Readers can tell a business under attack from a business with a problem, but only if you sound like the first one.
If someone is impersonating your business outright, using your name on another listing or spoofing your number, report that to Google as impersonation, its own policy, rather than burying it inside a review complaint. Expect some to come down and some to stay. It is maddening, and it is still better than paying someone to lean on the people who wrote them.
### Can I sue someone for a false Google review?
Sometimes, and the line is narrow. An opinion (“worst service in the city”) is not the same as a false statement of fact (“they stole my wallet”). If a review asserts a fact that is false and damaging, Missouri sets a clock: an action for libel must be brought within two years, under section 516.140. Talk to a Missouri attorney early, and weigh that new fee-shifting rule before anyone files anything.
For everything short of that, the quiet truth is that the reply does more work than the lawsuit ever could.
### Your reply is for the next customer, not the last one
Think about who actually reads it: someone on a lunch break, thumb hovering over your number, deciding whether to call you or the next name down. They aren’t grading whether the complaint was fair. They’re watching how you act when something goes sideways, which is the exact thing they’re nervous about before hiring a stranger.
Two calm lines beat a defensive paragraph every time. Thank them, say you have no record of the visit or that you want to make it right, and give a real way to reach you. No relitigating. No form letter. If the reviewer simply picked the wrong pin, say so kindly; people often delete their own review once they realize, and that is the fastest removal there is.
Write it the next morning, not at midnight with your jaw clenched. Read it out loud once before you post. If it sounds like something you would say across the counter to a customer you respect, it’s ready.
Close the review tab for an hour. Go find dinner in Ellisville - the one-star will still be there, and you’ll answer it better fed.
### Before you pay anyone to make reviews disappear
Ask three questions, and treat silence as the answer:
Which specific Google policy will you cite? If they can’t name one, they are selling the report you can file yourself.
Will you contact the reviewer? If yes, ask exactly what will be said. That is where the FTC’s review suppression section lives.
What happens if Google keeps it up? “Permanent” is a sales word, not a promise anyone controls.
Here’s the math that matters more than any one review. One sour rating on a profile with four reviews is the whole picture. The same rating buried under a steady stream of real, recent customers is barely a ripple. That isn’t about deleting anything; it’s about more of the right people seeing you, in more places they already look, so the next review is from someone who found you on purpose.
Got a one-star you can’t sleep on? Start with the report, then the reply. If a contractor is pitching you “reputation management” off the back of it, read what to ask before you hire them. Setting up properly while you’re at it? See what licensing you actually need, hiring your first employee, or browse the local pros listed on St Louis Near Me Directory to see who your neighbors call.
If you’re the shop, the kitchen or the one-person crew still answering reviews at midnight after the second shift, this part is for you. You do good work. One stranger shouldn’t get the loudest voice on your name, and the answer is more customers who actually walked through your door. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it possible to remove a bad Google review?
A.  Only if it breaks a Google policy, or if the person who wrote it deletes it. Google’s help page says you can report any review, but only those that violate its policies are eligible for removal. A review that is merely negative or unfair stays, so a calm public reply is your strongest move.
### Q. Can an owner delete Google reviews?
A.  Not directly. Google lets you report any review, but only those that violate its policies are eligible for removal. Report it from your Business Profile, pick the specific policy it breaks, and check the status in the Reviews Management Tool. If Google finds no violation, you get a one-time appeal.
### Q. How to get a fake review removed from Google?
A.  Report it under the policy it breaks. Google’s contribution policy says content not based on a genuine experience is fake engagement and will be removed, and it counts current or former employment as a conflict of interest. Screenshot the review and the reviewer’s profile first, and describe any pattern of similar reviews in your report.
### Q. Can you legally pay a company to remove bad reviews from Google business?
A.  Paying someone to file policy reports buys nothing you can’t do yourself, since Google lets you report any review. The risk is in the method: the FTC rule bars unfounded legal threats, intimidation and false public accusations aimed at reviewers, and it bars paying for reviews, positive or negative. The longer-term fix is more real customers; a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your name where those customers already look.
### Q. How many 5 star reviews to cancel a 1 star on Google?
A.  There’s no magic number. The more real reviews a profile carries, the less any single rating moves it: a single bad review on a thin profile is the whole story, so more real customers matter more than any one rating. That’s why owners put their name in more places, including St Louis Near Me Directory, where neighbors search by category and neighborhood.
### Q. Why is my Google review not deleting?
A.  If you are the owner, a flagged review only comes down when Google finds a policy violation, and evaluation typically takes several days. If you wrote the review, open Google Maps, click Menu, then Your contributions and Reviews, click More next to the review and select Delete review.
