## Chimi’s in Wentzville Is Still Sizzling. The St. Peters One Closed.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-authentic-flavors-of-chimi-s-wentzville
The skillet hisses before you see it. You hear it come out of the kitchen, a hard, spitting sizzle that cuts right through the talk at every table it passes, and then the steam hits your face as it lands. Beside it sits a little bowl of salsa the kitchen made itself and a scoop of guacamole that is still bright green. That is the plate Chimi’s Fresh-Mex puts first when it describes itself on its own website: sizzling fajitas, house-made salsas, fresh guacamole.
Here is the part a lot of people out past the Missouri River have not caught up with yet. The Chimi’s in St. Peters is gone. STL.News reported that the St. Peters location closed and that a new restaurant, Casa del Maiz, opened in the same space with a smaller, spicier menu. The paper also said nobody has confirmed whether the two share owners.
And the chain’s own locations page still prints a St. Peters address on Cloverleaf Drive. Look closer and it gets stranger. The phone number on that St. Peters line, 636-317-1399, is the same number Chimi’s gives for its kitchen in a Dierberg’s shopping center on Mid Rivers Mall Drive.
So if you type “Chimi’s” into your phone and tap the first pin, you can end up in a parking lot staring at a sign with a different name on it, with hungry kids in the back seat asking why you stopped. The Wentzville kitchen at 8 Wentzville Center Drive is the one to aim for. Wentzville is on the restaurant’s current list of locations. Two moves save the night: put the street address in the map, not the brand name, and call (636) 887-4422 before you leave the house, since the restaurant’s own pages say hours are subject to change without notice.
### What is Chimi’s Fresh-Mex in Wentzville?
Chimi’s Fresh-Mex in Wentzville is a locally owned Mexican restaurant at 8 Wentzville Center Drive, phone (636) 887-4422. It is one of a handful of Chimi’s kitchens around St. Louis, known for sizzling fajitas, street-style tacos, hearty burritos and enchiladas, with house-made salsas and fresh guacamole on the side.
### Who this place is for
The honest answer is: the table that cannot agree. One person wants a heavy plate off the grill, one wants a couple of light tacos, one does not eat meat, and one is seven years old. Chimi’s menu has room for each of them. The restaurant says it runs from quick lunch specials to full dinner platters, with vegetarian dishes, combination plates and customizable meals, and its menu headings include seafood and soups and salads. That spread is why it works for families out west, where the strip along the highway leans hard on national chains and the independent kitchens are the ones worth seeking out.
It also works for the night nobody wants to cook. Order for pickup, swing by the Wentzville Center, and the smell fills the car before you are out of the lot. By the time you are home the bag is warm against your lap and somebody has already stolen a chip.
“Fresh-Mex” is right there in the name. In the restaurant’s words, the idea is to balance traditional Mexican recipes with a fresh, contemporary approach. In practice that shows up in the small bowls: salsa that tastes of tomato and chile instead of a jar, guacamole you can see was mashed, not poured. It is not a white-tablecloth place and does not pretend to be. It is a neighborhood kitchen that wants you back on a random weeknight.
### A chimichanga is a burrito that took a swim
The place is named after one dish, so start with it. Cambridge Dictionary defines a chimichanga as a Mexican dish made from a folded flour tortilla filled with rice, beans, cheese or meat, and fried. That is the whole difference between a burrito and a chimichanga. Same tortilla, same kind of filling. One goes straight to the plate soft; the other goes into hot oil and comes back with a shell that crackles when your fork breaks it, steam leaking out of the crack.
If you only order one thing on a first visit, make it a chimichanga, the dish that matches the name on the sign. A restaurant that names itself after a plate is telling you where it puts its pride.
People who grew up on soft burritos sometimes balk at the idea of frying one. Try it once with salsa spooned over the top. The shell goes from glassy to soft where the sauce lands, and the inside stays hot long after the first bite. It is the kind of plate you finish slowly because it never cools down fast enough to rush.
### What to order on your first visit
Keep it simple the first time. Here is a plan that covers the whole menu’s range without overwhelming the table:
Chips, salsa and guacamole to start. The house-made salsa is the fastest test of any Mexican kitchen. If the first bowl is good, relax; the rest usually follows.
One sizzling fajita platter for the table. It arrives loud, gives everyone a taste of the grill, and buys you time to decide on the next round.
A chimichanga. The dish that matches the name on the sign. Split it if you want to save room.
Street-style tacos. The restaurant calls out carne asada and grilled chicken tacos among its signature dishes. Order a couple of different fillings and compare.
Enchiladas for the comfort eater. Enchiladas are on the restaurant’s own short list of what it serves, and they are the easy order for anyone who wants something rich and saucy.
Something from the seafood side. The menu has a Mariscos section, and the restaurant lists seafood specialties among its signature dishes.
Menus change, and specials rotate with the season. Check what is on the board when you sit down rather than counting on any one dish being there forever.
### The lighter side of the menu
If someone at your table asks what the healthiest Mexican dish to order is, point them toward the grill and away from the fryer. Grilled chicken or steak with salsa, beans and a few tortillas gives you all the flavor without the crackling shell. Pile on the salsa and go easy on the cheese, and you will still walk out full.
Vegetarians are covered here, not handed a single afterthought plate. Between the vegetarian dishes, the guacamole and the beans, a meatless meal is a real meal. That matters for mixed groups. Nobody has to make a speech about what they do not eat; they just order.
Kids are easy too. The restaurant says its menu is built for individuals, families and groups alike, and a basket of chips does a lot of quiet work while the grown-ups read the menu.
Still hungry for more Mexican kitchens worth the drive? Our guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis rounds up local favorites across the metro, picked by locals, not by an algorithm.
If you run the taqueria, the family kitchen or the one-truck operation with your name on the side, look at what happened in St. Peters. A name changed, and the map kept sending hungry customers to the old one. Who is telling your customers where you are right now? A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your menu, hours and photos where neighbors search and where AI assistants look, so the customers who want your food find your door. Claim your spot when you are ready.
### The fajitas came from Texas ranch country
That sizzling skillet has a history most diners never hear. The Handbook of Texas, published by the Texas State Historical Association, notes that fajitas, widely available in restaurants, are a common folk dish in South Texas but not in West Texas.
Which raises the question people really ask: is Tex-Mex actually Mexican food? The same Handbook says Tex-Mex foods are a combination of Native American and Spanish cuisines that came together to make a distinct new cuisine. So it is its own thing, born on the border, not a lesser copy of something from Mexico City. When the skillet lands in Wentzville, you are eating a ranch-country tradition that traveled a long way to get here.
### Patio nights and the to-go bag
Ask about sitting outside when the weather is good. The restaurant lists al fresco dining among the ways to eat with them, and a warm evening out west with a skillet still popping in front of you is one of those small pleasures that is easy to skip until you make a habit of it.
For the ride home, curbside pickup is on the restaurant’s own list of services, which means on a rainy night you can stay in the car with the wipers going while the bag comes to you.
### What is the most authentic thing on the table?
Look at the tortillas. The Handbook of Texas points out that corn tortillas form the basis of a long list of popular dishes, including enchiladas, tacos, chilaquiles, chalupas, quesadillas and tostadas, and that most Texas-Mexican corn dishes carry names that come from Nahuatl, the Aztec language. So the oldest thing on your plate may be the plainest: the tortilla wrapped around your taco.
That is worth a moment of attention next time a warm stack shows up. Tear one open and smell it. Corn, a little toast from the griddle, steam on your fingers. It is a thread that runs a lot further back than any restaurant chain.

The Wentzville Chimi’s is at 8 Wentzville Center Drive, Wentzville, MO 63385, phone (636) 887-4422. It is an easy stop for Wentzville, Lake Saint Louis, O’Fallon and Foristell, and its spot by the Wentzville Center makes it simple to pair with a shopping run or an errand at one of the other local businesses in Wentzville.
Hours can shift by day and by season. Call (636) 887-4422 before a big group drive, especially if you are counting on a late dinner. And search by the street address, not by the Chimi’s name alone, so the map does not hand you the old St. Peters pin.
If you are making a night of it, browse the full run of places to eat in Wentzville for dessert or a second stop, or head east toward the river for an evening on the old brick Main Street historic district.

A.  It is at 8 Wentzville Center Drive, Wentzville, MO 63385, phone (636) 887-4422. Search by that street address rather than the brand name, because the St. Peters Chimi’s has closed and a different restaurant now runs in that space.
### Q. What is the difference between a burrito and chimichanga?
A.  The frying. A chimichanga is a folded flour tortilla filled with rice, beans, cheese or meat, and then fried, per Cambridge Dictionary. A burrito is the same idea served soft.
### Q. What is traditionally in a chimichanga?
A.  Rice, beans, cheese or meat inside a flour tortilla, folded and fried, per Cambridge Dictionary. Most kitchens finish it with salsa or a sauce spooned over the crisp shell, which softens it just where the sauce lands.
### Q. Is Tex-Mex actually Mexican food?
A.  It is its own cuisine. The Handbook of Texas, from the Texas State Historical Association, describes Tex-Mex foods as a combination of Native American and Spanish cuisines that came together to make a distinct new cuisine. Fajitas, for example, are a common folk dish in South Texas.
### Q. What is the healthiest Mexican dish to order?
A.  Go to the grill side of the menu instead of the fryer: grilled chicken or steak with salsa, beans and tortillas, light on the cheese and sour cream. Chimi’s also lists vegetarian dishes for meatless eaters.
### Q. What is the most authentic Mexican dish?
A.  No single plate owns that title, but the corn tortilla is the foundation. The Handbook of Texas notes that corn tortillas form the basis of dishes such as enchiladas, tacos, chilaquiles, chalupas, quesadillas and tostadas, and that most Texas-Mexican corn dishes take their names from Nahuatl, the Aztec language.

## A $750 Wedding at Busch Stadium and Other St. Louis Venues That Print Their Prices
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-event-venues-in-st-louis-for-your-next-celebration
You open the first tab and find a room you love. You scroll for a price. There isn’t one, only a button that says Inquire.
You open another. Same button. By the fifth tab you are guessing: is this $500 or $5,000?
Some St. Louis venues do print the number. Busch Stadium posts a price for each of its clubs, and its micro-wedding package for up to 10 guests starts at $750. A Forest Park pavilion is $85 a day, reserved by permit through the city’s Permit Section at 314-289-5330. Sort your tabs into those two piles and planning gets calmer: open the rooms with numbers first, and send the rest one short, specific question.
Fall for the number before you fall for the room.
### What to consider when choosing a venue for an event?
Start with three numbers: your headcount, your date and the ceiling for the whole bill. Then ask what the number covers. At Grbic Events, the packages include china, flatware, linens, full-service staff and a hosted bar. At one municipal civic center, the rental fee includes the set-up of tables and chairs, trash receptacles and custodial services. Capacity also moves with the layout: the National Car Rental Club at Busch Stadium seats 100 for dinner and holds 160 for a cocktail reception, and the Century Room at Grbic fits 150 for a reception but 120 for a ceremony. Check the season, check the rules on outside food and alcohol, and check whether the price on the page will still be the price when you sign, because Busch Stadium says plainly that its pricing is subject to change at any time.
### Which St. Louis venues print their prices?
The CommunityAmerica Cardinals Club at Busch Stadium greets you with a baby grand piano in the entrance, then marble hallways, then an expansive room decorated in magnificent wood. The National Car Rental Club is modeled after the historic Eads Bridge. And the stadium posts its numbers the way a hotel does: the Perficient Red Jacket Club is $1,250 for four hours and seats 50, with room for 100 at a cocktail reception, and the National Car Rental Club is $2,250 for four hours. For a wedding, the micro-wedding packages are $750 for up to 10 guests and $1,250 for up to 25, offered between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Thursday, on non-game days only, and the Gold Glove ceremony is $5,500 for up to 300 guests. Prefer reviews? Traveler reviews of Busch Stadium are one click away.
Grbic pitches the Century Room as dining al fresco beside rustic brick and glowing candlelight, and the room does have brick fireplaces. The Luxe Room, a building that was once the Old Bailey Dairy Farm, sets exposed brick against modern chandeliers. Grbic Events, a family-owned banquet venue in South City, prints its packages: buffet prices start at $100 per person and plated prices start at $155, and each package includes a four-hour reception, a one-hour cocktail hour and a five-hour hosted bar. The Century Room holds up to 150 guests for a reception and the Luxe Room holds 300 or more. The Century Room’s food and beverage minimums are $10,000 on Friday, $12,000 on Saturday and $8,000 on Sunday, and Grbic says it has smaller party and shower packages, with pricing and dates available if you inquire.
Upstairs at The Cheshire, a vaulted ceiling with dark wood beams, original to the historic landmark building, stretches over a room for up to 250 guests, and the smaller rooms hide behind giant sliding barn doors. Its wedding packages list mirror tiles, floating candles, a parquet wood dance floor, a private tasting for up to four guests and a complimentary night’s stay for the couple, with the Shakespeare at $115 and the James Joyce at $130. Confirm whether those prices are per guest before you budget.
At Olivette Lanes, the party is the point, and the prices are on the page. A kids’ bowling birthday party is $17 per child, with a minimum of eight kids, which the page prices at $136. That covers an hour and a half of bowling, shoe rental, two slices of pizza and a small soda per child, with a $25 deposit. An adult weekend party is $89.95 per lane for up to six people, and the page welcomes family reunions.
At the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station, the Shark Canyon viewing window is the backdrop for a full bar set-up, and birthday parties run $150 for up to six guests, $300 for up to 12, and $525 for up to 12 in the Shark Canyon party, with ninety minutes in a private party space. The Saint Louis Zoo sells the iconic backdrop of animal habitats for anniversary celebrations, milestone birthday parties and class reunions, says children’s birthday packages are not available, and starts its catered birthday events at $1,200 for a daytime event.
### Which St. Louis venues make you ask for a quote?
St. Louis Union Station lets you hold a wedding reception, ceremony or bridal shower under the sweeping archways and mosaics of the Grand Hall, where a 65-foot ceiling plays a light show of 30 video vignettes set to music. The Midway runs from weddings with 200 guests to trade shows with 3,000, in natural light through a steel trussed glass roof, across 43,000 square feet. To start, it gives a phone number, (314) 923-3900, and an email, info@stlouisunionstation.com. Guests can also book rooms at the hotel.
The Pageant turns a 33,000-square-foot concert room into a gala backdrop, with a tiered main floor, a balcony of more than 300 theatre-style seats and a flexible capacity of up to 2,000. Delmar Hall holds up to 750, and The Halo Bar, with a private entrance, a full bar, an outdoor patio and a sound system, holds up to 150. Its event page invites you to ask your event planner or contact the venue to plan a party, reception or wedding.
The Original Schlafly Tap Room sits at 2100 Locust Street in downtown St. Louis. Its North Bar, Club Room and Hale Room all have city skyline views, windows over the courtyard Biergarten and their own private bars, with original brick walls and twelve-foot windows. The page lists a capacity of 156 for dinner and 250 for a cocktail party, with staffing, audio-video, tables and linens included, and it offers set and custom packages. Contact the events manager at events@schlafly.com or 314-241-2337 extension 243, and know that popular days fill up quickly. Directions are on Google Maps.
Luxury Events Venue, at 810 Lumiere Place Boulevard on Laclede’s Landing, describes an industrial chic room with views of the Gateway Arch, high ceilings, chandeliers, exposed brick and an accent wall made for photos. It holds 85 guests, lets you bring your own food and caterer, does not allow outside alcohol because it has a fully stocked bar and bartenders, and promises a custom proposal by email within 24 hours of your inquiry. ### What do people rent venues for?
Almost everything. The Saint Louis Zoo markets its rooms for anniversary celebrations, milestone birthday parties and class reunions. ### What are some affordable wedding venues in St. Louis?
The honest answer is a park. Tower Grove Park’s Sons of Rest Shelter is $140 a day with electric outlets and room for 100, and the Gurney Picnic Site is $50 a day and holds 75. A Forest Park pavilion is $85 a day and holds 100, though pavilion reservations run only from May 1 to Sept. 30, need two weeks’ notice and can be made up to a year ahead. The Jewel Box in Forest Park is the cheapest true reception hall with a posted price: $1,750 for a Sunday through Thursday evening, $3,250 for a Friday or Saturday, plus a $1,000 security deposit, with room for 100 guests when there is a dance floor and 160 when there is not. Every event at the Jewel Box must be catered by a company from the city’s authorized caterers list.
Indoors on a smaller budget, a municipal civic center rents a room for up to 100 people at $450 for residents and $525 for non-residents, an eight-hour block that includes set-up, use time and cleanup. And if the wedding is tiny, Busch Stadium’s $750 micro-wedding is ten guests, a home-plate memory, and a price you can put in a spreadsheet today.
### Is it cheaper to rent a tent or a venue?
Not reliably. Zola’s tent guide says tent weddings often cost similar amounts to traditional venues once you add the required rentals, permits and services, and that flooring, lighting, climate control, generators, tables and chairs can easily double or triple your initial tent budget. One local rental company’s 20 by 40 foot tent seats up to 66 for a formal sit-down dinner or up to 160 for a cocktail reception, and all-day rentals start at $1,000 with installation and takedown included. For 100 seated guests you would need more than that tent, plus tables, chairs, linens and catering.
### What a Party for 100 People Can Cost
Add it up from posted numbers. A Forest Park pavilion that holds 100 is $85 for the day. Restaurant catering priced by the pan does the rest: at Osteria Forto, a full pan of rigatoni bolognese is $140 and a full pan serves 16 to 20, so six pans, $840, serve 96 to 120. Six full pans of Forto salad at $100 each add $600. Add the pavilion at $85, six pans of rigatoni bolognese at $140 each and six pans of Forto salad at $100 each, and the day comes to $1,525 before tax, delivery, plates and drinks, or about $15 a guest across 100 guests.
Move indoors and the numbers climb in steps. Grbic’s buffet packages start at $100 per person with a five-hour hosted bar, so 100 guests starts at $10,000. Busch Stadium’s National Car Rental Club is $2,250 for four hours for a seated group of 100, before food. The cheapest all-in plan is rarely the most beautiful one, and the most beautiful one is rarely the cheapest, so decide which of those two you are buying.
### Booking Windows and Seasons
Zola says you should book your venue around nine to 14 months in advance, and its planning checklist says 12 to 18 months out. June is when most couples marry in St. Louis, so venues fill fast in peak season. Public spaces run on their own clocks: the Jewel Box takes reservations up to two years in advance, Forest Park pavilions can be booked up to a year ahead with two weeks’ notice, and Tower Grove Park requires reservations at least seven days in advance, with prime dates and locations filling quickly.

## Filthy Knees, Free Museums: Indoor St. Louis When It Pours
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-indoor-activities-in-st-louis-for-any-weather
Your kid is gone. Vanished up a multi-story slide somewhere over your head, and you’re on scraped knees in a tunnel deep in City Museum’s caves, jeans filthy, laughing too hard to care. You can’t even hear the rain pounding the roof of this 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse downtown, which a sculptor turned into tunnels, caves and slides built from salvaged scrap. Bring clothes you can crawl in.
Then the good news lands: four of the best rainy-day stops in town cost nothing to walk into. The Saint Louis Science Center, the Saint Louis Art Museum and the Missouri History Museum charge no general admission, because since 1971 City and County property owners have paid for them through the Zoo-Museum District tax, and the Contemporary Art Museum in Grand Center is free on its own. Most big cities charge $20 or more a head at their flagship museums, so a family of four is out $80 before anyone sees a dinosaur. Here they spend the whole gray day in Forest Park and pay for nothing but parking. In St. Louis, the rainy day is the cheap day.
Live in the City or County? Two more freebies most residents never use. The steamy rainforest under the Climatron dome at the Missouri Botanical Garden is free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon, and the Butterfly House in Chesterfield lets residents in free for the first two hours on the first Tuesday of every month, butterflies landing on your sleeve while it sleets outside.
One more that visitors walk right past: after dark, step into the Grand Hall at Union Station and look up. On the hour from 5 to 10 p.m., a 3D light show plays across the 65-foot ceiling, flowers swaying and fireworks bursting overhead, with John Goodman narrating the old station’s story. It costs nothing to stand there and watch, except on nights the hall is booked for a private event.
Before you grab the umbrella: check the day. The Art Museum and History Museum are typically closed Mondays, the Science Center on Tuesdays. For City Museum, buy tickets online because the morning ticket line gets long, park in the serpent-fenced lot at 16th and Delmar for a flat $15, and write your phone number on your kid’s wristband before they vanish into a tunnel. Knee pads are for sale in the gift shop by the door. Then dry off at Union Station with the aquarium’s shark tank and a ride on the 200-foot St. Louis Wheel, which is climate-controlled and runs in a downpour.
### The Rainy-Day Cheat Sheet
### The Free Big Three, Paid For Before You Walked In
Start on the glass Sky Bridge at the Saint Louis Science Center, wet I-64 traffic hissing past beneath your feet while the kids aim radar guns at it. The rest of the building is experiments, dinosaurs and the McDonnell Planetarium (the Omnimax and some simulators are paid add-ons; note it’s closed Tuesdays). Across Forest Park, run up Art Hill and shake the rain off inside the Saint Louis Art Museum, thousands of years of art in one free building. The Missouri History Museum tells the city’s story, from the 1904 World’s Fair to Chuck Berry, at no charge.
Add a fourth free stop in Grand Center: the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis is always free, with rotating modern and experimental shows that can be strange in the best way. From there you’re a short walk from the Fabulous Fox and the rest of the arts district if the rain hangs on into the evening.
### City Museum: Wear Jeans You Can Ruin
You hear it before you find your way in: kids hollering through tunnels somewhere over your head, sneakers squeaking on metal. If you do one paid indoor thing in St. Louis, make it the City Museum. Housed in a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse and dreamed up by the late artist Bob Cassilly, it works as a museum and a playground at once, though neither word quite covers it: caves and tunnels, multi-story slides, a rooftop school bus hanging off the edge, and endless salvaged-material art to climb through. It’s as fun for adults as for kids (wear clothes you can crawl in). On a miserable-weather day, you can lose three or four hours here without noticing. A tip from locals: it’s busiest on weekend afternoons, so go at opening or on a weekday if you can, and know that much of the fun is physical - this is a climb-crawl-slide kind of place, not a look-with-your-eyes museum. There’s even a pinball and arcade room tucked inside if your crew needs a breather from the tunnels, and if that ends up being everyone’s favorite part, the city’s barcades and pinball halls are worth a trip of their own.
### For the Kids: Sharks, a 200-Foot Wheel and 2,000 Butterflies
Families have easy wins downtown. The St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station brings touch pools and a shark tank under one roof, and the St. Louis Wheel right outside is a climate-controlled, 200-foot observation wheel that runs year-round - a fun, dry way to see the skyline even in a downpour. Out in Kirkwood, The Magic House (the St. Louis Children’s Museum) is a beloved hands-on playground for younger kids, and in Chesterfield, the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House is a warm indoor tropical conservatory with roughly 2,000 free-flying butterflies - a real mood-lifter on a gray day. Little kids tend to love it: butterflies land right on you, it’s warm and calm, and it’s an easy hour that doesn’t require a nap-time meltdown recovery afterward.
Total tangent - St. Louis Hills, quietly one of the best neighborhoods in the city.
### For Grown-Ups: a Rainforest Dome, a Food Hall and the Fox
Indoor doesn’t have to mean kid-focused. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s Climatron - a geodesic-dome rainforest conservatory - is a lush, humid escape when it’s cold and gray outside (and St. Louis city and county residents get in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings). City Foundry STL in Midtown packs a food hall, the Alamo Drafthouse cinema, Puttshack’s high-tech mini golf, and more under one roof - a whole indoor date without moving your car. And for a classic grown-up rainy afternoon, the free Art Museum plus a long lunch is hard to beat. Grand Center, the arts district around the Contemporary Art Museum, is also home to theaters, jazz at the Dark Room, and the Fabulous Fox - so a gray day can easily turn into a culture-packed evening if you let it, and those same theaters and music rooms turn up again when the city makes its New Year’s Eve plans.
### Retro Bowling on the Loop, Mini Golf at the Foundry
Rained out and craving a show anyway? Here is where music DVDs still turn up in St. Louis.
Planning a cold night out for two instead? Here are St. Louis winter date ideas and what to reserve.
When you just want to do something, St. Louis delivers. Pin-Up Bowl in the Delmar Loop pairs retro bowling with a cocktail lounge; Puttshack at City Foundry does tech-tracked mini golf; and Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, laser tag, and a big arcade for an all-day rainy-weather option. If your crew wants active indoor fun - escape rooms, climbing, arcades - St. Louis has a whole scene for that, too (see our separate guide to active indoor things to do), and come October that same appetite for a scare fills the region’s haunted houses and Halloween events.
A rainy-day outing is better with the right lunch or coffee stop nearby - and that’s what a local directory is for. You can search St Louis Near Me Directory to find spots near any of these attractions before you head out.
If you run a café, a lunch spot or an escape room within a few minutes of Forest Park or Union Station, list your business with us and turn the soaked families coming out of the Science Center into customers.
### A Rainy Weekend Plan: One Free Day, One Paid Day
The beauty of St. Louis for bad weather is how the attractions cluster, so you can chain several without much driving. In Forest Park, the free Art Museum, History Museum, and Science Center sit within a few minutes of each other - you could spend an entire rainy day going museum to museum and never pay admission. Downtown, the City Museum and Union Station (aquarium, wheel, mini golf, ropes course, mirror maze) are a short hop apart, enough to fill a family weekend on their own, and Union Station turns into a holiday destination in its own right once the Christmas lights and seasonal events arrive. And Grand Center / Midtown pairs the free Contemporary Art Museum with City Foundry’s food hall and entertainment for an easy adult day.
A smart rainy-weekend plan looks like this: one day of free museums (Forest Park’s big three plus the Contemporary Art Museum), one day of paid play (City Museum in the morning, Union Station in the afternoon). Mix in a warm break at the Climatron or the Butterfly House if the gray really sets in, and the worst-weather weekend of the year turns into one of the more memorable ones.
### Know Before You Go: Closed Mondays, Closed Tuesdays
A couple of planning notes save headaches. Hours and prices drift, so it’s worth a quick check of each attraction’s website before you drive out - especially the Science Center, which is closed Tuesdays, and the Art Museum and History Museum, which are typically closed Mondays. The free museums can get busy on rainy weekends and school breaks, so arrive early for parking. And remember that “free admission” sometimes still means paid parking, paid special exhibitions, or paid add-ons like the Science Center’s Omnimax - the core visit is free, but budget a little for extras.
### Which Indoor Day Is Right for You?
Free rainy day: the Science Center, Art Museum, History Museum, and Contemporary Art Museum - all $0. Restless kids who need to move: City Museum or The Magic House. Toddlers: the Butterfly House or the Magic House. A whole family day under one roof: Union Station’s aquarium and wheel. An adult rainy date: the Climatron or City Foundry. Something active indoors: Pin-Up Bowl, Puttshack, or Main Event. There’s no such thing as a washed-out day here - only an indoor one, and usually a cheap one at that. Keep this list handy on your phone; the day the forecast falls apart is exactly when you’ll be glad you already knew where to go. And most of these spots are close enough together that you can chain two or three into a single day if the rain really settles in - a museum in the morning, lunch, and a bowling alley or aquarium in the afternoon.

Two questions come up every time the forecast turns. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis that won’t cost a fortune? Start with the free big three in Forest Park. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What can we do inside when it's raining?
A.  In St. Louis, plenty. Climb through the City Museum, explore the free Saint Louis Science Center, Art Museum, or History Museum, visit the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station, or warm up in the Missouri Botanical Garden’s Climatron rainforest. City Foundry STL adds a food hall, cinema, and mini golf under one roof.
### Q. What are 5 indoor activities?
A.  Five great St. Louis indoor activities: climb through the City Museum, explore the free Saint Louis Science Center, tour the free Saint Louis Art Museum, meet the sharks at the St. Louis Aquarium in Union Station, and walk the humid Climatron rainforest at the Missouri Botanical Garden. All work rain or shine.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis?
A.  The free institutions carry the day here - a major art museum, a history museum and a science center that cost nothing to walk into. Add City Museum for something no other city has, plus aquariums, bowling and indoor mini golf when you want the day structured around one stop.
### Q. What can couples do together on a rainy day?
A.  Go somewhere steamy first. Walk the rainforest under the Climatron dome at the Missouri Botanical Garden, which is free for City and County residents on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon. Then head to City Foundry STL in Midtown for the food hall, a movie at the Alamo Drafthouse or a round of Puttshack. If it’s still pouring, finish with jazz at the Dark Room in Grand Center. Three stops, zero ball pits.
### Q. What to do when I'm bored on a rainy day?
A.  Pick the format first: something to look at, something to climb or something to eat and linger over. Look: the free Art Museum on Art Hill. Climb: the tunnels and slides at City Museum. Linger: the food hall at City Foundry. Or go somewhere warm. At the Butterfly House in Chesterfield, City and County residents get in free for the first two hours on the first Tuesday of every month.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Missouri?
A.  Go underground. Missouri has roughly 7,500 recorded caves, which is why it’s called the Cave State, and about 20 are show caves with guided tours. Meramec Caverns in Stanton, the largest commercial cave in the state, is an easy day trip down I-44, and a cave holds the same temperature all year, so the rain up top stops mattering. Check tour times before you drive.

## Remember the Warrenton Denny’s? It’s a Family Cantina Now: Casa Tequila
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/experience-authentic-flavors-at-casa-tequila-cantina-grill-winghaven
Remember the Warrenton Denny’s? Seventeen years of coffee refills and Grand Slams on Veterans Memorial Parkway, and then one afternoon the signs came down and the doors were locked. “Well guys, after 17 years at Warrenton Denny’s... We are closed for good,” a longtime employee wrote on Facebook.
It didn’t stay dark. Walk into that room now and it smells like charred peppers and lime; a skillet of fajitas comes hissing past your booth, steak and onions still spitting, and somebody at the next table turns to look. Jessenia Lopez and Leo Carmona, who run Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill, didn’t lease the old Denny’s. They bought it. “If this is like the long haul, and we’re gonna do this for the rest of our lives, we might as well just buy something,” Lopez told the Warren County Record. It’s the small-town turn people forward to each other: the diner closes, and the family down the road buys it so they never have to leave.
That move trips people up, so text this part to whoever’s driving: map apps may still send you to the family’s old unit in the Shoppes at Warrenton outlet center, and that unit is closed. The Warrenton kitchen is 429 E Veterans Memorial Pkwy now, the former Denny’s, and the sister kitchen is 905 Caledonia Dr in the Winghaven neighborhood of O’Fallon. Both open at 11 every morning.
Then order like a regular. Street tacos, carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa or shrimp. A skillet of fajitas for the table. The Trash Can Nachos, exactly as over-the-top as the name promises, with a margarita on the rocks, salt crusted on the rim and cold against your lip. Ask which tequilas behind the bar say “100% agave” on the label, because the word “tequila” alone promises less than people think: under Mexico’s official tequila standard, a bottle labeled just “Tequila” only has to get 51 percent of its sugars from blue agave, and up to 49 percent can come from other sugars, as the Tequila Regulatory Council spells out. Same glass, same salt, same lime, and nearly half the sugar that tequila was distilled from can be something other than agave. Screenshot that for whoever always orders the house margarita without asking. Those nachos are the dish people post about: Atly’s review-based roundup of Missouri’s best queso and nacho spots lists the Winghaven kitchen first. Ask for a to-go box early, because the portions win. And if you’re the one planning the graduation party or the backyard birthday, the same family will roll a taco truck up your driveway: email casatequilawinghaven@gmail.com with the date, the place and a head count.
### Two kitchens, one family, one new address
Walk into Winghaven on a warm night and the patio is the first thing you hear. Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill is one restaurant with two kitchens on the western edge of the metro. Winghaven: 905 Caledonia Dr, O’Fallon, (636) 284-7385. Warrenton: 429 E Veterans Memorial Pkwy, (636) 377-1269. Both run 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 on Fridays and Saturdays. “Winghaven” isn’t a separate town, just the name of the O’Fallon store’s neighborhood.
The Warrenton story is the one locals repeat. The couple’s first home there, in the outlet center, came with little more than tables and booths; they built out a bar and bought about 90 percent of the restaurant equipment themselves before the Denny’s down the road came up for sale.
And if a friend says Casa Tequila closed, they’re thinking of Casa Tequila Bar & Grill in St. Peters, a different restaurant. Both Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill kitchens are open and cooking.
Both kitchens answer to the same couple, so the menu and the standards travel between them, and regulars order the same plate at either door without a second thought.
### What to order when the skillet hits the table
Five things on the menu earn the drive out I-70 or down Caledonia:
Street tacos: carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa or shrimp, small enough that you order three and argue over the last one.
Sizzling fajitas: steak or chicken, arriving loud enough that the whole room knows what you ordered.
The Trash Can Nachos: the signature, and big; Atly’s review roundup calls the portion large, and it’s the plate that gets photographed before anyone touches it.
Carne asada and chunky guacamole: the guac comes cold and bright with lime against warm chips.
The margaritas: the reason the place is named for tequila, poured from a deep shelf that runs from a clean blanco to a slow-sipping añejo.
Portions run big enough that the to-go box is part of the meal, and the chips keep coming warm while you decide.
Eating at home? Both kitchens do takeout and deliver through the major apps, and tacos and fajitas ride out the drive across O’Fallon or out to Wright City better than most food does. On a weeknight when nobody wants to cook and everyone is tired of the pizza rotation, that’s the call.
### Tequila: why “100% agave” on the bottle matters
The name isn’t an accident. Casa Tequila leans into its bar with a deep tequila selection - the kind of range that lets you drink your way from a familiar blanco to a smoky, sipping-quality añejo. If tequila has only ever meant the burn of a bad college shot, this is a good place to be gently corrected. Two label words do most of the work. “100% agave” means every sugar in the bottle came from blue agave; without it, the rules allow up to 49 percent other sugars. Then the age: under the same standard, a reposado rests at least two months in oak, an añejo at least a year, and an extra añejo at least three years, so the darker the pour, the longer it sat in the barrel.
The margaritas are the headliner for most tables, and regulars are loyal to them - classic on the rocks, blended with fruit, or built up into something more ambitious. Pair one with the Trash Can Nachos to start and you’ve got the platonic ideal of a St. Charles County Friday night. For anyone not drinking, the usual Mexican-restaurant standbys and soft options are on hand too, so the designated driver isn’t stuck with water. It’s the kind of bar program that makes the place work equally well for a casual weeknight and a birthday worth celebrating - you can keep it simple or make a night of it, and the room flexes to match.
### A patio, a pitcher and a game on in Winghaven
Casa Tequila leans into a warm, upscale-casual feel - comfortable enough for a family dinner, lively enough for a night out with friends. The Winghaven location in particular plays up the social, patio-and-sports side of things, with outdoor space and an easygoing atmosphere that suits a summer evening and a pitcher of margaritas. It’s the kind of place where a quick weeknight dinner and a leisurely celebration both feel right at home.
Service gets consistent praise, which matters as much as the food for a neighborhood restaurant. When people describe why they keep returning, it’s usually some combination of the flavors, the generous plates, the drinks, and staff who make you feel like a regular even on a first visit - a rare combination that’s harder to find than it should be. That’s the quiet advantage of a family-run place: the owners are often on the floor, and it shows in how the room is run.
Waiting on the skillet? Lewis Place, back in the city, has a story worth the ten minutes.
### Why the names over the door matter
It’s easy to default to a national chain when you’re hungry and don’t want to think. But there’s a real case for a place like Casa Tequila instead. When Jessenia Lopez and Leo Carmona own the restaurant, the quality is personal - their name is on it, their neighbors are the customers, and a bad night isn’t a data point on a corporate dashboard, it’s a face they’ll see at the grocery store. That accountability is exactly why independent restaurants so often out-cook their chain competition on flavor and care.
It’s also where your money goes further for the community. Dollars spent at a locally owned restaurant circulate back through the local economy far more than dollars spent at a chain, and the character it adds to a place like Winghaven or Warrenton - a real gathering spot, not an interchangeable box - is the kind of thing a suburb misses only after it’s gone. Choosing the family-run taco spot over the drive-thru is a small vote for the kind of town you want to live in.
### First visit: chips, guac, then the nachos
Never been? Keep it simple. Start with chips and the chunky guacamole while you look at the menu, and put in an order of the Trash Can Nachos if you’re with a group - it’s built to share and it’s the signature for a reason. For the main event, the street tacos are the easiest crowd-pleaser (get a mix - carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa), while the sizzling fajitas make the whole table turn to look when they arrive. Add a margarita, pace yourself, and you’ve had the full Casa Tequila experience on the first try. Bring the family or a crew - the portions are generous and the room is built for a good time, not a hushed one. And if the weather’s good, ask about patio seating at the Winghaven location; a margarita outdoors on a warm St. Charles County evening is hard to beat, and it’s exactly the sort of small, local pleasure that’s easy to overlook until you make a habit of it.
Craving another basket of warm chips somewhere else in the metro? Our guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis rounds up local favorites across the region - real places, real reviews, no algorithm deciding what you see.
If you’re the taqueria, the cantina or the family kitchen behind the sizzling skillets, the Gold plan keeps your address, hours and photos in front of more customers, so a move like Casa Tequila’s sends diners to the new door, not the old one.
### Winghaven or Warrenton: which one to drive to
The two locations quietly cover a lot of ground on the western side of the metro. The O’Fallon store sits in Winghaven, a master-planned community of homes, offices, and green space in one of the fastest-growing parts of the metro - the kind of neighborhood with plenty of families looking for a go-to dinner spot that isn’t a chain. It draws easily from O’Fallon, Lake Saint Louis, Dardenne Prairie, and Wentzville, which has its own family-run favorite in Chimi’s Fresh-Mex on Wentzville Center Drive.
The Warrenton location, the original, anchors the western edge of the metro along the I-70 corridor, where good sit-down Mexican is genuinely harder to come by. For folks out that way - Warrenton, Wright City, and the surrounding towns - having a from-scratch, family-run cantina nearby is no small thing. Between the two, Casa Tequila has become the reliable answer to “where should we get Mexican tonight” across a wide stretch of the western suburbs and the I-70 towns beyond them.
### The food truck, for your backyard party
Casa Tequila also runs a food truck for private events - a fun way to bring the tacos, fajitas, and margarita energy to a birthday, office party, graduation, or backyard get-together without anyone having to cook or clean up. There’s something about a taco truck pulling up to your own driveway that turns an ordinary afternoon into an occasion; guests remember it in a way they don’t remember a tray of grocery-store sandwiches. Rates and availability vary by date and event size, so the move is to email casatequilawinghaven@gmail.com with your date, time, location, and rough head count, and let them put together a menu that fits. It’s a simple way to make a gathering feel like a party without you doing the work.

## $9.60 Toasted Ravioli, All Day Sunday: Why Sunday Beats Friday at Satchmo’s
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-satchmo-s-chesterfield-mo-a-taste-of-local-flavor
The toasted ravioli steams when you break one open, the breading crackles, and the draft beside it sweats onto the bar while a game murmurs on the TV overhead. At Satchmo’s, in the Woodchase Shopping Plaza at 13375 Olive Boulevard, that basket is $9.60 during happy hour: 2 to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and all day Sunday from the 11 a.m. open.
That’s why Sunday beats Friday here. Happy hour means 20 percent off every appetizer, $2 off drafts, $3 wells and $4 house wine, and on the current online menu that turns the $12 toasted ravioli into $9.60 and the $16 eggroll trio, buffalo chicken, pizza and taco, into $12.80, so two people can split both with two well drinks on a Sunday for $28.40 before tax and tip. Send that to whoever’s picking the Sunday spot. And if you’re reading old reviews, check the dates: new owners took over in mid-2024, and their operating manager, Matt Mitchell, had opened 27 restaurants for chains like Applebee’s and Red Robin before this one, St. Louis Restaurant Review reported.
The name over the door is Louis Armstrong’s. In 1919 he came up the Mississippi on a Streckfus excursion steamer with Fate Marable’s band, looked up at downtown St. Louis and asked whether all those tall buildings were colleges, historian William Howland Kenney recounts in Jazz on the River; on those boats, the National Mississippi River Museum notes, he learned to read music. Satchmo’s says on its own site that it’s named for him and quotes him there: “What a wonderful world.” When the second basket lands, raise a $3 well drink to the kid on the steamer deck.
Then pick your night by how you want it to sound. Monday, the chicken and steak fajita skillet hisses across the room. Wednesday, kids eat free and the turkey melt comes off the grill. Thursday at 7, free trivia starts and a Philly cheesesteak sits next to your answer sheet until 8:30. Most Saturdays at 6, a local act plugs in, no cover. Tuesday’s steakhouse salad and Friday’s golden fish and chips fill in the week. Specials rotate, so call (314) 392-9401 before you build a night around one.
### A riverboat name on a bar-and-grill menu
Powdered sugar is the first clue: the Monte Cristo comes deep-fried and dusted with it, and some of it ends up on your shirt. The rest of the menu is built for a bar stool: a double cheeseburger called the Big Mo, an 8-ounce sirloin, a full bar and TVs for the game. Its current site is satchmosgrill.com, and the old satchmosbarandgrill.com address is dead, so ignore any listing that still points there.
### Toasted ravioli first, then the eggrolls
Toasted ravioli ($12). The breading cracks and the filling steams when you bite through. This is St. Louis, so order the city’s own appetizer first; at happy hour it’s $9.60.
The eggroll trio ($16). Grilled buffalo chicken, pepperoni pizza with marinara, and beef taco with avocado crema, one of each; the wrappers shatter, and the buffalo one is the plate St. Louis Restaurant Review gave five stars.
The Big Mo ($17). The menu’s signature double cheeseburger, American cheese and thousand island running toward your wrist, with tots or onion rings on the side.
Prices are from the restaurant’s own menus and can change. Sides run $5. Save room for the apple wontons ($8): fried, filled with apple pie filling, and dusted in cinnamon sugar under a drizzle of caramel.
### A game on, a draft in hand
Come on a Thursday at 7 and you’ll hear the room before you see it: free trivia, hosted by Unleashed Entertainment, with prizes every round until 8:30. Wednesday is the night to bring the kids, because they eat free, and the turkey melt special comes off the grill with the cheese still sliding. Save room for the chocolate chip cookie skillet, baked to order and slumping under vanilla ice cream, fudge and caramel ($8).
Saturdays are getting louder. The owners are booking local musicians for most Saturdays at 6, no cover and all ages, so a bar named for a trumpet player gets live music in the room; the lineup goes up on the bar’s Facebook page first. Before 6 on any day, a $4 glass of house wine or a $3 well drink is the cheapest seat in the house.
### The 2 o’clock rule
Two questions come up every time: what’s actually included in the happy hour, and what time it starts. Plenty of places advertise one and then discount two drafts and a basket of fries, and most don’t start until you’ve already left work.
That 2 p.m. start is the part people miss. Most happy hours wait until 3 or 4; this one catches the early shift, the retirees and the parents between school pickup and practice, with 20% off all appetizers, $2 off drafts, $3 wells and $4 house wine, and Sunday running all day. It turns an ordinary weeknight into an affordable one, and it’s a smart window to try the place for the first time without committing to a full dinner.
Monday’s fajitas are the special you hear coming, still hissing on the skillet as they cross the room.
As with any restaurant, exact happy-hour times and daily specials can shift, so it’s worth a quick call to (314) 392-9401 or a look at the current menu before you go - especially if you’re building a night around the deals. A two-minute check beats showing up on the one night the schedule changed.
Unrelated, but someone still owes you an explanation of Provel cheese.
### A note on the menu, so you’re not surprised
Because Satchmo’s changed ownership and reworked its menu, some older write-ups and stale online listings still describe dishes that aren’t part of the current kitchen. If you’ve seen a review promising a particular sandwich or dessert that isn’t on the menu when you visit, that’s why - the food evolved with the new team. When in doubt, the menu at satchmosgrill.com and a quick call to (314) 392-9401 are the sources to trust, not a years-old blog post or a stale listing.
We’d rather tell you that plainly than send you in chasing a dish that’s no longer served. The upside of a menu reset is that what’s there now reflects a kitchen that chose it on purpose - and the savory burgers and from-scratch touches are the pieces regulars are talking about.
### Fine dining for the anniversary, Satchmo’s for a Tuesday
Ask around for the must-try restaurants in Chesterfield and you will mostly hear about two things: the fine dining rooms - the steak houses and chef-driven places out toward the airport road - and the restaurants out in Chesterfield Valley. Those are real, and they are worth the reservation. But they answer a different question than the one most people are actually asking on a Tuesday, which is closer to: where is the best place to eat in Chesterfield when nobody wants to dress up, plan ahead, or spend ninety dollars a head?
West St. Louis County is thick with national chains - the same signs, the same menus, the same everything you’d find in any suburb in the country. An independently owned bar and grill like Satchmo’s is a different animal. The people who own it are running one restaurant, in one community, and staking their name on it - which tends to show up in the details, from a house-made sauce to a server who actually remembers you.
There’s a real story in the reopening, too. Taking over an existing restaurant, gutting and remodeling it, and betting months of work on winning a neighborhood back over is no small thing. Choosing a place like this over the interchangeable option down the road is a small vote for the kind of local dining scene worth having - and, happily, you usually eat and drink better for it. It’s exactly the sort of neighborhood spot a good local directory exists to help people find.
Looking for more Chesterfield and west-county spots? Our Wentzville and St. Charles County dining guides and the wider roundup of St. Louis restaurants locals love point you to more independent kitchens worth the drive.
If you’re the owner of a neighborhood bar like this one, notice how Satchmo’s gives nearly every night of the week its own special, and the Gold plan puts yours, with your hours and photos, in front of more customers picking a place tonight.
### Your first visit, start to finish
Never been, or coming back after the remodel? Keep it simple. Start with a shareable appetizer for the table while everyone settles in and looks at the menu. For your main, a burger is the safe, crowd-pleasing move on a first visit - it’s the signature, and it’s the fastest way to judge whether a new-to-you bar and grill knows what it’s doing. If you want to see the kitchen stretch a little, ask what they are proudest of - there is more here than pub standards.
Time it around the daily happy hour if you can - it’s the friendliest way to sample the place without committing to a full dinner tab, and it’s an easy sell for talking a few friends into joining. Finish with something sweet if you’ve got room - a fitting end to a local night out. Go in relaxed, plan to linger, and you’ll get the point of the place quickly.
### Making a night of it in west county
One of the quiet advantages of a spot like Satchmo’s is location. Chesterfield is an easy hub for the western suburbs, so it’s simple to fold dinner here into a larger evening - a movie, some shopping, a walk, or an event nearby - without anyone having to trek downtown and back. A dependable, unfussy bar and grill is exactly the anchor a casual night out needs: somewhere you can land before or after whatever else you’re doing.
It also works for the range of occasions real life actually throws at you - a low-key date, a family dinner where the kids and the grown-ups both find something they like, a place to watch the game with friends, or a quick weeknight meal when nobody feels like cooking. That flexibility is underrated. The restaurants that become genuine regulars aren’t usually the fanciest ones; they’re the reliable, comfortable spots that fit however the evening is shaping up.
### The bet the new owners made
Satchmo’s opened in 2013, and a new ownership group took it over in mid-2024. They spent five months remodeling, swapped the old sports-bar menu for a short one that runs from burgers to steaks, and inherited hundreds of online reviews written about the old place, which is why the dates on those reviews matter.
There’s an art to this kind of restaurant that’s easy to take for granted. A great neighborhood bar and grill has to be a lot of things at once: casual enough to walk into after work in whatever you’re wearing, but good enough that you’d happily bring an out-of-town friend. Affordable enough to be a habit, but with a few dishes that feel like a small treat. Familiar every time, without getting boring. That’s a harder balance to strike than it looks, which is why the ones that get it right earn such loyal regulars.
The reopening under new ownership is really a bet on exactly that balance - taking a place with an established name in the community and sharpening it into somewhere people want to return to week after week. Whether any restaurant pulls that off is ultimately decided one meal at a time, by whether the burger’s right and the service is warm and the room feels good to sit in. On the strength of the refreshed menu and the care that clearly went into the remodel, Satchmo’s has given itself a real shot at becoming that kind of Chesterfield regular.

## The $4.25 St. Paul Sandwich and the Chop Suey Counters Still Frying It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-taste-of-tradition-exploring-the-enduring-appeal-of-old-st-louis-chop-suey
“Lucky, I need one more bowl of chili.”
A man in the crowd shouted it in December 2024, half joking, while a demolition crew sorted good brick out of what was left of Lucky Inn. A storm the week of November 4 had brought down the back of the building, kitchen and all. Hing Yee opened the place in 1932. His son, Robert “Lucky” Yee, ran it for 65 years, and Peter Tao, writing for the Missouri Historical Society, called it the longest continually operating chop suey restaurant until that storm. In the demolition photos, the pots are still on the stove near the cash register.
Lucky Inn is gone. The St. Paul isn’t. Somewhere in this city an egg patty is hissing in hot oil right now, about to be slapped onto white bread. St. Louis’s strangest cheap sandwich, a hot egg foo young patty on plain white bread with mayo, dill pickle, lettuce and tomato, still comes out of small family kitchens like that one, and it still costs counter money: $4.25 to $7.25 on the shop menus checked for this guide. At two of those counters it’s cheaper than the egg foo young plate its patty comes from.
Below: where to get one this week and what each counter charges, what’s actually in it, the two stories about the name (neither one proven), and the old Chinatown a lot of St. Louisans picture buried under Busch Stadium. It isn’t. Its heart became a parking lot.
### Where to get a St. Paul sandwich this week, and what it costs
Who has the best St. Paul sandwich in St. Louis? Argue about it after you’ve tried three. Every price below comes from the shop’s own online menu or website, and these are small kitchens that can change a price or close early without notice, so call before a long drive. Mondays are the trap: China King and Mai Lee are both closed. On Sundays, the Bridgeton shop is.
And order two. The bag comes back warm and heavy at the bottom, the car fills with the smell of fried egg and onion, and the first sandwich won’t make it out of the parking lot.
Old St Louis Chop Suey, Bridgeton. 12454 St Charles Rock Rd., (314) 298-2411. The cheapest board on this list: chicken or vegetable $4.25, ham or pork $4.45, beef, shrimp or crab $4.75, and a Special for $5.00. A chicken egg foo young lunch on the same menu is $7.75. It’s open 10 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and 11 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. Saturday, and it’s closed Sunday. It also pours bubble tea.
Park Chop Suey. 1321 Chouteau Ave. This is the name the famous legend points to. Its own online menu starts with a plain St. Paul at $5.00; chicken, ham or pork is $5.50, duck $6.00, beef or vegetarian $6.50, shrimp $6.75 and mixed meat $7.00. The plain egg foo young dinner on the same menu is $7.50, so the sandwich is the cheaper way to eat that patty.
China King, Telegraph Road. 6051 Telegraph Rd., Suite 5, (314) 293-2888, for south county. Its online menu lists seven St. Pauls: pork, chicken, ham or vegetable at $6.65, beef or shrimp at $6.85, and the House at $7.25. It’s closed Monday, open 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday, 10:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday.
Mai Lee. 8396 Musick Memorial Drive in Brentwood, steps from the Brentwood MetroLink stop: the sit-down version, with a bar and more than 200 Vietnamese and Chinese dishes. When KCUR reported on it in 2021, Mai Lee sold the original St. Paul plus six other versions, including barbecue pork and shrimp. Open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday.
Old St Louis Chop Suey, Chippewa. A second shop with the same name, and its own website, sits at 4600 Chippewa St. in south city. I couldn’t confirm a shared owner or load its prices, so check its menu first.
### What’s in a St. Paul sandwich, bite by bite?
Peel back the paper and the smell gets there first: fried egg, onion, a little hot oil. The patty is egg foo young, the same patty the chop suey houses serve with gravy and steamed rice, fried crispy-brown so the edges crunch while the middle stays soft and full of bean sprouts. Then the cold half: a slather of mayonnaise, a leaf of iceberg lettuce, sliced tomato and dill pickles, all of it between two soft slices of white bread that start giving way under the heat the second you pick it up.
If anyone asks what sandwich St. Louis is famous for, this is the one, and that collision is the whole point. Hot against cold, crunch against cream, pickle brine cutting through fried egg. The St. Louis Post-Dispatch once called it “an odd combination” and a favorite St. Louis original in the same sentence. NPR’s Sandwich Monday tried one in 2013 and filed it under St. Louis tradition.
You order it by what goes into the patty. A plain St. Paul has only vegetables in the egg; for a little more, add a meat. A Special or mixed-meat version piles several in. Park Chop Suey on Chouteau Avenue even sells a duck St. Paul, lists salad dressing where the classic build calls for mayo, and will add cheese for an extra charge.
Even the crunch has a St. Louis back story. After Army service in Vietnam, William Hong decided to supply the city’s Chinese restaurants with bean sprouts while knowing nothing about growing them. He set up in the basement of a family-owned building at 927 Tyler Street, and his family says he worked and slept down there, in the dark and the damp, to keep the sprouts watered. The Missouri Historical Society reports the business grew to 5,000 pounds a week for nearly 150 restaurants.
The St. Paul price board
Across the counter menus above, a St. Paul runs $4.25 to $7.25. The meat you pick moves the price most, and the loaded version sits at the top of every board: the Special at $5.00 in Bridgeton, mixed meat at $7.00 at Park Chop Suey, the House at $7.25 at China King. Order from the shop’s own menu and you see the shop’s own price.
### Who named it St. Paul? Two stories, no proof
Ask where the Saint Paul sandwich originated and you’ll get one of two stories. The version every St. Louisan has heard goes like this: a cook named Steven Yuen invented the sandwich in the 1940s at Park Chop Suey and named it after his hometown, St. Paul, Minnesota. KCUR’s Hungry For MO calls it the most popular theory. It has a hole in it. St. Louis Magazine pointed out in 2016 that the 1940s are several decades before Park Chop Suey opened, and that the shop’s current owner was loath to discuss the folklore.
The second story is bigger. James Beard thought the St. Paul was a play on the Denver sandwich, which he believed Chinese cooks created decades earlier in logging camps. If he was right, the St. Paul is the St. Louis branch of something much older than any one chop suey house.
Neither story can be proven, and the sandwich doesn’t care. Here is what is on the record. After leaving Vietnam in 1978 and spending years in refugee camps, the Tran family landed in St. Louis, and in 1982 they opened a chop suey called China Wall with the St. Paul on the menu. Nearly every Chinese restaurant in the city already sold it. “We knew we needed to put it on the menu because we’d seen it at other chop sueys,” Qui Tran told KCUR.
His mother, Lee Tran, had learned the trade waiting tables at Chinese restaurants around town. In 1985 she opened Mai Lee in a tiny six-table room with a full Chinese menu, slowly added Vietnamese dishes, and Mai Lee became the first Vietnamese restaurant in St. Louis. The St. Paul came with her, and KCUR found it still a constant at Mai Lee 36 years later. Jennifer 8. Lee, who produced the documentary The Search for General Tso, told KCUR what sandwiches like this one mean: “It tells a story of immigrants who arrived in a new place and cooked to survive.”
### Hop Alley: the Chinatown that became a parking lot
St. Louis chop suey had a downtown address before it had corner counters. Hop Alley, St. Louis’s Chinatown, was a neighborhood of family-owned grocery stores, restaurants and laundries, with storefronts on 8th Street between Market and Walnut. Alla Lee, the first Chinese man to arrive in St. Louis, came in 1857. By 1935 a chop suey sign hung over the Orient Restaurant at 400 North Seventh Street.
Ed Shew’s father waited tables at the Orient for decades, and Shew’s memory of the place is pure sense. The smell of garlic, ginger and soy sauce at the door. Mounds of rice so hot the steam rose to the second-floor balcony. Waiters balancing large round metal trays. Chef and co-owner Eng Mow sending out chicken chow mein, egg foo young and chop suey. Plate lunches were $1.25.
Now the part most people get wrong. Plenty of St. Louisans believe Busch Stadium was built right on top of Chinatown. A 2024 essay on the Missouri Historical Society’s blog calls that a pervasive misunderstanding. The 1962 stadium plan helped doom the neighborhood, but the Chinatown core “literally became a parking lot in the 1960s and remained that way for more than a decade.” The Orient served its famous chicken chow mein for the last time in late December 1967, and a high-rise bank building took its place.
You can stand on the spot today. The Board of Aldermen voted in June 2024 to give South 8th Street from Walnut to Market the honorary name On Leong Way, effective that July. The old neighborhood would know the name: the St. Louis chapter of the On Leong Chinese Merchants Association was one of its community organizations. Walk that block, notice how ordinary it looks now, then go eat something that came out of that history.
Make it a two-stop afternoon. Start on On Leong Way, South 8th Street between Walnut and Market, then drive to whichever counter above is closest and order a St. Paul with the meat you grew up on. When you want the rest of the food this city invented, our guide to the dishes St. Louis actually invented picks up where this one stops.
If you’re the family behind a counter like these, with the St. Paul on the board and regulars who order without looking up, here is a question worth sitting with. When somebody new in town asks their phone where to get a St. Paul sandwich, does your name come up, or somebody else’s? See who AI names instead of you, then decide whether your counter deserves to be easier to find.
### Chop suey went where it was welcome
The Missouri Historical Society describes how, under Jim Crow, Chinese grocers, restaurants and laundries welcomed Black customers that white businesses shut out, and built loyal followings in Black neighborhoods in St. Louis and across the country. Across from the Peoples Finance Building in Mill Creek Valley, at Jefferson Avenue and Market Street, stood a popular takeout spot called King Hong Cafe, close to the Star movie theater and busy with Black youth. Then urban renewal took Mill Creek Valley too.
Lucky Inn, on the north side, had its own regulars for decades, officers from the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department among them. Robert Yee said the menu barely changed in his 65 years there. What changed was the order. Fried rice became the constant favorite, perhaps outselling the chop suey the place was built on.
The St. Paul is one door into this city’s Chinese food. The dim sum carts are another.
### The counters close one family at a time
Chop suey was a hit long before it was a memory. It got so popular that it was commercialized in a big way in the 1930s and repackaged in the 1950s as convenience food people ate at home in front of the TV. George Lee, a Chinese American farmer who grew Chinese vegetables for St. Louis restaurants and markets, had a short answer for that: “Canned chop suey? Not for me.”
The bigger threat is quieter. Robert Yee didn’t want his children working the unforgiving restaurant life, and he never made them carry on the family business. So he and his wife, Wing, kept driving into the city every day from their suburban home until the storm made the decision for them. On December 19, 2024, the demolition began. Robert stood by the rubble calling out to the crew, “Have you found the cash yet? It’s somewhere under there.” Before it was over, the Yees picked up a few of the salvaged bricks to keep.
No scandal. No bankruptcy notice. Just a family that had earned the rest, and one less kitchen in the city frying egg foo young. Go this week, not someday.
### How to order a St. Paul like you grew up on one
Lead with the meat. Say “chicken St. Paul” or “shrimp St. Paul.” Plain means vegetables in the egg patty and nothing else.
Go big with the Special at Old St Louis Chop Suey in Bridgeton ($5.00) or the mixed-meat version at Park Chop Suey ($7.00).
Add cheese at Park Chop Suey, where the menu offers it for an extra charge.
Get a side. Park Chop Suey’s egg roll is $1.75, and three crab rangoon are $3.75.
Eat the first half in the car. The hot patty against the cold lettuce is the best part, and it fades as the heat soaks into the bread.
Check the day. China King and Mai Lee are closed Mondays; the Bridgeton shop is closed Sundays.
