### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where did the Saint Paul sandwich originate?
A.  In St. Louis, by most accounts: KCUR credits a Chinese American chef in the city in the mid-1900s. The popular story names Steven Yuen at Park Chop Suey in the 1940s, but St. Louis Magazine noted that date falls decades before Park Chop Suey opened. James Beard tied it to the older Denver sandwich instead.
### Q. Who has the best St. Paul sandwich in St. Louis?
A.  There is no official winner; it’s a taste argument. For a fair test, try three: Old St Louis Chop Suey in Bridgeton (chicken, $4.25), Park Chop Suey on Chouteau Avenue (plain, $5.00) and China King on Telegraph Road (House, $7.25). Judge the patty first: crisp edges, plenty of sprouts, hot all the way through.
### Q. What sandwich is St. Louis famous for?
A.  The St. Paul sandwich: a fried egg foo young patty with mayo, dill pickle, lettuce and tomato on white bread, still sold in restaurants all over St. Louis. KCUR reported that some consider it the most iconic sandwich in Missouri history, and St. Louis Magazine found it nowhere to be found in Minnesota.
### Q. Where can I find chop suey in St. Louis?
A.  Park Chop Suey, 1321 Chouteau Ave., lists chicken, pork or ham chop suey at $9.50, and Old St Louis Chop Suey in Bridgeton, 12454 St Charles Rock Rd., lists chicken or pork chop suey at $10.50. Both sell St. Paul sandwiches too, so you can order the old-school plate and the sandwich in one bag.
### Q. Does St. Louis have a Chinatown area?
A.  St. Louis lost its Chinatown. Hop Alley, the downtown Chinatown around 8th Street between Market and Walnut, was lost to urban renewal, and its core became a parking lot in the 1960s. In 2024 the city gave that stretch of South 8th Street the honorary name On Leong Way so the neighborhood isn’t forgotten.
### Q. Why is chop suey no longer popular?
A.  Tastes moved and the family kitchens aged out. At Lucky Inn, open from 1932 until a 2024 storm, fried rice outlasted chop suey as the favorite, and the owner didn’t want his children in the unforgiving restaurant life. Documentary producer Jennifer 8. Lee calls chop suey “the biggest culinary joke that one culture has played on another.”
### Q. How much does a St. Paul sandwich cost?
A.  On the counter menus checked for this guide, $4.25 to $7.25. Old St Louis Chop Suey in Bridgeton lists chicken or vegetable at $4.25 and a Special at $5.00. Park Chop Suey runs from $5.00 plain to $7.00 mixed meat, and China King on Telegraph Road runs from $6.65 to $7.25.

## New Year's Eve in St. Louis: The Arch Fireworks Go Up at 8, Not Midnight
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ring-in-2026-your-ultimate-guide-to-new-year-s-eve-in-st-louis
It’s a quarter to 8 on December 31, you’re on the ice in Kiener Plaza, and your fingers have quit. A s’more has welded itself to your glove. The DJ is still going, the fire pits are still glowing, and every head in the plaza is tipped back toward the same dark patch of sky above the Arch. In fifteen minutes it lights up. Not at midnight. At 8 p.m.
That’s the early New Year’s Eve clock, and St. Louis keeps two. The early one belongs to the park and the museum: fireworks at Winterfest at 8, a balloon drop at City Museum at 8, both finished by 9. The late one belongs to the concert hall and the ticketed rooms, and it counts down to midnight the way you’d expect. Pick your clock first. Kids in the plan? Work backward from 8. No kids? Work forward from 9. Who can come, what it costs and how you get home all follow from that.
### What to do for New Year’s Eve in St. Louis?
Start with who is coming. A family with a six-year-old wants the early clock. Winterfest at Kiener Plaza costs nothing to walk into, the ice is free if you bring your own skates, and the fireworks are free too. City Museum runs its party from 5 to 9 p.m. and folds it into the price of admission. A couple who want a dressed-up night, or friends who want a countdown and a toast, want the late clock: a ticket, a reservation, or a seat at Powell Hall (718 N. Grand Blvd., box office 314-534-1700), where the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra plays a New Year’s Eve concert. MetroLink runs until about 1 a.m., so the train home is still on the table. Plenty of people do both: skates and fireworks at 8, then somewhere with a tablecloth by 9:30.
### Winterfest: skates, s’mores and fireworks at 8
Winterfest takes over Kiener Plaza every winter, and on December 31 it throws a party called Neon Nights from 4 to 8 p.m. Blades scrape the ice, marshmallows toast over the fire pits, and a heated igloo waits if your fingers give out, all in the shadow of the Arch. There’s a live concert, a DJ, fire dancers and visiting characters, and this year’s page promises 3-D glasses and glow products while supplies last. The page lists one fireworks time for the night: 8 p.m.
Rentals cost extra. On the Winterfest page this year they’re $15 for adults and $10 for kids ages 3 to 15, so a family of two adults and two kids that brings its own skates keeps $50 in the cooler. The night also comes with an RSVP button, so hit it before you go, then dress for standing still. Skating keeps you warm. Waiting for fireworks does not.
### City Museum: a balloon drop at 8 and a toast made of juice
By 7:58 at City Museum, the dance party in Architecture Hall is loud, somebody is mid-chorus at karaoke in Beatnik Bob’s, and the holiday lights have been on all day. Then the balloons drop. The party is part of Weirdly Wonderful Holidays: a countdown kicks it off at 5, face painting and balloon twisters keep the kids busy, and the toast is sparkling juice, the non-alcoholic kind. It comes with general admission or a member pass, so the new year arrives on the ticket you were going to buy anyway. The museum is at 750 N. 16th St., and questions go to 314-231-2489.
If the forecast turns ugly, our guide to indoor spots when the weather turns has backups for the days around it.
### You can’t be in two places at 8
The catch: Winterfest’s fireworks and City Museum’s balloon drop land at the same hour. You get one. If you have kids who love a crowd, a rink and a sky full of light, give the 8 o’clock to Kiener Plaza and let the museum be the plan for another day. If your kids would rather spend the night inside a building that already feels like a holiday, give it to City Museum, where the lights and decorations stay up all day and the party starts at 5.
Either way you finish by 9 and the hard part is over: the car, the coats, and one very awake child. Nobody has to defend a bedtime at 12:15. It’s a small thing and it is most of the reason these two parties exist.
### If you want to sit down at Winterfest
If your toes have had enough, reserve a heated igloo. An igloo seats up to six, and this year the page lists reservations starting at $100 for 90 minutes. Book the igloo after your skate, not before, so you get the full time inside. No outside food or drink is allowed in the igloos, which means the s’mores kit comes after, by the fire pit, with everyone else.
### Later in the night: Powell Hall, ticketed rooms and one good dinner
For the late clock, start with a sound instead of a sale: the quiet in a concert hall just before the first note. The St. Louis Symphony Orchestra books Powell Hall, at 718 N. Grand Blvd., for a New Year’s Eve concert. This year’s listing has it at 7:30 p.m., and the box office takes calls at 314-534-1700. Hearing the year out with an orchestra is a different kind of loud than a DJ.
For the bar, hotel and rooftop parties, go to each venue’s own page, such as the events list at Ballpark Village. Packages and prices are the part that moves from one December to the next, so buy from this year’s page, not from a guide. Not even this one.
Would you rather sit down? The tablecloth rooms book first. Casa Don Alfonso, the Italian restaurant inside the Ritz-Carlton, is one to check, and our guide to date-night restaurants has more. Ask for the late seating if you can get it. Dinner at 9:30 feels like the start of the night instead of the opening act.
### For adults who want the night to surprise them
Not everyone wants glow products, a DJ or a plate of something with a name. If you’d rather end the year somewhere with a little more edge, start with our list of offbeat things to do beyond the Arch, then finish at one of the craft cocktail bars and speakeasies. The trick on December 31 is to pick the second stop before you leave the first. Otherwise you spend the best hour of the night on a sidewalk, scrolling, with everyone else who didn’t decide.
Confetti at midnight
### Getting there, and getting home
The best parties sit in the worst places to park. Downtown, Ballpark Village and Soulard are all spots where parking is a headache, and many of the celebrations there are steps from a MetroLink or MetroBus stop. Winterfest is a short walk from the Eighth & Pine or Stadium MetroLink stations. MetroLink runs seven days a week until about 1 a.m., which covers a late dinner and a drink afterward. Leave the car at home, or at one of the free Park-Ride lots at a MetroLink station, and the trip home stops being a decision you make with cold hands and a long line for the ride-share.
Check the last trip time for your train or bus before you leave the house. A schedule that ends mid-party strands people, and a plan that depends on a ride-share surge price is not a plan. Metro’s Transit Information desk answers trip questions at 314-231-2345, or by text at 314-207-9786, Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Ask a week ahead, not on the night.
### How to read a New Year’s Eve ticket page
A New Year’s Eve ticket page is mostly adjectives. Look past them for four plain facts. When is the toast, exactly, and does it happen at midnight or at some other hour? What does the price cover: food, drinks, both or neither? Is it 21 and over, and is there a table or only standing room? And what happens to your money if someone in your group gets sick on the 30th?
If the page doesn’t answer one of those, email the venue and keep the reply. An open bar that closes at 11 is a very different night from one that stays open to 1, and you want that in writing before you pay, not after.
Do the same with a hotel package. A room is the cleanest answer to the ride home, but only if check-in, checkout and the party all line up with the way you plan to spend the night. Read the fine print the way you’d read it if a stranger were paying and you were the one signing.
Then do one small thing that saves the evening: screenshot every ticket and confirmation before you leave the house, and send them to the person who is driving or leading the group. Cell service gets thin when a crowd stands on one block, and a doorman will not wait while your email reloads.
Mark the calendar - the big night books up fast

Dates, start times and programs change every year, and the organizers know their own schedule better than any guide does, this one included. These are the pages that carry it:

City Museum’s New Year’s Eve party: hours, the balloon drop and what’s included.

Metro Transit: schedules and last trips for MetroLink and MetroBus.
Side road for the road-trip crowd: when every table downtown is gone, here’s where to eat in Elsberry, Missouri.
Open these pages a week out, then again the morning of. A start time that moved is a start time you miss, and the organizer’s own page is the first place a change shows up.
Pick the clock, open the page, and book the part that sells out. The Arch will light up at 8 whether you planned it or not. The only open question is whether you’re standing under it, with warm hands, a ride home and a story to tell on January 1.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can I see fireworks in St. Louis?
A.  On New Year’s Eve, the show to know is Winterfest at Kiener Plaza, where the fireworks go up with the Arch in the frame and walking in is free. It’s an early show, so don’t save the trip for midnight, and plan to arrive before the sky goes dark so you can find a clear spot. For anything later in the evening, check the host venue’s own page for this year’s plan.
### Q. What time do fireworks start in St. Louis?
A.  At Winterfest’s New Year’s Eve party, the fireworks start at 8 p.m., after a 4 p.m. kickoff for skating, a DJ, a live concert and fire dancers. That makes it a family-hour show rather than a midnight one. Confirm the schedule on the Winterfest page before you leave.
### Q. Where to see fireworks on New Year’s Eve?
A.  Kiener Plaza downtown, with the Arch behind the show. It’s a short walk from the Eighth & Pine or Stadium MetroLink stations, so you can skip downtown parking. Winterfest has an RSVP button for the night, and you can bring your own skates to use the ice for free. Aim to be standing still by a quarter to 8 so you aren’t hunting for a sightline when the fireworks start at 8 p.m.
### Q. What is something fun to do on New Year’s Eve?
A.  Pick a clock. For an early night, skate and watch the fireworks at Winterfest or head to City Museum for karaoke, a dance party and the balloon drop at 8. For a late night, hear the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra at Powell Hall or book a dinner reservation first.
### Q. How do I get home after a New Year’s Eve party in St. Louis?
A.  Plan it before you go. Many downtown celebrations are steps from a MetroLink or MetroBus stop, and Metro Transit’s advice is to check when service ends for the night so you aren’t stranded. Park at a free Park-Ride lot at a MetroLink station if you’d rather not park downtown.

## A Locked Door at 3:05: When (and What) to Eat at Thai Kitchen Florissant
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-authentic-flavors-at-thai-kitchen-florissant
3:05 p.m. on a Wednesday, and the door at 8458 N. Lindbergh won’t open. There’s still lemongrass and chili on the air, your stomach growls in the parking lot, and nobody warned you about the gap.
At 4 the lock turns, and by 4:15 the wait has paid for itself. Order the khao soi first. The crispy noodles on top crackle when your spoon breaks through to the yellow curry, and then the heat arrives late: Riverfront Times critic Cheryl Baehr found this one spicier than most, its warmth “more haunting than assertive,” creeping up the back of your palate and staying. Then the Gang Quah shrimp, a tangier, tomato-forward curry with chunks of pineapple warmed through in the broth, spooned over rice so the sweet and the sour hit together.
Those recipes have a name behind them. They’re Andie Ongartsutthikue’s, passed down through her mother’s family for generations, Baehr wrote when she put this kitchen on her list of St. Louis County favorites. What the menu doesn’t say: this is a family branch. Andie, as the Thai Kitchen founder is known, ran her own restaurant in Bangkok for five years before coming to the U.S. in 1995, and the Florissant kitchen, opened in April 2018, belongs to her brother and sister-in-law, St. Louis Restaurant Review reported. That’s why the family’s group site, thaikitchenco.com, takes online orders for its other kitchens, from O’Fallon to Overland, but not this one. Order Florissant on its own page or by phone. One more for the table: the Nam Tok Beef with sticky rice. Nam tok means waterfall in Thai, for the juices that drip off the grilled beef.
So you only learn it once: closed Tuesdays; Monday and Wednesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and 4 to 8:30; Saturday and Sunday, noon to 8:30 straight through. On the Saturday we checked, online orders stopped at 8:15. Call (314) 695-5039 if you’re cutting it close.
Here’s the North County twist. Two Thai kitchens share this stretch of Lindbergh, and both go dark in the afternoon: Pearl Cafe, a few doors down at 8416, breaks from 2:30 to 5 on weekdays. Thai Kitchen’s one-hour gap is the short one. And if the lock still beats you, or it’s a Tuesday, the founder’s own new carryout kitchen, Thai Kitchen Overland at 9440 Midland Blvd, cooks from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day, Ladue News reported when it opened, with moo ping pork skewers and sticky rice you can only get there. Send that to the friend who always suggests Thai at 3:30.
Then the surprise. This Thai kitchen in North County keeps a whole section of pho, big bowls that come with bean sprouts, basil, jalapeños and cilantro on the side. And on its own online ordering page, the most-liked item isn’t a curry at all. It’s the crispy spring rolls, still crackling when the box opens, with pad Thai right behind them.
Ask how much heat you want; the staff will dial a dish up or down. Plan on a box for tomorrow, because portions run big. Budget-wise, most curries, noodles and fried rice list at $17.94 on the online ordering page and the spring rolls at $8.34, so two plates and a starter run about $44 before tip.
### Lunch on a clock
Weekday lunch runs 11 to 3, and plates come out fast enough for a lunch hour. Order the Thai basil stir fry and the basil still smells green when it lands. Get the last order in by about 2:45, before the gap.
### The bowls and plates regulars come back for
### Tom yum, Crying Tiger and the specialties page
The tom yum noodle soup arrives so hot you lean back from the steam, and the first spoonful, sour with lime and lemongrass, clears your sinuses on the way down. The rest of the house specialties run to Panang grouper, spicy catfish and Crying Tiger, and the duck spicy basil fried rice is the plate to split when the table can’t decide.
### Big soup bowls, pho included
With the pho, you build the bowl yourself: tear the basil, push the bean sprouts under the broth, and drop the jalapeño slices in one at a time until it bites back. There’s chicken pho, rare-beef pho and a seafood noodle soup beside the tom yum, and the steam on your face is the point.
Red curry over rice
### The curry that comes home in a box
The red curry arrives orange-red and glossy with coconut milk, deep and slightly sweet, with your choice of meat and fresh vegetables over rice. Panang runs thicker and nuttier, green brighter and sharper. Whatever’s left goes home in a box, and tomorrow’s lunch is handled.
### A long menu, and a pho section nobody expects
The spring rolls are the sound of this place: the box opens, the wrappers crackle, and somebody at the table has already taken two. They’re the most-liked thing on the online ordering page, and the pho bowls and a kids’ menu mean the whole table gets fed, including the friend who only eats pho.
### Delectable Appetizers and Salads
Before the main courses arrive, start with a few appetizers. Crispy spring rolls, flavorful chicken satay, or a plate of Thai dumplings all make an easy opener. If you want something lighter to lead off, the salads are a strong choice. The Papaya Salad, for one, brings a bright mix of textures and a chili kick that wakes up your palate before the bigger dishes land. It’s a smart first move, especially on a warm afternoon. And if you’re weighing whether Thai is healthier than Chinese takeout, this end of the menu, the salads and the broth-based soups, is where Thai cooking runs lightest; the coconut-milk curries and fried rice are the rich end.
### Rich Curry Selections
Curry is the heart of this menu, and Thai Kitchen Florissant handles it well. You can pick from several rich, aromatic options, each with its own distinct profile. The Red Curry runs creamy and slightly sweet, the Green Curry brings a brighter, sharper spice, and the Panang leans thick and nutty. Each one arrives with your choice of protein and a generous pile of rice, which makes for a genuinely comforting meal. Pick based on how much heat you’re after, then work through the rest on later visits.
Rich Curry Selections
### Flavorful Fried Rice Varieties
Don’t sleep on the fried rice, because they do it exceptionally well here. There are several variations worth ordering, including the popular Spicy Basil Fried Rice, which hits hard with heat and herbs, and the sweet-and-savory Pineapple Fried Rice, which plays fruit against fluffy grains. It’s hard to go wrong with any of them; each one lands as a filling, satisfying order. The full menu is posted online, which is handy when you’re deciding ahead of time. It’s an easy way to taste the range of St. Louis flavors without ever leaving Florissant.

It’s that steady, genuine hospitality that turns a decent dinner into a visit you actually look forward to repeating.

## Tell a Joke, Get the Candy: St. Louis Halloween Events, Haunts and Pumpkin Patches
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/unforgettable-halloween-event-st-louis-your-guide-to-spooky-fun
“Why didn’t the skeleton go to the party? He had no body to go with.” A seven-year-old in a cape delivers it on your porch, dead serious, and only then holds out the pillowcase. That’s Halloween in St. Louis. Here, trick-or-treaters tell a joke before they get the candy, a habit that goes back to just after World War II and still baffles every transplant on the block. Teenagers do it too, usually with the worst pun they can find. New in town? Have the kids practice one before the 31st, because a St. Louis porch expects it.
The rest of October piles on around it: screams leaking out of The Darkness onto the sidewalk near Soulard, a haunted hayride rattling through the dark at Creepyworld in Fenton, the glow of Jack’s Lighted Trail at Eckert’s in Belleville while your breath fogs and your kid clutches a pumpkin bigger than their head.
Pick by the most nervous person in the car.
Wants to be genuinely scared? Strobe light, a scream right behind you, a hand on your shoulder that isn’t your friend’s. That’s The Darkness, at 1525 South 8th Street next to Soulard Market, or Creepyworld’s scream park at 1400 South Old Highway 141 in Fenton. One combo pass covers both. Everyone walks through a metal detector, and ticket sales are final, no refunds. Both go from weekends in late September to nightly as Halloween gets close, and the last two weekends sell out, so buy timed tickets ahead or go on a weeknight.
Is five years old? Glow sticks bobbing through Forest Park after dark: Boo at the Zoo, select October nights from 5 to 8:30 p.m. (last entry at 8). It’s $16 this season, $13 for members and free under age 2, parking in the park is free, scary costumes stay home, and there’s a sensory-friendly night with quiet areas and sensory maps. The insider catch: on Boo nights the zoo clears everyone out at 4 p.m. and reopens at 5, so a daytime zoo visit can’t just roll into the party.
Just wants a pumpkin and something warm? Mud on your boots and a hay wagon bumping out to the field: Eckert’s in Belleville, about 25 minutes east of downtown, or Thies Farm’s Pumpkinland, Stuckmeyer’s in Fenton and Rombachs in Chesterfield, generally late September through October 31. Go early on a weekend, before the best pumpkins are picked over.
Before you plan around an old list, four things have changed. Union Station’s Trick or Train isn’t on the calendar anymore; the St. Louis Aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins, with underwater pumpkin carving, runs there from mid-September into November 1 instead. Six Flags St. Louis is now Mid America Adventure, and Fright Fest still takes over the park after dark. Purina Farms’ kids’ Halloween event is on hold while tornado damage keeps its visitor center closed. And St. Charles turns Main Street into Legends & Lanterns on October weekends, free.
### The whole season at a glance, scary to not-scary
Here’s a Saturday in late October. The line outside The Darkness stretches down the sidewalk near Soulard, fog rolling out every time the doors open. Out in Fenton, Creepyworld’s hayride wagons rumble past in the dark to a soundtrack of screams. And in Forest Park the zoo’s lights come up at 5 for a crowd of very small superheroes. Most of it runs from late September through late October or early November.
### For the fearless: haunted houses and scream parks
You hear the flagship before you see it: screams leaking out the doors and a line of people laughing a little too loudly to prove they aren’t nervous. Then you’re in the first black corridor, hand on the shoulder in front of you, fog thick enough to taste. The Darkness, in the Soulard area near Ballpark Village, has been terrifying visitors for more than three decades, and it has been featured on the History Channel’s Modern Marvels and on the Travel Channel. Haunt owners in town for the industry’s Transworld trade show have toured it to see how it’s done. A short distance away, the same company’s Lemp Haunted House on Lemp Avenue leans into the neighborhood’s real haunted lore for a second, distinct scare.
Need something to wear first? Here’s how to choose a Halloween costume.
For a bigger, outdoor-heavy experience, Creepyworld in Fenton (off Highway 141) is a sprawling “scream park” with multiple attractions including a haunted hayride - a full night out rather than a single walk-through. And for scares wrapped inside a theme park, Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure (the former Six Flags St. Louis) in Eureka overlays the whole park with haunted mazes and scare zones after dark while the coasters keep running. These ramp up from weekend nights in late September to nightly as Halloween approaches, so buy timed tickets ahead and expect lines on the closest weekends.
### For families: not-scary Halloween fun
Plenty of the best local Halloween is built for little ones: tiny bumblebees and dinosaurs waving glow sticks, costumes encouraged, scares dialed all the way down. The classic is Boo at the Zoo, the Saint Louis Zoo’s after-hours family event in Forest Park, where costumed kids ride the Emerson Zooline Railroad in the dark and the Primate House stays open after sunset. It’s a themed evening rather than a trick-or-treat event, scary costumes stay home, and guests 14 and older can’t wear full-face masks or face-covering makeup. It runs select evenings through most of October and is a beloved rite of the season for St. Louis families.
Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm in Grantwood Village is another family favorite - an after-dark experience with a haunted tram ride (watch for the headless horseman), decor, and shows, plus a daytime Fall Fest at the Clydesdale stables for the younger set. Downtown at St. Louis Union Station, the St. Louis Aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins season runs from mid-September into the first day of November, with underwater pumpkin carving plus a Trick or Treat Night and a Trick, Treat & Toast evening on the aquarium’s calendar. Purina Farms in Gray Summit used to run a not-so-scary kids’ Halloween event, but its visitor center has been closed since the March 2025 tornadoes, so check the farm’s own site before you plan around it.
### For the harvest crowd: pumpkin patches and farms
Some of the most reliable fall fun around St. Louis skips the scares completely: hayrides, corn mazes, and the annual hunt for the perfect pumpkin. The regional heavyweight is Eckert’s in Belleville, Illinois (about 25 minutes east of downtown), an eighth-generation family farm with pick-your-own pumpkins and “Ecktoberfest” festival weekends; its newer Jack’s Lighted Trail, a walkable illuminated pumpkin path, has become a fresh evening draw.
On the Missouri side, Thies Farm & Market’s Pumpkinland brings a straw castle, corn maze, and rides; Stuckmeyer’s Farm in Fenton (near the junction of Highways 141 and 21) runs Saturday “Halloween Family Fun Days” with farm animals and hayrides; and Rombachs Farm in Chesterfield opens daily in October with its “Great Pumpkin Pyramid.” These are the low-key, daytime, all-ages side of the season - perfect for younger kids, photos, and a wagon full of pumpkins - and they generally run from late September through October 31.
Random, but: every O’Fallon business worth knowing is one click away.
### The St. Louis Halloween calendar, week by week
It starts with fog machines in Soulard and ends with kids counting candy on the living-room floor. The exact dates slide a little each year, but the rhythm holds. Mid-to-late September: The Darkness opens, Creepyworld kicks off with a late-September “Slasher Weekend,” and the aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins season starts at Union Station. Late September into October 1: the farms open their pumpkin fields and corn mazes, and Stuckmeyer’s Saturday fun days get rolling. The first full weekends of October: Boo at the Zoo opens for select nights, Grant’s Farm’s Halloween Nights are in full swing, and St. Charles turns historic Main Street over to Legends & Lanterns, a free festival of storybook villains, ghost stories and a Day of the Dead plaza that runs on October weekends. The last two weekends: everything is open at once, the haunts go nightly, and the best tickets sell out. Halloween and just after: trick-or-treat hours are set town by town, and the St. Louis rule still holds on every porch: tell a joke, get the candy, a habit that goes back to just after World War II. Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure runs through the first day of November.
Planning the rest of the season? Our guides to the best St. Louis Christmas lights and exploring St. Louis year-round pick up where October leaves off.

### Trick-or-treating and neighborhood happenings
Beyond the ticketed attractions, the oldest Halloween tradition of all is still going strong across the metro: door-to-door trick-or-treating. One thing that surprises newcomers - there’s a local wrinkle to it. In much of the St. Louis area, kids are expected to tell a joke before they get their candy, a “St. Louis trick” that generations here grew up with and that puzzles visitors from anywhere else. It’s a small, charming piece of local culture worth knowing before your first Halloween in town.
Because trick-or-treat night and its hours are set locally, they vary by municipality - each city and suburb tends to announce its official window, so check your city’s page or social media as the date nears. Many neighborhoods, churches, and business districts also host trunk-or-treats and fall festivals - safer, contained, weather-friendly alternatives that are great for younger kids - and shopping centers and malls sometimes run daytime candy events. A quick local search in the days before Halloween usually turns up several within a short drive.
For the grown-ups, the season has its own nightlife: costume parties and Halloween-themed events pop up at bars, breweries, and event spaces across the city and suburbs in the days around the holiday, and the metro’s genuine haunted-history spots lean into the season with tours and special evenings - a seasonal turn on the unique, offbeat St. Louis outings adults seek out year-round. Between the daytime family traditions and the after-dark options, the only real question left is how spooky you want to get.
### What to expect at a haunt (and how to survive it)
If you’re new to the big haunted attractions, a little know-how makes the night better. The premium haunts are a real production: expect elaborate, multi-room sets, live actors whose whole job is to make you jump, plenty of fog, strobe effects, and loud sound design. They’re intense by design - genuinely too scary for young children, and worth being honest with yourself about if you spook easily. A scream park like Creepyworld bundles several attractions and a hayride into one ticket, so plan for a couple of hours on your feet, outdoors, in whatever the late-October weather is doing.
The practical playbook: buy timed tickets online in advance (the closest weekends to Halloween sell out and the lines are long), wear comfortable closed-toe shoes, dress for the actual temperature after dark, and go earlier in October or on a weeknight if you want smaller crowds. If you’re bringing a group with mixed nerves, know that most haunts don’t let you bail mid-attraction easily - so match the outing to the least brave person in your party, or split up and regroup after.
### A morning at the pumpkin patch
The harvest farms deserve a little extra attention because they’re the most flexible, all-ages option of the season. A typical visit is a half-day out: a hayride to the pumpkin field, a corn maze to get lost in, a straw-bale playground or barnyard animals for the little kids, and cider, kettle corn, or apple-cider donuts on the way out. They’re built for photos - the wagons, the pumpkin pyramids, the fall color - and they’re a gentle, no-scares way to mark the season with toddlers and grandparents alike.
A few tips make the morning smoother: go early on weekends before the crowds and the best pumpkins thin out, bring cash for the stands that prefer it, dress the kids for mud after any recent rain, and check the farm’s page for whether admission, the maze, and hayrides are separate tickets or bundled. Weekdays, if you can swing them, are dramatically calmer than sunny Saturday afternoons.
### How to plan your Halloween season
With this much on offer, a little planning goes a long way. Match the outing to your crew first: a genuine haunt like The Darkness or Creepyworld for teens and thrill-seekers, Boo at the Zoo or Grant’s Farm for families with young kids, and a pumpkin-patch morning at Eckert’s, Thies, Stuckmeyer’s, or Rombachs for the harvest crowd. Many families do one of each over the month - a patch early, a family night mid-month, and a scarier outing for the older kids as Halloween nears.
A few practical notes: the haunted attractions get busiest on the weekends closest to Halloween, so go early in October or on a weeknight if you can, and buy tickets in advance. The farms are weather-dependent and busiest on sunny weekend afternoons, so it pays to keep a few indoor St. Louis attractions built for a rainy day in your back pocket in case the forecast turns. And because exact dates, hours, and ticket prices change every year, always confirm on each venue’s official page before you head out - the events are annual, but the calendar isn’t identical two years running.
The range is what makes the metro so easy to plan around. Within a short drive you can go from a gentle pumpkin-patch morning to a genuinely terrifying scream park to a friendly night at the zoo, mixing and matching by the weekend. Book the haunts the day tickets go on sale - the weekends nearest Halloween are the first to sell out, and those are exactly the ones your teenagers will want.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best haunted house in St. Louis?
A.  The Darkness, next to Soulard Market about a mile from Ballpark Village, is the region’s most famous haunted house, running for more than three decades and regularly ranked among the best in the country. Its sister attractions, the Lemp Haunted House and Creepyworld scream park in Fenton, round out the top tier, and Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure in Eureka adds scares inside a theme park.
### Q. What events are happening in St. Louis in October?
A.  October in St. Louis is Halloween season: The Darkness, Creepyworld and the Lemp Haunted House for scares, Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure, Boo at the Zoo on select nights, Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm, Pirates and Pumpkins at the St. Louis Aquarium, pumpkin patches all month, and the free Legends & Lanterns festival on historic Main Street in St. Charles.
### Q. What events are happening in St. Charles, Mo. for Halloween?
A.  The big one is Legends & Lanterns, a free festival on historic Main Street over several October weekends. Costumed storybook and folklore villains like Lizzie Borden, the Big Bad Wolf and the Queen of Hearts roam the street, you can write a scary story with Edgar Allan Poe, and a self-guided video tour points out Main Street’s paranormal hotspots.
### Q. What can adults do for fun on Halloween?
A.  Go get scared: The Darkness, the Lemp Haunted House and Creepyworld are built for grown-ups, and Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure adds coasters after dark. Bars and breweries across the city throw costume parties in the days around the holiday, and the Lemp Mansion leans into its own haunted history with paranormal tours and a Halloween bash.
### Q. What to do on Halloween that isn’t partying?
A.  Make it a pumpkin-patch morning at Eckert’s, Thies, Stuckmeyer’s or Rombachs, then go back after dark for Eckert’s Jack’s Lighted Trail. Boo at the Zoo is a costumed family night with no trick-or-treating, Legends & Lanterns in St. Charles is free, and on Halloween itself there are trunk-or-treats and the old St. Louis rule of telling a joke for your candy.

## Trout in Forest Park? Yes. Grandpa Needs a $12 Permit to Keep One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-good-fishing-spots-in-st-louis
The line goes tight at Jefferson Lake in Forest Park, and your knuckles already ache from the cold. Breath hangs over flat gray water. Something silver throws itself clear of the surface. A rainbow trout. Not in an Ozark stream, hours down the highway. In a city park, inside St. Louis, in the dead middle of winter.
That fish was put there on purpose. The city’s parks department lists trout from November through February in exactly three city lakes: Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park, Jefferson Lake in Forest Park and O’Fallon Park Lake. The Missouri Department of Conservation says it normally stocks almost 40,000 rainbow trout across its St. Louis-area winter lakes each November through January, and it slips in a few brood-stock lunkers, some as large as 10 pounds. Rainbows aren’t native here. MDC says that in winter the water is simply cold enough to support them.
Here’s the part worth saying out loud at the next family dinner. Grandpa, if he’s a Missouri resident 65 or older, fishes without a permit. The grandkid, 15 or younger, fishes without one too. But the moment either of them wants to carry a trout home, MDC says they need a trout permit “regardless of age.” The youth trout permit is $6. For the grandkid, six dollars is the whole difference between a fish fry and handing that trout back to the lake.
So this guide starts where almost nobody else does, with the winter trout, then works out to the bigger water: Creve Coeur Lake, the Busch Conservation Area lakes and the Mississippi itself.
### Where to fish around St. Louis?
Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park is 3 acres by the city’s count, small enough that a kid on the bank can see the whole shoreline and never lose sight of you. Jefferson Lake in Forest Park is 9 acres and the only Forest Park lake MDC stocks. Creve Coeur Lake in Maryland Heights spreads across 320 acres, a lake left behind when the Missouri River cut off one of its own bends. And the August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area, off Route D in St. Charles County, gives you a whole day of lakes and woods. Most anglers 16 and older need a Missouri fishing permit; Missouri residents 65 and older don’t.
### The permit rule that trips up grandparents
Settle this at the kitchen table the night before, not in a gravel lot with your phone at 4 percent. A resident Missouri fishing permit is $14, and MDC sells it online, by phone and in the MO Fishing app, where the permit appears on your screen right after you buy it. Anyone 15 and younger, resident or nonresident, may fish without one, MDC says, and Missouri residents 65 or older may fish without one as well.
Read the fine print on that last exemption, though. MDC’s own wording is that residents 65 or older may fish “except trout permit or daily tags in areas where required.” So the free ride ends at the trout. A resident trout permit is $12, the youth version is $6, and you need one to keep a trout no matter how many birthdays you’ve had. Release every fish and the basic rules are all you’ll ever touch. Tuck a printout or a screenshot of the permit where cold fingers can find it, so nobody is digging through a glove box while the bobber drifts.
### Winter trout run on a calendar, so fish by it
The season has two halves. Between Nov. 1 and Jan. 31, MDC says some lakes are catch-and-release only and some are catch-and-keep, so read the sign at the water before the cooler comes out of the trunk. After Feb. 1, trout may be harvested from all of the winter trout lakes. That makes February the month to go if you want trout on the table.
Keep it legal while you’re at it. MDC’s St. Charles County agent put the daily limit at four trout, with eight in possession, and said trout or other gamefish eggs are not allowed as bait. Corn, dough bait and small spinners all go back in the tackle box ready for next time.
Then use the one tool most people never hear about. MDC’s Fish Stocking Hotline, 636-300-9651, is updated immediately after each stocking run, and a recorded message tells you when and where fish went in, how many and what species. Call it with the coffee brewing. If the truck just came through your lake, that’s your morning.
### Creve Coeur Lake, a river bend that got left behind
Stand on the shore at Creve Coeur and you’re looking at a piece of the Missouri River that lost its way. MDC calls it an oxbow lake, formed when a tight curve of the river was cut off and separated from the main channel. What’s left is 320 acres of open water where the wind pushes ripples across and the far bank goes soft in the haze.
MDC lists white bass, sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass here. Boats are allowed, but only electric motors may be used, so the loudest thing on the water is usually a goose. The area is open from 8 a.m. to a half hour after sunset.
### August A. Busch: bring a kayak, leave the bass boat
The Busch area is 6,950.8 acres of woods, gravel roads and lakes you reach one at a time, each with its own quiet. Five of them, Lakes 3, 7, 21, 22 and 23, get MDC’s winter trout. The area page also lists muskie, sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass.
Know the boat rule before you hitch up a trailer. On the Busch area, only department-owned boats may be used and only electric motors are permitted. Hand-launched canoes and kayaks are the exception, allowed on Lakes 6, 34, 35, 36 and 38 from April 1 through September 30 with a valid area boating tag, and you register at headquarters before you launch. The area itself opens at 4 a.m. and closes at 10 p.m., which means you can be on the bank in the dark, listening to the woods wake up.
Off the water for a second: Southwest Garden is the neighborhood you keep driving past.
### Forest Park: one lake yes, one lake no
Forest Park fools people. Fishing is permitted in its lakes and lagoons except where restrictions are posted, according to Forest Park Forever, but fishing is not permitted in Post-Dispatch Lake. Walk over to Jefferson Lake instead.
The city’s parks department says nine park lakes are stocked every two to four weeks under the St. Louis Urban Fishing Program: channel catfish from March through September, hybrid sunfish in May and September, and trout from November through February in Carondelet’s Boathouse Lake, Jefferson Lake and O’Fallon Park Lake. So a summer evening at Jefferson Lake is a catfish evening, with a worm on the bottom and the light going orange behind the trees.
### The big river
The Mississippi fishes nothing like a park lake. No dock, no stocking truck, just brown current sliding past and the hum of barges. At Confluence Point State Park you can fish from the banks of both the Mississippi and the Missouri, but not within 300 feet of the confluence point itself, and the park lists carp, buffalo, catfish and drum as the catch.
Your Missouri permit stretches farther than you’d think. Under MDC’s reciprocal rules with Illinois, you may fish the flowing waters of either state on the Mississippi, either state’s adjacent backwaters and shared oxbow lakes, and from the bank of either state. On the other state’s waters, the more restrictive of the two states’ regulations applies. Planning a river morning up by the dam? Our guide to Melvin Price Locks and Dam covers the visit. And if you’re curious what else might be down there, read up on sharks in the Mississippi.
### Before you head out
Buy the permit first, and add a trout permit if anyone in the car plans to keep a trout, kids and grandparents included.
Call the stocking hotline at 636-300-9651 the night before a winter trip.
Read the sign at the lake. Catch-and-release rules, motor rules and limits are posted at the water.
Keep the kit simple. A rod, hooks, a bobber and a cup of worms will catch something almost anywhere on this list.
Pack it out. Cut line and hooks left on the bank are brutal on birds.
Need bait, a rod or breakfast on the way to the lake? Look up the shops and diners near your spot on St Louis Near Me Directory before you load the car.
If you run the bait shop, the tackle counter or the guide service anglers pass on the way in, the people reading this page are your next customers. List your business so they can find you before they hit the water, or see what a listing can do for you.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can I fish in Missouri without a license?
A.  Yes, if you’re 15 or younger, or a Missouri resident 65 or older. Everyone else needs a Missouri fishing permit, which is $14 for a resident. Both exemptions stop at trout you keep: that takes a trout permit.
### Q. Do I need a trout license in Missouri?
A.  Only to keep trout. MDC says anglers who want to catch and keep trout at the St. Louis winter trout lakes need a trout permit regardless of age, on top of a fishing permit if they aren’t exempt. A resident trout permit is $12 and the youth permit is $6.
### Q. What is the best month to go trout fishing?
A.  Around St. Louis, February. From Nov. 1 through Jan. 31 some winter trout lakes are catch-and-release only; after Feb. 1, MDC says trout may be harvested from all of them. Call the stocking hotline at 636-300-9651 to time your trip to a fresh stocking.
### Q. Where is the best place to fish without a boat?
A.  The city lakes are made for the bank: Jefferson Lake in Forest Park and Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park both get winter trout from November through February under the St. Louis Urban Fishing Program. For river fish, Confluence Point State Park allows fishing from the banks of both the Mississippi and the Missouri.
### Q. Where can I fish in the Mississippi River near St. Louis?
A.  Confluence Point State Park lets you fish from the banks of both rivers, though not within 300 feet of the confluence point. Under MDC’s reciprocal rules, a Missouri permit lets you fish the Mississippi’s flowing waters and fish from the bank of either state.
### Q. What kind of fish do you catch in the Mississippi river?
A.  At Confluence Point, Missouri State Parks lists carp, buffalo, catfish and drum. Bring heavier line than you’d use at a park lake, fish the slower water near the bank, and watch your footing on wet rock, because the current never takes a day off.
### Q. Is there any free fishing?
A.  For some people, yes. Anyone 15 and younger and Missouri residents 65 or older can fish without a fishing permit. Keeping a trout still takes a trout permit.

That cold-knuckle, line-goes-tight feeling is closer than the Ozarks. Find the bait shops and outfitters near your favorite spot in the St Louis Near Me Directory, and if you run a local outdoors business, list it here so anglers planning their next trip become your customers.

## Low-Income Apartments in St. Louis: The Voucher List Is Closed, These Doors Aren’t
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/finding-low-income-apartments-in-st-louis-your-guide-to-affordable-housing
“Accepting Applications.” Two plain words, printed beside Laurel Park on the Housing Authority of St. Louis County’s own properties page: 352 garden-style apartments in North St. Louis County, one, two and three bedrooms, and a leasing office you can call at (314) 868-8220. Most people looking for a cheap apartment in St. Louis never see that line, because they stop at a different one. The St. Louis Housing Authority’s voucher page says its Section 8 waitlist “is currently closed and not accepting applications until further notice,” and that sentence lands like a door shutting in a cold hallway.
Here is what that sentence does not tell you. A voucher is only one way into an affordable apartment. Some buildings set their rent around low incomes and take applications at their own front desk, on their own timeline, whether or not any voucher list is open. On the day we checked, County Housing listed Laurel Park, Stratford Commons, Stratford Manor and Wellington Family Homes as accepting applications. Over in the city, SLHA says its Elderly-Only waiting list “remains open throughout the year.” Different doors. Same goal: a lease you can actually pay.
If you have been sitting on the edge of a borrowed couch, phone at four percent, scrolling listings that ask for three times the rent in income, take a breath. You are not behind. You have been looking at the wrong list. This guide is about the other ones: the buildings that take applications directly, the numbers that decide whether you qualify, and the calls to make this week.
### What salary do you need to afford $1200 rent?
To keep $1,200 rent at 30% of income, you need about $4,000 a month before taxes ($1,200 divided by 0.30), or $48,000 a year. That 30% is the line HUD uses: households paying more than 30% of income for housing count as cost-burdened. That is the income a $1,200 rent quietly asks for. SLHA’s posted income limits are $45,400 for two people and $51,100 for three, and they are adjusted each year.
So if your paycheck is under that line, you are not failing at budgeting. You are exactly who income-based housing is built for. And the gap between what you earn and what a market-rate place costs is the gap these buildings close. The arithmetic is simple and a little brutal: $1,200 times 12 is $14,400 a year in rent, and $14,400 is 30% of $48,000. Every dollar of rent above what you can carry comes out of the grocery cart, the bus pass, or the light bill.
### The apartments that do not wait on a voucher
When a building’s rent is tied to income, you apply to that building. Not to a citywide lottery, not to a list that opens once in a long while. You call the leasing office, ask whether they are taking applications, and ask what the income limit is for your household size. The phone call takes ten minutes. The hold music is the worst part.
County Housing’s properties page is the clearest place to start in St. Louis County, because it shows status next to each property. It describes Stratford Commons as a townhome community in North St. Louis County with 114 units and two to four bedrooms, with a management office at 314-260-9008. It lists Wellington Family Homes as newly renovated family housing with modern amenities and playground space, at (314) 332-2543. For older adults it lists Stratford Manor, a 52-unit senior community in North St. Louis County (314-381-8081), plus Elm Ridge (314-395-2024) and Scott Manor (314-867-0010). Status changes, so treat the list as a reason to call, not a promise.
It also tells you who is not taking applications right now, and that saves you a wasted bus ride. On the same page, its public housing communities, including Arbor Hill and Fee Fee Manor, were marked “Not Accepting Applications.” Better to learn that from a web page than at a locked office door with your folder of pay stubs going soft in the rain.
### Do housing projects still exist in St. Louis?
Yes, though most people now call it public housing. SLHA says approximately 2,790 individuals and families are currently living in SLHA housing. Its family public housing list is closed for now; the agency’s public housing page says so in the same breath as the one exception that matters most to older renters.
That exception is the senior list. SLHA says its Elderly-Only waiting list remains open throughout the year, and its senior building waiting list accepts applications on an ongoing basis. For most of those buildings, you or your co-head and everyone in your household must be at least 62. One is different: SLHA lists Parkview Apartments at 4451 Forest Park Ave. as Elderly Only (50+), with studio and one-bedroom units, phone (314) 533-3350. If you are 50 and tired of climbing three flights to a hot attic apartment, that line is worth reading twice.
### SLHA’s senior buildings, with the numbers to call
These are the buildings SLHA lists on its Apply for Housing page. Each office is listed with hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.:
Cahill House. Elderly only (62+), one and two bedrooms. (314) 436-5061.
Les Chateaux, 1330 Chouteau Ave. Elderly only (62+), one and two bedrooms. (314) 436-7524.
Parkview Apartments, 4451 Forest Park Ave. Elderly only (50+), studio and one bedroom. (314) 533-3350.
Sr. Living at Cambridge Heights, 728 Biddle St. Elderly only (62+), one and two bedrooms. (314) 436-9091.
Sr. Living at Renaissance, 3217 Martin Luther King Dr. Elderly only (62+), one and two bedrooms. (314) 652-8900.
SLHA says applications must be submitted online through its RentCafe portal, each household may apply only once, and applying through SLHA is always free. If a disability or other circumstance keeps you from applying online, SLHA says paper applications are available; call (314) 531-4770.
People are asking
### Are there low-income apartments in St. Louis with no waiting list?
Few have no list at all, but some are taking applications right now. On the day we checked, County Housing’s properties page marked Laurel Park, Stratford Commons, Stratford Manor and Wellington Family Homes as accepting applications. In the city, SLHA says its Elderly-Only waiting list remains open throughout the year. Call the office first, because a status can change overnight.
### What qualifies as low income here
SLHA’s income limits page spells out three tiers. A low-income family earns no more than 80 percent of the area median income, a very low-income family no more than 50 percent, and an extremely low-income family no more than 30 percent. Its posted chart starts at $39,750 for one person and reaches $56,750 for a family of four. HUD sets the limits and they are adjusted each year, so check the page the week you apply.
Buildings with their own income rules may use different cutoffs. Ask the leasing office the plain question: “What is the most a household of my size can earn and still qualify here?” Write the answer on the back of an envelope. You will be making a lot of these calls.
Still want a voucher too? The city list is closed, but you can be ready the day it opens. Here is how Section 8 works in St. Louis and how reopenings are announced.
### Before you tour: paperwork and the walk-through
Eligibility usually turns on a few things. County Housing says it typically includes income, family size, and U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status. SLHA says eligibility for its programs is set by comparing a family’s annual income with HUD’s published income limits. Keep your pay stubs, benefit letters and IDs in one folder so you can answer fast when an office calls back.
On the tour, use every sense you have. Open the kitchen cabinets and look for droppings. Run the shower and wait for hot water. Stand still in the bedroom and listen for the neighbor’s television through the wall. Smell the hallway. Then walk to the nearest bus stop and time it, because a cheap apartment an hour from your job is not cheap. Our guide to getting around St. Louis by public transit helps you check the route before you sign.
Then do the slow, unglamorous part: keep a call log. A sheet of notebook paper taped inside the folder works fine. Write the property name, the date, who you spoke with, whether they are taking applications, and the income limit they gave you. After a week of calls the names blur together, and the log is what keeps you from re-applying somewhere you already applied, or missing the callback from the one office that said yes. When an office tells you to call back on the first of the month, write that down too, and set an alarm on your phone for 9 a.m. that day. The people who land these apartments are rarely luckier. They are usually just the ones who called back.
Once you are on any list, keep your contact information current. SLHA says you must notify it within 10 business days of changes to your name, address, phone, email, income or family size. County Housing warns that failing to report changes may result in removal from the waitlist. A moved mailbox has cost people their place in line.
### Who helps pay rent near St. Louis while you look?
Start with 2-1-1. United Way 211 of Missouri and Illinois calls itself a 24/7 connection to resources and agencies near you: dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626 and you reach a trained resource specialist. Tell them your ZIP code, your household size and the date the rent is due. Then lean on these guides:

### Q. What is needed for low income apartments?

Bring pay stubs, benefit letters and ID, and ask each leasing office for its own list.

A.  For SLHA’s programs, low income means no more than 80% of the area median income, very low income no more than 50%, and extremely low income no more than 30%. SLHA’s posted chart lists $39,750 for one person and $56,750 for four. HUD adjusts the limits each year.

### Q. Do housing projects still exist?

A.  It depends on household size. SLHA’s posted income limits run from $39,750 for one person to $74,900 for eight. HUD bases them on area median family income, which it estimates annually. SLHA’s voucher waitlist is currently closed until further notice.

## Kids Eat Toasted Ravioli Here: Millwoods, Maryland Heights
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/explore-the-delicious-millwoods-sports-bar-and-grill-in-maryland-heights-menu
Hot Honey on your fingers, darts thudding into a board, a pool break cracking somewhere behind you, and at 8:30 on Saturday night the band starts. Millwoods Sports Bar & Grill sits at 12068 Dorsett Rd. in Maryland Heights, and its own tagline is “Not just a Sports Bar.” One customer quoted on the bar’s Maryland Heights page counted “at least 50 TVs!” Fridays belong to a DJ.
Here’s what you can’t see from the parking lot: the bar’s own contact page takes questions about dart and pool leagues, and it says, “We love group events and gatherings!” I could not find league nights, team sizes or fees posted anywhere, so call (314) 222-9876 and ask those three things. When St. Louis Magazine covered the plans for this building, partner Keeley Walker put the goal plainly: “Maryland Heights’ new home bar.” Leagues are how a sports bar becomes one.

### Customizing Your MeYou Webster Groves Experience
### Navigating Spice Levels for Every Palate
Not everyone wants the same heat, and MeYou plans for that. Several spice options let you dial in the meal. If you’re unsure, start milder. Ask your server for a recommendation based on what you’re ordering; they’re usually happy to guide you.
Here's a general idea of what to expect:
No Spice: Perfect for those who want pure flavor without any heat.
Mild: A gentle warmth, good for most people.
Medium: A noticeable kick, but still manageable for many.
Hot: For those who truly love a fiery experience.
Thai Hot: Proceed with caution! This is for serious spice enthusiasts.
Don't be afraid to experiment, but remember, you can't un-spice a dish once it's made. It's better to be a little underwhelmed by the heat than overwhelmed.

Gluten-Free: Rice is a staple, so many dishes are naturally gluten-free. However, it's always best to confirm with your server about sauces and any potential cross-contamination if you have a severe sensitivity.

## Busch Stadium Allows Outside Food but No Backpacks: Where to Stay
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-rated-hotels-close-to-busch-stadium-for-your-next-st-louis-visit
The sandwich is still warm through the paper when you step out of the hotel lobby. A sealed bottle of water in one pocket, a card in the other, and the sidewalk red with jerseys all the way to the corner. You hear the crowd before you see the stadium.
Here’s the turn most first-timers miss. Busch Stadium lets you carry that sandwich in. The Cardinals allow outside food and beverages everywhere but the luxury suites, as long as drinks are in sealed containers. What won’t get through the gate is the bag on your back. “Reminder that backpacks are not allowed,” the Cardinals’ gameday guide says. And the concession stands are cashless, card only.
So the hotel you pick isn’t just a bed. It’s the locker for your backpack and the kitchen for your lunch. Live! by Loews says Busch Stadium is directly across the street. The Drury Plaza Hotel at the Arch lists the ballpark at 2 blocks, and it puts out a free hot breakfast and a free 5:30 Kickback with hot food and cold drinks. That’s two meals you don’t buy inside the park, and a bag you never have to explain to a gate attendant.
### How early should you get to Busch Stadium?
Earlier on weekends. The Cardinals say Busch Stadium gates open 1.5 hours before game time Monday through Thursday and 2 hours before game time Friday through Sunday, and they note that gate times are subject to change. Stay a few blocks away and you can leave the room when the gates open instead of an hour before, with nothing on your back but the jersey. Walk up early on a summer night and you get the whole slow build of it: the field still bright and the seats filling around you.
Want to start even earlier? Cardinals Nation hosts the official Cardinals Pre-Game Party before every home game, a ticketed pep rally with a full buffet, an all-inclusive bar and a DJ, starting 2.5 hours before first pitch and ending at game time. Read the fine print: the party ticket does not include admission to the game itself.
### Across the street: Live! by Loews in Ballpark Village
Live! by Loews says the stadium is directly across the street. Live! by Loews sits in Ballpark Village, the entertainment district next to Busch, and the hotel says the stadium is directly across the street. Ballpark Village and the hotel are separated only by an outdoor “mock” baseball diamond used for events,, so on game day the crowd is right outside.
The hotel lists 216 guestrooms, including 19 suites, and some of those rooms have walkout balconies. If you’re planning a birthday or a once-a-year trip around one game, this is the room where you step outside and the stadium is right there. It’s also the one that books first, so if the date matters, it’s the first call you make.
The location works on the off day too. The hotel says the Gateway Arch, Enterprise Center, America’s Center Convention Complex, Union Station and City Museum are all within walking distance, which turns a one-game trip into a weekend you never need the car for.
### Two blocks out, with free food: Drury Plaza Hotel at the Arch
Here’s the budget play nobody on a first trip thinks about. The Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch lists Busch Stadium at 2 blocks, the Gateway Arch at 1 block and the MetroLink Stadium Station at 3 blocks. It also lists a free hot breakfast and a free 5:30 Kickback with hot food and cold drinks.
Think about what that means on a night game. You eat breakfast at the hotel, see the Arch before lunch, come back for the 5:30 spread, and walk two blocks to the gate with the money you didn’t spend on dinner still in your pocket. For families, there’s an indoor pool and two whirlpools waiting after the last out, which is how you get a tired kid to stop talking about the seventh inning. Check-in is 3 p.m. and check-out is 11 a.m., and late check-out runs $40 when it’s available, worth it after a late game.
### A bird’s-eye view of the field: Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark
If you want to look down into the stadium, go up. Three Sixty, the bar atop the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark at One South Broadway, says it sits almost 400 feet up and gives guests a bird’s-eye view of Busch Stadium plus views of the Gateway Arch and the Mississippi River. It says it opens two hours before all home day baseball games.
That makes the Hilton a strong pick for a day game: a drink with the whole field laid out below you, then the elevator and a short walk to your seat. On a hot afternoon, that elevator ride down into the noise is half the fun.
### The Westin, MetroLink and the ride home after a long game
The Westin St. Louis has a quiet advantage: the train. According to the Cardinals, the closest MetroLink station is next to the Westin on the 8th Street side of the stadium. MetroLink normally runs until midnight, and if the Cardinals game goes past midnight, the Cardinals say MetroLink will keep running until the downtown platform is cleared. For MetroLink and bus schedules, the number the Cardinals give is (314) 231-2345.
That matters if your hotel is farther out on the line, or if you’d rather not pay to park downtown at all. A hotel near any MetroLink stop can work as a ballpark hotel, as long as you know where the train lets you off: right by the Westin, a short walk from the gates. Extra innings don’t strand you. You file out with the crowd, the night air finally cool, and the train is still there.
Hungry on the drive in from the south? Here’s where to eat in South County before you hit downtown.
### Getting dropped off or picked up
Rideshare is the other easy way in, and the Cardinals spell out exactly where to stand. Drop-offs happen on the west side of the stadium on 8th Street north of Gate 3, or on the east side on Broadway just south of Clark Street. After the game, rideshare, taxi and personal-vehicle pickups are on the east side on Broadway, just south of Clark Street, and Clark Street is closed between the stadium and Ballpark Village.
Set your pickup pin on Broadway before the ninth inning ends. Then you’re the one standing on the curb with your phone up while everybody else is still arguing with the map. And if anything feels off on the walk in or out, the Cardinals say you can text security at 314-300-1000.
### What you can carry through the gate
Pack for the gate, not for the trip. The Cardinals allow outside food and beverages except in the luxury suites, but no alcohol, glass, aluminum or hard-sided coolers, and beverages must be in sealed containers. Backpacks are not allowed. Concession stands are cashless and take only credit and debit cards, so leave the cash envelope in the room safe.
A short walk from your hotel turns those rules into a non-issue. You pick up a sandwich, keep the water sealed, slip your card in your back pocket, and leave everything else in the room.
### If you’re driving in for the day
The Cardinals say stadium parking can be purchased online or over the phone at 314-345-9000. Buy it before you leave the house, so the last mile of the drive isn’t a hunt for a sign with a price on it. And if you’re staying the night, park once at the hotel and forget the car until checkout. ## Escape Rooms, Rock Climbing, VR & Barcades in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-indoor-activities-in-stl-beat-the-boredom-indoors
Some days you don’t want to look at things in a museum — you want to do something. Maybe it’s a first date that needs a spark, a group of friends who can never agree on a plan, a birthday, or just a restless Saturday when the weather won’t let you outside. You want to move, compete, and laugh a little.
St. Louis has a deep bench of active indoor entertainment — escape rooms, rock climbing, virtual reality, retro barcades, bowling, and axe throwing — all under a roof and open whatever the sky is doing. This is a local’s guide to the best active indoor things to do in St. Louis, sorted by the mood you’re after. Some nights call for a puzzle and a team. Some call for a wall to climb, others for a cocktail and a pinball machine. St. Louis covers all of them within a short drive.
### St. Louis Active-Indoor Spots at a Glance
### Escape Rooms: Turn a Night Into a Team Sport
Escape rooms are the perfect active indoor plan for a date or a small group — an hour of puzzles, teamwork, and a ticking clock. St. Louis Escape in Soulard runs eight themed rooms and even adds blacklight 3D mini golf and a pinball arcade if you want to make a night of it. Downtown in the Loft District, Escape the Room STL offers several themed rooms for around $35 a person. Both are ideal for four-to-eight people who want to laugh, argue about clues, and (maybe) beat the clock together. They’re also a great equalizer for mixed groups — there’s a job for the detail-spotter, the big-picture thinker, and the person who just enjoys yelling “try that key in that lock.” Book a slot ahead, show up a few minutes early, and plan to grab food or drinks afterward to rehash how you did.
### Indoor Rock Climbing: Surprise Yourself
You don’t need to be an athlete to have fun on a climbing wall — the good gyms are built for beginners. Upper Limits in Maryland Heights is a big, well-equipped gym with 45-foot walls and auto-belays, so you can climb even without a partner. Climb So iLL runs a dramatic downtown location inside a former power plant (plus a St. Charles gym), pairing climbing with yoga and fitness. Rent shoes, take the intro, and you’ll be surprised how quickly a rainy afternoon turns into a real workout you actually enjoyed. Climbing is also a sneaky-great date or group activity: you’re cheering each other up the wall, there’s a built-in sense of accomplishment, and no experience is required to have a genuinely good time.
### Barcades: Beer, Quarters, and Zero Boredom
For grown-ups, St. Louis’s barcades are some of the best nights out in the city. Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, and console classics, with a rooftop bar (it’s 21+ in the evenings, with family hours during the day). Over in The Grove, Purple Quarters is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a well-loved local team, with comedy and karaoke nights mixed in. Both nail the same trick: cheap games, good drinks, and the instant nostalgia of a machine you haven’t touched since childhood.
### Bowling and Games, Grown-Up Edition
Bowling still holds up, and St. Louis does it with character. Pin-Up Bowl in the Delmar Loop pairs retro lanes with a full cocktail lounge and runs late into the night — a great low-key date or group hang. For a bigger, do-it-all option, Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, open late daily — ideal for families or big groups who want variety without venue-hopping.
### Virtual Reality: The Group Adrenaline Hit
VR has grown up, and St. Louis has real options now. Sandbox VR, which opened inside City Foundry in late 2025, is the premium pick — full-body motion capture and haptics that drop your group into a shared virtual world (zombies, space, the works). In south county, STL Virtual Reality in Oakville is an all-ages spot where up to six players can team up or compete across co-op, competitive, and escape-style games. Either way, it’s a genuinely modern, high-energy activity that groups and older kids love.
### Axe Throwing and Other Ways to Blow Off Steam
If your idea of active indoor fun involves throwing something, St. Louis has you covered. Top Notch Axe Throwing runs locations in St. Louis and St. Charles where a coach gets you sticking axes into a target in minutes — a surprisingly fun group or date activity. Amp Up Action Park combines an axe range with other action attractions under one roof. It’s the kind of thing that sounds intimidating and turns out to be the highlight of the night.
Nothing to do with axes — there are surprisingly good restaurants in Hazelwood.
### City Foundry STL: When You Can’t Agree on One Thing
If your group can’t settle on a single activity, City Foundry STL in Midtown solves it. This food-hall-and-entertainment complex — which drew more than two million visitors in 2025 — packs Puttshack’s tech-tracked mini golf, Sandbox VR, The Escape Game, and the Alamo Drafthouse cinema around a huge food hall. You can throw an entire evening together here: dinner, a game, a movie, a drink, all without moving the car. It’s the easiest answer to “what do you want to do?” in the whole city — and because it keeps adding new tenants, there’s usually something you haven’t tried yet. For a group with mixed ages and interests, it’s hard to beat: the little kids do mini golf, the teens do VR, and the adults get a proper dinner and a drink, all in one building.
### The Deeper Pinball and Games Scene
St. Louis has a genuinely serious pinball culture worth knowing about if you catch the bug. Beyond the big barcades, spots like the Silver Ballroom in Bevo (a punk-rock pinball bar in a former bowling alley) and Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton (all-ages) draw dedicated players, and there are league nights around the metro. The point is that “playing some games” in St. Louis can be a five-dollar lark with a beer or a genuine hobby — the machines and the community are here either way. If arcades and pinball are your thing, it’s worth exploring the full lineup across the city and into the Metro East.
### Know Before You Go
A few quick tips make an active-indoor night smoother. Book escape rooms and VR ahead — they run on timed slots and sell out on weekends. Check age policies: barcades like Up-Down STL and Purple Quarters are 21+ in the evenings (Up-Down adds daytime family hours), while family centers like Main Event and all-ages spots like STL Virtual Reality welcome kids. Wear the right clothes for climbing or City Museum-style crawling. And call ahead for the smaller venues — independent spots occasionally change hours or host private events, so a two-minute check saves a wasted drive.
### Which Active Indoor Plan Fits Tonight?
A memorable date: an escape room or Up-Down’s barcade. A group or party: Main Event or Sandbox VR. Actually getting active: rock climbing at Upper Limits or Climb So iLL. Can’t agree on one thing: City Foundry. Low-key and cheap: Pin-Up Bowl or a barcade with a roll of quarters. Whatever the mood, there’s an active indoor plan in St. Louis that beats sitting at home. And most of these are surprisingly affordable — an escape room, a climb, or a night at the barcade runs about the price of a movie and popcorn, but you’ll actually remember it. When the group text asks “what should we do?”, you’ll have a real answer.
