## Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-personal-injury-lawyer-in-st-louis
Two cars crash the same way on the same afternoon. One wreck happens on Kingshighway, the other on a street in Belleville, twenty minutes east.
The Missouri driver has five years to file. The Illinois driver has two. And if a jury later decides each driver was 60% at fault, the Missouri driver still collects a substantial check while the Illinois driver collects nothing at all.
St. Louis straddles a state line, which means the single most important fact about an injury claim here is one almost nobody explains: which side of the river it happened on.
### How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis?
In Missouri, generally five years for personal injury, three years for wrongful death from the date of death, and two years for medical malpractice. In Illinois, it’s two years for personal injury and wrongful death, and only one year for a claim against a local public entity. If your claim is against the City of St. Louis for a street or sidewalk defect, written notice must reach the mayor within 90 days. And a work injury must be reported to your employer in writing within 30 days. Which deadline applies is a legal question — don’t self-diagnose it.
### Missouri’s five years is a trap
Missouri’s general five-year window is unusually generous, and that generosity is exactly what hurts people. Someone hears “five years,” relaxes, and blows through every shorter deadline that actually governs their case.
Because the five years is the exception in this list, not the rule:
Wrongful death: three years from the date of death, not from the injury. Medical malpractice: two years from the act, with a ten-year outer limit. A work injury: 30 days to notify your employer in writing. Street or sidewalk defect in the City of St. Louis: 90 days written notice to the mayor. Anything that happened in Illinois: two years — or one year against a municipality.
One more that surprises people: for a minor, the Missouri clock is paused until the disability is removed — and the statute sets that at age twenty-one, not eighteen. Medical malpractice has its own separate rule for minors.
### The 90-day rule almost nobody knows
If you were hurt by a defect in a street, sidewalk, bridge, boulevard or thoroughfare in a Missouri city of 100,000 or more — which in this metro essentially means the City of St. Louis — you must give written notice to the mayor within 90 days of the occurrence. The notice has to state the place, the time, the character and circumstances of the injury, and that you will claim damages.
Two limits worth being precise about, because they get blurred constantly. It applies only to cities over 100,000 — St. Louis County is a county, not a city, so this particular provision doesn’t reach it. And it applies only to those specific kinds of defects, not to every claim against a city.
Suing a public entity is harder in another way, too. Missouri governments are generally immune, with narrow exceptions — principally the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by a public employee on the job, and injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property. Outside those windows the claim often does not exist at all.
Where immunity is waived, damages are capped, and the cap is adjusted for inflation every year. For 2026 the Department of Commerce and Insurance publishes it at $532,148 for any one person and $3,547,658 for all claims from a single occurrence. Those numbers change every January 1 — if you see them quoted without a year attached, they’re probably stale.
### Partly your fault? It depends which state
This is the single biggest practical difference across the river, and it’s the reason people who assume they have no case sometimes do.
Missouri uses pure comparative fault. There is no cutoff. Your recovery is reduced by your share of the blame, and that’s all. (Worth noting for accuracy: for ordinary negligence this comes from a 1983 Missouri Supreme Court decision rather than a statute, so anyone citing “the Missouri comparative fault statute” for a car wreck is misinformed.)
Illinois uses modified comparative negligence with a bar. If you are found more than 50% responsible, you recover nothing at all. At 50% or less, your damages are reduced proportionally.
Put actual numbers on it. Say your damages are $100,000 and a jury finds you 60% at fault:
Missouri: you recover $40,000. Illinois: you recover $0.
Same facts. Same injury. Same jury. Opposite outcomes, decided by geography. Which state’s law applies is a choice-of-law question and depends on more than your home address — another reason not to talk yourself out of a claim because you think you were partly to blame.
### Why the other driver’s insurance usually isn’t enough
Missouri requires drivers to carry $25,000 per person, $50,000 per accident, and $25,000 for property damage. That is the floor the state demands of an at-fault driver. It is not a measure of what an injury costs.
An ambulance ride, an emergency room visit, imaging and a single surgery can exhaust $25,000 before anyone counts a lost paycheck. If the at-fault driver carries the minimum and has nothing worth pursuing, that policy is effectively the ceiling on your recovery.
Which is why the coverage that matters most is often your own. Missouri requires uninsured motorist coverage on every auto policy, at the same $25,000/$50,000 limits. Missouri does not require underinsured motorist coverage — that one is optional, and it is precisely the coverage that carries a serious claim when the at-fault driver is insured but nowhere near adequately.
Go read your own declarations page tonight. Ten minutes, and it tells you more about your protection than the other driver’s policy will.
### Hurt at work? Two clocks, running at once
A work injury runs on an entirely separate track, and the first deadline is brutally short.
Written notice to your employer within 30 days. Missouri’s Division of Workers’ Compensation says plainly that failing to report within 30 days may jeopardize your benefits — and advises keeping a copy of the notice with the date, time, and who received it. There is a narrow exception where the employer wasn’t prejudiced, but the burden falls on you. Treat 30 days as hard.
The claim itself must be filed with the Division within two years, extended to three if your employer never filed its report. The Division also notes the period can run from the last payment made on account of the injury — which matters if you received benefits for a while.
Now the part most injured workers never hear. Workers’ compensation is generally your exclusive remedy against your employer — that’s the trade. But it does not bar a claim against a negligent third party: another driver who hit you while you were working, a subcontractor on the site, the manufacturer of a machine that failed.
Those third-party claims run on the ordinary injury clock, not the comp clock. So you can have two live cases at once, with different deadlines, and the third-party case is frequently where the real recovery is.
Apropos of nothing: Rock Hill, Missouri is tiny and eats surprisingly well.
### The one sentence in the fee agreement that costs you thousands
Injury lawyers work on contingency — a percentage of what they recover, nothing if they lose. We are deliberately not going to tell you what percentage is “normal” in Missouri, because no neutral source establishes one. Every number you’ll find comes from law firm marketing.
You don’t need the average anyway, because Missouri’s rules of professional conduct require your contract to spell it out. A contingency agreement must be in writing, signed by you, and must state:
• the percentages for settlement, trial and appeal, separately — they are often different • the litigation and other expenses to be deducted • whether those expenses come off before or after the fee is calculated • any expense you owe even if you lose
That third item is the one to read twice, because Missouri sets no default. The contract decides — and the rule requires the contract to say which. Here is what it’s worth, on a $100,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $10,000 of case expenses:
Expenses first, then the fee: $10,000 comes off, the fee is one third of $90,000 — $30,000 — and you net $60,000. Fee first, then expenses: the fee is one third of the full $100,000 — $33,333 — then $10,000 of expenses, and you net $56,667.
Same settlement, same percentage, same expenses. A $3,333 difference, decided entirely by one sentence. If a fee agreement doesn’t address it, that agreement doesn’t comply with the rule.
Expenses are separate from the fee and typically include filing fees, depositions and court reporters, expert witnesses, medical records, investigators and exhibits.
### Why your settlement shrinks, and the cap that protects you
A $100,000 settlement never lands in your account as $100,000, and the reason isn’t just the fee.
When someone injures you, your health insurer or the hospital usually pays the bills up front. If you later recover from the at-fault party, those payers can claim reimbursement out of your settlement — otherwise the same bill gets paid twice. That’s a lien.
Missouri law puts a real limit on it, and it is stated correctly almost nowhere. Health care provider liens are capped at 50% of the net proceeds — and “net” is defined as what remains after attorney fees and the expenses of recovery. Providers do not get to take the settlement. Where the liens exceed the cap, they share the available amount proportionally.
If MO HealthNet paid your bills, the state has its own lien, with no fixed percentage cap — but attorney’s fees take priority over the state’s claim, and courts apportion based on equitable factors including your age, the permanence of the injury and your future needs.
### Can a lawyer call you after a crash? No.
This is the question people actually have after a wreck, and it has an unambiguous answer.
Missouri’s rules prohibit a lawyer from initiating in-person, telephone, or real-time electronic solicitation of legal business under any circumstance — with narrow exceptions for existing clients, other lawyers, close friends and relatives. Not “discouraged.” Prohibited.
Written solicitation has rules too. In an injury or wrongful death matter, a lawyer may not send one within 30 days of the accident. And any solicitation letter must be marked ADVERTISEMENT on the envelope and at the top of the first page.
So: a call or a knock at the door from a lawyer you don’t know is a violation. A letter that shows up a week after your crash is a violation. A letter at six weeks with no ADVERTISEMENT marking is a violation. You can report any of them to the Office of Chief Disciplinary Counsel.
Related, and worth knowing: Missouri lawyers generally may not pay anyone for recommending them, and may not practice through a business a non-lawyer owns or controls. If a “case manager” from a marketing company signs you up and then assigns you a lawyer, ask directly who owns the firm.
### Checking a lawyer, and what the lookup won’t tell you
For Missouri, the Office of Chief Disciplinary Counsel is the Supreme Court agency that investigates lawyer misconduct, and public discipline imposed since January 1, 2006 is posted through the courts. The Missouri Bar maintains an official directory to confirm someone is a member and authorized to practice. For Illinois, use the ARDC lawyer search.
Three limits to understand, because misreading these does real harm:
The Missouri Bar’s LawyerSearch tool is opt-in — it lists only lawyers who asked to be listed and are taking new clients. A lawyer’s absence from it means nothing. Use the official directory for the “is this person licensed” question.
Public discipline online runs from 2006 forward. Older matters aren’t in that set.
And pending, dismissed and confidential complaints are not public — so a clean record means no public discipline, not that nobody ever complained.
For a Metro East crash, check both states. A Missouri license is not an Illinois license.
### You probably don’t need legal aid
This surprises people, so it’s worth saying directly: legal aid organizations in this metro generally do not handle personal injury cases — and that isn’t a gap in the system.
Injury work is done on contingency, which means someone with a real claim can hire a lawyer without any money up front. Cost isn’t the barrier here the way it is for an eviction or a custody fight.
Where legal aid matters enormously is the wreckage that follows an injury — the eviction when you can’t work, the debt collectors, the denied benefits. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri covers 21 counties of eastern Missouri; Land of Lincoln Legal Aid covers the entire Metro East from its East St. Louis office. The Missouri Bar also runs a free, confidential fee dispute resolution program if you end up in a disagreement with your own lawyer over a bill.
This is general information about Missouri and Illinois law, not legal advice, and deadlines have exceptions that turn on facts specific to your case. If you were injured, talk to a lawyer licensed in the state where it happened — most will tell you where you stand at no charge.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What percentage do most injury lawyers take?
A.  There is no Missouri cap and no neutral source establishing a local norm — every percentage you will find online comes from law firm marketing. What Missouri’s rules do require is that your written agreement state the percentages for settlement, trial and appeal separately, since they often differ. Ask for those three numbers in writing.
### Q. How much will I get from a $50,000 settlement?
A.  It depends on the fee percentage, the case expenses, whether expenses come off before or after the fee, and any medical liens. On a $50,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $5,000 of expenses, expenses-first nets you about $30,000 while fee-first nets about $28,333. Missouri also caps health care provider liens at 50% of your net proceeds after fees and costs.
### Q. What not to say to a personal injury lawyer?
A.  Don’t guess or minimize. Saying “I’m fine” or estimating speeds and distances you aren’t sure of can follow a case for years. Also avoid assuming you have no claim because you were partly at fault — Missouri uses pure comparative fault, so being 60% responsible reduces recovery rather than ending it.
### Q. How hard is it to win a personal injury lawsuit?
A.  Most injury claims settle rather than going to trial. The harder practical questions are usually whether the deadline was met, whether fault can be proven, and whether there is enough insurance to collect against — Missouri only requires $25,000 per person in liability coverage, which frequently becomes the real ceiling.
### Q. How long do I have to file an injury claim in Missouri?
A.  Generally five years for personal injury, three years for wrongful death from the date of death, and two years for medical malpractice. Shorter deadlines override these: 30 days to report a work injury in writing, and 90 days’ written notice to the mayor for a street or sidewalk defect claim in the City of St. Louis.
### Q. Is the deadline different if my accident happened in Illinois?
A.  Yes, and dramatically. Illinois allows two years for personal injury and wrongful death, against Missouri’s five and three. A claim against an Illinois local public entity must be filed within one year. For a Metro East crash the Illinois clock is the one that likely matters.
### Q. Can I still recover money if the accident was partly my fault?
A.  In Missouri, yes — it uses pure comparative fault, so if you are 60% at fault on $100,000 of damages you still recover $40,000. In Illinois, being more than 50% at fault bars recovery entirely, so the same facts would yield nothing. This is the sharpest legal difference across the river.

A.  Fighting an insurer rather than a driver? Here is when to call an attorney about a denied claim.
Facing charges rather than a claim? Here’s what a criminal defense attorney costs in St. Louis.
If the harm came from treatment rather than a crash, start with whether you have a medical malpractice case in St. Louis.
Hurt on the job rather than on the road? Here is when to call a workers’ compensation attorney in St. Louis.
No. Missouri’s rules prohibit a lawyer from initiating in-person, telephone or real-time electronic solicitation, with narrow exceptions for existing clients, other lawyers, friends and relatives. Written solicitation is also barred within 30 days of an accident, and any solicitation letter must be marked ADVERTISEMENT.

## Kicked Out at 1:30? The Grove Is Just Getting Loud. Where to Dance in St. Louis Tonight
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-dance-clubs-in-stl-your-ultimate-guide-for-2026
1:30 on a Saturday night in a bar out in St. Charles. The house lights slam on mid-chorus, the bartender is already stacking stools, somebody is still clutching a half-finished Busch Light, and a bouncer is holding the door open to the cold. Your shirt is still damp. Your feet are still going. And twenty-some miles east, in the Grove, the bass is only now getting loud.
Same city, same night. The difference is a line on a map, and almost nobody explains it until you’ve been kicked out on the wrong side of it. The scene moves fast, too: Attitudes, the Grove’s longtime staple, is closed for good, Europe on Washington Avenue lost its 3am permit, and Pop’s in Sauget isn’t the 24-hour club the old lists swear it is. And the cheapest good night out costs nothing at the door: Soulard’s DJ bars skip the cover and the velvet rope, and Club Viva throws in a free salsa lesson at 8:15. Here’s where the floor is full tonight, and how late it stays that way.
Last call, by zone: most of the Missouri metro, 1:30am. Licensed clubs in the City and St. Louis County, 3am. Sauget, Illinois, somewhere between 5 and 8 in the morning.
The best places to go dancing in St. Louis span a few districts: Washington Avenue downtown (EDM and hip-hop at Europe, dressy dancing at Pepper Lounge), The Grove (the heart of LGBTQ+ nightlife and Latin nights), Soulard’s DJ bars, Latin dancing at Club Viva, country line-dancing at PBR in Ballpark Village, and true after-hours clubs across the river in Sauget, Illinois. Most are 21+.
### The Local Quirk That Shapes Your Whole Night: Last Call by Zone
Here’s how it plays out on a real Saturday. At 1:30 the lights come up in a Soulard bar without the late license, and you spill onto the sidewalk smelling like beer and somebody else’s cologne. Ten minutes later you’re on Manchester in the Grove, Just John is open until 3, and the bass is only getting louder. When the music stops depends entirely on which side of which line you’re standing on. Across most of the Missouri metro, last call is 1:30am. But qualifying high-volume venues in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County can serve until 3am, which is why the downtown and Grove spots keep going after the suburbs have gone dark. And if you’re still not ready to quit? Cross the Mississippi into Sauget, Illinois, where the clubs run until 5 or 6am, and one legendary spot keeps the music going until 7 or 8 in the morning.
So the shape of your night comes down to one early choice. A normal-hours neighborhood bar, a 3am downtown club, or a dawn run across the river and a drive home over the Poplar Street Bridge with the sun at your back and the Arch catching it. Plan the finish before you plan the start, and line up your rides accordingly.
### Which St. Louis Dance Clubs Are Open Tonight?
It depends on the night, and weeknights are where people get burned: you show up dressed and ready, the door is dark, and the only sound on the block is your own shoes. Here’s the rhythm, taken from the venues’ own posted hours:
Sunday and Monday: the Grove carries it. Just John opens in the afternoon and runs until 1:30am, Rehab has something going seven days a week, and HandleBar stays open until 2:30am. Pepper Lounge also opens at 10pm on Sundays.
Tuesday: the quietest night. Just John (open until 3am) and Rehab are your best bets; HandleBar is closed Tuesdays. And yes, Pop’s in Sauget still runs its overnight party from midnight to 7am, even on a Tuesday.
Wednesday: reggae night at Club Viva from 8pm, plus the Grove.
Thursday: Latin night and the free lesson at Club Viva, PBR from 8pm, and Oz in Sauget from 11pm until 5am.
Friday and Saturday: everything. Club Viva and PBR open at 8pm, the Soulard DJ bars get going around 9 or 9:30, Europe and Pepper Lounge open at 10pm, and Oz and Pop’s run from 11pm until 6 to 8 in the morning.
Want a club that’s already open at 9pm? Head to the Grove, Club Viva or PBR. The big downtown rooms don’t open their doors until 10, so skip the 9:15 wait on an empty sidewalk. Sauget doesn’t start until 11. And if it’s a Sunday-through-Thursday night and you’re still going at midnight, Pop’s runs its overnight party every night of the week. Hours shift for holidays, private events and big game nights, so check the venue’s socials the day you go.
### Downtown & Washington Avenue: The Club District
Washington Avenue was St. Louis’s marquee club strip for years, and while it’s thinned out, its anchor is still standing and still packed. Europe Night Club (710 N 15th St) is the survivor - a proper nightclub running house, techno, bass, hip-hop, and Latin nights, open Friday and Saturday nights, and big enough to land touring names when the trance and EDM crowd comes to town. It inherited the crowds from the downtown clubs that have closed around it, which is exactly why it still feels alive on a Saturday at midnight. One caution: the city’s excise commissioner has revoked Europe’s 3am permit, so check its current closing time before you plan to finish the night there.
For something a little dressier, Pepper Lounge brings an all-night dance floor with hip-hop, R&B, house, and EDM and a cocktail-and-heels crowd - a good pick if you want to dance but also want the night to feel like an occasion. On Clark Avenue a couple of blocks from Ballpark Village, Tin Roof mixes live bands and DJs for a rowdier, no-pretense party, and a short walk away sits the metro’s wildest curveball (more on that below).
### The Grove: St. Louis’s Nightlife Heart (and LGBTQ+ Home Base)
If you want the densest concentration of dance floors in one walkable stretch, go to The Grove on Manchester Avenue - the center of St. Louis’s LGBTQ+ nightlife and one of the most welcoming, high-energy scenes in the region for absolutely everyone. Just John Nightclub (4112 Manchester) is the flagship: a real dance floor, a performance stage, rotating DJs and theme parties, and doors open until 3am Tuesday through Saturday. A few doors down, the bike-themed HandleBar pairs a real dance floor and a two-story patio with DJ sets, karaoke, drag shows and regular Latin dance nights.
Round out the Grove crawl with Rehab Bar & Grill on Chouteau (drag shows, a big patio, DJ nights, open seven days a week). If an old guide sends you to Attitudes, the Grove’s longtime staple, skip it: it’s closed for good. One geography note so you find it: the beloved Grey Fox Pub - a gay pub and drag venue going strong since 1988 - is just south in Tower Grove South, not in the Grove proper, but it’s well worth the short hop.
Nothing to do with nightlife: nobody talks enough about the Southampton neighborhood.
### Soulard: Where the DJ Sets Sneak Up on You
Soulard is famous for its bar-crawl energy, and several of its spots turn into genuine dance parties after dark. Social Bar & Grill on South 7th throws a bass-heavy EDM night on Thursdays and an industry party on Sundays. Duke’s hides a Friday-and-Saturday DJ dance party upstairs (Cajun food downstairs, if you need fuel), and Molly’s spins DJ sets on its patio on weekend nights. It’s the move when you want dancing without a cover charge or a velvet rope - just wander until you hear the beat.
### Latin Night: Salsa, Bachata, and Free Lessons
St. Louis has a warm, growing Latin dance scene, and the anchor is Club Viva at 408 N Euclid in the Central West End - salsa, bachata, merengue and cha-cha on its Thursday and Saturday Latin nights (Wednesdays are reggae, Fridays Afro-Caribbean), with a free intro salsa and bachata lesson around 8:15pm so first-timers aren’t thrown in cold. It’s 21+ with a small cover, and its Thursday and Saturday Latin nights are the reliable heart of the scene. Add La Calle on Manchester for its Saturday Latin dance night and HandleBar’s Latin nights, and you’ve got a full rotation. Can’t dance a lick? That’s what the free lesson is for - show up early.
### Boots and a Mechanical Bull: Country Line Dancing
Want to two-step instead of two-turntable? PBR St. Louis: A Cowboy Bar in Ballpark Village (601 Clark Ave) is the big, loud answer - live country and southern rock, a giant dance floor, a mechanical bull, and hours that run to 2am on Thursdays and 3am on Fridays and Saturdays. It’s the perfect pairing with a Cardinals game or a bachelorette party, and no, you don’t need to know how to line dance before you get there - you’ll pick it up (or fake it) by the second song.
### Across the River: The After-Hours Clubs of Sauget, Illinois
This is the part where St. Louis stops playing by Missouri’s clock. Because Sauget, Illinois sits outside Missouri’s closing laws, its clubs run when everything else is locking up. Oz Nightclub (300 Monsanto Ave) is the big EDM-and-hip-hop room, open until 5am on Thursdays and 6am on weekends, pulling touring DJs and the crowd that isn’t ready to call it. And then there’s Pop’s (1403 Mississippi Ave), the legendary concert venue and nightclub whose overnight party runs from midnight to 7am Sunday through Thursday and 11pm to 8am on Fridays and Saturdays, with cover bands and DJs still going at 5:30 in the morning for the diehards. Cross the river when the metro closes and the night simply keeps going.

## Whose Name Does Google Show After a St. Louis Hailstorm?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/local-seo-for-contractors-in-st-louis
The hail stops, and the street goes quiet except for water running down the downspouts. A homeowner steps off the porch, squints up at a roofline that has changed color, and does what everybody does next: thumbs a phone and types “roofer near me.” Whoever Google shows first gets the call. Everyone else finds out on Monday how busy the week was.
That is a St. Louis scene. The National Weather Service says thunderstorms normally occur here on between 40 and 50 days a year, with usually a few severe ones that produce “large hail and damaging winds.” So what decides which name the phone shows? Not the retainer. Google answers in one sentence the pitch deck leaves out: “There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”
That is Google’s own help page, not anyone’s opinion. So if somebody has pitched you a bought ranking, or is holding your profile under their own login, they are selling something Google says does not exist. You do good work. Why should the phone showing your name depend on a stranger’s password? The rest of this page is Google’s own rules, with the St. Louis parts filled in.
### Is it worth having a Google Business Profile?
Google calls it “your free Business Profile” on Search and Maps, and it is the one local listing Google lets you control directly. Google says businesses “with complete and accurate info are more likely to show up in local search results,” and that verifying tells Google you are “authorized to represent the business.”
What the profile will not do is buy you a spot, as that opening sentence says. It also will not be yours if somebody else set it up and walked away. Google’s rules for anyone managing a profile on a business’s behalf, a “third-party SEO/SEM company” included, say they must “never claim a Business Profile without express consent from the business owner” and must “transfer Business Profile ownership to the business owner immediately upon request.” Whose email address owns your profile right now? If you cannot say, that is this week’s first job. If it is not yours, ask for the keys. Google has already told them to hand them over.
Here is the step path, from Google’s own help page. If you have a shop, go to business.google.com/add, enter your name and address, pick your business, and select Request Access. The current owner gets an email and has 3 days to respond. If you drive to customers and have no shop, that form is not your route: Google says a service-area business should contact Google and enter Transfer ownership of listing in the “Tell us what we can help with” field. With no response after 3 days, you may have the option to claim the profile, though Google notes that option “isn’t always available.”
### The Missouri license rumor, and the lists your name is already on
Before a careful homeowner lets a stranger onto her roof, she types the company name into her phone and looks for a license. So your license is a listing too, and one rumor about it is wrong. If you searched for what license a contractor needs in Missouri, you may have read that the state licenses HVAC or mechanical contractors statewide, maybe even that it started in 2026. The bill is Senate Bill 957, which would establish “the Missouri Statewide Mechanical Contractor Licensing Act.” Its page lists an effective date of August 28, 2026 and a status of “Second Read and Referred” to a committee. A bill’s effective date is the day it would take effect if it passed, which is easy to mistake for law. Even the bill’s training standard points home: it would require criteria “equal to those of the mechanical code of St. Louis County as of April 18, 2023.”
Drive an electrical truck from Florissant to Ballwin and the paperwork can change under your tires. Missouri’s statute defines a local license as “limited to practice within the political subdivision issuing the license,” and a statewide license, issued through the Division of Professional Registration, as one that “allows the licensee to practice in any jurisdiction regardless of local licensing requirements.” In a county with 88 municipalities, that difference is not trivia, and almost nobody frames it that way.
Inside the City of St. Louis, contractors answer to the License Collector, in Room 104 of City Hall at 1200 Market Street, phone 314-622-4528. The City’s license page says a construction contracting business “requires a Construction Industry Contractor Graduated Business License (GBL),” and that “a separate Graduated Business License is required for each business location or trade name.” Keep the trade name on that license, on the truck and on your Google profile identical. And here is free credibility you already qualify for: the state “shall publish via electronic media and update on a weekly basis a list of valid statewide license holders,” and the Division keeps a public licensee search. A careful homeowner can check you in a minute. Make sure your entry is correct, because a name that does not match or a lapsed status reads as a red flag.
### How does local search ranking actually work?
Google says local results are “mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity.” Relevance is how well a profile matches what someone is searching for. Distance is how far each business is “from the customer who’s searching.” Prominence means “how well-known a business is,” and Google adds that it is based on things like how many websites link to you and how many reviews you have. You can work on relevance and prominence. You cannot touch distance, and you cannot buy position. Sit with that for a second: if nobody can pay for the top spot, the contractor ahead of you is not paying for it either. Something on his profile is easier for Google to read. What?
### The service-area rules, and the geometry nobody mentions
Two job tickets are clipped to the visor, a gutter repair in Ballwin and a furnace in Florissant, and Google gives you one profile to cover both. Most trades have no shop customers walk into. You drive to them. Google calls that a service-area business, and the rules are published. You can set “up to 20 service areas based on the cities, postal codes, or other areas you serve,” and you cannot use a radius: “You can’t set your service area as a radius distance around your business.” The whole area “shouldn’t be more than about 2 hours of driving time from where your business is based,” and East-West Gateway describes a St. Louis region of more than 4,400 square miles across Missouri and Illinois, so that limit rarely stops a St. Louis contractor. Distance still does. If customers don’t come to your address, Google says to remove it from your profile.
Then the rules that get trades suspended. “Do not create more than one page for each location of your business, either in a single account or multiple accounts.” That kills the scheme somebody will eventually pitch you: a separate listing for Ballwin, one for Florissant, one for O’Fallon. A rented mailing address you don’t operate from, a virtual office, “isn’t eligible for a Business Profile.” And your name has to be your real-world name “as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers.” Not Smith Plumbing - Emergency Plumber St. Louis Ballwin Kirkwood. Google says that kind of extra information “could result in the suspension of your Business Profile.”
Put three facts together. Distance from the searcher is a ranking factor. A service-area business hides its address. You get exactly one listing. So you cannot rank equally across the whole St. Louis metro, and no budget changes that: a plumber based at one end of town will have a harder time surfacing for a customer at the other end than the plumber who lives there. That is geometry, not effort. It is a reason to distrust anyone promising metro-wide dominance, and a reason to think hard about which 20 areas you name, in a county that has 88 municipalities.
### Reviews: what Google says, versus what you will be told
The last customer of the day is still on the porch with her phone out, promising she will leave you a review tonight. Tonight turns into never unless it takes one tap. Google’s whole public statement on reviews and ranking is one sentence: “More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” It adds that “positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out.” No threshold. No number. No recency formula. Anyone quoting you a figure, “you need 40 reviews to rank,” is not quoting Google.
Here is the easy part. Google says “you can ask customers to visit a Google link or scan a QR code,” so put the code on the invoice, on the clipboard, on the truck. Reply to every review, too. BrightLocal found that 42 percent of consumers are unlikely to use a business that never replies.
Now the part that gets people punished, all in Google’s words. Merchants may not “offer incentives - such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services” in exchange for a review. They may not “selectively solicit positive reviews from customers.” If a tool decides who gets your review link based on how happy the customer seems, that second line is the one to read twice. Reviews “paid for, directly or in kind,” reviews posted “from multiple accounts by or at the request of one person,” and “unusual volumes or patterns of review contributions” are out too, and Google says incentivized reviews “will be removed from Maps.” The gift card feels harmless. It is the prohibited case.
Hard left turn: the work van still has to stop for lunch in Jennings.
### What a local SEO retainer costs, and what Google says about hiring one
The pitch usually comes at suppertime, and it promises page one. Ahrefs polled 439 SEO providers and reported that “Local SEO costs $1,557 per month on average.” Agencies typically charge $1,819 and freelancers around $1,150. At the average, that is $18,684 a year. Google’s own advice for a business your size is blunt: “If you run a small local business, you can probably do much of the work yourself.” And on the sales pitch: “No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google.”
Do not read that as never hire anyone. Google lists real work a good SEO does, from technical advice to content. Read it as a price tag for the questions Google tells you to ask: what will you do, how will I see it, and who owns the profile when you leave?
### About those local SEO statistics
You will see a widely cited ranking-factors study that assigns percentage weights to profile signals, reviews, on-page factors and links. Worth knowing what it is. It comes from a company that sells local SEO software, it surveys 47 local search experts who score each factor from 0 to 5, and its own text says “none of the experts have special access to the internal workings of Google’s local search algorithm.” Useful as a read on what practitioners believe. It is not evidence, and it is not Google.
### The AI question, answered honestly
You are being told AI is changing how customers find you. Here is what is documented. BrightLocal’s 2026 survey found that use of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools for local recommendations rose “from 6% last year to 45%,” making it the third most popular source of business recommendations. That is real and moving fast. What I could not find is any survey showing that people hire plumbers or roofers through AI assistants, so anyone saying they do is extrapolating.
What Google says about its own AI features is plain: “The best practices for SEO remain relevant for AI features in Google Search,” and “there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary.” Whitespark’s 2026 report adds that local search “has remained somewhat insulated from this AI upheaval.” Getting your profile, hours and service areas right serves both.
### When St. Louis actually breaks things
Back to the weather, because it is the part that drives the phone call. Beyond the 40 to 50 thunderstorm days, the National Weather Service says temperatures of 90 degrees or higher occur on about 35 to 40 days a year, and snowfall has averaged “a little over 18 inches per winter season.” I could not find data showing search volume spikes by a specific percentage in any of those windows, so I will not invent one. The practical move needs no number. Set your hours before the storm, not after it.
### What is actually worth your time
Stripping out everything unsourced, here is what survives. All of it is free, and all of it comes from Google’s documentation.
Verify the profile. Google says verification tells it you are authorized to represent the business, so it is more likely to show up.
Fill in every field, accurately. Hours, category, service areas. Complete and accurate beats clever.
Choose your 20 service areas on purpose. Name the places you want work, not the places you could technically reach.
Ask for honest reviews and answer them. No incentives, no filtering. A QR code on the invoice is enough.
Claim Bing too. Our Bing Places guide covers the traps.
Check your state listing. If you hold a statewide electrical license, make sure the public record is right.
And be skeptical of anyone whose pitch needs a statistic they cannot source, a review shortcut Google prohibits, or a ranking Google says cannot be bought.
Fix the profile first, then everything else. Start with how to optimize your Google Business Profile and how to respond to reviews.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I get a Google Business Profile for free?
A.  Google calls it “your free Business Profile” on Search and Maps. What is not free is anything a third party sells around it. Google also says it “never accepts money to include or rank sites in our search results,” and local rankings cannot be bought either, so treat any pitch that promises a purchased position as a misrepresentation.
### Q. Do you need an LLC to have a Google Business Profile?
A.  No. Google’s test is whether “a business must make in-person contact with customers during its stated hours,” and a service-area business that visits customers qualifies. Its naming rules even tell you to leave irrelevant legal terms like LLC out of your profile name unless your signs, cards and invoices consistently show them. Whether you form one for liability or licensing is a question for a lawyer and the City.
### Q. Can I have multiple businesses under one Google account?
A.  Yes, if they are genuinely separate businesses. Google recommends that anyone new to Business Profile who manages several create a business group. But each location gets one profile: “Do not create more than one page for each location of your business, either in a single account or multiple accounts.” An HVAC company and a separate excavation company can share your login. Two profiles for the same shop cannot.
### Q. How much does it cost to hire an SEO company?
A.  In Ahrefs’ survey of 439 providers, local SEO averaged $1,557 per month, with agencies at $1,819 and freelancers near $1,150. That is a national, self-reported sample, so treat it as a rough benchmark. Google adds that a small local business “can probably do much of the work yourself,” and that no one can guarantee a number one ranking.
### Q. Is SEO dead now with AI?
A.  Not according to Google. Its documentation says SEO best practices remain relevant for AI features, with no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. BrightLocal reports AI use for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in a year, but I found no survey showing contractors get hired that way yet. Accurate listings serve both.
### Q. Will SEO exist in 5 years?
A.  Nobody can honestly promise a five-year forecast. What is documented today: Google says SEO best practices remain relevant for AI features, and its own list of what SEOs do now includes “Optimizing for generative AI.” The durable part is the part you control, an accurate profile, honest reviews, and a website that says what you do and where.
### Q. What is SEO in construction?
A.  Google describes SEO as “helping search engines understand your content, and helping users find your site.” For a contractor that means a verified Google Business Profile, service areas that match where you actually work, reviews you earned honestly, and a website that names your trades and your towns. Google’s own starter guide adds that “there are no secrets here that’ll automatically rank your site first.”
### Q. Can you pay Google for a better local ranking?
A.  No. Google states that “there’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.” Anyone promising a purchased position is misrepresenting how the system works.

## How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in St. Louis (After the 2024 Rule Change)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-real-estate-agent-in-st-louis
The rules for hiring a real estate agent changed in August 2024, and the lawsuit that changed them was decided in a Missouri federal courtroom — the Western District, in Kansas City.
If you are buying a house in St. Louis right now, you will be asked to sign something before you are allowed to walk through your first front door. Most people sign it without reading it.
Here is what actually changed, what didn’t, and the specific things worth checking before you pick anyone.
### How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis?
Start by verifying the license. Missouri’s public lookup is at mopro.mo.gov, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp — both free, both take a minute. Then interview at least three, and before signing anything, get the compensation figure written as an actual number. Since August 2024 a buyer must sign a written agreement before touring a home, and that agreement’s compensation term must be, in the National Association of Realtors’ own words, “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended.” A blank, or “standard rate,” or “whatever the seller offers” does not meet that standard.
### What actually changed in 2024
The case was Burnett v. National Association of Realtors. NAR agreed to pay $418 million, and a judge granted final approval in November 2024. The practice changes took effect on August 17, 2024. Two of them matter to you.
One: offers of buyer-agent compensation came off the MLS. This is the change that gets described wrong more than any other. Compensation was not banned. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent — it just can’t be advertised through the multiple listing service anymore. Seller concessions toward your closing costs can still appear there, though nothing in a listing tells you what movers actually cost in St. Louis, which stays its own line in your budget.
Two: you sign before you tour. An agent working with you must have a signed written agreement in place before showing you a home. There are exceptions — an open house hosted by the seller’s agent doesn’t require one, and neither does a showing where you’re unrepresented.
What did not change: commissions were always negotiable. The settlement didn’t create that, cap anything, or set a rate. NAR now requires agents to conspicuously disclose that compensation “is not set by law and is fully negotiable” — which was true before, and is now something they have to say out loud.
### Commissions did not go down
You will read that the settlement drove commissions down. The data doesn’t support it, and you should know that before you sit across from anyone.
Redfin’s research tracked the average buyer’s-agent commission at 2.38% in the second quarter of 2024, dipping to 2.36% in the third quarter as the rules took effect — and back to 2.42% by the third quarter of 2025. Slightly higher than before the change. A separate analysis by AccountTECH, covering more than 224,000 closed transactions across roughly 1,300 offices, found the same shape: a real dip in late 2024 that round-tripped within about five months.
Two independent datasets, same conclusion. Anyone telling you the market has settled this for you is wrong.
And there’s a detail in that data that lands directly on St. Louis. Broken out by price, the average buyer-agent commission in the third quarter of 2025 ran 2.52% on homes under $500,000, 2.32% between $500,000 and $999,000, and 2.22% above a million. The cheaper the house, the higher the percentage. Nearly every St. Louis transaction sits in that first tier — so buyers and sellers here are in the segment paying the most, proportionally, and have the most to gain from asking.
Which almost nobody does. A survey conducted by Ipsos for Redfin in spring 2025 found 37.4% of sellers negotiated or tried to negotiate commission — against just 27.2% of buyers. Buyers are leaving the most on the table, in the tier where the percentage is highest.
### Verify the license in about a minute
Two free public tools, and almost nobody uses either.
License status: the Missouri Division of Professional Registration portal at mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search. You can confirm the license is real, active, and whether the person is a salesperson or a broker. (If you find an older link floating around, note that Missouri migrated portals — the legacy address redirects here.)
Disciplinary history: a separate page, pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp, which posts actions taken since June 30, 2011 as downloadable PDFs you can search by name.
Know the limits of what you’re seeing. You cannot see pending or unresolved complaints, sales volume, transaction history, or anything before mid-2011 without digging into archives. A clean record means no public discipline — not that someone is good at the job.
### Agent, REALTOR, broker — three different things
These get used interchangeably and they are not interchangeable. There are actually two separate systems running at once.
The state licensing system. Under Missouri law, a broker is licensed to conduct real estate business, and a salesperson must be affiliated with a broker who is responsible for their conduct. A salesperson cannot operate independently. That’s state law, and violating it is a licensing matter.
The trade association. “REALTOR” is a registered membership mark belonging to the National Association of Realtors. It is not a license and not a job title — it means the person pays dues and is bound by NAR’s Code of Ethics, first adopted in 1913. A licensed agent who isn’t a member is not bound by that code.
The practical consequence is that you have two different complaint paths. Legal violations go to the Missouri Real Estate Commission, which can act against a license. Ethics complaints against a REALTOR go to the local association — here, St. Louis REALTORS — which can only discipline membership. Knowing which is which saves you months.
### The word that decides how much they owe you
Missouri law draws a line between a client and a customer. A client has entered a brokerage relationship. A customer is involved in the transaction but has not.
There is also a role called a transaction broker, who assists with the deal without an agency or fiduciary relationship to either side. That is a legitimate, legal arrangement — and it means nobody in the room owes you a fiduciary duty.
Ask the question directly: Am I your client or your customer, and are you acting as a single agent, a limited agent, or a transaction broker? If the answer is vague, that is the answer.
Unrelated, and we know it — where to eat in Creve Coeur.
### What a seller has to tell you in Missouri — and what they don’t
Missouri leans toward caveat emptor. There is no broad statutory duty for a seller to volunteer every defect. There are specific exceptions in both directions, and they surprise people.
Must be disclosed: if methamphetamine was produced on the property and the seller knew, that has to be disclosed in writing — and it applies whether or not anyone was ever convicted.
Need not be disclosed: Missouri law says a property is not required to be disclosed as “psychologically impacted.” That covers a homicide, felony or suicide having occurred there, and an occupant having had a disease unlikely to be transmitted by living in the house. The statute goes further and bars a cause of action against an agent for not telling you.
Now the part worth reading twice. The agent’s duty is broader than the seller’s. A Missouri licensee must disclose adverse material facts actually known, or that should have been known — to clients and customers both. But the same law says the licensee has no duty to conduct an independent inspection, no duty to discover adverse facts for a customer, and no duty to verify what the seller told them.
So it is a duty not to conceal. It is not a duty to investigate. Nobody in the transaction is required to go find the problems for you. Get your own inspection.
### Which St. Louis number are they quoting you?
If an agent quotes “the St. Louis median” without saying which geography, they may not be misleading you on purpose — but the figures differ enormously.
For June 2026: the median sale price in St. Louis City was about $261,000, up roughly 0.8% year over year, on 292 homes sold. In St. Louis County, about $325,000, up roughly 6.6%. Meanwhile the median list price across the whole St. Louis MO–IL metro area ran about $290,000, down 3.3% — and that one is an asking price, not a sale price. They are not the same measurement and should never be compared to each other.
Two more metro figures worth having: median days on market around 44, four days longer than a year earlier, and active listings up about 10.3%. More inventory, sitting slightly longer. We’re reporting those as recorded, not predicting where they go.
City and county are different markets. An agent who closes constantly in one may know very little about the other — so ask which municipalities they actually close in.
### What to ask before you sign
Do the license and discipline lookups first, quietly, before the meeting. Then:
1. What exact rate or dollar figure goes in the compensation blank, and how long does this agreement run? 2. Can I cancel it, and on what terms? 3. If the seller offers compensation off-MLS, does that reduce what I owe you dollar for dollar, or do you keep the difference? 4. Am I your client or your customer, and what is your agency role? 5. Will you show me homes where the seller offers little or no buyer-agent compensation? 6. Are you a REALTOR, or licensed only? 7. Which municipalities do you actually close in?
Question three is the sharpest one on the list, because it is precisely the ambiguity the off-MLS change created — and a straight answer to it tells you most of what you need to know about the person.
Two red flags worth naming: anyone who tells you the commission is standard or set by law, and anyone who pressures you to sign before you’ve read it. The signature is required. The terms in it are not.
This is general information about Missouri real estate practice, not legal advice. For advice about your situation, talk to a Missouri attorney.

### Q. How much does a realtor make off of a $300,000 house?
A.  At the 2.52% average buyer-agent commission for homes under $500,000, a $300,000 sale is about $7,560 to the buyer’s agent, before their brokerage takes a share. ### Q. What not to say to a real estate agent?
A.  Avoid revealing your maximum budget or your deadline pressure before you understand who the agent represents. Under Missouri law a transaction broker owes no fiduciary duty to either party, and a “customer” is owed less than a “client” — so establish your agency relationship in writing first, then share strategy.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule in real estate?
A.  It is an informal rule of thumb that circulates online in several conflicting versions — sometimes about touring three homes, sometimes about savings or budgeting. It is not a Missouri regulation, an NAR rule, or a lending standard, and no authoritative source defines it. Treat it as folklore rather than guidance.
### Q. What annoys real estate agents?
A.  Common complaints are touring homes far outside your approved budget, working with several agents at once without disclosing it, and missing scheduled showings. ## 200-Amp Service Change? St. Louis Won't Let You Permit It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/old-house-wiring-in-st-louis
The basement light is a bare bulb on a pull chain, and when you yank it the bulb hums before it settles. Over the washer, two separate wires run side by side through white porcelain knobs nailed to the joists, a few inches apart. Upstairs the window unit kicks on, and the bulb dips. The air smells like damp brick and old dust.
You follow the wires with a flashlight to a splice wrapped in masking tape gone brown and brittle. Your thumb is already on the hardware store app.
Stop there, and read the City of St. Louis permit page before you buy anything. What you can’t permit yourself: “You may not apply for permits for service changes, rehab, or new construction.” If the electrician’s quote says service change, that permit is not yours to pull, and the page says those jobs need to be performed by a licensed contractor. What you can: pass a short test from the Building Division’s Electrical Section, and you can get a permit for a room addition, repair or modification to an existing system on an owner-occupied single-family home. An extra outlet on the bedroom circuit? Possibly yours, after the test. A service change at the panel is a permit no homeowner may apply for. Read that twice before you text the brother-in-law with the voltage tester. The Electrical Section is at 1200 Market, Room 425, at 314-622-3313.
Upstairs, the warning signs are things your hand and nose catch first. Put the back of your hand on the outlet cover that feeds the power strip, the phone charger and the space heater. A plate that feels warm, a lamp that dips when something big kicks on, a whiff of hot plastic near a switch: those are the things to write down and show an electrician.
In this city, those signs live in very old houses. When University of Missouri-St. Louis researchers studied older homeowners in St. Louis, the average age of their homes was 97 years. Over 80% had an electrical outlet used for more than two devices, which the researchers flagged as a fire risk, and the most common needed repairs they found were installing electrical plugs and weatherization. Tell that to the neighbor with the extension cord snaking under the rug: one of the repairs these houses need most is simply more outlets.
The City’s side of the bill is small. Every electrical permit carries a $25 application fee; a residential repair or modification inspection is $60, and $100 when it comes with a new service. The real money is the electrician: HomeAdvisor’s national cost data puts a 200-amp panel upgrade at $1,300 to $2,000. The rest of this page is how to know what you are paying for.
### Is knob and tube wiring still safe?
Original knob-and-tube can keep working, but it was built for a house with toasters and irons, not a modern load. According to home inspectors at InterNACHI, its dangers come from its age, improper modifications, and building insulation that envelops the wires, and it has no ground wire. Have a qualified electrician evaluate it, and replace any wire that is brittle or cracked.
Here is the surprise. The original work is often better than what came after it: inspectors write that the original installation of knob-and-tube is often superior to modern Romex, and the porcelain lasts almost forever. The trouble is everything people did to it later, in the damp basements of brick houses that have outlived three owners.
Knob-and-tube runs the hot and neutral wires separately, usually 4 to 6 inches apart, so the wires can shed heat into free air. Blow insulation into that attic and the heat has nowhere to go, which is why the 2008 National Electrical Code requires that this wiring not be covered by insulation. Then come the decades of handiwork. It is not uncommon to find connections wrapped with masking tape or Scotch tape instead of electrical tape, and that many homeowners installed fuses rated too high for the wiring so they would blow less often, which let the wire itself take the heat.
Think of beige masking tape gone brown and brittle on a splice above the basement stairs. That is the realistic hazard: not the old copper, but the tape, the oversized fuse and the insulation someone packed around it without knowing.
### How to tell what is in your walls, without touching anything
Take a flashlight to the unfinished basement or attic and look up at the joists. Knob-and-tube is insulated copper wire passing through porcelain tubes where it crosses the framing, supported along its length by nailed-down porcelain knobs. You will see two separate wires running parallel, inches apart, instead of one flat modern cable. Where the wires enter a device, they are wrapped in a flexible cloth or rubber sleeve called “loom.” Two-prong outlets everywhere are the other giveaway, since the system has no ground wire to serve three-pronged appliances.
If your house is newer, look for a different metal. InterNACHI writes that between approximately 1965 and 1973, single-strand aluminum wiring was sometimes substituted for copper branch-circuit wiring because of the sudden escalating price of copper. It quotes the Consumer Product Safety Commission: homes wired with aluminum wire manufactured before 1972 are 55 times more likely to have one or more connections reach “Fire Hazard Conditions” than a home wired with copper.
Either way, read the label on the outside of the panel and leave the cover on. What is behind it is the electrician’s job.
People are asking
### What does a 200-amp electrical panel upgrade cost in St. Louis?
HomeAdvisor’s national cost data puts a 200-amp panel upgrade at $1,300 to $2,000, with a new power supply and meter adding $100 to $650 and permits and drywall repair adding $150 to $300. In the City of St. Louis, every electrical permit carries a $25 application fee, and the inspection fee for a residential service-only job is $60. Homeowners may not apply for City permits for service changes, so a licensed contractor has to do the job. Replacing a fuse box with a breaker box costs $1,500 to $2,000 in the same national data, and up to $4,500 if the wiring needs a complete overhaul.
### The sounds and smells that mean call today
Old wiring rarely fails silently, and the warnings are things you can hear and smell. HomeAdvisor’s list of signs that a panel needs an upgrade includes an age of over 25 years, persistent flickering lights, overheating appliances, electric shocks upon contact, unusual hissing or crackling sounds, burn marks around the panel, and frequent breaker trips with high-load devices. Add the warm face plate and the whiff of hot plastic from the top of this page, and you have a checklist you can run with a flashlight and your nose.
Stand in the basement and listen while someone upstairs runs the microwave and the hair dryer at once. A faint buzz from the panel, a click and a dark room, a brown scorch mark on the panel door: none of those are “just an old house.” Write down what you saw and heard, and when. An electrician can diagnose a pattern far faster than a vague “the lights act funny.”
And a word about the way these houses got this way. InterNACHI’s inspectors note that when knob-and-tube was first introduced, common household appliances were limited to little more than toasters, tea kettles, coffee percolators and clothes irons, and that existing systems are notorious for modifications made to keep up with televisions, refrigerators and everything after. Many of those changes were made by insufficiently trained handymen rather than experienced electricians. Every owner of a century-old St. Louis house inherits a few of them.
### Do you actually need 200 amps?
Not always. HomeAdvisor notes that most homes have electrical service between 100 and 200 amps. Amperage is how much your whole house can draw at once, so the question is what you plan to run. An electric range and dryer, central air added to a crowded panel, a heat pump, a hot tub, an EV charger: each one is more for the panel to carry. A gas house with one air conditioner often does fine.
Ask the electrician for a load calculation before you sign anything. A contractor who skips that step and quotes a bigger service anyway is guessing with your money.
### Buying a house that sat empty? Read this first
If the house you love sat dark for a while, the meter cold and the basement smelling of damp plaster, know this rule before you set a move-in date. The City charges a re-inspection fee for structures whose electrical service has not been in use for six months or more, and if the re-inspection isn’t applied for, the power company can be ordered to keep the service disconnected until the City says otherwise. Ask the seller how long the power has been off, and budget for an electrician’s walk-through before the inspector’s.
Power’s off for the panel swap and the stove is dead? Eat in Glendale, Missouri tonight.
### Fixing aluminum wiring the right way
The danger with aluminum lives at the connections, where outlets and switches meet the wire. According to InterNACHI, the CPSC recommends two methods for correction: rewire the home with copper wire, or use COPALUM crimps. Pigtailing with an ordinary twist-on connector is not one of them, and InterNACHI says that method is only effective if the connections between the aluminum wires and the copper pigtails are extremely reliable. That is worth knowing when a quote looks suspiciously cheap.
COPALUM is not a weekend fix. InterNACHI describes a specially designed metal sleeve and powered crimping tool that can be properly installed only with the matching AMP tool, typically around $50 per outlet, switch or light fixture. It also warns that not all licensed electricians are properly trained to deal with defective aluminum wiring, so ask how many aluminum jobs a contractor has done.
### Fuse boxes, Federal Pacific and Zinsco
A fuse box is not automatically dangerous. The hazard is the one InterNACHI describes: a fuse rated too high for the wire, screwed in so the nuisance stops. A fuse protects the wire, so the wrong one turns the wire inside your wall into the weakest link. If you are replacing the whole thing, HomeAdvisor puts replacing a fuse box with a breaker box at $1,500 to $2,000, up to $4,500 if the wiring needs a complete overhaul, and replacing a Federal Pacific or Zinsco panel at $1,500 to $4,000.
### Checking that your electrician is real
Because homeowners can’t permit a City service change or rehab, the license on the truck matters. Before you hand over a deposit, read our guide on how to check whether a contractor is licensed in Missouri, then get itemized bids that separate the electrical work from the plaster patching.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is knob and tube wiring still legal?
A.  Owning a house with it is not against the law, but working on it is regulated. The City of St. Louis has adopted the 2017 National Electrical Code, and homeowners may not apply for City permits for rehab or service changes, so those jobs need a licensed contractor. InterNACHI also notes that the 2008 National Electrical Code requires that this wiring not be covered by insulation.
### Q. Is it okay to buy a house with knob and tube wiring?
A.  It can be, if you price it in before closing. Have a qualified electrician evaluate how much original wiring is still in use, whether insulation covers it, and what the panel is. If the house sat empty, ask about the City’s re-inspection rule for service unused for six months or more.
### Q. Can you get home insurance on a house with knob and tube wiring?
A.  Sometimes. InterNACHI says many insurance companies refuse to insure houses that have knob-and-tube wiring due to the risk of fire, with exceptions sometimes made where an electrical contractor has deemed the system safe. Ask your own agent before you commit, and get that electrician’s assessment in writing.
### Q. Is 100 amp electric good?
A.  For many houses, yes. Most homes have service between 100 and 200 amps, and what decides it is your load: a gas house with one air conditioner is very different from one with an electric range, a heat pump and an EV charger. Ask an electrician for a load calculation.
### Q. How do I know if I have aluminum wiring?
A.  Check when the house or its additions were wired. InterNACHI says single-strand aluminum was sometimes substituted for copper between approximately 1965 and 1973. Warm face plates, flickering lights and a hot-plastic smell at outlets are reasons to call an electrician.

## Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine: A Hazelwood Middle Eastern Favorite
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/explore-the-delicious-kaslik-mediterranean-cuisine-menu-for-2025
Refreshed September 2026
There’s a particular kind of restaurant that a neighborhood quietly falls in love with: unassuming from the street, packed with regulars, serving food made with obvious care. In north St. Louis County, Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine is exactly that spot. This is an honest look at what it is, what to order, and why it’s spent more than a decade earning a loyal Hazelwood following.
If you’ve driven North Lindbergh and never stopped, you’ve been missing some of the best Middle Eastern food on the north side — shawarma, kebabs, hummus, and mezze made from scratch by a family that’s been doing it right for years. It’s the sort of place that doesn’t advertise much because it doesn’t have to; word of mouth and a loyal regular base keep it going, which is usually the best possible sign about a restaurant.
### What Kaslik is
Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine sits at 7847 North Lindbergh Boulevard in Hazelwood, MO 63042, phone (314) 972-8282. It’s a family-owned Mediterranean and Middle Eastern restaurant serving Levantine classics — the shawarma, kebabs, and mezze of the eastern Mediterranean. It first opened in Florissant around 2013 and moved to its Hazelwood home a couple of years later, and it’s been a north-county fixture ever since.
A note on the name and the food, because it’s a nice story: “Kaslik” is a town in Lebanon, and the menu draws on that whole Levantine tradition — but the family behind the restaurant is Palestinian, having come to St. Louis from the West Bank. The result is honest, home-style Middle Eastern cooking rooted in real heritage rather than a corporate concept, which is exactly why it tastes the way it does.
### What to order
The menu covers the Levantine greatest hits, and a few dishes anchor any good order:
Shawarma — chicken or beef, sliced from the spit, wrapped or over rice. The gateway dish and a reliable favorite.
Kebabs and grilled meats — lamb shish kebab, chicken kabob, kefta, and a mixed grill platter for the table that wants a bit of everything off the fire.
The mezze — hummus, baba ganoush, fattoush, and stuffed grape leaves. Order a few to share; they turn a sandwich run into a proper spread.
Falafel and vegetarian options — crisp, herby falafel and a genuinely good veggie platter make this an easy call for meatless eaters.
Baklava — the classic sweet, flaky finish. Save room.
The kebabs and the hummus are the fundamentals that tell you whether a Middle Eastern kitchen is the real deal, and Kaslik passes the test — the grilled meats come off the fire juicy and well-seasoned, and the dips taste made-that-day because they are. If you’re new to the cuisine, a mixed grill with a couple of mezze and warm pita is the perfect introduction. It’s the kind of food that tends to surprise skeptics: fresh, satisfying, and far more interesting than the fast-casual chain versions of “Mediterranean bowls” that have popped up everywhere. This is the real, from-the-source version, and once you’ve had it, the mall-food-court imitation never quite measures up again.

### A quick primer on Levantine food
If Middle Eastern food is new to you, here’s the short version of what makes it so satisfying. The Levantine tradition — the cooking of the eastern Mediterranean, from Lebanon and Syria through Palestine and Jordan — is built on fresh, bright, generous flavors: grilled meats seasoned simply and well, fresh herbs, lemon and garlic, olive oil, and a whole family of dips and salads meant for sharing with warm bread. It’s food that feels both healthy and deeply comforting, which is a rare combination — you can eat well here without the heavy, over-full feeling a lot of restaurant meals leave you with, and still walk out satisfied.
It’s also a cuisine built for the table, not the individual plate. A proper Middle Eastern meal is a spread — several mezze in the middle, a platter of grilled meats, a stack of pita, everyone reaching and passing. That communal, unhurried style is part of what makes a place like Kaslik feel welcoming, and it’s why it works so well for a group. You don’t just eat here; you graze, you share, you linger.
### Great for takeout, catering, and feeding a crowd
One underrated thing about this style of food: it travels beautifully. Shawarma, kebabs, and mezze hold up far better in a takeout container than most restaurant meals, which makes Kaslik a smart call for a family dinner at home, a working lunch, or a spread for a group. The dips, the pita, the grilled meats — nothing here goes soggy or sad on the drive back to Florissant or Bridgeton, and much of it reheats the next day without complaint.
That’s also what makes it a genuinely good catering option for anyone hosting. A Middle Eastern spread — platters of grilled meats, bowls of hummus and baba ganoush, fresh fattoush, warm bread, and a tray of baklava — is generous, colorful, and easy for a crowd to graze on, and it quietly accommodates the vegetarians and lighter eaters in the group without anyone having to think about it. For an office lunch, a graduation party, or a family gathering in the north county, it’s a more interesting and more inclusive choice than the usual pizza-or-sandwiches default, and it feels like an occasion without being fussy or expensive.
### A first-timer’s game plan
Never had much Middle Eastern food, or bringing someone who hasn’t? Keep it simple. Start with hummus and warm pita — it’s the universal on-ramp, familiar and irresistible. Add a baba ganoush or fattoush to round out the mezze, then anchor the meal with a mixed grill so the table gets a taste of the different kebabs and grilled meats at once. It’s proof that some of the metro’s most authentic, worth-the-trip food is tucked into unassuming strip-mall storefronts far from the trendy districts, waiting for anyone willing to look.
For north-county residents, it’s a reminder that you don’t have to drive to the city or the fashionable suburbs for a genuinely great meal — there’s a real one right on Lindbergh. And for anyone from elsewhere in the metro who considers themselves a serious eater, it’s a nudge to broaden the map. ## Candicci’s: A 40-Year St. Louis Italian Favorite, Reinvented

The short version: after more than 40 years as a full-service restaurant, Candicci’s closed its longtime Ballwin dining room in 2024 and reopened as Candicci’s Catering & Express — a takeout-and-catering operation built around the pizzas, pastas, and family favorites that made its name. If you’re picturing the old white-tablecloth veal-and-seafood dining room with its patio and sit-down service, gently update that picture; the format is different now, but the pizzas, pastas, and toasted ravioli you love are still here, just served a new way.
### What Candicci’s is today
Candicci’s Catering & Express operates from 14870 Clayton Road, on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border in west St. Louis County (ZIP 63017), phone (636) 220-8989. It moved here in 2024 into the former Chirco’s Pizza space at Clayton and Baxter — not in Old Town Chesterfield or the Valley, but along the Clayton Road corridor between the two communities, an easy hop from the rest of Chesterfield’s shops and services.
The concept shifted from sit-down dining to takeout, delivery, and catering. Owner Bob Candice has been candid in local coverage about why: staff shortages, rising lease costs, and food-cost pressure made the full-service model untenable, so the family reinvented the business around what it does best rather than closing the doors for good. It’s a genuinely admirable pivot — keeping a 40-year name alive by changing the format instead of giving up, and a reminder that the restaurants worth rooting for are often the ones that find a way to keep going when the easy choice would be to walk away.

Starters and salads — spinach-artichoke dip, mozzarella sticks, house salad.
Family specials and a kids’ menu — built to feed a household without a big-night-out bill.
Catering trays — the same favorites scaled up for a crowd, from pastas to pizzas to sliced-meat spreads.

## Your Casino Floor Is Floating: All 6 St. Louis Casinos, Compared
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-casinos-in-st-louis-mo-a-comprehensive-guide
The river wind is still in your collar when the doors slide shut behind you, and here’s what almost nobody on this floor knows: you’re standing on water. Warm air, carpet soft enough to swallow your footsteps, a wall of slot chimes, and somewhere past the cashier cage a table goes up in one big shout. You walked here over the cobblestones of Laclede’s Landing with the Arch at your back. No boarding pass. No resort fee. No $18 airport beer.
The water part is literal. Missouri’s constitution lets casino games run on the Mississippi and Missouri rivers only, and it counts “artificial spaces that contain water” within 1,000 feet of the main channel, so even the big land-style rooms sit over man-made basins of water. The heading on that section of the constitution says it outright: “boats in moats.” It plays like any Vegas floor. Legally, it floats.
Most St. Louisans price out a Vegas weekend, close the tabs somewhere around the resort fee, and forget there are six casino floors right here in the metro. One you can walk to from Busch Stadium, and the Caesars Rewards card still in your wallet from that last Vegas trip works there. One is an honest-to-goodness riverboat in Alton. And one across the river will drive its hotel guests and rewards members to big St. Louis home games for free.
Going tonight? Do it in this order.
Pick by where you are. Downtown or at a Cardinals game: Horseshoe. South county: River City. West county or St. Charles: Hollywood or Ameristar. Metro East: DraftKings at Casino Queen or Argosy.
Bring a photo ID. You must be 21 on both sides of the river; Casino Queen, for one, takes a driver’s license, state ID, military ID or passport.
Park free or ride. River City and Argosy both advertise free parking. Or take MetroLink to the Laclede’s Landing or East Riverfront stop: $2.50 a ride, or $5 for a one-day pass.
Get the players card before your first spin. Sign up at the desk before you play. Missouri’s gaming commission lists “If you put your player’s card in, you will win less” as a myth; the card only changes the rewards you earn.
Check the clock. Hollywood and River City run 24 hours except a short closing early Wednesday mornings; the two Illinois casinos keep set hours (details below).
Set your number before you sit down. If it ever stops being fun, the free, confidential National Problem Gambling Helpline is 1-800-GAMBLER.
### What’s the Nearest Casino to Downtown St. Louis?
Horseshoe St. Louis. It sits at 999 N. 2nd Street on Laclede’s Landing, steps from the Gateway Arch, and it’s the only casino in downtown proper. Staying at a hotel near Busch Stadium or catching a show downtown? You can walk it, finishing over the Landing’s cobblestones with the casino lights ahead and the river on your right, or ride MetroLink to the Laclede’s Landing stop.

DraftKings at Casino Queen sits on the East St. Louis riverfront at 200 Front Street, “just minutes from downtown St. Louis” in its own words, and MetroLink’s East Riverfront station is on the same street, at 100 S. ### Why You Don’t Need Vegas (or Biloxi)
Do the honest math. A Vegas weekend is a flight, two burned vacation days, a resort fee and a card statement you don’t want to open, all before you’ve touched a chip. A St. Louis casino night is a tank of gas and whatever you decide to lose. Drop a hundred bucks at the tables and that’s the whole night, and you’re asleep in your own bed by two.
