### Six Casinos, Two States, One River
The St. Louis area has six casinos: four in Missouri, Hollywood Casino (Maryland Heights), River City Casino (Lemay), Horseshoe St. Louis (downtown, formerly Lumière Place) and Ameristar (St. Charles), plus two in Illinois, DraftKings at Casino Queen (East St. Louis) and Argosy Casino Alton. You must be 21, and Missouri now allows legal sports betting, too. That state line matters more than you’d guess, and it explains the floor you were standing on a minute ago.
Every Missouri casino is, on paper, a floating casino: the constitution allows the games only on “excursion gambling boats and floating facilities.” The state created its gaming commission in 1993 to regulate “excursion gambling boats,” and the commission still counts 13 “riverboat gaming casinos” in Missouri, sleek land-style rooms like Hollywood and Ameristar included. You’d never feel it on the floor - it plays like any Vegas room - but that quirk is why every one of them hugs a river. Illinois plays it more literally still: up in Alton sits an honest-to-goodness riverboat.

### The Slot Machine Questions Everyone Googles
Be honest - you’ve typed at least one of these into your phone in a parking lot. Here are straight answers, no mysticism, with help from the Missouri Gaming Commission’s own slot myth list.
What’s the “$20 method”? It’s a bankroll trick, not a loophole: you put $20 in a machine, play a set number of spins, and if you don’t hit a target you cash out the ticket and move on - protecting whatever’s left instead of feeding it all back. It won’t beat the house math, but it’s a genuinely good way to make a small budget last and stay in control.
Which slot machines “hit” the most? No machine is ever “due,” and none is warm because the last person left. Every Missouri slot runs on a random number generator, and the commission says a jackpot that just hit “has no impact on the outcome of the next play.” By law each machine has to pay back at least 80% of what’s wagered over 10 million games, not on any one night, and the commission posts each casino’s actual slot payout every month on its website. Play the ones you enjoy, set a limit, and treat any win as a happy surprise.
Are the machines rigged? Not in the cheating sense. In Missouri the game software has to be tested and certified by a licensed independent lab, it sits in a locked compartment, and only a Gaming Commission agent can break the seal on it. “Casinos flip a switch to loosen or tighten the slot machines” is on the commission’s myth list. The house edge is built into the math legally and openly - that’s just how casinos make money, the same way the lottery does. The real trap is online: the commission warns that online casinos are illegal in Missouri, and fake ones use real casino photos to look legit. At the six casinos above, the game is square; the odds simply favor the house, which is exactly why you set a budget.
### Sports Betting Is Finally Legal in Missouri
This is the big recent change. Missouri voters approved Amendment 2 on November 5, 2024, and legal sports betting - both at retail sportsbooks inside the casinos and through online apps - officially launched on December 1, 2025. For the first time, you can place a legal sports bet at a retail book inside a Missouri casino or on a mobile app, as long as you’re physically in Missouri. All four Missouri-side casinos here run retail books, but the phone is where the action went: in August, Missouri’s retail counters took about 39,000 bets while the mobile apps took about 6.8 million. Illinois’ sports betting law took effect June 28, 2019, so the Casino Queen and Argosy books had a long head start. Minimum age in Missouri is 21, same as the casino floor.
### Before You Go: ID at the Door, Free Parking, a Players Card
You must be 21 to gamble in both Missouri and Illinois, and to bet sports in Missouri. Bring a valid photo ID.
Hours: Hollywood and River City are open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, except early Wednesday mornings (Hollywood closes 5am-7am, River City 5am-6am). Casino Queen runs 8am-3am, to 5am on Fridays and Saturdays; Argosy runs 9am-2am, to 3am on Fridays and Saturdays. Check the property before a late-night run.
Parking is free in River City’s covered garage and lots, and Argosy advertises free self-parking - one more Vegas headache you get to skip.
Join the players club. Sign up before you play. Hollywood, River City and Argosy run PENN Play. Horseshoe runs Caesars Rewards. Casino Queen runs Bally Rewards. The state says your card has no impact on the outcome of the game, only on the rewards you earn.
Gamble responsibly. Set a budget before you walk in and treat it as entertainment money, not income. If it ever stops being fun, the free, confidential National Problem Gambling Helpline is at 1-800-GAMBLER, and Missouri’s own line is 1-888-BETSOFF.

You’ll find slots, table games, poker rooms and sportsbooks without leaving the metro, so there’s no need to travel to Vegas for a night out.
### Q. Is River City Casino in downtown St. Louis?
A.  No. River City sits in Lemay, south of downtown. For a casino downtown, you want Horseshoe St. Louis. It sits on Laclede’s Landing, steps from the Gateway Arch.
### Q. Is there a Caesars casino in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, under a different name. Caesars renamed the old Lumière Place Horseshoe St. Louis in 2022, and it runs on Caesars Rewards - so a card earned in Las Vegas works downtown, along with its WSOP poker room and Caesars sportsbook.
### Q. Is there a Harrahs casino in St. Louis?
A.  Not anymore. Hollywood Casino in Maryland Heights was a Harrah’s until Penn bought it and renamed it Hollywood Casino in 2012. Today the metro’s Caesars casino is Horseshoe St. Louis downtown, alongside Hollywood, River City and Ameristar on the Missouri side, and DraftKings at Casino Queen and Argosy across the river in Illinois.
### Q. Is River City Casino worth visiting?
A.  It is the pick if you want a strong all-around floor without the downtown crowd: 1,600-plus slots, a baccarat room open 24 hours a day, a 200-room AAA Four Diamond hotel and a friendlier, less-touristy room. South-county players tend to make it their regular rather than a night out.

## 9 St. Louis Restaurants Locals Actually Love (Not the Chains)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-top-fast-food-spots-in-st-louis-a-2025-guide
Refreshed September 2026
Picture a Friday night when nobody at the table wants a drive-thru. Maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend around, or you’re just tired of the same three chains off the highway in Chesterfield, Kirkwood, or Florissant. You want somewhere that actually tastes like St. Louis — a place a local would send you, not a logo you could find in any city in America.
This is that list. A quick honesty note first: despite how it sometimes gets labeled, none of these are “fast food” in the drive-thru sense. They run the range from order-at-the-counter barbecue to sit-down, special-occasion kitchens — the common thread is that they’re independent, they’re beloved, and they’re the opposite of an interchangeable chain. Here are nine St. Louis spots worth going out of your way for.
### Nine St. Louis restaurants worth the drive
St. Louis’s most beloved local restaurants span every price point and craving: Pappy’s Smokehouse for Memphis-style barbecue, Hi-Pointe Drive-In and Stacked STL for standout burgers, The Frisco Barroom in Webster Groves for elevated tavern food, Havana’s Cuisine in the Central West End for a real Cuban sandwich, Menya Rui for Tokyo-style shoyu ramen, The Golden Hoosier for sandwiches with a side of taxidermy, and, when you want something more refined, Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood. Below is what to order at each.
### 1. Pappy’s Smokehouse
If you only eat at one place on this list, make it Pappy’s. This is the St. Louis barbecue institution — old-school, Memphis-style, and worth every minute of the line that regularly forms out the door. The dry-rubbed ribs are the headliner: smoked low and slow, tender without turning to mush, with that deep bark that tells you someone who cares was tending the pit.
Don’t stop at ribs, though. The brisket comes off moist and thinly sliced, the pulled pork is smoky and piled high, and the sides pull their weight — rich baked beans, sweet potato fries, and applesauce that tastes homemade. Go early; the most popular cuts sell out, and when the meat’s gone for the day, they close. It’s casual, family-friendly, and about as St. Louis as a plate of food gets.
### 2. Hi-Pointe Drive-In
Part burger joint, part retro movie set, Hi-Pointe Drive-In leans into a fun, nostalgic vibe — pop-culture touches everywhere and a menu built around genuinely excellent burgers. You can build your own or order one of the signature creations, and the staff are happy to walk a first-timer through it.
A few crowd favorites to point you in the right direction: the Frisco Melt, a rich, melty burger on sourdough; the Arch D-Lux, a stacked, bold-flavored classic; the Taco Burger for something crunchy and a little different; and the Cowboy Burger loaded with fixings. Add a thick shake — the flavors get creative — and you’ve got the whole experience. It’s a burger a step above the usual, in a room that makes you smile.
### 3. Stacked STL
Stacked STL is for the person who wants their burger built exactly their way. You pick the patty — beef, pork, turkey, or a beef-pork blend — then the bun (brioche, pretzel, gluten-free, or a lettuce wrap), the cheese, the sauces, and a genuinely long list of toppings. If decision fatigue sets in, there’s a lineup of a dozen signature burgers ready to go.
People rave about the juicy patties and the crispy fries, and the vibe is laid-back and friendly, with customer artwork on the walls. It gets busy at peak hours and parking can take a lap or two, but for a burger made precisely to your spec, that’s a small price. Not in the mood to go out? It’s an easy one to get delivered.
### 4. The Frisco Barroom
Over in Webster Groves, on Big Bend Boulevard near Webster University, The Frisco Barroom does elevated tavern food in a warm, rustic room — and its upstairs patio is one of the better places in the area to lose an afternoon. There are heaters up there, so it works well past the first cold snap, too.
Curious why a griddle patty beats a grilled one? This is what actually makes a good burger.
The kitchen keeps it fresh and consistent: the burgers get real praise (the double cheeseburger with horseradish cheese has a following), the salads are surprisingly good, and they turn out solid pierogies and kielbasa when you want something heartier. There’s a deep whiskey list with generous pours, and live music turns up now and then. It’s the kind of place you settle into for a few hours.

If you’re the one providing it, get listed. Run a restaurant in the St. Louis area? This is exactly how diners find you when they search “best local restaurants near me” or ask an AI assistant where to eat tonight. ### 5. Havana’s Cuisine
For a genuine Cuban sandwich — no trendy reinvention, just the classic done right — Havana’s Cuisine, now in the Central West End, is the answer. The sandwich is built the traditional way: quality ham, slow-roasted pork, Swiss, pickles, and yellow mustard, all pressed between bread imported from Tampa’s legendary La Segunda Bakery. They’ll even do the Tampa version with salami if that’s your style.
Beyond the sandwich, the menu sticks to satisfying Cuban classics rather than chasing food trends, and that focus is exactly the point. Sometimes you just want food that tastes the way it’s supposed to, made by people who care about getting the tradition right — and Havana’s delivers that in every bite.
### 6. Menya Rui
Menya Rui has earned a serious reputation for one thing done exceptionally well: Tokyo-style shoyu ramen. Rather than chase every ramen style at once, the kitchen focuses on a clear, soy-based broth built on real technique — savory, layered, and balanced — the kind of bowl that rewards a place that takes its time.
The details are where it shines: a perfectly cooked egg, tender meat, noodles with the right chew, and toppings arranged with obvious care. Add a starter or two and you’ve got a meal that feels considered rather than thrown together. It’s a standout example of St. Louis’s independent food scene — a specialist doing specialist work, and doing it right.
### 7. The Golden Hoosier
Sometimes you want a place that’s a little weird in the best way. The Golden Hoosier is a grill and cocktail bar whose walls are lined with taxidermy — equal parts charming and delightfully odd, and a fun way to show a visitor that St. Louis has more character than the tourist checklist suggests.
Random, but — ever actually looked at the Gate District?
The real draw is the food. The sandwiches are done right — a standout BLT dressed up with pesto aioli is a good place to start — and the cocktails hold their own. It doesn’t take itself too seriously, which is refreshing, and it lands as a reliable, memorable pick for a casual meal with a personality all its own.
### 8. Acero
When you want a meal that feels like an occasion, Acero in Maplewood is worth the reservation. This is upscale Italian, not fast food — a chef-driven kitchen that plates food as beautifully as it tastes, with bright colors and careful composition that make you want a photo before the first bite.
A dish like the Chicken Milanese shows the approach: a lightly floured chicken breast cooked so it stays juicy, served with Yukon potatoes and leeks in a caper sauce with just the right tang. The care shows in every element, main course to sides. It’s the kind of place that reminds you what a genuinely thoughtful, ingredient-first restaurant can do — a special-night spot rather than a quick bite.
### 9. Peppe’s Apt. 2
Rounding out the list, Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood offers something a little different — a curated, course-based dining experience that lets you choose your way through a multi-course meal. It’s a smart middle ground for anyone who likes a structured menu but still wants some say in what lands on the table.
The result is a chance to taste a variety of dishes in one sitting without the stiffness of a formal tasting menu. It leans more refined than a quick counter meal, and that’s the appeal: a memorable, slightly special evening in one of the metro’s most walkable downtowns. Pair it with a stroll around downtown Kirkwood and you’ve got a full night out.
### How to use this list
Notice how much ground these nine places cover: smoky barbecue and build-your-own burgers on one end, chef-driven Italian and a course-based Kirkwood dinner on the other, with Cuban sandwiches, ramen, and taxidermy-lined cocktails in between. That range is the point. St. Louis’s best eating isn’t concentrated in one neighborhood or one price bracket — it’s spread across the whole metro, from Webster Groves to Maplewood to the Central West End, waiting for anyone willing to look past the chains.
If you’re building your own rotation, mix it up: a casual counter night at Pappy’s or Hi-Pointe one week, a special-occasion dinner at Acero or Peppe’s the next, a ramen or Cuban-sandwich run when you want something specific and done well. And when you find your own favorite — the little independent spot that becomes your regular — that’s the real win. Those are the places that give a city its flavor, and the ones most worth supporting.
### Why local spots beat the chains
There’s a reason a list like this skips the drive-thrus. Independent restaurants are cooked by people making the food they know and love, for a community they’re part of — and that shows up on the plate in a way a corporate spec sheet never can. Every dollar you spend at one of them stays closer to home and keeps a real local business, and a real local family, going.
It’s also just better eating. The chains are engineered to be the same everywhere; these places are memorable precisely because they’re not. So the next time the easy move is the familiar logo off the highway, take the small detour instead. Your taste buds — and your neighbors running these kitchens — will thank you for it. And if you have a go-to that isn’t on this list, that’s the whole idea: St. Louis has far more great independent restaurants than any nine-spot roundup could hold, and the fun is in finding your own.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  A few things are close to mandatory: Memphis-style barbecue ribs at Pappy’s Smokehouse, a St. Louis-style burger at Hi-Pointe Drive-In or Stacked STL, and a genuine Cuban sandwich at Havana’s Cuisine on Tampa-imported La Segunda bread. Round it out with Tokyo-style shoyu ramen at Menya Rui. Between them you’ll taste why locals are so loyal to their independent spots.
### Q. Where do famous people eat in St. Louis?
A.  There’s no single celebrity hangout, but well-regarded, chef-driven rooms like Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood draw the special-occasion crowd, while institutions like Pappy’s Smokehouse pull everyone from families to visiting musicians — its walls are covered in photos of the bands who’ve stopped in. In St. Louis, the best tables are democratic; anyone can grab one.
### Q. What is Saint Louis famous for food?
A.  St. Louis is known for a distinctive local canon: thin-crust St. Louis-style pizza with Provel cheese, toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, and a strong barbecue tradition. But the everyday reality is a deep bench of independent restaurants — barbecue, burgers, ramen, Cuban, Italian, and more — spread across neighborhoods from the Central West End to Maplewood, Webster Groves, and Kirkwood.
### Q. What food is unique to St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, the St. Paul sandwich, frozen custard concretes, pork steaks, and cracker-crust pizza with Provel. Most of it came out of working neighborhoods rather than restaurant kitchens, which is why it is still best at corner places.
### Q. Where do locals eat in St. Louis?
A.  Neighborhood streets rather than destination districts — South Grand, Cherokee, The Hill, Delmar in the Loop. The pattern is that locals eat where parking is annoying and the room is small, which is usually a good sign about the kitchen.
### Q. What restaurants is St. Louis famous for?
A.  The city is better known for its dishes than for any single restaurant — toasted ravioli, Provel pizza, gooey butter cake, the St. Paul sandwich. Ask which place does one of those well and you will get a real answer; ask for the famous restaurant and you will get an argument.

## Sharks Took the Mall: What's Left to Buy at St. Louis Union Station
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-unique-finds-your-guide-to-st-louis-union-station-shopping
Sharks swim where the shops used to be. Remember the old Union Station mall: warm chocolate drifting under the train shed, a guy in an apron at the Fudgery singing while he worked a slab of fudge across the counter, a cart around every corner? Walk in today and the St. Louis Aquarium fills that old interior mall space, and the loudest sound is a kid gasping at the glass of the 250,000-gallon Shark Canyon.
This building has outlived two lives now, first as the busiest railroad terminal in the world, then as the mall. Life number three has fins. What’s left to buy fits in one breath: a plush shark from the Aquarium gift shop, fudge and a cupcake in a paper bag from Cookies and Cupcakes next door, and an over-the-top Freak Shake at the Soda Fountain that starts melting down the glass before you find the straw. No mall directory, no stand-alone candy store. And if you came for a train, you’re a few blocks off: Amtrak pulls into Gateway Station on South 15th Street. The only train boarding here now is the Polar Express ride at the holidays.
The best thing in the building was never for sale. Walk into the Grand Hall on the hour, any hour from 5pm to 10pm, tip your head back, and watch fireworks and deep-sea creatures pour across a gold-leaf ceiling 65 feet up in a free 3D light show. Check Union Station’s calendar first, because the hall sometimes closes for private events. Out on the lake, the Fire and Light Show shoots fire 25 feet into the air from eight lotus-shaped pods, also on the hour and also free, but it was paused for maintenance at our last check, so look before you promise the kids.
The $5 parking stamp most people miss. Park in the South Lot (enter from Market Street on 18th or 20th). If you do the Aquarium, take your lot ticket to the gift shop at the Aquarium’s exit, by the photo counter, and get it stamped: the lot then charges a $5 flat rate when you leave. Without the stamp, hourly and event rates apply. The lots are credit card only, and the Aquarium itself is cashless.
Two rules that surprise people. After 3pm every day, anyone 16 or younger on the property needs a parent or supervising adult 21 or older, and that adult needs an ID. And yes, you can sleep next to the sharks: the Union Station Hotel built rooms that look into the aquarium, which the Aquarium says no other aquarium in the country offers. The Aquarium itself is open Sunday through Thursday 9am to 5pm and until 6pm on Friday and Saturday, with last entry 45 minutes before close.
### So where did all the stores go?
No - the traditional shopping mall at Union Station is gone. The festival marketplace with its dozens of stores, the place half of St. Louis remembers by the smell of fudge, emptied out as shopping moved elsewhere. In a fitting twist, the St. Louis Aquarium literally took over the old interior mall space when Union Station was redeveloped into an entertainment destination. So if you’re picturing a day of retail browsing, that’s not what Union Station offers anymore.
What replaced it is, for most kids, a lot more fun: an aquarium, a 200-foot observation wheel with climate-controlled gondolas, a ropes course, mini golf, a mirror maze, nightly light and fire shows, a slate of restaurants and a restored historic hotel. Listen on a Saturday and you can hear the change: squeals from the ropes course, the clink of sundae spoons at the Soda Fountain, the hush in front of the shark glass. The shopping today is the gift-shop-and-treats kind, an add-on to a day of attractions rather than the main event.
### What shopping and gifts you’ll find at Union Station today
Think gift shop and sweets counter, not department store. You’ll smell the sugar at Cookies and Cupcakes before you see the case, and the plush sharks are stacked where small hands can reach them. Here’s all of it:
The St. Louis Aquarium gift shop - the biggest “store” at Union Station, packed with plush sharks and otters, toys, apparel, and souvenirs. It sits at the Aquarium’s exit, by the photo counter, and it’s the go-to for a kid’s keepsake.
Cookies and Cupcakes - a bakery counter next to the Aquarium gift shop with cupcakes, cookies, fudge and coffee to go; you’ll smell the sugar before you see the case.
The Soda Fountain - part restaurant, part sweets stop, famous for over-the-top “Freak Shakes,” sundaes and old-fashioned sodas.
Attraction shops and kiosks - small gift and photo stands tied to the Wheel and the other attractions, good for souvenirs and mementos.
Grab a gift or a sweet on your way through, a little paper bag of fudge going soft in your hand by the time you reach the car, and you’re covered.
Looking for a keepsake? The best Union Station souvenirs skew local and kid-friendly: a plush shark or otter from the aquarium shop, a St. Louis Wheel photo, gooey-butter-flavored treats, or fudge from Cookies and Cupcakes. It’s enough to satisfy the “can we get something?” request without a full shopping trip - and the aquarium store in particular is roomy and genuinely fun to browse.
### Stores at St. Louis Union Station: then vs. now
Here’s the map you still carry in your head, next to what stands in those spots now. Every name in the right-hand column is on Union Station’s own map today.
Looking for a candy store? There isn’t a stand-alone one anymore. Your sweet stops are Cookies and Cupcakes for fudge and a cupcake to go, and the Soda Fountain for a Freak Shake or a sundae you eat on the spot. Both sit inside the building, so you can grab one between the sharks and the Wheel.
And yes, Union Station is still open and busy every day. The Grand Hall and the plaza cost nothing to walk through. Each attraction and restaurant keeps its own hours, and several outdoor rides are seasonal, so check the hours on Union Station’s site the morning you go.
### What happened to the Union Station mall?
The story is a St. Louis landmark’s reinvention. Union Station opened in 1894 as the largest and busiest railroad terminal in the world, serving 22 railroads beneath its jaw-dropping Grand Hall. As passenger rail faded, the last train pulled out in 1978, and the station sat looking for a purpose.
In 1985 it reopened as a festival marketplace mall - the era most St. Louisans remember, full of shops and restaurants. That format thrived for a while, then slowly declined as retail changed, until the stores emptied out. Rather than let a National Historic Landmark fade, developers reimagined it: beginning around 2018–2019, Union Station was redeveloped into a family entertainment and hospitality destination, anchored by the new St. Louis Aquarium (opened Christmas Day 2019) and the St. Louis Wheel. The Grand Hall became the centerpiece for a spectacular free 3D light show. The building was saved - just with a new job.
It’s a history worth soaking in while you’re there. Soldiers shipping off to war, families bound for the West, dignitaries, everyday St. Louisans on an ordinary errand: all of them passed beneath that Grand Hall ceiling. Stand in the same room today, now full of kids on their way to see sharks, and you catch an only-in-St.-Louis moment.
### What Union Station is now - the real reason to visit
Come for a full day, not a shopping trip, and Union Station shines. Under one roof (and one lakefront plaza) you’ll find:
The St. Louis Aquarium - six galleries including the 250,000-gallon Shark Canyon.
The St. Louis Wheel - a 200-foot observation wheel with enclosed, climate-controlled gondolas.
A ropes course, mirror maze and Selfie Express indoors, plus mini golf, a carousel and seasonal rides like the Wave Swinger outside, great for mixed-age groups.
The free Fire & Light Show on the lake and the free 3D light show in the Grand Hall - two of the best no-cost experiences in the city.
Restaurants and the Soda Fountain, plus the landmark St. Louis Union Station Hotel, part of Hilton’s Curio Collection.
For the full rundown, see our guides to planning your St. Louis Aquarium visit and everything there is to do at Union Station.
Union Station is also a year-round calendar of its own. The holidays bring the Polar Express Train Ride and festive lights, summer adds outdoor rides and lakeside food stands, and the free Fire & Light Show runs nightly whatever the season. It’s worth checking the events calendar before you go - there’s often something special layered on top of the regular attractions, and plenty of it is free to enjoy.

### Where to eat at Union Station
Miss the old food court? The dining lineup today runs from sit-down rooms to grab-and-go counters:
The Train Shed - American plates, shareables, and cocktails under the historic train-shed canopy.
The Soda Fountain - retro diner fare and those famous Freak Shakes.
Station Grille - breakfast and lunch in the beautifully restored Fred Harvey restaurant space.
Landry’s Seafood House - Gulf Coast seafood with boardwalk seating on the lake.
The Grand Hall - dinner and drinks beneath the 65-foot archways, one of the most striking rooms in St. Louis.
The Pitch Athletic Club & Tavern and Cookies and Cupcakes, plus seasonal outdoor stands.

Even if you buy nothing and ride nothing, walk into the Grand Hall and look up. Designed by architect Theodore Link and opened in 1894, its Romanesque, barrel-vaulted ceiling soars 65 feet, dressed in gold leaf, mosaic, and stained glass - a genuine cathedral of the railroad age. Each night it becomes the canvas for a free 3D light show of more than 30 video vignettes projected across the ceiling. The room also carries real history: the on-site Station Grille occupies the restored space of the original Fred Harvey restaurant, part of the legendary “Harvey Girls” era of railroad dining. It’s the best free thing to do at Union Station, no ticket required.

### Sweet St. Louis: treats worth taking home
If your idea of “shopping” leans delicious, St. Louis delivers. The Soda Fountain at Union Station is the spot for sundaes, old-fashioned sodas, and those famous shakes - a sweet souvenir you eat on the way out. And it fits the city’s legacy: St. Louis has a genuinely sweet history, from gooey butter cake (the beloved local specialty) to the ice cream cone, famously popularized at the 1904 World’s Fair right here in town. Grab a treat at Union Station, and you’re part of a long St. Louis tradition.
### Stay the night: the Union Station Hotel
You can also sleep inside the landmark. The St. Louis Union Station Hotel, part of Hilton’s Curio Collection, occupies the historic head house, with the breathtaking Grand Hall serving as its lobby bar and lounge. It blends the grandeur of the railroading age - original architecture, soaring ceilings, old-world detail - with modern rooms and amenities. For a special-occasion stay or an easy base for a downtown weekend, waking up steps from the aquarium, the Wheel, and the nightly light shows is hard to beat. (Aquarium members even get a discount on rooms.)
### Making a trip of it
The move is to treat Union Station as a half- or full-day outing. Arrive mid-morning, do the aquarium, browse the gift shop, grab lunch and a Freak Shake, ride the Wheel toward sunset, and stay for the free Fire & Light Show after dark. A few tips to make it smooth:
Bundle your tickets - combo passes cover the aquarium, the Wheel, and the rides for less than buying separately.
Validate parking if you visit the aquarium: take your lot ticket to the Aquarium gift shop for the $5 flat rate before you leave (the lots are credit card only).
Time the free shows - check the daily schedule for the Fire & Light Show and Grand Hall light show so you don’t miss them.
Go by MetroLink if downtown parking isn’t your thing - the Union Station stop is a short walk away.
Union Station is at 1820 Market Street, right in the heart of downtown - close to the Gateway Arch, Ballpark Village, and the rest of a St. Louis weekend.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is there still a mall at Union Station in St. Louis?
A.  No. The old festival-marketplace mall closed, and the St. Louis Aquarium was built into the former interior mall space when Union Station was redeveloped. Today Union Station is a family entertainment and dining destination, and the shopping is limited to the Aquarium gift shop and sweet stops like Cookies and Cupcakes and the Soda Fountain.
### Q. What’s inside St. Louis Union Station?
A.  Union Station holds the St. Louis Aquarium, the 200-foot St. Louis Wheel, a ropes course, a mirror maze, Selfie Express, mini golf and a carousel, plus restaurants, the Soda Fountain, the Aquarium gift shop, and the landmark St. Louis Union Station Hotel (Curio Collection by Hilton). It’s also home to a free nightly Fire & Light Show and a 3D light show in the historic Grand Hall.
### Q. What restaurants are in Union Station in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  The sit-down choices are The Train Shed, The Pitch Athletic Club & Tavern, the Soda Fountain, Station Grille for breakfast and lunch, Landry’s Seafood House on the lake, and the Grand Hall for evening drinks under the 65-foot ceiling. Cookies and Cupcakes covers a quick sweet, and seasonal stands like the Taco Container and Fairground Eats open on the plaza.
### Q. Is Union Station still open in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Union Station is open every day as a family attraction, dining and hotel complex, even though the mall and the passenger trains are long gone. The Grand Hall and the plaza are free to walk, while the aquarium, the Wheel, the rides and each restaurant keep their own hours, and some outdoor rides are seasonal, so check the hours before you go.
### Q. Is St. Louis Union Station still a train station?
A.  Not for regular passenger trains. The last one left in 1978. Amtrak now stops at Gateway Station, 430 South 15th Street, a few blocks east, and MetroLink’s Union Station stop is a short walk from the entrance. The only train you’ll ride at Union Station itself is the seasonal Polar Express Train Ride at the holidays.
### Q. Is Union Station in St. Louis worth visiting?
A.  Yes, especially for families and visitors. Just come for the attractions, dining, and free light shows rather than shopping. Between the aquarium, the St. Louis Wheel, the rides, the historic Grand Hall, and the nightly Fire & Light Show, it’s an easy half- or full-day out. The building itself, a restored 1894 landmark, is worth seeing on its own.

### 6. Deep Tissue Massage
Stubborn knots and aches that will not quit call for something firmer. Deep tissue massage reaches the deeper layers of muscle and connective tissue. Therapists use slower strokes and heavier pressure, zeroing in on the specific spots that give you trouble.
This type of massage is particularly effective for chronic muscle tension and pain. It can help break up scar tissue that forms after an injury and can also reduce inflammation. If you've been dealing with back pain, stiff shoulders, or leg tightness, a deep tissue session could offer some serious relief.
Here's what you can generally expect:
Targeted Pressure: The therapist will use their fingers, thumbs, elbows, and forearms to apply firm pressure.
Slower Pace: Strokes are typically slower than in a Swedish massage, allowing the therapist to work out deeper tension.
Focus Areas: Sessions often concentrate on areas where you're experiencing the most discomfort or tightness.
It's important to communicate with your therapist during the session. While some discomfort is normal as the muscles release, it shouldn't be unbearable. Staying hydrated afterward is also key to helping your body flush out any toxins released during the massage.
Many spas in St. Louis offer this service, and it's a great option if you're looking for more intense therapeutic work. You can often find deep tissue massage services listed alongside other massage types on spa websites.
### 7. Swedish Massage
Therapy and Wellness Massage
Swedish massage is probably what most people think of when they hear the word “massage.” It's a really popular choice for a reason. This type of massage focuses on relaxation and easing muscle tension using long, flowing strokes, kneading, circular movements, and tapping. The primary goal of a Swedish massage is to promote relaxation and improve circulation.
Here's what you can typically expect during a session:

Vibration: Shaking or trembling movements that help to relax muscles and relieve pain.

## Crackling Fish, Tingling Lips: Cate Zone in University City Is Not Sichuan
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cate-zone-stl-your-guide-to-authentic-chinese-cuisine-in-st-louis
The hot crisp fish lands still crackling, and two bites in, the Sichuan peppercorn starts its slow, tingling hum across your lips. Somebody reaches for the guo bao rou, pork cutlets fried until they shatter, in a light sauce snapped with ginger. The dumplings come next, thick-skinned, folded by hand in the kitchen.
That’s a weeknight at Cate Zone Chinese Cafe, 8148 Olive Boulevard in University City, and despite what half the listings say, it isn’t a Sichuan restaurant. The kitchen cooks Dongbei food, the hearty pickle-and-pork cooking of China’s far northeast, on the stretch of Olive that became St. Louis’s second Chinatown. A roomier sibling opened in Chesterfield’s Four Seasons Shopping Center in February 2024, and both kitchens close on Mondays.
Second Chinatown? Here’s the St. Louis secret. The first one, Hop Alley, filled the downtown blocks between Seventh and Eighth streets from Walnut to Market, and by 1914 more than a dozen Chinese grocers there sold dried shrimp and noodles you couldn’t buy anywhere else in town. It was cleared in the 1960s to make way for Busch Stadium. By the 1990s the cooks had regrouped out here, along Olive near I-170, as Feast Magazine traced with the Missouri Historical Society. That’s why the city’s most talked-about Chinese kitchens sit in suburban strip centers: St. Louis traded its Chinatown for a ballpark. Send that to the friend who swears the city never had one.
Don’t show up on Olive at 3:30. The University City kitchen closes from 2:30 to 5 every day it’s open, then comes back for dinner with a separate skewers menu; call (314) 738-9923 if you’re unsure. Craving it mid-afternoon? Chesterfield runs straight through, 11 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. Sunday and Tuesday through Thursday and until 9 on Fridays and Saturdays, at (314) 392-9624.
Save two names to your phone and point at them: 老式锅包肉, the guo bao rou the menu itself calls “traditional,” glazed in sweet soy instead of the bright-orange sauce, and 东北杀猪菜, the sour cabbage and pork belly the northeast named the “pig-killing dish” after the winter slaughter feasts it was cooked for. The table next to you will ask what you ordered. And if you can only get one dish, make it the hot crisp fish, $19.99, the plate the Riverfront Times singled out.
Most plates run $17 to $22. For two people, three plates and the handmade dumplings is plenty, served family-style: three of the $19.99 plates and the $17.99 dumplings come to about $78 before tax and tip, with leftovers. There’s strip-center parking right out front.
### At a Glance: What to Order
### What Cate Zone Actually Is
This is Northeastern Chinese food - a point of confusion worth clearing up, because plenty of listings mislabel it as Sichuan. It isn’t. Dongbei cooking is heartier and homier than the mouth-numbing spice most Americans associate with Sichuan, and the menu here first attracted notice for that Northeastern focus, even if it also reaches into other regions with dishes like Yangzhou fried rice and spicy Chengdu chicken.
The restaurant is owned by Daniel Ma and Quincy Lin, and it has quietly become one of St. Louis’s most respected authentic Chinese kitchens - a longtime pick on Ian Froeb’s STL 100 list of the region’s best restaurants (named in 2018, 2019, 2020, and 2023), and the subject of a glowing Riverfront Times review that singled out its hot crisp fish as the dish it’s best known for. It’s the kind of unassuming strip-mall spot that food-obsessed St. Louisans send their out-of-town friends to.
The storefront is modest, and that’s the point. There are no trend dishes and nothing plated for a photo. The kitchen cooks the food of one specific place, and that single-region commitment is why the dishes carry such a clear point of view: sour cabbage you can smell from the next table, cumin lamb that leaves your fingers fragrant, a sweet and sour pork that tastes nothing like the takeout version.
### What to Order at Cate Zone
Start with the hot crisp fish - the dish Cate Zone is best known for, lightly battered and fried with a Sichuan-pepper kick that sneaks up on you. The guo bao rou (sweet and sour pork) is the Northeastern version done right: crisp pork cutlets in a light, ginger-snapped sauce, nothing like the neon takeout goo you’re picturing. The housemade dumplings are a must - hand-folded in-house, thick-skinned and satisfying, and a specialty the second location leaned into even harder.
From there, don’t skip the sour cabbage with pork belly, a true Dongbei signature where fermented cabbage and fatty pork stew into something warming and a little tangy, and the cumin lamb, fragrant with toasted cumin, a little heat, and fresh cilantro. If your table is adventurous, ask what’s good that day - the kitchen’s homestyle Northeastern dishes are where it shines. Everything is meant to be shared family-style, so bring people and order across the menu; portions are generous and half the fun is passing plates around.
### A quick primer on Northeastern (Dongbei) Chinese food
If “Dongbei” is new to you, here’s the short version. Dongbei means China’s northeast: the provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning, up against the Russian and North Korean borders. It’s a cold-winter region with a short growing season, so the cooking leans on preserved and pickled vegetables, wheat as much as rice, and pork as the favorite meat. The result is hearty, savory, generous food built on a few bold flavors rather than delicate ones.
The region’s history shows up on the plate: Dongbei cooking carries influences from neighboring Russian, Mongolian, and Korean kitchens, and it grew out of the older Shandong and Manchu traditions. Cold-weather staples (wheat-flour breads and dumplings, crocks of fermented cabbage, big braises) make sense the moment you picture the winters they were built for.
A few dishes tell the whole story. Guo bao rou, crispy fried pork in a bright sweet-and-sour sauce, is the Northeastern original that the gloopy American-Chinese “sweet and sour pork” was loosely descended from; tasting the real one is a small revelation. Suan cai, fermented sour cabbage, gets stewed with fatty pork belly into something deeply comforting. Di san xian braises potato, eggplant, and green pepper into a savory, glossy classic. And dumplings, thick-skinned, pan-fried or boiled, are the heart of the table, often served with chilled noodles alongside. Compared with fiery Sichuan or light, seafood-forward Cantonese cooking, Dongbei food is the rustic, warming, pickle-and-pork cousin. Skip the shock-and-awe spice. This is deep, satisfying, cold-night flavor.
Nothing to do with dumplings - but here’s Shaw, block by block.
### Before You Go: Hours & Tips
Cate Zone Chinese Cafe is at 8148 Olive Blvd in University City; the phone is (314) 738-9923. It’s closed on Mondays, and it runs a mid-afternoon break, with lunch and dinner service the rest of the week - so if you’re coming mid-afternoon, call first (the kitchen closes from 2:30 to 5 p.m. between services). It’s a small, popular room, so expect a wait at peak times and consider going a little early or a little late. Takeout is a solid option if the dining room is full, and there’s plenty of strip-center parking right out front. Cash and card are both fine, and the prices are gentle for how much food you get - this is a place where a table can eat well without spending much.
### There are now two Cate Zones
Cate Zone got popular enough to expand. In February 2024, the owners opened a second, larger location in the western suburbs - Cate Zone Chinese Cuisine, at 24 Four Seasons Shopping Center in Chesterfield - with a bigger, more modern dining room and a real focus on those handmade dumplings. The University City original (branded “Cate Zone Chinese Cafe”) is still the cozy, no-frills flagship; the Chesterfield spot (“Cate Zone Chinese Cuisine”) is the sit-down version for the west county crowd. If you’re out toward Chesterfield, you don’t have to drive to Olive to get the food.
Which should you pick? If you want the original strip-mall room - and a reason to explore the Olive corridor afterward - go to University City. If you’re bringing a bigger group, want a roomier table and a proper dining room, or you simply live out west, Chesterfield is the easier call. Either way you’re getting the same Northeastern roots and the same handmade dumplings; the difference is the setting, not the cooking.
### Make a day of it on Olive Boulevard
Cate Zone sits in the middle of something bigger. The stretch of Olive Boulevard through University City - roughly from I-170 west to Midland - is St. Louis’s de facto Asian food and grocery district, often called the city’s “unofficial Chinatown.” It grew into that role after St. Louis’s original downtown Chinatown, Hop Alley, was demolished in the mid-1960s to make way for Busch Memorial Stadium; by the 1990s, Olive had become the new hub.
That means a meal at Cate Zone can anchor a whole afternoon of eating and shopping, and it’s one of many reasons University City is worth a dedicated dining trip. Within a few blocks you’ll find Lu Lu Seafood & Dim Sum and Soup Dumplings STL for the dumpling-and-dim-sum crowd, Wonton King and Royal Chinese BBQ for Cantonese roast meats and duck, Tang Palace for Shanghai fare and hot pot, ChiliSpot for Sichuan heat, and bubble-tea cafes scattered between them. When you’re ready to cook at home, a full-size Asian grocery like Olive Supermarket stocks the sauces, noodles, and produce you won’t find at a regular store. It’s one of the most rewarding food corridors in the metro - and Cate Zone is one of the best reasons to start exploring it.
If the tingle of Sichuan has you curious about the rest of Asia’s table, here’s what to order when you find Malaysian food in St. Louis.

There’s something worth appreciating in that, too. A neighborhood that lost its original Chinatown to a stadium parking lot rebuilt an even bigger one a few miles west, one family restaurant and grocery at a time. So eating your way down Olive does double duty. You get a great afternoon, and you help the immigrant families who made this corridor what it is.

## A 1960s Camper on Highway P Pours Wentzville’s Best Coffee
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-coffee-shops-in-wentzville-mo-your-local-guide
“Sips of Sunshine.” That’s what Faith McDonald wanted to call her coffee camper. Then she and her dad drove to Maryland to pick up a 1960s Nomad trailer that came already painted with another name, Flower Coffee Collective, and the paint won. She was 19, and she tested about 1,200 drinks before she opened.
Pull up to 5020 Highway P at 6 on a weekday morning and the espresso machine is already hissing inside that little trailer. Her own favorite at launch, the Golden Hour Latte, is white chocolate mocha under a salted-caramel drizzle and vanilla cold foam, sweet enough to count as breakfast. Take it to an outdoor table or drive off with it. The camper opens at 6 on weekdays and 7 on Saturdays, and it’s closed Sundays.
Here’s the part to tell whoever’s riding shotgun: Wentzville ran on tobacco long before it ran on coffee. The city’s own history counts seven tobacco plants in the area at one time, says many of the men behind them became millionaires, and says one, Caleb Dula, went on to become the first president of Liggett & Myers. Tobacco money built the town; now the coffee at the top of this list comes out of a camper a 19-year-old found in Maryland. Screenshot that one. The town is closing in on 50,000 people, and the fuel is espresso, because so much of life here happens in the car: the commute east on I-70, a shift at the GM plant, the ballfields on Saturday.
So sort it by the morning you’re having:
The camper, for the story. Flower Coffee Collective’s window on Highway P: 6 a.m. to 4:30 weekdays, 7 to 4:30 Saturdays, closed Sundays.
Ellbee’s General Store, for sitting. The room smells like fresh coffee, and the shelves are lined with old-fashioned candy. 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., until 8 Thursday through Saturday from June to September, closed Sundays, and next door there’s a nine-hole mini golf course, Downtown 9, Wednesday through Saturday, 10 to 4. Coffee, then a putter. On the second Saturday of each month, April through November, Ellbee’s throws a free makers market from 9 to 1.
7 Brew, for speed. The cup comes through the drive-thru window already sweating into your palm, from 5:30 a.m., and still pouring until 10 p.m., 11 on Fridays and Saturdays, when everything else has gone dark.
Long Row Lavender in Wright City, for a whole Saturday. The café runs Wednesday through Saturday, 10 to 4, March to mid-December, so a lavender latte is off the table in January and February. Its 1,000 lavender plants bloom in June, by the farm’s own account; go then and the air smells like a sachet before you’re out of the car. Every spring the family replants the lavender that didn’t survive the Missouri winter, so the purple you see was earned.

### Which independent shops stand out?
Start with the one you’ll tell people about. At Flower Coffee Collective you can drive up to the camper window or park and sit outside, and the homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes have a real following. At launch the beans came from Electric Fountain Brewing, up the river in Quincy, Illinois. Call (636) 290-6481 if the weather looks rough; a trailer is a trailer.
Heading into the city instead? Our metro guide covers how to pick a St. Louis coffee shop by neighborhood and errand.
Downtown on Main Street, Ellbee’s General Store is the sit-down-and-linger pick. Part old-fashioned general store, part café, it does espresso drinks, frappes, milkshakes, and ice cream alongside candy and sandwiches - the stop where you actually stay a while, a frappe sweating on the table, instead of grabbing and running. Between the two, the camper is for the drive and Ellbee’s is for the chair.
At Ellbee’s the milkshake blender whirs behind the counter while somebody at the register buys candy for the drive home. Order a frappe and a sandwich and take a table; this is the stop built for staying. If you only have time for one independent, make it the camper. Locals rotate through both.
### Where are the reliable drive-thrus?
Sometimes you just need caffeine, fast. 7 Brew Coffee on Wentzville Parkway is the fast one, a drive-thru-only stand known for fast, customizable orders, infused energy drinks, Italian sodas, and shakes, open early morning to late at night, which matters in a metro where only a handful of coffee shops stay open late. The newest option, Ziggi’s Coffee (which opened off I-70 in early 2026), splits the difference: it’s a full cafe and a drive-thru with WiFi, handcrafted espresso, and the trendy “dirty soda” drinks, so you can grab and go or come in and sit. And there’s the dependable Starbucks on Wentzville Parkway (drive-thru plus seating), with a second grab-and-go kiosk inside the Target. None of these will surprise you - that’s exactly the point on a rushed morning.
The drive-thru stands earn their place here because the morning happens in the car: a GM shift change, a school drop-off, a ballfield at 8. Order ahead in the app where you can, and the line on Wentzville Parkway stops mattering.
Nothing to do with coffee - but Clifton Heights is worth a Saturday.
### Do you want a drive-thru or a sit-and-work room?
Pure drive-thru speed: 7 Brew. Drive-thru or a table with WiFi: Ziggi’s or the Wentzville Parkway Starbucks. Grab-and-go kiosk: the Starbucks inside Target. The quirky, sit-outside camper: Flower Coffee Collective. Sit down and stay a while: Ellbee’s General Store downtown. Match the spot to your morning and you’re never stuck. Two minutes to spare or a whole lazy Saturday, there’s a right answer either way.
### Is Long Row Lavender worth the short drive?
Just up the road in Wright City - near Wentzville, not in it - Long Row Lavender is a destination lavender farm with a real café and coffee bar. The signature draw is the lavender latte, and the farm serves coffee, desserts, and a light lunch on a pretty patio, generally Wednesday through Saturday. It’s less a quick-coffee run than a little outing - a lovely way to turn a morning coffee into a half-day escape when the weather’s nice. Wander the lavender rows, grab a latte and a dessert on the patio, and you’ve got the makings of a genuinely pleasant Saturday that just happens to start with coffee. Just check the days and hours before you go, since the farm keeps a limited, seasonal schedule rather than café hours.
### From seven tobacco plants to a coffee camper
It’s no accident Wentzville’s coffee scene keeps expanding. The town was founded in 1855 beside a new railroad and named for Erasmus Livingston Wentz, the New York man who supervised building the line, and for decades its money came from tobacco. The city has been one of the fastest-growing in Missouri for two decades - its population has ballooned to nearly 50,000 by the Census Bureau’s latest estimate, a jump of several hundred percent since 2000 - and all those new neighbors mean new cafes keep opening to serve them, alongside the other shops and services in our Wentzville city guide. What was once a small crossroads town now has everything from a vintage coffee camper to a brand-new franchise cafe, and the options only keep improving. For a suburb its size, that’s a genuinely good coffee map.
It also reflects a broader shift in how a fast-growing town builds its identity. Coffee shops are often the first “third places” a booming suburb gets - somewhere that isn’t home or work where neighbors actually run into each other. As Wentzville has filled in, the independents like Flower Coffee Collective and Ellbee’s have quietly become community anchors, the kind of small businesses that give a growing place its character. Supporting them is part of how a suburb keeps a little soul as it scales, and it’s a big reason a “best coffee in Wentzville” list is worth keeping current.

### Which One Should You Try First?
New to Wentzville coffee? Start with the camper. Flower Coffee Collective hands you the story and the best local cup in one stop. When you’d rather sit, sip, and soak up some downtown charm, Ellbee’s General Store is the one. Running late is exactly what 7 Brew and the Wentzville Parkway Starbucks are for. Need room to work at the newest spot in town? That’s Ziggi’s. Save Long Row Lavender in Wright City for a free morning with nice weather - a lavender latte on the farm is its own small event. Work through all five and you’ll have tasted everything the area does well, from vintage-camper charm to a lightning-fast drive-thru window.
### How do you make a morning of it?
Coffee in Wentzville pairs naturally with the rest of a laid-back suburban morning. Grab a cup from the camper and walk it over to one of the parks - Rotary Park and the Quail Ridge area give you trails and green space to sip and stroll. Downtown around Main Street, an Ellbee’s coffee goes hand-in-hand with browsing the little shops, and if the morning stretches toward lunch, our guide to where to eat in Wentzville picks up right where the coffee leaves off. And if you’re headed out to the wine country or the Katy Trail for the day, a drive-thru on Wentzville Parkway is the logical fuel stop on the way out of town. Good coffee here is where the good Saturday starts.
One more practical tip: hours vary a lot between the fast drive-thrus (open early to late) and the sit-down spots (which keep more limited, daytime hours, and the lavender farm is only open a few days a week). A quick check before you drive out saves a disappointing locked door, especially for the destination spots.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is there a coffee shop in a camper in Wentzville?
A.  Yes - Flower Coffee Collective serves espresso and specialty drinks out of a restored 1960s Nomad camper trailer, with outdoor tables where you can sit. It pours beans from a small roaster and is known for homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes. It’s the most distinctive, only-in-Wentzville coffee stop in town. Find it at 5020 Highway P, open from 6 a.m. weekdays and 7 a.m. Saturdays until 4:30 p.m., closed Sundays.
### Q. Where can I find the best coffee in St. Charles County?
A.  Wentzville, St. Charles, O’Fallon and St. Peters each have independents worth a stop, and the county is spread out enough that drive time usually decides it for you. Rather than chase one county-wide winner, work out whether you want a fast window, a table for an hour, or a weekend destination, then pick the closest shop that does that one thing well.
### Q. Which coffee shop has the best WiFi?
A.  The shops that mean it advertise it - outlets along the wall, tables sized for one, and staff who do not mind a second refill. The tell for the opposite is a room of tall stools and a queue at nine. If working is the point of the trip, call ahead and ask whether laptops are welcome at the hour you plan to arrive; most places will tell you plainly.
### Q. Do coffee shops have secure WiFi?
A.  Treat every shop network as open, because most are. That is fine for ordinary browsing and a bad idea for banking or anything you would not want read over your shoulder. Use your phone’s hotspot or a VPN for anything sensitive, avoid saving the network, and log out of accounts when you pack up.
### Q. Why are coffee shops closing early?
A.  Afternoon trade in a commuter town is thin and staffing it is expensive, so a lot of independents now run a strong morning and shut mid-afternoon rather than pay for quiet hours. Hours also move with the season and with staffing, which is why any list of times goes stale fast. Check the shop’s own page the morning you go.

## Takumi Fairview Heights: Leave a Piece, Pay 50 Cents
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-delicious-dishes-at-tasty-bowl-fairview-heights-il
Two pieces of Hot Mess Roll sit on the plate, still crackling from the fryer, eel sauce gone sticky, jalapeño heat still in your mouth. You are full. Nobody at the table can face them. And at this restaurant, those two pieces just cost you a dollar.
That is the line printed at the top of the menu, and it changes how hungry you think you are: uneaten items are charged at $0.50 a piece, and nothing on the all-you-can-eat menu leaves in a to-go box. So you learn to play it the way the BND advises. Tap a small round into the tablet at your table - a couple of salmon nigiri, a Sweetheart Roll in its pink soy paper, a plate of takoyaki - and tap in the next round before the last one is gone.
This is Takumi All In One Eatery, at 51 Lincoln Hwy in Fairview Heights, Illinois. If you knew this storefront as Tasty Bowl, the place we once wrote up for its robot-cooked stir-fry, that restaurant now goes by Takumi. It closed for a remodel, the row of automated stir-fry cookers came out, and owner Sean Lin told the Belleville News-Democrat he was switching to an all-you-can-eat sushi concept. The phone number is the same: (618) 206-6123. Almost everything else is new, including the rules, and the rules are where a first visit gets expensive.
So here is the short version before anything else. An adult pays $17.95 for weekday lunch and $27.95 for weekday dinner or any time on a weekend. The catch most people miss is that the sushi and sashimi, the sushi appetizers and a handful of other items are dinner only. Walk in at 1 p.m. on a weekday expecting a sashimi spree and you will be ordering fried rice, lo mein and maki rolls instead. The $10 jump to dinner is what buys the raw fish.
### What kind of food does Tasty Bowl in Fairview Heights serve?
Nothing under that name now: the restaurant formerly known as Tasty Bowl reopened as Takumi. As Tasty Bowl, it sold made-to-order sushi and sashimi, ramen and build-your-own stir-fry bowls cooked in a row of automated stir-fry cookers. Lin told the BND the business was switching concepts because of the challenge of competing with similar stir-fry and sushi places, and in its place at the same address is Takumi, an all-you-can-eat restaurant that is mostly Japanese, with Chinese, Thai and Vietnamese dishes on the same menu.
That menu runs two long pages, bold red headings on black, and it reads like a dare. Start with something hot to hold: miso, mushroom or wonton soup. Something cold and briny: seaweed salad, spicy kani salad. Then the crunch: crab rangoon, gyoza, sweet potato tempura, Japanese popcorn chicken, a fried bun. Sesame chicken and General Tso’s. Soupy dumplings and crystal shrimp dumplings from the dim sum list. Beef pho. Pad thai. Hibachi chicken or shrimp or salmon. Skewers of yakitori. Then the rolls, dozens of them, and a dessert list that ends with fried Oreos and green tea ice cream.
The BND reported that everything is made to order, so a round can take a few minutes to land. The paper’s advice is to place the next order before you finish the one in front of you. Manager Feng Pan also said the menu is in a testing phase and will be adjusted as they learn what people like, so treat any single item as here-for-now.
### How does all-you-can-eat sushi work at Takumi?
You sit down, the tablet glows at the edge of the table, and you pay one price per person no matter how many rounds you order from it or from your server. That is the whole system, and it sounds simple until you see how the details stack up. Here is how to get the most out of it without a surprise on the bill.
First, choose your time. Lunch runs 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday and costs an adult $17.95. Dinner starts at 4 p.m. on weekdays, and on Saturday and Sunday the dinner menu runs all day, both at $27.95. If cool, soft salmon over rice is the reason you are coming, come at dinner or on a weekend. Nigiri, sashimi, the sushi appetizers like Tuna Tataki and Yellowtail Jalapeño, the steak and scallop hibachi and several special rolls are dinner only. If you mostly want rolls, fried appetizers, noodles and dumplings, weekday lunch is the cheaper seat.
Second, order small and often. The menu itself asks guests to order responsibly, and it means it: uneaten items are charged at $0.50 a piece. Ten forgotten pieces of a roll you over-ordered is another five dollars on the check. The rhythm that works is a few items per person, eat them, then tap in the next round while the last couple of pieces are still on the plate. You lose nothing by ordering twice. You can lose a lot by ordering once, big.
Third, plan to finish it there. The all-you-can-eat menu is dine-in only, and leftover items can’t be packed to go. If you want sushi to take home, Takumi’s website has an online ordering link, and that is a separate thing from the buffet price.
Fourth, bring the kids, but know the price chart. Children under 3 eat free at every meal. Ages 3 to 8 pay $10.95 at lunch and $13.95 at dinner, and ages 9 to 12 pay $12.95 at lunch and $17.95 at dinner. Call (618) 206-6123 if you want to confirm a price before you drive over.
So what are the rules of all-you-can-eat here, boiled down? One price, rounds from the tablet, dinner for the fish, nothing to go, and 50 cents for every piece you leave behind.
### Where the robot stir-fry went
The short video above shows what used to be here: you built a stir-fry bowl and an automated cooker tumbled it hot, right where you could watch. The BND reported that part of the remodel was removing the multiple automated stir-fry cookers and building that space out as the front kitchen, with the back kitchen still in use.
So can a robot chef cook food? This building is the answer: yes. Tasty Bowl cooked its stir-fry in a row of automated cookers until the remodel took them out. Lin told the paper his struggle was competing with a similar stir-fry and sushi restaurant in O’Fallon, so instead of running the same idea as the place up the road, he changed the idea. Food made to order by people in a front kitchen replaced food tumbled in a barrel.
One more change worth knowing before you plan a night out. When the BND visited after the reopening, the bar side of the restaurant was closed so staff could focus on the dining tables, and manager Feng Pan said the cocktail menu was still in the works and drinks weren’t available yet, though the restaurant still holds a liquor license. If a drink with dinner matters, ask when you call.
Making a night of it on the Illinois side? Our guide to the best restaurants in Belleville, IL covers more of the Illinois side, close to Takumi.
If you run the sushi bar, the stir-fry counter or the family kitchen two exits over, read this page again. Tasty Bowl’s owner told the paper his struggle was competing with a similar concept restaurant nearby. When two restaurants sell the same thing, the one that shows up first gets the table, and the other one never even hears about the night it lost. ### What to order on a first visit
The safest way into a menu this long is to treat round one as a sampler and let the table vote. A few picks, all pulled from Takumi’s own menu:
Hot Mess Roll - white tuna, crab meat salad, cream cheese and jalapeño, deep-fried and finished with eel sauce, spicy mayo and hot sauce. Crunch first, then heat.
Fairview Heights Roll - white tuna, avocado, cream cheese and crab meat with eel sauce, spicy mayo, green onion and fish egg. The one named for the town.
Sweetheart Roll - spicy crunchy tuna and avocado in pink soy paper with spicy mayo, the roll that makes the table look up.
Baked Baby Octopus and Takoyaki - the two items the BND singled out for daring diners. “Tako” is Japanese for octopus, and the takoyaki comes off the kitchen appetizer list, so it is there at lunch too.
Soupy Dumpling - from the dim sum list, next to the crystal shrimp dumplings.
Fried Oreo or green tea ice cream - order dessert in its own small round so the last thing on your plate isn’t 50 cents of rice.
If anyone at the table is wary of raw fish, the cooked rolls are marked on the menu, and Dragon, Queen, Volcano and Yum Yum are among them. The hibachi, fried rice, lo mein and Chinese entrees give a picky eater a full meal without a single piece of sashimi.
The bill, before you sit down
An adult pays $17.95 at weekday lunch and $27.95 at weekday dinner or all day on weekends. Kids 9-12 pay $12.95 or $17.95, kids 3-8 pay $10.95 or $13.95, and under 3 eat free. What moves your total: the clock, the kids’ ages, and $0.50 for each uneaten piece.
### Sushi manners that also save you money
What are the etiquette rules for eating sushi at a place like this? The one that matters most at Takumi is the one on the menu: order what you will actually eat. Share a roll across the table rather than each ordering your own, and you will taste more of the menu with less left on the plate.
Is it disrespectful to not finish your sushi? Here it is also expensive. Leaving a plate of half-eaten rolls is exactly what the 50-cent charge is there to stop, and it is a fair trade for a menu where you can keep ordering. Pace yourself. Order the next round when the table is nearly done, not when everyone is already full.
The menu also carries the standard warning that eating raw or undercooked seafood, shellfish or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness, especially with certain medical conditions. If that warning applies to someone in your party, the rolls marked cooked and the kitchen menu are the way to go.
Rather pay by the piece and take the leftovers home? Our guide to sushi and Japanese food in St. Louis has the order-what-you-want spots.
### Before you go: hours, address and phone
Takumi is at 51 Lincoln Hwy, Fairview Heights, IL 62208, phone 618-206-6123, online at fairviewheightsbuffet.com, where you will also find the menu and an online ordering link. Hours are 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 11 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Weekday lunch pricing runs 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., weekday dinner from 4 p.m. to close, and Saturday and Sunday are all-day dinner.
It is an easy stop from anywhere in the Metro East, and if you are crossing the river from Missouri for it, from Bevo Mill or anywhere else on the south side, the drive is the cheap part. Go hungry, go at dinner if you want the fish, and keep an eye on the plate. It is one more name on our list of places to eat in Fairview Heights.

### Q. How long are you allowed to stay at an all-you-can-eat buffet?
A.  Ask your server when you sit down. The practical limit at Takumi is the clock: lunch pricing ends at 4 p.m. on weekdays, and the restaurant closes at 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Call 618-206-6123 if you are planning a long table.
### Q. Is it disrespectful to not finish your sushi?

## $35, Cash Only at the Exit: St. Louis Drive-Through Lights
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-ultimate-guide-to-drive-through-christmas-lights-in-st-louis-this-year
Cash only, paid as you exit. You take Exit 261 off I-44 and, as the park’s own directions say, drive toward the lights. The defroster roars. The back seat goes quiet. Brake lights stretch ahead in a slow red ribbon, and the first animated scene flickers on outside the window while a small voice behind you says whoa.
Then the exit booth comes into view, and the car ahead of you already knew. Santa’s Magical Kingdom charges $35 per family vehicle, $40 on Saturdays, tax included, and its own site says admission is cash only at the ticket booth, paid as you exit. The card in your hand does nothing there. The park says an ATM is available inside the General Store, but tuck the bills in the cupholder before you back out of the driveway.
And here is the part worth forwarding to whoever is planning the trip: the cheaper night is also the calmer one. The $40 price is Saturdays only, and the park says that except for the week of Christmas, it always has fewer visitors during the week than on weekends. Skip the Saturday, keep the five dollars, and spend less of the night staring at the bumper ahead.
### What are the best drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis?
Two drive-throughs make the biggest claims. Santa’s Magical Kingdom, off I-44 at Exit 261, calls itself the Midwest’s most spectacular holiday light display, with animated scenes and millions of lights for $35 a carload ($40 on Saturdays), cash only, paid as you exit. WonderLight’s Christmas, at World Wide Technology Raceway, bills itself as the area’s largest drive-through show and syncs over 1 million LED lights to your car stereo for $35 a car.
Both stay open on the holidays: WonderLight’s is open nightly, holidays included, and Santa’s Magical Kingdom stays open on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas and New Year’s Eve, so neither one asks you to plan around a closed gate. After that, the choice comes down to mood. Santa’s Magical Kingdom is the storybook one, scene after scene rolling past the window. WonderLight’s is the concert, the bass from your own speakers thumping while the lights jump with the beat.
### Santa’s Magical Kingdom: animated scenes and a cash-only exit
Animated scenes, dazzling special effects and millions of shimmering lights roll past the window at Santa’s Magical Kingdom. It says it is open every single night of its season, including Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas and New Year’s Eve. Gates open at 5:30 p.m. and close at 10:30 p.m. through Dec. 24, then at 10 p.m. from Dec. 25 on. Its exact season dates post each fall on its site, so check there before you go.
Two tips straight from the park. First, arrive at least 20 to 30 minutes before closing so you have time to drive through, and more if you want to browse Kringle’s General Store. Second, except for the week of Christmas, it always has fewer visitors during the week than on weekends. If you can swing a school night early in the season, you will crawl less and see more.
Price is by the carload, and the park says it plainly: one price entertains the entire family. That is why the grandparents end up wedged in the third row, knees up, pointing at the same reindeer the kids just spotted, while the windows fog every time someone laughs.
### WonderLight’s Christmas: lights that play your radio
Someone in the front seat turns the dial until the static clears. The bass comes up through the seat, and a whole field of lights jumps on the beat of a song playing out of your own speakers. At WonderLight’s Christmas, over 1 million LED lights sync to traditional and newer, rocking Christmas music played through your own car stereo. Roll the window down an inch if the kids can stand the cold: a line of cars playing the same song at the same moment is half the show.
It sets up at World Wide Technology Raceway. This season’s dates are already posted: Nov. 13 through Jan. 3, 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., open nightly, holidays included.
Pricing is $35 per car for up to 8 passengers, $50 for limos and activity vans, and $100 for large vehicles such as buses, RVs and trolleys. Check the vehicle rule before you borrow the church van: the large-vehicle price applies to vehicles with full-height standing entry, dual rear wheels, a cutaway chassis or standing room inside. Same eight people, two prices: $35 in a regular car, $100 in a shuttle with standing room.
### Where are the best places to see Christmas lights in St. Louis on foot?
Some of the best lights in town make you leave the car, and two of them are worth it. Does the STL Zoo do Christmas lights? Yes. Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo runs select nights from Nov. 27 to Dec. 30, 5 p.m. to 8:30 p.m., with last entry at 8 p.m. Tickets are $19 general admission and $16 for Zoo members, and children 0-23 months get in free. The Zoo says more than 1 million twinkling lights cover the walk, with s’mores over open firepits, Santa visits every night through Dec. 23, and parking on both Zoo lots included in admission, as available.
The Missouri Botanical Garden’s Garden Glow is the other one. It features more than two million lights on select nights, and the path is about a mile long and takes 45 minutes to an hour. The Garden warns that tickets tend to sell out well in advance, especially from mid-December through Jan. 1, so this is the one to book first. Cold cheeks, mittens wrapped around a hot drink, and a kid riding your shoulders for the last quarter mile.
Making a full night of it? Find dinner, a cocoa stop and a late dessert along your route on St Louis Near Me Directory, then hit the lights after the kids have eaten.
If you run the diner, the bakery or the cocoa stand those light-show lines drive past, those families are hungry on the way home. A Gold listing puts you in front of them and turns that traffic into customers: see the Gold plan, list your business or see who AI names instead of you.
### Way of Lights: the quiet one
Then there is the Way of Lights at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows. Its season details post on the Shrine’s site each fall, so check there for this year’s schedule before you go.
This is the stop for the car that wants the radio off. Slow tires on the drive, the hush of a family that just stopped arguing about the playlist, and the Christmas story coming up in the windshield.
### Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park and the rest of the list
Tilles Park’s Winter Wonderland is the other name every St. Louis family asks about. I could not confirm this season’s dates or per-car price, and its official page does not load for me, so check St. Louis County Parks before you go rather than trusting an old number from a past season.
Out past the city, the Grove of Lights at Lost Hill Lake and Christmas Traditions each post their own schedules every season. For the walk-through classics, check Brewery Lights at Anheuser-Busch and Grant’s Farm on their own pages before you plan around them, and browse more seasonal listings on a local family events calendar.
### Lights downtown: Union Station after dark
If the car needs a break, St. Louis Union Station has two light shows of its own. The Fire and Light Show on the lake runs on the hour, with eight lotus-shaped pods shooting pillars of fire 25 feet into the air, choreographed to music. Inside the hotel, the Grand Hall Light Show runs on the hour from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. daily, except on days the Grand Hall is rented for private events. Flowers sway, fireworks burst and other images dance across the ceiling while everyone stands with their heads tipped back.
The season adds more. On THE POLAR EXPRESS Train Ride, riders board real vintage train cars, dancing chefs serve hot chocolate, and Santa boards at the North Pole. Pancakes with Santa runs in the Grand Hall. Parking is in its own lots, at hourly and special-event rates, credit card only.
### How to plan the night so nobody melts down
Eat first. A hungry kid in a slow line of lights is a long night for everyone. Pick one drive-through and one stop, not four. Bring cash for Santa’s Magical Kingdom, and count it at the kitchen table: a Saturday carload is $40 and any other night it is $35, and the exit booth is the wrong place to find out you are five short. Charge the phone, and find the radio station before you reach the entrance.
Pack the back seat like a living room: blankets, a pillow for whoever falls asleep first, a roll of paper towels for the cocoa, and a bag for the wrappers. Turn the dome light off, crack a window when it fogs, and let the kids call out every reindeer they spot.
Then go early. Santa’s Magical Kingdom says its weeknights are quieter except for the week of Christmas, and Garden Glow says its tickets go fastest from mid-December on. The sweet spot is a school night in early December, a full tank, and a back seat full of blankets.
Want the walk-throughs ranked too? Our full St. Louis Christmas lights guide covers both.
And if the night runs long, let it. The best part is often the drive home, the windows dark again, the radio low, and someone in the back seat asleep with their face against the glass.
