### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where are the best places to see Christmas lights in St. Louis?
A.  For a drive-through, start with Santa’s Magical Kingdom ($35 a carload, $40 on Saturdays, cash only) and WonderLight’s Christmas ($35 a car). On foot, Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo and Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden each cover their grounds with more than a million lights. For a quieter, faith-centered night, add the Way of Lights at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows.
### Q. Does the STL Zoo do Christmas lights?
A.  Yes. Wild Lights runs select nights from Nov. 27 to Dec. 30, 5 p.m. to 8:30 p.m., last entry 8 p.m. Tickets are $19 general admission and $16 for Zoo members, free for children 0-23 months, and admission includes parking on both Zoo lots as available.
### Q. How much does it cost to see the lights at Tilles Park?
A.  I could not confirm this season’s price. St. Louis County Parks posts Winter Wonderland details on its site each season, so check there before you go. If you want a posted price today, WonderLight’s Christmas lists $35 per car for up to 8 passengers.
### Q. How long is the light show at Union Station St. Louis?
A.  Plan on catching one at the top of the hour. Union Station says the Grand Hall Light Show runs on the hour from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. daily, except when the Grand Hall is booked for a private event, and the Fire and Light Show on the lake also runs on the hour.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in St. Louis, Missouri in December?
A.  Drive Santa’s Magical Kingdom or WonderLight’s Christmas, walk Wild Lights at the Zoo or Garden Glow, and catch the free Fire and Light Show at Union Station, where THE POLAR EXPRESS Train Ride and Pancakes with Santa also run for the season.
### Q. Is there free parking at Union Station, STL?
A.  Union Station says its West and South lots charge hourly and special-event rates, credit card only. St. Louis Aquarium visitors can get the ticket validated in the Aquarium gift shop for a $5 flat rate.
### Q. Do I need cash for drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis?
A.  At Santa’s Magical Kingdom, yes. Admission is cash only at the ticket booth and is paid as you exit, and there is an ATM inside the General Store. Bring bills anyway: it is the fastest way through any exit line.

## A Bean Bag Decides the Balloon Race: St. Louis Festivals, Season by Season, Mostly Free
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-annual-events-a-season-by-season-guide-to-the-citys-best-festivals
The first sound is a whoosh. A pilot blasts a propane burner, a burst of flame lights the balloon from the inside, then the next one fires, and the next, until Emerson Central Fields in Forest Park is full of balloons glowing, as the organizers put it, like huge fireflies. That’s the Friday Balloon Glow of the Great Forest Park Balloon Race in mid-September. For part of the night, weather permitting, the rope line comes down and the organizers invite everyone onto the field to walk among the balloons, take photos and talk with the pilots and crew.
On the organizers’ schedule the field opens at 5 p.m. and the glow runs about 6:45 to 8:45, with fireworks after. Admission is $0, parking inside Forest Park that weekend is free, and two MetroLink stops, Forest Park-DeBaliviere and Central West End, sit just under a mile away.
Then comes the part most of the crowd never learns. Saturday’s race isn’t won by the fastest balloon. The field opens at 1 p.m., and around 4:30 one “hare” balloon launches and lands wherever the wind takes it. Its pilot and crew lay an X on the ground, and the “hound” pilot who drops a bean bag closest to the center wins. Balloons have come down in every corner of the metro, so one might land on your street. The country’s oldest and largest free balloon event, by the organizers’ count, comes down to a bean bag. The Library of Congress even keeps it in its permanent collection as a Local Legacy.
Summer nights in Forest Park have their own free-seat secret. The line for The Muny’s free seats forms at the upper entrance, and the theater tells you to bring chairs, blankets and snacks, because a picnic in that line is a St. Louis tradition. At 7 p.m. the gate opens to the last nine rows, nearly 1,500 seats, free and first come, first served, for an 8:15 curtain. Over more than a century, one in four Muny audience members has gotten in without paying.
On July 3 and 4, cross the river and watch the shells burst over the Arch from the Illinois side. Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park in East St. Louis sits directly across from the Arch and the downtown skyline, and it has stayed open until the Celebrate STL fireworks end, so check its hours for the year. And St. Patrick’s Day gets two parades: the big one downtown at noon on the Saturday before, and Dogtown’s at 11 a.m. on the 17th itself.
Add it up and six of the city’s biggest traditions cost $0 at the gate: beads on South Broadway, bagpipes in Dogtown, Shakespeare on the lawn, fireworks over the Arch, balloons over Forest Park and Santa at the Thanks-For-Giving Parade. The one big ticketed festival is the Japanese Festival at the Missouri Botanical Garden over Labor Day weekend.
### Late winter: Mardi Gras season
On Grand Parade Saturday, Soulard smells like beer and grilled brats by mid-morning, the brick sidewalks are slick with confetti, and a float rolls by close enough that the beads smack your coat before you can catch them. It fits a city the French founded. The Bud Light Grand Parade of Soulard Mardi Gras steps off at 11 a.m. the Saturday before Fat Tuesday near Busch Stadium and rolls almost three miles down South Broadway to the Anheuser-Busch Brewery, free to watch the whole way. The season also brings the Purina Pet Parade and family-friendly events in the weeks before; parade day is the rowdy one. The insider move: the narrow Soulard streets jam early, so get dropped off or ride in and walk, claim a curb on Broadway well before 11, and dress for standing still in February for hours.
### Spring: parades and green rivers of people
Bagpipes bounce off the brick two-flats, somebody’s already in a green wig at 9 a.m., and the whole block smells like corned beef. That’s Dogtown on March 17. St. Louis runs two beloved St. Patrick’s Day parades, and locals have strong opinions about them. The Downtown St. Patrick’s Day Parade is the big civic one: the Saturday before St. Patrick’s Day at noon, marching bands and giant character balloons heading west on Market Street from 8th to 22nd, after the Parade Run takes over downtown that morning. Out in Dogtown, the historically Irish neighborhood near Forest Park, the Ancient Order of Hibernians parade on March 17 is the neighborhood-party version, a wall-to-wall street celebration that’s as much block party as parade. Downtown’s is the bigger show; Dogtown’s is the one people call in sick for. The insider timing: Dogtown’s parade steps off at 11 a.m. at Tamm and Oakland and runs down Tamm to Manchester, and the streets start closing around 6 a.m., so park well outside the neighborhood and walk in.
### Late spring and early summer: culture in the park
The lawn at Shakespeare Glen at dusk: blankets edge to edge, somebody uncorking a bottle, fireflies coming up, and then a hillside of people going quiet at the same moment as the first actor walks on. The St. Louis Shakespeare Festival’s “Shakespeare in the Park” has staged a free, professional production there every late May and June since 2001, for nearly 40,000 people a season. The Glen sits off Fine Arts Drive on the east side of Art Hill, between the Zoo and the Art Museum. Bring a blanket, a picnic and a bottle of wine, and come early for a spot on the grass. In late June, PrideFest, the region’s largest Pride celebration, fills downtown with drums, whistles and rainbow flags snapping in the wind as the parade turns onto the festival grounds.
### Summer: fireworks over the Arch
The first shell goes up over the Arch, the riverfront crowd says “ohhh” in one breath, and the boom lands a half-second later, rolling off the stainless steel and back across the water. The annual Fourth of July celebration downtown, now run by Celebrate Saint Louis (the group behind the old Fair Saint Louis), sets off fireworks over the Gateway Arch on July 3 and 4, sends America’s Birthday Parade down Market Street on the Fourth, and fills the week with concerts. The local trick: cross the river. Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park in East St. Louis has an overlook that puts the whole Arch and skyline in front of you, with far more lawn and far less elbow-to-elbow than the riverfront. Smaller municipal fireworks light up communities all across the metro the same week if downtown feels like too much.
### Late summer: the world comes to St. Louis
Late August and early September are the city’s most gloriously international stretch. The Festival of Nations in Tower Grove Park - a free, decades-old celebration put on by the International Institute - gathers dozens of cultures for food stalls, music, and dance, and it is a food-lover’s dream. Over Labor Day weekend, the Japanese Festival at the Missouri Botanical Garden (running since the 1970s) turns the Garden’s 14-acre Japanese Garden into a showcase of taiko drumming, tea ceremonies, and lantern-lit evenings, while the Big Muddy Blues Festival has brought free live blues to Laclede’s Landing on many a Labor Day weekend (check whether it’s on this year). Between them, you could eat and listen your way around the globe without leaving town.
### Early fall: art, balloons, and beer
September and October are arguably peak festival season. The Saint Louis Art Fair transforms downtown Clayton into one of the top-ranked juried art fairs in the country, free to browse. Nearby, the Great Forest Park Balloon Race - and its can’t-miss Friday-night Balloon Glow, when the balloons light up after dark - is a free St. Louis tradition dating to 1973 that packs Forest Park with spectators. Saturday’s race is a chase, not a sprint: the “hare” lifts off first, and the “hounds”, more than 50 balloons by the organizers’ count, follow in waves, each pilot trying to drop a bean bag closest to the X the hare’s crew lays out where it lands. Emerson Central Fields opens at 5 p.m. Friday for the glow, which runs from about 6:45 to 8:45 with fireworks after, and at 1 p.m. Saturday, with the launch around 4:30; bring a blanket and get there early for a spot near the rope. Then the season turns to beer, with Oktoberfest celebrations bringing German food, music, and steins to neighborhoods across the metro; Soulard has long thrown one near its historic market, so check this fall’s lineup before you go. Cooler air, big crowds, and a lot to do outdoors before winter.
Wildly off-topic - Benld’s restaurants, all in one place.
### Late fall: the bridge to the holidays
As the leaves drop, downtown kicks off the holiday season with the Ameren Thanks-For-Giving Parade - a giant-balloon, marching-band Thanksgiving parade the Saturday before the holiday, ending at Kiener Plaza and rolling straight into the downtown Winterfest festivities. From there, the metro lights up for the winter holidays: for that whole stretch - the light displays, the Christmas markets, New Year’s Eve - see our dedicated seasonal guides, which pick up right where this calendar leaves off.
### The St. Louis festival calendar at a glance
The whole festival year fits on one screen. Scan the Cost column first: almost every row says free. The weekends slide a little each year, so plan the month here, then confirm the date on the event’s own page.
### Before you go: the date, the parking, cash and layers
A few habits turn a good festival day into a great one. Confirm the exact date the week before - most of these move by a weekend or two each year. Plan the parking or take transit for the big draws (Mardi Gras, the parades, July 4, the Balloon Race all snarl traffic), and consider MetroLink for downtown events. Get there early for anything free and popular, both for a good spot and easier parking. Bring cash for food and craft vendors, sunscreen and water in summer, and layers in the shoulder seasons. And follow the event’s official page or the venue for the current year’s schedule - lineups and hours are set fresh each season even when the tradition itself is a fixture.
### Free, and the fastest way to feel like a local
There’s a reason St. Louisans organize their calendars around these events. Most are free, which makes them some of the best entertainment value in the region. They’re how a big metro of distinct neighborhoods actually comes together - Soulard, Dogtown, Tower Grove, Clayton, and downtown each get their moment to host the whole city. And they’re the fastest way for a newcomer to feel like a local: show up to a couple of these, and the year stops feeling like a stranger’s calendar and starts feeling like yours. Pick one from the next season on the horizon, and go.
### Festivals by neighborhood: who hosts what
One of the charms of the St. Louis calendar is that the celebrations are spread across the city’s distinct neighborhoods, each with a signature event it’s known for. Soulard owns the bookends of the outdoor year - Mardi Gras in late winter and, traditionally, an Oktoberfest in the fall - both anchored around its historic market. Dogtown is synonymous with its St. Patrick’s Day street party. Tower Grove Park hosts the international food-and-culture sprawl of Festival of Nations. Forest Park is the setting for Shakespeare in the Park and the Great Forest Park Balloon Race. Clayton’s downtown becomes a top-tier art fair each September. And the Gateway Arch grounds and downtown host the civic big-hitters: the July 4 fireworks, PrideFest, and the Thanks-For-Giving Parade. If you want to get to know St. Louis’s neighborhoods, following the festival calendar is one of the best ways to do it - each event is also an introduction to the place that throws it.
### A whole summer of weekends without buying a ticket
It’s worth saying plainly: a remarkable number of these events cost nothing to attend. Festival of Nations, the Great Forest Park Balloon Race and Balloon Glow, the Saint Louis Art Fair, Shakespeare in the Park, and the parades are all free at the gate. That makes St. Louis’s festival season one of the best entertainment values anywhere - you can fill a whole summer of weekends without buying a ticket. To do it smart: bring your own water and snacks where allowed (and cash for the food you can’t resist), arrive early to skip the worst parking, and check each event’s page for free-admission details versus paid add-ons like reserved seating, rides, or beer gardens. For families especially, the combination of free entry and genuinely top-tier programming - a professional Shakespeare production, dozens of balloons rising over Forest Park, dozens of cultures under one park’s trees - is hard to beat anywhere in the country.

### Pick one festival a season and go every year
The locals who love this city most tend to have their handful of non-negotiable events - the ones they go to every single year, rain or shine, until they become as much a part of the season as the weather. Maybe it’s the Balloon Glow every September, or Festival of Nations for the food, or the Dogtown parade with the same crew. The invitation here is simple: pick one or two from this calendar, go this year, and go again next year. That’s how a new arrival turns into a St. Louisan - not all at once, but one beloved annual tradition at a time, until the whole year has a familiar, welcome shape to it. And the beauty of a calendar this full is that there’s almost always something on the horizon: finish one season’s festival and the next is only a few weeks out, which is a quietly wonderful thing to realize about the place you live.
People are asking
### What is there to do in St. Louis between March and September when no festival is on?
Eat dinner at a farmers’ market on a weeknight. From May through September, Tower Grove Farmers’ Market runs a Tuesday evening market in Tower Grove Park from 4 p.m. to dusk, stocked with prepared food and drinks for dinner in the park, and a Thursday evening market in Francis Park, tucked next to the Rockwell Beer Garden with its cold drinks and wood-fired pizza. Saturday mornings, the main market fills Tower Grove Park from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., April through October, with about 120 vendors of local produce, handmade goods and treats. Check the market’s own schedule for this season’s exact opening and closing days before you go.
### Why you check the date the week before
Festivals aren’t permanent fixtures, and it’s worth going in with clear eyes. Beloved events do sometimes pause, move, or end - rising costs, staffing, and safety logistics have all reshaped the local calendar in recent years, and a festival that ran for a decade can go on hiatus without much warning. That’s exactly why the single most useful habit for any of these is to check the event’s official page or social media before you make plans, rather than assuming last year’s date and location still hold. The events in this guide are the sturdy, long-running anchors of the St. Louis year - the ones most likely to be there season after season - but even they set fresh details annually. A two-minute check saves a wasted trip, and it’s the price of admission for a city whose calendar is alive and always evolving.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the biggest annual festivals in St. Louis?
A.  Soulard Mardi Gras (late winter), the Downtown and Dogtown St. Patrick’s Day parades (March), Shakespeare in the Park and PrideFest (late spring and June), the Fourth of July fireworks over the Arch, Festival of Nations and the Japanese Festival (late summer), the Saint Louis Art Fair and Great Forest Park Balloon Race (September), and the Thanks-For-Giving Parade (November). Most are free.
### Q. What events are happening in St. Louis on Labor Day weekend?
A.  The Japanese Festival at the Missouri Botanical Garden is the anchor, with taiko drumming and sumo across the holiday weekend, and it’s ticketed. Festival of Nations in Tower Grove Park usually lands a weekend or two earlier, the Saint Louis Art Fair fills downtown Clayton in early September, and it’s worth checking whether Big Muddy Blues is on at Laclede’s Landing.
### Q. What are some free events happening in St. Louis today?
A.  It depends on the day, but the free anchors are predictable: parades in March, June, July and November, Shakespeare in the Park in June, Festival of Nations in late August, and the Art Fair and Balloon Race in September. For today’s smaller events, check the City of St. Louis events calendar, and remember the Zoo is free every day it’s open.
### Q. What is happening in St. Louis next week?
A.  Start with the calendar table above for the season you’re in, then confirm the exact date on the event’s own site, since most of these move by a weekend or two each year. For the smaller stuff, like walking tours, neighborhood festivals and concerts, the City of St. Louis events calendar lists the next seven days at a glance.
### Q. What are some fun things to do near St. Louis this weekend?
A.  Match it to the season. If a festival from the calendar above is on, go; most are free and easy to reach by MetroLink. If not, the free Zoo and the Forest Park museums work any weekend, and the day-trips guide linked below has more escapes within two hours of the city when you want to get out of town.

## Golden Chicken St. Peters: The $15.99 Chicken Takes an Hour
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/golden-chicken-a-beloved-st-peters-eatery-for-flavorful-meals
$15.99. That is what Golden Chicken’s online menu charges for a whole rotisserie chicken, with garlic sauce and pita in the bag. Now look one line down. The half chicken plate is also $15.99. Same price, half the bird, though the plate does bring rice, hummus and pickles with it. And both carry the same four words in parentheses that decide your whole evening: 1 hour wait time.
That is the thing nobody tells you about the little Mediterranean kitchen at 632 Jungermann Rd in St. Peters. The chicken that gives the place its name is not sitting under a heat lamp waiting for you. If you walk in at 6:30 with a hungry family and ask for a whole chicken, you are in for a long wait, or a change of plans. If you order it from the website as you leave work in O’Fallon or Cottleville, an hour out, you walk in, the bag is warm, the garlic hits you before you get it to the car, and nobody in the back seat has started complaining yet.
The second thing nobody tells you: Golden Chicken is closed on Thursdays. Every other day it runs 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Plan a Thursday shawarma run and you will be reading the hours on a locked door.
Get those two facts right and the rest is easy. Here is the money version for a couple: two half chicken plates come to $31.98. One whole chicken, plus a side of basmati rice and a side of hummus, comes to $29.97, and you get the whole bird instead of two halves. Order ahead, skip Thursday, and the bill stays small. The restaurant’s phone is (636) 244-3031, and its own website takes orders directly for pickup.
### What kind of food does Golden Chicken in St. Peters serve?
Halal Mediterranean food, made from scratch, despite a name that sounds like a fried-chicken drive-thru. In its own words, the main dishes are chicken shawarma, beef shawarma, rotisserie chicken and baklava, served with falafel, gyro meat, warm pita, hummus, salads and seasoned rice. The menu runs from wraps and bowls to kebab plates, wings, loaded fries and family trays, then ends somewhere you would not expect from a place called Golden Chicken: Dubai strawberry cups and pistachio bubble waffles on the same dessert list as the baklava.
Unwrap a chicken shawarma wrap in the parking lot and you get the whole idea in one bite: warm chicken, a sharp swipe of garlic sauce, the cold snap of a pickle. Nothing else is in it, and nothing else needs to be. The beef shawarma wrap is louder, with tahini, hummus, parsley and pickled turnips that bite back.
What makes Golden Chicken worth a detour is not one dish. It is how cheap it is to eat well here if you know the menu. A chicken shawarma wrap is $9.99 on the online menu, and it is nothing fancy: chicken, garlic sauce and pickles, rolled tight. A gyro wrap is also $9.99. A falafel wrap is $7.99. That is lunch for under ten dollars, and there is even a Gyro Tuesday item listed at $9.99.
### What is the difference between a gyro and a shawarma here?
This is the question first-timers stand at the counter trying to answer, and Golden Chicken’s menu answers it more clearly than most explainers do. The gyro wrap is beef and lamb with onions, tomatoes, lettuce and tzatziki, the cool, yogurt-based sauce. The chicken shawarma wrap is chicken with garlic sauce and pickles. The beef shawarma wrap is beef with onions, tomatoes, parsley, hummus, pickles, pickled turnips and tahini sauce.
So in practice, on this menu, the difference you will taste is the sauce. Gyro means cool and creamy. Chicken shawarma means sharp garlic and the snap of a pickle. Beef shawarma means nutty tahini and the bright pink crunch of pickled turnip. If you like one, you will probably like all three, and the cheapest way to find out is to order two wraps and split them.
And what does a shawarma consist of when you order it crunchy? The menu has a “Viral Crunchy” version of both shawarma wraps, listed as the Amo Amjed Wrap, at $10.99 for chicken and $11.99 for beef. The crunchy chicken version sits at the very top of the restaurant’s most-ordered list, ahead of every plate and bowl.
### How to order the rotisserie chicken without the wait
Every item in the rotisserie section of the menu carries that one-hour wait, so the move is to order online and show up when it is ready. The whole chicken is $15.99 and includes garlic sauce and pita, the best deal on the board if you have rice or a salad at home. The half chicken plate is also $15.99 and adds rice, hummus and pickles, a full dinner for one. The whole chicken plate is $24.99 and brings the bird with rice, hummus, pickles, pita, garlic sauce and spicy garlic, enough for two with leftovers. For a cookout, three whole chickens and a fry tray run $54.99, and the rice trays with three, four or five whole chickens run $65.99, $89.99 and $109.99.
The math is the reason to read this page. A whole chicken at $15.99 costs the same as a half chicken plate, so if your household is two or more, the whole bird plus a $5.99 order of basmati rice and a $7.99 hummus beats two plates. The difference is about the price of the drinks.
Feeding a crowd this weekend? Golden Chicken’s family trays and catering need 24 hours’ notice, so call ahead. For more Mediterranean kitchens around the metro, our guide to the best Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis is the next stop.
If you run the kebab grill, the bakery or the one-room kitchen people only find by accident, this page is for you too. Golden Chicken’s best trick, the one-hour chicken, only works because people know to order ahead, and they only know because someone told them. ### What to order on a first visit
If the table is new to Mediterranean food, build outward from the familiar. Start with something everyone recognizes, add one thing that is new, and share everything. A plan that works:
Chicken Shawarma Bowl - $14.99. Chicken, garlic sauce, rice and fresh veggies. The safe, filling middle of the menu.
Mix Kebab Plate - $21.99. Chicken, shish and kufta kebab with tahini salad, rice and pickles. Three meats, one plate, the best way to find your favorite.
Falafel Plate - $13.99, with hummus, tahini salad, pickles and pita. The vegetarian at the table eats as well as anybody.
Appetizer Tray - $17.99. Hummus, spicy hummus, garlic sauce and baba ghanoush with pita bread. Put it in the middle and watch it go.
Lemon Mint - $4.99. The drink one reviewer on the restaurant’s catering page called “amazing.”
Chnafa - $8.99, or the baklava at $4.99, for the end of the meal.
Dinner math on Jungermann Rd
On Golden Chicken’s online menu, wraps run $7.99-$13.99, plates and bowls $13.99-$21.99, and a whole rotisserie chicken is $15.99. What moves the bill: wrap or plate, how many chickens, and whether you add sides like a $3.99 order of fries.
### Is rotisserie chicken healthy to eat?
That depends on the rest of the plate more than the bird, and I am not going to pretend a menu can settle a nutrition question. What Golden Chicken’s site does say is that it lists healthy options among what it offers, and its menu gives you room to choose: a garden salad is $8.99, a tabouleh salad $7.99, and the half chicken plate comes with hummus and pickles rather than fries. If you want the rotisserie bird lighter, order the whole chicken and build your own sides at home.
Bringing kids? One guest review on the restaurant’s home page says the staff helped them order and that “Kids get spoiled with a special treat!” Another reviewer wrote that the employees explained what was in different menu items and made suggestions based on what they liked, which is exactly what a nervous first-timer needs at the counter. If you are not sure what tahini or tzatziki is, ask. Nobody here will make you feel silly for it.
If you order online often, Golden Chicken runs a rewards program: you earn points every time you order online and can redeem them for free food. For a household that makes the one-hour chicken a weekly habit, that adds up.
The restaurant also says it will make its best attempt to accommodate dietary restrictions such as gluten-free, vegan or allergies, and asks you to call directly for specific requests. That is worth doing before a catering order for a mixed crowd.

### Catering, family trays and feeding a crowd
Golden Chicken does a surprising amount of big-table cooking for a small room. The family trays on its online menu include a kebab tray at $99.99 with four each of shish, kufta and chicken kebab skewers plus hummus, tahini sauce and pita, a shawarma box at $109.99 with four beef and four chicken shawarma wraps, fries and sauce, a gyro tray at $99.99 with eight gyro wraps, and 36 pieces of falafel for $29.99.
For bigger events, the catering page lists corporate lunches, weddings, private parties and holiday parties. The catering team works the same days as the dining room, every day but Thursday from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., and serves events in St. Peters and O’Fallon, from an office lunch for 20 to a wedding for 200, by the restaurant’s own description. It asks for 24 hours’ notice for catering orders and says there is no minimum order amount to place one, though there may be a minimum to have it delivered. A tray of rotisserie chickens and a gallon of lemon mint, which the drinks list shows at $20.00, turns a backyard birthday into the kind of spread people photograph.
### Before you go: hours, ordering and the drive
Golden Chicken is at 632 Jungermann Rd, St. Peters, MO 63376, phone (636) 244-3031. Hours are 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sunday through Wednesday and Friday through Saturday. It is closed on Thursdays. It offers dine-in, takeout and delivery, and its own website takes online orders for pickup, which is the easy way to time the rotisserie chicken.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between a gyro and a shawarma?
A.  At Golden Chicken in St. Peters, the gyro wrap is beef and lamb with onions, tomatoes, lettuce and tzatziki sauce, while the chicken shawarma wrap is chicken with garlic sauce and pickles, and the beef shawarma wrap comes with hummus, pickled turnips and tahini sauce. The sauce is the difference you taste first.
### Q. What does a shawarma consist of?
A.  On Golden Chicken’s menu, a chicken shawarma wrap is chicken, garlic sauce and pickles. The beef shawarma wrap is beef, onions, tomatoes, parsley, hummus, pickles, pickled turnips and tahini sauce. Both also come in a bowl with rice and fresh veggies.
### Q. What are the two types of shawarma?
A.  At Golden Chicken, the two shawarma choices are chicken and beef. Each comes as a wrap, as a bowl, and in a “Viral Crunchy” wrap version, and there is also a butter chicken shawarma wrap and bowl.
### Q. What does shawarma taste like?
A.  Golden Chicken’s chicken shawarma leans on its garlic sauce and pickles, so expect garlic up front and a sour, crunchy bite. The beef version is built around tahini, hummus and pickled turnips. If you want heat, the menu lists a spicy garlic sauce and shatta, a spicy chili sauce, at $0.99 each.
### Q. Is Golden Chicken open on Thursdays?
A.  No. Golden Chicken is closed on Thursdays and open 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. the other six days. Call (636) 244-3031 to confirm holiday hours.

## 1,500 Free Seats and a Sold-Out Arch: How to Plan a Trip to St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-ultimate-guide-how-to-plan-a-trip-to-st-louis-missouri
Did you book the Arch yet? Not the trip, the tram. The Gateway Arch’s own site warns that tickets for the ride to the top sell out early and often, and plenty of visitors find out standing on the riverfront, necks craned at 630 feet of stainless steel they won’t be riding up today.
Book it and here’s the payoff: the door of a five-seat capsule clicks shut, you’re knee to knee with strangers, and the little pod rattles and tilts its way up the inside of the leg until the windows at the top show you Illinois on one side and the whole city on the other. Then the rest of the trip is easy. Two to three days covers it.
### The Arch, done right
In July the walk from the garage to the Arch is seven to ten sticky minutes, so get the details straight before you leave the car:
Tickets: the tram runs $15 to $19 for adults and $11 to $15 for kids 3 to 15, priced by date. Allow 45 to 60 minutes, with under 10 minutes at the top. Sold out online? A batch of same-day tickets goes on sale at 9 a.m. each day, when available, and on National Park Service fee-free days such as Veterans Day the $3 park fee comes off adult tickets.
Get there 30 minutes early and walk in at the entrance plaza facing Fourth Street and the Old Courthouse. The legs are exits only, and everyone goes through airport-style security.
The free part: the museum under the Arch costs nothing, and neither does the Old Courthouse across the street, where Dred and Harriet Scott first sued for their freedom.
Parking: there’s no lot at the Arch. Prepay the Stadium East Garage at 200 S. Broadway online and it’s $10 for the first five hours. On a Cardinals home game day, the discount only holds if you prepay by 11:59 p.m. the night before.
The rest of the trip comes down to three moments. Walk through the Saint Louis Zoo gate without paying a cent, because general admission is free, and follow the barking to the sea lions. Sit on the Art Museum steps at the top of Art Hill with the Grand Basin below you and kids tumbling down the grass; the museum behind you is free, and so are the History Museum and the Science Center. Then bite into toasted ravioli on The Hill, crust crackling, a cup of warm marinara on the side, before live blues downtown or on Laclede's Landing.
The summer secret locals guard: The Muny, the huge outdoor musical theater in Forest Park, gives away nearly 1,500 seats at every performance. They’re the last nine rows, first come, first served, no ticket needed, so bring a cushion and get in line early. Broadway-style musical, warm night air, the price of zero.
Get around on MetroLink, which runs from Lambert airport to downtown and the Central West End for $2.50 a ride or $5 a day, with MetroBus and rideshares for the gaps, and sleep downtown or in a neighborhood like the Central West End.
### When to come and how the city lays out
### Best Times To Visit St. Louis
Spring and fall are the sweet spots. In April and May the redbuds and dogwoods light up Forest Park and you can walk all day without melting. September and October bring crisp nights and festival season, including the Great Forest Park Balloon Race, when the hot-air balloons lift off over the park and the whole city looks up. July and August are the trade-off: the shirt sticks to your back before you reach the car, so do the Arch and the Zoo early and save the afternoon for air conditioning. Winter is cold and gray, with fewer crowds and lower hotel prices, and a sleety Saturday is made for City Museum, a maze of slides, tunnels and climbing towers built out of the city’s own salvage. The Arch closes on Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year’s Day.
### Understanding St. Louis's Layout
The Mississippi forms the city’s eastern edge, with downtown and the Arch on the riverbank and Illinois across the water. Forest Park sits a few miles west, a straight shot on I-64 or MetroLink, with the Central West End along its eastern side and The Hill and the Missouri Botanical Garden to the south. Group your days by zone: the Arch, the riverfront and Busch Stadium together; Forest Park and the Central West End together; the Garden, Tower Grove Park and dinner on The Hill together. Grouping your stops by area is the single easiest way to cut down on drive time.
### Budget-Friendly Travel Tips
The best money news in St. Louis is how much is free. The Zoo, the Art Museum, the History Museum and the Science Center in Forest Park charge no general admission, and neither do the museum under the Arch, the Old Courthouse or the sculptures and splash fountains of Citygarden downtown. Street parking is usually free on Sundays and state holidays. A $5 MetroLink day pass beats a downtown hotel’s nightly parking rate, so ask what the hotel charges before you book. And when you do want a guide to local shops or services, you might find what you need on a local directory.
People are asking
### What are the best travel tips for a first visit to St. Louis?
Touch the Arch: the National Park Service’s own FAQ says “go right ahead,” and local legend says a touch means you’ll never be able to leave St. Louis. But know before you buy a tram ticket that the top has no restrooms or snack bar, and no strollers or wheelchairs are allowed on the observation deck. On MetroLink, set up Tap & Ride in the Transit app or on a Ride On card: Metro says it caps what you pay at the price of the best-deal pass, such as the $5 one-day pass, and children 4 and younger ride free. And Forest Park is 1,300 acres with over 30 miles of paths, so treat its five big institutions as a menu of two a day, not a checklist.
### Getting around: car, train or scooter
Getting around St. Louis is pretty straightforward once you know your options. You've got a few main ways to see the city, and each one suits a different kind of day and budget.
### Getting Around By Car
If you prefer having your own wheels, renting a car is a solid option. St. Louis isn't as overwhelming with traffic as some bigger cities, so driving can be quite manageable. You'll find parking garages and street parking available, though downtown street parking often has time limits and meters. Sundays and state holidays usually mean free street parking, which is a nice bonus. Having a car gives you the freedom to explore beyond the city center easily, like taking a trip out to Missouri Wine Country.
### Utilizing Public Transportation
St. Louis has a public transit system that can get you to many key spots. The MetroLink light rail has two lines that connect major attractions, and the MetroBus system covers a wide area. It's a good way to save money and avoid parking hassles, especially if you're sticking to the main tourist areas. You can check routes and schedules to plan your journeys.
### Rideshare and Scooter Options
For quick trips or when public transport isn't convenient, rideshare services are readily available throughout the city. You'll also see electric scooters zipping around in many neighborhoods, which can be a fun and fast way to cover short distances, especially in the downtown area or along the riverfront. Just be sure to check local regulations and designated parking areas for scooters.
Here's a quick look at your main transportation choices:
Car Rental: Offers the most flexibility for exploring the wider region.
MetroLink/MetroBus: A cost-effective way to reach popular attractions and downtown.
Rideshare/Scooters: Convenient for short trips and last-mile travel.
### Driving In and Reserving Parking
The Arch slides into view before your exit, and that’s usually when someone in the passenger seat asks where you’re parking. Most visitors arrive by car, and the drives are easy: about four and a half hours from Chicago on I-55, three and a half to four from Kansas City or Indianapolis on I-70, and around four and a half from Memphis or Nashville. Just passing through? I-270 and I-255 loop around the metro, so you never have to touch downtown. If the Arch is on your list, book the tram ride to the top before you leave home, because the Arch’s own site warns those tickets sell out early and often. The same site points visitors to the Stadium East Garage at 200 S. Broadway, and buying that spot online at least a day ahead gets you the discounted rate. For a Cardinals game or a big downtown event, reserve a garage space ahead through a parking app instead of circling the blocks around Busch Stadium. And if your hotel charges for parking, ask the nightly rate when you book. Over a long weekend it adds up.
Changing the subject entirely: local SEO in University City decides who finds you.
### Where To Stay In St. Louis
Finding the right place to rest your head after a day of exploring St. Louis shapes the whole trip. Want to be steps from the action, or tucked into a quieter neighborhood away from the crowds? St. Louis makes both easy, and the right pick usually comes down to your budget and how you like to travel.
### Boutique Hotels And Downtown Stays
If you like a hotel with a bit of personality and history, downtown has some genuine standouts. These are places that feel a step above the average chain hotel, with distinctive architecture, thoughtful room design, and staff who actually look after you. Many of these are super close to major sights like the Gateway Arch and Busch Stadium, so you can just walk to a lot of places. It's a great way to soak in the city's atmosphere right from your doorstep.
Hotel Saint Louis, Autograph Collection: This place calls itself “Hip-storical,” and it really lives up to that. It's got modern touches mixed with old-school charm, like a restored stained-glass roof. The rooms are comfy, and it's walking distance to lots of downtown attractions and eateries.
Magnolia Hotel St. Louis: A classic choice built in 1925, this hotel has hosted some famous guests. It offers that old-world luxury feel with beautiful architecture and thoughtful details throughout. It's right downtown, making it easy to get around.
Live! By Loews St. Louis: For a more contemporary feel, this hotel is right across from Busch Stadium. It's got a modern vibe, a rooftop spot to hang out, and all the amenities you'd expect. Plus, it's just a couple of blocks from the Gateway Arch.
### Charming Neighborhood Accommodations
Beyond the downtown core, St. Louis has some really lovely neighborhoods that offer a different kind of stay. These spots often feel more local and can give you a better sense of everyday life in the city. You might find smaller inns or guesthouses in nearby St. Charles here that provide a more intimate experience. It's a nice change of pace if you're looking for something a bit quieter or want to explore areas outside the main tourist hubs. You can discover unique shops and local eateries that aren't in the guidebooks.
### Family-Friendly Lodging Choices
When you're traveling with kids, you need a place that's comfortable for everyone and maybe has a few extra perks. St. Louis has hotels that cater to families, offering amenities that make traveling with little ones a bit easier. Think about places with pools, larger rooms, or even complimentary breakfast to help keep everyone happy and fed. Some hotels are also located near family attractions like the zoo or museums, cutting down on travel time. The Missouri Botanical Garden is also a fantastic spot for families to explore.
Here are a few things to consider when looking for family-friendly lodging:
Location: Is it close to attractions your kids will enjoy? Less travel time means more fun time.
Amenities: Does it have a pool? Free breakfast? These can make a big difference.
Room Size: Can everyone spread out comfortably? Look for options with suites or adjoining rooms if needed.
Reviews: See what other families say about their stay. Did the kids have a good time? Was it easy for the parents?
### The Arch, City Museum and the rest of the must-sees
St. Louis is packed with sights worth your time, and most of them cluster close enough to string together in a day. Towering monuments, deep history, and wide-open green space all sit within a short drive of each other. Keep your camera handy, because a few of these spots photograph beautifully.
### Iconic Landmarks And Monuments
The Gateway Arch is the landmark everyone comes for, and it earns the attention. This incredible stainless steel monument stands at 630 feet, making it the tallest man-made monument in the Western Hemisphere. You can take a tram ride to the top for amazing views of the city and the Mississippi River. It's a pretty unique experience, and the photos you'll get are excellent. Beyond the Arch, consider a visit to Busch Stadium, home of the St. Louis Cardinals. Even if there isn't a game, you can often take a behind-the-scenes tour to see where the magic happens. For a different kind of historical perspective, check out Laclede's Landing with its cobblestone streets and old brick buildings; it's a great spot for photos.
### Museums For Every Interest
St. Louis has a fantastic array of museums. For art and history fans, the free museums in Forest Park - the Saint Louis Art Museum, the Missouri History Museum, and the Saint Louis Science Center - are all worth a visit and cost nothing to enter. Music lovers can still soak up the city's deep blues heritage at live shows around town. If you're looking for something a bit different, the City Museum is an absolute blast. It's an eclectic mix of playground, art installation, and architectural salvage, built from repurposed materials. It's fun for all ages, though be prepared for some climbing and exploring. For a dose of nature and history combined, the Missouri Botanical Garden is a national historic landmark. It's 79 acres of beautiful landscapes, including a Japanese strolling garden and a vast orchid display. It's a peaceful escape from the city bustle.

### Toasted ravioli, live blues and the neighborhoods
Culture in St. Louis shows up in three places especially: on the plate, on the stage, and in the character of its neighborhoods. Each part of town carries its own personality, and moving between them is half the fun of getting to know the place.
### A Taste Of St. Louis Cuisine
When you think of St. Louis food, barbecue probably comes to mind. While “St. Louis-style” ribs are more about a cut than a specific cooking method, you can find some fantastic BBQ joints. Places like Pappy's Smokehouse offer a taste reminiscent of Memphis style, while Sugarfire Smokehouse blends techniques from around the country. Don't shy away from a line at these popular spots; they tend to move fast and serve up hearty meals quickly. Beyond BBQ, St. Louis has a dynamic food scene. You might find a spot like Winslow's Table, which has a cozy, neighborhood feel and serves farm-to-table dishes. It's a great place to grab breakfast or lunch, and it's often busy with locals, which is always a good sign.
### Discovering The Blues Scene
St. Louis has deep roots in the blues, and the best way to experience it is live. The city helped shape the genre, and its clubs and bars still host blues acts year-round, from intimate neighborhood joints to festival stages in the warmer months. Many places around town also host live blues music, so be sure to check local listings for evening shows. It's a great way to connect with the city's musical heritage.
### Exploring Historic Neighborhoods
St. Louis is often called a “city of neighborhoods,” and for good reason. Each area has its own unique vibe and history. Taking a narrated trolley tour can be a great way to get an overview of the city and discover some of these distinct areas. You'll learn about historic spots, local hangouts, and places that might not be on the typical tourist map. It's a good way to get your bearings and find inspiration for where you want to spend more time. You can find more on specific neighborhoods, block by block, in the St Louis Near Me Directory neighborhood guides.
### When you want a change of scene: day trips
Day Trips From St. Louis
St. Louis itself has plenty to fill your days, but sometimes you just want a change of scene. The city makes a good home base for that. Point the car in almost any direction and you'll hit wine country, historic river towns, or an easy family outing inside a comfortable drive.
### Wine Country Excursions
Missouri actually has a pretty decent wine scene, and you can reach a good chunk of it without going too far. The Augusta and Hermann areas are the go-to spots for a laid-back afternoon out of the city.
Charming towns, nature spots, and historic sites all sit within a short drive, and any one of them makes a solid half-day escape from the city. When you're ready to line up an itinerary, the travel directory linked below is a good place to start pulling the pieces together.
### A weekend or a week: how it comes together
A weekend covers the essentials: ride the tram to the top of the Arch, work your way through a barbecue joint or two, and catch a set of live blues before you head home. A full week gives you room to slow down for Forest Park, the free museums, and a day trip out toward wine country. Either way, build your plan around a few anchor neighborhoods, and you'll spend less time in the car and more time actually in the city. Most people who visit St. Louis end up circling a return trip on the calendar before they've even left.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What’s the best time of year to visit St. Louis?
A.  Spring (April and May) and fall (September and October) bring the best weather, and fall adds festival season, including the Great Forest Park Balloon Race. Summer is hot and humid but packed with outdoor events, while winter is cold and quieter, with fewer crowds, lower hotel rates and the free indoor museums to fall back on.
### Q. How do I get around St. Louis?
A.  Fly in and you can ride straight from the airport: MetroLink’s Red Line runs from both Lambert terminals to the Central West End, Forest Park, Union Station and downtown, so a hotel near a station makes a rental car optional. You’ll still want a car or a rideshare for the Hill, the Missouri Botanical Garden and day trips, and Uber and Lyft are easy to find across the city.
### Q. What is a must see in St. Louis?
A.  The Gateway Arch comes first: ride the tram to the top, and book it ahead, since tickets sell out early and often. Then give Forest Park a full day for the free Zoo, Art Museum, History Museum and Science Center, add City Museum for something no other city has, and catch a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium in season.
### Q. What is the best place to take a road trip from St. Louis?
A.  For a day, drive the Great River Road north through Alton to Grafton, with limestone bluffs along the Mississippi the whole way. Missouri wine country around Augusta and Hermann is the other classic. History fans head to Hannibal for Mark Twain or cross the river to Cahokia Mounds, and families pick Mid America Adventure (formerly Six Flags St. Louis) in Eureka.
### Q. How many hours is it to drive to St. Louis?
A.  It depends where you start. Chicago is about four and a half hours down I-55, Kansas City and Indianapolis are roughly three and a half to four hours on I-70, and Memphis and Nashville each run about four and a half. Build in a little extra if you’re rolling into town during weekday rush hour.
### Q. Is there a bypass around St. Louis, MO?
A.  Yes. I-270 arcs around the north and west sides of the metro, and I-255 finishes the loop through south county and across the river in Illinois, so through-traffic on I-70, I-55, I-44 or I-64 can skip downtown entirely. If St. Louis isn’t your stop, the loop is usually the easier drive.
### Q. Is it safe to walk in downtown St. Louis at night?
A.  The busy parts are your best bet: the Arch grounds, Ballpark Village and the blocks around Busch Stadium fill up on game and event nights. Downtown thins out quickly once the offices close, though, so stick to lit, busy streets, take a rideshare for longer hops after dark, and never leave a bag visible in a parked car.
### Q. Is St. Louis an expensive city?
A.  Not for a visitor. The Zoo, Art Museum, History Museum and Science Center in Forest Park are free, so are the Arch grounds, and hotel rates drop in the off-season. The costs that add up are the Arch tram, City Museum, ballgames and parking, and Arch parking runs cheaper when you buy it online a day ahead.

## Heritage Closed, Its Order Button Didn't: Watch Here Now
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/experience-the-best-game-day-at-heritage-sports-bar-grill
Click. Order placed. Card charged. And nobody in the kitchen at 118 E. Main St. in Collinsville to fry a single wing.
That was Heritage Sports Bar & Grill after it closed, and the strangest part of its ending wasn’t the dark windows. It was the order button. According to St. Louis Restaurant Review, “online ordering remained available even though Heritage was no longer operating normally.” People typed in their card numbers for wings that no kitchen was ever going to fry. The Review, whose affiliated eOrderSTL service Heritage used, says it refunded those customers.
Somewhere on Collinsville’s Main Street a room still roars when the Cardinals score. It just isn’t that one. So think about it the next time you tap “order” at a place you haven’t walked into for a while. A website can outlive a bar by weeks.
Heritage had opened in a historic building that had already housed several bar and restaurant concepts, with what the Review called “considerable optimism.” Then came the abrupt closing, which the Review traces to “trouble within its ownership structure.” Local business coverage reported the doors shut for good without public notice. No last call. Just a group text with nowhere to land.
So here is where it lands now. Every bar on this page was checked against its own website before we named it, and we pulled the details that actually decide a game day: who opens early, who has 30 screens, who doesn’t unlock the door until evening, and who lets you bring the dog.
### What makes a great sports bar?
You can hear the answer before you see it: a room that goes dead quiet on a full count, then a bartender turning up your game because you asked before first pitch, not during it. After that it’s sightlines, enough screens for every game your table cares about, and a kitchen that is still frying when the game goes long.
Here is how to use this page today. Pick the game first, then the bar. If it’s a noon kickoff on a weekend, you need a place that is already open, and Sloan’s Pub House in Collinsville opens at 10am on Saturday and Sunday. If it’s a Monday game in Troy, know that Time Out doesn’t open until 6pm on Mondays. If your table follows four games at once, go to either Hotshots, where both locations list 30 large HDTVs. If the dog is coming, the Wooden Nickel in Glen Carbon says both its patios are dog friendly. Then make one phone call before you leave, because hours move with the season, and a thirty-second call beats a wasted drive across the county.
### Collinsville: stay on Main Street
Heritage’s regulars don’t have to leave the street. Sloan’s Pub House sits at 119 West Main Street, more pub than warehouse of TVs, and that is the point. Its own site lists a main menu, a brunch menu, a fish menu and a cocktail list, with hours running to 2am on Friday and Saturday. Call 618-855-9100.
The kitchen runs till 10pm, and a fried-food late-night menu keeps going till midnight. That matters more than it sounds. Extra innings, a West Coast start, a double-overtime game that nobody planned for: the fryer is still hissing when the other kitchens on the block have gone quiet. If the old place felt like yours, give this one three visits before you judge it. One for a big game, one for a nothing game, one for brunch.
### Edwardsville: park once, walk the strip
Downtown Edwardsville is the deepest game-day bench on the Illinois side, and you can hear it from the sidewalk on a warm evening: a cheer drifting out of a patio, a door swinging open on a different game, somebody yelling a score down the block.
Big Daddy’s opened its Edwardsville location in August of 2008. It has a beer garden with an outside bar and 9 HD TVs spread inside and out. On a mild night with a full slate, the beer garden is the seat you want.
Foundry Public House at 126 N. Main St. is the pick when half the table cares more about the food than the score. One honest flag, and it is the Heritage lesson in miniature: the bar is under new ownership, and the Edwardsville City Council granted the new owner a liquor license. Its website did not load when we checked. That doesn’t mean anything is wrong. It means you call before you build a night around it.
Hotshots Edwardsville at 2511 South State Route 157 is the machine built for watching everything at once: 30 large HDTVs, an 82-inch mega HDTV, a large patio and pool tables. It stays open till 2am on Friday and Saturday; call (618) 307-9723. This is where you take the friend who follows three teams and refuses to choose.
The smart Edwardsville move is to park once and walk. Start with a drink in the Big Daddy’s beer garden while the early game plays out, eat at whichever kitchen your table agrees on, and finish wherever the late game sounds loudest. Three rooms, three moods, and you never move the car.
### Glen Carbon and Troy
The Wooden Nickel Pub & Grill at 171 S. Main Street in Glen Carbon is the small-room option, with a front patio and a back patio, both dog friendly by its own account. Call (618) 288-2141 to check hours. Less spectacle, more sound: one game on, a regular calling the play before the replay does, a dog asleep under the table with its chin on somebody’s shoe.
Time Out Sports Bar & Grill at 111 West Market Street in Troy runs 11:30am to 1:30am most days, but on Mondays the doors open at 6pm. Its site pitches it as a venue for holiday parties, which matters if your watch party outgrows a table. The number is (618) 667-2221.
Still hunting for your new home bar? Browse bars, restaurants and local favorites on both sides of the river at St Louis Near Me Directory, with photos and hours in one place.
If you’re the one pouring the beer or running the fryer at a Metro East bar, read this twice. Every Heritage regular is looking for a new spot right now, and plenty of them are asking ChatGPT instead of a friend. A Gold listing puts your room, your screens and your specials in front of those customers for under a dollar a day. See who AI names instead of you, or put your bar on the map.
### O’Fallon: the biggest screen on the list
Hotshots O’Fallon at 1319 Central Park Dr. pairs 30 large HDTVs with a 105-inch projector screen, plus pool tables and dart boards. Call (618) 624-4200. It runs till 1am Sunday through Thursday and till 2am on Friday and Saturday. When a whole room tilts toward one screen and goes silent on a 3-2 count, you will understand why people make the drive.
The posted draft list opens with a run of IPAs, Sierra Nevada Hazy Little Thing first, and it is long enough to settle most arguments at the table. Get there before kickoff if you want a seat facing the projector. Once the room fills, the best view is wherever you happen to be standing, and on a big night that is a cheerful kind of crowded, shoulder to shoulder, the whole place counting down the last two minutes together.
### What we left off, and why
We cut every bar we could not confirm through its own channels, including spots in Belleville, Granite City and downtown O’Fallon that earlier versions of this page named. Some of them may be pouring right now. We just couldn’t prove it from the source, and after what happened with Heritage’s order button, “probably open” isn’t good enough to send you there. If your favorite is missing and still pouring, tell us and we will check it.
The same goes for you as a customer. Before you pay online at a bar you haven’t visited in a while, look for signs of life: a recent post, a phone that rings and someone who answers, a menu with this season’s specials. Thirty seconds of checking protects your card from a kitchen that isn’t there.
Unrelated, but nobody in the history of the Metro East has won the Provel argument at a bar. Settle it over late-night eats instead.
### Adopting a new bar
Losing a home bar is a small grief, and the cure takes more than one visit. Go for a nothing game, not the playoff crush, and listen to what the room sounds like when it’s half full. Learn the bartender’s name; they’ll learn your order faster than you expect. Sit in the same spot twice, and order the same thing the second time so the kitchen starts to know you. By the third game, somebody will save you a stool without being asked, and that is the moment a bar starts to feel like home again. Tip like you want the place to still exist next season, because Heritage is proof that no bar is guaranteed one.
And when the chalkboard says trivia night or a booster-club fundraiser, go to one. That’s the difference between a bar you go to and a bar that’s yours.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What’s the difference between a sports bar and a bar?
A.  A sports bar is built around the broadcast. Screens are placed for viewing rather than decoration, the sound system can carry a game, and the schedule drives the staffing. A regular bar may have a TV; a sports bar arranges the room around it. Hotshots, with 30 large HDTVs at each Metro East location, is the far end of that scale. The Wooden Nickel in Glen Carbon is closer to a pub that happens to have the game on.
### Q. What is sports bar etiquette?
A.  Ask before you claim a table on a big game day, and ask early if you want your game on sound, not at kickoff. Don’t stand in someone’s sightline. Keep the rivalry good-natured. And if you’re holding a table for three hours, keep ordering.
### Q. How much should you tip at a sports bar?
A.  The usual restaurant standard applies. Tip on the pre-discount total when a special or happy-hour price is involved, because the work is the same. A long stay on a busy game day is worth more, since you’re holding a table the server would otherwise turn.
### Q. What is the most ordered item at a sports bar?
A.  Wings, with nachos and a shareable fried platter close behind: food built for a table watching a screen rather than each other. During a rush, order before halftime, because the kitchen will run long.
### Q. Where is the best place to watch sports in St. Louis?
A.  On the Illinois side, it depends on the game. For every game at once, either Hotshots, with 30 large HDTVs at both locations. For a beer garden, Big Daddy’s in Edwardsville. For an early weekend kickoff close to the old Heritage spot, Sloan’s Pub House on Collinsville’s Main Street.
### Q. Where are the best bars in St. Louis?
A.  The best bar is the one where the room sounds right for the game you came to watch. For the Metro East, this page is our honest shortlist. For the Missouri side, browse bars by neighborhood on St Louis Near Me Directory and call ahead.
### Q. What network do the St. Louis Cardinals play on?
A.  Major League Baseball now produces and distributes in-market Cardinals games. Fans can watch on traditional cable and satellite providers or through Cardinals.TV, the MLB streaming platform in the MLB app, according to the Cardinals’ announcement. Any of the bars above can tell you which channel they have it on when you call.
### Q. Can I bring food into Busch Stadium?
A.  Yes. The Cardinals’ ballpark guide says guests may bring their own food and drinks into Busch Stadium for all games, within the bag policy. Non-alcoholic drinks must be in factory-sealed clear plastic containers no larger than 2 liters, and outside food is not allowed in some premium areas such as the Cardinals Club.

### Choosing the Right Bandana for You
Two bandanas can look identical on the shelf and wear nothing alike once you own them. Fabric, size, and print each change how one sits and where it works. A few minutes of thought up front saves you from a drawer full of squares you never reach for. Here is what actually matters.
### Material Matters: Cotton vs. Silk
This is probably the biggest decision you'll make. Cotton bandanas are the workhorses. They're durable, breathable, and easy to wash. If you plan on wearing your bandana for practical reasons, like keeping sweat out of your eyes during a St. Louis summer festival or tying it around your head for a hike, cotton is your best bet. It's also generally more affordable. You can find some really nice cotton ones at local markets.
Silk, on the other hand, is all about luxury and style. It feels amazing against your skin and has a beautiful sheen. A silk bandana is more of a fashion statement, perfect for dressing up an outfit or adding a touch of elegance. They're delicate, though, so you'll want to handle them with care and probably get them dry-cleaned. They're less common in everyday shops, but you might find them in more upscale boutiques.
### Size and Shape Considerations
Bandanas come in different sizes, and the size you choose will affect how you can wear it. A standard 22x22 inch bandana is pretty versatile. You can tie it around your neck, wear it as a headscarf, or even tie it to a bag. Smaller ones might be better for wrist wraps or as accents. Larger ones can be folded into more elaborate headwear or even used as a makeshift bag.
### Color and Design Selection Tips
This is where you get to have fun! Think about your personal style and what you'll be wearing your bandana with.
Solid Colors: Classic and easy to match. A black or white bandana goes with almost anything. Red is bold, blue is calming.
Patterns: Paisley is the traditional choice, but don't be afraid to explore other patterns like florals, geometrics, or even novelty prints.
St. Louis Themed: Keep an eye out for bandanas featuring local landmarks or colors. You might even find some custom options that incorporate St. Louis pride.
When picking a design, consider where you'll be wearing it. A busy pattern might be great for a casual outing, but a more subtle design might be better for a slightly dressier occasion. Think about how it will look with your St. Louis culinary scene adventures.
Color and Design Selection Tips
Ultimately, the best bandana for you is the one that makes you feel good. Go to Mom Said No in Alton IL and don't be afraid to experiment! Try different materials, sizes, and patterns until you find your perfect match.

## The Bridge the Army Eyed for Demolition Practice: Outdoor St. Louis, Mostly Free
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-outdoor-activities-in-st-louis-for-every-adventure-level
Sixty feet above the Mississippi, the wind shoves at your jacket and the steel bridge under your shoes kinks 30 degrees in the middle of the river. Army demolition teams once eyed this exact walk, the old Chain of Rocks Bridge on Route 66, as something to blow up for practice. It survived the 1970s only because scrap steel got too cheap to bother. Cars haven’t crossed it since 1968. You can, free. Interstate traffic hums from the newer bridge upstream, the river churns brown below, and the bend is there because riverboat men refused to steer between its piers and two water intake towers.
Most of outdoor St. Louis works that way. By the second overlook at Castlewood your shoes are white with limestone dust, your calves burn, the Meramec slides past far below, and a freight train grinds along the tracks down in the valley. Downtown is about twenty minutes behind you. A century ago St. Louisans rode out here on weekends to dance at riverside clubs; the clubs are long gone, the bluffs aren’t.
Back in town, here’s the part most guides skip. Forest Park is bigger than Central Park and the zoo inside it is free, because since 1971 City and County property owners have paid for it through the Zoo-Museum District tax. Live here? You already bought your ticket. Visiting? A St. Louisan bought it for you. Same deal at the Missouri Botanical Garden: City and County residents walk in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon, which saves two adults $32 (kids 12 and under are always free).
Do this today: hike the River Scene Trail at Castlewood (about three miles; the park entrance is 1401 Kiefer Creek Road in Ballwin), eat lunch on a blanket in Forest Park, then catch sunset on the bridge from Chain of Rocks Park at 10840 Riverview Drive, open until half an hour after sunset. Everything else, from the Katy Trail to Cahokia Mounds, is below, sorted by the kind of day you want.
### The Free-Day Cheat Sheet
### Easy Does It: Art Hill, the Arch Grounds and Tower Grove
Start with the park St. Louisans measure every other park against. On a warm evening in Forest Park, blankets dot Art Hill, the Grand Basin goes gold below the Art Museum, and bikes tick past on the paved paths. Inside its 1,300 acres sit four free attractions (the Zoo, the Saint Louis Art Museum, the Saint Louis Science Center and the Missouri History Museum), plus boating on the Grand Basin. You could spend a dozen weekends here and not repeat yourself.
Downtown, the grounds of Gateway Arch National Park are free to roam, with riverside paths beneath the country’s tallest monument (the tram to the top is ticketed, the walk around is not). And in the city’s south side, Tower Grove Park - a 289-acre Victorian landmark next to the Missouri Botanical Garden - is a favorite for a farmers-market morning or a shady picnic. For manicured beauty, the Missouri Botanical Garden (paid admission) is one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country, and Laumeier Sculpture Park pairs 105 free acres with more than 60 large outdoor sculptures - it’s celebrating its 50th year in 2026. North of the Arch, the St. Louis Riverfront Trail follows the river about 16 miles to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge.
Tower Grove Park’s West Gatehouse at the Kingshighway entrance - look for the “TGP” worked into the slate roof. (Photo: Lane Forman)
### Bring the Kids: A Free Zoo and the Clydesdales
The rope climber at Lindenwood Park in St. Louis, MO, photographed for St Louis Near Me Directory by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026.
The playground at Lindenwood Park in St. Louis, MO, photographed for St Louis Near Me Directory by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026.
Few cities make family days this affordable. The Saint Louis Zoo is consistently ranked among the country’s best - and general admission is free. Grant’s Farm, the Busch family’s historic animal preserve, is also free to enter (you just pay for parking), with a tram ride past roaming deer and bison, a goat corral, and the famous Clydesdales. For a quieter outing, Suson Park in south county has a small working farm with animals kids can meet, and Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park - the largest lake in St. Louis County - offers flat trails, sailing and rowing, and plenty of room to run.
Unrelated, and we know it - but St. Louis Place has a story.
### Real Adventure: The Bluffs Above the Meramec
Think St. Louis is all flat? The bluffs will fix that. Castlewood State Park, about twenty minutes west, is the local hiker’s favorite, with switchback trails up to dramatic overlooks above the Meramec River. Cliff Cave Park in south county offers rugged riverbluff trails (the cave itself is usually closed, and trails occasionally close after flooding, so check the county’s status first). For a woodsy, wildflower-filled ramble, Shaw Nature Reserve in Gray Summit protects 2,400+ acres of Ozark-border landscape with miles of trails.
### On Two Wheels: 240 Miles of Crushed Limestone
St. Louis is a genuinely great trail city. The Katy Trail is the longest developed rails-to-trails path in the country - about 240 crushed-limestone miles running from near Kansas City to the St. Louis suburbs - and the stretch through the Missouri River wine country near Augusta is a bucket-list ride. Closer in, the Great Rivers Greenway network links more than 140 miles of paved greenways across the region, and the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge carries walkers and cyclists across the Mississippi on a historic Route 66 span with skyline views. Rent a bike or lace up your shoes; the mileage is there. And you don’t have to be a serious cyclist to enjoy it - the crushed-limestone Katy Trail and the paved greenways are flat, shaded, and beginner-friendly, so a casual family ride is just as doable as a long training day. Several outfitters near the trails rent bikes by the hour if you don’t have your own.
### Out of Town for a Day: Monks Mound and Billion-Year-Old Granite
When you’ve got a full day, a few destinations are worth the drive. Just across the river in Illinois, Cahokia Mounds is a UNESCO World Heritage Site - the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, where you can climb Monks Mound, the biggest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. (Note: the site’s Interpretive Center is currently closed for renovation, but the grounds, mounds, and trails remain open.) South of the city, Elephant Rocks State Park lets you scramble over billion-year-old granite boulders the size of small houses. And to the west, the Augusta wine country and Klondike Park pair Katy Trail access with river-valley views and a tasting or two.
### What to Do Outside Today, Season by Season
The metro rewards every season. In spring and fall, hit the bluff trails at Castlewood or a long stretch of the Katy Trail when the weather’s perfect. In summer, go early for the Zoo or a paddle at Creve Coeur Lake before the heat, and save shady Tower Grove or the Botanical Garden for the afternoon. In winter, Forest Park’s paths and the free museums keep you moving even on gray days. There’s no wrong season to get outside here - only different versions of a good day. Fall may be the secret best season: the bluff trails light up with color, the Katy Trail is perfect, and the summer humidity has finally broken. Spring brings wildflowers to Shaw Nature Reserve and the Botanical Garden into full bloom. Even a mild winter day is worth a walk around Forest Park or a climb up Monks Mound with the crowds gone.

St. Louis sits at the meeting of two great rivers, and there’s more water play than newcomers expect. Creve Coeur Lake is the county’s largest, with sailing, rowing, kayak rentals, and a flat paved loop that connects into the greenway system. The Great Rivers Greenway keeps adding paved miles that link parks, neighborhoods, and the riverfront - you can ride for hours without touching a road. And for a only-in-St.-Louis photo, the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge lets you walk or bike a mile across the Mississippi on a retired Route 66 span. Add in fishing lakes at county parks like Suson and you’ve got a whole warm-weather category most visitors never discover.

### The Prettiest Outdoor Spots in St. Louis
If the goal is pretty rather than sweaty, start at Art Hill in Forest Park around sunset, when the light drops over the Grand Basin below the Art Museum and half the neighborhood is out on blankets. Tower Grove Park is the other postcard: its Victorian pavilions and gatehouses look like nothing else in town, and the paths are flat enough for a stroller. The Missouri Botanical Garden hands you its Japanese Garden, the Climatron dome and the rose gardens in one loop, and if you live in the City or the County it’s free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings from 7 a.m. to noon ($16 otherwise, kids 12 and under free). Want a view you earn? Climb to the bluff overlooks at Castlewood State Park and watch the Meramec curl past below. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge is the photographer’s pick, a mile of retired Route 66 that bends in the middle of the Mississippi because riverboat men fought a straight route past two water intake towers. John Carpenter filmed Escape from New York on it. Park on the Missouri side at Chain of Rocks Park, 10840 Riverview Drive, open 7 a.m. to half an hour after sunset. And for strange and beautiful, Laumeier’s giant outdoor sculptures and the 1.5-billion-year-old granite boulders at Elephant Rocks photograph better than they have any right to; the paved Braille Trail winds right through them. Nearly all of it is free. Bring the good camera anyway.
### Make a Full Day of It for the Price of Gas and a Sandwich
The nicest thing about outdoor St. Louis is how easily you can stack a day. A classic combo: a morning walk or bike through Forest Park, a picnic by the Grand Basin, then the free Art Museum up on Art Hill when you need a break from the sun. Another: hike the bluffs at Castlewood in the morning, then cool off with lunch in nearby Kirkwood or a float on the Meramec. Out west, ride a stretch of the Katy Trail from Augusta and reward yourself with a winery stop. Because so many of these spots are free or nearly free, you can build a full, memorable day for the price of gas and a sandwich.
