### Q. What are 5 outdoor activities?
A.  Five great St. Louis outdoor activities: walk or bike Forest Park, visit the free Saint Louis Zoo, ride the Katy Trail, hike the bluffs at Castlewood State Park, and meet the animals at Grant’s Farm. Nearly all are free or nearly free, so you can stack several in one day.
### Q. What is the most popular outdoor activity?
A.  Walking and biking through Forest Park is arguably the most popular outdoor activity in St. Louis - the roughly 1,300-acre park is the beating heart of the city’s outdoors, larger than Central Park, with paved paths, boating on the Grand Basin, and four free attractions. Best of all, it’s free.
### Q. What are some fun things to do outside of St. Louis?
A.  For day trips outside the city, cross into Illinois for Cahokia Mounds, a UNESCO World Heritage Site where you can climb Monks Mound. Head south to Elephant Rocks State Park to scramble over giant granite boulders, or west to the Augusta wine country and Klondike Park along the Katy Trail.
### Q. What are the best parks in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Forest Park is the anchor at roughly 1,300 acres, with the Zoo, the Art Museum and miles of paths inside it. Tower Grove Park is the walkable Victorian favorite, Laumeier Sculpture Park puts large-scale art outdoors for free, and Castlewood State Park about twenty minutes west has the bluff-top overlooks above the Meramec River.

## $75 for a $150 Bottle: Wednesday at Roberto’s, Where the Regulars Own the Bar
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/experience-authentic-italian-dining-at-roberto-s-trattoria
$75 for a $150 bottle. The white cloth is crisp under your wrists, a plate of toasted ravioli lands in the middle of the table, and the Italian reserve you’d have saved for an anniversary is suddenly a Wednesday wine, poured beside a 9-ounce prime filet in gorgonzola cream. On Wednesdays at Roberto’s Trattoria & Chophouse, in the Concord Plaza shopping center just south of Sunset Hills, every bottle on the list priced at $150 or less is half off.
Rest your forearms on the granite-topped bar and you’re where the owners sat. For about ten years, Matt and Jami Hines ate Wednesday dinner right there, and Matt had been eating founder Roberto Zanti’s cooking for more than twenty years. After long conversations with Zanti, who had built the place since opening Zanti’s on Gravois Road in Affton, the couple bought it to carry on what he started. Zanti once told St. Louis Magazine his goal was “to do the impossible to make people happy,” and the Hineses say they’ve kept their promise to him.
End the night the way they did, with a small glass of the house limoncello. It’s made in house from organic, hand-peeled lemons, pure cane sugar and grain alcohol: bright peel first, real sweetness, then warm all the way down. They’ll sell you a 500ml bottle to take home, too.
The short list before you book:
Dinner is Tuesday through Saturday, 4:30 to 10 p.m.; lunch is Tuesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; closed Sunday and Monday.
Reservations are recommended. Use OpenTable or call (314) 842-9998; nine or more must call, with a $200 deposit. Cancel inside 48 hours and the deposit isn’t lost: it comes back as a gift certificate.
Corkage is $25, so on a Wednesday a $50 bottle off their list costs the same as opening your own.
The half-off skips 375ml half-bottles, and the site doesn’t say whether it covers Wednesday lunch. Ask.
No children’s menu, no high chairs or booster seats. Casual clothes are fine.
### From Zanti’s in Affton to Concord Village
Zanti opened Zanti’s on Gravois Road, renamed it Roberto’s, then moved a few miles west to a bigger space in Concord Village and later added “Chophouse” to the name. For families in Mehlville, Oakville, Sunset Hills and Crestwood, it’s the white-tablecloth night out that doesn’t start with a parking garage downtown, and its lunch menu, dinner menu and wine list are online to read before you go. ### Half trattoria, half chophouse
### Pasta on one side of the menu, steak on the other

### Q. What makes a restaurant a trattoria?
A.  In Italy, a trattoria is a casual, family-run restaurant a step below a formal ristorante: regional home cooking, a short menu, house wine and fair prices. Roberto’s uses the word loosely. ## Nothing at the Door: 6 St. Louis Must-Sees, and the Tax That Opens 3
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-ultimate-guide-to-explore-st-louis-must-see-attractions
Your calves start burning about halfway up Art Hill in Forest Park. At the top you pull open the heavy door of the Saint Louis Art Museum, step into stone-cool air, and nobody asks you for a ticket. Somebody already paid for your visit, and you will never meet them.
They are the property owners of St. Louis City and St. Louis County. Their property tax supports the Zoo-Museum District, and that is why the Art Museum, the Saint Louis Zoo and the Science Center charge no general admission. Voters in the city and county approved it themselves. So when your cousin from out of town asks what St. Louis is famous for, here is the line worth repeating at dinner: the best day in this city is one some St. Louis homeowner’s tax bill already covered for you.
### What are the must-see attractions in St. Louis?
So run the numbers at the kitchen table before you load the car. Say it’s two adults and two kids between 3 and 15. Three of the six charge no general admission at all: the Zoo, the Art Museum and the Science Center. The Arch tram is the ticket you plan around, from $15 for adults 16 and up and $11 for children 3 to 15, about $52 for the family at the starting price. Book it ahead at gatewayarch.com, because prices vary by date, and know that the museum under the Arch and the Old Courthouse are free with no ticket at all. The Missouri Botanical Garden is the gate where living here pays: $16 for ages 13 and up, or $6 at the STL Resident Rate with proof of residency.
Then the parking arm goes up, and the free morning gets its first price. The Zoo’s own lots charge non-members $20 per car, and the Science Center’s main lot at 5050 Oakland Avenue is $15, debit or credit only. Free doors, paid asphalt. Put it in the budget before you pull a ticket at the gate.
### The free ones, and why they stay free
The bill for your free afternoon lands in somebody else’s mailbox: a property tax bill in St. Louis City or St. Louis County. The Zoo’s own history page puts it plainly: the district leads cultural institutions that are supported by property tax from St. Louis County and St. Louis City. The district was set up so city and county residents would support three of them: the Zoo, the Art Museum and the Science Center. The Missouri Botanical Garden and the Missouri History Museum joined later, also with the voters’ approval. Five institutions, one tax, and a city that decided culture should not have a cover charge.
Inside, nobody is checking tickets, because there are none. The museum’s own line is short and blunt: admission to the Museum is free every day.
At the Zoo you hear it before you see it: a kid shrieking at the first thing with fur, gravel crunching under stroller wheels, a gate you walk straight through with your wallet still in your pocket. The Zoo’s own visit page says it in capital letters: admission is FREE. That means you can leave at nap time without feeling like you wasted a ticket.
The Science Center is the rainy-day answer. Kids tip their heads back under the McDonnell Planetarium dome and press close to the glass. General admission is always free; the OMNIMAX films, the planetarium shows and the special exhibitions are the ticketed part, so decide which one before the kids see the posters.
### The Arch is the one that costs, and is worth it
Stand between the legs of the Arch and tilt your head back until your neck complains. The top is 630 feet up, and that ride is the one St. Louis does not hand you for free. Here is the honest answer to the question every visitor types into a phone: no, the tram to the top of the Gateway Arch is not free unless you are 2 or under. The National Park Service lists the Tram Ride to the Top starting at $15 for adults 16 and up and $11 for kids 3 to 15. Prices vary by date, and tickets sell through gatewayarch.com, so book before you drive downtown on a busy weekend.
What you get for it: a slow, humming climb inside the curve of the steel, your knees nearly touching a stranger’s, and then the window. The Mississippi spread brown and wide below, the barges crawling, Illinois flat to the horizon on one side and the whole city stacked up on the other. The park asks you to allow 45 to 60 minutes for the whole tram experience.
The part people miss: the museum under the Gateway Arch is always free for all visitors and needs no ticket. Entrance to the Old Courthouse is free too. If the tram is sold out, you still walk away with the Arch overhead, cold and silver against the sky, and a museum day that cost you nothing.
### City Museum, where adults forget to act like adults
City Museum is housed in an old shoe factory in Downtown St. Louis, and it does not behave like any museum you have been dragged through. Slides, caves, climbers, even a bus. You will hear it before you see it: a roar of kids and grown-ups shrieking down chutes and calling to each other through the dark. It is loud, and the people who complain about their scraped knees are the same ones planning a return trip on the drive home. Wear jeans. Leave the nice shoes in the hotel.
### The Garden: the one big exception at the gate
The Missouri Botanical Garden joined the same tax district later, but it still sells tickets. General admission is $16 for ages 13 and up. The STL Resident Rate is $6, with proof of residency. If you live here, put that proof in your pocket before you leave the house: it is $10 back on your ticket at the gate. Then go anyway. Step through the gate and the traffic noise drops away behind the walls. The air turns damp and green, gravel crunches under your shoes, and for an hour the city you just drove through feels very far off.
People are asking
### Which St. Louis attractions are truly must-see on a first trip?
Start with the Gateway Arch, where the tram to the top starts at $15 for adults and the museum underneath is always free. Then add City Museum, the playground built inside an old downtown shoe factory. The Saint Louis Zoo and the Saint Louis Art Museum are free to enter, and so is the Science Center, which credits the residents of the Zoo-Museum District for its free general admission. Finish at the Missouri Botanical Garden, which joined the same tax district later; check its ticket page for current rates.
### What are some cute neighborhoods to visit in St. Louis?
The attractions are the postcard. The neighborhoods are the trip. Pick one, park once, and walk until your feet ache:
The Delmar Loop - a stretch of record stores, theaters and restaurants from half the countries on earth, loud on a warm night. Our Delmar Loop dining guide maps it.
Soulard - red brick, narrow streets, the clatter of the farmers market and blues leaking out of corner bars. Start with our Soulard guide.
The Central West End - big old houses, shaded sidewalks and cafe tables full of people who look like they have nowhere to be. The Central West End guide covers the food.
The Hill - the smell of garlic and baking bread on every block. Go hungry and read the guide to The Hill first.
### Is Saint Louis a walkable city?
Between districts, not really. Plan on driving between districts. Inside a district, absolutely. The Loop, Soulard, the Central West End and the Hill all reward the person who parks once and wanders, because the good stuff is in the side streets you would blow past in a windshield tour. Plan your day as two or three walkable pockets connected by short drives, and you will see more and sit in less traffic. Bring the comfortable shoes, not the cute ones.
### One day, three pockets, almost no ticket stubs
If you only have one day, here is the route locals give their own relatives. Start downtown early, while the riverfront is still cool and quiet, with the Arch tram and the free museum underneath. Drive west to Forest Park and spend the middle of the day at the free Zoo or the free Art Museum, whichever your group will argue about less. Pack water; Art Hill is steeper than it looks. Then pick one neighborhood for the evening, the Loop or the Central West End, park once, and let dinner run long. You will end the day with tired feet, a camera roll full of the Arch, and most of your attraction budget still in your pocket.
### Eat like you live here
St. Louis food is its own dialect. Order toasted ravioli and get the crunch, the hot meat inside and the marinara on your fingers. Try a square of gooey butter cake that sticks to the roof of your mouth. Eat a thin, cracker-crisp pizza with Provel and decide for yourself which side of that argument you are on. On a sticky summer night, line up for a frozen custard concrete so thick the spoon stands up. Rather than list a hundred places here, our best-restaurants guide and the neighborhood guides above do the heavy lifting.

### A rainy day plan that costs almost nothing
Weather turns fast here. When it does, the free Science Center is the move, and if the stars are calling, read our guide to the McDonnell Planetarium first. The Art Museum is a second free indoor stop. Add City Museum and you have a full rainy day where the only wet thing is your umbrella in the car.
### When to go
St. Louis is a four-season city, and each season changes the plan. Spring puts color back in the Garden and Forest Park and pulls everyone onto the patios. Summer is hot and heavy, so do the outdoor stops in the morning and the cool, quiet museums in the afternoon. Fall is the best patio weather of the year. Winter is quieter, and it is when the free indoor museums earn their keep. Whenever you come, check hours on each attraction’s own site before a long drive, because schedules shift by season.
Quick test for out-of-towners: if you leave without trying toasted ravioli, did you even visit? Start on the Hill.

### How much is it to go up the STL Arch?
The Tram Ride to the Top costs $15 to $19 for adults 16 and up and $11 to $15 for kids 3 to 15, set by the date you pick, and peak days cost the most. Infants 2 and under ride free, and an America the Beautiful pass takes $3 off each tram ticket, up to four tickets per pass.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is the zoo in St. Louis still free?
A.  Yes. The Saint Louis Zoo’s own visit page says admission is free. It stays free because the Zoo is part of the Zoo-Museum District, which is supported by property tax from St. Louis City and St. Louis County.
### Q. Can you go up the St. Louis Arch for free?
A.  Not unless you are 2 or under. The Tram Ride to the Top starts at $15 for adults 16 and up and $11 for kids 3 to 15, with prices that vary by date. The museum under the Gateway Arch is always free and needs no ticket, and so is the Old Courthouse.
### Q. What are the top 10 things to do in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Ride the Arch tram, walk the free museum underneath, lose an afternoon at City Museum, spend a free morning at the Saint Louis Zoo, climb Art Hill to the free Art Museum, take kids to the free Science Center, pay the gate at the Missouri Botanical Garden, walk the Delmar Loop, eat your way across the Hill, and wander Soulard.
### Q. Is Saint Louis a walkable city?
A.  Inside its neighborhoods, yes; between them, you will want a car. The Loop, Soulard, the Central West End and the Hill are made for walking, but plan on driving between them.
### Q. What are some cute neighborhoods to visit in St. Louis?
A.  Soulard for red brick and blues, the Central West End for shaded sidewalks and cafes, the Hill for Italian food, and the Delmar Loop for shops, music and restaurants from around the world.
### Q. Which neighborhood in St. Louis is the most walkable?
A.  For a visitor, the Central West End and the Delmar Loop are the easiest to explore on foot, with restaurants and shops packed close together. Soulard is a close third if you like old brick streets and live music.

## $76 to Walk, $35 to Drive: The Best St. Louis Christmas Lights for a Family of Four
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-christmas-lights-in-st-louis-this-holiday-season
“Burning wood embers and smoke will be present.”
The Missouri Botanical Garden puts that smoke warning on its own Garden Glow page. It’s meant as a caution. It reads like an invitation. S’more roasting and warming fire pits burn at the Central Axis and Linnean Plaza, so your coat comes home smelling like a campfire. Over at the Saint Louis Zoo, the Wild Lights page promises open firepits too, and a specialty hot chocolate in naughty or nice versions. And at the Anheuser-Busch brewery, the Clydesdales come through behind a marching band at 7:30 every night, weather permitting.
Then the bill comes, and it splits the season in two.
The walk-throughs charge by the head. The drive-throughs charge by the car. Four $19 tickets to Wild Lights at the Zoo come to $76. That same family of four, with room for four more, rolls through WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway for $35, the price on its own page for a car of up to eight people.
Three money facts most families miss. Garden Glow has Family Nights when kids 3 to 12 pay $6 instead of $12 and nonmember adults pay $22 instead of $24, so two adults and two kids pay $56 instead of $72. Its same-day tickets go up $2 after 4:30 p.m., so buy at lunch, not in the parking lot. And the cheapest night at the brewery comes after Christmas, not before: for a few nights Anheuser-Busch opens the main gate at Busch Place and Arsenal and lets cars drive Pestalozzi Street free, 5 to 10 p.m.
Neither one is the wrong night. They are different nights. On foot, it’s wood smoke, cold fingers and a kid choosing between naughty and nice. In the car, it’s the whole family together in the dark, headlights off, Christmas music coming through your own stereo on 89.5 FM, the car creeping along at around 2 to 5 mph while about 2 miles of LED lights pulse past the windshield. Decide which night you want first. Then let the head count pick the show.
### What are the best Christmas lights in St. Louis?
For a walk, Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden puts its lights on a path about a mile long, and the walk takes 45 minutes to an hour. Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo and the Grant’s Farm walk-through are the other walks, and Brewery Lights fills the Anheuser-Busch brewery with a light tunnel and a Clydesdale parade. In the car, WonderLight’s Christmas costs $35 a carload and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka starts at $35. For the homemade version, there’s Candy Cane Lane in St. Louis Hills.
### Three walking nights, from the parking lot to the last fire pit
Garden Glow starts on a street corner. You park free in one of the Garden’s two lots at Shaw Boulevard and Vandeventer Avenue, one block west of the Garden, and ride the nonstop shuttle to the entrance. On busy evenings the Garden says to allow extra time for parking and the shuttle, so the night starts with kids bouncing on their heels in the cold. Then the path, about a mile of it, 45 minutes to an hour by the Garden’s own count. The lights are animated and flashing, and the Garden notes they may affect anyone susceptible to photosensitivity. Inside, the Holiday Flower and Train Show is included with your ticket: model trains running through miniature landscapes and poinsettias, open nightly during Garden Glow hours. That’s the stop a five-year-old has to be pried away from. Near the end the smoke finds you, at the fire pits on the Central Axis and Linnean Plaza. S’more roasting kits are sold at retail spots around the grounds. By then the cold is in your toes, and the shuttle back to the car is the last stretch.
Wild Lights at the Zoo runs on no clock at all. Wild Lights has no timed entry. Doors open at 5 p.m., last entry is 8, and parking is free on both Zoo lots as available, so you pull in whenever the kids are ready. Up on Historic Hill the Zoo counts over 1 million twinkling lights. Go to Penguin & Puffin Coast first, because it closes at 8 p.m., and it’s one of the animal exhibits still open after dark. Then the firepits. Roast s’mores, or let each kid pick the naughty or the nice hot chocolate and hold it in both hands. Kris Kringle takes pictures every night until just before Christmas, so the photo line is part of the walk.
Brewery Lights is the night that ends with horses. At 7:30 the parade comes through the red-brick brewery: floats, a trolley, a marching band and the Clydesdales, weather permitting. Everything before it is the warm-up. You show up within the hour of your time slot, park free, and stand about 10 minutes in line at the check-in tent, where every guest 21 and up gets a complimentary beer before going in. Inside are two 50-foot digital holiday trees, giant nutcrackers and a light tunnel in the Kids Winter Wonderland. The Biergarten sells toasted ravioli and pretzels from 5 to 8 p.m.
One warning: Brewery Lights has no entry after 8 p.m., so a late start can cost you the horses.
Grant’s Farm runs its holiday walk-through on select nights, 5 to 10 p.m., with last entry at 9. A tram takes you in. From there it’s live carolers on the steps of the Busch family home, a 50-foot animated Christmas tree synchronized to holiday music, Santa and Mrs. Claus in the Tiergarten, and complimentary carousel rides when the weather cooperates. Tickets are $15 a person, and children 3 and under are free.
Wild Lights: $19, or $16 for Zoo members; children 0 to 23 months free; last entry 8 p.m.
Brewery Lights: reservations required; a $25 Flex Ticket works on any available night, even a sold-out one; children 5 and under enter free with a general admission ticket.
Garden Glow: same-day admission goes up $2 after 4:30 p.m.; the full price breakdown is further down.
### Which drive-throughs are worth the gas?
These are the short versions. For routes, timing and how to prep the car, our full drive-through Christmas lights guide goes show by show.
WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway is the big synchronized one: over 1 million LED lights set to Christmas music you play through your own car stereo, on 89.5 FM. The full song selection lasts about 45 minutes, and its producer bills it as the area’s largest drive-through Christmas light show. It’s open nightly, holidays included, rain, shine or snow. At the entrance every car turns off its headlights, so the whole line rolls through by the glow of the displays. It’s $35 a car for up to eight passengers, tickets are sold in two-hour time slots, and the dog can come if it stays in the car. Learn how to tune the radio and kill the headlights before you reach the ticket booth; check-in goes faster when nobody is hunting for the switch.
Santa’s Magical Kingdom sits at Jellystone Park off I-44 at Exit 261 in Eureka. Its 35 acres hold four-story doors, a 300-foot waterfall of lights, an elves’ village in the trees, a Tunnel of Dancing Lights the length of a football field, and a lighted Gateway Arch with a fireworks effect. Family-vehicle admission starts at $35, it charges by the carload so squeezing Grandma in costs nothing extra, and you pay cash at the exit booth. Here’s the move worth knowing: book the open-air holiday wagon or the Santa Express Train, $18 a person, for two or more riders, and your car’s admission is waived. Public wagon rides have their own start times and several December blackout dates, so check the calendar first.
Grant’s Farm from the car is the short one. It opens its drive-through on just four nights a season, and it costs $30 a vehicle. You wave at Santa and Mrs. Claus, roll through a tunnel of twinkling lights, pass the Busch Family Estate in full holiday dress, and play the music for the 50-foot animated tree on your radio. No RVs, limos or passenger vans.
Celebration of Lights in O’Fallon loops through Fort Zumwalt Park, and every scene is designed and funded by local organizations, churches and businesses, so the whole drive reads like a town’s Christmas card. A car is $18, tickets must be bought in advance, and the city runs a few walk-through Holiday Stroll nights at $10 a person, with fireworks over Lake Whetsel.
Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park: check St. Louis County Parks for this season’s drive-through details. The St. Louis County Parks Foundation also sells a preview night, when you see the lights by horse-drawn carriage or on foot without the December traffic. Tickets for that night start at $200.
### Where can you see Christmas lights for free?
Candy Cane Lane. The lights live on the 6500 block of Murdoch Avenue in St. Louis Hills. Residents put out information about their charities, and an organizer told PBS NewsHour that donating is completely optional. Park and walk it. St. Louis Magazine reported the street got so choked with traffic that sightseers started parking at the nearby Ted Drewes and walking down Murdoch, and St. Louis Public Radio put it plainly: go in a car and you’ll be stuck for hours. Even in winter, people line up at the Ted Drewes on Chippewa for a concrete before wandering down to the lights.
These lights are hung by neighbors on their days off. “I will not stop until you can see my house from space,” Candy Cane Lane organizer Matt Mauschbaugh told PBS NewsHour, standing near the 16-foot tree he built in his yard. Residents told the same reporter they take days off in the month of November to hang thousands of lights. The big pin oaks get wrapped like candy canes, a look that grew out of a neighborhood block contest. You walk it with your breath fogging and your kids sprinting ahead to the next yard.
Brewery Lights after Christmas. For a few nights right after Christmas, Anheuser-Busch lets the public drive in and out of Pestalozzi Street free, 5 to 10 p.m., through the main gate at Busch Place and Arsenal. Same brewery, same lights, seen through your windshield, and the ticket money stays in your pocket. Check the Brewery Lights FAQ for this year’s nights.
The Way of Lights. Across the river in Illinois, the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows lights its grounds to tell the Journey to Bethlehem and the birth of Christ. It’s the Shrine’s largest fundraiser, and donations are accepted rather than tickets sold. The outdoor display stays open on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas even when the buildings close. Inside, a room of decorated Christmas trees is open noon to 9 p.m. at no charge. Out back there are camel and pony rides for $10 a person, a petting zoo at no charge, and kettle corn and hot chocolate from RayRay’s.

Run the numbers for two adults and two kids ages 3 to 12, using each show’s own posted prices. Prices are set each season, so check the official page before you go.

And the two free nights are not consolation prizes. One is a brewery lit up like a Christmas card, and the other is a street the neighbors have turned into a small city of light.

Buy Garden Glow tickets early in the day, not in the parking lot. Every same-day ticket bought after 4:30 p.m. costs $2 more, and Garden Glow tickets are good only for the date and time you pick. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where to see Christmas lights in STL?
A.  On foot, try Garden Glow, Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo or Brewery Lights. To stay in the car, WonderLight’s Christmas is $35 a carload and Santa’s Magical Kingdom starts at $35. For the homemade version, there’s Candy Cane Lane in St. Louis Hills.
### Q. Is Candy Cane Lane St. Louis free?
A.  Yes. Candy Cane Lane is the 6500 block of Murdoch Avenue in St. Louis Hills, decorated by the people who live there. Residents post information about their charities and some visitors give, which an organizer told PBS NewsHour is completely optional. St. Louis Public Radio’s warning: go in a car and you’ll be stuck for hours, so park and walk.
### Q. Where is the best Christmas light trail?
A.  For a walking trail, Garden Glow is the pick: a path of about a mile through the Missouri Botanical Garden that takes 45 minutes to an hour. Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo, with no timed entry, and the Grant’s Farm walk-through, at $15 a person, are the other strong walks.
### Q. Where can I find the best Christmas lights in Missouri?
A.  On the Missouri side of St. Louis, start with Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden on foot and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka, 35 acres of displays by car or open-air wagon. O’Fallon’s Celebration of Lights at Fort Zumwalt Park is the $18-a-car choice.
### Q. What are the Christmas lights at Anheuser-Busch Brewery?
A.  That’s Brewery Lights. Reserved nights come with free parking, a complimentary beer for guests 21 and up, brewery tours, two 50-foot digital trees and a 7:30 p.m. parade with the Clydesdales, weather permitting. For a few nights right after Christmas, Anheuser-Busch says the public is free to enter and exit Pestalozzi Street by car from 5 to 10 p.m.
### Q. How long is the garden glow in St. Louis?
A.  The Garden Glow path is about a mile long and takes 45 minutes to an hour, according to the Garden, so add time for hot drinks and photo stops. The season usually runs from mid-November into early January; check the Garden’s page for this year’s nights.
### Q. Where to park for garden Glow in St. Louis?
A.  Use the Garden’s two free lots at the corner of Shaw Boulevard and Vandeventer Avenue, where a shuttle runs every Garden Glow evening. Skip private lots, where the Garden warns cars can be towed.
### Q. Where is the biggest display of Christmas lights?
A.  Around St. Louis, WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway bills itself as the area’s largest drive-through light show, with over 1 million LED lights along roughly 2 miles. Santa’s Magical Kingdom covers 35 acres, and the Zoo counts over 1 million lights at Wild Lights. The biggest depends on whether you count miles, acres or bulbs.

## Still a Quarter a Game: The Best Arcades in St. Louis, Kids or 21+
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-arcades-in-st-louis-mo-from-classic-games-to-modern-fun
Still a quarter. That’s the price of every game at Up-Down on North Euclid, so five dollars buys you twenty of them. Behind you a skee-ball rattles up one of the four lanes and thunks into the 50 ring. Your slice of house-made pizza is going cold on the ledge, the joystick is worn smooth by a thousand other hands, the cabinet hums warm against your knees, and the attract screen keeps flashing a high score you are absolutely going to take down. How is it still a quarter, when a modern redemption game costs several times that per play? The old cabinets are paid for, and the beer covers the rent.
And that’s only one lane of a surprisingly deep arcade city. On Monday nights the pinball is free at the Silver Ballroom, a punk-rock pinball bar on Morgan Ford. Fenton has a pinball museum where you actually play the collection. The City Museum hides an 18-machine pinball hall on its third floor. And here’s the parent move almost nobody knows: Up-Down, 21+ the rest of the month, lets kids in one Sunday a month from 10am to 2pm, and Two Plumbers in St. Charles goes all-ages on weekend afternoons.
One warning first. If an older list sends you to Purple Quarters in the Grove, it’s closed, and so is Magic Mini Golf on the Loop. What follows is what’s actually open, split the only way that matters: are you bringing kids or a cocktail?
### The Two Kinds of Arcade Night
St. Louis arcades split into two camps, and you can hear the difference from the door. The 21+ barcades sound like pint glasses and 8-bit music: Up-Down on North Euclid, Two Plumbers and Rec Hall out in St. Charles, where the games are cheap and the drinks are the point. The all-ages family entertainment centers sound like sirens and a ticket ribbon spooling into a kid’s arms: Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights, Main Event in Chesterfield, Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton, with redemption games, laser tag and prize counters built for a birthday. Pinball runs through both, with a devoted St. Louis scene of its own. Know which one you want, and the choice gets easy.
Before you drive over, the details that save a wasted trip. Up-Down is at 405 N. Euclid, open 3pm to 1:30am on weekdays and 11am to 1:30am on weekends, 21+ except its family Sundays: one Sunday a month, 10am to 2pm, with the dates posted on Up-Down’s St. Louis page. The Silver Ballroom is at 4701 Morganford Road, with 19 machines listed on Pinball Map; Monday is the free-play night, but a bar’s specials can change, so check its socials that afternoon. And across the river, Wood River, Alton and Edwardsville have a whole second cluster, so Illinois-side players don’t need the bridge.
### The Barcades: Beer, Nostalgia, and 25-Cent Classics
Sit down at a barcade with a beer sweating on the ledge and the evening plans itself. Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the flagship - more than 60 arcade games from the ’80s and ’90s, a dozen pinball machines, four skee-ball alleys and Nintendo 64 on a projector, so the couch battles of your childhood play out wall-size. Every game still costs a quarter, which means a $5 bill buys twenty of them. It’s 21+ except for one family Sunday a month (10am to 2pm), and it nails the nostalgia-plus-cocktails formula. Out in St. Charles, Two Plumbers Brewery + Arcade pairs house-brewed beer with a room of retro cabinets and pinball, and it opens to all ages on weekend afternoons. Rec Hall, also in St. Charles, runs the format at full scale: roughly 70 arcade machines, free-roam VR and a full bar. One update if you’re working from an older list: Purple Quarters in the Grove has closed.
What makes a barcade such an easy win is the low pressure. No reservation, no skill required. Drop in for one drink and a round of Mario Kart on the N64 projector, your friend’s kart blown up wall-size, or stay till close working a pinball table until the flipper buttons leave a dent in your thumbs. It’s fun sober or not, because the games carry the evening either way. First date, small group, or a “we don’t know what we want to do” night after a Cardinals loss: a barcade almost never misses.
### The St. Louis Pinball Trail
If pinball is your thing, St. Louis over-delivers. The legendary Silver Ballroom on Morgan Ford in the Bevo neighborhood, a punk-rock pinball bar, keeps around 20 machines, free play on Monday nights, and a fierce local following. Murphy’s On 21 in south county and the Benton Parkade in Benton Park are favorites for league players, and Red Fish Blue Fish in St. Charles keeps a solid bank of tables. For an all-ages pinball fix, the Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton is a dedicated collection you can play, and there’s even a pinball-and-arcade room tucked inside the City Museum. St. Louis runs real pinball leagues, so if you catch the bug, there’s a whole community waiting. The scene stretches into the Metro East too, where Atomic Pinball Arcade and the Pump House in Wood River keep dozens of machines for Illinois-side players.
What’s great about the pinball trail is how welcoming it is to newcomers. You don’t need to be good - most of these spots keep older, easier tables alongside the brutal modern ones, and the regulars are usually happy to show a first-timer the ropes. Drop a few dollars in, learn to nudge without tilting, and you’ll understand why pinball, of all things, became one of the city’s most durable nightlife hobbies.
### Family Game Centers: Bring the Kids
When the point is to wear kids out (and win a plastic prize), the big all-ages centers deliver. Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights is the reliable classic - a wall of games, sports on the screens, and a full menu. Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, and Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton adds go-karts and mini golf to its 80-game arcade. For the youngest kids, Chuck E. Cheese has several metro locations with the tokens-and-tickets formula that never dies. Out at Ameristar in St. Charles, the Hi-Vi Arcade has 60-plus video games, air hockey and a prize counter the whole family can use. (Magic Mini Golf on the Delmar Loop, a family pick in older guides, has closed.)
### Don’t Forget the Metro East
Cross the river into Illinois and the arcade options keep coming. Edison’s Entertainment Complex in Edwardsville is a big all-ages spot with a 70-plus-game arcade, bowling, and laser tag; Game Over in Alton packs 200-plus games across three levels; and the pinball crowd has Atomic Pinball Arcade and the Pump House, both in Wood River. If you’re on the Illinois side of the metro, you don’t have to drive back across the river for a great arcade night. Edison’s in particular works well for a mixed-age group or a birthday, since it combines the arcade with bowling and other attractions in one place - the Metro East answer to a Dave & Buster’s night.
Wildly off-topic: The Grove sits inside a neighborhood called Forest Park Southeast.
### Why St. Louis Is Quietly a Great Arcade Town
It wasn’t always like this. St. Louis watched its old mall arcades fade, the way a lot of cities did. Then the barcade boom brought the games back for grown-ups, and a passionate pinball community rebuilt the scene from the machines up. Today the metro spans the whole spectrum: national chains, indie neighborhood barcades, dedicated pinball museums, and bars that keep a few tables in the corner for the regulars. The result is a city where “let’s go play some games” can mean almost anything, on almost any budget, any night of the week.
Part of the fun is how the arcades reflect their neighborhoods. A barcade in the Central West End feels different from a pinball bar in Bevo, which feels different from a brewery-arcade in St. Charles or a big family center out in Chesterfield. Chasing them down is a low-key way to see parts of the metro you might otherwise skip - and to end up somewhere new with a controller in your hand.

### Before You Go: Age Rules, Pricing and Quieter Nights

With kids, aim for Up-Down’s monthly family Sunday or Two Plumbers on a weekend afternoon. And for the smaller independent spots, a quick check of hours or Facebook before you go is smart, since game bars sometimes host private events or league nights.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Which St. Louis arcade has the best reviews?
A.  There’s no single winner, but a few St. Louis spots earn the most devotion. Up-Down STL is the flagship barcade, and the Silver Ballroom in Bevo keeps a fierce local following. For families, Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights and Main Event in Chesterfield are the reliably popular picks. The best fit depends on whether you want cocktails, pinball, or kids.
### Q. How much does an average arcade game cost?
A.  Classic cabinets on quarter or token play are the cheapest entertainment in the building, while modern ticket-redemption and motion games cost several times as much per play. Every game at Up-Down STL is still a quarter, and Game Over in Alton sells $20 for 80 credits. Card systems make this harder to feel, so decide your spend before you load the card, not after.
### Q. Why are arcade games so expensive now?
A.  Newer cabinets cost operators far more to buy and maintain than an eighties machine did, and redemption games are priced around the prizes they pay out. That is why the barcades leaning on restored classics can still run cheap play - the machines are paid for and the beer covers the rent.
### Q. What are some tips for choosing an arcade bar?
A.  Check whether the machines are on free play or coin, whether food is served or you can bring it, and how loud the room gets after nine. If pinball is the draw, ask whether the tables are maintained in-house - a well-kept table plays completely differently from a neglected one.
### Q. What are some fun adult things to do in St. Louis?
A.  Barcades and pinball are the obvious ones on this page, and they pair well with the rest of a night out because they are clustered near bars and food rather than stranded in a strip mall. Weeknights are the move if you want to actually get on a machine.

## How Much Does a Bookkeeper Cost? (And Why Missouri Licenses None of Them)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-bookkeeper-cost
### How much does a bookkeeper cost?
For most small businesses, somewhere between $200 and $400 a month for straightforward monthly bookkeeping, rising toward $1,500 or more as the work gets more involved. Hourly, the reported median sits around $24, with freelancers commonly quoting $25 to $50.
A word on those numbers before you rely on them. Almost every page publishing bookkeeping rates is published by an outsourced bookkeeping company, and their in-house-versus-outsourced comparisons are marketing. The ranges above appear consistently enough across sources to be useful as a sanity check. Treat any single figure — including a quote you are given — as a starting point rather than a market rate.
What actually drives your price is not your revenue. It is transaction volume, number of accounts, and how bad the shoebox is. A consultant billing four invoices a month is cheap to keep straight. A restaurant with daily deposits, tips, vendor accounts and a payroll run is not, at any revenue level.
### The thing nobody tells you: anyone can call themselves a bookkeeper
This is the part worth knowing before you hand someone your bank logins. Which is the line that should make you sit up: the person you trust with every number in your business needs no license at all. So how do you tell the good ones apart?
Missouri does not license bookkeepers. There is no state exam, no registry, no board, and no complaint process. The title is unregulated, and a person who took a weekend course and a person with twenty years in the trade may describe themselves identically.
“CPA” is different. Certified Public Accountant is a protected title in Missouri — only licensees may use it, or any designation implying it. That protection is what makes the letters meaningful, and it is why the distinction matters when you are comparing quotes.
Worth being precise about what that protection does and does not do, because the internet gets this wrong in both directions: a non-licensee may still perform a great deal of legitimate accounting work, including preparing tax returns, advisory work, and preparing non-attest financial statements. The restriction is on calling yourself a CPA, not on doing bookkeeping.
If this pattern feels familiar, it should — it is the same structure as the trades here. Missouri does not license contractors either, which is why verifying a contractor works differently in this state. In both cases the vetting is yours to do.
### What to look for instead of a license
Since there is no state credential, these carry the weight:
Voluntary certification. The AIPB Certified Bookkeeper and NACPB Certified Public Bookkeeper credentials are the recognized ones. Neither is required, which is rather the point — someone who obtained one chose to be tested.
Professional liability insurance. Ask directly. Someone touching your financial records without it is asking you to carry the risk.
References from businesses like yours. Restaurant books and contractor books are different animals; experience in one does not transfer cleanly.
A named CPA they work with. Good bookkeepers usually have one, and are quick to say where their scope ends.
### Bookkeeper, accountant, CPA — what you are actually buying
These get used interchangeably and they are not the same purchase.
A bookkeeper handles the ongoing record: categorizing transactions, reconciling accounts, chasing invoices, producing monthly statements. This is the recurring work, and it is what most small businesses are actually short of.
An accountant works on what the records mean — financial statements, tax planning, structure. Often seasonal or periodic rather than monthly.
A CPA is a licensed accountant, and the license matters most where independence and attestation are required — audits, reviewed statements, representation before tax authorities.
Most small businesses need the first regularly and the second occasionally. Paying CPA rates for monthly transaction categorization is a common and expensive mistake; so is having nobody look at the year until March.
### In-house, freelance, or a service
A service or a freelancer is where nearly every small business should start. You pay for the hours the work takes, not for a person’s day, and you can leave.
A full-time in-house bookkeeper reportedly runs roughly $45,000 to $60,000 in salary before benefits and overhead, which is commonly estimated to add another 25% to 40%. That is a real employer decision — and if you are contemplating it, note that the obligations attach the moment you hire anyone. We covered them in hiring your first employee in Missouri.
The honest test is not cost, it is volume. If the work genuinely fills a week, hire. If it fills two afternoons a month, hiring for it is expensive in a way the salary figure understates.
### How do you know when it is time?
Most owners do their own books at the start, and that is usually correct. The question is not whether you can keep doing it — it is what it costs you to keep doing it. A few honest signals:
You are doing it at 11pm on a Sunday. That is the real price, and it never appears in a comparison. Your own hour has a value, and if bookkeeping is displacing the work that actually earns, you are already paying more than a bookkeeper charges.
You do not know this month’s number without adding it up. Not the bank balance — the balance is not profit. If you cannot say roughly what you made last month without an evening of work, you are flying on instruments you have not read.
You are behind, and being behind makes you avoid it. This is the loop that turns three messy months into two messy years, and it is exactly what makes cleanup expensive later.
Something outside is about to require clean books. A loan application, a lease, an insurance policy, a buyer, an accountant asking for last year. This is the most common trigger and the worst possible timing — the books need to have been kept, not reconstructed under a deadline.
You have started paying people. Payroll changes the risk profile immediately. The obligations we covered in hiring your first employee come with filings and deadlines, and missing them is expensive in a way a late invoice is not.
### What bad books actually cost
The costs are rarely a penalty. They are quieter:
Deductions you cannot prove. An expense you cannot substantiate is an expense you did not really have, at tax time. Owners routinely overpay because the receipt was lost, not because the money was not spent.
Sales tax filed on a guess. If you sell goods, you file whether or not you sold anything, and the arithmetic has to be right. Our guide to the Missouri sales tax license covers the obligation; the books are what make it accurate.
Decisions made on the balance. Treating the bank account as profit is how a good month funds a purchase that a tax bill was supposed to cover.
A sale you cannot close. If you ever want to sell the business, the books are the asset. A buyer doing the due diligence we described in buying a business in Missouri is going to ask for three years of returns — and what they find determines the price, or whether there is one.
### What makes the quote go up
If your number came back higher than the ranges above, it is usually one of these:
Cleanup. Months or years of uncategorized transactions are billed separately, often at a premium, and it is the most common reason a first quote shocks people.
Payroll. Usually a separate line, and more so with multiple pay rates or contractors.
Sales tax filing. Relevant if you sell goods — see our guide to the Missouri sales tax license, including the requirement to file even in a zero-sales period.
Multiple accounts or entities. Each one is another reconciliation every month.
Cash-heavy operations. More manual work, more room for discrepancy.
Mixed personal and business spending. The single most avoidable cost driver, and the reason a separate business account pays for itself.
### How to hire one without regretting it
Four questions, and the answers tell you most of what you need:
What exactly is included each month, in writing? Reconciliation, categorization, monthly statements, sales tax, payroll — itemised. “Bookkeeping” as a single line on a quote is how scope disputes start.
Whose software is it, and whose data? Make sure the file is in your name and you retain access. Businesses discover the answer to this at the worst possible moment, when they are trying to leave.
What is the cleanup cost, separately stated? Get it before you sign, not after they open the books.
What happens at tax time? Do they hand off to your CPA, and have they done that handoff before? A tidy file that arrives in a form the accountant can use is most of the value.
And ask how they prefer to receive things. A bookkeeper who wants receipts photographed as they happen will cost you less than one reconstructing a quarter from bank memos, because you are paying for their time either way. The cheapest arrangement is almost always the one where you do the five seconds of work at the moment of the transaction.
Apropos of nothing: the books can wait until after lunch in Dupo.
One last thing, since Missouri leaves the vetting to you: keep the bank logins in your own name and grant access, rather than handing over credentials. Nothing about that implies distrust — it is the same reason you would not give a contractor the deed. It just means you can end the arrangement on a Tuesday without losing control of your own accounts.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a bookkeeper cost for a small business?
A.  Commonly $200 to $400 a month for straightforward monthly work, rising toward $1,500 or more as volume and scope grow. Hourly, the reported median is around $24, with freelancers often quoting $25 to $50. Price tracks transaction volume and number of accounts far more than revenue.
### Q. Do bookkeepers need a license in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri does not license bookkeepers — there is no state exam, registry or board, and anyone may use the title. “CPA” is different: it is a protected designation only licensees may use. Since there is no state credential to check, look instead for voluntary AIPB or NACPB certification, professional liability insurance, and references.
### Q. What is the difference between a bookkeeper and an accountant?
A.  A bookkeeper maintains the ongoing record — categorizing transactions, reconciling accounts, producing monthly statements. An accountant interprets those records for statements, tax planning and structure. A CPA is a licensed accountant, which matters where attestation or representation is required. Most small businesses need bookkeeping monthly and accounting occasionally.
### Q. Is it cheaper to outsource bookkeeping or hire in-house?
A.  For most small businesses, outsourcing — you pay for hours worked rather than a salary. A full-time in-house bookkeeper reportedly runs about $45,000 to $60,000 before benefits and overhead of roughly 25–40%. Be skeptical of dramatic savings comparisons, though: they are usually published by outsourcing companies. The real test is whether the work fills a week or two afternoons.
### Q. Why is my bookkeeping quote so high?
A.  Usually cleanup — back months of uncategorized transactions are billed separately and often at a premium. Payroll, sales tax filing, multiple accounts, heavy cash handling, and mixed personal and business spending all add to it. Ask for cleanup to be quoted as its own line before you sign anything.
### Q. What should I ask before hiring a bookkeeper?
A.  What is included each month, itemised in writing; whose software the file lives in and whether you keep access; what cleanup costs, stated separately; and how they hand off to your accountant at tax time. Also keep bank logins in your own name and grant access rather than sharing credentials.

## Find Quality Roof Tiles Near Me: A St. Louis Buyer's Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/find-quality-roof-tiles-near-me-a-2025-buyer-s-guide
Refreshed September 2026
Updated June 21, 2026.
Imagine standing at the curb looking up at your roof, knowing it’s on borrowed time. You’ve seen tile roofs — the kind that make a house look like it belongs in a magazine spread — and you’re wondering if that’s the move. It’s a big decision, and an expensive one — likely among the largest single purchases your house will ever ask of you — so it’s worth understanding what you’re getting into before you call anyone.
Here’s an honest, St. Louis-minded guide to roof tiles: the types, what they really cost, how to find someone who can install them right, and what our Midwest weather means for the decision.
### First, an honest word about tile in St. Louis
Tile roofs are everywhere in the Southwest and Florida, but they’re less common here — most St. Louis homes wear asphalt shingles, with slate and clay showing up mainly on historic and higher-end houses. That doesn’t make tile a bad choice; it means two things matter more locally: weight (many of our older homes weren’t framed for heavy tile and may need structural reinforcement) and freeze-thaw durability (our winters cross above and below freezing constantly, so you want a tile rated to handle it). A good local installer will steer you right on both — and a bad one will skip the conversation entirely, which is itself the tell.
### Your roof tile options
The main players, each with its own look, weight, and price:
Concrete — the workhorse: tough, versatile, can mimic clay or slate, and the most budget-friendly tile. Heavy, though.
Clay / terracotta — classic, warm, and long-lasting, with that Mediterranean charm. A bit more fragile and pricier.
Slate — the premium, natural look that can last a century. Beautiful, very heavy, and the most expensive.
Composite — made from recycled materials, lighter and more impact-resistant; a great way to get the slate look without the weight.
Metal — lightweight and durable, and it can be shaped to resemble tiles or shakes.
Solar tiles — generate electricity while protecting the home; a big investment with long-term energy payback.
### The St. Louis look: matching tile to the house you actually own
Tile reads differently on different St. Louis housing. On the metro’s historic stock — the grand homes of Compton Heights and the Central West End, the century-old brick throughout the city — slate and clay are period-correct: that’s what many of those roofs wore originally, and restoring the look adds real character value that appraisers and future buyers both notice. On mid-century ranches across the county, a heavy Mediterranean profile can look borrowed from another climate — flatter concrete or composite profiles usually sit more naturally. And on newer builds out in St. Charles County or the Metro East, composite “slate-look” tile delivers the upscale effect without the framing drama.
Two practical notes before you fall in love with a photo: drive your own neighborhood and see what tile actually looks like on homes shaped like yours, and if you’re in a historic district or an HOA, check approval requirements before ordering samples — some districts care a great deal about roof materials, and finding out after the deposit is the expensive way to learn. Ten minutes with your municipality or HOA board now saves a standoff later.
### What tile actually costs
Tile is a premium roof, and the price reflects it. Installed costs vary widely by material, and the figures below are national ballpark ranges — your real St. Louis quote will depend on your roof’s size, pitch, and complexity, so treat these as a starting point and get real local bids:
Concrete: roughly $11–$28 per square foot installed
Clay / terracotta: roughly $9–$26
Slate: roughly $8–$35
Composite: roughly $8–$15
Solar tile: roughly $21–$25
Three things push the number up: roof complexity (lots of valleys, dormers, and steep pitches mean more cuts, waste, and labor), structural support (heavy tile may require reinforcing the framing), and tear-off and disposal of your old roof. Ask for an itemized estimate so you can see exactly what’s included — and what conveniently isn’t.
### Tile versus the alternatives, honestly
Tile isn’t automatically the right answer, and a guide that pretends otherwise isn’t helping you. The honest comparison:
Asphalt shingles cost a fraction of tile up front and install on any framing — which is why most of the metro wears them. Their trade-off is lifespan: decades shorter than tile, meaning you (or the next owner) buy the roof again. If you plan to move within ten years, asphalt’s economics usually win.
Metal roofing splits the difference: lighter than tile, longer-lived than asphalt, excellent in storms. It’s tile’s real competitor for buyers thinking in decades.
Tile and slate win on lifespan, fire resistance, and looks — the fifty-to-hundred-year roof — and cost the most up front, sometimes plus structural work. They make the most sense for forever homes, historic restorations, and owners who’d rather buy once.
The clarifying question isn’t “which roof is best?” It’s “how long will I own this house, and what’s the roof’s job while I do?” Answer that honestly and the material usually picks itself.
### Finding an installer who actually knows tile
This is the part that makes or breaks the job. Tile isn’t asphalt — it has to be laid, flashed, and sealed correctly, on a structure that can bear the weight, or you’ll be chasing leaks and slipped tiles for years. So:
Get at least three quotes from local contractors who specialize in tile, not just any roofer.
Interview, don’t just price-shop. Ask why they recommend a given tile or method for your roof. The cheapest bid that skips a needed step isn’t a deal.
Confirm licensing and insurance, and ask for recent local references and a workmanship warranty.
### Hail, insurance, and paperwork — the Midwest fine print
This is hail country, and that changes the tile conversation in three ways. First, ask about impact ratings: tiles carry impact classifications, and some insurers offer premium discounts for higher-rated (Class 3 or 4) roofing — while clay in particular can crack under severe hail. Ask your agent how each material you’re considering affects your policy before you choose. Second, document everything: photograph your roof when it’s new and after major storms, because a clean before-and-after record makes any future claim dramatically smoother. Third, permits: reroofing commonly requires a permit in both the city and county, and structural reinforcement work certainly does — requirements vary by municipality, so confirm with your local building department, and expect a reputable installer to pull the permit themselves and say so in the quote.
### A few ways to save
Tile is an investment, but you can be smart about it: schedule in the off-season (late fall or winter, when crews are slower and more flexible on price), ask about reclaimed tile or lighter materials that may skip costly structural work, and bundle the job with other projects like gutters while the crew is already on-site.
Random, but: De Soto has more places to eat than you’d think.
### Five questions that sort real tile installers from pretenders
“How many tile roofs have you installed in the last two years — and can I see one?” Recent, local, visitable work beats any brochure.
“Will my framing carry this tile, and how will you verify that?” The right answer involves an actual structural assessment, not a glance and a shrug.
“What underlayment and flashing system are you using, and why?” Tile sheds water; the layers beneath it keep your house dry. An installer who can’t explain them fluently is telling you something.
“How do you handle repairs later — do you stock matching tile?” A cracked tile in year eight shouldn’t require a scavenger hunt.
“What exactly does the workmanship warranty cover, and for how long?” In writing, in the contract, alongside the manufacturer’s material warranty.
For the general vetting layer under all of this — insurance certificates, three estimates, red flags — our step-by-step hiring guide applies to roofers as much as any trade, and the roofing contractor guide goes deeper on the trade itself.
### What the project actually looks like, start to finish
Owners are often surprised by the shape of a tile job, so here’s the honest arc. It starts with an assessment visit — measurements, framing check, photos — then a detailed quote (expect a week or two for a good one; instant quotes on premium roofing are a yellow flag). Material lead times vary: common concrete profiles may be days away, while specific clay colors or slate can take weeks, which is why off-season planning pays. The installation itself typically runs longer than an asphalt job — tile is laid piece by piece, flashed carefully, and often preceded by structural work — so budget for more days of crew presence, protective tarps over landscaping, and a dumpster in the driveway for the duration.
Two things worth insisting on: a written schedule with weather contingencies (this is St. Louis; there will be weather), and a final walkthrough where the installer shows you the flashing details, ridge work, and cleanup — including the magnet sweep for dropped nails. A crew proud of its tile work enjoys that walkthrough. A crew that resists it is telling you something too.
### Built to last — with a little upkeep
Done right, a tile roof can last 50 to 100 years, often outliving your time in the house. It’s low-maintenance, not no-maintenance, and the distinction matters: look it over once or twice a year and after big storms for cracked or slipped tiles, and clear debris and any moss from the valleys (our humid summers love to grow it). When something’s off and you’d rather not climb up there, a local pro is worth the call — tile repair is precisely the kind of job where an hour of expertise beats an afternoon of ladder bravery.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can my roof structure support tile?
A.  Maybe — and that’s a question for measurement, not guessing. Tile weighs several times what asphalt does, and many older St. Louis homes were framed for shingles. A qualified installer or structural engineer can assess your framing and price any reinforcement; lighter composite and metal tile-look options often avoid the issue entirely.
### Q. How do tile roofs handle hail?
A.  It depends on the tile: concrete and composite generally fare well, and some products carry Class 3 or 4 impact ratings that insurers like, while clay can crack under severe hail. Ask about impact ratings before you buy, check how your insurer treats each material, and photograph the roof after major storms so any claim starts with evidence.
### Q. Are tile roofs common in St. Louis?
A.  Less so than asphalt shingles — tile and slate show up mainly on historic and higher-end St. Louis homes. Tile is a fine choice here, but because of our freeze-thaw winters and older framing, weight and cold-weather durability matter, so work with an installer who knows local conditions.
### Q. How much does a tile roof cost?
A.  It varies widely by material and roof size. Installed costs run roughly $8 to $35 per square foot depending on the tile, which puts many home roofs in the tens of thousands. Get itemized local quotes — complexity, structural support, and old-roof tear-off all affect the final price.
### Q. How long do tile roofs last?
A.  With proper installation and occasional upkeep, 50 to 100 years — slate and clay are especially long-lived. They’re fire-resistant and low-maintenance, though heavier tiles may require structural reinforcement.

A.  Yes, we work with all sorts of garage doors and openers! Our technicians are trained to handle many different brands and models, so no matter what kind of garage door you have, we can likely help you fix it.
### Q. How can I avoid needing emergency repairs in the future?
A.  Regular check-ups and maintenance can really help prevent big problems down the road. Things like lubricating the moving parts, making sure everything is tightened up, and checking the springs and cables can keep your garage door running smoothly and avoid unexpected breakdowns.

## Credit Card Processing Fees: What Missouri Businesses Actually Pay
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/credit-card-processing-fees-small-business
### What do credit card processing fees actually cost a small business?
Between 1.5% and 3.5% of each transaction, and where you land inside that range depends less on luck than most owners think. Which is oddly good news: if it isn’t luck, then the gap between 1.5% and 3.5% is something you can actually control — once you know where to look.
That range is the one point everyone agrees on — NerdWallet, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and OnDeck all publish the same figures independently. Roughly:
In person, tapped or swiped — about 1.8% to 2.6%, plus 8 to 15 cents
Online or manually keyed — about 2.25% to 3.5%, plus 25 to 30 cents
Debit — about 0.5% to 1.5%, lower because debit interchange is regulated
So the same $100 sale costs you roughly $2 across the counter and closer to $3.50 typed into a form. If a meaningful share of your work is invoiced or taken over the phone, that difference is not rounding — it is a line item worth managing.
And the question almost everyone is really asking: in Missouri, you are allowed to pass it on. More on that below, because it is the part page one does not answer.
### Where the money actually goes
Your rate is not one fee. It is three, stacked, and only one of them is negotiable — which is the single most useful thing to understand before any sales call.
Interchange. The largest slice, and it goes to the bank that issued your customer’s card — not to your processor. It is set by the card networks, it is the same for everyone, and nobody can discount it for you. Rewards cards carry higher interchange, which is why the customer paying with a premium travel card costs you more than the one with a plain debit card.
Assessments. A small cut to the network itself — Visa, Mastercard, and so on. Also fixed, also not negotiable.
The processor’s markup. This is the only part that is actually up for discussion, and it is the entire basis of every competing quote you will ever receive.
When a salesperson promises to “beat your rate,” they are talking about that third layer. Anyone claiming they can cut the first two is either confused or counting on you being.
### The three pricing models, and the one to avoid
Flat rate. One blended percentage for everything — the Square and Stripe model. You pay the same whether the customer used a debit card or a premium rewards card. It is simple, predictable, requires no negotiation, and for low volume it is genuinely hard to beat on total cost once you account for your own time.
Published rates as of this writing: Square 2.6% + $0.15 in person on the free plan, 3.3% + $0.30 for online and invoices, 3.5% + $0.15 keyed. Stripe 2.9% + $0.30 for standard online domestic cards. Both change their pricing periodically, so check current rates rather than trusting any article, including this one.
Interchange-plus. You pay the real interchange, whatever it happens to be for that card, plus a stated markup. A competitive markup for a small or mid-sized merchant runs roughly 0.20% to 0.50% plus 10 to 20 cents. It is the transparent option — you can see exactly what the processor is making — and as volume grows it usually wins. It also requires you to read a statement.
Tiered. Your transactions get sorted into vague buckets labeled something like “qualified,” “mid-qualified” and “non-qualified.” The advertised rate is the qualified one. A great deal of your volume will mysteriously not qualify.
Avoid tiered. The structure exists to make comparison impossible, and the headline number it advertises is the one you will rarely pay.
### Can you charge customers the fee? In Missouri, yes.
This is the most-asked question on the topic and the least well answered, because the answer genuinely depends on your state — and nearly every guide ranking for it is written for nobody in particular.
Missouri has no state law prohibiting or regulating credit card surcharging. A Missouri business may add a surcharge to credit card transactions. You are still bound by the card networks’ own rules, which generally cap surcharges in the region of 3–4%, require advance disclosure, and require that you register the practice with the networks.
For context on why this varies at all: in Expressions Hair Design v. Schneiderman, the Supreme Court held unanimously that surcharge bans regulate speech rather than conduct — they govern how a business is allowed to describe its prices. That reasoning dismantled outright bans in states that had them. Missouri never had one to dismantle.
### Surcharge or cash discount?
They sound like the same thing and they are not, legally or in how customers receive them.
A surcharge adds a fee on top of the posted price when someone pays by credit card. A cash discount posts the higher price for everyone and takes something off for cash. Same arithmetic, different framing — and the cash-discount structure sits outside most surcharge rules entirely, which is exactly why many businesses choose it.
Two practical notes. Debit is different: surcharging debit cards is not permitted the way credit surcharging is, so a blanket “card fee” applied to everything is a mistake. And disclose it before the sale, visibly — at the door, on the menu, on the estimate. The complaint customers make is almost never about the 3%. It is about finding out at the till.
### If you take orders through a delivery app, that is a different number
Worth separating, because restaurant owners routinely blame their processor for something else entirely. Go and read what owners post about this and you will find figures like “we have 14.81% come out of every sale” — and then a reply blaming the card processor. It almost never is.
Card processing runs 1.5% to 3.5%. Third-party delivery marketplace commission is an entirely different order of magnitude — Uber’s own published pricing lists marketplace delivery in the region of 20–30%, against roughly 2.5% plus 29 cents when the order comes through your own website using their tooling.
So an order placed on the app and the same order placed on your own site are not remotely the same transaction, and no amount of renegotiating your card rate touches the gap. If your effective cost per sale looks impossible, check which channel the orders are arriving through before you fire your processor.
One Missouri-specific trap that rides along with this. Missouri Department of Revenue Letter Ruling LR 8316 addressed whether delivery platforms act as the marketplace facilitator for sales tax purposes — and concluded they do not, in the arrangement examined. The practical consequence is that the restaurant generally retains primary liability for the sales tax on those orders, even though the platform collected the money from the customer.
That is not a processing question, it is a remittance one, and getting it wrong compounds monthly. If a meaningful share of your revenue arrives through a delivery platform, confirm with your accountant who is remitting what — and see our guide to the Missouri sales tax license for the underlying obligation.
### The fees that are not on your rate sheet
The percentage is the part people compare. The monthly extras are where a “cheaper” processor quietly becomes expensive:
Monthly minimum — charged if your fees fall short of a floor. Brutal for seasonal businesses.
PCI compliance fee, and worse, a PCI non-compliance fee if you never completed a questionnaire you may not know exists.
Statement, batch and gateway fees — small individually, permanent collectively.
Chargeback fees, charged per dispute whether or not you win it.
Early termination fees, which is why the contract length matters more than the rate.
The only number that means anything is your effective rate: total fees for the month divided by total card volume. Work it out from an actual statement. It is frequently 0.5 to 1 point above whatever rate was quoted, and it is the only figure worth comparing between providers.
Random, but: Old North St. Louis is having a quiet comeback.
### When switching is worth the hassle
Run the effective rate before you do anything else. If it is close to the flat rates above, a switch will save you very little and cost you a week.
Interchange-plus generally starts to win as volume grows, because the flat-rate blend that protects a small merchant becomes an overpayment once you are processing steadily. Rather than trusting anyone’s threshold — including a processor’s, whose threshold is always conveniently just below your volume — take one month of real statements and price it both ways.
One more thing worth checking before you switch anything: how quickly the money actually lands. Two processors quoting the same rate can settle days apart, and for a business managing payroll against a thin balance, funding speed is worth more than a tenth of a point. Ask what standard settlement looks like, whether next-day funding costs extra, and what happens to deposits over a weekend or a holiday. It rarely appears on a rate comparison and it is frequently the thing you notice most.
Before signing anything, ask four questions and write down the answers: what is the markup over interchange, what is the contract term, what are the monthly fees in full, and what does leaving cost? A processor that will not answer the fourth in writing has told you what you need to know.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it illegal to charge the 3% credit card fee?
A.  Not in Missouri. The state has no law prohibiting or regulating credit card surcharges, so a Missouri business may pass the cost on. You must still follow the card networks’ rules — which generally cap the surcharge around 3–4%, require clear advance disclosure, and require registering the practice. Legality genuinely varies by state, which is why national guides dodge this question.
### Q. Can I pass on credit card fees to my customer?
A.  In Missouri, yes. You can either surcharge credit card payments or run a cash discount, where the posted price applies to everyone and cash customers pay less. The cash-discount structure avoids most surcharge rules. Either way, disclose it before the transaction — customers object far more to the surprise than to the amount.
### Q. Can merchants charge 2% extra on credit card payments?
A.  Yes, provided the surcharge does not exceed your actual cost of acceptance and stays within the networks’ cap, generally around 3–4%. A 2% surcharge on credit cards is well inside that. Note that debit cards are treated differently and cannot be surcharged the same way, so avoid a blanket fee on all card payments.
### Q. Is a 3% credit card fee normal?
A.  It is at the high end but not unusual, particularly for online, invoiced or keyed transactions, which run about 2.25% to 3.5% plus a fixed amount. In-person card-present rates should be lower, around 1.8% to 2.6%. If you are paying near 3% for mostly in-person sales, your effective rate is worth auditing.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to accept a credit card payment?
A.  Card-present beats keyed every time — taking the card in person is meaningfully cheaper than typing the number into a form, because keyed transactions carry more fraud risk. Beyond that: encourage debit where practical, since regulated debit interchange is lower, and match your pricing model to your volume rather than to whichever advert reached you first.
### Q. How to avoid the 3% credit card fee?
A.  You cannot avoid interchange — it goes to the card-issuing bank and nobody discounts it. What you can do is reduce the processor’s markup, take payments in person rather than keyed, steer toward debit, and in Missouri either surcharge or offer a cash discount. Start by calculating your effective rate from a real statement; most owners have never done it.

## The Cash-Only Bakery That Takes Cards: What to Order at Missouri Baking Co on The Hill
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/explore-the-delicious-missouri-baking-co-menu-what-s-new-for-2025
“Just mix them, by the pound.” Butter and warm sugar hang in the doorway, the woman up front is pointing down the case at chocolate drops and amaretto macaroons, and behind the glass a cannoli gets filled while she watches, so the shell will still crack when she bites into it in the car. ### Screenshot This: What to Order and How to Pay
### A Genoa Baker’s Shop That Outlasted a Family Fight
Missouri Baking Company is a family-owned Italian bakery at 2027 Edwards Street, right in the heart of The Hill - the historic Italian neighborhood that’s been feeding St. Louis fresh bread and red sauce for generations. It was founded in 1924 by Stefano Gambaro, a baker from Genoa in northern Italy, and it has stayed in the family for a full century.
That century wasn’t without drama. After a court fight that began in late 2024, when one sibling sold his half of the business to an outside partner, a St. Louis court in January 2026 placed the bakery entirely in the hands of Camille “Mimi” Lordo - a granddaughter of the founder - keeping the 100-year-old institution family-run and intact. So the cannoli you carry out today still comes from the founder’s family.
You can taste that stubbornness in a shell that still shatters. A place this old has watched The Hill change around it, watched grocery-store bakeries and national chains come and go, and kept filling cannoli to order. The court fight could have ended with the doors locked and the recipes sold off. Instead the lights stayed on and the case stayed full.
### Why the Line Is Worth It
The white box on the passenger seat never makes it home full, and the awards back that up: it was named best bakery in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch’s 2024 “Headliners,” and St. Louis Magazine readers keep voting it an A-List finalist for best bakery. Honors are nice; the cannoli is the proof.
That’s what you’re standing in line for on a cold Saturday: the same handful of Italian classics, the same white box tied with string, the same cash drawer, decade after decade. When people say a place is “worth the line,” this is the spot they mean.
### What to Order From the Missouri Baking Co Menu

### The Cannoli
The shell cracks first, then the sweet ricotta cream, faintly citrus and chocolate.
