### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is it worth getting your roof cleaned?
A.  For looks, often yes. ARMA calls algae streaks an aesthetic irritant, so cleaning is mostly about appearance, curb appeal and peace of mind. It is worth it only if it’s done gently: high pressure and scrubbing can strip granules and shorten shingle life.
### Q. Is it better to pressure wash or soft wash a roof?
A.  Soft wash. The Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association says high pressure washing systems for algae removal should not be used. Soft washing lets a cleaning solution do the work, followed by a gentle rinse.
### Q. How much does it cost to soft wash your roof?
A.  This Old House lists soft washing at $0.30-$0.75 per square foot, so a 1,500-square-foot roof works out to about $450-$1,125. Fixr says soft-washing a 1,500-square-foot roof can reach $1,326 at the high end. Get two written local quotes.
### Q. What is soft wash roof cleaning?
A.  It’s cleaning with a solution instead of force. A crew gently applies a mix of bleach, trisodium phosphate and water, then rinses the roof with a gentle spray. No high-pressure wand on the shingles.
### Q. How often should a house roof be cleaned?
A.  There’s no fixed calendar. Because the streaks are cosmetic, clean when they come back enough to bother you. Shady slopes that stay damp tend to streak first. Algae-resistant shingles, many made with copper, are the preventive option when you re-roof.
### Q. Can I clean my roof myself?
A.  Yes, using ARMA’s bleach, TSP and water mix and a gentle rinse, but ARMA warns the process makes the roof slippery and hazardous to walk on. Work from a ladder, protect your plants, and hire a pro for steep or two-story roofs.
### Q. Is it okay to pressure wash asphalt?
A.  Not asphalt shingles. ARMA says high pressure washing should not be used for algae removal, and warns that friction can loosen and remove granules, shortening the life of the shingle.

## 15-Year-Old Furnace, $400 Quote: St. Louis Repair or Replace
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hvac-repair-vs-replace-a-st-louis-homeowners-guide
The furnace is 15. The fix is $400. Your socks are already cold on the basement concrete of a South City brick flat, and the tech’s flashlight is still resting on top of the cabinet. Upstairs, the floor registers have stopped breathing, and the kids are asking why their room is cold. No click, no whoosh, just the fridge humming in the kitchen. You flip the repair quote over and do the math in pen: 15 times 400 is 6,000.
That 6,000 is over a line. Trane, the furnace and air conditioner maker, calls it the $5,000 rule: multiply the age of your equipment by the estimated repair cost, and if the number is more than $5,000, consider replacing the unit. Screenshot that. It turns a panicked basement decision into kitchen-table arithmetic.
Then hold on to a second number, a St. Louis one: $65, which is the city’s $40 residential furnace permit plus its $25 application fee. The city issues those permits to licensed mechanical contractors who are certified by the City of Saint Louis. Here’s the turn: the city’s fee schedule lists a combination furnace and condensing unit at $40 too. Swap the furnace and the outdoor AC unit together and the permit costs no more than the furnace alone. So when a replacement quote comes in low and never says the word permit, you’re not looking at a bargain. You’re looking at a permit nobody has mentioned yet. Ask about it.
### Should I repair or replace my HVAC system in St. Louis?
In St. Louis, start with the $5,000 rule: multiply the furnace’s age by the repair quote, and if the result tops 5,000, start pricing a replacement. ENERGY STAR says to consider replacing a furnace that is more than 15 years old, or an air conditioner or heat pump that is more than 10. Inside the city, a new furnace needs a mechanical permit, $40 plus a $25 application fee, pulled by a City-certified licensed contractor.
### The permit only a city-licensed contractor can pull
Here’s the St. Louis piece of this decision, and it protects your wallet and your family. Mechanical permits in the city are required to install things like boilers and furnaces, and to apply, a contractor needs a Mechanical Contractor’s license issued by the City of St. Louis Building Division. The rules behind it are the 2018 International Mechanical Code as the city adopted it, through Ordinance #70800.
It isn’t an excuse for a slow job, either. The city says most applications are approved within 1 to 3 business days, and once a permit is approved, the contractor prints it from the STL City Permits dashboard and schedules the inspection. So ask every bidder the same blunt question, out loud, at the basement stairs: are you licensed with the city, and are you pulling the permit?
Want to check for yourself? The city’s Permit Section is at 1200 Market, Room 425, at (314) 622-3313, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The city even posts residential mechanical permits by neighborhood on its open data dashboard, so you can see how busy furnace work has been on your side of town. Write the Permit Section number in marker on the furnace cabinet, right next to the filter size, so the next time a stranger with a clipboard is standing in your basement, the question is already waiting for you.
### When the furnace goes, look at the whole system
Stand at the furnace and look up. If you have central air, that sheet-metal box riding on top, sweating in August and silent in January, is part of the air conditioning, and out back the condenser sits on its slab by the alley. The furnace doesn’t live alone down there. It shares ductwork, a blower and usually a thermostat with the air conditioner outside, so a furnace decision is really a whole-house decision. That’s why the honest quote asks about the AC’s age before it prices a furnace. In the city, the permit math even leans that way: the fee schedule charges $40 for a combination furnace and condensing unit, the same as a furnace by itself.
Pay attention to the air itself. ENERGY STAR notes that poor equipment operation, inadequate equipment and leaky ductwork can make the air too dry in the winter or too humid in the summer. In this town you feel both: the static shock off the doorknob in February, the clammy sheets in August. If your house does both, ask the contractor to look at the ducts and the sizing, not just the box.
And ask how they sized it. “Same size as the old one” is a guess, not a measurement, and a house that has had new windows or insulation since the last furnace went in may not need the same equipment at all.
One more thing to picture before you sign. A brand-new furnace paired with a tired old air conditioner is a mismatched couple, and you’ll be back in the basement with a flashlight sooner than you’d like. If the AC is already past its own line, ENERGY STAR’s threshold for an air conditioner or heat pump is more than 10 years, then price both and decide with the whole picture on the kitchen table, not one box at a time. You may still fix only the furnace. You just won’t be surprised next July.
### What is the $5000 HVAC rule?
It’s a multiplication problem you can do on a napkin while the tech packs up. Age times repair cost. A 15-year-old furnace with a $400 repair scores 6,000, over the line, so you price a replacement before you sign anything. Run the same $400 repair on a 6-year-old furnace and you get 2,400, well under it, so you fix it and go back to bed.
Trane pairs it with a second check. If repair costs are near or above 50% of the price of a new system, it says, consider HVAC replacement, particularly for older HVAC equipment. That’s the rule that catches the one expensive repair on a younger unit, the quote that makes your stomach drop even when the age math looks fine.
Keep the size of these bills in perspective. Trane puts the cost to repair a furnace anywhere from $100 to $3,000 and up, depending on the problem, the age of the system and whether parts are still available. A small part on a young furnace is a Tuesday, the kind of thing you fix and forget before the Blues game starts. A four-figure repair on a 17-year-old furnace is the furnace telling you something.
### The 15-year line, and the smell of the first cold night
Every fall it happens the same way. The first truly cold night, the thermostat clicks, the burner lights, and the house fills with that scorched-dust smell of a furnace waking up after a long summer. If that smell is coming from a furnace that went in before your oldest kid started school, you’re already in the zone where the math changes.
ENERGY STAR draws the line plainly: if your furnace or boiler is more than 15 years old, consider replacing it with an ENERGY STAR qualified furnace, which it says is 15% more efficient than a conventional furnace. Picture that 15% on the Spire bill that lands in February, the one you open standing at the kitchen counter with your coat still on. Trane lands in the same place. Well-maintained central AC units and furnaces can last up to 20 years, it says, while heat pumps can last up to 15 years. Fifteen isn’t a death sentence. It’s the point where a repair stops being routine and starts being a bet.
The other tells are ones you can feel without a gauge. ENERGY STAR lists equipment that needs frequent repairs while your energy bills keep going up, rooms that are too hot or too cold, and a system that’s noisy. You know the room. It’s the back bedroom where the kids sleep under two blankets in January while the living room feels like July.
The furnace can wait an hour. Dinner can’t: where to eat in Wildwood.
### How often should you get HVAC replaced?
Less often than the guy with the clipboard would like. Trane says that, in general, an HVAC system will last 10-20 years, and that for any system more than 15 years old, replacement may be recommended. The gap between 10 and 20 is mostly maintenance, and most of that maintenance is boring.
Trane’s list starts with changing the HVAC air filter every 30-90 days and keeping indoor supply registers and return air vents clear. Pull the filter and hold it up to the basement light. If you can’t see the bulb through it, your blower is breathing through a pillow.
Then walk outside to the condenser, the big metal box humming next to the patio. Trane’s same list says to keep the area around the outdoor unit clear on all sides. Pull the leaves out of the fins, cut back the hostas, move the recycling bin. It takes ten minutes on a Saturday, and it’s the cheapest repair you’ll ever make.

For a repair, Trane puts the cost to fix a furnace anywhere from $100 to $3,000 and up. For more costly repairs, Trane suggests getting multiple quotes, just like you would for a replacement. Get the failing part diagnosed and priced in writing. Run the $5,000 rule and the 50% rule on it at the kitchen table, not in the basement with the tech waiting. If it fails either one, or the furnace is past 15, get replacement quotes from more than one contractor. Trane suggests getting multiple quotes and comparing them, and thinking about who answered your questions and was most responsive, not just who was cheapest.
Ask every one of them the same three things: who pulls the permit, how they sized the new equipment, and whether the price covers the inspection. The one who answers all three without flinching is usually the one worth hiring. For a deeper walk through comparing bids, see our guide to getting and comparing HVAC estimates in St. Louis.

### What is the average lifespan of a furnace?
Lennox, the furnace maker, says the average lifespan of furnaces is 15-20 years. It adds that gas furnaces can last 15-20 years, boilers 15-30 years and electric furnaces 20-30 years. ENERGY STAR suggests you consider replacing a furnace or boiler once it is more than 15 years old.
### Frequently Asked Questions

A.  Multiply the age of your equipment by the estimated repair cost. Trane says that if the number is more than $5,000, you should consider replacing the unit, and if it’s less, a repair may be the answer. A 15-year-old furnace with a $400 repair works out to 6,000, so it’s time to price a replacement.
### Q. What’s the average lifespan of an HVAC system?
A.  Trane says that, in general, an HVAC system will last 10-20 years. Well-maintained central AC units and furnaces can last up to 20 years, while heat pumps can last up to 15 years.
### Q. Is it worth replacing a 30 year old furnace?
A.  Usually, yes. ENERGY STAR suggests considering a replacement once a furnace is more than 15 years old, and that furnace is well past the line. ENERGY STAR says a qualified furnace is 15% more efficient than a conventional one, so the new unit starts paying you back on the gas bill.

The city’s fee schedule lists a residential furnace at $40, plus a $25 application fee, and most applications are approved within 1 to 3 business days.

## St. Louis Section 8 Is Closed, and the Reopening Will Run in the Newspaper
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/navigating-section-8-in-st-louis-city-your-comprehensive-guide
Who hears first when the St. Louis Section 8 list reopens? Whoever still reads the newspaper. The St. Louis Housing Authority says open waitlists “will be disclosed via phone, our website, and local newspapers.” Not a text alert. Not an app. The paper, the one your aunt still unfolds next to a cup of coffee going cold. Tell her to call you.
Is the list open right now? No. SLHA’s own Housing Choice Voucher page says it in one line, and it said the same thing when we checked it today: “The HCV waitlist is currently closed and not accepting applications until further notice.” If you have been refreshing that page on a cracked phone screen at the kitchen table, thumb hovering, hoping this is the night it changes, you are not doing anything wrong. The list is simply shut. To ask about an application you already sent, SLHA’s number is 314-531-4770.
On the county side, the Housing Authority of St. Louis County promises something more useful still: it posts reopenings on its website, social media, partner agencies and in the newspaper 30 days in advance, and its waitlist page has an email sign-up that tells you when either list reopens. Two minutes on that form today could be the whole head start. The county’s main line is (314) 428-3200. This page covers the rest of what you need before that day comes: what you would pay, why your ZIP code sets what the voucher is worth, who qualifies, and what to do while the list stays closed.
### How does Section 8 work in St. Louis and how do I apply?
A Housing Choice Voucher pays part of your rent straight to a private landlord, and you usually pay about 30% of your adjusted income. In the City of St. Louis, applications go through the St. Louis Housing Authority’s online RentCafe portal, and today its voucher list is closed until further notice. Sign up for alerts, watch the newspaper, and apply the first day it opens.
### Your ZIP code decides what the voucher is worth
This is the fact that surprises people, and it is worth saying out loud to anyone you know on a list. HUD does not give St. Louis one voucher price. Its fair market rent page for the region says: “All Housing Choice Voucher programs operated in the St. Louis, MO-IL HUD Metro FMR Area will use Small Area FMRs as defined by ZIP Codes.” Same voucher, same family, different street, different number.
Look at the two-bedroom column. HUD’s fair market rent is $990 in 63106, the ZIP where SLHA’s own office sits on Page Boulevard, and $1,730 in 63105. That is a $740 gap for the same two bedrooms. These are HUD’s benchmarks, not a promise of what the housing authority will pay, and they are adjusted each year. But they tell you why a landlord in one neighborhood says yes and one across town says the rent is too high. When you get a voucher, ask for the limit in the exact ZIP you want before you fall in love with a porch.
### How much rent will I pay on Section 8?
Your share is not a flat fee. Federal rules set your total tenant payment as the highest of a few amounts, starting with “30 percent of the family’s monthly adjusted income” and “10 percent of the family’s monthly income.” If your adjusted income is $1,500 a month, 30% of that is $450. The voucher covers the rest, up to the limit.
There is one guardrail worth knowing before you sign anything. When you first rent a place and its gross rent is above the payment standard, federal rules say your share must not exceed 40 percent of your adjusted monthly income. That rule is what stops a pretty apartment from quietly eating your grocery money. If the numbers on the paper make your stomach drop, that is your signal to keep looking.
### Who qualifies for Section 8 in Missouri?
SLHA posts its income chart on its own income limits page. Right now it lists $39,750 for a one-person household and $56,750 for a family of four, and those figures are adjusted each year when HUD publishes new limits. Income is the gate, but not the only one. County Housing says eligibility typically includes income, family size, and U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status.
The program is also built to reach the lowest incomes first. Federal rules say not less than 75 percent of the families a housing authority admits to its voucher program from the waiting list in a year must be extremely low income. So if your paycheck feels impossibly small next to your rent, you are exactly who the program was written for.
### When the list opens, the first day counts
An older version of this page told you selection was a lottery and speed did not matter. SLHA’s own Apply for Housing page says otherwise. When funding is available, applications are selected based on preferences, and “Applications resulting in a tie in preferences will be sorted on the waiting list in date and time order.” Ties go to whoever applied earlier. Apply on day one.
Applications go online through SLHA’s RentCafe portal, and each household may apply only once. You get a confirmation number; write it on paper and tape it inside the folder where you keep every letter, because a phone dies and a screenshot gets lost. Applying through SLHA is always free. If a disability or another hardship keeps you from applying online, SLHA offers paper applications through its reasonable accommodation process at 314-531-4770 (TDD 314-286-4223).
After you apply, the paperwork is on you. SLHA says you must report changes to your name, address, phone, email, income or family size within 10 business days. County Housing warns that failing to report changes may get you removed from the waitlist. Moving in with your sister? Tell SLHA that week.
Do one thing tonight: get on the alert lists. Sign up for County Housing’s waitlist email, bookmark the SLHA voucher page, and dial 2-1-1 for rent help while you wait. Our St. Louis help and assistance hub gathers food, housing and emergency support in one place.
If you run a building that rents to voucher holders, or a nonprofit that walks families through the application, the people reading this page are looking for you right now. List it on St Louis Near Me Directory so renters on a long wait have one more door to knock on, and you get more customers.
### City, county or the Illinois side: one list does not cover all three
Apply to the authority for the place you actually live. Getting this wrong means waiting on a list that cannot help you.
City of St. Louis: the St. Louis Housing Authority, 3520 Page Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63106, phone 314-531-4770. To check whether an application you already sent was received, SLHA says to call that number.
St. Louis County: the Housing Authority of St. Louis County, 8865 Natural Bridge, St. Louis, MO 63121, phone (314) 428-3200. It keeps two lists, one for public housing and one for vouchers, and says it has no exact date for reopening.
Illinois side of the river: apply through the Illinois housing authority that serves your town. The rules on rent and eligibility are federal, so most of this page still applies.
If you already hold a voucher and want to move outside SLHA’s area, its page notes the agency bills for portability. Ask before you sign a lease across the county line.
### What can stop an application cold
Most denials come down to income or paperwork. A few are absolute. Federal rules require housing authorities to refuse admission if anyone in the household is subject to a lifetime sex offender registration requirement, or has ever been convicted of manufacturing or producing methamphetamine on the premises of federally assisted housing. Other history is screened case by case under each authority’s policy, so tell the truth on the form. SLHA’s fraud warning is blunt: signing a form you know is false is fraud.
And guard your wallet. County Housing posts its own warning to beware of online scams about the voucher waitlist. SLHA says applying is always free, so anyone asking for a fee, a gift card or a wire to “move you up” is lying. Hang up, then call the number printed on the agency’s own site.
### The day the voucher arrives, a clock starts
Getting picked is the start of a search, not the end of one. Federal rules say a voucher’s first term must be at least 60 calendar days, and the housing authority may grant extensions. You find the place yourself. SLHA’s page puts it simply: the family is responsible for finding housing where the owner agrees to rent under the program, and SLHA then pays a portion of the rent each month directly to the property owner.
Start calling landlords the same week the envelope comes. Walk the unit with the voucher’s ZIP limit in your pocket, open the windows, run the tap, look under the sink. The place still has to pass the authority’s inspection before the lease is approved. And once you are in, SLHA runs a Bridge to Homeownership program that helps voucher families use their FSS escrow savings toward a mortgage, so the voucher can be a first step, not the last stop.
Can’t wait years for a voucher? Some St. Louis apartments take income-based applications directly. Here is how to find a low-income apartment without the voucher list.
### While the list stays closed
Do not hang your whole year on one list. The wait is long and nobody can tell you how long, so the families who get housed soonest are usually the ones with four or five irons in the fire at once, each with its own folder and its own reminder on the fridge. Stack your options:
Call 2-1-1. United Way 211 of Missouri and Illinois is a 24/7 connection to resources and agencies near you: dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626 and a trained resource specialist picks up.
Look at income-based buildings. Many properties set rent by income without a voucher. See our guides to income-based housing and low-income housing in St. Louis.
Facing eviction? Do not wait on Section 8. Start with emergency rent assistance in St. Louis.
Searching in North County? Get a feel for the area around Black Jack with our Black Jack dining guide.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is the St. Louis Section 8 waiting list open?
A.  No. The St. Louis Housing Authority’s voucher page says the HCV waitlist is currently closed and not accepting applications until further notice. SLHA says open waitlists will be announced by phone, on its website and in local newspapers. County Housing’s waitlist page lets you register to receive an email when either of its waitlists reopens.
### Q. How do I apply for Section 8 housing in St. Louis?
A.  City residents apply online through SLHA’s RentCafe portal while the list is open; each household may apply once, and applying is free. Paper applications are available as a reasonable accommodation at 314-531-4770. On the county side, County Housing says that when a waitlist opens you can apply online through the RentCafe portal.
### Q. How much rent will I pay on Section 8?
A.  Usually the highest of 30% of your monthly adjusted income or 10% of your monthly income. When you first rent a unit priced above the payment standard, your share cannot exceed 40% of your adjusted monthly income.
### Q. How much is a 2 bedroom Section 8 voucher in Missouri?
A.  In the St. Louis area it depends on your ZIP code, because HUD uses Small Area Fair Market Rents here. HUD’s two-bedroom fair market rent is $990 in 63106 and $1,730 in 63105. Ask the housing authority for its payment standard in the ZIP you want; the figures are adjusted each year.
### Q. How long is the waiting list for Section 8 in Missouri?
A.  I could not find a published wait time from either agency. County Housing says waiting time varies with program availability and the number of applicants, and SLHA’s list is closed until further notice. Use the wait to get on every list you qualify for and to look at income-based apartments.
### Q. What disqualifies you from Section 8?
A.  Income above the limit is the most common reason. Federal rules also require a denial if a household member is subject to lifetime sex offender registration or was convicted of making methamphetamine in federally assisted housing. False information on the application is fraud.

## Call Before the Ceiling Drips: Who Qualifies for St. Louis Home Repair Grants
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/who-is-eligible-for-government-home-improvement-grants-a-comprehensive-guide
The bucket under the kitchen ceiling is half full again, and every few seconds it pings. The furnace clicks, hums, and gives up. Who pays to fix a house like this when the money is already gone? In the city of St. Louis, the honest answer starts with one phone call, 314-657-3888, and it starts before the ceiling gives way, because the program on the other end of that line has a waiting list.
It does not start with a check in the mail. The federal government’s own help site says flatly that it does not offer “free money” to individuals to repair or improve their homes, and that the sites claiming otherwise are often scams. Read that again the next time a video tells you to click for your free home grant. What St. Louis does have is a real City program that pays for real repairs. It is slow, and its paperwork trips people long after they thought they were in, including families living in a parent’s house whose name is still on every bill. The people who get the most out of it are the ones who called while the stain on the ceiling was still just a stain.
### Who is eligible for government home improvement grants?
It depends on the program. In the city of St. Louis, the Healthy Home Repair Program takes homeowners who have owned and lived in their home at least 2 years, hold clear title, are current on taxes, mortgage and homeowner’s insurance, and earn under 80% of Area Median Income. Seniors 60 and older can also call (314) 612-5918. Call 314-657-3888 to join the waiting list.
That last sentence is the one that matters most, and it is the one nobody puts in the headline. The program is run by the City’s Community Development Administration, and it blends loans and grants to pay for essential repairs; it is not a check in the mail. The City’s own enrollment page says that once your intake is received you go on a waiting list, and that because so many homeowners are already on it, there may be a significant delay before you can take part. Emergency repair needs get priority. Everyone else waits for a notice that their name has reached the top.
### The waiting list is the program
So here is the move most people miss: get on the list now, while the furnace still clicks on and the roof is only stained, not open. You can call 314-657-3888 or start online through the City’s application site, and you will get periodic updates as you move up. The call takes a few minutes and some basic information. The wait is the long part. Start the clock before you need it. That is the line worth passing to the neighbor with the blue tarp on the roof.
Write down the day you called and the name of whoever took your information, and keep that scrap of paper in the same folder as your deed. When the updates come, you will know exactly how long you have been in line, and nobody can tell you that you never called.
When your turn comes, an evaluator visits and writes up a list of qualified repairs. The program is honest about its limits: it can only address problems that threaten health and safety, it may not fix everything you want, and it cannot repair a home that is structurally unsound or one that goes past its funding limits. A new kitchen is not on the table. A furnace that has gone cold in January, wiring that smells hot behind the outlet, a roof letting water into the walls: that is the work it was built for. The City’s partner agency, Mission: St. Louis, then builds the repair plan, explains the costs and the financial help available, prepares the legal documents and manages the contractors until the work is done.
### What the City asks of you, line by line
For the City program, the rules are short and strict. You have to live in the City of St. Louis, have owned and lived in the home for at least 2 years, have clear title, be current on your real estate taxes and mortgage payments, and have homeowner’s insurance. Because federal dollars fund it, the household has to be low or moderate income, under 80% of Area Median Income. The dollar limits by household size are adjusted each year, so check the City’s current income limits table rather than a number you saw somewhere else.
Now the trap that catches families. When you reach the top of the list, the City asks for a stack of papers, and two lines on it sink applications that looked fine on the phone: a recorded warranty deed, and Ameren and Spire bills in your name and at your address. If you are living in the house your mother left you and the gas bill still carries her name, or the deed was never changed, the clear-title rule and the bill rule will stop you cold. Fix that while you wait, not the week the letter finally comes. It is the paperwork, not the roof, that usually decides who gets helped first.
If insurance is the snag, the City points homeowners who cannot get a policy to the Missouri FAIR Plan at 314.421.0170. The deed copy comes from the City’s Recorder of Deeds at 314.622.4610, and paid tax receipts from the Assessor’s Office at 314.622.4050.
Here is the full list the City asks for, so you can start a folder tonight:
Recorded warranty deed to your home (all pages)
Missouri driver’s license or state ID, and a copy of your Social Security card
Last year’s federal income tax return (1040 and W-2s)
Last year’s paid real estate tax bill or receipt, and your mortgage statement
Ameren, Spire and MSD sewer bills in your name and at your address
The last three months of checking and savings statements (all pages)
Proof of income: your last 4 pay stubs, or TANF, Social Security, SSI and pension letters
Key Eligibility Criteria for Home Improvement Assistance
### If you are 60 or older in the city
Seniors have a second door that moves differently. Through the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging, volunteers provide minor home repairs for people 60 or older living in their own home in the City of St. Louis. The program also covers heating and cooling repairs, basic plumbing and electrical work, and simple home modifications like ramps, handrails and grab bars. Think of the grab bar by the tub that means you stop holding your breath every time you step out. You need proof of home ownership or a current paid property tax receipt, and for contracted work you may have to cover part of the cost. Call (314) 612-5918, and the agency puts you in touch with a referring agency to schedule the work.
### A cold house and a high gas bill
If the problem is the draft that makes the curtains move with the windows shut, look at weatherization. The Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis runs a Weatherization Assistance Program for qualified homeowners and renters living in St. Louis City, at no cost to them, with an emphasis on elderly people on fixed incomes, people with disabilities and families with children. The work can include insulation, sealing air leaks, weather stripping, window and door repair, and furnace repair or replacement. Renters count here, which surprises people. Its St. Louis City division is at 1408 N. Kingshighway Blvd., (314) 615-3646, and it asks for proof of homeowner’s insurance from owners along with ID and income papers.
Waiting on a list while the gutter overflows? Our step-by-step home repair guide helps you decide what to fix first.
### What about the USDA 504 program, veterans and other federal help?
You will see the USDA Section 504 Home Repair program on every national list. It is real, but it is for people who live in a rural area and have a very low income, according to USAGov’s page on home repair programs for special groups. So before you count on it, check your exact address with USDA, because it only reaches homes in eligible rural areas.
Veterans have their own lane. The VA offers disability housing grants for veterans with qualifying service-connected disabilities, and changing a home might mean installing ramps or widening doorways. USAGov also lists Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA) grants for medically necessary changes such as wider doors or accessible bathrooms. If a disability is part of your story but not a military one, the federal benefit finder for disability is a calmer place to start than a search engine full of ads.
When no grant fits, a loan might. HUD’s Limited 203(k) mortgage lets homebuyers and homeowners finance up to $75,000 into their mortgage to repair, improve or upgrade a home. That is borrowed money, paid back with interest, so read the terms closely; this 203(k) explainer walks through how lenders handle it. For everything else, USAGov is the one place to check a program’s name before you hand anyone your Social Security number.
Call 314-657-3888 today, even if the roof is holding. While you wait, browse the St Louis Near Me home services directory for local repair pros, or start with our home services listings.
If you’re the roofer, electrician, plumber or heating-and-cooling crew who fixes these houses, the City’s program has been asking for contractors like you, and the homeowners on its list are looking too. List your business with us so they can find you.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Does the government give grants for home improvements?
A.  Not as free money for anyone who asks. USAGov says the federal government does not offer free money to individuals to fix their homes, and ads that promise it are often scams. Targeted help does exist: the City of St. Louis Healthy Home Repair Program blends loans and grants for low and moderate income homeowners, and the VA has disability housing grants for qualifying veterans.
### Q. What is the Healthy home repair Program in St. Louis?
A.  It is the City of St. Louis home repair program, administered by the Community Development Administration with Mission: St. Louis as its partner agency. It blends loans and grants to pay for repairs that threaten health and safety, for low and moderate income homeowners in the city. Call the Home Repair Hotline at 314-657-3888 to be added to the waiting list.
### Q. How to get a grant for house repairs?
A.  In the city of St. Louis, call the Home Repair Hotline at 314-657-3888 or apply online through the City to join the Healthy Home Repair waiting list. Gather your deed, ID, tax return, paid tax bill and utility bills in your name while you wait. When your name reaches the top, the City asks for that paperwork and an evaluator visits your home.
### Q. What grants are available for home repairs in Missouri?
A.  In St. Louis, the main ones are the City’s Healthy Home Repair Program, the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging’s minor home repair help for people 60 and older, and the Urban League’s free weatherization for qualified city homeowners and renters. Rural Missourians with very low incomes may qualify for USDA Section 504, and veterans with qualifying disabilities can apply for VA housing grants.
### Q. What is the 504 home repair program?
A.  It is a USDA program for people who live in a rural area and have a very low income. According to USAGov, Section 504 provides funds to improve or modernize your home or remove health and safety hazards. Because it is limited to rural areas, check your exact address with USDA before you apply from anywhere in the metro.
### Q. What if I can’t afford to fix my house?
A.  Get on the City’s Healthy Home Repair waiting list at 314-657-3888 now, since emergency repairs get priority and everyone else waits. If you are 60 or older, call the Area Agency on Aging at (314) 612-5918. For drafts and a failing furnace, the Urban League’s weatherization program at (314) 615-3646 is free for qualified city households.
### Q. What is considered a major home repair?
A.  For St. Louis repair programs, the line is health and safety. The City’s program says it can only address problems that threaten health and safety, and it asks contractors such as roofers, electricians, plumbers and heating and cooling crews to apply to do the work. A failing roof, furnace or wiring counts. Cosmetic updates do not, and a house that is structurally unsound is beyond its reach.

## Don’t Call. Walk In: The Side Door at 800 N. Tucker Where St. Patrick Center Help Starts
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-patrick-s-center-in-st-louis-missouri-services-and-community-impact
The strap of the bag digs into your shoulder. The papers that prove who you are sit folded in the front pocket, gone soft at the creases from being checked so many times. Downtown is waking up around you, and the only thing you need to know is where the door is.
It’s a side door. St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center is on the north side of the building at 800 N. Tucker Blvd., the left side as you face it from Tucker, at the corner of Convention Center Drive. Intake starts every weekday at 8 a.m. and again at 1 p.m., first come, first served, and the door closes for lunch from noon to 1. No appointment. What happens inside is called a discovery session: a private sit-down with a specialist who works out what you need and which programs fit. Here’s the part that surprises people: you can’t call ahead. Intake won’t start by phone, email or a message on social media, so the whole first step is walking through that door.
Bring a photo ID, anything that shows where you’ve been staying, and a utility shutoff notice if that’s the emergency. Don’t have any of it? The center says to come in anyway. If you’re driving, there are meters on the surrounding streets and a $3, cash-only lot across the street from the Tucker entrance.
Need a bed tonight? The center isn’t an overnight shelter. Call 2-1-1 or (314) 802-0700 for tonight’s shelter options. It also has no rental assistance available right now, so if a past-due rent notice is what brought you here, ask the intake specialist where to take it next. One visit can still reach well past this building. St. Patrick Center has led the joint City and County coordinated entry process for years, the system that matches people to housing programs across the region. That’s also why its get-help page posts an HMIS release of information: it’s the consent that lets your intake go into the region’s shared homeless-services database, so the next agency doesn’t make you tell the whole story again.
Screenshot this: St. Patrick Center Welcome Center, side door on the north side of 800 N. Tucker Blvd. Weekdays at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m. No appointment. A bed tonight: 2-1-1 or (314) 802-0700. Veterans: 314-356-0657.
St. Patrick Center has been one of St. Louis’s main front doors for homeless and housing services for more than 40 years, all from that one building. It’s a ministry of Catholic Charities, and housing usually comes first. It’s hard to keep a job or a clinic appointment when you don’t know where you’ll sleep.
### Key Takeaways
Help starts with a walk-in intake at the Welcome Center, weekdays at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m. There are no phone or email intakes.
The Hospital to Healthy Housing (H2H) program, run with Barnes-Jewish Hospital, moves people who keep landing in the ER into apartments. Their emergency visits fell 53% once they had permanent housing.
Project HERO sets aside 47 apartments for veterans facing trauma and homelessness, with one-on-one case managers.
It isn’t an overnight shelter and has no rental assistance right now. For a bed tonight, call 2-1-1 or (314) 802-0700.
Volunteers serve meals, sort donations and cook casseroles and salads for clients; donations go to the dock on Hadley Street.
### What St. Patrick's Center Does in St. Louis
### Mission and Core Values
The discovery session is private, just you and a specialist. You set the folded papers down, or you say you don’t have any, and you start talking. What comes back is one plan instead of three waiting lists: a place to live, steady work and healthcare, usually in that order. Respect is part of the method, not a slogan. People who have been talked down to at enough counters stop coming back, and a housing plan only works if they come back.
### Serving St. Louis City and County
The center serves people from both St. Louis City and St. Louis County. It’s one door in a wider local safety net, and when it isn’t the right one, the intake specialist can point you to the next, including neighborhood groups like Better Family Life and its community resource programs.
### Support Across Three Areas
Housing, income and health tend to come apart together. The eviction costs the job, and the lost job costs the prescription. So the center works on all three at once instead of one symptom at a time.
Housing: from a referral to emergency shelter, to a lease through its network of more than 200 St. Louis-area landlords, to 47 apartments set aside for veterans through Project HERO.
Work: job training, resume help, interview practice and introductions to local employers who are hiring.
Health: help finding doctors, specialists and mental health care, plus the Hospital to Healthy Housing partnership with hospitals like Barnes-Jewish.
### Housing First: How Does St. Patrick Center Get People Inside?
A safe place to live is the first step for most people trying to rebuild. Without it, holding a job or keeping up with your health gets much harder. St. Patrick's Center runs several housing paths for exactly that reason, each built to fit a different situation.
### The Hospital to Healthy Housing (H2H) Program
Some people land in the emergency room again and again for one underlying reason: they have nowhere to live. H2H goes straight at that pattern. The center partners with hospitals like Barnes-Jewish to move homeless patients into apartments, then links them with the health and social services they need. Fewer costly ER trips follow, and the hospital spends less.
Reduces frequent ER visits: Participants saw roughly a 63% drop in emergency room visits in the first 90 days after getting housing, and about a 43% drop a year later.
Cuts down hospital stays: Stable housing also cuts down on avoidable hospital stays.
Lowers readmissions: Fewer people cycle back through the emergency room when they have a safe place to live.
### Project HERO: Support for Veterans
Coming home from service and then finding nowhere to live is a brutal combination. Project HERO answers it with 47 apartments set aside for veterans facing trauma and homelessness. Residents work one-on-one with case managers on personal goals, managing money, working through emotions, landing a job. The center partners with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and the Missouri Department of Mental Health so support never hinges on a veteran's finances. Residents put a share of their income toward rent, building financial footing while they heal.
### Finding Stability Through Landlord Partnerships
The center has built a network of over 200 landlords across the St. Louis area, and that network is what makes it possible to place people quickly. Staff handle much of the legwork, matching clients to a home that fits their budget and getting them settled faster than most expect. Landlords who want to help can join the network and list your property.
Here's a quick look at how we help:
Apartment identification: We actively search for suitable apartments based on client needs.
Lease assistance: We help with the paperwork and understanding lease agreements.
Ongoing support: We connect you with resources to help you maintain your housing long-term.
Totally unrelated, but - window companies across St. Louis are mapped here.
### Help With Jobs and Healthcare
Housing is only one piece of the puzzle. People also need their health and a way to earn a living before things hold steady. So the center connects clients with medical care and job support, treating the two as part of the same recovery rather than separate errands.
### Healthcare Coordination and Access
Getting the right medical care is hard when everything else is unstable too. The center helps clients work through the system: finding doctors, specialists, and mental health services, then keeping care on track. Staff connect people with help for chronic conditions, prescriptions, and preventive visits. The coordinated approach is built to keep people healthier and out of the hospital.
### Job Training and Placement Services
A job that pays the bills and means something is a big step forward. The center runs training programs that build the skills employers actually ask for, whether someone is starting fresh or returning to work after time away. Support includes resume building, interview practice, and introductions to local businesses that are hiring, work with room to grow.
### Addressing Complex Social and Medical Needs
Sometimes it all hits at once. Health problems, past trauma, or substance use can pile up while someone is also trying to find housing and work. The team builds a single plan that covers the full set of needs instead of one at a time, then connects the person with services that range from day-to-day help to support groups. The whole person, not one slice of the problem.
Here's a look at how our programs have made an impact:
Reduced Hospital Visits: For individuals in our Hospital to Healthy Housing (H2H) program, emergency room visits dropped by 53% after they secured stable housing and received support services.
Fewer Inpatient Stays: Inpatient hospital days for H2H participants decreased by 67%.
Lower Readmission Rates: The rate of patients being readmitted to the hospital fell by 42%.
The numbers point to a simple truth: stable housing and steady care change how well people do overall. Veterans get the same combination through Project HERO, a place to live plus the tools to rebuild, so recovery has somewhere to take root. You can read more about the center's housing solutions and how they contribute to a healthier St. Louis.
### Want to Help? Where Volunteers Fit
Community Engagement and Volunteer Impact
Much of what the center does depends on people giving their time. Volunteers keep programs running day to day and help the work reach further than paid staff alone ever could. There's a real role here for anyone willing to show up.
### Volunteer Opportunities and Contributions
Volunteering is the most direct way to pitch in. Each year, nearly 3,000 volunteers give over 29,000 hours, and the center leans on every one of those hours. The jobs vary: serving meals, sorting donations, helping at fundraising events, backing up the office, even cooking casseroles and salads for clients at home. Every hour given helps build a stronger St. Louis.
### Host a Group Volunteer Project
Want to bring friends, family, or coworkers along? Hosting a group project, like assembling care kits, is a good way to do it. A group gathers and packs essential kits for the individuals and families the center serves, a hands-on afternoon that puts needed items straight into people's hands. The center tells you which supplies are running short so your event matches what's actually needed right now.
### Building a Stronger St. Louis Together
The center works as a hub for community action, not only a place that hands out services. Volunteer a few hours or run a kit pack and you become part of the response to homelessness and poverty in the city. Paired with the center's core programs, that effort helps people reach self-sufficiency and hold onto their dignity. To find current openings, support the mission of St. Patrick's Center on their website.
### Does It Work? What the Center Tracks
### Program Effectiveness and Outcomes
How does the center know its work is landing? It watches both the numbers and the stories. Staff track how many people find stable housing, how many land jobs, and how their wellbeing shifts over time. The measure isn't one night off the street. It's whether someone builds a life. Results get compared against peer organizations to keep the programs sharp.
Tracking client progress from entry to exit.
Gathering feedback through surveys and interviews.
Analyzing long-term housing stability rates.
### Strategic Planning for Growth
The center plans to reach more people and serve them better. That means identifying which programs do the most good, making sure those programs are funded, and finding new revenue so the work can continue. Careful with its resources, deliberate about what comes next.
### Collaborations for Regional Impact
No single organization solves homelessness in St. Louis on its own. So the center works closely with other groups, sharing ideas and resources and coordinating who does what with fellow homeless service providers. Those partnerships knit a stronger safety net across the region. The center also aligns its strategy with Catholic Charities of St. Louis to keep the shared message consistent. To pitch in, look into donor engagement opportunities.

### St. Patrick Center Drop-In Hours: The Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker
The front door for help is the Welcome Center, a side entrance on the north side of St. Patrick Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd., at the corner of Convention Center Drive. Bring a photo ID, proof of where you live or that you’re homeless, and any utility shutoff notice, if you have them. If all you’ve got is the bag on your shoulder, come anyway. A specialist assesses your situation and routes you to housing, health or job programs. St. Patrick Center has led the joint City and County coordinated entry process for years, so one visit can open doors well beyond its own programs.
