### What your kids get when you stay
Addressing Root Causes Through Fatherhood Engagement
Too many programs treat symptoms and leave the source untouched. Involved fathers change that math. When a dad is present and engaged, he addresses several problems at once, at the root rather than the surface. Being there for the kids is a big piece of it. The bigger piece is a family unit sturdy enough to hold together when life gets rough.
### Combating Family Instability and Its Societal Effects
A stable home underpins a healthy society, and the reverse holds just as firmly. When fathers are absent or checked out, families tend to struggle, and the effects spread, from a child’s grades to their long-term well-being. Supporting fathers attacks that instability directly. Fewer kids grow up without a consistent male role model, and research ties that consistency to better outcomes.
Reduced likelihood of children experiencing poverty.
Lower rates of juvenile delinquency.
Improved academic achievement for children.
### Cultivating Essential Character Traits in Fathers
Showing up is step one. Showing up with the right skills is the harder, more useful part. Fatherhood programs spend real time on character: responsibility, patience, steady communication, the knack for solving a problem instead of escalating it. Those traits carry past the living room. A dad who learns to defuse a conflict at home tends to handle one at work better too, and the family, the job, and the block all gain from it.
### Reducing Crime and Improving Worker Productivity
The connection is less of a leap than it sounds. Children with engaged fathers are less likely to end up in the justice system, a straight gain for public safety. And a father who has steadied his own life usually brings that to the job, showing up reliable and focused. That lifts the local economy and the workplace at the same time, and it all traces back to supporting dads in the role.
Fix the root and the surface problems tend to ease with it. Engaged fathers make families and communities stronger, and that is the entire premise the center runs on. It is also why the programs stack employment, reentry, and relationship help together instead of treating each one in isolation.
People are asking
### At what age can a child choose which parent to live with in Missouri?
In Missouri the judge makes that call, not the child. The custody statute lists “the unobstructed input of a child, free of coercion and manipulation” as one factor in deciding the child’s best interests, and the judge may interview the child in chambers. The same law says no preference goes to either parent because of that parent’s sex, so a dad starts even. What you control is the Sunday drive: keep the who-do-you-want-to-live-with question out of the car, because pressure is the one thing that factor is written to keep out.
### How to Get Started at the Fathers & Families Support Center
Call 314-333-4170 or fill out the Get Started form at fatherssupportcenter.org. The headquarters is downtown at 1601 Olive Street, and services run at several locations around St. Louis. Moms are welcome too: the flagship Family Formation program enrolls men and women.
Family Formation is the big commitment, and the center doesn’t hide it. It’s a no-cost, six-week, Monday-through-Friday program, with day and evening classes, covering parenting and co-parenting, family therapy, job skills, health, legal help and substance-use prevention, followed by a year of follow-up support. Can’t take six weeks of weekdays? Fathers’ Rap, a peer support group at 1601 Olive, meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m. and covers child support, custody and visitation, relationships and work. That’s a slot a dad can make straight off a shift, still in his work boots.
The other doors: Employment Development & Mentoring pairs job seekers with trained mentors and works toward placement; the Re-Entry Project runs with the Missouri Department of Corrections at the Transition Center of St. Louis; and the Youth Leadership & Development Program mentors young people ages 14 to 24. Since its first class more than 25 years ago, the center has worked with nearly 23,000 fathers, and it reports a 7% recidivism rate for its graduates, against a Missouri average of about 35%.
### Know a dad who needs this?
The Fathers and Families Support Center turns uncertain dads into the role models their kids need, steadies families, and leaves whole neighborhoods better off. A more present father, a calmer household, a more connected block: that is the sequence, and it starts with support. You can add to it. Volunteer an hour, send a donation, or point one father toward the door. Any of those keeps the work going and helps build stronger families, one dad at a time.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What types of family support services are available?
A.  In St. Louis, the Fathers & Families Support Center alone offers parenting and co-parenting classes, family therapy, job training and placement, legal assistance, substance-use prevention, reentry help after prison, youth mentoring for ages 14 to 24 and a twice-weekly support group for dads. For food, housing or utility help on top of that, dial 2-1-1 to reach United Way’s referral line.
### Q. What support groups are available in St. Louis?
A.  For fathers, Fathers’ Rap meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Fathers & Families Support Center, 1601 Olive Street, with talk on child support, custody and visitation, relationships and work. The center’s Neighborhood Healing Network also runs monthly trauma workshops for people hurt by crime or violence. For other kinds of groups, 2-1-1 keeps a current list.
### Q. What are the legal rights of a father in Missouri?
A.  If you’re married to the mother, you’re presumed the legal father. If not, paternity has to be established first, by both parents signing an acknowledgment of paternity or through a court or child support order. Once it is, Missouri law presumes that equal or roughly equal parenting time is in the child’s best interest, though a judge can find otherwise.
### Q. How do I contact child support services in Missouri?
A.  Call the Missouri Department of Social Services’ Child Support Customer Service line at 866-313-9960 about a case with an order, or 800-859-7999 for general information. You can also manage a case through the Child Support Customer Portal at dss.mo.gov. The state program serves both parents, including help establishing paternity and changing an existing order.
### Q. How to cope with being a father?
A.  Don’t do it alone. Talk with other dads who’ve been there, like the men at Fathers’ Rap, keep a simple routine with your kids even on hard weeks, and look after your own sleep and health. If stress turns into hopelessness, call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. Asking for help is part of the job.
### Q. What kind of job help does the center offer?
A.  Its Employment Development & Mentoring program covers job readiness, resume writing and interview coaching, occupational training, financial education and job placement, with trained mentors for career guidance. It shows up in paychecks: in its most recent annual report, the center says 267 participants gained or kept a job, at an average of $18.65 an hour.

## St. Louis Women's Shelters: You Don't Need a Packed Bag to Get In
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/finding-support-a-guide-to-st-louis-women-s-shelters-and-resources
You do not have to pack a bag first.
Saint Martha’s, a confidential St. Louis shelter for women and children, says it on its own page: the most important thing is a woman’s safety, “even if that means leaving behind the necessities.” The shelter provides meals, toiletries, emergency clothing, linens and personal care items. So if the duffel is still half-zipped on the closet floor, or never got packed at all, that is not a reason to wait for a better night.
What helps tonight is one phone number, and the phone can stay on silent while you look it up. Saint Martha’s answers at 314-533-1313, open 24/7, 365 days a year. Safe Connections runs a 24-Hour Crisis Helpline at 314-531-2003, and you can text it as well as call. ALIVE’s 24-hour crisis line for St. Louis is 314-993-2777. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788. If you are in danger right now, call 911.
One detail worth a screenshot. Safe Connections has two numbers, and only one of them is the crisis line. 314-646-7500 is the number listed with its office address on Hampton Avenue. The 24-Hour Crisis Helpline is 314-531-2003. Save that one in your phone under a name nobody would look twice at, the pharmacy, a cousin, the dentist, and send it to a friend who might need it someday without having to ask.
The rest of this page is the plain version of what happens next: who picks up, what a shelter room actually looks like, how long you can stay, what to do if the shelter is full, and where to turn if it is not violence at all, just nowhere to sleep. Read it in pieces. Close the tab when you need to. It will still be here.
### How do I get into a women’s shelter in St. Louis?
Call a 24-hour line and let an advocate do the searching with you. In St. Louis that means Safe Connections at 314-531-2003, ALIVE at 314-993-2777, or Saint Martha’s shelter at 314-533-1313. Saint Martha’s says that if it has no open bed, it can still help you safety plan and work to find openings elsewhere. In immediate danger, call 911.
### What happens when you call
That helpline has a St. Louis history worth knowing. Safe Connections says it started with a single phone in a small apartment, answered around the clock by volunteers, and fifty years later it still answers 24/7. Somebody has been picking up that phone at 2 a.m. in this city for half a century.
The first voice is not a form. Safe Connections names three main purposes for its helpline: empathetic, emotional support, because sometimes you just need someone to listen and believe you; safety planning, to help you decide on your next steps when you feel trapped or unsafe; and shared resources, from its own no-cost counseling services to medical professionals, legal professionals and shelters. Its words: “There is no reason too small to reach out.” You can call about your own safety, your kids, a pet, or a friend you are worried about.
If English is not your first language, Safe Connections says it may be able to arrange phone interpreters for more than 140 languages, and callers who are Deaf or hard of hearing can reach it through Relay by dialing 711.
A call can be short. You can hang up mid-sentence if a door opens. Advocates on these lines are used to that, and the number will still work the next time you dial it, from the parking lot at work or the bathroom with the fan running.
And if the first shelter you reach is full, that is not the end of the call. Saint Martha’s says that when it has no open beds, it can still help a woman safety plan and work to find openings elsewhere. A full shelter is a reason to keep talking, not a reason to go home.
### How a domestic violence shelter works, from the inside
Most people picture a gym floor full of cots. Saint Martha’s describes something quieter. Under the heading Individual Bedrooms, it says each family has a separate, private space where they can rest without fear, in addition to shared living and dining rooms, a kitchen and a play room. That first night it may simply be a closed door, clean sheets, a toothbrush you did not have to bring, and a kitchen where somebody else already made dinner.
Look at how Saint Martha’s lists itself and you see the safety at work. The address it lists is a post office box, P.O. Box 4950. The shelter itself has a private address and 24/7 security monitoring. You will not find it on a map, and the person you left will not either. You get the location from the people on the phone.
The days after that move at your pace: counseling for you and your kids if you want it, and a plan for what comes next that you write with staff, not one handed to you. The program runs 12 weeks. One resident put the feeling plainly on the shelter’s page: “There is no judgement here.”
### Are children allowed in women’s shelters?
Saint Martha’s shelter serves women and their children, and it says a safe place is provided for each child who enters. Staff talk with kids about physical and emotional safety, teach coping skills and support the whole family. Many shelters built for survivors plan for children the same way, so ask about your kids’ ages on the first call.
If you are pregnant and have nowhere to live, The Haven of Grace serves pregnant women who are unhoused, with a maternity shelter and long-term support for mother and child. For young mothers, Almost Home says it has served more than 1,900 young St. Louis moms since 1993.
And the dog asleep by the back door counts too. Lydia’s House, a transitional housing program in St. Louis for women and children leaving domestic violence, describes its housing as confidential, safe and pet-friendly.
Save one number tonight, even if you never use it. Safe Connections’ 24-hour helpline is 314-531-2003, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233. If you are rebuilding after leaving, start with free food in St. Louis, income-based housing and help with utility bills.
If you run the shelter, the counseling practice or the legal clinic standing beside women who have left, list your organization with us so the next woman can find you. Here is how a local listing earns trust, and what the Gold plan adds for a practice or a small business.
### If you are not ready to leave yet
A call does not have to be about leaving tonight. Under Why Call, Safe Connections lists reasons that include guidance on being safer while living in an unsafe home, and discussing the safest options for leaving an unhealthy relationship, whenever that day comes. It also takes calls about bullying, gaslighting and other controlling behavior, the kind of thing that leaves no bruise and still keeps you awake at 3 a.m. replaying a conversation.
A plan can be small. Which door you would use. Which friend would answer at midnight. Where the car keys live, and whether the spare is somewhere only you know about. Advocates help you think it through without pushing you toward a decision you have not made. Saint Martha’s puts the hard questions plainly on its own page: when is it safe for a woman to leave, where will she go, how will she get there. Those are the questions a crisis line is built to answer with you, one at a time.
If someone you love is the one in danger, the same lines take your call. Safe Connections says its helpline is also there for family and friends worried about someone who may be struggling.
### How long you can stay
It depends on the kind of program, and it helps to know the difference before you call. An emergency shelter is the first stop. Saint Martha’s runs a 12-week program. Transitional housing is the next step: Lydia’s House offers confidentially located, fully furnished apartments for up to two years, and it is clear that it is not an emergency shelter. It describes itself as a critical link between emergency shelters and safe, independent living.
So the order usually runs: a crisis line, then an emergency bed, then, if you need it, transitional housing while you get work, school and a lease lined up. The apartment with your own key comes at the end, not the beginning.
### If it is not violence, just nowhere to sleep
Not every woman searching for a shelter is leaving a partner. Sometimes it is an eviction notice taped to the door, or a couch that is not available anymore. The City of St. Louis runs a Housing Help Line at (314) 802-5444, and says the city has a baseline of 400 year-round shelter beds, with more emergency beds opened during extreme cold.
United Way 211 is the other door. Dial 2-1-1, or 1-800-427-4626, and a resource specialist can connect you to food pantries, shelters, rent assistance and utility assistance across the St. Louis area and Missouri. If the first call does not land, a general helpline can point you in the right direction for local resources.
For families, Gateway180 states its vision as ending family homelessness in the St. Louis community. Another place to look is this list of shelters for women, and the county keeps a page on its human services department.
### After the first night
Safety comes first. Then the ordinary things come back one at a time: groceries, a job, a quiet hour with someone to talk to. These links are a place to start when you are ready for them.
Food: Operation Food Search and the St. Louis Area Food Bank

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are some women’s homeless shelters in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  Saint Martha’s runs a confidential shelter for women and children (314-533-1313). The Haven of Grace serves pregnant women who are unhoused, Almost Home says it has served more than 1,900 young St. Louis moms since 1993, and Gateway180 works to end family homelessness in St. Louis. For women leaving abuse, call Safe Connections at 314-531-2003 or ALIVE at 314-993-2777 and an advocate can help find an open bed.
### Q. Where can I find emergency housing in St. Louis?
A.  Call the City of St. Louis Housing Help Line at (314) 802-5444, or dial 2-1-1 for United Way 211, which connects people to shelters and rent help. The city says it keeps a baseline of 400 year-round shelter beds and opens more emergency beds during extreme cold.
### Q. How long do people stay at women’s shelters?
A.  It depends on the program. Saint Martha’s emergency shelter runs a 12-week program. Lydia’s House, which is transitional housing and not an emergency shelter, offers furnished apartments for up to two years.
### Q. What should I bring to a shelter?
A.  Whatever you can grab safely, and nothing if that is what it takes. Saint Martha’s says safety comes first even if it means leaving the necessities behind, and it provides meals, toiletries, emergency clothing, linens and personal care items.
### Q. How does a domestic violence shelter work?
A.  You call a crisis line, an advocate helps you plan, and the shelter gives you a confidential place to stay. At Saint Martha’s that means a private address with 24/7 security monitoring, a separate, private space for each family, meals, individual, group and family therapy for adults and children, and a plan for your next steps.
### Q. Are children allowed in women’s shelters?
A.  Often, yes. Saint Martha’s serves women and their children and provides a safe place for each child, along with counseling and coping skills. Ask about your children’s ages when you call.
### Q. What is Lydia’s house?
A.  Lydia’s House is a St. Louis transitional housing program for women and children who are survivors of domestic violence. It offers confidential, pet-friendly, fully furnished apartments for up to two years. It is not an emergency shelter, so start with a crisis line if you need a bed tonight.

## St. Louis Food Pantries: Most Want an ID. This Trailer Does Not
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/navigating-food-pantries-in-st-louis-your-guide-to-resources-and-support
Thursdays only, 10:30 to 12:30. That is the whole window at Estell Ministries Food Pantry on Page Boulevard, according to the city’s own list of food help. That’s it. Miss it because the bus sat at the light too long, and the cupboard with the one can of beans and the half bag of rice stays that way until next Thursday.
Or you make the trip on the right day and find the side door locked, a sheet of paper taped to the glass, the words by appointment only in marker. Your breath fogs the window while you read it twice. That is how most pantry doors in this city work, and the St. Louis Area Foodbank, which works with nearly 600 pantries, agencies and organizations in 26 counties in Eastern Missouri and Southwestern Illinois, says so on its own help page: for most food pantries, an appointment is required, and for most, a photo ID is required too. The people who walk out with a full bag are not luckier than you. They called first.
Now the two lines to screenshot and send to the friend who has been skipping lunch so the kids can eat. First: you never pay. The Foodbank’s exact words are that you do not need to bring any money to a food pantry or a food distribution event. Second, and almost nobody knows this one: there is a door with no paperwork at all. The Foodbank runs a program called Food on the Move, where neighbors walk through a custom-built trailer and choose the foods they need, and it says verification of personal information is not required to participate. No ID. No proof of address. You climb the step up into the trailer, an empty bag over your shoulder, and you reach for the cans and boxes your family will actually eat, not whatever someone packed for you.
Those trailers are not a once-a-year thing. Each month, the Foodbank and its partners hold over 80 food distribution events through Food on the Move and its Food Access and Resource Markets, and the stops are posted on the Foodbank’s distribution event calendar. And if the fridge is humming over nothing but ketchup and a jar of pickles tonight, there is hot food in this city today, too.
### Where can I get free food in St. Louis?
Dial 2-1-1, United Way’s line that answers 24/7, or type your ZIP code into the St. Louis Area Foodbank’s Pantry Locator. For a meal today, St. Patrick Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. serves lunch seven days a week, noon to 12:30 p.m., and Gateway 180 at 1000 North 19th St. hands out brown bag lunches all day. Most pantries want an appointment and a photo ID. You never need money.
### A hot lunch today, before any paperwork
A pantry fills the shelf for next week. Sometimes the problem is the next three hours: the growl that starts around eleven, the headache that comes with it, the paper bag you would trade almost anything for. The City of St. Louis keeps a list of food banks and free meals. Start with these three.
St. Patrick Center, 800 N. Tucker Blvd., lists lunch seven days a week from noon to 12:30 p.m. That is a thirty-minute window, so get in line a few minutes early. Gateway 180, at 1000 North 19th St., lists brown bag lunches seven days a week, all day, which makes it the closest thing to an open door you will find. And St. Peter and Paul Parish, in its Mid-Level Hall at 1919 S. 7th St., lists meals Monday through Friday from 5 to 5:45 p.m., with weekend meals from noon to 12:45 p.m. The city notes its list comes from Start Here STL and says to check there for the latest, so give the number a quick call before you go: St. Patrick Center is 314-802-0700, Gateway 180 is 314-231-1515 and St. Peter and Paul is 314-231-9923.
Eat first. A full stomach makes the next phone call a lot easier to make.
### Can you just show up to a food pantry?
Usually not, which is why the taped sign on that locked door catches so many people. The Foodbank says that for most food pantries an appointment is required, and that you should check the website of the pantry you want before you go. Guardian Angel Settlement, at 3300 South Jefferson Ave., is listed by the city as by appointment only, at 314-773-9027. That is normal, not a brush-off.
The exception is the shortcut from the top of this page. Food distribution events run the other way. The Foodbank describes them as walk-through or drive-through events that are temporary, planned in advance and placed in areas with low access to food. An appointment is usually not required, it is first come, first served, and an ID is usually not required either. At the drive-through markets, it looks like this: hazard lights blinking down the lot, the trunk popping open, a volunteer in a reflective vest sliding a box in while you keep both hands on the wheel. Find the dates and places on the Foodbank’s distribution event calendar, look for a Food on the Move stop if you have no ID with you, and get there early.
### The two-minute call that saves the trip
What is the difference between a food pantry and a food bank? The bank is the warehouse; the pantry is the door you walk through. The Foodbank itself puts it this way: supplied by a food bank, a food pantry is a distribution center for individuals and families in need to receive food free of charge. You will almost never shop at the warehouse. You will shop at a church basement, a school room or a storefront that the warehouse stocks.
That is why the call matters. Each pantry sets its own hours, its own service area and its own paperwork. Ask three things: are you open this week, do I need an appointment, and what do I bring. The Foodbank says to bring the documentation your pantry asks for, which may include a photo ID and proof of income, and it suggests a reusable bag, although bags are usually provided. Some doors are not where you would expect. The city lists Isaiah 58 Ministries at 2149 South Grand Blvd. with its entrance around the back, at 314-776-1410. Knowing that before you circle the building twice in the cold is worth the call by itself. To see which pantries open on which day, start with our day-by-day list of food pantries open today in St. Louis.
### Find the pantry closest to your front door
The fastest search is the St. Louis Area Foodbank’s Pantry Locator. Its instructions are simple: enter your address or ZIP code, press Find Pantries, and see what food outlets are near you. Write down two, not one. If the first is closed or full, the second is already on your list, and you are not starting over with the kids asking what’s for dinner. If the map is not working for you, the Foodbank’s phone number is (314) 292-6262.
Can’t get across town? Mobile markets bring the food to the neighborhood. Check mobile pantry schedules and the Foodbank’s calendar, and if you would rather talk to a person, our guide to where to turn for help walks through another free search tool.

### Your first visit, start to finish
The first time is the hardest, mostly because you do not know what happens behind the door. Here is the usual shape of it. Someone at a folding table asks your name, maybe your address and how many people live with you. You show your ID if they asked for it on the phone. Then you wait, often in a hallway that smells like cardboard and floor cleaner, while other people from your own neighborhood wait beside you. Some pantries hand you a packed box. Others let you walk the shelves with a cart and choose, the way you would at a small store.
Nobody is grading you. The volunteers have seen every kind of week, the layoff, the medical bill, the car that died on Gravois. Ask the questions you came with: when can I come back, do you have diapers, is there fresh produce today. Say thank you if you want to. Then carry the bag to the car and let yourself breathe. You did the hard part.
### Don’t throw out the can with yesterday’s date
You get home, unpack the bag on the counter, and a box of crackers says best by last week. Keep it. The Foodbank says “Best By,” “Sell By” and “Expiration” dates do not mean food is unsafe to eat after the date on the package. The one hard rule is infant formula, which the Foodbank says must be used before the date on the package. Check that can every time.
Groceries put away and five quiet minutes to yourself? Go read what Boulevard Heights is like.
### Help that lasts longer than one bag
A pantry gets you through the week. SNAP gets you through the month. The Foodbank says it works with partner organizations and government agencies on everything from SNAP applications to Medicaid resources. When the paperwork feels like a wall, ask the pantry volunteer handing you the bag who helps with SNAP forms nearby. For more options, see the Franciscan Sisters of Our Lady of Perpetual Help and St. Louis Public Radio’s guide to SNAP alternatives.
Health coverage is often the next bill hiding behind the grocery bill. For help with applying for Medicaid and MO HealthNet renewals, ask the same person who helped with your SNAP form. And when it is 2 a.m. and nothing is open, United Way 211 of Missouri and Illinois says you can dial 211 to reach a trained resource specialist 24/7, including for food assistance programs.
### For the neighbor who keeps asking how to help
Every reader of this page knows someone who has said, “Tell me what I can do.” Here is something specific to tell them. The Missouri Department of Revenue says any taxpayer, individual, corporation or trust, that donates cash or food supplies to a local food pantry, homeless shelter or soup kitchen may take a credit of 50 percent of the donation, up to $2,500 per taxpayer, per year. Give $200 to a pantry and the credit is worth $100 against Missouri income tax. The state says the credit is nonrefundable and scheduled to sunset, so donors should read the Department of Revenue’s food pantry credit page before counting on it. Volunteers can plug into the effort too. For who qualifies and how to claim the credit, see our guide to the Missouri food pantry tax credit.
Make one call before you close this page. Dial 2-1-1 or the pantry nearest you, ask if you need an appointment, and put your photo ID by the door tonight. For rent, utilities and family help in the same place, browse the St Louis Near Me public services directory.
If you run the corner grocery, the church kitchen or the catering van that drops off its extra trays, you already feed this city. Your business still needs to get more customers to keep doing it. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory helps neighbors find you, for under a dollar a day. List your business.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can you just show up to a food pantry?
A.  At most pantries, no. The St. Louis Area Foodbank says an appointment is required at most food pantries, so check the pantry’s website or call first. Food distribution events are the exception: an appointment is usually not required, and food goes out first come, first served.
### Q. Do you pay for food at a food pantry?
A.  No. The Foodbank says you do not need to bring any money to a food pantry or a food distribution event. A food pantry gives food free of charge to individuals and families in need.
### Q. What are the requirements to use a food pantry?
A.  Each pantry sets its own. The Foodbank says most pantries require a photo ID, and some ask for proof of income. Many also serve only certain ZIP codes, so ask whether your address is in their area when you call.
### Q. What is the difference between a food pantry and a food bank?
A.  A food bank is the supplier; a food pantry is where you pick up food. The St. Louis Area Foodbank works with nearly 600 pantries, agencies and organizations in 26 counties, and those pantries hand the food to families free of charge.
### Q. Is there any way I can get free food right now?
A.  Yes. Gateway 180 at 1000 North 19th St. lists brown bag lunches seven days a week, all day, and St. Patrick Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. serves lunch daily from noon to 12:30 p.m. Any hour, dial 2-1-1 to reach a trained resource specialist.
### Q. Who is eligible to receive the food pantry tax credit in Missouri?
A.  Any taxpayer, individual, corporation or trust, that donates cash or food supplies to a local food pantry, homeless shelter or soup kitchen. The Missouri Department of Revenue says the credit is 50 percent of the donation, up to $2,500 per taxpayer, per year, and it is nonrefundable.

## St. Louis Voucher List Closed. Some Voucher Units Aren't
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/finding-low-income-housing-in-st-louis-mo-resources-and-options
About 7,000. That is how many housing vouchers the St. Louis Housing Authority administers, and the waiting list to get the next one reads, in plain type, closed and not accepting applications until further notice.
You can feel that sentence land. The coffee has gone cold next to the late-rent notice, and your thumb keeps dragging the page down to refresh it, as if the word might change. Out in St. Louis County, the housing authority has no date yet for reopening its two lists either.
Here is the turn that notice leaves out. A closed list is one door, not the building. The city keeps a senior list open all year. A handful of County Housing properties are taking applications directly right now, on their own lists, and three of them, Elm Ridge, Scott Manor and Wellington Family Homes, are Project-Based Voucher Housing, where the assistance stays with the apartment instead of following you. And when a big list does reopen, you want your folder already sitting on the kitchen table.
If the trouble is tonight, not someday, write this number on the fridge before you read another word: the St. Louis Housing Help Line, (314) 802-5444.
### How do you get approved for low income housing?
You get approved by applying where a list is open and proving you qualify. Pull out your last pay stub and count the people who live with you, because those two numbers decide most of it. SLHA compares your household’s yearly income with limits HUD sets for this area and adjusts each year: right now $39,750 for one person and $56,750 for a family of four, with the full chart further down. Every adult must also meet HUD’s citizenship or immigration rules, pass a screening that looks at criminal activity and past rental history, and owe no balance to SLHA or any other housing authority. That last one trips people up quietly. An old balance with another housing authority counts against you, so if you owe one, call that agency before you apply.
What to do today, in order. First, open County Housing’s waitlist page and type your email into its alert form, so your phone buzzes the moment either county list reopens. Second, call the County Housing properties that are taking applications now, listed below, and ask each leasing office one question: do you have project-based voucher units, and how do I get on your list? Third, build the folder: pay stubs, bank information, any SSI or SNAP letters, proof of citizenship and a Social Security card for everyone in the house. Fourth, when a list opens, apply online through the housing authority’s RentCafe portal, once per household, and write the confirmation number SLHA gives you in pen, on paper, not just in your phone.
Applying through SLHA is always free. Anyone who asks you for money to get on a list is not the housing authority.
### Is the St. Louis Housing Authority waiting list open?
Not for families right now. The St. Louis Housing Authority (SLHA) lists both its Public Housing and its Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) waiting lists as closed. When a list does open, SLHA announces it by phone, on its website and in local newspapers, so if a paper still lands on your porch, that is one more place to watch.
The exception is real, and it is the one most guides skip. SLHA’s Elderly-Only waiting list stays open all year. Everyone in the household must be at least 62, except at Parkview Apartments on Forest Park Avenue, which takes residents 50 and up. If a parent or grandparent is the one who needs a home, that call can be made this afternoon. Scroll down for the buildings.
Out in the county, the Housing Authority of St. Louis County (County Housing) runs two lists, one for public housing and one for vouchers. Neither has a reopening date, and County Housing says it doesn’t know one yet because it depends on funding and how many people are already waiting. The useful part is the warning it gives: when a list reopens, County Housing posts it on its website, its social media, through partner agencies and in the newspaper 30 days ahead. Use that month for the folder. If a birth certificate went missing two moves ago, start hunting for it now.
### Open right now: properties that take applications directly
Lunch break in a parked car, engine off, phone pressed to one ear and a pen in the other hand, and a leasing office picks up. That call can do more for you this week than any closed list. Project-based voucher is the phrase to listen for. HUD explains that with a project-based voucher, the rental help stays with the unit, and those properties can keep their own waiting lists, separate from the housing authority’s. That is how, in St. Louis County right now, Elm Ridge, Scott Manor and Wellington Family Homes are taking applications even though County Housing has no reopening date for its voucher list. County Housing lists these properties as accepting applications today:
Laurel Park, North St. Louis County: 352 garden-style apartments with 1, 2 and 3 bedrooms. (314) 868-8220.
Stratford Commons I and II, Pine Lawn: 114 townhomes with 2 to 4 bedrooms. 314-260-9008.
Stratford Manor, Pine Lawn: a 52-unit senior community with 1 and 2 bedrooms. 314-381-8081.
Elm Ridge, Hazelwood: senior apartments with 1 and 2 bedrooms, part of the Project-Based Voucher program. (314) 395-2024.
Scott Manor, St. Louis County: senior apartments with 2 bedrooms, also Project-Based Voucher. 314-867-0010.
Wellington Family Homes, Wellston: newly renovated family housing in the Project-Based Voucher program. (314) 332-2543.
Vacancies change, so call before you take a bus across the county. For a wider search, County Housing points renters to the MHDC Affordable Housing Locator and AffordableHousing.com, along with the big rental sites. One tip from County Housing worth keeping: if you hold a voucher and find a place anywhere other than AffordableHousing.com, ask the owner up front whether they accept Housing Choice Vouchers.
### Three quiet ways people lose a spot they waited for
None of them takes doing anything wrong on purpose. Each one starts with an envelope, a phone number or an apartment you didn’t expect:
The letter comes back. SLHA writes when your name reaches the top, and that envelope may be the one you never see. If you’ve moved and the letter is returned, or you don’t respond, your name comes off the list.
The update comes late. A new phone number, address, email, income or household size has to reach SLHA within 10 business days, through RentCafe or on SLHA’s change form. County Housing has the same rule: missed updates can mean removal from its list.
You say no to an efficiency. SLHA combines its one-bedroom and zero-bedroom lists. Turn down a zero-bedroom offer without good cause, and you’re removed. If an efficiency won’t work for you, talk to SLHA before you turn one down.
### The senior buildings with an open list

Sr. Living at Cambridge Heights (62+), 728 Biddle St., (314) 436-9091

### A pay stub and a head count: what counts as low income here
HUD publishes new limits every year, so check SLHA’s income limits page before you apply. The limits SLHA posts today:
1 person: $39,750
2 people: $45,400
3 people: $51,100
4 people: $56,750
5 people: $61,300
6 people: $65,850
7 people: $70,350
8 people: $74,900
Behind those numbers sit three terms you’ll see on every form. A low-income family earns no more than 80 percent of the area median income. Very low income means no more than 50 percent, and extremely low income means no more than 30 percent. For Section 8, HUD says families generally have to be extremely low-income or very low-income to qualify, so a household near the top of that chart may fit public housing better than a voucher.
What help costs you
### How much do you get for a housing voucher?
It depends on your income, where you rent and which utilities you pay. With a voucher you usually pay about 30% of your income toward rent, and County Housing covers the rest up to its payment standard. Applying through SLHA is always free, and County Housing warns of online scams around its voucher waitlist, so never pay anyone to put you on a list.
### The folder on the kitchen table, and the other ways to apply
Both SLHA and County Housing take applications through RentCafe portals. SLHA allows one application per household and gives you a confirmation number when it receives yours. If a disability or another hardship keeps you from applying online, SLHA has paper applications: call (314) 531-4770, or TDD (314) 286-4223. County Housing offers paper applications only while a list is open; request one at (314) 428-3200.
To check on an SLHA application, log in to RentCafe or call 314-531-4770.

If you’re the landlord, the property manager or the moving crew who helps families start over, think about the parent who finally holds a voucher and asks a phone who rents to voucher holders nearby. Does your name come up? See how a listing works.
### Where do I live if I can’t afford rent?
If the eviction notice is already taped to the door, a waiting list is not your answer this week. Start with the St. Louis Housing Help Line at (314) 802-5444. The City of St. Louis lists it as the St. Louis Housing Help Line. St. Louis County calls 314-802-5444 its Emergency Shelter Hotline. An intake specialist interviews you and, if you’re in crisis, refers you to emergency shelter or to rent, mortgage or utility assistance. United Way 2-1-1 is the other call, available 24/7, connecting you to agencies across the St. Louis area.
If you need a bed tonight, our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis covers where to go and how intake works, and our guide to St. Patrick Center’s services explains one of the city’s main doors to housing help. If you’re behind but still housed, see our guide to emergency rent assistance in St. Louis.
Facing eviction? Legal Services of Eastern Missouri offers free civil legal help to low-income Missourians, including a Housing Law Program that defends tenants against eviction. Call 800-444-0514. Missouri Tenant Help, at www.MoTenantHelp.org, offers free do-it-yourself forms for tenants facing eviction, and legal aid groups across Missouri support it.
### Can you buy a house on a low income in St. Louis?
Sometimes, yes, and the path is concrete: the weight of a key ring in your palm is further off than a lease, but it is on a map.
SLHA’s Bridge to Homeownership lets eligible Housing Choice Voucher families put their voucher toward a monthly mortgage payment instead of rent. You need at least one full year in SLHA’s voucher program, must be a first-time buyer (waived when a household member has a disability), and must earn at least $15,000 a year with a year of steady full-time work. Seniors and families with a disability get flexibility on the work and income rules. The down payment is at least 3% of the price, with at least 1% from your own money.
Habitat for Humanity Saint Louis offers an affordable mortgage to buyers living at or below 80% of the area median income. In return, every signer puts in at least 250 hours of sweat equity, earned building their own home and other Habitat families’ homes and in workshops on personal finances and home maintenance. Habitat builds and rehabs 3- and 4-bedroom homes in Hyde Park, where buyers may qualify for up to $50,000 in down payment help for homes inside city limits. Call the homeownership line at 314-371-0400, ext. 632.
The Missouri Housing Development Commission’s First Place Program offers first-time buyers and qualified veterans mortgages at interest rates below regular market rates, with an option for cash help toward the down payment and closing costs. The loans come through MHDC Certified Lenders, so ask any lender you talk to whether they’re certified.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How do I qualify for low income housing in Missouri?
A.  Your household income has to fall under the limits HUD sets for your area, which change each year. In St. Louis, SLHA posts $39,750 for one person and $56,750 for four. Adults must also meet citizenship or immigration rules, pass criminal and rental-history screening, and owe nothing to any housing authority.
### Q. Can I apply for St. Louis low-income housing online?
A.  Yes. The St. Louis Housing Authority takes applications online through its RentCafe portal, and County Housing uses RentCafe too, but only while a list is open. If a disability keeps you from applying online, call SLHA at (314) 531-4770 for a paper application.
### Q. How fast can you get a housing voucher?
A.  There is no set timeline. Your turn depends on how many vouchers are available, when you applied and any preferences you qualify for, and right now SLHA’s voucher list is closed while County Housing has no reopening date. Once you’re selected, HUD says you usually get 60 to 120 days to find a home.
### Q. Are there any low-income apartments in St. Louis that don’t have a waiting list?
A.  A few take applications directly. County Housing lists Laurel Park, Stratford Commons, Stratford Manor, Elm Ridge, Scott Manor and Wellington Family Homes as accepting applications. Vacancies change, so call the leasing office first, and ask whether it has project-based voucher units with their own list.
### Q. Is $31,000 a year considered low income?
A.  For St. Louis Housing Authority programs, often yes. SLHA’s posted income limit for one person is $39,750, higher than that salary, and larger households have higher limits: $56,750 for four. HUD resets the limits every year, so check SLHA’s income page before applying.
### Q. What is the highest you can make for Section 8?
A.  It depends on household size. SLHA’s posted income limits run from $39,750 for one person to $74,900 for eight. HUD says families generally must be extremely low-income or very low-income to get a voucher, and it adjusts those limits every year.
### Q. How to apply for housing assistance?
A.  Gather pay stubs, bank information, benefit letters, proof of citizenship and Social Security cards. Apply online through SLHA or County Housing when a list opens, apply directly to properties accepting applications now, and report any change in address, income or household size quickly so you keep your place.
### Q. Who can help me find a place to live in St. Louis?
A.  Call the St. Louis Housing Help Line at (314) 802-5444. An intake specialist interviews you and, in a crisis, refers you to emergency shelter or rent, mortgage or utility help. United Way 2-1-1 answers 24/7, and County Housing’s properties page shows which buildings are taking applications.

## Missouri’s Age Law Stops at 69: Laid Off Late in a Career in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/exploring-fulfilling-jobs-for-seniors-over-60-in-2026
The gooey butter cake is on the counter, still in the bakery box, and there is already powdered sugar on your sleeve. Seventy candles would set off the smoke detector, so somebody bought a 7 and a 0. The grandkids are loud in the next room. It is a good morning.
And on that morning, without a card or a phone call, one Missouri law lets go of you. The Missouri Human Rights Act defines age as forty or more years but less than seventy years. The day you turn 70, the state’s age-discrimination protection stops covering you.
Unless you work in the City of St. Louis. The City’s own civil rights agency lists older age as a protected class and defines it as age 40 and older. Seventy is still 40 and older. Same birthday, same cake, and the City’s protection is still there when the candles go out.
If you’re 60 or 63 or 66 and the job just ended, that birthday may feel far off. The clocks running right now are not.
Maybe it went the usual way. “We’ve decided to go in a different direction,” in a conference room with the blinds half down. The badge that stopped working at the side entrance. The cardboard box with the coffee mug and the good stapler you bought with your own money. The drive home that has never felt so long. And on top of the box, a thick envelope with a signature line on the last page, and somebody saying they’d need it back “as soon as you can.”
Don’t sign it in the car.
Whatever that envelope says, you have more time than the person who handed it to you implied. Weeks, not minutes. And a second clock, a Missouri one, started in that conference room.
### I lost my job at age 60. What should I do now?
Don’t sign anything on the spot, and start two calendars. If a severance agreement waives age claims, federal law gives you at least 21 days to consider it and at least 7 days to revoke it after signing. Missouri gives you 180 days to file an age discrimination complaint with the Missouri Commission on Human Rights. Then register at MoJobs and, if you live in the City, call SLATE’s Job Center on Market Street at (314) 589-8000.
The first weeks after a layoff feel like fog. You wake up at the old alarm time and lie there listening to the furnace kick on with nowhere to drive. The days get long and the decisions get rushed. The people who come out of this best are rarely the ones who move fastest. They’re the ones who know which deadlines are real.
### Missouri’s age law stops at 69. The City’s and the federal one don’t.
Back to that birthday cake, because it is the part that surprises people. Missouri’s protection runs from 40 up to the day before you turn 70.
Federal law keeps going. The Age Discrimination in Employment Act forbids age discrimination against people who are age 40 or older, with no upper cutoff written into that rule. So a 72-year-old who is passed over still has the federal law, even after Missouri’s has run out.
Inside the City of St. Louis there is a third layer. The Civil Rights Enforcement Agency answers inquiries into possible discrimination in housing, employment and public accommodation taking place in the City, and provides a free impartial investigation into claims based on federal, state and local protected classes, including older age, age 40 and older. Its number is (314) 622-3301. If the job you lost was inside the City limits, the agency provides a free impartial investigation.
The clocks are short, and they start the day it happens. Complaints under the Missouri Human Rights Act must be filed with the Missouri Commission on Human Rights within 180 days of the alleged discrimination, and if a complaint misses that window, the commission lacks jurisdiction to act on it. Federal law allows 300 days for filing employment discrimination complaints with the EEOC. Don’t gamble on the longer clock. Write the date of the meeting in that conference room on the calendar, count forward 180 days, and circle it in red. The commission takes calls at (573) 751-3325, runs a toll-free complaint hotline at 1-877-781-4236, and asks new filers to complete the Complaint Assessment on the Missouri Commission on Human Rights site.
While the memory is fresh, make a folder. The termination letter. The severance packet. Your last two performance reviews, if you can still get to them. The names of the people in the room and what each one said, written down the same night in plain words. If somebody younger was moved into your job, note when you heard it and from whom. A folder like that takes an hour to build and can be impossible to rebuild six months later.
None of this means you have to sue anybody. Most people don’t want to. It means you get to decide, instead of letting the deadline decide for you.
### Start at 1520 Market Street, not on a job board at midnight
The midnight job search is its own kind of lonely. The laptop glow, the same listing reposted six times, the “we’ll be in touch” that never comes. A person across a desk does more for you than another hundred clicks.
If you live in the City, that desk is at SLATE, up on the third floor at 1520 Market, where you trade the glow of a laptop for a chair across the desk from a real person. It’s formally the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment.
The Job Center sits at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor, and it’s open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Wednesdays, when it opens at 9. The number is (314) 589-8000. SLATE says its training programs help St. Louisans who are minorities, women, and long-term unemployed enter careers in growing industries.
Do one thing before you go: register at MoJobs and update your profile. SLATE says doing that before your visit will save you time at the Job Center. In the same building, Room 4086, the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging works to encourage the independence of older persons by providing opportunities for employment, socialization and volunteer activities; its number is (314) 612-5918. Bring the work history you’d put on a resume, even a rough one, and the honest answer to a hard question: do you want the same work somewhere else, or something that finally means more?
### The envelope on the kitchen table
Now the federal clock. If that agreement asks you to give up age-discrimination claims under federal law, the law is on your side for once. The individual is given a period of at least 21 days to consider the agreement. If the layoff is part of a program offered to a group of employees, it’s at least 45 days. After you sign, you get at least 7 days to revoke it. The agreement must also advise you in writing to consult with an attorney before you sign. That “as soon as you can” was a request, not a deadline.
So put the envelope on the kitchen table, under the fruit bowl if you have to, and sleep on it more than once. You gave this company years. It owes you at least 21 days to consider the agreement.
### A second career that means something
Sometimes a layoff turns out to be the push you would never have given yourself. Not because losing the job felt good. It didn’t. But the question it forces is a fair one: if you’re going to start over anyway, why start over at the same desk?
The work that tends to feel meaningful later in life has one thing in common. Your years are the qualification, not the problem. A former manager who has untangled a hundred bad projects. A retired nurse’s aide who can calm a scared patient in one sentence. A machinist who can teach a nineteen-year-old to read a micrometer by feel. Those are not skills a younger applicant can fake.
Try a direction on before you buy it. Volunteer one Saturday at the kind of place you think you want to work. Take a former coworker who made the jump to lunch and ask what the first year was really like, the boring parts included. An afternoon of honest answers can save you a year of retraining for the wrong thing.
A few directions worth a real look, each tied to people who are hiring or helping in St. Louis:
Care work. Helping older neighbors stay home is steady, human and in demand. Look at Circle of Care St. Louis careers, Senior Care Authority St. Louis careers and FreedomCare Missouri.
Teaching and mentoring. If you trained people for years, browse mentoring and tutoring roles.
Nonprofit and staffing work. See The Rome Group job listings.
Consulting and project management. Search consulting jobs near St. Louis and project manager openings in St. Louis.
Your own small business. If you want to turn your past professional skills into a small business, start with this small-business resource.
A detour, because you’ve earned an afternoon off: take a slow walk through Botanical Heights and let the job search wait an hour.
### How do you talk about your age in an interview?
You don’t apologize for it, and you don’t hide it. You make it specific. “Thirty years of experience” is a phrase interviewers forget before you finish saying it. “I took over a project that was four months behind and shipped it on time” is a story they repeat to the next person in the room.
Write down three of those stories tonight, longhand, while the house is quiet. One about a mess you cleaned up. One about a person you trained. One about money you saved or made. Those three stories are your resume, your cover letter and your interview, and they are the reason focusing on your accomplishments works better than listing duties. If you want more practice, talk about what you accomplished, not how long you were there.
### Where to look, and what to keep in the cupboard while you do
Job boards are a tool, not a strategy. Use a few, set alerts and get back to calling people. These are the searches and reading from earlier versions of this guide:
St. Louis Near Me jobs board, including part-time, remote and customer service listings
Age-friendly job listings

Side gigs to supplement your income
Our guide to second-chance jobs
And if the severance runs thin before the next paycheck shows up, there is no shame in using what the city offers. You paid into it for years.
Free food giveaways in St. Louis
Utility-bill assistance in St. Louis
Local coupons and deals and our service categories on St Louis Near Me Directory
Somewhere down the road there’s a first morning at the new place. A new badge that works on the first try. Somebody showing you where the coffee is. You’ll walk in knowing exactly what you’re worth, because you took the time to find out.
Ready for the next chapter? Browse second-career and part-time openings on the St. Louis Near Me jobs board, and keep this page open while you call SLATE at (314) 589-8000.
If you run the care agency, the nonprofit or the small shop that would hire someone who has seen it all, make sure they can find you, and so can the customers who come with them. List your business on St Louis Near Me Directory, look at the Gold plan, or read why local businesses join to get more customers.
Know someone holding a severance envelope right now?
Send them this page before they sign. A senior center, a union hall, a church job ministry or a caseworker can share it too.
