### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is my age stopping me from getting a job?
A.  It might be, and if it is, that can be illegal. Federal law forbids age discrimination against people who are 40 or older, and Missouri’s law covers ages forty up to seventy. If you think it happened, write down the date and remember Missouri’s 180-day filing deadline.
### Q. Is it hard to get a job after age 60?
A.  It can take longer, especially through online applications. It gets easier when you lead with specific results instead of years, ask people who know your work for introductions, and get help from a job center such as SLATE in the City.
### Q. Is it hard to get a job at 65 years old?
A.  Harder through resume portals, easier through people. At that age you are still inside Missouri’s protected age range of forty to under seventy, so you have the same right to a fair shot as anyone else. Use it, and keep a record of every application.
### Q. What is a good career to start at age 60?
A.  One where your experience is the credential: care work, training and mentoring, consulting, project management or a small business built on your old trade. Pick the one you would still want to do on a gray Monday in February.
### Q. What jobs can elderly get?
A.  Almost any job they are able to do. Care work, tutoring, customer service, office support, consulting and part-time retail are all worth a look. Browse our St. Louis Near Me jobs board to see what is open now.
### Q. What can a 70 year old do to make money?
A.  Part-time or consulting work in a former field, care work, tutoring and small side businesses are common paths. One thing to know: Missouri’s age-discrimination law covers ages forty to under seventy. The federal law covers people age 40 or older.
### Q. What are some suitable jobs for seniors in St. Louis?
A.  Care work for older neighbors, nonprofit and office support, teaching and mentoring, consulting and customer service. SLATE’s Job Center at 1520 Market St. can point City residents toward training and employment.
### Q. What companies hire retirees?
A.  Care agencies, nonprofits, staffing firms and small businesses that need someone reliable on short notice are good places to start. Look for postings marked part-time or flexible, and ask directly whether a company hires retirees.

## Find Your Furry Friend: A Guide to St. Louis Pet Rescues
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/find-your-furry-friend-a-guide-to-st-louis-pet-rescues
💥Organizations, shelters, and community groups are welcome to link to and share this blog with their members, clients, and friends if they believe it will help more people discover and support pet rescues and other pet service providers.
Walk into almost any St. Louis shelter and you’ll see the same thing: kennels of dogs who lost their homes through no fault of their own, and cats waiting for someone to notice them. Dozens of rescue groups across the city and county exist to match those animals with the right people.
This guide walks you through where to look, how the adoption process actually works, and what to expect when you go searching for your next companion among the many St. Louis pet rescues.
### Key Takeaways
St. Louis adoption runs through three layers: the City and County shelters, big nonprofits like the Humane Society of Missouri, the APA and Stray Rescue, and dozens of foster-based cat, breed and small-animal rescues.
Understanding the adoption process, including requirements and what to expect, is key to a successful match.
Fees run from $0 at fee-waived events to $600 for some puppies. An adult cat or a big adult dog is often under $200, and the fee already covers spay or neuter, vaccines and a microchip (check each shelter’s current price).
Adopting a rescue pet provides a second chance to an animal in need and brings immense joy to the owner.
Beyond adoption, resources are available for pet owners in St. Louis, covering lost pets, responsible rehoming, and veterinary care.
Supporting local St. Louis pet rescues can involve volunteering, donating, or fostering animals.
### Navigating St. Louis Pet Rescues
Bringing a rescue pet home gives an animal a second chance at a happy life, and it tends to change yours too. Before you fall for the first pair of puppy eyes you see, though, it helps to understand how St. Louis rescue organizations actually operate.
### Understanding the Adoption Process
Most rescues have a process to make sure the pets go to good homes. It’s usually not super complicated, but it does take a little time. You’ll likely fill out an application that asks about your living situation, experience with pets, and what you’re looking for in an animal. Some places might also do a home visit or require references. The goal is to find the best fit for both you and the animal. They want to make sure the pet’s needs are met and that you’re prepared for the commitment.
Here’s a general idea of what to expect:
Application: This is where you share details about yourself and your home.
Meet and Greet: You’ll get to spend time with the animal you’re interested in.
Interview/Home Visit: A volunteer or staff member might chat with you more or visit your home.
Adoption Fee: Most rescues charge a fee that covers part of the cost of care, vaccinations, and spaying/neutering. In St. Louis that ranges from free during fee-waived events to several hundred dollars for a puppy; the FAQ below breaks it down.
Finalization: Once approved, you’ll sign the adoption papers and take your new friend home!
None of this is meant to be a hurdle. The paperwork exists so the match sticks, and a pet you thought hard about before adopting is a pet you’re far less likely to return.
### Finding the Right Match for Your Lifestyle
This is a big one. Think honestly about your daily routine. Are you super active and looking for a hiking buddy, or do you prefer quiet evenings on the couch? Do you have kids or other pets? Answering these questions will help you narrow down your search. A high-energy dog might not be happy in a small apartment with owners who work long hours, just like a shy cat might get overwhelmed in a busy household. Rescues often have staff who know the animals well and can offer great advice on which pet might fit in best with your lifestyle.
Consider these points:
Energy Level: Match the pet’s energy to your own activity level.
Size and Breed: Think about space and any specific needs related to breed traits.
Temperament: Some pets are independent, others are very social. What works for you?
Time Commitment: Pets need daily care, training, and attention.
### The Benefits of Adopting a Rescue Pet
Adopting a pet from a St. Louis rescue is incredibly rewarding. You’re saving a life, plain and simple. Plus, many rescue animals are already house-trained or have basic obedience skills, which can be a nice bonus. You’re also often getting a pet that has been vet-checked, vaccinated, and spayed or neutered, saving you some initial costs. Beyond that, there’s a special bond that forms when you give a deserving animal a loving home. It truly makes a difference.
### Where to Find St. Louis Pet Rescues
Where to Find St. Louis Pet Rescues
The sheer number of adoption options in St. Louis can feel overwhelming at first, from big municipal shelters to tiny volunteer-run groups working out of foster homes. Dogs, cats, rabbits, even the occasional pot-bellied pig: the metro has a group that handles it.
### City and County Animal Care and Control
Your first stop might be the official animal care and control facilities for St. Louis City and St. Louis County. These shelters often have a wide variety of animals needing homes, from playful puppies and kittens to older, calmer companions. They are usually the first point of contact for stray animals found within their jurisdictions, meaning they often have the largest number of animals available for adoption.
St. Louis City Animal Care and Control: The City’s shelter is run by the nonprofit CARE STL under a city contract it has held since 2019 and renewed in July 2026. It must take in every animal Animal Control brings, adopts out of 2700 Walnut Place in Midtown, and welcomes walk-ins daily from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. It charges one flat fee for every animal, waives it often when kennels are full, and dogs in its LifeSavers program always go home free.
St. Louis County Animal Care and Control: The Saint Louis County Pet Adoption Center at 10521 Baur Blvd. in Olivette is a government shelter that cannot turn animals away. Its adoption fee doubled from $40 to $80 in October 2025 and still covers vaccinations, a microchip and spay or neuter. When it runs over capacity it holds emergency fee-waived adoption events, and it held several in 2026.
These facilities are great places to start your search, and the staff can often provide information about the animals’ temperaments and histories.
### The Humane Society of Missouri and the APA
Two private nonprofits sit alongside the government shelters, and both post standing deals worth knowing before you pick a place to visit.
Humane Society of Missouri: Adoption centers at 1201 Macklind Ave. in the city and on Administration Drive in Maryland Heights. Cats nine months and older are pick-your-price with a $35 minimum, pit bulls and pit mixes five months and older go home fee-waived, and adult dogs over 35 pounds are $190, plus a $10 rabies tag.
APA Adoption Center: 1705 S. Hanley Rd. in Brentwood. Adult cats are about $125, two kittens are $300, dogs run $100 to $600, and dogs 30 pounds and up, five months and older, are fee-waived every Tuesday. APA pets are also on view at PetSmart stores in Brentwood, Florissant, South City and Bridgeton.
Both run weekly specials, so check their current adoption pages before you go.
### Dedicated Cat and Dog Rescues
Beyond the official shelters, St. Louis is home to numerous rescue organizations that focus specifically on dogs or cats. These groups are often run by dedicated volunteers who pour their hearts into saving, rehabilitating, and rehoming animals. They might have fewer animals at any given time compared to county shelters, but they often provide extensive medical care and behavioral support before adoption.
Some well-known organizations include:
Stray Rescue of St. Louis: a shelter at 2320 Pine St. downtown that takes in about 3,000 dogs a year. Adult fees have been around $50, and local sponsors often cover them for a month at a time (a sponsor covered adult dog and cat fees for all of October 2026, for example).
Tenth Life Cat Rescue: a cat-only rescue that prioritizes special-needs cats, with an adoption lounge at 3202 Cherokee St. Adult cats are $160, kittens six months and under are $185, and two cats adopted together get $50 off.
Gateway Pet Guardians: based in East St. Louis, in a former elementary school turned 54,000-square-foot Pet Resource Center with a low-cost vet clinic and a free pet food pantry.
Five Acres Animal Shelter: a private shelter at 1099 Pralle Lane in St. Charles that takes in more than 1,600 cats and dogs a year and reports a 99% placement rate.
These rescues often have detailed profiles of their animals online, giving you a good sense of their personalities before you even visit. You can often find them through online adoption platforms like Petfinder or by searching directly for their websites. For example, St. Louis Pet Rescue holds Saturday adoption events at the PetSmart in Sunset Hills and the Petco at Gravois Bluffs in Fenton; check its site for this week’s schedule.
Cat people have one more door. Several cat cafes in St. Louis double as adoption floors, with lounge cats you can apply to adopt through each cafe’s partner rescue. An hour of coffee and lap time tells you more about a cat’s personality than a kennel card ever will.
Total swerve: where Warrenton eats might genuinely surprise you.
### Breed-Specific Rescue Organizations
If you have a particular breed in mind, St. Louis also has rescue groups that specialize in certain types of dogs or cats. These organizations have a deep understanding of the specific needs, temperaments, and potential health issues associated with particular breeds. They are fantastic resources if you’re looking for a specific companion, like a Greyhound, a German Shepherd, or even a smaller breed like a Chihuahua.
Here are a few examples of what you might find:
Midwest Border Collie Rescue: a foster network based in the Chicago suburbs that places border collies across the Midwest, so ask whether it adopts into Missouri.
Serendipity German Shepherd Dog Rescue: an all-volunteer, state-licensed rescue founded in 2004 that keeps its dogs in foster homes around St. Louis.
These specialized rescues can be incredibly helpful in matching you with a pet whose traits align perfectly with your lifestyle and experience. Most have no building at all, which is why the application comes before you ever meet the dog.
### Resources for Pet Owners in St. Louis
Resources for Pet Owners in St. Louis
Even the most devoted owners hit rough patches. A pet slips out an open gate. A job loss makes the rent-plus-vet-bill math impossible. A senior dog needs surgery nobody budgeted for. St. Louis has real help for each of these, and knowing where to turn before a crisis hits saves the time you can’t get back.
### Lost and Found Pet Resources
Losing a pet is a heart-wrenching experience. The first few hours are critical. If your pet has gone missing, act fast. Check your immediate surroundings thoroughly, and then expand your search.
Then go to the shelters. STL Lost Pets, the shared database run by the APA, St. Louis County Animal Care and Control and the Humane Society of Missouri, says about 90% of lost, stray and unwanted pets in the St. Louis area end up at one of its partner shelters. Cats are the hard case: nationally only 6% of stray cats taken in by shelters in 2025 went home to an owner, against 34% of stray dogs (Shelter Animals Count), which is why a microchip with current contact details matters even for an indoor cat. Our guide to lost pets in St. Louis covers which shelters to check first and how long each one holds a stray.
Here are some steps and resources to help you find your lost companion:
Secure your pet safely if you find a lost animal, just as you’d want someone to do for your own.
Check for identification like collars and tags. If the pet is microchipped, contact the microchip company with your information.
Visit local shelters and animal control facilities regularly. Don’t just rely on phone calls; go in person.
Utilize online platforms and social media. File a lost pet report with STL Lost Pets, search its found dogs and found cats lists, and share your pet’s photo on its Facebook page and in neighborhood groups.
If you’ve found a pet, try to locate its owner by checking for ID and posting on local lost and found pages. Taking the animal to a vet or shelter for a microchip scan is also a good idea.
### Rehoming Your Pet Responsibly
Sometimes, circumstances change, and you may find yourself unable to keep your pet. This is a tough situation, but responsible rehoming is key to your pet’s well-being. Avoid simply giving your pet away to strangers. Instead, explore options that ensure a safe transition.
Consider these approaches:
Reach out to local rescues and shelters that may be able to take your pet or help you find a suitable new home.
Network with friends, family, and colleagues who might be looking to adopt.
Use reputable rehoming services that screen potential adopters carefully.
In St. Louis, the APA’s rehoming page points owners first to Adopt-a-Pet’s Rehome tool, which lets a pet go straight from your home to a screened adopter, and it lists a $30 fee to surrender a single pet if you live in St. Louis City or County. The City’s fee schedule charges $150 to relinquish an owned dog or cat to Animal Care and Control, so check current fees before you decide.
It’s important to be honest about your pet’s history, temperament, and any medical needs to ensure a good match with a new family.
### Veterinary Care and Financial Assistance
Unexpected veterinary emergencies can be financially straining. Fortunately, there are organizations in the St. Louis area and beyond that offer assistance to pet owners facing financial hardship.
Payment Plans and Credit: Many veterinary clinics offer payment plans or accept veterinary-specific credit lines like CareCredit.
Non-Profit Assistance: Several foundations and funds exist to help cover veterinary costs for pets in need. These often have specific criteria, so it’s worth researching options like The Mosby Foundation or Frankie’s Friends, both national charities with their own eligibility rules (Mosby helps dogs only).
Low-Cost Clinics: For routine care, vaccinations, and spay/neuter services, look into the Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic, a low-cost spay, neuter and wellness clinic that has performed more than 150,000 surgeries since 2012, or Gateway Pet Guardians’ low-cost clinic in East St. Louis. To help pay for the surgery itself, BARC St. Louis, an all-volunteer nonprofit, subsidizes spay and neuter for privately owned family pets.
Don’t hesitate to ask your veterinarian about financial assistance options; they often have a list of resources available to their clients.
### Beyond Adoption: Supporting St. Louis Rescues
Adopting a pet is a wonderful way to give a deserving animal a loving home, but the support for these organizations doesn’t have to stop there. Many St. Louis rescues rely heavily on community involvement to keep their operations running smoothly and to provide the best care possible for the animals. There are several ways you can contribute, even if you’re not in a position to adopt right now.
### Volunteer Opportunities
Local shelters and rescue groups are always looking for helping hands. Volunteering is a direct way to make a difference in the lives of animals waiting for their forever homes. Tasks can range from walking dogs and socializing cats to assisting with cleaning, administrative work, or helping out at adoption events. Your time and effort are incredibly valuable.
Here are some common volunteer roles:
Animal Care: Direct interaction like walking dogs, playing with cats, and grooming.
Event Support: Helping set up, manage, and break down adoption events or fundraisers.
Administrative Tasks: Assisting with paperwork, answering phones, or data entry.
Outreach: Helping to spread the word about adoptable animals or the rescue’s mission.
### Donating to Local Shelters
Financial contributions are vital for rescues to cover the costs of food, medical care, shelter, and enrichment for the animals. Every little bit helps, and many organizations offer different ways to donate, from one-time gifts to recurring monthly pledges.
Beyond monetary donations, many shelters also have wish lists for specific items they need. These can include food, blankets, toys, cleaning supplies, and specialized medical equipment. Checking a rescue’s website or social media pages is usually the best way to see what they currently need most.
Cash gifts give rescues something in-kind donations can’t: flexibility. That flexibility might pay for a sick animal’s emergency surgery one week and a pallet of prescription food the next. It’s the most direct way to keep an operation running.
### Fostering Animals in Need
Fostering is a temporary, yet incredibly impactful, way to help. It involves opening your home to an animal for a short period, providing them with a safe and loving environment outside the shelter. This is especially important for animals who may be too young, recovering from surgery, or simply need a break from the kennel environment to decompress and show their true personalities.
Fostering can be a rewarding experience, allowing you to directly care for an animal and help prepare them for adoption. Rescues typically provide the necessary supplies and cover veterinary costs, so you can focus on giving the animal love and attention. It’s a fantastic way to help more animals get adopted faster.
Here’s what fostering typically involves:
Providing a safe space for the animal.
Following the rescue’s guidelines for care and behavior.
Transporting the animal to vet appointments if needed.
Socializing the animal and helping them adjust.
Working with the rescue to find a permanent adoptive home.
### Specialized St. Louis Animal Shelters
### Small Animal Rescue Options
Beyond the usual cats and dogs, St. Louis is also home to organizations dedicated to helping smaller critters find their way to loving homes. If you’re looking for a rabbit, guinea pig, hamster, or other pocket pet, these specialized rescues are a great place to start. They often have a wealth of knowledge about the specific needs of these animals, which can be quite different from those of dogs and cats. Finding the right small animal rescue means you’re more likely to find a healthy, well-socialized pet and get the support you need to care for them.
Missouri House Rabbit Society of St. Louis: An all-volunteer rescue that runs the Bunny House shelter and specializes in rabbits left outside. It also teaches rabbit care and offers members boarding and nail trims.
Local Pet Stores with Adoption Programs: Some larger pet store chains partner with local rescues. The APA shows adoptable pets at four St. Louis-area PetSmart stores, and smaller rescues hold weekend events at PetSmart and Petco, so ask the store which partner handles its animals.
General Animal Shelters: Don’t overlook your local city or county animal shelters. While they might not have a dedicated ’small animal’ section, they often take in rabbits, guinea pigs, and other small pets when they are surrendered. The Humane Society of Missouri’s posted adoption fees list rabbits at $15 and guinea pigs and hamsters at $10.
### Farm Animal Sanctuaries
For those with a bit more space and a different kind of heart for animals, farm animal sanctuaries offer a unique adoption experience. These places typically rescue animals like horses, goats, pigs, chickens, and cows who have been neglected, abused, or are no longer wanted. Adopting from a sanctuary means you’re directly contributing to the well-being of an animal that might otherwise have nowhere to go.
Longmeadow Rescue Ranch: The Humane Society of Missouri’s 165-acre ranch near Union, about an hour from St. Louis, has taken in horses and farm animals since 1988. It is free to visit on Fridays from noon to 3 p.m. and Saturdays from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., and its animals are available for adoption or Barn Buddy sponsorship.
Local Farms with Rescue Efforts: Sometimes, individual farms or small groups operate informally to rescue farm animals. Networking with local agricultural communities or checking online forums can sometimes lead to these opportunities.
### Assistance for Military Pet Owners
Military life can be complicated, and sometimes service members face difficult decisions when it comes to their beloved pets. Whether it’s due to deployment, housing restrictions, or other service-related challenges, several national programs serve military families in the St. Louis area. These programs provide temporary or long-term solutions to keep pets with their military families or ensure they are cared for during times of separation.
Dogs on Deployment: A national nonprofit, founded in 2011, that connects active-duty service members and veterans with volunteers who board their pets during deployments, training and emergencies. It also offers veterinary and moving help.
Operation Foster: Run by PACT for Animals, Operation Foster places the pets of deploying service members and of people going through medical treatment into volunteer foster homes, and reports helping more than 3,000 pets in all 50 states.
Guardian Angels for Soldier’s Pet: This program focuses on providing a safe haven for pets whose owners are serving in the military, helping to bridge the gap during deployments or other temporary situations.Additionally, Guardian Angels for Soldier’s Pet assists veterans who are hospitalized, in treatment, or experiencing homelessness, ensuring care during difficult circumstances. It is an all-volunteer national group that matches pets with foster homes through state coordinators. Read the Guardian Angels for Soldier’s Pet mission statement.
Most of these specialized programs run on shoestring budgets and volunteer hours. Expect detailed applications and, in some cases, a home visit. A little patience goes a long way with groups stretched this thin.
Some St. Louis shelters go further still, taking in exotic pets or animals with chronic medical conditions that would struggle in a general kennel. A parrot who outlived his owner, a diabetic cat, a three-legged rabbit: these are the animals that need a specialized landing spot. Tenth Life Cat Rescue, for one, prioritizes cats with medical or behavioral needs. Those are the groups worth seeking out when your future pet comes with particular requirements.
### How Do You Choose Where to Adopt?
The choice between a large county shelter and a small breed rescue matters less than you might think. Both are staffed by people who want the exact outcome you do. So visit more than one. Ask blunt questions about an animal’s history and quirks. Sit on the floor and see who climbs into your lap. That moment, when a particular dog or cat decides you’re theirs, is worth every application form you filled out to get there.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much to adopt a dog in St. Louis?
A.  Adopting a dog in St. Louis usually costs $50 to $325, and some puppies reach $600. St. Louis County charges a flat $80, Stray Rescue’s adult fees have run about $50, the Humane Society of Missouri charges $190 for adult dogs over 35 pounds, and the APA ranges from $100 to $600. Fees include spay or neuter, vaccines and a microchip; check current prices.
### Q. Where can I find a free cat adoption in St. Louis?
A.  Free cat adoptions in St. Louis come through shelter specials. The APA waives fees for its working cats, St. Louis County and CARE STL waive fees when their kennels fill up, and Stray Rescue’s sponsors cover adult cat fees for whole months. The Humane Society of Missouri’s adult cats are pick-your-price from $35. Follow shelter social pages for short-notice events.
### Q. Where to get a cat in St. Louis?
A.  Start with Tenth Life Cat Rescue’s lounge on Cherokee Street, Stray Rescue downtown, the Humane Society of Missouri’s city and Maryland Heights centers, the APA in Brentwood, the County shelter in Olivette and CARE STL in Midtown. For a lower-pressure first meeting, several St. Louis cat cafes keep adoptable cats from partner rescues in their lounges.
### Q. How to get a pet cat for free?
A.  Adopt during a fee-waived event, ask the APA about its fee-waived working cats, or take in a friend’s rehomed cat. But a “free” cat is rarely the cheapest: Tenth Life puts spay or neuter alone at $160 to $220 at a regular vet, before testing, vaccines and a microchip, which a $35 to $160 shelter adoption already includes.
### Q. What is the least adopted pet?
A.  Nationally it is dogs, not cats. Shelter Animals Count found 57% of dogs entering U.S. shelters in 2025 were adopted, against 63% of cats, and more dogs than cats were euthanized. In St. Louis, look at where fees get waived: big adult dogs and pit bull mixes. Research finds only weak evidence for the famous black-cat bias.
### Q. What are red flags when adopting a dog?
A.  Walk away from a “rescue” that skips the application and meet-and-greet, won’t share vet records, pushes same-day payment, has no return policy or has no Missouri license; the state requires every shelter and rescue to hold an Animal Care Facilities Act license. With the dog itself, ask about food guarding, fear of strangers and any bite history.
### Q. How do I start the adoption process?
A.  Start with an online application. Most St. Louis shelters, including CARE STL and Stray Rescue, let you apply before you visit, which speeds up the meeting. Expect questions about your home, your other pets and your landlord’s pet rules; Stray Rescue needs written landlord approval before it can proceed. Bring a photo ID when you go.
### Q. Can I help a rescue even if I can’t adopt?
A.  Absolutely. You can volunteer to walk dogs or socialize cats, foster an animal for a few weeks, or take a CARE STL shelter dog out for the day through its Doggy Day Out program. Donations of money, food and supplies help too, and cash goes furthest because it covers whatever the animals need that week.

## Belly Tight at 1 A.M.? St. Louis Emergency Vets Open 24/7
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-every-second-counts-finding-reliable-emergency-veterinarian-service-near-you
Belly tight as a drum, 1 a.m., and your big dog is heaving over and over and bringing up nothing. He paces the kitchen, drool strung off his lip onto the tile. You’re in socks with the car keys already in your fist, wondering if this is an overreaction you’ll be paying off for months. Waiting until morning feels like the cheap, sensible choice. It isn’t. The American College of Veterinary Surgeons calls this, gastric dilatation-volvulus, a rapidly progressive life-threatening condition of dogs that requires immediate medical attention, and it lists clinical signs for more than 6 hours among the factors that raise the death rate.
Here is the St. Louis part almost nobody knows. If that twisted stomach has damaged the blood vessels around the spleen, the surgeons’ college notes that a blood transfusion may be indicated. VEG’s hospital at 250 Mid Rivers Mall Circle in St. Peters is a VEG Blood Bank location, which provides blood for canines, and its page says those donations help save the lives of dogs in need of transfusions. So the healthy dog snoring on somebody’s couch tonight, paws twitching through a dream about squirrels, could be the reason yours comes home.
### What is considered an emergency for a vet in St. Louis?
Anything that threatens your pet’s life or gets worse by the hour: trouble breathing, a swollen belly with dry heaving, a cat straining in the litter box with little or no urine, poisoning, seizures, being hit by a car, or collapse. Around St. Louis, VEG in Brentwood, Animal Emergency Clinic in Kirkwood and Veterinary Specialty Services in Manchester all list 24/7 emergency care. Call on the way.

### Why is waiting until morning the expensive choice?
Because the bill follows how sick your pet is when you walk in, not what time it is. Pet Poison Helpline says it flat out on its own site: the sooner an exposure or poisoning is addressed, the easier, less expensive, and safer it is to treat. The ER exam is not the scary number. CareCredit’s state-by-state table puts the average emergency exam in Missouri at $115 for a dog and $122 for a cat. The same page lists one night of hospitalization at a vet clinic at $619 for a dog. The exam is the cover charge. The overnight stay, the IV line, the monitors beeping in a back room while you drive home alone - that is what waiting tends to buy.
Cats make the same point more quietly. He walks in and out of the litter box, squats, strains, and leaves almost nothing behind. You hear the litter scratch, then silence, then the scratch again. It looks like constipation. Cornell’s Feline Health Center says a urethral obstruction is an absolute emergency, requiring immediate veterinary treatment. A cat crouched in the box at 11 p.m. is not a morning problem.

Emergency hospitals see the sickest patient first, not the first one through the door, so a dog in respiratory distress goes ahead of a limping cat that came in earlier. That wait can feel unfair from the chair. It’s the same rule that will put your pet first on the worst night.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are signs my pet needs immediate care?
A.  Check the gums and the breathing first. Pale, gray or blue gums, fast or noisy breathing at rest, a hard swollen belly with dry heaving, a cat straining in the litter box with little or no urine, a seizure, or a pet that can’t stand all mean go now, not in the morning.
### Q. What are three signs your dog is suffering?
A.  Watch breathing, behavior and body. Panting while resting; hiding, restlessness or snapping when touched; and a hunched posture, limping or refusing food are classic signs of pain. Any one that is new and lasting deserves a same-day call to your vet, and alongside other red flags, a trip to the ER.
### Q. How long should a dog be sick before going to the vet?
A.  Not long. A bright, playful adult dog that vomits once may only need watching, but call your vet the same day if the vomiting or diarrhea keeps coming back, shows blood, or your dog stops drinking, and call sooner for a puppy or a senior. Weakness or a swollen belly means go now.
### Q. How much does an emergency vet visit cost?
A.  In Missouri the emergency exam alone averages $115 for a dog and $122 for a cat, according to CareCredit’s published cost table. Tests, treatment and hospitalization come on top, and the same table lists a night in a vet clinic at $619 for a dog. Ask for a written estimate before treatment starts.
### Q. How much does urgent vet cost?

A.  Tell the front desk your budget before treatment starts. ### Understanding Your Auto Repair Needs
Understanding Your Auto Repair Needs
A funny noise on startup. A check engine light that's been glowing for a week. These are the moments that send most of us looking for a shop. Before you start stressing about the cost or where to take it, it helps to understand what might be going on under the hood.
### Common Car Issues and When to Seek Repair
Cars are complex machines, and over time, parts just wear out. Some issues are minor annoyances, while others can turn into big problems if ignored. Here are a few common things to watch out for:
Brakes: Squealing, grinding, or a soft pedal are clear signs your brakes need a look. Don't wait on this one – your safety is on the line.
Tires: Uneven wear, bulges, or constant low pressure mean it's time for new tires or at least a rotation and alignment.
Engine: Strange smells, rough idling, or warning lights usually point to something more serious under the hood.
Exhaust: Loud noises from the back of your car or a rotten egg smell could mean a leak or a catalytic converter issue.
The key is to not ignore those little signs. A small fix now can prevent a much larger, more expensive repair down the road.
### Preventative Maintenance for Your Vehicle
Think of preventative maintenance like going to the doctor for a check-up. It's all about catching potential problems before they become actual problems. Regular check-ups can save you a lot of headaches and money in the long run.
Here are some basics:
Oil Changes: This is probably the most common one. Fresh oil keeps your engine running smoothly. Stick to the schedule recommended in your owner's manual.
Tire Rotations: Helps your tires wear evenly, making them last longer and improving your car's handling.
Fluid Checks: Coolant, brake fluid, power steering fluid – they all play a role. Make sure they're at the right levels and aren't leaking.
Filter Replacements: Air filters and cabin filters get dirty over time, affecting your engine's performance and the air you breathe inside the car.
### Signs Your Car Needs Professional Attention
Sometimes, it's obvious your car needs help. Other times, it's a bit more subtle. Trust your gut feeling if something seems off.
Here are some red flags:
Warning Lights: That dashboard light isn't just for decoration. If it's on, something needs checking.
Unusual Noises: Clunks, rattles, grinding, or squealing sounds are your car's way of telling you something's wrong.
Changes in Performance: If your car feels sluggish, hesitates, or handles differently, it's time for a mechanic.
Leaks: Puddles under your car are never a good sign. Different colored fluids can indicate different issues.
Smells: Burning smells, a strong gasoline odor, or even a sweet smell can point to specific problems.
This isn't about being paranoid behind the wheel. Catching the warning signs early keeps you, and everyone sharing the road, safer. Handle the small issues promptly and your car stays dependable.

### What to Expect During Your Auto Repair Visit

### The Diagnostic Process
First, the shop needs to pin down what's actually wrong. This is the diagnostic process. Plugging in a computer is part of it, sure. But a good mechanic does more: they listen to your description, maybe take the car for a quick spin, and run a visual inspection. They're hunting for clues to pinpoint the issue. Sometimes it's obvious, like a flat tire. Other times it's detective work, especially with weird noises or intermittent problems.
Listen to your description: Be as detailed as possible about when the problem started, what it sounds like, and when it happens.
Visual inspection: They'll look under the hood, check tires, brakes, and other visible components.
Computer diagnostics: Many modern cars have onboard computers that can store error codes indicating specific issues.
Test drive: Sometimes, the best way to understand a problem is to experience it firsthand.
### Understanding Repair Estimates
Once they've diagnosed the problem, you'll get an estimate. This is super important. Don't be afraid to ask questions about it. A good estimate should break down the costs, including parts and labor. It should also give you an idea of how long the repair might take.
Here’s what you should typically see:
Parts: A list of the parts needed and their individual costs.
Labor: The estimated hours of work and the hourly labor rate.
Taxes and Fees: Any additional charges.
Total Estimated Cost: The final price you can expect.
Get that estimate in writing before you authorize any work. A written estimate protects you and the shop if the final bill ever comes up for debate.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What's the difference between regular maintenance and a repair?
A.  Think of maintenance like going to the doctor for a check-up to stay healthy. It's things like oil changes and tire rotations to keep your car running smoothly. A repair is like going to the doctor because you're sick – something's broken and needs fixing.
### Q. How do I know if my car needs a repair?
A.  Listen for weird noises, pay attention to warning lights on your dashboard, or if your car just doesn't feel right when you drive it. If you notice anything strange, it's best to get it checked out by a pro.
### Q. Should I always get multiple quotes for a repair?
A.  It's a really good idea! Getting quotes from a couple of different shops helps you compare prices and makes sure you're getting a fair deal for the work needed. Don't just go with the first one you call.
### Q. What does a mechanic mean by 'diagnostics'?
A.  Diagnostics is basically the mechanic's detective work. They use special tools to figure out exactly what's wrong with your car. It's like a doctor running tests to find out why you're feeling sick.
### Q. Why is it important to keep records of my car's service history?
A.  Keeping records is super helpful! It shows you (and any future owner) what work has been done on the car. Plus, regular maintenance records can help your car last longer and might even be good for its resale value.
### Q. How to find a mechanic that won't rip you off?
A.  Get the same job quoted by three shops and compare the line items, not the totals — an oil change at $50 against $90 usually means different oil or a different filter. Ask for the old parts back; the request alone tells you something about the shop.
### Q. How do I know if a mechanic is trustworthy?
A.  They show you the problem, put the estimate in writing before starting, and call before exceeding it. Illinois puts this in statute — under the Automotive Repair Act, no repair over $100 starts without your specific authorisation. Missouri relies more on the shop’s own practice.
### Q. How to pick a good auto repair shop?
A.  Match the shop to the job: dealers for warranty and complex electronics, independents for everything else, specialists for transmissions and bodywork. Then check they will diagnose before quoting. A shop that prices a repair without looking is guessing with your money.
### Q. What is the 30-60-90 rule for cars?
A.  Scheduled maintenance intervals at 30,000, 60,000 and 90,000 miles, each with its own checklist of fluids, filters and belts. Follow the manufacturer’s schedule rather than a shop’s menu — the two are not always the same, and the difference is usually upsell.
### Q. What are the red flags when choosing an automobile repair shop?
A.  Pressure to authorize work before anything has been diagnosed. No written estimate, or one with vague line items instead of parts and labor. Refusal to show you the old part. A price quoted over the phone for a problem nobody has looked at yet. Any one of those is reason enough to call the next shop.

Root canals: To save a tooth that's badly infected.

### Advanced Technology for Better Outcomes
### Modern Dental Equipment

### Addressing Dental Emergencies Promptly
Addressing Dental Emergencies Promptly
A tooth cracks on a popcorn kernel. A kid catches an elbow at the basketball hoop. When it happens, you want to know where to turn before the pain sets the agenda. Dental emergencies need quick attention to prevent further problems and relieve pain. Don’t wait out severe discomfort or an accident involving your teeth or jaw.
### Immediate Pain Relief
When a dental emergency strikes, the pain can be intense. The first priority is usually to get that pain under control. ### Urgent Care Availability

For instance, if you're in the St. Louis area and need immediate help, St Louis Urgent Dental is a place to consider.
### Handling Unexpected Dental Issues
Dental emergencies can range from a chipped tooth to a knocked-out tooth, or even severe infections. Here are some common scenarios and what to do:
Knocked-out tooth: If a tooth is completely dislodged, try to gently place it back in its socket if possible. If not, store it in milk or saliva and see a dentist immediately.
Broken or chipped tooth: Rinse your mouth with warm water and apply a cold compress to any swelling. Save any tooth fragments if you can.
Severe toothache: Rinse your mouth with warm salt water. If there's swelling, a cold compress can help. Avoid putting aspirin directly on the gum.
Lost filling or crown: Try to cover the exposed area with dental wax or sugar-free gum to protect it.
Even when the pain fades, the cause usually hasn’t. A quiet tooth can still be an infected one, so get it checked before it turns into something worse.

## The $225 Day That Starts at 5 a.m.: Flexible Jobs for St. Louis Seniors
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-flexible-jobs-for-seniors-your-guide-to-staying-active-and-earning
The alarm goes off in the dark, and for once you don’t reach for snooze.
Coffee in the travel mug. Reading glasses in the shirt pocket. A sandwich in a paper sack, because you already know you won’t get far from the table today. By 5 a.m. you’re signing in at a polling place in the City of St. Louis, a school gym or a church hall depending on your ward, with a handful of people you first met at training, unfolding booths, squaring up the sign-in books, testing a pen that refuses to write. The doors open at 6. Somewhere out front a car heater is idling, because somebody wanted to be first.
The polls close at 7 that night. You’ve been on your feet and in your chair, back and forth, since before the sun came up. Your voice is a little hoarse from saying “Name and address, please?” a few hundred times. And the City’s Board of Election Commissioners owes you $225, paid two weeks after the election.
That is the honest shape of flexible work after a career. Nobody tells you this part: the most flexible jobs are not the softest days. They’re the jobs you can say yes or no to, date by date, without asking anybody’s permission and without anybody taking it personally. One long day, then your calendar is yours again.
### What’s the best part-time job for seniors?
The best part-time job for a senior is one you can say yes or no to, date by date, without losing it. In St. Louis, the City’s Board of Election Commissioners says no experience is required for election judges, training lasts 1.5-2 hours, and an election judge is paid $225 per election. From home, tutoring, bookkeeping and customer service fit best when you already have the skill. If you claimed Social Security before full retirement age, earnings over an annual exempt amount can reduce your benefits.
### The $225 day: how City election work actually goes
The City’s requirements are short, and they’re printed in plain English on the Board of Election Commissioners’ page. You must be 18 years of age or older and a registered Missouri voter. You must be able to read, write and speak English, be available from 5:00 a.m. until the polls close, attend a training session before the election, and declare a political party: Democrat, Republican or Independent.
Notice what is not on that list. No resume. No interview about where you see yourself in five years. After you apply, the Board sends a letter or email with training dates. After training, you’re assigned to a polling location or serve as an alternate.
To start, apply online through the Board’s election judge application page, or call the Board of Election Commissioners at (314) 622-4336 during office hours. One honest caveat: this is the City’s board and the City’s pay. If you live in St. Louis County, ask your own election office about pay before you count on the same check.
Is it worth it? Do the math out loud. The polls open at 6 a.m. and close at 7 p.m., you report at 5, so $225 works out to roughly $16 an hour before you count the training session. That won’t make anybody rich. But it is paid civic work, it ends when the polls close, and it puts you at a folding table across from your neighbors all day long, which is more conversation than some retirees get in a week.
Then take the kitchen calendar off the fridge and find a pencil, because Missouri law sets the election days years ahead. The general municipal election falls on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in April, every year. In even-numbered years, add the primary on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in August and the general election on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Circle them. Those are the days the City needs you, and you can see them coming a long way off.
### The Social Security catch: 100 election days, or one steady job
Here is the letter nobody wants to open. If you started Social Security before your full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 you earn over an annual exempt amount. A higher exempt amount applies in the year you reach full retirement age.
The amounts change. Social Security publishes new exempt amounts for the coming year every October, and the current lower annual exempt amount, the one for people under full retirement age, is $24,480. That figure is adjusted each year, so check the Social Security page on working while you get benefits instead of trusting a number a friend quoted at church. Here is the scale that matters: a single $225 election day is a long way from $24,480. Twenty steady hours a week at a desk job is a different story.
### Flexible means two different things. Most job ads only offer one.
Some work is flexible by the hour. You open an app or a laptop when you feel sharp, close it when your back says so, and the week bends around grandkids, doctor visits and the Tuesday you just don’t feel like it. Freelance bookkeeping, online tutoring and editing live here. So does driving for a delivery app, if you don’t mind the car smelling like somebody else’s fries.
Other work is flexible by the date. The job itself is rigid, start time and all, but it only happens on certain days, and you decide which of those days you want. Election work is the purest St. Louis example. Seasonal retail, tax season and substitute shifts follow the same rhythm. You trade a hard day for a wide-open month.
Know which kind you want before you apply anywhere. A retiree who wants long mornings with the paper and a second cup will hate a job that needs you at 5 a.m. A retiree who wants the week clear for travel will hate a job that pings him every afternoon. Neither is lazy. They just want different things from the same word.
### Working from the kitchen table without getting played
The laptop warms your knees. Out on Highway 40 the brake lights are stacked up in the sleet, and for once you are not in them. The dog has given up on a walk and gone back to the rug. This is the dream version of retirement income, and it is real, but it rewards a skill you already have far more than a skill an ad promises to teach you.
If you kept books for thirty years, a small business with a shoebox of receipts needs you. If you taught, a parent with a struggling seventh grader needs you. If you spent a career on the phone calming people down, customer service work is mostly patience, and you have plenty. Browse remote listings and part-time listings on our St. Louis jobs board, and read every posting twice.
One rule protects you better than any checklist: a real job pays you. If anyone asks you to pay first, for training, a starter kit or a “certification,” walk away. If anyone mails you a check and asks you to send part of it back, walk faster.
Unrelated, and still good advice: after a long day at a folding table, Benton Park is a fine place to walk it off.

### Choose the days first, then the job
Get a paper calendar and a pencil. Cross out what is already spoken for: the standing lunch, the grandkids on Wednesdays, the week at the lake. What is left is what you are selling. Then pick one door this week, not five. One application to the Election Board, one call to an old colleague who runs a small shop, or one profile on a jobs board with your real hours on it.
The pencil matters. It is the difference between a job that fits around your life and a life that fits around a job, and after the career you just finished, you have earned the first one.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the easiest job for seniors with no experience?
A.  Look for jobs that train you on their own dime. The City of St. Louis Board of Election Commissioners says no experience is required for election judges and that training is provided, in a session that lasts 1.5-2 hours. Browse entry-level listings on our jobs board for more.
### Q. What is the easiest job for seniors?
A.  The easiest job is the one built on something you already do well. A retired bookkeeper will find freelance books easier than a warehouse shift, and a retired teacher will find tutoring easier than retail. Match the work to the skill and to the hours you actually want.
### Q. Are there any legitimate work from home jobs for seniors?
A.  Yes. Tutoring, bookkeeping, editing and remote customer service are real paid work. The simplest test of legitimacy: a real employer pays you, never the other way around. If a posting asks for money up front, skip it and browse our St. Louis jobs board instead.
### Q. How can a 70 year old make money from home?
A.  Sell the skill you spent a career building, by the hour, to people who need it: books for a small business, homework help for a family, proofreading for a local nonprofit. Tell former colleagues you are available. Most first clients come from people who already trust you.
### Q. What jobs can a 70 year old get?
A.  More than most people assume. The City of St. Louis election judge requirements ask that you be 18 years of age or older. Seasonal retail, tutoring, part-time office work and driving roles also fit, depending on your energy and the days you want free.
### Q. How hard is it for a 70 year old to get a job?
A.  It depends on the door. Online applications that sort resumes by keywords are a long shot at any age. Jobs with a short, published requirement list, and jobs you hear about from people who know your work, are far easier, because you either meet the requirements or someone vouches for you.
### Q. What’s a good side hustle for seniors?
A.  One with no startup cost that uses what you know. Paid election work in the City, freelance books, tutoring or pet sitting for neighbors all start with a phone call, not an investment. If a side hustle asks you to buy inventory or a kit first, be careful.
### Q. Can a 70 year old woman get a job?
A.  Yes. Employers who need reliability, patience and judgment have every reason to hire her. Start with roles that list their requirements plainly, like City election work, and with people who already know her work, then widen the search to part-time and remote listings.

## What a Small Business Website Actually Costs (and When You Don't Need One Yet)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/small-business-website-cost
### What does a small business website actually cost?
Somewhere between about $200 a year and about $35,000, and that spread is not because anyone is confused. It is because “a website” is not one product. It is at least three, sold by three different kinds of business, and the price you are quoted tells you which one you are being sold. Which is the question hiding under every quote: not “how much is a website,” but “which of the three am I actually buying — and do I even need it yet?”
You build it on a platform: roughly $17 to $49 a month, billed yearly, plus your time.
A freelancer builds it: commonly $500 to $8,000 once, then hosting on top.
An agency builds it: commonly $5,000 to $35,000 or more, usually with a retainer attached.
All three can be the right answer. None of them is the right answer for everybody, and a good number of small businesses in this metro do not need any of them yet.
### Why every number you find is different
Search this question and look at who is answering. Every result on the first page is published by a company that sells websites, sells a tool for building them, or earns a commission when you sign up for one.
Here is what each one says, with its stake in the answer named:
Wix — $17 to $100 a month. Wix sells website subscriptions.
GoDaddy — $145 to $640 a year. GoDaddy sells domains, hosting and website subscriptions.
Forbes Advisor — $0 to $450 do-it-yourself, from around $1,500 professional. Forbes Advisor is an affiliate publisher; the links pay it.
Agency blogs — $4,000 to $15,000. Agencies sell $4,000 to $15,000 builds.
Elementor — $10,000 to $35,000, with e-commerce starting at $20,000. Elementor sells a page builder used on large custom projects.
Development shops — $1,000 to $50,000. The widest range comes from the firms that take work at every point in it.
Google’s own AI summary splits the difference and lands on $16 a month at the low end and $5,000 to $15,000 at the high end — assembled from exactly those sources.
The tell that this is unsettled: a Reddit thread from a decade ago outranks most of the commercial pages. When a ten-year-old forum post beats the professionals on a pricing question, search is telling you it does not trust the professionals on that question.
None of these companies is lying. Each is quoting the honest price of its own product. The problem is that all six answers wear the same label.
### You are not buying one thing
Sorting the products apart makes the numbers stop looking random.
### A platform subscription
You choose a template, type in your own words, and upload your own photos. Checked directly against their published pricing at the time of writing: Wix runs $17 a month for its Light plan, $29 for Core, $39 for Business and $159 for Business Elite, priced for a year paid up front. Squarespace runs $19, $29, $49 and $99 a month on the same annual basis. Both include a free custom domain for the first year on a paid plan.
What you are actually paying for is hosting, security patching, and the fact that you never have to think about either. What you are not paying for is anyone writing your content or taking your photographs. That is your weekend, and for most owners it is the real cost.
### A freelancer
Five hundred to eight thousand dollars, depending less on page count than on how much of the work is genuinely yours: your words, your photos, your services list, your booking flow. A freelancer who hands you a template with your logo dropped in is worth the low end. One who interviews you, writes the copy, shoots the space and sets up the booking is worth the high end and frequently charges the middle.
### An agency
Five thousand to thirty-five thousand. At this level you are buying a team — strategy, design, development, content, and usually a monthly retainer afterwards. For a business with several locations, a real e-commerce catalog, or compliance obligations, that is money well spent. For a two-truck HVAC company, it is a truck.
### The costs nobody quotes you
The quoted price is the part you can compare. These are the parts that show up later.
The domain after the first year. “Free domain” almost always means free for twelve months. In month thirteen it renews at the registrar’s standard rate, and standard rates vary enormously between registrars for an identical product. Some also sell you WHOIS privacy as an add-on. Cloudflare Registrar, by contrast, publishes at-cost registration and renewal with no add-on fees and includes WHOIS redaction and SSL at no charge. Same domain, different bill, and nobody mentions it during the sale.
Payment processing. If you sell anything through the site, the platform’s cut is separate from the card network’s cut. Squarespace publishes card rates starting at 2.9% plus $0.30 and adds a 2% online store transaction fee on its entry plan, dropping to 0% one tier up. That upgrade can pay for itself long before you notice, which is worth understanding before you sign anything.
Maintenance. On a platform this is included. On a custom build it is not, and a site nobody patches becomes a liability rather than an asset. Ask directly who is responsible for updates and what it costs, and get the answer in writing before the build starts.
The move. Content typed into one platform’s editor does not lift cleanly into another. Changing platforms in three years usually means rebuilding, which is a cost you incur when you are least expecting it.
### Renting versus owning
This is the distinction that matters most and gets discussed least.
On a platform subscription you are a tenant. Stop paying and the site goes dark. You keep the domain, because the domain is registered to you, but the pages, the layout and the structure stay behind. That is not a scam — it is what a subscription is — but plenty of owners discover it during a cash-flow squeeze, which is the worst possible moment.
A custom build on your own hosting is yours. So is the responsibility for it: updates, security, backups, and someone to call when it breaks at nine on a Friday night.
Renting is the right call for most small businesses, and there is no shame in it. Just make the choice deliberately, and keep the domain registered in your name and your own account — not your web designer’s. A domain held in a departed contractor’s account is one of the more painful and avoidable problems in small business.
### When you honestly do not need one yet
Not every business needs its own website on day one, and a lot of the pressure to build one comes from people who sell them.
Consider holding off if everything below is true of you:
You do not sell anything online — customers call, book, or walk in.
You have no storefront to send people to, because you work from home or travel to jobs.
Your work is found through referrals and search, not through a catalog.
You cannot yet name what a visitor is supposed to do on the site.
That describes a great many home-based businesses, consultants, freelancers and one-van trades across Missouri and Illinois — real businesses serving a real region without a front door to photograph. For that owner, a claimed Google Business Profile and a complete directory listing cover the same ground a five-page brochure site would: who you are, what you do, where you work, how to reach you, and proof from customers.
Say plainly what that is and is not. It is a genuine, findable presence for a business without one, and it costs a fraction of a build. It is not ownership, it is not a substitute for a real website once you have something to sell, and anyone who tells you a listing replaces a website in every case is selling listings.
Nothing to do with budgets — but here’s where to eat in Brooklyn.
### When you genuinely do need your own site
Build one, and stop deliberating, if any single item here applies:
You sell products online. A catalog, a cart and a checkout have to live somewhere you control.
You take bookings or deposits. Scheduling with money attached needs to be yours.
You are selling to other businesses. A procurement officer will look for a site, and its absence reads as risk whether that is fair or not.
You are in a field where people research before they call — legal, medical, financial, anything where a stranger is weighing whether to trust you with something that matters.
You have content worth publishing. If you are answering customer questions in writing, that work should accumulate on property you own.
### What to actually budget
If you are opening a business in this metro and want a number to plan against, here is an honest one.
First year, doing it yourself: roughly $200 to $600. That is a platform plan billed annually, with the domain free for the first twelve months, and your own time on the words and the photographs. This is the correct starting point for most new businesses, and it is easy to underestimate how far it goes.
First year, hiring a freelancer: roughly $1,500 to $5,000 all in. Budget the build, plus about $250 to $600 a year in hosting and domain afterwards, plus something for the changes you will want in month four.
First year, hiring an agency: $8,000 and up, plus a retainer. Justify this with revenue, not ambition. If the site is not going to carry transactions or a real content operation, the money buys more elsewhere.
Fold whichever figure you land on into your wider opening costs rather than treating it as separate — it belongs in the same column as registration, licensing and insurance, and it competes with them for the same dollars.
### How to hire without getting taken
Whoever you hire, four questions separate the professionals from the rest, and all four are fair to ask before you pay anything.
Who owns the domain and the hosting account? The answer must be you. If it is not, walk.
What happens if we part ways? Ask specifically what you keep. Get it in writing.
Who writes the words? This is where projects stall for months. If the answer is “you send us the copy,” that is fine — but now you know the real timeline.
What does year two cost? Hosting, maintenance, updates, and the hourly rate for changes. A vague answer here is the most reliable warning sign there is.
Two red flags worth naming: a quote given before anyone has asked what your business does, and a monthly fee with no stated term. The first means you are getting a template. The second means the meter runs until you notice.
And whichever route you choose, do the free things first. Claim your profile, get your name, address and phone identical everywhere they appear, and get listed where people in your area actually look. Those cost nothing and they work whether or not you ever build a site.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a website worth it for a small business?
A.  It is worth it when you can name what a visitor should do there — buy, book, apply, or read something only you can tell them. If you cannot name that action yet, a website will not create it, and the money is better spent on being findable. Revisit the question the moment you start selling or scheduling online.
### Q. Is $1500 a good price for a website?
A.  For a freelancer building a small custom site with your own words and photos, $1,500 is a fair market price. It is high for a template with your logo dropped in and low for anything with e-commerce or custom functionality. Judge it by who writes the content and who owns the accounts, not by the page count.
### Q. How much does it cost to set up a small website?
A.  Doing it yourself on a platform, roughly $200 to $600 for the first year — a plan billed annually, with the domain usually free for twelve months. Hiring a freelancer, roughly $1,500 to $5,000 all in. The setup is rarely the expensive part; year two, when the free domain renews and changes start costing hourly, is where budgets break.
### Q. What can I use instead of a website?
A.  A claimed Google Business Profile plus a complete listing on a local directory covers what a small brochure site covers: who you are, what you do, your service area, contact details, photos and reviews. It works well for home-based businesses and service-area trades. It does not work if you need to sell, schedule with deposits, or publish your own content.
### Q. What is a fair price for a website?
A.  Fair depends on which of the three products you are buying. Platform subscriptions are $17 to $49 a month billed yearly. Freelance builds are $500 to $8,000. Agency builds start around $5,000. A price is unfair mainly when it is quoted before anyone has asked what your business does, or when year-two costs are left vague.
### Q. Do I need an LLC to run a website?
A.  If the answer turns out to be an app rather than a site, the pricing works nothing like this — see what it costs to build an app in St. Louis before you ask anyone for a quote.
No. Neither Missouri nor any platform requires a business entity before you can register a domain and publish a site. Forming an LLC is a liability and tax decision that stands on its own, separate from your website — and if you are weighing it, look at how the entity forms actually differ rather than at what a website builder tells you.

## What Business Insurance Does Missouri Actually Require? (Less Than You Think)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-insurance-missouri-what-is-required
### What business insurance does Missouri actually require?
Far less than the search results suggest. Missouri compels exactly two things for most small businesses:
Workers’ compensation, once you have five or more employees — or one or more if you are in construction.
Commercial auto, for vehicles the business owns.
That is close to the whole legal list. General liability insurance is not required by the state of Missouri. Neither is professional liability, nor cyber, nor a business owner’s policy.
You would not learn that from page one. We pulled the current results for what business insurance costs, and every organic result is an insurance carrier or broker — Progressive, The Hartford, Hiscox, ERGO NEXT, Insureon, biBerk. Each quotes its own book, and each has an obvious commercial interest in the phrase “highly recommended” sitting as close as possible to the word “required.”
So the useful version of this page is the distinction nobody selling a policy is motivated to draw: what the state makes you carry, versus what your landlord, your customers and your city make you carry. The second list is longer, and it is the one that actually decides what you buy.
### Workers' compensation: the threshold, and the trap inside it
Under RSMo 287.030, an employer becomes subject to Missouri’s workers’ compensation law at five or more employees.
Construction is the exception, and it is severe: one employee. If you erect, demolish, alter or repair improvements, coverage is required from your first hire, not your fifth. Given how much of this metro’s small-business economy is trades, that single sentence is the most consequential one on this page.
Now the trap, which catches family businesses constantly. Relatives count. The statute expressly provides that an employee who is a member of the employer’s family within the third degree of affinity or consanguinity is included in the employee total. Your brother, your daughter-in-law, your nephew on the crew — all counted. Owners who assume family “does not count toward the five” can be over the line without realizing it.
If you are subject to it, the coverage has to be with a carrier authorized in Missouri by the Department of Commerce and Insurance, or you have to qualify to self-insure. There is no informal version.
We covered the wider first-hire obligations separately in hiring your first employee in Missouri — the 20-day reporting rule catches people just as often.
### What actually forces you to buy general liability
Not Missouri. These three, in roughly this order:
Your landlord. Commercial leases routinely require general liability at a stated limit, with the landlord named as an additional insured. This is the most common reason a small business buys its first policy, and the lease usually specifies the number.
Your customers. Any commercial client, general contractor, property manager, hospital, school or municipality will ask for a certificate before you set foot on site. In the trades this is not occasional — it is the price of being allowed to bid. Plenty of work is lost not on price but on being unable to produce a certificate that afternoon.
Your city. Some municipal licensing and permitting requires proof of insurance, and requirements vary from one St. Louis County municipality to the next in the same way business licensing itself does. Ask the city that governs your address rather than assuming.
Which reframes the question usefully. You are rarely deciding whether to carry general liability. You are discovering what limit somebody else has already decided you need — and the answer to “how much coverage?” is usually written in a contract you have already been handed.
### What it costs, and why every number you find is different
Here is the published range from the carriers currently ranking for this question, each describing its own customers:
That is a tenfold spread, and none of it is dishonest. “Starts at” describes the cheapest customer a carrier will write — typically a low-risk, home-based, single-person operation. An average describes that carrier’s particular mix of customers, which is not your business.
What actually sets your premium is your trade, your payroll, your revenue, your claims history, and whether you work at height, with fire, with vehicles, or in other people’s homes. A bookkeeper and a roofer are not adjacent on any rate table. Treat every published figure as evidence that quotes vary, not as your price.
### The coverages worth understanding before you shop
General liability — third-party bodily injury and property damage. The customer who trips, the pipe that floods the unit below. This is the one contracts demand.
Business owner’s policy (BOP) — general liability bundled with property coverage, usually cheaper than buying both. Worth asking about if you own equipment or occupy space.
Commercial auto — required for company-owned vehicles, and worth a specific question if you use a personal vehicle for work. Personal auto policies often exclude business use, which owners discover at claim time.
That commercial auto point deserves more than a line, because it is the gap that surprises people most. If you drive your own truck to jobs, your personal auto policy very likely excludes business use — and exclusions are not discovered when you buy, they are discovered when you claim. A service business running errands, hauling tools, or visiting customers in a personally-owned vehicle can find the whole loss uncovered after an accident, with no warning beforehand. Ask your agent the question directly and in those words: am I covered driving this vehicle for work? The answer is frequently no, and the fix is usually cheaper than people expect.
Professional liability — for advice and services rather than physical damage. Consultants, bookkeepers, designers.
Workers’ compensation — the one that is genuinely mandatory at the thresholds above.
### The certificate is the part you will actually use
Day to day, almost nobody asks whether you are insured. They ask for a certificate of insurance — the one-page summary your carrier or agent issues showing coverage type, limits and dates. Understanding it is worth more than understanding the policy. Which flips the usual worry around: are you paying for coverage you’ll never use, while missing the one line a customer’s contract will actually demand?
Certificate holder is not the same as additional insured. Naming someone as certificate holder just means they get a copy. Naming them as additional insured extends your coverage to them for claims arising out of your work, and that is what commercial clients and landlords actually want. It is an endorsement, it usually costs something, and it is the line people get wrong when they forward a certificate and get told it is insufficient.
Ask your agent how fast they can issue one. In the trades, work is won and lost on this. A general contractor asking for a certificate before Friday is not going to wait until Tuesday, and the business that can produce one within the hour gets the job. Know the process before you need it, and keep a current copy on your phone.
It is a snapshot, not proof of anything continuing. A certificate shows the policy was in force the day it was issued. It says nothing about whether you cancelled it the following week — which is exactly why we tell homeowners on the other side of this to call the insurer directly rather than trust the PDF. Anyone can edit a PDF, and in a state that licenses no contractors, a certificate is one of the few verifiable signals a customer has.
Which is the quiet argument for carrying it even where nothing compels you to. In Missouri there is no state registry proving you are legitimate. Insurance you can evidence on request is one of the very few things that does — and the businesses that treat the certificate as a sales asset rather than an annoyance tend to be the ones winning the work.
Nothing to do with insurance — but here’s what’s in O’Fallon, Illinois.
### Getting quotes without wasting a week
Have these ready before you call anyone, because every quote depends on them: your exact trade or classification, annual revenue, payroll, number of employees, whether you own or lease your premises, whether you own vehicles, and any required limits from a lease or contract.
Then three practical notes:
Get the contract requirement first. If a lease or client agreement dictates a limit and an additional-insured endorsement, that is your specification. Shopping before you know it wastes the exercise.
Compare like for like. A cheaper premium with a higher deductible and narrower coverage is not cheaper. Ask what is excluded, not just what it costs.
Use an independent agent as well as the online quoters. The direct carriers are fast and fine for simple risks. For a trade with real exposure, someone who can place you across several carriers usually does better — and the ones on page one are the ones who bought their way there, not necessarily the ones who will write your class of business well. An agent who works with trades in this metro every week will know which carriers are comfortable with your classification and which will decline it, and that knowledge saves more money than an hour of comparison shopping.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should I pay for small business insurance?
A.  There is no honest single figure. Carriers currently publish anything from about $14 a month to $141 a month, and all of those are true of somebody — a low-risk home-based business and a business owner’s policy for a premises-based operation are different purchases. Your premium is set by trade, payroll, revenue, claims history and exposure, so get several quotes for your specific classification.
### Q. How much does $1,000,000 general liability insurance cost?
A.  Published general liability figures cluster in the $30 to $55 a month range across carriers, but the limit is only one input — trade and risk matter far more. Moving from a $1M to a $2M limit usually costs proportionally less than doubling, since the first dollar of coverage is the expensive part. Check what limit your lease or client contract actually requires before pricing anything.
### Q. How much does business insurance cost for an LLC?
A.  Being an LLC does not change your premium. Insurers rate on what you do and how risky it is — trade, revenue, payroll, claims history — not on your entity type. An LLC limits liability legally; insurance covers the loss financially. They solve different problems, which is why most businesses carry both.
### Q. What is the best insurance for a small business?
A.  For most, general liability — usually bundled into a business owner’s policy with property coverage. It is what landlords and clients require and it covers the most common claims. Add workers’ compensation if you meet Missouri’s threshold, commercial auto for company vehicles, and professional liability if you sell advice rather than physical work.
### Q. Is business insurance required in Missouri?
A.  Only narrowly. Missouri requires workers’ compensation at five or more employees — one or more in construction — and commercial auto for company-owned vehicles. General liability is not required by the state. What compels most businesses to carry it is a landlord, a client contract, or a municipal licensing requirement.
### Q. Do family members count toward Missouri's workers' comp threshold?
A.  Yes. RSMo 287.030 provides that an employee who is a member of the employer’s family within the third degree of affinity or consanguinity is counted in the total. Family businesses that assume relatives are excluded can cross the five-employee line without realizing it — and in construction the threshold is one employee regardless.
