## Missouri Sales Tax License: Free, Fast, and No Bond (Despite What Google Says)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-sales-tax-license
### Do I need a Missouri sales tax license?
If you sell goods or a taxable service to an end customer from a location in Missouri, yes — and you need it before your first sale, not after. The Department of Revenue puts it plainly: any person or company with a business location in Missouri from which they sell or lease goods, or provide a taxable service to a final consumer, is required by law to collect and remit Missouri sales tax. Which means the real question isn’t whether you need one — it’s whether the scary-sounding parts you half-remember (a bond? a big fee?) are even real.
Two things surprise almost everyone who looks this up.
It is free. There is no application fee for the retail sales license itself.
You almost certainly do not need a bond — despite what page one of Google will tell you. We pulled the live results for this exact search, and the sixth organic result is still advertising help with “the mandatory tax bond.” That requirement was eliminated. Missouri’s own guidance is unambiguous: effective August 28, 2018, bonds are no longer required for businesses that collect and pay sales or vendors use tax.
Under the old rule you had to post a bond worth roughly three times your average estimated monthly tax. That is a real amount of money to tie up, and people still walk into the process braced to pay it. You do not have to. The Department can still require a bond from a business that goes delinquent — that exception survives — but a new business registering in good faith is not posting one.
### Wait — what is a tax bond?
Worth answering properly, because “you need to post a bond” is one of those phrases people nod along to without knowing what it means, and it sounds far more alarming than it is.
A sales tax bond is a financial guarantee that you will hand over the tax you collect. Think about what the state is actually worried about: you are collecting their money from your customers all month. If you spend it and disappear, the state is out the tax and the customers already paid it. The bond is their insurance against that — not against your business failing, specifically against you keeping money that was never yours.
### The three parties, and the part people get backwards
A surety bond is an agreement among three parties:
The principal — you, the retailer.
The obligee — the Missouri Department of Revenue, the one being protected.
The surety — the company that issues the bond and pays out if you don’t.
Here is the part almost everyone misreads: a bond is not insurance for you. If the state makes a claim, the surety pays — and then comes after you to be repaid in full. You are buying the state a guarantee, not buying yourself protection. That is why sureties run a credit check before issuing one.
### What it costs and how you get one
Today a bond can only be required from a business in default, and it’s capped at two times your average monthly tax liability (it was three times under the pre-2018 rule) — so it scales with how much tax you collect, not with your profit.
The state accepts four forms, and they are very different experiences:
A cash bond — cashier’s check, money order, or certified check. Simple, and the full amount sits with the state doing nothing for you.
A surety bond from an insurance company licensed in Missouri. You pay a premium rather than the whole amount, which is why most businesses choose it.
A certificate of deposit from a state or federally chartered institution.
An irrevocable letter of credit from a commercial bank.
You obtain a surety bond through a surety company or a bond agent, not from the state. They check your credit and business history, quote a premium, and file the bond with the Department. Better credit, lower premium.
### When it ends — and the money you may be owed
A bond is not permanent, and this is where real money goes unclaimed.
Under the current statute and the bond rule amended in February 2026, the Department may refund or release a bond after one year of satisfactory tax compliance (it was two years under the old rule). “Satisfactory” has a precise meaning: no tax due, and every return filed and paid on time. A bond is also released when you close the account, file a final return, and owe nothing.
So it is not a fee you paid and forgot — it is your money, held conditionally, returnable once you have proven yourself.
And plenty of businesses never asked for it back. A 2015 Missouri State Auditor report found the Department holding about $19.4 million in cash bonds for businesses that had already closed, and urged it to return them. Release generally is not automatic; someone has to request it, and the Department’s bond refund request (Form 472) exists for exactly this.
If you have been in business since before August 2018, registered back when bonds were required, and have filed cleanly since — go find out whether the state is still holding your money. That is a five-minute phone call with a genuine chance of a four-figure answer, and it is the most valuable sentence on this page for an established business.
### What the license actually is (and what it is not)
This is the single most common mix-up in Missouri, and it costs people time at the wrong counter.
A sales tax license comes from the state, through the Department of Revenue. It authorizes you to collect sales tax on the state’s behalf and obliges you to remit it. It is about tax.
A business license comes from your city. It is permission to operate there at all. Missouri issues no general statewide business license, so if someone tells you they “got their Missouri business license,” they usually mean one of these two very different things. We broke that apart in a separate guide to what licensing you actually need in St. Louis.
You will often need both. They are separate applications, to separate governments, on separate timelines. And the order matters: the City of St. Louis wants your state sales tax number before it will process a Graduated Business License, so the state step comes first if you sell a product.
### Who is exempt, and who thinks they are but isn’t
Genuinely exempt: pure wholesalers. If you are 100% wholesale — selling only to other businesses that will resell the goods — you are not required to register for a retail sales tax license. You will instead be handing your suppliers a resale exemption certificate.
The trap is the word only. Sell wholesale all year and then do one holiday market, one pop-up, one direct sale to a neighbor, and you have made a retail sale. The exemption describes a business that never sells to a final consumer, and a great many “wholesale” businesses quietly do.
Not exempt, though people assume otherwise: selling from home, selling at markets and craft fairs, selling only online to Missouri buyers, or being very small. There is no minimum-revenue floor that lets a Missouri seller skip the license. Being tiny is not an exemption; it just means the numbers on the return are small.
Services are the genuinely confusing part. Missouri taxes some services and not others. If you are unsure whether what you sell is taxable, that is the one question worth taking to an accountant rather than guessing, because guessing wrong compounds monthly.
### What happens if you skip it
This is not a paperwork scold. The Department of Revenue states that making retail sales without a Missouri retail sales license carries penalties of up to $10,000 and potential criminal prosecution.
In practice, the more common outcome is quieter and still expensive: you were required to collect tax you never charged. The state does not care that you did not collect it — the obligation to remit is yours either way. So the money comes out of your margin, backdated, with interest. A year of unremitted sales tax on a small retail operation is the kind of number that ends a business that was otherwise working.
### How to register
The process is genuinely short.
Online through the Department of Revenue’s business registration portal, or on paper using Form 2643, the Missouri Tax Registration Application. Online is faster and it is the same registration — you can add withholding tax at the same time if you have employees.
Have ready: your federal EIN (or SSN for a sole proprietor), your legal business name and any fictitious name, your physical business address, the ownership details, and your taxable begin date. That last one matters more than it looks — a retail sales tax license cannot be issued without it, so know the date you started or will start selling.
Timing: allow 10 business days for a retail sales tax application to process, and up to 15 calendar days for other application types. Register before you plan to open, not the week of.
When you are approved, a welcome letter arrives with your license number and your assigned filing frequency. You do not choose that — the Department sets it. Read the letter and put the due dates in a calendar the day it arrives.
Totally unrelated, but your brain needs a break — where to eat in Spanish Lake.
### The rule that catches people in year one
You must file a return even when your sales were zero.
Every business holding a Missouri sales tax license files for every period, whether or not it sold anything. A seasonal shop closed for the winter still files. A business that had a terrible quarter still files. A business that opened, registered, and has not made a sale yet still files.
Missing a zero return produces exactly the same non-filing consequences as missing a real one, which is a genuinely irritating way to acquire a penalty on $0 of revenue. If your business is seasonal or slow to start, this is the single thing to put in your calendar.
### What rate do you actually charge?
Not one rate. Missouri’s combined rate is the state portion plus local add-ons — county, city, and in many places special taxing districts layered on top.
In the St. Louis metro that stacking gets unusually fine-grained, because Community Improvement Districts and Transportation Development Districts can apply to specific developments. The practical consequence: two shops a few blocks apart can owe different combined rates, and a rate you learned at a previous location may not be the rate at your new one.
Do not carry a number over from a friend’s store or from something you read. Look up your rate by your exact address using the Department of Revenue’s rate lookup, and re-check it if you move or open a second location. Living here as well as selling here? Our St. Louis money guide maps the rest of the local tax picture, from the yearly tax on your car to the city earnings tax.
### A sane sequence for a new St. Louis seller
Confirm what you sell is taxable — goods almost always, services sometimes.
Get your EIN from the IRS. Free, same day.
Register with the Department of Revenue for sales tax, and withholding too if you have employees. Allow 10 business days.
Take that sales tax number to your city for the local business license. In the City of St. Louis, the Graduated Business License step needs it.
Look up your combined rate by address before your first sale.
Calendar every filing date, including the periods you expect to be zero.
None of it is difficult, and the whole state layer costs nothing. The expensive version is the one where you sell for eight months first and register afterward — because the tax you should have collected is owed regardless of whether you charged it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is a sales tax license in Missouri?
A.  There is no fee — the Missouri sales tax license is free to apply for and free to hold. And since August 28, 2018 there is no bond requirement either, despite guides that still say otherwise. The Department can require a bond from a business that becomes delinquent, but not from a new registrant in good standing.
### Q. How do I get a sales tax license in Missouri?
A.  Register online through the Department of Revenue’s Online New Business Registration, or file Form 2643 by mail. Have your EIN, legal and fictitious business names, physical address, ownership details, and your taxable begin date ready — the license cannot be issued without that date. Allow about 10 business days for a retail sales tax application to process.
### Q. What is the difference between a business license and a sales tax license?
A.  Different governments, different purposes. The sales tax license is issued by the state and authorizes you to collect and remit sales tax. A business license is issued by your city and is permission to operate there. Missouri has no general statewide business license, so most sellers need the state tax license plus whatever their municipality requires.
### Q. Is the Missouri tax ID the same as the EIN?
A.  No. An EIN is a free federal identifier from the IRS for federal tax and payroll purposes. Your Missouri tax ID is an eight-digit number the Department of Revenue assigns when you register for sales tax or withholding, and it arrives in your welcome letter with a PIN. You will typically need the EIN first, because the state registration asks for it.
### Q. What does a sales tax license mean?
A.  It authorizes you to collect sales tax from customers on the state’s behalf, and it obligates you to remit that tax and file returns on the schedule the Department assigns you. It also lets you hand suppliers a Form 149 exemption certificate so you can buy inventory for resale without paying tax on it. It is not permission to operate a business — that is a separate, local question.
### Q. Do I still need a bond for a Missouri sales tax license?
A.  Almost certainly not. Bonds have not been required for businesses collecting and paying sales or vendor’s use tax since August 28, 2018. The Department can still require one from a business that falls into default, capped at two times its average monthly tax, and temporary or traveling vendors should confirm with the Department before their first event. If you posted a bond before 2018, ask for it back with Form 472: the current rule allows release after one year of satisfactory compliance.
### Q. What happens if a business does not charge sales tax?
A.  You still owe it. Missouri law says a seller’s failure to collect the tax doesn’t relieve it of the obligation to pay, so the uncollected tax comes out of your own margin, plus interest and additions: 5% if you filed but didn’t pay, and 5% a month up to 25% if you didn’t file at all. Selling without a license adds its own penalty, $500 for the first day and $100 a day after, up to $10,000.
### Q. Can you pay sales tax online in Missouri?
A.  Yes. File and pay through MyTax Missouri, the Department of Revenue’s online portal; an e-check costs 50 cents and a card costs 2% plus 25 cents. Businesses with three or more locations must file electronically. File every period on the schedule in your welcome letter, even when you had no sales: a missed zero return draws the same non-filing penalties as a missed real one, while returns filed on time keep a 2% timely-filing discount.

## Where to Get Help Finding Work in St. Louis: Employment Resources
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-get-help-finding-work-in-st-louis-employment-resources
Looking for work can be one of the loneliest things a person does. You send applications into a void, you wonder if your résumé is even being read, and if you’re coming back to work after time away — raising kids, a health setback, retirement, prison, a layoff — it can feel like everyone else already knows a secret you missed. Here’s the good news St. Louis doesn’t advertise well enough: the metro is full of free help, staffed by people whose entire job is to help you find yours.
This is a guide to that help — the job centers, nonprofits, and training programs across greater St. Louis that will sit down with you, at no cost, and actually work the problem. Whatever your situation, one of these is built for it.
### Start here: the free public job centers
The backbone of the region’s job-search help is the public workforce system, and it costs you nothing. SLATE — the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment (a City of St. Louis department, downtown at 1520 Market Street, 314-589-8000) is a full American Job Center: free job-search help, résumé and interview workshops, weekly job fairs, computers to use, and funding for training in fields like healthcare and construction. Its services are available in person and virtually. Across the county and the rest of the metro, the state runs Missouri Job Centers — find your nearest one through jobs.mo.gov, which keeps the current locations and hours (some are appointment-based, so call ahead). Both plug into MoJobs (jobs.mo.gov), Missouri’s free online job-matching system. If you do only one thing after reading this, make it a call to SLATE or your nearest Missouri Job Center.
### Help built for a specific situation
Some of the best help in St. Louis is aimed squarely at people the big job boards leave behind:
Coming back after incarceration: the Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis runs an Adult Re-Entry program (and its well-known Save Our Sons / Save Our Sisters job-readiness programs), and SLATE administers re-entry employment grants. Judgment-free, and built for exactly this.
Living with a disability: Missouri Vocational Rehabilitation offers assessment, individualized employment plans, job placement, supported employment, and assistive technology, with offices around the metro. MERS Goodwill also specializes in employment services for people with disabilities and other barriers — evaluation, counseling, training, and real job placement.
New to the country: the International Institute of St. Louis has a Workforce Solutions team that helps immigrants and refugees with job placement, job-readiness, ESL, and credential help — free to the job seeker.
Age 55 and older: the Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP) provides paid training and placement for lower-income job seekers 55+, across the city, county, and St. Charles.
No diploma yet: both MERS Goodwill (through its Excel Center) and the Urban League offer paths to a free adult high-school diploma alongside job help.
### Free and low-cost training that leads somewhere
Sometimes the fastest route to a stable job is a short, targeted credential — and you don’t have to pay full freight for it. St. Louis Community College’s Workforce Solutions runs short-term, low- or no-cost training in high-demand fields: CDL truck driving, skilled trades, healthcare (with partners like Mercy and BJC), and advanced manufacturing (with Boeing). Ranken Technical College has trained St. Louisans in hands-on trades — automotive, electrical, construction, IT, manufacturing — since 1907. And the job centers above can often help fund training through federal workforce dollars, so ask. A six-week certificate that leads to a $20-an-hour job beats a year of applying into the void.
### Who’s hiring across the metro
It also helps to know where the region’s jobs actually are. Greater St. Louis’s largest employers cluster in a handful of sectors: healthcare is the giant — BJC HealthCare is the region’s largest employer, with SSM Health and Mercy close behind — followed by education and research (Washington University is one of the metro’s biggest employers), defense and manufacturing (Boeing’s huge north-county presence, GM’s Wentzville assembly plant), logistics and distribution (the metro’s river, rail, and highway crossroads make it a national shipping hub), and finance and professional services (Edward Jones, Enterprise Mobility, and others). You don’t have to work at a giant — but knowing which industries are hiring hard helps you point your search, and many of these employers list openings on our jobs board and their own career pages. It’s also worth knowing that the region has been actively courting growth in geospatial and tech (around the new federal NGA campus in north St. Louis), bioscience (the Cortex district and the plant-science corridor), and skilled trades — all areas where training programs and apprenticeships are expanding to fill real, well-paying openings. If you’re choosing a direction to train toward, those are good bets in this metro.
### What to expect at a job center (it’s less intimidating than it sounds)
A lot of people never walk into a job center because they don’t know what happens there. Here’s the honest version: you show up (or call), and a real person helps you figure out a plan. There’s no cost, ever — these are publicly funded, and you’ve already paid for them with your taxes. Bring a photo ID and, if you have one, a copy of your résumé (if you don’t, they’ll help you build one). You can use their computers, printers, and internet for your search, sit in on free workshops on résumés and interviewing, and get matched to openings and, often, to training money. You do not need to be receiving unemployment, you don’t need a degree, and you won’t be judged for gaps or a rough patch — helping people through exactly those is the whole point of the place. Call ahead to check whether your nearest center takes walk-ins or appointments, and go in with a couple of honest questions about what you want. You’ll leave with more of a plan than you walked in with.
### Help for young people and first-time workers
If you’re young or looking for your first real job, there’s targeted help too. SLATE and the Missouri Job Centers run youth and young-adult programs (typically for roughly ages 16–24) that combine job-readiness training, work experience, and sometimes paid opportunities. The region also has growing apprenticeship pathways — earn-while-you-learn programs in the skilled trades, healthcare, and IT that pay you a wage while you train toward a credential and a career, often with little or no student debt. A job center or a program like Ranken can point you toward registered apprenticeships. For a first-time worker, that combination — a job center’s coaching plus an apprenticeship or entry-level role — is one of the surest footings there is.
Apropos of nothing: Metro East neighbors can’t find you without local SEO in Edwardsville.
### Which resource is right for you?
To make it simple, here’s the shortest path for a few common situations. Just need general job-search help? SLATE (city) or your nearest Missouri Job Center (county/metro) — start there. Coming back after incarceration? The Urban League’s Adult Re-Entry program and SLATE’s re-entry services. Living with a disability? Missouri Vocational Rehabilitation and MERS Goodwill. An immigrant or refugee? The International Institute’s Workforce Solutions. 55 or older and lower-income? The SCSEP senior employment program. Need a diploma or a quick credential? MERS Goodwill’s Excel Center, STLCC Workforce Solutions, or Ranken. Young or a first-time worker? SLATE’s youth programs and registered apprenticeships. Most of these can also refer you to the others, so there’s no wrong door — walk into any one and they’ll help you find the rest.
### You don’t have to do this alone
If there’s one thing to take from all of this, it’s that the loneliness of a job search is optional. St. Louis has quietly built a real safety net of people and programs whose job is to help you find work — free, local, and used to meeting people wherever they are, whatever they’re carrying. Reaching out isn’t a sign you’ve failed; it’s what the people who land good jobs actually do. Pick one resource above that fits your situation, make the call this week, and let someone help you work the problem. The metro is rooting for you more than it lets on.
### Making your search work
A few habits move things faster. Tailor the résumé to each role instead of blasting one version everywhere — the job centers above will help you do this for free. Use your network, awkward as it feels; a huge share of jobs are filled through someone who knew someone, and a simple “I’m looking, do you know anyone hiring?” works. Apply where you actually want to be — go straight to the career pages of specific local employers, not just the aggregators. And pace yourself: a job search is a grind, and the people who land well are usually the ones who treated it like a routine and asked for help rather than white-knuckling it alone.
And be patient with yourself on the hard days — a job search almost always takes longer than feels fair, and a string of no-answers says far more about a broken hiring process than about your worth. Set a couple of small, doable targets each week (two tailored applications, one workshop, one call to a job center), celebrate finishing them, and let the professionals above carry some of the weight. That’s not giving up; it’s working smart — and it’s exactly what these free St. Louis resources exist to do.
If you are weighing where to point your effort, ask which jobs are in high demand in Missouri before you retrain for anything. Healthcare, skilled trades and logistics have been the consistent answers. If you want examples of resources to start from, the Job Center, the county library system and the state’s re-employment services are the three most people actually use.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is there job help for people re-entering the workforce after prison?
A.  Yes. The Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis runs an Adult Re-Entry program plus its Save Our Sons and Save Our Sisters job-readiness programs, and SLATE administers re-entry employment grants. This help is judgment-free and built specifically for people coming back to work after incarceration.
### Q. What employment resources exist for people with disabilities in St. Louis?
A.  Missouri Vocational Rehabilitation provides assessment, individualized employment plans, job placement, supported employment, and assistive technology, with offices around the metro. MERS Goodwill also specializes in employment services — evaluation, counseling, training, and placement — for people with disabilities and other barriers to work.
### Q. Can I get free job training in St. Louis?
A.  Often, yes. St. Louis Community College’s Workforce Solutions and Ranken Technical College offer short-term, low- or no-cost training in high-demand trades and healthcare, and the Missouri Job Centers can frequently help fund training through federal workforce dollars. Ask a job center about what you qualify for.
### Q. Do I have to be on unemployment or have a degree to use a job center?
A.  No. Missouri Job Centers and SLATE are free and open to everyone — you don’t need to be receiving unemployment benefits, you don’t need a college degree, and you won’t be turned away for employment gaps or a rough patch. Bring a photo ID (and a résumé if you have one), and they’ll help with the rest at no cost.
### Q. What are the biggest employers and industries hiring in St. Louis?
A.  Healthcare leads — BJC HealthCare is the region’s largest employer, with SSM Health and Mercy close behind. Other major sectors include education and research (Washington University), defense and manufacturing (Boeing, GM’s Wentzville plant), logistics and distribution, and finance and professional services (Edward Jones, Enterprise Mobility). Knowing which industries are hiring hard helps you focus your search.
### Q. What jobs are in high demand in Missouri?
A.  Healthcare, skilled trades and logistics have been the consistent answers rather than anything faddish. The American Job Center downtown at 1520 Market Street, 314-589-8000, keeps current local demand data and the training that goes with it — free.
### Q. Why is it so hard to get a job right now in 2026?
A.  Application volume per opening has risen sharply and automated screening filters most of it before a person looks. That makes the free help more valuable, not less — resume screening for the systems that read it first is exactly what the Job Center does.
### Q. What are 5 examples of resources?
A.  The American Job Center at 1520 Market Street for the full service, SCSEP for paid training if you are 55 or older, the public library for computers and classes, 2-1-1 for wraparound help, and community college short-course programmes.
### Q. What is a good resource?
A.  One that is free, local and staffed by a person. The American Job Center qualifies on all three: 1520 Market Street, 314-589-8000, offering free help with searching, resumes and training referrals rather than a website that hands you a list.

## Nobody Scrolls Instagram for a Water Heater: Digital Marketing, in the Right Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/digital-marketing-for-small-business
Nobody scrolls Instagram deciding whose water heater to replace. They stand in a cold basement in Florissant in January, phone flashlight on a pilot light that won’t catch, and they search. Then they call one of the first names that comes back.
Google’s own ad-planning numbers for the city of St. Louis show the pattern: about 1,900 searches for “furnace repair” in January, about 170 in June. Nobody scrolled their way into those 1,900. The furnace quit, the house went cold, and they typed. And if you try to rent that moment instead, the same Google data prices one top-of-page click on “water heater repair” in St. Louis at roughly $42 to $82. Per click.
One rented click: $42 to $82. A complete Google profile in the same search: free, for as long as you keep it.
That one sentence would have saved Dana a lot of Sundays. Dana is a composite, not a customer: two vans, heating and cooling, North County. Sunday, 9:40 p.m., the van keys on the counter, the laptop the only light in the kitchen, and a guide written by a company with a hundred-person marketing department is telling her to build a content calendar, start a newsletter, run ads, post three times a week and get on video. She tries it for five weeks, typing posts in the van between service calls. By week six she has quit and decided she’s bad at marketing.
She isn’t. She was handed a menu with no order to it. So what if the first thing on it were the only thing she needed for a while?
### What does digital marketing actually mean for a small business?
Less than the guides imply, and in a specific order. Every article on this subject hands you the same four-item menu - search, social, email, paid ads - as though a two-person business could run all four. For a local business, three of them do very little until the first one is real.
First: be findable. A complete Google profile and listing, written in the words customers actually type, town included. In a city of 79 neighborhoods next to a county of 88 municipalities, “furnace repair Florissant” and “furnace repair Ferguson” are different searches. Nothing else works before this.
Second: be believable. Reviews that mention the job and the street, photos of real work in real basements, plain answers to the questions you hear on every call.
Third, and only then: be everywhere. Social, email, ads - the channels that amplify something that already exists.
The menu puts the third step first. That’s the expensive part, and it’s the menu’s doing, not yours.
Here’s what “findable” looks like from the other side. Seven on a January morning, a man in a Ferguson driveway in his robe, breath fogging, thumb on “furnace repair Ferguson.” Three names come up on the map. One shows real reviews that mention streets he knows; one shows none. He calls the first. Google’s own help page says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, and that more reviews and positive ratings can help a business’s local ranking. That’s the whole job of the first two weeks.
The first two weeks, in order. Week one, findable: pick your Google categories with Google’s own test, finishing the sentence “This business IS a ___,” not “HAS a ___,” and use as few as describe your core work. Name every town you actually serve, inside Google’s limit of about two hours’ drive. Add ten photos of real jobs, taken on your phone. Week two, believable: text your last five customers a review link and ask them to mention the job and the street. Everything on the rest of the menu can wait until those two weeks are done.
And skip the course in your inbox. When you’re ready to learn the rest of the menu, your library card already covers it. St. Louis Public Library and St. Louis County Library cardholders get LinkedIn Learning free, video courses on marketing, software and business; the city library counts more than 16,000 of them. Sign in with your library card, or use the app with library code slcl for the County, stlouispubliclibrary for the city. Dana could have watched one on her phone in the van between calls, instead of paying somebody to hand her the same unordered menu. Want a person instead of a video? The Missouri SBDC office at STL Partnership offers confidential, no-cost, one-on-one consulting that covers marketing; the counselor’s line is 314-615-7694.
### Belief one: you do not need all of it
Dana’s guide handed her five jobs: the calendar, the newsletter, the ads, the posts, the video. How many of those have you started, felt guilty about and quietly dropped? That pile isn’t a discipline problem. It’s a stack of channels with no order, sold as one job.
### Why the menu fails
At 9 p.m. Dana checks the ad dashboard from the driver’s seat, engine ticking: clicks, no calls, because every click landed on a profile with no photos and last winter’s hours. The four-channel list isn’t wrong. It’s unordered, and unordered advice is no advice when you have four hours a week. It fails specifically because those channels are not peers. Search is demand capture: somebody already wants what you sell and is looking for it right now. Social and email are demand nurture: they keep you in mind for later. Paid ads are demand rental: they work while you pay and stop when you stop.
A local service business lives almost entirely on the first one. People search at the moment something breaks, and they call one of the first few results. Rented clicks stop the minute you stop paying. A complete profile showing up in that same search costs nothing. Advice that treats a nurture channel and a capture channel as equally urgent is advice written for a brand, not for a trade.
### Who writes the menu
Look at who fills page one for this question: enterprise software companies, a national bank, a business magazine, accounting software and course sellers, organizations whose own marketing runs on budgets and headcount a two-van shop will never have. Every one lists the same four channels. Not one puts them in order. The most useful result is a forum post from someone handed a small business with almost no online presence, which is the real starting line for most St. Louis shops, and almost nothing above it is written for them.
### Even if you are not convinced
Even if your competitors really are on every platform, you are not competing with their posting schedule. You are competing for the person searching at nine at night, and that person never opens Instagram before calling.
Even if you genuinely enjoy social media, keep doing it - just stop counting it as the work. It is the reward for having the foundation, not a substitute for it.
Even if you already tried and it did not work, that is evidence about the order you tried it in, not about your ability. Almost everyone who quits marketing quit at channel three.
Totally unrelated, but - Patch is the south-side neighborhood nobody mentions.
### Belief two: the order matters more than the effort
Now picture a different owner - a one-woman bookkeeping practice working out of a spare room in O’Fallon. Call her Renee. She has no storefront, no staff, and no interest in becoming a content creator.
She spends a single Saturday on the unglamorous version instead. She fills in every field of her profile, in the words her clients actually use rather than the words on her business card. She lists every town she serves. She writes out the six questions she gets asked on every intro call, and answers them plainly. She asks four past clients for a review, at the moment each of them said thank you.
She does no posting at all. Within weeks she is turning up for searches she never targeted, because she finally gave a search engine something to match against.
### Why order beats effort
Because search engines and answer engines cannot recommend what they cannot describe. This is the mechanism underneath everything else, and it is almost never explained to owners.
A profile with three fields filled in gives a search engine nothing to match a customer against, so it sits there no matter how long you wait. A profile that tells the whole story - every service named the way a customer would say it, every town covered, real photos, honest hours, the questions you answer daily - gives it dozens of things to match. Same platform, same week, completely different outcome.
This is why “it takes three to six months” is only half true. The foundation is fast, if you actually build it. What takes months is authority and competitive rankings. Confusing the two is how a finite job gets billed as an ongoing one - the timeline breaks into three separate clocks, and only the last one is slow.
### What supports this
Words beat effort. “Contractor” is what you are; “basement egress window installation” is what somebody types. If the second phrase appears nowhere in your profile, no amount of posting fixes it.
Coverage beats frequency. A listing supporting up to 10 categories across up to 40 locations produces as many as 400 combinations a customer might search - against the handful of phrases most businesses ever think to target.
Completeness compounds. Every photo, service, event and update is one more thing that can be indexed and one more reason to surface you. Posting once more this week is not.
Proximity is doing more than you think. You rank differently for someone in Belleville than for someone in St. Charles, because distance is part of the calculation. Defining your service area properly does more for a traveling trade than months of content.
No storefront required. Home-based businesses, consultants and service-area trades are exactly the ones traditional local search handles worst - and exactly the ones a properly built listing helps most, because it does not depend on having an address to photograph.
### Even if you are not convinced

### What Google Business Profile Management Really Is
Sunday, 11:40 a.m. Your phone sits quiet on the counter in Florissant while, three miles away, somebody asks Maps whether you’re open, and the AI, reading hours you set two winters ago, tells her you close at noon. It matters because the three pins that pop up when someone in Clayton or Chesterfield types your trade are profiles, and Whitespark’s ranking-factors study rates the profile itself as the top driver of who gets those three spots.
The key word is ongoing. A profile with last spring’s photos and a newest review from two winters ago reads like a shop with the lights off, and Whitespark’s research shows the algorithm increasingly rewards profiles that “look alive” through fresh posts, photos, and steady review activity (Whitespark via Street Fight, 2025). The core elements of professional GBP management:
The facts, exactly right: name, address, phone, website and hours, including the snow-day closure in January and the early close before a Cardinals home opener, so the AI never sends someone to a locked door.
Real photos: the crew in the van, the finished kitchen in Kirkwood, the storefront in daylight. Not stock.
Review replies: answered within a day, in your own words, the way you’d talk to a neighbor over the fence.
Posts: a short update when something changes, like a new service area or a holiday special, so the profile looks alive.
The numbers: the calls, direction requests and website clicks Google reports, checked monthly so you know which month the phone actually rang.

### What Changed in Google Business Profile (2024–2026)
If your GBP playbook is more than a year old, part of it is broken. Google has quietly retired features many owners still rely on, and added ranking signals that weren’t there before. Here’s what actually changed:
The Google-built website is gone. The free “business.site” websites were shut off in March 2024, and the redirects stopped in June 2024 - so any old link now lands on a dead page (Search Engine Journal, 2024). If that was your only site, customers are hitting a wall right now.
Chat and call history were removed. Google turned off Business Profile chat and call history on July 31, 2024 (Google Business Profile Help, 2024). Messaging now has to run through your website, WhatsApp Business, or social DMs instead.
Social signals officially count now. For the first time, Whitespark’s 2026 report confirmed social signals as a measurable local ranking factor (Street Fight, 2025) - another reason your directory listings and social profiles need to line up with your GBP.
### Essential Optimization Strategies
The fastest lever you control is your primary category - it’s treated as the single most important GBP-level ranking factor (Rio SEO, 2025; corroborated by Whitespark 2026). Pick the one category that most precisely matches your core business, then add secondary categories for everything else you do. An Italian spot on The Hill might run “Italian Restaurant” as primary, with “Pizza Restaurant” and “Catering Service” as secondary.
Complete profile optimization checklist:
Fill out every section - hours, contact info, website, and a detailed description
Add high-quality photos - storefront, products, services, and team
Select accurate categories - one precise primary plus relevant secondary ones
List every service - Google can’t match you to a service you never listed
Incorporate location terms - naturally include neighborhood names and landmarks
Post regular updates - keep the profile active with news, offers, and events
Consistency across platforms is non-negotiable. Your name, address, and phone must match exactly across your website, social media, and directory listings. Even small mismatches - “Street” versus “St.,” an inconsistent suite number - erode Google’s confidence in where you actually are, and NAP inconsistency is one of the most common (and costly) mistakes owners make (Rio SEO, 2025).
### Reviews: Your Single Biggest Trust Lever
Reviews decide more sales than almost anything else on your profile. Standards are climbing, too - 68% now require at least a 4-star rating, and 31% won’t consider a business under 4.5 stars (up from 17% a year earlier).
Two things most owners miss:
Recency is a live signal. 74% of consumers only trust reviews from the last three months (BrightLocal, 2026), and Whitespark calls review recency one of the most underrated ranking factors going (Whitespark, 2025). A wall of five-star reviews from two years ago doesn’t carry the weight you think it does.
How you reply matters as much as the review. 80% of consumers are more likely to use a business that responds to all reviews - but 50% are turned off by generic, templated replies, and 19% now expect a same-day response (BrightLocal, 2026).
The takeaway: keep new reviews coming, and answer every one like a human. We break down exactly how in our guide to responding to Google reviews.

## The City Nearly Threw Away Your House’s Birth Certificate: How to Find the Real History of a St. Louis Home
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-the-history-of-your-st-louis-house
Someone else’s name is pencilled on a joist in your basement. Upstairs, a strip of wallpaper peels back to show another pattern underneath, and another under that. The back bedroom has a door that opens onto nothing.
So you look up your address, and the listing says 1920. Something about that doesn’t sit right. The trim is heavier than 1920, the lot is oddly shaped, and the house two doors down looks fifty years newer.
Trust that itch. Whether you’re in a brick four-family in Dutchtown, a frame house in Ferguson, a bungalow in Affton or a farmhouse that got swallowed by a subdivision out past Wentzville, the odds are decent that the year you were handed is wrong. Count how many old houses on your block are listed as built in exactly 1900 or 1920. That isn’t a building boom. It’s where somebody filling in a tax record didn’t know, and rounded.
Here’s what most house-history guides never mention, because it only exists here. The St. Louis Public Library’s St. Louis Room holds about 112,000 house-numbering certificates the City’s Building Department issued from around 1880 to 1976. Each one gave a new building its street number, and each lists the city block, the lot, the owner and the contractor, with a rough sketch of the lot and a dated stamp from the Street Department. The Building Division planned to throw the whole collection away. A library patron suggested donating it instead, and in 2010 the library took it in.
Find your address in that collection and the house stops being a listing. There’s the contractor who framed it, the owner who paid him, your lot drawn out by hand, and the day the Street Department stamped it real.
Then the permit. City building permits were filed by street address starting in 1900; before that they name only the street and the block, so for an older house the trail runs through the city block number on your parcel record. Permits from before 1940 are on microfilm at the Landmarks Association of St. Louis library, by appointment on weekdays, and from the 1890s the St. Louis Daily Record printed permit summaries that often name the builder, the architect and the estimated cost.
And you can start tonight, from the couch. A free St. Louis Public Library card, open to City, St. Louis County and St. Charles County residents, unlocks the library’s Digital Sanborn Maps database: more than 1,400 digitized fire-insurance maps of Missouri towns, the maps that show a house’s footprint edition by edition.
### How do you find out when your house was really built?
Not from a real estate listing. Those pull from assessor records, and assessor records are frequently estimates entered decades after the fact - which is why so many old houses are listed as 1900 or 1920 on the nose.
Four record types give you the real answer, and they work best in this order:
Sanborn fire insurance maps - show your house’s actual footprint, materials and outbuildings, block by block, year by year.
City directories - who lived at your address, in almost every year.
Deeds and property records - when the land changed hands and what it sold for.
Newspaper archives - the human material: the sale, the fire, the wedding, the obituary.
All four are free to use in St. Louis, and three of them are within a short drive of Forest Park.
### Why the year you were given is probably wrong
This is worth understanding before you start, because it explains most of the confusion.
Assessor records exist to value property for taxation, not to document history. In many jurisdictions a build year was entered in bulk when records were computerized, sometimes a century after the house went up, and when nobody knew the real date they rounded. That is why round years like 1900 and 1920 cluster so heavily in old neighborhoods - not because a remarkable number of houses were built in those exact years, but because those were the shrugs.
Real estate portals then repeat that number, and so does everything downstream of them. The number is not a lie; it is just a placeholder that got treated as a fact.
Two other things muddy St. Louis specifically. Houses were often built in stages - a small structure first, with additions over the following decades, so there may be no single build year at all. And the metro annexed and re-platted aggressively, meaning your house may predate the municipality it now sits in.
### Start with Sanborn fire insurance maps
If you do only one thing, do this one. Sanborn maps were produced for insurance underwriters from the late 1800s onward, and they are absurdly detailed for the purpose you are now using them for.
Each map shows individual buildings with their footprints, how many stories they had, what they were built of - brick shaded one color, frame another - plus porches, outbuildings, and often the house number. They were reissued periodically, which is what makes them powerful: find the earliest edition your house appears in, and the last edition it does not, and you have bracketed the construction date to a few years using primary evidence.
They also explain oddities. A garage that seems too old for the house. A neighbor’s addition that is clearly newer. The stable that became a garage. The building that used to be a corner store, which is why your ground floor has a door where a window should be.
### Then read the city directories
St. Louis had two long-running annual directory series, Gould’s St. Louis Directory and Polk’s City Directories. They listed residents and businesses with addresses and occupations - a printed version of the job search engines do now.
The trick most people miss: many directory volumes can be searched by address, not just by name. That reverses the whole exercise. Instead of hunting for a person, you look up your own address year after year and watch the occupants change - a machinist in 1911, a widow in 1919, a family that stays through the 1940s.
Two traps to know about. Street names and numbers changed. St. Louis renumbered, and streets were renamed. An address that returns nothing may simply have been called something else, which is exactly what Sanborn maps and plat records help you untangle. And spelling was inconsistent, especially with immigrant surnames - the same family may appear as Schmidt, Schmitt, Schmit and Smith across four volumes. Search by sound, not by spelling.
The original brick paving on North Main Street in St. Charles, still in service. Photographed by Lane Forman, July 26, 2026.
### How to look up your house’s history by address, free
Start with the address itself and work backward. The first time you see your house number printed beside a stranger’s name in a century-old city directory, you’ll be hooked. Every step below costs nothing but time.
Pull the parcel record. For a house in the City of St. Louis, the city’s online Address & Property Search shows ownership, assessed value and permit activity for any address (it doesn’t allow searches by owner name). The year built you see there is the assessor’s number, so treat it as a lead, not the answer.
Bracket the date on a Sanborn map from your couch. With a St. Louis Public Library card (residents of the City, St. Louis County and St. Charles County qualify), the library’s Digital Sanborn Maps database, more than 1,400 maps of 376 Missouri towns and cities from 1867 to 1970, and Fire Insurance Maps Online open from home. Find the first edition that shows your footprint and the last one that doesn’t.
Walk the deed chain. City deeds sit with the Recorder of Deeds at City Hall, 1200 Market St., Room 128, whose Archives Department handles historical land records. St. Louis County deeds are at the Recorder of Deeds, 41 South Central Ave. in Clayton, where every recorded document is open for public research.
Look the address up in old city directories at the Missouri Historical Society or the Central Library, year by year, to see who lived there and when the listings begin.
Check the 1950 census. It’s the newest census open to the public, free online from the National Archives, and it shows who was in the house on census day.
Ask for help. The Missouri Historical Society’s Library & Research Center offers house history workshops, and its staff will point you to the right map, directory or deed book.
One caution: if the address returns nothing in an old record, the street may have been renumbered or renamed. Check a Sanborn map before you decide the house wasn’t there yet.
Total tangent - where to eat in Wood River, whenever you surface.
### Where to go, specifically
### Missouri Historical Society Library and Research Center
The best starting point in the region, at 225 South Skinker Boulevard, just west of Forest Park - in a 1920s former synagogue that reopened in 2023 after renovation. Admission is free.
Check the hours before you drive over, because they catch people out: closed Mondays, open Tuesday through Friday from noon to 5pm, and Saturday from 10am to 5pm. You can reach them at (314) 746-4500, and if you are coming from out of town it is worth calling first so they can pull materials. Their city directory and property research help is one of the most-used things they do.
### State Historical Society of Missouri, St. Louis Research Center
On the UMSL campus, inside the Thomas Jefferson Library, and reachable on the MetroLink Red Line. Strong on manuscript collections, photographs, maps and neighborhood histories - useful once you know who lived in the house and want to know what the neighborhood was doing around them.
### St. Louis Public Library
The Central Library downtown holds genealogy and local history collections, census records, newspaper archives and historic directories, and the staff there are used to exactly this question. This is also where the free database subscriptions live that would otherwise cost you money at home.
### Missouri Digital Heritage
A Missouri Secretary of State project that puts digitized records from institutions across the state in one place - useful for the evening-on-the-couch phase of the research, before you commit to a Saturday.
### Finding old photographs of your house
This is the part everybody actually wants, and it is the least predictable.
Straight-on photographs of ordinary houses are rare, because nobody photographed ordinary houses. What exists instead is incidental: your house in the background of a street scene, in a real estate or auction listing, in a newspaper photo of a parade or a flood or a snowstorm on your block. Assessor photographs from mid-century surveys exist in some jurisdictions. Neighborhood association archives and church anniversary booklets are quietly excellent and almost never searched.
The other source is people. Long-time neighbors have shoeboxes, and the family that sold you the house may have photographs they never thought to hand over. It costs a knock on a door and a polite letter.
### Newspapers fill in the humans
Once you have names from the directories, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch and the long-defunct St. Louis Globe-Democrat turn them into people.
Search the surname alongside the street. Property transfers were printed. So were engagement notices, funeral arrangements held at home, small-business advertisements with your address in them, and the occasional item you were not expecting. This is the stage where a research project becomes a story, and where most people stop being able to put it down.
### When the house tells you itself
Documents are the proof, but the building offers hints worth reading alongside them.
Look at what is structural rather than decorative, since decoration gets replaced: the framing in the attic and basement, whether floor joists are sawn or milled, the shape and mortar of the foundation, window openings that have been altered, brick coursing and the mortar color, and how the additions meet the original block. Old plumbing and wiring can be dated roughly. A datestone or a builder’s mark is a gift.
Treat all of this as directional. Styles persisted for decades and materials were reused, so architectural evidence narrows the window - it does not close it. The records close it.
Found out your house is older than the paperwork says? That usually changes who should work on it. Century homes in this metro come with their own foundations, brick, mortar and wiring, and the trades who understand them are worth finding deliberately - browse local pros on St Louis Near Me Directory or the home services coverage map.
If you’re the mason, plasterer, electrician or carpenter who can read old brick and soft mortar by hand, list your trade with us and turn more of the old-house owners reading this into customers.
### What to do with what you find
Write it down while you have it. A one-page timeline - build date, owners in order, alterations, sources - is worth more than a folder of screenshots, and it is the thing you will hand to the next owner.
It also has practical value. Knowing your house is genuinely older than the listing says changes how you approach renovation: what is behind the plaster, whether the brick has been repointed with the wrong mortar, why the basement behaves the way it does. If you are about to work on an old house here, that context matters - older foundations have their own problems, and the trades who work on century homes are not always the same ones who work on new construction.
And a note on the archives themselves: they are free, they are staffed by people who like this question, and they are underused. The institutions above have spent generations keeping these records so somebody would eventually come and ask.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I find when my home was built?
A.  Start with Sanborn fire insurance maps to bracket the date between the earliest edition showing the house and the last one that does not. Confirm with city directories and deed records. Treat the year on a real estate listing as a starting hypothesis, not an answer, because it usually comes from assessor data that was estimated.
### Q. Who used to live at my house?
A.  Look your address up, not a name, in the old city directories at the Missouri Historical Society or the Central Library, and you’ll see the occupants change year by year. The 1950 census, free online from the National Archives, shows the household on census day, and deeds at the Recorder of Deeds name every owner.
### Q. How can I find old photos of my house?
A.  Rarely head-on, usually incidental. Look for your house in the background of street scenes, newspaper photographs of events on your block, auction and real estate listings, and mid-century assessor surveys where they exist. The Missouri Historical Society’s photographs and prints collection is open by appointment, and long-time neighbors’ shoeboxes are the most overlooked source of all.
### Q. How do I find old pictures of my house on Google Maps?
A.  Google only goes back so far. On a computer, drop into Street View at your address and use the date option in the box at the top left to step through older captures, which on most St. Louis streets start in the late 2000s. For anything older than that you need newspapers, archives and neighbors.
### Q. How do I find the history of my house online for free?
A.  Online gets you most of the way. The City of St. Louis Address & Property Search, the St. Louis Public Library’s Digital Sanborn Maps and Fire Insurance Maps Online (with a library card), the 1950 census and Missouri Digital Heritage all work from the couch. Older deeds, directories on microfilm and local photograph collections still mean a trip, so do the online phase first and arrive at the archive with specific questions.
### Q. Is there a way to check my address history?
A.  Yes, two ways. For the property, the city’s Address & Property Search shows ownership and permit activity for a city address, and the Recorder of Deeds holds every transfer. For the address itself, remember St. Louis renumbered and renamed streets, so old directories and Sanborn maps show what your house used to be called.
One practical payoff of knowing your house is older than the listing suggested: there is a real chance there is original hardwood under the carpet. Hardwood, laminate or vinyl covers how to check before you price anything new.

## Hiring Your First Employee in Missouri: What You Actually Owe in 2026
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-your-first-employee-in-missouri
### What do you actually owe when you hire your first employee in Missouri?
Search this and you will get a very reasonable national checklist — EIN, W-4, I-9, payroll, workers’ comp. Page one right now is the SBA, Indeed, Reddit, a California coach, and a Michigan nonprofit. All fine. None of it tells you what Missouri requires, and Missouri has changed twice in the last two years in ways that catch employers out. Which is exactly why guessing gets expensive here. So before that first hire starts, do you actually know what Missouri now requires — and what it quietly stopped requiring?
The short version, current as of today:
Minimum wage is $15.00 an hour, effective January 1, 2026.
You do not owe statewide paid sick leave. That mandate was repealed. A great deal of advice still says otherwise.
Workers’ comp kicks in at five employees — unless you are in construction, where it is one.
You must report the hire to the state within 20 days. Most first-time employers have never heard of this one.
### The paid sick leave whiplash, explained once
This is worth getting straight, because employers are still being told to budget for something they no longer owe.
In November 2024, Missouri voters passed Proposition A. It did two things: raised the minimum wage on a schedule toward $15, and created a statewide paid sick leave mandate — an hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked.
Then the legislature undid much of it. House Bill 567 was signed on July 10, 2025 and took effect August 28, 2025. It repealed the paid sick leave mandate, which employers were only obligated to provide through August 27, 2025, and it removed the inflation-indexed raises that would have begun in 2027.
What survived: the $15.00 minimum wage that took effect January 1, 2026.
So the accurate position today is: pay at least $15.00, owe no statewide sick leave, and expect no automatic annual increase after this one. Any guide written between late 2024 and mid-2025 — which is most of what is still ranking — will tell you something different. You can of course offer paid sick leave; plenty of employers do, and it competes well for staff. You are simply not required to.
### Workers’ comp: the number that changes everything if you are in the trades
Missouri sets the threshold at five or more employees. Under five, most employers are not required to carry workers’ compensation insurance.
Construction is the exception, and it is a big one: one employee triggers it. If you run a roofing, framing, concrete, electrical, plumbing or general contracting operation and you hire a single person, you need coverage from that hire — not from your fifth.
Given how much of the metro’s small-business economy is trades, this is the single most commonly missed obligation on this page. It pairs with a reality we covered separately: Missouri does not license contractors at the state level, so nobody checks your insurance at a licensing desk. That does not make the requirement optional; it just means the discovery happens after an injury instead of before.
One deadline to file away now rather than later: once covered, a work injury must be reported to your insurer within five days of the injury or of the employee telling you, whichever comes later.
### The 20-day rule nobody warns you about
Here is the requirement first-time employers almost never see coming, because it has nothing to do with taxes or insurance.
Under RSMo 285.300, every Missouri employer must report each newly hired or rehired employee to the Missouri State Directory of New Hires within 20 days of their start date. It runs through the Department of Social Services, and the purpose is child-support enforcement — locating parents and establishing orders.
Two details that trip people:
Rehires count. A seasonal worker returning after being separated for 60 or more consecutive days is a new hire for this purpose. Restaurants, landscapers and shops with a winter lull hit this constantly.
It is not payroll. Running payroll software does not automatically satisfy it unless that provider files on your behalf — ask them directly rather than assuming.
Reporting is free and takes minutes through the state’s employer portal at missouriemployer.dss.mo.gov, or by phone at 888-663-6751.
### The registrations, in the order that avoids backtracking
Nothing here is difficult; it is just spread across three governments.
1. Federal EIN from the IRS — free, same day, online. You need it before payroll exists.
2. Employer withholding with the Missouri Department of Revenue. If you already registered for sales tax, this is the same registration system and you can add withholding to your existing account. Our guide to the Missouri sales tax license covers that portal.
3. Unemployment insurance with the Missouri Division of Employment Security. Rates for new employers change periodically, so get your assigned rate from them rather than from an article.
4. Workers’ compensation, at the threshold that applies to you — five employees generally, one in construction.
5. Payroll. Software or an accountant. For one employee, the software is usually cheaper than the first mistake.
### Day-one paperwork
Three documents, and two of them are federal:
Form W-4 — federal withholding. Missouri also has its own withholding certificate for state tax.
Form I-9 — identity and work authorization. There is a deadline: complete it within three business days of the start date, and keep it on file. You do not send it anywhere.
A written offer stating the wage, the title, the schedule, and the start date. Missouri is an at-will state, but “at will” does not mean “unwritten” — most first-hire disputes are about what someone believed they were promised.
### Employee or contractor? Get this one right
The tempting move with a first hire is to call them a 1099 contractor and skip everything above. It is also the most expensive mistake available to a new employer.
The test is control, not paperwork. If you set their hours, direct how the work is done, supply the tools, and they work only for you, they look like an employee no matter what the agreement says. Getting it wrong exposes you to back taxes, penalties, and — if someone gets hurt — an uninsured injury claim, because a misclassified worker was never on a workers’ comp policy.
Genuine contractors exist and are perfectly legitimate. If you are unsure which you have, that is a specific question for an accountant, and it is much cheaper to ask before the hire than after an audit.
Random, but: here’s every place to eat in New Melle.
### Where St. Louis employers actually find people
The compliance side is the part with deadlines. Finding the person is the part that takes longer than anyone plans for, and a first hire is unusually hard because you have no reputation as an employer yet — nobody has worked for you and told anyone what it was like.
What tends to work for a first hire in this metro, roughly in order of hit rate:
The people already around you. Customers, suppliers, the person who does your books, other owners on your block. A first hire is a trust hire; you are going to be alone in a van or behind a counter with this person. A name from someone you already trust outperforms a stranger from a job board almost every time.
Trade schools and community colleges, if the work is skilled. St. Louis Community College and the region’s apprenticeship programs graduate people specifically looking for a first employer, and their career offices will post a role for free. We wrote about the local pipeline in our guide to trade schools and apprenticeships in St. Louis.
Your own front window and your own customers. Underrated and free. People who already like your business are a warmer applicant pool than a job board delivers, and they show up already knowing what you sell.
Neighborhood-level channels — the community groups and neighborhood pages where people actually talk. A role posted where someone in Maplewood or Florissant already reads is worth more than the same role buried on a national site alongside a thousand others.
One thing worth knowing before you post anywhere: candidates look you up. They read your reviews and look at your photos before they apply, the same way customers do — and a business that is hard to find or looks abandoned online gets fewer and worse applicants. Your visibility is doing recruiting work whether or not you meant it to.
Be specific in the posting, too. “Competitive pay” reads as evasive when the state floor is $15.00 and everyone knows it. Naming the wage, the hours, and whether the schedule is fixed will filter your applicants better than any screening question.
### A first-hire sequence for a St. Louis business
Decide employee vs contractor, honestly.
Get the EIN.
Register withholding with the Department of Revenue and unemployment with Employment Security.
Get workers’ comp if you are in construction, or if this hire puts you at five.
Set up payroll and confirm whether it files new-hire reports for you.
Written offer at $15.00/hr or better.
W-4 and I-9 on day one; I-9 completed within three business days.
Report the hire within 20 days.
Then the part no checklist covers: you now have someone whose rent depends on your revenue being steady. That changes how much a quiet week costs you, which is why most owners find that the hire and the marketing problem arrive in the same month.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What do I need to do to hire my first employee?
A.  Get a federal EIN, register for employer withholding with the Missouri Department of Revenue and unemployment insurance with the Division of Employment Security, obtain workers’ compensation if it applies to you, set up payroll, collect a W-4 and I-9, and report the hire to the Missouri State Directory of New Hires within 20 days. Pay at least $15.00 an hour.
### Q. Do I need an LLC to hire employees?
A.  No. A sole proprietor can hire W-2 employees without forming an LLC or corporation — you just need the EIN and the registrations above. An LLC changes your liability exposure, not your ability to employ people. Since hiring adds real risk, it is a reasonable moment to revisit the question, but it is not a prerequisite.
### Q. Does Missouri require paid sick leave?
A.  Not anymore. Proposition A created a statewide paid sick leave mandate, but House Bill 567 repealed it effective August 28, 2025 — employers were obligated only through August 27, 2025. Guides written in that window still say it is required. You may offer it voluntarily, and many employers do because it helps them compete for staff.
### Q. When does a Missouri business need workers' compensation?
A.  At five or more employees for most employers — but at one or more if you are a construction contractor. That exception catches a lot of trades businesses making a first hire. Once covered, report any work injury to your insurer within five days of the injury or of being told about it, whichever is later.
### Q. How to hire someone for the first time?
A.  Define the role and the hours before you advertise, decide honestly whether it is an employee or a contractor, complete the registrations, then make a written offer stating wage, title, schedule and start date. Missouri is an at-will state, but most first-hire disputes come from things that were said rather than written.
### Q. How much does it cost to hire your first employee?
A.  Beyond wages at $15.00 an hour or more, budget for the employer share of payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, workers’ compensation if it applies, and payroll software. The registrations themselves are free. Costs vary enough by industry — a roofer and a bookkeeper are not comparable on comp premiums — that you should get real quotes rather than trust an average.

## AI for St. Louis: How Local Businesses Can Actually Use It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ai-for-st-louis-how-local-businesses-boost-visibility-with-a-hyper-local-near-me-directory
Two shops sit on the same St. Louis street. One owner spent the past year letting AI draft her social posts, field after-hours questions, and tidy up her online listings. Now, when someone asks ChatGPT for “a good option near me,” her business is the one that comes up. Her neighbor still isn’t sure whether “AI” is a real tool or just hype, and he’s slowly going invisible to a whole new way people search. The gap between them didn’t take a computer-science degree or a big budget. Just a willingness to use a few tools well.
That’s the real story of AI for small business in 2026. Robots aren’t taking over. Ordinary local owners are quietly getting an edge. What follows is an honest, practical guide to how St. Louis businesses can actually use AI: the wins that are real, how to get found by AI, and where it still falls on its face.
### How Can Small Businesses Use AI?
The most useful AI for a small business is ordinary. It’s a handful of everyday tools that save hours and sharpen your marketing. Here are the practical wins St. Louis owners are actually getting:
Marketing and content — drafting social posts, email newsletters, and website copy in minutes instead of hours (marketing is the most common entry point for small-business AI).
Customer service — chatbots and automated replies that answer common questions and capture leads after you’ve gone home.
Reviews — drafting thoughtful, personalized responses to every review, fast, so none go ignored.
Operations — scheduling, appointment reminders, bookkeeping help, and summarizing the busywork that eats your day.
Getting found — the newest and most overlooked: making sure AI assistants recommend you when a customer asks for a local option.
Adoption has moved fast. Industry surveys in 2026 put generative-AI use among small firms above half, with marketing the most common first use. You don’t need all of it, though. Picking even one or two of these frees up real time and levels the field against bigger competitors.
### How Do Local Businesses Get Found by AI?
This is the shift that matters most, and the one most owners are missing. People increasingly skip the search box and just ask an assistant: BrightLocal’s 2026 research found about 45% of consumers now use AI tools like ChatGPT for local recommendations, up from just 6% a year earlier — the third most-used local-discovery channel behind Google and directories. If AI doesn’t know your business exists, you’re invisible to nearly half the market. So here’s the question that should stop you cold: when someone asks an AI for the best in your field near them, does it even know you exist?
The good news: getting recommended by AI rests on the same foundations as good local SEO, because that’s where these tools pull their answers. AI assistants favor businesses with a complete, consistent presence (matching name, address, and phone everywhere), real reviews, and citations across trusted local sources and directories. In other words, you don’t optimize for the AI directly — you make your business easy for it to find, verify, and trust. A complete listing in a hyper-local directory is one of the clearest signals you can send, because it hands the AI exactly the structured, consistent local data it’s looking for.
### What AI Actually Looks Like on a Tuesday
Strip away the buzzwords and “using AI” is refreshingly ordinary. Take a small St. Louis contractor on a normal week. Monday, he pastes a few bullet points into a chatbot and gets a month of social captions back in five minutes. Tuesday, a customer messages at 9 p.m. asking about pricing, and an automated assistant answers the basics and books a callback while he’s asleep. Wednesday, three new reviews come in, and instead of ignoring them, he drafts warm, personal replies to all three in the time it used to take to write one. None of that is science fiction or a big investment. It’s a few free or cheap tools handling the small stuff so he can spend his day doing the actual work. AI isn’t replacing him. It’s clearing the busywork off his plate so the human parts get his full attention.
### Which AI Tools Should a Small Business Try First?
You don’t need a stack of software to start — you need one tool aimed at one problem. A general assistant like ChatGPT (or a similar chatbot) is the natural first step: it drafts posts, emails, and review replies, brainstorms promotions, and answers “how do I…” questions about running your business. From there, the highest-value additions are usually a customer-facing chatbot or auto-responder for your website and social messages, and whatever scheduling or bookkeeping tool you already use — most now have AI features built in. The trap is buying five tools you never learn; the win is picking one, using it daily for a month until it’s a habit, and only then adding another. Training matters, too: even a few hours spent learning to prompt a tool well dramatically changes what you get out of it.
### What Are the Things AI Can’t Do for Your Business?
Honest guardrails matter, because the hype outruns reality. AI can’t replace your judgment, your relationships, or your accountability. Specifically, it can’t reliably get facts right on its own (it invents confident-sounding details — every output about your business, prices, or the law needs a human check), it can’t build genuine trust or handle a delicate customer situation the way a real person can, it can’t make strategic decisions that depend on knowing your market and your goals, it can’t guarantee compliance or accuracy in regulated fields like law, medicine, or finance, and it can’t replace your voice — over-automated content reads like everyone else’s. Use AI to draft, speed up, and assist; keep a human in charge of anything a customer sees or that carries real consequences.
### Why Do So Many AI Projects Fail?
It’s widely reported that a large majority of AI initiatives fail to deliver their intended value — and for small businesses, the reasons are usually mundane, not technical. The common traps: starting with a shiny tool instead of a real problem (buying “an AI” with no clear job for it); skipping the human check and getting burned by a confident-but-wrong output; no training, so the tool gets used badly or abandoned; and expecting magic instead of a modest, compounding efficiency gain. The businesses that succeed with AI do the opposite: they pick one painful, repetitive task, apply a tool to that, keep a person reviewing the output, and expand only once it’s clearly working. Start small, stay honest about results, and AI becomes a quiet advantage instead of an expensive disappointment.
