### What are the best indoor activities for kids in St. Louis when December weather turns bad?
Make The Magic House your December plan: its Holiday Magic celebration is listed for December 1-24 and included with admission, with the house decorated and aglow with festive lights, a Winter Wonderscape of an Ice Castle slide, a Snow Maze, the Elves’ Workshop and Santa’s Sleigh, and extended holiday hours. The dates are set each year, so confirm them on its Holiday Magic page. For a free backup, the Saint Louis Art Museum says museum admission is free, and it hosts a Winter Celebrations weekend of art making and live performances each December.
### For kids bouncing off the walls: trampolines, slides and auto-belays
When the couch cushions are already on the floor, it’s time to jump. Trampoline parks lead the way: Sky Zone in Fenton (631 Gravois Rd., 636-364-4444) and Urban Air Adventure Park - with locations in Sunset Hills, Cottleville, and Fairview Heights on the Illinois side - pack in trampolines, foam pits, obstacle courses, and climbing walls, with dedicated toddler times at slower hours. Socks are required at both. Sky Zone allows only its own, and Urban Air doesn’t publish its prices, so call your location.
Slick City Action Park is an all-indoor slide park - think a dozen giant slides plus air-jump courts - with metro locations in Chesterfield and St. Peters, and it suits kids who’ve outgrown the ball pit. For climbers, Climb So iLL (downtown St. Louis and St. Charles) has walls and auto-belays sized for families.
Older kids and tweens gravitate to Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country (indoor go-karts, laser tag, a ninja course) and Puttshack at City Foundry, which reinvents mini-golf with tech-enabled scoring and a full menu. That makes it a rare spot that entertains a squirrelly nine-year-old and a couple of adults at the same table.
### Little ones and play cafés
Got toddlers? Go Play! in Chesterfield (140 Long Rd., Suite 108, with a second spot in Lake St. Louis) offers a three-story play structure, slides, and ball pits with coffee for the grown-ups. Ages 1 to 15 are $21, ages 6 to 12 months are $10, under 6 months are free, and adults are always free. Sessions run 9 to 1 and 2 to 7. The site lists Wednesday as the closed day while another page says Tuesday, so call 636-893-8134 before you go.
TotSpot Social in Clayton’s DeMun neighborhood is a play-space-and-café built for newborns through age six, with timed sessions. And We Rock the Spectrum in Fenton is a sensory-inclusive gym designed so kids of all abilities - including those with autism or sensory needs - can play side by side. These smaller spots are the sanity-savers when you have a napper and a runner in the same stroller.
### Union Station: a rainy day in one building
St. Louis Union Station is more than the aquarium. Under the same historic roof you’ll find a mirror maze, a ropes course, mini-golf, a carousel that costs $5 a ride (not the $2 survivor at Faust Park), a Build-A-Bear Workshop, and the giant St. Louis Wheel just outside. That’s enough to build a whole rainy day around without going back to the car. The Wheel is $18 and up for ages 13 and older, $12 and up for ages 3 to 12, and free at 2 and under.
An Aquarium-plus-Wheel combo ticket exists, but its price appears only at checkout and no savings figure is published, so price it against buying each separately before you commit. Aquarium members get unlimited visits for less than the cost of two general admission tickets, plus 15% off Union Station rides and a parking voucher.
### Indoor playgrounds near you, by part of town
Nobody types “indoor playground near me” with time to spare. There’s a kid bouncing off the couch cushions and maybe twenty minutes of patience left in the house. So here’s the metro sorted by drive, not by brand. Downtown: City Museum, Union Station’s aquarium, mirror maze and ropes course, and the climbing walls at Climb So iLL are a short hop apart, the easiest answer for an indoor play place downtown. Midtown and the central corridor: the free Science Center in Forest Park, Puttshack at City Foundry, and TotSpot Social on Clayton Road in DeMun. South County and Fenton: Sky Zone on Gravois Road, Urban Air in Sunset Hills, and We Rock the Spectrum. Kirkwood and Town and Country: The Magic House and Amp Up Action Park.
West County: Go Play! and Slick City in Chesterfield, plus the Butterfly House and the Carousel at Faust Park. St. Charles County: Urban Air in Cottleville, Slick City in St. Peters, and the second Go Play! in Lake St. Louis. Metro East: Urban Air in Fairview Heights. Pick the cluster closest to home and your backup is one exit away.
Nothing to do with kids - but Soulard is worth a wander.
### What to check before you load the car
Two checks save every indoor-play outing. First, check the ticket rules before you leave the driveway. The Magic House sells admission at the front desk and the Aquarium no longer uses timed ticketing, so neither needs an advance purchase. City Museum is cheaper online, and the Science Center’s Blue Whale exhibit sells timed entry every 15 minutes. Second, pack the right gear: Sky Zone and Urban Air require socks (Sky Zone allows only its own), closed-toe shoes make City Museum far more fun, and a change of clothes is never a bad idea.
### Go early, keep a backup, pack the bag
Go early. The Aquarium opens at 9, the Science Center at 9:30 (11 on Sundays), and the Magic House at 10:30 (9:30 on Saturdays). Have a backup that’s open the same day. The Monday and Tuesday closures above are the easiest way for a plan to fall apart, and the carousel and Butterfly House also close for a few weeks each January. Pack a bag. Water bottles, a snack, your Sky Zone socks, and a change of clothes cover most disasters, and they keep you from paying concession prices for a forgotten juice box.
It also helps to match the venue to your window of time. If you’ve got ninety minutes before a nap, a play café or the Carousel is perfect; if you’ve got a whole miserable-weather afternoon to fill, City Museum or Union Station will happily eat all of it. And don’t underestimate the smaller neighborhood spots - a quiet play café on a weekday morning can save your sanity just as well as a big-ticket attraction on a Saturday.
### By age: what actually works when
The right indoor spot depends a lot on who’s in the back seat. For babies and young toddlers, the winners are the calm, contained spaces: TotSpot Social, the soft-play areas at Go Play!, the Carousel at Faust Park, and the toddler hours at the trampoline parks, where the big kids aren’t bouncing them off the mats. For preschoolers and early grade-schoolers, The Magic House is a strong pick, and the Aquarium, Butterfly House, and City Museum’s lower levels hit the sweet spot of “amazing but not overwhelming.”

### Budgets, memberships, and keeping it cheap
Indoor play adds up fast with a couple of kids, so start with the cheap doors. The Science Center is free to enter, though parking is $15 (card only, free for members). The Magic House drops to $3 a person from 3 to 5 p.m. for residents of the counties listed above, and Free Family Night covers up to two adults and four children on the third Friday of the month. The Butterfly House is free for St. Louis City and County residents during the first two hours on the first Tuesday of each month.
Memberships come down to arithmetic. The Magic House Family tier is $175 against $60 at the door for four, so it wins on the third visit. The Magic House also honors the ACM Reciprocal Network at 50% off, not free, for Family, Family Plus and Grandparent memberships, up to six people with the cardholder present. Because Science Center entry is free, its membership is really about parking and shows: the $100 Family tier includes free parking plus four free OMNIMAX, planetarium and Discovery Room tickets per visit. The ASTC Passport program excludes venues within 90 miles and never covers the planetarium, the large-screen theater or special exhibits.
The other passes follow the same math. City Museum’s $39.99 Gold Pass costs less than two $20 tickets, and an Aquarium membership gives unlimited visits for less than two general admission tickets. For the pay-to-play spots, buy Sky Zone socks once and reuse them.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best indoor activities for kids in St. Louis on a rainy day?
A.  Top picks are the City Museum ($20, children 2 and under free), The Magic House in Kirkwood ($15 for age 1 and up), the Saint Louis Science Center (free admission, closed Tuesdays) and the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station. All four are indoors, but their closed days differ, so check before you go. For high energy, add a trampoline or slide park like Sky Zone, Urban Air, or Slick City.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis on a rainy day?
A.  Sort it by energy. Curious kids: the Saint Louis Science Center (free admission, $15 parking) or The Magic House in Kirkwood. Kids bouncing off the walls: Sky Zone, Urban Air or Slick City, with the right socks on. Toddlers: Go Play! or TotSpot Social. Can’t decide? Union Station puts an aquarium, a mirror maze, a ropes course and mini-golf under one roof, so one parking spot covers the whole wet day.
### Q. Is there an indoor playground for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, several, and they are not interchangeable. Go Play! in Chesterfield and Lake St. Louis has a three-story play structure for younger kids, TotSpot Social in DeMun is a play café with a soft area for babies, and Sky Zone, Urban Air and Slick City are big trampoline and slide parks for older kids. Match the venue to the age, not the drive time.
### Q. How much does it cost for an indoor playground?
A.  Prices are per person, and some places charge adults while others don’t. Go Play! in Chesterfield is $21 for ages 1 to 15 with adults always free, Sky Zone Fenton requires $4.99 socks on top of the ticket, the Saint Louis Science Center is free to enter with $15 parking, and The Magic House is $15 for everyone age 1 and up, or $3 a person from 3 to 5 p.m. for qualifying local residents.
### Q. What are some fun winter games for kids to play indoors?
A.  The ones that work are the ones with a physical outlet: obstacle courses down a hallway, indoor bowling with soft balls, scavenger hunts with written clues for readers. Save screens for the recovery hour. If the walls are closing in, the venues above exist for exactly that afternoon.

## Hot Towel, Straight Razor, Cash Only: South City Barbershops Since 1907
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-barbershops-in-south-city-st-louis-2026
The hot towel lands first, heavy and steaming, and Union Barbershop on Gravois goes quiet except for the scrape of a straight razor making its first pass along your jaw. Then the second pass. That two-pass hot-towel shave is the house ritual near Benton Park; its booking listing on Squire prices it at about $50 to $80 for 45 to 75 minutes, so call 314-328-2411 before you go.
Over on South Grand, at Wyoming Barber Shop, you wait your turn on a bench that looks like it came out of a church, under vintage photos from the day the shop opened in 1907. Every station has its own retro sink. The South Grand business district calls 3192 S. Grand the oldest barber shop in Missouri, and the man behind the first chair, Marco, has been cutting hair for 45 years and has owned the place since 2000. His daughter Reece, who grew up in the shop and learned the trade from him, works the next chair over. It’s cash only, and they’d rather you call ahead at 314-772-6675.
Here’s the move most people never make: before a stranger puts a straight razor to your throat, look the barber up. Missouri’s Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners licenses every barber in the state, and the free MOPRO license search at mopro.mo.gov shows whether a license is active. Almost nobody checks. It takes a minute.
Then the nick. It stings, the razor stops mid-stroke, and in Missouri what happens next is spelled out by rule: the barber has to stop, glove up, clean the cut and reach for antiseptic and liquid or spray styptic, without letting the bottle touch the wound. The chalky styptic pencil old-time barbers rubbed on a razor cut is banned in Missouri barbershops. The same rules want a clean towel or paper on the headrest, a fresh towel or neck strip between your skin and the cape, and every tool disinfected before it touches you. That fresh paper behind your head is the rule, not a courtesy.
Tip math worth a screenshot: 15 to 20 percent is about $4 to $5 on a $25 cut and $12 to $16 on an $80 shave.
### The old-school chairs: a shop open since 1907
Wyoming Barber Shop is the reason to walk South Grand with a few twenties in your pocket: classic cuts, clean skin fades and straight-razor shaves from a father and daughter who know most of the room by name. Make it part of a stroll through the South Grand International District, where lunch can be pho or falafel down the block. When it’s Sunday morning and the interview is Monday, head to Bevo Mill: St. Louis Barber & Beauty Salon takes walk-ins seven days a week, so the clippers are already buzzing when everyone else is at brunch.
### Hot towels and two passes of a straight razor
Union Barbershop, on Gravois near Benton Park, builds its shave the slow way: hot towels, lather, two passes with a straight razor, then a beard trim and skin products, with sharp fades in the next chair for everyone else. In Tower Grove South, Yasser’s Barbershop does the full routine, cuts, shampoo, facials and hot-towel shaves, from a barber with one of the better reputations on the south side. Bring cash; Yasser’s doesn’t take cards.
### Fades, appointments and a design-forward chair in Shaw
The cape snaps around your neck and the clippers start their low buzz at SOHA Barbershop in Southampton, opened by two longtime barbers who cut for years before going out on their own. It runs by appointment, so book instead of dropping in. In historic Shaw, Idle Hands Grooming Company is co-owned and pairs barbering with high-end styling, the kind of appointment where you talk through the cut in the mirror before the first snip. On Cherokee Street, Nisus Barbershop is the walk-in stop: sit down, listen to the clippers in the chair ahead of you, and you’re next for a fade or an everyday cut. In Dutchtown, Legacy Barber & Beauty handles clean cuts, shaves and razor lining, that crisp edge along the hairline you keep touching for days.
### A few more South City chairs worth knowing
Out toward Macklind, on the St. Louis Hills edge of Southampton, Angelo’s Barber Collective literally brands itself “south city barbers,” with sharp fades in a different pocket than the Grand and Cherokee crowd. Back on Cherokee Street, Latin Barber Shop is the long-tenured mainstay, open seven days and walk-in friendly, the place to walk in on a Sunday and walk out with the sides tight again before Monday’s meeting.
### Walk-in or appointment? Know before you go
South City shops split fairly cleanly into two camps, and knowing which is which saves you a wasted trip. The walk-in mainstays - St. Louis Barber & Beauty in Bevo Mill (open seven days), Nisus and Latin on Cherokee Street (long daily hours) - are built for “I need a cut today.” The appointment shops - SOHA in Southampton and Idle Hands in Shaw - run on a booked schedule and are worth planning around, especially for a first visit or a more involved cut-and-style. A few, like Wyoming and Yasser’s, take walk-ins but book up fast, so a quick call ahead is the move. When in doubt, check the shop’s Instagram or booking page; most post their current hours and their booking link right there.
Random, but: Alton across the river is worth a Saturday.
### What a real barbershop cut costs - and how to tip
South City barbering is still a bargain compared with a salon. A standard men’s cut at these shops generally runs in the range of a chain price to modestly above it, a beard trim or lineup adds a little, and a full hot-towel straight-razor shave - the real ritual, hot lather and all - is priced as the small luxury it is. The unwritten rule: tip like you would at a good restaurant, around fifteen to twenty percent, more if your barber squeezed you in or nailed a tricky cut. Cash is always appreciated and, at a cash-only shop like Yasser’s, required - so hit the ATM first. And the single best money-saving habit is also the best-grooming habit: rebook on a regular cadence (every two to four weeks depending on your style) so you’re never walking in shaggy and hoping for a miracle.
People are asking
### Should you get your hair cut at a barbershop or a salon?
Pick by the job you want done, not by the sign on the door. Missouri’s barber law defines a barber as anyone who will “shave the beard or cut and dress the hair” for the public, requires at least 1,000 hours of barber school or 2,000 as an apprentice before the license exam, and lists shaving and haircutting among the skills a barber must have, while the hairdresser license behind a salon chair is written around cutting, waving, permanent waving, bleaching and coloring. So book the salon for color or a perm, and the barber for a skin fade, a sharp lineup or hot lather and a straight razor along your jaw. For both in one chair, look for the state’s cross-over license, issued to anyone who meets the licensing and exam requirements for barbering and cosmetology, and ask which license your stylist holds before the cape goes on.
### Why South City is a barber town
There’s a reason the south side has this many good shops. South City is a dense grid of walkable, fiercely local neighborhoods - Tower Grove, Southampton, Bevo, Cherokee, Shaw, Dutchtown - where a corner storefront still means something and people are loyal to businesses within a few blocks of home. That’s exactly the soil a great barbershop grows in: repeat customers who come every three weeks for years, know the barber’s kids’ names, and send their brothers and coworkers. It also reflects the area’s mix. You’ll find century-old straight-razor traditions a few blocks from a design-forward grooming lounge, an immigrant-run shop that’s anchored a block for a generation, and a brand-new studio built by two barbers who trained under the old guard before striking out on their own. A barbershop isn’t just where you get a haircut here - it’s one of those third places where the neighborhood actually talks to itself.
That density is good news for you, the customer, because it means competition on craft rather than just price. When there are eight excellent shops within a couple of miles, the way a barber keeps your business is by genuinely being good - listening, remembering how you like it, and sending you out looking sharp enough that someone asks where you got it done. It’s worth trying a couple before you settle, precisely because the bar is high enough that you can afford to be picky.
Looking for a barber, stylist, or grooming spot in another part of the metro? Browse the Personal Care listings in the St Louis Near Me directory.
If you run a chair in South City, or a whole shop, list your shop with us and turn more of the new neighbors in Tower Grove and Bevo into regular customers.
### Getting the cut you actually want
The single biggest predictor of a good haircut is communication, not the shop. Bring a photo - two, ideally: one of the length and shape you want, one of a look you want to avoid. Learn a little vocabulary so you and the barber mean the same thing: a fade blends from skin up gradually, a taper is a subtler version around the edges, and “scissors on top” versus “clippers” makes a real difference in how a cut grows out. Be specific about the parts people usually get wrong - how tight you want the sides, whether you want the neckline squared or rounded (a “blocked” vs. “natural” nape), and how much to take off the top, in inches or fingers rather than a vague “not too much.” Speak up early if something’s going a direction you don’t love; a good barber would much rather adjust mid-cut than send you home unhappy. And when they nail it, tell them what you liked and book your next visit before you walk out - that’s how you become a regular who never has to re-explain your head again.
### Between visits: making a good cut last
The chair is only half of it. A sharp cut that grows out fast is worth less than a slightly simpler one you can maintain, so ask your barber what to do at home - most will happily tell you which products and routine suit your hair. For beards, a little oil or balm keeps things from getting scraggly between trims; for the neckline, a cheap trimmer and a mirror will buy you an extra week before the “forgot” stage. And if you like the straight-razor shave, know that it’s as much relaxation as grooming - the hot towels, the ritual, twenty minutes of doing nothing - which is exactly why plenty of South City regulars book one not because they need it, but because it’s the best twenty dollars of self-care in the neighborhood.
A quick word for anyone new to the ritual: a real straight-razor shave is a multi-step process - hot towels to soften the beard, a pre-shave oil, a careful pass with the grain, more lather, and a second pass - so it takes time and shouldn’t be rushed. Book it when you’re not squeezing it between errands, mention any skin sensitivity up front, and let the barber work. Done right, it’s the closest, most comfortable shave you’ll ever get, and it’s a genuinely different experience from dragging a cartridge razor across a dry jaw at seven in the morning.

The Southwest Garden neighborhood marker in south St. Louis, MO, photographed for St Louis Near Me Directory by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026.

### How to pick your barber
The best barber is the one who listens. Bring a reference photo, be clear about how short you want the sides, and ask whether a shop prefers walk-ins or appointments - some of these book up fast. And once you find someone who nails it, do what every well-groomed local does: tip well and rebook before you leave.

## Failed St. Louis Emissions? Your Report Names 10 Shops
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-a-trustworthy-auto-repair-shop-in-st-louis-2026
You nodded.
The inspector at the emissions station handed you the printout, the check-engine light still glowing amber on the dash, and said the car failed. You nodded like you knew what any of it meant. Then you folded the paper into the glove box, drove to the first shop with an open bay, and signed the work order without reading past the total. The lobby smelled like burnt coffee and tire rubber, and an air gun screamed behind the door.
Most of us have done some version of that. Here’s what almost nobody unfolds. When a car fails the Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program test, the emissions check for vehicles registered in the St. Louis area, the station gives you a repair facility performance report that lists the ten nearest Missouri Recognized Repair Stations. Those are shops with a Missouri-recognized repair technician: employed full time, certified by the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence in the A6, A8 and L1 areas, and approved by the state program. It matters for your wallet too. Labor costs only count toward a cost-based waiver if a Missouri Recognized Repair Technician did the work. The state says plainly the list is not a recommendation, and choosing a shop is still your call. But it is a short list of trained hands, printed for you, sitting in your glove box.
If your car fails the St. Louis emissions test, the printout already names the ten nearest Missouri Recognized Repair Stations. Unfold it before you call anyone.
### How do I find a trustworthy auto repair shop in St. Louis?
Find one before you need one. Ask a neighbor which shop they’ve used for years, then take it a small, non-urgent job. Ask for a written estimate and your old parts back, and watch whether they call before going past the estimate. For emissions work, start with the recognized repair shops on your failed-test report. Two places to start: St. Louis Auto & Truck Repair on Delmar and EcoTECH Import Auto Service on Watson Road.
And read the work order before you sign it. Under Missouri law, section 430.020, a shop that furnishes labor or material on your vehicle and gets a written memorandum of the work signed by the owner has a lien, and that lien is only for the work written on the order you sign: the amount of work or material ordered or stated in that memorandum. A vague order leaves the job wide open. A clear one is the line the shop agreed to, and it’s the first thing you’ll want in your hand if the bill comes back bigger than the words on the page. If the shop won’t make it right, the Missouri Attorney General takes consumer complaints; the Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222.
The small-job test works because it moves the vetting to a calm, ordinary afternoon instead of the morning your car dies on the shoulder with the hazards ticking and trucks shaking the car as they pass. When the car is already broken, you take the first place that answers the phone. When it isn’t, you get to be picky.
### Two St. Louis shops worth a first visit
Start with these and run your own small-job test. St. Louis Auto & Truck Repair, at 2701 Delmar Blvd, is listed as an AAA Approved Auto Repair Facility, and AAA members receive a 10% labor and 10% parts discount on repairs there, up to a cap. If you drive an import, EcoTECH Import Auto Service at 8512 Watson Road describes itself as an independent repair facility in St. Louis, minutes from downtown Webster Groves, and lists Subaru, Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Volkswagen, Audi, BMW and Porsche among its specialties. Call ahead to confirm hours and that they work on your make before you drop the keys.
### The signs of a good mechanic show up before the repair
The signs of a good mechanic are mostly about how they talk to you, not how the shop looks. A good one writes the work order in words you can read back to them. They tell you what’s urgent and what can wait, and they say it without the tone that makes you feel stupid for asking. They’ll walk you into the bay, or hold up the part at the counter, and show you the crack in the belt or the brake pad worn down to the metal. You can feel the difference in your shoulders: you walk out of a good shop looser than you walked in.
The best car mechanic for you is also the one who calls before going past the estimate. That phone call is the shop respecting the paper you both signed. If the work order says brakes and the bill says brakes plus a list of “while we were in there” extras nobody approved, the shop skipped the call, and that tells you everything about the next visit.
Here’s the habit that makes all of this easier. Before you sign, read the work order out loud at the counter, slowly, as if you’re double-checking a delivery address. It feels awkward for about three seconds. Then it changes the whole conversation, because the person behind the counter now knows you read what you sign.
### Red flags of a bad mechanic, and how to tell if one is lying
You can usually hear the first red flag before you see the bay. The phone rings, the voice is in a hurry, and the price is a shrug. The red flags of a bad mechanic sound a lot alike. “We can’t give you a price until we tear into it,” with no offer to call you once they know. A rush to fix everything today, when only one item is truly about safety. A bill with one lump number and no breakdown of parts and labor. A shrug when you ask to see or keep the old parts. And a work order you’re asked to sign that is mostly blank.
That last one matters more in Missouri than most people realize, because the signed memorandum is what the shop’s lien rests on. A blank or vague work order leaves the scope of the job wide open after you’ve already signed it.
How do you tell if a mechanic is lying? You rarely catch it in the moment, so build the proof in. Ask to see the worn part before you approve the work, and ask for the old part back afterward. Get the diagnosis in writing, then take that paper to a second shop for anything expensive. Two honest shops usually describe the same problem in the same plain words, even if their prices differ. A story that changes every time you ask a question is your answer.
For more ways to build a short list, this guide to finding top-rated auto repair near you walks through where to look. Cross-check what neighbors say against the shop’s recent reviews, and pay attention to how the owner answers the angry ones. A calm, specific reply to a complaint tells you more than a wall of five-star ratings.
### What not to say to your mechanic
Three phrases cost people money at the counter. “Just do whatever it needs” turns a work order into a blank check. “I don’t really know anything about cars” invites a bigger list. And “I need it today no matter what” takes away your time to get a second opinion.
Say these instead. “Please write down exactly what you’re doing and the price before you start.” “Call me before you go past that number.” “Which of these is about safety, and which can wait a month?” “Can I see the old part?” None of that is rude. A good shop hears it and relaxes, because it means you’ll be easy to work with when the job gets complicated.
### Dealer or independent shop?
Dealers carry factory tools and training that matter for recalls, warranty claims and newer cars packed with electronics. Good independents usually win on price and on the simple pleasure of a mechanic who remembers your car. And using an independent for routine work does not cost you your warranty: under the federal Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, no warrantor of a consumer product may condition its warranty on your using a brand-name article or service unless that article or service is provided free under the warranty. Plenty of St. Louis drivers split it that way: the dealer for recall and warranty work, a trusted independent for everything else.
Keep every invoice in one folder in the glove box. The paper trail protects your resale value, settles warranty arguments, and lets the next mechanic see what the last one did.
Hard left turn: if the car is stuck in the bay for the afternoon, here is where to eat on South Grand while you wait.
### What to do if a mechanic is scamming you
Stay calm and get paper. Ask for an itemized invoice, and compare it line by line with the work order you signed. If the bill includes work you never approved, say so in writing and keep a copy. Pay attention to what you signed, because the shop’s lien is tied to the work ordered or stated in that memorandum.
If talking it through goes nowhere, the Missouri Attorney General takes consumer complaints. The office asks you to send copies of important documents such as contracts, invoices, warranties and canceled checks, and not to send originals. For questions about filing, call the Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-392-8222. If real money or damage is involved, a private attorney can tell you what your rights are; the Attorney General’s office mediates complaints but does not act as your lawyer.
And if a mechanic ruins your car, the same rules apply, only faster: photograph the damage before you drive away, ask the shop in writing what it will do to fix it, get a second shop’s written opinion on what went wrong, and keep every receipt. The cleaner your paper trail, the shorter the argument.
### Keep the good one
Once you find an honest shop, stay. Bring it the oil changes and the tire rotations, not just the emergencies, and the shop starts to know your car the way a family doctor knows your blood pressure. Here is how often to get an oil change in St. Louis and why the schedule matters. The reward is the day something really breaks, when you call a number you already know and hear a voice that already knows you.
Body work is a different trade from mechanical repair, with a different relationship to your insurer. If the damage is cosmetic or structural, what an auto body estimate actually means is the guide to read instead.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How to find the best car mechanic?
A.  Ask neighbors which shop they’ve trusted for years, then test it with a small, non-urgent job. Watch whether the shop writes a clear work order, explains it plainly, calls before going past the estimate, and shows you the worn part. If your car failed the St. Louis emissions test, the report lists the ten nearest Missouri Recognized Repair Stations to start from.
### Q. What are the signs of a good mechanic?
A.  A good mechanic writes the work order in plain words, separates safety repairs from things that can wait, shows you the old part, and calls before adding work. You leave feeling informed, not pressured.
### Q. What are the red flags of a bad mechanic?
A.  No price in writing, pressure to fix everything today, a lump-sum bill with no parts and labor breakdown, refusing to show or return old parts, and asking you to sign a mostly blank work order.
### Q. How to tell if a mechanic is lying?
A.  Ask to see the worn part, ask for the old part back, and take the written diagnosis to a second shop for anything expensive. Honest shops describe the same problem the same way; a story that keeps changing is the tell.
### Q. Can a mechanic not let you leave?
A.  Missouri law, section 430.020, gives a shop that furnishes labor or material on your vehicle and has a written memorandum of the work signed by the owner a lien for the amount ordered or stated in that memorandum. Read the work order before you sign it, and if a dispute starts, get legal advice rather than arguing at the counter.
### Q. What to do if a mechanic is scamming you?
A.  Get an itemized invoice, compare it to the signed work order, and put your objection in writing. If that fails, file a complaint with the Missouri Attorney General; for questions, the Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222. Send copies of your documents, not originals.
### Q. What not to say to your mechanic?
A.  Skip “just do whatever it needs” and “I need it today no matter what.” Say “write down the work and price before you start” and “call me before you go past that number.”
### Q. What happens if a mechanic ruins your car?
A.  Photograph the damage before you leave, ask the shop in writing how it will fix it, and get a second shop’s written opinion. Keep every receipt. If the shop won’t make it right, the Missouri Attorney General’s consumer complaint process or a private attorney is the next step.
### Q. Will using an independent shop void my car’s warranty?
A.  No. Under the federal Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, a warrantor may not condition its warranty on your using a brand-name service unless that service is provided free under the warranty, so routine work at an independent shop does not void it.

## The Best Yoga Studios in St. Louis: A Guide for Every Style and Budget
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-yoga-studios-in-st-louis-2026-a-guide-for-every-style-and-budget
Maybe you’ve been meaning to start. Maybe your back has been begging you to. Or maybe you’ve practiced for years and just moved to a new corner of the metro and need to find your people again. Whatever brought you here, the question is the same: which studio is right for me?
St. Louis has an unusually rich yoga scene — donation-based community spaces, sweaty power studios, and decades-old institutions among them. Here’s a guide to some of the best, by what you’re looking for.
### Community-first and donation-based
If cost or intimidation has kept you off the mat, start here. Brick City Yoga in Benton Park West keeps classes accessible with a flat low price and donates monthly revenue to local nonprofits. The Collective STL in Old North is a donation-based, Black-owned nonprofit studio — pay what you can — with welcoming community classes. And the Solar Yoga Center, teaching traditional Hatha since the late 1960s, is the oldest yoga center in the city, run by volunteer instructors.
### Bring the heat: hot and power yoga
Like to sweat? Namaste Yoga Studio in Kirkwood offers approachable hot, warm, and non-heated classes and a respected teacher-training program. Pure Hot Yoga on Clayton Road (at the Clayton/Richmond Heights edge) is a long-running hot-yoga mainstay, and FLY Yoga Studio in Midtown runs alignment-based classes in a modern, infrared-heated space.
### Specialty practices and deeper study
For something specific: Joy of Yoga in Brentwood blends yoga with Ayurveda, meditation, and energy work, plus teacher training and retreats. Urban Breath Yoga in Maplewood is known for its prenatal offerings and a scholarship program that keeps the practice within reach — an easy pairing with a wander through Maplewood’s food scene. And Shanti Yoga + Wellness (Tower Grove and Maplewood) focuses on restorative, nervous-system-calming practice for life’s transitions.
### Metro East options
Illinois practitioners have good choices too: Vive Yoga Studio in Edwardsville offers Vinyasa, Power, Sculpt, and Yin in a welcoming all-levels space, Go Yoga Express (Belleville/Swansea and Edwardsville) adds hot yoga, hot Pilates, and an infrared sauna, and Yoga on West Main in Belleville is a boutique studio with small-group power, barre fusion, and restorative classes.
### More studios worth knowing (and a few more styles)
The list above leans south-city, community, and Metro East — so here are a few that widen the map and the menu of styles. In West County and St. Charles County, YogaSix (Town & Country and the Streets of St. Charles) offers six clearly-labeled class types — hot, power, sculpt-and-flow, restorative, slow, and TRX-style — which makes it easy to know exactly what you’re walking into, and it fills the western-suburb gap the rest of this list leaves open. Out in Lake Saint Louis, Studio Aire specializes in aerial yoga (plus aerial hoop and pole) — a genuinely different practice using suspended silks, great for anyone bored of the mat. On the south side, Yoga St. Louis in Lindenwood Park has taught Iyengar yoga — a precise, prop-supported, alignment-first method — since 1984, which makes it one of the best choices in the metro for beginners, older students, or anyone working around an injury. And on Cherokee Street, Marbles Yoga Studio runs traditional, progressive Hatha classes (Levels I through IV) in a walkable arts-district setting.
### Which style is right for you?
“Yoga” covers a lot of very different rooms, so it helps to know the vocabulary before you book. Hatha is slower and foundational — great for beginners. Vinyasa (or “flow”) links movement to breath at a steadier pace. Power yoga is the athletic, strength-building end. Hot yoga (including the fixed Bikram sequence) runs the room to 95–105°F for a deep sweat and looser muscles — energizing for some, too much for others, so hydrate and go in rested. Iyengar is precise and prop-supported, ideal for alignment and injuries. Restorative and yin are slow, deeply relaxing, and nervous-system-calming. And aerial uses a hammock to take pressure off the joints while you build strength. If you’re not sure, start with a Hatha, gentle, or explicitly “all-levels” class — you can always chase the heat or the challenge once you know the basics.
### Yoga on any budget: from free to premium
One of the best things about St. Louis’s scene is that cost is rarely a real barrier. At the free-to-low end, The Collective STL in Old North is fully donation-based (pay what you can), Brick City Yoga keeps a low flat rate and gives back to nonprofits, and the volunteer-run Solar Yoga Center charges only minimal fees. In the middle, most independent studios sell class packs or monthly memberships, and nearly all offer an intro deal or a free first class — the single best way to sample a room before committing. At the premium end, chain and boutique studios (YogaSix, hot studios, specialty aerial) cost more but bundle amenities, standardized classes, and lots of scheduling options. The move for a newcomer: ride the intro offers. You can practice at a different studio every week for a month on first-timer deals, figure out which style and vibe fit you, and only then pay for a membership where you know you’ll actually show up.
### Your first class: what to expect (and how not to feel lost)
The hardest part of yoga is walking in the first time, so take the pressure off. Book a beginner or all-levels class, and message the studio ahead to say you’re new — every place on this list is used to it and will look out for you. Arrive ten minutes early to meet the teacher, mention any injuries, and get set up. Bring a mat if you have one (most studios rent or lend them), wear comfortable clothes you can move in, and skip a big meal beforehand — especially for a hot class, where you’ll also want water and to expect to sweat. Once you’re in the room, the only real rule is to listen to your own body: rest in child’s pose whenever you need to, ignore what anyone else is doing, and know that “I can’t touch my toes” is a reason to start yoga, not a reason to skip it. Nobody is judging the new person; they were all new once.
Random, but: Kirkwood’s whole dinner lineup lives right here.
### Why it’s worth starting
Beyond the flexibility everyone associates with it, a regular practice tends to deliver the things people actually stick around for: less back and neck pain from desk life, real gains in strength and balance, and — the one most students mention first — a genuine drop in stress. The breathing and the deliberate slowness do something a treadmill doesn’t, which is why so many people who try it for their body stay for their head. In a busy metro, a studio also becomes a rare hour with your phone in a cubby and nowhere to be but on your mat. You don’t have to be flexible, calm, or “a yoga person” to begin — those are results, not prerequisites. Pick a welcoming room from this guide, take the free first class, and let the rest follow. And if the first studio isn’t quite right — too hot, too fast, too far — that’s useful information, not a failure. With this many distinct rooms, styles, and price points across the metro, the practice that finally clicks is almost always just one more intro class away.
### A quick map by area
Practicing close to home makes you far more likely to keep going, so here’s the shorthand by region. South city: Brick City (Benton Park West), Marbles (Cherokee St), Shanti (Tower Grove), Yoga St. Louis/Iyengar (Lindenwood Park). North side: The Collective STL (Old North). Central corridor: Solar Yoga Center (DeBaliviere/Skinker), FLY (Midtown), Pure Hot Yoga (Clayton Road). Inner-ring suburbs: Urban Breath and Shanti (Maplewood), Namaste (Kirkwood), Joy of Yoga (Brentwood). West County / St. Charles County: YogaSix (Town & Country and St. Charles), Studio Aire (Lake Saint Louis, aerial). Metro East (Illinois): Vive (Edwardsville), Go Yoga Express (Swansea and Edwardsville), Yoga on West Main (Belleville). Whatever corner of the metro you’re in, there’s a welcoming mat within a short drive — and picking the studio closest to your home or commute is the single most reliable predictor of whether you’ll actually keep the habit past week three.
### Studios for specific needs
If you’re looking for something particular, the metro has it. For prenatal yoga, Urban Breath Yoga in Maplewood is well known for its pregnancy offerings and prenatal teacher training. For a calming, trauma-informed or restorative practice — helpful during grief, burnout, or big life transitions — The Collective STL and Shanti Yoga + Wellness both build classes around gentleness and the nervous system. For beginners, seniors, or anyone rehabbing an injury, the prop-supported precision of Iyengar at Yoga St. Louis is hard to beat, and the volunteer-run Solar Yoga Center’s traditional Hatha is famously unintimidating. And for accessibility on a tight budget, the donation-based and give-back studios (The Collective, Brick City) make sure cost is never the reason someone can’t practice. Whatever you’re carrying onto the mat, there’s a room in St. Louis built for it.
### How to choose your studio
The best studio is the one you’ll actually return to. If you’re new, look for a beginner or all-levels class and arrive ten minutes early to meet the teacher. Most studios offer an intro deal or a free first class, so try two or three before you commit — the right room, temperature, and teaching style make all the difference.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can I find affordable or donation-based yoga in St. Louis?

### Q. Which St. Louis studios offer hot yoga?

### Q. I'm a total beginner, where should I start?
A.  Look for a class labeled “beginner” or “all levels,” arrive early to meet the instructor, and take advantage of intro deals to try a few studios. Community-focused spots like Brick City and The Collective are especially welcoming.
### Q. What’s the difference between the main styles of yoga?
A.  Hatha is slow and foundational (great for beginners); vinyasa or “flow” links movement to breath; power yoga is athletic and strength-building; hot yoga (including Bikram) heats the room to 95–105°F; Iyengar is precise and prop-supported for alignment and injuries; restorative and yin are slow and deeply relaxing; and aerial uses a suspended hammock. If unsure, start with a Hatha, gentle, or all-levels class.
### Q. Where can I find hot, aerial, or Iyengar yoga in St. Louis?
A.  For hot yoga, try Namaste (Kirkwood), Pure Hot Yoga (Clayton Road), FLY (Midtown), or Go Yoga Express (Metro East). For aerial, Studio Aire in Lake Saint Louis specializes in suspended silks. For precise, alignment-focused Iyengar, Yoga St. Louis in Lindenwood Park has taught it since 1984 — a strong pick for beginners or anyone working around an injury.
### Q. What should I bring to my first yoga class?
A.  Comfortable clothes you can move in, a water bottle (especially for hot classes), and a mat if you own one — most studios rent or lend them. Skip a heavy meal beforehand, arrive about ten minutes early to meet the teacher and mention any injuries, and know you can rest in child’s pose anytime. You do not need to be flexible or experienced to start.
### Q. Which yoga class is best for beginners?
A.  Look for anything labeled gentle, basics, slow flow, restorative or level one. Those are built to be taught, meaning the instructor names each pose, offers a modification and does not assume you already know the sequence. Hatha classes move at a pace that lets you check your alignment. Avoid a hot power class as your first ever visit, not because it is beyond you but because heat plus unfamiliar poses makes it hard to tell effort from strain. Call the studio and say it is your first class — they will point you to the right one on the schedule.
### Q. What yoga should a beginner start with?
A.  Start with a style that prioritizes alignment over speed. Hatha and gentle or basics classes teach the shapes, Iyengar goes deep on precision and uses props heavily, and restorative teaches you to hold and breathe. Any of the three gives you a vocabulary you can carry into a faster vinyasa class later. The style matters less than the teacher and the room, so try two or three before you commit to a membership anywhere.
### Q. Where can I find free yoga classes in St. Louis?
A.  Several channels run free or donation-based sessions across the metro: public library branches, parks and recreation departments, community centers, some employers and health systems, and studios that hold a weekly community class on a pay-what-you-can basis. Outdoor series pop up seasonally in warm months. Schedules change constantly and spots fill, so check the hosting organization’s own calendar and register ahead rather than showing up cold.
### Q. What is the best yoga for older beginners?
A.  Chair yoga, gentle, restorative and Iyengar are the usual starting points, and all four are widely taught. Chair and gentle remove the floor-to-standing transitions that are the actual barrier for many people, while Iyengar uses blocks, straps and bolsters so a pose meets you where your body is. Tell the instructor before class about joints, balance, blood pressure or any recent surgery, and clear a new activity with your clinician first.
### Q. Is 20 minutes of yoga a day enough exercise?
A.  It is enough to build a habit and to notice real changes in mobility, balance and how you carry tension, which is more than most people get from an occasional long class. Whether it is enough on its own depends on what you are after: general movement guidance points to a mix of aerobic work and strength training across the week, and a gentle 20-minute practice does not fully cover either. Treat it as a foundation and add walking or something that raises your heart rate.

## A Red Bulb, a Bookcase, a $12 Cocktail: St. Louis Speakeasies
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-s-best-craft-cocktail-bars-and-speakeasies-2026
“Just look for the red light.”
That’s the whole set of directions a friend gives you for None of the Above, and it turns out to be enough. An unmarked, street-level door at City Foundry. One industrial-style red light burning over it. Then a graffiti-lined tunnel, a ramp, a flight of stairs, and a windowless room where the cold glass in your hand is the only clock you trust. Gerard Craft, whose Niche Food Group is behind the place, put the whole idea plainly: “We want people to feel transported a little bit.”
### What are the best craft cocktail bars and speakeasies in St. Louis?
For the drink itself, start at Planter’s House at Chouteau and Mississippi, home of the In A Pickle cocktail and a 350-plus spirits list. For the hunt, go to None of the Above behind a red-lit door at City Foundry, Mother May I behind a bookcase on South Grand, and Bemiston Cocktail & Social Club down a long hallway in Clayton. Thaxton Speakeasy keeps an underground lounge going downtown.
Here’s the part the red light leaves out. Missouri law shuts the taps at 1:30 a.m. A separate section of state law, section 311.176, carries St. Louis City in its own title: a bar inside the city’s convention trade area can apply for a special permit to stay open until 3:00 a.m., and it pays an additional fee of three hundred dollars a year for the privilege. That’s why plenty of St. Louisans call them “3 o’clock bars,” and it’s why the city’s excise office keeps a table of wards with “No New 3am Closing Permits.” The cocktail rooms on this list are not 3 o’clock bars. They wind down well before that, so the St. Louis way to do this night is backwards from what you’d guess.
The best cocktail in St. Louis is usually poured before ten. The 3 a.m. bars didn’t make a better drink. They bought a permit.
So plan it like a local. Planter’s House pours until 11 p.m. on its latest nights, Bemiston until midnight, and Mother May I until 1 a.m. Get to your first door by seven, while there’s still a stool at the bar and the bartender has time to talk you through the menu. Bemiston also books private events, so a glance at its Facebook or Instagram before a big night saves you a walk down an empty hallway. Save the 3 o’clock bar for the last stop, not the main event.
### The bookcase on South Grand
Walk into Monstera Mezcaleria, bartender Fricker’s agave spirit and natural wine bar, and the room upstairs is bright and airy. The trick is a door made to look like a bookcase. Behind it, stairs drop into Mother May I at 3194 S. Grand, a basement lit in cool blue that St. Louis Magazine called a “cocktail dive.” The menu features cocktails for $12 and under, which is the first thing you’ll say out loud to whoever came with you.
Cheap doesn’t mean lazy. The Drink Dirty martini takes several days to prepare: sous vide olive-washed Hayman’s Gin, vermouth, and a house brine made with confit olives. You taste the olive before the gin, salty and round, and the glass sweats on the bar. The snacks come off a roller grill like a gas station at midnight: hot dogs, taquitos, egg rolls, cheddar popcorn, cheese puffs, Twinkies, and pork rinds tossed in hot sauce. It’s the only room on this list where your fingers smell like cheese dust and your drink was built over days.
Fricker also splits his time with Natasha Bahrami running the restaurant side of The Gin Room, so the same stretch of South Grand hands you two very different nights: a gin-obsessed bar room on one side, a blue-lit basement under a bookcase on the other. Mother May I stays open until 1 a.m. on its two latest nights, which makes it the closest thing to a late finish among the rooms here.
### Down the hallway in Clayton
Bemiston Cocktail & Social Club, at 14 S. Bemiston, is the one you walk past twice. There’s a solid wooden door at the end of a long hallway, marked only with three small windows, the letter “B,” and a single red lightbulb hanging above it. Push through and the street noise drops away into exposed brick, wood paneling and strings of bare lightbulbs. It’s a 60-seat room that shares a kitchen with Louie’s Wine Dive next door, so the food is real food.
Order the Cafe Jalisco and the cold brew reaches your nose before the glass reaches the bar: house vanilla-infused Casamigos Reposado, cold brew and orange bitters. The Paper Crane is the brighter pick, blood orange-infused Toki Japanese whiskey with Amaro Nonino, yuzu liquor and citrus, tart enough to make you sit up.
### Where the city’s cocktail habit got serious
Sit at the bar at Planter’s House and the first thing you hear is the shaker, a hard rattle cutting under the dinner noise. The place calls itself an award winning, seasonal bar and restaurant, and its own site leads with three drinks it calls world famous: In A Pickle, Industry Sour and Purgatory. The back bar is the show. The 350-plus spirits list features 39 Planter’s House exclusive bourbons, ryes and rums, so the bottle you point at may not exist on any other shelf in town. Let the bartender talk you through one of those exclusives and pour you a taste of something you can’t get across town.
This is also the clearest example of the early-night rule. On its latest nights, Planter’s House runs 4 p.m. to 11 p.m., with the kitchen closing at 10. Show up at nine expecting to settle in for the long haul and you’ll be on your last round before you’ve warmed up.
If you’re new to rooms like this, here’s the quick test. Order one classic you already know, an old fashioned or a daiquiri, and pay attention to the first sip. At a craft bar the juice was squeezed that day, the syrup was made in-house, and the ice is big and clear, so the drink stays cold and sharp instead of going watery by the third sip. The same name at a chain tastes like sugar and melt. That gap is what you’re paying a few extra dollars for: somebody who obsesses over the details so you don’t have to, and who will happily tell you why if you ask.
### The tunnel under City Foundry
None of the Above sits within the old underground tunnels at City Foundry, 3730 Foundry Way. The tunnels turned up during construction, when crews tried to drain water and found it went far deeper than anyone expected. The graffiti on the tunnel walls is original street art recovered when work on City Foundry began. Niche Food Group bar manager Fionna Gemzon curates a list built on luxury spirits and technique-driven cocktails, with a short run of hors d’oeuvres. Craft described the point of the windowless room plainly: you could be sitting there in the middle of the day, but it could also be nighttime.
Downtown, Thaxton Speakeasy describes itself as a downtown, underground cocktail lounge in the lower level of an old building. It’s the room to pick when you want the speakeasy idea without the food-hall crowd on the way in.
### Dress code, door etiquette and what not to order
The dress code for a speakeasy in St. Louis is mostly about the room, not a rulebook. Wear what you’d wear to a good dinner. These rooms are dark and small, and a hoodie under a red bulb just feels like the wrong costume. If a bar does post a code, it’s on its own site or social page, so check there before a big night.
Inside, the etiquette is the hush. Keep the group small, keep your voice under the music, and keep the phone flash off; the guy two seats down is on a first date. Tip like the drink took work, because at Mother May I it literally took days.
As for drinks not to order at a bar like this: skip the vodka soda and anything you’d order from a sour-mix gun. Instead, give the bartender two things, a spirit and a mood. “Gin, something salty.” “Whiskey, not sweet.” Then let them build to it. At Planter’s House, ask for one of the exclusive bottles. At Mother May I, the dirty martini is the order. At Bemiston, the Paper Crane.
### A cocktail night that fits the clock
Because these rooms close early, plan the night like a short walk instead of a marathon. On South Grand, The Gin Room and the bookcase at Monstera sit on the same stretch, and you can finish downstairs at Mother May I. In Clayton, Bemiston covers the whole evening, with dinner from the kitchen next door. If you want a dance floor afterward, that’s when the late rooms make sense, and our guide to St. Louis’s best dance clubs picks up where the cocktails stop. For dinner first on the same street, see our South Grand dining stretch.
Whatever the route, line up a rideshare or a sober driver before the first drink. The tunnel, the hallway and the bookcase are all easier to find than a parking spot at midnight.
Hard left turn: the car you leave parked outside tonight has its own exam coming. Here is what fails a Missouri car inspection.
### Which room for which night
For a date, pick a door you find together: the bookcase at Monstera or the red bulb at the end of Bemiston’s hallway. For a special dinner with serious drinks, Planter’s House. For the full disappear-for-an-evening effect, the tunnel at None of the Above. For a cheap round that still tastes like somebody cared, Mother May I.

Hidden is charming at the door and costly online, because the couple asking their phone where to go tonight should hear your name. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the dress code for a speakeasy?
A.  In St. Louis, dress like you’re going to a good dinner and you’ll fit any of these rooms. They’re small and dim, so the vibe matters more than a rule. If a bar sets a formal code, it posts it on its own site or social page.
### Q. What was the worst kept secret of Prohibition?
A.  The speakeasy itself. The whole neighborhood knew where the hidden bar was; the secret was a wink, not a wall. St. Louis keeps the wink alive with a bookcase door at Mother May I, a red light over an unmarked door at None of the Above, and a hallway door marked with a single “B” at Bemiston.
### Q. What drinks are not to order at a bar?
A.  At a craft cocktail bar, skip the vodka soda and anything that comes out of a sour-mix gun. Name a spirit and a mood instead and let the bartender build it. Order the house signature first: the In A Pickle at Planter’s House or the Drink Dirty martini at Mother May I.
### Q. What are some good date ideas around St. Louis?
A.  Find a hidden bar together. Walk through the bookcase at Monstera Mezcaleria into Mother May I, or follow the long hallway to the red bulb at Bemiston in Clayton, where the kitchen next door handles dinner. Start early, because these rooms close well before 3 a.m.
### Q. What is the #1 cocktail bar in the world?
A.  On the current World’s 50 Best Bars list, No. 1 is Bar Leone in Hong Kong. Closer to home, Planter’s House says its In A Pickle is world famous, and it costs you a drive, not a flight.
### Q. Why do some St. Louis bars stay open until 3 a.m.?
A.  Missouri law stops liquor sales at 1:30 a.m. Under section 311.176, a bar in St. Louis City’s convention trade area can apply for a special permit to stay open until 3:00 a.m. and pays an additional fee of three hundred dollars a year. Some city wards refuse new 3 a.m. permits.

## America's First Wine Region Is a Day Trip From St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-day-trips-from-st-louis-2026-15-escapes-within-two-hours
Napa lost this one. You’re on a winery patio in Augusta, Missouri, and the wind comes up the bluff carrying the smell of warm dirt from between the vine rows. A glass sweats in your hand. Somebody’s kid is chasing a dog across the grass, and the river bottoms run flat and green to the tree line. It feels like any easy afternoon in the country. Augusta is also the place that beat California.
Seven California districts and one in Oregon had filed applications with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. The honor went to the 15 square mile area surrounding Augusta, on June 20, 1980, making it the first American Viticultural Area in the United States.
Now the part you can repeat at a dinner table. In the 1880s an aphid-like parasite was killing France’s prized vineyards, and hundreds of thousands of rootstocks were gathered from Missouri vineyards and shipped to France. Missouri was credited with helping to save the French wine industry.
Most of us have never heard that. We say Napa and picture the real thing a plane ticket away, while the actual first sits 45 minutes west of the city. That is the trick of a day trip from St. Louis. The good stuff isn’t far. It’s just unannounced. Here is the order to drive it in, nearest first, with the clock starting in St. Louis.
Cahokia Mounds, 8 miles. Up a stairway to the top of a 100-foot mound, the wind comes flat across the bottomland, and a reconstructed circle of posts nearby lines up with the sunrise to mark the season. The site puts it eight miles from downtown St. Louis. There is no admission or parking fee, the grounds stay open from dawn until dusk, and the lobby, with restrooms and the gift shop, opens Wednesday through Sunday from 9:00 am till 3:00 pm.
Augusta, 45 minutes west. Gravel under the tires, a glass in your hand by noon, live music on the weekends. Visit Augusta calls it “just 45 minutes” from St. Louis. Augusta Winery is open daily 11am-5pm at 5601 High St, and the live weekend music runs from April through October.
Meramec State Park and Fisher Cave, about an hour. The cave air hits your face first, then the dark beyond the beam of a hand-held light, then a bear’s claw mark on the wall and a calcite column over 30 feet tall. Missouri’s tourism division calls the park “just an hour from St. Louis.” Tours cost $14 for adults, $12 for teens, $10 for kids 6 to 12 and nothing for kids under 6, before tax.
Ste. Genevieve, 1 hour. Walls of upright logs, still standing: the Green Tree Tavern here is Missouri’s oldest verified building, dated to 1790 by its tree rings. The town’s visitor site calls it a short 1 hour drive from St. Louis. Start at the Welcome Center at 66 S Main St, where admission is free and rangers give free guided tours.
Kimmswick, about 35 minutes south. Brick underfoot, then a slice of apple pie stacked over a dozen layers high at the Blue Owl. It is open from 10 AM to 3 PM, so the pie stop comes before the afternoon, not after.
Hannibal, 100 miles north. Paint Tom Sawyer’s famous fence yourself and board a raft with Huck and Jim in the exhibits. At the Mark Twain Boyhood Home & Museum, one two-day ticket covers all eight buildings: $20 for adults, $15 for seniors and veterans, $6 for students 6 to 17, and free for kids 5 and under. Summer hours run 9:00 am to 5:00 pm, winter hours 10:00 am to 4:00 pm. Leave early.
Elephant Rocks State Park is where you get to climb. Giant granite boulders stand end to end, and underfoot is St. Louis history: from 1880 to 1900, millions of paving blocks for the St. Louis levee and downtown streets came from the quarry just outside the park, each roughly the size of a shoebox. Entry is free, the park is open year-round, and dogs stay on a leash. I could not find an official drive time from St. Louis, so put 7406 Highway 21 in your map app first.
### What are the best day trips from St. Louis within two hours?
Ste. Genevieve, a short one-hour drive from St. Louis, was the first permanent European settlement in Missouri, established by 1750 by French Canadian settlers. Hermann is a picturebook village of red brick buildings and rolling vineyards in the Missouri River Valley. Augusta holds the first American Viticultural Area, named in 1980. And Hannibal, 100 miles north of St. Louis on the Mississippi, is the boyhood home of Mark Twain.
### Wine country, because it came first
Start with Augusta, because almost nobody you know realizes what they are looking at there. Fifteen square miles won that fight against California and Oregon. Tell that to the friend who just got back from Napa, then hand them the keys and let them taste the argument for themselves. Go on a weekday if you can, when the patios are quiet enough to hear the gravel crunch under the next car pulling in. Mount Pleasant Estates in Augusta offers tours of its historic wine cellar.
Hermann has its own claim. By the late 19th century Stone Hill Winery there had grown to become the second largest winery in the country, and its arched cellars still give tours. Hermann’s own visitor bureau calls it a picturebook village where red brick buildings and rolling vineyards welcome you to Missouri Wine Country, and on a fall afternoon the description is not oversold. If you want a lunch stop with a downtown to walk off the meal, our full guide to things to do in Washington, MO covers it street by street.
### Eight miles from downtown, a city with a sun calendar
Fill your bottle at the fountain by the Monks Mound parking lot, grab a paper map from the holder, and start climbing. Your calves notice before you’re halfway up. At the top the wind comes across the flat bottomland with nothing to stop it, and you are standing on a 100-foot mound that is the largest earthwork in North America. Then go find Woodhenge, a circle of posts around a large central post, set so the sunrise lines up with it to mark the season and time of year.
Cahokia Mounds World Heritage and State Historic Site describes itself as the largest pre-Columbian site north of Mexico. At its peak, around 1100, this metropolis stretched over 4,000 acres, encompassed about 120 earthen mounds, and hosted a population of nearly 20,000 individuals, larger than London at that time. Look down at the grass and try to picture it full of people, cooking smoke, voices. The site was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, and the State of Illinois now protects roughly 2,200 acres of the central portion. Bring water. Bring the kid who says history is boring. Ask them to count the mounds from the top.
### The rocks that paved the St. Louis levee
Put your palm flat on the stone at Elephant Rocks State Park on a sunny afternoon and it gives back the day’s heat. Missouri State Parks says the rocks were formed from 1.5-billion-year-old granite, giant boulders that stand end-to-end like a train of circus elephants. The park says they fascinate children who love to climb on and between the boulders, which is a polite way of describing the sound of sneakers slapping warm stone and a parent saying “not that high.” The Braille Trail there was especially designed for people with visual and physical disabilities, so a grandparent with a cane can come along too.
Now the St. Louis part. Just outside the park is the oldest recorded commercial granite quarry in the state, opened in 1869. It furnished facing stone for the Eads Bridge piers on the St. Louis levee, and from 1880 to 1900 millions of paving blocks for the levee and downtown streets came from it. Each block was roughly the size of a shoebox and sold for about 8 cents. A good block maker turning out 50 a day earned $4, a pretty good wage for a very hard day’s work.
Meramec State Park is the one for the kid who wants something a little spooky. The state describes how the Meramec River flows by majestic bluffs, wooded areas and a dramatic cave entrance, with more than 13 miles of hiking trails. The headliner is Fisher Cave, toured with hand-held lights. Inside are well-preserved bear claw marks, cave wildlife and calcite columns over 30 feet tall. Cool air on your face at the entrance. Dark beyond your beam. A bear’s claw mark, right there on the wall.
And when you only have half a day, Castlewood State Park is the history lesson nobody expects. In the early 1900s, the area that’s now Castlewood State Park was a popular retreat for partying St. Louisans. The dance clubs are gone, but the winding Meramec River and the lush valley that surrounds it remain. Stand on the bluff and try to hear the band.
### South to the French town, north to Twain’s
Ste. Genevieve’s own visitor site sells it as wineries, history, events and charm, just a short 1 hour drive from St. Louis. The National Park Service tells the deeper part: established by 1750, Ste. Genevieve was the first permanent European settlement in Missouri, and early French Canadian settlers were drawn here by the rich farmland they called le Grand Champ, the Big Field. At the Bauvais-Amoureux House, upright cedar logs are set directly into the ground, one of the few surviving examples of that building technique in the United States. Walk the old streets slowly and read the plaques.
On the way back, Kimmswick earns a stop for one reason you can taste. The Blue Owl there is famous for its Levee High Apple Pie, made with over a dozen layers of apples, and with a 10 AM to 3 PM day, you plan the drive around the pie and not the other way around. Our Kimmswick guide has the rest of the town.
People are asking
### What cities are within 5 hours of St. Louis, Missouri?
Chicago, Memphis and Kansas City are all within five-hour drives of St. Louis, according to Washington University’s guide to life in St. Louis. Closer in, Hannibal is 100 miles north of St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve is a short 1 hour drive. For a day trip, the closer towns win, because you spend the day there instead of on the interstate.
Go north instead and the river carries you to Hannibal. Its visitor bureau says it is located 100 miles north of St. Louis along the mighty Mississippi, celebrated around the world as the boyhood home of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, better known as Mark Twain. That is a long drive, so leave early, and let the kids read the first chapter of Tom Sawyer in the back seat. Inside the museum campus the exhibits let you ride a raft down the Mississippi with Huck and Jim, explore a cave with Tom and Becky, and pilot a steamboat.
For the history buff in the car, Springfield, Illinois holds the Lincoln Home National Historic Site, where visitors go inside the only home that Abraham Lincoln ever owned. Inside, his bedroom has a reproduction of the original wallpaper pattern on the walls.
Not every escape needs a vineyard at the end of it. Some Saturdays the trip is just across the river to Fairview Heights, Illinois.
### How to build the day so it doesn’t fall apart
Pair stops by the clock. Cahokia is eight miles out, so it slots in before or after anything else. Augusta is 45 minutes away, and Meramec and Ste. Genevieve are each about an hour, which makes any one of them a full day with a pie stop. Hannibal, 100 miles north, deserves a day of its own.
Check the official page the night before. Cave tours post their own hours, and the Blue Owl closes at 3 PM. A wasted drive stings worse than a skipped one.
Pack like the countryside won’t have what you forgot. Water, sneakers with grip for the boulders, a light layer for the cave, and a little cash for small-town shops. Leave room in the schedule for the stop you didn’t plan: the roadside stand, the overlook, the antique store with the screen door that slaps shut behind you. That is usually the part everyone remembers.
And plan the ride home as carefully as the ride out. Pick the stop you want to end on, not the one that happens to be last on the map. A slice of pie in a paper box on the passenger seat. Sunburned arms against the window. A kid asleep before the first exit with a pocket full of creek rocks. The drive back in the dusk light, with the city glowing ahead of you and nobody talking much, is the part of a day trip that actually resets a week. Give it time. Don’t schedule a thing for that evening.
