### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can my child take music lessons in St. Louis?
A.  The Community Music School of Webster University (Webster Groves and Chesterfield) offers lessons on nearly every instrument plus Suzuki and Kindermusik, and Shock City School teaches group and private lessons starting in preschool.
### Q. What is the best all-around arts program for kids in St. Louis?
A.  COCA (Center of Creative Arts) in University City is the metro’s premier multidisciplinary arts center, offering dance, theater, visual art, and music for ages preschool through high school, plus summer camps.
### Q. Where can kids take dance classes in St. Louis?
A.  The Saint Louis Ballet School in Chesterfield (ages 2-18), the Dance Center of Kirkwood, and Central Studio Academy in the Central West End and Webster Groves all offer strong kids’ dance programs.
### Q. Where can babies and toddlers take classes in St. Louis?
A.  For ages 0–5, look for caregiver-involved, play-based programs: Music Together (offered around the metro by providers such as Little Music Makers) and Kindermusik through the Community Music School of Webster University are the go-to early-childhood music options. Suzuki strings, also at the Community Music School, can begin as young as four.
### Q. How much do kids’ classes cost in St. Louis, and what should I ask?
A.  Costs vary widely by discipline and format — group classes and camps are generally more affordable than private lessons or company-track programs. Most studios offer a free trial class or tour, so use it. Ask about class sizes, recital or performance opportunities, make-up policies for missed classes, and any recital, costume, or materials fees on top of tuition before you enroll.
### Q. Should I start my child in a camp or a year-round class?
A.  A camp is the lower-risk way to test interest — programs like COCA, Metro Theater Company, Craft Alliance, and STL Rock School run week-long summer and break camps that end in a showcase, so your child gets real immersion without a season-long commitment. If they come home excited, roll into the year-round classes, where weekly practice is what actually builds skill over time. Popular camps and fall sessions fill early, so plan ahead.

## No Tax Waiver, No Missouri Plates: Your First 30 Days in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/new-to-st-louis-your-move-in-setup-checklist-2026
No waiver, no plates, and the City won’t email you one. It mails it. Your out-of-state title, soft at the creases from the ride in the moving folder, won’t get you Missouri plates without that paper, and neither will the car in the driveway still wearing another state on its bumper.
The paper is a statement of non-assessment, which the City calls a tax waiver, and it costs nothing. It shows you owe no personal property tax here, and a new resident to the State of Missouri qualifies. Go in person, and the Assessor’s virtual lobby texts you to confirm your place in line, then texts again when you may enter the building, so you can sit in the parked car outside City Hall with the engine off and the phone on the dash until the second text buzzes. Or email the request from the couch and watch the mailbox, because the City mails the waiver back. Either way, a free piece of paper is the one thing holding up your plates.
The clock is already running. The Missouri Department of Revenue gives you 30 days from the date of becoming a Missouri resident to title your vehicle. Count from that date, not from the day the last box gets unpacked.
Screenshot this one for the glove box: if the car was owned and operated in another state for at least 90 days before you title it in Missouri, no additional sales tax is due. Owned it for less than 90 days? Missouri can ask for the difference between its tax and what you already paid the other state.
The second catch shows up on a pay stub. Your first one lands, and you read it at the kitchen table between the takeout containers. There may be a line you didn’t have back home: the City of St. Louis collects a one percent earnings tax from its residents, regardless of the location of their employer. It has done that since 1954. Do the math on a $60,000 salary: 1% is $600 a year to the City. Live in the city, drive out to a job in the county, and the City still counts it. If your employer skips the withholding, the tax doesn’t skip you. The City says the responsibility sits with each taxpayer, penalty and interest included.
So read that stub slowly. The City’s 1% follows your address, and it follows your desk. Work in the city while living in the county and you owe it on those wages, because even part of a day inside the limits counts as a full day worked in the City.
There is a little mercy in it. If you move in partway through the year, the City says you’re only liable for the wages earned while living or working in the City. Whatever your employer didn’t withhold goes on Form E-1, due April 15. Write that date on the side of a box with the marker that’s already in your hand.
### What is the first thing you should do when moving to another state?
For the car, start with the waiver, today, before the first box is open, because the City mails it back and the 30-day clock is already running. Everything else on this page can wait a week, except the two dates that carry penalties: April 1 for your personal property declaration and April 15 for the earnings tax.
### The paper chase that comes before Missouri plates
Walk up to the license office counter with nothing but your old title and you’ll walk back out to the parking lot without plates. Build the stack on your kitchen counter first, one sheet at a time. On top goes the tax waiver. Under it, a Missouri safety inspection not more than 60 days old. If you live in St. Louis City or St. Louis County, add an emissions inspection, also not more than 60 days old. Then there’s one more check newcomers don’t expect: every motor vehicle previously titled in another state must be inspected to verify its vehicle identification number and odometer reading, and a Missouri safety inspection will satisfy that requirement. So one stop at an inspection station can cover two lines on the list. Hand over the keys, sit with the old title in your lap, and let someone verify the VIN and read the odometer. Bring your old title, proof of insurance and Form 108, the Application for Missouri Title and License, and the counter visit goes fast.
Newer cars catch a break. Missouri exempts vehicles from the safety inspection for the first ten years after the model year, as long as they have fewer than 150,000 miles. The identification number and odometer inspection still applies to a car with another state’s title, so don’t skip the station entirely.
### Where to take the waiver request, and what goes in the envelope
In person, it is City Hall, 1200 Market St., Rooms 115 and 117. By email, send a copy of your driver’s license, each car title and registration front and back, and confirmation of your current address to assessor-personalproperty@stlouis-mo.gov, then wait for the mail. Questions go to (314) 622-4171. Live in St. Louis County instead of the city? Missouri asks for the statement from your county of residence’s assessor’s office. Moved here from elsewhere in Missouri? The City says to get your waiver from the county where you lived on January 1.
### Trash, water and one bill for both in the city
The first night you haul a bag out to the alley, you’ll wonder who you’re supposed to pay for this. Inside the City of St. Louis, the City itself collects residential trash. It charges $14 per month per unit, collected quarterly on your water bill. That flat fee is more generous than it sounds: the City’s service list includes weekly collection of yard waste March-December and a monthly pickup of bulky items like furniture, appliances and tires, and the fee covers 12 drop-offs a year at a transfer station. So the busted box spring the last tenant left in the basement doesn’t need a truck rental. Bought the house? When you purchase a new home, the City creates the refuse billing account automatically, so nothing is required of the new homeowner. If your block uses alley dumpsters, the City ended alley recycling on Aug. 15, 2025, so find the nearest drop-off site before the flattened boxes take over the porch.
Moving to the county instead? Call the city hall of the municipality you landed in and ask who hauls your trash, and which day.
### The envelope that shows up in January
You’ll get through the first winter, and then the mail brings a form you’ve never seen. In the City, the Assessor’s Office mails assessment lists in January, and your declaration is due by April 1. File it late, or not at all, and the City adds a 10% penalty. Your car goes on that list, along with trucks, motorcycles and boats. The bill itself comes from the Collector of Revenue in November and is due no later than December 31, so put a sticky note on the fridge now.
People are asking
### What do I need to set up when I move to St. Louis?
Set up the things with deadlines first. Missouri gives you 30 days from becoming a resident to title your car, and the license office will want a statement of non-assessment, plus a safety inspection and, in St. Louis City or St. Louis County, an emissions inspection. Inside the City, trash is a $14-a-month fee per unit on your water bill, and residents owe the 1% earnings tax no matter where their employer is.
### Live in the county and work downtown? The 1% finds you too
Your new house is in the county, your new job is downtown, and your pay stub still has a line for the City. The City collects its earnings tax from employees of businesses located or performing work or services within the City of St. Louis, regardless of where they live. The City counts the day generously in its own favor, too: if any portion of a day is worked within the City, that day is considered a day worked in the City. Drive in for a two-hour meeting, and that whole day counts. If you split your weeks between a city office and somewhere else, keep a simple log of your days now. It’s a lot easier than rebuilding it from memory with a coffee going cold next to a stack of pay stubs next spring. Skip the tax and the penalty is 5% of the tax for each month, up to 25%, plus interest at 1% a month.
### Save the number that fixes the block: 311
Sooner or later the streetlight in front of your new place flickers out, or the trash truck rolls past your cart without stopping. Inside the City limits, you can dial 311 to reach the Citizens’ Service Bureau, whose staff place service requests and send concerns to the right City department. Calling from outside the City limits, say from your desk at a county job, use 314-622-4800 instead. Put it in your phone under something you’ll remember on a dark porch at night. County residents have their own municipal lines, so look yours up once you know which city hall you belong to.
### A first-week list for the rest of it
Put the utilities in your name before move-in day: electric, gas, water and sewer. In the City, the refuse fee rides on your water bill.
Switch your driver’s license. Bring proof of identity, date of lawful status, proof of your Social Security number and proof of your Missouri address.
Forward your mail and update your bank, insurance, employer and subscriptions.
Ask about sewer backups if the house has an older basement, and whether your insurance covers them.
Learn your trash and recycling day so your cans aren’t the only ones out on the wrong morning.

### Budget for the first month
A move always costs more than the truck. Plan for utility deposits, the title, plate and inspection fees for the car, and that first water-refuse bill if you’re in the city. Renters should keep the security deposit and renters insurance in mind; owners will meet the personal property tax bill in November. For the taxes that follow you past move-in week, see our St. Louis money guide. Knock out the deadline items first, the ones that cost you a penalty if you wait. Eat takeout off a moving box for one more week if you have to. The perfect couch can come later, once the bills settle into a rhythm you recognize and the paper stack on the counter is gone.
### Then go meet the people on your block
Once the last box is broken down, the fastest way to feel at home is to plug in. Find your neighborhood association, try the corner spot you keep walking past, and start your own list of go-to places. A bakery, a park you didn’t know about, a mechanic you trust: that’s what turns a new address into home.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What documents do I need to switch my license to Missouri?
A.  A new Missouri resident with an out-of-state license, valid or expired no more than 184 days, brings proof of identity, date of lawful status, proof of Social Security number and proof of a Missouri residential address. Take your out-of-state license with you, and ask the license office which papers count as your proof of address before you go.
### Q. How do I know if my car needs an inspection in Missouri?
A.  Look at the model year. Even model year vehicles are inspected in even calendar years and odd model years in odd calendar years, unless exempt. To title a car that came from another state, you need a safety inspection not more than 60 days old, plus an emissions inspection if you live in St. Louis City or St. Louis County.
### Q. What vehicles don’t need an inspection in Missouri?
A.  Vehicles in their first ten years after the model year, with fewer than 150,000 miles, are exempt from the safety inspection. A car titled in another state still needs the identification number and odometer inspection when you title it here, and a Missouri safety inspection covers that.
### Q. Why do you have to pay personal property tax?
A.  Because the City levies personal property tax each year against tangible personal property such as cars, trucks, motorcycles and boats. In the City, you declare by April 1, and the bill is due no later than December 31. Your first year, you’ll show a tax waiver instead of a paid receipt to get your plates.
### Q. What is the 183 day rule in Missouri?
A.  For state income tax, someone not domiciled in Missouri is still a resident if they had permanent living quarters here and spent more than 183 days of the taxable year in the state.
### Q. How long do you have to stay somewhere to be considered a resident in Missouri?
A.  For income tax, if Missouri is your domicile, you’re a resident unless you keep no permanent home here, keep one elsewhere, and spend no more than 30 days of the year in the state. For your car, the 30-day titling clock starts the day you become a Missouri resident.

## A First-Time Homebuyer's Guide to St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-first-time-homebuyer-s-guide-to-st-louis-2026
The sticker shock runs backwards here. A typical St. Louis home sells for far less than the national median, so it remains one of the most affordable major metros in the country, and ownership stays within reach for first-timers who’d be priced out almost anywhere else. Affordable isn’t the same as easy, though — not in this market. Going in prepared is what separates the buyers who close from the ones who keep getting outbid.
This guide runs through it in plain English: what the market looks like right now, the down-payment help that actually exists, the older-home quirks worth knowing, and where to find honest guidance before you sign anything. Start with the market, because it shapes every decision that follows.
### St. Louis is affordable — but it’s a seller’s market
The U.S. median home sells for around $400,000. In the city of St. Louis, it’s been running closer to $250,000 — one of the best affordability pictures of any large metro. Tight inventory is the catch. Homes have been going in about a month, selling at roughly 98% of asking, and better than a third close above list price. Cheap and competitive, in the same breath. Line up your financing before you fall for a place, not after.
Price alone can mislead you. Some of the lowest numbers sit in North County and North City neighborhoods that have absorbed decades of disinvestment, so read a price next to schools, commute, and the home’s condition rather than on its own. Property taxes deserve a line in the budget too. St. Louis County’s effective rate lands on the higher end for Missouri, and it feeds straight into your monthly payment.
### Get help with the down payment
First-timers here leave more money on the table at this step than anywhere else, usually because nobody told them the help exists. The programs worth knowing:
Missouri Housing Development Commission (MHDC) — its First Place and Next Step programs pair a competitive 30-year fixed mortgage with down-payment assistance of up to about 4% of the loan amount, given as a second loan that’s fully forgiven after 10 years in the home. You can take the forgivable assistance or a discounted interest rate. What you cannot do is combine a First Place loan with a Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) — MHDC’s First Place operations manual states plainly that the two may not be used together. An MCC turns a chunk of your annual mortgage interest into a federal tax credit, so if that is worth more to you than the down payment help, it is a decision to make before you apply rather than after. Minimum credit score is generally 640. First Place is aimed at first-time buyers; Next Step allows higher incomes and repeat buyers. Income and price limits apply (roughly a $510,000 purchase-price cap and household income limits in the low-to-mid $100,000s for the St. Louis area — check the current figures).
HomeSTL (City of St. Louis, via the St. Louis Development Corporation) — relaunched in 2026 and much bigger than it used to be: a forgivable, 0% interest loan of up to $40,000 citywide, or up to $50,000 in a HUD Qualified Census Tract, with no monthly payments and forgiveness over ten years. You need to be a first-time buyer (no ownership in three years), at or below 80% of area median income, buying within the City of St. Louis, and completing HUD-approved homebuyer education. It’s funded from a fixed pot and reservations run until the money is gone (or the program’s 2026 deadline), so move early and use one of its approved lenders.
Beyond Housing — the metro’s largest HUD-approved counseling agency and its biggest down-payment-assistance provider, offering roughly $7,000–$10,000 as a 5-year forgivable loan. Important: Beyond Housing serves St. Louis County, St. Charles County, and Jefferson County — not the City. You’ll need to finish its homebuyer education and one-on-one counseling first.
St. Charles County runs its own Down Payment Loan Program — up to $10,000, 0% interest, forgivable after five years, for buyers in the county’s program area (first-time status isn’t even required).
USDA, FHA, and VA loans — if you’re buying in an outer county (Franklin, Lincoln, Warren and similar), a USDA loan can mean zero down. FHA lets first-timers put down as little as 3.5% with a 580+ score (lenders often want ~620–640 in practice), and VA loans give eligible veterans 0% down with no monthly mortgage insurance.
Because terms, income limits, and availability change, work with an MHDC-approved lender and confirm the current details before you count on any single program.
### Which program works where
A quick map, since eligibility is mostly about location:
City of St. Louis: HomeSTL + MHDC (+ possible MCC).
St. Louis County: Beyond Housing + MHDC.
St. Charles County: the county HOME program + Beyond Housing + MHDC.
Outer/rural counties: USDA zero-down + MHDC.
MHDC is the common thread almost everywhere, so it’s a smart first call no matter which county you’re shopping.
### Know the steps
The sequence rarely surprises anyone. Check your credit and budget, get pre-approved for a mortgage (St. Louis sellers rarely take an offer seriously without a pre-approval letter), find a buyer’s agent, tour homes, make an offer with earnest money, get a home inspection and a lender appraisal, then close — usually about a month after your offer is accepted. Plan for closing costs of roughly 2–5% of the price on top of your down payment.
A couple of Missouri specifics work in your favor. Missouri has no real-estate transfer tax — a genuine savings compared with many states. And most closings here are handled by a title company; a real-estate attorney is not required, though you’re free to hire one.
### Figure out your real budget first
Get clear on what you can actually carry each month before you tour a single house. Sticker price is the least of it. Lenders weigh your debt-to-income ratio (many programs cap it around 45%), so your car payment, student loans, and credit cards all shape how much home you qualify for. The monthly payment covers principal and interest, then keeps going: PITI — principal, interest, taxes, and insurance — plus PMI if you put less than 20% down.
Those extras add up fast around here. In higher-tax St. Louis County municipalities, taxes and insurance can pile on a few hundred dollars a month, so run the full number, not just the mortgage. Keep a cushion after closing, too. Older St. Louis homes have a way of needing a water heater or a furnace the week after you’ve spent everything, so don’t drain your savings to the last dollar for the down payment.
### Making a competitive offer without overpaying
When a third of homes sell above asking, first-timers tend to do one of two things: overbid in a panic, or keep losing out. A good buyer’s agent threads that needle. They pull recent comparable sales so you know what a home is really worth, advise on earnest money, and shape an offer that stands out without wrecking your budget. Your single biggest advantage is a strong, current pre-approval letter — it tells a seller the financing is solid.
Price is not the only lever, either. Flexibility on the closing date, a slightly larger earnest deposit, or trimming small repair requests can all make an offer more appealing without raising the number. One move to skip: waiving the inspection to win a bid. On a century-old brick home, that’s how a “deal” turns into a five-figure surprise. Assistance programs like MHDC and HomeSTL work with normal financed offers, so getting help and staying competitive aren’t a trade-off.

### Two St. Louis quirks to budget for
Older homes need a real inspection. St. Louis has one of the largest stocks of pre-1940 brick homes in the Midwest. They’re charming and solid, but watch for foundation movement (our clay soil swells and shrinks), aging knob-and-tube wiring, old plumbing, and lead paint. A thorough inspection — and sometimes a specialist for the foundation or electrical — is money well spent. Once you’re in, our seasonal home maintenance checklist helps you protect the investment, and if repairs are looming, see our guide to government home improvement grants.
Occupancy inspections. Some St. Louis-area municipalities require a point-of-sale occupancy inspection before a home can change hands — separate from your buyer’s inspection. Rules vary city by city and the waits can run several weeks, so ask early which apply to your address.
### Get free, honest guidance first
Sit down with a HUD-approved housing counselor before you talk to a single lender. It’s low-cost or free, and it’s often required to unlock the assistance programs above anyway. In St. Louis, Justine Petersen (314-533-2411) and Beyond Housing both run homebuyer education and one-on-one counseling that connects you to lenders, agents, and down-payment help. Habitat for Humanity St. Louis offers a sweat-equity path to ownership for qualifying families. A counselor reads your real numbers, flags what could trip up your loan, and gets you shopping on facts instead of guesswork.

First-timers cluster in a handful of value pockets. North County suburbs like Florissant and Hazelwood, mid-county Overland, and in-city neighborhoods like Tower Grove South and Dutchtown all pull them in; over in St. Charles County, growing suburbs such as St. Peters and O’Fallon trade a higher price point for newer homes. Dozens of metro neighborhoods still list homes under $200,000, rare for a major city. Inventory is tight, though, so move fast and lean on that pre-approval when the right one surfaces.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much do I need for a down payment in St. Louis?
A.  Often far less than you’d think. MHDC’s First Place and Next Step programs offer up to about 4% in forgivable assistance, the City’s HomeSTL program offers up to $40,000 (or $50,000 in some areas), and Beyond Housing offers $7,000–$10,000 in the surrounding counties. FHA needs as little as 3.5% down, and VA and USDA loans can mean zero down for those who qualify.
### Q. What credit score do I need to buy a home in St. Louis?
A.  It varies by loan, but many first-time programs start around a 640 credit score (MHDC’s minimum), while FHA can go lower in theory — though lenders often want roughly 620–640 in practice. A HUD-approved housing counselor can help you strengthen your score before you apply.
### Q. Is St. Louis a good place to buy a first home?
A.  Yes — it’s one of the most affordable large metros in the U.S., with a median home price well below the national figure and many neighborhoods still under $200,000. Just know it’s currently a seller’s market, so come pre-approved and ready to act.
### Q. What should I watch out for when buying an older St. Louis home?
A.  Get a thorough inspection. Many area homes predate 1940, so watch for foundation issues (clay soil), knob-and-tube wiring, old plumbing, and lead paint — and check whether your municipality requires a point-of-sale occupancy inspection before closing.
### Q. Does Missouri charge a real-estate transfer tax?
A.  No. Missouri has no state or local real-estate transfer tax, which saves buyers and sellers money compared with many other states. Most St. Louis closings are handled by a title company, and hiring a real-estate attorney is optional.
### Q. How long does it take to buy a home in St. Louis?
A.  Once your offer is accepted, closing usually takes about a month while the lender finalizes your loan and the appraisal and title work are completed. Getting pre-approved first can take a few days to a couple of weeks, and finding the right home varies — but in this tight market, buyers who are pre-approved and ready tend to move fastest.
### Q. What are the key things I should know as a first-time homebuyer?
A.  Three that change the math: your credit score sets the rate more than the price sets the payment, the down payment is rarely the 20% people assume, and closing costs are a separate number nobody warns you about. Everything else is negotiable. Those three decide what you can actually carry.
### Q. What is the first-time homebuyer assistance program in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single one. Missouri runs MHDC First Place and Next Step, the City of St. Louis runs HomeSTL, Illinois has IHDA, and Madison and St. Clair counties run their own. Which you qualify for depends on your county, income and whether you are inside the city limits — so check them in that order rather than applying blind.
### Q. What grants are available for first-time homebuyers in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  Almost none, in the way the word implies. What gets called a grant is usually a forgivable or repayable second lien recorded against your house. Forgivable means it disappears on a schedule; sell before that schedule ends and recapture applies. Get the recapture terms in writing before you accept anything.
### Q. What are the biggest first-time home buyer mistakes?
A.  Shopping for a house before shopping for a lender, budgeting the mortgage payment and forgetting taxes and insurance, and treating an assistance program as free money without reading the lien terms. The other one around here is skipping the sewer scope on an older home — the cheapest inspection add-on and the most expensive thing to miss.

## Why Your St. Louis Trees Need a Regular Arborist Checkup
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-your-st-louis-trees-need-a-regular-arborist-checkup
A mature oak can shade a St. Louis backyard for decades and get exactly one close look in its whole life: the morning a limb is already down on the garage roof. That’s the expensive way to find out the tree was in trouble. The logic your doctor uses at a checkup — catch the small stuff before it becomes the big stuff — works just as well on the tree in the yard, and hardly anyone applies it.
The big mature trees that make a St. Louis yard worth sitting in are also the ones that do the most damage when they fail. A regular checkup from a certified arborist is preventive care aimed at exactly those trees. It finds the weak branch union or the hidden pocket of decay that a summer storm will happily finish off. What follows is what an arborist actually does, the local pests and diseases worth knowing by name, and how to tell a real one from a guy with a chainsaw and a fresh business card. In tree care, that difference can be your roof.
### What a Certified Arborist Actually Does
A certified arborist does far more than run a chainsaw. The good ones work like a doctor for your landscape, and the job covers a lot of ground:
Assess risk and health — evaluate root stability, branch structure, and overall condition to flag hazards before they fail.
Prune for structure — make the specific cuts that improve a tree’s form, reduce wind resistance, and remove weak or dead limbs (without ever topping it).
Cable and brace — support a weak branch union with hardware so a valuable tree can be saved instead of removed.
Diagnose pests and disease — identify what’s attacking a tree and whether it can be treated, plus advise on soil, planting, and species selection.
That last point matters more than most homeowners realize. St. Louis trees are under real pressure from a handful of specific threats right now, and a trained eye catches what a homeowner can’t: the early bark-blonding of an ash under attack, a hairline crack in a major limb, the fungus at the base that gives away decay in the roots. At that stage there are still options. By the time the trouble is obvious from the porch, the cheap fixes are usually gone.
This is where a standing relationship beats a panic call. Instead of dialing someone the morning after a limb drops on the garage, you have a professional who already knows your trees and checks them on a schedule. Small problems get flagged while they’re still a pruning cut, not a full removal. Over the life of a mature tree, that steady attention almost always costs less than one emergency. It’s the difference between keeping a decades-old shade tree and losing it to something a season’s earlier notice would have caught.
### The St. Louis Threats an Arborist Watches For
Missouri trees have a few named enemies. Knowing which ones are genuinely dangerous and which are mostly headlines is exactly what a professional sorts out for you:
Emerald ash borer (EAB) — the big one. This invasive beetle was first found in Missouri in 2008 and is now widespread across the state, and it kills untreated ash trees. If you have an ash, an arborist can tell you whether it’s worth treating or should come down before it dies and gets brittle.
Oak wilt — a lethal fungal disease that can kill an oak fast. A crucial local rule an arborist follows: don’t prune oaks in the spring and early summer (roughly April through June), when the beetles that spread it are active.
Bagworms — they defoliate evergreens like junipers, arborvitae, and red cedar, and because conifer foliage doesn’t grow back, they can kill a shrub or young tree if ignored.
Spotted lanternfly — you’ve probably heard the alarm, but here’s the honest status: the Missouri Department of Conservation says there are no known established populations in Missouri yet. It’s approaching, not here — worth watching, not panicking over.
### Why “Certified” Matters
Anyone can call themselves an “arborist.” The word on its own implies no skill and carries no accountability. A Certified Arborist is a different thing entirely: the title is a credential from the International Society of Arboriculture (ISA), earned through at least three years of experience and a rigorous exam covering tree biology, diagnosis, pruning, cabling, and safety, then kept current with ongoing education every three years. For the narrower question of whether a tree is safe, there’s a further credential still, the Tree Risk Assessment Qualification (TRAQ).
That gap shows up fast in the yard. An uncertified crew might top your tree, over-prune it, or talk you into removing a healthy one, either because they don’t know better or because removal is where the money is. A certified arborist answers to a standard and a testable body of knowledge instead. As one arborist group nicely put it, certified arborists are “healthcare providers for trees.”
### What Actually Happens During a Checkup
A tree checkup is less mysterious than it sounds. A certified arborist walks your property and looks at each significant tree from the roots up: the soil and root flare for heaving or decay, the trunk for cracks and cavities, the branch unions for weak, included-bark attachments, and the canopy for deadwood, imbalance, and signs of pest or disease pressure. They’ll tell you which trees are sound, which need pruning, which need watching, and which — honestly — should come down before they fail. A good arborist is as willing to tell you a tree is fine as to sell you work; that’s part of how you know they’re the real thing.
You come away with a plan instead of a worry: prune this one this winter, treat that ash, keep an eye on the leaner by the driveway, no action needed on the rest. For the price of a nice dinner out, you trade a vague anxiety about “the big tree” for a clear, professional read on it.
### When to Schedule a Checkup
You don’t need an arborist on retainer, but a few moments call for one. Have your mature trees looked at every few years as a baseline, and always after a major storm, a drought, or nearby construction that may have damaged roots. Call sooner if you notice any of the warning signs a homeowner can spot: a new lean, cracks or cavities, mushrooms at the base, lots of dead limbs, or soil heaving around the roots. And if you have ash trees or aging oaks, get on a professional’s radar now rather than after the damage is visible. The best time to find a problem is while it’s still cheap to fix.
### How to Hire the Real Thing (and Spot the Fakes)
Vetting an arborist is straightforward once you know what to check:
Verify the credential. You can confirm any ISA Certified Arborist’s status online at treesaregood.org — ask for their certification number.
Require insurance. Ask for current proof of liability insurance and workers’ compensation, and don’t be shy about verifying it. Tree work is dangerous; an uninsured injury on your property can become your problem.
Get it in writing. A detailed written estimate (get two or three), a clear scope, and local references.
Red flags to walk away from: anyone who knocks on your door after a storm claiming to be “working in the neighborhood”; anyone who recommends topping (a certified arborist never will); anyone pushing you to remove a healthy tree; cash-only lowball bids; and pressure to sign or pay a big deposit today. The good ones don’t rush you.

### It Pays You Back
A checkup feels like an optional expense until you price the alternative. An emergency removal after a tree fails — often at night, in a storm, onto a structure — costs far more than the proactive pruning or treatment that would have prevented it, and that’s before the roof repair. Healthy, well-kept trees also add real curb appeal and value to a home. Spending a little to keep a big tree sound is one of the better returns in home maintenance, and it’s a lot less stressful than the 2 a.m. version.
There’s an environmental payback, too. A mature shade tree cools the house through a St. Louis summer and soaks up stormwater, and it takes decades to replace. Lose one to a preventable pest or an avoidable split and you’re out far more than a repair bill. You’re out something that made the whole yard better and can’t be bought back at any price. Keeping your big trees sound is the rare home project that pays you back in shade, in resale value, and in not standing in the driveway at 2 a.m.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is hiring an arborist worth it?
A.  Yes. A checkup feels optional until you price the alternative: an emergency removal after a tree fails onto a structure costs far more than the pruning or treatment that would have prevented it. Healthy, well-kept trees also add curb appeal and value, making proactive tree care one of the better returns in home maintenance.
### Q. What is the difference between an arborist and a tree service?
A.  An arborist is trained to diagnose tree health, assess risk, and prune for structure — more like a doctor for your landscape. A tree service focuses on the physical work of cutting and removal. The strongest providers combine both, but only a Certified Arborist carries a tested credential in tree biology and care.
### Q. What does an arborist charge per hour?
A.  Pricing varies by arborist and scope, and most price by the job or consultation rather than a fixed hourly rate. A basic consultation or tree assessment typically runs a modest few-hundred-dollar range, and some companies waive that fee if you hire them for the work. Detailed written or insurance-grade reports cost more.
### Q. Is the emerald ash borer in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle that kills untreated ash trees, was first found in Missouri in 2008 and is now widespread across the state, including the St. Louis area. If you have ash trees, a certified arborist can advise whether treatment makes sense or the tree should come down before it turns brittle.
### Q. Can I prune my oak trees any time of year?
A.  No — timing matters for oaks in Missouri because of oak wilt, a lethal fungal disease. Avoid pruning oaks in spring and early summer, roughly April through June, when the beetles that spread it are active. The dormant season is the safer window. After storm damage in that period, an arborist can advise on protective steps.
### Q. How do I verify an arborist is certified?
A.  Ask for the arborist’s ISA certification number and verify it online at treesaregood.org, the ISA’s public site. Also require current proof of liability insurance and workers’ compensation, get a written estimate, and check local references. Walk away from anyone who solicits door-to-door after a storm, recommends topping, or demands a large deposit up front.
### Q. What's the difference between an arborist and a tree service?
A.  An arborist diagnoses; a tree service removes. Plenty of good crews do both, but the incentive differs — if the only service offered is cutting, the recommendation will tend toward cutting. Get the assessment from someone who is not bidding on the removal when the tree is worth saving.
### Q. What questions should I ask an arborist?
A.  Ask what specifically they are seeing and where, what happens if you do nothing for a year, whether the work can be staged, and who carries the insurance if a limb goes through the roof. A good one will answer the do-nothing question honestly instead of treating it as a trick.
### Q. How much does an arborist charge to inspect a tree?
A.  An inspection is usually billed as a modest flat visit fee, and many will credit it against work you go on to book. That fee is the cheapest part of the whole business — it is what tells you whether you are looking at a pruning job or a removal.
### Q. Can seniors get trees cut down for free?
A.  Sometimes, but it varies by municipality rather than being a statewide program. Some cities and non-profits run assistance for hazardous trees on owner-occupied property, usually means-tested and limited to trees that threaten a structure. Call your city forestry office before paying for a removal you might qualify for help with.

## Whose Tree Is It? Storm-Proofing Trees in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/storm-proofing-your-trees-a-st-louis-homeowners-guide
Not your tree. The huge one between your curb and the sidewalk, the one that groaned over the roof all night while you lay awake listening, may well belong to the City of St. Louis. The city’s Forestry Division says city-owned trees sit between the curb and sidewalk, or typically within 10 feet of the curb, and its crews manage them. That dead limb hanging over your car may be a phone call, not an invoice.
Usually you learn it in the dark. In south city in July, the sound comes first. A crack like a rifle shot somewhere behind the garage, then a long tearing groan, then a thud you feel in the soles of your feet before you hear it. The rain is coming sideways off the back porch. The lights flicker twice and hold. You stand at the kitchen window with your hand flat on the cold glass, trying to see which tree it was, and your stomach already knows the answer: the big silver maple, the one you’ve been meaning to have someone look at for three summers.
Most St. Louis homeowners meet their trees this way. Not on a calm Saturday with a cup of coffee and a ladder, but in the dark, during the five minutes of wind that decides whether a limb lands on the lawn or through the roof over a kid’s bedroom. The work that changes how those five minutes go happens months earlier, and it is less dramatic than you’d think. It starts with the question nobody asks until the limb is already down: whose tree is it?
If it’s the curb tree and it’s sick, dropping limbs or leaning toward your porch, report it instead of paying a crew to cut a tree you don’t own. Call the city at 314-622-4800 or start the request online from the city’s Report a Problem with a City Tree page. The city asks for the address or intersection, a description of the conditions, and photos if possible, so stand on the sidewalk and take two pictures before you dial. On a narrow street in Tower Grove South or Dutchtown, that curb tree is often the biggest one hanging over your roof. Here is the line worth texting your neighbor: the cheapest tree job in St. Louis is the one you report instead of pay for.
The wire is the opposite story. Ameren Missouri states plainly that trees near the line running from the main power line to your house, the line it calls a service drop, are the property owner’s responsibility. The branch rubbing that wire every time the wind gusts is yours to deal with. Through the Contact Our Team link on its Trees and Your Service page, Ameren will set an appointment to disconnect the service drop so the trees can be trimmed safely, and the same page says only qualified line clearance contractors may work within 10 feet of higher voltage lines. So the tree out front may be the city’s problem, while the limb on your own wire is yours, and you’ll want to sort out which is which in October, not during a July warning.
If that sounds like overthinking a few trees, walk through Forest Park. On May 16, 2025, an EF3 tornado crossed the park, and Forest Park Forever counts more than 5,200 trees damaged there, with 3,100 of them toppled or harmed past saving. Those were some of the most professionally cared-for trees in the region, and the storm still flattened whole stands. Your backyard maple won’t beat a tornado. What it can beat is the ordinary summer thunderstorm, the kind that leaves snapped limbs at the curb from the Hill to Holly Hills while the sound trees beside them barely lose a leaf.
### How can I protect my trees from high winds?
The honest answer is mostly boring: keep the tree well structured so wind slips through it instead of shoving it like a sail. That means removing dead wood, thinning crowded interior branches, shortening the long heavy limbs that reach over the roof, and having a certified arborist brace or cable a weak split trunk. Do it in the dormant months, from leaf fall to early spring, when you can actually see the shape of the tree and the cuts close well once growth starts.
Stand under your tree in February and look up. Bare branches tell you everything leaves hide in July: the dead limb with no buds at its tips, the two trunks squeezed together in a tight V with bark pinched between them, the long branch that runs thirty feet sideways with almost no taper. That tight V is where trees split. The sideways branch is the one that tears off in a gust and swings into the gutter.
And one thing to never pay for. The Missouri Department of Conservation is blunt that topping is the worst thing to do to a tree. Cutting a canopy back to stubs feels like safety, a smaller tree that can’t fall as far. It works the other way. MDC notes that the regrowth after topping is weakly attached and breaks easily in storms, so a topped maple drops more limbs in three years than it did before, and every one of them is a thick, fast-growing sprout. If someone offers to “take the top out so it’s safer,” thank them and close the door.
The trees that worry arborists most in St. Louis yards are the fast growers. MDC says Callery pear, the tree sold as Bradford pear, has a poor branch structure and doesn’t fare well in storms, often losing limbs or splitting apart. You’ve seen it: the white-flowered pear on the corner, split down the middle like a wishbone after one spring storm. Silver maple is the other one. Missouri State University’s tree guide calls its wood weak and prone to decay if damaged, often injured in ice or wind storms. Those two shade a lot of St. Louis houses, which is why they fill the curb piles every time a line of storms crosses the river.
When you plant, plant slow. Oaks take longer to give you shade, but the trade is a tree that holds. And think about where it would land. A big tree twenty feet from the house is a gift. The same tree right over the bedroom is a bet you make every summer.
People are asking
### Do young trees grow better in a windy yard?
They grow sturdier, if not taller: a young tree that bows in a gust and springs back answers with a thicker, more tapered trunk and more roots, while one lashed tight to a stake grows taller and thinner and is more likely to snap once the stake comes off. So if your new tree goes in where the wind rakes across an open yard, MU Extension says to stake it no higher than one-third of its height so the top of the trunk can still sway, using rubber hose or fabric straps so no rope or wire touches the bark. Cut the supports loose one season after planting, before they girdle the trunk.
### The ten-minute walk that finds the dangerous tree
Do this twice a year, once with leaves and once without. Bring your phone and take a picture of anything that bothers you, because next spring you’ll want to know whether that crack got longer. Look for:
Cracks or cavities in the trunk, soft wood that gives under your thumb, or a hollow that sounds dull when you knock on it.
A new lean, or soil at the base that is lifting, cracking or mounded on one side. That is the root plate starting to let go.
Mushrooms or shelf fungus at the base, often the only outside sign of decay inside.
Dead or hanging limbs, especially the broken ones still caught up in the canopy.
A tight V-shaped fork with bark pinched inside it, the classic split point.
Any one of those on a big tree near the house, the driveway or a wire is worth a certified arborist’s eyes before storm season.
Found something on that walk that made your stomach drop? Get a certified arborist out before the next warning, not after it. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for local tree services and arborists, compare a few, and get written estimates while nobody is in a hurry.
If you’re the arborist, the tree crew or the one-truck stump grinder who answers the phone at 6 a.m. after a storm, the homeowners reading this are looking for someone exactly like you. Put your business where those customers are already searching and get more customers before the storm season does it for you.
### The knock on the door the morning after
The chainsaws start before the coffee is done. The street smells like wet sawdust and bar oil. By nine there is a pickup with a magnetic sign on the door idling at the curb, and a man on your porch with a clipboard saying they’re working on your block and can fit you in today if you sign now. Your heart is still racing from last night, which is exactly what he’s counting on. MDC’s storm advice is short: do not hire anyone that knocks on your door to do tree work. They may or may not know what they’re doing, and they may not carry the insurance that protects you if a limb goes through the neighbor’s roof. Already handed one of them a deposit, and now his phone just rings? Here’s what to do when a contractor takes your money and disappears.
Before you hire anyone, ask for proof of liability and workers’ compensation insurance, look for an ISA Certified Arborist on the crew, and take thirty seconds on your phone to check that name at TreesAreGood.org, where the International Society of Arboriculture lets you verify an arborist’s credentials. A real one won’t mind. Get more than one written estimate, and don’t hand over a big deposit to a stranger. If the tree out front turns out to be a city tree, call 314-622-4800 and let Forestry handle it.
Then slow down. Treat every downed wire as live and stay away from anything touching one. Look up before you walk under a damaged tree, because broken limbs caught in the canopy can let go without a sound. Leave the big cuts to insured pros. A limb under tension can whip back hard enough to break bones. Photograph everything before you clean up: the Missouri Department of Insurance says homeowners insurance generally provides some coverage for removing trees that damage your home or other insured property, including a neighbor’s tree that fell on your property, and pictures help that claim.
### A broken tree isn’t always a lost tree
Morning light makes the damage look worse than it is. The torn limb lies across the patio, leaves still green, and the raw yellow wound up on the trunk is so bright it looks like the whole tree is finished. The urge is to have it all gone by dinner, to stop looking at it. Wait.
MDC’s storm advice puts it simply: if you have more pressing issues to tend to, the trees can wait awhile. Proper pruning is what helps a damaged tree recover. A clean break on a healthy oak, cut back properly to the branch collar, often closes over and the tree goes on shading the house for decades. A tree you rush to remove in a panic is gone for good, and so is the shade that kept your upstairs bearable in August.
The ones that usually can’t be saved are easier to read than you’d think. A trunk split down the middle. A tree that was straight on Friday and leans on Saturday, with the soil heaved up on one side like a lifted rug. A canopy where most of the big limbs are gone. Those go on the arborist’s list first. Everything else deserves a second opinion from someone who isn’t standing on your porch with a contract, and a calm look a week later, once the wires are fixed and the street is quiet again.
The tree’s handled and the gutter’s still hanging by one bracket? The handyman map has people who fix that.

People are asking
### What is the 10-20-30 rule for planting trees?
It’s a diversity cap for a whole community’s trees: no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of any one genus and 30% of any one family, so one insect or disease can’t devastate the canopy all at once. The city has lived the reason: ash made up 17% of its street trees when the emerald ash borer showed up, a beetle expected to kill every untreated ash in its path, and bright yellow tags went up on the ones that had to come down. The city’s replanting plan replaces every removed ash from a palette of about 40 species. Before you replace the tree you lost, do the same math on your block: if every big tree in sight is a maple, plant an oak or another genus.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which type of trees are most vulnerable to storm damage?
A.  Fast growers with weak wood and tight forks. In St. Louis that mostly means Callery pear, sold as Bradford pear, which MDC says often loses limbs or splits apart in storms, and silver maple, whose weak wood is often injured in ice or wind storms. Any tree with a tight V-shaped fork is more likely to split.
### Q. What should I do after a windstorm damages my trees?
A.  Stay away from any wire and anything touching one. Photograph the damage before anything moves. Then have a certified arborist decide what can be saved, and don’t hire whoever knocks first. If the tree stands between the curb and the sidewalk in the city, report it to Forestry at 314-622-4800.
### Q. Will insurance pay for tree removal after a storm?
A.  Often, when the tree hit something insured. The Missouri Department of Insurance says a homeowners policy generally provides some coverage for removing a tree that damages your home or other insured property, even a neighbor’s tree. A tree that just fell in the yard is a different story, so read your policy and call your agent.
### Q. What trees are storm resistant?
A.  No tree is storm proof, but slow-growing, strong-wooded trees hold up far better than fast growers. Ginkgo is one example: Missouri State University notes its ginkgos came through the 2007 Springfield ice storm with little to moderate damage. Native oaks are the classic choice for a St. Louis yard if you can wait for the shade.
### Q. At what wind speed do trees fall down?
A.  There’s no single number, because a decayed tree can fail in an ordinary gust. For a benchmark, the National Weather Service’s Beaufort scale lists trees uprooted at storm force, winds of 55 to 63 mph. A well-pruned, healthy tree gives you the best odds at any speed.

## A Margarita in a Whole Pineapple: What to Order on Cherokee Street, St. Louis’s Mexican Row
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-authentic-mexican-on-cherokee-street-st-louis
Tongs click against a metal tray at Diana’s Bakery, and the hard part is stopping: a concha with its sugar shell cracking, a churro, a square of tres leches, a few dollars all in. Down the block, La Manganita is pressing tortillas to order, so the one under your taco hits the plate warm and soft. And at La Vallesana, the margarita comes out in a whole pineapple. That’s a Saturday on west Cherokee Street, roughly Jefferson to Nebraska, the stretch Feast Magazine has called one of America’s best Latin American dining districts.
Four family-run anchors sit within a couple of blocks of each other, and each has the one thing to order:
A margarita in a whole pineapple, two straws sticking out: La Vallesana, 2801 Cherokee. The straws are a suggestion, not a rule. Then a paleta from the ice cream counter it grew out of.
Carne asada beside two scrambled eggs, rice and beans: Taquería El Bronco, 2817 Cherokee, winner of Calle Cherokee’s first Taco de Oro taco competition, per the district’s own food guide, and one of the few Mexican breakfasts on the street, from 9 a.m. Friday through Sunday.
Poblano, squash blossoms and melted cheese on a tortilla just off the press: La Manganita’s vegetarian taco, a deconstructed chile relleno, at 2812 Cherokee.
Barbacoa under radish, cucumber, onion and a squeeze of lime: the taco stand at El Torito, 2753 Cherokee. Ask for the verde and the roja too.
A crackling bag of chicharrones: Latino Americana, 2800 Cherokee, the carnicería that bags its own. Get hot sauce on the side.
For the ride home: a tray of pan dulce at Diana’s (2843) and watermelon cookies at El Chico Bakery (2634).
The counterintuitive part: some of the best tacos in St. Louis come from a stand inside a grocery store. That’s El Torito, and a crowd forms outside it at lunch. A dollar or two of pan dulce is the cheapest good souvenir in town.
Two updates the old lists miss. The Taco & Ice Cream Joint at 2738 Cherokee closed in 2024. And the Cinco de Mayo festival, an 18-year street party that drew around 30,000 people, was canceled over rising costs, St. Louis Public Radio reported; the district hopes to bring it back in some form.
So circle early November instead. That’s when the panaderías bake pan de muerto, the sugar-dusted bread made for Día de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, and when Diana’s Bakery puts out the Día de los Muertos altar it’s known for. Miss that week and the pan de muerto waits a year. Three more clocks worth knowing: Diana’s opens at 6 a.m., hours before the taco stands, and Wednesday is the street’s weak day, when La Vallesana and La Manganita both list themselves closed (El Torito and El Bronco stay open). And the cheapest parking on the street is on a Sunday: City of St. Louis meters, the ones lining Cherokee included, charge Monday through Saturday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. and are free all day Sunday and on city holidays.
And the plate most people walk right past isn’t Mexican. At 2818, Sueño Latino, which Feast Magazine called Cherokee’s only Honduran restaurant, is known for pollo con tajadas, chicken over a pile of crisp fried plantain chips, plus baleadas and, on Fridays only, yuca con chicharrón. It’s open every day from 10 to 9, so it’s the Wednesday answer when La Vallesana and La Manganita are dark. And a few doors down at La Manganita, owner Manny Garcia cooked in Italian restaurants before he opened his own, which is why a taquería on Cherokee has pasta on the menu.
### Why Cherokee Street? Park Once, Eat Six Blocks
Walk it once and you get it. Inside six blocks you pass a carnicería selling bags of its own chicharrones, a taco stand inside a grocery store, panaderías with pan dulce stacked in the windows, a candy shop hung with piñatas, and, just off the street, a snack shop charring elotes and dusting them with chili and Cotija. Nearly all of it is independent and family-owned. It’s the closest thing St. Louis has to a Mexican mercado district.
### A Neighborhood Built by Its Restaurants
Nobody planned this street. El Chico Bakery opened at 2634 Cherokee in 1998 and still sells the watermelon cookies people come back for. La Vallesana started as a small ice cream counter and grew into a restaurant with two big patios. Sueño Latino, at 2818, was opened by three brothers from Honduras and their mother, and the recipes on the menu are hers. One family business at a time, a row of affordable south-city storefronts became Calle Cherokee.
You can taste that history. Tortillas pressed by hand while you wait, salsas built from family recipes, conchas on Diana’s trays like the ones in Mexico City panaderías.
### The Sit-Down Anchors: Pineapple Margaritas to a Supermarket Bar
Start with the restaurants that have defined the street. La Vallesana (2801 Cherokee) is the anchor. It grew from a small ice cream shop into one of the street’s biggest restaurants, with two large patios, serving tacos, tortas, quesadillas, and margaritas (order the one served in a whole pineapple), and it still works as a nevería for paletas and ice cream. El Torito (2753 Cherokee) is the grand-dame: a Mexican supermarket, a sit-down taquería, and a bar all under one roof, with an on-site grill, brightly painted walls, a patio, and fútbol on the TVs.
Taquería El Bronco (2817 Cherokee) is a bona fide institution - it won the inaugural “Taco de Oro” and does Mexican breakfast, pozole, tortas, and the classics as well as anyone in town. And La Manganita (2812 Cherokee) is the spot for made-to-order handmade tortillas and some of the best vegetarian tacos on the street, with a Taco Tuesday worth planning around. Any one of these four is a full, satisfying meal; together they’re a crash course in why Cherokee earns its reputation. If it’s your first time, El Bronco or El Torito is the safe, always-good starting point; regulars tend to have a favorite and defend it.
Headed north with a box of conchas on the passenger seat? Florissant has its own guide.
### Tacos & Street Food
If you’re here to graze, the tacos are the move. El Torito’s taco stand turns out barbacoa, carnitas, tripa, pollo, and al pastor with full toppings and house verde and roja salsas - regularly called some of the best tacos in the city. One update for return visitors: the Taco & Ice Cream Joint at 2738 Cherokee closed in 2024, so for something sweet after your tacos, walk over to La Vallesana’s ice cream counter or grab an elote at Botanas La Michoacana. The beauty of Cherokee is that you can order two tacos here, a torta there, and a paleta down the block, sampling as you walk instead of committing to one table.
A few ordering tips for first-timers. Al pastor (marinated pork, often with pineapple), carnitas (slow-cooked pork), and barbacoa (rich, tender beef) are the crowd-pleasers if you’re new to the lineup; the more adventurous should try tripa (crispy tripe) or lengua (beef tongue), both done well here. Ask for the salsas - the verde and roja are where the kitchens show off - and don’t skip the pickled onions and radishes. Tacos here are small and cheap by design, so order a few different kinds and figure out your favorite. It’s a low-stakes, high-reward way to eat, and it’s a big part of what makes the street so fun.
### The Panaderías (Mexican Bakeries)
Do not leave Cherokee without stopping at a panadería. Diana’s Bakery (2843 Cherokee) is the standout - a family-owned shop turning out more than a hundred traditional treats: conchas, churros, bolillos, telera, tamales, and tres leches, and it’s especially known for its Día de los Muertos pan de muerto. Grab a tray and tongs (that’s how it works), load up on pan dulce, and thank yourself later. Nearby, Lilly’s Panadería (2819 Cherokee) offers pan dulce, donuts, and tres leches, and El Chico Bakery (2634 Cherokee), family-owned since 1998, is known for its watermelon cookies and fruit-filled empanadas. A dollar or two of pan dulce is the best cheap souvenir in St. Louis.
### Mercados & Sweets
Part of the fun of Cherokee is stocking your own kitchen. The El Torito supermercado is the quintessential Mexican grocery - produce, a full butcher counter, imported goods, baked goods, and housewares - the place to find the dried chiles, masa, and Mexican Coke you can’t get elsewhere. Latino Americana (2800 Cherokee) is a carnicería and grocery with imported products and house-made chicharrónes, and Dulcería Medina (2734 Cherokee) is a Mexican candy shop stocked with imported sweets and party supplies (the go-to for a piñata). For a treat on a hot day, La Vallesana’s paletas and nieves are the classic, and Botanas La Michoacana (just off Cherokee on California) does elote - Mexican street corn - fresh fruit, and grab-and-go antojitos.
### Cinco de Mayo on Cherokee: Where It Stands
For 18 years, the Cinco de Mayo festival on Cherokee between Nebraska and Jefferson was one of the biggest street parties in the region, with a parade, music stages, Lucha Libre wrestling, and margaritas served in a whole fresh pineapple. Organizers canceled the 2026 festival, citing rising costs and production fees for what had grown into a roughly 30,000-person event, and the street’s improvement district has said it hopes to bring the celebration back in some form. On the holiday itself, the restaurants and bars still run their own specials, which is honestly a calmer way to eat here: a pineapple margarita on La Vallesana’s patio with room to breathe. The street keeps other events on the calendar too, like the Brewed Arts Festival in the fall and the Jazz Crawl, so check cherokeestreet.com before you plan a trip around one.
Exploring St. Louis’s food neighborhoods? Family-run restaurants, taquerías, and bakeries like these are exactly what a good local directory helps you find. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for spots on Cherokee Street and across the whole metro before you go.
If you’re the taquería, the panadería or the paleta counter on Cherokee, the Gold plan puts your hours, menu and photos of your pan dulce case in front of more customers planning a walk down the street.
### Make a Day of It
Because everything sits within a few blocks - roughly 2634 to 2843 Cherokee - the best way to do the street is on foot. Park once and make a loop: tacos at El Torito or El Bronco, a torta at La Vallesana, a walk through the supermercado, pan dulce from Diana’s, and a paleta for the road. Cherokee is also an arts-and-antiques corridor, so you can browse murals, vintage shops, and galleries between bites. Give yourself a couple of hours and an empty stomach; it’s one of the most rewarding, affordable food outings in the whole city.
One more St. Louis secret, for after the tacos, runs under the same street. At its far east end, near Broadway, the Lemp brewery once aged its lager in natural caves, and the remains of the Lemp family’s underground theater still lie beneath Cherokee Street, sealed off since the state bought the cave entrance for I-55 in 1961, according to the nearby Chatillon-DeMenil Mansion.
A practical note on timing and payment: many of these are small, family-run spots that keep their own hours, and a few are cash-friendlier than card-first - it never hurts to have a little cash for the taco stands, bakeries, and paleta carts. Weekends bring the biggest crowds and the fullest bakery cases; a weekday visit is quieter if you’d rather linger, and on a night you don’t want the drive into south city, Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill out in Winghaven is a sit-down Mexican option in St. Charles County. And come hungry but pace yourself - the whole appeal is trying a little from several places rather than filling up at the first stop. If you’re bringing friends from out of town, this is the walk that turns them into believers about St. Louis food.
One more reason to make the trip: it’s cheap. A couple of tacos, a torta to split, a bag of pan dulce, and a paleta will run a fraction of what a sit-down dinner costs elsewhere, and you’ll eat better. In a city full of underrated food, Cherokee Street might be the most underrated stretch of all - a few blocks where the tortillas are fresh, the prices are fair, and the whole thing feels like a small trip to somewhere else without leaving town.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What to do on Cherokee Street, St. Louis?
A.  Eat your way down the street. Cherokee’s western end packs taquerías, sit-down restaurants, Mexican bakeries, a supermercado, candy shops, and paleta stands into a walkable six blocks. Park once, grab tacos, a torta, and pan dulce, then browse the murals, vintage shops, and galleries between bites. Weekend late mornings are the sweet spot, when the bakery cases are full.
### Q. What are some good Mexican restaurants on Cherokee Street in St. Louis?
A.  The must-try anchors are La Vallesana (tacos, tortas, quesadillas and paletas), Taquería El Bronco (the first Taco de Oro winner and one of the few spots on the street serving Mexican breakfast), La Manganita (tortillas pressed to order and great vegetarian tacos) and El Torito, a taquería, bar and Mexican supermarket in one. All four sit within a few walkable blocks.
### Q. What stores are located on Cherokee Street in St. Louis?
A.  On the Mexican stretch you’ll find El Torito’s full supermarket (2753 Cherokee), Carnicería Latino Americana for marinated meats and house-made chicharrones (2800 Cherokee), Dulcería Medina for Mexican candy and piñatas, and three panaderías. Farther along, Cherokee is known for vintage and antique shops and art galleries, so it’s easy to shop between meals.
### Q. What is popular Mexican street food?
A.  Tacos lead: al pastor, carnitas, barbacoa and lengua on small corn tortillas, which you can try side by side at El Torito’s taco stand. Close behind are tortas, quesadillas, elote (grilled corn slathered in chile, garlic and cotija, a specialty at Botanas La Michoacana just off Cherokee) and paletas, the fruit ice pops La Vallesana is known for.
### Q. What is a famous street in St. Louis?
A.  Cherokee Street is one of the best known, for its Mexican dining district and its antique row. The others locals name first are the Delmar Loop, home of the St. Louis Walk of Fame and Blueberry Hill, Washington Avenue’s loft district downtown, and South Grand’s international restaurant row. Each one makes a good half-day on foot.

## Dogs Were Banned From St. Louis Patios. Now These Breweries Bring the Water Bowl
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-friendly-patios-and-breweries-in-st-louis
Before August 24, 2007, the dog sighing under your patio table at a St. Louis restaurant was breaking city health rules. Not bending them. Breaking them. The city Health Department had kept dogs out of indoor and outdoor eateries for years, and it took a raid on the open-air dining area at the Forest Park Boathouse to shake the rule loose.
So the next time a server sets a steel bowl down on the concrete with that cold little clank, and your dog drinks so loudly the next table laughs, know that somebody fought for that sound. The leash looped twice around a chair leg, the sweating pint, the warm weight of a dog leaning on your shin while the sun drops behind the brick: in this city, that whole scene is legal because of one ordinance, and it still runs on one small rule most people never notice.
### Are there any dog friendly breweries in St. Louis?
Yes, and plenty of them treat a dog as a regular, not a nuisance. The thing that decides your afternoon is not the brewery’s reputation. It is the patio. St. Louis City Ordinance 67611, sponsored by Alderwoman Lyda Krewson, lets a food service establishment allow a customer to be accompanied by a dog in its permitted outdoor dining area, under certain conditions. The Board of Aldermen passed it 25 to 1. Read that again and you find the catch: outdoor dining area. Inside is a different question, and every place answers it for itself.
That is why the same city can feel wide open one Saturday and strangely closed the next. Krewson put it plainly when the bill passed: the restaurant owner has to post a sign saying whether they allow dogs. Owners can also ask you to remove a dog that is causing trouble. The sign is the real answer, not the review you read last spring.
Here is the part almost nobody mentions. The bill only got through after Krewson added a waterless hand sanitizer requirement, made owners responsible for any unsanitary condition caused by a dog, and let seven wards opt out. The city has since redrawn its wards, and I could not confirm which blocks, if any, still sit outside the rule. So skip the guesswork and do three things before the dog even sees the leash. Put a collapsible bowl, a bottle of water, a short leash and a few bags in the car. Pick two patios, not one, so a no at the first door doesn’t end the day, and check each place’s own page or call that morning, because a policy can change faster than any guide. Then, at the door, ask the host the one question the sign can’t answer: is the dog welcome at any outdoor table, or only a certain section? That question saves you the awkward shuffle with a full pint in one hand and sixty pounds of dog in the other.
### Where the bowls come out on their own
Start in Tower Grove South, on Holt Avenue, at Civil Life Brewing Co. at 3714 Holt Ave. Leashed, well-behaved dogs are welcome on its spacious outdoor patio, and the menu runs to chips and dips, soups and sandwiches, which matters when a dog is watching every bite you lift. Pour, sit, and feel the leash go slack as your dog finally lies down. Questions before you go can go to info@thecivillife.com.
Then head west to Francis Park in St. Louis Hills, where Rockwell Beer Garden sits by the lily pond. Walk the loop first so your dog has sniffed every tree, then settle in with a pint. On a crisp evening the fire pit snaps, the hollow tock of pickleball drifts over from the courts next door, and your dog drops its chin on your boot and watches the smoke. Bringing a group? Rockwell lets you reserve a fire pit party, and you can email hello@rockwellbeer.com to ask about the dog side of it first.
Urban Chestnut is the lesson in reading the patio, not the brewery. At the Grove Bierhall on Manchester Avenue the house lists a dog-friendly terrace and patio, and at the Midtown spot on Washington Avenue it lists a dog-friendly biergarten. Inside is off the table. Dogs used to wander the Grove hall until a Post-Dispatch writer saw a puddle on the floor and wrote about it, and the brewery ended indoor dogs after that. One puddle, one article, one new rule. It is a small story with a sharp point: every dog on a patio is quietly voting on whether the next dog gets in.
### When a patio isn’t enough for your dog
Some dogs don’t want to lie under a table. They want to run until their tongue hangs sideways. For them there is K9 Garden at 4565 McRee Ave, an indoor-outdoor dog park, bar and café with off-leash play areas, a climate-controlled indoor park and a spacious outdoor yard. Food and drinks can be ordered from the patio. Membership is required, and day passes are available, so you can try it once before you commit. Call (314) 530-9990 or email info@k9garden.com before you drive over to ask what the day pass needs from you and your dog.
The building has a history. It was the St. Louis home of Bar K, and after that closed, the owners of 4565 McRee and The Rail Apartments announced a new pet emporium and sports bar for the same site. Be honest with yourself about your dog before you go. A pack of strange dogs is heaven for a social one and a nightmare for a shy senior who would rather nap in the shade at Civil Life. If your dog flinches at a slammed door, pick the patio.
### The ten seconds that keep a patio dog-friendly
Every rule above comes down to what happens in the first ten seconds after you sit. Your dog smells fries at the next table and the leash goes tight. You can feel it in your wrist. That is the moment the staff is watching, whether they say so or not, because the ordinance lets an owner ask you to leave and nobody wants to be that table.
So tuck the leash short under your thigh. Bring your own collapsible bowl and a bottle of water so your dog isn’t sharing a communal bowl with the whole neighborhood. Keep paws on the ground, never on a chair. Carry more bags than you think you need. And if the barking starts and won’t stop, take a lap around the block. Leaving early once costs you half a pint. Staying costs every dog owner who comes after you.
Walked the dog past every patio on your street already? Fountain Park is a different walk worth taking.
### What that little sign is really promising you
Most people glance at the dog sign the way they glance at a fire exit. It deserves a second look, because the rules behind it explain why some patios feel so easy. To get the ordinance passed, the owner took on the job of cleaning up any unsanitary condition a dog leaves behind, and a waterless hand sanitizer requirement came along with it. That is why a good patio often has a pump bottle near the host stand and a staffer who arrives with paper towels before you can even apologize.
It also explains the flip side. A patio that says yes is taking a small risk on you every afternoon. When a dog lunges at a toddler’s pizza crust, or a puppy leaves a puddle by the rail, the owner is the one on the hook. After enough of those moments, the sign comes down, and nobody at the next table ever learns why. So when you see that sign, read it as a favor somebody is still willing to do, not a right you walked in with.
And if there is no sign at all? Ask. A ten-second question at the host stand is better than the slow walk back to the car with a confused dog and a pint you already paid for.
People are asking
### Can a dog go behind the bar at a St. Louis brewery or restaurant?
Not under Ordinance 67611, the city’s patio law: it lets a restaurant welcome a customer’s dog in an outdoor dining area only if the dog reaches it directly from the exterior and does not enter the interior, and it keeps the dog off any seat, table, countertop or similar surface and away from plates or utensils. So the shortcut through the taproom, past the taps and the smell of the fryer, is out: if the only way to the patio runs through the dining room, ask the host how to reach it from the street before your dog sets a paw inside.
### One easy dog day, start to finish
If you want a plan instead of a list, here is a day that works for most dogs. Start in the late morning with a long walk around Francis Park, past the lily pond, letting your dog check every bench and every tree trunk. By the time you reach Rockwell Beer Garden, the edge is off. Get a pint and a pizza, take a table in the shade, and let the dog stretch out on the cool ground while the pickleball paddles pop next door.
In the afternoon, if your dog still has gas in the tank and loves a crowd, drive over to K9 Garden on McRee and buy a day pass. Watch the play yard for a few minutes before you unclip the leash. You will know in a minute whether your dog is in heaven or wants to leave. Trust what you see.
Finish at Civil Life on Holt Avenue as the light goes gold, when the patio is full of conversation and the dogs are too tired to care about the next table’s sandwich. That last hour, with a quiet dog asleep against your foot and a cold glass in your hand, is the whole reason people in this city fought for the patio rule.
### Timing it so your dog actually relaxes
Saturday afternoon at a busy beer garden is loud: kids, strollers, a dozen dogs, somebody’s birthday. A social dog loves it. A nervous one shakes. If yours is the second kind, go on a weekday or right when the doors open, while the chairs are still cool and the staff has time to say hello. In July and August, put your palm on the concrete before your dog lies on it. If you can’t hold it there, find shade or come back in the evening.
Planning a patio day with your dog? Check the sign at the door, pack the bowl, and search St Louis Near Me Directory for patios, taprooms and dog-friendly stops near you before you load the car.
If you’re the taproom, the beer garden or the corner patio bar that puts the water bowls out every afternoon, dog owners want to know. A listing that says so is how you get more customers who walk in with a leash in one hand and a thirst for a second round. See how a listing works.
### More ways to fill a dog day in St. Louis
Beyond the brewery patios, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis covers the rest of the map, and dog-friendly restaurants in St. Louis covers sit-down patios with water bowls.
Making a full day of it? Let the dog run first at one of the dog parks in St. Louis, grab a treat at one of the dog bakeries in St. Louis on the way home, or stretch it into an overnight with dog-friendly getaways from St. Louis.
