Where to eat on South Grand
Beyond the Arch: unique things to do for adults
Two things settle whether a place is the real thing: what should I order at a dive bar without slowing the room down, and whether the dive bars making a comeback on every list are the ones that were here all along. A short list and a cheap pour answer both, and the comeback is mostly people noticing again.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between a regular bar and a dive bar?
A.  A dive bar is defined by being unpretentious rather than dirty. Compared with a regular bar, a dive keeps drinks cheap and poured strong, decor that is accidental and accumulated over decades, and a mix of neighborhood regulars. You come for the price and stay for the characters.
### Q. Are dive bars usually cash only?
A.  Often, yes. Many St. Louis dives are cash-only or strongly prefer cash, and some have unreliable card readers with no ATM nearby. Iowa Buffet is famously cash-only. Bringing cash is always smart: you’ll tip more easily and won’t get caught out if the machine is “down” for the night.
### Q. What not to order at a dive bar?
A.  Skip the cocktail menu and table service, because most dives don’t offer either. Order a beer or a simple well drink, keep it uncomplicated, and you’ll fit right in. Don’t expect a list of craft anything; these are neighborhood bars built for cheap, strong pours, not mixology.
### Q. What is the oldest bar in St. Louis MO?
A.  Pop’s Blue Moon (5249 Pattison, near the Hill) is the one locals most often name among the oldest bars in the city. It’s reportedly built partly from lumber salvaged from the 1904 World’s Fair. Several old corner taverns go back generations, but Pop’s wins for sheer history and cheap drinks.
### Q. Which St. Louis dive bar has the best pinball?
A.  The Silver Ballroom (4701 Morgan Ford, Bevo) is the pinball dive: a full wall of well-maintained machines, horror-movie decor, and a punk-and-metal atmosphere. Tick Tock Tavern in Tower Grove also has pinball and a photo booth. For a night built around games and cheap drinks, the Silver Ballroom is the pick.
### Q. What’s the best dive bar in St. Louis for live music?
A.  The Heavy Anchor (5226 Gravois, Dutchtown) pairs a comfortable dive bar with a back-room music venue hosting local bands, comedy, and trivia. Nick’s Pub in Dogtown and Pop’s Blue Moon also feature live music regularly. For a genuine dive-bar-plus-stage experience, the Heavy Anchor is the most reliable bet on any given night.
### Q. Is The Venice Cafe really a dive bar?
A.  Sort of: it has dive prices and an unpretentious, come-as-you-are crowd, but it’s wrapped in one of the most extraordinary settings in St. Louis, a mosaic-and-found-object outsider-art wonderland with a legendary patio. Think of it as a dive with a soul and an art budget. It’s a must-visit either way.
### Q. What should I order at a dive bar?
A.  Whatever is on tap and cheap, or a simple pour with one mixer. Dive bars are built around a short list done fast, and a complicated cocktail order slows a one-bartender room down. If there is a kitchen and it has been there for decades, order from it.
### Q. Are dive bars expensive?
A.  That is close to the definition — if the drinks are priced like a cocktail lounge, it is a themed bar wearing the look. Expect to pay noticeably less than downtown, expect cash to be welcome or required, and expect the tip to matter more than the tab.
### Q. What is a dirty dive bar?
A.  Usually a compliment about wear rather than an actual hygiene complaint: scuffed floors, taped stools, decades of stickers. Worn is character; sticky is a warning. The bars that last are the ones where the room looks its age and the glassware does not.
### Q. Are dive bars making a comeback?
A.  They never left here, which is why this list exists. What has changed is attention — rising prices elsewhere sent people looking for a cheap stool and a jukebox, and the corner bars that survived the last twenty years were waiting. The risk now is imitation rather than extinction.

## Eight Stories Up, for Free: The Great River Road From Alton to Grafton
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/great-river-road-best-stops-from-alton-to-grafton
Eight stories above the Mississippi, the wind finds the gap at the top of your jacket. Below the railing, a towboat shoves a raft of barges into the lock, so slowly you hear the engine long before you see it gain a foot.
Nobody charged you to stand up here.
Free, public tours of the Melvin Price Locks and Dam leave from the National Great Rivers Museum in East Alton every day at 10 a.m., 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., and they begin promptly. Only 25 people get on each public tour. Groups of 10 or more call the Alton Visitor Center at 1-800-258-6645 to schedule a tour outside those times; everyone else, just get there early.
The main lock down there is 1,200 feet long, built for tows of up to 15 barges at once, and Melvin Price is one of the largest locks on the Mississippi River. What rides through it is the stuff on your table and under your tires: soybeans, corn, grain, asphalt.
You can drive past it for years and never know you are allowed up there. The same goes for the road’s other famous sight, on the bluff above Route 100 in Alton: the red-eyed monster on the bluff that every car slows down for.
That monster is a copy. The Piasa Bird you will photograph was repainted on the cliff in the 1990s. The one Father Marquette described in 1673 had nearly disappeared from exposure to the elements by around 1700, and rock quarrying and powder mills chewed into the bluffs through the 19th century, possibly destroying the very stone it was painted on. In between, it came back as colorful paintings and even metal cutouts.
Send that to whoever is driving. Then start the day on top of the dam and follow the river west to Grafton.
### Is the Great River Road worth it?
Yes, if you give it a whole day and start early. The drive is short, but the stops are not: the visitor bureau says to allow at least 1 1/2 hours for the National Great Rivers Museum and the lock and dam alone. Catch the 10 a.m. tour, eat lunch in Alton, and save Elsah, the Grafton SkyTour, the Brussels Ferry and Pere Marquette State Park for the afternoon. In January and February, bald eagles winter there in the hundreds.
### Under the barge, then up top
Inside the museum, walk under the life-size barge frame and look up. Standing beneath it is the fastest way to feel how vast one barge really is, and then remember the lock outside takes 15 of them.
The National Great Rivers Museum sits at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam, at 2 Lock and Dam Way in East Alton, and it is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Plan on 45 minutes to an hour for the tour itself, a half-mile walk, and a climb to heights of about 80 feet. The Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau says to allow at least 1 1/2 hours to visit both the museum and the locks and dam, so do not book lunch tight.
Wear real walking shoes and bring a layer, because the half-mile is outside and the top is exposed. Kill the wait before the tour inside: there is an exhibit where you try for yourself to move the water in the locks to balance the levels, which is exactly what you are about to watch happen for real, from the top. Our guide to the Melvin Price Locks and Dam covers what to know before you go.
### Lunch at the bar that sells a thousand burgers a day
Back in Alton, push open the door of the yellow brick building on the corner of 4th, Pearl and Broadway and the noise hits you first: a band tuning up, glasses knocking, somebody yelling an order over the grill smoke. Anheuser Busch opened it in 1921. Today it is Fast Eddie’s Bon Air, with live music and cheap eats like peel-n-eat shrimp, and its own history page claims an average of 1,000 burgers sold per day. It also says nearly 7,000 people celebrate their 21st birthday there every year, which tells you two things: it is loud, and you must be 21 to walk in. If the kids are along, our rundown of where to eat in Alton has the sit-down places instead.
### The monster on the bluff is a copy
Roll west out of downtown Alton on Route 100 and the bluff comes up on your right. The Mississippi spreads wide and brown on your left, and then there it is, painted high on the limestone: a red-eyed, winged thing with antlers, staring down at your windshield.
That is the Piasa Bird, and the story behind it goes back to 1673. When Father Jacques Marquette came down the Mississippi with Louis Jolliet that year, he described the Piasa as a bird-like monster painted high on the bluffs near what is now Alton. In Marquette’s telling, it was as large as a calf, with antlers like a deer, red eyes and a beard like a tiger’s. The painting you are looking at went up in the 1990s, high on the cliff where it watches over the river and the road. Look past it at the water. That brown, wide river is the one Marquette came down.
Pull over where it is safe and take the photo.
### Elsah, the village that stopped the clock
Turn off the engine in Elsah and the first thing you notice is the quiet. Watch for the small turn, because it is easy to miss. The road dips into a narrow valley between the bluffs and there it all is: stone walls, steep roofs, a church steeple, the river hidden behind the trees. James Semple founded the village in 1852, and Elsah was one of the first villages added to the National Register of Historic Places in its entirety, 48 buildings from the 19th century, all of it tucked into that one small valley.
Park and walk it. Put your hand on a stone wall in the shade and it is cool even in August. A slow loop is enough to see the whole village, and you will hear your own footsteps on the street the entire time.
### Grafton, from the chairlift
The chair swings a little when it scoops you up, and then the ground just falls away. Grafton sits where the Illinois River meets the Mississippi, and the best way to understand that is from above. The Grafton SkyTour carries you to the top of the hill near Aerie’s winery, and Aerie’s Resort sits on a bluff overlooking the confluence. A day pass is $12 a person with unlimited rides that day, in an open chair or an enclosed gondola cabin. Riders under 48 inches tall need to ride with someone who is at least 48 inches.
Pick the open chair if the weather lets you. Your feet dangle over the treetops, the lift hums under you, and the two rivers open up below like a map somebody unrolled across the valley. Aerie’s Alpine Coaster, with nearly 4,000 feet of track, is there if anyone in the car still has energy.
Back down in town, walk the riverfront, find a patio, and let the afternoon slow down. Grafton is built for exactly that.
Opposite direction, we know, but Sullivan’s restaurants are worth the drive.
### Cross on the free ferry
The steel ramp clanks under your front tires as you roll on. About a mile past Grafton, the Brussels Ferry crosses the Illinois River from Route 100 to Calhoun County near Brussels. The Illinois Department of Transportation owns and runs it, it is free, and it operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week. You drive onto the deck, cut the engine, and for a few minutes the only sound is the motor and the river slapping the hull. Even if you have nowhere to be in Calhoun County, the ride is the point. Our guide to ferries near St. Louis covers the other crossings and how to check that a boat is running before you drive to the landing.
### Finish at Pere Marquette
Last stop: Pere Marquette State Park. Walk into the lodge even if you are not staying. The Civilian Conservation Corps built it in the 1930s, and the stone fireplace in the lobby rises to a roof height of 50 feet and is said to weigh 700 tons. Stand in front of it on a cold day and you can feel the heat on your face from across the room.
Outside, the park offers horseback riding, camping, hiking, fishing, hunting and boating, with views of the Illinois River and its backwaters from points atop the bluffs. Climb to one of those overlooks late in the day and watch the light go copper on the water before you head home.
### Come back in January for the eagles
January on the river is a gloves-on, breath-in-the-air kind of cold. If you only make this drive once, make it twice. Start the winter trip at the dam again, because the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau calls Melvin Price a great place to watch American bald eagles as they hunt on the Mississippi. In January and February, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources says Pere Marquette is a hotspot for bald eagle watching, with wintering bald eagles in the hundreds along the Mississippi and lower Illinois River near the park. Bring binoculars and a thermos. Scan the bare trees along the river for a white head that does not move, then wait. Sooner or later one drops off the branch and skims the water, and the whole car goes silent.
### How to run the day without rushing it
The whole trick is the 10 a.m. tour. Leave St. Louis early enough to be standing in the museum lobby well before the 10 a.m. tour, and you will be back on the ground before the lunch crowd fills the stools at Fast Eddie’s. If you miss it, the 1 p.m. tour works just as well, and you simply flip the order: lunch first, dam second.
After lunch, give the drive itself room. The stretch of Route 100 between Alton and Grafton is short, but it is the part people remember, so do not treat it like a commute. Pull off where it is safe and legal, roll the windows down, and let the river noise into the car. Elsah is a short walk. Grafton can take the whole afternoon if you let it, and you should.
Save the ferry and the lodge for last. The ferry is a short crossing that feels like a much bigger trip, and the lodge is where the day winds down: boots on stone, the smell of wood smoke in winter, tired kids sprawled on a bench in the great room. If you time the overlook for the end of the afternoon, the drive home comes with the sun going down over the river behind you.
Pack a few things the night before. Binoculars, even in summer, because the bluffs are full of birds. A jacket for the top of the dam and the chairlift, where it is always windier than it looks from the ground. Cash and cards both. And a full tank, so the only stops you make are the ones you want.
One last tip for St. Louisans who think they have done this drive already: do it in a different season. The road in October, with the bluffs gone orange and gold, and the road in January, with eagles hunched in bare trees, feel like two different places. Neither one looks anything like the road on a hot summer weekend, when the patios are full and the river is busy with boats.
Want more river towns and easy escapes like this one? Explore more of the region on our maps and line up your next day trip before the eagles come back.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you see bald eagles in Alton, Illinois?
A.  Yes. In January and February the river corridor up from Alton is eagle country. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources calls Pere Marquette State Park a hotspot for bald eagle watching in those months, with wintering eagles in the hundreds along the Mississippi and lower Illinois River near the park. Go early and bring binoculars.
### Q. What is the myth of the Piasa Bird?
A.  The Piasa is a winged monster painted on the bluff above Route 100 in Alton. Father Jacques Marquette, on his 1673 trip down the Mississippi with Louis Jolliet, described it as a bird-like monster painted high on the bluffs: as large as a calf, with antlers like a deer, red eyes and a beard like a tiger’s. The original had nearly disappeared by around 1700, and the painting you see today was repainted on the cliff in the 1990s.
### Q. Where does the Brussels Ferry take you?
A.  Across the Illinois River. The ferry sits about a mile west of Grafton and links Illinois Route 100 to Calhoun County, near Brussels. The Illinois Department of Transportation runs it free, 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
### Q. What is there to do at Pere Marquette State Park?
A.  Horseback riding, camping, hiking, fishing, hunting and boating, plus bluff-top views of the Illinois River. Do not skip the lodge the Civilian Conservation Corps built in the 1930s, with its 700-ton stone fireplace. In January and February, it is one of the best places on the route to see bald eagles.
### Q. How much is the Grafton Sky Tour?
A.  A day pass is $12 per person and covers unlimited rides that day, in an open chair or an enclosed cabin. A SkyTour Passport is $59.99 per person for unlimited rides for 365 days from purchase.
### Q. What is the history of Elsah, Illinois?
A.  James Semple founded Elsah in 1852. It was one of the first villages added to the National Register of Historic Places in its entirety, with 48 19th-century buildings tucked into a small valley between the bluffs.
### Q. What two rivers meet in Grafton, Illinois?
A.  The Mississippi and the Illinois. Aerie’s Resort sits on a bluff overlooking the confluence of the two, above downtown Grafton. Ride the Grafton SkyTour up and you can see why Aerie’s calls it The Best View in the Midwest.

## 58 Inches or 54: The Kart Line at St. Louis Fun Centers
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-family-fun-centers-across-the-st-louis-suburbs
A Honda engine coughs awake behind the fence at Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton, and your kid is already walking toward the kart gate with his chin up. Then he backs against the height sign. Fifty-eight inches. That is the line to drive a single kart there, and the driver also has to be at least 10 years old. Miss it by a finger and he rides shotgun in a double kart with a grown-up, or he watches.
Every parent in the metro has lived some version of that moment: the long drive, the wristband, the face that falls at the measuring post. It is avoidable. The rules that decide whether your day goes well are printed on each fun center’s own website, and almost nobody reads them before loading the car. This guide does, place by place, from Fenton and Town and Country to Richmond Heights and across the river to Belleville and Edwardsville.
### What are the best family fun centers near St. Louis?
Ask the parents at a soccer sideline where to take kids for fun in St. Louis and you hear the same five places, usually with a story attached about a meltdown at a height sign or a kid who would not leave the arcade. Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton mixes indoor and outdoor fun, with go-karts, mini golf and bumper boats. Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country runs karts, laser tag and a ropes course with no admission charge. Tropicana Lanes in Richmond Heights is the old-school bowling house. On the Illinois side, The Edge in Belleville puts everything under one roof, and Edison’s Entertainment Complex in Edwardsville packs bowling, laser tag and a massive arcade into one building.
The best one for your family is the one whose height rules, hours and prices fit the kids you actually have. That is where the rest of this page earns its keep.
### The number on the post decides the day
Measure your kids at home, in socks, against the kitchen doorframe, before you pick a place. The two big kart tracks on the Missouri side draw their lines in different spots, and four inches is a lot of birthday disappointment.
At Swing-A-Round in Fenton, a single-kart driver must be 58 inches tall and at least 10. Younger or shorter kids who are 3 or older and at least 36 inches can ride in a double kart with an adult driver who is 16 or older. The kiddie karts take drivers from 35 inches and are recommended for ages 3 to 8. Those karts run on 9 hp Honda engines at speeds up to 20 mph around a quarter mile with four turns, a tunnel and a bridge, and in the winter months they only run when it is warmer than 50 degrees outside.
At Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country, the single pro kart line is lower: age 10 and 54 inches. Kids between 7 and 11 can drive a junior kart, and a double-kart passenger has to be between 35 and 54 inches tall with a driver who is 18 or older. So the tall nine-year-old who strikes out in Fenton can still drive in Town and Country, and the short ten-year-old who cannot reach 58 inches may clear 54. That one comparison has saved more than one birthday.
### The free birthday pass most parents never hear about
Picture the counter on a birthday: a kid in a paper crown, a parent digging through a purse, a line forming behind you. Swing-A-Round runs a Birthday Club, and it is free to join. Members get a complimentary 2-hour Fun Pass on their birthday at the Fenton location, covering go-karts, mini golf, kiddie karts, bumper cars and boats, and the indoor playground. Winter birthdays, or bad-weather ones, get a $10 arcade card and two hours of bumper cars and the indoor playground instead.
Here is the catch that sends families home annoyed. You have to register for the pass, kids under 13 must be signed up by a parent, and you bring the confirmation email plus proof of the birthday when you come in. For children, that means an original or certified copy of a state- or hospital-issued birth certificate. The club’s own page says school IDs and kids’ security IDs will not be accepted. Put the birth certificate in the glove box the night before and the day stays free.
### The cheapest hours are printed on the door
Walk into a bowling alley before lunch and you can hear your own ball roll. Fun centers price the clock. The same lane, the same arcade and the same laser tag arena cost less when the building is quiet, and the deals are posted, not secret.
Tropicana Lanes runs an Early Bird Special from Sunday to Friday, 10am-1pm, at $3 per game. Edison’s in Edwardsville sells a Doorbuster pass for the first three hours of any day: laser tag, arcade and one hour of bowling, all for $22, and a Doorcloser pass on Sunday evenings from 4pm-8pm at the same price. The Edge in Belleville shows every movie for $6 every Tuesday and Wednesday in its Grand and Bistro theatres, holidays excepted. And Swing-A-Round sells a 3-hour Fun Pass at $29.99 a person that bundles the go-karts, mini golf, bumper boats, kiddie karts and the indoor playground.
Where can children go for free? The pay-to-play places above are not the only answer. Admission to the Saint Louis Zoo is free, and the Saint Louis Science Center says entry is always free. On a gray afternoon when the budget is spent, those two are still open to you.
### Missouri side: karts, lanes and a ropes course
### Swing-A-Round Fun Town, Fenton
Swing-A-Round has served the St. Louis area for more than 30 years, and it still feels like the summer you remember: the slap of bumper boats, the ping of the batting cages and the whine of karts coming out of the tunnel. It runs three mini golf courses, bumper boats, batting cages it calls St. Louis’ largest, bumper cars and an arcade inside a 12,000 square foot indoor facility. Single karts cost $9 for the driver, $2 per passenger and $6 for kiddie karts. It is at 335 Skinker in Fenton, 636-349-7077, and there is a second location at 3541 Veterans Memorial in St. Charles, 636-947-4487.
### Amp Up Action Park, Town and Country
Amp Up is the place for the kid who wants to go fast and the parent who does not want to pay to stand around. There is no admission charge: you pay as you go for the activities, food and drinks you choose, and the viewing area for people who only want to watch is free. Beyond the karts there is three-level laser tag, an elevated ropes challenge, axe throwing for ages 14 and up, patio games and pickleball.
### Tropicana Lanes, Richmond Heights
Tropicana has been a St. Louis bowling tradition since 1960, and you can hear it from the parking lot: the rumble of a ball down one of its 52 lanes and the crash of pins a beat later. Bumpers and assist ramps are available, so a preschooler can push a ball down the ramp and watch it actually reach the pins. Hourly bowling covers up to 5 people per lane, and the party menu leans local, with toasted ravioli next to the pizza and sliders. It is at 7960 Clayton Rd, (314) 781-0282.
### Illinois side: the two big rooms across the river
### The Edge, Belleville
The Edge is 85,000 square feet under one roof, and its centerpiece is Laser Rock, a multi-level laser tag arena of more than 14,000 square feet that can play up to 60 people at once. Picture a pack of cousins in vests shouting across ramps in the dark. Add go-karts, bowling, bumper cars, VR, an arcade and movie theaters, and a mixed-age group can split up and still meet for food. It is at 701 South Belt West, 618-236-2101.
Want more places to burn off a whole afternoon’s worth of energy? Browse the St Louis Near Me directory for family attractions and things to do across the metro, then check each one’s height and age rules before you drive.
If you run the kart track, the bowling house or the party room, the parent reading this is deciding where to spend the afternoon right now. List your place with us and get more customers from families who have already made up their minds to go out.
### Edison’s Entertainment Complex, Edwardsville
Edison’s is the polished one. Its Pharaoh’s Quest laser tag sends kids through an ancient-Egypt arena of 4,000 square feet, with sarcophagi and catacombs. There are more than 70 arcade games, from air hockey and Skee-Ball to VR, and bowling lanes with huge projection screens and automatic bumpers. It has eight party and event spaces and a full-service restaurant. It is at 2477 S. State Route 157, 618-307-9020.
### How to pick the right one for your crew
Match the place to the shortest kid, not the oldest. If your youngest is too short for a single kart, lean on the kiddie karts and the indoor playground at Swing-A-Round, or a double kart at Amp Up. If everyone clears the line, the speed and the laser tag open up. If money is the tight part, plan around the early hours at Tropicana and Edison’s, or the free birthday pass. If the weather is ugly, head for the indoor rooms in Richmond Heights, Belleville or Edwardsville, since Swing-A-Round’s karts stop below 50 degrees.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where to take kids for fun in St. Louis?
A.  For go-karts and mini golf, Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton. For karts, laser tag and a ropes course with no admission charge, Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country. For bowling, Tropicana Lanes in Richmond Heights. For everything under one roof, The Edge in Belleville or Edison’s in Edwardsville. Check height rules before you go.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in St. Louis with a baby?
A.  Most fun-center rides have a height floor, so a baby is a passenger to the day, not a player. The free options carry the most value here: admission to the Saint Louis Zoo is free, and entry to the Saint Louis Science Center is always free, so you can leave the moment nap time hits without feeling you wasted a ticket.
### Q. How to have fun with kids without spending money?
A.  Start with the free doors: the Saint Louis Zoo and the Saint Louis Science Center. At Amp Up Action Park, watching from the viewing area costs nothing, which works for a sibling who is too small to drive. And if a birthday is coming, Swing-A-Round’s free Birthday Club pass covers two hours in Fenton.
### Q. Where can children go for free?
A.  The Saint Louis Zoo, where admission is free, and the Saint Louis Science Center, where entry is always free. On their birthday, Swing-A-Round Birthday Club members get a complimentary 2-hour Fun Pass at the Fenton location, as long as you register first and bring the right proof of age.
### Q. How much does it cost to open a family entertainment center?
A.  I could not find a St. Louis figure I would stand behind, and national numbers swing wildly with building size and attractions. The honest way to price one is to get real quotes for the lease or land, the attractions you want, insurance and staffing, and to study how local centers price by the hour, the game and the pass.
### Q. Are family entertainment centers profitable?
A.  They can be, but notice how the St. Louis-area centers make the math work: party packages, food and drink, and off-peak deals like early-bird bowling and first-three-hours passes that fill quiet hours. Busy weekends alone rarely carry a building that big.
### Q. How to open a family entertainment center?
A.  Pick the anchor attraction first, because karts, laser tag and bowling each need very different space. Then check zoning and permits with the city or county where you want to build, line up insurance before you sign a lease, and plan the party rooms and the kitchen early. Every center on this page leans on birthdays and groups.

## Best Tutoring and Learning Centers Across the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-tutoring-and-learning-centers-across-the-st-louis-metro
Report cards come home, and suddenly the kitchen table turns into a battleground. Maybe it is fractions in third grade, or chemistry that stopped making sense in October, or the looming ACT that decides which scholarships your high schooler qualifies for. If you have ever Googled “math help near me” at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, you are in very good company across the St. Louis metro.
The good news: the region is loaded with quality tutoring and learning centers, and they are spread out from St. Charles County to the Illinois Metro-East. You do not have to drive downtown or settle for whoever a neighbor happened to mention. Here is a practical look at where to find help, how to choose, and what it actually costs.
### When it is time to get a tutor
A rough patch on one quiz is normal. The signs that point toward outside help are more persistent: grades sliding two quarters in a row, homework that triggers tears or shutdowns, a kid who says “I am just bad at math” (a confidence problem, not an ability one), or a standardized test on the calendar with real stakes attached. Tutoring is not a punishment or an admission of failure. It is the same logic as hiring a swim coach. Some skills are easier to build with a trained outside eye.
The other common trigger is timing. Reading and math gaps compound. A second grader who never locked in place value will struggle with long division in fourth grade and algebra in eighth. Catching it early is almost always cheaper and faster than catching it late.
### The national learning centers, town by town
The familiar chains run on proven systems, and the St. Louis suburbs have plenty of them. What matters is finding the specific location near you, because quality and hours vary by franchise owner.
Mathnasium focuses purely on math, K-12 through pre-calculus, with a free assessment that maps a student's exact gaps before any lessons begin. You will find centers in St. Charles, St. Peters (the St. Peters North location on Mexico Road), and Kirkwood (technically on Manchester Road in Des Peres, serving Kirkwood and Webster Groves families). Across the river, Mathnasium of O'Fallon, Illinois serves the Metro-East including Belleville families.
Kumon takes a different angle: a worksheet-based, self-paced method in both math and reading that builds independent study habits over the long haul. Metro centers include Chesterfield (on Olive Boulevard), Wildwood, Manchester (located in Ballwin on Manchester Road), and Clayton (on Ladue Road). Kumon tends to reward consistency. It is a marathon, not a quick fix.
Sylvan Learning covers the widest subject range: math, reading, writing, science, and ACT/SAT prep, with personalized plans tied to local school curriculum. The Ballwin center serves Ballwin, Chesterfield, and Kirkwood, there is a dedicated Chesterfield location, and Sylvan of O'Fallon, Illinois serves the Metro-East. Sylvan is a strong pick when a student needs help across several subjects rather than just one.
### Local independents and specialized programs
The national chains aren’t the whole picture. St. Louis has homegrown independents and specialty programs that fill gaps the big brands don’t. Mackler Associates in Frontenac is a longtime local name in academic tutoring and ACT/SAT prep, the kind of established, one-location practice families pass along by word of mouth. Huntington Learning Center, another established brand with metro locations, runs K-12 tutoring and intensive, diagnostic-driven test prep, and is often a fit when a student needs a structured, results-focused plan rather than casual help.
A different category worth knowing: Brain Balance, which has a presence in the metro, is not subject tutoring at all — it’s a drug-free program aimed at focus, attention, and behavior for kids who struggle to sit still and absorb material in the first place. If the real obstacle is attention rather than the algebra itself, a focus-and-executive-function program can matter more than another hour of math. Beyond any brand, plenty of independent one-on-one tutors — retired teachers, graduate students, and subject specialists — work across the metro, and they often cost less and flex around your schedule.
### Match the help to the subject
The best choice depends on what’s actually hard. For reading struggles or dyslexia, look specifically for a tutor or center trained in a structured, multisensory method like Orton-Gillingham — it’s the researched approach for stubborn reading gaps, and not every general tutor offers it. For math, a diagnostic center that pinpoints the exact missing building block usually beats generic homework help. For writing, you want someone who’ll coach the process, not just fix a paper the night before it’s due. And for ACT and SAT prep, ask about real practice tests, score tracking, and whether the tutor knows the current test format cold. Naming the specific problem before you shop saves money and false starts.
Unrelated, and we know it — Collinsville’s local-search page is right here.
### Lower-cost and free options first
Before you commit to a monthly membership, know that real help exists for little or nothing. Most St. Louis County Library and St. Louis Public Library branches offer free homework help and, in many cases, free live online tutoring with a library card. Many high schools run National Honor Society peer tutoring at no cost, and area universities often have students who tutor affordably. Online, Khan Academy is genuinely free and strong for math and test prep. None of this replaces a dedicated center when a student has a deep, persistent gap — but for a single tough unit or a confidence dip, the free tier is often all you need, and it’s the honest first stop before spending real money.
### Making tutoring actually work at home
The center does the teaching, but whether it sticks is decided at your kitchen table. Kids read the adults around them, so the single most useful thing a parent can do is frame tutoring as normal and even a little enviable — the academic version of a coach — rather than a punishment for a bad report card. Protect the sessions like any other commitment; the families who see results are almost never the ones who cancel every time something else comes up. Ask your tutor what to reinforce between visits, and keep it light: ten focused minutes a night beats a tense hour on Sunday. And watch for the real early win, which usually isn’t a grade at all — it’s a kid who stops saying “I’m bad at this” and starts asking questions again. Confidence tends to arrive before the A does, and it’s the thing that keeps the A coming.
### What to ask on the free assessment
Nearly every center offers a free assessment or trial, and it’s the best hour you’ll spend before committing a dime. Go in with questions. Ask who will actually work with your child — a certified teacher, a trained staffer, or a college student — and whether it’s the same person each week, because continuity matters more than credentials for a nervous kid. Ask how they measure progress and how often you’ll hear about it. Ask about the total cost, including any registration, assessment, and materials fees stacked on top of the monthly rate, and about the cancellation policy before you sign anything. Then watch the room: are the other kids engaged or bored, is the staff warm or rote? Trust your read on how your own child responds in that first session — it tells you more than any brochure.
### In-person versus online
Most of these centers now offer both. In-person wins for younger kids, students who are easily distracted, and anyone who needs the structure of a dedicated space away from home and phones. Online works well for busy high schoolers, families juggling several activities, and rural-edge towns where the nearest center is a 25-minute drive. Online math tutoring has improved a lot. Shared digital whiteboards mean a tutor can watch a student work a problem in real time, the same as sitting beside them. If you are unsure, many centers let you start in person and shift online later, or mix the two.
### How to choose the right one
Match the method to the kid. A worksheet system like Kumon suits a disciplined child who needs reps. A diagnostic, plan-driven center suits a student with specific gaps to close. Ask how they assess and how they measure progress.
Ask about the tutors. Are they certified teachers, college students, or trained staff? There is no single right answer, but you deserve a clear one.
Visit before you commit. Take the free assessment most centers offer. Watch how they talk to your child. Warmth matters as much as credentials.
Check the contract. Understand the monthly cost, the minimum commitment, and the cancellation policy before you sign.
Mind the drive. A center two towns over with a perfect program still loses if you cannot reliably get there twice a week. Convenience drives consistency, and consistency drives results.
### What it costs
Expectations help. Center-based memberships in the St. Louis metro generally run in the range of a few hundred dollars a month for two to three sessions a week, depending on the brand, subject, and session length. Private one-on-one tutors often charge by the hour, which can be cheaper for a quick fix but adds up fast for ongoing help. Intensive ACT or SAT prep packages are usually priced separately and can be a meaningful investment, though a score bump that unlocks scholarship money frequently pays for itself many times over. Always ask about assessment fees, materials fees, and any registration cost on top of the monthly rate.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does tutoring cost in the St. Louis area?
A.  Center memberships commonly fall in the few-hundred-dollars-per-month range for two or three weekly sessions, while private hourly tutors vary widely. Test-prep packages are typically priced on their own. Always confirm the total, including any assessment or materials fees, before enrolling.
### Q. What age should my child start tutoring?
A.  There is no single right age. Some families start as early as kindergarten to build reading and number sense, while others wait until a specific subject becomes a struggle. The better question is whether a real gap exists. If it does, earlier is almost always easier and less expensive than later.
### Q. Is online tutoring as effective as in-person?
A.  For motivated, focused students, yes. Online sessions with shared whiteboards let a tutor watch and guide work in real time. Younger children and easily distracted students usually do better in person, where the structure of a dedicated space keeps them on task.
### Q. How long until I see results?
A.  Most families notice improved confidence within a few weeks, with grade improvements typically following over a semester of consistent attendance. Worksheet-based programs reward the long haul. Targeted gap-closing and test prep can move faster. Consistency is the biggest single factor.
### Q. Should I pick a chain or an independent tutor?
A.  Chains offer proven systems, structured assessments, and accountability. Independent tutors can offer more flexibility and a personal touch. Neither is automatically better. Match the format to your child's needs, your budget, and your schedule.
### Q. How do I find help for a specific need like reading, dyslexia, or ACT prep?
A.  Match the specialist to the problem. For reading struggles or dyslexia, look for a tutor trained in a structured, multisensory method such as Orton-Gillingham. For the ACT or SAT, ask about full practice tests and score tracking, and confirm the tutor knows the current format. Longtime local independents like Mackler Associates and diagnostic centers like Huntington are common starting points for test prep.
### Q. Are there free or low-cost tutoring options in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. St. Louis County and St. Louis Public Library branches offer free homework help and often free live online tutoring with a library card, many high schools run free National Honor Society peer tutoring, and Khan Academy is free online for math and test prep. These are a smart first stop for a single tough unit before you pay for a monthly membership.

## The Best Local Credit Unions in the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-local-credit-unions-in-the-st-louis-metro
The bank statement finally lands on a Saturday morning. There it is: a $12 “maintenance” fee, an ATM charge, a savings rate that rounds to nothing. Then a neighbor in Florissant mentions the car she just financed through her credit union — a full point below what your big bank quoted. You start doing the math on how many years you’ve been leaving money on the table.
St. Louis is a good place to fix that. Both sides of the river are thick with strong, member-owned credit unions, several founded right here for local workers and neighborhoods. This guide walks through the best of them across the metro: who’s allowed to join each one, and why so many St. Louisans quietly bank this way.
### What Makes a Credit Union Different From a Bank
The short version: a credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative that’s owned by its members, not by outside shareholders. When you open an account, you become a part-owner with a vote. Because there are no stockholders to pay, the money a credit union earns flows back to members as lower loan rates, higher savings rates, and fewer fees. A bank, by contrast, answers to investors who expect a profit.
That difference shows up in real numbers. According to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the federal regulator, credit unions nationally averaged a 6.27% rate on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and paid 3.26% on a one-year $10,000 CD versus 2.41% at banks (NCUA, 2025). On a car loan or a mortgage, a point or more adds up to real money over the life of the loan.
And your money is just as safe. Deposits at federally insured credit unions are protected up to $250,000 by the NCUA — the credit-union equivalent of FDIC insurance, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. The coverage amount is identical to a bank’s; only the insuring agency’s name changes.
### The St. Louis–Headquartered Credit Unions
These are the home-grown institutions — founded and headquartered in the St. Louis area, most now open to anyone who lives or works in the metro.
First Community Credit Union (Chesterfield) is the largest credit union headquartered in St. Louis — roughly $4.78 billion in assets, more than 408,000 members, and about 42 branches. It celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024, and its community charter covers St. Louis City plus a wide sweep of Missouri and Illinois counties, so most metro residents can join.
Together Credit Union (St. Louis) began in 1939 as the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union — a beer-industry credit union that grew into a roughly $2.64-billion institution with about 145,000 members and 26 branches. It rebranded to Together in 2020 and is now a founding and official banking partner of St. Louis CITY SC. Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families.
Vantage Credit Union (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, worship, or attend school in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois.
Neighbors Credit Union (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro.
Alliance Credit Union (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river.
### A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers
The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign.
West Community Credit Union (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. Alltru Credit Union (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County.
And there’s a big new entrant: CommunityAmerica Credit Union, Missouri’s largest credit union at roughly $5 billion in assets, planted its flag in St. Louis by merging in Electro Savings Credit Union on January 1, 2025. It now runs branches in Maryland Heights, Manchester, South County, and St. Peters, with membership eligibility inherited from Electro’s metro charter.
### The Metro East (Illinois) Anchors
Cross the river and the Metro East has its own strong, locally rooted credit unions.
Scott Credit Union (Edwardsville) is the Metro East’s largest home-grown credit union, with roots at Scott Air Force Base and a field of membership spanning more than 30 Illinois and Missouri counties; a $5 minimum share opens the door. 1st MidAmerica Credit Union (Bethalto) serves around 64,000 members across some 21 Illinois counties from about 10 branches, and recently expanded into Granite City through a local merger. Both are worth a look if you live or work on the Illinois side of the river, and both reflect a whole-metro reality: “local” in St. Louis stretches well into Illinois.
### A St. Louis Story Worth Telling: St. Louis Community Credit Union
If you want a credit union that doubles as a force for the neighborhoods, St. Louis Community Credit Union is the standout. With about $427 million in assets and more than 51,000 members across 14 branches, it’s the region’s largest CDFI and one of the nation’s larger Minority Depository Institutions — meaning it deliberately banks underserved parts of North City and North County that big banks have long overlooked.
The impact is concrete: more than $40 million in business loans, roughly 90% of them to Black-owned businesses, plus payday-loan alternatives and its “Sure Rides” affordable auto-loan program. It even reopened a historic Gateway branch honoring one of the nation’s first African American–owned banks. For a lot of St. Louisans, joining here is as much a vote for the community as it is a smart financial move.
### How to Choose — and How Membership Works
The old idea that you need a special connection to join a credit union is mostly history. Every credit union has a “field of membership” — the rules for who can join — but most of the St. Louis institutions above now hold a community charter, which typically means anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a given county is eligible. In practice, nearly every metro resident qualifies for several of these.
To choose, start with what you actually do at a bank. Want branches near your home and work? Compare locations. Carry a car loan or plan to buy a house? Compare loan rates. Keep a big savings balance? Compare CD and savings rates. Also ask whether the credit union participates in the CO-OP shared-branching and ATM network, which lets members use thousands of other credit unions’ branches and surcharge-free ATMs nationwide — a quiet perk that makes a local credit union feel a lot bigger than its branch count. Opening an account usually takes a small deposit (often $5 to $25) that represents your ownership share.
Wildly off-topic — here’s downtown St. Louis, block by block.
### Are There Any Downsides?
To be fair, credit unions aren’t perfect for everyone. Because membership is tied to a field of membership, you have to be eligible to join — though, as noted, most metro residents qualify for several. A single local credit union also has fewer branches than a national megabank, so if you travel constantly or move out of state, that can matter (the CO-OP shared-branch network softens this a lot). And historically, some smaller credit unions lagged big banks on app features and digital tools, though most St. Louis institutions have closed that gap and now offer solid mobile banking, Zelle, and online account opening.
The honest takeaway: for the vast majority of St. Louisans — anyone who wants better loan and savings rates, lower fees, and a say in how their institution is run — the tradeoffs are minor next to the upside. It’s worth pulling up two or three of the credit unions above, comparing their rates and branch maps against your current bank, and seeing for yourself what a switch would save you.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the biggest credit union in Missouri?
A.  CommunityAmerica Credit Union is Missouri’s largest credit union, at roughly $5 billion in assets; it planted its flag in St. Louis in 2025 by merging in Electro Savings. Among credit unions actually headquartered in St. Louis, First Community is the largest, with about $4.78 billion in assets and over 408,000 members.
### Q. What is the best credit union in Missouri?
A.  There’s no single best — it depends on what you need. By size, CommunityAmerica is Missouri’s largest. In the St. Louis metro, First Community and Together lead on branches, Vantage has an especially open charter, and St. Louis Community Credit Union stands out for community impact. Compare rates, branches, and eligibility.
### Q. What credit union is the highest recommended?
A.  No single credit union is universally the highest recommended — the right one depends on your priorities. For branch access, First Community and Together stand out; for the most open membership, Vantage; for community impact, St. Louis Community Credit Union; and on the Illinois side, Scott and 1st MidAmerica. Compare rates and locations for your situation.
### Q. What are the top 3 credit unions?
A.  By asset size in the St. Louis area, the three largest are CommunityAmerica (Missouri’s largest, roughly $5 billion), First Community (about $4.78 billion, the largest headquartered in St. Louis), and Together Credit Union (about $2.64 billion). Bigger isn’t always better, though — the best fit depends on your rates, branches, and eligibility.
### Q. What is the hardest credit union to get into?
A.  In today’s St. Louis metro, almost none are truly hard to join. Most local credit unions now hold a community charter, so anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a covered county is eligible. A few still lean on employer or labor-union groups, like Alliance’s trades roots, but most residents qualify somewhere easily.
### Q. How safe is it to keep $500,000 in a credit union?
A.  Very safe, if you structure it right. The NCUA insures up to $250,000 per depositor, per credit union, per ownership category. To fully cover $500,000, spread it across different ownership categories — individual, joint, retirement — or across two credit unions. Every dollar within those limits is backed by the U.S. government.
### Q. Can anyone join a credit union in St. Louis?
A.  Almost anyone can. Most St. Louis credit unions now hold a community charter, meaning anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a covered county can join — and between them they cover the entire metro on both sides of the river. Opening an account usually requires a small share deposit, often $5 to $25.
### Q. Do credit unions have better interest rates than banks?
A.  Generally, yes. Because credit unions are not-for-profit and member-owned, they tend to pay more on deposits and charge less on loans. NCUA figures for 2025 show credit unions averaging 6.27% on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and 3.26% versus 2.41% on a one-year $10,000 CD.

Salt + Smoke prints the whole ladder on its wedding page: $18.99 per person for one meat and one side, $20.99 for two and two, $22.99 for three and three, and $24.99 for four and four. Its final quote, it says, depends on your guest count, appetizers, desserts and the service style you choose.
That last part is where the number moves. Salt + Smoke offers three levels: drop-off, with hot, ready-to-serve barbecue delivered and set up; a staffed buffet, where its team sets up, serves your guests and cleans up after; and full service, which adds staff, bar, rentals and venue. The Pasta House Co.’s catering menu asks you to call or email for pricing. I could not find a posted per-plate price for a plated, fully staffed dinner on the full-service houses’ own sites, so ask each one for an itemized quote that splits food, staff, bar, rentals and service charge into separate lines.
### The last hour of the night
Guests remember how the night ended. By the last hour the dance floor is sticky, the heels are under the table, and somebody’s uncle is asking whether there’s any food left. Salt + Smoke sells late-night bites for exactly that moment, something smoky to refuel the dance floor before the send-off. It’s worth pricing at the start rather than adding in a panic the week before.
The night before matters too. SqWires lists rehearsal dinners alongside weddings and showers, which makes it an easy call if you want the families around one long table in an old Lafayette Square factory. And if the cake is the part you care about most, Cravings lists wedding cakes and gourmet desserts right alongside its dinner catering, so you can ask about both in one call.
Out-of-town guests asking what to do the morning after? Hand them the St. Louis city guide.
### Not a wedding? The office party, the gala and the graduation
The same kitchens feed the rest of the calendar, and the format changes more than the food. For the office, Ces & Judy’s corporate catering runs from hot breakfast and boxed lunches up to a served dinner with a cocktail hour and tray-passed hors d’oeuvres. Salt + Smoke does boxed lunches, hot buffets and drop-off spreads for the all-hands meeting, and its party menu covers graduations, birthdays, holiday parties and tailgates. Cooler lids popping in a parking lot before kickoff, a sheet cake going soft in a June backyard: that’s the job too, and a drop-off order is usually all it takes.
Raising money is its own kind of event. Butler’s Pantry has a non-profit arm for fundraisers, galas, dinner parties and cocktail parties, and Callier’s keeps a separate menu for schools, churches and nonprofits next to its corporate box lunches. Across the river, Cygan-Delaney’s list runs from banquets and business meetings to golf outings. If your board, your parish or your booster club is planning, ask the same first question a couple would: does the room already have a caterer?
Barbecue for a hundred, priced out
### What is a reasonable budget for a 100 person wedding?
Say your list lands at 100 guests. At Salt + Smoke’s posted wedding buffet rates, those 100 guests come to $1,899 at $18.99 a person, or $2,499 at $24.99 a person with four meats and four sides. Appetizers, desserts, staff, bar and rentals move the total from there. Then add the room: at the Jewel Box, where 100 is the reception limit with a dance floor, the city charges $1,750 Sunday through Thursday or $3,250 on Friday and Saturday, plus a security deposit and insurance.
### Questions to ask before you sign anything
Bring these to every tasting, and get the answers in writing:
Exclusive, approved or open? Ask the venue first, then ask the caterer whether it has worked that room.
What’s inside the per-person price? Food, staff, bar, rentals, service charge and gratuity should each have their own line.
Which service style is this quote? Drop-off, a staffed buffet and full service change who sets up, who serves and who cleans up.
What’s the plan for allergies? Vegan, gluten-free and nut-free guests need a written plan, not a nod at the tasting.
When does the food come out? Agree on a timeline that leaves room for photos, so dinner isn’t drying out under a heat lamp.
Clear, itemized answers are a good sign. A single number scribbled on a napkin is not.
