### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How to pick a wedding caterer?
A.  Start with the room, not the menu. Ask your venue whether it has an exclusive caterer or a preferred list, because the Jewel Box requires a company from the city’s authorized caterers list, and Butler’s Pantry is the exclusive caterer at The Coronado. Then pick a service style, taste two or three finalists, and compare itemized quotes line by line instead of headline prices.
### Q. What are the red flags to look for in wedding catering?
A.  A quote with one number and no lines for staff, bar, rentals or service charge. A caterer who says yes to your date without asking where the reception is, or who can’t say whether your venue allows outside caterers. No written timeline for when food comes out, and no written plan for allergies. Each one moves a surprise from the contract to the wedding day.
### Q. What are common catering mistakes to avoid?
A.  Paying a deposit before checking the venue’s caterer rules is the expensive one. The others: pricing only the buffet and forgetting appetizers and desserts, which Salt + Smoke says shape its final quote, plus any late-night food; waiting too long for a spring or fall date, the seasons Butler’s Pantry calls peak; and guessing the guest count instead of waiting for real RSVPs.
### Q. How much should catering cost for a 50 person wedding?
A.  For barbecue, St. Louis has posted numbers to work from. Say 50 guests say yes. At Salt + Smoke’s posted wedding buffet prices, those 50 guests come to $949.50 at $18.99 a person and $1,249.50 at $24.99 a person. Pass two burnt end toasted ravioli to each of the 50 at $1.75 apiece and cocktail hour adds $175. Staff, bar, rentals and dessert come on top of that.
### Q. How far in advance should you book a caterer in St. Louis?
A.  As soon as the date is set. Butler’s Pantry tells hosts to call and book once they’ve chosen a date, especially in the peak seasons of spring, fall and the holidays. If your venue has an exclusive caterer, call that caterer the same week you sign with the venue, because no other kitchen can take the job.

## “Please Do Not Leave Your Car”: MoDOT’s Advice After a St. Louis Crash
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-do-after-a-car-accident-in-st-louis
The bang is louder than you thought a car could be. Then the quiet, which is worse. A fine white dust hangs in the air from the airbag, your wrists sting, the hazard button is somewhere under your shaking finger, and in the side mirror the traffic on the interstate keeps coming at seventy like nothing happened. Every nerve says get out of the car.
On a St. Louis interstate, the people who clear wrecks for a living say the opposite. MoDOT’s own instruction is to move your vehicle to the right shoulder as far as you safely can, turn on your hazard lights, call 911, and wait in your vehicle for help to arrive. In MoDOT’s words: “Please do not leave your car, especially on the interstate.” If the car can’t move, or someone is hurt, it stays where it is. If there’s smoke or fire, trust your eyes and get clear.
Here’s the part most people around here never hear until the day they need it. MoDOT runs Motorist Assist operators who patrol the St. Louis region’s interstates: I-64 from I-70 to downtown, I-44 from west of Six Flags to downtown, stretches of I-55 and I-70, the entire route of I-170, and the I-270/255 loop from Riverview Drive to the Jefferson Barracks Bridge. They back up fire, police and EMT crews at major incidents, and they can change a tire, bring fuel or handle minor repairs. The number to report a crash or a breakdown is 1-888-ASK-MODOT (275-6636). Save it in your phone tonight, under “crash,” and text it to the new driver in your house.
And if it was a small bump with nobody hurt, get out of the lane. The state calls it Steer It, Clear It: unless there are injuries or the car won’t move, you move it out of the driving lane. Two people standing in the left lane of I-270 comparing bumpers is exactly the scene that law was written to stop.
This is general information to help you stay organized after a wreck. It isn’t legal advice, and every crash is different. For your own situation, talk with a licensed Missouri attorney.
### Is Missouri a no-fault state for car accidents?
No. Twelve states and Puerto Rico have no-fault auto insurance laws, and Missouri isn’t one of them. Here, fault decides who pays: the driver who caused the crash, through their liability insurance, is generally responsible for the damage. If you disagree with how an insurer assigned fault, Missouri’s insurance department says you can ask the courts to rule or pursue the claim under your own policy.
That one fact explains why the next ten minutes matter so much, while the glass is still crunching under your shoes and the other driver is pacing by their bumper on the phone. In a fault state, the story of what happened is the claim. The photos you take with trembling hands, the name of the woman who saw it from the gas station, the exact words you do or don’t say to the other driver: all of it ends up in front of an adjuster deciding who owes whom.
It also explains why the insurance card in the other driver’s glove box matters more than their apology. Missouri requires liability coverage of at least $25,000 for injury to one person, $50,000 for injury to two or more people, and $25,000 for property damage in any one accident. Missouri auto liability policies must also include uninsured motorist coverage, which protects you when you’re hurt by a driver who has none. Those are floors, not promises. A serious injury can blow past them fast, which is why it’s worth knowing your own limits before you ever need them.
### The first ten minutes, once you’re safe
Check yourself, then everyone else. Neck, head, the passenger who’s gone too quiet. If anyone is hurt, that call comes before anything else. Adrenaline is a strong painkiller, so “I’m fine” is not a diagnosis. Plenty of people feel okay at the scene and wake up the next morning with a neck that won’t turn.
When it’s safe, your phone becomes the most useful thing in the car. Shoot wide, then close: every vehicle from several angles, both license plates, the debris on the pavement, the traffic signal or sign that matters, the weather and the light. Photograph the other driver’s insurance card and license rather than copying them by hand while your fingers shake. If a stranger stops and says “I saw the whole thing,” get their name and number before they drive away. They will drive away.
Then the hard part: stay kind and say less. “I’m so sorry, I didn’t see you” is how decent people talk, and it’s also a sentence that can follow you into the claim. You may be rattled and missing half the picture. Swap names, phone numbers, addresses, license numbers, plates and insurance details, and let the facts settle on their own.
### Police reports and the state’s accident form
Call the police for any crash with an injury, a death or real damage. If officers come, ask how to get a copy of the report and write down the report number before they leave. That number is the thread every later phone call hangs on. If police don’t come to a small crash, document everything yourself as if they had.
There’s a separate state form most people mix up with the police report. The Missouri Department of Revenue’s Motor Vehicle Accident Report, Form 1140, is the one you may file when the other driver was uninsured. Under Missouri law you may file it if the accident happened less than one year ago, it involved an uninsured motorist, and it caused property damage costing more than $500, or someone was injured or killed. You can print the form yourself or get a copy from your insurance company or the Department of Revenue.
### Telling your insurer, and what to keep
Call your own insurance company soon, even if the other driver was plainly at fault. Reporting a crash isn’t admitting blame. Give the facts you have and skip the guessing. If the other driver’s insurer calls asking for a recorded statement, you’re allowed to slow down, ask questions and get advice before you agree to anything.
From that night on, keep one folder, paper or on your phone, for everything:
The police report number and the officer’s name
Every photo, even the blurry ones
Medical visits, bills and notes
Repair estimates and invoices
A log of missed work
Every letter and email from any insurer
A few lines each day about how you feel, while it’s fresh
Unrelated, and we know it - every rug eventually meets a St. Louis carpet cleaner.
### Getting the car fixed
The tow lot smells like coolant and wet cardboard, and the person behind the counter wants to know where the car is going. You get to decide. Missouri’s insurance department says it is always your option to go to the repair shop of your choice. The catch it spells out in the same breath: your insurer may only be obligated to pay for the lowest estimate, so you’d be responsible for any difference. Get your own estimate, ask the shop about a warranty on the work, and keep every invoice in the folder.
Rental cars are another surprise. When you claim against the other driver’s liability coverage, the department says the other insurer doesn’t have to pay for a rental in all situations, but if you have no other vehicle available, the insurer should cover a rental at least until it determines the loss on your car. If your own policy has rental coverage, ask how to set it up today. The estimate itself is its own process, and the first number is rarely the last. How an auto body repair estimate actually works explains why it moves and who should do the negotiating. If the other vehicle was a commercial rig, read who is liable in a St. Louis truck accident before you talk to any adjuster.
### The deadline, and the check that comes too fast
For most lawsuits over an injury to a person, Missouri’s time limit is five years, under section 516.120 of Missouri law. Some claims run on different clocks, so don’t assume five years fits every situation, and confirm your own timeline with an attorney.
The faster danger is a friendly phone call a few days after the crash with a check attached. With a car in the shop and bills on the counter, signing feels like relief. But an early offer often arrives before anyone knows how your neck will feel in a month, and once you sign a release, you usually can’t go back for more. Nothing says you have to take the first number. If you want a lawyer’s view, the Missouri Bar’s site at mobar.org has LawyerSearch, a free tool for finding a lawyer in good standing who is accepting new clients.
Need a body shop, a mechanic or a tow you can trust? Browse the St Louis Near Me Directory automotive listings to find help close to home.
If you run a body shop, a tow truck or a repair bay in St. Louis, the customers reading this need you this week, so make sure they can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How does insurance work when it’s not your fault?
A.  In Missouri, you usually file against the at-fault driver’s liability insurance, which pays for the damage its driver caused. If that insurer drags its feet or disputes fault, you can use your own coverage, such as collision, and let your insurer sort it out with theirs. Missouri’s insurance department says that if you disagree with an insurer’s fault decision, you can ask the courts to rule or pursue the claim under your own policy.
### Q. Should I pay the deductible if not-at-fault?
A.  If the other driver’s insurer accepts the claim and pays for your repairs, your deductible usually doesn’t come into it. If you go through your own collision coverage to get the car fixed faster, you’ll typically pay your deductible up front. Ask your insurer whether it will try to recover that money from the other side, and how you’ll be told if it does.
### Q. How long does it usually take to settle a car accident claim?
A.  There’s no set clock. A property-damage-only claim with clear fault can wrap up fairly quickly. An injury claim usually waits until you’ve finished treatment, because nobody knows what it’s worth until then. Disputed fault, multiple cars and low policy limits all slow things down.
### Q. How to win a car accident claim?
A.  Most claims are won or lost on paper. Photos from the scene, witness names, a police report number, prompt medical care and an organized folder of bills and estimates do most of the work. Stay factual, don’t guess about fault, and don’t sign a release until you understand what you’re giving up.
### Q. Will physical therapy increase my settlement?
A.  Treatment is for healing, not for the claim, and it should be what your doctor recommends. What therapy does is create a record. Visits, notes and progress reports show what the injury was and how long it lasted. Skipping care you were told you need can make it easier for an insurer to argue you weren’t really hurt.
### Q. Do you have to use all the money from an insurance claim?
A.  It depends on the payment and your paperwork. If you have a loan or lease, the lender may be listed on a repair or total-loss check and have a say in where the money goes. Ask your insurer and your lender before you decide not to repair a financed car.
### Q. Do I lose no claims if not my fault?
A.  “No claims bonus” is mostly a British term. Here, the question is whether a not-at-fault crash affects your rate or any safe-driver discount, and insurers handle that differently. Ask your own insurer directly, and get the answer in writing. If you’re shopping for a new policy anyway, ask every company the same question so you can compare the answers side by side.
### Q. How long do I have to file a claim after a car accident in Missouri?
A.  Tell your insurer right away, because policies expect prompt notice. For a lawsuit over an injury to a person, Missouri’s general window is five years under section 516.120, though some claims have different deadlines. Confirm yours with an attorney before time gets short.

## Two O’Fallons, One Wrong Click, $1,650 a Year: St. Louis Suburbs Compared
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-suburbs-compared-find-the-right-town-for-you
It’s 11 p.m., the laptop is the only light in the kitchen, your coffee went cold an hour ago, and two O’Fallon listings look perfect. Then you notice one is in St. Charles County, Missouri, and the other is across the Mississippi in Illinois. Troy pulls the same trick. Click the wrong one and you haven’t just picked a house. You’ve picked a state, a tax system and a bridge you’ll be sitting on every morning.
So you open another tab, and one number stops you. At typical rates, the same $300,000 house runs about $5,490 a year in property tax in St. Clair County, Illinois, and about $3,180 in St. Charles County, Missouri: 1.83% of value versus 1.06%, per the Tax Foundation’s county figures. Even after Missouri’s yearly tax on a $30,000 SUV, about $657, the Illinois side costs roughly $1,650 a year more. Houses are cheaper over there. The tax bill isn’t.
Same $300,000 house: St. Clair County, IL, about $5,490 a year. St. Charles County, MO, about $3,180 a year, plus about $657 on a $30,000 SUV.
That car bill is Missouri’s catch. In November the envelope lands on the kitchen counter, one bill for every car you owned on January 1, due by December 31.
Each car is assessed at a third of its value and taxed at your local rate. The $657 comes from running St. Charles County’s own published example rate on a $30,000 SUV.
Illinois abolished personal property taxes in 1979, so no envelope waits on that side of the river.
And inside the City of St. Louis, 1% of every paycheck goes to the earnings tax, even for people who only work there.
Before you close the laptop, add one line to the moving list. Missouri won’t title your car without a statement of non-assessment from your county assessor: St. Louis County takes requests online or in Clayton, St. Charles County online or at 201 N. Second St., and the City of St. Louis assessor answers at 314-622-4800. Request it as soon as you have your title or current out-of-state registration in hand, bring both to the license office, and you won’t sit in its plastic chair twice.
Shop by school district, not town name. Two houses a mile apart can sit in different districts, so ask for the exact district on every listing and check it against that district’s own boundary map. Then drive the commute for real: leave the open house at 7:30 on a weekday morning, merge onto I-270 or I-64 with everyone else, watch the brake lights stack up red, and check the clock when you park.
### West County: walkable main streets, big lots and the price of both
Friday night in downtown Kirkwood, the patios are full, a freight train rumbles past the old depot and kids on bikes cut across the sidewalk. West County is the part of St. Louis County most people picture when they think suburbs: bigger lots, strong schools and home prices toward the top of the metro.
Dinner smells drift out onto the sidewalk, and you can walk home after. That’s Kirkwood and Webster Groves, the walkable-downtown stars, with historic main streets and school districts that consistently rank among the best in Missouri. You pay for that combination of charm and schools.
Drive west and the lots get bigger, until in Wildwood you hear tree frogs instead of traffic at night. Chesterfield, Town and Country, Wildwood and Des Peres lean more spread-out and newer, with larger homes and a higher price point. Chesterfield Valley is where the big-box shopping and a lot of the jobs are; Wildwood is the greener, more rural one.
Cul-de-sacs, basketball hoops over the garage and kids on scooters until the streetlights come on: that’s Ballwin and Ellisville, generally a step more affordable than Town and Country or Chesterfield, with access to the same well-regarded districts.
Out where the subdivisions give way to wooded hills along I-44, Eureka and Manchester stretch the dollar further still. Eureka is more rural and newer, out toward Mid America Adventure (the former Six Flags) with Rockwood schools. Manchester sits between Ballwin and Kirkwood at a middle price, with Parkway and Rockwood access and none of the Town and Country premium.
### Mid County: Clayton, Ladue and a shorter drive to work
Every September the white tents of the Saint Louis Art Fair fill the streets of downtown Clayton. The rest of the year you can walk to lunch, the county courthouse and a MetroLink platform without touching your car keys. Mid County sits between the city and West County, and it trades big lots for shorter commutes and walkable, character-rich neighborhoods.
Clayton is where the county does business: the county seat, a true walkable downtown, and one of the very top school districts in Missouri (Ladue and Clayton routinely trade the number-one and number-two spots). It’s also one of the most expensive places to live in the area, so it fits buyers who put schools and walkability ahead of square footage.
A few minutes west the streets go quiet and the driveways get long. Ladue, Frontenac and Huntleigh are the prestige addresses: estate-scale lots, the highest household incomes in the metro and, in Ladue’s case, the top-ranked school district in Missouri for several years running. Close-in luxury, big, private and expensive, for buyers who want space without leaving Mid County.
Independent restaurants and shops line the revitalized main streets of Maplewood and Brentwood, compact, older streetcar suburbs where city energy comes with a short commute, and you can walk it all.
University City, Richmond Heights, Creve Coeur and Maryland Heights round out the area: U. City has the Loop and a diverse, urban feel, Creve Coeur skews more upscale and corporate, and Maryland Heights is convenient to the airport and Westport.
### St. Charles County: new subdivisions and the metro’s fastest growth
Fresh sod, a new elementary school with the paint barely dry, and a longer drive across the Missouri River every morning. St. Charles County is where much of the metro’s new construction and population growth has gone: since 2020 the county has grown about 5% while the City of St. Louis shrank almost 8%, per the Census Bureau. Expect newer subdivisions, newer schools and a longer-but-manageable commute to downtown.
St. Charles itself anchors the county with its historic brick Main Street along the riverfront.
O'Fallon (Missouri), St. Peters, Wentzville, Lake St. Louis, Cottleville, and Dardenne Prairie are the growth engines. Wentzville has been among the fastest-growing school districts in the entire state. Lake St. Louis is built around its lakes; Cottleville and Dardenne Prairie are smaller and newer.
If you want a newer home and a yard for a more reasonable price than West County, this county is usually the first place to look - just budget for the extra drive time.
Total tangent - driveways crack, patios sag, and St. Louis concrete crews fix both.
### South County and Jefferson County: more house for less, down I-55
Down I-55, a stretched budget finally gets room to breathe. South St. Louis County offers steady, established neighborhoods at gentler prices than West County.
Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, and Sunset Hills are dependable, family-oriented communities. Sunset Hills sits a bit higher on price; Affton and Mehlville are among the more budget-friendly inner-ring choices.
Further south, Jefferson County stretches the dollar further. Arnold is the county's largest community and a common landing spot for first-time buyers; Festus and Imperial offer a more semi-rural feel with highly rated Festus schools. (One common mix-up: Fenton is actually in St. Louis County, not Jefferson County, though it borders the line.)
### North County: lower prices and a short drive to the airport
The mid-century house you would pay far more for in West County is often the one you can afford in Florissant, Hazelwood and Ferguson. North County offers some of the most affordable housing in the metro.
The region has historically carried economic and racial divides (some describe a similar divide along Olive Boulevard, echoing the city’s Delmar Divide), and headlines have shaped outside perceptions.
The fair, accurate take: these are real communities with engaged residents, established housing stock, and genuine value. Visit the specific neighborhoods, talk to people who live there, and judge each block on what you actually see.
Narrowing it down? Explore the metro city by city in our local guides, and find the dentist, mechanic, and coffee shop that make a new neighborhood feel like home.
If you run a business in one of these towns, list it with us and turn the new neighbors shopping for a dentist, a mechanic and a coffee shop into customers.
### Illinois Metro-East: more house for the money
The Illinois listing from your 11 p.m. search wins on sticker price: across the river, your budget often goes further. The tax bill is another story, because property taxes work differently in Illinois. Factor the full monthly cost, not just the sticker price.
Edwardsville and Glen Carbon are the Metro-East's standouts - Edwardsville District 7 is one of the most respected districts in the region, and Edwardsville's walkable, historic Main Street (home to the restored Wildey Theatre) gives it real downtown life.
Waterloo and Columbia in Monroe County are known for low crime, strong homeownership, and well-rated schools, just south of the river.
Belleville, Collinsville, O'Fallon (Illinois), and Highland round out the choices - Belleville has a large historic district and Main Street, Collinsville is central and convenient, and O'Fallon, Illinois, the other O’Fallon, is a growing community near Scott Air Force Base.
### Property taxes: the Missouri-vs-Illinois math
The sticker price is only half the story. Illinois leans more heavily on property taxes than Missouri, so a house that looks cheaper across the river can cost about the same - or more - once the monthly tax bill is baked in.
Two homes at the same list price can carry very different payments depending on the county, the school district, and any special assessments. Before you fall for a bargain on either side of the river, ask your lender or agent to run the full monthly cost - principal, interest, taxes, and insurance - for the specific address, not the town average.
Within Missouri, too, rates vary between the City, St. Louis County municipalities, and the outer counties, and don’t forget Missouri’s separate annual personal-property tax on vehicles.
### New construction vs. historic character
One of the clearest dividing lines in the metro is new versus old. St. Charles County and the outer edges are where you’ll find newer subdivisions: bigger closets, open floor plans, low early maintenance, and often an HOA - at the cost of smaller lots and a longer commute. Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Maplewood, University City, and much of South City offer the opposite: brick, character, mature trees, and walkable streets, but also older systems that need upkeep. Neither is better; it’s a genuine trade-off between move-in-ready convenience and established charm. Be honest about which one actually fits how you live before you tour a single house, because it quietly rules half the map in or out.
### Match the town to where you are in life
It helps to think in terms of who’s buying. First-time buyers stretching a budget tend to land in North County, Jefferson County (Arnold, Festus), or the Illinois side. Move-up families chasing space and newer schools gravitate to St. Charles County. Schools-first buyers aim for Clayton, Ladue, Kirkwood, or Webster Groves and accept the price. And downsizers or walkability-seekers love Maplewood, Webster, Kirkwood, and Edwardsville, where you can park once and live on foot. There’s no wrong answer - just the one that fits your stage and your commute.
### How to actually choose
Personality aside, four practical filters narrow the field fast:
Schools: Even if you do not have kids, district reputation drives resale value. Look up the specific district (not just the town) and check current ratings - you can also see where schools sit across the metro on our St. Louis area schools map.
Commute: Drive your real route at your real rush hour before you commit. Ten miles in West County can feel very different from ten miles across the river.
Budget: Compare total monthly cost, including property taxes, which vary a lot between Missouri and Illinois.
Walkability: If a walkable downtown matters, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Clayton, Maplewood, and Edwardsville should be near the top of your list.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which suburbs in St. Louis are considered the best to live in?
A.  It depends what matters most to you. For schools and walkable downtowns, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Clayton and Ladue lead. For space and newer homes, look at Chesterfield, Wildwood and St. Charles County towns like O’Fallon and Wentzville. For value, Arnold, Florissant and the Illinois side. Edwardsville is the Metro-East standout. Pick the school district first, then the town.
### Q. Which St. Louis suburbs have the best schools?
A.  Ladue, Clayton, Kirkwood, and Webster Groves consistently rank near the top in Missouri, and Edwardsville District 7 leads the Metro-East. Always confirm current ratings for the exact district that serves a specific address, because one town can be split between districts.
### Q. What is the most expensive suburb in St. Louis?
A.  Ladue, with tiny Huntleigh and Frontenac next door, sits at the top: estate-size lots, the highest household incomes in the metro and, in Ladue’s case, a top-ranked Missouri school district. Clayton and Town and Country follow close behind. In all of them you pay for the address and the district as much as the house.
### Q. What city is 30 minutes from St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Plenty. With no traffic, St. Charles, Chesterfield, Edwardsville, Belleville and Arnold are all roughly 25 to 35 minutes from downtown St. Louis, and inner suburbs like Clayton, Kirkwood and Webster Groves are closer. Rush hour on I-64, I-70 or a river bridge can stretch any of those, so drive it at your real commute time before you decide.
### Q. Is St. Louis growing or shrinking?
A.  Both, depending on where you draw the line. Census Bureau estimates, adjusted each year, show the City of St. Louis down about 7.7 percent since the 2020 census, to roughly 278,000 people, while St. Charles County grew about 5 percent to roughly 426,000. The growth is in the suburbs, which is why the newest subdivisions and schools are out there.

## Soulard Has Six Local Farms: St. Louis Farmers Markets by Town
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-guide-to-st-louis-metro-farmers-markets-by-town
Six.
That is how many local farms the City of St. Louis counts among the more than 100 vendors at Soulard Farmers Market. Six. The rest sell meat and fish, baked goods, honey, candy, prepared meals, flowers and crafts. Soulard is a grand old public market, the longest continuously operating market west of the Mississippi by the city’s own account, and it is worth every Saturday you give it. It is just not mostly farmers.
And it is only full one day a week. The city’s posted hours put vendor participation at 10% on Wednesday and Thursday, 35% on Friday and 100% on Saturday. You feel that number the second you walk in on a Saturday: the shoulder-to-shoulder crawl down the aisles, a crate of peppers thumped onto a stall, somebody calling out the price of a bag, cold concrete under your shoes.
If you want to shake the hand that pulled the carrot out of the ground, you want a growers-only market. Tower Grove, for one, says everything sold there must be grown, made or created by the vendor within 150 miles of St. Louis. Soulard for the spectacle, Tower Grove for the farmer. That is the whole map in one line.
### Where are the farmers markets in the St. Louis metro?
In the city, Soulard runs year-round, Wednesday through Saturday, and Tower Grove Park hosts the big Saturday growers-and-makers market. In the county, Saturday markets run from Kirkwood out to Wildwood, with a Sunday market in Richmond Heights. Across the river, the Metro-East has its own, further down this page. Soulard stays open all year.
### Which St. Louis farmers markets stay open in winter?
Fewer than you would think. Soulard, at 730 Carroll Street, is open year-round, Wednesday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., says the city, and Saturday is the full day. The U City Farmers Market runs outdoor Saturdays, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., through November 21, then moves indoors to the Heman Park Community Center, 975 Pennsylvania Avenue, for winter markets January through March on the 2nd and 4th Saturdays, 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. And Tower Grove says its off-season markets, November through March, are smaller but still vibrant, typically at Tower Grove Park, The Boulevard, Rockwell Beer Garden and 4 Hands Brewing Co. downtown. Check the market’s site for winter dates the week you go.
A warm room in January, folding tables of eggs and greens, and wet boots squeaking on the floor. That is a winter market, and plenty of St. Louisans have never been to one.
### Soulard, and the day to go
The City of St. Louis runs Soulard Farmers Market at 730 Carroll Street, and it is closed Monday and Tuesday. Sunday it is closed too, with the exception of one produce stand, and the city tells you to call the market at (314) 622-4180 before coming down on a Sunday.
So go on a Saturday, the 100% day. Vendors sell produce, fresh meat and fish, baked goods, honey, candy, beverages, snacks and prepared meals, with flowers, apparel and arts and crafts among the non-food stalls. Go hungry. Bring a bag with handles, because you will buy more than you meant to. The city also notes that individual vendor hours may vary, so the stall you loved last month might pack up before you get there.
One more Soulard detail worth knowing: the city describes it as a small business incubator, with affordable rent and a steady stream of customers, and says Freddie Lee’s Gourmet Sauces, now sold in 1,000 stores, made its start there. Some of what you taste at a Soulard stall today ends up on grocery shelves later.
### Tower Grove and its sister markets
Folding tables under the trees of Tower Grove Park, a cooler of eggs at your feet, a farmer who can tell you which field the beets came out of. Tower Grove Farmers’ Market calls itself a makers-only, growers-only market, and that changes the conversation at every table. Ask why the tomatoes look lumpy and the person who grew them tells you. The Saturday market in Tower Grove Park runs 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., April 4 through October 31, and a Tuesday evening market runs 4 p.m. to dusk from May 5 through September 29. 2026 marks its 21st season.
Tower Grove’s market site lists two more you should know by town. In Richmond Heights, the Boulevard Farmers’ Market runs Sundays, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., May 3 through October 25. In the city’s Francis Park, the Rockwell Beer Garden Farmers’ Market runs Thursdays, 4 p.m. to dusk, May 7 through September 24, and you can probably guess what people drink while they shop.
### Mid-County and North County, Missouri
Kirkwood. The Kirkwood Farmers’ Market was founded by the City of Kirkwood in 1976 as a bicentennial project, and this year it celebrates 50 years downtown. The Saturday Vendor Market opened April 4 and runs from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. The Summit Market on site keeps longer hours: weekdays 9:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., Saturdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sundays 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
University City. The U City Farmers Market runs Saturdays, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., April 11 through November 21, so it outlasts most of the suburbs. A Wednesday market ran 4 to 7 p.m. through September 30. And here is the one most people miss: indoor winter markets at the Heman Park Community Center, 975 Pennsylvania Avenue, January through March on the 2nd and 4th Saturdays, 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Warm room, muddy boots, eggs in January.
Ferguson. The Ferguson Farmers’ Market at Plaza at 501, 501 S. Florissant, runs every Saturday, 8 a.m. to noon, May through October. It was founded in 2002 and is now celebrating its 25th season, which makes it the North County habit for a whole generation of shoppers.
### West County and the next county over
Wildwood. The city-run Wildwood Farmers Market sits at 221 Plaza Drive and is open every Saturday between May and October, 8 a.m. to noon. Coffee in one hand, a flat of berries balanced on the other arm, and the whole thing over by lunch.
Lake Saint Louis. The Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market runs Saturdays, rain or shine, 8 a.m. to noon, April through October. It describes itself as producer only, and it lists SNAP and Double Up Food Bucks among the food assistance programs it keeps going for low income families and individuals. For more of what that county has, our guide to easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis makes a good second half of the morning.
### Illinois Metro-East
Alton. Start here if you use SNAP. The Alton Farmers’ & Artisans’ Market says SNAP benefits are accepted by most vendors, and recipients can receive an unlimited dollar for dollar match. Unlimited. The 2026 season ran every Saturday from 8 a.m. until noon, May 9 through October 17, in the lot at Landmarks Boulevard and Henry Street downtown, rain or shine.
Edwardsville. The Land of Goshen Community Market runs Saturdays, 8 a.m. to noon, May 9 through October 17. This season it gathered in City Park around the Edwardsville Public Library, with vendors along Kansas and Park Streets. It accepts SNAP and Link Match vouchers, and Illinois LINK cards buy tokens in $1 increments.
O’Fallon, Illinois. Mind the state; there is an O’Fallon in Missouri too. The Vine Street Market at 212 E. 1st Street runs Saturdays, 8 a.m. to noon, from the 2nd Saturday in May to the 3rd Saturday in October, with 60-plus vendors each week and a focus on local food within 100 miles of O’Fallon. The Illinois side has far more than markets, too; our Illinois coverage map shows the rest of it.
Pick your market by the day you are free, not the town you live in. Then fill the rest of the morning from the St Louis Near Me shopping directory, where local food shops, bakeries and farms sit by neighborhood.
If you’re the grower, the baker or the honey stand at the market, a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory keeps the customers who met you at the market able to find you all week.
### Do farmers markets run year-round?
Most around here do not. Every suburban Saturday market on this page wraps up between mid-October and late November, and the three winter options above carry the season to spring. In January the produce turns to what keeps, and a quiet weekday at Soulard is quiet enough to hear your own footsteps on the concrete.
When the markets close, the same shopping instinct moves indoors. This is how to shop a health food store in St. Louis without paying for the label.
### What is the best farmers market in St. Louis?
It depends on what you came for. For the spectacle and a Wednesday option, Soulard. For growers-only tables, Tower Grove on a Saturday morning. For a Sunday, the Boulevard. For winter eggs, U City’s indoor markets. For the strongest SNAP match on this page, Alton. And for a fifty-year-old habit, Kirkwood. The best market is the one you go back to so often that the honey guy starts setting a jar aside.
Nobody at the produce stand will defend Provel. Somebody in St. Louis always will.
### How to shop a farmers market like a regular
Go early. The good tomatoes, the berries and the sweet corn go first, and the first hour is when the tables are still full.
Bring cash and small bills. Breaking a twenty for a three-dollar bunch of radishes is nobody’s favorite moment, and some stalls are cash-first.
Bring your own bags. A sturdy tote beats juggling an armload of peaches across a gravel lot.
Ask the grower. What was picked yesterday, what is at its peak this week, and how to cook the strange green thing you have never tried. Two minutes at the table beats an hour of recipe scrolling.
Use SNAP where it is matched. Ask at the information table wherever you shop.
Thinking of working those markets from your own kitchen on wheels? Start with what a St. Louis food truck really costs.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a farmers market in St. Louis this weekend?
A.  Almost always, yes. Soulard is open year-round, Wednesday through Saturday, and Saturday is the day all of its vendors are there. In the colder months, Tower Grove runs smaller off-season markets from November through March, and U City holds indoor winter markets on the 2nd and 4th Saturdays from January through March.
### Q. Is Soulard Market cash only?
A.  I could not find a payment rule on the City of St. Louis Soulard page, which is where the market posts its hours and stand rental details. Treat it like any big market: bring small bills for the produce stands, carry a card as a backup, and ask before you bag up a pile.
### Q. Is Soulard Market still open?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis says the market is open year-round, Wednesday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., at 730 Carroll Street. It is closed Monday and Tuesday, and the city asks you to call (314) 622-4180 before coming down on a Sunday.
### Q. What does Soulard Farmers Market have?
A.  More than 100 vendors, according to the city, including six local farms. Expect produce, fresh meat and fish, baked goods, honey, candy, beverages, snacks and prepared meals, plus fresh flowers, apparel, health and beauty accessories, and arts and crafts.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy food at farmers markets?
A.  Sometimes. I could not find a St. Louis price comparison worth quoting, so here is the clearest win instead: if you use SNAP, a match doubles your produce money. The Alton market offers an unlimited dollar for dollar match from most vendors, which no grocery store coupon will touch.
### Q. Should you bring cash to a farmers market?
A.  Yes, bring some, in small bills. Small growers often prefer cash, and small bills keep the line moving. If you use SNAP, find the information booth first for tokens; Goshen in Edwardsville sells LINK tokens in $1 increments.
### Q. Do you haggle at the farmers market?
A.  Not really. A grower’s table is not a flea market, and arguing over a two-dollar bunch of kale lands badly. The better move is to ask whether there is a deal on a bigger quantity or on seconds, the bruised fruit that is perfect for jam, especially near closing time.
### Q. What are the downsides of buying from a farmer's market?
A.  Short hours and short seasons. Tower Grove’s Saturday market closes at 12:30 p.m., most suburban markets end by fall, and at Soulard only about 10% of vendors show up on a Wednesday or Thursday. You also shop what is in season, which means no tomatoes in February.
### Q. Are you supposed to tip at a farmers market?
A.  No, tipping is not part of buying produce. If a prepared-food stand has a tip jar for its cooks, that is a nice extra. The thanks a grower notices most is coming back next week and telling a friend where the good peaches came from.
### Q. What is the difference between O’Fallon, Missouri and O’Fallon, Illinois markets?
A.  This guide covers the Vine Street Market in O’Fallon, Illinois, at 212 E. 1st Street. Add the state when you search, or you will drive the wrong direction across the river.

## St. Louis Chambers of Commerce and Networking, by Suburb
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-chambers-of-commerce-and-networking-by-suburb
Most small-business owners in St. Louis end up running everything alone — the invoicing, the marketing, the quiet stretches between jobs. The oldest cure for that isolation still holds up: get in a room with other local owners. Across the metro, on both the Missouri and Illinois sides, that room has a name. Sometimes it is a chamber of commerce. Sometimes it is a weekly referral group built to pass leads. Here is who does what, where they meet, and how to get real value without wasting money. Before you write another membership check, ask: is that room actually sending you customers, or just costing you a Tuesday morning and a fee?
### What a chamber of commerce actually does
A chamber of commerce is a membership organization of local businesses in a defined area — a city, a cluster of towns, or a county. You pay annual dues, and in return you get a mix of the following: networking events where you meet other owners, a public member directory that links to your website, ribbon cuttings and grand-opening support, referrals when residents call asking who to hire, advocacy with city hall on issues that affect business, and educational workshops on things like taxes, hiring, and marketing.
A chamber gives back roughly what you put in. Owners who show up to a few events a year, introduce themselves, and follow up tend to win work. Owners who pay dues and never attend shrug at renewal time and walk away. The membership is a tool. It only pays off when you actually pick it up.
### Chamber vs. referral group vs. industry association
Owners mix these three up constantly. The plain difference:
A chamber of commerce is broad and local. Any kind of business in the area can join — a plumber, a bakery, a law firm, a nonprofit. The point is community connection across industries.
A referral group (sometimes called a leads group) is small, structured, and built to pass business directly. The best-known is BNI, which runs chapters around St. Louis. Most groups allow only one person per profession — one realtor, one electrician, one insurance agent — so members refer work to each other without competing. Meetings are usually weekly and attendance is expected.
An industry association is national or regional and tied to one trade — restaurants, home builders, accountants. You join for industry training, standards, and contacts in your own field, not for local cross-referrals.
Many owners belong to more than one. A common combo is one chamber for community visibility plus one referral group for steady leads.
### Chambers in St. Charles County (Missouri)
The fast-growing western side of the metro has several active chambers. The St. Charles Regional Chamber in St. Peters serves the St. Charles County region and is part of the Missouri Chamber Federation. The O'Fallon Chamber of Commerce and Industries covers O'Fallon, Missouri (not the Illinois O'Fallon — both exist). Out west, the Western St. Charles County Chamber of Commerce serves Wentzville and the growing communities around it. These are good first stops if your customers live in St. Charles, St. Peters, O'Fallon (MO), or Wentzville.
Total swerve: noon is coming, and Eagle Park, Illinois has lunch covered.
### Chambers in West and Mid St. Louis County
If you work the western suburbs, the Chesterfield Regional Chamber is one of the larger chambers in the region and covers the Chesterfield business corridor. Further along Manchester Road, the West St. Louis County Chamber of Commerce in Ellisville serves Ballwin, Ellisville, Manchester, Wildwood, Valley Park, and several neighboring towns — a strong choice for home-service pros and retail owners across far West County.
Closer in, the Kirkwood-Des Peres Area Chamber of Commerce serves Kirkwood, Des Peres, Warson Woods, Glendale, and Oakland, and has been around since the 1940s. The Mid County Chamber of Commerce, based in Maplewood, covers the Maplewood and Richmond Heights area, which is a busy small-business and restaurant pocket. And in the region’s business hub, the Clayton Chamber of Commerce serves downtown Clayton — the county seat, packed with law firms, agencies, and finance offices — a strong fit if your clients are professional-services businesses.
### Chambers in South County and the Webster Groves area
The Quad Chamber of Commerce — the rebranded name for the longtime Webster Groves, Shrewsbury, Rock Hill and Brentwood chamber — covers that string of inner-ring suburbs (“the Quad”) along the south-central corridor. Head into Jefferson County and the Arnold Chamber of Commerce serves Arnold and the surrounding Jeffco communities. Both are practical fits for trades, shops, and service businesses that draw from those neighborhoods.
### Chambers in North County (Missouri)
In North St. Louis County, the Greater North County Chamber of Commerce, based in Florissant, serves Florissant, Hazelwood, Black Jack, Spanish Lake, and the wider north-county area. If your customer base sits north of the city, this is the local network to look at first.
### Chambers in the Illinois Metro-East
The Illinois side has its own strong set of chambers, and they matter if you serve customers across the river:
The Edwardsville/Glen Carbon Chamber of Commerce is one of southern Madison County's largest business associations, covering Edwardsville and Glen Carbon.
The Greater Belleville Chamber of Commerce serves Belleville and surrounding communities in St. Clair County.
The O'Fallon-Shiloh Chamber of Commerce covers O'Fallon, Illinois (again, the Illinois one) and Shiloh.
The Collinsville Chamber of Commerce serves Collinsville, home of the Italian Fest and the International Horseradish Festival.
The RiverBend Growth Association acts as the chamber and economic-development organization for the Riverbend communities, including Alton, Godfrey, Bethalto, Wood River, and Grafton.
### The metro-wide regional organization
One more layer sits above the local chambers. Greater St. Louis, Inc. is the bi-state regional business and economic-development organization, formed in 2021 by merging several older groups (including the former regional chamber and the partnership). It works at the scale of the whole 15-county metro — site selection, workforce, downtown revitalization, and big-picture advocacy — rather than ribbon-cuttings on Main Street. For most small businesses, your neighborhood chamber is still the right day-to-day network, but it helps to know Greater St. Louis, Inc. exists: it’s the group shaping the regional economy your business operates inside, and its research and events can be worth following even if you never join at the corporate tier.
### Referral and leads groups across the metro
Beyond chambers, BNI Mid America runs structured referral chapters across St. Louis and southern Illinois, including groups on the Illinois side in St. Clair County. These weekly groups are built for one thing: passing qualified leads to one member per profession. They take more commitment than a chamber — weekly attendance, a brief presentation, and a habit of bringing referrals — but for trades and service pros, a single good chapter can become a steady pipeline.
### How to get real value from any of these
Pick by where your customers are, not where you live. Join the chamber that covers the towns you want to work in.
Visit before you pay. Most chambers and referral groups let you attend an event or two as a guest. Go, talk to people, and see if the room is your kind of crowd.
Show up consistently. The owner who attends six events beats the one who attends one. Relationships, and the referrals that follow, are built over months.
Use the member directory link. Most chambers link to your website, which is a small but real boost to how customers and search engines find you.
Give before you ask. Refer other members first. The fastest way to get referrals is to send them.
### Free ways to network too
Dues are not the only path. Many chambers run free or low-cost public events you can attend as a guest. Local Facebook groups, neighborhood business associations, and main-street merchant groups are often free to join. And plain visibility does the same work — sponsor a youth team, table at a community festival, partner with the shop two doors down. It all serves one aim: becoming the familiar name in your own backyard.
### Your first 90 days in a chamber, done right
Joining is the easy part; the return comes from a simple, repeatable habit. In your first three months, aim to attend every event you reasonably can — not to sell, but to be seen. People refer businesses they recognize, and recognition is just repetition. Wear a name tag, learn a handful of members by name, and get comfortable answering “what do you do?” in one clear sentence a stranger could repeat to someone else later. That last part matters more than most owners think: your referrals travel through people who half-remember you, so make yourself easy to describe.
Then follow up like it’s the actual job, because it is. After each event, send two or three short, genuine notes to people you connected with — no pitch, just “good to meet you, here’s my card, happy to send business your way.” Offer a referral before you ever ask for one; nothing builds goodwill faster in a room of small-business owners. Volunteer for a committee or a ribbon-cutting within the first couple of months, since the members who run things get known fastest. Do that for a season and the chamber stops being a line item and starts being a pipeline. Skip the follow-up and it’s just an expensive lunch club.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I have to join a chamber to network locally?
A.  No. Chambers are one option. Referral groups, free community events, merchant associations, and local online groups all build connections. A chamber simply packages a lot of that into one membership with a directory listing attached.
### Q. How much does chamber membership usually cost?
A.  It varies by chamber and by the size of your business, generally ranging from low hundreds of dollars a year for a small business up to more for larger companies. Ask each chamber for its current dues tiers, and weigh them against how many events you will realistically attend.
### Q. What is the difference between a chamber and BNI?
A.  A chamber is broad, local, and community-focused, and welcomes any business in its area. BNI is a structured weekly referral group that allows only one member per profession and exists specifically to pass leads. Many owners join both.
### Q. There are two O'Fallon chambers — which one do I want?
A.  There is an O'Fallon, Missouri in St. Charles County and an O'Fallon, Illinois in St. Clair County. Each has its own separate chamber. Pick the one in the state where your customers are.
### Q. Can a brand-new or home-based business join?
A.  Yes. Chambers welcome startups, solo operators, and home-based businesses. For a new owner with no local network yet, a chamber or referral group is one of the fastest ways to meet customers and referral partners.
### Q. Will joining a chamber actually get me customers?
A.  It can, but not automatically. Members who attend events, follow up, and refer others tend to win work. Members who pay and never show up usually do not. Treat it as a relationship-building tool, not an ad you buy once.
### Q. What is Greater St. Louis, Inc., and should my small business join it?
A.  Greater St. Louis, Inc. is the bi-state regional business and economic-development organization for the wider metro — it works on site selection, workforce, and regional advocacy rather than local ribbon-cuttings. For most small businesses, a neighborhood chamber is the better day-to-day fit, but it is worth following Greater St. Louis, Inc.’s research and events because it shapes the regional economy you operate in.
### Q. Which chamber covers Webster Groves and Brentwood now?
A.  The Quad Chamber of Commerce. It is the rebranded name for the longtime Webster Groves, Shrewsbury, Rock Hill and Brentwood chamber — the four inner-ring suburbs known as “the Quad.” If you serve customers in those towns, it is your local network.

## Water Up the Floor Drain? Call MSD Before a Waterproofer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/basement-waterproofing-in-st-louis-a-homeowners-guide
The floor drain gurgles first, and in St. Louis that sound can start a 30-day clock nobody tells you about. It is a low, wet cough from the corner by the water heater, the kind of sound you half hear over the rain on the windows, and by the time you get down the stairs there is a gray tongue of water sliding across the concrete toward the boxes of Christmas ornaments. Your socks are soaked before you find the light switch. The smell hits a second later, sour and swampy, the smell of the street’s sewer line and not the clean smell of rain.
That smell tells you which water you have. Water gets into a St. Louis basement two very different ways. It can push in sideways, through the block or the poured wall or the seam where the wall meets the floor, because the clay outside is holding rain against your house like a sponge pressed to a window. Or it can come up from below, out of that floor drain, because the sewer line under the street filled faster than it could empty and had nowhere else to go. The first kind is a waterproofing problem. The second kind is a sewer problem, and no amount of sealer, drain tile or membrane on your walls will stop it.
The two problems send you to different people, and only the sewer one comes with a deadline: the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District gives you 30 days to report a backup, and the clock runs while you are still pulling wet cardboard off the floor. Get the order wrong and you can spend thousands on a system aimed at the wrong water, then miss the window to have the sewer district look at the part that might have been theirs.
### Is waterproofing a basement worth it?
Usually yes, when the water is coming through the walls. If you see a dark line along the bottom of the wall after a storm, damp patches that track the rain, white chalky crust on the block or paint that keeps bubbling off, the water is getting in from outside, and it rarely stays small. Clay keeps swelling when it is wet and shrinking when it dries, and that push and pull works the same cracks every spring. Fixing it while it is still a drainage job is the cheap version. Waiting until it is a bowing-wall job is not.
It is not worth it, at least not yet, in two cases. One is when your gutters overflow and your downspouts dump water right at the foundation, because that is a Saturday-afternoon fix, not a contract. The other is when the water rose out of the floor drain. That is a backup, and the answer starts with a plumber, a backwater valve and a phone call to the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District, not a waterproofer.
### The first phone call, before the shop vac
Stand in the wet for a minute and look at where the water is thickest. Around the drain, with the toilet or the laundry tub burping? Or along a wall, spreading out from a crack or the cove joint? Take photos of both, and of anything ruined, before you clean.
If it came up through the drain, call MSD at (314) 768-6260. MSD says that to be eligible for coverage you have to contact it within 30 days of the backup. When heavy rain overloads a public sewer line and it backs up into a building, MSD says it will reimburse up to $3,000, with a $100 deductible, for the damage, and it recommends homeowners carry extra coverage through their insurance company because damage can run past that. If a public line collapsed or got blocked by roots or debris, MSD says it will reimburse the homeowner for the adjusted losses. The district’s Building Cleanup Guide explains how to document your losses, so read it before the soaked carpet goes to the curb.
Now the part that stings. MSD is just as plain about what it does not cover. Stormwater that comes in through doors, windows or cracks in the foundation after a heavy rain is, in MSD’s words, not considered a building backup, and that damage is the homeowner’s responsibility. Same storm, same soaked socks, a completely different answer depending on which way the water traveled. A clog in your own lateral line, the pipe from your house to the main, is also on you, and MSD tells people to call a certified plumber for that.
If the backups keep coming from the public sewer, MSD offers what it calls a Sewer Separation Program for properties with a history of building backups caused by MSD issues, and through it MSD pays for plumbing modifications such as a backflow device or check valve. MSD describes a backwater valve as a gate-like device on your private lateral that lets sewage leave your home but not come back in. That is the fix for water from below. It does nothing for a weeping wall.
### Why does St. Louis clay keep pushing water at the wall?
When your house went up, the builder dug a hole, poured the foundation and shoveled loose dirt back in around it. That backfill never packs as tight as the undisturbed clay beyond it, so it drinks rain faster and holds it right against your wall, a moat with the house in the middle. People in the trade call it the clay bowl. After a soaking week the wet soil leans on the foundation with real weight, and water squeezes through pores in the concrete, through every hairline crack and through the cove joint where the wall sits on the floor slab.
You can hear it in an old basement on a wet night if the house is quiet: a faint tick of water somewhere behind the paneling, or the sump pump kicking on every few minutes like a refrigerator that will not settle down. That pump is doing its job. It is also telling you how much water is sitting in the ground outside.
### Damp wall or a real leak? Tape up a square of plastic
A lot of St. Louis basements that feel wet in July are not leaking at all. Thick summer air drifts down the stairs, hits a cool block wall and the cold water pipes, and beads up like sweat on a glass of iced tea. People pay for wall systems to fix that, and it never works, because the water was in the air the whole time.
The test costs nothing. Tape a square of clear plastic tight against the damp spot on all four edges and leave it a day or two. If drops form on the room side, the moisture is coming from the air, and a dehumidifier is your first fix. The EPA suggests keeping indoor humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50. If the wall side of the plastic is wet, water is coming through the concrete from the ground outside, and you are in waterproofing territory. Whatever you find, dry wet materials fast: the EPA says that if wet or damp areas are dried within 24-48 hours after a leak, in most cases mold will not grow.
### Start outside, with a ladder and a garden hose
Walk the house in the next hard rain with an umbrella and watch. You will learn more in fifteen minutes than any sales visit will tell you. Look for gutters spilling over the front like a waterfall, a downspout that ends in a splash block six inches from the brick, a flower bed that dips toward the wall and holds a puddle. The EPA’s own advice is short: clean and repair roof gutters regularly, and make sure the ground slopes away from the building foundation so water does not collect around it.
So clean the gutters. Add extensions so the downspouts empty well out into the yard and downhill, never onto the neighbor’s side. Build the soil up against the foundation so it falls away from the house, and keep mulch from piling into a dam. On a lot of homes that is the whole fix, and it costs a weekend and a few trips to the hardware store.
### When the outside fixes are not enough
If the plastic test says the wall is wet and the gutters and grading are already right, the real systems come in. An interior drain tile is a perforated pipe set along the footing under the edge of the floor, feeding a sump pump that lifts the water out before it can build pressure. It appeals in an older St. Louis house because it does not tear up the yard and can go in any month of the year. Crack injection seals a single leaking crack from inside. Exterior waterproofing means digging down to the footing, coating the wall with a membrane and laying a drain outside it. It stops the water before it ever touches the wall, and it also means your hostas, your sidewalk and maybe your porch steps come out for a while.
One line matters more than the rest. Waterproofing manages water. Foundation repair stops a wall that is moving. A little seep at the cove joint is a water job. A wall that bows inward, a stair-step crack that gets wider, a gap you can slide a coin into that was not there last year - those are structural, and they call for anchors, bracing or straps, sometimes piers. If someone points at a damp corner and starts talking about your house caving in, thank them, let them leave, and get a structural engineer’s opinion before you sign anything big.
Different subject entirely, we know - St. Charles businesses, get seen.
### The kitchen-table test for a waterproofing bid
Most of the people who do this work are honest. The few who are not all use the same script, and it is easy to spot once you know it. Sit at the table with each bidder and listen for these:
Do they ask where the water came in? A pro who never asks about the floor drain, the gutters or the timing after rain is selling one package to every house.
Is the diagnosis in writing? You want the cause, the method, the materials and the length of wall covered on paper. Get at least three, and be wary when they disagree wildly.
Can you read the warranty? Ask who pays if it leaks again, and whether the warranty moves to the next owner if you sell.
Is there pressure? “Today only” pricing, cash only, the full amount up front, or talk of imminent collapse over a damp wall are all reasons to walk them to the door.
Licensing and insurance. Ask for proof of liability insurance and check what your city or county requires for the work.
If the water already got past the drain and into the drywall, here’s what to do in the first 48 hours of water damage restoration.
If a job goes sideways after you have paid, keep the contract, invoices and canceled checks. The Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222 for questions about filing a complaint.
Want three honest looks at your basement instead of one scary one? Search St Louis Near Me Directory for waterproofing contractors, plumbers and foundation pros around the metro, call two or three, and ask each one the same question first: where is my water coming in?
If you’re the waterproofing crew, the plumber or the one-truck foundation outfit who actually asks that question, the homeowners standing in wet socks tonight are your next customers. A listing helps them pick you before the fear-sellers call back. Add your business, or see who AI names instead of you.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Will insurance pay for basement waterproofing?
A.  Generally no. Waterproofing is prevention, and standard policies tend to treat slow seepage as maintenance. Sudden damage like a burst pipe is a different question, and flood coverage is a separate policy. For sewer backups, MSD itself recommends additional coverage through your insurance company, because damages may exceed what it reimburses. For what a true river flood did here, see our story of the 1993 flood in St. Louis.
### Q. What are common waterproofing mistakes?
A.  Paying for a wall system when the water came up the floor drain. Sealing the inside of a wall that water is pushing through from outside. Skipping the gutters and grading before spending on interior work. Treating a moving wall as a water problem. And signing a bid with no written scope, which is how a cheap price grows on the day.
### Q. How to choose a basement waterproofing contractor?
A.  Choose the one who asks the most questions. A good contractor wants to know when the water shows up, where it pools and whether the floor drain has ever backed up, then puts the cause, method, materials and warranty in writing. Get at least three written assessments, check insurance, and walk away from anyone who quotes over the phone or pushes a same-day signature.
### Q. How much should I expect to pay for basement waterproofing?
A.  It depends on which water you have, and I could not find a St. Louis price survey from a neutral source worth repeating. The range runs from downspout extensions you can put on in an afternoon, to crack injection, to an interior drain tile and sump system, to full exterior digging at the top. Get written quotes from three local contractors for the same scope so you are comparing like with like.
### Q. Who do I call when water comes up through my basement floor drain?
A.  Call MSD at (314) 768-6260 and report it within 30 days of the backup, take photos before you clean, and follow MSD’s Building Cleanup Guide to document your losses. If the problem is in your own lateral line, MSD says to call a certified plumber. A waterproofer is the wrong first call for this one.

## How to Optimize Your Google Business Profile: A St. Louis Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-optimize-your-google-business-profile-2026-st-louis
For a St. Louis small business, your Google Business Profile is the closest thing there is to a free storefront on the busiest street in town. It’s what shows up when someone nearby searches for what you offer — the map, the reviews, the hours, the “call” and “directions” buttons — and for most local businesses it drives more customers than the website ever will. Yet the majority of profiles sit half-finished, quietly losing business to competitors who took an afternoon to fill theirs out. One afternoon is the whole gap. So which side of it are you on right now — the finished profile getting the calls, or the half-built one getting scrolled past?
The good news is that optimizing your Google Business Profile is free, it doesn’t require any technical skill, and a complete profile routinely out-performs a bigger competitor’s neglected one. This is a practical, step-by-step guide to doing it right in 2026 — from claiming and verifying to the specific sections that move the needle, plus the common mistakes that hold St. Louis businesses back.
### How Do You Optimize a Google Business Profile?
Optimizing your Google Business Profile means claiming it, filling in every section completely and accurately, and keeping it active — so that Google trusts your information and shows you to nearby customers. Google ranks local results on three factors: relevance (how well you match the search), distance (how close you are), and prominence (how established and trusted you appear). You can’t change your distance, but you directly control relevance and prominence, and a well-optimized profile is how you do it. The whole job comes down to a handful of steps done thoroughly, then maintained.
Here’s the sequence that works: claim and verify your profile, complete every field, load up quality photos, build and respond to reviews, post regularly, and keep it all current. Let’s walk through each.
### Step 1: Claim and Verify Your Profile
You can’t optimize what you don’t control. Search for your business on Google — if a profile already exists (Google often auto-creates them), click to claim it; if not, create one, though it’s worth first ruling out the other reasons a business doesn’t turn up in a Google search so you don’t create a duplicate of a listing that already exists. Then verify ownership, usually by phone, email, or a postcard code. Verification is non-negotiable: it’s what unlocks editing and tells Google you’re the legitimate owner. Until you’re verified, you’re at the mercy of whatever incomplete information Google guessed. This first step trips up more businesses than any other, so if you do nothing else today, claim and verify your profile.
### Step 2: Complete Every Single Section
This is where most of the optimization happens, and where most businesses quit early. Fill in everything: your exact business name (as it really appears, no keyword stuffing), address, phone, and website; your primary category (the most important single choice — pick the most specific one that fits) plus relevant secondary categories; your full list of services or products with descriptions; your hours, including special and holiday hours; a keyword-natural business description; and the attributes that apply (wheelchair accessible, women-owned, free Wi-Fi, outdoor seating, and so on). Every field you complete gives Google more to match you against and more reason to trust you. A profile that’s 100% complete simply gets shown more than one that’s 60% done — and completing it is entirely free.
### Step 3: Add Real, Quality Photos
Profiles with photos get significantly more clicks, calls, and direction requests than those without — people want to see what they’re walking into. Add a clear logo and cover photo, then real images of your storefront, your interior, your team, and your actual products or work. Authentic photos beat stock every time, because they build trust and set accurate expectations. Refresh them periodically; a profile with recent photos signals an active, open business. This is one of the highest-return, lowest-effort moves available — a handful of good photos taken on your phone can measurably lift how many people choose you.
### Step 4: Build and Respond to Reviews
Reviews are one of the strongest prominence signals Google uses, and they’re the deciding factor for many customers choosing between you and the next option. Make asking a routine part of the job — a friendly request after a good interaction, with a direct link — and aim for a steady trickle of recent reviews rather than a one-time push. Just as important: respond to every review, positive and negative. A warm thank-you to a happy customer and a calm, professional reply to a critical one both show prospective customers (and Google) that you’re engaged and care. For the full playbook, see our guide to responding to Google reviews.
### Step 5: Post Regularly
Google Business Profile posts — short updates, offers, and events that appear on your profile — keep it active and give searching customers one more reason to choose you. They don’t transform your ranking on their own, but the activity signals a live, engaged business, and a timely offer can be the nudge that turns a browser into a customer. Aim for a post or two a week. If you’re not sure what to share, our guide to Google Business Profile posts has ideas and a simple approach.
### Use the Q&A and Messaging Features
Two underused features quietly win customers. The Questions & Answers section on your profile lets anyone ask a question — and anyone can answer, which means if you don’t, you risk a wrong or unhelpful reply representing your business. Get ahead of it: seed the common questions yourself with accurate answers, and monitor for new ones. The messaging feature lets customers text you directly from your profile; if you turn it on, commit to responding quickly, because a fast reply often wins the job while a slow one loses it. Both features signal to Google that you’re responsive and engaged, and both remove friction for a customer who’s ready to reach out but has one quick question first.
Random, but: where to eat in Des Peres is one tab away.
### Optimize for St. Louis Specifically
Generic optimization gets you partway. Local specificity gets you the rest. Make sure your profile reflects the actual St. Louis-area communities you serve. If you have a storefront, your address and map pin do the work; if you’re a service-area business (a plumber, a cleaner, a contractor), set your service areas to the specific towns and neighborhoods you cover — Kirkwood, Florissant, St. Charles, the Metro East, wherever you actually go. Work your real service area and neighborhood names naturally into your description and posts, and gather reviews from customers across those areas. In a spread-out metro like St. Louis, a business optimized for the specific communities it serves shows up for far more “near me” searches than one that only says “St. Louis.” For the bigger picture, see the complete GBP management guide.
### How Long Until Optimization Shows Results?
Some of it is nearly immediate and some compounds. Completing your profile and adding photos can start improving how often you appear within days to a couple of weeks, because Google simply has more to work with and more reason to trust you. The prominence-building pieces — a steady flow of reviews, consistent activity, and consistent listings elsewhere — build over weeks and months into durable ranking. Plenty of owners treat optimization as a one-time task and expect instant top placement. It doesn’t work that way. You get a quick lift from completeness, then steady gains from consistency. Keep at it, and your profile climbs and holds rather than spiking and fading.
### What Are Common Google Business Profile Mistakes?
Avoiding a few common errors puts you ahead of most local competitors. The big ones: never claiming or verifying the profile in the first place; keyword-stuffing the business name (a Google guidelines violation that can get you suspended — use your real name only); inconsistent name, address, and phone across the web, which erodes trust; choosing the wrong or too-broad primary category; letting hours go stale, especially around holidays, which frustrates customers and hurts you; ignoring reviews entirely; and setting it and forgetting it — a profile that never changes looks dormant. Most of these are quick fixes, and correcting even one or two can lift your visibility. If your profile has been suspended, don’t panic — see our guide to GBP suspension and reinstatement.
### Keep It Active — Optimization Is Ongoing
A Google Business Profile rewards steady attention and quietly slips without it. Update your hours the day anything changes. Add fresh photos now and then, keep asking for and responding to reviews, post regularly, and answer the questions customers submit through the Q&A. Check your profile’s free performance insights to see how people are finding and contacting you, and do a quick monthly audit to catch anything outdated. This ongoing upkeep is exactly the part that slips when you’re busy running a business — and exactly the part that separates the profiles quietly winning customers from the ones sitting idle. A few minutes of attention a week is all it takes to stay on the winning side of that line.
Your Google Business Profile works best as part of a complete, consistent local presence. A listing on the St Louis Near Me Directory reinforces the same information Google and AI assistants use to trust and rank you - a consistent citation that makes your whole online presence stronger.
