### Q. How to survive in an apartment with no AC?
A.  Close the blinds on the sunny side during the day, run fans to move air, and drink water before you feel thirsty. Fans alone won’t protect you in a real heat wave, so spend the hottest hours at a library, community center or cooling center (dial 2-1-1 for the nearest one). Seniors and people with disabilities should apply to Cool Down St. Louis for a free unit.
### Q. Is a broken AC considered an emergency?
A.  For a senior, a baby, or anyone with a heart, lung or other heat-sensitive condition, a dead AC during a heat advisory is a health emergency. Get to a cooling center (dial 2-1-1), call Cool Down at 314-241-0001 about a replacement unit, and if you rent, tell your landlord in writing. Call 911 for confusion, fainting or a body temperature above 103°F.
### Q. What types of grants are available in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  For cooling and utility costs, the main ones are Cool Down St. Louis (free window AC units plus Ameren-funded bill help up to $600), LIHEAP crisis help (up to $300 in summer and $800 in winter), and Ameren’s Dollar More (up to $600) and Keeping Cool credits. For rent, food or medical bills, dial 2-1-1 for current programs.
### Q. What are signs that your AC unit is going out?
A.  Warm air from the vents, weak airflow, a unit that runs nonstop or keeps clicking on and off, water leaking indoors, ice on the coils, and a power bill that jumps for no reason. Change the filter first. If it still struggles and you are a senior or have a disability, apply to Cool Down St. Louis before it quits in July.

## St. Louis Union Station Runs on Two Clocks: Things to Do, Prices and When to Go
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-at-st-louis-union-station-the-complete-2026-guide
The gondola door clicks shut, the plaza noise drops away, and the St. Louis Wheel lifts you over downtown in the dark. That’s how a good day here ends.
Get to St. Louis Union Station after lunch, though, and the sharks have already eaten.
The feed is on the St. Louis Aquarium’s posted daily schedule for 10:00 to 10:15 a.m., in Shark Canyon, the 250,000-gallon habitat where sharks, rays and sea turtles glide past the glass while small hands smudge it from the other side. By then, the aquarium, the ropes course and the mirror maze are already counting down to closing time. Out on the plaza, meanwhile, the St. Louis Wheel didn’t start turning until noon on a weekday, and it will still be lifting gondolas into the dark at 9.
Nobody tells first-timers this: Union Station runs on two clocks. The indoor attractions keep museum hours. The Wheel Park keeps carnival hours. Roll in after lunch and you spend the afternoon racing one of them. Roll in at 9, take a long lunch and stay past dark, and you get both. Below: the day that works, every price before tax, the pass that costs $27.75 less than seven separate tickets, the 3 p.m. rule that catches parents of teenagers, and the free fire show that’s on pause right now.
### What time of day is best to go to St. Louis Union Station?
Early, then late, with a slow middle. Here’s that day, scene by scene.
Morning, in the blue. The aquarium opens at 9 a.m. Stand at the glass of Shark Canyon and the whole room goes blue while a ray folds past at eye level. The ray and fish feed is posted for 9:45 and the shark feed for 10:00, though the aquarium notes its schedule can change. At the shark and ray touch pool, a $5 cup of fish lets your kid feed the stingrays. Your aquarium day pass allows re-entry all day, so you can walk out for lunch and come back.
Late morning, three stories up. The ropes course puts you three stories up on rope bridges and swinging logs, and the log moves the second you trust it. Next door to that nerve, the mirror maze turns every corner into a kaleidoscope of LED light and reflections. The ropes course and the mirror maze both run 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, and the ropes course sells its last ticket one hour before closing.
Noon, on the plaza. The Wheel Park opens at noon Monday through Friday and at 10 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday. In season, Fairground Eats serves crispy funnel cakes and 30-ounce fresh-squeezed lemonade from noon, powdered sugar on your fingers and a cup too big to hold one-handed. The Soda Fountain opens at 11 a.m. for diner burgers and Freak Shakes.
Mid-afternoon, the rule. After 3 p.m., visitors 16 and younger must be with a parent or supervising adult age 21 or older, a valid ID is required, and one adult can bring up to six youths. If the plan was to drop a pack of teenagers off for the evening, this is the rule that ends it.
Late afternoon, look up. The aquarium closes at 5 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and at 6 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Walk into the hotel lobby, tip your head back, and on the hour from 5 to 10 p.m., fireworks and flying birds sweep across the 65-foot ceiling of the Grand Hall.
After dark, the Wheel. The gondola door closes and the plaza noise drops away. A Wheel ride is a 10-12 minute flight, 200 feet up, in an enclosed, climate-controlled gondola, with the Gateway Arch and the downtown skyline lit outside the glass. Down below, the carousel glows against the old 1894 station. Take one more lap before you go.
And if a storm rolls in, or a toddler hits the wall at 4 p.m., the money isn’t gone. Tickets for the Wheel, mini golf, the carousel, Loco Motion, Flying Louie and the Wave Swinger are valid for 90 days. An aquarium day pass you miss because of illness or weather can be exchanged any time in the next 90 days. Screenshot that paragraph for the next meltdown.
### Union Station runs on two clocks
Here’s every ticketed attraction and both light shows in one place, sorted by the clock they keep. Prices are adult tickets before tax, taken from Union Station’s own ticket calendar and attraction pages. The aquarium prices by date.
Read it top to bottom and the line jumps out. Every ticketed attraction under the station roof shuts by 5 or 6 p.m. Everything out under the sky runs into the night. By the time the aquarium halls are emptying, the Wheel’s gondolas are still climbing over the plaza and the carousel is starting to glow. Plan around that line and nothing gets missed.
### What are the attractions at Union Station in St. Louis?
Here’s what each one is like up close, plus the price or rule that matters before you go.
The St. Louis Aquarium. Six habitats that follow the water from the creatures of local rivers out to The Deep, the twilight world of the ocean’s depths. River otters frolic in Changing Rivers. Sharks, rays and sea turtles glide through Shark Canyon. The aquarium bills itself as the nation’s most interactive, and the touch pools are where kids lose track of time. Allow at least 1 to 3 hours. Children under 3 get in free.
The St. Louis Wheel. It climbs 200 feet with 42 fully enclosed, climate-controlled gondolas, so January wind and July heat stay outside. You ride only with your own group, up to eight to a gondola. The splurge is the VIP gondola: leather bucket seats and a glass floor for a view straight down. Strollers stay on the ground, and there’s a spot to park them.
The Ropes Course. Three stories up over the old station floor, 30-plus obstacles: narrow balance beams, rope bridges and swinging logs, all suspended high above the retail floor below. Kids under 48 inches get Sky Tykes, a low course where parents walk alongside. The rules to check before you pay: closed-toe and closed-heel shoes, 48 inches to 6 feet 8 inches tall for the big course, under 300 pounds, and 13 to go alone. No phones, keys or wallets on the course; the lockers are free.
The Mirror Maze, and where to find it. If you went looking for it out with the rides, that’s why you missed it: it’s indoors. The A-Maze-Ing Discoveries Mirror Maze sits inside the historic 1894 station, a 1904 World’s Fair-themed run of mirrored corridors and LED light that turns every corner into a kaleidoscope. The Mirror Maze is No. 12 on Union Station’s own property map.
The Carousel. Out on the plaza, steps from the Wheel. A ride is $5, and parents can stand next to small children for free. In the daylight it’s a quick spin; after dark it glows against the old station walls.
Mini Golf. The course has 18 holes directly beneath the historic train shed, in the shadow of the 200-foot Wheel. The course is fully lit, so a night round works.
The seasonal rides. The Wave Swinger lifts riders up to 25 feet; you need to be 48 inches to ride alone, or 42 inches with a companion 16 or older. Flying Louie is a swinging pirate ship. Loco Motion is a mini spinning coaster. Union Station lists the Wave Swinger, Flying Louie and Loco Motion as seasonal, so check before you promise them.
Selfie Express. A train-themed walk-through of more than 10 photo rooms, built for the kid with the phone.
### What is the schedule for the Union Station Light Show?
The Grand Hall Light Show is the one visitors walk right under without knowing it’s there. In the hotel lobby, look up: fireworks, flying birds and an aquarium scene sweep across the 65-foot barrel-vaulted ceiling in 30 video vignettes set to music. It was created by Technomedia, a collaborator with Cirque du Soleil, and Union Station calls it the first of its kind in the U.S. One vignette tells the station’s story, narrated by John Goodman; others feature Jon Hamm, Bob Costas, Dan Dierdorf, Joe Buck and Chris Kerber. Shows run on the hour from 5 to 10 p.m. daily, except when the Grand Hall is rented for a private event. Union Station’s own holiday guide says admission is included for hotel guests and dining patrons, so the easy way in is a drink or dinner in the Grand Hall, which serves from 4 p.m. to midnight.
The Fire & Light Show is the free one: eight lotus-shaped pods on the lake shooting pillars of fire 25 feet into the air, timed to a pounding soundtrack, on the hour. Fire that tall throws its heat across the water. But when we checked Union Station’s show page, it said the show was “taking a brief pause” for routine maintenance on the lake elements. Check the Fire and Light Show page the day you go. When it’s running, Landry’s boardwalk tables give you a front-row view.
### Combo tickets: the math that saves real money
This is the part people get wrong at the ticket window, standing in line with a kid tugging their sleeve and five separate prices in their head. Union Station sells bundles, priced per person and not transferable:
All-Access Pass: $70 adult, $59.99 child. Unlimited aquarium, Wheel, carousel, Selfie Express, mirror maze, Flying Louie, Loco Motion, Wave Swinger and mini golf, plus one run on the ropes course. Bought one at a time on a $29.75 aquarium day, the aquarium, the Wheel, the ropes course, Selfie Express, the mirror maze, mini golf and one carousel ride cost an adult $97.75 before tax. At $70, the All-Access Pass costs $27.75 less than those seven separate tickets, and it makes the rides unlimited, so you can ride the Wheel twice.
Aquarium + Wheel: $40 adult, $30 child. The two big ones. Separately, on a $29.75 aquarium day, that’s $47.75 for an adult.
Indoor Pass: $50 adult, $45 child. Aquarium, ropes course, mirror maze and Selfie Express. The rainy-day bundle.
Groups of 10 or more can book group tickets instead. If you searched for a Wheel group combo, start there.
Building the day around the aquarium? Check one thing first. Our aquarium tickets guide shows which day is cheapest and who gets in free, so you buy the right pass before you buy the combo.
If you’re the diner, the bar or the gift shop a few blocks from the station, the families reading this are about to decide where to eat once the Wheel stops turning. Be in front of them when they look: see what a Gold listing puts on their screen.
### Where to eat at Union Station, kitchen by kitchen
The smell hits first: fried dough from the plaza, burgers from the diner. You never have to leave the property, but the kitchens keep different hours, so match the meal to the clock.
Station Grille - breakfast 6 to 11 a.m. on weekdays (7 a.m. on weekends) and lunch until 2 p.m.
Soda Fountain - daily 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Classic diner burgers and the famous Freak Shakes.
The Train Shed - apps, entrées, cocktails and rotating taps, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 on Friday and Saturday.
Landry’s Seafood House - Gulf Coast plates like Blackened Snapper and Lemon-Pepper Catfish, from 11:30 a.m.
The Grand Hall - 4 p.m. to midnight under 65-foot archways and mosaics, with the light show overhead.
The Pitch Athletic Club & Tavern - for fans, across the street from Energizer stadium.
Fairground Eats (seasonal) - crispy funnel cakes, soft pretzels with cheese and 30-ounce fresh-squeezed lemonade, noon to 8 p.m.
Cookies and Cupcakes - 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., next to the aquarium gift shop.
Leave the cooler in the car. Union Station’s code of conduct prohibits outside food and alcohol, and it prohibits coolers, hard or soft-sided.
Saving a grown-ups’ night for later? Start with where to eat on The Hill.
### Parking and MetroLink: get the ticket stamped before you leave the fish
South Lot - directly behind Union Station, entered from Market Street on 18th Street. It’s the closest lot to the aquarium and the outdoor attractions, with accessible spaces, a drop-off and a complimentary parking tram.
West Lot - entered from Market Street on 20th, closest to the hotel and dining.
What it costs - both lots charge hourly and special event rates, and both are credit card only at the exit.
The $5 rate - it’s an aquarium perk. Take your parking ticket to the aquarium gift shop near the photo counter and get it stamped, and the fee is $5 when you exit. Do it on your way out of the aquarium. Once you’re back at the car with a hungry kid, nobody walks back in.
MetroLink - the Union Station MetroLink stop is at 301 S. 18th Street.
### Where is Union Station? Downtown, not Dogtown
If you searched whether Union Station is in Dogtown: it isn’t. It sits in the heart of downtown at 1820 Market Street, St. Louis, MO 63103. Dogtown is a different part of the city, the area around Clayton-Tamm directly south of the Saint Louis Zoo; our Dogtown guide covers it. For GPS, the Wheel and the aquarium both list 201 S. 18th Street.
One more mix-up worth heading off. If you’re here to catch a train, you’re at the wrong building: the final Amtrak train left Union Station in 1978.
### The clock tower is still taller than the Wheel
Stand on the plaza at dusk and look from the Wheel to the old clock tower. The Wheel is 200 feet tall and the clock tower is 230 feet, so the old clock tower still wins by 30 feet.
When Union Station opened on September 1, 1894, it was the world’s largest and busiest train terminal: Theodore Link’s Romanesque design, serving 22 railroads, with the Harvey Girls in crisp black-and-white uniforms running trackside meals. The station expanded for the 20 million visitors of the 1904 World’s Fair, and by the 1940s it handled more than 100,000 passengers a day. In 1948, Harry Truman held up the “Dewey Defeats Truman” headline on its platform.
Then the interstates and the airlines won. The building became a National Historic Landmark in 1970, the last Amtrak train pulled out in 1978, and in 1985 it reopened as a “festival marketplace” after a $150 million restoration, the largest adaptive re-use project in the country at the time. The aquarium, the Wheel and the rides are its next act. Curious what’s left of the shopping? See our Union Station shopping guide.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the attractions at Union Station in St. Louis?
A.  Inside: the St. Louis Aquarium, a ropes course three stories over the main floor, the A-Maze-Ing Discoveries Mirror Maze and Selfie Express. Outside: the 200-foot St. Louis Wheel, a carousel, 18-hole mini golf and seasonal rides like the Wave Swinger. Add the Grand Hall light show and, when it’s running, the Fire & Light Show on the lake.
### Q. What time is the light show at Union Station in St Louis?
A.  The Grand Hall light show runs on the hour from 5 to 10 p.m. daily, unless the hall is booked for a private event. It plays across the 65-foot ceiling of the hotel lobby, and Union Station says admission is included for hotel guests and dining patrons, so order a drink in the Grand Hall and look up.
### Q. How often is the fire show at Union Station St Louis?
A.  The Fire & Light Show on the lake runs on the hour and is free: eight lotus-shaped pods shooting fire 25 feet into the air, set to music. When we checked, Union Station’s show page said it was paused for routine maintenance on the lake elements, so check that page before you plan a night around it.
### Q. How much does it cost to ride the Ferris wheel at Union Station St. Louis?
A.  A Wheel ticket is $18 for ages 13 and up and $12 for kids 3 to 12, before tax, and children 2 and under ride free. The Aquarium + Wheel combo is $40 for adults, and a Wheel ticket stays valid for 90 days if the weather turns on you.
### Q. How long does it take to ride the St. Louis ferris wheel?
A.  One ride is a 10-12 minute flight in an enclosed, climate-controlled gondola that climbs 200 feet, with the Gateway Arch and downtown in view. You ride only with your own group, up to eight to a gondola. The Wheel opens at noon on weekdays and at 10 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday.
### Q. How much does it cost to park at Union station St. Louis?
A.  The South and West lots charge hourly and special event rates, credit card only. If you visit the aquarium, take your parking ticket to the aquarium gift shop near the photo counter and get it stamped, and you pay $5 when you exit. Or ride MetroLink to the Union Station stop at 301 S. 18th Street.
### Q. How old is Union Station in STL?
A.  Union Station opened on September 1, 1894, as the world’s largest and busiest train terminal, serving 22 railroads. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1970, saw its last Amtrak train in 1978, and reopened in 1985 after a $150 million restoration. Its 230-foot clock tower still stands taller than the 200-foot Wheel.
### Q. Is Union Station in St. Louis worth visiting?
A.  Yes, if you time it. Get there by 9 or 10 a.m. for the aquarium and the indoor attractions, which close by 5 or 6 p.m., then stay for the Grand Hall light show on the hour and a Wheel ride after dark. The $70 All-Access Pass covers most of the ticketed list for one adult.
### Q. Is Union Station in Dogtown?
A.  No. Union Station is in the heart of downtown at 1820 Market Street, St. Louis, MO 63103. Dogtown is the area around Clayton-Tamm, directly south of the Saint Louis Zoo. To reach the station, MetroLink stops right there at 301 S. 18th Street, and the South parking lot is entered from Market Street on 18th Street.

## Started With No Factory, Now in Every Target: 10 St. Louis Businesses to Watch
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-businesses-in-st-louis-to-watch
“Power outages, equipment breaks. We aren’t making our numbers.” That was the Katie’s Pizza & Pasta team with 50 days left on a 400,000-pizza order for Target, every crust stretched by hand and slid into a wood-fired oven at 800 degrees, heat you feel on your face before you smell the char. They went from 1,000 pizzas on day one to 7,000 a day by day 45, and they made the deadline in 96 days. The frozen line started during the pandemic, when the St. Louis dining room became an assembly line and the servers and bartenders became delivery drivers. No factory, no funding. Now it’s a reported $20 million retail deal and a pizza in every Target in the country. That’s what a business to watch looks like up close. It rarely looks like the old standbys that already anchor the metro’s economy: the brewery, the pet food, the bread.
The other nine are just as easy to miss from the street: a fence line along Cass Avenue, a startup rebuilding seeds inside the chloroplast, a WashU cancer spinout under a new name. Every one earned its spot with a recent win you can check yourself, and one once-hyped name, Benson Hill, got cut after its bankruptcy, because yesterday’s buzz doesn’t count.
One St. Louis secret hides in these stories: the city pays founders to stay. Arch Grants gives winners of its startup competition $75,000 with no equity taken, plus $25,000 more to relocate, and asks one thing back: headquarter in the City of St. Louis for at least a year. Buck Surgical, No. 6 below, won one, then a $100,000 Growth Grant. Arch Grants hasn’t announced its next window; the last one ran about six weeks, Feb. 18 to March 31. If you’re building something that can scale, sign up for the reminder at archgrants.org tonight.
Run something smaller? Here’s the night these ten never have. Your phone face-down on the counter at 9 p.m. A homeowner in Florissant tapping a request into a lead-farm app. Three other contractors’ phones lighting up in three other trucks, because the app sold that one request to all of them and will bill every one. That middleman is standing in the doorway the ten companies below made sure to own: when a customer, an investor or a new hire went looking, the search ended at their door. Your work was never the question. So here’s the question worth asking: when a neighbor in Kirkwood asks her phone for what you do, does the answer reach you, or an app that resells her request?
Five minutes, tonight, free: what would you find if you searched your own trade plus your neighborhood the way that neighbor does, on Google, on the map, and in the AI app on her phone? How many of the names that come back are apps reselling the job instead of people who’d do it? And if you’d rather sell to companies like the ten below, they gather in two places worth a visit: T-REX downtown for geospatial startups and the 39 North district in Creve Coeur for agtech.
### 1. Next NGA West & T-REX (geospatial): a $1.7 billion campus in north city
Lunch hour at Jefferson and Cass, traffic easing past a security fence that runs around 97 acres of the St. Louis Place neighborhood. Behind it sits the new $1.7 billion Western headquarters of the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, opened in September 2025. NGA turns satellite images, drone footage and maps into geospatial intelligence, the analysis of anything tied to a place on Earth, used by the military and disaster-response teams; it helped pinpoint Osama bin Laden’s compound. With T-REX, the downtown tech incubator, and the geospatial startups it’s pulling in, NGA is pulling mapping and location companies to the city that used to have to court them. For owners: a campus that size changes who’s driving down Jefferson at lunch. If you feed, fix or move people on the north side, add St. Louis Place and the streets around Jefferson and Cass to the places your profile and listings name.
### 2. Katie’s Pizza & Pasta (food): 400,000 pizzas in 96 days
Early on, the phone rang and a federal agent was on the line: pull the pizzas off the grocery shelves. The pepperoni meant USDA inspection, a detour most founders never hear about. Chef Katie Lee went through it and kept going. Her premium frozen line, a consumer packaged goods brand sold on grocery shelves, is now in all roughly 1,800 Target stores nationwide, after her team hand-made a reported 400,000 pizzas in 96 days. Frozen-entrée sales are up 82% and sauces 91%, more major retailers are signed, a dedicated plant in Bridgeton should triple frozen-pizza output, and a fourth restaurant is open in Crestwood.
### 3. Plastomics (agtech): a better seed, built inside the chloroplast
Hold a leaf up to a window and every green speck you see is a chloroplast, the tiny structure where photosynthesis happens. It carries its own strand of DNA, and that’s where Plastomics loads new traits. Most genetically modified crops get the new gene in the plant’s main genome, its complete set of DNA. Putting it in the chloroplast instead makes the trait more stable, lets several traits stack together, and keeps it from drifting to other plants through pollen. The St. Louis startup raised roughly $6 million in Series B funding to push toward commercial seeds.
### 4. Pivot Bio (agtech): fertilizer pulled out of thin air
Those white anhydrous tanks parked at the edge of spring cornfields along I-70 hold one of farming’s biggest costs and pollutants: nitrogen fertilizer. Pivot Bio wants to shrink that bill. The company engineers microbes - microscopic soil bacteria - that perform nitrogen fixation, pulling nitrogen straight out of the air to feed a corn plant the way nature intended, so farmers can use less synthetic fertilizer. The company has committed to a $7 million-plus expansion adding about 40 jobs, with manufacturing in Hazelwood and R&D in the 39 North agtech district in Creve Coeur. Its global headquarters now sits in the Twin Cities, but the lab work and the production run here, another sign St. Louis is the center of gravity for the future of farming. For owners: forty new jobs in Hazelwood means forty more people looking for lunch, a mechanic and a barber near the plant.
### 5. Allotera Therapeutics, formerly Wugen (biotech): cancer-fighting cells, off the shelf
Allotera Therapeutics, the company most of St. Louis still knows as Wugen, is a spinout of WashU Medicine chasing a holy grail of cancer treatment. It’s developing CAR-T therapy - treatment that re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to hunt and kill cancer - but in an “off-the-shelf” version. Today CAR-T is custom-built for each patient, which is slow and enormously expensive; Allotera is working on a universal, ready-to-use form that any eligible patient could receive. Its lead therapy, sofi-cel, is now in a global pivotal Phase 2 clinical trial for hard-to-treat T-cell leukemia and lymphoma, backed by roughly $150 million in Series C money. If it works, it’s a very big deal - and it’s happening here.
### 6. Buck Surgical (medtech): tools for vessels thinner than spaghetti
Buck Surgical builds tools for microvascular surgery - operating on blood vessels and structures thinner than a strand of spaghetti, the delicate work behind reconstructive and transplant procedures. Precision at that scale is brutally hard, and Buck’s technology aims to make it faster and more reliable. The startup was named a 2026 “Startup to Watch” by the St. Louis Business Journal, raised $4.2 million, and won a growth grant from Arch Grants, the St. Louis nonprofit that hands promising startups equity-free cash to stay and build in the city. Buck reads like a case study in how the region’s medtech pipeline works: a highly technical, patient-serving company born from St. Louis’s deep bench of surgeons, engineers, and university research.
Totally unrelated, but if you’re suddenly hungry - where to eat in Chesterfield.
### 7. DeepSight (medtech): ultrasound that steers the needle
DeepSight, an imaging company with offices in Clayton and California’s Bay Area, tackles a problem every clinician knows: guiding a needle to exactly the right spot inside the body. Its NeedleVue system uses medical ultrasound - imaging that bounces sound waves off tissue to see beneath the skin in real time - to help doctors place a needle accurately for procedures like biopsies and injections. In 2025 the company earned FDA clearance for the device, the regulatory green light that lets it actually reach patients - a milestone many medtech startups never hit. For patients, better needle guidance can mean fewer failed attempts and less pain during a routine biopsy or injection; for the company, clearance is what turns a promising idea into a real product.
### 8. Take Root Hospitality, Vicia (food): a Beard finalist that got leaner
If one of these companies is where you want to work next, start with where working adults in St. Louis build new skills.
On the culinary side, few St. Louis names carry the weight of Vicia, the vegetable-forward, farm-driven restaurant from chefs Michael and Tara Gallina under their Take Root Hospitality group. Vicia was a 2026 James Beard Award finalist for Outstanding Restaurant - the culinary world’s equivalent of an Oscar nomination - and while Philadelphia’s Kalaya took the medal, making that final five puts St. Louis’s food scene squarely on the national stage. The group has gotten leaner, not bigger: Taqueria Morita has closed, and Take Root now runs two restaurants, Vicia and Winslow’s Table. Fewer rooms, sharper focus.
Curious what else is happening across the metro? Explore local businesses and community on the St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you run something smaller, start here. Katie’s frozen pizza started as a pandemic plan to keep one restaurant’s doors open, with no factory and no funding. Now it’s in every Target. So when a neighbor searches for what you do at 9 p.m., does that search end with your phone buzzing on the counter, or with an app that rents your own customers back to you? See what Gold does for $357 a year, under a dollar a day, or see who gets named instead of you. Refuse to be invisible.
### 9. Orise Distribution (logistics): 40 new jobs in medical supply
Not every business to watch is a lab or a kitchen. Orise Distribution, a medical-supply distributor, announced a $6.2 million expansion adding about 40 new jobs in 2025 as it builds out nationwide distribution and adds textile-manufacturing lines. It’s the kind of quiet, job-creating growth - real facilities, real hires - that keeps a regional economy healthy underneath the flashier headlines. Medical-supply distribution is a steady, recession-resistant business, and Orise’s move to add its own manufacturing means more of that supply chain runs through St. Louis.
### 10. HJ Enterprises (manufacturing): 150 jobs headed to High Ridge
St. Louis’s comeback runs well past the downtown redevelopment story, out into the exurbs. HJ Enterprises broke ground on an expansion set to bring roughly 150 jobs to Jefferson County, in High Ridge, in 2025 - a meaningful boost for a part of the metro that doesn’t always get the spotlight, and a vote of confidence in local manufacturing. For families in Jefferson County towns like High Ridge, Arnold, and House Springs, a growing local employer means good jobs close to home - the kind of win that rarely makes national headlines but genuinely changes a community.
### A note on who’s not here
A “to watch” list is only useful if it’s honest, so we vetted every entry - and deliberately left off some names you might expect. The clearest example: Benson Hill, once one of St. Louis’s most-hyped agtech companies. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2025, was delisted from the Nasdaq, and converted to liquidation later that year, with its assets sold off. Including a company on the way down would defeat the purpose. Every business above was checked for real, current momentum - a recent raise, expansion, approval, or award. Yesterday’s buzz didn’t count.
### Why St. Louis - the bigger picture
Notice the pattern: plant science, biotech, medtech, and geospatial keep coming up. That’s not a coincidence. St. Louis has quietly assembled one of the country’s densest innovation ecosystems, and these companies are its output:
The Donald Danforth Plant Science Center and the 39 North district make the region a global hub for agtech - the science of feeding the world.
The Cortex Innovation Community in the Central West End anchors tech and biotech startups near Washington University and its medical school.
T-REX downtown and the new NGA headquarters are building a national geospatial cluster.
Arch Grants and BioSTL pour equity-free funding and support into founders who agree to build here.
Add it up and you get a city that punches far above its size in exactly the industries that will define the next decade. The businesses above aren’t flukes - they’re the product of a machine St. Louis has been quietly building for years. For a city long known mostly for what it used to be - the gateway west, the brewery town - that’s a genuine shift: St. Louis is increasingly known for what it’s building next. The proof is the ten companies above, each with a 2025 or 2026 milestone already on the board.
One more name worth watching is yours. Remember the habit from the top: every company above made sure that when someone went looking, it was there. The Florissant bakery pulling its first trays at 5 a.m. and the two-truck HVAC crew in Fenton deserve the same shot, and too often a middleman takes it. Nobody there is bad at the work. They’re just hard to see. A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts one business in up to 10 categories across 40 St. Louis communities, about 400 search combinations, with no public address required.

### Q. Which companies have headquarters in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty of big ones. The region is home to Centene, Reinsurance Group of America, Emerson, Edward Jones, Graybar, Ameren, Stifel, World Wide Technology, Post Holdings, Energizer, Build-A-Bear and Purina, plus Bayer’s North American crop science hub in Creve Coeur. Panera has announced it is moving its headquarters to the Boston area. This list skips those household names for the smaller companies to watch.
### Q. What Fortune 500 companies are in St. Louis?
A.  Eight St. Louis-area companies made Fortune’s most recent 500, ranked on the prior year’s revenue. Centene leads at No. 19, followed by Reinsurance Group of America at No. 193, Emerson at No. 245, Edward Jones at No. 249, Graybar at No. 342 and Ameren at No. 466, which returned to the list after a year off. The rankings change every June, so check Fortune’s current list.
### Q. What are the top 10 companies in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the yardstick. By revenue, the top names are Fortune 500 firms like Centene, Reinsurance Group of America, Emerson and Edward Jones. By headcount, BJC HealthCare and Washington University lead. By momentum, which is what this St Louis Near Me Directory list measures, watch NGA’s new campus, Katie’s Pizza & Pasta, Plastomics, Pivot Bio, Allotera and Buck Surgical.
### Q. What are the top workplaces in St. Louis?
A.  The best-known scorecard is the St. Louis Post-Dispatch Top Workplaces list, built from employee surveys. Its latest edition named 160 employers. Among the large ones are Benjamin F. Edwards, Moneta, Lou Fusz Automotive Network, St. Louis County Library, Waterway Carwash and CarShield. The list turns over every year, so check the current edition before you apply anywhere.
### Q. Is St. Louis a good place for startups?
A.  Increasingly, yes. St. Louis offers a low cost of living, major research anchors in Washington University and the Danforth Plant Science Center, and startup support that’s hard to match. Arch Grants gives founders equity-free cash to build here, while Cortex, 39 North, T-REX and BioSTL provide space, funding and mentorship. The region is especially strong for agtech, biotech and geospatial startups.

## Missouri's Largest Office Tower Sold for $3.6 Million: Why Downtown St. Louis Is Ripe for Development
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-downtown-st-louis-is-ripe-for-development
Forty-four floors stacked over Chestnut Street, and since AT&T consolidated its offices in 2017, almost nobody working behind the windows. Walk past at quitting time and the only footsteps on that block are yours. In 2006 that tower, the former AT&T building at 909 Chestnut, sold for $204.9 million. In April 2024 the Goldman Group of Boston bought it for about $3.6 million. Less than two cents on the dollar, for the largest office building in Missouri.
Now the number most people outside City Hall have never heard. Stephen Westbrooks runs the St. Louis Development Corporation, the independent economic development agency serving the city. He told St. Louis Public Radio that downtown is “at about maybe 12,000 residents” and needs to be “closer to maybe 25,000” before the neighborhood has the density to carry the grocery stores and restaurants people expect to walk to. That is the real gap downtown. Not a shortage of buildings. A shortage of neighbors.
So here is the line worth repeating at the next tailgate: the biggest office tower in Missouri sold for less than two cents on the dollar, and the city’s own development chief says downtown needs about twice the people it has. Cheap buildings plus a missing crowd is exactly what ripe looks like.
We are not going to cheerlead. The problems are real and we name them below. But the setup is more real than it has been in a long time, and most of the people who drive past it every day on the way to the highway have not noticed.
### Why is downtown St. Louis ripe for development?
Because three things lined up at once, and they rarely do. The first is price. When a 44-story tower changes hands for about $3.6 million, the cost of getting in the door is no longer the obstacle. The second is help. The city set aside $55 million of its Rams settlement money for downtown, and Missouri’s historic tax credit can stack with the federal one to cover up to 45% of qualified rehab costs on a certified historic building in St. Louis. The third is a signal: Cordish Cos. plans a roughly $670 million redevelopment of the old Millennium Hotel site downtown.
Somebody built these buildings to last a century, in stone and brick that still holds a chill on a winter morning. Most of the walls are fine. What they are missing is people inside them, and every dollar of public money in this story is aimed at that one problem.
None of that is a finished comeback. It is a starting line. The question for anyone who lives here, works here or is thinking about moving here is simple: do you read that $3.6 million price as proof of collapse, or as the cheapest entry a downtown this size will offer in our lifetime?
This is not only developer news. You can act on it this week. Missouri’s historic credit is available to both commercial properties and owner-occupied homes, according to the State Historic Preservation Office, so a city homeowner with a certified historic house can use the same tool as a tower developer. The office strongly encourages applicants to meet with its Architectural Preservation Services team before submitting an application, and those consultations are available Tuesday afternoons and Thursday mornings by appointment. Book one before you price the windows, the tuckpointing or the roof. The pre-application review is where you learn what qualifies.
### Why are there so many empty buildings in downtown St. Louis?
Walk the blocks between the Old Courthouse and Union Station and you can hear it: your own footsteps bouncing off stone that was carved for a much busier street. The Brookings Institution, in a study of office-to-residential conversion that used St. Louis as its case, put it bluntly. Downtown “suffers from highly concentrated vacancies in highly visible properties, such as the Railway Exchange Building (vacant since 2014) and the AT&T Tower (vacant since 2017).”
Highly visible is the key phrase. Two giant empty towers make a whole district feel empty, even on blocks where people are living, working and eating lunch. The buildings were made for a world of big single-company headquarters, and that world left. What stays behind is a lot of square footage with good bones and no tenant.
Shopping went the same way. If you are old enough, you may remember riding the escalators at St. Louis Centre. When it opened in 1985 it was the largest urban shopping mall in the United States. It closed in 2006 as an almost-vacant dead mall. That is the honest history: downtown has lost big things before, and it has also turned them into something else.
### The tax credit that pays St. Louis less than the rest of Missouri
Here is a detail that surprises almost everyone who hears it. Missouri created its own historic preservation tax credit in 1997. According to the State Historic Preservation Office, the state credit is 25% for certified historic structures in St. Louis and Kansas City, and 35% if the property sits outside those two cities. Add the federal program’s 20% credit and the total reaches 45% in St. Louis and Kansas City, or 55% everywhere else in the state.
So the two big cities get the smaller number. Even so, 45% of qualified rehab costs is a very large share of a renovation bill, and it is the reason a money-losing restoration can turn into a project a bank will finance. You can see what that looks like on Washington Avenue in Downtown West, where developers have acquired many buildings in the Washington Avenue Historic District and redeveloped them as loft condos and apartments. Brick that once smelled of machine oil and bolts of cloth now holds somebody’s kitchen.
That same credit is still available today. It is the lever that makes converting an empty office tower possible at all. For the full stack, read our guide to St. Louis downtown development incentives.
### Is downtown St. Louis safe to walk?
This is the question underneath every other question, so here are the police department’s own numbers instead of a vibe. In its year-end report, the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department said homicides declined to 141 incidents in 2025. Overall Part I crime fell 16% compared to 2024 and 28% compared to 2023. Shooting incidents fell 28%, and robberies dropped 15% year over year.
Two honest caveats. Those are citywide figures, not a downtown-only count, and a lower number is not the same thing as a low number. And remember who gets counted. St. Louis voted in 1876 to separate from the county and become an independent city, according to the St. Louis County Library, so the city’s crime numbers cover only the old city line, not the suburbs around it. That frozen border is a big part of why St. Louis shows up on scary national lists.
For a walk downtown, do what locals do. Go where people already are: the Arch grounds, a ballgame crowd heading up the street, Washington Avenue at dinner time. Keep your phone in your pocket at a crosswalk and your eyes up. Use the same street sense you would use in any downtown.
### Will St. Louis ever recover? Follow the money
You can argue about vibes forever. Money is easier to read. The Board of Aldermen voted 12-3 to send a plan for the city’s $255 million Rams settlement to Mayor Cara Spencer, and she signed legislation authorizing it. Downtown will receive $55 million of it. That money is aimed at redeveloping larger vacant buildings, such as the Railway Exchange, and at pushing redevelopment of the riverfront.
He also pointed to new statewide incentives and local legislation. His words: “That legislation, if we’re able to execute, gives us a running start to facilitate investment.” He went further: “I think it makes our downtown nationally competitive.” Note the “if.” Westbrooks said the challenge now is to capitalize on those opportunities, and that is the honest place to stand.
Then there is the riverfront. Demolition of the 28-story Millennium Hotel began in November 2025, St. Louis Public Radio reported. The Gateway Arch Park Foundation bought the 4.2-acre site, and a redevelopment by Cordish Cos. is expected to cost roughly $670 million, with a 1.3 million-square-foot structure holding residential, office, commercial and public space. That nearly 60-year-old building is coming down. Nobody spends $670 million on a district they think is finished.

### So why is downtown St. Louis ripe for development right now?
Because the buildings are cheap and the help is stacked. The former AT&T tower, the largest office building in Missouri, sold for about $3.6 million in April 2024. The city set aside $55 million of its Rams settlement for downtown, and state plus federal historic credits can reach 45% of qualified rehab costs in St. Louis.
### The catalyst that has not fired yet
The wild card sits north of downtown. The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency opened its new St. Louis campus on September 26, 2025, with the move of its workforce expected to wrap up by spring 2026. A large federal employer settling into the city is the kind of anchor that, in other places, pulls contractors, startups and lunch traffic in its wake.
Here is the honest part. That spillover has not clearly shown up downtown yet. The campus opened in 2025. The boom around it is still potential. And that is the pattern across downtown: the ingredients are on the counter, and the oven is not on.
Call it the chicken-and-egg standoff. Residents wait for more shops and restaurants. Shops and restaurants wait for more residents. Developers wait for proof of demand. Westbrooks’ 25,000 number is really a description of how to break that loop: enough people living downtown that a grocery store and a dozen restaurants can pay their rent. Whoever moves first while prices sit this low is the one who looks smart in ten years.

You do not need a development budget to read this story early. You need to know where to look. Picture-perfect renderings come and go. These are the signals that tell you the comeback is real:
The Railway Exchange. It is named in the plan for the $55 million downtown money. When work starts on that building, the plan is moving.
The Millennium site. Demolition is the easy part. Watch for the Cordish construction to start on the 4.2-acre site.
The 909 Chestnut tower. The Goldman Group has said the project would rely heavily on incentives. A financing announcement there would be the clearest sign that the new state and city tools work.
Downtown population. 12,000 today by the city’s estimate, 25,000 as the goal. Every new loft building moves that number.
Your own walk. Go on a weeknight, not just game day. Count the lit windows on Washington Avenue. Notice which restaurants are full. You will feel the trend before any report prints it.
Thinking of living downtown? The gap is the point. A neighborhood that needs twice the residents it has is a neighborhood that will compete for you: loft rents, new restaurants trying to win regulars, and the first pick of the buildings that come back. A $670 million plan for the Millennium site. A city development chief with a number on the wall: 25,000. Downtown is not dying. It is waiting for people.

## St. Louis Downtown Development Incentives Explained
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-downtown-development-incentives-explained
Buy a grand old building downtown for a fraction of its value, then watch the government hand back nearly half the cost of fixing it up. In downtown St. Louis in 2026, that’s roughly how the math works. Between long-standing tax credits and a fresh wave of city money, St. Louis has assembled one of the most aggressive redevelopment-incentive stacks of any major American downtown. Which raises the question worth real money to get right: of that whole stack, which incentives can a single project actually combine — and which quietly cancel each other out?
This is the companion money-and-mechanics guide to our broader case that downtown St. Louis is ripe for development. Here we get specific: exactly what the widely-reported $55 million is, the tax-credit engine that makes rehabs pencil out, the other tools stacked on top, and the honest caveats every developer should keep in mind. Anyone weighing a downtown project will want the nuts and bolts, so that’s what this is.
Bookmark this - incentive programs change, and we keep it current. Confirm the latest details with the city before you commit capital. Then read why downtown St. Louis is ripe for development.
If you’re the lender, the attorney or the general contractor who turns an incentive into a building, list your firm where developers start their search.
### What is the $55 million for downtown St. Louis?
The number gets thrown around loosely, so let’s be precise. The $55 million is not a new tax or a mystery fund. It’s the downtown share of a $255 million spending plan the Board of Aldermen passed on July 2, 2026 — the city’s cut of the legal settlement it won when the Rams NFL franchise left for Los Angeles (STLPR). Mayor Cara Spencer and Board President Megan Green unveiled the full plan, which spreads across the whole city. The downtown slice breaks down like this:
That $15 million for acquiring vacant buildings targets exactly the kind of stuck, high-profile properties that have dragged downtown down. The long-empty Railway Exchange Building is one named target. The city takes control of dead assets, then hands them to developers who will actually revive them. One honest note: like every public commitment, this $55 million is current as of 2026 and subject to the usual political process. Budget fights and political pressure can reshape or delay incentives, so treat this as a strong signal of intent backed by a passed bill, not an ironclad guarantee.
Context matters here: the $55 million is one slice of a citywide plan. The larger $255 million package directs its biggest share, roughly $120 million, toward North St. Louis, including recovery from a 2025 tornado, plus about $70 million for infrastructure across the city. Downtown’s $55 million is meaningful. But it’s a targeted bet inside a broader effort to stabilize a shrinking city, not a downtown-only windfall. That’s another reason private capital will ultimately decide how far downtown’s comeback goes. The city money is a spark, not the whole fire.
### The real engine: historic tax credits
The city money grabs headlines, but the workhorse that actually makes downtown rehabs viable is older and bigger: historic tax credits. Two of them stack:
The Missouri Historic Tax Credit returns 25% of the qualified cost of rehabbing a certified historic building (Missouri State Parks / SHPO).
The federal Historic Tax Credit returns another 20% (via the National Park Service).
Stacked, they can offset close to 45% of a rehabilitation’s cost. Here’s why that matters: a tax credit — a dollar-for-dollar reduction of taxes owed, and often sellable to investors for cash — is far more powerful than a deduction. When nearly half your renovation budget comes back, a project that would lose money at full cost suddenly turns a profit. That single mechanism is what turned dozens of derelict downtown warehouses into the occupied Washington Avenue loft district between 1998 and 2008 — and it’s still on the books, ready to do it again for today’s empty office towers.
Here’s the math on a real scale. Say a developer buys a vacant historic office building and budgets $20 million to rehab it into apartments. The 25% state and 20% federal historic credits together can return close to $9 million of that — credits the developer can sell to investors for upfront cash to fund the work. Layer in an Opportunity Zone for the equity and tax abatement on the finished building, and a deal that looked impossible at $20 million out-of-pocket becomes one that actually clears. That gap — between the sticker cost and the after-incentive cost — is the entire reason a 100-year-old building gets a second life instead of a wrecking ball.
### The new frontier: office-to-residential conversion
The specific challenge in 2026 is downtown’s glut of empty office space — vacancy hit 31.7%, the highest since 1999. The national fix is office-to-residential conversion: gutting an obsolete office tower and rebuilding it as apartments, which downtowns desperately need. Missouri moved in 2026 to sweeten this specifically, advancing new downtown “innovation zone” incentives aimed at conversions (STLPR). The exact terms and timing of the state’s conversion incentives have been in flux — some pieces are phasing in, and at least one project (the AT&T Tower) paused waiting on the details — so confirm the current program before you underwrite a deal. But the direction is unmistakable: both the city and the state are steering money toward turning empty desks into front doors.
### The rest of the stack: OZs, TIF, and abatement
Beyond historic credits, downtown developers can layer several more tools. They’re alphabet soup, so here’s each in plain English:
Opportunity Zones (OZs) — a federal program where investors who put capital gains into projects in designated lower-income areas (much of downtown qualifies) can defer and reduce the taxes on those gains. It rewards patient money that stays invested.
Tax Increment Financing (TIF) — the city lets a project use the future increase in tax revenue it generates to help pay for its own upfront costs. The bet is that a rebuilt building throws off far more tax than the empty one it replaced.
Property-tax abatement (Chapter 353 and similar) — a temporary freeze or reduction on property taxes for a redeveloped building, so an owner isn’t punished with a huge tax jump the moment they improve it.
Used together — historic credits plus an OZ plus abatement, say — these programs can dramatically change a project’s return. That’s the whole point: downtown’s buildings are cheap and the public sector is willing to co-invest in fixing them, a combination that’s rare in a major U.S. city.
### What the money is actually targeting
Each incentive points at a specific downtown problem:
Stuck landmark buildings: the vacant Railway Exchange and the enormous, empty AT&T Tower — Missouri’s largest building, which sold for about $3.6 million after being worth $205 million in 2006 — are exactly the assets the acquisition money and conversion incentives aim to unstick.
The riverfront: $15 million backs riverfront economic development, alongside the privately-led $670 million redevelopment replacing the demolished Millennium Hotel near the Arch.
Street life: the $7.5 million in retail and restaurant incentives targets the chicken-and-egg problem directly — you need shops and dining to attract residents, and the money is meant to help the first movers open.
### How a developer actually taps this
The high-level path looks like this: identify a building (ideally one already on, or eligible for, the National Register of Historic Places, which unlocks the historic credits), work with the city’s development arm (the St. Louis Development Corporation) and the State Historic Preservation Office on the applications, and stack the programs that fit — historic credits for the rehab, an OZ for the equity, abatement or TIF for the ongoing costs. It’s paperwork-heavy and slow, and most developers use consultants who specialize in the credits. But the payoff is a project that simply wouldn’t exist at market math — which is the entire reason St. Louis’s historic core is even convertible.
On timing, set realistic expectations: a historic-tax-credit deal isn’t a weekend flip. Getting a building certified, lining up the credit financing, and completing a full rehab commonly runs a year or more from purchase to occupancy, and the credit cash flows as the project hits milestones rather than on day one. That’s exactly why the low purchase prices matter so much — they give a project the cushion to absorb a long, complex timeline and still pencil out. Patience is part of the price of admission, and it’s priced in.
Nothing to do with tax credits — Clifton Heights dinner options, right this way.
### How small businesses fit in
Read all this as a game for people who buy skyscrapers, and you’d miss half the story. The $7.5 million in retail and restaurant incentives in the city’s downtown plan aims squarely at small operators, the coffee shop or the neighborhood restaurant, because a downtown revives on street life. And street life comes from independent businesses, not office leases. Pair those incentives with downtown’s unusually cheap commercial rents, and the barrier to opening a storefront here is lower than in almost any comparable big-city core.
There’s a real first-mover advantage in it, too. The businesses that open before a district fills in are the ones that become its anchors — the spot everyone already knows by the time the new residents arrive. In a downtown with thousands of apartments in the conversion pipeline and a city actively subsidizing the first wave of retail, an entrepreneur with a good concept and some nerve has a genuine shot at planting a flag early and cheaply. That’s a very different proposition than fighting for overpriced space in a market that’s already peaked.
Add it up and St. Louis has stacked cheap real estate, deep public incentives, and active political will into one of the more compelling redevelopment setups in the country. It’s still early enough that being first actually pays.
### The buildings already coming back
The incentive stack already has a track record, and it points to occupied buildings rather than paper promises.
The Washington Avenue loft boom of 1998–2008 ran on these exact credits. Along the lower stretch of Washington Avenue alone, developers claimed roughly $82.9 million in historic tax credits against about $332 million in total rehab costs — more than $100 million of private investment poured into buildings everyone had written off, creating a living neighborhood where there had been empty warehouses.
Today, the Butler Brothers building has reopened as “The Victor,” a 384-unit apartment conversion in the Downtown West neighborhood.
The Jefferson Arms — vacant for 19 years — is finishing a roughly $104 million conversion into apartments, a hotel, and retail.
These are leased buildings with residents and businesses inside them, all made possible by the same tools now aimed at downtown’s empty office towers. The model is proven; the open question is only how fast it scales.
### How St. Louis stacks up against other cities
What makes St. Louis unusual is the depth of the whole stack, not any single program. Plenty of cities offer the 20% federal historic credit, because it’s national. Far fewer add a 25% state credit on top. Missouri’s is among the most generous historic-preservation credits in the country. Combine that with Opportunity Zones covering much of downtown, tax abatement, TIF, and now fresh city money and state conversion incentives, and the total subsidy available on a St. Louis rehab runs deeper than in most major markets. Meanwhile the buildings themselves cost a fraction of comparable historic stock in Chicago, Denver, or Nashville. Cheap real estate paired with a deep incentive stack is genuinely uncommon, and it’s the core of the St. Louis pitch.
### Who should be paying attention
The audience here reaches well beyond billion-dollar developers. Several kinds of players stand to gain:
Developers and investors who can navigate the credits and take on a full building — the obvious audience.
Out-of-state and coastal investors priced out of their own markets, who can buy far more building per dollar here and let the incentive stack carry much of the cost.
Local entrepreneurs and small businesses — the retail and restaurant incentives, plus cheap downtown space, lower the bar to opening a storefront in a district that badly needs first movers.
Owner-occupants and small landlords who can rehab a single historic building and still tap the credits, not just the big syndicated deals.
If any of that describes you, the combination of low prices and deep incentives is worth a serious look before the wider market catches on. The best deals in a turnaround happen before the turnaround is obvious.
### The honest caveats
None of this is free money, and we’re not going to pretend otherwise:
Incentives can change. The $55 million and the state conversion credits are subject to political and budget pressure. Programs get capped, delayed, or altered. Build your model with a margin.
Projects stall. The AT&T Tower’s conversion paused waiting on incentives — proof that even a marquee deal can hang on a single program’s timing.
Credits are complex and take time. Historic-tax-credit deals involve certification, syndication, and long timelines; the cash doesn’t arrive on day one.
Demand is still early. Incentives lower your cost, but downtown’s residential and retail demand is still building. This rewards conviction, not a quick flip — you may be buying into a district a year or two ahead of the crowd.
Not every building is savable. Some vacant structures are too far gone, contaminated, or structurally compromised to rehab economically. The incentives help, but they can’t rescue a building past the point of no return — due diligence on the physical asset matters as much as the incentive math.
Weigh all that, and the picture is still unusually favorable: cheap buildings, a deep incentive stack, and a city actively trying to say yes. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the $55 million for downtown St. Louis?
A.  It’s the downtown share of a $255 million spending plan the Board of Aldermen passed in July 2026 — the city’s cut of the Rams relocation settlement. The downtown $55 million funds vacant-building acquisition ($15M), the riverfront ($15M), infrastructure ($15M), retail and restaurant incentives ($7.5M), and a public-private events fund ($2.5M).
### Q. Where is the St. Louis Rams settlement money going?
A.  The full $255 million plan spreads across the city: roughly $120 million toward North St. Louis recovery, about $70 million for infrastructure, $55 million for downtown, and around $10 million for vacant-property reduction. It stems from the legal settlement St. Louis won after the Rams left for Los Angeles.
### Q. What tax credits are available for rehabbing historic buildings in Missouri?
A.  Two stack together: Missouri’s state Historic Tax Credit covers 25% of qualified rehabilitation costs on a certified historic building, and the federal Historic Tax Credit covers another 20%. Combined, they can offset close to 45% of a rehab — the financial engine behind most downtown St. Louis conversions.
### Q. What is an Opportunity Zone?
A.  An Opportunity Zone is a federally designated lower-income area where investors who reinvest capital gains into local projects can defer and reduce the taxes owed on those gains. Much of downtown St. Louis qualifies, so it’s a common layer developers stack on top of historic tax credits to improve a project’s returns.
### Q. What is Tax Increment Financing (TIF) in St. Louis?
A.  TIF lets a redevelopment project use the future increase in tax revenue it generates to help pay its upfront costs. The reasoning: a rebuilt, occupied building produces far more tax revenue than the vacant one it replaced, so the city captures that growth to help finance the improvement.
### Q. Is St. Louis offering incentives to developers?
A.  Yes, and aggressively. Beyond the $55 million in Rams-settlement downtown money, developers can stack the 25% state and 20% federal historic tax credits, Opportunity Zone benefits, tax abatement, and emerging office-to-residential conversion incentives. It’s one of the deeper redevelopment-incentive stacks of any major U.S. downtown.
### Q. What is happening with the Railway Exchange Building?
A.  The long-vacant Railway Exchange, a massive historic downtown building, has been named a target of the city’s $15 million vacant-building acquisition money. The city has moved to take control of it so a developer can revive it, though as of 2026 no developer had been finalized. It’s a test case for the whole strategy.
### Q. Can I convert a St. Louis office building into apartments?
A.  That’s exactly the play the city and state are encouraging. Office-to-residential conversion turns empty office towers — downtown vacancy is 31.7% — into needed housing, supported by historic tax credits and emerging state conversion incentives. Terms and timing have been evolving, so confirm the current programs before underwriting a conversion.
### Q. Will St. Louis’s development incentives last?
A.  The historic tax credits are long-standing and stable, but the newer money — the $55 million and state conversion incentives — is subject to political and budget pressure, and can be capped, delayed, or altered. Treat the passed programs as strong signals of intent, build a margin into your model, and confirm current terms with the city.
### Q. Why is downtown St. Louis a good place to invest?
A.  The combination is rare: historic buildings selling for a fraction of replacement cost, an incentive stack that can cover close to half a rehab, fresh public money, and a city actively trying to attract developers — all in a metro with below-average costs and rising job growth. The catch is that demand is still early-stage, so it rewards patient, conviction-driven capital.

## Why St. Louis Real Estate Is So Affordable: 8,000 Empty Lots
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-st-louis-real-estate-is-so-affordable
8,000. That is how many vacant lots the City of St. Louis’s land bank owns, by its own count on the Land Reutilization Authority’s front page, along with about 2,000 unoccupied buildings in its care. Walk almost any north or south city block and you can find one: a square of chicory and tall grass between two brick houses, a chain-link gate nobody has opened in years, cicadas so loud in August you stop hearing the traffic on the boulevard.
Here is the part a lot of people moving here never hear. If you own the house next to one of those lots and the lot is too small to build on, the land bank sells it as a side lot, and its programs page says adjacent owners can expand their property for under $200. Under two hundred dollars, for a piece of the city. Say that to a friend in Denver and watch the face they make.
That number is the whole story of why St. Louis real estate is so affordable, and it is not a sign that something is wrong with the houses. It is a sign of supply. There is more city here, more land and more brick, than there are buyers to fill it. You feel it the first time you tour a two-family flat with nine-foot ceilings, a basement that smells like cool limestone and old paint cans, and a backyard deep enough for a garden, and then look at the price on the listing sheet.
### Why is St. Louis real estate so affordable?
Because the city has more houses and land than buyers. The City of St. Louis’s land bank owns 8,000 vacant lots and about 2,000 unoccupied buildings, and that surplus holds prices down. Missouri’s own cost-of-living data puts St. Louis metro housing at 80.0 on an index where the United States is 100.0, so housing here runs about a fifth below the national average.
That’s the short answer. The long one is more useful if you’re deciding whether to pack a truck, because cheap can mean a bargain or it can mean a block nobody wants, and in St. Louis it can mean both within a few streets of each other.
### The land bank nobody outside the city has heard of
The Land Reutilization Authority calls itself the oldest land bank in the U.S. It has the authority to manage, maintain, market and sell the vacant and abandoned buildings and property it owns in St. Louis. When a property goes unclaimed long enough, this is where it tends to end up, and over decades the pile has grown into thousands of parcels.
Think about what that does to a single street. A row of brick houses, most of them lived in, porch lights on, a dog barking behind one fence. Then a gap where a house used to be. Then a boarded two-story with plywood over the windows, gray from the weather. Every one of those gaps and boards sits on the market in some form, and every one of them pulls on what the occupied houses around it can sell for. That’s the supply side of St. Louis prices, and it’s visible from the sidewalk.
It also means opportunity for some buyers. The land bank lists purchase programs and an offer process on its site, so a buyer who wants a project, or a homeowner who wants the yard next door, deals directly with the city’s own agency. One program that used to get a lot of attention, Mow-to-Own, is gone: the land bank says the Mow-to-Own and Garden Lease policies were discontinued. If an older article promises you a lot for mowing it, that door is closed.
### What Missouri’s own numbers say about the cost of living
The Missouri Economic Research and Information Center, MERIC, publishes a cost-of-living table built on the Council for Community and Economic Research survey. In its most recent table, the St. Louis MO-IL metro scored 89.8 overall against a United States baseline of 100.0. Housing, the line that matters most when you move, came in at 80.0. Groceries were close to the national line at 98.7, and health care actually ran above it at 103.9.
That last number is worth sitting with for a second. St. Louis isn’t cheap at everything. It’s cheap where it counts most in a monthly budget, which is the roof over your head. The state as a whole is in the same position: MERIC says Missouri had the seventh lowest cost of living in the United States for the latest quarter it reports.
For a mover, that translates into something you can feel. A rent or mortgage payment that leaves room at the end of the month. A grocery run that costs about what it did back home. A doctor’s bill that may not.
### What a house actually sells for here
St. Louis REALTORS publishes a monthly housing report for the City and County combined, and in its July report the median sales price for a single-family home was $350,000, up 5.9% from the year before. Those are combined city and county figures, so the price on any one street can sit well above or well below them.
So don’t move here expecting every house to be a steal. Move here expecting range. The same budget can buy a renovated brick bungalow on a quiet south city street, a fixer with original woodwork and a slate roof that needs a roofer’s attention, or a newer house farther out with a two-car garage and a lawn you’ll mow every Saturday from April to October.
### Is the market cheap because it’s falling?
No, and this is where the numbers surprise people. The same Realtors report shows the median sale price up from a year earlier, while the inventory of homes for sale grew 15.2%. More houses to choose from, and prices still rising slowly. That’s not a market in collapse. It’s a market where buyers have a little more room to negotiate than they did a year ago.
What you’re really buying in St. Louis is a low starting point, not a falling one. The land bank lists 168 or more vacant buildings stabilized for future rehab under Prop NS, which means empty houses kept standing until someone can bring them back. Cities that have given up don’t do that.
Weighing a move and want to see the neighborhoods for yourself? Browse local businesses, services and neighborhoods on the St Louis Near Me Directory, and read why downtown St. Louis is ripe for development for the bigger picture.
If you’re the agent, the inspector or the title office newcomers will need, the people reading this are the customers you want before they ever land at Lambert, so list your business where they’re already looking.
### Who comes out ahead
The affordability helps different movers in different ways:
Remote workers. If your paycheck is set somewhere else and your housing line drops toward that 80.0 index, the difference stays in your pocket every month.
First-time buyers. A house with a yard and a basement is still a realistic goal on a normal income in a lot of St. Louis neighborhoods.
Rehabbers and patient buyers. The land bank’s purchase programs and its stabilized buildings are a real path for someone willing to take on a project.
Neighbors who want more yard. If an eligible side lot sits next to your house, the land bank says you can expand for under $200.
### The honest trade-offs
Cheap housing comes with real costs, and pretending otherwise would waste your moving budget:
Block by block matters more than city by city. A street of lived-in brick houses and a street with three empty lots can be four blocks apart. Walk it at night before you buy.
Old houses need old-house money. Slate roofs, tuckpointing, original windows and century-old plumbing are part of the charm and part of the bill. Get an inspection, and budget for the first big repair.
Not everything is cheap. MERIC’s health-care index for the metro sits above the national baseline.
Summers are humid and winters bite. Window units hum all of July; the furnace earns its keep in January.
A cheap house is half the budget. Here’s the other half.
### How to shop St. Louis like someone who lives here
Start with the street, not the listing. Drive it on a weekday evening and again on a Saturday morning. Count porch lights. Notice who’s cutting grass, whose recycling bin is out, whether the corner store has its lights on. Then look up the empty lots on the block and find out who owns them, because a lot owned by the land bank next door is a different future than a lot owned by an absentee speculator.
Next, read the price against the house, not against the city median. A $200,000 brick two-family that needs a roof and tuckpointing may cost more in the end than a $260,000 one that doesn’t. Have an inspector climb up and look. Ask about the sewer lateral, the electrical panel and the age of the furnace before you fall for the woodwork.
Finally, give yourself a season. St. Louis rewards people who learn it slowly: which neighborhoods smell like barbecue smoke on Sunday afternoons, which streets flood in a hard rain, which block has a neighbor who will lend you a ladder. The affordability is real, and it lasts long enough for you to choose carefully.
### How buying from the land bank works
If a lot or an empty building caught your eye on a walk, the land bank lays out its path to purchase step by step on its own site. First, search for the property: do your research, pick the parcel, and get access to see it in person. Second, choose one of its purchase programs and make an offer, using the offer checklist and forms it posts. Third, for its Development Program, gather feedback from the neighborhood, which in practice means knocking on doors and talking to the people who will live next to whatever you build. Fourth, the LRA Commission reviews the offer and may accept it, counter it or deny it.
None of that is fast, and none of it is a shortcut around inspections, permits or a rehab budget. But it is a real door into a city where the land itself is not the expensive part, and for a patient buyer standing in the tall grass of an empty lot with a tape measure, that changes the math.
