### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the basic steps for a cleanup?
A.  Five steps: (1) choose a target area and date; (2) recruit volunteers and confirm supplies; (3) coordinate disposal/hauling with your city’s refuse or 311 service ahead of time; (4) run the event with a safety briefing and assigned zones; (5) document before-and-after photos and schedule the next one. Small grants (like Love Your Block) can fund tools and dumpsters.
### Q. What are some tips for a successful cleanup?
A.  Keep the area small enough to finish and see results, start early before the heat, provide water and gloves, and make it social — food or music brings people back. Partner with a neighborhood association for reach, line up disposal in advance so bags don’t sit, and celebrate the before-and-after. Recurring monthly cleanups beat one big annual push.
### Q. How to clean up the neighborhood?
A.  Combine quick wins with lasting systems: organize regular volunteer cleanups, adopt chronic-problem blocks and alleys, report illegal dumping to the city, and pursue small grants (like Love Your Block) to fund tools and lot transformations. The most effective neighborhoods pair hands-on work with a bit of seed money and strong local ownership.
### Q. How to start a community clean up?
A.  Rally a core group through your neighborhood association, pick a date and a specific area, and line up supplies and disposal in advance (Brightside St. Louis and the city’s Refuse Division can help). Publicize it widely, make it welcoming and social, and document the results. To go bigger and more lasting, pursue a small grant — the Love Your Block model — to fund tools, dumpsters, and lot improvements.
### Q. Are there grants to clean up your neighborhood?
A.  Yes. Programs like Love Your Block give residents micro-grants (typically $500–$2,500) for neighborhood cleanup and beautification projects — Columbia, Missouri runs one now. Many cities also offer neighborhood or block-grant funds, and local foundations and business sponsors sometimes chip in. Start by asking your neighborhood association and city’s community-development office what’s available in your area.
### Q. How to start a neighborhood cleanup?
A.  Pick one block and one date, not a whole district. Line up bags, gloves and a disposal plan before you invite anyone — the failure mode is twenty volunteers and nowhere to put the trash. Tell the city; many will supply materials or haul the pile if asked in advance.
### Q. What can you do to improve your neighborhood and keep it clean?
A.  Small and repeated beats big and occasional. A standing monthly hour does more than one heroic Saturday, because the block starts to look maintained, and maintained blocks attract less dumping. Reporting problem properties and broken lights matters as much as picking up litter.
### Q. What are three things that make a good neighborhood?
A.  People who know each other by name, somewhere to walk to, and visible upkeep. The third is the one residents can move fastest — it signals that somebody is paying attention, and that signal changes behavior more reliably than any ordinance.

## How Pay-As-You-Throw Cuts a City's Trash
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-pay-as-you-throw-cuts-city-trash
The first five ideas in this series ran on pride, coordination, and neighborly momentum. This last one runs on something colder, and for some people more powerful: price. It’s the most controversial tool on the list, and the one St. Louis should approach most carefully. The principle behind it, though, is rock-solid, and worth understanding before you dismiss it.
### What Pay-As-You-Throw actually is
Under a Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) system — also called unit-based or “save-as-you-throw” pricing — households pay for trash collection based on how much they actually throw away, usually by buying official bags or stickers, while recycling stays free. In most cities, trash feels free: you make as much as you want and the bill never changes. PAYT flips that. Suddenly the second and third bag costs you something, and recycling and composting become the obvious way to save money.
The behavior change is real and measurable. According to the U.S. EPA and researcher Lisa Skumatz’s widely-cited data, PAYT communities average roughly a 28% reduction in the garbage they send for disposal (studies range from about 25% to 50%), and their recycling and diversion rates run meaningfully higher than non-PAYT towns — about 29% versus 21%. When people have a direct financial stake in making less trash, they make less trash.
### The honest catch
Here’s where we level with you, because telling the truth is the whole point of this series. PAYT is a fee, and fees are politically hard: residents can read it as a new tax on top of what they already pay. It also has to be implemented carefully, or it can backfire. Middletown, Connecticut is the cautionary tale. The city ended its bag program in late 2025 after an independent review found household trash had fallen only about 8%, far short of the roughly 30% reduction officials had previously claimed. The concept can work, but the numbers and the politics have to hold up to scrutiny. There, the program came apart.
### How the price signal actually changes behavior
The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple, which is why it works. A flat trash bill reads the same whether you set out one bag or five, so your own waste never registers as a cost. Put a price on each extra bag and two things happen on their own: people start noticing how much they throw away, and the free options, recycling and composting, turn into the cheap way out. Nobody gets lectured about the environment. The household budget does the persuading.
That’s why the behavior change holds up: it doesn’t depend on anyone caring about landfills. It runs on the same everyday logic that makes people flip off the lights when they pay the electric bill. Give a household a direct financial stake in producing less garbage, and it produces less garbage. That’s exactly what the roughly 28% average reduction, and the higher recycling rates, reflect.
### Where it works, and where it breaks
PAYT doesn’t drop into place on its own, and pretending it does is how cities get burned. It works best paired with easy, free alternatives: robust curbside recycling, convenient composting, and accessible bulk-item drop-off, so residents have somewhere for their diverted material to go. Strip those away and you get the failure mode every skeptic warns about. People dodge the bag fee by dumping illegally, which is the last thing a city like St. Louis, already fighting dumping, can afford.
The politics are the other trap. Because it looks like a new fee, PAYT invites backlash unless residents see the trade clearly: lower base costs, or the genuine ability to pay less by recycling more. Middletown’s reversal made the point. A program that can’t prove its results, or sell them to residents, won’t survive contact with a budget hearing. The design and the buy-in matter as much as the concept.
### Why it still matters for St. Louis
Even if St. Louis never adopts full PAYT, the principle underneath it is one the city can’t afford to ignore: the cost of trash is real, and someone always pays it. Right now, a dirty city taxes itself twice. Once in what illegal dumping and litter do to property values and business, and again in the millions the city spends hauling away mattresses, tires, and overflowing waste that could fund parks, rec centers, or public safety instead.
PAYT’s deeper lesson is that incentives shape behavior at city scale. You don’t have to charge by the bag to use that insight. You can reward the behavior you want, recycling drop-offs, composting programs, bulk-pickup days that make legal disposal easier than illegal dumping, instead of only punishing the behavior you don’t. Handled with care and honesty, price signals are a legitimate tool. Handled carelessly, they’re a political landmine. St. Louis should file this one under “powerful, but proceed with eyes open.” It rounds out the full strategy in our complete St. Louis cleanliness playbook.
Concretely, St. Louis can chase PAYT’s results without necessarily charging by the bag. Make the legal, low-waste choice the easy one: expand and simplify curbside recycling, stand up convenient composting and yard-waste options, and run frequent, well-publicized bulk-pickup and drop-off days so a resident with an old couch has an obvious free path that beats hauling it to an alley. Every one of those moves attacks illegal dumping from the demand side. When legal disposal is genuinely easier than dumping, dumping drops, and it does so without the political fight a per-bag fee triggers.
The bigger takeaway is a mindset rather than a single policy: reward the behavior you want, don’t just punish the behavior you don’t. Cameras and fines catch a dumper after the fact. Incentives and easy alternatives help head the dump off before it happens. A city serious about clean streets needs both, and PAYT’s real gift to St. Louis is the reminder that the “carrot” half of that equation is the one cities most often forget.
PAYT makes recycling the money-saving choice — but it’s a fee, so implementation and buy-in are everything.
### A middle path: incentives without the fee
Because full Pay-As-You-Throw is politically heavy, it’s worth spelling out the lighter menu: the carrot-based moves that borrow PAYT’s insight, that incentives shape behavior, without charging households by the bag. None of these require a fee fight, and several attack illegal dumping at the same time:
Free, frequent bulk-pickup and drop-off days — the single most direct anti-dumping tool. When getting rid of a mattress legally is easier than hauling it to an alley, most people choose legal.
Convenient recycling and composting — expand curbside recycling and add yard-waste and food-scrap options, so the low-waste choice is also the easy one.
Recycling rewards — small perks, coupons, or recognition for households and blocks that recycle well, turning diversion into a visible, rewarded behavior.
Block and school competitions — friendly “cleanest block” or “most recycled” contests that use pride and a little prize money to drive participation.
Business take-back and packaging partnerships — enlist the retailers and restaurants whose packaging becomes waste, the way the UK’s Love Essex did.
The thread through all of them is the one PAYT teaches: make the behavior you want the easy, rewarded choice, and the behavior you don’t the inconvenient one. St. Louis spends real money hauling illegally dumped tires and mattresses and chasing dumpers after the fact, money that could fund parks, rec centers, or public safety. Every one of these incentive moves attacks that cost from the front end, before the dumping happens, and none of them requires the political capital a per-bag fee would burn. That’s the honest, usable takeaway from Pay-As-You-Throw for a city like ours: you don’t have to adopt the fee to steal the idea.
Hard left turn — the restaurants in Pacific, Missouri will surprise you.
The trade-off deserves a clear eye, though. The carrot menu is politically easier and genuinely effective, but it doesn’t generate the revenue or the sheer behavior-change punch of full Pay-As-You-Throw. That roughly 28% average reduction comes from people feeling the cost directly. The carrots nudge; the fee shoves. For a city like St. Louis, still fighting entrenched illegal dumping and wary of anything that looks like a new tax, the honest recommendation is to lead with the carrots, prove the city can make legal disposal genuinely easy and rewarding, and only then have the harder conversation about unit-based pricing, from a position of trust rather than surprise. Earn the buy-in first. The tool works far better when residents don’t feel ambushed by it. St. Louis doesn’t have to choose one path forever, but it does have to choose where to start, and starting with the easy, trust-building wins is what earns a city the credibility to attempt the harder reforms later.
Trash is never free - St. Louis pays for it either way. Whether or not the city ever charges by the bag, the lesson holds: reward less waste, make legal disposal easy, and stop letting dumping drain money better spent elsewhere. See the whole approach in our St. Louis cleanliness playbook.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Which action reduces waste the most?
A.  At the household level, reducing what you buy and reusing what you have beat recycling, because they prevent waste entirely. At the city level, unit-based pricing (Pay-As-You-Throw) is one of the most effective single levers — it cuts disposed garbage by about 28% on average by giving households a direct financial reason to reduce, reuse, and recycle.
### Q. What are 5 ways to reduce waste?
A.  (1) Buy less and choose durable, low-packaging goods; (2) reuse and repair before replacing; (3) recycle correctly for your area; (4) compost food and yard waste; (5) support systems that reward less waste, like Pay-As-You-Throw pricing, recycling drop-offs, and composting programs. The first two prevent the most waste; the rest divert what’s left from the landfill.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to dispose of waste?
A.  For everyday household waste, recycling and composting are usually the cheapest routes because they divert material from paid trash disposal — and under Pay-As-You-Throw pricing they literally save you money. For bulky items, use your city’s scheduled bulk-pickup or drop-off days rather than a hauler; in St. Louis, check with the Refuse Division. Never dump illegally — the fines dwarf any savings.
### Q. How to get rid of large amounts of waste?
A.  For big volumes, rent a dumpster or use a licensed hauler, or take loads to a transfer station or the city’s scheduled bulk-collection days. Separate recyclables, metal, and yard waste to cut disposal costs. Whatever you do, dispose legally — illegal dumping in St. Louis carries steep fines and is caught on roughly 275 alley and vacant-lot cameras.
### Q. What are 10 ways to reduce waste?
A.  Buy less and choose durable goods; avoid single-use plastics; reuse and repair; buy secondhand; compost food and yard waste; recycle correctly; go paperless; donate instead of trashing usable items; buy in bulk with less packaging; and support systems that reward less waste, like Pay-As-You-Throw, recycling drop-offs, and composting programs. The first few prevent the most waste; the rest divert what’s left from the landfill.
### Q. How to get rid of junk for free?
A.  Donate usable items to charities or thrift stores, list them free on community marketplaces or “buy nothing” groups, and use your city’s scheduled bulk-collection and recycling drop-off days rather than a paid hauler — in St. Louis, check with the Refuse Division. Never fly-dump to save money: illegal dumping carries steep fines and is caught on roughly 275 alley and vacant-lot cameras. Many scrap-metal buyers will take appliances or metal at no charge, and some retailers offer take-back on old electronics or mattresses when you buy new — always worth a quick call before you pay anyone to haul something away.

## The Best Wedding Venues in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-wedding-venues-in-st-louis
Say yes on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday you’ve learned the first hard truth of wedding planning: almost everything — the date, the guest count, the budget, the vibe — hangs on one decision. The venue. In St. Louis you’re spoiled for choice, from a 1920s movie palace to a glass greenhouse in Forest Park to a garden with 79 acres of blooms. Plenty are beautiful. The right one fits your guest count and your budget, and looks like the day you actually picture.
What follows: the best St. Louis wedding venues by style, what a wedding really costs here, and the questions that keep a booking from turning into a budget blowout.
Geography narrows the list faster than anything. St. Louis’s best venues cluster in a handful of areas — Forest Park and the Central West End for gardens and grand hotels, Midtown and downtown for historic landmarks and lofts, and the wine country to the west for vineyards and barns. Pick a general part of the metro early, ideally near where most of your guests will stay. Everyone’s drive stays shorter, and your shuttle bill stays sane.
### Grand & historic: for the show-stopper wedding
If you want jaws to drop the moment guests walk in, St. Louis’s historic landmarks are hard to beat.
St. Louis Union Station is the classic grand choice. Its 1894 Grand Hall, with a 65-foot barrel-vaulted ceiling and a nightly light show, ranks among the most dramatic rooms in the Midwest, and the on-site Curio Collection hotel makes it easy on out-of-town guests. The Coronado in Midtown is the Art Deco stunner: built in 1925 and lovingly restored, with high ceilings, terrazzo floors, and multiple ballrooms that put the ceremony and reception under one roof. Then there’s The Royal Sonesta Chase Park Plaza in the Central West End. Old-world glamour, full-service polish, rooms for the whole party upstairs. It’s the pick for couples who want the hotel to handle everything.
### Garden & greenhouse: for the outdoor-at-heart couple
St. Louis does green as well as any city, and two spaces let you marry surrounded by it — rain or shine.
The Missouri Botanical Garden spreads across 79 acres of meticulously kept gardens with several event spaces, so an outdoor ceremony comes with an indoor backup that still feels special. The Jewel Box in Forest Park needs almost no added decor. It’s a 1930s Art Deco glass greenhouse packed with tropical greenery, photogenic in every season because the greenery lives inside, safe from the weather. At either one, the setting does half the work in your photos.
### Modern & industrial: for the design-forward wedding
Not into chandeliers? St. Louis’s converted warehouses and modern spaces trade them for exposed brick, tall windows, and a blank canvas you fill yourself.
Wild Carrot leads the industrial-beauty group, with exposed brick, high ceilings, and a team that’s good at helping couples pull off the non-traditional. Neo on Locust and Windows on Washington carry downtown and loft-district character, their open, flexible layouts built for a personal design touch. Here the room is a backdrop for your ideas, not a look you have to decorate around.
### Wine country, barns & the great outdoors
Just west of the city, the rolling hills of Augusta and Defiance form one of the oldest wine regions in the country. Its wineries have turned into some of the most sought-after wedding settings in the metro: a ceremony in the vines, a reception in the tasting room, photos with the Missouri River bluffs behind you. It’s the pick for a relaxed day in the country that’s still a short drive from St. Louis.
Barn and farm venues in the surrounding counties offer the same rustic warmth with string lights and open space, and they often come with flexible, bring-your-own-vendor policies that help a budget stretch — room to hire one of the best wedding and event caterers across the St. Louis metro instead of taking whatever the house serves. The trade-offs to weigh: most are a drive from downtown (plan transportation or nearby lodging for guests), and outdoor-heavy venues live and die on the rain plan — always ask what happens if the sky opens.
### Unexpected & budget-friendly spaces
Some of the most memorable St. Louis weddings happen in places that aren’t “wedding venues” at all. Forest Park’s Boathouse puts your reception right on the water, in the middle of the city’s best-loved park. City Museum throws a party nobody forgets, for couples who lean playful over formal. Breweries like Schlafly and Urban Chestnut, restaurant private rooms, downtown lofts: they bring built-in character and often a lower all-in cost than a ballroom, because the space, the bar, and sometimes the food arrive together.
Some of the most memorable St. Louis weddings happen in unexpected spaces — lofts, breweries, and the Boathouse — where the character comes built in.
These non-traditional spaces are the secret weapon for a smaller budget. A venue that already includes tables, chairs, a bar, and in-house food removes the rentals and vendor coordination that quietly inflate a “cheap” blank room. If your number is tight, start here rather than at the grand ballrooms.
### When to get married in St. Louis
Timing is one of the biggest levers on both price and experience. Late spring and fall are peak season here — comfortable weather, gorgeous light, and the highest venue demand and prices, so the best spaces book a year or more out. Winter and mid-summer are the value windows: St. Louis summers run hot and humid (a real consideration for outdoor plans), and January–March dates can save thousands at the very same venue. A Friday or Sunday instead of a Saturday is another quiet discount most couples overlook. If flexibility on date matters less to you than budget, off-peak is where the savings live.

### What a St. Louis wedding actually costs
Money drives every other decision, so start here. A wedding in the St. Louis area typically lands in the low-to-mid five figures, roughly $25,000 to $35,000, generally below the national average. The range is wide, and it hangs on two things: how many people you invite, and where you host them. Venue plus catering usually eats about half the total, which is why the venue decision is really a budget decision in disguise.
The good news for St. Louis couples is real flexibility. A modest, meaningful wedding can be done for well under $20,000 by keeping the guest list tight and choosing an affordable or all-inclusive space; a marquee celebration at a landmark venue climbs past $30,000 fast. The single biggest lever you control is the guest count — every additional head multiplies catering, rentals, and the size of room you need. Cut the list before you cut the dream.
Watch the fine print, too. The quoted venue price is rarely the price you pay: a service charge (often 18–22%), sales tax, gratuity, and sometimes a bar minimum or a cake-cutting fee get layered on top. When you compare two St. Louis venues, ask each for an all-in estimate with those charges included — the “cheaper” room sometimes ends up costing more once the add-ons land. Building a 5–10% cushion into your budget for the surprises is the difference between a plan that holds and one that blows up the month before.
### How to choose the right venue (the questions that matter)
Beautiful photos sell a venue; the fine print determines whether it works. Before you sign, ask:
What’s actually included? Tables, chairs, linens, setup, teardown, and a coordinator can be bundled or billed separately — an all-inclusive space often beats a “cheaper” blank room once you add up the rentals.
Catering: in-house, preferred list, or open? This is a huge cost and flexibility factor. Some venues require their caterer; others let you bring your own.
What’s the real capacity — seated, with a dance floor? The “holds 200” number rarely accounts for a band, bars, and room to move.
Off-peak and off-day pricing? A Friday, Sunday, or winter date can save thousands at the same venue.
What’s the rain plan, and the noise/end-time rules? Outdoor venues live or die on the backup, and some spaces have hard cutoffs.
### How far ahead to book (and the guest details people forget)
In St. Louis, the marquee venues — Union Station’s Grand Hall, the Coronado, the Chase Park Plaza, the Botanical Garden — get claimed 12 to 18 months out for peak spring and fall Saturdays. If you have your heart set on a specific space and date, start touring the moment you’re engaged; the popular ones fill first and rarely have a cancellation to catch. For an off-peak or weekday date, you have more room, but the best pricing still rewards booking early.
Once the room is yours, the day becomes about the guests moving through it. The details couples forget until late: a hotel block near the venue for out-of-town guests (Union Station and the Chase have rooms on-site, a real advantage), transportation if your ceremony and reception are in different spots, honest parking for the headcount, and simple accessibility — ramps, elevators, and restrooms that work for elderly and disabled guests. Ask every venue how it handles these before you fall for the chandeliers; a stunning room with a parking nightmare turns into your guests’ only memory.
Once the venue is booked, the transportation quote is the next line that surprises people, and it pays to understand why a limo’s quoted hourly rate is never the final bill before you sign anything.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much does the average wedding cost in St. Louis?
A.  A St. Louis wedding often runs in the low-to-mid five figures — roughly $25,000–$35,000, generally below the national average — though it swings widely with guest count and venue. The venue and catering together typically account for about half the total, so the space you choose is the single biggest factor in your final number.
### Q. What is a realistic budget for a wedding?
A.  A realistic wedding budget hinges on guest count, with venue and catering eating roughly half of it. In St. Louis, a modest wedding is very doable for well under $20,000 with an affordable or all-inclusive venue and a trimmed guest list, while a larger celebration at a landmark space runs $30,000 or more. Set the guest count first — it drives everything else.
### Q. Is $10,000 enough for a wedding?
A.  Yes — $10,000 can host a lovely St. Louis wedding if you keep the guest list tight and choose the venue wisely. All-inclusive spaces, non-traditional venues (a loft, a brewery, a park pavilion), and off-peak dates stretch the budget furthest. At this level, fewer guests and a venue that includes the essentials are what make it work.
### Q. Is $5,000 enough for a wedding?
A.  It’s tight but doable for an intimate St. Louis wedding — think a small guest list, a low-cost or free venue (a park, a family home, an off-peak restaurant room), and DIY touches. At $5,000 the strategy is fewer guests and a space that already includes tables, chairs, and catering so you’re not renting every piece separately.
### Q. What do the groom’s parents typically pay for?
A.  Traditionally the groom’s family covers the rehearsal dinner, and often the officiant, the marriage license, and sometimes the honeymoon or the bar — but modern couples split costs however works for them. When you tour St. Louis venues, ask exactly what’s included so both families can divide the real line items without surprises.
### Q. What is the 50/30/20 rule for weddings?
A.  The 50/30/20 wedding rule is a budgeting guide: put about 50% toward the reception (venue, food, and drink), 30% toward the “experience” (attire, photography, flowers, and music), and 20% toward everything else (stationery, favors, and a contingency cushion). Because the venue anchors that biggest 50% slice, picking the right St. Louis space is the highest-leverage decision you’ll make.
### Q. How to pick the perfect wedding venue?
A.  Work from constraints inward: guest count, season, and whether you need a rain plan. Then ask what the venue includes — tables, chairs, staff, and whether catering is open or exclusive. A cheaper room that forces a full rental order is rarely cheaper once the invoice arrives.
### Q. How much should I budget for a 100 person wedding?
A.  Build it from the per-head costs rather than a headline number: catering and bar scale directly with the count, while photography, music and flowers are closer to fixed. Set the guest list first — it is the single lever that moves the total most, and it moves it in both directions.
### Q. Is $10,000 a reasonable wedding budget?
A.  It is workable here, especially at a smaller count, on an off-peak date, or in one of the unexpected spaces above that do not carry a full venue fee. What it does not stretch to is a large guest list with full service — so decide which of those two you care about.
### Q. Is $5000 a reasonable budget for a wedding?
A.  Yes, with a short guest list and a venue that is not charging a wedding premium. Ceremony plus a meal for a small group is very achievable; a hundred guests is not. Off-peak dates and a Friday or Sunday do more for this budget than any single vendor negotiation will.

## The Window Salesman Won't Mention This: 18 St. Louis Districts Need City Approval
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-window-company-in-st-louis
The curtain moves. Nobody touched it. The furnace kicked on a while ago, and the hem is still drifting off the sill, pushed by air that is coming through the window, not around the room. Hold the back of your hand near the bottom sash and you can feel it: a thin, steady cold, like a freezer door somebody left cracked. The glass is cold enough to fog where you breathe on it. The sash is painted shut. And the gas bill on the counter says this has been going on all winter.
So you start calling window companies. A few days later a salesman is at your kitchen table with a binder, a sample corner of vinyl he lets you hold, and a price that drops by thousands if you sign tonight. You want the draft gone. You also want to not be the person who got talked into the wrong windows. Both feelings are right.
Here is the thing most window pitches in St. Louis never mention, and it can sink a contract you already signed. The City of St. Louis has 18 local historic districts, among them Soulard, Lafayette Square, Benton Park, Fox Park, the Shaw neighborhood, Tower Grove East and the Central West End, and each district’s ordinance has its own set of rehabilitation and design standards, developed with the neighbors who live there. If your house sits in one, the city has a say in your windows before any salesman does. The Cultural Resources Office, the city’s preservation agency, is responsible for review of exterior work within the city’s local historic districts, and its own permit page is blunt about it: no permit may be issued without the Cultural Resources Office or the Preservation Board’s approval. The office even keeps an Approved Historic Window List, a list of replacement windows it has approved for use in local historic districts.
That gives you the one question worth more than any discount. Before you sign anything for an old city house, look the salesman in the eye and ask: “Is this exact window on the city’s Approved Historic Window List?” A company that works these neighborhoods every week answers in a breath. A company that hesitates, or says the city won’t care, just told you everything about how the rest of the job will go. Say that line to a neighbor on a block of old brick houses and watch them reach for their phone.
Not sure whether your address is in a district? The city’s City Historic Districts page has an interactive map of local districts and landmarks. Or call the Cultural Resources Office at (314) 657-3865, or walk into its CRO Hotspot desk in City Hall (12th & Market) Room 424, where staff help with over-the-counter applications and permit review. The office says applications in its areas are referred automatically by the Building Division and approved within a few days, unless the work does not comply with the standards or more information is needed. A few days of patience costs nothing. A row of windows the city won’t accept costs a great deal, plus the cold you were trying to escape.
Outside the districts, the rules are looser and the job is the same: get the price itemized, compare it line by line, and hire the crew, not the binder. Here is what that costs and how to tell the good companies from the loud ones.
### How much are new windows in St. Louis?
Then comes the part no national price chart can tell you. In most cases, changes to building exteriors in a local district must be reviewed by the Cultural Resources Office for compliance with that district’s standards, and for larger projects the Preservation Board may weigh in. The quote that looks cheapest on the kitchen table is not cheap if it names a window the city turns down. So in a district, the first line of every quote you compare should be the same: a window from the approved list, or a written answer from the company on how it will get one approved.
The other big lever is what gets replaced. Full-frame window replacement includes a new window frame and sashes, while pocket-window replacement includes a window that fits inside the existing frame. In a century-old brick house with out-of-square openings and decades of paint, that choice decides how much of the old trim gets torn out, how much dust drifts through the living room, and how long the crew is in your house. Ask which one you are being quoted, in writing.
### Who to hire: the crew matters more than the brand
No single window company is best for every house. You will mostly choose between big national brands sold through local dealers and independent local installers. Either can be excellent, and either can disappoint, because even a great window performs badly when it is set badly. You feel a bad install the first cold night: the same thin draft, now coming around a brand-new frame.
Look for a company that is licensed and insured and shows you proof without being asked twice, has reviews from real local customers you can read, puts the product warranty and the labor warranty in writing, and gives you a clear written quote with no same-day-only discount. For an old city house, add one more: they have worked with non-standard openings and historic district reviews before, and they can tell you how the city permit fits into their schedule.
Shortlist before anyone sits at your kitchen table. Browse local installers on the St. Louis window companies map, or see every trade across the metro on the home services coverage map, then invite three of them to quote the same windows.
If you’re the window crew homeowners should be calling, list your business so more customers find you before the salesman with the binder does.
### Old brick, odd openings
St. Louis is a city of old brick: four-families, bungalows, tall narrow houses with tall narrow windows, many of them a little out of square after a century of settling. Run a tape measure across the top of one of those openings and again across the bottom, and the two numbers often disagree. That is why the crew matters. An installer who mostly drops stock sizes into newer suburban frames can make an old opening look fine on day one and leak by the first hard freeze.
Ask any company you are serious about to measure every opening itself, top, middle and bottom, before it orders a single window. Ask how it handles plaster returns, brick sills and the weights hiding in the walls of an old double-hung. And watch how they move through the house. The good ones run a hand along the old sash, tap the sill, look at the paint lines and ask what year the house was built. The ones in a hurry never touch the window at all.
### What time of year are windows cheapest?
Window companies are busiest in late spring through early fall, when demand and pricing run highest. The quieter stretch is late fall and winter, when many installers are hungrier for work and more willing to sharpen a bid. Crews replace windows one opening at a time, so the house is never standing open to the cold, and a winter install is practical. The bonus: you can feel the difference that same night, standing where the draft used to be.
If the windows are not an emergency, gather quotes in the off-season and let the historic-district review, if you need one, run while you compare. And don’t let a price that is only good today rush a decision this big. A real company honors a fair quote for more than an evening.
### Vinyl, fiberglass or wood?
Material is the biggest lever on both price and look, so understand it before a salesperson frames the choice for you. Vinyl and fiberglass are popular mid-range choices, while wood is the most expensive but offers a classic look. HomeGuide puts vinyl windows at $350 to $1,500 per window, including labor, and fiberglass windows at $400 to $2,000 each with installation. Vinyl is the low-maintenance default for most houses. Fiberglass costs more, and HomeGuide says it tends to last longer than all other window frame materials. Wood is the one you notice with your hand on the sash, warm and solid, and it is often what an old brick facade calls for. Composite frames aim for the look of wood with less upkeep.
No material is right for every home. The honest answer depends on the house, how long you will live there, your budget, and, in a local historic district, what the city will approve. Knowing the trade-offs lets you push back when someone insists their most expensive line is the only sensible option.
### Red flags when hiring a window company
Watch for a marathon in-home pitch that ends with a sign-tonight price dropping thousands of dollars. Watch for no license or insurance, or a refusal to show proof. For a vague or verbal-only estimate. For a big cash demand up front. For a quote far higher or far lower than the others, and a shrug when you ask for local references or a written warranty. That stomach-drop moment when the price suddenly falls is manufactured urgency, not a deal. A good company gives you a clear written quote, answers questions without theatrics, and lets you take your time.
Three quotes in, need a break from binders? Go eat: Ballwin’s whole restaurant lineup is a good place to argue about vinyl.
### Questions to ask before you hire
Is this exact window on the city’s Approved Historic Window List? (local historic districts)
Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof?
Is the quote itemized and in writing, and how long is it good for?
Full-frame or pocket replacement?
Which brand and product line, and which glass package?
What does the warranty cover on labor, not just the glass?
Who does the installation: your crew or a subcontractor?
Can you share local references?
A reputable company answers all of these plainly and never resents the questions. The ones to avoid get cagey the moment you ask them to slow down and write it down.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the average cost of a good replacement window?
A.  HomeGuide puts window replacement at $450 to $1,500 per window on average. Larger windows, custom sizes and premium wood windows fall at the high end. Ask for options at more than one price point so you can see what the extra money buys.
### Q. What is the average cost to replace windows in a 2,000 sq ft house?
A.  Square footage matters less than the number of openings. Count your windows, then use the per-window range: HomeGuide puts 10 to 15 windows in a house at $4,500 to $22,500. Bay windows and custom sizes push the total up.
### Q. Is it worth replacing 20 year old windows?
A.  Often, but check the failure first. Fog between the panes means the seal has gone and that unit is done. A sticking sash or a draft sometimes needs only hardware and weatherstripping. At twenty years it is a real question, not an automatic yes.
### Q. Is it cheaper to replace all windows at once?
A.  Per window, usually yes: one trip, one crew and better pricing on volume. Whether it is right depends on cash flow. Doing the worst side of the house first is a fair middle path, as long as you get the whole house priced so you know what you are putting off.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy windows and have someone install them?
A.  Sometimes on paper, rarely in practice. Many installers will not warranty labor on windows they did not supply, and a wrong measurement on a window you bought is your problem. In a local historic district, make sure the window you buy is one the city will approve before you pay for it.
### Q. What is a professional window installer called?
A.  Most people just say window installer or replacement contractor. A glazier is the tradesperson who cuts and sets glass. For a whole-house replacement, you are usually hiring a window company with its own install crew.
### Q. What to ask a window salesman?
A.  Ask whether it is full-frame or pocket replacement, who does the installation, what the labor warranty covers, and what the price is without the discount that expires tonight. If the house is in a local historic district, ask whether the window is on the city’s Approved Historic Window List.

## How to Hire a Concrete Contractor in St. Louis (Cost Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-hire-a-concrete-contractor-in-st-louis
Another St. Louis winter has left the driveway a jigsaw of cracks and heaved slabs. Coffee in hand on a Saturday in Florissant or Oakville, you stand there doing the math. Or maybe the plan is a patio out back for summer cookouts, and three quotes have landed that range from “that seems fair” to “are they pouring gold?” Concrete looks simple. A gray slab, poured and done. But the gap between a good pour and a bad one shows up a year or two later, when one is still flat and solid and the other is spiderwebbed with cracks.
Hiring the right concrete contractor is what separates those two outcomes. This guide walks through how to find a good one, what concrete actually costs per square foot in St. Louis, what the trade is even called, the classic negotiation mistakes to avoid, and the red flags that should send you looking elsewhere — so your driveway or patio outlasts the next decade of freeze-thaw.
### How Do You Find a Good Concrete Contractor?
The short answer: hire a licensed and insured contractor with a real portfolio of finished local work, strong recent reviews, and a clear written estimate — and be skeptical of anyone whose bid is dramatically cheaper than the rest. Concrete is unforgiving. Once it’s poured and cured, fixing a bad job usually means tearing it out and starting over, so experience and craftsmanship matter enormously. Ask to see driveways or patios they’ve poured in the area, read reviews that mention how the work held up over time (not just how friendly the crew was), confirm they carry insurance, and get everything — scope, thickness, reinforcement, prep, and price — in writing. Two or three detailed bids for the identical scope will quickly show you who’s serious and who’s guessing.
### What Does Concrete Cost in St. Louis?
Pricing is usually by the square foot, and it varies with the type of project. In the St. Louis area, a plain concrete driveway runs about $7 to $13 per square foot for standard, un-reinforced concrete — roughly $4,700 to $6,400 for a 500-square-foot driveway. A basic concrete patio runs about $4 to $8 per square foot, while decorative or stamped concrete with color, patterns, and borders jumps to $15 to $30 per square foot. If an old slab has to come out first, budget another $2 to $6 per square foot for demolition and disposal. And don’t forget permits — the City of St. Louis requires a permit for a new driveway, with a fee around $110, and many municipalities in the metro have their own requirements. A trustworthy contractor builds prep, reinforcement, thickness, and permits into the quote rather than surprising you later.
### What Is a Concrete Contractor Called?
You’ll hear a few names, and they’re worth knowing so you hire the right specialist. The tradesperson who places and finishes concrete is often called a concrete finisher or cement mason; a company that manages the whole job — forming, pouring, finishing, and cleanup — is a concrete contractor or flatwork contractor (“flatwork” means horizontal surfaces like driveways, patios, and sidewalks, as opposed to foundations or structural work). For a driveway or patio you want a residential flatwork contractor with a strong finishing reputation. For structural work — foundations, retaining walls, basement repair — you want someone who specializes there instead. Matching the specialty to the job is half of hiring well.
### What Is the Difference Between Cement and Concrete?
People use the words interchangeably, but they’re not the same — and a contractor who explains the difference clearly is usually one who knows their craft. Cement is an ingredient: a fine powder (typically Portland cement) that acts as the binder. Concrete is the finished building material — a mix of cement, water, and aggregates like sand and gravel that cures into the hard, durable surface you actually walk and park on. So your driveway isn’t “cement,” it’s concrete; cement is just the glue inside it. It sounds like trivia, but the mix design — the ratio of cement to aggregate to water, and any additives for our freeze-thaw climate — is exactly the kind of detail that separates a slab that lasts from one that flakes and cracks early.
### What Not to Tell a Contractor
None of this is about being adversarial. It’s about not handing away your leverage. A few things are better kept close. Don’t lead with your absolute maximum budget; “I can go up to $12,000” has a way of becoming the price. Don’t signal that you’re in a desperate hurry, or that theirs is the only bid you’re getting. And don’t tell them exactly what the other guy quoted before you’ve heard their honest number. It’s also wise not to reveal that you have no idea what the work should cost — which, having read the pricing above, you no longer don’t. What you should share is your scope, your timeline flexibility, and that you’re comparing a few detailed bids. That framing invites a fair, competitive price without inviting anyone to pad it.
### What Is Poor Man’s Concrete?
“Poor man’s concrete” is a budget alternative you’ll sometimes hear about — usually a soil-cement or dry-pour mix, where Portland cement is blended with on-site soil or gravel and compacted, or where dry concrete mix is poured and left to draw moisture from the ground. It’s cheaper up front and can work for a rustic shed pad, a footpath, or a temporary surface. But for a driveway or patio you’ll actually rely on, it’s generally a false economy: it’s weaker, less predictable, and far more prone to cracking and crumbling under our freeze-thaw cycles and vehicle weight. If a contractor proposes something like this to hit a low number, ask pointed questions about longevity and whether it’s truly appropriate for the load — because the money you save now often comes back as a full tear-out later.
### Repair or Replace? When Cracked Concrete Can Be Saved
Before you pay for a full tear-out, it’s worth knowing that not every crack means replacement. Hairline surface cracks are normal as concrete cures and rarely a structural problem. Minor cracks and small settled sections can sometimes be sealed, patched, or lifted back into place with slabjacking (also called mudjacking) for far less than a new pour. But when a slab is badly heaved, deeply cracked across large areas, crumbling, or pooling water, repair becomes a losing game and replacement is the honest call. A trustworthy contractor will tell you which camp your driveway or patio is in — and a good one won’t push a $6,000 replacement when a $600 repair would genuinely do. If someone insists on tear-out without even considering repair, get a second opinion before committing.

### Red Flags When Hiring a Concrete Contractor
Certain signs should give you pause. Be cautious of a bid dramatically lower than the others (often thin slabs, no reinforcement, or skipped prep you can’t see until it fails), no license or insurance, no written contract, large cash-only upfront demands, high-pressure “we’re in your neighborhood today” door-knockers, no local portfolio or references, and vagueness about slab thickness, base prep, or curing. Concrete work has a lot of quality hidden below the surface — the gravel base, the compaction, the rebar or mesh, the pour thickness — so a contractor who won’t spell those out in writing is asking you to trust what you’ll never be able to inspect. The good ones put it all on paper, because that’s exactly how they win jobs against the cut-corner crowd.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before committing, ask: Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof? Can I see driveways or patios you’ve poured nearby? How thick will the slab be, and what reinforcement do you use? How will you prep and compact the base? Will you pull the required permit? Is the estimate itemized and in writing? What’s your policy if it cracks — is there a warranty? How long before I can use it? A reputable concrete contractor answers these confidently and in detail. Vague or annoyed responses — especially about base prep, thickness, and permits — tell you they may be planning to cut exactly the corners that cause early failure.
### St. Louis-Specific: Clay Soil, Freeze-Thaw, and Permits
Our region throws two real challenges at concrete. First, much of the St. Louis metro sits on expansive clay soil that swells when wet and shrinks when dry, moving whatever sits on top of it — which is why proper base prep and compaction matter so much here and why a cheap, thin pour on unprepared ground so often cracks. Second, our freeze-thaw winters repeatedly expand and contract concrete and any water that seeps into it, punishing weak mixes and poor drainage. A contractor who knows St. Louis will talk about base preparation, adequate thickness, control joints to manage cracking, air-entrained mix for freeze resistance, and drainage that moves water away from the slab. Add local permitting — requirements and fees vary by municipality across the metro — and you can see why hiring someone who genuinely knows this ground beats hiring the lowest bid from out of town. Browse established local concrete contractors before you sign, and you’ll shortlist crews who’ve already proven their work survives our winters.

## How to Choose a Tile Installer in St. Louis (Cost Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-tile-installer-in-st-louis
The box of porcelain tile sits in the corner of your half-finished Kirkwood bathroom, and the whole result now rides on the hands that set it. Tile punishes shortcuts. The material can be flawless and the job still fails: crooked lines, lippage you catch with a bare toe, grout that cracks in a month, a shower that leaks behind the wall where you can’t see it. A great tile job quietly lasts for decades. A bad one announces itself every single day.
That makes the installer the most consequential finish decision in the whole remodel. Below: what tile installation should cost per square foot and per day, what the trade is called, how to spot real skill (including a clever test you can ask about), the mistakes that wreck jobs, and how to hire a St. Louis setter whose work you’ll be glad to look at for years.
### How Much Should You Expect to Pay for Tile Installation?
Here’s the direct answer: tile labor typically runs about $8 to $15 per square foot in 2026. The full range stretches from roughly $5 to $22 per square foot once you factor in tile type, pattern, and where you live — and that’s labor alone, sitting on top of what the tile itself costs. Standard 12×12 or 12×24 ceramic in a simple layout lands at the low end. Small mosaics, natural stone, and intricate patterns like herringbone or diagonal push toward the top, often adding 15 to 25 percent to labor. Prefer an hourly setter? Expect roughly $50 to $120 per hour, with most independents in the $65 to $90 range. One figure beats every national average: a written, itemized quote for your exact room, tile, and layout.
### What Is a Person That Installs Tiles Called?
Call them a tile setter, tile installer, or just a tiler — all three mean the same thing. A company that handles the full job (surface prep, waterproofing, setting, grouting) is a tile contractor. Tile setting is a real craft. A good setter reads substrate prep, waterproofs a shower properly, picks the right thinset and trowel, plans the layout, and keeps a long run dead straight and level. So hire a specialist, not a general handyman who tiles now and then. The difference turns up in the cuts and the grout lines.
### How Much Should You Pay a Tiler Per Day?
For smaller or hard-to-measure jobs, some setters quote by the day instead of the square foot. Working from typical hourly rates, a full day of skilled tile work generally lands around $500 to $700 for one experienced setter. Add a helper or intricate detail and it climbs. Day rates carry a catch, though. A slower setter simply bills more days, so a per-square-foot or per-job quote usually protects you better: it ties the price to the finished result, not the clock. Quoted by the day? Ask how many days your job should take, and what happens if it runs long. A confident pro answers straight.
### How Much Does Lowe’s Charge to Install Tile?
Lowe’s and Home Depot both sell tile installation, farmed out to third-party contractors. Their pricing usually sits in the same per-square-foot ballpark as hiring independently, sometimes a touch higher once service fees stack up, and you get less say over which crew shows up. What you’re buying is convenience and a corporate warranty. What you often trade away is the personal accountability and craftsmanship of a well-reviewed independent setter. Plenty of St. Louis homeowners find a skilled local tiler with a strong portfolio delivers a better result for the money. If you do go big-box, still pin down who’s actually setting the tile, whether they’re insured, and what the warranty covers. The store isn’t the one on its knees on your floor.
### What Is the 3-4-5 Rule for Tiling?
Want a quick read on whether a setter knows layout? Ask about the 3-4-5 rule. It’s a simple geometry trick that confirms a perfectly square (90-degree) corner before a single tile goes down. Measure 3 units along one line, 4 units along the perpendicular line, and if the diagonal between those two points is exactly 5 units, the corner is truly square — the 3-4-5 right triangle from geometry class. Setters use it to strike accurate reference lines so the whole floor or wall runs straight. Most older St. Louis homes sit slightly out of square. Tile off the crooked wall instead of a squared layout line, and you get tapering grout lines and a job that looks “off” for reasons nobody can name. A tiler who lights up at this question plans layouts properly.
### Common Tiling Mistakes to Avoid
Learn what goes wrong and you’ll spot the setter who gets it right. The classic mistakes: skipping or rushing surface prep (tile is only as good as what’s under it), inadequate waterproofing in showers and wet areas (the leaks you can’t see are the expensive ones), poor layout planning that leaves ugly sliver cuts at the most visible edges, the wrong trowel or too little thinset causing hollow spots and loose tiles, uneven tiles (lippage) from rushing, wrong or badly mixed grout, and skipping spacers or expansion joints so the finished surface has no room to move. Almost every one traces back to the same thing: prep and patience. Which is exactly why the cheapest, fastest bid so often turns into the priciest one after the redo.
Total tangent — here’s where to eat in Godfrey.
### Porcelain, Ceramic, or Stone: Matching Tile to the Room
A good setter also steers you toward the right tile for the spot it’s going, so a little background helps you weigh the advice. Porcelain is denser and more water-resistant than standard ceramic, the workhorse for floors, heavy traffic, and wet zones. It costs a bit more and cuts harder, which is part of why skilled labor matters. Ceramic is kinder to the budget and perfect for walls and quieter floors. Natural stone (marble, travertine, slate) is beautiful but porous, so it wants sealing and careful upkeep — wrong choice for a busy mudroom. Glass and mosaic tiles sing as accents and backsplashes, yet they demand extra skill to set cleanly. No single tile wins outright. The setter who asks how you’ll actually use the room before naming a tile is the one thinking about how the job holds up, not just how it photographs on day one.
### Red Flags When Hiring a Tile Installer
Some warning signs show up before you ever sign. Be wary of no portfolio or references, no insurance, a bid far below the others, vagueness about surface prep and waterproofing, unwillingness to put scope and price in writing, large cash-up-front demands, and anyone who talks only about how fast they’ll finish rather than how well. A setter who can’t show you bathrooms and floors they’ve actually done, or who waves off your questions about the substrate and shower waterproofing, is telling you exactly where they’ll cut corners. Good tilers are proud of the work. Their portfolio is the best sales pitch they’ve got.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Bring this short list to the estimate: Can I see photos of showers and floors you’ve tiled? Are you insured? How will you prep the surface, and how will you waterproof the wet areas? Is the quote per square foot or per job, and what’s included — prep, setting, grouting, sealing? How do you handle layout in a room that’s out of square? What tile types do you specialize in? Do you offer any warranty on the workmanship? A skilled setter answers with specifics, and usually some enthusiasm. Thin answers, especially on prep and waterproofing, are your cue to keep looking. Those invisible steps are where a beautiful tile job is won or lost.
### St. Louis-Specific: Old-House Floors, Basements, and Bathrooms
Tiling here carries a few local quirks worth paying for. Our century-old homes come with floors and walls that are rarely flat or square, so a setter who can level a subfloor and plan around an out-of-square room earns the rate. Our humid summers and finished basements raise the stakes on waterproofing and on picking the right materials for below-grade, moisture-prone space — get it wrong and you invite mold and loose tile. Bathroom and shower work is where corner-cutting hurts most, because one hidden leak can rot a floor or a ceiling. A setter who’s worked older St. Louis homes brings exactly that judgment. Browse experienced local tile pros before you commit, and you’ll shortlist setters whose finished work you can go stand in front of.

## Custom Cabinets in St. Louis: How to Choose a Cabinet Maker (Costs)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-cabinet-maker-in-st-louis
The coffee’s gone cold. You’re standing in your Ballwin or Tower Grove South kitchen doing the mental math on a remodel, and your eye keeps landing on the cabinets: the dated doors, the drawer that never quite closes, the layout that fights you every time you cook. So you start pricing it out. One company says $8,000. Another says $30,000. And you genuinely can’t tell whether you’re comparing the same thing or getting played.
Cabinets are almost always the single biggest line item in a kitchen remodel, which makes the cabinet decision the one most worth getting right. This guide breaks down what cabinets really cost — stock, semi-custom, and fully custom — whether it’s cheaper to buy or build, what a $10,000 budget realistically covers, which cabinet styles are aging poorly, and how to choose a St. Louis cabinet maker who’ll deliver quality that lasts.
### Is It Cheaper to Buy Cabinets or Have Them Built?
Straight answer: buying pre-made (stock) cabinets is almost always cheaper up front than having them custom built. Stock cabinets get mass-produced in standard sizes, so they cost the least. Custom cabinets are built to your exact kitchen and specs, which costs more in both materials and skilled labor. Price isn’t the whole story, though. Custom fits your space with no filler strips or awkward gaps, uses higher-grade materials, and lasts far longer — often 40 years or more versus 10 to 15 years for stock. Stock wins on today’s price. Custom wins on fit and durability. For a lot of kitchens, semi-custom is the middle ground: more sizes and styles than stock, better quality, without the full custom price tag.
### What Is the Average Cost for Custom Kitchen Cabinets?
Cabinets get priced per linear foot — the run of cabinetry along your walls — installed. Here are the 2026 tiers. Stock runs about $100 to $300 per linear foot. Semi-custom runs about $150 to $650 per linear foot. Fully custom runs about $500 to $1,200+ per linear foot. Scale that up to a whole kitchen and the picture gets clearer: stock or basic semi-custom often runs $8,000 to $15,000; a mid-range semi-custom kitchen with finished interiors, soft-close hardware, and professional installation averages $16,000 to $22,000 nationally; and fully custom cabinets run roughly $18,000 to $30,000 for an average-sized kitchen. Your number comes down to size, materials, and how custom you go. That’s why an itemized, per-linear-foot quote is the only honest way to compare bids.
### Will Home Depot Make Custom Cabinets?
Sort of. Read the fine print. Home Depot (and Lowe’s) mostly sell stock and semi-custom cabinet lines from major manufacturers, plus design and installation services. What they label “custom” is usually semi-custom: you pick from set door styles, finishes, and modular sizes with some configuration room, but it’s not a true one-off built from scratch to your exact specs. For many kitchens that’s perfectly fine, and often a good value. The gap shows up when your kitchen is unusual: an odd layout, a specific wood or finish they don’t stock, cabinetry that has to wrap around old-house angles. That’s the job a genuine local custom cabinet maker handles and the big box isn’t set up for.
### Can Lowe’s Make Custom Cabinets?
Same story at Lowe’s. They offer stock and semi-custom cabinet lines with design and installation, not true built-from-scratch custom cabinetry. Got a straightforward kitchen with standard dimensions? Their semi-custom options can be a reasonable, convenient choice, backed by a corporate warranty. Need real customization — exact sizing, unique materials, built-ins for a tricky St. Louis old-house kitchen? Then you want an independent cabinet maker or a cabinetry-focused contractor. And remember, as with tile and windows, the store isn’t the installer. Ask who actually builds and installs, whether they’re insured, and what the warranty covers before you sign.
### Is $10,000 Enough for a Kitchen Remodel?
Honestly? $10,000 is a tight but workable budget for a modest kitchen refresh — not a full gut renovation. Cabinets alone can eat most or all of $10,000 at the stock-to-semi-custom level, so a budget that size means choosing carefully. Keep your existing layout, because moving plumbing and gas gets expensive fast. Go with stock or semi-custom cabinets. Or reface instead of replace if the boxes are still sound. Then add countertops, a backsplash, hardware, and labor, and the $10,000 disappears quickly. It can still produce a big visual jump — new cabinet fronts, counters, and paint transform a room. What it won’t cover is a full custom kitchen with new appliances and a reworked layout. A good cabinet maker or remodeler will tell you straight what your budget can and can’t stretch to, and help you spend it where it shows most.
### What Cabinet Color Is Outdated?
Cabinets are a long-term investment, so style longevity matters, especially if resale is on your mind. Trends shift. A few looks are widely considered to be fading: very dark, heavy cherry and orange-toned wood finishes from the early 2000s, honey oak in its dated golden form, and starkly all-white kitchens, all giving way to warmer, more natural palettes. Aging well right now: warm neutrals, soft greens and muted blues, natural wood tones, and two-tone kitchens. Chasing the trend of the moment is its own trap, though. A color that’s “in” this year can date just as fast. The safest long-term bet is usually a timeless neutral on the main cabinets, with color and personality added through paint, hardware, and accents you can swap cheaply later. A good cabinet maker can walk you through what holds up in both style and resale value.
Total tangent — Fenton’s dinner options are better than you think.
### Stock, Semi-Custom, or Custom: How to Decide
The three tiers are genuinely different products with different lifespans, and matching the tier to your kitchen saves both money and regret. Stock cabinets come in fixed sizes and a limited set of styles. They’re the budget choice, they install fast, and they make sense for a rental, a flip, or a basic kitchen — just expect a lifespan around 10 to 15 years and some filler gaps where standard sizes don’t quite fit. Semi-custom cabinets start from standard boxes but add far more sizes, door styles, finishes, and modifications, with better construction. They last roughly 20 to 30 years and suit most homeowners doing a real, lasting kitchen. Fully custom cabinets get built from scratch to your exact space and taste, in whatever materials and configuration you want. They cost the most and take the longest. They also fit perfectly, use the best materials, and can last 40 years or more. Staying in the home long-term with an awkward or period kitchen? The step up to semi-custom or custom usually pays you back in fit, durability, and daily satisfaction. On a budget, or moving before long? Stock does the job.
### How to Choose a St. Louis Cabinet Maker
Custom, semi-custom, hybrid — whatever tier you land on, the maker matters more than the label. Look for someone licensed and insured, with a real portfolio of finished kitchens you can actually go see, strong verifiable reviews, clear communication about materials (solid wood vs plywood vs particleboard, dovetail joints, soft-close hardware), and a detailed written quote and timeline. Ask about construction quality, not just the door style. The box, the joinery, and the hardware are what decide whether cabinets last 15 years or 40. Watch for the usual red flags too: no insurance, no portfolio, a bid far below the rest, big cash-up-front demands, vague answers about materials or timeline. Custom cabinetry is a months-long relationship. Hire someone whose work and communication you trust.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Bring this list to the first meeting: Can I see kitchens you’ve built or installed? Are you licensed and insured? What materials do you use for the boxes, doors, and drawers — and why? Is this stock, semi-custom, or fully custom? What’s the itemized cost per linear foot and the total? What’s the timeline, and what could delay it? What warranty covers the cabinets and the installation? Do you handle removal and disposal of the old cabinets? A quality cabinet maker answers every one of these in detail and welcomes the scrutiny, because their materials and craftsmanship are the whole selling point. Vague answers about what’s inside the boxes? That’s your sign to keep looking.
### St. Louis-Specific: Old-House Kitchens and Built-Ins
St. Louis’s older homes make cabinetry a genuinely local problem. Our century-old brick homes, bungalows, and four-families tend to have kitchens with non-standard dimensions, plaster walls that aren’t plumb, quirky nooks, and charming but awkward footprints. Those are exactly the spots where stock cabinets leave gaps and a skilled custom or semi-custom maker earns the fee by building to fit. Plenty of owners of historic St. Louis homes also want cabinetry that respects the period character of the house, from Shaker doors to furniture-style built-ins. That’s a job for a craftsman, not a modular kit. Own one of these homes? Prioritize a cabinet maker with real experience in older construction and creative built-ins. Look at their finished work before you commit. The right one turns an awkward old kitchen into the best room in the house.
