### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the average cost for custom kitchen cabinets?
A.  Fully custom cabinets run about $500 to $1,200+ per linear foot installed, or roughly $18,000 to $30,000 for an average-sized kitchen. By comparison, stock runs about $100 to $300 per linear foot ($8,000 to $15,000 for a kitchen) and semi-custom about $150 to $650 per linear foot, with a mid-range semi-custom kitchen averaging $16,000 to $22,000 nationally. Always get an itemized per-linear-foot quote.
### Q. Will Home Depot make custom cabinets?
A.  Home Depot primarily sells stock and semi-custom cabinet lines plus design and installation. What they call “custom” is usually semi-custom — set door styles, finishes, and modular sizes with some configuration, not a true one-off built to your exact specs. That’s fine for many kitchens, but for unusual layouts, specific materials, or old-house quirks, a genuine local custom cabinet maker is what you actually need.
### Q. Is $10,000 enough for a kitchen remodel?
A.  It’s a tight but workable budget for a modest refresh, not a full gut renovation. Cabinets alone can consume most of $10,000 at the stock-to-semi-custom level, so it usually means keeping your existing layout, choosing stock or semi-custom cabinets, or refacing rather than replacing. It can deliver a big visual improvement, but a full custom kitchen with new appliances and a reworked layout typically costs well beyond it.
### Q. What cabinet color is outdated?
A.  Widely considered to be fading: very dark or orange-toned cherry finishes from the early 2000s, dated golden honey oak, and starkly all-white kitchens. Warmer, more natural palettes — warm neutrals, soft greens and muted blues, natural wood, and two-tone kitchens — are aging better. But chasing any single trend is risky; a timeless neutral on the cabinets with color added through paint and hardware is the safest long-term bet.
### Q. What is the average cost of cabinets for a 12x12 kitchen?
A.  In 2026 the tiers run roughly $100 to $300 per linear foot for stock and $150 to $650 for semi-custom. Translated to a whole kitchen, stock or basic semi-custom often lands at $8,000 to $15,000, which is where most 12x12 kitchens fall.
### Q. What is the most affordable way to buy kitchen cabinets?
A.  Stock cabinets in standard sizes, ordered to fit the layout you already have. Cost climbs when the room forces custom widths or when you move plumbing. Refacing is cheaper still if the boxes are sound — it is the doors and fronts people actually see.
### Q. What makes a kitchen look cheap?
A.  Filler strips and awkward gaps where stock sizes did not quite fit, visible hinge hardware, and thin doors that flex. Custom avoids the gaps because it is built to the room — which is most of what you are paying the premium for.

## St. Louis Tuckpointing: What It Costs and How to Hire (Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-tuckpointing-cost-and-how-to-hire
Walk almost any block in Benton Park, Dutchtown, or Old North and you’re surrounded by it: the deep red brick that makes St. Louis, well, St. Louis. People fall in love with these homes for it. Then they run a thumb along an old mortar joint and feel it crumble — sandy, soft, giving way. That mortar is the glue holding a century-old wall together. When it fails, water gets in and bricks loosen, and a cheap maintenance job you could have scheduled becomes an expensive structural one you can’t ignore.
Tuckpointing — repairing and renewing those mortar joints — is practically a rite of homeownership in this brick city. This guide walks through what it costs in St. Louis, how it differs from repointing, whether a handyman or a DIY weekend can handle it, whether insurance helps, and how to hire a mason who gets it right the first time.
### How Much Does Tuckpointing Cost in St. Louis?
Here in the St. Louis area, tuckpointing and brick repair generally run about $8 to $25 per square foot. The broader range lands anywhere from roughly $5 to $25 per square foot, driven by the condition of the existing mortar, how hard the work area is to reach, and whether the mortar needs color-matching. For a standard residential job, most homeowners spend between $500 and $2,500. A full facade, significant structural damage, or hard-to-access upper walls pushes well past that. One number reframes the whole decision: labor is 80 to 90 percent of the cost. This is skilled, hands-on work, not a materials game, so the mason you hire matters far more than shaving a few dollars off the mortar. Get two or three detailed, in-person estimates. A real quote depends on a mason actually looking at your joints.
### What Is the Difference Between Tuckpointing and Repointing?
People use these words interchangeably, but there’s a technical distinction worth knowing. Repointing is the core repair: grinding or raking out old, deteriorated mortar and packing in fresh mortar to restore the joint. Tuckpointing, in its strict traditional sense, is a decorative technique. It uses two colors of mortar — one matched to the brick and a thin contrasting fillet line — to fake the crisp look of very fine, neat joints. In everyday St. Louis usage, though, “tuckpointing” has come to mean any mortar-joint repair, and most homeowners and even many masons use it as a catch-all for repointing. What matters for you is the substance: fresh, properly matched mortar packed into cleaned-out joints. When you get quotes, ask what the mason means by the term so everyone’s pricing the same work.
### Can a Handyman Do Tuckpointing?
Generally, no. This is one to take seriously. Tuckpointing is a skilled masonry trade, not a general-handyman task. Done right, it means removing old mortar to the correct depth without damaging the brick, then mixing mortar of the appropriate strength and composition — critically important on soft, old St. Louis brick, more on that below. Add color-matching, packing the joints properly, and tooling them to shed water and match the original profile. A handyman without masonry experience can easily use too-hard modern mortar, smear the brick faces, or do a surface “skim” that looks fine for a year and then fails — sometimes causing more damage than the original problem. For anything beyond a tiny cosmetic patch, hire an actual masonry or tuckpointing specialist.
### Can I Do Tuckpointing Myself?
You can tackle a small, accessible, non-structural patch if you’re handy and patient — a few crumbling joints at ground level, say. Go in with clear eyes, though. It’s physically demanding, dusty, and unforgiving work. The two most common DIY mistakes are using the wrong (too-hard) mortar and failing to rake the joints deep enough for the new mortar to bond. On St. Louis’s soft historic brick, hard modern Portland-heavy mortar can trap moisture and crack the brick faces over time. That’s an expensive lesson. Anything up high (ladders and scaffolding add real danger), anything structural, or any large area is squarely a job for a pro. Unsure whether your brick needs a soft lime-based mortar? That uncertainty is itself a good reason to call a specialist.
### Is Tuckpointing Covered by Insurance?
Usually not. Standard homeowners insurance treats tuckpointing as routine maintenance, the gradual wear of mortar over decades, and maintenance is exactly what policies exclude. So the everyday “my old joints are crumbling” repair comes out of your own pocket. There are exceptions. If the mortar or brick damage results from a sudden, covered peril — a vehicle strikes the wall, say, or a covered event causes specific damage — a claim may apply to that damage. But you can’t neglect brick for twenty years and expect insurance to fund the catch-up. So budget for tuckpointing as planned maintenance, and address it before water intrusion turns cosmetic decay into structural repair. If a sudden event caused the damage, read your policy or ask your agent.
### Signs Your St. Louis Brick Needs Tuckpointing
Catching it early saves money, so learn the tells. Watch for mortar that’s cracked, crumbling, receding, or sandy to the touch, visible gaps or missing chunks between bricks, and bricks that feel loose or have shifted. White chalky staining (efflorescence) signals water moving through the wall. So does any dampness or water intrusion on interior walls that back up to brick. Here’s the logic: mortar is built to be the sacrificial layer that fails before the brick does, so deteriorating joints are the wall doing its job and warning you. The moment water gets behind the brick, freeze-thaw cycles accelerate the damage fast. Seeing these signs? Get a mason out to assess before another winter works on it.
Nothing to do with brick — but the yard? Every St. Louis landscaper, mapped.
### How Long Does Tuckpointing Last?
Done properly, tuckpointing is a genuinely long-lasting repair. Quality work with the right mortar can last 25 years or more, and historically, good lime-mortar joints on well-maintained brick have lasted far longer. The catch is that “done properly” is carrying a lot of weight in that sentence. Joints raked to the correct depth, the right mortar for your brick, careful tooling, proper curing: those buy you decades. A rushed surface smear with the wrong mortar might look fine through one summer, then start failing by the second or third winter. This is the whole argument for hiring a real mason over the cheapest bid. The difference between a 3-year patch and a 25-year repair hides in craftsmanship you can’t fully see once the scaffolding comes down. Pay a bit more for someone who knows St. Louis brick, and the job becomes a once-a-generation expense instead of a recurring headache.
### Red Flags When Hiring a Tuckpointing Contractor
Masonry attracts its share of door-knockers and corner-cutters, so vet carefully. Be wary of unsolicited “we noticed your mortar” door-to-door pitches, no license or insurance, or a bid dramatically cheaper than the others — often a thin surface smear over unraked joints that fails within a couple of winters. Watch too for large cash-up-front demands and no written scope. The big one on an old St. Louis home: any contractor who can’t speak intelligently about mortar type for old brick. Using the wrong hard mortar here is a genuine, brick-cracking mistake, so a mason who shrugs at the question is a real risk. Look for local specialists with brick-repair portfolios, verifiable reviews, and a written scope that spells out how deep they’ll rake the joints and what mortar they’ll use.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before hiring, ask: Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof? Can I see brick repair you’ve done nearby? What mortar type will you use, and is it appropriate for my home’s age and brick? How deep will you rake the old joints? Will you match the mortar color and joint profile? Is the estimate itemized and in writing? Do you offer any warranty on the work? How will you access the upper walls safely? A true masonry pro answers the mortar-type question in particular with real knowledge — mentioning softer lime-based mortar for older brick — and welcomes the scrutiny. Vagueness there is the single biggest warning sign on a St. Louis brick home.
### St. Louis-Specific: Why the Brick City Needs Tuckpointing
Few cities are as defined by brick as St. Louis, and that heritage comes with a maintenance reality. Much of our building stock is a century old or more, built with soft, locally-fired brick and lime-based mortar that behaves nothing like modern materials. It’s more porous, and it needs a compatible softer mortar so the joints, not the irreplaceable brick, stay the sacrificial layer. Then our punishing freeze-thaw winters go to work on any joint that’s let water in, expanding and contracting until soft mortar crumbles and bricks spall. Old soft brick plus hard freeze-thaw: that combination is why tuckpointing is such a constant here. It’s also why hiring a mason who genuinely understands historic St. Louis masonry — not one who’ll slap hard modern mortar on a 120-year-old wall — protects both your home and its character. Browse experienced local brick and tuckpointing specialists before you commit, and you’ll shortlist masons whose repairs have survived our winters and respected our brick.

## Missouri Licenses No Dog Groomers. How to Choose One in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-dog-groomer-in-st-louis
The dryer in the back room of a St. Louis grooming shop sounds like a leaf blower running inside a closet. You slide the leash across the counter, your dog plants all four paws on the tile and looks back at you once, and a person you met forty seconds ago walks her through a swinging door. The door swings shut. For the next two to four hours you won’t see the table, the clippers working near her eyes, or how long she sits in a crate with her fur still wet.
Here’s the part almost nobody in St. Louis knows. No state agency regulates that back room. The Missouri Department of Agriculture says it in one flat line: dog or cat grooming is not regulated in Missouri. No state license required. The boarding kennel down the road is licensed and inspected by the state, and the person holding scissors an inch from your dog’s eye needs nothing at all.
Read that twice, then text it to whoever in your house books the dog’s appointments. In Missouri, you are the inspector.
Unless you live in the right county. St. Charles County writes its own rules. St. Charles County’s code makes it unlawful to keep a grooming shop in unincorporated St. Charles County without first obtaining a valid registration, and before that registration is issued the county must issue a certificate of inspection. Both have to be conspicuously displayed at the shop. So if your groomer is out there, look at the wall by the register before you hand over the leash. Anywhere else, ask your groomer what license their city or county requires, if any, and listen to how fast the answer comes.
There is one exception, and it’s the most useful sentence on this page. The same state page says that if animals are also being boarded by their groomer overnight, a license is required. So the groomer who offers to keep your dog until morning because you’re stuck at work has stepped into the world of Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act program, where all licensed facilities are inspected at least once per year or upon complaint, routine inspections are unannounced, and inspection reports are available to the public upon request. If your dog will sleep anywhere but your house, ask to see that license before you say yes. The program’s office answers at (573) 751-3076.
### How much should I pay for a dog groom in St. Louis?
Use a real St. Louis price sheet as your yardstick. Silver Maple Pet Center lists its prices online: baths run $42 to $114 depending on size, and full haircuts run $62 to $125, with the bath, brush-out and nail clip included in the haircut price. A small dog like a Chihuahua or Westie lands at $42 to $58 for a bath. Matting, a nervous temperament and add-ons raise the bill.
### Reading the price sheet like a groomer would
Run your hand down your dog’s back on the kitchen floor, feel the knot hiding behind one ear, then make the call. When the groomer reads you a number, hold it next to that menu and the menu starts to talk. At Silver Maple, a bath for a large dog like a Labrador or German Shepherd runs $56 to $68, while a haircut for a Poodle or Irish Setter jumps to $84 to $125. That gap is the scissors. A coat that keeps growing needs a person standing over it with shears for an hour, and a coat that just sheds needs soap, water and a dryer. If a groomer quotes you a haircut price for a Lab, ask what the cut is for.
Silver Maple says its grooming clients come from all over St. Louis, including families from Kirkwood and Webster Groves, so it’s a fair local yardstick. For a second one, look at a van. Furry & Fabulous Mobile Grooming in St. Louis lists its Bath Service starting at $100, its Bath & Trim Service starting at $110, and its Haircut Service starting at $130. Same soap, same nail clip. The extra money buys a driveway instead of a waiting room full of barking.
The little line items tell you even more. Silver Maple lists a de-shedding treatment at $32 to $37, a nail grind with a bath at $13, a flea bath at $19.50, and yes, a blueberry facial at $14. Your dog comes home smelling like a muffin. That’s a nice extra. It is not the reason you picked the place.
The one cost you control is the mats. Silver Maple says matted or severely tangled coats require extra time and effort, which may increase the price, and that regular brushing at home helps prevent mat formation and reduces the time needed for de-matting during grooming. After a muddy spring walk in Forest Park, ten minutes on the kitchen floor with a slicker brush, the dog sighing and leaning into your knee, is cheaper than paying a stranger to pick knots out of a squirming dog on Saturday.
Reading the groomer's menu
### How much should I pay for a dog groom?
At Silver Maple Pet Center a bath runs $42 to $114 by size and a full haircut $62 to $125, with the brush-out and nail clip included. A van costs more: Furry & Fabulous Mobile Grooming starts its bath service at $100. Mats and a nervous dog push any price up.
### The five-minute walk-through that replaces a state inspector
Since no state agency regulates the room behind the swinging door, you check it, and you do it before the first appointment. Call ahead and ask if you can see the grooming area when you drop off. A good shop says “sure, come on back.” Then use your nose and your ears. The room should smell like shampoo and warm towels, not ammonia. Dogs waiting in crates should be dry or being dried, not shivering. You should hear clippers and somebody talking softly to a dog, not one person yelling over six dogs barking.
Expect to be asked for your dog’s rabies paperwork, and be glad when you are. In the City of St. Louis, rabies inoculation is the only vaccination required by City ordinance, and failure to maintain the required vaccination and registration can result in a ticket and a fine. A shop that checks it is checking the one thing the law already asks of you. A shop that never asks isn’t checking anyone else’s dog either. Then ask three questions while you’re standing there. Who stays with a dog while it’s under a dryer? What do you do with a dog that panics on the table? And what happens if my dog is badly matted, do you call me before you shave? Listen to how fast the answers come. The groomer who has thought about this answers in one breath. The one who hasn’t starts with “well, usually.”
Then book something small. A bath or a nail trim tells you nearly everything a full groom would, for a fraction of the price. Watch your dog at pickup. A dog that trots out wagging and leans on the groomer’s leg has already given you the review. A dog that bolts for the car, tail tucked, has given you one too.
Random, but: Highland, IL’s dinner lineup is worth a look.
### Red flags that should send you back to the car
Most of these you’ll feel in your stomach before you can name them, standing at the counter with the leash still looped around your wrist.
They won’t let you see where the grooming happens, ever.
They don’t ask about your dog’s vaccinations.
Nobody can explain how they handle an anxious, senior or reactive dog.
Dogs are left alone in crates under heated dryers.
They offer to keep your dog overnight but can’t show you a state license.
Recent reviews mention nicks, razor burn or a dog that came home shaking.
If your dog ever comes home with an unexplained cut or won’t walk toward the shop door again, believe the dog. Don’t go back, and leave an honest review so the next owner on the block knows too.
### Salon, van or the tub at a self-serve wash
A salon is the cheapest full groom, and it’s also the loudest: other dogs, other dryers, a crate while your dog waits. A grooming van pulls into your driveway and works on one dog at a time, which is a gift for the old dog with bad hips or the rescue who shakes at the sound of a bark. You pay for that quiet, as the van prices above show. And if your dog only needs a scrub, a self-serve wash gives you the raised tub, the warm water and the sprayer, and you go home with the wet sleeves instead of the groomer. None of these is the right answer for every dog. The right one is whichever leaves your dog calm at pickup.
### Which dogs shouldn’t be shaved for a St. Louis summer
Grooming and shaving are not the same thing. Nearly every dog does well with baths, brushing and nail care, but thick double coats, the kind on Huskies, Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds and Pomeranians, are usually better brushed out than buzzed down. That plush undercoat is part of how those dogs handle a St. Louis August and a January wind off the river, and a shave can change how it grows back. A good groomer will tell you that to your face instead of just doing what you asked. Take extra care, too, with very old, sick or badly anxious dogs, who may do better with shorter sessions in stages.
### Can grooming help with allergies?
It helps, but it’s management, not a cure. A bath and a thorough brush-out pull out loose hair and dander your dog would otherwise leave on the couch, and they rinse off the pollen and dust a dog picks up on a spring walk. Pair it with washing the dog’s bedding and keeping the bedroom dog-free, and an allergic person in the house will usually notice the difference.
### How much should you tip a St. Louis groomer?
Pickup is the moment. Your dog comes through the swinging door fluffed and wiggling, smelling of shampoo, and the card reader swivels toward you with a tip screen. NerdWallet says the industry standard for tipping service professionals, according to etiquette experts, is 15% to 20% of the bill. On a $62 haircut that’s about $9 to $12. On a $100 groom, $15 to $20. Go higher for the matted, wiggly or nervous dog that took real patience, and if you can’t swing a tip, a detailed review with your groomer’s name in it is worth more than you’d think.
### How often to book, from spring blowout to winter salt
Coats that keep growing, like Poodles, Bichons and doodle mixes, need regular professional grooms to stay ahead of mats. Thick double coats do well with regular de-shedding through the spring blowout. Short coats can often get by on an occasional bath and a nail trim, plus a rinse of the paws after a walk on salted winter sidewalks. If you hear nails clicking on the kitchen floor, it’s time, whatever the calendar says. Your groomer should be glad to suggest a schedule for your dog in particular.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much does it cost to groom a 20 lb dog?
A.  Most 20-pound dogs fall in a groomer’s small or medium row. On Silver Maple Pet Center’s menu, a small-dog bath runs $42 to $58, a Maltese or Bichon haircut runs $62 to $84, and a Cocker Spaniel haircut runs $72 to $98. Matting or a nervous dog pushes it higher.
### Q. Why does it take 4 hours to groom a dog?
A.  NerdWallet, citing PetSmart, says a grooming appointment can last two to four hours. Most of that isn’t hands-on time. Your dog waits a turn, gets bathed, then dries, and a thick coat can take a long time under a dryer. If the wait matters, ask for the first appointment of the day or a one-on-one mobile groomer.
### Q. What is the hardest dog breed to groom?
A.  Price sheets answer this one. Silver Maple’s most expensive haircut tier is giant coats like the Bouvier and Giant Schnauzer at $104 to $125, with Poodles in the $84 to $125 large tier. Coats that never stop growing take the most scissor time, and heavy double coats take the longest to dry.
### Q. Do dog groomers expect a tip?
A.  Most do. NerdWallet puts the standard for service professionals at 15% to 20% of the bill. Tip on the high side for a matted, anxious or senior dog that took extra patience.
### Q. Is a $5 dollar tip good for a dog groomer?
A.  On a small-dog bath it’s a little light. At 15% to 20%, a $42 bath works out to about $6 to $8, and a $62 haircut to about $9 to $12. Five dollars beats nothing, and a kind review with the groomer’s name in it adds a lot.
### Q. Do you tip a dog groomer if she’s the owner?
A.  You don’t have to, since an owner sets her own prices. Plenty of owner-operators still appreciate one, especially at a small shop where she does every groom herself. If a tip doesn’t fit the budget, a detailed online review helps her just as much.
### Q. Is it hard to groom your own dog?
A.  Baths and brushing are easy to learn. Haircuts and nails on a squirmy dog are where people get nervous, and where a nick happens. Many owners split it: brush at home between visits, which Silver Maple says helps prevent mat formation and reduces de-matting time, and leave the scissors to the pro. A self-serve dog wash covers the messy part.
### Q. How much can a dog groomer charge?
A.  Whatever the market will pay. Missouri doesn’t regulate grooming at all. That’s why comparing two posted menus, like the one at Silver Maple, is the fastest way to tell a fair quote from a padded one.
Grooming and boarding are different services with different questions to ask. Dog Boarding and Daycare in St. Louis: Real Prices, and How to Check a Kennel covers overnight and daycare options.

## The City-County Transfer Door Is Shut. Here’s What’s Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-school-in-st-louis
The door is shut. The city-to-county transfer program you may have heard about from a neighbor is closed to new students. The Voluntary Interdistrict Choice Corporation, which oversees the program, says it plainly: “No more applications are being accepted.” Students already enrolled can stay in their county district or magnet school through high school graduation. Nobody new gets in.
So if you are on the couch after bedtime, laptop warm on your knees, a lunchbox still drying in the rack, you can close that tab. The doors that are still open in St. Louis work differently than most people assume, and the biggest one runs on luck and a calendar, not on test scores.
Saint Louis Public Schools says admission to its magnet schools is based on a lottery system, and any student living in the city of St. Louis is eligible to apply. The placement window opens each fall. Once it closes for the lottery and results go out, the application reopens for first come-first served applicants, which means the families who apply late are picking over whatever seats are left. The window opens each fall and closes weeks before the lottery - check the date on the SLPS enrollment page before you plan around it. Confirm this year’s dates on the SLPS magnet schools page, or call 314-633-5200.
What you can do this week: if you live in the city, log in to or create your Focus parent account, which SLPS uses to submit a placement request for a magnet school, so you are ready the day the window opens. If your child may qualify for gifted programs, call the SLPS Gifted and Talented Office at 314-345-4548 before you apply. If you live in the county, your assigned public district is your starting point, so look up its enrollment steps tonight. And whichever side of the city line you live on, write down the three things that matter most for your kid before you open a single ranking site.
### How do you pick the best school for your child?
In St. Louis, start with what is actually open. The Voluntary Interdistrict Choice Corporation says no more applications are being accepted for new students to enroll in a county school, and SLPS runs a placement lottery for its magnet schools, with seats left after it going first come-first served, so the calendar matters as much as the school. Then rank what your child needs most: the teaching, safety and culture, special support, the commute and the cost. Tour your finalists and ask current parents if they would choose it again.
Look at your kid’s backpack slumped on the hook by the door, the one with the broken zipper pull. That is who you are choosing for. The best school for the family down the street can be the wrong school for yours, and that is not a failure on anyone’s part. A shy reader, a kid who needs to move, a teenager who lights up in a robotics lab: each one points somewhere different. Start with the child in front of you and work outward. If your child has a disability or you suspect one, the process runs on its own rules, so begin with what parents need to know about special education here.
### Are magnet schools only for smart kids?
No, and this is the myth that keeps a lot of good families from ever applying. SLPS describes magnet schools as public schools without school boundaries, each with something its traditional schools do not offer, and it fills most seats by lottery. Your child does not have to be a straight-A student to get a number drawn.
Some programs do ask for more. SLPS posts recommendation forms and essay information for Collegiate School of Medicine and Bioscience High School, McKinley Classical Leadership Academy High School and Metro Academic and Classical High School, and gifted programs run through the Gifted and Talented Office. If you are aiming at one of those, start the paperwork early, while there is still time to ask a teacher for a recommendation without rushing them.
The honest downside of magnets is not who gets in. It is the commute, a theme your child may outgrow, and the simple fact that a lottery can say no. Have a second choice you would be glad to get, and tell your child about both before the results come, so a no lands softer at your kitchen table.
### Charter schools: public, free and run differently
Missouri’s education department, DESE, defines charter schools as independent public schools that are free from some rules and regulations that apply to traditional public school districts. They may not charge tuition or fees, and DESE says there is no cost to parents for sending their children to a charter school.
Where they can open is limited by state law: Missouri says charter schools may be operated only in certain kinds of districts, such as a metropolitan school district. DESE’s charter list places St. Louis charters, like Atlas Public Schools, in the St. Louis Public School District. So yes: DESE lists charter schools, such as Atlas Public Schools, in the St. Louis Public School District.
Stand in a charter’s pickup line once, engines idling and kids spilling out with their coats half on, and you will learn more than any brochure tells you. Because each charter is independent, quality and culture vary more from one to the next than they do inside a single district. Judge each one on its own: who runs it, how long it has been open, and whether the families you meet at pickup would choose it again.
### Charter, private or your neighborhood school?
Parents ask which is better, charter or private school, as if one label could answer it. It cannot. A charter is public and costs nothing in tuition. A private or parochial school sets its own tuition, admissions and philosophy, and that bill comes every year for as long as your child is enrolled.
What tuition can buy is smaller classes, a faith community or a particular way of teaching. What it does not automatically buy is a better fit. If your child needs special-education services, ask every private school directly what it provides and get the answer in writing, because private schools do not all offer the same supports a public district does.
Run the real numbers. Add up tuition for every year your child would attend, then compare it with the commute, the activities and the friendships you would trade for it. Sometimes the neighborhood school a few blocks away, where your kid can walk home with friends, is the quiet winner.
Wildly off-topic: when the tours are done and everybody is cranky, find an indoor afternoon in St. Louis and let the kids run.
### Reading the numbers without letting them decide
State data is the most honest place to start. On the Illinois side, the Illinois Report Card promises to go beyond test scores and give a snapshot of every Illinois public school, which helps Metro East families compare districts side by side. On the Missouri side, ask the district or school for its most recent state report and read it yourself.
Rating sites repackage that data into neat rows of stars, the kind you scroll at midnight until they blur. Use them to build a short list, not to make the call. Ratings lean hard on test results, and test results follow neighborhood income closely enough that a high number can tell you more about the zip code than about the classroom. A school a notch lower on a list might have the reading specialist, the dual-language track or the arts program your child would thrive in.
Treat every number as a question to ask on the tour. If a score dropped, ask why. If attendance looks low, ask what the school is doing about it. The way a principal answers tells you a lot.
### What to look for when you walk the halls
Nothing replaces walking through the building. Go during the school day if they will let you. Listen at the classroom doors: a low hum of kids talking about the work is a good sound. Watch the hallway at passing time. Notice whether the person at the front desk looks up and smiles when you walk in.
Bring questions and write the answers down. How do you help a child who is behind, and one who is bored? How do teachers reach parents, and how fast? What happens when a kid is bullied? How many teachers left last year? What does before-care and after-care cost, and when does the bus come? Then find two parents in the pickup line and ask them one thing: would you choose this school again?
Trust your read. You know your kid. A place that feels warm and busy and a little loud in the right way usually is.
### Special needs, commutes and the long haul
If your child has a disability or a learning difference, ask early and ask specifically about special-education support, who provides it and how often. Get it in writing before you commit. For families navigating hearing loss, the choice narrows fast, so start with our guide to schools for the deaf in St. Louis.
Be honest about the drive. A slightly better school that adds an hour of traffic every day costs your family something real: the dinner that gets rushed, the practice that gets skipped, the kid asleep against the car window. A strong school close to home makes it easier to show up for the play and the parent conference.
And think past this year. Ask about enrollment trends and staff turnover, because schools change. You are not choosing a building for one year. You are choosing a place your child will walk into hundreds of mornings in a row.
See every school near your front door before you start touring. The St. Louis Schools Map plots public district, magnet, charter, private and Catholic schools on both the Missouri and Illinois sides, so you can build your short list in one sitting. Save the schools map to your phone for the week of tours.
If you run the tutoring center, the after-school program or the uniform shop these families call next, a Gold listing helps you get more customers from the parents already searching, so see who AI names instead of you or list your business.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Are there charter schools in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Missouri law limits where charter schools may operate, and DESE’s charter list places St. Louis charters, such as Atlas Public Schools, in the St. Louis Public School District. DESE calls them independent public schools, and they may not charge tuition or fees.
### Q. What is the difference between a charter school and a public school?
A.  A charter school is a public school, but an independent one. DESE says charter schools are free from some rules and regulations that apply to traditional public school districts. Both are free to attend; the difference is who runs the school and how much freedom it has over how it teaches.
### Q. Is a magnet school better than a regular school?
A.  Not automatically. A magnet is a public school without school boundaries built around something special, which can be a great match for a child with a strong interest. A regular neighborhood school can be the better fit when the commute, friendships or support services matter more. Compare the two schools, not the labels.
### Q. Does magnet school cost money?
A.  SLPS describes its magnet schools as public schools, and you get in by applying, not by paying: seats are filled by lottery. Ask the school you choose about supply lists, uniforms and activity costs so nothing surprises you on the first day.
### Q. What are the downsides of magnet schools?
A.  A lottery can say no, so you may not get your first choice. The commute can be long, a theme can stop fitting as a child grows, and a few programs ask for recommendations or essays. Apply on time, list a second choice you would be glad to get, and ask how transportation works.
### Q. Are magnet schools only for smart kids?
A.  No. SLPS fills its magnet seats by lottery, and any student living in the city of St. Louis can apply. A few programs, such as gifted schools and selective high schools, add recommendations, essays or gifted eligibility, so check the specific school before you apply.
### Q. Which is better, charter or private school?
A.  Neither wins on the label. A charter is public, and DESE says there is no cost to parents to send a child there. A private school charges tuition and sets its own rules, which can buy smaller classes or a faith community. Compare the actual schools, the yearly cost and the support your child needs.

## Your Address Can Cost $2,940 at St. Louis Community College
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-college-or-trade-school-in-st-louis
Pull the last envelope off your counter, the electric bill or the lease renewal, and look at the address in the little plastic window. Now hold that address up against St. Louis Community College’s fees page. STLCC’s Associate in Arts takes 60 credit hours, so at the in-district rate of $127 a credit hour the tuition comes to $7,620, at the out-of-district rate of $176 it comes to $10,560, and the gap is $2,940.
Same classes. Same credits. Same degree. The rule that moves the price is simply your address. On STLCC’s fees page the $127 rate carries an asterisk, and the footnote names who gets it: residents of St. Louis City, St. Louis County or portions of Franklin and Jefferson counties.
It is the kind of detail a careful shopper catches before an open house, not after the first bill. The rest of this guide works the same way: the rules that move the price, so you can compare a community college, a university and a trade school on real numbers.
Check your district: STLCC says you are eligible to enroll as a resident if you live in St. Louis City, St. Louis County or portions of Franklin and Jefferson counties in the school districts it lists, and it adjusts the rates each year, so read the current ones on the STLCC tuition and fees page.
If you live outside the district, look hard at online sections, because STLCC prices online courses at $130 an hour for out-of-district students instead of $176.
Pull your high school transcript and look for the A+ seal; if it is there, the A+ Scholarship may pay the unpaid balance of your tuition and general fees at a participating community college or technical school.
File the FAFSA, which A+ asks you to complete each academic year.
Questions about a bill? STLCC says your campus cashier’s office is just a call or visit away at 314-539-5015, and its payment plan lets you spread fall and spring payments out for a small fee.
### Is it better to go to a community college or a university?
Neither wins for everyone, and you can do both. Under Missouri’s CORE 42, general-education courses that match a CORE 42 transfer number are guaranteed to transfer one-to-one among participating schools, so you can start at a community college and finish the bachelor’s at a university. If you graduated from an A+ designated high school, the A+ Scholarship can pay the unpaid balance of tuition and general fees at a participating community college. Go straight to a university when your field needs it from day one.
Spread the options across the table, course lists side by side, and the deciding question gets clearer: which path gets you to the work you want, in the time you want, at a price you would happily pay again? Answer that first. The school almost picks itself. And if you would rather learn where the air smells of hot metal and cutting oil than in a lecture hall, trade school sits on the same map: Ranken Technical College, on Finney Avenue, has been training students since 1907.
### The 2.5 that is really a price tag
Slide your high school transcript out of its folder and look for one small mark: the A+ seal or stamp. In Missouri that mark, and the 2.5 GPA behind it, is a money line. The state’s A+ Scholarship Program pays the unpaid balance of tuition and general fees, after non-loan federal aid like the Pell grant, at participating public community colleges and vocational or technical schools.
To get it, you graduate from an A+ designated high school with an unweighted 2.5 GPA or higher, at least 95% attendance for grades 9-12 and at least 50 hours of unpaid tutoring or mentoring. Then you enroll and attend full-time at a participating school and complete the FAFSA each academic year. To keep it, you hold a 2.5 cumulative GPA in college. Drop under that line and the help can stop, which is why a 2.5 matters more here than it does almost anywhere else.
There is no paper application. Instead, check with your community college or technical school to see what materials it requires along with the A+ seal on your high school transcript.
### What A+ will not pay for
Here is the part worth knowing before you reach the bookstore counter and hear the register add up a stack of textbooks. A+ covers tuition and general fees. It does not cover the rest of your life.
STLCC’s own cost-of-attendance estimate lists $2,000 for books, materials, supplies and equipment, and $9,494 for food and housing for an independent student. Budget for both alongside tuition, so the full cost of each option sits side by side.
The program has two traps worth taping to the fridge. You must complete at least 12 credit hours in each fall and spring term you receive an A+ award. And repeat coursework, including a class you already failed, will not be reimbursed. Take the load you can actually finish, and if a class is going sideways, talk to the financial-aid office before you drop or retake it.
### Going back at 30, 40 or 50
If you have been out of school for years, the first night back can feel like walking into a room where everybody else already knows the rules. The fluorescent light, the syllabus, the login you swear you typed right. That feeling passes, and a well-chosen price is still working for you long after it does.
If A+ is not part of your story, the in-district rate and the online price matter even more. One class at a time is still progress. Plenty of people finish a certificate first, get the raise, and let the next semester pay for itself.
Before you sign up, ask the admissions office three blunt questions: what does this certificate or degree actually lead to, how many people who start it finish, and can my work or military experience count for credit? The answers tell you more than the course catalog.
### Is the two-years-then-transfer route worth it?
It is the quietest money move in the region. Missouri built a 42-credit-hour general-education block called CORE 42, and the state says courses that match a CORE 42 transfer number are guaranteed to transfer one-to-one among all participating schools. The University of Missouri-St. Louis publishes the same Missouri Core 42 requirements in its own catalog.
So the English comp you take at an STLCC campus at night can count the same as the one at a university at noon. Your diploma still comes from the university. The catch is honest: a course can transfer and still not fit your major, so sit down with an advisor in your first semester, not your last.
### Trade school: grease, sparks and a paycheck sooner
Some people learn best with a wrench in hand and the hum of a shop around them. That is not a lesser path. It is a shorter one to a paycheck, and often a cheaper one.
Stand in any welding bay for a minute and you hear it before you see it: the steady crackle of an arc, the hiss of a grinder, a hood snapping down. Ranken Technical College, at 4431 Finney Ave. in St. Louis, has been training students since 1907 and is accredited by the Higher Learning Commission. St. Louis Community College runs programs in machining, welding and auto repair, with campuses including Florissant Valley, Forest Park, Meramec and Wildwood. If you qualify for A+, ask any technical school whether it participates before you sign anything.
And ask about apprenticeships. In many building trades you are paid to learn on the job while you finish classroom hours, which turns the debt question upside down.
### Certificates: months, not years
Not every good job needs a full degree. A certificate is short, focused training, sometimes a single semester, built to get you hired in one field. For someone working two jobs, that matters: a finish line you can actually see keeps you showing up on the nights you are tired enough to quit.
The smart way to use one is as a first rung, not the whole ladder. Pick a certificate whose credits can stack into an associate degree later, so nothing you pay for now is wasted if you decide to keep going. Ask the program in writing which of its courses count toward a degree, and keep that answer.
Then compare it honestly with an apprenticeship in the same field. One costs tuition and pays later; the other pays you now and costs time. Neither is the wrong answer. The wrong answer is the one you pick because a recruiter called twice and sounded friendly. Call the employers who hire for that job in St. Louis and ask which credential they want to see. They will tell you, and that call is free.
Off the subject entirely: when the forms start to blur, get outside somewhere in St. Louis for an hour.
### How to choose without the brochure doing the talking
Glossy viewbooks all smell the same, like fresh ink and promises. Cut through them with five questions counselors often call the five C’s: cost after aid, curriculum (does it teach the exact thing you want?), career outcomes, culture and convenience for a person who also has to work.
Then check two things no salesperson can fake. Look the school up on the federal College Scorecard, which lets you search and compare colleges. And confirm accreditation, because credits from an unaccredited school may not move anywhere. Talk to someone who finished the program last year, not someone paid to recruit you. Ask one question and listen to how long they pause before answering: would you do it again, knowing what it cost?
See every campus and training program near your address before you choose. The St. Louis Schools Map puts community colleges, universities and technical schools across Missouri and Illinois on one screen. Save the schools map to your phone so the short list is one tap away.
If you’re the welder, the tutor or the one-truck HVAC crew these programs turn out, a Gold listing puts your name where neighbors and AI look for help, so you get more customers from the work you already do; see who AI names instead of you or list your business.
