### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is downtown Kirkwood known for?
A.  Downtown Kirkwood is known for its historic 1890s train station, the open-air Kirkwood Farmers Market, and a walkable core full of independent shops and restaurants. Founded in 1853, it was the first planned suburb west of the Mississippi and remains one of the St. Louis area’s most charming, pedestrian-friendly downtowns.
### Q. Is Kirkwood, MO a wealthy area?
A.  Kirkwood is an established, well-off St. Louis suburb known for high property values, top-rated schools, historic homes, and safe, tree-lined neighborhoods. It blends that affluence with a genuinely walkable, small-town downtown, which is a big part of its appeal to both residents and visitors.
### Q. What are the best new restaurants in Kirkwood?
A.  Recent standout openings include Café Amalia (Greek, 2025), Salt + Smoke (barbecue, 2025), Napoli Kirkwood (Italian), and, down by Grant’s Trail, 4 Hands + Peacemaker Lobster & Crab and the Perennial on the Trail taproom. The 1947 landmark Spencer’s Grill also reopened under new ownership.
### Q. Where can I get barbecue in Kirkwood?
A.  Salt + Smoke, which opened a Kirkwood location in 2025, is the downtown barbecue spot — known for brisket smoked 16 hours over post oak and its white-cheddar cracker mac. It joins the brewery-and-seafood 4 Hands + Peacemaker for a strong casual, beer-friendly lineup near the train station.
### Q. Is downtown Kirkwood walkable?
A.  Yes. Downtown Kirkwood is built around its historic train station, with shops, restaurants, and the farmers market clustered within a few walkable blocks. It’s one of the most pedestrian-friendly suburban downtowns in the St. Louis area — park once near the station and you can spend the whole day on foot.

## Central West End Restaurants by the Clock: Where Locals Eat and Drink on Euclid
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-the-central-west-end-st-louis-a-locals-guide
The first happy hour on Euclid Avenue pours at 6:30 in the morning. Kingside Diner calls it Third-Shift Happy Hour: mimosas and Bloody Marys on weekdays, set down in front of whoever’s night just ended. The last call comes around midnight, when the Jujube Inn on North Euclid clears its final glasses and Scarlett’s Wine Bar on Laclede, open since noon, finally turns out the lights.
Between dawn and midnight, the Central West End runs on a clock most visitors never learn. The street meters stop charging at 7 p.m. and don’t charge at all on Sundays. Mainlander, the supper club at 392 N. Euclid, puts next month’s tickets on sale at noon on the first. A French bistro pours a $6 glass of house wine for exactly one hour, Sunday through Thursday. Miss the clock and you’re circling the block with a hungry date in the passenger seat, or standing at a locked door on a Monday.
So this guide to Central West End restaurants runs hour by hour, with what to order when you get there. Every hour, price and address below was checked against the restaurant’s own website or menu. Where we couldn’t confirm something, we left it out.
### Morning: Where to Find the Best Breakfast in the Central West End
Kingside Diner, at 236 N. Euclid Ave., opens at 6 a.m. every day and runs until 2 p.m. Sunday through Wednesday, then until 8 p.m. Thursday through Saturday. On weekdays from 6:30 to 10:30 a.m., it pours that Third-Shift Happy Hour: mimosas, Bloody Marys, Bud and Bud Light, house wines, beside the diner’s breakfast plates, for the people whose workday just ended.
Bowood by Niche is the softer morning. It’s tucked inside Bowood Farms at 4605 Olive St., a light-filled room beside the greenery, and Gerard Craft’s kitchen sends out cacio e pepe eggs, a soft scramble heavy with pecorino and cracked black pepper on sourdough, for $18, or a crab cake Benedict for $26. The insider move is the 8 a.m. happy hour, Monday through Thursday: an $8 buttermilk pancake, an $8 mimosa, warm butter sliding off the stack. Bowood’s own menu says those hours can change, so check its social pages before you set the alarm. Park in Holliday’s lot across the street at 4600 Olive.
On weekends, two brunches are worth the wait. Evangeline’s at 512 N. Euclid serves a jazz brunch on Saturday and Sunday, in a room that bills itself as a bistro and music house. Yellowbelly serves Saturday brunch from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., and the plate to order is maple-glazed fried chicken on coconut-pecan brioche French toast for $18: crackling crust, sticky maple glaze, soft sweet bread underneath.
### Midday: Lunch Places Near the Central West End That Don’t Rush You
The best lunch trick in the neighborhood is a window. Edera Italian Eatery, at 48 Maryland Plaza, serves lunch Monday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., and its own site spells out the move: order at the carryout window, then carry your meal into the courtyard. That courtyard is walled in towering ivy, so a weekday sandwich turns into a long, quiet lunch in green shade. Order The Ted, a pistachio-crusted chicken “street sandwich” with prosciutto and arugula, for $20.
At 11 a.m. the door of The Noble Crown unlocks, every day of the week, and the first lunch crowd drifts in off the sidewalk. Dressel’s Public House on North Euclid follows at noon, Monday through Saturday. Around the corner at 4253 Laclede Ave., Scarlett’s Wine Bar slides pizzas out of an imported Mugnaini wood-fired oven, the edges blistered and smoky, for a $26 lunch that runs every day until 2:30 p.m.: a small salad of your choice plus an entree of your choice. Walk-ins only, and you can smell the wood fire before you sit down.
### Happy Hour: Where the Neighborhood Drinks for Less
Brasserie by Niche calls its happy hour Cinq à Six, and it means it: Sunday through Thursday, 5 to 6 p.m. A glass of house wine is $6, a carafe $20, and a single Brasserie cheeseburger with fries is $12. Sit at the bar while the dining room fills and the garlic and shallot from the mussel pots drift out of the kitchen: a burger with fries plus a glass of house wine comes to $18.
Yellowbelly, at 4659 Lindell Blvd., runs happy hour Tuesday through Friday from 5 to 6:30 p.m. The cocktails drop to $10, and the raw oysters are $4 each, dressed with kimchi water and pickled daikon or with tepache, chili flake and lime, cold and briny and gone in one tip of the shell. The Nashville hot fried oysters are $4 each too. Scarlett’s pours its happy hour Monday through Friday from 4 to 6 p.m., and on Tuesdays happy hour runs all day. Evangeline’s does it twice: Wednesday through Friday from 4 to 7 p.m., then again from 10 p.m. to close.
### Where to Eat Dinner Outside in the Central West End
Edera’s courtyard is the patio people mean when they say “outside in the CWE.” The restaurant describes it as lush greenery and twinkling lights, an Italian-style courtyard alongside towering ivy walls, and on a warm night the little lights come up against the ivy as the sun drops. Dinner runs Monday through Thursday from 5 to 9 p.m. and Friday and Saturday until 10. It’s closed Sundays.
Retreat Gastropub, at 6 N. Sarah St., opened in 2015 and does outdoors two ways. Its “patio” is a screened-in sunroom that keeps the rain off and the breeze in, and there’s sidewalk seating as well. Inside, the centerpiece is a bar of concrete poured on site and wood reclaimed from St. Louis sites, under old gas lanterns repurposed as light fixtures. Retreat’s site says it’s closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays.
Scarlett’s patio is weather permitting and takes no reservations, so the play there is simple: walk up early on a soft evening and stay put.

### After Seven: The Meters Stop and the Big Dinners Start
Here’s the parking rule that changes the night. Brasserie by Niche notes that metered spaces line most of Laclede and Euclid and stay active until 7 p.m., except on Sundays, and Evangeline’s says the same: meters run until 7 Monday through Saturday and are free on Sundays. Book a table after seven and the meter is your friend. Brasserie also offers valet for $10, and Evangeline’s opens a complimentary private lot on Washington on Friday and Saturday from 5 p.m. to midnight.
Then eat. Brasserie by Niche, at 4580 Laclede Ave., is the French bistro from James Beard Award-winning chef Gerard Craft. Start with the French onion soup under a lid of melted Comté ($16.95), then the mussels in white wine, shallot and crème fraîche with garlic toast for dragging through the broth ($33.95). Finish with the floating island, poached meringue drifting on crème anglaise. Dinner runs Monday through Saturday from 5 to 10 p.m. and Sunday until 9.
The Tenderloin Room has been inside the Chase Park Plaza since 1962, and its bar sits beneath the original stained-glass ceiling. Look up before you order. The Senate Bean Soup is still on the menu, billed as a house classic since 1962, at $10. The steak to order is the Pepperloin à la Tenderloin, $74 for eight ounces. It’s open Sunday through Thursday from 5 to 9 p.m. and Friday and Saturday until 10.
Bar Italia has been pouring since 1983. Its grilled New Zealand lamb chops come with a balsamic glaze and mashed potatoes for $52, and it’s open Tuesday through Sunday from 4:30 to 9 p.m., closed Mondays. At Edera, the pappardelle Bolognese is $29, and the Neapolitan pizzas come blistered from a hot oven. For a menu you don’t have to choose from, drive to Vicia at 4260 Forest Park Ave., where “Let Us Cook For You” brings three family-style courses for $85 a person, Tuesday through Saturday, 5 to 9 p.m., with a validated lot across from the door.
### Is Mainlander Worth Setting a Noon Alarm For?
Yes, if you like your dinner to be an event. Mainlander, at 392 N. Euclid Ave., seats dinner by ticketed appointment, Wednesday through Saturday at 6:00 and 8:30 p.m., and its reservations open at noon on the first of each month for the month after. Supper comes family style, shared down the table, and the cooking blends a mid-century Midwestern supper club with French technique, German comfort food and a distinct Taiwanese flair.
Three things make it different from anywhere else on this list. Mainlander is a tipping and gratuity-free restaurant, with no service charge, ever. It changes its entire menu every month, drink pairings included. And you can bring your own bottle for a $20 corkage fee if you tell them first. Can’t get a ticket? The Jujube Inn bar is a la carte and first come, first served, Wednesday through Saturday from 5:45 p.m. to midnight.
### Good Bars Near the Central West End, From Cocktails to a Pint
For a proper cocktail, Lazy Tiger at 210 N. Euclid pours Tuesday through Thursday from 5 to 10 p.m. and Friday and Saturday until 11. Retreat’s spirit-forward list, built on a beverage program founded by Tim Wiggins, leans on aged spirits and house-made shrubs and syrups. The Tenderloin Room’s bar pours bourbon and whiskey under that stained glass.
For music with your drink, Evangeline’s calls itself a bistro and music house, and its bar runs until midnight on Fridays and Saturdays. Scarlett’s has live music almost every Friday and Saturday and stays open until midnight every day. For a pint and a chair, Dressel’s Public House at 419 N. Euclid keeps a poem by Jon Dressel on its homepage that ends “Where food loves drink, And life and art embrace,” and it’s open Monday through Saturday from noon to 10 p.m. The Scottish Arms at 8 S. Sarah St. is walk-in only and closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

### Where exactly are the CWE restaurants in St. Louis?
Many of the places in this guide sit on North Euclid Avenue: Kingside Diner at 236 N. Euclid, The Noble Crown at the corner of Maryland Plaza and Euclid, Mainlander at 392 N. Euclid and Evangeline’s at 512 N. Euclid. Edera is at 48 Maryland Plaza, while Brasserie by Niche and Scarlett’s sit on Laclede Avenue at 4580 and 4253.
### New on Euclid: The Noble Crown, and What’s Coming Underneath It
The newest big room in the neighborhood is The Noble Crown, which opened June 10 in the former Culpepper’s space at the corner of Maryland Plaza and Euclid, a collaboration between restaurateur Kevin Brennan and the Saint Louis Chess Club. It’s a modern American bistro open seven days a week for lunch and dinner, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 11 on Friday and Saturday, and walk-ins are always welcome.
The part worth watching is downstairs. The restaurant’s site describes the Under Ground Crown as a Mediterranean small-plates room with a dedicated burrata bar, an intimate six-seat chef’s counter and a private dining room set inside the building’s historic boiler room. Check its site for an opening date before you plan around it. Make it a chess day while you’re here: the World Chess Hall of Fame sits at 4652 Maryland Ave.
### Know the Day Before You Go
Bar Italia is closed Mondays. Yellowbelly is closed Sundays and Mondays. The Scottish Arms is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Mainlander seats only Wednesday through Saturday, and Lazy Tiger’s hours start on Tuesday.
Kingside Diner, Bowood by Niche and Scarlett’s are open every day, and The Noble Crown is open seven days a week. Edera serves lunch Monday through Friday and dinner Monday through Saturday. Brasserie by Niche serves dinner Monday through Saturday, and Dressel’s opens at noon on those same days. The Tenderloin Room opens at 5 p.m. every night of the week.
On Sundays the meters are free, Brasserie by Niche serves both brunch and dinner, and Scarlett’s and The Noble Crown keep their regular hours. Just skip Edera, Dressel’s and Yellowbelly, all three closed on Sundays.

### Which Table for Which Night?
A first date with a budget: Cinq à Six at Brasserie by Niche, then a walk up Euclid.
The anniversary: The Tenderloin Room under the stained glass, or a Mainlander ticket bought at noon on the first.
Dinner outside: Edera’s ivy courtyard, or Retreat’s screened sunroom.
Dining alone: Mainlander’s own FAQ answers “Can I dine alone?” with a yes and a party of one.
A big group: Scarlett’s asks groups of 10 or more to call after 11 a.m., and Brasserie adds a 20% gratuity for parties of eight or more.
Coming off a night shift: Kingside’s Third-Shift Happy Hour, weekdays from 6:30 a.m.

## Where to Eat in Webster Groves, MO: A Local's Guide to Old Webster & Old Orchard
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-webster-groves-mo-a-locals-guide
Webster Groves is the kind of St. Louis suburb that makes you slow down. Tree-lined streets, century-old homes, a college campus, and two little walkable business districts — Old Webster and Old Orchard — each packed with independent shops and restaurants where the owner might be the one taking your order. It’s a town that has quietly become one of the metro’s most rewarding places to eat, without ever losing its friendly, family-first feel.
What makes it special is the range. In the span of a few walkable blocks you can get a genuinely world-class Bosnian flatbread, a plate of handmade Italian pasta, a Thai curry, a craft cocktail, and a scoop of something sweet — and lately, a wave of stylish newcomers has landed right beside the longtime favorites. You can browse the famous local bookstore, then eat remarkably well without ever moving your car.
So whether you live in Webster, you’re in for a show at one of its theaters, or you’re just exploring, here’s where to eat — district by district.
📌 Eating your way through Webster? Keep this — and share it.
Bookmark this guide and send it to whoever you’re meeting — the friend you’re browsing the bookstore with, the family deciding on dinner, the group that always ends up at the same spot.
Every share helps one more person discover how well this little town eats. That’s the idea.
### Old Webster: Dining Along Lockwood
The heart of Webster Groves is Old Webster, the walkable stretch around Lockwood Avenue. Its anchor is Olive + Oak ($$–$$$), the polished modern-American room where locals go for oysters, the celebrated O+O burger, and a special-occasion dinner. Next door, its newer sibling Perennial on Lockwood ($$) is an easygoing brewpub — get the pretzel monkey bread and a house beer. For a stylish Italian night, Madrina ($$–$$$) does midcentury Italian-American with handmade pastas and a lively aperitivo hour.
Round out Lockwood with Cyrano’s Cafe ($$), the beloved dessert-and-wine spot famous for its caramel brioche bread pudding; Dewey’s Pizza ($$), the reliable wood-fired family favorite; and Llywelyn’s Pub ($$), a Welsh pub for a burger and a Scotch ale. It’s a district built for wandering — and a good excuse to browse the neighborhood bookshops between courses.
### Old Orchard: Dining Along Big Bend
Webster’s second walkable district, Old Orchard, clusters around Big Bend, and it might be the more exciting of the two right now. Its crown jewel is Balkan Treat Box ($$), a nationally praised Bosnian and Turkish spot turning out wood-oven pide (boat-shaped flatbread) and ćevapi that you genuinely can’t find done this well anywhere else in the region — expect a line, and be glad for it. Nearby, Big Sky Cafe ($$–$$$) has been a New American neighborhood favorite for years, and The Frisco Barroom ($$) does rustic American with scratch breads and a rooftop deck.
For flavor from farther afield, MeYou ($$) turns out excellent Thai — the khao soi and pad see ew have a devoted following; we walk the whole menu in our MeYou guide — and the relocated DD Mau ($–$$) does modern Vietnamese fast-casual with roti-shell tacos and bánh mì. It’s a compact district that eats far bigger than its size.
### Webster’s New Wave
A genuine fresh wave has landed in Webster over the last couple of years. The standout is Off Elm ($$–$$$), a stylish craft-cocktail bar with seasonal drinks and raw-bar snacks that opened in late 2024 and instantly became the neighborhood’s go-to for a grown-up night out. Add the relocated and expanded DD Mau, the midcentury-cool Madrina, and the Perennial on Lockwood brewpub, and you’ve got four genuinely new reasons to eat in Webster — all opened since 2023. It’s proof that a historic family suburb can still surprise you.
### An Only-in-Webster Meal
If you do one thing on this list, make it Balkan Treat Box. What started as a food truck became one of the most acclaimed restaurants in the entire St. Louis region, earning national attention for its wood-fired Bosnian and Turkish cooking. The pide comes out blistered and bubbling from the oven, the ćevapi (little grilled sausages) arrive with warm somun bread and ajvar, and the whole thing tastes like nothing else in town. It’s the rare neighborhood spot that food lovers drive across the metro for — and the single best argument for putting Webster Groves on your dining map.
### Just West: Rock Hill
Webster’s dining scene spills right into neighboring Rock Hill, a short drive west on Manchester. The big draw is Katie’s Pizza & Pasta Osteria ($$–$$$), a wildly popular wood-fired Italian spot known for its seasonal pizzas — think fig or dandelion greens — and wild-boar pasta. For a more old-school St. Louis-Italian experience, Farotto’s ($$) is the neighborhood classic, famous for its meatball sandwich on garlic-cheese bread. Both are close enough to fold right into a Webster food day — a short hop west on Manchester and you’ve doubled your options without really leaving the neighborhood. Locals treat Rock Hill and Webster as one continuous dining zone, and you should too.
Unrelated, and we know it — Highland, IL businesses have their own visibility playbook.
### Great for Families
Webster is a family town through and through, and plenty of its tables are built for exactly that. Dewey’s Pizza is the everyone-agrees pizza night, DD Mau keeps kids happy with fast-casual Vietnamese, Big Sky Cafe handles a family dinner with a little polish, and Farotto’s over in Rock Hill is a longtime kid-friendly favorite. Even Balkan Treat Box, for all its acclaim, is a genuinely welcoming, casual counter-service spot. In Webster, eating well and bringing the whole family are rarely at odds.
### Coffee, Sweets, and the Bookstores
Eating in Webster isn’t only about sit-down meals — it’s about the stroll between them. Both Old Webster and Old Orchard are made for grazing: a coffee and a pastry to start, a scoop of something sweet later, and Cyrano’s legendary desserts whenever the mood strikes. And no Webster afternoon is complete without ducking into the neighborhood’s beloved independent bookstores, which sit right among the restaurants and the rest of the local shops and businesses in Webster Groves. The natural rhythm here is browse, snack, browse some more, then settle in for a real meal — the kind of unhurried afternoon that makes people fall in love with this town in the first place. Bring a tote bag and an appetite, and let the day wander.
### Catch a Show, Then Dinner
Webster Groves has a genuinely deep arts scene, and pairing a performance with a meal is one of the best ways to experience the town. Home to Webster University’s acclaimed conservatory and a hub for local theater and music, the community keeps a busy cultural calendar year-round. That makes for an easy, elevated night out: an early dinner at Olive + Oak or Madrina, a show nearby, and a nightcap at Off Elm to close it out — all within a walkable few blocks. If you’re coming into Webster for a performance, build in time to eat well before or after; the district is designed for exactly that kind of evening, and the restaurants are used to the pre-show rush.
### How to Plan a Webster Food Day
A little strategy makes a Webster food day even better. Pick a district to anchor your visit — Old Webster (Lockwood) leans toward sit-down dinners and bookshops, while Old Orchard (Big Bend) skews a bit more casual and buzzy, with Balkan Treat Box as the must-do. Parking in both is a mix of free lots and street spaces, easy on a weekday and busier on weekend evenings, so arrive a little early if you’re aiming for a popular room. Best of all, once you’re parked in either district, everything is walkable, so you can browse, snack, and dine without moving the car. If you want to see both districts in one visit, they’re a short drive apart — and easily worth the hop for a town that punches this far above its size at the table.
### The Best Table for the Occasion
To match the room to the night: for a date night, Madrina, Olive + Oak, Off Elm, and Big Sky Cafe set the tone. For a family dinner, Dewey’s, DD Mau, and Farotto’s keep everyone happy. For a genuinely memorable, only-here meal, it’s Balkan Treat Box. And for drinks and a grown-up night out, Off Elm, Perennial on Lockwood, and The Frisco Barroom’s rooftop are the moves. Webster makes it easy to find the right table, whatever the occasion.
### A Little About Webster Groves
A bit of context on why Webster feels the way it does. One of St. Louis’s oldest and most established suburbs, it’s known for tree-lined streets, historic homes, excellent schools, and a genuinely deep arts scene — home to Webster University and its acclaimed conservatory, plus longstanding cultural anchors. Its two walkable districts, Old Webster and Old Orchard, grew up around the old rail lines and kept their small-town, storefront character, which is exactly why they’re such a pleasure to eat and stroll through today. For visitors, the formula is simple: pick a district, park once, and wander — ideally with a stop at the neighborhood’s famous bookstores worked in between meals.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is Webster Groves known for?
A.  Webster Groves is known as one of St. Louis’s oldest, most charming suburbs — tree-lined streets, historic homes, excellent schools, and a strong arts scene anchored by Webster University. Its two walkable districts, Old Webster and Old Orchard, are full of independent shops, bookstores, and a growing roster of well-regarded restaurants.
### Q. What is there to do in Webster Groves?
A.  Beyond dining, Webster Groves offers walkable shopping in Old Webster and Old Orchard, live theater and arts through Webster University and local companies, historic architecture, and neighborhood parks. It’s an easy, pleasant place to spend an afternoon browsing bookstores and boutiques before a good meal.
### Q. What are the best restaurants in Old Webster?
A.  Along Lockwood Avenue in Old Webster, the standouts are Olive + Oak (modern American), Madrina (Italian), the Perennial on Lockwood brewpub, Cyrano’s Cafe (desserts and wine), Dewey’s Pizza, and Llywelyn’s Pub. It’s a compact, walkable strip, so it’s easy to browse a few before deciding.
### Q. What is the best new restaurant in Webster Groves?
A.  Off Elm, a stylish craft-cocktail bar with raw-bar snacks that opened in late 2024, is the buzziest recent arrival. It joins other newcomers like the relocated DD Mau (Vietnamese), Madrina (Italian), and the Perennial on Lockwood brewpub — four fresh reasons to eat in Webster, all since 2023.
### Q. Where can I get the best unique meal in Webster Groves?
A.  Balkan Treat Box, in the Old Orchard district, is the region’s most acclaimed only-here meal — nationally praised Bosnian and Turkish cooking with wood-oven pide and ćevapi. It started as a food truck and became a destination that food lovers drive across the metro to try. Expect a line at peak times, and know that it’s well worth the wait — there’s truly nothing else quite like it in the St. Louis area.

## Chesterfield, MO Restaurants: Dinner Where the Valley Once Went Under Water
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-chesterfield-mo-a-locals-guide
Every lobster roll at Stoney River’s Sunday brunch and every whiskey poured at Westchester lands on ground that was under water the morning after the levee broke. Both restaurants say so on their own sites: they’re in the Chesterfield Valley.
“I thought there was a tsunami coming.” That’s how Michael Herring described the night of July 30, 1993, to St. Louis Public Radio. He had been out with the sandbagging crews when the levee broke, and on the drive back to city hall he kept checking his rearview mirror at an intersection, waiting for the water. The next morning he rode a helicopter over the valley. “The valley was now under water,” he said.
Volunteers came from across the nation to help clean it up. That November, Mayor Jack Leonard told the Associated Press, “They saved the valley. They turned our desolation into optimism.” Today the levee is taller and wider, backed by pumps that can move 20,000 gallons of floodwater a minute, and the outlet mall that sat against it is now The District, where The Factory books concerts and teams shout answers in Game Show Battle Rooms.
Now the valley is noise and traffic again. At Westchester you can hear the pans in the open kitchen from your seat, and at Stoney River’s Sunday brunch the lobster roll lands next to an $8 brunch cocktail.
Chesterfield’s best tables also run on things a map app won’t tell you. A hospital cafe opens again at 1 a.m. A steakhouse welcomes your ball cap only at its first-floor bar. A butcher counter still works inside a market that opened in 1937 as the Chesterfield Mercantile. And the roads around the old mall may not match your phone. So this guide sorts Chesterfield, MO restaurants by where you’re standing when you get hungry. Every hour, price and address below was checked against the restaurant’s own website or menu; where we couldn’t confirm something, we left it out.
### Nice Restaurants in Chesterfield, MO, for the Night That Has to Go Right
Start at Annie Gunn’s with the potato pancake: peppered, pecan-wood smoked bacon draped over crisp Yukon Gold, house-made pear chutney sweet against the salt, $14. Then a cup of what the menu calls Annie Gunn’s Incredibly Famous Potato Soup, $7, and an aged filet mignon, $48 for six ounces. Annie Gunn was a real person, the restaurant says, and her hospitality was legendary. For the full show, Chef Lou’s prix fixe is four courses with wine pairings at $300 a person, everyone at the table in, and the menu warns the selections “change nightly, sometimes hourly.”
Come early and walk next door first. Smokehouse Market opened in 1937 as the Chesterfield Mercantile, and the butchers still work a full-service meat counter with freshly baked pies up front. It closes at 6 p.m., so the pie goes in the car before dinner, not after.
At Ruth’s Chris in the Wildhorse village, you hear the steak before you see it. It comes out of an 1,800-degree oven onto a 500-degree plate and is still hissing when it’s set down. The room is one of its franchise group’s most expansive, 15,000 square feet indoors and outdoors, with free valet at the curb. One rule before you dress: the house asks guests not to wear gym wear, bucket hats or baseball hats, and hats and team jerseys are welcome on the first-floor bar only. That makes the bar the most relaxed seat in a dressed-up house.
At Westchester you can watch the line work in the open kitchen from an intimate dining room while the bar pours from a huge selection of hand-picked wines and whiskeys. The place was inspired, its site says, by a couple of cocktails and a desire for seasonal fare “in a sea of chain restaurants,” and Chesterfield native Matthew Glickert cooks a menu that never sits still.
At Paul Manno’s the pasta arrives al dente, boiled in water salted with Sale Rolando salt, under a tomato sauce made only from Poma Rossa San Marzano tomatoes: Italian cooking the way the owner’s grandmother made it. Ask whether Mamma’s Lasagna is on tonight. The menu marks it limited.

## Gumbo, a Flood, a Bordello and a Toy Frog: Cajun and Creole Restaurants in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cajun-and-creole-restaurants-in-st-louis
The rice comes on the side. At Gumbo 2 Geaux in Alton, Illinois, a scoop of white rice sits next to a 16-ounce bowl of chicken-and-sausage gumbo, and you decide how much of it goes in. Steam off the bowl, a spoon, and your call on the rice. That is how the traditional gumbo is served here, as a soup, with the rice on the side.
Troy and Kyndra got to Alton by way of a flood. After the 2016 flood in Baton Rouge they packed up what was left, took a $1,200 FEMA check and moved to Illinois to rebuild their lives. In 2018 they started serving gumbo from their home kitchen. In October 2022 they opened the restaurant at 1808 Washington Ave., (618) 208-7048, which is open Monday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Order the fried gator po’boy, then take the menu’s advice and add the seafood cream sauce, loaded with crab, shrimp and crawfish, for $5. The menu says the sauce is especially good smothered over a po’boy.
One St. Louis boil caterer admits the heat is tuned for us. His standard spice level is “tuned to the St. Louis palate,” and if you want a more authentic Louisiana level you have to ask for increased spice on the crawfish only, because the sides absorb heat fast.
### What are examples of Cajun and Creole food?
The usual list runs gumbo, jambalaya, étouffée, red beans and rice, boudin, po’boys, remoulade and beignets. In the St. Louis area that list reads like a map, and some of the stops are strange. Webster Groves has fresh-fried beignets dusted with powdered sugar, and one topping, Linda’s Special, comes with a honey drizzle and a toy frog. Gumbo comes with the rice on the side in Alton. In the Central West End, Evangeline’s builds its Championship Gumbo on a blonde roux and sells boudin balls. Cajun and Creole overlap on that list more than the labels admit, which is why the tomato test further down matters.
### Two South Broadway buildings with a past
Peel, twist, and the lemon garlic butter is on your fingers: Broadway Oyster Bar serves a bucket of boiled crawfish, a pound and a half of them, for $25.75. The bucket lands in a bar that books live music twice a day every night except Friday. The bar is at 736 S. Broadway, (314) 621-8811, and the kitchen is open every day. The building is from the mid 1840s and has been a family home, a boarding house, a Chinese laundry, a record store and a bordello, and its own history page adds that some people feel it is haunted by spirits who play good-hearted jokes on the staff late at night. Order the alligator sausage and shrimp cheesecake, which the menu itself warns is very addictive, and any po’boy, because they come on Gambino’s bread from New Orleans.
Cotton candy grapes go into the County Fair Sangria at Sister Cities Cajun, and the chicken and sausage jambalaya is made with 100% chicken andouille and no pork. The restaurant, at 3550 S. Broadway, says its building was built in 1887 by Paul Oehler and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It bills itself as country Cajun, and the menu also lists a shrimp remoulade, a sauce that Mississippi River Country’s Cajun-versus-Creole guide says would not typically be found in Cajun kitchens. Plan around the calendar. It is closed on Wednesdays, and Sunday and Monday are counter service.
### The tomato test, and who it is really about
The one-liner you will hear is that Creole is city food and Cajun is country food. Louisiana food writer Jay D. Ducote, in that Mississippi River Country guide, calls that a vastly simplified way to describe the two cuisines, then says the real difference is the people behind them.
Cajun comes from les Acadiens, French colonists from the Acadia region of Canada. The guide says the Acadians were forcibly removed in what became known as Le Grand Dérangement, the Great Upheaval, and that many settled in the swampy region of Louisiana now called Acadiana. Creole describes the people born to settlers in French colonial New Orleans, and the word grew to include native-born enslaved people of African descent and free people of color. The guide says Creole food is a blend of Italian, Spanish, African, German, Caribbean, Native American and Portuguese cooking, and that traditionally enslaved cooks prepared the food in the kitchens of well-to-do families. A history that credits only the French has left out the people at the stove.
The test for the plate is simple. Creole cuisine uses tomatoes and proper Cajun food does not. Sauce piquant is a Cajun exception that does include tomatoes. That is why you find tomatoes in Creole jambalaya and not in Cajun jambalaya, and why a Creole roux is often made with butter and flour while a Cajun roux is made with oil and flour.
You can taste the argument on St. Louis menus. Evangeline’s lists its chicken saucisse jambalaya with Creole tomato. Evangeline’s builds its Championship Gumbo on a classic blonde roux. Gumbo 2 Geaux, which calls its recipes Acadian, builds its traditional gumbo on chicken breast, smoked pork sausage, onion and bell pepper. Sister Cities Cajun says its chef is from well south of New Orleans, which is why the kitchen takes pride in showcasing the differences between Cajun and Creole food.
### Food hall, market stall, jazz room: the rest of the city
A Swamp Thang, Slapp’n Shrimp and N’awlins bread pudding share one menu at 4 Hens Creole Kitchen, in the City Foundry food hall at 3730 Foundry Way. A table of people who cannot agree on dinner can still eat together. Its site also names shrimp and grits. City Foundry says everything is made from scratch, down to the remoulade sauces and the Little Chicks Lemonade. The site lists hours Monday and Wednesday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Under a 1929 Renaissance-style hall, Soulard’s Cajun Corner cooks from stand 2 inside Soulard Market, 730 Carroll St., a market that has been running since 1779. MapQuest’s listing describes the cooking as authentic New Orleans Cajun. The city lists market hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Wednesday through Saturday, and says vendor participation is 10% on Wednesday and Thursday, 35% on Friday and 100% on Saturday. We could not find the stand’s own hours, so Saturday, at 100% vendor participation, is the safest day to go.

### Crawfish, and the St. Louis palate
Cajun Boil Co. cooks crawfish and shrimp boils on site or delivers them fresh, and Stephen Robichaux runs the entire boil. His father is from Thibodaux, Louisiana, and he went to his first crawfish boil before he was a year old. The company says live crawfish run February through June, with shrimp year-round, and LSU AgCenter says Louisiana harvests peak March through May. The company describes an on-site boil as watching the boil happen, smelling the seasoning fill the air and eating straight from the pot. Every boil comes with potatoes, whole garlic, corn, sausage, mushrooms and pineapple. A one-sack boil of about 35 pounds of live crawfish is $600 for fresh-boiled delivery.
Robichaux’s tips are plain. Keep the sides at standard heat and ask for the extra spice on the crawfish only. Pour a portion out onto butcher paper or a newspaper-covered table, let people dig in, then bring out the next batch.
You can also eat a boil without hosting one. Cajun Kitchen’s seafood boil is preorder only, pickup only, with crawfish at $16 a pound and the Full Boil Experience at $41. Evangeline’s says the crawfish for its annual boil festival are flown in from Louisiana that morning. Broadway Oyster Bar keeps a bucket of boiled crawfish on its regular menu. For the full field of boil houses, seafood boils and crawfish across the metro covers them.
Still hungry after the gumbo? Try soul food in St. Louis, the Black-owned restaurants guide, or the whole metro on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you own a spot like these, a boil crew or a beignet stand, the customers typing “gumbo near me” are choosing between the kitchens a guide like this one could check. Put your hours, your menu and your story where those customers look, and the answer is waiting before they have to call. List your restaurant.
### What closed, and what we could not confirm
Gayot lists The Gumbo Shop, 9501 Manchester Rd., as closed. Creole With A Splash Of Soul at 4353 Manchester Ave. has changed hands: St. Louis Magazine’s September openings list has La Crazy Margarita opening at that address on September 2, with Creole With A Splash Of Soul in parentheses.
Gulf Shores’ Edwardsville location at 215 Harvard Drive was set to close Nov. 23, The Intelligencer reported, and the owners planned to reopen the restaurant at 6900 N. Illinois St. in Fairview Heights, in the former TGI Fridays. We could not confirm that it opened, and the company’s own contact page lists the Creve Coeur and St. Peters locations. Shay’s Creole Smokehouse in St. Charles is not on this list because we could not check it against a page of its own.
One distinction keeps these lists honest: a boil caterer is not a restaurant. Cajun Boil Co. is here because it cooks a Louisiana family recipe, though you book it through a request form rather than walking in. If a boil is what you want, the seafood boils guide above has the field.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is New Orleans food Creole or Cajun?
A.  Mostly Creole. The Mississippi River Country guide says Creole describes the people born to settlers in French colonial New Orleans, and that Creole food is a blend of the various cultures of New Orleans. The two styles overlap: Sister Cities Cajun calls itself country Cajun and still lists a shrimp remoulade, a sauce the same guide says would not typically be found in Cajun kitchens.
### Q. Is gumbo considered Creole or Cajun?
A.  Both. Louisiana law names gumbo the official state cuisine, and each tradition makes it its own way. The Mississippi River Country guide says the tomato is how you tell a Cajun gumbo from a Creole one. In St. Louis, Evangeline’s builds its gumbo on a classic blonde roux, while the Alton restaurant serves an Acadian-recipe gumbo with chicken breast and smoked pork sausage.
### Q. Is jambalaya Cajun or Creole?
A.  Both, and the tomato decides again. The guide says you find tomatoes in Creole jambalaya and not in Cajun jambalaya. Evangeline’s lists Creole tomato in its jambalaya, while the Alton restaurant cooks its pork jambalaya with smothered pork roast, smoked pork sausage, onion, bell pepper and celery.
### Q. What is the most famous Cajun dish?
A.  Gumbo is the safest answer, since Louisiana law names it the official state cuisine. Boudin is the other one to know: the guide describes it as a Cajun sausage of pork, rice and seasoning stuffed into a casing. In St. Louis you can find boudin balls at Evangeline’s and Gator’s Louisiana Kitchen.
### Q. What is typical Creole food?
A.  The guide describes Creole cooking as an array of spices from many regions and creamy soups and sauces, with tomatoes and often a butter roux. It says a remoulade of nearly a dozen ingredients would not typically be found in Cajun kitchens. In St. Louis, look for the shrimp remoulade at Evangeline’s and the shrimp and grits at 4 Hens Creole Kitchen.
### Q. Where do the locals eat in St. Louis, MO?
A.  For Louisiana cooking, the rooms people plan nights around include Broadway Oyster Bar, with live music twice a day every night except Friday, Evangeline’s Sunday jazz brunch, and the stalls at Soulard Market, which the city lists at 100% vendor participation on Saturday. For soul food and Black-owned restaurants across the metro, see the guides linked above.
### Q. Which Cajun and Creole restaurants in St. Louis are closed on Mondays?
A.  Cajun Kitchen of St. Louis is closed Sunday and Monday, Beignet All Day is closed Mondays, and Soulard Market is closed on Mondays. Evangeline’s lists hours Wednesday through Sunday and Fresh Catch Cajun Kitchen lists Tuesday through Saturday. Broadway Oyster Bar, Gulf Shores and the Alton restaurant list Monday hours, and Sister Cities is open Monday with counter service.

## Chili or Gravy? A Local's Guide to the Best Breakfast & Brunch in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-breakfast-and-brunch-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
Half a pound of beef, before noon, under a blanket of chile. That’s the Southwest Slinger at Southwest Diner on Southwest Avenue: two quarter-pound burgers, home fries and two eggs under New Mexican chile and longhorn cheese. The kitchen makes its chile red and green, so your first decision of the weekend is how much heat you want with your coffee.
In Kirkwood, under the neon at Spencer’s Grill, the grill’s own website puts the classic order in a regular’s mouth: “I’ll take a #11 and a #12 please!” The #11 is the Slinger: two eggs, your choice of meat, hash browns and toast, all covered in chili, cheese and onions. The #12 is the Slammer, the same plate under house-made gravy. Chili or gravy. A whole city’s breakfast loyalties, sorted by number.
Downtown, Rooster takes the gravy side, with andouille, eggs and potatoes under sausage gravy on thick-cut toast. On Hampton, Courtesy Diner keeps the chili version coming; Explore St. Louis says Courtesy will have a slinger waiting for you 24 hours a day. Its Catherine Neville told Tasting Table the dish is “a full plate of ‘yes’ when you should probably be saying ‘no.’”
That’s the part most brunch lists miss. The best brunch in this city isn’t one restaurant. It’s one dish, built differently at every counter, and a clock that runs out earlier than you think.
### Where is the best brunch in St. Louis?
Start with the slinger, and start early. For the city’s own dish, go to Courtesy Diner on Hampton at any hour, order the #11 at Spencer’s Grill in Kirkwood, or get Southwest Diner’s New Mexican chile version. For brunch with a drink, Rooster downtown and on South Grand pours an award-winning Bloody Mary made with a house blend of 17 secret ingredients, and Egg in Benton Park and Midtown sets its benedicts on corn bread. For a slow morning outdoors, Winslow’s Table in University City has a shaded patio. Of all of those, only Courtesy is still cooking breakfast after 3 p.m.
### Booth #4 and the girl who watched the grill
Spencer’s Grill has stood at 223 South Kirkwood Road since 1947, and Explore St. Louis says its glowing neon sign carries a vintage clock. When current owner Meredith Shadwick was a little girl, her grandpa brought her there on breakfast dates. They sat at the bar or in booth #4 so they could watch the cooks work the grill top. She dreamed of owning the place, and when the chance came, she and her husband jumped at it. So when a short stack lands in front of you, fluffy with crisp edges, you’re eating inside a little girl’s wish that came true.
### The 2 p.m. wall, and the Tuesday trap
Sleep in on a Sunday and you can miss brunch entirely. Rooster serves 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily. Egg’s weekend hours are 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Spencer’s runs 6:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. every day, and Southwest Diner stops at 2 p.m., too. Courtesy is the outlier. It never closes.
Weekdays have their own trap. Southwest Diner is closed Tuesdays. Egg’s posted hours start on Tuesday, with no Monday listed. Downtown, Chris’ @ The Docket opens Wednesday through Monday. On a Tuesday off, go where the sign says every day: Spencer’s, Rooster, Courtesy, or the original Chris’ Pancake & Dining, serving 6:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily.
Now the move that saves you a cold sidewalk. Rooster’s website has a waitlist button for each location, and Chris’ has a Join Waitlist button on its site. Southwest Diner says there isn’t always a wait, but to be safe, join Yelp Waitlist before you arrive, or call 314-260-7244 and they’ll put you on the list. One call, and you finish your first cup at home instead of on the curb.
One more worth texting the group chat. Rooster belongs to the Baileys’ Restaurants family, whose loyalty program gives you 25 points just for signing up and 1 point for every $5 spent at any Baileys’ location. Thirty points takes $5 off. Say your first brunch tab comes to $25: that’s 5 points, plus the 25 for joining, and you’re already at 30.
### Pancakes with a comeback on Kingshighway
The happiest breakfast news on the south side smells like butter and coffee. When Bill Choi retired after 37 years running Uncle Bill’s Pancake House, hundreds of people lined the sidewalk on the final day. The kitchen ran out of food. The doors closed early. Now it’s back at 3427 S. Kingshighway Blvd, and its own site says it plainly: same corner, new griddle, new chapter. Ivan and Berto Garcia bought it and made a commitment to turn the lights back on and do it right: expanded cypress wall paneling, a Germanic cuckoo clock above the register, and the classics back with the pancakes: the thick-cut bacon, the 2X2X2X2 and the Slingshot. Uncle Bill’s has been a St. Louis original since 1961. It doesn’t take reservations, but if you’re bringing a big group, it asks you to call ahead.
The original Chris’ Pancake & Dining has been holding it down since 1987, with hot-off-the-griddle breakfast from 6:30 a.m. every day. Breakfast runs all day, from The Classic Breakfast and golden-brown pancakes to originals like breakfast fried rice. There’s also Chris’ South, plus Chris’ @ The Docket downtown, so there’s usually one within reach of a weekday morning.
### Benedicts, crepes and orange juice squeezed by hand
When the slinger feels like too much, the dressed-up brunch rooms take over. Egg’s Benton Park location sits in the historic Polar Ice building on Gravois near Jefferson, and the menu says its Valencia orange juice is “freshly squeezed by a human!” The benedicts come on corn bread: spinach and avocado, or house-smoked Missouri pork belly, each with two poached eggs and hollandaise. If you want something no diner on this page makes, the Tunisian Breakfast section of Egg’s Benton Park menu has chakchouka, a tomato and bell pepper stew with two eggs cracked on top and baked. Midtown’s Egg is at 3100 Locust.
Rooster calls itself a European-style urban cafe. Its crepes are made from scratch with its own batter, all of its breads are baked in house, and its eggs are farm fresh and cooked to order. It’s the place for a sweet crepe and a savory one, split down the middle of the table.
At Winslow’s Table, you order at the counter, then pick a seat inside or out; there are no reservations. Pastries are baked fresh every morning, the coffee is Sump, and breakfast runs 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily. On a mild morning the shaded patio is the whole point.
### Where can you still get chicken and waffles?
Start back at Uncle Bill’s, where the menu promises crispy chicken, fluffy waffles and syrup worth slowing down for. Up in Ferguson, Elicious Southern Style Breakfast and Brunch calls itself Ferguson’s go-to destination for bold Southern flavors and warm hospitality, and it was built to bring Southern comfort food to the Ferguson community. For more of that cooking, see our guide to soul food in St. Louis.
One stop to cross off older lists: St. Louis Public Radio reported that Grace Meat + Three would close the doors of its Grove location after nine years, with its last day on Sept. 13. If a list still sends you to The Grove for that plate, it’s out of date.
### Cafe mornings from Maplewood to Main Street
Some mornings want a mug and a quiet table more than a mountain of chili. In Maplewood, Living Room Coffee & Kitchen roasts all its own beans and serves breakfast all day off a seasonal, rotating menu. It’s family and queer owned, open 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday, at 2810 Sutton Blvd. On weekends there’s no public wifi, on purpose, to better serve the people actually in the room.
On South Main Street in St. Charles, Frontier Perk Cafe serves Thursday through Monday, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., at 336 South Main Street. Its own site warns that holidays, festivals and nature may affect those hours, so check before a festival weekend.
Across the river at 120 S. Main St in Edwardsville, Illinois, Café Birdie is open every day from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., cooking heartland classics with a West Coast twist. Owner Jenny Levi grew up in Edwardsville and came home after more than 20 years working in West Coast kitchens. And Birdie? She’s the family dog, the canine familiar of Jenny’s daughter and business partner, Hannah.
Side trip for anyone running a shop on Main Street in Edwardsville: here’s how Edwardsville businesses show up in local search.
### Why a St. Louis brunch costs what it does
Read the menus and the price starts to make sense. Spencer’s lists its suppliers: bacon from Behrmann Meats, milk from Rolling Lawns farm, coffee beans from La Cosecha and eggs from a Missouri farm called the Egg Basket. Rooster bakes its breads and makes its crepe batter in house. Egg squeezes its oranges by hand. You’re paying for those hands, and you can taste it in the first bite of real bread.
There are still ways to spend less. Spencer’s advertises free coffee refills, so the second and third cups cost nothing. Rooster’s loyalty program earns you points at any Baileys’ restaurant location. And Egg sells a Mimosa Kit, 16 ounces of fresh-squeezed orange juice plus a bottle of Cava, so you can pour brunch at home on the mornings you don’t want to leave the couch. If home breakfast is the plan, start with what makes a good bagel.
Brunch done by 2 and already thinking about dinner? Pick up where the griddle leaves off with our guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis.
If you run the griddle, the cafe or the brunch room with a Saturday line out the door, this part is for you. A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your menu, hours and photos in front of hungry St. Louis searchers for $357 a year, under a dollar a day, and every photo and post on it can be indexed and cited by AI on its own - see how it brings more customers to your counter.
Whatever you order, order it before the clock in the neon sign tells you it’s too late. Chili or gravy, red or green, crepe or pancake: pick a counter, put your name on the list from the couch, and go eat the dish this city made its own.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where’s the best place to get brunch?
A.  Pick by mood. For a classic St. Louis plate, go to Spencer’s Grill in Kirkwood, open every day from 6:30 a.m. to 2 p.m., or Courtesy Diner on Hampton, which Explore St. Louis says serves a slinger 24 hours a day. For crepes and a Bloody Mary, try Rooster downtown or on South Grand. For benedicts on corn bread, Egg in Benton Park or Midtown. For pastries and a shaded patio, Winslow’s Table in University City.
### Q. Where to get a slinger in St. Louis?
A.  Courtesy Diner on Hampton serves the chili classic around the clock. Spencer’s Grill in Kirkwood calls it the #11, and its gravy-covered #12 is the Slammer. Southwest Diner at 6803 Southwest Avenue makes the Southwest Slinger with two quarter-pound burgers under New Mexican chile and longhorn cheese. Explore St. Louis says Rooster’s version features local andouille and sausage gravy over thick-cut toast, and that Rooster’s two locations also serve a vegan slinger.
### Q. What is a STL slinger?
A.  It’s St. Louis’s signature diner pile-up. At Spencer’s Grill, the #11 Slinger is two eggs, your choice of meat, hash browns and toast all covered in chili, cheese and onions. Explore St. Louis calls the slinger an amalgamation of potato, egg, chili, cheese and protein that is inexplicably linked to St. Louis. Some kitchens swap the chili for gravy or New Mexican chile.
### Q. What place has the best chicken and waffles?
A.  In St. Louis, start at Uncle Bill’s Pancake House at 3427 S. Kingshighway Blvd, whose menu promises crispy chicken, fluffy waffles and syrup worth slowing down for. Uncle Bill’s has been a St. Louis original since 1961 and is back on the same corner. For a Southern-style brunch in North County, Elicious in Ferguson is built around bold Southern flavors.
### Q. Why is brunch so expensive?
A.  Part of the answer is on the menus. Spencer’s Grill buys bacon from Behrmann Meats and milk from Rolling Lawns farm, Rooster bakes its breads in house and makes its crepes from scratch, and Egg squeezes its Valencia oranges by hand. To spend less, join a loyalty program: the Baileys’ Restaurants program that covers Rooster gives you 25 points for signing up, and 30 points takes $5 off. Spencer’s also offers free coffee refills.
### Q. What are some must-eat places in Saint Louis?
A.  For breakfast, start with Courtesy Diner for a slinger at any hour, Spencer’s Grill in Kirkwood for the neon sign and the #11, and Southwest Diner for New Mexican chile and sopapillas, pillowy donuts you eat with honey. For brunch with a cocktail, Rooster and Egg. After breakfast, Explore St. Louis points visitors to The Hill for a toasted ravioli crawl. For dinner ideas, see our guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis.
### Q. What foods is St. Louis known for?
A.  Explore St. Louis’s guide to the city’s emblematic eats covers the slinger, toasted ravioli, St. Louis-style pizza with Provel cheese and gooey butter cake. At breakfast, the slinger is the one to order: an amalgamation of potato, egg, chili, cheese and protein, and Courtesy Diner serves it 24 hours a day.

## Mission Taco Lost Its Name. The Best Mexican Food in St. Louis Is a Soaked Torta on Page Avenue
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-mexican-food-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
Carnitas and onions in a sandwich soaked so deep the bread gives in your hand. A fiery red salsa on one side of the tray, a piquant green one on the other, and sauce already running toward your wrist. That’s the torta ahogada at Taqueria Durango, 10238 Page Ave in Overland, and it’s where this guide starts now that Mission Taco is gone for good.
Here’s the line to send your group chat: the tortilla brand in your grocery cart is the reason Mission Taco had to change its name. In 2023, Gruma Corp., the parent company of Mission Foods, sued over the Mission name; the parties settled, and the restaurant became Session Taco in September 2024. Then on Saturday, Oct. 17, Session Taco closed its last two St. Louis restaurants, in the Delmar Loop, where it opened in 2013, and in Soulard. LaPez Mod Mex in the Central West End, a former Session Taco, closed with them.
It didn’t happen overnight. The group behind it once ran as many as nine restaurants across the St. Louis and Kansas City areas. Its location in the next county over became Sobremesa in June 2026 and closed in September, less than four months after opening. So if your saved taco list still says Mission, delete it, and use this one.
### What is the most popular Mexican restaurant in St. Louis?
The name many people still say first is Mission Taco, and that door is locked. So pick by craving, and screenshot this part: at Malinche, Monday and Tuesday tacos run 3 for $19 or 5 for $27. For the soaked torta and two house salsas, Taqueria Durango on Page Avenue; call 314-429-1113. For street tacos and a cantarito at lunch, Mestiza at 3279 Hampton Ave, open Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 9 p.m. and Sunday until 8. For a sit-down dinner, Malinche at 15939 Manchester Road in Ellisville, Monday through Saturday from 5:30 to 9 p.m., with reservations on its website. For a mezcal you’ve never tasted, Nixta at 5232 Delmar Blvd, Wednesday through Saturday from 5 to 10 p.m. and Sunday from noon to 6. For a birthday table of twelve, The Mexican STL at 9615 Watson Rd in Crestwood; call (314) 525-5025. And for the Cherokee Street classic, La Vallesana at 2801 Cherokee St.; call (314) 776-4223.
### Page Avenue: Two Salsas and a Soaked Sandwich
No host stand, no valet, no hostess with a tablet. Taqueria Durango sits in a plain strip mall set back from Page Avenue at 10238 Page Ave, and the Post-Dispatch’s STL 100 praised the fiery red and piquant green salsas, the earthy, spicy tacos al pastor, and the signature torta ahogada, a sandwich of carnitas and onions soaked through. The bread goes soft. The sauce runs down your wrist. You keep eating anyway.
This is the order for a first visit. Get the torta ahogada, get an al pastor taco to judge the kitchen by, and try both salsas before you decide which one is yours. Ask for extra napkins. Don’t wear a white shirt.
### Hampton Avenue: Street Tacos and a Clay Cup
At Mestiza on Hampton Avenue in Lindenwood Park, you wrap your hand around a cantarito, the tequila drink named for its clay cup, and it’s cold all the way through. Then the birria fundida lands, rich and steaming, and you reach for a tostada before it cools. Mestiza calls itself a place for street tacos, bright cantaritos and easy charm. Its own site names the four orders that matter: Del Trompo, Birria Fundida, Casi Alucinógenos and churros.
Start with the guacamole, which comes with chicharrónes and tostadas, so you get the crunch and the cool in one bite. Save the churros for last. Mestiza is at 3279 Hampton Ave and opens Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 9 p.m. and Sunday from noon to 8 p.m. That makes it the easy weekend lunch pick, the place you go when someone says “tacos?” at 1 in the afternoon and nobody has a reservation.
### Ellisville: The Dinner Worth the Drive West
A corn flat pressed by hand, pastor negro, pineapple and cucumber on top, set down in the middle of the table for everyone to reach for. That’s the Del Trompo at Malinche, $16 on the menu, and it’s the plate to order first. Malinche is at 15939 Manchester Road in Ellisville, and it serves Monday through Saturday from 5:30 to 9 p.m.
Read the menu slowly, because the good stuff is in the descriptions. The Birria Fundida ($19) is steamed lamb with quesadillas doradas and a spicy birria consommé for dipping. The Mole Ozumbeño ($19) is built on a pile of dried chiles and chocolate, over rice and chicken. The guacamole with chicharrones and tostadas is $11. Go on a Monday or Tuesday and the taco deal runs 3 for $19 or 5 for $27, which is the cheapest way to taste half the kitchen in one sitting. Finish with the churros at $8. Come hungry.
Got a friend still planning a Mission Taco night?
Text them before they drive to the Loop: the last Session Taco closed Saturday, Oct. 17, and the name change came from a lawsuit by the company behind Mission tortillas. Then send them this page so dinner still happens.
### Delmar: A Library of Mezcal
The first sip of a good mezcal tastes like smoke you can drink, and it warms you all the way down. Nixta calls itself a library Mecca for mezcal and tequila drinkers, with both extensive and rare selections, and pairs them with contemporary chef-driven food. It now lives in the Maker’s Locale in the Delmar Maker District at 5232 Delmar Blvd, not far from the Loop where Session Taco just went dark.
The room has two bars. One is the cocktail bar with the live-edge wooden bar top carried over from the old location. The other is Bar Limón, a five-seat seafood bar in the middle of the room, where St. Louis Magazine counted four ceviches and five aguachiles, including an aguachile negro made with octopus. Inside seats 65, and the patio and green space out back hold at least that many again. Nixta opens Wednesday through Saturday from 5 to 10 p.m. and Sunday from noon to 6 p.m. Take a seat at Bar Limón, order the octopus, and ask the bartender to pour you something you can’t find anywhere else.
### Crestwood: Big Room, Big Group
Where Crestwood Mall used to stand, there’s now a Mexican restaurant built for the birthday table of twelve. The Mexican STL opened at Crestwood Commons, the redeveloped site of the former Crestwood Mall, with seating for 370 guests inside and out. On a warm night, four hangar doors fold up into the ceiling and the dining room opens straight onto the patio air.
The bar carries 40-50 tequilas. The cocktail list has six margaritas at $14-$16. There’s a small party room for 14 if your group wants its own door. It sits at 9615 Watson Rd, and you can call (314) 525-5025 to book. This is the room for the family dinner where Grandma wants a real table and the cousins want a loud one.
Off the taco trail for one second: Ballwin businesses, start here.
### A Quick Word on Cherokee Street
No honest Mexican-food conversation in St. Louis skips Cherokee Street. La Vallesana at 2801 Cherokee St. is the place to start if you’ve never walked that stretch. Cherokee already has its own full guide, so we’ll point you there for the deep dive and keep the spotlight here on the rest of the metro.
### Three More for the List
A few more names to keep in your phone. Up on Midland Boulevard, King Burrito sits at 11084 Midland Blvd, and you can call 314-427-5580 to ask what’s good before you drive. In Soulard, a few blocks from where Session Taco just closed, Chava’s at 925 Geyer Ave is a lively spot known for classic Mexican dishes and a long run of margaritas. And across the river, Rio Grande MX Cocina in Fairview Heights is the name to look up on the Illinois side. Before your first trip to the Page Avenue counter or the Ellisville dining room, read what regulars say about Taqueria Durango and Malinche, then go hungry.
### Why Your Saved Taco List Is Probably Wrong
If smoke is more your speed than salsa, here is a St. Louis BBQ sauce recipe and what makes the style different.
This is the month to stop trusting any list you bookmarked. The Tilford Restaurant Group, owned by brothers Adam and Jason Tilford, closed more locations in late 2025 and early 2026 before the final Session Taco doors shut on Oct. 17. Restaurants change faster than the lists that rank them. Before you drive anywhere a list sends you, open the restaurant’s own website and check the hours. It takes ten seconds, and it saves you the long walk back to a cold car. A restaurant’s own page is the one place that changes the day the doors do, so make it the last thing you check before you grab your keys.
Hungry for tacos near you, from a kitchen that’s still open? Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Mexican restaurants, taco counters and panaderías across the metro, and check hours before you drive out.

### How to Eat Like a Regular
Order the house specialty first and judge a place by it: the torta ahogada on Page, the Del Trompo in Ellisville, the octopus aguachile on Delmar. Ask which salsas they make in-house and try every one. Sit at the bar when the room is full, because the bartender knows what’s good tonight. And when a kitchen earns your loyalty, go back often and tell your friends. This month is the reminder: the places you love only stay open if people keep walking in. Pick one room from this page, go this week, order the dish it is known for, and bring someone who has never been there before. Then do it again next month with a different room, until the whole list feels like your own neighborhood and every counter knows your face.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What makes Tex-Mex different than Mexican food?
A.  Tex-Mex is the Texas-born, American take: flour tortillas, yellow cheese, ground beef and big combo platters. Regional Mexican cooking leans on corn tortillas, fresh chiles, slow-cooked meats and sauces like mole. St. Louis has plenty of both, and the rooms in this guide lean regional.
### Q. What’s the best Mexican restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  There isn’t one winner, there’s a best room for each craving. Taqueria Durango on Page Avenue for the torta ahogada and two house salsas. Mestiza on Hampton for street tacos and cantaritos. Malinche in Ellisville for a sit-down dinner. Nixta on Delmar for mezcal and aguachile. La Vallesana for the Cherokee Street classic.
### Q. What is the most popular Mexican restaurant?
A.  Popular and best are not the same thing. In St. Louis, the name many people still say first is Mission Taco, and it’s gone: Session Taco, its renamed successor, closed its last St. Louis locations on Saturday, Oct. 17. The independent rooms in this guide are where to go instead.
### Q. What is the name of the new Mexican restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  The one drawing the most attention is The Mexican STL, at 9615 Watson Rd in Crestwood, on the old Crestwood Mall site, with seating for 370 guests inside and out. New spots open and close often around here, so check hours before you make the drive.
### Q. What is not authentic Mexican food?
A.  Most of what Americans picture first: hard-shell tacos, ground-beef burritos under yellow cheese and nachos with liquid cheese. For the real thing in St. Louis, look for corn tortillas, al pastor, birria, mole and tortas at the restaurants in this guide.

## Best Sushi & Japanese Food in St Louis: A Local's Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-sushi-and-japanese-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
Something quietly remarkable has happened to Japanese food in St. Louis over the last few years: the ramen got serious. Not the packet-and-a-microwave kind — the real thing, tonkotsu broth simmered for the better part of a day until it turns silky, poured over noodles made to order. A handful of obsessive cooks turned this into a genuine ramen town, and the sushi scene grew up right alongside it.
So if your mental map of St. Louis sushi stops at the strip-mall spot near your house, it’s time to redraw it. There’s a chef-driven izakaya in Maplewood, a conveyor-belt sushi bar with robot servers out in St. Charles, six locations of a beloved local sushi chain, and destination ramen counters where people happily wait in line on a Tuesday. This is a scene with real range — from a $9 bowl of noodles to an omakase splurge.
This guide spreads across the whole metro — South City, Maplewood, University City, West County, St. Charles, and the Metro East — so wherever you are, there’s a great bowl or a fresh roll within reach. Grab your chopsticks.

### The Ramen Renaissance
Start here, because this is what changed everything. Nudo House ($$), from the Mai Lee family (chef Qui Tran and Marie-Anne Velasco), is the gateway drug — a Vietnamese-Japanese mashup doing rich tonkotsu ramen and killer banh mi, with locations in Creve Coeur and the Delmar Loop. For the purist’s bowl, Menya Rui ($$) in the Southampton neighborhood is the one ramen obsessives drive across town for — chef Steven Pursley trained seriously, and the tonkotsu and shoyu bowls show it. Down in Oakville, Ichiro Ramen Bar ($$) gives South County its own steaming, comforting bowl. These rooms proved St. Louis would line up for real ramen — and the whole Japanese scene leveled up because of it.
### Where to Eat Sushi Right Now
For sushi with personality, a few spots lead the pack. On South Grand, Cafe Mochi ($$) is a longtime favorite for creative maki — the Volcano roll is a rite of passage — in one of the city’s most walkable international dining strips. In Webster Groves, Sushi Station ($$) keeps regulars happy with dependable rolls and a friendly room. And for a modern, chef-driven experience, Robata ($$$) in Maplewood is the standout — an izakaya where the sushi shares the menu with a live robata grill (more on that below). Whether you want an inventive roll or clean, simple nigiri, the metro delivers.
Totally unrelated, and worth a click — local search in O’Fallon, Illinois.
### Izakaya & Japanese Beyond Sushi
Sushi is only part of the story. An izakaya — a Japanese pub built for sharing small plates over drinks — is one of the best ways to eat, and Robata in Maplewood is the metro’s flagship, with a robata (charcoal grill) turning out skewers of chicken, vegetables, and seafood alongside sushi and sake. It’s the spot for a long, grazing dinner with friends. Look also for donburi (rice bowls), katsu (panko-fried cutlets), gyoza (dumplings), and takoyaki (octopus fritters) popping up on menus around town. The point: order a spread of small plates, share everything, and you’ll eat far better than sticking to a single roll.
### The Suburbs: Wasabi & West County
Out in the county, the anchor is Wasabi Sushi Bar ($$), a homegrown local chain with roughly half a dozen locations — Kirkwood, Town & Country, Rock Hill, and more — making it the reliable, close-to-home sushi option for a huge swath of the metro. It’s consistent, family-friendly, and does a solid creative-roll menu. In Chesterfield, Ninja Japanese Steakhouse ($$) pairs a full sushi bar with the theatrics of hibachi (teppanyaki) — the knife-flipping, onion-volcano show that’s a hit with kids and groups. West County isn’t a sushi desert; it’s quietly well-covered.
### St. Charles & the Novelty Factor
Across the Missouri River, St. Charles County brings some genuine fun to the table. Sushi Boat ($$) in St. Charles is a conveyor-belt (kaiten) sushi spot where plates circle the room — and it’s leaned into the gimmick with robot servers gliding food to your table, making it a favorite for families and first dates alike. For a more traditional sit-down experience, Sushi Ai ($$) has built a loyal St. Charles County following with fresh fish and generous rolls. If you’ve got kids who are sushi-curious, the conveyor belt is a low-stakes, high-delight way to get them hooked.
### The Central West End: Rolls & Cocktails
For a night out with a scene, the Central West End has long been sushi-and-cocktails territory. Drunken Fish ($$$) does big, creative rolls and a lively bar in the CWE and at Westport — a reliable group spot, if not the purist’s pick. Nearby, Sushi Koi ($$) draws a following for chef-driven rolls, and the veteran Kampai ($$) has been slinging sushi in the neighborhood since the 1980s. This is the lane for a date night: order a couple of showy rolls, get a cocktail, and enjoy the buzz of one of the city’s liveliest dining districts.
### The Metro East
The Illinois side has its own steady options, so eastsiders don’t need to cross the river for a fix. In Edwardsville, Wasabi Edwardsville ($$) brings the same crowd-pleasing sushi-bar formula to the Metro East, and a handful of pan-Asian rooms around O’Fallon and Belleville round out the rolls-and-ramen options. It’s not the deepest scene in the metro, but for a weeknight sushi craving on the east side, it more than does the job.
### What St. Louis Sushi Does Best
Every sushi town has its signature, and St. Louis leans hard into the creative Americanized roll — the tempura-crunch, spicy-mayo, eel-sauce maki that locals love. Cafe Mochi’s Volcano and Wasabi’s specialty rolls are prime examples, and yes, you’ll find a “St. Louis roll” on plenty of menus (typically a fried, cream-cheese-forward roll that nods to the city’s love of Provel and rich flavors). If you prefer the pristine, traditional side — clean nigiri and sashimi that let the fish speak — the chef-driven rooms like Robata and Menya Rui’s neighbors deliver. And thanks to the ramen boom, tonkotsu ramen now belongs on this list of local strengths too. Range is the whole point.
### How to Order Like a Regular
A few tips to eat well. If you’re new to raw fish, start with a cooked or tempura roll and work your way toward nigiri and sashimi — there’s no shame in easing in. At a good sushi bar, sit at the counter and ask the chef what’s freshest; omakase (“chef’s choice”) is the move if you trust the kitchen. For ramen, eat it fast — the noodles keep cooking in the hot broth, and a bowl is best in its first ten minutes. Use the pickled ginger to cleanse your palate between pieces, not as a topping, and go easy on the soy sauce so you taste the rice and fish. And at the conveyor-belt spots, keep your stack of plates — that’s how they tally the bill.
### Sushi on a Budget — and the Splurge
One of the best things about the metro’s Japanese scene is how it stretches across price points. On the budget end, a bowl of ramen at Nudo House or Ichiro runs well under $15 and eats like a full meal, and the conveyor belt at Sushi Boat lets you graze plate by cheap plate — a great trick for feeding kids or sampling widely without committing to a big order. Lunch specials at Wasabi and Cafe Mochi are another quiet bargain, pairing a roll or two with soup and salad for not much money. At the splurge end, a chef-driven dinner at Robata — sushi, robata skewers, and sake shared across a table — is a genuine occasion, and asking for omakase at a good bar puts your meal in the chef’s hands for a memorable (if pricier) experience. The point: you can eat Japanese food here on a weeknight budget or make a real event of it, and both ends of that range are well served.
### Great for Groups, Dates & Families
Japanese food happens to be some of the most social eating around, and the metro has a room for every occasion. For a group, an izakaya like Robata — built for sharing small plates over drinks — or a hibachi table at Ninja, where the chef performs right in front of you, keeps everyone entertained. For a date, the Central West End’s sushi-and-cocktails spots bring the buzz, or a quiet counter seat at a good sushi bar lets you talk over beautiful nigiri. And for families, the conveyor belt and robot servers at Sushi Boat turn dinner into a low-stakes adventure that even picky kids get a kick out of. Match the room to the occasion and Japanese food rarely disappoints.
### A Note on What’s Closed
Raw fish in this town does not stop at the sushi counter — here is what to know about poke bowls in St. Louis.
One honest update for anyone chasing an old favorite: a few well-known names have changed. Nippon Tei, the longtime upscale Japanese spot, has given way to a successor concept, Sado, on The Hill — worth knowing if you go looking for the old room. Tani Sushi Bistro in Clayton and BaiKu in the Central West End have also closed. It’s a reminder that even beloved restaurants come and go — so when a sushi bar or ramen counter earns your loyalty, go often and bring friends. That’s how the good ones stay open.
