### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How to eat Ethiopian food for beginners?
A.  Wash your hands, then eat with your right hand only — no utensils needed. Tear off a small piece of the injera flatbread, use it to pinch and scoop up a bite of stew or meat, and pop the whole thing in your mouth. Meals are shared from one communal platter, so start from the section closest to you. If you’d rather use a fork, just ask — every St. Louis Ethiopian spot will happily provide one.
### Q. What is the most popular Ethiopian dish?
A.  Doro wat is widely considered Ethiopia’s national dish and its most iconic — a rich, spicy chicken stew slow-cooked with caramelized onions and the berbere spice blend, traditionally served with a hard-boiled egg. Other favorites include tibs (sautéed beef or lamb), kitfo (spiced minced beef), and shiro (a creamy chickpea puree). For a taste of everything, order a beyaynetu combo platter.
### Q. Is Ethiopian food healthy?
A.  Generally, yes. Ethiopian cuisine is built around lentils, split peas, vegetables, and lean stews, with injera made from nutrient-dense teff. The many vegetarian and vegan dishes (thanks to the Orthodox fasting tradition) are naturally high in fiber and plant protein and low in processed ingredients. Some meat stews and spiced butter add richness, but a veggie-forward Ethiopian meal is a genuinely wholesome, balanced choice.
### Q. Which hand do you eat Ethiopian food with?
A.  Traditionally, you eat Ethiopian food with your right hand only — the left is considered unclean for eating. You tear injera with your right hand and use it to scoop the stews. It’s also customary to wash your hands before and after the meal, since everyone eats by hand from a shared platter. If this feels unfamiliar, don’t stress — restaurants are welcoming and a fork is always available.
### Q. How is Ethiopian food traditionally eaten?
A.  Ethiopian food is traditionally eaten communally — a single large platter lined with injera and topped with several stews is placed in the middle of the table, and everyone shares it by hand, no individual plates. A gesture called gursha, hand-feeding a bite to a companion, is a sign of friendship and respect. The shared, hands-on style is central to the culture: Ethiopian food is meant to be eaten together, not alone.

## Seven Pounds of Crawfish for One Pound of Meat: Where to Get a Seafood Boil in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/seafood-boils-and-crawfish-st-louis
Mostly shell. That’s the bucket in front of you at Broadway Oyster Bar on South Broadway: a pound and a half of spicy boiled crawfish with lemon garlic butter, a band playing somewhere behind you, and juice running down your wrist as you twist the first tail loose. Pinch, pull, reach for the next one.
About 15 percent of a medium crawfish’s body weight is tail meat, according to LSU AgCenter and Sea Grant agent Mark Shirley. It takes about 7 pounds of medium crawfish to make 1 pound of meat, and about 8 pounds of big ones, because of their big claws and heavier shells. Bigger isn’t better.
That math runs the whole seafood boil scene in St. Louis. At Hook & Reel on Chippewa Street, the seafood is listed as MP, market price, every boil has a 1-pound minimum, and the printed menu adds an 18% service charge for parties of six or more. So order like you’re buying shells, ask for medium crawfish when you can, and read the bottom of the menu before a table of six writes in a second tip.
Timing matters too. Louisiana’s wild crawfish season generally runs from mid-January through early July and peaks in March, April and May, according to the crawfish guide We Love Crawfish. Below are the boil houses and crawfish counters we could confirm from their own websites and menus, with hours and phone numbers. Places that show up on older roundups but that we couldn’t confirm are left out, so call before you drive across the river for one.
Six or more? Call ahead and ask whether a service charge is added. Hook & Reel’s is 18%.
Order a pound per adult, then add sides. A pound is the minimum per boil at Hook & Reel and Crafty Crab.
Pick your heat one level below your pride. The sauce coats everything in the bag.
In spring, ask for medium crawfish. More meat for the weight.
Wear something washable. Shells spray when they crack.
### Where can you get a seafood boil in St. Louis?
Start with Hook & Reel on Chippewa Street or Crab’s Landing on North Tucker Boulevard. Broadway Oyster Bar serves a bucket of boiled crawfish on South Broadway, and Peacemaker Lobster & Crab in Benton Park puts andouille and a biscuit in its boils. North and west, La Juicy Seafood has kitchens on West Florissant Avenue and in O’Fallon, and on the Illinois side, Crafty Crab is in Fairview Heights.
Hook & Reel Cajun Seafood & Bar, 4680 Chippewa St. This is the build-your-own boil at full volume. You pick your catch by the half pound or pound, then one of seven sauces, from Plain to the house Special Blend, which the menu calls its most requested, then Mild, Spicy or Fire. The Garlic Butter is “a creamy buttery sauce with a garlic punch.” Lemon Pepper is “a citrus sauce with an infusion of peppercorns.” Or go Dry, an Old Bay-only rub of sweet paprika, cloves, cardamom and dry mustard, and your fingers smell like a spice drawer on the drive home. Dine-in hours are 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Call (314) 282-0770.
Crab’s Landing, 701 N. Tucker Blvd. A boil house built around combos. Its online ordering menu leads with them: snow crab and shrimp; shrimp, snow crab and sausage; shrimp, snow crab and black mussels; and a lobster combo. Snap a snow crab cluster at the joint and the steam comes out with the meat. If someone in your group would rather not crack anything, there are fried shrimp, catfish and chicken tender baskets, plus hush puppies for whoever’s waiting on the crab to cool. Online ordering opens at 11 a.m.
Broadway Oyster Bar, 736 S. Broadway. The New Orleans room from the top of this page. That bucket of boiled crawfish is $25.75, and the kitchen keeps going with Crawfish Enchiladas, which the restaurant promises are always on the regular menu, even during its food festivals. It lists Louisiana crawfish and shrimp among its seafood. There’s live music twice a day every night except Friday, when one act plays the evening, so you’re peeling tails to a band. Call 314-621-8811.
Peacemaker Lobster & Crab, 1831 Sidney St., Benton Park. A different kind of boil. Chef Kevin Nashan’s kitchen draws on the Acadians of the Northeast and Gulf coasts, and every lobster or shrimp boil comes with potatoes, corn, andouille and a biscuit. The raw bar is built around a 130-year-old stone oyster trough, and the restaurant says its catch is flown in daily. Tear the biscuit and drag it through whatever’s left in the bowl. Crawfish shows up here as a buffalo crawfish poorboy. Call 314.772.8858.
La Juicy Seafood, 10732 W. Florissant Ave. and 373 Winding Woods Dr., O’Fallon. Louisiana-style Cajun boils, from crawfish to Dungeness crab, and a house rule printed on its own site: prepare to eat “the Louisiana way, with your hands.” Roll your sleeves up before the bag opens. The West Florissant kitchen is open daily from noon to 10 p.m. (314-942-6668). O’Fallon runs noon to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and noon to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday (636-294-9171).
Crafty Crab, 51 Ludwig Dr., Fairview Heights, Ill. The Metro East pick. Its online menu walks you through three steps: your catch, then your seasoning (Crafty Cajun, butter garlic, lemon pepper or “the boom!!!,” all three mixed), then your heat, from mild to “fire (my mouth on fire).” Order the boom and you get garlic butter, lemon pepper and Cajun heat in the same bite. Each pound comes with potatoes and corn on the cob, with a 1-pound minimum, and it sells crawfish by the pound. The Fairview Heights Crafty Crab is open noon to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and noon to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Call (618) 489-1153.
### Where the butter came from: the Viet-Cajun boil
The bag-and-butter boil isn’t straight Louisiana. Texas Highways magazine traces Viet-Cajun crawfish to Houston, a style that combines Cajun spices with Southeast Asian flavors. After the fall of Saigon in 1975, many Vietnamese refugees settled along the Gulf Coast to work in the seafood industry. Houston restaurants were serving the style by the early 2000s, and it took off after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 sent an influx of Louisiana-based Vietnamese to Houston.
The magazine’s scene would look familiar here: a crowd digging into plastic bags “dusky with seasoning.” A festival organizer it quoted, Tinh Trinh, explained the difference in one line about the finish, more salt, pepper, garlic and onion, then butter: “The Vietnamese like a lot of butter.” Look back at the sauce lists above and you’ll taste the same idea.
Not every night out should end with butter to the elbows. Date-night restaurants in St. Louis
### How ordering by the pound actually works
Think of it as building the meal, not choosing it. At Hook & Reel and Crafty Crab, you order seafood by weight, at least a pound per boil, and the corn and potatoes ride along: two potatoes and an ear of corn with every Hook & Reel boil, potatoes and corn on the cob with each Crafty Crab pound. Then you choose the sauce, then the heat.
Is 1lb seafood boil enough for 2 adults? Here’s the arithmetic nobody prints on the menu. A pound of crawfish is mostly shell. With medium crawfish, the LSU AgCenter figure is about 7 pounds of whole crawfish for 1 pound of tail meat. Crab legs and shrimp come in their shells too, and you pay for those by the pound as well. For two hungry adults, a pound is a starter, not dinner.
On heat, believe the names. Crafty Crab labels its top level “fire (my mouth on fire)” for a reason, and the sauce coats everything in the bag, so there’s no scraping it off later. Order one level below your pride.
First crawfish? Hold the head in one hand and the tail in the other, twist, and pull them apart. Peel the first ring or two of shell off the tail, pinch the end, and pull the meat out with your teeth. The head is full of seasoned juice; plenty of people suck it before they toss it on the pile. Crab legs are easier: snap at the joint and the meat slides out. Either way, wear something you can wash. The sauce travels, and shells spray when they crack.
Extras are where a table customizes. Hook & Reel’s sides run from fries and Cajun fries to sausage, broccoli, corn on the cob, rice, noodles and ramen noodles. Peacemaker sends its boils out with andouille and a biscuit already in the mix.
### Why is seafood boil so expensive?
Because the seafood is priced like seafood, and the market moves. Hook & Reel’s menu lists its snow crab, Dungeness, king crab, lobster, shrimp, crawfish, clams, mussels and scallops at market price, so the price moves with the market. Add the shell weight above and you’re paying a lot per bite of meat.
The other line to read is the service charge. Hook & Reel’s printed menu adds 18% for a party of six or more. That’s not a reason to skip it. It’s a reason to check the bill before you add a tip on top, and to ask about the rule anywhere you’re booking a big table.
If you want a fixed number, Broadway Oyster Bar’s bucket is the clearest one we found on any menu here: $25.75 for a pound and a half of boiled crawfish.
### What months are best for crawfish?
Spring. We Love Crawfish puts Louisiana’s wild season at mid-January through early July, peaking in March, April and May, and notes that farm crawfish are available over a longer stretch of the year. When the calendar turns to April, the LSU AgCenter says, the Louisiana season is usually beginning to heat up.
So in fall and early winter, a crawfish craving is a gamble on whoever’s still serving it. Broadway Oyster Bar keeps boiled crawfish on its menu, Hook & Reel and La Juicy list crawfish among their boils, and Crafty Crab sells it by the pound. When spring comes, ask for the medium ones: an LSU AgCenter agent says larger crawfish carry less meat for their weight, because of their big claws and heavier shells.
### If somebody at the table doesn’t eat shellfish
Sort this out before you book, not at the table. Hook & Reel’s menu runs to po’ boys, baskets, wings, pasta, soups and salads, including a chicken po’ boy. Crab’s Landing has chicken tender and catfish baskets. Peacemaker has a smoked brisket poorboy and a corn dog.
A shellfish allergy is a different conversation. Hook & Reel’s menu asks you to tell your server if anyone in your party has a food allergy. Do that everywhere, and call ahead to ask how the kitchen handles it before anyone orders.
### Why a boil works for a group
Most group dinners are separate meals at one table. A boil is one pile. Nobody waits on an entree, nobody compares plates, and the mess is shared, so it isn’t embarrassing. Trinh, the Houston festival organizer, called crawfish “a thing we come together for,” and that’s the whole pitch. For a table of six, call ahead and ask about the service charge while you’re on the phone.

## Dim Sum Carts and the $4.95 Sandwich Minnesota Never Got
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-chinese-food-and-dim-sum-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
A hot, crispy egg foo young patty goes between two soft slices of white bread, with pickles, lettuce, tomato and a slather of mayo, and you eat it with both hands. That is a St. Paul sandwich. At Fortune Express on Chippewa Street the pork version is $4.95, and it is named for a Minnesota city where it is nowhere to be found.
That is not a typo. When St. Louis Magazine went looking for the reason in 2016, it reported that the sandwiches are sold at Chinese restaurants throughout St. Louis but are nowhere to be found in Minnesota. Nobody has proved where the name came from, and the best theories are below.
The other half of Chinese food in this city rolls on wheels. On weekends, on Olive Boulevard in University City, servers push dim sum carts between the tables. Around them you will find noodles pulled by hand in the Delmar Loop, a Dongbei kitchen, and a newcomer that opened in January and cooks with Sichuan numbness and Hunan heat. Every place below was checked against its own site or a current listing before this page went up, and the ones that have closed are named so you don’t drive to a dark window.
### Where do the locals eat in St. Louis, MO?
Locals eat Chinese food in two modes, and the day of the week picks the mode. The weekend mode is steam and tea; the weekday mode is a hot patty, a bowl of noodles, a bag of takeout. Saturday and Sunday are for dim sum on Olive Boulevard: Wonton King at 8116 Olive, whose own site puts dim sum at 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., and Lu Lu at 8224 Olive, which opens at 10:30 a.m. on Sundays. The other days are for the counters: noodles at Corner 17 in the Loop, a St. Paul sandwich at Fortune Express, a takeout order from a West County restaurant that has been delivering since 1988.
Skip Tuesday. Corner 17 and Wei Hong are both closed that day.
### Weekend dim sum on Olive Boulevard
Pots of tea sit on the table. Then the carts arrive, steam-heated, pushed between tables of families and friends, and every stop is a small offer: steamed char siu buns, shrimp dumplings, sweet egg tarts, steamed buns filled with rich custard. Lift a lid and the steam rolls up. That is dim sum at Wonton King, where Sauce Magazine says tables fill almost from the moment the doors open and the only challenge, once you hit your stride, is knowing when to stop.
Wonton King’s own site says dim sum is served Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., and that the restaurant has been serving Cantonese food in St. Louis for decades. The same page also says daily, so call 314-567-9997 before a weekday trip. Bring a group, because sharing is the point.
Lu Lu Seafood & Dim Sum, at 8224 Olive, keeps longer hours: its ordering page shows 11 a.m. to 9:10 p.m. most days, opening at 10:30 a.m. on Sundays, and the number is (314) 997-3108. One local dining guide says Lu Lu runs cart-rolled dim sum on weekends and advises arriving before noon for the fullest carts.
For the baked half of Cantonese cooking, Wei Hong on Olive is a family-owned bakery and BBQ shop. Its site says the dining room and kitchen are closed and only the bakery and take-out BBQ are available, Wednesday through Monday from 10:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday it is closed.
### The St. Paul sandwich is a habit here, not a stunt
When the Tran family opened a Chinese chop suey in 1982, they noticed that nearly all of the Chinese restaurants in St. Louis sold this one dish, so they put it on their menu too. St. Louis Public Radio told that story in 2021 and priced the sandwich at about $6, against about $11 for a normal order of egg foo young. The patty is egg with mung bean sprouts and minced white onion folded in, fried, then closed up in soft white bread.
Fortune Express lists eight versions on its ordering page, every one dressed with mayo, pickles, tomatoes and lettuce: pork, ham, beef, chicken and vegetable at $4.95, shrimp at $5.25, a plain at $4.85, and a special with chicken, beef and shrimp at $5.50. Order the plain and you get the vegetable patty. For a few cents more, you add the meat.
Where did it come from? The tidy legend says a cook named Steven Yuen invented it at Park Chop Suey in the 1940s and named it for his hometown of St. Paul, Minnesota. St. Louis Magazine noted that the 1940s fall decades before Park Chop Suey opened, and that the current owner was loath to discuss the folklore, possibly because it isn’t true. The other popular theory belongs to James Beard, who thought the St. Paul descends from the Denver sandwich, built by Chinese cooks feeding logging camps and railroad crews. Pick the one you like, then ask the person at the counter, because no one has proved either.
### Noodles, Dongbei and Sichuan heat
Corner 17, at 6623 Delmar Boulevard in the Loop, lists hand-pulled and hand-shaved noodles on its ordering page, dumplings dyed with beets or carrots, and a tea egg, slowly boiled with tea and Asian herbs in soy sauce, for $1.99. Its site tells a family comeback story: the previous restaurant failed in 2007, and the name stands for family, growth and dreams. The site runs a waitlist you can join by scanning a code.
Cate Zone Chinese Cafe, at 8148 Olive, cooks the food of Dongbei, China’s cold northeast, where the thick, rich stews are built for the weather. St. Louis Magazine’s 2016 first look described dishes arriving in heavy ceramic donabe pots that hold in the heat, and a chicken and mushroom soup traditionally served to a new groom by his in-laws, with long, slippery noodles that are supposedly hard to eat on purpose. The restaurant’s own site lists the University City original and a second location in Chesterfield. We wrote up what to order in our Cate Zone guide.
Down the road, Spicy Chef at 8080 Olive debuted on January 15 with Jianghu cooking that combines Sichuan’s numbing spice, Hunan’s heat and Guizhou’s sour kick. St. Louis Magazine’s highlights include chicken with nine-leaf Sichuan pepper, and it reported that owner Tony Liu hinted at more local openings to come.
Tai Ke Shabu Shabu, at 9626 Olive in Olivette, is the hot-pot room: a white bar lined with induction cooktops, a choice of original or spicy broth, and Taiwanese popcorn chicken tossed in white pepper and fried basil. Sauce Magazine says it will keep you reaching for your cold beer as if you were in a Taiwanese night market instead of an Olivette strip mall.
Nothing to do with noodles: Maryland Heights business owners, this one is for you.
### How to order dim sum when you have no plan
Dim sum is a large range of small dishes traditionally eaten in restaurants for brunch, and the tea matters as much as the food. At a cart house you don’t need a plan: order a few things, then take what rolls past. If you want a place to start, order shrimp dumplings, a steamed char siu bun and an egg tart. The carts are not a gimmick, either. In the Guangzhou tea pavilions where dim sum took shape, servers balanced dishes on their arms or on trays as they climbed up and down the stairs, and eventually carts took over the steamers and plates.
Is dim sum usually lunch or dinner? Lunch. In the Cantonese tradition it is a breakfast and lunch meal, never dinner, and more traditional restaurants typically serve it until mid-afternoon. It is now commonplace for restaurants to serve dim sum at dinner too, but Wonton King’s cart window closes at 3. The difference between dumplings and dim sum is scope. Dumplings are one family on the table, alongside steamed buns and rice noodle rolls.

### West County, and the delivery experiment of 1988
Dynasty tells its own origin story. In 1988 its owner and a couple of friends noticed that pizza delivery was working and asked why Chinese food couldn’t be delivered too. The restaurant says that made it the first Chinese delivery and takeout restaurant in St. Louis County, and that people loved the new concept of having the food delivered straight to their doors. It now has two locations, in Manchester and Chesterfield.
88 China, at 14823 Clayton Road in Chesterfield, takes online orders for pickup and lists itself as closed on Mondays.
### What closed
Private Kitchen, the Shanghai-style room at 8106 Olive that Sauce Magazine reviewed in 2015, where reservations were a must, is permanently closed, according to Restaurant Guru. Shu Feng at 8435 Olive and Guo Bin at 8600 Delmar both show as closed on MapQuest, and Wei Hong’s dining room is closed too, per its own site. When an old list sends you to one of them, believe the dark window.
If you only have one weekend, do it in this order:
Saturday or Sunday, 11 a.m.: dim sum at Wonton King, 8116 Olive Boulevard.
On the way home: a $4.95 pork St. Paul sandwich at Fortune Express, 6738 Chippewa Street.
Any day but Tuesday: hand-pulled noodles at Corner 17, 6623 Delmar Boulevard.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is dim sum?
A.  Dim sum is a large range of small Chinese dishes traditionally eaten in restaurants for brunch, most of them tied to Cantonese cooking. Wonton King’s website calls it a Cantonese tradition in which small plates are shared at the table. Think steamed dumplings and buns, savory and sweet plates, and a pot of tea in the middle of the table.
### Q. How are you supposed to eat dim sum?
A.  Go with a group so you can share. Sauce Magazine’s advice for Wonton King is to order a few items from the menu to get started, then save room for the carts servers wheel around the dining room. Keep the tea coming, because in dim sum culture the tea is just as important as the food.
### Q. What to order at a dim sum place?
A.  Start with the classics Sauce Magazine lists for Wonton King: steamed char siu buns and shrimp dumplings, then sweet egg tarts and steamed buns filled with custard. Add whatever else rolls past on the carts, and stop when the table is full.
### Q. Is dim sum usually lunch or dinner?
A.  Lunch, or earlier. Cantonese tradition has it for breakfast and lunch but never for dinner, though restaurants now commonly serve it at dinner too. In St. Louis, Wonton King’s site says dim sum is served Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., though another line on the same page says daily, so call ahead before a weekday trip.
### Q. Do people eat dim sum for breakfast?
A.  In southern China, yes. Many Cantonese restaurants serve dim sum as early as five in the morning. In St. Louis it is a late-morning habit: Wonton King starts at 11 a.m., and Lu Lu opens at 10:30 a.m. on Sundays, so plan a brunch, not a breakfast.
### Q. What is the difference between dumplings and dim sum?
A.  Dumplings are one kind of dim sum, and dim sum is the whole style of eating. A traditional dim sum brunch includes steamed buns, rice or wheat dumplings, and rice noodle rolls, with many other small plates alongside.
### Q. Is dim sum Chinese or Korean?
A.  Chinese. Dim sum grew out of Cantonese teahouse culture in Guangzhou, in southern China, where teahouses served small portions of food with tea. Most modern dim sum dishes are still associated with Cantonese cuisine.
### Q. What is a St. Paul sandwich?
A.  A St. Paul sandwich is an egg foo young patty, made with mung bean sprouts and minced white onion, served between two slices of white bread with pickles, mayonnaise, lettuce and tomato. It is sold at Chinese restaurants in the St. Louis area, and Fortune Express lists eight versions from $4.85 to $5.50.
### Q. Why is it called a St. Paul sandwich if it comes from St. Louis?
A.  No one knows for sure. The popular legend credits Steven Yuen of Park Chop Suey in St. Louis, who is said to have named it after his hometown of St. Paul, Minnesota, but St. Louis Magazine pointed out that the 1940s date given for the invention is decades before that restaurant opened.

## Cunetto’s Is Dark on Monday: Italian Food in St. Louis Beyond The Hill
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-italian-food-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
You promised somebody lasagna. All afternoon you’ve been tasting it: the red sauce, the garlic bread, the corner of the pan where the cheese goes crisp. So on a Monday evening you point the car at The Hill and find parking right out front, which should have been the clue. Cunetto House of Pasta is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Zia’s is closed Mondays too. The windows are dark, the engine is idling, and the lasagna is still only an idea.
Here’s what the usual lists skip. That same Monday, Louie in Clayton starts dinner at 5. Pastaria and Cafe Napoli are both cooking on Forsyth Boulevard. In Soulard, Pizzeoli seats you from 4 to 9:30, seven days a week. The best Italian food in this metro isn’t one neighborhood. It’s a schedule.
So here is the guide that lasagna deserved: a quick bow to The Hill, then the rooms in Clayton, Maplewood, Soulard, St. Peters and across the river in Edwardsville, with the nights each one goes dark. Every hour comes off the restaurant’s own website, read this week.
### What is the Italian neighborhood in St. Louis called?
The Hill. Charlie Gitto’s calls it the historic Italian neighborhood, and the legend of toasted ravioli starts in that kitchen: sometime in the 1940s, as legend has it, an unnamed chef at Angelo’s on the Hill dropped a ravioli into hot oil instead of water. Angelo’s is now Charlie Gitto’s. Charlie’s father was its maitre d’, Charlie helped peel the potatoes and polish the brass from about age nine, and in 1981 he opened the restaurant under his own name, having bought it from Angelo himself. A boy peels potatoes in a kitchen, then owns the room. That is The Hill in one family.
The neighborhood’s other landmark fits in your hand. The James Beard Foundation, which gave the deli Gioia’s a 2017 America’s Classics award, says its hot salami is hot as in temperature, not as in spice: a fresh, boiled sausage with a texture like coarse pâté and a flavor that is porky, earthy and a little funky.
### Lasagna is a Sunday thing, and Cunetto’s and Zia’s share only four nights
Cunetto House of Pasta opened in October 1974, started by two brothers who had been pharmacists, and it has never taken reservations. Dinner runs Wednesday through Sunday from 4:45, and every Sunday is lasagna, so the lasagna you were promised isn’t lost. Zia’s on Wilson Avenue is open Tuesday through Saturday, which means the two Hill classics are both open on exactly four nights: Wednesday through Saturday. Charlie Gitto’s is the one that never goes dark, with dinner every night of the week.
### Two ovens tell the St. Louis pizza story
The first oven cost almost nothing. In 1964, Ed and Margie Imo opened a pizza parlor on The Hill, at Thurman and Shaw, and Imo’s says its first kitchen was a used oven, two refrigerators and a stove they bought for $75. The squares and the Provel came with it: a thin, crispy crust, a cheese blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone, and a cut that is simply how St. Louis slices a pizza.
The second oven weighs three tons. It stands in the middle of the dining room at Noto in St. Peters, hand-built in Naples, and a Neapolitan pie spends about 90 seconds inside it. What comes out has a puffed, charred rim and a hot, soupy center, and the restaurant says to eat it with a knife and fork. Noto opened January 6, 2020, in the same spot as the family’s J. Noto Bakery, after Wayne and Kendele Sieve ran a mobile pizza trailer starting in 2017. Plan around the calendar: it serves dinner Wednesday through Saturday only, 4 to 9.
In Soulard, Pizzeoli serves a charred, flimsy-crusted pie by candlelight out of a 900-degree wood oven, and its site says joining the waitlist is highly encouraged. It is open daily, 4 to 9:30. On Finkman Street, Onesto sells more than pizza, with entrees, salads and pasta, plus a sangria of the month club. Onesto is open Tuesday through Sunday, 4 to 9.
At City Foundry, Fordo’s Killer Pizza makes its sourdough dough by hand and finishes with house-made gelato. It opens at 11 every day. And Farotto’s in Rock Hill began in 1956 as a family pizzeria with carryout and car-hop service, and it’s open every day from 11.
### Handmade pasta, and the nights each room goes dark
Start in Clayton, where two kitchens share a boulevard. Pastaria, at 7734 Forsyth, cooks handmade pastas and wood-fired pizzas in an open kitchen under James Beard Award-winning chef Gerard Craft, every night, 4 to 9, with a happy hour from 4 to 5:30. The garage is complimentary if you bring your ticket in for validation. At 7754 Forsyth, Cafe Napoli serves Monday through Saturday and closes on Sundays. Owner Tony Pietoso says on the group’s site that he remembers his customers’ names, and his kids do too. Valet starts at 5:30 for $12 a car.
Over on DeMun Avenue, the patio tables at Louie go first come, first served, weather permitting, so on a warm night the people who arrive early get the air. Dinner runs Monday through Saturday, and Sunday is dark. There is a free lot south of the building. Book through OpenTable or by phone, and know that a voicemail request isn’t a booking until someone calls you back.
In Maplewood, Acero on Manchester Road opened in 2007, and its own story says the name means maple in Italian. It promises people serving people instead of rushing diners through, and it prices like it: the pastas run $40 to $43 a plate, and a four-course tasting menu starts at $75. The cheaper way in is the gnocco fritto, fried dough draped in prosciutto di Parma, olive oil and sea salt, at $18. Acero serves dinner Tuesday through Saturday.

### Where can I get oven repair in St. Louis?
If it is a gas oven and you smell gas, skip the repair shop for now: Spire says to leave the area immediately and call Spire or 911, and its eastern Missouri line, 800-887-4173, takes gas emergencies around the clock. For a dead element or a flaky thermostat, our guide to appliance repair in St. Louis explains when a fix is worth paying for and when to replace the oven.
And on Watson Road sits the smallest week of all. Trattoria Marcella has belonged to brothers Steve and Jamie Komorek since 1995 and is named for their mother, Marcella Slay Komorek. Its site calls the cooking Italian “soul food” with a twist. Dinner is Tuesday through Thursday until 8:30, Friday and Saturday until 9:30, and Sunday and Monday it’s closed. Call ahead and plan for an early table.
### Toasted ravioli runs $10 at Mio Osteria, $13 at Vito’s and $16 at Charlie Gitto’s
Order it as the table’s opening move. Charlie Gitto’s describes its version as handmade ravioli, breaded and fried, crispy outside and soft and savory inside: the first bite cracks, then gives. The recipe is shorter than the legend. Bread a filled ravioli, deep-fry it until it’s golden, dust it with Parmesan and put warm marinara beside it.
Here is the price ladder, straight from the menus. In Edwardsville, Mio Osteria lists meat-filled toasted ravioli with marinara for $10. Vito’s, at 3515 Lindell, serves fried beef ravioli with Parmigiano and a side of marinara for $13, under the line “Saint Louis Favorite!” Charlie Gitto’s lists The Original, a handmade meat-filled ravioli, for $16. Same appetizer, three prices. Vito’s full name is Vito’s Sicilian Pizzeria & Ristorante, and in St. Charles, Pio’s says its founder was the first to bring thin-crust pizza, toasted ravioli and pizza burgers to the St. Charles area. It began in 1954 as the Continental Cafe.
Off the menu for a second: Godfrey, IL business owners can see how to get more customers here.
### Across the Mississippi and out to St. Charles County
You don’t have to cross the river to leave The Hill behind. In Edwardsville, Mio Osteria at 224 S. Kansas St. describes itself as bringing a taste of The Hill to Edwardsville, just 30 minutes from the real thing. Chef Micah Hopkin cooks homemade pastas, and the lunch menu carries a family-recipe Italian beef. It serves lunch and dinner Monday through Friday, dinner only on Saturday, and is closed Sunday. Also in Edwardsville, Sugo’s Spaghetteria at 243 Harvard Drive cooks recipes from Sicily and northern Italy that its listing says three generations of mammas passed down.
West of the river, Pio’s at 403 First Capitol Drive in St. Charles is open Tuesday through Saturday, 11 to 10, and Sunday from 3 to 9. It’s closed Mondays. In O’Fallon, Osteria Forto at 2509 Highway K takes dinner Tuesday through Saturday, and our notes on Osteria Forto’s menu cover the details. Gioia’s has grown past the neighborhood, too: besides the original on Macklind Avenue, its site lists four more doors, one of them at 9955 Winghaven Boulevard in O’Fallon.
### Who takes a reservation, and who makes you wait
Italian dinners fall apart at the host stand, so know the rules before you park. Cunetto doesn’t take reservations at all, so go at 4:45 when it opens or bring patience. Onesto takes reservations only for its private dining room, for parties of 10 to 20, and seats everyone else first come, first served. Pizzeoli runs a waitlist you can join online. Farotto’s takes reservations only for groups of 8 to 14, by calling and asking for a manager. Louie takes reservations through OpenTable or by phone. At Charlie Gitto’s, parties of six or more go on one check with a 20 percent gratuity added, and the dress code is smart casual.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What makes a St. Louis pizza?
A.  A thin, cracker-crisp crust covered edge to edge with toppings, cut into squares, and topped with Provel, a blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone that melts without stringing. Imo’s, which opened in 1964, calls itself the creator of the original, and says Provel was invented in St. Louis in 1947, though the cheese’s origins are debated.
### Q. How to make St. Louis toasted ravioli?
A.  Bread a meat-filled ravioli, deep-fry it until golden and crisp, and serve it hot with Parmigiano and marinara for dipping. Charlie Gitto’s describes its version as handmade ravioli, breaded and deep-fried, crispy outside and soft inside, and Vito’s lists fried beef ravioli with Parmigiano and a side of marinara.
### Q. What is St. Louis’ signature dish?
A.  Toasted ravioli is the dish most people name, and its legend begins on The Hill in the 1940s. Charlie Gitto’s calls its own version an icon of St. Louis cuisine. Provel-topped, square-cut pizza runs a close second, and Imo’s has been selling it since 1964.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Order the toasted ravioli first, then a square of Provel pizza, then a Gioia’s hot salami sandwich, which the James Beard Foundation honored as an America’s Classic in 2017. For Italian beyond those three, book a pasta room in Clayton or Maplewood.
### Q. Which Italian restaurants in St. Louis are open on Monday?
A.  Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill, Pastaria, Louie and Cafe Napoli in Clayton, Pizzeoli in Soulard and Farotto’s in Rock Hill all list Monday hours on their own sites. Cunetto House of Pasta and Zia’s are both closed that day.

## Best Patios in St Louis: A Local's Guide to Outdoor Dining
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-patios-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
St. Louisans take patio season seriously. The moment the weather turns, we abandon our indoor tables and chase every string-lit courtyard, rooftop, and beer garden we can find — because a good patio isn’t just where you eat, it’s where a summer evening actually happens.
But here’s an honest heads-up before you make a plan: the patio scene has changed a lot recently, and several of the spots people still recommend are gone. A few beloved rooftops and gardens have closed or gone private, so this guide leads with the truth about what’s no longer there — then points you to the great patios that are very much still open and worth your evening.
From the last iconic downtown rooftop to the biggest party patio in the city, the DeMun garden row, the German beer gardens, and the best dog-friendly spots, here’s where to spend your patio season across the whole metro. Grab a cold drink and a seat outside.
📌 Patio-season lover? Keep this — and share it.
Bookmark this guide and send it to the friend who lives for patio weather, the group planning a golden-hour hangout, or anyone still trying to make a reservation at a patio that closed two years ago.
Every share points one more person to a great seat outside. That’s the whole idea.
### First, an Honest Word: What’s Gone
Because so many outdated lists are still floating around, let’s clear the air. Several once-famous patios are no longer options: Vin de Set, the beloved Chouteau’s Grove rooftop, closed after a 2022 fire and hasn’t reopened as a restaurant. Cinder House at the Four Seasons is not the sure thing it once was — its status has been in flux, so call ahead before counting on it. The Boathouse in Forest Park is closed for a major renovation, running only a seasonal pop-up beer-and-wine garden. And Das Bevo, the windmill biergarten, now operates mostly as a private event space. Knowing what’s gone saves you a wasted trip — now let’s get to the good stuff that’s open.
### Rooftops & Skyline Views
If you want a view, one spot now stands above the rest. Three Sixty ($$$), atop the Hilton at the Ballpark downtown, is the last of the great iconic rooftops — a 6,000-square-foot terrace with panoramic views over Busch Stadium, the Arch, and the Mississippi. It’s the go-to for a Cardinals-game drink or a special night out. For a more exclusive perch, The Last Rooftop ($$$) at The Last Hotel offers an 11th-floor terrace and pool (day-pass or guest access). And out in DeMun, Sasha’s ($$) pairs a popular patio with rooftop seating, heaters, and blankets. For skyline drama, Three Sixty is the answer.
### The DeMun Garden Row
The prettiest cluster of patios in the metro is the DeMun/Clayton stretch. Louie ($$$) has a coveted, intimate patio to go with its handmade pasta and top wine list. Next-level for romance, Edera ($$$) has an ivy-lined, garden-like courtyard (with heated igloos in winter). Nearby, Winslow’s Table ($$) has a beautiful shaded patio, and in University City, plant-based Frida’s ($$) does a patio with fresh flowers and tabletop fire. In Clayton, Bar Napoli ($$$) hosts a lively weekend patio scene. This is the row for a leisurely, beautiful outdoor meal.
### The Big Social Patios
Sometimes you want a scene, not a quiet corner. Molly’s in Soulard ($$) is the king — around 11,000 square feet, one of the largest patios in the city, with multiple bars and string lights strung over the whole thing. It’s the ultimate big-group, all-afternoon patio. Katie’s Pizza & Pasta ($$) in Rock Hill (and beyond) has large, lively patios perfect for families and groups. And near Cherokee Street, The Whiskey Ring ($$) offers an expansive secured patio. These are the spots for a loud, happy, sun-soaked afternoon with friends.
Nothing to do with patios — Brentwood owners, here’s how locals find you.
### Beer Gardens
St. Louis’s brewing heritage means world-class beer gardens. In Maplewood, Schlafly Bottleworks ($$) has a massive covered patio and a beloved beer garden that runs spring through fall. In The Grove, Urban Chestnut’s Grove Bierhall ($$) has an elevated terrace and front patio attached to its 400-plus-seat hall, with a traditional German biergarten also at its Midtown location. And in Tower Grove South, Civil Life ($) is a laid-back, family- and dog-friendly beer garden pouring English-style ales. Pull up a communal table, order a pretzel, and settle in.
### Dog-Friendly Patios
Bringing your best friend along? Several patios roll out the water bowls. In the Central West End, Narwhal’s Crafted ($$) has a covered patio with fire pits and a genuinely dog-welcoming vibe. The beer gardens are your other best bets — Civil Life in Tower Grove South is famously dog- and family-friendly, and Schlafly Bottleworks and the Urban Chestnut biergartens welcome well-behaved pups too (policies shift seasonally, so it’s worth a quick check). For a relaxed evening where the dog is part of the plan, these spots make it easy. (For more, see our guide to dog-friendly patios and breweries in St. Louis.)
### Riverfront & Beyond
For water views, the metro’s edges deliver. Across the river in Alton, Illinois — a scenic river town about 25 minutes north — spots like Great Rivers Tap & Grill ($$) and Chez Marilyn ($$) offer Mississippi River views and inviting patios. Back in Forest Park, the Boathouse Beer & Wine Garden ($) runs as a lakeside pop-up while the restaurant is renovated. And St. Charles’s Historic Main Street district has a cluster of patios worth exploring near the riverfront (call ahead, as a couple of longtime spots there have been in transition). A river breeze and a cold drink is a summer combination that’s hard to beat.
### A Few More Patios Worth Knowing
Beyond the headliners, the metro is full of great outdoor seats. In Benton Park, Peacemaker Lobster & Crab ($$$) pairs excellent seafood with pleasant outdoor seating. In The Grove, the bike-themed HandleBar ($$) has a lively, late-running patio, and in the Shaw neighborhood, Bailey’s Range ($$) does burgers with patio space. Clayton’s Bar Napoli and the Central West End’s Brasserie by Niche both do a classic sidewalk-cafe scene. And nearly every brewery in town — there are dozens — has some form of patio or beer garden, so when in doubt, your neighborhood taproom is a safe bet for a seat outside. The point: on a nice St. Louis evening, a good patio is never far away. And don’t overlook the coffee shops, wine bars, and neighborhood cafes with a few sidewalk tables — some of the most pleasant outdoor sitting in the city is the low-key kind, a cup or a glass and a bit of people-watching on a quiet street.
### What St. Louis Patios Do Best
A few things this scene has really come to own. Beer gardens are a genuine strength, thanks to the city’s brewing roots — Schlafly and Urban Chestnut lead a deep field. Garden courtyards, especially the DeMun row, offer some of the prettiest outdoor dining anywhere. The big social patios like Molly’s are built for groups and all-day hangs. And dog-friendly options mean nobody in the family gets left home. What St. Louis lost in a few iconic rooftops, it more than makes up for in the sheer number and variety of great outdoor spaces — there’s a patio here for every mood.
### How to Make the Most of Patio Season
A few tips. Patio season in St. Louis runs roughly April through October, with the sweet spots in late spring and early fall when the humidity eases. Go early or reserve on nice evenings — the best patios fill fast the first warm week of the year. Chase the golden hour for the prettiest light (and, on rooftops, the skyline glow). Check for heaters, fire pits, or igloos if you want to stretch the season into the shoulder months (Edera, Narwhal’s, and Sasha’s all have you covered). And always call ahead for a specific patio — outdoor spaces open and close with the weather and, as this guide shows, with the years. Then relax and enjoy the evening.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. When is patio season in St. Louis?
A.  Patio season in St. Louis runs roughly from April through October. The most comfortable stretches are late spring (April–June) and early fall (September–October), when temperatures are mild and the humidity eases. Midsummer can be hot and humid, so shaded patios and evening seatings are best then. Many spots extend the season with heaters, fire pits, or winter igloos, so you can dine outside comfortably even in the cooler shoulder months.
### Q. What is the best rooftop bar in St. Louis?
A.  Three Sixty, atop the Hilton at the Ballpark downtown, is the definitive St. Louis rooftop — a large open-air terrace with panoramic views of Busch Stadium, the Gateway Arch, and the Mississippi River. It’s the go-to for a game-day drink or a special night out. Note that a few former rooftop favorites, like Vin de Set and (in flux) Cinder House, are no longer reliable options, which makes Three Sixty the clear skyline choice.
### Q. Which restaurant has the biggest patio in St. Louis?
A.  Molly’s in Soulard has one of the largest patios in the city — around 11,000 square feet, with multiple bars and string lights overhead. It’s a favorite for big groups, weekend afternoons, and all-day hangs. For beer-garden scale, Schlafly Bottleworks in Maplewood and Urban Chestnut’s Grove Bierhall also offer expansive outdoor space that can handle a crowd.
### Q. Which restaurants have dog-friendly patios in St. Louis?
A.  Several. Narwhal’s Crafted in the Central West End has a covered, fire-pit patio that welcomes dogs, and the beer gardens are reliably pet-friendly — Civil Life in Tower Grove South is famously dog- and family-friendly, and Schlafly Bottleworks and the Urban Chestnut biergartens generally welcome well-behaved dogs too. Policies can shift seasonally, so it’s always worth a quick call before bringing your pup.
### Q. Where are the best beer gardens in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis’s brewing heritage gives it excellent beer gardens. Schlafly Bottleworks in Maplewood has a big covered patio and beloved garden; Urban Chestnut runs a Grove Bierhall terrace and a traditional Midtown biergarten; and Civil Life in Tower Grove South is a laid-back, dog-friendly garden pouring English-style ales. All three are great for a relaxed, communal, warm-weather afternoon.

## Your 1am Taco Is Gone: What Still Cooks in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-late-night-eats-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
It’s 12:40 on Delmar, the bars are emptying, your stomach is loud, and the taco counter you walk to without thinking has its lights off. For good. Session Taco, the St. Louis brand that began as Mission Taco Joint, closed its remaining restaurants on Saturday, Oct. 17, and the Delmar Loop was one of them.
The old lists haven’t caught up. iTap Soulard’s own web page still tells you to order tacos from Mission Taco Joint to your table. Courtesy Diner on Hampton, the slinger counter, lists Monday through Saturday 6am-9pm on its own site. That’s a breakfast-and-supper diner now, not a 2am one.
So here’s a map that matches the clock. Nearly every hour below was read off the business’s own hours page the week the tacos stopped, and anything that couldn’t be confirmed got cut. Screenshot the short version: after midnight in this city, trust a griddle that never cools, and check the kitchen, not the bar. And the late-night math worth repeating: hashbrowns ($3.95) and a large coffee ($2.65) at the 24-hour Waffle House on S. Lindbergh come to $6.60.
### What are the best 24 hour restaurants in St. Louis?
Three in the morning on S. Lindbergh, and the Waffle House there is still lit, because its own page lists it open 24 hours, every day. You slide onto a stool, the flat-top hisses, and the Cheese N’ Eggs come out the way the menu promises, cheese melted all the way through two scrambled eggs, with raisin toast for $8.50. The pecan waffle has been on that menu since 1955. Nobody hurries you. Text this to whoever’s driving tonight: kitchen closed? White Castle on Gravois, Waffle House on Lindbergh.
### The Griddles That Never Go Dark
Pull into the White Castle at 3601 Gravois at one in the morning and you already know the sound: the drive-thru speaker crackling, the sack handed out the window going soft with onion steam before you hit the light. White Castle lists that Gravois location as open around the clock, every day of the week. It’s the closest thing South City has to a promise after midnight. One reviewer on MapQuest put the downside plainly, describing “extremely long lines after a night of drinking.” Go anyway. At 1am, a hot slider in a paper sack beats a locked door.
If you want a booth and a fork, the Waffle House at 5330 S. Lindbergh lists itself open 24 hours, and its own menu page reads like a small mercy at 3am: hashbrowns for $3.95, a Two Egg Breakfast for $7.50, a large coffee for $2.65. You hear the spatula scrape the flat-top before you’ve sat down. If the night was long, the All-Star Special is $13.35 for eggs with toast and jelly, a choice of grits, hashbrowns or sliced tomatoes, a waffle, and your choice of bacon, sausage or ham. That’s a whole table’s worth of breakfast on one ticket. The chain’s St. Louis locator also lists stores at 3154 Telegraph Rd. and 10221 Page Ave.; check that store’s own page before a late run, because the 24-hour listing we confirmed is the Lindbergh one.
### Yaqui’s on Cherokee: The Late Slice Worth Crossing Town For
Cherokee Street goes quiet early. You walk past dark storefronts, your footsteps loud on an empty sidewalk, toward one warm, lit window at 2728 Cherokee St., the one still lit when the rest of the block has gone dark. Yaqui’s posts its hours like a regular would want them, kitchen and bar listed separately. The kitchen runs until midnight Wednesday through Saturday and until 10pm Sunday, Monday and Tuesday. The bar stays open until 1:30am on Friday and Saturday. So the move is simple: get your pizza order in before 12, then sit with it, the box warm on your knees or the slice folding in your hand, while the room stays loud. Show up at 12:15 on a Friday and you’ll get a drink, not a slice.
### What Closed, and Who Quietly Changed Their Hours
The big one is Session Taco. Sauce Magazine reported that the brand “is closing its remaining locations,” with a closing date of Saturday, Oct. 17, and that the two remaining Session Taco restaurants were in the Delmar Loop and Soulard. Session Taco’s own site said it plainly: “We will be closing our remaining locations this Saturday, Oct. 17th.” The same report said LaPez Mod Mex in the Central West End, which formerly operated as a Session Taco, will also close. If an app or an old guide still sends you to either taco counter, it’s sending you to a dark door. And if you ever carried a basket of carne asada fries from Mission Taco across the patio at iTap, that late order is over.
It ended fast. Sauce reported the closure was announced Monday, Oct. 12, in a social media post, with the last service set for Saturday, Oct. 17, and that the brand had run in the city for more than a decade. For that final week, Session Taco’s own site said its hours would be limited to dinner and late night. Plenty of people never got the message, which is exactly why the old lists are dangerous for a while yet.
That leaves the Delmar Loop thin after midnight. We couldn’t confirm a single Loop kitchen cooking past midnight from any restaurant’s own hours page this week, so if you’re hungry on Delmar after the bars let out, the honest advice is to point the car toward Cherokee or Gravois.
The quieter change is the diner. Courtesy Diner on Hampton still does the slinger, that plate of hash browns, eggs and chili St. Louis swears by the morning after, but its own site now lists Monday through Saturday 6am-9pm and Sunday 6am-3pm. Eat it at dawn, not at 2am. And if Tiffany’s Original Diner in Maplewood is your habit, call before you drive over: we couldn’t confirm its overnight hours from the diner itself.
### Bars That Pour Late, Kitchens That Don’t
Here’s the trap that sends people home hungry: the bar and the kitchen keep different clocks. Broadway Oyster Bar at 736 S. Broadway posts it in black and white. The bar is open until 1:30am every night. The kitchen closes at 10pm Monday through Thursday, 11pm Friday and Saturday, and 9pm Sunday. On a Tuesday, that’s three and a half hours of music and drinks with the fryer already cold. Eat there early, then stay.
In Soulard, iTap’s page still points you to two food neighbors in its L-shaped building. One of them, Mission Taco Joint, is the brand that became Session Taco, and Session Taco’s Soulard restaurant closed on Oct. 17. The other, Epic Pizza, is the one to order from now: iTap says that most times your order gets delivered right to your table. A slice and a pint on the patio is still a good Soulard night. Just skip the taco line on their page.
Unrelated, and we know it - does your Troy, IL business show up?
### Your Late-Night Plan, Night by Night
Most late-night guides give you one list for the whole week. The clocks don’t work that way, so here’s the week the way the hours pages actually read. Pick your night, then pick your stop, and you won’t end up idling in a dark lot.
Sunday through Tuesday are the hard nights. Yaqui’s kitchen stops at 10pm on all three, even though the doors stay open until midnight. Broadway Oyster Bar stops cooking at 9pm on Sunday and 10pm on Monday and Tuesday. After that, your hot food comes off a 24-hour griddle: the White Castle on Gravois or the Waffle House on S. Lindbergh. Order the hashbrowns, get the coffee, and don’t feel bad about it. That counter is open for exactly this.
Wednesday and Thursday are better at Yaqui’s: its kitchen runs until midnight both nights, so a slice on Cherokee at 11:30 is a real option, and the bar closes at midnight with it. Broadway Oyster Bar’s kitchen still closes at 10pm on Wednesday and Thursday, so if you want oysters, eat first and stay for a drink.
Friday and Saturday are the long nights. Yaqui’s cooks until midnight and pours until 1:30am. Broadway’s kitchen runs to 11pm with the bar open until 1:30am. Yaqui’s also opens at noon on Saturday and Sunday, instead of the 4pm weekday start, which matters if your late night turns into a late lunch.
One more wrinkle: holidays. Broadway Oyster Bar lists Thanksgiving Day and Christmas Eve among its closed days, so on those nights skip the downtown plan entirely and go straight to the griddle.
### Game Nights, Concerts and the Downtown Crowd
The crowd pours out of a Cardinals game or a show at Enterprise Center or Stifel Theatre, the sidewalks fill, and everyone has the same idea at the same minute. Plan the food before the last song, not after. If Broadway Oyster Bar is your stop, remember its kitchen hours above: on a Friday or Saturday you have until 11pm to order. After that, the downtown play is a drink, and then the drive to a griddle that never cools.
### How to Eat Late Like a Regular
Call, every time. Late hours are the least reliable thing online, and a two-minute call beats a locked door and a cold parking lot. Ask “is the kitchen still open?” not “are you open?”, because the bar almost always outlasts the grill. Weekends run later than weeknights at the spots above. And when you’re out in the county with nothing nearby, a 24-hour chain is the plan, not the failure.
Want dinner before the clock runs out? Start with the best restaurants in St. Louis, then save this page for the night the craving hits at 12:40.
If you run the kitchen that’s still hot at midnight, tell the people standing on the sidewalk right now. Hungry people ask their phone, and ChatGPT, who’s open, and too often the answer is an old list that still names a closed taco counter. A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your real late hours, your photos and your menu in one place neighbors and AI assistants can read, so it brings you more customers instead of sending them to the dark door down the street. Already on Google? Good. This makes that work harder; it doesn’t replace it. List your spot, or see who AI names instead of you.
The best late food in this city was never fancy. It’s a sack of sliders on Gravois, a slice on Cherokee ordered at 11:50, and hashbrowns at a counter that never turns its lights off. The round-the-clock griddles we could confirm today are chains: the Waffle House at 5330 S. Lindbergh and the White Castle at 3601 Gravois Ave. We can’t speak for each owner’s reasons, so call before you drive.

Downtown, Broadway Oyster Bar at 736 S. Broadway is open until 1:30am every night, but eat early, because its kitchen closes by 11pm even on weekends. If dinner is running late, Broadway Oyster Bar’s kitchen takes orders until 10pm Monday through Thursday and 11pm Friday and Saturday, and Yaqui’s on Cherokee cooks until midnight Wednesday through Saturday. ## Best Cheap Eats in St Louis: A Local's Guide to Eating Well for Less
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-cheap-eats-in-st-louis-a-locals-guide
One of the best things about eating in St. Louis is how far a few dollars go. This is a city where you can get three street tacos for the price of a fast-food combo, split a foot-long Italian sub that feeds two, or sit down to a 24-hour diner slinger for under ten bucks. Great cheap food is everywhere here — you just have to know where to look.
And the range is the real joy. Cheap eats in St. Louis means Cherokee Street taquerias, Hill delis, North County hot-dog stands, South Grand shawarma, University City Chinese, a Korean-Mexican taco, and iconic local treats like a Ted Drewes concrete. You can eat your way around the world for the price of a single fancy entree.
This guide rounds up the metro’s best budget-friendly spots — genuinely delicious food where you can eat well for roughly under $10 to $12 a person — across the city and suburbs and across a dozen cuisines. Bring cash (some of the best spots prefer it) and an empty stomach.
📌 Love a great cheap meal? Keep this — and share it.
Bookmark this guide and send it to the friend who’s always broke but always eating well, the group looking for a payday-eve dinner, or the newcomer who thinks eating out has to be expensive.
Every share points one more hungry person to a great cheap meal. That’s the whole idea.
### Taquerias & Tacos
Few things beat cheap tacos, and St. Louis delivers. On Cherokee Street, the city’s historic Mexican corridor, La Vallesana ($) does street tacos around $3-4, plus tortas on fresh French bread and house-made ice cream, and El Torito ($) — a taco stand inside a Mexican supermarket — slings barbacoa, carnitas, and al pastor for a couple bucks each. Out in Overland (North County), Taqueria Durango ($) is a beloved institution for big-portion birria and street tacos around $3. For a full deep-dive, see our guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis. This is the cheapest great eating in town.
### Sandwiches & Delis
St. Louis is a serious sandwich town, and a split sandwich is a budget secret weapon. On The Hill, Gioia’s Deli ($$) makes the iconic Hot Salami sandwich (a century-old recipe) — grab a foot-long and split it to stay cheap. Nearby, Adriana’s ($$) does famous foot-long Italian subs and Sicilian soups at lunch. In Benton Park, Blues City Deli ($$) is a landmark for New Orleans po’boys, muffulettas, and Italian beef. For a true bargain, Fortune Express ($) in St. Louis Hills makes the St. Louis-only St. Paul sandwich (egg foo young on white bread) for around $5-6. And in the suburbs, DD Mau ($) does fast-casual banh mi in Webster Groves and Maryland Heights.
### Diners, Dogs & Comfort Food
For cheap comfort, St. Louis’s old-school spots are unbeatable. Courtesy Diner ($) — a 24-hour institution since 1935, on Hampton and Laclede Station — makes the definitive slinger (a burger patty, two eggs, hash browns, and chili, all on one plate) for around $9-11. In Brentwood, Carl’s Drive-In ($) is a cash-only, 16-stool 1950s gem for griddle burgers and house root beer in frosted mugs — a combo runs well under $10. And in Overland, Woofie’s ($) has done Chicago-style Vienna Beef dogs since 1977, with a loaded dog around $5-7. These are the timeless, wallet-friendly St. Louis classics.
Nothing to do with tacos — Florissant, get found first.
### Global Cheap Eats
The metro’s international spots are where cheap eating gets truly exciting. In Brentwood, Mai Lee ($-$$) — the city’s oldest Vietnamese restaurant — does lunch bowls of pho and vermicelli around $9-12. On Olive in University City, Cate Zone ($-$$) serves generous Dongbei (Northeastern Chinese) plates. For value vegetarian, Gokul ($$) does an all-you-can-eat Indian buffet, and on South Grand, The Vine ($-$$) makes shawarma and falafel plates in the $8-12 range. Don’t miss Sameem ($-$$), Missouri’s only Afghan restaurant, in The Grove. And in the Delmar Loop, Seoul Taco ($) does Korean-Mexican gogi tacos around $3.50-4, with K-Bop ($-$$) nearby for Korean rice bowls and Gyro House ($) for a 40-year-old gyro under $10.
### Iconic Cheap St. Louis Staples
Some of the cheapest food here is also the most famous. Ted Drewes ($) on Route 66 has served its legendary frozen-custard “concrete” — so thick they hand it to you upside down — for nearly a century, and it’s a couple of bucks a cup. In North County, C&K Barbecue ($) serves the true St. Louis specialty of fried, sauced snoots at budget prices. The slinger at Courtesy is the definitive cheap diner plate. And a plate of toasted ravioli — the fried-ravioli appetizer St. Louis invented — is the perfect cheap bite to split at a bar or casual Italian spot. These are the flavors that define eating cheap and well in St. Louis.
### Markets, Food Halls & Frozen Custard
A few more ways to eat cheap and well. The historic Soulard Farmers Market — open since the early 1800s — has vendor stalls turning out affordable prepared plates, produce, and snacks, especially on weekends. At City Foundry in Midtown, a food hall gathers a dozen stalls under one roof, so a group with different cravings can each grab something in the $8-12 range and share a table. And for the cheapest happy ending of all, St. Louis’s frozen custard tradition — Ted Drewes on Route 66, plus neighborhood custard stands all over the metro — delivers a genuinely iconic treat for just a few dollars. Markets, halls, and custard stands are proof that eating cheap here can also be an experience.
### What St. Louis Cheap Eats Do Best
A few genuine strengths define the budget scene. Tacos are the ultimate cheap thrill, especially on Cherokee Street and in North County. Split-worthy delis — Gioia’s, Adriana’s, Blues City — let two people eat for one sandwich’s price. The slinger and the diner tradition deliver hot comfort at any hour for under $11. The metro’s global variety — Vietnamese, Chinese, Afghan, Korean, Mediterranean, Indian — means you can eat a different cuisine every day of the week on a budget. And the iconic local treats, from Ted Drewes to snoots, are cheap by design. Eating well here truly does not require a big budget.
### Lunch Specials: The Bargain Hunter’s Secret
One of the best cheap-eats tricks in St. Louis is simply eating at lunch. Many spots that feel like a splurge at dinner offer lunch specials at a fraction of the price — a full plate of the same food, plus rice and a side, for well under the dinner tab. This is especially true at the metro’s international restaurants: Vietnamese pho houses, Chinese spots on Olive, Indian buffets, Thai kitchens, and Mediterranean cafes almost all run weekday lunch deals. The move is to save your fancier cravings for midday, when the prices are friendliest, and treat a nice sit-down lunch as the budget alternative to an expensive dinner. Your wallet will thank you.
### How to Eat Cheap Like a Regular
A few tricks to stretch your dollars. Split the big sandwiches — a Gioia’s or Adriana’s foot-long easily feeds two. Bring cash to the taquerias and old-school spots like Carl’s (some are cash-only or cash-preferred, and it moves the line). Hit the ethnic corridors — Cherokee Street, South Grand, and Olive Boulevard in University City are wall-to-wall value. Go for lunch specials, which are often the same food at a fraction of dinner prices. And order the house specialty — the taqueria’s birria, the deli’s signature sub, the diner’s slinger — because that’s where the value and the flavor both live. Eat adventurously and cheaply; in this city they go hand in hand.
