## Who Qualifies Now — Medicaid Expansion Changed the Rules

This is the part people miss. Thanks to **Medicaid expansion**, adults ages 19–64 can qualify based on income alone — you no longer have to be pregnant, disabled, or a parent to get covered. The cutoff is roughly **138% of the federal poverty level**: about **$1,730 a month for one person** or roughly **$3,588 a month for a family of four** (higher for larger households). Children and pregnant women qualify at higher income levels still. These figures shift yearly, so if you’re anywhere close, apply — MO HealthNet checks the current numbers for you at **mydss.mo.gov**.

## What You’ll Need to Apply

- Social Security numbers for those applying
- Proof of identity (a driver’s license or state ID)
- Proof of Missouri residency (a lease, utility bill, or mail)
- Proof of household income (recent pay stubs, benefit letters, or a statement if you have none)
- If you’re 65 or older, blind, or disabled — the Aged, Blind, and Disabled (ABD) Supplement form
- Immigration or citizenship documentation, if applicable

Applying online lets you send these straight through the myDSS Document Uploader, which is the quickest way to avoid back-and-forth.

## What MO HealthNet Covers

Coverage is comprehensive — not a stripped-down plan. MO HealthNet includes doctor visits, hospital and emergency care, prescriptions, lab and X-ray, maternity and newborn care, mental health and substance-use treatment, and preventive care like checkups and immunizations. Most members pick a **managed-care health plan** — in the St. Louis area that includes **Home State Health, Healthy Blue, and UnitedHealthcare Community Plan** — which comes with a member card, a network of local doctors, and a nurse line. Kids get extra benefits through MO HealthNet for Kids (Missouri’s CHIP), including dental and vision.

## Special Paths to Coverage

Beyond the standard adult pathway, Missouri has targeted programs worth asking about:

- **Pregnant women**— MO HealthNet for Pregnant Women and Show-Me Healthy Babies cover prenatal care, delivery, and postpartum at higher income limits; coverage can start quickly so care isn’t delayed.
- **Children**— MO HealthNet for Kids (Missouri’s CHIP) covers children in families that earn too much for regular Medicaid but can’t afford private insurance, and includes dental and vision.
- **Adults 65+, blind, or disabled**— the Aged, Blind, and Disabled programs cover long-term care, in-home services, and help with Medicare costs.
- **Working people with disabilities**— the Ticket to Work Health Assurance program lets you earn more and keep coverage.
- **Young adults who aged out of foster care**— may qualify for coverage up to age 26 regardless of income.

## Need Care Before You’re Approved?

Don’t skip a real emergency waiting on paperwork. By federal law, hospital emergency rooms must screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency, insured or not. If you deliver a baby or face a medical crisis while your application is pending, tell the hospital — MO HealthNet coverage can often be **backdated up to three months** before your application date, wiping out bills you thought you’d be stuck with. Community health centers also treat patients on a sliding fee scale, so a lack of coverage today never has to mean no care today.

## What Does It Cost?

For most people, MO HealthNet is **free or nearly free** — there’s no monthly premium for the majority of members, and copays for covered services are small or zero. Some programs (like MO HealthNet for Kids at higher income tiers, or Ticket to Work) may involve a modest monthly premium on a sliding scale, but nothing like private insurance. That’s the whole point of the program: cost should never be the reason you skip the care you need. Compared with a marketplace plan’s premiums and deductibles, Medicaid is by far the most affordable coverage available to those who qualify — which is exactly why it’s worth ten minutes to find out if you do.

## What If You Don’t Qualify?

Even if your income is a little too high for MO HealthNet, you’re not out of options — and you should never assume “no coverage” is the end of the road. Most people who don’t qualify for Medicaid **do** qualify for subsidized private insurance through the Health Insurance Marketplace at **HealthCare.gov**, where tax credits can bring premiums down to a few dollars a month; a free Cover Missouri navigator can walk you through it. Your children may still qualify for MO HealthNet for Kids even when you don’t. And regardless of insurance, St. Louis **community health centers** like Affinia Healthcare, CareSTL Health, and Family Care Health Centers treat everyone on a **sliding fee scale** based on income — so a checkup, a prescription, or a dental visit stays affordable while you sort coverage out. Ask; the door is rarely fully closed.

## Get Free Help Enrolling in St. Louis

If the forms feel overwhelming, trained local navigators will walk you through it for free — no cost, no pressure:

- **Community health centers**like Affinia Healthcare, CareSTL Health, Family Care Health Centers, and People’s Health Centers have enrollment specialists on site and will see you whether or not you’re insured yet.
- **Cover Missouri navigators**offer free, unbiased enrollment help by phone and in person.
- **Your hospital’s financial counselor**— if you have unpaid bills, ask; they can often help you apply and backdate coverage.

## Already Applied? What Happens Next

After you submit, the Family Support Division reviews your case and requests anything missing — respond fast to keep it moving. A decision usually comes within about **45 days** (longer for disability-based cases that need medical review). If approved, you’ll get a MO HealthNet ID and choose or be assigned a managed-care plan. Keep your address and phone current, and watch for your **annual renewal** notice — returning that form on time is the single most important thing you can do to avoid a coverage gap. If you’re ever denied, you have the right to appeal, and a community health center or legal aid can help.

## Myths That Stop People From Applying

Plenty of eligible Missourians never apply because of outdated fears. A few worth retiring: **“I make too much money”** — expansion raised the limit dramatically, and many full-time workers now qualify. **“I own a car and a home, so I’m out”** — for expansion adults, eligibility is based on income, not assets, and your home and vehicle don’t count. **“Applying will hurt my immigration case”** — using Medicaid you’re entitled to does not, on its own, make you a “public charge,” and emergency Medicaid is available regardless of status. **“It’s charity I shouldn’t take”** — MO HealthNet is coverage your taxes already fund, built so a health scare doesn’t become a financial one. When in doubt, apply and let the state decide.

## Cover the Rest of the Basics Too

Health coverage is one piece of the safety net. While you’re getting set up, it’s worth checking whether you also qualify for SNAP food benefits — many households qualify for both — and if rent is tight, our guide to emergency rent assistance points you to programs that pay back rent. Applying for one often makes the others easier, since much of the same information carries over.

**Ready to get covered?** Apply at **mydss.mo.gov/healthcare/apply**, call the Family Support Division at **855-373-9994**, or dial **2-1-1** to be matched with a free local enrollment helper. See all St. Louis help resources.

**Run a clinic or nonprofit that helps people get covered?** If your organization offers health services or enrollment help, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so patients searching for care can find you.

## No Bed Tonight in St. Louis? Don’t Call the Shelter First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/emergency-homeless-shelters-in-st-louis-where-to-go-tonight
Your phone says 6%. The bus shelter glass is fogging from your own breath, or you’re in the car with the engine off to save gas, listening to it tick as it cools. You have one call left in that battery, maybe two. Use it on the call that can actually match you to a bed.
Here’s the backward truth about finding a bed in St. Louis: the shelter is usually not the first call. Beds here are matched to people through a referral system, and even Gateway180, the family shelter on N. 19th Street, puts the hotline number above everything else on its own website. The city’s own shelter page names three doors in. Call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444. Dial 2-1-1. Or walk into the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. on a weekday. Write them on the back of your hand if your battery is dying.
One more thing worth knowing before winter. When the temperature hits 25 degrees or below, or the wind chill drops under 10, the City of St. Louis calls Code Blue. Depending on how bad it gets, that can mean 24-hour shelter access, warming buses and rides to a bed. On the worst nights the city’s plan adds 600 surge beds to the 400 it keeps open all year. If you know someone who has been sleeping on a different couch every week, these numbers are worth passing along quietly.
When someone answers, you don’t have to explain how you got here. Say where you are, who is with you, and whether anyone is in danger. That’s the whole script.
### What’s the fastest way to get emergency housing in St. Louis?
Call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444, dial 2-1-1, or walk into the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. on weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Those are the three shelter referral routes the City of St. Louis lists. Ages 16 to 24 can call or drop in at Covenant House Missouri, open 24 hours. In danger at home? Call ALIVE at (314) 993-2777.
### Door one: the Housing Helpline
The phone rings, and a housing specialist picks up. On the Housing Helpline, (314) 802-5444, they interview you and, if you’re in crisis, refer you to an emergency shelter or to help with rent, mortgage or utilities. The line is a joint effort of St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis, so it doesn’t matter which side of the city limits you’re standing on.
This is the number Gateway180, at 1000 N. 19th St., lists as its Housing Resource Hotline, written there as 314.802.5444. The shelters don’t want you guessing which one has a bed; the hotline is how beds get matched to people.
### Door two: 2-1-1, any hour
It’s 2 a.m., the helpline’s staff have gone home, and the cold is coming up through your shoes. That’s what 2-1-1 is for. United Way 211 of Missouri and Illinois says you can dial 211 to reach a trained resource specialist 24/7, and the call is free and confidential. If 211 won’t connect from your phone, dial 1-800-427-4626 instead; some older guides print it without the 1, as 800-427-4626, and it’s the same line.
When they answer, lead with the three things that decide where you go: where you are right now, who is with you, and whether anyone is hurt or in danger. A single man, a mom with two kids and a 19-year-old are routed to different doors, so saying it first saves you minutes when minutes matter.
### Door three: the Welcome Center on Tucker
Some people need a face, not a phone. Downtown, the morning traffic is just starting on Tucker, your breath shows in the air, and if you’re carrying what you own in one bag, that’s fine. The St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. is where people who are homeless or about to be come to meet intake specialists, and it works as a walk-in access point. The city lists its hours for shelter referral as Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Go early. Bring whatever papers you have, even if it’s just a crumpled piece of mail with your name on it.
From there, a single adult man may be referred to the Biddle Housing Opportunities Center at 1212 N. 13th St., a city-owned emergency shelter for single adult men, run by the Magdala Foundation. Its number is (314) 612-1675, but the city says referral comes through the helpline, 2-1-1 or the Welcome Center, so start with one of the three doors. If you’re a man on your own tonight, our guide to homeless shelters for men in St. Louis walks through where to go next.
### What to grab in the next ten minutes
If you still have a minute before you walk out the door, use it. Grab the phone charger before the phone, because a dead phone is how people miss the callback that has their bed in it. Grab your medications in their bottles, so whoever checks you in can read the labels. Grab any ID, a Social Security card, a birth certificate, a lease, a piece of mail with your name on it. Put them in one plastic bag and keep that bag on your body, not in the bottom of a duffel.
Then grab a layer you can sleep in. Shelter rooms can run warm or cold, and a hoodie you can pull over your face at night is worth more than anything else you could carry. If you have kids, bring the one stuffed animal or blanket that makes them sleep. That smell of home matters more than you think on the first night.
And if you have to leave in a hurry, leave. Papers can be replaced. You can’t. A case manager can help you track down a birth certificate next week; nobody can give you back a night spent somewhere dangerous.
### Shelter for who you are
The doors are the same. The bed you land in depends on who is standing next to you.
Youth ages 16 to 24: Covenant House Missouri, 2727 N. Kingshighway Blvd., (314) 533-2241. It’s open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and young people can call or drop in; for bed availability, call (314) 351-4866.
Families with children: Gateway180, 1000 N. 19th St., (314) 231-1515, works to help women, children and families reach stable housing. Call the helpline first for a referral.
Young moms: Almost Home, 3200 St. Vincent Ave., (314) 771-4663, gives motivated young moms housing support and a path to stability.
Single adult men: the Biddle Housing Opportunities Center, by referral through the three doors above.
Anyone in danger at home: ALIVE’s 24-hour crisis line is 314.993.2777, written here as (314) 993-2777. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233.
Veterans: the St. Patrick Center connects veterans who are homeless or at risk with its SSVF program at 314-356-0657.
Live in St. Louis County? The county’s Supportive Housing Program is listed at (314) 615-4450.
### Code Blue nights, step by step
You can feel Code Blue before you hear about it: the air hurts to breathe and the metal bench burns cold through your jeans. The city calls Code Blue its emergency response to dangerous cold for people experiencing homelessness, and it runs between December 1 and March 1. The trigger is 25°F or below, or a wind chill below 10°F, expected for two hours or more. At the higher levels the city activates rally points around town, timed transportation circuits and warming buses.
On those nights, call 2-1-1 or the helpline and ask one question: “Where is the nearest warming center or rally point tonight?” You can also check the City of St. Louis website for current Code Blue updates.
### Once you’re inside
The first night is the hardest. The lights are bright, the blanket smells like industrial soap, and someone down the hall is snoring like a truck. It’s okay to just sleep. Tomorrow, ask for a case manager and say the words “permanent housing.” That’s the next door.
When you’re ready, the help that pays for the next step is close. Our guide to emergency rent assistance lists the St. Louis programs that pay back rent and deposits, and the St. Patrick Center offers financial help with past-due rent, utility bills, or first month’s rent and a deposit when funding is available. For a free printed list of nearly every service in town, START HERE is the St. Louis Area Resource Directory, distributed by Criminal Justice Ministry.
### If school is part of your night
A kid doing homework by phone light in the back seat is still a student with rights. Missouri’s education department says the federal homeless education law covers children and youths who are sharing the housing of other persons due to loss of housing, economic hardship or a similar reason, or living in motels or hotels. Ask the front office who handles homeless education for the district, and let that person handle the paperwork.
Tonight, make one call. The St. Louis Housing Helpline is (314) 802-5444, and 2-1-1 answers every hour. Save this page, and when you’re ready for the next step, our St. Louis help guide and our list of free food giveaways happening today are waiting.
If you’re the diner, the laundromat or the corner store where people come in out of the cold, you already know what a warm room means. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory helps neighbors find you and helps your business get more customers, for under a dollar a day. List your business.
### If you’re helping someone find shelter
Sit next to them and make the call together. A person who has been turned away before often can’t face the phone alone, and your calm voice on speaker can carry the first two minutes. Offer a charged phone, a ride to Tucker Blvd. in the morning, a place to keep their ID safe. Tonight’s only job is a bed.
And if the weight of it is too much for either of you, call, text or chat 988 at any hour, a line Missouri’s Department of Mental Health points people to. A night like this ends. People get through it every week in this city.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What happens when you call the homeless hotline?
A.  On the St. Louis Housing Helpline, (314) 802-5444, a housing specialist interviews you about your situation. If you’re in crisis, they refer you to an emergency shelter or to help with rent, mortgage or utilities. Have your location, the people with you and any safety concerns ready to say first.
### Q. Do homeless shelters make you leave during the day?
A.  It depends on the shelter, so ask at intake. Covenant House Missouri, for ages 16 to 24, is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. During Code Blue cold, the city says it may extend shelter hours, including 24-hour access, and open daytime warming options.
### Q. Is sleeping on a couch considered homeless?
A.  For school purposes, often yes. Missouri’s education department says the federal homeless education law covers children and youths sharing the housing of other persons due to loss of housing, economic hardship or a similar reason. If that’s your family, ask your school for its homeless liaison. Adults on a couch should still call the helpline, (314) 802-5444, and describe their situation honestly.
### Q. Do homeless people need ID?
A.  Don’t let a missing ID stop you from calling. I could not find a St. Louis shelter referral page that says you need an ID just to call the helpline or 2-1-1. Bring whatever you have, even a piece of mail, and ask your case manager about replacing lost documents once you’re safe.
### Q. What to do if homeless with no money near me?
A.  Start with a free call. 2-1-1 is free and confidential and answers 24/7, and the Housing Helpline, (314) 802-5444, can refer you to an emergency shelter. Youth 16 to 24 can walk into Covenant House at 2727 N. Kingshighway Blvd. at any hour, and Covenant House says its shelter, meals and clothing come at no cost to them.
### Q. Where can I find help for homeless people in St. Louis?
A.  The St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. is a walk-in access point where people meet intake specialists and get referred to programs. The City of St. Louis Homeless Services Division, (314) 657-1704, leads the city’s Continuum of Care. For a list of local services, see the Start Here St. Louis Area Resource Directory, distributed by Criminal Justice Ministry.

## Start Here: One Call for a Bed Tonight

You don’t need to guess which shelter has space — these lines check for you:

- **2-1-1 or 1-800-427-4626**— the United Way regional line, 24/7, for emergency shelter intake anywhere in the bi-state metro.
- **City of St. Louis Homeless Services**— coordinates year-round and cold-weather overflow beds for people in the city.
- **St. Louis County Supportive Housing Program: (314) 615-4450**— Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–4:30 p.m., for county residents facing a housing crisis.

In extreme heat or cold, the city and county open **additional emergency and warming/cooling beds** — hundreds beyond the year-round baseline — so always call even if you’ve been told shelters are full.

## Emergency Shelters in St. Louis

These are among the region’s core emergency and crisis shelters. Call ahead when you can, since intake and openings change daily:

- **Gateway180 (Gateway Homeless Services)**— 1000 N 19th St; (314) 231-1515; open 24 hours. Missouri’s largest emergency shelter for women, children, and families.
- **Covenant House Missouri**— 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd; (314) 533-2241; 24 hours. Emergency and crisis shelter for youth and young adults (through their early twenties).
- **Almost Home**— 3200 St Vincent Ave; (314) 771-4663. Housing and support for young mothers and their children.
- **St. Patrick Center**— downtown; the region’s leading nonprofit for adults who are homeless or at risk, with shelter, housing, and job programs.
- **START HERE STL / Biddle House**— emergency shelter for single adult men; for intake call 2-1-1 or 800-427-4626.
- **Salvation Army Family Haven**— a family-focused shelter serving St. Louis County families.
- **Loaves & Fishes for St. Louis**— emergency shelter and support for families facing homelessness.

## Shelter by Who You Are

Different shelters serve different people, which is why one call to 2-1-1 saves time — they route you to the right door:

- **Families with children**— Gateway180, Salvation Army Family Haven, and Loaves & Fishes keep families together.
- **Single women and women with children**— Gateway180 and, for young mothers, Almost Home.
- **Single men**— Biddle House / START HERE and Peter & Paul Community Services.
- **Youth and young adults**— Covenant House Missouri’s Genesis emergency shelter.
- **Survivors of domestic violence**— call the National DV Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or ALIVE at (314) 993-2777 for safe, confidential emergency housing.
- **Veterans**— ask about the St. Patrick Center’s veteran programs and SSVF for rapid rehousing.

## What to Expect — and What to Bring

Walking into a shelter for the first time is intimidating, so here’s the reality: it’s **free**, staff are used to helping people in crisis, and **you won’t be turned away for lack of an ID or money** (though a photo ID helps if you have one). Expect a short intake conversation about your situation, a safe place to sleep, and usually meals and a shower. Bring any medications, important documents, and a change of clothes if you can grab them — but don’t delay getting to safety over packing. Most shelters connect you with a case manager who starts working with you on the next step: stable housing.

## How Shelters Actually Work

A few practical questions come up for almost everyone:

- **How long can I stay?**Emergency shelters are short-term — often a set number of nights — while your case manager works on next steps, but transitional programs can last months. No one is put back on the street without help finding the next placement.
- **Can my family stay together?**Family shelters like Gateway180 are built to keep parents and children together rather than splitting them up.
- **What about my belongings or pet?**Space for belongings is limited; ask at intake, and mention a service animal or pet so staff can help with options.
- **Is it safe?**Shelters have staff on site around the clock, secure entry, and rules that exist to keep everyone safe.
- **Do I need to be sober?**Many shelters are low-barrier, meaning you won’t be turned away for a substance-use issue — getting you safe comes first.

## Understanding Homelessness — and Why Asking for Help Is Normal

Homelessness generally takes three forms: **sheltered** (staying in an emergency shelter or transitional housing), **unsheltered** (sleeping in a car, outside, or somewhere not meant for living), and **chronic** (long-term homelessness, often alongside a disability). Most people who experience it are in it briefly, because of a single hard shock — a lost job, a medical bill, a family breakup — not because of anything they did wrong. The entire shelter system exists precisely so a temporary crisis doesn’t become a permanent one. Reaching out isn’t failure; it’s the fastest way back.

## Once You’re Safe: The First Steps Back

A shelter is also a launchpad. Using a shelter or drop-in center’s address, you can receive mail, replace a lost **ID or birth certificate**, and apply for benefits that speed your path to housing — you can get rent help, SNAP food benefits, and MO HealthNet coverage even while homeless. Your case manager can connect you with job programs (the St. Patrick Center is known for these), a Continuum of Care housing assessment, and, when you’re ready, move-in help. One step at a time, in a specific order, is how thousands of St. Louisans have found their way back to a place of their own.

## If Shelters Are Full: Staying Safe Tonight

Sometimes beds fill up — but you still have options. Keep calling **2-1-1**, since openings shift hour to hour. In dangerous heat or cold, the city and county run **warming and cooling centers** and open overflow shelter, and public spaces like libraries offer daytime refuge. A hospital emergency room will not turn away someone in medical crisis. And if the weight of this feels like too much, the **988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline** is free and available every hour of the night. This situation is temporary, and you deserve to get through it safely.

## Keeping Kids in School Through a Housing Crisis

If children are part of your situation, one federal protection matters a lot: under the **McKinney-Vento Act**, kids who are homeless — including families staying in shelters, motels, or doubled up with others — have the right to **stay enrolled in their same school** even if they’ve moved, and to get **transportation to and from it**. Every school district has a **homeless liaison** whose job is to make this happen, remove enrollment barriers like missing records, and connect families to resources. Tell your child’s school or your shelter case manager that you’d like to reach the McKinney-Vento liaison. Keeping the classroom, the friends, and the routine steady gives kids an anchor while the rest of life is in motion — and it’s their legal right, not a favor.

## Beyond Tonight: From Shelter to Housing

Emergency shelter is the first step, not the destination. Every program above can connect you to **rapid rehousing, transitional housing, and permanent supportive housing** through the St. Louis Continuum of Care — the coordinated system that moves people from crisis to a place of their own. Ask your shelter case manager about it on day one. And as you stabilize, our guides to emergency rent assistance and free food across St. Louis can help you cover the basics while you get back on your feet.

## If You’re Helping Someone Find Shelter

Watching someone you care about lose their housing is its own kind of helpless feeling — but you can do real good in a few minutes. Sit with them and call **2-1-1** together; a person in crisis often can’t face the phone alone. Offer a ride to intake, a charged phone, or a safe place to keep documents. Resist the urge to solve everything at once — tonight’s job is simply a safe bed. Save this page and pass it to anyone who might need it: a neighbor, a coworker, a client, a fellow parent at school. The difference between a night outside and a night indoors is often just one person who knew which number to call. Tonight, that can be you.

**Need shelter now?** Call **2-1-1** or **1-800-427-4626** any hour, or reach Gateway180 at **(314) 231-1515**. County residents in crisis: **(314) 615-4450**. See all St. Louis help resources.

**Run a shelter or outreach program?** If your organization provides shelter, meals, or housing help, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so neighbors in crisis — and the people helping them — can find you fast.

## Text Your ZIP to 785-503-3310: Free Food in St. Louis Today, and Which Giveaways Need No Appointment
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-residents-your-guide-to-free-food-giveaways-happening-today
Two hundred thousand people. Every month. That’s how many Operation Food Search says it feeds across the St. Louis bi-state area. So if you’re standing at an open fridge right now, cold air on your shins, staring at a jar of mustard and the last two eggs, you are not the only one. You are one of a crowd that size, and the help built for that crowd is closer than it feels.
Here’s the fastest move almost nobody knows about: text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310. Operation Food Search runs that number for finding free food near you. No app, no account, no hold music, just your thumb and a phone with a little battery left. Screenshot that number now and send it to the one friend who’d never ask out loud. If you’d rather hear a human voice, its 24-hour Hunger Hotline is (314) 726-5355, and extension 1 is the line for food locations near you.
Now the catch that sends people home with empty hands. Walking into most pantries cold does not work. The St. Louis Area Foodbank, which works with nearly 600 partners in 26 counties, says it plainly: for most food pantries, an appointment is required. Its food distribution events run the other way. Those are first come, first served, usually with no appointment and usually no ID. Know which kind of door you’re heading to before you spend the bus fare or the last quarter tank getting there.
### Can I just show up to a food pantry?
Usually not at a pantry, but yes at a distribution event. The St. Louis Area Foodbank says most pantries require an appointment and most ask for a photo ID, so call first. Its walk-through and drive-through food distribution events are first come, first served, and usually need no appointment and no ID. Neither one costs you a cent.
Write that down somewhere you’ll see it. It’s the difference between a wasted afternoon and a trunk with groceries in it.
### The call that saves you a wasted trip
Here’s the version that goes wrong, because it happens to people every week. You ride two buses with a toddler on your hip, find the pantry, pull the handle, and the door doesn’t give. Not because nobody cares. Because that pantry books its visits ahead, and nobody told you. One phone call the night before fixes that.
When you do call, ask three things: are you open tomorrow, do I need an appointment, and what should I bring. The Foodbank’s own answer on that last one is short. Bring what your pantry asks for, which may include a photo ID and proof of income. Bring a reusable bag if you have one, though bags are usually provided. And do not bring money. You do not need any money at a food pantry or a food distribution event. Not a dollar, not a donation, not a fee.
Here’s the line worth passing to the neighbor who throws food away too soon. The Foodbank says “Best By,” “Sell By” and “Expiration” dates don’t mean food is unsafe to eat after that date. That can of green beans stamped last month is still dinner. The one exception it names is infant formula, which must be used before the date on the package. Check the formula. Trust the beans.
### Free food giveaways you can walk up to
If today is the day and you can’t wait on a callback, a distribution event is your best bet. The Foodbank describes them as walk-through or drive-through events that are planned in advance and placed in areas with low access to food. Look for two names on it. Food On The Move is the walk-through one, set up shopping style, so you walk the tables and pick what your family will actually eat instead of taking a box of whatever. A Food Access and Resource Market is the drive-through version, where you stay in your seat with the heater running and the food comes to your trunk.
Browse the Foodbank’s Food Distribution Event Calendar to find a mobile market or distribution event that fits your schedule. It covers the whole bi-state area, including towns well outside the city, so scan for the one closest to you before you set out. Events can shift with weather, and the Foodbank posts schedule changes on its social media, so a quick look the morning of is worth the thirty seconds.
Can’t find one that fits today? Go back to the text line or the Hunger Hotline. Operation Food Search says that 24-hour line connects you to immediate food assistance through its partner agencies. That is the honest answer to “where can I eat tonight” when the calendar comes up empty.
### When the pantry covers today but not next month
A pantry bag is a bridge. It gets you to Friday. SNAP, the program people still call food stamps, is what gets you through the month after that, loaded onto a card you swipe at the grocery store like anyone else in line. The Foodbank describes it as a federally funded program that helps approved people buy food at grocery stores, convenience stores and some farmers’ markets.
In Missouri you apply through the Department of Social Services at mydss.mo.gov, or call its Family Support Division Information Center at 855-373-4636, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. If the online form feels like a wall, call. A person on the other end can walk you through it.
And when benefits get tangled up, neighbors step in. A local news report described one giveaway that handed out 500 hot meals and 900 cans of formula to families on SNAP. That’s this city on a hard week: folding tables, steam coming off foil pans, strangers handing strangers dinner.
### No car, kids at home, or both?
Getting there is half the battle, and it’s the half nobody plans for. A bag of canned goods weighs more than you think by the third block, handles biting into your fingers, and a winter wait at a bus shelter with a full cart is its own small misery. So solve the ride before you solve the food.
Operation Food Search points people to MoRides for transportation help, at morides.org or 844-836-7433. Call before the day you need it, not the morning of. If a ride is the thing standing between you and a pantry, say so when you call the pantry too. Some will tell you about a closer site you didn’t know existed.
If there are kids in the house, there’s a separate map just for them. Operation Food Search lists free meals for children and teens on the same Find Food map at FindFood.OperationFoodSearch.org. For the in-between weeks, when you can pay a little but not a full grocery bill, its mobile market sells a mix of free and reduced-price groceries at stops around the area, listed at OFSMetroMarket.org. That’s the option for the parent who doesn’t think of themselves as someone who goes to a pantry, and maybe would rather pay something. No shame either way. Food is food.
### What to say when you call
The first call is the hard one. Your mouth goes dry, you rehearse it twice, and you almost hang up on the second ring. Keep it short. Something like: “Hi, I need food for my family this week. Are you open, do I need an appointment, and what should I bring?” That’s it. The person who answers has heard it a thousand times, and the answer is usually kinder than the voice in your head expects.
Write down the day, the time and the address while they’re still on the line. Ask if they serve your ZIP code, because some pantries only take neighbors from certain areas. And if they say no, ask the one question that turns a dead end into a lead: “Who should I call instead?”
### More doors to knock on
If the first door doesn’t open, the next one often does. These are worth a call before you go, since every one sets its own hours and rules.
Operation Food Search: the Hunger Hotline at (314) 726-5355 and its online Find Food map at FindFood.OperationFoodSearch.org, which shows pantries and community meals.
The Salvation Army: its Greater St. Louis office runs community food pantries. Call your nearest corps for its schedule.
LifeWise STL: lists a Food Market on its site.
Sts. Joachim & Ann Care Service: runs a food pantry along with housing help and street outreach.
Cornerstone United Methodist Church: one of many church pantries. Call the church for hours before you go.
FISH food pantry: call 636-856-5151 for a referral voucher, then (636) 447-5482 for an appointment, Monday, Wednesday and Friday mornings.
O.A.S.I.S. drive-up pantry (also listed as Powell Terrace Food Pantry): (636) 724-3036.
If the gas or electric bill is what ate the grocery money this month, there’s help for that too: utility assistance programs in St. Louis.
### Have food to give instead?
Some readers land here from the other side of the table, with a full pantry and a heavy heart. Operation Food Search’s food and fund drive page shows how to host a food or fund drive, or drop off much-needed items at its warehouse. And dial 2-1-1 any time you’re helping someone who needs more than food: United Way 2-1-1 connects people with help for housing, utilities and health care.
Hungry today and not sure where to start? Text your ZIP to 785-503-3310 for food near you, then keep our St. Louis Help & Assistance hub open for rent, utility and health help.
If you run a pantry, a church kitchen or a corner grocery that hands out bags on Saturdays, people are searching for your door right now. List it on St Louis Near Me Directory so the next family finds you before the shelves run bare.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is there a free food giveaway in St. Louis today?
A.  Check the St. Louis Area Foodbank’s Food Distribution Event Calendar for today’s walk-through and drive-through events, which usually need no appointment. If nothing fits, text your ZIP to 785-503-3310 or call Operation Food Search’s 24-hour Hunger Hotline at (314) 726-5355 for food near you.
### Q. What food pantries are in my area?
A.  Use the St. Louis Area Foodbank’s pantry locator or Operation Food Search’s Find Food map at FindFood.OperationFoodSearch.org. You can also text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310, or call (314) 726-5355, extension 1, for locations near you.
### Q. Can anybody get food at a food pantry?
A.  A food pantry exists so people in need can get food free of charge. Each pantry sets its own rules, and some serve only certain areas or ask for a referral, so call ahead and ask whether you qualify.
### Q. Do food pantries require proof of income?
A.  Some do. The St. Louis Area Foodbank says to bring the documents your pantry requires, which may include a photo ID and proof of income. Food distribution events usually don’t ask for ID at all.
### Q. Can I go to two food pantries in one day?
A.  Each pantry sets its own visit rules, so ask when you call for an appointment. A food distribution event usually needs no appointment, so it can be another stop that day.
### Q. What does the Hunger Hotline do?
A.  Operation Food Search’s 24-hour Hunger Hotline, (314) 726-5355, connects you to immediate food assistance through its partner agencies and points you to food near you.
### Q. What can I do if I have no money and no food?
A.  Go anyway. You don’t need money at a food pantry or a distribution event. Text your ZIP to 785-503-3310, dial 2-1-1, and apply for SNAP at mydss.mo.gov so next month is steadier.
### Q. What should I bring to a food pantry?
A.  Bring whatever your pantry asks for, often a photo ID and sometimes proof of income, plus a reusable bag if you have one. Bags are usually provided, and you never need to bring money.
### Q. Is food past the Best By date safe?
A.  The St. Louis Area Foodbank says Best By, Sell By and Expiration dates don’t mean food is unsafe after that date. The exception is infant formula, which must be used before the date on the package.

### Most Needed Food Items

When you're gathering items to donate, it's helpful to know what's most needed. Operation Food Search is asking for non-perishable items that are easy to store and use. They specifically request that you **please avoid glass containers and ramen noodles.**

- **Pop-top cans:**These are super convenient.
- **Canned proteins:**Think light tuna or salmon, canned chicken, or meat.

- **Fruits and vegetables:**Canned fruits (in natural juices) and canned vegetables.

## Government Assistance Programs

Sometimes, getting help with food means looking into programs offered by the government. These programs are designed to provide a safety net for individuals and families facing food insecurity. It's good to know what's available, even if you're just looking for a little extra support.

### SNAP Benefit Information

SNAP, which stands for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, is a federal program that helps low-income individuals and families buy food. Think of it as a way to stretch your food budget further. To figure out if you qualify, you'll need to look at your household income and certain expenses. The Missouri Department of Social Services handles SNAP applications for residents of Missouri. They can help you understand the process and what documents you'll need. **Applying for SNAP can make a real difference in your ability to get nutritious food on the table.**

### Missouri Department of Social Services

The Missouri Department of Social Services (DSS) is the main agency you'll interact with for state-level assistance programs, including SNAP. They have various offices and resources to help you. If you're unsure about the application process or need help with an existing case, reaching out to them is a good first step. They also often have information about other support services that might be available to you and your family. You can find more details about their services and how to apply on their website. They also help with processing applications and scheduling interviews, which can be a big help when you're trying to get benefits quickly. For instance, they were involved in distributing 500 hot meals and 900 cans of formula to families in need recently. Check DSS services.

Here's a general idea of what you might need:

- **Proof of Identity:**Like a driver's license or state ID.
- **Proof of Income:**Pay stubs or a letter from an employer.
- **Proof of Household Expenses:**Rent receipts, utility bills.
- **Social Security Cards:**For all household members.

Applying for government assistance can sometimes feel complicated, but remember that these programs exist to help people like you. Don't hesitate to ask questions and seek clarification from the Department of Social Services. They are there to guide you through the process.

Looking for help with government programs? We can guide you to the right resources. Visit our website today to learn more and find the support you need.

## Shut-Off Date Circled in Red? Missouri Opens LIHEAP Oct. 1 for 60+, Nov. 1 for Everyone
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-apply-for-liheap-in-missouri-energy-assistance-in-st-louis-2026
A red circle around the shut-off date. You drew it on the Spire bill, and the bill has been sitting on the kitchen counter ever since. The furnace kicks on for the first time this season, the house fills with that burnt-dust smell, and you stand there doing math that won’t come out. You haven’t called anyone yet, because you aren’t sure who to call.
Make one call before that bill goes back under the magnet on the fridge. In the City of St. Louis or Wellston, it’s the Urban League at 314-615-3632, weekdays 8 a.m. to noon. In St. Louis County, it’s CAASTLC’s energy line, 314-446-4420. What you’re applying for is LIHEAP, the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, and it pays the utility directly, so the money lands on that Spire bill, not in your hand.
If you, or anyone in your home, is 60 or older or has a disability, that door opened October 1, a full month before everyone else. Everyone else can apply starting November 1.
Then ask Spire or Ameren for the form almost nobody asks for: the elderly or disabled customer registration. Anyone 65 or older qualifies, and so does a household with a federal disability award letter or a doctor’s form saying the home needs gas or electric service to stay healthy. Under Missouri’s Cold Weather Rule, from November 1 through March 31 the utility can’t shut off a registered household under 150% of the federal poverty line that’s on a winter payment plan and pays at least half of each month’s bill; the rest gets spread into later payments. You can list a second person on the form, a daughter or a neighbor, and the utility has to notify that person too before any shut-off. It runs out every year, so renew it each fall. Text that to anyone you know over 65 who heats with Spire or Ameren.
The gap nobody circles for you: crisis help (ECIP) doesn’t open until November 1 for senior and disabled households, and December 1 for everyone else. If your shut-off date comes sooner, the bridge is your utility and a charity. Call Spire or Ameren and ask for a payment arrangement, and apply to Heat Up St. Louis, which pays past-due bills straight to the utility.
Ask for this season’s form, MO 886-4576, because the agencies turn away last year’s.
And don’t rule yourself out on a guess. The income line is higher than you might think: a household of four can bring in up to $5,657 a month before taxes and still qualify, on the state’s chart that changed October 1.
Already on SNAP? Skip the proof of income on the LIHEAP form. Working mornings in the city? The Urban League’s drop box on North Kingshighway is open from noon to 5 p.m.
### What is LIHEAP in Missouri?
A few weeks after you’re approved, you open the next bill and the balance is smaller; the money never touches your hands. LIHEAP is a federally funded program that helps income-eligible households pay their home heating and cooling bills. In Missouri it’s administered by the Department of Social Services (DSS) Family Support Division, and it comes in two parts:
Energy Assistance (EA) - a one-time payment each season toward one heating fuel, paid directly to your utility company. You never touch the money; it lands on your account.
Energy Crisis Intervention Program (ECIP) - emergency help when you’re facing disconnection, already shut off, or watching the propane gauge sink toward empty. Winter crisis help can reach up to $800 and opens November 1 for senior and disabled households, December 1 for everyone else. Shut-off date before then? Tell the agency when you apply, and call Spire or Ameren about a payment arrangement while you wait. Once the Cold Weather Rule starts November 1, a LIHEAP pledge for the amount due counts as the payment the utility asks for on a winter plan.
Because it pays the utility straight away, LIHEAP pairs well with every other program out there. Many people use it alongside charity help like Heat Up St. Louis and their own utility’s payment plans. One quick note on geography: this is Missouri’s LIHEAP. If you live across the river in Illinois, you’ll apply through Illinois’ own LIHEAP program instead - dial 2-1-1 and they’ll route you to the right one.
### Do I qualify? The income chart that changed October 1
Pull last month’s pay stubs and benefit letters out of the drawer before you read this chart. Two things decide eligibility: your household income and your countable assets. Missouri sets the income cutoff at 60% of the state median income, set by household size and adjusted each year. The agency counts everyone’s gross income from last month, before taxes. Here are the monthly limits on the state’s current chart:
These limits are adjusted each year, so confirm your household’s row on the Missouri DSS Benefit Program Income Limits chart before you rule yourself out. On top of income, there’s an asset test: you generally need $3,000 or less in bank, retirement, and investment accounts. And you must be responsible for paying your home’s energy costs - if heat is included in your rent, LIHEAP usually isn’t your program.
One rule people trip on: everyone living in your home counts as your household, and their income counts too - even roommates who aren’t related to you. Add up the whole household’s income before you decide you’re over the limit, and don’t rule yourself out on a guess. Renters can qualify as long as the utility bill is in your name.
Random, but somebody has to say it - Columbia, Illinois eats well.
### How much does LIHEAP pay in Missouri?
The amount depends on your income, household size, fuel type and available funding. Here’s what the state lists right now, so you know what to expect:
Regular Energy Assistance (EA): one payment per season toward one heating fuel, applied to your utility account. The most it pays is $326 for natural gas, $318 for electric and $495 for tank propane, caps that are adjusted each year.
Winter crisis (ECIP): up to $800 when you’re facing disconnection or out of fuel.
Summer crisis (ECIP): up to $300 toward cooling, available in the warm months - see our guide to Cool Down St. Louis and summer cooling help.
It’s not a fortune, but it’s often exactly enough to stop a shut-off and reset your footing - and you can receive EA and apply for crisis help in the same season.
Waiting on a decision, with the shut-off date still circled? Read our guides to Heat Up St. Louis and the Cold Weather Rule while you wait.
If you’re the agency or the nonprofit that walks families through a heating season, list it with us, and the next family searching for heating help can find your door.
### How do I apply for LIHEAP in Missouri?
You have three ways to apply, and none of them require internet skills you don’t have:
Online - the fastest route. Start on the state’s LIHEAP page at dss.mo.gov, which links the online application and a printable copy.
By phone - call the Family Support Division at 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO) to ask questions or request a paper application by mail.
In person, by mail or by fax - bring, mail or fax the paper form to the agency that serves your address (see the St. Louis agencies below).
Whichever way you go, use this season’s form, MO 886-4576. The application changed, and versions from previous years aren’t accepted. Applications are typically reviewed within about 30 business days, faster when you’re in an active crisis. Apply as early in the season as you can, because crisis funds are limited and run out as winter deepens.
### Urban League or CAASTLC: where to apply in the St. Louis area
LIHEAP runs through one agency per area, so your application goes to the one that covers your address. In the city and the county, that’s one of these two. Call first to confirm hours:
St. Louis County → Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) 2709 Woodson Rd., Overland, MO 63114 • energy line 314-446-4420 • fax 314-446-4480 • energyhelp@caastlc.org • caastlc.org/energy-services Mail it, fax it, email it, or drop it off at Woodson Road or at 26B North Oaks Plaza in Northwoods.
City of St. Louis & Wellston → Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis 1408 N. Kingshighway Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63113 • 314-615-3632 • ulstl.com It takes applications weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon. Working mornings? A drop box is open from noon to 5 p.m., or you can mail it there.
Live in one of the outlying counties - Jefferson, St. Charles, Franklin, Lincoln? Every Missouri county is served by a Community Action Agency. Call 2-1-1 (United Way) and they’ll connect you to the one that covers your address.
### What documents do I need?
Gathering everything before you apply is the difference between a smooth approval and weeks of back-and-forth. Have these ready for everyone in your household:
Proof of last month’s gross income (pay stubs, an SSI or Social Security award letter, an unemployment or pension statement). Anyone already on SNAP can skip this one.
Proof of a Social Security number for every household member
Your current gas and electric bills, plus any shut-off notice
This season’s application, form MO 886-4576, filled out
Looking for more local resources? A tool like findhelp.org can point you to food, housing, and health programs near you, and you can search the St Louis Near Me Directory for St. Louis organizations and community resources.
If you run a nonprofit, a weatherization crew or a service that helps families keep the heat on, list it with us so more of the neighbors and customers who need what you do can reach you.
### When can I apply for LIHEAP this season?
Timing matters, and the calendar has a head-start built in for the people who feel the cold hardest:
Energy Assistance (EA) runs October 1 through May 31. Households with a member age 60 or older, or who has a disability, can apply starting October 1; everyone else starts November 1.
Winter crisis (ECIP) opens November 1 for senior and disabled households and December 1 for everyone else, and runs while funding lasts.
Summer crisis (ECIP) runs June through September.
The takeaway: don’t wait until February. Apply in the fall, and if a crisis hits later in the season, you can still come back for ECIP.
### The 30 business days after you apply
Once your application is approved, the payment goes straight to your utility company and shows up as a credit on your account - you won’t receive a check to cash. Regular applications are reviewed within about 30 business days; crisis (ECIP) cases move faster because a disconnection clock is ticking. You can check your status by calling 855-373-4636 or the agency that took your application.
A detail worth knowing: getting approved for regular Energy Assistance does not use up your crisis eligibility. If an emergency hits later in the winter, you can come back and apply for ECIP on top of the EA payment you already received. And while you wait, it’s always worth calling your utility to let them know an application is in - it shows good faith and can buy you time.
People are asking
### What happens if you don’t pay your utility bill on time in Missouri?
It happens in steps, and the last one hangs on your door: before your gas or electric company can shut you off, the Missouri Public Service Commission says it must send a shut-off notice, try to reach you in person, and then put a hang-tag on your door or make at least two phone calls. Paying late on five bills in 12 straight months is enough for the utility to require a security deposit just to keep the service you already have. If it does shut you off, getting it back can cost a reconnection fee and a deposit, and if you broke an earlier payment arrangement, the company can ask for the full balance. So the cheapest day to call your utility is the day you know you’ll be short, not the day that tag shows up.
### Stack it with Heat Up, Spire and Ameren help
LIHEAP is the foundation, but it’s rarely the only help you qualify for - and if a disability is what put your household on a fixed income, it’s worth learning how to apply for SSI and SSDI disability benefits in St. Louis while you’re at it. Because it pays the utility directly, it stacks cleanly with charity grants and your provider’s own programs. Here’s what else is on the table in the St. Louis area:
### Don’t forget free weatherization
Here’s the part almost nobody applies for: if you qualify for LIHEAP, you likely qualify for Missouri’s Weatherization Assistance Program, too. It pays for free energy-efficiency upgrades - attic insulation, air sealing, and furnace repair or replacement - that permanently lower your bills instead of just paying this month’s. The income limit is even more generous (up to 200% of the federal poverty level), and the same Community Action Agencies handle it. When you apply for energy assistance, ask CAASTLC or the Urban League to add you to the weatherization list. Few things in the safety net pay back this well, and the wait is worth taking.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How do I apply for LIHEAP in Missouri?
A.  Apply online from the state’s LIHEAP page at dss.mo.gov, or send this season’s paper form, MO 886-4576, to your local agency: the Urban League (314-615-3632) for the City of St. Louis and Wellston, or CAASTLC (314-446-4420) for St. Louis County. Households with someone 60 or older or disabled can apply from October 1, everyone else from November 1. Have last month’s income proof, Social Security numbers and current bills ready.
### Q. Is there a way to apply for LIHEAP online?
A.  Yes. The state’s LIHEAP page at dss.mo.gov links an online application, and it’s the fastest route. Prefer paper? Print form MO 886-4576 from the same page, or call 855-373-4636 and they’ll mail one. In St. Louis County, CAASTLC also takes a finished form by email at energyhelp@caastlc.org or by fax at 314-446-4480.
### Q. What is the phone number for LIHEAP in Mo?
A.  The statewide line is the Family Support Division at 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO). Call it with questions, to check on an application, or to get a paper form mailed to you. Around here, the agency that takes your application is the better call: the Urban League at 314-615-3632 for the City and Wellston, or CAASTLC’s energy line at 314-446-4420 for St. Louis County.
### Q. What is the income limit for LIHEAP in Missouri?
A.  It’s 60% of the state median income, set by household size. On the current DSS chart, gross monthly income can be up to $2,942 for one person, $3,847 for two, $4,752 for three, $5,657 for four and $6,562 for five, rising to $8,146 for ten. There’s also a resource limit of about $3,000. The limits are adjusted each year, so check the live chart before you rule yourself out.
### Q. What income is counted for LIHEAP?
A.  Everyone who lives in your home counts, roommates included, and so does their income. The agency looks at last month’s gross income, before taxes: paychecks, Social Security or SSI, unemployment, pensions. Add it all up and compare it to the chart row for your household size. One shortcut: anyone already on SNAP doesn’t have to send income proof.
### Q. How much does LIHEAP pay in Missouri?
A.  Regular Energy Assistance is one payment per season for one fuel, paid straight to your utility. The current caps are $326 for natural gas, $318 for electric and $495 for tank propane, adjusted each year. Crisis help (ECIP) can go higher when you’re facing disconnection: up to $800 in winter and up to $300 for summer cooling. Your exact amount depends on income, household size and fuel type.
### Q. How many times can you use LIHEAP in Missouri?
A.  Regular Energy Assistance pays once per season, for one fuel. Crisis help is separate, so the regular payment doesn’t use up your chance at ECIP if a shut-off notice lands on the counter in January. When the next season opens, you apply again on that season’s form.
### Q. What are common reasons for LIHEAP denial?
A.  Most trace back to the rules on this page. Household income over the chart for your size (count everyone in the home), more than about $3,000 in bank, retirement or investment accounts, or heat that’s included in your rent instead of billed to you. Paperwork sinks plenty of applications too: missing income proof, a missing Social Security number, or an old-year form instead of MO 886-4576.
### Q. What if my income is a little too high?
A.  Don’t give up - LIHEAP isn’t the only help. Charities like Heat Up St. Louis, your utility’s own programs (Ameren’s Keeping Current, Spire’s DollarHelp, which reaches up to 300% of poverty), and the Salvation Army each set their own limits. Dial 2-1-1 to be matched to a program that fits your household’s numbers.
### Q. What is the $500 direct cash assistance program in Missouri?
A.  If you see this phrase online, know that it is not LIHEAP - LIHEAP pays your utility company directly, never you in cash. Missouri has no standing program that simply mails eligible residents a flat $500. One-time relief funds and guaranteed-income pilots do appear from time to time, but be cautious of any site that charges a fee to apply; legitimate assistance never does. Dial 2-1-1 to find what is actually available to you right now.

## What is LIHEAP in Missouri?

LIHEAP is a federally funded program that helps income-eligible households pay their home heating and cooling bills. In Missouri it’s administered by the Department of Social Services (DSS) Family Support Division, and it comes in two parts:

- **Energy Assistance (EA)**— a once-a-year payment toward your primary heating (or summer cooling) cost, paid- *directly to your utility company*. You never touch the money; it lands on your account.
- **Energy Crisis Intervention Program (ECIP)**— emergency help when you’re facing disconnection, already shut off, or about to run out of fuel. This is the one to reach for when the situation is urgent.

Because it pays the utility straight away, LIHEAP pairs well with every other program out there. Many people use it alongside charity help like Heat Up St. Louis and their own utility’s payment plans. One quick note on geography: this is **Missouri’s** LIHEAP. If you live across the river in Illinois, you’ll apply through Illinois’ own LIHEAP program instead — dial 2-1-1 and they’ll route you to the right one.

## Do I qualify? Income limits and the asset test

**Two things decide eligibility: your household income and your countable assets.** Missouri sets the income cutoff at roughly 60% of the state median income, which changes every year and is set by household size. Here are the current monthly gross-income limits (chart effective April 1, 2026):

Bigger household? The limit keeps climbing with each person — check the live figure on the Missouri DSS Benefit Program Income Limits chart, which updates annually. On top of income, there’s an **asset test: you generally need $3,000 or less** in bank, retirement, and investment accounts. And you must be responsible for paying your home’s energy costs — if heat is included in your rent, LIHEAP usually isn’t your program.

One rule people trip on: **everyone living in your home counts as your household, and their income counts too** — even roommates who aren’t related to you. Add up the whole household’s income before you decide you’re over the limit, and don’t rule yourself out on a guess. Renters can qualify as long as the utility bill is in your name.

## How much does LIHEAP pay in Missouri?

The amount depends on your income, household size, fuel type, and available funding — but here are the current 2026 figures so you know what to expect:

- **Regular Energy Assistance (EA):**a heating payment of- **$153 to $495**, applied to your utility account.
- **Winter crisis (ECIP):**up to- **$800**when you’re facing disconnection or out of fuel.
- **Summer crisis (ECIP):**up to- **$300**toward cooling, available in the warm months — see our guide to Cool Down St. Louis and summer cooling help.

It’s not a fortune, but it’s often exactly enough to stop a shut-off and reset your footing — and you can receive EA *and* apply for crisis help in the same season.

## How do I apply for LIHEAP in Missouri?

**You have three ways to apply, and none of them require internet skills you don’t have:**

- **Online**— the fastest route. Apply through the state portal at mydss.mo.gov/utility-assistance (available in English and Spanish).
- **By phone**— call the Family Support Division at- **855-373-4636**(855-FSD-INFO) to ask questions or request a paper application by mail.
- **In person**— take your documents to a local Community Action Agency, which will fill out the application with you (see the St. Louis agencies below).

Applications are typically processed within about 30 days — faster when you’re in an active crisis. Apply as early in the season as you can, because crisis funds are limited and run out as winter deepens.

## Where to apply for LIHEAP in the St. Louis area

If you’d rather sit down with someone, two agencies handle most LIHEAP intake in the metro. Call first to confirm hours and whether you need an appointment:

- **St. Louis County → Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC)**
 2709 Woodson Rd., Overland, MO 63114 • 314-863-0015 • caastlc.org/energy-services
- **City of St. Louis & Wellston → Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis**
 1408 N. Kingshighway Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63113 • 314-615-3632 • ulstl.com

Live in one of the outlying counties — Jefferson, St. Charles, Franklin, Lincoln? Every Missouri county is served by a Community Action Agency. Call **2-1-1** (United Way) and they’ll connect you to the one that covers your address.

## What documents do I need?

Gathering everything before you apply is the difference between a smooth approval and weeks of back-and-forth. Have these ready for everyone in your household:

- A **photo ID**for the applicant
- **Social Security numbers or cards**for every household member
- **Proof of income**from the prior month (pay stubs, SSI or Social Security award letter, unemployment or pension statement)
- Your **most recent gas and electric bills**(and a disconnection notice, if you have one)

## When to apply: the 2025–2026 deadlines

Timing matters, and the calendar has a head-start built in for the people who feel the cold hardest:

- **Energy Assistance (EA)**runs- **October 1 through May 31**. Households with a member- **age 60 or older, or who has a disability, can apply starting October 1**; everyone else starts- **November 1**.
- **Winter crisis (ECIP)**opens in November (elderly and disabled first, all others from December 1) and runs while funding lasts.
- **Summer crisis (ECIP)**runs June through September.

The takeaway: don’t wait until February. Apply in the fall, and if a crisis hits later in the season, you can still come back for ECIP.

## What happens after you apply

Once your application is approved, the payment goes **straight to your utility company** and shows up as a credit on your account — you won’t receive a check to cash. Regular applications are reviewed within about 30 business days; crisis (ECIP) cases move faster because a disconnection clock is ticking. You can check your status by calling **855-373-4636** or the agency that took your application.

A detail worth knowing: getting approved for regular Energy Assistance does *not* use up your crisis eligibility. If an emergency hits later in the winter, you can come back and apply for ECIP on top of the EA payment you already received. And while you wait, it’s always worth calling your utility to let them know an application is in — it shows good faith and can buy you time.

## Stack LIHEAP with other help

LIHEAP is the foundation, but it’s rarely the only help you qualify for. Because it pays the utility directly, it stacks cleanly with charity grants and your provider’s own programs. Here’s what else is on the table in the St. Louis area:

## Don’t forget free weatherization

Here’s the part almost nobody applies for: if you qualify for LIHEAP, you likely qualify for Missouri’s **Weatherization Assistance Program**, too. It pays for **free energy-efficiency upgrades** — attic insulation, air sealing, and furnace repair or replacement — that permanently lower your bills instead of just paying this month’s. The income limit is even more generous (up to 200% of the federal poverty level), and the same Community Action Agencies handle it. When you apply for energy assistance, ask CAASTLC or the Urban League to add you to the weatherization list. It’s one of the best deals in the entire safety net, and the wait is worth it.

## Missouri Cold Weather Rule: How to Stop a Winter Utility Shutoff
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-cold-weather-rule-how-to-stop-a-winter-utility-shutoff-2026
It usually arrives on the coldest possible week. A shut-off notice with a date on it, and a pit in your stomach. Maybe a medical bill put you behind in Overland. Maybe a family in Crystal City is stretching one paycheck across two months of winter. Or your hours got cut in Washington, right when the furnace started running nonstop.
Here’s something Missouri utility companies don’t always volunteer: during the winter, they can’t just cut your heat off whenever they want. A state law called the Cold Weather Rule stands between you and a freezing house — but only if you know it exists and take the one step it requires. This guide explains exactly how it works, who it covers, and what to do the moment you’re worried about a disconnection, verified against Missouri’s current rule for the 2025–2026 winter.
Worried about a shut-off? Call your utility today and ask for a Cold Weather Rule payment agreement - before the disconnection date, not after. If the bill itself is the problem, our utility assistance guide walks through who helps pay it.
If you’re the agency, the church fund or the furnace crew that keeps a family’s heat on through the cold months, list it with us so more neighbors can find you.
### What is the Missouri Cold Weather Rule?
The Cold Weather Rule is a Missouri regulation that limits when regulated electric and natural gas companies can disconnect your heat-related service during winter. It runs every year from November 1 through March 31. Its most important protection: a utility cannot shut off your service on any day the National Weather Service forecast predicts the temperature will drop below 32°F within the next 72 hours.
That 72-hour window is new. In 2025, Senate Bill 4 tripled it from the old 24-hour rule — so a single warm afternoon in the forecast no longer opens a window for disconnection. It’s a meaningful upgrade for families living paycheck to paycheck through a Missouri winter. The rule covers whatever you use to heat your home, natural gas or electricity, so gas-heated and all-electric households are both protected.
The rule is not free money, and it won’t forgive your balance. It delays disconnection and gives you a structured way to catch up — it doesn’t erase what you owe. Think of it as a legal timeout that keeps the heat on while you get back on your feet.
### Which utilities does the Cold Weather Rule cover?
The rule applies to investor-owned electric and gas utilities regulated by the Missouri Public Service Commission (PSC). In the St. Louis area, that covers the big ones:
If you’re served by a city utility, a co-op, or you heat with delivered propane, you’re not automatically covered — but don’t assume you’re out of luck. Many municipal utilities and co-ops adopt their own winter moratoriums voluntarily. Call your provider and ask directly what winter protections they offer.
### What you must do to stay protected
The rule protects you, but it isn’t automatic — you have to act. To keep or restore service during the cold-weather months, you generally need to enter a Cold Weather Rule payment agreement with your utility. Here’s how it works:
You agree to pay your current arrears spread over about 12 months, on top of your ongoing monthly bills.
If you genuinely can’t afford that budget amount, you can ask for a longer term by mutual agreement — utilities are expected to work with you.
Staying on the plan is what keeps the protection alive. Miss the agreed payments and you can lose it.
The single most important move is timing: call before the disconnection date. Once you’re on a payment agreement, the utility can’t disconnect you for the covered balance as long as you’re keeping up your end.
### How to get reconnected if you’ve already been shut off
If your service is already off, the Cold Weather Rule still helps — you don’t have to pay the entire past-due balance to get the heat back on. Reconnection for less than the full amount owed is allowed under the rule.
The exact down payment depends on your history. If this is your first time needing help, entering a standard payment agreement is usually enough. If you previously defaulted on a Cold Weather Rule agreement, you’ll typically need to pay an initial amount — often 50% of the past-due balance or $500, whichever is less — and spread the rest over a new 12-month plan. Some utilities set higher down payments for repeat situations, so confirm the exact figure with Ameren, Spire, Evergy, or Liberty directly.
Once you make the required payment and enter the agreement, the utility must reconnect you promptly — and faster when temperatures are dangerous. One tip that saves people money: if you’ve applied for LIHEAP or a charity pledge, tell the utility. A pending pledge can count toward your reconnection and sometimes covers the down payment entirely, so ask whether it can be applied before you drain your own savings.
### How to set up your payment agreement
When you call your utility, being specific and organized is the difference between a smooth agreement and a runaround:
Say the words. Tell the representative you want to set up a Cold Weather Rule payment agreement. Naming it signals you know your rights.
Know your numbers. Have your account number ready and a realistic sense of what you can pay each month on top of your regular bill.
Get the terms in writing. Ask for the down payment, the monthly amount, and the length of the plan confirmed by email or mail.
Don’t over-promise. Agree to a monthly amount you can actually sustain — defaulting on the plan is exactly what costs people their protection.
Keep every confirmation number and receipt. If there’s ever a dispute, that paper trail is your proof.
The call itself is usually short. The hard part is making it before the disconnection date — so put it at the top of today’s list.
### What happens when the rule ends on March 31?
This is the trap that catches people every spring: the Cold Weather Rule’s disconnection protection ends on March 31, and utilities can begin shutting off past-due accounts again starting April 1. If you rode out the winter on the rule’s protection but never got onto a payment plan, that first warm week is when the shut-off notices go out.
Don’t let winter’s breathing room lull you. Before the end of March, make sure you’re either caught up or locked into a payment agreement that carries you past April 1. If you’re on a Cold Weather Rule plan and keeping up with it, you stay protected — the plan doesn’t expire just because the season does.
### Lower the bill so this doesn’t happen again
A payment plan handles this winter; free weatherization handles every winter after. If you qualify for LIHEAP, you likely also qualify for Missouri’s Weatherization Assistance Program, which pays for free insulation, air sealing, and furnace repair or replacement that permanently cut your heating costs. The same Community Action Agencies — CAASTLC in St. Louis County, the Urban League in the City — handle it, and it’s worth the wait list. Also ask your utility about Budget Billing, which averages your yearly usage into a flat monthly amount so a brutal January doesn’t blindside you.
### Extra protection for serious illness
Missouri’s utility rules provide added protection when a disconnection would endanger someone’s health. If a member of your household has a serious illness, a licensed medical professional can certify that losing service would be especially dangerous, which can extend your protection. Ask your utility how to register a medical certification on your account, and have your doctor’s office ready to provide it. This lives in Missouri’s formal regulation (20 CSR 4240-13.055), so it’s a right, not a favor.
### The Cold Weather Rule buys time — use it
The rule is a shield, not a solution. The smartest thing you can do with the breathing room it gives you is line up real help to pay down the balance:
Apply for LIHEAP (Missouri Energy Assistance) — the state program that pays your utility directly, up to $800 for a winter crisis.
Reach out to Heat Up St. Louis for charity grants toward past-due heating bills.
Ask your utility about its own help — Ameren’s Keeping Current bill credits or Spire’s DollarHelp.
Use the timeout to stack these up. That’s how a winter emergency turns into a manageable plan instead of a shut-off in February.
### If your utility won’t work with you
Utilities are required to follow the Cold Weather Rule. If you believe yours is violating it — refusing a payment agreement you’re entitled to, or threatening a disconnection during a cold-weather window — you have somewhere to turn. Contact the Missouri Public Service Commission Consumer Services line at 1-800-392-4211, or file a complaint at psc.mo.gov. You have rights as a utility customer, and the PSC exists to enforce them.
Looking for more local resources? A tool like findhelp.org can point you to food, housing, and health programs near you, and you can search the St Louis Near Me Directory for St. Louis organizations and community resources.
If you run a nonprofit or a service that helps neighbors in need, listing it is how the people looking for you actually find you.
