### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best job for a convicted felon?
A.  The strongest options are fields that hire on skills and offer stability: skilled trades through unions and apprenticeships (you can try out trades via the BUD/Missouri Works program), warehousing and manufacturing, commercial driving (CDL), food service, and landscaping. In St. Louis these roles often pay about $16–$35 an hour and are among the most open to applicants with records.
### Q. Does the city of St. Louis hire felons?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis “banned the box,” so its job applications no longer ask you to check a box for a felony conviction, and a record won’t automatically screen you out. It’s a recognized second-chance employer for many municipal roles.
### Q. What employers are felon friendly?
A.  In the St. Louis area, employers known for hiring on skills over background include Amazon warehouses, MOD Pizza, Icon Window Cleaning, Spectrum Brands, and many skilled-trade and manufacturing companies, with roles often starting around $15–$28 an hour. You can browse current second-chance-friendly openings on the St. Louis Near Me jobs board.
### Q. Can a felon work at a dispensary in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the offense. Under Missouri’s constitution, a marijuana offense that has been expunged or is currently eligible for expungement is not automatically disqualifying for cannabis-industry work. Other felonies and out-of-state offenses are treated differently, so check your specific eligibility before applying. For how the industry itself is regulated on both sides of the river, see what to know about cannabis dispensaries in St. Louis.
### Q. What's the deal with background checks when I'm looking for a job?
A.  So, employers can look into your past. It's a normal part of hiring for many jobs. But, you have rights! They can't just say 'no' because of a past mistake. They should look at the job and what happened. Sometimes, there are 'ban the box' laws that say they can't ask about your record right away. It's good to know if those apply where you are.
### Q. Are there special websites for people with a record?
A.  Totally! There are websites out there that are all about helping folks like you find work. They often partner with companies that are more open to hiring people who have a past. Think of them as a shortcut to finding places that are willing to give you a chance. Just search for 'felon friendly job boards' or 'second chance employment'.
### Q. What kind of jobs are usually more open to hiring me?
A.  Good question! Many jobs that involve working with your hands or in industries that are always busy tend to be more welcoming. Think about construction, manufacturing, warehouses, and even some jobs in healthcare or helping professions. These places often focus more on your skills and your willingness to work hard.
### Q. How can I make my past less of a hurdle when applying?
A.  It's all about how you present yourself. Focus on what you *can* do now. Highlight skills you learned, even if it was during a tough time. Be honest, but frame it positively. Maybe explain what you learned from your past and how you're ready to be a reliable employee. Practice talking about it calmly and confidently.
### Q. What if I don't have a lot of recent work experience?
A.  No worries! Think about skills you have that don't come from a job. Did you learn anything in programs? Are you good at problem-solving or working with others? Even volunteer work or personal projects count. You can also look into training programs or apprenticeships that can give you new skills and recent experience.
### Q. Where can I get help if I'm feeling stuck or discouraged?
A.  You're not alone! There are lots of groups and people who want to help. Look for re-entry programs in your community. They often have job counselors, workshops on interview skills, and even support groups where you can connect with others going through similar things. Sometimes just talking to someone who gets it makes a huge difference.

## Navigating the Job Market After Incarceration

Navigating the Job Market After Incarceration

Okay, so you've done your time and you're ready to get back out there and find a job. That's awesome! But let's be real, the job market can feel like a maze sometimes, especially when you've got a record. It's not always straightforward, and you might run into some hurdles. The good news is, there are ways to tackle this head-on.

### Understanding Your Rights and Protections

First off, it's good to know that you have some rights. Depending on where you live, there might be laws in place to help prevent employers from automatically saying 'no' just because of your past. These are often called 'ban the box' laws, and they usually mean an employer can't ask about your criminal history right at the very beginning of the application process. They typically have to wait until later, like after they've decided they're interested in you.

It's also worth looking into 'fair chance' hiring initiatives. These aren't everywhere, but they're popping up more and more. They aim to give folks with a criminal record a fairer shot at getting hired by encouraging employers to look at the whole picture, not just the conviction.

### Building a Strong Resume and Cover Letter

Your resume and cover letter are your first impression, so you want them to shine. Think about what skills you picked up, even if it was during your incarceration. Did you learn a trade? Did you take any classes? Did you manage anything or work with others? These are all transferable skills that employers want to see.

When writing your resume, focus on what you *can* do now. Instead of dwelling on the past, highlight your strengths and what you're looking for. For your cover letter, this is your chance to tell a bit of your story (if you're comfortable) and explain why you're a great fit for the job. You can briefly address your background if you feel it's necessary, but always spin it positively, focusing on what you learned and how you've grown.

### Highlighting Transferable Skills

This is a big one. Think about all the things you've done that could apply to a job. For example, if you had to manage your time well in a structured environment, that's a skill. If you worked on a team, that's a skill. Problem-solving, communication, reliability – these are all valuable.

Here are a few examples:

- **Reliability:**Showing up on time, every time. This is huge for employers.
- **Teamwork:**Working well with others to get a job done.
- **Problem-Solving:**Figuring things out when they go wrong.
- **Following Instructions:**Doing what you're asked to do accurately.
- **Learning New Things:**Being open to training and picking up new skills.

Don't underestimate the skills you've developed. Many of them are exactly what employers are looking for, even if they don't seem like 'job skills' at first glance. Think about how you managed your daily life, interacted with others, and handled responsibilities. These are all transferable.


## Resources for Finding Felon Friendly Jobs

Okay, so you're looking for work after incarceration, and the thought of where to even start can feel overwhelming. Don't sweat it! There are definitely places out there designed to help folks like you get back on their feet. Think of these as your go-to spots for finding opportunities that are more open to giving second chances.

### Online Job Boards Specializing in Second Chances

These websites are pretty cool because they're specifically set up for people who might have a criminal record. They know the challenges, and they work with employers who are willing to look past a past mistake. You can often filter by industry or location, making your search a bit more focused. It's a good idea to check these out regularly because new jobs get posted all the time.

- **Second Chance Job Search:**This is a general term for platforms that focus on re-entry employment. Many list jobs that don't require background checks or are willing to consider applicants with a record.
- **Industry-Specific Boards:**Some sites might focus on particular fields, like skilled trades or manufacturing, which are often more open to hiring individuals with a criminal history.
- **Local Initiatives:**Keep an eye out for local or state-run job boards that specifically aim to connect formerly incarcerated individuals with employers in your area.

### Local Workforce Development Centers

These centers are usually government-funded and are all about helping people find jobs. They often have staff who are trained to help individuals with barriers to employment, including those with a criminal record. They can help with:

- Resume building and interview practice. 
- Connecting you with local employers who are known to be re-entry friendly. 
- Information on training programs that can boost your skills and make you more marketable. 
- Access to computers and internet for your job search. 

Don't be shy about visiting your local center. They're there to help, and the services are usually free.

### Non-Profit Organizations Supporting Re-entry

There are tons of non-profits out there dedicated to helping people successfully re-enter society after incarceration. These organizations often provide a wide range of support, and finding a job is usually a big part of that. They might offer:

- Job placement assistance. 
- Mentorship programs. 
- Workshops on life skills and job readiness. 
- Help with things like transportation or work attire. 

Doing a quick search for "re-entry programs" or "felon employment services" in your city or state should bring up some great options. These groups are often passionate about what they do and can be a real lifeline.

## Industries That Welcome Formerly Incarcerated Individuals

It can feel like a huge hurdle trying to figure out where to even start looking for work after incarceration. You might be wondering if anyone will give you a chance. The good news is, there are definitely industries out there that are more open to hiring folks with a past. It's not about finding a 'felon-friendly' industry, but rather finding industries that value skills and a willingness to work, and are increasingly recognizing the benefits of second-chance hiring.

Industries That Welcome Formerly Incarcerated Individuals

### Skilled Trades and Manual Labor

This is often a go-to for many reasons. Think about construction, plumbing, electrical work, welding, and auto repair. These jobs often require hands-on skills and a strong work ethic, which many individuals develop during their time inside or through vocational training. The demand for skilled tradespeople is high, and many companies are looking for reliable workers. Plus, the work itself can be very rewarding, and you can often see the results of your labor.

- **Construction:**From framing to finishing, there's a lot of work here.
- **Manufacturing:**Building things, operating machinery.
- **Landscaping and Maintenance:**Keeping outdoor spaces looking good.
- **Auto Repair:**Fixing cars and trucks is always needed.

### Manufacturing and Warehousing

These sectors are often looking for people to fill roles in production, assembly, and logistics. Think about factories, distribution centers, and shipping companies. These jobs can offer steady work and opportunities for advancement. Many companies in this area are actively looking to fill positions and are open to individuals who are ready to contribute. The nature of the work often involves following procedures and working as part of a team, which can be a good fit.

Manufacturers are increasingly adopting second-chance hiring practices, offering employment and training opportunities to formerly incarcerated individuals. This approach has yielded positive results across various sectors, demonstrating the value of integrating this talent pool into the workforce. You can find more information about this trend and how it benefits businesses by looking into second-chance hiring.

### Healthcare and Social Services

While some roles in healthcare require extensive background checks, there are many positions in support services, patient care, and administrative roles that can be accessible. Social services, in particular, often value individuals who have personal experience with the challenges faced by those seeking to re-enter society. Roles like case management aides, community support workers, or even administrative staff in non-profits can be a great fit. Your lived experience can be a real asset here.

### Technology and Creative Fields

Don't count out the tech world or creative industries! While it might seem less obvious, many tech companies and creative agencies are starting to look beyond traditional backgrounds. If you have skills in coding, web design, graphic design, writing, or digital marketing, these fields can be very welcoming. Online courses and certifications can help you build a portfolio, and many companies are realizing that talent can come from anywhere. The ability to problem-solve and think creatively is highly valued.

It's worth noting that many local businesses are actively seeking to connect with the community. Directories like the St Louis Near Me Directory can help you find businesses in various sectors that are looking for local talent. By understanding the types of industries that are more open, you can focus your job search more effectively.

## Strategies for a Successful Job Search

Okay, so you've got your resume ready and you're feeling good about your skills. Now comes the part where you actually go out and find that job. It can feel like a big hurdle, but with the right approach, you can totally make it happen. Let's break down some smart ways to go about it.

### Networking Effectively

Think of networking as just talking to people and letting them know you're looking for work. It's not about being pushy; it's about building connections. Start with people you already know – friends, family, former colleagues, even neighbors. Let them know what kind of work you're looking for. You never know who might have a lead or know someone who's hiring.

- **Reach out to your existing contacts:**Don't be shy about telling people you're on the job hunt.
- **Attend local events:**Look for job fairs or community gatherings where you can meet new people.
- **Join online groups:**Many industries have online forums or social media groups where professionals connect.

Building a network takes time, but even small connections can lead to big opportunities. It's about being visible and letting people know you're ready to work.


### Preparing for Interviews

Interviews can be nerve-wracking, but preparation is key. Think about common interview questions and practice your answers out loud. It helps to have a few stories ready that show off your skills and how you handle challenges. Remember, they want to see that you're reliable and a good fit for their team.

- **Research the company:**Know what they do and why you want to work there.
- **Practice your "elevator pitch":**A short summary of who you are and what you can do.
- **Prepare questions to ask them:**This shows you're engaged and interested.

### Addressing Background Checks

Background checks are a common part of the hiring process, and it's best to be upfront about any past issues. If you have a record, consider getting a copy of your background check beforehand so you know exactly what an employer will see. When the time comes, you can address it honestly and explain what you've learned and how you've changed. Many employers are willing to give second chances, especially if you can show you're committed to being a good employee.

- **Be honest and direct:**Don't try to hide anything.
- **Focus on the positive:**Talk about your growth and what you've learned.
- **Highlight your skills and work ethic:**Show them you're ready to be a valuable team member.

## Leveraging Community Support Systems

Getting back on your feet after incarceration isn't a solo mission. There are tons of folks and groups out there who want to help you succeed, and tapping into them can make a huge difference. Think of these as your personal pit crew, ready to give you a boost when you need it.

### Mentorship Programs

Having someone who's been through something similar and made it out the other side can be incredibly helpful. Mentors can offer advice, share their own experiences, and help you see possibilities you might have missed. They've walked the path, so they know the bumps and how to get around them. It's like having a guide who can point out the best routes and warn you about dead ends.

### Support Groups for Re-entry

Connecting with others who are also navigating the re-entry process can be really powerful. You can share stories, frustrations, and successes in a safe space. Knowing you're not alone in this journey can be a huge comfort and a great source of motivation. These groups often have members who have found jobs and can offer practical tips.

### Financial Literacy and Job Readiness Workshops

Sometimes, the practical stuff is what trips people up. Workshops focused on things like budgeting, managing money, and getting ready for job interviews can give you the skills you need to feel more confident. They can cover everything from how to dress for an interview to how to handle tricky questions about your past. Plus, learning to manage your finances is key to staying on track once you land that job.

Building a solid support network isn't just about finding a job; it's about building a stable foundation for your future. These resources are there to help you not just get back on your feet, but to stand tall and move forward.


## Overcoming Common Challenges

Overcoming Common Challenges

### Dealing with Stigma and Discrimination

Let's be real, facing stigma and discrimination after incarceration is tough. It's like you're constantly trying to prove yourself, and sometimes, it feels like no matter what you do, that past is always going to be a shadow. Employers might have their reservations, and that's a hurdle. It's not fair, but it's the reality for many. The key is to be prepared. Think about how you'll address your record honestly and concisely if it comes up. Focus on what you've learned and how you've grown. Remember, there are employers out there who are willing to give second chances. You just need to find them. Resources like online job boards specializing in second chances can be a lifesaver here.

### Maintaining Motivation

Job searching can be a marathon, not a sprint, and it's super easy to get discouraged. You might face rejections, or maybe the jobs you're qualified for just aren't paying enough. It's important to celebrate the small wins. Did you get an interview? That's a win! Did you update your resume? Another win! Try to keep a routine, stay connected with supportive friends or family, and remember why you're doing this. Setting realistic goals for yourself each week can also help. Maybe it's applying to a certain number of jobs or reaching out to one new contact. Breaking it down makes it feel more manageable.

### Building Trust with Employers

Building trust is huge, especially when you have a criminal record. Employers worry about reliability, honesty, and workplace safety. Your goal is to show them you're a dependable and trustworthy employee. This starts with being upfront and honest during the application and interview process. Highlight your transferable skills and any training or certifications you've obtained. Showing up on time, being prepared, and demonstrating a strong work ethic in any job you get will go a long way. Sometimes, starting with temporary or contract work can be a good way to prove yourself and build that trust over time. It gives both you and the employer a chance to see if it's a good fit without a long-term commitment right away.

Facing tough spots? Don't let common problems stop you. We've got the tips and tricks to help you push through. Ready to find solutions and keep moving forward? Visit our website today for more helpful advice!

## Wrapping Things Up

So, finding a job after a conviction can feel like a really tough climb, but it's definitely not impossible. We've talked about a bunch of ways to get started, from looking into specific programs to just getting your resume in shape and practicing your interview skills. Remember all those resources we mentioned? Keep them handy. It might take some time and a lot of persistence, but there are people and places out there ready to give you a fair shot. Don't give up on yourself, and keep putting one foot in front of the other. You've got this.

## The Diaper Bank Won’t Hand You a Diaper. These St. Louis Libraries Will.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-diaper-bank-essential-support-for-families-in-need
Three diapers left in the pack on the dresser, and it’s 11 at night. Daycare wants a full day’s supply in the bag tomorrow morning, payday is Friday, and the baby goes through eight to twelve a day. SNAP won’t buy a box. Neither will WIC. You do the math on the back of an envelope and it doesn’t come out.
What most parents never get told about the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank is that you can’t walk into its warehouse and pick up a pack. It never hands diapers straight to families. It sends them out through partners you can walk into, and the easiest ones to reach are public libraries. One of them, Julia Davis Library on Natural Bridge, hands out diapers on Tuesdays until 7 p.m., late enough to make it after work.
Tonight: dial 2-1-1, which answers around the clock, and ask about emergency diapers near you. Then ask the daycare whether a partial day’s supply will get your child in the door while you restock.
This week: free diaper pickups in St. Louis
St. Louis Public Library (households at or below 200% of the federal poverty level; once a month per child; sizes newborn to 6, training pants 2T to 4T):
Julia Davis, 4415 Natural Bridge Ave.: Tuesdays, 4 to 7 p.m.
Walnut Park, 5760 W. Florissant Ave.: Tuesdays, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Carpenter, 3309 S. Grand Blvd.: second Wednesday, 9:30 to 11:30 a.m.
Central, 1301 Olive St.: first Saturday, 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
Bring a library card or ID, and call 314-241-2288 before you go, because supplies run out and schedules change.
St. Louis County Library (kids 4 and under): Florissant Valley, Grand Glaize, Lewis & Clark, Natural Bridge, Parkview and Weber Road branches. The county lists the six branches but not set days, so call your branch before you go.
Everywhere else: the Find Supplies map at stldiaperbank.org lists partner pantries, clinics and programs, or dial 2-1-1.
Buying a pack anyway? Diapers are now free of Missouri state and local sales tax. If the register rings up tax on them, ask the cashier to take it off.

### Why running out of diapers costs a family more than diapers
Back at the dresser with three diapers left, the math runs further than the baby. Run short and the trouble stacks up: a rash by morning, a daycare that can turn your child away at the door, a shift you can’t make. Diapers rank with food and shelter as a basic need, yet they slip through nearly every safety net.
### What a month of diapers really costs
The numbers add up fast. A single baby goes through 8 to 12 diapers a day, and over a year that can top $1,000. For a household already stretching every paycheck, that is a serious line item. Worse, SNAP or WIC benefits can't be used to buy them. Missouri has at least stopped taxing them: diapers, period products and incontinence supplies are now exempt from state and local sales tax. The pack still costs what it costs.
### No diapers, no daycare, no shift
The shortage reaches parents as hard as it reaches babies. Many daycares and childcare centers require a full day's supply of diapers, and without them a child can be turned away at the door. That leaves parents, mothers especially, unable to work or even job-hunt. The trap closes quickly: you need diapers for childcare, childcare to work, and work to afford diapers.
### What a short pack does to a baby, and to you
Stretch a diaper too long and by morning there’s an angry red rash, a baby who won’t settle, and a parent who feels like they failed. The St. Louis Area Diaper Bank notes that many mothers who go through diaper need rate it as more stressful than running short on food. None of that is a parenting failure. It’s math: about $100 a month to diaper one child, just over $1,000 a year, with no safety-net program that pays for it.
### How the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank actually gets diapers to you
### Like a food bank, but for diapers
It runs like a food bank where the shelves hold diaper boxes instead of canned corn. The St. Louis Area Diaper Bank collects donated and bulk-bought diapers, many of them Huggies that arrive through the National Diaper Bank Network, then sends them to partner agencies that already know the families: home-visiting programs, clinics, pantries and libraries. A child enrolled with a partner that provides case management or home visits gets 50 diapers a month for as long as they’re enrolled. The Diaper Bank says plainly that 50 won’t cover a whole month. It’s sized to close the gap most families report, about 10 to 12 diapers short each week.
### From Wentzville to Belleville: who it serves
The Diaper Bank doesn't just serve the city itself. Their reach extends across a wide area, including St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson, Lincoln, Warren, and Montgomery counties in Missouri. They also help families in Madison and St. Clair counties in Illinois. This broad service area means they're able to support a lot of families who might otherwise struggle to find these items. It's about making sure that no matter where you live in the greater St. Louis area, help is available. You can find out more about their work and the communities they serve on their website.
Serving the Greater St. Louis Region
### The Period Supply Program
Beyond diapers, the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank also recognized another overlooked need: menstrual hygiene products. In 2020, they launched the Period Supply Program. This program provides monthly kits with period education and a supportive note to individuals who menstruate. These kits are distributed through schools, shelters, food pantries, and healthcare centers. It's a thoughtful addition that addresses another basic need, showing a commitment to the overall well-being of women and girls in the community.
Here's a look at what they provide:
Diaper Program: Offers 25-50 diapers and 10-20 training pants monthly per family.
Period Supply Program: Distributes monthly kits with educational materials and supportive notes.
Service Area: Covers multiple counties in both Missouri and Illinois.
When money is tight, some families cut back on food or utilities just to keep diapers on hand. Removing that trade-off is the whole point of the program.
The volume is staggering: the Diaper Bank moves between 250,000 and 300,000 diapers each month. That scale tracks the size of the need. Around 75 partner organizations, local libraries among them, help get these supplies into the hands of families who need them most.
Nothing to do with diapers - Forest Park Southeast rewards a slow walk.
### Who keeps the shelves full
You might be wondering how the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank keeps up with the constant demand for diapers and period products. It's a community effort, really. The need is growing, and so are the costs. Think about it: diapers aren't cheap, and for families already stretched thin, it's a huge worry.
### Growing Demand and Rising Costs
It's a tough situation. Many families find themselves unable to afford enough diapers to keep their little ones clean and dry. This comes down to health, not comfort. Babies can develop rashes and infections if they aren't changed frequently enough, and that's a real concern for parents. Plus, many daycares require a stash of diapers before they'll accept a child, which can be a barrier to parents working or attending school. The price of diapers has gone up, too, making it even harder for families to manage.
### The Role of Partner Organizations
The Diaper Bank doesn't work alone. They team up with a whole network of local groups – think libraries, community centers, and other non-profits. These partners are on the front lines, helping to get the diapers and period products out to the families who need them most. It's a coordinated effort to make sure supplies reach every corner of the St. Louis region. If you're looking to help, organizing a diaper drive with your workplace or community group is a fantastic way to contribute. The Diaper Bank can even help you get started with organizing collection events.
### How the Diaper Bank Distributes Diapers
So how does it work? You ask a partner, not the warehouse. The partner orders from the Diaper Bank, and the diapers reach you through that partner, whether it’s your home visitor, your clinic or the children’s desk at the library. Hundreds of thousands of diapers move that way every month, built on donations, diaper drives and a lot of volunteer hands.
Down to the last few diapers in the pack? Find the nearest free pickup on the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank’s Find Supplies map (stldiaperbank.org), call 2-1-1, or ask about a library pickup day (St. Louis Public Library: 314-241-2288). Also see our guides to free food and affordable housing.

### The sales tax break, and the research behind the next fix
You know, it's easy to think of diaper need as just a lack of a product, but it's really a bigger issue that affects families in so many ways. That's why looking into research and policy solutions is so important. It's about finding ways to make sure everyone has what they need without it breaking the bank.
### Saint Louis University's Research Initiative
Saint Louis University is actually doing some great work right here in Missouri, looking into how to get more diapers to families who need them. They received a pretty significant grant to study this very problem. The goal is to figure out the best ways to improve access to diapers across the state, which is a huge step. They're partnering with the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank and other groups to really get a handle on the situation and find practical solutions. This kind of research helps us understand the scope of diaper need and how it impacts maternal and infant health.
### Advocating for Policy Changes
Beyond research, there's a push to change policies that make it harder for families. Did you know that many government assistance programs, like SNAP and WIC, don't cover diapers? It's true. And Medicaid only covers them if they're medically necessary, which isn't always the case. This leaves a big gap. Organizations are working to advocate for changes, like making sure diapers are included in these programs or finding other ways to provide direct support. It's about making sure basic necessities are actually covered.
### Exempting Diapers from Sales Tax
This one already happened. Under Section 144.029 of state law, diapers, period products and adult incontinence supplies are now free of Missouri state and local sales tax, for every buyer, with no form to fill out. If a register still rings up tax on a pack, the Missouri Department of Revenue says to ask the store to take it off. It won’t pay for a month of diapers, but on a bill that can top $1,000 a year per child, every dollar counts. You can find more information on the Diaper Bank Model and how it helps address these gaps.
The math forces impossible choices. Parents stretch each diaper too far, which invites rashes and infections, or they miss work when a childcare center turns the child away for showing up short. Either way, the whole household feels it.

By providing a consistent supply of diapers, the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank helps ease that worry, allowing caregivers to feel more in control and less anxious. ### Who will take extra diapers in St. Louis, even an opened pack?
The Diaper Bank on Etzel Avenue will, and it takes opened packs too. Its donation page says it accepts any size and any brand of disposable diapers in unopened and opened packages, so the half-used box your baby outgrew last week still goes to another family, and its greatest need is the bigger sizes, 4 to 7 plus 2T and 4T training pants. The warehouse at 6141 Etzel takes drop-offs weekdays from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., and if that window doesn’t fit your shift, its map lists “Ambassador” homes and businesses that collect donations closer to you.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can I get diapers if I have no money?
A.  Start with the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank’s Find Supplies map at stldiaperbank.org, which shows the pantries, clinics and programs that hand out its diapers free. St. Louis Public Library runs pickups at its Carpenter, Central, Julia Davis and Walnut Park branches for households at or below 200% of the federal poverty level. Still stuck? Dial 2-1-1.
### Q. How does a diaper bank work?
A.  Like a food bank, but for diapers. It collects donated and bulk-bought diapers, then passes them to partner agencies that already know the families. The St. Louis Area Diaper Bank never hands diapers to individuals at its warehouse. Families get them through partners, and a child enrolled with a case-management or home-visiting partner receives about 50 diapers a month.
### Q. How to get a free pack of diapers?
A.  Go to a partner pickup. St. Louis County Library hands out Diaper Bank diapers or training pants for kids 4 and under at six branches, including Florissant Valley, Grand Glaize and Weber Road. City library pickups run on set days, like Carpenter Library’s second Wednesday from 9:30 to 11:30 a.m. Call 314-241-2288 first, because supplies run out.
### Q. Does EBT cover diapers?
A.  No. SNAP benefits on an EBT card only buy food, so diapers, wipes and period products are off the list, and WIC doesn’t cover them either. That gap is the whole reason diaper banks exist. The one break Missouri does give you is at the register: diapers are now free of state and local sales tax.
### Q. Does WIC give free diapers?
A.  No. WIC pays for specific foods and formula for pregnant women, new moms and children under 5, not diapers. It’s still worth asking your WIC clinic, caseworker or home visitor whether their office is a St. Louis Area Diaper Bank partner, since many family programs are. If not, the library pickups and 2-1-1 are your next calls.
### Q. Can you get free baby diapers on Medicaid?
A.  Not for everyday baby diapering. MO HealthNet, Missouri’s Medicaid program, can cover diapers or pull-ons as incontinence supplies when a doctor documents a medical need, which usually means an older child with a disability or medical condition, or an adult. For a typical baby or toddler, the Diaper Bank’s partner sites are the free option.
### Q. How to get free diapers from Huggies?
A.  Huggies doesn’t hand out free packs on request, and its rewards and sweepstakes offers change often, so check huggies.com for what’s running before you count on it. The steadier route is local: through the National Diaper Bank Network, Huggies-donated diapers help stock the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank, and those reach families free through its partner sites.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to get diapers?
A.  Free, through a diaper bank partner, if your family qualifies. If you’re buying, the price per diaper drops with bigger boxes and store brands, and a subscribe-and-save order can shave off a little more. Missouri also stopped charging sales tax on diapers, so if a receipt shows tax on a pack, ask the store to remove it.
### Q. Where to donate in St. Louis?
A.  For diapers, wipes and period supplies, give to the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank at 6141 Etzel Ave. Call 314-624-0888 or email info@stldiaperbank.org before you drop off. Money stretches further than a store-bought pack, because the Diaper Bank buys through national wholesale programs, and it always needs volunteers to sort and pack. A diaper drive at work or church is the other easy way in.
### Q. What exactly is diaper need?
A.  Diaper need means not having enough diapers to keep a baby or toddler clean, dry and healthy. In real life it’s a diaper left on hours too long because it’s the last one in the box. The St. Louis Area Diaper Bank says half of St. Louis families sometimes can’t afford enough, diapering one child runs about $1,000 a year, and many moms rate it as more stressful than going short on food. No public benefit program pays for everyday diapers.

It might seem like a simple thing, but for many families right here in St. Louis, having enough diapers for their little ones is a real struggle. ### The Financial Burden of Diapers

Let's talk numbers for a second. Diapers aren't cheap. For a baby, you're looking at using anywhere from 8 to 12 diapers a day. That adds up fast. Over the course of a year, families can spend over $1,000 just on diapers. That's a huge chunk of change, especially when you're already trying to make ends meet. And here's a kicker: you can't even use SNAP or WIC benefits to buy them. Plus, in Missouri, diapers are taxed like a luxury item, which just makes them even more expensive for families who are already struggling to afford life's basics. It's a tough spot to be in.

### Impact on Childcare and Parental Employment

This diaper shortage doesn't just affect the baby's comfort; it has a big impact on parents' lives too. Many daycares and childcare centers require parents to provide a full day's supply of diapers. If you don't have enough, your child might not be able to attend. This can make it really hard for parents, especially mothers, to work or even look for a job. It's a cycle that's tough to break out of. You need diapers for childcare, you need childcare to work, and you need to work to afford diapers. See the problem?

### Diaper Need as a Public Health Crisis

When babies aren't changed frequently because there aren't enough diapers, it can lead to health issues. Skin irritation, rashes, and even infections can become a real concern. Keeping a baby clean, dry, and healthy is so important for their development and well-being. Diaper need isn't just a convenience issue; it's a public health concern that affects the health of our youngest and most vulnerable residents. It's something we really need to pay attention to in our community. ## FindHelp.org in St. Louis: Your Shutoff Notice Can Unlock Up to $800
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/connecting-communities-to-hope-the-life-changing-benefits-of-findhelp-org
Is the notice on the counter yet? The one in the window envelope you keep turning face down, so you don’t have to see the red print every time you reach for the coffee. Maybe it’s the fridge instead, humming over three eggs and a jar of mustard, with payday still nine days away. Either way, you are here because you typed something like “help paying bills St. Louis” at an hour when every office in town is closed.
Don’t throw that envelope away. In Missouri, a disconnect notice with a specific date on it is one of the papers that qualifies you for the state’s Energy Crisis Intervention Program, and winter ECIP can pay up to $800 toward your energy bill, based on funding. Ameren Missouri says a disconnection notice is required for ECIP but not for the regular Energy Assistance payment, and it recommends applying for LIHEAP even if your bill is not past due. The paper you are hiding from is the key to the door.
The door has a St. Louis address. If you live in the City of St. Louis, the Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis takes LIHEAP applications Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to noon, at 1408 North Kingshighway Blvd., with a drop box from noon to 5 p.m. The number is (314) 615-3632. In St. Louis County, Ameren Missouri partners with the Community Action Agency of St. Louis County to help customers apply.
For everything else, food, rent, a ride to the clinic, there are two tools worth knowing. Findhelp.org is a free search site that lists programs near any ZIP code, and its own privacy policy says you are free to search through and use the website without providing any information about yourself. No name, no email, no story you have to tell a stranger first. And when a list feels like a wall, United Way 211 of Missouri and Illinois says you can dial 211 to get connected to a trained resource specialist 24/7, free and confidential. Search findhelp when you want to look quietly. Call 211 when you need someone to sort it out with you.
### What is Findhelp and what does it do?
Findhelp.org, whose privacy policy still uses the name Aunt Bertha, is a search site that matches people with need-based service providers: food pantries, housing, financial help, health care and more. Type a St. Louis ZIP code and search without giving any information about yourself. For a live person any hour, dial 211.
### Search it without giving your name
Open findhelp.org on your phone. The home page asks one question: what are you looking for today? The buttons are plain words. Food. Housing. Goods. Transit. Health. Money. Care. Education. Work. Legal. Tap the one that is keeping you up, type your ZIP code in the box that asks “Where?” and press Find Programs.
What comes back is a list of programs near you. Read the eligibility lines before you fall in love with one. Some programs serve only seniors, only families with kids, only one ZIP code. That’s not a door closing on you; it’s the list telling you to skip ahead.
Then do the one thing that saves the most heartbreak: call before you go. Hours change, pantries run out, a bus ride across the county with a toddler on your hip is a lot to spend on a locked door. A two-minute call that starts with “Are you open today, and what do I need to bring?” protects your whole afternoon.
If you are on a library computer or a borrowed phone, you can close the tab when you’re done. You didn’t make an account, so there’s nothing to log out of.
### When a list is not enough: dial 211
There is a specific kind of tired that comes from calling five numbers off a list and getting five voicemails. That’s when you dial 211, the line Missouri’s social services department lists as 2-1-1 Missouri, United Way.
The 211 FAQ says that when a person calls 2-1-1, a trained specialist will determine the area the person is calling from and what services are needed, and then give contact and program information for all available services in the person’s community. In other words, you say what is wrong, and they do the sorting.
A few details that matter when your phone is your lifeline. If 211 won’t go through from your cell phone, the 211 FAQ says to call 1-800-427-4626 instead. Some workplaces block three-digit numbers like 211; the same toll-free number works from there. If talking out loud isn’t safe or isn’t possible right now, 211 also takes text messages at 1-800-427-4626 and has an online chat, both Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. You can also email 211@unitedwaystl.org.
One thing 211 is not: an emergency line. The 211 FAQ says residents should keep calling local emergency numbers for medical emergencies, fires and police help. For a medical emergency, a fire or police help, call 9-1-1.
### The shutoff notice: what to do this week
The house goes quiet in a particular way when the power is cut: no fridge hum, no furnace click, just your own breathing. Most people never get that far, and the reason is usually one application or one phone call made in time.
Missouri’s Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program has two parts. Energy Assistance is a one-time payment for one fuel type for your heating or cooling costs. The Energy Crisis Intervention Program, or ECIP, helps pay your energy bill when you have a termination or disconnect notice indicating a specific disconnect date, among other crisis situations. The Missouri Department of Social Services says winter ECIP is available November through May, based on funding, with a maximum of $800. Summer ECIP runs June through September, based on funding, with a maximum of $300. Ameren Missouri says the deadline to apply for the annual Energy Assistance program and winter ECIP is May 31.
Renters, this includes you. The state says you may be eligible if you are responsible for paying the utilities for your home, including if you rent. You also need to be a Missouri resident, a U.S. citizen or legally admitted for permanent residence, have $3,000 or less in your bank accounts, retirement accounts or investments, and meet the income guidelines for your household size. Applications are reviewed within approximately 30 business days unless it is considered a crisis, and the state asks you to keep paying what you can on your bill while you wait. You can also call 855-373-4636 to have an application mailed to you.
Before you head to the Urban League on Kingshighway, put these in a folder: photocopies of the Social Security cards for everyone in the household, the prior month’s proof of income, and your most recent gas and electric bills. That is the Urban League’s own list. Walking in with the folder complete is the difference between one trip and three.
Ameren Missouri runs its own help on top of LIHEAP. Its Dollar More Program can help eligible customers with up to $600 a year for a past-due bill. Veterans Energy Assistance is open to active-duty military, veterans and their families, with up to $600 toward past-due utility bills; Ameren says to call 211 for details.
Water works differently. United Way 211’s utility page says Missouri American Water offers an installment plan for residential customers in financial hardship, and that it’s important to contact the company before your water is shut off to keep your eligibility for the plan. The arrangement requires paying 25% of your balance up front and the rest on a schedule of up to 6 months. The same page points City of St. Louis water customers to their own assistance page. The pattern is the same everywhere: call before the date, not after.
Random, but: here’s the West End, block by block.
### Food tonight, and food next month
An empty pantry has a sound: the cabinet door that swings open on nothing, the kid asking what’s for dinner in a voice that already knows. Tonight and next month are two different problems, so solve them separately.
For tonight, search the Food button on findhelp with your ZIP code, or call 211 and say “I need food today.” Ask the pantry what time to arrive and whether to bring ID or a piece of mail. For next month, apply for SNAP. The Missouri Department of Social Services’ food assistance page is where you apply for SNAP, and where you can also find your local food pantry. Our step-by-step guide to applying for SNAP in Missouri walks you through the application.
### Rent, a bed, and the next step
Rent trouble has its own weight: the knock you dread, the note taped to the door, the math you do at 3 a.m. that never comes out right. Findhelp’s Housing button and 211 both lead to local programs, and our St. Louis guides go deeper.
Emergency rent assistance in St. Louis covers who pays back rent and how to apply.
Emergency shelters in St. Louis covers where to go tonight if you have no bed.

### How to ask so people can say yes
Asking for help is hard in the body before it’s hard in the head. Your throat tightens. You rehearse the call twice and hang up before it rings. That’s normal, and it passes faster than you think once a real voice answers.
Here is a script that works on almost any help line, pantry or agency. Say where you live, by ZIP code. Say who is in the house: “me and two kids,” “just me,” “my mom, who is 78.” Say the one thing that is most urgent, with the date if there is one: “My electric is set to be shut off on the 14th.” Then stop and let them ask questions. You don’t have to explain how you got here. Nobody on a help line needs your whole story to do their job.
Keep a notebook or a note on your phone. Write the date, the name of the person you talked to, and what they told you to do next. When you call back, read it to them. It turns “nobody helped me” into “on Tuesday, the caseworker told me to bring my lease,” and that sentence gets things moving.
And if the first place says no, ask one more question before you hang up: “Who would you call if you were me?” People who work in help know other people who work in help. That question has opened more doors than any website.
### Is it legit? What the fine print says
When you’re already stretched thin, the last thing you need is a website that sells your name to someone who calls you about loans. So it’s fair to ask if findhelp.org is a legitimate website.
The site’s own privacy policy describes it as a software application designed to match interested persons with need-based service providers. It says you can search without providing any information about yourself, and that the company currently does not sell your personal information. The same policy still names the company Aunt Bertha, a Public Benefit Corporation, which answers the other question people ask: yes, findhelp and Aunt Bertha are the same service under an older and a newer name.
The usual cautions still apply. No legitimate pantry or rent program will ask you to pay a fee to get help. If anyone does, hang up and call 211.
### For the caseworker, the pastor, the neighbor who helps
Maybe you’re not the one in trouble. Maybe you’re the one people call. You can search findhelp on someone’s behalf, with their ZIP code and their permission, and sit with them while they make the first call. Your calm voice on speaker can carry the first two minutes.
If you run a program, findhelp says that when you claim your program, your organization can more easily receive referrals, follow up quickly and track your impact at no cost to you, and it offers free training sessions on searching, referring and claiming your listing. Its organizations page is where to start.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is Findhelp.org a legitimate website?
A.  Yes. Its privacy policy describes it as a software application that matches people with need-based service providers. You can search without giving any information about yourself, and the policy says the company currently does not sell your personal information. No real help program should charge you a fee to get help.
### Q. Is Findhelp the same as Aunt Bertha?
A.  Yes. Findhelp.org’s own privacy policy still names the company Aunt Bertha, a Public Benefit Corporation, and refers to its older website, auntbertha.com. The same policy lists its website as www.auntbertha.com or www.findhelp.org.
### Q. How can I get money if I am struggling?
A.  Start with the bill that has a date on it. If it’s a utility shutoff notice, Missouri’s Energy Crisis Intervention Program helps pay energy bills when you have a disconnect notice with a specific date; winter help is capped at $800, based on funding. In the City of St. Louis, the Urban League takes those applications at (314) 615-3632. Ameren Missouri’s Dollar More Program can help eligible customers with up to $600 a year for a past-due bill. For other bills, search the Money button on findhelp.org or dial 211, which is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day.
### Q. Where do I ask for help?
A.  In St. Louis, dial 211 to reach United Way 211, or 1-800-427-4626 if 211 won’t connect. A trained specialist figures out where you are and what you need, then gives you contact and program information. To look on your own first, search your ZIP code at findhelp.org.
### Q. What to do when no one helps you?
A.  Write down every call: the date, the name and what they said. Then call 211 and read it to them, so they can skip what already failed. Before you hang up on any office that says no, ask, “Who would you call if you were me?” For a medical emergency or police help, call 9-1-1.
### Q. How to ask for help and actually get it?
A.  Lead with three facts: your ZIP code, who lives with you, and the most urgent need with its date. Then stop and let them ask questions. Have your ID, a piece of mail and the bill or notice nearby. You don’t have to explain how you got here to get help.

## The Problem: A Broken Safety Net

Before we understand the transformative benefits of the platform, we need to recognize the problem it addresses. The American social safety net, while extensive, has long been fragmented and difficult to navigate. Community organizations, food banks, housing assistance programs, healthcare services, and government benefits exist in silos, often with outdated contact information, confusing eligibility requirements, and no clear pathway for people in need to find them.

Erine Gray, founder and CEO of **FindHelp.org**, witnessed this breakdown firsthand. While working in state government for four years after earning his Master's in public policy, Gray saw the wide technology gap in social services. But the defining moment came when his mother contracted encephalitis, a rare brain disease that left her requiring 24-hour care and reliant on the social safety net. "The light bulb moment for me was realizing the safety net is broken still," Gray reflected in an interview with Forbes. This personal experience, combined with his professional insights, led him to ask a critical question: "What do people do when life throws them a curveball, and how do they connect to social services?"

**Put your business on the local map**

In 2010, Gray founded FindHelp (formerly known as Aunt Bertha) with a mission that remains at its core today: to connect all people and the programs that serve them, with dignity and ease. What started as an idea to create a better way has evolved into a comprehensive technology platform that is fundamentally reshaping how Americans access social services.

## How FindHelp.org Works: Simplicity at Scale

At its heart, FindHelp.org is elegantly simple. The platform operates as a free, user-friendly search engine that connects individuals to social care services across the United States. Here's how it works:

**For People Seeking Help:** Users simply enter their ZIP code on the main page at **FindHelp.org**. Within seconds, they receive a tailored list of available resources based on their location and specific needs. The platform organizes services into easy-to-understand categories including food assistance, housing, healthcare, care services, transportation, financial assistance, employment support, and more. Users can filter results by eligibility requirements, service type, and availability, then view detailed information about each program including contact details, hours of operation, and next steps for accessing services.

A standout feature is the "Connect" button, which allows users to send referrals directly to programs, notifying providers of interest and facilitating follow-up. This process is designed to be intuitive and accessible, with mobile apps available for iOS and Android devices. Importantly, searches can be conducted anonymously and completely free of charge—no registration required, no data sold, and no advertisements cluttering the experience.

**For Organizations:** Community-based organizations (CBOs), healthcare providers, government agencies, and other service providers can claim their program listings at no cost. This allows them to update information in real-time, manage referrals, track client interactions, and access powerful analytics dashboards. Organizations benefit from closed-loop referrals that track service delivery from initiation to completion, providing crucial feedback on whether assistance was actually received. These tools help organizations demonstrate impact to funders, identify unmet community needs, and streamline their operations—all without any subscription fees for basic services.

In New York State alone, there are more than 13,800 programs listed. This comprehensive coverage, combined with support in over 100 languages, ensures that FindHelp.org truly serves America's diverse population.

## Addressing Food Insecurity: A Critical Mission

Food insecurity remains one of America's most pressing challenges, and the platform has become an essential tool in combating it. In 2021 alone, food-related searches on the platform exceeded 250,000, highlighting both the desperate need and the platform's vital role in connecting hungry families to nourishment.

Through the platform, users can locate food pantries, apply for SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits, find meal delivery services, and connect with nutrition assistance programs. The platform has forged strategic partnerships to enhance food access, including a collaboration with GA Foods to provide medically-tailored meals and nutritious options through a streamlined referral system. Users can order and track meal deliveries directly through the platform, with a focus on reaching high-need populations.

Programs like those operated by A Gift From Ben, Inc., which offers free food to anyone in need—including low-income families, seniors, and veterans—with no eligibility restrictions, exemplify the accessible, dignity-centered approach that FindHelp.org facilitates. The platform also simplifies access to government benefits through integrations with services like mRelief, which offers a quick SNAP eligibility screener via text or website, guiding users through the application process across most U.S. states.

## Technology with a Human Touch

What sets FindHelp apart from other resource directories is its commitment to accuracy through human curation. While many competitors rely on automated bots that can propagate outdated information, FindHelp employs real people to verify and update program data regularly, with a target cycle of every six months. This human touch ensures that when someone searches for help, the information they receive is current and reliable—critical when a family is facing an immediate crisis.

The platform's technology approach prioritizes user-centric design, interoperability, and data-driven decision-making. Robust APIs enable seamless integration with existing systems like electronic health records (EHR), allowing healthcare providers, governments, and other organizations to manage social care directly within their established workflows. This interoperability has made FindHelp the platform of choice for major healthcare systems, with the company earning the distinction of being rated #1 "Best in KLAS" for social determinants of health (SDoH) networks—an award based on direct customer feedback evaluating healthcare technology vendors.

Privacy and security are foundational to the platform's design. FindHelp protects social care information under the same strict standards required for personal health information (PHI), maintaining compliance with HIPAA and FERPA regulations. As Gray emphasizes, "I am a big believer that we'll protect people's data as a cornerstone for the operation and for the business. We don't charge the people seeking help and we don't monetize their information through ads."

This commitment to privacy means that someone searching for help doesn't have to worry about their personal struggles being commodified, sold to advertisers, or exposed publicly. In a digital age where data exploitation is common, this ethical approach to technology is both refreshing and essential for maintaining the dignity of vulnerable individuals.

## Real Impact: Voices from the Field

The true measure of FindHelp.org's value comes from the people who use it every day. Healthcare providers, community organizations, and individuals consistently share stories of how the platform has transformed their ability to connect people with essential services.

Findhelp's referral platform and patient-facing website for staff is a powerful new tool in our toolbox to help our patients connect with community services and resources."

I can send families information via text or email and refer them to outside organizations at a later time. It is like a virtually interactive encyclopedia of the 21st century."

**Lauren Butler** from Harmony House's New Beginnings program shares how FindHelp.org addresses immediate needs: "When clients are housed through our program, sometimes they are in a completely new area that they have never lived before. They are in need of immediate access to resources in the area, especially food banks. The fastest way to provide these resources is through Findhelp. It has been a huge time saver, and has shown us all resources we didn't even know existed."

Client referrals continue to grow monthly through Findhelp!"

## A Sustainable Business Model Aligned with Mission

One of the most innovative aspects of FindHelp.org is its business model, which manages to be both mission-driven and financially sustainable. The platform offers **completely free access to individuals seeking help** and to community-based organizations providing services. No advertisements clutter the experience, and no user data is sold or monetized.

So how does FindHelp sustain itself? The answer came through an evolution that Gray describes in the Forbes interview. Initially, the plan was to charge nonprofits $50 per month for screening tools, but that proved insufficient. The breakthrough came around 2014 with the passage of the Affordable Care Act, when healthcare systems began massive cost restructuring efforts focused on preventing hospitalizations through social care interventions.

"Health plans started hiring tens of thousands of social workers and care coordinators to get to know their members and to try to help them connect to services," Gray explains. FindHelp began offering white-labeled software with advanced integrations that larger customers—healthcare systems, insurance companies, government agencies, and employers—could subscribe to. Today, FindHelp works with 450 customers nationwide, including eight of the top ten largest health plans and nearly 200 hospital systems in the United States.

This approach allows the revenue from large institutional customers to subsidize free access for individuals and smaller organizations. It's a model that Gray is passionate about: "We don't charge the people seeking help and we don't monetize their information through ads. And the nonprofits, we don't charge them either." By serving multiple stakeholders—individuals, CBOs, healthcare providers, governments, and employers—FindHelp has created a sustainable ecosystem where everyone benefits.

## Addressing Social Determinants of Health

Healthcare providers increasingly recognize that health outcomes depend on more than medical care alone. Social determinants of health—factors like food security, stable housing, transportation access, and financial stability—profoundly impact whether someone stays healthy or ends up repeatedly in the emergency room.

the platform has become essential infrastructure for healthcare organizations addressing these social determinants. By enabling seamless screening, referral, and tracking of social needs within clinical workflows, the platform helps healthcare providers deliver whole-person care. When a doctor identifies that a patient's diabetes management is failing not due to lack of medication but due to food insecurity, they can immediately connect that patient to food pantries, SNAP benefits, and meal delivery services—all tracked to ensure the person actually receives help.

This approach is proving effective at reducing costly hospital readmissions and emergency department visits. As Gray notes, healthcare systems and plans began investing heavily in social care because "somebody's paying for the safety net. The question is how much pain does somebody have to go through to get there?" By proactively addressing social needs, healthcare organizations can improve outcomes while reducing costs—a true win-win that FindHelp.org makes operationally feasible at scale.

## Dignity, Privacy, and Empowerment

Beyond the impressive statistics and partnerships, what truly distinguishes FindHelp is its unwavering commitment to human dignity. The platform's design choices consistently prioritize the experience and privacy of vulnerable individuals seeking help.

The option for anonymous searches means someone doesn't need to register, provide personal information, or risk exposure to access critical information about available services. The absence of advertisements means someone searching for emergency food assistance won't be confronted by targeted ads exploiting their vulnerability. The prohibition on data sales means someone's most difficult moments won't be commodified and packaged for profit.

This dignity-centered approach extends to the language and interface design. Services are organized intuitively, eligibility requirements are stated clearly, and the process for connecting with help is straightforward. Support in over 100 languages ensures that language barriers don't prevent someone from accessing their safety net. The mobile app means someone without home internet access can still search for resources using a smartphone.

Gray's personal experience caring for his mother clearly informs this emphasis on dignity. He understands that when someone is in crisis—whether due to illness, job loss, natural disaster, or any other challenge—they need help that is accessible, respectful, and effective. the platform embodies these values in every aspect of its design and operation.

## Looking Forward: A Vision for the Future

After fifteen years of operation and exponential growth, FindHelp continues to innovate and expand its impact. Recent developments include launching statewide digital infrastructure in states like Tennessee and Minnesota, supporting Medicaid redetermination efforts, expanding the Marketplace fulfillment services for direct delivery of goods and services (**including transportation, meals, diapers, car seats, and more**), and continuously enhancing the platform's analytics and reporting capabilities.

Gray remains optimistic about the future: "It's an area that hasn't gotten a lot of innovation with technology. I think that's where the new wave of investment will happen. Imagine maybe a health plan or a hospital system, or even a county government, might just make that problem go away. Because at the end of the day, somebody's paying for the safety net. The question is how much pain does somebody have to go through to get there? And I'm just an optimist about the future."

The company, now with 220+ employees and continuing to grow, has built more than a platform—it has built essential infrastructure for modern social care delivery in America. By connecting all stakeholders—individuals, community organizations, healthcare providers, governments, and businesses—FindHelp.org is creating an integrated ecosystem where social care is coordinated, effective, and humane.

### Academy / Sherman Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Academy / Sherman Park, St. Louis
Academy / Sherman Park serves as a historic professional and educational corridor in North St. Louis — positioned just outside the Central West End and within easy reach of the Cortex Innovation Community, Washington University, and downtown — offering high-caliber AI, consulting, workforce training, B2B marketing, and managed IT services for residents and businesses across the metro.
Academy / Sherman Park is a neighborhood in North St. Louis positioned at 38.6584° N, 90.2673° W , just outside the Central West End. The official boundaries are Dr. Martin Luther King Drive on the north, Delmar Boulevard on the south, North Kingshighway Boulevard on the east, and Union Boulevard on the west — a compact 0.44 square miles bounded on every side by some of the most heavily traveled corridors in the city. As of the 2020 Census, the neighborhood was home to 2,355 residents living in 1,276 housing units. Its surrounding neighborhoods read like a roll call of historic North City: Fountain Park to the east, the Central West End to the south, Visitation Park, West End, and Hamilton Heights to the west, and Kingsway West to the north.
The land that today contains Academy / Sherman Park was originally part of a large tract owned by Jean Pierre Cabanné , a French fur trader who arrived in St. Louis in 1798 and married Julie Gratiot, a descendant of the prominent Chouteau family. Their sons, Lucien and Francis, inherited the farm and called it “Mount Cabanne.” The neighborhood was developed during the rapid westward expansion of the city before and after the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition — St. Louis’s legendary World’s Fair — with most residential buildings constructed between 1890 and 1910 for the growing middle class. Today, the majority of the neighborhood (everything except the area north of Page Boulevard) falls within the Mount Cabanne / Raymond Place Historic District , listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
The defining streets of Academy / Sherman Park are Cabanne Avenue and Raymond Avenue — tree-lined showplaces of brick and stone-fronted four-square homes with turrets, corner towers, triple dormers, and curved bay windows; Page Boulevard , a wide east-west corridor; Union Boulevard on the west, which carries the neighborhood’s two most prominent civic landmarks; and Delmar Boulevard at the southern boundary, the famous east-west spine connecting Academy / Sherman Park to the Delmar Loop and Washington University. The architectural character of the neighborhood is remarkably consistent: two- and three-story tightly constructed homes, with an unusual concentration of stone-fronted four-squares that distinguish Academy / Sherman Park from comparable South City neighborhoods like Shaw or Tower Grove South.
The neighborhood’s civic anchors sit along Union Boulevard. Soldan International Studies High School (originally Soldan High School), opened in 1909 and designed by celebrated St. Louis architect William B. Ittner , was praised by the United States Bureau of Education for its Tudor Gothic detailing and built to complement the nearby William Clark School (1906) — also designed by Ittner. Soldan was attended for a year by playwright Tennessee Williams , who later used the school as a setting for The Glass Menagerie , and graduated notables including William McChesney Martin Jr. (longest-serving Chairman of the Federal Reserve), Clark Clifford (U.S. Secretary of Defense), singer Fontella Bass, actress Agnes Moorehead, and St. Louis Rams owner Georgia Frontiere. The Cabanne Branch Library , a Beaux-Arts Carnegie library built in 1906–1907 on Union Boulevard, was the second of the original six St. Louis branch libraries funded by Andrew Carnegie and was renovated in 2019 — the last active Carnegie-funded St. Louis library to undergo restoration.
Academy / Sherman Park also has a deep literary and cultural footprint. Sally Benson , author of the autobiographical stories that inspired the 1944 MGM film Meet Me in St. Louis , grew up at 5135 Kensington Avenue in the neighborhood (the house was demolished in 1994). The neighborhood was home to a substantial Jewish community in the 1920s and 1930s, anchored by the B’nai Amoona Temple on Academy Avenue (now a Missionary Baptist church). Other historic religious and civic buildings in the immediate area include the Pilgrim Congregational Church (1906) and the former Church of the Messiah (1907).
Walk Cabanne or Raymond Avenue today and the architecture still argues for itself: turret-topped four-squares and bay-windowed brick homes that would be six-figure showpieces almost anywhere else in Missouri, some meticulously kept, others boarded and waiting for an owner willing to take them on. Academy / Sherman Park, like much of north St. Louis, has far fewer residents than it did when Soldan opened its doors in 1909, and it has no commercial strip of its own — not because the housing stock or the history don’t warrant one, but because retail, restaurants, and everyday services followed the city’s population south of Delmar decades ago. That is the honest picture: a neighborhood built for a much larger population, still carrying real architectural and civic weight, presently served more by its neighbors than by itself. It is also one of the least-written-about pockets of the city, which is exactly why it belongs in a guide instead of being skipped.
Academy / Sherman Park is geographically compact and almost entirely residential — there is no commercial strip inside its own boundaries, and no St Louis Near Me Directory member is headquartered here. Because the neighborhood sits at the seam between several major St. Louis service corridors, the businesses that serve its residents and professionals are located just across the boundary: everyday needs like coffee, food, and pet grooming a few blocks south in the Central West End, West End, and DeBaliviere Place, and professional and institutional services in the Cortex Innovation Community on Duncan Avenue and downtown St. Louis along Washington Avenue. The listings on this page reflect that practical reality — real businesses, each labeled with its actual neighborhood and distance, drawn from the closest service area that Academy / Sherman Park residents and professionals actually use.
Image: Houses on Cabanne Avenue in Academy — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0, Paul Sableman

Academy / Sherman Park sits in the mid-western section of the City of St. Louis on relatively level ground in the area historically known as the Cabanne District, and the climate follows a classic Midwest four-season pattern — warm, humid summers with highs regularly reaching the upper 80s°F, cold winters with periodic snow and ice along Page Boulevard and Cabanne Avenue, and transitional springs and falls that make the tree-lined residential blocks particularly photogenic. The neighborhood’s position along the Delmar Boulevard corridor and just north of Forest Park gives it a slightly more urban, exposed microclimate than the parkside neighborhoods directly to the south.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Academy neighborhood? 
A. Academy / Sherman Park is defined by the Mount Cabanne / Raymond Place Historic District — tree-lined streets of stone-fronted four-square homes built mostly between 1890 and 1910, developed on land once owned by French fur trader Jean Pierre Cabanné. It’s a compact 0.44-square-mile, almost entirely residential neighborhood with no commercial strip of its own, anchored instead by Soldan International Studies High School and the Cabanne Branch Library.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Academy? 
A. Academy / Sherman Park has no businesses of its own — it’s almost entirely residential, with no St Louis Near Me Directory member based there. Its guide is honestly labeled by actual location and distance: Alambda Systems and Mind Safety Management LLC in the nearby Cortex Innovation Community, plus pet grooming, coffee, and dining options a few blocks south in the Central West End and DeBaliviere Place.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Academy? 
A. Academy / Sherman Park has no dining, retail, or recreation inside its own boundaries — it’s geographically compact and almost entirely residential. The closest options are just blocks away: Wolfgang’s Pet Stop and Evangeline’s Bistro and Music House in the Central West End, Crema Coffeehouse in DeBaliviere Place, and Deli Divine on the Delmar corridor in the West End, all within a mile of Cabanne and Raymond Avenue.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Academy? 
A. Yes — Soldan International Studies High School (1909), designed by William B. Ittner, is the neighborhood’s civic anchor, attended for a year by playwright Tennessee Williams and later used as a setting for The Glass Menagerie. The Cabanne Branch Library, a 1906 Beaux-Arts Carnegie library on Union Boulevard, was restored in 2019, and the neighborhood south of Page Boulevard sits within the Mount Cabanne / Raymond Place National Historic District.

Q. What is it like to live in Academy? 
A. Living in Academy / Sherman Park today means turret-topped, stone-fronted four-square homes that would be showpieces almost anywhere else in Missouri — some meticulously kept, others boarded and waiting for an owner. The neighborhood has far fewer residents than when Soldan opened in 1909, and no commercial strip of its own, so daily life leans on the Central West End and West End nearby for coffee, food, and services.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Academy? 
A. Residents and visitors get around Academy / Sherman Park via its four boundary streets — Dr. Martin Luther King Drive to the north, Delmar Boulevard to the south, North Kingshighway Boulevard to the east, and Union Boulevard to the west — with Delmar connecting directly to the Delmar Loop and Washington University. Its position just outside the Central West End puts the Cortex Innovation Community and downtown within easy reach.
