### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Is Central West End a good neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. Yes — the American Planning Association named the Central West End one of America’s Great Neighborhoods, and it’s consistently rated the most walkable neighborhood in St. Louis. It combines architecturally distinguished streets like the gated Westmoreland and Portland Places with a genuinely walkable commercial core along Euclid and Laclede Avenues, anchored by the Cortex Innovation Community, Washington University Medical Center, and the Cathedral Basilica.

Q. What is the Central West End known for? 
A. The Central West End is known for being one of St. Louis’s most walkable, architecturally distinguished neighborhoods — home to the gated 1887 Westmoreland and Portland Places mansion streets, the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis and its enormous mosaic interior, the Cortex Innovation Community tech district, and a literary legacy that includes T. S. Eliot, Tennessee Williams, William S. Burroughs, and Kate Chopin.

Q. What to do in the Central West End? 
A. Start with a walk down Euclid Avenue, where more than 75 independent businesses — including Northwest Coffee Roasting, Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Ice Cream, and the 125-year-old Straub’s Market — line a genuinely walkable commercial strip. Tour the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis for its mosaic interior, visit the World Chess Hall of Fame on North Maryland Avenue, or catch dinner and live music at Evangeline’s Bistro on North Euclid.

Q. Is Central West End St. Louis walkable? 
A. Yes — the Central West End is consistently rated the most walkable neighborhood in St. Louis. Its level ground above the culverted River des Peres, dense Euclid and Laclede Avenue commercial core, and MetroLink stations at Central West End and Cortex make it possible to run errands, eat, and get a haircut without a car — while the residential edge toward Kingshighway and Vandeventer moves at a slower pace.

Q. What are some good places to eat in the Central West End of St. Louis? 
A. Euclid and Laclede Avenues carry the neighborhood’s dining scene: Brasserie by Niche serves French bistro plates on Laclede, Evangeline’s Bistro and Music House pairs dinner with live music on North Euclid, and Narwhal’s Crafted anchors Laclede’s western end with cocktails and a patio. For dessert, Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Ice Cream on North Euclid and Straub’s Market’s prepared foods on Kingshighway round out the corridor.

Q. What is considered Central West End St. Louis? 
A. The Central West End’s official boundaries run Delmar Boulevard on the north, I-64/US 40 on the south, North Vandeventer Avenue on the east, and Union Boulevard along the eastern edge of Forest Park on the west, across the 63108 and 63110 zip codes. Within that footprint, residents describe two distinct halves: the walkable Euclid and Laclede Avenue commercial core, and the quieter mansion district toward Kingshighway and Vandeventer.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Central West End businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses that serve the Central West End by combining local content with curated listings. Joining connects a Central West End business to stronger “near me” signals tied to the Cortex Innovation Community, the Cathedral Basilica, Forest Park, and the Euclid, Laclede, and Kingshighway corridors — helping it stand out to nearby residents, scientists, students, and medical professionals.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Central West End? 
A. Central West End’s business mix reflects its split identity: coworking and lab space in Cortex, fine dining and live music, salons and personal care, art galleries and modern furniture design, and upscale grocery, ice cream, and specialty coffee along Euclid and Laclede. Many providers operate out of restored historic buildings on Euclid, Laclede, McPherson, Kingshighway, and Duncan Avenues, serving residents, scientists, students, and medical professionals.

### Cheltenham Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Cheltenham, St. Louis
Cheltenham is a small, history-rich neighborhood in southwest St. Louis — a former clay-mining and firebrick district tucked just south of Forest Park, and part of the wider Dogtown cluster. Its modern streets are quiet and residential, but the ground beneath them once fed one of the largest fire-brick industries in the country.
Cheltenham sits in the southwest corner of the City of St. Louis, bounded roughly by Oakland Avenue on the north, Manchester Avenue on the south, Macklind Avenue on the east, and Hampton Avenue on the west. Forest Park lies immediately to the north, and the neighborhood is woven into the “Dogtown” cluster alongside Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, and Hi-Pointe. At roughly a third of a square mile, it is one of the City’s smaller official neighborhoods.
The area’s recorded history reaches back to around 1798. In the 1830s a Sulphur Springs resort opened here, and the neighborhood took the name Cheltenham after the English spa town of the same name — the birthplace of the resort’s manager. For a brief moment Cheltenham was a place people traveled to for its mineral waters, long before it became a place defined by its clay.
Cheltenham also hosted an unusual social experiment. Between 1858 and 1864 a band of French utopian communards known as the Icarians — followers of Étienne Cabet — settled here. In February 1858 the remaining members purchased a few hundred acres and set up communal workshops for tailors, joiners, blacksmiths, and shoemakers. Internal disputes over strict governance, including votes to reinstate bans on smoking and drinking, splintered the group, and the depleted commune disbanded by 1864, with some families later joining the Icarian settlement in Iowa.
What truly defined Cheltenham was clay . Beneath the area lies the bowl-shaped Cheltenham Syncline , a geologic formation south of Forest Park holding large reserves of high-quality fire clay. The 1852 extension of the Pacific Railroad line to Cheltenham supplied the transport that, paired with the clay and an immigrant workforce, turned the district industrial almost overnight.
The firebrick industry grew quickly. The earliest and largest firm, the Laclede Fire Brick Company , was founded in 1844 , and about a dozen companies followed. The Cheltenham Fireclay Works — operating on the site from 1855 and incorporated in 1867 as Evens & Howard Fire Brick Co. — produced fire bricks, sewer pipe, and gas retorts that shipped as far as Quebec and Africa. By 1895 roughly 50 brick yards operated in the area, making St. Louis the state’s chief clay-products center.
The clay and brick boom drew Irish and Italian immigrants whose families helped establish the neighboring Dogtown and The Hill communities. Today the kilns are long gone, and Cheltenham is a modest residential and light-industrial pocket — but the Manchester and Macklind corridors that frame it still carry working businesses, from manufacturers and trades to studios and an STLCC campus on its northern edge by Forest Park.
A quiet residential street in Cheltenham. Photo: “Tiny Cheltenham Street” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Flickr.

Cheltenham shares St. Louis’s humid subtropical climate — hot, humid summers with July highs near 90°F , and cooler winters averaging near 40°F in January, spread across roughly 42 inches of precipitation a year.
What the neighborhood is for has changed more than what it looks like. The clay ran out and the brickyards closed decades ago, but Cheltenham never emptied out — it settled into a quiet, small residential pocket wedged between Forest Park, Dogtown, and The Hill. Its edges now do double duty as a practical stop for the surrounding blocks: a hair salon and a dentist on Oakland Avenue, a plumber and a pizza counter close by — the kind of everyday businesses a resident actually uses rather than visits.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Cheltenham neighborhood? 
A. Cheltenham is a small, roughly third-of-a-square-mile neighborhood in southwest St. Louis, bounded by Oakland Avenue, Manchester Avenue, Macklind Avenue, and Hampton Avenue, just south of Forest Park. It was once a major clay-mining and firebrick district built on the Cheltenham Syncline, and today it’s a quiet residential and light-industrial pocket within the wider Dogtown cluster.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Cheltenham businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory is a hyper-local, SEO-optimized directory that helps Cheltenham businesses get found by nearby searchers, expanding rather than replacing their existing Google Business Profile. It offers a free 7-day trial, simple Gold, Platinum, and Diamond tiers, no long-term contracts, and never sells competitor ads against a listing, so shops along Manchester and Macklind can start small and grow.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Cheltenham? 
A. Cheltenham’s 10 listed businesses lean practical and service-based: a hair salon, plumber, emergency dentist, pizza restaurant, towing company, yoga studio, vintage and home-goods store, animal shelter, and community college campus. Most sit along the Oakland, Manchester, or Macklind Avenue edges, reflecting the neighborhood’s legacy as a working clay and firebrick district turned quiet residential pocket.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Cheltenham? 
A. Dining is limited to Imo’s Pizza on Hampton Avenue, the well-known St. Louis-style chain. Retail centers on Cool Stuff Period, a vintage and home-goods shop on Manchester Avenue. For recreation, YogaSix on Oakland Avenue offers classes from gentle to heated flow, and Forest Park sits immediately to the north for a bigger green space.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Cheltenham? 
A. Cheltenham has no parks of its own, but Forest Park borders it directly to the north. Its real landmark is underground: the Cheltenham Syncline, the clay formation that fed the Laclede Fire Brick Company and Evens & Howard Fire Brick Co., once part of roughly 50 area brickyards that made St. Louis a major clay-products center.

Q. What is it like to live in Cheltenham? 
A. Living in Cheltenham means quiet, small-scale residential streets close to Forest Park, with everyday services like Colorwheel Hair, STL Urgent Dental, and Tony LaMartina Plumbing nearby rather than a business district to visit. At roughly a third of a square mile, it’s one of the city’s smaller neighborhoods, so most other needs mean a short drive into Dogtown or The Hill.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Cheltenham? 
A. Cheltenham is compact and walkable within its own blocks, framed by Oakland, Manchester, Macklind, and Hampton avenues, with Forest Park and the STLCC campus reachable on foot from the northern edge. The 1852 Pacific Railroad line once served the neighborhood’s industry; today, getting around beyond Cheltenham typically means a short drive into Dogtown, The Hill, or Forest Park.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Cheltenham? 
A. Cheltenham’s own directory of 10 ranked businesses, from Colorwheel Hair to St. Louis Community College’s Forest Park campus, covers the essentials close to home. For more, St Louis Near Me Directory’s full guide to all 79 St. Louis neighborhoods, linked from this page, covers the wider Dogtown cluster and surrounding areas beyond Cheltenham’s small footprint.

Q. Which famous people live in Cheltenham? 
A. This page does not name current residents of Cheltenham. Its most notable people are historical: the unnamed manager of the 1830s Sulphur Springs resort, born in Cheltenham, England, who gave the neighborhood its name, and the French Icarian communards who ran workshops here from 1858 to 1864 before the settlement disbanded.

### Clayton-Tamm Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Clayton-Tamm, St. Louis
Clayton-Tamm sits at the heart of St. Louis’s beloved “Dogtown” — a working-class Irish-American enclave directly south of Forest Park and the Saint Louis Zoo, anchored by St. James the Greater Catholic Church on its dramatic hill, the 1942-era Pat Connolly Tavern with its iconic neon Budweiser sign, Bob Cassilly’s Turtle Park, and the annual Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade down Tamm Avenue — offering historic neighborhood taverns, craft breweries, family-owned hardware, custom display manufacturing, technology consulting, and walkable retail for residents and businesses across the west-central St. Louis corridor.
Clayton-Tamm sits along the western edge of the City of St. Louis at 38.6264° N, 90.2933° W in zip code 63139. Its boundaries form a compact rectangle: Oakland Avenue and Interstate 64/U.S. Highway 40 to the north (separating it from Forest Park), Hampton Avenue to the east, Manchester Avenue (Old Route 66) to the south, and Louisville and Dale Avenues to the west. The neighborhood’s defining streets are Tamm Avenue (the residential and parade spine), Clayton Avenue (the commercial east-west spine), Oakland Avenue (the northern boundary along the Zoo), and Manchester Avenue (the southern industrial-historic edge). The name comes from the intersection of Clayton Avenue and Tamm Avenue, the center of the neighborhood’s business district. Clayton-Tamm is one of five official city neighborhoods — along with Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham, and a small slice of Ellendale — that together form the informal area known as Dogtown , which is not itself an official St. Louis neighborhood. The neighborhood sits within zip code 63139 alongside surrounding Hi-Pointe to the west, Franz Park and Cheltenham to the east, and Forest Park directly across I-64 to the north.
Ask a lifelong resident where Dogtown actually ends and the answer changes depending on which bar you’re standing in. City records recognize only five official neighborhoods in the area — Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham, and a corner of Ellendale — and “Dogtown” itself has never been one of them. Locals use the name far more loosely and don’t agree on its edges: some draw the line at Hampton Avenue, some stretch it east into Franz Park, and some count only the blocks immediately around Clayton and Tamm. What almost nobody disputes is that the Clayton-and-Tamm intersection is Dogtown’s actual downtown — the highest concentration of bars, taverns, and shops, and the starting line for the AOH Parade. Search “Dogtown, St. Louis” instead of “Clayton-Tamm” and this corridor is almost always what people mean.
The earliest development in what would become Clayton-Tamm was a 1785 Spanish land grant to Charles Gratiot , a Swiss-born early settler related by marriage to St. Louis’s founders, “to cultivate wheat, hemp, corn, tobacco, etc.” The grant was formalized in 1798 and reaffirmed by the US in 1808 after the Louisiana Purchase. Major growth came in 1852, when the Pacific Railroad extended into Cheltenham, opening the area’s clay-rich subsurface to industrial-scale mining. The first clay mines were established in 1845, and by the early 20th century two major operations were running in Clayton-Tamm: the Roberts Mine and the Gittins Mine , the latter reaching 100 feet deep just west of Tamm Avenue. The mining industry drew waves of Irish, Italian, German, French, and Balkan immigrants who built the housing stock around the mines. The Pacific Railroad, the 1849 St. Louis Fire (which triggered stricter brick-building codes), the 1876 founding of Forest Park, and the 1904 World’s Fair all accelerated the build-out of the neighborhood that would soon be called Dogtown. The clay mined here supplied much of the red brick that gives St. Louis its “Brick City” nickname.
The Dogtown name itself is the subject of one of St. Louis’s most enduring legends. While a popular tale ties it to Filipino Igorot tribespeople at the 1904 World’s Fair allegedly hunting dogs for ceremonial purposes, the Dogtown Historical Society — through historian Bob Corbett — has documented the name’s appearance in a Missouri Republican article dated August 14, 1889 , five years before the Fair. The most credible origin describes coal miners displaced from Forest Park when the city acquired the land in 1876, who built shacks south of the new park and used watchdogs to defend their squatters’ homes — giving rise to the “Dogtown” label. The neighborhood’s housing stock primarily consists of early-20th-century red-brick workers’ cottages, two-family flats, and Craftsman bungalows packed densely along tree-lined streets. Closer to Clayton and Tamm Avenues, rows of original miners’ cottages reflect the area’s industrial origins; further out, three-bedroom Craftsman bungalows and frame homes intermingle with brick construction. Clayton-Tamm is notably hilly by St. Louis standards — neighboring Hi-Pointe to the west is named for sitting on one of the city’s highest points, and Clayton-Tamm’s own slopes are unusual in this otherwise flat Mississippi River city.
The neighborhood’s defining institution is St. James the Greater Catholic Church at 1360 Tamm Avenue, founded as a mission in 1860 to serve the Irish Catholic miners. The current English Gothic Revival church , with its cut ashlar stone facing and dramatic hilltop perch on some of the highest ground in Dogtown, was built during the Great Depression entirely funded by parishioners. St. James the Greater School , the attached private K-8 Catholic school across Tamm Avenue from the Sisters of Charity Seminary, has served the parish for over 160 years. Clayton-Tamm contains no public schools — residents are served by the Saint Louis Public School District. The neighborhood’s other religious landmark is the 1911 Memorial Congregational Church , now home to St. Louis Bible Fellowship. Each March 17, Tamm Avenue becomes the route of the Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade , established in 1984 and held in Dogtown since 1986 — widely regarded as the more authentic of St. Louis’s two St. Patrick’s Day parades, drawing tens of thousands for Irish Schools of Dance, pipe bands, and clan floats. The parade kicks off at Tamm and Oakland in front of Pat’s, runs the length of Tamm Avenue to Manchester Road, and remains a multi-generational celebration of Irish-American heritage.
Public green space in Clayton-Tamm itself is famously limited — none of St. Louis’s 108 official city parks fall within the neighborhood’s boundaries. But the trade-off is extraordinary: Forest Park lies directly across Interstate 64 to the north, one of the largest urban parks in the United States, drawing roughly 13 million visitors annually and home to the Saint Louis Zoo (free admission), the Saint Louis Art Museum , the Missouri History Museum , the Saint Louis Science Center , The Muny outdoor theatre, the Norman K. Probstein Golf Course , and miles of trails. Older Dogtown residents also remember The Highlands , the amusement park that operated at the western end of Forest Park from the 1890s until a 1963 fire destroyed it; the site is now home to the Dwight Davis Tennis Center, just across I-64 from Clayton-Tamm. Connecting Clayton-Tamm to the park is Turtle Park , the beloved sculpture playground at Oakland and Tamm Avenues, opened in August 1996 . Sculpted by Bob Cassilly — the artist behind City Museum — and funded by philanthropist Sonya “Sunny” Glassberg as a gift to St. Louis’s children, the park features seven oversized concrete turtles native to Missouri (a 40-foot snapping turtle, a soft-shelled turtle, a red-eared slider, three box turtles, and a stinkpot turtle), seven concrete eggs, and a sinuous snake taking a bite out of the Tamm Avenue overpass. Cassilly borrowed a live snapping turtle from the Saint Louis Zoo to model the largest sculpture, and Turtle Park was voted “Best Picnic Spot” by the Riverfront Times in 2011.
The intersection of Clayton and Tamm forms the unofficial “Downtown Dogtown” — a tight commercial core of independent bars, taverns, breweries, and small specialty shops centered on the Pat Connolly Tavern at 6400 Oakland Avenue (in continuous operation since Irish immigrant Pat Connolly opened it in 1942 , marked by an iconic neon Budweiser V-9 sign), Seamus McDaniel’s , Felix’s Pizza Pub , Heavy Riff Brewing Company (opened 2013 in the former Gewinner’s grocery space), Tamm Avenue Bar , Hogtown Smokehouse , Mac’s Local Eats , and Sugaree Baking Co . The 2010 Census recorded 2,251 residents in Clayton-Tamm, a 9% decline from 2000, with 1,415 housing units at an impressive 90% occupancy rate , split roughly 53/47 owner/renter . The 2020 Census reported a population that remained 85.2% White, 4.6% Black, 2.2% Asian, 6.8% two or more races, and 4.8% Hispanic/Latino; surveys show over 20% of residents claim Irish ancestry , the highest concentration in the city. The median age is 32, with a strong young-adult presence aged 25-44. Median home sale prices over the trailing 12 months are around $220,000 , with three-bedroom cottages near Clayton and Tamm Avenues running $215,000 to $300,000. That renter share shows up on the ground at properties like Oak Park Apartments on Oakland Avenue, which puts Forest Park and the Saint Louis Zoo within a short walk for residents who want Dogtown’s character without owning a century-old cottage.
Clayton-Tamm’s compact, walkable footprint and its position south of Forest Park, between the corporate density of Clayton and the residential pockets of South City, give the neighborhood a distinctive role as the commercial “downtown” of broader Dogtown. The intersection of Clayton and Tamm is the town square; the Pat Connolly Tavern is the unofficial living room; the AOH Parade is the calendar’s most important date; and the brick cottages climbing Clayton-Tamm’s unusual slopes are physical evidence of the immigrant mining families who built them. Many of the businesses serving this corridor straddle the wider Dogtown area or the nearby Class A office market in Clayton, reflecting the practical service ecosystem Clayton-Tamm residents and professionals use every day. The listings on this page draw from that broader Clayton-Tamm and Dogtown footprint, presenting the bars, breweries, retail, professional services, and consulting providers in their natural geographic relationship to the corridor.
Image: Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade in Dogtown — the more authentic of St. Louis’s two St. Patrick’s Day parades, held annually on March 17 down Tamm Avenue in Clayton-Tamm — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.5 by Agent-88

Clayton-Tamm sees a classic Midwest four-season climate — hot, humid summers and cold winters — with the calendar built around one date: March 17, when the Ancient Order of Hibernians Parade runs down Tamm Avenue rain, shine, or snow.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Why do they call it Dogtown in St. Louis? 
A. The most credible explanation, documented by the Dogtown Historical Society to an 1889 Missouri Republican article predating the 1904 World’s Fair, traces the name to coal miners displaced from Forest Park when the city acquired that land in 1876. They built shacks south of the new park and kept watchdogs to defend their squatters’ homes, giving the area its “Dogtown” label.

Q. Is Dogtown a good neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. Dogtown is the informal name for five official St. Louis neighborhoods — Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham, and a slice of Ellendale — and Clayton-Tamm, its commercial core, carries a strong identity built around the Pat Connolly Tavern, Turtle Park, and the annual AOH St. Patrick’s Day Parade. It sits directly south of Forest Park and the Saint Louis Zoo.

Q. What defines the Clayton-Tamm neighborhood? 
A. Clayton-Tamm is defined by its position as “Downtown Dogtown” — the Clayton-and-Tamm intersection that forms the commercial heart of the wider Irish-American Dogtown area. The neighborhood is anchored by St. James the Greater Catholic Church on its hilltop, the Pat Connolly Tavern, open since 1942, and Bob Cassilly’s Turtle Park across from Forest Park.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Clayton-Tamm businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Clayton-Tamm businesses a hyperlocal listing tied to the neighborhood’s own landmarks — Turtle Park, the Pat Connolly Tavern, and St. James the Greater — helping bars, breweries, and bakeries along Clayton and Tamm avenues stand out to residents, Zoo visitors, and the AOH Parade crowds who fill this corridor every March.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Clayton-Tamm? 
A. Independent neighborhood bars and breweries, barbecue and baked goods, and lawn and home services dominate Clayton-Tamm’s business mix. On-page options include Hogtown Smokehouse, Tamm Avenue Bar, Sugaree Baking Company, and Heavy Riff Brewing Company, nearly all sitting directly on Clayton, Tamm, Oakland, or Manchester Avenue inside the neighborhood’s own boundaries.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Clayton-Tamm? 
A. Clayton-Tamm’s dining runs from Hogtown Smokehouse’s barbecue to Sugaree Baking Company’s fresh-baked goods and Heavy Riff Brewing’s house-smoked BBQ and craft beer. For recreation, Turtle Park’s Bob Cassilly-sculpted playground anchors the neighborhood at Oakland and Tamm, with the 1,326-acre Forest Park and the Saint Louis Zoo directly across Interstate 64.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Clayton-Tamm? 
A. Yes — Clayton-Tamm has no city parks of its own, but Turtle Park, Bob Cassilly’s sculpture playground at Oakland and Tamm, opened in August 1996, serves as its outdoor anchor. St. James the Greater Catholic Church on its hilltop, the Pat Connolly Tavern with its 1940s neon Budweiser sign, and the 1911 Memorial Congregational Church round out the neighborhood’s historic landmarks.

Q. What is it like to live in Clayton-Tamm? 
A. Living in Clayton-Tamm means a hilly, walkable neighborhood of century-old red-brick cottages and Craftsman bungalows, with over 20% of residents claiming Irish ancestry, the highest concentration in the city. The 2020 census recorded a population that is 85.2% White, with a median age of 32, and roughly 47% of housing units renter-occupied.

### Clifton Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Clifton Heights, St. Louis
Clifton Heights serves as one of southwest St. Louis’s most topographically distinctive Victorian-era residential neighborhoods — an 1885 Julius Pitzman-platted Methodist subdivision atop the Gratiot League Square, anchored by the 4.4-acre Clifton Heights Park and its iconic lake (originally a private park dedicated to the City in 1912), the Fry Memorial Methodist Church (now a boutique inn), and the curving streets that flow down through Queen Anne and Arts & Crafts homes toward the park — offering general contracting, plastering, marketing, industrial supply, and real estate services across the Hampton and Arsenal corridors.
Clifton Heights is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6143° N, 90.2916° W in southwest St. Louis City. The neighborhood is bounded by Interstate 44 on the north and west, Hampton Avenue on the east, and Arsenal Street on the south. Surrounding neighborhoods include Ellendale to the north and west, The Hill and Southwest Garden to the east, and Lindenwood Park to the south. The neighborhood sits within ZIP code 63139 and lies in the 4th Ward of the City of St. Louis. The neighborhood spans approximately 0.48 square miles and is home to roughly 2,836 residents (2020 census). Clifton Heights has arguably the most unique topography in all of the city — a large hill that naturally slopes north and west toward the ancient valley of the River des Peres (long since channelized along the railroad and I-44), with a natural “dimple” or mini-valley at its center forming the bowl that holds Clifton Heights Park and its small lake. The unconventional winding streets are uncommon for St. Louis, where the rectilinear street grid rules in most of the city.
The area that now constitutes Clifton Heights was originally part of an approximately 3-mile by 3-mile tract of land called the Gratiot League Square , granted to the Swiss-born merchant Charles Gratiot in 1798 . Gratiot had requested the land grant in 1785 from the authorities of New Spain, who then governed the region, so that he could “establish a habitation on the River des Peres, to cultivate wheat, hemp, corn, tobacco, etc., etc.” This land was relatively remote from the village of St. Louis, which then consisted of only a few dozen structures along the Mississippi riverfront and common land that extended a couple of miles to the west and south. After the 1803 Louisiana Purchase , Gratiot’s ownership of the land was recognized by the U.S. government in its process of reviewing the Spanish land grants. The land in present-day Clifton Heights retained its rural character until the middle of the 19th century, when the arrival of railroads and the discovery of coal and clay deposits transformed much of the area. While these mines and factories are more closely associated with the Dogtown neighborhoods and The Hill , some were established within Clifton Heights as well.
In 1851 , ground was broken in St. Louis for the Pacific Railroad , using land granted to the newly formed company by the state of Missouri. As construction proceeded westward along the valley of the River des Peres, trains began running in 1853 along roughly the northwestern boundary of present-day Clifton Heights. The development of Clifton Heights as a residential neighborhood took off in the 1880s . An 1876 map shows just a handful of streets in present-day Clifton Heights; by 1884 , the area was served by streetcars along Arsenal Street to the south and (New) Manchester Road to the north. A major catalyst of this development in the northern part of the neighborhood was a community of Methodists led by Benjamin St. James Fry . The group hired the Prussian-born surveyor and city planner Julius Pitzman in 1885 to lay out their subdivision, which covered an area listed by the Recorder of Deeds as D. W. Graham’s Sulphur Springs Tract . Pitzman — whose work also influenced the development of Lafayette Square’s Benton Place (1866), Westmoreland and Portland Place, and several other St. Louis private streets — designed the distinctive curving streets surrounding the park that give Clifton Heights its uniquely Victorian, almost Webster Groves-like feel. The original construction included a Methodist church on Clifton Avenue, named the Fry Memorial Methodist Episcopal Church after Fry’s death in 1892. The church on that site, built in the early 20th century after the original burned, was sold to private owners in 2004 and is now a boutique inn.
Commercial buildings began to appear in the neighborhood by the turn of the 20th century. One example is the Clifton Pointe Building at the corner of Columbia Avenue and Clifton Avenue, built between 1903 and 1907 . At the time of a 1991 survey by the Landmarks Association of St. Louis, a Rexall Drugs store occupied the building; as of 2025, it is home to a hair salon and law office. In the 1920s and 1930s , another wave of home building occurred. Based on information from building permits, scores of Clifton Heights homes were constructed during this period by local builder Harry C. Vollmar , whose family had lived in the neighborhood since at least 1910. The last part of Clifton Heights to be developed for residential use was the Clifton Hills subdivision north of Southwest Avenue and west of Tamm Avenue in the 1940s and 1950s . When Interstate 44 was built in St. Louis in the late 1950s and 1960s (in service by 1972), about 50 of the neighborhood’s houses ended up confined between the new highway and the railroad tracks , and a small park called Frisco Park was effectively eliminated. I-44 now constitutes both a physical and psychological border for Clifton Heights. In 1991 , the Landmarks Association of St. Louis conducted a 455-page survey to assess the historical significance of the architecture within the neighborhood.
The 4.4-acre Clifton Heights Park at the geographic center of the neighborhood — located between Columbia Avenue, Sulphur Avenue, Elizabeth Avenue, and the winding Clifton Avenue — began life as a private park developed for the residents of the 1885 Clifton Heights Subdivision . The original 4.4-acre tract was dedicated to the City of St. Louis in 1912 , with an additional 1.25 acres added during the early 1920s. The City later bought adjoining property to the south and east, enlarging the park to its present size. Today the park features a charming lake with ducks, geese, two fountains, a viewing deck, and a “boat house,” as well as a basketball court, playground, and walking paths that wind down through the surrounding Victorian homes toward the lake at the bottom of the bowl. The lake is part of the St. Louis Urban Fishing Program , although it is not regularly stocked like the program’s nine other park lakes. In 2018 , the City of St. Louis released a master plan to guide future improvements to the park, prioritizing infrastructure repair, restoration of the park’s Victorian character, and improved accessibility. The Clifton Heights Neighborhood Association (cliftonheights-stl.org) holds several annual events in the park, including an Easter egg hunt, a fall festival, and a candy cane hunt.
Clifton Heights is also home to the Mason School of Academic & Cultural Literacy on Southwest Avenue (an SLPS pre-K to 6th grade project-based magnet school designed by district architect Rockwell M. Milligan and opened in 1921 ; former U.S. Representative and 1988 / 2004 presidential candidate Richard Gephardt grew up on Reber Place and attended what was then called Mason Elementary), Epiphany of Our Lord Catholic Parish (founded 1911, celebrated 100 years in 2011), Mount Tabor United Church of Christ on Arsenal Street (formed 1928 by a merger of two congregations dating to 1889), an AMVETS Post 6 , and a Drury Inn and Suites at the intersection of I-44 and Hampton Avenue. The neighborhood’s key business anchors today include Independents Graphic & Display at 6331 Knox Industrial Drive (the 35,000-square-foot custom printing, sewing, prototyping, and POP-display manufacturer), The St. Louis Plastering Company LLC at 6841 Manchester Avenue (the high-rated specialty plaster contractor for the neighborhood’s Victorian and Arts & Crafts homes), Hof Construction, Inc. at 3137 Jamieson Avenue (the 100-year, multi-generational family-led general contractor and construction-management firm with GSA, educational, and institutional project experience), S. M. Wilson & Co. at 2185 Hampton Avenue (the century-old employee-owned construction-management firm specializing in healthcare, industrial, retail, and municipal projects), STL Pest Control at 2525 Hampton Avenue (family-owned since 1989, the neighborhood’s most-reviewed business at 3,764 Google reviews), Maplewood Plumbing & Sewer, LLC. at 2725 Watson Road (licensed residential plumbers on the job since 1985), and Erker Realty at 6242 Columbia Avenue (a 40-year, independently owned real estate office a block from the park).
Clifton Heights Park — the 4.4-acre park and lake at the heart of the Clifton Heights neighborhood, St. Louis, Missouri. Photo: St Louis Near Me Directory.

Clifton Heights experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate — hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season — same as every other neighborhood in the city.
What sets Clifton Heights apart has nothing to do with weather and everything to do with shape. Walk in from Hampton or Manchester and the ground drops away beneath you, curving streets peeling off Pitzman’s 1885 plat and winding down toward the lake at the bottom of the bowl — a sensation few other St. Louis neighborhoods offer, since almost everywhere else in the city the grid stays flat and straight. It reads less like a slice of a big city than a small hillside village that got absorbed into one. That village is still mostly what it looks like: modest Victorian and Arts & Crafts homes on quiet curving streets, a handful of small owner-run businesses along the edges (a pest control company, a plumber, a real estate office, a piano studio, a plastering contractor for the old houses), and a working light-industrial strip on Knox Industrial Drive that keeps blue-collar jobs on land that has been zoned for that use since the neighborhood’s earliest coal and clay days. It is not a destination neighborhood — there is no commercial strip to browse — it is a residential one, and a resident walking down into the park at dusk, past the boat house and the two fountains, is doing exactly what the neighborhood was built for in 1885.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Clifton Heights neighborhood? 
A. Clifton Heights is a small, 0.48-square-mile southwest St. Louis neighborhood bounded by Interstate 44, Hampton Avenue, and Arsenal Street, home to about 2,836 residents. It’s defined by unusual topography: an 1885 Julius Pitzman-platted subdivision whose curving streets wind down into a natural bowl holding Clifton Heights Park and its lake.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Clifton Heights businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Clifton Heights businesses a Gold, Platinum, or Diamond listing — schema-optimized, up to 400 keyword combinations, Google Business Profile support, and review management — built to expand, not replace, their existing Google presence. Every paid plan includes a 7-day free trial, no long-term contract, and no competitor ads running on the listing.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Clifton Heights? 
A. General contracting, plaster restoration, plumbing, pest control, and real estate dominate the Clifton Heights business mix. Anchors include Hof Construction, S. M. Wilson & Co., The St. Louis Plastering Company, STL Pest Control, Maplewood Plumbing & Sewer, and Erker Realty, plus Independents Graphic & Display’s custom sewing and POP-display shop on Knox Industrial Drive. It’s a residential neighborhood, so most commerce serves the housing stock directly.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Clifton Heights? 
A. Clifton Heights has almost no dining or retail of its own — residents head into neighboring The Hill, Southwest Garden, Ellendale, or Lindenwood Park for restaurants and shops. Recreation centers entirely on Clifton Heights Park: its lake with ducks and two fountains, a boat house, basketball court, playground, and the winding walking paths through the park’s mini-valley.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Clifton Heights? 
A. Yes — the 4.4-acre Clifton Heights Park and its lake anchor the neighborhood, originally a private park for the 1885 subdivision before its 1912 dedication to the city. Nearby landmarks include the Fry Memorial Methodist Episcopal Church (now a boutique inn), the 1903–1907 Clifton Pointe Building at Columbia and Clifton, and the 1921 Mason School of Academic & Cultural Literacy.

Q. What is it like to live in Clifton Heights? 
A. Living in Clifton Heights means a quiet, densely built residential neighborhood of Victorian and Arts & Crafts homes on curving 1880s-1950s streets, centered on the lake and boat house at Clifton Heights Park. There’s no commercial strip to browse, but a handful of long-tenured, highly rated local businesses like STL Pest Control and Maplewood Plumbing serve the housing stock directly.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Clifton Heights? 
A. Hampton Avenue and Arsenal Street frame the neighborhood’s eastern and southern edges, with Interstate 44 forming its northern and western border. Streetcars once ran along Arsenal and Manchester as early as 1884, and today the winding streets Julius Pitzman platted in 1885 still curve down from those corridors toward Clifton Heights Park at the center.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Clifton Heights? 
A. Clifton Heights’ own directory of 10 ranked businesses, from Hof Construction to Erker Realty, covers home services and real estate close to home. For dining and retail, neighboring The Hill, Southwest Garden, and Lindenwood Park are a short trip away, and St Louis Near Me Directory’s full guide to all 79 St. Louis neighborhoods covers the wider area.

### College Hill Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
College Hill, St. Louis
College Hill anchors a historic, hilly stretch of North St. Louis built on Saint Louis University’s 1836 College Farm and the 1820s riverfront estate of Captain Lewis Bissell — anchored today by the towering 1871 Corinthian-column Grand Avenue Water Tower (designed by George I. Barnett) and the 1887 Bissell “New Red” Water Tower (designed by William S. Eames), the 1820s Bissell Mansion (one of St. Louis’s oldest standing brick homes), Mount Grace Convent (home of the “Pink Sisters”), and the William B. Ittner-designed 1912 Bryan Hill Elementary — offering chambers of commerce, professional consulting, business publications, marketing services, and neighborhood anchors like a Black history museum and a family-run barbershop for residents and businesses across the North St. Louis corridor.
College Hill sits in north St. Louis at 38.6733° N, 90.2195° W in zip code 63107. The neighborhood’s boundaries form an irregular pentagon: East Warne Avenue and Adelaide Avenue on the northwest, Interstate 70 on the northeast, Ferry Street on the southeast, and West Florissant Avenue on the southwest. The neighborhood’s defining streets are East Grand Boulevard (the historic commercial spine bisecting the southern hill), West Florissant Avenue (the southwestern boundary), Blair Avenue (running south of the Bissell Water Tower), and Bissell Street . College Hill is bordered by Hyde Park to the south, O’Fallon to the west, the Mark Twain/I-70 industrial corridor and Bissell Point sewage treatment plant to the east (separating it from the Mississippi River), and Mark Twain neighborhood to the north. The neighborhood’s near-perfect street grid is bisected by two hills — the larger southern hill anchored by the Grand and Bissell Water Towers, and the northern hill anchored by Mount Grace Convent. The 2020 Census recorded the neighborhood as 92.2% Black, 4.3% White, 1.7% Asian, and 0.6% Hispanic/Latino , with a 2010 Census count of 1,871 residents — a 36% decline from 2000 reflecting decades of population loss across North St. Louis.
The neighborhood’s name comes from its former use as the College Farm of Saint Louis University . The area, generally bounded by Warne, Carter, and Linton Avenues and Broadway, was acquired by SLU in 1836 for garden and recreation purposes, though the University ultimately decided not to build a campus there. The land was subdivided into residential lots in the early 1870s. Before SLU’s purchase, the area was rural, consisting of several large farm estates owned by Colonel John O’Fallon (whose 600+ acre holdings became the present O’Fallon Park ), Dr. John Gano Bryan, Edward Hempstead, and Captain Lewis Bissell . Bissell — born in Connecticut in 1789, nephew of General Daniel Bissell, and a War of 1812 veteran who came to St. Louis in 1808 to serve under his uncle at Fort Bellefontaine — built his Greek Revival and federalist mansion atop a Mississippi River bluff between 1823 and 1828 on what became known as Bissell Point . He partnered with Colonel John O’Fallon to supply goods to frontier troops, eventually acquiring approximately 1,500 acres at Bissell Point.
The neighborhood’s most distinguishing architectural features are its two historic standpipe water towers — engineered to equalize the surging water pressure from the new Bissell Point pumping station, and now among only seven such surviving towers in the entire United States (with St. Louis home to three of them, the third being the 1898 Compton Hill Tower). The Grand Avenue Water Tower at 20th Street and East Grand Avenue was placed in service in 1871, designed by George Ingham Barnett (the first St. Louis architect to receive training abroad) and considered the largest perfect Corinthian column in existence at 154 feet tall — in the late 1920s, lights were placed at its top to serve as aviation beacons for what became Lambert Field. The Bissell “New Red” Water Tower at Bissell Street and Blair Avenue, built in 1886-87 at a cost of $79,798 from red brick, light gray stone, and terra cotta, stands 194 feet high — designed by William S. Eames (founder of the St. Louis chapter of the American Institute of Architects), often likened to a Moorish minaret. Both towers are listed on the National Register of Historic Places; in 1997, the Gateway Foundation added nighttime lighting to both, making them visible from the interstates.
The Bissell Mansion at 4426 Randall Place — one of St. Louis’s oldest standing brick homes, possibly the oldest — is a nearly 6,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, four-bathroom Greek Revival and Federalist structure with walls at least a foot thick, intact stained glass, a dumbwaiter, fireplaces in each room, and a central staircase. Captain Bissell lived there for over 40 years until his death in 1868 at age 79. The home was nearly demolished in the early 1950s for the construction of the Mark Twain Expressway (now I-70), but preservationists saved it. It became a designated St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 and operated for over four decades as the Bissell Mansion Restaurant & Murder Mystery Dinner Theatre before closing at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The home is widely reported to be haunted by Captain Bissell himself.
College Hill’s other major institutions reflect its early-20th-century immigrant religious heritage. Mount Grace Convent and Chapel at East Warne Avenue, home of the contemplative cloistered “Pink Sisters” (Sister Servants of the Holy Spirit of Perpetual Adoration, named for their distinctive pink habits), was founded in 1928 and anchors the northern hill of the neighborhood. St. Paul’s Lutheran Church on East John Avenue dates its congregation to 1862, with the present church building constructed in 1926. Bryan Hill Elementary School at 2128 Gano Avenue, built in 1912, was designed by William B. Ittner — the prolific Building Commissioner for the St. Louis Public School District who designed 45 elementary schools and 5 high schools for the district starting in 1897. Lowell School at 1409 Linton Avenue (built 1926) now houses the KIPP St. Louis Triumph Academy Charter School . The St. Louis Academy at East Linton Avenue and 21st Street opened in September 2001 on the former Perpetual Help Catholic School site.
The neighborhood’s housing stock dates predominantly from between 1880 and 1920 and is dominated by red-brick townhouses, four-family flats, and single-family brick dwellings — many with comparatively large yards, with properties near the crest of the hillside bluff overlooking the Mississippi River and its surrounding valleys. The architecture is notably varied; College Hill developed slowly over decades, producing blocks where homes from 1870 sit next to homes from 1950. Two unusual clusters of wood-frame houses survive in violation of the city’s post-fire brick-only building codes — one cluster around West Florissant on DeSoto Street, another on Conde Street at College Street. Nearly half of residential units are owner-occupied. Historically, commercial activity was concentrated along East Grand Avenue near the Old Water Tower and along a strip on West Florissant Avenue. The neighborhood’s 1849-platted predecessor settlement, Lowell , originally extended from Adelaide Avenue, Broadway, East Prairie Avenue, and the river — annexed by the City of St. Louis without ever being incorporated.
College Hill’s modern business activity has been deeply shaped by the North Spring Empowerment Center , which borders the neighborhood and serves as the home of the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce . The neighborhood has access to MetroLink and Metro bus service via the Grand Avenue corridor, with quick I-70 access at Adelaide Avenue, West Florissant, Broadway, and East Grand exits — placing College Hill within minutes of downtown, the airport, and Interstates 55, 44, and 170. With its 1,871 residents (2010), unique combination of two nationally landmarked water towers, the centuries-old Bissell Mansion, the William B. Ittner-designed Bryan Hill School, the Pink Sisters at Mount Grace, and the layered architecture spanning eight decades, College Hill represents one of St. Louis’s most historically significant North Side neighborhoods. The listings on this page draw from the broader College Hill and surrounding service ecosystem.
Image: The Bissell Street Water Tower (the “New Red”), built 1886-87 — the 194-foot Victorian standpipe tower designed by William S. Eames, anchoring College Hill and listed on the National Register of Historic Places — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

College Hill sees the same hot, humid summers and cold, snowy winters as the rest of St. Louis, with the hillside views from the two water towers the one thing that changes the way the seasons feel here.
What’s more useful to know is that College Hill today is overwhelmingly residential, and its own commercial footprint is thin. What anchors the corridor now is civic and professional rather than retail — the North Spring Empowerment Center, the chamber of commerce and consulting offices clustered around it, and a handful of small operations working out of converted storefronts and homes along East Grand. That’s an honest reflection of a neighborhood that lost more than a third of its population between 2000 and 2010 and never fully rebuilt the commercial strip that once ran along East Grand Boulevard near the Old Water Tower. For groceries, personal care, and culture, residents typically head a mile or two south and west — to Jeff Vanderlou, where Clark’s Barbershop has cut hair across three generations since 1962, and to St. Louis Place, home to the Griot Museum of Black History. Both sit just outside College Hill’s boundary rather than inside it, but both are a short drive away, and both speak more directly to who lives in College Hill now than a downtown consultancy ever could.

Henry Clark opened the shop in 1962; his son Vincent took over after working there since 1981, and today it’s run by third-generation owner Chris Clark, who grew up in the chairs. More than sixty years in, it still functions as much as a neighborhood gathering spot as a barbershop — the kind of place where regulars sit and talk between cuts. Services include standard, senior, and kids’ haircuts, beard trims and razor lines, and scalp treatments. Closed Sundays.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Where is the College Hill neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. College Hill sits in north St. Louis at approximately 38.6733° N, 90.2195° W, zip code 63107. Its irregular pentagon-shaped boundaries run East Warne and Adelaide Avenues on the northwest, Interstate 70 on the northeast, Ferry Street on the southeast, and West Florissant Avenue on the southwest — bordered by Hyde Park to the south, O’Fallon to the west, and the Mark Twain neighborhood to the north.

Q. What defines the College Hill neighborhood? 
A. College Hill is defined by two rare landmarks — the 1871 Grand Avenue Water Tower and 1887 Bissell “New Red” Water Tower, two of only seven surviving 19th-century standpipe towers in the U.S. — alongside the historic Bissell Mansion, Mount Grace Convent’s Pink Sisters, and William B. Ittner’s Bryan Hill School. Its 1880-1920 brick housing and hill-split street grid round out a neighborhood shaped more by landmarks than commerce.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help College Hill businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses serving College Hill by combining local content with curated listings. Joining connects a College Hill business to stronger “near me” signals tied to the Grand and Bissell Water Towers, the Bissell Mansion, Mount Grace Convent, and the East Grand, West Florissant, Blair, and Bissell Street corridors — helping it stand out to North St. Louis residents searching online.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in College Hill? 
A. College Hill’s own businesses lean civic and professional rather than retail: the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce and St. Louis Small Business Monthly anchor the North Spring Empowerment Center corridor, alongside consulting firms like Luther’s Consulting and Collaborative Strategies. The neighborhood’s commercial footprint stayed thin after losing more than a third of its population between 2000 and 2010.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in College Hill? 
A. College Hill has little dining or retail within its own boundary today. Residents typically head about a mile and a half to Jeff Vanderlou for Clark’s Barbershop, cutting hair across three generations since 1962, or to St. Louis Place for the Griot Museum of Black History. The neighborhood’s own draw is its landmark water towers rather than shops or restaurants.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in College Hill? 
A. Yes, several major ones. The 1871 Grand Avenue Water Tower and 1887 Bissell “New Red” Water Tower are two of only seven surviving 19th-century standpipe towers in the U.S., both on the National Register of Historic Places. The Bissell Mansion, a St. Louis City Landmark since 1971, Mount Grace Convent, and the Ittner-designed Bryan Hill Elementary round out the neighborhood’s landmarks.

Q. What is it like to live in College Hill? 
A. Living in College Hill means red-brick townhouses, four-family flats, and single-family homes dating mostly from 1880 to 1920, with nearly half owner-occupied. The 2010 census recorded 1,871 residents, down 36% from 2000, and the neighborhood is 92.2% Black. Its own commercial footprint is thin, so residents rely on nearby Jeff Vanderlou and St. Louis Place for everyday shops and services.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around College Hill? 
A. College Hill has access to MetroLink and Metro bus service along the Grand Avenue corridor, with quick Interstate 70 access at the Adelaide Avenue, West Florissant, Broadway, and East Grand exits. That puts the neighborhood within minutes of downtown St. Louis, the airport, and Interstates 55, 44, and 170.

### Columbus Square Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Columbus Square, St. Louis
Columbus Square anchors a small but historically deep stretch of near-north downtown St. Louis built on the city’s first wave of German Catholic, Irish, and Italian immigrant settlement — anchored today by the 1844 Shrine of St. Joseph (the only Vatican-authenticated miracle site in the Midwest and the only example of Baroque church architecture in St. Louis), the William B. Ittner-designed 1906 Patrick Henry Downtown Academy, the iconic Vess Bottle visible from I-70, the 1927 Cass Bank and Trust building, and the layered 1936 Neighborhood Gardens / 1952 Cochran Gardens / 1985-87 Columbus Square Townhomes and Castles housing legacy — offering coworking, marketing agencies, business brokerages, and chambers of commerce in the corridor that bridges Downtown St. Louis and the Bottle District.
Columbus Square sits just north of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6372° N, 90.1957° W in zip codes 63101 and 63106. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood’s boundaries are Cass Avenue on the North, Interstate 70 on the East, Cole Street on the South, and N. Tucker Boulevard / N. 13th Street on the West. Columbus Square is bordered by Old North St. Louis and the Bottle District beyond Cass to the north, Carr Square to the west (separated by Tucker), the St. Louis Post-Dispatch building and Downtown St. Louis across Cole Street to the south, and I-70 plus the Mississippi River industrial corridor to the east. The neighborhood sits within a short walk of the Gateway Arch grounds and the Central Business District. The 2020 Census recorded Columbus Square as 88.7% Black, 5.8% White, 0.6% Asian, 3.3% Two or More Races , with 2.2% Hispanic/Latino, and a 2010 Census population of 1,869 residents . In 2010, Columbus Square ranked last among the 79 St. Louis neighborhoods for median household income at $18,800 .
Columbus Square was settled by successive waves of immigrants . The first wave — a group of German Catholics — settled in the vicinity of 11th and Biddle Streets in the 1840s. The first Irish immigrants then colonized the land around 6th and Biddle, an area that subsequently became St. Patrick’s parish. After 1840, the area from the river west to 12th Street was built up with high-density tenement quarters and two- and three-story row houses for newly arriving immigrant laborers. Many of these structures fell to commercial and industrial development after the Civil War; those that remained had deteriorated into overcrowded slums by 1870, with tenement enclaves carrying nicknames like “Castle Thunder,” “Crabber Alley,” and “Wild Cat Chute.” An Italian community emerged near 7th and Carr Streets after the turn of the century — making the southern portion of today’s Columbus Square (along with the area along Cole Street) the original “Little Italy” of St. Louis . By 1920 the whole area north and west of downtown took on a polyglot character, with immigrants from Russia and the Balkan countries adding to the mix.
The neighborhood holds the distinction of being the birthplace of much of St. Louis Italian culinary history. The Bommarito family operated St. Louis’s first Italian bakery at 7th and Carr Streets, plus a spaghetti factory at 10th and Carr. The legendary Tony’s restaurant — created by Anthony Bommarito in 1946 as a small café — was originally Tony’s Spaghetti House and later Tony’s Steak House, growing from this Little Italy corridor to eventually become St. Louis’s top restaurant. By the mid-1900s most of the Italian community had relocated to The Hill on the south side of the city, but the Little Italy foundation in Columbus Square is commemorated on the SW corner of 11th & Carr by a plaque to Frank A. Cammarata Sr. and his wife Antonia “Lena” Cammarata — Italian immigrants who contributed to the original development of the neighborhood.
The neighborhood’s defining religious landmark is the Shrine of St. Joseph at 1220 N. 11th Street. Founded in 1843 by Austrian Jesuits to serve the rapidly expanding German Catholic immigrant community, the church was built on land donated by Mrs. Ann Biddle — wealthy widow and daughter of John Mullanphy , St. Louis’s first millionaire. The cornerstone was blessed by Bishop Kenrick on April 14, 1844, and the church was dedicated in August 1846 with Father James Van de Velde (later Bishop of Chicago) officiating. The Shrine is the only example of Baroque church architecture in St. Louis and the only church in the Midwest to host a Vatican-authenticated miracle . On March 16, 1864, dying German immigrant Ignatius Strecker was instantly cured after kissing a relic of Blessed Peter Claver — a healing the Vatican formally declared authentic in 1887, becoming one of the two miracles required for the canonization of Peter Claver in 1888. A second miracle followed when parishioners who pledged $4,000 toward a monument during the 1866 cholera epidemic were all spared, leading to the installation of the Altar of Answered Prayers in 1887. The third major expansion in 1881 added the twin towers; the Friends of St. Joseph saved the church from demolition in the late 1970s.
Public schooling in Columbus Square centers on Patrick Henry Downtown Academy at 10th Street, opened in 1906 and designed by William B. Ittner — the prolific St. Louis Public Schools architect responsible for 45 elementary schools and 5 high schools. Other architectural and visual landmarks include the Cass Bank and Trust building at 13th and Cass Avenue (a 1927 Beaux Arts structure that housed a bank founded in 1906 by St. Louis businessmen, nominated for the National Register of Historic Places), and the iconic Vess Bottle — the giant orange soda bottle that has become a Columbus Square landmark, visible as drivers exit I-70 onto Broadway. The neighborhood also includes three small parks: the 0.45-acre Columbus Square Park (established 1980), the 4.30-acre Father Filipiak Park (established 1980, named for a beloved local priest), and the 1.27-acre Fourteenth Street Mall (established 1976).
Housing in Columbus Square reflects nearly a century of public and subsidized development. After truck terminals and industries replaced many of the original tenement homes in the early 20th century, housing staged a comeback with the erection of the Neighborhood Gardens apartments in 1936 — an early example of garden-style multifamily housing. Cochran Gardens public housing followed in 1952. The Columbus Square Townhomes and the Castles were both constructed between 1985 and 1987, and the former Columbus Square apartments (now known as CitySide ) date from the same era. The 1980s townhomes are noted for hugging the sidewalks and framing the 19th-century Shrine of St. Joseph quite well, contributing to a streetscape that maintains historic continuity despite the dramatic 20th-century clearance.
Columbus Square’s modern commercial profile reflects its position bridging Downtown and the Old North St. Louis corridor. Few traditional retail businesses operate within the boundaries — a Schnucks grocery served the area until closing in 2000, leaving an enormous abandoned surface parking lot at 10th and Cass that falls within the McKee NorthSide plan’s Phase B redevelopment boundaries. The St. Louis Post-Dispatch building sits just across Cole Street from Columbus Square, while the former Rams stadium-area surface lots and the Bottle District (Paul McKee’s NorthSide plan) sit just north and east. The renaissance of Downtown St. Louis, the proximity to One Metropolitan Square (the tallest tower in St. Louis), and the corridor’s adjacency to the Gateway Arch grounds make Columbus Square a small but strategic professional crossroads — even though almost none of that commerce actually sits inside the neighborhood’s own boundary lines.
Image: The Shrine of St. Joseph entrance at 1220 N. 11th Street — the 1844 Austrian Jesuit-founded Baroque church, site of the only Vatican-authenticated miracle in the Midwest and the only example of Baroque church architecture in St. Louis — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 by Marcus Qwertyus

So where does Columbus Square actually begin and end, commercially speaking? Inside the boundary lines — Cass Avenue, I-70, Cole Street, and Tucker Boulevard — the neighborhood today is almost entirely housing and institutions: the Shrine of St. Joseph, Patrick Henry Downtown Academy, three small parks, and the Cochran Gardens-to-Columbus Square Townhomes housing legacy described above. St Louis Near Me Directory found exactly one standalone commercial address inside those lines — STL Luxury Ride, a limousine service on Cole Street, the neighborhood’s own southern edge. Everything else a resident, Shrine visitor, or Patrick Henry family reaches for day to day — coworking space, a sit-down dinner, a dentist, a tattoo — sits a few blocks south, across Cole Street, on the Washington Avenue and Locust corridor of Downtown St. Louis proper. That is not a knock on the neighborhood; it is the honest shape of a place built as housing first and commerce a distant second.
Columbus Square runs the same four-season Midwest pattern as the rest of St. Louis — humid summers push activity toward the Gateway Arch grounds and Father Filipiak Park, while cold winters shift what little indoor commerce is nearby to the coworking floors and storefronts a few blocks south on Washington Avenue.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Columbus Square neighborhood? 
A. Columbus Square is defined by its layered immigrant and religious history: German Catholic, Irish, and Italian settlement dating to the 1840s, anchored today by the 1844 Shrine of St. Joseph, the Midwest’s only Vatican-authenticated miracle site. ### Compton Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Compton Heights, St. Louis 
Compton Heights is one of St. Louis's grandest planned residential districts — a quiet enclave of turn-of-the-century mansions on the near-south side, just northeast of Tower Grove Park (ZIP 63104). Laid out in 1888–1889 by celebrated city surveyor Julius Pitzman, it was designed from the start as an exclusive retreat of curving private boulevards, deep lawns, and architectural showpieces.
The Compton Hill Improvement Company assembled the tract in 1888 for about $400,000, and Pitzman broke sharply from the city's rigid street grid — laying out the graceful, curving Hawthorne and Longfellow Boulevards and writing some of Missouri's first deed restrictions to protect the neighborhood's scale and setbacks. The gamble worked: beer barons and industrialists tied to Anheuser-Busch, Falstaff, Magic Chef, Monsanto, and Pet built landmark homes here, many of which still stand.
The neighborhood's crown is the Compton Hill Water Tower, an ornate 179-foot Romanesque standpipe completed in 1898 above a reservoir finished in 1871. One of only seven decorative standpipe towers left in the country, it still opens its 198-step observation deck to the public on select days, offering one of the best skyline views in the city. It anchors Compton Hill Reservoir Park, home to the bronze “Naked Truth” memorial.
Compton Heights is bounded by Interstate 44 on the north, Nebraska Avenue on the east, Shenandoah Avenue on the south, and Grand Boulevard on the west. It borders Fox Park and McKinley Heights to the north, Tower Grove East to the south, and the bustling South Grand business district just across its western edge.
Who is it for now? Largely the same kind of household Pitzman was building for in 1888 — buyers with the means and patience to restore a century-old mansion on a private, city-maintained-but-neighborhood-governed street, rather than families needing a corner store within walking distance. It remains one of the smallest of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods by business count, and that scarcity is itself the point: this is one of the only near-south-side districts where the 1889 street plan, not a strip of storefronts, is the main attraction.
Because Compton Heights is first and foremost a residential landmark district, it has no commercial zoning, no corner store, and no school of its own — something almost no other guide about it says plainly. Strictly within its boundary, exactly two businesses operate: SOMA Therapeutic Massage on South Compton Avenue and the Gallery 3450 apartment community on Russell Boulevard, both detailed below. Everything else a resident actually walks to — a beloved used bookstore, a comic lounge, vegetarian and Mediterranean kitchens, a global grocery, and neighborhood coffeehouses — sits one block west, across Grand Boulevard, in Tower Grove East and the South Grand International District. That is not a knock on Compton Heights; it is the trade the district’s original owners made in 1888, choosing curving private streets and deep lawns over storefronts, and their successors are still making it today.
The Compton Heights neighborhood, St. Louis. 
Like the rest of St. Louis, Compton Heights sees humid 90°F summers and cold-but-manageable winters, with a spring severe-weather season that keeps the neighborhood’s century-old roofs and trees on local contractors’ radar.

### Covenant Blu-Grand Center Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Covenant Blu-Grand Center, St. Louis
Covenant Blu-Grand Center serves as the premier cultural and artistic hub of St. Louis — home to the Grand Center Arts District (the city’s “Broadway” corridor), anchored by the 1929 Fox Theatre, Powell Symphony Hall, the Sheldon Concert Hall, the Contemporary Art Museum, St. Alphonsus “Rock” Church (1867), Third Baptist Church (1885), Saint Louis University, and the Grand Center Community Improvement District — offering theaters, museums, breweries, restaurants, professional services, and arts organizations across midtown St. Louis.
Covenant Blu-Grand Center is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located in the center of the city at 38.6435° N, 90.2427° W . Its official boundaries run north along Dr. Martin Luther King Drive , south along Olive Street and Lindell Boulevard , east along North Compton Avenue , and west along Vandeventer Avenue . The neighborhood is bordered by JeffVanderLou to the north, Vandeventer to the southwest, Midtown and Saint Louis University to the south, Central West End to the southwest, and The Greater Ville to the northwest. The 2020 census recorded the neighborhood’s population at 2,710 residents . Notable internal streets include North Grand Boulevard, Washington Avenue, Delmar Boulevard, Locust Street, Olive Street, Lindell Boulevard, North Spring Avenue, and North Theresa Avenue . The neighborhood includes the famous “Bright White Way” corridor of Grand Boulevard between Lindell and Delmar.
The neighborhood’s most consequential cultural era began in the 1920s , when Grand Boulevard between Lindell and Delmar emerged as St. Louis’s “Bright White Way” — a glittering corridor of nightclubs, ballrooms, restaurants, and six grand theatres that dominated the city’s nightlife from the 1920s through the 1950s. The most spectacular of these was the Fox Theatre at 527 North Grand Boulevard, built in 1929 by movie pioneer William Fox (founder of 20th Century Fox) as the second-largest theatre in the United States with 5,060 seats (4,500 after restoration). It was designed by architect Howard Crane in a striking “Siamese-Byzantine Baroque” style with a 90-foot grand lobby modeled after ancient Indian religious buildings, columns, crimson and gold accents, a signature elephant carpet, and a 2,000-pound chandelier. The Fox opened on January 31, 1929, was one of five spectacular Fox Theatres built in the late 1920s (alongside Brooklyn, Atlanta, Detroit, and San Francisco), and was designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1975 and added to the National Register of Historic Places on October 8, 1976 .
After decades of decline, the Fox Theatre was completely restored in 1982 in a one-year, $2 million-plus restoration spearheaded by St. Louis philanthropist Mary Strauss — the elephant carpet was rewoven, the chandelier was lowered and relamped, and all 4,500 seats were renovated and reinstalled to bring the theatre “as closely as possible to its 1929 state of magnificence.” The Fox reopened in September 1982 and has anchored the modern Grand Center Arts District ever since. The neighborhood’s primary coordinating body, Grand Center Inc. , was established in 1981 as a non-profit urban redevelopment corporation; it manages the Grand Center Community Improvement District with over 100 property and business owners and maintains a master database of hundreds of arts organizations, restaurants, and community institutions throughout the district. The Kranzberg Arts Foundation operates several eclectic contemporary venues including The Marcelle Theatre and High Low , providing affordable performance and gathering space for grassroots artists and smaller arts organizations.
The Grand Center Arts District’s performing arts anchors today include Powell Symphony Hall (home of the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra), the Sheldon Concert Hall , the Grandel Theatre , Jazz St. Louis (formerly Jazz at the Bistro), the Centene Center for the Arts , and the Metro Theater Company (a nationally recognized professional theater for young audiences and families). The visual arts cluster includes the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis (CAM) , the Pulitzer Arts Foundation , the Saint Louis University Museum of Art (SLUMA) , the Vaughn Cultural Center , the Bruno David Gallery , and the Kranzberg Arts Center . The Moto Museum uniquely dedicates an entire facility to motorcycles. Part of the neighborhood falls within the Midtown Historic District , listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
The neighborhood’s historic religious institutions include the Third Baptist Church at the heart of the Arts District (congregation established 1850, present building completed 1885) and the St. Alphonsus Liguori “Rock” Catholic Church on North Grand Boulevard — a striking Gothic Revival landmark whose cornerstone was laid in 1867 and whose walls were built of locally quarried limestone, earning its nickname “The Rock” and designation as a St. Louis City Landmark . The neighborhood’s educational anchors include the Clyde C. Miller Career Academy high school, the Grand Center Arts Academy (opened 2010, an arts-focused independent public charter school serving grades 6–12), Cardinal Ritter College Prep High School (private co-ed Catholic), Loyola Academy of St. Louis (private Catholic middle school for boys), and Preclarus Mastery Academy (5–12 independent charter). Just south of the neighborhood lies Saint Louis University , whose campus extends along Lindell Boulevard.
The neighborhood’s community life is anchored by annual events centered on Strauss Park at the intersection of Grand and Washington. Summer brings the free “Thursdays @ the Intersection” outdoor concert and movie series; spring features the Art Walk on the third Friday in May with simultaneously open museums and galleries plus live entertainment; fall hosts the “Dancing in the Street Festival” on the last Saturday in September with 85+ performances spanning ballet, hip-hop, flamenco, salsa, belly dance, tap, and more across multiple outdoor stages; and the annual First Night celebration runs each New Year’s Eve. According to the 2020 census, 97.3% of the neighborhood’s housing stock is studios or one- and two-bedroom units (one of the highest concentrations of small living spaces in America), 92.1% of real estate is classified as apartment complexes or high-rise apartments (among the highest in the nation), and 95.2% is renter-occupied — reflecting both the district’s student population (Saint Louis University, Grand Center Arts Academy) and its growing urban-redevelopment housing pipeline. Many historic residences in the neighborhood predate 1939, with new construction also occurring between 2000 and the present.
Image: The Fox Theatre at 527 North Grand Boulevard — designed by architect Howard Crane in Siamese-Byzantine Baroque style and opened January 31, 1929 by movie pioneer William Fox as the second-largest theatre in the United States, restored in 1982 by St. Louis philanthropist Mary Strauss, designated a St. Louis City Landmark 1975, and added to the National Register of Historic Places 1976 — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA

Covenant Blu-Grand Center sits on the central plateau of midtown St. Louis at 38.6435° N, with Grand Boulevard’s historic “Bright White Way” corridor running north-south through its heart. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers with frequent 90°F days, cold winters with regular freezing temperatures, and a notably active spring severe weather season including real tornado corridor exposure. Peak outdoor activity falls during spring and fall, when Strauss Park’s “Thursdays @ the Intersection” outdoor concert and movie series, the May Art Walk, the September “Dancing in the Street Festival”, the Saint Louis University campus events, and the Fox Theatre marquee draw the heaviest neighborhood and visitor use. 
Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at the Fox Theatre Broadway series, Powell Symphony Hall concerts, the Sheldon Concert Hall, Jazz St. Louis, the Grandel Theatre, the Contemporary Art Museum, the Pulitzer Arts Foundation, the Saint Louis University Museum of Art, the Kranzberg Arts Center, High Low and The Marcelle, the Moto Museum, and the area’s restaurants including Stage Left Grill, Curtain Call Lounge, and Urban Chestnut’s Midtown Brewery and Biergarten. Winter shifts commerce indoors to the First Night New Year’s Eve celebration, the indoor arts venues, the Saint Louis University academic year, and Saint Alphonsus Liguori “Rock” Church and Third Baptist Church services. The neighborhood’s 1920s “Bright White Way” theatre district, the 1867 Rock Church, the 1885 Third Baptist Church, the 1929 Fox Theatre, and the modern Kranzberg-era contemporary venues anchor more than 150 years of layered midtown architectural and cultural heritage.

#6 
The Fox Theatre 

527 N. Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63103, USA
Historic Venue $$$ National Register of Historic Places Best for: Broadway productions and concerts 

The Fabulous Fox Theatre at 527 North Grand Boulevard is the crown jewel of the Grand Center Arts District — a 4,500-seat performing arts center designed by Howard Crane in Siamese-Byzantine Baroque style and opened January 31, 1929 by movie pioneer William Fox as the second-largest theatre in the United States. After decades of decline, the Fox was completely restored in 1982 under the leadership of philanthropist Mary Strauss, with the signature elephant carpet rewoven, the 2,000-pound chandelier relamped, and all seats renovated. It was designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1975 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.
The Fox today hosts the city’s premier Broadway touring productions, concerts, comedy acts, and major touring events. The 90-foot lobby modeled after ancient Indian religious buildings remains one of the most iconic interiors in St. Louis. Best suited for theatergoers, concertgoers, and visitors looking for the marquee Broadway experience in the city.
