### The Ville Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
The Ville, St. Louis
The Ville is the historic 42-square-block north St. Louis neighborhood that served from 1911 to 1950 as the cultural center of Black St. Louis — home to Sumner High School (the oldest Black high school west of the Mississippi), Homer G. Phillips Hospital (which trained more Black doctors than any institution in the world), and Annie Malone’s Poro College. Notable alumni include Chuck Berry, Tina Turner, Arthur Ashe, Dick Gregory, Grace Bumbry, and Robert Guillaume. The corridor today is almost entirely residential, with commercial activity limited to the chamber-advocacy and business-district organizations tied to the neighborhood’s legacy, plus a handful of small businesses — a barbershop, a corner store — in the immediately surrounding blocks.
The Ville is one of the most historically significant neighborhoods in American urban history — a compact 42-square-block rectangle centered at 38.6591° N, 90.2446° W in zip codes 63113 and 63107 on the city’s north-central plateau, bounded north by St. Louis Avenue , south by Dr. Martin Luther King Drive , east by Sarah Street , and west by Taylor Avenue . Interior streets including Whittier Street (formerly Wash), Annie Malone Drive (formerly Goode Avenue, renamed to honor the neighborhood’s greatest entrepreneur), Cottage Avenue , W. Kennerly Avenue , Aldine Avenue , Maffitt Avenue , and St. Ferdinand Avenue form a tight residential grid that, at its peak in the 1930s and 1940s, was among the most prosperous Black communities in America. The name itself is a shortening of “Elleardsville,” the old settlement named for horticulturist Charles M. Elleard who arrived from San Francisco in the 1860s; the area was annexed by St. Louis in 1876, and Black residents coined “The Ville” in the late 1880s as the neighborhood became one of the few parts of St. Louis free of racially restrictive covenants.
The transformation was rapid and well-documented. In 1873, St. Louis built Elleardsville Colored School No. 8 (later renamed Simmons School) — the neighborhood’s first Black institution and the earliest African American institution in the community. After Missouri’s 1911 introduction of racially restrictive housing covenants concentrated Black residents in the few open neighborhoods, The Ville’s African American population went from 8% in 1920 to 86% by 1930 and reached 95% by 1950 — the Ville of proud Black St. Louis folklore. James Kennerly had owned a large Cote Placquemine (Persimmon Hill) plantation near present-day Kennerly and Taylor avenues, which was destroyed by fire in 1863. Original street names like Kennerly, Wash (now Whittier), Goode (now Annie Malone Drive), and Taylor preserve traces of those early landowners.
The institutions that defined The Ville’s golden era are without parallel in the story of Black St. Louis. Sumner High School (4248 West Cottage Avenue) was founded in 1875, named for abolitionist U.S. Senator Charles H. Sumner, and relocated to The Ville in 1910 (current building constructed 1908). It is the oldest Black high school west of the Mississippi River , and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in December 2025. Sumner alumni include Chuck Berry , who was born and raised in The Ville before recording the songs that shaped rock and roll; comedian and activist Dick Gregory , born at 1803 N. Taylor Avenue; actress and singer Tina Turner (born Anna Mae Bullock), who moved to The Ville at 16 and graduated from Sumner in 1958; opera diva Grace Bumbry ; tennis champion Arthur Ashe , who completed his senior year at Sumner; Emmy-winning actor Robert Guillaume ; civil rights attorney Frankie Freeman ; activist Julia Davis; African Methodist Episcopal pioneer Charleton Tandy; and operatic baritone Robert McFerrin. Lloyd Lionel Gaines — plaintiff in the 1938 Gaines v. Canada Supreme Court case — was also tied to the neighborhood.
Across St. Ferdinand Avenue from Sumner stood Poro College , founded in 1917 by Annie Turnbo Pope Malone — one of America’s first Black female millionaires, whose hair-care and cosmetics empire (the “Poro System”) employed nearly 200 African Americans in St. Louis alone and reached 75,000 worldwide. Annie Malone arrived in St. Louis from Illinois in 1902; one of her early salespeople was Sarah Breedlove, who later became Madam C. J. Walker . The Poro Building — a million-dollar complex housing her Poro College of Beauty Culture, manufacturing plant, and numerous community organizations — became the symbol of African American enterprise in St. Louis. Malone was a generous philanthropist to the St. Louis Colored Orphans’ Home (which moved to The Ville in 1922 thanks to her gift and was later renamed the Annie Malone Children’s Home , now the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center at 2612 Annie Malone Drive, NRHP-listed), St. James A.M.E. Church, and successfully pushed the city to pave streets in The Ville.
Homer G. Phillips Hospital (2601 North Whittier Street, NRHP-listed) opened in 1937 after a 15-year campaign led by attorney Homer G. Phillips — who was assassinated in 1931 , four years before he could see the hospital built in his name. By 1961, Homer G. Phillips had trained more Black doctors and nurses than any other institution in the world, employing more than 800 people at peak as a fully Black-staffed teaching hospital at a time when racial segregation barred Black physicians from white St. Louis hospitals. It closed in 1979 amid community protests and is now a 220-unit senior living facility; its red brick towers remain the visual anchor of the neighborhood, with the Homer G. Phillips Ambulatory Care Center continuing health services in the building. The Ville was designated a local historic district in 1987 .
Tandy Park (5.6 acres, established 1918, at Kennerly and Billups) is the neighborhood’s central green space, featuring the Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts , the Tuskegee Airman Football Field , basketball courts, a skating rink, and a playground. The adjacent Tandy Community Center (4206 West Kennerly Avenue, built 1938 as Public Works Administration Project No. 8483 by the same architect who designed Homer G. Phillips Hospital) is an Art Deco recreation facility on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP since 1999), remaining in active use. St. James African Methodist Episcopal Church (organized 1885) and Antioch Baptist Church (organized 1884) anchor the neighborhood’s spiritual and civic life. Other landmarks include the Marshall School (4342 Aldine Avenue, built 1918, NRHP-listed), Turner Middle School (4235 Kennerly, originally the Charles Henry Turner Open Air School for Crippled Children, opened 1925 and named for the distinguished entomologist who taught at Sumner from 1908-1922), and the former Lincoln University Law School (1939-1955, later absorbed into the University of Missouri Law School).
The Ville today faces real challenges alongside real momentum. An EF3 tornado struck the neighborhood on May 16, 2025 , causing significant damage including the temporary displacement of Sumner High School students. A “Stronger Northside” neighborhood revitalization plan was formally adopted in December 2025, a $3.2 million ARPA-funded modular housing pilot is underway on Aldine Avenue, and community organization 4theVille is developing an MLK Cultural Boulevard project to anchor the southern corridor. The 2000 census recorded 97% Black residency among 2,695 residents; that number kept falling, to 1,868 residents by the 2010 census and 1,427 by the 2020 census — a neighborhood that once anchored a thriving Black business and cultural district now counts under 1,500 residents. The Ville today continues working to rebuild and reinvest at a fraction of its mid-century population. The Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center continues its century-long mission, and the work of rebuilding is ongoing.
Image: Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the 1937 NRHP-listed landmark at 2601 North Whittier Street that trained more Black doctors than any institution in the world and is now a 220-unit senior living facility — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

North St. Louis runs the region’s full humid continental range — hot, humid summers and cold winters — but for The Ville that exposure hasn’t been abstract: the EF3 tornado of May 16, 2025 tore directly through the flat, open plateau the neighborhood sits on, and the rebuilding is still underway.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is “The Ville” known for? 
A. The Ville is known as the historic cultural center of Black St. Louis, the 42-square-block neighborhood that from 1911 to 1950 produced an unmatched roster of institutions and residents — Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital, and Annie Malone’s Poro College, plus alumni Chuck Berry, Tina Turner, Arthur Ashe, Dick Gregory, and Grace Bumbry.

Q. Where is The Ville neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. The Ville sits in north-central St. Louis, a compact 42-square-block neighborhood in zip codes 63113 and 63107 centered near 38.6591° N, 90.2446° W. Its four boundary streets are St. Louis Avenue to the north, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive to the south, Sarah Street to the east, and Taylor Avenue to the west.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help The Ville businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Ville-area businesses a hyperlocal listing tied to the neighborhood’s own landmarks — Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center, and Tandy Park — so providers show up in searches from residents, history visitors, and the community partners rebuilding the corridor after 2025’s tornado.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in The Ville? 
A. The Ville today is almost entirely residential — a local historic district of homes, churches, schools, and NRHP-listed institutions rather than a commercial strip. The closest verified options are the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce, the Locust Central Business District, Clark’s Barbershop in neighboring JeffVanderLou, and Kingz Korner Store in neighboring Penrose.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in The Ville? 
A. The Ville itself has no dining or retail corridor of its own — the closest options are Clark’s Barbershop and Kingz Korner Store just outside its boundary. For recreation, Tandy Park anchors the neighborhood with the Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts, the Tuskegee Airman Football Field, basketball courts, a skating rink, and a playground.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in The Ville? 
A. Yes — The Ville holds an extraordinary concentration of landmarks: Sumner High School (NRHP-listed December 2025), the former Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center, Tandy Park with its Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts, the Art Deco Tandy Community Center, and the neighborhood’s anchor congregations, St. James A.M.E. Church and Antioch Baptist Church.

Q. What is it like to live in The Ville? 
A. Living in The Ville today means a quiet, historic residential street grid still rebuilding after an EF3 tornado struck the neighborhood in May 2025. The “Stronger Northside” revitalization plan and a $3.2 million ARPA-funded modular housing pilot on Aldine Avenue are underway, while population has fallen to under 1,500 residents from its mid-century peak.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around The Ville? 
A. The Ville is built on a tight residential grid — Whittier Street, Annie Malone Drive, Cottage Avenue, W. Kennerly Avenue, Aldine Avenue, Maffitt Avenue, and St. Ferdinand Avenue — framed by its four boundary streets, which connect directly to St. Louis Avenue and Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, the main routes linking the neighborhood to downtown and the rest of north St. Louis.

### Tiffany Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Tiffany, St. Louis
Tiffany is the south-central St. Louis neighborhood named for the 1890 Tiffany streetcar line that ran along the former Tiffany Street (now 39th Street) and transformed Mary McRee’s 1888-sold farmland into a middle-class commuter suburb. The neighborhood’s 215-structure Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District (NRHP-listed December 1978) is anchored by the $550 million SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital that opened in 2020 on Grand Boulevard. Tiffany’s own commercial footprint is small — a city park, a veterinary clinic, and a gym on its own boundary streets — while the wider SLU Medical Center corridor around it supplies everything else.
Tiffany is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, centered at 38.6218° N, 90.2459° W in zip code 63110 on the city’s south-central section. Its boundaries run north to Chouteau Avenue , south to Interstate 44 , east to Grand Boulevard , and west to 39th Street — the same corridor once called Tiffany Street, from which the neighborhood takes its name. That western boundary, 39th Street, was home to the massive United Railways Company car shop complex, the hub of St. Louis’s entire streetcar network, and the Tiffany streetcar line that gave the area its identity long before the neighborhood was formally named. The eastern spine, Grand Boulevard , carries the region’s most-used bus route and anchors the SLU/SSM Health medical campus that now defines the neighborhood’s eastern face. Interior streets — McRee Avenue, Lafayette Avenue, Blaine Avenue, and Folsom Avenue — weave through a residential fabric that has been on the National Register of Historic Places since December 1978 . Adjacent neighborhoods include Forest Park Southeast to the north, Shaw to the south across I-44, the medical district to the east, and Botanical Heights (the rebranded former McRee Town) to the west.
The name Tiffany has nothing to do with jewelry. It derives from Louis and P. D. Tiffany , a family of landowners whose tract ran along what is now 39th Street. That street was called Tiffany Street until 1926; the Tiffany streetcar line took the same name. Before any of this, the land was part of the French colonial Prairie des Noyers , laid out in 1769 as communal agricultural strips west of the early St. Louis settlement. After the Louisiana Purchase, the tract passed through various hands before William McRee — a retired Army officer and Surveyor General of the Missouri and Illinois District — assembled most of it between 1825 and 1832. His widow Mary Urquhart McRee developed a subdivision called McRee City in 1869 (Mary married Samuel McRee at age 14, lived in New Orleans during the Mexican-American War, and inherited the land when Samuel died of cholera). Mary sold her remaining land in 1888, just before her death at 83. The purchaser was the Dundee Land and Investment Company , run by Thomas A. Scott , a young Canadian real estate developer described by contemporaries as “one of the most daring real estate operators St. Louis has ever known.”
Scott platted the land as Dundee Place in June 1889 (covering the area between McRee and Park Avenues, westward from Grand to Old Manchester Road, now Vandeventer) and held a grand auction in June 1891, naming two new streets in a deliberate bipartisan gesture: Folsom (for Frances Folsom Cleveland, wife of President Grover Cleveland) and Blaine (for James G. Blaine, the Republican nominee Cleveland had just defeated). With the completion of the Grand Avenue Viaduct in 1890 and electrified streetcar lines by the turn of the century, Tiffany developed rapidly as a middle-class commuter suburb. Nearly all of the 215 contributing structures in the Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District were built between 1891 and 1928 — a catalogue of late-Victorian and early-20th-century brick construction, from the celebrated rows of blonde brick homes on Blaine Avenue to Dutch colonial houses on Rutger Street to classical ornament reflecting the post-1904 World’s Fair confidence in the city’s future.
Architectural landmarks within Tiffany include the Bell Telephone Exchange Building (1902, architect F.C. Bonsack) at McRee and Grand and the Marquette Apartments (1912, Lafayette and Spring) which anchor the historic commercial and residential character of the neighborhood’s core. Parallel to all of this, the medical corridor on Grand Boulevard was taking shape: the Josephine Heikamp Hospital opened in 1900, Saint Louis University acquired its medical school in 1903, and the landmark Firmin Desloge Hospital — a 15-story green-roofed tower — opened in 1933. The $550 million SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital that replaced Desloge opened September 1, 2020 , and a new $300 million Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital is planned for the former Pevely Dairy site at Grand and Chouteau with a projected 2027 completion. As one local urbanist put it, “residential Tiffany is in reality a different neighborhood than ‘Tiffany’” — the neighborhood is more than half owned by SSM Health and Saint Louis University, with the residential core compressed into the six square blocks south of the medical campus.
The neighborhood’s single park, Tiffany Park (3801 McRee Ave, 1.1 acres, established 1980), was created by the Midtown Medical Center Redevelopment Corporation as part of a late-1970s stabilization effort. Its western boundary was deliberately designed to block through-traffic on Blaine Avenue — a practical crime-reduction measure that also gave the park an unusual triangular presence on the residential block. The park features a tiered concrete semi-circle, a pavilion, a playground, and a basketball court, and remains the neighborhood’s primary outdoor gathering point. The Tiffany Community Association , formed in the early 1990s when the MMCRC program stalled, developed the long-range plan that helped stabilize reinvestment through the 2000s and into the present. In 2017, the Association partnered with Park Central Development on a new neighborhood plan addressing the residential core’s future.
Today Tiffany is anchored on its eastern edge by the SLU/SSM Health medical campus — a Level 1 trauma center that draws patients from across the region — while the residential core continues to fill in with renovations and adaptive reuse along McRee, Folsom, and Blaine Avenues. About 75% of Tiffany residents rent their properties , with many being SLU medical residents who buy homes during residency and either sell upon graduation or stay as permanent neighborhood residents. Downtown St. Louis sits just over 3 miles to the east; Forest Park is approximately 2 miles to the west; the Missouri Botanical Garden is just across I-44 in adjacent Shaw.
Image: Skyline of the Tiffany Neighborhood showing the SLU/SSM Health medical campus along Grand Boulevard and the surrounding 215-structure NRHP-listed historic district — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

Tiffany sees St. Louis’s full humid continental swing — hot summers, a real spring tornado season, cold winters — with Interstate 44’s southern edge and the elevation drop toward 39th Street doing more to shape daily life here than any one season does.
The honest count for Tiffany is four verified connections, not eight: Tiffany Park itself, St Louis Veterinary Center and The L.A.B. Gym on the neighborhood’s own Chouteau and Grand boundary streets, and Park Central Development, the nonprofit that partnered with the Tiffany Community Association on the 2017 neighborhood plan. That is genuinely all of it — more than half of Tiffany’s land belongs to SSM Health and Saint Louis University, and the residential core is compressed into roughly six square blocks with almost no retail of its own.
What fills the gap sits just outside the boundary, and is worth naming honestly rather than pretending it’s Tiffany’s own: Fresh Gatherings Cafe + Farm is about half a mile northeast in The Gate District , and Fiddlehead Fern Cafe is about 0.7 miles south in Shaw . Both are real, well-reviewed options a short walk or drive from Tiffany’s residential core — not Tiffany businesses, but close enough that residents use them routinely.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Tiffany neighborhood? 
A. Tiffany is a small, south-central St. Louis neighborhood named for the 1890 Tiffany streetcar line, bounded by Chouteau Avenue, Interstate 44, Grand Boulevard, and 39th Street in zip code 63110. Its 215-structure Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District (NRHP-listed 1978) sits beside the $550 million SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital, with more than half the neighborhood’s footprint owned by the hospital and university.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Tiffany businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives businesses serving Tiffany a dedicated, schema-optimized listing tied to Tiffany Park, the SLU/SSM Health medical campus, and the historic district — capturing “near me” searches from residents, medical staff, and students that a generic profile would miss. Join St Louis Near Me Directory to get listed.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Tiffany? 
A. Tiffany’s own commercial base is genuinely small: Tiffany Park is the neighborhood’s only true landmark, joined by St Louis Veterinary Center and The L.A.B. Gym on its own boundary streets and Park Central Development, the nonprofit that helped plan the neighborhood’s future in 2017. That is four verified connections, not the eight a padded list once suggested.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Tiffany? 
A. Tiffany has almost no retail or dining of its own — the neighborhood’s footprint is mostly residential and hospital land. Recreation centers on 1.1-acre Tiffany Park with its playground and basketball court. For dining, Fresh Gatherings Cafe + Farm sits about half a mile away in The Gate District and Fiddlehead Fern Cafe about 0.7 miles away in Shaw.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Tiffany? 
A. Yes — the 215-structure Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District (NRHP-listed December 1978) includes blonde-brick homes on Blaine Avenue and Dutch colonial houses on Rutger Street, the 1902 Bell Telephone Exchange Building, and the 1912 Marquette Apartments. Tiffany Park at 3801 McRee Avenue, established 1980, is the neighborhood’s only public green space.

Q. What is it like to live in Tiffany? 
A. Tiffany is small and hospital-adjacent: about 75% of residents rent, many of them SLU medical residents who stay through their residency. The residential core is compressed into roughly six square blocks south of the SSM Health medical campus, surrounded by a historic district of 1891-1928 brick housing rather than a commercial strip.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Tiffany? 
A. Grand Boulevard, Tiffany’s eastern edge, carries the region’s most-used bus route and connects directly to the SLU/SSM Health medical campus. Interstate 44 borders the neighborhood to the south and Chouteau Avenue to the north, with McRee, Lafayette, Blaine, and Folsom Avenues carrying local residential traffic through the historic core.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Tiffany? 
A. ### Tower Grove East Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Tower Grove East, St. Louis
Tower Grove East serves as one of south St. Louis’s most architecturally splendid Victorian-era neighborhoods — a 0.51-square-mile residential and commercial corridor settled by 1850s German Catholic dairy farmers and built up by the relatives of the prominent German immigrants who founded Compton Heights and Flora Place — anchored by Tower Grove Park (the 289-acre 1868 Henry Shaw gift just across South Grand Boulevard), the South Grand Business District’s internationally renowned restaurant row, Roosevelt High School, the Carpenter Branch Library, Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey, and the four-square Victorian and Italianate flats with carved fretwork, stained-glass windows, and elaborate staircases — offering community and immigrant-service organizations, custom floral design, live theatre, scratch-kitchen restaurants and cocktail bars, and neighborhood corner taverns across the South Grand, Shenandoah, Arsenal, and Gravois Avenue corridors.
Tower Grove East is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6029° N, 90.2364° W in south-central St. Louis City. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Shenandoah Avenue on the north, Nebraska Avenue on the east, Gravois Avenue (MO Route 30) on the south, and South Grand Boulevard on the west. Total area is 0.51 square miles , with a 2020 census population of 5,708 residents and a density of approximately 11,000 per square mile . ZIP codes are parts of 63104 and 63118 , and the neighborhood sits in the 7th Ward of the City of St. Louis under Alderwoman Alisha Sonnier. Surrounding neighborhoods include Compton Heights to the north across Shenandoah, Fox Park and Benton Park West to the east, Gravois Park and Dutchtown to the south across Gravois, and Shaw and Tower Grove South to the west across South Grand. The neighborhood is approximately six miles south of downtown St. Louis.
Tower Grove Park itself belongs to neither neighborhood — it’s an independently governed 289-acre place, run by its own Board of Commissioners under the terms of Henry Shaw’s 1868 gift, not a piece of Tower Grove East’s own 0.51-square-mile footprint. Tower Grove East runs along the park’s eastern flank, its South Grand Boulevard boundary facing the park’s Grand Avenue entrance directly across the street. Tower Grove South, on the park’s opposite side, borders its southern edge along Arsenal Street — and shares a border with Tower Grove East of its own, along Grand Boulevard south of the park.
Tower Grove East was originally part of La Petite Prairie , settled by the French in the early 1700s. Grazing land was held in common, and farming land was divided into long narrow tracts. The commons system was abandoned around 1800, and the land began to be sold into private hands. By the 1850s , much of the property was owned by German Catholics — recent immigrants fleeing the aftermath of Germany’s 1848 civil war — who found the area ideal as pasture land for their dairy farming operations. The neighborhood takes its name from its position bordering the east entrance of Tower Grove Park across South Grand Boulevard. The park was deeded to the City of St. Louis in 1868 as a gift from Henry Shaw (1800–1889), the 19th-century English-born businessman and botanist who owned much of the surrounding land and also founded the adjacent Missouri Botanical Garden .
As the German immigrants prospered, the wealthiest began building mansions in the adjacent Compton Heights and along Flora Place — the city’s exclusive private streets just north of Shenandoah. Their siblings, cousins, and extended family members later settled the pastures of what is now Tower Grove East and built beautiful homes and flats of their own, using similar architectural detail to what is found in the wealthier Compton Heights and Flora Place. The typical Tower Grove East house was built on the four-square plan — a pyramid or hipped roof on a two-story cube, often with a pressed-brick or limestone course separating the stories. Buyers chose architectural elements from pattern books that illustrated multiple styles of windows, doors, stairways, and fireplace mantels. The often austere exterior facades typically hide a wealth of richly designed entries with carved fretwork , built-in hall benches, mirrors, and bookcases, wood paneling, stained-glass windows , and elaborate staircases.
The neighborhood’s civic and educational anchors include Roosevelt High School on Hartford Street (opened 1925, designed by Rockwell M. Milligan in an impressive Collegiate Gothic style), Shenandoah Elementary School on Shenandoah Avenue, and the Carpenter Branch Library on South Grand Boulevard (one of 15 branches in the St. Louis Public Library system). The neighborhood is also home to the Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey on Tennessee Avenue. A monument in nearby Reservoir Park commemorates The Westliche Post , the German-language newspaper that Joseph Pulitzer later acquired and merged to form the St. Louis Post-Dispatch . Houses of worship include St. Wenceslaus Church on Oregon Avenue, St. Pius V Catholic Church and Messiah Lutheran Church on South Grand Boulevard, Holy Trinity Baptist Church on Minnesota Avenue, and the Body of Christ Temple on Louisiana Avenue.
The neighborhood’s commercial heartbeat is the South Grand Business District (also known simply as South Grand ) — a six-block stretch of South Grand Boulevard that has been branded and improved through the South Grand Community Improvement District. The district anchors one of the most internationally diverse restaurant rows in the Midwest, with Vietnamese, Thai, Ethiopian, Italian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Japanese, Lebanese, Afghan, and Mexican restaurants alongside specialty grocers, rare bookstores, jewelry boutiques, natural food stores, and international gift shops. Many storefronts retain their original late-19th-century commercial architecture, and most restaurants offer outdoor dining that animates the streetscape year-round.
Tower Grove East’s history through the second half of the 20th century followed the trajectory of many south-side St. Louis neighborhoods. The 2000 census recorded 7,211 residents across 3,485 housing units (79% occupied, 39% owner-occupied, 61% renter-occupied). Like much of south St. Louis, the neighborhood lost 8% of its population between 1990 and 2000. By 2020, the population had stabilized at 5,708 residents with a racial makeup of 55.6% White, 28.9% Black, 5.0% Asian, 5.3% Hispanic/Latino , and other backgrounds. The neighborhood’s late-20th-century recovery accelerated in the 2010s and 2020s, with extensive historic restoration along Shenandoah, Arsenal, Humphrey, and the smaller cross streets, and with the South Grand business district’s emergence as a regional destination for international dining and independent retail.
Today, Tower Grove East’s active redevelopment is driven by neighborhood and immigrant-service organizations, floral and hospitality businesses, live theatre, and the steady pull of Tower Grove Park’s programming next door. The businesses listed on this page include the Tower Grove East Neighborhood Association (TGENA) , the St Louis Near Me Directory , Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey on Tennessee Avenue, the International Institute of St. Louis on Arsenal Street (the 1919-founded immigrant and refugee service hub and host of the Festival of Nations), Botanicals Design Studio on South Grand (the custom florist founded by Keith McDonnell and Dean Riebeling), Riley’s Pub on Arsenal Street, Tick Tock Tavern and its next-door neighbor Buzz’s Hawaiian Grill on Magnolia Avenue, and Crafted. and Sheesh , two of the newer additions to South Grand’s international restaurant row. Tower Grove Park itself, just across South Grand, adds 2,185+ Google reviews of its own, 13 restored early-20th-century picnic pavilions, the Piper Palm House, the Tower Grove Farmers’ Market, “sip and stroll” events, and Food Truck Friday to the neighborhood’s doorstep.
Roosevelt High School — the 1925 Collegiate Gothic landmark on Hartford Street, designed by district architect Rockwell M. Milligan, in the Tower Grove East neighborhood of St. Louis, Missouri. Photo: St Louis Near Me Directory.

Tower Grove East follows the same four-season Midwest climate as the rest of St. Louis — humid summers that fill Tower Grove Park and the South Grand patios, and cold winters that push commerce indoors to South Grand’s restaurants, Riley’s Pub, Tick Tock Tavern, and Stray Dog Theatre at the Abbey.
Tower Grove East is Tower Grove South’s opposite in almost every way that matters to a resident. It’s a third the size — 0.51 square miles against 1.49 — and its German Catholic settlers were the relatives and employees of the families building mansions in neighboring Compton Heights and along Flora Place, not the mine and brickyard workers who built up Tower Grove South. There’s no equivalent to South Grand’s restaurant row or Morganford’s retail strip inside its own boundary; instead, Tower Grove East’s commercial life is a handful of long-running institutions — a neighborhood theatre in a converted church, a florist, two corner bars — clustered a short walk from the park and from South Grand next door. It suits residents who want that South Grand access without living inside the commercial corridor itself.

The Tower Grove East Neighborhood Association (TGENA), founded in 1965, is a nonprofit, volunteer-run organization serving the residents of the Tower Grove East neighborhood. As a steward of one of south St. Louis’s most historic and architecturally rich neighborhoods, the association is the central civic resource for residents, new neighbors, and businesses looking to connect with the Tower Grove East community.

Live Irish music sessions on Wednesday nights and rotating nightly specials give the place a warm, lively, regulars-filled atmosphere. Reviewers consistently cite the welcoming, family-like environment, the friendly bartenders, and the quality of the pizza and beer. It’s an ideal spot for neighbors and visitors looking for an authentic, unpretentious corner pub a short walk from Tower Grove Park and the South Grand restaurant row.

The International Institute of St. Louis (IISTL) is the region’s immigrant and refugee service and information hub, located on Arsenal Street in Tower Grove East. A 501(c)(3) United Way agency established in 1919, the Institute serves roughly 7,500–8,000 new Americans from about 75 countries each year, with locally and nationally acclaimed programs spanning English and citizenship classes, refugee resettlement, employment and training, immigration assistance, and services for vulnerable populations including elderly refugees and trafficking survivors. The Institute anchors the city’s thriving International District and hosts the celebrated annual Festival of Nations and the Race for Refugees in Tower Grove Park, reaching tens of thousands of area residents through its outreach. It is an essential resource for newcomers building independence in St. Louis and for community members seeking to connect across cultures.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Tower Grove East neighborhood? 
A. Size and lineage. At just 0.51 square miles — a third the size of Tower Grove South next door — Tower Grove East was settled in the 1850s by German Catholic dairy farmers related to the wealthier families who built Compton Heights and Flora Place. It’s defined today by its four-square Victorian flats, Tower Grove Park across South Grand, and a tight cluster of civic and community institutions.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Tower Grove East businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Tower Grove East businesses a schema-optimized listing built for local and AI search, plus optional Google Business Profile cleanup and review management. It strengthens “near me” visibility tied to Tower Grove Park, South Grand, and the Tower Grove Abbey — with no competitor ads on any member’s listing and no long-term contract required.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Tower Grove East? 
A. Community and immigrant-service organizations, live theatre, custom floral design, and a handful of corner bars and restaurants define Tower Grove East, alongside the South Grand corridor’s international dining. The neighborhood is too small for a shopping strip of its own — its commercial identity comes from a few tightly clustered, long-running institutions rather than a continuous retail row.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Tower Grove East? 
A. Dining ranges from Turkish (Sheesh) and Hawaiian (Buzz’s Hawaiian Grill) to a cocktail-and-kitchen spot (Crafted.) and two classic corner bars, Riley’s Pub and Tick Tock Tavern. Botanicals Design Studio covers custom floral work. For recreation, Tower Grove Park sits just across South Grand with its Farmers’ Market, Food Truck Friday, and 13 restored Victorian picnic pavilions.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Tower Grove East? 
A. Yes. Stray Dog Theatre performs inside the Tower Grove Abbey, a former 1912 German Evangelical church on Tennessee Avenue. Roosevelt High School’s 1925 Collegiate Gothic building and the Carpenter Branch Library anchor the neighborhood’s civic core. Tower Grove Park, across South Grand Boulevard, isn’t technically inside Tower Grove East’s boundary but borders it directly along the park’s east side.

Q. What is it like to live in Tower Grove East? 
A. Quiet and tightly knit. At 5,708 residents packed into 0.51 square miles, it’s one of the denser pockets of south St. Louis, but its scale keeps it feeling like a small town rather than a commercial strip. Residents live in four-square Victorian flats with carved fretwork and stained glass, walk to South Grand for dinner, and lean on TGENA, active since 1965, for neighborhood life.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Tower Grove East? 
A. Tower Grove East is entirely walkable at 0.51 square miles, with South Grand Boulevard as its commercial spine and fast access to Interstates 44 and 55 for the rest of the metro. Most residents walk or bike to South Grand’s restaurants and Tower Grove Park across the street; the neighborhood’s compact grid makes a car unnecessary for daily errands within its own boundary.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Tower Grove East? 
A. Residents and visitors can browse StLouisMissouriNearMe.com for neighborhood guides and business listings across the region. St Louis Near Me Directory highlights trusted Tower Grove East providers — from Stray Dog Theatre and the International Institute to Riley’s Pub and Botanicals Design Studio — alongside ratings and service details, making it easier to plan a visit around the park, South Grand, or a night at the Abbey.

### Tower Grove South Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Tower Grove South, St. Louis
Tower Grove South sits in the heart of south St. Louis as one of the city’s most populous and culturally diverse neighborhoods — formerly known as Oak Hill, anchored by the 289 acres of Henry Shaw’s Tower Grove Park (one of the largest existing Victorian walking parks in America), bordered by the international South Grand Business District and the Morganford Road corridor — offering sustainable retail, craft brewing, boutique design and creative agencies, an old-world German butcher shop, international dining and historic event venues along South Grand, weekly farmers’ markets, and historic-neighborhood community amenities for residents and businesses across the central-south St. Louis corridor.
Tower Grove South sits in south-central St. Louis at 38.5968° N, 90.2681° W in zip code 63116. Its boundaries form a rectangle: Arsenal Street to the north (along the southern edge of Tower Grove Park), Chippewa Street to the south, Grand Boulevard to the east, and Kingshighway Boulevard to the west. The neighborhood’s defining streets are South Grand Boulevard (the international restaurant and retail spine on the east), Morganford Road (the secondary commercial corridor running roughly north-south through the western half), Arsenal Street (the northern boundary along the park), and Chippewa Street (the southern boundary). Tower Grove South is bordered by Tower Grove East across South Grand Boulevard, Shaw and Southwest Garden across Tower Grove Park to the north, Dutchtown and Bevo Mill to the south, and Southampton to the west. The neighborhood encompasses approximately 1.49 square miles and is one of the most densely populated neighborhoods in St. Louis, with a 2010 Census count of 13,333 residents — placing it consistently among the top three most populated neighborhoods in the city.
Tower Grove Park itself is not part of Tower Grove South — it’s a separate, independently governed place, run under Henry Shaw’s will by its own Board of Commissioners rather than by either neighborhood. Tower Grove South’s boundary runs along Arsenal Street, hugging the park’s southern edge, while Tower Grove East sits on the opposite side of the park along South Grand Boulevard, facing its eastern entrance. The two neighborhoods border each other too, along Grand Boulevard south of the park — so a Tower Grove South address and a Tower Grove East address can sit two blocks apart with the same park in view from both, but neither one owns it.
The neighborhood’s earliest known name was Prairie des Noyers , a rich agricultural area in the nineteenth century divided into long strips called “common fields” and sold to anyone willing to farm the land. The Russell family acquired a significant portion of these common fields to build their family estate, Oak Hill — the name by which Tower Grove South was originally known. Shortly after building their estate, the Russells discovered coal in the fields and founded the Parker-Russell Mining Company , employing many in the community as miners. The 1849 cholera epidemic decimated the community and effectively closed the mines; Parker-Russell shifted to extracting fire clay, and the successful brick industry brought jobs and German immigrants to the area in the 1850s. Many of these German immigrants were dairy farmers from the 1848 civil war who found Prairie des Noyers ideal as pasture land. In 1876 the city limits of St. Louis expanded to include Tower Grove South , and following the opening of the Grand viaduct and the 1872 dedication of Tower Grove Park, the area saw rapid real estate speculation. The McDonalds were the first major landowners between Grand and Gustine to sell out to a major subdivision — Tower Grove Heights .
Most of Tower Grove South was built between the 1860s and the 1930s, following the extension of streetcar lines from downtown St. Louis. The neighborhood’s housing stock is dominated by two-and-a-half-story Italianate and Victorian brick homes featuring stained glass, intricate staircases, and the red brick mined from the surrounding clay fields. Closer to the park in the Tower Grove Heights sub-neighborhood (extending from Arsenal to Utah Street, east of Gustine to Grand), single-family brick Victorian houses are most prominent, complete with their own neighborhood association and branding. The 1920s brought Cape Cod-style houses , while older shotgun houses are still found in the western part of the neighborhood near Kingshighway. The architectural showpiece of the Grand Boulevard business district is the 1928 South Side National Bank building — one of St. Louis’s best examples of Art Deco architecture — which nearly faced the wrecking ball before grassroots preservationists rescued it. Today this 10-story structure houses The Noble by Culinary Canvas , an elegant event venue retaining the original bank vault, high ceilings, and ornate gold detailing inspired by Greek and Roman design.
The defining institution of Tower Grove South is Tower Grove Park , the 289-acre Victorian-era walking park donated to the City of St. Louis by Henry Shaw on October 20, 1868 and opened to the public in 1872. Shaw — the English-born merchant, botanist, and philanthropist who also founded the adjacent Missouri Botanical Garden — designed the park with conditions that it “shall be used as a park forever” and that the city make an “annual appropriation” for its maintenance. As per Shaw’s estate, Tower Grove Park remains the only public city park in St. Louis managed by an independent Board of Commissioners. The park features 32 picturesque Victorian-era pavilions , including the chinoiserie Chinese Pavilion (Pagoda), the Turkish Pavilion with its onion-domed roof, the identical Cypress Pavilions, the large Sons of Rest Pavilion, and the 1931 Henry Shaw Memorial Pavilion. Other landmarks include the Piper Palm House (1878) — the oldest standing greenhouse west of the Mississippi River, designed by George I. Barnett, the “dean” of Missouri architects — its identical 1885 sister the Piper Plant House , The Ruins (constructed by Shaw from limestone blocks of the 1867 Lindell Hotel fire), the three-tiered cast-iron Fountain, and Café Madeleine . The park is home to nearly 400 species of trees, bushes, and flowering plants, is part of the Mississippi Flyway , and is widely renowned for spring and fall bird migration watching.
The South Grand Business District on the eastern edge of the neighborhood is one of St. Louis’s most beloved international destinations. After a serious slump in the 1970s, the district became a magnet for new Vietnamese immigrants who opened restaurants and shops along Grand Boulevard, beginning what locals describe as having “more ethnicities represented on one street than Epcot.” Today the corridor hosts Café Mochi (Japanese/Vietnamese), King & I (Thai), Grand Bistro (Andrew Trinh reopened his parents’ legendary Pho Grand here in April 2025 — same family, same recipes — after Michael and Tami Trinh ran it for 33 years until 2022), Cafe Natasha’s (Persian), Snō (modern Asian dim sum), Meskerem Ethiopian Restaurant , Sameem Afghan Restaurant , Apotheosis Comics & Lounge , The Gin Room (founded by Natasha Bahrami, the only American inducted into the Gin Hall of Fame), and Dunaway Books . Each August, Tower Grove Park hosts the Festival of Nations , the region’s largest multicultural celebration, with 75 nations represented through food, dance, and music across the Centene Charitable Foundation Forest Stage, the Enterprise Magnolia Stage, and the World Music Stage. The Tower Grove Farmers’ Market has run from May through October every Saturday morning since 2006, just west of the Wading Pool Pavilion, and is widely regarded as the best farmers’ market in the St. Louis region.
The Morganford Road business district on the western flank of the neighborhood emerged after 2000 with substantial reinvestment in restaurants, bars, retail, and a neighborhood-scale storefront grocery store specializing in natural and locally grown foods. Civil Life Brewing Co. (established 2011 by Jake Hafner) anchors the southern end on Holt Avenue, serving Cask Marque-certified traditional English and American ales. Other key Morganford businesses include Black Sheep Whiskey & Wine , Road Crew Coffee & Cycles , Mama 2’s Biscuits , and the 45-year-old A&M Cyclery . Tower Grove South’s children attend Mann Elementary , Fanning Middle Community Education Center , and Roosevelt High School in the St. Louis City School District. The neighborhood is also home to Artscope , a non-profit offering art classes and camps from a small cottage surrounded by nature, and several active community organizations through the Tower Grove South Neighborhood Association .
Tower Grove South’s most recent census data (2020) records the neighborhood as 57.6% White, 21.8% Black, 7.7% Asian, 7.6% two or more races, and 8.4% Hispanic/Latino — making it one of the most racially and ethnically diverse neighborhoods in St. Louis. The median age is 36 , with 35.2% of residents between 25 and 44, average household size of 2, and approximately 5,027 households. Median home values are approximately $225,600 , with park-front renovated brick homes commanding premium prices. The neighborhood is a major urban-revitalization success story — once in decline by the 1970s and 1980s, it has been steadily rehabilitated since the 1990s, with the South Grand corridor leading first followed by Morganford after 2000. Today Tower Grove South is consistently ranked a top-10 place to live in St. Louis. Because of its walkability, mixed-use commercial spine, and proximity to Tower Grove Park, the neighborhood draws a service ecosystem of restaurant, retail, brewing, design, and event-venue providers that reflect both its historic stock and its young, diverse, urban resident base. The listings on this page draw from that broader Tower Grove South ecosystem.
Image: The Turkish Pavilion at Tower Grove Park, with its distinctive onion-domed roof — one of the 32 Victorian-era pavilions in the 289-acre park donated to the City of St. Louis in 1868 by Henry Shaw — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 by TMS63112

Tower Grove South sees the same four-season Midwest climate as the rest of St. Louis — humid summers that fill Tower Grove Park and the South Grand patios, and cold winters that push commerce indoors to the Piper Palm House, South Grand, and Morganford Road.
What actually separates Tower Grove South from its smaller neighbor across Grand Boulevard is scale. At 1.49 square miles and roughly 13,000 residents, it has room for a genuine commercial spine — South Grand’s restaurant row on the east, Morganford Road’s post-2000 retail revival on the west — where Tower Grove East, a third the size, has only a handful of corner businesses clustered near the park. That size is also why Tower Grove South reads as a shopping-and-dining destination first and a residential neighborhood second, even though most of its 1.49 square miles is still the same brick Italianate and Victorian housing stock the German brickmakers built in the 1850s and 1860s.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Is Tower Grove South a good neighborhood? 
A. Yes, and it’s consistently ranked one of St. Louis’s top-10 neighborhoods to live in. Tower Grove South pairs walkable density — it’s among the city’s three most populated neighborhoods — with the 289-acre Tower Grove Park, the international South Grand restaurant row, and a Morganford Road corridor that has added craft brewing, boutique retail, and specialty grocers since 2000.

Q. Is Tower Grove considered south St. Louis? 
A. Yes. Tower Grove South sits in south-central St. Louis, ZIP code 63116, bounded by Arsenal Street, Chippewa Street, Grand Boulevard, and Kingshighway Boulevard. “Tower Grove” can mean either of two separate neighborhoods, Tower Grove South and Tower Grove East, plus the 289-acre park that sits between and borders them both without belonging to either.

Q. What defines the Tower Grove South neighborhood? 
A. Tower Grove South is defined by its size, density, and the park at its northern edge. At 1.49 square miles and roughly 13,000 residents, it’s among St. Louis’s three most populated neighborhoods, shaped by 1850s German immigrant brickmakers, Henry Shaw’s 1868 gift of Tower Grove Park, the international South Grand Business District, and the post-2000 revival of Morganford Road.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Tower Grove South businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Tower Grove South businesses a schema-optimized listing built for local and AI search, plus optional Google Business Profile cleanup, review management, and citation syncing. It strengthens “near me” visibility tied to Tower Grove Park, South Grand, and Morganford Road — with no competitor ads on any member’s listing and no long-term contract required.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Tower Grove South? 
A. Sustainable and specialty retail, craft brewing, international restaurants, and boutique creative agencies define the mix. South Grand carries the international restaurant row and gift shops; Morganford Road carries craft brewing and neighborhood retail; and side streets hold specialty grocers like a Bavarian sausage maker and a longtime beauty supply store serving the neighborhood’s diverse residents.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Tower Grove South? 
A. South Grand’s restaurant row spans Vietnamese, Thai, Persian, Ethiopian, and Afghan kitchens alongside a Mediterranean café and market. Morganford Road adds Civil Life Brewing and neighborhood retail. For recreation, Tower Grove Park supplies 289 acres of walking paths, pavilions, and tennis courts, the Saturday Farmers’ Market, and August’s Festival of Nations, the region’s largest multicultural celebration.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Tower Grove South? 
A. Yes. Tower Grove Park borders the neighborhood’s north edge with 32 Victorian pavilions and the 1878 Piper Palm House, the oldest greenhouse west of the Mississippi. On Grand Boulevard, the restored 1928 Art Deco South Side National Bank building now houses The Noble event venue. Tower Grove Heights, nearest the park, holds the neighborhood’s grandest single-family Victorian homes.

Q. What is it like to live in Tower Grove South? 
A. Dense, walkable, and diverse — one of St. Louis’s most racially mixed neighborhoods, with a median age of 36 and roughly 5,000 households. Residents live in Italianate and Victorian brick homes built from locally mined clay, walk to South Grand or Morganford for dinner, and treat Tower Grove Park as a backyard. Median home values run about $225,600.

### Vandeventer Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Vandeventer, St. Louis
Vandeventer is the historic north-central St. Louis neighborhood that gave its name to Vandeventer Place (the 1870 Julius Pitzman-designed Gilded Age private street whose limestone gates now stand in Forest Park) and was the West Belle Place childhood home of Lloyd Lionel Gaines, whose 1938 Supreme Court case Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada became a landmark precursor to Brown v. Board of Education . The corridor today is thin on its own commercial footprint — its real anchor is chamber advocacy and senior housing, with event venue rental a few blocks over in Grand Center and everyday options a few blocks south in the Central West End.
Vandeventer is City of St. Louis Neighborhood #58 , centered at 38.6500° N, 90.2516° W on the city’s north-central plateau in zip code 63113/63108. Its official boundaries run north to Dr. Martin Luther King Drive , south to Delmar Boulevard , east to N. Vandeventer Avenue , and west to N. Newstead Avenue — a compact rectangle of rectilinear streets that local urbanists have called a “true rectilinear beauty.” The neighborhood’s internal spine, N. Sarah Street , runs north-south through the center and anchors the area’s primary park (Turner Park) and most significant recent development. N. Spring Avenue runs parallel one block west, serving as the address of the Urban League’s North Spring Empowerment Center at 929 N. Spring. The neighborhood lies between the Central West End to the south, The Ville to the north, and just west of the Grand Center Arts District (home to the Fox Theatre and Powell Symphony Hall) — within easy reach of every Vandeventer address.
The land that became Vandeventer began as part of St. Louis’s French colonial Grande Prairie Commonfield , organized into long narrow arpent strips that extended westward from the original riverfront settlement and were maintained under common enclosure until about 1800. By 1850 the strips had been consolidated into larger tracts suitable for subdivision. In the mid-1850s, the Cote Brilliante subdivision was laid out to the west and Prairie Place along Belle Glade to the north. In 1858 , florist and horticulturist Charles M. Elleard purchased a tract bounded by present-day Martin Luther King Drive, Annie Malone Drive, Cote Brilliante, and Newstead Avenues just north of today’s Vandeventer, establishing a conservatory and greenhouses. By 1870, a small town called Elleardsville — later known as The Ville — had emerged around Elleard’s floral nursery, with its town hall at the corner of present MLK Drive and Whittier Street. An Abbey Trotting Race Track occupied the neighborhood’s northern section between roughly Page, Whittier, MLK, and Taylor avenues until about 1877. German and Irish immigrants settled the area through the turn of the 20th century, and streetcar lines — including the Hodiamont line — linked Vandeventer to the rest of the growing city.
The neighborhood’s most celebrated landmark was Vandeventer Place , a privately maintained gated enclave platted on June 4, 1870 , on land purchased from the estate of New York stockbroker Peter Lewis Vandeventer (who came to St. Louis in the 1860s with his brothers William and Henry Barnum Vandeventer from their Wall Street firm at 6 Wall St., New York City). Funded by businessmen Napoleon Mulliken, Charles H. Peck, and John McCune, the street was designed by Julius Pitzman — St. Louis’s most influential private street designer — with a rigid rectilinear plan featuring a grass-median boulevard, fountains at each end, and lavish mansions on each side. The first houses were built in 1871. The monumental limestone entry gates were added in 1894, designed by architect Louis Mullgardt . At its peak, the enclave’s 50 mansions housed the city’s wealthiest citizens: Governor and U.S. Ambassador to Russia David R. Francis (mansion No. 16, designed by Charles K. Ramsey in 1880), oil magnate H. Clay Pierce (whose mansion at No. 40 reportedly cost $800,000), chemical patriarch Edward Mallinckrodt (No. 26), banker John Lionberger (No. 27, designed by the great American architect Henry Hobson Richardson in 1886), and tobacco heir Hiram Shaw Liggett (No. 32).
Vandeventer Place declined after 1900 as its residents moved west to the newer private places of Portland and Westmoreland (where David Francis and the Mallinckrodts built new Central West End mansions), and by the 1920s the rise of Grand Center as a theater and streetcar hub had largely emptied the street. By 1947 the Veterans’ Administration demolished the eastern half for the John Cochran VA Hospital; the western half fell to the Juvenile Justice Center around 1950 . Only the east Grand Boulevard limestone gate by Louis Mullgardt was preserved and relocated to Forest Park near the Jewel Box , where it stands today as a Forest Park Statue & Monument. The story is captured in the 2024 book Vandeventer Place — Gilded Age St. Louis: A Social, Economic, Architectural and Urban History of the Legendary Post-Civil War Enclave by Mike Boyd and Thomas Grady.
Vandeventer carries one of the most important civil rights histories of any St. Louis neighborhood. Lloyd Lionel Gaines (1911–1939?), who lived with his family in a house on West Belle Place within the neighborhood, graduated first in his class from Vashon High School and became the first African American to apply to the University of Missouri School of Law — then a segregated institution. After rejection, with NAACP support, he pursued the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. The resulting Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938) ruling held that Missouri must provide Black students equal legal education within the state — a landmark precursor to the eventual dismantling of Plessy v. Ferguson through Brown v. Board of Education . Gaines disappeared in Chicago on March 19, 1939 , and was never found; his case remains among the most consequential and haunting in American legal history.
Turner Park , the neighborhood’s 1.4-acre public park placed into ordinance in 1937 , is located just southwest of the intersection of C.D. Banks Avenue and N. Sarah Street. It is named for James Milton Turner (c. 1839–1915), born into slavery in St. Louis County in 1839 or 1840, freed in 1843, educated in secret schools (despite the 1847 Missouri law prohibiting teaching Black people), and a graduate of Oberlin College. Turner became Missouri’s foremost post-Civil War Black leader: he established 32 schools for African Americans statewide , helped found Lincoln University , and was appointed by President Ulysses S. Grant in 1871 as the first African American U.S. Minister to Liberia . He died from blood poisoning in Ardmore, Oklahoma on November 1, 1915, after a tank-car explosion injury, with large crowds attending his funeral in St. Louis. The park today features a picnic pavilion, modern playground with splash pad and musical instruments, soft safe playground surface, a softball field, and a loop trail winding around the 1.4-acre property.
Today Vandeventer is a neighborhood in active renewal. The North Sarah Apartments — 120 mixed-income units developed by McCormack Baron Salazar — anchor a residential revitalization along N. Sarah Street. Pamoja Preparatory Academy at Cole Elementary School is the only district school in the neighborhood, providing African-centered education with Swahili language instruction. The Guardian Angel Settlement Association provides early childhood education and social services, and the Advanced Manufacturing Innovation Center (AMICSTL) — a $60 million facility near the neighborhood’s eastern edge — is bringing aerospace, transportation, and agricultural manufacturing training jobs to the area. After eighth grade, students head a mile north to Sumner High School in The Ville. The neighborhood is anchored on its east side by Firehouse 282 on Vandeventer Avenue — a former fire station now serving cold drinks, live music, and fried buffalo fish filets.
The 2020 Census recorded 2,041 residents , an 18% gain from 2010’s low of 1,682, reflecting renewed confidence in a neighborhood with an exceptional depth of story. As Vandeventer resident and urban planner Judith Arnold notes, the neighborhood has been on the revitalization path for decades, resulting in a stable community full of personally invested residents who can mobilize quickly: “I can snap my finger and have 100 residents ready to come help clean up.” Vandeventer aspires to serve as a model for neighborhoods to the north still working on redevelopment.
Image: Vandeventer Place — the 1870 Julius Pitzman-designed Gilded Age private street that gave the neighborhood its name, demolished 1947-1950; its 1894 Louis Mullgardt limestone gate now stands in Forest Park near the Jewel Box — Wikimedia Commons , Public Domain

Vandeventer sees the same hot, humid summers and cold winters as the rest of St. Louis, with a notably active spring severe-weather season, and Turner Park’s playground, splash pad, and loop trail busiest in spring and fall.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is Vandeventer Place in St. Louis? 
A. Vandeventer Place was a privately gated, Gilded Age enclave platted in 1870 on land from stockbroker Peter Lewis Vandeventer’s estate, designed by Julius Pitzman with a grass-median boulevard and fountains. Its roughly 50 mansions housed St. Louis elites like Governor David R. Francis and chemical patriarch Edward Mallinckrodt. Demolished by 1950, only its 1894 limestone entry gate survives, relocated to Forest Park near the Jewel Box.

Q. What defines the Vandeventer neighborhood? 
A. Vandeventer is City of St. Louis Neighborhood #58, a compact rectilinear district on the north-central plateau bounded by Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Delmar Boulevard, N. Vandeventer Avenue, and N. Newstead Avenue. It takes its name from the 1870 Vandeventer Place private street and carries deep civil-rights history, sitting between the Central West End and The Ville, just west of Grand Center.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Vandeventer businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds neighborhood-specific pages that tie a Vandeventer business to local search signals around Turner Park, the North Spring Empowerment Center, and the Vandeventer Place Gates. Plans expand a business’s existing Google Business Profile rather than replace it, with plain-English service, no competitor ads, and no long-term contracts — helping providers stand out to nearby residents and visitors.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Vandeventer? 
A. Vandeventer itself has very little retail footprint inside its own boundary — its real anchors are chamber advocacy and senior housing: the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce at the North Spring Empowerment Center, and Vandeventer Place Senior Living on Pendleton Avenue. For everyday shopping and dining, residents head a few blocks south into the Central West End.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Vandeventer? 
A. Genuinely inside Vandeventer, options are thin — this is mostly a residential, institutional neighborhood. For dining and retail, residents go about two-thirds of a mile south into the Central West End, home to The Boxing Gym and Black Mountain Wine House STL, or east into Grand Center for the Center on Vandeventer event venue. Recreation centers on Turner Park’s playground, splash pad, and loop trail.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Vandeventer? 
A. Yes — Vandeventer carries an unusual concentration of history for its size. Turner Park, its 1.4-acre green space, honors civil-rights pioneer James Milton Turner; the relocated 1894 Vandeventer Place Gates stand in Forest Park; and West Belle Place was the childhood home of Lloyd Lionel Gaines, whose 1938 Supreme Court case became a landmark precursor to Brown v. Board of Education.

Q. What is it like to live in Vandeventer? 
A. Vandeventer is a neighborhood in active renewal: the 2020 Census counted 2,041 residents, an 18 percent gain from 2010’s low of 1,682. New mixed-income housing at the North Sarah Apartments, the African-centered Pamoja Preparatory Academy, and a stable, mobilized resident base point toward continued momentum, even though day-to-day shopping and dining still mean a short trip into the Central West End or Grand Center.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Vandeventer? 
A. Vandeventer sits on a compact rectilinear street grid anchored by N. Sarah Street running north-south through its center, with N. Spring Avenue one block west. Its edges — Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Delmar Boulevard, N. Vandeventer Avenue, and N. Newstead Avenue — connect directly to the Central West End, The Ville, and Grand Center, all within easy walking or short driving distance.

### Visitation Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Visitation Park, St. Louis
Visitation Park is a compact half-mile-square historic district on St. Louis’s north-central side — anchored by the 1909 Soldan High School, the 1908 Carnegie-funded Cabanne Branch Library, three private places (Windermere, Beverly, Savoy), and Ivory Perry Park (formerly Visitation Park) named for the civil rights activist who led the 1963 Jefferson Bank protests and authored St. Louis’s first lead-paint legislation in 1970. The corridor offers neighborhood retail, HIPAA-compliant telecommunications, regional tourism services, and commercial logistics for residents and businesses across the broader West End and Central West End area.
Visitation Park is a compact residential neighborhood on St. Louis’s north-central side at 38.6552° N, 90.2831° W in zip code 63112. Its boundaries run north to Maple Avenue , south to Delmar Boulevard , east to Union Boulevard , and west to Belt Avenue — a roughly half-mile-square pocket that sits just north of Forest Park and west of the DeBaliviere corridor, approximately six miles outside downtown St. Louis. The neighborhood’s internal spine, Cabanne Avenue , runs east–west through its core and once served as the primary address for the institutions that gave the area its identity. The quiet residential lanes of Windermere Place , Beverly Place , and Savoy Court — three of the city’s historic private places — add a distinctive character that distinguishes Visitation Park from the broader West End grid. Adjacent neighborhoods include the West End to the north, the Academy neighborhood to the east, the Skinker-DeBaliviere neighborhood to the south, and Hamilton Heights to the west.
The land that became Visitation Park was historically part of Survey 378 , held by early St. Louis figures including Lucien Cabanne, James Clemens Jr., and Emanuel de Hodiamont — names that still echo in the neighborhood’s street names and legal descriptions. Much of the area was originally uncultivated meadow land owned by Dr. J. Sheppard Cabanne , with Windermere Place developed beginning in 1895 on what had previously been a farm owned by the Thomas Wright family. By the 1870s, the western edge of Union Boulevard north of Delmar was lined with substantial family estates belonging to the Blossom, Monks, Cabanne, Colman, and Gay families. Most of the rest of the neighborhood was developed during and just prior to the 1904 World’s Fair , producing an eclectic mix of architectural styles and an unusual concentration of large institutional buildings primarily located along Union Boulevard — what local historians call the “Union Avenue Promenade.” 
The neighborhood’s defining moment came in 1892 with the opening of Visitation Academy , a French Renaissance chateau-style institution at Cabanne and Belt designed by the prominent firm Barnett, Haynes & Barnett (the same firm that designed the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis). The Academy of the Visitation had been incorporated in 1858 by Visitation Nuns who arrived in St. Louis from Kaskaskia following the flood of 1844, originally housed on Cass Avenue on land donated by Mrs. Anne Biddle. The 1892 westward move educated daughters of St. Louis society as well as children of South American diplomats whose families were in the city during and after the 1904 World’s Fair. After 70 years, the Academy made another westward move in 1962 to 3020 North Ballas Road in St. Louis County, and the City demolished its French Renaissance chateau to create what was originally Visitation Park — the small public park (city ordinance 1961) that gave the neighborhood its name.
In 1989 , the park was renamed Ivory Perry Park to honor the civil rights activist who had spent decades fighting for racial justice from this very neighborhood. Ivory Perry arrived in St. Louis in 1954, led the landmark Jefferson Bank protests of 1963 demanding the hiring of Black bank tellers, championed tenant rights throughout the 1960s, and discovered the connection between lead paint and childhood health problems while visiting renters in their homes — spearheading the city’s first lead-paint legislation in 1970 and becoming a nationally recognized pioneer in what would later be called environmental justice and “environmental racism.” The park today (officially 0.29 acres but the working footprint is closer to 10 acres including surrounding green space) features basketball courts, a softball field, a picnic pavilion, and a playground — bordered by Cabanne Avenue to the north, Belt Avenue to the west, Arlington Avenue to the east, and Clemens Place to the south. The park hosts an annual summer concert series June through August.
The neighborhood’s institutional legacy is remarkable for its scale. Soldan High School , opened in 1909 at 918 N. Union Blvd on the neighborhood’s eastern edge, was celebrated at its founding as the “brightest gem in the city’s public school system.” The school reopened in 1993 as Soldan International Studies Magnet School , today featuring six foreign languages, a science-focused magnet curriculum, and strong partnerships with St. Louis University, Washington University, and the University of Missouri-St. Louis. At roughly the same time as Soldan’s opening, Smith Academy & Manual Training School (1905, originally built for Washington University) operated as an elite boys’ preparatory school — the male counterpart to Mary Institute — and St. Philomena’s Technical School (1910) provided vocational training for young women. The Cabanne Branch Library , designed in 1908 by the distinguished firm Mauran, Russell & Garden and funded through a Carnegie grant , became the second Carnegie library built in St. Louis. The William Clark Elementary School (1906) and Frederick von Harten House (1896) are additional city landmarks within the district.
Visitation Park’s religious and cultural institutions include the St. Louis Artists Guild (1908) and the Young Men’s Hebrew Association (1927), which added cultural and civic dimensions that drew residents from across the region. A wave of development starting in 1906 saw the creation of four separate churches within the neighborhood: Pilgrim Congregational Church (1906), Union Avenue Christian Church (1907), the former Church of the Messiah (1907), and Westminster Presbyterian Church (1913). The neighborhood was further distinguished when Pilgrim Congregational Church became, in 1953 , one of the first St. Louis congregations to formally welcome integrated membership, choosing to remain in the area rather than follow other institutions to the western suburbs. The Visitation Park Historic District , first designated in 1975 by Alderman C.B. Broussard and expanded in 1987, recognizes this layered architectural and social history.
Among Visitation Park’s most celebrated childhood residents is poet, playwright, and novelist Ntozake Shange , whose landmark choreopoem for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf brought national attention to Black women’s experiences, and whose novel Betsy Brown draws directly from her girlhood in St. Louis during the court-ordered school integration era of the 1950s and 1960s. Her life here — in a neighborhood shaped equally by academic excellence, civic activism, and architectural ambition — speaks to the uncommon depth of character that defines Visitation Park. The neighborhood’s demographic trajectory shifted significantly in the 1950s and 1960s as the removal of restrictive covenants in the late 1940s greatly increased housing options for African American families and many white middle-class residents moved out of the city. As of 2020 , Visitation Park’s racial makeup was 77.6% Black, 18.1% White, 0.2% Native American, 1.2% Asian, 2.3% Two or More Races, and 0.7% Some Other Race , with the neighborhood’s total population well under 1,000 residents.
Today, the neighborhood is experiencing a renewed wave of restoration and investment alongside long-standing community organizations like WeCollab that are working on 20-year preservation plans across Visitation Park and the adjacent West End. New businesses like Deli Divine on Delmar Boulevard reflect the corridor’s growing momentum, while restoration projects in the Winston Churchill Apartments (1927) and 1898-era Foursquares continue the work of preserving Visitation Park’s extraordinary architectural inheritance.
Image: Soldan High School, 918 N. Union Blvd — opened 1909 by architect William B. Ittner, celebrated at its founding as the “brightest gem in the city’s public school system,” reopened as Soldan International Studies Magnet School in 1993 — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 2.0 by Paul Sableman

Missouri’s four-season swings just move the neighborhood’s activity around — concerts and ballfield use at Ivory Perry Park in the warmer months, the Delmar corridor and Cabanne Branch Library carrying the traffic once the weather turns.
There is no commercial strip to speak of here, and that is the point. Visitation Park is a place people live, not a place people shop — a few hundred households behind the gates and hedges of Windermere Place, Beverly Place, and Savoy Court, three of St. Louis’s handful of surviving private streets, still governed by their own residents’ associations rather than the city. That is unusual even by St. Louis standards, where private places are themselves a regional rarity. For everything else — a coffee, a sandwich, a night out — residents walk or drive a few blocks into the West End, DeBaliviere Place, or Skinker-DeBaliviere, which is exactly how the businesses below are framed.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Visitation Park? 
A. Yes — remarkably many for a half-mile-square neighborhood. Ivory Perry Park sits on the 1892 Visitation Academy site and honors civil-rights activist Ivory Perry; Soldan High School opened in 1909; the Carnegie-funded Cabanne Branch Library dates to 1908; and three historic private places — Windermere, Beverly, and Savoy — preserve the district’s Gilded Age character, all within the 1975/1987 Visitation Park Historic District.

Q. What is it like to live in Visitation Park? 
A. Quiet and residential: a few hundred households, many behind the gates of Windermere Place, Beverly Place, and Savoy Court — three of St. Louis’s rare surviving private streets, still self-governed. There’s no commercial strip, and the neighborhood’s own history calls that the point; for a coffee, a sandwich, or a night out, residents walk or drive a few blocks into the West End or DeBaliviere Place.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Visitation Park? 
A. The neighborhood’s internal spine, Cabanne Avenue, runs east-west through its core, with Delmar Boulevard and Union Boulevard as its southern and eastern edges. The MetroBus system runs along both Delmar and Union, connecting Visitation Park directly to the West End, DeBaliviere Place, Skinker-DeBaliviere, and Forest Park just to the south.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Visitation Park? 
A.
