By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Collinsville is the Metro East town that grows about 60% of the world's horseradish — yes, really, it's the self-declared Horseradish Capital of the World — with an Italian-immigrant heritage to match (the Italian Fest has run since 1983). It's also home to two landmarks you've definitely seen: the world's largest catsup bottle (a 170-foot Route 66 water tower) and Cahokia Mounds , the UNESCO World Heritage site that was the largest city in pre-Columbian North America.
A town with that much character eats well. Here's where to go in Collinsville.
The independents cluster in Uptown / downtown along Main Street , with a couple out near the I-55/70 plaza. A few close a day midweek (Mungo's is dinner-only, closed Mondays; Carisilo's closed Wednesdays), so check first. Time it for the International Horseradish Festival in early June or Italian Fest in September — both genuine Collinsville institutions.

### Old Herald Brewery & Distillery
Start with the showpiece. Old Herald is a brewery and craft distillery and restaurant inside the former Collinsville Herald newspaper building — exposed-brick adaptive reuse, a pet-friendly patio, and a “Cold Herald” ice creamery. The anchor of the Uptown drinks scene.
📍 115 E Clay St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Kruta Bakery
A century-old institution: Kruta Bakery was founded in 1919 , moved to Collinsville in 1974, and is now run by the third and fourth generations — gooey butter, peanut cake, stollen, and rye breads. A genuine living landmark.
📍 300 St Louis Rd, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Mungo's Italian Eatery
Mungo's is the Italian spot with a heart — owner Tony Mazzola named it for his late friend and mentor, Charlie “Mungo” Mugavero. Dinner-only, closed Mondays, and a real reflection of the town's Italian roots.
📍 100 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Ravanelli's Italian Steakhouse & Wine Bar
Ravanelli's has been “comfort food since 1964” — family-owned Italian and steakhouse with huge portions and famous broasted chicken. The big-occasion, leave-full classic.
📍 26 Collinsport Dr, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Bert's Chuckwagon
Don't let the name fool you — Bert's Chuckwagon is a beloved Tex-Mex institution, a Collinsville fixture since 1963 , known for its tacos, chimichangas, and hand-breaded onion rings. (It's Tex-Mex, not BBQ.) Pure local nostalgia.
📍 101 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Porter's Steakhouse
For the upscale night, Porter's is the independent steakhouse near the I-55/70 plaza — hand-cut steaks and chops, seafood flown in daily, and a 200-plus-bottle wine list. The dress-it-up option.
📍 1000 Eastport Plaza Dr, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Verona Coffee Company
Verona Coffee is the independent downtown coffee house (since 2017) — espresso, hand-brews, pastries, and a little brunch, giving Uptown its own morning anchor.
📍 101 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Carisilo's Mexican Restaurant
Carisilo's is the family-owned authentic Mexican spot with the longest track record of the local taquerias — the dependable fajitas-and-margaritas pick. Closed Wednesdays.
📍 1978 Vandalia St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Heritage Sports Bar & Grill
The newcomer: Heritage opened in 2025 in a restored historic Main Street building (exposed brick) — kabobs, brats, a covered patio, and a game-day room. Fresh energy in Uptown.
📍 118 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Why this little town matters
Collinsville is a town with genuine identity — horseradish capital, Italian-fest heritage, the world's biggest catsup bottle, and an ancient UNESCO city in its backyard — and the food lives up to it: a brewery-distillery in an old newspaper building, a 1919 bakery, a 1964 Italian steakhouse, a 1963 Tex-Mex landmark, and a new sports bar in a restored brick storefront. ### FAQ
What's Collinsville, IL famous for?
It's the “Horseradish Capital of the World” (about 60% of the global supply grows here, celebrated at the June Horseradish Festival), home of the world's largest catsup bottle water tower, and next to Cahokia Mounds, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
What's the oldest restaurant in Collinsville?
Bert's Chuckwagon (Tex-Mex, since 1963) and Ravanelli's (Italian steakhouse, since 1964) are the longtime institutions, and Kruta Bakery dates to 1919.
Does Collinsville have a brewery?
Yes — Old Herald Brewery & Distillery, a combined brewery, craft distillery, and restaurant inside the former Collinsville Herald newspaper building Uptown.
Is Bert's Chuckwagon a BBQ place?
No — despite the name, Bert's is a beloved Tex-Mex spot (tacos, chimichangas, hand-breaded onion rings), a Collinsville fixture since 1963.

Columbia is a growing Metro East town on the Illinois bluffs, about twelve minutes south of downtown St. Louis — platted in 1820, settled hard by German immigrants in the mid-1800s, and still wearing that heritage on its menus. It sits on a plateau between the Mississippi bottoms and bluffs rising to 700 feet, which is exactly why the area's best sunset-and-a-glass spot is here.
From a German pub to a farm-to-bottle distillery to a café in a former church, here's where to eat in Columbia.
The independents cluster downtown on Main Street , with the distillery and the bluff-top bar a short drive out. A few spots close a day or two midweek, so check first. Time a fall trip for FestiFall at Metter Park — German potato pancakes and all.

### Tiny's Pub & Grill
Start with the heritage pick. Tiny's has been a Columbia bar-and-grill since 1975 , and it's leaned hard into the town's German roots — Sauerbraten, Jägerschnitzel, sausages, Currywurst, ten biers on tap, plus American fare and a Main Street patio. A multi-generation community staple.
📍 602 N Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Stumpy's Spirits Distillery
The signature landmark. Stumpy's is a true farm-to-bottle craft distillery on an eighth-generation family farm — award-winning bourbon, vodka, and whiskey made from grain grown on-site and limestone-well water, with guided tours and a tasting room. One of the few genuine farm-distilleries in the country.
📍 1727 Centerville Rd, Columbia, IL 62236

### Sunset Overlook
Sunset Overlook is the wine, craft-beer, and cocktail bar in an 1850s farmhouse on Bluff Road — small plates (flatbreads, warm pretzels, charcuterie, gourmet grilled cheese), live music, and the best sunset view in the area, just minutes from the city. Kid- and dog-friendly outdoors.
📍 11604 Bluff Rd, Columbia, IL 62236

### Cafe on the Abbey
The most distinctive room in town: Cafe on the Abbey serves coffee and all-day breakfast and lunch inside a former Catholic church and convent — specialty drinks, from-scratch desserts, and Keto options under the old bones of the building. Worth it for the setting alone.
📍 322 S Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Washy's Pub
Washy's is the hometown bar-and-grill (since 2019) — handmade, charbroiled-to-order burgers, fried chicken, wings, and grilled cod, breakfast through dinner daily. The friendly everyday spot on Main.
📍 210 S Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Miller's on Main
Miller's on Main is the American restaurant with a genuine Columbia lineage — formerly Reifschneider's, rebranded with the same menu — doing burgers, pizza, pasta, steaks, hand-cut filet, and Cajun shrimp pasta. The reliable sit-down dinner.
📍 608 N Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Marie's Ice Cream Shoppe
For the sweet finish, Marie's is the local ice cream shop — the classic small-town scoop to cap a Columbia visit.
📍 1220 Columbia Centre, Columbia, IL 62236

### A local pizza name to know
For pizza, Joe Boccardi's (117 S Main St) has anchored downtown since 1992 — hand-rolled St. Louis-style pizza and toasted ravioli. It's part of a small, family-owned St. Louis-area group (four locations), so a local favorite rather than a one-off independent.

### Why this little town matters
Columbia is a German-rooted bluff town the apps treat as a commuter exit — but it keeps a 1975 German pub, a farm-to-bottle distillery, a bluff-top sunset bar in an 1850s farmhouse, and a café in a former church. That's a real, distinctive food scene built on genuine local history, and it deserves more than a list of chain logos.

Sunset Overlook on Bluff Road — a wine, beer, and cocktail bar in an 1850s farmhouse with small plates, live music, and the best sunset view in the area, minutes from St. Louis.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Cottleville is the rare St. Charles County town that kept its old bones. Back when Boone's Lick Road — the trail Daniel Boone's sons cut west — crossed Dardenne Creek right here, travelers kept getting stranded in the mud and ending up in town for the night. Two hundred years later, people still come to Cottleville to linger, except now it's for a walkable little strip of Highway N where nearly every door is an independent restaurant, brewery, coffee roaster, or wine garden.
This is one of the best pure food-and-drink strolls in the metro — and the local-ownership stories run deep, right down to a BBQ joint named for the year Captain Cottle got his land grant. Here's where to eat in Old Town Cottleville.
Most of these sit shoulder-to-shoulder on Highway N in Old Town, so park once and wander. A few keep their own rhythm (the coffee roaster is mornings; some kitchens close Mondays), so glance at hours first. Come on a Twilight Tuesday in summer and the amphitheater concerts plus food trucks turn the whole town into a block party.

### Plank Road Pizza
Start with the cornerstone. Plank Road Pizza does from-scratch craft pies and gets called the best pizza in St. Charles for a reason. It's owned by local operator Andrew Brewer — who also runs the cookie shop and the BBQ joint next door — making this stretch of Old Town a genuine one-family labor of love.
📍 5212 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### 1798 BBQ
Right next door, 1798 BBQ slow-smokes pulled pork, ribs, and brisket — and the name is pure Cottleville: 1798 is the year Captain Warren Cottle received his Spanish land grant on this ground. History you can eat, from the same owner as Plank Road.
📍 5210 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Exit 6 Pub & Brewery
Exit 6 was St. Charles County's first nano-brewery — five house beers, a couple dozen taps, no kitchen (bring or order your own food), and a cheeky streak that once made it briefly internet-famous. A true beer-first neighborhood taproom.
📍 5055 Highway N, Ste 113, Cottleville, MO 63304

### The Rack House Kitchen Wine Whiskey
For the upscale night, The Rack House does from-scratch modern American plus weekend brunch — and a wine-and-whiskey list so deep it's been named one of America's Top Whisky Bars by Whisky Advocate. The dress-it-up option without leaving Old Town.
📍 5065 State Hwy N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Bemo's Grill
Bemo's Grill is the locally owned, all-things-to-everyone neighborhood favorite — burgers, sandwiches, steaks, pasta, seafood — with a near-perfect local reputation across thousands of reviews. The reliable family pick on the strip.
📍 5373 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Upshot Coffee
Upshot Coffee is the independent specialty roaster and café — espresso, cold brew, matcha, baked goods, even bone broth, plus a mural by a local artist on the wall. The morning anchor of Old Town, and the S'mores Croffle is the indulgence to split.
📍 5326 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Cottleville Wine Seller
Cottleville Wine Seller is the Old Town wine shop, wine garden, and live-music spot rolled into one — 200-plus labels, an outdoor garden, and bands on weekends. The easy, lingering middle of a Cottleville afternoon.
📍 Old Town Cottleville (Highway N), Cottleville, MO 63304

### Cottle Village Farmstead + Distillery
On the eastern edge of town, Cottle Village is the ambitious new destination — a restaurant (The Tavern), a distillery, and an outdoor venue across a few acres, built by a St. Louis hospitality couple who moved to Cottleville and made it an homage to the area's farmstead past. Kentucky-bourbon-country energy, twenty minutes from the airport.
📍 6470 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Why this little town matters
Cottleville proves a small town doesn't have to trade its history for a strip mall. The same Boone's Lick crossing that stranded travelers two centuries ago now anchors a walkable Old Town where a single local family runs the pizza-cookies-BBQ corner, the county's first nano-brewery pours next to a top-rated whisky bar, and a returning hometown couple just built a distillery as a love letter to the place. The national apps will sell you the nearest chain; they'll never tell you that story.
We will. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Cottleville and St. Charles County before you go — and our Augusta guide is the natural next stop deeper into Missouri wine country.
And if you run a Cottleville spot — a café, a tasting room, a food truck — a listing is how the next carful wandering Old Town finds you .

### FAQ
What's the best area to eat in Cottleville?
Old Town Cottleville along Highway N — a walkable strip with pizza, BBQ, a brewery, a top whisky bar, a coffee roaster, and a wine garden, mostly within a couple of blocks.
What's the story behind 1798 BBQ's name?
1798 is the year Captain Warren Cottle received his Spanish land grant on the land that became Cottleville — the BBQ joint (same owner as next-door Plank Road Pizza) named itself after the town's founding year.
Does Cottleville have a brewery or distillery?
Both — Exit 6 Pub & Brewery (St. Charles County's first nano-brewery) in Old Town, and Cottle Village Farmstead + Distillery on the town's eastern edge.
When is the best time to visit Cottleville?
Summer Twilight Tuesdays bring amphitheater concerts and food trucks to Legacy Park — a great night to pair with an Old Town dinner.

Creve Coeur runs along Olive Boulevard, one of the most internationally diverse restaurant stretches in all of St. Louis County. One drive turns up Syrian kebabs, two Korean BBQ houses, vegan Indian street food, a French patisserie that's been here since 1981, and Italian with real Hill pedigree. The chain apps see a strip mall; locals see a passport. (Heads-up: some of these show “St. Louis 63141” on Google but physically sit inside Creve Coeur.)
From a Syrian grill to a karaoke-and-bulgogi hybrid, here's where to eat in Creve Coeur.
It's all about Olive Boulevard (63141) — a single corridor with one of the metro's deepest benches of international food. A few spots close Sundays or Mondays, and lunch out here is a steal. Don't be thrown by “St. Louis” mailing addresses on a few of these; they're Creve Coeur.

### Layali Halab
Layali Halab is one of the only dedicated Syrian kitchens in the whole region — chef Mustafa Mustafa cooked professionally in Syria for a decade before opening this Aleppo-style spot. Charcoal kebabs, falafel, hummus, and a complimentary lentil soup for dine-in. Named for the “nights of Aleppo.”
📍 10477 Old Olive Street Rd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Bombay Food Junkies
Bombay Food Junkies is the area's only fully plant-based Indian spot — founded by Bombay natives Krupa and Sid, who ran St. Louis's first all-vegetarian Indian food truck back in 2013. Bombay-style chaats, a vegan “chicken” sandwich, samosas, and dairy-free shakes.
📍 12955 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Il Bel Lago
Il Bel Lago is brothers Frank and Carmelo Gabriele carrying their family's Hill pedigree out to Olive — they grew up at their father's landmark Giovanni's. The broiled veal chop with black truffle sauce is the dish that converts truffle skeptics. The dressy Italian.
📍 11631 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### La Bonne Bouchée Patisserie & Café
La Bonne Bouchée has been St. Louis's trusted French bakery since 1981 — a genuine Parisian-style patisserie with café classics like Croque Monsieur, Quiche Lorraine, and French onion soup. Pastry, coffee, and a long local history.
📍 12344 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Joo Joo Restaurant & Karaoke
Joo Joo is the Korean BBQ-and-karaoke hybrid — grill your own meat, then book a private karaoke room. Sauce Magazine has called its barbecue some of the finest in St. Louis; the kori gom tang oxtail soup is a standout. The fun night out.
📍 12937 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Seoul Garden
Seoul Garden is the family-owned all-you-can-eat Korean BBQ spot with a grill built into every table — cook your own bulgogi and spicy pork ribs, with bibimbap and soft tofu soup on the side. Hands-on and generous.
📍 10441 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Orzo Mediterranean Grill
Orzo is the Greek and Mediterranean fast-casual spot from Nick and Laura Cowlen — the duo behind the “Go Gyro Go!” food truck — tucked by the fountain in the City Space strip. Gyros, wraps, salads, and bowls. The great quick lunch.
📍 11627 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

### Timothy's
Timothy's is the “fine-casual” American spot punching above its strip-corridor address — a small seasonal menu with a lobster pot pie, steak frites, an exceptional wine program, and superb service at approachable prices. The neighborhood sleeper.
📍 12710 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur, MO 63141

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Drive about half an hour south of St. Louis along the Mississippi and you hit Crystal City — a town that exists because of glass . They mined silica sand out of the ground here, built what was once the largest plate-glass plant on earth, and named the place for the crystal-clear product it made. The plant's gone now, but the town it built is still standing, still independent, and — turns out — still feeds you well.
Crystal City and neighboring Festus blur together so completely that locals just say “the Twin Cities,” but Crystal City has its own two main drags — Truman Boulevard and Bailey Road — lined with the kind of spots that don't exist anywhere else: a 1948 burger stand that's cash-only on purpose, a bike shop that's also a wood-fired pizzeria, a Chinese place that's been family-run since 1982. Here's where to eat on the Crystal City side.
A couple of these keep old-school habits — Gordon's is cash only (there's an ATM inside), and a few of the diners close Mondays. Worth a heads-up before you go. One update to the old local advice: the Crystal City Underground , the flooded silica mine beneath the old glassworks, is closed after flooding and opens only for special events, with no reopening date announced. For the rest of the day, see things to do in Festus next door.

### Gordon's Stoplight Drive-In
Start at the landmark. Gordon's Stoplight Drive-In has been griddling “the best hamburgers in the world” since 1948 — same corner, same simple idea, cash only, and a line that proves the formula still works after 75-plus years. This is a genuine piece of Jefferson County, served on a tray.
📍 500 Bailey Rd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Pedal'N Pi
Only in a town like this: Pedal'N Pi is a bike shop and a wood-fired Neapolitan pizzeria under one roof. Owner Chris Creed opened it in 2021, and the crust earns the raves — including from gluten-free eaters, who swear it's the best GF pizza they've had anywhere. Fix a flat, eat a pie, leave grinning.
📍 514 Bailey Rd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Kettelhut's Smokehouse
For smoke, Kettelhut's is the family-owned Memphis-style smokehouse on Truman Boulevard, putting out brisket and pulled pork that regulars describe as melt-in-your-mouth — and a sleeper burger that surprises everyone who orders it. Everything's smoked fresh on-site daily, the way BBQ is supposed to be.
📍 1267 N Truman Blvd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Lam's Garden
Some places earn their spot just by lasting. Lam's Garden has served family-style Chinese here since 1982 — four-plus decades of one family feeding the same town. In an era when restaurants flicker out in eighteen months, that kind of staying power is its own recommendation.
📍 510 Bailey Rd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Thai Rama
When you want something cooked precisely to order, Thai Rama does from-scratch Thai on Truman Boulevard, every dish built with fresh produce and dialed to your heat tolerance — all the way up to “Thai hot” if you're feeling brave. It's the kind of careful, independent cooking a small town is lucky to have.
📍 606 N Truman Blvd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Main Street Cafe
For the home-style breakfast-and-lunch routine, Main Street Cafe on Truman is the early-morning diner locals have leaned on for years — fried chicken, BBQ, seafood, and a 6 a.m. open Tuesday through Saturday. Closed Mondays; otherwise, it's the town's reliable plate.
📍 902 N Truman Blvd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Iguanas Mexican Grill
Iguanas brings the street tacos, fajitas, enchiladas, and seafood, plus late hours for when the night runs long — an authentic family Mexican spot that opened in 2021 and quickly became a Truman Boulevard regular.
📍 907 N Truman Blvd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### P'sghetti's Pasta & Sandwiches
If you want something unmistakably St. Louis, P'sghetti's does Provel-laden Italian subs, homemade sweet bread, and big plates of pasta — a locally owned, St. Louis-family operation that opened its Crystal City spot in the old frozen-custard building. Toasted ravioli energy in the best way.
📍 101 S Truman Blvd, Crystal City, MO 63019

### Why this little town matters
Crystal City was built as a company town for the glassworks, a place that literally manufactured something you could see through. The plant closed in 1990, but the town didn't — and the proof is on Truman and Bailey, where a 1948 drive-in, a bike-shop pizzeria, a 1982 family Chinese restaurant, and a daily smokehouse all hold their corners. That's a kind of resilience the chain-logo maps off the highway will never show you.
That's the whole reason we built a hyper-local directory. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Crystal City and Jefferson County before you go — and if you're working your way through the county, our De Soto guide and Hillsboro guide are close by.

### FAQ
What's the most famous place to eat in Crystal City?
Gordon's Stoplight Drive-In — griddling hamburgers since 1948, cash only, and still drawing a line. It's a genuine local landmark.
Is the food in Crystal City actually in Crystal City, or Festus?
The twin cities blur together, but everything in this guide is confirmed in Crystal City proper (ZIP 63019) — on Truman Boulevard and Bailey Road — not over the line in Festus.
What's the unique thing to do in Crystal City besides eat?
The Crystal City Underground, the flooded silica-sand mine left from the glass industry, used to be the answer, but it is closed after flooding and opens only for special events. For more to do nearby, see things to do in Festus .
Are there independent restaurants in Crystal City, or mostly chains?

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Have you ever found yourself driving through a small town and wondering where the locals actually eat — not the highway chain with the glowing sign, but the place with six trucks parked out front at noon and a regular's name half-remembered by the woman behind the counter?
In De Soto, that place isn't hard to find. Tucked into southwest Jefferson County along Joachim Creek, this old railroad town has quietly held onto something a lot of suburbs traded away years ago: a real, walkable Main Street where almost every kitchen is somebody's livelihood, not a corporate franchise. Whether you grew up here, you're passing through on the way to the lake, or you just like hunting down the genuine article, here's where to eat in De Soto.

### Junction Cafe
Start where De Soto starts its mornings. Junction Cafe opens early — 6 a.m. on weekdays — and trades in exactly what a railroad-town diner should: all-day breakfast, hearty "Junction" sandwiches, and an open-face roast beef that arrives under a quilt of gravy. It's the kind of counter where the coffee never quite runs dry.
📍 106 S Main St, De Soto, MO 63020

### El Lobo Rojo
Right across the Main Street divide, chef Jose Maria Lopez cooks the Jalisco-style Mexican food he grew up on at El Lobo Rojo — tacos, burritos, fajitas, chimichangas, the works. It's independent, it's got its own loyal following, and the portions don't apologize for themselves.
📍 106 N Main St, De Soto, MO 63020

### Sherwood's Classic Eats
A De Soto success story in motion: Sherwood's has been feeding the area since 2018 and moved onto Main Street at the end of 2024, bringing along its handmade pizzas, pasta, and a stacked signature sandwich called "The John Wayne." Subs, salads, wraps — it's the dependable, made-to-order kind of spot every town needs and not every town has.
📍 122 N Main St, De Soto, MO 63020

### Cafe Smok N Pi
Just outside downtown on Route 21, Cafe Smok N Pi does the thing St. Louis-area smokehouses do best — and the move here is the pork steak , that gloriously regional cut you won't find done right just anywhere. Brick-oven pizza rounds out the menu, and live music takes over Friday and Saturday nights from 6 to 9.
📍 12636 State Route 21, De Soto, MO 63020

### Pogolino's
When De Soto wants pizza, a lot of De Soto goes to Pogolino's — the local Italian-leaning pizzeria and Chamber of Commerce mainstay that opens daily at 11. Nothing flashy, just the neighborhood pizza joint doing what it's done for years.
📍 530 N 2nd St, De Soto, MO 63020

### Just Be Kind Café
For a slower morning, Just Be Kind Café is the exposed-brick, plant-filled coffee shop and bakery the town didn't used to have. Specialty coffee, house-baked goods, and custom cakes, open weekday mornings into the afternoon. The name pretty much tells you the vibe.
📍 426 S Main St, De Soto, MO 63020

### LaChance Vineyards
And when you want to make an evening of it, LaChance Vineyards is the destination — an 80-acre family farm winery in De Soto's rolling hills, founded in 2010 by Harold and Tami Hamby and named for Harold's French great-grandfather. Roughly 8,000 vines, a farm-to-table menu, and live music; it's been named the St. Louis area's #1 winery more than once by the local food press.
📍 12237 Peter Moore Ln, De Soto, MO 63020

### A town with more going on than you'd guess
De Soto wears its history on its sleeve — the Iron Mountain railroad rolled in back in 1858 and made this a genuine "train town," and the place still sits along Joachim Creek , where the locals race rubber ducks every fall. (Trivia for your table: in 1980, De Soto was the U.S. town closest to the mean center of the entire country's population.) The De Soto Fall Festival each September turns N Main Street into a street fair, food vendors and all.
It's a lot of character for one small Jefferson County town — and a perfect example of why a hyper-local directory beats a generic national app. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for De Soto and you'll turn up the businesses the big platforms never bother to list. ### FAQ
Does De Soto have good local restaurants, or just chains?
The Main Street core is overwhelmingly independent — diners, a Mexican spot, pizza, a coffee bakery, a smokehouse, and a destination winery, all locally owned. That's the reason to get off the highway.
Where's the best breakfast in De Soto?
Junction Cafe is the early-riser favorite, open at 6 a.m. weekdays with all-day breakfast and big diner plates.
Is LaChance Vineyards in De Soto or Kimmswick?
Both — the main 80-acre estate and restaurant are in De Soto, with a second tasting location up in Kimmswick.
When is the De Soto Fall Festival?
Each September on N Main Street — arts and crafts, a car show, a 5K, food vendors, and the famous Joachim Creek duck race. Check the current year's date before you go.

The landmark. London's Wing House has been frying since 1963 — one of the oldest Black-owned wing joints in St. Louis, founded by Dale and Hildred London and now run by their son Patrick. Cathy's Kitchen To-Go is the Dellwood carryout sibling of the famous Ferguson restaurant — Cajun chicken pasta, blackened shrimp alfredo, crispy catfish — built on 30 years of family recipes owner Cathy collected traveling the country. The flagship became a national symbol of community resilience; this is its West Florissant window.
📍 10198 W Florissant Ave, Dellwood, MO 63136

Hunan Chop Suey is the Dellwood Village strip's go-to fast Chinese counter — chop suey, fried rice, wings, St. Louis-style — and it's right in the City of Dellwood's own business directory. The dependable neighborhood takeout.

### Village Bar
Village Bar is the corridor's living history — the building started as an 1872 post office and feed store and has poured beer since just after Prohibition, arguably the oldest watering hole on Manchester. Get the "Better Burger" (fresh, never-frozen) and the award-winning hand-breaded onion rings. Open till 1 a.m.
📍 12247 Manchester Rd, Des Peres, MO 63131

### Surf & Sirloin
Surf & Sirloin is the family-owned old-school steakhouse Larry Karagiannis opened in 1994 — filet mignon with classic Béarnaise, seared Maine scallops, fish bought whole and inspected on-site. The brickwork-and-high-ceilings room where West County couples have celebrated anniversaries for 30 years.
📍 13090 Manchester Rd, Des Peres, MO 63131

### Three Kings Public House
Three Kings is the gastropub whose breaded chicken wings earned national attention — plus award-winning burgers and a deep craft-beer list, ingredients from Missouri and Illinois farmers. It's a small St. Louis-grown group (four locations), and this is the Des Peres one.
📍 11925 Manchester Rd, Des Peres, MO 63131

### Rosalita's Cantina
Rosalita's is the big-blue-marble-bar Tex-Mex and tequila spot — tableside guacamole, Cadillac Fajitas, and a house margarita locals routinely call the best in town, under starry light fixtures with a patio.

### Casa de Tres Reyes
Casa de Tres Reyes is the colorful, genuinely kid-friendly independent Mexican spot doing birria tacos, cheese-crusted burritos, and empanadas — one of the few places doing Mexican breakfast plus birria and margaritas under one roof.

### Tiger Soup Dumplings

### Tiger 88 Banh Mi & Boba

Dupo is a small rail town in the American Bottom flatlands south of East St. Louis — its odd little name a worn-down version of Prairie du Pont ("bridge prairie"), from the French colonists who settled here around 1750 and built one of Illinois's first wagon-road bridges. It grew up around the Missouri Pacific switching yards, and it still feels like a railroad town. Here's the pleasant surprise: for a village of about 4,000, Dupo punches well above its weight on food — a women-owned scratch café, a lakeside tavern with live music, an independent Mexican spot the town adores.
When you're down by the bluffs and hungry, here's where to eat in Dupo.
Most spots sit along Main Street and the side streets just off it, with a couple out toward the lakes. The café is a morning operation; the taverns run late. A few are newer, so a quick hours check helps. Dupo sits about ten miles from Cahokia Mounds — the UNESCO World Heritage site — so it's an easy pairing with a visit there.

### Sugar & Sage Cafe
Start at the town's new darling. Sugar & Sage is a family- and women-owned scratch café — locally roasted coffee, made-from-scratch breakfast and lunch, and homemade baked goods, with a kids' play area. It got a St. Louis TV feature, sources from local small businesses, and has quickly become the heart of Dupo's mornings.
📍 115 N 2nd St, Dupo, IL 62239

### Triple Lakes Tavern
The destination spot. Triple Lakes Tavern sits out by the lakes with a patio and live music — smoked cheeseburgers, chicken dumplings, "Fried Chicken Sundays," and a Friday fish-and-wings spread. The lean-back, stay-a-while pick.
📍 8055 Triple Lakes Rd, Dupo, IL 62239

### The Mexican
The Mexican on South Main is the independent Mexican spot the town genuinely loves — reviewers rave about the garlic shrimp fajitas, the margaritas, and a signature white dip with the chips. One regular called it "such an amazing addition to our little town," which is exactly the vibe.
📍 200 S Main St, Dupo, IL 62239

### Dairy Land
Dairy Land (you'll also see it as Dawn's Dairyland) is the classic small-town walk-up — burgers, hot wings, cheese sticks, corn dogs, fried cauliflower, malts, and soft-serve. The owner-run treat-and-a-burger window every rail town should have.
📍 501 S Main St, Dupo, IL 62239

### 5th Street Billiards Bar & Grill
5th Street Billiards is the pool-hall-and-grill — burgers, wings, Italian beef, "coldest beer in town," and year-round pool leagues. The casual hang for a game and a plate.
📍 200 N 5th St, Dupo, IL 62239

### Judy's Corner
Judy's Corner is the spotless little neighborhood bar where owner Judy runs the room and the kitchen turns out pizza — a genuine local corner spot with a loyal following.
📍 534 S Main St, Dupo, IL 62239

### Why this little town matters
Dupo is a 270-year-old French-rooted rail town that the apps reduce to a couple of listings and a gas station — but it quietly fields a women-owned scratch café, a lakeside tavern with live music, a beloved independent Mexican spot, and a classic ice-cream-and-burger stand. By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Let's be straight about Eagle Park: it's not a town with a Main Street — it's a small residential neighborhood in Madison County wedged where Madison, Granite City, and Pontoon Beach meet, just north of St. Louis. Homes, mobile homes, and a neighborhood improvement association — and no restaurants of its own. But people here get hungry too, and the good news is real local food is a few minutes away in every direction. Here are the closest authentic spots.
From fresh birria tacos to a 30-year Vietnamese institution, here's where to eat near Eagle Park.
Eagle Park (ZIP 62060, a Madison postal address; some maps list it as Eagle Park Acres) has no commercial strip — residents drive a few minutes into Granite City or Pontoon Beach for a meal. The closest authentic cluster runs along Nameoki Road in Granite City. Everything below is labeled by its real town; call ahead at the smaller spots.

### Tacos El Manny (Granite City)
A family-owned Mexican spot on Nameoki Road — fresh tacos and birria that locals rate highly. Distinctive and genuinely local (closed Mondays).
📍 2800 Nameoki Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Vin Hoa (Granite City)
A 30-plus-year Vietnamese-and-Chinese institution — cash-only takeout that the neighborhood has leaned on for decades. The kind of quiet, reliable spot only regulars know.
📍 3212 Nameoki Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Taqueria Z (Granite City)
An authentic Mexican spot popular with locals — another fresh, family-run option in the Nameoki Road cluster minutes from Eagle Park.
📍 Nameoki Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Why this town matters
Eagle Park is a tiny residential pocket with no restaurants — and saying that plainly is the honest answer searchers deserve, instead of mislabeling Granite City spots. By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
East Alton is a small working Riverbend town wedged between Alton, Wood River, and Bethalto — and its food scene is genuinely compact. But "small" doesn't mean "skip it," because the locals here punch above their size: a farm-to-table wood-fired pizzeria that doubles as a morning pastry shop, a chef's comfort-food kitchen with a daily-changing special board, two family Mexican rooms, and a corner tavern with an award-winning chili and a Friday fish fry.
From a husband-and-wife wood-fired pizzeria to an award-winning tavern chili, here's where to eat in East Alton.
East Alton's dining sits in two small clusters — Eastgate Plaza and Airline Drive (62024) — walkable or a short drive between. The scene is honestly thin, so we lead with the six real locals and point you next door to Alton and Wood River for more. Several keep limited hours (closed Sun/Mon, breakfast-to-afternoon).

### 1929 Pizza and Wine
The standout. 1929 Pizza and Wine is the husband-and-wife (Matt and Amy Herren) farm-to-table, wood-fired pizzeria — a seasonal, locally-sourced menu, and the same space runs as a morning pastry shop ("Patisserie '29") before flipping to dinner at 5. The destination spot people drive in for. Dinner Tue–Sat.
📍 7 Wood River Ave, East Alton, IL 62024

### Food A Fare
Food A Fare is Chef Mike Hollis and Nyla Hollis's chef-driven comfort-food kitchen — a flaky-crust chicken pot pie, plus rotating specials like Brunswick stew, Tuscan sausage stew, and shrimp chowder. A small Eastgate Plaza storefront with a real chef behind it. Closed Sun–Mon.
📍 139 Eastgate Plaza, East Alton, IL 62024

### Casa Romero Mexican Restaurant & Cantina
Casa Romero is the full-bar cantina where the salsa hits the table before you've finished sitting down — Tequila Fiesta Shrimp, seafood nachos, and margaritas. An East Alton fixture on Airline Drive.
📍 521 E Airline Dr, East Alton, IL 62024

### Mr. Pancho's Mexican Restaurant and Grill
Mr. Pancho's is the other family Mexican spot — a full traditional menu (tacos, fajitas, combination plates) with a steady local following, holding down the Eastgate Plaza side of town.
📍 119 Eastgate Plaza, East Alton, IL 62024

### Rosewood Café
Rosewood is owner Tija Hunter's breakfast-and-lunch coffee café — a breakfast power bowl, soup flights served in bread bowls, and specialty lattes. She even gives free delivery to teachers and staff in the local school districts midweek. Closed Mondays.
📍 961 E Airline Dr, Suite B, East Alton, IL 62024

### The Airliner Bar & Grill
The Airliner is the true Riverbend corner tavern — an award-winning chili, all-you-can-eat whitefish on Fridays, and hot burgers, wraps, and melts, with the kitchen and bar running past midnight most nights. Closed Sundays.
📍 573 E Airline Dr, East Alton, IL 62024

### Why this town matters
East Alton is small and easy to drive past — which is exactly why a farm-to-table wood-fired pizzeria, a chef's comfort kitchen, and a Friday-fish-fry tavern deserve a spotlight. All six are locally owned, no chains. We map the Riverbend town the apps overlook.

### FAQ
What's the best place to eat in East Alton, IL?
1929 Pizza and Wine — a husband-and-wife farm-to-table, wood-fired pizzeria that doubles as a morning pastry shop. In a town this small, it's the destination-worthy spot.
Is East Alton's food scene big?
It's honestly compact — about six real independents, clustered at Eastgate Plaza and along Airline Drive. The upside: Alton and Wood River are right next door for more options.
Where's the Friday fish fry in East Alton?
The Airliner Bar & Grill — all-you-can-eat whitefish on Fridays, reflecting the Metro East's deep Catholic, working-class tavern culture. Fish fries here are a ritual, not a gimmick.
Where should I go for more food near East Alton?
Alton (the historic tourist-and-dining hub) and Wood River are both minutes away — see our Alton and Wood River guides for deeper benches.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
East St. Louis has a real but thin food scene, and what survives is deeply local: old-school BBQ and soul food, defined less by ribs than by snoots — crispy fried pig snouts, a Metro East tradition. Two long-running pit institutions still serve them, alongside a late-night fish-and-chicken counter and the riverfront casino dining. People here get hungry too, and these are the genuinely local spots worth knowing — plus where to go nearby for more.
From a drive-through line wrapped around the building to cash-only ribs since the '70s, here's where to eat in East St. Louis.
This is a thin market with a lot of mislabeled listings — many “East St. Louis” results are actually in Washington Park, Cahokia Heights, or across the river. We kept to verified East St. Louis ZIPs (62201/62203/62205/62207). Hours are limited and a couple of spots are cash-only — a same-day check helps. For a fuller sit-down meal, Belleville and Fairview Heights are a short drive southeast.

### Big Mama's BBQ Express
Big Mama's has been smoking since 2001 — crispy snoots, meaty rib tips, and the over-the-top “Cooter Comeback Sammich” (double patties or pulled meat, “cooter sauce,” loaded with fries), plus house-made cakes. The drive-through line famously wraps around the building; locals plan around the wait.
📍 5900 St. Clair Ave, East St. Louis, IL 62203

### Sandy's Bar B Q
Sandy's is the old-school BBQ shack in business since the 1970s — crispy snoots with perfect texture and juicy, tender ribs under homemade sauce. It's cash only, no cards, no call-aheads: you show up, you order at the counter. A genuine decades-old neighborhood institution. (Use the 327 S 15th St location; verify the limited hours.)
📍 327 S 15th St, East St. Louis, IL 62207

### Pop's Fish & Chicken
Pop's is the casual local fish-and-chicken counter — fried catfish-nugget dinners, ten-wing dinners, plus burgers, Philly steak, and gyros — and it's open late, until about 11:30 p.m. most nights, one of the few genuinely late-night bites in the city.
📍 2413 State St, East St. Louis, IL 62205

### Bridgeway & That Chickn' Place (at the Casino)
The riverfront option. Bridgeway (New American sit-down) and That Chickn' Place (wings and chicken) operate inside the downtown casino at 200 Front St — casino-run, not locally owned, but the only riverfront dining in the city, with downtown St. Louis skyline views and a kitchen open into the early-morning hours.
📍 200 Front St, East St. Louis, IL 62201

### Why this town matters
East St. Louis is a thin, high-turnover market — which is exactly why the surviving local pits matter. A 50-year cash-only BBQ shack and a snoot-famous drive-through are the real story here, and the chain apps are a minefield of closed and mislabeled spots. We verify what's actually open, and point you to Belleville and Fairview Heights for more.

### FAQ
What's the signature food in East St. Louis, IL?
Snoots — crispy fried pig snouts — are the regional BBQ tradition, and both surviving pit institutions (Big Mama's and Sandy's) are known for them. It's the dish that defines local BBQ here more than ribs.
What's the most old-school spot in East St. Louis?
Sandy's Bar B Q — in business since the 1970s, cash-only and in-person-only. A 50-year neighborhood holdout in a city that's lost most of its sit-down restaurants.
Is East St. Louis's food scene big?
Honestly, no — it's a thin market with high turnover and lots of mislabeled listings. A handful of genuine local BBQ and soul-food spots, plus the riverfront casino dining. For a fuller meal, Belleville and Fairview Heights are a short drive southeast.
Are some “East St. Louis” restaurants actually in other towns?
Yes — in 2021 Centreville, Cahokia, and Alorton merged into Cahokia Heights, and many southern-edge listings fall there or in Washington Park (62204). Real East St. Louis ZIPs are 62201, 62203, 62205, 62206, and 62207.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Edwardsville is the Madison County seat and a genuine college town — home to SIUE, a historic Main Street, a Route 66 alignment, and the 1890 Leclaire model-village district. All of that adds up to one of the strongest independent food scenes in the Metro East: chef-driven New American, hand-pulled pasta, scratch bakeries, and a cocktail-and-brunch culture that punches well above a town of 27,000.
From a Beard-pedigree kitchen to the town's oldest bar, here's where to eat in Edwardsville.
The independents split between historic downtown (Main Street, Vandalia, St. Louis Street) and the newer Plum Street / Route 157 corridor — both in 62025. A few are dinner-only or brunch-focused, so check first. Time a June trip for the Edwardsville Route 66 Festival (the 2026 edition coincides with Route 66's 100th birthday).

### Cleveland-Heath
Start at the flagship. Cleveland-Heath is downtown's chef-driven New American room — gourmet comfort food that earned its founding chef James Beard “Best Chef” semifinalist nods. A genuine destination, and the anchor of Edwardsville dining.
📍 106 N Main St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Mio Osteria
Mio Osteria is the family-owned Italian spot from Micah and Aerika Hopkin — casual lunch, upscale dinner, and a thoughtful cocktail-and-wine program, with a real owner-history pedigree in St. Louis kitchens. The grown-up Italian night.
📍 224 S Kansas St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Brick + Bramble
Brick + Bramble is the craft-cocktail bar and shareable-plates spot with a popular weekend brunch — a community staple on Plum Street. The place for a good drink and small plates.
📍 2323 Plum St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Café Birdie
Café Birdie is the breakfast-and-brunch café opened in 2023 by Edwardsville native Jenny Levi, who came home after 20-plus years cooking on the West Coast — a great local-roots story and a bright daily breakfast.
📍 120 S Main St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Sacred Grounds Cafe
Sacred Grounds is the downtown independent coffeehouse — organic breakfast and lunch, walls full of local art, a longtime community hangout. The morning anchor.
📍 233 N Main St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### 222 Artisan Bakery & Cafe
222 Artisan Bakery (on St. Louis Street, not Main) is the family-owned scratch bakery — fresh bread, cinnamon rolls, pastries, breakfast and sandwiches, plus sourdough pizzas on weekends. Run by a mom-and-son team.
📍 222 St. Louis St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Chava's Mexican Restaurant
Chava's is the family-owned authentic Mexican spot — recipes from Guadalajara, run by the Ybarra family since 2013. The dependable, made-fresh Mexican pick.
📍 217 E Vandalia St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Stagger Inn Again
Stagger Inn Again is Edwardsville's oldest continuously operating watering hole — a restaurant by day, a bar with live music by night. The historic local hang.
📍 104 E Vandalia St, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Peel Wood Fired Pizza
Peel is the neo-Neapolitan wood-fired pizzeria that started right here in Edwardsville in 2008 (founded by two ex-pastry chefs) before growing into a small regional name. It's a local-born chain rather than a one-off, but the Edwardsville original is the real deal.
📍 100 Quartz Knoll, Edwardsville, IL 62025

### Why this little town matters
Edwardsville is a college town that quietly built a destination food scene — a Beard-pedigree New American kitchen, hand-pulled pasta, scratch bakeries, a craft-cocktail brunch culture, and the town's oldest bar — across a historic downtown and a Route 66 alignment. The national apps reduce it to logos near campus; we map the real Main Street.

### FAQ
What's the best restaurant in Edwardsville, IL?
Cleveland-Heath downtown — a chef-driven New American kitchen with James Beard “Best Chef” semifinalist pedigree, the anchor of the local scene. For Italian, Mio Osteria.
Where do locals get breakfast or coffee in Edwardsville?
Café Birdie (brunch, opened 2023 by a hometown chef), Sacred Grounds Cafe (organic coffeehouse), and 222 Artisan Bakery (scratch bakery on St. Louis Street).
Did Peel Wood Fired Pizza start in Edwardsville?
Yes — Peel was founded in Edwardsville in 2008 by two former pastry chefs before expanding; the Edwardsville location is the original.
What's the oldest bar in Edwardsville?
Stagger Inn Again on Vandalia Street — Edwardsville's oldest continuously operating drinking establishment, a restaurant by day and live-music bar by night.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Part of West County — explore the whole region in our West County restaurant guide .
Ellisville sits in far West County where Manchester Road runs past Clarkson, and its food packs into about a mile of that corridor — a stretch with serious staying power. A St. Louis pizza institution from 1968, a 30-year Chinese-Thai-Vietnamese spot, a golf-themed wing joint since 1993, plus newer stars like a Mexico City small-plates room and a Filipino mochi-donut shop. The trick out here is the city line: Manchester straddles Ellisville, Ballwin, and Winchester, so plenty of "Ellisville" listings aren't.
From a 1968 Provel-and-cracker-crust pizza to Mexico City small plates, here's where to eat in Ellisville.
Nearly every independent worth visiting sits along a one-mile stretch of Manchester Rd (roughly 15300–16100, 63011), with Mulligan's just off it on Clarkson. Watch the city line — a 63011 ZIP doesn't guarantee Ellisville (some nearby spots are Ballwin or Wildwood). Several are decades-old family institutions; a couple close Sundays or Mondays.

### Malinche Mexican Culinary Experience
The critics' darling. Malinche isn't your average taco shop — it's small plates inspired by the culinary traditions of Mexico City, in an intimate, elevated room that earned Feast Magazine and KSDK coverage. Order several plates and the chips-and-salsa with its local cult following.
📍 15939 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Faraci Pizza
Faraci is a genuine 1968-vintage St. Louis pizza institution — thin, square-cut, cracker-crust, Provel-topped — still run by the family, with specialty pies like buffalo chicken and Mediterranean. The real St. Louis article. Closed Sundays.
📍 15430 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Mulligan's Grill
Mulligan's has been the family-owned, golf-themed bar and grill since 1993 — menu items named after golf terms, and locals insist the only way to order the wings is "trashed" (extra-crispy). The neighborhood hang on Clarkson.
📍 11 Clarkson Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Golden Wok
Golden Wok is the 30-plus-year fixture that quietly grew from a Chinese carryout into a three-cuisine spot — Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese under one roof. The dependable pan-Asian standby. Closed Sundays.
📍 15941 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Tatva Cafe
Tatva is the vegetarian South Indian room where the dosas — crispy fermented rice-and-lentil crepes — are the draw, alongside South Indian curries and breakfast. A genuinely different option on the corridor.
📍 15801 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Mochi Donut Factory
Mochi Donut Factory is the Filipino-family shop from high-school sweethearts Carlo and Jaen Henson (born and raised in Manila) who brought the chewy mochi donut to West County — churro, Fruity Pebbles, pineapple-passionfruit. Morning-and-early-afternoon only.
📍 16023 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Fallon's Grill and Tap
Fallon's is the family-run Irish bar and grill — authentic pub fare (burgers, sandwiches, plus steak and seafood) and a whiskey bar, in a room that aims family-friendly. Closed Mondays.
📍 15850 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, MO 63011

### Why this town matters
Ellisville's one-mile Manchester stretch is deeper than it looks — a 1968 pizza institution and a 1993 wing joint sharing the road with Mexico City small plates and Filipino mochi donuts. The apps can't tell which side of the city line they're on, and they flatten the family institutions into logos. We map the real corridor.

### FAQ
What's the best restaurant in Ellisville, MO?
For a special meal, Malinche Mexican Culinary Experience — Mexico City-style small plates that earned real critical attention. For a St. Louis classic, Faraci Pizza (since 1968).
Where's the independent food in Ellisville?
Along a one-mile stretch of Manchester Rd (roughly 15300–16100), plus Mulligan's on Clarkson. Faraci, Malinche, Golden Wok, Tatva, Mochi Donut Factory, and Fallon's are all on Manchester.
Are some "Ellisville" restaurants actually in other towns?
Yes — Manchester Rd straddles Ellisville, Ballwin, and Winchester, with Wildwood just west. A 63011 ZIP doesn't guarantee Ellisville (e.g., spots on Clayton Rd are Ballwin; some are Wildwood), so confirm the city.
Which Ellisville spots have deep roots?
Faraci Pizza (1968), Golden Wok (1991), and Mulligan's Grill (1993) are all decades-old family businesses — genuine generational neighborhood institutions.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Elsberry is a small far-north Lincoln County town of about 1,800 on Highway 79 — the Great River Road along the Mississippi — and for its size, the food scene is genuinely healthy: a real cluster of locally owned independents on North Main and Broadway. Every spot below appears on the City of Elsberry's own business-license list, the strongest “still open” signal there is. People here, and travelers on the river road, get hungry too — these are the real local favorites, no padding needed.
From a 6 a.m. biscuits-and-gravy diner to a deli-ice-cream-florist all under one roof, here's where to eat in Elsberry.
Most of the independents sit within a few walkable blocks on North Main Street and Broadway (63343), so a meal pairs naturally with a Great River Road / bald-eagle-watching trip. Several keep small-town hours — a couple are Thu–Sun only or daytime only — so call ahead. The only chain in town is a gas-station Hunt Brothers Pizza.

### The Pickle Barrel
The town's most-loved spot and the best hook anywhere — a wonderfully odd hybrid that's a deli counter, a hand-scooped ice-cream shop, AND a full florist/gift shop under one historic Broadway roof, with pinball and arcade machines. The chicken-bacon-ranch wrap, ice cream, and apple pie are the orders. Daytime only.
📍 401 Broadway St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### AJ's Tex-Mex & BBQ
The other point of local pride — a Tex-Mex-and-barbecue fusion named Elsberry Chamber Small Business of the Year two years running. Smoked BBQ plates alongside Tex-Mex, open late Thu–Sat (to ~1 a.m.) so it doubles as the evening hangout.
📍 451 N Main St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### Dos Primos
The family-run Mexican room — fajitas (chicken, steak, shrimp, Hawaiian), carne asada, and a white queso reviewers call “to die for.” Open daily 11–9, the most consistent full-week hours in town. (One reviewer flat-out called it the best taco they've ever had.)
📍 457 N Main St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### Rachel's Restaurant
The home-cooking diner — open at 6 a.m. for biscuits and gravy and breakfast-for-lunch plates, where reviewers say they're treated “like family.” The classic everybody-knows-everybody Main Street morning room (weekend hours shorten).
📍 447 N Main St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### Cadillac Bills
The burger joint — big smashed double cheeseburgers, chili cheese fries, a pork tenderloin sandwich, and fried catfish, with both dine-in and a drive-through (rare for a town this size). Closed Mondays.
📍 403 N Main St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### Shooters Saloon
The town's social hub on Broadway — boneless and “naked” wings, a French dip, and a Friday/weekend ribeye Steak Night, with a pool table, darts, and Wednesday poker. Kid-friendly until 9, then the late-night tavern.
📍 213 Broadway St, Elsberry, MO 63343

### Why this town matters
Elsberry punches way above its size — five strong sit-down independents plus a saloon, a local coffee shop (Southern Grace), and a BBQ trailer (Low N Slow), almost all on a couple of walkable blocks. For a far-north river town nobody writes about, that's a real food map, and it's the perfect lunch stop on a Highway 79 drive. We map it honestly.

### FAQ
What's the best place to eat in Elsberry, MO?
The Pickle Barrel is the most-loved (and most charming) — a deli, ice-cream shop, and florist in one historic Broadway storefront with arcade games. AJ's Tex-Mex & BBQ is the other local pride, twice named the Chamber's Small Business of the Year.
Does a town the size of Elsberry really have good food?
Yes — Elsberry isn't thin. Five strong independents (Rachel's, Cadillac Bills, AJ's, Dos Primos, the Pickle Barrel) plus Shooters Saloon, all locally owned and mostly on North Main and Broadway. The only chain is a gas-station Hunt Brothers Pizza.
What's a good food stop on the Highway 79 river road?
Elsberry — most of its restaurants cluster a few blocks apart on North Main and Broadway, an easy walk-the-block lunch stop on the Great River Road, near bald-eagle-watching and river recreation. Winfield and Troy are the nearest larger towns.

Most people know Eureka for Mid America Adventure, the old Six Flags, and its screaming coasters off I-44 — but the far-west St. Louis County town has a real historic downtown on Central Avenue , a stretch of Route 66 history, and the strange, quiet story of Times Beach (the dioxin town the EPA erased, now Route 66 State Park) just across the Meramec. After the roller coasters, this is where the locals actually eat.
From Colombian coffee to an Irish pub to a 1971 Italian original, here's where to eat in Eureka.
The independents cluster downtown on Central Avenue , with a couple of spots out toward Hilltop Village and I-44. A few keep limited days (the café and the breakfast dive close early-week), so check first. Make a day of it with Route 66 State Park , the Endangered Wolf Center , or — if the kids insist — Mid America Adventure.

### Sarah's on Central
Start downtown. Sarah's on Central is the café-and-cake shop doing breakfast, lunch, scratch desserts, specialty coffee, and cocktails — the brunch-and-dessert anchor of Central Avenue (the local outpost of the beloved Sarah's Cake Shop family). Closed Monday–Tuesday.
📍 127 S Central Ave, Eureka, MO 63025

### La Finca Coffee
La Finca brought authentic Colombian-style coffee to Eureka — fresh-roasted coffee, empanadas, breakfast burritos, the “La Finca Frappe,” and vinyl Latin music. A genuinely distinctive independent and a local favorite.
📍 104 S Central Ave, Eureka, MO 63025

### Chick-N-Elly's
Chick-N-Elly's is the beloved local breakfast spot and dive bar — all-day weekend breakfast, omelettes, and wings, with the kind of well-worn character a chain can't manufacture. A genuine Eureka institution.
📍 122A S Central Ave, Eureka, MO 63025

### O'Dell's Irish Pub & Ale House
O'Dell's is the downtown Irish pub doing homemade Irish-American comfort — corned beef, bangers and mash, a Frisco melt, a bourbon pork chop — with a warm, authentic room and a big local following.
📍 141 S Central Ave, Eureka, MO 63025

### Poor Richard's Restaurant & Sports Club
A family-owned bar and grill since 1982 , Poor Richard's is the wings-and-steaks game-day spot — decades of Eureka loyalty behind it. Just off the Central strip near Hwy 109.
📍 108 Hilltop Village Center Dr, Ste A, Eureka, MO 63025

### Joe Boccardi's Ristorante
Here's the heritage pick: Joe Boccardi's original location opened in Eureka in 1971 — hand-rolled St. Louis-style pizza, toasted ravioli, and pasta from the Boccardi family. It's since grown into a small regional family group, but this is the one that started it all.
📍 128 Boccardi Ln, Eureka, MO 63025

### Exit 11 Coffee Company
For the drive-thru fix, Exit 11 Coffee is the locally owned, award-winning roaster — small-batch beans and house-made organic syrups, “fast, fresh, organic, homemade.” Eureka is its flagship, a homegrown St. Louis-region coffee name.
📍 527 N Central Ave, Eureka, MO 63025

### Why this little town matters
Eureka is more than the exit for Mid America Adventure — it's a real Route 66 town with a downtown full of independents: Colombian coffee, an Irish pub, a 1982 family bar-and-grill, a breakfast dive, and the 1971 original Boccardi's. Here's a St. Louis secret hiding in plain sight: tiny Fairmont City is one of the most authentically Mexican places in the entire metro. For a village this small, the density is remarkable — a tight cluster of family-owned taquerias, mariscos joints, and grocery-and-kitchen combos line Collinsville Road, reflecting an established Latino community. This is real regional-Mexican food, not Tex-Mex: al pastor cut with pineapple, cabeza tacos, weekend posole, seafood tostadas. People here eat well — here are the spots.
From the best al pastor a Sauce critic had locally to birria pizza, here's where to eat in Fairmont City.
The taquerias cluster along Collinsville Road (62201). Heads up: Fairmont City shares the 62201 ZIP and that road with part of East St. Louis, so listing sites flip the same spot between the two cities — the places below are confirmed Fairmont City. Several are cash-friendly and a couple are tucked inside grocery stores or trailers; the "tienda plus taqueria" format is the local signature. For more, Collinsville is minutes east.

### Tienda El Ranchito
The standout. You walk through a Mexican market — deli case, handmade sweets, pan dulce — into a back dining room dressed in bright murals and green-tiled faux roofs. The al pastor (guajillo and pineapple) was called the best a Sauce Magazine critic had locally, and the braised-pork tamales with crema are "stunningly elegant." Weekend posole and siete mares seafood soup, too.
📍 2565 N 32nd St, Fairmont City, IL 62201

### Mi Tierra Bonita
Half grocery, half kitchen, open 9 to 9 daily — grab Mexican pantry staples and a plate of street tacos in one stop. Tacos de tripa, al pastor, carne asada, birria, mole de olla, tortas, ceviche, and posole. The full neighborhood taqueria experience.
📍 3203 Collinsville Rd, Fairmont City, IL 62201

### Mariscos Mi Tierra y Mas
The mariscos specialist — Mexican-style seafood tucked in the back of a grocery store, praised locally for some of the best seafood platters around. Seafood tostadas and a cult Birria Pizza, in big, well-seasoned portions.
📍 3121 Collinsville Rd, Fairmont City, IL 62201

### El Gallo Jiro
A Collinsville Road taqueria open daily (from 9 on weekends) — tacos and mariscos the focus, a dependable stop in the cluster.
📍 5606 Collinsville Rd, Fairmont City, IL 62201

### Taqueria Mi Rodeo
About as genuine as a taco stand gets — a humble trailer with tented seating on the Collinsville Road corridor, where the tacos de lengua and al pastor get called the best in the area, washed down with homemade horchata. Cash only.
📍 5703 Collinsville Rd, Fairmont City, IL 62201

### Why this town matters
Fairmont City is tiny, and it punches so far above its size it's almost unfair — a true cluster of family-owned, regional-Mexican kitchens that most of the metro drives past on the interstate. This is exactly the kind of overlooked, genuinely-great local food we live to map. Skip the Tex-Mex; this is the real taco run.

What's the best place to eat in Fairmont City, IL?
Tienda El Ranchito — a grocery-and-taqueria whose al pastor a Sauce Magazine critic called the best he'd had locally, with "stunningly elegant" tamales. For seafood, Mariscos Mi Tierra y Mas (try the birria pizza).
Why does a town this small have so much Mexican food?
Fairmont City has a large, established Hispanic/Latino community, so a dense cluster of family-owned taquerias, mariscos joints, and Mexican grocery-kitchens lines Collinsville Road — real regional-Mexican cooking, not Tex-Mex. It's one of the most authentically Mexican spots in the whole St. Louis metro.
What's the "tienda plus taqueria" format?
Several of the best spots (Tienda El Ranchito, Mi Tierra Bonita, Mariscos Mi Tierra) are grocery stores with a kitchen in back — you shop for pan dulce, chiles, and pantry goods, then sit down for tacos. Two birds, one stop.

### Frida's Cocina
Frida's Cocina is the standout — the Post-Dispatch ran a review calling it home to “St. Louis' best, wildest burrito.” NW Baja-style Mexican, family-owned: a birria taco plate with consommé for dipping, crispy chicken flautas, and chips and salsa diners rave about. Start here.

Royal Palm is the owner-run Mediterranean and Levantine spot reviewers call “an amazing alternative to the chain restaurants” — falafel, brick-oven pizza, charcoal-grilled meats, and manakeesh flatbread, with a café and lounge attached. Warm, personal, genuinely local.

### Taqueria Olvera
Taqueria Olvera presses its own corn tortillas fresh in-house every day from family recipes — the detail that separates a real taqueria from a Tex-Mex chain. Build-your-own tacos and burritos at the counter. Fast, cheap, and authentic Mexican.
📍 341 Market Pl Dr, Fairview Heights, IL 62208

### Lilly Gyros
Lilly Gyros is the long-standing, no-frills family-owned gyro counter locals treat as a neighborhood staple — Greek and Mediterranean lunch plates done right, with a kids' menu. The dependable everyday spot.

### Sushi Tatsu
Sushi Tatsu is the low-key, family-run sushi bar that quietly became the locals' answer to “where do you actually get good sushi out here” — specialty rolls plus Japanese and Korean dishes. (Closed Tuesdays — verify hours.)
📍 5725 N Illinois St, Fairview Heights, IL 62208

### Tong Phoon Thai Restaurant
Tong Phoon has been family-owned and serving the same neighborhood since 2007 — classic Thai curries and noodle dishes, an independent that has outlasted plenty of chains around it. The reliable Thai.
📍 5900 N Illinois St, Suite 7, Fairview Heights, IL 62208

### Pho Noodles & Sandwiches
Pho Noodles & Sandwiches is the small independent Vietnamese kitchen — the place to know when you want a steaming bowl of pho or a banh mi instead of another mall food-court tray. (Closed Sundays.)

### Frank's Restaurant
Frank's is the locally owned daytime diner doing hearty home-cooked plates — breakfast specials, beef tips, generous portions, the kind of independent breakfast counter the chains can't replicate. Open roughly 6 a.m. to 3 p.m.
📍 200 Lincoln Hwy, Fairview Heights, IL 62208

Fenton sits on the west bank of the Meramec River just south of I-44 — a small, parks-rich St. Louis County town founded back in 1818 and named for a settler's Welsh grandmother. For decades it was a Chrysler factory town (that plant is gone now, replaced by a logistics park), but the historic Gravois Road core still nods to Route 66, and the independent food scene is more interesting than its strip-mall surface suggests.

Maggie's Lunchbox has been the family-run scratch breakfast-and-lunch spot since 2008 — a Cuban sandwich, buffalo chicken salad, gooey butter cake, and from-scratch pastries. A genuine local institution tucked in Fenton's business park.
📍 867 Horan Dr, Fenton, MO 63026

### Tiger Soup Dumplings
The standout. Tiger Soup Dumplings brought Shanghai-style soup dumplings to Fenton — owners Yue Zhai and Victor Lai earned a Feast Magazine feature for the steamed XLB, spicy wonton noodles, and cucumber salad. A genuinely distinctive independent you won't find in the chains.
📍 98 Gravois Bluffs Cir Dr, Ste D, Fenton, MO 63026

### Viviano's Festa Italiano
Viviano's is the old-world Italian restaurant and Italian grocery — baked pasta, meatballs, Italian wedding soup, cannolis, plus a deli counter of breads, meats, and cheeses, with karaoke and live music. Eat in, then shop for dinner ingredients.
📍 62 Fenton Plaza, Fenton, MO 63026

### Sushi & K Fusion
On the historic Gravois Road corridor, Sushi & K Fusion does Japanese sushi and Korean BBQ — rolls, bento, bibimbap, and grilled Korean plates. A nice change of pace, right on the old Route 66 stretch.
📍 515 Gravois Rd, Fenton, MO 63026

### Azteca Mexican Restaurant
Azteca is the locally owned family Mexican spot (since 2009) — fresh salsa, fast service, and margaritas. The casual taco-night option for the west side of town.
📍 34 Western Plaza, Fenton, MO 63026

### Why this little town matters
Fenton looks like another I-44 suburb, but the independents tell a better story — a scratch bakery-café, a 2008 lunch institution, a soup-dumpling spot that made the food press, and an Italian restaurant with its own grocery counter. The national apps bury all of it under the chains; we'd rather send you to the real ones along the Meramec.

Russell's Cafe & Bakery (scratch café with a famous pastry case) and Maggie's Lunchbox (family-run since 2008, known for gooey butter cake).

Viviano's Festa Italiano — an old-world Italian restaurant with an attached Italian grocery and deli.

Ferguson is one of St. Louis's original railroad suburbs — it started in 1855 when William Ferguson traded ten acres to the Wabash Railroad for a depot and the naming rights, making it the first rail stop connected straight to the city. That depot-town downtown still runs along South Florissant Road , the heart of the Ferguson CityWalk, and on a Saturday morning it fills up around one of the most beloved farmers markets in the region.
It's a tight-knit, proud little downtown, and the independent food here is genuinely good. Here's where to eat in Ferguson.
The walkable core is South Florissant Road downtown — most spots below are within a few blocks. The famous Ferguson Farmers Market runs Saturday mornings (8–noon, May–October) at Plaza at 501, moving indoors monthly in winter — a destination in itself. A couple of spots keep limited days, so check before you go.

### Cathy's Kitchen Restaurant & Diner
Start at the flagship. Cathy's Kitchen is the downtown diner owner Cathy Jenkins built from the recipes she gathered on a cross-country road trip — American comfort food with Cajun-Southern leanings, from shrimp and grits to Cajun chicken pasta to catfish. It's become the symbol of this downtown's heart and resilience, and the food more than earns the visit.
📍 250 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson, MO 63135

### King of Soul Cafe
King of Soul Cafe does exactly what the name promises — genuine soul food, locally owned, a few blocks down South Florissant. The kind of from-the-heart cooking that anchors a neighborhood.
📍 423 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson, MO 63135

### The Garden Studio Cafe
The newest gem: The Garden Studio Cafe opened in early 2025 in the former Corner Coffee House — a coffee shop, café, and art gallery rolled into one, with local-partner coffee, lattes, and a from-scratch breakfast-and-lunch menu. A bright, creative addition to the downtown morning.
📍 100 N Florissant Rd, Ferguson, MO 63135

### Good News Brewing – Ferguson
In 2026, Good News Brewing took over the longtime Ferguson Brewing space on South Florissant — craft beer and wood-fired pizza, family-friendly, run by longtime Ferguson residents. A new chapter for the downtown's craft-beer corner. (It's a fresh opening, so confirm current hours.)
📍 418 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson, MO 63135

### The Ferguson Farmers Market
Not a restaurant, but the heart of eating in Ferguson: the Ferguson Farmers Market runs Saturday mornings May through October at Plaza at 501 — produce, prepared food, baked goods, and live music, with a monthly indoor Winter Market the rest of the year. It's consistently ranked among the best markets in the metro and is reason enough to plan a Saturday here.
📍 501 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson, MO 63135

### Why this little town matters
Ferguson is a historic railroad suburb with a downtown that has shown the whole country what resilience looks like — and the food is a big part of that. A diner whose owner the neighborhood literally rallied to protect, a soul-food café, a new coffee-and-art studio, a craft brewery, and a Saturday market locals treasure. The national apps can't capture any of that community; they just list logos.

What's the most famous place to eat in Ferguson, MO?
Cathy's Kitchen — owner Cathy Jenkins's downtown diner on South Florissant Road, known for comfort food with Cajun-Southern flair (shrimp and grits, Cajun chicken pasta) and as a symbol of the downtown's resilience.
When is the Ferguson Farmers Market?
Saturday mornings, 8 a.m.–noon, May through October at Plaza at 501 (501 S Florissant Rd), with a monthly indoor Winter Market the rest of the year. It's one of the most beloved markets in the metro.
Where do locals get coffee in Ferguson?
The Garden Studio Cafe on North Florissant Road — a coffee shop, café, and art gallery that opened in 2025 in the former Corner Coffee House space.
Is there a brewery in Ferguson?
Yes — Good News Brewing took over the former Ferguson Brewing Company space on South Florissant in 2026, serving craft beer and wood-fired pizza.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Festus has one of the best small-town downtowns in the St. Louis metro — and a name with a story. It grew up next to the glass-factory town of Crystal City, and locals jointly call them the “Twin Cities.” Festus was first nicknamed Tanglefoot (legend says for glass-plant workers whose feet tangled in the brush staggering home), then got the name Festus — supposedly when a preacher opened the Bible at random and landed on the name in the Book of Acts.
What matters today: there are no chains on Festus's Main Street. It's a genuinely walkable strip of independent restaurants, a brewery, a meadery, and bakeries. Here's where to eat in Festus.
Most of these sit on or just off Main Street , so park once and wander. (Heads-up: Truman Boulevard is the boundary with Crystal City — addresses there can land in either town, so this guide sticks to Festus-proper spots; for the Crystal City side, see that guide.) Time it for the Firecracker Festival in late June — carnival, drone show, and fireworks that draw tens of thousands.

### Pogolino's Pizza Place
Start with the anchor. Pogolino's has done family-owned thin-crust pizza and Italian since 1970 — fifty-plus years of crispy crust and specialty pies (the “Italian Stallion” among them) right on Main Street. The town's pizza institution.
📍 29 E Main St, Festus, MO 63028

### Petit Paree Restaurant & Lounge
The special-occasion room. Petit Paree has served French-inspired steak and seafood since 1960 — old-school lounge, white-tablecloth energy, a genuine Festus classic that's outlasted nearly everything.
📍 228 E Main St, Festus, MO 63028

### Main & Mill Brewing Company
Main & Mill is the downtown craft brewery and taproom that's become a true community hub — house beer, a friendly room, and a second “Central Tap” spot in town. The anchor of Festus's drinks scene.
📍 240 E Main St, Festus, MO 63028

### Taytro's Bar & Bistro
For something different, Taytro's brings “a taste of NOLA without leaving Missouri” — Cajun and Creole plates that have earned one of the strongest local followings in town. Just off Main, and worth the half-block.
📍 331 N Creek Dr, Festus, MO 63028

### The Brick Bistro & Brew
The Brick Bistro & Brew is the locally owned bistro-coffee-pizza combo (since 2018) — homemade soups, the “Popper” sandwich, thin-crust BBQ pizza, beer, and smoothies. The do-a-bit-of-everything daytime spot.
📍 218 E Main St, Festus, MO 63028

### Krabby Daddy's Seafood Eatery
Krabby Daddy's is the fast-casual Cajun seafood-boil spot — crab legs, shrimp, lobster, by the bag. It started right here in Festus (it's since grown, but this is the local original), and it scratches the seafood-boil itch the rest of Jefferson County can't.
📍 102 Pine St, Festus, MO 63028

### The Corner Cup Micro-Bakery
For the sweet stop, The Corner Cup is the cozy corner coffee-and-treats shop in a historic Main Street building — Kaldi's coffee, cupcakes, pies, hand pies, and scones, run by a local family. (Bread fan? The Braided Bakery a few doors down does challah, pretzels, and bagels a couple of days a week.)
📍 2 E Main St, Festus, MO 63028

### Why this little town matters
Festus is proof a small downtown can still be all its own — a Main Street with no chains, anchored by a 1970 pizza place, a 1960 French lounge, a craft brewery, a meadery, and a clutch of bakeries. That's a real local economy, the kind the national apps flatten into a list of interstate exits. We'd rather walk you down Main Street.
Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Festus and Jefferson County before you go — and since Festus and Crystal City are physically one town, our Crystal City guide is the natural companion, with De Soto and Herculaneum close by.

### FAQ
What's the oldest restaurant in Festus, MO?
Petit Paree (French-inspired steak and seafood, since 1960) and Pogolino's Pizza Place (family-owned since 1970) are the two longtime Main Street institutions.
Does Festus have a brewery?
Yes — Main & Mill Brewing Company on E Main Street, plus Four Brothers Mead (an award-winning meadery) downtown. The drinks scene is a real anchor of the no-chains Main Street.
Is Festus the same as Crystal City?
They're separate towns but physically continuous — locals call them the “Twin Cities.” This guide covers Festus-proper spots; Crystal City has its own where-to-eat guide.
When is the Festus Firecracker Festival?
Late June — a carnival, drone show, and fireworks that draw tens of thousands downtown.
