A.  Say what you like in plain terms and give a price range, and let them steer. Something like dry, not too heavy, similar to what you drank last time is enough to work with. Asking for a taste first is normal, and a flight is the fastest way to compare.
### Q. What appetizer pairs with wine?
A.  A cheese and charcuterie board is the safe default because it works across the list. Beyond that, match weight: lighter bites with something crisp and white, richer or cured things with a bigger red, salty snacks with sparkling. Most wine bars will suggest a pairing if you ask.

## Wineries in the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/wineries

### Call ahead about tastings, since many now take reservations only, and ask whether the tasting fee is waived with a bottle purchase.
### Common questions
### Q. What are the 5 S’s for wine tasting?
A.  See, swirl, sniff, sip and savor. Look at color and clarity, swirl to release aroma, smell before tasting, take a small sip and let it cover the palate, then note what lingers. Tasting rooms expect you to spit or pour off between pours.
### Q. What is the 30/30 rule for wine?
A.  A serving temperature shorthand: put a red in the refrigerator for about thirty minutes before pouring, and take a white out about thirty minutes before. Most reds are served too warm and most whites too cold, and temperature changes what you taste more than the glass does.
### Q. Can I drink red wine opened 2 weeks ago?
A.  It is unlikely to taste good. An opened bottle oxidizes within days, and after two weeks most reds turn flat, sharp or vinegary. It is not usually harmful, but pour a small amount and smell first. Recorking and refrigerating buys a few extra days, not weeks.

## Yoga in the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/yoga

### Shortlist two or three yoga studios, decide what pace, style and attention you want from a class, and compare that against what each teacher actually delivers when you show up.
### Common questions
### Q. What are common yoga mistakes to avoid?
A.  New students often rush their breathing, push too hard into a stretch, or skip the warmup. Watch a class before joining and notice whether the instructor corrects form gently, offers modifications, and paces the session so beginners are not left struggling to keep up.
### Q. What to say at the end of a yoga class?
A.  Many classes close with a quiet thank you to the instructor, sometimes paired with a small bow or a hands-together gesture. There is no required phrase, so a simple nod or spoken thanks works fine if a chant or greeting does not feel natural to you.
### Q. How do you say thank you to your yoga teacher?
A.  A brief spoken thank you after class is always appropriate, and lingering a moment to mention what helped you goes a long way. If a studio allows it, leaving a short positive review afterward is another simple way to show you valued the session.

## Roof Replacement Cost in St. Louis, and the Deductible Offer to Refuse
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-roof-replacement-cost-in-st-louis
Did the roofer on your porch just offer to take care of your deductible?
Look at him for a second. Clean boots, a clipboard, a pickup idling at the curb, and your gutters still dripping from last night. The morning after hail sounds the same in Affton, in Florissant, in Webster Groves: aluminum ladders clanking against siding, a nail gun popping three streets over, the gray sand of shingle granules piled at the bottom of the downspout. He is friendly. He is quick. And the sweetener he just offered you is something Missouri law says a roofer shall not promise.
Section 407.725 of the Missouri statutes says it plainly: a contractor shall not advertise or promise to pay or rebate all or any portion of any insurance deductible as an inducement to the sale of goods or services. So the friendliest line on the porch is the one to turn down. Screenshot that sentence. Send it to the neighbor with the new yard sign stuck in his wet grass.
Then breathe, because you came here for a number, and the number is less scary than the knock on the door made it feel.
### What is the average cost to replace a roof in St. Louis?
Replacing a roof in St. Louis costs an average of $8,155, according to Angi’s St. Louis cost data, and most new roofs land between $5,433 and $11,032. Asphalt shingles run about $3 to $11 per square foot, metal $5 to $22, and slate an average of $10 to $30, so the size of the roof, its pitch and the material move the price more than anything a salesman says.
The number moves most on the roof you actually have. Walk any South City block and look up at the brick two-stories, steep and close together, chimneys at every angle, and you can see why one crew bids high and another bids low. Angi’s guide puts labor at about half of the total, with materials making up the difference, so a cheap bid is almost always cheap on one of those two halves. Your job is to find out which.
And if you live in the city, here is a check worth making. A contractor working here needs a Construction Industry Contractor Graduated Business License from the License Collector, Room 104 of City Hall at 1200 Market Street. To get it, the contractor has to bring proof of workers’ compensation coverage or sign a statement saying he has it or is not required to. And every general contractor has to give the License Collector a list of the subcontractors on any job. So ask the man on your porch for his City license before he gets the ladder off the truck, and if the crew that shows up is not his, ask whose it is. The License Collector’s office answers at (314) 622-4528, Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM.
### The five-day clock your insurer’s letter starts
Here is the part nobody on the porch brings up. If you sign with a roofer and the work is meant to be paid through your homeowners policy, Missouri gives you a way back out. Under the same section 407.725, you may cancel that contract before midnight on the fifth business day after your insurer tells you in writing that all or any part of the claim is not a covered loss.
The letter is usually thin. You open it standing at the mailbox, and the words you were dreading are right there: part of the claim is not covered. That is the moment the clock starts, and it is your clock, not his. You cancel by giving written notice to the contractor at the address stated in the contract. Within ten days after that, the law says the contractor has to hand back any payments, partial payments or deposits you made. If the money does not come back, the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222.
He is also supposed to have told you all this already. The statute makes the contractor attach a notice of cancellation form to the contract, easy to tear off, in boldface type of at least ten points. If the paper he slid across your kitchen table has no such page, you have learned something useful about him before a single shingle comes off.
Two more lines from the same law are worth knowing before anyone sets a ladder against your gutter. A contractor shall not represent or negotiate your insurance claim on your behalf. And any violation of the section counts as an unfair practice under the Missouri merchandising practices act. None of that makes the roofer a crook. Most are not. It just means the person holding the clipboard should be selling you a roof, not a claim.
### Why one bid is thousands higher on the same roof
Start with size, because it fools almost everyone. Angi’s St. Louis guide makes the point that roof size does not always match your home’s square footage: the pitch, the roof over a porch or garage, and the overhang all add to it. Stand in the yard and look up at a steep two-story in Webster Groves and you can feel it in your neck. That is more roof than the floor plan admits.
Then complexity. A roof with chimneys or skylights poking through it, gables or dormers, or sections with different pitches costs more to replace, by the same guide’s account. Every one of those is a seam, and every seam is a place for March rain to find its way into a bedroom ceiling. A crew that bids the simple version of your roof has not seen it yet.
And then the part you cannot see from the driveway: what is new and what is staying. Listen to a tear-off and you will hear it, the shriek of old step flashing being pried off brick, the thud of rotten decking hitting the dumpster. A low bid often keeps the old flashing and the old pipe boots and promises no decking at all. Ask each roofer, in writing, which pieces are new. The bids start to make sense the minute you do.
### What is the 25% rule, and when does the City want a permit?
You will hear roofers say you cannot just patch it. Here is the local version of why. According to Angi’s St. Louis guide, the City of St. Louis requires a permit if you are replacing your roof with a different material, or if you need to replace more than 25% of the roof sheathing. Permit and application fees start at $44 and rise with the total project cost. The city’s Permit Section is at 1200 Market, Room 425, at (314) 622-3313. Watch the roofer pull up the first sheet of old shingles and find the boards underneath gone soft and dark. That is the moment a repair becomes a replacement.
That rule is the City’s. Ask the roofer, before you sign, who is pulling the permit and from which office. A good one answers without looking up from the tape measure.
### What a bid you can actually compare will list
Lay three bids on the kitchen table and they should all name the same things. If one is missing a line, it is not cheaper. It is less finished.
Your roof, by the foot
### How much does it cost to put a shingle roof on a 2000 sq ft house?
Angi’s St. Louis data puts about 2,000 square feet of roof at $4,600 to $14,400, with asphalt shingles at $3 to $11 per square foot. Ask for the roof area, not the house size: pitch, porches and overhangs can add more roof than the floor plan shows.
Roof area, and the pitch
How many old layers come off, and who hauls them away
Decking: the price per sheet and how many sheets are included before a change order
Underlayment, and where ice-and-water shield goes
Drip edge, flashing and pipe boots, each marked new or reused
Ventilation, intake and exhaust
Shingle maker, product line and color
The manufacturer’s warranty and the roofer’s own workmanship warranty, with the years written down
The permit, and who pulls it
Cleanup, including a magnet sweep for nails in the grass
One more line belongs on every bid, and it is the one people forget to read: the start date and how long the crew expects to be on the roof. A tear-off is loud. The house shakes a little with every sheet that drops, the dog will not stop pacing, and by noon there is a fine black grit on the porch rail. Knowing when it starts and when the dumpster leaves is worth having in writing, too.
The decking line is where surprise money hides. Nobody can see the boards until the old roof is off, so a careful roofer writes in an allowance and a per-sheet rate. When the crew finds a soft spot that gives under a boot, you already know what it costs.

### How much should a roof replacement cost in St. Louis?
Angi’s St. Louis data puts the average roof replacement at $8,155. By roof size, about 1,500 square feet of roof runs $3,500 to $10,800 and about 2,000 square feet runs $4,600 to $14,400. If a bid sits far outside the band for your roof, ask which line items explain the difference.
### After the storm: keep the claim and the contract apart
Hail brings knocks on the door, and some of them come from trucks with out-of-state plates. Your insurer decides what it owes after its own adjuster has been on the roof. A roofer is there to price and build the roof. When one person starts doing both jobs, slow down.
Read the contract at the kitchen table, not on the porch with the engine running. Look for the cancellation notice. Look for a stated price, not a promise to do whatever the insurance company approves. If the roof truly needs replacing, it will still need replacing on Thursday, after you have read every page.
Waiting on an adjuster all afternoon? Here’s where to eat in Berkeley.
### How to choose between three bids
Get three written bids from established local roofers and ask each one the same short list: what is new and what is reused, how much decking is included and at what rate, which underlayment goes where, what the workmanship warranty covers and for how long, and who pulls the permit. Then compare the answers, not the bottom lines.
The low bid is usually missing something. The high bid is often selling an upgrade you may or may not want. Once you can see what each price buys, the right roofer tends to be obvious, and nobody has to rush you to the signature line with the storm still dripping off the eaves.
Three bids on the same roof, and not one of them matches? Browse roofing companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory and put another local name on the ladder before anyone asks for a signature today.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 25% rule for roofing?
A.  Around here it is the line where a patch stops being a patch. According to Angi’s St. Louis guide, the City of St. Louis requires a permit if you replace more than 25% of the roof sheathing, or if you switch to a different roofing material. If you live outside the city limits, ask your roofer which office the permit comes from.
### Q. How much does it cost to put a shingle roof on a 2,000 sq ft house?
A.  Angi’s St. Louis data puts about 2,000 square feet of roof at $4,600 to $14,400. Watch the starting number: a 2,000 square foot house can carry more roof than that once pitch, porches, garages and overhangs are counted, so ask for the roof area itself.
### Q. Is $30,000 too much for a roof?
A.  For most St. Louis houses, yes. Angi’s St. Louis size table tops out at $6,900 to $21,600 for about 3,000 square feet of roof, so a bid like that sits above even the top of the table. Slate, at an average of $10 to $30 per square foot in the same guide, is the kind of job that can get there. Ask what the extra money buys.
### Q. How to tell if a roofer is lying?
A.  Listen for three things Missouri law covers. A promise to pay or rebate your deductible is something section 407.725 says a contractor shall not make. An offer to negotiate your insurance claim for you is another. And on an insurance-paid job, the contract should come with a detachable notice of cancellation form. If any of those is off, keep your pen in your pocket.
### Q. Does a 20 year old roof need to be replaced?
A.  Not on age alone. Granules piling up in the gutters, shingle edges curling, and daylight showing in the attic are what tell you, not the birthday. Have it looked at by a roofer who will put the findings in writing.
### Q. What is the cheapest time of year to get a new roof?
A.  I could not find a St. Louis source that names the cheapest month, so I will not invent one. My advice: if the roof is not leaking, take the time to get three written bids, and do not sign anything on the porch the morning after hail.

## Don’t Pay Yet: That Tree Might Be the City’s. St. Louis Tree Removal Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-tree-removal-cost-in-st-louis
The silver maple that just split over your Tower Grove South bungalow might belong to the city, and nobody tells you that until after you’ve paid. You heard it before you saw it. A dry crack like a rifle shot, a long tearing sigh, then a thud that rattled the storm door in its frame. By morning its biggest limb is lying across the yard and into the alley, leaves still green, the torn wood pale and wet and smelling sharp, like a fresh-cut board at the lumberyard. It missed the garage. Barely.
So now you’re standing in damp grass with your coffee going cold, looking up at the rest of that tree the way you’d look at a dog that just bit somebody. The question sitting in your chest isn’t about species or crown structure. It’s simpler and it’s heavier. What is this going to cost me?
Before you call anyone, do the one thing almost nobody does first, because it can take the bill to zero. Walk out to the curb and look at where the trunk actually comes out of the ground. In the City of St. Louis, city-owned trees are located between the curb and sidewalk, or typically within 10 feet of the curb, and the Forestry Division manages them. If the tree that scared you stands in that strip, it isn’t yours to pay for. You report it to the city at 314-622-4800 or online, and you get an email with a request ID so you can follow it.
That strip matters in the other direction too. A private crew can’t just walk up and cut a city tree for you. Under the city’s Forestry Ordinance, Ordinance 68607, pruning, spraying or removing any City tree takes a Permit to Maintain, and the city only issues it to a commercial tree service with at least one ISA Certified Arborist on staff. Hold on to that last detail. It comes back later.
If the trunk is clearly on your side of the sidewalk, it’s yours. Here’s what yours costs.
### What is a fair price for cutting down a tree?
A fair price is one that matches the job, and the job is almost never just “the tree.” One cost guide puts the typical range to remove a tree in St. Louis at $614 to $832. The stump is usually its own line: the same guide lists stump removal at $60 to $350 and grinding at $75 to $1,000, depending on the diameter and how deep the wheel goes.
Treat those numbers as a floor to reason from, not a promise. The three quotes you get on the same tree can land far apart, and most of the time nobody is cheating you. They’re pricing different jobs. One includes the stump and the other doesn’t. One hauls every chip away and the other leaves a mountain of mulch by the alley. One crew saw a limb leaning toward your neighbor’s roof and priced the risk.
In this city the price is mostly about the alley. A redbud by the front walk is a couple of hours, one saw and a chipper whining at the curb. A big old pin oak behind a two-family flat, crown spread over a detached brick garage and the service drop sagging through its branches, is a climber in a harness and a groundman leaning on a rope all day, lowering it piece by piece. Every piece is labor.
Then the lot itself. Old city lots run deep and narrow between brick walls, and if the truck can’t back down the alley, every branch goes through the side gate by hand, scraping the siding on the way. You’ll hear that in the quote. Condition is the counterintuitive one: a dead tree often costs more than a live one, because dead wood snaps without warning and nobody wants to tie a rope to it.
### The ash in your yard is on a clock
If the tree is an ash, the price conversation has a deadline built in. The city’s own emerald ash borer guidance says plainly that no permit is required for removing or treating ash trees on private property. Easy enough. But it also says that if a privately owned ash dies or becomes hazardous, it’s subject to a nuisance violation under Ordinance 68607, and the owner gets a notice to remove it.
Think about what that means for your wallet. A living ash is a choice: treat it, or take it down on your own schedule, in the slow season, at a calm price. A dead ash is a brittle, peeling hazard that gets pricier to climb every month, and eventually the city may be the one setting your timeline. The cheap version of this decision is the early one. You can feel the difference standing under it - firm bark versus bark that flakes off in your hand.
Before the saw starts
### What is the typical cost of removing a tree in St. Louis, MO?
One cost guide puts a typical St. Louis tree removal at $614 to $832. The stump is its own line: $60 to $350 to pull it or $75 to $1,000 to grind it. A tree leaning over the roof or the wires costs more, because it comes down in roped sections.
### The insurance question that protects your house, not theirs
Remember the arborist detail? Here it pays off. The city won’t let anyone touch a street tree without a certified arborist on staff. That’s a useful bar for the tree in your back yard too, especially when the real question is whether it needs to come down at all. A company that only removes trees tends to find that trees need removing.
Then ask about workers’ compensation, and don’t take a shrug for an answer. Missouri’s rule surprises people: you must carry workers’ comp with five or more employees, or with one or more if you’re in the construction industry. So a small crew can sometimes be completely legal and still carry none. That’s not a reason to panic. It’s a reason to ask the question out loud, in your driveway, before a man with a running saw climbs up over your roof.
Ask for the certificates to come straight from the insurance agent, not as a crumpled photocopy from the truck’s dashboard. A legitimate crew will send them without blinking.
### What a quote you can hold someone to actually says
The quotes that turn into arguments are the ones with two words and a number. A quote worth signing names:
Which tree, described so there’s no doubt - species, rough height and where it stands
Whether the stump is included, and ground to what depth
What happens to the wood and brush - hauled, chipped and left, or cut and stacked
Whether the crew repairs ruts or lawn damage from the equipment
Liability and workers’ comp certificates, with dates that cover your job
Who calls in the underground utility locates before any stump grinding
That last line gets skipped all the time. Stump grinding puts a spinning toothed wheel into ground that can hide gas, water, electric and fiber lines. If a company waves the question off, picture that wheel a foot from your gas service and find another company.
Waiting on a crew all morning works up an appetite. St. Ann’s restaurant lineup is a good place to spend the wait.
### Sometimes the cheapest tree job is no removal at all
Not every scary tree has to go. A limb that tore out in a storm may have come from one weak fork that can be pruned out, with a cable added to steady what’s left. Roots heaving a walkway are often a paving problem more than a tree problem. Some deadwood in a healthy, leafy crown is normal for big old hardwoods, and it gets trimmed, not felled.
The signs that do argue for removal are structural: a cavity or real decay through the main trunk, a lean that changed recently with the soil cracking and lifting on the far side, roots cut by nearby digging, much of the crown dead, or an ash that’s already past saving. Pruning doesn’t fix those. If you knock on the trunk and it sounds hollow, like rapping on an empty barrel, take that seriously and have someone qualified look before the next windy night.
If you’re trimming instead, mind the calendar with oaks. The Missouri Department of Conservation’s rule is short: don’t prune oaks mid-March through June, when fresh wounds draw the insects that carry oak wilt.
People are asking
### Who pays when tree roots clog your sewer line in St. Louis?
Inside city limits, you do - the City says the entire sewer lateral from your house to the MSD main is private property. Its Sewer Lateral Repair Program, paid for by a $28 fee on the tax bills of residential properties with 6 or fewer units, fixes breaks under the public right of way, but it “does not cover clearance of clogs/tree roots along ANY portion of the lateral line.” Many city sewer lines are clay pipe over 100 years old, so when the floor drain gurgles and the basement smells like the street, ask the plumber to show you the camera video, not just describe it. If that video shows a break under the street, the Street Department wants the plumber’s statement and the video.
### When to call, and how to get a fair number without a fight
The worst week to buy tree work is the week after a big storm. Every crew is booked, phones go to voicemail, and door hangers from outfits you’ve never heard of show up on your knob. If your tree isn’t an active hazard, let that wave pass. Late winter, with the leaves down and the schedules thin, is a calmer time to get quotes, and a climber can see every fork in bare branches.
Get three written quotes with the same scope - removal, stump, debris, cleanup - and compare them line by line instead of total to total. The honest levers are real ones: flexible timing, letting the crew leave the wood, bundling several trees into one visit. What backfires is pushing a company below the cost of its own insurance.
If money is the wall, call your city forester or public works office and ask whether there’s any help for hazardous trees or for older residents. Help like that varies by city and by year, so ask the question directly instead of assuming the answer is no.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to cut down a 40 ft tree?
A.  It depends less on the 40 feet than on what’s under it. One cost guide puts the typical range to remove a tree in St. Louis at $614 to $832. A 40-footer standing clear in an open yard sits toward the easy end; the same tree over a roof or wires has to come down in roped sections and costs more.
### Q. How big of a tree to charge $1000 for removal?
A.  There’s no fixed height that hits that number. A tree bigger than average, past the typical St. Louis range of $614 to $832, or an ordinary tree that needs roping over a house, can cross it, and so can adding stump grinding, which runs $75 to $1,000 on its own.
### Q. Is it cheaper to have a tree cut down or trimmed?
A.  Trimming is almost always cheaper that day, and it’s the right call when the tree is sound and the problem is clearance or deadwood. It’s the wrong call when the trunk is decayed or the tree is dying, because you pay for the trim now and the removal later.
### Q. What months should you not trim trees?
A.  For oaks in Missouri, the Department of Conservation says don’t prune mid-March through June, when fresh cuts attract the beetles that spread oak wilt. Storm damage and real hazards are the exception and get handled when they happen.
### Q. What is the cheapest time of year for tree removal?
A.  Late winter tends to be the calmest time to book, with the leaves down and crews less swamped. The priciest stretch is the week after a big storm, when every crew in town is booked solid.
### Q. Can seniors get free tree cutting service?
A.  Possibly, if the tree belongs to the city. In St. Louis, trees between the curb and sidewalk are managed by the Forestry Division, so report those to the city at 314-622-4800. For a tree on your own lot, ask your city forester or public works office whether any help exists before you pay.
### Q. How to negotiate tree removal?
A.  Get three written quotes that list removal, haul-away and stump work as separate lines, then compare line by line. Bundle several trees into one visit, let the crew leave the wood, and book outside storm season. Don’t push a crew below what its insurance costs.

## The $28 Already on Your Tax Bill: What a St. Louis Plumber Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-plumber-cost-in-st-louis
Gurgle. Then the smell. The floor drain in the basement of a brick two-family off Gravois is coughing up grey water every time somebody upstairs flushes, it’s Sunday night, and your socks are already wet because you went down the stairs before you found the light string.
You call the first number that comes up. A real person answers, and the relief in your chest is almost embarrassing. There’s a service call fee, the voice says, and a tech can be there tonight. You say yes. Nobody mentions a price for the actual work, and you don’t ask, because the water is still creeping out from the drain cover and asking feels like haggling with a lifeguard.
That silence on the phone is where most plumbing bills go wrong. Not the rate. The silence. And if you own a house inside the City of St. Louis, there’s a second thing nobody on that call will mention: you have been paying toward part of a sewer repair on your property tax bill for years. Most people find out after they’ve paid a plumber for the whole thing.
So before you say yes on that call, with the phone warm against your ear and the drain still burping, say three sentences. “What does the service fee cover?” “Will you give me the price before you start?” And if it smells like the sewer line: “Are you licensed with the City, and will you send me the camera video?” That last one isn’t fussiness. A plumber’s statement plus that video is what the City asks you to send before its sewer fund will pay for a break under the street.
### How do you calculate labor cost for plumbing?
Plumbing labor gets billed one of two ways. Hourly means the time on the job, multiplied by the shop’s rate, plus parts. Flat rate means the repair carries one set price whether it takes the tech twenty minutes or the whole afternoon. Nearly every bill also starts with a service call fee, and the only thing that matters about that fee is whether it buys you work or just a visit to your driveway. You aren’t buying hours. You’re buying a drain that stops gurgling, so for routine work like a toilet rebuild or a water heater change-out, a flat price set before the wrench comes out keeps a slow tech or a stubborn fitting from becoming your problem.
One St. Louis number you can check for yourself before the van pulls up: the City’s application fee for a plumbing permit is $30, and the other plumbing permit fees are set by City ordinance and posted by type. Ask for the permit as its own line on the quote, so you can hold the number up against that page at your kitchen table.
And the hourly rate is not the plumber’s wage. The billed hour carries the truck, insurance, workers’ comp, the license, the drive between jobs and the person who picked up your call on a Sunday. When a rate sounds too good, something on that list usually isn’t being paid for. In an old brick basement on the south side, the bigger number on your invoice usually isn’t labor anyway. It’s the sewer lateral. Which brings us to the money you’ve already paid.
### The $28 you already paid
Here’s the part that stings. The whole sewer lateral, the pipe running from your house out to the MSD main under the street, is your private property, and so is every root and crack in it. But the City runs a Sewer Lateral Repair Program, and every owner of a residential property with 6 or fewer units pays a $28 fee on their real estate taxes to fund it. That money repairs broken laterals under the public right of way, the stretch under the sidewalk and street, which is often the most expensive stretch to dig.
The catch is order of operations. The program won’t pay to clear clogs or tree roots, anywhere on the line, and it won’t touch a break under your yard. It wants a plumber licensed in the City of St. Louis to inspect the line, and if the break sits under the right of way, you send the plumber’s statement and the video to the Street Department at 1900 Hampton. Your property taxes have to be fully paid to qualify. Call the Department of Streets at (314) 647-3111, Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30, before anyone starts digging up the sidewalk on your dime.
So when the camera goes down the line and the tech turns the screen toward you, the question that can save you the most money on this whole page is a short one: “Where exactly is the break - under my yard, or under the sidewalk?” Ask it while the picture is still on the screen.
### Who’s allowed down your basement stairs
Inside the City, plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors certified by the City of Saint Louis. The City’s permit page lists the kind of work that needs a permit and an inspection: new plumbing fixtures, soil pipe connections, and the replacement of sewer laterals, soil stacks, vent pipes and water supply lines. In an old brick house on the south side, that list covers most of the jobs that turn into real money.
Now the number that ends an old excuse. The application fee for all plumbing permits is $30, and most applications are approved within 1 to 3 business days. So when someone offers to “save you the hassle” of a permit, you know exactly how much hassle they mean. Work done without a required permit doesn’t vanish. It waits behind the drywall until you sell, and then it’s your problem at the closing table.
Before you sign anything bigger than a drain clearing, call the City’s Permit Section at (314) 622-3313, 1200 Market, Room 425, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM. Ask two things: is this contractor licensed with the City, and does this job need a permit. A few minutes of hold music in your ear is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy on a plumbing job. If you live out in the county, the question stays the same: ask the contractor who issued their license and who pulls the permit, then check.
### What an old St. Louis house adds to the bill
The plumber didn’t make your house old. But age is the line item nobody quotes on the phone, and it shows up the moment a wrench touches metal.
Galvanized supply pipe is the classic. It rusts from the inside, so the first symptom is an upstairs shower that dribbles while the kitchen tap runs fine. The cost problem is that galvanized often won’t survive being disturbed. You call about a faucet, the tech gives the old fitting a quarter-turn, and the pipe behind it crumbles like wet cardboard. Now the faucet job is a repipe of that run. A good plumber warns you before touching it, not after.
Cast iron drain stacks rust the same way, inside out, and they tend to fail as a damp patch low on a basement wall instead of an obvious drip. Clay sewer laterals are the third. Roots find the joints, the line snakes clear, life is fine for months, and then that gurgle comes back on another Sunday night. Snaking treats the symptom. A camera run down the line tells you whether you’re looking at routine maintenance or a lateral that needs replacing, and where the break sits decides whether that $28 fund can help.
### Three questions that make any quote honest
You don’t need to know what a fair price is. You need a process that makes an unfair one obvious. Ask these out loud, every time.
“What does the service fee cover?” Trip only, trip plus diagnosis, or trip plus the first stretch of work. The answer tells you what the first line of the invoice will say before anyone gets wet.
“Will you give me the price before you start?” On anything past the diagnosis, you should hear a number and say yes to it. A plumber who works first and prices afterward has quietly taken away your right to say no.
“Can I see it?” If someone says the whole sewer line has to go, ask to watch the camera footage. A legitimate company turns the screen around without a pause. Being told to replace a lateral with no camera run is the loudest alarm in residential plumbing.
Water shut off and nothing to cook on until the plumber leaves? St. John’s whole food scene is a short drive and one click away.
Also listen for manufactured urgency. Real emergencies exist: water you can’t shut off, sewage coming into the living space, no water in the house at all, a water heater leaking from the tank body. A discount that “expires tonight” on anything else is a sales move, not a diagnosis.
People are asking
### Q. Does an emergency plumber charge more on a holiday or weekend in St. Louis?
A.  Not always, and you want that answer while the water is still ankle-deep, before anyone backs a van into the driveway. Roto-Rooter’s St. Louis branch says on its own site there is “no extra charge for nights, weekends, or holidays,” and that it gives upfront pricing before any work begins. Ask every shop you call the same two things - is there an after-hours fee, and what’s the price before the work starts - and get the answer in a text you can hold up when the invoice comes.
### Tonight, or Monday morning?
After-hours dispatch costs more almost everywhere, so the cheapest plumbing decision you’ll make is knowing what can wait. A single slow drain, a running toilet, a dripping faucet, low pressure at one fixture, a drip you can catch in a bucket with the supply valve closed - all of that can usually wait for a daytime appointment and a second quote.
What turns most emergencies into Monday appointments is a valve. Find your main water shutoff on a calm, dry afternoon, with a flashlight and no panic. In a lot of older St. Louis houses it sits in the basement on the wall where the water line comes in from the street. Give it a turn so you know it moves. If you ever smell gas, skip all of this: get out of the house first and call the gas utility from outside.

A short warranty on workmanship tells you how confident the shop is in its own work. And ask what happens if the job changes once a wall is open. The right answer is “we stop and call you.” The wrong answer is silence, followed by an invoice.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a normal call out fee for a plumber?
A.  It varies by shop and by hour, and it climbs at night and on weekends. The useful question isn’t the amount but what it buys: trip only, trip plus diagnosis, or trip plus the first stretch of work. A company that won’t tell you the fee on the phone is one to skip.
### Q. How to tell if your plumber is overcharging you?
A.  Judge the process. You should hear a price before work begins, get an invoice that separates parts from labor, and see evidence for any big diagnosis. Nobody should recommend replacing a sewer line without running a camera and showing you the footage. Pressure to sign tonight is a sales tactic.
### Q. What is the normal cost to replace a hot water heater?
A.  It depends on the unit, the fuel, the venting and whatever code upgrades your house needs, so get a written flat-rate quote that lists all of it. Going tankless usually costs more because gas lines and venting often have to change too. Ask whether the job needs a permit and who pulls it.
### Q. What is the labor cost to install a 50 gallon hot water heater?
A.  Labor is the part that swings. A straight swap in an open basement is a simple job for a plumber. A unit wedged in a tight corner, venting that has to be reworked, or old galvanized connections that crumble when they’re removed all add time, which is why a flat-rate quote is the safer way to buy it.
### Q. What is the hourly rate for a plumber in Illinois?
A.  The Illinois side of the St. Louis area draws on the same pool of plumbers, so the same rules apply: compare finished-job quotes, not hourly rates, and ask what the service fee covers. Licensing works differently across the river, so ask where the contractor is licensed.
### Q. Why do plumbers charge so much to replace a water heater?
A.  The tank is only part of it. The rest is licensed labor, venting, code upgrades, permits where they’re required, and hauling the old tank up the basement stairs and away. A quote that lists each piece is easier to trust than one lump sum.
### Q. How much does Home Depot charge to replace a hot water heater?
A.  Big-box stores usually send local installers, so the price tracks your market and the crew rather than a national sticker. Whatever the quote, ask what it leaves out. Permits, venting changes and haul-away are the usual carve-outs.

## You Can’t File This Permit: What a St. Louis Electrician Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-an-electrician-cost-in-st-louis
Twenty-five dollars, and you’re not allowed to pay it. That is the city’s fee for the electrical permit on a new service, and in St. Louis city only a licensed contractor can file it for you.
It starts with a sound. A south city breaker goes with a flat little snap, like a knuckle cracking, and the window unit in the back bedroom stops mid-hum. July in St. Louis. A brick two-family, plaster walls warm to the touch, and a gray panel in the basement that smells faintly of dust and old rubber. You flip it back on. It holds for twenty minutes. Then snap again.
So you call someone. The electrician stands in front of that panel with a flashlight for a few minutes, says “yeah, this is full,” and the number they give you on the stairs back up is bigger than the number you had in your head. Your chest tightens. Is that fair? Is it padding? You have no idea, and they can tell you have no idea.
Here is the thing nobody says on that staircase: the price of an electrician in St. Louis is mostly not the price of the person holding the flashlight. It is the price of the paper behind them - the city license, the permit, the inspection - and in the City of St. Louis, some of that paper you are not even allowed to carry yourself.
### What do most electricians charge per hour?
Look past the person on your basement stairs to the van idling in the alley, ladder rattling on the rack, a bin of breakers in the back. All of that is in the number. Start with what the electrician actually takes home, because that is the floor under every quote. Federal wage data for electricians puts the hourly median for the St. Louis, MO-IL metro at $37.10 an hour in wages. The bottom tenth earn about $22.54, and the top tenth earn about $50.39. That is pay, not price. It is what lands in the paycheck before the shop has bought a single breaker, insured the truck, paid for the permit or set aside money for the callback when something needs a second look in March.
So when a billed rate comes in well above that median, that is not proof anyone is padding. The shop is carrying the van that idles in your alley, the liability policy, the license renewals, the apprentice, and the drive across the river and back. When a billed rate comes in close to the wage itself, ask the harder question: who is covering all of that, and is it anyone? I could not find a primary source that publishes billed residential rates for St. Louis shops, and I am not going to invent one. What I can tell you is the wage under it, and that the rest is overhead you can ask about out loud.
### The $25 form you can’t file for yourself
This is the St. Louis detail that changes how you read every panel quote. In the city, the Building Division issues electrical permits to licensed electrical contractors certified by the City of St. Louis, and to owners of single-family homes who meet certain requirements. That homeowner door is narrow. If you live in the house and it is an owner-occupied single-family dwelling, you can apply for some repair or modification work. Then the city says it plainly: “You may not apply for permits for service changes, rehab, or new construction. Those need to be performed by a licensed contractor.”
Read that again with your panel in mind. A service change is exactly the job that snapping breaker is pointing at. In the city, that permit belongs to a licensed contractor. The application fee for every electrical permit is $25, and walk-in permits are handled in Room 425 at City Hall, 1200 Market, between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. You can call the permit section at (314) 622-3313 and ask whether a permit has been pulled at your address.
That phone call is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy. The real money goes into the work the permit forces: the inspection, the grounding brought up to code, the breakers that will actually pass. An electrician who offers to “skip the permit and save you some” is not handing you savings. They are handing you their risk, wrapped in a smaller number, and it comes due when you sell the house or file a claim after a fire.
Here is the line worth texting your sister before her own panel job: in St. Louis city, the cheapest electrician is the one whose name is already on the permit.
The license matters for the same reason. The city’s Committee of Electrical Examiners decides, by written and oral exam, who has the knowledge to get a certificate or license to do electrical work in the City of St. Louis. So the useful question is never “are you licensed?” in the abstract. It is “are you licensed in the city, and will your name be on the permit?” If your house sits outside the city line, ask the same question of whoever issues permits where you live, because the rules change at the border.
People are asking
### How much does a 200 amp electrical panel upgrade cost in St. Louis?
The number that tightens your chest on the basement stairs has a public cousin: First Choice Electric puts a typical 100-amp to 200-amp upgrade in the St. Louis area at $2,500-$4,500, with the panel, breakers, permits, utility coordination and inspection included. Then look at the meter box outside: the shop says a 100-amp meter base can’t support 200-amp service, and replacing it adds $1,200-$2,500, so ask every bidder whether it is in their price. The city’s cut is small, a $25 application fee plus a $100 inspection fee for the first unit when a residential job includes new electrical service. Treat it as one shop’s ballpark, not your quote.
### Why two quotes on one panel sound like two different houses
You get two quotes. One is a sticky note. The other is a page and a half. The gap between them makes your stomach drop, and you assume the long one is the rip-off. Often it is the other way around.
A panel job sounds like one thing and is really several. Is the service entrance being replaced too, with a new meter base and cable, and the utility scheduled to cut and restore power? Is the grounding still the original from decades ago, or has the old water-pipe bond been interrupted by a plastic repair somewhere in the basement? Are existing circuits simply being moved to the new panel, or is crumbling cable at the panel end being replaced? Does the quote include arc-fault and ground-fault breakers where the code calls for them, or a box full of standard breakers that may not pass inspection? And where does the panel live - an open basement, or a finished closet where every inch costs time?
The sticky note usually answers none of those. The page and a half answers all of them. The cheaper quote is often a different, smaller job wearing the same name. Ask the sticky-note shop to write down what it left out, and watch how fast the gap closes.
What the hour pays for
### How much do electricians charge per hour in St. Louis?
Federal wage data puts the median St. Louis electrician at $37.10 an hour in pay, and a shop’s billed rate sits above that because it also covers insurance, the truck and the license. For scale, First Choice Electric puts a 100- to 200-amp panel upgrade around St. Louis at $2,500-$4,500, permits and inspection included.
### What the wiring behind your plaster adds
Older St. Louis houses are beautiful and they keep secrets. Pull a cover plate in a city brick home and you may find cloth-wrapped wire that crackles if you bend it.
Knob and tube. No ground conductor, insulation that turns brittle with age, and real trouble when it is buried under attic insulation. Ask your insurance agent how they treat it before you call an electrician. Partial rewiring of the worst runs is often the sensible middle path.
Aluminum branch wiring. Not automatically unsafe, but the connections at outlets and switches can loosen and run hot. The usual fix is properly rated connectors at each device - slow, fussy labor, and far cheaper than rewiring.
Two-prong outlets. A three-prong outlet with no ground wire behind it only looks grounded. The honest fixes are running a ground or adding ground-fault protection and labeling the outlets.
None of this makes an old house a problem house. It just means a quote for a plaster-and-brick home is not comparable to the same job in a newer build, and anyone who quotes them the same has not looked.
Breaker fixed, lights back, and nobody wants to cook in a hot kitchen? Here’s what Swansea, IL has to eat.
### Read the quote like the inspector will
Lay the quotes side by side at the kitchen table and look for these lines. Any one that is missing is a question, not a deal.
Panel make, model and amperage, and whether the service entrance is included
Breaker count and type, with arc-fault and ground-fault breakers called out
Grounding and bonding work needed to meet current code
Who schedules the utility disconnect and reconnect
Who pulls the permit, in whose name, and when the inspection happens
How long your power will be off
Whether they patch the drywall or plaster, or leave the holes for you
The workmanship warranty, with the term written down
The patching line catches people. Some electricians close up the wall and some leave you staring at a ragged hole by the light switch. A quote that leaves it to you is not the same price as one that does not.
To save real money, batch small jobs into one visit so you pay for one trip instead of four, offer to do the demo and patching yourself and say so before they price it, and book non-urgent work away from the week after a big storm when every crew is chasing outages. Skipping the permit is not on that list. Neither is the cheapest box of breakers.
### When the panel really is the answer
You called about one circuit for a garage freezer. You were told you need a whole panel. Upsell or truth? Usually you can see it with your own eyes. No empty breaker spaces, tandem breakers doubled up in slots that were not designed for them, a small main in a house that has since gained central air - those are real limits. Open slots, a large main and one low-draw circuit? Then the circuit is the whole job, and a second opinion is fair.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a fair price for an electrician?
A.  Judge the scope, not the rate. A fair quote names the panel, the breakers, the grounding work, the permit and who pulls it, and the patching. Two quotes with the same list are comparable. A much cheaper quote is usually missing one of those lines.
### Q. How much do electricians charge to change an outlet?
A.  Small jobs are rarely billed at true hourly cost, because the trip is the expense, not the twenty minutes of work. Expect a minimum service charge that covers the visit, with extra outlets on the same visit costing much less each. Turning a two-prong outlet into a grounded one is a bigger job if no ground exists.
### Q. How much should you pay for an electrician?

### Q. How much should I pay my electrician per hour?

A shop’s billed rate sits above that because it also covers insurance, the truck, licensing and permit costs. A rate close to the wage itself is worth a careful question about who is covering all of that.
### Q. Why are electricians so expensive?
A.  Most of the bill is not the person in your basement. Licensing, liability insurance, a stocked truck, permit fees and warranty callbacks all sit inside the rate. The low end is often unlicensed or uninsured, which is a different product, not a better price.
### Q. What is a reasonable day rate for an electrician?
A.  Work it back from the wage and the overhead. A day rate has to cover eight hours of licensed pay plus the truck, insurance and the paperwork. If a day rate sounds like wages alone, ask who is actually doing the work and whether their name can go on the permit.

## $25 Permit, $10,400 Slab: What a 20x40 Driveway Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-concrete-driveway-cost-in-st-louis
Your toe finds it before your eyes do. Dark morning, coffee in one hand, keys in the other, and the front of your shoe catches the lip where one slab of the driveway has heaved up over its neighbor. You stumble, you swear, you look down. The crack that was a pencil line last spring is now a step, packed with grit and old rock salt, and the panel by the garage has tipped toward the door.
That lip is the St. Louis winter doing its work. Water gets into the crack, freezes, swells, thaws, and comes back the next night to do it again, while the clay underneath swells in the wet months and shrinks in the dry ones. The concrete is not failing all at once. It is being pried apart a little at a time, and every cold snap that lands near freezing gives it another nudge.
So you call for quotes, and the first thing to know is the number. The second thing is smaller, and almost nobody prices it in.
### How much does a 20x40 concrete driveway cost?
A 20x40 concrete driveway is 800 square feet, and at St. Louis rates of $7 to $13 per square foot for un-reinforced concrete, that comes to about $5,600 to $10,400 before any tear-out. Reinforced concrete runs $8 to $14 per square foot, and breaking out an old slab adds $1.40 to $2.30 per square foot. In the City of St. Louis, the permit to rebuild a residential driveway is $25.
### The $25 line on the whole job belongs to City Hall
Here is the part that makes contractors in the county laugh when they hear it. If your house is inside the city limits, the Street Department’s fee to reconstruct a residential driveway is $25. A brand-new residential driveway is $50. And if the work pulls up the old granite curb at the street, the City will cart that granite to storage for $5.
Think about that for a second. Thousands of dollars of concrete, a crew of four, a ready-mix truck idling at the curb with its drum turning, and the line item that keeps you legal costs less than a pizza. Skip it, and an inspector or a neighbor can stop the job while the forms are still wet.
The Department of Streets takes applications online, and you can reach it at (314) 647-3111 or at 1900 Hampton Ave, St. Louis, MO 63139, Monday thru Friday, 8:00 to 4:30. Ask your contractor, before anything else, who is pulling the permit and whether that $25 is already in the bid. If you live outside the city, call your own city hall before the old slab comes out.
### Why the base matters more here than the concrete
Walk past any ranch house in Crestwood or Ferguson on the morning of a pour and you can smell it before you see the truck: wet gravel, diesel, the cold mineral smell of the mix sliding down the chute. Everyone on the sidewalk watches the concrete. The gravel under it decides how long you keep it.
St. Louis homes sit on clay-dense soil that expands and contracts with the freeze-thaw cycles, which is why a slab here needs more than a quick scrape and a pour. A good job digs below the slab, brings in compacted aggregate base, and packs it in layers, not one pass with a truck tire. A slab laid on loose fill cracks along the line where the fill gave way, usually within a few winters.
When one quote is thousands under another, the base is often where the money went. It is also the one part of the job you will never see again once the truck pulls away.
### What moves the price up or down
On a city lot the job starts with a saw. It screams through the old apron where the driveway meets the granite curb, the gray dust settles on every parked car on the block, and the neighbors come out to look. The plain broom finish that follows is what the per-foot rates above assume. Staining and stamping are priced on top.
Steel is the next line. Un-reinforced concrete is the low number; rebar or wire pushes you into the reinforced range. Ask how the steel will sit. Mesh lying flat on the dirt does nothing, and rebar held up on chairs in the middle of the slab does its job. Thickness matters too: a thicker slab, 6 to 8 inches rather than 4 to 5, costs more and earns it where a truck or a dumpster will park.
Then the tear-out. Breaking up the old drive is loud, dusty work, the jackhammer rattling your windows for a morning, and at $1.40 to $2.30 a square foot it adds $1,120 to $1,840 to an 800-square-foot drive. If the old slab only sank and never broke apart, ask whether it can be lifted back into place instead. Slab lifting is a different trade at a different price, and on settling clay it is worth the question before you sign for a full replacement.
What a slab runs here
### How much for a 200 sq ft concrete patio?
A reinforced concrete patio in St. Louis runs $7 to $11 per square foot, so 200 square feet lands around $1,400 to $2,200; stamped runs $9 to $16 a foot, or about $1,800 to $3,200. Driveways run $7 to $13 un-reinforced, and steel, thickness and tearing out an old slab push either job toward the top.
### Four questions that sort the bids
Lay the quotes side by side on the kitchen table and they blur together. Four questions pull them apart fast. How deep will you dig, and what goes in for a base? How thick is the slab? What steel goes in, and how is it held up off the ground? Where will the control joints go, and how soon after the pour will you cut them?
A contractor who answers all four without a pause has done this a few hundred times. One who waves them off as details is telling you which parts of the job he plans to rush, and those are the parts that decide whether you are standing in this same spot, toe on a fresh crack, a few winters from now.
Listen for drainage too. Stand at the garage door after a hard rain and watch where the water goes. If it pools against the door or runs back toward the foundation, the new slab has to be pitched to send it away, and that may mean regrading or a trench drain at the apron. That work belongs in the written quote, not in a phone call after the concrete has set.
### Concrete or asphalt, said plainly
On an August afternoon you can feel the difference through your sneakers. Asphalt goes soft and gives off that hot tar smell; concrete stays pale and hard. Up front, asphalt in St. Louis runs $5 to $8 per square foot, and that price includes demolition of an existing asphalt driveway. Concrete costs more to put in and asks less of you for years after. On a house you plan to keep, that usually tips it toward concrete. On a short hold, asphalt can be the sensible call.
### What a written quote should spell out
The quote with one number and no detail is the one that keeps you up at night. A good one reads like a recipe:
Square footage and the slab thickness
Removal and disposal of the old surface
Depth of the dig, the base material, and how it is compacted
Reinforcement type and how it will be held off the ground
The concrete mix, and whether it is air-entrained for freeze-thaw
Where the control joints go and when they are cut
Finish: broom, exposed aggregate or stamped
Grading and drainage away from the house and garage
Who pulls the permit, and whether the fee is in the bid
The warranty, and exactly what it says about cracks
No honest contractor promises concrete that never cracks. What a good warranty covers is failure: settling, heaving, flaking and cracks past a stated width. The one who swears you will never see a crack is telling you what you want to hear.

### The first winter decides a lot
The new slab looks perfect the day the crew rolls up the hoses, pale gray and smooth, the joint lines crisp. Then the first ice storm comes, and the bag of rock salt in the garage starts calling your name. Leave it there. Spread sand for grip through that first winter instead. Salt damage on young concrete shows up later as a flaking, pitted surface that looks exactly like bad workmanship, and no warranty will cover it.
Keep heavy trucks and dumpsters off it until your contractor says it is ready, and ask them how the slab will be cured. A crew that has a plan for a hot, windy pour day has seen one go wrong before. Sheeting, curing compound or a slow soak from the hose all keep the surface from drying out faster than the slab beneath it.

A.  Between the two paved choices, asphalt. If you already have an asphalt drive that is worn but sound, an overlay is cheaper still: resurfacing runs $2 to $4 per square foot for a 2-inch overlay in St. Louis, against a full new pour.
### Q. How much would a 20x20 concrete patio cost?
A.  At St. Louis rates of $7 to $11 per square foot for reinforced concrete, a 400-square-foot 20x20 patio costs $2,800 to $4,400 with a plain finish. Stamped at $9 to $16 a foot, that 400-square-foot patio runs $3,600 to $6,400.
### Q. What is the average cost of a 12x12 concrete patio?
A.  At $7 to $11 per square foot for reinforced concrete in St. Louis, a 144-square-foot 12x12 slab costs $1,008 to $1,584. Stamped at $9 to $16 a foot, that 144-square-foot slab runs $1,296 to $2,304.
### Q. What are the downsides of having a concrete driveway?
A.  It costs more up front than asphalt, you wait before you can park on it, and patches never fully disappear. It will crack, so the control joints decide where. And it hates rock salt, especially in its first winter, so spread sand instead.

## A $135 St. Louis Car Detail Can Hit $230 Before the Van Leaves. Read the Add-Ons.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-car-detailing-cost-in-st-louis
How does a $135 car detail turn into a $230 bill before the van even leaves your driveway?
You find out standing next to the driver’s door in March. The floor mat crunches under your boot, gritty with the white crust that rode in on every slushy trip to work. The cupholder is tacky enough to hold a pen upright. Crouch by the rear tire and the inside of the wheel well is frosted chalk-white, like somebody dusted it with flour.
That crust has a source. MoDOT says its St. Louis region keeps over 30,000 tons of salt on hand, and in an average snowfall more than 200 trucks with plows, salt brine and rock salt spreaders go out to fight snow, ice and frost. Stretch MoDOT’s St. Louis roads out into one lane, the agency says, and it would run from New York to San Francisco and back. Your car drives through what those trucks leave behind all winter.
So you go looking for a detailer, and the prices make no sense. A mobile detailer’s St. Louis price list shows $135 for inside and outside on a car and $160 for an SUV or truck. Auto Detail STL, a shop on Baptist Church Road in south St. Louis County, writes that full packages combining interior and exterior work in St. Louis generally range from $275 to $400.
Now read the small lines on that $135 list. Buffing is $75 more. Odor elimination is $20 more. An engine detail is $40 more, and the gas fee to drive out to you is another $20. Add the buffing and the odor work to a salty, stale-smelling car and you are at $230 before the gas fee. The gap between the cheap quote and the shop package is not a ripoff on either side. It is a list of jobs, and the only question that matters is which ones are on yours.
### How much does a full car detail typically cost?
In St. Louis, a full inside-and-out detail typically costs $135 to $400. One mobile detailer’s St. Louis price list starts at $135 for a car and $160 for an SUV or truck, before add-ons like buffing and odor work, while Auto Detail STL says full packages here generally run $275 to $400. Paint correction or ceramic coating is a separate job, at $800 to $2,000 depending on the vehicle’s size and condition.
### What the low number leaves out
Run your fingertips across the hood after a quick wash. If it feels like fine sandpaper instead of glass, the dirt is still in the paint, and a wash alone will not pull it out.
That gritty feel is what separates a wash-and-wipe from a real detail. Auto Detail STL puts it plainly: clay bar treatments can remove embedded contaminants that ordinary washing cannot address. If the clay step is not on your quote, the wax or sealant goes on over the grit, and the smooth shine fades long before you expected it to.
Inside the car, the gap is the same. A quick package vacuums the open floor and wipes the dash. A real one gets the crumbs out of the seat tracks, the grime out of the vents and the stain out of the carpet where the coffee went over on a hard brake. The St. Louis shop lists its own basic interior detailing starting at around $120, covering vacuuming, cleaning mats, wiping down the dashboard and window cleaning, which tells you how much of the full-package price is the extra labor beyond that.
None of this makes the low quote dishonest. It makes it a different product. A mobile detailer working in your driveway at $135 can be exactly what a commuter car needs between big cleanings. Just know which one you are buying before the van pulls away.
### Winter is the job St. Louis cars actually need
Crouch down beside the rear wheel in March and look up into the wheel well. That chalky white rim on the plastic liner and along the rocker panel is road salt, and it has been sitting there through every freeze and thaw since the first snow.
Salt is the thing a spring detail should go after first. It packs into wheel wells, seams and the underside, places no one sees from the driver’s seat, and it rides into the cabin on boots and soaks into the carpet. When you ask for a quote after winter, ask whether the price covers the wheel wells and the floor mats, or just the paint you can see.
Spring brings its own mess. Sap drips and bird droppings bake onto a dark hood on the first hot afternoon, and the longer they sit, the harder they are to lift. Getting them off quickly is cheaper than paying someone to polish out the dull rings later.
### Paint correction is a different purchase
Stand at a gas pump at night and look down the side of a dark car under the canopy lights. Those fine circles that look like spider webs in the paint are swirl marks, and no wash removes them.
Paint correction is the machine polishing that takes them out, and a ceramic coating is the protective layer that often goes on afterward. Auto Detail STL lists these premium treatments in St. Louis at $800 to $2,000, depending on the vehicle’s size and condition. That is not an upgrade to a detail; it is its own project, and it is quoted separately for a reason.
Whether it is worth it depends on how long the car stays in your garage. A lease you are handing back soon is a poor candidate. A car you plan to keep for years, especially a dark one that shows every swirl in the afternoon sun, is where the money makes more sense.

### Mobile or shop: where the money goes
A mobile detailer pulls into your driveway, unrolls the hose and gets to work while you finish your coffee. You never sit in a waiting room. That convenience is real, and the price lists show it can cost less, with the trade-off spelled out in a travel or gas fee.
Picture the difference in your own week. With a mobile crew, you hear the van door slide open at nine, you hand over the keys, and by the time your last meeting ends the cabin smells like clean vinyl instead of wet boots. With a shop, you drop the car, find a ride, and pick it up later with the floor mats lined up on the hood to dry. Neither is wrong. One costs you an extra fee, the other costs you a morning.
The weather is the catch. A mobile crew works in whatever heat, wind and light the day brings. For a wash, a vacuum and a wax, that is fine. For polishing or a coating, a shop with a roof, steady lighting and controlled conditions is the safer bet.

### How to get a quote you can compare
Take four photos before you call: the driver’s floor, the back seat, a wheel well and the hood up close. A detailer who sees the real mess can give you a real number. One who gets surprised in your driveway either rushes or raises the price.

Is the clay step included? If not, the protection goes on over grit.
Wax, sealant or coating? All three are fair choices. They last different lengths of time and cost different amounts, so know which one is on the invoice.
What costs extra? Odor work, buffing, engine bays and pet hair are the usual add-ons, and they are where a $135 quote turns into a $230 bill.
Is there a travel fee? Mobile crews often charge one to reach you.
How long will you have the car? A real full detail is not a while-you-wait job. If the promise sounds like a car wash, it probably is one.
Are you insured? Polishers and strong cleaners near trim and glass carry real risk, and a professional carries coverage for it.
### When a detail pays you back
Open the door of a freshly detailed car and the first thing that hits you is what is missing: no stale fries, no wet dog, no dust on the vents. That first breath is what a buyer gets when they look at a car you are selling.
If the car is going on the market, put the money into the interior first. A buyer will forgive a faint swirl in the paint long before they forgive a smell, and clean photos draw more clicks than dirty ones.
Small things carry the most weight in that first look. The gray line of grime along the inside of the door sill, the film on the inside of the windshield that glows when the sun hits it, the fog of dust in the vent slats. A buyer will run a thumb along all of them without thinking about it. A detail that gets those spots is doing more for your asking price than one more coat of wax on the hood.
If you are keeping it, think of a spring detail as cleanup after winter: salt out of the carpet and wheel wells, grit out of the paint, a fresh layer of protection before summer sun.

## Three St. Louis Libraries Have Walk-In Study Rooms for When the Cafe Gets Too Loud
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-coffee-shops-to-work-remotely-in-st-louis
The steam wand screams right behind your left ear, the wifi page spins for the third time, and the battery icon on your laptop has just turned red. You picked a cafe off South Grand to get one report finished. You got a mocha, a wobbling two-top and a stranger’s phone call about her kitchen remodel, every word of it.
So you start the quiet math everybody does. Pack up and drive home to the dog and the laundry pile? Hunt for another cafe and buy another drink? Or sit tight and fake it for an hour?
Here is the move most people working around St. Louis never think of. There is a room with a door on that same street, inside the Carpenter Library at 3309 South Grand Boulevard. The St. Louis Public Library keeps study rooms at Carpenter, at Buder on Hampton Ave and at Schlafly on North Euclid Avenue in the Central West End, for exactly this moment. And you do not book them. The library’s own room page says they cannot be reserved but are available on a first-come, first-served basis in two-hour blocks.
Read that again, because it is the part people get wrong: no reservation system, no form, no waiting a week. You walk in, and if a room is open, it is yours. A door that clicks shut, a table that does not rock, and no grinder. The catch is the clock on the other end: study rooms must be cleared 30 minutes before the library closes, so a late-afternoon plan needs a check first. The library takes room questions at 314-241-2288.
That changes how a working day out in this city should go. Use the coffee shop for what it is great at, the warm cup, the low hum, the change of scenery that gets your brain moving again. When the call, the deadline or the spreadsheet needs real quiet, carry the laptop to a room built for it.
### What is the best coffee shop to do work in St. Louis?
The best one is the room that passes a ten-second look at the door: outlets along the walls, tables big enough for a laptop and a mug, people already typing, and a free seat far from the grinder. If none of those show up, or you need a door and real quiet, walk into a study room at the Buder, Carpenter or Schlafly branch of the St. Louis Public Library, first come, first served, in two-hour blocks.
### Ten seconds at the door tells you everything
Stand inside the door for a breath before you order. Smell the roast, listen to the room, and look at the walls instead of the pastry case. It works on the narrow storefronts along South Grand and Cherokee Street just as well as in the big-windowed corner rooms in the Central West End.
Look low first. Outlets along the baseboard and under the window counter mean the owner expects people to stay. Two outlets, both behind the bar, mean the opposite, and on a small room with a line out the door that is a fair choice.
Then look at the tables. A laptop, a mug and a notebook need real surface. Little round bistro tops were built for two cups and a conversation, and you will spend the afternoon catching your coffee before it slides off the edge.
Then look at the people. If three of them are bent over laptops in the soft glow of their screens, you belong. If it is all pairs leaning in and talking, you will feel the stares inside twenty minutes, and you will be right.
Last, find the grinder and the espresso machine. That shriek and rattle runs all day. Sit at the far wall or in a corner, away from the pickup counter, and your shoulders will come down a full inch.
### Wifi that works until it doesn’t
Nearly every cafe has wifi. The better question is whether it will hold up when it matters.
Email and documents need almost nothing. A video call is different, because cafe wifi often handles watching far better than being watched, and your face freezes mid-sentence while everyone waits. The portal kind is the worst: it drops without a sound, and you find out when a file refuses to save.
So treat the house connection as a bonus. Tether to your phone for anything important, and test that hotspot once at home so you are not fumbling with settings while a meeting starts without you.
### The hours that make or break a session
The same room can feel like a library mid-morning and a train station at lunch. The milk pitcher clangs, the line backs up to the door, and the chair across from you never stays empty.
Your best shot is a weekday morning after the commuter rush and the slow middle of the afternoon. Weekend mornings belong to people meeting each other; one person with a laptop at a four-top while a family waits is the exact scene that gets time-limit signs taped to the register.
Closing time is the other trap. Plenty of independent shops close earlier than you would guess, so check the hours for that day before you plan a late session. If you need somewhere after dark, that is its own search.
Watch the room, not just the clock. When the barista starts wiping down empty tables and stacking chairs by the back wall, the shop is telling you the day is winding down, and the best move is to save your work and go before anyone has to ask.
### The unwritten deal with the owner
Working from a cafe is normal and welcome in most of them. The deal is simple, and it is not written on the chalkboard.
Keep buying. When the cup is empty and you are staying, order the next thing. That is the rent on the seat.
Take calls outside. All of them. A room can absorb typing and low talk; it cannot absorb half of your status meeting. Headphones do not fix this, because the problem is your voice, not what you hear.
Match the table to your party. One person at a four-top during a rush annoys everyone, the staff included.
Ask before you move furniture to reach an outlet, and never run a cord across a walkway.
Tip for the time, not just the drink, and leave when the room turns. When every seat is full and a line forms, pack up kindly and you will be welcome next time.

### When the cafe is the wrong room
Being honest about this saves you a wasted afternoon and a cold, untouched second coffee.
Back-to-back video calls do not belong in a cafe, for your sake and everyone else’s. Neither does paperwork you need to spread out, or anything confidential on screen with strangers walking behind your chair. And no cafe can promise you a seat at a set time.
That is where the library study rooms earn their place. Walk in, close the door, and the only sound is your own keyboard. Two rules keep it smooth. First come means first come, so the rooms go to whoever walks in first, and a busy branch may have every door already shut when you arrive; have the cafe as your backup, not the other way around. And two-hour blocks mean you plan in two-hour chunks. That turns out to be a gift. A hard stop on the wall clock does more for a stalled report than a fourth refill ever will.
Plan the day around it. Start at the cafe with the first cup while the room is still quiet and the light is coming low through the front window. Answer the easy email there, where a little noise helps. Then, when the real work starts, drive over, take the room, shut the door and let the silence press in. When your block is up, you will have something finished, and the second coffee will taste like a reward instead of rent.
A coworking day pass is the other option when you need a guaranteed desk for a full day. Most people do best with a mix: the cafe for a focused stretch and a change of scene, a room with a door for the work that cannot be interrupted.
