## Lawn Care Cost in St. Louis: About $48 a Mow, or a $100 City Fine
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-lawn-care-cost-in-st-louis
The most expensive lawn cut in the City of St. Louis is the one you skip. Let the yard run wild and the Forestry Division sends a violation notice that gives you 10 days to deal with it. Miss that window and, in the city’s own words, the city will abate the property and issue an abatement fee and a fine of $100. Get labeled a chronic violator and that fine can be $100 per day it stays out of compliance.
And the abatement fee isn’t a flat number. The city bills it by the hour, at different rates depending on what it sends: mowers, hand crews, tractors, bobcats. If a notice is already on your door, call the Forestry Division at (314) 613-7200, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., ask exactly what was flagged, and get it cut and cleared inside the 10 days. A $48.20 mow on day nine beats a city crew on day eleven.
Nobody plans to end up on that list. It happens one wet week at a time. The mower coughs and dies on the second pull. The grass along the fence is past your ankles and still holding last night’s rain, so your socks are soaked by the time you reach the gate. And every evening a crew rolls down the block, trailer rattling over the expansion joints, and lays a clean edge along the curb across the street while you stand there smelling cut grass that isn’t yours. You tell yourself Saturday. Then it rains Saturday.
So here is the math with real St. Louis numbers, before the city does the math for you. LawnStarter, where St. Louis homeowners order mowing online, publishes its St. Louis lawn care facts: the average yard is 9,025 square feet and the average mowing price is $48.20. Only 31% of those customers cut weekly. 48% cut every other week, and 21% cut monthly.
Then the number that stings. Only 9% of those lawns are fertilized. Most of those yards are paying someone to cut grass, not to grow it, and then wondering why the bare patch by the driveway never fills in.
### What is the average cost of lawn care per month?
Thumbtack’s St. Louis price examples put weekly mowing at $120 a month for a property up to 8,000 square feet, $140 for 8,001 to 15,000 square feet and $160 for 15,001 to 20,000. LawnStarter’s St. Louis average of $48.20 a mow works out to about $193 a month at four weekly cuts, or about $96 a month at two cuts every other week. Fertilizer and weed treatments are billed on top.
Those examples come from Thumbtack’s St. Louis lawn care page, and its weekly prices include mowing all the turf, trimming along fences, trees and lawn edges, and blowing the clippings off the driveway, sidewalk and curb. Read that list twice when a quote comes in low. A crew that skips the trimming and leaves the driveway green with clippings is cheaper for a reason.
The yard itself moves the number more than the zip code does. A flat rectangle with a wide gate is the cheap version of any size. What pushes a quote up is everything that makes a crew climb off the mower: a steep front bank, a retaining wall, a swing set, raised beds, a gate too narrow for the commercial deck, a big tree they trim around by hand, a dog that has opinions. Walk your own yard once with that list in your head before you call anyone, and you’ll know which end of the range you’re on.
### Every other week is what most St. Louis yards buy
Nearly half of LawnStarter’s St. Louis customers cut every other week, and on paper it halves the bill. In May it often doesn’t work. Tall fescue grows fast in a wet spring, and one skipped cut turns the next mow into a hay harvest: wet clumps in rows across the lawn, a yellowed stripe under every row a few days later.
MU Extension’s cool-season lawn calendar spells out why. The standard guide is to never remove more than one-third of the green leaf area with a single mowing, and if a mowing is missed, cut only half the way back to the intended height, then finish the job a couple of mowings later. For tall fescue, the summer mowing height MU recommends is 3 to 4 inches. A crew that scalps your fescue to two inches in July to stretch the time between visits is costing you the lawn to save themselves a trip.
So the honest answer is a split schedule. Weekly through the spring flush, when the grass is racing. Every other week in the dry heat of midsummer and again late in the fall, when growth slows. Ask any crew whether it will price that way. Many will, and it’s cheaper than a full season of weekly cuts.
### The 9% problem: paying for treatment at the right time
If you’re in the 9% who fertilize, the calendar matters more than the brand on the truck. LawnStarter lists St. Louis fertilization at $47 to $140 a service, and the same dollars can feed the lawn or feed the weeds depending on the month they go down.
MU Extension is blunt about it. For cool-season grass like fescue, September is the most important time to fertilize. Crabgrass preventers go down by April 15, before you ever see a crabgrass seedling, because after you see it the barrier is useless. And MU says not to apply nitrogen fertilizer, especially quickly available soluble forms, past May 1, because it encourages foliar diseases. A program that sells you a heavy green-up feeding in June is selling you a pretty lawn for a little while and a fungus problem after that.
That’s the share-worthy part of this whole page: the cheapest treatment plan that works in St. Louis is the one built around April and September, not the one with the most visits. When a company quotes you a program, ask it to name the month of every application. If it can’t, it’s selling a schedule, not a lawn.
### Aeration, clay and the patch that never fills in
St. Louis lawns sit on heavy clay, the sticky orange-brown kind that clings to your boots after a rain and bakes hard as a brick in August. Clay compacts. Compacted soil chokes roots, and choked roots are why the thin patch by the driveway stays thin no matter how much fertilizer you throw at it.
Core aeration pulls actual plugs of soil, and you’ll see them scattered across the lawn like broken chalk for a week afterward. A spike machine just pokes holes and can press clay tighter. If you’re paying for aeration, ask which machine is coming, and book it for late summer or early fall alongside overseeding, when fescue seed actually takes.
Wondering if the whole crew is worth it? Here’s which lawn jobs are worth your own Saturday.
### The August problem
Most summers bring a hot, dry stretch when unwatered fescue gives up and goes dormant. The lawn turns the color of a paper bag, it crunches under your feet, and the crew has nothing to cut.
This is the most common billing argument in lawn care, and one sentence in the first conversation heads it off: what happens to my bill when the grass stops growing? Fair answers are that the crew skips the visit and doesn’t charge, or comes anyway at a reduced rate to trim and blow the drive. The answer to walk away from is a full mowing charge for dragging a deck over dormant grass, which only stresses it more.
### Leaves, cleanups and the bill nobody budgets for
Older St. Louis neighborhoods came with mature oaks, sycamores and sweetgums, and every fall they bury the yard in a crisp, ankle-deep layer that turns to a slick brown mat after the first cold rain. Leave that mat on fescue through winter and you’ll be paying to reseed in spring.
The lever you control is the number of passes. Mulch the early leaf drop into the turf with the mower, which costs nothing extra and feeds the soil, then pay for one thorough cleanup after the last leaves come down. If the leaf problem is really a tree problem, that’s a different budget, and our breakdown of what tree removal costs in St. Louis covers it.
Hourly yard help, St. Louis rates
### How much for 2 hours of yard work?
Thumbtack’s St. Louis price examples list an hourly rate of $25 an hour, travel, equipment and labor included, which puts two hours at about $50. LawnStarter lists St. Louis cleanups at $60 to $177, and yard size, leaf volume and whether the debris gets hauled away decide where you land.
### Make three quotes comparable before you sign
Almost every lawn pricing complaint comes from comparing two numbers that never measured the same work. Ask every company the same short list:
Is this per visit or per month, and how many visits does a month include?
Does mowing include trimming, edging and blowing the hard surfaces?
Are clippings mulched or bagged, and is there a charge for bagging?
Did you measure the turf, or estimate it from a satellite photo?
Is treatment separate, and can I buy mowing without it?
Which month does each treatment go down?
What happens to my bill in August when growth stops?
Do you carry liability insurance, and are the people on my property employees or subcontractors?
The measurement question is the sneaky one. A satellite estimate can count the roof, the driveway and the patio as lawn. A crew that walked your yard is quoting the grass you actually have.
And if the neglected yard is next door rather than yours, the city takes reports through its Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800. That’s the same process that ends in the $100 fine, so it’s worth a friendly knock first.
Done fighting the pull cord? Browse lawn and garden services near you on St Louis Near Me Directory, and ask each crew whether it prices per cut, per month or per application before you compare a single number.
If you run the mowing crew, the two-person outfit or the truck-and-trailer side hustle that works every evening after the day job, the neighbor watching you lay that clean curb edge is your next customer. List your business and get more customers on your route before the next quote goes to someone else.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should you pay somebody to mow your lawn?
A.  LawnStarter’s St. Louis average is $48.20 a mow on an average yard of 9,025 square feet. Thumbtack’s St. Louis examples run $35 for a smaller subdivision lot, $50 for a half acre and $100 for an acre. Slopes, narrow gates, heavy tree cover and bagging push you toward the top.
### Q. Is $50 for lawn mowing good?
A.  Yes, it’s close to fair. LawnStarter’s local average is $48.20 a mow, and Thumbtack’s St. Louis examples show $50 for a half-acre lot. Confirm that trimming, edging and blowing the drive are included before you agree, because those are what cheap quotes leave out.
### Q. Is mowing every 2 weeks enough?
A.  Not through a St. Louis spring. MU Extension says never to remove more than one-third of the green leaf area in one mowing, and fescue racing through a wet May can outgrow that before the next cut comes around. Every other week usually works in midsummer heat and late fall, which is why a split schedule is the smart buy.
### Q. How often should you mow your lawn in Missouri?
A.  As often as it takes to stay within the one-third rule, which in spring usually means weekly. MU Extension recommends a summer mowing height of 3 to 4 inches for tall fescue, so let the height guide you rather than the calendar. Mowing high also shades out weeds and helps the lawn ride out August.
### Q. How much should lawn treatment cost?
A.  LawnStarter lists St. Louis fertilization at $47 to $140 a service, depending mostly on lawn size. More important than the price is timing: MU Extension calls September the most important time to fertilize cool-season grass and says crabgrass preventers should go down by April 15.
### Q. Are lawn treatment services worth it?
A.  They are when the program is built around the right months. A fescue lawn gets the most from a crabgrass preventer by April 15 and a September feeding. A program that pushes nitrogen after May 1, which MU Extension warns against, can buy you disease instead of grass. Ask for the month of every application before you sign.
### Q. Is $100 an hour too much for landscape work?
A.  For routine mowing, yes. Thumbtack’s St. Louis examples list an hourly rate of $25 an hour, travel and equipment included. For a crew bringing commercial equipment, hauling and design work to a bigger landscape job, a higher hourly rate can be fair, so ask what the hour includes and get the total in writing.

## What Hair Salon Services Cost in St. Louis (2026 Price Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-hair-salon-services-cost-in-st-louis
It is a Thursday afternoon in Kirkwood and someone is standing on the sidewalk outside a salon, reading a price list taped to the inside of the window. Cut, it says, from $55. Color, from $95. Balayage, consultation required. She wanted a number before she walked in, and what she got instead was a floor — the smallest amount anyone in that building has ever charged for that service, on the fastest head of hair, with the newest stylist on the schedule. She is standing on the sidewalk doing arithmetic she does not have enough information to do.
Across the metro in Maplewood, a guy who has had the same cut for nine years just paid a little over thirty dollars and handed his stylist a ten because she squeezed him in on a Saturday. A few miles east on the Delmar Loop, a college student is booked for a full head of highlights and has budgeted $120, which is roughly a third of what that appointment is going to ring up once the toner, the bond treatment, and the blow-dry land on the ticket. And out in Florissant, a woman who colored her hair at home two weekends ago is working down a list of salons and getting the same sentence every time: we would need to see it in person first.
Four people, one metro, four completely different relationships with the same set of numbers. Nobody in that story is being cheated. Hair pricing is genuinely confusing — deliberately vague in a few places, accidentally vague in most — and almost none of it gets explained on the website. So here is the explanation, in the order it actually costs you money.
### What a salon appointment actually costs in the St. Louis metro
Start with the honest ranges. These are what services commonly run, and the spread is wide because the spread is real: a dry trim from a newer stylist in a strip-mall suite and a full restyle from a twenty-year colorist in a boutique studio are not the same product, and they will never carry the same price.
Women’s haircut: roughly $40 to $165 across the St. Louis area depending on the salon and the stylist. Nationally the average sits closer to $69, with most cuts falling between $40 and $120.
Men’s haircut: commonly $20 to $50, with the national average around $43.
Root touch-up: about $50 to $100.
Single-process color, all over: about $60 to $150.
Foil highlights: roughly $70 to $150 for a full head, with longer or thicker hair landing at the top of that band.
Balayage: commonly $150 to $350, and it can climb past that on long or previously colored hair.
Toner or gloss: $20 to $60 on top of the color service.
Bond-building treatment: $30 to $80 added to a lightening service.
Blowout or finish styling: $30 to $70, and it is frequently not included in the color price.
Keratin or smoothing treatment: $150 to $600 or more, driven almost entirely by hair length and density.
Extensions: tape-in installs commonly start around $400, and hand-tied work often runs $800 to $1,500 before any maintenance.
That first line is where most of the frustration in this whole category lives. Why are ladies hairdressers so expensive? It is not mystique. A women’s appointment usually bundles a shampoo, a sectioned wet cut, a blow-dry, and finish styling onto longer hair that needs more of every product, and the men’s number on the same menu is often a dry clipper cut with none of that attached. Compare the same service and the gap shrinks fast.
Two other things jump out of that list. The first is that the add-ons are not small. A color appointment with a toner, a bond treatment, and a blow-dry can carry $80 to $200 of services that never appear in the headline price. The second is that the ranges overlap, which means the number on the sign tells you far less than you think it does.
### Why the same haircut has three different prices inside one salon
Most full-service salons in the region price by stylist level, not by service. A cut is a cut on the menu, but the person holding the shears is priced into it. The tiers usually look something like new talent or associate, then stylist or designer, then senior, then master or artistic director.
A new-talent stylist has a cosmetology license and has tested out on the services they are booked for — they are not practicing on you. They are simply early. Senior stylists typically have several years and a stack of continuing education behind them, and they are the ones who take on complicated color. Master stylists are usually eight years and up. The price gap from the bottom tier to the top is commonly thirty to fifty dollars on the same service, in the same room, using the same product.
This matters more than any coupon. If you want a one-length trim and a blow-dry, a lower-level stylist is not a compromise, it is correct budgeting. If you are going from box-dyed dark to lived-in blonde, booking the cheapest chair in the building is how a $180 appointment turns into a $600 repair.
Random, but: Wright City’s food scene is worth a detour.
### How to read a price list that says “from”
When a menu says cut “from $55,” that is a starting price, not an average. It is calculated on the shortest realistic version of that service, performed by the least expensive stylist, on the least demanding hair. Almost nobody pays the from-price.
Here is what silently moves the number up:
Length and density. Nearly every salon has a long-hair or thick-hair upcharge, sometimes posted, often not. More hair means more product and more time.
Stylist level. Covered above, and it is usually the single largest variable.
Bowls of color. Some salons charge per bowl or per tube once a formula exceeds the standard amount, and long, dense hair routinely needs a second bowl.
Whether styling is included. A cut price that ends at a rough dry may be twenty-five dollars cheaper than one that ends with a finished blowout. That is not a trick, it is a different service.
Add-ons offered at the bowl. Deep conditioning, scalp treatment, bond builder. These are real services with real value, and they are also where a ticket quietly grows by fifty dollars.
The fix is one sentence, delivered when you book rather than when you check out: based on my hair, what is the realistic total for everything, including styling and any add-ons you would recommend? A good front desk will answer that, or hand you to the stylist who can. A salon that will not attach any number to it before you are in the chair is telling you something worth hearing.
### Color is where the budget actually goes
Every consultation eventually arrives at the same question. How much should it cost to get your hair colored? Honestly, that depends less on the color you want than on the color you already have. Applying a single tone to virgin hair is a chemistry problem with one step. Lightening hair that has been colored before, especially with box dye, is a chemistry problem with several steps, and each one takes time and product.
Roughly in order of cost and complexity:
Root touch-up — maintenance on an existing formula, the cheapest and fastest color appointment.
Single-process — one color, all over, usually going darker or matching to a tone.
Partial highlights — foils around the face and part line only.
Full highlights — foils throughout, more time and more product.
Balayage — hand-painted and freehand, slower to place, and priced accordingly.
Color correction — a different category entirely, priced by the hour rather than by the service.
Balayage typically costs fifty to a hundred dollars more per session than traditional foils, but the maintenance math flips it. Foils generally want a touch-up every four to six weeks. Balayage grows out softly and often stretches to twelve to fourteen weeks. Over a full year the two can land in the same place, and balayage sometimes lands lower. If you are comparing prices, compare the annual cost, not the appointment.
### Why the cheapest quote for color is often the most expensive outcome
Color correction is billed by the hour, commonly starting around $100 an hour and running to $150 an hour in busier markets. Most corrections take two to three hours, which puts them in the $200 to $300 range, and difficult ones run six hours or more and pass $600. That is not a markup for the word corrective. Corrective work often requires several times the pigment of a standard session, and going from light back to dark is genuinely harder than the reverse, because bleached hair has little pigment left for the new color to hold onto.
Which is why the lowest bid on a big color change deserves a second look. If a salon quotes a full transformation on previously box-dyed hair at a price that would barely cover a single-process, one of a few things is true: they are planning fewer steps than the job needs, they have not actually seen your hair, or they intend to add to the ticket later. Any of those can end with you paying for the cheap appointment and then paying for the correction.
The stylists who quote high in that first conversation are usually the ones who have already counted the sessions. A colorist who tells you the look you brought in will take two visits eight weeks apart is not upselling you. They are describing physics.
### Smoothing, keratin, and the long-appointment services
Keratin and smoothing treatments run about $150 to $600 and up, with short hair at the bottom of the band, medium hair in the $200 to $350 range, and long or dense hair at the top. Results generally last one to six months depending on the formula, your hair, and how faithfully you use the aftercare products.
Two questions are worth asking before you book one. First, what is the actual chair time, because these are long appointments and some salons block them as a half day. Second, what does the aftercare require, because a smoothing treatment maintained with the wrong shampoo is a service you paid for twice.
### Extensions: the install is not the price
Extensions are the service where people most often budget for the wrong number. A tape-in install commonly runs $400 to $800, and hand-tied wefts often land between $800 and $1,500 once you count both the hair itself and the labor to put it in.
Then the real cost starts. Tape-ins need moving every four to eight weeks at roughly $150 to $300 a visit. Hand-tied maintenance typically runs $250 to $650 every six to eight weeks. Add replacement hair and the professional shampoo you are now committed to using, and the annual number for permanent methods commonly lands somewhere between $1,500 and $4,500.
None of that is a reason to avoid extensions. It is a reason to ask for the twelve-month number before the first appointment rather than after the third.
### The consultation is the step people skip, and it is the cheap one
Most salons will do a consultation for free, or for a small fee credited toward the service. It takes about fifteen minutes, it usually does not require a chair, and it is the single highest-value part of the entire process.
Bring photographs — several, of the same look, in different lighting, so the stylist can see what you actually mean rather than what one filtered image implies. Be honest about your hair history. Box dye, henna, a rough bleach two years ago, a keratin treatment last spring: all of it changes what is chemically possible today, and a stylist who does not know about it is formulating blind.
What you want out of a consultation is three specific things. A realistic total, in dollars, for the appointment as it will actually be performed. A count of how many sessions the look will take. And a plain description of what the maintenance costs per year. Walk out with those three numbers and you have removed almost every unpleasant surprise from the process.
It is also the moment to ask what happens if you are not happy. Many stylists will fix an issue at no charge if you come back within a set window and say so. That policy is easy to get in advance and awkward to negotiate afterward.
### Tipping at a St. Louis salon
Twenty percent is the working standard at a full-service salon. Fifteen percent reads as adequate but unremarkable. Twenty-two to twenty-five percent is for genuinely exceptional work, a stylist who stayed late, or the person who fit you in the day before a wedding.
The mechanics matter more than the percentage:
Tip on the pre-tax total, not the after-tax total.
Tip on the original price even when you used a coupon, a gift card, or a first-visit discount. The work was the same work.
If an assistant shampooed you or a second stylist did your blow-dry, tip them separately and directly. Five to ten dollars is normal.
If you are unhappy, say so before you pay. A reduced tip communicates nothing useful, and most stylists would far rather fix it.
Then the arithmetic everyone is quietly doing in the chair. How much do you tip a $50 hair stylist? Ten dollars at twenty percent, seven-fifty at fifteen. On a $200 color, twenty percent is forty dollars, and it is entirely normal to split that between the colorist and whoever else touched your hair that day.
### A quick word on licensing
Cosmetologists and barbers in Missouri are licensed through the state Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners, and those licenses renew every two years. You can look up a person or a business, and see whether there are disciplinary actions on record, through the state’s renewal and verification portal. It takes about a minute, and it is worth doing before a chemical service with someone new.
### Before you book: the short list
Ask for a realistic total including styling and add-ons, not the from-price.
Ask which level of stylist you are booked with, and whether that matches the difficulty of what you want.
For any color change, ask how many sessions it will take.
Ask what the annual maintenance costs, especially for highlights, balayage, and extensions.
Disclose your full hair history, including anything you did at home.
Ask about the redo policy and the window for it.
Bring several photos of the same look, and one photo of something you definitely do not want.

If you’re the stylist with an open chair at nine on a Tuesday night, the person searching for a cut right then is your next client, so list your salon where they look first.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should it cost to get your hair colored?
A.  Root touch-ups generally run $50 to $100, single-process all-over color $60 to $150, full foil highlights roughly $70 to $150, and balayage $150 to $350 and up. Then budget for the extras that are usually charged separately: toner or gloss at $20 to $60, a bond-building treatment at $30 to $80, and a finish blowout at $30 to $70. Longer or denser hair sits at the top of every one of those bands.
### Q. How much do you tip a $50 hair stylist?
A.  Ten dollars is the standard twenty percent. Seven dollars and fifty cents is fifteen percent, which reads as acceptable rather than generous. Tip on the pre-tax amount, and tip on the original price even if you used a discount or a gift card. If someone else shampooed or styled you, hand them five to ten dollars separately.
### Q. Why are ladies hairdressers so expensive?
A.  Because you are usually comparing two different products. The women’s line on a salon menu typically bundles services that the men’s line does not, and it runs on longer hair, which means more chair time, more product, and often a long-hair upcharge on top. Layer in the stylist level and the add-ons that attach to color work — toner, bond treatment, finish blowout — and the totals separate quickly. Book a dry cut with no styling at a lower level and the price lands much closer to a barbershop cut.
### Q. Is it worth it to dye hair at a salon?
A.  For maintenance on a shade close to your natural color, home color is a reasonable choice and plenty of people do it well. For anything involving lightening, moving more than a couple of shades in either direction, or fixing something that already went wrong, the salon is almost always cheaper in the end. Color correction is billed hourly, commonly $100 to $150 an hour, and two to three hours is normal — which means one bad box of dye can easily cost more to undo than the professional service would have cost to do right the first time.
### Q. What is the normal price of a haircut?
A.  Nationally, men’s cuts average about $43 and generally fall between $20 and $50, while women’s cuts average about $69 and typically fall between $40 and $120. In the St. Louis metro the women’s range runs wider, roughly $40 to $165, because the market spans everything from a suite rental in North County to a senior stylist in a boutique salon. If you are being quoted well above that band, you are paying for the stylist’s level, not for the haircut itself.
### Q. Is $30 for a haircut expensive?
A.  For a men’s cut in St. Louis, no — $20 to $50 is the normal range and the national average sits near $43. For a women’s cut it is well under market, where $40 to $165 is typical. A $30 women’s cut generally means a walk-in chain rather than a booked stylist.
### Q. How much does it cost for a hairdresser to dye your hair?
A.  In this market a root touch-up runs about $50 to $100, and single-process color all over about $60 to $150. Highlights and corrective work climb well past that, which is where budgets usually get broken. Ask whether the quoted price includes the blow-dry and toner, because often it does not.
### Q. How much tip for $200 hair?
A.  Eighteen to twenty percent is standard, so roughly $36 to $40 on a $200 appointment. If more than one person worked on you — a colorist plus an assistant who shampooed — split it rather than handing it all to the stylist. Tip on the pre-discount total when a promotion applied.

## One Whole St. Louis Room, Designed, for $1,349: What Designers Cost
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-does-an-interior-designer-cost-in-st-louis
You’ve moved the couch four times. Go ahead and admit it. In a brick bungalow in Southampton, it can’t go under the front window, because that’s where the cast iron radiator lives, painted the same cream as the plaster and ticking every time the boiler wakes up. It can’t float in the middle, because the rug is too small. So it’s back against the wall where it started, and you’re standing in the doorway with your coffee going cold, staring at the dead corner, knowing the room is wrong and not knowing why.
And you haven’t called a designer. Not because you don’t want help. Because you assume the first word out of her mouth is a number with a comma in it, and you’re a little afraid of her face when she sees the rug.
Here is the number, and it’s printed right on a St. Louis studio’s own website. Olive + Opal Interiors lists its Room Revival package at $1,349: an in-home design consultation, a full room floor plan and layout strategy, a visual design board for one room with shoppable product links, up to 3 rounds of revisions, and in-home styling. One whole room, planned on paper, with a designer standing in it twice. The couch question and the radiator question both live inside that price.
If you’d rather carry the plan out yourself, the same studio’s Style Jumpstart is $749 for an in-home design consultation and a follow-up email of shoppable links. Across town, PureWave Designs, another St. Louis studio, lists a $395 design consultation right on its home page. The scariest number in interior design turns out to be one you can read before you ever pick up the phone.
Color and placement do more than people expect in these houses. St. Louis Homes & Lifestyles once featured a Joni Spear project in which, with only cosmetic changes, the designer turned an uninspired house into a home bursting with colorful style. No walls moved. That matters here more than almost anywhere, because the walls in an old St. Louis house are the expensive part: plaster over wood lath that cracks and dusts when you cut it, brick that carries the floor above, radiators that can’t move without a plumber. The cheapest fix is usually the one that leaves them alone.
You aren’t paying for taste. You’re paying to stop guessing. Before that first hour, snap a photo of every wall in the room, measure the radiator and the windows, and decide the number you won’t go past. Bring the rug too. She’s seen worse.
### How much should I budget for an interior designer?
Most homeowners spend $1,900 to $11,200 on an interior designer, or $5 to $12 per square foot, according to HomeGuide’s cost survey, with hourly rates of $50 to $200 before furniture. In St. Louis, Olive + Opal Interiors prices one fully designed room at $1,349 and an in-home consultation package at $749, and PureWave Designs lists a $395 design consultation. Furnishings are billed on top of the design fee.
Here is what that money looks like at night in a plaster-walled front room in Dutchtown: a floor plan spread across the coffee table, a design board with links you can actually click, a list of what stays and what goes, and a designer who is coming back to style the room. That’s the St. Louis package. Read it twice, because you get the plan whether or not you buy a single new piece. National numbers run much wider: the HomeGuide cost guide puts flat-rate fees at $1,000 to $12,000 per room and design-only work at $450 to $1,500 per room.
The same guide says most design firms charge between $1,500 and $4,900 a room on a flat fee, which makes that $1,349 St. Louis room package sit just under the band. Picture what the number is buying in a Shaw four-family where you own the top floor: plaster walls, a narrow front parlor, one good window. A plan you carry out yourself costs a fraction of a finished room, so decide which one you want before the first call.
### Five ways the meter can run
Three neighbors can hire three designers for nearly the same living room and get three bills that look nothing alike. The work isn’t different. The meter is.
Hourly is the honest one and the dangerous one. You pay for exactly the time you use, which is perfect when the problem is a paint color and a furniture layout and the designer can solve it while standing on the oak floor of a Tower Grove South bungalow with a fan deck in her hand. It gets dangerous on a big job with no ceiling, because the clock runs during the weeks when nothing seems to happen: the emails, the backordered fabric, the call to the vendor. Ask for a not-to-exceed number in writing.
A flat fee per room is the friendliest for a fixed budget and the most likely to hide a scope fight. The number only means something if the paper behind it says how many revision rounds, how many site visits and whether install day is included. Olive + Opal’s published package is a good model of a clean scope: it names the 3 revision rounds and the 2 styling hours right next to the price. Cost-plus is the one that confuses people: the designer buys at trade pricing, shows you that cost, and adds a percentage. Done cleanly, you see both numbers on every line. A percentage of the whole project scales with the job, and you should ask exactly what it’s calculated on. Per square foot fits gut renovations and new builds, and it fits a single small room badly.
The question that saves the most money is the plainest one. Before you compare any two quotes, ask each designer which of these meters you are on, and whether a furniture markup stacks on top of it.
### What the first paid hour should leave in your hands
A good first hour sounds like floorboards creaking in a Webster Groves Victorian. The designer walks every room you want touched, opens the closet, looks up at the light fixture, asks where you actually sit at night and where the dog sleeps. She is not selling. She is diagnosing.
By the end you should know what is possible in the space and what isn’t, a rough budget for the work you described, what has to happen before what, and any red flags she spotted, like a wall that may be carrying the floor above or wiring that won’t take a dozen new lights. If you walk away with none of that, you learned something useful for the price of one hour. And ask whether the fee comes back to you: Yours by Design, a St. Louis firm on Thumbtack, charges $150 for a one-hour consultation and credits it to the design fee if you hire the firm.
### The St. Louis house changes the bill
National cost articles stop being useful at the front door of a brick two-story in south city. Our housing stock is old, masonry-heavy and specific, and it changes both the design work and what it costs.
Plaster over wood lath is harder and more brittle than drywall, and running new wiring through it means real patching, the gritty white dust on every sill, not a quick mud-and-tape. Good designers plan runs to keep the plaster demolition small and price the patching honestly. If paint is part of the plan, our guide to interior painting in St. Louis covers the prep older walls need.
Cast iron radiators sit exactly where you want the sofa, tick and knock when the boiler kicks on, and can’t move without touching the piping. Any designer working an older St. Louis house should raise them without being asked. Old wiring is the other quiet budget killer: a lighting plan with recessed cans and new outlets is also an electrician’s bill, and our breakdown of what an electrician costs in St. Louis covers panel upgrades and what moves that price.
Reading a price list is a skill. Here’s the same trick on what a St. Louis hair salon really charges.
Then there’s the brick. A load-bearing brick wall isn’t a partition you knock out over a weekend while the neighbors listen to the sledgehammer. Cutting a new opening means a header, a structural professional and usually tuckpointing around the cut, and exterior brick limits where new windows can go. That one fact quietly rewrites a lot of open-concept dreams, and a designer who knows these houses will tell you in the first hour, before you’ve fallen for a plan the walls won’t allow.
Small original kitchens are the third St. Louis problem. They were built as work rooms, closed off, often next to a pantry or a back stair. The best design money in these houses is usually spent on space, not decoration: borrowing from the next room, reworking a doorway, moving the sink so it finally faces the window and the morning light over the backyard.
### Decorator, designer or architect?
A decorator works with the room as it is: furniture, fabric, color, lighting, layout. No walls move. If your rooms work and just look wrong, a decorator or a few paid designer hours may be all you need. An interior designer also works on the space itself, with built-ins, cabinetry, lighting plans and drawings a contractor can build from. When a bearing wall, a new opening in brick or an addition is on the table, you need an architect or structural engineer too.
Missouri’s Interior Design Council answers at 573.522.4683, so ask any designer whether they are registered before your job needs signed drawings. The builder is a separate check, and we walk through it in how to check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri.

### What color makes a house look expensive?
The honest answer is the color chosen in your own light, on your own walls, by someone who has stood in the room. More rooms, more site visits and furnishing on top push the bill up from there.
### Make two quotes comparable before you sign
Almost every design dispute traces back to a vague scope. A quote isn’t a scope. Get these in writing from every designer you talk to:
Which rooms are included, listed by name.
The deliverables: concept boards, floor plans, lighting plan, finish schedule, furniture specs.
How many revision rounds and site visits, and what one more costs.
The fee structure stated plainly, and whether a furniture markup is added on top.
Whether you’ll see trade cost and markup as separate lines.
The payment schedule, and what happens to money and drawings if either side walks.
Then think about the whole bill as three buckets: the design fee, the furnishings and the construction. The design fee is usually the one that scares people, and it’s often the smallest of the three once walls start moving. A one-room refresh with no construction is a design fee plus furniture. A kitchen or a whole first floor is all three, and the designer’s job is to keep the other two from running away. A light-touch engagement, one paid hour and a plan you carry out yourself on weekends, can be the best money in the whole project.
Two quotes aren’t comparable until they describe the same job. It’s the same discipline we argued for in our St. Louis concrete driveway cost guide.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should I pay for an interior designer?
A.  Nationally, HomeGuide puts most projects at $1,900 to $11,200, with hourly rates of $50 to $200. In St. Louis, Olive + Opal Interiors prices one fully designed room at $1,349, and PureWave Designs lists a $395 design consultation. Furniture is extra.
### Q. What is a normal budget for interior design?
A.  For one room on a flat fee, HomeGuide reports $1,000 to $12,000, and design-only help without furnishing runs $450 to $1,500 per room. Most design firms charge between $1,500 and $4,900 a room, and a St. Louis studio prices one fully designed room at $1,349, so decide first whether you need a plan or a finished room.
### Q. Is it worth paying for an interior designer?
A.  If your rooms work and simply look unresolved, a single paid hour is often worth it, because it ends the guessing. If you are moving walls or redoing a kitchen, a designer earns the fee by catching the expensive mistakes before they are built, and in an old brick St. Louis house those mistakes hide behind plaster.
### Q. Is it cheaper to use an interior designer?
A.  Rarely on the total, since you are adding a professional fee. Sometimes on furniture, when the designer buys at trade pricing and passes some of that through. Ask to see the trade cost and the markup as separate lines so you can tell.
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a designer?
A.  A designer who won’t disclose the furniture markup. A quote with no written scope or revision count. A large retainer with no milestones. A percentage fee and a markup on the same furniture without saying so. And in an older house, a designer who never asks about the plaster, the radiators or the electrical panel.

## You Have Weeks, Not Hours: St. Louis Termite Treatment Averages $416
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-pest-control-cost-in-st-louis
The screwdriver is supposed to knock. You push it into the wood sill along the basement wall, the way the inspector just did, and instead of a hard little tock you hear a soft, dry crunch, like stepping on a stale cracker. The blade sinks to the handle. Behind you, the man with the clipboard is already saying the words “today only.”
That sound is the most expensive noise a St. Louis house makes, and it is also the moment people spend the most money they didn’t need to spend. So breathe first. Missouri’s own extension guide says you can.
University of Missouri Extension puts it plainly in its guide to subterranean termites: if you find damage, there is no hurry to apply control measures. Termites work slowly, and a few weeks of delay are of little consequence. Use that time, the guide says, to choose a treatment and a professional carefully. The same guide tells you how to do the screwdriver test yourself: probe wood near the foundation, and termite-damaged wood offers little resistance.
Weeks, not hours. That changes the whole negotiation. It means you can get a second and third bid, ask who holds the termite license, and compare the treatment against what the job usually costs here. According to Angi’s St. Louis cost data, termite treatment in St. Louis averages $416, with most homeowners paying somewhere between $162 and $691. A quote far above that range is not automatically wrong, but it has to explain itself, line by line, before anyone signs. A termite price that is only good today is the one price you can always walk away from.
Three phone calls belong before any of that, and none of them is to a pest company. Rats, roaches or bed bugs inside a building in the City of St. Louis go to the city’s Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800. Mosquitoes in St. Louis County go to the county at 314-615-0680, the number county cities give residents for spraying requests. And for termites anywhere in Missouri, the state Pesticide Control Program at 573-751-5504 oversees the Category 7B license for termite pest control, so you can check the person holding the drill before you let him near your foundation.
Write those three numbers on the inside of the cabinet door under the sink.
### How much does pest control typically cost in St. Louis?
Most one-time pest control visits run $108 to $261, with an average of about $172, according to Angi’s national cost data. Ongoing plans bill per visit: about $40 to $70 for a monthly visit and $100 to $300 for a quarterly one. Termites are their own line. Angi puts termite treatment in St. Louis at an average of $416.
Those are the ordinary numbers, the ones for ants marching along the baseboard under the sink and the spider in the corner of the shower you pretend not to see. The bill turns ugly in two places: a specialty pest like termites or bed bugs, and the fees that sit around the plan rather than inside it. Both are easy to see coming once you know where to look, and neither one is something you have to decide in the driveway.
### One visit or a plan: which meter is running
It starts with a line of ants crossing the counter of a south city two-family toward the sugar bowl, the morning after the first warm rain. You call, you agree to a monthly price on the phone, and the first invoice shows up stuck to the storm door with a second line above that price that you don’t remember anyone saying out loud.
A one-time visit fits a problem you can point at: that ant trail, a wasp nest humming under the back porch rail, a single mouse that slipped in through a gap in the old brick when the nights turned cold. A plan is a subscription, and the price on the phone is only the monthly part. Angi’s national figures for a 1,500-square-foot home put the initial visit of an ongoing plan at $150 to $300, then $40 to $70 for each monthly visit or $100 to $300 for each quarterly one. That initial visit is the second line on the invoice.
Inspection fees can stack on top as well. Angi says pest inspections run $125 to $450 on average, that some companies inspect for free, and that the fee is sometimes waived or deducted from the bill if you go ahead with treatment. Ask which of those it is before the truck pulls into your driveway, not after.
St. Louis gives you a way to check that fee. Rottler Pest Solutions, which has been protecting St. Louis-area homes since 1956, says on its own St. Louis page that it gives a termite inspection free of charge before beginning treatment. So when a company wants a fee just to shine a flashlight into the damp back corner of a brick bungalow basement, where the paint flakes off the foundation wall and the air smells like wet cardboard, you know at least one local company that prices that look at zero. Ask the others to match it, or to take the fee off the treatment.
Over a full year, Fixr puts regular pest control treatments at $471 to $867. Put that next to whatever you are quoted, add the first-visit charge, and the real yearly cost of the plan is finally on the table.
### Why termites are the line item a St. Louis house cannot skip
Four species of termites are reported to occur naturally in Missouri, according to MU Extension, and all of them are subterranean. They live in the soil and come up into the house from below. The most common house-infesting termite in the United States, the eastern subterranean termite, is one of them.
You usually meet them in spring. MU Extension says swarming flights happen in Missouri during the spring months, usually on a warm, sunny day following rain. That is the morning you find a scatter of shed wings on a basement windowsill, light as dandruff, and a few more caught in the window track.
Old St. Louis houses give them a lot of doors. Foundations made of hollow block, or of masonry and rock, give termites several ways to reach the wood unseen, and consistently moist soil along a foundation wall is good termite habitat. The extension guide’s advice is the same advice that keeps a basement dry: slope the grade away from the house and point the downspouts away from the walls. Our guide to basement waterproofing in St. Louis covers that side of it.
One thing the guide is blunt about: there are no do-it-yourself termite control measures that effectively achieve the desired results. Treatment belongs to a licensed professional.
### Ask for the 7B, not just a business card
Missouri splits structural pest work into license categories. Category 7A covers general structural pests, with the exception of wood-destroying organisms. Category 7B covers wood-destroying organisms, including termites, carpenter ants and powderpost beetles. A company can be perfectly good at spiders and still not be the one you want drilling along your foundation.
So when the termite bid comes, ask a plain question: who on this job holds a 7B? If the answer is vague, the Missouri Department of Agriculture’s Pesticide Control Program is at 573-751-5504. It is a short call, and it separates a termite company from a general pest company taking a swing at a termite job.
### The scratching in the wall, and the city number to call first
Mice announce themselves at night. A light scrabble behind the drywall, a pause, then again, usually right where the headboard sits. By morning there is a dusting of droppings in the back of the cabinet under the sink.
Angi puts rodent extermination at $180 to $600, and Fixr puts a one-time rodent removal at $225 to $500, more if you want rechecks or live trapping. That pays for the mice in the house today. It does not seal the gap they came through.
In the City of St. Louis, that first number from the top of this page is the step before the exterminator. The Citizens’ Service Bureau takes reports of rats inside a building, rats seen on the exterior of a property, roaches inside a building and bed bugs, at 314-622-4800 or online. The city’s Vector Control program, which works to reduce mosquitoes and rats, is at 314-657-1500. I could not find on the city’s pages exactly what happens after each kind of report, so ask when you call.
Half of these problems start in the yard. Here’s what lawn care costs in St. Louis.
### Mosquitoes: call the county before you buy a season
You hear them before you see them, that thin whine at your ear on the patio after dark. Angi puts mosquito removal at $350 to $500.
In St. Louis County, check the public program first. Cities that contract with the county health department tell residents to call St. Louis County at 314-615-0680 to request mosquito spraying or report a mosquito concern. One of them lists the county’s work, which includes inspecting properties, sampling water for larvae, trapping adult mosquitoes to test for disease and ultra-low volume mist spraying when outbreaks are found. In the city, a mosquito breeding site or a spraying request goes to the Citizens’ Service Bureau.
Public spraying covers a neighborhood, not your shady side yard. But a phone call about the standing water two doors down costs nothing, and it is the honest first move before you sign a season-long program.
### Bed bugs: the most expensive routine pest
Bed bugs are the job that keeps people up in every sense. Angi puts bed bug extermination at $1,000 to $4,000 and says a major treatment can cost as much as $6,000. Fixr puts the range at $300 to $3,500, from chemically treating one bedroom on the low end to heat treating a whole four or five-bedroom home on the high end.
Before you compare those numbers, ask every company the same question: are follow-up visits in the price, or billed separately? That one answer moves the real total more than the method does.
The plan, priced in full
### How much does pest control charge?
A one-time visit typically runs $108 to $261, per Angi. On a plan, add an initial visit of $150 to $300 to the $40 to $70 monthly or $100 to $300 quarterly rate; the pest, the size of the house and how bad the infestation is move it most.
### Six questions that make three quotes comparable
Lay the bids on the kitchen table and ask each company the same six things. The quotes stop being three numbers and start being three offers you can rank.
What is the initial visit fee, and is it waived if I sign up for a plan?
Is there an inspection fee, and is it deducted if I hire you?
Does each scheduled visit include the inside of the house, or only the outside unless I ask?
Are return visits between scheduled ones included, or billed as extra visits?
For termites, who on the job holds a Category 7B license?
For bed bugs, are follow-up treatments in this price?
If you are still deciding who to call rather than what to spend, our companion piece on how to choose a pest control company in St. Louis covers red flags, guarantees and the questions to ask before anyone treats your home.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $50 a month good for pest control?
A.  Yes, it sits inside the normal range. Angi puts a monthly pest control visit at $40 to $70. Before you judge it, add the initial visit, which Angi puts at $150 to $300 on an ongoing plan, and ask whether the inside of the house is treated or only the outside.
### Q. Why is my monthly pest control bill so high?
A.  Usually because something sits around the monthly rate: an initial visit of $150 to $300, an inspection fee of $125 to $450 that was never waived, or more visits than the problem needs. Angi says a one-off problem shouldn’t need regular service, while a persistent, significant problem may need quarterly or monthly visits. Ask for an itemized statement.
### Q. Is it expensive to get rid of termites in your house?
A.  Less than most people fear. Angi’s St. Louis data puts termite treatment at an average of $416, with most homeowners paying between $162 and $691. The expensive part is the damage: Angi says termite repairs average about $1,000 to $3,000.
### Q. Is it worth paying for pest control?
A.  For termites, there is no real alternative. MU Extension says there are no do-it-yourself termite control measures that effectively achieve the desired results. For a one-off problem like a single wasp nest, a single visit is enough and a standing plan usually isn’t worth it.
### Q. How much should you spend on pest control?
A.  For ordinary pests, Angi puts the average at about $172 a visit, with most homeowners paying $108 to $261. Fixr puts a full year of regular treatments at $471 to $867. Much more than that should mean a specific problem, like termites or bed bugs, priced on its own line.
### Q. Is pest control a rip-off?
A.  Not when you can read the meter. The bad deals hide in the fees around the plan and in pressure to sign the same day. For termites, MU Extension says a few weeks of delay are of little consequence, so take the time to get three bids and check the 7B license at 573-751-5504.
### Q. How fast do I need to act after finding termites?
A.  You have weeks. MU Extension says that if you find damage, there is no hurry to apply control measures, because termites work slowly. Use the time to pick a treatment and a licensed professional.

## Old Tile Under St. Louis Carpet May Be Asbestos. Lift a Corner Before You Pay.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-new-flooring-cost-in-st-louis
Your thumbnail catches the edge of a cold, hard square under the carpet, and that is the moment a St. Louis flooring budget can change. You’ve pried the carpet back in the bedroom closet of a south city brick two-family, the tack strip bites your knuckle, the old pad crumbles in your fingers, and under all of it the floor is one of two things: narrow strips of wood with a dull gray sheen, or hard, cold squares of old vinyl tile with a crust of glue along the seams.
That one touch, before any showroom or sample board, decides which flooring bill you’re about to get.
Wood means you might be shopping for the wrong job. HomeAdvisor’s cost data puts refinishing at about $3 to $8 a square foot, while most new installs fall between $3 and $22. Squares mean stop. The EPA lists vinyl floor tiles, the backing on vinyl sheet flooring and the adhesives among the places asbestos may be found, and it tells homeowners not to sand or try to level asbestos flooring.
Here is the part the national price guides never mention, and it splits right at the city line. Missouri’s own asbestos rule exempts a single residential structure with four or fewer dwelling units, which on paper covers that two-family and most four-families too. The city doesn’t stop there. In the City of St. Louis, asbestos abatement projects of more than 10 square feet of asbestos-containing material fall under Ordinance 71332, and the Health Department’s Air Pollution Control Program lists a $100 fee for an asbestos abatement notification. That is not much floor. Demolition, renovation and abatement projects in the city must be reported on the STL City Permits website. I could not confirm whether the city ordinance carries the state’s small-building exemption, so call the program at (314) 657-1479 before the first square comes up with a flat bar. Or do what the EPA suggests: when asbestos flooring needs replacing, put the new floor covering over it if you can.
### How much does it cost to floor 1000 sq ft fully installed?
For 1,000 square feet installed, HomeAdvisor’s cost data puts vinyl at $2,000 to $14,000, laminate at $3,000 to $13,000, carpet at $3,500 to $11,000, hardwood at $6,000 to $25,000 and tile at $15,000 to $20,000 or more. Those prices include ripping up and hauling away the old floor, but not subflooring, underlayment, baseboards or trim.
Read those ranges the way you’d read a contractor’s face when he steps on the soft spot by the bathroom door. The low end is a flat, square room with nothing hiding underneath. The high end is everything else. Labor is the bigger half of the money: HomeAdvisor says to plan on putting roughly 60% of the total toward the flooring pro, with materials covering the rest. That is why two quotes for the same plank can land thousands apart, and why the cheapest one usually just hasn’t looked under your carpet yet.
### What the wood under your carpet is worth
In a south city bungalow, run your palm across a strip of old oak once the carpet is gone and you can feel every tack hole and the gritty line where the pad glue dried. It looks tired. It usually isn’t finished. Solid hardwood can take several refinishings over its life, while engineered planks reach their limit after one or two, according to HomeAdvisor.
The money gap is wide. Refinishing averages $1,892, with most projects between $1,107 and $2,681. Installing new hardwood averages $5 to $15 a square foot. On a 1,000-square-foot main floor, that is roughly $3,000 to $8,000 to sand and finish what you already own against $5,000 to $15,000 to start over, before anyone touches a subfloor.
A board or two will be shot, maybe by a radiator that leaked or a dog that never made it outside. Replacing a floorboard runs $6 to $12 a square foot, which is pocket change next to a tear-out. If you’re still deciding between wood, laminate and vinyl once you know what’s down there, our guide to hardwood, laminate, or vinyl in St. Louis homes picks up right there.
### The basement floor starts with the water, not the plank
Go down the basement steps of a St. Louis brick house after a hard rain and put your hand flat on the bare slab. If it feels cool and faintly damp, that slab is telling you what it will do to whatever you lay on it. Luxury vinyl plank is the usual answer down there, and a vapor barrier under any floating floor on a slab is cheap insurance against the musty smell that shows up a year later.
For vinyl, HomeAdvisor puts materials at $2 to $7 a square foot on most jobs, with labor adding another $3 to $10. Wear layer and plank rigidity drive most of the spread. A thin, floppy plank telegraphs every bump in an old slab, and you feel it underfoot every time you walk to the laundry.
If the lower level has ever taken water, fix that first. Our St. Louis basement waterproofing guide covers the drainage and grading side, and the order of operations is simple: water first, then floor.
### The lines that quietly grow a flooring quote
The plank price is the number everyone shops. The prep is the number that decides whether you stay on budget, and in an older house it starts the minute the crew pulls up the first row and goes quiet.
Somebody always asks where the couch goes while the floors cure. Here’s what a storage unit costs in St. Louis.
Ask for each of these as its own line, with a dollar figure beside it, so you can lay three bids side by side on the kitchen table:
What is not in the per-foot price. HomeAdvisor’s installed prices include tear-out and disposal of the old floor, but not subflooring, underlayment, baseboards or trim.
Prep and furniture moving. HomeAdvisor says to account for $150 to $300 for extra prep and moving furniture.
Carpet removal before a refinish. Carpet removal averages $120 to $720, plus $75 to $150 to haul it away.
Board repair. Hardwood floor repairs run $200 to $600.
Stairs. Refinishing stairs and railings runs $4.50 to $8 a square foot.
Old-house edges. Radiator feet, framed floor registers, pocket door tracks and shoe molding someone caulked to the floor all eat finish-carpentry hours. Ask how they were counted.
### Tile, carpet and the rooms that get wet
Tile is the cold, solid floor you feel through your socks on a January morning, and it is priced like it. Tile installation can run from $3 to $30 a square foot, according to HomeAdvisor, and it still earns its place in baths, entries and mudrooms. Substrate prep drives a big share of the bill in an older house, so read our guide to choosing a tile installer in St. Louis before you sign.
Carpet is still the softest, quietest way to cover a bedroom. Builder-grade olefin and polyester cost less than wool, and the pad underneath is where cheap bids cut corners you won’t feel until the second winter.
Holding a big-box quote up
### How much does Home Depot charge to install a floor?
I could not find a per-square-foot installation rate Home Depot publishes, so measure its quote against the market. HomeAdvisor puts most installs at $3 to $22 a square foot, with labor taking roughly 60% of the total; material quality and room size move it most.
### When the old tile stays where it is
There is a quieter way through the asbestos question, and it costs less than abatement. Leave the old squares down, sealed under a new floor, and nobody breathes what is in them. The EPA says that when asbestos flooring needs replacing, new floor covering should go over it if possible, and that you should not sand it, scrape it or try to level it.
That points you toward floors that float. HomeAdvisor calls the biggest advantage of laminate the fact that it can be installed over existing floors, and installed laminate runs $1.70 to $17 a square foot. Underlayment is necessary for vinyl, laminate and carpet, and it costs $0.50 to $5.40 a square foot to install. If the subfloor itself has gone soft, the kind of give you feel through your shoe near a toilet or an old radiator, subfloor replacement runs $3 to $10 a square foot. On an old tile floor, that work is exactly what disturbs the tile, so it is the moment to have the material tested first.
Ask every bidder the same plain question while you stand in the room together: are you going over the old floor, or taking it out? The answer changes the price, the dust and, inside the city, possibly the paperwork.
### What one room costs, and how fast it goes in
Most homeowners don’t floor a whole house at once. They do the living room first, the one where the carpet has a path worn from the couch to the kitchen. For a typical 320-square-foot living room, HomeAdvisor says to expect about $4,000, with a budget pick as low as $960 and a high-end makeover at $7,000 or more.
The install itself is faster than the shopping. A straightforward 200-square-foot room of laminate can wrap up in roughly three hours once the boards have acclimated for at least three days, while stone or ceramic tile stretches into a full day. Clear the room yourself if you can: pros usually charge $60 to $120 an hour to move furniture, and a packed room turns into a line on the bill.
### How to read a flooring quote before you sign
A quote you can compare names the product and its wear layer or thickness, splits labor from material, says who hauls the old floor, sets a subfloor repair allowance, and spells out what happens if they open the floor and find more. If one bid is far lower than the other two, look for what it left out. On an old house, the low bid is usually the crew that skipped the subfloor conversation.
### Lift the carpet, then line up three bids
Know what is under your carpet before anyone prices it. Then compare refinishers and installers in the St Louis Near Me Directory flooring category and ask each one for the same scope, line by line.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood floors or replace them?
A.  Refinishing is cheaper in nearly every case. HomeAdvisor puts refinishing at $3 to $8 a square foot against an average of $5 to $15 a square foot to install new hardwood. Replacement starts to make sense with severe water damage, warping or board separation.
### Q. How much does it cost to refinish 1000 square feet of hardwood floors?
A.  At $3 to $8 a square foot, 1,000 square feet comes to roughly $3,000 to $8,000. Dustless equipment adds an average of $2 a square foot, and bigger jobs often get a lower per-foot rate.
### Q. Can I stay in my house while floors are refinished?
A.  Many people do, but plan to live around a sealed-off room. Even dustless sanding is not dust-free. Water-based topcoats take two to four hours to dry, while oil-based topcoats take up to 10 hours, so the finish you pick sets how long you tiptoe around it.
### Q. How much does a contractor charge to install LVP?
A.  HomeAdvisor puts vinyl labor at $3 to $10 a square foot, with materials adding $2 to $7 on most jobs. Add a vapor barrier over a basement slab and leveling if the floor is wavy.
### Q. What are the downsides of luxury vinyl plank flooring?
A.  Vinyl can gouge more easily than harder flooring materials, according to HomeAdvisor, and a thin plank shows every hump in an old subfloor. There is no sanding it back like oak; when the wear layer is gone, you replace it.
### Q. Is it cheaper to do tile or hardwood floors?
A.  Per 1,000 square feet, HomeAdvisor puts tile at $15,000 to $20,000 or more and hardwood at $6,000 to $25,000, so hardwood usually starts cheaper. Tile wins in rooms that get wet.
### Q. Can old floor tile under carpet contain asbestos?
A.  Yes. The EPA lists vinyl floor tiles, the backing on vinyl sheet flooring and the adhesives among the places asbestos may be found. Do not sand or level it. In the City of St. Louis, abatement of more than 10 square feet falls under Ordinance 71332; call Air Pollution Control at (314) 657-1479 first.

## A $40 St. Louis Storage Unit Becomes $80 in Month Five
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-self-storage-cost-in-st-louis
$24. That is what the payment screen says in month five for a 5x5 at Public Storage on Gravois Road, the unit you booked online at $12 a month. Nobody snuck it past you. It was printed on the listing the day you clicked Reserve: $12 a month online, $24 in-store rent for months five through twelve.
You read it standing in the corridor, phone in one hand, padlock key in the other. The listing calls this one a ground-floor inside unit with a swing door, near the door or elevator, so the Gravois traffic is only a muffled hiss behind you. The hinge squeaks when you pull the door open. Inside is the box marked KITCHEN in your own handwriting, the rolled rug, the lamp with no shade, all of it exactly where you left it the week you swore this would be temporary.
It isn’t one building. On the same Public Storage page, a climate-controlled 10x10 downtown on South 3rd Street lists at $40 online and $80 in-store for months five through twelve. A 10x20 on Watson Road lists at $121 online and $242 in-store. Every new rental adds a one-time $29 admin fee. North side of the map or south, small unit or big, the same doubling.
Same unit. Same lock. Twice the rent.
And here is the Missouri part nobody tapes to the office window. If that higher bill goes unpaid, state law gives the facility a lien on everything in the unit, and once you are in default for more than forty-five days the operator may sell what is stored there. The rug. The lamp. The kitchen box. If the sale brings in more than you owed, the extra is held for you, and if nobody claims it within a year after the sale, Missouri law sends it to the state treasurer. You can still pay what you owe and take your things home any time before the sale, but the clock is real, and it can start with a bill you never budgeted for.
So make one call before you sign, and say it just like this: “What is the in-store rent on this exact unit for months five through twelve, and can you email it to me?” Then set a reminder for just before month five and call again: “Your website shows my unit size for new customers at a lower price than I am about to pay. Can you do better, or should I move to a smaller unit?” Public Storage says all rentals are month to month, so you are never stuck, and the person who picks up knows it.
### How much is a storage unit in STL?
On Public Storage’s St. Louis listings, online prices start as low as $12 a month for a 5x5 and $40 for a climate-controlled 10x10 downtown, but those are welcome rates. The same listings show in-store rent for months five through twelve of $24 for that 5x5 and $80 for that 10x10, plus a one-time $29 admin fee on every new rental.
So budget on the second number, not the first. Do the math in the parking lot with the engine running and the air on your face. If the in-store rent fits your month without a wince, the welcome rate is a bonus. If only the welcome rate fits, you are not renting a $40 unit. You are renting an $80 unit with a coupon that runs out before month five, and it runs out right about when you still haven’t decided what to do with the things inside.
### The calendar trick that beats the price jump
The fix costs nothing but a phone reminder. The day you sign, open your calendar and count forward to the start of month five. Set an alert for two weeks before it. When it goes off, drive over on a cool morning, roll up the door, and look at what is actually in there. The air inside will smell like dust and old paper. Some boxes you will not even remember packing.
That is the moment to decide. Keep paying the higher rent with your eyes open. Move to a smaller size. Sell, donate or haul away the things nobody in the family wants, then turn in the key. Every one of those is a fine answer. The only expensive answer is the one where the alert never existed and month five turns into year three.
If the honest answer is that most of it should go, compare a year of rent against what it costs to clear it out once. That comparison ends a lot of storage bills.
### What each size really holds
Renting one size too big is the most common money leak in storage, and it happens because square feet are abstract while a pile of furniture in the driveway is very real. Public Storage’s own size guide puts it in rooms:
5x5: a large closet. Seasonal bins, boxes of books and papers, golf clubs. Not furniture.
5x10: one room. The furniture from a studio or a light bedroom.
10x10: three rooms.
10x15: four rooms.
10x20: five rooms.
Rooms are a rough ruler, so do the driveway test. Stack everything you plan to store in the garage or on the driveway, step back, and look at the footprint of the pile. Count the big rigid things, not the bedrooms: a sectional, a treadmill, a washer and dryer and a dining table will eat a unit no matter how small the apartment they came out of. Leave a path down the middle of whatever you rent. You will need the thing in the back corner some cold Saturday, and you will not want to unload the whole unit onto wet pavement to reach it.
Maybe the unit isn’t the answer at all. Here is what hiring a home organizer costs in St. Louis.
### What Missouri lets a facility do if you fall behind
This is the part people learn too late, usually from an envelope that sits unopened on the kitchen counter under the car keys for a week. Missouri law gives the operator of a self-service storage facility a lien on everything in your unit for unpaid rent and charges. The rules are written into state statute, and they run on a calendar:
If you are in default for more than forty-five days, the operator may enforce the lien and sell what is stored in your space.
The operator has to notify you of the default at least forty-five days before disposing of anything, by first-class mail or email to your last known address.
A second notice comes no sooner than ten days after the first, and it has to give you at least ten days to pay.
At least seven days before the sale, the operator has to advertise it in the classified section of a newspaper.
Any money left over after the debt is paid is held for you for one year.
At any time before the sale, you can pay what is owed and get your things back.
That last line matters most. It is not over until the sale. If money gets tight, the worst move is silence. Call the office the week you know you will be short, not the week the second notice arrives. A phone call is a much easier conversation than an auction.

Whoever’s welcome rate you catch, for a few months. Size, location and climate control move the number most.
### Is climate control worth it in a St. Louis summer?
Stand inside a metal drive-up unit on a July afternoon with the door rolled up and you will have your answer for some of your things. The air is thick. The walls tick as they heat. Cardboard goes soft at the corners.
What is in the box decides it, not what it cost. Solid wood furniture, electronics, photographs, vinyl records, leather, instruments and artwork are the things heat and damp ruin slowly, and slow damage is the kind you discover a year later when the drawer won’t close. Yard tools, bikes, ladders, patio furniture and sealed plastic bins of clothes mostly ride out a summer fine. And climate control is not a mold guarantee: anything that goes in damp, like a rug, a mattress or a tent, needs to be bone dry first, conditioned building or not.
Price the difference at the facility you are actually considering, on the same size, and compare in-store rent to in-store rent. That is the only comparison that will still be true in month five.
### Questions to ask before you sign
Ask these by phone or email from your couch, before move-in day, when you still have time and leverage, not at the counter with a loaded truck idling outside:
What does this rate become, and when? Get the in-store rent for the unit, in writing.
What is due at move-in besides the first month? Admin fee, lock, insurance, itemized.
Is insurance required, and will you accept my homeowners or renters policy instead?
How much notice do I owe when I leave, and how do I give it?
What are the gate hours, and are they different from office hours?
Is this unit climate controlled or only temperature controlled? They are not the same thing.
Ask every facility the same questions, word for word, and the prices finally line up side by side. It is the same habit that makes moving quotes comparable.
### What not to put in the unit, and the one thing you can’t do there
Every lease has a prohibited list, and it is close to the same everywhere: gasoline and propane, aerosols and paint thinner, perishable food that draws pests to the whole building, plants and animals, and hazardous chemicals. Drain the mower and leave the grill tank at home. Keep passports, car titles, medication, tax records and hard drives with you too. They aren’t banned, but a locked unit across town is the wrong place for anything you might need at ten at night.
And the question people ask quietly: you can’t live in a storage unit. Missouri law says an occupant may not use a leased space for residential purposes, and an operator may not knowingly allow it. If housing is the real problem behind the search, that is a different search, and there is real help in this metro for it.

## Same Hour, $30 Less: The St. Louis Deep Tissue First-Visit Rate
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-therapeutic-massage-costs-in-st-louis
“Tell me if it gets to be too much.”
Then her forearm sinks into the back of your right calf, slow as a closing door, and the sound that comes out of you is half laugh, half groan. The sheet is warm. The lotion smells like nothing in particular, and you notice that because for once your brain is quiet enough to notice anything. That calf has been a clenched fist since you started running the Forest Park loop. The foam roller didn’t touch it. Neither did stretching against the kitchen counter or the heating pad on the couch. Ten minutes in, something under her arm finally lets go, and you feel it spread up the back of your knee like warm water.
That hour cost $100 at StlMassageWorX on South Kingshighway, the same price the studio charges for 60 minutes of Swedish. On Chouteau, Richmassagestl.com charges $130 for an hour of deep tissue. Same city. Different bill.

Before you trust anybody’s hands, though, spend a minute on their license. The City of St. Louis adds its own gate: anyone applying for a massage therapy business license in the city must first be licensed by the State of Missouri. A good studio will tell you on the phone, without a pause, that every therapist there is licensed.
### How much does a massage typically cost in St. Louis?
At two City of St. Louis studios, an hour of massage runs $100 to $130 and ninety minutes runs $140 to $180, by each studio’s own booking page.
