A 30-minute express session there is $65.
The real bill shows up an hour later, in the car. Your shoulders sit an inch lower. You check the mirror and back out slowly because your neck turns farther than it did when you parked. That is what you are paying for, and it is why the cheapest hour is not always the right one and the priciest is not always better. Studios change rates, so read the number off the studio’s own page or hear it on the phone before you book.
### Deep tissue without the deep-tissue markup
You feel deep tissue in your teeth a little: the slow lean of a forearm, the therapist’s weight coming down through one point, your breath going shallow until she says “breathe into it.” It is hard work on the therapist’s own body, and most people assume it always costs extra because of that. Sometimes it barely does. At StlMassageWorX, 90 minutes of deep tissue and 90 minutes of Swedish are both $140. At Richmassagestl.com, deep tissue is $130 against $125 for its stress relief massage, and $180 against $175 for ninety minutes.
So the premium you have been bracing for can be zero, or the price of a coffee. Ask on the phone: do you charge extra for deeper pressure, or is pressure part of the hour?
Deep tissue should feel like the good ache after a hard workout, never sharp, never the kind of pain that makes you hold your breath. Pressure is a conversation. The client who says “lighter there” gets a better hour than the client who lies still and suffers politely.
### The extra half hour is the cheapest one you will buy
An hour on the table is never an hour of hands-on work. You talk through where it hurts, you undress, you settle under the sheet, and at the end you sit up slowly and find your socks. Those minutes come out of your session whether it is sixty or ninety long.
That is why the longer booking tends to win for therapeutic work. At StlMassageWorX, going from 60 to 90 minutes of deep tissue takes the bill from $100 to $140. At Richmassagestl.com, deep tissue goes from $130 to $180. Either way you pay for the setup once, and nearly every added minute is hands on muscle. ### Thirty minutes for one stubborn spot
Sometimes you don’t need the whole body done. You need the one knot under your shoulder blade that has been pinching since you started hauling the laundry basket up the basement stairs. Richmassagestl.com sells an Express Session of 30 minutes for $65, and the booking page asks you to pick the area you want to prioritize when you book. That is a fair way to try a therapist before you commit to a longer hour, and a smart buy when the problem is one spot. It is a poor buy for full-body deep tissue, which needs time to warm the surrounding muscle before the real work starts. Book it for the knot, and you walk back out to the car with one shoulder sitting lower than the other, rolling it in small circles at the stoplight, surprised by how lopsided relief can feel.

### What five hundred hours buys you on the table
A cheap hour from someone unlicensed is the most expensive hour on this page. Missouri law spells out how a licensed therapist’s five hundred hours of supervised instruction break down: three hundred hours of massage theory and practice techniques, one hundred of anatomy and physiology, and the rest in business, ethics, hygiene, Missouri law and ancillary therapies including CPR and first aid.
The quick check, step by step:
Search the therapist’s name in the state MOPRO license search.
Make sure the license is current and shows no discipline.
Can’t find a record? Call the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage at 573-522-6277 or email massagether@pr.mo.gov before you book.
When you call a studio, ask it plainly: is every therapist here licensed by the state? A good shop answers before you finish the sentence.
If the answer is a pause and a change of subject, you just saved yourself a bad hour, and it cost you nothing.
One more reason the license matters for your wallet. A licensed therapist went through anatomy and physiology, so they know when deep pressure is the wrong call: a fresh injury, a recent surgery, a medication that thins your blood, a swollen leg that should be seen by a doctor first. Tell them about all of it on the intake form, even if it feels unrelated. The cheapest massage is the one that doesn’t send you to urgent care afterward.

## Die Without a Will in Missouri and Your Spouse Does Not Get Everything: What a Will or Trust Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-will-or-trust-costs-in-missouri
Die married in Missouri without a will, and your spouse does not inherit everything. Not the whole house. Not the whole checking account. The kitchen goes quiet after the funeral luncheon: casseroles stacked in foil by the sink, the refrigerator humming, his reading glasses still folded on the counter next to a folder of bank statements nobody wants to open. The house still smells like him. And under Missouri law, part of it now belongs to the kids.
Here is the rule nobody tells you at the funeral home. When there are children and all of them are also the surviving spouse’s children, Missouri’s intestacy law gives the spouse the first $20,000 of the estate plus one-half of the balance, and the children split the rest in equal parts. If even one child is from an earlier relationship, the spouse’s share is one-half of the estate. On a $220,000 estate with shared children, that comes to $120,000 for the spouse and $100,000 for the kids, and some of the kids’ share may be sitting inside the house their mother still sleeps in.
Then comes the bill nobody quoted you. Without other planning, that property moves through probate, and the lawyer’s fee comes with a floor written into state law. Section 473.153 of the Missouri statutes sets the attorney’s minimum compensation as a percentage of the personal property administered and the proceeds of real estate sold under the court’s order: 5 percent of the first $5,000, sliding down to 2 percent on the largest estates. The personal representative is allowed a minimum on the same schedule. Say the probate base is $300,000 in accounts and sale proceeds: by that schedule, the floor works out to $8,800 for the attorney and another $8,800 for the personal representative.
The fix for the house is one recorded page. A Missouri beneficiary deed, part of what the statutes call the Nonprobate Transfers Law of Missouri, names who gets the house at your death, as long as it is filed with the recorder of deeds before you die. For a city house, the Recorder of Deeds takes land records at City Hall, Room 126, 1200 Market St., (314) 622-3260, and a standard deed records for $25 for the first page plus $5 for each additional page. Set $25 next to $8,800 and you can feel the floor shift under the whole conversation.
For the rest of the plan, here is a price tag you can actually read. TuckerAllen, a St. Louis-area estate planning firm that posts its prices, lists a will package at $1,649 for an individual and a trust package at $2,795. If a death has already happened, the estate goes to the probate division where the person lived: in St. Louis County, the 5th Floor of the Courts Building at 105 South Central in Clayton (general information 314-615-2629); in the city, the 10th floor of the Civil Courts Building at 10 North Tucker Boulevard (314-622-4238). Estates of $40,000 or less after debts may qualify for a small estate affidavit instead. This is cost information, not legal advice.
### Is it cheaper to do a will or a trust?
A will is cheaper to write and can cost more later. One St. Louis-area firm, TuckerAllen, lists its will package at $1,649 for an individual and its trust package at $2,795. A will still goes through probate, where Missouri law sets a minimum attorney fee as a percentage of the estate.
Read what’s in each box before you compare the numbers, ideally at a table with the quotes spread out flat and a pen in your hand, because the names sound alike and the contents don’t. TuckerAllen’s will package includes a last will and testament, a healthcare directive (living will), a medical power of attorney, a HIPAA release, a financial power of attorney and a deed. Couples pay $2,499. The trust package adds a revocable living trust and a pour-over will to the same health and financial documents. Its list ends with “Trust Funding Instructions,” and couples pay $3,995. Its power of attorney package on its own is $650 for an individual, and the firm lists a one-hour appointment as free.
Notice those last three words of the trust list. Instructions. A trust only skips probate for what you actually move into it, and the deed signing and the trips to the bank are often yours to finish. When one office quotes you a number and another quotes you twice that, ask each one for its document list in writing and ask, out loud, who does the funding. That one question explains most of the gap between two quotes that sound like the same thing.
Do I need a lawyer for a will in Missouri, though? Start with what the statute itself asks for. Missouri’s will law asks for a will in writing, signed by you or by someone at your direction and in your presence, and attested by two or more competent witnesses who sign in your presence. What the fee buys is the drafting judgment and a signing done right, which you only notice the day someone challenges the paper.
### What Missouri’s probate fee schedule charges your family
Here is the full ladder from section 473.153. On the first $5,000, 5 percent. On the next $20,000, 4 percent. On the next $75,000, 3 percent. On the next $300,000, 2.75 percent. On the next $600,000, 2.5 percent. On everything over $1,000,000, 2 percent. It is a floor, not a cap: when reasonable compensation runs higher, the statute tells the court to allow the additional amount.
Prices one firm posts
### How much does a lawyer charge for estate planning?
TuckerAllen, a St. Louis-area estate planning firm that posts its prices, lists $1,649 for an individual will package and $2,795 for a trust package. A will can cost more later, because it still goes through probate, where Missouri law sets a minimum attorney fee as a percentage of the estate.
Do the math once and it stops being abstract. On $100,000 in the probate base, the attorney’s minimum is $250 plus $800 plus $2,250, or $3,300. The personal representative is allowed a minimum on the same schedule, though a family member serving in that role may choose to waive it. That’s why the trust pitch exists, and on those numbers it isn’t a crazy pitch.
But read the base, because this is where marketing gets sloppy. The percentages apply to the personal property administered and the proceeds of real estate sold under the probate court’s order. Property that never enters probate isn’t in that number at all. And in Missouri, keeping the house out of probate can cost a lot less than a trust.
Random, but: Bridgeton’s dinner options are worth a look.
### The deed that keeps a Missouri house out of court
It’s called a beneficiary deed, and the statute covering it is titled “Deeds effective on death of owner.” A deed that expressly states it is not to take effect until the death of the owner transfers the property to the beneficiary you named, effective at your death, as long as it is signed and filed with the recorder of deeds in the city or county where the property sits before the owner dies. It doesn’t have to be delivered to the beneficiary, and it can even point the house into a trust.
The word that matters is “before.” A beneficiary deed signed at the kitchen table and slid into a desk drawer, under the takeout menus and the old checkbook, is the classic way this goes wrong. Record it. For a city house that means the walk up the steps of City Hall to Room 126 with the original in a folder, and a fee that starts at $25 for a standard deed. City records require the legal description to include the City Block Number and Lot Number, so copy it straight off your current deed. Then make a copy and tell the person you named where the original is.
One more trap undoes more plans than any other. In Missouri, a beneficiary designation may not be revoked or changed by a will unless the designation itself expressly gives you that right. So if an old life insurance policy, a payable-on-death account or a beneficiary deed still names an ex-spouse, the new will you sign next month doesn’t fix it. The designation wins. Pull every one of them out and read the names before you pay anyone to draft anything.
### Does a will in Missouri need to be notarized?
Not to be valid. Missouri’s will statute asks for two or more competent witnesses. A self-proving affidavit is the extra step. Under Missouri’s self-proved will statute, a written will can be made self-proved by the acknowledgment of the testator and the witnesses, each made before an officer authorized to administer oaths, at the signing or any time after. That short affidavit means your family isn’t hunting down two witnesses years later to testify about an afternoon they barely remember.
It’s also the reason a handwritten page in a drawer worries lawyers. Missouri’s will statute requires two or more competent witnesses who sign in the testator’s presence, and a page written alone at a desk has none. If that page is all there is, assume the intestacy split in the opening is what your family will be living with.
Signing day is where a lot of people meet a notary for the first time, so it helps to know where to get a document notarized in St. Louis before you need one.
### How long probate holds the money
Cost is half of it. Time is the other half, and the floor is set by statute. Under section 473.360, creditor claims not filed in the probate division within six months after the first published notice of letters testamentary or of administration are forever barred. That window is the practical minimum for an estate that goes through full administration, however simple it is.
Picture what six months means in a real house. The thermostat set low to keep the gas bill down. The mail piling on the mat. A lawn somebody has to mow every other week. The estate still pays the insurance and the utilities while everyone waits.
### When a small estate can skip full probate
Missouri has a short path for modest estates. Under section 473.097, a small estate affidavit can work when the value of the entire estate, less liens, debt and encumbrances, does not exceed $40,000, and thirty days have passed since the death with no application for letters pending. That covers a car and a checking account. A paid-off house usually blows through it.
That’s one more reason the cheap documents matter most. A recorded beneficiary deed and a payable-on-death designation on each account keep those assets out of the estate count altogether, which can be the difference between a short affidavit and a six-month case.
### Questions to ask before you hire anyone
Take these to the first meeting. The answers will tell you more than the price does.
Is this a flat fee, and what exactly is in it? Ask for the document list in writing.
Does the trust fee include funding: preparing and recording the deed and changing the accounts over, or only instructions?
What falls outside the flat fee, and how is that billed?
Given what I own, would a beneficiary deed and payable-on-death designations do most of this for less?
Will you check my existing beneficiary designations against the new plan?
Who will be at the signing, and will the will be self-proved?
The fourth question separates a counselor from a salesperson. A good answer works through your facts. A bad one changes the subject. Hearing that a deed and a few beneficiary forms may cover most of what you own is not a lesser plan. For a lot of St. Louis families with one house and a few accounts, it is the plan.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a lawyer for a will in Missouri?
A.  Start with the statute. A valid Missouri will must be in writing, signed by you or by someone at your direction in your presence, and attested by two or more competent witnesses who sign in your presence. A lawyer’s fee buys drafting judgment, a proper signing and a check of your beneficiary designations.
### Q. Does a will in Missouri need to be notarized?
A.  No. Missouri requires two witnesses for a valid will. A will can also be made self-proved by the testator and the witnesses acknowledging it before an officer authorized to administer oaths, which spares your family from tracking down the witnesses later.
### Q. What happens to a bank account when someone dies without a will in Missouri?
A.  If the account has a payable-on-death beneficiary, a will couldn’t have changed that designation anyway unless the designation allowed it. If it has no beneficiary, it becomes part of the estate and Missouri’s intestacy law divides it: with a spouse and shared children, the spouse gets the first $20,000 plus half the balance and the children share the rest. Estates of $40,000 or less after debts may use a small estate affidavit after thirty days.
### Q. Do you have to go to probate if you have a will in Missouri?
A.  Often, yes. Under Missouri law, a will, to be effective as a will, must be presented for and admitted to probate. What stays out of probate is property that passes another way, such as a house with a beneficiary deed recorded before death or an account with a named beneficiary.
### Q. How much does a living trust cost in Missouri?
A.  Prices vary by firm and complexity. As one published St. Louis-area benchmark, TuckerAllen lists its trust package at $2,795 for an individual and $3,995 for a couple, including a pour-over will, health care and financial powers of attorney, and trust funding instructions. Ask any firm whether funding the trust is included or left to you.
### Q. What is the downside of having a living trust?
A.  It costs more up front than a will, and it only works for what you actually move into it. A trust package that ends with funding instructions leaves you to retitle the house and the accounts.
### Q. What is the biggest mistake with wills?
A.  Assuming the will controls everything. In Missouri, a will can’t revoke or change a beneficiary designation unless the designation expressly allows it, so an old policy or account naming an ex-spouse still pays the ex-spouse. The second mistake is a handwritten page with no witnesses, when Missouri’s will statute requires two or more competent witnesses.

## What Car Insurance Costs in St. Louis (and Why Your ZIP Code Moves the Price)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-car-insurance-costs-in-st-louis
A driver in Affton opens the renewal notice at the kitchen counter and reads it twice. Same 2016 sedan. Same clean record. Same job, same commute, same everything. The premium went up anyway, and nothing on the page explains why.
Fifteen miles west in Chesterfield, a friend with a nearly identical car and a nearly identical driving history pays noticeably less for the same coverage. Not because of anything either of them did behind the wheel. The gap opened up before either of them ever asked for a quote.
And somewhere in Dutchtown, a third driver is shopping for the cheapest number a computer will produce, buying the bare state minimum, and quietly hoping the person who eventually rear-ends them is insured. In Missouri, that is a real gamble with real odds attached to it.
Three drivers, one metro, three very different bills. This is a plain-English breakdown of what car insurance actually costs around St. Louis, what Missouri legally requires, why your ZIP code moves the price so hard, and which of the money-saving moves you have heard about actually do anything. It is consumer cost information, not insurance advice — the last section is a list of questions to take to a licensed agent, because that is who should be answering them for your situation.
### How much does car insurance cost in St. Louis?
St. Louis drivers pay more than the Missouri average, and the size of that gap depends on whose data you read. Two of the most widely cited 2026 rate studies land in different places:
MoneyGeek (2026) puts Missouri full coverage at about $124 a month, or $1,486 a year, and Missouri minimum coverage at about $62 a month, or $740 a year. It shows St. Louis full coverage at roughly $200 a month — about $76 a month above the state figure — with Columbia at the low end near $120.
NerdWallet (2026) puts St. Louis full coverage at about $3,175 a year against a Missouri average near $2,365 a year.
Insurance.com reports a Missouri minimum-coverage average around $544 a year, or roughly $45 a month.
Those numbers do not agree, and that is worth understanding rather than ignoring. Every rate study builds a fictional driver — a specific age, credit tier, vehicle, mileage, coverage limit, and deductible — then prices that driver across carriers. Change the assumed profile and the average moves by a thousand dollars without anyone being wrong.
The useful takeaway is not a single number. It is the shape of the thing: full coverage in the city runs somewhere in the neighborhood of two to three thousand dollars a year for an average adult driver, state-minimum liability runs a fraction of that, and St. Louis sits above the Missouri average in every study that separates them. Treat any published average as a sanity check on a quote you are holding, never as the price you should be getting.
### What Missouri actually requires — and what changed
Missouri law sets a floor, and the floor is lower than most drivers assume. Under Missouri Revised Statutes section 303.190, a motor vehicle liability policy has to provide at least:
$25,000 for bodily injury to or death of one person in any one accident
$50,000 for bodily injury to or death of two or more people in any one accident
$25,000 for injury to or destruction of the property of others in any one accident
That is the shorthand you will hear from agents as 25/50/25. The property damage figure is the part that moved: the current version of the statute took effect July 1, 2019, raising Missouri’s property damage minimum to $25,000 from the much lower requirement that had been on the books since the 1990s. If you have carried the same policy for a decade without re-reading it, this is one of the few numbers in your life that changed while you were not looking.
Missouri also requires something most states do not. Every auto policy issued in Missouri has to include uninsured motorist bodily injury coverage of at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident, per the Missouri Department of Revenue. That coverage exists to pay you when the at-fault driver has nothing. It is not optional here, and there is a reason for that, covered further down.
One more piece of the legal frame matters for cost. Missouri is an at-fault state, operating under pure comparative negligence. The driver found responsible for a crash is financially responsible for the damage, and each party’s recovery is reduced by their own share of the blame. There is no no-fault system quietly absorbing the first layer of loss. Whoever caused it, pays — through their liability coverage, or out of their own assets when the coverage runs out.
### Why your ZIP code moves the price more than your driving does
This is the part that frustrates people most, and it is the part with the hardest evidence behind it. NerdWallet’s 2026 St. Louis analysis priced the same hypothetical driver — a 35-year-old with good credit — across the city’s most populated ZIP codes. The results ranged from about $2,277 a year at the low end to about $3,784 a year at the high end.
That is a spread of roughly $1,507 a year for one person, one car, one driving record. The only variable that changed was the mailing address. Cross Kingshighway and the number moves. That single fact explains more about St. Louis premiums than any conversation about safe driving ever will.
Carriers price geography because geography predicts claims. The inputs they weigh include:
Vehicle theft and break-in frequency in the immediate area, which drives comprehensive claims
Traffic density and intersection volume, which drive collision frequency — more cars in the same square mile means more chances to hit one
Local repair labor rates and parts costs, which set how much each claim costs to close
Uninsured driver concentration, which determines how often your own uninsured motorist coverage has to pay instead of theirs
Weather and hail claim history, which in Missouri is a genuine line item rather than a footnote
Litigation patterns in the venue where a claim would be handled
None of those are within your control, and none of them are personal. A garaging address in a high-claim ZIP is priced as a high-claim risk even for a driver who has never filed anything. It also means moving across the metro is a rate event. When you change your address, your premium is being recalculated whether or not anyone calls to tell you.
Totally unrelated — but Fenton’s whole restaurant lineup is here.
### Why is Missouri car insurance so high?
Drivers ask why is Missouri car insurance so high after every renewal cycle, and the honest answer is that it is a stack of pressures, not one villain. Several of them are national and several are specifically Missouri.
The national pressures are simple arithmetic. Vehicles carry more technology than they used to, which means a bumper tap now involves sensors and calibration rather than a bumper. Repair labor costs more. Parts cost more and take longer to arrive. Medical costs attached to injury claims keep climbing. Every one of those raises the average cost to close a claim, and premiums follow claim costs with a lag.
The Missouri-specific pressures are the ones that hit St. Louis hardest:
Uninsured drivers. Missouri’s uninsured motorist rate sits around 16 percent, roughly the eighth highest in the country, based on Insurance Research Council data. Nationally the IRC put the figure at 15.4 percent in 2023, with about one in three drivers either uninsured or underinsured. Every uninsured driver on the road is a claim that has to be paid by somebody else’s policy.
Severe weather. Hail and wind events generate large volumes of comprehensive claims across the region in a single afternoon, and those losses are recovered through everyone’s renewal.
Urban claim density. The city of St. Louis concentrates traffic, theft exposure, and repair demand in a way that the exurbs do not.
Low statutory minimums. A 25/50/25 floor means a meaningful share of at-fault drivers cannot cover the damage they cause, which pushes cost back onto the other driver’s uninsured and underinsured coverage.
### What actually lowers a premium versus what people think does
Ask how can I lower my car insurance rate and you will get a pile of tips of wildly uneven value. Here is the honest sorting, based on what the rate data shows moves a number and what does not.
Things with real, measurable leverage:
Credit-based insurance score. This is the sleeper. MoneyGeek’s Missouri data shows full coverage averaging about $121 a month with good credit and about $280 a month with poor credit — a difference of roughly $159 a month, or nearly $1,900 a year, for the same coverage. Missouri permits credit-based insurance scoring. Nothing else on this list comes close to that swing.
Shopping the whole market at renewal. Carriers file rates independently and each one weighs your ZIP, vehicle, and history differently. The same driver can be a preferred risk at one company and a surcharge at another. This costs an afternoon and nothing else.
Deductible level. Real, immediate, and covered in detail below.
Age and years licensed. Not a lever you can pull, but worth knowing the scale. MoneyGeek shows a 16-year-old male in Missouri averaging about $383 a month, or $4,600 a year, against about $189 a month, or $2,263 a year, at 25. Adding a teen driver is the single largest premium event most households will experience.
Annual mileage and garaging address accuracy. If your commute genuinely shrank, the carrier does not know unless you tell them.
Bundling and multi-vehicle. Modest but real, and it costs nothing to price it.
Time. Tickets and at-fault accidents age off the rating window. A surcharge is not permanent.
Things people believe move the price but mostly do not:
The color of the car. It is not a rating factor. It has never been a rating factor.
Paying the bill early. Paying in full for the term can avoid installment fees, which is a real but small saving. Paying a monthly bill three days early does nothing.
Being a naturally cautious driver. Carriers rate what they can verify — claims, violations, and mileage. Self-assessment is not an input.
Dropping uninsured motorist coverage. Not available in Missouri anyway, and the reason it is mandatory is the same reason cutting it would be a poor trade.
Buying a cheaper car outright. Sometimes true, often not. Repair cost, parts availability, and theft frequency for that specific model matter more than the sticker price. Some inexpensive vehicles are expensive to insure precisely because they get stolen.
One more piece of the picture: can I ask my insurance company to lower my premium? You can ask for a policy review, and it is worth doing annually. What that review can actually find is unapplied discounts, an outdated mileage figure, a vehicle you no longer own, a driver who moved out, or a coverage level that no longer matches the car. What it cannot do is negotiate the filed rate. Insurance pricing is filed with the state, and the person on the phone has no authority to discount it because you asked nicely.
### Is it better to have a $500 deductible or $1000?
The deductible is the clearest cost trade in the whole policy, and it is one of the few dials you fully control. Carinsurance.com’s analysis puts the average savings at:
$250 to $500 deductible — about $168 a year, roughly a 9 percent reduction
$500 to $1,000 deductible — about $188 a year, roughly a 10 percent reduction
$250 to $1,000 deductible — about $356 a year, roughly a 17 percent reduction
So the question is it better to have a $500 deductible or $1000 has a math answer rather than an opinion answer. Moving from $500 to $1,000 typically saves somewhere near $188 a year and increases your out-of-pocket exposure by $500 per claim. The break-even is a bit under three years. If you file a comprehensive or collision claim less often than roughly once every three years, the higher deductible is the cheaper path over time.
The catch has nothing to do with math. A deductible is only affordable if the cash exists on the day of the crash. A $1,000 deductible on a household that cannot produce $1,000 on short notice converts a covered loss into an unrepaired car. The workable number is the largest one you could write a check for tomorrow without borrowing — and that is a household budgeting question, not an insurance question.
One detail worth checking on your declarations page: comprehensive and collision carry separate deductibles, and they do not have to match. Hail damage and a parking lot collision may bill you differently than you expect.
### The honest math on dropping collision on an older car
Collision coverage pays to repair your own vehicle after a crash you caused, regardless of the other driver. WalletHub puts the national average cost of collision coverage at about $382 a year. On an older car, that number starts to look strange relative to what the coverage can ever pay out.
Here is why. Collision pays actual cash value minus your deductible, and it is capped by what the car is worth. On a vehicle with a book value of $3,000 carrying a $1,000 deductible, the absolute maximum the coverage can hand you is $2,000 — and only in a total loss. Anything less than a total loss pays less than that.
The widely cited heuristic, used by Consumer Reports and repeated across the industry, is the 10 percent rule: when your annual collision and comprehensive premium reaches about 10 percent of the vehicle’s book value, the coverage has stopped being efficient. WalletHub frames the same idea a second way — if three to five years of collision premiums would exceed the value of the car, the coverage is questionable. Consumer Reports adds a second trigger: a vehicle more than about ten years old.
Run your own numbers rather than borrowing someone else’s conclusion:
Look up your vehicle’s actual cash value, not what you paid and not what you think it is worth
Ask your agent for the exact annual dollar cost of the collision and comprehensive lines alone, separated from liability
Subtract your deductible from the vehicle value — that difference is the true maximum the coverage can ever pay
Divide the annual premium by that maximum payout
Ask the harder question: if the car were gone tomorrow, could the household replace it out of savings, and is there still a loan or lease on it
Two hard stops apply regardless of the arithmetic. If the vehicle is financed or leased, the lender almost certainly requires collision and comprehensive as a term of the contract, and dropping it is a default. And if the car is genuinely the only way anyone in the household gets to work, the replacement cost is not really the book value — it is the book value plus everything that breaks while there is no car. The math is the starting point, not the verdict. Walk the result through a licensed agent before changing anything.
### Why the cheapest liability-only policy can be the most expensive outcome
This is the section that matters most, and it is the one the price-comparison screens are structurally unable to show you.
Missouri’s minimum liability caps out at $25,000 per person for bodily injury and $25,000 for property damage. Consider what those numbers buy in practice. A single newer vehicle totaled in an at-fault crash can exceed the $25,000 property damage limit on its own, before anyone is treated for anything. An injury claim involving an ambulance ride, an emergency room, imaging, and any surgical intervention can pass $25,000 quickly.
In a no-fault state, some of that first layer gets absorbed by each driver’s own policy by design. Missouri does not work that way. Missouri is an at-fault state, so when the damage you caused exceeds your limits, the coverage stops and you do not. The remainder is a claim against you personally — savings, wages, and assets — and pure comparative negligence means partial fault still carries proportional financial responsibility.
Now stack the other half of the problem on top. With roughly 16 percent of Missouri drivers uninsured and about a third of drivers nationally either uninsured or underinsured, the odds that the person who hits you cannot cover your damage are not remote. They are ordinary. That is precisely why Missouri makes uninsured motorist bodily injury coverage mandatory at 25/50, and why the underinsured question — what happens when the at-fault driver has coverage but not enough — is worth raising with an agent explicitly rather than assuming it is handled.
The math that gets missed: the gap between minimum limits and substantially higher limits is usually a modest number of dollars per month, because the expensive part of a liability claim is the first dollar of coverage, not the last. Doubling or tripling a limit does not double or triple the price. Ask for the quote both ways and look at the actual difference before deciding — that comparison is free, and most drivers have never seen it.
None of that is a recommendation about what you should carry. It is a description of where the risk sits. What you buy depends on what you have to lose, and a licensed agent who can see your full picture is the right person to work that out with.
### What to ask an agent before you sign anything
Walk into the conversation with these, and take the same list to every agent so the answers line up next to each other:
What are my current liability limits, in writing, and what does it cost per month to step them up one level and two levels
What are my comprehensive and collision deductibles, and are they the same number
What is the annual dollar cost of collision and comprehensive alone on each vehicle, separated from liability
Do I carry underinsured motorist coverage in addition to the required uninsured motorist coverage, and at what limits
Which discounts am I currently receiving, and which ones exist that I am not getting
What annual mileage and garaging address are on file for each vehicle, and are they still accurate
Is a credit-based insurance score being used in my rate, and where does that place me
What would a single at-fault claim do to this premium at renewal
Does my policy include rental reimbursement or towing, and what does each one cost per month
If I move within the metro, how do I find out what the new address does to this rate before I sign a lease
Covering the house as well as the car? Here is what drives a St. Louis home insurance premium.
Get every answer in writing, and get a full quote sheet rather than a monthly payment. Monthly payment figures hide installment fees, term length differences, and coverage that was quietly trimmed to make the number look better. It is the same discipline that makes car detailing quotes comparable — ask everyone the identical questions and the prices finally line up next to each other.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $300 a month too much for car insurance?
A.  It depends entirely on what is in the policy. For a single adult with a clean record and one modest vehicle, $300 a month is well above the St. Louis full-coverage averages of roughly $200 a month in MoneyGeek’s 2026 data or about $265 a month implied by NerdWallet’s $3,175 annual figure. For a household with two vehicles, a teen driver, or a recent at-fault claim, $300 can be entirely normal — MoneyGeek shows a 16-year-old male in Missouri averaging about $383 a month on his own. Compare against a policy with the same limits and deductibles before deciding it is too high.
### Q. Is it better to have a $500 deductible or $1000?
A.  Moving from $500 to $1,000 saves roughly $188 a year on average, about a 10 percent reduction, per carinsurance.com. That means the higher deductible pays for itself in a little under three years without a claim. The limiting factor is cash, not math: a $1,000 deductible only works if you can produce $1,000 the day of the crash without borrowing. The workable choice is the largest deductible you could genuinely cover tomorrow.
### Q. How can I lower my car insurance rate?
A.  The levers with real measurable effect are your credit-based insurance score, shopping the entire market at every renewal, raising your deductible, correcting outdated mileage or garaging information, bundling policies, and simply letting old violations age off the rating window. In Missouri, credit is the largest single swing — MoneyGeek shows about $121 a month with good credit against about $280 a month with poor credit for the same full coverage. Car color, paying a monthly bill a few days early, and considering yourself a careful driver do nothing at all.
### Q. Can I ask my insurance company to lower my premium?
A.  You can request a policy review, and it is worth doing once a year. That review can find unapplied discounts, a mileage figure that no longer matches your commute, a vehicle you sold, a driver who moved out, or coverage that no longer fits the car’s value. What it cannot do is negotiate the filed rate itself — insurance pricing is filed with the state, and no representative has authority to discount it on request. If the review does not move the number, comparison shopping is the remaining lever.
### Q. Why is car insurance suddenly so expensive?
A.  Premiums lag claim costs, so a sharp renewal increase usually reflects losses the carrier absorbed a year or two earlier rather than anything you did. Repair costs rose as vehicles gained sensors and cameras that require calibration after even minor damage, parts and labor got more expensive, and medical costs on injury claims climbed. Regionally, hail and wind events add large comprehensive loss volumes. A move to a different ZIP code, an added driver, or a claim on the policy will amplify all of it — and within St. Louis alone, NerdWallet found the same 35-year-old driver quoted between about $2,277 and $3,784 a year depending only on address.
### Q. Is $200 a month for car insurance bad?
A.  In St. Louis it is close to typical for full coverage — one 2026 study put the city around $200 a month, roughly $76 above the Missouri average, with Columbia near $120. Bad depends on your coverage and record, not on the number alone.
### Q. Is $300 a month bad for insurance?
A.  It is above the local norm for full coverage, so it is worth asking what is driving it: recent claims, a young driver, low deductibles, or lender-required coverage on a financed car. Any of those can be legitimate; all of them are worth re-shopping annually.
### Q. What not to tell your insurance company?
A.  Never speculate about fault or injuries at the scene — report the facts and let the adjusters determine liability. What you must not do is understate mileage or hide a household driver; that is misrepresentation and it can void the claim you are paying for.
The driver in Affton, the one in Chesterfield, and the one in Dutchtown are not being priced on how carefully they drive. They are being priced on where the car sleeps, what a credit file says, what deductible they picked, and how much of somebody else’s uninsured risk their policy is quietly carrying. Three of those four are things you can look at this week — and the fourth is the reason it is worth looking at all.

## The Wire Was Bigger Than the Down Payment: St. Louis Closing Costs, and Missouri's $0 Transfer Tax
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-closing-costs-actually-cost-in-st-louis
The wire-transfer form is one page, and your hand still shakes on it. The bank counter is cold under your wrist. The teller reads the title company’s account number back to you twice, slowly, and you check every digit against the email, because everyone has told you about wire fraud. Then she reads the amount, and it is not the down payment you memorized to the dollar. It is bigger. That gap is closing costs, and almost nobody rehearses it.
Here is the part that makes St. Louis different from almost anywhere else in the country: which side of the river your house sits on changes the bill. Missouri’s constitution prevents the state, counties and other political subdivisions from imposing any new tax on the sale or transfer of homes or any other real estate. Cross into Illinois and the state charges 50 cents for each $500 of value, and a county can add 25 cents more. If you buy a $300,000 house in the Metro East, that is about $450 in transfer stamps at 75 cents per $500. On the same price in Missouri, it is zero.
Same metro. Same commute. Different bill. Say that to the friend shopping both sides of the bridge.
And inside the city limits, a blank strip of paper has a price. The City Recorder lists a standard deed at $25 for the first page and a nonstandard deed at $50, and what makes a deed standard is mostly a 3-inch blank top margin on page one. Ask your title company whether every document you record is standard format. Below: what the bill holds, how big it gets, what you can move, and how to read your two federal forms side by side.
### What are typical closing costs in Missouri?
Plan on 2% to 5% of the purchase price, the range Freddie Mac tells buyers to prepare for: if you buy a $300,000 St. Louis home, that is roughly $6,000 to $15,000, on top of the down payment. Missouri adds no transfer tax, because its constitution bars any new tax on selling real estate, so the government line is mostly recording fees. In the City of St. Louis, a standard deed is $25 for the first page.
The number feels worse than it is, and here is why. Part of that 2% to 5% is not a fee at all. Prepaid interest, the first year of homeowners insurance and the opening escrow deposit are your own money moving forward in time; you were going to owe taxes and insurance anyway. Ask your lender to split the total into money spent and money prepaid, and watch your shoulders come down an inch.
Freddie Mac’s own closing cost explainer says the amount varies greatly depending on your location and the price of your home, which is exactly why a range is a sanity check and your Loan Estimate is the real number. The CFPB’s guide to sizing your down payment is the place to plan both piles of cash together.
### The City deed that costs double
This one is pure St. Louis, and almost nobody outside a title office knows it. The City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds lists a standard deed at $25 for the first page plus $5 for each additional page. A nonstandard deed costs $50 for the first page. What makes a deed standard is mostly formatting: the City’s land records requirements call for a 3-inch blank top margin on the first page, void of any text, writing or graphic. A stamp, a scribble or a logo in that strip, and the fee doubles.
Your title company prepares the documents, so this is usually their problem, not yours. But it is a fair question at the closing table: are all of our documents standard? The City Recorder’s land records office is in City Hall, Room 126, at 1200 Market St., and the line is (314) 622-3260. The land records page carries the current fee list; check it, because fees change.
### The river line: $0 on one side, stamps on the other
Drive east over the Poplar Street Bridge, the river brown and wide under the deck, and the rules for your closing bill change before you reach the other bank. Read the Missouri rule in its own words. Article X, Section 25 of the Missouri Constitution says the state, counties and other political subdivisions are prevented from imposing any new tax, including a sales tax, on the sale or transfer of homes or any other real estate. So on a purchase in the city, St. Louis County or Jefferson County, the taxes-and-government-fees section of your disclosure holds recording charges and little else.
Illinois works the other way. The Illinois Department of Revenue explains that the state tax is imposed on the privilege of transferring a beneficial interest in real property located in Illinois. The statute sets the state rate at 50 cents for each $500 of value, and the Counties Code lets a county add 25 cents for each $500. Every Illinois sale is reported on Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, and the IDOR instructions for that form are worth a skim before you budget. Then call city hall in the town where the house sits and ask whether it adds a stamp of its own, before closing week rather than during it.
Who pays those stamps is a line in your contract, not something to assume. Read it with your pen in hand before you sign.
### The line items, one section at a time
The Loan Estimate breaks costs into lettered sections, and once you learn them you can read any lender’s paperwork. The paper smells like toner and the font is small, so take it slow.
Section A, origination charges. The lender’s own fees, plus any discount points you chose. The cleanest number to compare between two lenders.
Section B, services you cannot shop for. The appraisal, the credit report and similar items the lender picks.
Section C, services you can shop for. Title work, settlement fees and the lender’s title policy. If you are allowed to shop, the lender has to give you a written list of providers and tell you that you may choose a different one.
Section E, taxes and government fees. Recording, plus transfer tax in Illinois.
Sections F and G, prepaids and escrow. Your own money, collected early.
Section H, other. Often the owner’s title policy, HOA documents and any attorney fee.
The bill on each riverbank
### What's the typical closing cost on a $300,000 house?
Budget 2% to 5% of the price; if you buy a $300,000 home, that is about $6,000 to $15,000. On the Missouri side the transfer tax is $0 and a standard City deed records for $25 for the first page. On the Illinois side, state and county stamps at 75 cents per $500 add about $450 if you buy that same $300,000 house, and the town may add its own.
Section C is where the quiet savings live. Most buyers take the first settlement company on the list without a second look, and never ask what a second quote would say. A phone call costs you nothing but a few minutes on a lunch break.
What moves your number most is not the state line, though. It is points, the size of the escrow deposit, and the day of the month you close, since prepaid interest runs from closing to the end of the month. Ask your lender which date in the month makes your cash to close smallest.
### Who pays closing costs in MO?
Your purchase contract decides it. The buyer usually carries the costs tied to the loan and their own due diligence, and the seller carries the costs of handing over a clear title, but every line can be negotiated. A seller credit toward your costs is a common ask, and sometimes an easier one for a seller to say yes to than a lower price. Your loan program caps how big that credit can be, so ask your lender for your exact limit before you write the offer.
Short on cash for the table? Some help covers closing costs, not just the down payment: see the St. Louis assistance programs.
### Reading your Loan Estimate against your Closing Disclosure
This is the part with federal teeth. Federal rules say you must receive your final loan disclosures no later than three business days before consummation; the CFPB’s Closing Disclosure guide walks through the form. Use those days. Lay the two forms side by side on the kitchen table, section letter against section letter, and circle every line that moved.
Some lines may move and some may not. Charges for certain third-party services, such as recording fees, can rise only so far: the rule lets them grow by no more than 10 percent in total. The CFPB explains which final costs can increase from the estimate. If a lender goes over a limit, it can cure it by refunding the excess to you no later than 60 days after consummation, which is why a buyer who never compares the forms may never learn a check was owed.
For more on fees, read the CFPB on junk fees in housing costs. Question anything you cannot name.
### What to ask before you sign anything
What is the total in Section A, and what is each line inside it?
How much of my cash to close is fees, and how much is prepaids and escrow?
What is the largest seller credit my loan allows?
Can you quote this with a lender credit, with no points, and with one point, with the break-even in months?
Where is your written list of settlement providers?
If the house is in Illinois, which transfer stamps apply, and who is buying each one?
Are all of the documents we are recording standard format?
Which day of the month would make my cash to close smallest?
Get the answers in writing, and ask two or three St. Louis mortgage lenders the identical questions so the answers line up side by side.
Bring this list to the table, not just your checkbook. If you are earlier in the process, start with the first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis, then read what St. Louis home inspections miss before you waive anything to win a house.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are typical closing costs on a $250,000 house?
A.  If you buy a $250,000 house, the 2% to 5% range Freddie Mac uses works out to about $5,000 to $12,500. In Missouri there is no transfer tax on top. If you buy that $250,000 house in Illinois, state and county stamps at 75 cents per $500 add about $375.
### Q. How much would the closing cost be on a $300,000 home?
A.  If you buy a $300,000 home, the 2% to 5% range Freddie Mac gives buyers works out to roughly $6,000 to $15,000. If that $300,000 home is in Illinois, add about $450 in state and county transfer stamps at 75 cents per $500, plus any stamp the town charges. Missouri charges no transfer tax, so a Missouri buyer at the same price skips that line entirely. Your Loan Estimate is the real number; the range is the sanity check.
### Q. What would closing cost be on a $400,000 house?
A.  If you buy a $400,000 house, 2% to 5% works out to about $8,000 to $20,000. The high end usually means points, a large escrow deposit or an early-month closing. If that $400,000 house is in Illinois, state and county stamps at 75 cents per $500 add about $600.
### Q. How much are closing costs on a $500,000 property?
A.  If you buy a $500,000 property, the 2% to 5% range works out to about $10,000 to $25,000. If it is in Illinois, state and county stamps at 75 cents per $500 add about $750 on that $500,000 price, and a town may add its own; in Missouri, the transfer tax line is $0. At this price, points and the escrow deposit swing the total more than anything else, so ask for the loan quoted more than one way.
### Q. Can a seller refuse to pay closing costs?
A.  Yes. A request for seller-paid costs is a term in your offer, and the seller can accept it, counter it or turn it down. If you need the credit to close, put it in your first offer rather than asking after the inspection.
The wire form will still make your hand shake. But you will know what is inside the number: a lender’s pricing, a recorder’s fee list, a state line that decides whether there is a transfer tax at all, and a stack of your own money collected a little early. Three business days is how long the law gives you to look. Take every one of them.

## St. Louis Down Payment Help Runs Out Fast: The $50,000 Loan Is Reserved, the $8,000 Isn't
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/down-payment-assistance-programs-st-louis-buyers
The biggest down payment check in the St. Louis area is the city’s HomeSTL loan, worth up to $50,000, and right now you cannot reserve a dime of it. The St. Louis Development Corporation’s own HomeSTL page says it is no longer accepting reservation requests, because all funds are fully reserved.
Tonight the kitchen table is the office. The lender’s estimate sits under a coffee mug ring, the cash-to-close line circled twice in blue pen. The pre-approval letter is still warm from the printer. Your phone lies face up beside it with the savings balance open, and the gap between those two numbers is a figure you could say out loud, and would rather not. That gap is exactly what down payment help was built to close.
Here is the part that should make you sit up. The money that is still on the table is smaller, quieter, and almost nobody asks for it. In Florissant, Beyond Housing offers up to $8,000 toward a down payment and closing costs, and its own page says applicants there are not required to be first-time homebuyers. Owned a house before? In Florissant, that does not shut the door. Tell the friend who sold their first place and assumes they are locked out.
Everything below is the help a St. Louis buyer can actually reach, on both sides of the river, and the timing rules that cost people more money than any income limit. Program terms change without warning, so treat every number here as the place to start the conversation with a lender and a HUD-approved housing counselor, not the last word.
### What grants are available for first-time home buyers in Missouri?
Almost none of it is a true grant. Missouri help comes as forgivable or deferred loans: MHDC’s First Place program offers cash assistance for down payment and closing costs statewide, Beyond Housing adds up to $7,000 in St. Louis County and up to $8,000 in Florissant as zero percent, five-year forgivable loans, and the city’s HomeSTL has offered up to $50,000 when funded. HomeSTL and the Beyond Housing loans both require a homebuyer education course first.
The pen at the closing table is heavier than you expect. The word grant is what trips people. A grant sounds like something you keep no matter what. These are liens recorded against your new house, and you keep the money by staying put long enough for it to be forgiven. Sell early and part of it comes back out of your sale proceeds at the closing table, on a day you were hoping to feel like you came out ahead.
### The city’s HomeSTL loan: the biggest number, and the first to run dry
If you are buying inside the city limits, behind a brick front and a limestone stoop worn smooth by old winters, HomeSTL is the one to watch. The city’s ARPA office describes a base loan of $40,000, with an additional $10,000 possible for homes in HUD Qualified Census Tracts. The SLDC page calls it a forgivable loan with 0% interest and no monthly payments for up to 10 years, and it can go toward closing costs, down payment, a permanent rate reduction, prepaids or principal reduction, with no cash back to you.
The rules are tight. You cannot have owned or co-owned a home in the last three years. Your household income cannot exceed 80% of the area’s median income. You have to finish an approved homebuyer education course and borrow through an SLDC-approved mortgage lender. The HomeSTL program guidelines are the document your lender will read line by line.
And SLDC processes requests in the date order each eligibility packet was completed. When the program came back, it was resuming with $1 million in American Rescue Plan Act funds. That pot is now fully reserved. If it opens again, the buyers who get it will be the ones whose education certificate is already dated and whose lender is already on the approved list, not the ones who start reading the rules that week. Bookmark the HomeSTL page, and call SLDC at 314.657.3700 to ask how it will announce the next round.
### St. Louis County, Jefferson County and Florissant: the quiet $7,000 to $8,000
Out in the county, where the yards get wider and the lawn mowers start early on weekends, the suburban money runs through Beyond Housing, a HUD-approved housing counseling agency. Its program page lists up to $7,000 in St. Louis County, up to $7,000 in Jefferson County and up to $8,000 in the City of Florissant. The assistance is a zero percent interest, five-year forgivable loan, and it requires no monthly payment. Beyond Housing does not offer these funds for the City of St. Louis.
The price cap is where most buyers fall out. In St. Louis County, including Florissant, the limit is $219,000 for an existing home and $371,000 for new construction. Jefferson County runs $226,000 existing and $329,000 new. If the Affton ranch you toured, fresh paint still sharp in the hallway, is listed above that line, the county money is simply not in play.
Then come the two timing rules that sink people who did qualify. You must have already completed a HUD-certified homebuyer education course and one-to-one homeownership counseling before you apply, not while you are under contract. And your closing has to be scheduled at least 30 days out from the date you apply for the assistance. When the listing agent pushes for a fast close, that is the moment this money quietly slips off the table, and nobody calls to tell you. So call first: Beyond Housing’s line for questions is 314-376-5822, and the right question is how soon you can book the counseling session, before you tour a single house.
### Across the river: Illinois money comes with a menu
Across the river, IHDA Mortgage offers several kinds of down payment help. It is several, and they are not equally good deals. As listed on the IHDA Mortgage program directory:
IHDAccess Home - 6% up to $15,000, a deferred loan for first-time homebuyers with no monthly payment; repayment is due when you sell or refinance.
IHDAccess Deferred - 5% up to $7,500, no monthly payment, due when you sell or refinance.
IHDAccess Forgivable - 4% up to $6,000, no repayment unless you sell or refinance before the 10-year forgiveness period ends.
Opening Doors - a flat $9,000, forgivable, with no repayment unless you sell or refinance before the 5-year forgiveness period ends.
IHDAccess Repayable - 10% up to $10,000 at zero interest, but monthly repayment is required.
Read that last one twice. Zero interest is real value, but it is still a second bill in the mailbox every month on top of the mortgage. And look at the directory itself: the programs carry a “limited funds remain” banner. The newest, IHDAccess Home, was announced by the governor’s office as a zero-percent second mortgage with repayment deferred for up to 30 years unless the home is sold or refinanced earlier. Limits are set county by county, so use IHDA’s county lookup rather than a number you read anywhere else, including here.
IHDA programs require all homebuyers to take a pre-purchase education course; the education requirements page lists the approved providers. Do it before you write an offer.
### Madison County and St. Clair County
Madison County runs its own HOMEbuyer Assistance Program with financial assistance of up to $15,000. Household income must be at or below 80% of Area Median Income, the minimum credit score is 620, the property must be a one- or two-unit home or condominium, and a HUD-certified homebuyer education course is required. The maximum property value is $219,000 for an existing home and $329,000 for new construction. You apply through a qualifying lender, not the county. Its first-time definition also covers someone who previously owned a home with someone else and was displaced by a life-changing event such as divorce or death. If Glen Carbon is on your list, its restaurant lineup is a fair preview of a Saturday night there.
St. Clair County has a Homebuyer Assistance Program too, providing funds for a down payment and closing costs to eligible clients buying in eligible areas of the county, with homebuyer counseling required. The county page lists the program; call the department for current amounts and which areas qualify.
### Statewide Missouri help, and the loan underneath it
The Missouri Housing Development Commission’s First Place program serves first-time homebuyers and qualified Veterans, and for buyers with limited savings it offers cash assistance for down payment and closing costs. Loans come only from MHDC Certified Lenders, and MHDC sets no minimum down payment. The First Place operations manual spells out how the assistance is repaid or forgiven, and the income and purchase price limits tell you whether your household fits. Shopping a manufactured home? Read up on mobile home parks in St. Louis and ask the lender how MHDC treats one before you fall for it.
The loan underneath changes what the help is for. A VA-backed purchase loan often needs no down payment as long as the sales price is not higher than the home’s appraised value, so for an eligible Veteran the assistance is really about closing costs. On an FHA loan, read HUD’s own answer on the minimum down payment before you guess at it.
Your rate can cost you more over the life of the loan than any of this help saves you, so read what a mortgage rate really is before you lock one.
### What is the biggest negative when using down payment assistance?
It is not the money. It is the flexibility you did not price in. Almost every program here records a lien on the house with strings tied to how long you stay. The county loans through Beyond Housing are forgiven over five years. HomeSTL carries no monthly payments for up to 10 years. IHDAccess Home and IHDAccess Deferred come due when you sell or refinance, and IHDAccess Repayable bills you every month. Take a job in another city in year three and you could be writing a check you thought you would never see.
Your lender list also gets shorter. HomeSTL requires an SLDC-approved lender, MHDC works only through Certified Lenders, and Madison County requires a direct lender that closes the loan in its own name. Comparison shopping still matters; you are just shopping a smaller room.
### The order that actually gets you the money
Finish homebuyer education first. Find a course through HUD’s counselor directory, and add one-to-one counseling if you want the St. Louis County or Florissant money.
Know which county your target street sits in. The county line decides which program you can touch.
Get pre-approved with a lender already approved for that program, and ask in writing whether funds are open today.
Write offers with a closing date that leaves room for the program’s timeline.
Keep checking program status. Rounds reopen quietly, and nobody sends a letter.
Questions to put to every loan officer: which programs are you approved to originate, is the money forgivable, deferred or repayable, over how many years, what happens if I sell early, and what happens if the funds run out between contract and closing? Asking two or three mortgage lenders the same questions is the only way the answers line up side by side.
Line up the lender before you line up the house. Browse mortgage lenders on St Louis Near Me Directory and ask each one the questions above; the ones who answer clearly about fund status are worth the second call. New to all of it? Start with the first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the biggest negative when using down payment assistance?
A.  Lost flexibility. Most programs record a lien with a stay-put clock: the Beyond Housing county loans are forgiven over five years, HomeSTL runs up to 10 years, and several Illinois loans come due when you sell or refinance. Leave early and you may repay part of it. You also borrow from a shorter list of approved lenders.
### Q. What are the requirements for a first-time homebuyer in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the program. For HomeSTL you cannot have owned or co-owned a home in the last three years, household income cannot exceed 80% of the area’s median income, and you need an approved education course and an SLDC-approved lender. The Beyond Housing county loans require HUD-certified education and one-to-one counseling before you apply, plus a closing at least 30 days out.
### Q. What is the $7500 first time home buyer grant in Illinois?
A.  That is IHDAccess Deferred, and it is a loan, not a grant: 5% of the price up to $7,500, no monthly payment, due when you sell or refinance. IHDA also lists IHDAccess Home at 6% up to $15,000 and IHDAccess Forgivable at 4% up to $6,000.
### Q. What disqualifies you from first time home buyer?
A.  Usually owning a home in the past three years. But the rule bends: Beyond Housing does not require first-time status in Florissant, and Madison County counts you as first-time if you were displaced from a jointly owned home by divorce or death. Income over the cap, a price over the limit or a credit score under the floor (620 for Madison County) can also rule you out.
### Q. Is down payment assistance worth it?
A.  If you are sure you will stay through the forgiveness period, a forgivable loan is close to free money toward closing. If a job or family change could move you in a few years, a deferred or repayable loan can turn into a bill at the worst time. Run your own numbers with a licensed loan officer and a HUD-approved housing counselor.
The buyer in Belleville, the one in Florissant and the one eyeing a brick two-family in the city are each eligible for something different, on a different clock, from a different pot. Finish the course now, while it costs you nothing but an evening, so the next time a round opens your paperwork is already dated.

## Close Your Old Bank Last: How to Switch Banks in St. Louis Without a Bounced Bill
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-switch-banks-in-st-louis-without-missing-a-bill
The car payment comes back unpaid on a gray morning, and the email from the lender sits on top of the inbox in bold. Returned item. Late fee pending. You stare at it over cold coffee in Belleville, because the money was there. It was just in the new account, and the lender was still pulling from the old one, the one you closed three weeks ago because closing it felt like crossing the finish line.
Then the second shoe. The old bank also let the insurance draft go through after you thought the account was done, and now you owe a bank you already left. You call. Forty minutes of hold music. The person who finally answers is polite and cannot undo any of it.
The federal regulator of national banks has heard this exact story. On its HelpWithMyBank site, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency answers a customer who closed a checking account and watched the bank keep accepting recurring charges from an insurance company. The answer is blunt: it is your responsibility to cancel all recurring charges with third parties before closing the bank account you authorized for payment. The bank is not your safety net here. The order you do things in is.
A St. Louis credit union has quietly built that order into a piece of paper. St. Louis Community Credit Union’s switch kit runs in three steps, and the third one is the tell. Its Checking Account Closure Notice is the last form, and the kit says to mail it to your old institution only once your direct deposit and payments are coming to the new account AND you know all of your checks have cleared the old one. Then the credit union says the remaining balance will be sent to your new checking account. You can ask for the application in person or by phone at 314-534-7610.
A St. Louis bank puts a number on it. Midwest BankCentre tells people switching to keep your old account open for 30-60 days to catch any lingering automatic payments or deposits. Its close-out step on its switch page reads like the credit union’s form: confirm your checks have cleared, confirm the automatic payments and deposits have moved, then close.
Two St. Louis institutions, one rule. That capital AND is the whole lesson in one word. Close last. Close only after the money has proven it moved. Send that line to anyone halfway through a switch right now.
### How quickly can you switch banks?
You can open a new account in minutes, but a safe switch takes one to two full billing cycles. Open the new account, move direct deposit first, wait for a full paycheck to land, move each autopay at the company that charges it, keep the old account open and funded until every item has drafted from the new one, then close it in writing.
Most bounced payments during a switch come from the gap between those two speeds. Fast to open, slow to finish. People act on the first number and get burned by the second.
### Why the money is fast and the switch is slow
The plumbing is not the problem. Nacha, which runs the rules for the ACH network behind direct deposit and autopay, reports that the significant majority of ACH payments settle in one business day or less, and it has rolled out Same Day ACH on top of that.
Under Regulation CC, money from an electronic payment must be available by the business day after your bank receives it.
So the deposit can ping your phone before your alarm goes off. The slow part is people and calendars. Payroll runs on a cutoff, and a change that misses it waits a whole pay period. Many employers first send a small test entry to confirm the new account is real; Nacha lists the ACH prenotification as one way to validate account information. And somewhere on your list there is one biller with a clunky website and a draft that only hits once a year. That one sets your schedule. Not the bank. Not the network. The homeowners premium you forgot about.
Benefit deposits have their own lane (here is a notice on direct deposit changes). Either way, watch a full payment land in the new account before the old one goes anywhere.
### The kitchen-table hour that saves the switch
Start with the end of it, because that is the moment St. Louis Community’s closing rule is built for. The old statement is flat on the kitchen table under the light, a pen in your hand, coffee going cold beside the closure form you have not signed yet. You run the pen down the page. Paycheck: moved, ticked. Car loan: moved, ticked. Then the last autopay, the insurance draft, and it pulled from the new account this cycle. Tick. Nothing left on the old statement. Only now does the form get a signature and a stamp.
Getting there is an hour with a highlighter, a stack of statements and the radio on. Pull twelve months, not three. Three months catches the monthlies and misses the annual car insurance, the term life policy, the alarm monitoring, the tax software that renews itself in the dark. Build two columns: money that leaves on its own, and money that arrives on its own. Write the day of the month next to every line.
Then split the outgoing column in two, because the two kinds break differently. Payments tied to your routing and account number, like a mortgage, a car loan, insurance and most utilities, stop working the moment the old account closes, and the only fix is giving that company your new numbers. Payments tied to your debit card number, like streaming, apps and delivery, keep working right up until the old card dies, then fail all at once. Two lists, two fixes. One list is how a switch that looked finished falls apart six weeks later.
When the list is done, the order is simple. Deposits before debits, always. Reroute the paycheck first, wait until a full paycheck lands, then move bills in order of what a failure costs you: housing, car loan, insurance, utilities, cards, then everything else. A streaming service can fail without damage. A mortgage cannot.
### What to bring when you open the new account
Federal customer identification rules at 31 CFR 1020.220 require a bank to get your name, date of birth, street address and a taxpayer identification number before it opens your account.
An unexpired government photo ID, such as a driver’s license, state ID or passport.
Your Social Security number or ITIN.
Proof of your current address if the ID shows an old one.
An opening deposit. Ask the amount before you go.
Twelve months of old statements for the list above.
One step before you apply: banks often check a checking-account screening report, and an old unpaid overdraft can sink an application. Here is how to get a copy of the report banks use. Pull it first if you have any doubt.
Before you move a dollar, look the new place up on BankFind Suite or the NCUA locator.
Then read up on how deposit insurance works and share insurance for credit unions.
### The first month of a new account is different
A brand-new account does not get the same treatment as an old one. Under Regulation CC’s new account exception, an account counts as new during its first 30 calendar days, and the usual availability rules loosen for the bank in that window. If a big deposit is due mid-switch, ask the new bank how long it will hold it.
Thinking about a house once the money is sorted? Read how to choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis before you call one.
### Keep the old account alive longer than feels right
A short overlap sounds like plenty. It only catches the weekly and every-other-week items. Your monthly bills get one shot to prove they moved, and the yearly ones get none. Keep the old account open and funded until every line on your list has drafted from the new account at least once. That fits Midwest BankCentre’s 30-60 days; for most households that is one to two full monthly cycles, longer with a quarterly or yearly bill.
Leave a real cushion in it, enough to cover checks still out there and payments not yet moved. Read the old statement every cycle; anything still hitting it is something you missed. Keep the old debit card until the very end. A full cycle with nothing on the old statement is your green light.
Keep one emergency brake in your pocket. Regulation E lets you stop payment on a preauthorized transfer by telling your bank at least three business days before the scheduled date. That is a backstop for a draft you spot early, not a plan.
Shop the new account with the same three questions everywhere. Browse banks across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory and ask each one: what waives the monthly fee, where is the branch nearest my job, and what does it cost to close in the first six months. Leaning toward a credit union? Start with local credit unions in the St. Louis metro.
If you run the branch, the credit union or the tax office people lean on when money gets moved, this reader is choosing where to bank this month. List your business and get more customers at the moment they decide.
### Close it in writing, then keep the paper
When a full cycle goes by with nothing on the old statement, close it on purpose. Move the last of the balance, ask for closure in writing or in person, and get written confirmation that the account is closed. File that page with your tax papers. It ends every future argument about a fee you supposedly owe.
Draining an account to zero and walking away is not closing it. A drained account can still charge a monthly fee and go negative. And an account you simply forget eventually goes to the state as unclaimed property, on a clock that depends on the river: Missouri’s State Treasurer lists a 5-year dormancy period for most property, and Illinois law presumes a demand or savings deposit abandoned after 3 years.
Two fee traps to check before you leave. If the account you are leaving is fairly new, ask whether it carries an early account closure fee. And a free account is often free only because your direct deposit waives the monthly fee. Move the paycheck and that waiver can vanish while the old account still holds your cushion. Read the old fee schedule first.
### Switching on both sides of the river
Branch geography is the real variable here. Plenty of banks are thick on one side of the river and thin on the other, so if you live in Edwardsville and work in Clayton, or live in Webster Groves and work in Fairview Heights, check branches near both ends of the commute, not just near home. Credit union membership can also stop at a county line, so ask before you plan around one.
If a closing goes wrong, who hears the complaint depends on the charter. For Missouri, the Division of Finance takes complaints against banks in its jurisdiction. In Illinois, the Division of Banking accepts consumer complaints about state banks. National banks answer to the OCC through HelpWithMyBank.gov.
Looking for a low-cost account to switch into? The Bank On certified account list is a good place to start, and the program’s national data hub was built with the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
