### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I transfer everything from one bank to another?
A.  Open the new account, list every automatic payment and deposit from twelve months of statements, move direct deposit and wait for a full paycheck to land, then move payments one at a time, starting with housing and loans. Change each one at the company taking the money. Close the old account last, in writing.
### Q. What documents do you need to switch banks?
A.  A bank must collect your name, date of birth, street address and taxpayer identification number to open an account. Bring a government photo ID, your Social Security number or ITIN, proof of address if your ID is out of date, and an opening deposit.
### Q. How long does a bank transfer take between different banks?
A.  Nacha reports that the significant majority of ACH payments settle in one business day or less. The full switch takes longer, because payroll cutoffs and once-a-year bills set the pace.
### Q. What are the downsides to switching banks?
A.  Time, mostly, and a window of a month or two where a missed payment can bounce. You can also lose a fee waiver tied to your old direct deposit, and a brand-new account can carry longer holds in its first 30 days.
### Q. Is it hard to switch banks?
A.  Not hard, just ordered. List every automatic payment first, move deposits before debits, and close the old account only after everything has cleared from the new one.
### Q. How do I switch to another bank?
A.  Open the new account and leave the old one funded. Move direct deposit, then each autopay, confirming each one has drafted from the new account. Then close the old account in writing and keep the confirmation.

## $0 a Month Isn’t Free: The $7 Missouri Form Your Bank Skips
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-bank-for-small-business-checking-in-st-louis
Seven dollars. That’s the Missouri form your bank will want and never brings up.
Tuesday afternoon in a Florissant cul-de-sac. The mower’s still ticking as it cools in the trailer. Grass clippings on your boots. An $85 check going soft at the corners in your hand. It’ll go into the same account that pays the car note, the way every check has since the first yard, because nobody ever handed you a better map.
The ad said “free checking.” “Free” means no monthly fee. Not no fees. The culprit is the fee schedule, the one document that says what free costs, sitting four pages back where the ad never points. One line on it caps how much cash you can deposit before the overage starts, and the overage waits on next month’s statement. For a business paid in $85 checks and twenties, that line is where the “free” quietly ends. Nobody walked you through it. That’s on the process, not on you.
Same story from a different chair. A stylist renting a station in Kirkwood takes half her money through a payment app and half in twenties, folded into an apron pocket that smells like hairspray by closing. Those twenties count against the same cash allowance.
Here is what that cash line looks like in print. Two published examples count the same twenties two ways: U.S. Bank’s Business Essentials is $0 a month but includes only 25 cash units per statement cycle (a deposit of less than $150 equals one unit), then $0.35 per $100, while Bank of America’s Business Advantage Fundamentals gives the first $5,000 in cash free per statement cycle, then 30 cents per $100. Twenty-five small deposits can use up the first allowance, which is the lawn crew and the stylist’s apron pocket all over again.
One more, from a bank with branches that include Clayton: Simmons Bank’s Business Core Checking lists $5,000 in cash deposits per month without a fee, then $2.50 per additional $1,000. These are published examples, not recommendations, and schedules change, so check the current one before you decide.
So which account was actually built for a business like that? Before any account can answer, the bank wants one piece of paper the ad never mentions: a Missouri fictitious name registration, $7, good for five years, filed at bsd.sos.mo.gov. Do business under any name but your own and you file it. It doesn’t reserve the name for you, since two businesses can register the same one. It makes doing business under that name legal, and it’s the proof that the name on the account is yours. Questions about the form can go to the Missouri Secretary of State’s St. Louis office at (314) 340-7490.
Work Belleville too, and the rules change at the river. Illinois has sole proprietors file with the county clerk in every county where they do business, then publish notice in a local newspaper once a week for three weeks. A lawn crew that mows Belleville and Edwardsville is working St. Clair County and Madison County: two filings, not one. The St. Clair County Clerk answers at 618-277-6600 ext. 2363, and the Madison County Clerk at (618) 296-6200.
The order that saves a second trip starts with three numbers no bank will ask for, all sitting on last month’s statement: your lowest daily balance, how many checks and transfers moved through, and how much paper cash came in. Next comes the $7 name filing, then the EIN, which the IRS hands out free in minutes even though some websites charge for it. With photo ID for every signer and the ownership details in hand, those three numbers pick the account.
### Three numbers pick your bank. The sign-up bonus isn’t one of them
The Friday teller window settles this, not the app store. The right account is the one whose fee structure matches the way money actually moves through your business. Not the one with the sign-up bonus, and not the one your cousin uses. Three numbers do almost all of the work.
Start with the lowest your balance sinks. Your January number, when the grass stops and the phone goes quiet, usually decides whether the monthly maintenance fee gets waived. It counts for more than your best week in May, and it’s the single biggest lever.
Then comes how many items move through. A spring stack of forty yard checks rubber-banded on the dash counts against a monthly item allowance, along with checks written, ACH credits and debits, and sometimes card swipes. Forty of those lands very differently than four transfers a month.
Last is how much paper cash you deposit. A bank bag of twenties goes through the counting machine with that fast paper flutter, every bill counted against the cash allowance. It’s the fee line that quietly ruins the math for salons on Cherokee Street, food trucks working Food Truck Friday in Tower Grove Park, lawn crews, and anyone who takes twenties.
Three more things come after those. A night drop three miles from your last stop, when that stop is a cul-de-sac in Hazelwood at 6:40 p.m. and the cash bag is riding on the passenger seat, is worth real money to a trade business and nothing to someone paid by transfer. A deposit relationship can open the door to a small line of credit later, the kind that buys the second mower before the April grass comes in. And when a customer taps her card on your phone in her driveway, three companies take a slice, so card processing is worth pricing separately, for reasons covered further down.
Whichever of those three is loudest for your business is where the comparison starts, before a single account page. A caterer who deposits $4,000 in currency a month and a business paid by four ACH transfers a month are shopping for two different accounts. (Any bank named on this page is a published example from its own fee documents, not a ranking or a recommendation, and none paid to be here. This is general education, not financial, tax or legal advice for your situation.)
Before the account, the paperwork - here is what business licenses you actually need in St. Louis.
### Bring these four things or make a second trip
Plan on four categories of paperwork: a tax identification number, government photo identification for everyone who will sign, whatever documents prove your business exists under the name you are using, and ownership details for anyone holding a meaningful stake. Walk in with all four and the appointment takes forty minutes. Walk in with two of them and you are making a second trip.
### Why do websites charge for an EIN the IRS gives away?
An Employer Identification Number is the business equivalent of a Social Security number, and the IRS issues it online in minutes for free. The agency says it plainly on its own page: beware of websites that charge for an EIN, because you never have to pay a fee for one. Paid EIN services exist entirely because people do not know that.
A few practical details from the IRS application itself. The responsible party listed on the application needs a Social Security number or ITIN. You can apply for only one EIN per responsible party per day. The online tool is not open around the clock - it runs Monday through Friday from 6:00 a.m. to 1:00 a.m. Eastern, Saturday 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and Sunday 6:00 p.m. to midnight. Print the confirmation letter the moment it appears on screen, because the bank will want to see it and getting a replacement later is slower than it should be.
Which raises the question people actually ask at this point: can I open a business bank account using only an EIN? Almost never. The EIN is one required piece of a file, not the file. You will still need photo identification for every signer, whatever registration or formation document proves the business name belongs to you, an operating or partnership agreement if more than one person owns a share, a business license where your municipality requires one, and ownership details for anyone with a meaningful stake. The EIN is the key that fits the lock. It is not the door.
### Do I need an LLC to get a business checking account?
No. A sole proprietor can open a business checking account, and the U.S. Small Business Administration lists a Social Security number as an acceptable substitute for an EIN if you are a sole proprietorship, alongside your formation documents, ownership agreements, and business license. Whether you should form an LLC is a separate question with liability and tax consequences, and it belongs in front of an attorney or a CPA rather than a blog post.
The practical reason people think an LLC is required is different from the legal one. If you want customers to write checks to a trade name - the name on the truck, the name on the sign - rather than to your own legal name, the bank needs a document connecting that trade name to you. That document is a fictitious or assumed name registration, and it is not the same thing as forming an LLC.
### What is the $7 Missouri form nobody mentions?
If you are operating in Missouri under any name other than your true name, you are required to register it. The Missouri Secretary of State points to Section 417.200 of the Revised Statutes: anyone doing business under a name other than their true name must register that fictitious name. The filing fee is $7.00, the registration is good for five years, and renewals happen within six months before expiration.
The part worth reading twice: the Secretary of State says failure to register your fictitious name is a misdemeanor under Missouri law. It also warns that registering a name gives you no exclusive rights to it - two businesses can hold the identical registered name at the same time. So the filing is a compliance step and a banking step, not trademark protection.
The filing, start to finish: go to bsd.sos.mo.gov, file a fictitious name registration with your business name, business address, and every owner’s name and percentage, and pay $7. Paper works too: the form is on the Secretary of State’s forms page, signed by every owner and mailed with the fee. Renew in the six months before the five years run out; let it lapse and you start over with a new filing. Screenshot this for the glovebox: Missouri name, $7 for five years. Work Belleville too, and Illinois wants a county filing plus three weeks of newspaper notices. The EIN, $0, straight from the IRS.
If you formed an LLC or a corporation, your articles filed with the Missouri Secretary of State’s Corporations Division are what the bank wants to see, plus your operating agreement if more than one person owns a piece.
### What changes when you work the Illinois side of the river?
Across the river the structure is genuinely different, and this catches people who moved a business from St. Louis County to St. Clair or Madison County. LLCs, corporations, and limited partnerships register with the Illinois Secretary of State. But sole proprietors and general partnerships do not. Under the Illinois Assumed Business Name Act, they file a certificate with the county clerk in every county where they conduct business, listing the assumed name, the true legal name of each owner, and each business address in that county.
There is a second step Missouri does not have. The Act also requires that notice of the filing be published in a newspaper of general circulation in that county, once a week for three consecutive weeks. Fees are set at the county level and vary. If your lawn crew mows in Belleville and Edwardsville, that is St. Clair County and Madison County - two filings, not one. Budget the time before you promise a bank appointment. We walk through the whole two-state cost picture in what it actually costs to start a business in St. Louis.
### Does the bank still ask who owns the business?
This is the one to read carefully, because the rule moved twice in eighteen months and most of the advice online is now wrong.
On August 11, 2026, FinCEN issued a final rule that permanently removes the requirement for U.S. companies and U.S. persons to report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act. The rule took effect on publication in the Federal Register on August 14, 2026. All entities created in the United States - the ones previously called domestic reporting companies - and their beneficial owners are exempt from filing initial reports and from updating or correcting reports already filed. FinCEN has said it will delete information previously reported by U.S. persons from the database. Foreign reporting companies still report beneficial ownership for foreign individuals.
Now the part people get wrong. That change is about reporting to the government. It has nothing to do with what your bank asks you. Under FinCEN’s separate Customer Due Diligence rule, a covered financial institution still has to identify and verify the beneficial owners of a legal entity customer when that customer first opens an account, when it learns something that calls the old information into question, and as its own risk-based procedures require. A February 2026 exceptive relief order eased the requirement to re-collect the same information at every subsequent new account, but the first-account obligation is intact.
Translation for the person sitting at the desk in the branch: bring the ownership details anyway. Legal name, address, date of birth, and identification number for anyone owning 25 percent or more, plus one individual with significant control - a managing member, a president, a general partner. Being told you no longer file with FinCEN and then arriving without that information is how a Tuesday appointment becomes a Thursday appointment.
### Can I use a personal bank account for my LLC?
You can physically do it. It is also the mistake on this list that costs the most money, and the bill arrives in April rather than the day you make it.
Start with what the IRS says in Publication 583, Starting a Business and Keeping Records: one of the first things you should do when you start a business is open a business checking account, use it for business purposes only, and never pay personal expenses from it. The same publication explains why - for most small businesses the business checkbook is the main source for entries in the books, and your books have to show gross income, deductions, and credits. A commingled account is not a set of books. It is a puzzle.
Three costs follow from that, and none of them are theoretical:
Read the cash line
### How much does it cost to open a business checking account?
Often $0 a month, but the fee schedule decides the real cost. U.S. Bank’s Business Essentials is $0 a month with 25 cash units per cycle, then $0.35 per $100, and Simmons Bank’s Business Core Checking allows $5,000 in cash deposits a month, then $2.50 per additional $1,000. Using a business name? Add the $7 Missouri fictitious name registration the bank will ask for.
Reconstruction labor. Somebody has to go line by line through twelve months of a mixed account and decide which charges were business. That somebody bills by the hour. Our breakdown of what a bookkeeper actually costs shows what that hour is worth, and cleanup work is priced above ordinary monthly bookkeeping for exactly this reason.
Deductions you quietly abandon. Expenses that cannot be substantiated are expenses that do not get claimed. People undercount their own business spending every year because the receipt is gone and the charge looks personal.
The liability question. If you formed an LLC specifically to keep business problems away from your house, whether mixed funds undercut that separation is a legal question with real consequences. Ask an attorney. Do not ask the internet, and do not assume the answer is comfortable.
There is also a mundane logistical reason. A check made out to a business name generally cannot be deposited into a personal account held in your own name. The first time a commercial client pays you by check instead of by app, you find that out at the teller window.
### Read the fee schedule, not the brochure
Ask for the full fee schedule in writing before you open anything, and read the deposit agreement rather than the marketing page. Here is why that matters more for a business account than it did for your personal one: the federal consumer disclosure rules largely do not reach you.
Truth in Savings, Regulation DD, defines an account as a deposit account held by or offered to a consumer. Regulation E, the rule behind the familiar protections on unauthorized electronic transfers, covers accounts established primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. A business checking account is neither. So the terms of your account - including what happens when someone drains it through a fraudulent transfer - are governed by the contract you sign, not by the consumer rules you have in the back of your head. Ask directly what the fraud reporting window is and what the bank’s obligation is once you report. Get the answer in writing.
With that established, these are the lines to pull off every fee schedule and put side by side:
Monthly maintenance fee, and the exact conditions that waive it
How the waiver balance is measured - minimum daily balance, average monthly balance, or combined balances across linked accounts. These are not the same thing and the difference is real money for a business with a lumpy cash cycle.
Monthly transaction allowance, and precisely which items count against it
Per-item fee once you go over
Cash deposit allowance per statement cycle, and the fee per additional $100 or $1,000
Incoming and outgoing wire fees, domestic and international
ACH origination cost if you will pay contractors or run payroll out of the account
Overdraft and returned item fees, and whether there is a daily cap
Stop payment, paper statement, and account research fees
Cost of fraud tools such as positive pay, dual authorization, and ACH debit blocks
Minimum opening deposit
Early closure fee if you leave within the first several months
Then do one piece of arithmetic that almost nobody does. Take the waiver requirement and price it. As a purely illustrative example, if an account charges $20 a month and waives it at a $5,000 minimum daily balance, you are choosing between $240 a year in fees and $5,000 of your working capital sitting still. For a business that runs tight in February and flush in June, the fee is sometimes the cheaper option. Run your own numbers with the actual figures on the actual schedule.
A published example shows how that trade works. The Bank of America schedule above lists a $16 monthly fee for Business Advantage Fundamentals, waived with any one of three things: a $5,000 combined average monthly balance, at least $500 in new net qualified debit-card purchases, or Preferred Rewards for Business membership. That is $192 a year in fees, set against $5,000 of working capital, $500 of debit-card spending or a membership, and only your own January balance can say which costs you less.
### What is the downside of a free business bank account?
Free almost always means no monthly maintenance fee. It rarely means no fees. The revenue has to come from somewhere, and the usual places are a low transaction allowance with per-item charges past it, a small or nonexistent cash deposit allowance, no interest on balances, higher wire and expedited-service pricing, fraud controls sold as add-ons, and in the case of app-based accounts, no branch and no way to deposit currency at all.
None of that is a trick. It is a fit question. A consultant in Clayton who gets four ACH payments a month and writes six checks will genuinely pay nothing on a free account for years. A food truck operating out of Maplewood that deposits $6,000 in currency a month will find that the same free account is the most expensive one on the table. Match the structure to the deposit pattern and the word free stops being a selling point and becomes a data point.
### What happens when your cash outgrows the free allowance?
If your customers hand you money, this section decides your account. Two separate ceilings apply, and they are easy to confuse.
The first is the bank’s own cash deposit allowance. Business accounts typically include a set dollar amount of currency you can deposit per statement cycle at no charge, with a fee per additional increment after that. Ask two follow-up questions the brochure will not answer: does the allowance reset monthly or accrue, and does a deposit made at a night drop or through a smart safe count differently than one made at the teller line. Then estimate your own monthly cash honestly - not your best month, your typical month - and price all three candidate accounts against that number.
Published examples show how wide that range runs. Commerce Bank’s small business fee schedule lists free cash deposits up to $5,000, $10,000 or $20,000 per cycle, depending on the account. Bank of America’s Relationship Banking tier lists $20,000 free, then 30 cents per $100. These are examples, not recommendations, and each schedule changes, so check the current one.
The second ceiling is federal and has nothing to do with fees. Under the Bank Secrecy Act, a financial institution files a Currency Transaction Report on currency transactions above $10,000. This is routine paperwork, not an accusation, and it happens constantly to legitimate cash businesses. You show identification, the bank files the form, life continues.
What is genuinely dangerous is the workaround people invent. Deliberately breaking a deposit into smaller pieces to keep the bank from filing that report is called structuring, and it is a federal crime under 31 U.S.C. 5324 even when every dollar involved is clean. Banks watch for the pattern and file suspicious activity reports when they see it. If you take a lot of currency, deposit it as it comes in and let the paperwork be paperwork.
### What is the $3000 rule for banks?
People hear about a $3,000 threshold and assume it is a deposit limit. It is not. It is a recordkeeping rule for buying certain paper instruments with cash. Under 31 CFR 1010.415, no financial institution may issue or sell a cashier’s check, bank draft, money order, or traveler’s check for $3,000 or more in currency without recording specific details - the purchaser’s name, the date, the type and serial number of each instrument, and the dollar amount. The rule covers currency purchases from $3,000 through $10,000 inclusive.
Two practical consequences for a small business. If you are not already a deposit customer, the institution has to verify your identity from a document acceptable in the banking community showing your name and address, which is why buying a large cashier’s check somewhere you do not bank takes longer. And depositing currency into your own account first and then buying the instrument does not sidestep the rule - the transaction is still subject to it.
### Card fees come in three layers, and you can haggle one
Card acceptance is three stacked layers, and only one of them is negotiable. Interchange goes to the bank that issued your customer’s card. Network assessments go to Visa or Mastercard. The processor’s markup goes to whoever sold you the terminal. When someone quotes you a rate, they are quoting the third layer wrapped around the first two, and the wrapping is where the differences hide.
The only number worth comparing is your effective rate: total card processing fees for a month divided by total card volume for that month. Every quoted headline rate describes one card type under one condition. The effective rate describes what actually left your account. Compute it from a real statement and the sales pitches sort themselves out quickly. We go deeper on this in what Missouri businesses actually pay in credit card processing fees.
One structural detail that surprises people. The Federal Reserve’s Regulation II caps debit interchange at 21 cents plus 0.05 percent of the transaction, plus a one-cent fraud-prevention adjustment for eligible issuers - but only for issuers holding $10 billion or more in assets. Cards issued by smaller community banks and credit unions are exempt from that cap. You do not choose which card a customer hands you, so a merchant in a metro full of community institutions can see a different mix of debit costs than the averages suggest. It is a reason to look at your own statement rather than a national benchmark.
Last thing: do not let a bundled merchant offer pick your checking account. Price the deposit account on the twelve fee lines above and price card processing on its own effective rate. Bundles are sold together because the weaker half is easier to move that way.
### When a credit union or a small local bank beats a national one
Three situations, mostly: when you deposit currency, when you want to talk to a person who can decide something, and when you will eventually need a modest loan from an institution that knows your name.
Deposit insurance is not the differentiator people think it is. The National Credit Union Administration insures share accounts at federally insured credit unions to $250,000, the same standard maximum the FDIC applies at banks. A business account is generally insured separately from the owner’s personal accounts, provided the entity is engaged in an independent activity rather than existing to multiply coverage.
There is one exception with real planning consequences. The FDIC insures a sole proprietorship’s account as the single account of the owner - meaning it is combined with that person’s other single accounts at the same institution under one $250,000 limit, not given its own. If you are a sole proprietor who occasionally parks a large deposit before paying subcontractors, that is worth knowing before the balance gets there.
Where the local institution genuinely wins for a cash business: branch density in the neighborhood you actually work in, a night drop you pass on the way home, staff who recognize a recurring deposit pattern instead of flagging it, and lending decisions made by people in the same ZIP code rather than a scoring model three time zones away. Where the national bank wins: operations in multiple states, heavy software integrations, treasury and cash management services, branch coverage while traveling, and larger credit facilities.
Two caveats on credit unions specifically. You have to be eligible for membership, which is usually easier than people assume - we cover the field-of-membership rules in how to join a credit union in St. Louis. And not every credit union offers business accounts or business lending, so ask before you fall in love with the rate sheet. If you want a sense of the local field, our roundup of credit unions in the St. Louis metro is a starting point for your own research, not a recommendation.
On the two-state question: banking across the river is ordinary and nothing about the Mississippi limits where you can hold an account. What the state line does control is your registration, your licensing, and your tax obligations. Those follow where you operate, not where your deposits sit.
### Why would I get denied for a business checking account?
Usually not for the reason people fear. Business checking approval is rarely a credit score decision. The common causes are banking history, paperwork mismatches, and industry risk policy. Which is worth a pause: a mismatch in how your business name reads from one place to the next can sink more than a bank application. So - does your information actually agree everywhere it appears?
Account screening companies such as ChexSystems and Early Warning Services keep records of closed accounts, unpaid negative balances, and account abuse. They are consumer reporting agencies, which gives you rights most people never use. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains that nationwide account screening agencies must give you a free report on request, and that you can dispute inaccurate or incomplete information for free. A bank that denies you based on one of those reports has to give you an adverse action notice under the Fair Credit Reporting Act - which tells you which company to go ask.
The other frequent causes are fixable in advance. Your name on your ID, on your state or county registration, and on your IRS EIN letter all need to match. An expired fictitious name registration will stop the process cold. Missing beneficial ownership details will pause it. And some business categories sit outside a given institution’s risk appetite, which is a policy decision rather than a judgment about you - the next institution may say yes to the same file.
If you have ever had an account closed by a bank, pull both screening reports before you apply anywhere. Finding a stale entry after a denial is a much worse afternoon than finding it before.
### How do you compare three banks in one afternoon?
Pick three institutions - and make one of them a credit union or a community bank, because the fee structures diverge most there. Put the twelve fee lines above into a column for each one, using your own honest monthly numbers rather than a good month. Then add four rows the fee schedule will never tell you:
Your realistic monthly overage on transactions and on cash, multiplied by the per-item and per-increment fees - this converts an abstract allowance into a dollar figure
Nearest branch to the last stop of your working day, and whether it has a night drop
Whether the institution does business lending at all, and to businesses your size
Total estimated annual cost for your actual usage
Before you chase funding, read which small business grants a St. Louis owner can actually apply for.
That last row is the answer. Not the headline rate, not the bonus, not the branding. The account with the lowest total annual cost for the way your money actually moves, at an institution you can reach when something goes wrong. If two come out close, break the tie on the branch and on whether you will ever want to borrow from them.

If you run the lawn crew, the chair or the catering van yourself, a separate account is the day that $85 check stops landing next to the grocery money and starts looking like a business. The next step is the phone. Tonight a neighbor in Affton will search for your trade, and a lead-farm will happily sell that request to three to eight shops, then rent your own customers back to you. ### What should you ask before you sign?
May I have the complete fee schedule and the deposit account agreement in writing before I open
Exactly how is the balance that waives the monthly fee calculated
Which items count against the monthly transaction allowance, and which do not
What is the free cash deposit allowance per cycle and the fee beyond it
If someone initiates an unauthorized transfer out of this account, what is my reporting deadline and what is your obligation
What fraud controls are available, what do they cost, and which are on by default
Does opening this account establish a relationship for future business lending, and what would you want to see from me
Are merchant services priced independently of this account, and can I see a sample statement
What documentation do you need from a Missouri fictitious name registration versus an Illinois county assumed name certificate
Is there a fee for closing the account within the first year
Ask all ten at every institution. Identical questions are the only thing that makes two quotes comparable.
Business accounts carry the same fee architecture as personal ones, only larger. Everything in the full list of bank fees and how to kill them applies here, with higher balance thresholds attached.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need an LLC to get a business checking account?
A.  No. Sole proprietors open business checking accounts routinely, and the Small Business Administration lists a Social Security number as an acceptable substitute for an EIN if you operate as a sole proprietorship. What the bank needs is proof that the name on the account belongs to you - which for a trade name means a Missouri fictitious name registration or an Illinois county assumed name certificate. Whether forming an LLC is right for you is a liability and tax question that belongs with an attorney or CPA, not a banking requirement.
### Q. Can I use a personal bank account for my LLC?
A.  It is possible and it is the costliest habit on this list. IRS Publication 583 tells new business owners to open a business checking account, use it only for business, and never pay personal expenses from it - because for most small businesses the business checkbook is the primary record behind the tax return. Mixing funds means paying someone to untangle a year of statements, losing deductions you cannot substantiate, and raising a separation question your attorney would rather you never raised. Checks written to a business name also cannot generally be deposited personally.
### Q. Why would I get denied for a business checking account?
A.  Most often it is banking history rather than credit. Account screening companies such as ChexSystems and Early Warning Services report closed accounts and unpaid negative balances, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes that nationwide screening agencies must provide a free report on request and investigate disputes at no charge. A bank that denies you based on a report must send an adverse action notice under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Other common causes are name mismatches across your ID, registration, and EIN letter, an expired fictitious name filing, or an industry outside that institution’s risk policy.
### Q. What is the $3000 rule for banks?
A.  It is a recordkeeping rule, not a deposit limit. Under 31 CFR 1010.415, a financial institution may not issue or sell a cashier’s check, bank draft, money order, or traveler’s check for $3,000 or more in currency unless it records the purchaser’s name, the date, the type and serial number of each instrument, and the amount. It applies to currency purchases from $3,000 through $10,000. Depositing the cash into your own account first and then buying the instrument does not avoid it, and non-customers face additional identity verification.
### Q. What is the downside of a free business bank account?
A.  Free normally means no monthly maintenance fee rather than no fees at all. The cost usually reappears as a low monthly transaction allowance with per-item charges beyond it, little or no free cash deposit allowance, no interest on balances, higher wire and expedited service pricing, fraud tools sold separately, and sometimes no branch access at all. That structure is genuinely cheap for a service business paid by transfer and genuinely expensive for a salon, food truck, or lawn crew depositing currency every week. Match it to your deposit pattern before calling it free.
### Q. What qualifies for a business checking account?
A.  Generally an EIN, your formation or registration paperwork, and personal ID for anyone with signing authority or meaningful ownership. If you operate in Missouri under any name other than your true name, you are required to register that fictitious name first - a $7 filing good for five years, and banks do ask.
### Q. Is it hard to get approved for a business bank account?
A.  Usually straightforward with an EIN, formation paperwork and ID. It gets harder in high-cash or high-risk categories, where banks apply extra scrutiny. In Missouri, operating under any name other than your true name means registering that fictitious name first - a $7 filing good for five years, and banks do ask for it.
### Q. What bank account is best for an LLC?
A.  A business checking account in the LLC’s own name, opened with the LLC’s EIN, never a personal account with business money running through it. Beyond that, match the account to how you actually transact: cash deposit allowances matter for a caterer, ACH and transaction limits matter for a consultant. To build a shortlist, browse banks across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick three and ask each the same ten questions.
The lawn crew in Florissant, the stylist in Kirkwood, the caterer in Belleville, and the handyman in O’Fallon do not need the same account, and there is no single institution that is right for all four. What they need is the same forty-minute exercise: count the cash, count the transactions, name the balance they can leave alone, and then make three fee schedules answer for themselves. Do that once and the account stops being a decision you avoid and becomes one you already made.

## St. Louis Bank Fees: Switch Off the Overdraft Fee You Said Yes To
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-avoid-bank-fees-in-st-louis
You never chose the overdraft fee. You said yes to it, once, at a desk on account-opening day, and forgot.
The phone buzzes on the nightstand at 2 a.m. and the screen lights up the ceiling. The banking app shows a number in red. A gas pump in Florissant put a hold on the card, a streaming renewal hit the same afternoon, and the paycheck landed a day late. The shortfall was eleven dollars. The fee was not.
Here is the turn. A bank can charge an overdraft fee on an ATM withdrawal or an everyday debit swipe only if you opted in to that service. The FDIC says it in one blunt line on its consumer page on overdraft and account fees: if you don’t opt in, you can’t be charged a fee. The same page puts a typical overdraft fee at around $35 per transaction. So the thing that turned eleven dollars into a cold stomach-drop sits on a switch, and the switch is yours.
St. Louis has a second answer most people searching this never hear. A farmers’ bank founded in 1906 to serve a small farming community near St. Louis grew into today’s First Bank, and it sells a checking account called Imagine Checking. First Bank’s own product page says it is designed to prevent overdrafts, with no overdraft fees and no NSF return item fees, and it opens with $25. It sits on the national list of Bank On certified accounts, a program built around low-cost checking with no overdraft fees. And the national scoreboard for that program is kept from here: the Cities for Financial Empowerment Fund and the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis partnered to build the Bank On National Data Hub.
Tell the friend who just ate a fee: the fix for overdrafts has a St. Louis address.
### How do I avoid overdraft fees?
Call your bank and opt out of overdraft coverage for debit card and ATM transactions, then ask for that in writing. After that, a short balance means a declined card instead of a fee. Turn on low-balance alerts, link savings for automatic transfers, and if fees keep coming, move to a no-overdraft account such as a Bank On certified one.
The words to say on the call, word for word: “Please opt me out of overdraft coverage for debit card and ATM transactions, and send me written confirmation.” That is the whole job. It takes less time than the hold music.
### What a declined card actually feels like
People worry about opting out because they picture the worst moment: the line at the register in Kirkwood, a cart already bagged, the little terminal beeping no. That moment is real. Your face goes warm, you hand over another card or put the ice cream back, and the cashier has seen it a dozen times that week. Then it is over. Nothing lands on your statement.
The opted-in version feels fine at the register and terrible at 2 a.m. The card approves, the groceries go home, and a fee lands for a shortfall of a few dollars. Pick which of those two moments you would rather have.
### The St. Louis clock nobody warns you about
This metro sits on two sides of a river, and the river changes the rules for the account you forgot. Leave an old checking account untouched and the bank eventually hands the balance to the state as unclaimed property. Missouri’s State Treasurer lists the dormancy period as 5 years for most property. Illinois law treats a demand or savings deposit as abandoned after 3 years without owner contact. So the account you left behind in Belleville goes to the state two years sooner than the same account in Kirkwood, and inactivity fees can nibble it the whole way there. One real deposit or withdrawal a year on every account you own stops both.
### The fee your opt-out does not stop
Checks and automatic payments live under different rules. The FDIC is plain about it: banks are not required to obtain your opt-in for non-sufficient funds fees. So if the rent autopay or the car payment pulls from an account that cannot cover it, the payment can bounce and still cost you a fee, opted out or not. That bounced-payment notice in the mailbox, the one with the landlord’s name on the envelope, is the fee people never see coming.
This is also where the money really piles up. The National Consumer Law Center reported that banks and credit unions took over $12 billion in overdraft and NSF fees from families in a single year. The fix here is timing: know the day each autopay pulls, know when your deposit really posts, and ask your bank exactly what happens to a returned payment before you need to know.
Watch for repeat charges on one payment, too. When an automatic payment comes back unpaid, a merchant can send it again, and some banks charge a separate fee each time. The FDIC once issued guidance on this practice in Financial Institution Letter 40-2022, and has since rescinded that guidance. Your own fee schedule is now the only answer that counts, so ask: if a payment is returned and sent again, am I charged twice?
### Are overdraft fees illegal?
No. A federal rule that would have cut most overdraft fees to $5 was issued and then overturned by Congress, and it never went into effect. What stays illegal is the consent problem: an overdraft fee on an ATM withdrawal or a one-time debit card purchase you never opted in to. If that happened to you, you are not asking for a favor. Ask the bank to show you the opt-in record.
The federal rule, Regulation E, spells out how that consent must work in 12 CFR 1005.17: the bank has to describe the service, give you a reasonable chance to opt in, get your affirmative consent, and confirm it in writing, including your right to revoke. People who do not opt in must get the same account terms, conditions and features as people who do, so opting out cannot cost you a worse account. And opting in does not even promise the purchase goes through: in the FDIC’s words your bank may pay it, not must, and a bank can still decline a debit purchase even after you opted in.
Somebody else just got a letter about a card they never opened - here is how to freeze your credit before that letter is yours.
### The moves that stop overdraft fees, in order of power
Opt out of debit card and ATM overdraft coverage. Free, reversible, and it turns a fee into a declined card.
Link savings for overdraft transfers. The FDIC notes the transfer fee is typically less than an overdraft charge. Ask what it is.
Turn on low-balance alerts. They catch the most common cause: a deposit landing a day later than you expected.
Learn your deposit cutoff time. A late deposit posts the next business day, and that gap is where fees are born.
Watch card holds. Gas pumps, hotels and rental counters can hold more than the final charge.
Move to a no-overdraft account if fees keep coming. Look for Bank On certified accounts.
The price of a short balance
### Which banks do not charge fees?
The FDIC says an overdraft fee may cost around $35 per transaction, and using an ATM outside your network averages $4.86 in total fees, per Bankrate’s study. A no-overdraft account takes the first number to $0: First Bank’s Imagine Checking opens with $25 and charges no overdraft or NSF return item fees. What moves your real cost is which account you hold and whether you opted in.
### How long will a bank let you overdraft?
Two clocks can run at once. Some banks charge an extra fee for each day the account stays negative, and the FDIC calls these continuous or daily overdraft fees. The second clock is closure: leave an account negative long enough and the bank can close it. If you are negative and cannot fix it today, call before either clock runs out. A conversation about a repayment date is a far easier call than one about a closed account.
### How to get bank fees waived?
Call once, calm, with the date and the amount in front of you. Something close to this works: “I was charged an overdraft fee on the ninth. My deposit posted a day later than I expected. This is the first time it has happened on my account. Would you reverse it as a one-time courtesy?” If the first person declines, ask whether a supervisor can approve a courtesy adjustment. Then fix the cause before you hang up: “While I have you, please opt me out of debit card overdraft coverage and turn on a low-balance alert.” That last sentence is worth more than the refund.
A first request has a fair shot. A fourth one, on an account that keeps going negative, is asking the bank to stop charging for the product the way it is priced. If that is you, the answer is the opt-out and a different account, not another call.
### The quiet fees that renew without asking
Monthly maintenance fees are the price of the account you hold, and most come with a way to make them zero: a direct deposit, a minimum balance, or a set number of card purchases. Bankrate’s yearly checking account and ATM fee study tracks what those fees and waivers average, and its roundup of common bank fees and how to avoid them covers paper statements and the rest. The cleanest fix is to ask, in these words: which of your checking accounts has no monthly fee at all?
Wires add up fast; Bankrate’s look at wire transfer fees shows how they stack. And before you send any wire, confirm the instructions by calling a number you looked up yourself, never one from an email.
### If the bank says no, who to call
The right regulator depends on how your bank is chartered. Start with this guide to finding your state’s bank regulator.
Missouri: file a complaint against a bank with the Missouri Division of Finance.
Illinois state banks: the Illinois Division of Banking.
Deposit insurance: the FDIC insures deposits to at least $250,000 at each insured bank, and the NCUA share insurance fund covers federally insured credit unions up to $250,000.
The CFPB once wrote an overdraft fee rule that Congress reversed, and a credit union is one way out of these fees. Our guide to local credit unions in the St. Louis metro covers how membership works around here.
### What to ask at the branch
Highlight every line with the word fee on three months of statements.
Ask which checking account has no monthly fee and no overdraft fee.
Ask to be opted out of debit card and ATM overdraft coverage, in writing.
Ask what happens to autopays and checks after you opt out.
Ask whether a returned payment sent again means a second fee.
Turn on low-balance alerts before you leave.
This is general consumer information, not personal financial advice.
Take the same six questions to every bank you are weighing. If the fees are structural rather than a bad month, the fix is a different account. Here is how to switch banks without missing a bill, in the order that keeps an autopay from bouncing.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do banks charge a monthly fee for checking accounts?
A.  Many do, but most list a way to waive it, and some accounts have no monthly fee at all. Accounts in the Bank On program feature low costs and no overdraft fees. Ask any bank which of its checking accounts has no monthly fee and no overdraft fee.
### Q. Are overdraft fees illegal?
A.  No. A federal rule to cut most overdraft fees to $5 was overturned by Congress and never took effect. A fee on an ATM withdrawal or one-time debit card purchase is not allowed unless you opted in to overdraft coverage first.
### Q. How long will a bank let you overdraft?
A.  Check your account agreement first. Some banks add daily overdraft fees for each day the balance stays negative, and an account left negative long enough can be closed. Call the bank before either happens.
### Q. How to get bank fees waived?
A.  Call with the date and the amount, explain the cause in one sentence, and ask for a one-time courtesy reversal. If the first person says no, ask for a supervisor. Then opt out of debit card overdraft coverage on the same call.
### Q. How can you avoid monthly maintenance fees on a checking account?
A.  Meet the waiver condition your account lists, such as a direct deposit, a minimum balance, or a set number of transactions. Or switch to a checking account that has no monthly fee to waive.
### Q. Why is my bank charging me a monthly maintenance fee?
A.  Because your account is a paid product and you are not meeting the condition that turns the fee off. Check the disclosure for the waiver rule, then meet it or ask for an account with no monthly fee.

## Financial Planner Fees in St. Louis: The 1% You Never Get a Bill For
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-financial-planner-costs-in-st-louis
$5,000 a year: say your retirement account holds $500,000, and that’s what one percent of it costs you, with no bill ever showing up. It comes out a quarter at a time, $1,250 at a go, inside a statement most people open at the kitchen counter, glance at, and slide back into the envelope with the electric bill.
Now walk it downtown. Stifel’s headquarters sits at One Financial Plaza, 501 North Broadway, in the heart of downtown St. Louis, and the firm’s own relationship summary, the short form every firm has to hand you, says the quiet part in plain type. In advisory accounts, you will typically pay Stifel an asset-based fee at the beginning of each quarter. And its financial advisors are compensated based upon a percentage of advisory fees and commissions and other transaction-based fees that Stifel receives.
Read that twice. The person across the desk is paid out of the same percentage that leaves your account. It isn’t hidden. It’s printed, on a form most people never unfold. That’s exactly why you do the math in dollars.
Now hold that against a schedule a firm actually prints. Edward Jones publishes its Advisory Solutions fee schedule: a program fee of 1.35% a year on the first $250,000 and 1.30% on the next $250,000, plus a platform fee of 0.05% on fund-model accounts. On that same $500,000, the program fee alone works out to $6,625 a year, while the 0.96% survey average works out to $4,800. Same half-million, $1,825 apart, every single year, before the platform fee. The same sheet says the fee may be discounted or reduced at the firm’s sole discretion, which is your cue to ask.
Before you compare a single price, make one phone call. Missouri’s Securities Division, part of the Secretary of State, says its registration staff registers approximately 1,822 investment advisers and 11,566 investment adviser representatives annually. Its Investor Protection Hotline is (800) 721-7996, and the general line is (573) 751-4136. Ask whether the person you are about to hire is registered and whether there is anything on their record. The fee you are about to agree to will cost you every year.
General cost education, not advice about your money. Here are the numbers.
### What is the normal fee for a financial advisor?
The normal fee is just under 1% of the money managed each year: an Envestnet and Datos Insights survey of 491 financial advisors put the average bundled AUM fee at 0.96%. Advisors who charge a set price instead averaged $6,815 a year for an ongoing retainer, $2,926 for a one-time flat-fee plan and $595 a month for a subscription. Say you have $500,000 invested: 0.96% is $4,800 a year.
Those figures come from the State of Financial Planning Fees study, and the part to carry into any first meeting is this: 53% of the advisors surveyed raised their fees in the past 12 months. The retainer average jumped from $4,484 to $6,815. If you signed years ago, the number on your agreement may not be the number coming out of your account.
Hourly work is the cheapest door in. Kitces fee research found median hourly rates near $250, with the median shifting up from around $200. A two-hour session on whether to take a pension lump sum is a few hundred dollars, paid once, with a receipt you can hold.
### Four meters, one service
The first meeting usually ends the same way: a folder slid across the desk, a pen set on top, and a fee page with one of four meters on it. The meter decides who comes out ahead. A percentage of assets grows with your balance whether or not the work does; the survey’s 0.96% average is the only model that got cheaper, down from 1.05%. A retainer is a set yearly price no matter your balance, which favors big portfolios and pinches small ones. A flat-fee plan is a one-time document and a meeting or two, then you carry it out yourself. A subscription is a monthly charge for ongoing access, and it moved fastest of all: from $215 a month to $595.
None of those is the right answer by default. A retiree with $1.2 million and a messy tax picture may get a bargain from a retainer. A 40-year-old in south city with $60,000 in a workplace retirement plan and one big question would be paying for years of service she doesn’t need. Picture the meter running while you sleep, and ask which one fits the work you actually want done.
The firm type matters too. In the same survey, registered investment adviser firms averaged $7,550 for a retainer while other firms averaged $5,237. Bigger price, different business model, and the brochure will tell you which one you are looking at.
### The fee you feel and the fee you don’t
A check for $4,800 would hurt. You’d feel the pen drag. The same $4,800 pulled from an account in four quarterly slices of $1,200 barely registers, which is exactly why percentage pricing is described as painless. It isn’t cheaper. It’s quieter.
And it compounds. The SEC’s investor bulletin on fees runs a $100,000 investment growing at 4% a year for 20 years. With a 0.25% annual fee, it ends near $208,000. With a 1.00% fee, near $179,000. That is about $29,000 gone on a $100,000 start, the price of a decent used car, without one bill ever crossing your kitchen table.
That doesn’t make a one percent planner a bad deal. It makes the fee a real cost that has to be beaten by real value: a tax move, a smarter withdrawal order, or the phone call that talks you out of selling everything in a bad month. The bulletin’s number is the bar, not the verdict.
### One percent, in dollars
At a flat one percent, the yearly fee is the balance divided by one hundred. Write your own number next to the closest line:
$100,000 - $1,000 a year, about $83 a month
$250,000 - $2,500 a year, about $208 a month
$500,000 - $5,000 a year, about $417 a month
$1,000,000 - $10,000 a year, about $833 a month
Most percentage schedules step down as balances grow, with breakpoints that work like tax brackets, and many carry an annual minimum fee. A minimum of $2,500 on a $150,000 account is not 1%. It’s 1.67%. Ask whether household accounts can be added together to reach a breakpoint sooner, and ask for the all-in yearly cost, including the expense ratios of the funds underneath, as one figure you could write on a napkin.
Spreadsheet break: here’s what Tower Grove South is actually like on foot.
### Is 2% fee high for a financial advisor?
Say a planner quotes you 2%. Against a 0.96% average, that’s roughly double, and whoever charges it should be able to say why. Two honest complications. Two percent of $80,000 is $1,600 a year, less than the average flat-fee plan, and small accounts often carry higher rates because there is a floor below which the work doesn’t pay. And an all-in fee that already includes fund costs is a different animal from an advisory fee stacked on top of expensive funds.
Budget before the first meeting
### Is one fee for a financial advisor worth it?
Compare it in dollars first. Survey averages run from $2,926 for a one-time flat-fee plan to $6,815 a year for an ongoing retainer, with hourly work at a median near $250. The firm type and the fee model move it most, so get each St. Louis planner’s own written schedule before you compare.
### Fee-only, fee-based and commission: one word changes the money
Fee-only means you are the only one paying the planner. Fee-based means fees and commissions, a legitimate model that sits one syllable away from fee-only. Commission means the product company pays them, and your cost hides inside what you bought. None of these is automatically honest or dishonest. Each puts different pressure in the room. So ask it out loud: how are you paid, by whom, and do you ever receive money from anyone other than me? Then get the answer in writing. For the vetting side of that conversation, read our guide on how to choose a financial advisor in St. Louis.
Brokers work under a different standard than advisers. The SEC’s Regulation Best Interest requires broker-dealers to act in the best interest of the retail customer at the time a recommendation is made. Ask whether the person across the table is acting as a fiduciary on everything they recommend, every time, and ask them to put that in writing.
### Where the real fee schedule is written down
Registered advisers must prepare a narrative brochure, Part 2 of the Form ADV, with plain English disclosures of their business practices, fees, conflicts of interest and disciplinary information. Go straight to the fees and read the schedule yourself.
There’s a shorter sheet too. Registered broker-dealers and registered investment advisers are required to give retail investors a Form CRS relationship summary, which tells you the types of services a firm offers and the fees and costs you will pay. Read it on your phone in the parking lot before the first meeting.
Then check the person:
Investment Adviser Public Disclosure for investment advisers
FINRA BrokerCheck for brokers
CFP Board verification to verify a CFP certification
The Missouri Securities Division hotline above, or the Illinois Securities Department at 800-628-7937 if you live on the Metro East side
Smaller firms are usually overseen by a state, not the SEC; Investor.gov’s adviser registration page explains where that line sits. If a planner works both sides of the river, ask which states they are registered in and check it.
### How much money should you have to see a financial advisor?
Less than you think, if you shop by fee model instead of by firm. Account minimums belong to percentage pricing, because a percentage of a small balance doesn’t cover the work. Hourly and flat-fee planners aren’t paid out of your balance, so it matters less to them. What matters is whether you face a decision worth paying to get right: a pension lump sum, a rollover after a layoff, an inheritance, when to claim Social Security.
If money is tight, start with free tax preparation programs around St. Louis and a local credit union before you pay anyone.
### Questions to ask before you sign
What would I pay in dollars in year one, with my actual numbers?
What is the all-in yearly cost, including fund expenses, as one number?
Is there an annual minimum, and what percent is that at my balance?
Do you receive money from anyone other than me?
Are you a fiduciary on everything you recommend, and will you put it in writing?
Can I have your Form ADV brochure and Form CRS today?
How much notice do I get before a fee increase, and how do I leave?
Get the schedule on paper. A rate said out loud has no minimums and no fund costs attached. A written one has both.
Take the dollar figure, not the percent, into every first meeting. Read how to choose a financial advisor in St. Louis before you sit down, and what a will or trust costs in Missouri if estate planning is why you started looking.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth paying a financial advisor?
A.  It depends on your situation. The cost side is measurable: the SEC’s illustration shows $100,000 growing at 4% for 20 years ending near $179,000 with a 1.00% annual fee, against about $208,000 at 0.25%. A fee tends to earn out when the decisions are complex and hard to reverse, and rarely when the service is an annual rebalance and a statement.
### Q. How much money should you have before getting a financial advisor?
A.  It depends on the fee model, not the balance. Firms charging a percentage of assets often set minimums. Hourly and flat-fee planners are not paid out of your balance: survey averages put a flat-fee plan at $2,926, and Kitces found median hourly rates near $250.
### Q. What is a red flag for a financial advisor?
A.  Anyone who won’t put the fee in writing, can’t say plainly whether they are a fiduciary on everything they recommend, or isn’t registered. Check registration and history on Investment Adviser Public Disclosure, FINRA BrokerCheck, or with the Missouri Securities Division at (800) 721-7996.
### Q. What are the downsides of using a financial advisor?
A.  Cost, mainly, and it compounds. Retainers averaged $6,815 a year in the Envestnet survey, and 53% of advisors raised fees in the past 12 months. Some pay structures also carry conflicts where compensation depends on which products you buy.
### Q. Is $100,000 enough to have a financial advisor?
A.  Yes, if you pick the right fee model. At 1% a year, $100,000 costs $1,000 annually. A one-time flat-fee plan averaged $2,926 in the Envestnet survey, and hourly work at a median near $250 lets you pay only for the decisions you need help with.
### Q. Are fee-only financial advisors worth it?
A.  Fee-only describes who pays the planner, not how much. A fee-only planner can charge a percentage, a retainer, a flat plan fee or hourly. What it buys you is a simpler conflict picture, because you are the only source of their pay. Price still has to be compared in dollars.

## Retired in St. Louis? Your Social Security Break Eats Your Pension Break
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-missouri-taxes-retirement-income
Who gets a cut of the 1099-R sitting on your kitchen table? It came in a thin envelope you almost tossed out with the grocery flyers. Now it’s propped against the sugar bowl, Box 1 staring up at you, the furnace kicking on behind you, and three governments are in the room: the IRS, Jefferson City and, if you live inside the city limits, City Hall.
Start with City Hall, because most people guess wrong in the gloomy direction. The City of St. Louis describes its earnings tax as a one percent tax on earned income such as salaries, wages, commissions, tips and other compensation. A pension is not a paycheck. The Collector of Revenue’s own earnings tax page settles it in one line: retired and unemployed individuals do not pay the tax.
The catch is work. Pick up a few shifts behind a hardware store counter in the city and the one percent comes right back on those wages, because the city’s earnings tax rules collect it from city residents wherever their employer is, and from anyone working inside the city, wherever they live. The pension check stays clean. The side-job paycheck does not.
Jefferson City is next, and Missouri is kinder than its reputation on one line and sneakier on another. Social Security comes off the state return once you are 62. A government pension gets its own exemption. But the two don’t stack. The Missouri Department of Revenue’s pension FAQ says it flatly: if you also claim the Social Security deduction, your public pension exemption will be reduced by that amount. That one sentence is where a retired teacher’s refund quietly shrinks.
Then there’s the river. Cross it to Belleville and the same envelope gets a different answer. The Illinois Department of Revenue says Illinois does not tax the federally taxed portion of 401(k) plans, IRAs, government retirement plans or Social Security benefits. Same Box 1. Same hum from the furnace. A different set of rules, one bridge away.
Here it is, one check at a time. General information, not tax advice.
### Does Missouri tax social security and pensions?
Missouri does not tax Social Security for anyone 62 or older, as long as the benefits are in federal adjusted gross income. Public pensions can be subtracted up to the maximum Social Security benefit amount, minus any Social Security deduction you take. Private pensions, IRAs and 401(k)s get an exemption of at most $6,000, which shrinks once income passes $25,000 single or $32,000 married filing combined.
The pension lines sit on Form MO-A, the page of small boxes that rides behind your MO-1040, and the Department points you there to work out each exemption. On the tax year 2025 form, the public pension line reads: amount from Line 1 or $47,633 (maximum social security benefit), for each spouse. Use the form for the year you file.
Do this tonight, before anyone files anything: set your SSA-1099 next to the 1099-R, find the Social Security amount and the pension amount, and subtract the first from the second. That rough number is closer to your real Missouri public pension exemption than the one you have been carrying around in your head.
Missouri letting your Social Security go does not stop the IRS. The IRS says your benefits may be taxable if one-half of your benefits plus all your other income passes a base amount: $25,000 for a single filer, $32,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
### The trap: two Missouri breaks that eat each other
Here’s the arithmetic nobody mentions at the retirement party. Say you retired from a county job with a $30,000 pension, under the yearly cap, and you also deduct $20,000 of Social Security on the same return. Follow the Department’s rule and the public pension exemption starts at $30,000, then drops by the $20,000 you already took for Social Security. You shelter $10,000 of that pension, not $30,000. The other $20,000 sits on your Missouri return as taxable income.
Screenshot that paragraph for anyone in your family with a public pension and a Social Security check. It is the single line most likely to make two retired neighbors with the same income get two different refunds.
If you spent a career in a public job where Social Security was cut, read this twice. The Social Security Fairness Act repealed the Government Pension Offset and the windfall elimination provisions. If either one ever shrank your check, a bigger Social Security payment now means a bigger Missouri Social Security deduction, and by the rule above, a smaller public pension exemption. Last year’s return is not a template for this one.
### Private pensions, IRAs and 401(k)s: $6,000 at most, often nothing
This is the rule that covers the 401(k) from a private employer, the rollover IRA, the company pension: the statements in the manila folder that took a working life to fill. The Department’s pension FAQ sets the private pension exemption at $6,000 at most, with full eligibility only under these Missouri adjusted gross income limits:
$25,000 - single, head of household or qualifying widow(er)
$32,000 - married filing combined
$16,000 - married filing separately
Above the limit, the exemption is reduced by the amount your income goes over it. A single filer far enough past the line gets nothing, so the exemption mostly helps people living on small checks.
Done squinting at boxes for one day? Here’s where to eat in Ste. Genevieve on a slow drive down the river.
### Withdrawals, rates and the capital gains break
The Department posts each year’s rate on its individual income tax year changes page; check it for the year you are filing.
One newer break matters if you are selling stock or a rental. According to the Department’s capital gains subtraction FAQ, eligible individuals can subtract 100% of their federally reported capital gains from their federal adjusted gross income on the Missouri return. Ask your preparer whether you qualify before you plan a sale around it.
### Illinois: the list, and where it ends
Illinois is broad, but it’s a list, not a blanket. Publication 120, Retirement Income lets you subtract the federally taxed portion of:
Qualified employee benefit plans, including 401(k)
IRA distributions, including converting a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA
Social Security benefits
Railroad retirement
Government retirement and governmental disability plans, including military plans
What you may not subtract is just as specific: income that is not from a qualified employee benefit plan, including third-party sick pay and deferred compensation or disability plans that are not government plans. If you had an executive deferred pay deal or a private disability policy, read that line slowly.
Income outside the list does not get the subtraction. The state’s withholding tables put it at 4.95%, so a Glen Carbon retiree doing contract work two days a week pays it on that work like anyone else. Illinois also gives a personal exemption, and the Department’s form-change bulletin shows that exemption amount increased.
### Why a short move counts: the federal law behind it
Retirement income is taxed where you live, not where you earned it. Title 4, Section 114 of the U.S. Code says no state may impose an income tax on any retirement income of an individual who is not a resident or domiciliary of that state. A career spent in a downtown office tower gives Missouri no claim on the retirement income of someone who now lives in Belleville. Wages are a different story, which is why the city earnings tax still follows a part-time job.
### The city earnings tax, case by case
Put the city rules from the top of this page side by side and they sort out cleanly:
A city resident living only on a pension, Social Security and IRA money is a retired individual, and retired individuals do not pay the tax.
A city resident who takes a part-time job anywhere owes the one percent on those wages.
A Ballwin or Belleville resident who works part-time inside the city limits owes the one percent on what they earn there.
More on how the tax is filed is in our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax.
### Property tax: where retirees actually find money
None of this is income tax, but it’s where a lot of Missouri retirees get real dollars back. The City of St. Louis runs a Senior Citizen Property Tax Freeze Credit Program that limits future increases from residential property tax increases for seniors. Missouri law lets a county grant this kind of credit only if it adopts it, so county homeowners should start at St. Louis County’s freeze application page and confirm the deadline there.
The state’s Missouri Property Tax Credit is for a maximum of $750 for renters and $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home, for certain seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals, with household income limits. If your income is low enough to qualify, look at free tax preparation in St. Louis before you pay anyone to file.
### Who gets the $6,000 tax break for the elderly?
Two different $6,000 breaks are floating around, and they get mixed up at every kitchen table in town. The federal one, per the IRS, is an additional $6,000 deduction for individuals age 65 and older, or $12,000 for a married couple if both spouses qualify, phasing out above $75,000 of modified adjusted gross income, $150,000 for joint filers. It is temporary, so check the IRS page for the years it covers. The Missouri one is the private pension exemption above. Same number, different government, different form. A retiree in Ferguson with a small 401(k) could qualify for both; a retiree in Chesterfield with a big one may get neither.
### What to bring to a CPA or an enrolled agent
Last year’s full federal and state returns, including Form MO-A or Illinois Schedule M
Your SSA-1099 and every 1099-R, even the small ones
A list of every account you draw from, pre-tax or Roth, and what you took out
Your exact move dates if you crossed the river during the year
Pay records from any part-time work, and where the work was done
Your property tax receipt, or your rent statement if you rent
Then ask one question before any other: is my Social Security deduction reducing my public pension exemption, and by how much? Ask every preparer you interview the same thing. That habit is also how you go about choosing a financial advisor without a leap of faith.
