### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much of Social Security is taxable in Missouri?
A.  None of it for Missouri purposes if you are 62 or older and the benefits are included in federal adjusted gross income, and none of your Social Security disability benefits. Federal tax is separate: the IRS may tax part of your benefits once one-half of them plus your other income passes $25,000 single or $32,000 married filing jointly.
### Q. Are public pensions taxable in Missouri?
A.  Partly. Missouri lets eligible taxpayers subtract public retirement benefits up to the maximum Social Security benefit amount. If you also claim the Social Security deduction, your public pension exemption is reduced by that amount, so the two breaks do not stack.
### Q. How is income tax treated on pensions in Missouri?
A.  It depends on who paid the pension. A government pension gets the public pension exemption, capped and reduced by your Social Security deduction. A private pension, IRA or 401(k) gets an exemption of at most $6,000, reduced by every dollar your income runs past $25,000 single or $32,000 married filing combined.
### Q. What income is not taxable in Missouri?
A.  For retirees: Social Security at 62 and older, Social Security disability benefits, public pension income up to the yearly cap minus the Social Security deduction, up to $6,000 of private pension income if your income is under the limits, and, for eligible individuals, federally reported capital gains through Missouri’s capital gains subtraction. Wages from a part-time job are taxable, and in the city they also carry the one percent earnings tax.
### Q. Who gets the $6,000 tax break for the elderly?
A.  Federally, individuals age 65 and older can take an additional $6,000 deduction, or $12,000 for a married couple if both qualify, phasing out above $75,000 of modified adjusted gross income or $150,000 for joint filers, per the IRS. Missouri’s separate $6,000 is the private pension exemption, which phases out above $25,000 single or $32,000 married filing combined.
### Q. How much of my retirement income is taxable?
A.  It depends on which bucket each dollar comes from and which side of the river you live on. In Missouri, Social Security at 62 and older is exempt, government pensions are partly exempt, and private pension, IRA and 401(k) money gets an exemption of at most $6,000. In Illinois, the federally taxed portion of qualified plans, IRAs, government pensions and Social Security is subtracted.

## Eight Anheuser-Busch Employees Pooled $55. Joining Their St. Louis Credit Union Takes $5.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-join-a-credit-union-in-st-louis
The fee sits on your statement in small gray type, one line between the grocery run and the gas. Monthly maintenance. You read it twice, then you do the math on a year of it, and something in your chest goes tight, because you did nothing to earn that charge except leave your paycheck where it lands.
Now drive down to Soulard with the windows cracked. On the days the brewery is cooking, the air around Lynch Street smells like warm bread and wet grain, and that smell is part of this story. In 1939, eight Anheuser-Busch employees pooled their savings, which totaled $55, and petitioned the state of Missouri to open a credit union so they could give sound financial advice and credit to their co-workers. Their first branch opened in Soulard, at 10th and Lynch Streets.
That credit union is Together Credit Union now, headquartered at 423 Lynch Street, and it serves more than 142,000 members. Here is the part almost nobody in St. Louis knows: you do not have to work anywhere near a bottling line to join it. If you live or work in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County or Jefferson County, or across the river in Madison or St. Clair County, you are eligible. Immediate family or household members of current members are eligible too. It takes a $5 minimum deposit.
Read that once more. Eight brewery workers needed $55 to open the door. You need five dollars to walk through it.
### Can anyone just join a credit union in St. Louis?
Not anyone, anywhere, but close to it here. Every credit union has a field of membership that spells out who may join, and around St. Louis those fields are wide. Together Credit Union, for one, accepts anyone who lives or works in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson, Madison or St. Clair County, plus immediate family of members, for a $5 minimum deposit. Read the eligibility page, bring photo ID, and fund the share account.
That one paragraph is most of the job. The rest of this page is the fine print people trip over: the wording on the eligibility page, the Missouri law that was written with St. Louis in mind, and the little deposit that quietly turns you from a customer into an owner.
### Do credit unions have membership requirements?
Yes. According to the NCUA’s consumer site, members of a credit union share a common bond, also known as the credit union’s field of membership. That bond can come from your employer, your family, where you live, work, worship or go to school, or a group you belong to.
For most of the last century, the bond was a job. You worked at the plant, the hospital or the school district, and the credit union was down the hall from the time clock. That is exactly how the Lynch Street credit union began. What changed is the community charter, which serves everyone tied to a defined place. The NCUA’s Chartering and Field of Membership Manual says a community charter must be based on a single, geographically well-defined local community, and the agency has published guidance on statistical areas that requires a community drawn that way to have a population of 2.5 million or less. That cap is one reason charters around here read like a list of named counties instead of “the St. Louis metro.”
So open the eligibility page and read the verbs slowly, the way you would read a lease. “Live or work” means you qualify through either one. A person who sleeps in one county and clocks in two counties over has two chances, and needs only one.
### The Missouri law with a line for one city
Here is the strange local fact that makes all of this easier for us. Missouri’s credit union membership statute, Section 370.080, RSMo, lets a state-chartered credit union serve a geographic area that may include all those persons who reside or work in “a city not within a county” or a county where its main office is located. Since 1876, St. Louis has been an independent city, meaning it is not part of any county. That phrase in the law is describing us.
Two more lines in that statute are worth knowing before you sit down at a member services desk. A membership share must have a par value of not less than one dollar nor more than one hundred dollars, so the buy-in at a Missouri state-chartered credit union can never be more than $100. And a membership share shall not be pledged as security on any loan. Your ownership stake cannot be used as collateral against you.
One more line from that statute is the reason people stay members for decades. Once you are admitted, you may remain a member until you choose to withdraw. Change jobs, move to Wentzville, it does not matter. The only thing that reliably closes the door behind you is closing the account yourself.
### Your family may already be your way in
The quietest door is the one at your own kitchen table. Most credit unions allow members’ families to join. For the legal fine print, the NCUA has legal opinions on the eligibility of immediate family members and on household members, which it defines as persons living in the same residence maintaining a single economic unit. If your mother has banked at the same credit union since before you could see over the counter, ask. Together Credit Union’s own list of family members runs from spouses and children to in-laws, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces and nephews.
People are asking
### What’s the phone number for a St. Louis credit union?
It depends which one you want. Together Credit Union, the one that started with Anheuser-Busch employees, lists 800-325-9905. Vantage Credit Union’s general support line is 314.298.0055, and First Community Credit Union lists (636) 728-3333. Call before you go and ask the one question that matters: “Does my address or my job qualify me?”
### Missouri charter, Illinois charter, or federal?
It matters the day something goes wrong, because that is the day you need to know who to call. On this side of the river, the Missouri Division of Credit Unions is the regulatory agency responsible for the examination, supervision, chartering, merger and liquidation of all state-chartered credit unions, and it responds to consumer requests or complaints about credit union services. In the Metro East, the Illinois Division of Financial Institutions licenses, charters and examines state-chartered credit unions. Ask your credit union which charter it holds, and write the answer on a sticky note now, while nothing is wrong.
Completely off topic, but if you end up in Jefferson County tonight, here is where Hillsboro eats.
### The five dollars that makes you an owner
At a credit union, you buy in. As the NCUA’s consumer site puts it, credit unions are owned and controlled by their members. The NCUA explains in a legal opinion on membership rights and par value of shares that federal credit union bylaws let the board of directors set the par value of a share. At Together, the minimum deposit is $5. It is not a fee and it is not gone. It sits in your savings account with your name on it.
New words come with the new card in your wallet. If the paperwork says “share draft,” read this explainer on what a share draft account is before you sign. The words feel odd for about a week.
Then leave that first deposit alone and let it sit there with your name on it.
### What to bring to the counter
The paperwork is the same kind you would bring to any bank. If you like a list on paper, print this account-opening checklist. Put these in a folder the night before:
A government photo ID, such as a driver’s license or passport.
Your Social Security number or another taxpayer ID number.
Proof of address, like a recent utility bill or lease.
Proof you qualify: a pay stub for a job-based path, or the member’s name if you are joining through family.
The opening deposit, plus whatever you want in checking on day one.
Going straight to the teller window with a fat envelope of cash for a cashier’s check? Expect a few extra questions. Under 31 CFR 1010.415, no financial institution may sell a cashier’s check, money order or traveler’s check for $3,000 or more in currency unless it keeps records on the buyer. Nobody is accusing you of anything. Bring your ID and expect the questions.
### Is the money as safe as at a bank?
Yes. The NCUA’s Share Insurance Fund is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States and provides up to $250,000 of federal share insurance. The FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor at an insured bank. Same ceiling, different sticker on the door. The NCUA’s share insurance FAQ walks through how joint accounts and retirement accounts get their own coverage.
Take sixty seconds before you move a paycheck: look the credit union up on the NCUA’s credit union locator. If it shows up there, you know who stands behind it.
### Where credit unions fall short
Honesty first: there are trade-offs. The branch map can look small next to a big bank’s. The counterweight is shared branching: the NCUA’s final rule on the definition of a service facility provides that shared locations are service facilities for certain federal credit union purposes, whether or not the credit union owns a piece of the network. Together Credit Union, for instance, points members to thousands of Shared Branch locations. Ask any credit union whether it is in a shared network before you write it off over branch count.
Not-for-profit does not mean fee-free, either. Ask for the full fee schedule in writing and lay it next to that statement with the small gray line on it. Compare them line by line.
### If a bank once turned you down
Eligibility and account approval are two different tests. Your field of membership asks where you live or work. A separate screen can stop a checking account, so before you apply anywhere new, read why a checking account gets denied and how to get a copy of the report banks use. On ChexSystems’ own site you can request and view your ChexSystems report and dispute errors. Do that first, with a cup of coffee, before you sit across from anyone.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it difficult to get into a credit union?
A.  Rarely, in St. Louis. Together Credit Union’s communities include St. Louis City and St. Louis County in Missouri and Madison and St. Clair counties in Illinois, and immediate family or household members of its members can join too. At Together Credit Union, living or working in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson, Madison or St. Clair County qualifies you, with a $5 minimum deposit.
### Q. What is the easiest credit union to join?
A.  The one whose eligibility page already names your county and the relationship you actually have to it. A charter that says “live or work” gives you two ways in. If a parent, spouse or sibling is already a member, that can open a door your own address does not.
### Q. Can I join a credit union if I have bad credit?
A.  Often, yes. Membership is about where you live, where you work or who you are related to. What can block a checking account is a separate screening report, and ChexSystems lets you request and view your report and dispute errors. Clean that up first, then apply.
### Q. Why would you get denied from a credit union?
A.  Usually one of two reasons. Either you fall outside the field of membership, which you fix by finding a credit union that does cover your county, job or family, or the checking account screen turned something up. Ask which reason applies, then pull your ChexSystems report and dispute any errors.
### Q. What is the $3,000 bank rule?
A.  It is the federal rule that no financial institution may sell a cashier’s check, money order or traveler’s check for $3,000 or more in currency unless it keeps records on the buyer. Bring your ID and expect the questions.
### Q. Is there a downside to joining a credit union?
A.  A few honest ones. You have to fit a field of membership, the branch map can look small, and you still have to read the fee schedule. Ask about shared branching, and ask for the full fee schedule in writing.
### Q. Is it better to use a credit union or a bank?
A.  It depends on what you need, and that is your call. The federal insurance limit is the same $250,000 either way. The difference is ownership: credit unions are owned and controlled by their members. Compare fees and loan rates side by side before you move anything.

## On a $35,000 Car, a St. Louis City Buyer Owes $3,387.65 in Tax at the License Office
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/credit-union-vs-bank-auto-loan-in-st-louis
Thirty days after the new-car smell, a Missouri buyer stands at a license office counter with a paper number ticket going soft in a sweaty hand, and learns the sales tax was never inside the loan. On a $35,000 car, the state’s 4.225 percent is $1,478.75. Live in the City of St. Louis and the Department of Revenue’s motor vehicle local rate chart adds 5.454% more, another $1,908.90 on that $35,000. That is $3,387.65 in state and city tax on a $35,000 car, owed at the counter, and it was nowhere on the monthly payment you circled in blue ink.
Screenshot this before you sign: $35,000 car, City of St. Louis address, $3,387.65 due at the license office. Trading one in? The Department of Revenue figures the tax on the purchase price less any trade-in allowance, so your number drops. Put three things in the folder now: the title or manufacturer’s statement of origin, a signed Form 108, and a paid personal property tax receipt.
That is the St. Louis catch, and it sits right next to a second one. When a dealer arranges your financing, it sends your application to banks and credit unions, and the lender that wants the deal quotes the dealer a rate. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau calls that the buy rate. The rate printed on your sheet is the contract rate, and the CFPB says plainly that the rate offered to you may be higher to compensate the dealer. The lender quoted the dealer one number. The dealer can quote you another.
Both catches have the same fix: walk in holding your own written number, with the tax already counted. And the lender most likely to give you a lower number is a credit union. Not because of a promotion. Because of the federal numbers.
### Is it better to get an auto loan from a bank or credit union?
On price, a credit union usually wins. The NCUA’s rate survey for December 26, 2025 put the national average new-car loan at 5.44% at credit unions and 7.41% at banks for a 60-month term, a gap of almost two full points. Used-car loans showed the same pattern. Averages are not your quote, so get a written offer from a credit union and a bank, and make the dealer beat the better one.
Those are federal numbers, not a sales flyer. They come from the NCUA’s Credit Union and Bank Rates report, built on S&P Global Market Intelligence data for the last Friday of the quarter. The 48-month used-car loan showed 5.53% at credit unions against 7.73% at banks.
Two points sounds like nothing until it turns into dollars leaving your checking account. Run that $35,000 through any loan calculator at both averages and read the total-interest line, not the payment. The gap is real money, for the same car, the same driver and the same credit file. Same Saturday. Different building.
Getting in the door is easier than most people think. St. Louis Community Credit Union, for one, is open to anyone who lives or works in St. Louis City or St. Louis County, along with several neighboring counties on both sides of the river. You join by opening a regular savings account, and the minimum deposit is $1. One dollar bill slid across a teller counter. Do that a few days before you shop, not at the dealership.
Here is the line worth saying out loud at the dinner table: the payment that fits your budget can still be the expensive one. A payment a little higher fits almost every budget the lower one fits. That is exactly why nobody notices.
### Missouri makes you pay the car sales tax yourself, 30 days later
The license office line moves one number at a time, folders and envelopes pressed to chests, a printer clacking somewhere behind the glass. That is where the tax gets paid. In Missouri, you title the car and pay the sales tax at a license office after the sale. The Missouri Department of Revenue says you have 30 days from the date of purchase to title and pay sales tax, at a state rate of 4.225 percent plus your local sales tax, on the purchase price less any trade-in allowance. Miss the window and there is a $25 title penalty on the 31st day, rising another $25 for every 30 days late, up to $200. Bring the title signed over to you or the manufacturer’s statement of origin, a signed Application for Missouri Title and License (Form 108), and a paid personal property tax receipt.
The local piece follows your home address, not the dealer’s. For a City of St. Louis address, the DOR chart lists 5.454%; in St. Louis County, St. Charles or Jefferson County, the rate depends on the town you live in, and the same chart lists each one. Either way, a buyer who got preapproved for the car price only can come up thousands of dollars short at that counter. In Illinois it usually runs the other way. The Illinois Department of Revenue says a purchase from a registered Illinois retailer is reported on Form ST-556, and generally the retailer will complete and file that return along with the title forms for you. A Belleville or Edwardsville buyer tends to see the tax inside the deal. Either side of the river, ask every lender one blunt question: does this preapproval cover tax, title and fees, or only the vehicle?
### How the dealer markup works, and the one question that changes the room
Nothing about the buy rate is a scandal. Arranging a loan is real work, and the markup is how the dealer gets paid for it. But it is your money. The CFPB puts it in a sentence worth taping to the dashboard: dealers and lenders are not required to offer the best rates available, and you may save hundreds or thousands of dollars over the life of the loan by getting quotes directly from other lenders, comparing offers, and negotiating for the best interest rate available to you.
Here is the moment it works. You slide a credit union’s written offer across the desk. The finance manager reads it, his keyboard goes quiet for a beat, and then he starts typing again. Sometimes the dealer comes back lower, and that is fine. Take it. You only know it is the better deal because you had a number to beat. The CFPB’s plain-language guide, Take control of your auto loan, is worth printing and folding into your glovebox for exactly this conversation.
And ask the question out loud, even if you do not get a straight answer: what is the buy rate on this approval, and what rate am I being charged? Asking costs nothing. It tells the room you know there are two numbers.
Totally unrelated, but here’s where to eat in Crystal City.
### Your credit score moves the rate more than the lender does
If two points between lenders got your attention, the gap between credit tiers is bigger. Experian’s table of average car loan rates by credit score shows a new-car APR of 4.41% for super prime borrowers (781 or above) and 13.52% for subprime borrowers (501 to 600). Put both rates through a calculator on the same car and the gap dwarfs anything between two lenders.
Nobody publishes credit-union-versus-bank rates split by credit score, so read the two sources together. Your credit tier decides which neighborhood your rate lives in. The lender you pick decides which house on the block. Pull your own credit before you shop, so the first person to see your score is you and not a finance manager.
### Shop three lenders inside one two-week window
The fear that keeps people from comparing is that every application dings their score. For auto loans, the scoring models expect you to shop. FICO says older versions of its score allow a 14-day span for rate shopping, and newer versions expand the window to 45 days. Experian notes that VantageScore treats multiple auto loan inquiries within a 14-day period as one inquiry.
Plan for 14 days, not 45. You do not get to choose which scoring model a lender uses, and two weeks is safe under all of them.
Bunch it up. A credit union quote this week, a bank quote next week, and the dealer pull on Saturday all land inside one window.
Get every offer in writing, with the APR, the term and the total finance charge in dollars, so the offers line up side by side.
### Is it smart to do a 72 month car loan?
It is the most expensive way to make a payment fit. Keep the $35,000 at the 5.44% credit union average and change only the term, stretching it a year longer. The payment drops. The total interest climbs, because you pay the rate for an extra year. Long notes are normal now: the Federal Reserve’s G.19 consumer credit release shows new-car loans at finance companies running 66 to 67 months. Normal is not the same as cheap.
The trap is that the term is the easiest lever anyone has. If the payment comes in $60 over your target, twelve more months fixes it in a keystroke. So every time a new sheet slides across the desk, write down five things: price, trade-in, rate, term and payment. If the only one that moved is the term, nothing got better.
A long term also keeps you underwater longer, and that hurts at trade-in time. The CFPB’s report on negative equity in auto lending describes what happens when the trade-in value offered is less than what you still owe and the unpaid balance is rolled into the new loan: it can place you further underwater on the next one. If you are upside down, GAP coverage is the product the CFPB describes as optional and intended to cover the difference between what you owe and what the insurer pays if the car is stolen or totaled. Price it with your own insurer and your own lender before you buy it in the finance office.
### Why credit unions price lower, and the catch
It is built into how they are owned. The NCUA’s consumer site, MyCreditUnion.gov, describes a credit union as a not-for-profit financial institution owned and controlled by its members, with profits returned to members as reduced fees, higher savings rates and lower loan rates. No outside shareholders are waiting for their cut.
The catch is that you have to belong. Members share a common bond, which the NCUA calls the field of membership, and you may qualify through your employer, your family, or where you live, work, worship or go to school. Joining usually means opening a savings account first, so do it a few days before you shop, not at the dealership. The other honest trade-offs: smaller branch networks than the biggest national banks, sometimes a thinner app, and averages that are only averages. One credit union can be above the line. That is why you get two quotes, not one.
### What to ask before you sign anything
Take the same list to every lender, so the answers sit next to each other on the kitchen table:
What is the APR, and what is the total finance charge in dollars over the full term?
What would the payment and the total interest be one term shorter?
Can I pay extra toward principal any time without a fee?
Does this preapproval include tax, title and fees, or only the vehicle price?
If the dealer arranged this loan, what is the buy rate and what am I being charged?
Is any balance from my trade-in being rolled into this loan, and exactly how much?
Which add-ons are on this contract, what does each cost, and which can I remove right now?
How long is this preapproval good for?
Then compare total cost, not the payment. A payment is a number somebody chose for you. The total is the truth. Insurance is the other half of the monthly bill, and it swings by ZIP code here, so check what car insurance costs in St. Louis before you settle on a payment you can carry. This is general consumer education, not advice for your household; a licensed lender or a nonprofit credit counselor who can see your whole budget is the right person to pressure-test the plan.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does a credit union have better interest rates than a bank?
A.  On average, yes, on auto loans. The NCUA’s survey for December 26, 2025 showed new-car loans at 5.44% for credit unions and 7.41% for banks on a 60-month term, and used-car loans at 5.53% against 7.73% on a 48-month term. A single credit union can still be above average, so compare written offers.
### Q. How much would a $30,000 car loan cost a month?
A.  Put $30,000 into any loan calculator over 60 months at the NCUA’s averages, 5.44% for credit unions and 7.41% for banks, and compare the total interest, not just the payment. Your own rate depends on your credit, the car and the term.
### Q. How much is a $40,000 car loan monthly payment 72 months?
A.  The NCUA survey lists new-car rates for 48- and 60-month terms, so plug its 60-month averages, 5.44% and 7.41%, into a loan calculator as a rough guide. Then run the same $40,000 over 60 months. At the same rate, the longer note always costs more in total interest.
### Q. Is it smart to do a 72 month car loan?
A.  Only if the lower payment is worth the higher total. At the same rate, stretching from 60 to 72 months lowers the payment and adds a year of interest, and it keeps you owing more than the car is worth for longer.
### Q. What is needed to get a car loan from a credit union?
A.  Membership first. Credit union members share a common bond, called the field of membership, and you may qualify through your employer, family, or where you live, work, worship or go to school. After you join, expect to show identification, income and your existing debts, the same as any lender.
### Q. What are two disadvantages of a credit union?
A.  You have to qualify and join before you can borrow, which is a step a bank does not ask for. And branch networks are usually smaller than the biggest national banks. A third, quieter one: the lower rate is an average, not a promise, so one credit union may not beat your bank.
### Q. What not to say when financing a car?
A.  Don’t open with the monthly payment you want. It invites a longer term instead of a better rate. Negotiate the price first, the financing second, and bring a written preapproval. The CFPB notes that dealers and lenders are not required to offer the best rates available.
### Q. What's the smartest way to pay for a car?
A.  Cash, if it leaves your emergency fund standing. If not, the shortest term you can carry, at a rate you shopped yourself before the dealer ran your credit, with tax, title and fees already counted in the budget.
The sheet will still come off the printer warm. The pen will still be sitting there. The only difference is whether the number in your pocket is lower than the one circled in blue.

## A Block of Provel on Loan: How St. Louis Pizza Got Its Cheese
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-style-pizza-provel-cracker-crust
The knife goes across, then down, then across again, and the pie falls apart into a grid. Nobody waits for plates. A hand goes straight for the edge, for one of the little crispy triangle corners, and the cheese does not follow it up in a long rope the way it would off a New York slice. It just lets go. Soft, creamy, a little glossy, sitting on a crust that cracks when you bite it.
That cheese is Provel, and the most famous pizza in town has a better story about it than most St. Louisans have ever heard. By Imo’s own history, the Provel that made the chain arrived in the trunk of a man’s car, and the young couple who ran the place could not pay him for the first block. He left it with them on loan anyway.
There is a second surprise in that same history, and it is the one worth saying out loud at the table. By Imo’s own account, mozzarella was the cheese traditionally layered on South St. Louis style pizza. The Provel that now defines the style came in as a swap a neighborhood chef made in their kitchen. The most St. Louis thing on a St. Louis pizza started as a substitution.
### What is Saint Louis style pizza?
St. Louis-style pizza is a thin, crispy, crunchy crust covered edge to edge with toppings and Provel cheese, then cut into squares instead of wedges. Provel is a blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone with a low melting point, so it melts without turning stringy. The squares give you crispy triangle corners at the edge and softer center squares in the middle.
That is the whole definition, and it is shorter than the arguments it starts. Thin crust alone is just thin crust. Squares alone are a party cut. It is the three together, with that particular cheese melting into the toppings, that people mean when they say St. Louis pizza.
### How to order it like you grew up here
Start with the cheese question, because it changes everything else. When you call a place you have not tried, ask whether they use Provel on their thin crust or mozzarella. A St. Louis pizzeria will not be offended by the question. It is the first thing a regular would want to know, and the answer tells you which pie is about to land on your counter.
Then think about who is eating. Squares are made for a crowd, so a thin-crust pie stretches further around a table than the same size cut in wedges. If you have kids, the center squares go first. If you have corner people, and every family does, order a size that leaves enough edge pieces to keep the peace.
Eat the first squares fast, while the cheese is still glossy and the crust still cracks. That crispy, crunchy base is the point of the style. Leave it in a closed box for twenty minutes and the steam softens it. Crack the lid a little on the drive home and the crust has a better chance of arriving the way the oven left it.
Want it at home without a delivery driver? Imo’s sells its own Shredded Provel Cheese and its frozen pizzas in grocery stores, and the company’s own advice for the frozen pie is the local rule in one line: cut your pizza into squares to get the parlor experience in your own kitchen. Pile the cheese to the edges on the thinnest crust you can find, slide it into a hot oven, and listen for the crackle when the knife goes through.
### A block of Provel in the trunk of a car
The Imo’s history starts small enough to feel like a family story told at a holiday table. Ed and Margie Imo, a young couple, spent five years saving $1,500 and opened their first parlor on the corner of Thurman and Shaw. The year was 1964. Their first kitchen was a used oven, two refrigerators and a stove, bought for $75.
Think about the work in that room the way the company describes it. Ed kept his day job as a tile setter, slicing squares of linoleum by day and pizza by night. Margie answered the phones, scooped salads into cups and ran the cash register, which was an old tackle box they repurposed. Margie’s brother drove every delivery. Then they hired a chef from the neighborhood to cook the pizzas, and that chef made the call that stuck: Provel instead of mozzarella.
It sold. It sold so fast they needed more of the cheese than they could find, and word got around town that they were looking. One day a man the company remembers only as Mr. John showed up with a block of Provel in the trunk of his car. They could not pay him for that first block, so he gave it to them on loan the first week. The next week they paid him back. According to Imo’s, Mr. John returned every week for the next three years, until his death.
There are bigger, more official histories of St. Louis pizza. None of them have a better scene than a man opening his trunk outside a corner pizza parlor and trusting two strangers with a block of cheese.
### Why the squares, and why the corner piece?
Here is the part even the company keeps modest. On its own page about the style, Imo’s answers “why squares?” simply: it is how pizza gets sliced in St. Louis. The linoleum line in its history is a nice echo, the tile setter cutting squares all day and then cutting squares all night, but it is told as a detail of Ed’s life, not as a patent.
What the squares really do is change how a pizza gets eaten. A round pie cut into a grid gives you two kinds of pieces. The edge pieces are the crispy triangle corners and slim strips with a dark, crunchy rim. The center squares are smaller, softer, and carry more cheese and toppings than crust. At any St. Louis table you will see people go for one or the other on instinct.
Imo’s says squares make for the perfect shareable pizza, and you can see why in any living room on a game night. Nobody has to wrestle a floppy wedge. A kid can take one square. Somebody watching their carbs can take two center pieces and call it dinner. The pizza stops being eight equal slices and turns into a bowl of snacks everyone reaches into.
### What Provel actually does when it melts
Pull a square off a fresh pie and look at the cheese. It does not stretch into strings. It slumps and sheets across the toppings, creamy and slick, and it stays put on the square instead of sliding off in one piece. That is the low melting point Imo’s describes: Provel melts without being stringy. The company calls it gooey and creamy, and that is about right.
Imo’s lists its Provel facts plainly. The blend is cheddar, Swiss and provolone. It was invented in St. Louis, Missouri in 1947. More than 2 million pounds of it are eaten each year. The company also says the cheese’s origins are debated, which is an unusually honest line for a pizza chain to put on its own website.
If you did not grow up on it, the first bite can surprise you. It is not the clean, milky pull of mozzarella. It is softer and more buttery, with a tang that sits under the sauce. People who were raised on it taste a whole childhood. People who were not tend to have an opinion within one square. Both reactions are part of the experience.
And if Provel is not for you, that is a preference, not a verdict on the city. Ask whether the kitchen will build the same thin crust with mozzarella. Many local kitchens will make it either way if you ask.
Hungry for dessert after? A walk to one of the St. Louis bakeries is a good way to settle the table after a big round of squares.
Provel is only one of the local foods outsiders squint at - here is the rest of what this city invented.
### Is the pizza different on the Illinois side of the river?
Sometimes, and the fastest way to find out is to ask. A thin, square-cut pizza in Belleville, Edwardsville or Collinsville can arrive with Provel or with mozzarella depending on the kitchen. Neither is wrong. They are just different pies, and a minute on the phone saves a disappointed face at the table when the box opens.
The same goes for the Missouri side. A shop in Affton, Florissant, Kirkwood or Maryland Heights might be a lifelong Provel house, or it might be the place your mozzarella-loving cousin swears by. The style is a shared language across the metro. Each kitchen still has its own accent.
### Can you get it outside St. Louis?
You can, if you are willing to ship it. Imo’s says it will ship its squares anywhere in the US, and its history describes packaging and shipping St. Louis style pizza, Toasted Ravioli and Provel Bites across the country to loyal customers. That is how a lot of former St. Louisans in other states get their fix, and how a lot of people who never lived here get their first taste.
Shipped pizza is a box, a freezer and an oven, not a corner parlor with the crust still crackling. It is still the closest a homesick St. Louisan in another state can get without a drive. For a gift with more than one local flavor in it, these two help:
Sending a taste of St. Louis to someone far away
How to order a Philly cheesesteak in St. Louis, for melted cheese done a different way
Settle the Provel argument at your own table. Browse pizza across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then order two thin-crust pies from one kitchen, one with Provel and one without, and let the room vote square by square.
If you run the pizza place people should be calling, the hungry customers searching tonight should find your squares before anyone else’s. Put your hours, menu and phone in front of them with a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is different about St. Louis pizza?
A.  Three things together: a thin, crispy, crunchy crust, Provel cheese instead of mozzarella, and a cut into squares instead of wedges. Provel is a blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone that melts without being stringy, so each square stays neat. The edge pieces come out as crispy triangle corners and the center squares stay soft.
### Q. Is Provel cheese only in St. Louis?
A.  It is a St. Louis cheese at heart. Imo’s says Provel was invented in St. Louis, Missouri in 1947 and that more than 2 million pounds of it are eaten each year. The company also admits its origins are debated. Where it is eaten most is not up for debate: on squares of thin crust, right here.
### Q. Who has the best St. Louis style pizza?
A.  There is no settled answer, and anyone who says otherwise grew up on one particular pie. Imo’s is the name most people know, but plenty of St. Louisans have a neighborhood favorite they defend just as hard. Judge a shop on the crust, the cheese and whether the corner pieces still crack.
### Q. Can you buy Provel Cheese outside of St. Louis?
A.  The easiest way to taste it outside the region is in a pizza that ships. Imo’s says it ships its squares anywhere in the US, and it has shipped Provel Bites across the country too. If you want the block itself, call a store near you and ask before you drive.
### Q. Did Imo’s start the Provel tradition?
A.  Imo’s own history says a chef from the neighborhood chose Provel in place of the mozzarella traditionally layered on South St. Louis style pizza, and that the switch was such a hit they had to hunt for more cheese. Imo’s says Provel itself dates to 1947, years before the first parlor opened in 1964.

## Three Chiropractor Visits a Week? Missouri Insurance Draws a Line at Visit 26
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-chiropractor-st-louis
Your lower back locks up on the highway near the Hampton exit, and every tap of the brake sends a hot line down one leg. By the time you limp into the waiting room you’d sign almost anything. Then the front desk says it kindly, sliding a clipboard across the counter: “We’ll want to see you three times a week to start.” The pen is on a little chain. Under the intake form sits a payment page.
Before you sign, count. Three a week adds up fast, and Missouri law puts a marker at visit 26. RSMo 376.1230 says an in-network patient can get 26 chiropractic office visits in a policy period, and after that the insurer may require prior authorization. The next visit is where a plan you agreed to on day one can quietly become a bill you pay yourself.
Nobody at the counter is lying to you. Most people just never hear about that marker until an explanation-of-benefits letter lands in the mailbox. Knowing it turns the first appointment around: you stop asking “how many visits?” and start asking “what happens at 26?”
### How much does it cost for a session with a chiropractor?
Prices vary office to office, so get three numbers by phone: the cash price of the first exam, of a routine follow-up adjustment, and of x-rays. The bigger cost is the count. Missouri law lets an insured patient see an in-network chiropractor for 26 office visits per policy period and lets the insurer require prior authorization past 26, so a long plan can turn into visits you pay for yourself.
A front desk that answers all three numbers in one call, without steering you straight to a booking, is telling you something good about the office behind it.
### The teaching clinic most St. Louis lists skip
Logan University runs academic teaching clinics in the St. Louis area, and one sits inside the city at 5200 Berthold Ave., in the Stephen A. Orthwein Center at Paraquad. Advanced chiropractic students treat patients there under the direct supervision of licensed doctors of chiropractic. You do not need a referral. The clinic says it accepts most major insurance plans and files the forms for you, and it tells new patients to plan for about an hour.
That hour is the point. A long first visit, with a supervising doctor checking a student’s work, is the opposite of a two-minute screening and a package pitch. Call 314-274-3367 and ask the same questions you would ask anyone else.
### Find the chiropractic page in your own policy first
Do this in the parking lot, engine off, phone glowing in your lap. The same Missouri statute says the certificate of coverage for a health plan must clearly state the availability of chiropractic coverage and any limitations, conditions and exclusions. So the answer is already in a document you own. Open your insurer’s app, pull up the plan document, and search the word “chiropractic.”
Then call the member number on the back of your card and ask one plain question: “Do you need prior authorization for chiropractic visits after 26?” Write down the name of the person who answers. If the office later proposes a plan that runs past that number, you will know before the visit past 26 whether anyone has asked permission, and whether you should.
Two limits on that rule. It covers health plans the statute reaches, so a self-funded employer plan or a cash-only practice can work differently. And it is a line for authorization, not a promise that the first 26 visits cost you nothing; your copay and deductible still apply.
### How do you check a Missouri chiropractor’s license?
Missouri chiropractors renew their licenses through the state Board of Chiropractic Examiners in Jefferson City, one of the boards of the Division of Professional Registration. The division’s Licensee Search lives at pr.mo.gov, and you can run it from the parking lot. Type the name on the business card, confirm the license is current, and look for discipline. Questions go to the board at 573-751-2104, or by mail to 3605 Missouri Boulevard in Jefferson City.
Across the river it is a different system. A chiropractor in Belleville or Edwardsville answers to Illinois, and the place to check is the IDFPR License Lookup run by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. One metro, two state boards. A strip-center office on Manchester Road in Kirkwood and one off Main Street in Belleville can look identical online and sit under different rules.
### What should the first visit include?
The paper on the table crinkles under you. Before anyone pushes on your spine, you should get a history, a physical exam and a working diagnosis you could repeat in plain English on the drive home. The plan should connect to that diagnosis and carry a re-evaluation date: the day someone checks whether you are actually better.
It also helps to know what a chiropractor is not licensed to do here. Missouri’s definition of chiropractic in RSMo 331.010 excludes operative surgery, obstetrics, osteopathy and podiatry, along with prescribing any drug or medicine. If your pain needs a prescription, a scan read by a physician, or a surgical opinion, a good chiropractor will say so and refer you rather than add visits.
X-rays deserve their own question. Ask why you need them, what the chiropractor expects them to show, and whether the answer would change the plan. If every new patient gets films on the first day no matter what brought them in, that is worth a polite follow-up. You are not being difficult. You are the one lying on the cold plate, and you are the one getting the bill. A clear answer sounds like a reason tied to your symptoms. A vague one sounds like routine. Either way, you will hear the difference, and you can decide before anyone turns the machine on.
### Treatment plan or contract?
A treatment plan has an end and a checkpoint. A contract has a dollar total and a signature line. If the paper asks you to prepay a block of visits before your second appointment, at a price that is only good today, you are holding the second thing with the first thing’s name on it.
None of that makes a series of visits wrong. Back pain often does take more than one appointment. The test is whether the plan can shrink. Ask whether unused prepaid visits are refunded if you get better early, and what changes if several visits change nothing. Take the paper home overnight; an honest plan survives a night on the kitchen counter. Then go clear your head at a good coffee shop before you decide.
### The two-minute phone call that sorts the offices
Hold music, a click, then a real voice. This is the cheapest test you will run, and it costs nothing but the call. Ask the same questions of every office, in the same order, and write the answers on one sheet of paper so you can compare them at the kitchen table instead of in a gown.
Start with money: what is the cash price for the first exam, for a routine follow-up, and for x-rays? Then the plan: will I get a written plan with a re-evaluation date, and does anything have to be paid in advance? Then the line: if my plan runs past 26 visits, who asks my insurer for authorization, you or me? An office that bills insurance every day will know the answer. One that goes quiet has told you something too.
Last, the person. Ask for the chiropractor’s full name as it appears on the license, so you can type it into the state search before you go. It feels fussy. It takes less time than finding a parking spot.
### Neck adjustments: you can ask for the gentler version
If the pain is in your neck, say what you want out loud on the first visit. You can ask how the chiropractor plans to work on the neck, whether there is a lower-force option, and what they would do instead if you are not comfortable with a quick twist. A good practitioner hears that as an ordinary request and explains the choices. One who treats it as an insult has answered a bigger question than the one you asked.
### If something goes wrong after a visit
Most problems are about money, not injury: a plan you did not understand, a refund nobody will discuss. Ask in writing first, and keep every receipt and the plan sheet in one envelope. If the problem is how you were treated, the Missouri board’s own page links to its complaint forms, and the board office in Jefferson City answers at 573-751-2104. In Illinois, start with the IDFPR License Lookup to confirm who holds the license, then follow the department’s complaint process.
### Is chiropractic worth it for back pain?
Sometimes, and the honest framing is modest. The American College of Physicians’ guideline on low back pain starts from a fact most offices skip: most patients with acute or subacute low back pain improve over time regardless of treatment. For those patients it lists spinal manipulation as one nondrug option alongside superficial heat, massage and acupuncture, and it rates the evidence for manipulation as low quality.
If the chiropractor’s best advice is “get stronger,” here is when a trainer beats another adjustment.
That cuts both ways. It means manipulation is a legitimate choice, and it means a plan that promises your spine will fail without dozens of visits is selling certainty the research does not hold. Weigh hands-on options side by side:
How a chiropractor differs from an osteopathic physician (DO) in St. Louis
What an eye exam runs without insurance
Make two calls before you lie down on anyone’s table. Browse chiropractors across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask two offices the same things: the first-visit price, the re-evaluation date, and what happens at visit 26.
If you run the practice that answers those questions straight, the patients searching tonight should find you before they find the clipboard down the street. A complete listing puts your hours, services and side of the river in front of new customers - put your practice on St Louis Near Me Directory.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth spending money on a chiropractor?
A.  It can be, for back pain especially, if the plan is short, checked and honest. The American College of Physicians lists spinal manipulation as one nondrug option for acute low back pain, alongside heat, massage and acupuncture. Spend on a plan with a re-evaluation date, not on a prepaid block sold before anyone knows how you respond.
### Q. Does insurance cover chiropractic?
A.  Often, with conditions. In Missouri, RSMo 376.1230 lets an insured patient see an in-network chiropractor for 26 office visits per policy period, and lets the insurer require prior authorization for visits past 26. Your certificate of coverage has to spell out the limits, so search it for “chiropractic” and call the number on your card.
### Q. Is paying for a chiropractor worth it?
A.  Judge it at the re-evaluation, not on the first day. Most acute low back pain improves over time regardless of treatment, so the real question is whether visits are helping faster than time would. If several visits change nothing and the plan does not change either, stop paying and ask for a referral.
### Q. What are red flags for chiropractors?
A.  A demand to prepay a block of visits before your second appointment, a price that is only good today, and a plan with no re-evaluation date. Add an office that will not quote a cash price by phone, or a license you cannot find in the Missouri Licensee Search or the Illinois IDFPR License Lookup.
### Q. What is a red flag in chiropractic?
A.  Any promise that goes past what chiropractors are licensed to do. In Missouri the practice excludes surgery and prescribing any drug or medicine, so a pitch to treat everything with adjustments, or a refusal to refer you to a physician when your symptoms call for it, is a reason to walk out.
### Q. Why do doctors discourage chiropractors?
A.  Not all of them do. The American College of Physicians includes spinal manipulation among first options for acute low back pain, but rates its evidence as low quality, which is why many physicians treat it as one choice among several rather than a cure. The friction usually comes from long prepaid plans and claims that reach past the evidence.
### Q. How do I check whether a St. Louis chiropractor is licensed?
A.  Use the state the office sits in. On the Missouri side, search the Licensee Search at pr.mo.gov, run by the Division of Professional Registration, or call the Board of Chiropractic Examiners at 573-751-2104. On the Illinois side, use the IDFPR License Lookup. Search the full name exactly as it appears on the business card.
### Q. What should I ask before my first chiropractic appointment?
A.  Five things, all by phone. What does the first exam cost in cash? What does a follow-up cost? Are x-rays extra? Will I get a written plan with a re-evaluation date? And if the plan runs past 26 visits, who requests prior authorization from my insurer? A front desk that answers all five without hedging has told you plenty.

## The Soda Won’t Ring Up: What Missouri SNAP Still Buys at a St. Louis Corner Store
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-corner-stores-snap-wic-and-prices
The bell over the door rings behind you. The cooler hums along the back wall, the lottery screen flickers by the register, and you have a gallon of milk in one hand and a cold soda in the other. You set them both on the counter, slide the EBT card, and wait for the little beep.
Today, both go through. Missouri’s Healthy SNAP rules will change that. The Department of Social Services is taking soda, candy, energy drinks and pre-packaged desserts off the list of things the card can buy. A bottle of Gatorade stays, because the state carved out drinks sold mainly for hydration. The soda in your other hand does not. The state has already extended the launch date, so the date to watch is the one on the DSS Healthy SNAP page.
Here, that rule lands hardest at the corner store. OneSTL counts more than 329,000 people in the St. Louis region living in census tracts that meet the food desert definition, where the corner store two blocks away is often the closest food there is. And the Metro East has no hot-meal workaround: Illinois runs its Restaurant Meals Program in Cook and Franklin counties only. One more number to save before you read on: if your card is lost, stolen or suddenly empty, Missouri DSS says to call 800-997-7777.
Nobody at the counter explains any of this before the card gets declined, so here it is, plainly: what a St. Louis corner store must keep on its shelves to take your card, what it can and cannot ring up, and where WIC fits.
### What stores allow SNAP?
Any store USDA has authorized to take SNAP, and that includes plenty of convenience stores. Look for the SNAP or EBT sign at the door, or type your address into USDA’s SNAP Retailer Locator to see every authorized store nearby. To stay authorized, a corner store must stock at least seven varieties in each staple food group: dairy, grains, protein, and vegetables or fruits.
### The shelf a corner store has to keep
Walk past the chips and the phone chargers and look for the quiet stuff: the half gallon of milk, the loaf of bread, the can of beans, the bag of rice, a few onions in a wire basket. That shelf is not an accident. USDA’s stocking standards rule says every SNAP store other than a specialty shop must stock, on a continuous basis, at least seven varieties in each of the four staple food categories.
Continuous means any day the store is open, not just the day an inspector walks in. The rule also requires one perishable variety in at least three of the four categories, meaning food that would spoil within two to three weeks at room temperature. So if your corner store takes EBT, there should be something fresh or frozen in the cooler, not only cans.
If the shelf looks bare week after week, that is worth knowing. Use the SNAP Retailer Locator, which lets anyone find nearby SNAP-authorized stores by street address, city or ZIP code, and keep a second store in your back pocket.
### What can you buy with Missouri food stamps?
The short version: groceries you take home. Fruits and vegetables, meat, poultry and fish, dairy, and breads and cereals all count. Seeds and plants that grow food count too. What does not count, under USDA’s list of what SNAP can buy, is food that is hot at the point of sale, plus nonfood items like pet food, cleaning supplies, paper products and other household supplies.
The hot rule is the one that trips people up at a corner store. The chicken under the heat lamp smells like dinner, and it will not go through on the card. Cold food from the case is a different story. When the warmer is the only thing open, the cooler next to it is usually your SNAP aisle.
### What are the new snap restrictions in Missouri?
Missouri asked USDA to classify certain foods and drinks as restricted, and the state’s Healthy SNAP definitions spell out what goes. Read them like a label, because that is how the register will read them.
Soft drinks are out when they are sweetened with more than 10 grams of sugar per serving, carbonated or not. A drink made with milk, soy or rice milk is not a soft drink under the rule. Candy is out, but the definition does not include items containing flour or requiring refrigeration. Energy drinks with stimulants like caffeine or guarana are out. Sports drinks sold mainly for hydration, such as Gatorade, are not included, and neither are medically necessary nutrition products.
You do not need to sign up for anything. DSS says anyone already getting SNAP or SuN Bucks in Missouri moves to the Healthy SNAP rules automatically. The state has already extended its launch date, so check the DSS page for the current start date before you plan a shopping trip around it.
Across the river it is a different list, so check with Illinois if you shop in the Metro East.
### Why the corner store feels so expensive
Look at what people actually carry out. USDA’s SNAP redemption data shows convenience stores handled 20.2% of SNAP transactions but only 5.3% of the benefit dollars. Convenience stores had the smallest average transactions of any store type, about $10. Supermarkets and super stores took 78% of the money.
That is the corner store’s real job: the fill-in trip. Milk for the morning. Eggs when the carton is empty. Bread before school. Small baskets at small-store prices add up fast, so the money stretches furthest when the corner store covers the gaps and a bigger store covers the week.
A few habits help. Buy staples in normal grocery sizes, where small stores tend to stay closest to supermarket prices. Skip single-serve packs, where the premium hides. Read the unit price on the shelf tag when there is one, not the big number on the sticker.
### A two-minute check before you fill the basket
Stand inside the door for a moment and look before you grab. Is the SNAP or EBT sign on the glass or by the register? Is there milk in the cooler with a date that is not tomorrow? Are the eggs cold to the touch, not sitting on a warm shelf? Is there anything green or orange in the produce basket, even if it is just onions, potatoes or a few bananas going spotty?
If the answers are yes, that store is probably worth your regular business. If the cooler is half dark and the bread is stale, buy the one thing you came for and save the rest of your benefit for a bigger store. Ask the clerk which day the milk truck comes. Corner store staff usually know, and fresh stock on delivery day is the best the shelf will look all week.
Keep a short running list on your phone of the two or three stores you can reach on foot, which ones take the card, and which ones keep milk and eggs. On a cold night with a sick kid, you will not want to guess. Share the list with whoever else in the house does the shopping.
### Can you use WIC at a corner store?
Sometimes, but never assume it. WIC is not a food budget like SNAP. It covers specific foods in specific sizes, and a store has to be approved as a WIC vendor on its own, separate from SNAP. Plenty of small stores take SNAP and not WIC.
On the Missouri side, the Department of Health and Senior Services publishes the list of authorized Missouri WIC retailers and pharmacies. Check it before you walk in with the WIC card and a baby on your hip. On the Illinois side, you can call the Illinois State WIC Office at (844) 901-0962.
### Where St. Louis runs short on grocery stores
For a lot of families here the corner store is not a convenience. It is the closest food there is. The OneSTL access indicator counted 79 census tracts in the St. Louis region that met the food desert definition, home to more than 329,000 people.
You can feel that number on a bus route. A grocery run that should take twenty minutes becomes a transfer, a wait in the cold, and a walk home with the bags cutting into your fingers. That is exactly when the corner store two blocks away matters most, and why it is worth knowing what it is required to stock.
Unrelated, but it saves a trip: find out what St. Louis will actually take in the recycling bin.
### If your EBT money disappears
It happens, and it feels awful: you swipe at the counter, the screen says insufficient funds, and you know the balance was there yesterday. Call to freeze the card right away. Missouri’s Department of Social Services says to call 800-997-7777 if your EBT card has been lost, stolen or damaged, and ask for a replacement. Then change your PIN, and check your balance before you shop.
### For the people behind the counter
The owner who opens before dawn, stocks the milk and keeps the EBT reader working is doing a neighborhood a real service. They also count staple varieties, track perishables, and will soon have to sort out which drinks the card can buy. Many corner stores also sit near a pharmacy counter, and between the two, a family can cover most of the week without a car. Owners can add their store to St Louis Near Me Directory and keep their hours current.
Need a store near you that takes EBT tonight? Browse convenience stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the two closest to you and ask two things: do you take SNAP, and do you have milk and eggs in the cooler.
If you run the corner store that keeps milk cold and the card reader working, the neighbor calling around is a customer you can win. List your store so more customers can find your door.
