### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is not allowed to buy with SNAP?
A.  Food that is hot at the point of sale, plus nonfood items like pet food, cleaning supplies, paper products and other household supplies, according to USDA. In Missouri, the Healthy SNAP rules will also exclude sugary soft drinks, candy, energy drinks and pre-packaged desserts.
### Q. What can you buy with Missouri food stamps?
A.  Groceries to take home: fruits and vegetables, meat, poultry and fish, dairy, and breads and cereals, plus seeds and plants that grow food. Sports drinks sold for hydration, such as Gatorade, stay allowed under the Missouri definitions.
### Q. Do any fast food chains accept EBT?
A.  Only in states that run the Restaurant Meals Program, a state option for SNAP households where everyone is elderly, disabled or homeless. Illinois runs it in Cook and Franklin counties only, so the Metro East is not covered.
### Q. Can you buy McDonald’s with SNAP?
A.  Not on the Illinois side of the metro. Restaurant meals are hot, prepared food, which SNAP does not cover unless a state runs the Restaurant Meals Program for elderly, disabled or homeless recipients, and the Illinois program covers only Cook and Franklin counties.
### Q. Can I use Missouri SNAP in Illinois?
A.  Yes. Healthy SNAP benefits can be used at approved retailers located in the United States that display the Quest Mark logo, according to Missouri DSS, so a SNAP store in Belleville can take a Missouri card.
### Q. What are the key differences between a corner store and a supermarket?
A.  Distance, hours and the size of the trip. USDA data shows the average SNAP purchase at a convenience store is about $10, while supermarkets and super stores take 78% of SNAP dollars. The corner store covers the gaps; the supermarket covers the week.
### Q. Can you buy rotisserie chicken with EBT at Walmart?
A.  Not when it is hot. USDA does not let SNAP buy food that is hot at the point of sale, so a chicken pulled from the warmer is declined at any store. A cold, packaged chicken from the refrigerated case is a grocery item, and grocery items are what the card is for.
### Q. What do I do if money disappears from my EBT card?
A.  Call 800-997-7777 to report the card lost or stolen and ask for a replacement, as Missouri DSS directs. Change your PIN, check your balance before every trip, and keep the card in your wallet instead of a pocket or the car, where it is easy to lose and easy to forget.

## Illinois Taxes Gas at 70.4 Cents a Gallon, Missouri at 29.99, and Missouri Pays 12.5 Cents Back
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-gas-prices-missouri-vs-illinois
The nozzle clicks into the tank at a station in Belleville, the gas smell hangs in the cold air, and the digits on the pump roll past the point where you meant to stop. Inside that number, Illinois takes 70.4 cents a gallon in state taxes and fees, the second-highest bite in the country, according to the Tax Foundation’s state-by-state count, while Missouri’s number on the same chart is 29.99 cents.
You feel that gap before you understand it. Fifteen gallons later you are back on the Poplar Street Bridge, the Arch catching the last light, and the tax difference alone on that one fill was about six dollars.
Here is the turn most drivers never hear about. Missouri will send part of its own gas tax back to you, 12.5 cents on every gallon you pumped, if you ask between July 1 and September 30. The state’s revenue director says the average refund came to $162.74. Fewer than 1 in 100 Missouri drivers file for it.
### Why is gas so much higher in Illinois than Missouri?
Mostly taxes. Illinois charges 48.3 cents a gallon in state motor fuel tax, a rate it adjusts each year, plus a prepaid sales tax per gallon. Missouri charges a flat 29.5 cents and stops. The Tax Foundation puts combined state taxes and fees at 70.4 cents in Illinois and 29.99 cents in Missouri. All of that is baked in before any station sets a price.
### Two states, one gallon, two very different receipts
Stand at a pump on either bank and the hose, the handle and the smell of the fuel are the same. The paperwork behind the price is not. Missouri’s rate is a single per-gallon excise that climbed two and a half cents a year from 17 cents until it reached 29.5 cents, and the Missouri Department of Revenue’s motor fuel FAQ lists every step of that climb in one table.
Illinois runs two meters at once. The Illinois Department of Revenue sets the motor fuel tax on gasoline at 48.3 cents a gallon right now, and it normally moves that rate every July with inflation. Then the state adds a prepaid sales tax on motor fuel, set in cents per gallon for each half of the year. Two charges, both baked into the number on the sign, both invisible on your receipt.
That gap rides inside the number on every Metro East price sign, with the same crude oil in both tanks. The station owner in Belleville is not the villain. The tax code is.
### The 12.5 cents Missouri hands back, if you ask
When Missouri raised its gas tax from 17 cents to 29.5 cents, lawmakers attached a refund to the increase. Every gallon you pumped into a car or truck rated 26,000 pounds or less can earn back the full 12.5-cent difference. Think of the crumpled receipts in your cup holder as cash you have not picked up yet.
Do the math on your own tank. Five hundred gallons a year, a normal commute, is $62.50. A two-car household burning a thousand gallons is looking at $125. Yet according to reporting on the state’s claim counts, only 11,801 claims came in during a year when Missouri had more than 4 million drivers. Less than one percent. The money sits in Jefferson City because almost nobody fills out the form.
One catch matters on this side of the river. Missouri’s Director of Revenue, Trish Vincent, said in an interview with KY3 that the refund is only for Missouri residents. If you live in Edwardsville and top off in Missouri, you get the cheaper pump price, not the refund.
### How to file the refund without a shoebox of receipts
The form is Form 4923-H, filed with the Missouri Department of Revenue. Claims must be submitted on or after July 1 and no later than September 30, for fuel bought during the state fiscal year that ended June 30.
For each purchase the worksheet wants the date, the gallons, the seller’s name and address, and the VIN of the vehicle the fuel went into. You do not have to send in the original receipts. You keep them for at least three years after you file. The easy way to build the list is a fuel app or loyalty account that logs every fill-up for you; the department accepts account printouts that carry the required details, and Vincent pointed drivers to exactly that so they can skip the paper slips.
Start this week, not in September. Pick one card or one app for every fill-up, and the list builds itself while you drive. Snap a photo of any paper receipt the day you get it, before the ink fades, and drop it in one folder on your phone. Ten seconds at the pump saves an evening of guessing next summer. Keep the folder simple, one per car, and the worksheet almost fills itself by July.
### The money Missouri expected to give back, and didn’t
When the increase was written, original budget estimates projected that about 20% of the new gas tax revenue would be refunded, with out-of-state drivers carrying a larger share of the cost. That is not what happened. The refunds paid out came to $1.562 million in one year, from a driving population of more than 4 million. The gap between the forecast and the reality is your money, sitting unclaimed.
Why does a refund this simple go unclaimed? The receipt is the reason. It curls up in the console, fades in the summer heat on the dash, and by July it reads like a blank strip of thermal paper. Nobody remembers the gallons from a February fill-up on the way to work. The claim never gets started because the list never got kept.
### Mistakes that sink a refund claim
The first mistake is filing through the wrong door. KY3 reported that the rebate application should be done only through the Department of Revenue’s own website, and Vincent cautioned drivers about apps that offer to help with it. A fuel app is fine for keeping the record. The claim itself goes to the state.
The second is padding the numbers. The state denied a record $3.3 million in what it said were fraudulent claims in a single year, so every line on your worksheet should match a real purchase you can show. The third is mixing vehicles: the records must show the VIN of the vehicle the fuel was delivered into, so a household with two cars keeps two clean lists. And the fourth is the calendar. A claim that arrives after September 30 does not count for that year, no matter how good the records are.
### What is Unleaded 88, and why is it cheaper in Illinois?
Unleaded 88 is E15, a blend of 15% ethanol and 85% gasoline that retailers sell under the 88 name to highlight its higher octane. The EPA says it can be used in flexible-fuel vehicles and in model year 2001 and newer cars, light-duty trucks and SUVs. It cannot be used in motorcycles, in vehicles with heavy-duty engines such as school buses and delivery trucks, or in nonroad gear such as boats.
On the Illinois side there is a quiet bonus. The state’s prepaid sales tax table charges gasohol (E15 only) fewer cents per gallon than it charges ordinary motor fuel, so the pump with the orange-and-black E15 label can carry a smaller tax bite than the regular one beside it. If your car is on the EPA’s list and you are already filling up in the Metro East, it is worth a look at the price on that button.
### Is crossing the river for gas worth the trip?
Only when you were going anyway. On a 15-gallon fill, the state tax gap alone is about six dollars. A dedicated 12-mile round trip burns some of that back in fuel and eats half an hour of your evening. If you work in Clayton and sleep in Edwardsville, fill up before you hit the bridge. If you never cross the river on a weeknight, the refund is the bigger win.
Gas is the cost you watch. Road salt is the one you don’t - see what a St. Louis winter costs your car.
### For the people behind the counter
The station owner hears the complaints about the price on the sign, and almost none of it is theirs to set. The tax arrives with every load of fuel. What the owner controls is the coffee that is hot at 5 a.m., the clean restroom, the light over the canopy, and whether a driver searching late at night can find them at all. They also collect that tax for the state and pass it along, and the price war with the station across the street happens in pennies, not dimes. A family-run station on a busy corner lives on the people who come back: the contractor who grabs the same coffee every morning, the nurse coming off a night shift who wants a lit lot and a working pump, the parent who needs a restroom that is actually clean. Drivers who need more than a fill-up can also find a trusted auto repair shop nearby. If you run a station, being listed and complete on St Louis Near Me Directory is how you turn that late-night search into a customer.
Which two stations do you pass every day? Browse gas stations across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick your regular stop, and run every fill-up through one card or app so next July’s refund claim takes ten minutes instead of a Saturday.
If you own the station, the car wash or the repair bay those drivers pass, a complete listing helps you get more customers from the drivers searching on the way home. List your business and turn that late-night search into a sale.
Gas is the price everyone watches. For why the rest of the receipt keeps climbing, see what causes inflation, or read the corner store math on everything else.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is Missouri gas so cheap?
A.  Missouri’s state gas tax is a flat 29.5 cents a gallon, and the Tax Foundation ranks its combined state taxes and fees at 29.99 cents, well below Illinois at 70.4. Missouri residents can also claim 12.5 cents a gallon back with Form 4923-H, which makes the real cost lower still for anyone who keeps a record of their fill-ups.
### Q. Are taxes higher in MO or IL?
A.  On gasoline, Illinois by a wide margin: 70.4 cents a gallon in combined state taxes and fees against Missouri’s 29.99, per the Tax Foundation. Illinois also adds a prepaid sales tax per gallon on top of its motor fuel tax. Income and property taxes are a separate comparison.
### Q. What are the current gas prices in Illinois?
A.  Pump prices change daily, often by a few cents between morning and evening, so check a live tracker before you drive instead of trusting a number you saw last week. What stays steady is the tax built into them: Illinois charges 48.3 cents a gallon in state motor fuel tax on gasoline right now, plus a prepaid sales tax per gallon.
### Q. Is gas cheap in Missouri?
A.  Cheaper than across the river. Missouri’s state taxes and fees come to 29.99 cents a gallon on the Tax Foundation’s count, against 70.4 cents in Illinois, and residents can claim 12.5 cents a gallon back each year.
### Q. Is it cheaper to live in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  At the pump, Missouri wins: its state gas taxes and fees are less than half of Illinois’, per the Tax Foundation. Housing, income tax and property tax decide the rest, so compare those for your own household.
### Q. How do I get money back from the Missouri gas tax?
A.  File Form 4923-H with the Missouri Department of Revenue between July 1 and September 30. List each purchase’s date, gallons, seller name and address, and your vehicle’s VIN, and keep the original receipts for three years after you file. The refund is for Missouri residents only, and the claim itself should go through the Department of Revenue’s own website, not a third-party app that offers to file it for you.

## A New Battery Can Fail Your St. Louis Emissions Test: Where to Buy Auto Parts
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-auto-parts-in-st-louis
Click-click-click-click. That fast, dry chatter under the hood is a starter begging for power the battery doesn’t have anymore. The dome light sags while you hold the key. Your breath fogs the inside of the windshield. Half an hour later you’re at a parts counter that smells like new rubber and cardboard, a fresh battery is sitting on the mat in front of you, and somebody behind the counter offers to plug a scanner in and clear that check engine light while they’re at it. It feels like the problem just ended.
In St. Louis, it might have just started. If your car is registered in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County or Jefferson County, it goes through the Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program, and Gateway’s own page on readiness monitors lists two common reasons a car’s self-checks read “Not Completed”: the battery was replaced or disconnected, and the memory was cleared by a repair shop. A gasoline car from 2001 or newer fails with two or more of those monitors not completed. So you can swap a battery in a parking lot, roll into a test lane the same day, and pay $24 to fail an emissions test over a car that has nothing wrong with it.
Nobody at the register is hiding this. It just isn’t their job to know when your plates expire. The fix is order, not avoidance. Test first, then swap the battery or clear the code. Or do the repair and then drive the car the way Gateway describes, “in a way that allows the self-test to complete,” before you go in. And if you fail only on monitors, Gateway says you can legally drive up to 30 days past your registration expiration to reset them, as long as you keep the test report in the car to prove it.
That’s the St. Louis wrinkle almost no national guide mentions. The rest is the buying question every driver here faces sooner or later: which counter, which yard, new or used or rebuilt, and when the wrench belongs in your hand instead of a shop’s. Get the order right and a repair becomes a cold afternoon in the driveway. Get it wrong and you buy the same part twice, or pay for the same test twice.
### Where is the best place to buy auto parts in St. Louis?
Match the store to the part. A chain counter is best for common parts you need today: batteries, pads, sensors, filters. An independent parts house finds the odd and professional-grade parts. A licensed salvage yard wins on body panels, mirrors, glass and trim. In the Gateway counties, put a new battery in after your emissions test, not the week before.
The chain is the right first stop when the part is common and the clock is running. They stock deep on the fast-moving numbers, and the receipt lives in their system, which matters two winters later when a warrantied part dies and the paper is long gone from the glovebox. The test bench is the other reason to go. O’Reilly’s own Saint Louis store page lists battery testing, alternator and starter testing and check engine light testing, and its Gravois Rd store also lists drum and rotor resurfacing.
Use that bench before you spend a dollar. A car that won’t crank on a frozen morning can be a battery, a corroded cable end, a starter or an alternator that quit charging, and they all feel the same from the driver’s seat: the clicking, the dash flickering, the sinking feeling in your stomach. Test the cheap explanation before you buy the expensive one.
The independent parts house, the jobber if you’ve heard a mechanic use the word, is where you go when the chain says special order, a few days out. These counters supply working shops all morning, so the person across from you has usually heard which brand of the same part comes back in a box. Bring your VIN. Read it off the corner of the dashboard through the windshield, or off the sticker in the driver’s door jamb, and the lookup gets a lot shorter.
### Why does a brand-new battery fail a Gateway emissions test?
Because the car forgets. Modern engines run a set of self-tests, called readiness monitors, on the emissions system while you drive. Gateway’s test reads whether those self-tests have finished. Pull the battery or wipe the trouble codes and the computer starts over from zero, so every monitor reports “Not Completed” until the car has been driven enough to rerun them.
The thresholds are on Gateway’s readiness page. A gasoline car from model year 1996 to 2000 fails with three or more monitors not completed. A gasoline car from 2001 or newer fails with two or more. The program covers gas-powered vehicles 1996 and newer and diesels 1997 and newer, 8,500 pounds or less, registered in the four Gateway areas. The emissions test is $24 and a safety inspection is $12, and Gateway asks drivers to report any station that charges more.
Picture the printout coming out of the machine with the word that ruins the trip on it. If you fail, the station hands you a report that shows what part of the inspection failed and a list of the ten nearest Missouri Recognized Repair Technicians. If the only failure is monitors, what you need is miles, and the 30-day window.
So the counter’s offer to clear the light is a decision, not a favor. Read the code, write it down, take a photo of the screen. Clear it only if your Gateway test is behind you or far enough ahead that normal driving will finish the self-tests. A light that comes straight back on is telling you the part you bought wasn’t the problem.
### What’s the difference between OEM, aftermarket and remanufactured parts?
OEM is the part the factory installed, and the dealer parts counter is where you buy it new. Aftermarket is made by another company to fit the same car. Remanufactured means a used core was taken apart, cleaned, and rebuilt to work like new. Recycled means a used original, pulled from another vehicle at a yard.
You can hear the difference at the counter if you listen for it. “Reman” and “rebuilt” get used like the same word, and they aren’t always the same job: a rebuild may replace only what was broken. Ask which one is in the box and what the warranty paper says, then hold the old part and the new one side by side before you leave the lot. Same bolt holes, same plug, same pulley.
One fear you can set down. A non-dealer part does not by itself kill your new-car warranty. Federal law, the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, says a warrantor may not condition a written or implied warranty on your using a part or service identified by brand, trade or corporate name, unless it’s provided free under the warranty. The dealer can still deny a claim when the part itself caused the damage, so keep the receipt.
Nothing to do with brake pads, but St. Louis barbecue deserves its own afternoon.
### A core charge is your money in the trunk
Buy an alternator, a starter or a brake caliper and the receipt often carries a second line: the core charge. It’s a deposit on your old part, because the old one is worth something to the people who remanufacture them. Bring it back and the deposit comes back to you.
The ways people lose that money are all ordinary. The old part rides around in the trunk, sliding into the spare-tire well every time you take a corner, until the return window closes. The housing comes back cracked. The receipt goes through the wash in a jacket pocket. Drain it, put it in the box the new one came in, and take it back the same week. Ask the counter how long you have before you walk out, because the window isn’t the same everywhere.
If a shop does the job, ask who keeps the core. Usually the shop returns it and keeps the refund, which is normal. It just belongs on the estimate where you can see it.
### When does a salvage yard beat a new part?
When the part is cosmetic, sheet metal, glass or discontinued. A used factory door, fender, mirror, tailgate or seat came off the same assembly line as yours, so the gaps line up and the color code can be matched before you pay. Wheels, trim pieces and interior panels are where a yard usually wins outright.
A yard is its own kind of morning. Gravel under your boots, rows of cars sitting on stands with their hoods up, the faint smell of old coolant in the air. Bring gloves, your own sockets, a photo of the part still on your car and the VIN. Ask what other years and models used the identical part, because the yard’s computer often knows interchanges the counter at a chain store never asks about.
Buy from a licensed yard. Missouri law says no one may carry on the business of selling used parts, or of salvaging, wrecking or dismantling vehicles for resale of their parts, unless licensed to do so by the Department of Revenue. The director of revenue issues separate licenses for a “used parts dealer,” a “salvage dealer or dismantler,” a “rebuilder or body shop” and a “scrap processor.” You can read it yourself in section 301.218 of the Missouri statutes. A licensed yard has records and an address to come back to when the part doesn’t fit.
### Do it yourself, or hand it to a shop?
Look at the labor line on the estimate, then look at what happens if you get it wrong. A battery, wiper blades, an air filter or a headlight bulb is a driveway job with cold fingers and a flashlight in your teeth. Pads and rotors are a driveway job if you own a jack, stands and a torque wrench and you know how to use all three.
Some jobs belong to a shop regardless of skill: anything that holds the car to the road or stops it when you haven’t done it before, fuel and airbag work, and anything that needs a scan tool to program a new module. If you’re in the Gateway counties, add one more reason to let a shop handle it the month your test is due: they deal with readiness monitors every day and can tell you whether the car is ready before you pay for a test lane.
If you do it yourself, borrow the odd tools instead of buying them. O’Reilly’s Saint Louis store page lists a Loaner Tool Program. Ask at the counter what the deposit is and when you get it back.
### The view from behind the counter
One of the names on the signs around here has Missouri roots. O’Reilly Automotive officially started in the auto parts business in Springfield, Missouri, in November of 1957, according to the company’s own history.
The walk-in isn’t where a parts counter makes most of its day. The shop account is: the call that comes in first thing because a car is already up on a lift. The test bench and the loaner tools turn a guess into a sale. A yard’s real product isn’t metal, it’s information: which part fits, what grade it is, and whether a stranger can find it. Same logic for the counters and yards themselves. People look for this category by neighborhood, and a shop that’s easy to find and list gets the call.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I buy real OEM parts?
A.  New OEM parts, the ones the factory installed, come from a dealer parts counter. A licensed salvage yard sells the same factory part used, often for far less, and it is the best place to look for body panels, mirrors and trim. Bring your VIN either way.
### Q. Where can I find used auto parts in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  At licensed salvage yards on both sides of the river. In Missouri, selling used parts or dismantling vehicles for parts requires a license from the Department of Revenue under section 301.218. Call ahead with your VIN, ask what other models used the same part, and buy brake, airbag and seat belt parts new.
### Q. Where is the nearest Advance Auto Parts store in Saint Louis, MO?
A.  Store lists change, so use the chain’s own store locator and call before you drive. The better question is which store has the bench you need: check the store page for battery, alternator and starter testing before you buy the part.
### Q. Which store is better, AutoZone or O'Reilly's auto parts?
A.  Neither wins every job. Pick the store that has your part on the shelf and the service you need at that location. O’Reilly’s Saint Louis store page has a filter by store services, including check engine light testing and the Loaner Tool Program. Keep every receipt in the chain’s system for the warranty.
### Q. Who is the number one auto parts retailer?
A.  It depends whether you count stores or sales, and the rankings shift year to year. The local answer is simpler. O’Reilly Automotive started in the auto parts business in Springfield, Missouri, in November of 1957.
### Q. What's the best place to buy auto parts?
A.  The one that matches the part. Chain counters for common parts you need today, an independent parts house for hard-to-find and professional-grade parts, and a licensed salvage yard for body panels and glass. In the Gateway counties, time a battery swap or a code clear so it doesn’t land right before your emissions test.
### Q. Are there any junkyards in Missouri?
A.  Plenty, and the licensed ones are businesses with records and addresses. Missouri issues separate Department of Revenue licenses for used parts dealers, salvage dealers or dismantlers, rebuilders or body shops, and scrap processors. Ask to see the license if a yard seems informal.

## A St. Louis Car Wash Plan Pays for Itself on Wash Two. Here's the Catch
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/car-wash-cost-st-louis-monthly-membership
Two washes. That is when the monthly plan at one St. Louis-area car wash starts paying you back, and in February you can feel why: the hiss of slush off the tires on Lindbergh, the grit that comes back on your fingertip when you touch the rocker panel, the doors gone the color of sidewalk.
You back out of the driveway in Affton on the first sunny day in weeks and the car looks dusted with chalk. White crust is packed into the wheel wells. There is a tide line across the tailgate where the slush rode. That crust is salt, and it doesn’t care whether you meant to get to the wash this week.
It has a source. MoDOT says it has over 30,000 tons of salt on hand for the St. Louis area and more than 200 trucks with plows, salt brine and rock salt spreaders, working before and during a storm. Its St. Louis region maintains 6,400 lane miles, which MoDOT says would stretch from New York to San Francisco and back in one lane. A lot of that salt ends up under your car.
Now the menu. Country Club Car Wash, which lists a location in Chesterfield, posts its prices side by side: a basic touchless exterior wash is $13 for a single visit or $25 a month for unlimited. Two basic singles at $13 is $26, so the plan wins on trip two. The top exterior wash is $26 once or $45 a month, and the full-service basic is $33 once or $55 a month. Two singles beat the monthly price on every tier of that board. It’s one wash’s menu, so check the one on your own route.
So the question isn’t whether a plan is cheaper. On paper it almost always is. The question is whether you’ll actually go twice, every single month, including the dry, sleepy ones when the car looks fine.
### Are unlimited car wash plans worth it?
Yes, if you will really wash at least twice a month. On Country Club Car Wash’s published menu, every monthly unlimited price is less than two single washes: $25 a month against a $13 basic exterior wash, and $45 against $26 at the top exterior tier. Wash less than twice a month and paying per wash is cheaper.
That last line is the whole trap. A plan is a bet on your own habits, and most of us are optimists about our habits. The people who win are the ones whose commute already rolls past the tunnel, so stopping costs them a turn signal instead of a trip.
### Run the break-even on your own commute
The math takes ten seconds. Take the monthly price, divide it by the single-wash price for the same tier, and round up. That is how many washes a month you need before the plan stops costing you money.
Then do the honest part. Picture the last three months, not the next three. How many times did you actually pull in? If the answer is “once, maybe,” the plan is a gym membership with soap. If you drive salted roads every day from Florissant to a job across the county, two a month is easy, and four is normal after a snow.
The tier matters more than people expect, too. On that same menu, the basic exterior wash is a touchless wash and a spot-free rinse. The underbody spray, which the menu calls the Bottom Blaster & Salt Shield, shows up starting at the next tier: $18 once or $32 a month. If you’re buying a plan for winter, that’s the line on the menu that does the real work, because it hits the frame rails and brake lines you never see.
### Is it good to get a car wash every month?
Through a St. Louis winter, once a month is the floor, not the goal. Salt sitting dry on a cold car does less harm than salt that thaws, turns to brine and soaks into every seam. Our winters do a lot of freezing at night and thawing by the afternoon, and every one of those thaws puts wet salt to work on the underside of your car.
The best time to wash is the first day it climbs comfortably above freezing after a storm, when the roads have dried and the crews have stopped spreading. Wash during the storm and you’re paying to rinse off salt you’ll pick up again on the drive home. Wash on a bitter morning and water can freeze into door seals and locks. You know the sound: the door handle that won’t give, then the crack of ice letting go.
In summer, monthly is plenty for most cars unless they live under a tree that drips sap or near a construction zone. That’s the season a plan quietly earns less. Pollen, bugs and bird droppings are worth washing off quickly, but they rarely add up to two trips a month for a commuter.
### Are unlimited car washes actually unlimited?
Usually yes on the wash count. Scrubbles, another express chain in the area, tells members on its plan page “you have unlimited washes every day!” What’s limited is everything around the wash: the plan generally covers one vehicle, the tier you signed up for, and only that company’s tunnels. Read the terms for the one detail that matters to you, whether that’s a second car in the household or a location near your office.
What one St. Louis menu charges
On Country Club Car Wash’s menu, a single exterior wash runs $13-$26 and a full-service wash with a vacuumed interior runs $33-$46. Monthly unlimited runs $25-$45 for exterior and $55-$75 for full service. The tier you pick moves the price most, so buy the one you actually need.
Those numbers are one operator’s board, not a citywide rate. Check the menu on your own route before you sign, because a cheaper plan at a tunnel you never pass is the most expensive plan there is.
### What are the disadvantages of car subscription?
You pay in the months you don’t use it, and you have to remember to stop. That’s the business model, and it isn’t a secret. A plan that renews on its own every month only needs you to forget about it for a summer.
Cancelling is rarely hard, but it has fine print. Scrubbles says its plans carry “No contracts, cancel anytime!” and that you can cancel by email, by phone or text, or through the Manage Membership tab. It also asks for 4 days notice when your anniversary date falls on a weekend. That’s exactly the kind of line that turns into one more charge if you wait until the night before.
The fix is boring and it works. When you sign up, put a reminder in your phone a few days before the renewal date for the month you expect to stop, probably late spring. When it buzzes, look at the car and decide. Keeping a plan should be a choice you make on purpose, not the default you drift into.
### Both sides of the river get the same salt bill
It doesn’t matter much whether you commute out of Belleville or out of Kirkwood. Both sides of the metro salt their roads hard, and the brine kicks up off the pavement and coats everything behind the front bumper. If you cross the river every day, you’re collecting it from two sets of trucks. Factor that into the break-even: a daily bridge commuter in a salty month is the person a plan was built for, and a retiree who drives to the grocery store twice a week is not. Be honest about which one of those you are in January, and again in July.
### Touchless or soft-touch: what you’re paying for
A touchless wash never lays a brush on your paint, so it can’t leave swirl marks. It makes up for that with stronger soaps, which strip wax faster. A soft-touch tunnel uses foam or cloth and pulls stubborn road film off better, and how gentle it is depends on how well the operator keeps that material clean. You can usually tell from the lot: tidy bays, fresh-looking foam, an attendant prepping cars at the entrance.
Dark paint on a car you love leans touchless through the salt months. A white crossover that sits in traffic on the way into Kirkwood every morning can live happily in a soft-touch tunnel. Neither choice is wrong. A dirty car through a whole winter is the only wrong answer.
Shopping for a car that already spent winters on salted roads? Here is how to spot rust before you buy.
### When a detail beats another month of washes
A wash removes what’s on the car. A detail fixes what the winter left behind: the white salt rings dried into the floor mats, the haze on the paint, the swirl marks from a season of quick washes. Those are different jobs, and a plan doesn’t do the second one.
A sensible rhythm for a St. Louis car is a wash plan through the salt months and one proper detail when spring finally settles in, then a hard look at whether you need the plan through summer. If you want the numbers for that spring visit, here’s what car detailing costs in St. Louis.
### A quick plan for buying a plan
Before you sign anything at the pay station, do these five things:
Find the menu with both columns. You need the single price and the monthly price for the same tier, side by side.
Do the division. Monthly price divided by single price, rounded up, is the number of washes you need each month.
Check the tier for the underbody spray. In winter that line is worth paying for. In summer it rarely is.
Pick a tunnel on your route. A plan near home that you pass only on weekends is a plan you’ll stop using.
Read the cancellation line. Note how and when you have to cancel, then set the reminder.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are unlimited car washes actually unlimited?
A.  The wash count usually is. The limits are around it: the plan generally covers one vehicle, one tier and one company’s locations. Read the terms before you count on using it for a second car or at another brand’s tunnel.
### Q. Is it good to get a car wash every month?
A.  Yes, and through a St. Louis winter monthly is the minimum. Wash on the first dry day above freezing after a storm, and pick a tier with an underbody spray so the salt comes off the frame and brake lines, not just the paint.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of car subscription?
A.  You pay in months you don’t use it, and the plan renews until you cancel. If you wash fewer than two times a month, single washes usually cost less. Set a reminder before the renewal date so the decision stays yours.
### Q. Who has the best car wash subscription?
A.  The best one is the one on the road you already drive, at a price where two washes a month cover it. Compare two operators on your route using the same tier on each menu, and check which tier first includes the underbody spray.
### Q. What is the best car subscription service?
A.  If you mean a car wash subscription, judge it by the break-even: the monthly price divided by the single-wash price at the same tier. The lower that number and the closer the tunnel sits to your daily drive, the better the plan is for you.
### Q. Is it cheaper to wash my car at home?
A.  In summer it can be, if you have the time and the buckets. In winter it rarely works: a hose can’t reach under the car the way a tunnel’s underbody spray does, and washing in a cold driveway invites frozen locks and door seals.

## That Flower Site May Not Be a Florist: How to Order From a Real St. Louis Shop
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/order-flowers-real-st-louis-florist
The cellophane crackles first. Then the little plastic fork with the card in it, and your mother turning the vase toward the porch light on a South City street, looking for the arrangement she saw on your phone. It isn’t quite there. Fewer stems. A carnation where the rose was supposed to be. She says it’s lovely, in the voice people use when it isn’t, and you hear that voice all the way through the phone.
Nothing went wrong with the flowers. Something went wrong with the money. The Society of American Florists warns that people ordering online can “discover that only a portion of the amount they paid was transmitted to the florist fulfilling the order.” The rest stayed with a website that took your card and never touched a stem.
Here is the part that flips the usual advice. The internet is not the villain. According to its own family history, Walter Knoll Florist, a St. Louis shop whose story starts with an 1883 photograph of a funeral the family decorated, became the first florist to sell flowers on the internet. That family says it has been at it for well over a century.
So the question was never website or shop. A website is fine. A website that isn’t a florist is the problem.
### Is it better to order from a local florist or online?
Order from a local florist, online or by phone, as long as the site belongs to the shop that will design and deliver it. Order-gathering sites take your order, keep part of what you paid and pass a smaller budget to a real florist. Before you pay, call and ask: Is this the florist that will design and deliver my arrangement?
That one question sorts the field fast. A shop with a humming cooler in the back and a van out front says yes without thinking about it. A call center has to think about it.
### Sending flowers to a St. Louis hospital room
Mercy Hospital St. Louis says it plainly on its own flower shop page: plants and cut flowers are not permitted in ICU or Burn Unit rooms. Its in-house floral designers deliver free to patients on the Mercy campus during weekday hours, and the shop does not carry latex balloons because of patient allergies. An order-gathering site in another state doesn’t know any of that. Send roses to an ICU bed through a site like that and the flowers you paid for never reach the person you sent them to.
At Barnes-Jewish Hospital it works the other way. If the person you love is a patient at Barnes-Jewish Hospital, the hospital has its own Plaza Gift and Flower Shop in its Plaza Tower, selling fresh flower designs and delivering to patients, at 314-362-4300. The hospital itself suggests its in-house shops when the patient may be released within 3-5 business days. The person arranging the stems works under the same roof as the person in the bed.
### Where the missing part of your money goes
SAF spells out what it considers deceptive: representing a business as local without maintaining a physical presence in the community, collecting undisclosed service fees, and transmitting orders below stated retail prices and standard delivery fees. Read that last one twice. It is the thin vase on your mother’s porch.
Somewhere in a back room in the metro, a designer pulls a printout off the machine, wet hands, buckets of stems at her feet, and finds a budget smaller than what you paid and a photo she has never seen. Good designers do a lot with that. They can’t do the photo, because the photo was never a picture of anything her shop made.
Shops hand orders to each other all the time, and it is the right move when the flowers are going to another state. The trouble starts when a website dresses itself up as the florist down the street from you.
### How do you know you’re ordering from an actual local florist?
Give every site the St. Louis test first: a real shop here has a corner you can stand on. Walter Knoll’s own timeline says it opened at Holly Hills and Idaho and later moved its main office to the city’s historic Florist Row, where it occupies more than 70,000 square feet. That is the kind of address you can drive past.
Then ask the questions the Society of American Florists prints for consumers. Is this the florist that will design and deliver my arrangement? Do you have a physical location in my community? Are there service fees? A shop with a real counter can answer all three before you finish asking.
Then spend thirty seconds on the address. Paste it into Google Maps and check that it lands in the neighborhood the site claims to serve, Dutchtown or Kirkwood or the Central West End, then drop the little yellow figure onto Street View. You want a storefront with buckets by the door, not an office park somewhere you have never been. Look hard at the checkout, too. Every shop charges delivery. A separate service charge stacked on top of it is the line that usually pays someone who never saw your flowers. And don’t let a local-looking phone number settle it, because SAF lists caller ID spoofing among the tactics these operations use.
If you want that shop as a starting point, Walter Knoll lists its offices at 2765 LaSalle St. in St. Louis and its number as (314) 352-7575. Then compare it with a smaller shop closer to the person getting the flowers. Close matters more than famous.
### Tell the florist three things, not a photo
A dollar number, who it’s for, and one thing to avoid. “Here’s my budget, it’s for my mother’s birthday, she can’t stand lilies.” That sentence beats any picture on any website. The designer is standing at the cooler looking at what actually came in this week, which roses opened overnight, which tulips are still tight, and a photo can’t see any of that.
Then say the words “designer’s choice” and get off the phone. Florists aren’t offended by a budget. They’re relieved by one, because now they can build something with their hands instead of chasing someone else’s picture.
### When the flowers are for a funeral
Here the real deadline belongs to the funeral home, not the florist. Call the funeral home first and ask when deliveries need to arrive before the visitation, then call the shop. Name the piece you want: friends and coworkers usually send a standing spray or a vase arrangement, and the casket spray is the family’s.
If the obituary asks for donations instead of flowers, do that. And think about the house a while later, when the casseroles have stopped coming and the kitchen has gone quiet. That is when a small arrangement on the doorstep lands hardest. It is an old St. Louis errand. Walter Knoll traces its own start to a funeral it decorated.
Flowers are one way to send love home. Here are gifts that actually come from here.
### Same-day orders: whose clock are you on?
Every shop sets its own same-day cutoff, and it is earlier than most people think, because the driver’s route gets built in the morning. Call instead of clicking. A person on the phone can tell you in five words whether today is still possible, and a checkout page will happily take an order nobody can fill.
Then remember the building has a clock too. Hospitals and care facilities only take deliveries at the front desk during certain hours, and some units don’t allow fresh flowers at all. A quick call to the nurses’ station saves the driver a wasted trip and saves you an awkward call later. Schools and offices close their doors earlier than you’d guess, so ask for a delivery window rather than an exact time.
Distance moves the clock as well. A shop near the recipient can make a late-morning order work. A shop on the far side of the metro is making a route decision before you’ve finished your coffee. That is one more reason close beats famous.
### The holidays every florist dreads a little
Walk into any shop in the days before Valentine’s Day or Mother’s Day and you can feel it: extra hands at the bench, buckets stacked three deep, the phone ringing while someone is already on the other line. A year of demand lands in a couple of days, on a product that can’t be stockpiled.
You can make that crunch work for you. Order several days ahead, because shops buy flowers to match their order book and early orders get built from stems bought with you in mind. Skip the long-stem red roses if you want the budget to stretch, since they are the most sought-after flower of those weeks. Ask for a garden-style mix or tulips instead, and say designer’s choice. On a peak day that phrase is the difference between a designer fighting a photo and a designer working for you. And if the date can move by a day, move it. The day before or after is calmer for the shop and the driver alike.
### Sending flowers to someone in another city
Here a relay order is honest and useful. The trick is to do the relaying yourself. Look up a shop in the recipient’s town, check the address on Street View, and call it directly, just as you would at home. You get a real person who knows the local funeral homes and hospitals, and the whole budget stays with the people building the arrangement.
It works the other way too. When a cousin in another state wants to send something to a St. Louis address, send them the name of a shop here instead of a link to a national site. You know the neighborhood. They don’t.
### Keeping the arrangement alive once it’s on the table
The flowers from a real shop usually come with a little packet of food and a short card of instructions. Use them. Give the stems a fresh cut, keep the water clean and topped up, and move the vase away from the sunny window and the fruit bowl. A cool spot on the dining room table does more for a bouquet than any trick on the internet. And if something wilts early, call the shop. A real florist would rather hear about it than lose you to a website, and many will make it right.
### What a real shop gives you that a website can’t
A person who can fix it. When the delivery is late or the color is wrong, the shop that built it can send a driver back that afternoon. An order-gathering site can open a ticket. That difference is worth more than any coupon code, and it is the reason to keep one florist’s number in your phone the way you keep a plumber’s.
Planning something bigger than a birthday bunch? Flowers are usually one of several vendors you book together:
Wedding and event caterers across the St. Louis metro

The sympathy etiquette that makes an arrangement land right
Nail salons across the metro, for the day of
Want every dollar to turn into stems? Browse florists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the two closest to the recipient’s address, and call the one that picks up.
If you’re the florist with the cooler, the van and your name on the door, the people hunting for a real local shop should reach you before they reach a website pretending to be you. Put your shop where those customers are already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can I tell if a flower website is a real local florist?
A.  Find the street address on Street View, call the number and ask whether they are the florist who will design and deliver your arrangement, and ask whether there are service fees.
### Q. Is it cheaper to call a local florist?
A.  Often you pay a similar total and get more flowers, because nothing is skimmed before the designer starts. Calling the shop directly also skips the separate service charge some order-gathering sites add on top of delivery.
### Q. What is the best company to order flowers from?
A.  The shop that will actually build and deliver the arrangement, as close to the recipient as you can find. A national brand name matters less than whether the flowers come from a real cooler in the same metro.
### Q. Who is the best florist in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Nobody can rank that honestly for you, and the right answer changes with the address. Pick two shops near the person receiving the flowers, call both, and order from the one that asks you good questions about who it’s for.
### Q. What are the unspoken rules of flower etiquette?
A.  Give a budget, the occasion and one boundary, then let the designer choose the stems. At a funeral the casket spray belongs to the immediate family. If the obituary asks for donations in lieu of flowers, honor it, and remember that something sent to the house a couple of weeks later often means the most.
### Q. What time should I order flowers for delivery today?
A.  As early in the morning as you can, and always by phone. Same-day cutoffs vary by shop, and funeral homes and hospitals set their own delivery windows, so ask the building first and the florist second.
One phone call, one honest budget, one shop near the person you are trying to reach. That is how the vase on the porch ends up looking like somebody meant it.

## Photographer Cost in St. Louis: $325 to $500 a Session, and the Arch Permit Is $0
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/photographer-cost-st-louis
$0. That is what the National Park Service asks for a family photo under the Gateway Arch, in most cases, as long as there are eight or fewer of you. No permit, no permit fee. Just the wind coming up off the river, the kids squinting into the sun, and that long curve of steel turning gold behind your photographer’s shoulder.
Now drive across town to the Missouri Botanical Garden with the same family in the same outfits. There, a formal session needs a photo permit, reserved at least 24 hours ahead, good for that one date only, and nonrefundable. Same city. Same golden hour. A completely different set of rules, and nobody tells you until you are standing at the gate with a garment bag over your arm.
That is the part of photographer pricing most quotes leave out. The session fee is only half the bill. Where you shoot, how many people you bring, and what the contract says about the files all move the real cost, and in St. Louis the answer changes from one patch of grass to the next.
So here is the honest version, built from what local studios actually post and what the parks and the Garden actually say. Start with the price, then pick the place, then read the fine print before you hand anyone a retainer.
### What is a reasonable price for a photographer?
For a family or portrait session around St. Louis, posted studio prices run about $325 to $500. One Metro East studio lists $325 for a 30-minute mini session and $500 for a one-hour session, both with edited high-resolution downloads and a print release. Another charges $450 for a 90-minute session with 30 edited images.
### Where the permit is free, and where it is not
Stand on the Arch grounds in the evening, the river barges sliding past and joggers looping the paths. The Park Service rule is plain: in most cases, permits and fees are not required for still photography that involves eight or fewer people. To stay in that free lane, the shoot has to happen in areas open to the public, use hand-carried equipment only, and not require exclusive use of a site. Bring a tripod you can carry. Leave the lighting rig and the rented arch of flowers at home.
One honest catch. The Park Service also notes that people doing still photography are subject to entrance or recreation fees that may apply even when a permit is not required. Free to shoot is not always free to walk in.
City parks are their own office. Before you bring a big group or anything that looks like a production into a city park, call the City of St. Louis Department of Parks, Recreation, and Forestry at 314-289-5300 and ask what applies to your date. It is a quick call, and it saves the moment where somebody in a uniform walks over mid-pose.
Across the river, the grassy terraces of Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site draw a lot of engagement sessions at dusk. The site’s own policy says arrangements must be made with site personnel and a Photography Permit should be obtained and filled out before a photo session. The number is 618-346-5160.
Head west across the Missouri River and the county parks there keep their own rules, so do not assume what worked in Tower Grove Park carries over. Call the county’s Parks and Recreation Advisory Board at 636-949-7535 before you promise a client a spot on the trail. A photographer who has to pack up mid-session because of a permit question loses more than the hour; the family loses the light, the toddler’s patience and the one evening everybody was free.
The pattern across all of these is the same. Small group, hand-held gear, public ground: usually simple. Bigger group, lights, props, a spot you want to yourself: ask first, in writing, and keep the answer on your phone. When you get a quote, ask the photographer which of these places they shoot most often and whether a permit cost is already built into the price, or whether it lands on you.
### What a Garden photo permit actually buys you
The Garden permit sounds like a hassle. It is also quietly a deal for big families, and almost nobody reads far enough to notice. The Garden says the permit level includes admission for your entire party while visiting. Grandma, the cousins, the toddler in the stroller: one permit covers the whole group’s way in for that date.
Members get a break, too. Permit fees for members of the Garden Giving Societies, at the $600 Contributor level and higher, are either waived or discounted depending on group size, though a reservation is still required. If your family already gives at that level, check before you pay twice. And if you are getting married there, a permit is not required for a booked ceremony or private event at the Garden.
Now the rules that change the pictures. Photography is permitted only in the outdoor, public areas of the Garden, not inside any buildings or conservatories, and that includes the Climatron. Photography is not permitted on any of the islands in the Japanese Garden. Lighting equipment and reflectors are not permitted. Props are limited to one per person, no larger than two feet by two feet. Wardrobe changes are strongly discouraged. And photography is not allowed during evening public events, including the Whitaker Music Festival and Garden Glow evenings, so a family card shot under the holiday lights is off the table there.
Sessions must be completed and groups departed by close, no exceptions. If your photographer loves that last soft light before the gates shut, build the schedule backward from closing time, not forward from when everybody finally finds parking.
### Why a cheap quote and a $500 quote are different jobs
The shoot you see is the short part. You hear the shutter for one short session. What you do not see is the evening after, when the photographer sits in a dark room scrolling through a long run of near-identical frames to find the one where nobody blinked, then fixes the skin, the stray hair, the sky. That is the work a session fee pays for, and it is the first thing that disappears from a bargain quote.
So read what each quote delivers, not just the dollar figure at the top. The Metro East studio that posts $325 and $500 sessions spells it out: an online gallery for viewing, sharing and ordering, downloadable fully edited high-resolution images, and a print release. The 90-minute session at $450 from another local photographer promises 30 edited images, with the option to buy more. Those are numbers you can compare. A quote that says only “digitals included” is not.
Ask three questions of every quote. How many finished images will I get? Do I get downloads or only prints? Is a print release included? Line the answers up side by side on one sheet of paper and the cheapest quote is often not the cheapest at all.
Travel moves it too. The same Metro East studio serves the general metropolitan St. Louis area and adds a small mileage fee past its 40-mile radius. If your dream spot is an hour out, ask about that line before you fall in love with the location.
What local studios post
Posted family session prices from studios serving the St. Louis metro run about $325 to $500: $325 for a 30-minute mini session and $500 for an hour at one Metro East studio, and $450 for 90 minutes with 30 edited images at another. Session length, the number of edited images, and travel past the studio’s mileage radius move the price.
### Who owns the photos after you pay?
Not you, in most cases, and paying the invoice does not change that. The U.S. Copyright Office says a work is under copyright protection the moment it is created and fixed in a tangible form. The photographer pressed the shutter, so the photographer holds the copyright.
Moving that copyright to you takes paper. Under 17 U.S.C. 204(a), a transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless it is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights or an authorized agent. A gallery link in your inbox is not that.
What families actually need is a print release: permission to print the pictures, frame them over the couch and post them for the grandparents. Make sure the contract says you get one, and if the photos are for a business, ask separately whether commercial use is covered.
Thinking you could just do it yourself? Start with what photography classes cost in St. Louis.
### Five questions to ask before you hand over a retainer
Ask them on the phone, not by text, and listen for how fast the answers come. Are you insured, and can you send my location a certificate if they ask for one? Who actually shows up on the day? How many weeks until the full gallery? What happens if you are sick? Is my payment a retainer or a deposit, and what comes back if I cancel?
That last one matters most. A retainer usually holds a date and is often kept if you cancel; a deposit is usually treated as an advance on the work. The word in your contract decides it, so read it before you sign, sitting at your own kitchen table rather than at a coffee shop with the photographer watching you read.
### What the price looks like from behind the camera
If you shoot for a living here, you already know the hour in the park is the easy part. The nights at the screen, the backup drives, the gas to the Garden and back, the permit you build into the quote: none of it shows up in a parent’s mental math. And none of it helps if the family searching for a photographer at 10 at night never finds you. That is the argument for keeping a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $100 an hour good for a photographer?
A.  It is well under what local studios post. One Metro East studio lists $325 for a 30-minute mini session and $500 for an hour, with edited downloads and a print release included. At that rate, ask what gets cut, starting with editing and the number of finished images.
### Q. How much should a 20 minute photoshoot cost?
A.  Short shoots are usually sold as mini sessions with a flat fee, not by the minute. A Metro East studio lists a 30-minute mini session at $325, including fully edited high-resolution downloads and a print release.
### Q. How much should you expect to pay for a photographer?
A.  For a family session in the St. Louis area, plan on about $325 to $500, based on posted local studio prices. Add any location costs: a Missouri Botanical Garden photo permit is required for formal sessions, while small groups at the Gateway Arch usually need no permit at all.
### Q. How much does a 2 hour photo shoot cost?
A.  Many local studios publish sessions of an hour or 90 minutes and quote longer shoots individually. One Metro East studio lists $500 for an hour and customizes quotes for extended family sessions, and another charges $450 for 90 minutes with 30 edited images - ask each one to put your full time in a written quote.
### Q. Do I need a permit to take photos at the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  Yes, for formal photography such as weddings, family sessions, prom and quinceañera photos. Reserve at least 24 hours ahead; the permit is for one date, nonrefundable, and includes admission for your whole party. It is not required for a ceremony or private event booked at the Garden.

## Closed by Noon Saturday: Where St. Louis Buys Lumber, Trim and Brick
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-building-supplies-in-st-louis
12:15 on a Saturday. You’re standing outside a lumberyard on Tesshire Drive with a snapped piece of baseboard in your fist, and the yard closed fifteen minutes ago. Back home, the new trim you bought last week sits a sliver taller than the old trim it’s supposed to meet. You can feel the step with a thumbnail.
In a Kirkwood bungalow or a Florissant ranch, nobody else will ever notice. In a brick house with trim milled before your grandparents were born, you will see that seam every time you walk down the hall.
That seam is the real question behind where you buy building supplies in St. Louis. Price per board is the part everybody compares. The part that costs you is the second trip, the board that won’t lie flat, and the piece nobody makes anymore.
Here is the thing most weekend lists miss. The two places that solve an old St. Louis house best keep hours built for the trades, not for your Saturday. Norrenberns Lumber & Hardware, a lumberyard on Tesshire Drive in business since 1946, opens at 7:30am on weekdays and closes at noon on Saturday. Refab, the salvage warehouse at Gravois and California, is open Thursday through Saturday only, 10am-4pm, and closed the other four days.
And the brick? In this city even used brick is policed like a pawn shop. A licensed City of St. Louis brick dealer has to photograph every person who sells it brick and see a demolition permit before taking a single used one.
Plan the job around their clocks, not yours. The yard that can match your trim and the warehouse that has your 100-year-old door are both shut on a Sunday afternoon, the one time most of us finally have free.
### Where’s the cheapest place to get lumber?
It depends on what the board has to do. For a stack of studs on a Sunday, a big-box store is hard to beat. For straight stock in volume, hardwood and trim that has to match, a lumberyard usually wins on the total job. For old wood, doors and profiles nobody mills anymore, salvage is cheapest because it may be the only place. Price the same written list everywhere.
### Three counters, three different jobs
Stand at the end of a big-box lumber aisle and you know the routine. Pull a 2x4 off the stack, sight down the edge, set it back. Pull another. The pile smells of fresh-cut pine and the forklift beeps two aisles over. You do the sorting, and that is fine when you need eight studs at 6pm on a weeknight and a store open late. The big box wins on hours, small quantities and easy returns.
A lumberyard is a different room. It smells like cedar and sawdust and the counter has a pencil behind somebody’s ear. Norrenberns lists more than 100 moulding profiles in stock, plus hardwoods like walnut, white oak and cherry, and special-order profiles in almost any wood. That is the counter you take the broken piece of trim to. You hold it up, somebody turns it over in their hands, and you find out in a minute whether the house can be matched or has to be fudged.
Walk in, ask, bring the piece.
Salvage is the third room, and in St. Louis it is a big one. Refab calls its warehouse 140 years of St. Louis building history in a 37,000-square-foot re-use center. Doors with the old paint still in the panel grooves. Stacks of reclaimed lumber, hardwood flooring, barn wood, cabinets, light fixtures and brick. It is cold in winter and quiet except for somebody dragging a door across the concrete to see it in the light.
The rules are blunt and printed on their own page: they will hold a purchase for up to two weeks while you arrange transportation, and there are no returns or exchanges. Their sign-off is the best advice in this whole guide. Measure twice, buy once.
### Reading a board before it reads you
Whichever counter you choose, learn to read the wood in your hands. Lift one end to eye level and sight down the long edge like a pool cue. A gentle bow along the edge is crown; framers set it up on a joist so the floor settles flat. A board that spirals like a propeller is twisted, and it will fight you on every nail. Look at the face for cup, where the board curls across its width like a shallow gutter.
Then run your hand down the corners. A missing corner with bark or a rounded edge is wane, and it leaves nothing for trim to sit on. Loose knots near the edge rattle when you tap them, and that is where a joist cracks under load. Your palm will tell you about wet wood before your eyes do: it feels cool and heavy, and it will shrink after it is nailed up.
At a big box you will put back three boards for every one you keep, and that is normal. At a yard, tell the counter what the piece is for and let them pull from the stack. Either way, reject the bad ones before they leave the lot. A twisted stud is free to refuse and expensive to install.
### How do you know which one your job needs?
Walk the job before you walk any aisle. Stand where the new piece will go and ask one question: will this be seen next to something old?
If the answer is no, the job is commodity. Framing in a basement nobody sees, blocking, a shed floor. Buy where it is cheapest and most convenient, sort your own boards, keep the receipt.
If the answer is yes, the job is a match. Baseboard, casing, a stair tread, a door in a 100-year-old opening, a patch of brick on a front wall. That is where a yard with a moulding wall or a salvage floor saves the job, because the cheap board that doesn’t match costs you the whole room.
For a deeper side-by-side on board quality, see our guide on whether lumber yards really have better lumber than Home Depot.
### Used brick in St. Louis is regulated like a pawn shop
Old red brick is the material this city is made of, and that makes it worth stealing. The City of St. Louis treats used brick accordingly. Under Ordinance 67392, a brick dealer gets its Brick Dealer Permit through the Director’s Office of the Department of Public Safety, and the dealer has to:
Photograph each person selling or otherwise transferring bricks to them, and show the photos to police on request.
Keep a register of all purchases and sales open to inspection.
Require the seller to show a demolition permit and a valid City business license before accepting used brick.
Every permit expires October 15 of each year, and the rules sit on the city’s Brick Dealer Permit page, issued through the Department of Public Safety. So when a pallet of soft, rust-red brick turns up cheap from a stranger with a pickup, ask where it came from. A legitimate dealer can tell you, and has the paperwork to prove it.
Bring a whole brick from your wall when you shop, not a photo. Color shifts in daylight and size varies by era, and you want to hold the two side by side in your palm before you buy a pallet. Buy extra the same day. Salvage stock on the floor is the entire supply.
### Decks, porches and anything that lives outdoors
Outdoor wood is where the wrong purchase hurts the slowest and the most. A deck that looked fine the summer you built it goes soft at the posts a few winters later, and you find out with your heel. When you buy treated lumber, ask whether it is rated for ground contact or above ground, and put that rating on your written list. Posts, anything buried and anything that sits wet against the ground need the ground-contact product.
Composite decking is a special order more often than people expect. Norrenberns, for one, says most colors of the Deckorators lines it carries are available to order within a week lead time. Ask about lead time the day you get the quote, not the day the crew shows up.
### Salvage without regret
A salvage floor rewards patience and punishes impulse. Before you carry a door to the counter, check it for square by measuring both diagonals; if they disagree, the door will rub. Look at the hinge edge for old mortises and plan on filling them. Pull the reclaimed lumber into daylight and look for nails and screws left in it, because one hidden nail will chip a saw blade in a second.
Old paint deserves respect. Assume a painted door or piece of trim from an old building may carry lead paint, and test it before you sand. Strip it outdoors or hire it out if the test comes back positive.
And buy enough. If you find flooring or brick that matches, buy more than your takeoff the same day, because what is on the floor is the whole supply. There is no reorder at a salvage counter.
The trim you can match yourself. The leak behind the wall you’re about to close up is a job for a plumber.
### Price the list, not the store
Write the spec, not the product. Species, grade, size, length, count, and for anything outdoors, whether it is rated for ground contact. Hand the identical list to every counter and ask for a line-by-line quote with any substitution flagged in writing. That one sheet of paper is your whole defense against a friendly upgrade.
Then compare the delivered and taxed total, not the shelf price. A cheaper board that needs two trips, a rented truck or a sorting session in a cold aisle is not cheaper. Ask what delivery costs to your street and what day they run your area, and whether the load lands at the curb or where you need it.
And if the project crosses the river, a yard in Belleville and one in Maryland Heights are both local to somebody and a long drive from each other. Ask about delivery zones before you fall for a price.
### Before you leave the house
Carry a sample: a piece of the old trim, a whole brick, a photo of the stamp on an existing board.
Check the hours and call ahead. Norrenberns, (314) 843-0700: Monday-Friday 7:30am-4:30pm, Saturday 8:00am-Noon. Refab, 314-357-1392: Thursday-Saturday, 10am-4pm.
Measure the opening, then measure it again. At a salvage floor there is no taking it back.
Know who installs it. Some work needs a permit or a licensed trade; for small jobs, a trusted handyman may be the right call.
Still hunting for the yard that has your board? Browse building supplies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then send the same written list to two of them and compare the quotes line by line.
If you run the yard, the salvage floor or the one-truck delivery outfit, the rehabber holding a broken piece of trim is searching for you right now. A Gold listing puts your stock, hours and photos where those customers look. Put your yard in front of more customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do lumber yards have better lumber than Home Depot?
A.  Often the stock is more consistent, because a yard serving the trades carries more species, grades and lengths and someone else does the sorting. A big box can still have good boards; you just pick them yourself. For a full comparison, read our guide on lumber yards versus Home Depot.
### Q. Is lumber cheaper at a lumber yard?
A.  Not automatically. Commodity studs are often close in price or cheaper at a big box. A yard tends to win on the total job: fewer rejects, delivery that saves trips, and trim or hardwood you cannot get on a big-box shelf. Price the same written list at both.
### Q. Is it cheaper to get lumber from a lumber yard?
A.  Per board, sometimes not. Per project, often yes, once you count the boards you throw out, the extra trips and the time spent culling a pile. On a large or visible job, ask the yard for a quote before you decide.
### Q. Is Lowes or Home Depot better for lumber?
A.  They carry similar grades, so the real difference is the individual store, how fast its pile turns over and how much sorting you have to do. For anything structural or in volume, a dedicated yard usually gives you more consistent stock.
### Q. Where can I legally buy used brick in St. Louis?
A.  From a dealer holding a City of St. Louis Brick Dealer Permit. Ordinance 67392 requires those dealers to photograph sellers, keep a register of purchases and sales, and see a demolition permit and a valid City business license before accepting used brick. Permits expire October 15 each year, so ask to see it.
