## Free Preschool in St. Louis Has Two Rules: An August 1 Birthday and Potty Training
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-preschool-in-st-louis
Does my kid really have to be out of diapers to get free preschool in this city? At St. Louis Public Schools, yes. The district’s own admissions page says it offers free preschool for students who are fully toilet trained and have turned 3 or 4 prior to August 1st of the upcoming school year. Two lines. One is a birthday. The other is a bathroom.
If you are reading this with a sticker chart on the fridge and a pile of tiny underwear on the dryer, you already know which line is harder. The timer on your phone goes off every forty minutes. The little step stool scrapes across the tile. Somebody announces, proudly and too late, that they had to go. You are not doing anything wrong. You are just on the clock, and almost nobody told you there was a clock.
That is the leverage point for a St. Louis parent picking a preschool: before you tour a single lobby, know which free door your child can walk through, which record to pull, and what a real month of tuition costs. The tour comes last.
### Is preschool free in St. Louis?
It can be. Saint Louis Public Schools offers free preschool for children who are fully toilet trained and have turned 3 or 4 before August 1 of the school year they start. The district lists a 10:1 student to teacher ratio in every classroom, free breakfast and lunch served at school, before and/or after care at all schools, and district transportation for eligible 4-year-olds. Registration runs through Focus, the district’s student information system.
Outside the city line, call your own school district and ask the same question. If the answer is no, you are shopping private, and the price changes the whole conversation.
### The birthday line and the bathroom line
Do the birthday math first, because it is the line you cannot move. A child who turns 3 before August 1 fits the district’s cutoff for that fall. A child who turns 3 in mid-August waits a year for the free seat. Same height, same vocabulary, same love of the big slide. Different calendar. Put the August 1 date on the fridge next to the sticker chart and count backward.
Then the bathroom line. “Fully toilet trained” is the district’s phrase, and it is worth asking the school office what it means in practice before you enroll, so the first week does not end with a phone call and a bag of wet clothes at pickup. Ask it plainly: what happens if my child has an accident in the first month?
There is a quieter benefit on that same SLPS page that matters to working parents: the district lists the ability for preschool students to attend the same school as older siblings. One drop-off line instead of two. One car door, one wave, one coffee going cold in the cupholder instead of two.
Here is the line worth texting the friend who is about to put down a deposit: in St. Louis, the difference between free preschool and a private tuition bill can come down to a birthday before August 1 and a kid who can make it to the bathroom alone.
### Pull the record before you fall for the lobby
A tour is built to make you feel something. The bright cubbies, the smell of crayons and floor cleaner, the tiny chairs, the teacher who kneels to say hello to your kid by name. All of it is real, and none of it tells you what an inspector found on the last visit. So look first.
In Missouri, the state’s Child Care Search lets you search for a facility by name. Read its own warning, too: the records available for review on that site may not reflect the complete history of a child care facility’s compliance. Public records on a licensed or license-exempt program can be requested from the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, Office of Childhood. A thin record online is a reason to ask for the full file, not proof that nothing is in it.
In the Metro East, the Illinois Sunshine website is the state’s resource for anyone interested in licensed child care in Illinois, with a monitoring report search and a page on how to make a licensing complaint. Families in Belleville get the same advice as families in Affton: read what the inspector wrote, then ask the director about it by name.
Rather talk to a person? Illinois DCFS lists a Day Care Information line at 1-877-746-0829. Have the program’s exact name and address in front of you when you call, and a pen, because the person on the other end will move faster than you can type.
That question changes the tour. You stop being a guest and start being the parent who did the homework. A good director answers without flinching and tells you what changed. A defensive one has just told you something too.
### Church preschools and home daycares play by different rules
Plenty of St. Louis families end up in a church basement classroom, and plenty of them love it. Know what it is. The state education department describes a child care center operated by a religious organization as “a regulated, license-exempt facility.” Programs under the exclusive control of a religious organization are license-exempt under Section 210.211, RSMo, and must still comply with certain child care laws and regulations.
Among the documents the department lists for these religious organization child care centers is a Notice of Parental Responsibility. Ask for yours at enrollment and read it at the kitchen table, not in the hallway with a toddler pulling on your sleeve.
Home daycare sits on a threshold. The same Missouri statute says its licensing rules do not apply to a person caring for six or fewer children, including a maximum of three children under the age of two, at the same physical address. So the warm living room with the gate across the stairs may be perfectly good, and may never have seen an inspector. Ask how many children are there on a full day, and how many are babies.
### What a month of preschool really costs in Missouri
If the free seat is not an option, here is the number to brace for. Child Care Aware of Missouri puts average monthly costs at $750 to $900 for preschool care, $850 to $1,000 for toddler care and $1,000 to $1,200 for infant care. Feel that in the checkbook: preschool alone can run past a car payment, every month, for years.
Three things move the bill. Hours: five half-days is a different product from a full day. Calendar: a school-year program and a year-round center are not the same price, even when the monthly rate looks close. Fees: registration, supplies and a deposit sit on top of the quoted rate. Ask for the rate sheet, in writing, before you fall in love with the reading corner.
Building a shortlist tonight? Browse preschools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pull each one’s state record before you book a single tour.
If you run the preschool, the church program or the in-home daycare these parents are hunting for, they are searching by neighborhood right now, and every one of them is a family who could be your next customer. Put your program on St Louis Near Me Directory and get more customers from the parents already looking.
### Help paying, and the waitlist nobody mentions
Missouri’s Office of Childhood monitors participation in the state’s Child Care Subsidy Program, the program families lean on when tuition outruns the paycheck. Know this before you count on it: Missouri now places new Child Care Subsidy applications on a waitlist. Families are placed based on the date their application was submitted and by a priority ranking, with children with special needs first.
The practical move is the same every time: apply early, because the date counts, then keep looking at programs while you wait. Questions go to the families line at 573-415-8605. And ask every program on your list whether it accepts subsidy before you tour it. Some don’t, and you want to know that before your kid falls for the sandbox.
Somewhere between the sticker chart and the first day of school, the first dentist visit sneaks up too.
### What to watch on the tour
Go mid-morning, when the room is doing what it really does. Stand still for ten minutes. Listen. A good room has a hum, not a roar: a teacher crouched at eye level, a kid narrating a block tower, someone singing the clean-up song slightly off-key. Then watch the adults, not the toys. Notice who looks up when your child walks in, and who keeps their eyes on the kids already in the room. Both answers tell you something.
Count the room. Children and adults in the room your child would join. Compare it with what the director told you on the phone.
Ask how long the lead teacher has been here. It is the one question most parents skip, and the answer tells you more than the curriculum binder.
Watch a hard moment. A three-year-old will melt down while you are standing there. How an adult handles that is the whole tour.
Look at the bathroom. Unglamorous, and the fastest read on how a place actually runs. It matters double if your child just learned to use one.
Name what you found in the record. Ask what changed. Listen to the tone of the answer as much as the words.
Ask the sick-day rule out loud. The fever threshold, how long a child stays home, and how fast they expect you at the door.

### What is the average cost of daycare in St. Louis?
Plan on a payment the size of a car note, every month. Child Care Aware of Missouri averages $1,000 to $1,200 a month for infant care, $850 to $1,000 for toddlers and $750 to $900 for preschool, with registration, supplies and a deposit due on top.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which type of preschool is best?
A.  The one your child can get into, that you can afford, with a clean record and a lead teacher who has stayed. In the city, check the free St. Louis Public Schools seat first. Then compare private, church and in-home programs on the same three things: the state record, how many children each adult watches, and how long the teachers have been there.
### Q. What are the signs of a good preschool?
A.  A room that hums instead of roars, adults at a child’s eye level, a lead teacher who has been there a while, and a director who can talk about the inspection record without getting defensive. A clean, well-stocked bathroom says more than the art on the walls.
### Q. What is the best age for a kid to start preschool?
A.  Readiness matters more than the number. In St. Louis Public Schools, the free program takes children who have turned 3 or 4 before August 1 and are fully toilet trained, so for many city families those two lines set the start date.
### Q. Which is better, Montessori or regular preschool?
A.  Neither wins on the label. If the method matters to you, ask where the lead teacher trained in it and how long they have taught that way. Then judge a Montessori room by the same things as any other: the state record, the adult-to-child count and the way a hard moment gets handled.
### Q. How much does preschool cost in Missouri?
A.  Child Care Aware of Missouri puts average monthly costs at $750 to $900 for preschool care, $850 to $1,000 for toddlers and $1,000 to $1,200 for infants. Registration, supply fees and deposits sit on top of the monthly rate.
### Q. What are red flags in a daycare?
A.  A director who won’t discuss the inspection record, a room with more children than adults can watch, a tour that steers you away from the bathroom, and a church or home program that cannot hand you its paperwork. Vague answers about the sick-day rule are a warning too.
### Q. How to look up daycare licensing violations?
A.  In Missouri, use the state Child Care Search site, and remember its own note that the records shown may not reflect a facility’s complete history. In Illinois, use the Illinois Sunshine website’s monitoring report search.
### Q. Are daycare licenses public record?
A.  In Missouri, public records on a licensed or license-exempt child care facility can be reviewed or requested from the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, Office of Childhood.

## Buying a Car in St. Louis: Missouri's Sales Tax Isn't on the Dealer's Sheet
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-a-car-st-louis-dealership-missouri-illinois
The finance manager turns the contract around on the desk and clicks a pen open for you. The coffee in the paper cup went cold an hour ago. The new keys are already warm in your fist, the monthly payment is circled in blue ink, and your signature is the last thing standing between you and the drive home down Manchester Road.
Look at that sheet once more. On a Missouri deal, one big number usually is not on it.
The sales tax. In Missouri it is yours to go pay. The Department of Revenue gives you 30 days from the date of purchase to title the car and pay the sales tax at a license office, and if you miss it, a $25 penalty lands on the 31st day and grows another $25 every 30 days, up to $200. Nobody mails you a reminder. The dealer hands you a temporary permit and a folder, and the tax rides home with you, unbilled.
Cross the river and the rhythm flips. An Illinois dealer registers with the Illinois Department of Revenue to collect Illinois sales tax and reports the sale on Form ST-556, so the tax is settled at the desk. That one difference is why a Missouri deal sheet can look a few thousand dollars friendlier than the same car in Fairview Heights, right up until you stand in line at the license office with your checkbook.
Here is the line to say out loud to anyone shopping this week: in Missouri, the dealer sells you the car, and the state sends you the tax bill by way of a 30-day clock.
### What happens if I buy a car in Illinois and live in Missouri?
Missouri still taxes it. When you title the car at a Missouri license office, you pay 4.225 percent state sales tax plus your local sales tax on the purchase price, less any trade-in allowance. You have 30 days from the purchase date to do it. Day 31 brings a $25 penalty that climbs $25 every 30 days, to a $200 maximum.
### The tax follows your driveway, not the dealership
Your local rate is the one where you live. Missouri’s own list of what you pay at titling says it plainly: state tax of 4.225 percent, plus your local sales tax, on the price less your trade. A buyer in Webster Groves who finds the right SUV on a lot in Granite City, still settles up at a Missouri counter.
It runs the other way too, and this is the part the Metro East forgets. An Illinois resident who drives a car home from a Missouri lot files Form RUT-25 and pays within 30 days after the car is brought into Illinois. The rate is set by the buyer’s address, and the Illinois instructions carve out our own corner of the map: in the two Metro East counties right across from the Arch, the rate is 6.5 percent, except outside the Metro East Transit District, where it is 6.25 percent. Illinois allows credit for tax already paid to another state only if it was properly due and separately stated on your proof of payment, so keep every page of that bill of sale.
So shop both sides of the river for price, inventory and how a salesperson treats you when you say no. The tax is decided by the street you park on.
### How much is sales tax on a $30,000 car in Missouri?
Do the math at the kitchen table, not the dealership desk. The state share alone is $1,267.50 on a $30,000 car, which is 4.225 percent of the price, and your local rate stacks on top of that. Put a $10,000 trade-in against it and Missouri taxes you on $20,000 instead, because the tax is figured on the purchase price less the trade-in allowance.
Then add the counter fees you will hand over the same morning: an $8.50 title fee and a $9 title processing fee, plus plates. If you bought a temporary permit, it was a $5 permit fee and a $9 processing fee at a license office. Bring a pen of your own. The line moves faster when you are not borrowing one.
### Sell your old car yourself and keep the tax break
This is the one most people in a Kirkwood showroom have never heard. Missouri extends the trade-in tax credit to a car you sell yourself. Under RSMo 144.025, the credit applies when you sell your old vehicle yourself and buy the next one within one hundred eighty days before or after that sale.
Put it in plain money. If a neighbor on your block will pay more for your old sedan than the number scribbled on the appraisal slip, you can take the neighbor’s cash and still get taxed only on the difference, as long as the dates land inside the window. Carry the bill of sale from your private sale to the license office with the rest of the paperwork.
Shopping for a pickup instead? Read what to check on a used truck before you shake anybody’s hand.
### The doc fee is capped, and the law says some of it is profit
You will see an administrative or doc fee on the sheet. Missouri lets dealers charge one under RSMo 301.558, and the statute says out loud what the fee is: a portion of the administrative fee may result in profit to the motor vehicle dealer. The ceiling rises every year with the Consumer Price Index, so check the current cap against your sheet before you sign. A fee above it should not be there.
The bigger money sits on the menu that comes after it: service contracts, gap coverage, paint and fabric plans. Ask for each price on its own line, not folded into the monthly payment, and walk in with a preapproval from your own bank or credit union so the dealer has a rate to beat. Our guide to a credit union versus bank auto loan in St. Louis walks through getting one.
### What to carry into the license office, and when
The license office has its own sound: the number board chiming, a printer grinding out plates paperwork, somebody two seats over realizing they left the insurance card on the kitchen counter. Do not be that person. For a car from a dealer, Missouri asks for the title signed over to you or the Manufacturer’s Statement of Origin, a signed Application for Missouri Title and License (Form 108), and a current insurance identification card, which can be the original, a copy or a legible one on your phone.
Two inspections can trip you up. The safety inspection must be not more than 60 days old, or not more than 90 days old if the seller is a Missouri dealer. And if you live in St. Louis City, St. Louis County or Jefferson County, you also need an emissions inspection not more than 60 days old. A car that sat on a back row for a while can age out of both before you get to the counter, so check the dates on the inspection paperwork the day you buy.
The temporary permit is the other clock. It runs 30 days from the purchase date, and only one temporary permit may be purchased per vehicle. There is no second paper tag. If your title paperwork is stuck, start calling on day ten, not day twenty-nine.
One small sting at the window: pay by card and the card vendor adds a convenience fee of 2.0 percent plus $0.25 per transaction. On a tax bill in the thousands, that is real money for the privilege of not writing a check.
### The private seller who is not really private
The cheapest-looking car in the St. Louis listings is sometimes parked in a grocery store lot off Gravois with a phone number taped to the glass. Missouri’s Department of Revenue has a word for the worst version of that deal: curbstoning, the sale of used vehicles by unlicensed dealers who pretend to be private parties in order to evade regulation. The state warns that their customers often get saddled with damaged, dangerous or uninsurable vehicles.
The tell is a seller whose name is not on the title, or who has three other cars for sale this month. Walk away from that one, however good the price. A licensed lot at least hands you paperwork the license office will take.
### What a dealership owner sees from the other side of the desk
Every unit on the lot is money waiting to move, and a car that sits gets more expensive to carry by the day. That is why a store wants to be the first name a buyer finds when they search for a dealer near them, and why a complete directory listing earns its keep.
Knowing that helps you as a buyer, too. A salesperson who has watched the same trade-in sit under the lot lights for weeks has a reason to talk. Ask how long a car has been on the lot. Ask whether the price on the window is the price before the doc fee, the add-ons and the tax you will pay later at the license office. Write the answers on the back of the worksheet in your own handwriting, and make them say the out-the-door number to you before anybody slides a contract across the desk. Then go home and sleep on it. The car will very likely still be there in the morning, and the 30-day clock does not start until you sign.

The tax does not end at the license office. Missouri bills St. Louis County personal property tax on that car every year after you buy it, and your next renewal will ask for a personal property tax receipt or waiver.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the difference in sales tax on cars between Missouri and Illinois?
A.  Missouri charges 4.225 percent state tax plus your local rate, paid by you at a license office. An Illinois buyer who brings a car in from out of state uses 6.25 percent unless instructed otherwise, and 6.5 percent in the two Metro East counties inside the Metro East Transit District. Illinois dealers register with the state to collect Illinois sales tax and report the sale on Form ST-556.
### Q. Do I have to pay Missouri sales tax on a car purchased out of state?
A.  Yes. When you title the car in Missouri you pay the 4.225 percent state tax plus your local sales tax on the price less your trade-in, and you have 30 days from the purchase date to do it.
### Q. Do I pay taxes twice if I buy a car out of state?
A.  Illinois allows credit for tax you already paid to another state, but only if it was properly due and is separately stated on your proof of tax paid. Keep the bill of sale that shows it.
### Q. Is it better to buy a car in Illinois or Missouri?
A.  Shop on price and inventory, not tax. Your rate follows your home address, so a Missouri buyer pays Missouri tax and an Illinois buyer files Form RUT-25 for a car bought here.
### Q. Is Missouri a good state to buy a car?
A.  On paperwork, it is friendly. The title fee is $8.50 plus a $9 processing fee, and RSMo 144.025 keeps your trade-in credit when you sell your old car yourself within 180 days. The catch is that the sales tax is on you to pay within 30 days.
### Q. How much is sales tax on a $30,000 car in Missouri?
A.  The state share is $1,267.50, which is 4.225 percent of $30,000, plus your local sales tax. A trade-in lowers the taxable amount, because Missouri taxes the price less the trade-in allowance.

## The Cheap Sofa Costs You Twice in St. Louis: How to Buy One That Lasts
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-furniture-in-st-louis-that-lasts
In the City of St. Louis, a sofa that dies early gets one ride out a month.
That’s the part nobody mentions on the showroom floor. You find out later, on a cold morning, walking a dead couch backward down your own back steps while somebody you love says “left, LEFT” and the armrest scrapes the railing. The cushion that stopped springing back two winters ago is still dented where you sat. The fabric has gone shiny at the edges. It cost less than the one you almost bought, and now it’s sitting in the alley.
Here is how the city actually handles it. Bulky items are picked up once a month. You place your items, not more than three, out by 6:00 am on the Monday of your collection week. Residents with alley collection put their bulk in the alley behind their home, away from the refuse containers, and collectors are not permitted to pick up items on private property. The service is included in the solid waste fee of $14 a month per unit, collected quarterly on your water bill. Miss your Monday, and that sofa sits by the garage until next month, collecting rain.
So the cheap sofa is not cheap. You pay for it at the register, you pay for it every time you sit down on it, and you pay for it again the morning you haul it out. The fix is not spending more. It’s knowing what to touch, lift and ask in the store, so the next one outlasts the mortgage instead of the warranty. If you need your own pickup week, the city’s Refuse Division answers at (314) 622-4800.
### How can I tell if furniture is high-quality?
Check four things on the showroom floor: the frame, the springs, the cushion foam and the fabric’s rub count. Ask what wood the frame is and how the corners are joined, lift one front corner to see whether the frame twists, ask for the foam density as a number, and look for a Wyzenbeek double-rub figure. The Association for Contract Textiles rates 15,000 double rubs as suitable for commercial low traffic.
Start with your hands, not the price tag. Grab one front corner of the sofa and lift it a few inches off the carpet. A solid frame comes up as one piece, and the far leg lifts with it. A weak one twists like a cardboard box, and you can feel the joints give under your fingers. That flex is what eventually cracks a corner, usually right around the time the store’s warranty runs out.
Then ask the salesperson three plain questions. What wood is the frame, and is it kiln-dried? How are the corners joined: glued and screwed blocks, dowels, or staples? And what’s under the seat: hand-tied coils or heavy-gauge sinuous springs, the zigzag wire you can feel through the deck? A store that sells good furniture answers those in a sentence. A store that doesn’t will talk about the color.
Foam is where the vague words live. “High density.” “Premium comfort.” Ask for the density as a number, in pounds per cubic foot, and get it written on the order. If nobody can find the number, that tells you what you need to know about the cushion. Sit, stand, and watch the seat: good foam comes back up while you’re still looking at it.
Fabric has a number too. Durability is tested in Wyzenbeek double rubs, a machine scrubbing the cloth back and forth. The Association for Contract Textiles rates 15,000 double rubs as suitable for commercial low traffic and private spaces, and 30,000 for commercial high traffic and public spaces. It also warns that a fabric with twice the abrasion cycles does not mean double the service life, so treat the number as a floor, not a scoreboard. If you have a dog who naps on the arm, start there.
### Open the drawer: dressers, tables and bed frames
Pull a drawer all the way out and look at the corner where front meets side. Interlocking dovetails, the little fanned fingers of wood, mean someone built a real box. Staples and a strip of glue mean the drawer bottom will sag the first time you overload it with jeans. Run your thumb under a raw edge, too. Solid wood shows grain all the way through. A gray or brown crumbly core is particleboard, and once the surface chips there’s nothing underneath to repair.
Veneer isn’t automatically a bad word. A thin sheet of good wood over a stable core can move less with the seasons than one wide solid plank. What fails is cheap veneer over cheap board. Knock on a tabletop: a dull hollow tap and a light lift usually tell you which one you’re looking at. And anchor every dresser to the wall, new or old, the day it comes into a house with kids.
### Chain store, local independent, or an estate sale in Webster Groves?
Each one sells you something different. A big chain out by the highway stocks deep and can often deliver fast; you’re buying a model number off a warehouse shelf. A small independent in Kirkwood, with a handful of sofas and a wall of fabric swatches, usually sells you choices: the frame, the fabric, the cushion fill, and the same person on the phone if something goes wrong.
Estate sales and consignment floors are the sleeper. An old walnut dresser in a Webster Groves dining room, smelling faintly of cedar and lemon oil, is often solid wood with dovetailed drawers, and it already survived decades of somebody else’s family. The trade is simple: no warranty, no return, no delivery. Bring a tape measure, a flashlight and a friend with a truck.
Used mattresses and pillows are the one place the law steps in. Missouri’s RSMo 421.038 says bedding may not be manufactured in whole or in part from any secondhand material unless that material has been sanitized, germicidally treated or cleaned by a method approved by the state. Look for the label before you load anything into the car.
### Will it fit through an old St. Louis doorway?
Measure the narrowest point of the whole route, not the front door. In an older brick house in Florissant or the city, that’s usually the turn at the stair landing, the handrail you can’t take off, or the low ceiling over the basement steps. Measure the clear opening with the door swung open, because the door and hinges steal width. Then get the sofa’s diagonal depth off the spec sheet and compare it to the tightest number you wrote down.
A contractor can widen a drywall opening in a Maryland Heights ranch in an afternoon. Nobody is cutting into a load-bearing brick stairwell for a sectional. So ask before you buy whether the legs unbolt and whether the back comes off. A couple of inches is often the whole ballgame, and you only want to learn that once.
Hardwood in the showroom, but is it the real thing? How to tell if Amish furniture is real.
### That “going out of business” banner: what Missouri law says
You’ve driven past the store with the banner that never seems to come down, flapping over the parking lot. Missouri has a rule for that. Under RSMo 407.800, a business holding a going-out-of-business sale has to inform the attorney general in writing not less than ten days before the sale, the inventory can’t be supplemented after the sale begins, and the sale can’t run more than sixty days unless an extension is registered with the attorney general’s office by affidavit.
So if a liquidation looks like it’s in its fifth month and the floor keeps filling with fresh stock, believe your eyes. The percentage on the sign is not the deal. The deal is the exact model number, priced at two other stores, written on a scrap of paper in your pocket.
### Can you return it after it’s delivered?
Usually only if the store says so. The federal Cooling-Off Rule, the three-business-day right to cancel, covers sales made somewhere other than the seller’s place of business, like your living room or a hotel ballroom. It applies at a purchase price of $25 or more when the sale is made at the buyer’s residence, or $130 or more at other temporary locations. Buy in the showroom, and the return policy on your receipt is your protection.
So read it before you pay, standing at the counter, while the salesperson is still being friendly. Ask what happens if it won’t fit through the door, whether there’s a restocking fee, and whether special orders are final. Then, when the truck comes, look the piece over with the delivery crew still in the room, before you sign anything that says it arrived in good condition.
### When the old one finally has to go
Back to the alley. The city’s rules are short and strict: large items need not be dismantled, but smaller loose pieces go in a container or bundle, and no container or bundle may weigh over 100 lbs., be over 6 ft. long, or be over 2 ft in diameter. Don’t put bulky items in your regular trash container, and don’t block the alley. Pickups happen during the week of the indicated Monday each month, depending on where you live.
One more alley lesson: a sofa left out the wrong week soaks up rain like a sponge, and a wet one is a lot heavier to drag back to the garage. Check your collection week before you carry anything out, not after the first storm rolls across the river.
If the old piece still has good bones, a solid frame or a dovetailed dresser, it may be worth more to a neighbor or an upholsterer than to the truck. The point of buying well is that, years from now, you’re the one with the walnut dresser somebody wants.
Shopping frames instead of price tags this time? Browse furniture stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and call ahead with your stairwell measurement and the three frame questions already written down.
If you’re the shop that builds, sells or reupholsters furniture that outlasts the alley, the customers asking about frames and dovetails are looking for you. Put your shop where St. Louis shoppers search.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What brand of furniture lasts the longest?
A.  Construction predicts lifespan better than the nameplate. Ask any brand for the frame wood and joinery, the spring system, the foam density as a number and the fabric’s double-rub rating. A brand that can answer all four in writing is worth a second look.
### Q. What brand of furniture is built to last?
A.  The one whose specs you can see. In St. Louis, a local independent or upholsterer can often show you the frame, the springs and the cushion fill on a cutaway or in the back room, which a big box rarely will. Lift a corner and open a drawer before you trust any label.
### Q. What to avoid when buying a couch?
A.  A frame that twists when you lift one front corner, staples at the corners, a cushion tag that says “high density” with no number, and a fabric with no double-rub figure. Also avoid buying before you measure the tightest turn on the way in.
### Q. What is the 2/3 rule furniture?
A.  A sizing guideline: a coffee table about two-thirds the width of the sofa, so a 72-inch sofa pairs with a table about 48 inches wide. The same idea is used for a sofa against a wall or art over a sofa, as a guide rather than a strict formula.
### Q. What items make your house look cheap?
A.  Usually materials that fail early, not taste: cushions that stay dented, fabric gone shiny at the arms, drawers that sag, chipped particleboard edges. Buying fewer, better-built pieces fixes more of that than any accessory.
### Q. How often does the City of St. Louis pick up old furniture?
A.  Once a month. Put no more than three items out by 6:00 am on the Monday of your collection week, at the curb or in the alley behind your home, and call the Refuse Division at (314) 622-4800 if you don’t know your week.

## The $200 City Inspection Your Property Manager’s Fee Sheet Leaves Out
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-property-manager-in-st-louis
The phone buzzes on the nightstand after ten. The screen lights the ceiling blue. Three words from the tenant in the little brick two-bedroom: no heat again.
Now you’re standing in the kitchen in socks, the floor cold through them, scrolling for a furnace guy who answers at that hour, doing the math on tomorrow’s shift. The rent was never the hard part. The phone is.
So you start pricing property management, and the fee sheets all look tidy: a percentage, a placement fee, a smiling stock photo. What the tidy sheet leaves out is the rule that only exists inside the city line.
The City of St. Louis says 100% of property in St. Louis is located in a Housing Conservation District. For rental units, a Certificate of Inspection must be obtained before occupancy of the unit. That means an inspector walks the unit before the next tenant gets keys, and water and electric must be operable at the time of inspection, so the faucet runs and the lights come on while they watch. The application is $120 for a vacant unit. If a resident is found living there without a current certificate, it jumps to $200. And a reinspection is required every three years or upon a change in occupancy for rental dwelling units.
Every turnover, then, is a city inspection, and the process doesn’t wait for anyone’s schedule. Keys handed over before the certificate is in hand don’t save a week. That skipped step books the $200 version.
A fee sheet that skips the city inspection isn’t cheaper. It’s just quieter. So ask the questions the brochure won’t. Who applies for the certificate when a tenant moves out? Who pays if it’s late? And would you rather find out on the phone with the city’s Building Division at (314) 622-3313, or before you sign?
### How much do property managers charge in Missouri?
Published St. Louis fee sheets mostly run 8% to 10% of monthly rent, or a flat plan of $89 to $179 a month. Placing a tenant often costs 100% of the first month’s rent, and lease renewals run $99 to $275. One St. Louis firm on South 39th Street lists 8% of monies collected plus 75% of the first month’s rent at leasing. Ask every manager whether the fee comes off rent collected or rent due.
That last question is the quiet one. On rent collected, an empty unit costs you nothing in management fees. On rent due, the fee keeps running through a month of silence and an unlit porch.
### The fee stack nobody reads until the first statement
The monthly percentage is the number on the website. The owner statement is where you feel the rest, the PDF you open on your phone in the break room and scroll twice because the total doesn’t match the number in your head. Tenant placement is the big one, because it comes back every time a tenant leaves. Renewal fees are next. Then whatever the agreement calls onboarding, inspections or setup; one St. Louis firm lists a $99 onboarding and inspection fee.
Do the arithmetic on your own house before a salesperson does it for you. If the rent is $1,400 and placement is a full month’s rent, every new tenant costs you $1,400 up front, before the first monthly fee. Two turnovers in three years and the placement fee alone can outweigh the difference between an 8% and a 10% manager. That is why the cheapest percentage on a website is so often the most expensive deal by the second lease.
Then read what the percentage is charged on. Some fee sheets say rent, some say monies collected, and the difference shows up the month a tenant pays late or not at all. Ask for the exact line in the agreement to be read out loud while you’re on the phone.
Ask for the entire fee schedule on one page, in writing, before you sign. If that page doesn’t exist yet, ask for it before anything else.
### The turnover clock inside the city line
Here’s the part that makes a vacant month longer than it has to be. The city’s own page says the earliest your inspection may be scheduled is 3 business days from the day you apply, and the latest is 15 days from the application day. So the clock starts when someone applies, not when the last tenant’s moving truck pulls away from the curb.
Inspectors examine a building’s exterior, interior and interior common areas, and they set the dwelling’s occupancy load. If a Certificate of Inspection is issued with violations, the property owner has 30 days to make the necessary repairs. Own a two-family in the city? Each additional application at the same address is $65 per unit, and a Certificate of Inspection is valid for 12 months. Owner-occupied properties are exempt, which is why so many first-time landlords who used to live in the house never hear about it.
If you would rather ask a person, the Building Division answers at (314) 622-3313, and in-person applications go to City Hall, 1200 Market, Room 425. The city clock rewards whoever has the application in before the old tenant’s last box is out the door, while the rooms still smell like cardboard and cleaning spray.
### Should you hire a property manager for one St. Louis rental?
Hire one when the distance, the door count or the day job stops working. One house twenty minutes away, plus a plumber you trust, is a real case for doing it yourself. A duplex in Florissant and a house in Affton on top of a full-time job is not.
A manager does four jobs: price and market the unit, screen and place the tenant, collect the rent, and run the repairs. Only rent collection runs itself. The repairs are the late-night buzz you’re really paying to hand off, so ask how repair calls get answered after hours before you ask about anything else.
### Does a property manager in Missouri need a real estate license?
Almost always, if they manage your property for a fee. Missouri law, RSMo 339.010, defines a real estate broker as someone who, for another and for compensation, rents or leases real estate or negotiates its rental or leasing. The owner managing his own house is exempt, and so are the owner’s regular employees and licensed attorneys. The company running your Affton house from across town is not.
So ask for the license number, and look it up yourself before you hand over a key ring.
### Your tenant’s deposit: the Missouri rules on the clock
The deposit is your money on paper and the tenant’s money in law. Under RSMo 535.300, a landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of two months’ rent. Within thirty days after the tenancy ends, the landlord has to return the full deposit or furnish an itemized list of damages. Get it wrong and the tenant recovers twice the amount wrongfully withheld.
Here’s how a move-out actually goes: the echo in an empty living room, a nail hole behind where the TV hung, a fridge somebody unplugged with the door shut. Every one of those is a judgment call about wear and tear versus damage, and every one ends up on that itemized list or it doesn’t. The manager who photographs the unit on move-in day is the one who wins that argument on move-out day, without a raised voice.
Someone does the walk-through with the flashlight and the camera. You carry the liability if it’s late. Ask how they document move-out, and how fast.
### When the rent doesn’t come: Missouri notice rules
The worst version of the late-night buzz is the one that never comes: the rent that just doesn’t land, and the tenant who stops answering. Missouri moves faster here than most owners expect. To end a month-to-month tenancy, RSMo 441.060 calls for one month’s notice, in writing, terminating on a periodic rent-paying date not less than one month after the notice is received.
Unpaid rent works differently. Under RSMo 535.020, giving the notice in section 441.060 is not required before filing a rent and possession case. That speed is only useful if someone is watching the ledger the day rent is late. Ask a manager who files, who shows up at the courthouse, and whether that is in the monthly fee or billed per case.
### What the job looks like from the manager’s side
Turn the desk around for a second. The person who runs your house is usually a small shop: a couple of people, a truck, a phone that rings at every hour. Cheap units are the hardest to serve, because one after-hours call plus a vendor run can eat a month of a percentage fee. That math is why minimums exist. The late-night repair call is the real product, and the fee sheet rarely says how it gets answered.
And the good ones are not hard to spot once you know the tells: a fee sheet on one page, a license number they offer before you ask, and a plan for the city inspection at every turnover. When you find that shop, keep them. If you run one, a complete listing where owners already search does more than another flyer at the hardware store.
Want the phone to stop buzzing at night? Compare property management companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and open every call with two questions: rent collected or rent due, and who pulls the city inspection at turnover.
If you’re the property manager who actually picks up when the furnace quits, landlords are searching for you right now. A Gold listing works without a public address, so a two-person office counts the same as a tower downtown. Put your company where those customers look. Refuse to be invisible.
### What to ask before you sign
Seven questions, one phone call, a pen on the counter. Is the fee charged on rent collected or rent due? Can I see every fee on one page? Who applies for the city Certificate of Inspection when a tenant moves out, and who pays if it’s late? What can you spend on a repair without calling me? Who keeps the late fees? How do I end the agreement, and what does that cost? And what’s your license number?
Get the answers into the agreement, not an email thread. Then decide whether you want full management or just someone for the repairs; here is what property maintenance services actually cover.
One more thing worth hearing out loud: you are not being difficult by asking. The firms worth hiring have answered every one of these before, usually in under a minute, and they would rather you ask now than call angry after the first statement lands in your inbox.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What percentage do most property management companies charge?
A.  Most published St. Louis fee sheets show 8% to 10% of monthly rent, and some firms offer flat plans of $89 to $179 a month instead. You can compare property management companies side by side on St Louis Near Me Directory before you call.
### Q. How much is a reasonable management fee?
A.  Judge the whole stack, not the headline. In St. Louis, a fair deal is a monthly fee in the 8% to 10% range, a placement fee you can see in writing, and no surprise line items. Placement often equals a full month’s rent, so it matters more than a point on the percentage. Inside the city line, add the $120 Certificate of Inspection application at each turnover, and ask who files it.
### Q. Do you need a real estate license to manage rental property in Missouri?
A.  Generally yes. RSMo 339.010 defines a real estate broker to include anyone who, for another and for compensation, rents or leases real estate. Owners acting on their own property and their regular employees are exempt, as are licensed attorneys.
### Q. What is the 2% rule for rentals?
A.  It is a quick screen: a rental passes if the monthly rent is at least 2% of the purchase price. Treat it as a filter for bad deals, not a target, and remember management fees and the city inspection come off whatever the house actually brings in.
### Q. What is the 50% rule in rental property?
A.  Many investors assume about half of the rent goes to operating expenses. If the rent is $2,000 a month, expect about $1,000 in total expenses, and the property manager’s fee is one of them.

## Missouri Protects Your Down Payment From Your Closer, Not From a Fake Email: Choosing a St. Louis Title Company
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-title-company-in-st-louis
If the company holding your down payment lets it disappear the night before closing, who pays you back?
Most buyers never ask, because by then they are too tired to. You have signed your name so many times it has stopped looking like yours. The pen is warm from use, the conference room is cold, and your phone shows a wire confirmation for more money than you have ever moved in one tap. The closer slides another page across the table, and you sign that one too, because everyone in the room seems to know what it means except you.
Here is what that page could be, if you are buying on the Missouri side of the river. Missouri law, section 381.058 of the Revised Statutes, requires a title insurer to issue a closing protection letter in favor of the buyer, lender or seller in all residential real estate transactions where its policy is issued and its own agent is handling the settlement. That letter covers losses up to the amount of the settlement funds when the insurer’s named title agent steals the money, commits fraud with it, or fails to follow written closing instructions it agreed to.
Read the limit twice. The protection runs to what the named title agent does. A criminal who fakes that agent’s email and sends you new wiring instructions is not the agent. That is why the one call that matters most happens before closing day, to a phone number you already had.
Picking the title company is not a formality you inherit from your agent. It is the one hire that decides whether you own what you just paid for, and whether your money is protected on the way there. Here is how to choose it, and what changes when the house sits in Kirkwood instead of Belleville.
### Who chooses the title company, buyer or seller?
Whoever writes it into the contract, and buyers usually have more say than they think. Federal law, RESPA Section 9, bars a seller from requiring you to buy title insurance from a particular company as a condition of sale when a federally related mortgage is involved, and a seller who does is liable for three times the title insurance charges. If your lender lets you shop, it must hand you a written list of providers and say you may choose a different one.
So a referral from your agent or lender is a suggestion, not an assignment. You can say yes to it. You can also call two other companies first and see whose closer answers the phone like a person.
### A St. Louis title search can reach back to colonial deeds
Old brick has old paper. Walk past the soot-dark two-families in south city and every one of them has a line of owners behind it, each sale a document somebody had to get right. The French and Spanish official recordings of colonial St. Louis run from 1764 to 1804, according to the National Park Service, and they are mainly deeds, wills, marriage contracts, inventories and mortgages. Nobody is going to dig those out for a bungalow sale. But they are a reminder that this city has been recording who owns what for longer than most of the country has existed, and a chain of title here can be long.
If something odd shows up on a city property, the land records sit with the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds and Vital Records Registrar, (314) 622-4610. You will rarely need to call. Your title company should. Ask which recorders it works with every week, because a company that moves fast in one office is not automatically fast in the next.
### The letter that guards your down payment, and the gap it leaves
The wire leaves your account with a soft chime, and for a few hours that money sits with people you have met once. The closing protection letter is what stands behind them, and it is not a favor. Missouri treats it as a priced product: the rate for issuing one in a residential deal is filed with the state’s insurance director, filed separately for buyers and lenders than for sellers, and the entire fee is kept by the title insurer rather than the local agency. In plain terms, the company standing behind your policy is also standing behind the closer.
That changes what you should ask for. Ask which underwriter the agency writes for, and ask to see the closing protection letter with your name on it before you wire anything. A good closer will email it without a sigh. A closer who has never been asked may need a minute, and that minute tells you something too.
Then close the gap the letter leaves. Wiring instructions arrive by email in most closings, and that is exactly where a fake one hides: same logo, same signature block, one changed account number. Before you send a dollar, call the title company at a number you found yourself, on its own website or on the paperwork you signed at contract, and read the account number back out loud. It is a short call. It is the cheapest insurance in the whole transaction.
### Why an Illinois closing comes with a lawyer and a Missouri one usually does not
Drive east over the Poplar Street Bridge, the Arch shrinking in the mirror, and the closing room changes. Someone at the table now works only for you, and so does someone across from you. On the Illinois side, the state Supreme Court decided Chicago Bar Association v. Quinlan & Tyson on January 25, 1966, and held that the drawing or filling in of blanks on deeds, mortgages and other legal instruments requires the peculiar skill of a lawyer and constitutes the practice of law. A broker may complete the purchase contract. The deed belongs on an attorney’s desk. That is why a Metro East closing so often seats a lawyer for the buyer and another for the seller.
Missouri drew the line wider. In In re First Escrow, decided October 27, 1992, the Missouri Supreme Court held that escrow companies may fill in the blanks of standardized form documents prepared or reviewed by Missouri attorneys, under the supervision of and as agents for an entity with a direct financial interest in the transaction. The same opinion set the fence: escrow companies may not draft legal documents, select the form of documents used, or provide legal advice to customers.
So on the Missouri side the person across the table is usually a closer, not your lawyer. That is legal and normal. It also means nobody in that room is there to tell you whether a strange easement on Schedule B is a problem. If you want that answer, you bring your own attorney or you ask for it well before the closing date.
One more difference people repeat at the closing table: Missouri voters adopted a constitutional amendment on November 2, 2010, that prevents the state, counties and other political subdivisions from imposing any new tax on the sale or transfer of homes or any other real estate.
### What is the purpose of a title company?
Most of what you are paying for happens in a quiet office weeks before you see a conference room. Four jobs. Search the public record for everything filed against the property. Examine what turns up and put it in a title commitment, which lists what must be fixed before a policy issues and what the policy will never cover. Insure the result. And run the money: hold the earnest money and the lender’s funds, pay everyone at closing, and record the new deed.
The middle part is where the hours go. A loan paid off years ago but never released of record. A contractor who filed a lien and was never paid. An estate nobody finished closing. None of it is dramatic, and every one of those can push your move-in date while the moving truck idles at the curb.
Read the exceptions list on your commitment the day it arrives, not at the table. It is the one page that tells you what you are not buying protection for.
Want a second quote before the referral becomes the default? Browse title companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two of them, and ask each for the all-in number in writing on the same address.
If you run the title agency, the closing desk or the small escrow office that never misses a date, this part is for you. Buyers go looking for you the week they go under contract, and the ones who find you become customers who tell their friends. Put your office where they are looking.
### Lender’s policy or owner’s policy: which one is yours?
The owner’s policy is the one that protects your equity if a forged deed, a missed heir or an old lien surfaces after you move in, and unlike every other insurance you carry, you pay for it once, at closing.
Buy both at the same time and ask whether a simultaneous-issue rate applies. Then file the policy somewhere you will find it years from now, next to the deed, not in a box marked kitchen.
### Who pays is a line in your contract
Custom sets a default, and custom bends. Who pays for the owner’s policy, the settlement fee and the rest is whatever the purchase contract says. Federal rules give you that Closing Disclosure no later than three business days before consummation. Spend that time reading it next to your contract, line by line, with a pen. For the dollar side, our breakdown of what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis walks through the line items, and if you have not picked the loan yet, start with how to choose a mortgage lender.
### Five questions to ask before you commit
What is the all-in number, in writing? Premium, settlement fee, search and exam, wire and recording, on one page you can set beside another company’s quote for the same address.
Which underwriter do you write for, and can I see my closing protection letter? In Missouri residential deals the insurer shall issue the letter when its own agent is performing the settlement. Ask for it by name.
Who is my closer, and what is their direct number? A human name before there is a problem, not after.
How will you send wiring instructions, and what number do I call to confirm them? Write that number down now, before any email arrives.
On the Illinois side: are you working with my attorney, and who prepares the deed? A vague answer is your answer.
Changing subjects: when the keys are finally yours and the kitchen is the first thing you want gone, read how to hire an architect here first.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the purpose of a title company?
A.  To confirm the seller can actually hand over clean title, to insure against defects that surface later, and to hold and pay out the money at closing. In Missouri the title or escrow company may run the closing itself, within limits the Missouri Supreme Court set in In re First Escrow in 1992.
### Q. What should a title company not do?
A.  Give you legal advice. Under In re First Escrow, Missouri escrow companies may not draft legal documents, select the form of documents used, or provide legal advice to customers. In Illinois, drawing or filling in the deed is the practice of law, so it comes from an attorney.
### Q. Who pays for the title company at closing?
A.  Whoever the purchase contract says pays. Local custom sets a starting point, but nothing in it is fixed. You get the Closing Disclosure no later than three business days before consummation; read it against the contract.
### Q. Can I get my money back from a title company?
A.  Sometimes. In a Missouri residential deal, the closing protection letter covers losses up to the settlement funds if the insurer’s named title agent steals them, commits fraud with them, or fails to follow written closing instructions it agreed to. Separately, under RESPA Section 9, a seller who required you to use a particular title insurer is liable for three times all charges made for that title insurance.
### Q. What does a title company usually charge?
A.  There is no single price for the whole bill, so get the all-in number in writing and compare two companies on the same address. One piece is regulated in Missouri: the rate for a closing protection letter in a residential deal is filed with the state insurance director.
### Q. Do you need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Illinois?
A.  In practice, for the deed, yes. The Illinois Supreme Court held in Chicago Bar Association v. Quinlan & Tyson that drawing or filling in blanks on deeds, mortgages and other legal instruments constitutes the practice of law. Metro East buyers should plan for a lawyer.

## You’re Paying Sales Tax on Straws That Missouri Says Aren’t Retail
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-wholesale-in-st-louis
Cherokee Street, after close. The cup sleeves crackle on a checkout belt, then the straws, the napkins, the to-go boxes and the toothpicks for the club sandwiches. The scanner beeps, the receipt curls out long enough to brush your shoe, and at Missouri’s 4.225% state rate, every $1,000 on it carries $42.25 in state sales tax.
Here’s what that register can’t know, because nobody built it to ask what you do for a living. Missouri law, RSMo 144.011, says that when an eating or food service establishment buys nonreusable items to furnish to its customers with their food or beverage, the purchase is not a sale at retail. Then it names them, the way you’d read them off a stockroom shelf: containers, trays, napkins, dishes, silverware, cups, bags, boxes, straws, sticks and toothpicks. Paper, wood, plastic and aluminum, in the statute’s own words. Everything on that belt. Exactly how it fits a particular counter is worth confirming with the Department of Revenue or an accountant, but the law is right there on the page.
A weekly $1,000 restock makes that tax line $2,197 over 52 weeks. Cities, counties and certain districts may stack local sales taxes on top; inside city limits, the city even keeps an interactive map of its TDD, SBD and CID taxing districts. The cashier isn’t hiding anything. The register simply can’t tell a lunch counter from a graduation-party run, and the sites that pop up when you search “wholesale license” would rather sell you a filing package than mention that the state’s forms sit on the Department of Revenue’s own page, ready to download.
None of that is on you. Nobody hands a new owner this rule along with the keys. Getting it off the receipt takes paper, not connections.
### How do I get wholesale prices for my business?
It ends at a counter. You slide a signed certificate across to the account rep at a restaurant-supply house, the rep files it with your account, and the next invoice comes back without the sales-tax line on the cups. That’s wholesale buying in practice: proof, on file before the first order, that you’re a business buying to resell. It takes paper, and all of it fits in one folder riding on the passenger seat next to the bank bag.
First in the folder: Missouri’s Form 2643, the Tax Registration Application, from the Department of Revenue. Second, if the shop sits inside city limits the way a Cherokee Street counter does, the city’s Graduated Business License. The City of St. Louis says all businesses, unless exempt, require one, and the Office of the License Collector handles it at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 102-104, (314) 622-4528. Third, the page every supplier wants: Missouri Form 149, the Sales and Use Tax Exemption Certificate, or, for a supplier a bridge away in Illinois, Form CRT-61, the Certificate of Resale.
That folder is the whole gate. A real wholesaler asks to see it before it sells you a single untaxed case, and that question is how you know you’ve found a real one.
One surprise waits at the city counter: LLC paperwork isn’t a license. The city’s own page says registering for an LLC does not qualify as a business license in the City of St. Louis. Questions piling up? The city’s Business Assistance Center sits in the same building, 1200 Market, Room 421, (314) 622-4120, there to help with licensing and permitting for a new or expanding business. Same building, same folder.
### The pause on the phone while a rep looks you up
You call a distributor, give your business name, and the line goes quiet. Keys click. It can feel like suspicion. It isn’t. Missouri law, RSMo 144.210, puts the burden of proving a sale was not a sale at retail on the seller, and tells the seller to obtain and maintain exemption certificates signed by the purchaser as evidence. Your certificate is the wholesaler’s audit shield. Without it, the tax you didn’t pay becomes their problem.
Illinois runs the same check from its side. The CRT-61 instructions say it’s the seller’s responsibility to verify that your Illinois account ID number is valid and active, and they point sellers to the Verify a Registered Business link at mytax.illinois.gov. That’s the clicking. When you call registered, folder open on the seat beside you, the conversation turns from “who are you?” to “what do you need on the truck?”
### Cups, straws, toothpicks: the line Missouri drew for food counters
The napkins blow off the counter every time the door opens, and the law still has a place for them. A food business buys two kinds of things, and one invoice mixes them. The food you cook and sell is inventory, a resale purchase. The nonreusable things that leave with it, the clamshell, the straw, the napkin, are the items RSMo 144.011 keeps out of the definition of a sale at retail. The mop, the dish machine and the office printer stay behind when the customer leaves, and they’re a different story. Same invoice, different lines, different answers.
Run a guesthouse or a small inn? The very next clause of the same statute covers nonreusable items furnished to guests in their rooms, when those items are included in the charge for the room. Either way, the certificate carries your signature, so it’s worth having your accountant look over how you fill out Form 149 before the first supplier files it.
### A state form, and the people who’d charge you to fill it in
A resale certificate is a signed statement that tells a supplier you’re buying goods to sell again, so the supplier doesn’t charge you sales tax on that purchase. You fill it in, you sign it, and the supplier keeps it on file. Missouri’s Form 149 is listed on the Department of Revenue forms page, the same page that lists Form 2643. When a site offers to “process” it for a fee, it helps to know what the fee buys: a download and your own signature.
Across the river, Illinois has a quirk that saves real paper. According to the Illinois CRT-61 instructions, a purchase order signed by the purchaser may be used as a Certificate of Resale if it contains all of the required information: name and address, a description of the property being purchased, a statement that the property is being purchased for resale, the purchaser’s signature and date of signing, and either the purchaser’s Illinois retailer account ID number, Illinois reseller account ID number, or a Certificate of Resale to an out-of-State purchaser. Build those lines into your own purchase order template once, and every Illinois order carries its own certificate.
Every untaxed invoice rests on a certificate with your name signed at the bottom. A good accountant reads the first one before an auditor ever does.
### Four kinds of wholesale counters, four different deals
A cash-and-carry aisle smells like cardboard and floor wax. A distributor is a voice on the phone and a truck at the back door. They run on different deals, and the wrong one costs real money.
A true wholesaler buys deep and sells to the trade. It usually delivers, often sets a minimum, and is the account you open once and reorder from for years.
A distributor is the authorized channel for particular brands. You get a rep, often the only legitimate source for that line, and the brand’s rules along with it.
A cash-and-carry is a warehouse you shop yourself. Certificate at the desk, flatbed through the aisles, your own van at the dock.
A buying group pools your volume with other independents so a small shop can bargain like a bigger one. The membership terms are worth reading twice.
Most small operators end up with two or three at once: a standing delivered order for the predictable stuff, a cash-and-carry run for the Saturday that ran hotter than planned, and one specialty source for the thing that makes the shop different.
### Two numbers to get in writing before you fall for a product line
The samples are lovely, the catalog is glossy, and the line you want comes with a number attached. Two numbers, really. The opening order is what it takes to open the account. The ongoing minimum is what it takes to earn a delivery. Both exist because picking, packing and driving one stop costs about the same whether the box is small or huge.
Three follow-ups settle the rest. Is the minimum counted in dollars or in cases? Does it reset per delivery, per week or per month? Is there a small-order fee under the line? Then case pack: you may want a dozen when the only unit they sell is a carton of six dozen. That one question has kept more than one back room from filling up with things nobody buys.
The folder is ready. Now it needs two phone numbers. Browse wholesalers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two, and put the same pair of questions to each: what is the minimum opening order, and what are the terms for a brand-new account?
If you’re the restaurant-supply house, the distributor or the cash-and-carry that opens accounts for small shops, the owners holding a fresh Form 149 are your next customers. They’re searching right now. Put your business where those customers look, so the next call with paperwork in hand comes to you.
### How a shop with no history earns credit terms
The credit application asks for the one thing a new shop doesn’t have yet: a track record. Credit terms mean the supplier ships now and you pay later, so the supplier is quietly financing your shelves. Brand-new businesses rarely get that on the first order, and it isn’t personal. The usual path: pay by card for the first several orders, fill out the credit application, offer two or three trade references, and ask again after a few clean months.
Expect a request for a personal guarantee while the history is thin. It stings a little, signing your own name under the shop’s. It’s how a stranger’s risk gets priced. A couple of small accounts paid early, and the next supplier you call answers in a different tone.

### What terms do St. Louis furniture dealers give a commercial buyer?
Start with one question: will you resell the sofa, or seat your customers on it? Form 149’s resale box is for retailers buying property for resale, and Missouri generally taxes retail sales of tangible personal property, so chairs for your own dining room don’t fit that box. After that the terms are the dealer’s: Arhaus (Brentwood) sells under contract terms for commercial use, not resale, with 50% down on stocked pieces and 100% at order for pieces made to your specifications, which can’t be canceled. IKEA offers business credit through Slope on net 30 or 60 day terms at 0% interest, but only after a year in business and $85K+ in annual revenue, so a brand-new shop should ask every dealer, in writing, what it takes to open an account.
### The candle that goes home with you
A case of candles comes in for the shelf, and one of them ends up flickering on your own dining table. That candle was never resold, and a resale certificate covers only goods you resell. Missouri use tax is imposed on the storage, use or consumption of tangible personal property in the state, so that one candle owes it. One candle is not the worry. The habit is what shows up in an audit. A withdrawal log on a clipboard by the back door is the cheapest insurance in the building.
