### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can a regular person buy wholesale?
A.  Not as a private shopper. Under RSMo 144.210 the seller carries the burden of proving a sale was not retail, so a real wholesaler needs a signed exemption certificate on file before it sells anything untaxed. Registering the business comes first.
### Q. How do I qualify to buy wholesale?
A.  Register with the Missouri Department of Revenue using Form 2643, get the City of St. Louis Graduated Business License if you operate inside city limits, then give each supplier a signed Form 149. If your business is located in the City of St. Louis, you also need an Occupancy Permit from the Building Division, and if you pay by check, the license application may be held for several working days until the check clears. In Illinois, the supplier will want a CRT-61 with your Illinois account ID, and it will verify that number is active.
### Q. Do I need an LLC to buy wholesale?
A.  An LLC is not on the list. The Illinois CRT-61 instructions spell out what proof of resale must contain: name and address, a description of the property, a statement that it’s being purchased for resale, a signature and date, and an account ID number. Entity type isn’t one of them. Choose your structure for liability and taxes, and talk it through with an accountant.
### Q. How much do I need to start wholesale?
A.  It varies widely by trade, which is exactly why the question comes before the shopping. Get two figures in writing: the minimum opening order and the ongoing minimum per delivery. Then confirm whether it’s counted in dollars or cases and whether a small-order fee applies below the line. The wholesaler listings on St Louis Near Me Directory put enough names in front of you that two calls can settle it.
### Q. What are the four types of wholesalers?
A.  For a small shop, the useful four are the true wholesaler that sells to the trade and delivers, the brand distributor, the cash-and-carry warehouse you shop yourself, and the buying group that pools independents. Each comes with its own minimums and terms.
### Q. Can I use Missouri Form 149 at an Illinois wholesaler?
A.  Illinois has its own form, CRT-61, the Certificate of Resale. Its instructions call for the purchaser’s Illinois retailer account ID number, Illinois reseller account ID number, or a Certificate of Resale to an out-of-State purchaser, and a signed purchase order can serve as the certificate if it carries all the required information.

## The 1943 Ad That Breaks St. Louis' Toasted Ravioli Legend, and What Else This City Really Invented
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-food-traditions-what-this-city-invented
The breading cracks first. Then the steam, then the burn on the roof of your mouth, because nobody at a table on the Hill waits for toasted ravioli to cool. You drag the next one through warm red sauce, a little Parmesan still clinging to the crust, and somebody across the table starts telling you who invented it.
Let them. Then know this.
The city’s own tourism bureau, Explore St. Louis, tells the story as a cook who dropped a few ravioli into a fryer one day in the 1950s. But Oldani’s, the restaurant now called Mama’s on the Hill, was already advertising toasted ravioli in the St. Louis Star and Times in 1943. The paper trail beat the official legend to the table by years.
That is the honest shape of St. Louis food. This city invented a lot of what it eats and wrote down almost none of it. Most of the famous origin stories are a cook, an accident and no date. One dish has a name, a year and a witness: the concrete, handed through a custard window on Chippewa in 1959.
### What food is only found in St. Louis?
Three plates, mostly. A slinger at a diner counter after midnight, chili running over hash browns and eggs. A St. Paul sandwich, a hot egg foo young patty on cold white bread with mayonnaise, lettuce, tomato and pickles. And a frozen custard concrete so thick it is served upside down. Toasted ravioli and gooey butter cake started here too, but they travel.
### How to settle it yourself in one weekend
You do not need a food tour. You need an appetite, a car and a willingness to eat dessert in a parking lot. Check current hours before each stop; these are stands and dining rooms, and they keep their own schedules.
Saturday lunch on the Hill: order toasted ravioli at two of the three claimants and compare the crust while it is still too hot to hold. Charlie Gitto’s is at 5226 Shaw Ave, (314) 772-8898; Mama’s on the Hill, the old Oldani’s from the 1943 ad, is the other side of the argument.
Saturday after dinner: drive to Ted Drewes at 6726 Chippewa Street, get a concrete, and eat it standing in the lot. Watch the cup come through the window upside down.
Saturday, late: find a diner counter and order a slinger. Ask what goes under the chili, because no two kitchens build it the same way.
Sunday breakfast: buy gooey butter cake at a bakery counter, then eat a corner out of the box before you are home. Everyone does.
Sunday lunch: a St. Paul sandwich from a Chinese carryout, wrapped in paper, eaten in the car.
Keep a note of which ravioli you liked. Locals will ask, and the answer tells them which side of the argument you are on.
### The toasted ravioli fight nobody can win
Three restaurants want the credit: Mama’s on the Hill, Charlie Gitto’s and Lombardo’s. The first two tell nearly the same tale, a chef dropping ravioli into hot oil instead of boiling water in the 1940s. The trouble is that Charlie Gitto’s, then called Angelo’s on the Hill, did not open until 1947. Lombardo’s says its menu carried the dish in the 1930s, and no one has shown that the menu really dates from that decade.
So look hard at that 1943 ad. Read it carefully: an ad proves the dish was for sale. It does not prove who fried the first one.
None of that changes the plate. Ground beef inside a pasta pillow, a crust that shatters, a ramekin of sauce going cold because the basket empties first. Locals call them t-ravs, and Explore St. Louis calls them the city’s quintessential bar food. Order a second basket before you settle anything.
Here is the part worth repeating at the table. Every one of these stories is about a mistake: wrong pot, wrong oil, a cook in a hurry. Nobody claims a chef sat down and designed the thing. In this city, being an accident is part of the pedigree, and the family that can prove the earliest accident wins.
### Why a concrete comes through the window upside down
Summer night, hot asphalt still breathing under your sandals, a line at the Ted Drewes stand on Chippewa along historic Route 66. The cup comes through the window flipped over, and nothing slides out. That is the whole test.
This is the one St. Louis invention with a witness. In 1959, according to the Missouri Encyclopedia, a neighborhood teenager named Steve Gamber kept demanding that his malts be made thicker. Ted Drewes Jr., managing the Chippewa stand, tinkered until he had a malt that could be held upside down without spilling. Gamber asked what to call it. Drewes told him: a concrete.
The thickness has a legal side, too. Under the federal standard at 21 CFR 135.110, frozen custard must contain 1.4 percent egg yolk solids by weight of the finished food, and ice cream contains less. That yolk is the density you feel when the spoon stands up on its own.
The stand is part of the story. Ted Drewes opened it in 1941 at what is now 6726 Chippewa Street, where Route 66 passed down Chippewa on its way through St. Louis. Imitators, the Missouri Encyclopedia notes, keep chasing its ratio of milk fat to eggs and honey. You can taste the honey if you slow down, which nobody does in July.
Then the line people screenshot. Dairy Queen credits the concrete at Drewes as the inspiration behind its Blizzard, according to the Clio historical guide. A national chain’s best-known cup traces back to one south city teenager who would not stop asking for a thicker malt.
The family also filled the idle winter season by selling fresh-cut trees, grown on land it bought in Nova Scotia. Same lot, cold air, pine instead of vanilla.
### The slinger is closing-time food
It arrives heavy. Hash browns on the bottom, eggs and a meat patty on top, chili poured over all of it until it pools at the rim, shredded cheese going soft in the heat. You break a yolk and it runs into the chili. Nobody orders one at noon.
The point is ballast. It is the plate you want after a long shift, a ballgame that ran late or a night that should have ended an hour earlier, eaten at a counter under bright lights while the grill hisses behind you and the coffee keeps coming.
Explore St. Louis puts it plainly: the slinger is inexplicably linked to St. Louis, and it is our midnight snack. I could not find a dated record of the first one, which fits. A dish built to be slung together on a plate at two in the morning was never going to come with paperwork.
Hungry enough to go settle one of these arguments tonight? Start with American food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory for the slinger and the pork steak, and keep Mexican food in your back pocket for the next night out.
If you run the diner, the custard window or the carryout kitchen frying egg foo young at midnight, this part is for you. Hungry customers search by the dish, not your name. A Gold listing puts your plate in front of them, or start by putting your business on the map.
### A St. Paul sandwich is egg foo young on white bread
Hot and cold in one bite. A crisp egg foo young patty, still spitting from the fryer, pressed between two slices of white bread with cold lettuce, tomato, pickles and a smear of mayonnaise. The bread goes soft where the patty touches it.
It is a Chinese-American carryout staple served all over St. Louis, built for American taste buds, and it is named for a city in Minnesota that never made it famous. Ask for one anywhere else and watch the face across the counter.
Order it the way regulars do: wrapped in paper, eaten in the car before the steam fogs the windshield, a pickle slice sliding out the back of every bite.
### Gooey butter cake and the baker who doubled the butter
Powdered sugar on your fingers, on your shirt, on the car seat. A firm edge, then a center that sags under a fork and sticks to the roof of your mouth.
The legend, as Explore St. Louis tells it, is an absentminded baker who forgot he had already added butter to his yellow cake mix and doubled the amount. Ask any local, the bureau says, and you will get the same story. I could not find the baker’s name in any record from the time. Enjoy the cake. Hold the legend loosely.
What matters more is where you buy it. A slab from a bakery counter, cut into squares still warm enough to fog the plastic lid, is a different food from the shortcut version baked at home. Bring one to a St. Louis office on a Monday and watch it disappear before the coffee finishes brewing. Bring one to a family party and someone will tell you their aunt makes it better. They will be wrong, and they will say it anyway.
Different question entirely: when a visitor wants to carry some of this home, here is what is actually from here.
### Pork steaks are the shoulder St. Louis puts on the grill
Charcoal smoke drifting over a south city backyard, sauce blistering black at the edges, fat popping on the coals. A pork steak is cut from the shoulder of the pig, the same meat sold as Boston butt or pork blade steak, and its marbling is why it stays juicy when a chop would dry out.
Explore St. Louis calls a grilled pork steak slathered in barbecue sauce a sign of summer around here, and nobody who has stood next to a Weber in July would argue. It is less an invention than a habit: a cheap cut this city decided to love.
The way most backyards cook it: sear the steaks over hot coals until the edges char, then move them into a pan with beer and barbecue sauce, cover the grill and let them go slow until a fork slides through. The sauce thickens into something sticky that ends up on your wrist, your plate and the dog.
Pizza gets its own fight. Provel, a processed blend of Cheddar, Provolone and Swiss, divides every visitor, and the full case is below.
St. Louis-style pizza: Provel, cracker crust and the square cut
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What foods originated in St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, the slinger, the St. Paul sandwich and the frozen custard concrete are the dishes locals claim. The concrete has the clearest record: 1959, at the Ted Drewes stand on Chippewa. Toasted ravioli has the next best evidence, a 1943 newspaper ad on the Hill.
### Q. What is St. Louis’ signature dish?
A.  Toasted ravioli. The dish is ravioli breaded and deep-fried, topped with Parmesan and served with dipping sauce, and three restaurants still argue over who made it first. Explore St. Louis calls t-ravs the city’s quintessential bar food.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the hour. Toasted ravioli at a table on the Hill, a concrete eaten in the parking lot on Chippewa on a summer night, a St. Paul sandwich from a Chinese carryout, and after midnight, a slinger at a diner counter.
### Q. What is St. Louis food famous for?
A.  Thrift and accident. A cheap shoulder cut turned into a summer ritual, an egg foo young patty went onto white bread, and nearly every origin story involves a cook doing the wrong thing with the right ingredient. The food is famous for being filling, a little messy and stubbornly local.
### Q. What food is St. Louis famous for?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, pork steaks off the grill, the slinger, the St. Paul sandwich, the concrete and thin square-cut pizza topped with Provel, a processed blend of Cheddar, Provolone and Swiss.
### Q. What is the difference between a concrete and a milkshake?
A.  A concrete is made from frozen custard and blended so thick it is served upside down. Under 21 CFR 135.110, frozen custard must contain 1.4 percent egg yolk solids by weight; ice cream contains less. A milkshake is thinner and meant for a straw.

## St. Louis Sign Permit: $25 to File, 30 Days If You Skip It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-sign-permit-st-louis-metro
Thirty days.
That is how long the City of St. Louis gives you, once the Cultural Resources Office sends a citation letter, to apply for the permit you skipped. After that, the city’s own FAQ says, your project is referred to Housing Court. And before the letter ever comes, an inspector can stop you on the sidewalk, and all work must cease immediately until a permit is obtained.
Think about who is on that ladder. Not a corporation. You, maybe, after a shift at the other job, the new sign leaning against the brick, still wrapped in shrink film that squeaks when you peel a corner back to look at your own name. You paid for those letters out of the money that was supposed to be breathing room. Then a stranger with a clipboard tells you to climb down.
Here is the turn nobody mentions. The permit is not the expensive part, and it is usually not the slow part either. For most work in a City Historic District, the Cultural Resources Office says permits are approved within 5 working days. The delay that hurts owners is the one they walk into by building first and asking second. The process is not on your side. But it is predictable, and predictable can be beaten.
### Where is it legal to place business signs?
Wherever the city or town that governs your exact address says, and only after that government issues a permit. In the City of St. Louis, installing or modifying a sign on your property or building needs a building permit to ensure it meets local safety and zoning rules, and a building in a City Historic District needs a permit for all exterior work, except painting wood trim. Outside the city line, call that town’s zoning office before anyone cuts metal.
### The permit costs less than the vinyl on your truck door
Run the City’s own math once and the fear shrinks. Permit fees are based on estimated construction cost. Work up to $1,000 is $44 total, $1,001 to $2,000 is $48, and $2,001 to $3,000 is $55. Above $3,000 it is a $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated construction cost, or fraction thereof.
Say your lit storefront sign is quoted at $9,000: the City’s $25 application fee plus $10 for each of those nine thousands puts the permit at about $115. You do not even pay most of that up front: only the $25 application fee is due when you file, and the permit fee comes when final approvals are in and the permit is ready to be issued. One catch to know cold: all fees paid to the City for building permits are non-refundable. File the right drawing the first time.
Hold that permit fee next to the cost of a sign sitting in a back room for weeks while the grand opening date slides, and it is plain which one is the real bill. The money you lose to a stalled sign is days of customers driving past a blank wall.
### Is your storefront inside a City Historic District?
Walk outside and look at the block. Old brick, tall front windows, a cornice somebody restored by hand. If the building sits in a City Historic District, the Building Division will automatically refer your sign application to the Cultural Resources Office. Every district has its own unique standards, and the office reviews permit applications to ensure the proposed work complies with them.
This is where owners lose a month without knowing why. Most permits clear in about a week, but a project that cannot comply with the standards gets scheduled for a hearing before the Preservation Board, which meets the fourth Monday of each month. Miss one meeting and you wait for the next. Ask the Cultural Resources Office before you approve a final proof, at 314-657-3865, and bring photos of the facade. A sign drawn to the standards from day one stays on the fast track.
### What to carry into Room 425
City permits are filed with the Building Division Permit Section, Room 425, City Hall, 1200 Market Street, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with the Hot Spot Desk open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Questions go to (314) 622-3313.
At a minimum, the City asks for the address of the project, the $25 application fee per application, and a letter of authorization from the property owner if the owner of record is not the one applying. That last item is the one tenants forget. If you lease, get the landlord’s signature before the sign shop starts drawing. Paying in person? The City accepts only check or cash at the counter, so leave the card in your wallet and bring the checkbook.
Then add the project plans: a scaled drawing of the sign, where it mounts on the building, its size and materials, and whether it lights up. The clearer the drawing, the fewer trips back to the counter.
### A lit sign means a second permit and a licensed electrician
Channel letters that glow at dusk are what make a storefront look open for business from a block away. They also bring the wiring into it. In the City, electrical permits are issued to licensed electrical contractors certified by the City of St. Louis, and to owners of single-family homes who meet certain requirements. A storefront is not a single-family home, so the electrician pulls that one. Ask your sign shop who their electrician is before you sign the quote, not after the letters arrive.
Completely different problem, same storefront: if the shelves behind that new sign are still half empty, here is how to buy wholesale in St. Louis.
### Outside the city line, the rules change at the curb
Drive fifteen minutes in any direction and you can cross into a different town with a different sign code, a different fee table and a different person who signs off. The sign your competitor put up across the boundary tells you nothing about what you are allowed to build. Your address decides.
So make the first call to the town, not the sign shop. In Chesterfield, the Planning Department’s Planner of the Day line is (636) 537-4733. On the Illinois side, the City of Belleville’s main line is (618) 233-6810. Ask three questions: is a permit needed for this sign, does the site sit under any special district or review board, and how long does review usually take. Write down the name of the person who answered.
If you are in a multi-tenant center, ask one more: does the center already have its own sign rules that the landlord enforces? Many do, and they can be stricter than the town’s.
### Read the lease before you fall for the proof
The sign shop emails a proof at 11 p.m. and your name is on it in letters two feet tall, and it is hard not to say yes on the spot. Wait for the lease. The signage clause may require the landlord’s written approval of the design, the size, the colors and how it mounts. Get three things in writing: approval of this exact proof, who owns the sign when you move out, and who patches the wall when it comes down.
Because the City wants the owner’s authorization letter with the permit application, a slow landlord does not just delay the sign. It delays the permit that the sign depends on. Chase that signature first. If a property manager runs the building, here is how property management works in St. Louis, so you know who actually holds the pen.
### Already got stopped? Here is the way back
Maybe it already happened. The drill is still in your hand, two letters are up, and the inspector’s words are still ringing in your ears. Breathe. This is fixable, and the clock is longer than it feels in that moment.
Stop the work, because the City’s rule is that all work must cease until a permit is obtained. Then call the office that stopped you the same day and ask exactly what the permit needs. If a citation letter from the Cultural Resources Office arrives, you have 30 days from receiving it to apply, so the goal is to file well inside that window, not to argue about it. Pull together the owner’s authorization letter, photos of the facade with the half-hung sign, and the shop’s drawing, and file. The sign you already paid for is not lost. In most cases it just needs paperwork to catch up with it.
And next time, the order flips: permit first, then the ladder.
### What sign shops wish every buyer knew
Two quotes for the same storefront can look wildly different, and the cheap one is often missing the hard parts. Design time before you ever see a proof. Aluminum, acrylic faces, LED modules. A bucket truck, a crew, insurance, an electrician for anything lit. And the line that rarely gets written down: somebody has to read the code, redraw the layout until it fits, and stand at the counter on Market Street, sometimes twice.
Ask every shop to itemize the permit work. A shop that pulls the permit for you is selling you weeks of your life back, and that is worth more than the gap between two quotes.
Want a shop that pulls the permit, not just prints the panel? Browse sign dealers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory and call two or three with your street address in hand. The shop that asks for the address first already knows the code decides the job.
If you run the sign shop that handles the drawings, the counter and the install, the sign is what people see driving past, and your listing is what they find when they search. Put your shop on St Louis Near Me Directory and get more customers who already know they need the permit done right.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a sign for a business cost?
A.  It depends on how it is built, how big it is, whether it lights up and how high it has to be installed, so get itemized quotes. In the City of St. Louis, the permit is the small line: say a sign is quoted at $9,000, and the City’s $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated construction cost puts the permit at about $115.
### Q. How much should a shop sign cost?
A.  Compare quotes line by line rather than by the bottom number: design, materials, lighting, installation and permit handling. A quote that leaves out permit work or the electrician is not cheaper, it is unfinished, and the missing part lands on you later.
### Q. How much does it cost to get a sign?
A.  Budget three lines, not one: making the sign, installing it, and permitting it. In the City of St. Louis, permit fees follow estimated construction cost, starting at $44 total for work up to $1,000, and all City building permit fees are non-refundable.
### Q. How much should I charge for a sign?
A.  If you are the shop, price the whole job, not the panel: design hours, materials, the install crew and equipment, the electrician for anything lit, and the hours spent getting the permit approved. Itemize the permit work on the quote so the buyer sees what an online price leaves out.
### Q. Is sign making profitable?
A.  It can be, when the shop recovers the costs that do not show up in a printed panel price: design time, installation, insurance and the hours spent at the permit counter. Shops that itemize that work protect their margin. Shops that give it away to match a low quote usually do not.
### Q. Does a sign in a St. Louis historic district need extra approval?
A.  Yes. In a City Historic District, all exterior work except painting wood trim needs a permit, and the Cultural Resources Office reviews it against that district’s standards. Most permits are approved within 5 working days, while projects that cannot comply go to the Preservation Board, which meets the fourth Monday of each month.

## Your Adjuster Can't Pick Up Your St. Louis Police Report. You Can.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-police-report-guide
“Do you have the police report number?”
That is usually the first question from the insurance adjuster or the bank’s fraud line, and it often comes while you are still standing beside the car, little cubes of window glass crunching under your shoes. The short answer: the department that wrote the report keeps it. In the City of St. Louis you can order it online and pick it up at 1915 Olive Street, and a simple request normally costs less than $5.
One detail explains why the adjuster asks you instead of getting it themselves. The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department’s records page says attorneys and insurance companies are not eligible to access reports at the Service Center and must submit a Sunshine Request. You are. Walking out with that sheet of paper is often the moment the rest of the claim starts moving.
### How do I look up a local police report?
Ask the department that wrote it. In the City of St. Louis, request it through the SLMPD Public Records portal or at the Records Service Center, 1915 Olive Street, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays, 314-444-5551. For St. Louis County Police reports, use the county’s Sunshine request portal or Central Police Records at 7900 Forsyth Boulevard in Clayton, 314-615-5317. A simple city request normally costs less than $5.
### Order it online, then walk in for it
SLMPD calls it Express Pick-up. You submit the request on the SLMPD Public Records portal from your kitchen table, and the department notifies you when the record is ready. Then you go to the first floor at 1915 Olive with a photo ID and payment, hand it over, and leave with paper in your hand instead of a number on a ticket. The page says it plainly: the online request is there to avoid long wait times.
Do not race downtown the morning after, though. SLMPD says police reports cannot be made available until they are completed and approved, and for crash reports that usually happens within 5 days. You can check a crash report’s status on the department’s online traffic accident page before you make the trip.
Bring a state-issued photo ID or a valid passport. If the report belongs to someone else who was involved, bring a notarized release from that person; no notary is needed when you are picking up your own record. Personal checks are not accepted, so carry another way to pay. Hours and fees can change, so glance at the SLMPD records page before you go.
The bill is small. SLMPD charges $.10 a page plus $15 an hour, prorated, for the time it takes to find the report, and says a simple request is normally less than $5. That follows Missouri’s Sunshine Law, which caps a standard paper copy at ten cents a page.
### Which department wrote your report?
The one that showed up. Most people remember the flashing lights in the window better than the patch on the officer’s sleeve, so this is the step that trips them. It sounds obvious until you remember how this region is stitched together: one side of a street can be city and the other side a separate town with its own badge on the car door. Look at the patch on the officer’s sleeve, or the name on the card they handed you, before you request anything.
If it was SLMPD, the Olive Street office has it. If St. Louis County Police responded, the record sits with Central Police Records in Room B-013 at 7900 Forsyth Boulevard, open 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding holidays. If a city’s own department came, ask that department for it.
Across the river, the same rule holds: ask the Illinois city’s own department. In Collinsville, the police department’s line is 618-344-2131.
### The ten minutes before you call anyone
Your hands may still be shaking a little, and the cold air through the broken window smells like the street. That is normal. Breathe, and stand still for a second. Do not pick up the glass yet, do not wipe the door handle, and do not start hauling the damaged things to the trash. Walk around once with your phone camera running. Get the broken window, the open glovebox, the empty spot on the back seat where the bag used to be, and a wide shot that shows the street and the house number.
Then write it down while your memory is still sharp: what time you last saw everything fine, what time you found it, and every item that is gone. Brand, color, what was inside it. If neighbors on the block have doorbell cameras, knock or text now, because footage gets recorded over. None of this is required to get a report. All of it makes the report, and the claim that rides on it, stronger.
When the officer or the dispatcher is done, ask one question before you hang up or they drive off: what is the report number, and which department is it filed with? Write the answer on something you will not lose. That one line is the whole difference between a ten-minute errand on Olive Street and a week of phone tag.
### When should you call 911 instead of the non-emergency line?
Think about what is happening in front of you. A stranger still in your backyard at 2 a.m. is 911. A busted car window you found over coffee is not. SLMPD puts it this way: 911 should be used during emergency situations that warrant immediate police response, and the non-emergency number when police assistance is needed, but not urgent.
Save these two before you need them. SLMPD non-emergency is 314-231-1212. St. Louis County Police non-emergency is 636-529-8210. The call that starts your report is also the call that gives you the number everyone else will ask for.
Off topic for a second: once the glass is swept up and the ruined stuff is in a pile by the curb, here is what you can recycle in St. Louis.
### What the adjuster needs from you
The report number opens the file. Everything after that is proof you control. Before you sweep the glass off the driveway, photograph it. Write down what is gone the same day, while you can still picture where the laptop bag sat on the back seat, and dig out receipts or serial numbers.
If a Missouri insurer stalls on your claim, the Department of Commerce and Insurance runs an Insurance Consumer Hotline at 800-726-7390.
### Getting a report for someone else
Maybe it was your mother’s car on her driveway in South City, or your teenager’s bike lifted off the porch, and you are the one doing the running around. In the City, that takes one more piece of paper. SLMPD asks for a notarized release from an involved party when you request a report on their behalf, along with your own state-issued photo ID or valid passport.
Get the release signed and stamped before you drive downtown. Most banks and many shipping stores keep a notary on hand, and it is far easier to sit across a desk from one for five minutes than to be turned away at the counter.
### If the report gets something wrong
You read it at the kitchen counter with your coffee going cold and spot it: a misspelled name, the wrong plate, a stolen item missing from the list. Do not argue it with the officer on the street. Call the records unit of the department that wrote it and ask how to add a correction or a supplemental statement, then request the updated copy. Send the adjuster the corrected version, not the first draft.
### If it was your shop, not your car
The call comes before sunrise. The alarm company, or the neighbor who opens the bakery next door, telling you the front glass is gone. You are standing in your own doorway in a coat over pajamas, smelling cold air where the heat should be, and everything in you wants to start cleaning. Take the photos first. Then get the report number, exactly like anyone else would, because your business insurer will ask for it before a board-up crew’s invoice or a stack of receipts means anything.
Price the missing stock honestly and list it item by item. If the break-in happened in the City, request it the way anyone else would: online for Express Pick-up, or at the counter on Olive Street.
### Can a department refuse to give you the report?
Sometimes it can hold part of it back. Missouri law says all incident reports and arrest reports shall be open records, but investigative reports stay closed until the investigation becomes inactive. So you may get the basic facts of what happened without the detective’s notes, and on a crash report, plate numbers, addresses and phone numbers can be blacked out.
The clock is on your side. Under the Sunshine Law, a request must be acted on no later than the end of the third business day after the custodian of records receives it. If the narrative is withheld, ask for the report number and the basic incident facts. That is usually what the adjuster or the bank wanted in the first place.
Still not sure which badge came to your door? Browse police departments across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, find the one that covers your address, and save its non-emergency number while you are calm.
If you run the auto glass shop, the locksmith truck or the law office people call after a break-in, put your business on St Louis Near Me Directory so the next person standing in broken glass can reach you.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I get a copy of a police report in Missouri?
A.  From the department that wrote it, not the state. Missouri’s Sunshine Law caps a standard paper copy at ten cents a page and requires the custodian of records to act on your request no later than the end of the third business day after receiving it.
### Q. How to obtain a St. Louis city police report?
A.  Order it on the SLMPD Public Records portal and pick it up when you are notified, or go to the Records Service Center, first floor at 1915 Olive Street, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays, 314-444-5551. Bring a state-issued photo ID or valid passport. Personal checks are not accepted.
### Q. Where can I get a police report in St. Louis County?
A.  For reports written by St. Louis County Police, use the county’s online Sunshine request portal or visit Central Police Records, Room B-013, 7900 Forsyth Boulevard in Clayton, 314-615-5317, 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays. If a city’s own police department responded, ask that department instead.
### Q. How long does it take to get a police report?
A.  It has to be finished first. SLMPD says reports cannot be made available until they are completed and approved, and for crash reports that usually happens within 5 days.
### Q. Is filing a police report worth it?
A.  If you plan to file an insurance claim or dispute a charge, usually yes, because the report number is what the adjuster or the bank asks for first. It also puts the date, place and loss on paper while they are fresh.
### Q. Are police reports public record in Missouri?
A.  Incident reports and arrest reports are open records under Missouri law. Investigative reports stay closed until the investigation becomes inactive, and on crash reports some personal details such as plate numbers and phone numbers can be redacted.
### Q. How to access local police records?
A.  Start with the department that responded. In the City, that is SLMPD on Olive Street; for St. Louis County Police, it is Central Police Records in Clayton; across the river in Collinsville, call the police department at 618-344-2131.
### Q. What is the non-emergency number for St. Louis police Department?
A.  SLMPD’s non-emergency number is 314-231-1212. St. Louis County Police non-emergency is 636-529-8210. Save 911 for emergencies that need an immediate police response, and use the non-emergency line for a break-in you discovered after the fact. Calling it is also how a report usually gets started.

## Towed in St. Louis? $25 a Day Until You Get It Back
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/car-towed-in-st-louis-cost-and-what-to-do
Twenty-five dollars a day. That’s what the City of St. Louis charges to store a towed car, on top of a $100 tow fee, and the meter does not care that you found out at eleven at night with your keys already in your hand.
You know the moment. You walk back to where you parked and there’s a clean, dry rectangle of pavement where your car should be. First thought: stolen. Your stomach drops, your face goes hot, and four seconds later you look up and see the small sign bolted to the light pole you parked under.
Breathe. This is a solvable problem with a known order and, mostly, a known price. The fastest way to keep the bill small is to find the car today, bring the right papers, and know which rules cover the lot you parked in. Here it is in that order.
### How much is it to release an impounded car?
If the City of St. Louis towed it, the published rates are a $100 tow fee and $25 per day for storage, plus $60 for a dolly (four-wheel drive, missing wheels, flats) and $80 an hour for labor. The City asks you to call (314) 383-7546 for your exact charge. Tickets and a police hold come on top of that.
City tows go to the City lot at 7410 Hall Street. It releases cars Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday from 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Miss the Saturday window and the next posted opening is Monday morning, and the storage line on your bill keeps adding a day at a time.
Here is the number that matters most if money is tight. The City’s Towing Division holds vehicles 30 days before they are sold at auction, and public auctions run every Wednesday at 9:30 a.m. Thirty days of storage alone at $25 a day is $750, more than seven times the tow.
### Who towed it? Find the car first
Call the police agency covering the exact spot where you parked, because the tower had to tell them. In the City, check the Towing Division’s towed car lookup or call (314) 383-7546. In St. Louis County, the police non-emergency line is 636-529-8210.
That reporting duty is why the call works. Under Missouri’s RSMo 304.157, a tow from a signed private lot must be reported to law enforcement within two hours; other tows get twenty-four. Across the river, 625 ILCS 5/4-203 says the towing service must notify the law enforcement agency with jurisdiction within 30 minutes of finishing the tow. In the Metro East, call the department for the town where the car was parked, not the one where you live.
One detail trips almost everyone. A car hooked from an apartment complex or a restaurant lot is a private-property tow, and Missouri requires the sign there to carry the phone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency. The sign you just noticed is telling you who to call. Take a photo of the sign before you do anything else, in focus, with the whole thing in the frame.
### What to bring to the City lot so you only make one trip
The City lists exactly what it wants at the window: a copy of the vehicle’s registration, a valid driver’s license, a receipt for any tickets, and a release order if police put a hold on the car. You also pay all towing and storage fees there.
Look closely at the payment list: Mastercard, Visa, a company or cashier’s check, or a money order. Cash is not on it. If your card is maxed, stop for a money order on the way so the ride out to Hall Street isn’t wasted.
Make the call before you leave the house. Ask for the exact total, confirm the car is actually at Hall Street, and ask whether a police hold is on it, because a hold means you need the release order before the lot can hand over the keys. Write the total on your hand if you have to. Standing at a window in the cold, short by twenty dollars, is the worst version of this night.
Bring a licensed driver too. Showing up with a dead license or a friend who can’t legally drive the car out means another day on the meter.
### Does Missouri cap what a private lot can charge?
Not with a statewide dollar figure. RSMo 304.155 makes the owner responsible for “all reasonable charges for towing and storage” and does not define reasonable. So in Missouri, the sign is the cap.
A private-property tow under RSMo 304.157 needs a sign in plain view at all entrances, at least seventeen by twenty-two inches, with lettering at least one inch high, warning that unauthorized vehicles will be removed at the owner’s expense and disclosing the maximum fee for all charges related to towing and storage. It also has to list the phone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency.
Stand under it with your phone light if it’s dark. If there is no sign at the entrance you drove through, or the invoice beats the maximum printed on it, you have something real to argue with.
Missouri also aims a penalty at the property owner. Under RSMo 304.158, an owner who causes a car to be removed is liable to that car’s owner for double the storage or towing charges whenever the rules in that section were not followed.
Cash in your pocket? RSMo 304.158 says the people running a storage facility that holds a car towed under that section “shall accept cash for payment of towing and storage” from the registered owner or the owner’s agent. The City’s own lot, as above, publishes a different payment list, so bring a card or money order there.
### The truck is hooking up your car right now
You hear the winch before you see it, that grinding whir and the clank of the chain. In Missouri, get to the car before it leaves the lot. RSMo 304.158 lets a towing company charge not more than one-half of the regular towing charge if the owner returns before the car is removed from the private property, and says “the regular towing charge may only be imposed after the abandoned property has been removed from the property and is in transit.”
That is statute, not a favor. Say it early and say it calmly. Photograph the truck, the sign, where the car sits and the time on your phone. Raising your voice rarely helps; the law already did the arguing for you.
A side thought for later: if the hook scraped a bumper, auto body work is its own separate errand.
### How do you dispute a tow you think was wrong?
Watch the mailbox, because the clock runs off a letter. Missouri gives the towing company five working days to send written notice of the removal, the grounds for it and where the car went to the registered owner and any lienholder.
Under RSMo 304.156, the owner may file a petition in the associate circuit court within ten days after receiving the towing company’s notice to decide whether the car was wrongfully taken or withheld, and the petition must name the towing company among the defendants. You can get the car back while the case runs by posting a cash or surety bond equal to the towing and storage charges.
Start a folder the night it happens, even if it’s just an envelope on the kitchen counter. Put in the sign photo, the photo of the empty space, the receipt from the lot, the letter when it arrives, and a short note of what time you parked and what time you came back. Write it down while it’s fresh and you’re still angry, because two weeks from now the details blur and the paperwork is all that speaks for you. A judge or a hotline worker can act on a timeline. They can’t act on a feeling.
File a complaint alongside it. The Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline is 800-392-8222. In Illinois, the Attorney General lists a Carbondale hotline at 1-800-243-0607 and a Springfield hotline at 1-800-243-0618. Send the sign photo, the invoice and the time stamps.
The Hall Street bill
### What happens if you can't afford to get your car out of impound?
At the City of St. Louis lot the storage keeps running at $25 per day on top of the $100 tow fee, with $60 added for a dolly and $80 an hour for labor. After 30 days the car is sold at a Wednesday auction. Call (314) 383-7546 for your exact total, and go the day you can cover it.
### Next time, pick the truck yourself
Three kinds of tow exist, and they price differently. A consent tow is one you call: you pick the company, agree on the rate and choose where the car goes. A police-ordered tow follows a crash, an arrest or a blocked lane, and the agency picks the company. A private-property tow is ordered by a lot owner, and you were never the customer.
Only the first one gives you a price before the hook goes on. Put two towing numbers in your phone tonight, while you’re calm, and check whether your auto policy or roadside plan covers a tow. Those plans cover breakdowns, not the storage meter at an impound lot.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does an impound fee cost?
A.  At the City of St. Louis lot, the published rates are a $100 tow fee and $25 per day of storage. A private lot can charge up to the maximum its sign discloses, so the photo you took of that sign is your price sheet. The cheapest day to get the car out is always the first one.
### Q. How much do I have to pay if my car gets impounded?
A.  For a City of St. Louis tow, start with the $100 tow fee and add $25 for each day of storage, plus $60 for a dolly or $80 an hour of labor if they were used. Add any tickets. The Towing Division will give you the exact figure at (314) 383-7546.
### Q. How to get impound fee waived?
A.  Relief here comes from statute, not from asking nicely. In Missouri, a tower may charge no more than half the regular towing charge if you return before the car leaves the private lot. An invoice above the maximum on the lot’s sign is worth disputing, and if you think the tow was wrongful you can petition the associate circuit court within ten days of the tower’s notice.
### Q. Will Impounds do payment plans?
A.  Don’t count on it. The City lot tells you to be prepared to pay all towing and storage fees at the facility, and it lists cards, checks and money orders as payment. Ask the Towing Division directly, and do it on day one, because every day of waiting is another $25.
### Q. What if I can’t afford impound fees?
A.  Move on the cheapest piece first: call for the exact total so you know the real number, and check a private-lot invoice against the sign. If you are disputing the tow in Missouri, you can get the car released while the case runs by posting a bond equal to the towing and storage charges.
### Q. Can a tow truck take my car if I get back before it drives off?
A.  In Missouri, not at full price. RSMo 304.158 limits the charge to one-half of the regular towing charge when the owner returns before the car is removed from the private property. The full charge applies only once the car has left the lot and is in transit.

## Used Car in St. Louis: The Plates Stay With the Seller
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-check-a-used-car-before-buying-st-louis
The screwdriver squeaks on the last bolt and the seller’s license plate drops into his palm. He keeps it. The title he hands you is soft from his back pocket, signed on the back, and the car at the curb is yours now, bumper bare, engine still ticking as it cools.
Nobody tells you about that bare bumper until it happens. In Missouri, when a car changes owners completely, the seller’s plates cannot be transferred to or used by the buyer. You drive away on a temporary permit or on plates moved from a car you already own.
And a clock started the second that title changed hands. You have 30 days from the date of purchase to title the car and pay the sales tax. On the 31st day, Missouri adds a $25 title penalty, then another $25 for every 30 days you’re late, up to $200.
So the real work happens before the handshake. Every check you run while the money is still in your pocket is leverage. Every problem you find after is yours.
### How to properly inspect a used car before buying?
Type the 17-digit VIN into the free NICB VINCheck, then pull a federal NMVTIS title report. Ask to see the paper title and the Missouri inspection slips before you talk price. Get under the car with a flashlight and look for silt and flaking rust. Then pay an independent mechanic you picked to put it on a lift.
That order saves you gas and money. The two VIN checks take minutes at your kitchen table and can kill a bad car before you drive across the county. The paperwork test happens in the seller’s driveway, with the car still cold. The lift comes last, on the one car that survived everything else.
One more thing makes this metro different. A car that crossed the Mississippi lived under two titling systems, and the gap between them is where the surprises hide.
### The Missouri paperwork a St. Louis seller has to hand you
A thin stack of paper on the hood is your first warning. To title the car, Missouri wants a safety inspection not more than 60 days old, or 90 days if a Missouri dealer sold it and did that inspection within 60 days before the sale. A car less than eleven years old with under 150,000 miles is exempt.
If you live in St. Louis City or St. Louis County, you also need an emissions inspection not more than 60 days old. The Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program covers 1996 and newer gas vehicles and 1997 and newer diesels at 8,500 pounds or less gross vehicle weight rating. State law requires private sellers to give the buyer a current emissions approval or waiver before the sale, and the program says the seller, not the buyer, should pay for that test. You then have 60 days from the test date to register the car.
Here is the line almost nobody in a driveway knows. Missouri’s emissions program says the statutes behind that rule supersede “as is” declarations on sales contracts or bills of sale to individuals.
So read it as a lie detector. A seller who shrugs and says you can get the test done yourself is asking you to pay for whatever the test finds: a dead catalytic converter, a bad oxygen sensor, a check-engine light somebody cleared last week. Not sure what you’re owed? MoDNR’s Inspection and Maintenance office answers at 314-416-2115, and its dealer and private-sale rules are one page long.
Bring your own paper too. For plates, the state asks for a paid personal property tax receipt or a statement of non-assessment from your county or the City of St. Louis for the previous year. Sales tax and dealer fees get their own walk-through in the guide to buying from a St. Louis dealership.
### What do Missouri and Illinois title brands actually mean?
Hold the title under the porch light and read the front, not just the signature lines on the back. A title brand is a permanent note that something serious happened to this car. Missouri’s core brand is salvage: under RSMo 301.010, that means repairs back to legal road condition would exceed 80 percent of what the car was worth immediately before the damage. Once repaired and examined, the new Missouri title reads prior salvage.
Missouri also prints designations for reconstructed, motor change, specially constructed and non-USA-std vehicles under RSMo 301.190. None of those words is flood. A Missouri salvage brand tells you an insurer wrote the car off; it doesn’t tell you water did it.
Illinois names the water. Under 625 ILCS 5/3-117.1, a car submerged until water rose over the door sill into the passenger or trunk compartment is a flood vehicle. Its title must indicate the word flood, and Illinois law says flood “shall be conspicuously entered on subsequent titles for the vehicle.”
Now the trap inside that same statute. An Illinois owner may keep a totaled vehicle by agreement with the insurer if it is 9 model years of age or older, or if the damage was hail only. So a hard hit on a 12-year-old car can settle, get patched, and never produce a salvage certificate. A clean title is not a clean history.
### How does title washing work, and how do you catch it?
Title washing means moving a branded car to a state that doesn’t see the brand and getting a fresh clean title issued there. The federal answer is NMVTIS, the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System, which the Justice Department says is designed to protect consumers from fraud and unsafe vehicles. Before you buy, an NMVTIS report shows the car’s title, its most recent odometer reading and its brand history.
This is not a theory. After Hurricane Katrina, the department notes, truckloads of flooded vehicles left Louisiana for states as far away as the upper Midwest, where they were dried out, cleaned and readied for sale in states that do not brand flood vehicles.
Missouri adds a checkpoint of its own: under RSMo 301.190, certain vehicles previously registered in other states get an inspection before Missouri titles them. Useful, but it happens after you’ve paid. The report happens before.
Nothing to do with cars: martial arts classes fill up faster than you’d guess.
### How to spot a flood car in a two-river town
Look where a detailer wouldn’t. Lift the spare tire and run a finger around the well. Peel back a corner of carpet by the pedals. Shine the flashlight along the seat rails and into the glove box. Gritty, grey, dried-mud dust in any of those places is the river talking.
Then use your nose with the windows up. A musty smell counts. So does a cabin that reeks of air freshener on a car that otherwise looks unloved.
The free NICB VINCheck tells you whether a participating insurer reported the car as stolen, salvage or flood-damaged. Know what that means: a car that flooded and never got claimed comes back clean.
### How bad is undercarriage rust on a car that has wintered here?
Bad enough to end an otherwise healthy car. The parts that go are the ones you can’t see from the driveway: brake lines, fuel tank straps, exhaust hangers, floor pans, subframe mounts.
So get low, on cardboard if you have to. A light orange film is normal on steel that has seen a few winters. Flakes that drop onto your face when you tap a brake line are not. Press a thumb into the rocker panels and the rear wheel arches. Anything that gives under that pressure is structural, and it is the seller’s problem until you sign.
### What the test drive tells you if you turn the radio off
Ask for the car cold. Put your hand on the hood before the seller starts it; if the metal is already warm, somebody ran it to hide a hard start, a rattle or a puff of blue smoke. Then turn the key yourself and listen for the first five seconds.
Keep the radio off for the whole drive. A whine that rises with speed, a clunk over a pothole, a grinding hum on a long curve: each one is a repair bill speaking early. Brake hard once on an empty stretch and feel whether the car pulls or the pedal sinks. Take it up to highway speed if you can, because some shakes only show up there.
When you park, leave it running and walk around the back. Sniff for sweet coolant or burning oil. Look under the car for a fresh drip on the pavement. Write down anything you heard so you can hand the list to your mechanic.
### Why an independent inspection matters most
It’s the only step where somebody with a lift, a scan tool and no stake in the sale tells you the truth. Pick the shop yourself, never one the seller suggests. Ask for the car on a lift, a scan for stored and pending codes, and a written summary you keep whether you buy or walk.
The report is not even the main prize. The clearest red flag in a used-car deal is a seller who refuses the inspection. That refusal has already answered your biggest question. Walk away from a no.
### What does “as is” really mean in Missouri versus Illinois?
Two different things, and the gap is worth real money. Under 815 ILCS 505/2L, an Illinois dealer cannot disclaim the implied warranty of merchantability on a used car until the 15th calendar day after delivery or until it has been driven 500 miles, whichever comes first, regardless of any “as is” language in the contract.
Read the exclusions, though. That section does not apply to a vehicle with more than 150,000 miles at the time of sale, or to one with a title branded rebuilt or flood. Buy a flood-branded car from an Illinois dealer and you’ve given up the one protection that law hands you.
On the Missouri side, read the “as is” box literally, with the one exception above: it does not cancel the emissions approval a seller owes you. If a dealer won’t make an emissions problem right, the Gateway program points buyers to the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline at 800-392-8222.
The two slips, priced
In the St. Louis emissions area, the emissions test is $24 and the Missouri safety inspection is $12, and the program asks you to report any station that charges more. On a private sale the seller should be paying for the emissions test. Skip the title for months and the late-title penalty can reach $200, far more than both slips together.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a red flag when buying a used car?
A.  A seller who will not let your mechanic put the car on a lift. That one ends the conversation. After that: a Missouri seller with no emissions approval in a county that requires one, a clean Illinois title on a car 9 model years or older, silt in the spare tire well, and flaking rust on the brake lines.
### Q. What is the $3000 rule for cars?
A.  It is one of several budgeting rules of thumb that circulate online, and none of them tell you whether the car in front of you is sound. A cheap car with a solid frame, a readable service history and no rust through the rockers can be a fine buy. A pricier one hiding flood damage is not. Spend the inspection money first, then let the number follow the car.
### Q. What not to tell a used car dealer?
A.  Don’t tell them you’re in a hurry, and don’t promise to skip the inspection. Say the opposite out loud: the deal depends on your own mechanic seeing the car first. A lot that hears that and gets quiet has told you something.
### Q. What not to say to a used car salesman?
A.  Less than you think, and the wording matters less than you think. What actually protects you is the title check, the inspection by a mechanic you chose, and your willingness to leave. A seller who resists any of those has told you more than any script could.
### Q. How to check if a car had flood damage?
A.  Start with the paper, then the car. Illinois prints flood on the title and on every title after it, so an Illinois history is worth pulling through NMVTIS. Then run the free NICB VINCheck. On the car itself, lift the spare tire, peel back the carpet by the pedals, check the seat rails, and smell the cabin with the windows up.
### Q. Is it worth buying a rebuilt title car?
A.  Sometimes, and only with your eyes open. A rebuilt or prior salvage title means the car was written off and repaired, so you are buying somebody else’s repair work. If you go ahead, get the inspection from a shop you chose and ask what was damaged and who fixed it. In Missouri, a car sold with a junk, salvage or rebuild title is also exempt from the dealer emissions requirements, so any emissions repair is yours. From an Illinois dealer, a rebuilt brand also means the state’s used-car implied warranty rule does not apply.

## UMSL Puts a $95 Value on an Eye Exam. Some St. Louis Exams Cost Nothing.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/eye-exam-cost-st-louis-optometrist
$95. That is the number UMSL’s eye clinic puts on one yearly eye exam, in writing, on the page where it tells its own students theirs is free: “a $95 value.” Hold onto it. It is a real St. Louis number from a real St. Louis clinic, and it is more than most front desks will say out loud before they see your insurance card.
You probably landed here because something went soft. The street sign you used to read from the light now swims until you are almost under it. The menu gets held at arm’s length, then tilted toward the window. The headache shows up behind your eyes around three in the afternoon and leaves when you close the laptop. None of it is an emergency. All of it is a bill you have been putting off, because nobody will tell you what the bill is.
So here are the numbers, the free door most people never hear about, and the one federal rule that keeps the frame wall from closing in on you.
### Where is the cheapest place to get an eye exam in St. Louis?
The cheapest exam is the free one, and in St. Louis it exists. The WashU Medicine Free Eye Service is a student-run mobile eye clinic that offers free vision screenings, eye exams and referrals for uninsured and underinsured patients, and no appointment is needed. If you can pay something, UMSL Eye Care, the clinic of the University of Missouri-St. Louis, takes most major medical insurance plans. Paying cash anywhere else, VSP says, can run $50 to $200 or more.
### The exam a student gives you, with a doctor checking
Here is the St. Louis detail that makes people sit up. At UMSL Eye Care, comprehensive eye exams are performed by advanced level students under the guidance and expertise of doctors. Your chin goes on the cool plastic rest, the big black phoropter swings in front of your face, and a voice asks the oldest question in eye care: better one, or better two? Then a second set of eyes, a licensed doctor’s, signs off on what the student found.
That is not a discount gimmick. It is how optometry gets taught, and it means the person in the chair next to you is working hard not to miss anything. Plan on the visit taking longer than a strip-mall exam. Bring a book. Bring your current glasses, a list of your medicines and, if you wear contacts, the box they came in.
UMSL runs three locations. The University Eye Center sits at 7840 Natural Bridge Road. The Lindell Eye Center is in the Central West End. A third clinic sits on a community college campus across the river, for the Illinois side. One number books all of them: (314) 516-5131. Its accepted-plan list runs from Blue Cross Blue Shield and EyeMed to Medicare, MOCare, Healthy Blue and IDPA, and the clinic says to call and ask if yours isn’t listed.
The line worth saying to a friend who has been squinting for a year: in this city, the exam you are scared to price might be one phone call to a university away.
### Why one office says $50 and another says $200
Because “eye exam” is a bundle, and every office packs it differently. VSP puts it plainly: a basic eye exam can cost around $50, while a more full-service exam with an independent optometrist, including a dilated eye exam, can cost upwards of $200. Extra tests, such as a contact lens fitting or a glaucoma test, add to the cost.
You feel the difference in the room. The basic version is the letters on the wall and the click-click of lenses. The full version adds the drops that sting for a second, then twenty minutes in the waiting room while the lights get too bright, then the drive home in borrowed sunglasses with the world blurred at the edges. The fitting for contacts is its own appointment-within-an-appointment, because how a lens sits on the curve of your eye is not part of a glasses exam.
So do not call and ask “how much is an eye exam.” Ask one narrow question: what is your self-pay fee for a comprehensive exam, and what costs extra? A front desk can answer that in a sentence.
### No insurance at all? Walk in to the WashU clinic
The WashU Medicine Free Eye Service was founded in 2022 by WashU Medicine physicians and medical students. Its clinic locations are Casa de Salud on Chouteau Avenue, the WashU Medicine Pro Bono Health Clinic on Forest Park Avenue and St. Patrick’s Center on North Tucker. It offers reading glasses, and when you need more than a screening, it helps connect you to partner clinics for further comprehensive care.
Screenings are available on a walk-in basis, and the clinic lists its upcoming dates and locations on its own page. Check that page before you go, not a flyer you saw months ago. Then go. A folding chair, a chart on the wall, a medical student with a penlight. Ten quiet minutes that can tell you whether the blur is just your prescription or something that needs a doctor this month.
Eyes rested and dilation worn off? Go find a plate of Italian food you can actually read the menu for.
### Your prescription walks out the door with you
This is where the bill usually grows. The exam ends, you blink back into the hallway, and the frame wall is right there, lit like a jewelry case. Federal law is on your side. Under the FTC’s Eyeglass Rule, the eye doctor must hand you one copy of your prescription immediately after the refractive exam and before offering to sell you anything, whether or not you ask for it.
They cannot make the exam conditional on buying glasses from them. They cannot charge any fee on top of the exam fee to release that prescription. Fold it into your wallet and price it at two other places before you pay for frames anywhere. That single slip of paper is the cheapest pair of glasses you will ever own.

### Medicare and the routine-exam gap
If you are on Original Medicare, read this before the appointment, not at the checkout counter. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer vision as an extra benefit, so call the number on your plan card first.
A visit for a medical problem is a different conversation from a visit for new glasses. Floaters, an injured eye, a sudden change: say so when you book, and ask the office how they will bill it.

### The two-minute call that saves the surprise
Most bad eye-care bills are not scams. They are a missing question. You hear the hold music, the receptionist comes back on, and you have maybe a minute of her attention before the next line lights up. Use it on four things: the self-pay fee for a comprehensive exam, whether dilation or retinal photos cost extra, the separate price of a contact lens fitting if you wear contacts, and whether they will bill your medical plan if the visit turns out to be medical.
Write the answers on the back of an envelope. Call a second office and ask the same four. Now you are not guessing at a number, you are comparing two of them, and that is the whole game. When you walk in, you already know what the card reader is going to say. No flinch at the counter, no quiet math in your head while the receipt prints.
### Optometrist, ophthalmologist or optician?
For a routine exam, glasses or contacts, start with an optometrist. That is who you will see at a school-of-optometry clinic like UMSL’s. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who does eye surgery and treats eye disease, and you usually reach one on a referral when the exam turns up something like a cataract. An optician fits and adjusts glasses from a prescription someone else wrote, which makes them the person who fixes the frames that keep sliding down your nose.

## Anyone Can Design a Missouri House: When St. Louis Projects Need an Architect
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-an-architect-in-st-louis
Missouri lets anyone design your house, as long as one sentence is on the plans. The tape measure snaps back into its case with a crack that bounces off the brick. Twelve feet. That’s how far you want to push the kitchen out the back of an old bungalow in Affton, and you’re standing in wet grass at dusk wondering whose name has to be on the drawings.
Here’s the answer most people never hear. On the Missouri side, the law that licenses architects lets anyone design a house, as long as one sentence appears on the plans. Cross the river into Illinois and the same two-family flat can need a licensed architect for one reason: what its walls are made of.
That’s the fork, and it decides who you hire, what you pay and whether the permit counter slides your plans back across the desk. Find out which side you’re on before you hand anyone a deposit.
### Can you draw your own house plans without an architect?
In Missouri, usually yes for a home. RSMo 327.101 lets an unlicensed person design a dwelling house, or a flat with no more than two families, as long as every drawing states the designer is not a licensed architect. Other small buildings qualify only if they hold nine people or fewer, stay under 2,000 square feet and stand alone. In Illinois, a detached single-family home or a wood-frame two-family qualifies; anything else may need a licensed architect.
### The one sentence that makes Missouri plans legal
Read the statute and the surprise is how little it asks of a homeowner. Under RSMo 327.101, a person who isn’t a licensed architect may render architectural services for a dwelling house, or for a multiple family dwelling, flat or apartment containing not more than two families. The condition is printed right in the law: the drawings, specifications and other documents have to state that the person is not a licensed architect.
So when your contractor’s “plans guy” hands you a roll of drawings, unroll them on the kitchen table and look at the title block. No seal and no such statement is your first red flag. It costs you thirty seconds and a cup of coffee going cold.
Everything else gets a much tighter test. A non-residential building escapes only if it provides for the employment, assembly, housing, sleeping or eating of not more than nine persons, contains less than two thousand square feet, and is not part of another building. All three at once. Turn the back half of a storefront into a 2,400-square-foot space and that test fails, however few people work inside.
Three- and four-family buildings get a narrower break: an unlicensed person may handle remodeling or repairing only when the work does not affect architectural or engineering safety features. If you own a south city four-family, ask that question before anyone moves a wall.
The teeth are real. Under RSMo 327.461, a contract for architectural services with someone who needed a license and didn’t have one is unenforceable by that person. And under RSMo 327.077, the state board can seek civil penalties of up to five thousand dollars for each offense, where each day of a continued violation counts as a separate offense, up to twenty-five thousand dollars.
### Why a brick two-flat is different across the river
Illinois writes it differently. Section 3 of the Illinois Architecture Practice Act exempts farm buildings, the construction, remodeling or repairing of a detached single-family residence on a single lot, and a two-family residence of wood frame construction on a single lot, not more than two stories and basement in height.
Two words do the work. Run your hand along the soft old brick of a two-flat in Belleville, Alton or Granite City and you’re touching the reason it falls outside that exemption. The same brick two-flat on a south St. Louis street sits inside Missouri’s rule for a flat containing not more than two families. For a small landlord, that’s the sharpest practical difference between the two states.
If the drawings do need a licensed architect, the seal is the proof. Missouri law requires each architect to have a personal seal and to affix it to all final technical submissions, drawings and specifications included. A stamp is a person putting their license on the line, not a decoration.
### What the City of St. Louis permit counter will ask for
Whoever draws it, the plans still have to get through City Hall. The city’s Building Division asks for the project address, project plans, a letter of authorization if you’re not the owner of record, and a $25 application fee per application. If you apply in person, bring five copies of the plans, and know that only check or cash is accepted at the counter.
Then the math. Above $3,000 of estimated construction cost, the city charges the $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated cost. So a $60,000 kitchen addition runs $25 plus $600, or $625 in permit fees, and every dollar paid to the city for a building permit is non-refundable. Get the drawings right the first time, before you ever file.
That’s also why the cheapest plans can be the most expensive. A set that gets bounced costs you weeks of a torn-up kitchen, the microwave on the dining room floor, and a contractor who moved on to his next job.
### Architect, draftsperson or design-build?
On an exempt house project, an unlicensed designer such as a draftsperson can legally draw your plans, and for a straightforward remodel that is often the right, cheaper hire. Once a project falls outside the exemption, you need a licensed architect, and Missouri requires that architect to seal the final drawings. Thinking of drawing them yourself? Here’s what Missouri lets a homeowner draw without an architect.
A design-build contractor can feel like the easy answer: one phone number, one truck in the driveway, one person to blame. That can work well on an exempt house. On a building that needs a licensed architect, ask who is actually drawing the plans and whose seal will be on them, and get that name in writing before the first payment. The question takes ten seconds. The answer tells you whether the bid in your hand is a design-build bid or just a build bid with drawings to be figured out later.
How architects charge matters too. Architect Bob Borson, writing at Life of an Architect, says percentage-of-construction fees vary by firm but generally fall in the 8% to 15% range. Hourly is the honest structure for the fuzzy front end, when nobody can scope a zoning question yet; a fixed fee buys predictability and gets renegotiated when the scope moves.
If the designer works through a company, check the company too. Missouri requires a corporation or company that practices architecture to obtain a certificate of authority from the state board for each profession named in its articles. A slick website and a truck wrap are not that certificate.
### Five questions to ask before you sign anything
The first meeting usually happens at your kitchen table, with the old floor plan spread out and a coffee mug holding down one curling corner. Watch how they listen. A good designer walks the house before talking price, opens the basement door to look at the joists, and asks what bothers you about the place at 7 a.m. on a weekday. Then put these on the table:
Does my project fall inside the exemption? Make them say which part of the law they’re relying on, out loud.
Who stamps the drawings, and can I see that license? If the answer is “nobody,” the plans should say the designer is not a licensed architect.
How is the fee built? Percentage, hourly or fixed, and what triggers a change.
What happens if the permit reviewer sends comments back? Revisions should be in the price, not a surprise invoice.
Will you visit during construction? Drawings answer most questions; the ones they don’t answer show up with a framing crew standing around waiting.
After you file, the city routes the plans to whichever staff and agencies the project calls for, and that depends on the specifics of the project itself. A designer who has walked plans through City Hall before will tell you who is likely to comment, and that knowledge is worth more than a slightly lower fee.
A different trade, same addition: the concrete work under it decides whether that new kitchen floor stays level.
### How to check a license in a minute
In Missouri, call the state board that licenses architects at 573-751-0047, or start from its page on pr.mo.gov. In Illinois, architects are licensed by IDFPR, and its site has a License Look Up. Check the person, then check that the name on the search matches the name on the seal.
Exempt Missouri house plans: look for the statement that the designer is not a licensed architect.
Anything outside the exemption: look for a licensed architect’s seal on the final drawings.
City of St. Louis permit: five copies in person, $25 to file, the rest when the permit is ready.
