### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a cheaper alternative to an architect?
A.  When the project is exempt, yes: in Missouri, an unlicensed designer such as a draftsperson may design a dwelling house or a flat of up to two families, provided the drawings state that the person is not a licensed architect. In Illinois, the exemption covers a detached single-family home on a single lot. Outside those lines there is no legal shortcut: final drawings need a licensed architect’s seal.
### Q. What is the average fee for an architect?
A.  For full-service work priced as a percentage of construction, architect Bob Borson says fees vary by firm but generally fall in the 8% to 15% range. Hourly billing is common for early feasibility and zoning questions, and fixed fees show up once the scope settles. Ask every firm which method it uses and what phases the fee covers.
### Q. How much does an architect cost for a small project?
A.  Small jobs are often quoted hourly or as a flat fee rather than a percentage, because a small addition still needs every wall and header drawn. Get the scope in writing first. And budget the city’s side too: in the City of St. Louis, work over $3,000 pays a $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated cost.
### Q. Is AI replacing architects?
A.  Not where the law is concerned. Software can sketch a floor plan, but Missouri requires each architect to have a personal seal and affix it to all final technical submissions, and a seal belongs to a licensed person, not a program. For a project outside the exemption, a licensed human still has to put a name on it.
### Q. What is the correct order to renovate a house?
A.  Plans and permits first, then demolition, structure, the rough-in trades, inspections, insulation and drywall, and finishes last. In the City of St. Louis, the building permit application is where you’ll be asked about any associated plumbing, electrical or mechanical permits, so line those trades up before you file.
### Q. What is the 30% rule for renovations?
A.  It’s a budgeting rule of thumb, not a law or a code: keep a renovation’s cost to a modest share of the home’s value so you don’t over-improve for the street. What decides whether you need an architect is the building type, not the budget.
### Q. How do I check whether an architect is licensed in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  In Missouri, call the state board that licenses architects at 573-751-0047. In Illinois, architects are licensed by IDFPR, and its site has a License Look Up. Then match the name on the license to the name on the seal.

## Your Trainer Ten-Pack May Not Get Missouri's 3-Day Cancel
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-personal-trainer-in-st-louis
The pen clicks. The contract slides across the front desk, still warm from the printer, a ten-session package with a signature line at the bottom and a sticky note marking where your initials go. Through the wall, plates clank back onto a rack. The person behind the counter is already reaching for your card.
Stop on that signature line for one breath. There is a three-month line buried in a Missouri definition, and it decides whether you can change your mind.
Under section 407.330 RSMo, a health spa contract must let you cancel within three business days, penalty-free, with every dollar refunded. That sounds like a safety net. But section 407.325 RSMo defines that contract as one for services rendered over a period longer than three months.
Read that twice. The ten-pack you plan to finish before the season changes may not be covered at all.
There is a second gap. Section 407.325 also leaves out nonprofits like the YMCA, private clubs owned and operated by their members, colleges and universities, and any facility owned or operated by the state of Missouri or any of its political subdivisions. So ask who runs the place before you count on that three-day window. If the law doesn’t cover you, the paper in your hand is the whole deal. And if a gym won’t honor terms it put in writing, the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection hotline is 800-392-8222.
Then check the price against a real one. At Saint Louis University’s Simon Recreation Center, a single session with the rec center’s certified trainers is posted at $35, and ten sessions run $280. It is a yardstick, not a coupon: Simon Rec says all clients must be members, and its membership list runs to students, faculty and staff, alumni, spouses and dependents, with the faculty-and-staff tier including SSM employees. Most people will pay a gym or an independent trainer instead. Now you know what the floor looks like.
So before you hand over a card, do four things, in this order. First, ask which certification the trainer holds and look it up yourself in the NCCA’s directory of accredited certification programs; the letters on a polo shirt are a claim, the directory is a check. Second, say this at the desk, word for word: “How many months does this contract run, and where is the buyer’s right to cancel?” Longer than three months at a commercial gym, and Missouri law requires the cancellation terms to be set forth under a conspicuous caption: “BUYER’S RIGHT TO CANCEL.” Shorter than that, and your exit is whatever the paper says, so read it while the pen is still capped. Third, ask what the first session includes. A real one starts with an assessment, not a workout. Fourth, if anything hurts, call a physical therapist before you call a trainer.
### How much should you spend on a personal trainer?
The rate card is usually laminated, a little sticky from the last hand that held it. Spend what a certified session is worth to you, and use a posted St. Louis rate card to check the rest. At SLU’s Simon Recreation Center, new clients start with a $75 package that includes a fitness assessment and two 60-minute sessions, then pay $35 for a single session or $280 for ten. A partner package of ten runs $168. Commercial gyms and independent trainers will charge more, and the gap is what you are paying for: the location, the hours, the specialty. Ask what you get for it.
### The four letters worth checking: NCCA
Look up from the drinking fountain and there it is: a framed certificate behind glass, a little crooked on its nail, a row of capital letters under somebody’s name. You will see the same wall of acronyms on trainer bios and stitched on sleeves. Even the campus option is careful about who counts: Simon Rec says no outside personal trainers are allowed to train in the Simon Recreation Center, and all personal instruction there must be scheduled through the fitness coordinator. The one that sorts them is NCCA, the National Commission for Certifying Agencies. It doesn’t train anybody. It accredits certification programs that assess professional competency, it calls itself an independent resource recognized as the authority on accreditation standards for professional certification programs, and its accreditation follows a five-year renewal cycle.
The useful part is that NCCA publishes an Accreditation Certification Programs Directory, so you don’t have to take anybody’s word for it. Type in the certification the trainer named. If it is there, the exam behind it was held to a standard. If it is not, ask what the trainer’s exam looked like and who graded it.
Read brand names slowly. ISSA sells a Certified Personal Trainer program whose own page says it includes NCCPT’s NCCA-Accredited Certification Exam. That means the name on the certificate and the name of the accredited exam behind it may be two different organizations. Ask which exam the trainer actually sat. A good trainer answers that in one breath and doesn’t flinch.
Then ask the boring question: is it current? Certifications lapse on a schedule, and the letters stay on the business card long after the card in the wallet expires. Ask to see it. Ask to see the CPR card next to it.
### What should you read twice before you sign?
The paper is thin and the type is small, and the paragraph that matters may be on the back. Read the cancellation clause, then the renewal clause, then the price. In that order. The chair is too low, the music is too loud, and the person across the desk is smiling, and none of that is a reason to skip a paragraph. Three business days is not long. They can be gone while your legs are still sore.
On the Missouri side, the health spa law is specific. A covered contract must let you cancel within three business days of signing and get back all the money you paid. To cancel, you notify the gym in writing, by certified mail with return receipt requested or by personal delivery, to the address printed in the contract, and the refund is due within thirty days of the gym receiving your notice. The contract must also provide for cancellation if you die or become permanently disabled and unable to use a substantial portion of the services for sixty or more consecutive days, with a refund figured by the weeks remaining in the term. A temporary disability gets the membership term extended.
One more Missouri check takes a minute. The same chapter makes it unlawful for a health spa to offer or sell a health spa contract unless it is registered with the Missouri attorney general, and each separate location files its own registration, renewed every year. Ask the gym whether its location is registered. A business that sells long contracts and can’t answer that has told you something.
Signing on the Illinois side of the river? Illinois law sets its own rules: every contract for physical fitness services there must let you cancel within 3 business days after the first business day after you sign, with all monies refunded, and a plan bought at a facility that hasn’t opened yet gets seven calendar days. Move farther than 25 miles away with no comparable center offered within 25 miles of your new home, and you can cancel, owing a fee of no more than 10 percent of the unused balance or $50, whichever is less.
Is the ache in your back a trainer problem at all? Read the chiropractic side of the same ache before you sign anything.
### What does a good first session look like?
The first good session smells like a clipboard and hand sanitizer, not sweat. Paperwork and questions before a single rep. Simon Rec says its initial fitness assessment will consist of five screenings, and they make a fair checklist to hold any trainer to: a blood pressure screening, a body composition screening, a three-minute step test, a flexibility screening and a muscle strength screening. It says the assessment takes about 60 minutes. That is an hour of the cuff tightening on your arm and the step box under your feet, and not one minute of being yelled at.
At Simon Rec, every service must be paid before participation, and a copy of the receipt must be presented to the personal trainer, so the paperwork is done before the first rep. Then your goals, out loud, with a date attached. Then a scaled-down version of the real program: light, unhurried, mostly teaching. You should leave knowing what next week looks like, and the trainer should leave with numbers to compare against. Simon Rec even prices a follow-up baseline assessment, $25, which tells you how seriously a good program takes measuring progress instead of guessing at it.
A first session that leaves you easing down the stairs sideways afterward proves very little. Soreness is a sensation, not a measurement. Good trainers write down loads, reps and what to change. Ask to see the notes.
Pay attention to how the hour feels, too. A good trainer watches your feet and your breathing more than the clock on the wall. They stop you mid-set to fix a grip, they ask how the last rep felt, and they say your name more than they say their own. If the session felt like a sales meeting with dumbbells in it, you already have your answer, and it cost you only one hour to learn it.
Pricing works the same way. Simon Rec’s card climbs in plain steps: $35 for one session, $99 for three, $180 for six, $280 for ten, and $168 for ten with a partner. A commercial gym’s card will look different, and that is fine, as long as it is on paper. Ask for it in writing, take it home, and read it at your own kitchen table, where nobody is waiting for you to sign.
### When do you need a physical therapist instead of a trainer?
You feel it on the third step down: the knee that catches, the hip that pinches. If you have pain, a recent injury, a surgery in your history, or a symptom you can’t explain, that belongs to a clinician first. The shoulder that won’t let you reach the top shelf is the same kind of question for someone licensed to examine them.
In Missouri you may not need a doctor’s referral to start. Section 334.506 lets a physical therapist evaluate and begin treatment without a prescription or referral, as long as the therapist has a doctorate of physical therapy degree or five years of clinical practice. There are limits. A patient who shows no measurable or functional improvement after ten visits or thirty days, whichever comes first, has to be referred to an approved health care provider, and the therapist can’t keep treating after that referral.
The same section lets a physical therapist develop fitness or wellness programs without a referral, which is the hand-off people miss. A therapist can set the guardrails, and a trainer worth keeping will ask for those restrictions in writing and program inside them. One caveat that costs people money: your insurance may still want a referral before it pays, even when the law doesn’t require one to treat. Call the number on the back of the card first.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth paying for a personal trainer?
A.  It is when you are buying something you can’t do alone: technique you can’t see in your own mirror, a program built around your history, and a person expecting you at the gym when you’d rather stay in bed It is not when you are buying motivation you could get from a friend with a gym membership. Decide which one you need before you sign.
### Q. Is 1 month of personal training enough?
A.  Enough to learn the form and leave with a program you can run yourself, which is a real goal. Plan the month around that: an assessment at the start, a program in writing, and a retest at the end so you can see what changed. Remember that in Missouri, a package that short may fall outside the state’s three-day cancellation law, so read the refund terms.
### Q. Is 30 minutes with a personal trainer enough?
A.  For a focused session on two or three lifts, often yes. For a first visit, no: Simon Rec says its initial fitness assessment alone takes about 60 minutes. Ask a trainer what they would actually do with the half hour before you decide the length.
### Q. Is a personal trainer actually worth it?
A.  It is worth it when you can check what you are paying for. Look the certification up in the NCCA directory, get the contract length and the cancellation terms on paper, and make sure the first session measures something. A trainer who welcomes all three is usually the one worth paying.
### Q. Can I cancel a personal training contract in Missouri?
A.  If it is a health spa contract, yes, within three business days, penalty-free, by written notice sent certified mail with return receipt requested or delivered in person. Missouri defines that contract as one for services over a period longer than three months, and the law excludes nonprofits like the YMCA, universities and government-run facilities. For anything else, the contract’s own terms decide.

## Never Bag It: Half the City’s Alley Recycling Got Thrown Out
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-can-you-recycle-st-louis
That neat white kitchen bag in your blue cart is going to the landfill. You rinsed the sour milk out of the jug for it. You scraped the peanut butter jar and flattened the delivery boxes, tied it shut and felt good about it. Once it’s bagged, none of that counts.
That isn’t a guess. In the first five months of the year the City of St. Louis ended alley recycling, its own count found that more than half of what it pulled from the blue alley dumpsters was rejected for contamination, and a tied bag of perfectly good bottles is exactly what a sorting line throws out as trash. Rule one, everywhere in this metro: never bag it.
Then comes the harder call. Saturday morning in Affton, you’re standing over the cart with the lid up, a dead drill battery heavy in one hand and a pizza box in the other, the bottom gone see-through with grease and the cheese welded on. The battery feels like something that ought to be recycled. The box is cardboard, and cardboard is supposed to be the easy one. Both answers are no, and the battery is the dangerous one. The rest, from the half can of deck stain to the tube TV in the garage, depends on which side of a city line you’re standing on. Across the river in Illinois, that TV can’t legally go in the trash at all. In Missouri, it can. Here’s the short version, made to stick on the fridge.
For the fridge door If it clinks or folds flat, it goes in loose: paper, flattened cardboard, plastic bottles and containers, glass bottles and jars, cans, cartons. If it tangles, stretches or squeaks, keep it out: bags and film, hoses, cords, string lights, foam. Greasy pizza box: tear off the clean lid, trash the bottom. Paint, oil, pesticides: book a hazardous-waste slot at 314-615-8958 (291 E. Hoffmeister, or 4100 Seven Hills Drive in Florissant; no TVs). An old fridge that still hums: Ameren Missouri pays its customers $50 and hauls it off. A dead drill battery or vape: tape the terminals, because crushed lithium starts garbage-truck fires. Your own rules: the City’s Refuse Division has an address lookup; in unincorporated St. Louis County, call 314-615-HAUL.
### What can you actually put in the recycling bin?
Five things, in nearly every program around here: paper and flattened cardboard, plastic bottles and containers, glass bottles and jars, metal food and beverage cans, and food and beverage cartons. You can hear a good load going in: a rinsed jar clinking against the cans, a flattened box sliding down flat. The City of St. Louis squeezes the rest of the rule into four words: loose, clean and dry. Nothing in a bag.
Clean means a quick rinse under the tap, not a scrub with the good sponge. Dry matters because one wet yogurt cup soaks the newspaper riding next to it, and soggy paper is worth less at the sorting line. Flatten the cardboard every time, until the box lies flat under your palm.
What are 5 things that cannot be recycled? Plastic bags and film, Styrofoam, food waste, needles and sharps, and one-time-use disposables. Styrofoam is technically recyclable somewhere in the world. There is no local processor for it, so here it is trash, and that includes the squeaky takeout clamshell.
### The rules change at every city line
Stand on a boundary street on pickup morning and you can watch it happen: one hauler’s truck groans down your curb, and a different company’s truck works the curb across the street. Kirkwood, unincorporated St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis run three different systems, and the Illinois side is a fourth, because curbside recycling here belongs to whoever holds the contract.
In St. Louis County, the waste ordinance sets a floor you can see from the porch: weekly trash, weekly recycling and a bulky pickup twice a year, all for one monthly fee. That floor covers only one- and two-family homes, and the county runs trash districts only in unincorporated areas. Every city inside the county signs its own hauler contract, so in Ballwin, Ballwin’s hauler writes the rules. The City of St. Louis runs its own refuse division. Across the river, Belleville empties a 32-gallon can marked RECYCLE once a week and takes glass bottles and jars, newspaper, office paper, unwaxed flattened cardboard, aluminum and tin, and no electronics of any kind.
So before you argue with a neighbor over a yogurt cup, look up your own address. The City’s Refuse Division has an address search for collection days, the county’s unincorporated trash-district map names your hauler, and every other city posts its own rules. Two people across a boundary street can both be right.
### What sinks a whole truckload: bags, hoses and greasy boxes
On the sorting line, one garden hose winds around a spinning screen like thread on a spool, and the line waits while somebody climbs in with a knife to cut it free. Plastic bags, extension cords, string lights and rope do the same thing. They’re called tanglers, and they’re the ones nobody guesses. Grease and cheese wreck paper fiber, so tear off the clean lid of the pizza box and trash the soaked bottom.
The local numbers are brutal. From January through May 2025, more than half of everything the City of St. Louis collected from alley recycling dumpsters was rejected at the recycling center for contamination. When the city tested collecting from roll carts and drop-off sites only in July 2025, contamination fell to 25% or less.
That is why alley recycling ended in August 2025 and those blue alley bins became trash dumpsters. Since the change, the city reports contamination down 83% and the tonnage actually recycled up 8%. Wishcycling, tossing in the hopeful maybe, is how a load that would have paid becomes a load somebody pays to bury.
People are asking
### Do plastic grocery bags actually get recycled?
Yes, once they skip your blue cart and ride back to the store. Saint Louis City Recycles says the city takes no bags or film at the curb, even ones stamped with recycling arrows or a resin number, while many grocery and retail stores take them in a drop-off box near the entrance marked with Recycle Responsibly images, along with bread bags, zip-lock bags, newspaper sleeves, deflated bubble wrap and the crinkly wrap off a toilet paper pack. Stuff them all into one bag hung on the pantry doorknob and drop it off on the next grocery run. To see what film can become, sit on the Bags2Bench in Brightside’s Demonstration Garden, a bench made from 13,500 recycled plastic bags and wood fibers.
### Is glass still worth recycling in St. Louis?
Yes. The City of St. Louis and Belleville both take glass bottles and jars at the curb. But glass has been the troubled material here for years, and the reason is mechanical rather than moral. In a single-stream truck glass breaks, the shards migrate into paper and plastic, and a bale of paper with glass in it is worth less to a mill.
So a separate channel exists. Ripple Glass - started in Kansas City in 2009 by the owners of Boulevard Brewing, bought by Strategic Materials in 2022 - expanded into St. Louis and runs free purple drop-off bins around the metro, open to anyone. Glass left there is crushed into cullet for manufacturers instead of screened out as residue.
### Where do old electronics and TVs actually go?
It depends which state you’re in, and the difference is legal rather than cultural. Illinois has banned electronics from landfill disposal since January 1, 2012 under the Electronic Products Recycling and Reuse Act, tightened by the Consumer Electronics Recycling Act in 2017. Televisions, monitors, computers, tablets and printers cannot go in an Illinois trash can at all.
Missouri has no residential landfill ban. The Missouri Department of Natural Resources says plainly that most electronics from a home can legally be thrown away, while recommending you don’t. What Missouri has instead is manufacturer takeback: under the state’s Electronics Scrap Management Rule, computer equipment bought in Missouri after July 1, 2010 carries a recovery plan, and the manufacturer has to collect and recycle it at no cost to a household.
One trap before you drive anywhere: the region’s two permanent household hazardous waste facilities list electronics, televisions and monitors among the things they will not take. E-waste is a separate errand.
Nothing to do with bins - lawn and garden season arrives sooner than expected.
### Where does household hazardous waste go in St. Louis?
Two permanent facilities, appointment only, open to residents of St. Louis City, St. Louis County and Jefferson County. The South facility sits at 291 E. Hoffmeister and runs Thursdays and Fridays plus alternating Saturdays. The North facility is at 4100 Seven Hills Drive in Florissant, Wednesdays plus alternating Saturdays. Weekday slots are 8:30 to 11:45 a.m. and 1:00 to 5:20 p.m.
Bring proof of address - a utility bill or your driver’s license. The first 50 pounds are subsidized; past that it runs $1.70 per pound, and latex paint is 50 cents per pound. Saturday dates alternate between the two sites, so book before you load the car. The scheduling line is 314-615-8958.
They accept paints, stains and varnishes, pesticides and herbicides, gasoline, motor oil and filters, antifreeze, transmission fluid, and alkaline and car batteries. They refuse explosives, ammunition, radioactive material, appliances, electronics and medical waste. Waste from a business, church, school or government office isn’t accepted here at all.
### What about paint, tires, mattresses and old appliances?
Latex paint doesn’t have to be an errand. Missouri’s DNR says to open the can, stir in kitty litter, sand, shredded newspaper or a paint hardener, leave the lid off until it dries into a hard crumble, then put it in the household trash. Oil-based paint is flammable in any state and belongs at a hazardous waste facility.
Tires have been banned whole from Missouri landfills since the 1990 law that also banned major appliances, waste oil and lead-acid batteries. The 50-cent fee on every new tire sold in Missouri funds the state cleanup program. A tire shop will take your old ones for roughly $3 to $5 each. Missouri does allow a homeowner to trash a tire cut through the tread or with the sidewalls removed.
Mattresses have no statewide recycling program in Missouri or Illinois, unlike the handful of states that fund one through a purchase fee. A recycling center that takes them charges by the piece, a hauler charges more and comes to you, and a retailer delivering a new set will usually take the old one if you arrange it at purchase.
Refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners have been banned from Missouri landfills since January 1, 1991, and the refrigerant has to be recovered by a certified technician rather than vented. If the unit still runs, Ameren Missouri pays $50 and hauls it away free through its fridge and freezer recycling program.
### Which batteries start fires in garbage trucks?
Lithium-ion. The rechargeable cell inside a laptop, a cordless drill, a phone, a hoverboard, a disposable vape. Crushed in the back of a packer truck or inside a baler, it enters thermal runaway, and that fire feeds itself and shrugs off water. Industry tracking counted 448 publicly reported fires at North American waste and recycling operations in 2025, with roughly $2.5 billion in estimated damage.
So none in the recycling cart, and none in the trash either. Tape the terminals with clear packing tape, bag it on its own, and take it to a hazardous waste facility or a retail battery drop-off. A swollen or damaged cell should go promptly rather than sit in a kitchen drawer.
Car batteries are the older, easier problem. Lead-acid has been banned from Missouri landfills since 1991, and nearly anywhere that sells one takes one back - the core charge on your receipt is the deposit that makes that happen.
### Where do motor oil, propane tanks and old pills go?
Used motor oil is banned from Missouri landfills and is simple to hand off. Most auto parts stores and quick-lube shops accept do-it-yourself oil free, commonly up to five gallons at a time, so long as it hasn’t been mixed with antifreeze, solvent or water. Once it’s mixed it stops being recyclable oil and becomes hazardous waste. Filters can be recycled too, but call ahead.
Propane tanks never go in a cart, a dumpster or a drop-off bin, because nobody downstream can be certain they’re empty. For a standard 20-pound grill tank, the exchange cage at a gas station or hardware store is the industry’s take-back loop: swap it, and the old shell becomes their problem. To be rid of one for good, ask an exchange or refill dealer to retire it. The one-pound camping cylinders are the awkward case.
Leftover medication should not be flushed. Many area police departments run permanent drop boxes, the St. Louis County Police Department keeps collection bins at several sites, and thousands of pharmacies take medication back year round. On the DEA’s April 25, 2026 take-back day, more than 30,000 pounds came in across the 323 collection sites in its St. Louis Field Division.
Still holding the thing you don’t know what to do with? Browse recycling centers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and read your item out loud before you load the car.
If you’re the one who hauls junk, runs a scrap yard or recycles electronics, list your business with us and turn more of the people reading this with a dead TV in the garage into customers.
### Why the shop on your corner pays for its own dumpster
Commercial waste is a contract, not a service the city owes you. A shop signs for a front-load dumpster - nationally, a four-yard container on weekly pickup runs around $110 to $200 a month - and the fine print bites: a one- to three-year term, an annual escalator, and fuel and environmental surcharges outside the quoted rate. A compactor costs real money up front and pays back only above roughly one pickup a week.
Cardboard is the one stream that can pay instead of cost. Baled old corrugated has traded near $100 to $130 a short ton through 2026, under the five-year average around $140 - real money at volume, on a clean bale, with a baler you own. And a Missouri business cannot do what a household can with retired computers: businesses, schools, churches and nonprofits are barred from landfilling certain electronics, and a serialized certificate of destruction settles the customer-data question two years later. Operators who are easy to find locally get the call, and being listed and complete is the cheap half of that.
Electronics are the big exception to everything above - here is what to do with old electronics in St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does the City of St. Louis still pick up recycling in the alley?
A.  No. The city ended alley recycling in August 2025, after more than half the material collected from alley dumpsters between January and May 2025 was rejected for contamination. Those blue bins are trash dumpsters now. Residents without a roll cart use the city’s single-stream drop-off sites, most open around the clock.
### Q. What are 5 things that cannot be recycled?
A.  Plastic bags and film, food-soaked cardboard, tanglers like hoses and cords and holiday lights, anything with a lithium-ion battery in it, and household hazardous waste such as paint or motor oil. None of those belong in a curbside cart anywhere in the metro. The last two are not just rejected - they start fires in trucks and at sorting facilities.
### Q. Which items cannot be recycled?
A.  Beyond the obvious five, the routine offenders here are bagged recyclables, greasy pizza boxes, polystyrene foam, disposable cups with a plastic lining, and ceramics or window glass mixed in with bottles. Bagging is the big one locally - more than half of what the City collected from alley dumpsters in early 2025 was rejected for contamination, which is why alley recycling ended that August.
### Q. What items can you not recycle?
A.  Anything that contaminates the load: greasy pizza boxes, plastic bags and film, styrofoam, ceramics, garden hose, needles. Contamination is the actual problem here - more than half of what the City collected from January through May 2025 was unusable, and it dropped to 25% or less once collection moved to roll carts and drop-off sites only.
### Q. What are 10 things you can recycle?
A.  Cardboard, paperboard, newspaper, office paper, magazines, aluminum cans, steel cans, plastic bottles and jugs, cartons, and glass bottles and jars - though glass is the one that varies most by municipality. Belleville takes it weekly in the marked 32-gallon can; check your own hauler before assuming.

## The St. Louis Gift That Won't Ship Inside St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-gifts-that-are-actually-from-here
One Ted Drewes shipping cooler holds fifteen 8-ounce concretes. Pack it on Chippewa, and UPS Overnight can set it on a porch on the far coast by morning, the lid squeaking open and the cold breathing out over somebody’s homesick face. Try to send that same cooler across the county and the answer is no. Ted Drewes says it plainly on its own shipping page: “We do not ship orders within the St. Louis Metro Area.”
Locals get pointed to the grocery freezer instead, at Schnucks or Dierbergs. Everyone else pays for the trip, and the trip is not cheap. Ted Drewes puts the average shipping cost at $120 to $200 per package, orders go out Monday through Thursday only, and they have to be placed at least 48 hours in advance. Plan the ride before you pick the flavor.
That one page tells you how to shop for the whole trip. The famous cold things cost more to move than to buy, so you either let the maker ship them or you hand them over in person, a cooler riding on the back seat. Everything else should be sealed, flat and happy in a suitcase.
So here is what to do today. Decide first whether the gift leaves in a suitcase or a shipping box, because that one answer cuts the list in half. Suitcase: buy chocolate, coffee, a book or a print, all of which shrug off a checked bag. Box: let the maker do it. For custard, call Ted Drewes at (314) 481-2652 before 5 PM, at least 48 hours ahead, and know that every shipped order runs through its Chippewa location. For a guest who is still in town, skip the shipping fee entirely: grab a pint at Schnucks or Dierbergs on the way to drop them off.
And for the guest still at your kitchen table, there is a gift that never needs a box. A Gus’ pretzel tears soft, and the salt comes off on your thumb. It was twisted by hand at 1820 Arsenal Street, where the family has been hand-twisting them since 1920 and where Gus Jr. is the third generation to bake them.
### What’s a good souvenir from St. Louis?
Something made here that survives the trip. Chocolates from Crown Candy Kitchen, gooey butter cake or coffee from Park Avenue Coffee, cured meats from Volpi, a pretzel from Gus’ for the people still in town. Shelf-stable goods ride in a suitcase. Frozen favorites like Ted Drewes ship overnight from the maker, at an average of $120 to $200 a package, and never within the St. Louis metro. A keychain from the airport gate can come from anywhere. These can’t.
### Four makers who will put the real thing in your hands
Start where the smell hits you at the door, chocolate and warm sugar before you’ve let go of the handle. Crown Candy Kitchen sits at 1401 St. Louis Avenue in Old North St. Louis, a soda fountain and candy counter that also runs an online store of chocolates and handmade creations: assorted chocolate gift boxes and hand-dipped clusters among them. It ships Monday through Thursday, and for custom or large orders the shop asks you to call 314-621-7229. That is the box for the person who can’t come back to the counter.
Volpi is the gift for the relative who judges a city by its deli case: a dry-cured salami, firm in the hand, that slices thin on the cutting board. John Volpi came to America from Milan in 1899, and the company says it has been crafting its foods since 1902, with the family now more than four generations in and still hand-making its products with the methods and recipes John used. The retail store is at 5263 Northrup Avenue, closed Sunday. Its website also has a Buy Online link for the people you can’t drive to.
Gooey butter cake leaves powdered sugar on your fingers and a sticky square on the plate, and it is the sweet this city calls its own; Explore St. Louis calls it St. Louis’ iconic dessert. Park Avenue Coffee lists its gooey butter cake by flavor, from Mom’s Traditional to Triple Chocolate to White Chocolate Raspberry, plus Bake At Home versions for someone who wants the kitchen to smell like it. Its cafes are in Lafayette Square, The Hill, Cortex and at 6th & Olive, and when you ship a gift the shop will put your message on a card in the box.
And Gus’, for the ones still here. The pretzels are made fresh daily, and the shop invites you to stop in and watch them twist. Frozen varieties sit in the freezer case at Gus’ and at St. Louis grocery stores, which makes a bag of them the easiest cold gift in town to hand to a houseguest.
### What ships well, and what should ride home on your lap?
Shelf-stable ships. Frozen is a project. The cooler lid coming off on a porch two states away, the cold breathing out of it: that moment is real, and Ted Drewes sells it, but read the fine print first. A standard cooler holds fifteen 8-ounce concretes or eight pints. Costs vary by delivery ZIP code and package weight, most deliveries arrive by 10:30 AM the next day, and Kansas City and Chicago addresses can now use UPS Ground for lower rates.
For everything else, think about what a checked bag does to a box. Chocolate in a gift box, a bag of coffee beans, a sealed package of cured salami, a book about the Arch, a print rolled in a tube. They travel without drama and land looking like a gift instead of an apology.

### Five questions to ask before you pay for the box
The phone call to the maker is where a good gift is won or lost, and it takes about as long as the hold music at a big-box store. Ask what day it ships, because a box that leaves late in the week can sit in a warehouse over the weekend. Ask what the recipient has to do when it lands: put it in the freezer within the hour, or let it sit on the counter until dinner. Ask whether there is a card, and what it says. Ask what it costs to send to that exact ZIP code, since the custard stand, the candy counter and the coffee roaster all price by where the box is going. And ask the question that tells you the most about a small shop: what do people from here usually send?
The answers come back fast and plain, and you can hear the room behind whoever picks up: a register drawer, a mixer, someone calling an order. That is the part of a local gift you can’t get from a warehouse. The person on the line has packed this box before, and they know which flavor gets the thank-you text.
One more thing to settle before you hang up: who is the box from? A gift that arrives with only a store name on the label reads like a bill. A card with your name and one line about why you picked it, the pretzel shop you walk past or the candy counter your grandmother liked, turns the same box into a phone call back to you.
### Match the gift to the person, not the city
A visitor flying out tomorrow needs flat and sealed: a chocolate box, a bag of beans, a print. Someone who moved away needs the thing they can’t get where they live now, and that is the frozen column, shipped by the maker or handed over at the holidays in a cooler. A homesick relative needs the exact one they remember. Nostalgia does not take substitutions; the second-best brand tastes like a stranger. If you don’t know which one they mean, ask them before you buy, and listen to how fast they answer. That speed is the gift telling you it’s the right one.
Twelve identical client gifts are their own puzzle. Skip anything frozen, because somebody will be out the day it lands, and skip anything with a size. A shelf-stable box from one local maker clears both, and the shop that made it can usually tell you how far ahead to order. ## Your Daughter Can Be the Paid Caregiver in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/home-health-care-cost-st-louis
The discharge papers are on the kitchen table, half out of the plastic bag from the hospital, under the car keys. The house is too quiet, and the phone is in your hand because somebody has to call and set up care. Before you dial, know this: $0. That is what you pay for covered Medicare home health care, the nurse who comes to check the incision and the therapist who walks your mother from the kitchen to the bedroom and back until her legs remember how. You pay nothing for covered home health services, in Medicare’s own words.
The catch lives in one word: covered. Medicare does not pay for 24-hour-a-day care at home, for home meal delivery, or for custodial help with bathing and dressing when that is the only care needed. So the help most families actually picture, somebody in the house in the long afternoon while you are at work, is the part that costs money.
Here is the Missouri rule almost nobody hears in the hospital hallway. If that ongoing help comes through the state’s Home and Community-Based Services program, under its Consumer Directed Services option you can hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian to be the caregiver (Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services). That means the adult daughter already driving over after her shift can be the one who gets paid. The state also says you do not have to be homebound to receive those services. The front door is one phone number: HCBS Intake at 866-835-3505.
Medicare will not bring dinner. The city has a program that does. The St. Louis Area Agency on Aging runs a Senior Nutrition Program, with meals for the elderly and disabled delivered to the home or served at senior centers, and a Senior Minor Home Repair Program, where volunteers make minor home repairs for people 60 or older living in their own home in the City of St. Louis. Think of the loose handrail on the back steps, the one everybody grabs on the way in. The office is at 1520 Market, Room 4086, and the line is (314) 612-5918. In the county? Call anyway. The agency works with the Mid-East Area Agency on Aging to refer city and county residents to the right resources.
### Is home health care cheaper than a nursing home?
Usually, as long as the paid hours stay short. The whole comparison fits on a sticky note on the fridge: nine hours of paid help at a national median of $35 an hour is $315, the same as one day in a semi-private nursing home room. The skilled visits Medicare covers cost you nothing on top of that.
Those are national medians from CareScout, and St. Louis agencies set their own rates, so call two and ask. But the shape holds. A private nursing home room ran $355 a day in the same survey, so that line sits a little higher. Above it, the facility usually wins on price, because the daily rate also buys the building, the meals, the laundry and somebody awake at 3 a.m.
Most families never get near that line, and the two prices are rarely a choice anyway. They run at the same time. Medicare pays the nurse and the therapist for the skilled part after a surgery or a hospital stay, and the family pays, or Medicaid pays, for the hours in between when somebody simply needs to be there.
What to do before the discharge papers are signed: ask the doctor or nurse practitioner to order home health care. Medicare says a provider must see the patient in person, confirm the need and order the care, and a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide it. No order, no visit. Then look the agency up on Medicare’s Care Compare before you say yes to the first name on the list. If the need is ongoing help with daily tasks, call HCBS Intake at 866-835-3505 the same day. On the Illinois side, the Department on Aging’s Senior HelpLine is 1-800-252-8966.
### What are the two types of home care?
Skilled home health, and non-medical home care. Missouri draws the line plainly in its HCBS FAQ: home health is when a doctor orders care for a sudden illness or injury, for instance after surgery, and it is short-term. Home and Community-Based Services is longer-term, hands-on help for older adults and people with disabilities who need ongoing assistance with daily tasks like bathing or getting dressed.
You can hear the difference in the house. Skilled care sounds like a blood pressure cuff tightening and a therapist counting steps. Non-medical care sounds like the shower running, eggs in a pan, the car door on the way to an appointment. Illinois names it bluntly: its Department of Public Health says home services are not medical. Before you ask a company what it charges, ask which kind of help it is licensed to give.
### Does Medicare pay for in-home care in Missouri?
In practice it sounds like a knock at the door, a nurse with a bag and a cold stethoscope, a short visit at the kitchen table, and the door again. So does Medicare pay? Yes, for the skilled kind, and the rules are the same in Illinois because this is a federal benefit. According to Medicare’s coverage page, it covers medically necessary part-time or intermittent skilled nursing care, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, medical social services, and part-time or intermittent home health aide care only if you are also getting a skilled service. If you qualify, you can get unlimited home health visits.
There is a ceiling almost nobody hears about until the second week. Part-time or intermittent means skilled nursing and home health aide services up to 8 hours a day combined, for a maximum of 28 hours a week. For a short time it can go up to 35 hours a week if the provider says it is needed. If your father needs someone in the house all day, Medicare is not the program that solves it, and arguing with the agency will not change that.
The one routine bill is equipment. After you meet the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for Medicare-covered medical equipment, the walker parked by the front door or the hospital bed that takes over the living room. The deductible is adjusted each year; Medicare posts the current figure on its costs page. On a Medicare Advantage plan, Medicare tells you to check with your plan about home health benefits, so call the number on the card before the first visit.
### Who qualifies for home health care services in Missouri?
Two tests, both federal. You must need part-time or intermittent skilled services, and you must be homebound. Homebound does not mean shut in. Medicare says you may leave home for medical treatment or for short, infrequent absences for non-medical reasons, like attending religious services, and you can still get home health care if you attend adult day care. A trip to church does not cost anyone the benefit.
Medicaid’s in-home program runs on different logic. Missouri’s minimum requirements for every HCBS program are being 18 years of age or older, enrolled in Medicaid, and assessed at a nursing facility level of care, which measures how much help someone needs with bathing, dressing and getting around. No homebound test. The point of the program is to keep people living in their homes and part of their community.
While the paperwork is out on the table anyway: an older homeowner in the county may qualify for the senior property tax freeze and the Missouri property tax credit.
### When the savings will not stretch
This is the conversation that happens at the kitchen table after everyone else has gone to bed, the bank statements spread out under the light. Look to Medicaid. In Missouri it is called MO HealthNet, and its Nursing Home Coverage helps residents of nursing homes pay for room and board. On the home side, Missouri’s HCBS programs are funded through Medicaid, and enrollment in Medicaid is one of the minimum requirements, so that application comes first. On the in-home side the state adds a useful rule. If you are approved for Home and Community-Based Services, you will not be required to spend down your MO HealthNet coverage (Missouri Department of Social Services).
There is a limit at home, and the state is honest about it. HCBS has a cap on the amount of services, called the cost maximum, and the monthly cost of caring for someone in a skilled nursing facility serves as the guide for it. Past that point the arithmetic itself points toward the facility. That is not a failure of the family. It is how the program is built.
The price of an hour
### What happens if an elderly person can't afford a nursing home?
Look to Medicaid: in Missouri, MO HealthNet’s Nursing Home Coverage helps nursing home residents pay for room and board, and the in-home HCBS programs are funded through Medicaid. Meanwhile, a covered Medicare home health visit costs you $0. Paid help is where the bill grows: CareScout’s national medians are $35 an hour for a non-medical caregiver and $90 an hour for skilled nursing in the home, against $315 a day for a semi-private nursing home room and $355 for a private one. What moves your number is hours per day, nights and weekends, and whether Medicaid picks up the long-term part. St. Louis agencies set their own rates, so get two quotes in writing.
### Paying a family member, and the Illinois side of the river
Missouri gives families two very different conversations. Under Consumer Directed Services you can hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian. Under the agency model, the caregiver cannot be an immediate family member. Either way, all caregivers must pass a background check. If a daughter is about to cut her hours at work to cover afternoons, that one choice decides whether the afternoons come with a paycheck.
Illinois runs its own version through the Department on Aging. The Community Care Program, established in 1979, is for people 60 years old or older who live in Illinois, have non-exempt assets of $17,500 or less, and have an assessed need for long-term care. The home, the car and the furniture are exempt assets and do not count. The Senior HelpLine, 1-800-252-8966, is where an Illinois family starts.
### How do you check an agency before you hand somebody a key?
Start on Care Compare, then go to the raw record. If you like spreadsheets, here is the raw federal file. Either way, read the ratings for the agencies that actually cover your mother’s address, not the ones with the biggest ads.
Then check the license and the person. Missouri’s home care directory covers all providers licensed and/or certified by the Bureau of Home Care and Rehabilitative Standards. Read it closely: Medicare says a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide the care. Missouri’s Family Care Safety Registry began in 2001, and by law certain care workers must register within 15 days of hire. Illinois keeps its Health Care Worker Registry, which shows information for certified nursing assistants and displays administrative findings of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of property. Five minutes on these pages, before a stranger has the spare key, is worth it.
### Why the agency keeps asking for paperwork
It is not stalling. Medicare pays home health agencies in 30-day units, a system CMS put in place on January 1, 2020 (CMS), so the order, the face-to-face visit and the care plan all have to line up before anything gets paid. Illinois agencies carry one more layer: Illinois is one of the states in Medicare’s Review Choice Demonstration for home health services. When the office calls back for one more signature, that is usually why.
If the hospital stay also left the family without a regular doctor to manage follow-up, deal with that now, not at the next crisis. Our guide to finding a primary care doctor in St. Louis covers how to actually get an appointment.
Sitting in a hospital hallway with a list of names and a phone that is almost dead? Browse home health care across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then check each agency on Care Compare before you agree to the first assessment.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Medicare pay for homecare for seniors?
A.  For the skilled kind, yes: part-time or intermittent nursing, physical and occupational therapy, speech-language pathology and medical social services. The person must need part-time or intermittent skilled services and be homebound, and a provider must order the care. Medicare does not pay for 24-hour-a-day care at home, home meal delivery, or custodial help with bathing and dressing when that is the only care needed.
### Q. Does Medicare pay for in-home care in Missouri?
A.  Yes, for covered home health services, and you pay nothing for them. It is a federal benefit, so the rules match Illinois. Ongoing non-medical help in Missouri usually comes through Medicaid’s Home and Community-Based Services instead; call HCBS Intake at 866-835-3505 to start.
### Q. How much will Medicare pay for home health?
A.  All of it, for covered services: you pay nothing, and if you qualify you can get unlimited home health visits. The routine out-of-pocket cost is equipment. After the Part B deductible, which is adjusted each year, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for covered medical equipment.
### Q. Who qualifies for home health care services in Missouri?
A.  Someone on Medicare who needs part-time or intermittent skilled services, is homebound, has seen a provider in person who orders the care, and uses a Medicare-certified agency. Leaving home for medical treatment, religious services or adult day care does not disqualify anyone.
### Q. How to qualify for home health care in Missouri?
A.  Ask the treating provider for a home health order at the appointment or at discharge. For ongoing help with daily tasks, enroll in MO HealthNet and request services through the state’s HCBS online portal or by calling 866-835-3505.
### Q. What are the two types of home care?
A.  Skilled home health, which a doctor orders after an illness or injury and which is short-term, and non-medical home care, which is longer-term help with bathing, dressing and daily life. Medicare pays for the first. For the second, Missouri’s HCBS programs are funded through Medicaid.
### Q. Can a family member be paid to provide the care?
A.  In Missouri, yes, under Consumer Directed Services, where you can hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian. Under the agency model the caregiver cannot be an immediate family member. All caregivers must pass a background check.

## Why St. Louis Pretzels Were Made to Stick Out of the Bag
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-a-good-bakery-in-st-louis
St. Louis pretzel sticks were made to stick out of the bag. Look at one at the counter on Arsenal Street, coarse salt on top, poking up out of a brown paper bag, while on the other side of a viewing window somebody rolls a rope of dough and twists it by hand. Gus’ Pretzels has made them that way, the same recipe and the same method, since 1920, in the Benton Park neighborhood on the south side, in the shadow of the Anheuser-Busch Brewery.
That stick in the bag is not a design choice. It is a sales trick from the street. According to the shop’s own history, the peddlers who sold Gus’ pretzels on street corners could not show off a twist pretzel hidden in a brown bag, so the stick was made to peek out of the top and let customers see the salty treat. St. Louis grew up on a pretzel built to be seen.
Hold on to that, because it is the whole secret of finding a good bakery here. The good ones let you see the work. A window onto the bench, a case that runs thin by late afternoon, a person at the counter who can tell you what came out of the oven this morning. The ones that hide the work are usually hiding a freezer.
### How do I find a good bakery?
Ask two questions before you buy: what did you bake here this morning, and what comes in frozen? A shop that bakes on site answers both in a sentence. Then buy one plain item, like a croissant, a cake donut or a loaf of white bread. Plain things have nowhere to hide. If the plain thing is good, order the fancy one.
Here is the short version you can use this afternoon. Pick two bakeries close to you. Call both and ask the frozen question out loud; the pause before the answer tells you plenty. Walk into the better one and buy the plainest thing in the case. Tear it open in the car. A real croissant shatters and leaves flakes all over your lap. A tired one bends.
Before you drive across town for a birthday cake, check the shop’s public record too. The City of St. Louis Department of Health keeps food inspection reports issued after May 10, 2012 in its online system, and older ones in an archive (City of St. Louis). Shop out in the county? Try the county’s page too. One bad visit means little. A pattern means something.
Two more things almost nobody checks. A cake from a Missouri home kitchen must say on its label that the food is not inspected by the state or the local health department, so read the sticker before you admire the frosting (Missouri law). And that donut still warm from a grocery store bakery case is taxed at Missouri’s reduced food rate of 1.225%, not 4.225%, warm or not (Missouri Department of Revenue).
### Watch the case, not the sign
Every bakery sign says fresh. The case tells the truth. A shop baking small batches for the day sells down as the hours go, and by late afternoon the trays have gaps, a lone muffin, a smear of powdered sugar where the gooey butter cake used to be. That empty tray is a good sign. A case that looks the same at opening and at closing is usually holding product built to sit.
Frozen dough is not a scandal. Plenty of honest shops bake some items off from frozen, and a good counter person will tell you which ones without flinching. The red flag is the shrug. If nobody behind the counter can say what was mixed in that building, you are buying from a warehouse with a pretty front window.
Then match the shop to the job. The place with the crackly bread is rarely the place with the buttercream roses, and neither is where you go for a dozen donuts at dawn. A decorating shop, a bread bakery, a donut fryer and an old-world Italian bakery are four different trades that happen to share a word.
### The cake St. Louis claims as its own
Gooey butter cake. Its place of origin is St. Louis, and the legend goes like this: during the 1930s a German baker making coffee cake added too much butter to the batter, and rather than throw the mistake away, he sold it by the square (Atlas Obscura). Which baker, and which bakery, nobody has ever settled.
What matters at the counter is this: the name covers more than one cake. It also goes by ooey gooey butter cake, and a bakery square and a home-kitchen pan can be very different things. The top crackles under your fork, the middle sticks to your teeth, and the powdered sugar ends up on your shirt either way. When you order for a party, ask the shop to describe theirs, buy a single square first, and taste it before you commit to a sheet.
### How far ahead should you order a cake?
As soon as you know the date. Small shops run on a few pairs of hands and a fixed amount of oven, and the books fill around the big holidays and the graduation and wedding stretch first. The quiet weeks after the new year are easy. The weekend before a holiday is not.
Put six things on the order ticket, not in somebody’s memory: how many people it feeds, the flavor and filling, any allergy, the pickup window, the deposit, and what happens if you cancel. Custom work is often paid up front because the shop buys ingredients and blocks its time for you. That is fair. Just know the terms before you hand over a card.
### Where the old-world bakeries are
Go to The Hill. It is a fifty-two square block section of the near south side of the city, and the Italian immigrants who built it first arrived in the 1880s to work in the clay mines (The Hill neighborhood association). The neighborhood association’s own business directory lists Vitale’s Bakery at 2130-32 Marconi (business directory). Park once and walk it, with an empty bag for whatever is still warm on the racks.
Then cross back toward Benton Park for the pretzels. Gus’ lists its hours on its own site, and the counter is at 1820 Arsenal Street (Gus’ Pretzels). The shop says its pretzels are made fresh daily, and its own sign-off is the best bakery advice in town: stop in and watch us twist. Grab a bag, then find a cup to go with it at one of the metro’s coffee shops.
Pastry needs a partner. If the coffee at home is the weak link, here is where to buy fresh coffee beans in St. Louis.
### What can a bakery tell you about allergens?
Less than a label would, so ask more. Under the FASTER Act, sesame is the ninth major food allergen, and as of January 1, 2023 it must be labeled as an allergen on packaged foods (U.S. Food & Drug Administration). That rule covers packaged food. A cookie handed to you across the counter on a square of wax paper carries no label at all.
So ask two things. What is in it, and what else runs through the same mixer, fryer and racks. In a small kitchen one bench does everything, and flour hangs in the air like fog. A good shop will tell you flatly that it cannot promise nut-free or wheat-free. That honest answer is worth more than a cheerful one. For a severe allergy, look for a dedicated facility, not a careful one.
### Buying from a home baker in Missouri
The cake lady down the block may be perfectly legal, and perfectly uninspected. Missouri law says a cottage food production operation is not a food service establishment and is not subject to the state’s food code beyond that statute. Its label has to carry the operation’s name and address and a statement that the food is not inspected by the department or the local health department, and it can sell online only when both the baker and the buyer are in Missouri (Missouri Revised Statutes 196.298).
None of that makes a home cake worse. A birthday cake from a home kitchen can taste like the one your grandmother made. It just means the questions are yours to ask: what is in it, how it was stored, and when it was baked. Read the label. If there is no label, ask why.
### Across the river, the rules flip
Drive over the bridge to an Illinois home baker and the paperwork changes completely. In Illinois a cottage food operation has to register with the local health department where it operates, and the person preparing or packaging the food must hold an ANSI-accredited Certified Food Protection Manager certificate. The local health department may charge a registration fee of no more than $50 (University of Illinois Extension). So the home baker in Illinois cleared a bar the home baker in Missouri never had to.
The receipt changes too. Missouri taxes qualifying food at a reduced state rate of 1.225% instead of 4.225%, and the Department of Revenue’s own example is a sweet one: donuts sold in a grocery store bakery department are taxed at the reduced rate even when they are still warm from baking. The catch is the 80% line. In the department’s restaurant example, when food prepared for immediate consumption is more than 80% of total sales, the restaurant should charge the regular tax rate on all its food sales (Missouri Department of Revenue). On the Illinois side, the state eliminated its 1% sales tax on groceries but authorized municipalities and counties to impose a local grocery tax of exactly 1% by ordinance, and the state had received more than 600 of those ordinances (Illinois Department of Revenue). Same warm donut, different line on the receipt.
Hungry for something that came out of an oven this morning? Browse bakeries across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the two closest to you, and call both with the frozen question. Buy the plain thing at whichever one answers it best.
If you run the bakery whose ovens are lit before sunrise, the people asking that question are looking for you. A Gold listing puts your bread, your gooey butter cake and your photos in front of new customers at the moment they are deciding where to drive. See what the Gold plan includes, or start by adding your bakery.
