### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best bakery in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single answer, because bakeries specialize. The shop with the best crusty bread rarely has the best buttercream, and neither one is the best donut. Decide what you need first, then pick the shop that treats that item as its main business. Ask what was baked on site that morning, and judge it on something plain.
### Q. What dessert is St. Louis famous for?
A.  Gooey butter cake. Its place of origin is St. Louis, and the story goes that a German baker making coffee cake in the 1930s added too much butter, then sold the mistake by the square. Nobody has proven which baker it was, so treat the origin story as local legend and the cake itself as required eating.
### Q. What is the best butter cake in St. Louis?
A.  The one that matches the cake you have in mind. The name covers more than one recipe, and the gooey butter cake from a bakery case can be very different from the ooey gooey pan someone brings to a potluck. Buy a single square from two shops, taste them side by side, then order the party size from the winner.
### Q. Is there a bakery on the Hill in Saint Louis, MO?
A.  Yes. The Hill neighborhood association’s business directory lists Vitale’s Bakery at 2130-32 Marconi. The Hill is a fifty-two square block section of the near south side, settled by Italian immigrants who arrived in the 1880s to work the clay mines. Check the bakery’s hours before you go, then park once and explore on foot.
### Q. Where can I find the best donuts in St. Louis?
A.  At whichever shop near you fries earliest and sells out fastest. Donuts are a timing product, not a shelf product, and the best one at dawn may be gone by lunch. Go early, and treat a case that is picked over by mid-morning as a recommendation, not a letdown.
### Q. What cake is famous in St. Louis?
A.  Gooey butter cake, the dense, sticky square the city claims as its own. When you order one, ask the shop to describe its version, because the name covers more than one recipe, and buy a single piece before committing to a whole pan.

## Same Van, Different Rights: Temp Jobs Across the River
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-staffing-agency-in-st-louis
Same vest, same van, different rights. The vest is still creased from the plastic bag. Someone clips a badge to your lanyard and restarts the safety video because nobody in the back row could hear it. Your new boots are already rubbing a heel.
A week later the first pay stub arrives from a company you have never heard of. Here is what nobody at that folding table mentions: which side of the river the dock doors face decides what that company has to put in writing. If your ride out crosses the Mississippi River on the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge, the 400-foot-tall cable-stayed towers sliding past the van window, you have changed rulebooks before the heater warms up.
Take the assignment in Illinois and the state’s Day and Temporary Labor Services Act rides along with you. The Illinois Department of Labor’s required worker notice says the agency shall provide, on a paycheck stub, a detailed statement with contact information about each client company where you worked, the number of hours worked at each worksite each day, your rate of pay for each hour worked, total pay period earnings and all deductions. On the Illinois side, that stub has to explain itself.
Slide that stub across the counter and put a finger on each line: client, hours, rate, deductions. That is only the first of five. Under the same Act:
An Illinois temp agency has to register with the Illinois Department of Labor. Ask to see it, and watch whether the recruiter looks up from the screen.
It cannot charge you for a ride it provides to the worksite. The seat in the agency van, knees against the seat in front, costs you nothing.
It owes you safety training at no cost to you. That video playing twice to the back row is on the agency’s dime, not yours.
And once you pass 720 hours at one client within a 12-month period it has to pay you at least what a comparable direct hire earns. That could be the worker at the next station, swiping in on the client’s own badge.
Each of those is a sentence you can say to a recruiter tomorrow morning, across the desk, with the stub folded in your pocket.
### Is it worth it to go to an employment agency?
Usually yes, as a second channel next to the free city and county job centers, not your only one. An agency earns your time when it staffs the kind of work you do, names the client, the county and the pay rate before it sends you, and puts you on its own payroll. If it asks you for money, hang up and let the phone go dark on the table.
Three moves you can make today, before the next call comes in.
Look the agency up if the job is in Illinois. The Illinois Department of Labor posts its list of currently licensed staffing and temporary labor agencies on the Act’s page, and runs a Day Labor HOTLINE at (877) 314-7052 (toll free). Not on the list? That is your answer. The same department licenses private employment agencies under the Private Employment Agency Act and publishes a list of suspended and revoked agencies, so an office across the river that feels wrong gets checked there too.
Get the county’s own desk right on the Missouri side. The Missouri Department of Higher Education and Workforce Development announced that the St. Louis County Job Center moved from The Crossings at Northwest to 6347 Plymouth Ave., Room 206, St. Louis, MO 63133, phone 314-377-0445. Hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on Friday, and it offers a full range of no-cost employment and training services to Missouri job seekers, including people who are unemployed or underemployed. If an old flyer on the fridge still says The Crossings, throw it out.
Read the first stub at the kitchen table, line by line. On an Illinois assignment, look for the client’s contact information, your hours at each worksite each day and every deduction, and ask about any line that is missing. On a Missouri assignment, ask the agency to list in writing anything it will deduct from your pay. A desk that hesitates over either request has told you something.
### What an Illinois pay stub has to show you
Flatten it on the counter under the kitchen light, because on the Illinois side the paper has a checklist behind it. The Illinois worker notice says each agency shall post the notice in an area easily accessible to all workers at each work location or branch office, so look for it on the wall while you wait for your badge.
Two more lines on that poster are worth a photo on your phone. The agency shall also provide each worker an annual earnings summary within a reasonable time after the preceding calendar year. And temporary workers have the right to request that their agency issue weekly, bi-weekly or semi-monthly checks. If your stub reads like a riddle, the same notice says you can file a complaint or report a violation with the Department of Labor by calling toll-free at 1-877-314-7052.
### Gear, the ride and the safety class: who pays
Turn the pay stub over and look for the deductions, because this is where a first week quietly shrinks. On both sides of the river, federal rule 29 CFR 531.35 says that when an employer requires an employee to provide tools of the trade specifically required for the employer’s particular work, there is a violation of the Act in any workweek when the cost of those tools cuts into the minimum or overtime wages required.
The math fits on the kitchen table. The Missouri Department of Labor lists the Missouri minimum wage at $15.00 per hour, and the Illinois Minimum Wage Law guarantees $15.00 per hour for workers 18 and older. Both are adjusted over time, so check the pages before you count on the figure. Multiply your hours by the floor, subtract every gear line, and see what is left.
Illinois goes further on three costs a temp feels in the body.
The ride. The Illinois worker notice says that if your agency or the client company provides transportation to a worksite, or refers you to a particular person, company or carpool that provides it, you cannot be charged for that transportation. The Department’s FAQ puts it plainly: staffing agencies and their agents are not allowed to charge for rides.
Meals and gear. The same FAQ says the Act prohibits excessive deductions for meal and equipment charges.
The safety class. On or before your first day working at a client company each year, the agency must give you general safety training for that worksite, according to the Illinois worker notice. The training will cover all known and existing hazards, it is provided at no cost to you, and you must be paid for time spent in training. That safety video you sat through twice? On the Illinois side, those minutes go on the clock.
Back on the Missouri side, same creased vest, same early ride in, the floor you lean on is the federal gear rule and the state’s complaint line. Missouri’s Division of Labor Standards takes calls at 573-751-3403 and says that if you feel you are not being paid the correct wages, you can file a minimum wage complaint. Illinois wage questions go to the Illinois minimum wage toll-free hotline at (800) 478-3998.
Nothing to do with jobs, but if the kitchen sink backs up the night before your first shift, here is a plumber.
### 720 hours: the number to keep on your phone
Count shifts the way you count down to a weekend. Per the Illinois Department of Labor FAQ, Section 42(a) requires a temp assigned to one third-party client for more than 720 hours in a 12-month period to be paid at least the straight-time hourly rate of the lowest-paid comparable worker the client hired directly. The FAQ adds “substantially similar benefits,” or the “hourly average cash equivalent of the actual cost of the benefits.”
So keep a running count in your phone’s notes app, shift by shift. The person on the next line over, wearing the client’s logo instead of a visitor badge, may be the number your pay is measured against. When your count crosses 720, ask the agency in writing what rate it is now paying you and why.
### Five questions for any desk, on either side of the river
Ask these in the first ten minutes, on either bank of the Mississippi, with a pen in your hand and the answers going on paper. You are far from alone in that chair: the American Staffing Association reports that nearly 2.2 million temporary and contract employees worked for America’s staffing companies during an average week.
1. Is this assignment in Missouri or Illinois, and what county? The answer tells you which rulebook you are under. 2. Who is the client and what is the rate? An agency that will not say either before dispatch cannot be judged. 3. Temp, temp-to-hire or direct placement? In temp work the agency is your employer of record and the job ends when the client says so. In temp-to-hire, get the hours to conversion and the conversion pay in writing. In direct placement, the client hires you from day one and pays the agency for the search. 4. Am I on your payroll, or are you calling me a contractor? For shift work under someone’s supervision, you should be on the agency’s payroll. 5. What happens if the first assignment does not fit? Good desks re-place people, on whichever side of the river the next opening is. Weak ones stop returning calls.
Worth knowing: federal EEOC guidance explains that placed workers typically qualify as employees of the staffing firm, the client they are assigned to, or both, so neither may discriminate against you.
Want a desk that already knows which side of the river your shift is on? Browse employment agencies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two of them, and ask both the county question first.
If you run a staffing desk that fills shifts in Missouri and the Metro East, the workers and the employers looking for you are asking Google and ChatGPT before they pick up the phone. See who AI names instead of you, then put your agency on the directory so more customers on both sides of the desk can call you.
### The no-cost desks on both sides of the river
Start with the free option before any private desk, and bring a folder so you are not digging through a bag at the front counter. In the city, the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment, known as SLATE, lists its Job Center at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor. The Job Center is open Monday through Friday, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except on Wednesdays, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. SLATE calls registering at MoJobs the first step for job seekers, and says registering with MoJobs and updating your profile before you visit will save you time at the Job Center. Questions go to (314) 589-8000.
SLATE is more than a job board. If you are 17 to 24 and live in the city, ask about YouthBuild, which SLATE describes as a program for disadvantaged City of St. Louis youth ages 17-24 to earn pay, help build affordable housing and learn leadership skills: real sawdust, with a paycheck. It also lists registered apprenticeship opportunities in the City of St. Louis, where you earn while you learn and receive paid training. Start on the SLATE page, or use the state’s Missouri Job Centers directory to find the closest office.
Live or work on the Illinois side? Start with Illinois workNet. These offices feed private agencies more than they compete with them: a certificate or a rebuilt resume is what lets a recruiter place you at a better rate.
Looking for care work, or hiring it for a parent? Our guide to choosing home health care in St. Louis walks the same ground from the family’s side.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do employment agencies cost?
A.  For a job seeker, the answer should be nothing; the hiring employer pays. Employers pay either an hourly markup over the worker’s pay rate on temp assignments or a one-time fee on direct hires. On an Illinois temp assignment, the agency also cannot charge you for the ride to the work site.
### Q. Can I just walk into an employment agency?
A.  Sometimes, but call first. Many agencies want an online application on file before an in-person meeting, and some run appointment-only offices. If you get an appointment, bring your photo ID and work-eligibility documents so the paperwork does not hold up your first shift.
### Q. Is it cheaper to hire through a temp agency?
A.  Cheaper per hour, almost never. Cheaper overall, sometimes, because the markup covers payroll taxes, screening and the ability to end an assignment without a severance conversation. In Illinois, an employer should also plan for the 720-hour equal pay rule on long assignments.
### Q. What is the average cost per hire for recruiters?
A.  One benchmark you will see is SHRM’s benchmarking report figure of $4,129 average cost per hire. Treat it as a rough anchor, not your number. Add internal and external recruiting costs over a period, divide by hires made, then weigh that against what an open seat costs you each week.
### Q. What are some good staffing agencies in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  There is no single best one, and published lists go stale fast. Sort by fit instead: firms that staff your exact function, name client industries and put you on their own payroll. If the work is in Illinois, check the agency against the Illinois Department of Labor’s registered list before your first shift.
### Q. What companies are currently hiring in St. Louis?
A.  Openings change fast, so use sources that refresh rather than a list inside an article. MoJobs carries job postings and hiring events, Illinois workNet is the place to start on the Illinois side, and the Missouri Economic Research and Information Center names some of the top private employers for the region: Washington University, Boeing, Barnes Jewish Hospital, General Motors and St. Louis University.

## 51,781 St. Louis City Residents Live in a Pharmacy Desert
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-pharmacy-in-st-louis
How far is the nearest pharmacy counter from your front door, and could you get there tonight without a car?
Most people never have to answer that until the orange bottle in the kitchen cabinet rattles with two pills left. Then it matters a lot. The store down the road may still have its lights on and its cooler humming, while the metal gate over the pharmacy window is already pulled down.
Here is the number nobody prints on the drugstore ads. In a geospatial analysis of pharmacy deserts in St. Louis City, researchers from the City of St. Louis Department of Health, GreaterHealth Pharmacy & Wellness and Washington University School of Medicine found 51,781 residents, 17.2 percent of the city, living in a pharmacy desert. Their definition is blunt: more than 1 mile from a pharmacy, or more than half a mile in a tract where at least 20 percent of households lack vehicle access. Black residents made up 80 percent of that desert population, against 43 percent citywide.
Then the study admits what its own map could not see. It did not account for home delivery. That blind spot is the most useful thing on this page, because it is the first question to ask any pharmacy you are thinking about: will you bring it to me?
### How do I know which pharmacy to go to?
Sort it on five things, in this order. Does your plan count the pharmacy as in-network? Can you reach it in a normal week, or will it reach you? Is the counter, not just the store, open when you are free? Will a pharmacist there spend five minutes with you? And what is the cash price on the day your plan says no?
Network status comes first because it moves the number more than anything you can say at the register. Your copay is set by your plan’s contract, not the store manager. Call the member number on the back of your card, sit through the hold music, and ask which pharmacies near you are in-network. Then ask the pharmacy itself to run a test claim on one prescription so you see the real price before you move anything.
Then make the money move most people never make. Before the tech behind the counter runs your card, ask one question out loud: what is the cash price? You only learn that number if you ask before the receipt prints, and then you can pick the lower of the two. If you fill on the Illinois side, read this part twice. The Illinois Department of Insurance explains that under its Prescription Drug Affordability Act, a consumer must not pay more for a drug than the least costly option. That one line is worth a screenshot if you fill prescriptions on the Illinois side.
Reach is the test people skip and regret. A counter three miles off that you can only get to by car at 5:40 p.m. is worse than one that drives the bag to your porch. Delivery exists here. GreaterHealth Pharmacy & Wellness, which took part in the study, says it offers free home delivery services for all of its patients. Ask every pharmacy on your shortlist the same question, then ask a pharmacist to review everything you take and flag overlaps. A counter that does that on a calm afternoon is the one you want on a bad night.
### How do you move a prescription without losing a week?
You know the sound: the drive-thru speaker crackles, and the voice on the other end says they never got the prescription. Most of that is avoidable. Call the pharmacy you are moving to, not the one you are leaving. Read them the drug name, the strength and the prescription number printed small on the label, and they request the transfer themselves. For an ordinary maintenance medicine that is usually a same-day errand.
Controlled substances work differently. Under a DEA final rule, electronic prescriptions for schedule II-V controlled substances can move between registered retail pharmacies for initial filling, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis. It is one move, not a standing arrangement, so ask both pharmacies before you switch.
Missouri pharmacies also report schedule II, III and IV dispensing to the state’s prescription drug monitoring program. That is not an obstacle to switching. It is why the person in the white coat may ask a question that feels personal.
### Is the counter in a drugstore the same as the pharmacy?
Look past the reading glasses and the candy rack to the back wall, where someone in a white coat is counting pills by fives on a plastic tray. That is the pharmacy. Not quite the same as the drugstore, and the gap is the license. The drugstore is the retail business: the aisles, the greeting cards, the candy by the register. The pharmacy is the licensed prescription department behind the counter. That same license sits inside grocery stores, big-box stores, clinics, hospital outpatient windows, independents and mail-order operations, which is why the two words are not interchangeable.
On the Missouri side, start with the state’s licensee search. Across the river, Illinois offers Check a License through the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.
Ordering online? The FDA’s BeSafeRx pages show how to locate a state-licensed online pharmacy and spot the warning signs of sites that only look like one.
### Why are drugstores so expensive?
Because most of the number on the register screen, the one that makes your stomach drop, was set several steps before the box reached the shelf. Pharmacy benefit managers, the middlemen between your plan, the drug makers and the counter, decide a lot of it. The Federal Trade Commission laid out how that works in its interim staff report on prescription drug middlemen and a second interim staff report.
Which side of the river you fill on changes a few things. Missouri’s Department of Revenue says a drug legally dispensed by a licensed pharmacist on a practitioner’s written authority is exempt from sales tax. Shopping in Illinois? Read the Illinois Department of Revenue answer on medicine before you assume it works the same way.
Off-topic, but if the bathroom outlet trips every time the hair dryer runs, here are St. Louis electricians.
On Medicare, Medicare.gov sets a ceiling on how high a Part D deductible can go, adjusted each year, and once your out-of-pocket spending reaches the yearly limit you pay nothing out-of-pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.
So get a real answer in ten minutes. Call two or three counters, ask the cash price for the exact drug, strength and quantity, and hold those numbers against your copay. If someone offers a discount card, ask whether that price will count toward your plan’s deductible before you pay it.
### What happens if your pharmacy closes?
Your prescriptions do not vanish, but the warning you get depends on which state you are standing in when the paper sign goes up on the door. Illinois requires a closing pharmacy to notify customers at least 15 days before the closing date and say where their records will be kept, under Illinois Administrative Code section 1330.790. Missouri’s rule, 20 CSR 2220-2.015, has the pharmacy send written notice to the State Board of Pharmacy within fifteen days after it stops operating.
Keep a printed medication list in a kitchen drawer, with each drug, strength and prescriber on it. If the counter you rely on goes dark, that sheet of paper is what lets a new pharmacist pick up where the old one left off. And if you are coordinating refills for a parent across town, our guide to home health care in St. Louis covers that job.
### When is the counter actually open?
Store hours and pharmacy hours are two different numbers. The front door can stay unlocked late while the counter closed hours earlier. Ask the specific question when you call: is the pharmacy counter open, or only the store? Drive-thru windows often keep their own shorter hours too. Write the counter’s closing time on a sticky note inside the cabinet door, right next to the bottles, so nobody in the house has to guess at night.
Treat any list of overnight pharmacies you find online as out of date, and check it by phone the same day for the exact address you plan to drive to. If it is late and you are holding a new prescription, ask the prescriber’s office or the urgent care to send it somewhere open right now instead of to your usual counter.
### What to bring the first time you walk up to a new counter
Bring the bottles themselves, in a grocery bag, not a list from memory. The labels carry the prescription numbers, the prescriber’s name and the strength, which is everything the new pharmacy needs to call the old one. Bring your insurance card and, if you have Medicare, the separate drug plan card that people forget lives in a different slot of the wallet.
Add the things that never show up on a label: the vitamin you take with breakfast, the allergy pill from the grocery aisle, the cream your dermatologist handed you as a sample. A pharmacist can only flag an overlap they can see. Then ask three questions before you leave. Who do I call after hours? Will you text me when a refill is ready? Can you line my refills up so they come due on the same day? A counter that says yes to the last one turns four trips a month into one, and on a sleeting January afternoon that is the whole point.
Not sure who should be holding your prescriptions? Browse drugstores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the two closest and ask each one three things: do you deliver, when does the counter close, and what does my prescription cost without insurance? The same questions about hours and who answers the phone apply on the animal side of the counter too - see choosing a vet for routine care.
If you run an independent pharmacy where a person still picks up the phone, the neighbors comparing counters are asking Google and ChatGPT before they ever call. See who AI names instead of you, then put your counter on the directory so more customers find the pharmacy that answers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are pharmacies and drugstores the same thing?
A.  A drugstore is the retail store; the pharmacy is the licensed prescription department inside it. Plenty of pharmacies sit inside grocery stores, big-box stores, clinics and hospitals instead. The license belongs to the counter, not the aisles.
### Q. Which is better for prescriptions, CVS or Walgreens?
A.  Neither wins as a rule. The better one for you is whichever your plan treats as in-network, keeps counter hours you can reach, and staffs a pharmacist willing to review everything you take. Run those checks on both, plus any independent nearby, and ask each whether it delivers.
### Q. Which drugstore is cheaper, CVS or Walgreens?
A.  It shifts by drug, by plan and over time, so a printed answer goes stale fast. Get a current one yourself: call both, ask the cash price for the exact drug, strength and quantity, then compare it with your copay.
### Q. Which pharmacy is usually the cheapest?
A.  There is no permanent cheapest. Price depends on your plan’s contract, the drug, whether a generic exists, and any discount program in play. Price one specific prescription at two or three places, including an independent, and re-check whenever your plan or your prescription changes.
### Q. Are local pharmacies cheaper than CVS?
A.  Sometimes on cash prices, often not on insured copays, because the copay is set by your plan rather than the store. The NCPA Digest counted 18,960 independent community pharmacies nationally as of July 2025, and many compete on delivery and time with the pharmacist rather than price alone. Price the exact drug at both.
### Q. Why are drugstores so expensive?
A.  Most of the price is set before the box reaches the shelf, by contracts between your plan, the pharmacy benefit manager and the drug maker. The counter you stand at controls less of it than it seems.
### Q. Who are the big 3 pharmacies?
A.  Most people mean the national retail chains, starting with CVS and Walgreens. The bigger three for your wallet are the pharmacy benefit managers that sit behind most prescription plans, which is why your copay can differ from one counter to the next.
### Q. What is the 5 rule in pharmacy?
A.  People usually mean the five rights of medication safety: the right patient, medication, time, dose and route. It is a safety habit built into nursing training, and it makes a fair checklist for you at the counter too.
### Q. Are there any 24 hour pharmacies in St. Louis?
A.  Overnight counters come and go, so any list you find online is likely out of date. Call the exact location the same day and ask whether the pharmacy counter runs around the clock or only the store. If it is late, ask your prescriber to send the prescription somewhere open now.

## The Price Is on the Last Page: St. Louis Consultant Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-business-consultant-costs-in-st-louis
Page one is your logo. Page two is a cloud of words: growth, alignment, strategy. Then come the arrows, the circles, the methodology with a trademark symbol. The price is on the last page, under a heading that says “Investment,” next to the word “retainer” and nothing that says what the retainer buys.
Why does the number come last? Why does a monthly fee show up with no hours, no deliverable and no end date attached? Would you ever quote one of your own jobs that way? That’s not how good work gets priced. It’s how unposted pricing works, and it only holds up as long as nobody compares.
So compare. Consulting Success, which studied nearly 1,000 consultants, calls $100 an hour “a common starting point” for a consultant’s rate. Now fold that proposal into your bag and take it to someone in St. Louis with nothing to sell you.
Downtown, the Missouri SBDC in the St. Louis Region works out of the Lammert Building at 911 Washington Ave., Ste. 815. The St. Louis Business Empowerment Center calls itself “St. Louis’ resource hub for small business success,” registration is free, and it offers live, on-demand and one-on-one training with an SMB coach; it counts 1000+ small businesses launched since 2010. Across the river, the Illinois SBDC for the Metro East at SIUE provides confidential, no-cost advising to entrepreneurs and existing business owners.
Lay the last page on their desk. Ask one question: what is this retainer buying that I couldn’t have asked about here first?
### How much should I pay for a business consultant?
Expect hourly quotes to start around $100, and expect most serious offers to come as a project price instead of a clock. In the Consulting Success study of nearly 1,000 consultants, 30% charge project-based, 29% hourly, 16% on a monthly retainer, 15% value-based and 10% daily. So the hourly rate you’ve been hunting for is the answer for fewer than a third of the people you’ll talk to.
The rate also moves. The same study found 79% of consultants are actively looking to increase their fees. Treat any number you see, including this one, as an opening position. The price that matters is the one tied to a single decision in your business: what will it cost to find out why the margin slipped, and what will it cost to fix it? Ask for those two prices separately. A consultant who can’t split them hasn’t scoped your job yet.
### The no-cost first hour most owners skip
Before you sign anything, sit down with someone who isn’t selling you a contract. On the Missouri side, that Washington Avenue SBDC office answers at 314-241-1005. Call and ask what a first session costs and how to sign up. The Missouri SBDC says all one-on-one counseling is confidential. In the Metro East, the SIUE center’s advising is no-cost, and its sessions may include business plans, financing options, marketing and management. And according to the SBA, SCORE mentors offer area-specific advice at no cost, by email, telephone and video.
Here’s how to use that hour well. Bring last year’s numbers, even if they live in a shoebox: what came in, what went out, and the three biggest bills. Write one sentence that names the problem in plain words, like “we’re busier than ever and keeping less.” Ask the advisor to tell you which part of that sentence is a do-it-yourself fix and which part needs a paid specialist. Then leave with a written list of the questions you’d ask that specialist.
That list is the most valuable thing you’ll carry into a paid meeting. It turns “help me grow” into “price this specific problem,” and that one change is what keeps a four-figure invoice from turning into a five-figure one. Sometimes the no-cost session answers the question outright. Then you just kept the fee.
None of this replaces a good paid engagement. Advising at no cost tends to be general and moves at the speed of a busy calendar, while a consultant you hire is accountable to a deliverable and a date. The point is order: sharpen the question for nothing, then pay someone to answer it.
### What is the rule of 3 in consulting?
Two different things wear that name, and only one touches your invoice. The one you’ll hear most is a rule of thumb for setting a rate in thirds: part of the hourly number is the consultant’s actual pay, part covers their expenses, and part absorbs the admin, the unbilled hours and the clients who never pay. The other version is a multiplier, where a former employee charges a few times what they used to earn by the hour doing similar work.
Both exist because working for yourself costs money a paycheck hides. The IRS sets the self-employment tax rate at 15.3%, made of 12.4% for social security and 2.9% for Medicare, and an independent pays for their own health insurance, software and retirement out of the same rate they quote you. You know this math already if you’ve ever run a side business out of a truck cab or a spare bedroom.
Why should you care about the seller’s arithmetic? Because it tells you what a very low quote means. Someone far under the going rate is subsidizing you from other income, is brand new, or is running a practice that won’t be around when the work is half done. That last one is the expensive kind of cheap, because you end up paying a second person to finish the first person’s job.
### Why the hour on the invoice isn’t the hour they work
A consultant doesn’t bill forty hours a week, any more than a plumber bills for the drive between jobs. Consulting Success tells consultants to start from the market salary for their role and convert it to an hourly figure based on realistic billable hours, not a full 40-hour week. The rest of the week goes to proposals, scoping calls, chasing invoices and pitches that never close. Your hourly rate pays for those too.
So the red flags run in both directions. Someone billing a premium rate who can’t name three recent jobs that look like yours is selling a brand, not a result. Someone quoting a bargain rate who swears they bill every hour of every week is describing a calendar that almost nobody in this trade really has. The honest middle sounds boring: a clear scope, a clear price, a clear end date.
### How to find a good business consultant?
Start by assuming the title guarantees nothing. Anyone can print the card, so the vetting is on you, and it takes about an hour. Ask for three clients from the last two years whose business looked like yours, then actually call them: what changed, how long it took, and what it cost. Ask who will do the work, by name. Ask the consultant to describe your problem back to you before quoting anything. If the description is generic, the plan will be too.
Somewhere between the second job and the spreadsheet, book the haircut you keep pushing back. St. Louis hair salons fill up when you wait.
Ask what they don’t take on, because someone who accepts every job accepts yours badly. Watch for the pitch that leans on screenshots of other people’s revenue. Real operators talk about your numbers, not their lifestyle. If hiring is the real problem under the problem, that’s its own project with its own economics, and how to choose a staffing agency walks through that side.
Then start small on purpose. A short paid diagnostic that ends in a written finding tells you more about a consultant than any reference call, and it caps what you can lose at a number you already agreed to. The good ones offer it before you ask. The ones who need a six-month commitment before they’ll look at your books are telling you something.
The St. Louis price spread
On one end, the Illinois SBDC for the Metro East at SIUE advises at no cost, and SBA says SCORE mentors offer advice at no cost. On the other, Consulting Success calls $100 an hour a common starting point, and most consultants quote by the project instead. What moves your number is scope, how fast you need it, and whether you are buying a diagnosis or the hands to carry out the fix.
### What should the agreement say before you sign?
A retainer that doesn’t list what it buys is a monthly bill for a promise. Five things, and you can check them over one cup of coffee. The deliverable, written as an object you could hold: a pricing model, a hiring plan, a documented month-end close, never “strategic guidance.” The date it lands. Who does the work, by name, and how many of that person’s hours you’re buying. The payment terms, and what triggers each payment. And the exit: how either side ends it, and what you keep when they do.
That last one matters more than the rate. Ownership of the work product should be written down, not assumed, and so should confidentiality in both directions. If a consultant tells you to grow into a bigger space, read the lease before you take the advice; what leasing commercial space here really involves covers the fine print most advice skips.
### The consultant across the table is an owner too
Most of the consultants you’ll meet aren’t firms. They’re one person with a laptop bag and a parking receipt, working the same late nights you are. The enemy here isn’t them, and it isn’t you. It’s the process: a market where prices hide, hype stands in for proof, and the good independent operator is just as hard to find as the right client. The fix on both sides is the same. Prices you can see. Work you can check. A name you can find when the problem finally gets loud.
Price the problem before you pay for the solution. Browse business management consultants across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the first three the same two questions: what would the diagnosis cost, and what would the fix cost.
If you’re the consultant who quotes the diagnosis before the fix, the owners searching tonight can’t hire you if they can’t find you. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a reasonable consulting fee?
A.  Reasonable is set by scope, not by an hourly figure. The same consultant may quote an hourly rate, a day rate, a project price or a monthly retainer for the same work, and those numbers don’t compare to each other. Ask what is being delivered, by when, and what happens if it runs long. A fee tied to a written deliverable and a date is the reasonable one.
### Q. Is $100 an hour good for consulting?
A.  It’s a normal place to start, not a steal and not a scam. Consulting Success calls $100 an hour a common starting point, and notes that only 29% of consultants still bill hourly. Remember the consultant pays the 15.3% self-employment tax and their own insurance out of that rate, and can’t bill every hour of the week.
### Q. What is the rule of 3 in consulting?
A.  Usually it means splitting a rate into thirds: one part is the consultant’s pay, one covers expenses, and one absorbs admin, unbilled time and clients who don’t pay. A second version is a multiplier on an old employee hourly rate. Neither is a law. Both explain why an independent’s rate looks high next to a paycheck.
### Q. How to find a good business consultant?

Call three past clients whose business looked like yours, have the consultant describe your problem back before quoting, confirm by name who does the work, and buy a small paid diagnostic before any long contract. ## Four Roommates Is One Too Many in St. Louis City Rentals
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renting-an-apartment-in-st-louis
The key sticks in the deadbolt, then gives. Fresh paint. Your footsteps too loud on bare floors. The leasing agent flips on the bathroom fan to prove it works, and it rattles like a coffee can full of screws. You’re already measuring for the couch in your head, and the application is waiting on a clipboard by the door.
Four friends splitting this place four ways? In the City of St. Louis, that’s one roommate too many.
The city’s rule is one blunt sentence: no more than three unrelated persons may live in the same dwelling. Most renters never hear it until the lease is signed. So before you touch that clipboard, ask for one piece of paper. In the City of St. Louis, a rental unit must have a Certificate of Inspection before anyone moves in. The city says 100% of its property sits in a Housing Conservation District, and Ordinance No. 71835 requires an inspection there that checks for minimal interior building code violations and minimum exterior standards.
That same inspection sets the number of people who may safely live in the unit. Ask for the paper before you ask about the pool. Know the head count before the deposit leaves your account, not after.
### How much do apartments cost in St. Louis?
It swings by ZIP code more than by building. HUD’s small-area fair market rents for the St. Louis metro, adjusted each year, list a one-bedroom at $800 in 63111 and $1,480 in 63108. Same city. The gap between those two is a car payment, every month.
Use the HUD figure as your gut check when a listing looks too good or too steep, then get the real number from the building. For the slower picture, the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey is the premier source of detailed information about the nation’s people and housing, and a survey of every lease in a county rarely matches what a listing app shows tonight.
### Before you sign: the city paper, the head count, the photos
Start with the certificate. Ask the leasing office to show you the unit’s Certificate of Inspection, the paper described on the city’s residential occupancy page. Rental units need a reinspection every three years or upon a change in occupancy, so a new tenant moving in is exactly the moment a fresh one is due. A landlord who gets caught with a resident already living in a unit without a current certificate pays $200 for the application instead of $120. If the office goes vague, that’s your answer. Want to ask the city directly? The Building Division answers at (314) 622-3313, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:45 PM, at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 426.
Then count heads. If you’re moving in with people you aren’t related to, remember that the limit of three unrelated persons in one dwelling comes from the city, not the landlord. Two couples sharing a duplex is a different conversation than four college friends, so ask before you apply. If the unit sits in a St. Louis County town instead, call that town’s city hall and ask whether it runs its own occupancy inspection.
Next, the move-in photos. Walk every room with your phone the day you get the keys: the stained carpet corner, the cracked outlet cover, the window that won’t latch. Email the photos to the landlord that evening so they carry a timestamp. In Missouri, those pictures are what stand between you and a deposit you’ll never see again, and the deposit itself is capped at two months’ rent.
Last, read the five clauses that do the damage before you read the rent: the auto-renewal, the notice-to-vacate window, who pays which utility, the pet and parking add-ons, and the early-termination formula. A lease that renews on its own unless you give sixty days’ written notice can quietly cost you a month you never planned to pay.
### On the tour, test it like you already live there
A showing is staged to feel good, so don’t just look. Turn on the kitchen tap and the shower at the same time and watch what the pressure does. Flip every switch. Open the cabinet under the sink and breathe in; a musty smell there tells you more than the fresh paint upstairs. Run the window unit or the central air for a full minute, because a St. Louis August will find every weak spot in it. Check your phone’s signal in the bedroom, not just the lobby, and look at the windows for painted-shut sashes and missing screens.
Then ask the questions that never make the listing: where packages go, where you park when the lot is full, how maintenance requests get logged, and who answers the phone at night when the water heater lets go. Write the answers down while you stand there. You’ll compare three buildings later, and memory blurs them together by the drive home.
### What is the landlord checking when you apply?
Bring photo ID, recent pay stubs or an offer letter, a bank statement, and contact details for your last two landlords. The office will pull a credit or tenant-screening report. If they turn you down because of what’s in it, federal law requires a notice of your right to get a free copy of that report from the company that supplied it, so you can dispute an error. Federal law says the Federal Trade Commission is authorized to enforce compliance with those requirements.
Screening has limits. The federal Fair Housing Act bars housing discrimination because of race or color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status or disability, and you can file a complaint with HUD. On the Missouri side, the Missouri Commission on Human Rights enforces the state’s own ban on housing discrimination; across the river, the Illinois Department of Human Rights investigates discrimination in housing.
### What should you read in the lease before you sign it?
Check how a month-to-month lease ends, because that is where most surprises live. In Missouri, either side can end a month-to-month tenancy with one month’s notice in writing under RSMo 441.060.
Illinois works differently. There, a landlord can end a holdover tenancy with 30 days’ written notice under 735 ILCS 5/9-207, and a landlord chasing unpaid rent must give a written demand of not less than 5 days first under 735 ILCS 5/9-209.
Side note from a neighbor: the fitness room in the brochure is two treadmills and a fan. Here’s a better gym near your new place.
Old brick has its own rule. If the building went up before 1978, federal law requires the landlord to disclose known lead-based paint hazards before you sign a lease, per the EPA disclosure rule. In a city full of century-old flats, that form should be in your packet. If it isn’t, ask.
And reset one expectation: your leverage at renewal is the lease term you negotiate going in. Illinois goes as far as barring home rule units from controlling the amount of rent charged, under the Rent Control Preemption Act. Ask for a longer term if the rent is one you can live with.
### How much deposit can a landlord hold, and when do you get it back?
In Missouri, a landlord may not demand a deposit above two months’ rent. Within thirty days after the tenancy ends, they must return it in full or send you an itemized list of damages along with the balance. You have the right to be present at the move-out inspection, and a landlord who wrongfully withholds money owes you twice the amount wrongfully withheld, under RSMo 535.300. Show up for that walkthrough with your move-in photos open on your phone.
Illinois runs a tighter clock. Under the Security Deposit Return Act, a landlord who wants to keep part of the deposit for damage must send an itemized statement within 30 days of the date you moved out. Without it, the full deposit is due within 45 days. In a building or complex of 25 or more units, the Security Deposit Interest Act requires the landlord to pay interest on the deposit.
Shortlist two buildings, then make one phone call each. Browse apartment buildings across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call the two closest to your commute, and ask what opens up soon and whether the unit’s Certificate of Inspection is current.
If you’re the landlord, the property manager or the leasing office, renters are searching for exactly what you have. Put your units where they look and get more customers through the door before the next vacancy sits empty.
### What are your rights if the furnace quits and nobody calls back?
January, the radiator stone cold, your breath fogging in the kitchen. Both states give you a narrow repair-and-deduct remedy, and both are easy to blow. Missouri’s version, RSMo 441.234, only applies after six consecutive months of lawful residence with all rent paid, for a condition that violates a local housing or building code. The landlord gets fourteen days after your written notice. The repair has to cost less than three hundred dollars or one-half of the rent, whichever is greater, and you can’t deduct more than one month’s rent in any twelve-month period.
Illinois sets the ceiling at the lesser of $500 or one-half of the monthly rent under the Residential Tenants’ Right to Repair Act, and the notice to the landlord goes in writing.
What you should not do is simply stop paying rent. That’s the fastest road to an eviction filing that follows you through screening reports for years. Put every repair request in writing and get advice before you act. The Missouri Attorney General publishes a landlord-tenant guide, and Missouri Legal Services provides free legal help to Missourians.
### Why an empty unit gives you room to ask
The leasing agent across the desk is working on a thinner margin than most renters assume. The National Apartment Association says only 6 cents of every dollar of rent comes back as profit to owners. An empty month hurts them. That’s your opening to ask, politely, for a waived fee, a parking spot or a longer lease at today’s rate.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where do the wealthy live in St. Louis?
A.  If rent is your yardstick, HUD’s ZIP-level benchmark is a quick map. It lists a one-bedroom at $1,410 in 63105 and $1,480 in 63108, against $800 in 63111. Higher benchmarks track pricier blocks, and for a renter that is the number that matters.
### Q. Where is Millionaires Row, St. Louis?
A.  I could not find that nickname on an official city page, so here is the closest thing on the record. The City of St. Louis says that in the late 1870s, a 1400-acre park west of town began to attract the area’s wealthy elite, and the Central West End developed Westmoreland and Portland places, along with Forest Park Terrace, all grand and lavish in style. Apartments sit within a short walk of those gates.
### Q. How much does an apartment building usually cost?
A.  There’s no usable national average, because land, unit count, construction type and the rent the units actually produce set the price locally. A four-family in south city and a garden complex in the county are not the same asset. Serious buyers price per unit against nearby sales, then confirm with an appraisal and a lender.
### Q. How much is an average apartment building?
A.  Buyers rarely price off averages. They work from net operating income and a capitalization rate drawn from comparable local sales, which is why two buildings with the same unit count can trade far apart. Start from the rent roll and the real expenses, not a headline number.
### Q. How much does it cost to build an entire apartment complex?
A.  Budget it as stacked line items rather than one number: land, hard construction costs, soft costs such as design and permits, financing during construction, and a reserve for lease-up. Construction type moves the total the most. Local bids and a lender’s term sheet are the only figures worth planning around.
### Q. How much does a 100 unit apartment complex cost?
A.  Unit count alone doesn’t set the price. A 100-unit garden community on suburban ground, a 100-unit rehab of an older city building and a new mid-rise with a parking deck can differ by multiples. Land, parking, construction type, labor and financing move the number, and all of them are local.

## Missouri's Gym Contract Law Leaves Out Karate Schools: How to Choose a Martial Arts School in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-martial-arts-school-st-louis
Slap. A white belt goes over onto her back and both palms smack the vinyl at once, flat and loud, exactly the way she was taught twenty minutes ago. From the folding chair by the door you flinch before she does. She’s already up, grinning, hair stuck to her forehead, looking for you to make sure you saw.
You did. And now the person at the front desk is sliding a clipboard across the counter, a membership agreement, twelve months, a line for your signature. The mat smells like disinfectant and feet. The room is still ringing with that slap. This is exactly the moment a contract gets signed without being read.
So read it, because in St. Louis the river changes what that paper can do to you. In Illinois, the Physical Fitness Services Act names martial arts outright: its definition of physical fitness services includes instruction in “judo, karate, self-defense training, or any similar activity.” Under that law, the contract may be cancelled by the customer within 3 business days after the first business day after signing, with all monies paid refunded, and the initial term may not run more than one year.
Missouri goes the other way. Its health spa law, RSMo 407.325, is the one that covers gyms, and its definition leaves out “any organization primarily operated for the purpose of teaching a particular form of self-defense such as judo or karate.” Same kid. Same slap on the mat. Sign in Illinois and a state statute is standing behind you. Sign in Missouri and the protection is mostly whatever that clipboard says.
### How do I know which martial art is right for me?
Start from the outcome you want, not the name on the sign. Choose a striking art for conditioning and stand-up skill, a grappling art for control and lower-impact sparring, or an Olympic-movement art for ranked competition. Then judge the school, not the style: watch a class, check the instructor and read the contract before you pay a dollar.
Most people do this backwards. They pick a discipline they saw in a movie, then hunt for a school that teaches it. Flip it. Write down the one thing you want twelve months from now. My kid follows instructions and isn’t scared of other kids. I can get through three rounds without seeing spots. I want a reason to leave the house on Tuesday nights. Let that sentence pick the room.
And don’t let anyone hand you the answer without asking about your body, your schedule and your goal first. A beginner needs classmates at their level, an instructor who corrects instead of performs, and a pace that doesn’t produce an injury in month two. Several arts supply that. Plenty of individual schools don’t.
### Karate, taekwondo, muay thai, judo, BJJ: what actually differs
Karate and taekwondo are structured striking arts built on forms, drills and rank, and the room sounds like it: counted reps, sharp yells, bare feet squeaking on the mat. Muay thai is full-contact striking with knees, elbows and clinch, and you hear it as the heavy thud of shins on pads. Judo is throwing and pinning. Brazilian jiu-jitsu is ground control and submissions, quieter, mostly breathing. Krav Maga and the broader self-defense category borrow from all of them and skip the sport.
Rank means different things in each. Some arts run through national federations, so ask the school whether it belongs to one. Brazilian jiu-jitsu has the IBJJF, which posts its own Graduation System for belts. Many schools sit outside any federation. Not worse, just unaffiliated. The certificate on the wall is only as good as the organization behind it, so ask which one.
Impact matters more than parents expect. Judo and BJJ mean constant close contact and very little getting hit. Muay thai and full-contact karate mean less grabbing and far more impact. Taekwondo sits between and is kick-heavy: hard on knees, wonderful for kids with too much energy. If a shoulder already complains, say so before you sign, and if it’s been complaining for months, get it looked at first by one of the chiropractors around St. Louis.
### What should a trial class actually show you?
A trial class is an audition, and you’re the judge. Watch four things: how much of the hour is moving versus talking, who the new person gets paired with, whether the head instructor teaches or only shows up at the end, and what happens when a technique goes wrong. Correction that is specific and calm is the product. Volume isn’t.
Then go watch a class you aren’t in. A weeknight advanced session tells you more than the sales-friendly beginner hour. Look at the mats, and at whether anyone wipes them down between classes. Listen for whether kids are taught to tap and to stop the instant they hear the word. That one rule is the difference between safe sparring and the other kind.
Ask two questions before you leave. What happens the week my kid doesn’t want to come? And can I sit and watch any class, any time? A school that welcomes parents in the room has nothing to manage.
### How do you check out a martial arts instructor in Missouri or Illinois?
Start with what the state does and doesn’t watch. Missouri’s Office of Athletics exists to protect the health and safety of participants in professional boxing, sparring, professional wrestling, professional and amateur kickboxing, professional and amateur mixed martial arts and professional full-contact karate contests. That’s the fight on a card, not the school your kid walks into after dinner.
There is one real public record worth a search. The U.S. Center for SafeSport keeps a Centralized Disciplinary Database you can search, and its work is aimed at the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Movement. A coach whose sport sits inside that movement may show up there; a coach outside it may not, so a clean result is a start, not a verdict.
On the Missouri side, the Family Care Safety Registry links to seven data systems maintained by Missouri state agencies to provide background results. Certain Missouri care workers must register by law, but the registry lists voluntary associations mainly for recreation or education among those not required to. So screening at a dojo is a choice the owner makes, which makes it a fair question to ask out loud: who do you background check, how often, and what would disqualify someone?
Kid still bouncing off the walls after class? Hand them a board and point them at a St. Louis skate park instead.
### What a martial arts contract can legally do, side by side
Set the two clipboards side by side. They might use the same template from the same software company. The law under them is not the same.
Illinois first. Because the Physical Fitness Services Act, 815 ILCS 645, names judo and karate, a dojo there gets the gym rules: the three-business-day cancellation with a full refund, and an initial term capped at one year. There’s a second layer for auto-renewing deals. Under the Automatic Contract Renewal Act, 815 ILCS 601/10, written notice of an automatic renewal must reach you no less than 30 days and no more than 60 days before the cancellation deadline.
Missouri second. The health spa rules are real, and they have teeth for gyms: the Attorney General’s office says health spas must be registered with it, and health spas new to Missouri should also file a bond or letter of credit of $10,000, $20,000 or $25,000 depending on how many unexpired contracts they hold. But the definition in RSMo 407.325 excludes schools primarily teaching self-defense such as judo or karate. A Missouri dojo usually sits outside all of that.
Translation for a Missouri signature: the cooling-off period you assume exists may not. Before the pen touches paper, ask for the term length, how it renews, the exact way to cancel (email, certified letter or in person), and whether a free trial converts into a paid month on its own. Take a photo of the signed page with your phone before you walk out to the car.
### Belt fees, testing fees and gear: where the money goes
Tuition is rarely the whole number. Budget five buckets: monthly or term tuition, a testing fee each time you grade, association dues if the school is affiliated, uniform and protective gear, and tournament entries. Some schools add an upgrade tier that stacks on top of everything else.
So don’t shop the monthly rate. Ask for the twelve-month all-in total in writing, at the promotion pace the school actually uses, including every testing fee, dues payment and required piece of gear. Divide it by the classes you will realistically attend, not the ones you hope to. That per-session number is the only one that compares fairly across schools.
Belt structure is the tell. If promotions land on a calendar instead of on demonstrated skill, and each belt costs more than the last, you’re buying certificates. Ask how many students tested last cycle and how many didn’t pass. A school that never holds anyone back isn’t really testing.
### How often should you train?
Two classes a week builds a habit. Three starts to build skill, because you come back before your body forgets what it learned. For kids, think of class as one piece of their week, not the whole of it; the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, now in their second edition, lay out how much activity children and adults need.
For adults starting out, the honest limit is recovery. Sore forearms the next morning are normal. A knee that swells is not. Pick the schedule you can keep for six months, then add a day once the first one feels easy.

Choosing a music school in St. Louis
Picking up golf in St. Louis, if the fit on the mat turns out wrong
Sit in on a class before you sign anything. Browse martial arts schools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two, and ask to watch a class you are not signed up for. The one that says yes without hesitating is the one to try first.
If you run the dojo, the boxing gym or the jiu-jitsu academy that lets a stranger sit in on class, that parent is already searching for you. A complete listing with your hours, the ages you teach and your disciplines puts you on their shortlist before they pick up the phone, which is how you get more customers from the calls you never knew you missed. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best martial art for a beginner?
A.  There isn’t one universal answer. Judo and Brazilian jiu-jitsu let a beginner train hard with very little getting hit. Taekwondo and karate give the most structure, which suits kids and anyone who likes a clear ladder. Muay thai builds conditioning fast at the highest impact. Pick by what you want twelve months out, then judge the school.
### Q. Is 27 too late to start martial arts?
A.  No. What changes with age is recovery, not whether you can learn. Look for a school that scales intensity, lets you sit out a round without commentary, and has other adults at your level. Ask how many adult white belts train in the class you would join.
### Q. Are martial arts classes expensive?
A.  It depends on format, class size and how often the school promotes students. Instead of comparing monthly rates, ask for a twelve-month all-in total in writing covering tuition, every testing fee at the school’s real promotion pace, dues, uniform and gear. Divide by the classes you will attend. That per-session number is the fair comparison.
### Q. Is $30 for 45 minutes good for a martial arts class?
A.  That depends on what is inside the 45 minutes. Six students with the head instructor teaching is a different product from thirty students and an assistant. Ask the class cap, who teaches, and the annual total including testing fees, then compare per-session cost between two schools you have actually watched.
### Q. Is martial arts 3 times a week enough?
A.  For most beginners, yes. Three sessions is where skill starts to stick instead of resetting between classes, and it leaves room for recovery. If you can only make two, keep them consistent; a steady two beats an on-and-off four.
### Q. Is martial arts worth the money?
A.  That turns on what you are buying, so define it before signing. If the goal is a weekly habit, weigh it against the gym membership you skip. If the goal is competition or self-defense skill, judge instructor quality, live resistance in training and how many adults stay past a year. Set a six-month checkpoint and a measurable outcome.
### Q. Why is Krav Maga not taken seriously?
A.  Krav Maga is a broad label, and the quality you get depends on the school in front of you. Plenty of Krav Maga instruction is rigorous. Sort it yourself by asking which organization certified the instructor and whether students train against a genuinely resisting partner.

## Last Call Is 1:30 a.m. in Missouri: Types of Bars in St. Louis and How to Pick One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/types-of-bars-in-st-louis-how-to-pick-one
1:30 a.m. Your ears are still ringing from the Duck Room, the pinball machines are chiming behind you, and the glowing walls of pop-culture memorabilia at Blueberry Hill look a little softer than they did at nine. Then the bar closes. That is not the bartender being strict. Wednesday through Saturday, Blueberry Hill’s bar hours end at 1:30 a.m., which is exactly the line Missouri law draws: no licensee may sell, give away or permit the consumption of intoxicating liquor between 1:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.
Cross the river and the rules change under your feet. In Illinois a two-for-one drink special is flatly illegal, and the liquor license on the wall comes from the town or county. In downtown Belleville, Shoehorn Brewing at 225 E. Main St. pours from 20 rotating taps and posts noon to 10 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, three and a half hours before a Soulard tavern has to stop pouring. So before you argue about the best bar in St. Louis, settle the three things that actually decide the night: the type of room, the hour you walk in, and which side of the Mississippi you are standing on.
### What are the five types of bars?
Most bars fall into five types: the neighborhood or corner tavern, the sports bar, the cocktail bar, the brewery taproom, and the music or late-night room. The St. Louis metro has all five, often within a mile of each other, and plenty of rooms here are two types at once, which is why the hour you arrive matters as much as the label.
### Five rooms, five different nights
The tavern with a past. Hammerstone’s, at 9th & Russell in Soulard, sits in a building with history dating back to 1884, and legend has it that during Prohibition it was a drug store in front with bootleg liquor out back. Call ahead for its hours. Down Russell, John D. McGurk’s Irish Pub & Garden at 1200 Russell Boulevard does post them: 4 p.m. to 1:30 a.m. Tuesday through Thursday, 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 a.m. Friday and Saturday. The fryer quits first, at 10 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday and 11 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, so a late table gets the band, a cold pint sweating on the rail and no dinner.
The music room. Blueberry Hill has been open in the heart of the Delmar Loop since 1972, and Chuck Berry duck-walked across its Duck Room stage over 200 times. It goes 21+ after 9 p.m. except for all-ages shows, and late-night food is ordered at the bar.
The sports room. Ballpark Village sits just steps from Busch Stadium and lists college football watch parties at its Live! Arena every Thursday, Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Go for the roar when a whole room stands up at once. Do not go to catch up with an old friend.
The taproom. Schlafly calls itself St. Louis’ original craft brewery. Its Tap Room at 2100 Locust Street posts 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Monday through Saturday and noon to 10 p.m. Sunday, with the kitchen closing at 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday. It is a dinner-hour plan: beer bread with bacon jam warm in the middle of the table, flights lined up beside it.
The cocktail bar. At Yellowbelly, 4659 Lindell Blvd in the Central West End, the shaker rattles over pineapple, coconut and lime, and the list leans on sugarcane and agave spirits. Most cocktails are $15, the bar runs 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday and to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and it is closed Sunday and Monday. You are paying for time and technique, not volume, which is why it works for a first date.
The shortcut, for when you are on the sidewalk with your phone out and four people waiting on you: a first date goes to the cocktail room, early. Dinner and a flight goes to Schlafly before the kitchen quits. A late band goes to the Duck Room or to McGurk’s in Soulard, where the bar runs to 1:30 and the kitchen does not. A game goes to Ballpark Village. And anything across the bridge gets checked against that bar’s own posted hours first, because Shoehorn’s 10 p.m. close and Blueberry Hill’s 1:30 a.m. one are two different nights. Hours change, so look again the day you go.
Here is the line to text the group chat before anyone orders a ride: in St. Louis the kitchen quits before the bar does, and in Belleville the bar can quit before you do.
### The river changes the rules
On the Missouri side, 1:30 a.m. is the default, but a room can buy more time. Missouri’s extended-hours law lets a bar in the City of St. Louis, in an area the city has designated a convention trade area, apply for a special permit to stay open until 3:00 a.m. It costs an additional $300 a year on top of the regular license fees, and the business needs $150,000 or more in gross sales for the year before, or has to be a resort. That is how a downtown Friday can outlast your neighborhood one: Ballpark Village lists Freedom Friday at PBR St. Louis from 8 p.m. to 2:30 a.m.
Illinois runs on local control. Even the state’s own retailer license application asks which municipality or county issued the bar’s local liquor license, so in the Metro East the honest way to learn closing time is that bar’s own posted hours, not a Missouri habit. What is the same everywhere in Illinois is the drink-special law: no bar may sell more than one drink for the price of one, sell unlimited drinks for a fixed price to the public, or pour a bigger drink without raising the price. That is why a drink special in Maplewood can look nothing like the one in Belleville.
### How do you pick a bar for the occasion?
Pick for the one thing that would ruin the night if you got it wrong: noise, seating or the clock. A group of nine needs a room that seats nine. A conversation you actually want to have needs a room where you can hear each other without leaning in. A 10 p.m. arrival needs a kitchen that has not closed.
Groups are a phone call, not a gamble. Call around 3 p.m., before the rush, and ask three things: do you seat a party this size, how late does the kitchen run, and will you split checks. If you want the sound on for a game, ask that too, because a room full of screens usually has one audio feed. And if the group is big, ask about a reserved section; Blueberry Hill, for one, takes parties of up to 60 guests with their own reserved tables.
### Can you smoke inside a St. Louis bar?
Not in Illinois. Under the Smoke Free Illinois Act, bars and taverns are smoke-free inside and smokers have to stand at least 15 feet from the entrance, so the smokers in Belleville stand out on the sidewalk under the streetlight, coats zipped. Missouri’s state law is far looser. It says bars, taverns, and restaurants that seat fewer than fifty people are not considered public places for its smoking rules when they conspicuously post a sign stating “Nonsmoking Areas are Unavailable.” Local rules can be stricter than the state, so if smoke matters to you either way, call ahead and look at the door before you sit down.
### A taproom night, done right
Taprooms are the early plan, not the midnight one. Schlafly’s Tap Room shuts at 10 every night, and on Sunday through Thursday the kitchen goes an hour before that. Order the beer bread, the house-made pale ale bread with bacon jam and bleu cheese cream, and let it go around the table while the flights come out. Get there before dinner, and you get the good tables, a kitchen still cooking, and a friend who is not drinking still has plenty to order.
If you like the brewing side, Schlafly runs public tours at its Bottleworks location on Saturdays at 11 a.m., noon and 1 p.m.; tickets are $10 a person and each tour runs 50 minutes. Only those 21 or older join the tasting. If wine is more your speed, the same early-evening logic works at the tasting rooms in Missouri wine country.
### Read the room from the doorway
You can tell which of the five types a room is running tonight in about ten seconds, before you take off your coat. Listen first. If you can hear the ice in a shaker from the door, it is a cocktail night, and you will be talking. If the noise hits you as a wall with a crowd groan inside it, there is a game on, and you will be watching. If the first thing you hear is a guitar being tuned, settle in, because nobody is leaving before the encore.
Then look at the bar rail. Empty stools with coats on them mean regulars who stepped out to smoke or take a call; that is a tavern, and it will be friendly once somebody nods at you. A rail three deep with people holding cash in the air is a late-night room at its peak, which is fun if you came for it and miserable if you came to catch up with an old friend. Smell tells you the rest: a fryer working hard means the kitchen is still open, and a room that smells only of beer and cold air has probably stopped cooking. None of this needs a review site. It needs one honest look before you commit to a table.
Off topic, but after a night out on dusty streets your car could use a car wash.
### What makes a good local?
A good local is a room you can get to without a highway, on a night you did not plan anything. The bar rail matters more than the tables, because a rail is where you can show up alone and not feel odd about it. The same bartender three months running is the whole difference between a bar and a business that happens to sell beer.
Some smaller tells hold up everywhere: water arrives without asking, a tab closes in under a minute, the taps change a few times a year, and the room has a second personality after ten that you actually like. Check the bathroom on your first visit. It tells you what the owner spends money on when nobody is watching.
Want a bar where the entertainment is you? Here is what to expect at a karaoke bar before your first song.

Beyond it, fame here tends to follow a brewing history, an old brick building, or a stage with a long booking calendar, so search by neighborhood and read recent reviews.

### Q. How to pick a bar for a first date?
A.  Use three filters: can you hear each other at a normal speaking volume, is there an easy way to leave after one drink, and is parking or a ride simple for both of you. ### Q. What are some unique bars in Saint Louis?
