## Clothes Under $100 Go Tax-Free in Missouri One August Weekend: How to Shop St. Louis in Person
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-shop-for-clothes-in-st-louis
A zipper runs down the middle of Washington Avenue. It’s set into the pavement, a zipper-and-stitch pattern along the center of the street, and after dark a line of LED-lit buttons glows down it like somebody stopped halfway through sewing downtown shut. Most people drive right over it on the way to a game.
It’s there on purpose. The pattern pays tribute to the old garment district, from a time when, as the American Planning Association tells it, those sidewalks filled with window-shoppers and buyers. Now the corridor is full of lofts and boutiques again. Walk in and you’re trying on clothes inside the same brick walls the buyers once came to.
Compare that with the gray poly mailer by your front door, the return label half peeled, the jacket inside that looked right on a screen and pulled across your back the second you zipped it. The National Retail Federation estimated that 19.3% of online sales would be returned, against 15.8% of retail sales overall. A fitting room settles that before you leave the store.
And one weekend a year, the fitting room also wins on price. Under Section 144.049 RSMo, Missouri’s Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday begins on the first Friday in August and continues through the following Sunday. The Department of Revenue says any article of clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less is exempt from all state and local sales or use taxes for that stretch, not just the state’s share.
That last part is where the river matters. In its most recent holiday, Illinois reduced the state’s portion of sales tax from 6.25 percent to 1.25 percent, on clothing under $125. So the $90 jacket is cheaper on the Missouri side of the bridge that weekend, even if the price tag reads the same. Two catches to say out loud at the register: items normally sold in pairs can’t be separated to qualify, so a pair of shoes counts as one $100 item, and ties, belt buckles, scarves, jewelry and handbags never qualify at all.
### Where is the best place to shop in St. Louis?
Pick a walkable business district before you pick a store, so one parking spot gets you several fitting rooms instead of one. Downtown, start on Washington Avenue, a corridor of lofts, boutiques and restaurants. Then shop the first weekend in August if you can, when Missouri takes state and local sales tax off any piece of clothing priced $100 or less.
### Walk the old garment district first
Look up from the zipper and the buildings still wear their old trade on their faces. The American Planning Association’s write-up of Washington Avenue describes fifteen blocks between Eads Bridge to the east and 18th Street to the west, lined with late 19th and early 20th century warehouses clad in brick, stone and terra cotta. Some still carry their fashion-industry names: Bee Hat, Knickerbocker, Fashion Square. You can run a hand along the cool stone on the way into a shop that sells the thing those buildings used to make.
Go on foot, slowly, and go in with a plan. Know your measurements before you leave home, because a boutique buyer can pull three sizes off the rack faster when you can say your waist and inseam out loud. Wear something easy to change out of. And if a kid tags along, the same write-up notes that City Museum opened in 1997 in a former shoe factory, which makes it the one stop on the street that fits everyone.
### Six kinds of stores, six different problems
Each kind of store sounds different when you walk in. A general boutique is hangers clicking along a short rail, a curated mix of brands, shallow in sizes and refreshed often. A menswear shop is the snap of a tape measure, because tailored clothing is the point. Resale, consignment and thrift smell like cedar and other people’s closets, and they sell secondhand. Western and workwear stores carry boots, denim and outerwear, and the leather hits you at the door. Formalwear and bridal shops often work by appointment, with a steamer hissing in the back. Specialty-fit stores cover extended sizes, maternity, uniforms and dancewear, and they’re the ones where nobody makes you ask twice.
The secondhand three get mixed up constantly, and the difference is who owns the jacket on the rack. A consignment shop holds clothes for the people who brought them in. A buy-outright resale shop pays on the spot and owns the piece from then on. A thrift store usually runs on donations. NARTS, is the professional association for resale, consignment and thrift stores. Clearing out your own closet? Ask each kind of shop how and when it pays before you haul the bags in.
### How do you find a shop that will actually fit you?
You know the moment. The curtain slides shut, the mirror is honest, and somebody on the other side asks, “How’s the shoulder?” That question is the whole reason to drive. Judge a store on four things, in this order: whether it carries your size in more than one brand, whether anyone looks at the garment on your body, what the written return policy says, and whether alterations happen in-house or by referral.
A size number is a suggestion, not a measurement, and it drifts between brands. Bring the shoes you’ll wear with the thing, and the undergarments too. Go early on a weekday if you want real attention, because a Saturday afternoon in a two-person shop is triage. And say your budget out loud. Nobody in a small store is offended by one.
### What a tailor can fix, and what nobody can
Pins in the waistband, chalk on the hem, a tape measure cold against your wrist. A tailor can take in a waist, taper a body, shorten sleeves, hem trousers and move buttons. A tailor can’t add fabric that isn’t in the seam, and reworking a shoulder is a big job because the whole garment hangs from it. So buy for your largest measurement and alter down. A jacket that fits the shoulders and gaps elsewhere is a good buy. One that fits everywhere but the shoulders isn’t.
Ask three things before you leave a garment: the written quote, the turnaround, and whether the store that sold it covers the first alteration. Then read the care label while you’re still deciding, because that’s the running cost. The Federal Trade Commission’s Care Labeling Rule at 16 CFR Part 423 requires a label that stays legible during the useful life of the product, and the maker must have a reasonable basis for the care instructions on it. A blazer that visits the cleaner every month costs more than its price tag.
Buying for a wedding? Get the suit fitted first, then order the boutonniere from a real florist once you know the color of the tie.
### Can you return it? What Missouri and Illinois actually say
The receipt crinkles in your pocket on the walk back to the car, and that’s the moment to read it. In both states, as FindLaw’s state-by-state summary puts it, whether you can get a refund depends on the retailer’s return and refund policies. A small shop may offer exchange or store credit instead of cash, or sell markdowns final. In Illinois, consumers may still seek action under the Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act when a practice is unfair or deceptive.
The FTC’s Cooling-Off Rule covers sales of $25 or more at the buyer’s home and $130 or more at other places away from the seller’s place of business, such as a rented hotel room. A boutique’s own storefront is its place of business. So ask about returns before you pay, and ask for the answer on the receipt.
Shopping bags cutting into your fingers? Set them down at one of the coffee shops in Maplewood for a while.
### When is clothing cheapest in Missouri and Illinois?
On the Missouri side, set a reminder for 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August and shop through midnight Sunday. One more line from the Missouri Department of Revenue worth knowing: the clothing exemption doesn’t cover watches, watchbands, jewelry, handbags, handkerchiefs, umbrellas, scarves, ties, headbands or belt buckles. Pay full tax on the tie. Save on the shirt, the coat and the school uniform.
Illinois runs its version differently. In its most recent holiday, set out in an Illinois Department of Revenue informational bulletin, the state’s share of sales tax dropped from 6.25 percent to 1.25 percent on qualifying clothing and footwear priced under $125 per item, from August 7 through August 16.
Outside those weeks, watch the clearance racks, and expect a small shop to mark those pieces final sale. Ask the clerk when the next markdown lands, write it on the back of the receipt, and come back that morning before the good sizes walk out the door.
### What to wear in St. Louis, Missouri?
Summer here is the shirt sticking to your back before you reach the car, then the air conditioning inside a restaurant raising goosebumps on your arms. Dress in breathable fabric and carry one light layer for over-cooled rooms. Winter turns. The National Weather Service in St. Louis puts the chance of measurable snowfall on Christmas Day at 13%, and a real coat earns its hook by the door.
Shoes are their own errand with their own stores. Here’s where to buy shoes that fit across the metro.
Packing light for a visit? One minimalist answer comes from Project 333, the minimalist fashion challenge Courtney Carver first wrote about in 2010, which invites you to dress with 33 items or less for 3 months, with accessories, jewelry, outerwear and shoes counted in.

The last piece is usually the one that fits worst. Fit matters with underwear too, so here’s how to get a bra that actually fits in St. Louis. And for the thing that tops it off, here’s how to buy and care for a hat in St. Louis.
Shop owners feel the calendar in their bones. By the National Retail Federation’s count, November and December have averaged about 19% of total annual retail sales over the past five years. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for clothes?
A.  People use it two ways. As a packing trick, it means a few tops, a few bottoms and a few pairs of shoes that all mix together. As a wardrobe challenge, it points to Project 333, which Courtney Carver first wrote about in 2010: dress with 33 items or less for 3 months, shoes and accessories included. Both are ways to stop buying duplicates.
### Q. What are some good clothing stores in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  That depends on your size, your budget and what you wear to work, so search by type and neighborhood instead of chasing a ranked list. Pick the type first, whether that’s a boutique, menswear, resale, extended sizes or formalwear, then call the two closest and ask whether they stock your size in more than one brand. Ten minutes on the phone beats a wasted Saturday.
### Q. What to wear in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Layers, and plan for humidity. Breathable fabric and one light layer for over-cooled rooms carry the summer. The National Weather Service puts the chance of measurable snowfall on Christmas Day at 13%, so a real coat earns its keep in winter.
### Q. What is the 5 5 5 rule for clothing?
A.  You’ll see it described as a capsule-wardrobe shorthand, and the exact split changes with whoever is explaining it. The useful part isn’t the number. It’s the habit of buying against what’s already in your closet instead of whatever is on the rack in front of you.
### Q. Do small clothing stores in St. Louis accept returns?
A.  Many do, on their own terms. Whether you get a refund depends on the store’s own return policy, so store credit, exchange-only and final-sale clearance are all common in independent shops. Read the policy on the receipt or at the register before you pay, and ask whether markdowns are final.

## The Screening Copay Illinois Waives and Missouri Keeps: How to Choose a Urologist in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-urologist-in-st-louis
Six digits in, you hang up. Again. The referral slip sits by your elbow with a coffee ring on it now, nine days on the kitchen counter, half under the gas bill: a specialist’s name, a fax number, the word UROLOGY in gray toner. You set the phone face down and tell yourself the same thing as yesterday. Tomorrow.
It isn’t the doctor you dread. It’s saying it out loud to a stranger with a clipboard. How many times you get up at night. What color it was. How long it’s been going on. So the slip sits there, and whatever it was written about keeps going on too.
Here’s the part that changes your bill, and it has nothing to do with which office you pick. In this metro, the river can decide it. Illinois insurance law, 215 ILCS 5/356u, requires the policies it covers to pay for an annual prostate cancer screening without imposing a deductible, coinsurance or copayment, for asymptomatic people 50 and over, African-American people 40 and over, and people 40 and over with a family history of prostate cancer. Missouri’s law, RSMo 376.1250, also requires coverage of a prostate examination and lab tests for men without symptoms. Then it says that coverage is subject to the same deductible and co-payments as your other benefits.
Same metro. Same blood draw. One side of the river waives the copay by law; the other side bills it like anything else. So before you dial, flip your insurance card over and ask the plan one question: which state’s rules does my policy follow? If you’re covered through a big employer, ask one more, because the answer may be neither. The Illinois Department of Insurance says it does not have jurisdiction over self-insured employer plans, and many large employers provide health benefits for their employees through self-insured plans.
### How do I choose the best urologist?
Check three things, in this order: board certification, your insurance network, and what the physician treats most. Certification is a free ABMS search, no log-in needed. Network status decides whether the bill is a copay or a shock. Subspecialty fit decides whether the person across the desk sees your problem every week or twice a year. Star ratings are tiebreakers, nothing more.
Urology has real internal lanes: kidney stones, prostate care, incontinence and pelvic floor, cancer surgery, male fertility. Ask the scheduler which way a physician leans. It costs you one sentence on a call you were making anyway. Follow it with the question people skip. When is the next new-patient opening, and who sees me if my doctor is in surgery?
### What does a urologist actually treat?
The urinary tract in everyone, kidneys down to the bladder, plus the male reproductive system. Stones that fold you over in the shower. Infections that keep coming back. Leaking when you laugh. An enlarged prostate, blood in the urine, and cancers of the prostate, bladder and kidney.
It isn’t a men’s clinic, either. Sit in the waiting room and you’ll see women there too, for the bladder that wakes them at 3 a.m. or the infection that won’t quit. A referral to urology says nothing embarrassing about you. It says your doctor wants a specialist’s eyes on it.
The prostate is where a lot of first visits start. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases calls benign prostatic hyperplasia, an enlarged prostate, the most common prostate problem in men older than 50, and estimates it affects 29% to 33% of men ages 65 and older.
### Where can I find a urology specialist in St. Louis?
Use three lists and let them check each other. Your doctor’s referral comes first, because it carries your records. Your insurer’s provider directory comes second, because it is the only list that governs what you pay. A local directory comes third, to see who practices near your commute.
Living in a metro is an advantage here. The American Urological Association’s annual Census found that most U.S. counties (62%) do not have a practicing urologist, and only 10% of practicing urologists keep their primary practice outside metropolitan areas. If you live out past the edge of the metro, plan on driving in. Pick the office near work, not home, so the follow-ups don’t eat a whole vacation day.
And check the network by state. An Illinois plan and a Missouri office twenty minutes across the bridge are not automatically a pair.
### Do you need a referral, and what is pre-authorization?
Your plan type decides the referral question, and the phone number on the back of your card is the only binding answer. Call it before you call the urologist. It costs you one stretch of hold music and saves a wasted trip.
Pre-authorization is a different animal, and mixing the two up costs people appointments. A referral is permission to see the specialist. Pre-authorization is your insurer agreeing ahead of time to pay for a specific test, drug or procedure, and the practice is the one that asks for it. That paperwork is heavy. The American Medical Association’s physician survey found that physicians complete an average of 40 prior authorizations per week, and that prior authorization consumes an average of 13 hours of physician and staff time each week.
So ask two things when you book: does this visit need pre-authorization, and has my records request gone out? Getting both moving on day one is the difference between one visit and three.
### What are red flags in urology?
Only a clinician who examines you can judge your own case. There is guidance on when not to wait, though. For an enlarged prostate, NIDDK says to tell a health care professional right away if you cannot urinate at all; if you feel painful, frequent and urgent needs to urinate and have a fever and chills; if you have blood in your urine; or if you feel great discomfort or pain in your lower abdomen or urinary tract.
Blood you can’t see counts too. The AUA and SUFU publish a Microhematuria Guideline covering its initial evaluation and risk-based follow-up. A dipstick test at an urgent care can turn into a urology appointment while you feel completely fine. Call the office and describe it plainly. Don’t triage yourself from a search bar at midnight.
### What does a urologist visit cost out of pocket?
Coverage decides it, not the office. On Medicare, there’s an annual Part B deductible; check the current figure on the CMS fact sheet. On a commercial plan it’s a specialist copay or coinsurance. And for the prostate screening itself, go back to the river: which state wrote your policy matters more than which office draws the blood.
Stuck on hold with the insurer? Somewhere in this city a dog is having the best afternoon of its life at one of these St. Louis dog parks.
Paying cash changes the playbook. Under federal rules, providers usually must give you a good faith estimate if you request one or schedule services at least 3 business days in advance, and you may be able to dispute your bill if it’s at least $400 more than the estimate. Ask which CPT codes the office expects to bill, then run them through the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Look-Up Tool to see what the services are worth before anyone hands you a statement.
### What happens at a first urology appointment?
A long conversation, a urine sample, and a focused exam. You’ll fill out a questionnaire on a clipboard in the waiting room, then hand over a plastic cup with your name on a sticker. Depending on the referral there may be a bladder ultrasound or bloodwork. You usually leave with a plan and orders, not a final answer.
Bring five things and the visit goes faster: your insurance card and photo ID, a written list of medications and supplements, any prior labs or imaging, your referring doctor’s name and fax number, and three questions written down so you don’t blank in the paper gown. Ask when you book whether to arrive with a full bladder. Some tests need one.
If the phone call itself is the wall, write the first sentence on the back of the referral slip and read it word for word: “My doctor referred me for a urology consult, I’d like a new-patient appointment, and I need to know whether you take my plan.” That’s it. The scheduler takes it from there, asks for your date of birth and your member number, and the hardest thirty seconds of this whole process are behind you before the hold music starts again.
The awkwardness is real, and it’s all on your side of the room. Whatever you dread saying, that staff has heard it before lunch. Vague answers just buy you a second visit.
### Two free checks before you book
Board certification and a clean license are different things, so check both. For certification, use ABMS Certification Matters, a free search tool with no log-in required, or the ABMS verification page.
Licenses take two bookmarks in a two-state metro. For Missouri physicians, use the state’s licensee search. On the Illinois side, use the IDFPR license lookup. For a national cross-check, try DocInfo and Medicare Care Compare.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who is the best urologist in St. Louis?
A.  There isn’t one answer, because the best urologist for kidney stones is rarely the best one for incontinence. Build your own shortlist: verify board certification through ABMS Certification Matters, confirm the office is in your network, then ask which conditions that physician treats most often.
### Q. Where can I find a urology specialist in St. Louis?
A.  Start with your primary care doctor’s referral, since it travels with your records. Cross-check the name against your insurer’s provider directory, which controls what you pay, then widen the search with a local directory to see who practices near your commute. Confirm the network by state; an Illinois plan and a Missouri office are not automatically a pair.
### Q. How much does a urologist visit cost out of pocket?
A.  It turns on your coverage, not the office. On Medicare there’s an annual Part B deductible, set by CMS. On a commercial plan it is a specialist copay or coinsurance. Paying cash, ask for a good faith estimate before the visit.
### Q. How much is the consultation fee for an urologist?
A.  Ask whether a quoted consultation fee includes the urine test, any ultrasound and any scope, and ask which CPT codes the visit should generate. Then check those codes in the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Look-Up Tool so the statement holds no surprises.
### Q. At what age should men start seeing a urologist?
A.  There’s no single age, and symptoms at any age are reason enough to call. Screening has its own clock, and Illinois law spells it out: its no-copay annual prostate cancer screening covers asymptomatic people 50 and over, and African-American people or those with a family history from 40.
### Q. What is the most common urological problem?
A.  No single condition owns the title across every age and sex. One is documented clearly: NIDDK reports that benign prostatic hyperplasia, an enlarged prostate, is the most common prostate problem in men older than 50.
### Q. What are red flags in urology?
A.  Only a clinician who examines you can judge your case. NIDDK advises telling a health care professional right away if you cannot urinate at all, if you feel painful, frequent and urgent needs to urinate with a fever and chills, if you have blood in your urine, or if you feel great discomfort or pain in your lower abdomen.

## Finding a Primary Care Doctor in St. Louis: Call the Office, Not the Main Line
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-a-primary-care-doctor-in-st-louis
Four pills left in the orange bottle on the windowsill. The pharmacy’s recorded voice says the refill needs a doctor’s sign-off, and the doctor who wrote it is gone: retired, out of network, or back on the other side of the river from the place you live now.
So you dial the big health system’s main number. Hold music. A transfer. More hold music, a little tinnier this time. Then the sentence everyone who has tried this has heard: “That physician isn’t accepting new patients at this time.”
Here is the part nobody tells you. The switchboard is not the schedule. The schedule lives at the practice, and in St. Louis the systems post it office by office. BJC Medical Group at the Highlands, on Highlands Plaza Drive in the 63110 ZIP, says on its own location page that it is accepting new patients for both primary care needs and chronic illness treatment, and its office line is 314-273-0195. BJC says its primary care side has both family and internal medicine providers and online scheduling. That is the whole trick: find the practice page, then call the office on it, not the main line.
No insurance card in your wallet right now? The first call in the city can be Affinia Healthcare, which says it provides essential services to patients regardless of their ability to pay and has a sliding fee scale. Its sites include Biddle, Lemp, South Broadway and Page Avenue, and appointments run through 314-814-8700.
### What is the best way to find a new primary care physician?
Start in your health plan’s own provider directory, not a search engine. Then make one call to the office and confirm three things: the physician is accepting new patients, the practice is in network for your exact plan name, and when the next new-patient slot opens. Ask the plan to confirm network status in writing, then check the doctor’s license and board certification before the first visit.
The order matters because each step can undo the one before it. A search engine sorts by popularity and ads. Your plan’s directory sorts by the thing that moves your bill. And a correct listing still doesn’t mean the schedule is open. A doctor can be contracted with your plan and closed to new patients.
Two filters narrow the list fast. Family medicine sees adults and children in one practice; internal medicine sees adults. Then be honest about the drive. The office you can reach without sitting in rush-hour traffic on Kingshighway, or crossing the river, is the one you will keep going back to when the cough won’t quit. Plans also re-verify their directories on a schedule, not daily: the law says not less frequently than once every 90 days, so a listing can be months behind the front desk.
### How do I know if a doctor is within my network?
Ask twice, and write it down. Kitchen table, insurance card flipped over so you can read the member number, a pen that has quit on you. Call the number on the back of the card, then call the practice, and use the plan name printed on the card, not just the insurer’s logo. One insurer can sell many plans with different rosters of doctors. Same company, different plan, different answer.
When the plan’s voice says “yes, that doctor is in network,” don’t hang up relieved. Federal law requires your plan to answer a phone question about a provider’s network status within 1 business day, in a written electronic or print communication if you ask for one. That email is your receipt. If you relied on the plan’s answer and it was wrong, the plan cannot charge you more cost sharing than it would have in network. Screenshot this part and send it to whoever in your family just switched jobs.
On the practice call, get the name of the person you spoke with and the date. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services explains the wider No Surprises Act protections at cms.gov/nosurprises. And if the plan won’t honor what it told you, Missouri has a referee. The state Department of Commerce and Insurance says it welcomes any questions or complaints you may have, and its Insurance Consumer Hotline is 800-726-7390.
Ask the office one more thing: does the physician, the practice and the building all bill under the same contract? In practices owned by a hospital system, a separate facility charge can show up on the bill.
### Getting in sooner than the first date they offer
The first opening they read you may be months out. You hear the keyboard clicking on the other end, a pause, then a date so far away you write it on the calendar in pencil. Three questions can pull it closer.
Ask to go on the cancellation list and say you can come on short notice. Ask whether a nurse practitioner or physician assistant in the same practice has an earlier new-patient visit, which gets you into the chart and onto the panel. And ask for the first opening with any clinician in the group rather than one named doctor. Once you are an established patient, getting in for a sick visit is usually far easier than getting in the door the first time.
If a sore throat or a twisted ankle can’t wait for that date, BJC says its convenient care is open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and you can walk in or reserve a time online for same-day or next-day care for minor illnesses and injuries. That is a stopgap, not a doctor who knows your history, so keep the new-patient appointment on the calendar.
### What happens at a new-patient visit?
Mostly paperwork and listening. The crinkle of the paper on the exam table, a blood pressure cuff tightening, and a lot of questions about you and your family. A first visit builds the chart: intake forms, a full medication review, personal and family history, vitals, and a talk about which preventive screenings fit your age and history. Arrive early enough to fill out the forms without rushing.
Bring five things. Photo ID and your insurance card. A written list of every medication and dose, including anything over the counter. Your pharmacy’s name and location. Dates of past surgeries and hospital stays. And your questions, written down, most important first, because that is the one that gets answered.
One billing wrinkle is worth knowing ahead of time. Marketplace plans and many other plans must cover a list of preventive services without charging you a copayment; the adult list is at healthcare.gov/preventive-care-adults. If the visit turns to a new or ongoing problem, that part can be billed as a separate office visit. Ask about it when you schedule.
### Moving your records to the new doctor
Request them yourself, even if it means digging up a portal password you last used years ago. It is the fastest route, and it comes with a clock. Under the HIPAA access rule, a provider must act on your request for access no later than 30 days after receiving it. Ask the new practice for its records-release form at the same time.
Ask for specific things instead of “everything.” The useful bundle is your problem list, current medications, immunizations, the last few lab and imaging reports, any operative reports and recent specialist notes. If the old practice has a patient portal, download what you can before you leave. Federal information blocking regulations exist to keep health data shared appropriately without improper barriers; read more at healthit.gov.
Card in one hand, phone in the other? Browse doctors across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask every office the same two questions: are you accepting new patients, and are you in network for this exact plan?
If you run a practice that is taking new patients, say so where people are looking. A full, current listing puts your open schedule in front of new customers at the exact moment they are working down a list of offices. List your practice on St Louis Near Me Directory.
### Urgent care, primary care, or the emergency room?
At 2 a.m., with a fever that won’t break and a child asleep on your shoulder, the choice feels impossible. It is simpler than it looks. They do three different jobs. Primary care is the office that holds your history, manages ongoing conditions and sends referrals. Urgent care is same-day help for things that can’t wait for a primary appointment but don’t need a hospital. The emergency room is for emergencies.
If you think you are having an emergency, get emergency help right away, and don’t let a cost question make that call for you. For everything short of that, use the number people forget they have: your own practice’s after-hours line. Once you are established, a clinician who can see your chart is a phone call away, and that call often settles whether something can wait until morning.
### How do you check a doctor’s license and board certification?
Do this from the parking lot before the first visit, phone propped on the steering wheel. For Missouri, start at mopro.mo.gov. For Illinois, use the state’s license lookup. You can also try DocInfo.
A license and board certification are different things. A license is the state’s permission to practice. Board certification is a specialty credential; to ask “Is my doctor ABMS board certified?” use the Certification Matters site. It takes about as long as reading the doctor’s name off the directory listing.
### What if you don’t have insurance right now?
Start with a right most people never use. If you don’t have or use health insurance, providers usually must give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost, and you may be able to dispute the bill if it is at least $400 more than the estimate. Ask for the estimate when you book.
Next, a community health center. Affinia Healthcare is one St. Louis option that serves patients regardless of their ability to pay, with locations that include Biddle, Lemp, South Broadway and Page Avenue. To find a health center near you, use findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov.
Then check Medicaid. On the Missouri side, you can apply for MO HealthNet at mydss.mo.gov; on the Illinois side, healthcare help is listed at ABE. And whatever your situation, you can always ask a practice for its self-pay rate before you book.
Nothing to do with doctors, but if the check-engine light is the other thing you’ve been putting off, here’s how to find a trustworthy auto repair shop in St. Louis.
### What the front desk wishes you knew
Call the practice itself, not a health system’s main number. The central line often can’t see whether one doctor in one office has a new-patient slot open. The front desk can, and they hear the phone ring all day with people asking the wrong number the right question.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who is the best primary care doctor in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single answer, and a ranking can’t know your plan or your commute. The right doctor for you holds a valid license, is board certified in family or internal medicine, is in network for your exact plan, is accepting new patients, and is close enough that you keep the follow-up. Build a short list against those five, then judge the first visit.
### Q. Where can I find a primary care doctor in St. Louis?
A.  Start inside your plan’s directory so cost is settled first, then go to the health system’s page for that one office and call the number on it. BJC Medical Group, for example, lists its practices location by location, and the Highlands office says it is accepting new patients. Without insurance, a community health center such as Affinia Healthcare is a good first call.
### Q. Is there a low-cost clinic in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Affinia Healthcare says it provides essential services to patients regardless of their ability to pay, and you can schedule at 314-814-8700. To find a health center beyond Affinia, use findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov.
### Q. How much will it cost to see a doctor without insurance?
A.  It depends on the practice, the length of the visit and whether labs or imaging get added, so get the number in writing. If you don’t have or use insurance, providers usually must give you a good faith estimate when you schedule in advance or ask for one.
### Q. What happens if you see a doctor outside of your network?
A.  You usually pay more, sometimes all of it, depending on your plan. The exception is when you relied on your plan’s directory or its answer to your question and it wrongly said the doctor was participating; then the plan cannot charge you more than in-network cost sharing.
### Q. What are red flags for doctors?
A.  Start with what you can check: a license that has lapsed or shows public discipline in the state lookup, or a specialty claim that doesn’t show up in Certification Matters. Then the practical ones: an office that won’t confirm network status, quote a self-pay fee or release your records. How a practice handles a simple question is how it will handle a hard one.
### Q. When should you switch primary care physicians?
A.  When your plan changes and the doctor drops out of network, when you can’t get a timely appointment, or when you leave visits feeling unheard. Line up the new doctor before you leave the old one, and download your records from the old portal first.

## Don't Rent a Guitar Yet: St. Louis County Library Lends Them Free
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-music-lessons-st-louis
Bzzzt. That flat, rattling buzz is what a first G chord sounds like when the fingertips are still guessing where to press. You hear it through the bedroom door, then a sigh, then the snap of a case closing.
Most parents answer that buzz with a credit card: a rental contract, a semester of lessons, a starter guitar from a big-box shelf. Here is the step almost nobody takes first. St. Louis County Library will lend you the guitar.
Acoustic, electric and bass guitars are on its instrument list. So are keyboards, ukuleles, banjos, cajons, djembes and xylophones. The library’s musical instruments are free to check out with a library card, and instruments may be borrowed for 3 weeks. Most come with an instruction book, a DVD and a hard case. The library says the program exists so you can experiment with new instruments before deciding to purchase one.
Three weeks is long enough to learn the only thing that matters before you spend real money: does the buzz turn into a chord, or does the guitar go quiet in the corner? Tell a friend whose kid is begging for drums. A practice pad kit is on the list too.
Borrowing has one more quiet benefit. When the library guitar goes back, you know which hand your kid reaches for the neck with, whether the strings hurt their fingers, and whether they actually pick it up without being asked. That is the information a music store can’t give you before the contract is signed. Look the instruments up in the library catalog and check one out the same way you would a book.
### Is there a music school in St. Louis?
Yes: the Community Music School of Webster University has taught since 1925 and has more than 1,200 students, with individual lessons on every band and orchestra instrument plus piano, guitar and voice. Around it sit private studios, music-store teaching rooms and teachers who work from home. Borrow an instrument from St. Louis County Library first, then pay for a trial lesson with two teachers before you commit.
A private teacher usually wins for an adult beginner or a kid with one clear instrument in mind: one familiar face, a flexible calendar, no front desk to pay for. A school usually wins for a young child, a family with two or three kids, or anyone who wants ensembles, a recital calendar and a substitute when their teacher has the flu. Webster’s Community Music School, for one, lists early childhood classes, Suzuki strings, orchestras, chamber music and a jazz collective next to its private lessons, so a sibling who wants a group and a sibling who wants one-on-one can end up under the same roof.
And don’t skip the band room. A school band or orchestra puts a beginner in a room full of squeaks and tuning notes every week, and private lessons work best layered on top of that, not in place of it. The band director is also the cheapest consultant you will ever get. Ask which instrument the program is short on, which rental shops they trust, and which private teachers their strongest players study with. Directors hear every beginner in the building, and they usually know exactly who to call.
There is a St. Louis reason to stay in that band room, too. To play in the St. Louis Symphony Youth Orchestra, musicians must be enrolled in their school music program, if one exists, and string players must take part in their school orchestra. The kid squeaking through a first-year method book in the back row is on the path that leads to the Symphony’s youth orchestra. Private lessons alone are not.
### What a good first lesson sounds like
Listen at the door. Within the first ten minutes you should hear the instrument, not a lecture. The student should walk out able to do one small thing they couldn’t do walking in, even if it is three clean notes. A first lesson that is half an hour of a teacher explaining their philosophy is a fair preview of the next thirty.
Ask for a trial lesson and expect to pay for it. A free first lesson is a sales call; a paid one is a lesson. While you sit in the corner chair, watch four things. Does the teacher talk to the student or to you? Does a correction come with a demonstration? Does the student leave with written practice notes? And does the teacher ever ask what the student actually listens to in the car?
The red flags are quiet. A studio that won’t let a parent watch. A teacher who can’t say what the next three months look like. A policy sheet that only shows up after you’ve paid.
### How studios bill, and where the real cost hides
Studios quote a 30-minute lesson three ways: per lesson, monthly tuition, or a semester package. They aren’t comparable until you turn each one into a cost per lesson actually taught. Then add the registration fee, the books, the recital fee, and ask about make-ups.
That last one is where the money goes. A lower rate with no make-ups can cost more per lesson taught than a higher rate that lets you reschedule, and you find out in the winter, when your kid is on the couch with a fever and the lesson you already paid for goes by without you.
### Should you rent an instrument or buy one?
Borrow first, if the library carries it. After that, rent for the first year on anything with moving parts, band and orchestra instruments especially, and think about buying mainly for keyboards and guitars. Most rental programs work as rent-to-own: a monthly payment, a damage plan, and credit toward purchase if the student sticks with it.
Two questions outrank the monthly number. Does the shop do its own repairs, and will the school’s band director accept the instrument? A cheap online instrument with keys that stick or strings that sit too high makes a beginner sound bad, and a beginner who sounds bad decides they have no talent.
### The phone call: five questions before you book
Most families pick a teacher off the first friendly voice that answers. Slow down for five minutes. Have a pen ready, put the call on speaker so your kid can hear it too, and ask the same five questions of every studio you call.
What does a trial lesson cost, and can I watch it? A yes to watching is a good sign. A no is worth a second thought.
How do you bill? Per lesson, monthly or by the semester. Write it down so you can turn it into a cost per lesson later.
What happens when we miss a week? Ask for the make-up and cancellation rules in writing before you pay anything.
What else will I buy? Registration, books, sheet music, recital fees. Get the all-in number.
What will my kid be able to play in three months? A good teacher answers this one without stalling. You can hear the difference between a plan and a pitch.
Then hang up and compare. Two studios that sound the same on the website almost never sound the same on the phone, and the one that asked about your kid before it quoted a price is usually the one to try first.
### How much practice should you expect?
Short and often beats long and rare. Five short sessions a week do more than one long Sunday session, because the skill is in the hands, and hands learn by repetition. For a young beginner that might be a few minutes at the kitchen table before dinner, with a parent close enough to hear.
For small children, a parent is part of the practice, not the audience for it. If nobody at home can sit with them most days, a group class may fit better for now. Weeknight activities all run on that same math, which is why picking lessons feels a lot like choosing a martial arts school.
### Can adults learn music as well?
Yes. Adults learn differently, not worse. They read faster, ask why, and catch their own mistakes. They also quit faster when progress feels invisible, usually after practicing hard on the weekend and not at all midweek. Put short sessions on an actual calendar, tell the teacher the one song you want to play, and expect a few clumsy weeks before your fingers stop arguing with you.
The library list works for grown-ups too. A borrowed keyboard on the dining room table for three weeks will tell you more about your patience than any studio tour.
Library guitar back on the shelf and the kid still asking for more? Browse music schools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two and ask the same three questions: what a trial lesson costs, how make-ups work, and how often students perform.
If you run a music school or teach from a home studio, this is where the next parent is looking. Families search by instrument and by town, so a full listing puts your studio in front of new customers right when they are ready to book. Add your studio to St Louis Near Me Directory.
### Recitals, and where to hear the music first
A recital is a deadline, and a date on the calendar produces more practice than any amount of nagging. Ask a teacher how often students perform and whether it is required. The answer tells you what kind of studio you are in.
Before the first lesson, take the student somewhere the music lives. At the Scott Joplin House State Historic Site, a player piano fills the air with Joplin melodies as you walk through the modest flat on Delmar Boulevard where he rented a room in 1902. Ragtime rolling out of a piano nobody is touching is a strong argument for learning to play one.
Off-key, we know: when did anyone last climb up and check your roof?
### What music teachers wish families knew before the first call
A teaching studio fills most of its year in a few weeks at the end of summer, and an empty after-school slot can’t be saved and sold later. That is why studios push monthly tuition instead of pay-as-you-go: tuition holds the slot. Make-up rules and late-cancellation rules are the same argument about that hour. Call early, ask both questions before you pay, and if a slot you love opens up midyear, grab it before the next family on the waitlist does.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a 30 minute music lesson cost?
A.  It depends on the teacher, the format and how the studio bills, so compare on one unit: cost per lesson actually taught. Convert monthly tuition and semester packages to that number, then add registration, books and recital fees. Ask about make-ups before you compare anything, because a cheap lesson you lose to a sick day is not cheap.
### Q. Can adults learn music as well?
A.  Yes. Adults grasp concepts and correct themselves faster than kids, build physical habits more slowly, and quit sooner when progress feels invisible. Short, frequent practice beats one long weekend session, and naming the song you want to play gives the lessons a destination.
### Q. At what age is it recommended to start music lessons?
A.  Readiness matters more than a birthday. Can the student sit and focus for the length of a lesson, take direction from an adult who isn’t a parent, and show some interest of their own? If you aren’t sure, borrow an instrument from St. Louis County Library for 3 weeks and watch what happens.
### Q. Why do piano students quit?
A.  Usually because progress feels invisible, practice has no routine, or the music has nothing to do with what they love. A teacher who builds technique under a song the student chose, plus a recital date on the calendar, fixes more of that than talent ever will.
### Q. Are 30-minute piano lessons worth it?
A.  For most young beginners, yes. Half an hour matches a small child’s attention span, and steady short lessons plus practice at home add up. As the music gets longer and harder, many students move to longer lessons.
### Q. How much is a private music teacher?
A.  Rates vary with training, performing experience and whether the teacher travels to you. Get the all-in number, fees and make-up policy included, from two teachers, and compare cost per lesson taught rather than the headline rate.
### Q. What is St. Louis known for in music?
A.  Scott Joplin, for a start. Joplin rented a room in 1902 in a modest flat on Delmar Boulevard, and at the Scott Joplin House State Historic Site an authentic player piano fills the air with his melodies as you walk through.

## Napa Came Second: A Winery Day Trip From St. Louis to the First U.S. Wine Region
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-winery-day-trip-guide
Seven California districts and one in Oregon filed to become the country’s first official wine region. On June 20, 1980, the federal government gave the title to Augusta, Missouri, a river town on the bluffs west of St. Louis. Napa Valley got its turn on January 28, 1981.
Drive out on a weekday and you can taste why that stings California. The road climbs out of the river bottom, the gravel pops under your tires in the lot, and the first pour of Norton, Missouri’s official state grape, lands in the glass dark and dry and bites back with acid. It is not trying to be a Cabernet. That’s the point.
The catch that ruins more of these days than bad wine is the ride home. Missouri’s RSMo 577.017 makes it an infraction to drink while operating a moving vehicle, which speaks to the driver. Cross into Illinois and 625 ILCS 5/11-502 wants alcohol in the passenger area sealed in its original container, for passengers as well as the driver. Same bottle, same back seat, different answer depending on which side of the river you’re on.
So settle the driver on Thursday, not in a gravel lot at dusk. And the next time someone calls Missouri wine a punchline, give them the date. Napa came second.
### Are there any wineries in St. Louis?
Yes, and the real surprise is next door. The Augusta AVA, in the Missouri River area just west of St. Louis, became the first American Viticultural Area in the country on June 20, 1980, and Napa Valley was second. The Hermann AVA adds 51,200 acres of vineyard country between St. Louis and Jefferson City.
### Ten dollars, four pours and your own picnic basket
Here’s one real afternoon, priced. At Noboleis Vineyards, 100 Hemsath Road in Augusta, a curated wine flight is $10 and a fully customizable one is $12, four 1.5-ounce pours served on a board. The board travels with you. Carry it out to the patio or the hilltop pavilion, set it on the table with the vineyard rows running away below you, and let the wind coming up the hill cool the glass.
No reservation is needed at the tasting bar. Bring a picnic if you like, because the winery encourages it, but leave the cooler of beer in the trunk: outside beverages aren’t allowed. Large groups should reserve ahead. Hours are 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and the number is 636-482-4500. Call it the template for every other room you try: flight price, food rule, group rule, closing time.
### How far is Missouri wine country from St. Louis?
Closer than most people think. The Augusta AVA sits in the Missouri River area just west of St. Louis. It covers roughly 15 square miles, close enough that you can leave after breakfast and be holding a glass before the lunch crowd.
Keep going west and you reach the Hermann AVA - 51,200 acres on the south bank of the Missouri, recognized August 18, 1983, in the stretch still called the Missouri Rhineland. Missouri has five AVAs. The other three, Ozark Mountain, Ozark Highlands and the Loess Hills District, are large rural appellations well outside the metro, and the Missouri Wine and Grape Board maps all of them.
Two other directions matter. Ste. Genevieve County, about an hour south on I-55, has its own cluster of tasting rooms and is the oldest permanent European settlement in Missouri. And the Augusta corridor - Defiance, Augusta, Dutzow, Marthasville - runs alongside Katy Trail State Park, which is why plenty of people on those patios arrived by bicycle.
### What are Norton and Chambourcin, and why does this region grow them?
They’re the two red grapes you’ll meet first here, and neither is European. Norton - also sold as Cynthiana - is Vitis aestivalis, an American species grape traced to Virginia in the 1830s. Missouri made it the official state grape under RSMo 10.160, effective August 28, 2003. It runs dark, dry and high in acid, with a wild streak a Cabernet drinker either loves on the first sip or never warms to.
Chambourcin is a French-American hybrid whose parentage was never fully documented. It’s a teinturier grape - the juice runs dark rather than clear - so the wine lands deep ruby with black cherry and plum. It ripens around the same time as Concord, fights powdery mildew in a wet year, and isn’t reliably hardy in northern Missouri. On the white side, Vignoles does most of the work, bottled both bone dry and frankly sweet.
The reason is climate and soil, not stubbornness. Cabernet and Chardonnay are Vitis vinifera, bred for a Mediterranean summer, and they buckle under cold snaps, humid fungal pressure and a root louse that lives in American ground. American species and hybrids handle all three. Walk in expecting Napa in a bottle and you’ll miss what this region is genuinely good at.
### Why does Missouri have wine history at all?
Because German immigrants planted the Missouri River valley in the mid-1800s and built one of the country’s largest wine regions out of it, decades before Prohibition. That isn’t local boosterism, and the proof left the state. When the phylloxera louse was killing French vineyards, Missouri’s state entomologist Charles V. Riley worked with French scientists on the cause and the cure.
By the winter of 1872, George Husmann of Hermann and the St. Louis nursery firm Bush & Son & Meissner had shipped nearly 400,000 American vine cuttings to Montpellier, France. Grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstock was the fix, and it is still standard practice in vineyards worldwide. The University of Missouri keeps that record in its own archives.
Prohibition ended the run. Vines came out, cellars went quiet, and the revival didn’t start until the 1960s. When the federal AVA system arrived in 1980, Augusta’s petition rested partly on that history - which is how a 15-square-mile patch of Missouri farmland beat every California district to the first appellation.
### How much do you typically spend at a winery?
It turns on your group size and whether you eat there, and any figure printed online goes stale fast - fees move with the season and with what’s in the flight. Treat a published price as a starting point and confirm it on the winery’s own page the week you go.
Three things move the bill. The tasting flight fee, which many places waive or credit toward a bottle you buy, and which is rarely posted anywhere obvious. Glasses versus bottles at the table - once three people are drinking, a bottle usually wins. And food, which is where a modest afternoon quietly turns expensive.
Three questions on the phone save more than any coupon. Is there a tasting fee, and does it come off a bottle purchase? Is outside food allowed, and does that change on event days? Is there a group minimum or a deposit for a party over six on a weekend? Whoever answers can settle your whole afternoon in ninety seconds.
### Where can I go for a wine tasting in St. Louis?
Four directions, and they don’t feel alike. West along the river through Defiance, Augusta and Dutzow gives you bluff views, bike traffic and the shortest drive. Hermann is a whole town organized around it. South toward Ste. Genevieve stays quieter on a fall Saturday. And the metro itself has tasting rooms, some run by producers whose vines are an hour away.
The Illinois side deserves a note. Neither Illinois appellation is near the metro - Shawnee Hills was designated in December 2006 near Carbondale, and the Upper Mississippi River Valley AVA, established in 2009, covers the Galena corner. So an Illinois tasting room 30 minutes from downtown isn’t inside an AVA. That’s a fact about federal boundary lines, not about your glass.
The metro-east drive is its own argument. The Great River Road along the bluffs above Alton toward Grafton is one of the better hours of scenery in either state. Statewide, Illinois counted more than 130 tasting rooms as of 2024.
### How do you get a group out there and home again?
Decide the ride before you decide the winery. Rideshare coverage thins out fast west of Defiance and south of Ste. Genevieve, and the car that dropped you at one o’clock may have no twin at five. Book a driver, draft one, or make sure somebody is genuinely not drinking - getting everyone home safely is a Thursday problem, not a dusk-in-a-gravel-lot problem.
The open-container rules differ across the river, and that catches people out. Missouri has no statewide open container ban covering passengers. RSMo 577.017 makes it an infraction to consume alcohol while operating a moving vehicle - it speaks to the driver, not the back seat. Plenty of metro municipalities ban open containers by ordinance anyway, so legal under state law is not legal on every street you park on.
Illinois runs the other way. Under 625 ILCS 5/11-502, alcohol in the passenger area must sit in the original container with the seal unbroken, for passengers as well as the driver. Subsection (c) exempts passengers in a limousine, a chartered bus or a motor home used for its ordinary purpose - and even then the driver may not have alcohol in the driver’s area. That exemption is why the party-bus model exists, so ask how a vehicle is licensed before you book.
If you’d rather hire the ride than draft one, our guide to booking transportation in the St. Louis metro covers what to confirm before a deposit changes hands.
Half the fun is the road out. Here’s the Route 94 drive along the Missouri River, stop by stop.
### When should you go, and when will it be packed?
October weekends are the busiest of the year on the Missouri River bluffs, and it isn’t close. Harvest runs from late summer into fall, the bluff timber turns, and Hermann holds Oktoberfest every weekend in October. Want a patio table on an October Saturday? Reserve it, and expect a wait anyway.
May through early July is the underrated window: green, warm, far less crowded, easy to walk into without a reservation. Late winter is the opposite - between January and March many tasting rooms cut hours or close on weekdays, so confirm the day before instead of finding a locked door 45 minutes from home.
A weekday afternoon buys you something a Saturday can’t: the person pouring has time to talk, and that conversation is most of what separates a winery visit from drinking wine on your own patio. Bring a layer - bluff-top wind in April is colder than the forecast sounds.
### What the owner is watching when your group walks in
Here’s the math from behind the bar. Missouri and Illinois both run three-tier alcohol systems, and a bottle that travels producer to distributor to retailer comes back to the winery at a fraction of shelf price. The same bottle poured across its own bar keeps the whole margin. That one fact shapes everything: a small winery here is an agritourism business that also farms, and the tasting room, the event calendar and the wine club carry the year. WineAmerica’s 2025 study counted 127 wine producers, 1,318 acres of vineyards and 1.08 million wine-related tourist visits in Missouri. October pays for February. What owners trade complaints about isn’t customers - it’s late spring frost and herbicide drift off neighboring row crops, which the University of Missouri’s Grape and Wine Institute has worked on for years. When a storm drops a limb across the patio, the first call goes to tree services, not the winemaker. The avoidable one is a party of fourteen arriving unannounced at two o’clock on an October Saturday. And since people search this category by place, a room 40 minutes out reaches new customers across the metro only if it’s listed and complete.
Ready to pick a direction instead of a link? Browse wineries across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the two that fit your drive, and ask each the same three things: tasting fee, group policy, outside food. If you are making a day of it, a stop for bread and pastry on the way out beats gas-station food - our guide to finding a good bakery here covers who bakes early enough to catch.
If you run a winery or a tasting room within a day’s drive of St. Louis, list your winery on St Louis Near Me Directory so the groups planning Saturday become customers at your bar.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I go for a wine tasting in St. Louis?
A.  Pick a direction first. West through Defiance, Augusta and Dutzow means bluff views and Katy Trail traffic. Hermann is a town built on it. South toward Ste. Genevieve runs quieter. The Illinois side pairs tasting rooms with the Great River Road above Alton. Then filter by what you want: dry reds, food service, a patio, or a room quiet enough to talk in.
### Q. What are some good wineries in the St. Louis area?
A.  Good depends on what you came for, and any ranking you read online ages badly as staff, menus and hours change. Decide first whether you want dry reds or sweet whites, a view or a quiet room, food on site or a cooler you bring. Then check three current things: hours, group policy, and whether tastings need a reservation.
### Q. How much do you typically spend at a winery?
A.  It depends on group size and whether you eat there, and printed prices go stale quickly. The tasting flight fee is often waived or credited toward a bottle, a bottle usually beats glasses once three people are drinking, and food is where the bill really grows. Call ahead about the fee, the credit, outside food, and any weekend group minimum.
### Q. How much does it cost to have a winery?
A.  Too variable for a useful number, and published figures age fast. Land and vines come first, and vines need about three growing seasons before a real crop. Then tanks, licensed production space and a tasting room. Licensing is layered: a federal TTB basic permit plus a state manufacturer license from Missouri’s Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Control or the Illinois Liquor Control Commission. Get the licensing checklist before the land.
### Q. What winery does Eric Trump own?
A.  Trump Winery, near Charlottesville, Virginia, in Albemarle County. The property was bought at a foreclosure auction in 2011, and Eric Trump has run it since 2012 through Eric Trump Wine Manufacturing LLC. It surfaces in winery searches nationwide, but it has no connection to Missouri or Illinois wine - different climate, different grapes, a thousand miles apart.
### Q. What is the best time of day to arrive at a winery?
A.  Earlier than you think. Tasting rooms fill through the afternoon, especially on a weekend with live music, and an early arrival buys you an unhurried pour and a staff member with time to actually talk you through what is in the glass. Check the day’s hours before you drive out - seasonal schedules change and some close earlier than the website suggests.

## $2 Rides, Free Rides and a 3-Day Rule: Getting Around St. Louis Without a Car
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/getting-around-st-louis-rides-shuttles-metrolink
The Red Line pulls out of Forest Park-DeBaliviere and the car rocks as it picks up speed, your bag pinned between your knees, when your phone buzzes against your leg. It’s your mother. Her cardiology follow-up is the day after tomorrow at 7:40 a.m., she hasn’t driven in two winters, and she wants to know who’s taking her.
If she’s on Missouri Medicaid, that ride may be covered the whole time. But the state wants the call at least three calendar days before the appointment. You just missed it by a day, standing in a swaying train car with one hand on the pole.
For this one, call a licensed cab tonight and give the dispatcher the exact door. If a medical problem has come up and her doctor says they can see her, ask the Medicaid line about an urgent care ride, because it takes those calls 24 hours a day. Then put every appointment after this one on the three-day clock.
That’s the whole St. Louis ride map, riding with you on one train. Around here, the cheaper the ride, the earlier you have to ask for it. A cab or a rideshare will come tonight, and you pay for the hurry. Almost everything cheaper wants a phone call first, and every one of those calls has a clock on it. Learn the clocks and a car stops being the only answer.
### What is the best way to get around St. Louis?
Match the ride to the clock. MetroLink is $2.50 and runs from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m.; Via Metro STL is $2 for trips up to seven miles in parts of St. Louis County; licensed cabs and rideshare cover the hours the trains don’t. Book the rest ahead: a Missouri Medicaid ride needs three calendar days’ notice, and Call-A-Ride’s reservation line closes at 5 p.m.
### The booking clock, cheapest ride first
Tape this inside the cabinet where the coffee mugs live, because some night you’ll want it at 9 p.m. again. A Medicaid ride to the doctor in Missouri costs least and asks most: call (866) 269-5927 at least three calendar days before the appointment, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., or the number on the card if you’re in a health plan. Metro Call-A-Ride, the $2 lift-equipped van for riders whose disabilities keep them off the bus and train, takes reservations at 314-982-1505 from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day, holidays included. Via Metro STL is a $2 shared ride you hail in an app, or by phone at 636.251.3328, inside zones in North, South and West St. Louis County, up to seven miles a trip.
MetroLink, at $2.50, needs no booking at all, but the trains run only from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m. A group shuttle or a wedding van needs a written quote from a company you’ve checked, booked weeks out. A cab or a rideshare takes minutes, and the price is whatever the meter or the app says that night.
Miss a window and you don’t lose the trip. You slide down the list, and the meter starts sooner. Everything below is how to stay near the top of it.
### Who pays for a ride to the doctor?
Hold music. A pen with no cap. The appointment letter flattened under your palm on the counter. That’s what booking a covered ride sounds like, and it goes faster when the right papers are in front of you before you dial.
In Missouri, MO HealthNet’s Non-Emergency Medical Transportation program, NEMT, gets eligible participants to covered appointments when they don’t have free, appropriate transportation of their own. The ride might be a bus pass, a van, a taxi, a rideshare, an ambulance, or, if it’s truly necessary, an airplane. The broker picks the least expensive mode that fits the medical need, though you can ask for a provider you like.
Fee-for-service participants call (866) 269-5927 at least three calendar days ahead, weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. If a medical problem comes up and the doctor says they can see you, that urgent care trip can be called in 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Managed care members call the number on their health plan card instead.
Have the rider’s name, date of birth, address, phone number and MO HealthNet ID on the counter, along with the provider’s name, address and phone number. Know the date and time of the appointment and the medical reason for the trip, mention any walker, cane or wheelchair, and say whether a rider under 21 needs someone along.
Three details change how the day goes, and they’re easy to miss on the first call.
A neighbor can drive. NEMT may help with gas costs when a friend or neighbor takes you, but the broker has to approve it before the appointment. MTM Health, the company that books Missouri’s Medicaid rides, says it reimburses at least $0.55 a mile when you choose gas mileage reimbursement.
No texting means no rideshare. If the broker assigns an Uber or Lyft, the rider has to be able to send and receive text messages. If Grandma carries a flip phone, call (866) 269-5927 and have rideshare excluded from her file.
The ride is late. Once a scheduled ride is more than 15 minutes past its time, call (866) 269-5944. And you should hear your pickup details, the time, the address and the type of vehicle, no later than 24 hours before the trip.
One more wrinkle worth knowing. MTM Health’s own Missouri page says two days’ notice is enough if you live in an urban county and three in a basic or rural one, and it lets you schedule rides in the MTM Link mobile app or web portal. The state’s FAQ says three calendar days. Call three days out and you’re covered either way.
Across the river, Illinois works differently, which trips up families with someone on each side. Fee-for-service Medicaid customers call Transdev at 877-725-0569, but Transdev doesn’t schedule the ride. It gives you a list of providers to call yourself. Managed care members call the number on the back of their card, and each plan sets its own scheduling rules.
### Two $2 rides worth knowing by name
The van door folds open and the lift whines down to the curb. Metro Call-A-Ride runs more than 120 wheelchair-lift equipped vans for riders whose disabilities keep them off MetroBus and MetroLink. You qualify under the Americans with Disabilities Act first, and then each trip is $2. Book at 314-982-1505, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day, holidays included, or schedule and cancel trips online with MetroGo!
It’s a shared ride, so the van may pick up someone else on the way. Your trip can be scheduled up to an hour before or after the time you asked for, with a 30-minute pickup window, so be at the door with your shoes on and keys in your pocket when that window opens. Dropped off early with time to kill near the clinic? Look up nail salons near you and sit somewhere warm. Cancel at least two hours ahead or it counts as a no-show, and repeated no-shows can cost you riding privileges. Trips that aren’t ADA-mandated can be reserved only up to one day ahead, and same-day trips happen only if there’s room. Text 314-742-3051 to check on a ride or cancel it.
Here’s the money part. Once you qualify for ADA paratransit, Metro’s On The Way With ADA card lets you ride MetroLink and MetroBus for free. Call ADA Services at 314.982.1510 to apply. On a day the bus works, that’s a ride for nothing instead of $2.
Via Metro STL works more like a rideshare with a bus fare. You hail a vehicle from the Via app, walk a short way to the pickup spot it picks, and share the trip with people headed the same direction. A ride is $2, anywhere inside a service zone during operating hours, with a seven-mile limit per trip. The zones cover parts of North, South and West St. Louis County. No smartphone? Call 636.251.3328 to set up the ride. Need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle? Switch on the “Wheelchair Accessible” option in your profile. Bringing a bike? Request two seats.
Booking a van, a car or a shuttle for a date you can’t miss? Start with transportation companies across the St. Louis metro, call two of them with your date, headcount and pickup address in hand, and ask each one for the quote in writing so the numbers line up.
If you’re the shuttle owner, the limo driver or the one-van medical transport crew those riders are calling, a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory that spells out your service area, your vehicles and your wheelchair access gives the rider comparing two quotes a reason to call you and become one of your customers.
### Where does MetroLink actually go?
The platform hums, the bell dings twice, and the doors slide open on a train that costs $2.50 to ride. Nobody needs to be called the day before, and for plenty of riders it’s the spine of a life without a car.
It runs seven days a week from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m., on two lines and 38 stations through the City of St. Louis, St. Louis County and St. Clair County, Illinois. The Red Line runs between the airport and Shiloh-Scott in Illinois; the Blue Line runs between Shrewsbury-Lansdowne I-44 and Fairview Heights, Illinois. If your day starts or ends far from that line, plan the gap with a bus, a Via ride or a cab.
People ask, “Can I live in St. Louis without a car?” Yes, if home and work both sit near that corridor or a busy bus line, and if you build the late nights around a cab company’s phone number instead of the last train.
Two things catch first-timers. Every MetroLink station now has automated security gates, and the validators that open them don’t support tap to pay with a debit or credit card. Buy the fare in the Transit app or at a ticket machine first. Our St. Louis public transit guide has the full fare table, the bus routes and the trick that caps what a day of riding can cost.
### The airport run, door by door
A suitcase wheel clicking over sidewalk seams in the dark is a lonely sound. At Lambert, the TSA checkpoints open at 3:30 a.m., and MetroLink’s first trains run before 5 a.m. On an early flight, don’t build the morning around the first train. Book the car the night before.
Check Metro’s Rider Alerts before you count on the train at all. Metro is closing both airport stations: Terminal 1’s MetroLink station closed October 12 for airport construction expected to finish in mid-December, and Terminal 2’s station closes November 2 for track maintenance, also expected back in mid-December. Until November 2, ride a westbound Red Line train to Terminal 2, head to Exit 10 and take the free airport shuttle to Terminal 1. Leaving Terminal 1, the shuttle to the train goes from Exit 12. Metro says it will share how riders can connect during the Terminal 2 closure before it begins. Questions: 314-231-2345, or text 314-207-9786, weekdays 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Know your door before you book anything, because “the airport” is not an address a driver can use:
Rideshare (Uber and Lyft): Terminal 1, Door 6 on the Departure level. Terminal 2, Door 12 on the Arrivals level.
Taxi: Terminal 1, Door 14 to the garage Yellow Level. Terminal 2, across from Door 12 in the garage. Every taxi pickup adds a $4 Airport Use Fee.
Your terminal: Southwest flies from Terminal 2’s E gates. American, Delta, United, Alaska, Frontier and Air Canada use Terminal 1.
Car services: the airport lists nine car service and limousine companies, with phone numbers, among its ground transportation providers.
One more trick for when the trains are back. Metro offers free long-term parking, up to 14 days, in marked spaces at nine MetroLink stations. One of them is Shrewsbury-Lansdowne I-44, the end of the Blue Line, so change to a Red Line train at Forest Park-DeBaliviere. For the dollars-and-cents comparison, see how to get to the St. Louis airport and what it costs.
### Cabs, apps and the one list to check first
Rain ticks on the bus shelter roof as the crowd spills out after a game, and the price in your rideshare app jumps while you watch. That isn’t your imagination. Uber’s own explanation of surge pricing says prices may increase when demand outruns drivers, and it names bad weather, rush hour and special events as the usual causes.
“Is Uber or taxi cheaper in St. Louis?” Check both. Get the app’s quote, then call a licensed cab company and ask what the trip to your address usually runs. Taxis picking up at the airport add the $4 fee. For how a cab meter adds up across town, see what a taxi costs in St. Louis.
Before you get into anything for hire, though, check one list. The St. Louis Metropolitan Taxicab Commission publishes the companies it licenses and says they are the only legal for-hire transportation companies in the St. Louis Metropolitan area, licensed and insured. It names five airport cab companies and six on-call cab companies, then its premium sedan services, each with a phone number. Not sure about a company? The commission takes questions at 314-535-7700. Airport taxis answer to that same commission.
### How do you book a group shuttle that actually shows up?
Eleven people in a South City driveway in their good clothes, checking their phones, listening for an engine that isn’t coming. Too many group-transport horror stories start with a verbal price. Get the quote in writing, confirm the exact vehicle, and check the paperwork before you pay a deposit.
The paperwork is checkable. A for-hire carrier moving passengers entirely within Missouri needs Missouri intrastate operating authority from MoDOT: a USDOT number, an application through MoDOT Carrier Express, proof of insurance sent in by the insurance company, and, for passenger carriers, a financial statement. Inside the city and county, look for the company on the Taxicab Commission’s list. Crossing into Illinois or beyond? Federal rules set minimum liability coverage for for-hire passenger carriers at $1.5 million for a vehicle seating 15 or fewer, driver included, and $5 million for 16 or more.
Then ask the four questions that decide your night:
What happens if the vehicle breaks down on the way?
Does the clock start at your door or at their garage?
What are the overtime and cancellation terms, in writing?
Is gratuity already in the quote?
A van that seats your whole party may not hold their suitcases too, because seats and cargo space are different things. Count bags along with people. Our guides to what a limo costs in St. Louis and renting a party bus walk through the contract line by line.
Missed the last train and need somewhere warm to wait it out? Here are the coffee shops open late in St. Louis.
### Leaving town without a car
Two doors out of town, and neither needs a parking spot. Amtrak’s Gateway Station sits at 430 South 15th Street downtown, in an intermodal center Amtrak describes as serving Amtrak, light rail, and intercity and local buses. Greyhound, according to the airport, picks up at the Bus Port at Lambert, just south of Terminal 1. A terminal shuttle runs there from Terminal 1, Door 12, and Terminal 2, Door 10.
Whatever you’re booking, the rule from the kitchen table holds. Call early, write down who you talked to, and keep the confirmation where you can find it with one hand while the other holds a coffee.
