### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can I live in St. Louis without a car?
A.  Yes, if home and work sit near the MetroLink corridor or a busy MetroBus line and you plan around the hours: trains run from before 5 a.m. to about 1 a.m. Via Metro STL covers short trips in parts of St. Louis County for $2. Keep a licensed cab company’s number for late nights, and book medical rides days ahead.
### Q. Is Uber or taxi cheaper in St. Louis?
A.  Neither wins every time. Uber says its prices may increase with demand, naming bad weather, rush hour and special events, and a taxi picking up at Lambert adds a $4 Airport Use Fee. Check the app’s quote, then call a cab company on the Metropolitan Taxicab Commission’s list and ask what the same trip runs.
### Q. How do I schedule a ride with MTM?
A.  MTM Health arranges rides for eligible MO HealthNet participants. Call 1-866-269-5927 at least three calendar days before the appointment, with your MO HealthNet ID, the provider’s name and address, and the appointment time, or schedule in the MTM Link mobile app or web portal. Health plan members call the number on their card instead.
### Q. Can you get free Uber rides if you have Medicaid?
A.  Not on your own app. But Missouri’s Medicaid ride program may assign an Uber or Lyft for a trip to a covered appointment you book through (866) 269-5927. To use the rideshare option, the rider must be able to send and receive text messages. If not, ask the broker to exclude rideshare from the file.
### Q. How to get a ride somewhere with no money?
A.  Start with coverage you may already have. Missouri’s Medicaid ride program gets eligible participants to covered medical appointments, and Illinois fee-for-service customers can get a provider list from Transdev at 877-725-0569. Riders who qualify for ADA paratransit can ride MetroLink and MetroBus free with Metro’s On The Way With ADA card.
### Q. Is Southwest terminal 1 or 2 at STL?
A.  Southwest flies from Terminal 2, out of the E gates, where the TSA checkpoint opens at 3:30 a.m. Rideshare pickup there is at Door 12 on the Arrivals level, and the taxi zone sits across from Door 12 in the Terminal 2 garage. American, Delta and United use Terminal 1, so tell your driver which one.
### Q. Does St. Louis have a metro system?
A.  Yes. Metro Transit runs MetroLink light rail, with two lines and 38 stations in Missouri and Illinois, plus MetroBus and Call-A-Ride. A train ride is $2.50. A credit card won’t open the station gates, so buy the fare in the Transit app or at a ticket machine before you reach the platform.

## St. Louis Wants Your Signed Lease Before It Says You Can Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/leasing-commercial-space-st-louis-metro
I’ll sign today and sort out the permit after. Be honest: you’ve said it in your head, standing in an empty storefront with your footsteps echoing off bare walls, a drop ceiling humming overhead, dust in the light from the front glass, and a rent number that finally fits the spreadsheet you built at the kitchen table after your shift.
You want it. Your hand is already reaching for the pen.
Here’s the order of operations nobody walks you through. In the City of St. Louis, the Permit Office will not take a commercial occupancy application until you bring either a signed lease or a notarized letter from the property owner. Only after the application is in does the Zoning section review whether the use you wrote down is allowed at that address. The City wants your signature before it tells you yes.
That’s the trap, and it isn’t your fault. The process runs backward. But the same City page lists the second door: the notarized owner’s letter. Ask the landlord for that letter before you sign the lease, file the application, and write the lease so rent starts on the later of a fixed date or the day your occupancy permit issues. Then a zoning “no” costs you an application fee instead of a five-year lease.
### What is the best way to find commercial real estate?
Work three channels at once: the listing sites for space owners chose to market, a tenant-side broker licensed in the state where the building sits, and a slow drive down the corridor you want, because some owners only put a sign in the glass. In the City of St. Louis, add one step before you sign: confirm with the Permit Office that your use is allowed at that exact address.
### The permit nobody tours with you
Inspection day is you on a folding chair in an empty room, coffee going cold, listening for a truck door outside. The City sets the date, and someone has to be at the property between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. to let the inspectors in. The ones who always look at a commercial space are the Building, Electrical, Mechanical and Plumbing inspectors and the Fire Marshal, and Air Pollution can join depending on the business.
Before that, you write a check at the counter. The application costs $80 for a unit of 3,500 square feet or less and $160 above that. Bring cash or a check, because that’s all the Permit Office accepts. If you pay $80 and the inspector measures more than 3,500 square feet, you owe the other $80 before the permit issues. And the clock runs: an application is valid for 60 days, then it’s treated as abandoned.
A permit also doesn’t follow the building. It stays valid only until the business changes, the business’s owner changes or the property’s use changes, so buying an existing shop means a new application, not a handoff. Call the Permit Section at (314) 622-3313 with the exact address and the exact use before you sign anything. If your address sits outside the City limits, make the same call to whichever building department covers it.
### What to carry into Room 425
The Permit Section sits at 1200 Market, Room 425, in City Hall, open weekdays from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and the application is made in person with a Customer Service Representative. The application is made in person, so walk in with everything in one folder.
Bring the signed lease, or the notarized letter from the owner granting permission to occupy, and either one should say what type of business will use the space. Bring contact information for the property owner and for your business, know whether the space is under or over 3,500 square feet, and be ready to describe exactly what kind of activity happens in the business. Be specific. The City’s own examples are manufacturing and an automotive painting facility. And bring cash or a check for the fee.
Starting a brand-new business in the City? The Business Assistance Center in City Hall, Room 421, will access all the information needed to open your business and process the applications with the various City departments for you.
### What happens if Zoning says no?
It’s the phone call that turns your stomach over. If Zoning denies the application because the use isn’t allowed in that zoned area, a Conditional Use or Board of Adjustment hearing may be set. That’s more waiting on a room you may already be paying for, which is exactly why the lease should not start the rent clock until the permit issues.
Inspectors can stop you too. If any one of them finds major violations, you don’t get the permit. You get a violation letter, you fix the problem, and you schedule a re-inspection that has to be passed by the same inspector who wrote the violation. Before you sign, ask the landlord in writing who pays to fix what an inspector finds in the building itself.
### Triple net or gross: what will you actually pay each month?
The flyer number is the smallest one you’ll see. The real one shows up later, in an envelope you open standing at the counter, and your shoulders drop an inch. A triple net lease is base rent plus your share of property taxes, building insurance and common area maintenance. A gross lease folds those into one number. Compare buildings on the all-in cost per square foot per year, never on base rent, and feel how different the two quotes look once the extras land on the same page.
In Missouri the tax piece runs heavier than tenants expect. Section 137.115 RSMo assesses subclass (3) real property, the commercial class, at thirty-two percent, against nineteen percent for subclass (1), the residential class. Section 139.600 RSMo then charges an extra levy against that same subclass (3) property. On a triple net lease, that bill is yours.
Across the river the math changes. Except in counties of more than 200,000 people that classify property, 35 ILCS 200/9-145 values each tract or lot at 33 1/3% of its fair cash value. The rate is what moves, so pull the actual tax bill on the actual parcel before you compare two buildings.
### What does CAM cover, and what should you cap?
Common area maintenance is the parking lot in February: the plow scraping at dawn, the salt crunching under your boots, the lights over the lot that never quite all work. You pay a share of it based on your square footage against the building’s. Ask for the actual CAM statements from past years, not the leasing flyer’s estimate.
Then ask for four things in writing: a cap on the costs the landlord controls, an exclusion for big replacements like a new roof or a repaved lot, a ceiling on the management fee, and the right to audit the bill. And ask how the space was measured, because rentable square feet include a slice of the hallways and you only work inside the usable ones.
Still a year from signing anything? Here are the coffee shops that let you camp with a laptop in the meantime.
### Build-out money isn’t a gift
You can smell a build-out before you see it: drywall dust, fresh paint, the hot-plastic smell of new conduit. A tenant improvement allowance pays for some of that, and it gets priced right back into your rent, your term and your free months. A longer term and a space the owner badly wants filled push the number up.
Read the parts nobody reads. Who owns the improvements when the lease ends. Whether a restoration clause makes you tear out what you built. Whether unused allowance disappears. If the allowance pays back after the work is done, you float the contractor yourself, so plan the cash for that gap before you sign.
### Who should sit on your side of the table?
It might start with a handshake in a parking lot. Make it happen before the first tour. You want a broker who works for you, picked early so nobody argues later about who brought you in. In Missouri, broker and salesperson licenses carry continuing-education rules set by the Missouri Real Estate Commission, so ask for the license and check it. Ask how many deals like yours they closed in the past year, in your building type, and ask in writing who pays them and when.
If the building is in Illinois, ask whether your broker holds an Illinois license. Starting January 1, 2026, the IDFPR Division of Real Estate has brokers and managing brokers from outside Illinois apply through an Endorsement Process, which replaced the old reciprocal process with specific states.
Want someone on your side of the table before you tour anything? Browse commercial real estate across the St. Louis metro and call two. Still weighing a storefront against working from home a while longer? Here’s what renting actually costs here.
If you’re the shop, the studio or the one-truck crew moving to a new address, the move is when regulars lose track of you. List your business with us so the customers searching for you find the new door, not the old one.
### Should you buy the building instead of leasing it?
Owning means the roof leak at 2 a.m. is your phone ringing, not the landlord’s. Buy when the business is steady, the spot is truly long-term and you have cash left after the down payment. Lease when you’re still learning how much room you need. An SBA 504 loan can be used for the purchase, construction or renovation of existing buildings or land, and SBA says a 504 loan cannot be used for “speculation or investment in rental real estate.” If the real question is whether the business can carry ten years of fixed rent or a mortgage, that’s worth an outside opinion. Here’s what a business consultant costs in St. Louis.
### The keys aren’t the finish line
Opening day comes, the paper sign in the window says “Now Open,” and the street walks past it. The lease process is built to get you into a room. Nothing in it gets people through the door. Every regular who knew the old address has to be told, whether you run a salon or one of the auto repair shops already listed with us, every search that still points at the old spot has to be fixed, and that work lands in the same weeks as the inspections.
That’s where a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory earns its keep. It doesn’t need a public address, so you can be listed while the build-out is still dust and plywood, and you can list in up to 10 categories with up to 40 location tags, so the neighborhood you move into knows you’re coming. You signed for the space. Refuse to be invisible in it.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What to look for when choosing a commercial real estate broker?
A.  Ask which side they usually represent in your building type, how many similar deals they closed in the past year, and whether they’re licensed in the state where the property sits. Get the representation agreement in writing before the first tour, and pick them before you call a single sign.
### Q. What is the best website to find commercial real estate?
A.  No single site holds everything. The big listing sites show space owners chose to market. To find the people who know the rest, search commercial real estate on St Louis Near Me Directory for brokers working the St. Louis metro, then drive the corridor you want and write down every sign in a window.
### Q. How can I estimate the value of a commercial property?
A.  Start with the income it produces: net operating income divided by a capitalization rate. The cap rate is the part that moves, so any number printed in an article ages fast. Cross-check against comparable sales, then pay for an appraisal before you commit.
### Q. What is the 2% rule in commercial real estate?
A.  It’s a rule of thumb borrowed from rental houses that compares one month’s rent with the purchase price as a quick screen. It ignores lease terms, tenant credit and debt cost, so treat it as a five-second filter, never a valuation.
### Q. Is commercial real estate a good investment now?
A.  That depends on how long you can hold, what the debt costs you and how solid the tenant is. If you’re buying a building your own business will occupy, the better question is whether the business could carry a year with no other tenant paying in.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule in real estate?
A.  It’s a home-buyer readiness check people pass around: savings set aside, payment reserves beyond the down payment, and several comparable properties reviewed before you offer. For a commercial space, stretch every one of those cushions, because empty months and build-outs both run longer than owners plan.

## Rabies Is the Only Shot St. Louis City Requires. The Tag Costs $4 or $50.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/choosing-a-vet-st-louis-routine-pet-care
Click, click, skid. Your dog’s nails scrabble for grip on the stainless exam table, her whole weight leaning into your hip, and the room smells like rubbing alcohol and somebody else’s nervous cat. The vet hasn’t walked in yet. You are already wondering whether this is the right place, and whether you will be back here at 2 a.m. some night wishing you had asked more questions.
Here is the thing almost nobody in this city is told when they adopt. Inside St. Louis city limits, the city says rabies inoculation is the only vaccination required by city ordinance. Every other shot your clinic offers is a medical recommendation you get to talk through. And rabies comes with paperwork: puppies and kittens must get their first rabies shot and be registered with the city between the ages of 3 and 4 months, and new arrivals get a 30-day grace period to register.
Then the line that makes people stop scrolling. The city’s registration fee is $4.00 for a spayed or neutered pet and $50.00 for an intact one. Same dog, same shot, a $46 difference that sits on whether one surgery happened.
If the vet who gave the shot did not have City of St. Louis tags available, you register in person at Animal Care and Control, 1520 Market St., Suite 4051, downtown, Monday-Friday from 8am - 4:30pm, and you bring proof of the rabies shot. They take a cashier’s check, personal check, money order or card. Questions go to (314) 657-1500. Lose the tag off the collar and a new one costs $1.00, with proof of a current rabies shot. So ask a new vet one extra question: do you carry City tags?
That is the shape of the whole decision. Almost everything that separates a clinic you will keep for ten years from one you quit in ten months is knowable before you book. Licenses are public. The rabies rules are published. Estimates are documents you can read line by line. Spend a boring hour now, so you are not spending a frantic one later with a whimpering animal in the back seat and the hazards on.
### How do I choose the right vet for my pet?
Use three filters, in this order: does the practice routinely see your species and life stage, is the veterinarian currently licensed in the state where the clinic sits, and what exactly happens when your animal needs care after hours. Everything else, from the parking lot to whether they text reminders, is preference.
Checking a license takes about as long as the hold music. In Missouri, the Veterinary Medical Board page carries a Licensee Search link, and vets themselves renew through the state’s MOPRO site.
Across the river, Illinois runs its own IDFPR License Lookup. If the clinic you are eyeing sits on the Illinois side, that is the one to use.
Accreditation is a separate, voluntary layer. Some animal hospitals earn accreditation from the American Animal Hospital Association. It is a real signal, though plenty of good clinics never apply, so its absence proves nothing. AAHA’s own guide to choosing a veterinarian is worth ten minutes on the couch.
### Book the first exam before anything is wrong
The worst time to meet a vet is the night your cat stops eating. A new-client exam at a busy practice can book out for days, and a same-day sick slot at a clinic that has never seen your animal may simply not exist. Establishing care means there is a chart, a weight history, and a voice on the phone that recognizes your name.
It also explains the thing that frustrates people most. The front desk usually will not tell you what to give the dog over the phone, because the doctor has not examined her. They are not being difficult. They are being careful with a license.
So make the small move. Adopted, just moved, or still driving the interstate back to your old clinic? Book a wellness exam this month. What it buys is access. If the car ride is the real obstacle, a dog who pants and shakes the whole way or a cat who flattens under the bed at the sight of the carrier, mobile vets in St. Louis make house calls.
### What happens at a first visit with a new vet?
The paper on the exam table crinkles under four paws, a cold stethoscope presses into fur, and a treat appears from a scrub pocket at exactly the right moment. A first visit is mostly history and hands. Expect the scale, the thermometer nobody enjoys, a nose-to-tail physical, a look at teeth and gums, and a long talk about food, parasite prevention and how your animal actually lives. Have the old clinic email records ahead, and carry the rabies certificate yourself. If you live in the city, Animal Care and Control asks for proof of that rabies shot too.
Confirm the practice sees your species before you book, not at the counter with a rabbit in a box. Rabbits, guinea pigs, birds and reptiles tend to hide illness until they are quite sick, and plenty of general practices see only dogs and cats. If your household runs scaly, feathered or pocket-sized, start with exotic vets in St. Louis.
Ask two things at the desk before you leave. What does the new-client exam include, and what is billed separately? Then ask whether rechecks are charged. Those two answers explain most of the gap between two clinics quoting the same exam fee.
### Which vaccines are actually required around St. Louis?
Rabies is the one written into law. Everything else is matched to risk. Veterinary vaccination guidelines, on the dog side the AAHA Canine Vaccination Guidelines, sort shots into core and noncore: the ones nearly every animal gets, and the ones chosen by how your animal lives. A dog who boards, swims and hikes river bluffs has a different conversation than a lap dog who never leaves the block.
How rabies is handled depends on where you live. Missouri lets county commissions set the rules: section 322.090 of the Revised Statutes empowers them to adopt rules and regulations to control rabies. The next county over has its own animal control ordinance, which requires dogs and cats to be vaccinated against rabies and the vaccination registered with its Division of Humane Services.
Inside the city, the vaccine you pick sets the calendar. Most veterinarians offer a 1-year or a 3-year rabies vaccine, and the city says registration must be updated every 1 or 3 years to match. Ask which one your clinic uses, and put the renewal on the fridge next to the takeout menus.
You survived the waiting room. Go reward yourself with the metro’s Mexican food.
### Are wellness plans better than paying per visit?
A wellness plan is a payment schedule, not insurance. You pay monthly and the practice bundles the predictable care, like exams, core vaccines and routine testing, at a package price. It smooths out the bills and nudges you to show up. It does not cover the surprise limp or the swallowed sock.
Do the arithmetic at the kitchen table before you sign. Add up twelve payments, then ask for an itemized list of what the plan includes. Ask whether it is a contract you must finish, what happens if you move or the pet dies mid-term, and whether membership discounts anything outside the bundle. If the yearly total lands near what you would spend anyway, it is a budgeting tool. Well above that, you are prepaying.
Ask where you will fill prescriptions, too. The price for the same medication can vary a lot between a clinic pharmacy, an online pet pharmacy and a retail counter, the same dynamic that plays out on the human side of the counter.
### Is pet insurance worth it for routine care?
Pet insurance pays you back for the unexpected. It is not a discount card for the routine. You pay the clinic, file a claim, and the insurer reimburses a share after the deductible. Wellness coverage, where it exists, is usually an add-on.
Plenty of people are buying it. The North American Pet Health Insurance Association reports 7.6 million pets insured in North America at the end of 2025, up from 7.03 million a year earlier.
Premiums move with species, breed, age and ZIP code, so pull live quotes and judge the contract, not the price. How does the insurer define a pre-existing condition? Is there a longer waiting period for orthopedic problems? Is reimbursement based on your invoice or a benefit schedule? The insurance commissioners’ consumer overview of pet insurance is a good place to start. Buy while the animal is young and healthy, before anything is on the chart.
### What should you ask before a dental cleaning?
You smell it before you see it: the breath that clears the couch. A real cleaning happens under general anesthesia, and the estimate is where two quotes split apart. Ask whether it includes pre-anesthetic bloodwork, monitored anesthesia, cleaning below the gumline, full-mouth dental X-rays and pain control. A much cheaper number usually means fewer of those, not a better deal.
The AAHA Dental Care Guidelines for Dogs and Cats are written for clinics, but they are worth a skim. The trouble that loosens teeth lives under the gumline, out of sight on an awake animal, which is why a tooth can look clean while the problem underneath goes untreated.
Fair questions: who watches the anesthesia, will the estimate carry a range for extractions found on the X-rays, and will somebody call you mid-procedure if the plan changes.
### What should you ask about after-hours coverage?
Ask it as one sentence: what do I do at 2 a.m.? The answers vary more than people expect. Some practices rotate their own on-call doctors. Many send you to a dedicated 24-hour hospital, the kind covered in our guide to finding an emergency vet in St. Louis. Others post a number that reaches a triage line. None of those is wrong. Not knowing which one you have is.
Do it tonight, not that night. Look up the 24-hour hospital your clinic names, drive past it once on an errand so you know which entrance to pull into, and save the number in your phone under the pet’s name, where a panicked thumb will find it. Then the follow-ups. Does the emergency hospital send records back? Will your regular vet see the discharge notes before the recheck? Write that number on the fridge while your animal is healthy and snoring on the rug.
### What veterinary practice owners wish clients knew
The exam fee buys a doctor’s time and a technician’s, and it is the part of the invoice people argue about most. What clients most often get wrong is comparing a written, itemized estimate against a single number someone else quoted over the phone. Good clinics head that off with a range instead of a guess and a callback with lab results before anyone has to chase. Owners in this trade grumble about the same two things: no-shows, and being asked to diagnose by phone. When people search for a vet, the listed hours, species seen and services are what turn that search into a booked appointment, which is the whole case for a complete listing.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it difficult to switch vets?
A.  Rarely. You need no permission from your current clinic and owe nobody an explanation. Book a new-client exam, then ask the new practice to request your records. Carry the rabies certificate yourself, since that is the document a new clinic usually wants first.
### Q. How to tell if a vet is good?
A.  Judge the first visit, not the lobby. A good vet examines nose to tail before recommending anything, explains why each test matters, hands you a written estimate with a range, and is patient with a scared animal. Then check the basics: a current license on the Missouri or Illinois lookup, and a straight answer to what happens at 2 a.m.
### Q. How often should cats go to the vet?
A.  At least once a year, and at least every 6 months for seniors, according to the AAHA/AAFP Feline Life Stage Guidelines. Kittens go more often during their vaccine series. Indoor cats still need the yearly exam, because cats are good at hiding pain.
### Q. Is it okay to not take your dog to the vet?
A.  Not for long. Inside St. Louis city limits, rabies vaccination and city registration are required, and Missouri’s animal-care statute defines adequate care to include health care as necessary to maintain good health. Medically, dogs hide dental disease and slow weight loss that a yearly exam catches.
### Q. What is the average cost of a vet visit?
A.  There is no honest single number, and published averages go stale fast. It swings with species, the clinic’s equipment, and whether the visit is a wellness exam or a sick workup. Ask each clinic what the exam fee is and what is billed separately, then compare the two lists.
### Q. Why are vets suddenly so expensive?
A.  Mostly because the medicine changed. Many general practices now do in-house bloodwork, dental X-rays and monitored anesthesia, and each of those needs equipment and trained staff. Ask for an itemized estimate so you can see where the money goes.
### Q. What would happen if I can’t afford vet bills?
A.  Say so early, before the estimate is final. Practices can often stage care, treating the urgent thing now and scheduling the rest, or suggest a lower-cost path. Ask about payment options and whether local humane groups run reduced-cost vaccine or spay-neuter programs. Our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis lists where to start.

## Your Heel Slips on Step Three. Missouri Lets You Swap the Size Tax-Free.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-shoes-that-fit-st-louis
Your heel lifts out of the shoe on the third step across the store carpet. Not much. A small slip, a breath of cool air against the back of your sock, and then the heel drops back into place as if nothing happened. Most of us keep walking, straight to the register, and spend the next season blaming our feet.
That slip is the shoe telling you the truth. So is the pinch at the little toe that you decide will “break in,” and the size you have been saying out loud since high school. The fix starts before you try on a single pair: get both feet measured, standing up, and fit the larger one. That is not a salesman’s line. It is printed in the maker’s own Brannock fitting instructions: “Be sure to measure both feet, then fit the larger foot. It is common to have feet of different sizes.”
And if you can wait for August, St. Louis hands you a second gift. Missouri’s back-to-school sales tax holiday runs from the first Friday in August through the following Sunday, and clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less is exempt from all state and local sales tax for those three days. Missed this year’s? The next one starts the first Friday of next August. The statute behind it, RSMo 144.049, writes footwear right into its definition of clothing.
Then it closes the loophole you were already thinking about. The law says, word for word: “Items normally sold in pairs shall not be separated to qualify for the exemption.” No, you cannot ring up the left shoe and the right shoe separately. Somebody in the legislature thought of it first.
Here is the part almost nobody knows, and it is the reason to care about fit in August. The same statute says that if you buy an eligible item during the holiday and later exchange it for a similar eligible item after the holiday ends, no additional tax is due on the new item. So the size 9 that pinches by the second week of school can go back for a 9 and a half, and the tax break rides along with it. Keep the receipt in the box.
This is a city that takes shoes personally. City Museum, where kids shriek down slides and crawl through wire tunnels over your head, is housed in an old shoe factory in Downtown St. Louis. Caleres, the company that owns Famous Footwear, keeps its headquarters at 8300 Maryland Avenue and says it has been “ferocious about fit since 1878.” The factories went quiet a long time ago. The habit of getting the fit right did not have to.
### Where are the best places to buy shoes in Saint Louis, Missouri?
The best store is the one with someone on the floor who reaches for the measuring device before reaching for a box. Match the shop to the shoe: a running store for running shoes, a boot dealer for safety toes, a comfort store for widths and orthotics, and a repair bench for the pair you already love.
St. Louis still has shops that work this way. Laurie’s Shoes was founded in 1951, and the family store says that from the start every customer was carefully measured and expertly fit, with extended sizes and widths on the wall. Call 314-961-1642 before you drive over. For the pair you already love, Cobblestone Quality Shoe Repair is family-owned and operated and lists shoe and boot re-crafting among its services; the number is (314) 727-4080.
Wherever you go, walk in and listen for one thing: does anyone offer to measure you before handing you a box? The good ones do it without being asked. You sit, peel off a shoe, and the cold metal plate of the measuring device presses against your heel. If nobody reaches for one, ask. If they do not have one, you have learned something about the store.
### How should a shoe store measure your feet?
Standing, on both feet, with your weight spread evenly, the carpet cool through your socks. Brannock’s instructions say the customer “should stand with equal weight on both feet to ensure that the foot being measured has elongated and spread to its maximum size.” Sit down for the measurement and you get a smaller number your foot will never wear.
The device takes two lengths, not one. Heel to toe is the number everybody knows. Arch length, heel to ball, is the one that decides the fit, because, in Brannock’s words, “Shoes are designed to flex at the ball of the foot.” The instructions say to compare the two and “generally you’ll use the larger of the two measurements as the correct shoe size.” A long arch with short toes can need a bigger shoe than the toe line ever suggests.
Two more habits finish the job. Bring the socks you will actually wear with the shoes, thick wool for boots, thin for dress shoes. And get measured every time you buy, because the same instructions say your foot size changes with age and weight. The number you memorized years ago may belong to a different pair of feet.
### Why your size changes from brand to brand
A shoe size describes the shoe, not your foot. Every shoe is built around a foot-shaped form called a last, and each brand cuts its own, so two companies can label different shapes a men’s 10 and both be telling the truth. That is why the size printed on the box is a starting point, not a verdict.
Trust the feel over the label. Expect to move half a size between a running shoe and a dress shoe. Expect width to shift when length does. And when a shoe pinches on the first lap around the store, believe it. Feet swell over a long day on the concrete floor of a warehouse or a hospital hallway, so a pair that is snug in the store will be tight by the end of a shift.
### What a good running-shoe fitting feels like
You get measured, then watched. A fitter looks at how you walk or jog, sometimes on a treadmill, and treats it as one clue rather than a diagnosis. Then you get three or four pairs and your feet decide. The right one disappears on your foot. The wrong one keeps announcing itself.
Check four things while each pair is on. Room in front of your longest toe while you stand. A heel that stays put when you push off, no slip, no cool air. The widest part of your foot sitting at the widest part of the shoe. And no hot spot anywhere, because a pressure point at the store turns into a blister a few miles later.
New shoes need a test walk. Point them toward a plate of Italian in St. Louis and call it research.
Runners ask fitters one question above all others: what brand do podiatrists recommend? A shoe store cannot honestly answer it, and a fitting is not a medical exam. Pain that outlasts a shoe change belongs with a clinician. Here is when to see a podiatrist in St. Louis.
### Work boots: read the label stitched inside
If your new job says safety toe, the federal rule behind it is OSHA’s foot-protection standard at 1910.136. It requires protective footwear where there is a danger of foot injuries from falling or rolling objects or objects piercing the sole, and it lists the consensus standards boots must meet, including ASTM F-2413-2005. The markings are on a label sewn inside the boot, not on the box. Pull back the tongue and read it before you pay.
Who pays catches people off guard. OSHA’s general rule has employers provide protective equipment at no cost, but standard 1910.132 says the employer is not required to pay for non-specialty safety-toe footwear, steel-toe boots included, as long as you are allowed to wear them off the job site. A plain steel toe is usually yours to buy. Ask human resources before the first shift, not after.
### Kids’ shoes: measure every single time
Children grow without sending a notice. A pair that fit in spring can be short by the first week of school, and the only warning is a kid who suddenly walks a little strangely. Measure both feet, standing, every time you buy. Same rule as the grownups, same device.
Resist buying two sizes up to stretch the money. A shoe that is too long trips a child, and the bend of the sole lands behind the ball of the foot instead of under it, the exact spot Brannock says a shoe is built to flex. If the August tax holiday lines up with the back-to-school trip, buy then, and check that each pair is $100 or less.
### Wide feet, narrow feet, and room for orthotics
Ask for widths by letter, and ask early, because width is the hardest thing to find on a shelf. A wide is not a longer shoe. Sizing up to buy room only moves the bend of the sole past your ball joint, which is how a good shoe gets blamed for a fit problem it did not cause.
If you wear a custom orthotic or a prescribed insert, bring it and fit the shoe around it. The factory footbed should lift out cleanly, and your insert should sit flat without crowding your toes or lifting your heel. Ask whether anyone on the floor is a certified pedorthist. A shop that has one will say so plainly.
### Returns: settle four things before the card comes out
Policies change from store to store, so ask before the receipt prints, not after the box has sat in the hall closet for a week. How many days do you have? Can the shoes be worn outside, or only on carpet at home? Do you need the original box and tissue paper? Is a sale pair exchange-only? Write the answers on the receipt in pen.
Then do the honest test at home that night. Wear the new pair around the house for an hour in the socks you plan to use, up and down the stairs, standing at the kitchen counter. If the heel lifts or a toe goes numb, you will know while the soles are still clean enough to take back.
### Is resoling worth it, or should you just replace them?
Construction decides it, and you can check before you buy. Turn the shoe over and look along the edge. A sole that is stitched on can usually be replaced. A sole that is only glued tends to cost more to rebuild than it is worth. Ask how the sole is attached while you are still holding the shoe.
Good shoes are worth keeping alive, which is where what leather repair costs in St. Louis picks up the story.
Ready to be measured instead of guessing? Browse shoe stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call ahead with two questions: do you measure both feet standing, and what is your return window on a shoe worn outside? The same fit-before-price habit works for the rest of the closet too, see shopping for clothes locally.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What's the best place to get shoes?
A.  A store that measures both of your feet standing up and lets you try several pairs. That matters more than the name on the sign. For running, go to a specialty run shop. For work, a boot dealer who can explain the safety label. For wide feet or orthotics, a comfort store that stocks widths.
### Q. What is the most reliable place to buy shoes?
A.  The one that measures you and will take them back. Reliability is a process, not a logo: both feet measured standing, the larger foot fitted, several pairs to compare, and a return window you understood before you paid. A store doing all four beats a cheaper price on a size you guessed.
### Q. What brand shoe do podiatrists recommend?
A.  No single brand fits every foot. The closest thing to a professional list is the American Podiatric Medical Association’s Seal program, which says it has been recognizing products that promote good foot health since 1967. Search the APMA Seal database, then get fitted from there.
### Q. What is a reasonable price for a pair of shoes?
A.  Whatever buys the fit and construction you need, and any number printed today ages badly. Budget by use: daily wear and safety footwear justify more, occasional dress shoes less. In Missouri, shopping the August sales tax holiday takes sales tax off a pair priced $100 or less.
### Q. Is $200 a lot for shoes?
A.  It depends on how many days you wear them, not the sticker. Divide the price by the days you expect to wear them before the cushioning packs flat or the sole wears through. A boot worn every workday for years costs pennies a day. The same money on a shoe that hurts is just gone.

## Golf in St. Louis for Beginners: $12 Rental Clubs, No Collar Needed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-start-playing-golf-in-st-louis
What are you supposed to wear to a golf course when you don’t own a single collared shirt? At Ruth Park, the municipal course on Groby Road, the honest answer is a shirt with sleeves and the sneakers already on your feet.
Then comes the walk, and it’s nothing like the worry. The clubs clank against each other on your shoulder, the grass is still wet enough to soak the toes of your shoes, and the only sound on the first tee is somebody’s ball cracking off a driver two groups ahead. Nobody checks your pedigree. They check that you registered.
Here’s the part nobody tells a nervous beginner. You don’t need your own clubs, a collar or golf shoes to play a real municipal course in this town. Ruth Park rents sets for both men and women at $12, bans only steel and ceramic spikes, and is in its 91st year of operation. A 91st season, twelve dollars and a shirt with sleeves: that’s the line to send the coworker who keeps saying golf isn’t for people like you.
Golf around here is not one thing, though. Some courses will sell a tee time to anybody with a phone. Some sell memberships and public rounds at once, with members holding the good hours. Some you cannot play at any price without an invitation. Ten minutes of sorting saves the whole awkward part.
### Which public golf course in St. Louis is considered the best?
Nobody hands out an official title, and every ranked list is somebody’s taste. For a first round, the best public course is the one that lets a beginner in without a fight: Ruth Park Municipal Golf Course on Groby Road rents full sets of clubs for $12, takes tee times up to seven days ahead at 314-727-4800, and lets men play in any shirt with sleeves.
Call the pro shop and say it plainly: first round, when’s a quiet time to come out. Show up at least 15 minutes before your time to register, start on the first hole like everyone else, and leave the steel spikes at home. Then rank the rest of the metro on your own terms: drive time, whether you can walk it, pace, and tee times at the hour you can get there.
### What kinds of golf courses can you actually play around St. Louis?
Three access types, and the difference is simply who is allowed to book. Public and daily-fee courses sell tee times to anyone paying a green fee, and that includes government-run courses - St. Louis County Parks operates three of them, Eagle Springs, Quail Creek and Quarry Golf Complex. Semi-private courses sell memberships and public tee times both, with members holding priority on weekend mornings. Private clubs are members and guests only.
That last category is where new golfers lose the most time. A private club will not sell you a round because you called and were polite about it. You get on through a member, through a reciprocal arrangement with your own club, or not at all. Bellerive Country Club and Norwood Hills Country Club are both private - buy a tournament ticket, sure, but you can’t book a Tuesday.
Both sides of the river carry real public golf, on the Missouri side and in the Metro East. What does not cross the river is a resident rate. County and city discounts follow where you live and pay taxes, so a Metro-East golfer pays the visitor price in St. Louis County, and the reverse holds too.
### How do you book a tee time in the St. Louis metro?
Two doors: the course’s own site or phone, and the third-party apps. Most metro courses book directly, and many also list slots on aggregators like GolfNow. Direct gets you the course’s own rate and a human to call when weather turns. An app sometimes gets you a discount on a time the course wants filled.
Prime time is roughly 7 to 10 a.m. Saturday and Sunday, and those slots go first, usually five to seven days out the moment the sheet opens. If you’re new, that is the block to avoid. A weekday afternoon or a twilight rate puts you on an emptier course with nobody behind you, and twilight pricing is cheaper almost everywhere.
Two practical notes. Know the cancellation window before you book - a no-show costs the course a slot it can no longer resell, and some now hold a card. And if you’re playing alone, say so; singles get paired with a twosome, which is the fastest way to learn how a round actually flows.
### What does a golf season look like in St. Louis weather?
Roughly March into November, with edges that move every year. The shoulders are the tricky part. In March, and again late in the fall, morning frost delays are routine, and a course will hold everyone in the parking lot until the turf can take foot traffic. That isn’t the starter being difficult - walking on frozen grass blades kills them, and the damage shows for weeks.
Late May through June, then September into October, are usually the best conditions of the year here. July and August bring the heat and humidity this region is known for, which pushes serious players to the first tee time and leaves afternoons open and cheap. After heavy rain, expect cart-path-only rules. Late summer and early fall bring aeration, when greens get punched so roots can breathe and then putt badly for about two weeks - worth a phone call before you book.
Winter doesn’t shut everything down. Mild January days pull courses open with temporary greens or mats, and layers buy you a course to yourself.
Twelve dollars still too steep for a maybe? Disc golf costs you one disc.
### Is there a PGA course in St. Louis?
Yes, in the sense people usually mean - courses that host PGA-sanctioned professional golf. Bellerive Country Club in Town and Country hosted the 2018 PGA Championship and hosted the BMW Championship in August 2026. Norwood Hills Country Club hosts the Stifel Charity Classic, a PGA TOUR Champions event.
Both are private. The realistic way onto either property is a spectator ticket or a volunteer shift - these tournaments run on hundreds of volunteers. What you cannot do is book a tee time.
The related question, what is the most prestigious golf course in St. Louis, gets settled by championship résumé, and Bellerive has the longest one: the 1965 U.S. Open, the 1992 and 2018 PGA Championships, the BMW Championship in 2008 and 2026, and the Presidents Cup scheduled for 2030. Prestige and playability are different measurements, though. The course that improves your golf this year is a public one twenty minutes from your house.
### Should you take lessons before you buy clubs?
For most new golfers, yes - one lesson before any equipment purchase, because a coach can tell you in ten minutes whether the hand-me-down set in your garage is close to the right length and lie angle. Bending a club is cheap. Replacing a bag you bought blind is not.
Instruction comes in three shapes: group clinics, the cheapest way in and full of other beginners; private lessons, usually sold in packages of three to six; and playing lessons, where a coach walks nine holes and fixes what a range never exposes. Look for a coach who belongs to the PGA of America - the association’s coach finder filters by area. The trial-lesson logic in our guide to choosing a martial arts school in St. Louis transfers straight across.
Once your swing repeats, fitting earns its keep. How can I determine which golf club is best for me? Not from a chart - from hitting into a launch monitor while a fitter changes one variable at a time: shaft flex and weight, club length, lie angle, grip size, head model. And what’s the 70/30 rule in golf? It’s the practice split coaches keep repeating: roughly 70% of practice time on the short game, 30% on full swings. Most amateurs do the reverse, which is why it keeps getting said.
### Where do you golf in St. Louis in the winter?
Indoors, and more people are doing it than ever. The National Golf Foundation’s 2026 Graffis Report, covering 2025 data, put total U.S. golf participation at an all-time high of 48.1 million once technology-enabled ranges, simulators and entertainment venues are counted alongside course play. Off-course formats alone accounted for 37.9 million participants, with 19 million people doing both.
In practice that means heated range stalls, indoor studios with launch monitors, simulator bays rented by the hour, and entertainment ranges built around groups. Winter simulator leagues run on weeknights. There’s a coaching argument for all of it too: a swing change holds better when you aren’t also managing wind, lie and score, so December through February is when a rebuilt grip actually sticks.
### What should a first-timer know before walking on?
Call the pro shop and say it plainly: first round, when’s a good time to come out. You’ll get a real answer, usually a weekday afternoon. Ask two more things while you have them - is there a dress code, and are metal spikes allowed. Plenty of courses want a collared shirt and soft spikes only, and learning that in the parking lot is the bad version.
On the course, pace is the entire etiquette conversation. Play the forward tees; they exist for exactly this. Play ready golf instead of strict honors - whoever is set hits. Pick up once you’ve reached double par and move on.
The rest is groundskeeping you do on the way past: rake the bunker behind you, fix your ball mark, fill divots from the sand bottle. Eighteen holes at a busy public course runs about four and a half hours. Fall more than a hole behind the group ahead and wave the group behind you through. People remember the golfer who does that, and nobody remembers the score.
### How do golf leagues and handicaps work around here?
Leagues are the cheapest standing tee time in golf, and they’re how most people find a regular group. A typical metro league is nine holes on a weeknight or weekday morning, priced for the season. The county course at Eagle Springs publishes a ladies league Tuesday and Thursday mornings, a Thursday night men’s league and a Friday couples league - a good template for what to ask other pro shops about.
A handicap is what lets a 24 and a 9 compete on the same card. You get one by joining a club or association that provides handicap service, then posting scores; the number recalculates as you play under the World Handicap System. You don’t need to be good to have one, just honest about posting.
### What a course operator sees from the other side of the counter
Green fees are the top line, but a lot of the margin lives in the cart, and food and beverage carries more of the year than golfers assume. The tee sheet is perishable inventory: an 8:10 Saturday foursome that never shows is revenue nobody can resell, which is why no-show policies keep tightening. Weekday mornings are the empty hours, and that is why operators chase leagues, corporate outings and shotgun-start charity scrambles. April through June and September through October pay for December through February, a rained-out Saturday in May is simply gone, and the maintenance budget runs whether anyone plays or not, right down to the cart paths and the concrete in the parking lot. Good operators manage pace with a real starter, price by demand, and build junior programs. People search for courses and coaches by neighborhood, so a complete, current listing is how a course turns up in a search that already happened.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best public golf course in St. Louis?
A.  Nobody agrees, and the honest answer depends on what you need from a round. Score candidates on drive time, walkability, pace, forgiveness for a new player, and tee times when you’re free. Then check reviews from the last three months, since conditions swing with weather, aeration and maintenance spending. A course that played rough two summers ago can be excellent now.
### Q. Which PGA event is taking place in St. Louis?
A.  The BMW Championship went to Bellerive Country Club in Town and Country in August 2026, and the Stifel Charity Classic, a 54-hole PGA TOUR Champions playoff event, followed at Norwood Hills Country Club. The next Stifel Charity Classic is set for Oct. 18-24, 2027.
### Q. What is the most prestigious golf course in St. Louis?
A.  By championship history, Bellerive Country Club: the 1965 U.S. Open, the PGA Championship in 1992 and 2018, the BMW Championship in 2008 and 2026, and the 2030 Presidents Cup. It’s private, so prestige here is something you watch rather than book. For a round you can play, judge on conditioning and pace instead.
### Q. What’s the 70/30 rule in golf?
A.  A practice guideline, not a rule of the game: spend about 70% of practice time on the short game - putting, chipping, pitching - and 30% on full swings and driving. The reasoning is that a large share of the strokes in any round happen inside a hundred yards. Most amateurs invert it.
### Q. How can I determine which golf club is best for me?
A.  Get fitted rather than guessing. A fitter puts you on a launch monitor and changes one variable at a time - shaft flex and weight, length, lie angle, grip size, head design - watching what your swing does with each. If you’re brand new, start smaller: have a coach check the length and lie of clubs you already own. Bending is inexpensive; a wrong full bag is not.
### Q. What is the poor man’s pebble?
A.  It’s a California nickname, not a St. Louis one. Golfers use “poor man’s Pebble Beach” for affordable coastal courses near Monterey and Santa Barbara that give you ocean views at a fraction of Pebble Beach money - Pacific Grove Municipal gets the title most often. The local version of the idea is a modest public course with genuinely good design.

## Choosing a Podiatrist in St. Louis: Medicare Won't Pay for the Nail Trim
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-podiatrist-in-st-louis
I bought the half-size-bigger sneakers instead of calling anybody. Then the gel inserts from the drugstore. Then I started taking the parking-garage stairs in Maryland Heights on the outside edge of my left foot so the heel would not land first, and told myself that was a choice.
If any of that sounds familiar, you know the morning version too. The first step off the bed onto a cold floor, and the heel answers like you stepped on a pebble that is not there. It eases by the time the coffee is done. It comes back after a long shift on concrete, louder, and you sit on the edge of the tub with your foot in your hand and finally type “foot doctor near me.”
Know the bill that stings before you book. Medicare doesn’t usually cover routine foot care, like trimming or clipping nails and cutting or removing corns and calluses, even when a podiatrist does it in the same chair where your covered heel exam happens. The heel pain is the covered visit. The nail trim on the way out can be the bill. Ask at the front desk which is which.
Then the list arrives: a wall of names with the same three letters after each one, DPM, from Chesterfield to Fairview Heights. Here is the part that list will not tell you. Missouri law is unusually specific about what those three letters allow. Under RSMo 330.010, a Missouri podiatrist’s “human foot” includes the ankle and the tendons which insert into the foot, and ankle surgery by a podiatrist can be performed only in a licensed acute care hospital or a licensed ambulatory surgical clinic.
Same three letters, two states, two rulebooks - and one question that sorts the whole list: how often does this office treat the thing that hurts me?
### What to look for when choosing a podiatrist?
Look for three things you can check before you call: an active license in the state where the office sits, a doctor who treats your specific problem every week, and network status for your exact plan. A podiatrist is a doctor of podiatric medicine who completes four years of podiatric medical school and three years of hospital-based surgical residency. Then ask whether X-rays happen on site.
Match the doctor to the problem first. A practice that spends its week on diabetic foot care and nail surgery is not the same practice as one built around runners and custom orthotics, even with identical letters on the door. Sorting by distance alone is how people end up limping into a second opinion two months later.
Five questions do most of the sorting on one phone call. Does this office see my problem weekly or a few times a year? Are X-rays taken here, or do I go somewhere else and come back? If orthotics come up, are they made for my foot or pulled off a shelf? Where does the doctor operate? And the one people skip: is the doctor personally in network, not just the group name on the building?
### Missouri or Illinois: two license lookups, one minute each
Checking a license takes less time than the hold music. On the Missouri side, type the doctor’s name into the state’s search page. On the Illinois side, use IDFPR’s license lookup. An office in Fairview Heights and an office in Chesterfield answer to different regulators.
Missouri’s statute also sets a bar for ankle surgery. A podiatrist doing it must either be board certified in foot and ankle surgery by the American Board of Podiatric Surgery or complete a twenty-four-month postgraduate clinical residency in podiatric surgery. For a Missouri podiatrist licensed after January 1, 2005 who wants to do ankle surgery, the residency is required. So if the word “surgery” comes up in the exam room, two questions belong in the same breath: which of those two does the doctor have, and which hospital or surgery center would do the procedure?
That is not you being difficult. It is the question the law already asks.
### A DPM or an orthopedic surgeon?
The American Podiatric Medical Association describes a DPM as a physician and surgeon who treats the foot, ankle, and related structures of the leg. An orthopedic surgeon reaches overlapping ground by a different road: medical school, a residency covering the whole musculoskeletal system, and often a foot-and-ankle fellowship on top. Both roads are legitimate. The useful question is not which letters win. It is how many feet like yours this person has had in their hands this month.
### What happens at a first visit
Expect a history, a hands-on exam, and often imaging in the same hour. The paper on the exam table crinkles, the doctor presses along the arch and the heel and asks where it lands, and then asks you to walk down the hall and back. Bring a list of symptoms, a list of every medication and past surgery, and any X-rays or MRIs from other doctors.
Bring the shoes you actually wear, not the good pair. The worn-down outside edge of a work sneaker tells a doctor things you cannot put into words. The flooring you stand on for ten hours matters too, so say what it is: concrete at a warehouse, tile on a hospital unit, hardwood at home. If your standing hours are about to change, say that out loud as well; our guide to choosing a staffing agency in St. Louis helps if a new job is part of the picture.
### The questions to ask before anyone makes you an insert
Orthotics are where a lot of people spend real money without a clear answer. You stand on a foam box or a scanner plate, it feels cool and a little strange under your bare foot, and a few weeks later a pair of inserts arrives. Before that happens, ask four things. What problem is this device meant to fix? Is it molded to my foot, or a prefabricated insert adjusted in the office? What does it cost if my plan says no? And when do we check whether it is working?
A good office answers all four without sighing. It also tells you what else is part of the plan, because an insert is rarely the whole plan: shoe changes, stretching, a follow-up visit. If the only answer to every question is the device, take a breath and get a second opinion before you pay for it.
The same goes for anything that sounds like a package. A practice that sells you a set of visits up front, before it has watched you walk, is asking you to trust a plan nobody has written yet. A practice that says “let’s see how the first two weeks go” is treating your foot.
Nothing to do with feet: what the river changes about buying a bottle for the next party. Here’s why.
### What Medicare covers, and the bill that surprises people
Medicare Part B covers podiatrist foot exams or treatment when you need medically necessary treatment for foot injuries or diseases, like hammer toe, bunion deformities and heel spurs. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. What Medicare does not usually cover is routine foot care: cutting or removing corns and calluses, trimming or clipping nails, and hygienic or other preventive maintenance. That one line explains most surprise podiatry bills. (Medicare foot care coverage)
For people with diabetes and severe diabetes-related foot disease, there is a separate therapeutic shoe benefit. Every calendar year it can cover one pair of custom-molded shoes and 2 more pairs of inserts, or a pair of extra-depth shoes and 3 pairs of inserts. The paperwork chain is the part that trips people: ask the office, before anything is ordered, who certifies the need and who supplies the shoes.
Custom arch supports for ordinary heel pain are a different story. Coverage varies widely by plan, so ask for the billing code before the device is made, then call the number on your card with that code in hand.
Paying cash? You have a federal right worth using. Under the No Surprises Act, if you do not have or do not use insurance, you can get a good faith estimate when you schedule care in advance or if you ask for one, and you may be able to dispute your bill if it is at least $400 more than the estimate. (CMS)
### Why the front desk asks so many questions
From the other side of the counter, a foot practice runs on a packed schedule and a lot of paperwork. The phone rings while someone in a walking boot waits to check out, and the staff are sorting which visits insurance will treat as medically necessary and which are routine care billed to you. Equipment like braces and therapeutic shoes comes with a documentation chain that runs back to another doctor’s chart. When the front desk asks for your other doctors’ names up front, that is why. Patients usually start by searching a category and a suburb, and a practice that keeps its listing complete and current is the one they reach first.
Not sure which foot doctor fits the problem you actually have? Browse podiatrists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two offices with the same three sentences about your symptom and see which one asks a follow-up question before quoting you a visit.
If you run the podiatry practice where the doctor watches a patient walk the hallway before writing anything down, those are the patients searching for you right now. List your practice and get more customers who already know what kind of foot doctor they need.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I go to a podiatrist without a referral?
A.  Often, yes, but your plan decides. Many HMO plans want a referral from a primary care doctor before a specialist claim gets paid, and some Medicare Advantage plans do too. Call the number on your card and ask about referral and prior-authorization rules before you book, so the first bill is not the way you find out.
### Q. How to know if a podiatrist is good?
A.  Look for signals you can check, not adjectives. Verify the license in Missouri or Illinois, ask whether the doctor is board certified and in what, and ask how often the office treats your problem. In the room, a good sign is a doctor who examines both feet, looks at your shoes, tells you what happens if you do nothing, and gives you a plan with a checkpoint.
### Q. Will a podiatrist remove an ingrown toenail?
A.  Yes. The APMA says a podiatrist will remove the ingrown portion of the nail and may prescribe a topical or oral medication to treat the infection. For ingrown nails that keep coming back, the corner of the nail that ingrows, along with the matrix or root of that piece of nail, can be removed. Skip the bathroom surgery with nail clippers.
### Q. What doctor to see for peroneal tendonitis?
A.  A podiatrist or an orthopedic foot-and-ankle specialist can both evaluate pain along the outside of the ankle, and in Missouri the podiatric definition of the foot includes the ankle and the tendons which insert into the foot. Start with whoever can examine you and image it soonest. Only the clinician who examines your ankle can say what is happening inside it.
### Q. Why don’t podiatrists like Skechers?
A.  That premise does not hold up as a blanket rule. Skechers USA, Inc is on the APMA Seal Program listing. Individual doctors have opinions about particular shoes for particular feet, and that is a judgment about your foot, not a verdict on a brand.
### Q. How much should a podiatrist visit cost?
A.  There is no single metro price, and any one number you read online is a guess. Cost turns on whether the visit is covered, whether X-rays or a procedure happen the same day, and whether the office is in network. Under Medicare Part B, medically necessary treatment runs 20% of the approved amount after the deductible. Paying cash, ask for a good faith estimate before the appointment.
### Q. Are podiatrists worth it?
A.  For a foot or ankle problem that has outlasted new shoes and a week of rest, usually yes, if only to trade guessing for an exam and an X-ray. The cheapest visit is the early one. Write down when the pain started, what makes it worse, and what you have already tried, from the bigger sneakers to the drugstore inserts. Then call two offices, read them the same three sentences, and book with the one that asks you a real question back.

## Illinois Taxes Your Bourbon at $8.55 a Gallon. Missouri Charges $2.00.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/independent-liquor-store-st-louis-missouri-illinois-rules
The rye goes down on the counter with a soft glass knock. The clerk reaches for the scanner, glances up at the clock behind the register, and slides the bottle back across to you. It has just gone past 1:30 in the morning.
Nobody is being difficult. Under RSMo 311.290, a Missouri retailer may not sell, give away or let anyone drink intoxicating liquor between 1:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. The clock on that wall is the law, and the clerk is the one who has to say it out loud.
That is the first of the quiet walls in this metro. The biggest one is the river. Missouri taxes a gallon of spirits at $2.00. Illinois taxes the same gallon at $8.55. Same bottle, same metro, and the Poplar Street Bridge decides when the doors open on a Sunday, how big a taste the clerk can pour, and whether a winery can ship a case to your aunt.
### What are the alcohol laws in St. Louis, Missouri?
In Missouri, licensed retailers may not sell between 1:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m., and spirits on a Sunday take a separate Sunday license that costs the store an extra $200 a year. You must be 21, and the clerk can accept a valid, unexpired driver’s or nondriver’s license, a uniformed services ID card, or a passport.
Sunday morning is where it bites. The shop lights are on, the coffee in your other hand is still hot, and the clerk shakes his head at the bottle anyway. Under RSMo 311.293, selling intoxicating liquor between 6:00 a.m. on Sundays and 1:30 a.m. on Mondays takes that special license, and a city or county can add its own fee on top. Inside the city limits, the City of St. Louis Excise Division puts it in one line: only establishments with Sunday Liquor Licenses are able to sell liquor on Sunday.
The city does keep a short list of exception Sundays, among them March 17th, July 4th and Superbowl Sunday. Read the fine print, though: on those days it is intoxicating liquor by the drink that may be sold. That is the bar down the block, not the bottle on the package-store counter.
Here is how to find a shop that can ring up spirits on a Sunday. The Missouri Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Control posts its license data to the Missouri Data Portal so anyone can sort, filter and download it. The file to open is “Active Primary/Secondary License,” not the primary-only one, filtered to your city or ZIP code. The state warns that these files do not include suspensions or revocations. I could not confirm how the Sunday license is labeled inside that file, so the phone finishes the job: call the shop and ask whether it holds a Sunday license. A yes means the spirits aisle is open.
Then the card. The clerk tilts your license under the counter light and looks up at your face, because RSMo 311.328 tells them to compare the photograph and physical characteristics on the card with the person standing there. Bring the plastic card.
### What changes once you cross the river?
Same bottle, two receipts. The one from the Missouri side and the one from the shop in Belleville can sit on your kitchen counter side by side and not agree. That is the tax. Missouri’s state excise on spirits is two dollars per gallon under RSMo 311.550. Illinois charges $8.55 per gallon on alcohol and spirits under 235 ILCS 5/8-1, before a county or city adds anything. Across a case for a wedding, that gap adds up to a nice dinner.
The cheapest move most St. Louisans never make: price the exact bottle on the Missouri side before you buy it in Belleville.
Then the pour. The clerk tips the bottle over a little plastic cup and stops almost before it starts. In Illinois that is the law, not stinginess: under 235 ILCS 5/6-31, a retail sampling is up to 3 samples of no more than 1/4 ounce of distilled spirits, one ounce of wine, or 2 ounces of beer, per consumer, per day. A quarter ounce barely coats the bottom of the cup. In Missouri, a package store can apply under RSMo 311.294 for a special permit to hold wine, malt beverage and distilled spirit tastings, for an extra twenty-five dollars a year. Everything here assumes 21 and over, and that the driver is not the one sampling.
### Is it cheaper to buy liquor at the liquor store or the grocery store?
The cart wheel squeaks past a pyramid of the famous bottle, priced low and stacked high near the front. Usually the grocery store wins on the dozen names everybody knows, and usually the bottle shop wins on everything else. A supermarket prices those names thin to pull carts through the door and makes it back in the rest of the building. A small shop cannot win that fight and mostly does not try. It earns on the middle and top of the shelf, where somebody who has actually tasted the thing beats fifty cents off.
So do it this way. Pick the exact bottle and size, price it at two stores on the Missouri side, then ask out loud whether a case break or a mixed-six discount applies. That last question is rarely posted on a shelf tag and is often the biggest number in the conversation.
### What a good bottle shop will do that a big-box won’t
Walk in, say the occasion and the ceiling - “retirement party, forty dollars, he drinks rye” - and a good clerk walks you to the shelf instead of pointing at an aisle. Ask for a bottle they do not carry and they can check whether their distributor has it. Ask how they release the hard-to-find whiskey - a list, a raffle, in person only - and ask early in the fall, not the week before Christmas, when the phone at the counter does not stop ringing.
### Can you ship liquor as a gift from St. Louis?
You stand at the parcel counter with the bottle wrapped in a towel, and the answer is still no. In Missouri, a winery holding a wine direct shipper license can ship up to two cases of wine per month to a resident who is at least 21, for personal use. In Illinois, a wine shipper licensee may ship not more than 12 cases of wine per year to a resident 21 or older under 235 ILCS 5/6-29. That is a wine rule. For the bourbon lover in Edwardsville, the gift that works is the bottle handed over in person, or a gift card from the shop.
Not sure which shop is worth the extra four minutes? Browse liquor stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and ask two things: do you do special orders, and do you hold a tasting permit. Those answers sort the list fast. If you would rather drink than buy, we walk through the kinds of bars this metro actually has.
If you run the shop where the clerk knows the rye shelf by heart, that is the shop people go looking for at five o’clock. A Gold listing puts your hours, your Sunday license, your tastings and your special orders in front of the customers already searching for them, so the shop gets more customers at the hour that counts.
### What are the rules on growlers and kegs?
The growler comes back across the counter cold and sweating, the cap still tacky. Missouri lets an original-package retailer fill 32 to 128 fluid ounces of draft beer to go under RSMo 311.201. Kegs carry more paperwork: under RSMo 311.082, the retailer has to see valid identification and take a minimum deposit of fifty dollars per keg. Lug it back with the tag on. On the Illinois side, ask the shop, because the local license decides more of this than the state does.
Totally unrelated: the kitchen you’ll pour it in probably costs less to fix than you fear. Here’s what remodels really run.
### How special orders and allocated bottles really work
The clerk writes your name and the bottle on a pad by the register and tapes the page to the wall. Nothing on that shelf arrived by magic. A Missouri shop buys from a wholesaler, the wholesaler buys from the producer, and a special order is really one question asked twice: does a distributor in this state carry the bottle, and will that distributor break a case so the shop can buy one instead of twelve? If the answer is yes, a good shop will tell you roughly when the truck comes and call you when it lands. If the answer is no, a good shop will say so instead of stringing you along for a month.
Allocated whiskey is the same system with less of it. The shop does not choose how many bottles of the famous release it gets; the distributor does. A store that receives a handful has to decide who walks out with them, and every shop decides differently. Some keep a list. Some raffle. Some hold them for regulars who buy the rest of the year. None of those is wrong. The only wrong move is getting angry at the clerk who has to tell forty people no, because the person who smiles, buys a bottle of something else, and asks how the list works is the one who hears first next time.
### Buying for a party without the second trip
The worst sound at a graduation party is the cooler lid opening on nothing but ice water. Avoid it the boring way: count adults, decide whether this is a beer-and-wine crowd or a cocktail crowd, and say both numbers to the clerk. A shop that does this every weekend will size the order faster than any calculator, and many will take back unopened, undamaged bottles if you ask before you buy. Ask. Policies differ shop to shop, and the time to find out is with the receipt still warm in your hand, not after the party.
Two more things save the day. Buy the ice last, from the same shop if it sells it, so it is still hard when you pull into the driveway. And if anyone at the party will be under 21, put the adult drinks somewhere the kids are not walking past with a plate. The rules on this page all assume the person holding the cup is old enough to be holding it.
### What running a bottle shop actually looks like
Beer is heavy, cold and dated, and the walk-in cooler hums all night on the owner’s electric bill. The margin lives in wine, in the middle and upper spirits shelf, and in the ice and mixers nobody price-checks. Under RSMo 311.280, a Missouri retailer may buy only from a licensed wholesaler in the state, so every shop draws from the same supply and wins on what it chooses to carry. People search by neighborhood at five o’clock, and a complete listing is how a shop gets more customers at the moment that counts.
