### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I find the cheapest alcohol in St. Louis?
A.  On the Missouri side, generally, and by comparing the exact bottle rather than the store. Missouri’s state excise on spirits is two dollars per gallon; Illinois charges $8.55 per gallon. After that, price one bottle at two nearby stores and ask about case and mixed-six discounts, which are rarely posted.
### Q. Who is the cheapest liquor store?
A.  It moves, so treat any name you read online as already out of date. Supermarkets usually win on the famous national brands they use to pull traffic. Independents win on the rest of the shelf and on knowing what is good at your number. Price the bottle you want at two stores and buy where the gap is real.
### Q. Where is the nearest liquor store in St. Louis?
A.  Search by neighborhood, then check hours before distance. Missouri sales stop between 1:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m., and in the City of St. Louis only establishments with Sunday Liquor Licenses are able to sell liquor on Sunday, so the closest shop is not always the open one. Call first on a Sunday morning.
### Q. How profitable is owning a liquor store?
A.  It depends on the mix, and any single margin figure you find online will be wrong for your store. Beer moves volume on a thin margin, while wine, the better spirits and the mixers and ice carry the profit. Rent, labor and the holiday season decide the rest. The owners who last tend to know their regulars by name and their walk-in cooler by sound, and they treat the stretch from Thanksgiving to New Year’s as the season that pays for the slow months.
### Q. How to price a liquor store?
A.  Start with the fact that the license does not come with the keys. Under RSMo 311.250, no Missouri liquor license is transferable or assignable except as the law provides, so the buyer has to qualify on their own. Then price the cash flow, the lease and the inventory at cost, with an accountant and an attorney who have closed one before.
### Q. Is liquor cheaper in Missouri or Kansas?
A.  From St. Louis, the border that changes your receipt is the Mississippi, not the Kansas line. Missouri taxes spirits at two dollars per gallon, and Illinois at $8.55 per gallon, plus whatever the county or city adds. Price the actual bottle on both sides of the river, and remember that a few dollars saved on one bottle is gone if you burn it in gas chasing a second store. For a case, the drive is worth it. For one bottle on a weeknight, the closest open shop with a clerk who knows the shelf usually wins.

## The $425 Permit on a $40,000 St. Louis Kitchen That Cheap Bids Skip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/kitchen-remodel-cost-st-louis
Your range hood roars and moves nothing. In a south city brick bungalow on a sticky August night, the steam rolls straight past it, beads on the painted-over cabinet doors and drips back onto the burner with a hiss, while the cold radiator under the window takes up the wall you wish were counter and the silverware drawer that swelled shut your first humid summer here sticks again. The only outlet that still works hides behind the toaster. And somewhere between the hiss and the drawer you say it out loud: we should just do the whole kitchen.
Two weeks later three bids sit on the counter you hate. One is eleven pages. One is a single handwritten sheet. One came over the phone from a company that never opened a cabinet door. The spread between them could buy a used car, and none of them describe the same kitchen.
Here is the line nobody puts on a bid. In the City of St. Louis, a building permit costs a $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated construction cost once a job runs over $3,000. On a $40,000 kitchen that is $425. So the bid that is cheaper because “we don’t bother with permits” is saving you about four hundred dollars, and handing you the risk of the whole kitchen when an inspector or a buyer’s home inspector asks for the paper trail years from now.
Four hundred dollars is the cheapest insurance in the whole job. Say that to the next contractor who offers to skip it and watch the price change.
### What is a realistic budget for a kitchen remodel?
Spread the three bids across the counter and hold them against the payback, because that is the part that should change your plan. In that same regional data the minor kitchen recouped 94.5% of its cost at resale. The midrange major remodel recouped 58.9%. The upscale gut job recouped 37.7%. Nationally the minor kitchen did even better, at 112.9%. The regional table is worth five minutes before you meet a single designer, because it tells you something a showroom never will: the smaller, sharper kitchen is the one that pays you back.
Those are averages, not a quote for your house in Maryland Heights or Edwardsville. The number worth trusting is the middle of three itemized proposals written against the same one-page scope, from companies that each stood in your kitchen and opened the doors.
### Cross the river and the kitchen paperwork changes
In the city, the permit starts with the sound of a check tearing out of the book. If you apply in person, that $25 application fee is a check or cash slid across the Building Division counter, because nothing else is taken there. The $10 per thousand waits until final approvals are in and the permit is ready to be issued, and none of it comes back if you change your mind. Before the first bid, call the Building Division at (314) 622-3313, weekdays 8:00 AM to 4:45 PM, and ask whether your kitchen needs a permit. Then ask the contractor who offered to skip it why he flinched.
Out in unincorporated county, the first stop is the county’s kitchen, bath and laundry remodel guide. And if a salesman sat at your kitchen table until you signed, Missouri’s RSMo 407.705 lets you cancel a home solicitation sale until midnight of the third business day.
In Belleville, the protection is a pamphlet you hold in your hand. Under the Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act, the contractor gives you “Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights” before you sign, and any job over $1,000 needs a written contract stating the total cost, parts and materials included. If that pamphlet never comes out of the folder, ask for it before you sign anything. The Illinois Attorney General’s home repair page is worth ten minutes at the kitchen table.
When the old trap under the sink comes out in Edwardsville or O’Fallon, smelling of old dishwater, the person on his back under there should hold a state license. The Illinois Department of Public Health licenses plumbers and plumbing contractors under the Illinois Plumbing License Law, so ask to see it before the water gets shut off.
### Four things that move the number
Everything you pick off a showroom shelf is rounding. These four are the money.
The layout. The moment the sink, range or refrigerator moves, you add drain and vent work, new supply lines, new circuits, and maybe a header if the wall you want gone is carrying load. Leaving the sink under the window where it already sits is the cheapest big decision you will make.
The cabinets. Usually the biggest line on the bid, and the one thing you cannot un-order. Stock, semi-custom and full custom are three separate price worlds; our guide to choosing a cabinet maker in St. Louis walks through that one decision.
The countertop. A fabricator cannot template until the cabinets are set and leveled, so the counter gets measured late and lands later still. Build that dead window into the schedule instead of discovering it with a sheet of plywood where your sink used to be.
What is behind the plaster. Brick four-families in south city, postwar ranches in Affton and Overland, century-old frame houses on the Belleville side: demo here turns up ungrounded circuits, galvanized pipe that rattles when the water shuts off, and floors that roll a marble to the low corner. That is not a contractor being difficult. Ask before you sign how the contract handles it: an allowance, a set unit price, or a change order at whatever it costs that day.
### What is the 30% rule in remodeling?
It is a guideline, not a hard-and-fast rule. The 30% rule suggests home renovations cost no more than 30% of your home’s value, so a house worth $400,000 would ideally see no more than $120,000 in renovation spending. Its job is to stop you pouring more into a house than the street will ever hand back.
Use it as a guardrail, then override it on purpose. Staying twenty years and cooking every night? The smell of onions in a pan on a range that finally vents outside is worth more to you than resale math. Selling in three years? Then the regional payback numbers above are the whole argument for the smaller job.
Off topic, but you’ll want it: the walnut hutch your new kitchen needs is probably sitting in a sale barn right now. Here’s how St. Louis auction houses work.
### The order the trades show up
A kitchen runs in a fixed sequence, and jumping it is what causes most delays:
Final selections - cabinets, counters, tile, fixtures, appliance model numbers - locked before anyone swings a hammer.
Permit application and approval.
Demolition and the temporary kitchen.
Framing, including any header for a wall that came out.
Rough-in: plumbing, electrical, HVAC and the range vent.
Rough inspection. Nothing closes up until it passes.
Insulation, drywall and first paint.
Flooring, when it runs under the cabinets.
Cabinets, shimmed and leveled.
Countertop template, fabrication and install - usually the longest wait.
Backsplash, plumbing and electrical trim, appliance hookup.
Final inspection and punch list.
What nobody warns you about: your sink is gone from demo day until the counter is set and the plumber comes back. Set up the temporary kitchen first - fridge in the dining room, microwave and coffee maker on a folding table, dishes in the laundry sink. Skip it and you will order pizza five nights a week and blow the budget sideways.
Three tiers, three price tags
Cost vs. Value figures for the West North Central region put a midrange minor kitchen remodel near $27,880, a midrange major remodel near $80,850 and an upscale major remodel near $159,347. What moves you between them is whether the layout and the cabinet boxes stay put.
### How do you read a kitchen remodel bid?
Compare scope, not totals. A bid you can judge names the cabinet line and door style, the counter material and edge, the appliance model numbers, who pulls the permit, and what is left out. When two bids land far apart, the gap is almost always in what one of them skipped.
Allowances. Placeholders for tile or fixtures you have not picked. Ask what happens when you go over, and whether unused money comes back.
Exclusions. Painting the next room, floor refinishing, a panel upgrade and appliance haul-away are the usual ones.
Permit. Who applies, and who pays the fee.
Payment schedule. Draws tied to finished milestones, not calendar dates.
Change orders. In writing, priced, and signed before the extra work starts.
Lien waivers. From the contractor and the subs with each draw, so a paid job cannot come back at you.
Red flags: a one-page lump sum, a deposit big enough to fund somebody else’s job, verbal change orders, a price that dies if you do not sign tonight, and anyone who will not put license and insurance in writing.
Want three bids you can actually compare? Browse kitchen remodelers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, write your scope on one page - layout change or not, cabinet grade, counter material, appliance list - and hand that same page to every company you call.
If you’re the remodeler who shows up with a tape measure and writes the bid line by line, homeowners comparing scopes are exactly the customers you want. Put your company where they’re looking and get more customers who already know what they’re buying.
### Where kitchens go over budget
Most kitchens go wrong on decisions, not craftsmanship. A crew cannot set cabinets around a tile you have not chosen, and a crew standing still moves to another job and comes back when its calendar allows. Lock every selection before demo and put the list in the contract.
Then there is “while we’re at it.” Refinish the hall floor since the sander is here. Repaint the dining room since the trim is off. Each one is reasonable alone; together they are the overage. Price them at bid time so they land in the plan instead of a change order.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I redo my kitchen for $10,000?
A.  You can refresh a kitchen at that budget. You cannot rebuild one. At that level you keep the cabinet boxes and the layout and spend on paint or refacing, hardware, a modest counter, a sink and faucet, and lighting. Move the sink or order new cabinets and you leave that range immediately.
### Q. Is $30,000 enough for a kitchen remodel?
A.  Often, for a kitchen that keeps its layout. The Cost vs. Value figure for a midrange minor kitchen remodel in the West North Central region is about $27,880, so that budget is real money for new fronts, counters, flooring and standard appliances. It stops being enough the moment walls or plumbing move.
### Q. How much remodeling can be done with $100,000?
A.  Generally a full midrange major kitchen, which the regional figures put near $80,850, with room left for a contingency. It does not reach the upscale tier, near $159,347. Whatever the number, never spend it down to the last dollar before demo.
### Q. What are some reputable kitchen remodeling companies in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  No honest article hands you a ranked list, because reputable depends on your scope and your jurisdiction. Build your own: companies that pull permits where you live, carry current liability and workers’ compensation coverage, give you references from recent kitchens, and put an itemized scope in writing. Then call those references.
### Q. Who are some reputable kitchen remodelers in St. Louis?
A.  Whoever hands you a name - a neighbor, a search result, a listing - run the same checks before you sign. Verify the trade licenses your town requires, get a certificate of insurance sent straight from the agent, confirm in writing who pulls the permit, and read the change order clause twice. On the Illinois side, ask for the consumer rights pamphlet.
### Q. How long does a full kitchen remodel take?
A.  Plan in two stages. Design, selections, cabinet ordering and permits often take longer than the construction, and cabinet lead time is the wild card, so get it in writing. Once demo starts, the countertop template and fabrication window is the built-in pause. Ask for a written schedule that shows the rough inspection and the template date.

## Choosing a Jeweler in St. Louis: Missouri Gold Buyers Must Post Their Prices
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-jeweler-in-st-louis
In Missouri, a gold coin is tax-free. Bend the same gold into a ring and it isn’t.
That is Section 144.815, which exempts purchases of bullion and investment coins from state and local sales tax, and defines bullion as metal whose value depends on its content rather than its form. A ring is all form. It is the first sign that jewelry runs on its own rules here, and most people find them out at the worst possible moment.
Like this one. You are rinsing plates on a weeknight in Affton when something small pings off the edge of the steel sink. You look down. One prong on your ring is bare, bent back like a tiny open hand, and whatever it was holding is somewhere between the drain and the floor. Your stomach drops before your brain catches up.
Or the quieter version: a watch in a Florissant nightstand that stopped years ago, your grandmother’s pearls gone slack on gray silk, a chain that let go at the clasp in Belleville. Sooner or later each of those ends at a counter, and some of them end at a scale.
Here is the rule worth knowing before you ever set old gold on one. Missouri’s Section 407.292 says that when a weighing device is used to buy gold, silver or platinum, a statement of prices has to be posted on a conspicuous sign close to the scale, with the price per troy ounce for twenty-four, eighteen, fourteen and ten karat gold. The buyer must copy your photo ID, have you sign the record, and keep each item in an unaltered condition for ten full days.
In Missouri, the price has to hang next to the scale. If you can’t read it from where you stand, you are at the wrong counter.
### Who is the best jeweler in St. Louis?
There isn’t one, and a shop that claims the title is selling you something. “Best” splits by job: the store that sets a beautiful engagement ring is not automatically the bench you want retipping worn prongs, restringing pearls or writing an insurance appraisal. Choose per task. Ask whether the work is done on site, get a written estimate split into metal and labor, and start with one small job before the ring that matters.
The on-site question is the one that tells you the most. Ask it plainly: “Do you do the work here, or does it ship out?” Neither answer is disqualifying, but shipped-out work means a longer wait and a middleman between you and the person holding the torch. When the bench is in the back room, you can sometimes hear it from the counter: the hiss of a torch, the tap of a hammer on a mandrel.
Then the real test. Will they talk you out of something? A jeweler who says “that chain isn’t worth soldering again, here’s why” is showing you how they think. Bring a battery, a clasp or a cleaning first. Watch how they handle a job too small to make them any money. Notice whether they clean the piece before they hand it back, whether they show you the worn spot under the loupe, and whether the estimate they write matches the number they said out loud. Small jobs are where a counter shows you who it is when the stakes are low.
### What a local bench does that a website can’t
Everything that happens after the sale. Sizing, prong retipping, a new shank, tightening a stone that clicks when you tap it, rhodium plating on white gold, pearl restringing, watch batteries and band links. A website ships you a ring. It cannot put your ring under a loupe and tell you a prong has worn thin.
Fit is the underrated one. Fingers swell in July heat and shrink in January cold, so a ring sized on a sticky August afternoon can spin by Christmas. A bench jeweler also knows when a ring cannot be sized at all: full eternity bands with stones all the way around and some tension settings usually have to be remade rather than adjusted.
### Is it cheaper to go to a local jeweler?
On the sticker, sometimes not. On the total, often yes, because the sticker is not the whole price. Add shipping, resizing an online ring somewhere else, a return that goes sideways, and repairs you now have no local relationship for.
Sales tax is a real St. Louis variable. The Missouri Department of Revenue puts the state sales tax rate at 4.225%, and cities, counties and certain districts may add local sales taxes on top. Ask for the out-the-door total in Kirkwood and in Edwardsville before you decide the bridge matters.
### How do you buy an engagement ring without being sold to?
Decide the number before the glass case lights up in front of you, say it out loud as soon as you sit down, and ask to see the grading report on any center stone. That one sentence changes the conversation from “what can we get you into” to “what can we build at this number.”
Know the disclosure rules so nobody can blur them. The Federal Trade Commission’s Jewelry Guides at 16 CFR Part 23 call for a clear and conspicuous disclosure, such as the words “laboratory-grown” or “laboratory-created,” conveying that a lab-made diamond is not a mined stone. If a stone’s origin stays vague after you ask twice, the vagueness is your answer.
Then ask what the ring costs to own: sizing, how often they want to inspect it, and whether the warranty requires you to bring it back on a set schedule to stay valid. Read that line twice, slowly, before you sign anything at all, even if the pen is already in your hand.
Wildly off-topic, but a good night’s sleep outlasts most purchases: how to buy a mattress without getting worked over.
### Which jewelry repairs are worth doing?
Almost always worth it: retipping or rebuilding prongs before a stone is lost, replacing a worn shank on a ring you wear daily, tightening stones, replacing a failed clasp, and restringing pearls. A prong repair costs far less than replacing a lost center stone, and stones that bounce off a kitchen floor are rarely found. Worth questioning: soldering a thin chain that has already broken twice, or plating a piece that will need it again every year.
Pearls tell you when they are due. If they slide loosely between the knots or the silk looks yellowed and frayed, take them in, and ask for a knot between every pearl so a break costs you one pearl instead of a strand rolling under the radiator. Keep pearls, opals and oiled emeralds out of ultrasonic cleaners.
### How do you get a watch battery and band done right?
Ask about the gasket, not just the cell. Opening a case back disturbs the seal that kept the watch water resistant, and old rubber gaskets dry out and flatten. A careful shop inspects or replaces the seal and tells you whether it can test the watch afterward. If the watch is dead, don’t assume the battery is the whole story; a movement that sat for years with a leaking cell may need more than a swap, and a good counter tells you that before charging for a battery that fixes nothing. For buying a new one, here is how to choose and buy a watch.
### What does an insurance appraisal actually do?
It gives your insurer a documented number. Many homeowners and renters policies cap what they pay for stolen jewelry, so call your agent and ask for your jewelry limit in dollars, then ask what scheduling a piece with an appraisal changes. Get the appraisal from someone whose interest is the document, not the merchandise; an appraiser who also wants to buy the piece has a reason to lean one way. Expect a full description with measurements, weights, grades and photographs, not a one-line value, and ask how often they suggest updating it.
### Before you sell old gold or buy estate pieces
Go back to that Missouri sign by the scale, and to the rest of Section 407.292. The buyer keeps the transaction record for one year for law enforcement inspection, and has a duty to inform law enforcement if there is reason to believe an item was obtained illegally. Buying from a minor requires written authority from a parent or guardian. The section does not apply to pawnbrokers or scrap metal dealers, so ask which kind of counter you are standing at.
Two checks on any older piece. Look for a maker’s mark beside the karat stamp: federal law at 15 U.S.C. 297 says a manufacturer or dealer who stamps a gold or silver quality mark on an article must also apply a registered trademark or the firm’s name. A stamp with nobody’s name next to it deserves a test, not trust. And get more than one offer. Estate pieces also move through the saleroom, so read how St. Louis auction houses work before you assume a store is the only buyer.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should jewelry cost?
A.  It depends on metal weight, stone quality and labor, so there is no single right number, but you can price it structurally. Ask for the quote split into metal, stones and bench time, ask what changes if you drop one grade of color or clarity, and compare two shops on the same specification rather than on a headline price.
### Q. Is $3,000 cheap for an engagement ring?
A.  It is a real budget, not a small one, and plenty of beautiful rings are built at that number. What matters more than the total is where it goes: cut quality and a setting built to hold the stone outlive an extra tenth of a carat. Say the number first and ask the jeweler to show you two different ways to spend it.
### Q. What month is jewelry cheapest?
A.  No month carries a guaranteed discount, because pricing tracks metal markets and inventory more than a sale calendar. What you can count on is that the weeks before the big gift holidays are crowded. Shop in a quiet stretch and you get an unhurried hour at the counter and a better shot at negotiating on a piece that has been sitting in the case.
### Q. What are the 5 C’s of jewelry?
A.  Most lists start with color, clarity, cut and carat weight, and the fifth people add is usually certification, meaning an independent grading report. Treat that one as buying advice rather than a grade, and ask to see the report before you fall for the stone.
### Q. What is the 2:1:1 rule in jewelry?
A.  It is a styling idea, not a valuation rule: balance a look by mixing quiet and bold pieces instead of piling everything in one place. Stylists describe it differently, which tells you it is a guideline. It has nothing to do with quality, price or how a jeweler quotes a repair.
### Q. What is the hottest jewelry right now?
A.  Lab-grown center stones are the change you will see in almost every case, and the FTC’s jewelry guides call for a clear disclosure that such a stone is not mined. Beyond bridal, more people are remounting stones they already own, buying vintage and estate pieces, and choosing lighter chains.
### Q. Can a local jeweler repair a ring I bought online?
A.  Usually yes, and this is where a bench relationship pays for itself. Sizing, prong work and stone tightening do not care where the ring came from. Ask first whether outside repairs void the online retailer’s warranty, and check that policy before you hand the ring over.
Ring in a drawer, waiting on a decision? ## Missouri Medicaid Now Covers Hearing Aids. Medicare Still Won't
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hearing-aids-st-louis-what-to-expect
How many times did you say “huh?” at dinner last night before somebody waved a hand and said never mind?
You know the moment. The fork stops halfway to your mouth while you lean toward the voice at the far end of the table at a family birthday in Affton. Everybody laughs. You laugh a beat late. On the drive home the radio sits louder than you would ever admit, your daughter repeats the same sentence twice, and nobody mentions it, which is worse than if they had.
Then, late one night with the phone glowing in the dark, you finally look up what this costs, and the first answer lands like a door closing. Medicare.gov says it in one line: Medicare doesn’t cover hearing aids or exams for fitting hearing aids, and you pay all costs for non-covered services. Most guides stop right there.
Here is what they skip. Missouri’s own Medicaid law, Section 208.152 in its version effective August 28, 2025, lists “medically necessary cochlear implants and hearing instruments” among the medical services MO HealthNet pays for, when they are prescribed by an audiologist or dispensed by a hearing instrument specialist. If you or a parent carries a MO HealthNet card, the first question for any clinic is not which brand. It is whether they bill MO HealthNet for hearing aids.
And then there is the river. In Belleville, Illinois law says all hearing instruments offered for sale must come with a 30-business day return privilege, and the receipt has to say you can return them for a refund within 30 business days of delivery. In Kirkwood, Missouri law only requires the purchase agreement to state the length of any trial period, and if no right exists to return the hearing aid, the seller has to say so in writing.
Same hearing aids, same price. One side of the Poplar Street Bridge guarantees your money back. The other side only guarantees you’ll be told if it won’t.
### Who is the best hearing aid supplier?
There isn’t one, and any list that names a winner is ranking products, not your ears. The best supplier for you holds a current Missouri or Illinois license, verifies the fit with a probe microphone in your ear canal, puts the trial period and return terms in writing, and tells you exactly what the price still includes after the fitting. Check the license first, then ask about real-ear measurement.
Here is what a fitting that goes right can sound like: the turn signal ticking in the car, a sound you forgot existed. Your own footsteps on the kitchen tile, suddenly too loud. That moment comes from the fitting, not the box. Two people with the same hearing test can walk out with very different results from the same model, because the fitting is the treatment and the device is hardware. So the phone call before you book should sound almost boring. Are you a licensed audiologist or a licensed hearing instrument specialist, and what is your license number? Do you do real-ear verification at the fitting? How many follow-up visits are in the price? What is the trial period, and what is nonrefundable if I send them back? Do you take MO HealthNet or my plan?
Both states let you check a license for free, from the same chair you are reading this in. The Missouri Board of Examiners for Hearing Instrument Specialists offers license verification, and it posts a notice that it continues to review complaints where purchase agreements do not meet the standards of Section 346.020. The board answers at 573.751.0240. In Illinois, the Illinois Department of Public Health licenses dispensers and responds to consumer complaints.
### Read the Missouri purchase agreement like a contract, because it is one
The clipboard comes across the desk with a pen clipped to it, the new hearing aids sitting in a little open case beside it, and everyone is smiling. Slow down right there. Sit with the paper before you sign, even if the clinic is warm and the coffee is good. Missouri’s Section 346.020 says the agreement must carry the licensee’s signature, business address and license number, plus the make, model and serial number of the hearing aid. It must state the exact amount of any down payment, the length of any trial period, any fees tied to that trial, and any right you have to return the device.
That last part is the one to put your finger on. If the line about returns is blank or vague, ask for it in writing before you hand over a card. In Missouri, the agreement is the protection.
### What is the difference between an audiologist and a hearing instrument specialist?
You will see both titles on the glass door and both on the business card, and from the waiting room they look identical. The difference is scope. Both can fit and sell you a hearing aid. The audiologist also performs diagnostic hearing evaluations on children and adults and may bill insurance, including Medicare, for medically necessary hearing and balance evaluations, per the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. In Illinois, dispensers are licensed by the Department of Public Health, while audiologists are licensed by the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.
Neither title settles quality. A meticulous specialist who runs real-ear measurements on every fitting will serve you better than anyone who skips them. The credential says what someone may do. The protocol says what they actually do.
### Why the probe microphone matters more than the brand
At a good fitting, a thin soft tube slides into your ear canal next to the hearing aid, and you sit still while a computer plays speech-like sound and reads what actually reaches your eardrum. It feels like nothing. It decides almost everything. ASHA’s practice guidance calls real-ear measures the gold standard in hearing aid fitting verification, and notes that the actual output of the manufacturer’s formula may vary considerably from prescriptive targets.
In plain words: the settings on the screen and the sound in your ear are not the same thing until someone measures them. Ask for it by name. If the answer on the phone is a pause, or “our software handles that,” you have learned something useful about the clinic before you ever sit in its chair. The same goes for follow-ups: hearing aids almost always need tuning once you have worn them in your own kitchen, your own car and your own church, so ask how those visits are scheduled and whether they cost extra.
Bring somebody whose voice you struggle with to the evaluation, and bring a written list of the rooms that beat you: the church basement, the shop floor, the restaurant with the tin ceiling, the graduation party under a white tent.
### What happens at a hearing evaluation?
Most of it happens sitting down. The clinician asks about your history, looks into your ear canals with a small light, and then seats you in a quiet booth with headphones. Tones come in, some so faint you are not sure you heard them, and you press a button or raise a hand each time. Then words: repeat what you hear, even when it sounds like mush. Results land on an audiogram, a chart of the softest sounds you can catch across pitches, and a good clinician walks you through it line by line instead of sliding a brochure across the desk.
This is where the money questions belong, before anyone mentions a model. Ask what the evaluation itself costs if you buy nothing. Ask whether the clinic is enrolled with MO HealthNet or your Medicare Advantage plan, and bring the card. Ask whether you can take a copy of your audiogram home. A test and a purchase are two separate decisions, and nothing about the first one obliges you to the second.
If a relative is coming along, give them a job: write down the answers. The appointment moves fast, the words are new, and the person whose hearing is being tested is the one least likely to catch every number.
### How are OTC hearing aids different from prescription ones?
They hang on a pharmacy peg near the reading glasses, in a plastic clamshell you need scissors to open. The FDA created over-the-counter hearing aids for adults 18 years of age and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, and that category went into effect on October 17, 2022. You can buy one in a store or online without seeing an ENT doctor or an audiologist. OTC devices are not meant for severe or profound loss, and a prescription hearing aid is only available through a licensed hearing health care professional.
Turn the box over before you pay. The FDA’s OTC rule requires important information on the outside package labeling, including the manufacturer’s return policy, and the FDA’s OTC regulations do not require manufacturers to provide a warranty. The return line on the box is the whole safety net.
Tired of asking people to repeat themselves? Browse hearing aid providers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two of them, and ask the same five questions from the top of this page, starting with the license number and whether they bill MO HealthNet.
If you run the clinic, the hearing practice or the one-chair dispensing office, these are the families looking for you this week. A complete listing helps a practice get more customers who already know what to ask - put your practice in front of them.
### How much does Medicare cover for a hearing aid?
This is the answer that makes people put the phone down and stare at the wall. Nothing toward the aids themselves. Medicare.gov is plain: Medicare doesn’t cover hearing aids or exams for fitting hearing aids. What Part B does cover is diagnostic hearing and balance exams. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, plus a hospital copayment in a hospital outpatient setting.
One wrinkle helps. You can visit an audiologist once every 12 months without an order from your health care provider, but only for non-acute hearing conditions, like hearing loss that happens over many years. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer extra hearing benefits that Original Medicare doesn’t cover, so call the number on your card and ask for the hearing allowance and the in-network clinics.
Veterans have their own road. Through VA audiology, if hearing aids are recommended and fit, the hearing aids, repairs and future batteries are at no charge as long as you maintain VA eligibility for care.
### What are the red flags for audiology referrals?
A wet pillowcase in the morning. A hiss in one ear that the other ear doesn’t share. The room tilting when you stand up too fast. Some signs mean a doctor first, ideally an ear, nose and throat physician, before anyone sells you an amplifier: pain or drainage from the ear, hearing that changed suddenly, worse hearing or ringing in only one ear, or real dizziness and spinning. A hearing aid fixes none of those. Nobody reading a web page can tell you which one you have, and that is exactly why you get looked at.
Nothing to do with ears: hosting the graduation party yourself? Start with what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the Trump hearing aid act?
A.  That phrase usually means the Over-the-Counter Hearing Aid Act of 2017, S.670, which directed the FDA to create a category of hearing aids adults could buy without a prescription. The FDA’s OTC category went into effect on October 17, 2022.
### Q. What is the best hearing aid available right now?
A.  No honest answer names a model. Hearing aids are matched to a pattern of loss, an ear canal and the rooms you live in, so the device that changes one person’s life underperforms for the next. Round-ups rank features and prices; they have not tested your ears.
### Q. What hearing aid do most audiologists recommend?
A.  There is no consensus brand. A clinic’s shelf is shaped by manufacturer relationships, insurance contracts and the fitting software its staff knows best. Ask which manufacturers they fit and why that one for your results. A specific answer about your hearing test tells you more than any logo.
### Q. What is the number one rated hearing aid?
A.  Ratings compare features, apps, batteries and price, and they turn over constantly. None of them ranks what decides your outcome: how accurately the device is programmed to your ears and how often you wear it. Treat a top rating as a shortlist and get the trial terms in writing.
### Q. How much should a decent hearing aid cost?
A.  It depends on what is folded into the price. A bundled quote pays for the device plus the fitting, follow-up visits and often a warranty; an unbundled quote is cheaper up front and charges for each visit. Ask for an itemized quote and compare the same things side by side.
### Q. What is the average cost of a behind-the-ear hearing aid?
A.  Style is a weak predictor of price. Behind-the-ear models span basic to premium, because the cost tracks the technology tier and the services bundled with it. Ask for the itemized number on two quotes rather than a style-based estimate.
### Q. Do I need a doctor’s order to see an audiologist?
A.  Not always. Under Medicare you can visit an audiologist once every 12 months without an order for non-acute hearing conditions. Private plans and MO HealthNet set their own rules, so call the number on your card first.

## Served Divorce Papers in St. Louis? You Have 30 Days to File a Parenting Plan
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-you-need-a-family-law-attorney-st-louis
Thirty days. In a Missouri case involving custody, each parent has thirty days after service of process to submit a proposed parenting plan, and for a lot of St. Louis parents that clock starts on a front porch in Affton, with a stranger saying your full name and handing over an envelope. You set it on the counter next to the coffee that has gone cold. The refrigerator hums. Upstairs, a child is still asleep.
That plan is the first draft of where your children wake up on a Tuesday for years. Here is what to do with the month, in order.
Today. Write the date you were served on the envelope itself. Then find your court. A St. Louis County case runs through the 21st Judicial Circuit, whose Family Court sits at 105 South Central Avenue, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 314-615-8029, and keeps its own Exchange Center and supervised visitation service. A case from inside the city limits goes to the 22nd Judicial Circuit Court, a separate court with its own judges.
This week. Put recent tax returns, pay stubs and every account statement in one folder, and book a consultation with a family lawyer. If paying one is the wall, Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes phone applications at 314-534-4200, but only from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday.
Before you move out, sign anything or change the kids’ routine, read the next two sections, on property and on parenting time. They are general information about Missouri and Illinois family law, not legal advice about your case, and nothing here predicts what a judge will do with your facts.
### Is Missouri a 50/50 state for divorce?
No. Missouri divides marital property and marital debts in whatever proportions the court deems just after weighing the factors in RSMo 452.330, and just is not a synonym for half. The even split people hear about lives somewhere else entirely: Missouri law presumes that equal or approximately equal parenting time is in a child’s best interests. Half the Tuesdays is the starting point. Half the house is not. In Missouri, the 50/50 lives in the calendar, not the bank account.
Look at your own kitchen the way the judge will. The mortgage statement under a magnet on the fridge, the minivan in the driveway with two car seats still buckled in, the years one of you stayed home so the other could work doubles. RSMo 452.330 tells the court to weigh exactly that: each spouse’s economic circumstances, including whether the family home should go to the parent who has the children, each spouse’s contribution to what you own, which the law says out loud includes the contribution of a spouse as homemaker, and the conduct of the parties during the marriage. No formula. No fixed weighting. A judge, your facts, and the word just.
What even counts as marital is its own fight. The condo you owned in Maryland Heights before the wedding starts outside the pot. So does your grandmother’s inheritance. Pour marital money into either one and the line blurs fast, which is why the first question a good family lawyer asks is where every account came from.
### The paper that decides where your kids wake up
Fathers walk into a first consultation braced for every other weekend. Missouri’s own words say otherwise. RSMo 452.375 forbids any preference for either parent in awarding custody because of that parent’s age, sex or financial status. And the equal-time presumption is rebuttable only by a preponderance of the evidence, so the parent who wants less than an even split for the other side has to prove it. It is a default, not a guarantee. But it is the default.
For unmarried fathers the gap is paperwork, not love. Under RSMo 210.823 a signed acknowledgment of paternity is considered a legal finding of paternity, and either signer can rescind it within sixty days of the last signature. What it does not do is set a schedule. A birth certificate makes you a father on paper; only a court order tells anyone when the kids are yours. Hold the first without the second and you have nothing to show a school front office at 3:15 when they ask who is allowed to sign the kids out. If you’re that dad at the front desk, read our guide to the Fathers & Families Support Center before your first hearing.
The judge also weighs the child’s adjustment to home, school and community, which matters more than people expect the week someone packs a bag. More on that below.
### When do you actually need a family law attorney?
When the other side disputes something, when a court order has to be created or changed, or when the money is complicated. No children, no house, no retirement accounts and both of you agreeing on paper is the narrow case people handle themselves. The facts that reliably mean hire someone: children whose schedule you two cannot agree on; a business, a pension or a 401(k) to split; a self-employed spouse who controls the books; any allegation of abuse; an order somebody is ignoring; or a spouse who already has a lawyer when you don’t. That last one is the quiet tell. If their attorney’s letterhead is already in your mailbox, you are negotiating against a professional with a pen you have never held.
Totally unrelated, but the outlet behind the couch went dead the same month? You need a licensed electrician, not a lawyer.
### How long does a Missouri divorce take?
Missouri sets a floor, not an average. Under RSMo 452.305 one of you has to have lived in the state for the ninety days before filing, thirty days have to pass after the petition is filed, and the court has to find the marriage irretrievably broken. Thirty days is the earliest a fully agreed case can close. A contested case runs on discovery, appraisals, custody evaluations and the court’s calendar, and those months feel longer than the calendar says when you are sharing a hallway with the person on the other side.
Orders do not freeze forever. Under RSMo 452.410 a custody order can be modified when facts that arose after the decree, or were unknown to the court then, show a change in the circumstances of the child or the custodian, and the change serves the child’s best interests. A handshake deal at a pickup in a gas station parking lot is not one of those facts. It is not an order at all.
People are asking
### Why do people say moving out is the biggest mistake in a divorce?
Moving out does not by itself hand over your share of the house: under RSMo 452.330, marital property means all property acquired by either spouse after the marriage, apart from the listed exceptions. The risk is the children. When a Missouri judge decides custody, one of the listed factors is the child’s adjustment to home, school and community, so the parent who stays with the kids in the same house can start to look like the stable arrangement. Talk to a family lawyer before the moving truck, not after.
### What changes if one of you lives in Illinois?
This metro straddles a river and two rulebooks. Everything above is Missouri law, and none of it carries across the bridge automatically. If one of you lives in Belleville and the other in Kirkwood, which state hears the case is not a small detail. It is the first question to put to a lawyer, and the lawyer should be licensed on the side of the river where the case will actually sit.
People are asking
### What assets cannot be touched in a Missouri divorce?
Nonmarital property, which the court sets apart to its owner before it divides anything else. Under RSMo 452.330 that covers property acquired by gift, bequest, devise or descent, property acquired in exchange for property you owned before the marriage, and property excluded by a valid written agreement. The increase in value of premarital property also stays out, unless marital assets, including labor, contributed to that increase.
### What a family lawyer costs, and how to spend less of it
There is no honest single number, and any figure pinned to a named firm would be stale within weeks. Four things do almost all of the work.
Contested or agreed. The biggest factor by a wide margin. A case with a signed settlement is mostly drafting; a contested one is discovery, depositions, motions and hearings, every hour billed.
The retainer is not the price. It is usually an advance the firm bills against, with a clause asking you to top it up. Think of it as the opening balance.
Children. A disputed parenting plan, a custody evaluation or a later modification each adds hours, plus outside fees separate from your attorney’s bill.
How tangled the money is. A family business, a pension, self-employment income or a spouse who keeps the records. Each one tends to bring an expert, and experts bill too.
One question worth asking on the first call: will the firm take limited scope work, such as drafting the parenting plan or appearing at a single hearing, instead of the whole case? Not every firm does. Asking costs nothing.
The parenting plan is due thirty days after service, so spend this week on three phone calls, not thirty browser tabs. Browse family law attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist three, check each license, and book the consultations close together so you can compare the answers while they are fresh. Family budgets get stretched by more than legal fees, too: how orthodontic costs and insurance actually work is worth reading before the next school year.
If you’re the family law attorney people trust with the hardest conversation of their year, they are searching for you the night the envelope lands, not after. List your practice so the next person on that porch has a name to call.
### Checking a lawyer before you sign anything
Start with fit, not badges. You want someone who handles family cases regularly in the county where yours will sit, St. Louis County, Jefferson, Franklin, St. Clair or Madison, because the local judges and the local habits are half the job. Then check the license: The Missouri Bar keeps an Official Directory of Lawyers, and Illinois attorneys show up in the Lawyer Search of the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission. Two minutes, both sides of the river.
Bring recent tax returns and pay stubs, a list of every account and debt, and any existing order, all in one folder. Ask how many cases like yours the attorney handled last year, who will actually work the file, how fast calls get returned, and what the written fee agreement says. Anyone who guarantees an outcome twenty minutes after hearing your facts is telling you something. If a business the two of you built is caught in the split, our guide to when a St. Louis business needs an attorney covers that side.
### What if you cannot afford a lawyer at all?
Free help exists, and it is income-qualified, so have your household income and assets ready before you call. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes applications online, or by phone at 314-534-4200 or 800-444-0514 in that narrow Monday, Wednesday and Thursday morning window. Set an alarm. Its Lasting Solutions program provides legal representation in family law cases, including divorces, custody and orders of protection, for survivors leaving abusive relationships in St. Louis City, St. Louis County and Jefferson County, among other areas.
On the Illinois side, Land of Lincoln Legal Aid offers free services to low-income and senior residents, and its Legal Advice and Referral Center takes intake calls at 877-342-7891.
If safety is the problem tonight, that is a faster, separate track. Missouri’s orders of protection come from Chapter 455, and RSMo 455.025 says the clerk’s duties in helping you file are performed without cost to the litigants. The National Domestic Violence Hotline answers at 800-799-7233. Neither path requires you to have hired anyone first.
Family law offices see the other side of this, too: the call comes when money is tightest and one household is becoming two. The practices that last are the ones that route the venting to a paralegal, quote truly agreed work plainly, and take limited scope cases instead of turning people away. If that is your practice, add or claim a listing so the person searching at midnight finds you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a divorce lawyer worth the cost?
A.  It depends on what is in dispute. With no children, no real estate, no retirement accounts and a signed agreement, a lawyer mostly buys correct drafting. Add children, a house, a pension or a spouse who controls the money, and the mistakes an unrepresented party makes tend to cost more than the fee. Some, like a vague parenting plan, follow you for a decade.
### Q. What rights do fathers have in Missouri?
A.  The same rights mothers have. Missouri forbids any custody preference based on a parent’s age, sex or financial status, and it presumes equal or approximately equal parenting time is in the child’s best interests. For unmarried fathers, RSMo 210.823 treats a signed acknowledgment of paternity as a legal finding of paternity.
### Q. How much does a divorce attorney cost in Missouri?
A.  There is no fixed rate. Cost tracks four things: whether the case is contested, how the retainer is billed against, whether children are involved, and how complicated the money is. An agreed case with a signed settlement costs a fraction of a contested one. Ask every firm for its hourly rate, its retainer amount and whether it takes limited scope work.
### Q. How do I find a good family law lawyer?
A.  Look for someone who handles family cases regularly in the county where yours will be filed, look the lawyer up in The Missouri Bar’s Official Directory of Lawyers or the Illinois ARDC Lawyer Search, then book two or three consultations close together. Bring tax returns, pay stubs and any existing order, and compare how each one explains your options.
### Q. Who is the top-rated family law attorney in St. Louis?
A.  Be wary of anyone who claims the title. A badge or a star count does not know your facts, your county or your budget. A better screen: confirm the license, then judge fit yourself in a consultation.
### Q. What are the three C’s of divorce?
A.  It is advice for getting through a divorce, not law. Missouri’s actual tests are different: whether the marriage is irretrievably broken, and how to divide marital property in the proportions the court deems just.
### Q. What should I do first after being served divorce papers in Missouri?
A.  Write down the date you were served, because a custody case gives each parent thirty days from service to submit a proposed parenting plan. Then gather tax returns, pay stubs and account statements into one folder, and get a lawyer’s read before you move out, sign anything or change the children’s routine.
### Q. Can a Missouri custody order be changed later?
A.  Yes, but not because somebody changed their mind. RSMo 452.410 requires new facts, or facts the court did not know, showing a change in the circumstances of the child or the custodian, and a finding that the change serves the child’s best interests.
None of this makes the year easier. It does make the first phone call shorter. Before anybody asks you in a conference room, sit at the kitchen table with the envelope and write down what you actually want on the other side of this: the schedule, the house, the retirement account, the holidays.

## A 20x40 Party Tent Is 800 Square Feet. In St. Louis, That Matters
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-ask-before-booking-party-rentals-st-louis
The tape measure snaps back into its case and you finally have your number. Forty feet from the side door of the parish hall to the curb, twenty across. Room for a 20x40. Room for the graduation party, the grill smoke drifting over the folding chairs, the sheet cake sweating in its box. You call the rental company, give them the South City address, and somewhere in the second sentence you say the words “parking lot.”
The line goes quiet for a beat.
Here is why. The City of St. Louis tent policy for special events says it in two flat sentences: “Tents must be placed on grass so they can be staked. Tents cannot be placed on pavement.” And the size you just measured is exactly where the paperwork starts. The city’s tent permit policy requires a permit whenever the area is 800 square feet or more, counting tents attached together. A 20x40 is 800 square feet on the nose.
Now the twist. That same policy exempts tents for private family events that are erected on the same lot with the residence. So the identical tent, for the identical party, in your own backyard needs no city tent permit. Move it two blocks to the church lot and you are into a permit, a $35 fee, a site plan and a city inspection before a single guest walks under it.
In St. Louis, the tent doesn’t decide whether you need a permit. The address does. That is the first thing to settle before any money changes hands, and it is the one question most people never think to ask.
### What size tent do you need for 100 guests?
For 100 guests at round tables, plan about 1,200 square feet: roughly 12 square feet a person, which makes a 30x40 the floor. A standing cocktail crowd of 100 needs about 800 square feet at 8 a head. A buffet event runs closer to 14 square feet a guest, and a dance floor or bar pushes you up a size. Anything 800 square feet or more needs a city permit off a residential lot.
Rental companies size from square feet per person, not from headcount, and the gap between seated and standing is bigger than people expect. A seated dinner needs room for elbows, chair backs and the walk to the buffet with a full plate. A cocktail crowd needs room to stand and turn around. Do the multiplication yourself, then add the footprint of everything that isn’t a person: the gift table, the DJ, the drink tubs full of melting ice.
Then hand the company three things: the guest count, the seating style and the extras. Ask them to confirm it fits your ground with room to stake. Inside the city, the policy also wants tent walls at least four feet from interior lot lines, which eats into a narrow South City yard faster than you would think.
### What size tent do I need for 50 guests?
Half the people, half the ground. Fifty seated guests at 12 square feet each is about 600 square feet, so a 20x30 is the floor and a 20x40 gives the plates and the folding chairs some breathing room.
Notice what that does to the permit math. A 20x30 sits comfortably under the city line. The 20x40 lands right on it. And if the caterer brings a 10x10 pop-up and the crew clips it to the main tent, the city counts the aggregate area of tents attached to each other. You just went from no permit to permit with one canopy.
### Six questions to ask before the deposit
Get each answer by email, not over the phone in a noisy kitchen. What is the delivery and pickup window? Does the crew set up and tear down, or is it a drop-off? What surface will the tent sit on, and does the price assume stakes or weights? What is the weather and cancellation policy, in writing? Who pulls the permit? And what does the damage waiver actually cover?
Each question maps to a way the day goes sideways. The truck rolls up while you are still in the shower. The chairs land stacked on the driveway and setting them out was extra. The only flat ground is asphalt. It rains and the deposit stays with the company. Somebody asks to see a permit nobody applied for.
### Does the price include setup, or is it a drop-off?
Ask directly, because both are common and they price differently. A drop-off means the crew unloads at the curb and leaves; you carry, unfold and stack, and you feel every one of those chairs in your shoulders that night. Full setup means they place the tables, open the chairs, stake the tent and come back to break it down. Plenty of companies do setup on tents and drop-off on everything else.
Then pin down the window. Many companies deliver on a range rather than a set time, and a weekend event can mean the gear arrives the day before and leaves the day after. Say so up front if a park shelter has to be clear by dark.
### The city rules that catch people under the tent
The permit is not the only line in the city’s policy. Tent fabric and decorative material have to be flame resistant. No open flames of any kind are allowed in the tent, which means the tea lights you bought for the centerpieces stay in the bag. Lighting, audio and visual systems run on electricity only. The tent has to be built to withstand a wind speed of 90 miles per hour, and the site has to be cleared of debris within 50 feet.
Where the city does require a permit, the tent cannot be occupied until a Fire Safety Unit inspector approves it, and the approval comes as a Certificate of Inspection plus an Occupancy Load Placard showing the maximum number of people allowed inside. Both get posted where guests can see them. A tent on city-owned property also needs a Board of Public Service permit, and that office answers at (314) 622-4627.
Outside the city limits, ask the rental company who pulls the permit and whose name goes on it. Good operators handle it routinely. Some contracts hand it to you in one quiet sentence.
### Do bounce houses need a permit in Missouri or Illinois?
Across the river, Illinois answers this one by name. The Illinois Department of Labor’s amusement ride FAQ says that if you operate inflatable rides or attractions at an event open to the public, you are subject to its rules, and an inspector affixes a permit decal to each approved ride. For your kid’s birthday in Belleville, it is just as plain: the person who rents the ride does not need a permit.
Illinois requires ride attendants to be at least 16 years of age and operators to carry $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate of general liability insurance. On the Missouri side, ask the company for its certificate of insurance, the manufacturer’s posted rider limits, and whether an attendant stays while the blower hums and the kids shriek.

### What happens if it rains on the day of your event?
Usually the party goes on and the deposit does not come back, which is why the tent is the rain plan rather than its casualty. Settle three things in writing: how late you can move the date and whether the deposit travels with it, what happens if the crew judges conditions unsafe, and whether sidewalls can be added at the last minute.
Wind is the real decision point, not rain. When the flags across the street snap straight out, a reputable crew will not raise a tent, and nobody should argue with them. If the site is a park, a rented lawn or one of the campgrounds around St. Louis, check its own rules on staking and vehicle access first.
### What are the most rented items for parties?
Tables, chairs, linens and tents carry most of any party order, because nearly every event needs them. After that come the things that make a party feel finished: sidewalls and string lighting for anything running past dusk, cocktail tables, chafing dishes, ice tubs, a dance floor, portable restrooms for open ground, heaters when the air turns sharp and fans when it turns thick.
Then the family category: inflatables, popcorn and snow-cone machines, yard games and a speaker somebody’s uncle will take over by the second hour. If the party is for kids, the bounce house gets booked first and carries the most rules.
### How can I reduce the cost of party rentals?
Shrink the tent, shrink the chair count, and widen the delivery window, in that order. None of them costs you anything the guests will notice.
Move the buffet and the bar outside the tent so you are not renting square footage to shelter a table. Swap a third of the seating for cocktail tables. Use one vendor instead of paying two delivery fees. Stake on grass instead of weighting on pavement. Ask what is already going out that weekend; a size sitting idle sometimes prices better.
### Are event rentals profitable?
They can be, and the margin isn’t where customers assume. A big frame tent is capital that pays back across seasons, not on one weekend. Linens carry good margins and miserable labor, because somebody launders and folds every one. The money is really made or lost on the truck: how many stops a two-person crew clears in a window. What operators grumble about is short: the call for a Saturday in May placed ten days out, and the tent booked for a driveway that cannot be staked.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a tent or a venue?
A.  A tent is cheaper on the invoice and more expensive in everything else. A venue rolls tables, chairs, restrooms, power, parking and a rain plan into one number. A tent covers ground and nothing more, so the honest comparison adds everything you put under it, any permit the address triggers, and the labor of running the day yourself.
### Q. How much does it cost to rent a 20x20 event tent?
A.  Get a written quote rather than trusting a number off the internet. The same 20x20 prices differently depending on how it is anchored, how tight the delivery window is, and whether the date falls in a busy season. Staking into grass is usually simplest; ballasting on pavement adds weights and labor. Sidewalls, lighting and the damage waiver move it further.
### Q. How much do chair rentals typically cost?
A.  Chairs price per chair, and that figure is only part of the bill. Style matters most: a white folding chair, a resin garden chair and a wooden crossback sit at very different prices. Then delivery, whether the crew sets them out or leaves them stacked, the waiver and quantity. Ask for the all-in total, delivered.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or rent a bounce house?
A.  Renting wins unless you use one many times a year. A purchased inflatable brings storage, a blower, cleaning, patching and the setup you were paying someone else to do. It also brings the liability. In Illinois, anyone who operates an inflatable at an event open to the public is subject to the state’s amusement ride rules.
### Q. What age is appropriate for a bounce house?
A.  Go by the unit, not a general rule. Ask the company for the manufacturer’s age, height and weight limits and the maximum riders at once, and keep the toddlers and the big kids on separate turns. Little kids and big kids bouncing together is where the tears start.
### Q. Where can I rent an event tent in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Search party equipment rentals by your own part of town rather than the whole metro, since delivery zones and fees are drawn tightly around a company’s yard. A vendor twenty minutes closer often quotes better than a bigger name across the river. Ask each the same three things: tent size, anchoring, and their written weather policy.
### Q. How much does an inflatable bounce house cost to rent?
A.  Ask for the number as a day rate plus delivery, because those are often quoted separately and the delivery half moves with your address. Size and type drive the rest: a plain bounce unit sits at the bottom, combo units with a slide cost more, and water units and big obstacle courses cost the most. The quote also moves with the rental window, an attendant, a generator if no outlet is within reach, and a long carry from the truck.

## Missouri Campsites Open 12 Months Out at 7 a.m. Illinois Gives You Six
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-book-a-campsite-near-st-louis
Twelve months, to the minute. At 7 a.m. Central, exactly one year before the first night of your trip, a Missouri state park campsite opens for booking. Not a week before. Not “sometime in spring.” Seven o’clock, a year out.
Here is how it usually goes instead. It’s March, the heat is still kicking on at night, and somebody in the group chat types “let’s camp Memorial Day.” Six thumbs up. Nobody books. Then it’s May, you finally open the reservation site with a coffee going cold next to the laptop, and the map of the park you wanted is a wall of taken sites. Your stomach sinks a little. You start bargaining with yourself about a tent site with no power.
Cross the river and the clock is different, which is the part almost nobody tells you. At Pere Marquette State Park in Grafton, Illinois, the park itself says reservations can only be made 180 days in advance, six months, and that its sites “go early in the fall months.” Same weekend, two states, two different alarms to set. Miss one and you can still catch the other.
That is the leverage on every camping trip within reach of St. Louis. The woods are easy. The calendar is where people get burned.
### What is the best campground near St. Louis?
The best one is the one you booked on the right morning. For the closest Missouri state park campground, start with Dr. Edmund A. Babler Memorial State Park at 800 Guy Park Drive in Wildwood, reservable 12 months out at 7 a.m. Central. On the Illinois side, Pere Marquette in Grafton has 80 reservable Class A sites with 20, 30 and 50 amp service and a shower building, bookable 180 days ahead.
Babler is the one you can reach after work on a Friday and still get the tent up before full dark. The park office number is 636-458-3813, and calling it is the fastest way to ask the question no website answers well: which loop is quietest and which sites drain after a hard rain. Pere Marquette is the bigger-trip pick, with the bluffs over the river road on the drive up and an all-in-one campground where everybody sleeps near the same shower house.
Here is what each one feels like. At Babler you roll in through a massive stone gateway that generations of Missourians have passed through, past Civilian Conservation Corps architecture, and by the time the car doors close the only sounds are gravel, birds and somebody’s cooler lid. At Pere Marquette you climb to the top of the bluffs and look out over the Illinois River and its backwaters, wind in your face, then walk back down to a campfire that smells like every good October you remember. Pick the park first. Then set the alarm for the right morning.
### How to grab a site the morning the window opens
Do the slow part the night before, while the house is quiet. Missouri’s own reservation page tells you to have your camping details and a card ready before you go online or call, and that is good advice. Pick your first-choice site and two backups on the park map. Write down the dates. Make an account and log in so you aren’t typing a password at 6:59 with your heart going.
At 7 a.m. Central, book. Online reservations run around the clock, and the call center at 877-422-6766 answers from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Central, seven days a week. If you are bringing friends, know that Missouri caps you at five campsites in one phone call or web session, so split the job between two people.
Missed it? Don’t give up on the trip. Missouri takes online reservations up to 7 p.m. on the day of arrival, and campsites that are not reserved stay open for walk-up registration. A cancellation on a Tuesday can turn into your Friday. Check the map again a few days out, and again the morning of. People’s plans change all the time.
### The two-state rules that decide summer weekends
Illinois runs tighter. Reservations there have to be made at least three days before the campsite is needed, so a spur-of-the-moment Illinois trip mostly depends on first-come sites. A site can be reserved for a maximum of 14 nights within a 30-day period. Memorial Day, Labor Day and some Fourth of July weekends require a two-night minimum stay.
Missouri is looser on the short end, with same-day booking until 7 p.m., but a few popular parks there also set two-night minimums on weekends. Read the park’s own page before you book a single Saturday night and then wonder why the checkout screen won’t take it.
And check the clock on the other end too. Missouri check-in begins at 3 p.m. and checkout is at 2 p.m. Quiet hours run 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. That last one matters more than it sounds when the site next to you is a family with a toddler and you brought a speaker.
### How much does it cost to camp, and what are you paying for?
You are paying for a spot of level ground and whatever plugs into it. Missouri says plainly that nightly rates vary from campground to campground and that rates are charged on the basis of available utilities, whether used or not. So if you book an electric site and never run a cord, you still pay for the electric. Book the site you actually need.
Know your cord before you choose. Look at the plug on the back of the trailer and match it to the site listing before you book. In a St. Louis August, power is the difference between a cool night and lying on top of the sleeping bag listening to the cicadas and sweating.
### What your first night out actually needs
Sleep warm first. The ground pulls heat out of you all night, so a real sleeping pad does more for an April or October night here than a fancier bag. Bring a tent with a full rainfly, two lights per person, and more water than seems reasonable. If you want the full list, our guide to what outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis covers it without the upsell.
Then buy your firewood instead of hunting for it. Missouri State Parks asks campers not to gather or cut firewood in the parks, so plan on picking up a bundle near the park. Pack trash bags too, because you’ll carry out what you bring in. Missouri also says no personal property may be left unattended longer than 24 hours, so you can’t hold a site with an empty tent.
The first night is always louder than people expect. Owls, a car door three loops over, rain ticking on the fly at 2 a.m. The second night you sleep like a rock. Book two nights if you can.
Set the alarm before you set up the tent. ### Changing or canceling without losing your shirt
Plans fall apart. The tent is packed, the cooler is iced, and then a kid wakes up with a fever, a storm parks over the Meramec, somebody’s shift changes. Missouri’s fee table lists $5.25 to change a reservation and $10 to cancel one, on top of losing the original reservation fee. But the reservation page adds the detail worth screenshotting: cancel online 31 or more days before arrival and there is no cancel fee. So if the trip is wobbly, decide early.
In Illinois, the $5 reservation fee is never refunded, but camping fees are refunded if you cancel on the website three days before arrival. Mark both deadlines in your phone the day you book. It takes thirty seconds and it is the cheapest insurance in camping.
Not ready to sleep outside yet? Start with a day out in the small towns around St. Louis and scout a park on the way.
### Camping with kids, dogs or a brand-new trailer
With small kids, book close. A park you can reach in under an hour means bailing at midnight is still an option, and knowing that makes everyone braver. Pick a site near the restrooms. Bring the same pillow they sleep on at home. Let them hold the flashlight. That is half the fun for a seven-year-old.
With a dog, bring a short leash, a stake and a water bowl, and walk the loop once before dark so the new smells aren’t all new at 10 p.m. With a new trailer, do a practice night in the driveway first. Find out what you forgot while your kitchen is still twenty feet away.
If camping is one leg of a longer trip, lock the campsite dates first, because those are the ones with a release date you can’t argue with, then build around them. For a bigger trip, here’s when a travel agent is worth it.
### What campground owners wish campers knew
A campground lives on weekends and holidays, and a rained-out holiday can’t be made up in November. The no-show who never cancels costs the family who would have taken that site. So if you aren’t going, cancel, even late. Someone is refreshing the map hoping you will.
Owners also wish you’d call. The person in the office knows which site floods, which one gets the morning shade and which one sits too close to the dump station. One short call beats an hour of squinting at a map. And if you just need to burn off a long week before you go, St. Louis gyms are a good place to start.
The bill behind one night
Nightly rates vary by campground and by the utilities on the site, charged whether you use them or not. Booking adds $6.50 per site online or $8 through the call center, and seniors 65 and older, people with disabilities and military families get $2 off every night.
