### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 200 rule for camping?
A.  It is the Leave No Trace guideline to camp at least 200 feet from lakes and streams, about 70 to 80 adult steps, so the ground near the water stays intact and wildlife keeps its path to it. It matters for backcountry and dispersed camping. In a developed state park campground, you camp on the pad the park assigns you.
### Q. How much does it cost to camp at a Missouri state park?
A.  It depends on the park and the site. Missouri says nightly rates vary from campground to campground and are charged on the utilities a site has, whether you use them or not. Each park posts its own rate sheet, so pull up the one for your park before you book and price the basic site against the electric one.
### Q. What is the cheapest campground?
A.  In Missouri’s state park system, look at the nine campgrounds that offer value camping, with lower rates that vary by the day and season. Then book the simplest site you can live with, since rates follow the utilities on the site. Seniors, people with disabilities and military families also get $2 off each night.
### Q. How much do campsites cost per week?
A.  At a state park, a week is simply the nightly rate times seven, plus the reservation fee, which Missouri charges for each site reserved: $6.50 online or $8 by phone. Illinois charges a $5 reservation fee. Price a weekday stretch against a weekend one, since some rates change by the day.
### Q. How much do most campgrounds cost per month?
A.  State parks are not built for month-long stays. Illinois lets you reserve a site for a maximum of 14 nights within a 30-day period. For a full month, you are looking at a private RV park, so call and ask for the monthly rate and whether electricity is billed separately.
### Q. Can I just show up, or do I have to reserve?
A.  In Missouri, you can book online until 7 p.m. on the day you arrive, and sites that aren’t reserved stay open for walk-up registration. In Illinois, reservations have to be made at least three days before you need the site, so a last-minute trip there depends on first-come sites.

## Illinois Makes Travel Agencies Hold 90% of Your Deposit in Trust. Ask Yours Where It Sits.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-use-a-travel-agent-st-louis
Most trips out of Lambert do not need a travel agent, and you can usually tell before the coffee in your mug goes cold. One flight, one hotel, three nights, booked in eight minutes on the couch with the TV murmuring and the dog asleep on your feet. Anyone who tells you that trip needs a professional is selling something.
Then the airport hands you a trip that does. St. Louis Lambert announced that Icelandair will fly nonstop between St. Louis and Iceland on a Boeing 737 MAX 8, up to four times a week from May 14 to October 24, with connections to more than 35 destinations in Europe. Read that with your own family in mind. One flight out, three dozen cities to pick from on the other side, a return that has to land before the first school bell, and a mother who needs the aisle seat near the front.
That is how the eleven browser tabs happen. Two of them show the same hotel at two different prices. The laptop fan whirs, the kitchen has gone quiet, your thumb hovers over the trackpad, and the deposit button glows at you like a dare.
Here is the part almost nobody in this two-state metro knows before they click. Illinois law says a travel promoter shall deposit 90 percent of all sums received from you into a trust account in a federally insured bank, and that trust exists for the benefit of the people paying. That is the standard Illinois wrote down. Hold every agency, on either bank, to the same question before it takes your money: where does my deposit sit until I travel, and who can touch it? A good advisor answers without blinking. A nervous one changes the subject.
If a deal goes bad on the Missouri side, the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222, and it asks you to keep your contracts, invoices and brochures. On the Illinois side, the Illinois Attorney General lists its regional consumer hotlines on its consumer protection page. Save both before you need them.
The rule of thumb is short enough to text your sister. A travel agent is worth it the moment one mistake would cost you more than the fee.
### How can I choose a reliable travel agency?
You are on the phone, card on the kitchen counter, pen in hand. Ask three questions before you read a single digit out loud: how do you get paid, what do you book most, and who picks up the phone if something breaks while I’m gone. Listen to the pause. A working advisor answers all three in about a minute. Vague answers about money are the loudest warning in this business.
Then check the plumbing, with the card still face-down on the counter. Pay by credit card, never by wire, Zelle, Venmo or personal check. Ask for the supplier’s own confirmation number, not just the agency invoice, and log in to the cruise line or tour company site yourself to see your name on the booking. Get the cancellation and change penalties in writing before a dollar moves.
Last, hire for the trip you are actually taking. If it is that first Iceland nonstop out of Lambert with a hop to somewhere past it, you want the advisor who books Europe connections every week, not the one who books river cruises and knows which cabins hum above the engine room. Ask how many trips like yours they booked this year. Then listen.
### The Iceland test: one flight out, 35 cities past it
Here is how a do-it-yourself Europe trip goes sideways. It is the way home. The passport line has not moved in twenty minutes, the overhead lights buzz, a toddler is wailing two rows of rope back, and the flight to St. Louis on your separate ticket is already boarding. The airline that sold you that ticket has no idea your first one ran late. Nobody is holding the door. You booked every piece yourself, in eleven tabs, and every piece was fine on its own.
That is the chain: a connection on a separate ticket, a rental car picked up in one country and dropped in another, a hotel that cancels free until a date nobody wrote down. It breaks at the weakest link, usually at a gate, usually when you are tired and your shoulders ache from the backpack strap.
That is the job a good advisor does. Not finding a secret cheaper fare, but seeing the whole chain at once and telling you, before you pay, which link snaps. If your trip is one city and back, keep the money. If it is three countries, two generations and a fixed date, the fee is cheap insurance against the phone call from a departure hall.
### Is it cheaper to book with a travel agent or yourself?
Two tabs, same hotel, two prices, and your stomach drops a little at the higher one. Here is the honest answer. Usually it costs the same, sometimes it is better value, and if you pay a planning fee it costs more by exactly that fee. What changes is what rides along with the price.
Where an advisor earns it back is in extras and in errors avoided. Onboard credit, an upgraded cabin at the same fare, a resort credit: those are real and paid for by the supplier. So is the mistake you never make, like the connection that was legal on paper and impossible on foot, or the shore excursion booked so tight a late tender leaves you squinting at the ship from the dock. Say your budget out loud. An advisor who won’t work inside a number is telling you something useful.
### When booking direct is the better call
Some trips are a click and a boarding pass. Book it yourself when the trip is one flight and one hotel, when you would happily rebook the whole thing in eight minutes, when you are chasing airline status that only counts on a direct booking, or when a planning fee would be a big slice of the trip. A weekend in Chicago does not need a professional.
Booking straight with the airline also keeps you inside the airline’s own promises. Read your carrier’s customer service plan (the federal rule on those plans is 14 CFR 259.5) before you assume a third-party booking gets the same grace.
### What ASTA and IATA after a name really tell you
The letters sit in an email signature, small and official-looking under a smiling headshot. They are trade credentials, not government licenses, and knowing the difference protects you. ASTA is the American Society of Travel Advisors, an association of travel professionals that advocates for travel agencies, the industry and the traveling public. An IATA or IATAN card is about supplier access, not about you. IATA’s own ID card eligibility rules ask a U.S. applicant to work at least 20 hours a week in travel sales and earn at least $5,000 in salary or commissions over the past 12 months. That tells you someone sells travel. It does not tell you they are good at your trip. For a first nonstop to Iceland, ask how many Europe trips with a connection they booked this year. That number tells you more than any logo.

### Travel insurance, waivers and the fine print
At checkout there is a little box, already half-tempting, offering to protect your trip for a little more. The Illinois Department of Insurance says it bluntly: a cancellation waiver sold by a cruise or tour operator is not an insurance policy, and waivers are not regulated by the department. If the operator that sold you the waiver becomes insolvent, you may not be able to collect. That checkbox at checkout feels like protection. Read what it actually is.
The same department warns that Medicare and Medicaid typically do not pay for medical care outside the United States, and that a policy may have set time periods when pre-existing conditions are not covered. Think of an ER waiting room abroad, the forms in another alphabet, the card you hand over that nobody there takes. That is the moment the fine print was about. For a plain-language overview of what policies cover, the insurance commissioners’ national guide is a good first read.

### What happens when something goes wrong mid-trip?
Rules cover part of it. The federal airline refund rule, 14 CFR Part 260, covers refunds for airline fares and ancillary service fees, and your credit card gives you a way to dispute a charge in writing. That is why a big tour deposit belongs on a card and not on a wire transfer.
The rest of it is a person. Rules do not rebook you. When a sailing is cancelled or a storm shuts an airport, you are standing on hard carpet with your phone at 4 percent, holding with hundreds of other travelers. An advisor is working the same problem from a desk back home while you find an outlet. That is what you are paying for on a multi-generation trip, a destination wedding, or any trip where a missed connection means the ship leaves without you.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it actually cheaper to use a travel agent?
A.  Rarely cheaper on the sticker price, often better value, and more expensive by exactly the fee if you pay one. The gap shows up as supplier-paid extras, like onboard credit or a better cabin at the same fare, and as the expensive mistake you avoided.
### Q. What is a normal fee for a travel agent?
A.  There isn’t one national number, so treat any figure you read as a guess about somebody else’s business. Fees are set by each advisor and scale with the work: less for one hotel booking, more for a multi-country itinerary or a group. Ask how much, what it covers, and whether it is credited back if you book, before any research starts.
### Q. What is the average cost of using a travel agent?
A.  For many leisure bookings the direct cost to you is nothing, because the cruise line, tour company or hotel pays the advisor out of the price you were already paying. Where a planning fee applies, a good advisor tells you before work begins. The real question is not the average. It is what this advisor charges you, in writing.
### Q. How much does a travel agent make on a $10,000 trip?
A.  It depends on what the $10,000 is made of. Taxes, port charges and some fees usually pay the advisor nothing, plain airfare often pays little, and many independent advisors share what they do earn with a host agency. If you are curious, ask. A good advisor will tell you how they are paid on your trip.
### Q. Who are the best travel agents in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single best one, because the right advisor depends on the trip. Pick for specialization: someone who books river cruises every week, or Disney every week, or Italy every week, beats a generalist on your trip. Ask how many trips like yours they booked this year, how they are paid, and who answers the phone at 2 a.m. overseas.
### Q. Is it cheaper to go through a travel agent?
A.  On a simple trip, no, and you will be faster on your own. On a complex one, the price is usually the same and the value is higher, because the advisor catches the broken connection or the wrong-date hotel before you pay for it.
### Q. Do I need travel insurance if my credit card already has it?
A.  Sometimes, but read the card’s benefit guide first. Card coverage often has limits well below a big trip’s cost and may only apply if you charged the trip to that card. Check whether it covers medical care abroad at all, then compare its covered reasons and limits against a standalone policy.

## $52 Buys a St. Louis Auctioneer License. Check Everything Else Yourself
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-auction-houses-work-st-louis
Crack. The gavel hits the block, the auctioneer says “sold,” and three rows back somebody’s stomach drops, because the walnut dresser they meant to bid “just a little” on is now theirs. Their hand is still half up. The paddle feels hot.
That sound is not decoration. In Missouri it is the moment the sale is complete. The state’s commercial code says a sale by auction is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary way, and a bidder may take back a bid only up until that announcement. Once the hammer lands, you have bought a dresser. Nobody in the room will tell you that before you raise your hand.
Here is the second thing almost nobody knows, and it is the one worth repeating to the next person who says “let’s just call an auction company.” In the City of St. Louis, an auctioneer’s license is bought over the counter at the License Collector’s office, Room 104 of City Hall, for $50 a year, or $10 for a single month, plus a $2 registration fee. The city honors a license from any Missouri county, but a house with an office inside the city has to buy the city one too. Fifty-two dollars. That is the whole price of the paper on the wall.
So the license proves someone cleared a legal bar, not that they are good. Whether it’s a brick two-family in South City or a ranch house in North County full of forty years of life, everything past that license you have to check yourself.
That is the whole game on both sides of the paddle: the license, the terms of sale, and the arithmetic nobody does until the bill comes.
### How do I find a reputable auction house?
Start with the license and the terms of sale. In Missouri, a public auctioneer must hold a license; in the City of St. Louis it is sold at the License Collector’s office in City Hall, so ask which county or city issued theirs and when it runs out. Then read the published terms of sale before you register or consign, and get the settlement window in writing.
Missouri treats the license seriously even if the fee is small. Selling goods, property or real estate as a public auctioneer without one is a class C misdemeanor, and a conviction bars the person from working as an auctioneer for a year. So the question “who licensed you?” is fair, normal and quick. Listen to how quickly the answer comes.
After that, the best signal is the conversation itself. Call and ask where the terms of sale are posted, whether you’ll get a settlement statement that lists every lot, which fees come out of a seller’s money, and what happens when a winning bidder never pays. A good operator has heard all four questions a hundred times. You will hear it in their voice: no pause, no shuffling papers, no “we’ll figure that out later.”
### The number the auctioneer shouts is never your bill
Most houses add a buyer’s premium on top of the hammer price, and sales tax lands on top of that unless you have an exemption on file. Some add a fee for paying by card. An online platform may add its own. Each one is printed in the terms of sale, and each one is easy to forget when the bidding gets loud and fast and your heart is going.
So bid backwards. Before the sale, decide the total you are willing to watch leave your bank account. Subtract the premium, the tax and any card fee listed in the terms. What is left is your top bid, and you write it on the back of your paddle or on your hand. Doing that math in the last forty seconds of a live lot is how people overpay for furniture they never sat in.
### What to check before you bid on anything
Go to the preview. Most auctions sell as-is, with no returns, and once the hammer falls the conversation is over, so the preview is the only time the item can talk to you. Pull every drawer and run it on its track. Smell the inside of the case for basement damp. Run a hand under the top for lifted veneer or fresh glue. If something has a plug and the room has an outlet, plug it in.
On an online-only sale, ask for a written condition report and ask the plain question: do these photos show all of the damage? A straight answer tells you more about the house than any review. And if it is a box lot, assume the best thing in the box is the thing on top.
### Reserve or absolute: what the auctioneer can and can’t do
Missouri law sets the default in the seller’s favor. A sale is with reserve unless the goods are put up, in explicit terms, without reserve, and in an auction with reserve the auctioneer may withdraw a lot any time before announcing the sale complete. In other words, if the bids don’t reach the seller’s floor, the lot can simply go home.
An absolute auction, announced without reserve, is different. Once the auctioneer calls for bids on a lot, it cannot be withdrawn unless no bid comes in within a reasonable time. That is why absolute sales pull a bigger, louder crowd. Everyone in the room knows the thing is really selling.
Two more lines from the same statute are worth carrying in your pocket. If you retract your bid, the bid before yours does not come back to life. And if the auctioneer knowingly takes a bid on the seller’s behalf without notice that this is allowed, the buyer may choose to cancel the sale or take the goods at the last good-faith bid.
### How online and absentee bidding really works
You leave a maximum and the system bids for you, one step at a time, only as high as it has to go. You can win well under your number. Many timed online sales also use a soft close: a bid in the final moments pushes the clock out, which is why a lot that was supposed to end while you brushed your teeth is still open when you get back to the screen.
Before you register, read three lines in the terms: the pickup window, the storage or abandonment fee if you miss it, and any hold the house places on your card. Winning a china cabinet from the couch is easy. Getting it down someone else’s basement stairs by the deadline is the real job. Bring blankets, straps and a friend, and if the lot came out of a dusty barn, plan a stop at a car wash on the way home.
Still fuzzy on what gets stacked on top of a winning bid? Here is how the buyer’s premium works in St. Louis, with the math.
### Selling: consignment, estate sale, or a buy-out?
Three routes, three different trades between price and certainty. With consignment, you stay the owner until the hammer falls and the house takes its commission out of what the lots bring, so a strong night pays well and a soft night does not. An on-site estate sale tags everything and brings the crowd through the front door, which handles a houseful of ordinary things better than one rare one. An outright buy-out is the fastest and usually the lowest ceiling, and for some families that certainty is worth every dollar of the difference.
What sells is rarely what a family expects. Tools, shop gear and sporting goods often find eager bidders. Big formal dining sets often disappoint. Small, dense things, such as coins, watches, good silver and estate jewelry, can outsell a whole room of furniture, which is why houses often pull them into their own sales. Ask the auctioneer what has been bringing money in their room lately, and listen.
### When does the seller actually get paid?
Not the next morning. Buyers have to pay, cards have to clear, the pickup window has to close, and the bidder who never pays has to be chased or the lot run again. The number of business days until settlement should be in your written contract before you hand over a single box. If a house won’t write it down, that tells you what you need to know.
Ask for a statement that lists every lot, not one net number at the bottom. You want the hammer price, the commission, and each charge for hauling, photos or unsold lots on its own line. And ask who eats the loss when a winner disappears, because in some contracts the lot just comes back to you weeks later.
### If you are doing this because someone died
Slow down by one day. The house smells like their coffee and their coat is still on the hook, and every choice feels urgent. It isn’t, not yet. Before anyone loads a truck, walk the rooms for paper: titles, deeds, insurance policies, savings bonds, tax records, photographs and address books. Check coat pockets, the backs of drawers, inside books and the freezer. Tell the auctioneer up front about firearms, prescription drugs or anything with a title, because those need their own handling.
Don’t polish, refinish or deep-clean anything to make it look nicer; on the wrong piece that strips value instead of adding it. Don’t toss the junk drawer or the garage shelf until somebody who does this for a living has looked. And if three siblings are deciding by group text at midnight, ask the house for a second walkthrough with everyone in the room. A good one will say yes.
### What the people running the sale wish you knew
The fees are the visible part. The invisible part is labor: sorting, hauling, photographing and listing hundreds of lots before a single bid exists, paid for whether the night is strong or soft. For an estate, what an auction house really sells is an empty house by the deadline, not a big price on one object. The winner who never pays and the winner who never picks up both cost real money after the gavel falls.
So be the bidder they remember for the right reasons. Pay on time. Show up inside the window. Say thanks to the crew carrying your dresser to the curb. It comes back to you the next time you want a straight answer about a lot.
Call two houses before you bid or sign anything. Browse auction houses across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, describe what you have or what you’re hunting, and ask each one who licensed them and when they settle.
If you run the auction house, the estate-sale crew or the one-truck pack-out business, the family reading this is picking who to call tonight. Get your company on St Louis Near Me Directory and get more customers who already know the right questions to ask.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What percentage do auction houses take?
A.  There is no single figure, because a house is usually paid from both sides of one sale. The seller pays a commission out of the hammer price, and the buyer often pays a premium on top of it. Rates vary by house, sale and lot value, so the published terms for that specific sale are the only number to trust.
### Q. What do most auction houses charge?
A.  The total take is split between a seller commission and a buyer premium, and one house’s rate tells you nothing about the next. Rates also shift with the format and the kind of goods. Get your number in writing, for your sale, before you register or consign.
### Q. What are typical auction fees?
A.  Beyond commission and premium, expect some mix of hauling, photography, a card fee, an online platform fee, storage if you miss pickup, and a buy-back fee when a reserve isn’t met. Ask which ones come out of a seller’s settlement and which are billed separately, and get the list on paper.
### Q. What are common auction mistakes?
A.  Bidding the hammer price instead of the all-in price. Skipping the preview and trusting a handful of photos. Forgetting that in Missouri the sale is done when the hammer falls. Winning something you can’t move by the pickup deadline. And on the selling side, refinishing an item before anyone who knows the category has looked at it.
### Q. What are the upcoming auctions happening in St. Louis?
A.  Sale calendars change week to week, so the current list lives with each house, not in any article. Check each auctioneer’s own calendar and email list, plus the online bidding platform they use. The preview time is posted with the catalog, and the preview is the part to put on your calendar.
### Q. How much money do you need for an auction house?
A.  As a buyer, less than you think, as long as you budget for the premium and tax on top of your bid. As someone starting a house, the license is the cheap part: Missouri sets the fee for a twelve-month auctioneer license at fifty dollars, paid to the county clerk. Trucks, storage, staff and insurance are the real money.
### Q. Can you provide me with a list of foreclosures in Saint Louis City?
A.  Foreclosures run on a different track from the auction houses on this page. Missouri’s auctioneer law does not cover sales held under a court’s authority or foreclosure sales of real estate. For the city’s land tax sales, the Sheriff posts the property list two weeks before each sale date; the Office of the Sheriff is on the 8th floor of the Civil Courts Building at 10 N. Tucker Blvd, (314) 622-4851.

## In Missouri, the Money You Pay a Gallery Belongs to the Artist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/visiting-buying-st-louis-art-galleries
Confession most of us never say out loud: we have slowed down at a lit gallery window on Washington Boulevard, looked at a canvas the size of a garage door, felt our face go warm for no reason, and kept walking. Not because we didn’t want to go in. Because the door looked like it was for somebody else.
It isn’t. A commercial gallery is a shop. You can walk in wearing the shirt you mowed in, stand in that cool white quiet, and leave without spending a dime. Nobody asks what you do for a living.
And here is the part almost nobody in town knows, the turn that changes how buying feels. In Missouri, a gallery selling an artist’s consigned work is legally that artist’s agent. State law, section 407.905 of the Missouri statutes, says the work and the money you pay for it are held in trust for the artist until the artist is paid in full, and the gallery’s creditors can’t touch it. When you hand over a check for a painting here, the law holds that money in trust for the painter.
Say that at the next dinner party. It is the opposite of what people fear about art buying.
### Is there an art district in St. Louis?
Yes. The Grand Center Arts District sits north of Highway 64/40 and Saint Louis University on Grand Avenue, with galleries and museums down several blocks around it. On the first Friday of every month, the district’s museums and galleries are free and open until 9 p.m. Venues there run from theater to street art to galleries.
Two Grand Center doors sit side by side on Washington Boulevard. The Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis at 3750 Washington is free, and tickets are not required for entry. The Pulitzer Arts Foundation at 3716 Washington is free too, with a free lot next door, and it stays open until 9 p.m. on First Fridays. Go on one of those nights and you hear it before you see it: the hum of a few hundred conversations bouncing off concrete floors.
### Walking in without buying is the normal thing
Most people who come through a gallery never buy anything, and the owners know it. Foot traffic today is how a collector shows up years from now. So take your time.
Walk the whole room once without reading a single label. Then go back to the piece that made your stomach drop a little. Ask for the price list, in exactly those words. It is a normal question, not a commitment. Don’t touch the work or the frames, ask before you take a photo, and know that a small red dot on the wall beside a piece means it has sold.
The person at the desk who asks if you have questions is not sizing up your wallet. They have been sitting in a silent room all afternoon. They want to talk.
### What’s the difference between art museums and galleries?
A museum owns a collection and exists to keep it and show it. The Saint Louis Art Museum in Forest Park, for one, is free every day. A commercial gallery owns almost nothing on its walls. It takes work on consignment from living artists and sells it.
There is a third kind people mix up with both: the artist-run space or co-op. Members hang their own shows and take turns at the desk, so the person handing you a cup of water may be the one who made the thing you can’t stop staring at. Ask them anything.
### What an opening night actually feels like
Warm room, white walls, plastic cups, somebody’s playlist a notch too loud. Arrive any time inside the window; nobody comes right at the start. Dress like you are going to dinner. If there is wine, one glass is the right number if you plan to talk to the artist, and you should talk to the artist. “What were you working from?” beats any art word you could memorize. If the artist is a friend, a small bunch of flowers is a kind way to say congratulations.
An opening is a bad time to look at art and a great time to meet people. If a piece is seriously in play, come back on a quiet weekday and stand in front of it alone. If you want it that night, say so early.
### How buying works, from the price list to the wall
Ask whether the price on the list is the out-the-door number, because sales tax still lands on art like anything else. A small courtesy discount is sometimes possible. Ask once, politely, and take the answer you get.
Payment plans are the least advertised thing in the trade. Many galleries will split a purchase into installments and hold the piece until the last one clears, but it is decided gallery by gallery, so you have to ask: is there any flexibility on payment? Get the terms in writing, including what happens if you stop paying.
Commissioning a piece? Settle size, medium, delivery date, total price and deposit before anyone touches a canvas, and bring a phone photo of the real wall with a lamp or chair in it for scale. One thing people get wrong: buying the painting does not buy the copyright. Under federal law, a transfer of copyright is not valid unless it is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights. You own the object. The artist still controls the prints.
Framing is mostly size and glass. On anything on paper you love, ask your framer about UV-filtering glass, the kind that keeps a print from fading in a sunny front room. Many galleries have a framer they trust and will point you to them.
### The two-minute price conversation
Most people freeze at this part, so here it is in plain words. You walk back to the desk. Your heart is going a little faster than it should over a rectangle of canvas. You say: “I keep coming back to the blue one by the window. Can you tell me about it?” That’s it. You have not promised anything.
Let them talk. You will hear where the artist lives, what the series is about, whether there are other pieces from the same run in the back. Then ask the three questions that matter: what is the total with tax, is there any flexibility on payment, and can I take it home or does it ship. If the answer to the first question makes your chest tighten, say so. “That’s more than I planned. Does the artist have smaller work?” is a sentence gallery staff hear every week, and it often leads somewhere good: a drawing, a study, a small print from the same hand.
If you need to think, say that too. Ask whether they can hold the piece for a day or two. Some will, some won’t, and nobody is offended by the question. Walk out, get a coffee, and notice whether you are still thinking about it an hour later. That feeling is the only appraisal that counts on a first purchase.
### Is it right for your wall? A quick test before you pay
Take a photo of the piece with your phone, then pull up a photo of the wall at home and look at them side by side. Is the room warm or cool? Does the light come in from the left in the afternoon? Will the piece hang across from a window that throws glare across the glass at dinner?
Then do the boring math. Measure the wall and the furniture under it before you go out, and keep the numbers in your notes app. A painting that feels huge in a gallery with tall ceilings can look small over a long couch, and the reverse happens just as often. Galleries are used to this question. Many will let you see a piece in a different light or even step outside with it.
### Caring for the piece once it’s home
Hang it where direct afternoon sun won’t hit it, away from the radiator, the fireplace and the bathroom steam. Keep works on paper out of damp basements. Dust a frame with a dry, soft cloth, never a spray. Keep the receipt, the artist’s name, the title and any certificate together in one folder, because the day you want to insure it, lend it or sell it, that paper is what tells its story.
And send the artist a photo of it on your wall. It costs you nothing. It might be the best email they get all month.
Then go back. The second visit to a gallery is easier than the first, and the third feels like stopping by a friend’s place. The staff remember a face that comes in to look, buys once, and keeps coming. That is how a city’s art scene actually stays alive: not a few big collectors, but a lot of neighbors who stopped walking past the door.
Thinking about bidding instead of buying off a wall? Read how St. Louis auction houses work before you raise a paddle.
### One free outdoor stop that started with a gift
If walls feel like too much, start outside. Laumeier Sculpture Park in St. Louis County shows more than 70 large-scale outdoor sculptures across 94 acres, free and open daily. Gravel under your shoes, wind in the trees, steel taller than your house. It exists partly because in 1976 local artist Ernest Trova gave 40 artworks, valued at about a million dollars, to St. Louis County to help form the park.
Pick one gallery close to home and go this week. Browse art galleries across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, walk in, and ask for the price list on the one piece you can’t stop looking at.
If you run the gallery, the frame shop or the studio with the open door, the visitor who just read this is deciding where to go Saturday. Put your space on St Louis Near Me Directory and get more customers through that door.
Planning more than one stop? Start with the small towns outside St. Louis that locals actually drive to.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do art galleries charge?
A.  The Contemporary Art Museum, the Pulitzer and the Saint Louis Art Museum are free to walk into, and looking around a gallery never obligates you to buy. The gallery earns its money from a commission on each sale, which comes out of the price the artist and gallery agreed on. If you buy, ask for the out-the-door total so tax doesn’t surprise you.
### Q. Why do galleries take 50%?
A.  When a gallery takes half, it is paying for everything the artist would otherwise carry alone: street-level rent, insurance on work it doesn’t own, lighting, hanging, the opening night and years of building a list of buyers. In Missouri, the artist’s share of that sale is held in trust for the artist under state law until it is paid.
### Q. What are some artsy things to do in St. Louis?
A.  Go to a Grand Center First Friday, when district museums and galleries are free and open until 9 p.m. Walk through the Contemporary Art Museum and the Pulitzer on Washington Boulevard, spend a free afternoon at the Saint Louis Art Museum in Forest Park, and take a slow loop of Laumeier Sculpture Park in St. Louis County.
### Q. What famous artists are from St. Louis?
A.  Ernest Trova is the name every local art lover should know. Laumeier Sculpture Park describes him as a local artist, and his 1976 gift of 40 artworks to St. Louis County helped create the park you can still walk through for free.
### Q. What is the 2/3 rule for art?
A.  It is a hanging rule of thumb, not an art-history term. A piece hung over a sofa or sideboard should be roughly two-thirds as wide as the furniture under it, so the wall looks finished instead of either crowded or lonely. Measure the furniture before you shop and bring that number to the gallery.
### Q. What is the 70/30 rule in art?
A.  It is a composition habit: let one element take up most of the picture and give a second element the smaller share, so your eye has somewhere to land. Painters use the same idea with color, one main temperature and a smaller counterweight. It is a starting point, not a law.

## At One St. Louis Bridal Shop, $3,000 Is the Top of the Rack
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/wedding-dress-shopping-timeline-st-louis
Three thousand dollars is not where a St. Louis wedding dress starts. At one boutique on South Big Bend Boulevard, $3,000 is the top of the gown price range. The Ultimate Bride’s own FAQ puts its gowns at $899 to $3,000, says many in the store run $1,699 to $2,499, and lists off-the-rack gowns starting at $699.
Sit with that for a second, especially if someone has already told you three grand is a modest number. Then think about the moment it actually matters. You are on the little round platform in socks or borrowed heels, the consultant is pulling clips tight down your back so a sample in somebody else’s size shows you a waist, and three people on a velvet couch have gone quiet. That silence is the dress. The price tag tucked in the sleeve is the part nobody wants to say out loud.
Here is the second surprise in that same FAQ, and it changes how you plan the money. To order your dress, the shop asks for a 75% payment, not a small deposit. It takes Visa, MasterCard, Discover, American Express and cash, and it does not accept checks. So the real question is not only whether you love the gown. It is whether three quarters of it is sitting in your account the day you say yes.
Everything below is built on that one idea: the budget and the calendar are the same decision. Get both right before the first appointment and the shopping turns into the fun part again.
### What are the most common mistakes brides make at a bridal appointment?
The most common mistakes are stacking too many appointments into one day, bringing too large an audience, arriving without a real budget number, and trying on gowns priced well above it. Add showing up without supportive undergarments or shoes near your ceremony heel height. Two or three shops in a weekend is plenty, and the ceiling gets said out loud at the start.
The audience one hurts most. Six opinions in a small fitting room produce a stalemate, and the person outvoted is usually the one wearing the dress. Bring the two or three people whose face you actually want to see when the curtain opens. Then say your number, and say whether it includes alterations and a veil. Nobody in the trade is offended by a budget. They are offended by hearing it at the register.
### How far ahead should you order a wedding dress?
Earlier than feels reasonable. The Ultimate Bride tells brides to allow 6-12 months before the big day, which leaves time for the dress to come in and for the alterations after it. When you say yes in a bridal shop, nothing usually comes off a shelf. The shop places an order, the gown gets made, it ships to the store, and only then does a seamstress put a pin in it.
Then a second clock starts. The same shop recommends booking alteration appointments at least three months before the wedding, because you will need 3-4 fittings. Count backward from the date on the invitation and the window for ordering shrinks fast. Ask every shop for the designer’s quoted ship window in writing, and ask what happens if it slips.
### What actually happens at a trying-on appointment?
At The Ultimate Bride, bridal appointments are an hour and a half and they are required. It also offers same-day appointments when there is room, so it is worth a call if you are close. That hour and a half goes fast: the rack, the curtain, the clips, the turn toward the mirror, the long breath out.
Sizes are where the nerves live, so ask before you go. That shop says its in-stock sizes range from 8-30, and it can order sizes 2-34. Samples are a fit tool, not a verdict. Your gown is ordered to your current measurements and then taken in or let out at the fittings, so there is no version of this where you order for a body you do not have yet. Bring the undergarments you plan to wear and shoes at the right heel height, and tell the consultant what you honestly think of each dress.
### Why alterations are a separate bill and a separate calendar
Alterations are skilled hand labor, priced by the job. The Ultimate Bride says plainly that alterations are an additional fee based on the amount of work your gown will need, and it only alters dresses bought at its store. Ask any shop the same two questions before you order: what does the fitting usually cost for a gown like this, and do you do it in-house?
What drives that bill is how much of the dress has to be rebuilt. Taking in a side seam on a plain crepe sheath is one job. Reshaping a beaded bodice means lifting the beadwork, moving what is underneath, then setting the beads back so the pattern still reads. A gown with a train needs a bustle. Cups and straps are their own line.
Bring the same shoes and the same undergarments to every fitting; change either one and the hem is wrong. At the last fitting, bring whoever is bustling the dress at the reception and have the seamstress teach them on the dress, with their hands. A bustle explained in words late at night in a hot reception hall is a bustle that comes down on the dance floor.
One shop’s real price tags
### Is $3000 a good budget for a wedding dress?
At The Ultimate Bride in St. Louis, $3,000 is the top of the range: its gowns run $899-$3,000, many in the store sit at $1,699-$2,499, and off-the-rack starts at $699. Designer, handwork and whether you buy off the rack move the price; alterations are billed on top.
### Off-the-rack gowns, sample sales and trunk shows
Three different things that all sound like a discount. Off-the-rack means you buy the actual gown in the shop and take it home. A sample sale is a store clearing floor samples it is retiring, sold as they are. A trunk show is a designer sending a bigger slice of a collection to one store for a short run; The Ultimate Bride says it hosts these a couple of times a year.
Off-the-rack is the answer when the wedding is close. You skip the production wait and go straight to alterations. The trade-off is real: the dress has been tried on, it may carry a floor mark or a loose bead, and you buy the size that exists. Check the hem, the underarms and the zipper in daylight by the window, and price the alterations before you call it a bargain.
Unrelated, but after a full day of fittings nobody wants to cook - here is St. Louis-style pizza, explained, and the metro’s gas stations for the drive home.
### What suits, bridesmaids and mothers need
Everyone else in the photos has a clock too, and theirs is shorter than the bride’s. Get every groomsman measured by a real tailor instead of guessing off an old shirt, and set that deadline well ahead of the date. Order all the bridesmaid dresses together at one shop, so the color comes out of the same run.
For the mothers, the etiquette is simpler than the internet makes it. Neither mother wears white, ivory, or a champagne pale enough to read white in a camera flash. Past that, the goal is coordination, not matching: the same level of formality and colors that sit comfortably beside each other. Tradition gives the mother of the bride first pick, and a short text between the two of them settles it faster than any rule. If you are also sorting rings and gifts, our guide to choosing a jeweler in St. Louis covers that half of the list.
### What does a bridal order commit you to?
A bridal order is a custom order, which is a different animal from a retail purchase. Once the shop sends it and fabric is cut to your measurements, there is nothing to restock, so the contract you sign is the deal. Read four things first: the cancellation terms, the ship-window language, whether alterations are included or separate, and what happens to your money if the shop closes. That last one is a fair question for anyone handing over most of the price months ahead.
Pay with a card and keep every receipt and the signed order form. If something goes genuinely wrong, Missouri shoppers can call the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-392-8222. On the Illinois side, the Attorney General lists consumer fraud hotlines that include its Springfield line, 1-800-243-0618.
### How soon should you clean and preserve the dress afterward?
Get the gown to a cleaner soon after the wedding, before invisible stains set. Sugar from champagne, cake and soda can dry clear and darken later, and sweat at the underarms does the same. Ask whether the cleaner works in-house or ships the gown out, and whether the box can be opened and closed again. Store it flat and indoors - not in an attic in August, not in a basement in a wet spring.
From behind the counter, the math is not what shoppers assume. Floor samples are inventory that gets tried on season after season and rarely sells at full price. A Saturday no-show is an hour nobody can sell again. Which is why a complete listing earns its keep: brides search this category by neighborhood, and hours, appointment rules, the size range on the floor and the designers carried are exactly what they want to know before they call. Shops can add themselves on St Louis Near Me Directory in a few minutes.
Call before you book, and ask the same three things everywhere. Browse bridal shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each one its price range, its size range on the floor, and how much it takes to place the order. Hair and makeup for the day are their own errand; what to buy at a beauty supply store is a separate guide.
If you own the bridal shop, the alterations studio or the tux counter, the bride counting backward from her date is searching for you right now. List your shop and get more customers through the door while her calendar still has room.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a bridal boutique in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, several. One example is The Ultimate Bride at 1115 South Big Bend Boulevard, (314) 961-9997, which requires appointments. Most bridal shops here work by appointment rather than walk-in, so call ahead, book a slot, and ask what size range is on the floor.
### Q. Is $3000 a lot for a wedding dress?
A.  It can be a generous one. At The Ultimate Bride, $3,000 is the top of its gown range, and many gowns there sit between $1,699 and $2,499. Set the ceiling as a total that includes alterations and a veil, then shop inside it.
### Q. How much does an average bridal cost?
A.  A national average will not tell you much about the shop you are standing in. Build your own number from three lines instead: the gown, alterations as a separate bill, and accessories such as the veil, undergarments and shoes. Ask each shop for its price range before you try anything on.
### Q. What are common red flags when choosing a wedding dress?
A.  Watch for a shop that will not put the ship window in writing, will not explain how alterations are priced before you order, or pushes you to sign today for a discount that ends at the door. A gown you only like clipped a size too tight is a flag. So is any consultant who talks about your body instead of the dress.
### Q. What color is the groom’s mom supposed to wear?
A.  Anything except white, ivory, or a champagne pale enough to read as white in photos. Beyond that there is no assigned color. Tradition gives the mother of the bride first choice, and the groom’s mother picks something that coordinates: the same formality, a shade that sits well beside the other dress without matching it.
### Q. How long do bridesmaid dresses take to arrive?
A.  Ask the shop for its quoted ship window when you order, then leave room for each person’s alterations after the dresses land. Place them as one order at one shop, because dresses ordered separately can come from different runs in slightly different shades.

## Gioia's Hot Salami Is Fresh Sausage: How to Order at a St. Louis Deli
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/types-of-delis-in-st-louis-and-how-to-order
“Just get it, you won’t be sorry.” That is not a review. That is the deli itself talking: Gioia’s on The Hill prints that line on its own menu, right next to the Hot Salami and Roast Beef, with one more piece of advice in quotes after it - try it on garlic cheese bread.
Stand on Macklind Avenue at a quarter to twelve and you understand why a sandwich shop would talk like that. The line runs back toward the door. The slicer hums. Garlic cheese bread comes out of the oven with the cheese still moving, and somebody ahead of you orders without even looking up at the board.
Here is the turn most visitors miss. The hot salami at Gioia’s is not the dry, hard salami in a grocery case. The menu calls it “Gioia’s fresh sausage, Sliced Fresh To Order,” and the shop’s own site signs off with two words: Since 1918. The menu lists it at two prices, $13.50 and $11. The counter on The Hill runs Monday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and it is closed on Sunday - so the craving that hits after church waits until the next day. The number is 314-776-9410. Feeding a crowd? Gioia’s asks for 24 hour notice on all catering jobs and lists a full case that feeds 10 for $100. Ten people fed from one phone call, the day before.
That is the leverage point for this whole category in St. Louis. The word deli covers several different businesses here, and each one is brilliant at one thing. Walk into the right one for your errand and lunch is the best part of the day. Walk into the wrong one and you get a fine sandwich and the nagging sense you missed something.
### What is the best deli in Saint Louis?
There is no single winner, because the metro runs several kinds of deli and each one wins a different errand. For cured meat by weight and olive salad, an Italian grocery on The Hill. For burek and smoked beef, a Bosnian market in south city. For a tray that feeds a party, a counter that takes catering calls. For a sandwich only this city makes, the hot salami above. Pick by errand, not by ranking.
Cured meat sliced to order and a jar of olive salad? Italian grocery. Corned beef stacked on rye? A Jewish-style sandwich house. Burek by the pan? A Bosnian market. A sandwich built while you fill the truck? The corner counter. A tray for eighteen people on Saturday? The grocery deli, with a phone number that answers.
### The sandwiches St. Louis invented
The Gerber is the one people from here defend. It is a half section of Italian or French bread spread with garlic butter, topped with ham and Provel, sprinkled with paprika and toasted until the top blisters and the edges go crisp enough to scrape the roof of your mouth. It was first made at the family-owned Ruma’s Deli and named for their customer and next-door neighbor, Dick Gerber, who ran a tire store beside them. The Rumas liked what he built so much they put it on the menu in 1973.
Provel is the cheese that makes it taste like home to some people and like a mistake to others. It is a white processed cheese made from cheddar, Swiss and provolone, with a low melting point and a gooey, buttery bite. It does not string. It slumps.
The St. Paul sandwich is the other Missouri original, and you will not find it at a deli at all. It is an egg foo young patty with dill pickle slices, white onion, mayonnaise and lettuce on white bread, sold at Chinese American carryouts. Hot, soft, crunchy and sour in one bite, wrapped in paper that goes translucent before you reach the car.
### What an Italian deli on The Hill does best
The bell over the door, the cold breath of the case on your hands, a wheel of cheese sweating on the counter under plastic. An Italian deli is a grocery first and a sandwich shop second. The counter exists to sell you a quarter pound of something sharp, fresh mozzarella in its own water, olive salad and bread with a crust that crackles when you squeeze it.
The neighborhood is built for it. The Hill’s own neighborhood history page says the Hill is home to more than 30 restaurants and four Italian grocery stores, plus bakeries and a gelato shop. You can park once and shop all of it on foot.
If one sandwich has to teach you the whole neighborhood, the Italian Trio on Gioia’s menu does it: mortadella, Genoa and hot salami on garlic cheese bread, garnished with pepperoncini, onions, and vinegar and oil. Soft, peppery, sharp and wet in the right way. Eat it standing up on the sidewalk with the paper peeled back, because it will not survive the drive home looking the way it did at the counter.
How to order: tell them what it is for. Salami for a sandwich gets sliced thin; salami for a board gets sliced thick enough to stand up. Ask for the ends if you are cooking with it.
### What a Bosnian market with a counter does best
Smoke hits you first, then butter and onion from the pastry tray. That is a Bosnian market: smoked and air-dried beef, cevapi by weight, and pastry by the pan. The Bosnian community here grew up first in the “Little Bosnia” neighborhood of Bevo Mill and has since spread into suburbs such as Affton, Mehlville and Oakville. The markets followed the families.
A Bosnian market is a grocery with a counter in the back, not a restaurant with a shelf out front. Behind the glass, look for smoked beef, sausage, soft cheese, red pepper spread and trays of burek sold by the piece. The pastry case smells like butter and onion and it empties first.
How to order: point, then say the weight. If you have never had it, buy small and come back - nobody minds a beginner, and the person at the counter will usually tell you how to cook it.
Jewish-style delis are the third pillar: brisket cured and steamed into corned beef or pastrami, cut across the grain and stacked on rye with mustard. Jewish-style and certified kosher are not the same thing, so if kashrut matters to you, ask about certification instead of reading it off a menu. Corner-store counters feed trades crews and second shift fast. Grocery delis win on trays and salads by the pound. To check any counter’s inspection record inside the city, the City of St. Louis runs a food-service ratings search.
### How do you order at a deli counter without holding up the line?
Say the weight, not the number of slices, and say the thickness. Those two habits are the whole difference between a smooth order and the sigh behind you. Take a number, decide before it is called, and lead with what the meat is for.
The vocabulary is short: shaved, thin, sandwich cut, thick. Shaved is for hot sandwiches where you want the meat to fold. Sandwich cut is the default. Thick is for cubing into salads. Ask for a sample slice before they run the whole order - it is a normal request - and order the meats before the cheese so the slicer is not cleaned twice.
Timing beats everything. Go before the noon crowd or after it, and on The Hill remember the clock: at Gioia’s, the doors on Macklind close at 4 p.m.
Wildly off-topic, but if the car gets towed while you wait for your number, here is what to do next - and where to find auto parts after.
### How do you order a catering tray from a deli?
Call early and ask the shop’s own rule. The Gioia’s numbers above - 24 hour notice, a full case that feeds 10 for $100, a half case that feeds 5 for $50 - make a useful yardstick when another counter quotes you a price for the same headcount.
Ask four things when you call: what is on the tray, whether condiments come on the side, what the pickup window is, and whether they hold trays cold until you arrive. Order bread separately if the party runs long, because pre-built sandwiches go soft by the second hour. The same plan-ahead logic applies to tables, tents and chairs.
### Why the same sandwich rings up differently across the river
Because Missouri and Illinois tax food on different rules, and a deli sits right on that line. In Missouri, the Department of Revenue says the state rate for qualifying food sales was reduced from 4.225% to 1.225%. The reduced rate does not apply to a business where food prepared for immediate consumption is more than 80% of its total gross receipts - which describes most standalone sandwich shops.
Illinois changed its own grocery rule. The Illinois Department of Revenue says that effective January 1, 2026, the state eliminated its one-percent sales tax on groceries, while local governments may adopt their own. Food prepared for immediate consumption was never in that grocery bucket. So on the east side, the cold-case sandwich and the counter-built one can be different tax animals.
### What a deli counter actually makes money on
Not the pound of ham. Sliced meat by weight runs on a commodity price the shop does not set, and every counter loses some yield on the slicer, the heels and whatever does not move out of the case. The margin lives in the built sandwich, the house salads and the catering tray. That is why a good counter would rather you order by weight and by purpose: it keeps the line moving and the case fresh.
Pick two counters, not one. Browse delis across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory: one near work for the sandwich, one near home for the by-weight run.
If you run the counter with the line out the door at noon, the people searching for lunch near them should see you first. List your deli and get more customers walking in hungry.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  On the deli side of town, make it a hot salami sandwich on The Hill and a Gerber, the garlic-buttered ham and Provel sandwich first made at Ruma’s Deli. Add a burek from a Bosnian market in south city. Those three cover real local traditions instead of a tourist checklist.
### Q. What sandwich is St. Louis known for?
A.  The Gerber: garlic-buttered Italian or French bread with ham and Provel, sprinkled with paprika and toasted open-faced. It went on the menu at Ruma’s Deli in 1973 and was named for a customer, Dick Gerber. The St. Paul sandwich, an egg foo young patty on white bread, is the other Missouri original, sold at Chinese American carryouts.
### Q. What is the average cost of a deli sandwich?
A.  Treat any single number as a guess. For one real data point, Gioia’s lists its original Hot Salami at $13.50 and $11, its two menu prices. Meat weight, built-to-order versus cold case, and tax treatment move the price from there.
### Q. What’s a good side to order at a deli?
A.  Whatever the case is turning over fastest, because sides are sold by the pound and freshness tracks volume. A vinegar slaw or pasta salad if the sandwich is rich, potato salad if it is not, a pickle spear either way. At an Italian grocery, olive salad doubles as a sandwich upgrade.
### Q. What is the unhealthiest lunch meat?
A.  There is no single worst one, but the cured, salty options - salami, bologna, pepperoni - are the ones to keep for a treat. Read the sodium line on the label or ask the counter. Roast turkey or roast beef sliced fresh is the easy everyday swap.
### Q. What is the best deli in downtown St. Louis?
A.  Downtown counters are built for office and courthouse traffic, so expect speed and a tight menu rather than a full grocery case. Judge them on turnover and hours. For a by-weight or catering run, the short drive to The Hill pays off.
### Q. Where can I find the best lunch in Saint Louis?
A.  Match the counter to the hour you have. Forty minutes near an office park means a corner or grocery counter. Ninety minutes means The Hill or a south city market where you can shop and eat. Going before or after the noon rush gets you a better sandwich from a calmer counter almost anywhere.

## St. Louis Beauty Supply: Sally Beauty Lists No Store Inside the City
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/beauty-supply-stores-st-louis-what-to-buy
Snap. That small, flat sound is the plastic band coming off a pack of braiding hair, and once you hear it, that pack is usually yours. So ask the return rule first. It is the cheapest sentence you will say all day.
Everything else in a beauty supply store comes at you at once. A wall of hair packs in shades of brown you did not know had names. Satin bonnets stacked by the register. The sharp, clean bite of developer somewhere in the back. Lace fronts on foam mannequin heads behind glass, the case locked, a key on a coil around somebody’s wrist. You walk in for edge control and a bonnet. You walk out with a plan for the next eight weeks of your hair.
Here is the part of that errand most people in this city never hear. The braids, locs, twists and Bantu knots that hair on the wall is bought for were protected by St. Louis law years before Missouri caught up. On May 7, 2021, Mayor Tishaura O. Jones signed Board Bill 222, the city’s CROWN Act, which bars denying someone a job or a seat in a classroom over hair texture or a protective style. The bill’s sponsor, 26th Ward Alderwoman Shameem Clark Hubbard, put it in her own words that day: a Missouri licensed cosmetologist for 26 plus years, and “THIS is where my passion and purpose meets policy.”
Missouri’s own CROWN Act, covering schools, was not signed until July 2025. So the city wrote that protection first, and the woman who carried it had spent more than two decades behind a chair.
### Is there a beauty supply in downtown St. Louis?
Not one we could confirm in the downtown core, and Sally Beauty, the national walk-in chain most people picture, lists no store under St. Louis itself. Its own Missouri store list names nearby towns like Florissant and Arnold instead. So from a downtown address, plan on a short drive, and call ahead before you go.
That call takes under a minute and it is the whole trick. Before you throw out the last pack you loved, take a photo of the label. Then ask three things: do you have this texture, length and color on the wall today, can opened hair come back, and do you sell pro-only color to the public. If the person on the line answers all three without a long hold, you have probably found your shop. If you shop the chain, its own site says joining Sally Beauty Rewards earns $5 for every $50 spent - sign up at the register before the first scan, not after.
The pin on the map matters less than the kind of store behind the sign. Two very different businesses use the same two words. One is open retail: anybody walks in and buys hair, tools, edge control and cosmetics. The other is a professional distributor that asks for a cosmetology or barber license before it rings up color and chemicals. Drive to the wrong one and you stand at a counter, keys still in your hand, being politely told no.
### The things a drugstore will never sell you
Walk the aisles slowly. A drugstore sells the finished product in one or two sizes, under bright light, in a box with a promise on it. A beauty supply sells the whole process, the back half included, and it smells like it: powder, fruit-scented gel, the faint ammonia edge of color. Developer in several strengths. Lightener by the tub. Toner, bond builders, applicator bowls and brushes, foil, sectioning clips, capes and gloves that smell faintly of powder when you tear the box.
Then the hair itself, which a drugstore barely touches. Braiding packs by the dozen. Bundles, closures, frontals, ponytails, clip-ins and full units on stands. Lace adhesive and the remover that goes with it, wig caps, T-pins, perm rods and flexi rods. And the tools: shears, clipper guards, flat irons with a real temperature setting instead of a dial marked low and high, rat-tail combs, edge brushes. Liter bottles of shampoo that make the drugstore size look like a hotel sample.
### What does “professional only” on the bottle mean?
It means the brand meant that product to travel from a distributor to a licensed stylist, and nowhere else. When it turns up on a discount shelf or a marketplace listing, the trade calls it diversion, and the brand usually will not stand behind it. That bottle could be old, repackaged or not what the label says. If pro-only color is sitting open on a public shelf at a price that makes no sense, put it back.
You do not need a license to buy consumer color, edge control, bonnets or hair. You only hit the license question at a professional distributor, and the fix is simple: call first and ask whether they sell to the public.
### How do you shop for bundles, wigs and extensions without guessing?
Four words decide almost everything: fiber, grade, density and lace. Fiber is human hair or synthetic. Synthetic holds a style straight out of the pack and costs far less, but a standard fiber melts under a flat iron unless the label says heat-friendly. You can smell the mistake before you see it. Human hair takes heat and color, and you care for it roughly the way you care for your own.
Grade is where the word Remy earns its price. Remy hair keeps every cuticle running the same direction, which is why it resists the tangling that shows up at the nape first. Hair collected without that alignment gets stripped and coated so it behaves for a few washes. It looks identical in the package. It stops looking identical a few weeks in.
Density is volume, written as a percentage on the box. Lower numbers read closer to hair growing from a real scalp, the middle numbers are the popular everyday choice, and the highest numbers are glamour volume that can read as a wig from across the room on fine hair. Density is not quality. A modest human-hair unit beats a huge processed one.
Lace is where people overpay without knowing it. HD lace is the thinnest and disappears best against the scalp, and it tears if you are rough with it. Transparent lace is sturdier and survives repeat cleaning. A closure covers a small parting area; a frontal runs ear to ear and buys you off-the-face styles. Hold the lace up to the light at the counter and ask which one the photo on your phone actually needs.
Care is unglamorous and it is most of the outcome. Detangle from the ends up with a wide-tooth comb. Wash in the direction the hair falls instead of piling it on your head. Keep heavy oils off the lace and use a real adhesive remover instead of picking at the glue line with a fingernail. Satin at night, every night.
Nothing to do with hair, we know - but when did anyone last look at what your roof would cost to replace, or who in town does roofing?
### What to buy for textured hair, and in what order
Start with what your hair does, not what the bottle promises. Hair that feels gummy and stretches like a rubber band when wet is usually asking for protein. Hair that snaps dry and rough between your fingers wants moisture. Get that one backwards and you can spend a lot of money making it worse.
Order matters as much as product. Cleanse, with a clarifying shampoo now and then and a cowash between. Deep condition with something that has real slip. Leave-in while the hair is still wet. Then a cream for softness, a light oil to seal, and a gel or custard only if you want definition. Edge control last, and less of it than you think.
If your scalp is flaking, sore, or shedding in a way that is new for you, that is a conversation for a licensed stylist first and a doctor if it does not settle. Nothing on that wall treats a scalp condition. Our guide to African hair braiding and natural hair salons in St. Louis covers what those appointments involve, and our salon price guide covers what the chair costs.
### How can you tell a good beauty supply shop from a bad one?
Listen to the counter. A good shop asks what your hair does before it sells you anything: texture, how it takes water, what chemical service you had last. Ask a specific question and you get a specific answer, not a finger pointed at aisle four.
Then look at the shelves. Developer labeled and rotated. Wigs out on stands where you can see the lace instead of guessing through a plastic sleeve. Foundation that runs genuinely deep, not three token shades. And the boring stock always there: end papers, neutralizing shampoo, base cream, T-pins. A shop that keeps the boring things is a shop working stylists trust. Dusty boxes, nothing labeled and nobody who can answer a texture question are your cue to leave.
From behind the counter, the money is not where shoppers assume. Hair is the anchor and the biggest cash commitment in the building, because one texture has to be stocked in several lengths and colors, and a wrong guess sits on the wall for months. The daily basket pays the rent: edge control, bonnets, combs, gel. Small, pricey items walk, which is why so much of the store lives behind glass.
Shopping for a hairpiece instead of a hair product? Start with what a good wig costs and how to buy one in St. Louis. And if this shopping is happening around a wedding, our guide to wedding dress shopping in St. Louis shows how early the rest of that calendar starts.
One phone call beats driving to three stores. Browse beauty supply stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the closest two, and call with your texture, your length and your color before you grab your keys.
If you run the shop - the wall of bundles, the glass case, the bonnets by the register - your next customers are searching by neighborhood right now. Make sure they find you, not the store across town: list your beauty supply and get more customers through the door.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there an online beauty supply store?
A.  Plenty, and they split the same way physical stores do. Professional sites ask for a license before they release pro-only color and chemicals; open retail sites sell to anyone. Hair is the harder thing to buy online, because texture and color are hard to judge on a screen. For a texture you have never worn, a store where you can touch it is worth the drive.
### Q. How much are bundles at beauty supply?
A.  There is no single price, and anyone quoting one number is quoting one product. Synthetic braiding packs are the cheapest thing on the wall. Human hair climbs steeply with length, texture and grade. Price the whole install, not one bundle: a sew-in usually takes several bundles plus a closure or frontal, so ask the counter what your look needs before you add it up.
### Q. Is owning a beauty supply store profitable?
A.  It can be, and the margin is uneven across the store. Fast-moving basics turn over constantly at a modest markup. Hair carries more margin but ties up the most cash, because one texture has to be stocked in several lengths and colors. For most owners it is an inventory question before it is a pricing one.
### Q. How much does it cost to start up a beauty supply store?
A.  It depends mostly on how much hair you stock on day one. Inventory is the line that swings the total, followed by rent and buildout, fixtures and glass cases, a register system, insurance, licensing, and enough cash to carry you through the first slow season. Price the inventory first and the rest of the plan follows.
### Q. Why are we boycotting beauty supply stores?
A.  When people say it, they usually mean a choice to move their hair and beauty spending toward Black-owned shops and brands. It is a personal spending decision, not a rule. If it matters to you, ask the shop who owns it - a good counter will tell you.
### Q. Do you need a cosmetology license to buy hair color in Missouri?
A.  Not for consumer color sold at open retail - anybody can buy that. The license question comes up at professional distributors selling pro-only lines. Call ahead and ask whether they sell to the public before you make the drive.

## No Sales Tax on the Receipt: Missouri's Tax Holidays and the St. Louis Department Stores Left
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-department-stores-guide
Zero dollars and zero cents. The register printer chatters, the receipt curls off the roll still warm, and on the line where Missouri normally adds its sales tax there is nothing. Not the state’s share. Not the local share either, because the law strips both.
In calendar order, the two windows run like this. From 12:01 a.m. on April 19 through midnight on April 25, the Show Me Green holiday under RSMo 144.526 takes the tax off ENERGY STAR certified new appliances, up to fifteen hundred dollars per appliance. Then, from 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August through midnight that Sunday, RSMo 144.049 does it for clothing at one hundred dollars or less per item and school supplies up to fifty dollars per purchase. Count forward from the end of summer and the next zero lands on April 19.
The line worth repeating to whoever shops with you sits in subsection 8 of the August law: the store’s own discount counts. A coat tagged one hundred twenty dollars and marked twenty percent off rings up at ninety-six, under the cap, and the tax falls away. A coupon the store gets reimbursed for by a third party doesn’t count. So on that weekend the clearance rack isn’t just cheaper. It’s the rack that can slide a coat under the line.
### What major department stores are left?
Those are the anchors. The easiest way to stand in one on that August Friday without fighting for parking: ride the MetroLink Blue Line to Richmond Heights station at 8001 Galleria Parkway and walk into the Saint Louis Galleria, where Dillard’s runs five floors. The escalator hums under your shoes, the bags knock against your knees, and the jeans, the shirt and the marked-down coat all print with nothing on the tax line.
### How to work the tax-free weekend
You’re holding the coat you actually came for, the tag says one hundred twenty, and your thumb is already on the markdown sticker doing the math. That math is the whole game. Clothing qualifies when the item’s taxable value is one hundred dollars or less, so the cap is per item, not per receipt. Three pairs of jeans at sixty dollars each all qualify. The same coat at full price doesn’t, and at ninety-six it does. And it isn’t only the state’s cut: the statute takes off state and local sales tax, so the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County’s local share comes off the same receipt. The Missouri Department of Revenue’s exemptions list carries both holidays if you want the official wording before you go.
School supplies work differently: the limit is fifty dollars per purchase. Computer software counts at three hundred fifty dollars or less, graphing calculators at one hundred fifty or less, and a personal computer with its peripherals up to fifteen hundred dollars. Check each price tag against the cap before you get in line. Layaway counts if the final payment is made and the item is handed to you during the weekend. You just have to be at the register between 12:01 a.m. Friday and midnight Sunday.
### Show Me Green week, for the dying washer
You know the sound: the washer banging across the basement floor on spin, the dryer that takes two cycles to dry one load of towels. Missouri gives you one week a year to replace it without the sales tax. From April 19 through April 25, the Show Me Green holiday exempts ENERGY STAR certified new appliances up to fifteen hundred dollars per appliance. The statute’s list covers clothes washers and dryers, water heaters, trash compactors, dishwashers, conventional ovens, ranges, stoves, air conditioners, furnaces, refrigerators and freezers. Walk an appliance floor that week, open the doors, listen to the seals, and look for the ENERGY STAR label before you pay. If tax still shows up on the screen, say so before you tap your card, because fixing it at the register takes a minute and fixing it later takes a phone call and a receipt you have to find.
### Getting to the Galleria without a car
Staying downtown? You don’t need to rent a car for an afternoon at the mall. MetroLink’s Blue Line has a Richmond Heights station on Galleria Parkway, and MetroBus serves the mall too. Ride out with an empty tote bag, watch the city slide by through the train window, and come back with it full.
Two small things make the trip easier. Check the return schedule before you start browsing, so you aren’t hauling bags around for an hour waiting on a train. And if you’re flying home, ask the store whether it ships, because a winter coat and two pairs of boots will not fit in the carry-on you packed for a long weekend.
### The anchors the metro has lost
Walk the Galleria’s upper level today and you pass a long wall where a department store used to breathe out cool air. Workers there are converting the entire two-floor Nordstrom footprint, and Dick’s House of Sport is replacing the store.
South County Center tells the longer story. Its dome-roofed Famous-Barr became Macy’s in 2006 and closed in 2025. The Stix, Baer & Fuller next door, added in 1973, became Dillard’s in 1984 and is still open. Two of the city’s own department-store names, gone from the signs, and the buildings still there for anyone who remembers.
### What can a department store still do that a website cannot?
Hand you the thing. A return at a counter takes a minute and you leave knowing the credit went through, instead of taping a box and waiting for a refund to post. Alterations get pinned on your actual body by someone with chalk and a mouthful of pins. A fragrance counter lets you spray a card, wave it, and smell it again an hour later in the parking lot before you decide. You open the refrigerator door on an appliance floor and hear how it seals.
Fine jewelry is the clearest case: sizing and a look under real light before you pay, the same reasons it pays to choose a jeweler carefully. Registries are the other one. Scanning gifts off a real shelf is faster than building a list in six browser tabs, especially if you’re already deep into wedding planning.
### Outlet or full-line, which is worth the drive?
Full-line stores carry the brands, the services and the deepest size runs. Clearance formats carry price. The catch is that some outlet goods are made for the outlet, with their own style numbers and sometimes their own return terms, so you only get burned when you assume it’s the same shirt. Rule of thumb: if you need a fitting, a shade match, a warranty or a human measuring something, go full-line. If you know your size and you’re buying basics or gifts, the clearance rack wins.
