Watch the edges of the floor, too. Some full-line stores tuck a clearance section into the same building, so twenty steps can take you from a full-price rack to a markdown one. Handy, but read the tag and the receipt, because a clearance item can carry a different return window than the dress hanging just across the aisle.
### How do returns, price adjustments and pickup orders work?
Your return window is whatever the retailer printed on the receipt or in the order email, and that is the piece of paper to keep. Windows vary by chain, by department, and by whether the item was clearance, jewelry, a mattress or electronics, so the number you remember from three years ago isn’t reliable.
A price adjustment, getting the difference back when something you just bought goes on sale, is a courtesy policy, not a right. Ask at the service counter with the receipt in hand, and ask early. Buy online and pick up in store is the sleeper move: the item is held so it isn’t sold off the floor while you drive in from Belleville or Kirkwood, you skip shipping, and anything wrong goes back at the same counter. Pickup orders are only held a set number of days, and that window is in the ready-for-pickup email.
Gift receipts are the most underused tool in the building. Asking for one takes about five seconds at the register. Ask for one at the register for anything you’re carrying home to someone else, especially on a visit when you won’t be back in town to swap a size. The person who opens it can exchange it without seeing what you paid and without calling you. Tuck it in the bag before you leave the counter, because tracking down a receipt from another state later is a headache nobody needs.
Rather dig through tables than ride escalators? Here’s what to know before you hit a St. Louis flea market.
### Holiday hours, and the counter that closes first
December at a St. Louis mall means wet boots on tile, a line at the gift-wrap table and the same three carols on a loop. Malls stretch their evening hours for the season, but anchor stores keep their own hours, separate from the mall’s. If your errand depends on a service desk, such as alterations, jewelry repair or returns, check that department’s hours, because a service counter can close before the sales floor does.
### Behind the counter
The ticket price was never the whole plan. Stores buy knowing a share of the goods will sell on markdown, cosmetics and fragrance keep the floor busy with repeat customers, and November and December decide the year. What staff grumble about is the pickup counter, where online orders turn salespeople into pickers. Independent shops feel all of it harder, and the ones that do well are easy to find: hours, departments and services listed where shoppers look, right next to the tree services, salons and every other trade in the directory.
Call the department, not the front desk. Browse department stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the one nearest you whether the department you need is still on the floor. Shopping for a new kitchen’s appliances? Start with what a kitchen remodel actually costs here.
If you run the boutique, the shoe store or the shop that still has real people on the floor, put your store where shoppers are searching and get more customers walking in already knowing what you carry.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What were some of the old department stores in St. Louis?
A.  Famous-Barr is the name most people reach for: headquartered in St. Louis, it was the flagship store of the May Department Stores Company. Stix, Baer & Fuller was the other big local name; its South County store became Dillard’s in 1984. St. Clair Square also had a Sears, which closed in 2019.
### Q. What happened to Famous Barr?
A.  It became Macy’s. Federated Department Stores acquired the May Department Stores Company on August 30, 2005, and Famous-Barr went defunct on September 9, 2006. Most stores didn’t close that day; the sign changed. The South County Center store that opened as Famous-Barr ran as a Macy’s until it closed in 2025.
### Q. Is Macy’s or Dillard’s higher end?
A.  There’s no clean answer, because it depends on the store and the department. Both carry a range from everyday brands to designer lines. Compare the specific department you care about at the specific address, and check whether that location has a clearance section mixed in, rather than judging by the logo.
### Q. Which mall in St. Louis is considered the best?
A.  It depends what you need. The Saint Louis Galleria in Richmond Heights covers about 1.2 million square feet, with Dillard’s and Macy’s. West County Center in Des Peres lists a Nordstrom. On the Illinois side, St. Clair Square in Fairview Heights keeps three department stores under one roof.
### Q. What are the best shopping areas in St. Louis?
A.  For department stores, the clusters are Richmond Heights, Des Peres, South County and Fairview Heights, Illinois. For independent shops it’s a different map: the walkable districts in Kirkwood, Maplewood and Webster Groves, the Delmar Loop and Cherokee Street. Most locals use both, the anchors for services and sizes and the districts for anything they want to be unusual.
### Q. Can I return an online order at a department store counter?
A.  Often yes for items the retailer sold itself, and it’s the fastest refund you’ll get. Bring the packing slip or pull up the order in the app. Items shipped by a third-party marketplace seller, and big items like appliances and mattresses, often follow a separate policy, so check the order confirmation before you load the car.

## In St. Louis, Getting Rid of the Old Mattress Is on You: How to Buy the New One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mattress-buying-guide-st-louis
So who carries the old one down the stairs?
Nobody asks that in the showroom. You’re on your back in Kirkwood with your shoes off, staring at ceiling tiles under the hum of fluorescent lights, the new cover cool and smooth under your palms, and the old bed is the last thing on your mind. Then the delivery date comes. The old queen is still in your South City bedroom, sagging in the middle, smelling faintly of years of you, and it’s too floppy to carry and too big to fit in the trash.
Here’s the part most mattress guides skip, because it depends on where you live. The Mattress Recycling Council runs statewide recycling programs in California, Connecticut, Oregon and Rhode Island. Missouri and Illinois aren’t on that list, so around St. Louis there is no state program waiting for your old bed. Haul-away is a store service, priced by the store. In the City of St. Louis, the Refuse Division picks up bulk items by region, one Monday a month, and you can reach it at 314-622-4800. In St. Louis County it depends on the hauler your town contracts with, so the answer in Ballwin isn’t the answer in Affton.
Ask about haul-away before you ask about price, and get it on the invoice. Then flip up the corner of the bed you like and read the law tag. Under RSMo 421.038, any bedding made with secondhand material must be sanitized by a method the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services approves, and it must carry a label that starts “THIS BEDDING CONTAINS PREVIOUSLY USED MATERIALS,” with the cleaning date and the cleaner’s permit number. Ten seconds, two questions, and you know more than most people who walk out with a receipt.
### How do I know what type of mattress is right for me?
Start with how you actually sleep, not a category name. Side sleepers generally want more give at the shoulder and hip; back and stomach sleepers generally want less. Heavier bodies sink further into every layer, so the same bed can feel medium to one person and soft to another. Then lie down in your real sleeping position for a full ten minutes before you decide.
After that it’s a short list of filters, and your own nights already know the answers. Wake up sticky at 3 a.m. with the sheets kicked off? Coil units and open-cell foams move more air than dense memory foam, which holds warmth by design. Partner flops like a landed fish? Pocketed coils isolate motion better than a connected innerspring. Sit on the edge every morning to pull on your shoes? Push down on the side rail and feel whether it collapses. Want the head to raise? Ask whether the bed flexes on an adjustable base.
One thing this guide won’t do is tell you a mattress fixes pain. If numbness, back trouble or a diagnosed sleep condition is what’s pushing you into the store, talk to your doctor or a physical therapist first. Firmness is a comfort choice. Anything past that belongs to someone with a license.
### Same bed, new name, different price
You lie on a bed in Kirkwood that feels like the one you tried in Maryland Heights an hour ago. Same give, same faint vanilla-plastic smell of new foam. Different name on the tag. That isn’t your memory failing. Manufacturers build a core mattress and let each retailer put its own exclusive name and cover on it, so the bed you liked in one store is technically a different product in the next. It stops you from price matching, and that is the whole point.
You beat it by shopping the build instead of the name. Ask for the spec sheet: coil count and gauge, whether the coils are individually pocketed, how thick each comfort layer is, foam density in pounds per cubic foot, whether any latex is natural or blended. Two beds with the same coil unit, layer thicknesses and densities are the same bed in different pajamas. Then ask it out loud, plainly: what base model is this one built from? A store that answers that question straight has earned your business.
### What actually drives the price of a mattress?
Materials and build first, then the cost of getting the thing up your stairs. On the build side it’s the coil unit, the density and thickness of the foams, whether latex is in the stack, the quilting and the fire barrier. Foam density is the durability number almost nobody asks for, and it’s the one that best predicts whether a bed still holds its shape years from now.
Some of that cost is federal. The Consumer Product Safety Commission’s open-flame standard at 16 CFR Part 1633 caps how much heat a mattress set may release during a 30 minute test.
The rest of the ticket is everything that isn’t the mattress: the lease, the truck, the two people carrying it up your stairs, the financing and the markdown structure. That last piece deserves suspicion. A compare-at number only means something if the bed really sold at that price. Ask what it costs today and what it will cost the week after the sale ends. If those match, the sale was scenery. Warranty length works the same way: a long warranty that turns prorated partway through can be worth less than a shorter one that doesn’t.
### What does a comfort trial actually commit the store to?
Less than the ad implies. A comfort trial is a store policy, not a legal right. The fine print often stacks conditions: a break-in period before you may exchange, one exchange instead of unlimited swaps, a restocking or pickup fee, a required protector, and a bed that must come back clean with its law tag attached.
The federal cooling-off rule is built for sales made away from the store. Under the Federal Trade Commission rule at 16 CFR Part 429, the right to cancel covers sales of $25 or more made at the buyer’s residence and $130 or more at other locations, meaning places other than the seller’s place of business, like a rented hotel room. Buy in a showroom and there is no federal window. The policy is your protection, so get five things written on the invoice before you sign:
How many nights before an exchange is allowed, and when the trial ends.
The dollar amount of any restocking, comfort or pickup fee.
Whether you get one exchange or more, and whether a refund is possible.
Whether a protector purchase is a condition, and which one counts.
Who comes to get the bed, and how long that takes.
### What should you check before delivery day?
Measure the path, not just the room. A king that fits your bedroom may not survive the turn at the top of the stairs in a South City flat or a Dogtown four-family, the crew grunting and the box spring scraping plaster. Check doorway width, stair width and the landing. A king foundation often ships as two split pieces for exactly that reason.
One local price ladder
On Mattress Direct’s own site, the featured beds run from $495 for a Campbell Ashby Firm to $3,495 for an MH Gray Legacy Plush Pillow Top, with several hybrids between $2,095 and $2,995. What moves your number: size, coils versus foam, latex in the stack, and whether delivery and haul-away are in the quote.
Then confirm three line items in writing: delivery, setup and haul-away of the old bed, with the dollar amount next to each. Some stores only take the old set if the new one arrives on the same trip, so ask that too, and ask whether they bag it before it goes down your stairs.
Doing it yourself? Call the city or your town’s hauler before you drag anything to the curb, and pick the pickup date first, because a mattress left out in a St. Louis thunderstorm turns into a waterlogged slab nobody wants to lift. Shopping for the frame and linens too? Our guide to department stores around the metro is the companion trip.
### Is a local store or a bed-in-a-box the better buy?
It depends on whether you trust your own back more than a product photo. A showroom lets you lie on two beds back to back inside ten minutes and gives you somebody to call when the crew is late. A boxed mattress arrives rolled tight, unfurls on your floor with a sigh, and usually comes with a longer trial. The difference shows up when something goes wrong: a trial is only as good as its return mechanics, so price both as a delivered, set-up, hauled-away total instead of comparing stickers.
Painting the bedroom before the new bed arrives? Read how long until it’s safe to sleep in a freshly painted room first.
### Behind the counter at a sleep shop
A sleep shop runs on an odd equation: a big ticket, very few of them. The promotional queen in the window opens the door; the rest of the margin lives in the adjustable base, the protector, the pillows and the financing. The industry is shrinking in units, too. The International Sleep Products Association’s trends report found total U.S. mattress market value fell 6.5% year over year while unit shipments fell 13.2%. Owners didn’t invent the model-name shell game, but they explain it all day, and people search for a mattress store late at night with a sore back, the same way they search for the nail salons across the metro already listed here. A complete listing with hours, delivery radius and haul-away terms is how an honest shop gets more customers. Listing a store takes a few minutes.
Shop the spec, not the sign. Browse mattress stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two with the same three questions - coil count, foam density, delivered price with haul-away - and buy from whoever answers plainly.
If you run the mattress store that answers the build question straight, put it in front of tired shoppers and get more customers who already trust you before they walk in.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where is the best place to buy a mattress in St. Louis?
A.  The best store does three things: hands you a real spec sheet, writes the trial and fee terms on your invoice, and quotes a delivered and hauled-away price instead of a sticker. That test works in Chesterfield, Florissant and Belleville alike. Shortlist a few shops near you, call each with the same build question, and buy from whoever answers straight.
### Q. Who has the best prices on mattresses right now?
A.  It shifts by weekend and by model, and exclusive names exist so you can’t settle it by comparing tags. Settle it yourself: fix your build spec, then get quotes from three stores on that spec, delivered and hauled away, financing included. Ask each one what the price will be the week after the sale ends.
### Q. What mattresses should I stay away from?
A.  Any bed a store won’t give you specs for. If nobody can name the coil count, the foam density or what’s in the comfort layers, you can’t compare it or judge how it will age. Skip anything missing its law tag, anything with previously used material sold without the sanitizing label Missouri requires, and any trial whose fees outweigh the discount that sold you.
### Q. What is the average cost for a good mattress?
A.  An average misleads here, because exclusive model names mean no two stores quote the same product. One store’s own price list is more useful: Mattress Direct’s featured beds run from $495 to $3,495. Pick the build you want, then compare delivered totals.
### Q. How much should I pay for a good mattress?
A.  Pay for the build, not the markdown. Decide what you want in coil count, foam density and warranty terms, then ask two or three stores to quote that build delivered and hauled away. The percentage off the sign tells you nothing; the delivered total and the trial terms tell you everything.
### Q. What type of mattress do 5 star hotels use?
A.  There’s no single hotel standard, and the bed you remember is usually a whole package: the mattress, a topper, heavy linens, blackout curtains and a quiet hallway. Ask the front desk for the model name, then run it through the same spec test you’d use in any showroom.
### Q. Does removing the law tag void a mattress warranty?
A.  Leave it on. It identifies the exact bed if you ever file a claim. A bed with previously used material carries a separate sanitizing label under Missouri law.

## Truck Repair in St. Louis: $149 an Hour, a 26,000-lb Line
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/heavy-duty-truck-repair-cost-st-louis
26,000 pounds. Around St. Louis, that one number decides more about your next shop visit than the $149-an-hour rate on the clipboard, and the quote sheet almost never has a line for it.
The tractor is up on the lift with the hood tipped forward. The bay smells like gear oil and cold concrete, and the air tanks hiss as they bleed down. A phone buzzes in a jacket pocket. It’s the broker, and the broker’s clock doesn’t stop because a truck is in a bay. The load still has a pickup window. The truck isn’t earning a cent, and the payment still lands on the first of the month.
Here’s why the weight matters. Missouri statute RSMo 307.400 applies the federal truck rulebook, Parts 390 through 397 of Title 49, to commercial vehicles “whether intrastate transportation or interstate transportation.” The same statute lets intrastate property haulers with a gross vehicle weight rating of twenty-six thousand pounds or less off that hook, unless they carry hazardous materials. Cross the line and the federal annual inspection follows your dump truck even if it never leaves St. Louis County.
Two more lines sit under it, and both are local. Missouri’s weigh-station law, RSMo 304.235, lets vehicles licensed for a gross weight of not more than eighteen thousand pounds roll past the scale unless an officer directs them in. And the Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program, the St. Louis emissions test, covers diesel vehicles 1997 and newer at 8,500 pounds or less registered in St. Louis City, St. Louis County or Jefferson County. Your hotshot pickup gets the emissions test. Your semi doesn’t. Three weights, three different rulebooks. So how many repair quotes have ever opened with the one question that decides which inspection a truck owes: what does it weigh?
### How much do truck repairs cost?
For a semi, repair and maintenance runs around 21.5 cents a mile, the 2025 industry average in ATRI’s operating cost research, with tires and towing on top. Shop labor runs near a $149-an-hour national median in Fullbay’s survey, and mobile work about 7.6% higher. Single jobs swing from a marker lamp to an engine overhaul. The bigger cost is usually the days the truck sits.
That 21.5 cents covers parts, labor and roadside service, and it rose 8.6% from the year before. The spread inside it is the useful part. A burned-out trailer lamp and a rebuilt engine both file under truck repair. Four things move a heavy-duty bill more than anything else: whether the fault is mechanical or emissions-related, whether the part sits on a shelf in this metro or two days out, whether the truck can be worked where it stands, and how many diagnostic hours a code burns before anyone picks up a wrench. Emissions work surprises owner-operators most, because a particulate filter, an SCR catalyst, a doser and their sensors throw overlapping codes, and the diagnostic clock runs the whole time nobody can name the failed part.
### Six things a dollars-only quote leaves out
A quote with nothing on it but a dollar figure hides the number that hurts most: days out of service. The quotes that hold up, the ones that come back while the coffee goes cold on the dash, answer six things. The heaviest GVWR the shop can lift and work on. Whether it has the factory diagnostic software for the engine and chassis. Whether its annual inspector is qualified under 396.19. The parts lead time for the make. How far its mobile service runs. And an estimate in hours out of service, not just dollars. The maintenance file is a separate matter, and it never belongs to the shop: 396.3 puts that duty on the motor carrier. A used unit bought at auction is its own gamble, and how St. Louis auction houses work covers the bidding side.
### The invoice is the smaller half
An empty dock door on a weekday hits the stomach before the math does. ATRI put the average cost to operate a truck at $2.336 per mile in 2025, the highest in the report’s history, and $1.854 of that was everything except fuel. The payment, the insurance, the plates and the permits are the quiet enemy here. They don’t pause because the tractor is up on a lift in Fenton doing zero miles.
Then there’s the load you couldn’t cover, the deadhead to get back under freight, and whatever the broker remembers next month. A three-truck outfit that loses one truck loses a third of its capacity, and the other two can’t absorb it. That’s why a slightly higher rate at a shop with your part already in the building routinely beats a lower rate at one that has to order everything.
### What actually drives a heavy-duty shop’s hourly rate?
Ten minutes in a heavy-duty bay explains the rate. The lift that can hold a loaded tandem-axle tractor. The rolling cart of laptops, one diagnostic tool per engine and chassis maker, each with its own subscription. The shelves of air dryers, wheel seals, slack adjusters and glad hands, which is money standing still until the morning it saves your week. The technician who is qualified to sign a federal annual inspection. The insurance on work that puts a loaded tractor back on the interstate. And, if the shop runs mobile service, somebody paid to be awake at 2 a.m.
So a rate by itself says almost nothing, and the rate quoted alone is the oldest trick on the counter. The useful version comes with what it includes, whether diagnostic time is credited once the repair is approved, and the current parts lead time for the make. A rate quoted next to a realistic completion time is information. A rate quoted alone is a fragment.
### What does a DOT annual inspection actually cover?
The clipboard again, the inspector walking the length of the trailer with a flashlight, tapping each slack adjuster. Under 49 CFR 396.17, every commercial motor vehicle must pass an inspection of the components in Appendix A to Part 396 at least once during the preceding 12 months, and documentation of that inspection has to be on the vehicle. Each unit counts on its own, so the tractor and the trailer each need one. The calendar doesn’t care how busy the season was.
Brakes and tires are what park trucks roadside, and the pickup in your own driveway runs on rubber too: what new tires cost in St. Louis.
Who signs it matters. Section 396.19 requires the inspector to understand the inspection criteria and to have completed a training program, hold a qualifying certificate, or have training and experience totaling at least one year. A carrier may inspect its own trucks or use a commercial garage as its agent. The report is kept for fourteen months from its date under 396.21. Separately, 396.3 requires maintenance records for every vehicle you control, kept where the vehicle is housed or maintained for 1 year and for 6 months after it leaves your control. Auditors ask for that file first, and it is the cheapest thing on this page to get right.
### Missouri, Illinois and the river in between
Cross the Poplar Street Bridge with a loaded trailer and the rules shift under your tires. Missouri leans on the federal rule and the 26,000-pound line above. Illinois adds a state layer: under 625 ILCS 5/13-101, owners of second division vehicles must submit them to a safety test and secure a certificate of safety. Section 13-109 sets the schedule at least every 6 months by default, with truck tractors, semitrailers and property-carrying vehicles registered for more than 10,000 pounds but less than 26,001 pounds on a 12-month cycle. Tests are conducted at an official testing station or by an official mobile safety testing company. For a yard in Granite City or Cahokia Heights, the second rulebook is the trap, and the shop worth the drive is the one that does the federal annual, the Illinois safety test, or both.
### Is scheduled maintenance actually cheaper than break-down repair?
Ask anyone who has watched the blue lights come on at a scale house. In CVSA’s 2025 International Roadcheck, inspectors conducted 56,178 inspections on May 13-15 across Canada, Mexico and the U.S., and the vehicle out-of-service rate was 18.1%. Brakes led: 3,304 brake system violations, 24.4% of all vehicle out-of-service violations, plus 2,257 for 20% defective brakes, together 41.1%. Tires came second at 2,899. On Missouri’s side of the river, the Highway Patrol’s Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Division is responsible for enforcing the laws, rules and regulations for the State of Missouri dealing with commercial vehicles. Its phone is (573) 526-6128.
Shop rate versus per-mile reality
### What’s the going rate for a mechanic right now?
For heavy-duty work, Fullbay’s survey puts the median shop labor rate at $149 per hour, with mobile repair about 7.6% higher than in-shop service. Across a year of driving, ATRI’s carriers spent 21.5 cents per mile on repair and maintenance, before tires and towing. What moves your bill: the make, whether parts are local, and whether the work happens in a bay or on the shoulder.
Every item on that list is something a preventive-maintenance interval or an honest pre-trip catches for a fraction of what it costs on the shoulder. An out-of-service order isn’t a repair bill. It’s a repair bill plus a tow plus a missed delivery plus a mark on your safety record. A workable rhythm for a small fleet: PM service on the engine maker’s interval, brakes and tires checked at every PM, the federal annual booked in a slow week you choose, and a written pre-trip the driver actually performs.

You do good work. The trouble is the fleet owner on the shoulder at 5 a.m. doesn’t know you exist, and he is searching his phone, not asking around. A website and a Google listing used to be enough; now a lot of people ask an app who to call and take the first name it gives them. It runs $357 a year, under a dollar a day, and listing your shop takes a few minutes. Refuse to be invisible.

If you run the diesel shop, the mobile rig or the one-bay heavy-duty garage, put your shop where fleet owners look and get more customers calling before the breakdown, not after.

### Q. Is $100 an hour fair for mechanic labor?
A.  For heavy-duty truck work, Fullbay’s shop survey puts the national median at $149 an hour. Judge any rate by what it includes, how diagnostic time is billed, and the shop’s parts lead time. A rate quoted without a completion time is half a quote.
### Q. What is the most expensive thing to fix on a truck?
A.  On a semi the big-ticket jobs are the engine, the transmission and the emissions aftertreatment system, which takes diagnostic hours to isolate. Frame and collision damage can run higher still. Brakes, tires and air system parts cost far less, which is exactly why putting them off is a bad trade.

### Q. Do I need a DOT annual inspection if I only drive in Missouri?
A.  If your truck hauls property inside Missouri only and its gross vehicle weight rating is twenty-six thousand pounds or less, RSMo 307.400 says the federal Parts 390 through 397 don’t apply, unless you carry hazardous materials. Above that line, the statute applies the federal rules whether intrastate transportation or interstate transportation, so the annual inspection under 49 CFR 396.17 rides along.

## The Non-Compete That Was Void Before She Signed It: When a St. Louis Small Business Needs a Lawyer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/small-business-attorney-st-louis-when-you-need-one
The new hire is sitting at your folding table in Belleville, pen hovering over a non-compete you pulled off the internet at midnight. Slide that same sheet across a counter in Affton and it is a different piece of paper. In Illinois, an employer may not enter into a covenant not to compete with any employee unless the employee’s actual or expected annualized rate of earnings exceeds $75,000 per year, and one signed in violation is void and unenforceable. Your first cook does not make that. The free midnight template never mentioned it.
That is the St. Louis problem nobody’s generic legal article mentions. This metro sits in two states, and a lot of owners run a business that crosses the river every day: the truck, the crew, the customers, the second location. The paperwork does not cross with you. It changes the moment you do.
So before that pen moves, do three things. Check the worker’s expected annual pay against the Illinois floor if the job is on the Illinois side. Put the advice to consult an attorney in writing and give the worker at least 14 calendar days to review the covenant. And ask any lawyer you call whether they are admitted in Missouri, Illinois or both, because the answer decides whether they can stand behind your paper at all.
### Why would someone need a business lawyer?
Because a handful of ordinary moments create liability that costs little to prevent and a great deal to unwind: forming the company, signing a lease, putting a partnership in writing, making the first hire, chasing a deal that went bad, and selling. The fifth is the one the templates never warn you about, and it arrives with a knot in your stomach.
The order matters more than the list. The first four are scheduled and mostly drafting. You see them coming, you can shop for help, and the bill is predictable. The fifth is a dispute, which means somebody else now controls half your calendar. A lawyer you meet at formation is doing prevention. A lawyer you meet mid-fight is doing damage control, and damage control is priced like it.
There’s a quieter reason too. Missouri law says a member or manager of a limited liability company is not liable, solely by reason of being a member or manager, for a debt, obligation or liability of the limited liability company (RSMo 347.057). That shield doesn’t maintain itself. Picture the opposite of it: one bank statement with the supplier payment, the kid’s cleats and the truck note on the same page. The shield holds because the company acts like a separate company: its own bank account, contracts signed in the company’s name, filings kept current. A lot of what a business attorney does is protect the thing you already paid to create.
Plainly: this page is general information about how business law works in Missouri and Illinois. It is not legal advice, and no article can tell you what your facts require. Only a licensed attorney who hears them can.
### Why does crossing the river change the paperwork?
Go back to the folding table. Illinois also bars a covenant not to solicit unless the worker’s annualized earnings exceed $45,000 per year, and the floors in that statute step up on a schedule written right into it. Even above those lines, a covenant is illegal and void unless the employer advises the employee in writing to consult with an attorney first, and gives the worker at least 14 calendar days to review it (820 ILCS 90).
Missouri wrote its rule from the other direction. Its statute says a reasonable covenant in writing promising not to solicit, recruit or hire away employees shall be enforceable, and that certain of those covenants are conclusively presumed to be reasonable if their postemployment duration is no more than one year (RSMo 431.202). One metro. Two rulebooks. Same pen, same new hire, and an outcome that turns on which side of the water your business sits.
That is the share-it-with-your-partner fact of this whole page: in St. Louis, the right lawyer is not just a good lawyer. It’s one licensed in the state where your paper will be enforced. If you operate on both banks, ask in the first call whether they are admitted in Missouri, Illinois or both.
### What exactly does a business lawyer do?
Three jobs, mostly. They draft and negotiate the documents that define your relationships: leases, operating agreements, customer contracts, employment terms, buy-sell provisions. They help keep the company in good standing so the liability shield stays intact. And when a relationship breaks, they either settle it or take it to court.
In practice the trade splits into transactional work and litigation, and those are nearly different careers. Transactional lawyers build things: the entity, the agreement, the deal. Litigators fight about things other people built. Plenty of small-firm business attorneys do the first and refer the second. Ask which one you’re hiring. The answer tells you how the work will be priced and how long it will run.
What a business lawyer does not do: run your books, file your taxes, or promise you a result. When a dispute has three plausible endings, a straight answer describes all three and what each is likely to cost. It does not pick a winner to make you feel better on the drive home.
### Which lawyer fits a small business, and when do you call a specialist?
For most small companies, a business or corporate generalist: someone whose practice is entity work, contracts and commercial disputes for owner-operated companies. One attorney like that covers most of what a small crew ever needs, and knows who to hand the rest to.
The rest is specialists. An employment lawyer when you’re letting someone go or writing a handbook. A real estate lawyer for a purchase or a complicated build-out. An intellectual property lawyer for trademarks and licensing. A tax attorney for elections and audits. A litigator once a dispute becomes a lawsuit. And there’s overlap people don’t expect: a divorce can put a co-owned business squarely in play, which is why some owners end up sitting across from a family law attorney and a business attorney in the same month.
### Do you need a lawyer to form an LLC in Missouri or Illinois?
The filing is the easy part. The operating agreement is the part that matters, and the two states treat it differently. Missouri’s statute says the member or members of a limited liability company shall adopt an operating agreement (RSMo 347.081). Where members don’t write their own terms, default rules fill the gap, and those rules were written for a generic company. They decide what happens when a member wants out, dies, divorces or quits showing up, and they decide it without knowing a thing about your business.
One more Missouri detail owners miss: if you do business under any name other than your true name, the statute says you shall, within five days after beginning business under that name, file in a format prescribed by the secretary of state, and the registration expires at the end of five years unless renewed (RSMo 417.210). A sign on the truck is a name. Check it.
### What moves the cost of a small business attorney?
The shape of the work, far more than the lawyer. Defined, repeatable matters such as forming a company, a standard operating agreement, a trademark application or a lease review are often quoted as a flat fee, because the attorney can predict the hours. Open-ended matters get billed hourly, because nobody can.
Four things move the number: whether the work is transactional or contested, how much of it a paralegal can carry, the attorney’s experience and specialty, and whether the other side is cooperating. Litigation is the expensive one for a structural reason. The opposing party controls half the calendar, and every motion you didn’t want lands on your invoice.
And sometimes the cheapest lawyer is no lawyer. In Missouri, when sitting as a small claims court, the judge has original jurisdiction of civil cases, tort or contract, where the amount in controversy does not exceed five thousand dollars, exclusive of interest or costs (RSMo 482.305). Equipment disputes land there constantly, which is its own argument for reading the fine print before you sign for a copier, as anyone who has compared buying against leasing office equipment can tell you.
Contracts make you hungry. We don’t make the rules: the metro’s Mexican food is the cure.
### Five questions for the first call
Start with fit rather than credentials. You want an attorney whose regular clients look like you, because if the practice is built around companies with hundreds of employees, your six-person shop becomes the file that waits. Ask these on the first call:
Who actually does the work, and what does each person on the matter bill?
Is this a flat fee or hourly, and what is excluded from it?
Are you admitted in Missouri, Illinois, or both?
What is a realistic response time on a normal email from me?
Have you handled this exact thing recently, and roughly what did it run?
Then watch the meeting itself. A business attorney worth hiring asks about your customers, your margins and how money moves through the company before offering an opinion, because the answer changes with those facts. And no attorney can guarantee an outcome. Anyone who implies otherwise has told you something useful about how they work.
### The other side of the desk: why good lawyers go unfound
A small-firm practice sells one thing it can’t restock: hours. The real economics live in the hours that never get billed, the call written off because invoicing it felt petty, the receivable that ages because a client had a slow quarter. Formation work is often priced close to cost on purpose. It’s the door, not the room. The relationship pays off years later, when that same client has a lease, a partner buyout and a deal.
Here is what burns them. The attorney who quotes a flat fee and means it often loses the owner at the kitchen table to whoever bought the loudest ad, or to a referral site that sells the same inquiry to a stack of firms. That’s not a skill problem. It’s an invisibility problem. Owners now ask a phone, or ChatGPT, who handles companies their size, and the answer comes from whatever is structured, local and findable. A website alone is a single thin thread.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to find a good small business lawyer?
A.  Look for fit first: an attorney whose clients are owner-operated companies your size, admitted in the state where your contracts will be enforced. Browsing the business attorney listings on St Louis Near Me Directory gives you local names to compare in one place. Then call two and ask the same questions about fees, staffing and response time. The one who asks about your business before quoting is usually the one to hire.
### Q. What are the four types of business law?
A.  There is no official list of four, and textbooks differ. A practical split for a small company: entity and governance (who owns what and who can sign), contracts and commercial work (customers, vendors, leases), employment (hiring, firing and the covenants that follow people out the door), and property, both real estate and intellectual property. Knowing which bucket you’re in tells you who to call.
### Q. How much does a lawyer cost for a small business?
A.  There’s no single number, and the fee structure matters more than the rate. Flat fees are common for defined work such as forming a company, an operating agreement or a lease review. Hourly is the norm for anything contested, because the other side controls part of the timeline. Get the arrangement in writing and ask what is excluded before any work starts.
### Q. Is $400 an hour a lot for a lawyer?
A.  On its own, that number means very little. Rates move with the practice area, the attorney’s experience and how much of the work a paralegal can carry. A higher rate that closes a matter quickly can cost less than a lower rate that drags. Ask for an estimate of total hours and a written fee agreement, not a rate comparison.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for lawyers?
A.  Think of it as a management idea, not a legal rule: the Pareto idea borrowed into practice management: a small slice of the work drives most of the results. Owners usually hear it in a useful form, that the modest document work done early is what keeps the expensive argument from ever happening.
### Q. What type of lawyer is needed for business?
A.  For day-to-day matters, a business or corporate attorney who works with owner-operated companies, with specialists brought in as the facts require: employment, real estate, intellectual property, tax, and a litigator once a dispute becomes a lawsuit. In this metro, add one question: admitted in Missouri, Illinois or both? Browse the business attorney listings on St Louis Near Me Directory to compare a few before you call.
### Q. Can the same lawyer represent me and my business partner?
A.  Often not, and it surprises people. When two owners want different things from the same document, such as a buy-sell, a departure or a valuation, their interests conflict, and one attorney may not be able to advocate properly for both. Firms run conflict checks before taking a matter for exactly this reason. Expect to hear that one of you needs separate counsel.

## Can't Pay a BJC Hospital Bill? You Have 240 Days to Ask for Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-hospital-billing-charity-care
The envelope from the hospital is thin, and the number in its little window has a comma in it. You read it at the kitchen counter with your keys still in your hand. Before you decide you’ll just have to pay it, know two numbers, both taken from BJC’s own written financial assistance policy.
The first is 40 percent: “Patients without insurance will automatically receive a 40 percent discount on the billed charges and will be considered for assistance.” The second is 240 days: you can apply for financial assistance “before, during or after your care, up to 240 days after your initial bill.” If the care was catastrophic, BJC caps what a patient pays in a 12-month period at no more than 20 percent of annual family income, even for people who would not normally qualify. The first step is one phone call to 314-362-8400. Ask for the financial assistance application.
Mercy posts its own income chart, based on the federal poverty guidelines. Under Mercy’s current guidelines, income at 0 to 200 percent of the poverty level gets a 100 percent hospital discount, and for a family of four that band runs up to $66,000 a year. Mercy also says eligibility is based solely on household income and family size, not on insurance status, so having insurance does not shut you out. If you are uninsured, Mercy asks you to call its screening line at 855-420-7900 before you apply.
If someone you love just came home from a hospital stay, this is the text to send them tonight: 40 percent off at BJC if you’re uninsured, 240 days to apply, and a 100 percent hospital discount at Mercy for a family of four earning up to $66,000.
Before you call, put three things on the table: the first bill, because the 240-day clock starts from it; proof of income, which BJC’s application asks for, such as a tax return or a paycheck stub; and a pen. Then say it plainly: “I’d like to apply for financial assistance. Please send me the application, and tell me which doctors on my bill your policy covers.” Write down the name of the person who answers.
Below are the federal rules that already protect you on both sides of the river, where hospital price files live, and what to bring before scheduled care. If you are deciding right now whether something is an emergency, stop reading and call 911 or your own clinician.
### How do I choose the right hospital?
When you have a choice, choose on the bill as well as the care. The paper wristband and the cold pre-op room feel the same at every hospital in town. What differs is the paperwork behind them: whether the building and the doctors working inside it are in your plan’s network for the exact service, what CMS Care Compare shows for the service line you need, and how generous the financial assistance policy is if things go sideways. Best for a hip replacement is not best for a stroke, and no list can tell you which one is in your network.
### The bill from a doctor you met for ninety seconds
The hospital’s contract with your insurer and the doctor’s contract with your insurer are two separate pieces of paper. A building can be in network while the anesthesiologist, the radiologist reading your scan, the pathologist reading your tissue and the hospitalist rounding on you every morning work for independent groups that negotiated their own deals, or none at all. You remember the anesthesiologist as a calm voice and a cold hand on your wrist while you counted backward. The bill remembers a group name you have never seen.
According to CMS, the No Surprises Act protects you from unexpected out-of-network bills for emergency room visits, for non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center, and for air ambulance services. You pay your in-network cost sharing, and the provider and the plan settle the rest without you in the middle.
Here is the part almost nobody knows. There is a consent form that asks you to waive those protections, and under 45 CFR 149.420 it can never cover certain services, no matter what you sign: anything related to emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pathology, radiology and neonatology; assistant surgeons, hospitalists and intensivists; diagnostic services including radiology and laboratory work; care from an out-of-network provider when no in-network provider at that facility could have done it; and unforeseen, urgent needs that come up mid-procedure. When a waiver does apply, the notice has to reach you at least 72 hours before a scheduled appointment, or on the day you schedule if the appointment is inside that window.
So the question for the scheduler is narrow: which groups practicing inside this hospital bill separately, and are they in my plan’s network? The same contract-versus-provider gap shows up well outside hospital walls. It is the reason people get blindsided by what their plan does and doesn’t pay toward hearing aids and audiology visits, too.
### ER, urgent care or nurse line: three different businesses
They carry three different legal duties. In 1986 Congress enacted EMTALA, now Section 1867 of the Social Security Act, to ensure public access to emergency services regardless of ability to pay. A Medicare-participating hospital that offers emergency services has to give you a medical screening exam when you ask, stabilize you, or arrange an appropriate transfer.
An urgent care is a walk-in clinic with posted hours and no duty to admit you upstairs. A nurse line is neither; most health plans and many clinics run one, and the number is usually on your card or on the practice’s after-hours voicemail. Two national numbers belong on the refrigerator door before you need them: the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222, and 988 for a mental health crisis.
One naming trap deserves a flag on both sides of the river. A freestanding emergency department can sit in a strip center, look exactly like an urgent care under the same buzzing parking-lot lights, and bill like a hospital emergency room, because that is what it is. If the sign says emergency, ask at the desk which one you are checking into before you hand over the card.
### What is a good faith estimate, and who gets one?
If you don’t have insurance, or you have it and choose not to use it, CMS says providers usually must give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost when you schedule at least 3 business days in advance or when you ask for one. Keep it in the same folder as the bills. If the final bill is at least $400 more than the estimate, you may be able to dispute it.
Ask whether the estimate includes the physician charges or only the facility charges. That one question is worth more than an hour of hold music later. CMS takes calls at 1-800-985-3059, 7 days a week, with language support, for questions or to submit a complaint if a facility, provider or insurer isn’t following these rules.
Unrelated, and we know it: sometimes after a day of phone trees you just want toasted ravioli.
### Where do I find a hospital’s prices?
Starting January 1, 2021, every hospital operating in the United States has been required to post its prices online in two ways: a comprehensive machine-readable file with all items and services, and a consumer-friendly display of shoppable services. Under the federal rule, the standard charges include the rate negotiated with each insurer and the discounted cash price, the charge that applies to someone who pays cash.
That cash number is the one people miss, and “self-pay rate” is a phrase worth saying out loud at registration. The rule has teeth: CMS audits a sample of hospitals, investigates complaints, and hospitals can face civil monetary penalties for noncompliance. Still, a price file is a starting point for a conversation, not a quote. The quote is the good faith estimate with your name on it.
### What is charity care, and how do I ask for it?
Section 501(r)(4) requires a nonprofit hospital organization to establish a written financial assistance policy, or FAP, for each hospital it operates, and the IRS says it must be widely publicized. It has to spell out who qualifies and whether the help is free or discounted care. Section 501(r)(5) limits what a FAP-eligible patient can be charged for emergency or medically necessary care to not more than the amount generally billed to people who have insurance, called AGB.
Section 501(r)(6) requires the hospital to make reasonable efforts to find out whether you qualify before it takes an extraordinary collection action. Those actions include selling your debt, reporting you to credit bureaus, placing a lien, seizing a bank account, starting a civil action against you, or garnishing wages. The FAP also has to list the providers other than the hospital itself who deliver care in that building, and say which ones the policy covers. Read that list. It is the plainest answer anywhere to the question of who else is going to bill you.
BJC’s policy shows what this looks like in a real St. Louis system. To get a discount, family income can’t be more than three times the federal poverty level, and families earning over $100,000 a year are not eligible regardless of size. Patients enrolled in Medicaid in the last six months automatically qualify for help with services Medicaid did not cover. And BJC notes that uninsured Illinois residents at its Metro East hospitals, including Memorial Hospital in Belleville, may get additional discounts under the Illinois Hospital Uninsured Patient Discount Act.
If you live on the Illinois side and have no insurance, ask for that state discount by name when you call. On the Missouri side, the federal 501(r) rules and each hospital’s own policy do the work.
What to actually say: ask for a financial counselor, and ask for the financial assistance policy by name. Apply in writing, keep a copy, note the date. Ask whether the hospital screens patients presumptively, and ask what the policy says about the physician groups that billed you separately. If a bill already went to collections, ask anyway.
### How do I get my medical records?
You have a federal right of access under HIPAA, at 45 CFR 164.524, and it comes with a clock. The provider must act on your request no later than 30 days after it gets it, and it may take only one extension. Any fee has to be reasonable and cost-based, limited to things like labor for copying, supplies and postage.
Ask for an electronic copy through the patient portal where the records already live; it is usually faster than paper. And ask for the itemized bill separately, in writing, because an itemized statement is a billing document, not a medical record, and it goes through a different department. The itemized bill is where duplicate charges and services you never received become visible, line by line, in small gray type.
### What to bring for a scheduled procedure
Photo ID and your insurance card, plus a secondary card if you have one.
The good faith estimate or written cost estimate, on paper, with the physician-charges question already answered.
A current medication list with doses, and your allergy list.
Your advance directive or healthcare power of attorney if you have one, and the cell number of the person driving you home.
Prior imaging on disc or the portal login, so nothing gets repeated and rebilled.
The name of the scheduler you spoke with, and the date.
Leave the rest at home. If a form appears at registration asking you to consent to out-of-network care, that is the moment to slow down and ask what it covers, not after.
Not sure which hospitals are even near you? Browse hospitals across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the number on your insurance card and ask whether the one you picked is in network for the exact service you need, and whether the physicians there are too.
If you run a clinic, a billing advocacy practice or a one-person medical billing service, this is the reader looking for you. Neighbors holding a confusing bill search for exactly that help; put your practice where they look.
### Before the scan, not after
The same questions that shrink a hospital bill also decide what a scan costs before it is ever run. Read what an MRI costs in St. Louis and how to pay less while you still have room to ask.
From the billing office side, the complaint is always the same: the policy already names which provider groups are covered and which are not, and hardly anyone reads it before the bill lands. Reading it first is the cheapest ten minutes in health care.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the main hospitals in St. Louis?
A.  The metro is served by several large nonprofit systems with campuses on both sides of the river, plus independent, specialty, psychiatric, rehabilitation and government hospitals. Rather than take anyone’s list on faith, search CMS Care Compare for hospitals near your own address, in Missouri and Illinois alike.
### Q. What is the number one hospital in St. Louis?
A.  We don’t rank hospitals. Ranking lists weight things that may have nothing to do with your situation. Check three things instead: whether the facility is certified and accredited, what its Care Compare measures show for the service you need, and whether it and its physicians are in your plan’s network. A hospital that fails the third test is the wrong hospital for you regardless of any list.
### Q. Which hospital system is considered the best in St. Louis?
A.  Different lists reach different conclusions because they measure different things, so this page doesn’t pick one. What is worth comparing system by system is public: accreditation, Care Compare measures for your service, network status, and what each system’s published financial assistance policy says about eligibility and about which physician groups inside its buildings it covers.
### Q. What is the biggest hospital in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Size is usually measured in licensed beds, and that count changes as facilities open, close or convert units, so any number in an article goes stale fast. Ask the hospital or check state licensing records for the current figure. Bigger also doesn’t mean better for any particular procedure.
### Q. How expensive is the hospital without insurance?
A.  Nobody can quote a real number without the service, the facility and your income. Ask for a good faith estimate before scheduled care, ask for the discounted cash price, and apply for financial assistance. At BJC, uninsured patients automatically get 40 percent off billed charges and are considered for more help. If you qualify under a nonprofit hospital’s policy, federal law limits emergency and medically necessary charges to the amount generally billed to insured patients.
### Q. How much does an average 3 day hospital stay cost?
A.  An average is close to useless here, because the same three nights can differ enormously by unit, procedure, drugs and coverage. Get your own number instead: request a good faith estimate if you are uninsured or self-paying, ask whether it includes physician charges, and if the final bill comes in at least $400 over that estimate, you may be able to dispute it.
### Q. What is the #1 hospital in Missouri?
A.  There is no single authoritative answer, and a statewide winner is the wrong thing to chase. A hospital that scores well statewide may be hours from you or outside your network. Search CMS Care Compare for hospitals near you, look at the measures for the service you actually need, and confirm the facility and its physicians are in network before anything else.
### Q. Which hospital in Missouri offers the best healthcare?
A.  Best healthcare is care for a particular condition. A strong cardiac program is not automatically the right place for a complex birth or a spine procedure, so match the facility to the diagnosis rather than the reputation. Then check the two things that decide what you pay: network status for both the building and the doctors, and what the published financial assistance policy says about who qualifies.

## Your Copier Died. Your St. Louis Lease Didn’t.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/copier-lease-traps-office-equipment-st-louis
The copier in the back room of a two-desk office off Hampton Avenue grinds, clicks and goes quiet. Toner hangs in the air, warm and dusty. A half-fed stack of invoices sits crooked in the tray, and the tech on the phone says the part is on back order. The machine is dead. The payment isn’t.
Pull the folder and two lines explain why. Missouri law first: under RSMo 400.2A-407, in a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee’s promises “become irrevocable and independent upon the lessee’s acceptance of the goods.” Then the tax line on the invoice. A Missouri Department of Revenue rule says payments for the lease of tangible personal property are subject to tax unless the lessor paid tax on the purchase of the property, and in the City of St. Louis the base sales tax rate, state and local combined, is 9.679%. The copier stopped. The payment, and the tax riding on it, did not.
That isn’t on whoever signed. The contract was written by people who draft these every day, for an owner who signs one between a delivery and a payroll run. The dealer gets paid up front. A finance company collects for years. A renewal clause ticks along on page four. Did anyone read page four out loud at the signing? Did anyone mention the tax? Should a machine nobody can use still collect on the first of the month?
There’s a third date the pitch skips if the office sits inside the City. The Assessor says all City of St. Louis taxpayers with tangible property are mandated by state law to file a list of all taxable tangible personal property by April 1st, and filing late brings a 10% assessment penalty. The Assessor counts business assets as personal property, so ask where your copier fits.
### How does a copier lease work?
A copier lease is usually two contracts and three parties: an equipment lease with a finance company, and a separate service agreement with the dealer whose van drops off the machine. The finance company pays the dealer, and every payment after that goes to the finance company, which will never hear your copier jam. Once you accept the machine, Missouri’s version of Article 2A of the Uniform Commercial Code says those promises are “not subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse, or substitution” without the consent of the party they run to. Drive across the Poplar Street Bridge and nothing changes: Illinois carries the same words at 810 ILCS 5/2A-407.
In plain words: a broken copier is a fight with the dealer, not a reason the finance company stops expecting a check. That is what the statute says, not a ruling on your paperwork, so have a business attorney read your own lease before you act on it.
Say it to every owner you know who leases a copier: the payment doesn’t stop when the copier does.
### Do this before you sign, or this afternoon if you already have
Put the folder on the desk under good light. Five sticky notes.
1. The notice window. Find how and when the lease says you must tell the lessor you won’t renew. Count back from the end date and set two phone reminders: a month before the window opens, and the day it opens. Send the notice exactly the way the contract says, and keep proof.
2. The end-of-term option. Fair market value means you own nothing at the end. A one-dollar or nominal buyout means you were buying it all along. Know which before anyone calls about an upgrade.
3. The tax question. Ask the dealer, in writing: did the lessor pay sales tax when it bought this machine? Staple the answer to the lease. Your accountant can tell you how it lands on your books.
4. The second contract. The service agreement has its own term, its own renewal clause and its own exclusions: network setup, moving the machine to another suite, damage blamed on paper the dealer didn’t supply. If its end date doesn’t match the lease, you can pay for service on a machine that’s gone.
5. The April 1 counter. First-time declarations must be submitted on a paper form: City Hall, Room 115, 1200 Market St., at the counter or the dropbox. The assessment is made as of January 1, at 33 1/3% of true value. The corporate personal property line is (314) 622-4181, and one call can settle how leased equipment in your office should be handled.
### The tax line nobody reads
Turn this month’s invoice over under the desk lamp and find the tax. The Department of Revenue rule behind it, 12 CSR 10-108.700, is quoted word for word in the department’s own letter ruling: “In general, payments for the lease of tangible personal property are subject to tax unless the lessor paid tax on the purchase of the property.” Which way your lessor went decides whether tax rides on every payment for the whole term.
And the rate depends on the address. The City’s base rate is 9.679%, but the department’s rate table lists special taxing districts inside the City, such as the 212 South Grand CID, at 11.679%. Two offices in the same city can pay different tax on an identical lease. Rates change, so check the current table before you sign. It costs nothing to ask the question in note 3.
### What cost-per-copy really covers
Every page that slides out warm into the tray is a click, and the contract is counting. Cost-per-copy, sometimes called cost per image or a click charge, bills a set amount for each page the machine counts, against a monthly allowance built into your payment. Print past it and the extra pages bill at an overage rate. Color usually meters separately, and a page counts whether it came out right or came out smeared.
Three questions save real money, and every answer belongs in writing. Does an unused allowance roll over or vanish at month’s end? Does a legal or tabloid sheet count as one click or two? Is there an escalator that lets the payment or the per-page rate rise every year? Tucked onto page four, a small yearly bump stacks up over a long term, and the tax line grows right along with it.
### Why a five-year lease keeps running after year five
Because most equipment agreements renew themselves unless you send written notice inside a set window before the end date, and that window can close months before your last payment. Miss it and the contract rolls, month to month or into a whole new term at the same payment.
These are evergreen clauses, and the consumer law people half-remember usually doesn’t reach them. Missouri’s private right to sue under the Merchandising Practices Act, RSMo 407.025, belongs to a person who buys or leases merchandise “primarily for personal, family or household purposes.” An office copier isn’t that. On the Illinois side, the Automatic Contract Renewal Act is written around the consumer too: its disclosure rules cover a contract that renews unless the consumer cancels. The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer office runs a Consumer Complaint Unit, but don’t build your exit plan around a complaint.
The real fix is the calendar on your phone. It’s boring. It works.
### Your real ways out early
There are four. Buy the lease out, roll it into an upgrade with the same dealer, transfer it to another business with the lessor’s written consent, or ride the term out and hit the non-renewal window on time. Only the last one is cheap. Nearly all your leverage sits before you sign: ask for a shorter term, a purchase option stated in dollars, and the evergreen renewal struck out.
A buyout quote is usually the remaining payments plus any residual, sometimes discounted. Get it in writing with a good-through date, then ask what returning the machine costs. Packing and freight are often on you, and damage in transit can be billed back.
Be wary of the upgrade rollover, not because the person offering it is crooked but because of the math. Rolling an unpaid balance into a fresh long agreement keeps the monthly number looking friendly while the total you owe grows. Do it twice and you’re paying for a machine that left two copiers ago.
While you’re out by the loading dock, look down. If the slab is cracking, call St. Louis concrete contractors.
### Before the truck backs up to take it away
The copier leaving your hallway still remembers your paperwork. A digital copier’s hard drive stores data about the documents it copies, prints, scans, faxes or emails, according to the Federal Trade Commission’s guide for businesses on digital copier data security, and deleting files or reformatting the drive doesn’t actually remove the data. The clause it tells you to look for: check that your lease contract states your company will retain ownership of all hard drives at end-of-life, or that the company providing the copier will overwrite the hard drive. It describes two protections: encryption, which encodes the data so it can be read only by particular software, and overwriting, which replaces existing data with random characters.
That matters more in a medical, legal or insurance office, because those machines handle exactly the kind of data Missouri’s breach law, RSMo 407.1500, covers, such as Social Security numbers and driver’s license numbers, and the law requires notice of a breach without unreasonable delay. Ask about the drive the day the machine arrives, not the morning it leaves.
Disposal is its own question. Missouri’s equipment recovery law defines a “consumer” as an individual using equipment bought primarily for personal or home business use, so a staffed office should line up its own recycler. Across the river, the Illinois EPA says its landfill ban applies to households, businesses, schools, and government agencies, and all must properly recycle covered electronic devices.
### Buy, lease or go refurbished?
Buying outright is usually cheaper over the machine’s life, because you aren’t paying a finance charge on top of the hardware. Leasing costs less in month one and bundles service and a planned replacement. Refurbished business-grade machines split the difference. Ask for the lifetime meter reading, what was replaced, and whether parts and toner are still easy to get.
The mistake is rarely the choice itself. It’s choosing on the monthly payment without multiplying by the term, adding the clicks and adding the tax. In the City, owning has one more line: a machine you own is tangible personal property, and it goes on the April 1 list.
So do the desks you buy to go with it. Used commercial furniture is the quiet bargain here, because companies shrink, merge and move, and a task chair built for full workdays can beat a new budget chair at the same price. Sit in it. Roll it. Listen for the creak in the cylinder. Measure the freight elevator and the door frames before anything big arrives. Clearing furniture out instead? Conference tables and chair lots often move faster through local auction houses than one listing at a time.
### What a good dealer sees from the other side of the counter
Ask an honest dealer where the money is and the answer usually isn’t the machine. It’s the years of clicks, toner and service calls behind it, which makes a good shop a service company with a delivery van attached. Its techs are both the asset and the bottleneck. What customers get wrong is shopping the monthly payment instead of the whole-term total plus the click rate, then guessing low on volume and blowing the allowance by spring.
The dealers who read the lease out loud with the customer, tax line included, are the ones offices remember. That kind of shop deserves to be the first name that comes up when a St. Louis office manager starts searching, and not just on the dealer’s own website.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or lease a copier?
A.  Buying is usually cheaper over the machine’s whole life, because a lease adds a finance charge on top of the hardware. Leasing costs less in month one and bundles service, toner and a planned replacement. Compare it honestly: payment times term, plus clicks at your real volume and any sales tax on the payments, against a purchase price plus a service plan. In the City of St. Louis, an owned copier also goes on your April 1 personal property declaration.
### Q. Is leasing a printer a good idea?
A.  It can be, if you print enough to need guaranteed service and you read the term, the click rate and the renewal clause first. It’s a poor fit for a low-volume office that could buy a desktop unit outright for less than a year of payments. Your page count and color needs decide it.
### Q. Can you get out of a copier lease?
A.  Usually only by paying. The common exits are a written buyout quote from the finance company, an upgrade rollover with the dealer, or a transfer to another business with the lessor’s written consent. Under RSMo 400.2A-407, in a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee’s promises become irrevocable and independent once the goods are accepted. Have an attorney read yours.

A.  It depends on how much you need. Furnishing a whole floor points you to used and liquidation warehouses. A few pieces you want to match for a decade point to a contract-furniture dealer who delivers and installs. One desk points to retail. Sit in any chair before you buy it, and check that replacement cylinders, casters and arm pads are still available. If you order online, confirm the return policy and who carries it upstairs.
