### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the average cost of a security system?
A.  There isn’t one meaningful average, because a quote is really three prices bundled together: equipment, installation labor and a monthly monitoring subscription. Published averages blur those. Ask each company to break the three apart on paper, state the contract length, and say whether you own the equipment at the end or are leasing it. In the City of St. Louis, add the $25 residential alarm permit, which a monitoring company collects for you.
### Q. What is the best security system without a monthly fee?
A.  A self-monitored setup, with sensors, a hub, a loud interior siren and alerts to your phone, is the no-fee route, and for many households it is enough. The tradeoff is real: nobody calls for help but you, and if you are asleep or your phone is on silent, nobody calls at all. In the City of St. Louis, a non-monitored system still has to be registered, and you mail that form and payment yourself.
### Q. Does home insurance go down if you have a security system?
A.  It can. State insurance regulators note that home security features such as burglar alarms, door deadbolts and window security devices may qualify for discounts. The amount depends on your carrier, so call your agent before you buy, ask whether a monitored alarm earns more than a local one, and get the answer in writing.
### Q. What are the downsides of home security systems?
A.  Multi-year contracts that are hard to leave, a monthly bill, batteries and radios that need care, and false alarms. In the City of St. Louis, false alarms after the first carry fees, and the fourth suspends your permit for 30 days, with denial of police response while it is suspended. Cameras add a privacy question about where footage is stored and who can see it.
### Q. Do you really need a security system?
A.  Not everybody does, and the honest order is to fix the cheap layers first: solid deadbolts, exterior lights, trimmed shrubs at the doors, and working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. A system earns its keep when the house sits empty for long stretches, when there is a rear alley or basement door you can’t see from inside, or when a monitored fire and CO signal truly matters to you.
### Q. Do I need a security system for my house?
A.  Ask what problem you are solving. If it is knowing what happened at the front door, a camera may be enough. If it is getting help when you can’t answer your phone, you need monitoring, and in the city that also means a permit your alarm company files. If it is smoke or carbon monoxide while you are away, a monitored panel is the piece that does that job.
### Q. What security system do burglars hate?
A.  Noise, light and the feeling of being watched. In practice that means a loud interior siren, motion lights over the back door and the alley side, a visible camera at the door people actually use, and sensors on the back and basement doors rather than only the front. A sign in the window with nothing behind it does far less than a siren that works.
### Q. What is the most highly rated home security system?
A.  Ratings roundups disagree because they weigh different things, and many earn a commission on the brands they rank. A better local question is which company will still answer the phone in year three, file your city permit and itemize the quote. Ask for references from homeowners near you, and ask how the company handles a false alarm before it becomes a fee.
### Q. Do I need a permit for a home alarm in St. Louis?
A.  Inside the city, yes. The City of St. Louis requires all residential and commercial alarm systems, monitored and non-monitored, to be registered, at $25.00 for a residential permit. If a company monitors your system, it is required to collect the fee and obtain the permit for you. In St. Louis County, call the non-emergency line of the department that would respond to your address and ask.
### Q. What happens to my alarm if the internet or power goes out?
A.  A properly installed panel has a backup battery and, in most current setups, a cellular communicator so it can still reach the central station when broadband or power drops. A system that calls out only over your home internet goes quiet in an outage. Ask which path yours uses, ask how long the backup battery lasts, and test it once a year with your monitoring company on the line.

## Free Wheelchairs and Hospital Beds in St. Louis: No Income Test, No Walk-Ins
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-get-medical-supplies-in-st-louis
8,058. That is how many pieces of medical equipment one St. Louis nonprofit loaned out in 2025: walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs, hospital beds, handed over free to people going home from the hospital or trying to stay out of one. Hold that number while you stand at the discharge desk with a printed list in your hand, the hallway smelling of hand sanitizer and reheated coffee, and a case manager asking which supplier you want.
Walker. Bedside commode. Maybe a hospital bed. Your dad goes home soon, and you have never once thought about where a bedside commode comes from.
The nonprofit is the St. Louis Health Equipment Lending Program, St. Louis HELP. It provides free home medical equipment regardless of insurance, age, diagnosis or income, and it says plainly that it is the only organization in the region that does not have any requirements. In 2025 it served 2,787 people across the St. Louis region. A working phone and email are the price of admission.
Here is the catch that trips up families, and it is the line worth screenshotting: there are no walk-ins. You request online or call 314-897-4357, its resource manager replies within 36 business hours, Tuesday through Saturday, and it is closed Sunday and Monday. So the day the discharge date gets set is the day you submit the request. Not the morning of. Equipment is cleaned and safety-checked before you get it, and pickup is by appointment at its warehouse or one of its HELP HUBs, including Cross Keys Baptist Church in Florissant on Thursdays and The Care Service in St. Charles on Fridays.
Free loan equipment is one door. The rest of the medical supply world runs through two other doors, and nobody explains them at the desk. One runs on prescriptions and suppliers enrolled with your insurer. The other is plain retail, where you hand over a card and carry the box to the car. Which door you use decides what you pay, how long you wait, and whether anybody shows you how to lock the brakes on that wheelchair.
### Where can I find medical supplies in St. Louis?
Start with who is paying. Free loan programs such as St. Louis HELP lend walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs and hospital beds at no charge. Suppliers enrolled in Medicare handle the equipment your doctor orders and Medicare pays for. Retail medical supply stores, pharmacies and online sellers cover everything you pay for yourself. Pick the door by who is paying, not by which store is closest.
That last sentence is the whole game. Anything you expect Medicare to cover needs your doctor’s order for use in your home and a supplier enrolled in Medicare. Buy it yourself at retail and ask for the money back later, and you will usually lose that argument. Anything you pay for out of pocket is a straight shopping decision: price against fit, delivery, and whether somebody will fix it when a wheel starts to squeal.
### What Medicare actually pays, and the question to ask first
Medicare Part B covers medically necessary durable medical equipment if your doctor orders it for use in your home. Medicare defines it as gear that is used for a medical reason, used in your home, typically only useful to someone who is sick or injured, and expected to last at least 3 years. Its own list includes canes, commode chairs, hospital beds, walkers, and wheelchairs and scooters. After you meet the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount if your supplier accepts assignment.
That “if” is the question to ask on the phone, before the delivery truck backs into the driveway: do you participate in Medicare, or will you accept assignment of my claim? Medicare itself tells you to ask the supplier that before you get the equipment. A yes keeps your share at that 20%. A shrug is your cue to call the next supplier.
The surprises live in the gap between medical and merely helpful. A grab bar can prevent the fall that sends someone back to Creve Coeur in an ambulance, and helpful is still not the same as covered. Medicare only pays for equipment from suppliers enrolled in Medicare, and if you carry a private plan, call the number on the card before you order a thing.
### What does Medicaid cover in Missouri?
The MO HealthNet Division covers the cost of durable medical equipment for participants, including items such as prosthetics, orthotics, respiratory care equipment, home parenteral nutrition, ostomy supplies, wheelchairs, wheelchair accessories and batteries, and hospital beds. The supplier does the paperwork with your practitioner’s order; you make sure the order exists before anyone loads a box.
Across the river the logic is the same even when the forms differ: written order first, an enrolled supplier submits it, and you wait for the answer before delivery. A family that skips the order and buys at retail usually ends up paying twice, once in cash and once in the long afternoon on hold trying to undo it.
### Where can I find free medical equipment in St. Louis, MO?
Start with St. Louis HELP, because it lends the big things: wheelchairs, walkers, shower chairs and hospital beds, with no age or income test. Request first, wait for the reply, then pick up at your scheduled time. When you are done, bring it back. Returns and donations need no appointment; you drop off at its listed locations and times, and the wheelchair that sat in your hallway goes to the next family.
If the hospital case manager or a therapist is helping, they can submit the request for you. St. Louis HELP has a separate path for healthcare pros: they complete the Request HELP form, then the patient or the patient’s representative completes a lending agreement, and the equipment is staged for pickup at a warehouse or HUB. Ask the case manager to send it before the discharge paperwork is even printed. One request per item, though; sending the same request by phone and online can slow things down for everyone.
For smaller and more specialized gear, Missouri Assistive Technology runs a device loan program built for trials, for times when your own device is in for repair, or for exploring options. Loans are shipped free of charge, and a prepaid UPS return label comes with every loan. It leans toward communication, computer access, vision and hearing devices rather than bath benches, so match the program to the item.
Caregiving eating your work hours? Someone in town is hiring through a staffing agency with shifts that might fit.
### How do you pick the right equipment the first time?
Measure before you shop. Doorway width, weight capacity and seat width cause the most returns, and none of them should be guesses. Bring the user’s height for a cane or walker, the tightest hallway turn for a wheelchair, and the bed height for a transfer bench. A tape measure on the kitchen counter saves a week of back and forth.
Then ask the questions that separate suppliers. Who delivers and sets it up? Who repairs it, and how fast? What is the return policy, since bath and hygiene items often cannot go back once used? If a hospital physical or occupational therapist already watched the transfer from bed to chair, take that advice seriously. You are the one who will be doing it at 2 a.m., barefoot, half awake. When equipment is part of a bigger decision about care at home versus a facility, look at how people pay for a retirement home in St. Louis.
### What moves the price, and how Missouri sales tax treats it
Four things move a cash price: new versus reconditioned, weight capacity and custom fitting, whether delivery and setup are bundled, and renting versus buying. A heavy-duty frame is a different product, not a fancier one.
Then there is tax, and Missouri is generous here. State law exempts all sales, rentals, repairs and parts of durable medical equipment, prosthetic devices and orthopedic devices as Medicare defines them, and spells out hospital beds, manual and powered wheelchairs including parts, and stairway lifts. If a register rings up sales tax on a wheelchair in Missouri, ask why before you sign.
### Who actually runs these stores?
Often a small local crew that knows exactly how a hospital bed fits through a 1950s bedroom door. A supplier that bills insurance is half a paperwork shop: an order that does not match the delivery ticket can sink a claim. The steady money is usually cash retail and service, compression, bath safety, lift chairs, repairs. People search for them in a hurry, often from a hospital hallway, which is why a complete listing matters. Owners can add their business so that search ends at their door.

## Under 21? One St. Louis Range Won't Rent You a Handgun Alone

Check the range’s age rule for handgun rentals, buy the range’s own ammunition for any rental gun, and wash your hands before you eat.
That last one matters more than it sounds. The Range St. Louis West posts it as a rule: always wash hands immediately after shooting, and there’s a sink in the check-in area so you don’t walk to the car with residue on your fingers. Use it. The cold water on your knuckles is part of the visit, same as the smell of burnt powder that follows you into the lobby.
The steps for a first trip, in the order you’ll meet them:
Call ahead. Ask three things: the age rule for renting a handgun, whether they rent to someone shooting alone, and whether you can bring your own ammunition. Policies differ from range to range. The Range St. Louis West posts weekday hours of 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., so a call on your lunch break settles it before the drive.
Dress for hot brass. Spent casings fly out of a semi-automatic pistol and they are hot. A casing that drops down a loose collar is how a nervous beginner flinches with a loaded gun in hand. High neckline, closed shoes, hair tied back.
Sign in and listen. Expect a waiver at the counter and a short safety talk. It isn’t a test you can fail by being new. It exists so staff know you’ll set the gun down and step back the moment someone calls a cease fire.
Start close and slow. Send the target out a short distance, load a few rounds, and fire one shot at a time. Stop when your grip starts to shake. Tired hands build bad habits.
Wash up before food. Hands, wrists and face, before the drive and before the burger.
### Do you have to bring your own gun to a shooting range?
No. Staffed indoor ranges keep a rental case for exactly this reason, and renting is the normal way a first-timer starts. At The Range St. Louis West, the posted walk-in deal lets you try out up to five guns for $15, which is the cheapest way to learn what actually fits your hand before you spend real money on one.
One policy catches newcomers off guard: only ammunition bought from the range is allowed in its rental guns. That isn’t a shakedown. They’re protecting a firearm a lot of strangers will shoot from ammunition they can’t inspect. Steel case, steel core, tracer and incendiary rounds aren’t allowed there at all, so if you bring your own box, read the label at home.
Bringing your own firearm? Every firearm entering that building has to be in a case, and personal firearms stay cased until you’re in your booth. Carry it in zipped and open it only at your lane.
### What are the rules for shooting ranges in Missouri?
The rules that govern your afternoon are the posted rules of the range you walk into, enforced by staff standing a few feet behind you. Every range runs on the same core: the muzzle stays pointed downrange, your finger stays off the trigger until the sights are on the target, and every hand comes off every gun during a cease fire.
When a cease fire is called, set the gun down with the action open and the muzzle downrange, step back, and touch nothing until the line goes hot again. Someone may be walking downrange to change a target. There’s no exception for tidying your bench or picking up your own brass.
Two more rules come straight off The Range St. Louis West’s posted list. Nobody is permitted on the range under the influence of drugs or alcohol, so the beer waits until after. And children must be at least 10 years old to shoot there with a parent or guardian, with a parent or guardian release signed for anyone under 18. If you’re bringing a teenager, ask the range you’re visiting what paperwork it wants before you go. Kids too young to shoot? Line up a sitter through St. Louis childcare and make it an adults-only afternoon.
### Eye and ear protection, and the part nobody mentions
Indoors, the room makes every shot louder. Concrete walls and a low ceiling throw the sound back at you, and the shooter two booths down hits you just as hard as your own gun. Wear foam plugs pushed in deep and muffs over them, every time. Electronic muffs are worth the money for a beginner: they let you hear the person coaching you while they clamp down on the blast.
Eye protection should wrap around the sides. Regular prescription glasses leave a gap where a casing can bounce in, so wear safety glasses over them or buy a pair made to fit over frames.
Then there’s lead, which you can’t see or smell. Don’t eat, drink or chew gum on the line. Wash before you eat afterward, and wash the clothes you shot in on their own. If you’re pregnant or bringing a child, ask the range about its ventilation before you book.
### What is the average cost for shooting range time?
Lane pricing in the St. Louis area isn’t standard. Some ranges sell an hour, some sell the day, and rentals and ammunition stack on top either way. Here is one posted walk-in rate so you have a real number to compare against when you call.
One posted walk-in price
At The Range St. Louis West, a walk-in shooter with no membership pays $25 to shoot all day, each additional shooter in the lane pays $10 with up to three per lane, and up to five rental guns cost $15. Ammunition is extra, and it is usually the biggest line on the receipt. Other ranges price by the hour, so ask before you go.
What actually decides your bill is how much you shoot. A box of ammunition goes fast once you stop being nervous, and two people sharing a lane can burn through several boxes without noticing. Buy one or two boxes for a first visit and stop when your hands get tired.
### How the first hour on the line actually goes
You sign in, get a booth number, clip a paper target to the carrier and send it out on its track. A staff member can walk you through loading the first magazine and watch your grip. The noise is bigger than you expected, even doubled up. If you’re right-handed, your first shots will probably land low and left. That’s a trigger habit, not a character flaw.
Most first-timers are ready to stop before they planned to. Concentration burns faster than ammunition. When you’re done, leave the action open, the magazine out and the gun on the bench until staff clears it. Then wash up at the sink, settle the tab, and walk out with a paper target you will absolutely keep.
Hands washed, ears still ringing a little, and suddenly starving? Here’s where St. Louis locals go for barbecue.
If it goes well and you start thinking about owning a firearm, the next question isn’t which gun. It’s where it lives when you’re not holding it. A safe or lockbox, anchored, belongs in the same conversation as the rest of your home security setup.
### Why you drive to a range instead of the backyard
Missouri law leaves part of this to local government. Section 21.750, Missouri’s firearms preemption statute, still allows a local ordinance, from a county, a city or another political subdivision, that regulates the discharge of firearms or the open carrying of firearms within its jurisdiction. So the rule on your street depends on which city or county you live in. A staffed range takes the guessing out of it: a backstop, a person watching the line, and posted rules you can read before you pay.
The same statute says that where open carry is banned by ordinance, a person with a valid concealed carry endorsement or permit still can’t be barred from carrying openly. For a first-timer driving home from the range, the simpler habit is the one the range itself asks for: unloaded, cased, zipped.
### Where are some free public shooting ranges in Missouri?
The Missouri Department of Conservation runs unstaffed ranges on its conservation areas where you shoot at your own pace, and MDC says no fee is required. They suit someone who already owns a firearm and knows the basics.
MDC also runs five shooting range and outdoor education centers with covered rifle and pistol booths. Each provides eye and ear protection, every user has to wear it, and fees must be paid before you shoot. If you want someone watching the line on your first public-range trip, start at one of those.

An indoor range pays to move air all day, every day, and to clean up lead it can’t see. That bill comes due whether two people or twenty are on the line, and a sticky St. Louis August arrives as a utility bill just like a January cold snap. The shops that win first-timers are the ones that post their rental rules and prices plainly and answer the phone, because a nervous new shooter picks the place that made the answer easy.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do you have to have your own gun to shoot at a shooting range?
A.  No. Staffed ranges keep a rental case so people without firearms can shoot, and trying several models is the cheapest way to learn what fits your hands. Expect to buy the range’s own ammunition for a rental, and check the age rule first. For an unstaffed public range, plan on bringing your own gear.
### Q. What do I need to go to a shooting range in Missouri?
A.  A photo ID, closed-toe shoes, a shirt with a high neckline, eye and ear protection, and money for the lane and ammunition. Protection can usually be rented or bought at the counter. If you’re bringing your own firearm, carry it in unloaded and cased. Call first about the rental age rule and any paperwork for minors.
### Q. Why are shooting ranges so expensive?
A.  Because the building is the product. An indoor range has to ventilate constantly, replace worn backstops, deal with lead cleanup and keep trained staff on every open line. Those costs run whether the lanes are full or empty. Ammunition, which the range doesn’t set the price of, is usually the biggest part of your own bill.
### Q. How often should you go to the shooting range?
A.  Regular short sessions with a plan beat one long session twice a year. Pick one thing to work on, like a smooth trigger press, and spend your ammunition on that instead of firing at a target you never look at closely. If you keep a firearm at home, steady practice plus an occasional class is a sensible floor.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule in self-defense?
A.  It’s range shorthand claiming most defensive encounters happen at about three yards, last about three seconds and involve about three shots. Treat it as a rough training saying, not data. Its origin is murky and instructors argue about it, so practice at varied distances instead of only the one the saying suggests.
### Q. Why do people go to gun ranges?
A.  Mostly practical reasons. Hunters sight in rifles before the season. People who keep a firearm at home practice so it isn’t unfamiliar under stress. Competitive shooters train for matches. And plenty go because it’s an absorbing skill with instant feedback, since the paper target tells you the truth on every shot.
### Q. Can you openly carry a gun in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on where in the metro you are. Missouri’s Section 21.750 still allows a local ordinance, from a county, a city or another political subdivision, that regulates open carry, but where open carry is banned, a person with a valid concealed carry endorsement or permit can’t be barred from carrying openly. Check the ordinance for the city you’re in, and keep a range trip simple: unloaded and cased.
### Q. Can you shoot a gun in your backyard in Missouri?
A.  Missouri’s Section 21.750 still allows a local ordinance, from a county, a city or another political subdivision, that regulates the discharge of firearms within its jurisdiction, so the answer can change at the city line. In a built-up St. Louis neighborhood, the backyard is the wrong place to learn. A range gives you a backstop and someone watching the line.
### Q. What should you wear to an indoor range?
A.  Closed-toe shoes, a shirt with a high, close neckline, and hair tied back. Ejected brass is hot and lands where it wants. Skip sandals and the ball cap with an open mesh back, and wash what you wore separately afterward.

## St. Louis Charges $150 to Surrender a Pet. Here's What Helps
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-st-louis-animal-shelters-do-and-how-to-help
The leash is looped twice around your wrist, and the dog is leaning his whole weight against your shin. He knows this lobby is wrong. Bleach, wet concrete, and somewhere behind a steel door a hallway of barking you can hear but can’t see. In the City of St. Louis, handing him over at the counter costs $150.
That’s the fee the city lists for relinquishing an owned dog or cat to its Animal Care and Control. Almost nobody hears the second half. The Commissioner of Health can waive fees case by case on proof of low income or financial hardship, and the city names the papers that count: current award letters for SNAP, SSI, TANF, Disability, WIC, unemployment or subsidized housing. If money is what put you in that lobby, bring the letter.
And here’s the number worth saying out loud to anyone who thinks shelters run on adoption fees: at the St. Louis County shelter, every dog costs $20 a day in food, medicine and staff time, and the average dog stays 32 days. That’s $640 a dog. The county council’s new adoption fee is $80.
So this is the plain version of what St. Louis shelters do, what they charge, and the help that actually moves a dog from that hallway to somebody’s couch.
### What happens to pets in animal shelters?
In the City of St. Louis, a stray brought to the Animal Care Center waits there for its owner, who pays $20 for the first three days of impoundment and $10 for each day after. CARE STL, the nonprofit that manages the shelter, oversees veterinary care, exercise and socialization, and runs adoptions, foster homes and volunteers. Owned pets can be surrendered too, for $150 in the city, a fee that can be waived for hardship.
The first job is identification, not adoption. A found dog is treated as somebody’s missing dog, which is why the scanner goes over his shoulders before anything else. Listen for the chirp. A registered chip with a current phone number can put a dog back in his own yard the same afternoon.
Then the daily fees start working against the owner. Every day a lost pet sits in the city shelter costs more to reclaim, so the person who checks every shelter in person, early, is the one who gets the shortest bill and the happiest dog.
### Before you hand over a pet, make this one call
Call the shelter before you drive. Ask two things: whether they take surrenders by appointment, and whether the fee can be waived for you. Then ask what they can do to help the animal stay home. A bag of food, a vet bill or a short-term problem is often the whole reason a healthy pet ends up on that counter, and there are pet food pantries in St. Louis and low-cost vet care in St. Louis built for exactly that stretch.
If the answer is still surrender, bring the paperwork: vaccine records, the microchip number, the name your pet turns his head to, what he eats, and how he does with kids, cats and strangers. Be honest about bites and health problems. The counselor who knows your dog hides from men in ball caps can place him with someone who doesn’t wear one.
Never tie a dog to a fence after hours or leave a carrier at a locked door. He spends the night scared, alone and loose on a dark lot, which is the opposite of what you wanted for him.
### What are some animal shelters in St. Louis?
The city’s own lost-pet page lists the shelters to walk through, in person, more than once if you have to. They are not interchangeable. The city shelter on Clark Avenue is a licensed shelter managed by a nonprofit, CARE STL.
Start with the city’s Animal Care Center at 2801 Clark Ave., managed by CARE STL, 314-612-5310. The county’s shelter, Saint Louis County Animal Care and Control, is at 10521 Baur Boulevard, 314-615-0650. The Humane Society of Missouri has its St. Louis City campus at 1201 Macklind Ave, 314-951-1562, and a Maryland Heights campus at 11660 Administration Dr., 314-951-1588. The Animal Protective Association of Missouri is at 1705 South Hanley Road, 314-645-4610, and Stray Rescue of St. Louis is at 2320 Pine Street, 314-771-6121.
Walk the kennel rows slowly. Lost dogs look different behind chain link than they do on your phone: thinner, quieter, sometimes too scared to come to the front. Say his name and watch the ears.
### Found a dog in the street? Who to call in the city
A skinny dog with no collar is standing at the end of your driveway, tail low, drinking the water you set down like he hasn’t seen any all day. Get him somewhere safe if you can do it without getting bitten, check for a tag, and get him scanned at a shelter or vet clinic.

### Where the $640 goes, and why fostering beats the fee
The county shelter’s own numbers tell the story. A dog costs $20 a day for food, medicine and staff time. The average dog stays 32 days. County Executive Sam Page said the shelter easily accommodates 80 dogs, and “We have too many.” Keep its population of 173 for a month and the bill runs easily over $100,000. Then an ordinance passed by the county council doubled the adoption fee from $40 to $80.
Read that as a volunteer and the lever jumps out. Every day a dog spends on your couch instead of in a run is a day the shelter isn’t paying for and a kennel someone else can use. Foster homes, not adoption fees, are the capacity. Ask any shelter on the list above about fostering, and ask what they actually need donated this week before you load the trunk with blankets.
If fostering doesn’t fit your life, the city shelter’s nonprofit manager, CARE STL, also runs its adoptions and volunteer program. Dog walking there means a leash that pulls hard for the first block and then goes slack, which may be the best part of that dog’s day.
Spent the afternoon kneeling on kennel concrete and woke up stiff? That one is on your mattress, not the dogs.
### What is the 3-3-3 rule for shelter dogs?
It’s the guideline shelters hand adopters for the first months at home. The San Francisco SPCA puts it plainly: the first 3 days are about adjusting to new surroundings, the next 3 weeks are for building a routine, and the first 3 months are about deepening trust. It is a pattern, not a deadline your dog agreed to.
The first weekend should be boring on purpose. A quiet room, the same bowl in the same spot, leashed walks even in a fenced yard. Skip the dog park and the family cookout. Then expect a wobble once he relaxes: the dog who was perfect suddenly tests the counter. He isn’t broken. He’s finally comfortable enough to be himself, and that’s the moment to call the group you adopted from.
### The city’s rule for street cats
The City of St. Louis passed Ordinance #69798 in 2014 to allow trap-neuter-return for feral cats. Colonies must be registered with the city through a sponsor, an animal welfare group approved by the Department of Health, and sponsors oversee the colony caregivers. If you’re the neighbor setting out kibble at dusk for the cats under the porch, ask a sponsor group about registering before animal control knocks.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What do I do with an animal I can’t keep?
A.  Call a shelter before you go and ask about appointments, help to keep the pet home, and the fee. In the City of St. Louis, relinquishing an owned dog or cat costs $150, and the Commissioner of Health can waive it on proof of low income or hardship, such as a SNAP or SSI award letter.
### Q. How long do pets stay in shelters?
A.  At the St. Louis County shelter, the average dog stays 32 days. A chipped stray can go home the same day it’s scanned, while a senior, a shy dog or one recovering from surgery can wait much longer. Fostering is what shortens that wait for the dogs who need it most.
### Q. What happens to animals at shelters if not adopted?
A.  Most keep waiting, and shelters work every angle: foster homes, adoption events, and transfers to partner rescues with more room. When a shelter is over capacity, the hard choices get harder, which is why the county executive’s plain “We have too many” was a call for adopters and fosters.
### Q. What do shelters do with animals they put down?
A.  Shelters handle remains through cremation or disposal services and keep a record of each outcome. If you’re bringing in your own pet at the end of its life, ask the shelter or your vet directly about private cremation and getting the ashes back. Staff will tell you how it works at their facility.
### Q. Can you go to a shelter just to pet the animals?
A.  Often you can walk through during public adoption hours, but handling is usually saved for adopters and trained volunteers, because a stream of strangers stresses kenneled dogs. For regular time with animals, sign up as a volunteer. In the city, CARE STL runs the volunteer program at the Animal Care Center.
### Q. What are the adoption fees in St. Louis County?
A.  The St. Louis County Council doubled the county shelter’s adoption fee from $40 to $80. Call Saint Louis County Animal Care and Control at 314-615-0650 to confirm today’s fee, what it covers and whether a fee-waived event is coming up.
### Q. Where can I find free puppies in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  A free puppy from a parking lot usually comes with no shots, no microchip and no surgery, and a sick puppy costs far more than any adoption fee. Follow the shelters on the list above instead. When they’re crowded they run fee-waived adoption pushes, and those puppies leave vetted.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for animals?
A.  Days to decompress, weeks to learn your routine, months to trust you: the first 3 days are about adjusting to new surroundings, the next 3 weeks are for building a routine, and the first 3 months are about deepening trust. Cats follow the same arc, often starting under a bed in one quiet room.
### Q. Is there a difference between a shelter and a rescue?
A.  Yes. A shelter is a building, and an animal control shelter like the city’s on Clark Avenue takes in animals brought by officers and the public. A rescue is usually a nonprofit that places animals through foster homes and often pulls dogs and cats out of shelters. Their intake rules, hours and adoption steps differ.

## St. Louis Inspection Fails a 3-Inch Crack. Fix the Chip Now
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/windshield-repair-vs-replacement-in-st-louis
Tock. One flat, hard knock on the glass, louder than a pebble that small has any right to be. You flinch, grip the wheel, scan the windshield at the next red light. Nothing. By the time you pull into the driveway you have forgotten it.
Then the renewal envelope from the Department of Revenue lands in the mailbox, and on a frozen morning, defroster roaring, ice scraper rasping, you see it: a silver star the size of a pencil eraser on the same glass that carries your Gateway emissions sticker. A few cold nights later it has grown a thin tail, wandering toward the middle.
Here is the line most St. Louis drivers never read. Missouri’s inspection rule rejects a windshield with any crack longer than three inches inside the sweep of your wipers, and any unrepaired star break there. That one word is the whole game. In St. Louis City and St. Louis County, the Gateway program lists the safety inspection at $12. Fill the star with resin while it is small and you walk in with a repaired chip. Let the tail run past three inches and you are shopping for a whole windshield before you can renew your plates.
The envelope is your clock. The Department of Revenue mails registration 60 days before the plates expire, and a passing Gateway test is only good for registration for 60 days. Questions about the emissions side go to the Gateway line at 314-416-2115.
### At what point can a windshield not be repaired?
A windshield stops being a repair job when the damage reaches the edge of the glass, goes through both the outer and inner layer, or sits on the driver’s side where it blocks your line of sight. Any one of those, and a good technician quotes a replacement instead of resin.
Run your fingertip over the break. If the outside is rough but the inside of the glass is smooth, only the outer layer took the hit, and that is the repairable kind. A windshield is two sheets of glass bonded around a thin plastic layer; a rock chip usually breaks only the top sheet and leaves a tiny air pocket. Repair pulls that air out and fills the void with clear resin cured under ultraviolet light. You will still see a faint mark at the right angle, like a dried water spot. The crack stops running. That is the point.
Edges are the quiet dealbreaker. The edges are the windshield’s strong holding points, so a crack that runs out to them weakens the whole pane. That is a structural problem, not a cosmetic one.
### What to do today, before the crack grows
Cracks grow from stress, and most of that stress is temperature. A blast of hot air on frozen glass is the classic way a quiet star turns into a long crack before you reach the highway. Five things, in order:
Cover it. A square of clear packing tape over the chip keeps water and grit out of the break. Peel it off right before the technician starts. Warm the cabin slowly. Start the defroster on low and let the glass come up gradually instead of hitting it on high. Skip the automatic car wash and park in a garage or shade until it is fixed.
Then make two calls. Your insurer first: is my deductible waived for a repair, what do I owe for a replacement, and does my policy cover camera recalibration. Then two local shops, asking each the same three things: repair or replace, which adhesive and what drive-away time, and does my car need recalibration. Same questions, side by side, and the vague answer stands out fast.
### Is it illegal to drive with a cracked windshield in Missouri?
Where a crack bites is the state safety inspection, and Missouri spells the standard out in its regulation, 11 CSR 50-2.270. The driver’s vision area is the area within the normal sweep of the wiper blades, above a line four inches up from the bottom of the windshield. Inside that zone, a car is rejected for any crack over three inches or any unrepaired star break, bull’s-eye or half moon. Outside it, those breaks fail when they are more than two inches in diameter. Distortion fails anywhere. So does any break with missing pieces or sharp edges.
Read the word unrepaired again. A star break that has been filled with resin is no longer an unrepaired star break. That is the screenshot-worthy part: a quick repair this week can be the difference between a $12 pass and buying a whole windshield, plus camera recalibration, before your plates run out.
Now the St. Louis wrinkle. Cars registered in St. Louis City and County also run through the Gateway emissions program, on a set rhythm: odd model years test in odd years, even model years in even years. The Gateway emissions test costs $24 on top of the $12 safety inspection. Missouri skips the safety inspection for a vehicle’s first 10 model years or until 150,000 miles, so the three-inch rule lands hardest on the older car, the high-mileage commuter, the truck you bought used. If yours is one of those, measure the crack with a tape measure tonight, not at the station.
### Who pays when a rock hits your windshield?
Usually your own policy, if you carry comprehensive coverage. Rocks, gravel, hail and vandalism are generally comprehensive claims rather than collision claims. If you carry liability only, the bill is yours, and you will never find the truck that threw the rock anyway.
How much you owe depends entirely on your policy language, which is why the call to your insurer comes before the call to a shop. Many policies treat a repair far more kindly than a replacement, and some sell a separate full-glass option. Ask, write the answer down, and get the claim number before anyone touches the glass. If your insurer offers to send a network shop, that is a convenience, not an order. The car is yours, and so is the choice of who works on it.
Still a star, not a crack? Book the repair this week. Browse auto glass repair shops across St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two of them, and ask both the same questions before you pick one.
If you run the glass shop, the mobile van or the one-truck chip-repair crew, the drivers reading this are looking for you right now, mid-panic, phone in hand. A Gold listing puts your shop in front of them so you get more customers from searches that already happen, or list yours and start there.
### Why does a new windshield need a camera recalibration?
On a lot of newer cars, the camera behind your rearview mirror runs lane-keeping, automatic braking and adaptive cruise, and it looks out through a precise patch of the windshield. Swap the glass and you have nudged the camera’s aim. Recalibration is how the car relearns where straight ahead is.
Some vehicles are calibrated in the shop, parked on a level floor facing printed targets. Others need a road drive on clearly striped lanes. Some need both. It adds real money to the invoice, which is one more reason a repair beats a replacement when repair is still possible. Do not let a shop skip it, and do not accept the dashboard light going dark as proof it worked. A camera that is aimed a little wrong can still sit there quietly while it misjudges the gap to the car ahead in rush hour.
Nothing to do with glass: someone you know is planning a wedding.
### Replacement day: why the wait matters
A repair is short, and you drive away when the resin is cured. A replacement is the bigger morning. The old glass is cut out, the frame is cleaned, new adhesive goes down, the new windshield is set, and then the car has to sit. That wait is called safe drive-away time: how long the adhesive needs before the glass can hold in a crash. The adhesive maker sets it, not the shop and not your schedule, and cold, damp weather stretches it.
That bond is holding a pane you look through at highway speed, so it is worth the wait. Ask what adhesive is going in and what its drive-away time is at today’s temperature, then actually wait it out. On an icy morning, take the in-shop appointment over the driveway.
### What about side windows and the back glass?
Different glass, different rules. Your windshield is laminated, which is why it spiders and holds together. Side and rear windows are tempered glass instead of laminated, and tempered glass breaks into fragments. You hear it as a hiss and a crunch, then keep finding glittering bits in the seat tracks. That is why a broken door window after a break-in means a replacement. Rear glass usually carries the defroster grid, so a good shop reconnects that too, and spends real time with the vacuum.
Winter roads deliver most of the rocks in the first place. If salt season is also wearing down your tread, our guide to what new tires cost in St. Louis covers the other half of the damage.
### How to read a windshield quote without getting burned
Lay the quotes on the kitchen table next to each other and read them line by line. The cheap one often looks cheap because something is missing. Look for four things on every quote: the glass itself (original-maker glass or aftermarket), the adhesive, recalibration, and any mobile or disposal fee. If a shop cannot tell you which adhesive it uses or how long the car must sit, that is your answer.
Ask, too, whether the quote is for a repair or a replacement, and whether the technician actually looked at the break or priced it from a phone description. A shop that wants to see the chip before it promises anything is usually the one you want. And if a shop tells you a small star must be replaced, ask why in plain words. Edge damage, damage through both layers, or damage in your line of sight are honest reasons. Anything else, get a second look. The shop that answers your questions plainly on the phone tends to be the one whose invoice holds no surprises when you pick up the keys.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it illegal to drive with a cracked windshield in Missouri?
A.  The rule that bites is the safety inspection. Missouri rejects a windshield with a crack over three inches inside the wiper sweep, or any unrepaired star break, bull’s-eye or half moon there. The safety inspection is not required for a vehicle’s first 10 model years or 150,000 miles.
### Q. Who pays when a rock hits your windshield?
A.  Usually your own comprehensive coverage, if you carry it. What you owe depends on your policy, and many treat a repair more kindly than a replacement. Call your insurer first and ask about the deductible for each, plus recalibration. With liability only, the cost is yours.
### Q. Can you fix just a crack in a windshield?
A.  Often, yes, if it is caught early. Where the crack sits matters more than how long it is. Cracks that reach the edge of the glass, sit in the driver’s line of sight or go through both layers usually mean a replacement.
### Q. What is the process for auto glass repair?
A.  The technician cleans the break, seals a small injector over it, pulls the trapped air out, and pushes clear resin into the void. Ultraviolet light cures it hard, then the surface is scraped flush and polished. The break stops spreading, though a faint mark stays.
### Q. At what point does a cracked windshield become a problem?
A.  Sooner than it looks, because cracks only grow. It is a safety problem once it crosses your line of sight or reaches the bonded edge. In Missouri it is an inspection problem at three inches inside the wiper sweep, if your car still needs inspecting.
### Q. How long does auto glass repair take?
A.  A chip repair is usually done while you wait, and you can drive as soon as the resin cures. A replacement takes longer: the install, then the adhesive’s safe drive-away time, then camera recalibration if your car needs it. Plan for a morning, not a lunch break.
### Q. Where can I get the cheapest auto glass repair in St. Louis?
A.  Start with your own insurer, because a covered repair can beat any advertised price. Then get quotes from two or three local shops and compare the same line items: glass brand, adhesive, recalibration and any mobile fee. A quote that leaves out recalibration is not really the lowest.

## Your First Colon Screening May Not Be a Colonoscopy
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-gastroenterologist-does-and-when-to-see-one-st-louis
Colon cancer is not waiting for your fiftieth birthday anymore. Up the road from the Arch, WashU Medicine says colorectal cancer rates in adults under age 50 have been increasing in the U.S. and globally, and the risk has been rising with each generation since the 1950s. Yin Cao’s team there holds an award of up to $25 million over five years to find out why.
Now the part that surprises people: your first screening may not start with a scope at all. Siteman Cancer Center’s colorectal screening program offers the full range of options, from at-home stool tests to comprehensive colonoscopy, plus a mobile screening unit. A stool test is done at home, with no bowel prep and no sedation. If it comes back positive, you will need a follow-up colonoscopy. The program’s line is 314-747-3046.
Hold that next to the folded referral slip on your counter, the one with “gastroenterology” printed across the top and a phone number you have not called. It has been in the junk drawer under the takeout menus because the appointment sounded like a project and nobody said what actually happens. This is general information, not medical advice. What it can do is make the phone call feel smaller.
### Why would someone need to see a gastroenterologist?
You get handed the slip at the end of a routine visit, almost as an afterthought, and it rides home in your coat pocket. Usually it means one of two things. A primary care clinician wants a specialist’s eyes on a digestive question, or screening is due. Neither is a verdict.
The territory is the whole digestive system, which the NIH describes as the GI tract plus the liver, pancreas and gallbladder. A gastroenterologist manages those conditions with medicine and performs scopes. And on screening, Siteman points to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force: all adults at average risk should begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45. If you are 45 and nobody has brought it up, bring it up yourself.
### Book it this week: three calls, in this order
First call: your insurer. The number is on the back of the card, in print small enough that you tilt it toward the kitchen light. Ask whether gastroenterology needs a referral on your plan and whether the practice is in network. Write down who answered and the date.
Second call: the GI practice, or Siteman’s screening line at 314-747-3046 if screening is the reason. Ask what the first visit includes, whether they need records from your doctor first, and whether a stool test is an option for you. Their care coordinators are nurses who help with scheduling and navigation, so ask them the question you were embarrassed to ask anyone else.
Third call, if money is the knot in your stomach: Affinia Healthcare, a community health provider across the St. Louis area, at 314-814-8700. Affinia says it provides essential services to patients regardless of their ability to pay and uses a sliding fee scale. Ask whether screening can be ordered there. Then put the appointment card on the refrigerator door where you see it every morning.
### Can I go straight to a gastroenterologist?
You are on hold with member services, the same four bars of music looping, and this is the question to ask when someone picks up. Your plan decides. HealthCare.gov describes an HMO as a plan that usually limits coverage to care from doctors who work for or contract with the HMO, and a PPO as a plan where you pay less if you use providers in its network. Neither definition tells you whether your plan wants a referral for gastroenterology, so ask it straight out and get the answer before you book.
If you are shopping for coverage right now, the plan type you pick shapes all of this. Our guide to how to get health insurance in Missouri walks through the marketplace and MO HealthNet basics.
### What will a gastroenterologist do on your first visit?
Most first visits are a conversation and an exam, not a procedure. You sit on the paper-covered table, the paper crinkling every time you shift, and the doctor asks for the timeline: what you noticed, when it started, what makes it better or worse, your family history, and every medication and supplement you take. Then comes an exam and a plan. That plan might be labs, imaging, a scope, a trial of treatment or simply a follow-up date.
Bring six things: a photo ID, your insurance card, a written list of medications with doses, the dates and results of any earlier GI procedures, the name of the clinician who referred you, and your questions on paper. Dates and patterns help a doctor more than adjectives do. If a family member has had colon polyps or colon cancer, find out the relative and roughly how old they were, because that history can change when screening should start.
### What should I avoid before seeing a gastroenterologist?
Do not stop, start or change a prescription on your own before the appointment. Call the office and ask. Some visits come with instructions and many come with none, and the practice’s instruction beats anything you read online, including this page.
If a colonoscopy gets scheduled, the prep instructions arrive in writing. Read them the day they arrive, not the night before, standing in the kitchen with a jug you have not mixed yet. If sedation is planned, line up a ride home early, and ask the facility exactly who counts as a driver, because each one sets its own rule.
Write your questions down the night before, while they are still loud in your head. In the exam room, with the clock ticking on the wall, they have a way of going quiet. A short list on your phone keeps the visit about what you came for.
Prep day means a long afternoon at home. If the garage door has been grinding every time it opens, St. Louis garage door services can come take a look.
### How the bill works, and what Missouri law already covers
An office visit is billed like any other specialist visit: a copay or coinsurance if you have insurance, a self-pay rate if you do not. A procedure is different. A colonoscopy can generate separate charges from the physician, the facility, the anesthesia provider and the lab. Ask which of those will bill you before the date, not after the envelopes start arriving.
Missouri already wrote screening into its insurance law. Under RSMo 376.1250, state-regulated health plans delivered, issued, continued or renewed on or after August 28, 1999, must cover a colorectal cancer examination and laboratory tests for any nonsymptomatic person, in accordance with American Cancer Society guidelines. It reaches plans the state regulates. If your employer self-funds its plan, ask human resources which rules apply.
If you are not using insurance, federal rules give you one more tool. According to CMS, your provider usually must give you a good faith estimate of expected charges if you request one or schedule services at least 3 business days in advance. Ask for it when you book, and keep it in the same folder as the referral.
### How to get a colonoscopy if you can’t afford it?
Start with the hospital billing office. The IRS says section 501(r)(4) requires a tax-exempt hospital organization to establish a written financial assistance policy. Ask for that policy and the application form by name, before the procedure if you can.
Next, ask your primary care clinician whether a stool-based screening test is reasonable for you. The Task Force lists stool-based tests such as the fecal immunochemical test, or FIT, among its screening strategies, and they are done at home. If it comes back positive, a colonoscopy is the usual next step, and that conversation belongs with your doctor.
Then check whether you qualify for Medicaid, and call a community health center near you to ask whether it offers reduced fees based on income. If you are paying cash, ask each place for one bundled self-pay price that states whether the physician, facility, anesthesia and lab are all included. A quote that covers one of the four is not a quote.

### Q. What is the first thing a gastroenterologist does?

A.  That is a clinical call, not a checklist. Most people arrive because a primary care clinician looked at their history, exam and labs and wanted a specialist’s view, or because screening was due. ### Q. What are the early warning signs of GI issues?
A.  There is no checklist that can sort one cause from another, and very different conditions can feel alike. What helps is a simple written record: what you notice, the dates, what you ate or changed, and what made it better or worse. Take that page to your own doctor and let a clinician read the pattern. ### Q. What is the most common diagnosis in gastroenterology?
A.  There is no single official scoreboard, so treat any one answer with caution. Reflux and irritable bowel complaints are among the conditions gastroenterologists see often in the office. How common a condition is across a population says nothing about you, though. Your own history decides that.
### Q. How much does it cost to see a gastroenterologist?

If you are not using insurance, CMS says your provider usually must give you a good faith estimate of expected charges when you request one or schedule at least 3 business days ahead. Ask for it in writing.
### Q. How much is a colonoscopy if you have no insurance?
A.  It varies enough by setting that one number would mislead you. The physician, the facility, anesthesia and the lab can each bill separately, and a hospital outpatient department and a freestanding endoscopy center may price the same procedure differently. ## Flashes in Your Eye Mean an Ophthalmologist Today. Blur Can Wait for an Evening Exam in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-an-ophthalmologist-in-st-louis
A flash at the edge of your right eye, like somebody set off a camera in the next room. Then gray specks, a little swarm of them, sliding across the page every time you blink. Your stomach drops a half second before your brain catches up.
So who do you call? The place that sold you your glasses, or a medical doctor? Tonight, or next week?
Here is the calm answer. The National Eye Institute names two signs of a possible retinal tear or detachment: a lot of new floaters that appear suddenly, sometimes with flashes of light, and a dark shadow, like a curtain, or a blurry area in your side or central vision. Its advice is to go to your eye doctor or the emergency room right away. That is the ophthalmologist lane, the medical doctor who can treat it. Almost everything else, from blurry menus to burning eyes at the end of a screen day, can start with an optometrist. And in St. Louis that door is wider and open later than most people know.
Missouri has exactly one optometry school, and it is here: the UMSL College of Optometry. Its University Eye Center sits in the Patient Care Center on the UMSL campus at 7840 Natural Bridge Road, is open to the public, and on Mondays keeps the lights on until 9 p.m. It runs an Eye Health Management service for patients with known or suspected cataracts, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Scheduling is 314-516-5131. Plenty of people drive past it on the interstate for years and never know it takes patients.
One more thing nobody tells you until the frames snap in your hand. If you carry MO HealthNet, Missouri’s Medicaid program, the state rule allows adults one eye exam and one pair of glasses every two years. A replacement pair inside that window can still be covered for listed reasons, broken, lost, destroyed or stolen among them, but for broken glasses the rule is blunt: you must show the provider the broken glasses or the program will not pay. Keep the pieces. Tape them in a sandwich bag if you have to. Cross the river and the clock is the same length: Illinois Medicaid limits adults 21 and older to one pair of eyeglasses in a two-year period, counted from the date the last pair was ordered.
Three professions handle eyes. Only one went to medical school. Here is how to tell them apart, and then take your actual symptoms to a person who can look inside your eye, because no article can.
### When should you see an ophthalmologist instead of an optometrist?
See an ophthalmologist when the problem is disease, injury or surgery: sudden floaters with flashes, a curtain over your vision, glaucoma, cataracts that are stealing your night driving. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor, an MD or DO, who can diagnose, treat and operate. For a vision exam or a glasses prescription, an optometrist is the right first call.
If it is blur, the fix can fit around a shift. The University Eye Center’s Monday hours run until 9 p.m., late enough to come straight from work with your name tag still clipped on, sit in the dark, read the letters off the far wall and leave with a prescription. Optometrists hold doctor of optometry (OD) degrees, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology says it plainly: optometrists are not medical doctors. For a curtain over your vision, you want the one who is.
A rule you can carry in your pocket: if the question is how well you see, start with an optometrist. If the question is what is wrong with your eye, you are heading for an ophthalmologist, often by way of an optometrist who spots it first and writes the referral. Many metro practices keep both under one roof, so the sign on the door rarely tells you who you booked. Ask when you call. It takes ten seconds and saves you a wasted morning in a dim exam room, chin on the plastic rest, waiting on the wrong doctor.
### The Missouri law that decides who can use a laser on your eye
Three jobs, one syllable apart in casual talk. The ophthalmologist is the physician and the only one of the three who operates. The optometrist handles primary vision care: exams, glasses and contact lens prescriptions, and catching changes early. Where that job ends is written into Missouri law, in the statute that defines optometry: an optometrist may not perform surgery, including the use of lasers for treatment of any disease or condition or for the correction of refractive error. So if someone in a Missouri office mentions a laser for your eye, the person holding it is an ophthalmologist. Illinois writes its own rules across the river.
Then there is the optician, the person you actually talk to while you try on frames under the bright mirror lights. Opticians are technicians trained to design, verify and fit eyeglass lenses and frames, and the Academy notes they do not test vision or write prescriptions and are not permitted to diagnose or treat eye diseases. Skilled, helpful, and not the person to tell about your flashing lights.
### Can I go straight to an ophthalmologist?
Usually yes. The gate is your insurance plan, not the profession. Ophthalmologists are specialists you can typically call directly, but some plans, HMO-style ones especially, want a referral from your primary care doctor before they pay. Skip that step and you can end up holding the whole bill. The number on the back of your card settles it in a few minutes on hold.
Some practices also will not book a new patient with a medical complaint until records arrive from the referring doctor, and some subspecialists see referred patients only. If coverage itself is the open question, start with how to get health insurance in Missouri, then come back to the eye appointment once you know what you hold.
### What are common eye problems ophthalmologists treat?
Cataracts, glaucoma, diabetic eye disease, macular degeneration, retinal tears and detachments, corneal disease, eye injuries, eyelid problems, and eye misalignment in children. Some get managed for decades with drops or injections. Some end in an operating room. A few are emergencies.
The quiet ones are the ones to respect. UMSL Eye Care puts it bluntly on its own site: many times, ocular diseases progress slowly without producing warning signs until irreparable damage has been done. No ache, no blur, nothing to warn you while you are reading the paper. How often you personally should be seen is a conversation with your own doctor, not something to read off a web page.
Squinting at the thermostat too? Your furnace may want a look before the first cold snap.
### Which eye symptoms should not wait?
Some eye complaints are a scheduling problem. Some are a same-day problem. Sudden floaters with flashes and a curtain across your vision sit at the top of the second list. Sudden vision loss, an eye injury, a chemical splash, or eye pain with nausea belong there too. None of this is a checklist for deciding you are fine. It is a short list of reasons to stop reading and pick up the phone.
It is the ride nobody wants: passenger seat, one hand cupped over the bad eye, headlights on the interstate smearing into stars. Most practices run an after-hours line, and a hospital emergency department can start the workup when nobody is answering at 11 p.m. Use the words “flashes,” “curtain” and “sudden” when you call, in that order, before you explain anything else.
### How to pick a good ophthalmologist in the St. Louis metro
Start with the license, the one credential you can check yourself in two minutes from the couch. Missouri and Illinois keep separate registries, which matters in a metro where plenty of people cross the river for care.
Missouri. The Division of Professional Registration runs a public licensee search at pr.mo.gov.
Illinois. Use the Check a License tool on the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation site, idfpr.illinois.gov.
Fit. Does the subspecialty match the referral? Where does the doctor operate? Who handles follow-up? How long is the wait for a new patient?
One logistical detail people forget: if your pupils get dilated, the parking lot will feel like staring into a flashlight. Bring somebody to drive. The same short checklist travels well to any specialist you get sent to, close to what you would run before seeing a dermatologist in St. Louis.
### What does an ophthalmologist visit cost, and what does insurance cover?
The confusing part is not the price. It is which insurance pays. A medical eye visit for disease, injury or monitoring goes to your health plan. A routine exam to update a glasses prescription is usually a vision-plan benefit. Same office, same chair, two different pots of money.
Medicare is the cleanest example. Medicare doesn’t cover routine eye exams, sometimes called eye refractions, for eyeglasses or contact lenses. Part B does cover one pair of eyeglasses with standard frames, or one set of contact lenses, after each cataract surgery that implants an intraocular lens. That is the exception, not the pattern.
On MO HealthNet, the two-year clock covers the exam too, but the state rule gives eligible children, pregnant women, people living in a nursing home and blind participants one exam a year. If your kid is squinting at the whiteboard, you do not have to wait out an adult schedule.
Paying cash? No number goes here, because it swings with the practice, the testing and whether a procedure happens. Ask for the self-pay rate before you book. If cost is the wall, two doors are worth knowing: UMSL Eye Care, where most major insurances are accepted, and EyeCare America, the Academy’s public service program that gives uninsured and underinsured individuals 18 years and older access to medical eye exams.

If you’re weighing surgery instead of glasses, start with who is a good candidate for laser eye surgery in St. Louis.
From the front desk, the recurring frustration is mismatch: a patient books a “routine” exam for a medical problem, or no-shows a dilated slot that held a chair, a technician and an hour. Say what is actually going on when you call. And if a practice is new to you, look it up by town and by symptom the way everyone does now. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to go to an ophthalmologist or optometrist?
A.  Neither is better; they answer different questions. An optometrist is the right first stop for a vision exam, a glasses or contact lens prescription and routine monitoring. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who diagnoses and treats eye disease and performs surgery. Most people start with an optometrist and get referred when something medical turns up.
### Q. Can an ophthalmologist treat floaters?
A.  Yes. Ophthalmologists evaluate floaters and treat the conditions behind them. Most floaters get watched rather than treated. The National Eye Institute treats a sudden burst of new floaters, sometimes with flashes of light, or a curtain-like shadow, as a reason to go to your eye doctor or the emergency room right away.
### Q. Should I see an ophthalmologist for astigmatism?
A.  Astigmatism on its own is a focusing problem, and an optometrist can usually diagnose it and prescribe glasses or contacts. An ophthalmologist comes in when it is tied to a corneal condition, when you are weighing refractive surgery, or when it is being corrected during cataract surgery.
### Q. What diseases can be detected by an ophthalmologist?
A.  Glaucoma, cataracts, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinal tears and corneal disease among them. A dilated exam also shows the blood vessels and optic nerve directly, so an eye exam sometimes turns up signs worth carrying to your primary care doctor.
### Q. What is the most common surgery performed by ophthalmologists?
A.  Cataract surgery is the one most people meet. The National Eye Institute says more than half of all Americans age 80 or older either have cataracts or have had surgery to get rid of cataracts. The clouded lens comes out and an artificial lens goes in.
### Q. Are ophthalmologists covered by insurance?
A.  Medically necessary eye care generally goes to your health insurance. The routine refraction that produces a glasses prescription often does not, and tends to be a vision-plan benefit. Confirm the practice is in network for your medical plan, not only your vision plan. Those two networks often differ.
### Q. Where is the least expensive place to get an eye exam?
A.  Ask two or three offices for the self-pay rate before you book, because prices swing. If you are uninsured or underinsured and 18 or older, EyeCare America is worth checking for a medical eye exam. A medical problem needs a medical exam, which is a different visit than a glasses check.
### Q. Where can I find an ophthalmologist in St. Louis?
A.  Start with your health plan’s provider directory, then verify the license in Missouri at pr.mo.gov or in Illinois through IDFPR. If you hold a referral, the referring office usually works with two or three practices regularly and can tell you which takes your plan.

## Missouri's Assisted Living Grant Tops Out at $292 a Month
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-pay-for-a-retirement-home-in-st-louis
$292 a month. That is the maximum Missouri’s Supplemental Nursing Care grant pays toward a resident of an assisted living facility, according to the state’s own Supplemental Nursing Care manual. A residential care facility tops out lower, at $156.
You find numbers like that late at night, at a kitchen table, with your mother’s bank statements fanned out under the lamp and a brochure on top that never quite says what anything costs. You have been told Medicare will help. You have been told Medicaid will help. Nobody has told you which bill each one actually touches, or that the answer changes with the license hanging by a building’s front door.
So here it is in the order it hits a family in St. Louis: what Medicare does not pay, what the five real sources are, and what to do this week before anyone signs anything.
### Does Medicare pay for a retirement home?
No. Medicare.gov puts it in six words: Medicare doesn’t pay for long-term care. Long-term care, also called custodial care, is help with daily living for people with a chronic illness or disability. That is most of what an assisted living or retirement community provides, and families find this out on the tour, with a pen already in hand.
What Medicare does cover is short and medical. After a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least 3 days in a row, Part A can pay for care in a skilled nursing facility, and it limits that coverage to 100 days in each benefit period. Days 21 through 100 carry a daily coinsurance that is adjusted each year; Medicare publishes the current figure. After day 100, you pay all costs.
So the rehab after a fall may be covered. The months afterward, in the same building, with the same parent needing help getting dressed, are not. That gap is where families get blindsided.
### The five sources that actually pay, and what to do this week
Almost every bill in St. Louis senior living gets paid from five places: the resident’s own income and savings, a long-term care insurance policy if one exists, VA Aid and Attendance for qualified veterans and survivors, Medicaid, and subsidized senior housing when the problem is rent rather than daily care. Which one opens depends on the building’s license and which side of the river it sits on.
Three moves this week will save you months. First, if your parent lives inside city limits, call the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging at (314) 612-5918. Its office is at 1520 Market, Room 4086, open Monday to Friday 8am - 5pm, and it offers help with Medicare needs. For County residents, the city’s agency works with the Mid-East Area Agency on Aging to refer people to the right resources, so the same call still gets you pointed somewhere useful.
Second, find the paperwork. Pension statements, bank statements, any insurance policy, discharge papers if your parent served. The drawer that smells like old paper and rubber bands is where half of this answer lives.
Third, before you tour, write down one question for every building: what license do you hold? Missouri’s own grant table pays different maximums to a residential care facility, an assisted living facility, and an intermediate or skilled nursing facility. The license on the wall decides which money can follow your parent through the door.
### What private pay and long-term care insurance really look like
Private pay is the default, and it is almost never one number. Most communities charge monthly rent, add a care-level fee after an assessment of how much help the resident needs, and many charge a one-time community fee on move-in. Ask for the rate sheet in writing, ask what triggers the next care level, and ask what the increases have been the last few years. Two places can quote the same base rent and land far apart once care levels are added.
If a long-term care policy is sitting in a drawer, read it before you tour anything. Look for when benefits start, the waiting period before the policy pays, the daily or monthly cap, and whether it covers assisted living or only nursing home care. An old policy without inflation protection may cover a small slice of today’s bill. Call the insurer with the policy number and ask them to say it back to you in dollars.
### VA Aid and Attendance: the benefit families forget to ask about
VA Aid and Attendance provides monthly payments added to the amount of a monthly VA pension for qualified veterans and survivors. It is for someone who needs help with daily activities like bathing and dressing, is in bed much of the day because of illness, is a patient in a nursing home due to loss of mental or physical abilities related to a disability, or has limited eyesight.
The paperwork is concrete. By mail, it is VA Form 21-2680, and a medical examiner must fill out the examination section. If your parent is already in a nursing home, the VA asks for an extra form about the facility too. If Dad wore the uniform, or Mom is a veteran’s surviving spouse, put this on the list before you assume the money is gone.
### What happens to the elderly if they can’t afford assisted living?
Usually, spend-down. Private savings pay until they are nearly gone, then the resident applies for Medicaid. The question that decides whether your parent has to move again at the worst moment is simple, and it belongs on the first tour: does this building accept Medicaid, and does it have Medicaid-certified beds?
Missouri’s Supplemental Nursing Care grant is the piece most families never hear about. It is a monthly cash grant toward care in a licensed facility, and the state manual sets the maximum by facility type: $156 for a residential care facility, $292 for an assisted living facility, and up to $390 in an intermediate or skilled facility when medical necessity is confirmed by a level of care determination. One catch is spelled out in the same table: a person in a MO HealthNet certified bed in an intermediate or skilled nursing facility is not eligible for the cash grant. It narrows a gap. It does not close one.
Across the river, Illinois built a different door. Illinois developed its Supportive Living Program as an alternative to nursing home care for low-income older persons and persons with physical disabilities under Medicaid, offering personal care and other services so residents can live independently. If your parent lives on the Illinois side, ask about it before you write off assisted living.
Driving Mom to six tours this month? Have a St. Louis auto repair shop look at that brake squeal first.
### Before you sign anything, ask these out loud
Sit in the lobby a few minutes before the tour starts. Listen to how staff talk to residents. Smell the hallway. Then ask, in this order: What license does this building hold? What does the current written rate sheet say? What triggers a move to a higher care level, and what does that cost? Is the community fee refundable? Do you accept Medicaid, and for which residents? If my mother’s needs outgrow your license, who decides, and how much notice do we get?
Visit twice: once on the scheduled tour, once unannounced around dinner, when the dining room is full and the real staffing shows. Take a sibling or a friend the second time so two sets of eyes see it. And if something you see later feels wrong, Missouri’s Adult Abuse and Neglect Hotline is 1-800-392-0210, answered seven days a week from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
If staying home a while longer is realistic, that can buy time and money both. Grab bars, a shower chair and a walker cost far less than a month anywhere, and they can make the next year safer while the paperwork catches up.
