### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Medicare cover retirement homes?
A.  Not for long-term stays. Medicare doesn’t pay for long-term custodial care. Part A can cover a skilled nursing facility after a qualifying hospital stay, limited to 100 days in each benefit period, and only while skilled care is needed.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in a retirement community?
A.  Under the federal Fair Housing Act rules, for a community to qualify as housing for older persons, at least 80 percent of its occupied units must be occupied by at least one person 55 years of age or older. The other units can house younger residents, which is why you may meet a 50-year-old neighbor in a 55-plus building.
### Q. Is it cheaper to live in a 55 and over community?
A.  Sometimes, but not for the reason people assume. A 55-plus community is housing, not care, so you are not paying for meals, staff or personal help. Compare the full monthly outlay, including any association fee, against what the current house really costs to heat, insure and keep up.
### Q. How much does a retirement home cost per day?
A.  Most communities bill monthly, so a per-day figure is the monthly rate divided by the days in the month, and it often leaves out the care-level fee and any move-in fee. Skilled nursing is usually quoted by the day. Ask three places for a current written rate sheet and compare the totals, not the base rent.
### Q. Where can I find affordable senior living in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging at (314) 612-5918 if your parent lives in the city; it works with the Mid-East Area Agency on Aging to refer City and County residents to the right resources. Ask about subsidized senior apartments and get on several waiting lists at once.
### Q. What is the point of a retirement home?
A.  Safety and company, mostly. Meals someone else cooks, help within reach at night, and neighbors in the next room instead of an empty house. For many families, the point is that the phone call in the middle of the night stops being theirs alone to answer.
### Q. At what age do most people go into a retirement home?
A.  There is no single age. The trigger is usually a fall, a diagnosis or a stretch where living alone stops being safe, not a birthday. Independent living tends to come earlier, assisted living later, when daily help becomes a real need.
### Q. Which assisted living facility in St. Louis is considered the best?
A.  The best one is the one whose license fits your parent’s needs today and next year, whose rate sheet you have in writing, and whose dining room feels right when you drop in unannounced. Ask whether it accepts Medicaid, how often care-level fees have changed, and how staff turnover has been. Then trust what you saw and smelled in the hallway more than the brochure.
### Q. How much is the cheapest retirement home?
A.  The lowest prices usually belong to subsidized senior apartments, which are housing rather than care, and they almost always come with a waiting list. Among licensed care settings, a residential care facility generally offers less help than assisted living, and Missouri’s Supplemental Nursing Care maximum is $156 for a residential care facility versus $292 for assisted living. Get written rates from several places before you decide what cheap really means.
### Q. What is the downside of living in a retirement community?
A.  Cost and inflexibility. Fees rise, care levels add charges as needs grow, and a building licensed for one level of care may not be able to keep a resident whose needs outgrow it. Some people also grieve the loss of a street and neighbors they knew for decades.

## Missouri Pawn Loans: Due in 30 Days, Then 60 More
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-pawn-shops-work-in-st-louis
The ring goes down on the glass. The clerk turns it under the lamp, weighs it, writes a number on a pad and slides the pad back across the counter. That number is a loan, not a price. Your stomach does the math before your head does.
Here is what most people standing at that counter are never told. In Missouri, a pawn loan is due in lump sum thirty days after you sign. If you miss that date, the law says the shop shall retain your ring for sixty days after default, and you can walk back in and redeem it the whole time. Title passes to the shop only on the day after those sixty days expire. Thirty days, then sixty more, written into state law.
And inside the City of St. Louis, the counters themselves are rationed. A city ordinance limits pawn shops to one license for every 30,000 residents, and the License Collector’s office says the quota is filled and no new licenses are being issued. You are not choosing from an endless strip of shops. You are choosing from a short list, so it pays to know the rules before you set anything on the glass.
### What should I know before visiting a pawn shop?
Bring a current photo ID and the item complete: the case, the charger, the cords, any paperwork. Decide at the kitchen table whether you want a loan against it or an outright sale, because those are two different deals at two different prices. Then ask the clerk for two things, out loud and in dollars: the total you must pay back, and the last day you can pay it.
Missouri law caps pawn interest at two percent per month on the amount of the loan. The same sentence of the statute lets the shop charge separately for storage and security of your item. That second line is where tickets differ from shop to shop, so make the clerk turn it into a dollar figure before you sign.
Expect your ID to be scanned. Missouri requires the shop to record your name, address, a physical description and your driver’s license or other official ID number on every pawn. Nobody is accusing you of anything. It is the same paperwork for every person who stands at that counter.
### The calendar on your ticket, step by step
Day one, you sign the ticket and leave with cash. The ticket is the contract, and it is also your key: under Missouri law, a person who properly identifies himself and presents the pawn ticket is presumed entitled to redeem the goods. Put it with your car title, not in a coat pocket.
Day thirty, the loan comes due. Most shops will extend it if you pay the interest and charges owed so far, and Missouri’s law spells out that an extended loan runs thirty days from the last extension. Ask for the extension terms on paper the day you pawn, not the day you are short.
The day after that, the loan is in default. This is the part that scares people, and it should not. The shop shall retain possession of your item for sixty days after default. Pay the principal, the fees and the interest due inside that window and the shop has to hand it back.
On the day after the sixty days expire, title passes to the lender without foreclosure, and your right of redemption is barred. That is the whole consequence. Missouri law says a pledgor has no obligation to redeem the goods or make any payment, and a pawnbroker may not make you personally liable for the loan. No lawsuit follows the ring out the door.
### Is it better to pawn or sell?
Sell if you never want it back. Pawn if you do, and you can see the money arriving on your own calendar. A sale usually pays more on the spot, because the shop owns the item that minute and carries the resale risk. A pawn pays less and adds charges, and what those charges buy is the right to get your property back.
The honest test takes two minutes. Open your phone calendar, count ahead to the due date and the end of the sixty days, and ask whether the money will really be there. If the answer is no, pawning is just the expensive way to sell. You take the smaller number, you pay the charges, and the guitar ends up on the wall anyway.
The exception is the thing that still smells like the person who owned it. A grandmother’s ring. A father’s watch with the band worn thin on one side. Those get pawned instead of sold on purpose, because a smaller loan and a ticket in the drawer beat never seeing them again.
### How much will a pawn shop give you for a $1000 item?
Far less than $1,000, and the reason is arithmetic, not insult. The offer starts from what the shop thinks it can resell the item for, here and fairly fast, then comes down again to leave room for margin and the chance you never return. A laptop that cost $1,000 new is not a $1,000 laptop three years later, and the loan comes off its used value, not the sticker.
Gold is the cleanest case. Its weight and purity set a floor under the offer no matter how the piece looks, which is why a broken chain still gets a real number. For gold, ask what the shop pays per gram, so you can compare one counter to the next.
What moves an offer up: the item powers on at the counter, it is complete, you brought the box, and the shop is not already holding four of them. What drags it down: no charger, cracked housings, dead batteries and phones locked to an account nobody can clear.
Cash in your pocket and an hour to kill? St. Louis Korean food makes a good reason to sit down.
### What sells at a pawn shop, and what gets turned away?
Shops take what they can resell without babysitting it. You can hear it in the back room: the clack of drills on a pegboard, a guitar somebody tunes before it goes on the wall.
Usually welcome: gold and diamond jewelry, watches, power tools, guitars and amps, laptops, tablets, game consoles, cameras and lenses, coins and bullion, lawn equipment.
Usually declined: furniture, older televisions, printers, car seats, most clothing, opened cosmetics, medical equipment, recalled goods, items with defaced serial numbers, and devices locked to someone else’s account.
Tools deserve a second thought. They are easy to pawn and painful to lose, because losing them can cost you work. If it is a tool you use twice a year, weigh the loan against renting equipment when you need it.
### When the due date gets close and the money is not there
Call the shop a week early, not a day late. Ask what it costs today to extend, and whether a payment toward the principal lowers what you owe at the end. A clerk who answers in dollars, without a sigh, is a clerk worth coming back to.
If you lose the ticket, go in anyway with your ID. The shop has your name, address and ID number on its own record, so a lost ticket slows a redemption down. It does not end it.
### What a fair counter sounds like
You can tell a lot in the first three minutes. A good clerk plugs the laptop in and lets it boot while you stand there, runs the drill until it whines, holds the chain to the light and says what it weighs. Then the number comes out plainly, with the payoff and the date attached, and nobody leans on you to decide before you have read the ticket.
Watch for the opposite. A rate quoted as a percentage with no dollar figure behind it. A storage or security charge nobody mentioned until the pen is in your hand. A clerk who wants to know why you need the money. You do not owe anyone that story. The shop is pricing the item, not you, and you are free to pick it back up off the glass and walk to the next counter.
Before you leave, read three lines on the ticket out loud: the amount you received, the total due, and the maturity date. If any of the three is blank or unclear, ask for it to be written in before you sign. That small pause is the cheapest protection in the whole transaction.
Call two or three counters before you drive anywhere. Browse pawn shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, have the make, model and condition ready, and ask each one for the payoff in dollars and the last day to redeem.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the point of a pawn shop?
A.  It is a lender and a resale store under one roof. The lending side hands you cash the same day against an object, and Missouri bars a pawnbroker from any agreement making you personally liable for the loan. The retail side sells what was forfeited or sold outright. That is why a pawn shop can say yes when a bank will not.
### Q. Can I pawn something at 17?
A.  No. Missouri law says a pawnbroker shall not accept a pledge from a person who is under eighteen years of age. Bring a parent who owns the item, or wait.
### Q. What items do pawnshops usually buy?
A.  Gold and diamond jewelry, watches, power tools, musical instruments, laptops, tablets, game consoles, cameras, coins and lawn equipment. The common thread is a known resale market and easy testing at the counter. If a buyer for it walks in most months, a shop will usually make an offer.
### Q. What will a pawn shop not take?
A.  Furniture, older televisions, printers, car seats, most clothing, opened cosmetics and medical devices are typical refusals. Shops also turn away anything with a defaced serial number, anything under recall, and phones or tablets still locked to another person’s account, because those cannot be resold.
### Q. What to pawn for $50?
A.  Small gold pieces are the steadiest answer, because the offer follows metal weight rather than style. After that, a name-brand cordless drill with a working battery, a decent set of hand tools or an entry-level guitar. Bring the charger and the case.
### Q. How much will a pawn shop give you for a $500 item?
A.  Well under $500. The shop starts from what the item would resell for used, not what it cost new, then leaves room for its margin and the chance you never come back. Gold is the exception that holds up best, because weight and purity set a floor under the offer.
### Q. What sells for $100 at a pawn shop?
A.  On the shelf, the $100 range tends to be mid-tier power tools, older game consoles with a controller, starter guitars and amps, and small gold chains. As a loan, an item usually needs a resale value well above $100 before the offer reaches that number, so bring the most complete version of whatever you have.
### Q. Is it worth selling items to a pawn shop?
A.  Often, when speed matters more than top dollar. You leave with cash, with no shipping, no stranger in a parking lot and no waiting on a marketplace buyer. A patient private sale usually nets more. If the money is needed this afternoon, that gap is often worth it.
### Q. Which pawn shop gives you the most money?
A.  There is no permanent winner. It shifts by item and by week, depending on what each shop already has too much of. Call three, describe the exact make, model and condition, and ask for a range. For gold, ask the price per gram so the quotes line up side by side.
### Q. What are some good pawn shops in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  Judge a shop by what predicts a fair deal: a clerk who says the payoff and the redemption date out loud, real testing at the counter, and reviews that mention people getting their items back without a fight. Compare pawn shops across the metro, then call two or three before you go.

## Ask for Bacon Fat: St. Louis Breakfast Ends at 2 p.m., Except Here
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-good-breakfast-and-brunch-in-st-louis
Bacon fat hisses under a ladle of blueberry batter, the edges go lacy and brown, and the smell of it rolls all the way back to the door. That is what you get at Half & Half on Maryland Avenue in Clayton if you read the small print. The menu lists blueberry pancakes at $11.50, and in brackets underneath: “ask to have cooked in bacon fat.” Ask. That bracket is the whole review.
Now the part that quietly ruins St. Louis mornings: four of the best breakfast rooms in town all close at 2. Half & Half runs 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Tuesday through Friday and 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on the weekend, closed Monday. Rooster, the crepe cafe on South Grand and downtown, is open daily 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. The Mud House at 2101 Cherokee Street posts 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., every day. Kingside Diner’s Clayton location, same thing, 7 to 2. Plan your morning on a dinner clock, roll in at 1:40 with four hungry people, and you’ll be eating drive-thru fries in the car with the windows fogging up.
So here is the rule worth texting the group chat: brunch in St. Louis isn’t late. It’s early with a deadline. Everything below is built around that clock.
### What timeframe is considered brunch?
There is no official clock. Brunch is the meal that bridges breakfast and lunch, so each restaurant’s own hours decide the window, and around here those hours end early. Every kitchen named above stops at 2 p.m. Sit down by noon and you have room for a second cup and a slow plate. Walk in at 1:45 and you’re asking a kitchen that is already scraping down the flat top to start one more ticket.
Two escape hatches, if the morning got away from you. Benton Park Cafe at 2901 Salena Street stays open until 3 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, a full extra hour of eggs. And a different Kingside Diner location, the one in the Central West End at 236 N. Euclid, runs 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. Thursday through Saturday, which makes it the late-breakfast answer when everyone finally wakes up hungry at 3. Save both in your phone before you need them.
One more thing nobody tells you: weekend and weekday hours are not always the same, even at the same restaurant. Half & Half opens an hour later on Saturday and Sunday than it does midweek. Check the day you’re going, not the day you’re reading.
### Soulard Market and breakfast: pick the right day
Cold air off the produce stalls, the thump of a crate set down on concrete, a paper bag of peppers getting heavy in your hand: a market-then-breakfast morning is one of the best things this city does. But the day matters more than the menu. The City of St. Louis lists Soulard Market as open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday and closed Sunday through Tuesday. Vendor participation is the number that changes everything: 10% on Wednesday and Thursday, 35% on Friday, and 100% on Saturday.
Translation: go Wednesday and most of the stalls are dark. Go Saturday and the whole hall is open, crates stacked high and vendors calling out prices. That is also the morning every curb in Soulard gets claimed. Walk in from a few blocks out, shop first while the produce is cold, then eat.
### Rooster: crepes from scratch and a Bloody Mary with 17 secret ingredients
At Rooster the sound is the crepe pan: a thin pour of batter swirled out to the rim, a quick flip, then a fold over eggs or fruit until the edge crackles under your fork. The kitchen makes its crepes from scratch with its own batter and bakes its breads in house, and the menu reads like a short promise: crepes, pancakes, scrambles, slingers.
Then the glass lands, cold and sweating. Rooster’s award-winning Bloody Mary is built on a house blend of 17 secret ingredients. You will taste tomato, heat and salt, and spend the rest of breakfast arguing about the other fourteen. It is the drink people order a second time just to keep guessing.
There are two of them, both open daily for dine-in and carryout from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.: Rooster South Grand at 3150 South Grand Blvd (314-772-3447) and Rooster Downtown. If you parked downtown for a game or a show, it is the easiest good breakfast within walking distance.
### Half & Half: the Clara Cakes and the bacon-fat trick
Half & Half describes itself as a breakfast, lunch and brunch destination in Clayton, and it is serious about two things: the food and the coffee, which it calls an equally focused program. Regulars come back for the Clara Cakes, plain pancakes with raspberry, mascarpone and granola at $12.25, and for a sausage biscuit made with housemade sausage. Cut into a stack and the mascarpone slumps into the warm cake, the raspberry goes bright and tart against it, and the granola keeps every bite from turning soft.
It sits at 8135 Maryland Ave. in Clayton, and you can call ahead at 314-725-0719. On a weekday morning it is the place to take the person you need to impress without trying too hard. On a weekend, get there early and bring patience.
### Diner or brunch spot? Know which morning you want
A diner opens early, runs the same breakfast menu every day, turns tables fast and keeps the check low. You hear the flat top before you see it. A brunch spot opens a little later, often runs a weekend-only menu, usually pours drinks, and expects you to sit a while. In a photo they look like the same plate of eggs. They are completely different mornings.
If you need to eat and get on with the day, pick the diner and sit at the counter. If the meal is the plan, pick the brunch room, book or join the waitlist, and leave the afternoon open. Two more options worth knowing: bakeries and coffee houses will feed you well for a fraction of the price when you don’t need table service, and a breakfast does not have to involve pancakes at all.
### Which neighborhoods make breakfast easy?
Aim for a walkable strip rather than a single address. In the city, Soulard, Benton Park, Lafayette Square, Tower Grove South and South Grand, the Central West End, The Grove, the Delmar Loop and downtown each put several breakfast kitchens close together. Park once, walk to plan B.
In the county, the old downtowns do the same job: Maplewood along Manchester, Webster Groves, Kirkwood, Clayton and University City. West county and Chesterfield lean toward shopping-center breakfast, less charming and much easier to park at with a group. Across the river, Belleville and Edwardsville have compact downtown blocks of their own.
### Waits, waitlists and the noon crush
Treat a quoted wait as a range, not a promise. Twenty minutes means the host is guessing how fast four tables will pay and leave, and one lingering party moves everybody. If the quote runs long, put your name in anyway, then try the next door down too. Whichever buzzes first wins.
Against a 2 p.m. close, a long wait is a real risk, not just an annoyance. If you are still standing outside at 1:15, the kitchen may be winding down by the time you sit. Call before you drive if your plan puts you anywhere near the last hour.
Nothing to do with pancakes - St. Louis drugstores, if you need one.
### How do you take a group or a couple of kids to brunch?
Call ahead for six or more, and give the real number. Small weekend kitchens often won’t seat a table until everyone has arrived, and a group that trickles in one car at a time loses the table it waited for. With kids, go early, before the room fills and the noise makes everyone tense.
Ask about split checks before anybody orders, and ask about high chairs the same way. Old storefront dining rooms are charming and often tight, so if someone uses a wheelchair or a walker, confirm the entrance and the restroom instead of assuming. Once the group runs past about a dozen, you have left brunch territory for private-room territory, and this guide to booking a banquet hall in St. Louis covers how those bookings work.
### Where do you get a good breakfast without paying brunch prices?
Go on a weekday, sit at a counter, and skip the two things that inflate the check: the specialty coffee drink and the brunch cocktail. A plain two-egg plate at an early-opening diner is the cheapest sit-down breakfast you will find, and often the most satisfying one. Bakeries and coffee houses are the next tier, with no wait and no table-service pressure. Craving something sweeter and thinner than a pancake? Here’s what to order at a creperie.
### What a breakfast house looks like from behind the counter
From the kitchen side, breakfast is a volume game. The checks are small, the coffee carries the margin, and the whole weekend rush is squeezed into a few loud hours before that 2 p.m. close. A room that is quiet at opening is drowning by late morning. And almost every new customer finds the place the same way: on a phone, in a parked car, searching for somewhere that is open right now.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the difference between breakfast, brunch, and lunch?
A.  Breakfast is eggs, griddle items and coffee, served from opening until late morning. Brunch is a hybrid that adds lunch plates and often drinks, usually on weekends and usually ending early afternoon. Lunch is the midday menu: sandwiches, salads and entrees. One restaurant can serve all three and keep them in separate windows, which is why the time you walk in decides what you can order.
### Q. Is brunch just a late breakfast?
A.  Not quite. A late breakfast is the same food eaten later. Brunch is a different menu built to bridge two meals, so you see pancakes next to a sandwich, plus a drink list that a breakfast counter usually doesn’t carry. It is also a longer sit, and brunch tables turn slower, which is why the wait feels so different.
### Q. What is the correct time to have brunch?
A.  There is no rule, but in St. Louis the safe answer is late morning, well before 2 p.m. Two favorites, Half & Half and Rooster, both close at 2. Arrive before the late-morning rush if you want to be seated quickly, and never plan to walk in during the last half hour.
### Q. Who has the best breakfast in St. Louis?
A.  No single place wins, because breakfast splits into kinds that barely compete. For a pancake you will think about later, Half & Half’s Clara Cakes in Clayton. For crepes and a Bloody Mary with 17 secret ingredients, Rooster on South Grand or downtown. For a fast, cheap plate, a counter diner that opens early. Pick the morning you want, then the place.
### Q. Where can I find the best brunch in Saint Louis, MO?
A.  Start with a neighborhood you can park in, then check which kitchens there serve the morning you want and what time they close. Comparing brunch spots by area beats chasing one recommendation, because the moment your first choice quotes a long wait you want the second option already picked on the same block.
### Q. Where’s the cheapest place to get breakfast?
A.  Counter diners, then bakeries, then taquerias and the hot counters inside international groceries, and on a weekday rather than a weekend. The cheapest sit-down breakfast is nearly always a plain two-egg plate at a place that opens early. Skipping the specialty coffee drink and the cocktail cuts the check a lot without changing the food.
### Q. What are the rules of brunch?
A.  No formal rules, only practical ones. Show up as the party you booked and give the host your full count. Don’t camp at the table long after paying while a line waits at the door. Ask about split checks before anyone orders. And watch the clock: in a town where good kitchens close at 2, the last half hour belongs to the cooks.

## Missouri Bankruptcy: The $15,000 Exemption Becomes $40,000
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-happens-when-you-file-bankruptcy-in-missouri
Fifteen thousand dollars. That is how much equity in the home you live in Missouri’s homestead statute protects from creditors today. The version of the same statute that takes effect on January 1, 2027 says forty thousand.
If you are reading this with the garnishment notice still on the kitchen table, the paper soft from being folded and unfolded, that number matters more than almost anything else on this page.
Missouri doesn’t let bankruptcy filers swap in the federal exemption list, so a St. Louis filer works from the state’s own figures. And Missouri’s figures are changing: the vehicle allowance goes from $3,000 to $5,000, household goods from $3,000 to $15,000, the any-property wildcard from $600 to $1,700. The date your petition is filed decides which set you get.
None of that makes the decision for you, and it shouldn’t be made alone. But it changes the first conversation. Waiting can cost money when wages are being garnished or a sale date is set. Rushing can cost money when your equity only fits under the new numbers. That is exactly the kind of timing question a bankruptcy attorney is there to answer, and you are allowed to ask it out loud.
For anyone in St. Louis City or St. Louis County, the case is filed in the Eastern Division of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse, 111 South 10th St., 4th Floor, downtown. You may never set foot in it. Most of what happens runs through paperwork, a trustee and one short meeting.
Here is what you can do today, before anyone files anything. Gather your recent pay stubs, your last two tax returns, your vehicle titles, your mortgage statement and any lawsuit papers, and put them in one folder. Write down every debt, including the ones you would rather not think about. Don’t pay back a relative, don’t move a car title into someone else’s name, and don’t run up new charges. Then book a consultation with an attorney who files consumer cases in this district and ask one question first: should I file before or after the exemptions change?
If paying a lawyer feels out of reach, start with a phone call that costs nothing. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, at 701 Market Street downtown, says its services are free; its number is 314.534.4200. Ask whether your situation fits what they handle. The court fee is not a wall either: with the court’s permission, individual filers may pay it in installments, and a court can waive the Chapter 7 fee for filers who qualify.
This is general information, not legal advice. Only an attorney who looks at your income, debts and property can tell you whether filing is right for you.
### Does Chapter 7 wipe out all debt?
No. A discharge releases you from personal liability for most debts, but not all of them. Debts that are not discharged include alimony and child support, certain taxes, certain loans made or guaranteed by a government unit for education, government fines and penalties, and debts for willful and malicious injury.
One distinction does more damage than the rest: a discharge ends your personal liability, but secured creditors may keep some rights to seize the property securing a debt even after a discharge is granted. If a lender holds a mortgage on the house or a title on the truck, talk through that collateral before you file. Medical bills are often a big part of the pile, which is why closing a coverage gap belongs on the same list: here is how to get health insurance in Missouri.
After the discharge, the law turns into a wall. A discharge operates as an injunction against any act to collect a discharged debt. The phone numbers you stopped answering have no lawful reason to call about those debts again.
### The day you file: the calls stop
Filing a petition operates as a stay against collection, under section 362 of the Bankruptcy Code. In plain terms, it stops most collection actions against you or your property. The court opens a case, a trustee is assigned, and your creditors get notice from the court, not from you. For a lot of people the first thing they notice is quiet. The phone sits face-down on the counter and doesn’t buzz.
The stay is a pause, not a ruling. Nothing about your debts has been decided yet, and a secured lender can ask the court for permission to move on a car or a house. If you have filed a recent earlier case, ask your attorney how that affects the stay, because it can.
### Chapter 7 or Chapter 13: two different tools
Chapter 7 is a liquidation. The trustee’s job under the Bankruptcy Code is to collect and reduce to money the property of the estate, but only property an exemption doesn’t protect. In many consumer cases the exemptions cover what the filer owns and nothing is sold at all.
Chapter 13 is a court-supervised repayment plan that runs for years: one payment, every month, the same day you learn to dread a little less. You keep your property and make one monthly payment to a trustee, who distributes it under a plan the judge confirms. People choose it for concrete reasons: they are behind on a mortgage and want to catch up over time, they have equity they would rather not risk, or their income is too high for Chapter 7. Neither one is the better chapter. They solve different problems.
### What the means test measures
The means test is arithmetic, not a judgment of your character. It is a calculator on a desk, not a person deciding whether you deserve help. It starts with your current monthly income, which the Bankruptcy Code measures over the 6-month period ending before the case is filed. If that income is more than the state median for your household size, the Bankruptcy Code requires a means test to decide whether a Chapter 7 filing is presumed abusive. The medians change, so have an attorney run the current ones.
That math is where an attorney earns the fee. The income window is also why a bonus or a severance check can change the answer, depending on when it landed.
### What can you keep? Missouri’s exemptions, before and after the change
Usually, everything. Exemptions mark out property a Chapter 7 trustee can’t sell. Under RSMo 513.427, Missouri filers claim Missouri’s list and are not authorized to claim the federal one. Here is how the main numbers move.
Every figure is measured against what the property would sell for on your filing date, not what you paid for it, and only your equity counts. A car worth $9,000 with $7,500 still owed is $1,500 of equity, and only that $1,500 needs covering.
Here is an illustration. Say a single filer with no kids owns a paid-off older sedan that would bring about $4,000 in a private sale and has about $20,000 of equity in her house. Under the current figures, the $3,000 vehicle exemption plus the $600 wildcard leave $400 of the car unprotected, and the $15,000 homestead leaves $5,000 of the house exposed. Under the new figures, the $5,000 vehicle exemption covers the car and the $40,000 homestead covers the house. Same person, same property, different filing date.
Retirement money sits on the protected list too. Missouri’s exemption statute protects money in a qualified retirement plan, including an inherited account. So is your right to receive Social Security, unemployment compensation or a public assistance benefit, a veteran’s benefit, and alimony or support up to $750 a month.
If collectors are the pressure point and bankruptcy is still a maybe, read up on debt collectors, the statute of limitations and wage garnishment in Missouri and compare debt consolidation in St. Louis before you pick a path. If you live on the Illinois side of the river, these Missouri numbers are not yours; ask an attorney who files there.
### From counseling to discharge, in the order you’ll live it
Every consumer case runs on the same spine. Chapter 13 adds a confirmation hearing and years of plan payments. Here it is step by step.
Credit counseling first. You must receive a briefing from an approved nonprofit budget and credit counseling agency during the 180-day period before you file.
The petition and schedules. Every debt, every asset, income, expenses, recent transfers. Nearly everything that goes wrong goes wrong here: a forgotten co-signed loan, a car titled in a relative’s name.
Filing day. The case opens, a trustee is assigned, and the stay begins.
The meeting of creditors. It is not a court hearing: bankruptcy judges are prohibited from attending the meeting of creditors under 11 U.S.C. § 341(c). The trustee asks you questions under oath about your paperwork. Bring photo ID and read your notice for where and how it is held.
A second course. After filing, there is a course on personal financial management. If you fail to complete it, the court can deny your discharge.
Discharge. It releases you from personal liability for most debts and prevents the creditors owed those debts from taking collection actions against you.
A different stack of paperwork entirely: if a move is part of the fresh start, local real estate agencies can walk you through it.
### Who should you call, and what should you ask?
Start with an attorney who files consumer cases regularly in the Eastern District of Missouri, because local practice and local trustees matter. Bring your folder. Then ask four questions. What does the fee cover, and what falls outside it? Do you recommend Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 for my facts, and why? Should I file before or after the exemption change? And what should I stop doing right now?
One check worth knowing. A bankruptcy petition preparer is not your lawyer: federal law says a preparer may not offer a potential bankruptcy debtor any legal advice. If the question is about timing, exemptions or which chapter, that is legal advice, and it needs an attorney.
Bankruptcy is one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, which covers the everyday money questions most of us learned the hard way. When you walk out of that first consultation and down the steps into the downtown air, the goal is simple: you should know your next step and your date.
Bring your folder and your one question. Browse bankruptcy attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, talk to two of them, and ask both whether your case should be filed before or after Missouri’s exemptions change.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Missouri?
A.  There isn’t a flat dollar cap. Your current monthly income is measured over the 6-month period before you file. If it is more than the Missouri median for your household size, the Bankruptcy Code requires a means test to decide whether a Chapter 7 filing is presumed abusive. Earning above the median is not an automatic no, so have an attorney run the test.
### Q. Will Chapter 7 take my car if I own it?
A.  Usually not. On a paid-off car the whole resale value is equity. Missouri protects $3,000 in motor vehicles under the current statute and $5,000 for cases under the version effective January 1, 2027, and the wildcard can cover more. If the value runs past what you can protect, talk to an attorney before you file.
### Q. What is the 90 day rule for Chapter 7?
A.  It usually means preferences. A payment to a creditor on or within 90 days before you file can be recovered by the trustee and shared among all creditors. For payments to an insider, such as a relative, the window stretches to one year. That is why paying back family right before filing is a mistake.
### Q. What disqualifies you from filing Chapter 7?
A.  A few things block a discharge. A Chapter 7 discharge in a case filed within 8 years before the new one, skipping credit counseling in the 180 days before filing, or failing the personal financial management course afterward. Failing the means test can push you toward Chapter 13 instead. An attorney can check each one against your history.
### Q. What assets do you lose in Chapter 7?
A.  Only what an exemption doesn’t protect. According to the federal courts, most Chapter 7 cases involving individual debtors are no asset cases, meaning nothing is sold for unsecured creditors. Missouri’s exemption amounts are in the table above. What tends to be at risk is equity above those limits, like a second vehicle worth more than the allowance covers.
### Q. What not to do before filing Chapter 7 bankruptcy?
A.  Don’t repay a relative, don’t move property into someone else’s name, don’t drain a retirement account to pay credit cards, don’t run up new charges, and don’t leave a creditor off your paperwork. Each one creates exactly the problem a trustee looks for. Bring the whole picture to a consultation, including the embarrassing parts.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of Chapter 7?
A.  It shows up on your credit report, so plan on a stretch of rebuilding afterward. Unprotected property can be sold. Co-signers stay on the hook, because your discharge protects you, not them. And some debts survive, including alimony and child support, certain taxes, government fines and certain government-backed education loans.
### Q. Can you be sued after Chapter 7?
A.  Not to collect a discharged debt. The discharge operates as an injunction against any act to collect it, and a collector who tries can be taken back before the bankruptcy court. Debts that are not discharged, like alimony and child support, can still be collected. Ask your attorney which of your debts fall where.

## Spot Getting Darker? Put a Penny Beside It, Then Call a St. Louis Dermatologist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-a-dermatologist-in-st-louis
The spot looked darker under the bathroom light again. You twist toward the mirror, faucet still running, and pull the skin tight with two fingers to see the edge. Was it this big last month? You honestly can’t say.
That small, cold drop in your stomach is the real problem. Not the spot. The not knowing, and the weeks between the phone call and the appointment, when all you can do is look at it again and hope you are remembering it right.
So here is the move that turns the wait into evidence, and it starts with a penny. Washington University’s dermatology division sends patients to a photo tutorial, and for a skin spot it says: “Use a penny to define relative size.” Then the part almost everybody gets wrong: “Do not use the zoom feature.” Take the close-up about six inches away instead, in a well-lit area, without flash, against a plain blue or white background, and skip the selfie if someone else can hold the phone. A white bath towel over your knee does the job.
Worried about a mole? Put a penny next to it, don’t zoom, hold the phone about six inches away, and turn the flash off. That is the photo a dermatologist can actually compare.
Why a coin from the junk drawer matters: the hardest thing to describe in an exam room is change. “I think it got bigger” is a feeling. A photo with a penny beside it is a measurement. And change is exactly what dermatologists are trained to look for. The American Academy of Dermatology’s ABCDEs of melanoma end on E for Evolving: the spot looks different from the rest or is changing in size, shape, or color.
WashU’s own instructions for sending those pictures through MyChart say: take up to 3 photos, have good lighting, and in the “To” section choose your dermatologist. Its scheduling page lists one number for general dermatology and skin cancer, 314-273-3376. So do two things today. Call and book, even if the first opening feels far away, and ask to be put on a cancellation list. Then take the penny photos tonight, and again in a few weeks in the same spot by the same window. Write down when you first noticed it and anything you have put on it. If your dermatologist isn’t on MyChart, bring the photos on your phone. You will walk in with something better than a memory.
No insurance, or no dermatologist at all? Don’t let that become the reason you keep waiting. In St. Louis, Affinia Healthcare says it provides essential services to patients regardless of their ability to pay, with a sliding fee scale and locations that include Biddle, Lemp and South Broadway; its appointment line is 314-814-8700. Casa de Salud serves uninsured and underinsured patients in St. Louis, with a focus on immigrants and refugees. A clinician at either can look at the spot, look at your photos, and refer you on if it needs a specialist.
### How do you know if you need a dermatologist?
You need one when something on your skin, hair or nails is changing, won’t clear up, hurts, or has started running your day, and you can no longer answer the question yourself. That last part is the real trigger. When you catch yourself searching for reassurance instead of an appointment, the appointment is the answer.
Hold the penny photo up next to the mirror and the letters stop being a poster in a waiting room. Is one half of the spot unlike the other half? Does the edge blur out like ink on a wet napkin instead of stopping clean? Do you see more than one shade in it, tan running into brown or black, or a patch of white, red, or blue? The penny helps with D, too: melanomas are usually greater than 6 millimeters, about the size of a pencil eraser, when diagnosed, though they can be smaller.
You don’t have to sort any of that out alone, and this page won’t try to make you your own doctor. The point of knowing the letters is simpler: when the scheduler asks why you’re calling, “a mole that has changed color” gets heard differently than “a spot I want looked at.”
Not every skin problem is a mole, of course. A rash that keeps coming back after the drugstore cream runs out, acne that has stopped answering anything on the shelf, hair coming out in the shower drain, a nail that has changed color and shape. All of those are reasons to call. So is the simple fact that something bothers you enough that you keep touching it.
### Do you need a referral first?
Flip your insurance card over and look at the back, because it decides, not your ZIP code. HealthCare.gov defines a referral as a written order from your primary care doctor for you to see a specialist, and notes that in many Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs) you need one before you can get care from anyone except your primary care doctor. Other plan types often let you book a specialist directly. The member services number on the back of your card is the fastest way to know for sure.
If you do need a referral, it can work in your favor. A primary care visit is often easier to get, primary care handles a lot of skin, and if the problem needs to go further, that visit becomes the referral, sometimes with notes and photos already attached. Plenty of dermatology offices ask for those notes even when the insurer doesn’t require them, simply because it makes the first visit faster.
Eye trouble raises the same referral question, and it gets answered the same way. There’s a companion piece on when to see an ophthalmologist in St. Louis if that is also on your list.
### Medical or cosmetic: the line that decides who pays
Two kinds of visit, and you can feel the difference at the front desk: one hands you a clipboard about allergies and family history, the other hands you a menu of services. Sometimes it is the same desk. Medical dermatology diagnoses and treats a condition, and it is generally billed to your health insurance. Cosmetic work changes how something looks when nothing is medically wrong, and you generally pay for it yourself. Same specialty, sometimes the same exam room, completely different money.
Medicare draws the line plainly. Part B covers medically necessary doctor services, and after you meet the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for most services. Commercial plans follow a similar logic, with their own definition of medically necessary tucked into the plan documents.
This is where bills go sideways. Book a cosmetic consult, then ask about the patch that has itched since spring, and the visit can turn into a medical one, or into charges under both headings. Say which you are coming in for when you schedule. If the honest answer is both, say that too, and ask how it will be billed before anyone picks up an instrument. Washington University’s own scheduling page keeps the two apart: aesthetic services schedule online, while general dermatology and skin cancer go through the phone line.
If what you want is surgical rather than medical, here’s how to choose a cosmetic surgeon in St. Louis.
### What happens at a first dermatology appointment?
The paper on the exam table crinkles when you sit down, and the room is a little cooler than you dressed for. A first visit is short and more ordinary than people expect. You fill out forms about medications, allergies, sun exposure and family history. The physician looks at what you came for, often under a bright lighted magnifier pressed gently against the skin. Photos may be taken for comparison later. You leave with a plan, a prescription, a follow-up, or a wait for results.
If a biopsy is needed, it usually happens the same day: a numbing sting, a small bandage, and a sample that goes off to a lab. Ask before you leave how you will hear the result and what to do if you don’t. A result that never reaches you is one of the most common ways the whole process breaks down.
Your photos earn their keep here. Pull them up when the doctor asks how long it has been there or whether it has changed. Then bring your questions written down, because the visit moves fast and the thing you meant to mention is the thing you remember in the parking lot with the keys already in your hand.
Unrelated, but it always happens the same week: the fridge starts humming wrong. Appliance help is local too.
### What does a dermatologist visit cost around St. Louis?
The fear that keeps a lot of people from calling is the envelope that comes after. Fair enough. There is no single St. Louis price, and I could not find a primary source that posts one, so this page won’t guess. What you can do is get your own number in writing. Under federal rules, if you are uninsured or not using insurance, providers usually must give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost when you schedule in advance or when you ask for one. If the bill comes in at least $400 more than the estimate, you may be able to dispute it through the federal process on CMS’s dispute page.
Three things drive what you actually pay. The visit itself, priced by how complicated the problem is. Any procedure done that day, billed on top of the visit. And lab work on a biopsy, which is often billed separately, so one appointment can bring two envelopes to your mailbox. When you call, ask the office-visit charge, ask whether pathology bills separately, and ask whether the office is in network for your specific plan, not just whether they “take” the insurance company’s name.
Take the photos tonight and make the call tomorrow. Browse dermatologists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two offices, and ask three things: the first available appointment, whether your plan needs a referral, and how the visit will be billed.

### What if you cannot afford a dermatologist?
Start with a community health center, like the two named near the top of this page. Walk in out of the cold with your phone in your pocket and your photos ready. A health center clinician can look at the spot, handle a lot of common skin problems, and refer you on when something needs a specialist. Bring your photos there too.
Free skin cancer checks are a second route. The American Academy of Dermatology keeps a locator called “Find a free skin cancer check” on its site. A screening is a check, not ongoing care, but it can tell you whether a worrying spot needs a follow-up visit.
Beyond that, ask any practice directly about self-pay pricing or a payment plan, and ask before the visit rather than after the bill. If the deeper problem is that you have no coverage at all, that is fixable with its own steps: see how to get health insurance in Missouri.
### How do you check that a dermatologist is board certified?
Do it on your phone in the parking lot before you walk in, engine still ticking. It takes about a minute. The American Board of Dermatology’s home page has a search box titled “Is My Dermatologist Board Certified?” Type the last name and you have your answer from the board itself, not from a review site.
Then run the Missouri check most people skip. The Missouri Board of Registration for the Healing Arts, based in Jefferson City, keeps a Licensee Search for physicians and surgeons, and right beside it a page of Disciplinary/Miscellaneous Actions. Board certification tells you about training. The state license page tells you whether the doctor is cleared to practice in Missouri.
One nuance worth carrying with you. “Board certified” on its own doesn’t say in what. Cosmetic skin procedures are done by clinicians from several specialties. If it matters to you which training sits behind the hands doing the work, ask which board and which specialty. A good office answers that without flinching.
Then judge the office the way you would judge anyone you trust with something that worries you. Did they explain what they were billing? Did they tell you how results would reach you? Did they look at your photos? Did you walk out to the car feeling heard, or rushed?
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When to see a dermatologist for a mole?
A.  When it matches any of the ABCDEs: an asymmetrical shape, an irregular or poorly defined border, several colors, a size usually bigger than a pencil eraser, or any change in size, shape or color. A new spot that looks different from your others counts too. Photograph it in good light and call; you do not need to be sure first.
### Q. Can I see a dermatologist without a referral?
A.  Often, but your plan decides. HealthCare.gov notes that many HMOs require a referral from your primary care doctor before you can see anyone else, while other plan types often let you book directly. Call the member services number on your card before you schedule, and ask the dermatology office whether it wants your primary care notes anyway.
### Q. How much do dermatologists charge per visit?
A.  It depends on the practice, how complicated the problem is and what gets done that day, so no honest single figure exists. Get the number from the office. If you are uninsured or paying cash, providers usually must give you a good faith estimate when you schedule or ask, and a bill at least $400 above it may be disputed.
### Q. Why is a dermatologist so expensive?
A.  Costs stack. The office visit is priced by complexity. A procedure during the visit, like a biopsy or a removal, is billed on top. Lab work is often billed separately by an outside group, so one appointment can produce two bills. Cosmetic services add another layer, because insurance generally doesn’t pay for them. Ask about each piece when you book.
### Q. What not to do before seeing a dermatologist?
A.  Don’t cover or treat the exact spot you want examined right before the visit. Skip makeup if it concerns your face and nail polish if it concerns your nails. Don’t throw away the creams you tried; bring them. And don’t rely on memory for how it changed. Photos taken in the same light tell the story better.
### Q. What are the most common things dermatologists treat?
A.  Acne, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea and skin cancer fill much of the schedule, along with hair loss, nail problems, hives, warts and skin infections. The specialty covers skin, hair and nails, so the range is wider than most people picture. If you are not sure something belongs there, call and describe it; the scheduler will tell you.
### Q. Is it possible to see a dermatologist for free?
A.  Sometimes. The American Academy of Dermatology runs a locator to find a free skin cancer check. For ongoing care without insurance, a community health center is steadier: in St. Louis, Affinia Healthcare says it serves patients regardless of their ability to pay and uses a sliding fee scale, and its clinicians can refer you onward.
### Q. How do I know if a dermatologist is good?
A.  Start with what you can verify. The American Board of Dermatology’s site has a search box, “Is My Dermatologist Board Certified?” After that, judge the office: whether it explains what it is billing, tells you how results will reach you, looks at the photos you brought, and answers questions without hurrying you toward the door.

## A Print Bill Can Tax Your Logo 9.679% in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-graphic-design-costs-and-covers-in-st-louis
The box of business cards slides across the counter still warm, and the smell of toner comes up when the lid lifts. The new logo is on every one of them, crisp, finally real. Under the box sits the invoice, and it has one total.
That one total is where the trouble lives. Missouri’s Department of Revenue publishes a tax matrix for graphic design companies, and the line is drawn in two rows. Graphic design fees incorporated into the sale of tangible personal property: taxable. Artwork sent electronically to the customer, or placed on the seller’s website for the customer to pick up: exempt. Same logo, same designer, same hours at the screen. When the design rides in on the same bill as the cards, the creative fee can be taxed like the paper.
In the City of St. Louis that is not a rounding error. The Department’s current rate table lists a 9.679% base sales tax rate for the city, and inside some of the city’s special taxing districts the same table reaches 11.679%.
Nobody at the counter did anything wrong. The bundle did it. Who decided a logo should ride in on the same total as the cardstock, one number that hides the tax, the revisions and who owns the file? And the scope underneath can be counted. IQComputing, which calls itself a St. Louis design office, posts its logo packages in plain numbers. It is one office’s price list, not a market rate, but it shows what a priced scope looks like: $398 for 3 concepts and 1 included revision, $597 for 5 concepts and 3 revisions, $996 for 11 concepts and 4 revisions. Every included revision is capped at up to a half hour each, on one selected logo, and extra revisions start at $48.
A revision there is a unit of time, half an hour of someone’s hand on the mouse, not a promise to keep going until the mark feels right. That is not a trick either. It is scope, written down, which is exactly what a bundled total never shows.
The paperwork that already exists spells out what a clean bid holds. That design office’s price list names the concepts, the included revisions, how long a revision lasts and the file formats: JPG, EPS and PDF in the $398 package, and JPG, PNG, GIF, EPS and PDF in the two higher ones. The EPS is the vector file a sign shop will ask for. The same table even gives copyright its own row, labeled Full Copyright. The state’s matrix adds the tax line, with business cards, flyers, banners and lawn signs on the taxable side. Federal law adds the last one: a transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless it is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights.
The request that keeps every one of those lines visible fits in a single sentence: “Design, printing and delivery on separate lines, please, with the file formats listed and the copyright transfer in writing.”
So when the next bid lands, how many of those lines are on it, and how many are folded into one number?
### How much does a graphic designer usually charge?
For a logo, the posted St. Louis numbers above are a fair anchor: $398, $597 and $996 at one design office, with the jump buying more concepts, more revisions and more file formats rather than a better designer. Beyond logos, design is sold by the hour, as a flat project fee, or monthly on a retainer, and the number on any quote describes how much work, how many rounds and which rights are in the box.
The formats matter the first day a sign shop asks for artwork. A fuzzy JPG saved off an old website will not stretch across a truck door, and the reply to the shop sits there with the cursor blinking, waiting on a vector file that was never part of the bill.
With the totals stripped off, two bids read as lines. Concepts. Rounds. Formats. Rights. Tax. Which bid puts all five in writing, and which one hides them inside a total?
### Do you pay sales tax on design work in Missouri?
In Missouri the design work itself is generally exempt, and the physical things it turns into are generally taxable. The Missouri Department of Revenue publishes a tax matrix for graphic design companies that lists graphic design services, including web design, advertising and marketing design, packaging and illustration, as exempt. So are webpage development, digital mockups, and artwork sent electronically to the customer.
The same matrix lists the taxable side just as plainly: business cards, flyers and brochures, laser prints, printed products like t-shirts, banners and lawn signs, and artwork sold on a disk or other physical media. The line that surprises people is the one from the opening: graphic design fees incorporated into the sale of tangible personal property are taxable. In the city, that means the base rate on the Department of Revenue’s rate table can apply to the creative fee too, not just the paper.
One small detail is worth knowing before you argue with an invoice. The matrix treats shipping, delivery, freight and postage charges as exempt, but handling charges as taxable, and a combined shipping and handling line as taxable too. An invoice with design and printing on separate lines keeps that question visible, and an accountant is the right stop for any filing question.
### Hourly, flat fee or retainer: match it to how well you can describe the job
Hourly suits work you can’t define yet: a pile of small edits, a run of ads, a project where you don’t know how many pieces you need. You carry the risk, so ask for an estimate range and a check-in point where the designer tells you where the hours stand before they keep going.
A flat project fee suits a defined deliverable, like a logo, a menu, a booth graphic or a short catalog. The designer carries the risk here, which is why the scope document matters so much. A flat fee with no named deliverables and no named revision limit is an argument waiting for week five. Expect a deposit up front and the balance at delivery.
A retainer suits work that never really ends: social graphics every week, seasonal signs, an ad that keeps changing. Before you sign one, ask two questions. Do unused hours roll over? And who decides what goes first when the queue is full?
Whichever shape you pick, remember what a solo designer’s number has to cover. Rent, software, a computer that wears out, self-employment taxes, and health coverage they buy for themselves. Knowing that makes a quote easier to read and much easier to negotiate without insulting anyone.
Posted logo prices near you
### How much do graphic designers typically charge?
Locally, the posted numbers are a useful anchor. One St. Louis design office lists logo packages at $398, $597 and $996, with extra revisions starting at $48. What moves the number is the count of concepts, how many revisions are included, and which file formats you walk away with.
### What are you actually buying when you buy a logo?
A logo purchase is a small set of files plus the rules for using them. A complete package for a working business usually covers the pieces below. Anything less and you will be paying someone to rebuild it the day you order your first banner.
The main version, plus a stacked or horizontal alternate, plus the mark on its own for small spaces like a profile photo
One-color and reversed versions, because sooner or later you need white on a dark truck door
Vector masters (AI, EPS or SVG) alongside JPG and PNG exports at the sizes you post most
Color values written three ways: HEX for screens, CMYK for print, and a Pantone reference if you plan on spot color
The typefaces named, with where they came from and what the license allows
A one-page usage sheet: minimum size, clear space, and the handful of things never to do to it
Know the ladder, too. A logo is one mark. A visual identity is the mark plus type, color, photo direction and the rules that hold them together. A full identity system adds the applied pieces: stationery, signs, vehicle graphics, packaging, social templates. Those are three different budgets, and a lot of frustration comes from paying for the first while expecting the third.
One practical note on print. Commercial printers want artwork built to their template, in CMYK, at full size, with bleed past the trim and text pulled safely inside it. A designer who works in print builds that in from the start. One who only works on screens may hand you a file the printer sends straight back, and that round trip is billable time for somebody. You will hear about it in an email with a red-circled screenshot and a polite, expensive question.
Different topic, same kitchen table: if the TV volume keeps creeping up at night, hearing aid providers are a short drive away.
### Who owns the files when the invoice clears?
Paying for a logo does not, by itself, make you the copyright owner. Federal law says a transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless it is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights, under 17 U.S.C. § 204(a). Without that signature, an independent designer generally keeps the copyright, and you hold whatever license the contract describes.
The phrase people reach for is “work made for hire,” and it does less than it sounds like. For commissioned work from someone who isn’t your employee, the statute at 17 U.S.C. § 101 limits work made for hire to a short list of specific kinds of work, and only if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them. What reliably moves ownership is a written assignment, signed.
Then there is the practical question of files. Finals are the exports: the PDF, the PNG, the print file. Source artwork is the editable original with its layers and paths intact, the one another designer could open in five years and change. Plenty of contracts deliver finals only and price source files separately. That is a fair way to work. You just need to know which one you bought before the sign shop asks, not after.
Two things travel with the work that aren’t yours to give away. Fonts are licensed, not sold, and a desktop license usually doesn’t cover putting the face on a website. Stock photos come in tiers, and the cheap tier often excludes packaging and merchandise. Ask which fonts and images are in the file and who holds each license.
Registration is cheap next to a dispute. The U.S. Copyright Office lists a $45 electronic filing fee for a single author, one work, not made for hire. Trademark is a different agency and a different errand: the USPTO base application fee is $350 per class. Copyright protects the drawing. A trademark protects your right to use it as your name in the market.
### How many revision rounds is normal?
Treat revisions as a unit of scope, not a courtesy. That posted price list makes the point better than any lecture: 1, 3 or 4 included revisions depending on the package, each up to a half hour, with more available as an add-on. A good proposal names how many rounds are included, defines what counts as one, and says what happens after.
A round is one consolidated set of feedback, sent once, from one decision-maker. That last part is the whole game. When feedback arrives as six texts over four days from three people who disagree, the designer is running six rounds while billing for one, and you are burning half-hours you already paid for. Pick one person to collect opinions and speak with a single voice.
Make the feedback usable. “Make it pop” sends someone guessing for hours. Say what is wrong in terms of the job the design has to do: the mark reads as a leaf and we sell tires; the phone number disappears at arm’s length; the letters blur on a truck passing at highway speed. Concrete problems get fixed in one pass.
Approve in writing, and say exactly what you are approving: the concept, the layout, the final press proof. Once ten thousand menus come off the press smelling of fresh ink, the typo is yours no matter who typed it.
Send the same brief to two designers this week. Browse graphic designers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, send your one-paragraph brief, and compare what comes back line by line: concepts, revisions, formats, rights.
