## After the First Freeze: When to Clean St. Louis Carpet
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-often-to-clean-carpets-in-st-louis
Spring is the wrong season to deep clean carpet in St. Louis. The right one starts the week the lawn turns white and crunchy underfoot for the first time.
Here is why. Ragweed pollen can cause hay fever, and ragweed typically blooms and produces its fine powder from August into November, usually peaking in mid-September. All fall it rides in on shoes, pant cuffs and the dog’s coat, and it settles into the base of the pile where a vacuum barely reaches. Then the first cold night comes. The National Weather Service’s own numbers for St. Louis Lambert put the first 32-degree freeze at a median of November 1, an average of November 2.
A few days after that, you hear the furnace click on, smell that first warm, dusty breath from the vents, and the house closes up for winter with a season of pollen still sitting in the floor. Clean in April and you scrub away a quiet winter. Clean in early November and you pull out the worst stretch of the year right before the blower spends all winter stirring it around.
There’s a second surprise most owners never read: the warranty. Shaw, the carpet maker, says its warranties require the homeowner to be able to show proof of periodic cleaning by hot water extraction. No receipt, and a stain claim on a newer carpet can get a lot harder. The cleaning invoice is not junk mail. File it with the carpet paperwork.
So here is the move, and you can make it today. Call two carpet cleaners now and ask for a slot in the week after the first freeze, instead of waiting for the frost and finding the calendar full. Tell both of them the same room list, stairs included, so the quotes compare. Ask each one to write “hot water extraction” and the date on the invoice. Until the crew shows up, vacuum the entry and the lanes often, so the deep clean has less to fight. The night before, clear anything you can lift alone off the floor and shut the dog in a back room.
### How often should carpet be cleaned?
For a typical household, every 12 to 18 months, depending on the number of residents and the amount of activity. That is Shaw’s guidance for a typical household. Shaw also recommends hot water extraction, commonly called steam cleaning, which will remove oils and particulates that accelerate soiling. Pets, toddlers and allergies all push you toward the short end of that range. In St. Louis, time the visit for just after the first freeze.
### Read the floor, not the calendar
Slide the couch out a foot and look down. The strip that sat under it is a shade lighter than the open floor, and the path from the back door to the kitchen reads like a trail through grass. That contrast is the best test you have, because it measures your house instead of an average one. If the traffic lane is visibly darker than the protected carpet, soil has reached the base of the pile.
Then use your other senses. Walk the first few feet inside the door in socks and feel for grit. Notice whether a smell comes back when the air turns damp, or the first time the heat runs in fall, because warmth and humidity both pull odor back out of the fibers. Watch whether the pile stands back up after you vacuum or the tracks fade within a minute. Any one of those beats a date on a calendar.
A spot that keeps coming back after you clean it is its own warning. It usually isn’t new dirt. The spill soaked into the backing or the pad, and as the surface dries it pulls the stain back up. Another round with a spray bottle won’t fix that. It needs real extraction.
### Pets, toddlers and allergies shorten the clock
Think about who actually lives on that floor. A dog that sleeps by the couch leaves skin oil that binds soil to the fibers, which is why dog-heavy rooms get a dull, greasy sheen in the lanes before anywhere else. A crawling baby spends hours with a face at pile level. An allergic kid wakes up stuffy in a house that seems clean.
Those homes belong at the 12-month end of the range, and the room the dog sleeps in can go sooner. A two-adult, shoes-off house with no pets can usually stretch toward the full 18 months, with an extra pass on the entry and the stairs.
For allergy households, two visits make more sense than one: once in late spring after the tree pollen settles, and once just after that first November freeze, when the ragweed season is finished and before the furnace runs all winter.
### Winter brings a different kind of dirt
Come the first snow, the grit changes. Road salt and the sand mixed with it ride in on boots and dry into a stiff, gray band a few steps inside the front door. Salt residue grabs moisture from the air, so that patch can stay faintly damp and attract more dirt all winter.
A boot tray and a good mat at the door do more than any cleaning schedule. If the band shows up anyway, treat the entry alone in late winter rather than paying for the whole house twice.
### Moving out of a rental?
Here the calendar doesn’t matter at all. The empty apartment echoes, the sun through bare windows shows every lane and every spot the couch used to hide, and the walk-through is days away.
Read your lease before you book anything. Some landlords want a professional cleaning at move-out and some don’t, and the wording is the only thing that settles it. If the lease asks for one, get the work done after the last box is out, keep the paid invoice, and photograph every room once the carpet is dry. A dated receipt and a set of photos are cheap insurance when the deposit comes up.
Landlords, the same logic runs the other way: a cleaning at every turnover, with the invoice on file, is how you show the next tenant got a clean floor, and how you keep a newer carpet’s warranty paperwork in order.
### What a vacuum can and can’t do
Listen to a vacuum on a gritty entry rug and you can hear it: the rattle of sand going up the hose. That is the loose top layer, and regular vacuuming is the single best thing you can do between deep cleans, especially in the entry and the lanes.
What it won’t touch is the oily film that glues fine soil to the fibers, which is exactly what hot water extraction is built to remove. Vacuum often so the deep clean has less to fight, and the 12-to-18-month schedule holds.
Different problem entirely: if the carpet turns out to be past saving, you’ll want junk removal to haul it to the curb.
### Steam or dry: which method should you book?
For the deep clean, hot water extraction is the method the warranty language is built around. The machine pushes heated solution into the pile and vacuums it straight back out, carrying the soil with it. Done well, it starts with a thorough vacuum and a pre-spray left to sit, then the rinse and extraction pass, then grooming so the pile dries standing up.
Low-moisture methods clean the upper pile and dry faster. They’re a fine touch-up between deep cleans, not a replacement for one, and if your carpet is under warranty, check whether a low-moisture visit counts before you book it.
The thing to ask any crew about is over-wetting. Too much solution and too little extraction, and water reaches the backing and pad, dries slowly, and can leave a sour smell or a stain that wicks back up. In a muggy St. Louis summer that risk climbs, which is one more reason to book in fall. A crew that sets air movers and tells you to run the HVAC fan is showing you how it works.
Renting a machine is a reasonable middle path for maintenance. Shaw’s warranty language even allows a do-it-yourself system, as long as the equipment is certified under the Carpet and Rug Institute’s Seal of Approval program. Rental units pull less water than a truck-mounted rig, so do extra dry passes and read how renting tools and equipment around St. Louis works before you load one into the car.
### Before the crew arrives
Move anything you can lift alone and anything water would ruin: lamps, plant stands, floor-level electronics, pet bowls, toy bins.
Vacuum thoroughly the day before.
Put pets in a closed room or take them out for the afternoon. Propped doors and loud machines make a bad day for a nervous animal.
Walk the crew to every spot and say what caused it: pet urine, coffee, red drink and grease all get treated differently, and anything already hit with a store-bought spotter needs flagging.
Ask for tabs or blocks under furniture legs that go back on damp carpet. Wood stain and metal rust both transfer.
Ask for the invoice to name the method. For a warranty, “hot water extraction” on paper is the point.
### Clean it, or replace it?
Get down on your knees in the hallway and part the pile with two fingers. If the fibers stand up and just look dirty, cleaning will help. If you see backing through crushed, split or matted fibers, that is wear, and no cleaning brings a worn fiber back.
Press a damp white cloth into a dull area and look at what comes up. Heavy transfer means there is real soil to recover. Check the seams and the edges along the walls too. Carpet that is coming apart is a replacement conversation no matter how clean it gets.
Put the first freeze on your calendar and book the week after. Browse carpet cleaning across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call two companies with the same room list, and ask each one to write the method on the invoice.
If you run the truck-mounted rig that books up every November, the customers who read this are about to call someone. Make sure it’s you, and get more customers in the weeks that matter most.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are signs I need to clean my carpet?
A.  Traffic lanes darker than the carpet under furniture, grit you can feel through a sock near the door, a smell that returns on damp days or when the heat first runs, pile that won’t stand back up, and any spill that soaked through to the pad. The furniture test is the most reliable: slide a chair out and compare.
### Q. Is it worth having your carpets professionally cleaned?
A.  For carpet that is still in good shape, yes. Grit at the base of the pile wears the fibers with every step, and a home vacuum only lifts the loose surface layer. Professional extraction pulls out the deeper soil and oils, and if your carpet is under a Shaw warranty, the invoice is your proof of periodic hot water extraction cleaning.
### Q. What happens if you never clean your carpet?
A.  It wears out faster and holds more of what you track in. Grit dulls and then mats the traffic lanes until they’re worn for good. Meanwhile pollen, pet dander and dust keep collecting, and a warm, humid day or a running furnace brings the smell back into the room.
### Q. How long do you have to stay off carpets after they are cleaned?
A.  Ask your crew, because it depends on the method, the airflow and the weather. After a hot water extraction clean, plan on staying off for most of the day, keep traffic to clean socks at first, and wait until the carpet is fully dry before furniture legs or rugs go back down. Running the HVAC fan speeds it up.
### Q. What type of carpet cleaning is most effective?
A.  For a deep clean, hot water extraction, which Shaw recommends to remove the oils and particulates that make carpet re-soil faster. Low-moisture methods dry quicker and work as touch-ups between deep cleans. Most homes do well with extraction on the 12-to-18-month schedule and touch-ups where traffic is heaviest.
### Q. How much do they charge to clean carpet per room?
A.  Companies quote either per room or per square foot, and most set a minimum for the trip. Room pricing often caps how big a room can be before it counts as two, and stairs, hallways, protector and pet treatment are usually separate lines. Ask which way you’re being quoted and get the total in writing before the hoses come off the truck.
### Q. Is it worth cleaning 15 year old carpet?
A.  Often, if the fibers are intact. Part the pile in a traffic lane: fibers that stand up and just look dirty will clean up noticeably. If you see backing through crushed or split fibers, that’s wear, and cleaning won’t reverse it. On carpet that old, ask the crew for honest expectations before you book.
### Q. How to choose the best carpet cleaning company?
A.  Ask what method they use and why for your carpet, whether they vacuum and pre-spray first, and exactly what the quote includes, down to stairs and spot treatment. Ask whether the invoice will name hot water extraction if you need it for a warranty. Then read reviews for how they handled a job that went wrong, not just the ones that went right.

## The City Wants a Week Before Your Rental Hits the Curb
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renting-tools-and-equipment-in-st-louis
Alarm chirping, the flatbed backs down your block, a skid steer chained to the deck, and the driver leans out the window looking for somewhere to set it down. There’s no driveway. There’s a row of parked cars, a strip of curb in front of your house, and a neighbor on the porch with a coffee, watching.
That strip of curb isn’t yours. In the City of St. Louis, the Street Department requires a permit to temporarily block any part of a street, sidewalk or curb lane, and its Blocking Right of Way permit covers exactly this: construction equipment, a dumpster, a storage container, a moving truck. Apply no later than one week before the date you need it, or two weeks for a job of significant size or length of time.
Then the line that catches weekend projects: blocking hours for sidewalks, curb lanes and traffic lanes run Monday-Friday, between 9am-3pm, with longer hours only considered depending on the traffic at your location. You also supply the barricades, with reflective tape and flashers during all hours of darkness. A rental counter will book you a machine in a five-minute call. The City wants a week.
If you’re in the County with a long driveway, this one may never touch you. If you’re in a brick two-family in the City where the street is the only flat ground you have, it’s the first call, before the rental yard. The Department of Streets is at (314) 647-3111.
### How does equipment rental work?
You reserve a machine for a block of time, show a photo ID and a credit card, leave a deposit hold, take it home or have it delivered, and pay for the time you hold it. The clock is what you buy, not the job. Fuel, worn blades and any damage are usually on you. The rental ends when the counter inspects the machine and closes your ticket, not when you drop it in the yard.
### Three calls before the machine shows up
Rent the machine last. Permit first, locate second, rental yard third. Write that on the fridge, because almost every ruined rental weekend is those three in the wrong order.
First, if anything will sit in the street in the City, start the Blocking Right of Way permit at least a week out. Second, if the machine digs at all, even a two-person auger for fence posts, file a locate request. Missouri law requires notice at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before you start digging, and a working day is every day except Saturday, Sunday or a legally declared state or federal holiday. Locate requests run 24/7 at 811 or 1-800-344-7483. Saturdays and Sundays don’t count toward that wait.
Third, call the rental yard with your dates, the width of your narrowest gate, and what your tow vehicle can actually pull. Book the machine for after the paint and flags are on the grass, not before. That one shift in order is the difference between a Saturday of work and a Saturday of watching a rented trencher sit in the driveway at full price.
One gap the free locate doesn’t fill: lines you own yourself, like the gas run out to the grill, the sprinkler system, the buried wire to a detached garage. Those are on you to find, and a private locator costs far less than the repair.
### Rent or buy for a one-off job?
The garage tells you the answer before the math does. If there’s already a tiller in the corner under a tarp, smelling faintly of old gas, you know how ownership goes for a tool you use once a spring.
Rent when the tool is bigger than the problem you have this month. Buy when you’ll reach for it again next season and the season after. The quick check: divide the purchase price by the day rate you were quoted. That is roughly how many days of use it takes to break even, before you count storage, a carburetor that gums up over the winter, and blades that cost real money.
Some rentals replace a service, not a purchase. A carpet cleaner is the classic one, and the cheapest rental is the one you didn’t need. Our guide to how often carpets actually need cleaning in St. Louis is worth two minutes before you haul one home.
### How rental time is priced
Counters sell time in blocks: a few hours, a day, a week, a month. Each longer block costs more in total and less per hour. A rainy St. Louis spring is the argument for the longer block: when the forecast turns and the yard goes to mud, a weekly rate buys rain days for not much more than a couple of single days would.
Read the return time printed on your contract instead of assuming what “a day” means. Some shops count it from checkout, some from opening to closing. Machines with an hour meter can also cap the engine hours included in a day, so a long, hard run can be billed even if the machine comes back on time. Ask both questions at the counter, out loud, before you sign.
### What do deposits and damage waivers actually cover?
The deposit is usually a hold on your card, released after the machine comes back intact. The damage waiver is different: an optional charge that limits what you owe for accidental damage. It is not insurance, and waivers commonly exclude theft, misuse, overloading and anything the contract calls neglect. Read the exclusions while you’re still standing at the counter.
Before you buy one, make a five-minute call to your own insurance agent. Some homeowner and renter policies extend to equipment in your care and some don’t. If the answer is no, a waiver on a machine you’ve never run before is often cheap peace of mind.
Nothing to do with trenchers: if the little one in your house is ready for school, start with St. Louis preschools.
### Delivery or pickup: which do you need?
Pick it up yourself if it fits in your vehicle and you can lift it alone. Take delivery for anything on tracks, anything needing a trailer with its own brakes, and anything you’d have to drive up a slope. Delivery is usually billed each way, and on many contracts the clock starts when the machine lands, not when you first pull the cord. In the City, if the machine will sit in the curb lane, that’s the Blocking Right of Way permit again.
If you tow it yourself, three things decide whether that’s a good idea: your vehicle’s rated tow capacity, the hitch class and ball size, and whether the trailer needs a brake controller. And if the tow vehicle is riding on tires you’ve been meaning to replace, deal with that first. Here is what new tires cost in St. Louis.
Ask about the delivery window before you agree to it. A long window on a weekend morning can eat the useful half of your day, and you want that conversation before the clock starts, not after.
### What to bring to the counter
A government photo ID and a credit card in the same name. Debit cards are often refused for the deposit hold.
The width of the gate, doorway or side yard the machine has to fit through.
What you’re cutting, breaking or drilling, so the blade or bit matches concrete, asphalt, tile or masonry.
A rough hour count, which decides the block you should buy.
A phone with a camera. Photograph every side of the machine at checkout and again at return.
Ask for the operating rundown instead of trusting the decal. A good counter person will start the machine with you, show you the kill switch, and tell you the one mistake everyone makes with that tool. Those two minutes are the most valuable thing on the lot.
### Is equipment rental taxed on both sides of the river?
Yes. Missouri law taxes the amount paid or charged for rental or lease of tangible personal property, with one exception: if the rental company already paid the tax when it bought the item, it shall not collect the tax again on the rental.
Illinois changed. Effective January 1, 2025, businesses that lease or rent tangible personal property in the ordinary course of business are treated as retailers there, and if you rent from an Illinois business, tax is itemized on your receipt. Renting in Belleville or Edwardsville now reads a lot like renting in Missouri once you see the ticket.
### How do you return it clean, fueled and on time?
Hose the mud and concrete slurry off before you load it, and you’ll hear the difference at the return counter: a quick walk-around instead of a long look. Bring the machine back at or above the fuel level you got it at, with every accessory in the box. Refueling and cleaning charges are where deposits go to die, and one missing pin or key can hold your ticket open.
Late is the expensive failure. Running past the return time can drop you into the next block. If you know by midday you won’t make it, call. Extending over the phone usually costs less than walking in late. Get the closed ticket in writing, and keep your return photos until the deposit hold drops off your card.
Got the permit and the locate on the calendar? Now find the machine. Browse equipment rental across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two yards with your dates, your gate width and your tow vehicle in hand.
If you run the rental yard that gets the panicked call for tomorrow morning, those customers are searching right now, usually late and close to home. Put your yard where they look and get more customers from the jobs that start this week.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to rent equipment?
A.  It depends on the machine and the block of time, and local rates move, so get a quote for your exact dates. You can predict the shape of the bill: the rate, plus sales tax, plus delivery each way if you use it, plus any damage waiver, plus fuel if the machine comes back low. In the City, add a Blocking Right of Way permit if it sits in the street. Ask for the out-the-door total, not the headline day rate.
### Q. Is renting equipment cheaper than buying?
A.  For occasional use, usually. The purchase price is only the opening bid: ownership adds storage, maintenance, replacement blades and the value you lose when you sell it. Renting also puts a better machine in your hands than you would have bought. Buying wins once you use the tool often enough that the day rates start acting like a payment plan.
### Q. What is the 5% rule for renting vs. buying?
A.  That rule comes from housing, not tools. It weighs the yearly cost of owning a home against a year of rent. Nothing like it is standard for equipment. The tool version is blunter: purchase price divided by day rate tells you how many days of use it takes to break even.
### Q. Is equipment rental taxable in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Missouri taxes the amount paid or charged for rental or lease of tangible personal property, unless the rental company already paid the tax when it bought the item. Across the river, Illinois began taxing rental receipts on January 1, 2025, and the tax shows up itemized on your receipt.
### Q. What are the risks of renting equipment?
A.  Three, mostly. Liability for damage, theft or a machine you overloaded, which a waiver only partly covers. Injury, because you’re running something unfamiliar against a clock. And schedule risk, since the clock runs whether it rains or not. Take the walk-around, buy one block longer than you think you need, and read the exclusions.
### Q. Is there an equipment rental app?
A.  Many rental companies let you reserve online, the big chains have their own apps, and peer-to-peer sites let owners rent tools to neighbors. No single app covers every yard around St. Louis, and what an app shows isn’t always what’s sitting on the lot. For a specific date, a phone call still wins.
### Q. What is considered equipment rental?
A.  Taking temporary possession of a machine or tool for a fee without owning it. In practice it runs from a floor sander, a carpet cleaner or a pressure washer through jackhammers, augers and stump grinders up to scissor lifts, dump trailers and compact excavators. If somebody hands you a machine and a return time, that’s an equipment rental.

## Book a St. Louis Hall: 31 Minutes Late Can Cost the Deposit
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-book-a-banquet-hall-in-st-louis
Thirty-one minutes. That is the line in the City of Florissant’s own hall rental rules where a late night turns into a lost deposit. Run thirty minutes or less past the time on your contract and you pay one more hour’s rent. Run thirty-one minutes or more and the entire deposit is forfeited. The same page says no additional time will be provided for set-up or clean-up.
Now stand in that room at the end of the party. The DJ is coiling cable across the floor. Somebody’s aunt is pressing foil over a half-pan of mostaccioli, your cousin is hunting for the lid to the cake carrier, and there are still centerpieces on every table and a stack of gift bags by the door. Nobody is looking at the clock. The clock is the only thing in the building that is keeping score.
Most families book a hall once or twice in a lifetime, for a fiftieth anniversary, a graduation, a quinceañera, a funeral lunch that has to happen before everyone flies home. Nobody hands you the glossary. The money people lose is rarely lost on the first phone call. It is lost in the fine print about the last half hour, the bar, the balloons and the head count, and every one of those rules is written down somewhere before you sign.
### Where can I rent a hall in St. Louis?
Across the metro you are choosing between dedicated banquet centers, hotel ballrooms, parish and church halls, veterans’ and union halls, country club rooms, city and park district community centers, and the event rooms behind breweries, wineries and restaurants. The type of room sets your rules far more than the address does, so sort by rules first.
A banquet center usually runs its own kitchen and bar, and you buy a package. A parish hall or veterans’ post more often rents a bare room and lets you bring the food, which is cheaper and hands you every problem that comes with a hot tray. A city-run room is the cheapest of all and the strictest. Florissant’s rules are a good example of how strict: the person who signs must be at least 21 years old, all alcoholic beverages must stay inside the rental room, and at no time may the tenant, caterers or vendors sell alcoholic beverages. Bring a cooler for the toast, fine. A cash bar, no.
The river matters too. If the hall you love sits on the Illinois side, ask who is allowed to pour before you price the bar, because everything below about permits is the Missouri side of the story.
### What a city hall’s rule sheet teaches about every hall
Private banquet centers rarely post their contracts online. Cities do, which is why Florissant’s rental page is worth reading even if you never set foot in its Celebration Hall. It is a plain-English version of the clauses every hall writes somewhere, and it shows you exactly where the money leaks.
The decorations rule is the one that surprises people most. Florissant allows table decorations only: no tape, putty, pins, nails or Command Strips on walls or windows, and nothing attached to the ceilings or floors. Confetti, glitter, sequins, table scatter, balloons, silly string, open flames and inflatables are strictly prohibited, and using them means forfeiting your deposit. Think about the bag of balloons in your trunk and the roll of painter’s tape you were going to use for the banner. Ask any hall, private or public, for its decoration list before you buy a single thing for the room.
The set-up rule is next. Florissant says tenants must stick to the pre-determined room set-ups and cannot make alterations on the day of the event. Private halls say it more politely, but the floor plan you approve two weeks out is usually the floor plan you get. If your grandmother needs a seat near the door, put it on the drawing.
### What does a per-head quote actually include?
A per-head price usually covers the food, the people who serve it, and the plates, glasses, silverware and house linen it lands on. It often leaves out the room rental, the bar, the service charge and sales tax, and those four are what turn a comfortable number into a tight one. Ask for every add-on in writing: cake cutting, chair covers, a microphone or projector, security, meals for your DJ and photographer, overtime and a cleaning fee. Inside the City of St. Louis, put security at the top of that list if anyone is pouring, for a reason the alcohol section below spells out.
Then ask the one question most people skip: does any of the service charge go to the staff? A service charge is not automatically a tip, and the people carrying trays at your party deserve to know which one you paid. The most useful document a hall can show you is a sample banquet event order, the sheet the kitchen and floor staff actually run the night from, with timing, counts, courses, bar hours and every fee on one page.
### In-house catering or your own caterer?
There are three models and they are not close substitutes. Some halls cook everything and sell you a package. Some keep an approved vendor list you must hire from. Some rent the room and let you bring anyone, often with a kitchen fee. Know which one you are buying before you tour.
In-house catering is the least work and the least flexible. One contract covers everything, which matters when the chafing dishes run dry with forty people still in line. The trade is the menu: you eat what that kitchen does well. Bosnian, Vietnamese, Indian, Mexican and soul food menus are often the whole reason a family goes looking for an outside-catering hall, and the smell of your own family’s food filling that room is worth fighting for. If the food is coming from a family kitchen or a church group rather than a licensed caterer, ask the hall what the health department allows before anyone starts cooking.
### What are the rules on alcohol, corkage and BYOB?
Alcohol is the most regulated thing in the building. In Missouri, a caterer or other business licensed to sell liquor by the drink can serve at your location under a temporary caterer’s permit. Under Missouri Revised Statutes section 311.485, that permit runs no more than one hundred sixty-eight consecutive hours, and the permit holder pays the director of revenue ten dollars for each calendar day or fraction of one.
Inside the City of St. Louis there is a second layer, and it has its own clock. The city’s special-event liquor rules charge $15 per caterer’s permit, per catered area, per day, and if an event goes past midnight it counts as an additional day. The city asks you to allow 10 days for processing, and it states that any event with alcohol requires security from a provider licensed in the City of St. Louis. That last line is the budget item families find out about late.
A sideways thought while you are reading contracts anyway: an estate planning attorney reads the one that matters most.
Which brings you to corkage. Many halls ban outside alcohol, and greed is not usually the reason. Their license and their liability ride on who poured. Where outside bottles are allowed, expect a corkage or setup fee, the hall’s own bartenders, and a hard cut-off time written into the contract.
### What does capacity really mean once you add a dance floor?
The number on a hall’s website is usually the most people the room can legally hold, not the number who can sit down to dinner with elbow room. Start subtracting: a dance floor, the DJ or band, a buffet line with space to queue, a head table, a cake table, a gift table, the bar and the line in front of it, and aisles wide enough for staff carrying trays.
Ask for a to-scale floor plan drawn with your real table count, your dance floor and your buffet in place. Walk it in your head. Can a server get from the kitchen door to the far table with a full tray without turning sideways? If the hall cannot produce that drawing, it has not run many events your size.
### What is in the contract, from deposit to teardown?
Read for six things: the deposit and whether any part comes back, the payment dates, the cancellation and postponement terms, the final head-count deadline, the set-up and teardown windows, and any insurance requirement. Those six decide almost every fight between signing and the party.
Florissant again shows the shape of it. A deposit is required at the time of booking, full payment is due at least 60 days ahead for venue rentals, and deposits come back within 14 business days. Cancel a meeting room less than 30 days out and you lose the rental fees plus a $25 cancellation fee. Private halls set their own numbers, often stiffer, but the questions are identical. The head count is the one that bites: most halls bill the final number you guarantee, so a guest who does not come still eats your money.
Then go back to the clock from the top of this page. Ask when vendors can load in, whether another party uses the room earlier that day, when the music must stop and when every last thing you brought has to be out. Write the answers down, assign one person to start packing before the last song, and if tables, chairs or a tent come from an outside supplier, line those windows up in writing too. Our guide to renting tools and equipment in St. Louis covers how rental periods get counted.
### Five calls to make before you sign anything
Do these with the contract open in front of you and a pen in your hand. Each one takes a few minutes, and each one closes a hole that costs families real money.
The hall. Ask four things and get the answers in writing: the exact end time, what happens in money if you run over, the decoration list, and the deadline for your final floor plan and head count.
A city-run room in Florissant. Florissant’s city contact line is 314-921-5700. Read the city’s facility rental rules first, because the overtime, decoration and alcohol rules are all on that one page.
A St. Louis County park pavilion. St. Louis County Parks takes reservation questions Monday through Friday from 9am-4pm at 314-615-4386. Its terms allow alcohol in a county park only with the reservation and only at the site you reserved, and no alcohol at all at Lone Elk Park.
An event inside the City of St. Louis with a caterer pouring. Read the city’s special-event liquor rules, which also point you to the Building Division at (314) 622-3313 to see whether the building needs an occupancy permit.
Your own family. Name the one person who starts packing before the last song, and give them the end time.
Holding a date and a head count with nowhere to put them? Browse banquet halls across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, tour two rooms the same day, and ask each one for its decoration rules and a sample banquet event order before you talk price.
If you run a hall, a parish room or a catering kitchen, the family reading this is already shopping for you. List your room with us and get more customers from the people holding a date right now.
### What the hall is thinking while you tour
A banquet hall sells a date that exists once. An empty peak night cannot be sold again in February, which is why minimums exist, why prime dates cost more, and why deposits are so often non-refundable: the moment the hall holds your date, it stops selling it. The heat, the insurance and the core staff cost the same whether the room is full or dark, so weekday lunches, trainings and funeral luncheons quietly carry a lot of halls through the year. If your date can move and your budget cannot, say so out loud on the first call. Families start that search on a phone, which is the case for a complete, current listing.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a banquet typically cost?
A.  There is no honest single number until the hall knows your date, head count, menu and bar. Five things move it: the day and season, the head count, an open bar or a cash bar, the room rental or minimum, and what the service charge and tax add on top. Ask for a sample banquet event order to see the whole bill.
### Q. How many banquet tables for 50 guests?
A.  Divide fifty by the number of seats the hall says each of its tables holds, then add one table for the late yes. Ask the hall for the exact table size, because round tables come in more than one size. Then leave floor space for the tables nobody sits at: gifts, cake, buffet and the DJ.
### Q. What permits are needed for a venue?
A.  Start by asking the venue what it already covers, because what falls on you is event-specific. In Missouri, a caterer serving drinks at a location other than its own licensed premises needs a temporary caterer’s permit under section 311.485, and the City of St. Louis adds its own caterer’s permit plus licensed security for any event with alcohol.
### Q. What caterers are available in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the hall, because it may have already decided for you. Ask whether it cooks in house, keeps an approved vendor list, or lets you bring anyone with a kitchen fee. If the choice is open, favor a caterer who has worked that exact room. They already know where the outlets are and how far the kitchen is from the buffet.
### Q. What are some cheap banquet halls in St. Louis that cost under $500?
A.  A full-service hall at a prime time is unlikely to land there once minimums and the bar are counted. A small budget goes furthest in a city or park district community room, a parish hall, a veterans’ post or a union hall, at an off-peak time, where you bring the food and do the clean-up yourself. Read the decoration and clean-up rules first.
### Q. What are some cheap and fun venues for small parties in Saint Louis?
A.  For twenty to forty people a banquet hall is often the wrong tool. Restaurant private rooms, brewery and winery back rooms, St. Louis County park pavilions, community center meeting rooms, and bowling or arcade party rooms handle small groups with less overhead. Ask about the alcohol rule before anything else, since many ban outside drinks.
### Q. How to get an event space for free?
A.  Free usually comes from membership, not luck. Parishes, veterans’ posts, fraternal lodges and union halls sometimes let members use a room for little more than a cleaning fee. Library branches and community centers may offer meeting rooms to residents, usually with no alcohol and set hours. Ask about a damage deposit anyway.
### Q. What are the advantages of a banquet?
A.  One room, one timeline, one bill. A banquet keeps a big group together instead of scattered across a loud restaurant, gives you a place for toasts and a slideshow, and hands cooking, serving and clean-up to someone else. It also gives you a per-person number to budget against before anyone sends an invitation.
### Q. Do banquet halls make good money?
A.  They can, but the money is lumpy. It piles up on a small number of prime nights, the bar tends to carry more of the profit than the food, and the building costs the same whether it is booked or empty. That is why weekday bookings often decide whether a hall has a good year or a thin one.

## Lost Health Coverage? 60 Days, and Free St. Louis City Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-health-insurance-in-missouri
The termination letter is on the kitchen table, under the mug, and somewhere in the second paragraph is a date. Not the last day of work. The other one: the last day your health plan covers you.
Don’t sort it out alone at that table. Dial (314) 612-5918 and you reach the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging, a City of St. Louis office at 1520 Market, not an insurance company.
The name says aging. The City’s own page says otherwise: SLAAA offers assistance for people of all ages with obtaining health insurance through the Affordable Care Act. Its federally trained and state licensed Navigators work one on one, and they can answer your questions or help guide you through the application itself. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8am-5pm.
Call before the calendar decides for you. Open enrollment at healthcare.gov starts November 1. Enroll or change plans by December 15 and pay the first premium, and coverage starts January 1. The last day is January 15. After that, between January 16 and October 31, the door only opens for a Special Enrollment Period.
Lose a job plan in any month and a second clock starts: 60 days to apply. The part almost nobody uses is that the window opens before the loss, too. If you expect to lose coverage in the next 60 days, you can qualify now, and pick the new plan while the old card is still in your wallet.
### What is the best way to pick a health insurance plan?
Go in order. Check MO HealthNet first, since you can apply for Medicaid any time of year. Then look at any job offer in the household. Then shop healthcare.gov. Before you click enroll, open the plan’s provider list and drug list and find your own doctor, your hospital and your prescriptions by name. If you qualify for cost-sharing reductions, you must pick a Silver plan to get them.
### The Silver rule that quietly costs families money
On the healthcare.gov screen, the Bronze plan sits at the top with the smallest monthly number, and after a layoff that small number looks like relief. For a lot of households it’s a trap.
If your income qualifies you for cost-sharing reductions, you must pick a plan in the Silver category to get them. Those reductions lower what you pay at the counter and the clinic desk, not just the premium. Buy Bronze to shave the monthly bill and you leave that help on the table for the whole year. A Navigator will run both side by side with you, so you see the real yearly cost instead of the sticker.
### Do the 60-day math tonight, not next month
Pull that letter out from under the mug and circle the date your plan ends with a pen. Count forward 60 days and write that date on the envelope too. That second date is the one that matters.
Then make three moves while the coffee is still warm. Call SLAAA at (314) 612-5918 and ask for a Navigator appointment. Apply for MO HealthNet through the state’s online portal at mydss.mo.gov or by phone at 855-373-9994, so you know whether you qualify before you pay for anything. Then start a healthcare.gov application with your best guess at this year’s household income.
Keep the termination letter somewhere you can find it. When you apply with a life event like this, you may be asked to send documents to confirm that you qualify, and you must send them before you can start using the coverage.
The good news on timing: with this Special Enrollment Period, your Marketplace coverage can start the first day of the month after you lose your job-based plan. Do it early and there is no gap at all.
### Who qualifies for MO HealthNet now?
More people than the old rules taught us to expect. Missouri’s Adult Expansion Group covers adults age 19 through 64 with income at or below 138% of the federal poverty level, who are not pregnant, not on Medicare Part A or B and not receiving SSI. That covers a lot of people working part time, between jobs, or self-employed in a slow stretch, and many of them talk themselves out of applying.
Don’t decide from memory that you’re over the line. The application costs nothing but an evening and a stack of pay stubs, and there is no enrollment season: you can apply for Medicaid and CHIP any time of year. And kids can qualify for CHIP even when their parents earn too much for Medicaid.
If you are the one losing MO HealthNet, say at a renewal that went wrong, you get a longer runway. Someone who lost Medicaid or CHIP coverage in the past 90 days may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period at healthcare.gov.
### Navigator or broker: who should you call?
Both can sit with you. The difference is who they answer to.
A Navigator, or any Marketplace assister, is trained and certified by the Marketplace to help you apply for a plan with any savings you qualify for, or to apply for free or low-cost coverage through Medicaid or CHIP. They are required to give fair, impartial and accurate information. That makes them the right first call when the situation is tangled: one spouse with a job offer, a teenager who might qualify for MO HealthNet, income that swings with every shift.
An agent or broker is trained and certified to sell Marketplace plans in the state where they are licensed, and they are generally paid by insurance companies. They answer your questions about the plans they sell. A good one is fast once you already know you want a Marketplace plan and need help comparing networks hospital by hospital. You still get the premium tax credit through a broker, as long as they enroll you through the Marketplace.
There is no wrong door here. There is only the cost of waiting while you decide which door.
### Covering the kids when the parents don’t qualify
The sound of a kid coughing in the middle of the night is when the coverage question stops being abstract. Here is the piece many parents miss: the Children’s Health Insurance Program provides low-cost health coverage to children in families that earn too much money to qualify for Medicaid but not enough to buy private insurance.
So a household can sit above the adult line and still have children who qualify. Parents on a healthcare.gov plan with kids on Missouri’s program is ordinary, not a loophole. Apply for them through MO HealthNet, and because you can apply for Medicaid and CHIP any time of year, you don’t wait for open enrollment to cover a child.
### What to bring to the table
The appointment goes faster when the folder is already full. Bring Social Security numbers and birth dates for everyone applying, recent pay stubs or self-employment records, your best estimate of this year’s household income, the termination letter, and details on any job-based plan someone in the house was offered.
The income estimate is the one that trips people. Work it out on paper before you sit down, including side work and any severance, and you can often finish in one sitting instead of three.
Different problem, same kitchen: the flickering light over that table probably needs an electrician, not another bulb.
### Is COBRA worth keeping after a layoff?
When you lose job-based coverage, your former employer may offer you COBRA, which can let you temporarily keep the health coverage you had. The first quote still makes people sit down hard, because you pay the full cost that your employer used to split with you.
Price a Marketplace plan before you sign. Marketplace plans may cost less than COBRA, especially if you qualify for savings based on your income, and a job loss usually lowers that income. Two rules to know:
You can still switch from COBRA to a Marketplace plan if it is within 60 days of when you lost your job-based coverage.
After that, voluntarily dropping COBRA doesn’t count as a reason to enroll. Choosing to stop paying the premiums on your own doesn’t qualify you either, so decide inside the first 60 days.
### Living in the Metro East? Different website, different rules
Cross the Poplar Street Bridge and the paperwork changes. Illinois has its own state-based marketplace, Get Covered Illinois, the state’s official health insurance marketplace, and that is where people in Belleville, Edwardsville or Granite City shop.
The trap for families who live in Illinois and work in Missouri: your plan follows where you live, but the network decides whether the St. Louis hospital you actually drive to is covered. Check the network before enrolling, not after the first bill. Big medical bills are one of the common roads into filing bankruptcy in Missouri, and a network mismatch is a quiet way to start down it.
Would rather sit across a desk from someone than a screen? Browse health insurance agents and brokers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and bring your pay stubs, your termination letter and a list of your prescriptions to the first meeting.
If you’re the broker who answers the phone in July, not just in open enrollment, families searching by their own neighborhood should be able to find you. Put your agency in front of them.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do you really need health insurance?
A.  For most people, yes, and not because of a fine. One ambulance ride, one broken ankle on an icy step, one night in a hospital bed can turn into a bill that follows you for years. Insurance is mostly protection against the bill you can’t pay, and the plan’s out-of-pocket maximum is the number that caps your worst year.
### Q. Should I choose HMO or PPO?
A.  An HMO usually costs less each month and keeps you inside a set network, often with a primary care doctor sending you to specialists. A PPO costs more and gives you wider choice plus some out-of-network coverage. Around St. Louis the bigger question is which hospital system and which specialists are inside the network. Settle that first, then pick the plan type.
### Q. What does health insurance not cover?
A.  Plans differ, but cosmetic procedures, routine adult dental and vision, and care the plan decides isn’t medically necessary are common gaps. Out-of-network care may be covered poorly or not at all. Read the plan’s benefits summary and its exclusions before you enroll, not after a claim comes back denied.
### Q. Does the US penalize you for not having health insurance?
A.  Not anymore at the federal level. The fee for not having health insurance no longer applies, so you no longer pay a federal tax penalty for going without coverage. The real cost of going without is the full bill, with nobody negotiating it down for you.
### Q. How long do I need to have health insurance before I can use it?
A.  You can use it the day coverage starts. During open enrollment, people who enroll by December 15 and pay their first premium are covered starting January 1. After losing job-based coverage, your Marketplace plan can start the first day of the month after the old plan ends, as long as you have sent any documents the Marketplace asks for.
### Q. What is the main reason to have health insurance?
A.  To keep one bad day from becoming a bad decade. Routine care matters too, but the main job is the big, unplanned bill: the surgery, the diagnosis, the hospital stay you never saw coming. Coverage turns a number with no ceiling into a number you can plan around, and it gets you the negotiated rate instead of the full list price. If cost is what stops you, start with a call to a Navigator before you decide you can’t afford it.
### Q. Is it actually cheaper to not have health insurance?
A.  It’s cheaper right up until it isn’t. Going without only works out if nothing serious happens, and nobody gets to pick that. Before you decide the premium is the problem, check MO HealthNet and the savings on healthcare.gov, or call SLAAA’s Navigators and let them run the numbers with you.

## No Reflectors, No Refunds: St. Louis Event Photo Fine Print
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-an-event-photographer-actually-covers-in-st-louis
No reflectors, and no refund. At the Missouri Botanical Garden, lighting equipment and reflectors are not permitted, and the permit required for formal photography for private personal use is good for the date you buy only and is nonrefundable. A package that says four hours, one photographer, an online gallery covers none of that. The permit is on you, and the big round reflector your photographer carries everywhere stays in the trunk.
Learn that in the parking lot, with Grandma already in her good shoes and the evening light going soft over the gardens, and the portrait is gone. Nobody lied to you. The quote just covered what quotes cover: time, people holding cameras, and files. Everything around it, the permit, the tax, the second room, the album, the overtime when the toasts run long, lives on separate lines, or nowhere at all.
So read a photography quote like a list of what is missing. Here is what an event booking in St. Louis actually covers, what it quietly leaves out, and the five questions that turn a vague price into a promise you can hold someone to.
### What is included in event photography?
Event photography is sold as a block of time, not a set of pictures. A typical booking names a window of coverage hours, the number of photographers on site, a set of edited digital images delivered in an online gallery, and a license that spells out how you may use them. Nearly everything else is extra: a second shooter, an album, prints, a USB drive, raw files, travel past a set radius, rush delivery and overtime.
None of that is a hidden fee when it is written down. It only becomes one when the quote said “coverage” and you heard “everything.” Image counts work the same way. A contract that promises roughly a certain number of edited images is promising a range, because a loud reception and a quiet awards dinner produce very different numbers of keepers. If one shot matters, the whole family on the steps, the retiring boss with her team, the sponsor banner, write it on a shot list and staple it to the contract.
### Five questions to ask before you sign anything
First: when does the clock start? At the contracted time, or when the shooting starts? Events run late and contracts do not, so a ceremony that slips forty minutes can eat forty minutes of coverage you paid for while the photographer stands in an empty room. Closing times do not slip either: at the Missouri Botanical Garden, permit sessions must be completed and groups departed by close, no exceptions, so a late toast can cost you the garden portrait entirely. Second: how many photographers, and where is each one standing? One person cannot be in two rooms. If the getting-ready happens in two places, or a conference runs breakout sessions side by side, a single shooter means one of them goes unphotographed.
Third: what comes back, and by when? Ask for the number of edited images as a range, the delivery date in weeks, and how long the gallery stays online before it comes down. Fourth: what can we do with the photos? Posting them is one thing. A recruiting brochure, a paid ad or a billboard is another, and is often priced separately. Fifth: what is the overtime rate, and in what increments does it bill? The night the speeches run long is the wrong night to learn the answer.
Then ask the one most families skip: will you send me a sample contract? A photographer who sends one quickly has usually written a good one. Read it at the kitchen table with a pen, not on your phone in a hurry between other errands.
### Who owns the photos, you or the photographer?
The photographer, almost always. The U.S. Copyright Office says the author and initial copyright owner of a photograph is generally the person who “shoots” or “takes” the photo, and paying for the session does not change that by itself. What you get is a license. The Copyright Office names one limited exception, a photograph created as a work made for hire, and it is not something that happens by accident on a party invoice.
That matters less than people fear for a family event. A personal-use license usually covers printing, sharing and posting, which is what most families want. It matters more for a business: if the photos from a company anniversary are headed for a website, a recruiting page or paid social, say so before the quote, so the license and the price match where the pictures are going.
And in St. Louis there is a second license in play that the photographer cannot sell you. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s policy says visitors agree not to use commercially any photography taken at the Garden. A family portrait among the roses is fine. The same frame on your company’s billboard is a different conversation, and it starts with the Garden, not the photographer.
Raw files are the other sore spot. Most contracts leave them out, and the reason is craft, not stinginess: an unedited file looks flat and wrong, and it carries the photographer’s name. If what you really want is more pictures, ask for a bigger edited set or a few specific extra edits instead.
If there is a second shooter, ask three more things. Who edits the second shooter’s images, the lead or the second? Do those frames land in the same gallery as everything else? And does the second shooter work under the lead photographer’s contract, or a separate one? The answers are usually fine. You just want them in writing before the day, not discovered afterward, when a set of pictures of your own family turns out to be governed by an agreement you never saw.
### The tax line nobody mentions in Missouri
Here is the part of the package that changes the bill and almost never comes up in the first phone call. The Missouri Department of Revenue’s Photographers Tax Matrix lists downloaded photos as exempt, and photography services that do not include receipt of tangible personal property as exempt. But photography services that include tangible personal property, such as CDs, DVDs, a USB device containing photographs or photo albums, are taxable. So are picture frames, ready-to-frame photographs and canvas images.
In plain terms: the same afternoon of shooting can be taxed differently depending on whether the photos arrive as a download link or in a leather album with a ribbon on the box. The album is not only a keepsake you can hold. It can change the tax character of the sale. The department’s own matrix says it may not cover every situation, so ask your photographer two simple questions: does the quote include tax, and which lines are taxable?
### Where you can shoot without a permit, and where you cannot
The rules change from one St. Louis landmark to the next, and the package covers none of them. At Gateway Arch National Park, the National Park Service says that in most cases permits and fees are not required for filming or still photography involving eight or fewer individuals, as long as the shoot meets the park’s conditions, including using hand-carried equipment only. A big family reunion with a light stand is a different conversation.
The Missouri Botanical Garden is the strict one, and the details are worth knowing before you promise anybody a garden portrait. Reservations should be made at least 24 hours in advance. Photography is permitted only in the outdoor, public areas, not inside the Climatron or other buildings and conservatories. It is not allowed during evening public events, including the Whitaker Music Festival and Garden Glow evenings. Props are limited to one per person, no larger than two feet by two feet. Sessions must be finished and groups gone by close, no exceptions.
One exception helps a lot: the Garden says a permit is not required for a booked ceremony or private event at the Garden. If you are holding the event there, ask your event contact for the photography guidelines instead of buying a separate permit. And if you would rather skip permits, weather and closing times altogether for the portraits, renting a photo studio in St. Louis is the controlled option.
Unrelated, but someone has to say it: after all this planning, the metro’s bakeries deserve a slow morning and a warm box on your lap.
### Hours, overtime and the clock nobody watches
Count backward from the moments you cannot lose, then pad both ends. For a birthday or anniversary party, that is usually the arrivals, the toast, the cake and the big group photo. For a company event, it is the empty room before doors open, the speeches, then the awards. Put the timeline in the contract so the photographer knows when the moment that matters is supposed to happen, and who to ask when it moves.
Overtime is the line people never read. Some photographers bill in half hours, some in full hours, and some have a hard out because the venue closes or they have another job in the morning. A photographer who tells you no ahead of time is doing you a favor. One who says “we’ll figure it out” is handing you an awkward conversation late in the evening with the DJ still going.
Last, ask about the sneak peek: a handful of images sent within a day or two, so you have something to post while the full gallery is being edited. Then, the week the full set arrives, download every file to two places. Galleries are hosted, hosting costs money, and most of them come down eventually.
Ask for the contract before you ask for the price. Browse event photographers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, request a sample contract from three, and check each one for hours, shooters, delivery date, license and tax.
If you’re the event photographer whose contract answers all five questions, the families reading this are about to call someone. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does “event photographer” mean?
A.  A photographer hired to document something that happens once, in real time, without stopping it. Unlike a portrait session, the event runs on its own schedule, and the photographer works around it, catching people, speeches, details and the room as they happen.
### Q. What is the purpose of event photography?
A.  To keep a day you cannot repeat. For families it is the faces, the toast and the group shot with everyone in it. For businesses and nonprofits the photos also become recaps, sponsor reports, recruiting material and next year’s promotion, which is why the license matters as much as the pictures.
### Q. What are some examples of event photography?
A.  Weddings and receptions, milestone birthdays and anniversaries, retirement parties, graduations, quinceañeras, bar and bat mitzvahs, galas and fundraisers, award banquets, grand openings, conferences and trade shows. Headshot stations at a conference are usually quoted as a separate service.
### Q. Where are some good locations for a photoshoot in St. Louis?
A.  Pick by the rules as much as the scenery. Gateway Arch National Park needs no permit in most cases for eight or fewer people using hand-carried gear in public areas. The Missouri Botanical Garden requires a permit for formal photography, limits sessions to outdoor public areas, and does not allow lighting equipment or reflectors. A rented studio skips weather and closing times entirely.
### Q. How much should an event photographer charge?
A.  There is no single right number, because the price is built from coverage hours, the number of photographers, editing time, delivery format and deadline, license, travel, and whether physical products make part of the sale taxable in Missouri. Ask for one total plus the itemized list behind it. For local ranges, see what a photographer costs in St. Louis.
### Q. How much to charge for a 4 hour event photography?
A.  Four hours is a block of time, not a package. The price depends on what sits around it: one photographer or two, how many edited images, how fast, what license, travel, and whether an album or USB drive is included. Price the whole scope as one total, then confirm the overtime rate before you sign.
### Q. What is the 20 60 20 rule in photography?
A.  People online use the phrase in conflicting ways, from splitting a frame into foreground, subject and background to sorting shots into strong, average and unusable. Because it means different things to different people, it is not a useful way to judge a booking. Judge the contract instead.

## Gelato vs. Ice Cream? The Gooey Butter Scoop Is Custard
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/gelato-vs-ice-cream-and-where-to-get-both-in-st-louis
Cream cheese, butter, a crumble of crust, all of it cold and slowly going soft on your tongue. The gooey butter cake scoop at Clementine’s in Lafayette Square tastes like the pastry, and the company says it is the most popular flavor at that shop. Now read its ingredient list. The base is not plain ice cream mix. It is a custard ice cream mix, with egg yolks.
So the scoop most people would call ice cream is quietly closer to the custard on Chippewa than to anything in a gelato case. And that one label is the easiest way to understand the whole gelato-versus-ice-cream question, because the difference is not magic or marketing. It is what goes into the base: milk, cream, or cream plus yolk.
Three local makers publish it. Gelato di Riso on The Hill says its Dolce gelatos are made with milk, instead of high-fat cream. Clementine’s standard ice cream mix starts with cream. And the frozen-custard concrete, the specialty of Ted Drewes on Chippewa, starts from a base with its own federal line for egg yolk. You can taste all three in one evening, in that order, for the price of three cups. Here is how.
### Is gelato basically just ice cream?
No. Ice cream has a legal floor in this country: under the federal standard, it must contain not less than 10 percent milkfat and weigh not less than 4.5 pounds to the gallon. What the good gelato shops do is spelled out by the shops themselves.
Gelato di Riso puts it plainly on its own site: its Italian gelato is made fresh every day, and it contains less air than American ice cream, making it more velvety in texture and rich in flavor. Less air is the part you feel first. The scoop sits heavier in the cup. It does not squeak against your teeth the way a hard-frozen ball of ice cream does. It slumps, and the flavor arrives all at once instead of after the cold wears off.
### Spoon one: milk, on The Hill
Gelato di Riso says its home on The Hill is where it makes all of its gelato, and it sells it there and at its second shop in downtown Kirkwood. The menu splits the case in two. Milk-based flavors run from Amaretto and Bacio to Stracciatella and Tiramisu. Water-based fruit flavors, Blood Orange, Lemon, Mango, Pink Grapefruit and more, carry no milk at all, which is why a lemon there can taste sharp enough to make your jaw tingle.
Two practical notes from the shop’s own menu. Flavors change daily, and it tells you to call the store for what is in the case, so do not drive across town for one flavor without calling. And if the evening is cool, order the affogato, espresso poured over your choice of gelato, and watch the hot coffee carve a little brown canyon through the scoop.
### Spoon two: cream, in Lafayette Square
Clementine’s publishes its ingredients, and the standard ice cream mix starts with cream, milk, skim milk, sugar and nonfat dry milk. That is the richer, rounder, coat-your-mouth feeling of American ice cream, the kind that leaves a film on the spoon. The company calls itself a maker of small-batch flavors, including Naughty, alcohol-infused ones, and non-dairy options.
At its Lafayette Square shop, the company says its most popular flavor is gooey butter cake, and that owner Tamara Keefe was the first to turn the classic St. Louis breakfast pastry into a frozen treat. Look at that flavor’s ingredient list and the base changes: a custard ice cream mix with egg yolks, then cream cheese, butter and crust folded in. So the most St. Louis scoop in that case is quietly closer to custard than to gelato.
### Spoon three: cream and yolk, on Chippewa
Frozen custard has a legal line of its own. The same federal rule says frozen custard shall contain 1.4 percent egg yolk solids by weight of the finished food, and ordinary ice cream contains less than that. The yolk is what makes custard eat silky and dense, and it is why a St. Louis concrete can hang upside down over a parking lot without falling out of the cup.
According to the State Historical Society of Missouri’s Missouri Encyclopedia, Ted Drewes opened its stand at what is now 6726 Chippewa Street in 1941, tapping the crowds on Route 66. In 1959, a neighborhood teen kept demanding thicker malts, and Drewes Jr., managing the Chippewa stand, tinkered until he had a malt that could be held upside-down without spilling. He called it a concrete. Stand in that line on a warm night and you will hear the cup get flipped before you see it.
### What to order at each stop
At Gelato di Riso, the cup sizes tell you how many flavors you get, not just how much: a Piccolo holds 1-2 flavors, a Medio 1-3 and a Grande 1-4, and the waffle cones take 1-2. That makes the Medio the smart order for a comparison night, one milk-based flavor and one fruit flavor side by side, so you can feel the cream-free richness against the clean, cold bite of the fruit. If someone in your group skips sugar, the Hill shop lists sugar-free chocolate and raspberry, and only that location carries them. Pints and quarts go home with you.
At Clementine’s, the gooey butter cake scoop is the obvious local order, and a good test of the custard question, since its own ingredient list puts egg yolks in the base. If you fall for a flavor, the company ships pints nationwide in the continental U.S. It also closes on Thanksgiving Day and Christmas Day, which is worth knowing before you promise the cousins a holiday scoop.
At the custard window on Chippewa, order a concrete and watch the hand-off. It is served upside down to prove the point. That is the whole show, and it comes with the order.
### How to run the three-spoon test in one evening
Pick one flavor you can find in all three styles, vanilla or chocolate works, and taste them in the order milk, cream, custard. Going lightest to richest keeps the first spoon from getting buried. Take a sip of water between stops. Let each spoonful sit on your tongue for a second before you swallow, and pay attention to two things: how fast the flavor shows up, and what is left in your mouth afterward.
The gelato tastes like the ingredient. The ice cream tastes like the ingredient wrapped in cream. The custard tastes like a dessert that happens to contain the ingredient. None of them loses. They just answer different cravings, and once you have tasted them in a row you will know which one you were actually craving the next time somebody in the back seat says the word.
One house rule makes it fair: call Gelato di Riso ahead about the flavor list, since it changes daily, and check each shop’s hours on its own site before you go.
Wildly off topic: that slow drip under the kitchen sink is not going to fix itself, so find a St. Louis plumber before the cabinet floor goes soft.
### Which is healthier, gelato or regular ice cream?
Neither is health food, and the honest answer depends on the shop. Ice cream carries a legal minimum of 10 percent milkfat. A gelato made with milk instead of high-fat cream, the way Gelato di Riso describes its Dolce flavors, is usually the lower-fat spoonful. A water-based fruit gelato drops the dairy entirely.
The catch is density. Less air means more actual dessert in the same size cup, so a small gelato is not automatically the lighter choice. If you are managing blood sugar, a dairy allergy or a doctor’s orders, ask to see the nutrition or ingredient information. Clementine’s posts ingredient lists flavor by flavor, which is exactly the kind of thing worth reading before you order.
### Where frozen custard fits in this town
The Missouri Encyclopedia lists gooey butter cake and frozen-custard concretes among the city’s signature sweets, next to toasted ravioli and Provel pizza on the savory side. Custard is the default summer stop here, a walk-up window and a line in the parking lot, with the line being half the point. It is where a lot of teams end up after a game, and where a lot of kids celebrate their first meet. If that is your household, our guide on signing your kid up for gymnastics in St. Louis covers the part that happens before the custard.
Gelato is the sit-down cousin, a cafe chair, an espresso, a long slow cup. Ice cream sits in between. Knowing that, you can pick the place by the night you want to have, not just the dessert.
Settle it with your own spoon this week. Browse ice cream and gelato shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick a gelateria, a creamery and a custard stand, and taste them in that order.
