### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is so special about gelato ice cream?
A.  Less air. Gelato di Riso says its gelato contains less air than American ice cream, making it more velvety in texture and rich in flavor. The scoop is denser, softer and quicker to taste, especially in fruit flavors made with water instead of milk.
### Q. Is gelato healthier than ice cream?
A.  Often lower in fat, not always lighter overall. Ice cream must contain at least 10 percent milkfat under federal rules, while a gelato made with milk instead of high-fat cream usually carries less. Gelato is denser, though, so the same size cup holds more dessert. Read the shop’s ingredient or nutrition information if it matters to you.
### Q. Why do people prefer gelato over ice cream?
A.  Texture and flavor. Less air makes it velvety rather than fluffy, and less fat coating your tongue lets fruit and nut flavors come through sharper. Plenty of people prefer ice cream for the opposite reason: it is richer and creamier, and it holds up better in a cone on a hot night.
### Q. Is gelato more expensive than ice cream?
A.  Prices vary shop to shop, so compare at the counter. When a cup does cost more, part of the reason is the air: a denser product means fewer cups from the same batch, and small batches made fresh daily take more hands than a tub from the freezer aisle.
### Q. Does gelato go in the freezer or refrigerator?
A.  The freezer. In the refrigerator it melts and the texture is ruined when it refreezes. A home freezer runs colder than a gelato case, so a pint from Gelato di Riso’s to-go menu will firm up at home. Let it sit on the counter a few minutes before you scoop.
### Q. Where is the best place to get gelato?
A.  The shop that makes it on site, in small batches, from a list that changes. Ask at the counter whether they make it there. In St. Louis, Gelato di Riso says it makes all of its gelato at its home on The Hill and changes flavors daily, and it sells it there and in downtown Kirkwood.
### Q. Who has the best ice cream in St. Louis?
A.  It depends which of the three you are craving. For velvety Italian gelato, go to a shop that makes it daily. For rich, cream-first ice cream with local flavors, try a small-batch creamery like Clementine’s. For custard, the concrete on Chippewa is the one people line up for.
### Q. What is the most famous custard in St. Louis?
A.  Ted Drewes. The Missouri Encyclopedia says its Chippewa stand opened in 1941 on Route 66. In 1959 Drewes Jr. tinkered there until he had a malt that could be held upside-down without spilling, and he called it a concrete.
### Q. What is a signature St. Louis dessert?
A.  Gooey butter cake and the frozen custard concrete. You can even get the first one frozen: Clementine’s says gooey butter cake is the most popular flavor at its Lafayette Square shop, built on a custard ice cream mix with egg yolks.

## Kids Gymnastics in St. Louis: The No Make-Up Rule to Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-signing-your-kid-up-for-gymnastics-in-st-louis
A registration form, half filled in on your phone, with a paragraph in capital letters near the bottom: ONCE A SESSION HAS COMMENCED YOU ARE IN CLASS FOR THE ENTIRE SESSION, regardless of attendance. Most parents scroll right past it to the signature box. That line is from St. Louis Gym Centre in Webster Groves, which calls itself the oldest gymnastics club in St. Louis, and it is the most useful sentence you will read before your kid’s first cartwheel on a real mat.
Here is what it means at the kitchen table. The club does not offer make-up classes for absences. Once a session begins, there are no refunds or credits for dropping a class mid-session. So the fever that keeps your four-year-old on the couch, wrapped in a blanket, sniffling through cartoons, costs you that class. Nobody is being unfair. Tuition, in the club’s own words, pays for your child’s place in class, not a specific number of classes.
And the spot itself has a clock on it. Current students have to pay by the Priority Due Date, and after it, the club’s registration agreement says the computer system electronically deletes unpaid students from the roster and new students are placed in the vacancies. The club does not invoice. It sends a reminder, and keeping track of the date is on you.
Another local club, St. Louis Spirits Gymnastics Club runs the opposite model: monthly tuition on automatic payment, with a digital payment method kept on file, and a 4-Class Trial of four consecutive weekly classes before your kid moves into an ongoing class. Neither model is the wrong one. They just fail in different ways for different families, and you want to know which one you are signing before the chalk dust is on your kid’s palms.
### At what age should you start gymnastics?
Earlier than most parents think, and with less pressure than they fear. St. Louis Gym Centre runs a 45-minute parent-and-child class for 1- and 2-year-olds, where the coach guides the class and parents lead their own kids through it. At 3 and 4, the class is still 45 minutes, but the coach leads and no parent joins. St. Louis Spirits starts ages 4 and under in its Tumbling Tigers program and opens Tumbling or All-Around Gymnastics at 6.
At that age it is rolling, hanging, balancing and waiting your turn in a wobbly line of small kids in leotards. It is genuinely good for coordination and confidence. It is not a head start on anything, and a kid who starts at seven is not behind. Start when your kid cannot stop moving and wants somewhere to put it.
### Five questions to ask before you hand over a card
First, is billing by the session or by the month? A session gym collects up front for a block of weeks; a monthly gym charges the card on file. Ask which, and write the date down. Second, what happens when my kid misses a class? Some gyms offer make-ups. St. Louis Gym Centre does not offer make-up classes for absences, and it says so plainly. Third, what happens if we stop halfway? At St. Louis Gym Centre, dropping a class mid-session gets you no refund or credit. Ask every gym the same question and get the answer before you pay.
Fourth, is there a trial? St. Louis Spirits builds one in, because, as its own FAQ puts it, one class does not tell the whole story. Four weeks lets a nervous kid stop clinging to your leg at the door. Fifth, do you discount siblings? St. Louis Gym Centre charges the most expensive class in the family at full fare and takes 20% off every class tuition after that, which matters fast once a younger sibling starts pointing at the mats.
Then go watch a class from the viewing area before you sign anything. Count the kids per coach. Watch whether a coach has hands on the kid on the beam or is talking from six feet away. You can tell within a few minutes whether the little ones are being taught or just kept busy.
### Session gym or monthly gym: which one fits your house?
Think about the last two months of your actual life, not the version on the fridge calendar. If your kid catches every bug that comes home from preschool, if a parent works rotating shifts, or if a grandparent does half the driving, a prepaid session with no make-ups will quietly eat money. You will pay for weeks your kid spends on the couch with a juice box and a thermometer. A monthly plan with a trial lets you test the drive, the coach and the kid before you commit, though it also keeps charging until you cancel, so ask exactly how and when to stop it.
If your weeks are steady and your kid never misses, the session model is simple: pay once, show up, done, and the due date is the only thing to guard. Either way, put the date in your phone the day you sign. The pain in this sport is rarely the price. It is the surprise.
### What the first class actually looks like
Loud. The thump of small feet landing on mats, a coach’s voice counting, the squeak of hands on a low bar, somebody crying over a stamp they did not get. Your kid will keep looking back at you to make sure you saw.
Dress them simply. St. Louis Spirits says your child does not need special equipment or an expensive uniform to get started. Clothing should cover the stomach and back and should not have zippers, snaps or buttons. No jewelry. Longer hair has to be pulled back securely and kept out of the face, which is a safety rule, not a style note, once your kid is upside down. Plan to arrive at least 10 minutes early for the first class so there is time to park, check in and peel a shy kid off your hip.
### Rec, pre-team and team are three different calendars
Rec is one class a week and no meets. Team is a season: more nights at the gym, competitions, a leotard you did not budget for, and weekends that belong to the sport. In between sits pre-team, the last low-commitment stop before the invitation that changes your family’s week. St. Louis Gym Centre fields Women’s DP, Women’s Xcel and Men’s DP teams. St. Louis Spirits lists Gymnastics Teams for ages 6 and up.
When a coach brings up team, ask for the practice schedule in writing, the full list of season fees, and how many meets are on the calendar. Not the range. The schedule. If you are still sampling activities, the best kids music, art and dance classes in St. Louis are worth a look before one sport takes over the calendar.
Off topic, and we know it: if that brown ring on the ceiling above the couch is growing, you need a roofer before you need a leotard.
### The safety check you can do tonight
Read the waiver before you tap agree. On St. Louis Gym Centre’s waiver, you and your child waive and release all rights and claims for damages, including injuries caused by the negligence or fault of the Centre or its workers. That language is common in youth sports, and it is still worth reading slowly, with your kid’s sneakers by the door, so you know what you are agreeing to.
Then look up the coaches. The U.S. Center for SafeSport publishes a Centralized Disciplinary Database that lists adults who have been suspended or deemed ineligible to participate in their sport. Checking it is an ordinary thing for a parent to do and nothing to feel awkward about. Ask the gym who on shift is trained in first aid, who decides when a kid sits out after a hard fall, and how often the equipment is checked. A gym that has thought about it answers fast. And if the same wrist or ankle keeps hurting, that is a doctor’s call, not a coach’s. Here is when to see an orthopedist in St. Louis.
The preschool price tag
### How much does gymnastics cost per class?
At St. Louis Gym Centre in Webster Groves, the 45-minute class for 3- and 4-year-olds is $196 per 8-week session, the parent-and-child class for 1- and 2-year-olds is $186, and there is a $60 yearly family registration fee. What moves the number: the class length and program, how many kids you enroll, and whether you miss weeks you have already paid for.
### When to switch tracks or stop
Watch for dread in the car on the way to practice that lasts more than a few weeks, a kid who used to talk about the beam at dinner and now goes quiet, and pain that keeps coming back to the same joint. None of those automatically means quit. Often it means a different track, a lighter schedule or a different gym. And plenty of kids do rec for years, never compete, and walk into middle school with better balance than anyone in the hallway.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What age is too late to start gymnastics?
A.  For recreational gymnastics there is no real cutoff. St. Louis Spirits enrolls ages 6 and up in Tumbling or All-Around Gymnastics, and St. Louis Gym Centre lists Adults’ Boot Camps and Open Workout on its own menu. A late start changes which track makes sense, not whether the sport is open to your kid.
### Q. Should I put my 3 year old in gymnastics?
A.  If your kid loves to climb and tumble, yes, for the fun and the coordination. At St. Louis Gym Centre the class for 3- and 4-year-olds is 45 minutes, the coach leads it, and no parent needs to join. Expect rolling, hanging and balancing, not a competitive head start.
### Q. Is 4 too old to start gymnastics?
A.  Not at all. St. Louis Spirits starts ages 4 and under in its Tumbling Tigers program, so a four-year-old walks in with kids the same age doing the same first skills.
### Q. What age should a girl start gymnastics?
A.  The same age as a boy. St. Louis Gym Centre’s class for 1- and 2-year-olds is coed, and for school-age kids it runs separate Girls’ Progressive Classes and Boys’ Progressive Classes. What matters more than age is whether your kid is itching to climb, roll and hang off things.
### Q. Is gymnastics an expensive sport?
A.  Rec is a predictable tuition bill. Team is where it climbs: season fees, meet entry fees, a competition leotard and warm-ups, and travel at the higher levels. Ask any gym for the full list in writing before your kid accepts a team spot, and ask what happens to that money if you leave mid-season.
### Q. Why is gymnastics so expensive?
A.  A gym needs a big, tall building, mats, bars and beams, and coaches who can spot small kids up close, and none of that shrinks when a class is half full. That is also why many gyms bill for your spot rather than for the classes your kid attends.
### Q. How to choose a gymnastics gym?
A.  Watch a class first. Then ask how billing works, whether missed classes can be made up, what happens if you drop mid-session, whether there is a trial, and whether siblings get a discount. Read the waiver before you sign it.
### Q. Is gymnastics worth the money?
A.  For most kids the payoff is balance, strength and the confidence of landing something that scared them last month. It is worth it when the billing fits your family’s calendar, so you are not paying for weeks your kid cannot make.
### Q. Where can I find adult gymnastics classes in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the gymnastics clubs themselves, since the equipment is the point. St. Louis Gym Centre in Webster Groves lists Adults’ Boot Camps and Open Workout. Call ahead to ask about times and whether true beginners are welcome.

## 48-Inch Fence First: The Real St. Louis Pool Cost
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-an-inground-pool-costs-in-st-louis
The pool plans the City of St. Louis wants on its counter show the fence twice: barrier type and height on the site plan, then gate and barrier type and height again on the pool details. The city cares about the fence before it cares about the water.
Walk it before anyone digs. Out the kitchen slider, across the yard in the July heat, shirt already stuck to your back, to the property line by the alley, gravel crunching under your shoes. Hook the tape on the line and pull it six feet toward the house. That strip stays grass: the city’s own residential pool guidelines put the pool wall at least 6 feet from any rear or side property line, and 10 feet from a street property line.
Now hold the tape up instead of out. Forty-eight inches. That is the city’s minimum barrier height, on all sides of the pool, measured on the side facing away from the water. Swing the gate in your head: it has to open outward, away from the pool, then close and latch on its own, with a clack behind you every time. Turn around and look at the slider you just walked out of. If the back wall of the house forms part of the barrier, every door with direct access to the pool needs an approved audible alarm, or every door has to be self-closing and self-latching.
A 48-inch fence on every side, a self-closing gate, maybe a door alarm, and a strip of yard you can’t build on. None of it is the pool. All of it comes first.
Then the counter at City Hall, where in-person payment is check or cash only. For a project over $3,000, the Building Division charges a $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand of estimated construction cost, and every dollar of it is non-refundable. Only the $25 is due when you file. The permit fee comes due once final approvals are in. And the pool guidelines add a line most quotes never mention: all pools require a permit from the City Health Department, on top of the building permit.
So when one metro builder’s published St. Louis-area guide says inground pools here typically run $35,000 to $110,000-plus, read its next sentence too: those ranges cover the pool and installation. Decking, fencing, upgraded steps, rails or lighting, electrical work, and permit and inspection fees typically fall outside that number. The fence the city requires first is the one the price leaves out.
### What is the average cost of an inground pool in St. Louis?
The same builder’s St. Louis-area guide lists average inground pool costs by type: vinyl at $35,000 to $68,000, fiberglass at $42,000 to $78,000, and gunite at $55,000 to $110,000-plus. It credits labor costs and permitting for pushing metro prices higher across all three.
The guide also names the cost driver your own yard controls: if your backyard is super sloped or rocky, construction may take longer, and labor costs may rise. Read the base range as the price of water in a hole, installed. Not the patio you’ll stand on with a hose. Not the fence the inspector will measure. Not the trench for the wiring. A quote that looks low next to two others usually is not cheaper. It is shorter.
### Write the scope before anyone writes the bid
Three proposals fanned out on the kitchen table, three totals, three different stacks of fine print. The fix is unglamorous and it works. Take a pad and write one page: pool size, shell type, distance from each property line, decking square footage, fence length and height, gates, equipment, cover. Hand that identical page to three builders and ask each one for an itemized total with a written list of everything it excludes.
Then ask four questions out loud, and listen for the pause. Who pulls each permit: the pool, the electrical, the plumbing, the fence? Who supplies the fence, and who makes sure it passes? What happens to the price if the excavator hits rock? And what is the total, not the monthly payment?
Walk the yard with each builder, too. Watch where they look: the width of the side gate, the slope toward the house, the wires overhead, the path a truck would have to take across the lawn. A builder who checks access before quoting is pricing your yard. One who doesn’t is pricing a brochure.
Compare the exclusion lists before you compare the totals. When the bids line up on paper, the real spread usually shrinks to something you can reason about.
### The City of St. Louis permit stack
The inspector’s clipboard at the edge of a fresh dig, dirt piled high beside the hole: in the city, that visit sits at the end of a paper trail. The applicant submits five sets of detailed construction plans drawn to scale to the Permit Section in Room 425 of City Hall. The site plan has to show the barrier type and height, and the pool details have to show the pool gate and barrier type and height again. Separate permits for plumbing, mechanical and electrical work are required when applicable, and new fences need their own permit too. Paying in person? The city takes only check or cash.
If you live in St. Louis County, call your own city hall and ask what it requires before you sign anything. The builder’s guide puts it plainly: most cities in the area require a building permit for any above-ground or inground pool, spa or hot tub capable of holding more than 24 inches of water, along with required inspections during installation.
None of this is the homeowner’s fault, and none of it is a trick. It is just a process that rarely shows up on the first page of a proposal. Ask for it on that page.
Own in one of the city’s historic districts? Add a step. The Building Division says property within a City Historic District, or a City Landmark, requires approval for all fences, among other exterior work. A pool barrier is a fence, so that approval belongs on your timeline before the dig, not after. Questions go to the Building Division Permit Section at (314) 622-3313, Room 425 at 1200 Market.
One more practical step: when a builder says “we handle the permits,” ask which ones, by name, and whether the fence and electrical work are in that sentence. Write the answer on the scope page next to their total. It takes thirty seconds and saves the conversation nobody wants to have in August.
### Can I get an inground pool for $30,000?
Not a finished, contractor-built one, if that builder’s local floor holds. Thirty thousand dollars sits under the $35,000 starting point for vinyl, and that starting point comes before decking, fencing, electrical work and permits.
That budget can still do real work. It can make a strong down payment on a financed build, or cover the whole surround on a pool you finance separately. It also lands inside the range the same builder gives for a semi-inground pool in the St. Louis area, which it says typically runs $18,000 to $60,000-plus depending on size, materials and customization. In a city where the pool season is short and loud and humid, a well-built semi-inground pool with a real deck is not a consolation prize.
### Vinyl, fiberglass or gunite: what you are paying for
Run your hand along each one at a showroom and you feel the difference before you read a tag. Vinyl is smooth and a little soft underfoot. Fiberglass is slick and hard. Gunite is plaster over concrete, the kind of surface you can feel through your feet.
The builder’s guide describes vinyl pools as coming as a kit, assembled on-site with steel or concrete walls and a stretched liner, which keeps costs lower. Fiberglass pools come as a single premade shell lowered into an excavated hole, so you pay more for the manufactured piece but often less for labor, and they are the least customizable of the three. Gunite pools are built entirely on-site with sprayed concrete and then plastered, which makes them the most labor-intensive.
So the question is not which one is best. It is which trade-off fits your yard, your timeline and how long you plan to stay in the house.

### What it costs to keep it blue
The smell of chlorine on the kids’ hair at dinner is part of the deal, and so is the bill behind it. The same St. Louis-area guide puts electricity at $70 to $350 a month during swim season and chemicals at $50 to $150 a month, for an annual total that typically runs $1,500 to $5,000. It adds that most owners spend about an hour a week on routine maintenance.
If you are weighing a salt system against chlorine, the guide prices salt systems at $1,100 to $2,500 upfront. Put that on the scope page with everything else, so it gets bid instead of upsold later. And if the dog plans to swim too, ask one of the vets about pool water before the first hot weekend.
Then make two calls before you sign: one to your insurance agent, because a pool changes your liability picture, and one to the person who does your taxes if anyone in the house has a medical reason for the pool. If you don’t have that person yet, here is what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis.
### What pads a pool quote, and where to push back
Start with allowances. A line that reads “decking allowance” is a placeholder, not a price, and the true number shows up after you have committed. Ask for actual square footage, an actual material and an actual unit price. Do the same for coping, tile and anything marked “to be determined.”
Next, the rock and unsuitable-soil clause. Read who pays and at what rate. Then the bundles: a cover, a heater and a water feature folded into one “package discount” are really three decisions you never got to make separately. And be wary of a quote built around a monthly payment instead of a total, because a payment can be stretched to look like almost anything.
It is the same discipline that protects you on any big back yard project, including solar panels in St. Louis, where the quote spread can be just as wide.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to choose the right pool contractor?
A.  Hand three builders one identical written scope, then compare their exclusion lists before their totals. Ask who pulls each permit, who supplies the fence and makes sure it passes, and exactly what happens to the price if the dig hits rock. The builder who answers those without a pause is usually the one who has done it many times.
### Q. What are common red flags when hiring a swimming pool contractor?
A.  A verbal-only price, a large deposit before permits are pulled, no written exclusions list, a quote framed only as a monthly payment, and a bid far below two others on the same scope. Vagueness about who handles the electrical, plumbing and fence permits is a warning too.
### Q. Can I get an inground pool for $20,000?
A.  Not a contractor-built one in this market, going by the local builder guide used here: $20,000 falls well under its $35,000 starting point for vinyl, before decking, fencing, electrical and permits. It does fit inside that builder’s $18,000 to $60,000-plus range for a semi-inground pool, and at the top of its above-ground range.
### Q. What does a $10,000 pool look like?
A.  An above-ground pool. The same builder says above-ground pools in the St. Louis area typically cost $6,500 to $20,000, a range that includes ladders, steps, equipment, labor and building accidentals. None of the price guides used here put a contractor-built inground pool anywhere near that figure.
### Q. Can I write off a swimming pool on taxes?
A.  Usually not. The IRS guide to medical expenses says you can include home improvements in medical expenses if their main purpose is medical care, and that the cost of the improvement is reduced by the increase in the value of your property. Medical and dental expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of adjusted gross income. Talk to a tax preparer before counting on it.
### Q. What not to tell a contractor?
A.  Don’t lead with your maximum budget, and don’t lead with the monthly payment you could handle. Both invite a quote to grow until it fits. Lead with the scope instead, then ask for one itemized total with the exclusions written down.
### Q. What do pool contractors do?
A.  They design the pool, pull or coordinate permits, excavate, set the shell or spray the gunite, plumb and wire the equipment, install coping and decking when it is in the contract, fill and start up the pool, and line up the inspections. Many also handle openings, closings and repairs in later seasons.

## Where to Buy Sporting Goods in St. Louis: Buy Used, Except the Helmet
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-sporting-goods-in-st-louis
The bat gets taxed. The cleats don’t. That is Missouri’s back-to-school sales tax holiday in one breath, and most St. Louis parents learn it at the register, receipt already curling out of the printer, a kid in shin guards tugging at their sleeve.
Here is the rule. The holiday starts at 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August and ends at midnight that Sunday, and state law exempts any article of clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less. The Missouri Department of Revenue lists “shoes or boots” among the clothing that qualifies. A few lines further down the same FAQ, it puts “sporting equipment” on the list of items that normally do NOT qualify. So the cleats in the box ride tax-free. The bat and the helmet are sporting equipment, and sporting equipment is on the do-not-qualify list.
Most of the money on a youth gear list is decided before you reach a register: which items ride used, which have to be new, and which wait for that August weekend. Make those three calls at the kitchen table and the coach’s one-page equipment list, printed out and stuck to the fridge with a magnet, stops reading like a ransom note.
Say it out loud at the next team meeting, because it saves real money: buy the glove used, buy the helmet new, and buy the cleats on the first weekend of August.
Before you leave the house, do three things. Photograph the certification line on the league’s equipment list, because that is the sentence the clerk will need. Trace your kid’s foot on paper and toss the outline in your bag with last season’s cleats, so the size question takes ten seconds. And if you are trading in outgrown gear, wipe it down and bring every piece of each set. Then shop in this order: used counter first, specialty fitter second, big box last for whatever is left.
### What are some good sporting goods stores in Saint Louis, MO?
The good store is the one that matches the item. For worn-in, slow-wearing gear, a trade shop wins. Play It Again Sports in Kirkwood buys, sells and trades used sports gear every day, with no appointment needed, and its own page promises cash on the spot for everything it accepts. Walk into any used-gear counter and you know it with your eyes closed: oiled glove leather, rubber bat grips, a mesh bag of scuffed softballs that rattles when somebody bumps it.
For running shoes, go where somebody watches you run. Big River Running has stores in West County, South City and University City, open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday and noon to 5 p.m. Sunday, and its fit specialists measure foot length, width and arch, run a treadmill analysis of your gait and generate a digital foot scan that shows pressure points and pronation. You feel the belt hum under your feet for a minute, then you see your own stride on a screen. It also runs a free START training program that takes beginners to their first 5K, and free coaching is hard to beat.
That shop has also turned into a running club with a cash register. Big River says it has hosted more than 1,500 runs with more than 20,000 program participants since it opened its doors, and its Wednesday workouts have met at Francis Park in South City, warm-up at 6:30 p.m., beginners in stiff new shoes breathing hard and finding their pace together.
For camping, paddling and ski gear, Alpine Shop lists boot fitting among its services, which matters more than the brand on the boot: you feel a good fit as a heel that stays put when you lean forward, not a shin bruise on the second run. A national big box still earns its trip for breadth: the cleat, the ball and the starter bat on neighboring aisles the night before a first practice.
Used is where families quietly save the most. Leather gloves get better with use, so a broken-in mitt at a trade counter is an upgrade, not a compromise. Cleats worn for one season by a kid who grew two sizes are barely creased. Dumbbells and golf clubs don’t age at all. And the crate of outgrown gear sitting in the garage, smelling faintly of dried turf and old sweat, is worth money if you wipe it down and bring it in complete.
### The one thing you should never buy used
The helmet. Pick one up at a garage sale and it feels fine: hard shell, foam that gives a little under your thumb, a chin strap that snaps shut with a satisfying click. None of that tells you what you need to know. So flip it over and read the inside of the shell before you read the price tag. NOCSAE, which publishes the recertification standards for football, lacrosse and baseball and softball batting helmets, requires a helmet that cannot be recertified to carry a permanent label that says when its original certification expires. A helmet that has been recertified gets a dated label with the name of the NAERA recertifying facility. No readable label, no deal.
Football helmets add a hard stop. NOCSAE says that if a certified helmet is not recertified within the interval the manufacturer specifies, the existing certification expires, and in most cases a football helmet can only be recertified until it is 10 years old, per NAERA and manufacturer guidelines. Federal rules require bike helmets to carry a labeled warning too: after an impact a helmet may be damaged to the point that it no longer protects the head, and that damage may not be visible. You cannot see a stranger’s crash. An old helmet on a folding table at a yard sale is not a bargain.
Buy it new, in person. A new helmet smells of fresh foam and plastic, with the tag still hanging off it. Have somebody set it on your kid’s head, snap the chin strap, and press down on the crown while your kid shakes their head. It should hug snug all the way around and move with the head, not slide over the eyebrows. That snug press is what you are paying for.
Bats are the middle case: used is fine if the stamp is right. USA Baseball says approved bats must feature a permanent certification mark on the barrel, and temporary labels, stickers and decals are prohibited. In youth baseball, bats with a USA Baseball mark are approved for play at any drop weight. So before you hand over cash for a used bat, tilt the barrel toward the light and look for a mark printed into it, not a sticker somebody smoothed on with a thumb.
Selling, not buying? Start with the bats. Dick’s Sporting Goods runs a bat trade-in with SidelineSwap that pays in Dick’s gift cards, and the company put the average payout at $70. Everything else in the garage crate goes to a trade shop like the one in Kirkwood, or to the next family on the team.
### Used or new: the short list
Buy used: gloves and mitts, cleats and skates for growing kids, golf clubs, weights and benches, kayaks and paddles, gear bags, and padding with no certification label (sliding shorts, shin guards, hockey pants).
Buy used, but check first: bats (look for the permanent mark on the barrel) and bikes (pay a shop for a safety check before the first ride).
Buy new: every helmet, mouthguards, and running shoes, since you can’t see the miles packed into somebody else’s midsole.
Timing helps the used pile most. Trade counters fill up right after a season ends, when garages get cleared out. If your kid can play a season behind the newest model, let them.
### How to walk out of a trade counter with more than you walked in with
Selling the crate takes ten minutes of prep at the kitchen table, and it changes the offer. Wipe the dirt off the cleats and knock the dried clay out of the studs over a trash can. Spray and air out the gloves and pads so the bag doesn’t hit the counter with that sour, closed-car smell. Bring each item complete: both shin guards, the bat with its grip intact, the skates with their guards.
Then decide before you walk in whether you want cash or credit. Cash is cleaner if the kid is quitting the sport. Credit is the move if you are trading up a size in the same sport, because you leave with the next glove in hand instead of an errand on the list. Either way, sort the crate first. Anything with a certification label you can’t read, or a helmet you can’t date, stays home.
Buying at the same counter, slow down. Bend the glove and listen for cracking in the laces. Run a thumb along the inside of a cleat for a worn heel cup. Spin a bike wheel and watch for wobble. Used gear tells you most of its story in the first thirty seconds, but only if you pick it up and handle it instead of just looking at it on the rack.
### How do league equipment lists actually get filled?
Two ways, and knowing which is which saves money before the first practice whistle. The league or school usually supplies the shared, expensive items, like catcher’s gear, team balls and goals. Families buy the personal-fit items: shoes, gloves, mouthguards, bats and, in most youth programs, the helmet.
The certification wording on that list is the line parents skim and the line that decides whether the gear is legal. Get it in writing before you shop, buy the helmet last and in person after somebody measures the head, and keep the receipt for anything with a warranty. Sign-up season is where the real costs hide in every youth sport, which is just as true when you are signing a kid up for gymnastics as it is at a baseball registration table.
Nothing to do with cleats - who to call about storm-damaged trees.
### Fit and returns: ask before you pay
Ask three things at the counter: does the store fit the item, can you return it after actually using it, and how long is the window. Those answers vary far more between store types than prices do. Big boxes generally want unworn goods with the tags still on and a receipt. Specialty shops are often the most flexible on shoes that have really been run in, which is half the point of buying there, and the same reason people still walk into neighborhood hardware stores. Used sales are frequently final or store credit only, a fair trade for the price and a nasty surprise if you assumed otherwise.
Fit beats brand every time. A helmet should sit level and snug, and not slide when your kid shakes their head hard. If a bad fit has already turned into a nagging ache in a knee or a heel, the shopping question has become a medical one, and that is when to see an orthopedist in St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is considered sporting goods?
A.  Sporting goods are the equipment, apparel and footwear used to play sports, train or get outdoors: balls, bats, sticks, racquets, gloves, pads, helmets, athletic shoes and uniforms, plus camping, fishing and water gear. Fan merchandise is not sporting goods. A jersey you wear to the ballpark is apparel; the jersey a team plays in is equipment.
### Q. What is considered a sporting goods store?
A.  A retailer whose main business is equipment, apparel and footwear for sport, fitness and the outdoors. That pulls in more storefronts than the sign suggests: bike shops, run specialty stores, golf pro shops, hockey shops, archery shops, fishing and hunting outfitters and used-gear traders. A fan apparel store is next door but different, because it sells team logos, not playing equipment. The difference predicts service: a store that sells equipment has to know sizing, certification marks and league rules, and usually staffs for it.
### Q. What are examples of sporting goods?
A.  A youth baseball bat, a catcher’s mask, soccer shin guards, molded cleats, a basketball, a tennis racquet, running shoes, swim goggles, a bike helmet, hockey skates, a golf bag, a life jacket, a rod and reel, dumbbells, a yoga mat, a kayak and a two-person tent. If you carry it, wear it or use it to play or train, it counts.
### Q. What are sport accessories?
A.  The small, fast-moving items around the main gear: socks, insoles, laces, grip tape, mouthguards, wristbands, glove conditioner, water bottles, gear bags, chalk and resistance bands. Each one is cheap. Together they quietly add a real chunk to an equipment list, and they are the items a coach assumes you already own.

It covers bats, not general used equipment. For gloves, cleats and the rest, a used-gear trade shop is the place to go.

Buy a season behind and you rarely pay list.
### Q. What do all athletes need?
A.  Whatever the sport: shoes matched to the surface, socks that don’t blister, a properly fitted helmet where the sport calls for one, a mouthguard wherever contact is likely, a water bottle, and a bag that keeps wet gear away from clean gear. ## Missouri Gives Mobile Home Park Families 120 Days to Leave. Illinois Gives 12 Months.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-mobile-home-parks-in-st-louis
One hundred twenty days. That is how long Missouri law gives a family that owns its home but rents the lot under it, once the owner of the land decides it should become something else. One window, to find another lot, line up a licensed installer and coax a house that has not moved in years back onto a truck. Or to sell it where it sits, to whoever will buy a home with that letter lying on the kitchen table next to the electric bill.
Drive east across the Mississippi, the Arch shrinking in the rearview mirror, and the rules change before the tires stop humming on the bridge. In Illinois, the same family gets at least 12 months’ notice when a park owner stops operating all or part of the park (765 ILCS 745/8.5). One river. Three times the clock.
Screenshot this before you sign anything in a park: Missouri, 120 days. Illinois, 12 months. Then ask the office one question out loud: who owns this land, and when did it last sell?
Here is why that question matters more than the countertops. In a park you own the house and rent the dirt. You own the furnace that kicks on with a thump at 5 a.m., the skirting you patched, the wooden steps you repainted twice. The ground under all of it belongs to somebody else. Two deals, two sets of rules, and in the St. Louis metro the rules change at the river.
Missouri’s statute does hand you one quiet guard. The community may not raise your rent, except for an increase based solely on higher property taxes, during the 60 days before it sends that change-of-use notice or at any time after. If more than 120 days remain on your lease, the longer period applies. Outside a change of use, a Missouri landlord can end a lot tenancy of less than a year with written notice that it ends no sooner than 60 days from the date your next rent comes due, whatever the lease says about earlier termination (RSMo 441.060). Past those lines, read a Missouri lease as if it were the whole deal, slowly, with a pen in your hand.
If a notice like that ever lands on your table, do not sit with it alone. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri provides free civil legal assistance to low-income people and the elderly in 21 counties of eastern Missouri. Call 314.534.4200 and ask for intake.
### Is it worth buying a mobile home in a park?
It can be, and for plenty of families across the metro it is. The math turns on one plain fact: you own a structure that sits on ground you rent, at a price you do not set. When the home is bought outright or paid off fast, and the park can show you a steady rent history in writing, the monthly cost can undercut an apartment, and the house payment eventually stops. The lot rent never does.
It goes badly in the mirror-image case. A long loan on an older home, on a lot whose rent climbs faster than your paycheck, in a park whose owner you never looked up. That one has no easy exit, because the home is hard to move and hard to sell with a rent increase hanging over it. You feel it first in the stomach, the morning a new notice is taped to the storm door.
### What the lot rent check buys, and what it never will
Lot rent buys the pad, the roads, and whatever services the park has promised in writing. It does not buy your roof, your water heater, your skirting or the insurance on the home. Those are yours, every one of them, including the cold morning the tap coughs air.
Illinois writes the bill into law. Under 765 ILCS 745/9, every charge, from ground or lot rent to services, has to be itemized in the lease and in every bill. Section 11 of the same Act makes every park lease bind the owner to maintain all subsurface water and sewage lines and connections in good working order. That matters, because the pipe that breaks under your pad is the one you cannot see until the yard turns to mud.
On the Missouri side, get the same list from the office before you sign: who fixes a water line under the pad, who pays for the road, and how water and sewer get billed. Skirting, steps, anchors and the shed land on you in either state, and for that kind of work a hardware store counter usually beats a big-box aisle for the right clip and a straight answer.
### How much warning before the lot rent goes up?
In Illinois, 90 days, every time. The park owner must give 90 days’ notice of any rent increase, and no increase takes effect until 90 days after that notice. Once it arrives you have 30 days to accept or reject it, and a month-to-month agreement must also carry at least 90 days’ notice before an increase (765 ILCS 745/6). The same section requires the park to offer you a written lease of at least 24 months, unless you waive that and agree to a different term.
Illinois also makes the park show its past. With every lease, sale and renewal, the owner must disclose in writing the rent charged for that home or lot over the past 5 years (765 ILCS 745/6.5). Hold that page in your hand and the future gets less foggy. In Missouri, ask for that same rent history anyway, and look for the rent-increase notice period in the lease itself. If it is not there, ask for it in writing before you hand over a deposit.
Lease papers can wait an hour. Spread them across a table at one of the metro’s coffee shops and read every page with a cup going cold beside you.
### What happens if the park is sold or closes?
In Missouri, the 120 days from the top of this page. In Illinois, the 12 months, with details that favor the tenant. If 12 months or more remain on your lease when the notice comes, you keep the balance of the lease up to the closing date. If less remains, you get the balance plus a written month-to-month tenancy, so the notice still adds up to a year. And within 20 days after a park sale closes and the ownership changes, Illinois requires the new owner to notify each homeowner in writing (765 ILCS 745/6.5).
Now the hard part, said out loud. Notice is not the same thing as somewhere to go. A home that has sat on one pad for years rarely moves cheaply, and a closure letter can mean selling for far less than the place is worth to you. So before you buy, find out who owns the land and whether it changed hands lately. That answer says more about your next ten years than the model of the home.
### Selling the home and leaving it where it sits
Illinois defends your right to sell. Under 765 ILCS 745/24, a park owner cannot interfere with your freedom to sell the home to a purchaser of your choice, and cannot require the home to leave the park on a sale to a qualified buyer unless it is less than 12 feet wide or significantly deteriorated, with the park owner carrying the burden of proving it. Section 9 bars a transfer or selling fee on a home that stays in the park unless the park renders a service.
On the Missouri side, read the lease’s resale section before you buy, not the week you list. Ask three things: is there a transfer fee, does the park screen your buyer, and can it make the home leave? Write the answers in the margin of the lease, in pen.
### Moving a home, and who is allowed to set it
If the home has to move, Missouri says who may touch it. No person may engage in the business of installing manufactured homes without a state installer license, and no local license is required on top of it (RSMo 700.656). Ask for the license before anyone backs a truck up to your steps.
The office that answers for that work is the Missouri Public Service Commission’s Manufactured Housing and Modular Units Program. Its page points to inspection requests, consumer complaints and a Manufactured Housing Consumer Recovery Fund. The toll-free line is 1-800-819-3180. Write it on the inside of a kitchen cabinet door, where the setup paperwork lives.
One more thing before you sign, and it costs nothing. Walk the park twice, once on a weekday evening and once after a hard rain. Listen for dogs, traffic and the hum of the road. Look at where the water stands, how the roads hold up, and whether the empty lots look cared for or forgotten. Knock on one door and ask a neighbor how the office treats people when something breaks. Five minutes on a porch will tell you what no lease can.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is rent in a mobile home park per month?
A.  It depends on the park, the lot and what is included, so get the current number from the office in writing, along with what it covers. In Illinois the park owner must disclose the rent charged for that lot over the past 5 years (765 ILCS 745/6.5). In Missouri, ask for the same history anyway.
### Q. Is buying a mobile home in a park a good idea?
A.  It is a good idea when the home is cheap enough to buy outright or pay off fast, the park itemizes its charges, and the lot rent has a history you can see. It is a poor idea when a long loan on an older home sits on a lot rent nobody will explain. The exit matters more than the entry.
### Q. What is the downside to living in a mobile home?
A.  In a park, it is structural. You own the home but rent the land, so a rent increase or a change of use can reshape your costs without you doing anything wrong. In Missouri, a change of use comes with 120 days’ notice (RSMo 700.600). Moving the home is slow and costly, and repairs are yours.
### Q. Is it cheaper to live in a trailer park or an apartment?
A.  Often month to month, if the home is paid off. The honest comparison adds what an apartment covers and you now carry: the roof, the furnace, the water heater, insurance and taxes on the home. Run both totals across a full year, loan payment included, before you decide.
### Q. What are common issues with mobile home park living conditions?
A.  Aging underground lines, rough roads, drainage, and arguments over how water is billed come up again and again. Illinois addresses the pipes directly: 765 ILCS 745/11 makes every park lease bind the owner to maintain subsurface water and sewage lines in good working order. In Missouri, get the repair duties written into the lease.
### Q. What is the cheapest price for a mobile home?
A.  A used home already sitting in a park is usually the least expensive way in, but the sticker hides the rest of the bill: skirting, steps, anchoring, any repairs a lender wants, and the lot rent for as long as you own it. If the home must move, add a licensed installer.
### Q. What are some good mobile home parks in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  We do not rank parks. Judge them on four things you can check: who owns the land and how recently it changed hands, how lot rent has moved over the years, how water and sewer are billed, and what the rules say about selling your home in place.

## St. Louis Fixture Swap: The $25 Permit Homeowners Can Pull
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-buying-lighting-fixtures-in-st-louis
No ground wire. You find that out at the top of the ladder, flashlight clamped in your teeth, breaker off, as the old dome light comes down in a little rain of plaster grit and dead moths. Behind it sits a shallow metal pan fastened to wood lath, two wires wrapped in crumbly cloth, and no bare copper anywhere.
The new fixture is still in its carton on the dining table. It looked perfect online. Now the question is not whether you like it. The question is whether this ceiling can hold it, and who is allowed to wire it.
In the City of St. Louis, that second question has a real answer most buyers never hear. The city’s own electrical permit page says a homeowner can receive an electrical permit after passing a short test given by the Building Division Electrical Section, as long as the work is on an owner-occupied, single-family dwelling and is a room addition, repair, or modification to an existing system. The application fee for all electrical permits is $25. Service changes, rehab and new construction are off the table for homeowners and need a licensed contractor. And the code the city points to on that page is the 2017 National Electrical Code, as adopted by Ordinance #70802.
Read that again if you own in the city: the cheapest line on a fixture swap can be the permit. Twenty-five dollars and a short test, and the work is yours to do legally. Everything in that paragraph comes from the City of St. Louis permit page, so it describes work inside city limits. In St. Louis County, ask your own municipality’s building department how it handles homeowner electrical work.
So before you fall for a fixture, look up first. What is in your ceiling decides more than what is in the showroom.
### How do I know what kind of light fixture I need?
Four things on the carton and one thing in the ceiling. Brightness in lumens. Color in Kelvin. Color honesty in CRI. The location listing, dry, damp or wet, that says where it may hang. Then the box overhead and whether it can carry the weight and the wiring of what you are about to put on it.
Everything else on the shelf is styling. Two fixtures with the same specs and different silhouettes light a room the same way. Two that look like twins with different Kelvin numbers do not. Turning the carton over takes about as long as reading the price tag.
### What to do before you buy anything
Start at the ceiling, not the store. With the breaker off and the circuit tested dead, drop the canopy of the fixture you plan to replace and take a phone photo of what is behind it: the box, the wires, how the box is fastened. If you see a bare or green ground wire and a solid metal or plastic box screwed firmly to framing, a like-for-like swap is usually in reach for a handy person.
If you see cloth-covered wire, porcelain knobs up in the attic, a box that wiggles when you push it, scorch marks, or no box at all, stop there. That is a licensed electrician’s job, and the fixture just became the least interesting problem in the room.
Next, walk to the wall switch and pull the dimmer’s faceplate or read the model number off its side, then snap a picture of that too. Note the bulbs already burning in the room, and the Kelvin number printed on them. Then go shopping with three photos in your pocket: the box, the dimmer, the bulb. Any counter worth your time will ask for all three.
If you live in the city and want to pull your own permit for a repair or modification, call the Building Division Electrical Section at 314-622-3313, or visit Room 425 in City Hall, and ask about the homeowner test.
### Lumens, not watts
Think about the last time you swapped a bulb and the room went oddly dim, even though the box said it was a “60-watt replacement.” Watts tell you how much power a bulb draws. The U.S. Department of Energy describes lumens as a measure of the total amount of visible light emitted by a source, and that is the number you are actually shopping for.
On most screw-in bulbs you don’t have to hunt for it. The Department of Energy notes that the packaging for medium screw-base light bulbs must contain the Lighting Facts label, established in January 2012 by the Federal Trade Commission. That label carries brightness in lumens, energy cost, life expectancy, light appearance, wattage and mercury content. Integrated LED fixtures, where the light source is built in, put these numbers on the carton or spec sheet instead. If a fixture will not tell you its lumens anywhere, that silence is information too.
Buy dimmable when you can, and aim a little brighter than you think you need. You can always take light away with a dimmer. You cannot add it once the fixture is on the ceiling.
### What does 2700K look like next to 4000K?
Stand in the front hall of an old brick house at dusk, one room glowing amber and the next one faintly blue through the doorway, and you have seen Kelvin at work. The Department of Energy lists 2,700 K as warm, with a friendly, personal effect suited to homes, and 3,000 K as soft, warm and pleasing. At 4,100 K it calls the light cool: neat, clean, efficient, the kind it pairs with offices, classrooms and showrooms.
Most living rooms, bedrooms and dining rooms look right at the warm end. Kitchens and baths can go either way, depending on whether you want flattering or crisp. Garages, laundry rooms and workbenches are where the cooler numbers earn their keep.
The mistake that ruins rooms is mixing. Your eye settles on one white and judges every other source against it, so a cool can light next to a warm pendant makes the pendant look dingy yellow and the can look surgical. The same DOE guidance warns that radically changing the color temperature, from 2,700 K to 4,100 K, is noticeable and can result in occupant dissatisfaction. Pick one Kelvin per sightline and hold it, table-lamp bulbs included.
### Why CRI decides whether the oak looks like oak
You hang the new fixture, flip the switch, and the room is bright enough but somehow wrong. The oak table reads gray. The red brick around the fireplace goes the color of cardboard. The paint color you argued over for a week looks flat. That is usually color rendering, not brightness.
The Department of Energy explains that light sources are rated on a 0- to 100-point scale for their accuracy in rendering colors compared with an ideal or natural light source, and that a higher color rendering index means a better light source. It is a separate question from Kelvin. A warm bulb can render colors honestly or badly, and only the CRI tells you which.
Spend for a higher CRI anywhere color gets judged: the bathroom mirror, the kitchen, the dining room, any room with real wood or brick. In the garage or the utility room, it matters far less.
### Why a new LED flickers or buzzes on an old dimmer
You hear it before you see it: a faint hum from the switch plate, or a shimmer at the low end of the slider. The dimmer in many older walls was built for incandescent bulbs, and LEDs draw a fraction of that load. The DOE puts it plainly: it is important to make sure LEDs are compatible with the dimming system.
The fix list is short. Confirm the bulb or fixture says dimmable, because a non-dimmable LED on a dimmer will misbehave. Look up your exact dimmer model on its maker’s compatibility list, which most dimmer makers publish. If it still buzzes, an LED-rated dimmer often solves it. And if you are eyeing a smart dimmer, check whether it needs a neutral wire in the switch box, because plenty of older switch boxes don’t have one.
Up on that ladder and something’s scratching in the attic? Pest control is a different call.
### Damp or wet: the line on the carton people skip
Think of the front porch light the morning after a hard summer storm, water beaded inside the glass like a terrarium. Every fixture carries a location listing, and it matters most where water lives. Dry is ordinary indoor space. Damp is for places that collect moisture or condensation without taking water directly, like a bathroom ceiling away from the shower or a deep covered porch. Wet is for anywhere rain, splash or spray can reach the fixture itself.
Be honest about exposure outdoors. A lantern on an open side wall that catches sideways rain in a summer storm wants a wet listing, not a damp one. And mount it the way the instructions show, because a wet-rated fixture hung upside down so it collects water will still fail. Over a tub or shower, ask your electrician what is allowed before you fall for a delicate pendant over the soaking tub.
### Size and hanging height, by eye and by tape
These are trade habits, not code, and they exist because they usually look right. For a chandelier over a dining table, a common rule adds the room’s length and width in feet and uses that sum as a rough fixture diameter in inches. Hang the bottom of it so people can see each other across the table without staring into glass.
In an entry or a hallway, keep the bottom of the fixture high enough that the tallest person in the house never clips it. In a bathroom, a single can light over the mirror lights the top of your head and drops shadows under your eyes. Sconces on either side of the mirror light your face instead. If you fix one lighting decision in a house, make it that one.
### When the swap is yours, and when it isn’t
A like-for-like swap onto a solid, properly fastened box, breaker off, circuit tested dead, similar weight and mounting, is within reach for many handy people. Call a licensed electrician when there is no ground at the box, when you find old cloth wiring or insulation crumbling off the conductors, when the box is loose, scorched or shallow, when you want a ceiling fan where a light was, or when you are adding new cans or a new switch.
A good hardware store counter can hand you the right brace and the right box, but it cannot see inside your ceiling. In the city, electrical permits are issued to licensed electrical contractors certified by the City of St. Louis, and to owners of single-family homes who meet the city’s requirements. Outside the city limits, call your own municipality’s building department and ask before you start. The same questions come up with bigger electrical projects, like solar on a St. Louis roof.
The good showrooms already work this way. Walk in with the three photos and a measuring tape reading of the room, and you will feel the difference at the counter: fewer guesses, a fixture that fits the box, and no second trip back with a carton under your arm.
Walk in with three photos and you’ll walk out with the right fixture. Browse lighting fixture stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and bring the ceiling box, the dimmer model on your wall, and the Kelvin already burning in that room.
If you run the showroom, the lamp-repair bench or the one-truck electrical crew that asks about the box before the sale, the homeowners standing on those ladders are customers looking for exactly you. Put your shop in front of them.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the four types of lighting fixtures?
A.  Designers usually sort fixtures by the job they do: ambient, task, accent and decorative. Ambient is the general fill that lets you cross a room. Task is aimed at one surface, like an undercabinet strip or a vanity light. Accent throws light on art or brick. Decorative fixtures are meant to be looked at as much as looked by.
### Q. What is the key difference between a lamp and a lighting fixture?
A.  In the trade, the lamp is the light source itself, what most people call the bulb, and the fixture is the housing, socket and wiring around it. In everyday speech, a lamp is the plug-in light on your end table and a fixture is wired into the house. That everyday difference is the one that matters when a house is sold.
### Q. Do light fixtures just stop working?
A.  They do, and the cause is usually findable. On integrated LED fixtures the electronics often give out before the light source, especially when heat gets trapped in a tight ceiling. On older fixtures it is often a worn socket or a brittle wire at the canopy. Check the switch and the breaker first, then call an electrician if the wiring looks tired.
### Q. What is the rule of thumb for lighting?
A.  Layer the light, then match the whites. Give each room more than one source instead of one center fixture doing all the work, and keep a single Kelvin number across one sightline. Put most of it on dimmers so the same room works for homework at dinner and a movie after.
### Q. Do all light fixtures in a house need to match?
A.  No, and a house where everything matches can look like a builder package. Keep the color of the light consistent and the finishes in a small, deliberate family. Rooms you can see into from one another benefit most from agreeing.
### Q. Where can I find a good light fixture store in St. Louis?
A.  You have three kinds of choices: big-box aisles for in-stock basics, dedicated lighting showrooms for special orders, design help and repair, and online sellers for range. A showroom earns its keep the moment you need something sized or fixed. Browse the lighting fixtures category on St Louis Near Me Directory and bring your three photos.

## The Third Return With No Envelope: St. Louis Tax Prep
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-tax-preparer-costs-in-st-louis
Phone in one hand, pen in the other, and the whole year spread across the kitchen table: one tidy W-2 from the day job, and next to it a loose stack of 1099s from the side work. The preparer on the line has already priced the W-2. The number sounds fine. Then comes the sentence that changes it: “I also do some work on my own.”
A pause. The sound of typing on the other end. The number starts to climb. In the 2025 NATP Fee Study, as reported by Accounting Today, one Schedule C, the form that holds side income, added $123 to $135 to the bill in larger communities. And the climb does not start at zero. Half of the preparers surveyed put their minimum fee at $150 to $350, and more for schedules.
### How much do most tax preparers charge?
The first number spoken on that call is mostly about who signs the return. The 2025 NATP Fee Study put the average fee for a base Form 1040 (Schedules 1-3) at $280 for CPAs and $228 for enrolled agents, versus about $185 for non-credentialed preparers, and the base return averaged $233 in communities of 50,000-plus. The second number, the one that arrives after the words about side work, is the Schedule C. The pen taps the table between them. Neither number has said a word yet about the city.
### The third return the stack on the table can’t show
Every sheet on that table came in an envelope. The W-2 did. The 1099s did. The return the side work owes the City of St. Louis has no envelope at all. The Collector of Revenue says it does not mail blank E-234 forms to all taxpayers. So the mail decides which returns reach a kitchen table, and the one written for side work is the one it never promised to bring.
The City’s rule is short. All businesses located in the City of St. Louis, and non-resident businesses that perform work, service or business activity there, are required to pay its 1% earnings tax, except those exempted by law. A contract worker, a self-employed person or a sole proprietor files it on Form E-234 as an E-2 return. For a calendar year, it is due April 15. The Earnings Tax Department sits in City Hall, Room 410, and answers at (314) 622-4101.
The day job already answers to that same one percent. The City collects it from residents of the city regardless of where their employer is, and from employees of businesses located or performing work in the city, regardless of where they live. The side work answers to it a second time, on a return of its own, and that return is the one with no envelope.
Back on the phone, the pen hangs over the blank line where a signature will go, and one short question finally gets said out loud: “Does this quote include the E-234?” The quote covered federal. It covered state. A quote gets built from the papers on the table, and the one return that never came in an envelope is the easiest one for a quote to leave out. Priced that way, it covers two returns when the work owes three.
Then the calendar on the fridge comes into it. April 15 is close, and the word extension floats up the way it does when a season runs tight. The City’s E-8 extension moves the E-234 to October 15. It moves the paperwork. It does not move the money. In the City’s own words, the extension only allows more time to file the return, and a payment of 100% of the estimated tax owed goes with it to avoid accruing penalty and interest. File later. Pay now.
And if the side work has grown to the point of paying helpers of its own, the Collector lists one more date before spring even starts: the Annual Business 1099 Report, Form E-6 or Schedule G, due March 1.
A W-2, a stack of 1099s, a third return with no envelope, and a quote that grew the moment the side work was spoken out loud. So which number on that call was the real one: the first quote, or the one that finally counted the city?
### What the higher fee for a CPA or enrolled agent buys
Down at the bottom of a Form 1040 there is a small box for the paid preparer: a signature and a PTIN. By law, a paid preparer has to fill it. The IRS is blunt about what it takes to get that number: anyone can be a paid tax return preparer as long as they have an IRS Preparer Tax Identification Number. That number is a registration, not a skill test.
The difference shows up the day a letter arrives. Per the IRS, enrolled agents, certified public accountants and attorneys have unlimited representation rights before the IRS, and may represent their clients on any matters, audits included. That is what the gap between $185 and $228 or $280 is paying for: a person who can sit across the table from the IRS on the owner’s behalf, instead of handing the envelope back.
### Four answers a straight quote already holds
Counted out loud, a side business inside the city limits has three returns, not two: federal, state, and the City E-234. A quote that covers all three tends to answer four things before anyone has to ask.
What is the minimum fee? What does each form cost, the Schedule C in particular? Does the office prepare the City of St. Louis E-234? And will the preparer sign the return with a PTIN? Four answers that fit on the back of an envelope, and an office that prices by scope can give all four on the first call.
The last check is five minutes at the keyboard, in the IRS Directory of Federal Tax Return Preparers with Credentials and Select Qualifications. The IRS says it can help you find preparers in your area who currently hold professional credentials recognized by the IRS.
### What is a reasonable amount to pay a tax preparer?
A reasonable fee is one whose shape you can see before the pen ever touches the signature line. Flat pricing per form is the most predictable. Hourly is fine when the work is genuinely open-ended: the NATP study put the average set hourly rate at $182, with half of preparers between $129 and $250 per hour.
The structure to walk away from is the one tied to your refund. The IRS tells taxpayers to avoid tax return preparers who base their fees on a percentage of the refund or who offer to deposit all or part of your refund into their financial accounts. A fee like that pays someone to make your number bigger, and the IRS adds that although the preparer always signs the return, you are ultimately accountable for the accuracy of every item on it.
That signature matters. By law, a paid preparer is required to sign the return and include their PTIN on it. An office that does the work and leaves the signature line blank is not saving you money.
Completely unrelated: if you’re moving before spring, find movers across the metro here.
Some returns pull in forms of their own. If panels are on your list, read up on solar panels in St. Louis before you budget the tax side of it. And if the problem is a notice rather than a return to file, here’s when you need a tax attorney in St. Louis instead of a CPA.
### From the preparer’s side of the desk
Tax prep makes up 65% of the average practice’s revenue in the NATP study, and 83% of preparers raise fees every one to two years, typically 6% to 10%. It is a business with one harvest, run by people who spend the quiet months paying for software and continuing education and hoping the phone rings in January.
The process works against the good ones. A preparer who quotes the minimum up front and asks about the E-234 on the first call loses the comparison to whoever comes up first in a search. That is why a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is built the way it is: up to 10 categories and 40 location tags, and no public address required, so an enrolled agent working from a spare bedroom can show up for the neighborhoods that office actually serves.
If your income is modest, you may not need to pay anyone at all. The IRS-sponsored Volunteer Income Tax Assistance program offers free tax help to individuals with low-to-moderate income, persons with disabilities, the elderly and limited English speakers. Our guide to free tax preparation in St. Louis walks through the local sites.

I could not find a St. Louis-only fee survey, so the closest benchmark is the 2025 NATP Fee Study: a base 1040 averaged about $185 to $280 depending on the credential, and $233 in communities of 50,000-plus. A Schedule C added $123 to $135 in larger communities. A City of St. Louis E-234 is one more return on top.
