### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What do tax preparers actually do?
A.  A paid preparer sorts your documents, works out your filing status and which forms apply, prepares the federal and state returns, and for a business in the City of St. Louis can prepare the E-234 earnings tax return too. By law the preparer must sign the return and include a PTIN on it. You are still accountable for every item on it, which is why you read it before you sign.
### Q. Is it better to go to a CPA or H&R block?
A.  It depends less on the sign over the door than on the person who signs your return. Ask whether that person is an enrolled agent, a CPA or an attorney, because those three have unlimited representation rights before the IRS. For a simple return, a non-credentialed preparer may be enough. For a Schedule C or a notice, the credential is what you are paying for.
### Q. How can I choose a reputable tax preparer?
A.  Check the credential in the IRS Directory of Federal Tax Return Preparers with Credentials and Select Qualifications, confirm the preparer will sign with a PTIN, and get the fee structure before work starts. To find local offices to call, browse tax services on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each the same four questions from this guide.
### Q. Who is the cheapest tax service?
A.  Free is the floor. The IRS-sponsored VITA program provides free tax filing assistance using IRS-certified volunteers for people with low-to-moderate income, persons with disabilities, the elderly and limited English speakers. Among paid options, non-credentialed preparers averaged about $185 for a base 1040 in the 2025 NATP Fee Study.
### Q. When should I use a tax service?
A.  When the return has a moving part you cannot check yourself: side-business income on a Schedule C, a business that owes the City of St. Louis E-234, or a letter from a tax agency. A notice answered badly costs more than the fee. A single wage form and nothing else rarely justifies one.
### Q. How much are taxes in St. Louis?
A.  On top of federal and state income tax, the City of St. Louis collects a one percent earnings tax from residents of the city, regardless of where their employer is, and from employees of businesses located or performing work in the city, regardless of where they live. Businesses located in the city, and non-resident businesses doing work there, pay the 1% earnings tax on the business’s earnings, filed on Form E-234.
### Q. What are the biggest tax mistakes people make?
A.  Waiting for a City E-234 form that never arrives in the mail. Treating side income as invisible because the paperwork was thin. Signing a return the preparer would not sign. And paying a fee that rises with your refund, which the IRS tells taxpayers to avoid.
Two quotes, two different products. One buys a return typed and filed. The other buys someone who can stand between you and the IRS when the letter comes. Know which one your side work needs, ask about the E-234 by name, and get the minimum in writing. Refuse to be invisible.

## BJC Will Estimate Your Test Before the Needle Goes In
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-lab-work-done-in-st-louis
No coffee. The order said fasting, so you sit in the vinyl chair with an empty stomach and a dry mouth while the tourniquet bites above your elbow.
A pinch. A cotton ball taped into the crook of your arm. Out the door in minutes.
Then, weeks later, the envelope. A bill from a laboratory you never chose, for a price nobody said out loud.
You can see a number before the needle instead. If your blood is going to a BJC hospital lab, BJC’s own cost-estimator page says: “If you would like an estimate in advance for procedures or tests performed at a BJC hospital, please call 314-747-8845.” The toll-free line is 844-747-8845, and there is a secure online Patient Cost Estimator Form too.
Have the order in your hand when you call. BJC asks for the hospital name and the procedure or service, and tells you to include the CPT code on your physician order, if known. It is the short code most people never look at, printed on the sheet you were handed. Insured? Have your policy and group number ready.
Know what the number covers. BJC says the estimate is for hospital costs only, which do not include physician or other professional fees that are billed separately by other providers. It will be a range of possible costs or an average cost, depending on your situation. A range is still a number you did not have yesterday.
Paying on a tight income instead? Affinia Healthcare is a federally qualified health center, and it lists laboratory services. A medical visit there starts at $25 for patients whose income does not exceed 100% of the federal poverty level, and additional fees may apply for other services, so ask what the lab adds. Proof of income is required. Payments are due at time of service. Discounts are also provided for patients with income between 100-200% of the federal poverty level. Call 314-814-8700; locations include Biddle and Lemp.
Now the turn most people on the Missouri side of the river never hear. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services says it on its own CLIA page: “Missouri does not have a licensure requirement for laboratories.” Someone who is only drawing blood or collecting specimens needs no CLIA certificate either. The testing itself must happen at a facility that is properly certified under federal rules.
So the room with the vinyl chair is often not the lab. Your tubes ride somewhere else, and that somewhere else may be the company that bills you.
For a yardstick, Quest’s consumer site lists a cholesterol (lipid) panel you order yourself at $59.00, plus a $6.00 physician service fee. No visit and no clinician who knows your history, but the price is on the screen before you click.
What to do today, in order. Call the office that ordered the test, or Affinia if you have no doctor yet, and ask them to read you the order, including whether you need to fast. Ask which laboratory will run the specimen. Call the member number on your insurance card and ask whether that laboratory is in network. If you are paying yourself, ask for a good faith estimate in writing. Then drink a glass of water, wear sleeves that push above the elbow, and go.
Say it word for word, because the person on the other end hears vague questions all day: “Before I come in, can you tell me what the lab work adds to my visit, the name of the laboratory that will run my blood, and the test codes on my order?” Write the answers on the order itself. That one sheet of paper is your price check.
### Can you walk into any lab test now?
The clipboard at the window, the pen on a chain, and the first question back: do you have an order? Sometimes you can walk in, and it depends on the route. A clinician writes an order and you take it to a draw station. A hospital or clinic draws and runs it in-house, often on the same morning as a visit. Or you buy a test yourself on a consumer site, which is where that $6.00 physician service fee comes in: a physician still stands behind the order, even when you are the one who picked the panel.
The first route is the ordinary one, and the order does quiet work you never see. It carries the list of tests and a diagnosis code that tells your insurer why they were ordered. That code is often the difference between a covered claim and a denial, and the ordering office writes it, not you. If a claim gets denied later, that code is the first thing to ask about.
The consumer route trades something for the up-front price. You get the number, but the person who knows your history did not decide whether it was the right question to ask. For a one-off cholesterol check, that tradeoff can be fine. For symptoms, it usually is not.
### How do you know the lab running your blood is legitimate?
The paperwork that matters is usually a framed certificate on a wall nobody looks at, behind the sign-in clipboard. Ask whose it is. Under the federal Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments, testing may only be performed by facilities that are properly certified. The Missouri CLIA program says it oversees this certification program in the state, carries out certain inspections of laboratories on a routine basis, and investigates complaint allegations.
If you want to check on a lab, or you think something went wrong, the Missouri CLIA Program takes calls at 573-751-6318 and email at CLIA@health.mo.gov. A real lab answers the certificate question without irritation. A front desk that cannot tell you which lab runs your specimen is telling you something too.
### What should you do the day before a blood draw?
The night before, the order sits on the counter next to the coffee maker, and the question is whether you are allowed to use it in the morning. Drink water. Take your regular medications unless the person who ordered the test told you otherwise. Only fast if the order says to. Most people fast when they did not have to and skip it when they should have, because nobody read them the order. A two-minute call to the ordering office prevents a second trip and a second stick.
Tell the lab about every supplement you take, gummies and hair-and-nail vitamins included, and do not stop a prescription on your own to make a number look better. If you fasted, pack a granola bar for the car. If needles make you light-headed, say it out loud at the chair; they would much rather lay you back than catch you. For a child, ask about numbing cream when you schedule, not when you are already in the chair. And give yourself something after the draw besides a bandage: a late breakfast, or the errand you keep putting off, like one of the nail salons near you.
### How do your results reach you?
Often on your phone before anyone calls. You open the portal at the kitchen table and there is a small red flag beside a word you have never seen. Take a breath. A value outside the reference range is not a diagnosis, and one number rarely means much without your history next to it. Write your question down and call the ordering office.
You also have a right to the report itself. Federal CLIA rules say that upon request by a patient, the laboratory may provide patients and their personal representatives with access to completed test reports. Under the federal patient-access rule, a covered entity must act on a request for access no later than 30 days after receipt of the request. If nothing has reached you within a week of the draw, call anyway. A result that never gets delivered is a real failure, and you are allowed to chase it.
When you do get the clinician on the phone, have three things in front of you: the report, the list of what you take, and the one question that scared you. Ask what the number means for you, whether it needs a repeat, and what would change the plan. Write the answers on the report itself. Next year, when the same panel comes around, that page is the most useful thing in the drawer.
Arm still sore where the tape came off? Read what a first massage visit costs in St. Louis before you book one.
### Why the same blood work can cost very different amounts
The tubes look the same everywhere. Purple top, gold top, a strip of tape with your name on it. The bill does not. Where you are drawn, which lab runs the specimen, and whether that lab is in your network all move the number, and the person holding the needle may work for a different company than the one that sends the invoice.
That is why the in-network question has to be about the laboratory, not the office. An in-network doctor can send your blood to a lab your plan does not contract with, and nobody in the room will mention it. Ask it exactly this way when you schedule: which laboratory will this specimen be sent to, and is it in network for my plan? If the answer is vague, get the lab’s name and call your plan yourself.
If you are paying without insurance, ask for a number in advance. CMS says that usually, providers must give you a good faith estimate of how much your health care will cost if you request one or schedule services at least 3 business days in advance. And you may be able to dispute your bill if it is at least $400 more than the estimate. Ask for the estimate in writing, and keep it with the order.
A posted price you can check
### How much does it cost to get something tested at a lab?
There is no single St. Louis price, but here is one posted number to compare against. Quest’s consumer site lists its cholesterol (lipid) panel at $59.00 plus a $6.00 physician service fee. A different panel, a hospital draw or an out-of-network lab can land somewhere else entirely, so ask for a written good faith estimate before the draw.
### Where to go if money is the hard part
If the last lab bill is still sitting unopened on the counter, you are not the only one. Start with a federally funded community health center. Under federal health center rules, a center must have prepared a schedule of fees with a corresponding schedule of discounts adjusted on the basis of the patient’s ability to pay, and must operate so that no person is denied service by reason of inability to pay. Bring proof of income if you have it; it speeds up the sliding-fee paperwork.
If the labs are part of a program you are already paying for, check whether they are bundled in before you pay for them twice. That comes up often in two kinds of care:

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is a lab without insurance?
A.  Ask for a good faith estimate. CMS says providers usually must give you one if you request it or schedule at least 3 business days in advance, and you may be able to dispute a bill at least $400 more than the estimate. Compare it against a posted consumer price before you book.
### Q. What should you not do before a lab test?
A.  Do not fast unless the order says to, do not skip water, and do not stop a prescription on your own to improve a number. Tell the lab about every supplement you take. If you are unsure about any of it, call the ordering office and ask them to read you the order.
### Q. How to know if a lab is good?
A.  Ask which lab runs your specimen and whether it holds a CLIA certificate. The Missouri CLIA program says it oversees this certification program in the state, inspects labs on a routine basis and investigates complaints; it takes calls at 573-751-6318. A good lab also tells you plainly how and when results will reach you.
### Q. How to get cheap lab tests?
A.  Try a federally funded community health center first. Federal rules require a schedule of discounts based on ability to pay, and no one may be denied service for inability to pay; findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov lists the nearest sites. Then compare a posted consumer price against a written good faith estimate.
### Q. What lab tests should I ask for?
A.  Ask what your history calls for rather than reading off a list. A useful line: given my age, my family history and what I have told you, what should we check, and how often? Buying a test on your own gets you a number, but nobody decides whether it was the right question.
### Q. What are common reasons for lab tests?
A.  Four, mostly. Screening looks for a problem before you feel anything. Diagnosis answers a question your symptoms raised. Monitoring tracks a known condition or a medicine over time. And pre-procedure work is what a surgeon or specialist wants to see first. The same blood count can serve any of the four, and the reason on the order shapes how the result is read and how the claim is coded.
### Q. What is the purpose of a laboratory test?
A.  To turn a guess into a number. A lab test measures something your clinician cannot see in the exam room, like blood sugar, kidney function or a cholesterol level, so the next decision rests on evidence instead of a hunch. It works best when the question is clear before the needle goes in.
### Q. Where can I get free STI testing in St. Louis?
A.  Before you buy a self-pay panel for sexual health testing, read our guide first. Who offers what, and how walk-in access works, is in our guide to free and low-cost HIV and STI testing in St. Louis.

## Saw Your Doctor First? That Can Rule You Out of a St. Louis Ortho Walk-In
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-an-orthopedist-in-st-louis
Pop. You hear it before you feel it, a wet little snap from inside the knee as you pivot on the last step of the deck stairs. Then the heat. Then the long, careful limp to the couch with a bag of frozen peas, telling yourself it is probably nothing.
Most people do the polite thing next. They wait a few days, then book their regular doctor. In St. Louis, that polite move can quietly close a door.
Mercy runs orthopedic walk-in care in town, and its own page spells out who it is for: children starting at age 10 and adults “with orthopedic injuries that have occurred within the past two weeks without being seen by your primary care physician for this injury.” Read the last part twice. The walk-in is built for the fresh injury that nobody has looked at yet. That is the St. Louis 2-week rule, and it is worth a text to every parent on a youth soccer sideline: the door opens at age 10, and it opens for new injuries. Wait three weeks, or get it checked somewhere else first, and you are outside the lane the page describes.
The same page lists what walk-in is not for: chronic pain lasting more than 2 weeks, back pain or injury, head injuries or concussions, open wounds, second opinions, multiple joints, or patients with hardware. What it does take is acute, new injuries, like fractures, sprains, muscle strains, swollen joints, dislocations and sports injuries, to the foot, ankle, leg, knee, hip, shoulder, elbow, arm, wrist or hand.
So here is the order of operations for a knee that just popped. Ice it, keep weight off it, and decide within days, not weeks. If it fits the walk-in list, check that location’s hours online and go. Mercy lists walk-in orthopedic care on S. New Ballas Road and on Southfork Road. If it does not, call your insurer before you call anyone else and ask one question: does my plan need a referral for an orthopedic visit? Then call the orthopedic office and ask whether they need that referral in hand before they schedule. And if the knee is cold, pale, numb, or bent the wrong way, skip all of this and go to an emergency room.
### Can I go straight to an orthopedic doctor?
You can book the visit yourself. Whether your plan pays for it without a referral is a separate question, and the answer lives in your insurance contract. HealthCare.gov puts it in one line for each plan type: POS plans require you to get a referral from your primary care doctor in order to see a specialist, while with a PPO you can use doctors outside the network without a referral for an additional cost.
An EPO, by the same HealthCare.gov page, covers services only if you use doctors, specialists, or hospitals in the plan’s network. That is the trap in plain sight. On an EPO, you can get through the door of an out-of-network office in a day and still end up with the whole bill.
The knee is throbbing on a pillow and you are on hold, listening to the same four bars of music. Stay on. The plan name is printed on your card, usually in small capitals near the group number. Turn it over. The member services number on the back is the fastest referral answer you will get. Ask two questions, write the answers on the back of an envelope with the date and the name of the person you spoke to, and keep it in the car.
On Missouri Medicaid, the state’s own FAQ answers the referral question with a pointer: check with your Primary Care Provider or your MO HealthNet Managed Care health plan to see if you need a referral to see a specialist. Questions about your options go to the MO HealthNet Managed Care Enrollment Helpline at 800-348-6627.
Missed the Mercy walk-in window, or need a different system? WashU Medicine Orthopedics takes appointments at 314-514-3500, with offices at the Center for Advanced Medicine on Parkview Place, and its page points people who need immediate care to its Orthopedic Injury Clinic or to online scheduling for same-day appointments at five area locations.
No primary care doctor to route a referral through? That gap is worth closing even if your knee heals on its own: how to find a primary care doctor in St. Louis.
### Signs the knee, shoulder or ankle needs an orthopedist
Your body tells you in mechanical language. A joint that buckles on the stairs. A knee that will not straighten all the way after a twist. A shoulder that clicks and catches when you reach for the top shelf. Swelling that comes back every time you use the joint. Those are structure problems, and structure is what an orthopedist works on.
Other signals are about time and sleep. Pain that wakes you up at night. Pain that hurts at rest, not just when you move. Weeks of ice, rest and drugstore pain relievers without real change. Numbness or tingling running down an arm or leg. A fracture somebody already found on an X-ray. Any of those is worth an appointment, and none of them is a reason to feel like you are overreacting.
Arthritis counts too. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons’ patient guide on knee arthritis says that although there is no cure for arthritis, there are many treatment options available to help manage pain and keep people staying active. That is exactly the conversation an orthopedic visit is for.
### When it is the ER, not an appointment
Some injuries do not get a phone call first. Bone through skin. A limb that goes cold, pale or numb below the injury. A joint that is obviously out of place. Those go to an emergency room.
Two conditions are worth knowing by name, because they hide inside ordinary-sounding pain. The first is cauda equina syndrome, a rare compression of the nerve roots at the bottom of the spinal cord that AAOS calls a surgical emergency. Its warning signs include being unable to urinate, being unable to hold urine, and what doctors call saddle anesthesia: numbness around the buttocks, the perineum and the inner thighs, the area a saddle touches. Back pain with any of that is not a walk-in visit. It is the ER, tonight.
The second is acute compartment syndrome. AAOS describes it as a medical emergency, usually caused by a severe injury and extremely painful, and warns that without treatment it can lead to permanent muscle damage. If a swollen shin or forearm hurts far more than the injury seems to justify, especially after a fracture or a crush, do not wait to see if it settles.
This is general information, not advice about your specific injury. If you cannot tell whether something is an emergency, treat it like one.
Those deck stairs are still out there. While the knee heals, find a handyman to put a real railing on them.
### Do you need a referral for physical therapy in Missouri?
The first therapy session is a padded table, a plastic goniometer against your knee, and someone asking you to bend until it pinches. You may not need a doctor’s note to get there. Not under state law, with conditions. Missouri’s statute, RSMo 334.506, says a physical therapist may evaluate and initiate treatment on a patient without a prescription or referral from an approved health care provider, provided that the therapist has a doctorate of physical therapy degree or has five years of clinical practice as a physical therapist.
The law builds in a checkpoint. The therapist must refer you to an approved health care provider if you do not demonstrate measurable or functional improvement after ten visits or thirty days, whichever occurs first. That is a useful clock to know about when the stiffness is the problem and nothing is broken. You can start the work sooner, and the system pushes you toward a doctor if it is not working.
State law is not insurance coverage, though. Your plan can still require a referral or an authorization before it pays for therapy. Ask the therapy office to run your benefits before the first visit.
### What happens at the first orthopedic visit
Expect questions first. When did it happen, what were you doing, what did you hear, what have you tried. Then hands on the joint, pressing and bending until something makes you wince, which is the point. An X-ray often happens in the building, and the plan that follows usually starts without surgery: a brace, an injection, therapy, time.
Bring the dates, any imaging you already have, and an honest list of what you tried, down to the brace from the drugstore and the weeks of ibuprofen. Before you leave the room, ask four things. What happens if I do nothing for six weeks? What is the nonsurgical option, and how long should it get? What would have to show up on imaging to change the plan? What does recovery look like in weeks?
You can also check the surgeon’s credentials yourself. The American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery’s site says you can verify if an orthopaedic surgeon is ABOS board certified. It takes about as long as finding parking.

### Why an orthopedic visit can cost more than you expect
The bill tends to arrive weeks later, after the swelling is gone and you have half forgotten the visit. The visit itself is the small part. Imaging and procedures move the number, and so does where the clinic bills from. If you are paying without insurance, you have a federal right to know the number first. CMS says that usually, if you don’t have or use health insurance, providers must give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost, when you schedule care in advance or if you ask for one. You may be able to dispute your bill if it is at least $400 more than the estimate.
Ask for the estimate in writing, and ask whether it includes the X-ray. Front desks hear that question all day. It is not rude.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you go to an orthopedist without a referral?
A.  You can book one; whether insurance pays depends on the plan. HealthCare.gov says POS plans require a referral from your primary care doctor to see a specialist, while PPO plans let you use out-of-network doctors without a referral for an additional cost. Call the member services number on your card and ask before the visit.
### Q. Does Mercy Ortho offer walk-in care in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Mercy’s orthopedic walk-in page says it treats children starting at age 10 and adults with orthopedic injuries from the past two weeks that a primary care physician has not seen. It is not for chronic pain over 2 weeks, back pain, head injuries, open wounds, second opinions, multiple joints or patients with hardware. Hours vary by location, so check before you go.
### Q. Should I go to an orthopedist for back pain?
A.  Often, but not through the walk-in door: Mercy’s walk-in page lists back pain or injury among the things not to choose walk-in for, so book a regular appointment. Trouble urinating, being unable to hold urine, or numbness across the buttocks and inner thighs is different. AAOS calls cauda equina syndrome a surgical emergency, so go to the ER.
### Q. Do orthopedists treat arthritis?
A.  Yes. AAOS patient guidance on knee arthritis says there is no cure for arthritis, but there are many treatment options available to help manage pain and keep people staying active. An orthopedic visit is where those options get matched to your joint and your life.
### Q. What are the signs I need to see an orthopedist?
A.  A joint that buckles, locks or catches. Swelling that keeps coming back. Pain at night or at rest. Numbness or tingling down a limb. A fracture already found on an X-ray. Weeks of rest and ice without real change. Any one of those is reason enough to book.
### Q. How much does it cost to see an orthopedist without insurance?
A.  It depends on the clinic and on imaging, so get it in writing first. CMS says providers usually must give a good faith estimate to people who don’t have or use insurance, when you schedule in advance or ask for one, and you may be able to dispute a bill at least $400 more than the estimate.
### Q. Is it better to go to a podiatrist or orthopedist for plantar fasciitis?
A.  Either can treat heel pain, and both usually start with a nonsurgical plan. A practical tiebreaker: pick the one who is in your network and can see you sooner, and bring the shoes you wear most days to the visit.

## Downloads Exempt, USB Taxed: St. Louis Studio Shoot Math
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renting-a-photo-studio-in-st-louis
A USB drive, light as a stick of gum, holds the whole edited gallery in the photographer’s hand at the studio door. In Missouri, handing it over puts the session on the taxable side. Sent as a download link, the same gallery is exempt.
That split is written down. The Department of Revenue’s tax guide for photographers lists downloaded photos as exempt. It lists photograph services when photographs are delivered by tangible medium as taxable, and it names the USB device containing photographs, and the photo album, on that same taxable side.
Same session. Same edit. Same face on the screen. The only thing that changed is how the files left the room.
The room has a row of its own. The Department’s guide for casting studios lists studio space that is regularly rented to the public as taxable.
Now set that next to a studio rate page. At Evocative Studios, a photography rental studio at 8120 Gravois Rd. in Affton, it is one number: $35 for occasional use, for a room with lighting equipment, backdrops, props, furniture, a hair and make-up area and a lobby for guests. Hourly rentals require a 2-hour minimum.
That is the whole problem, and it is not the photographer’s. The rate page shows one number. The rule that changes it sits in a state PDF on a different website, and neither page points to the other. The split pages keep half the bill out of sight.
Here is the other half, while the paper is still unrolling off the stand. Room: two hours at $35 is $70. Tax: the Department’s current sales tax rate table lists 8.738% for the St. Louis County rows in the Affton fire district. On a taxable $70 rental that is about $6.12, so the room comes to about $76.12.
Then the reset. Lights back to their original location, props and furniture back where they stood, the background paper clean and rolled up, the cardboard core turning between two hands. The rate page does not say whether that fits inside the two hours or after them.
And last, the line decided at the door. A download link adds $0 in tax to the session. A USB drive puts the session fee itself on the taxable side, so a rate from that same table lands on the photographer’s fee too.
Three small moves close the gap. First, send the gallery as a download link, since the photographers guide lists downloaded photos as exempt. Second, before booking, ask the studio one question in one breath: “Is tax inside the $35 or on top of it, and does putting the room back count inside my two hours?” Third, for anything the guides don’t settle, like a client who wants a drive anyway, the Department offers a letter ruling to businesses that want a firm answer; its casting-studios guide says it may not necessarily cover every situation, because taxability may depend on facts and circumstances.
One number on the rate page, the rule in a PDF a website away. What would change if the rate page carried the tax line?
### How much does a studio photoshoot cost?
Two bills, and they get mixed up all the time. The first is the room. The second is the person behind the camera. For the photographer, the room is the cost and the session fee is the income. The client’s side of that math lives in what hiring a photographer costs.
For the room, the real number is the hourly rate times the minimum, plus the time it takes to build and tear down. Rolling in a case, standing up two lights, taping cables, the pop of the first test flash, then striking it all and rolling the paper back up: every minute of it runs on the same clock as the shoot.
Covering an event instead of a sitting is a different structure again, with its own hours and deliverables, and it gets its own page: what an event photographer actually covers.
### The fee nobody puts on the booking page
Sales tax is the line that never makes the rate card. The casting-studios guide that lists rented studio space as taxable also says it may not necessarily cover every situation, because the taxability may depend on facts and circumstances around the specific transaction. That is why the most useful thing to know about any studio quote is whether tax is included or added on top.
The gear for a home setup sits on the taxable side too. The same guide lists photography equipment, including a camera, tripod, reflectors, light kit, studio backdrop and props, as taxable purchases. Part of why renting a lit room can beat building one is right there.
### What does “gear included” actually get you?
It depends on the room, and the details are worth having in writing. How many light heads. Strobe or continuous. Which softboxes, umbrellas and grids. Which backdrops, and whether paper is part of the rate or billed as you pull it. A listing that says lighting equipment and backdrops is a start, not an answer.
Strobes fire a burst. They freeze motion, they overpower window light and they give you clean files at low ISO. They also need a trigger on your camera, and a trigger for one brand of light will not always fire another. The strobe brand is worth knowing before the drive over. Continuous LED lights are what-you-see-is-what-you-get, easier if you are newer, and the only choice if you are shooting video in the same session.
Modifiers matter more than head count. One light in a big softbox beats three bare heads for a headshot almost every time. You can feel the difference on a subject’s face before you see it on the back of the camera: hard light makes people squint and tense, soft light lets their shoulders drop.

Backdrop paper is a consumable. Once a client walks across it in street shoes, that stretch is done, and it gets cut off and thrown away. Some rooms include it, some charge by the foot, and that difference is where a quote and an invoice drift apart.

### Is a home or garage setup a real alternative?
For a narrow slice of work, yes. Small product on a tabletop, a single headshot backdrop that never moves, editing at your desk. What a home setup buys you is no clock. Nobody knocks at the two-hour mark, and you can leave a set built overnight.
What it does not buy you is height, climate or a room a paying client takes seriously. A garage in a St. Louis July is a sauna by noon, and in January your client keeps their coat on. When you are charging real money, the room is part of what the client is buying.

## Compounded Shots Cost Almost What Brand Wegovy Does
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-medical-weight-loss-costs-in-st-louis
$299. Your thumb stops on it. That is the monthly semaglutide treatment price on The Shine Spa’s weight loss page, a St. Louis med spa, and the consultation is listed as free. For a second it feels like the door finally opened. You can almost hear yourself telling someone you started.
Keep scrolling. A line further down says the program uses compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, and that compounded medications are not FDA-approved. They say it plainly, which is to their credit. Then open a second tab: Novo Nordisk’s own self-pay price for the brand-name Wegovy pen is $349 a month, new patients pay $199 for each of their first two monthly fills of the starter doses, and the Wegovy pill starts at $149. The deal you were about to drive across the county for sits only a little below the real thing, sold by the company that makes it.
That is the field in one comparison. The cheap tier moved, and the price on the ad is rarely the price on your card statement. Here is how to get your real number in St. Louis, starting with two doors that cost nothing to walk through.
### How much do weight loss clinics usually cost?
Budget in two parts, because nearly every program bills in two parts: the service and the drug. A telehealth program can start at $59 a month on an annual plan, as Sesame’s Success by Sesame lists, with medication on top. A local clinic may bundle the two or split them. The drug is the big line: brand-name Wegovy at $349 a month self-pay, Wegovy pills from $149. Surgery is priced as a package, and it has its own rules.
The clinic fee is the figure nobody publishes the same way twice. One lists a monthly treatment price, another a membership, a third a package of four doses. So the useful move is not a range from the internet. It’s making each place put its total in writing.
### Two St. Louis doors that cost nothing to open
The first is at Washington University. Its Weight Management Program invites people to a complimentary informational session that walks through the whole program before you commit to anything. You schedule it by calling 314-286-2080. Sit in that room, take the handout, and you’ll leave with a sense of what a medical program looks like when it is not selling you a vial.
The second is a trick for anyone thinking about surgery. Washington University’s weight loss surgery program posts the exact codes your insurer will ask for: 43775 for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, 43644 for laparoscopic gastric bypass, and E66.01 as the diagnosis code for morbid obesity. Read those numbers to the person on your insurer’s phone line and the vague answer turns into a yes, a no, or a list of requirements. The program also warns that some policies require you to take part in a documented medical weight loss program first.
### Five questions to ask before you hand over a card
Call from somewhere quiet, with a pen and the back of an envelope. Ask: What is the monthly fee? Is the medication included in it, and is it brand-name or compounded? Who pays for labs, and are they billed by an outside lab? What happens if the drug price changes mid-month? What does it cost to cancel? A clinic that will answer all five in an email is telling you something good about how it runs.
Labs are where a quote and a bill split apart. If the clinic draws your blood but sends the tube out, the lab bills you directly, and the clinic may never see that invoice. Our guide to getting lab work done in St. Louis walks through how to learn what a panel costs before the needle goes in.
Then check your own coverage before you check anyone’s price list. Ask your plan, in writing, for its weight-management drug policy. If the drug is covered, a cash membership may be charging you for coordination you could get for a copay.
### Is compounded semaglutide still the cheap option?
Not by much, and the legal ground keeps moving under it. The FDA announced it is proposing to exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list, after finding no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound them from bulk substances. In the agency’s own release, the commissioner put it plainly: “When FDA-approved drugs are available, outsourcing facilities cannot lawfully compound using bulk drug substances unless there is a clear clinical need.” The FDA invited public comment and said it will consider those comments before making a final determination. Read the FDA’s announcement on the 503B bulks list for the current status.
If a clinic still offers a compounded version, you are allowed to ask hard questions. Which pharmacy fills it? Is that pharmacy a 503A or a 503B facility? What is the concentration, and how are the syringes marked? You want to draw up a dose at your own kitchen counter without squinting at tiny lines and guessing. A good operator answers without flinching.
### Will insurance pay for any of this in Missouri or Illinois?
Split it into three pieces: the visit, the counseling and the drug. Visits and labs usually ride on your regular medical benefits. Counseling has a federal floor under it. The drug is the fight, and it is decided by what your employer or your plan chose to buy, not by the clinic. It is usually settled on the phone, on hold, with the member ID card flat on the table in front of you.
The counseling floor comes from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which recommends that clinicians offer or refer adults with a BMI of 30 or higher to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions, and gives that a B grade. That grade is what gets preventive counseling covered in many private plans, so ask your plan whether you can use it with no cost sharing.
On Medicare, Part B covers obesity screenings and behavioral counseling for people with a BMI of 30 or more, delivered by a primary care provider in a primary care setting, and you pay nothing if that provider accepts assignment. Medicare also lists a newer route for medication: through the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, people with Part D who qualify pay a $50 copayment for a one-month supply of certain GLP-1 drugs.
### Medicaid on each side of the river
If you’re on Medicaid, your answer lives in a spreadsheet, not an ad. KFF explains why it varies so much: a long-standing statutory exception lets states choose whether to cover weight-loss drugs, so Medicaid coverage of GLP-1 drugs for obesity is optional for states, while coverage for diabetes, cardiovascular disease and sleep apnea is required. Read KFF’s Medicaid coverage report for the national picture.
Then go to the lists themselves: the MO HealthNet Preferred Drug List on the Missouri side and the Illinois Medicaid Preferred Drug List across the river. Search each one for the exact drug your doctor named, and ask the prescriber’s office whether a prior approval is needed before the pharmacy will fill it. Finding a drug on a list is the start of the paperwork, not the end of it.
Completely off topic: somebody in your life deserves flowers this week.
### What does surgery cost, and how do you get your own number?
Bariatric surgery is the one tier where the big bill is mostly one-time, and the one where a national average helps you least. Get your own quote instead. Medicare covers some bariatric surgical procedures, like gastric bypass and laparoscopic banding, for people who meet certain conditions, and its own guidance admits that for surgeries it’s hard to predict your costs in advance. Its advice: ask the doctor, hospital or facility how much you’ll pay for the surgery and any care afterward.
That advice works for everyone, not just Medicare. Ask the surgical program for a written self-pay price and, more important, the list of what it leaves out. Psychological evaluation, nutrition visits, scopes and follow-up care can each sit outside a package. Hold the paper in your hand before you say yes.
Local spa versus the maker
A St. Louis med spa lists compounded semaglutide at $299 for a monthly treatment and compounded tirzepatide at $399, with a free consultation. Brand-name Wegovy from Novo Nordisk’s self-pay program runs $349 a month, and the pill starts at $149. What moves your total is the dose you end up on, whether labs are billed separately, and whether your plan covers the drug at all.
### What happens to the bill when you stop?
Ask this one before you start, because it is the question people forget until month eight. Is this a course with an end, or a line in the budget that stays, like a phone bill? What does the fee look like once your dose is steady? Do visits get shorter, cheaper, or further apart? A clinic that has thought about your second year will have an answer ready, and you’ll hear it in how fast they say it.
Write the answer on the same envelope as the other five. Put it on the fridge. When the renewal email lands, you’ll know whether the number in it is the number you agreed to. If it isn’t, you have the envelope, the date of the call and the name of the person who said it, and that is a much shorter conversation than the one you would have without them.
### Where low-cost help actually comes from
Not from a discount code. Start with preventive counseling through coverage you already hold. Then, if a hospital bill is part of your plan, ask for its financial assistance policy by name. Under Section 501(r)(4), a hospital organization has to establish a written financial assistance policy, and the IRS says that policy must be widely publicized and spell out whether assistance includes free or discounted care.
And read every “free” twice. In this business it usually sits in front of the word consultation. A free consult is not free treatment, and you’ll feel the difference when the second invoice shows up.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I get weight loss shots in St. Louis, Mo?
A.  Three routes exist. Your own primary care doctor can prescribe and send it to your regular pharmacy. A local clinic or med spa can prescribe and monitor for a monthly fee, and some, like one St. Louis med spa, say outright that they use compounded medication. A telehealth service can ship to your door. Ask each one whether the drug is brand-name or compounded.
### Q. How much do weight loss centers cost?
A.  Budget by the year, not the visit. Ask what twelve months totals, including the first consultation, labs, dose increases and the medication itself. One St. Louis med spa lists $299 for a monthly semaglutide treatment, while a telehealth program like Success by Sesame starts at $59 a month on an annual plan with medication on top. The yearly figure decides whether you can keep going.
### Q. What is the cheapest GLP 1 without insurance?
A.  Among brand-name options, the manufacturer’s own pricing is the floor to beat. Novo Nordisk lists the Wegovy pill starting at $149 a month self-pay and the Wegovy pen at $349 a month, with $199 for each of a new patient’s first two fills of the starter doses. Confirm the price on the day you buy.
### Q. Is it worth going to a weight loss clinic?
A.  It depends on what the clinic adds. You’re paying for faster dose changes, someone watching side effects between visits, and staff who handle the paperwork. If your own doctor will prescribe and your plan covers the drug, a cash membership may be charging you for coordination you could get for a copay.
### Q. Does insurance cover weight loss centers?
A.  Often in part. Plans usually treat the medical visit and labs like any other office visit, then handle the drug and any membership as separate questions. Whether the medication is covered depends on your plan and what your employer bought, not on the clinic. Get the plan’s weight-management drug policy in writing first.
### Q. What is the least expensive weight loss program?
A.  Usually the one inside coverage you already have. Medicare Part B covers obesity screenings and behavioral counseling, and you pay nothing if your primary care provider accepts assignment. In private plans, ask whether the behavioral counseling the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force gave a B grade is covered without cost sharing.
### Q. Can I get free weight loss treatment?
A.  Parts of it. Behavioral counseling can cost nothing under Medicare Part B when your provider accepts assignment. Hospitals run by a hospital organization must have a written financial assistance policy, and it has to say whether it offers free or discounted care. Free medication is rare, and a free consultation is not free treatment.

## No, Your Ameren Bill Won't Hit Zero With Solar
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-solar-panels-in-st-louis
The Ameren bill lands after your first bright month with panels on the roof, and you open it already smiling. It is not zero. It is not close to zero. You read it twice, standing at the kitchen counter, and then you go looking for the salesman’s card.
Ameren Missouri says it outright, in capital letters, on its own solar page: “If your system produces more than you consume you WILL NOT have a zero bill. All other regular monthly charges will still apply.” The power your panels push back onto the grid is credited at “SUMMER (June through September) 3.84 cents per kWh” and “WINTER (October through May) 3.39 cents per kWh.” Hold that number up against the per-kWh price on your own bill and the whole Missouri solar question comes into focus.
In Missouri, solar pays you most for the power you use the moment the panels make it. Think of a sticky St. Louis July afternoon, the air conditioner grinding away while the sun beats on the south side of the roof: every kilowatt-hour the house burns right then is one you did not buy. A kilowatt-hour you send back while nobody is home comes back at a few cents. That spread, not the brand of panel, is what decides whether the porch pitch you just heard holds up.
And there is a trap almost nobody mentions before the contract. Ameren Missouri’s page says “net metering IS available with both the residential Anytime Saver rate and the Evening/Morning Saver rate but is not available with Overnight Saver, Smart Saver or Ultimate Saver rates.” If you switched to a time-of-use plan to charge a car cheaply overnight, find out which one you are on before anybody climbs a ladder. Ameren Missouri adds that “As part of the application process your Ameren account rate will be verified,” so this is not something an installer can wave away. The plan name is printed on your bill, and the rules are on Ameren Missouri’s solar page.
So before you sign anything, do this, in this order. Pull your last twelve months of Ameren statements and total the kilowatt-hours, because Ameren Missouri’s formula sets your maximum system size from your most recent 12 billing months. Look at the top of the bill for your rate plan name. Call your homeowners insurance carrier and ask, in writing, whether a rooftop array is covered as part of the house and what your wind and hail deductible is. Ask a roofer how many years your shingles have left, because panels that have to come off for a new roof are a bill nobody prints on the quote. Then ask every company to show you the math without a federal tax credit in it.
### Is the 30% solar tax credit going away in 2026?
It is already gone for anything placed in service after December 31, 2025. The IRS page for the Residential Clean Energy Credit says the credit “equals 30% of the costs of new, qualified clean energy property for your home installed anytime from 2022 through December 31, 2025” and that “The credit is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025.”
That means a quote that knocks 30 percent off the price for a federal credit, on a system going up now, is built on a number that does not exist for you. It is the most expensive line on the page, and it takes about a minute to check on irs.gov. Do it with the quote in your other hand.
If a company tells you the credit still applies through some other door, ask it to name the code section and show you where it lands on your own tax return. If the answer is that the company claims it, not you, then you are looking at a lease or a power purchase agreement, and that is a different product with different math.
### How Ameren Missouri decides how big your system can be
You do not get to pick a size off a brochure. Ameren Missouri’s page gives the formula: “Most recent 12 billing month load kWh/(8,760 hrs. x 15.6% Capacity Factor) = Maximum Allowable Nameplate Capacity in kW DC.” Its own worked example uses a home with a “Previous 12 month load = 13,512 kWh” and lands at “13,512/(8,760 x 0.156) = 9.887 kW.”
Two things fall out of that. Your size is anchored to what you already used, not what you plan to use, so if an electric car or a heat pump is coming, say so early. And a house that used a lot last year is allowed a bigger array than the same house after you swap out the old bulbs, which is worth knowing in both directions.
The paperwork has a clock, too. Ameren Missouri says it “will review the submitted application and approve or reply within 30 days (systems 10kW and below) or 90 days (11 kW and larger systems).” Any installer promising panels on your roof next week, with the utility approval still pending, is promising something it does not control.
### Hail, roofs and trees
Anyone who has stood in a St. Louis garage listening to hail hammer the gutters knows why this section exists. Call your carrier before you sign, not after the first storm. Ask three things and get the answers in an email: is a permanently mounted rooftop array covered as part of the dwelling or does it need its own endorsement, is your wind and hail deductible a flat dollar amount or a percentage of the house, and does adding panels change your premium or your deductible at renewal.
Roof age is next. A good array is built to sit up there a long time, and shingles that already curl at the edges are not. If the roof is near the end, replace it first, or you are buying a remove-and-reinstall job down the road. A local company that tells you to do the roof first and loses the sale for now is telling you something about how it works. If you are pricing parts of that roof job yourself, the counters at St. Louis hardware stores are still good for exactly that kind of question.
Then the trees. A big oak that keeps your back bedroom cool in July also throws shade across a roof, and shade does not cut output in a neat straight line. Ask for a shade study done on site, tied to your actual roof planes, at more than one time of day. A satellite picture with a sunny overlay is a sales graphic.
Before you add panels, cut the load: swapping old lighting fixtures is the cheapest kilowatt-hour you will ever save.
### Buying, leasing or a PPA
Panels can end up on your roof by different roads, and they are very different things to own. You buy with cash or a loan and the system is yours. You lease, paying a set monthly amount for equipment someone else owns. Or you sign a power purchase agreement and pay for the electricity the system makes, at a per-kWh rate, to the company that owns it.
If an offer leads with a lease and no money down, that can work for the right house. Just know what you are signing. Get five things in writing before the pen comes out: how long the term runs, the yearly price increase, what it costs to buy the system out in each year, who pays to take the panels off and put them back when the roof is replaced, and what happens at the end of the term. A small yearly increase feels like nothing in the first summer and feels very different when you are trying to sell the house.
That last point is where solar homes get stuck. An owned, paid-off system rides along with the house like a finished basement. A leased system is a contract the buyer has to agree to take over, or one you have to pay off, in the middle of a closing with a clock running. If there is any chance you move in the next several years, weigh that before you choose the road.
### What to watch once it is on the roof
Open the monitoring app once a month and look at the production line. A system that quietly stopped making power can sit dark for weeks with nobody noticing, while the bill creeps back up. Leaves and snow sitting on the panels after a storm do the same thing in a smaller way.
Keep one folder from day one: the signed interconnection paperwork with Ameren, the city or county permit and final inspection, every warranty with its registration confirmation, the monitoring login, and the installer’s contact information. When you sell, or when a storm hits, that folder is the difference between a phone call and a month of digging.
Want three real quotes instead of one porch pitch? Browse solar installation companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, hand each one the same twelve months of Ameren bills, and ask all three to show the math with no federal credit in it.
If you run a solar company that shows homeowners the honest math, put that where they are looking. A Gold listing helps more customers find the installer who says “do the roof first,” or you can start your listing here.
One last thing for the day the crew shows up: they will be on your roof for hours, and a cold lunch from one of the St. Louis sandwich shops nearby is a small thing people remember.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is solar worth it in Missouri?
A.  It can be, but mostly on the power you use as it is made. Ameren Missouri credits the surplus you send back at 3.84 cents per kWh in summer and 3.39 cents in winter, so a house that runs its air conditioning, laundry and dishwasher while the sun is up gets far more from the same panels than a house that sits empty all day. Run the numbers off your own twelve months of bills.
### Q. Why is my electric bill high if I have solar?
A.  Because solar shrinks the energy part of the bill, not the whole thing. Ameren Missouri says that even when your system makes more than you use, “you WILL NOT have a zero bill. All other regular monthly charges will still apply.” After that, check for new load like a car charger, panels covered in leaves or snow, and a system that stopped producing without anyone checking the app.
### Q. What is the biggest downside to solar electricity?
A.  It only makes power while the sun is up, so its value depends on what your utility pays for the surplus. In Ameren Missouri territory that surplus is credited at a few cents per kWh, at 3.84 cents in summer and 3.39 cents in winter, while you still buy power after dark at your normal rate. That timing gap, not panel quality, is what most often lets people down.
### Q. What is the 20% rule for solar?
A.  Ask whoever mentions it to define it in writing. The rule that actually binds an Ameren Missouri customer is the utility’s own formula: your most recent 12 billing months in kWh, divided by 8,760 hours times a 15.6% capacity factor, gives your maximum system size in kW DC.
### Q. What I wish I knew before getting solar panels?
A.  The regrets that come up most are avoidable in one afternoon of phone calls: not replacing an old roof first, not asking the insurance carrier about the hail deductible, not realizing that surplus power is credited at a few cents instead of what you pay, not checking whether your rate plan allows net metering, and signing a lease without reading the yearly increase and the buyout schedule.
### Q. Can you get free solar panels in Missouri?
A.  Be careful with the word free. The federal homeowner credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. When an ad promises free panels, ask one question: who owns them? If the answer is not you, it is a lease or a power purchase agreement with no money down. That can still work for the right household, but it is financing, so read the contract twice.
### Q. Will the government pay you to install solar panels?
A.  Not through the federal homeowner credit. The IRS says the Residential Clean Energy Credit is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025. What is left for a Missouri homeowner is the value of the power you stop buying, plus the small credit Ameren Missouri pays for the surplus you send back.

## Old Window Cracked? St. Louis Hardware Counters Still Fix It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-st-louis-hardware-stores-still-do-for-you
Don’t replace that window yet. You know the one. The old wooden sash that rattles in its track every time a truck rolls past, the cold draft you can feel on the back of your hand at the sill, and now a crack running corner to corner across the bottom pane. You have already priced a new window in your head and winced.
Here is what most people never think to ask. Schnarr’s Hardware, at 40 East Lockwood Ave, says it repairs wood and aluminum frame windows, and it also repairs wood sash windows and double strength glass windows, any shape any size. Read that twice if you live in an older house with rope-hung sashes and one pane that cracked last winter. That is not a part you buy off a shelf. It is a job somebody does for you, at a bench, with your window lying on it.
The same store will tell you why the bench still exists. Its own history says the Schnarr family started in business by repairing wagons and Model T cars, and sharpening reel lawnmowers when Clayton Road was little more than a country road. The tools changed. The idea did not: bring the broken thing in, and someone at the bench fixes it.
So before you price a replacement window, a new lamp or a whole new screen door, do this today. Pull the broken piece. Wrap it in an old towel so the glass doesn’t shift in the trunk. Call the store at 314.961.4522 and ask three questions: do you repair this kind of frame, how long will it take, and do I need to bring the whole sash or just the glass. Then drive it over. A cracked pane in an old sash is a repair. Do nothing and it becomes a replacement.
Schnarr’s lists a few more counter jobs that a self-checkout lane cannot touch. It cuts glass or plexiglass to your exact specifications. It cuts keys and can send you home with a spare set for your home or most vehicles. And it offers what it calls specialized lamp repair, which matters the first time a lamp your grandmother owned flickers and dies on the end table. You can feel the click of the switch go soft before it quits. That lamp is usually a cord, a socket and an hour of somebody’s time away from working again.
One more thing worth knowing before you hand a clerk a key: under federal law, whoever knowingly and unlawfully makes a key to a lock box or other authorized receptacle for the delivery of mail can be fined or imprisoned not more than ten years. More on that below. It is the kind of no that protects you.
And yes, screens. Schnarr’s puts it plainly: was Fido anxious to get to that squirrel? They can fix that also. Anyone who has watched a dog go through a back door screen in one leap knows exactly what that sentence means.
### What does a hardware store do?
It sells the small stuff a house eats up, one screw, one washer, one hinge pin at a time. And it does work for you at the counter: cutting keys, cutting glass, mending screens and windows, mixing and matching paint, cutting chain and rope to length, filling propane, sharpening blades and fixing the odd lamp. The second half is the part people forget, and it is the part that saves the most money.
Nothing about that service list is standard from store to store. One counter re-screens and repairs sash windows. Another cuts keys and mixes paint and nothing else, because nobody on staff runs the other machines anymore. So the most useful habit in this whole guide is the phone call. Ask before you load the frame into the car.
### Which keys can a hardware counter copy, and which can’t it?
Most house, padlock, cabinet and desk keys are routine work, as long as the store stocks the matching blank. What actually stops a copy is almost never the words stamped on the key. It is the blank. Some high-security key systems are built so the blanks are not sold to just anyone, and if the store cannot get the blank, no machine in the building will help you.
One category is off-limits by federal law, and it surprises people. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1704, whoever knowingly and unlawfully makes, forges or counterfeits a key to a Postal Service lock, or to any lock box, lock drawer or other authorized receptacle for the deposit or delivery of mail, can be fined or imprisoned not more than ten years, or both. If your mail comes to a cluster box, that lock belongs to the Postal Service. The clerk who sends you to the post office is not being difficult. That is the statute talking.
Car keys are their own job. A key cut on a regular duplicator is a mechanical copy. On many newer cars it will turn the lock and still not start the engine, because the car is looking for a chip inside the key, not just the right cuts. Some counters can handle certain chipped keys and some cannot touch a push-button fob. Call first, and bring a key that already works.
### How paint matching actually works at the counter
The counter reads your sample with a color-matching machine, finds the closest formula its tinting system can mix, and squirts colorant into a base. A shaker rattles the can loud enough to stop conversation. The match lives or dies on the sample you bring.
Bring something physical. A chip of old paint pried off a door jamb, a switch plate, a scrap of trim. A photo on your phone is a poor sample, because your camera and your screen both change the color before anyone sees it. Take the chip from a spot the sun hasn’t bleached. Paint off a south-facing wall reads differently than the same paint from inside a closet.
Sheen changes how a color reads, too. The same formula in flat and in semi-gloss will not look like the same color on a wall. If the match matters, buy a small sample, paint a patch, let it dry and look at it in the morning light and again at night before you commit to gallons.
### Can a hardware store fix a window or door screen?
Yes, and it is one of the most common counter jobs there is. Bring the whole frame, not just the torn mesh. The tech pulls the old spline out of its channel, lays new mesh across the frame, rolls fresh spline in with a little wheel and trims the edge with a blade. Done right, the new screen is drum-tight and hums faintly when you flick it.
The skill is tension. Too tight and the frame bows inward. Too loose and the mesh ripples in the first breeze. If the frame itself is bent or split at a corner, ask whether the shop can build a new one. And ask about mesh: heavier pet-resistant screen exists for exactly the dog and squirrel situation above.
Need the big tool for one afternoon, not forever? Read up on renting tools and equipment in St. Louis.
### What can the counter cut to size?
Glass, plexiglass, chain, rope, cord and, at some stores, pipe. Cutting to length is a small service that saves real money. You need a short run of something that only comes in a long package, and buying the whole package means paying for scrap you then have to store in the garage.
For glass, give the counter the exact opening, measured in two places each way, and say whether you measured the hole or the old pane. For a storm door or a pane next to a tub, ask whether the piece needs to be safety glass before anything gets cut. For chain and rope, tell the counter what it has to hold, not just how long it needs to be. A good clerk will steer you to the right grade instead of the cheapest reel.
### Should you exchange a propane tank or have it refilled?
Refill if you want to keep your own tank and pay for what goes in it. Exchange if you want speed. The difference is written into Missouri’s propane rules. The Missouri Propane Safety Commission registers a Class VI LP Gas Dispenser Operator as the retail operation of a dispensing station used to fill portable LP gas containers by weight. A Class VII Cylinder Exchange Dealer is a business where cylinders are stored in a secured cage or area and exchanged with customers, full cylinder for empty cylinder, and the commission says that does not include the filling of any cylinder or tank on premises.
In plain English: the cage by the front door and the fill station out back are two different kinds of business, registered separately. If you want your own tank filled, you need a store with a fill station, so ask before you haul the grill tank over. You will hear the hiss of the valve and watch the scale climb, and you leave with the tank you brought.
### Is a mower blade worth sharpening?
Usually, right up until the steel is thin, the nicks are deep or the back edge is worn round. What matters even more than the edge is balance. A sharpened blade that is heavier on one side shakes the whole mower, and you feel it in your wrists by the second pass across the yard. That is the step people skip with a grinder in the garage, and it is the reason to hand the job across a counter.
While the mower is on your mind, one fuel rule worth knowing. The EPA says E15 cannot be used in engines in nonroad equipment, such as lawnmowers and chain saws. A cheaper pump price is not a bargain if it gums up the carburetor on the machine you just paid to tune. Ask the counter about ethanol-free fuel or a stabilizer before the mower sits for the winter.
### When the counter beats the big box, and when it doesn’t
The counter wins when the job is small, odd, or needs a human being: one machine screw, a short run of chain, a screen re-mesh, a sash window, a lamp that went dark, a paint color matched off a chip, a blade sharpened and balanced. The big box wins on volume: sheet goods, appliances, bulk lumber and anything you would buy fifty of.
Be honest about the trade-off. Big stores tend to keep longer hours and deeper stock. Check the hours before you go, because at a small counter a broken screen can turn into a lunch-hour errand, not an after-dinner one. What the small counter gives back is parking by the door, a person who answers the phone, screws sold loose instead of a blister pack of twelve, and someone willing to look at the broken part in your hand and name it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What hardware store is located in St. Louis?
