### Q. What makes a good hardware store?
A.  Depth of service and depth of small parts. A good one cuts keys and matches paint, and it also mends screens, cuts glass, cuts chain by the foot and sharpens blades. It sells fasteners loose, by the piece, and somebody there will look at your broken part and tell you what it is called.
### Q. What are the most common things people buy at a hardware store?
A.  Fasteners, batteries, light bulbs, tape, glue, cleaning supplies, plumbing repair parts like washers and supply lines, electrical odds and ends, paint and brushes, hand tools, lawn and garden goods, and propane. Most trips are one broken thing plus two more items you remember standing in the aisle.
### Q. Is Home Depot considered a hardware store?
A.  In everyday speech, yes. In the trade it is usually called a home center. The practical difference is the counter: a home center is built around self-service aisles and volume, and a neighborhood hardware store is built around a service bench with someone behind it who runs the machines.
### Q. What store is cheaper, Home Depot or Ace Hardware?
A.  It depends on the item, and I could not find any public price comparison across St. Louis stores. Big home centers tend to win on lumber, sheet goods and bulk quantities. Smaller stores can win on small items sold loose, because you buy one screw instead of a sealed dozen. Check the item, not the sign.
### Q. How can I save money at the hardware store?
A.  Repair instead of replace. A sash window, a screen or a lamp can often be fixed at the counter for less than a new one. Buy fasteners loose. Have chain and rope cut to length. Sharpen a mower blade instead of buying another. And test a paint match on a small patch before you buy gallons.
### Q. Where’s the best place to buy hardware?
A.  Match the store to the job. Small, odd or repair work belongs at a neighborhood counter: one bolt, a screen, a sash window, a paint match, a sharpened blade. Bulk material and appliances belong at a home center. High-security keys and car fobs often belong with a locksmith.

## Missouri Won't Make Insurers Cover IVF. Illinois Will.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-fertility-treatment-involves-in-st-louis
You read the test under the bathroom light, then again by the window, as if the second line might show up if you gave it a minute. It doesn’t. You fold it into a tissue, push it to the bottom of the trash, and open the calendar on your phone to count forward one more time.
If you’ve been doing that long enough that you’ve stopped telling anyone you’re trying, this page is for you. Not a pep talk. The order things happen in, what each step asks of your body and your mornings, and the money question, which in this metro turns on something most people never think to check.
Start with the part that stings. In the most recent session of the Missouri House, St. Louis Rep. LaDonna Appelbaum filed a bill that “Creates provisions relating to insurance coverage for fertility treatments.” Another bill asked the state to seek approval for MO HealthNet coverage of fertility treatments. Both ended the same way: referred to a committee called Emerging Issues, and on each bill page the line still reads “Hearing not scheduled.” Nobody voted them down. Nobody heard them at all.
### Will insurance cover IVF in Missouri?
Only if your employer chose to buy that coverage. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine’s state table for Missouri lists no coverage mandate and no fertility preservation mandate, and notes that infertility coverage is expressly excluded from Medicaid. Illinois is different. Its law requires infertility coverage, IVF included, on group policies with pregnancy benefits that are written in Illinois. So for a St. Louis household, the state your policy was issued in can matter more than the state you sleep in.
That is not the same as having nothing. Plenty of employers here add a fertility benefit on their own, sometimes run by a separate company your insurance card never mentions. You find out by asking, and the asking is the first real step.
### Three calls to make before you book anything
First, human resources. Sit somewhere you can take notes through the hold music and ask four things: is there a fertility benefit, is it capped by dollars or by cycles, which state was our group policy issued in, and is the plan fully insured or self-funded. Then ask for the plan document itself, not the glossy two-page summary. Ask, too, whether testing is paid under your regular medical benefits even if treatment is not, because the testing alone sometimes answers the question.
Second, your OB-GYN or primary care doctor. Ask for a referral and ask whether the early bloodwork can be ordered now instead of after a first consult weeks away. Much of it is timed to a specific point in your cycle, so a missed window means waiting a month for the next one. If the order sends you out to a lab, our guide to getting lab work done around the St. Louis metro covers how orders, timing and billing usually go.
Third, if there is a male partner, book the semen analysis this week. It is one short appointment, it costs little next to everything that might come after it, and it is the test couples skip most often. Skipping it means the plan is built on a guess, and guesses get expensive when every month counts and every appointment means another morning off work.
### When is it time to ask for an evaluation?
The federal Office on Women’s Health puts it plainly: most experts suggest trying for at least one year, and women 35 or older should see their doctors after six months of trying. Starting earlier keeps more doors open, because every test and every treatment cycle runs on the slow clock of your own body.
If you’re single, or your partner is the same sex as you, that clock was never yours to wait out. Illinois wrote this into its insurance law: infertility there includes “a person’s inability to reproduce either as a single individual or with a partner without medical intervention.” Bring that line with you if a scheduler tries to make you wait a year for donor sperm.
### Why the river matters more than your ZIP code
Under 215 ILCS 5/356m, a group policy that provides pregnancy-related benefits can’t be issued or renewed in Illinois unless it covers the diagnosis and treatment of infertility, including in vitro fertilization, artificial insemination, embryo transfer and surgical sperm extraction, along with preimplantation genetic testing. The older version applied only to policies covering more than 25 employees. The newer one lifts the employer size requirement, so it applies regardless of employer size.
The IVF coverage has a count on it. It holds until you’ve had 4 completed egg retrievals, and if a live birth follows a retrieval, 2 more are covered. Religious institutions that find the procedures contrary to their teachings are exempt.
Here is the trap for this metro. The benefits firm NFP points out the rule applies only to policies written in Illinois, so an employer whose policy was issued elsewhere does not have to comply, even for Illinois residents, and self-insured plans are exempt too. So a family in Belleville can come up empty while a family in Kirkwood, on a policy their employer bought in Illinois, may be covered. Those two HR questions settle it.
### What the workup and the treatment ask of you
For the person who would carry the pregnancy, the first round is usually a long history, bloodwork early in the cycle, a transvaginal ultrasound, and an X-ray or ultrasound test to see whether the fallopian tubes are open. For a male partner, it’s the semen analysis. Because so much is cycle-timed, “the first round of tests” tends to take a month or two, not a week. Your cycle doesn’t care what day the lab is open. Write the test days on the paper calendar on the fridge, so the whole house knows which mornings are spoken for.
Treatment then climbs a ladder and stops at the lowest rung that fits what the tests found. Pills to help you ovulate, with an ultrasound to check the timing. Then intrauterine insemination, where washed sperm is placed in the uterus around ovulation, which for single people and same-sex female couples using donor sperm is often where things begin. Then IVF: daily injections, monitoring visits that come every few days and then most days, an egg retrieval under sedation, embryos grown in the lab, and a transfer, often a frozen one in a later cycle.
What people underestimate is the mornings. IVF monitoring means early appointments, weekends included, with a needle in your arm and an ultrasound wand before you’ve had coffee, and then the drive to work as if nothing happened. If your job can’t flex, sort that out before a stimulation cycle starts, not halfway through one. And the wait after a transfer or an insemination is its own kind of quiet. Nobody hands you a plan for that part.
Off topic, on purpose: the metro’s antique dealers make a good slow afternoon when you need one.
### What should you ask a clinic about its numbers?
Start by asking whether it reports its results, and where. Under 42 U.S.C. 263a-1, every assisted reproductive technology program has to report its pregnancy success rates each year to the Secretary through the Centers for Disease Control, along with the identity of each embryo laboratory it uses.
Then ask the questions that make the number mean something. What counts as a cycle in the rate you just quoted: a started cycle, a retrieval or a transfer? How does it break out for my age? Which embryo lab do you use? Who performs my retrieval and my transfer? How are weekend monitoring and after-hours calls handled? And what happens to my frozen embryos, and the storage bill, if I need to stop for a year? A practice that answers those directly, without a sigh, is telling you something a chart can’t. Write the answers down in the parking lot before you start the car, while the voice on the phone or across the desk is still fresh, and compare them that evening.
Not sure which practice to call first? Browse fertility providers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two and ask each one the same questions: what counts as a cycle, which lab, who does the retrieval, and what the quote leaves out.
If you run a fertility practice, a counseling office or a lab that families here depend on, the people sitting with that calendar are searching late at night for someone who will answer straight. A St Louis Near Me Directory listing puts your practice in front of those customers when they finally start looking.
### The money that can come back to you
Keep every receipt in one folder from the first visit on. IRS Publication 502 lists fertility enhancement among deductible medical expenses, including “Procedures such as in vitro fertilization (including temporary storage of eggs or sperm).” If you’re adding up a year of medical bills, our piece on what a tax preparer costs around St. Louis is a sensible next stop.
Then read the clinic quote line by line, at the kitchen table, with a pen. A base IVF price rarely covers medications, anesthesia, genetic testing of embryos, freezing, yearly storage or a later frozen transfer. Ask each practice for a written, itemized estimate and compare the same lines side by side.
The number before the extras
### How can I do IVF if I can’t afford it?
Know the size of the number first: a White House executive order on IVF access put the cost per cycle at $12,000 to $25,000. Then shrink it from every side - an employer benefit or an Illinois-issued group policy, testing billed under regular medical coverage, a clinic payment plan, HSA or FSA dollars, and the deduction for medical expenses. Medications, embryo testing, freezing and a later frozen transfer are what push a quote past the base fee.
None of this tells you how your story goes. It can’t. What it can do is let you walk into the first appointment with your plan document in your bag, your questions on a card, and the sense that you’re the one steering.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does IVF cost in St. Louis, MO?
A.  The federal reference point is the executive order on IVF access, which put the cost per cycle at $12,000 to $25,000. Ask each clinic for a written, itemized estimate that covers monitoring, anesthesia, embryo testing, freezing and storage, so you are comparing the same lines.
### Q. Is IVF cheaper now with Trump?
A.  The executive order on expanding IVF access told the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy to send policy recommendations within 90 days. Your bill still depends on your employer’s plan, where the policy was issued and the clinic’s own prices.
### Q. How to get free fertility treatment?
A.  Truly free is rare, and reduced is more realistic. The routes people use are an employer benefit, an Illinois-issued group policy, manufacturer assistance on medications, nonprofit grants and clinical studies at academic centers. Ask the clinic’s financial counselor what exists before you assume the full price is the only price.
### Q. Which fertility clinic in St. Louis is considered the best?
A.  Federal law requires every program to report pregnancy success rates to the CDC each year, but clinics treat different patients, so a raw comparison can mislead. Judge fit instead: how often they treat your diagnosis, who performs the retrieval, how monitoring is scheduled, and exactly what a quote includes.
### Q. At what age are 90% of your eggs gone?
A.  Around 30, by the most-cited model. A study in PLoS ONE estimated that for 95% of women, by the age of 30 only 12% of their maximum pre-birth population of non-growing follicles remains, and by 40 only 3%. That is a population model, not a forecast for you, and it says nothing about egg quality.
### Q. How many days after your period are you fertile?
A.  It follows ovulation, not the calendar. The Office on Women’s Health says you are most fertile two to three days before ovulation and 12 to 24 hours after it, and sperm can live for up to three days. The time before ovulation can vary from 13 to 20 days, even month to month in the same woman.

## First Tooth? Book the Dentist, and Bring Your Water Bill
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-pediatric-dentist-does-and-when-to-start-in-st-louis
Tink.
That tiny click of something hard against the rim of the sippy cup. You freeze, set down the dish towel, and hook a finger gently past the baby’s lip. There it is. A pale white edge poking through the bottom gum, sharp as a grain of rice, and suddenly your baby has a tooth and you have a question you did not have this morning.
The answer comes sooner than most parents guess. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry says your child should see a pediatric dentist when the first tooth appears, or no later than the first birthday. Not at three. Not when they start school. That first edge of enamel is the starting gun.
And in St. Louis there is a second question hiding behind the first one, sitting right there in the kitchen: what is in the water you just used to fill that cup? The AAPD tells parents to have the pediatric dentist evaluate the fluoride level of the child’s primary source of drinking water. Most parents never think to bring it up. Here, you can walk in with the answer already in hand.
If your water comes from the City of St. Louis Water Division, its latest water quality report says the city has been fluoridating customers’ drinking water in accordance with St. Louis City Revised Code Chapter 11.26. The same report lists its most recent fluoride results at a range of 0.21-1.15 ppm, sampled at each treatment facility, with the source listed as a water additive for dental health. If your bill comes from Missouri American Water instead, its latest St. Louis area report shows fluoride results of 0.49-0.59 ppm. Two utilities, two numbers, both printed in reports you can pull up on your phone before the appointment.
### When should a child see a pediatric dentist?
When the first tooth appears, or no later than the first birthday. That is the AAPD’s guidance, and its parent FAQ adds that the first dental visit should be scheduled by your child’s first birthday. After that, the AAPD says a check-up every six months is recommended to prevent cavities and other dental problems, though your pediatric dentist can tell you how often your child should come in based on their own oral health.
The point of that first visit is not a big cleaning. It is a baseline. One office starts to know your child’s mouth, and you leave with a plan for brushing, bottles and snacks that fits the kid you actually have, not a pamphlet kid.
### Your water changes the advice
Here is why the water matters. The AAPD says that if a child is not getting enough fluoride internally through water, especially if the fluoride level is deficient or the child drinks bottled water without fluoride, the pediatric dentist may prescribe fluoride supplements. So a family that mixes formula with bottled water, or keeps a filter pitcher in the fridge, may get different advice from a family pouring straight from the city tap.
Tell the dentist three things at the first visit: who your water utility is, whether your child drinks mostly tap or bottled water, and whether you use a home filter. It takes a moment to say. It can change what the dentist recommends for years.
### What to do this week
Start brushing before the appointment, not after. The AAPD says to clean your baby’s gums from birth with a soft infant toothbrush or cloth and water, then use a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste to brush baby teeth twice daily as soon as they erupt. Once children are 3 to 6 years old, the amount goes up to a pea-size dollop, and you still perform or assist the brushing. Children should spit out and not swallow excess toothpaste.
At bedtime, keep the bottle to water. The AAPD’s advice for preventing decay caused by nursing is to avoid nursing children to sleep or putting anything other than water in their bedtime bottle. The milk-sweet smell of a sleepy baby is lovely. On teeth overnight, it is not.
Then call a pediatric dental office, say your child just got a first tooth, and ask for a first visit before the first birthday. If you are still sorting out the medical side, here is how to choose a pediatrician in St. Louis.
### What the first visit actually feels like
Shorter and gentler than most parents brace for. Expect a lot of talking and very little drama. You will probably hold your child for much of it, and the dentist will take a careful look at the teeth and gums, ask about feeding and brushing, and tell you what they see. Crying is normal. Squirming is normal. The team has seen both many times before lunch.
Time it well. Book for the part of the day when your child is usually rested and fed, not right before a nap. Bring a favorite small toy and a list of your questions, written down, because the room will be bright and new and your baby will be grabbing at your shirt collar. Ask the dentist to tell you, before you leave, how often to come back and how much toothpaste to use at this age. Write both answers on the appointment card.
### What makes a pediatric dentist different
Training and focus. The AAPD says a pediatric dentist has two to three years of specialty training following dental school and limits the practice to treating children only. It describes pediatric dentists as primary and specialty oral care providers for infants and children through adolescence, including those with special health needs.
You feel that difference in the room. The chairs are smaller, the ceiling sometimes has something to look at, and the staff talk to a squirming two-year-old like it is the most normal thing in the world, because to them it is. A general dentist who sees kids regularly can be a fine choice too. What matters most is that your child gets seen, early and on a schedule.
### Sealants, and the back teeth that do the chewing
Later, when the permanent back teeth come in, ask about sealants. The AAPD explains that sealants work by filling in the crevasses on the chewing surfaces of the teeth, which shuts out food particles that could get caught there and cause cavities. It says the application is fast and comfortable and can effectively protect teeth for many years. For a kid who dreads the chair, that word comfortable matters.
Completely unrelated, but that first-tooth milestone still deserves frosting. Find a bakery.
### A Missouri insurance rule worth knowing before you need it
Most children never need to be put under for dental work. But if a toddler has extensive decay or simply cannot sit through treatment, the bill for the hospital and the anesthesia can be the part that scares parents most. Missouri law helps here. Statute 376.1225 requires covered health insurance policies to cover the administration of general anesthesia and hospital charges for dental care for a child under the age of five, a person who is severely disabled, or a person with a medical or behavioral condition that requires hospitalization or general anesthesia for dental care.
There is a catch to plan around. The same statute says nothing in it prevents a health carrier from requiring prior authorization for hospitalization for dental care procedures, the same way it does for other conditions. So if a dentist recommends treatment under general anesthesia, call your plan before the date is set, ask whether prior authorization is needed, and get the answer in writing. That one call can save a very long night of worry.
### Paying for it
HealthCare.gov says dental coverage is an essential health benefit for children, which means that if you are getting health coverage for someone 18 or younger, dental coverage must be available for your child either as part of a health plan or as a separate dental plan. It also notes you can’t buy a Marketplace dental plan unless you’re buying a health plan at the same time. If money is tight, our guide to free and low-cost dental care in St. Louis lays out the options.
### If you live on the Illinois side
Families across the river have two numbers worth saving. Illinois’ Department of Healthcare and Family Services says adults and children enrolled in Medicaid, but not enrolled in a Managed Care Plan, should visit DentaQuest or call 1-888-286-2447 for help finding a dentist. If your child is in a managed care plan, HFS points you to the number on the back of the membership card instead.
There is also a teaching clinic. The SIU School of Dental Medicine says its dental clinics are in two locations, its Alton campus and the SIUE East St. Louis Center campus, and it lists pediatric dentistry among its patient care clinics. Its clinic line is 618-474-7000, answered from 8 a.m.-5 p.m., Monday thru Friday. Call ahead and ask what a first pediatric visit there involves and how long to plan for, so nobody is hungry and cranky halfway through.
That first tooth is your cue to book. Browse pediatric dentists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick one close to home, and bring your water utility’s name to the first visit.
If you run a pediatric dental office or a family practice that loves little patients, parents are searching the week that first tooth shows up. Put your practice where they look and get more customers from families ready to book.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Should a 2 year old go to a dentist?
A.  Yes. The AAPD says a child should see a pediatric dentist when the first tooth appears or no later than the first birthday, so a 2 year old who has not been yet is overdue, not too young. After that, the AAPD recommends a check-up every six months unless the dentist advises otherwise.
### Q. What is the point of a pediatric dentist?
A.  Pediatric dentists are primary and specialty oral care providers for infants and children through adolescence, including those with special health needs, according to the AAPD. They spend two to three extra years training after dental school and treat only children, which shows in how they handle a nervous or squirming patient.
### Q. Do you really need a pediatric dentist?
A.  Not always. What your child needs is a dentist who sees children regularly and starts by the first birthday. A pediatric dentist is a strong choice for very young children, kids with special health needs, or a child who is anxious, because that is all they do.
### Q. What’s the difference between a pediatric dentist and a regular dentist?
A.  Training and patients. The AAPD says a pediatric dentist has two to three years of specialty training following dental school and limits the practice to treating children only. A general dentist treats all ages and may refer a child to a pediatric dentist for more complex care.
### Q. How much does it cost to see a pediatric dentist?
A.  It depends on your coverage. HealthCare.gov says dental coverage is an essential health benefit for children, so it must be available for anyone 18 or younger, either inside a health plan or as a separate dental plan. Ask the office for its self-pay rate before the first visit if you do not have coverage.
### Q. Who is the best pediatric dentist in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single best one, only the best fit for your child. Look for an office close to home that sees babies, explains its advice in plain words, and asks about your water. The AAPD also runs a Find a Pediatric Dentist search for families looking in their hometown.
### Q. Where can I find a free dentist in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  Start with children’s dental coverage, which HealthCare.gov says must be available for anyone 18 or younger who is getting health coverage. For clinics and sliding-fee options across the metro, see our guide to free and low-cost dental care in St. Louis.
### Q. When should a child stop going to a pediatric dentist?
A.  There is no single cutoff day. The AAPD describes pediatric dentists as oral care providers for infants and children through adolescence, so many kids stay through their teen years. When your child starts to feel too big for the small chairs and the cartoon ceiling, ask the office when it usually helps families move to a general dentist.

## Buying Plants in St. Louis: Tomatoes Wait Till May 1
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-buying-plants-in-st-louis
Did you put tomatoes in the ground the first warm weekend in April? Then came the cold night. By morning the leaves were dull and stiff, and for weeks the plant just sat there while you watered it, waited and wondered what you did wrong.
You did not do anything wrong except the calendar. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s planting guide for this city says, “In St. Louis this date is considered to be April 15,” meaning the average last killing frost. Average, not last. And its tomato advice is plain: “After the threat of frost is past and the soil is warm, around May 1, set out tomatoes, and plant seeds of beans and corn.” The peppers, squash, cucumbers and okra wait longer still, until “around May 10th.”
Here is the money part. A plant lost to one cold night is a plant you buy twice. So the April trip to the garden center is for the cool-weather crops, and the warm-weather flats can stay on the bench, or on your porch, carried into the garage on the cold nights, for a few more weeks.
The same guide names the bigger reason plants fail, and it should change how you shop: “Most failures with planting are generally caused by choosing a plant which is not well suited for the site and poor follow-up care.” Not the store. Not the brand of potting mix. The match between the plant and your patch of ground, decided before you ever reach the checkout.
So do the homework at home, before the trip. Stand in the spot at a few times of day and count the hours of direct sun on your face. Look at where the puddles sat after the last hard rain. Push a trowel in and see whether the dirt comes up crumbly or in slick gray clumps that hold the shape of the blade. Take two or three photos on your phone, the wide shot and a close one of the soil.
Then use the free help sitting a phone call away. The Garden’s Horticulture Answer Service takes questions by phone, “Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-noon Phone: (314) 577-5143.” If you would rather talk to someone in person, the Plant Doctor Desk at the Center for Home Gardening is a walk-in desk staffed by expert staff and Master Gardener volunteers, open “April-October open daily, 9 a.m.-4 p.m. November-March open Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m.”
One rule catches people. Do not show up with a sick branch in a grocery bag. The Garden says that for identifying a plant or diagnosing a problem, “only photos of the plant or issue are permitted. Please DO NOT bring plant material into the Garden to prevent potential contamination of our living collections.” Bring the photos you took. With the sun count, the drainage and those photos in hand, you shop with a short list instead of a cart full of hope, and the short list is cheaper.
### What gardening zone is St. Louis, MO in?
Zone 7 for the city and most of St. Louis County on the current USDA map. As one local garden columnist summed up the update, “The new map now places all of downtown St. Louis and almost all of St. Louis County in Zone 7.” The same column notes, “Only the westernmost edge of the county remains in Zone 6B.”
So the number on a plant tag means slightly different things depending on where you live in the county. Look up your own ZIP code on the USDA plant hardiness map rather than trusting a generic St. Louis number, and if your yard sits in a low spot where the cold settles on still nights and the frost lingers white on the grass after the rest of the street has thawed, treat a borderline plant as a gamble.
The zone tells you one thing only: whether a plant is likely to live through an average winter low. It says nothing about the wet, heavy August air that hangs over the city, or about clay that holds water like a bowl. A shrub that shrugs off January can still give up in July.
### When should I start my garden in Missouri?
Cool-season crops go first, while you still need a jacket to work outside. The Garden says that “With April 15 as your target date, seeds and transplants of hardy vegetables can be planted around March 20th,” including “lettuce, radishes, peas, spinach, mustard greens, collard, beets, carrots, potatoes, onions, early cabbage and broccoli.” Pansies can go out then too, which is why the benches fill with them while your coat is still on.
Warm-season crops follow the soil, not the first sunny afternoon. Tomatoes around May 1, then the heat lovers the Garden lists for around May 10th: “cucumbers, eggplants, okra, sweet potatoes, watermelons, peppers, summer squash and zucchini.” If the dirt still feels cold and damp in your fist, give it another week.
So if you are buying in April, buy the lettuce and the onion sets. If you are buying in May, that is when the tomatoes and peppers earn their price.
### Is it cheaper to buy plants at a nursery or Home Depot?
Compare the plant, not the tag. Two pots both labeled one gallon can hold very different amounts of root, so slide each plant partway out and look before you decide which is the bargain. A plant that has baked on a hot parking lot with spotty watering is not the same purchase as one that came off the truck this week, even at the same price.
A fair way to split it: buy the things that only have to last a season on price, and buy anything that has to live for years on condition and advice. Bagged mulch, a flat of annuals and basic vegetable starts are commodities. A tree that will shade your back window for decades is not, and the person who can tell you how it does in clay is part of what you are paying for.
Rather not dig at all? Here is what a gardener costs and does in St. Louis.
### Read the roots before you read the tag
Turn the pot over and ease the plant out. Healthy roots are pale and spread through the soil. Roots wound in a tight brown spiral around the outside mean the plant has sat in that pot too long, and they will keep circling in the ground unless you loosen or cut them at planting. A sour smell at the soil line or a stem that feels mushy when you pinch it is a plant to leave behind.
Then read the tag for the boring parts: hours of sun, water needs, mature height and width. The flower photo is the least useful thing on it. Check the hardiness number against your own ZIP. Look under a few leaves for insects. Ask when the shipment came in, and ask whether the place grew the plant or bought it in.
Buy fewer, better plants. Three shrubs that fit the spot beat nine impulse buys that do not, and you will spend the summer watching them fill in instead of watching them fade.
### Clay, and why the hole matters more than the plant
If your shovel comes up with slick, heavy clods that hold the shape of the blade, the hole you dig can turn into a bucket. Water runs into the loose soil you backfilled, cannot move out through the clay around it, and the roots sit in it. The plant leafs out on stored energy, then slides downhill through summer. It looks like a watering mistake. It is a drainage problem.
You can see this for yourself before you buy. Dig a test hole where you plan to plant, fill it with water, and watch how long it takes to drain. If it is still standing the next day, choose plants that tolerate wet feet, or build the bed up and plant on a low mound. Dig planting holes wide rather than deep, set the plant no lower than it sat in the pot, and work compost into the soil around it rather than making a rich pocket only in the hole.
The Garden flags the timing issue on wet ground, too: “Delay planting, however, if the soil is wet and will compact during planting.” If the clay smears like putty when you work it, wait a few dry days. Your back and your plants will both thank you.
### The best time to buy trees and shrubs
Early spring and fall, not the middle of summer. The Garden says spring planting “can be started in March and should be concluded at least by early June,” so roots have time to grow “before the hot St. Louis summer arrives.” Summer planting can work, but it warns that “follow-up care is very important as the plant’s root system may be inadequate to deal with the water demand of the leaves.”
Fall is the window people forget. “Fall planting should not be overlooked,” the Garden says, adding that “The cool soil temperatures of fall are ideal for root formation.” Picture the difference in the plant’s terms: warm soil under its feet, cool air on its leaves, and months to settle in before the next July. The exceptions are tender plants and ones that are hard to transplant, which the Garden says are “best planted in spring.”
Whatever season you buy in, the follow-up is the same, and it is the half of that first quote people skip. The Garden’s advice for success is to “select plants carefully, mulch after planting, check them at least once a week, and water if necessary until well established.” Put a weekly reminder on your phone. It is the cheapest insurance you will buy all year.
If you would rather hand the design and the heavy digging to someone else, here is how to choose a landscaping company in St. Louis. And if the reason you are outside every weekend is to get the car looking good after the pollen settles on it, the auto detailing listings are here.
