### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What month should you start planting a garden?
A.  March for cool-season crops in St. Louis, May for warm-season ones. The Missouri Botanical Garden uses April 15 as the city’s average last killing frost and says hardy vegetables can go in around March 20th. Tomatoes go out around May 1 once the soil is warm, and heat-loving crops like peppers and squash around May 10th.
### Q. How late is too late to start a vegetable garden?
A.  Count backward from fall. The Garden says to work backwards from October 20, the average first killing frost, and to add a couple of weeks for the shorter days of fall. For most vegetables, it says, that puts planting between mid-July and mid-September, so a late start is a fall garden, not a lost year.
### Q. Where is the cheapest place to get garden plants?
A.  Seed is cheapest per plant, then small starts, then end-of-season clearance on whatever is left. Divisions from a neighbor’s overgrown bed cost nothing at all. For anything meant to live for years, choosing the right plant for the spot saves more money than any discount, because a dead bargain is the most expensive plant you can buy.
### Q. Are plants more expensive at a nursery?
A.  Sometimes on the sticker, and the gap narrows once you compare what is actually in the pot. Check root mass, how fresh the plant is and whether anyone can tell you how it does in clay and full afternoon sun. Pay for advice on long-lived plants, and buy seasonal color wherever the flats look healthiest.
### Q. What is the difference between a nursery and garden center?
A.  A nursery grows plants; a garden center sells them, along with soil, pots and tools. Plenty of places are a bit of both, growing some stock and buying in the rest. Ask which a given plant is. A plant that came through a St. Louis winter on the property has already passed one test your yard will give it.
### Q. What does a garden nursery do?
A.  It propagates and grows plants, from seed, cuttings or young stock, until they are big enough to sell, then sells them to the public, to landscapers or to other stores. The good ones also tell you what will survive in your yard, which is the part of the purchase that never shows up on the tag.

## St. Louis Inspection Flags It. Whose Side Is Your Agent On?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-real-estate-consultant-does-and-what-it-costs-st-louis
When the city inspector writes up your house, whose side is the agent on?
The doorbell. A city inspector walks your rooms one at a time, flipping light switches, running the kitchen tap, looking hard at the stairs, while you stand in the hallway between stacks of moving boxes and try not to watch.
Then a sheet of paper with a list on it. Your stomach drops a little, because the buyer is going to see that list too.
In the City of St. Louis, that walk-through is part of selling a house. The Building Division puts it plainly: “For residential sales, a Certificate of Inspection must be obtained before occupancy of the unit is permitted.”
The application costs $120.00. Water and electric must be operable at the time of inspection. Inspectors examine a building’s exterior, interior and interior common areas, and set the dwelling’s occupancy load.
And if the certificate is issued with violations, the property owner has 30 days to make the necessary repairs.
So now there is a list, a clock, and a buyer. Somebody has to negotiate who fixes what and who pays. The only question that matters in that room is whether the licensee across the table is working for you at all.
Here is the part nobody says out loud while the list lies on the counter between the coffee mugs. Under Section 339.755 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri, a real estate licensee “may provide real estate service to any party in a prospective transaction without an agency or fiduciary relationship to one or more parties to the transaction.” The law calls that person a transaction broker. Their duties are real: present offers on time, use reasonable skill and care, disclose adverse material facts they know about. So the inspector’s list goes to both sides. Loyalty to you, when the two of you argue over who pays for it, is not on the list.
Turn the list over and do the math on the back. Clever Real Estate’s local survey puts total realtor fees due at closing here at 5.61% of the sale price. On a $276,000 home, the St. Louis median, Clever counts that as $15,500. That is a lot of money to hand to people who may owe you no loyalty, before anyone has told you whether selling is even the right call.
That is the opening a real estate consultant walks through. Pay someone a fee for advice and the question of who they work for gets a plain answer: you. Here is what that advice is, what it costs next to a commission, and where Missouri law says advice stops and licensed work begins.
### What is a real estate consultant vs. realtor?
One hands you a written report. The other hands you a pen and a listing agreement. A consultant sells you advice for a fee. A real estate agent sells you a transaction, usually for a commission paid when it closes. The consultant gets paid whether you buy, sell, or decide to sit still. That one difference reshapes every incentive at the table, and you can feel it in how fast the conversation turns to listing dates.
The title on the card tells you almost nothing. “Consultant” is a description, not a credential. In Missouri, what decides whether someone needs a license is what they do for the money, and that line is written into the statute, in a place most people don’t expect.
### Three things to do before you pay anyone
Clear a spot on the counter for three pieces of paper. First, ask for the form. In a residential transaction, Section 339.770 says that at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following first substantial contact, a licensee must give a buyer, seller, landlord or tenant who hasn’t signed a written services agreement a copy of the current broker disclosure form prescribed by the commission. It is short and easy to sign without reading. Read it anyway, slowly, with your coffee going cold. It is the page that tells you which relationship you’re in.
Second, check the license yourself on the Missouri Real Estate Commission’s page. If you would rather talk to a person, the commission’s general line is 573-751-2628. Either way it takes about as long as finding your reading glasses.
If you are selling in the city, ask one more thing on day one: who applies for the Certificate of Inspection, and who decides how the repairs get split? The earliest an inspection may be scheduled is 3 business days from the day you apply, and the Building Division takes calls at (314) 622-3313. Get the answer in writing before the inspector’s list arrives, not after.
Third, get an engagement letter before any advice starts. Three lines matter: what you get, the date you get it, and the fee. Ask, too, whether the fee credits against a commission if you later list with the same firm. Someone who won’t put scope and a date in writing is selling you a conversation.
### What does a consultant actually deliver?
Mostly four things, and each ends in a document, not a closing date. A written opinion of what a property or a plan is likely worth, with the comparable sales and assumptions spelled out. A strategy for a decision: sell now or wait, rent it or list it, which of three rentals to let go first. Preparation for a negotiation you’re about to have. And a portfolio review for someone who owns more than one door, with the rent roll spread across the table and a calculator in reach. None of it replaces the trades: when a repair list lands, you still need a roofer or a plumber, not an opinion.
There is a fifth kind of work that shades into a different job: feasibility advice on a project, closer to what a real estate developer does in St. Louis than to anything a listing agent handles.
### Where Missouri law draws the licensing line
Missouri defines a real estate broker in Section 339.010 as anyone who, for another and for compensation, does or attempts to do any of a list of acts. Two of those acts are worth reading closely. One is assisting or directing in the procuring of prospects calculated to result in a sale, exchange, lease or rental. The other is assisting or directing in the negotiation of any transaction calculated or intended to result in one.
Read those slowly, the way you’d read the fine print on a lease, because they are the whole answer. Building a spreadsheet, reviewing a rent roll, or explaining what prices have been doing on your street is not on that list. Sitting in on the negotiation and steering it, for a fee, is. So is lining up a buyer for you.
The consequences are spelled out too. Section 339.020 makes it unlawful to act as a real estate broker or salesperson, or to advertise or assume to act as one, without a license first procured from the commission. Section 339.170 makes knowingly violating those sections a class B misdemeanor. So if your paid adviser offers to “handle the negotiation,” ask to see the license before you hand over the offer.
One exemption matters a lot to anyone shopping for advice. Section 339.010 lists “any licensed attorney-at-law” among those the chapter does not apply to, so a real estate lawyer can advise you and negotiate for you without a real estate license.
Off topic, and we know it: if the inspector’s list says roof, read what a roof replacement costs in St. Louis before anyone quotes you.
### Is a consultant’s number the same as an appraisal?
No, and Missouri keeps them apart in law. Section 339.501 makes it unlawful to act as a real estate appraiser in the state without first obtaining a license or certificate from the Missouri real estate appraisers commission. Section 339.501’s exemption list covers any licensed real estate broker or salesperson who prepares a comparative market analysis or a broker price opinion.
Notice how that exemption is written: for licensees. A consultant’s pricing opinion, stapled at the corner and slid across the table, is excellent for deciding what to do and weak for binding anyone else. If a lender, a court or a tax appeal needs a value, you want the other document, and what a home appraisal involves in St. Louis walks through how that runs.
### What does advice cost next to a commission here?
Ask whether the quote is hourly, a flat fee for one named deliverable, or a monthly retainer. I could not find any published fee schedule for real estate consulting in St. Louis, so treat any range you see online as someone’s guess and get your own quote in writing.
What you can measure is what consulting competes against. Clever Real Estate, which sells its own 1.5% listing fee service, puts the average total realtor fees due at closing in St. Louis at 5.61% of the sale price, higher than its national average of 5.46%. That is a company survey, not a law, and commission has always been negotiable.
The percentage, in St. Louis dollars
### How much does a realtor make off of a $300,000 house?
Clever’s St. Louis survey works its 5.61% average out to $15,500 in realtor fees on a $276,000 home, the St. Louis median price, so a $300,000 sale lands a little above that, split between the listing side and the buyer side. Each agent then shares their side with their brokerage. What moves the number is the rate you negotiate, the sale price and whether the seller agrees to pay the buyer’s agent.
Now set a fee beside it. A flat fee for one written opinion is a single number, agreed up front, that doesn’t grow if the house sells for more. A percentage grows with the price of the house. A fee grows with the hours of thinking. Neither is cheaper in the abstract. Lay the two numbers side by side on the same sheet of paper, and the right one for your situation usually stops being a mystery.
### When paying for advice beats paying a percentage
When the decision is worth more than the transaction. If your real question is whether to do this at all, a commission is an odd way to buy the answer, because a commission only exists if you say yes.
A fee tends to win when you’re not sure you should sell, when you already have the buyer (a sibling, a neighbor, the tenant who wants the duplex), when you own several properties and the question is which one, when the property is odd, or when you’re a confident negotiator who needs preparation rather than representation. It loses when you need the house photographed, listed, shown on Saturdays and pushed hard for weeks. That is brokerage, and a percentage buys a lot of it.
If the property sits across the river in the Metro East, ask one more question on the first call: are you licensed in Illinois too? It’s a separate state with its own act, and plenty of metro professionals hold only one license.
Need the advice before you need the sign in the yard? Browse real estate consultants across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two and ask each for a written scope, a date and a flat fee on the same question before you choose.
If you’re the consultant, the broker or the one-person advisory shop, the people sitting at that kitchen table are searching for someone who will tell them straight who they work for. A St Louis Near Me Directory listing puts you in front of those customers while they’re still deciding who to call.
And if what you actually need is somebody to market and sell the house rather than tell you whether to, that is a different shopping trip. How to choose a real estate agent in St. Louis covers that side.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does a real estate consultant do?
A.  A real estate consultant gives paid advice about a property decision instead of brokering the sale. The work is usually a written opinion of value, a sell-or-rent analysis, negotiation preparation or a review of several rentals. You get a document and a recommendation, not a closing date. In Missouri, assisting in a negotiation for a fee is broker work that needs a license.
### Q. What is the difference between a real estate agent and a real estate consultant?
A.  An agent is licensed to handle transactions and is usually paid when one closes. A consultant is paid for analysis whether anything closes or not. Plenty of people do both. What carries legal weight in Missouri is the activity: assisting in a negotiation or procuring prospects for a fee is broker work under Section 339.010, title or no title.
### Q. How much does a real estate advisor cost?
A.  Ask whether the quote is hourly, a flat fee for one named deliverable, or a monthly retainer. I could not find a published fee schedule for this work in St. Louis, so get a written quote with the scope and delivery date. Compare it with the commission it would replace: Clever’s St. Louis survey puts total realtor fees at 5.61% of the sale price.
### Q. Is $100 an hour good for consulting?
A.  It depends on what the hour buys you. Measure it against the alternative: by Clever’s St. Louis survey, total realtor fees on a $276,000 median-priced home come to $15,500. If a few hours of advice change your decision, or keep you from a sale you didn’t need, the rate matters less than the outcome.
### Q. What is the best way to pick a real estate agent?
A.  Ask for the Missouri broker disclosure form at the first real conversation, so you know whether they would be your agent or a transaction broker. Look up their license through the licensee search on the Missouri Real Estate Commission’s site. Then interview at least two, and ask each the same questions about price, marketing and their commission.
### Q. Is it free to hire a real estate agent?
A.  No. Someone pays, usually at closing out of the sale. Clever’s St. Louis survey puts the average total at 5.61% of the price. The rate is negotiable, so the real questions are who writes the check, how much, and whether you asked.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of using a consultancy?
A.  You pay whether or not anything happens, and you may pay twice if you later hire a broker for the same property. In Missouri, acting as a broker without a license is unlawful, and assisting in a negotiation for a fee counts as broker work. And their pricing opinion isn’t an appraisal, so a lender or a court doesn’t have to accept it.

## Before the Mask Comes Down: Book Your Own Barnes-Jewish Anesthesia Visit
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-ask-about-anesthesia-before-surgery-in-st-louis
The surgery date is on the fridge now, circled in pen, and the scheduler has already hung up. Here is the call nobody tells you is yours. Barnes-Jewish Hospital’s Center for Preoperative Assessment and Planning says it plainly: “Please call and make your appointment as soon as your surgeon schedules your operation.” Not the surgeon’s office. You. And do it at least five to seven days before surgery, especially if your medical history is complex.
The number is (314) 362-4275. Save it before the calendar goes back on the magnet.
Why bother? Because the worst part of surgery, for most people, is the part they never get to rehearse. The IV taped to the back of your hand. The fluid running cold up your arm. A plastic mask settling over your nose and mouth while somebody you met ten minutes ago asks for a few deep breaths. This visit is where the anesthesia team meets you first, sitting up, dressed, in a chair instead of on a gurney. The center calls itself a unit of Barnes-Jewish Hospital where important information about your health can be gathered before surgery. The team includes anesthesiologists, advanced practitioners, resident physicians and nurses.
Getting there is its own small ritual. At the main campus you park in the Euclid Garage and cross the skywalk over Euclid Avenue to the Center for Advanced Medicine, traffic sliding by under your feet, the hospital towers ahead of you. If the city campus feels like too much, the center also has a CPAP desk at Barnes-Jewish West County Hospital, off Olive, and one at the Center for Advanced Medicine site near I-55 and Butler Hill Road.
Now the detail that surprises people. Before that visit, the center says to eat and drink normally and to keep taking your normal medications. The fasting comes later, on its own instructions. Walk in fed, with your coffee in you, not light-headed and rattled.
The night before, sweep the medicine cabinet into a grocery bag. Let the bottles rattle. Or fill in the center’s Home Medication Record with the dose and how often you take each one. Count the small stuff, too: vitamins, herbs, aspirin, inhalers. Add every current insurance card in your wallet, and the implant card for a pacemaker, defibrillator, stimulator or stent. If your recent tests were done outside the BJC health system, bring copies.
Text this to anyone with a surgery date: at an in-network hospital, an out-of-network anesthesia provider cannot use the No Surprises Act’s notice-and-consent waiver. If a clipboard comes at you asking you to sign away your balance-billing protection for anesthesia, do not sign it yet.
Having surgery somewhere else in the metro? Call the surgeon’s office today and ask one question: “Is there a pre-anesthesia visit, and who books it?”
### Does the anesthesiologist stay in the operating room?
The operating room is colder than you expect. Bright lights, steel, people in caps who all seem to know each other, and a narrow table that feels too small. The face at your head is the one that matters, and it may not be the doctor you met in the pre-op bay. That physician may be leading a care team across several rooms, coming back for the going-under and the waking-up.
In between, a nurse anesthetist, an anesthesiologist assistant or a resident is the person at the head of your bed, watching the screens. If knowing matters to you, ask it plainly in the pre-op bay: “Who is the physician responsible for my anesthetic, and will they be in the room when I go to sleep?” It is a fair question. You are allowed to hear the answer before the mask comes down.
### Who is standing behind your head while you are under?
It is quiet up there, behind the drape. The surgeon and the scrub team crowd the table; the anesthesia person sits at your head beside the monitors that beep with your heartbeat. That person might be a physician anesthesiologist, a resident in training, an anesthesiologist assistant, or a certified registered nurse anesthetist.
So who is watching that person? On the Missouri side of the river, the law spells it out. Section 334.104 of the Revised Statutes lets a CRNA provide anesthesia services without a collaborative practice arrangement while working under the supervision of an anesthesiologist or other physician, dentist, or podiatrist who is immediately available if needed. Read that list again. The supervisor does not have to be an anesthesiologist. In a small surgery center or a dental office, it may be the person doing your procedure. That is legal. It is also exactly why “who is responsible for my anesthesia?” is worth asking out loud at a freestanding center.
### What you have to tell them, even if it feels awkward
Your face gets hot saying some of it. Say it anyway, because the embarrassing items are the ones that change the plan. Every medication and supplement, including a weekly weight-loss or diabetes shot, and do not stop one on your own. Whether you snore, gasp at night, or use a CPAP machine, and whether to bring it. The honest number on drinking. Cannabis. Nobody in that curtained bay is grading you. They are planning around you.
Then tell them about past anesthetics. Was the wake-up rough? Did you throw up for hours? Did anyone say your airway was hard? And before the visit, call the relatives you can stand to call and ask one question: has anyone in the family ever had a dangerous reaction, a very high fever, or a death during or right after anesthesia? A rare inherited reaction called malignant hyperthermia runs in families, and the team can plan around it when they know. The Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States lists a 24-hour MH hotline, 1-800-644-9737, marked for emergencies only. That line is for the team in the room. Your job is the family history.
### When do you have to stop eating and drinking?
The night before, it can feel cruel. Your mouth goes dry, the coffee maker sits right there on the counter, and the sheet says no. Follow the written sheet you were handed, even if the internet says something looser. Some places still say nothing after midnight. Others allow clear liquids until a stated hour. If the sheet and your surgeon’s office disagree, call the number on the sheet.
For children the windows are often tighter and more precise. The National Library of Medicine’s MedlinePlus instructions for a child’s surgery say to give clear liquids up until 2 hours before the scheduled arrival time, to breastfeed until 4 hours before, and to stop formula 6 hours before. Ask which morning pills to take, and with how much water. Skipping a blood pressure pill because you heard “nothing by mouth” is a common, avoidable mistake.
Somebody has to feed the dog while you are in recovery. Line up one of the metro’s veterinarians before the surgery date, not after.
If the patient is your child, the clinicians who already know that kid are worth a call before the pre-op visit:
How to choose a pediatrician in St. Louis
What a pediatric dentist does, and when to start, since dental sedation for young kids raises the same questions
### Six questions to write on the back of the envelope
Your hospital may not book a sit-down visit. You may get a phone call from a nurse the evening before, while dinner is on the stove and a kid is yelling from the next room. Have the list where you can see it, or you will remember half of it in the car.
One: which type of anesthesia am I getting, general, a spinal or nerve block, or sedation, and why that one? Two: who will be with me in the room, and who is the responsible physician? Three: how will pain be handled when I wake up? Four: which medications do I stop, and on what day? Five: exactly when do I stop eating, and when do I stop drinking? Six: is the anesthesia group in my insurance network?
If you have a preference, say it on that call, not on the gurney. Some people want to be fully asleep for a procedure that is often done with sedation. Some want to stay awake with a block. The plan follows the procedure first and your health second, but there is often a real choice inside it, and the clinician who has read your chart is the one to make it with.
### What the morning itself feels like
You will say your name and date of birth more times than seems reasonable. Someone will ask what you are having done, and which side, and someone else will ask again a little later. That repetition is the safety check doing its job. The gown is thin, the blanket from the warmer is the best thing that happens all morning, and the anesthesia person will come by the bay to go over the plan one last time.
Use that minute. Say the awkward things again. Ask the question about who stays in the room. Then arrange the ride home before you need it, because after sedation or general anesthesia you are in no shape to drive, and the facility will tell you its own rule on who has to pick you up.
### Why does anesthesia arrive as its own bill?
Weeks later the envelope shows up with a name you have never heard. That is the anesthesia group, billing for its own professional work, separate from the hospital and the surgeon. And it is billed partly by the clock. Under Medicare’s anesthesia payment rule, the fee is built from base units for the procedure plus time units, multiplied by a conversion factor, and one time unit equals 15 minutes. The clock starts when the anesthesia practitioner begins to prepare you, not at the first cut, and stops when you can be placed safely under postoperative care.
That is where the waiver rule above earns its keep. Under the federal No Surprises Act rules, anesthesiology is one of the ancillary services where an out-of-network provider at an in-network facility cannot use the notice-and-consent exception. If a bill looks wrong anyway, the federal No Surprises Help Desk is at 1-800-985-3059.
Before surgery, make two calls. Ask your insurer whether the anesthesia group at that specific facility is contracted. Ask the facility which group staffs its operating rooms. If the procedure is oral surgery, the split bill works the same way:
What an oral surgeon does, and what it costs
Want a name and a face before the mask comes down? Browse anesthesiologists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask your surgeon’s office which anesthesia group staffs the rooms where you are scheduled.
If you run an anesthesia practice, a surgery center or a pre-op clinic, patients are searching for the group behind their surgery by name. A complete, current listing helps you get more customers who already know they need you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a difference between an anaesthetist and an anaesthesiologist?
A.  In the United States, yes. An anesthesiologist is a physician who trained in anesthesiology after medical school. Missouri law defines a certified registered nurse anesthetist as a registered nurse who is currently certified as a nurse anesthetist. The double-a spelling, anaesthetist, is common in British and Commonwealth usage, which is why search results mix the two.
### Q. Do anesthesiologists get called doctors?
A.  Yes. An anesthesiologist is a medical doctor, an MD or a DO, which is why many practices say “physician anesthesiologist” so patients can tell the roles apart. If you are not sure who is talking to you in the pre-op bay, ask. Nobody minds.
### Q. Do anesthesiologists stay during surgery?
A.  Someone from the anesthesia team is with you, but the physician may move between rooms. Under Medicare’s medical-direction rules, an anesthesiologist directing a team can direct up to four concurrent cases, personally takes part in induction and emergence, and must remain physically present and available for immediate treatment of emergencies. Ask who the responsible physician is for your case.
### Q. What is the 2 4 6 rule for anesthesia?
A.  It is shorthand for fasting windows before surgery: clear liquids up to 2 hours before, breast milk up to 4 hours, formula up to 6 hours. Your facility’s written sheet wins over any rule of thumb, so follow it and call if it is unclear.
### Q. What is a typical anesthesiologist fee?
A.  There is no flat fee. Under Medicare’s anesthesia payment rule, the charge is base units for the procedure plus time units, times a conversion factor, and private insurers negotiate their own rates. Ask the anesthesia group for a written estimate tied to your procedure, and confirm the group is contracted with your plan.
### Q. How much is anesthesia for 1 hour?
A.  An hour is four time units, since one unit equals 15 minutes, but the dollar figure depends on the procedure’s base units and on your plan’s rate. The clock starts when the anesthesia practitioner begins preparing you. Ask for the estimate in writing.

## St. Louis Pediatrician: First Ask Who Answers at Night
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-pediatrician-in-st-louis
The nurse line most St. Louis parents think they can call in the middle of the night stopped giving medical advice years ago.
St. Louis Children’s Hospital says it no longer provides health advice or nurse “triage” service to callers of its 454.KIDS phone line. Plenty of parents still have that number in their heads, passed down from their own parents along with the thermometer and the bulb syringe. But when the baby is hot to the touch and the house is dark and you are standing in the hallway with the phone glowing in your hand, the person who answers is whoever your pediatrician’s practice has arranged. Nobody else.
That changes what you are actually choosing. Most parents pick a pediatrician by reputation, a friend’s recommendation or a kind face at a meet-and-greet. Those matter. But the question that shapes your worst nights is plainer: who picks up when the office is closed, and what do they tell you to do?
### How can I choose a pediatrician before my baby is born?
Book a prenatal visit. It is not a luxury and it is not only for complicated pregnancies. The American Academy of Pediatrics puts Prenatal as the first column on its own schedule of children’s preventive visits, ahead of Newborn. Its footnote says a prenatal visit is recommended for parents who are at high risk, for first-time parents, and for those who request a conference. That last clause is the one to use. You do not need a reason. You need to call and ask.
The same footnote says what the visit should cover: anticipatory guidance, pertinent medical history, and a discussion of the benefits of breastfeeding and your planned method of feeding. Bring your questions on paper. The chairs in a pediatric waiting room are small and bright, and somewhere a toddler is always crying, and it is easy to forget the one thing you meant to ask.
### Start with the phone, not the bio
Before you read a single doctor’s profile, call the front desk and ask three things. Is the practice taking new patients on your exact insurance plan? Who answers the phone when the office is closed? And how fast can a brand-new baby be seen after you leave the hospital?
That last one has a clock attached. The AAP schedule says newborns should have an evaluation within 3 to 5 days of birth and within 48 to 72 hours after discharge from the hospital, to include evaluation for feeding and jaundice. Picture the real version of that trip, because you will make it. You will be a few days out of the hospital, running on broken sleep, buckling a newborn into a car seat that still smells new. A practice across the metro looks fine on a map. It feels very different at that point.
So write down the after-hours answer word for word. Some practices run their own on-call line. Some send calls to an outside service. Either can be fine. What matters is that you know, before the night you need it, what number you will dial and who will be on the other end.
If you are still collecting names, the same hospital says the 454.KIDS line, or 800.678.KIDS, continues to serve as a resource to help parents find a pediatrician or pediatric specialist. Use it for names. Just do not count on it for advice at midnight.
### The St. Louis question most guides skip: lead
Here is a second St. Louis fact that should shape your choice. The City of St. Louis says the entire city is considered a high-risk area for lead poisoning by the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, which is why guidelines call for universal testing of children under age six. The city ties that to buildings constructed before the 1970s, which it says includes the majority of the housing stock. Old plaster, old window frames, old porches. Beautiful houses. Real dust.
State law backs it up. Missouri statute says every child under six years of age shall be assessed annually using a questionnaire to determine whether the child is at high risk for lead poisoning. And in areas the state has determined to be high risk, child care facilities must, within thirty days of enrolling a child twelve months or older and under five, require the parent or guardian to provide evidence of lead poisoning testing.
That turns into a practical question for the front desk: how does the practice handle lead testing, and will it hand you the paperwork your child care center will ask for? A practice that answers that easily has done it many times. Lead starts mattering before birth, too. Missouri’s health department says women should be screened by their physician using the Prenatal Assessment Questionnaire to determine whether she and the fetus are at risk for lead poisoning. If your OB has not asked, bring it up. Lead screening for children is also on the federal list of preventive services for kids, which HealthCare.gov says are generally covered at no cost to you when provided by an in-network provider.
### Then check the doctor
Once a practice clears the phone, the network and the newborn timing, look at the people. The American Board of Pediatrics says board certification is a voluntary process that goes beyond state medical licensing, and it offers a public lookup so you can find out if a pediatrician is ABP-certified.
At the meet-and-greet, notice the small things. Does the doctor look at you when you talk? Is the nurse patient with a question you are embarrassed to ask? Does the waiting room separate sick kids from well ones? Nobody can hand you a ranking for this. You will know within a few minutes whether you could call this office worried and feel heard.
### What happens at those visits, and why one row is about you
The visits are more than a weigh-in on the paper-covered table. The AAP schedule includes developmental screening, autism spectrum disorder screening and developmental surveillance, and in the teen years it calls for hearing screens with audiometry that include high frequencies. Each check is a few quiet minutes in a small room, and each one is a chance to catch something early.
Then there is the row most new parents never expect. The schedule includes maternal depression screening. Your baby’s doctor may ask how you are sleeping, eating and feeling, and the honest answer is part of the visit, not a detour from it. A good pediatrician asks that question gently and waits for the real answer. Notice whether the one you are interviewing sounds like they would.
### What the first year looks like on the calendar
You will see this office a lot. After the newborn checks, the AAP schedule lists visits by 1 month and at 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24 and 30 months, then yearly from age 3 through 21. That is a long relationship with one front desk, one parking lot and one set of nurses. HealthCare.gov lists well-baby and well-child visits among the preventive services for children that are generally covered at no cost when you use an in-network provider. Sick visits are a different bill, so ask your plan how those are handled.
### Questions worth asking at the meet-and-greet
Keep it to a handful, and ask them out loud even if they feel awkward. How does the doctor like parents to reach them with a non-urgent question: a portal message, a nurse callback, or a visit? If your baby needs to be seen today, how does the office decide who gets the sick slots? Which hospitals does the doctor work with if your child ever needs to be admitted? Who covers when the doctor is on vacation, and will your child’s chart go with that person?
Then ask the one that tells you the most: what do you wish new parents knew before their first night home? Watch how long the answer takes. A pediatrician who has an answer ready, and gives it in plain words, is usually one who explains things well on the hard days too. If you leave the room feeling lighter than when you walked in, take that seriously. That feeling is information. Jot your impressions in the car before you pull out of the lot, while the details are still sharp: the wait, the tone at the desk, whether anyone smiled at the bump. Two visits blur together faster than you would think.
Totally off topic, but if a dead limb is hanging over the spot where the car seat comes out, call a tree service before the baby arrives.
The pediatrician is not the only new name on your list. If feeding is the worry that keeps you up, read when to call a lactation consultant in St. Louis. If you are still deciding who delivers, here is what a midwife does and how to choose one.
First teeth come sooner than anyone expects, and our guide to what a pediatric dentist does and when to start covers that next step. And if a hospital bill arrives that makes your stomach turn, start with how hospital billing works in St. Louis.
Make two calls this week, while you still have the energy to ask good questions. Browse pediatricians across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two close to home, and ask each front desk who answers after hours.
If you run a pediatric practice or a family clinic taking new patients, expecting parents are making exactly these calls right now. List your practice on St Louis Near Me Directory and get more customers from the families already searching.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. At what age should a child see a pediatrician?
A.  From birth. The AAP schedule starts with an evaluation after birth, then a visit within 3 to 5 days of birth and within 48 to 72 hours after leaving the hospital. Regular well visits follow through the first years, then once a year from age 3 through 21.
### Q. Is it okay to choose a pediatrician before my baby is born?
A.  It is more than okay. The AAP lists a prenatal visit as the first visit on its schedule and recommends it for first-time parents, parents at high risk, and anyone who requests a conference. Choosing early also means you know the after-hours number before you need it.
### Q. What to look for when picking a pediatrician?
A.  Start with what rules a practice out: whether it takes your exact plan, who answers when the office is closed, and how quickly it can see a newborn after discharge. In the City of St. Louis, ask how it handles lead testing. Then check board certification through the American Board of Pediatrics lookup.
### Q. How much does a typical pediatrician visit cost?
A.  Well-baby and well-child visits are among the preventive services HealthCare.gov says are generally covered at no cost when you see an in-network provider, and that includes Marketplace and Medicaid coverage. Sick visits can carry a copay or count toward a deductible, so call your plan before the first one.
### Q. When should my child first see a pediatrician?
A.  Before birth, if you book a prenatal visit, which the AAP recommends for first-time parents. After birth, the schedule calls for a visit within 3 to 5 days of birth and within 48 to 72 hours after discharge, including a check for feeding and jaundice.
### Q. Where can I find pediatrics in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis Children’s Hospital says its 454.KIDS line helps parents find a pediatrician or pediatric specialist, though it no longer gives nurse advice. You can also browse pediatric practices across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then confirm each one with your insurance plan.
### Q. What are the main duties of a pediatrician?
A.  Preventive care on a set schedule, plus care when your child is sick. The AAP schedule includes developmental screening, autism spectrum disorder screening and developmental surveillance, and it also includes maternal depression screening, so the parent gets checked on too.
### Q. Why would you go to a pediatrician?
A.  For the routine visits that track growth and development from birth through age 21, and for the fevers, rashes and coughs in between. One practice that knows your child’s history from the first week on is the quiet reason to choose carefully, and to choose once.

## $25 Symphony Seats, Nearly 1,500 Free Muny Seats: St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-see-live-theater-and-performing-arts-in-st-louis
Twenty-five dollars bought this seat. The house lights sink to half, a program slides off somebody’s knee, a cough gets swallowed, and a full room of strangers goes quiet at the same moment, so quiet you can hear the seat springs. Then the first chord hits, and you feel it in your ribs before your ears have sorted it out.
Most people assume a seat like that costs a night’s pay. At the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, it doesn’t have to. The orchestra says general rush tickets are available the day of listed performances for $25 each, and they must be purchased in person at the Box Office. Not online. Not on a resale site. You walk up to the window at 718 N. Grand Blvd. and ask for one.
Here is how to do it today. Pull up the SLSO concert calendar and find a performance listed for rush. The Box Office opens two hours prior to performances, so get to Grand Center early, bring a card, and ask for the rush ticket by name. The building you walk into is the Jack C. Taylor Music Center, and it sits in the middle of the Grand Center neighborhood, so dinner is a short walk either way.
If there is a student in your house, the number drops again. Students from grade school to graduate school can purchase select classical concert tickets starting at $15, and the tickets are available 10 days prior to the performance. Students 16 and up upload their ID to the SLSO app and the discount lands in the cart on its own. Students under 16 use the code STUDENT15. And if you wear a badge, police officers, firefighters and active or retired military can receive two complimentary tickets to a classical concert through the 2 for the Badge program, subject to availability. Call 314-534-1700 to check availability before you drive in.
Summer has an even better price: nothing. At The Muny in Forest Park, the last nine rows of the theatre, nearly 1,500 seats, are made available for each performance on a first-come, first-served basis. No tickets necessary. The line forms at the theatre’s upper entrance, and people bring chairs, blankets and snacks for the wait. The Muny itself calls a picnic in the free-seats line a St. Louis tradition. The gates for the free seats open at 7 p.m. in Kooyumjian Family Plaza, and showtime is 8:15 p.m. Arrive with the sun still on the pavement and you’ll be fine.
### What qualifies as performing arts?
The bows end, the curtain drops, the crew starts pulling cable, and by midnight the thing you just watched exists nowhere except in the people who were in the room. That is performing art. A painting is still on the wall after the painter goes home. A concert is not. That is also the plain logic behind a rush ticket. The show happens whether a seat is full or empty, and an empty seat at curtain time earns the house nothing.
In St. Louis the family is wide. Orchestras in Grand Center, touring Broadway on North Grand, plays built from scratch in Webster Groves, musicals under the open sky in Forest Park, Shakespeare on a lawn. Some of it costs $25. A surprising amount of it costs nothing at all.
### What are some free concerts in St. Louis?
Start at the Missouri Botanical Garden. Its open-air Whitaker Music Festival presents free Wednesday evening concerts under the stars every summer, and there is no charge for parking at the Garden. Bring a blanket and get there early enough to pick your patch of grass. So pack the cooler you never get to bring anywhere else, spread out on the grass, and let the heat come off the lawn as the band tunes up.
Then cross to Forest Park for words instead of music. The St. Louis Shakespeare Festival stages its performances at Shakespeare Glen in Forest Park from May to June, and admission is free. Nearly 40,000 attendees take advantage of that each season, which tells you two things: it is good, and you want to claim your patch of grass early.
Add The Muny’s free rows and a family can spend a whole summer of evenings on live performance without buying a single ticket. The only real cost is getting there before everyone else does.
### Buying a full-price ticket without getting burned
When you do pay, buy from the house. The Fabulous Fox says tickets may be purchased online through its primary ticket seller, MetroTix.com, and tells you to look for the on sale date posted on a show’s information page on fabulousfox.com. It also warns that secondary ticket sellers may be promoting tickets for sale before the show’s on sale dates, and it encourages you to wait for the official on sale date so you can see the actual price and seat availability. That one line will save some reader reading this a few hundred dollars.
For The Muny, the box office at #1 Theatre Drive answers at (314) 361-1900, 9 a.m.-4 p.m. Monday-Thursday. For plays built here rather than trucked in on a tour, The Rep, based in Webster Groves, stages its mainstage shows at the Loretto-Hilton Center. Same rule everywhere: the organization’s own site first, everybody else second.
### Three kinds of stage, three ways to buy
It helps to know who built the show you are watching, because that decides how the tickets behave. A touring house like the Fox hosts productions that arrive on trucks already built, play a short run and leave for the next city. Miss the run and it is gone. You will feel that urgency the moment you walk through the brass doors on Grand and look up into all that gold.
A resident company builds its own work here and keeps it on its own stage for weeks. That gives you time. You can read a review, talk a friend into it, and still get a seat for the second or third weekend.
Then there is The Muny, which is its own animal. Over 10 weeks each summer, it creates seven musicals from the ground up, and it calls itself the nation’s oldest and largest outdoor musical theatre. Its own history says it began as a grassy spot between two mighty oaks. Sit there on a July night with the cicadas going and the stage lights cutting through the humidity, and you understand why people have been coming back for generations.
The free rows are not a city handout, either. The Muny says that, unlike many Forest Park institutions, it receives no tax support from the Zoo Museum District or the Missouri Arts Council. Donors and paying ticket holders carry those free seats. Shakespeare in the Park works on the same generosity, and the festival says it has entertained over a million people since 2001.
### What should you wear, and when should you get there?
Relax about the clothes. The Fabulous Fox says it does not have a dress code, and you will see all kinds of outfits at most events. Dress for Broadway shows generally ranges from business casual to suits and dresses. Nobody is checking your shoes.
Timing matters more. At the Fox, the lobby opens one hour prior to showtime, and the auditorium generally opens for seating 30 minutes prior. Use that half hour. Look up. The ceiling is half the ticket.
At the symphony, the SLSO says nearby parking options are numerous in Grand Center, and there are designated areas for rideshares like Uber and Lyft. If you are chasing a rush ticket, that matters: you want to be at the window, not circling a block, when the Box Office opens.
Outdoors, dress for the weather rather than the occasion. A Forest Park evening in July holds its heat long after the sun drops, so bring water, something to sit on and something to fan yourself with. Indoors, bring a layer. A big hall is cooled for a full house, and you will feel it in your shoulders by the second act.
Same trick, darker room: here is how to get cheap movie tickets in St. Louis.

How to pick a steakhouse in St. Louis for dinner before the curtain
