### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best theater in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the night you want. For a Broadway show, it is the Fabulous Fox, where you walk in through the brass doors on Grand. For plays built here, The Rep, based in Webster Groves, stages its mainstage shows at the Loretto-Hilton Center. For a musical under the open sky with nearly 1,500 free seats at every performance, it is The Muny in Forest Park.
### Q. What musicals are playing in St. Louis?
A.  Check each house’s own site, because any list in an article goes stale. The Fox posts each show’s on sale date on that show’s page at fabulousfox.com, and The Muny’s box office answers at (314) 361-1900. Wait for the official on sale date rather than a reseller’s early listing.
### Q. What activities are free in St. Louis?
A.  In summer, a lot of live performance. The Muny gives away the last nine rows, nearly 1,500 seats, at each performance. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s Whitaker Music Festival presents free Wednesday evening concerts with no charge for parking, and the St. Louis Shakespeare Festival’s Forest Park performances are free.
### Q. What is going on in St. Louis this weekend for free?
A.  During the summer season, The Muny’s free seats are offered for each performance, with gates opening at 7 p.m. in Kooyumjian Family Plaza and showtime at 8:15 p.m. Off season, the cheapest reliable seat is the SLSO’s $25 day-of rush ticket, bought in person at the Box Office.
### Q. Is performing arts worth it?
A.  As an audience member, yes, and it does not have to cost much. A $25 rush ticket at the symphony, a $15 student seat, or a free night at The Muny or Shakespeare Glen all put you in the same room, hearing the same thing, at the same moment as everyone else.
### Q. What are 5 examples of performing arts?
A.  Theater, music, dance, opera and musical theater are five clear examples, and spoken word, puppetry and circus belong to the same family. In St. Louis you can see orchestral music in Grand Center, touring musicals on North Grand and Shakespeare on a lawn in Forest Park.
### Q. Is 17 too late for acting?
A.  No. Seventeen is early, not late. At any age, the fastest way in is to watch a lot of live work, notice what the people on stage are doing with their bodies and voices, then audition for anything that will have you.
### Q. Why is performing arts so important?
A.  Because it is one of the few things left that you cannot pause, skip or replay. A room full of strangers laughs at the same line, holds its breath at the same moment and walks out into the same night air talking about it. In a city that gives away free seats every summer, that experience is open to anyone willing to stand in line.
### Q. What jobs can I get with performing arts?
A.  Far more off stage than on it. Every production needs stage managers, carpenters, electricians, sound engineers, wardrobe and wig staff, props builders, box office and front-of-house crews, marketers and fundraisers. Teaching and arts administration absorb many more. A show that looks like ten people on stage is usually dozens of people behind it.
### Q. What do people do in performing arts?
A.  They rehearse far more than they perform. A production is built for weeks in a rehearsal room and a scene shop before an audience ever sees it. At The Muny, seven musicals are created from the ground up over 10 weeks each summer, which means one show is rehearsing while another is on stage that same night.

## In St. Louis County, Your School Doesn't Run Special Ed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/special-education-in-st-louis-what-parents-need-to-know
“We’d like to take a closer look.”
That is usually how it arrives. A few quiet words from a teacher who likes your kid, said across a table with a folder on it, or typed at the bottom of an email you read twice before you start the car. Your stomach drops before your brain catches up. Then the questions come fast. Is something wrong? Who decides? How long does this take? And who exactly are you supposed to call?
If you live in St. Louis County, that last question has an answer almost nobody hands you at the table. Special education in the county is not run by your school district. It is run by the Special School District of St. Louis County, which Missouri’s state plan describes as a distinct public school district for the purpose of providing special education and related services to students with disabilities within the component districts. SSD’s own handbook counts 22 public school districts in the county. Your child almost certainly stays in the same building. SSD says some 97 percent of its special education students attend the same neighborhood school their non-disabled peers attend. But the evaluation, the paperwork and much of the staff come from a second district most parents have never dealt with.
That second district runs on its own clock. Missouri’s Regulation XV says that when a parent referral is made to any certificated staff at either your home district or SSD, SSD must give you a copy of the Procedural Safeguards within five school days. A Joint Review Committee, made up of staff from both districts, then decides whether to evaluate, and its call is binding on both. Here is the line to tell every parent you know in the county: the people deciding whether to test your child may not work for your child’s school, and the clock does not start until you ask in writing.
### What are the three criteria used to qualify students for special education?
All three have to be true at once. Your child has a disability in one of the categories federal law lists, that disability adversely affects educational performance, and because of it your child needs special education and related services. Two out of three is not eligibility. A diagnosis on its own is not eligibility either.
The wording comes straight from the federal definition of a child with a disability: a child with one of the listed disabilities “who, by reason thereof, needs special education and related services,” with each category defined as a condition that adversely affects a child’s educational performance. So the pediatrician’s letter you bring in the folder matters. It is evidence for the team. It is not the team’s decision.
### Your first move, and the clock it starts
The house is quiet, the dishes can wait, and the laptop is the brightest thing in the room. Put the request in writing tonight, while the worry is still fresh. One St. Louis County district’s special education page says requests can be made verbally but recommends they be in writing and sent to the school counselor, the principal and the SSD special education coordinator. Email works, because the timestamp is your proof. If you are not sure who the coordinator is, the same page says SSD student intake can be reached through SSD Central Office at 314-989-8100.
Two sentences are enough. Copy these, fill in the blanks, and hit send before you talk yourself out of it: “I am requesting a full evaluation of my child, [name], [grade], for special education and related services, because I suspect a disability. Please confirm you received this request and tell me the date it was logged.” That email is the most important thing you will write all year, and it takes a few minutes.
Missouri’s Regulation III then sets the pace. The district must give you a Notice of Intent to Evaluate as soon as possible, but within 30 calendar days of the referral. If it refuses the request, it has to give you a Notice of Action Refused. Once you sign consent, the evaluation must be completed and eligibility decided within 60 calendar days. Delays are allowed only for just cause, such as school breaks or a child’s illness, and they have to be documented in your child’s record.
Calendar days matter here. Federal rules set 60 days from parental consent unless a state sets its own timeframe, and the two states on either side of the river did. Across the bridge in Illinois, state law counts 60 school days from written consent for both the eligibility decision and the IEP meeting. Sixty school days, with breaks stripped out, is most of a semester. Ask for every report before the meeting, so you read it on your couch, not for the first time under fluorescent lights with a room full of people waiting.
### Is it an IEP or a 504 plan?
Two different laws. An IEP is the written plan for a child with a disability who qualifies under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. The other route is section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which federal rules say is designed to eliminate discrimination on the basis of handicap in any program or activity receiving federal financial assistance. St. Louis Children’s Hospital lists special seating arrangements and curriculum adjustments among the examples of 504 accommodations.
If a 504 dispute goes nowhere, the U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights headquarters is at 800-421-3481. Under IDEA, a free appropriate public education means special education and related services provided at public expense and without charge.
### Will my child be pulled out of class?
Not by default. Federal law says removal from the regular classroom happens only if the nature or severity of the disability is such that education in regular classes with supplementary aids and services cannot be achieved satisfactorily. Removal has to be justified. Inclusion does not.
Missouri adds a line worth reading twice. Its Regulation IV says a student does not have to fail in the less restrictive options before being placed in a setting appropriate to his or her needs. Nobody has to fall apart first to earn help. In practice, most plans are a mix: the regular room for most of the day, a short pull-out for one skill, speech or occupational therapy on a set schedule.
Completely unrelated, but if something is scratching inside the attic wall in the middle of the night, here is pest control near you.
### Before kindergarten: First Steps and the third birthday
Under age three, this is not a school district job. First Steps is Missouri’s early intervention system for infants and toddlers, birth to age three, who have delayed development or diagnosed conditions associated with developmental disabilities. If the worry starts with a toddler who is not babbling or not walking, that is the door.
At three, the handoff to the school side happens, so start that conversation well before the birthday party. If your first conversation about any of this is with a pediatrician and you are still looking for one, our guide to choosing a pediatrician in St. Louis walks through it. Not sure a speech concern is worth acting on yet? Here are the signs your toddler needs speech therapy.
### When the answer you get is wrong
You can push back, and you do not need a lawyer to start. Missouri runs what it calls the child complaint process: you file a signed written complaint with DESE, it has to allege a violation that happened not more than one year before DESE receives it, and you send a copy to the school at the same time. DESE then has 60 calendar days to investigate and resolve it, and a finding can come with an order for corrective action and a timeline.
Mediation is the quieter route. If both sides settle there, they sign a legally binding agreement, and everything said in the room stays confidential and cannot be used as evidence in a later hearing. The formal option is a due process complaint, which must allege a violation that happened not more than two years before you knew or should have known about it. Keep every email in one folder. The paper trail you start this week is the one you will be glad you have.
### If your child goes to a parochial or private school
This is the part that catches St. Louis families who chose a parish school on purpose. Missouri’s Regulation XIII says no parentally-placed private school student with a disability has an individual right to receive some or all of the special education and related services that student would get in a public school. That is a real trade, and it is worth knowing before you sign anything.
What stays is still worth using. Each public agency must locate, identify and evaluate students with disabilities enrolled by their parents in private schools located inside its boundaries. Notice the word located. That can be a different district from the one you live in. If your child is designated to receive services, the paperwork is a services plan, and the public agency must make sure a representative of the private school attends each meeting about it.
### Who answers the phone when you need help
On the Missouri side, the state agency is DESE’s Office of Special Education at 573-751-5739. In Illinois, Family Matters Parent Training and Information Center says it is the only federally funded Parent Training and Information Center in Illinois, and its line is 1-866-436-7842. Call before the meeting, not after it.
For children whose needs go past what a neighborhood school can do, about 750 students with more significant disabilities are educated in one of SSD’s five special education schools. If you are weighing districts, charter and private options more broadly, our family guide to choosing a school in St. Louis handles that decision.
Send the letter first, then look around. Browse special education schools and services across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory while the evaluation clock runs, so you already know your options when the team calls.
If you run a tutoring center, a therapy practice or a school for kids who learn differently, the parent holding that evaluation letter is searching for you tonight. Put your practice in front of them and get more customers from the families already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to determine if a child needs special education?
A.  A school evaluation decides it, not a parent and not a doctor alone. The team asks whether your child has a listed disability, whether it adversely affects educational performance, and whether your child needs special education because of it. In St. Louis County, a Joint Review Committee from SSD and your home district decides whether to evaluate in the first place.
### Q. Do kids with ADHD get an IEP or 504?
A.  Either one, depending on what the child needs. The federal definition of other health impairment names attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, so an IEP is possible when the child needs special education because of it.
### Q. Are special ED and autism the same thing?
A.  No. Autism is one of the disabilities the federal definition lists, and special education is the set of services a qualifying child receives. An autism diagnosis alone does not make a child eligible. Federal law defines autism for this purpose as a disability that adversely affects a child’s educational performance, and the child still has to need special education.
### Q. Why would my child be put in a special education class?
A.  Only if the regular classroom, with supplementary aids and services, cannot work for that part of the day. Missouri’s state plan adds that a student does not have to fail in less restrictive settings first.
### Q. How long can special ED kids stay in high school?
A.  In Missouri, public schools are not required to provide a free appropriate public education to youth with disabilities who reach the age of 21, or to students who graduate with a regular high school diploma. A certificate or an alternative diploma does not end eligibility the way a regular diploma does.
### Q. What can autistic children get for free?
A.  Under IDEA, special education and related services are provided at public expense and without charge to the family. Before age three, Missouri’s First Steps program serves infants and toddlers with delayed development or diagnosed conditions.
### Q. What are some good special education schools in St. Louis?
A.  There is no ranking worth trusting, and for many children the family does not pick the school at all. In St. Louis County, SSD educates about 750 students with more significant disabilities in its five special education schools, and most other SSD students stay in their neighborhood school. Visit any program before you agree to it.

## Email a St. Louis Newsroom Yourself Before You Pay a PR Firm
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-pr-firm-actually-does-for-a-st-louis-business
Your stomach drops a little at the number at the bottom of the deck. The phone had buzzed face-down on the counter in the lull after the rush, and you flipped it over expecting a supplier. It was a public relations firm instead. Twenty minutes, the email said. The deck was glossy, full of logos from outlets you had actually heard of, and the word “placements” turned up more than once.
What would you want a newsroom to say about you, if it said anything at all? Look at where St. Louis newsrooms are now.
“It’s devastating for St. Louis,” Sarah Fenske, the Riverfront Times’ former executive editor, told St. Louis Public Radio on May 22, 2024. That was the day the alt-weekly was sold and she learned the entire writing and editing staff had been laid off. The station ran the story under a photo of a Riverfront Times newspaper box on Lindell Boulevard in Midtown. A metal box on a sidewalk, and fewer people writing what goes in it.
So which are you paying for: access, or judgment? Here is the part nobody pitching you has a reason to say out loud. The front door of a St. Louis newsroom is not locked. The St. Louis American’s site asks anyone with “a news tip, press release, event notice or community announcement” to submit it to its newsroom through a form on the page. St. Louis Public Radio’s contact page lists news@stlpr.org for press releases. The St. Louis Jewish Light’s contact page says all editorial submissions, news releases, event photos and Newsmakers items included, go to a single editorial email address. Your new hire, your anniversary, your expansion: those are submissions, not secrets. No retainer, no media database, no gatekeeper. A story, sent to the people who publish stories.
A retainer does not buy you the door. It buys you somebody who knows which story is worth carrying through it.
None of that makes hiring a firm a bad idea. What hurts owners is a pitch built on “guaranteed placements” and a long retainer, sold into a city where the reporters keep getting fewer. Often what the business needed first was a sharper story, or a first page on Google that tells a stranger the truth about you.
### Is public relations necessary?
For most small St. Louis businesses, not on a retainer, and not yet. Public relations becomes necessary when your reputation is under threat, or when someone who will never buy from you, a lender, a zoning board, a reporter, has to trust you first. Until then, send your own story: the St. Louis American takes press releases through an online form, and St. Louis Public Radio lists news@stlpr.org for press releases.
Want to test the door yourself before you sign anything? Tonight, after close, with the register counted and the lights half off, write three sentences. What happened, in plain words. Why it matters to people in a named St. Louis neighborhood or town. Who can talk about it, with a phone number that will actually be answered. Paste that into the St. Louis American’s submission form or an email to news@stlpr.org, and attach one good photo. If nobody bites, you learned something a retainer would have charged you months to learn: the story needs sharpening before it needs a publicist.
PR is an amplifier, and it only carries what is already there. Before you pay anyone, stand on the sidewalk outside your own door and search your business name on your phone. If the hours are wrong or the listing has one photo, a story in the paper just sends a stranger to a page that costs you the sale. If customers find you by searching for what you do, the next dollar usually works harder making you findable and well reviewed than it does on a media campaign.
PR starts earning real money when trust is your product and strangers decide: health care, financial services, child care, anything licensed. It earns it when you need a yes from a board rather than a buyer, when you are raising money or selling the company, when you have a story a reporter would run without being asked twice, and when you are already in the news and it is going badly. It can wait when your hours are wrong online, when your listings are thin, when you need revenue this quarter, or when nobody at the business can call a reporter back before their deadline passes.
### What exactly does public relations do?
It manages what other people say about you. The Public Relations Society of America’s definition, the one it says still stands today, is “a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.” Strip out the vocabulary and a firm does five jobs you would recognize.
Media relations: deciding what about you is genuinely news, as opposed to news only to you, and pitching the specific reporters who cover it. Message work: the two sentences you say every time, drilled until the person on camera stops wandering. Reputation: what fills the first page when a stranger searches your name, and what an AI assistant repeats when someone asks about you. Crisis: the holding statement, the order you tell people in, and what you do not say yet. And community relations: the neighborhood meeting, the chamber breakfast, the zoning hearing with the folding chairs and the bad coffee.
Notice what is missing. Selling. A firm that opens by promising you leads is describing a different service.
### How is PR different from advertising and SEO?
You pay for advertising and you control it. You pay for PR and you control almost none of it. An ad runs because you bought the space; a story runs because a reporter put their name on it. SEO is the part of marketing aimed at what search engines and AI assistants surface when someone is already looking.
For an owner with one budget, the order usually goes like this. Listings and search decide whether the person already hunting for you finds you. Advertising decides how many strangers see your offer this month. PR decides what those strangers think when they run into your name somewhere you did not pay to be. Most small businesses need the first two humming before the third earns its fee.
### What does a monthly retainer actually buy?
The invoice lands at the start of every month, whether or not a reporter called back. What it pays for is a block of somebody’s attention, spread across strategy, writing, pitching, monitoring and reporting. Not a number of stories. BuzzStream’s survey of about 70 digital PR agency leaders and freelancers put the average monthly contract at approximately $5,458, with 52.5% of contracts under $5,000. About 90% of agencies used the monthly retainer model, and agencies averaged $6,357 a month against $4,200 for freelancers. Over half the respondents were in the UK, so treat it as a survey of digital PR shops, not a St. Louis rate card.
A retainer with no hours written into it is a subscription to hope. Before you sign, get five things on paper: how many hours you get and what happens to unused ones, the names of the people doing the work rather than the ones in the pitch meeting, the fixed monthly deliverables, how often you get a report, and who owns the media list and the written materials when the relationship ends. That last one surprises people every time.
Project pricing fits more often than people expect. An opening, a relocation, a funding announcement, one media training day: those have an end date. Ask for the project number first. The same retainer-versus-project tradeoff shows up in other trades, as it does in what a real estate consultant does and what it costs.
Spent the week chewing your nails over a pitch deck? Book the repair: St. Louis nail salons.
### Why can nobody guarantee you a story?
Because the decision belongs to an editor, not a vendor. The moment money changes hands for editorial coverage, it stops being earned media and becomes advertising wearing a press release. Guaranteed placement is not automatically a scam. It is just not the thing you thought you were buying.
The shrinking newsroom is, oddly, the best argument for a good firm. The value is no longer the release. It is knowing which handful of people still cover restaurants, or health care, or Metro East development, and not wasting their afternoon. Ask any firm to name the reporters it would approach for you, and why. Logos instead of names means guessing.
### When does a small business need crisis help?
The moment someone else can publish your story before you can explain it: a lawsuit, a data breach, a failed inspection, a video with your sign in the frame. The phone keeps lighting up face-down on the counter, and every buzz is somebody who heard before you said a word.
A breach shows why the law is the floor, not the message. Under Missouri’s breach notice statute, a business that notifies more than one thousand consumers at one time must also notify the attorney general’s office and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. That tells you what you have to send. It says nothing about what your regulars, your staff and the reporter on line two are going to hear, and that gap is what a crisis communicator actually sells.
Whether or not you hire anyone: pick one spokesperson and route everything through that person. Write down what you know versus what you assume, and say only the first part out loud. Tell your own staff before they read it somewhere else. Call the reporter back before deadline, even if all you can give is what you can confirm right now. And never bury bad reviews or have friends post glowing ones. A cover-up becomes the second story, and it is always the more expensive one.
### How do you tell whether PR worked?
Not by counting clippings. Watch the numbers that move when people hear about you and never click anything: searches for your business name, direct visits, calls that mention where they heard of you, and what fills page one when a stranger looks you up. Record the baseline before the work starts, because a number nobody wrote down in month zero cannot be improved in month six.
Then the plain test the numbers miss: did a door open that was closed? A call back from someone who never returned yours. A banker who already knew the name. That is what earned media buys.
### What to ask a PR firm before you sign
Interview three firms. Ask each who does the work day to day, what they would do in the first month, what they would tell you not to spend money on, and for two references at roughly your size instead of their biggest logo. Vetting a firm is the same discipline as any big purchase; you would not buy a commercial truck without looking under the hood.
Walk away from a guarantee of placements, a media list they will not describe, and any refusal to write hours into the scope. Ask for a short exit window in the first contract. A firm confident about month three will not fight you on it.
### From the other side of the desk
If you run a small PR shop here, you already know the math. You sell hours, not outcomes, and salary is your cost of goods: the median annual wage for public relations specialists was $74,750 in May 2025, before benefits, rent and software. The pitch itself is the loss leader: a strategy deck written for free against other shops. And the complaint traded between owners is always the same, the client who goes quiet for weeks, judges you on a placement nobody controls, then cancels right as the relationships start paying. The shops that last write hours into the scope and report the same few numbers every month.
Want a local voice instead of a cold email? Browse public relations firms across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the first two for a project quote and the names of the reporters they would approach for you.
If you’re the owner holding that cold email, ask yourself one thing first: when a neighbor asks ChatGPT or Google who does what you do, does your name come up? Coverage fades in a week. A complete listing keeps working: a Gold listing gives you up to 10 categories across 40 location tags, so the website and Google profile you already pay for finally get more customers, for under a dollar a day. See who AI names instead of you, then start with Gold or claim your spot. Refuse to be invisible.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What exactly does public relations do?
A.  It manages what other people say about your business. PRSA defines it as a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics. Day to day that means pitching reporters, writing statements, preparing spokespeople, handling crises and running community relations. It earns attention rather than buying it.
### Q. What does a public relations department do?
A.  The same work an agency does, from inside the payroll: fielding media calls, writing press materials, employee and community communication, and crisis response. Most small St. Louis businesses never need one. The owner is the spokesperson until a full-time salary costs less than the retainer it would replace.
### Q. Why is public relations important?
A.  Because most decisions about your business get made by people you never spoke to. Coverage, community presence and a clean first page of results give a stranger a reason to trust you before they call. For a small local business, reviews and a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory often do that work sooner; PR is the version that reaches people who have never heard of you.
### Q. Is public relations free?
A.  Sending your own story is. The St. Louis American takes press releases and story ideas through a form on its site, and St. Louis Public Radio lists news@stlpr.org for press releases. What costs money is the strategy, the writing, the relationships and the hours behind them, which is what a firm sells.
### Q. How much do PR people charge per hour?
A.  Most PR is billed monthly, not hourly. BuzzStream’s survey of about 70 digital PR agency leaders and freelancers found an average monthly contract of approximately $5,458, with 52.5% under $5,000. I could not find a neutral published survey of hourly PR rates, so ask any firm for its blended hourly rate and how many hours your retainer includes.
### Q. How to choose the right PR agency?
A.  Interview three and ask who does the work day to day. Get hours written into the scope, the same few metrics reported monthly, two references at your size, and a short exit clause. Ask which reporters they would approach for you, by name. Walk away from guaranteed placements. You can start the shortlist with the public relations firms listed on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two.
### Q. What are the five main functions of public relations?
A.  Most versions come down to research, strategy, communication, relationship building and evaluation. In small-business terms: find out what people already think, decide what you want them to think, say it in the right places, keep the relationships warm, and check whether anything changed. A proposal with no research up front and no evaluation at the end is publicity, not public relations.
### Q. Is PR being replaced by AI?
A.  Reshaped, not replaced. AI drafts releases, builds media lists and monitors coverage faster than a junior staffer, which should shrink the hours a retainer needs. What it cannot do is take responsibility, earn a reporter’s trust or stand in front of a camera. Ask a firm which tasks it automates and whether your fee reflects that.

## Home Window Tinting in St. Louis: The 140-Degree Catch
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-home-window-tinting-in-st-louis
120 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit. That is how hot the room side of the glass ran on office windows at the Goodfellow Federal Center in St. Louis after a solar film went on the inside, according to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report written for the U.S. General Services Administration.
Think about what that means in your own west room. The film soaks up the sun, so the heat you paid to stop sits in the pane itself, warm against the back of your hand, a few feet from the couch. The blinds are down anyway.
Then the bill. In the zones where the film went on the inside of the double-pane windows, the lab found that “Total energy consumption (heating plus cooling) increased 10% or greater.” The manufacturer’s claim of 20-40% heating and cooling savings, in the report’s own words, “was not supported by the measured data or simulation results.” And the researchers picked this city on purpose: “The St. Louis climate was selected for the study to have access to a mixed heating and cooling demand.” Our summers and our winters, both on the meter.
None of that makes film a bad buy. It makes it a product you match to your glass before anyone opens a roll, and the order you do things in decides most of the outcome.
Start by naming the one problem. Glare on the TV, one room you cannot sit in by late afternoon, a floor bleaching by the patio door, a bathroom that needs daytime privacy. Each of those points to a different film, and a shop that sells you one film for all four is guessing.
Next, find out what glass you have: single-pane or double-pane, clear or tinted, low-e or not. The small etched mark in the corner of the glass, or the paperwork from when the windows went in, usually gives you the brand and the line.
Then ask your window maker, in writing, whether film is allowed on that line and which kinds. Glass maker Pilkington North America’s own bulletin says it “will not accept responsibility for glass performance following the application of ANY field-applied film or coating on Pilkington products.” Assume your brand has a rule too, and get it in an email you can find later.
Make the installer look at the glass before quoting. Pilkington’s advice is that “the film manufacturer or a factory-authorized dealer must be consulted for guidance” and that “Good practice would be to obtain specific recommendations and assurances in writing before proceeding with the application of the film.” Last, get the film warranty on paper, ask whether it covers glass breakage and seal failure on your windows, and ask for the film brand and product number on the estimate.
### What are the benefits of home window tinting?
Glare control, ultraviolet blocking that slows fading, some solar heat rejection, and daytime privacy. Glare is the one you notice the first afternoon: the white smear on the screen is gone and you can see the game again. Heat rejection depends on where the film sits and what glass it sits on, which is the whole point of the St. Louis test above.
Privacy from reflective film is daylight privacy. It works because the yard is brighter than the room. After dark, with the lamps on, it flips, and the street can see in. Frosted or decorative film is the honest answer for a bathroom or a sidelight. If what you are protecting from the sun is a photograph or a painting, the glass in the frame matters as much as the film on the window, which is covered in what custom framing costs in St. Louis.
### The double-pane surprise
Most people buy film for heat. On a double-pane window, inside film is mostly a glare product. Pilkington’s bulletin puts it flatly: “The application of solar control films to the room-side surface of an IG unit only reduces solar glare. It does little to reduce solar heat gain.” An IG unit is the sealed double-pane sandwich most newer windows use.
The same bulletin warns that these films “cause the inboard lite of glass to absorb a significant amount of the sun’s energy. This can easily lead to breakage from thermal stresses unless the glass has been heat-treated.” That is the crack that runs in from the edge of a pane on a hot afternoon. And on low-e glass it is blunter still: “Films should never be applied to the room-side surface of IG units with a surface 4 Low-E coating.”
Where film has real room to work is old single-pane glass, the wavy kind that makes the streetlight wobble when you walk past it. The Berkeley lab’s modeling found that “Simple payback analysis suggests a payback between 5 and 15 years for the four climates modeled, assuming single glazing base windows. Paybacks associated with double glazing were generally longer.”
### Dyed, metalized, ceramic, low-e: what the price gap buys
Dyed film is the entry product. It darkens the room and cuts glare, but it is weakest on heat, and the dye is what fades. That purple-brown cast on an old window is dyed film giving up.
Metalized film reflects solar energy back outside before the glass can soak it up, and it lasts. The trade-off worth asking about is radio signal: a metal layer across a window can weaken cell service or a garage remote in that room.
Ceramic film uses non-conductive particles instead of metal, so it rejects infrared heat without the signal problem and stays close to clear. It is usually the priciest per square foot.
Low-e film is aimed at winter as well as summer, bouncing room heat back inside off a cold pane. If your complaint is the chill rolling off the glass while the furnace runs, this is the family to ask about, and it is exactly the case where your glass type matters most.
Tinting the car, not the house? That is a whole different rulebook: what window tint costs and what’s legal in St. Louis.
Film is also one of three fixes for a room that cooks, and not always the cheapest. Exterior shade and interior treatments compete for the same job, and the numbers on the inside option are in what window blinds and shades cost in St. Louis. And if the real problem is a sash that rattles and leaks cold air, that is a job for the handyman list, not a roll of film.
### What to ask before anyone measures
You can sort the shops in one phone call. A good installer asks you questions before you ask any. What kind of windows are they? How old? Which way does the room face? Is there a tree out there, or an awning? If the first thing you hear is a price per square foot, you have learned something.
Then turn it around. Ask which film they would put on your glass and why that one. Ask whether the film maker’s chart allows it on your exact window, and whether they will put that in writing. Ask what the warranty covers if a pane cracks or a seal fogs, and who you call. Ask whether they do house windows regularly or mostly cars, because a beautiful job on a windshield is a different skill from a wall of old wavy glass.
Want the west room back without cracking a pane? Browse home window tinting across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and only shortlist the shops that ask what glass you have before they give you a number.
If you run a window film shop and you are the one who asks about the glass first, say so where homeowners are looking. A Gold listing puts that care in front of more customers in the months the phone goes quiet, or you can start your listing here.
### Doing it yourself
On a small, flat, clear single-pane window, a kit is a reasonable afternoon with a spray bottle and a squeegee. Anywhere else the odds turn. One speck of dust under the film is a bump you will see every morning for years, and nobody checks a kit against your glass. A kit leaves the glass check to you, so a thermal crack in the middle of summer is yours to argue about, on a window whose maker may already have stepped away from film.
If you do try it, practice on a pane you would not miss, work with the room as dust-free as you can get it, and leave the double-pane and low-e windows to someone who will check the glass first and stand behind it.
The one price the lab printed
### How much does it usually cost to tint a window at a house?
I could not find a verified St. Louis residential average. The Berkeley lab report put installed applied films at about $6.40 per square foot for simple tinted film up to $10 per square foot for spectrally selective reflective film, on commercial work. Your quote moves with the film family, the number of separate panes, ladder work and whether old film has to be scraped off first.
Treat that range as proof that good film and cheap film are different products, not as a quote for your house. Two or three itemized written estimates, each naming the film, will tell you more than any average you find online, and the shop that writes the clearest one is often the shop that will answer the phone later.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does tinting home windows void the warranty?
A.  It can, and you should assume so until your window maker tells you otherwise in writing. Glass maker Pilkington North America says it “will not accept responsibility for glass performance following the application of ANY field-applied film or coating on Pilkington products.” Call your window brand with the product line, ask what film is allowed, and ask the installer whether the film warranty covers glass breakage and seal failure.
### Q. What are the downsides of tinting house windows?
A.  Three that cost real money. Absorbing film on the wrong glass can crack it from thermal stress. Film can cloud your window warranty. And in a city with real winters, cutting solar heat can raise your heating bill: in the St. Louis federal building test, “Heating energy never decreased for windows with the subject film.” Reflective film also gives you privacy only by day.
### Q. Is residential window tinting worth it?
A.  For glare and one overheated room, usually yes. For the utility bill, it depends on your glass. The Berkeley lab modeled a payback between 5 and 15 years on single glazing, with double glazing generally longer. If you have newer double-pane windows, buy film for the room you cannot sit in, not for the bill.
### Q. How to choose the right house window tint?
A.  Start with the problem, then let the glass narrow it. Dyed for cheap glare control, metalized or ceramic for heat, low-e for a cold pane, frosted for privacy. Then ask the dealer which of those its maker allows on your exact glass, and get that recommendation in writing.
### Q. How much should home window tinting cost?
A.  Look at what moves the quote rather than chasing an average. Film family is the biggest lever, then total square footage, the number of separate panes, height and access, and whether old film has to come off. A quote that does not name the film brand and product number is not a quote you can compare.
### Q. What are the window tint rules in Missouri?
A.  Missouri’s tint rule, Section 307.173 RSMo, sits in the Motor Vehicles title and covers front side windows on a motor vehicle, allowing a sun-screening device with a light transmission of thirty-five percent or more plus or minus three percent. For a house, the rules to check are closer to home. A homeowners association or a historic district can still have rules about how windows look from the street, so ask before you go mirrored.
### Q. Where can I get my home windows tinted in St. Louis?
A.  Look for shops that do architectural film, not only car tint, and shortlist on three habits: they ask what glass you have before quoting, they hand you the film warranty in writing, and they put the film brand and product number on the estimate. The home window tinting listings on St Louis Near Me Directory are a place to start the calls.

## 4 to 5 Weeks or 10 Minutes: What Framing Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-custom-framing-costs-in-st-louis
The print slides out of the cardboard tube in a slow curl and tries to roll itself back up the second it touches the counter. You pin two corners flat with your palms. The framer pins the other two. Corner samples come down off the wall one at a time, gold, black, walnut, each laid against the edge of the paper, and the room goes quiet while the math happens. At Norton’s Fine Art & Framing on South Big Bend Boulevard, one St. Louis family has been running that quiet moment since 1949, when Ruth Norton, an interior decorator, and her husband Cecil, an architect and engineer, started a business to merge their two fields, according to the shop’s own history. Their website still shows Ruth at the original Central West End location, circa 1968.
Then the number arrives, and it is never the number you had in your head. Here is the one nobody leads with: time. Norton’s FAQ puts its current turnaround at around 4 to 5 weeks. Michaels will turn a phone photo into a printed, framed and gift-boxed keepsake for $29 in 10 minutes or less, per its November 18, 2025 announcement. Four to five weeks, or ten minutes. Both are honest. They are not the same product, and the gap between them is the whole story of a framing quote. One more number worth saying out loud at dinner: Norton’s says there are fewer than 500 PPFA Certified Picture Framers in the United States, and three of them work at that one shop.
So work it in this order, cheapest move first. Dig out any frame you already own: asked whether it will use a frame you bring in, Norton’s answers “Absolutely.” Bring the piece itself, not its measurements, because a framer needs to see the paper, the edges and the condition. Ask for a design and price quote; Norton’s says all of its design and price quotes are free of charge, and it schedules appointments Tuesday through Saturday, 10:30 to 5, at 314-645-4040. Ask whether your piece stays in the building. Ask what percentage of UV the glass blocks, and make them say the number. Then count back the full 4 to 5 weeks from the day you need it on the wall, and if that day is a birthday or a holiday, start now.
### How much should I expect to pay for framing?
Expect the quote to scale with size first. Norton’s own FAQ answers the question this way: the largest determining factor is the size of your art, because the larger the artwork, the more materials the project needs. After size, two choices move the number most, the grade of the glazing and the grade of the mat. What the piece means to you does not change the price at all. The same print can be framed three legitimate ways with a wide spread between the cheapest version and the most protective one, and the shop is not padding the difference.
You will notice no dollar range here for a custom job. That is deliberate. Custom framing is priced per shop, per moulding and per project, so the only fair comparison is two itemized quotes on the same piece. The one dated, published price in this category is that $29 Michaels photo frame, in an 8x8 or 8x10 with four finishes and an optional mat. It tells you what the floor looks like for a gift photo. It tells you nothing about the only copy of a family portrait.
What you can learn is the arithmetic behind the counter, so you can read your own quote and see which line is driving it.
### The arithmetic behind the quote
A quote is built from four buckets: moulding by the foot, mat and backing by size, glazing by area, and labor. You cannot argue a shop down on glass. You can absolutely redesign the mat.
Moulding by the foot. The footage is not the perimeter of your picture. Every mitered corner runs past the opening by the width of the moulding, on both pieces that meet there, so the stick you pay for is the perimeter plus eight moulding widths. A 16x20 opening has a 72-inch perimeter, but in a 2-inch moulding it uses 72 plus 16, or 88 inches. A wider frame costs you twice: more per foot, and more feet.
United inches. The trade’s shorthand for size is one long side plus one short side. A 16x20 is 36 united inches. Mats, backing and much of the fitting labor are priced off that figure, which is why a framer can quote fast once the tape comes off the piece.
Glazing by area. Glass and acrylic come from sheets, so their cost tracks square inches. That is why big pieces jump in price faster than they look like they should.
### How much does it cost to frame a 24x36 picture?
More than the size suggests, and the arithmetic shows why. A 16x20 is 36 united inches and 320 square inches of glass. A 24x36 is 60 united inches and 864 square inches. The figure the mat and labor are priced from rises about 67 percent, while the glass area nearly triples. Add a 3-inch mat all the way around and the outside size becomes 30x42, which is 1,260 square inches of glazing, close to four times the 16x20. If the budget is tight on a big piece, a narrower mat is the cheapest place to give ground.
### Which choices actually move the number?
Glazing and mat grade, and both are real protection rather than upsell. A fancier moulding, a second mat or a fabric wrap is taste, and taste is where you cut.
Glazing. The labels are slippery, so ask for the product name. Tru Vue, the glazing maker, says its Museum Glass blocks up to 99% of UV rays, with reflection under 1% and transmission over 97%. Stand in front of museum glass and the frame looks empty until you see the print sitting there, close enough to touch. If a shop just says “UV glass,” ask what percentage.
Mat grade. A decorative paper-faced mat, a conservation mat and a cotton rag museum mat are three different products at three different prices. Hobby Lobby’s custom framing page, for one, offers cotton rag museum mats for delicate photography and signed or limited-edition prints. For anything you could not replace, pay for the better board.
Mounting. Dry mounting bonds the piece flat to a board with heat and adhesive. It is cheap and it is permanent. Hinging with Japanese paper and wheat starch paste is the conservation route, chosen because it can be undone. For a poster, dry mount it. For anything signed, original or irreplaceable, do not.
The air gap. Nothing should press against the glass. A mat holds the glazing off the surface on its own; a float mount, where the torn or deckled edges show, needs spacers to do the same job, which adds depth and a step of labor. This matters in a river city. A St. Louis August pushes a lot of damp air through a house, and a photograph held tight against glass through enough humid summers can stick to it. Peeling it off is a conservator’s job, and the bill for that dwarfs the price of a mat.
Odd pieces. Jerseys, quilts and needlework need a different hand than paper. Norton’s FAQ says it frames all types of needlework, including cross stitch, needlepoint, crewel, hooked rugs and tapestries. A shadow box needs depth, and a diploma with a raised seal needs room so the glass does not crush it. Ask before you assume a shop takes the job.
Afternoon sun hitting that wall every day? Start with the window: what blinds and shades cost here.
### Where is the cheapest place to get custom framing?
The cheapest framing is the framing you do not buy custom. A piece already sized to a standard frame, 8x10, 11x14, 16x20, 24x36, goes in a ready-made frame for far less than any custom quote, and for a reproduction poster that is the right answer, not a compromise.
Let the mat do the fitting. For an odd-sized piece close to a standard, buy the ready-made frame and pay only for a custom-cut mat.
Print to a standard size. Size the photo file to a standard frame before you print it, not after.
Bring your own frame. Norton’s FAQ answers that question with one word, “Absolutely,” and says it is happy to use your frame or any framing materials you already have.
Spend the savings on glazing. A plain moulding with good UV glass protects your piece. An ornate moulding with ordinary glass does not.
And read the discount sign carefully. Hobby Lobby says its custom frames are always 50% off the marked price, and that this applies to frames only. That is a real saving on one of the four buckets, not half off the ticket.
### Is Hobby Lobby or Michaels cheaper for picture frames?
Nobody can answer that honestly as a blanket yes or no. Both chains price custom work per project, and neither publishes a list you could compare line by line. What each says about itself: Hobby Lobby says every store has a framing expert, and Michaels says its $29 10-minute framing is now in all U.S. stores, per its February 6, 2026 release. Get an itemized quote from each on identical specifications, then take the same list to an independent shop.
One question separates them more than price: does your piece leave the building? Norton’s FAQ says that unless advanced restoration is needed, all work is done by its staff on the premises. For a poster, who cares. For the only photograph of a grandparent, that is the whole question.
### Is the framer certified, and does it matter?
It is worth one question. The Professional Picture Framers Association runs a Certified Picture Framer credential, and Norton’s says there are currently fewer than 500 of them in the United States, three of them at that one shop on Big Bend: Doug and Mary Norton, charter members of the program, and their son Ty, certified in 2020. Plenty of excellent framers never sat the exam. But a framer who has will name the board, name the UV number, and tell you out loud whether the mounting can be undone.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I find custom picture framing in St. Louis?
A.  Independent frame shops, galleries with a framing counter, and craft chains with framing departments all do it. Norton’s Fine Art & Framing is at 2025 S. Big Bend Blvd., 314-645-4040, and schedules framing appointments Tuesday through Saturday, 10:30 to 5; it takes walk-ins but puts appointments first.
