### Q. Does Hobby Lobby still do framing?
A.  Yes. Hobby Lobby’s custom framing page says you can get your piece framed at any Hobby Lobby store and that every store has a framing expert. The same page lists cotton rag museum mats and Museum Glass for UV protection as options.
### Q. Does Hobby Lobby charge for framing?
A.  Yes. Hobby Lobby says its custom frames are always 50% off the marked price, and that the discount applies to frames only, so the mat, glass and labor are still on the ticket.
### Q. Why is framing necessary?
A.  For a poster you would happily replace, it is not. For anything you cannot replace, it is. A frame holds the piece flat, keeps fingers and dust off the surface, and with glazing like Tru Vue’s Museum Glass blocks up to 99% of UV rays.
### Q. What are the trends in picture framing?
A.  The clearest documented shift is speed. Michaels announced its $29, 10-minute photo framing in a November 18, 2025 release, and by February 6, 2026 said it was in all U.S. stores. At the other end, Norton’s FAQ puts its turnaround at around 4 to 5 weeks, with the work done by its staff on the premises.
### Q. Is a framer a good job?
A.  It is a skilled trade with a real credential behind it, the Professional Picture Framers Association’s Certified Picture Framer program. Some framers make a life of it: Norton’s lists Doug Norton with over 60 years of experience. Pay tracks the shop and the market, not the title.

## How to Pick a Steakhouse in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-pick-a-steakhouse-in-st-louis
Fat hits a hot broiler and spits. That sound starts every steak dinner in this town, and at Kreis’ on South Lindbergh the end of the story is already printed on the menu, at the bottom of a five-line doneness chart: “Not responsible for well done steaks.”
Read that line twice. A room that has served steak since the Kreis family opened it as a roadhouse in 1948 is telling you, in writing, exactly where its patience ends. That is the whole trick to picking a St. Louis steakhouse. The good ones put their rules on the page. You just have to read the page before you book, not after the check lands.
Here is what to read for, in order, using two menus that are live right now: Kreis’ in Frontenac and Citizen Kane’s, a family owned and operated steakhouse in a Victorian house.
### What are the signs of a good quality steak house?
A good steakhouse names its grade, says how its beef is aged, and tells you what each temperature means. Kreis’ does all three in print: its menu describes its beef as “USDA Prime Midwestern corn-fed Black Angus, aged in house,” and its chart spells out that medium rare is “Red or very pink on the inside.” A menu that commits to that much is a kitchen that expects to be checked.
The grade is the easiest tell, because it is a federal word, not a marketing one. USDA’s Agricultural Marketing Service says Prime beef “is produced from young, well-fed beef cattle” with “at least slightly abundant marbling” and “is generally sold in upscale restaurants,” while Choice “is high quality, but has less marbling than Prime.” Those white threads of fat are what melt on the broiler and make a strip taste like butter at the edges. A menu that says only “hand-cut” has promised you nothing you can check.
### The five-minute menu check, before you call for a table
First, find the grade next to the steak. Kreis’ splits its own menu down the middle: both New York strips are Prime, while the ribeye and the prime rib are labeled Certified Angus Beef. Same page, two different promises. If you are paying for Prime, make sure the cut you want is the one that carries the word.
Second, look for the aging. “Aged in house” means the restaurant holds the beef itself before it ever hits the grill. If the menu is silent, ask the server how long and where. A confident kitchen answers in one sentence.
Third, find out what comes with the steak. This is the line that moves your bill the most, and these two menus show why. At Citizen Kane’s, every entree includes “your choice of any side dish, plus Soup du Jour made fresh daily, Or Kane’s Rosebud Salad.” At Kreis’, the steak comes with a side, but salads are their own line, from an $8 house salad to an $11 iceberg wedge.
Fourth, read the fine print at the bottom. Kreis’ asks “Please no splitting of entrees,” reserves the right to add a 20% gratuity for parties of 8 or more, and does no separate checks for a table that size. Better to know that before you invite the whole office.
Fifth, look for the toasted ravioli. Half joking. Both menus carry it, Kreis’ calling it “A St. Louis classic” and Citizen Kane’s “A St. Louis tradition.” A steakhouse that keeps toasted ravioli on the same page as the shrimp cocktail is a local room, not a franchise wearing a local name.
### The $46 strip that costs more than the $52.95 one
Put the two menus side by side and the cheaper steak stops being cheaper. Kreis’ lists a 10 oz Prime New York strip at $46 with one side. Add its $9 Caesar salad and the strip, side and salad come to $55. Citizen Kane’s lists its New York strip at $52.95, and the side plus the soup or the Rosebud salad are already in that price.
That is not a knock on either room. Kreis’ strip is the one stamped Prime. It is a reminder that the steak line is never the dinner. Count what your table will actually order, add a drink, tax and tip, and then compare. The strip that looked cheaper on the page now costs more, before anyone opens the wine list.
The small upcharges add up the same way. At Kreis’, a béarnaise or hollandaise is $4, the brandy wild mushroom sauce $6, and asparagus carries a surcharge as your included side. At Kane’s, a béarnaise or brandy peppercorn is $3.95. None of it is hidden. All of it is printed. Most people just never scroll that far. Do it with the menu open on your phone and a pencil, and you will walk in knowing your number, which is a much better feeling than doing math under the table while the server waits with the check folder.
### What is the average cost per person at a steakhouse?
There is no honest single number, because menu structure swings it so far. Use the real St. Louis figures above as your yardstick: a strip, a side and a salad come to $55 at Kreis’ and $52.95 at Citizen Kane’s, before drinks, tax and tip. Order the 8 oz filet mignon at Kreis’ and the entree alone is $54; the 20 oz filet is $120.
The cheapest good steak night at Kreis’ is printed right on the home page. The Sunday night special is three courses for $55 per guest: a Caesar or house salad, a 12 oz Queen Cut of prime rib with au jus, creamy horseradish and a side, then amaretto cheesecake or apple strudel. It is dine-in only, internet only, you must mention it when you order, and it does not run on Easter, Mother’s Day, Father’s Day, Christmas Eve or New Year’s Eve.
At the other end of the same menu sits the 64 oz bone-in Extra Cut of prime rib at $145, with a flat house rule beside it: “No Splitting of Extra Cut.” The 32 oz King Cut at $82 gets the same rule. Somebody, at some point, tried. The menu remembers.
The cheapest great steak in town may be the one you sear at home - is a St. Louis butcher cheaper than the grocery store?
### How do you read the room before you book?
The building tells you the night. Citizen Kane’s sits in “a classic turn of the century Victorian home” and has served dinner there since 1993. That is a birthday-for-your-father kind of room. Citizen Kane’s steak seasoning is sold at Straubs, Dierbergs and Schnucks, so plenty of St. Louis home grills already taste a little like that dining room. Kreis’ history page describes “the ‘New York Style’ waiters” and a “relaxing country club atmosphere” that the Tompras family kept when they bought it in 1983. It also rents out a Private Dining Room with facilities for up to 75 guests, which is the answer when the rehearsal dinner outgrows a long table.
Say what the night is when you call. Anniversary, birthday, first client dinner: the host writes it down, and it changes which table you get. Both rooms recommend reservations on their own sites. If the evening needs flowers on the table, order them earlier in the day from one of the St. Louis florists on our directory. And if dinner comes before a show, our guide to live theater and performing arts in St. Louis helps you line the two up.
### What is the dress code for a steak house?
Kreis’ posts a Business Casual Dress Code and spells out exactly what that means. No athletic wear, sweatpants, cut-off shorts or exposed undergarments. “Mens shirts must have sleeves.” Take off the ball cap or beanie when you walk in. And one rule you will not find on many menus: management may delay seating “due to strong smoke odors.” Skip the cigar on the drive over. When in doubt anywhere else, call; a host will tell you straight in ten seconds.
### What if you are not a steak person?
Order the seafood and skip the apology. Kreis’ runs a full seafood list, from a $28 Icelandic cod with capers and lemon butter to $62 broiled sea scallops, and the German side of its history still shows in a $34 Vienna schnitzel and German potato pancakes with applesauce. Kreis’ even prints a $20 vegetable platter: broccoli, green beans, mushrooms, creamed spinach and your choice of potato. At Citizen Kane’s, the charbroiled Norwegian salmon comes topped with béarnaise and a grilled jumbo shrimp.
If you like your steak well done, take Kreis’ at its word and order something built for it, like the 18 oz Berkshire pork chop, charbroiled or breaded. And if a big beef dinner is wrong for the occasion altogether, this town has other answers; start with the dishes this city actually invented.
Booking a night that has to go right? Browse steak houses across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pull up the two menus you like most, and do the five-minute check above before you pick up the phone.
If you own the supper club, the chophouse or the corner bar with a strip on the chalkboard, your house rules and your Sunday special are exactly what diners are hunting for. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts that menu in front of the people deciding where tonight’s dinner goes, and that is how a room gets more customers who already know what they want to order.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best steak house in St. Louis?
A.  The best one is the one whose menu fits your night. For a big, old-school prime rib dinner, Kreis’ in Frontenac has been serving since 1948 and prints its grade, its aging and its doneness chart. For a smaller room with soup or salad and a side included in the steak price, Citizen Kane’s has served dinner in a Victorian home since 1993.
### Q. Where can I find the best cheap steak in St. Louis?
A.  Look for a fixed-price night. Kreis’ Sunday night special is three courses for $55 per guest with a 12 oz Queen Cut of prime rib, dine-in only, and you must mention it when you order. Its $20 Kreis’ Steakburger with steak fries is the lowest-priced beef on that menu.
### Q. What makes a steak house a steakhouse?
A.  Beef sits at the center of the menu and the kitchen is built around it, with steaks priced by cut and weight and the grade often printed beside them. The seafood, the sides and the sauces are arranged around the steak rather than beside it. Kreis’ even lists its prime rib under the heading “The Last Word in Prime Rib.”
### Q. What makes a steak house truly exceptional?
A.  Consistency you would bet an anniversary on. The kitchen hits the temperature you asked for every visit, the server can name the grade and the aging without looking it up, and the house rules are written down where you can read them. A printed doneness chart, like the one at Kreis’, is a kitchen putting its standard on paper.
### Q. What is the proper etiquette at a steakhouse?
A.  Order your steak the way you like it, and read the house rules first. Some rooms say no splitting entrees, and Kreis’ may add a 20% gratuity for parties of 8 or more with no separate checks. Agree on shared sides as a table. If a steak arrives wrong, say so at the first bite, not the last.
### Q. What is the dress code for a steak house?
A.  Business casual covers most St. Louis steakhouses. Kreis’ asks for no athletic wear, sweatpants or cut-off shorts, shirts with sleeves for men, and hats off at the door. When you are unsure, call and ask; the host will tell you.
### Q. What is the difference between a steak house and a chop house?
A.  Today the two words are used almost interchangeably on signs. A chophouse menu tends to lean harder on chops of lamb, veal and pork alongside the beef, the way Kreis’ lists double-boned Colorado lamb chops and a Berkshire pork chop next to its steaks.
### Q. Why are steak houses dark?
A.  Low light, dark wood and deep booths make a long, expensive dinner feel private, and they flatter both the room and the plate. It is a convention, not a rule. Plenty of newer steakhouses are bright, and a steak at the bar usually comes under ordinary lights.

## Your Finished Basement Is Not Living Area to an Appraiser
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-home-appraisal-involves-in-st-louis
The laser measure clicks on the top step. The appraiser heads down the basement stairs, past the carpet and the drywall you paid for, the stairwell air cooler than the kitchen, sweeps the red dot across the far wall, taps the tablet, and moves on. You stand at the top of the stairs doing the math in your head. That room was supposed to be the fourth bedroom.
On the report, it won’t be. The Fannie Mae Selling Guide says a level counts as below-grade “if any portion of it is below-grade, regardless of the quality of its finish or the window area of any room,” and that “a walk-out partially below-grade area with finished rooms would not be included in the above-grade square footage or room count.” The finished basement still has value. It just lands on its own line, the Basement & Finished Rooms Below-Grade line, not in the living area at the top of the page. Finished is not the same as counted.
Here is the part that only works in the City of St. Louis, and you can check it tonight from the couch. The City Building Division lists “the conversion of basement or below-grade space to living quarters” as work that requires a building permit. And the City Assessor’s Address & Property Search covers any property in the City of St. Louis: type in the address or parcel ID, pay nothing, and the record shows Building Permit Records next to the sale information and tax history. Questions about a permit go to the Building Division Permit Section at (314) 622-3313. If the house sits out in St. Louis County instead, this City search is the wrong door; ask the seller for the permit paperwork directly.
So look the house up before the appraiser’s car is in the driveway. Selling? If the basement finish shows up in the permit records, print that page and put it in a folder on the kitchen counter with the year the roof went on. If it doesn’t, you want to know that now, not when a buyer’s agent asks. Buying? Look up the address the night the contract is signed. A finished basement with no permit record on a City house is a question for the seller, in writing, before appraisal day.
Then the day itself. Unlock the attic hatch, crawlspace, furnace room, electrical panel and every bedroom; a locked door can mean a second trip. Never tell the appraiser the number you need. Hand over facts instead: permit dates, what the remodel included, a nearby sale you think compares. And if a loan is involved, ask your lender when you will see the report, because under 12 CFR 1002.14 the lender must give you a copy of the appraisal no later than three business days before closing.
### What is the point of getting a house appraised?
The appraiser’s car pulls away and you realize nobody asked what you think the house is worth. That is by design. When you borrow, the appraisal answers the lender’s question, not yours: is this house worth enough to back the loan? The Loan Estimate rule spells it out in the statement lenders must give you: “The creditor may order an appraisal to determine the value of the property” and may charge you for it. You pay for a report that protects someone else’s money. That is the quiet part, and it is worth hearing out loud before the visit.
You still get to read it. Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act rule at 12 CFR 1002.14, a creditor must provide a copy of each appraisal or other written valuation “promptly upon completion, or three business days prior to consummation of the transaction” on a first-lien home loan, whichever is earlier. Sit down with it at the kitchen table, not at the closing table.
Outside of a loan, the purpose flips. Divorce, an estate, a tax appeal, pricing a house before you list it: in those, you hire the appraiser, you are the client, and the report answers your question. In an estate, the furniture needs its own opinion too; that is a job for antique dealers, not the appraiser of the house.
### What the appraiser actually looks at, and why your basement lands on its own line
Three things: your house, the recent sales near it, and the market around both. They measure, sketch the floor plan, note condition, quality, age and room count, then adjust nearby sales up or down for each difference until a value comes out the other side. Fannie Mae requires them to follow the ANSI Z765-2021 measuring standard for above- and below-grade square footage, finished and unfinished, on single-family homes, and to report below-grade areas separately, with adjustments on the Basement & Finished Rooms Below-Grade line of the sales comparison grid.
That standard is why the number on the report may not match the number on the listing or the assessor’s card. Different method, different total. If the gap is big, it is worth asking which rooms were counted where, and the answer is usually on the sketch page.
An appraisal is not a home inspection. The appraiser forms an opinion of value and notes conditions that affect it. Nobody is running the furnace through a cycle or putting a camera down the sewer lateral. That is a separate hire, and a lot sits outside a standard inspection too, which is the subject of home inspections in St. Louis and what they miss.
### Who orders it, and why you cannot pick the appraiser
On a mortgage, the lender may order the appraisal and charge you for it. The appraiser’s opinion is supposed to be independent, and federal valuation rules at 12 CFR 1026.42 protect that: no covered person - the lender, or anyone providing settlement services - may try to make the value rest on anything other than the appraiser’s independent judgment “through coercion, extortion, inducement, bribery, or intimidation.” The rule is written for the people in the deal, but the lesson for a homeowner is the same: give facts, not a target.
The fee shows up on your Loan Estimate under the subheading “Services You Cannot Shop For,” and that heading is literal. For the rest of that page - title, settlement, transfer taxes and prepaids - see what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis. This post stays on the appraisal line.
The same federal rule also covers the person doing the work. The creditor and its agents must pay a fee appraiser a rate that is customary and reasonable for comparable appraisal services in the geographic market. The fee you pay is not always the fee the appraiser keeps, which comes up again in the FAQ below.
Unrelated, and we know it - once the number holds, the boxes start: what a move costs in St. Louis.
### When the number comes in low
The phone call is short and the silence after it is long. The lender lends against the appraised value, not your contract price, so a low number opens a gap somebody has to cover. The real moves: renegotiate the price, split the difference, bring cash, ask the lender to send the appraiser specific corrections, or walk away if your contract gives you that right.
Corrections run on facts. A sale near you that closed and was not used. A bedroom count that is wrong. Square footage that does not match the sketch. A condition rating that ignores the kitchen you permitted and paid for. What does not move it: needing the number to be higher.
Sellers have levers too: hold the price and let the buyer bring cash, meet in the middle, accept the lower number, or relist. Read your contract for the appraisal deadline and put it on the fridge.
### How to check that an appraiser is licensed in Missouri
It takes a minute. Missouri appraisal licenses and certificates are issued by the Missouri Real Estate Appraisers Commission, and its page on pr.mo.gov links to the state’s licensee search. The commission’s office in Jefferson City answers at 573.751.0038. Its application list covers trainee, certified residential, certified general and state license applicants.
The license is not a formality. Under section 339.501 RSMo, beginning July 1, 1999, it became unlawful for anyone in Missouri to act as a real estate appraiser without first obtaining a license or certificate from the commission. The same law says it shall not be construed to require a license for a licensed real estate broker or salesperson who prepares a comparative market analysis or a broker price opinion. So the free pricing opinion your agent emails over is useful, and legally it is not an appraisal.
If the real question is pricing strategy rather than value, that is advice work, covered in what a real estate consultant does and what it costs.
### A side note for owners who stay: the City tax hearing
Not selling? The same appraisal has a second life. In the City of St. Louis, a relative with a real estate license can sit beside you at a Board of Equalization hearing, but the Assessor’s own page says an agent “may not present an opinion of value unless they are licensed or certified as an appraiser.” You may give your own opinion of value. The board sits in Room 120 of City Hall, wants six copies of anything you want considered, and appeals are due by the second Monday in July.
Every other year the assessor puts a new value on your house, and if it reads high, the fight is at the Board of Equalization. The city lists common evidence as copies of sale contracts, information on comparable properties, income and expense statements and descriptive photographs. A licensed appraisal pulls the comparable sales, the measurements and the photos into one signed document, which is exactly the shape of evidence the board asks for.
Then the hearing itself: the board president asking whether you have documentation, the assessor or staff present with the right to present evidence of their own. That last part matters. You are not arguing with a form; there is someone across the room defending the number. Bring the six copies, signature page on top.
The assessed number itself is not market value, by design. Missouri assesses residential property at nineteen percent of true value under section 137.115 RSMo, and new values are set as of January first of each odd-numbered year. The statute also says that before the assessor raises a home’s value more than fifteen percent since the last assessment, excluding new construction or improvements, the assessor shall conduct a physical inspection. If your notice jumped and nobody came by, that is a question worth asking. Here is how to appeal your property assessment in St. Louis County.
Need a value nobody is going to argue with? Browse real estate appraisers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, check the license on the state site, then call two and ask each for the fee and the turn time in writing for your purpose - estate, divorce, tax appeal or pre-listing.
If you’re the certified residential appraiser people call when the number has to hold up at a hearing, the private work starts with a local search. See how a Gold listing helps you get more customers, or list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the typical cost of an appraisal in Missouri?
A.  I could not find a Missouri agency that publishes an average fee, so treat any single number you see online with care. On a mortgage, your fee is itemized on the Loan Estimate under “Services You Cannot Shop For.” For a private appraisal, call two licensed appraisers and get written quotes; acreage, an unusual floor plan or a rush job raises the price.
### Q. What should I do before an appraiser comes to my house?
A.  Open everything and gather paper. Unlock the attic hatch, crawlspace, furnace room, electrical panel and every bedroom. Put permits for the basement finish and any remodel in one folder, with the roof’s age. Skip the deep clean; access matters more than housekeeping. A locked room can mean a second trip.
### Q. What not to say to an appraiser?
A.  Do not name the number you need. Federal valuation rules at 12 CFR 1026.42 bar the lender and settlement service providers from trying to steer the value away from the appraiser’s independent judgment through coercion, inducement or intimidation, and a homeowner gains nothing by trying either. Facts are welcome: permit dates, what the remodel included, a nearby sale you believe is comparable. A target price is not a fact.
### Q. What devalues a home appraisal?
A.  Deferred maintenance, functional problems and square footage that does not count where you expected. Fannie Mae treats any level with a portion below grade as below-grade, regardless of finish, so a finished walkout is adjusted on its own line rather than counted as above-grade living area. Wrong facts on the report can hurt too, so read your copy.
### Q. What are the red flags for home appraisals?
A.  Factual errors first: wrong square footage, a wrong bedroom or bathroom count, a condition rating that ignores documented work, comparable sales from too far away, or a recent sale on your street that was never considered. Those are the points to send back through your lender, in writing, with proof.
### Q. Is there a downside to getting your house appraised?
A.  You pay up front, and the fee does not come back if you dislike the result. On a purchase, a value under the contract price opens a gap the lender will not cover. On a refinance, a low value can change the loan terms you were counting on. For a tax appeal or an estate, the downside is smaller: you hired the appraiser and you choose whether to use the report.
### Q. Is there a way to get a free appraisal?
A.  Not a real one. A licensed agent’s comparative market analysis is often free, and section 339.501 RSMo does not require an appraiser license for a broker or salesperson who prepares one, because it is not an appraisal. At a City of St. Louis Board of Equalization hearing you may give your own opinion of value at no cost, but an agent speaking for you must be a licensed or certified appraiser to offer one.
### Q. How much money does an appraiser make per appraisal?
A.  Often less than you paid, when a management company sits between the lender and the appraiser and keeps a share. I could not find a published figure for the split. What federal rules do require, under 12 CFR 1026.42, is that the creditor and its agents pay the fee appraiser a rate that is customary and reasonable for comparable appraisal services in the geographic market.

## St. Louis Dispensaries Take Illinois IDs - Not Expired Ones
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-cannabis-dispensaries-in-st-louis
“Will they take my Illinois license?”
That is the question people actually ask, usually in a low voice, standing in a small lobby with a counter, a camera in the corner, and a clerk holding out a hand for the card. Your thumb is already worrying the edge of your wallet. Out-of-town cousin, new neighbor, a St. Louisan who has driven past the same storefront a hundred times and finally pulled in: it is the same knot in the same spot.
The short answer is yes. Missouri’s own Division of Cannabis Regulation guidance says a dispensary confirms your age on “a valid (not expired) government issued photo ID,” and the examples it lists start with “a U.S. driver’s license” - not a Missouri one. A passport book or passport card works. So does a U.S. military ID. What does not work is the license that ran out last month and is still riding in your wallet. Expired is the word that turns people around at the counter, not out-of-state.
So before you go, check three things in under a minute. The expiration date on your license, which has to be in the future. The store itself, which should appear on the state health department’s list of licensed dispensary facilities - if it is not on the list, it is not a Missouri dispensary. And the plan for after, because a sealed bag stays sealed in the car and stays off the Arch grounds. The cap is three ounces, and the receipt will carry a state line and a local one. Each of those has a reason, and the reasons are below.
### What are the current cannabis regulations in Missouri?
Adults 21 and older may buy marijuana at a state-licensed dispensary, and the limit fits in one breath. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services puts it this way: “Up to three (3) ounces may be purchased in a single transaction, and consumers may be in possession of up to three (3) ounces of marijuana at any time.” The rule is written around age, not where you live.
The source behind all of it is Article XIV, Section 2 of the Missouri Constitution, which says its purpose is to make marijuana legal under state and local law “for adults twenty-one years of age or older.” The same section sets the state tax at “six percent of the retail price” and lets a local government add up to three percent more on adult-use sales. You will see both on the slip of paper the clerk folds into the bag.
The department warns that purchases outside a licensed dispensary are not authorized. A shop that is not on the state’s list is not a Missouri dispensary, whatever the sign in the window says.
### Why the receipt in one St. Louis County town reads different from the next
Hold two receipts side by side, one from a store inside Florissant and one from a store out in unincorporated county, and the bottom halves do not match. Same state, same county, same product. The difference is one line, and here is the part almost nobody outside a dispensary back office knows: at a store inside a city, the county cannot add its own marijuana tax on top of the city’s.
The constitution defines the “local government” that may add it this way: “in the case of an incorporated area, a village, town, or city and, in the case of an unincorporated area, a county.” After legalization, St. Louis County collected its own 3% at dispensaries inside cities that charged one too. A Florissant dispensary sued. In Robust Missouri Dispensary 3, LLC v. St. Louis County, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled 6-1 that counties could only levy the tax on marijuana sold in unincorporated areas, and Judge Mary Russell wrote that the constitution lets a county tax a dispensary in an unincorporated area “but not at a dispensary located within the boundaries of an incorporated village, town, or city such as Florissant” (Missouri Supreme Court, as reported by St. Louis Public Radio).
Run it on a $50 purchase, as a simple example. Six percent of that is $3.00, and the state levies that same rate at every licensed store in Missouri. A local three percent adds up to $1.50 more, and ordinary sales tax sits on top of both. Inside a city that approved its own tax, that $1.50 goes to the city. In unincorporated county, it goes to the county. Never both. Two stores a few minutes apart can print two different local lines, and now you know why. It is the kind of thing you can say out loud at the table and be right.
### From the lobby door to the counter
Most first visits go the same way. You step into the lobby, someone asks for the ID, and you wait the few seconds it takes them to read the birth date and the expiration date. That wait is the whole test. Then you are waved onto the sales floor, where glass cases and a menu board do the talking, and a clerk answers questions about what is on the shelf.
Say how much you want and the clerk rings it up. Three ounces is the ceiling for one adult-use transaction, and most people buy a small fraction of that. You pay, the package is sealed, and you are back outside in the time it takes to order a sandwich. Nobody needs your address or your reason.
One thing the clerk will not do is give you medical advice. They are retail staff. If you take blood thinners, are pregnant, or have a surgery coming up, that question belongs with your own doctor, not the person behind the glass.
### Where a legal bag still gets you a ticket
Legal to buy is not legal everywhere. Walk out into the parking lot, feel the cold air, and the rules change the second the bag opens. The constitution prohibits “Smoking marijuana in a location where smoking tobacco is prohibited,” so every no-smoking rule you already know now covers this too. Smoking in a public place, outside an area licensed for it, is subject to a civil penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars.
The car is its own line. Article XIV bars consuming marijuana while operating or being in physical control of a motor vehicle while it is being operated, and separately bars smoking inside one while it is being operated. Driving under the influence is prohibited outright. Keep the sealed package sealed until you are home.
Then there is the one that surprises visitors most. The Arch and the grass around it are Gateway Arch National Park, run by the National Park Service, and federal park rules at 36 CFR 2.35 prohibit “the possession of a controlled substance” unless it came from a practitioner or a valid prescription. The view from the top is the same either way; leave the bag in the room.
Nothing to do with any of this - the yard you came home to still needs a landscaping crew.
If you drive for a living, the rules that govern your job are a separate world from a consumer’s, and it pays to read them before anything else. Our post on what to know before buying a commercial truck in St. Louis covers more of that life.
### Can you grow your own in St. Louis?
Yes, but not casually. The constitution says a person at least 21 may obtain a registration card from the state health department to cultivate up to six flowering plants, six nonflowering plants over fourteen inches tall, and six clones under fourteen inches. The card comes first; the seeds come second.
The plants have rules of their own. They, and anything they produce beyond three ounces, must be kept at one private residence, in a locked space, and not visible by normal, unaided vision from a public place. A tomato-cage row along the alley fence in a south city backyard does not qualify. A locked closet with a grow light does.
Renters, read the lease before you buy a single pot of soil. Owners and landlords set their own rules for their own property, and a lease that bans smoking may be written to cover this too. Ask the landlord in writing and keep the answer.
### Who decides whether a store opens in your town?
Voters, and only on a hard schedule. Under Article XIV, a city or county that wants to ban non-medical dispensaries has to put the question on the general election ballot in a presidential election year, and the ban takes effect only if at least sixty percent of the votes cast are in favor. Anything less, and the jurisdiction has no power to ban them. It is a deliberately high bar, which is why storefronts turn up across so much of the county.
Your job is a different question. The same section says it does not require an employer to permit or accommodate marijuana use in any workplace or on the employer’s property, and it does not prohibit an employer from disciplining an employee for working while under the influence. Legal at home is not a promise about the break room.
### Does a Missouri medical card still matter?
It does, and you feel it at the register, where the clerk takes the patient card and the license together and matches the photos. Medical purchases are taxed at four percent instead of the six percent adult-use rate, and the department says approved patient ID card holders get a standard allotment of six ounces, or more with a physician recommendation, within a thirty-day period. Licensed dispensaries may also accept out-of-state patient cards.
Still deciding whether the card is worth keeping? Here is what a Missouri cannabis clinic does and what the card costs.
One more honest note: a card is also a medical record, and your surgical team will ask about cannabis use. The truthful answer protects you. Our guide to what to ask about anesthesia before surgery in St. Louis walks through that conversation.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a cannabis store the same as a dispensary?
A.  In Missouri, yes - people use both words for the same state-licensed retail store. The legal name in Article XIV is a dispensary facility, and only licensed dispensaries may sell. A shop that is not on the state’s list of licensed dispensary facilities is not a Missouri dispensary, whatever its sign says.
### Q. What is the difference between a cannabis store and a dispensary?
A.  Legally, none here - both are everyday names for a licensed retailer. The difference that matters is licensed versus unlicensed. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services keeps the list of licensed dispensary facilities on its website, and it cautions that purchases outside a licensed dispensary are not authorized under Article XIV.
### Q. What is a cannabis store called?
A.  Officially, a dispensary facility; Article XIV of the Missouri Constitution also defines a comprehensive marijuana dispensary facility. In everyday St. Louis speech, everyone just says dispensary.
### Q. What do people do at a dispensary?
A.  You show a valid, unexpired government-issued photo ID that proves you are 21 - a U.S. driver’s license from any state, a passport book or card, or a U.S. military ID. Then you order at the counter, pay, and leave with a sealed package. A single adult-use transaction is capped at three ounces, and you may not smoke it in a public place.
### Q. How much does 3.5 grams of bud cost?
A.  This page does not track prices; ask the store. What is fixed is the tax on top: a six percent state tax on adult-use sales, plus up to three percent local, collected by the city in an incorporated area or by the county in an unincorporated one - never both. Medical card holders pay four percent instead of six.
### Q. What to buy at dispensary for beginners?
A.  This page does not recommend products. The practical starting point is the label on the sealed package and a question to the clerk, and a health question belongs with your doctor. Whatever you choose, keep the package closed in the car and off the Arch grounds.

## Before You Replace Every Blind in St. Louis, Price the Cord
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-window-blinds-and-shades-cost-in-st-louis
$10. Angi lists a new lift cord at $10 to $30, materials only. A customized blind for the same window can run $650. In St. Louis that gap opens window by window, because the houses are old: the median home in the St. Louis metro is 50 years old, against a national median of 43, according to Construction Coverage’s American Cities With the Oldest Homes study. Old brick, old plaster, old shades that have hung through decades of humid Missouri summers.
You know the moment the bigger number lands. The tape measure snaps back into its case at the kitchen table, the estimate gets read out loud, and you start counting windows in your head: the one over the sink, the stair landing, the front bay, the bedroom shade that sits half-raised because a cord let go in spring and now stripes the afternoon sun across the bed. You can smell the dust when you finally tug it.
Half the time that shade is not dead. Angi’s own data says repairs start at $100 to $120 for the first set, with each additional set adding $40 to $50, and its rule of thumb is to replace only when the repair runs past 50 percent of the price of new.
And St. Louis has a shop built for exactly that call. Victor Shade Company was founded in 1908 by Harold Victor, according to a West Newsmagazine profile. “We specialize in custom-made shades, shutters and blinds, and their repair,” co-owner Scott Segall told the paper. “We’re the only full-service repair shop in St. Louis.” That is his claim, not ours. The profile lists the shop at 11477 Page Service Drive, (314) 428-7979, open 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays and 8 a.m. to noon Saturday. So here is the line worth repeating to anyone pricing a whole house: the median house here is 50, the shade shop dates to 1908, and the cheapest blind you will ever buy is the one you get fixed.
### How much do blinds typically cost?
Nationally, blinds run about $55 to $170 per window installed, which is $40 to $120 in materials plus $15 to $50 for the installation itself, according to Angi’s blinds installation cost guide. Those are national figures. Nobody publishes a St. Louis price sheet, so treat them as a yardstick for the quote in your hand.
The spread is wide because “blinds” covers wildly different products. In Angi’s breakdown, mini blinds run $20 to $140, cellular $65 to $380, and customized blinds $65 to $650. Removing and hauling off the old ones adds $10 to $30 per window if it is not already in the price, a line people forget until the invoice lands.
So before you price anything, walk the house once with a roll of painter’s tape. Mark each window that is truly broken, each one that only has a bad cord or a cracked slat, and each one that is fine but ugly. Call a repair shop about the second group first. Then ask for two in-home measures on the first group in the same week, so both quotes cover identical openings. Victor Shade’s free consultation, per that profile, includes expert measuring and a project plan with pricing, which is the itemized number you want to compare against. Get the labor line separated from the product line on every quote. A lump sum hides which half is negotiable.
### Repair first: what a fix costs against new
You can hear a dying blind before you see it. The lift cord rasps, the bottom rail tips to one side, the slats will not close all the way and a bar of light lies across the bedroom floor at dawn. That is usually a part, not a product. Angi lists materials-only repair costs of $10 to $35 per damaged slat, $10 to $30 for a lift cord, $8 to $20 for a tilt mechanism and $70 to $200 for a motor.
Run the 50 percent test on each window. A custom cellular shade near the top of Angi’s $65 to $380 band with a snapped cord is a repair. A $25 vinyl mini blind with three bent slats is a replacement, and a cheap one. The expensive mistake is the middle: tearing out a whole house of good custom shades because two of them stopped working.
If the fabric is not sun-rotted and the headrail is sound, a repair call costs you one phone conversation to find out.
### Which is cheaper, blinds or shades?
At the bottom of the market, blinds. Angi’s window treatment cost data puts blinds at $30 to $200 and shades at $50 to $150, so the cheapest thing on the wall is a basic slat blind. From the middle up, the two overlap almost completely. Cellular shades run $70 to $350 per window installed and custom shades $250 to $2,600 per window installed, per HomeGuide’s window shades cost data.
The real fork is stock versus custom. Stock comes in fixed widths and either fits your opening or leaves a gap down each side, and that gap is exactly where the morning sun comes in. Custom is built to your measurements, costs more, and is the only option once your window is not a standard size.
If drafts are the reason you are shopping, shades have the edge. Cellular shades “trap air within each cell, as well as between the shade and the window,” according to the U.S. Department of Energy factsheet Interior Cellular Shades Boost Home Energy Performance, which also notes that vinyl or metal blinds account for about 60 percent of all window coverings in U.S. homes. Put your palm near an old sash on a January night and you feel the reason.
### Why an older St. Louis house pushes the price up
Older houses mean fewer standard openings, and fewer standard openings mean more custom orders. With the metro’s median home at 50 years old, that is the normal case here, not the exception.
Run your hand down the casing of an old window and you can often feel it: the opening is not quite square, the plaster dips, the jamb is shallow. A custom blind is cut to the narrowest of its measurements, so an out-of-square opening either gets a sliver of light or gets mounted outside on the trim. A bay window in Shaw or Compton Heights is three or five coverings, not one. Transoms, arches and the tall narrow windows beside a stair are custom-only. This is where a dealer who measures earns the fee, because the shop that measures owns the mistake.
If the windows themselves are the problem and you are weighing replacement, that is a different project with different math. Our guide to choosing a window company in St. Louis covers it.
### Do motorized blinds cost a lot more?
Yes. Motorized blinds run about $300 to $1,000 per window installed, per HomeGuide’s motorized blinds cost data, against $55 to $170 for a standard installed blind in Angi’s numbers. The tech has moved fast. “At one time, remotes operated by an infrared sensor which required precise alignment. Now it’s all done through WiFi and Bluetooth,” Scott Segall told West Newsmagazine.
Motors earn their money on windows you cannot reach, shades too heavy to lift comfortably, and rooms you want on a schedule. Motorizing every window because the soft hum looked good in a showroom is how a modest project doubles.
Is the sun fading the print on that wall too? Here is what framing it behind UV glass costs.
### Are corded blinds still safe to buy?
Not in a house with small children. In its Federal Register rulemaking of November 28, 2022, the Consumer Product Safety Commission said it was aware of 209 fatal and near-miss strangulations on window covering cords among children 8 years old and younger from January 2009 through December 2021. If a toddler can reach the window, cordless is the floor, not an upgrade. Victor Shade, per the same profile, carries cordless and retractable systems in addition to automated systems for child and pet safety. Ask any dealer to confirm in writing that what you order meets the industry’s ANSI/WCMA A100.1-2022 standard, which the Window Covering Manufacturers Association says took effect on June 1, 2024.

### How much do blinds cost generally?
Nationally about $55 to $170 per window installed, according to Angi: $40 to $120 in materials plus $15 to $50 to hang them. Mini blinds run $20 to $140 and cellular shades $65 to $380, and in an old St. Louis house a snapped $10 lift cord is often a repair, not a replacement.
### Is there a tax credit for energy efficient blinds or shades?
No. The IRS credit page lists the qualified building envelope components, starting with new exterior doors, then windows, skylights and insulation materials. And the credit is gone regardless: the IRS says in its official FAQ that it will not be allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025. A salesperson who promises your shades a federal refund is wrong.
Sales tax, on the other hand, is real money on a four-figure order. Missouri’s state sales tax rate is 4.225 percent, and cities, counties and certain districts can add local tax on top, per the Missouri Department of Revenue. On the Illinois side, most tangible personal property counts as general merchandise for sales tax, per the Illinois Department of Revenue. Ask for tax broken out on every quote before you compare them side by side.
### Where is the most affordable place to get blinds?
There are four channels, cheapest to most expensive:
Ready-made off the shelf. Cheapest, fine for standard openings if you can live with a side gap.
Cut-to-size in the store. Exact width at a low price, good for newer houses where every window matches.
Cut-to-size online. Cheap and exact, but you supply the measurement, so you own every error.
A local dealer who measures and installs. The most per window, and the only channel that handles bays, arches, transoms and out-of-square plaster openings without buying twice.
Mixing channels in one house is normal: stock in the guest room, dealer on the front bay, a repair call for the shades that only need a cord.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do shades typically cost?
A.  Cellular shades run about $70 to $350 per window installed and custom shades $250 to $2,600 per window installed, according to HomeGuide’s window shades cost data. Ready-made shades cost a fraction of that. The spread comes down to whether the shade is built to your opening, the fabric you pick, and whether the lift is manual or motorized.
### Q. Are shades cheaper than blinds?
A.  Usually not at the entry level. Angi’s data puts blinds at $30 to $200 and shades at $50 to $150, so the least expensive thing you can hang is a basic slat blind. From mid-range up the two overlap, and stock versus custom sizing drives the price more than the shade-or-blind choice.
### Q. Is it better to have blinds or shades?
A.  Blinds win where you want to tilt slats for light and view without raising them: kitchens, home offices, street-facing rooms. Shades win on softness, insulation and wide openings. For a drafty bedroom window in an old house, a tightly fitted cellular shade does more than a slat blind.
### Q. What are the drawbacks of cellular shades?
A.  The honeycomb cells collect dust and cannot be wiped like a hard slat, so cleaning means a vacuum brush. There is no tilt, so the room is open or closed with nothing in between. Cordless lift mechanisms wear over years of daily use, which is where a repair shop earns its keep.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of blackout shades?
A.  Light still leaks around the edges unless you add side channels, so an inside-mounted blackout shade is rarely truly black. Heat builds in the pocket between shade and glass on a sunny exposure. And daylight in that room becomes all or nothing.
### Q. Where’s the cheapest place for blinds?
A.  Ready-made blinds off a big-box shelf are the cheapest, with Angi listing mini blinds from $20. Cut-to-size, in store or online, costs a little more for an exact width. But the cheapest blind of all may be the one already on your window: a $10 to $30 lift cord, in Angi’s materials-only figures, beats a new blind at any price.
### Q. Should blinds be lighter or darker than the walls?
A.  A covering slightly lighter than the wall makes a window read larger and keeps a small room from closing in. Darker reads as a deliberate frame and hides dust better. Standard whites are usually the cheapest colorways, so ask what a specialty color adds per window before you fall for it.

## Day 31 Costs $25: Buying a Work Truck in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-buying-a-commercial-truck-in-st-louis
The diesel ticks over at idle on the lot, a low clatter you feel in the soles of your boots. The salesman slides the paperwork across the hood: a bill of sale, a Manufacturer’s Statement of Origin, a Missouri Form 108. A signature, a handshake, keys. The ink is barely dry when a clock starts that nobody at the sales desk mentions.
Missouri’s Department of Revenue gives a buyer 30 days from the date of purchase to title and pay sales tax on a newly purchased vehicle. On the 31st day after purchase there is a title penalty of $25. It grows another $25 for every 30 days late, up to a maximum penalty of $200. The tax itself is state sales tax of 4.225 percent, plus local sales tax on the purchase price, less trade-in allowance, if any. That check is real money, and it is due on a calendar the sales desk never shows.
The desk’s job ends at the handshake. The 30-day clock, the January 1 tax line, the emissions weight line and the paper the license office wants all start after it. Is a missed date a sign of a careless owner? Or of a process that hands over keys and leaves the rest in fine print?
### What is the cheapest month to buy a truck?
On the sticker, no single month wins; dealer discounts move with quotas and model-year changeovers. On the tax bill, one day does. Missouri law says every person owning or holding tangible personal property on the first day of January, including property purchased on that day, is liable for taxes on it during the same calendar year. That is property tax, not the purchase price. The City of St. Louis assessor says the same thing from its side of the counter: the assessment is made as of January 1 for the current year’s tax and is predicated on 33 1/3% of true value.
Then the City adds a deadline of its own. Taxpayers with tangible property are mandated by State law to file a list of all taxable tangible personal property by April 1st of each year with the Assessor’s Office, and a 10% assessment penalty is added when the declaration comes in after April 1st. Individual declarations are mailed in January. And one line on the Assessor’s page matters most for a new truck or a new business: first-time declarations must be submitted on a paper form. That form goes to City Hall, Room 115, 1200 Market St, or the personal property desk answers at (314) 622-4171, Monday thru Friday 8:00 am to 5:00 pm.
### The 8,500-pound line only St. Louis trucks meet
The inspection bay sounds the same every time: the hiss of the lift, a tech leaning in with a tablet, the wait on a plastic chair. What changes is whether the truck has to be there at all. Missouri’s emissions rule, 10 CSR 10-5.381, covers vehicles operated on public roadways in the area containing the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County, along with neighboring counties.
The same rule carries a weight line. A light duty truck is any motor vehicle rated at 8,500 pounds GVWR or less, and when the emissions inspector verifies that a vehicle is over 8,500 pounds GVWR, the inspection record shows a GVWR exemption. Two trucks can look identical on the lot and sit on opposite sides of that line. The number that decides it is printed on the door-jamb label, a small sticker by the latch, not in the glossy brochure on the desk.
### What the license office stack asks for
The license office line moves at its own pace, the number board clicking, a folder going soft in a sweaty hand. The Department of Revenue’s stack is the certificate of title signed over to the buyer or the Manufacturer’s Statement of Origin, a signed Application for Missouri Title and License (Form 108), a safety inspection not more than 60 days old, and an original or copy of a paid personal property tax receipt or a statement of non-assessment from the county of residence, or the City of St. Louis, for the previous year. That last paper is the one that sends people home while the 30-day clock keeps running, and no dealer can print it.
### The trailer, not the truck, decides the license
This is the rule that blindsides good crews, usually on a hot morning with mud drying on the trailer deck, because nobody at the sales desk brings it up. Federal rules put a single vehicle with a GVWR of 26,001 pounds or more in Group B. Group A is any combination with a gross combination weight rating of 26,001 pounds or more where the towed vehicle is rated over 10,000 pounds. A truck whose door-jamb rating sits under that line by itself feels safe.
Then the skid steer gets hitched. Say the truck is rated at 19,500 pounds and the equipment trailer at 12,000. The combination is rated 31,500 pounds, and the towed unit is over 10,000. That is Group A territory, and it is the door-jamb rating and the trailer’s plate that count, not what happened to be on the deck that day. The trailer and the truck are really one purchase, and the trailer’s plate is half the math.
The river matters too. The federal definition of a commercial motor vehicle covers a vehicle used on a highway in interstate commerce with a gross vehicle weight rating or gross combination weight rating of 10,001 pounds or more. A one-ton dually can be rated past that line while still looking like a pickup. Does the first Metro East job across the bridge make a shop an interstate carrier that has to register? That is a question for FMCSA, and the answer belongs in the glove box.
Old box truck rusting behind the shop since the new one came home? Here is what hauling it off really costs in St. Louis.
### When a bigger rig needs different plates
The first loaded run across the river feels like a promotion: the bridge deck humming under the tires, the trailer chains settling behind you, a bigger job waiting on the Illinois side. Growth sneaks up on the paperwork, though. MoDOT says you are required to have apportioned plates if you operate in two or more jurisdictions and your vehicle meets any one of several conditions: the power unit licensing weight is 26,001 pounds or heavier, the power unit has more than two axles regardless of licensed weight, or it runs in a combination of 26,001 pounds or heavier.
For a St. Louis contractor, “two or more jurisdictions” can mean nothing more exotic than Missouri and Illinois. The same combination that pushed the driver into Group A can push the truck into apportioned plates. Both lines belong in the trailer spec at the desk, before the deal is done.
### The bill that comes every year after
The sales tax is a one-time sting. Personal property tax is the one that comes back. In the City of St. Louis, the assessor says taxpayers with tangible property are mandated by state law to file a list of all taxable tangible personal property by April 1st of each year, and a 10% assessment penalty is added when the declaration comes in after April 1st. The declaration shows up in January, usually on a day when the truck is cold enough that the diesel needs a minute before it stops knocking.
The first January 1 the truck is yours, it goes on the declaration. Pay the bill, and file the receipt where you can find it, because Missouri asks for the previous year’s paid receipt when you title the next vehicle. The step-by-step for getting that paper, or a waiver when you owe nothing, is in the St. Louis personal property tax receipt and waiver guide. County residents can see how their side works in St. Louis County personal property tax.
### Why the sticker is not the truck price
A lot of work trucks leave the factory unfinished. A chassis cab is a frame, a cab and a drivetrain, and whatever rides on the back, a service body, a dump, a flatbed, a stake bed, gets built on afterward by a body company. That is a second invoice and a second calendar, and it is where budgets break. You stand in a body shop that smells like welding smoke and fresh primer and realize the truck you bought last month still can’t carry a single tool.
So pick the body before you order the chassis. The cab-to-axle length has to fit it, and anything that runs on hydraulics, a dump bed or a liftgate, is cheaper planned at the build than bolted on later. Then watch the payload, not the towing number on the brochure. A steel service body, a ladder rack, a compressor and a full parts bin eat payload fast, and an impressive towing figure means little if the truck is already heavy before it leaves the yard. Ask the dealer and the body company for the finished weight in writing, and hold it up against the door-jamb rating you wrote down at the desk.
### Used, new or one more year on the old one
A used truck keeps cash in the business and spends reliability. A new one spends cash and buys a build that fits the work. Either way, the smell of a truck tells you something the listing won’t: burnt coolant, hot clutch, fresh undercoating sprayed over rust. Ask for the maintenance file and the last inspection, and walk away from a seller who can’t produce either. The full walk-around is in what to check when buying a used truck in St. Louis, and what keeping one running costs is in what truck repair really costs in St. Louis.
If the old truck is past saving, don’t let it sit and collect a personal property bill of its own. Find junk removal in the metro and get it off the lot and off your books. ### Q. What’s the best place to buy a truck?
A.  For a work truck, the dealer’s commercial or fleet desk, not the retail showroom, because that desk orders chassis and works with body companies. Bring your door-jamb GVWR target and your heaviest trailer, and ask whether the rating lands over 8,500 pounds, the line Missouri’s St. Louis-area emissions rule uses for its GVWR exemption. ### Q. How much is a $70,000 truck payment?
A.  At an illustrative 7 percent over 60 months, about $1,386 a month, with roughly $13,165 in interest over the loan. Stretch it to 72 months and the payment drops to about $1,193, but the interest climbs to about $15,927. In Missouri, budget the sales tax separately: 4.225 percent state plus your local rate, due within 30 days. Then budget the yearly personal property bill, assessed at thirty-three and one-third percent of the truck’s value, from the first January 1 you own it.
### Q. How many miles is too much for a used truck?
A.  Mileage is the wrong gauge on a work truck. A gas half-ton and a diesel chassis cab age on different curves, and idle hours on a service truck can do more harm than road miles. Ask for engine hours, the maintenance file and the last inspection, and read the odometer last.
### Q. Which state is cheaper to buy a truck?
A.  For a St. Louis business it is mostly not a choice. Missouri’s Department of Revenue titles the truck and collects state sales tax of 4.225 percent plus your local sales tax, and Missouri assessors tax personal property at thirty-three and one-third percent of true value each year. Price the truck where you shop, then price the tax where you live.
### Q. What should you never reveal to the dealer when negotiating?
A.  Your monthly payment target, and how badly you need the truck by next week. Negotiate the price of the truck first, then the trade, then the financing, one at a time. A payment number lets the deal stretch the term until the math works for the lot, not for you. And walk in with your Missouri paper stack already built, so the 30-day title clock is never part of the pressure.

## Your Estimate Promised a Lifetime Warranty. AI Wrote It.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-staff-is-already-using-ai-shadow-ai-st-louis
“I just had the app clean it up a little.”
That is what your office manager says when you walk the estimate back to her desk. It is a plumbing estimate for a sewer lateral under a brick two-family, two pages, still warm from the printer, and it reads better than anything that has left the shop in years. Except the customer just called asking about the lifetime labor warranty in the second paragraph. You have never offered a lifetime labor warranty in your life. You can feel the heat climb up the back of your neck while the printer ticks as it cools.
She is not hiding anything. She is a little proud of it, honestly. The phones were ringing, the customer was waiting, and a two-hour estimate took twenty minutes. Nobody ever told her there was a line, much less where it sits. That is the real problem in this story, and it is not her. It is the rule nobody wrote down.
She is also far from alone. In the Work Trend Index from Microsoft and LinkedIn, 78% of AI users said they bring their own AI tools to work, and the share was even higher at small and medium-sized companies, at 80%. And 52% of people who use AI at work said they are reluctant to admit using it for their most important tasks. Read those two numbers together and you get the shape of every small office in town: the tool is already in the building, and nobody is saying so out loud.
Here is the part the national articles skip. St. Louis City Hall and the St. Louis Housing Authority have both put this line in writing. City Hall’s IT agency told City employees, in its guidance on generative AI, to review content and validate information before relying on or publishing it. The second one went further, and it reads like it was written for a small office. The St. Louis Housing Authority posted an AI acceptable use policy on its website, and the lines that matter are blunt. Employees may only use a work account, not a personal account, with a license assigned by its IT department. Its list of prohibited uses includes entering confidential or personal information into a prompt for any AI tool, regardless of any incognito or privacy function that the tool promotes. And everything created or informed by AI must be reviewed and validated by the person who used it. Further down that same list of prohibited uses: copying and pasting AI-generated reports or correspondence without verifying facts. Sound familiar?
You do not need a policy as long as a public agency’s. You need the same ideas on one sheet, taped inside the office door, and you can write it tonight at the kitchen table:
1. Say yes first. “AI is allowed here, and you will never get in trouble for telling me you used it.” Put that line on top. If half your people are reluctant to admit it, every rule below depends on making the truth cheap.
2. Work account, not personal. Pick one tool, put it on the business, and turn off model training in its settings. A personal login on someone’s phone is the door you cannot see through.
3. Name what never goes in. Customer names, addresses and phone numbers. Card and bank numbers. Employee records. Anything you signed a confidentiality agreement over. Private mode does not change the answer, which is exactly why the Housing Authority wrote that line the way it did.
4. A named person reads it before it leaves. Not “the office.” A name. Then one line in the job file: drafted with AI, read by whom. Four seconds, and the next phantom warranty never reaches a customer.
### Why is shadow AI a problem?
Because three things happen without anyone deciding they should: customer or employee information leaves the business through a personal account, a draft nobody checked reaches a paying customer, and nobody keeps a record of which work a machine touched. None of that means your staff is reckless. It is what busy people do when nobody has written down the line.
Take the three one at a time, because each has a different fix.
Information walks out the door. A spreadsheet of customer names and job totals pasted in to be “cleaned up.” A complaint email pasted whole, address and all, so the tool can write a calmer reply. On a personal account, that customer’s details now sit with a company you never signed an agreement with. The practical boundaries are laid out in our guide to what is safe to paste into ChatGPT for your business.
Unchecked drafts reach customers. This one costs money soonest. A generated draft sounds sure of itself whether it is right or wrong. It will invent a warranty, promise a lead time your crew has never hit, or quote a code section that has nothing to do with your county. A homeowner holding that promise in writing does not care which software typed it.
No record of what a machine touched. Months later a dispute lands on your desk and you want to know how a sentence got into a contract. Nobody remembers. The file looks like every other file in the cabinet. That is a bookkeeping gap, not a technology gap, and it is the one owners underestimate.
Rather write your one-page rule with other St. Louis owners in the room? The AI workshops for St. Louis business owners are built for that. Bring the one document your staff already runs through a chatbot, the estimate, the review reply, the follow-up email, and leave with a rule for it.
If you own the plumbing shop, the landscaping crew or the six-person office where this is already happening, your customers are asking AI who to call, too. See who AI names instead of you, then put a Gold listing in front of them for $357 a year, under a dollar a day, with a 7-day trial.
### What it looks like inside a six-person shop
In a small company it never looks like software. It looks like a phone face-up on the desk next to the coffee ring, a browser tab behind the scheduling screen, and somebody trying to get out the door before rush hour on the interstate. In practice:
A quote drafted in a free chatbot and lightly edited before it goes out.
An angry customer’s email pasted in whole so the tool can write a calmer answer.
A spreadsheet of names, addresses and job totals dropped in to be sorted or summarized.
Review replies and social posts generated in a batch from one rough prompt.
A lease or insurance certificate uploaded so somebody can ask what it actually says.
A stack of resumes pasted in with “rank these for me.” Hold that one; it matters across the river.
None of it needs an IT department or a company card. The barrier for a staff member is a login. The barrier for the company is a decision, a budget and a conversation. That gap is the whole story, and if you want the adoption numbers taken apart properly, they are in what percent of small businesses actually use AI.
### Can you actually tell which work was AI-assisted?
Not reliably, so stop planning around it. OpenAI built its own classifier to flag AI-written text, and in its own tests it correctly identified only 26% of AI-written text, while labeling human writing as AI-written 9% of the time. The company later pulled the tool due to its low rate of accuracy. If the people who built the model could not catch the model, a free detector website will not settle an argument in your office.
Worse, detectors miss in the direction that hurts. They flag plain, careful writing, which is exactly what your best employee turns in. Accusing her off a website score is a fast way to watch her clean out her desk.
The answer is disclosure, and it is cheap. A one-line note in the job file answers the question for good. The shops that get this right do not have better software. They are the ones where saying “I used the app on this” is as normal as saying “I called the supply house.” If training is the next step, read how to judge an AI course before you pay for one first.
### Across the river, the resume pile is a legal line
If anyone on your payroll works in Illinois, this part is not optional. Illinois amended its Human Rights Act so that an employer may not use artificial intelligence that has the effect of subjecting employees to discrimination on the basis of protected classes, in recruitment, hiring, promotion, discipline, discharge and the other terms of employment. The same amendment bars using zip codes as a proxy for protected classes, and it covers an employer that fails to provide notice to an employee that the employer is using AI for those purposes. It is already in effect.
Look at what that does to the resume pile. An office manager in a Fairview Heights branch who pastes applications into a chatbot and asks it to rank them has used AI in a hiring decision, whether or not the owner ever heard about it. The law looks at the effect, not the intent. That is why the never-paste list on your one page should name resumes and applications outright. If your service area crosses the river, and for most St. Louis metro businesses it does, write the rule to the stricter side. One rule is easier to run than two.
### The one-page policy, filled in
Go back to the four lines from the top and give each one your own words. The Housing Authority’s version is a useful model for the tone. IT must review each request for a tool, including whether the subscription level allows for opt-out of model training. Translate that for a shop: one approved tool, training off, and no customer gets a message no person read.
Then do the part most owners skip. At the next staff huddle, with the coffee still too hot to drink, ask who is already using what, and do not flinch at the answer. You will usually learn two or three people have been doing it for months, one of them is genuinely good at it, and nobody meant to hide anything. That person just became your trainer.
### What this looks like from the owner’s chair
In a small service business the crew is rarely the bottleneck. The office is. One person answers the phone, schedules, orders parts, chases the adjuster, writes the estimates and follows up on the quiet ones, and almost none of that is billable. The free estimate is the loss leader of the whole trade. So when the first hard freeze hits, the pipes in old brick basements start to split and the phone will not stop, the unpaid work is exactly where the chatbot shows up. Not because anyone chose AI. Because nobody is paid for that hour.
There is a second unpaid hour you never see: the customer who asked an AI assistant for a plumber and heard someone else’s name. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are examples of shadow AI?
A.  A quote drafted in a free chatbot on someone’s phone. A customer spreadsheet uploaded to be summarized. A meeting recording run through a transcription app nobody approved. Review replies generated in bulk. A contract uploaded so somebody can ask what it means. The common thread is a personal login, no invoice, and no record at the company.
### Q. Can employers tell if you have used AI?
A.  Not from the writing alone. OpenAI’s own classifier correctly flagged only 26% of AI-written text in its tests, and the company pulled it for its low rate of accuracy. An employer can see account activity on company equipment and on a company AI account, which is one more reason to move everyone onto a work account.
### Q. Can an employee refuse to use AI?
A.  It depends on the job and on the law, and edge cases like a disability accommodation, a union contract or a licensed professional duty are a question for an employment lawyer, not a blog. In practice, most refusals are about accuracy or credit. Hear them out before they turn into a discipline problem; the person refusing may be the one who catches the next phantom warranty.
### Q. Is IT acceptable to use AI in the workplace?
A.  Yes, inside limits your business writes down: a work account instead of a personal one, a never-paste list, and a named person who reads anything before it reaches a customer. The St. Louis Housing Authority’s own policy lets approved, trained employees use approved AI tools, on work accounts only, and says all content created or informed by AI must be reviewed and validated by the user. Without the limits, it is not the AI that creates the risk. It is the silence.
### Q. What is a good AI policy for a company?
A.  One page, in your own words, specific enough to use when the phone is ringing. It says AI is allowed and disclosure carries no penalty, names one approved work account, lists what may never be pasted, and names the person who reviews customer-facing output. A short page taped inside a cabinet door beats a long one nobody opens.
### Q. How do I create an AI policy for my company?
A.  Ask your staff what they already use, with amnesty attached. Write the never-paste list first, since it is short and does the most work. Name the reviewer. Add the one-line note in the job file. Read it aloud at a meeting, take objections, revise once. If you would rather build it with other owners, the AI workshops listed on St Louis Near Me Directory walk through exactly this.
### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?
A.  It is a rule of thumb that circulates online, not a research finding, and the versions people quote do not agree with each other. Treat any tidy AI percentage rule as somebody’s framework until you see the study. Our companion post on the AI rules people quote traces each one back to where it came from.
### Q. What can AI do for small business owners?
A.  It drafts and it summarizes: first-pass estimates, follow-up emails, review replies, plain-English versions of long documents. It does not know your prices, your suppliers or your crew’s schedule, and it will guess confidently about all of them. It also decides, more and more, which local business a customer hears about, which is why St Louis Near Me Directory exists. See AI for St. Louis and how local businesses can use it.
### Q. Are people losing jobs due to AI?
A.  In a small local shop, the honest answer is that tasks move first, not whole roles. First drafts, summaries and routine replies. Hands-on, licensed, on-site work is a different question, covered in what AI will not replace in a local service business.
