## 77% or Under 20%? What Share of Small Businesses Use AI
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-percent-of-small-businesses-use-ai
Seventy-seven percent. You hear it on a sales call while you sit parked between jobs, engine off, ladder rack ticking as it cools, a half-written estimate on the clipboard against the wheel: 77% of US businesses now use AI regularly, so you are already behind. The number is real. It comes from Intuit’s AI Impact Report, built on survey responses from more than 34,000 business owners.
Here is the number the caller left out. When the U.S. Census Bureau asks businesses directly, the national AI use rate comes back at 19.8%. For firms with four or fewer employees, it is less than 20%. Neither side lied. They asked different questions of different people, and only one of them sells AI features.
Now look at who that small-firm number describes in Missouri. The SBA Office of Advocacy’s latest state profile counts 590,131 small businesses here, 99.4 percent of all Missouri businesses, and they employ 44.4 percent of the state’s workers. In construction alone there are 69,794 small businesses, and 55,698 of them have no employees at all. One person. One truck. One phone that rings while they are up on a roof in the St. Louis heat. That is the business the “under 20%” line is about, and this state is full of them.
Intuit is upfront about the difference, if you read past the headline. Its 77% includes any kind of AI use, from free tools and built-in features to dedicated paid subscriptions. By that definition, a built-in feature you barely noticed in your bookkeeping app can count. That is a fair thing to measure. It is not the same as a business deciding to run on AI, and it should never be the number used to rush you into a contract.
### What percentage of businesses have adopted AI?
Roughly 18 to 20 percent, counted the way the government counts firms. The Federal Reserve Board’s note on monitoring AI adoption says Census business survey data show about 18 percent of firms had adopted AI at its latest reading, and the Census Bureau’s own later reading put the national rate at 19.8% for the period ending May 3. Small firms sit at or below that line. Bigger firms sit well above it.
Size is the whole story. The Census Bureau reports that 37% of firms with at least 250 employees used AI in their business operations, and 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees. Between December and May, AI use rose among firms with at least 20 employees but did not change significantly among firms with fewer than 20. The boom is real. It is happening above a headcount line that the one-truck contractor, the corner shop and the two-chair salon sit well below. Sector matters too: as of May 3, Information was at 39.7%, while Retail Trade, the shop counter itself, was around 14%.
### The line to say back to the next caller
Keep this one ready, because it ends most pitches in a sentence: “Is that 77% of businesses or of workers, and does it count free features?” Then listen to the pause. A seller who knows the answer will tell you. A seller who does not was reading a slide.
Behind that line sit five questions that work on any AI statistic. Who ran the survey, and do they sell AI? What exactly was asked? “Ever touched an AI feature” and “runs part of the business on AI” are different questions. Who counts as one: a firm, a worker, or a job? What date does it describe? Does the trend cross the Census question change? Most numbers fall apart or become useful by the third.
The “who counts as one” question swings results hardest, and the most careful middle figure has a St. Louis name on it. The Fed note uses three publicly available surveys. One is the Real-Time Population Survey from economists Bick, Blandin and Deming, which puts work-related generative AI use at about 41 percent of workers, and the note thanks Alexander Bick of the St. Louis Fed by name. Another, the Survey of Business Uncertainty, estimates that 78 percent of the labor force works at firms that have adopted AI. It is easy to hear that as most businesses. It is not. It is weighted by employment, so one big employer counts for thousands of workers. The Fed note puts it plainly: the biggest driver of variation likely relates to differences in sampling distributions and units of analysis.
Line the three up and nothing contradicts anything. Most firms have not adopted AI. A large minority of workers use it anyway. Most people work somewhere that has. The caller simply picked the one that makes you sound late.
If you want to test the tools instead of the statistics, St. Louis has made that cheap. OpenAI Academy, working with SCORE, ran an in-person ChatGPT workshop for St Louis-area small business owners on July 24, with hands-on time to build one simple, reusable solution for each business. And St. Louis County Library says anyone with a valid card is eligible for a scholarship and free access to Coursera and Grow with Google, through its partnership with TechSTL.
### Why the government’s own number jumped without anyone buying anything
In November, the Census Bureau broadened its question. It used to ask about AI used in “producing goods or services.” Now it asks about AI used “in any of its business functions.” Drafting an email with a chatbot went from not counting to counting overnight.
The Fed note measured what that one edit did. The gap between the new and old series ranged from 47 percent (10.6 percentage points) for professional services to 159 percent (7.5 percentage points) for manufacturing. Nothing was installed. No one signed a contract. The wording moved, and the chart moved with it. Any trend line that shows AI adoption “doubling” across that change is two different questions stapled together.
### What a state of one-truck businesses should take from this
Those Missouri counts change two things for an owner here. First, when someone tells you most businesses like yours already use AI, the federal data says otherwise for firms your size, and you can say so out loud without flinching. Second, the pressure on a two-person shop is lighter than the trade press implies, which buys you time to learn this properly instead of buying something quickly. The honest dollar ranges are in what AI actually costs a small business, and the rules of thumb people trade at the counter get tested in which AI rules hold up.
### What to do with the honest number this week
Start by saying it back. The next time someone opens a pitch with “everybody’s using AI now,” ask them which survey, what it asked, and whether it counted firms or workers. Watch the pause. It tells you more about the pitch than anything that follows it.
Then pick the one task in your week that you would happily never do again. The reorder email to the same supplier. The reply to the same three questions about hours and parking. The quote you rebuild from scratch every time. Write it on the back of a receipt and tape it by the register. That scrap of paper is worth more than any adoption statistic, because it turns a national argument into one small job you can actually test.
Time that task once, the old way. Try it with an assistant for a few weeks. Time it again. If the number drops, you have adopted AI in the only sense that pays. If it does not, you have lost nothing but a few evenings, and you can tell the next salesperson exactly why you are not buying.
Last, look at the other side of the counter. Your adoption rate is your business. Your customers’ adoption rate is your visibility, and the 41% worker figure says a lot of them are already asking these tools questions every week. Make sure the answer they get includes your door.
Enough percentages for one sitting. Go find a St. Louis salon and let somebody else hold the scissors for an hour.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many companies are actually using AI?
A.  Roughly 18 to 20 percent, counted as firms. The Census Bureau put the national rate at 19.8% for the period ending May 3, and less than 20% for firms with four or fewer employees. Vendor surveys that count any feature use, like Intuit’s 77%, answer a much easier question.
### Q. Is AI being adopted by small businesses?
A.  Yes, but slowly and from a low base. The Census Bureau found AI use rose among firms with at least 20 employees between December and May but did not change significantly among firms with fewer than 20. For most St. Louis shops, there is time to learn it properly instead of buying in a hurry.
### Q. What is the biggest user of AI?
A.  By sector, Information, at 39.7% as of May 3, followed by Finance and Insurance at 33.9%, per the Census Bureau. Retail Trade sat around 14%. By size, the largest firms lead: 37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI.
### Q. What is the failure rate of AI adoption projects?
A.  There is no reliable single rate. The figures that circulate come from different studies that define failure differently, and many count a project as failed simply because no one measured a baseline first. For a small business, the useful test is simpler: pick one task, time it now, and time it again after a few weeks with the tool.
### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?
A.  There isn’t a standard one. The phrase gets used online for several unrelated ideas, so treat any number-plus-rule slogan as marketing until someone shows you the study behind it. Run it through the same five questions you would use on any AI statistic.
### Q. Which 5 jobs will survive AI?

### Q. Who are the big 4 of AI?
A.  There is no official list, and it changes depending on who is writing it. Some lists group the consumer chatbots, some the cloud platforms, some the chipmakers. For a small shop the question barely matters. The practical choice is which tool handles one repeating task, at what monthly cost, and what happens to your customers’ data.

## St. Louis Owners: Google's Free AI Is Naming Someone
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/google-ai-mode-explained-for-local-business
The water heater quit at suppertime. The basement smells like rust and wet concrete, the floor drain is gurgling, and a homeowner in south county is standing on the cold bottom step with her phone. She doesn’t type “plumber.” She types the whole sentence: who can look at a water heater tonight, near me, and won’t charge just to show up.
Across the county a plumber is wiping his hands on a rag at the end of a late call, phone face-down on the truck seat. He does good work. He has no idea that question was just asked, and Google’s AI Mode is about to answer it with somebody’s name. Whoever gets named gets the call. He never hears it ring somewhere else.
### Is Google AI mode free?
Yes. AI Mode is built into Google Search, and when it rolled out to everyone TechRadar called it Google’s new free AI search tool. Google’s help page lists three ways in: go to google.com/ai, ask a question on www.google.com and tap AI Mode, or tap AI Mode on the Google app home screen. For the business being described, Google says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary. Anyone who calls to sell you a way in is selling around that sentence.
So what does it do with that sentence from the basement step? Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a “query fan-out” technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources, then returning a comprehensive AI-powered response with links to supporting websites. One tired question becomes a handful of searches the plumber never sees. The answer is stitched together from whatever exists about him in public, and in St. Louis, “where” is the part that breaks.
### Google gives you 20 places. St. Louis has more than that before you leave the city.
Google’s own Business Profile help says you can set up to 20 service areas based on the cities, postal codes, or other areas you serve. Twenty. The City of St. Louis says it has 79 different neighborhoods, each with its own distinctive style and characteristics, and that count stops at the city line. Since 1876, when voters decided whether the City of St. Louis should separate from the county and become an independent city, as the St. Louis County Library tells it, “St. Louis” has meant two different governments and dozens of towns. Your customers don’t ask for a radius. They say Bevo Mill, Carondelet, Dutchtown, The Hill, south county. If nothing public ties your name to the place they say, the fan-out has nothing to grab.
That is the leverage point, and it isn’t your fault. The tools were built for a map with a pin in it. St. Louis talks in neighborhoods.
### The fifteen-minute check, tonight
Do this at the kitchen table after the last call, with a pen and the back of an invoice. First, open AI Mode and type the sentence your customer would really type, with the neighborhood in it: “who fixes a furnace that’s short-cycling in Dutchtown,” “who can rewire a two-family in Carondelet.” Second, write down every business it names and what it says about each one. Third, run the same search with the Web filter, so you see the plain links beside the written answer. Fourth, circle what is wrong or missing about you: old hours, a service you dropped, a neighborhood you drive to every week that appears nowhere next to your name.
Then fix it where you control it, in this order. In your Google Business Profile, open the service-area setting and spend your 20 slots on the neighborhoods and towns that actually pay you, then correct the hours. On your website, put those same place names in plain sentences on the page about each service, the way a customer would say them. Then give the neighborhoods that didn’t fit a page of their own: one service-area page per cluster you work, south side, south county, the central corridor, with each neighborhood named in a plain sentence about the job you do there. That is the whole job, and the sting of the first search is what makes owners finally do it.
### Can anyone sell you a spot inside the answer?
You know the call. It comes in while you’re under a sink or up a ladder, and the voicemail is waiting when you climb down, the voice warm and in a hurry. Your business is “missing from Google’s AI,” and for a monthly fee they can fix it. The voice sounds like it knows something you don’t. That is the whole trick.
Here is what Google itself says to site owners: there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary. So the pitch is one of three things wearing a costume: an ad account with a markup, ordinary marketing work described in spooky language, or nothing at all. You are not behind. You are being sold a fear, and the fear is the product.
Three questions end that call in under a minute. Ask what the Google product is called, and if they can’t name it, there isn’t one. Ask whether you’re paying them or paying Google, and listen to how long the pause runs. Then ask what happens the month you stop paying. If the answer is that you vanish, they are describing advertising, not visibility, and advertising is something you can buy yourself without a middleman taking a cut.
Notice how that call is built. It doesn’t ask about your work. It doesn’t care that you showed up on time to forty jobs last month or that half your customers came from a neighbor’s recommendation. It lands on the one thing you can’t see from the cab of the truck, the answer on somebody else’s phone, and it charges you rent on the not-knowing. The fifteen-minute check takes that leverage away. Once you have looked with your own eyes, nobody can sell you a fog.
None of that makes all marketing help a scam. It means the specific promise, a paid seat inside the written answer, runs straight into Google’s own line that there are no additional requirements to appear, and the voice on the voicemail either knows that or never checked.

## AI Got Your Business Wrong? You Can’t Edit the Answer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-ai-says-about-your-business-and-how-to-fix-it
The truck is still running in the supply-house lot, heater blowing on the windshield, a cold coffee sweating in the cup holder. Between the second call and the third, the owner of a two-van heating and cooling shop types his own company name into a chatbot, just to see. The answer scrolls up clean and confident. It has the Saturday hours wrong. It lists a phone number that rang at the old shop. And it calls him a heating company “in St. Louis County,” when his shop has sat inside the city limits the whole time.
That last one is the most St. Louis mistake a machine can make, and it’s the one that tells you where all the others come from. According to the St. Louis County Library, voters in 1876 decided whether the City of St. Louis should separate from the county and become an independent city. The split stuck, and the county got a newly built courthouse of its own. A century and a half later, a listing that only says “St. Louis, MO” still doesn’t say which St. Louis it means, and a chatbot stitching an answer together will guess.
Guessing is the whole problem. The answer didn’t come from someone who knows the shop. It was assembled from scraps scattered across the web: an old chamber page, a directory nobody updated, a profile Google tidied up on its own. Fix the scraps and the answer follows. You’re not doing anything wrong. The machine is reading old paper.
### How to correct incorrect AI information?
You can’t edit the answer. You fix the sources the answer is built from, then wait for the assistants to read them again. That means your own website first, then your Google Business Profile, then Bing and the directories where you already appear, then the old records nobody remembers making.
Here’s the fifteen-minute version you can do from the truck before the next call. Write down, on one sheet, the truth: your name exactly as it’s painted on the van, one phone number, your street address, your real hours including Saturday, the services that pay the bills today, and the neighborhoods and towns you actually drive to. If you’re in the city, write “City of St. Louis.” If you’re in the county, write the town. Then ask ChatGPT, Google and Microsoft Copilot the same few questions a customer would ask: what is this business, what are its hours, what’s the phone number, does it do the service you most want to sell, and is it still open. Screenshot each answer with the date showing. Write down every source each assistant cites. Those citations are your map, and the wrong fact is almost always sitting on one of them.
Google does give you a feedback button. Its Search help says that if you found an AI Overview inaccurate you can click Report a problem and choose a category. Use it. Just know that it is feedback, not a work order. The same help page says it straight: AI Overviews can and will make mistakes.
### Why does AI give incorrect information?
Because the answer is assembled, not looked up. An assistant pulls fragments from a search index and from listings, then writes smooth sentences over the top. If your hours are stale in one place and right in another, nothing in that process knows which one is current. It picks. The confident tone tells you nothing about whether the fact is true, the same way a clean invoice tells you nothing about whether the furnace was actually fixed.
The failure rate is real. The BBC reported on the largest study of its kind, coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union: 45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue, and 20% contained major accuracy issues, including hallucinated details and outdated information. That study was about news, not about whether a furnace company works Saturdays, so don’t treat 45% as your number. Treat it as proof that the wrong answer about your shop is a pattern in the machine, not bad luck and not your fault.
### Where the wrong answers come from
Go back to that truck cab and look at what’s riding on the dash: old invoices, a business card from the first shop, a magnet with a number you haven’t used in years. The internet keeps the same pile, and the assistants read all of it.
A Business Profile that changed without you. Google says that if it receives reports that your business info isn’t accurate, it might update your profile, and you’ll find an alert in the Edit profile section. Most owners never open that screen after the day they claimed the listing. Go look. A change Google made on someone else’s report is a wrong answer with a very respectable source behind it.
The ghost at the old address. You moved from one building to another and the old record stayed live. Now there are two of you, and an assistant will merge them, average them, or just pick one. Same thing when a shop changes hands and the previous owner’s profile never got closed.
The vague city line. Every listing that says only “St. Louis” leaves the city-or-county question open. If the city shop above is ever going to stop being filed in the county, the words “City of St. Louis” have to appear somewhere the machine reads.
Old pages nobody maintains. A sponsor page from a 5K, a supplier’s dealer locator, a chamber PDF. They sit for years, get read, and hand a machine your old number.
Reviews about a shop you used to run. Reviewers write about the visit they had. An assistant summarizes what they wrote, even when the policy they complained about is long gone.
Fixed what it says, and it still names the other guy? That’s a different machine at work. Here’s how AI decides which local businesses to name.
### The questions to ask every assistant, word for word
Use the same questions every time, so next quarter’s check lines up with this one. Fill in your own details:
What is [business name] in [your neighborhood or town]? Does it know you exist, and does it put you in the city or the county correctly?
What are [business name]’s hours? The costliest one to get wrong, because the customer who reads “closed” never calls.
What’s the phone number and address for [business name]? Watch for the old suite, the retired tracking number, the old shop.
Does [business name] do [your best-paying service]? Assistants often describe you by what you led with years ago.
What areas does [business name] serve? Especially across the river, where Missouri and Illinois get blurred.
Who are the best [your trade] near [your neighborhood]? Not checking facts here. Checking whether you’re named at all.
Is [business name] still open? This one catches the ghosts.
### What you can get corrected, and how long it takes
Some of these are levers. Some are walls. Know which before you spend a Saturday on them.
Your own website: total control, minutes. Put the name, address, phone, hours, services and the neighborhoods you serve in plain text on a page, not baked into a picture. If you’re a city shop, say City of St. Louis in words.
Your Google Business Profile: strong control, minutes to weeks. Google says edits usually take up to 10 minutes to review, but sometimes it can take up to 30 days. The mechanics of a complete profile are in our guide to optimizing your Google Business Profile.
A record you don’t own: partial control. For the ghost at the old address, Google Maps lets you select Suggest an edit, then Place closed or not here, and mark it permanently closed, a duplicate of another place, or moved to a new location. Your suggestion goes to Google as feedback, so check back on it.
Bing: free, and most owners skip it. Bing says Bing Places for Business is a free online platform where businesses can create and manage their listings to appear in Bing search results and Bing Maps. If you care what Microsoft’s assistant says about you, start there.
Old pages and reviews: you can ask, and you can reply. Email the webmaster of the stale page. Reply to the review that describes something you have since changed, and say what changed. The reply is text, and text gets read.
The AI answer itself: no form, no promised timeline. Don’t take anyone’s word for how fast a fix shows up in a given assistant. Re-run your questions at 30 days and 90 days and keep the screenshots side by side.
### Fix things in this order, because the wrong order wastes weeks
Write the one-sheet truth first. Everything else gets copied from it, word for word.
Fix your own website. It’s yours and it’s instant.
Kill the ghosts before you polish the real profile. Old locations and duplicates keep voting against you while you work.
Then your Google Business Profile. Hours, categories, services, service area, and any change Google made on its own.
Then Bing Places and the directories where you already appear. Start with the ones the assistants cited.
Then the stragglers and the reviews. Emails and replies. Don’t let a slow webmaster stall the rest.
Re-run the same questions at 30 and 90 days. Same assistants, same words.
The phone that doesn’t ring on a Saturday marked closed doesn’t leave a missed call. The day just looks slow, and you blame the weather. That’s why the hours line goes to the top of the sheet. If you’d rather work through this with your own business on the screen and other owners at the table, the AI workshops are built for it. For the bigger picture, start with AI for St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I trust Google AI mode?
A.  Treat it as a fast first draft, not a record. Google’s own Search help says AI Overviews can and will make mistakes, and tells you to check important info in more than one place. For anything about your own business, check it against your Business Profile and your website. The real risk isn’t an insult. It’s a confident wrong answer about your hours.
### Q. Can AI Search be trusted?
A.  For a quick summary, mostly. For a fact you’ll act on, check it. In the European Broadcasting Union study the BBC reported, 45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue. That research looked at news, not local listings, but the cause is the same: answers stitched from sources that disagree.
### Q. Is Google AI as good as ChatGPT?

### Q. What should I do if an AI gives me a wrong answer?
A.  Screenshot it with the date and the question showing, and note every source it cited. Then fix those sources instead of arguing with the assistant. In Google, Report a problem on an AI Overview sends feedback. It is not a correction ticket. Re-ask the same question a month later, and again a few months after that, and keep the before and after together.
### Q. How to correct business information on Google?
A.  Sign in to the Google Account that manages your Business Profile, open Edit profile, change the field and save. Google says edits usually take up to 10 minutes to review, but sometimes up to 30 days. While you’re there, look for alerts about changes Google made from outside reports, and correct any that are wrong.
### Q. How to correct incorrect information on Google?
A.  It depends who owns the record. Your own profile, you edit directly. A wrong fact on someone else’s website has to be fixed by that website. A complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory gives the machines one more correct source to read.
### Q. How much does it cost to amend your business name?
A.  Updating the name on your own listings is an edit, not a filing. ## St. Louis City Hall Told Staff Not to Paste This in ChatGPT
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/can-i-use-chatgpt-for-my-business
The dome light is the only thing lit on the block. You came down off a tear-off at dusk, the grit is still packed into the creases of your hands, and the homeowner in the red-brick bungalow, one of a whole row of them on her block, wants your estimate tonight, before she calls the next roofer on her list. So you open ChatGPT on your phone. You thumb in her name, her street, the square count and your price, and twenty seconds later it hands back a proposal cleaner than anything you have ever typed with one thumb in a truck cab.
Then the cold little question shows up on the drive home, the one that sits low in your stomach at the red light: where did her address just go?
St. Louis City Hall answered that for its own people before most contractors ever thought to ask. When the City’s Information Technology Services Agency wrote its guidance on generative AI for City employees, issued by the City’s Chief Technology Officer and the agency’s director, it named ChatGPT outright, and its rule on sensitive information is one sentence long: do not utilize, upload, or include sensitive, confidential, or personally identifiable information when using these systems. Another rule says that if you log on with your City email, do NOT use your City password. A third says to review content and validate information before relying on it or publishing it.
Read that again, because it is not a ban. The City did not tell its workers to put the phone down. It told them what stays out of the box and who checks the output. A roofer, a plumber or a one-truck painter can run the exact same rule tonight, at the kitchen table or in the cab, and keep the twenty-second proposal. Here it is as four moves you can make before you hit send.
1. Paste the job, not the person. The tool does not need her name or her street to write the scope. “Customer A, brick bungalow, two layers to tear off, 24 squares, architectural shingle” writes the same proposal. Type her name back in yourself, in the email, after the draft is done.
2. Flip one switch, once. In ChatGPT, open Settings, select Data controls, and turn off Improve the model for everyone. OpenAI says it uses data from ChatGPT and its other services for individuals to train its models, and that you control whether your chats are used to improve them. That switch is the control.
3. Read every number before it leaves the cab. The draft sounds sure of itself whether it is right or wrong. Check the price, the square count, the warranty line and any date it promises. If you would not sign it on her porch, do not send it from the truck.
4. Give the chatbot its own password. Same idea as the City’s rule. If that account ever gets cracked, the login should not also open your email, your bank or your supply-house account.
That is most of it. The rest of this page is the why behind each move, and what to do if a customer’s file already went in. If it did, the Missouri law to know is the state’s breach-notice statute, RSMo 407.1500, and it has a five-year paperwork rule most owners have never heard of.
### What happens if I put confidential information into ChatGPT?
On a personal ChatGPT account, OpenAI says it uses data from its services for individuals to train its models unless you switch that off. No stranger can search your chat, and no alarm goes off. But your customer’s details now sit with a company you never signed an agreement with. Business plans work differently: OpenAI says that by default, it does not use your business data for training its models.
So the damage is almost never the movie version, where your customer list pops out on a competitor’s screen. It is quieter. It is the email that comes back three weeks later asking why her insurance claim number was in a draft you sent, and the hot flush in your face while you try to remember what you pasted and where. It is a confidentiality line in a general contractor’s sub agreement that you broke without noticing. It is not being able to say, with a straight face, what happened to someone’s file. And if that file held a Missourian’s personal information and it turns into a breach, the state’s statute decides who you notify, which a section further down spells out.
If you need to paste something touchy just once, Temporary Chat is the narrower door. OpenAI says a temporary chat won’t appear in your history, create memories, or help improve its models. Narrower is not closed. The City’s rule still wins: personal information stays out.
### The plan you pay for is not the private plan
This is where good operators get tripped up, and it is not their fault. The receipt in your inbox says Plus, so it feels like a business tool. It isn’t, as far as your data goes. OpenAI files ChatGPT under services for individuals, and it says it uses data from those services to train its models. Your chats can help train it until you turn that off. Paying more buys a better model. It does not change who is allowed to learn from what you typed.
The line moves when the account is a business account. OpenAI says data from ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise and its API platform isn’t used for training its models by default. One catch owners should know before they move the crew over: in ChatGPT Business, OpenAI says workspace admins can view, access, export, and delete end user conversations in the workspace. That cuts both ways. You can check what went out the door, and your people should know you can. Google draws its line in plainer words than anyone. Its Gemini privacy page tells users that if the Keep Activity setting is on, don’t enter data that’s confidential or that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see.
Think about the office manager at a two-truck HVAC shop in a hot week, the phone ringing off the wall, pasting a service history into whatever app is already open. She is not being careless. She is being fast, on a tool nobody set up for her. The fix is a setting and a sentence, not a scolding, and our companion page on staff already using AI without the owner knowing walks through the one-page rule that keeps it from happening again.
### What is safe to paste? Most of your week
Almost everything that wears you out at night, the stuff you squint at under the kitchen light while the dishwasher hums, is safe. Your own marketing copy. Your public prices. The text on your website. A job posting with no names in it. A warranty letter template. A review reply where you leave the reviewer’s name out. A blurry photo of a manufacturer’s install sheet you want in plain English. If you would be fine seeing it taped to the counter at the supply house, it can go in.
And the redaction trick from move one frees up most of the rest. A collections letter does not need the customer’s name to sound firm and polite. A scope does not need the house number. Paste the shape of the problem, keep the identity on your side of the glass, and you get the same output with nothing at stake.
Totally off-topic, but if the breaker panel in your own basement is buzzing while you read this, call an electrician before you call it a night.
### What should never go into a consumer chatbot?
Six kinds of paper stay out of a personal account, switch or no switch, because each one carries a promise that lives with you, not with the software company.
Customer personal data. A name next to an address, phone number or account number. A route list. A spreadsheet of past jobs.
Employee records. Social Security numbers, tax forms, background checks, medical notes, write-ups with a real name on them.
Anything you promised to keep quiet. An NDA, a client contract, or a general contractor’s sub terms. The promise follows the document into the chat box.
Health information. Injury reports, treatment notes, insurance claim files.
Money credentials. Card numbers, bank and routing numbers, a screenshot of your processor dashboard.
Bids you haven’t submitted. The number you are about to hand a general contractor is confidential today and public next month, and the gap is exactly when it matters.
The short version for the sun visor: no names, no numbers that point to a person, no health, no money logins, nothing somebody else made you promise to protect.
### Somebody already pasted it. Now what?
Breathe first. Then write it down before you delete anything, because every call you make next depends on knowing what actually went in.
Write down what went in. Which file or text, roughly when, from whose account, personal or business.
Turn training off on that account now. It only covers new conversations, but it stops the next one.
Call before you decide. Your attorney or your cyber insurance carrier. Calling early does not commit you to filing anything.
Check your customer contracts. A notice clause in an agreement can run on a shorter clock than any statute.
Tell your people where the line is. If nobody ever drew it, nobody crossed it on purpose.
If it does turn out to be a breach of personal information, Missouri’s law is RSMo 407.1500. Notice to affected consumers has to be made without unreasonable delay. If you notify more than one thousand consumers at one time, you also notify the attorney general’s office and the consumer reporting agencies. And if, after an investigation, you decide notice isn’t required, that determination has to be documented in writing and kept for five years. Whether a paste into a chatbot counts as a breach turns on the facts, and this page can’t settle that for you. What it can tell you: start the paper trail the same night, at the same kitchen table.
### Health, legal and money files play by stricter rules
Think of the clipboard of intake forms on a chiropractor’s front desk in the county, or the accordion folder of W-2s on a tax preparer’s floor in February. A chiropractor, a tax preparer, a title office, a home health agency: each already lives under rules about what a vendor must sign before it touches a file. For health records, that paper is a Business Associate Agreement. OpenAI says it is able to sign BAAs for its API platform. The personal app on your phone is a different product, so never assume a chat window is covered because the company behind it signs agreements somewhere else. This isn’t legal advice. It is the question to put to your own counsel before a patient’s name ever goes near a prompt.

Nobody pays you for the estimate. The roof is billable; the paperwork is not. The scope, the follow-up, the review reply, the third nudge on an unpaid invoice all get done after dark, at a kitchen table that doubles as the office, by someone who has already worked a full day. That unpaid hour is exactly where AI moved in first, and it should. Getting your night back is the point.
But there is a second unpaid hour that no chatbot fixes. It is the hour you never see: the homeowner who searched for a roofer, or asked ChatGPT who to call, and got somebody else’s name. ## How AI Picks Local Businesses: It Matches Neighborhoods
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-ai-decides-which-local-businesses-to-name
Who did the AI name instead of you?
Not on some marketing chart. In a basement. Cold water creeping across the concrete toward the furnace, a phone glowing in one wet hand, and a person typing a whole sentence the way they would text a friend: plumber who can come tonight, Bevo Mill. Three names come back. Short reasons beside each one. No list of ten, no page two, nothing to scroll. The plumber who answered that call is already backing a van into the alley, and the one who wasn’t named will never know the call existed.
Here is the part nobody selling “AI visibility” over the phone will tell you. Google says its AI Mode uses a query fan-out technique, breaking down your question into subtopics and issuing a multitude of queries simultaneously. So that one wet-handed sentence quietly becomes a fan of searches, and one of them is almost certainly about the place: Bevo Mill. The answer gets built from whatever those searches find.
Now look at the line on your van door, your website footer and your Google profile. If it says “Serving Greater St. Louis,” you have plenty of company. It’s the line every sign shop and web template in this town hands out, and it made sense back when a phone book and a yard sign were the whole game. But the City of St. Louis says it has 79 different neighborhoods. Carondelet. Dutchtown. Tower Grove South. The Hill. Not one of those words is on your van door. A search for Bevo Mill has nothing to grab.
That is the leverage point of this whole page, and it costs you an evening at the kitchen table, not a contract. You’re not broken. You’re just written in a language the new machine can’t match.
### How do you get AI to recommend your business?
You can’t buy the sentence, and there is no form to submit. An assistant splits the customer’s question into many smaller searches and names the businesses those searches can find and confirm. So the work is plain: put the exact neighborhoods and towns you drive to, the hours you keep and the jobs you take into words, and make your name, phone and address match everywhere you already appear.
Do it tonight, in this order, with coffee and a legal pad. First, write down the neighborhoods and towns your trucks actually reach in a normal week, by name, the way a customer would type them. Not a radius. Names. Second, put that list in plain text on your website’s service page, as a sentence, not baked into a map image, because a map graphic gives a search nothing to read. Third, open your Google Business Profile and check that the phone number, hours and service area match that same page, character for character. Fourth, write one sentence about the job you take that the shop down the road doesn’t, and one about the job you turn down. Fifth, ask whoever built your website to confirm the robots.txt file is not blocking OAI-SearchBot, which OpenAI says is used to surface websites in search results in ChatGPT’s search features.
Five steps. None of them is a subscription. Google says it plainly: there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary. The fix is the words.
### Why the neighborhood name decides who gets the call
Think about how a St. Louisan actually talks. Nobody in a flooded basement says “metropolitan statistical area.” They say the neighborhood, the parish, the street they grew up on. That is what they type, too, now that they type full sentences. And each of those little fanned-out searches looks for a page that says the same words back.
Here is the honest line between what is published and what is inferred. Google has described the fan-out in its own announcement of AI Mode. It has not published a rule that says “the business that names the neighborhood wins.” Nobody has. But follow the mechanism. If a sub-search is about Bevo Mill and your pages never say Bevo Mill, you are relying on the machine to guess that “Greater St. Louis” includes it. Meanwhile the shop whose service page lists the south city neighborhoods it covers, one after another, has handed the machine the exact words. When an answer only has room for three names, the guess loses to the match.
It is the same instinct you already trust. When a neighbor asks you for a roofer, you don’t say “somebody in the area.” You say the guy who did the house on your block. Specific beats general, with people and now with machines.
### Where an assembled answer finds your business
Not from memory. From pages it fetches while the customer waits, that hum of a phone thinking in a quiet basement. Your own website. Your Google Business Profile. Directory and listing pages. Review sites. The chamber roster, the supplier’s dealer locator, the parish bulletin with your ad in the back. The answer is stitched across all of them, which is why the same details need to say the same thing in every one.
OpenAI uses separate robots.txt tags, OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot, for separate jobs. It says each setting is independent of the others, so a site can allow OAI-SearchBot in order to appear in search results while disallowing GPTBot, the one tied to training. Plenty of web templates and security plugins block bots in bulk. If yours blocks the search one, you have opted out of being named in ChatGPT search without ever deciding to. That is a ninety-second check, and it’s worth more than any monthly “AI package.” For the wide view of what AI does and doesn’t do for a local shop, the overview of AI for St. Louis businesses covers the ground floor.
### Why one mismatched phone number can cost you the slot
Look at the dash of any work truck: the clipboard, the gas receipts, the old magnetic sign in the back with a phone number from two vans ago. That old number is still alive somewhere online, on a listing nobody remembers making. So is the suite number from the last shop, and the business name written three ways, with LLC, without it, and with an ampersand.
This part is inference, and it deserves those words. An answer assembled from five sources has to decide those sources describe the same business. Five that match make that easy. Two that contradict make your name the expensive one to include, and an expensive name is the easy one to cut down to three. Pick one exact name, one phone number, one address format. Close the old listing instead of leaving it to rot. If a staff member drafts copy with an assistant, check the service area against what the crew really covers, because most owners have no idea which parts of their own copy are AI-assisted.

## $60,000 or One Morning: How to Judge an AI Course
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-judge-an-ai-course-for-business-owners
$60,000. That is the estimated tuition Washington University’s Olin Business School lists for its one-year Master’s in AI for Business. It is a real degree, built for people changing careers, and it is priced like one.
Now put that number next to a different St. Louis morning. OpenAI Academy, working with SCORE, ran an in-person workshop called ChatGPT for small businesses for St Louis-area owners on July 24. It started with breakfast at 9:30 AM, wrapped at 1:00 PM, asked people to bring a laptop or tablet, and spent its last stretch on hands-on time to build one simple, reusable solution for each business. Attendees walked out with 3 months of ChatGPT Plus.
Between those two prices sits every course that will find you on your phone this year. The countdown clock. The wall of logos. The price slashed for the next few minutes only. You read it in the truck with the engine off, the last job’s invoice still clipped to the visor and the cab going stale with coffee, and the only thing you want to know is whether this is training or a sales funnel with a video player bolted on.
Here is the leverage point most of those pages hope you miss. What pays you back is not AI knowledge. It is one working thing built on your own business: the estimate follow-up that writes itself in your voice, the callback script, the answer to the question customers ask you five times a week. A course that ends with that thing is worth paying for. A course that ends with “clarity” is not, at any price.
### Is there an AI course that will help my business?
Yes, if it passes three tests, and you can run all three before you pay a cent. Does it use your business as the working example? Do you leave with something built and running? Does the teacher use these tools on their own work every week? Fail any one and you are buying entertainment.
Test one: your business is the example. A course built around a made-up online store teaches you a made-up online store. You run a one-truck roofing outfit, or an HVAC crew that lives in attics from June to September, and the gap between the demo and your day is the whole problem. So write down the single task that eats the most of your week and bores you most. Quoting. Callbacks. The same long email you retype for every new customer. Send that sentence to the provider and ask them to show you, on a call, how their training would handle it. A good one asks three questions about how your jobs actually run before touching a keyboard. A weak one changes the subject to a feature list.
Test two: you leave with something running. Ask it in exactly this shape: what will I have built by the time this ends? Real training answers small and concrete, the way the St. Louis OpenAI and SCORE session did, with one reusable tool per business. A lead magnet answers with a roadmap, a framework, a mindset. You cannot save a mindset to your phone, and you cannot hand it to whoever answers your calls.
Test three: the teacher has been burned by it. Ask what they used AI for last week in their own work, and what went wrong. Anyone who works with these tools for real has a story ready: the confident wrong number, the summary that dropped the one line that mattered, the invented fact. An instructor with no failure story has not done enough of the work to teach it, because half of using AI well is knowing where it lies to you.
Put all three questions in an email, not a phone call, so the answers sit in writing where you can reread them at the kitchen table that night. A provider who will not answer in writing has answered.

### The red flags that should end the call
Five things, and each one is a signal about the seller rather than about AI, which is why they work even if you know nothing about the subject. A guaranteed result. A promised revenue number. Secret or “proprietary” prompts. A no-charge session whose only real content is the pitch for the paid one. Any hint of official certification or government backing.
The guarantee is the loudest. Nobody can promise what a tool will do inside your business, because the outcome rides on your margins, your crew, your customers and your follow-through. A clear refund policy is a good sign. A guaranteed outcome is a bad one, and they are not the same thing.
The secret prompt vault is the most durable nonsense in this market. Prompts are plain English sentences. They copy in one keystroke and go stale when the model changes. Four clumsy sentences you write about your own jobs beat a stranger’s polished template, because yours carry the context. Anyone selling secrecy is selling a scarcity that does not exist.
The upsell-only session you can spot before you register. Look for a long run time, no published agenda, and a “special offer” waiting at the end. That is not a crime, since every business sells something, but know which meeting you are walking into before you give up an evening you could have spent with your family. And be suspicious of any certificate described as official or required. Your customers will never ask to see it.
### What the price of an hour looks like from the truck
Course marketing never prices your hour, so do it yourself. For a lot of St. Louis owners the business is the second job, or the job after the job, and the hour a course asks for comes out of sleep, the books, or the kids. An HVAC company that earns its year in a St. Louis July is not learning anything new in July. A roofer after a hailstorm is not either. Training lands in the slow month or it does not land at all, and the slow month is when every dollar already has a name on it.
That is why the only fair measure is hours. Not revenue, which moves for a dozen reasons you will never untangle. Pick the one task you named, time it this week, and time it again in a month. If the number has not moved, the training did not work for you, however good the class felt. If a single reusable tool saves you an hour a week, it has already outperformed most of what gets sold on a countdown clock.

## One AI Rule Is Already Missouri Law: $1,000 a Violation
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-ai-rules-people-quote-and-whether-they-hold
One of the AI rules people pass around online is already Missouri law. Not the 70-20-10 split. Not Asimov’s robots. The one that says a person should read what the machine wrote before a customer does, and it sits in a statute that never mentions AI at all.
The draft comes back late, on the laptop at the kitchen table, after the second shift. It reads clean and sure of itself. Halfway down the new service page it promises “same-day service, guaranteed,” a promise this business has never once made. The fridge hums. The cursor blinks over the publish button, and the tired part of the brain says it looks fine.
Section 407.020 of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act makes it an unlawful practice to use any deception, false promise or misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise in or from the state of Missouri. It does not ask who, or what, typed the words. Under section 407.100, a court can award the state a civil penalty of not more than one thousand dollars per violation.
And the customer who feels misled has a door of their own, close to home. Section 407.025 lets them bring a private civil action in the circuit court of the county where the seller resides or where the deal took place. For a seller in the city, that is the 22nd Judicial Circuit. In the county, it is the 21st Judicial Circuit at 105 South Central Avenue.
Then comes the line almost nobody quotes. The same section says no civil penalty is imposed if the business shows that a violation resulted from a bona fide error notwithstanding the maintenance of procedures reasonably adopted to avoid the error. In plain words, Missouri’s own law rewards the owner who has a habit of checking. The folklore gets the likes. This sentence has a courtroom behind it.
### What is the 10/20-70 rule for AI?
It is a resource-allocation pattern from Boston Consulting Group: companies leading on AI dedicate 70% of resources to people and processes, 20% to technology and 10% to AI algorithms. It came from a survey of 1,000 senior executives, so it describes corporate rollouts. It is not a law.
A one-truck crew has no department to hand 70% of anything to. The idea underneath still holds, though: a tool nobody learns to use does nothing, like the new card reader still in its box by the register.
### What Missouri’s law asks of a kitchen-table business
“Procedures reasonably adopted” sounds like a binder in a corporate office. For a business run from a truck cab or a kitchen table, it can be four small habits, and every one of them answers a word in 407.020. Read aloud in a quiet kitchen, a made-up guarantee sounds wrong the second it leaves the mouth. A false promise is the guarantee the draft made up, so the habit is reading each promise out loud, the hours and the turnaround and the guarantee, against what the business really does. A misrepresentation is the wrong price, so the price and the coupon terms get matched to the real ones. An invented license, award or review is the kind of thing the tool slips in to sound impressive, so it comes out. And the corrected draft gets saved with the date it was checked, because a procedure the owner can show is worth more than one the owner remembers.
The law reaches the page whether the words appear before, during or after the sale, advertisement or solicitation. When it appears to the attorney general that someone is using an unlawful practice, the attorney general may seek an injunction in circuit court, and that is where the per-violation penalty lives. This is not legal advice. For a question about one real page, the Bar Association of Metropolitan St. Louis keeps a free online lawyer directory, and its attorneys are located in the St. Louis metropolitan area and charge fees for their services.
None of this asks an owner to stop using the tools. It asks for one honest read before a stranger trusts the page. So here is the only question worth asking about the last AI draft that went live: if a customer printed it out and read it back across the counter, which line would you want to change?
### So where did the 30% rule come from?
I could not source it. Two different rules share the name, one splitting a task between the machine and a person who keeps the judgment, the other a school cap on AI-written work, and neither has a named author, paper or date I could find. The advice in the first one is fine. The pedigree is folklore.
### Are the three laws of AI real laws?
No. They are Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics, formally stated in his story “Runaround” in Astounding, and they govern his fictional robots; the AI rule a Missouri owner actually answers to lives in the Revised Statutes, at 407.020.
### What about the four stages of AI adoption?
Whose four? Searching for the original turns up several unrelated maturity models from different organizations, with different stage names, some with four stages and some with five. They are separate maps drawn by separate firms, usually at the front of a service offering, and each one tends to place the reader somewhere in the middle, needing help to reach the end. Useful for a conversation. Not a measurement of where you stand.
### “Google punishes anything AI wrote”
This is the scare rule, repeated by the same people who sell you a fix for it. Google answered it directly in its Search Central guidance. Its words: “Appropriate use of AI or automation is not against our guidelines.” What Google does count against a page is using automation to generate content primarily to manipulate search rankings, which is against its spam policies.
The same guidance says Google’s ranking systems aim to reward original, high-quality content, however it is produced, and it points creators toward original, high-quality, people-first content. So the rule is not “no AI.” It is “no junk.” A page that answers a neighbor’s real question, in your own words about your own work, is the page that wins either way.
### Did Stephen Hawking really warn us about AI?
Yes, and this one is real and precisely sourced. In a BBC interview by technology correspondent Rory Cellan-Jones, Hawking said: “The development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race.” His warning came in response to a question about a revamp of the technology he used to communicate, which involved a basic form of AI.
Notice the word full. He was talking about a hypothetical machine that outgrows us, not software that drafts appointment reminders. When that quote gets pasted under a post about business tools, it borrows the weight of a very different argument. Hawking earned his warning. It was not about your invoicing.
The rule nobody posts: your staff may already be using these tools. Here is what shadow AI looks like in a St. Louis shop.
### What this looks like from behind the counter
Most people running a business in this town are not sitting in a corner office with an AI budget. They are working a job and building something on the side, or running the whole show from a truck cab and a kitchen table. The estimate gets written at the stove. The callback happens in a parking lot. The constraint was never a software line item. It is hours.
That is why these rules land strangely. They were written for companies with departments. And they skip the AI question that actually touches your bank account: when a neighbor asks ChatGPT or Google who to call, whose name comes back? People search for answers, not websites. A website is a single thread, and it stays invisible until something points to it. Being listed, complete and structured where the machines and the neighbors look is what turns the work you already do into calls. That goes for a two-truck HVAC outfit, a salon or one of the metro’s antique dealers.
You are not behind and you are not broken. You have just been handed the wrong rules by people with something to sell. The honest test for any AI tool is short. Does it handle one named task, like the follow-up after an estimate? Does a person check what it writes before a customer sees it, the habit Missouri’s own penalty section rewards? Would you notice within a week if it stopped? ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?
A.  Two different rules share the number and I could not trace either one to a named author, paper, firm or date. One says AI should handle most of a repetitive task while a person keeps the part that needs judgment. The other, from schools, caps how much submitted work should be AI-generated. Treat both as folklore with a decent idea inside, not a standard.
### Q. What are the four stages of AI adoption?
A.  There is no single canonical model. Different organizations publish their own maturity models with different stage names, some with four stages and some with five. Treat any list as one firm’s map for organizing a conversation, not as a measurement of where your business stands.
### Q. What are the three rules of AI?
A.  People usually mean Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics, formally stated in his story “Runaround” in Astounding. They govern his fictional robots. No statute contains them, and they are a storytelling device rather than a rule any AI product follows.
### Q. What is AI not allowed to do?
A.  For a Missouri business, the most important limit is not an AI law at all. Section 407.020 of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act makes deception, false promises, misrepresentation and omitting material facts in selling or advertising merchandise an unlawful practice, whether a person or a tool wrote the words. A court can award the state a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars per violation, though none is imposed for a bona fide error made despite procedures reasonably adopted to avoid it. On search, Google says appropriate use of AI is not against its guidelines, but using automation primarily to manipulate rankings violates its spam policies.
### Q. What was Stephen Hawking’s warning about AI?
A.  In a BBC interview, Hawking told correspondent Rory Cellan-Jones that “the development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race.” He was describing a hypothetical self-improving machine, not the business tools sold today, and the question that prompted it was about the AI-assisted system he used to communicate.
### Q. Which 5 jobs will survive AI?
A.  There is no authoritative list of five, and the ones circulating rarely name a source. Work that means showing up in person, holding a license and standing behind the result is hardest to hand to software, but that is reasoning, not a research finding. What is certain is that those trades still need to be found, which is why a complete St Louis Near Me Directory listing matters as much as the skill.

## AI Can’t Hold a St. Louis License. It Can Hide Your Name.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-ai-wont-replace-in-a-local-service-business
Once a month, on the fourth Monday, a board in the City of St. Louis sits down to hear complaints against plumbers. The Plumbers and Drainlayers Board of Examiners hears charges against Master Plumbers, Drainlayers and licensed Journeyman Plumbers. It has no chair for an app. And plumbing permits in the city are issued to licensed plumbing contractors who are certified by the City of Saint Louis.
Behind that board sits a state law from 1939. Missouri Revised Statute 341.010 says anyone working at the business of plumbing in a city of fifteen thousand or more shall first receive a certificate, and the next section says it comes from a board of examiners, after an examination the applicant is compelled to pass. Nobody wrote it with software in mind. It still says the one thing no app gets around: a named person earns the right to touch the pipe, and a named person answers for it.
Now set that against what lands on your phone. You climb out of a crawlspace with cobwebs in your collar and the knees of your jeans soaked through, sit in the truck with a gas-station coffee going cold in the cupholder, and the feed serves up a man in a rented office saying AI is about to make your trade obsolete. Also that you could clear a thousand dollars a day with it. Also that his course closes at midnight. You scroll. The next video says the same thing in a different room.
That pitch is not built for you. It is built to sell to you. The people making it earn their money from worry, not from fixing anything, and the law, the insurance policy and the customer at the door all tell a different story than their video does.
### Which business can AI not replace?
Any business whose product needs a licensed person on site and answerable afterward. In St. Louis that is not a theory. It is a permit counter that only serves certified contractors, a monthly board hearing, and a 1939 statute. Software cannot sit the exam, carry the insurance or take the blame, so that work stays human.
That is not a claim about how smart the software is. It is a claim about who signs, who is insured and who a board can discipline. Run your own work through three quick questions. Does somebody have to be physically there, in the attic, under the sink, with scissors in someone’s hair? Does the state issue a credential with a person’s name on it for this? And is somebody answerable a year from now when the joint drips or the color turns brassy?
Work that answers yes three times is protected, and the protection has very little to do with the technology being bad at it. Work that answers no three times (the estimate, the same phone question for the fortieth time, chasing the schedule) is exposed right now. Most local service businesses are some of each. Knowing which is which is what keeps you from buying a fix for the wrong half.
### A license is issued to a person, not a process
Plumbing is not the only trade where Missouri law points at a human being. Look at the chair in a salon. Under Missouri law, a cosmetology apprentice must serve no less than three thousand hours under the supervision of a licensed cosmetologist. Three thousand hours of wet hair, foils, the sting of developer on a nick in your knuckle, all of it logged to one name.
Veterinary medicine puts it in a single line of statute. Missouri’s definition of the veterinarian-client-patient relationship, in RSMo 340.200, requires that the veterinarian has assumed the responsibility for making medical judgments about the animal. Read that phrase twice. Assumed the responsibility. The law does not care how good the diagnosis software is. It cares who will stand in the exam room, with the dog panting on the cold steel table, and own the call.
Put the three side by side and the pattern is not “AI is bad at pipes.” The pattern is that the statute names a person, requires that person to show up, and holds that person answerable. Even if a model someday diagnoses a slab leak better than you do, a licensed human still has to own the result, because owning the result is what the license is. Changing that is not a software update. It is a legislature, and the insurance industry standing behind it.
### Somebody has to answer when it goes wrong
Your customer is buying two things, and only one of them is the work. The other is recourse. When a water heater lets go and the finished basement smells like a wet dog for a week, there is a name on the permit, a policy number, and a board that will take a written complaint. That whole system assumes a specific human being can be found and held to it.
Which is why “the software told me to” will never work as a defense. If you run an estimate or a diagnosis through a tool and hand it to a customer, you have adopted it. The liability did not move, because there is nowhere for it to go. You can be sued. The tool cannot. That gap is permanent in a way no capability chart is.
The wider question of where these tools fit in a local business is covered in AI for St. Louis: how local businesses can actually use it. This page is about the narrower thing underneath it: who the law can hold responsible, and why that line does not move.
### Where AI really is taking work
Here is the honest part, and it cuts both ways. The work AI is taking in a service business is the paperwork wrapped around the real work, and there is more of it than most owners say out loud. The estimate you type at the kitchen table late at night with the dishwasher running. The follow-up email you have been dodging since last week. The same question about your service area, asked over and over.
Take the paper by Tyna Eloundou and three other authors. It is worth reading for what it says rather than what gets quoted from it. Its headline estimate is that around 80% of the U.S. workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by large language models, and approximately 19% may see at least half their tasks affected. The authors say plainly that they do not make predictions about the adoption timeline. Anybody quoting that paper as a countdown clock is selling something.
For a service shop, the exposed list is short and specific:
Drafting: estimates from scrappy notes, letters to an insurer, job descriptions.
Summarizing: a long call, a warranty document, months of maintenance history.
First-pass questions: hours, service area, do you work on that brand.
Scheduling admin: confirmations, reminders, the reshuffle when a morning job runs long.
Marketing copy: service-page text and review replies.
If someone on your payroll does mostly those five things, that role is already changing. The good version of this is usually moving that person toward billable work, not cutting them, because the limit in most service shops is billable hours, not admin hours. Before you decide anything, find out what your crew is already doing with these tools on their own phones; that is the subject of your staff is already using AI. And for the real adoption numbers, without the hype, see what percent of small businesses actually use AI.
### What about the “make $1,000 a day with AI” videos?
They are selling the course. That is the business model, not cynicism. The money comes from people buying the method, not from people running it, which is why the price always expires at midnight and the urgency always sounds the same.
There is a federal rule you can hold up against them. The FTC’s Business Opportunity Rule, 16 CFR Part 437, makes it a violation for any seller to fail to give you the required disclosure in writing at least seven calendar days before you sign any contract or make a payment. If they have made an earnings claim, they owe you a single written earnings claim statement, titled “EARNINGS CLAIM STATEMENT REQUIRED BY LAW,” showing the dates those earnings were achieved and the number and percentage of all buyers who actually hit them. Ask for both, in writing. If the seller tells you the Rule doesn’t apply to what they sell, ask them to explain why, in writing, and watch how fast the midnight deadline stops mattering.
None of that makes learning the tools a scam. The line is whether you are being sold a skill or a rented outcome. A skill you keep, and you can test it on a slow afternoon against work you already understand. That is the idea behind the AI workshops: sit down with the tools, on your own jobs, and see where they help and where they quietly get it wrong.

### The judgment nobody sells a course on
The hardest parts of a trade to automate are the parts nobody ever wrote down. Every experienced operator knows them by feel.
Diagnosing an old house. So much of this metro is old brick with additions stacked on additions and generations of plumbing in one wall. The code is a lookup. The skill is holding six possible causes at once and picking the true one from a smell, a stain, the age of a fitting, the way the floor slopes, and one sentence the homeowner said about last winter. It is also saying, out loud, “I have to open the wall to know,” instead of guessing with confidence. A model is built to give a confident answer. You are allowed to say you don’t know yet.
Reading a person. A customer goes quiet, and the silence means they are lost and embarrassed to say so. Another says “do whatever you think” and means “I can’t afford this and I hope you notice.” A pet owner asks about cost and is really asking whether the dog is going to make it. You have the room, the face and the pause. A tool has a transcript.
Deciding what not to sell. Telling someone the small repair will hold for years, when you could have written a full replacement that afternoon, gives up this month’s money for a referral you will never see on a spreadsheet. Every recommendation engine optimizes the sale in front of it, because that is all it can see. An operator who has worked the same streets for years is optimizing something else.
Improvising when the plan breaks. The joist is where the drawing said it wouldn’t be. The part is discontinued and the supply house is closed. The client in the chair has a box-dye job nothing in school covered. Every trade is a long string of small recoveries, and the recovery is where the skill lives.
