### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is paying for a life coach worth it?
A.  It can be, if your problem is a stuck goal rather than a clinical one. Coaching buys structure, accountability and a thinking partner. It buys no diagnosis and no treatment. Ask for the total engagement price in writing, set an exit condition before the first payment, and judge the result against it. If you are struggling rather than stuck, the same money often goes further with a licensed therapist, and a sliding-scale clinic like UMSL’s Center for Psychological Growth starts at $20 an hour.
### Q. Will insurance cover a life coach?
A.  Don’t count on it. Ask your plan before you assume, and budget to pay a coach out of pocket. Therapy is different: HealthCare.gov says all Marketplace plans cover mental health services, including psychotherapy and counseling, as essential health benefits. Check your own plan’s network and copay, and ask HR whether an employee assistance program includes counseling sessions.
### Q. What does a life coach actually do?
A.  Goal-setting, structure, accountability and decision support for a functioning adult who wants to get from a stated goal to a finished one. A good coach asks more than they tell, and you leave each session with a small number of specific actions and a deadline on each. Common specialties include career, business, health habits and life transitions. Ask which one a coach actually does most, because many list far more than they practice.
### Q. How long should you have a life coach?
A.  As long as you are working toward an exit condition you named in writing at the start. Make it something you can check off, with a date. Long arrangements can be legitimate when the goal genuinely keeps changing. If your sessions a year in sound like the first month, it is time to stop.
### Q. Can you be a life coach without a license?
A.  Yes. The limits are on titles and on clinical work. Missouri bars anyone without a license from calling themselves a psychologist, a professional counselor or a counselor, or from practicing psychology or professional counseling. A professional counselor needs a degree with a major in counseling and, with a master’s, at least two years of supervised counseling experience after it. To check a therapist, use the Licensee Search listed on the Division of Professional Registration’s home page at pr.mo.gov.
### Q. What kind of questions do life coaches ask?
A.  Forward-looking ones. What does done look like? What have you already tried? What is the smallest step you could take this week? What happens if nothing changes? What did you commit to last time? Good coaching questions tend to be uncomfortable rather than clever. Questions digging into childhood, trauma or symptoms belong in a licensed therapist’s office, and a coach asking them has stepped past the line.

## Your Song Isn't Yours Until the Bill Is Paid: What St. Louis Studio Time Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-recording-studio-time-costs-in-st-louis
The last vocal take is still ringing in your headphones. Through the glass, the engineer bounces a rough mix, and the song you carried around in your phone for months finally exists, on a drive just out of reach. Until the bill is square, that is where it stays.
That is not a figure of speech. Shock City Studios, at 2200 Gravois Avenue, works out of the Polar Wave Ice & Fuel Building in Benton Park, built in 1927 as an ice manufacturing and storage plant, and its rate sheet says it plainly: $90 per hour with a 2-hour minimum, a 50% deposit at booking to reserve the studio and the engineer, and the remaining balance due at the end of your session or the files cannot be released. Two hours comes to $180.
The rate buys you an hour. The balance buys you your song. So before you set one hourly number against another, find out what the hour includes and the moment the file becomes yours.
### How much does a 2 hour studio session cost?
At Shock City Studios on Gravois Avenue, a 2-hour session costs $180: the studio posts a standard rate of $90 per hour with a 2-hour minimum, the same rate for any of its rooms, and a 50% deposit reserves the studio and the engineer. Other St. Louis rooms price differently, so ask every studio whether the hour includes the engineer, setup time and your files.
Here is the part worth repeating to your bandmates. Shock City’s rate sheet says the rates are the same for any of its studios, and the equipment list for Studio A includes an SSL 6000 Series console. The same $90 that books any other room books the big desk with the long rows of faders. If you were talking yourself into the cheap room because you assumed the serious one was out of reach, read the sheet before you settle.
The deposit is easy math, too. Half of $180 is $90, so the money that holds a two-hour date is the price of one hour, paid when you book. The other $90 is what stands between you and your files when the session ends.
Work that is not music has its own lines on the same sheet: audiobooks and voice-over at $100 an hour, podcast audio at $90 an hour and podcast video at $150.
Then pick up the phone. Shock City lists (314) 771-3099 for pricing, booking and tours. Call that room and two others, describe the exact project in one breath, and ask each the same three things: is the engineer included, does the clock start at load-in, and what do I walk out with? Three answers to the same questions are a comparison. Three hourly numbers are a guess.
### What does the hourly rate actually rent?
Three things at once: a room that sounds right, a signal chain of consoles, preamps and microphones, and a person who knows how to run both. Take away any one of them and the price drops. That is the whole reason two rooms can quote numbers that look nothing alike.
The room is the part people underrate. Shock City describes its Live Room as having a 20-foot ceiling, double-sided reversible sound baffles and movable rugs to change how it sounds, and a warm color scheme with natural light. Its rate sheet lists a $50 one-time fee for the Live Room on top of the hourly rate. That is construction you are renting, not gear, and it is why a garage full of nice microphones still sounds like a garage.
Then the engineer, which is where the money genuinely goes. The structure looks the same at any hourly creative space in town. If you have ever priced renting a photo studio in St. Louis, you already know the shape of it: room, equipment, operator, time.
### Is the engineer included in the hourly rate?
Ask this first, every single time. At Shock City the deposit reserves the studio and the engineer together, so the person in the chair is part of the price. Other rooms quote a room-only rate and expect you to bring your own engineer or run the session yourself. Those two numbers are not comparable, even when they look close.
Room-only pricing is a bargain or a disaster. With an engineer you trust, it is the cheapest way to work. Without one, the first stretch of a paid hour goes to learning somebody else’s routing while the clock runs and the singer stands in the booth with cold hands, waiting for a headphone mix that never quite arrives.
Setup is the other quiet cost. Shock City’s own preparation page puts it bluntly: “Remember that recording takes longer than just playing the song.” Mics go up, the console gets set, levels get chased, and that time is on the clock. Ask any room whether billing starts at load-in or at the first take.
### Hourly, a full day, or per song?
Book hourly for short, defined work: one vocal over a finished beat, a voiceover, an overdub. Book a full day when a band is tracking, because a drum kit only gets miked once if it stays up. Shock City posts a Day Rate of $640 when booking 8 continuous hours. The same eight hours at the standard $90 would come to $720, so the day rate saves $80 and works out to $80 an hour.
That saving only holds if the hours are continuous. Split a band across two short sessions on different dates and you pay for the kit to go up twice, which is the most common avoidable expense in this whole process. Leave the drums standing, eat lunch out of a paper bag, and keep going.
Per-song packages take the meter out of the room, which changes how everybody behaves in it. Many artists prefer them. The tradeoff is scope: a package defines what one song includes, and going past that has a price, so read the definition before you sign.
### What is billed separately from tracking?
Tracking, mixing and mastering are three different jobs, and usually only the first sits inside the hourly rate. Mixing is often priced per song. Mastering is often a separate person entirely. A low tracking rate with honest mixing fees behind it is a normal structure. You just want to see it coming.
Ask for the whole path to a finished song, priced: recording, editing and comping, mixing, revisions, mastering, delivery format. Then ask how many mix revisions come with the price and what one more costs. That single question separates rooms that have done this a hundred times from rooms that have not.
Editing is the sneaky line. Tuning a vocal, stitching a dozen takes into one pass, lining up a doubled chorus: that is real labor, billed by the hour or folded into a mix fee. Nobody enjoys finding out which one afterward.
Session ran long and you are starving? Here is where to find the best Ethiopian food in St. Louis.
### How much studio time does your project actually need?
Answer this before you shop rates, because it moves the budget more than any hourly figure. A single vocal over a finished instrumental is a short job when the artist knows the words cold. A band tracking live needs a day. A podcast with a prepared host and one guest fits comfortably in an afternoon.
Drums are where preparation pays. Shock City’s advice to drummers is specific: “Make sure you have a new set of heads, both top and bottoms. Tune them a day before the recording session.” Fresh heads, a tuned kit and a band that has rehearsed to a click will finish more songs in the same paid hours than a band that is still arguing about the bridge.
The cheapest hour in any studio is the one you never had to book, because the parts were already learned. If the playing itself is the bottleneck, fix that first. Our guide to how to choose music lessons in St. Louis is often a better first spend than a second session.
### What should you check in the deposit and cancellation policy?
Get it in writing before money moves. Shock City’s posted policy is a good model of what a clear one looks like: a 50% deposit at booking, and for 2-4 hour sessions, the deposit is returned if you cancel 48 hours before session time. Longer bookings need more notice, up to 10 days before the session date for 8+ hour sessions.
Ask every room three things and write the answers down. How much notice cancels without losing the deposit? Can the deposit move to another date? If we run over, what does the extra time cost, and is the room even free after us? A studio with an answer for all three has policies. A studio without them has arguments later.
### Who owns the recording when the session ends?
Ask before you book, not after. Practice varies room to room, so get whatever you agreed to in writing, even if writing means a text message.
The practical question matters more than the legal one: what do you physically walk out with? A stereo mix plus stems or the raw multitrack files, in a format any other studio can open, is the goal. Shock City’s sheet is frank that it cannot guarantee the safe storage of digital audio files and strongly advises clients to bring their own hard drive and take it home after each session. Do that anywhere. A drive in your coat pocket on the drive home is the only backup you control.
Before you sign anything with a label or a producer, read what an entertainment attorney does in St. Louis.
### Why the rate looks the way it does from behind the glass
From the owner’s side, the hourly rate is not what one hour is worth. It is what the whole week has to cover: rent on a treated room, gear that wears out, insurance, utilities, software, and the engineer’s time in the chair and outside it. No room is booked every hour it is open, so the booked hours carry the empty ones. That is why day rates exist: they fill the calendar.
And most bands who book a room heard about it from another band, usually standing in the back at one of the neighborhood venues locals actually love.

A.  Treat any single figure you see online as a claim until you see a rate sheet. Use that as a yardstick, then ask every other room what its hour includes, since an engineer-included hour and a room-only hour are different products.

Other rooms will differ, and some price in blocks once a session gets longer, so ask. Then ask the question that changes the total: does the clock start at load-in, and is mixing inside that price or billed separately?
### Q. How much does a recording studio cost per day?
A.  Shock City Studios posts a Day Rate of $640 when booking 8 continuous hours, which is $80 less than eight hours at its standard $90 rate. A day is the right call for drums or a full band, because microphone setup happens once. Ask any room what happens if you run past the block and what the extra time costs.
### Q. How much should a recording studio charge?
A.  Price the week, not the hour. A sustainable rate covers rent on a treated room, gear repair and replacement, insurance, utilities, software, the engineer’s paid time, and every hour that never gets booked. ### Q. How long does a studio session take?

A full band tracking live needs a day, because load-in, mic setup and headphone mixes eat the first stretch before a usable take exists. Rehearsing to a click before you book is the cheapest way to shorten it.
### Q. What should I do to prepare for a recording session?
A.  Rehearse until the parts are automatic, and practice to a click. Finish the lyrics at home, because writing in the booth is the most expensive writing you will ever do. Drummers, put on fresh heads and tune them the day before, as Shock City’s prep page advises. Bring spare strings, sticks, cables and a hard drive for your files. Show up early so load-in is not on the clock, and sleep: a tired voice is audible on every take.

## No Uniform Deductions Below $15: What Work Uniforms Cost in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-work-uniforms-cost-in-st-louis
$10.00 an hour. That was the City of St. Louis’s own minimum wage under Ordinance 70078, and the City’s FAQ still says the Supreme Court of Missouri determined the City’s law is valid. Then Jefferson City shut the door. Missouri statute 290.528, effective August 28, 2017, says no political subdivision, a city included, may require an employer to pay a minimum or living wage rate. The City’s minimum wage page now opens with a banner: archived for historical purposes and no longer maintained.
So the line that counts on a St. Louis paycheck is the state one. Missouri’s Division of Labor Standards posts it at $15.00 an hour. And a state rule, 8 CSR 30-4.050, says uniforms, the laundry or cleaning of uniforms, and the breakage or loss of uniforms may not be deducted by the employer as a credit toward the minimum wage.
Here is where that rule stops being paper. A new hire waits at the time clock on the first payday. The polo still holds the square creases from its plastic sleeve, and the embroidered logo sits stiff against the collarbone. The stub slides out of the envelope: hours, rate, taxes. Then one more line, a uniform charge nobody mentioned at the interview. If that line pulls the hour under $15.00, the payroll setup has just walked into a rule that the uniform rep’s clipboard never prints and the payroll template never flags.
Who was supposed to explain that? The rental agreement? The software? The same state page adds a wrinkle: retail or service businesses whose annual gross income is less than $500,000 are not required to pay the state minimum wage rate. The same page lists the Division of Labor Standards at 573-751-3403.
Three checks worth doing before the next payday, from one owner to another:
First, lay one pay stub next to the state number. Take the week’s pay after any uniform line and divide it by the hours. If it lands under the $15.00 the Division of Labor Standards posts, that uniform line is exactly what 8 CSR 30-4.050 says can’t be credited toward the minimum wage.
Second, call 573-751-3403 with one question: does the under-$500,000 retail or service line on the state page cover this shop? That answer decides who carries the shirt.
Third, pull the uniform agreement out of the drawer and look for the two things the City of St. Louis wrote into its own request. When the Treasurer’s Office asked vendors for uniform rental and laundry service, it said each employee would receive eleven uniform shirts and/or pants, and that the initial contract would run a two-year period with two options to renew for one-year terms. Garment count and renewal terms, on paper, before any rate. Find both in the agreement, and circle the notice date.
And that is only the wage side. The weekly rate per employee is the number every rental program leads with, and it sounds like the price of a gas-station coffee. Multiply it by four people and by every week of a multi-year term and it stops sounding like coffee. The clause that moves the most money rarely sits next to that rate. It sits further back: the auto-renewal language that can roll the whole agreement into a new term if a notice window slips past during a busy season.
The garment is the cheap part. The contract wrapped around it is where the money lives.
### How much do work uniforms typically cost?
The shirt is rarely the bill. A rental bin on pickup day at an auto bay smells of coolant and grease baked into cotton, and that smell is the real price: a route, a laundry and a replacement cycle, not a polo. Three pricing models sit underneath every quote, and a flat number that skips them is a guess.
Rental programs drop clean garments on hangers and haul the dirty ones away, billed per employee per week. That rate moves with garment type and with how many changes each person gets. A five-shirt rotation for a diesel tech costs more than two polos for a front counter, and flame-resistant or high-visibility garments sit at the top of the range. A rate only compares with another rate when the garment count and the delivery frequency travel with it.
Buying outright flips the shape of the spend. The day-one number is bigger, the garments belong to the business, and laundering, repair and replacement follow them home. Under the Missouri rule above, laundry, maintenance, and breakage or loss of uniforms can’t be credited toward the minimum wage either. The ongoing spend is smaller and lumpier: a new hire needs a set, somebody tears a knee on a trailer hitch, a size changes after the holidays.
Decoration is the third bucket, shared by both models. Embroidery carries a one-time digitizing fee for each logo plus a per-piece run charge that falls as quantity climbs. Screen printing charges by color and by run size, so a one-color back print on 96 shirts lands somewhere very different from a four-color print on 12. Any range read online, this page included, is a starting point that still owes a written quote.
### Rent or buy: who ends up owning the risk
Soil decides most of it. Grease, coolant, solvents, blood, fryer oil: the kind of shirt peeled off at the end of a shift that nobody wants in a home washer. For that work, an industrial laundry is selling consistency and a documented process, not just convenience. Garments that stay presentable, on a crew that rarely changes, point the other way.
The honest difference is who carries the risk. In a rental program the supplier owns the garments and the laundering, so it also owns the replacement cycle, the sizing swaps and the stain that will not come out, and that transfer is billed every week whether it gets used or not. Buying hands all of it back, including the part nobody budgets: somebody in the office now manages shirts.
Headcount swings are the tiebreaker. A landscaping crew that goes from six people to fourteen across a sticky St. Louis summer fits a rental program, because garments flex in and out with the roster. A stable five-person shop that has not hired in two years may be paying weekly for flexibility it never touches. Old payroll records settle the question faster than any sales call.
The hourly line no uniform crosses
In St. Louis the number that caps any uniform charge is Missouri’s, not the City’s: $15.00 an hour from the Division of Labor Standards, while the City’s old $10.00 rate sits on an archived page. Uniforms, their laundry and their loss can’t be credited toward that $15.00. What moves it: a retail or service business with annual gross income under $500,000 is not required to pay the state rate, and the state posts the figure again each year.
### What is actually inside a uniform rental contract?
The agreement belongs on a desk under a lamp, not on a counter while the delivery truck idles outside. Six terms move real money: term length and auto-renewal, per-garment loss and damage charges, prep or make-up charges for new hires, surcharges added to the weekly invoice, size-change fees, and what happens to the garments on the day of cancellation.
Term and auto-renewal gate everything else. Multi-year terms are normal in this industry and not automatically unfair, but the renewal language deserves the brightest highlighter in the drawer. How long does the first term run? Does it renew on its own? How many days of notice are owed, and in what form? Miss that window and the agreement can hand over another full term. The notice date belongs on the calendar the day of signing, not the day frustration sets in.
Loss and damage is the charge that surprises people. The garments belong to the supplier, so a shirt that disappears off a truck or comes back shredded gets billed at a replacement value set in the agreement. Who decides whether an item is damaged or simply worn out? Is there an allowance before charges start? And the Missouri rule applies here as well: breakage or loss of uniforms is on the list that cannot be credited against a minimum-wage worker’s pay.
Then the quiet lines. Prep charges cover setting up a new employee with emblems and hemming, so high turnover pays them constantly. Energy or environmental surcharges show up as a percentage on the invoice and can move without a conversation. Size changes may be free, free once, or billed every time. At cancellation: return every garment, buy them, or both, and at what price?
Not sure whether you want a weekly route or a local decorator? Compare both before anything gets signed. Browse uniform suppliers listed across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then carry the six contract terms above into every conversation you have.

### What do embroidery and screen printing add to the price?
Two moving parts and one trap. The parts are setup and run. Embroidery setup is digitizing, a one-time conversion of the logo into a stitch file, charged per logo and per size. Screen printing setup is a screen per color. The trap is that setup travels with the artwork, and most buyers never take possession of it.
Here is how it bites. A business pays to digitize its logo once, switches decorators a few years later for a better price on polos, and learns nobody ever asked for the stitch file. Same logo, same setup fee, second time. Ask for the digitized stitch file and a vector logo in writing, have them emailed, and store them somewhere that survives an employee leaving.
Run charges are predictable. Embroidery is priced by stitch count, so a dense logo with heavy fill costs more per piece than a clean one. Screen printing charges per color and per print location, while the per-unit price falls sharply as the run grows. Twelve shirts will never price like 144. ### When a work shirt is safety gear
Some uniforms are branding and some are equipment. The HVAC tech climbing into an attic that feels like an oven, the crew working beside moving traffic, the line cook at an open flame: for that work, ask whether a written safety standard covers what they wear, and confirm the exact standard for your trade rather than trusting any blog, this one included.
Protective garments carry a written performance standard, and standards specify performance, not looks. A shirt that happens to be orange is not high-visibility apparel. A cotton work shirt is not flame-resistant. Suppliers quote to whatever specification they are handed, so get the right one named on the quote.
Uniforms are one fee in a stack of them. The next one most owners trip on is the sign out front: business sign permits across the St. Louis metro.
### Why does the cheap quote usually cost more?
A weekly rate is not a garment price. It covers pickup and delivery on a fixed route, industrial laundering, inspection, repairs, replacement of worn garments, sizing changes, emblem work for new hires, and the standing inventory that puts a clean shirt on the truck the week it is needed. A quote that undercuts the market by a wide margin usually reappears somewhere else: a low garment count, a thin replacement allowance, surcharges left out of the quoted figure, or a term long enough to make the first-year number irrelevant. Same cost, parked somewhere quieter.
The useful number is the annual total at real headcount, prep charges, surcharges and expected replacements included. A supplier who cannot produce one on request has said something worth hearing. Two quotes from two different models, a rental route and a buy-outright decorator pricing the same crew, will look nothing alike, and that contrast is the point. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I buy custom work uniforms?
A.  Three routes cover nearly everything. Local decorators and embroidery shops sell blank garments and decorate them in house, which is the fastest path for small runs. Uniform rental companies supply and launder garments on a weekly route, which suits the dirty trades. Online catalog suppliers ship decorated apparel nationally, often cheapest per piece at volume and slowest to fix when something arrives wrong. In St. Louis, you can compare local uniform suppliers and decorators side by side on St Louis Near Me Directory before you call anyone.
### Q. How much do custom embroidered shirts cost?
A.  Embroidered shirts price in two layers, plus the shirt itself. The first layer is a one-time digitizing fee that converts your logo into a stitch file, charged per logo and per size. The second is a per-piece run charge driven by stitch count and quantity, which falls as the order grows. Underneath both sits the blank garment, and a moisture-wicking polo and a heavy twill work shirt are not the same starting point. Get a written quote at your real quantity before budgeting.
### Q. What are the three types of uniforms?
A.  The phrase usually means one of two breakdowns, so ask which one somebody is using. By function, uniforms split into identity apparel that makes staff recognizable, protective apparel required by a safety standard, and general workwear built mainly for durability. By supply model, they split into weekly rental-and-laundering programs, garments bought outright by the employer, and employee-purchase programs where staff buy from an approved list. In Missouri, 8 CSR 30-4.050 lists uniforms among the things an employer may not deduct as a credit toward the minimum wage, which matters for any employee-purchase plan.
### Q. Where can I buy embroidered workwear?
A.  Embroidered workwear comes from two very different vendors, and the choice sets your ongoing costs for years. A decorator sells you the garments outright, so you own them, you launder them, and you reorder whenever you hire. A rental program keeps ownership, delivers clean garments weekly, bills per employee, and folds emblems and name tags into the service. Dirty trades usually land on the rental side. Offices, retail and service businesses with presentable garments often land on the decorator side.
### Q. Where can I find custom-made work wear?
A.  Be precise about what custom means, because it changes minimums dramatically. Customized stock apparel, meaning catalog garments decorated with your logo, is what almost everyone actually buys, and minimums are usually modest. Genuinely custom-made clothing, cut and sewn to your own specification, involves pattern work, sampling, large minimums and long lead times. Unless you have a fit or fabric requirement no catalog meets, customized stock is the practical answer.
### Q. Where do small businesses get their clothes?
A.  Most small businesses in the metro start with a local decorator, because turnaround is the real constraint rather than price. A first order that includes digitizing takes longer than a reorder. Ask for a sample or a single decorated piece before committing to a full run, especially on sizing, since cuts differ between brands and a crew that hates the shirts will not wear them. Also ask how long the supplier stocks your blanks, so next year’s reorder still matches.
### Q. Where can I order custom embroidered shirts?
A.  Ordering goes smoother when you arrive prepared. Bring vector artwork, because a low-resolution image pulled off a website usually needs redrawing at your expense. Bring a size run collected from your actual employees instead of a guess. Confirm logo placement and size in writing, approve a digital proof, and ask for the stitch file once production is done. Owning your artwork is what lets you change suppliers later without paying a second setup fee.

## How to See a Cardiologist in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-see-a-cardiologist-in-st-louis
The visit ends the way most of them do. Your primary care doctor is already half standing, hand near the door, and says something that lands quietly: “I want you to see cardiology.” Two days later a portal message appears with the word referral in it and nothing else that explains what happens next.
Or you moved here. You had a cardiologist in another state who knew your history cold, and now you are unpacking boxes in Creve Coeur with a medication bottle that has two refills left and an insurance card you have not read yet.
Both situations feel medical. Mostly they are logistical. What follows is the paperwork side: how a referral actually moves, what to ask before you accept an appointment date, what to carry in with you, and what to do when the first opening is months away.
Before anything else, the part that is not about scheduling. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath while you are sitting still, fainting, or anything that feels like a heart attack means calling 911. Not booking an appointment. Not sending a portal message. Not reading a blog post. Call 911 and let someone with a monitor and an ambulance make the next decision.
This article is general information about getting care, and it is not medical advice.
### Can I just go see a cardiologist without a referral?
Sometimes, and it depends on your plan. PPO plans usually let you self-refer while still steering you to in-network doctors. HMO and many Medicare Advantage plans typically require a referral or prior authorization. Original Medicare Part B generally does not. Call the number on the back of your card.
That last sentence is the only advice on this page that binds. Plan rules vary by employer, by product year, and by network tier, so the person answering the member services line is the authority here, not a search result. Ask them plainly: do I need a referral to see a cardiologist, and do I need prior authorization for testing once I get there. Then ask them to note the call.
There is a second layer people run into even when the plan says self-referral is fine. Many cardiology practices still want a referring physician and a records packet before they will book a new patient, because someone in the office has to decide how soon you should be seen. That is a practice rule, not an insurance rule, and it catches a lot of people off guard.
Which is why having a regular doctor makes everything downstream easier. If yours retired, or you never replaced the one you had before the move, start there. Our guide to finding a primary care doctor in St. Louis walks through that step, and if the coverage question is still open, how to get health insurance in Missouri covers the enrollment side.
### How does a cardiology referral actually get sent?
A referral is usually two things traveling on two different tracks, and appointments stall when only one of them arrives. The first is the authorization, the permission your plan requires. The second is the records packet: the office note, recent labs, any EKG, any prior imaging.
The authorization is what people picture when they hear the word referral. The records are what actually determine when you get seen. A nurse or a physician at the cardiology office reads what came over and sorts you into a timeframe. Thin packet, no sorting. Your referral can be sitting in a queue, perfectly valid, while you sit at home assuming a phone call is coming.
So make two calls instead of waiting for one. Call the referring office and ask which cardiology group it went to, what day it was sent, and what records went with it. Then call the cardiology office and ask whether it arrived and whether anything is missing. Note the date and the name of whoever you spoke with.
That habit sounds fussy. In our experience it shortens more waits than any other single thing a patient can do, because it puts a name and a date on a request that otherwise has neither.
One more wrinkle worth knowing. Records do not always cross between systems automatically, even in 2026, and even between offices a few miles apart in south county. If you had testing done somewhere else, you may need to sign a release yourself and request copies directly. Ask for them on a disc or through the patient portal, and keep your own copy.
### What should you ask when you call to schedule?
Six questions, asked before you accept a date, prevent most of the unpleasant surprises. Ask them in this order and ask the scheduler to add the answers to your file.
Is this doctor in my network, and is the building in my network too? Those are two separate answers. A physician can be contracted with your plan while the location where you are seen bills as an outpatient hospital department, which changes the math on what you owe.
Is a facility fee billed separately? This is the follow-up to the previous question and it is the one people wish they had asked. A facility fee is a charge for the room, billed apart from the physician charge. Ask whether this location bills one, and get the answer before you agree to the visit.
How long is the wait for a new patient? Ask for the actual next available date, not a general range, and ask whether a different physician or a nurse practitioner in the same group has something sooner. Groups often have several providers and only one gets requested by name.
Will I need a separate imaging appointment? Echocardiograms, stress tests, and wearable monitors are frequently scheduled for a different day, sometimes at a different address. Knowing that up front lets you plan time off work once instead of twice.
What do you need from my other doctors, and do you have it yet? Ask this even if the referring office told you everything was sent. Confirmation from the receiving end is the only confirmation that counts.
Is there a cancellation list, and how do I get on it? More on that further down, because it is the single most underused option in the whole process.
### What should you bring to a first cardiology appointment?
Bring more than you think you need. A first cardiology visit is largely an information-gathering exercise, and the quality of the plan you leave with depends on the quality of what you walk in with.
Start with a complete medication list, including doses and how often you take each one. Include supplements, fish oil, over-the-counter pain relievers, and anything you take occasionally. Supplements matter more than people expect, because several of them interact with heart medications. The easiest version of this is to photograph every bottle on your kitchen counter and bring the phone.
Bring prior testing. Old EKG tracings, echocardiogram reports, stress test results, monitor summaries, cardiac CT or catheterization reports. Reports are useful, actual images and tracings are better. A cardiologist who can compare today to three years ago is working with something a brand-new test cannot give them.
Bring family history with specifics. Not “heart problems run in the family” but which relative, on which side, what happened, and at what age. Early events in close relatives carry weight that a vague summary does not.
And bring a symptom diary with dates. Write down what happened, when, what you were doing, how long it lasted, and what made it stop. Three lines per episode is plenty. Memory compresses everything under pressure, and a page of dated entries is worth more than an hour of trying to remember in the exam room.
Two practical extras. Bring your insurance card and a photo ID, and bring someone with you if you can. A second set of ears catches the half of the conversation you will not remember, and that is true at any age.
### What do the cardiology subspecialties mean in plain words?
Cardiology splits into narrower jobs, and the words on a practice website rarely explain themselves. You do not have to pick the right one yourself, but knowing the vocabulary makes the scheduling call go faster.
A general or noninvasive cardiologist is where most people start. They evaluate symptoms, manage medications, order and read testing, and follow you over time. If something narrower is needed, this is the person who points you there.
An interventional cardiologist works in the catheterization lab. Angiograms, stents, and related procedures through a catheter rather than open surgery. An electrophysiologist handles rhythm: monitors, ablations, pacemakers, and defibrillators. If the word arrhythmia is in your referral, this is often where it lands.
You will also see heart failure specialists, imaging specialists who focus on echo and nuclear studies, structural cardiologists who work on valves, and preventive or lipid specialists who concentrate on risk and cholesterol. And a cardiologist is not a cardiac surgeon; surgery is a separate specialty entirely, and most cardiology patients never need one.
Heart-healthy detour — the best Indian food in St. Louis.
### What can you do when the next opening is months away?
Assuming this is not an emergency, and emergencies go to 911, a long wait is a problem you can usually work on rather than simply accept. Five moves are worth making, and none of them require being difficult with anyone.
Get on the cancellation list, and ask how it actually works at that office. Some call from the top down, some text everyone at once, some only fill same-day gaps. Say clearly that you can come on short notice if that is true, and give them the number you actually answer. People who say yes to a Tuesday morning slot at nine the night before get seen months earlier than people who do not.
Ask the referring office to call over. A nurse or a physician describing why the referral was written often moves a patient up when a fax cannot. This is not a favor you are begging for; it is a normal part of how referrals get triaged.
Widen the map. Large groups run satellite offices, and the wait in O’Fallon MO or down toward Arnold can differ sharply from the wait at the main location, for the same group and the same insurance. Ask the scheduler to check every location, the far ones included.
Take the far appointment and keep looking. Book the date you can get, then keep the cancellation list working. Cancel only after something better is confirmed.
And solve the transportation question early rather than the night before. If driving to a suburban office is the obstacle, free and low-cost rides to medical appointments covers what exists in the metro, including options tied to certain insurance plans.
### Why new-patient waits run long, from the practice side
It helps to know what is happening on the other end of the phone, because it changes what you ask for. Schedulers are not gatekeepers holding out on you. They are working inside a template somebody else built.
A cardiologist’s week is divided into fixed blocks: clinic time, procedure time, reading time, hospital rounds. New-patient slots are a small share of clinic time, because a new patient takes far longer than a follow-up. When one physician leaves a group, those slots do not redistribute cleanly, and the backlog shows up for everyone.
Records are the other bottleneck, and it is the one patients can actually influence. Incoming referrals sit in a queue waiting to be triaged, and a referral with no note, no labs, and no tracing cannot be triaged. Somebody has to request the missing pieces, wait for them, and re-review. That round trip can add weeks, quietly, with nobody at fault.
So here is the honest division of labor. A scheduler can add you to a cancellation list, check other locations and other providers in the group, tell you what records are missing, flag your chart for the triage nurse, and tell you whether the practice is contracted with your plan. A scheduler cannot override clinical triage, promise what your visit will cost, tell you what your symptoms mean, or move you ahead of someone a physician ranked as more urgent.
Ask for the things in the first list and you will usually get them. Push for the things in the second and you will spend goodwill you may want later. Being pleasant and specific with the front desk is strategy as much as courtesy.
### How do you keep the cost from surprising you?
Ask before, not after. Cardiology bills arrive in pieces, and the pieces come from different places, which is why the total rarely matches what anyone expected.
A single visit can generate a physician charge, a facility charge if the location bills as a hospital department, a separate charge for each test, and a reading fee for whoever interprets the images. Confirm that the physician, the location, and the imaging site are all in network. Those can be three different answers.
If testing is ordered, ask the office for the procedure codes, then call your plan and ask what applies to your deductible and whether prior authorization is required. Advanced imaging often needs authorization, and a denial after the fact is far harder to fix than a phone call beforehand. If you are uninsured or paying cash, ask about a good faith estimate and about financial assistance, and ask before the appointment rather than at checkout.
Not sure who to call first? Whether you are self-referring, moving an existing condition to a new doctor after a move, or widening the search from Creve Coeur out to O’Fallon MO and down toward Arnold, it is easier when the options sit in one place. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the 8 signs you should see a cardiologist?
A.  There is no official list of eight, but the common reasons people get referred group neatly. Chest discomfort that appears with exertion and eases with rest. Breathlessness that is new for you. A racing, pounding, or skipping heartbeat. Fainting or near-fainting. Swelling in the ankles or legs. Blood pressure or cholesterol that will not come under control. A close relative with early heart disease. A murmur or an abnormal EKG someone noticed. Each is a reason to be evaluated, not a diagnosis, and the emergency symptoms described earlier still mean calling 911.
### Q. Is a cardiology referral serious?
A.  Usually it means your doctor wants a more specialized read, not that something dire has been found. Referrals are written for stable, routine reasons constantly: a number that drifted, a family history worth accounting for, a symptom worth ruling out before it becomes a question later. The signal to pay attention to is timing rather than the referral itself. If the office tells you to be seen within days, that is a message. Ask the referring nurse what urgency was assigned and what you should watch for while you wait for the appointment.
### Q. What are the three types of cardiologists?
A.  Most practices sort into three broad buckets. General or noninvasive cardiologists handle evaluation, medication, prevention, and follow-up, and they interpret the testing. Interventional cardiologists work in the catheterization lab, performing angiograms and placing stents. Electrophysiologists deal with rhythm: monitors, ablations, pacemakers, and defibrillators. Beyond those three you will find heart failure, imaging, structural, and preventive or lipid specialists. Most people begin with a general cardiologist, who refers onward if a narrower skill set is needed. You do not have to choose the right bucket yourself.
### Q. How do you know if a cardiologist is good?
A.  Start with what you can verify. Board certification in cardiovascular disease, an active state license, and hospital privileges are all things you can look up rather than guess at. Then judge what only you can judge: whether the doctor explains findings in words you actually follow, whether the office returns calls, whether your results reach your primary care doctor without you personally carrying them across town, and whether questions are welcomed rather than tolerated. A good visit ends with you able to repeat the plan back. Ranked lists are marketing; credentials, communication, and follow-through are evidence.
### Q. What not to do before seeing a cardiologist?
A.  Do not stop a prescribed medication on your own, and do not start a new supplement to look healthier on paper. Ask the office directly whether to fast, whether to hold caffeine, and whether to skip a morning dose, because instructions differ by test and only they know what is scheduled. Do not arrive without your medication list and prior records. Do not cancel because you happen to feel fine that morning, since a symptom that comes and goes is exactly what the visit is for. And do not spend the night before self-diagnosing online.
### Q. What can be mistaken for heart failure symptoms?
A.  Quite a lot, which is precisely why the workup exists. Breathlessness and swelling are not specific findings. Lung conditions, anemia, thyroid problems, kidney or liver disease, vein problems in the legs, sleep apnea, deconditioning, and side effects of certain medications can all produce a similar picture. The reverse happens too: heart problems sometimes show up as fatigue, a nighttime cough, or simply not being able to do what you could last year. That overlap is why a clinician orders tests instead of guessing, and why this page cannot tell you which one applies to you.
### Q. What are the five heart disease symptoms you should never ignore?
A.  Treat these as emergencies rather than reasons to book an appointment: chest pain or pressure, especially alongside sweating or nausea; shortness of breath while you are at rest; fainting or passing out; a sudden racing heartbeat with lightheadedness; and pain spreading into the jaw, neck, arm, or back. Symptoms can present differently in women and in people with diabetes, sometimes as unusual fatigue or discomfort that feels like indigestion. If any of these happen, call 911. Do not drive yourself, and do not wait to see whether it passes on its own.

## What a Limo Costs in St. Louis, and What the Hourly Rate Leaves Out
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-limo-costs-in-st-louis
The group text starts in March. Eight kids going to prom together, four sets of parents in Chesterfield trying to agree on a pickup order, and one mom who volunteered to make the calls because nobody else would. Three quotes come back. None of them are comparable in any way she can see.
A couple planning a September wedding hits a different version of the same wall. The shuttle quote covers four hours. Photos, the gap before the reception downtown, and the ride back out toward Sunset Hills add up to six. Nobody mentioned that the booking had a minimum on it, or where the clock starts.
Then there is the simplest math of all. Four friends in Cottleville, one night out downtown, wondering whether a car with a driver really costs more than two rideshares each way at surge pricing. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it does not, and the reason has almost nothing to do with the hourly rate.
### How much does it cost to rent a limo in St. Louis?
Almost every limo operator in the St. Louis metro bills by the hour with a minimum attached, commonly three to four hours on a weekend night and more on prom weekends and holiday dates. The hourly rate rises with vehicle size, and airport runs are often quoted as a flat point-to-point transfer instead.
Nobody publishes a verifiable rate card for this metro. Any single number you read online, including one in a guide like this, is a claim that owes you a written quote. What you can rely on is the shape of the pricing, which is remarkably consistent from one company to the next.
Price tracks the vehicle, and the ladder is easy to follow. A black sedan or a standard SUV sits at the bottom. A stretch sits above it. An executive sprinter, with the tall ceiling and individual seats, sits above that, and a full party bus usually sits at the top. Every step up adds passengers and adds hourly cost, so the useful question is not which vehicle you want. It is the smallest vehicle your group actually fits in.
Then the calendar moves the number again. A Tuesday airport transfer out of Chesterfield and a Saturday night in May are different products sold by the same company. Prom season, wedding season, graduation and New Year’s Eve all compress supply, and on those dates the minimum hours typically stretch. Airport work is the exception to the hourly rule, commonly sold as a flat fare priced on the pickup address, which is why a run from Sunset Hills and a run from Cottleville can be quoted differently for the same car.
### Why is the quoted hourly rate never the final bill?
Because the hourly rate is one line on an invoice with several. Gratuity is commonly added at eighteen to twenty percent, and it may or may not already sit inside the number you were quoted. Fuel or administrative surcharges, cleaning and damage deposits, overtime blocks and travel time all live alongside it.
Gratuity is the single most common misunderstanding. Some operators build the driver gratuity into the package and say so in the contract. Others add it at the end. A few manage both without meaning to, and the customer tips a second time in cash at the curb because nobody explained it. One sentence fixes this: is the driver gratuity already included in this total, and if it is, what percentage is it?
Surcharges are the next layer. A fuel surcharge, a booking or administrative fee, tolls, and parking at a downtown venue can each appear as a separate line. None of them are unreasonable on their own. What is unreasonable is finding out afterward, so ask for an all-in total in writing with taxes and fees already inside it.
Then there is the deposit that is not a payment. Most operators hold a refundable damage and cleaning deposit, and the cleaning clause is the one that bites. A spilled drink is usually forgiven. A sick passenger, glitter or confetti usually is not, and the fee is often fixed in the contract at a number nobody reads until it is charged.
### When does the clock actually start on a limo booking?
It may start before the car reaches you. Garage-to-garage billing means the meter runs from the moment the vehicle leaves the operator’s yard until it returns, not from your driveway to your last stop. In a metro this spread out, that difference can be an hour of billable time you never spent in the car.
Plenty of companies do not bill that way, and the ones that do are hiding nothing as long as it is on the contract. The trouble is the comparison. An operator quoting portal to portal and an operator quoting garage to garage can post similar hourly rates and land far apart on the total, and the cheaper-looking one is often the second. If your pickup is in Cottleville, ask where the yard is.
Overtime behaves the same way. Very few operators bill it by the minute. It is usually charged in blocks, commonly half hours or full hours, and the block starts the second you cross the line. Ten minutes late leaving a reception can cost the same as fifty. Build a cushion into the booking instead of hoping the night runs on schedule.
Nobody is driving tonight anyway — go eat the best Korean food in St. Louis.
### What should a written limo contract spell out?
Everything you agreed to on the phone. A usable contract names the exact vehicle or vehicle class, the passenger capacity, the pickup and drop-off addresses, the start and end times, whether billing is garage to garage or portal to portal, the all-in total with fees and gratuity broken out, the deposit, and the cancellation terms.
The clause people skip is vehicle substitution. Fleets break down, and every operator reserves the right to send something different. That is normal. What matters is what the contract promises when it happens: an equivalent or better vehicle at the same price, a refund, or nothing at all. If it promises nothing, you have agreed that a fourteen-passenger stretch can become two sedans on prom night.
Cancellation deadlines and weather policy belong in there too. Ask what happens if the wedding date moves, if a flight lands two hours late, if the passenger count drops. Get the answer in the document rather than in a text message, because the document is what governs after the person you spoke to no longer works there.
### How do you check that a limo operator is licensed and insured?
Ask for a certificate of insurance and read the name on it. A for-hire passenger vehicle should carry commercial auto liability rather than a personal policy, and the certificate should show the operator as the insured with coverage active on your event date. A legitimate company sends one without arguing about it.
Three more checks take a few minutes each. Confirm the chauffeur holds the license class required for the vehicle and passenger count being driven. Confirm the vehicle is registered and inspected for for-hire passenger service rather than as a private car. And confirm the business on the certificate is the business on the contract, because brokers who resell your booking to whichever operator is free that night are common and are not always disclosed.
This metro sits on a state line, and the rules are not identical on both sides. Missouri and Illinois regulate for-hire passenger carriers through their own agencies, and cities can add requirements on top. We are not going to tell you which rule applies to your booking, because those change and a blog post is the wrong place to learn them. Verify current requirements with the relevant state agency and your local authority, and ask the operator which authority licenses them.
One last signal, and it is a good one. Be wary of the quote that lands far below everybody else’s. Insurance, inspections, licensed chauffeurs and maintenance are the expensive parts of this business, and they are the parts a cut-rate operator trims first.
### What changes when the passengers are under twenty-one?
Alcohol changes the entire booking. When a vehicle is carrying minors, reputable operators run a dry car and enforce it, and many will end the night on the spot if alcohol turns up. The chauffeur is not being difficult. The company’s license, insurance and future are riding on that decision.
For the parent organizing eight kids in Chesterfield, that policy is the thing you are actually paying for. Ask what happens if alcohol is found, whether the car is searched, whether a chaperone is required or allowed, and whether the driver calls a parent or the police. Get the answer in writing, then forward it to the other three sets of parents before anyone pays a deposit.
Then handle the boring logistics, which are what usually go wrong. Fix one pickup address instead of six. Decide who signs the contract and carries responsibility for damage, because that is one adult, not eight families. Match the passenger count to the stated capacity, since fourteen passengers means fourteen seats and not fourteen plus two on laps. And book prom weekend months out.
### How do you fit a limo to a wedding timeline?
Work backward from the reception rather than forward from the ceremony. Most wedding transportation quotes fail on the gap in the middle: photographs, the drive downtown, the traffic, the twenty minutes nobody planned for. Count the hours the car is genuinely committed, add one, then compare that against the operator’s minimum.
The other trap is treating the wedding party and the guests as a single transportation problem. They are two. A stretch or a sprinter for the couple and the party is one booking. Shuttling sixty guests between a hotel and a venue is another, and shuttle work is often quoted its own way. Decide which one you are buying before you collect quotes, or you will compare two things that were never the same product.
Venue geography drives the whole number, which is why the venue decision and the transportation decision belong in one conversation. A ceremony and reception under the same roof can shrink the car down to a single transfer. Two sites on opposite ends of the metro can double it. If you are still deciding, start with our guides to the best wedding venues in St. Louis and the best event venues in St. Louis for your next celebration. The kitchen runs against the same clock the cars do, which our roundup of wedding and event caterers across the metro gets into.
### Why is the cheapest quote usually the one with the surprise on it?
Look at it from the operator’s side and the minimum stops looking greedy. A two-hour booking blocks the same Saturday evening slot as a six-hour one, because the vehicle and the chauffeur are committed either way. The minimum exists to price the slot, not the ride.
Run a Saturday in May from the yard. The vehicle is detailed before it leaves and again when it returns. The chauffeur is paid for the shift, not for the hours you sat in the car, plus the empty miles out to your driveway and back. Commercial insurance on a for-hire passenger vehicle is a fixed monthly cost that does not care whether the car moved. Fuel, inspections, maintenance on a heavy vehicle carrying people, and somebody answering dispatch at midnight all sit underneath that one hourly number.
If your group is larger or you want everyone riding together, compare a limo against renting a party bus in St. Louis.

Thinner coverage, a subcontracted vehicle, an older car, or fees that surface after you commit. In our experience the boring, itemized, slightly higher all-in total is frequently the cheaper one by the time the night ends.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is a limo for 7 hours?
A.  Seven hours is billed the same way three hours is: the hourly rate multiplied by the hours, plus gratuity, fees and any travel time. Because seven hours clears almost every minimum, the minimum stops mattering and vehicle size becomes the main driver of the total. Ask for an all-in written figure for the full seven hours rather than a rate, confirm whether the clock runs garage to garage, and confirm what an eighth hour costs, since overtime is usually charged in blocks rather than by the minute.
### Q. How much to hire a limo for 1 hour?
A.  Usually you cannot, at least not on a weekend. Nearly every operator applies a minimum of roughly three to four hours on Friday and Saturday nights, and longer on prom weekends and holidays, so a single hour still gets billed as the minimum. The exception is airport work, which is commonly sold as a flat point-to-point transfer priced on the pickup address rather than by the hour. If your trip is genuinely one leg, ask for the transfer price instead of an hourly quote and compare on that basis.
### Q. Are limos cheaper than Uber?
A.  For a short trip with two people, no, and it is not close. Rideshare wins point to point. The math shifts with group size, surge pricing and waiting. Four to fourteen people making several stops across an evening, with a driver who stays with the car between them, can land nearer a stack of surge-priced rides than most people expect, and nobody has to reorder at closing time. Run your own numbers for the specific night: passengers, stops, hours, and what surge does downtown after midnight.
### Q. Why does no one use Limos anymore?
A.  People do, just for fewer occasions. The stretch limo lost most of its everyday work to two shifts at once. Rideshare took over short trips and airport runs, while executive SUVs, sprinter vans and party buses took over group travel because they are easier to get in and out of and feel less dated. What remains is concentrated in weddings, proms, milestone birthdays, group nights out and corporate airport work. The category did not die. It narrowed to the events where arriving together is part of the point.
### Q. What replaced limos?
A.  Mostly three things. Black car and executive SUV service took the business sedan and airport work. Sprinter vans and party buses took the group celebrations, because a tall cabin with real seats beats a long bench when fourteen people are dressed up. Rideshare took nearly everything short and spontaneous. Most companies that used to be limo companies now run all of it out of one yard, which is why a request for a limo quote often comes back with three vehicle options and only one of them is a stretch.
### Q. When did limos go out of style?
A.  The shift is usually placed in the 2010s, when rideshare apps became the default for short trips and the long stretch started reading as dated rather than special. Corporate travel had already moved toward black sedans and SUVs, and group celebrations moved toward party buses and sprinters across roughly the same decade. Style is not the whole story, though. Prom and wedding demand held up, which is why a stretch is straightforward to book in this metro in January and hard to get on short notice in May.
### Q. Do rich people still ride in limos?
A.  Some do, mainly for weddings, formal events and occasions where a stretch is the look they want. Day to day, the money moved to chauffeured black SUVs and sedans, which are more discreet, easier to park downtown and simpler to step out of in front of a venue. The vehicle changed more than the habit did. Hiring a professional driver is still ordinary at the top of the market. The long white stretch simply became a celebration vehicle rather than a status one.

## Family of Four, Same Ice, $28 Apart: What Ice Skating Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ice-skating-in-st-louis-what-it-costs
Scrape. A blade catches, slides an inch farther than anybody planned, and a small hand slaps the boards hard enough to sting through the glove. Somebody laughs. Somebody else sits down on the ice whether they meant to or not, and the cold comes straight through the seat of their jeans.
That is the first five minutes of almost every family skate. The real question is what it costs, and around here the answer changes at the city line. Ice skating around St. Louis is billed in two pieces, and the biggest swing on that bill has nothing to do with which rink has the prettiest photos. It comes down to your address.
### What does ice skating cost?
Two charges, not one: admission to a public skate session, plus skate rental if you do not own a pair. At Brentwood Ice Rink a non-resident pays $7 admission and $3 for rental. At Centene Community Ice Center in Maryland Heights it is $12 and $5. Residents of the city that runs each rink pay less admission. Check the rink’s own page the day you go, because rates and sessions change.
Here is the part most rink roundups skip. Both of those buildings post a resident price and a non-resident price, side by side, on their own city pages. Brentwood charges its residents $4 for a public session and everyone else $7, with skate rental at $3 either way, and kids 3 and younger skate free with a paid admission. Maryland Heights charges its residents $5 at Centene and non-residents $12, with $5 skate rental for both.
Now put four people on the bench, rental skates thudding down beside them, laces still cold from the shelf. A Maryland Heights family of four, all renting, pays $40 at Centene. The family of four that drove in from the next town over pays $68 for the same session, on the same ice, under the same lights. At Brentwood, a Brentwood family of four pays $28 and a family from anywhere else pays $40.
Same frozen water, same cold on your cheeks: for a family of four, a $28 gap at Centene and a $12 gap at Brentwood, decided by which side of a city line you sleep on.
To check it yourself today, open the rink’s own fee page: Brentwood Ice Rink public sessions (the rink’s number is 314-963-8680) or Centene Community Ice Center page on the Maryland Heights city site. The resident price belongs to people who live in the city that runs the rink, so a Brentwood address gets the Brentwood rate and a Maryland Heights address gets the Centene rate. Everyone else pays the non-resident line. So do this today: if your own town runs a rink, open its fee page and find the resident line first, then call 314-963-8680 if you want Brentwood’s current fees confirmed before you load the car.
The add-ons are where an outing grows without anyone noticing, usually at the rental counter, with its smell of damp boot leather and a stack of skates warm from the last session’s feet. Some rinks rent helmets and some expect you to bring one from home. Brentwood says its skating aids, the plastic frames a beginner leans on and pushes across the ice, are free to use and handed out first come, first served, so on a busy session the early family gets them. Ask about lockers before you assume they are included. If you own skates you skip rental and pay for sharpening a few times a season instead.
There are other shapes for the same day. Brentwood sells public session pass packages at the front desk, and group rates and party packages price differently again, usually per head with a minimum. If you are pricing a birthday, compare the rink against the best family fun centers across the St. Louis suburbs, because the per-child math is rarely what you assume.
### Why is the public skate window so narrow?
Because the sheet is already booked. Listen to a rink between sessions: the low hum of the resurfacer crossing back and forth, the ice behind it wet and glassy, a hockey bag thudding onto a bench. A rink sells its ice in blocks, and hockey teams, figure skaters and learn-to-skate classes take a lot of them. Public skate is a scheduled session dropped into the gaps, not open ice all day.
That one fact separates a good outing from a wasted drive. Brentwood says it runs public sessions almost daily year-round, and in the same breath says sessions are subject to change with little to no notice. Check the rink calendar the morning you go. Not last week, and not the flyer stuck to the fridge.
If you have a nervous first-timer, pick the quietest-looking session on the calendar rather than the most convenient one. Fewer bodies, more wall to hold onto, and nobody whipping past at hockey speed while your kid is still learning to stand.
Show up earlier than the start time. The rental counter is where the line forms. At Brentwood the rental shelves run from hockey skates in size 1 through 14 and figure skates from youth size 7 through adult size 14, and somebody is always hunting for the last pair in their size. Every minute spent waiting for a size 2 is a minute of the session you already paid for.
### Which rinks does the St. Louis metro have?
More than most people realize, and they are not interchangeable. The metro has an outdoor rink in Forest Park, rinks run by city parks departments, and the Blues’ practice complex in Maryland Heights. Season length, public skate hours and fees differ at each one.
Steinberg Skating Rink sits in Forest Park and is the outdoor one, which makes it the postcard: breath clouding under the lights, cold air on your face. It is also the one most exposed to weather. Brentwood posts a monthly ice schedule on its city site. Centene Community Ice Center in Maryland Heights is the official practice home of the St. Louis Blues and runs public skating too.
We are not ranking them. Price is the reason to look twice: if your own city runs a rink, the resident rate is often the cheapest ice you can get. The arena’s own site is the only place that answer stays current.
### What should you wear to skate?
Dress for a cold, wet floor rather than a cold day outside. Long pants, never shorts, thin gloves for everyone, socks that come up past the boot line, and layers you can shed. The ice is cold, falling on it is wet, and the rail feels colder than the air around it.
Gloves are the item people skip and regret within fifteen minutes. Hands go down first in a fall, other skaters are wearing blades, and cold wet fingers end a session faster than tired legs ever will. They do not need to be ski gloves. Any thin, dry pair does the job.
Socks are the second one. One pair of thin-to-medium socks that reaches above the boot, not two thick pairs, which bunch up and rub. Throw a dry spare pair in the bag for the ride home.
Skip scarf ends, drawstrings and anything long enough to catch. A hat is fine. A heavy winter coat is usually too much indoors once a kid has been moving for ten minutes, so a fleece with a light jacket over it beats one enormous parka.
### How do you make a first time on the ice go well?
Keep it short and lace them tight. A first session of thirty to forty-five minutes ends on a good note instead of a meltdown. Rented skates have to be snug through the ankle, tight enough that a child cannot lift the heel, because a loose boot is why beginners say their ankles bend.
That tightness feels wrong to parents. Loose skates are not comfortable, they are unusable, and the wobbling ankles everyone blames on weak legs usually come from laces done up like sneakers. Snug at the toe, tightest across the ankle, and check them again twenty minutes in.
Helmets for young children, and a bike helmet from the garage is often fine. Confirm the rink’s policy before you go. Ice is unforgiving in a backward fall, and small kids fall backward.
Get a skate aid early if the rink has them. Leaning on that frame turns the first half hour from misery into visible progress, and on a busy session they go to whoever asks first.
Then teach the fall and the getting up, right at the wall. Bend the knees, keep the hands out of the way, go forward rather than backward, then get to hands and knees, plant one blade and push up. Ten minutes of that beats an hour of dragging a crying child along the rail. If it goes well and lessons come up, the questions worth asking are the same ones in our guide to what to know before signing your kid up for gymnastics in St. Louis.
Skating makes everybody hungry. Warm up afterward at the best restaurants in Edwardsville.
### How do you keep the calendar and the weather from wrecking the day?
Two checks, both on the day itself. Look at the rink’s public skate calendar that morning, and if the rink is outdoors, look at the temperature. Outdoor ice can close for warm spells and rain, and that call is often made only a few hours ahead. Indoors, read the session name as well as the time: Brentwood’s themed Galactic Glow Fridays cost more than a regular public session, $8 for residents and $10 for non-residents, with the same $3 skate rental.
Indoor rinks are weatherproof but not schedule-proof. A tournament or a private rental can swallow a block of public skate, and school breaks tend to bring both extra sessions and packed boards.
Have a backup that does not need ice. If the session is cancelled or the rental line is out the door, our roundup of the best indoor play places for kids in St. Louis covers the winter options that hold up with a carful of disappointed children.
Build the day around the session rather than the other way around. The session itself, plus rental time at the front end and prying boots off sore feet at the back, adds up to a solid block. Nobody skates well hungry.
### What it takes to keep a sheet of ice frozen
From the rink’s side of the counter, the building runs whether anybody is skating or not. An ice sheet is a refrigeration job: chilled lines under the floor, air kept dry so the ice stays hard, and a resurfacer with a trained driver.
That is why the public window is narrow. Contracted ice from hockey leagues, figure skating clubs and learn-to-skate programs helps pay for the building, and public skate is sold into what is left over.
None of that is a complaint about pricing. When you see a short public skate on the calendar and a wall of hockey filling the rest of the day, you are looking at a building paying for itself. And when your own city runs the rink, part of that building is already yours.
So the plan is short. Check the calendar the morning of, price admission and rental as two separate things, look for a resident rate, dress for a wet cold floor, lace the skates tight and keep the first session short. Do that and a cold afternoon on the ice is one of the cheaper good days a family gets all winter.
Not sure which rink fits your weekend? Start with what is near you, then work outward. Browse skating rinks listed across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then check that arena’s own public skate calendar for current session times, resident rates and fees before you get in the car.
If you run the rink, the skate-sharpening shop or the learn-to-skate class, families are hunting for you every cold weekend. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your sessions and lessons in front of them so you get more customers from those searches. Put your rink or program on the map.
