### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to get $5 movie tickets at AMC?
A.  Chain-specific discount days are the route, and at AMC that has long meant a weekly discounted showtime tied to the free AMC Stubs rewards account rather than an open public sale. The rate is not the same everywhere. Big-city and premium locations price differently than suburban ones, premium formats are typically excluded, and the program terms change. Sign up for the free tier, sign in before you check out, and confirm the current day and price for your specific location in the AMC app rather than trusting any figure you read online.
### Q. How to get 50% off movie tickets?
A.  Percentage-off savings usually come from how you pay, not from the showtime. Warehouse clubs, credit unions, employers and membership organizations regularly resell theater gift cards and ticket bundles below face value, and that discount applies before anything else. Rewards points are the other half: free tiers at every major chain accumulate points that convert to tickets or concessions. Stack a below-face gift card against a discount-day price and the effective savings can get steep. Verify blackout terms and format restrictions on the card itself, because the fine print controls whether it works.
### Q. How to get $1 movie tickets?
A.  Dollar-level pricing lives in summer children’s series and one-off industry promotions, not in the regular schedule. The big chains have run seasonal kids programs for years under names like Regal Summer Movie Express, Cinemark Summer Movie Clubhouse and the Marcus Theatres kids series, showing older family titles on weekday mornings at a token price. Industry-wide discount days have also run in recent years, with the date and price announced annually. Participation, pricing and titles vary by location and by season, so check the chain’s summer schedule page before you plan around it.
### Q. Where can I watch movies for $5?
A.  Look at the low-cost end of the physical screen map: weekday matinees at first-run multiplexes, second-run and discount houses that pick up titles a few weeks after release, and smaller independent single screens with simpler pricing and fewer upcharges. Second-run houses are the most reliable of the three because their entire model is lower pricing on older titles. You give up the recliner and the premium sound, and you accept that the film has been out a while. Prices are set locally, so call the theater or check its site.
### Q. How can I get 5 dollar movie tickets?
A.  Run the subscription math and think in effective cost per movie instead of sticker price. A paid monthly plan divides its fee across however many films you actually see, so a frequent moviegoer can push the real per-ticket cost far below the posted price while an occasional one pays more than they would have. Art-house annual memberships work the same way, trading a yearly fee for a lower rate on every visit. Divide the current fee by your honest monthly attendance, then compare that number to what you pay now.
### Q. What movies are free right now?
A.  Free screenings run all year in the metro, but they are scheduled by institutions rather than theaters, so they never show up in ticketing apps. Public library branches on both sides of the river host family and classic film afternoons. Municipal parks departments run outdoor movie nights through the warm months. College campuses and student organizations screen films that are often open to the public. Neighborhood associations and business districts add their own summer series. Check library event calendars, city parks pages and campus activity listings for what is playing this week.

## Pilates 3x a Week: $225. Every Day: $250. One STL Studio
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-pilates-three-times-a-week-enough-a-st-louis-guide
Sore thighs on the stairs the morning after. That is the first receipt from a reformer class: the carriage rolls out, the springs drag it home, and somewhere around the tenth rep your legs start to shake on the footbar. By the second week you know the sound of the room: the soft clunk of a carriage meeting its stopper, springs clipped and unclipped between exercises, an instructor telling you to slow down. By the third week the question in your head has changed from “can I do this” to “how often can I afford to do this.”
At Casa di Pilates on South Kingshighway, it costs $225. That is the studio’s 12-class monthly plan, with a 3-month minimum. Walk in at the $35 drop-in rate twelve times instead and the same month runs $420. At the same studio, twelve drop-ins at $35 come to $420, $195 more than the $225 plan. Now the line worth screenshotting: there, going every single day costs just $25 a month more than going three times a week. Unlimited, one class a day, is $250.
At Freeman Pilates on Morgan Ford Road in Tower Grove, the price works differently. Every monthly membership comes out to $25 a group class: 8 classes is $200 and 12 is $300. There is no discount for showing up more. So the third weekly class costs a flat $100 a month at Freeman, and $55 at Casa, where 8 classes is $170. Either way, you pay it in cash and in the walk back to the car with your legs still humming.
Which means the real question hiding inside “is three a week enough” is a quieter one: is that third class worth $55 to $100 a month to you? Your body will usually tell you two is enough. Your calendar, and your bank app, decide the rest.
### Is Pilates 3 times a week enough?
Yes, and for most healthy adults it is more than enough. The federal Physical Activity Guidelines say adults need muscle-strengthening activity at least 2 days each week, and reformer work, with springs and your own body weight as the load, is strength work. Two well-taught sessions cover that floor. Three gets you to the harder exercises faster and makes the machine start to feel like yours instead of something you are being talked through.
Your body adapts between sessions, not during them, so stacking classes back to back is not automatically better. The real test is the one you take in February, when it is dark by dinner and the car is cold. Two sessions a week for a year beats three a week for six weeks every time. Choose the number you will still be showing up for after the holidays.
There is one caveat worth taking seriously. If you are pregnant, recovering from surgery, or managing a back or spine condition, frequency is the wrong first question. Clear it with your physician or physical therapist and tell the studio before you book. Casa di Pilates says post-op clients need a doctor’s clearance before joining group classes, and that private sessions are ideal for tailored rehab.
Want to find out whether three a week fits your life before you sign up for it? Casa sells a one-week unlimited intro for $80. Use it hard: go as many times as your schedule really allows in that one week, then count. If you made it three times without wrecking your week, you have your answer and your plan. If you are brand new to the machines, Freeman offers a 50-minute introductory private session on the reformer for $45, built to teach you the equipment before you walk into a group class.
Then read the fine print before you pick a plan, standing in your grip socks on the studio floor if you have to, because this is where people quietly lose money. At Freeman, classes you do not use do not roll over into the next month’s membership. At Casa, the 12-class and unlimited memberships carry a 3-month minimum, and a group class needs 12 hours’ notice to cancel. A late cancel costs $10 and a no-show costs $15.
### The kinds of Pilates you can book around St. Louis
Walk into a studio and the floor tells you what you are buying: a stack of rolled mats against the wall, or a row of reformers with their springs hooked in a line. The word Pilates covers several different products at different prices, and booking the wrong one is the most common reason a beginner decides the method is not for them.
### Group mat classes
Mat Pilates is the entry point: you, a mat, and maybe a small ball, a ring or a light band. It is usually the cheapest option, and it turns up in gyms, community centers and studio side rooms all over the region. Plenty of independent gyms and studios around town fold a mat class into a regular membership, which makes it the least risky way to find out whether you like the work at all.
### Hot mat
Some studios heat the room. Casa di Pilates runs hot infrared mat classes under what it calls sunlit infrared panels, and asks you to bring fitted breathable clothing, a water bottle and a sweat towel. It advises against heated classes during pregnancy.
### Group reformer classes
The reformer is the sliding carriage with springs, straps and a footbar, and group reformer is what most people mean now when they say they do Pilates. Spring resistance makes it real strength work, and the moving carriage makes it unforgiving of sloppy alignment. Expect to pay more than mat. Grip socks are mandatory at Casa, along with leggings or shorts, nothing loose.
### Private and duet sessions
A private is one instructor, one client and the whole equipment set. A duet splits the session between two people. At Freeman, a single private session is $85. At Casa, a one-on-one mat or reformer private is $100 and a duet is $120 for the pair. A handful of privates up front, then group classes, is the usual way to learn fast without paying private rates forever.
### Clinical Pilates
Some physical therapy clinics use Pilates equipment in rehab, delivered by a licensed clinician rather than a fitness instructor. It looks similar and it is not the same thing. The same care you would put into choosing a chiropractor applies here: credentials, scope and a clear plan matter more than the room.
### How long before you notice anything?
Sooner than you would guess for some things, slower than you want for others. Most people feel more aware of their posture within the first few sessions, largely because an instructor has spent the hour telling them where their ribs are. That is coordination, not strength, and it fades if you stop.
Real strength follows the same timeline as any other resistance training. Early gains are mostly your nervous system learning to use muscle you already have. Visible change takes longer and depends on sleep, food and everything you do outside the studio. A rough arc:
The first few weeks. You learn the names of the exercises and stop feeling lost. Soreness shows up in muscles you did not know you had.
The second month. Movements feel coordinated instead of improvised. Plenty of people notice they sit differently at a desk.
A few months in. Stairs, grocery bags and getting up off the floor feel easier.
If nothing has changed after two solid months, the problem is usually the class, not the method. Too large, too easy or too mixed in level. Switch formats before you quit.
Price your own three-a-week month before you commit to it. Shortlist two or three studios close enough that you will really go on a cold night, then ask each one the same three things: the per-class cost after the intro offer ends, whether unused classes roll over, and the cancellation window. Start with Pilates studios listed across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you run a Pilates studio, teach classes or rent out a reformer room, the people doing this exact math are your next customers, and they are comparing you line by line. Put your studio where they look and get more customers.
### How do you pick a studio and an instructor?
By asking questions before you pay, the step almost nobody takes. Instructor training varies enormously, from short workshops to long programs with supervised teaching and testing. So ask directly: where did you train, and how long was the program? A well-trained instructor answers happily. Anyone who gets defensive has told you something useful.
Ask about class size, whether the first visit includes someone watching you move, how they handle an injury, and whether classes are leveled. Then take a class and watch one thing. Does the instructor correct you by name? An instructor who never leaves the front of the room is running group fitness on Pilates equipment. That might be exactly what you want. Just know what you are buying.
If you are weighing this against other options, the two disciplines often share buildings, and comparing the yoga studios across St. Louis alongside your Pilates shortlist is a sensible way to decide where the money goes.
### What a first class feels like
Less intimidating than the equipment suggests. Arrive early, fill out a health form, and someone will show you how the carriage, footbar, straps and springs work. Then you lie on your back and breathe, which feels like cheating for about a minute.
Footwork on the bar comes next. It looks easy and it is not. Somewhere in the middle you will be asked to do something that feels physically impossible while the person on the next machine makes it look effortless. That passes. You will be told to slow down more than you expect, because Pilates rewards small ranges done precisely over big ranges done fast. Strong lifters fail quiet sets of leg circles all the time. It is a control problem, and control is the whole point.
The next day, expect soreness in an odd map: deep abdominals, inner thighs, upper back, the sides of your hips. The second class feels far less confusing than the first, and that is usually the moment people decide whether they are staying.
Not Pilates at all, but routine vet care runs on the same rhythm question.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Pilates a good way to lose weight?
A.  It can support weight loss, but it is not an efficient calorie burner next to running, cycling or circuit training. Weight change follows your whole week: what you eat, how much you move and how you sleep. Where Pilates helps is the part people usually quit over. It builds strength and joint comfort that make the rest of your activity sustainable. Pair it with walking and reasonable eating, and it earns its place.
### Q. How much is a regular Pilates class?
A.  In St. Louis, two studio price lists show the range. Casa di Pilates charges $35 for a drop-in class, and Freeman Pilates sells a 5-class card for $150. Monthly memberships bring the per-class cost down: Freeman charges $25 a class on its memberships, and Casa’s 12-class month is $225. Intro offers are usually cheaper than what you will pay long term, so compare the per-class cost after the intro ends.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in Pilates?
A.  It is a rule of thumb about effort and control, not an official principle of the method. The common version says work at roughly eighty percent of your maximum and keep the rest in reserve for form, breath and precision. Push to failure on a reformer and your alignment collapses, which is the moment the exercise stops doing its job. Some instructors use the phrase differently, so ask yours which version they mean.
### Q. Does Pilates flatten your belly?
A.  Partly, and not the way the marketing implies. You cannot spot-reduce fat from one area. What Pilates builds is deep abdominal and postural strength, which changes how your midsection holds when you stand and sit. Many people look leaner through the middle after a few months without losing much weight, simply because they carry themselves differently. Actual fat loss follows your overall eating and activity.
### Q. What are the three C's of Pilates?
A.  Most instructors name concentration, control and centering. Centering means working from the deep muscles of the trunk. Control means every movement is deliberate, never flung. Concentration means paying attention instead of moving on autopilot. The lists vary: many teachers add precision, breath and flow, and studios rank them differently. If your instructor uses another set, that is a difference of tradition, not a mistake.
### Q. What are common mistakes in Pilates?
A.  Rushing is the big one. Close behind: holding your breath, gripping through the neck and shoulders instead of working from the trunk, and choosing springs by ego rather than by what lets you hold your form. Beginners also hide limitations from the instructor, which is how a manageable back issue turns into a bad week. And a money mistake: buying a membership with unused classes that do not roll over, then missing half of them.
### Q. Is Pilates basically yoga?
A.  No, though they overlap enough to confuse people and often share a building. Yoga centers on breath, held postures and, depending on the style, a meditative side. Pilates is built around controlled repetitions, often against spring resistance on equipment. Yoga generally leans toward flexibility and breath. Pilates leans toward trunk strength and movement control. Plenty of people do both, and they complement each other more than they compete.

## Where to Park at St. Louis Lambert Airport
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-park-at-st-louis-lambert-airport
It is 4:40 a.m. in St. Peters and the car is already loaded. Two bags, a car seat, and a boarding pass on a phone sitting at nineteen percent. The flight leaves at 6:15. You have driven to this airport a hundred times, and you still do not know, honestly, where you are going to leave the car for the next nine days.
A few miles east, somebody in Bridgeton is running the same problem in the other direction. Two nights. Home Thursday. Parking close to the door costs more per day, but the trip is short, so the total stays small. That is the whole calculation, and for that trip it is the right one.
And a family up in Godfrey IL is an hour north with a cousin who has offered to drive them down and drop them at the curb, if everybody can agree on which terminal. Nobody can agree on which terminal. That one is fixable, and it is the mistake that ruins the most mornings.
St. Louis Lambert International Airport, STL on your ticket, is not a hard airport to park at. It is an easy airport to park at wrong. Two terminals in separate buildings, several tiers of lots, a shuttle system, and a curb that changes depending on your airline. Here is how the choices actually break down, and what each one costs you in time.
### Should I park in short-term or long-term parking at the airport?
Let the length of the trip decide, not the sign at the entrance. One or two nights, park in the garage attached to your terminal and buy back the time. Three days or more, the daily maximum starts to dominate, so an economy, long-term or off-site lot with a shuttle wins. Confirm current rates at flystl.com.
The reason is arithmetic, not preference. Every option at STL settles into a daily rate once you are past the first few hours, and the difference between the closest garage and a remote lot is a per-day difference. On a two-night trip that gap is small enough that most travelers would rather walk sixty steps to the door in February. On a ten-day trip, the same gap multiplies by ten.
There is a second variable people skip entirely: what time you come home. A remote lot and a shuttle are a perfectly good idea at nine in the morning. They are a longer, colder idea at eleven at night after a two-hour delay, with a sleeping kid on your shoulder and a bag that lost a wheel in Denver. If the return leg lands late, weight the decision back toward the garage even on a longer trip.
And if you are only pulling in to hand somebody a bag or collect them from the door, the answer is neither. There is normally a brief free grace period in the garages for exactly that kind of quick in-and-out. Confirm the current terms at flystl.com before you count on it, because the airport sets that rule and it does change.
### What are your actual parking options at STL?
Six, broadly, and they sort by how much time you are buying back. Lambert runs two terminals, Terminal 1 and Terminal 2, and they are separate buildings with their own parking and their own curbs. A free inter-terminal shuttle connects them. Which side you want depends entirely on the airline printed on your boarding pass.
### The terminal garages
Closest, covered, and the most expensive per day. You park, you walk, you are inside. No shuttle, no waiting, no standing in weather with luggage. That is worth real money on a short trip, on a bad-weather day, with small children, with anybody who does not walk far comfortably, or on any return that lands after dark.
The catch is that each garage belongs to its terminal. Park in the wrong one and you have not lost your car, but you have added a shuttle ride to both ends of your trip. Check the boarding pass, then check the overhead signs on the airport roadway, which split the two terminals well before you commit.
### The airport’s economy and long-term lots
These are surface lots on airport property, priced below the garages and served by airport shuttles or a longer walk depending on the lot. The advantage that gets overlooked is simplicity: it is still the airport, so there is no third party in the loop, no separate reservation, and no outside company holding your keys or your dates.
The trade is exposure and time. Surface parking means your windshield sees whatever the week brings, and you are adding a shuttle leg at both ends. Lot names, locations and availability get adjusted from time to time, so pull the current list off flystl.com the week you travel rather than trusting a lot name you remember from two years ago.
### Off-site private lots and shuttles
Independent lots sit near the airport and run their own shuttles to the terminals. As a category they are usually the lowest daily rate, they often discount a reservation made in advance, and some offer covered spaces or a valet-style hand-off. For a long trip, that is a meaningful saving repeated across every day you are gone.
Read the terms before you book, because this is the option with the most fine print. Shuttle frequency, hours of operation, whether the shuttle runs overnight, what happens if your flight comes back a day late, and the cancellation policy all vary by operator. So does whether your reservation is tied to your license plate. Ask, and keep the confirmation on your phone.
### Valet
Valet is the shortest path from your driver seat to the terminal door, and where it is offered it sits at or above the top of the self-park range. You pull up, hand over the keys, and walk in. For a tight connection, a business trip measured in hours, or a traveler managing bags alone, that is sometimes exactly the right purchase.
### The cell phone waiting lot and curbside drop-off
The cell phone waiting lot exists so nobody circles the terminal loop. Your driver waits there, free, until you text that you are standing at the curb with your bag in hand. Then they pull up once, load, and leave. Waiting at the curb itself is not allowed, and enforcement is real.
Drop-off has the same terminal trap as parking. Departures and arrivals curbs are separate, and each terminal has its own. Tell your driver the terminal number, not the airline, and confirm the terminal on your boarding pass rather than on memory, because airline assignments do change.
### Hotel park-and-fly packages
Several hotels near the airport bundle a night’s stay with parking for the length of your trip and a shuttle to the terminal. For a 6 a.m. departure after an hour’s drive, or for a family that would otherwise be awake at three in the morning, the package can be a better deal than it looks once you count the night you would have slept badly anyway. Confirm how many parking days are included and how the shuttle runs at that hour.
### How do you decide between parking, a ride and being dropped off?
Three inputs decide it: how long you are gone, how many people are traveling, and what time you leave and land. Parking is priced per day, a ride is priced per trip. So the longer you are gone, the better a ride looks, and the more people you take, the worse it looks against one car.
Run it that way instead of guessing. A two-night trip for one person is almost always a parking trip, because two round-trip fares beat two days of parking only rarely. A two-week trip for one person flips completely, since the fare stays the same while the parking meter keeps counting. Rideshare, taxi and transit each behave differently at 4 a.m. and at midnight, which we cover in more detail in our guide to getting around St. Louis by rides, shuttles and MetroLink.
Party size is the variable people misjudge worst. Four adults with checked bags frequently do not fit in one standard rideshare vehicle, so you are buying two, or paying up for a larger class, and the math moves fast. At that point a single pre-booked vehicle can be the cheaper and calmer option, which is why it helps to know what a limo costs in St. Louis before you assume it is out of reach.
Being dropped off is free only on paper. Somebody is making two round trips to the airport, one of them at an hour nobody enjoys, and if your flight slips they are sitting in the cell phone lot burning their evening. Offer it as a favor with a real cost attached, and have a backup plan if it falls through the night before.
One more case worth naming. If the itinerary is complicated, several legs, a cruise connection, a group flying from different cities, the ground plan gets built at the same time as the flights, not the night before. That is one of the situations where knowing when to use a travel agent in St. Louis saves more than it costs.
Home from the trip? Next on the list: choosing an orthodontist in St. Louis.
### How much time should you actually leave?
Build the morning backward from boarding time, not from departure time. Boarding usually closes well before the plane pushes back, and everything ahead of it stacks: the drive, parking, the shuttle wait, the shuttle loop, the walk, bag drop, and security. Where you park changes that stack by a lot more than most people budget for.
Shuttles are the piece that surprises people. A shuttle is not a taxi. It runs on a headway, so you wait for it, and then it makes its loop, and both of those are dead time you did not spend when you parked in the garage. Add the walk from your row to the shuttle stop with your bags, and a remote lot can quietly cost you half an hour on each end.
Then there is the terminal question, which is the expensive one. Terminal 1 and Terminal 2 are separate buildings. If you park at the wrong terminal you ride the free inter-terminal shuttle to fix it, and that shuttle is time you never planned for, on a morning where you had none to give. Southwest Airlines operates out of Terminal 2. Everything else, check the boarding pass.
Security is variable and you cannot control it. Early morning banks, Sunday afternoons, spring break weeks and holiday Mondays all run heavy, and the expedited lanes keep their own hours, so the lane you counted on may not be open at 4:45 a.m. Plan for the slow version of the line and be pleasantly surprised.
Returning a rental car is its own step, not a rounding error. You are dropping the car, waiting for a bus or making a walk, then joining the same bag-drop and security lines as everybody else. Treat it as a separate block on the schedule.
### What goes wrong, and how do you avoid it?
Almost all of it is one of six things, and five of them are preventable from your kitchen table. The wrong terminal, a dead battery, a forgotten row number, a full lot, a reservation that does not match the car, and ice. None of these are exotic. They are just the ones nobody plans for.
Wrong terminal is number one by a wide margin. Two terminals, two sets of parking, two curbs, and a boarding pass that people glance at instead of read. Look at the terminal number the night before, tell whoever is driving, and then look at the overhead signs again on the airport roadway. Airlines do get reassigned, so last year’s answer is not this year’s.
A dead battery on return is the classic long-trip failure, and cold weather makes it worse. If your battery is already three or four years old and slow to crank, deal with it before the trip rather than at eleven at night in a dark lot. Make sure your dome light and any accessory are actually off when you walk away.
Photograph the sign. Every time. Row, aisle, level, section, lot name, and the shuttle stop number if there is one. You will remember it perfectly for four days and not at all on the eighth, and a photo with a timestamp takes three seconds. While you are there, take a picture of the entry ticket or the license plate on your reservation confirmation.
Lots fill. Thanksgiving week, the days around Christmas, spring break and big event weekends all put pressure on the cheaper lots first, because everybody had the same clever idea. If you are traveling in a peak window, reserve where reservations are offered and have a second lot in mind. Check lot status on flystl.com the morning you leave.
Not staying at a hotel? Here is what a St. Louis guest house actually is.
If the car is a rental rather than your own, read how to rent a car in St. Louis before you get to the counter.
Still shopping for the bag itself? Here is what to avoid when buying luggage in St. Louis.
Not sure parking is even the right call for this trip? Compare it against the other ways to get to the St. Louis airport and what each one costs.
Two smaller ones that bite. Off-site reservations are often tied to a license plate, so if you swap cars at the last minute, update the booking or you will be sorting it out at the gate. And a surface lot after an ice storm is a surface lot: your car may be under a sheet of ice, so throw a scraper and a pair of gloves in the trunk even on a summer departure, because winter travel is when this actually matters.
Still deciding how you are getting to the gate? Sort the ground plan before the travel week gets close, because the cheap options are the ones that sell out first. Start with airports and airport services listed on St Louis Near Me Directory, then confirm current rates, lot status and shuttle timing before you leave the house.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to park at Lambert Airport in St. Louis?
A.  Rates are set per lot and per day, so the structure matters more than any single number. The terminal garages are the highest, the airport’s economy and long-term lots come in lower, and off-site private lots are typically lower still. There is usually a short free grace period for a quick pull-in at the garage. On anything longer than a few hours, the daily maximum is the figure that actually decides your bill, not the hourly rate. Pull current rates from flystl.com before you travel, since they are adjusted from time to time.
### Q. Where is the best long term parking at Lambert?
A.  It depends on which trade you want to make. On-airport long-term and economy parking trades a longer walk or a shuttle ride for a lower daily rate, with no third party in the loop and no separate booking to manage. Off-site private lots trade a shuttle ride for a lower rate again, often with a discount for reserving ahead. The garage attached to your terminal costs the most and saves the most time. For a week or more, the lower daily rate usually wins. For two or three nights, the garage often does.
### Q. Where to park at Lambert Airport for Southwest Airlines?
A.  Southwest Airlines operates out of Terminal 2, so you want Terminal 2 parking: the garage attached to that terminal if you are buying time, or an economy, long-term or off-site lot with a shuttle that serves Terminal 2 if you are buying a lower daily rate. Follow the Terminal 2 signs on the airport roadway rather than the general airport signs. Terminal assignments can change, so confirm the terminal on your boarding pass and check flystl.com for the current lot list before you drive out.
### Q. Is Southwest terminal 1 or 2 in St. Louis?
A.  Terminal 2. Lambert runs two terminals, and they are separate buildings with their own parking, their own curbs and their own security checkpoints, connected by a free inter-terminal shuttle. If you park or get dropped at Terminal 1 by mistake, you can ride that shuttle over, but it costs you time you probably did not budget on an early morning. Airlines do get reassigned between terminals, so read the terminal number on your boarding pass and verify it on flystl.com rather than relying on what was true last year.
### Q. How early should I book airport parking?
A.  For an ordinary week, a few days ahead is usually plenty. For peak travel windows, book as soon as you buy the flight. Thanksgiving, the stretch around Christmas and New Year, spring break weeks and big event weekends put pressure on the cheapest lots first, because every traveler is making the same calculation you are. Reserving early also tends to be where the advance discounts live at off-site lots. Note the cancellation terms when you book, and check lot status on flystl.com the morning you leave in case anything has changed.
### Q. How to get the best deal on airport parking?
A.  Match the lot to the trip, then book ahead. Short trips reward the garage because you are buying time, and long trips reward economy, long-term or off-site lots because the daily rate compounds across every day you are gone. Reserve in advance where a lot offers a discount for it. Compare the daily maximum rather than the hourly rate. Consider a hotel park-and-fly package if you are driving in from an outer county for a very early flight. Then confirm current rates directly at flystl.com instead of trusting a number you saw quoted somewhere else.
### Q. What happens if I arrive early for airport parking?
A.  Usually nothing dramatic, but the details depend on where you booked. Airport lots normally charge from the moment you enter, so arriving several hours early simply starts the clock earlier and may push you into an extra day at the boundary. Off-site reservations are typically tied to a start time, and arriving well ahead of it can mean the extra time is billed, or that the space is not held yet. Read the terms when you book and call the lot if your plans shift, rather than assuming there is flexibility built in.

## What It Costs to Rent AV Gear for a St. Louis Event
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-it-costs-to-rent-av-gear-for-a-st-louis-event
A daughter in Fenton is putting together a memorial slideshow for her father. The hall is booked, the photos are scanned, and the funeral director told her the room does not have a projector. She calls an audio visual company, describes the service in two sentences, and gets a quote back with nine lines on it. Three of those lines are abbreviations she has never seen before.
Across the river in Edwardsville, Illinois, a parent volunteer is running a school auction in a gym. She needs a microphone that carries to the back wall, a screen the whole room can read, and music between items. Two companies quote the job. The totals are nowhere near each other, and neither document explains why.
Those are the same problem. Neither quote was written for somebody who rents AV once. They were written for planners who already know what a fast-fold is, what strike means, and why a labor line can cost more than the gear line sitting above it.
So this piece skips the prices on purpose. There are no dollar figures here, and you should be suspicious of any article that hands you them, because AV pricing moves with the room, the date, the gear tier and the labor. What you can learn is how to read the quote, what gear your event actually needs, and what to send two companies so their numbers finally mean the same thing.
### How much does it cost to rent a projector?
A projector rental is priced by what the room demands, not by the box. Brightness, screen size, cabling, delivery, setup, strike and whether a technician stays all move the number. Ask for the gear line, the labor line and the rental period separately, then compare two quotes on identical room details.
Notice what is missing from that list: the projector itself. On most small event quotes, the projector is not the expensive part. The expensive part is the hours. A driver loading a van, two people setting a screen and dressing cables, someone standing by during your program, and that same crew coming back at eleven at night to tear it all down are time. Time is what you are really buying.
That is why a company that quotes you over the phone in thirty seconds, before asking a single question about the room, is guessing. The right first questions are how big the room is, how high the ceiling is, how many people are coming, how much daylight gets in, where the power is, and when you can get in the door. If nobody asks those, the number is not a quote. It is a placeholder.
Dates matter too. Graduation weekends, gala season in the spring and fall, the run-up to the holidays and any Saturday in wedding season put the whole metro’s inventory and crews in play at once. Book late into a busy weekend and you are not just paying for gear, you are paying for the last available technician. Booking early is the cheapest thing you will do all month.
### What is actually on an AV quote?
A real AV quote separates gear from labor from time. Read it in that order. Everything else on the page, delivery, damage waiver, power, rigging and overtime, is a modifier on one of those three. If a company hands you a single lump sum with no breakdown, ask for the itemized version before you compare it against anything.
### The gear line
The gear line lists each item and how many of it. A projector, a screen, a stand or a rigging kit, a switcher, cables, speakers, a mixer, microphones, a laptop or a media player. Read for quantities, then read for spares. Ask directly whether a backup unit travels with the order, because a single lamp or a single wireless receiver is a single point of failure in front of your entire guest list.
Also ask what the gear is. Model names mean little to most of us, but the specs behind them do. You want the brightness figure for the projector, the screen size, the number of wireless channels and the speaker count written on the page. Those are the numbers you will use to check the second quote against the first.
### The labor line
Labor is usually where two quotes diverge. It can cover a delivery driver, a setup crew, an on-site technician for the length of your program, and a strike crew afterward. Some companies bundle a short setup into the gear price and charge separately for anyone who stays. Others quote a technician by the hour with a minimum. Neither approach is wrong, but you cannot compare totals until you know which model each company used.
Ask one blunt question: will a person be in the room during my event, and for how long? For a slideshow that plays once on a loop, you may not need anyone. For a program with live microphones, a video that has to roll on cue, and a speaker who hands the mic to somebody else, a technician is the difference between a smooth night and a long one.
### The rental period
Rental periods are not obvious. Some houses bill a day. Some bill an event day that spans your load-in through your strike even when that crosses midnight. Some price a weekend as one unit because the warehouse is closed Sunday anyway, and some quote weekly for a multi-day conference. It is the same clock you meet at the counter when renting tools and equipment in St. Louis, only with a crew attached to it. Get the start and the end written down.
Then ask what happens if the program runs long. Overtime is real, it is usually billed by the hour or the half hour per person on the crew, and it is the most common surprise on a final invoice. A reception that runs an extra hour is an extra hour of everybody standing in the back of the room.
### Delivery, setup and strike
These are three separate events and each one carries a cost. Delivery is the truck and the driver. Setup is the crew building the system in your room. Strike is taking it back out, and it usually happens the moment your guests leave, which is late. Confirm whether the quote includes all three or only a drop-off. A drop-off price with a pickup you were supposed to arrange yourself is the classic reason two quotes look nothing alike.
Delivery windows matter as much as the fee. If the venue only unlocks at four and your program starts at six, say so before you book, because a tight window can require more crew rather than less. Ask what time they intend to arrive, and put that time in writing.
### Damage waiver and insurance
Most quotes carry a damage waiver line, sometimes as a percentage of the gear subtotal, sometimes optional. Read what it actually covers. Waivers commonly exclude theft, water and damage from misuse, and a waiver is not the same thing as insurance. Separately, many venues require the AV company to carry liability coverage and to name the venue as an additional insured, and your own event policy may or may not extend to rented equipment sitting in a locked room overnight.
### Power, rigging and the venue’s own rules
Power is a question, never an assumption. A gym, a tent, a barn and a historic hall can all run short of circuits, and putting a projector, a lighting package and a sound system on one household circuit is how you find that out in front of guests. Ask where the power is and whether distribution or a generator is needed. Rigging is the other one: hanging anything overhead, flying a speaker or using a lift usually requires a rated point, a trained crew and the venue’s written approval.
Then there are house rules. Hotels and conference centers frequently have an in-house AV provider, and some contracts restrict outside vendors or add a fee for bringing your own. Some venues require house labor for load-in or for touching power. None of that is a scam, but all of it belongs on the quote. Ask the venue for its AV and vendor rules in writing, then forward that same document to every company you ask to bid.
### What gear does your event actually need?
Specify your event in units, not adjectives. Lumens for brightness, feet or inches for screen size, channels for wireless microphones, speaker count for the room. A company can price a specific unit. Nobody can price big screen and good sound. Deciding these before you call also keeps you from being sold a package built for a room twice the size of yours.
### Projection and screens
Brightness is decided by the light in the room, not by the size of the crowd. A dark ballroom with the house lights down is forgiving. A gym with a wall of windows at ten in the morning, a tent, or a hall where people need light to eat and read a program will eat a dim projector alive. If you cannot control the light, you need a brighter projector or an LED wall instead of projection. Say the words ambient light on the phone and listen to what the company asks next.
Screen size follows your farthest viewer. The common planning habit is that the last row sits no more than about six screen heights back, and the front row no closer than roughly one and a half, which turns the length of your room into a screen height and then into a diagonal. Ceiling height caps you, since the bottom of the image has to sit high enough that heads do not block it. Match the aspect ratio to your content too, because a widescreen deck on a square screen wastes the screen you rented.
Then choose a screen type. A tripod screen is small and fast. A fast-fold in a frame is what most event rooms use, and it can be ordered with skirting so it looks like an event rather than a classroom. Rear projection hides the projector and the beam completely but needs open floor behind the screen. Ask which one the quote includes.
### Sound and microphones
Count sound in channels and coverage. Every wireless microphone that can be live at the same moment is a channel, and channels have to be coordinated so they do not fight each other or the building’s own systems. A podium speech, a toast that moves around the room, an officiant who needs both hands free, and a band or a playlist are four different requirements. Write down how many people will be talking at once, then add one spare handheld. Somebody always needs it.
Speaker count is about coverage, not volume. A long narrow room, an L-shaped hall, a space with a hard ceiling and a tile floor, or a tent with no walls each need more than one point of sound so the back is not straining while the front gets blasted. Ask how many speakers the quote includes and where they will stand. Ask whether you also need a microphone for the audience during questions.
### Lighting
Lighting is the easiest line to cut and the one people regret when the photos come back. The practical asks are simple: enough light on whoever is speaking, uplighting if you want the room to change character after dinner, and a look for the dance floor if there is dancing. Each of those needs power and somewhere to hide cable. If you are recording or streaming, light on the speaker’s face stops being decoration and becomes a requirement.
### Streaming and recording
Streaming turns your event into a broadcast, and a broadcast needs its own gear and its own person. Decide how many cameras, whether anyone will switch between them live, and whether audio comes from the sound system rather than a camera microphone, which is the single biggest quality difference an online viewer will notice. Then check the room’s internet. A hardwired connection with a known upload speed beats guest wireless every time, and only the venue can tell you what exists. Recording with no live audience online is a much smaller ask.
Signing gear paperwork for the office too? Read the copier lease traps first.
### Should you rent, buy or use the venue’s in-house AV?
Rent for a one-off, buy for a routine, and check the venue’s in-house team before you do either. The deciding factor is not price, it is how often the room and the requirements repeat. A church projecting lyrics every Sunday and a family holding one memorial are not solving the same problem, even though both of them need a projector and a screen.
In-house AV lives at hotels, conference centers and some larger banquet halls. It is convenient, and it already knows the building’s power, ceiling and quirks, which is worth real money on a complicated day. It may also be contractually exclusive. Ask before you sign the venue contract, not after, whether outside AV is allowed and what fee applies if you bring your own. That question belongs on the same checklist you use when comparing the best event venues in St. Louis for your next celebration.
General party and event rental companies sit in the middle. Many carry a projector, a screen, a portable sound system and a microphone right alongside the tents, tables and linens, which is genuinely handy when you are already renting from them. What they usually do not carry is a technician who stays. The questions are the same ones in our guide to what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis: what is included, who sets it up, and when it comes back.
Dedicated AV production companies are the other end of the range. They own deeper inventory, they carry spares, they send people who have solved your exact problem in your exact venue before, and they will walk the room with you. For a program where something has to work on cue in front of an audience, that is precisely what you are paying for. For a slideshow at a family gathering, it may be more than you need.
Two more categories are worth knowing about. Tool and equipment rental counters sometimes stock basic projection or portable PA gear as a sideline, usually pickup only and usually without support. Universities, public libraries and some community organizations lend or rent media equipment to students, members or nonprofit groups, which is a legitimate option for a small meeting if you qualify. Neither one puts a person in your room.
Buying only makes sense when the same need repeats. Run the math on frequency rather than on the sticker. A projector you use monthly for years is cheap. A projector you use twice is a box in a closet with a light source that ages whether or not you turn it on, plus the cables, the stand, the screen, the case, and the person who has to learn how to run it. Renting also means somebody else owns the failure at seven in the evening.
### How do you get two quotes you can actually compare?
Send every company the same document. Not a phone call, a document. When the inputs are identical, the differences between the quotes become real information about scope and service instead of noise from two different conversations. This one habit protects your budget more than any negotiating you do afterward.
Include the room details: length, width and ceiling height; guest count and seating layout; how much daylight the room gets and whether it can be darkened; where the doors and the load-in path are, including stairs, elevators or a dock; where the power is and what circuits are available; and a timeline with your access time, program start, program end and the latest possible strike. Add whatever the venue already owns, because a house sound system or a mounted screen changes everything above it.
Then describe the program itself in plain sentences. A team lead in Union, Missouri, planning a company all-hands might write: ninety people in a rented hall, a laptop presentation for forty minutes, two people speaking with handheld microphones, a five-minute video with sound, then questions from the floor. That paragraph tells an AV company more than a gear list would, because it lets them tell you what you actually need.
Ask every bidder the same three closing questions. What is not included in this number? What happens if the program runs past the scheduled end? What happens if the venue changes the room or the layout after we book? The answers will differ, and those differences are usually the entire gap between the cheapest quote and the one that works.
Finally, compare the quotes line by line instead of total to total. Put them side by side and check gear against gear, labor against labor, period against period. Nine times out of ten the cheaper quote is cheaper because something is missing, and once you find the missing line you can ask for it to be added and priced honestly.
Not sure who to call for your room? Start near the venue and work outward, because a company that already knows the building saves you a site visit. You can browse audio visual companies listed across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory. Send the same room details, timeline and guest count to two or three of them, then compare the quotes line by line.
If you run a business in this trade, put your business on the map.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to hire a projector and screen?
A.  Ask for it two ways. A package quote bundles the projector, the screen, the stand, the cables and often a short setup window into one number, which is easier to read and frequently cheaper than assembling the same items piece by piece. An a-la-carte quote prices each item and each hour of labor separately, which is what you want when the room is unusual or the program runs long. Neither format tells you the price by itself, because brightness, screen size, delivery, setup, strike and whether a technician stays are what move it. Ask the same company for both formats and read them together.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or rent a projector?
A.  It comes down to how many times you will use it. Sketch a break-even by counting real events per year across the useful life of the gear, then add everything a rental quietly includes: the screen, the stand, the cables, the case, storage space, and somebody who knows how to set it all up. Light sources age on the calendar as well as on hours, and a projector bought for a big room this year may be wrong for the room you use next year. Frequent, repeating use favors buying. Occasional use, unfamiliar rooms and anything that has to work on cue favor renting.
### Q. Where can you rent a projector and screen?
A.  Think in categories rather than brands. Dedicated AV production companies carry the deepest inventory, spares and technicians. General party and event rental companies often stock a projector, a screen and a basic sound system next to the tents and tables. Tool and equipment rental counters sometimes keep simple projection or PA gear as a sideline, usually pickup only. Hotels and conference centers have in-house AV, occasionally on an exclusive basis. Universities, libraries and some community organizations lend media equipment to students, members or nonprofits. Match the category to how much support you need on the day, not to the lowest published rate.
### Q. Can you rent projectors from Best Buy?
A.  National consumer electronics retailers are built to sell hardware, not to rent it. Any rental-style or try-before-you-buy program they run tends to be limited, regional and subject to change, so treat that path as a purchase with a return window rather than as a rental house, and check the retailer’s current policy directly before you plan around it. The practical difference is support. A rental house delivers, sets up, brings the right cables and adapters, keeps a spare unit on the truck and can put a person in the room during your program. A return window does none of that at seven on a Saturday evening.
### Q. How much do projection screens cost?
A.  The screen is its own line on the quote, priced by type and size rather than folded into the projector. A tripod screen is the small, fast, classroom-style option. A fast-fold screen in a frame is what most event rooms use, and it can be ordered with skirting and a dress kit so it looks finished in photos. Rear projection screens hide the projector and the beam but need open floor behind them. Size is driven by your farthest viewer and capped by ceiling height, and the aspect ratio should match your slides. Ask which type, what size, and whether dressing is included.
### Q. How much should I pay for a projector?
A.  Judge the value, not the number. What is genuinely worth paying for is brightness that beats the light in your actual room, resolution that matches your content, a screen sized for your farthest viewer, and support: delivery, setup, the correct cables and adapters, a spare unit, and a technician in the room if anything has to happen on cue. What is not worth paying for is capability your room will never use, such as a projector specified for a ballroom when you are in a small meeting space. Ask each company to justify its recommendation in units, then pick the one that explains itself.
### Q. How much rate for projector rental?
A.  Rates are quoted against a defined period, so pin the period down first. Common structures include a single day, an event day covering load-in through strike even when it crosses midnight, a weekend priced as one unit because the warehouse is closed, and a weekly rate for multi-day conferences. Delivery windows are part of that clock, since a narrow access window at the venue can require more crew and a late strike can trigger overtime billed by the hour per person. Get the start time, the end time, the overtime rule and the pickup arrangement in writing before you compare any two rates.

## Is a St. Louis Butcher Cheaper? Not on Ground Beef
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-a-st-louis-butcher-cheaper-than-the-grocery-store
Thirty pounds of ground beef, cold through the packaging, stacked against your chest on the way out of Bolyard’s Meat & Provisions on Sutton Boulevard. That armload is what it takes to get the shop’s lowest ground beef price: $10.30 a pound. Buy ten pounds and it is $12.36 a pound.
Now hold that up against the grocery case. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ latest monthly average for a pound of 100% ground beef across U.S. cities is $6.792, or about $6.79. That is ordinary grocery beef averaged across the country, set against pasture-raised, dry-aged beef from one shop, so it is not a like-for-like price. The gap is still too wide to wave away: even at its deepest bulk discount, this butcher’s ground beef runs about $3.51 a pound more ($10.30 minus $6.792), or about $105 extra on the 30-pound order. Anyone who says the neighborhood counter is always the cheap option has not done the subtraction.
Then you look past the register and the math starts to wobble. Bolyard’s calls itself St. Louis’s only whole animal butcher shop. It says its animals are delivered through the front door from Missouri farms, and that all of the cutting, stuffing and grinding happens in an open cutting room. The shop invites customers to ask the butchers questions, so the grind in your bag was made in a room you can see into, by people you can talk to. A plastic-wrapped grocery tray cannot tell you where it was cut, because nobody at the store saw it happen either.
Here is the line worth repeating at the next cookout: the grocery store wins on price per pound, and the butcher wins on what is in the pound. Most people only ever ask the first question.
Here is how to run the test this week. Bring two things: your last grocery receipt and a card listing the five cuts your household really eats, with the per-pound price from the receipt next to each. Go on a weekend morning, when the shop serves brunch from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., eat first, then walk the case and ask the price of each cut on your card. Circle the wins, cross out the losses, and buy only the circles. The shop says it encourages customers to ask its butchers questions, so lead with the meal, not the cut: “Braising for six this weekend, what would you use?” For bulk ground beef or a beef bundle, call 314-647-2567 or check the shop’s bulk page for its posted bundle dates before you clear freezer space.
### Is it cheaper to buy meat from a local butcher?
Not on the everyday cuts, at least not at a whole-animal shop. A butcher earns its price on what a supermarket tray never hands you: soup bones, liver, tallow, braising cuts, a steak cut to the thickness you ask for, and meat you can trace to a farm.
The reason is plain. A supermarket prices a few popular cuts as loss leaders to get you through the door. A whole-animal butcher has the opposite problem: every animal arrives with all of its parts attached, and the whole thing has to sell.
That is exactly why the bulk page at Bolyard’s reads the way it does. The 30-pound ground beef price is 31% off, by the shop’s own math. Its eighth-of-a-beef bundle costs $13.65 a pound and comes with ribeye, strip steak and tenderloin, but also 10 pounds of soup and stock bones, 4 quarts of beef stock and 5 pints of tallow. Tallow is rendered beef fat, the kind that sets up white and firm in the fridge and makes a skillet of potatoes taste like a diner griddle. That is the part of the animal a supermarket mostly never sells you.
The bundle also carries cuts the shop calls butcher’s choice, picked from a list that includes Denver steak, teres major, picanha and flatiron steak. They come from seam butchery, which follows the natural lines of the muscle instead of sawing straight across. You will not find a teres major in a sealed tray, and the first time one hits a hot cast iron pan you will understand why people get loyal to a counter.
The same shop shows where a counter earns its keep in the fall. Its Thanksgiving turkeys are pasture raised by Buttonwood Farm in Missouri, fresh and never frozen, and taken off pasture and processed just days before delivery, at $10.30 a pound. That is not a grocery-store loss-leader bird, and it is not trying to be. If you want one, preorder now through the shop’s turkey page, since pickup is set for the days just before Thanksgiving, and plan on 1.5 to 2 pounds per guest, which is the shop’s own rule of thumb.
### Where does the extra money actually go?
Into labor you can watch: the rasp of butcher’s twine pulled tight around a roast, the crackle of paper folded over a fresh cut. Tying a roast, trimming a brisket, grinding to a blend, cutting a chuck into steaks and braising pieces. None of that happens in a case-ready store, where meat arrives pre-cut and pre-packed. Bolyard’s says most of its team has restaurant backgrounds, so the person who hands you the paper-wrapped parcel can usually tell you how to cook what is inside it.
Into aging and sourcing, too. Dry aging takes time and costs weight, and pasture-raised animals from small farms do not come at feedlot prices. You can decide that difference is worth something or worth nothing. Just do not pretend a $6.792 pound and a $10.30 pound are the same pound.
### The kinds of meat counters around St. Louis
“Butcher” covers several different businesses here, and they do not price alike. Knowing which one you walked into explains most of the confusion about cost.
### Whole-animal and full-service butcher shops
These are the shops with a saw in the back and someone who will cut to order. Ask whether they break whole animals or primals on site. The answer tells you a great deal in five seconds, and it predicts where the bargains sit: in the trim, the bones and the less famous cuts.
### Ethnic, halal and kosher meat markets
Neighborhood markets built around particular cuisines often carry cuts the mainstream case skips, from goat and lamb to oxtail and tripe, and they can be some of the best value in the category. Go with a plan and one question: ask what sells fastest. High turnover is the best proxy for freshness in any meat case.
### Farm-direct sales
Plenty of producers around the outer metro sell whole, half and quarter animals straight to households, and some of them set up at weekend markets, which is a low-stakes way to meet one before you order in bulk. Our guide to St. Louis metro farmers markets by town is a good place to find them.
### Processors and lockers
A processor is not a retail shop. It is the business that cuts and wraps an animal for the person who owns it, and when you buy a half beef from a farmer, this is usually who does the cutting and charges you a separate fee. Their schedules can book far out, so call the processor first, not last.
### Supermarket counters and case-ready meat
Some grocery stores staff a counter that will cut and grind for you. Others sell only case-ready meat, packed elsewhere. They look alike from ten feet away. The test: ask for a steak cut to a thickness you name. A shrug means case-ready.
Not cooking tonight? Grab a hot bowl in Fairview Heights instead.
### Which cuts win at the counter, and which lose?
Likely wins at a butcher: bones for stock, liver and other offal, shanks and braising cuts, the odd steaks like Denver or teres major, and anything you buy in volume. Likely losses: the handful of headline cuts a supermarket runs as a promotion, starting with boneless skinless chicken breast and family packs of ground beef. A butcher cannot beat a loss leader, and a good one will say so without flinching.
Steaks sit in the middle. A supermarket ribeye and a dry-aged ribeye cut from a whole rib section can differ in aging, trim and thickness, so the sticker comparison is not apples to apples. Our piece on how to pick a steakhouse in St. Louis covers the same vocabulary from the other side of the plate.
House-made sausage, bacon and deli meats are their own question, where ingredients matter as much as price. The same logic runs at a sandwich counter, which we broke down in types of delis in St. Louis and how to order.
### How a bulk beef order really works
Bulk is where per-pound savings usually live, and also where the biggest surprises hide, because a farm half or quarter is normally sold on hanging weight with a separate processing fee. Hanging weight is the carcass before it is cut into the meat you recognize. From there you lose bone, fat trim and moisture, so the pounds you carry home are well under the number you were quoted.
So ask for three numbers before you commit: the price per pound of hanging weight, the processing fee with any extras, and the expected take-home pounds. With all three you can figure a real cost per pound in your freezer and hold it up against your grocery receipt.
Measure the freezer, not your hopes. Bolyard’s says every cut in its beef bundle is vacuum packed and takes up approximately 3 cubic feet. The shop posts its bundle dates on its bulk page, so check those before you clear a shelf, and it will deliver on request for an additional $25 within a 3-mile radius. Splitting a bundle or a quarter with another household is the sensible first step: you find out whether your family really eats that much beef before you scale up.
### How to talk to a butcher
Lead with what you are cooking, not with a cut name. “Braising this for six people” gets a better answer than a name half remembered from a video. Ask what came in, because the best value in the case is often whatever the shop has a lot of right now. Order steaks by thickness, and ask for a coarse grind for chili or a particular blend for burgers.
Call ahead for anything that is not routine: a large roast, a specific bird, sausage for a party, a holiday order. A counter can get you almost anything with notice and almost nothing without it. And ask whether they sell bones and trim, since some shops keep them in the back until someone asks.
### Getting it home and keeping it good
A bargain you throw away was not a bargain. Ground meat and organ meats have the shortest life in the refrigerator, whole muscle cuts hold longer, and anything you will not cook soon belongs in the freezer, portioned the way you will cook it and labeled with the cut and the date.
Butcher paper is for the trip home and the next day or so. Rewrap or vacuum seal anything headed for the freezer. Bolyard’s says its vacuum-packed bundle cuts may be stored under refrigeration for up to a month or in the freezer for a year or longer. Treat that as the shop’s word on its own packaging, and trust your nose: sliminess or a sour smell that does not fade means it goes in the trash.

If you run a butcher counter, a meat market or a farm that sells by the quarter, your next customers are already holding their grocery receipt up against your case. Put your counter where they look and get more customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth buying meat from a butcher?
A.  For most households, yes, but selectively. A whole-animal butcher can cost more per pound on everyday ground beef than the grocery average, so the value shows up elsewhere: bones and stock, liver, braising cuts, steaks cut to your thickness, grinds you specify and meat you can trace to a farm. Treat the counter as the place you go for particular things, not a full replacement for the grocery run.
### Q. What's the difference between a butcher shop and a meat market?
A.  In everyday use the terms overlap, and plenty of businesses use them interchangeably. The useful distinction is what happens on site. A full-service butcher shop breaks larger pieces down in house and cuts to order. A market may focus more on packaged meat, often alongside groceries and often serving a specific cuisine. The question that settles it is whether they cut on the premises.
### Q. Can you buy meat straight from the farmer?
A.  Yes, and it is common around the outer St. Louis metro. Producers sell whole, half and quarter animals, and some sell smaller amounts at markets or by arranged pickup. Bulk purchases usually route through a separate processor that cuts and wraps the meat and charges its own fee, so ask how the sale is structured and what you receive at pickup before you agree to anything.
### Q. How much is a 1/2 cow in Missouri?
A.  Prices move, so get the structure first. A farm half beef is normally priced per pound of hanging weight, which is the carcass before cutting, plus a separate processing fee, and the take-home pounds come in well under the hanging weight. Ask for the hanging-weight price, the processing fee and the expected take-home pounds. For a smaller start, Bolyard’s on Sutton Boulevard sells an eighth-of-a-beef bundle at $13.65 a pound.
### Q. How long is meat good after buying from a butcher?
A.  It depends on the cut and how it is wrapped. Ground meat and organ meats go first, whole steaks and roasts last longer, and butcher paper is only meant for the trip home and the next day or so. Freeze what you will not cook soon. For vacuum-packed cuts, Bolyard’s says its bundle may be stored under refrigeration for up to a month or in the freezer for a year or longer.
### Q. What meat lasts longest in the fridge?
A.  Whole muscle cuts generally hold up best. A steak or roast has far less exposed surface than ground meat, so bacteria have less to work with. Ground beef, sausage and organ meats are the shortest lived. Cured and smoked products behave differently because salt and smoke change the picture. Keep meat in the coldest part of the refrigerator and keep it sealed.
### Q. Can meat go bad in a vacuum sealed bag?
A.  Yes. Vacuum sealing removes most of the oxygen, which slows the bacteria that need air, but it does not sterilize the meat, and some bacteria grow fine without oxygen. Sealed meat still needs refrigeration or freezing and still has a limit. Watch for a puffed bag, cloudy liquid, sliminess or a sour smell when you open it, and throw it out rather than gamble.

## $321 Buys 4 Hours of Driving School in St. Louis. Missouri Requires 40.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-driving-school-costs-in-st-louis
“Do I really have to sit in that passenger seat for forty hours?”
Yes. And you already know what those hours feel like. Your right foot pressing the floor mat where a brake pedal would be. Your hand finding the door handle as the car noses into the merge onto 270 at five o’clock, brake lights stacked red all the way to the river. The blinker ticking a beat too long while your kid decides whether that gap is a gap at all.
Here is the number that changes how you budget for all of it. The Missouri Department of Revenue says a teen must have received 40 hours of driving instruction, including a minimum of 10 hours of nighttime driving between sunset and sunrise, before moving from a permit to an intermediate license. Now look at what a class buys you. Lindbergh Schools Community Education lists its driver education course at $321, and the drive time included is a total of 4 hours in a Community Ed. vehicle. Four hours toward forty. The rest of that passenger seat is yours.
You are not buying your teen’s driving hours from a school. You are buying a few expert ones, and filling the rest yourself.
### How much money does it cost to go to driving school?
Around St. Louis, a school-district class like Lindbergh Schools Community Education’s driver education course runs $321 and includes 4 hours of drive time. Private lessons cost more per hour: Missouri Driving School posts private driving lessons at $94.50 per hour. Either way, Missouri requires 40 hours of driving instruction, including 10 at night, so most families pay for a few professional hours and drive the rest themselves.
Those two prices are two different products. The school-district class is a bundle: the classroom part held over Google Meet on evenings from 6:00 to 8:00 PM, the laptop glowing on the kitchen table while dinner goes cold, then a small block of drive time with a certified instructor, done in person. Its page says the course may help qualify for auto insurance discounts, so call your agent before you pick a school. Students must be at least 15 years of age with a valid Missouri driving permit. The private lesson is pure behind-the-wheel time, one-on-one, priced by the hour, and Missouri Driving School says its training cars have dual brake controls and $1 million in liability insurance. That second brake pedal is what you are paying for.
### Before you pay anyone: who signs for the 40 hours
Here is the step nobody warns you about. To move up to the intermediate license, the teen must hold the permit for a minimum of 182 days, and a qualified person or grandparent must go to the license office with them to verify the 40 hours, 10 of them at night. You are the receipt. Start a log tonight, a notebook in the glove box with the date, the minutes and whether the headlights were on, because guessing at the counter how many hours were after dark is no fun.
Read the DOR’s wording closely, too: the 40 hours of driving instruction can be with a qualified person, a grandparent or a qualified driving instructor. That matters for your wallet, because the instructor’s time is part of the count you are building, not a separate bill on top of it. Write those lessons in the notebook like any other drive.
Under 16, your teen may drive only with a licensed driver in the front seat who is a qualified person, a grandparent, a qualified driving instructor, or a qualified driver at least 25 years of age who has been licensed for a minimum of 3 years and has written permission from the parent or legal guardian. The instruction permit itself is available at 15.
### Spend the paid hours on the St. Louis roads that scare you
So the smart money question is not “how many lessons” but “which hours.” Spend the professional time where a calm stranger in the right seat beats a tense parent: the first on-ramp to 70 when the lane runs out, the first left across Hampton at rush hour, the first night when a summer storm turns the road into a mirror and the wipers can’t keep up. Do the easy miles yourself.
For those easy miles, a local tip from the St. Louis Roamer: Jefferson Barracks. Its roads are slow, not usually heavily trafficked, and a fair place for a new driver to practice turning corners. Windows down, the trees sliding by slow, nobody behind you honking.
The intermediate license has its own rules your teen will test. They may not drive alone from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. except to and from a school activity, job or an emergency, unless a licensed driver 21 or older is with them, and the DOR caps passengers under 19 who are not immediate family.
The next bill after the license is the policy: what car insurance costs in St. Louis.
### How to compare schools in one phone call
Prices mean little until you know what is inside them. Ask every school the same short list:
How many hours behind the wheel, exactly? Not sessions. Hours.
Is classroom time included, and is it online or in person?
Does the car have a dual brake?
Do you pick up from home or school?
What does one extra hour cost? For a nervous first-timer, that add-on rate matters more than the package price.
What is the cancellation policy, in writing? Teenagers get sick.
Write the answers down on one sheet, one column per school, and the quotes that sounded wildly different on the phone usually line up fast. A cheaper price that buys fewer minutes in the car is not cheaper. A pricier one that picks your teen up from school might save you an hour of driving across town every week, and that time is worth something too. Pick the school whose hours land on the skills you least want to teach yourself.
Then use the answers to plan your own hours. If the school covers four, the rest of the forty are evenings and weekends with you. Start the night hours early. The fall evenings get dark before dinner, and that is the easiest time to bank them.
Behind the wheel, by the hour
### How much is 10 hours of driving lessons?
Missouri Driving School posts private lessons at $94.50 an hour, so ten hours adds up fast. A school-district course like Lindbergh’s runs $321 with 4 hours of drive time included, and Missouri still requires 40 hours of instruction, 10 of them at night, before an intermediate license.
### A plan for the rest of the forty hours
Think of the forty hours as four rough stages, and only one of them needs a stranger with a second brake pedal.
The empty lot. A big school parking lot on a Sunday morning, light poles and painted lines and nobody else. Starts, stops, turns, the feel of how little the gas pedal needs. Teens are jerky here and that is fine. The car lurches, you both laugh or you both go quiet, and by the third Sunday the stops get smooth. This stage costs you gas and patience, nothing else.
The quiet street. Your own neighborhood on a weekday evening. Stop signs, parked cars on both sides, a dog that walks out from between two of them. Keep the radio off. You want your teen hearing the tires and the turn signal, not a playlist.
The hard stuff. This is where the paid hours earn their price. The first highway on-ramp, when the car has to get up to speed in a lane that ends. Heavy traffic at rush hour. Rain at night, when the road shines back and the lane lines disappear. A certified instructor has done these a thousand times and does not flinch, and your teen can feel that calm from the right seat.
The repetition. After the hard lessons, you drive the same kinds of roads together, over and over, until it stops being an event. Errands count. The drive to practice counts. This is where most of the forty actually happen, and it is the part no school can sell you.
Night hours fit into every stage after the first. Ten of the forty must be between sunset and sunrise, and they are the hours families most often come up short on at the license office. Bank them early in the season, while the evenings come dark before dinner, rather than cramming them at the end.
### Where the money is worth spending, and where it is not
Not every dollar here buys the same thing. A rough ranking from the passenger seat:
Worth it: professional time on highway merging and heavy traffic. These are the skills where a calm expert beats a nervous parent, and where mistakes cost the most.
Usually worth it: a lesson close to the road test. A fresh set of trained eyes catches the habits that crept in over weeks with you: rolling stops, wide right turns, mirrors checked a second too late.
Skip it: paying for basic parking-lot practice. You can do that yourself, for free, and most teens need several sessions of it before anything else sticks.
One more cost that never shows on a price sheet: your own time. Forty hours is a lot of evenings. Splitting them with a grandparent, who the state also counts as a supervisor for the hours, can keep everyone sane.
### The tests at the end of the permit
Before the permit, your teen passes the vision, road sign recognition and written tests at a Missouri State Highway Patrol driver examination station. The driving test comes later, on the way to the intermediate license. If the first try goes badly, find out exactly what was marked and practice that one thing. A second attempt that fixes one specific problem goes far better than another twenty comfortable miles.

### Q. Can a 15 year old learn how to drive?
