## Smile Drooping? Call 911, Not a St. Louis Neurologist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-a-neurologist-in-st-louis
The coffee mug tips out of your right hand and the spoon rings off the counter. You go to say “I’m fine” and the words come out thick, like your mouth is full of cotton. In the hallway mirror, one corner of your smile won’t lift. That is not a neurologist appointment. Mercy’s stroke checklist says one sign like that is enough: call 911 immediately, and note the time it started.
Here is what that call does in St. Louis that no clinic visit can. Under Missouri’s Time Critical Diagnosis system, a 911 call activates EMS, treatment begins as soon as responders reach the patient, and the hospital is alerted that a patient is on the way so its staff can begin treatment the moment the patient arrives. Patients are taken to a hospital with staff specially trained to handle stroke. Your car can’t phone ahead. Neither can the receptionist at your doctor’s office.
Barnes-Jewish Hospital says it was Missouri’s first Comprehensive Stroke Center and among the first hospitals the state certified as a Level I Stroke Center. Mercy Hospital St. Louis says the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services designated it a Time Critical Diagnosis Level 1 Stroke Center. Barnes-Jewish describes what that level means: Level I centers act as resource centers for a region, keeping specialized resources for the most complex patients. You don’t pick one from the floor of the kitchen. You call, and the system routes.
Barnes-Jewish puts the rule bluntly: “Call 911. Don’t drive yourself in. Don’t call your primary care physician to ask what to do.” Mercy puts the stakes in a number: nearly 2 million brain cells die every minute a stroke goes untreated.
Here is the relief, though. Most nervous-system symptoms are not that. Most headaches are just headaches, and a foot that falls asleep during a long Cardinals broadcast is just a foot. The skill is sorting three piles: 911 right now, a neurologist soon, or your regular doctor at the next visit.
### What symptoms require a neurologist?
The ones with a shape: they last, they change, or they sit on one side of the body. A headache that is new, getting worse, or different from your usual. Numbness, tingling or weakness on one side that doesn’t go away. A tremor, stiffness or a walk that has changed, often noticed first by the person walking beside you through the grocery store. Coordination that has slipped, so you are clipping doorframes and dropping keys on the porch. Thinking that has slowed, words that hide on the tip of your tongue. And any seizure, once the emergency has passed.
The pattern matters more than the symptom. Everyone gets headaches. The one that wakes you, or arrives with vision changes or confusion, is the one your doctor asks about in a different tone of voice.
For that pile in St. Louis, two front doors publish their own numbers. WashU Medicine’s adult neurology page lists 314-362-1408 for appointments, at the department on South Euclid Avenue. Mercy Neurology in Medical Tower B on New Ballas Road says to call to schedule, at 314-251-8892. Have the dates of your symptoms written down before you dial, so the first question doesn’t catch you flat.
### The 911 pile: run BE FAST at the kitchen table
Mercy calls BE FAST the quickest way to check for signs, and it takes about as long to run as it does to read. B is balance: is the person suddenly unsteady, stumbling or having trouble walking? E is eyes: did their vision suddenly change, are they seeing double or have they lost sight in one or both eyes? F is face: ask them to smile, and look for one side drooping. A is arms: ask them to raise both, and watch whether one drifts down. S is speech: ask them to repeat a simple sentence, like “The sky is blue,” and listen for slurring. T is time: if you notice any one of these signs, call 911 immediately, and note the time symptoms began.
Say the time out loud and write it on whatever is nearest, the back of an envelope, the margin of a bill. That number travels with the patient.
Mercy lists other warning signs too, including a sudden, severe headache with no clear cause, confusion, and numbness on one side of the body. One sign is enough.
And if the symptoms fade on their own, that is not the all-clear it feels like. Mercy calls stroke-like symptoms that resolve within minutes a transient ischemic attack, or TIA, and warns not to let the word “mini” mislead you: a TIA is a serious warning sign, and some people who have one will have a full stroke in the hours or weeks after. The hand works again, the words come back, the room stops tilting - and you still make the call.
Everything below this line is about the non-urgent piles.
### The neurologist pile: getting through the door in St. Louis
For the symptoms that need a specialist soon but not tonight, the St. Louis path usually starts with your regular doctor and a referral slip. WashU Medicine’s adult neurology specialists, in the department at 660 South Euclid Avenue, treat patients with a variety of neurologic disorders, and the adult neurology page lists one number for appointments: 314-362-1408. In west St. Louis County, Mercy Neurology’s office in Medical Tower B at 621 S. New Ballas Road says to call to schedule, at 314-251-8892. Write it on the back of the referral slip so it is there when your nerve to call shows up.
A neurologist diagnoses and treats problems of the brain, spine and nerves, and is usually not a surgeon. Neurosurgery is its own specialty. Most people sent to neurology are there for answers and a plan, not an operation, and knowing that takes some of the dread out of the word.
### What happens at the first appointment
Less drama than you are bracing for. The first visit is mostly conversation and a hands-on exam in a small room with a paper-covered table.
Expect a long history: when it started, what makes it better or worse, what else changed around the same time, what runs in your family. This is not small talk. For many neurological problems, the story you tell is the most useful test in the room, and the exam is there to confirm or challenge it.
Then the exam itself, and it is low-tech on purpose. Follow a finger with your eyes. Push against the doctor’s hands. Touch your nose, then their finger, then your nose again. Walk heel-to-toe down the hallway while someone watches your feet. The cold tap of a reflex hammer below the kneecap. It can feel almost childish, and it is how a good examiner narrows a problem to one part of the nervous system.
Imaging may follow, but usually after the exam and because of what it found, not instead of it.
Bring a witness if you can. The spouse who saw the tremor first, the grown kid who noticed the pauses mid-sentence at Sunday dinner. Neurology is one of the places where a second set of eyes routinely supplies what the patient genuinely can’t see.
### Referrals, insurance and the waiting
Some insurance plans require a referral from a primary care doctor before they will cover a neurology visit; others let you book on your own. Check yours before you book, because finding out afterward is an expensive way to learn.
Neurology waits can be long. Two moves help. Ask to go on the cancellation list, and ask plainly whether your symptoms should be seen sooner than the next open slot. Practices triage, but only on what you tell them, so say the specific thing: “the numbness is on one side and it’s spreading,” not “I’ve been having some issues.”
If something changes while you wait, call back. Don’t sit politely on a date months out while a symptom gets worse. And if what changes is sudden, you already know which number to call instead.
Dizzy, ringing ears, pressure behind the face? Sometimes it starts in the ear, not the brain. When an ENT beats your regular doctor.
### How to prepare so the visit is worth it
You get a limited window with a specialist. Preparation buys you more of it.
Keep a symptom log for two weeks. Date, time, what happened, what you were doing, how long it lasted. Patterns you can’t see from memory jump off the page.
Bring a complete medication list, supplements included.
Write your three questions down and ask them first, not as you stand up to leave.
Bring prior imaging on a disc, or know exactly where it was done.
Bring the witness. Their version of events is evidence too.
### What happens after the first visit
Many people leave a first neurology appointment without a diagnosis, and that is normal rather than a failure. Neurology often works by ruling things out, and the exam is a map of where to look next.
Three things commonly follow. Testing, such as imaging, blood work or nerve studies, chosen because of what the exam found. A trial of treatment, where how you respond is itself information. Or watchful waiting with a follow-up date, which is a real clinical decision and not a brush-off, because some conditions only show their shape over time.
Ask two questions before you leave: what would make you want to see me sooner, and what should I be writing down until then? Those answers turn the gap between appointments into useful time instead of anxious time.
If a diagnosis is serious or the treatment is major, a second opinion is reasonable. Bring the records. The value of a second opinion is a fresh reading of the same evidence, not a repeat of every test.
### Does telehealth work for neurology?
Partly. Follow-ups, medication adjustments, going over test results and managing a stable condition can work well on video, and save a drive across the metro for a short conversation. A first appointment usually doesn’t, because the exam needs hands, a hallway to walk and a reflex hammer. Ask at the first visit whether the practice offers video follow-ups, because that answer shapes how workable a long relationship with a distant specialist will be.
If the appointment sends you across the metro, make something of the trip. A specialist visit out west pairs well with a slow lunch afterward, somewhere like Satchmo’s in Chesterfield.
Put the 911 signs where the whole house can see them. Write BE FAST on an index card and tape it inside a kitchen cabinet, then find neurology and specialist practices on St Louis Near Me Directory for the non-urgent symptoms that still deserve a specialist.

### What this is not
This page is general information, not medical advice, and it can’t examine you. Nothing here should talk you out of care. If you are weighing whether a symptom is worth mentioning, mention it. The cost of raising it is one awkward sentence.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are early signs of neurological problems?
A.  Common early signals include headaches that have changed, numbness or weakness on one side, tremor or stiffness, a changed walk, slipping coordination, and slower thinking or trouble finding words. Most single episodes are harmless; it is persistence and pattern that matter, so mention them to your doctor.
### Q. What are the red flag symptoms for neurological conditions?
A.  The emergency ones follow BE FAST: sudden loss of balance, vision changes, a drooping face, a weak or drifting arm, or slurred speech. Mercy also lists a sudden, severe headache with no clear cause, confusion and one-sided numbness. If you notice any one of these signs, call 911 immediately and note the time symptoms began.
### Q. Why would someone be referred to a neurologist?
A.  Because a symptom has a pattern worth a specialist’s eye: it is persistent, changing, one-sided, or affects movement, memory or coordination. A referral means your doctor wants a closer look, not that a diagnosis has been made.
### Q. What will a neurologist do on your first visit?
A.  Take a detailed history, then run a hands-on exam: eye movements, strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination and walking. It is low-tech on purpose. Imaging, if ordered, usually comes after the exam and because of what it found.
### Q. Will a neurologist order an MRI?
A.  Sometimes, not automatically. Scans are chosen based on what the history and exam suggest, so many first visits end with a plan rather than a scan.
### Q. Is it serious if you have to see a neurologist?
A.  Usually less serious than it feels. A referral means a symptom deserves a closer look. Many visits end in reassurance or a manageable plan, and most neurology patients are there for answers and management, not surgery.
### Q. Can I see a neurologist without a referral?
A.  It depends on your insurance. Some plans require a primary care referral before they will cover the visit; others let you book directly. Call the number on your card before you book. In St. Louis, WashU Medicine’s adult neurology appointment line is 314-362-1408.
### Q. How long is the wait time for a neurologist?
A.  It varies by practice and can be long. Ask for the cancellation list, describe your symptoms specifically so the practice can triage, and call back if anything changes. If you notice any BE FAST sign while you wait, call 911 immediately.

## $1,646 or $171: Urgent Care vs the ER in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/urgent-care-vs-er-in-st-louis-what-it-costs
The kids’ after-hours clinic on Tesson Ferry Road closes at 7:30 on Sunday nights. You find that out at nine, standing in the kitchen with the car keys in one hand and your crying kid’s wrist in the other.
The wrist is puffing up and going warm under your palm. The crying has turned into that hiccuping kind. The fingers still wiggle when you ask. The pediatrician opens in the morning.
Now you have two doors, and the gap between them is brutal. In a Health Affairs study of roughly 29 million people in managed care plans, the average emergency department visit cost $1,646. The average urgent care visit cost $171.
Two doors. $171 or $1,646, on average. Pick your door before the night picks it for you.
On a weeknight, there’s a third door built for exactly this. Washington University Children’s After Hours, at 12436 Tesson Ferry Road, is staffed by specially-trained pediatric nurse practitioners and lists sprains, strains and fractures among what it treats. It calls itself a kid-focused, faster alternative to ERs for the same copay you’d pay at the pediatrician’s office. Monday through Friday it runs from 4 to 11:30 p.m. Saturday and Sunday it’s noon to 7:30 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an arrival time online.
The grown-up version of the same secret sits on Barnes-Jewish Hospital’s own emergency medicine page. The level 1 trauma center on S. Kingshighway says it is seeing high patient volumes, waits may be longer, and people with mild-to-moderate symptoms and minor injuries can consider BJC Convenient Care or Virtual Care instead.
BJC says a Convenient Care co-pay is often the same as a primary care visit. Its Virtual Care providers are available 24/7 for minor illnesses and injuries, for patients located in Missouri or Illinois, and you can start through MyChart or as a guest. On a Sunday at nine, that phone in your pocket may be the cheapest door you have.
For chest pain, none of this math matters. The ER is the only door that counts.
### Is it more expensive to go to the ER or urgent care?
The ER, almost always. MedlinePlus says emergency department care can cost 2 to 3 times or more than the same care in your provider’s office, and your insurance may require a higher copayment there. Urgent care can deal with minor injuries such as sprains and minor broken bones. For severe chest pain or sudden weakness on one side, call 911.
### Why the same sprain costs so much more in one building
An emergency room is not a clinic with brighter lights. The Barnes-Jewish Hospital Emergency Room at 400 S. Kingshighway Blvd. lists itself as open 24 hours, 7 days a week, and describes itself as a level 1 trauma center and comprehensive stroke center. Standing by for the worst thing that could come through the doors at 3 a.m. costs money every hour of every day, and part of that cost lands on everyone who walks in, including you and your swollen wrist.
The law adds a promise, too. Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, Medicare-participating hospitals that offer emergency services must give a medical screening exam to anyone who asks for one, regardless of ability to pay, and then provide stabilizing treatment for an emergency condition. That’s a good thing. It also means the ER works out the bill afterward, not before.
And the bill rarely arrives as one envelope. On its price estimate page, Barnes-Jewish says its estimates cover hospital costs only and do not include physician or other professional fees, which are billed separately by other providers. So when the first statement shows up, don’t assume it’s the last one. Keep the discharge papers in the same kitchen drawer as the bills.
### The cheaper doors for a swollen wrist at 9 p.m.
Urgent care is not the only alternative to the ER, and it isn’t always the cheapest one. Around St. Louis, the big health systems run a few other doors, and each one is worth a line in your phone.
Washington University Children’s After Hours. For kids, at 12436 Tesson Ferry Road: Monday through Friday 4 to 11:30 p.m., Saturday and Sunday noon to 7:30 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an arrival time online.
BJC Convenient Care. BJC says that at convenient care your co-pay is often the same as a primary care visit, and it’s often less expensive than a visit to an urgent care or emergency room. It’s meant for urgent, non-life-threatening needs.
BJC Virtual Care. BJC says its virtual care providers are available 24/7 for minor illnesses and injuries, for patients located in Missouri or Illinois, and visits are typically billed at the same rate as a primary care visit, depending on insurance.
Mercy-GoHealth Urgent Care. Mercy says its centers are open seven days a week, including holidays, and that you can reach virtual Urgent Care from anywhere in Missouri, Oklahoma and Arkansas.
Your own doctor’s after-hours line. MedlinePlus says that when the office is closed, your call may be forwarded to a nurse or other provider who is on call.
A video visit at the kitchen table, phone propped against the sugar jar, can answer the question you actually have at nine on a Sunday: which door do I need? That alone can save a wasted drive.

### Is there a 24-hour urgent care in St. Louis?

### When the wrist is not the worry: skip the math
Some nights the swollen wrist is the small problem in the house. MedlinePlus, from the National Library of Medicine, says to call 911 when you or someone with you cannot wait, such as for:
Severe chest pain or pressure
Severe shortness of breath
A seizure that lasted more than 1 minute
Suddenly not able to speak, see, walk or move
Suddenly weak or drooping on one side of the body
A head injury with passing out, fainting or confusion
It sends these to an emergency department rather than a clinic:
Coughing or throwing up blood
A severe allergic reaction with trouble breathing, swelling or hives
Severe pain anywhere on the body
A possible broken bone with loss of movement, especially if the bone is pushing through the skin
The rule under all of it, in MedlinePlus’s words: if a person or unborn baby could die or be permanently disabled, it is an emergency.
And for that wrist, MedlinePlus’s page on when to use the emergency room for a child lists this sign: a body part near an injured bone that is numb, tingling, weak, cold or pale. Touch the fingers. Look at the nails. If the hand below the swelling is cold, pale or numb, put the keys in the ignition and go to the ER.
### What urgent care handles, and where the wrist stops being minor
MedlinePlus says to go to urgent care when the problem is not life threatening or risking disability, but you’re worried and can’t see your own provider soon enough. It lists the kinds of things a clinic can take care of:
Colds, the flu, earaches, sore throats, minor headaches, low-grade fevers and limited rashes.
Sprains, bruises, minor cuts and burns, minor broken bones and minor eye injuries.
A trampoline wrist with warm, pink fingers is the kind of sprain-or-maybe-a-small-break that list is talking about. Past that line, the clinic will send you on, and now you’ve paid for two visits in one night. That double bill is the real cost of guessing wrong in the cheap direction. When you’re not sure, call the clinic first and describe what you see. It takes two minutes.
One honest twist from the researchers behind that $171 figure. Writing for Penn’s Leonard Davis Institute, they found that 37 urgent care visits were associated with the decline of one lower-acuity emergency department visit. Translation: because urgent care is so easy, people use it a lot more, and overall spending went up. The cheap door is only cheap if it replaces the expensive one. It is not a reason to go for every sniffle.
Think about it like odds, because that’s what it is. Anyone who has spent an evening at a St. Louis casino knows that a small chance of a very bad outcome is worth paying to avoid. Apply the same thinking to chest pain and the answer is easy. Apply it to a sore throat and so is the other answer.

### No insurance? Ask before anyone touches you
Being uninsured at a front desk, a kid on your hip with a bag of frozen peas on the wrist, feels like holding your breath. You can let some of it out. Federal rules give you real rights here, and asking about price is ordinary.
At a walk-in clinic, ask for the self-pay price first. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much is an ER visit out of pocket?
A.  It depends on your plan, but the full price is steep: the average emergency department visit cost $1,646 in a Health Affairs study of roughly 29 million managed care enrollees. MedlinePlus says your insurance may require a higher copayment for the emergency department. Physician fees can be billed separately from the hospital, so ask for an estimate where you can.
### Q. Why do people go to the ER instead of urgent care?
A.  Mostly hours and fear. An emergency room like Barnes-Jewish Hospital’s lists itself as open 24 hours, 7 days a week, and when you’re scared you want the place that can handle anything. A nurse advice line or a virtual visit can help you decide, and BJC says its Virtual Care providers are available 24/7.
### Q. What shouldn't you go to urgent care for?
A.  MedlinePlus says to call 911 or go to the emergency department for severe chest pain or pressure, severe shortness of breath, sudden weakness or drooping on one side, a seizure lasting more than a minute, a head injury with passing out or confusion, coughing up blood, or a bone pushing through the skin.
### Q. Can urgent care treat a broken bone?
A.  For minor ones, yes. MedlinePlus lists minor broken bones among the kinds of problems an urgent care clinic can deal with. Go to the emergency department for a possible broken bone with loss of movement, especially if the bone is pushing through the skin, or if the area near the injury is numb, tingling, cold or pale.
### Q. What are some disadvantages of urgent care?
A.  It stops where the problem turns life threatening, so a wrong guess can mean paying for two visits. Researchers writing for Penn’s Leonard Davis Institute also found that urgent care raised overall spending, because 37 urgent care visits were associated with the decline of one lower-acuity emergency visit.
### Q. Is it better to go to the ER or urgent care if you don't have insurance?
A.  For anything that isn’t an emergency, a walk-in clinic is usually the cheaper door, and you can ask for its self-pay price first. Uninsured patients can usually get a good faith estimate under federal rules. For a true emergency, go to the ER: hospitals must screen you regardless of ability to pay.
### Q. Is $100 copay for urgent care normal?
A.  There is no single normal; your plan sets it. HealthCare.gov says the Summary of Benefits and Coverage lets you make apples-to-apples comparisons of costs and coverage, so check yours. In St. Louis, BJC says a Convenient Care co-pay is often the same as a primary care visit, and often less expensive than a visit to an urgent care.

## Acupuncture in St. Louis: Medicare Covers It but Can't Pay Your Acupuncturist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/acupuncture-in-st-louis-what-to-know-before-you-go
Nobody says it at the front desk, but most people stalling on acupuncture aren’t stalling on the price. They’re stalling on the needles. You can already hear the paper sheet crackle under your back, feel the cold swab on your skin, and hear a calm voice say “little pinch” while every muscle you own braces for worse.
Missouri has an answer for half of that fear. It is unlawful for anyone to practice acupuncture in this state without a license, and the license requires the practitioner to be at least 21 and actively certified as a Diplomate in Acupuncture by the National Commission for the Certification of Acupuncture and Oriental Medicine. The Missouri Acupuncturist Advisory Committee licenses and regulates every one of them. The hand holding the needle answers to the state.
The other half is money, and here is the line to say out loud to the friend who swears Medicare paid for theirs: Medicare will cover acupuncture, but it can’t pay a licensed acupuncturist directly. In St. Louis that turns one decision into two doors, and the door you pick decides whether you get a claim or a bill.
### Will insurance pay for acupuncture?
Usually not, and a St. Louis hospital says so on its own page. WashU Medicine’s Living Well Center says insurance coverage varies, but acupuncture is usually not covered by most healthcare insurance carriers, and it asks you to call your carrier before the appointment. Make that call at the kitchen table with your card face-up and a pen ready, because the answer sets the whole budget.
Medicare is the exception, with sharp edges. Part B only covers acupuncture, including dry needling, for chronic low back pain: pain lasting 12 weeks or longer, with no known cause, and not tied to surgery or pregnancy. The stiff neck from a winter of shoveling, the knee that clicks on the stairs, the migraine that parks behind one eye - none of those fit. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.
And it runs on a stopwatch. Medicare covers up to 12 acupuncture treatments in 90 days for chronic low back pain. If you show improvement, it covers an additional 8 sessions, for a maximum of 20 in a 12-month period. If you are not improving, it stops paying.
### Two doors in St. Louis: the physician route or the acupuncturist’s office
Here is the catch most people find out from a bill. Medicare can’t pay licensed acupuncturists directly for their services. You have to get the treatment from a doctor or another health care provider, like a nurse practitioner or physician assistant, who also holds the acupuncture training Medicare spells out.
Door one is the medical route. At WashU Medicine’s Living Well Center, the first visit is a consultation: you meet with a physician who asks detailed questions about your medical history, and if your doctor decides acupuncture is right for you, you may get your first session at the end of that consultation. Mercy offers acupuncture inside its integrative medicine program too. If you are on Medicare with chronic low back pain, this is the kind of door to ask about first: “Will Medicare pay you for this, or will I be paying?”
Door two is the independent acupuncturist’s office, usually self-pay, often slower and quieter. Yong Kang Clinic in St. Louis posts its prices: a first visit is $177 and an hour and a half of your time; regular follow-up visits are $137 and usually take about an hour. No claim, no surprise. You know the number before you park.
Neither door is the better one. They are different deals, and the mistake is walking through one while expecting the other’s paperwork.
### What the first visit actually feels like
Slower than you expect, and mostly talking. Whichever door you pick, the first visit is mostly history and questions, which is why it runs longer than the ones after it.
Expect questions that seem off-topic. Sleep, digestion, stress, how cold your hands get. In traditional practice those answers shape the treatment, so give real ones instead of polite ones.
Then the part you have been dreading. Mercy describes acupuncture as thin, solid needles placed at specific points on the skin. Solid matters: nothing is injected, nothing is drawn out. Most people feel a quick tap, a dull heaviness, a faint warmth spreading under the skin, or nothing they could name. Then the lights go low and you lie still. A lot of people drift off, and you will hear it if you are one of them, because the room is quiet enough to catch your own breathing change.
Walking out, you may feel loose and drowsy or oddly bright. Both are common. Do not put a hard workout or a tense meeting right after the first one until you know which kind you are.
### How to judge it without fooling yourself
A single session tells you whether you can lie still with needles in. It tells you almost nothing about whether acupuncture helps you. Treat it like Medicare does: pick a course, decide before the first visit what “working” would look like, and write down where you are starting.
“My back is a bit better” is useless three months later. “In June I couldn’t sit through a Cardinals game at Busch without standing every inning, and now I can” is evidence. Make the goal that concrete, something your body either does or doesn’t.
Be wary of any practice that wants a big package paid upfront before you have a single data point. Ask three things: the price of one session, the price per session in a package, and what happens to unused sessions if you stop. That last answer matters most. A package that can’t be refunded turns a trial into a contract before you know anything.
Call your plan before you call the clinic. Coverage for specialist care is almost always plan-specific, the same trap people hit when they ask whether they need a referral to see an allergist in St. Louis. Five minutes on hold can decide whether a course costs you a copay or the full price.
If you run an acupuncture or massage practice, the nervous first-timer reading this is the customer still deciding where to book. When they ask an AI assistant for a licensed acupuncturist near them, is your name the one it gives? See who AI names instead of you.
### Choosing a practitioner in the metro
The license is the floor. Every acupuncturist practicing in Missouri needs a state license, so ask for theirs before you book. Then ask the questions a good practice answers without flinching:
Are you licensed in the state where this clinic sits? If you cross the river for care, the clinic’s state is the one that counts.
Are the needles single-use and disposable? The answer should be an instant yes.
How often do you treat my specific problem? Practitioners specialize like everyone else.
Do you bill insurance, or is it self-pay? And for Medicare, can you bill it at all?
Will you tell me when to stop? The one who will say “this isn’t working for you” is worth more.
Needles out, jaw unclenched, nowhere to be. Spend the next hour at a St. Louis tea house.
### How to prepare the day of
Eat something light first. An empty stomach is a common reason people feel woozy on the table.
Skip alcohol and go easy on caffeine beforehand.
Wear loose clothes that roll up past the knee and elbow.
Bring your medication list, especially blood thinners. The practitioner needs to know.
Tell them you’re nervous. It changes how they talk you through the first needle.
### The part nobody warns you about
Sometimes people cry on the table. Not from pain. It tends to come out of nowhere, a while into lying still with your eyes closed, when the shoulders you have been holding up since breakfast finally drop and something else drops with them. A tear runs sideways into your ear and you lie there wondering whether to wipe it.
If that happens, you have not done anything wrong, and a seasoned practitioner will not be thrown by it. Say so if you want a minute before you sit up. Ask for a tissue. Drink the water they hand you. Some people feel wrung out for the rest of the evening; some feel lighter than they have in weeks. Either way, it is worth a line in the notes you are keeping, because how you feel the night after is part of the evidence too.
The other surprise is the quiet. Most of us never lie still that long without a phone. The hum of a space heater, rain on a window, your own pulse in your ears. For some people that stillness turns out to be half of what they came for.
### Acupuncture or dry needling?
They look alike on the table: a thin needle, a held breath. Acupuncture works inside a traditional point system and is done by people licensed for it. Dry needling is mostly done by physical therapists aiming at tight muscle knots, described in Western anatomy terms. Medicare lumps them together for chronic low back pain only; private plans may treat them very differently. If a physical therapist offers “needling,” ask which one it is and how it will be billed.
### What it will not do
Acupuncture is not a diagnosis. If new or worsening pain has never been properly checked, get it checked first, because pain is a symptom and treating it blind can delay finding what caused it. It is not emergency care and not a reason to stop medication you were told to take. Alongside regular care for chronic pain, it has a place. Instead of regular care, it is a gamble.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Does acupuncture hurt first time?
A.  Usually less than you fear. The needles are thin and solid, nothing is injected, and most people feel a quick tap, a dull ache or nothing at all. Tell the practitioner you are nervous; a good one will talk you through the first needle and stop if you ask.
### Q. How long is a first time acupuncture session?
A.  Longer than the ones after it, because most of it is history and questions. One St. Louis clinic, Yong Kang, posts its first visit as an hour and a half and its regular follow-ups as about an hour.
### Q. What is the average cost for an acupuncture session?
A.  Prices vary by practice, so ask before you book. As one local example, Yong Kang Clinic in St. Louis lists $177 for a first visit and $137 for regular follow-ups. WashU Medicine’s Living Well Center notes acupuncture is usually not covered by most insurance carriers, so plan as if you are paying unless your plan says otherwise.
### Q. What should you not do before acupuncture?
A.  Don’t arrive on an empty stomach, skip alcohol, go easy on caffeine, and don’t book a hard workout right after the first session. Wear loose clothes and bring your medication list, especially if you take blood thinners.
### Q. Is it normal to fall asleep during acupuncture?
A.  Yes. The room is quiet, the lights are low and you are lying still, so many people drift off. It is not a problem, and nobody minds the snoring.
### Q. What are the signs that acupuncture is working?
A.  A change you can measure in your own life: sleeping through the night, sitting through a full game or a long drive, walking a distance you had given up. Write your starting point down before the first visit, because memory is a poor judge three months later.
### Q. When should acupuncture be avoided?
A.  Don’t use it in place of getting a new or worsening symptom diagnosed, in an emergency, or as a reason to stop prescribed medication. If you take blood thinners, are pregnant or have a bleeding condition, tell the practitioner before any needle goes in.
### Q. Where can I find the best acupuncture in St. Louis?
A.  Start with a license. Missouri makes it unlawful to practice acupuncture without one, so ask to see it, then compare an option like WashU Medicine’s Living Well Center or Mercy’s integrative medicine program with independent clinics on price, insurance and how often they treat your problem.

## The Maplewood Chocolate Shop With a Curry Award: Why Artisan Chocolate Costs More
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/artisan-chocolate-in-st-louis-what-makes-it-different
A chocolate shop on Manchester Road has a Good Food Award for Thai red curry. Another one on its list is for a wine jelly named after Norton, the grape Missouri law picked as its official state grape. Neither one is a truffle, and both tell you how this kitchen works.
Behind the glass at Kakao Chocolate in Maplewood, somebody is standing over a pot of caramel with a spoon, waiting for one temperature. A little short and the caramel runs. A little past and it turns chewy. The shop says it cooks its caramel to a specific temperature for a texture that is not too gooey and not too chewy, and that you can watch its confectioners stir the caramel, dip the truffles and make the marshmallows by hand, right in front of you. The air in there smells like warm sugar and cocoa.
That spoon is most of the answer to why the little box costs more than the grocery-store bag. You can go see it today: Kakao is at 7272 Manchester Road, open Tuesday through Friday from 12 to 6 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., 314-645-4446. Order the $7 marshmallow pie first. It is layers of vanilla bean marshmallow, chocolate and Missouri pecans, soft enough to give under your thumb, with the pecans cracking under the chocolate when you bite.
That is the same kitchen, and the same habit. Kakao’s list of Good Food Awards includes its Norton Pates de Vin and a Clean Plate Pantry Thai Red Curry, from the shop’s line of savory sauces. A chocolate shop on Manchester Road, winning for curry, because somebody there cooks everything by hand and will not hand the pot to a machine. Keep that in mind as we get to what you are paying for.
### Why is artisan chocolate so expensive?
Because a person makes it, in small batches, and nothing about that scales. Go back to the caramel pot. A factory runs that step by machine, in batches no kitchen pot could hold. A small kitchen runs it with one cook who cannot walk away, and a pot cooked past its point is a pot thrown out. That loss lands in the price.
The same math runs through the whole case. A hand-dipped truffle is somebody’s afternoon. Kakao says it makes everything from scratch with no artificial flavors, colors or preservatives, and that means less can be made weeks ahead, so more gets made fresh and less gets sold before it fades. Small batches mean no volume discount on anything, ever. You are paying for a person’s afternoon, not a factory’s minute.
The supermarket bar is cheaper because it was designed to be: long runs, shelf-stable fillings, a supply chain built around price. That is a fair product. It is just made for a different moment than the one you have at a glass case, breathing warm sugar.
### Sunday closes at 4, so go early
The single most useful tip for a first visit is about the clock. Kakao opens at noon on weekdays and closes at 4 p.m. on weekends, and its posted hours skip Mondays entirely. The Saturday afternoon stroll after a late lunch that ends at a locked door is a real way to miss it. Check the clock before you check the map.
Buy two things, not twelve. First, the piece that could not survive a warehouse: one of the shop’s award-winning truffles or that marshmallow pie. Let a truffle sit on your tongue a few seconds before you chew, and the flavor arrives in layers instead of all at once. Then taste something plain, a square of dark chocolate, and notice whether the flavor lingers after you swallow or vanishes. Two pieces, five minutes, and you know more about what you like than any ranking could tell you.
### A basement, a career change, and a curry award
The story behind the counter is part of what you are tasting. According to Kakao’s own history, owner and chief chocolatier Brian Pelletier spent twenty years in business marketing before he went looking for different work: making people happy with chocolate. It started in a windowless basement.
The award list reads like someone who never stopped experimenting. A lavender truffle. A Turkish coffee truffle. A raspberry goat cheese truffle, which sounds like a dare until you eat one: tart fruit first, then a cool tang, then the dark shell melting off your tongue. That is the kind of flavor work a craft chocolatier competes on.
Notice what Kakao is, too. It is a confectioner. Its craft lives in the truffles, the caramels and the marshmallows, which is where most excellent local chocolate shops put their skill. That is different from a bean-to-bar maker, and knowing the difference is the fastest way to stop overpaying.
### What “artisan” means, and the label that means more
“Artisan” on a box is not a guarantee of anything. It is a word, not a standard, so on its own it tells you very little. Look past it to what the shop actually does.
“Bean-to-bar” is a real claim about a real process. It says the maker starts with raw cocoa beans and handles everything after: roasting, cracking, winnowing, grinding, conching and tempering. If you have ever stood near a roaster, you know the smell, something between brownies and toasted nuts with a sharp, almost winey edge. A bean-to-bar maker competes on sourcing and roasting.
A chocolatier competes on flavor and finish. Many fine shops start from high-quality chocolate made by someone else and do their craft in what they build from it: the ganache, the fillings, the caramel, the dipping and finishing. That is a genuine craft. It is just a different one. Both can be superb. Only one of them is making chocolate from beans, and a good shop will tell you which one it is without blinking.
### How to tell craft from merely expensive
Price alone proves nothing. These do.
Read the ingredient list. Good dark chocolate has a short one: cocoa beans or cocoa mass, sugar, cocoa butter, maybe vanilla. If vegetable fats are standing in for cocoa butter, you are paying craft prices for a coating.
Check the snap and the shine. Well-tempered chocolate breaks with a clean, dry crack you can hear, and the surface is glossy enough to catch the light from the case. Dull, soft or crumbly means the temper failed somewhere.
Ask what they make and what they buy. Any good shop answers happily. The answer tells you which craft you are paying for.
Ask what they are proud of. Whatever they name first is usually where the skill is, and it is rarely the thing in the window.
### Is bean to bar chocolate better?
Not automatically. It is more traceable, because one maker controls every step and can tell you where the beans came from and how they were roasted. A great bean-to-bar bar tastes like a place: fruity, earthy, sometimes almost smoky. A poorly made one is still poorly made, however short the ingredient list. And a filled truffle from a skilled chocolatier is a different pleasure entirely. Judge the piece in your hand, not the label on the box.
The percentage on a dark bar trips people up too. It tells you how much of the bar came from the cocoa bean, cocoa solids plus cocoa butter, and the rest is mostly sugar. So a higher number means less sugar, not better chocolate. Use the percentage to predict sweetness. Use the ingredient list, the origin and the shop’s own recommendation to predict quality.
Dessert sorted. Now dinner: where to eat in downtown Kirkwood.
### Buying it without wasting money
Buy one piece first. A single $7 marshmallow pie tells you what a whole box would have.
Buy close to when you will eat it. Fresh cream fillings are at their best within days, not months.
Store it cool and dry, not cold. The refrigerator is the most common way people ruin good chocolate.
Find your shop before the holidays. Small kitchens have real capacity limits, and the good pieces sell out in the rush.
Buying for a gift is a different purchase from buying for yourself. For a gift that has to ride in a car or sit under a tree, ask the shop directly what holds up. Kakao, for one, says it ships in insulated boxes with frozen gel packs, which tells you how seriously a good shop takes heat. For yourself, buy the fragile thing, two pieces instead of twelve, and eat them that week. The most perishable items in the case are where the maker’s skill is easiest to taste, and they are exactly what no supermarket sells at any price.
### Why the holiday rush is the wrong time to discover a shop
A chocolatier who hand-dips every piece cannot simply double output for December. The kettle holds what it holds. The people at the counter have two hands each. So the best selection and the most attention both happen outside the weeks when everyone shows up at once, and the walk-in on the last Saturday before Christmas often meets a picked-over case and a line out the door, with the bell over the door ringing every few seconds.
That is how a lot of people decide artisan chocolate is overrated. They did not taste the shop at its best. They tasted what was left. The fix is simple: find your shop in the fall. Go on a quiet weekday afternoon, buy one or two pieces, and decide whether you like it while the people behind the counter have time to talk. Then order any gift boxes early, and ask how far ahead the shop wants custom orders. The same logic holds for Valentine’s Day and Easter, when small kitchens run at their ceiling again.
There is a quieter reason to go early, too. A shop that knows your face in October is a shop that will find you something good when the case is thin in December. That is the part of buying local that no price tag captures: the person who remembers you liked the lavender one.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What does “artisan chocolate” mean?
A.  On its own, not much. It describes a style, so look at what the shop actually does. The more meaningful label is bean-to-bar, which says the maker starts from raw cocoa beans and controls roasting, grinding, conching and tempering. Many fine chocolatiers instead start from quality chocolate and craft the fillings, caramels and finishing, which is a different skill, not a lesser one.
### Q. Is artisan chocolate worth it?
A.  For eating slowly, often yes. For baking or bulk snacking, usually not, because the hand labor and fresh ingredients get lost in a recipe. Buy one or two pieces before committing to a box. That single purchase tells you what the expensive version would have.
### Q. Which artisan chocolate brand is considered the best?
A.  There is no single answer, and anyone offering one is stating a preference. Awards are one honest signal: Kakao Chocolate in Maplewood has won Good Food Awards for several of its truffles. Beyond that, judge by process: a short ingredient list, a clean snap, a glossy surface, and a shop that will tell you plainly what it makes and what it buys.
### Q. What is bean to bar chocolate?
A.  Chocolate made from scratch by one maker, starting with raw cocoa beans and running through roasting, cracking, winnowing, grinding, conching and tempering into the finished bar. It is different from a chocolatier’s craft, which usually starts with finished chocolate and builds truffles, caramels and other confections from it.
### Q. Is bean to bar chocolate better?
A.  It is more traceable, not automatically tastier. One maker controls every step, so you can learn exactly where the beans came from and how they were handled. Whether the bar is better depends on the beans and the skill, so taste before you trust the label.
### Q. Is artisan chocolate healthy?
A.  It is still sugar and fat, so treat it as a pleasure rather than a health food. Higher-percentage dark chocolate carries more cocoa and less sugar than milk chocolate, and a shop like Kakao that skips artificial flavors, colors and preservatives means fewer additives. Portion matters far more than either.
### Q. Where can I find chocolate in Saint Louis?
A.  Kakao Chocolate is at 7272 Manchester Road in Maplewood, 314-645-4446, open Tuesday through Friday 12-6 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday 10 a.m.-4 p.m. For more shops across the metro, search chocolatiers on St Louis Near Me Directory, and call ahead near the holidays.
### Q. How should you store good chocolate?
A.  Cool, dry and sealed, not in the refrigerator. Cold storage invites condensation and sugar bloom, and chocolate picks up odors from everything around it. A cupboard away from the stove beats the fridge every time.
Go on a weekday afternoon and buy one piece. Watch what is being made behind the counter, ask what they are proudest of, and let a single truffle or marshmallow pie make the case before you buy the box. ## Fired in Missouri? A Certified Letter Can Make Them Say Why
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/fired-in-missouri-what-your-rights-actually-are
Red light on the badge reader. You swipe again, and it blinks red again, and the security guard at the Maryland Heights warehouse door is already walking over with a face that says he got a list this morning. By 9 a.m. you are back in the car with the heater ticking, a cardboard box on the passenger seat holding a desk fan, a coffee mug and a framed photo, and one question riding with you all the way down I-270: was that even allowed?
The honest answer stings before it helps. In Missouri, a job can end at any time and for any reason, unless the reason is one the law forbids. Your boss can let you go without a warning, without a meeting, without a reason said out loud.
But here is the part almost nobody hears in that first week, and it is written into state law. Under Missouri statute 290.140, if you worked at least ninety days for a corporation that employs seven or more people, you can send a request by certified mail, naming the statute, and the company has forty-five days to hand you a signed letter “truly stating for what cause, if any” you were let go. You have up to one year after the firing to ask.
Say it to the next friend who gets walked out: they did not have to tell you why in the room. They may have to tell you on paper.
And if the job was inside St. Louis city limits, you carry one more protection the state’s list does not name. City Ordinance 68715 outlaws discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, according to the city’s Civil Rights Enforcement Agency, which takes employment complaints at 314-622-4800.
That letter matters because the reason is the whole case. Fair or unfair is not the test here. The test is what the reason was, and whether it sits on a short list the law forbids.
### What qualifies as wrongful termination in Missouri?
A firing is wrongful only when the reason behind it is one the law bans. The Missouri Department of Labor puts the rule plainly: Missouri follows the employment-at-will doctrine, so either side can end the job “at any time and for any reason,” as long as no contract is broken and no civil rights law is violated. Arbitrary is allowed. A boss who fires you to make room for his nephew is a bad boss, not a lawbreaker.
Legal Services of Missouri lays out the exceptions: an employment contract to the contrary; discrimination based on race, color, age, national origin, religion, ancestry, sex or disability; or a firing that breaks Missouri public policy, which usually means you refused to do something illegal, blew the whistle on your employer, or used your workers’ compensation rights.
If your job was in the city and the jokes in the break room were about who you love or how you dress, that city ordinance is the door to try first. The agency provides a free, impartial investigation.
### What happens if you are fired for no reason?
Usually, nothing illegal happened. That is hard to hear at the kitchen table at midnight with the termination letter going soft at the corners from being reread.
But no reason given is not the same as no reason existed, and this is where the service letter earns its stamp. A reason that shows up for the first time months later, in front of an investigator, looks a lot thinner than one written down while it was fresh. Ask for it now, by certified mail, and you pin the company to one story. The letter can be three sentences: your name and job title, your start and end dates, and a line saying you are requesting a service letter under Section 290.140 of the Missouri Revised Statutes. Mail it to the manager, superintendent or registered agent, keep the green return-receipt card, and mark day forty-five on the calendar.
Two more things still happen even when nobody explains anything. First, the money you already earned is yours. The state labor department says to request wages due from your former employer by certified mail, return receipt requested; the employer has seven days to respond, and if it does not pay within those seven days it can owe you additional wages for up to sixty days. Second, you can apply for unemployment through the Division of Employment Security. The state decides whether you qualify, not your old manager, so file and let the agency make that call.
### The four exceptions that turn a legal firing into an illegal one
These are the only doors that open, and each one has its own tell. One clock runs on all of them: the Missouri Commission on Human Rights says complaints under the Missouri Human Rights Act must be filed within 180 days of the alleged discrimination, while federal law allows 300 days to file with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. That clock does not stop while you are sleeping badly and job hunting.
### Discrimination under the Missouri Human Rights Act
According to the Missouri Commission on Human Rights, the Missouri Human Rights Act makes it illegal to discriminate in hiring and firing because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or age (40 through 69). Those categories are the protected ones. A firing motivated by any of them is not a management decision, it is a legal problem.
Direct evidence is rare. Almost nobody says the quiet part in an email anymore. What tends to matter instead is pattern and timing: who else was cut and who was kept, what changed after you disclosed a pregnancy or a diagnosis, whether the stated policy was applied to everybody or only to you. One comment is a comment. A comment plus a sudden performance file plus an unusual exception to the usual process starts to look like something else.
### Retaliation for doing something protected
An employer cannot fire you for reporting illegal acts, for reporting safety violations, or for filing a workers’ compensation claim. This is the exception people talk themselves out of most often, usually with some version of “they would never be that obvious about it.” Sometimes they are exactly that obvious.
Timing is the tell here. If you were a solid employee for four years, reported something in June, and were managed out by August, the calendar itself is evidence worth showing to somebody. Write down the dates now, while you still remember which week was which.
### Refusing to break the law
Missouri’s public policy exception protects an employee who is fired for refusing to do something illegal. In real life this looks like being asked to falsify an inspection, alter a record, skip a required safety step, backdate a document, or misreport somebody’s hours. Saying no to that and losing your job over it is one of the clearest situations in this entire area of law.
### A written contract that promised something specific
If you have a written contract promising a set term of employment, or one saying you can only be dismissed for “just cause,” then at-will does not apply to you the same way. The contract governs instead. Check the actual document rather than your memory of the conversation, because a verbal assurance that you had a job for life generally does not carry the same weight as a signed term. Union members often have comparable protections through a collective bargaining agreement, along with a grievance process that runs on its own timeline.
### What evidence does HR need to fire someone?
In an at-will state, legally, none. HR is not a court and a firing is not a verdict. There is no burden of proof to meet, no hearing you can lose, and no rule that the reason be sensible. The one place the law asks for the truth is the service letter, which has to state the cause truly if you request it.
In practice most HR departments document heavily anyway, and it helps to understand why. The file is not built to convince you. It is built for the possibility that a state agency or an attorney asks, eighteen months from now, what the reason was. Write-ups, performance plans, attendance logs and coaching notes all exist so the company’s answer stays consistent under questioning.
Which is exactly why a paper trail that appears out of nowhere is worth noticing. A file that starts three weeks after you filed a complaint, requested a leave, or reported an injury reads very differently from one that goes back three years. Request a copy of your personnel file in writing, and keep your own dated notes about meetings, who was present, and what was said.
One caution on that. Keep your records, not the company’s. Walking out with confidential documents, client lists or system access is a reliable way to turn your case into their case.
### Does HR decide who gets fired?
Rarely on their own. In most organizations the operating manager drives the decision and HR administers it: reviewing documentation, checking that the process was followed, calculating final pay, sitting in the room as a witness. HR’s job in that meeting is to protect the company from a bad process. Sometimes that protects you as a side effect, and sometimes it does not.
This matters for one very practical reason. The person delivering the news is often not the person who made the call, so the tone in that room tells you almost nothing about the reasoning behind it. Someone can be genuinely sorry and still be reading a script. If you want to know why, ask for the reason in writing instead of trying to read the messenger’s face.
### Can a hiring manager override HR?
Often, yes, within limits. In most companies HR advises rather than commands, and a determined manager with budget authority usually gets the outcome they want on hiring and firing. The exception runs the other way: HR can stop or slow a termination that creates obvious legal exposure, because that is the risk they are paid to see coming. In smaller shops there may be no HR function at all, in which case the manager and the owner are the entire process, start to finish.
### What is the #1 reason that employees get fired?
There is no single authoritative answer, and any article handing you one tidy percentage is guessing at it. What can be said honestly is that the reasons employers actually write down cluster into a short list, and pure job performance is not always at the top of it.
Attendance and reliability. Chronic lateness and unexcused absences are the easiest thing in the world to document, which is part of why they show up so often.
Policy violations. Safety rules, expense rules, equipment use, confidentiality. Bright-line rules produce bright-line terminations.
Conduct toward other people. Harassment, threats, and the slow-burn kind of behavior that finally generates a complaint from a coworker.
Performance. Usually the slowest path, because it typically requires goals, documentation and a plan before anyone signs off.
Reduction in force. The budget changed, the contract ended, the department got restructured.
Worth noticing: only that last one has nothing to do with you at all, and it is the category most likely to arrive wearing a different label. If you were told your performance had slipped but three colleagues were cut the same week and none of the roles were backfilled, that was a layoff. What it gets called on the paperwork can matter later, especially for unemployment.
### What should you do in the first week after being fired?
The first few days are when you have the most leverage and the least composure, which is an unfortunate combination. A short, boring checklist beats improvising here.
Write the timeline down that same night. Dates, names, who said what, what was in your file before and after. Memory degrades fast and specifics are what anyone reviewing this will ask for.
Ask for the reason in writing. A polite email asking the company to confirm the stated reason for separation costs you nothing and creates a record.
Do not sign anything in the room. Severance agreements almost always include a release of claims. Take it home. Read it twice. Have somebody qualified read it once.
Request your personnel file in writing. Ask for write-ups, reviews and any documentation supporting the decision.
Save your own copies, not the company’s data. Your reviews, your emails about your own work, your notes. Nothing confidential.
File for unemployment right away. Do not wait for the severance conversation to resolve first.
Check your final paycheck against your records. Hours, commissions, and anything your written policy says about accrued time off.
And one more that people skip because it feels indulgent. Losing a job is a genuine stressor, and the metro has free and low-cost mental health support that does not require an employer plan to access. Nobody makes good decisions about a severance agreement at three in the morning.
Unrelated palate cleanser for a rough week: what makes St. Louis artisan chocolate different.
### What are you actually owed on the way out?
Less than most people assume, and more than most people claim. The wages you already earned are yours regardless of how the separation went, and that is not negotiable based on how the last meeting felt. Everything after that depends on documents.
Accrued time off generally follows your employer’s written policy or your contract rather than a universal rule, so the handbook is the place to look. Severance is normally something a company offers, not something the law hands you, which is precisely why it usually arrives attached to a release you are asked to sign. Continued health coverage is often available at your own cost, and the plan administrator is who explains the terms.
For questions about wages and the mechanics of final pay, the Missouri Department of Labor is the authority worth checking before you take anybody’s word for it, including a former manager’s. Deadlines and requirements vary by situation, and getting that from the source beats getting it from a group chat.
### When is it worth calling an employment attorney?
Not every bad firing is a case, and a good attorney will tell you that in the first ten minutes. But there are patterns that are worth a phone call rather than a shrug, and most of them are about reason and timing rather than about how unfair the whole thing felt.
You were fired soon after reporting something, filing a workers’ compensation claim, or requesting a leave or accommodation.
Comments were made about your age, pregnancy, disability, religion or national origin, by anyone involved in the decision.
You have a written contract, or you are covered by a collective bargaining agreement.
You were asked to do something you believed was illegal, said no, and were gone shortly afterward.
You have been handed a severance agreement with a release of claims and a signing window.
The stated reason is demonstrably false and you can show it.
Bring documents to that first conversation, not just the story. Your offer letter, the handbook, reviews, write-ups, the termination letter, and your dated timeline. Ask what an initial consultation costs when you call, because that varies from one practice to the next and there is no reason to guess. Employment law is a specialty, so look for someone who does this work specifically rather than a generalist who will take it on.
If the answer turns out to be that you have no case, that is still useful. It frees you to put the energy into the next job instead of into a grievance that was never going to move. Plenty of people in the metro have restarted from a standing stop, and there are practical places to begin, including part-time work while a longer search runs.
If the problem is the pay itself, start with the Missouri minimum wage, who is exempt, and how to file a wage complaint.
If a union or a collective bargaining agreement is part of the picture, here’s when you need a labor relations attorney in St. Louis.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What happens if you are fired for no reason?
A.  In Missouri, usually nothing illegal has happened, because at-will employment lets an employer end the job at any time and for any reason, as long as no contract is broken and no civil rights law is violated. You can still ask for the reason on paper: Missouri statute 290.140 lets an employee of a corporation with seven or more employees, after at least ninety days on the job, request a service letter by certified mail, and the company has forty-five days to answer. You can also apply for unemployment and let the state decide whether you qualify.
### Q. What evidence does HR need to fire someone?
A.  Legally, none in an at-will state. There is no burden of proof before the firing, though a service letter you request later must state the cause truly. Most HR departments document anyway, because the file exists to give the company a consistent answer if an agency or an attorney asks later. A paper trail that begins right after a complaint or an injury report is worth noting.
### Q. Does HR decide who gets fired?
A.  Usually not alone. The operating manager typically drives the decision and HR administers it: checking documentation, confirming the process, calculating final pay, and sitting in as a witness. The person delivering the news is often not the person who made the call, so ask for the reason in writing rather than reading the room.
### Q. How long does it take for HR to fire someone?
A.  Anywhere from the same afternoon to several months, and the timeline reflects documentation more than deliberation. A serious conduct issue can move in hours. A performance case with write-ups and a formal plan often runs weeks. Missouri law does not require a notice period or a waiting time, so a long process is company policy rather than a legal right.
### Q. What is the #1 reason that employees get fired?
A.  There is no reliable single answer, and precise percentages floating around online are usually invented. The reasons employers put in writing cluster into attendance and reliability, policy violations, conduct toward coworkers, performance, and reductions in force. Attendance issues appear often simply because they are the easiest thing to document cleanly.
### Q. Can a hiring manager override HR?
A.  Frequently, yes. HR normally advises rather than commands, and a manager with budget authority tends to get the outcome they want. The reverse also happens: HR can halt a termination that creates clear legal exposure. At smaller companies there may be no HR at all, leaving the manager and owner as the whole process.
### Q. What is the 12 hour rule in Missouri?
A.  This question usually comes from workers looking for a cap on shift length or a required gap between shifts. Missouri does not set a general daily hour limit for adult employees the way many people expect, and overtime is normally figured on hours worked across a week. Rules differ for minors and for certain regulated industries, so confirm your situation with the Missouri Department of Labor.

## The Staircase Comes Later. Check the Missouri License First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hypnotherapy-in-st-louis-what-to-know-before-you-book
The recliner tips back, and a voice you met forty minutes ago asks you to find a staircase. One step down, then another. Your shoulders drop an inch you didn’t know they were holding. A phone buzzes on a desk across the room, and you hear it. Hypnosis isn’t sleep. You were never going under the way the movies promised.
So the question people in Kirkwood ask first, will I be out cold, is the wrong one. The right one comes before the recliner: who trained that voice, and for how long?
Missouri has a court record on exactly that. Two days after a woman was attacked in her apartment in Cape Girardeau, a police officer hypnotized her to sharpen her memory of the man. According to a later federal appeals court opinion, his only training in hypnosis was a four-day course. She was his twenty-seventh subject. At the end of the session, he told her that her memory of the event would improve.
The court set the conviction aside, holding that denying the defendant a state-provided expert on hypnosis made the trial fundamentally unfair. In the same opinion it noted that, under the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling in Alsbach v. Bader, hypnotically enhanced testimony “is not now admissible in Missouri courts.”
Four days of training. A twenty-seventh subject. A promise that her memory would get better. That’s how a hypnosis session in Missouri ended up in a federal court opinion. Before anyone walks you down the staircase, check the training and the license, then check the price.
Here’s the law that makes the license the right thing to check. Missouri’s psychology law, RSMo 337.015, names hypnosis outright. It sits inside the statute’s definition of the practice of psychology, right between psychotherapy and biofeedback, and the same section says no person shall engage in the practice of psychology in Missouri unless licensed under that chapter or otherwise exempt.
This is general information, not medical advice. If anxiety, pain or insomnia has a real grip on your life, bring it to a clinician first and use what follows as background for that conversation. And if tonight feels like a crisis rather than a booking question, call or text 988. Behavioral Health Response, whose crisis specialists work alongside St. Louis Metro 911 operators, calls itself Missouri’s largest 988 provider.
### Is it normal to feel worse after hypnotherapy?
It can happen, and it’s uncommon. Cleveland Clinic calls side effects rare and lists the ones people report: dizziness, drowsiness or fatigue, headaches, increased anxiety and trouble sleeping. Some people walk back out to the parking lot loose and warm. Others feel foggy, or a little raw, the way you can after a hard conversation you didn’t plan on having.
Sit in the car for a few minutes before you pull out onto Lindbergh, engine off, hands in your lap, until the fog lifts and the brake lights ahead look sharp again. Then say it out loud at the next appointment; Cleveland Clinic’s advice is to tell your hypnotherapist about any side effects or negative feelings. If a symptom doesn’t go away or keeps coming back, the NHS says ask a doctor, not just the therapist.
### Missouri wrote hypnosis into its psychology law
Read RSMo 337.015 and the list is plain: counseling, psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, hypnosis, biofeedback. The statute treats hypnosis as part of the practice of psychology, and it reserves that practice for people licensed under the chapter, unless an exemption applies.
The exemptions sit one page over, in RSMo 337.045. It lets qualified members of other professions, among them practitioners of medicine, licensed professional counselors, licensed clinical social workers, licensed marriage and family therapists and nurses, do work of a psychological nature consistent with their training and their own code of ethics. That is the door a licensed counselor, social worker or nurse who uses hypnosis walks through: the license is in something else, and hypnosis is one tool inside it.
From across a waiting room, every framed certificate looks official. Only a state license comes with a name you can look up. The Missouri Division of Professional Registration runs a Licensee Search at pr.mo.gov. Type the practitioner’s name and watch what comes back, because the license type tells you which committee to look at. The State Committee of Psychologists, the Committee for Professional Counselors and the Committee for Social Workers all list the same address: 3605 Missouri Boulevard in Jefferson City.
The psychologists’ committee page goes one step further than most people ever look. It posts a Disciplined Licensees list and a Complaint Form, and its office answers at 573.751.0099. A look at that page, sitting in your kitchen with the booking site open in the other tab, is the cheapest insurance in this whole decision.
The three-step check, before you pay a deposit: type the name into the Licensee Search at pr.mo.gov. Note the license type and open that committee’s page. If it’s a psychologist, scan the Disciplined Licensees list. Do it with your coffee going cold beside the laptop; it’s faster than the intake form.
And if the name doesn’t come up? Ask why before you pay. A certificate from a hypnosis training school is not a Missouri license, and a practitioner who is licensed in another state should be able to tell you which one.
Cleveland Clinic’s advice on choosing a hypnotherapist points the same direction: look for a healthcare professional who is properly trained, licensed and credentialed in a field such as medicine, dentistry, psychiatry, psychology, social work or nursing. That background matters most when the thing you want help with is anxiety, panic or something heavier, because a licensed clinician can tell when hypnosis is the wrong tool.
Ask at the first phone call: what license do you hold, and which Missouri board issued it? A good practitioner answers in one breath. A vague answer, a pause, a change of subject - that tells you as much as the answer would have.
### What actually happens in the hour in that recliner
Your attention narrows and your body lets go. Cleveland Clinic describes hypnosis as a state of deep relaxation and focused concentration, and lays out four stages: induction, deepening, suggestions and emergence.
Induction is the settling. Slow, controlled breathing. Tensing your muscles as you breathe in and letting them go as you breathe out. Deepening is where the staircase comes in: your therapist might have you picture slowly walking down a staircase or sinking into a comfortable bed. Suggestions are the work itself, the changes you came in for. Emergence runs the picture in reverse, climbing back up the stairs, or pulling the covers off and getting out of that comfortable bed.
You stay present the whole way through. Cleveland Clinic says most people remember everything that happens during a session, and that you’ll always be in control of your mind and thoughts. Sessions usually last around an hour, and you’ll probably need several before you feel a change.
### A quiet room, not a stage show
Hypnotherapy isn’t a sham, and it isn’t a cure either. If your only picture of hypnosis is a stage show and a volunteer clucking like a chicken, the clinic version will feel almost boring: a quiet room, a box of tissues, a person taking notes.
Cleveland Clinic calls hypnosis a type of complementary therapy, meaning something you receive along with typical medical or psychological treatment, not instead of it. It lists stress or anxiety, phobias and panic attacks among the conditions people use it for, and it says hypnosis isn’t mind control or brainwashing. It is also clear that hypnotherapy is safe when you work with a trained, certified therapist.
So judge the practitioner, not the technique. Be wary of anyone who guarantees a result, promises to cure a serious illness, or wants a large package paid upfront before you know whether it helps you. Cleveland Clinic notes that your therapist won’t be offended if hypnosis isn’t working well for you. One who is offended has told you something.
### Who should avoid hypnotherapy?
The NHS gives the clearest line. It says hypnotherapy may not be safe for you if you have schizophrenia or a history of psychosis, or if you have epilepsy. If that describes you, or the person you’re booking for, the question belongs with a treating clinician, not on a practitioner’s intake form.
Symptoms nobody has checked yet. New or worsening pain, insomnia or panic deserves an evaluation first.
A crisis right now. Hypnotherapy is not urgent care.
A history of dissociation or strong reactions to deep relaxation. Say so before the first session and let the practitioner decide.
Cost is its own wall, since hypnotherapy is often paid out of pocket. If money is what has kept you from care for anxiety, start with free and low-cost mental health and substance use help in St. Louis before you fund a complementary service yourself.
### What are the three things hypnosis cannot do?
It can’t take control of you. Cleveland Clinic says hypnosis isn’t mind control or brainwashing, and that you’ll always be in control of your mind and thoughts.
It can’t put you to sleep. Losing consciousness under hypnosis is, in Cleveland Clinic’s words, a common myth. Most people remember the whole session.
It can’t replace treatment. It is complementary therapy, used along with typical medical or psychological care. It doesn’t mean stopping a medication or canceling therapy that is working.
And keep the Cape Girardeau case in mind. A voice telling you your memory will improve is not proof that it did.
### What are the potential side effects of post-hypnosis?
Mostly the quiet ones. The list Cleveland Clinic gives is short: dizziness, drowsiness or fatigue, headaches, increased anxiety and trouble sleeping. It calls them rare. What it doesn’t list is the thing people fear most going in, losing control, because that isn’t how hypnosis works.
Plan your first appointment like you’d plan a dental cleaning you’re nervous about. Leave the hour after it open. Don’t book a client call or a big meeting right behind it until you know whether you come out sharp or ready for a nap. Keep a note on your phone that night: how you slept, what came up, what felt different. That note is what you bring to session two, and it turns a vague “I don’t know, it was fine” into something your practitioner can actually adjust.
A practitioner who waves off a bad reaction, or pushes you to keep going without changing anything, has given you your answer about whether to book again.
### How do you choose a hypnotherapist in the St. Louis metro?
Start with the license, then work through the rest before you hand over a card number:
What license do you hold, and which board issued it? Then look the name up on the state’s Licensee Search at pr.mo.gov.
Do you treat my issue often? Smoking, phobias, pain and anxiety are different work.
Will you coordinate with my doctor or therapist? Someone who welcomes that is treating this as complementary care.
How many sessions before we review whether it’s helping? You want a checkpoint, not an open-ended commitment.
What happens to unused sessions in a package? Ask before you pay.
Before the first session, write down where you’re starting, in one sentence you could read back to yourself later. “My anxiety is a little better” is impossible to judge three months from now. “I drove to the airport without rehearsing it for two days” is something you can check. The same habit works for acupuncture in St. Louis or any other add-on to your care.
