## Your Oregano Smells Like Dust: When to Throw Out Spices, and Where St. Louis Restocks
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-throw-out-your-herbs-and-spices
You smell nothing. The oregano lid sticks, then gives with a dry little crack, and you lean in over the jar the way you would over a pot of sauce, and there is nothing there. Not a bad smell. Not a stale one. Just the faint dusty air of a closet nobody has opened in years. It is the rack above the stove in a Dogtown kitchen, or the back of a pantry in Florissant, and behind that oregano sit four jars of cinnamon, a paprika gone the color of a grocery bag, and a tin of poultry seasoning bought for one Thanksgiving, several Thanksgivings ago.
Now hold that cabinet up against one counter in Soulard that, by its own count, sells between 600 and 800 pounds of spices a week on average. Your cabinet moves maybe a jar a year. That gap is the whole story of why your chili tastes flat, and the cheapest spice in your kitchen is the one you actually finish.
Before anything goes in the trash, know this: almost none of that cabinet can hurt you. McCormick’s guide says spices go “not good” rather than bad, and only two things in the house last indefinitely. Salt, and vanilla extract, “and that’s about it.”
The people behind that Soulard counter have a test of their own, and it is stricter than anything printed on a supermarket jar. Soulard Spice Shop’s FAQ puts it in one line: “The aroma should reach your nose before your nose reaches the container.” For ground spices, herbs and seasonings, the shop’s rule of thumb is to replace them after one year, or give them the sniff test, because if you cannot smell it a few inches from your nose, you will not taste it either. One year. Not the two to four McCormick gives ground spices.
Crush a pinch of cumin in your palm. Fresh, it comes up warm and earthy before your hand reaches your nose. Old, you have to go looking for it. That is the shop’s test, done at your own stove, and most of the cabinet fails it.
Two dollars and a quarter. That is what the cumin problem costs to fix. Soulard Spice Shop, which sells inside Soulard Market at 730 Carroll Street, lists a 2-ounce bag of whole cumin seed at $2.25 in its online store, about $1.13 an ounce, and a 2-ounce bag of ground cinnamon at $2.00. Two dollars replaces all four of your tired cinnamons with one that actually smells like cinnamon. The shop’s history says the business opened in 1914 and its founder was the first lessee of the market’s Grand Hall when it went up in 1929. The retail shop is open only Wednesday through Saturday and still averages 600 to 800 pounds of spices a week, which is why a small bag from that counter is fresher than a big jar from anywhere. Its own homepage says it in four words: “The aroma is amazing!”
On South Grand, the draw is depth, not speed. St. Louis Magazine’s guide to the city’s spice shops calls Jay International Foods, at 3172 S. Grand, a mainstay of the international market scene since 1970, with a comprehensive selection of herbs and spices, a particularly impressive range of South Asian, Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian ones, and a friendly, knowledgeable staff. Go for the whole seeds, which hold their flavor longest, and ask that staff which ones move fastest. I could not find a store website with prices, so read the shelf tag.
So here is tonight’s job, start to finish. Pull every jar onto the counter. Tip a small pinch of each into your palm, crush it with a finger, and smell. Healthline’s guide to spice shelf life says to crush or rub a small amount in the palm of your hand, and it takes about ten seconds a jar. A clear hit of the thing on the label, keep it. Dust, it goes on a list. Hard and lumpy, it goes, period. Empty the dead ones into the trash, rinse the glass, and if you live in the city, the jar goes in the blue recycling bin, because the city’s single stream recycling takes glass bottles and jars. Then take the list to Soulard on a Saturday, which the city’s market page lists as the day with 100% vendor participation, or to South Grand, and buy small. Call the market office at (314) 622-4180 first if you want to be sure the stall you need is in.
### Can you eat 20 year old spices?
Almost certainly yes, and that is the strange part. Spices do not truly spoil. They lose flavor, aroma and color over time, so a twenty year old jar of coriander is tired rather than hazardous. Expect close to no smell and close to no taste. You would add a tablespoon where a teaspoon used to do, get a gritty pot of beans, and still wonder why it tastes flat.
The one real exception is water. Moisture can make spices cake or mold, and if you ever see mold in a spice container, throw that jar out without a second thought. Lumps are the warning shot. Do not chip them apart with a fork and keep going. That brick of garlic powder got wet somewhere, probably over a steaming pot, and it has told you everything you need to know.
Assuming the jar is dry and loose, the test is still your palm. Something identifiable coming back means there is still a little fuel left. A vague nothing means the jar finished years ago and nobody noticed, because noses adjust. You have smelled that weak oregano for six years, so it smells like oregano to you. Buy one fresh jar and smell them side by side. It is a humbling ten seconds.
### Which jars fade first, and why
For the record, McCormick’s shelf-life guide gives whole spices three to four years, ground spices two to four, and leafy herbs and most blends one to three. Treat those as the outside edge, not the target.
Whole spices outlast ground ones because less of their surface touches the air, which is the best argument for walking out of a South Grand grocery with a bag of cumin seed instead of a jar of ground cumin. A peppercorn or a cinnamon stick keeps its oils sealed inside. Grinding shatters all of that open at once, which is why fresh-cracked pepper hits your nose across the room and the pre-ground can smells like paper.
That makes whole spices the single cheapest upgrade most kitchens can make. Buy peppercorns, cumin seed and coriander seed whole, crack what you need right before it goes in the pan, and you get the oils at their peak. A cheap grinder covers most of it. A whole seed you grind a spoonful at a time keeps paying you back years after the pre-ground jar has gone to dust, and that is the money-saving move nobody prints on the label.
Think about what that means for a St. Louis summer, too. A pork steak on the grill wants a rub that smells like something when it hits the heat, and a two-year-old jar of blend on the shelf above a hot stove will not get you there.
Blends fade fastest, and they fade unevenly. A taco packet or an Italian seasoning is several herbs and spices in one container, each on its own clock. Any salt in it stays exactly as salty forever. The herbs go first. So an old packet does not just taste weaker, it tastes flatter and saltier, because the balance shifted while it sat in the drawer.
A new jar of cumin is a small bill. The brisket it goes on is not. See whether a St. Louis butcher beats the grocery store.
### The three signs a jar is finished
A weak smell when you crush it in your palm. A hard, lumpy texture. A color that has visibly faded. Two of those are about flavor. The lumps are about moisture, and moisture is the one sign that is not a judgment call.
Color is the slowest signal and the easiest to read from across the kitchen. Paprika drifting from brick red to pale rust. Oregano going from green toward gray-brown. Turmeric that looks like sand instead of sunshine. When the color goes, the aroma usually left a while ago.
### How do you bring a tired spice back to life?
Heat, mostly. McCormick’s guide gives three ways to wake up spices that are fading but not ancient. Toast a curry powder or five spice blend: dump the whole jar into a dry pan, heat it to medium-low and stir constantly until it gets noticeably more fragrant. Do not walk away, because ground spices burn easily, and let it cool before it goes back in the jar.
Or bloom them in oil. Heat the oil, add the spices, and stir as they warm and give up whatever aroma they have left, which works especially well for curry powder, coriander and cumin. The kitchen will smell like a restaurant for about thirty seconds, and then you carry on with the recipe.
And the jars that cannot be saved for cooking can still be a potpourri. Whole cloves and a cinnamon stick in a pot of water on the back burner do more for a cold January kitchen than they will ever do for a stew. When a jar is truly done, or caked, let it go. Keeping a dead jar because tossing it feels wasteful is how a cabinet ends up with four cinnamons and none that work.
### How should you store spices so they last?
Cool, dark, dry, and away from the stove. That little ledge above the burners is the worst seat in the house, because repeated heat is an enemy of every spice, whole or ground. Salt can live there. Nothing else should.
Keep them out of the sun and off the stove. A pantry, drawer or cupboard away from the oven beats any open shelf in a sunny window.
Never shake a jar over a steaming pot. Use a spoon to get spices out before adding them to hot food. That steam is how jars cake.
Close the lid all the way. Air and humidity are what wear down the oils.
Write the date on it. A permanent marker on the jar the day you open it ends every future argument about how old it is.
Consider the fridge for the red ones. Paprika and cayenne keep their color longer if refrigerated, and oily seeds like sesame and poppy can stay fresher there too.
The bigger lever is how much you buy. A club-size tub of a spice you use twice a year is a false economy, because most of it fades before you finish it. Small jar, used up, replaced. It is the same logic that runs through cutting a St. Louis grocery bill in general.
People are asking
### Which condiments should you never keep past their expiration date?
The date is not the danger: the USDA says that except for infant formula, dates are not an indicator of a product’s safety, and any food that has developed an off odor, flavor or texture should not be eaten, whatever the label says. Acid guards most of the fridge door, too: in University of Wisconsin-Madison research, all Salmonella died within 1 hour in mustard and sweet pickle relish, in the refrigerator or at room temperature, and typical mayonnaise has a pH of 3.7, so it should behave much like ketchup. What can turn a jar is what goes into it, like a basting brush that touched raw chicken or a knife licked clean and dunked back into the mayo. So while every spice jar is out on the counter tonight, open the fridge door, unscrew each lid, smell it, and toss anything that smells off.
### Where do you find herbs and spices near you?
Refill the cabinet one small bag at a time, from somebody who sells it fast. Browse herbs and spices sellers across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, including the small shops and international markets that sell whole spices in amounts a household can finish before they fade.
If you’re the spice stall, the international grocer or the market vendor scooping cumin by the ounce, the cooks reading this are your next customers, so put your shop where they look.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which spices never expire?
A.  According to McCormick’s shelf-life guide, salt and vanilla extract last indefinitely, “and that’s about it.” Other extracts fade in two to three years. Everything else has a flavor window, from one to three years for leafy herbs and most blends up to three to four years for whole spices. None of it turns unsafe on a date. It just stops tasting like much.
### Q. Can you keep spices for 10 years?
A.  You can keep them, since spices do not truly spoil, but even whole spices, the longest-lasting jars on McCormick’s list, top out at three to four years. Crush a pinch in your palm. If it still smells like itself, use extra in something long-simmered. If it smells like dust, replace it. If it has caked into lumps, throw it out regardless of age.
### Q. Can I use 10 year old cinnamon?
A.  It is safe, but McCormick gives ground spices two to four years, so a jar that old is long past its best. Rub a pinch first. Still warm and sweet means it can work in something forgiving if you use more. Cardboard means it is done. A cinnamon stick of the same age often holds up better, because whole spices keep their oils sealed in longer.
### Q. What to do with expired turmeric powder?
A.  Rub-test it first. If there is some aroma left, try a gentle toast in a dry pan or bloom it in hot oil before the rest of the dish goes in, which can wake up a fading spice. If it is pale and smells like nothing, replace it. If it has caked, moisture got in, and it goes in the trash.
### Q. What can you do with expired cloves?
A.  Whole cloves are whole spices, so they hold up longer than most jars, three to four years by McCormick’s guide. Scratch one and smell it. If there is anything there, cook with them. If not, McCormick suggests turning older spices into a potpourri, and a few cloves with a cinnamon stick simmering in water will make the house smell like the holidays.
### Q. Does taco seasoning go bad?
A.  It does not become unsafe, but blends fade fastest. McCormick puts most seasoning blends at one to three years. Because a blend mixes several spices that fade at different speeds, an old packet tends to taste flat. Rub-test it, and if it smells like very little, a fresh packet is the cheapest fix in the kitchen.
### Q. Do salt and pepper expire?
A.  Salt does not, according to McCormick. Pepper fades, and the form matters. Whole peppercorns fall in the three to four year range for whole spices, and cracking them right before cooking releases the oils at their peak. Pre-ground pepper loses its bite sooner, so a grinder of whole peppercorns is the easiest upgrade on the table.

## Nobody at the Dinner Table Does This Math: How Long It Really Takes to Become a Doctor
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-long-it-really-takes-to-become-a-doctor
Eleven years. That is the short version, the floor, the road with no detours, from the day a St. Louis kid tosses a graduation cap to the day that kid treats patients with nobody co-signing the chart. A tenth grader in Webster Groves can announce at dinner that she is going to be a doctor, and everybody nods, and somebody passes the bread, and nobody at the table does that math.
Do it in birthday candles. Eighteen on the cake when the cap goes up. Twenty-two at college graduation, folding chairs on a hot lawn. Twenty-six when medical school ends and the family takes the picture on the steps. Then residency, the paid and supervised years in a hospital, which runs three to seven years depending on the specialty, and a fellowship can stack one to three more on top. The shortest road ends around twenty-nine. Plenty of good doctors blow out thirty-five candles before anybody stops checking their work.
Saint Louis University’s own history marks 1836 as the year it established the first medical school west of the Mississippi, in a building on Washington Avenue at Tenth Street. Stand on that corner downtown today and all you get is bus brakes and old brick. The years are still being served a few miles west. More than 1,400 residents and clinical fellows train with WashU Medicine faculty in nearly 200 specialty and subspecialty programs. Those are the years nobody mentions at the dinner table: the badge clipped on before dawn, the cold sting of hand sanitizer on a cracked knuckle, the pager going off while the coffee is still too hot to drink.
Here is the part worth forwarding to the kid at that table. In St. Louis, the money wall can be lower than the time wall. WashU Medicine committed $100 million over a decade to scholarships so that as many as half of its future medical students could attend tuition-free, in entering classes of about 120. There is no lottery ticket to buy for it: the school says an admissions scholarship committee decides each award one student at a time, some on financial need, some on merit, some on both. Get admitted and you are in the conversation. Tuition has an answer for some students. The eleven years do not have one for anybody.
So test the years before you spend them, and start with a phone call this week. Barnes-Jewish Hospital Volunteer Services answers at 314-362-5324, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its rules are plain: 16 for the Summer Teens Program or high school community service, 18 for everyone else, a one-year commitment, two semesters for college students, then an orientation. Out west, Mercy Hospital St. Louis runs its own Volunteer Services office at 615 S. New Ballas Road, (314) 251-6180. Then go stand in that hallway under the fluorescent hum, smell the floor cleaner, and watch a nurse walk a frightened patient back to bed. One year of Tuesdays there will tell you more about the next eleven than any timeline, including this one.
### How old are doctors after med school?
About twenty-six, if you go straight through: college by twenty-two, medical school by twenty-six. That is the day the diploma says MD or DO. It is not the day you work alone.
That day comes later, and you will remember it. A pen, a chart, a patient you just examined, and for the first time there is no line under your name waiting for somebody senior to sign. After a three-to-four-year residency in internal medicine, family medicine or pediatrics, that moment arrives around twenty-nine or thirty. Choose a surgical residency at the long end of the seven-year range and add a fellowship, and the pen is in your hand somewhere in your middle thirties.
Then life adds its own years. A gap year to work and apply. A second application cycle after the first one comes back with the thin email. A research year. A career change that starts with a chemistry class at night, after a full shift, with a backpack on the kitchen chair. None of it is rare, and none of it means you are behind. It means you are on the long end of a wide road that everybody pretends is narrow.
Is thirty-four late? Ask the career changer finishing a night chemistry lab, safety goggles leaving a red line across the bridge of the nose, an hour after clocking out of a full shift. Only an imaginary schedule calls that late. A career that begins at thirty-four instead of twenty-nine still runs for decades. The people who feel the weight of this timeline worst are usually measuring it against a four-year degree, and that was never the right comparison. The right comparison is the work itself, and whether you still want it on a Tuesday night at 2 a.m. with a patient who is scared and a family that wants answers.
### Where the eleven years actually go
Split the number into its pieces and nothing in it is mysterious. It is just long.
College takes four years, and the science prerequisites and the MCAT both live inside it; the major matters less than finishing the required courses. Medical school takes four more, classroom science first and clinical rotations second, ending in an MD or a DO. Residency runs three to seven years of paid, supervised training in one specialty, with internal medicine and family medicine at the short end. A fellowship, one to three years, is optional and only for a subspecialty.
Add the shortest honest version and you get four plus four plus three. Add a seven-year residency and a three-year fellowship and you get eighteen. Every number between those two is somebody’s real schedule, and the University of Medicine and Health Sciences counts it the same way: 4 years of undergraduate education, 4 years of medical school and at least 3 years of residency. For a second read, try this physician timeline from Kaplan.
The college years are where a lot of people quietly lose ground, usually in chemistry or physics, usually late at night with a highlighter going dry. If the fundamentals need rebuilding before the MCAT, start early. Our rundown of tutoring and learning centers across the St. Louis metro covers the kind of help that shows up years before anybody is thinking about a white coat.
### Is there a difference between an MD and a DO?
Both are physicians, and those are the two types in the United States. A DO program includes everything an MD program does, plus added training in osteopathic medicine. For the timeline on this page the difference barely matters, and the choice between them belongs much further down the road than most high schoolers imagine.
### Residency is the part nobody can shorten
Residency is where the range comes from. The length is set by the specialty you choose, not by how well you did in school, and it runs anywhere from three to seven years. These programs are accredited by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education, and a resident is not a student anymore. A resident is a working doctor with a paycheck, a patient list and a supervisor, learning the job by doing it, on the night shift as often as the day.
Think about the hour that matters, not the year. The hallway is quiet except for a monitor chiming two rooms down. Somebody’s grandmother needs a decision. That is residency, repeated thousands of times, and it is why there is no shortcut worth chasing. A few accelerated programs combine a bachelor’s degree with an MD and shorten the front end of the timeline to about six or seven years. None of them removes residency.
Start with the schools you can actually drive to before you plan eleven years around one. You can browse medical schools and health science programs listed on St Louis Near Me Directory, and if you need a paycheck while you get clinical hours, check our jobs board for health care openings around town.
If you run the tutoring center, the scrubs shop or the clinic that hires pre-med students, these are years of future customers looking for you right now, so list your business where they already search.
### Is becoming a doctor hard?
Yes, and the hard part is not where people think. It is not one brutal exam or one impossible course. It is eleven or more years of showing up, which makes endurance matter more than raw brilliance for almost everybody who finishes.
Admission is competitive. The coursework is heavy in volume more than in difficulty, a stack of flashcards so tall the rubber band snaps. The standardized exams, the MCAT before medical school and the USMLE during it, are high stakes and studied for like it. Then residency adds hours and responsibility that school never did. And underneath all of it sits the quiet one: money. The earning years start late. Families who plan for that early tend to treat it like any other bill on the fridge, and our look at how St. Louis families afford private school tuition works the same planning muscle years earlier.
### What is the quickest doctor to become?
A primary care physician on the standard track. The shortest residencies last three years, in specialties like internal medicine and family medicine, which puts the shortest usual path for a practicing MD or DO at about eleven years, starting right after high school.
There is a wrinkle in the question, though. “Doctor” covers more than physicians. If what you really want is to be the person in the room with a patient, the other health careers deserve a hard look before you commit to the longest road on it.
### How many years to be a PA vs. doctor?
Far fewer, and that gap is why the comparison keeps coming up. A physician assistant needs a bachelor’s degree and then a master’s level PA program of about 27 months, roughly three academic years, with more than 2,000 hours of clinical rotations inside it. A physician on the shortest usual path needs about eleven years, starting right after high school. That is not a rounding error. It is most of a decade.
The trade is scope and independence, not caring for patients. PAs take histories, examine patients, diagnose and treat illness, prescribe medication and assist in surgery. Physicians carry broader independent authority and deeper specialty training, bought with the extra years. Somebody deciding at thirty-two with two kids asleep down the hall is answering a different question than a nineteen-year-old sophomore, and both answers can be completely right.
Eleven years is one road. Plenty of good careers start next month with a trade or an apprenticeship.
### Do most doctors retire as millionaires?
Nobody can honestly hand you a percentage, and anyone who does is guessing. What is real is the shape: a late start, often heavy debt, high earning years, a long career. Two doctors in the same specialty can finish in completely different places depending on when they started, what they borrowed and what they spent.
For the pay side, go straight to the government numbers. O*NET lists median wages of general internal medicine physicians at $256,560 a year, against $135,880 for physician assistants and $132,300 for nurse practitioners, and those figures are updated each year. You can also check the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook. And if money is the main reason you are choosing this road, sit with that for a while. It has never been enough fuel for a decade of 2 a.m. pages.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is becoming a doctor hard?
A.  Yes, though the difficulty is spread out rather than packed into one moment. Admission is competitive, the coursework is heavy in volume, the MCAT and USMLE exams are high stakes, and residency is demanding in hours and responsibility. Stretch that across eleven or more years and endurance matters more than brilliance. The best early test is time in a real clinical setting before you apply.
### Q. What is the quickest doctor to become?
A.  A primary care physician. The shortest residencies last three years, in specialties such as internal medicine and family medicine, so four years of college, four of medical school and three of residency add up to about eleven years after high school. A few accelerated programs combine the bachelor’s degree and the MD, but residency still has to be completed.
### Q. How many years to be a PA vs. doctor?
A.  A physician assistant completes a bachelor’s degree and then a master’s level PA program of about 27 months, with more than 2,000 hours of clinical rotations. A physician on the shortest usual path needs about eleven years, starting right after high school: four of college, four of medical school and at least three of residency, plus one to three more for an optional fellowship.
### Q. Who gets paid more, MD or PA?
A.  The physician, by a wide margin. O*NET lists median wages of $256,560 a year for general internal medicine physicians and $135,880 for physician assistants. Specialty, location and experience move both numbers, and the physician paid for that gap with years of extra training before earning a full salary.
### Q. Who gets paid more, NP or PA?
A.  They are close. O*NET lists median wages of $135,880 a year for physician assistants and $132,300 for nurse practitioners. That gap is small enough that specialty, setting, state and experience can flip it, so compare the specific job, not the title.
### Q. Do most doctors retire as millionaires?
A.  There is no reliable percentage, so treat any quoted figure with suspicion. Outcomes depend on specialty, debt, location, spending and how long someone practices. Physician earning years start late and often begin with significant debt, then run for decades, and two doctors in the same field can end up in very different places.
### Q. Can a doctor earn $1,000,000 a year?
A.  Some do, but they are the exception. O*NET lists median wages of $256,560 a year for general internal medicine physicians, about a quarter of that. Incomes at the very top usually come from high-paying procedural specialties, practice ownership and heavy workloads, not the typical path.

## Fear the Ankle, Not the Sting: What Paintball Really Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-paintball-actually-costs-in-st-louis
Snap. That is the sound, and the feeling, of your first paintball hit: a sting on the back of the arm, a splash of color on your sleeve, and somebody’s kid whooping from behind a bunker fifty feet away. Gateway Paintball Park, out on Missouri Bottom Road in Bridgeton, says some people compare it to “the snapping of a wet towel or rubber band.” Most of the dread about paintball is about that snap. It is the wrong thing to dread.
The park that calls itself the largest paintball facility in St. Louis says the injury it sees most is not a welt. It is a twisted ankle, usually in shoes without ankle support.
Not the sting. The ankle, turned while running, sliding and diving. So the first money-saving move on this page is free: lace your kid into boots or high-tops, not the slip-on sneakers by the door. The second one is about paint.
Here is the St. Louis catch: Gateway says every paintball field in the St. Louis area is field-paint-only, so a cheap bag from a sporting-goods store stays in the trunk. Your paint math happens at the counter, and that is where $15 more doubles your rounds from 500 to 1,000.
Gateway posts its open play prices online. $40 a player covers entry, all-day air fills, 500 paintballs and the rented mask, marker, tank and hopper. The Double Ammo package, with 1,000 rounds, is $55.
Paint is the cost that runs away from families, and the cheapest time to buy it is at registration, while everyone is still tugging on masks and nobody has fired a shot. Prices change, so confirm them first at (314) 298-3772. And check one rule before you promise anything: open play there is ages twelve and up. The ten-year-old riding along cannot just walk on.
Gateway has been running since 1998 on 102 acres with 12 playing fields, tucked between highways 70, 270 and 370 in St. Louis County. Open play needs no reservation: show up Saturday or Sunday between 10am and 4pm and register at the counter.
### Is 3 hours of paintball enough?
Yes, and the local fields are built around that clock. Gateway’s private group package for teenagers and up runs up to three hours of play at $40 a person with a ten-player minimum, and includes 500 paintballs per player, unlimited air fills and a referee who runs the games.
The paint matches the clock. A cost guide from Precision Paintball says most players use about 150 paintballs an hour. Three hours at that pace is about 450 balls, which is just under the 500 that come in the base package. So one base package covers the afternoon, and you have a straight answer for anyone who wants to buy more paint at hour two.
Your body will agree with the clock, too. By the third hour there is somebody else’s paint drying on your mask lens, your knees are damp from crouching behind a bunker, and you know the hiss of the air-fill station by heart. In open play at Gateway, a referee splits the crowd into two teams and walks the group from field to field; each game takes 10 to 15 minutes, and a field is usually played twice before everyone heads back up front to reload. Some fields are simple elimination games; others are attack and defend or capture the flag, which is where the screaming starts. Run hard, then rest. That is the rhythm of the day.
### How expensive is it to play paintball?
Less than people fear, as long as you pick the paint before you hear the first marker pop out on the field and everyone suddenly wants more. In St. Louis County the numbers are tidy, because Gateway rolls everything into three open play packages. Recruit is $40 with 500 paintballs. Double Ammo is $55 with 1,000. Veteran is $80 with 2,000. Each price includes entry, all-day air fills and the rented mask, marker, tank and hopper. For a parent bringing two kids to open play on a Saturday, that is $120 for all three of you on the base open play package, or $165 if all three double to 1,000 rounds. Private groups are a separate product, reserved in advance for ten or more.
Two rules shape the rest of the bill. First, you cannot bring paint from a store: Gateway is a field-paint-only facility, and its FAQ says all St. Louis area paintball fields have the same “Field Paint Only” policy, for insurance and liability reasons. Second, timing matters. The posted packages are the prices you choose at registration, so decide on 500 or 1,000 rounds in the parking lot, out loud, before the adrenaline gets a vote.
### Who can play, and what if your kid is younger?
Open play at Gateway is for ages twelve and up, according to the park’s FAQ. Private groups can start at eight. That gap catches families every spring: the ten-year-old who has been counting down to a sibling’s birthday cannot just walk on with the teenagers on a Sunday.
For younger kids the park offers a low impact option and a gellyball party, and each one needs at least 10 players. Low impact paintball uses a .50 caliber ball that the park says has about one third of the impact energy of a standard paintball, with a marker that weighs 70% less. Gellyball goes smaller still, for ages 8 to 12, at $30 a child for a two-hour party with unlimited ammo, and it only runs when it is above 50 degrees. Picture a nine-year-old who can actually lift the marker and laughs at the hit instead of crying at it. That is what you are paying for.
Too cold for gellyball? Take the party to a family fun center instead and skip the paint bill.
### Booking a birthday group
Private groups need a reservation, and the FAQ spells out the fine print parents miss. You need at least 72 hours of notice and a deposit, which you can pay over the phone or in person at the park, and deposits are non-refundable. If you reschedule more than 72 hours ahead, the deposit can move to a new date within 90 days. Cancel within 72 hours and the deposit is lost.
Do the math for the party before you send invitations. Ten teenagers at $40 is $400 for three hours. Ten kids at the $30 gellyball rate is $300 for two. If half the guests want 1,000 rounds, Gateway lets each player double to 1,000 for $15 more at initial registration, so collect that answer with the RSVP, not at the counter while the cake melts in the car.
Weather is part of the deal. Gateway plays year-round in all types of weather, and as an all-outdoor park it closes for extreme weather like tornadic thunderstorms or ice. Cold mornings mean fogged masks and numb fingers; August means sweat pooling inside the goggles. Pick the date with that in mind, and pack dry socks either way. Bring a towel and a trash bag for the ride home too; paint washes out, but it rides home on knees, elbows and the back seat first. Some kids will want to keep their splattered shirt as a trophy. Let them.
### Is paintball painful for beginners?
It stings, and pretending otherwise sets a kid up badly. Gateway’s FAQ says a lot of the time you will hardly feel it, but hits sting from closer range. The park does not allow shooting within 10 feet, which takes the worst shots off the table.
Clothing does the rest. The FAQ puts it plainly: you can always take off a layer, but you can’t add it if you don’t bring it. The park’s advice is a long-sleeved tee and pants when it is warm, the weather plus one layer when it is cool, and tennis shoes or boots on your feet. Chest protectors, gloves, jerseys and neck guards are available. Veterans show up wearing more clothes than the weather needs, and now you know why. A hit through a hoodie is a thump. A hit on a bare forearm is the one people talk about at dinner.
### Is paintball an expensive hobby?
As a few trips a year, no. As every weekend, yes, and the reason is paint. Buying your own marker and mask removes the rental, and Gateway’s FAQ permits players to bring their own gun and goggles if they meet its rules: full face protection from forehead to chin including both ears, a lens rated for paintball under the ANSI safety standard, and a .68 caliber pump or semi-automatic marker that chronographs under 280 feet per second. Paint is the cost that never leaves: only paintballs purchased at Gateway may be used on its fields. For a yardstick, public field admission alone runs about $15 to $30 nationally, according to a pricing breakdown from Sports Carnival, and Precision Paintball puts paint at $15 to $30 per 500-round bag and $50 to $75 per 2,000-round case. Against that, paying Gateway $15 more to double your rounds to 1,000 is the low end.
Compare it to other family outings before you decide. A $40 day that includes three hours of running, gear and 500 paintballs sits in the same neighborhood as a lot of weekend plans, and our rundown of what ice skating in St. Louis costs makes a useful benchmark.
### What to ask before you drive out
Prices change, so call first. Gateway’s number is (314) 298-3772. These are the questions that change your total:
Is open play running this Saturday or Sunday, 10am-4pm, or is the field closed for weather?
Which package should a first-timer pick, 500 or 1,000 rounds?
What does extra paint cost if we run out mid-day?
Are chest protectors, gloves or neck guards extra, and how much?
For a party: which date, which package, and how much is the deposit?
For kids under twelve: low impact or gellyball, and what is the weather cutoff?
Write the answers on a sticky note on the dashboard. Then set the paint budget out loud before the doors open. That one habit saves more than any coupon, and it saves the argument in the car on the way home too.
### Where do you find paintball near you?
Compare what is within driving distance before you plan the day. Browse paintball fields and parks across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call for a current price sheet and the age rules before you promise anyone a party.
If you’re the field owner, the ref or the one running the pro shop, put your packages where St. Louis parents are already comparing them and get more customers through the gate. List your field with us, or see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How expensive is it to play paintball?
A.  Nationally, field admission runs about $15 to $30, with paint at $15 to $30 per 500-round bag on top. In St. Louis County, Gateway Paintball Park bundles it: $40 a player for entry, air, rental gear and 500 paintballs, $55 for 1,000, $80 for 2,000. Call for current prices before you go.
### Q. Is paintball an expensive hobby?
A.  Occasionally, no. Weekly, it adds up, because paint is a consumable and Gateway says St. Louis area fields all have a field-paint-only policy. Owning a marker and mask removes the rental charge, but every game still costs paint. A few trips a year usually sits alongside other family outings.
### Q. Is paintball painful for beginners?
A.  It stings at close range and you may barely feel it at distance. Gateway compares it to a snapped wet towel or rubber band and bans shooting within 10 feet. Long sleeves, pants and a hoodie layer handle most of it, and low impact paintball hits much softer for younger players.
### Q. Why is paintball not popular anymore?
A.  Gateway in Bridgeton has run since 1998, plays on 102 acres with 12 fields, and says the St. Louis Blues came out to play for their 8th year. Open play runs every Saturday and Sunday from 10am to 4pm.
### Q. Can a paintball gun hurt somebody?
A.  Yes, which is why Gateway requires goggles with full face protection from forehead to chin and checks personal markers on arrival to chronograph under 280 feet per second. It says the most common injury it sees is a twisted ankle from running and diving.

## No License Number, No Call: What a Private Investigator Costs in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-private-investigator-costs-in-missouri
The first number to check is not the price. It sits at the bottom of the ad, small and easy to miss while the phone is warm in your hand and the house has gone quiet. In Missouri, that ad is supposed to carry the investigator’s license number. Section 324.1132 of Missouri law says nobody can advertise as a private investigator or private detective without including it.
No number, no call. That one line will save you more money than any rate comparison on this page.
Check the number first, then ask the price. In this business the price is built out of hours, and in St. Louis it can also be built out of a bridge.
### How much is a PI for a day?
About $600 to $1,600 for an eight-hour day, with an average near $1,100, according to Bark’s national private investigator price guide. The hourly figure underneath runs $68 to $125 on average, and specialized or complex cases can go as high as $400 an hour. Bark is clear that these are national averages that move with location, so treat any St. Louis quote as one investigator’s price, not the market’s.
Do the arithmetic before you pick up the phone. Eight hours at $68 is $544. Eight hours at $125 is $1,000. Write that range on the back of the envelope before you dial, and no quote will catch you off guard.
Then picture what that $544 to $1,000 buys in St. Louis. A parked car on a side street off Manchester Road. A July afternoon with the engine off and the windows cracked. Coffee going cold in the cupholder. A front door that does not open for four hours. You pay for every one of those hours, the dead ones too, because surveillance is billed by the time somebody sat there, not by the evidence they caught. A day where the subject never leaves the house costs exactly what the day that answers your question costs.
So ask what a day means to them, when the clock starts, and whether the drive to the address and the hour spent writing the report are inside the day or on top of it. Those three answers explain most of the difference between two quotes for the same job.
Then ask the question only a St. Louis client needs to ask: what happens if the car I am paying you to follow crosses the river? Illinois runs its own license: the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation licenses private detectives and private detective agencies on that side. On this side of the river, that is not trivia. Ask whether they hold an Illinois license too, or who they hand the job to on the other side, and what that handoff costs, before the brake lights you are paying to follow climb onto the Poplar Street Bridge toward the Illinois side.
### The license number tells you more than the price does
You are about to hand a stranger the most private worry you have, and maybe a photo of someone you love. Your thumb is on the call button, and the only thing you know about this person is a logo and a phone number. That small license number is the one thing in the ad you can check before you say a word.
Missouri licenses private investigators at the state level, and the board that does it works out of Jefferson City. To get that license, an investigator has to pass a written examination on investigator rules under section 324.1110, and section 324.1108 requires proof of liability insurance of no less than $250,000. The license is not decoration. Somebody tested this person, and somebody insured them.
Here is the part most St. Louis searchers never learn. Section 324.1114 says no municipality may make a state-licensed investigator pay a local license fee or pass its own examination. There is no separate city or county investigator badge to hunt for. The state license is the one that counts, whether the work happens on a cul-de-sac in Kirkwood or an office park in Maryland Heights.
Check it tonight, before anyone has your card number. Start at the board’s website, look up the name and number from the ad, and confirm the license is current. If the site fights you, the board’s phone is 573-522-7744. A real professional will expect you to check. Hesitation when you ask is the most useful red flag you will ever get for free.
### A retainer is a deposit, not the price
The invoice is the moment it gets real. You read the line with the dollar sign twice, then set the paper face down on the counter like that might make it smaller. Most of that sting comes from one misunderstanding: the retainer is not the bill.
Bark puts the usual upfront retainer at $500 to $2,500, and it spells out how the arrangement is meant to work: if money is left over when the job ends, you get it back, and if the money runs out before the job is done, the investigator may start charging monthly instead. That second part is where the sticker shock lives. It is the email that lands on a Thursday night telling you the balance is gone and the question is still open.
Treat the retainer as an opening balance and put a fence around it. Before money changes hands, get in writing how many hours it buys, what happens to the unused part, whether the work stops on its own when the balance hits zero, and the most you will spend without a new conversation. A written cap is ordinary to ask for. Anyone who bristles at it has told you something.
Then ask for updates on a schedule you choose: a short call every couple of days, or a written note at the end of each block of hours. Silence is the hardest part of this. A week of checking your phone in the grocery line and hearing nothing feels worse than a disappointing report, and a set check-in turns the retainer from a black box into a running tab you can actually read. It also gives you a natural place to say stop.
Get two or three quotes and ask every investigator the same questions. You can browse private investigation services across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, check each license number against the state board, then compare what each retainer actually buys. The cheapest hourly rate is not always the cheapest case.
If you’re the licensed investigator, the one sitting in that parked car with the cold coffee, make sure the person comparing retainers tonight can find you. List your agency with us so your license number and your work show up where St. Louis is already looking.
### What actually moves the number
A working firm, Whitesell Investigative Services, lists the drivers in one line: case type, hours required, travel, urgency, risk and reporting needs. Everything else hangs off those.
### Desk work or field work
A background check is screens, databases and courthouse files, the hum of a laptop in a quiet office. Surveillance is somebody else’s unpredictable schedule. Bark lists typical ranges by service: a criminal background check at $100 to $500, a general background check at $200 to $900, tracing a missing person at $700 to $1,200, and asset searches at $1,000 to $1,600. Two cases can share one hourly rate and land very far apart on the invoice, because one needs six hours and the other needs sixty.
### The person being watched
The hour count is set by the subject, not by you. Someone who leaves at 7:40 every weekday is cheap to observe, because the pattern shows up fast. Someone who works nights, leaves at random or already looks over a shoulder in the grocery lot takes more attempts to get the same answer.
### Distance and the drive
Travel gets billed as hours, mileage or a separate line, and Bark lists travel expenses, special equipment and specialist database access among the extra fees to ask about before you sign. A case that follows somebody from one end of the metro to the other on a Friday is a longer, more expensive day than one that stays on one street.
### Experience
Experience usually costs more per hour and often less per case. Someone who has run your kind of case a hundred times knows which two hours matter and stops burning the other six. When you compare quotes, compare the plan as well as the rate: how many hours they expect, what they will try first, and when they would call you to say the approach is not working. A higher rate attached to a tighter plan is often the smaller bill at the end of the month.
### Is it worth it to hire a private investigator?
Use one test. If the answer changes a decision you have to make anyway, a filing, a custody position, a claim, a hire, then a defined block of paid hours usually costs less than guessing wrong. If the answer changes nothing, you are buying certainty, and that is allowed to be worth money too, as long as you know that is the purchase.
The alternative most people try first is doing it themselves, sitting low in their own car at the end of somebody’s street with their heart pounding. That is unsafe, it can turn a calm situation into a dangerous one, and what you gather may count for less than the same thing documented by a licensed professional who can explain how it was obtained.
If this is heading for a courtroom, get the order right. An investigator gathers, a lawyer decides what is useful, and doing it backward wastes hours you paid for. Our guide to finding the right lawyer in St. Louis is worth reading first if you do not have one yet. And if the question is about a job rather than a person, read what your rights actually are after being fired in Missouri before you pay anyone.
### What to ask on the first call
Most bad outcomes here come from a vague scope, not a high rate. Whitesell’s own advice is to ask for budget controls before approving more time. Keep this next to the phone:
What is your Missouri license number, and may I check it with the state board?
Hourly or day rate, and how many hours is a day?
What is billed on top: mileage, database fees, report writing, court time?
What does the retainer buy in hours, and what happens to what is left?
Does the work stop when the retainer runs out, or does the bill keep running?
What do I get at the end: a written report, photos, video, timestamps?
What would make you tell me to stop spending money on this?
That last one tells you the most. An investigator willing to say “this is not worth your money” before taking any of it is the one worth hiring.
Before you pay anyone to dig, look at what is already public. Start with Missouri court records.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it illegal to hire a private investigator?
A.  No. What is regulated is the investigator: in Missouri, it is unlawful to run a private investigator business without a state license, and every advertisement has to show the license number. Ask for it, check it with the state board, and expect a professional to hand it over without fuss. This is general information, not legal advice.
### Q. Can a PI get phone records?
A.  Not the way people usually mean. Federal law, 18 U.S.C. 1039, makes it a federal crime, with up to 10 years in prison, to obtain someone’s confidential phone records by making false or fraudulent statements to a phone company employee. In a legal case, records normally come through a subpoena or court order instead. Anyone advertising that they will pull call logs for a fee is a red flag, and you are the one who hired them.
### Q. Can a private investigator read your text messages?
A.  Not lawfully. Message content sits behind accounts and devices a licensed investigator has no right to enter, and getting into them without authority can create legal trouble for the person who paid as well as the person who did it. If somebody offers that service, walk. Message evidence in a lawsuit comes through the court process, which is a question for your attorney.
### Q. Can you sue someone for hiring a PI on you?
A.  Lawful observation from public places is generally not, by itself, what people end up suing over. Claims tend to come from conduct: harassment, trespassing or unlawful access to private information. Whether any of that fits your situation depends on the facts and on state law, so take it to a lawyer. Nothing here is legal advice.
### Q. How to tell if a PI is watching you?
A.  Good surveillance is built to be forgettable, so most people never notice. What people do report is the same unfamiliar car parked nearby on different days, or hearing that someone has been asking neighbors, coworkers or a landlord about them. Lawful observation from a public place is one thing. Feeling followed or unsafe is another, and that belongs with the police.
### Q. How long does a PI investigation take?
A.  Records and background work can move in days, because it runs at the speed of databases and courthouses. Surveillance is open-ended, since it runs on the subject’s schedule rather than yours, which is why it is billed by time. Buy a defined block of hours, review what came back, and decide again from there.

## A Tavern That Feeds You at Noon, a Pub That Won’t Unlock Till 4: Pub vs. Bar in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-makes-a-pub-different-from-a-bar
“Is this place a pub or a bar?” The text buzzes in while you’re circling a Soulard side street for parking, and you realize you can’t answer it. Inside John D. McGurk’s, the rooms are brick and wood hung with Irish artifacts, Irish musicians play Wednesday through Sunday nights, and a garden out back runs past a fountain and a waterfall to three outdoor bars. It looks like a pub. It sounds like a pub.
Then read the door. McGurk’s opens at 4PM Tuesday through Thursday and at 11:30AM Friday through Sunday. On a Wednesday nobody gets in before 4PM. On a Saturday the door opens at 11:30AM. Same fiddles, same room, two different nights.
Over in Dogtown the sign says tavern. Patrick Connolly came to St. Louis from Dunmore, County Galway, in 1929 and opened the Pat Connolly Tavern in 1942. Tuesday through Sunday it opens at 11:30am, puts fried chicken and T-ravs on the table, and on Friday and Saturday keeps the lights on until 1:30am. A tavern that feeds you at noon. A pub that won’t unlock until four.
In St. Louis the pub can keep bar hours and the tavern keeps pub hours. Read the clock, not the sign.

Entrees and a kids menu mean a family dinner works. Wings, pretzels and nothing else mean a counter night. Three: the photos. Count booths against stools. Bringing six or more, you want booths. Below is where each word came from and what it still promises.
### What makes a pub a pub?
A pub is short for public house, and the idea is the house part: a kitchen you can smell at lunch, tables instead of stools, grandparents and kids at dinner, and a room quiet enough to talk in. A bar leans on the drink and the counter. The line is atmosphere and habit, not law.
What the word promises, in practice, is a room that works before dark, and you can taste the difference. At the Pat Connolly Tavern that means fried chicken and T-ravs, the dishes it brags about on its own homepage. At McGurk’s it means bangers and mash, corned beef and cabbage, and Guinness stew, steaming in a brick room while the garden fountain runs outside. A pub seats you at a table rather than a stool and keeps a kitchen going most of the day. Families come for dinner, and the room turns over to adults later.
The history explains the feel. A public house was literally that: a home in an English or Irish village that opened its front rooms to anyone who wanted a drink, with the family still living upstairs. Dark wood, low ceilings, snug corners and a fireplace you can warm your hands at are less decoration than leftovers from somebody’s parlor. That is why a good pub feels domestic and a good bar does not.
Three signals do most of the work, and you can sense each one from the doorway. Onions and fryer oil in the air at noon, not just last night’s spilled beer. Daylight on the tables, because the hours start with lunch instead of happy hour. And chairs scraping around four-tops instead of stools lined up at a rail, which is the most reliable tell in any photo you will find online.
### So what makes a bar a bar?
A brass rail under your shoe, a stool that spins a quarter turn, a bartender who can reach you without walking. Even the Pat Connolly Tavern started that way: its own history says that before the Budweiser sign went up, Pat’s was a Griesedieck Bros. bar, and the tavern recently worked with the Dogtown Historical Society to restore an original mural. A bar is named after its furniture. The bar is the long counter that separates the person pouring from the people drinking, and the room eventually took the name of the fixture. Everything else follows from that: stools instead of booths, service by the drink, and an evening that starts later and runs harder.
In American English, bar is the default word. It covers a hotel lobby, a dive on a corner, a cocktail room with a printed menu, and a sports room with nine screens. That breadth is exactly why the word tells you less than people assume. It describes a piece of joinery, not a mood.
Still, a place that calls itself a bar is usually telling you a few things on purpose. Later close. Louder room. A drink-forward menu with more spirits than taps. Food that is short, fried and built to keep you there rather than to be the reason you came. And a door policy that tightens after a certain hour, which matters if anybody in your group is under 21.
Plenty of exceptions exist, and some of the better kitchens in the metro sit behind signs that say bar. In our experience the sign is a starting guess, nothing more. What settles it is the hours page and the menu, and both of those are usually two clicks away.
### Where did the words pub, bar and tavern come from?
All three describe the same basic transaction and arrived by different routes. Pub is English and domestic. Bar is a piece of furniture that swallowed the whole room. Tavern is the oldest of the three, and in the United States it also became a licensing term, which is why it still shows up on so many old signs.
### The public house
Public house is a formal-sounding phrase that entered ordinary speech and then got clipped. Village alehouses, inns and taverns in Britain were folded together under the label, and the shortened form stuck so completely that almost nobody says the long version now. The word still carries an expectation of food, and of a landlord who lives with the consequences of a bad night.
### The tavern
Tavern comes down from the Latin taberna, meaning a hut or a shop. For centuries it meant a place selling wine, and later a place that fed and housed travelers as well. Colonial American taverns sat closer to inns than to bars: a public room, a hearth, a meal, a bed upstairs and the mail. That is why so many of them doubled as courtrooms and meeting halls.
### The saloon and the bar
Saloon is the American nineteenth century word, and Prohibition all but killed it off. Bar outlasted everything because it was the most literal term available. You drank at the bar, so you went to a bar. Modern spinoffs follow the same logic. A taproom is named for the taps. A brewpub is named for the brewery attached to the kitchen.
### Does any of this change what you order?
It changes what the room is set up to do well, which amounts to the same thing. A pub is built around beer and around food that goes with beer, so the taps are half the menu and the kitchen is not an afterthought. A bar is built around the pour, so spirits, cocktails and speed get the attention instead.
Order to the room and you will do better. In a pub, ask what is on cask or what the house pours most of, then order something that takes a few minutes to cook. In a bar, ask the person working what they make well, because a busy counter rewards a decision far more than it rewards a debate.
One small thing trips people up. The tall shaker glass most places use is measured to the brim rather than to a marked line. So a full-looking glass and a full pint are not always the same thing.
None of this is a hierarchy. It is a fit. The best beer list in a neighborhood might sit behind a sign that says bar, and the best cocktail might come out of a pub with a fireplace. The words point at the odds, not at the outcome.
Buying a place instead of drinking in one? Start with a Missouri real estate attorney.
### How do you tell which one you are walking into?
Four things settle it faster than the name on the sign: the opening time, the menu, the seating and the door policy. Every one of them is visible from your phone before you leave the house, and together they predict the room better than any label a marketing team picked out.
### Read the opening time
A place that unlocks at eleven in the morning is committed to lunch, and lunch means a kitchen, tables and daytime staff. A place that opens at four or later has decided the evening is the whole business. That single line on a listing tells you more about the room than the photo gallery does.
### Read the menu
Look for entrees, not just baskets. A menu with sandwiches, a soup, a few plates and a dessert is a kitchen. A menu that runs wings, pretzels and a frozen pizza is a snack program designed to keep people at the counter. Neither one is wrong. They simply point at different evenings.
### Read the seating
Count stools against tables in the interior photos. Booths, four-tops and a patio with real chairs mean the room expects you to stay and eat. A long counter with stools and a standing area near the taps means the room expects you to move around and talk to strangers. Bring a group of eight to the second kind and somebody stands all night.
### Read the door policy
Many rooms across the metro welcome all ages while the kitchen is open, then shift to adults only later in the evening. That cutoff is set by the venue and by local rules, and it is not always posted online. If anybody in your party is under 21, or you are bringing kids to dinner, call and ask. It takes a minute and saves a wasted drive.

### Which words does St. Louis actually use?
The metro leans on tavern more than most American cities do, and it uses pub loosely. A corner tavern here usually means a neighborhood room in an old storefront, often older than everyone standing in it, with a short menu and a bartender who knows the block. It is not a British word and it does not pretend to be.
Pub shows up in two different ways. Some rooms mean it in the Irish or English sense: dark wood, table service, a working kitchen, a Sunday crowd that settles in. Others use it as a friendlier synonym for bar because it reads as welcoming on a sign. Both are legitimate. Only one of them will feed your family at six.
Then there is the newer category. Brewery taprooms sit somewhere between the two: long communal tables, all ages during the day, beer made on site, and food that ranges from nothing at all to a full kitchen or a truck parked out front. If you are planning around dinner, check the food situation separately, because the taproom label says nothing about it.
Across the river the language shifts again, slightly. Rooms in Belleville, Edwardsville and Alton use tavern and pub with the same looseness, and hours or age policies can differ because the rules belong to a different state. Worth a look at the listing rather than an assumption carried over from the Missouri side.
### Which one fits the night you are planning?
Start from the night, not the noun. Six people, a birthday, and a table you can sit at for three hours is a pub problem. A stop after a show at half past ten with no plan to eat is a bar problem. Match the room to the evening and the word on the sign stops mattering much.
Family dinner with grandparents and a seven year old? Look for lunch hours, entrees and booths, then call about the age cutoff. Watching a game with four friends? Ask how many screens they have and whether the sound stays on, because a quiet pub with one television is a bad afternoon for that plan.
A first date where you want to hear each other calls for a smaller room with tables, early, before the volume climbs. A late night with a group calls for the later close, so the bar side wins. A slow Sunday where you want to read for an hour calls for a pub with a fireplace and nobody rushing you out of the booth.
One more piece of practical advice we give constantly. Call. A thirty second phone call answers hours, kitchen close, age policy, patio and whether the group of nine you are bringing needs a reservation. Websites go stale between updates. The person answering the phone knows what is happening tonight.
