### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is a pub called a bar?
A.  Because the counter took over the name. A bar was originally the barrier between the stock and the customers, and in Britain the room where you order and stand became the public bar, as opposed to the lounge or the snug. So a pub contains a bar, and American usage generalized the smaller word into the name for the whole building. Both are correct, which is exactly why the question keeps coming up.
### Q. What is a tavern?
A.  Historically a tavern sold wine, and later fed and housed travelers, which put it closer to an inn than to a modern bar. In American use it also became a licensing word in several states, generally covering a place that serves drinks and food without lodging. Around the St. Louis metro it usually means a neighborhood corner room with a short menu and a long memory. Rules vary by state and city, so check locally.
### Q. Is a pub a British bar?
A.  Close, but the emphasis sits in a different place. A British or Irish pub is a food and community room that also serves drinks, with table seating, daytime hours and mixed ages until evening. An American bar is a drinking room that may also serve food. American pubs borrow the look and often the menu, and the good ones borrow the hours too, which is the part that actually changes your experience.
### Q. What do British people call bartenders?
A.  Barman, barmaid, or bar staff as the neutral term for everyone working. The person who runs the place is the landlord or landlady, and licensee or publican is the formal version you see on the paperwork above the door. Bartender is understood everywhere and gets used more now than it once did, particularly in cocktail rooms. In a traditional pub you order at the bar rather than waiting for table service.
### Q. Who drinks more alcohol, Brits or Americans?
A.  Closer than the stereotype suggests. In international comparisons of alcohol consumed per adult, the United Kingdom and the United States land near one another, near enough that the ranking depends on the year and the source you read. We are not quoting a figure here because those numbers get revised. The World Health Organization and the OECD both publish current data. The real difference is pattern rather than volume.
### Q. Difference between a bar and a tavern
A.  In everyday speech a tavern is smaller, older and more likely to serve food, while bar is the broader word covering everything from a hotel lounge to a late-night room with a cover charge. In some states the distinction is also a licensing one, with tavern licenses carrying food requirements attached. Locally the useful test stays the same: check the kitchen hours and the seating rather than the sign.
### Q. Can I bring kids to a St. Louis pub or tavern?
A.  Often, while the kitchen is open, and the menu is the fastest tell. Llywelyn’s Pub in Webster Groves publishes a separate kids menu, which is a room planning for families at dinner. The age cutoff later in the evening is set by each venue and local rules and is not always posted, so call before you bring the stroller.

## Your Uncle Is Ruining the Burger. 16 Stools in Brentwood Know Why.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-actually-makes-a-good-burger
Hiss. Then a scrape. On a stool at Carl’s Drive In on Manchester Road in Brentwood, you hear your burger before you see it: a ball of beef hits the flat-top, a spatula comes down hard, and the edges spread into a dark, lacy fringe that crackles when it flips. Your homemade root beer lands in a frosty mug. By the time the glass starts to sweat, lunch is on the counter.
Now the backyard version, the one you have probably eaten in a Florissant driveway on the Fourth of July. Thick patty, lukewarm grill, and somebody’s uncle leaning on it with the spatula halfway through, so the juice hisses into the coals and the smoke rolls off. One gets you a crust you can hear. The other gets you a gray puck and a bottle of ketchup doing all the work.
That counter has a story, too. The building started in 1918 as a Lubrite Service Station. In 1959 a tornado badly damaged it, and the owner rebuilt. That same year a 25-year-old named Carl Meyer, whose family delivered meat to the place, bought it with his wife, Pat, and named it Carl’s Drive In. The family that delivered the beef ended up owning the griddle. A 1962 remodel closed it in for air conditioning and indoor seating for 16, and those 16 stools are still the whole dining room.
Press it in the first seconds, or never press it at all. That one rule is the whole gap between Carl’s and your uncle.
Here is the line to say out loud at the next cookout: USDA research shows that 1 in 4 hamburgers turn brown before they reach a safe internal temperature. The brown middle your uncle trusts is lying to him one burger in four. An instant-read thermometer reading 160°F settles it.
### Do it today: two ways
Taste it first. Carl’s menu calls it a crispy-edged, griddle-smashed double cheeseburger, and the double with cheese is $7.50. Grilled onions are 30 cents more. Skip the second stop for dessert: there’s a Ted Drewes concrete on the menu. Hours are Monday-Saturday 11am-7:30pm and Sunday 11am-4pm at 9033 Manchester Rd. Call (314) 961-9652 for curbside, because parking and seating are limited.
Then make it tonight. Mac’s Local Eats on Oakland Avenue prints its own burger math on the menu: 2 patties = ¼ pound. That works out to 2-ounce smash patties, and it is the number to copy. Buy one pound of 80 percent lean ground chuck and split it into eight loose balls with your fingertips, the same math scaled up. Put them back in the fridge. Heat a cast-iron skillet on high until a drop of water skitters and vanishes. Ball down, stiff spatula on it right away, lean your weight in for ten seconds. Salt the top. Flip once by scraping hard, cheese on, and stack two per bun.
### What’s the secret to a good smash burger?
Heat, contact, and speed. Drop a loose ball of 80/20 chuck onto a screaming hot surface, then flatten it hard within the first thirty seconds while the meat is still soft. Season after the smash, flip once, scrape up every bit of crust, and never press it again.
That early window is where home cooks lose it. You feel it through the spatula: soft raw beef gives under your palm for a few seconds, then the bottom sets and it stops spreading and starts tearing. Ball goes down, spatula goes on immediately, lean your weight into it, and hold for about ten seconds while the fat starts to spit.
The spatula decides it. A flimsy one bows under your hand and gives you a fat middle with burnt, brittle edges. A stiff one, or two stacked, goes down flat as a floor tile. Lay a square of parchment between the steel and the beef and it peels away clean, with no torn patty left behind.
Then leave it alone. That crust is the entire point: browned, lacy, faintly crunchy edges a thick grilled patty cannot produce. It forms because the beef is pinned flat against dry, hot metal with nowhere to steam. Slide it around and you start over.
Flip once, with the thinnest, sharpest spatula you own, and scrape rather than lift. The flavor you just built is stuck to the griddle, and a gentle lift leaves it there. Get under it hard and you bring the crust with you. Cheese goes on the instant it flips; a thin patty is done in about a minute a side, so cover the pan or splash in a little water to steam the cheese down.
### What actually makes a good burger?
Fat, heat, and restraint, in that order. Mac’s Local Eats at 5656 Oakland Ave. makes the beef case better than any recipe: it smashes whole-cow, dry-aged beef and toasts its buns in beef tallow. You taste the beef before you taste anything on it. A good burger is mostly decided before a single topping shows up: coarse ground chuck at roughly 80 percent lean and 20 percent fat, a surface hot enough to brown the outside fast, and hands that barely touch the meat. Mac’s is closed Mondays and Tuesdays, so plan the trip.
### The grind and the fat ratio
Fat is flavor, and it’s also insurance. An 80 percent lean blend melts as the patty cooks, carries flavor, and keeps things edible when somebody overcooks it. Lean 90/10 sirloin sounds like an upgrade. It cooks dry, and no sauce fixes dry.
Ground chuck is the workhorse. It tastes deeply beefy, and every meat counter carries it. If your butcher grinds to order, ask for chuck ground coarse the day you cook. Coarse gives you texture instead of paste, and beef ground that morning beats a pack that has sat pressed in a foam tray for days.
Blends add something once the basics are right: chuck for the base, brisket for richness, short rib for a deeper, almost roasted flavor. Fresh chuck that nobody overworked still beats a clever blend that was.
### How much you handle the meat
Every time you squeeze ground beef, you make it a little worse. Working the meat smears the fat and links up proteins, and the result is a patty with the springy, dense bite of meatloaf. Keep the beef cold, portion it with your fingertips, and form the loosest patty that will survive the trip to the heat.
Cold matters more than most people expect. Warm fat smears into the lean; cold fat stays in distinct pieces and melts during cooking, leaving little pockets of juice behind. Portion your patties, then put them back in the refrigerator until the pan or the grill is genuinely ready.
### Shape and size
A thick grilled patty needs a dimple. Press your thumb into the center to leave a shallow well, because the edges tighten as they cook and shove the middle up into a dome. The dimple relaxes flat instead. Make the patty a little wider than the bun, too, since it shrinks in both directions.
For a smash burger the math is different: 2 to 3 ounces per ball, and two thin patties on one bun beat a single thick one every time. Two patties means twice the browned surface, twice the crust, and a burger you can still fit in your mouth.
### How hot should the pan or griddle be?
Hotter than you think, and for a smash burger, as hot as your equipment safely allows. A flat surface holding somewhere around 400°F to 450°F browns the beef in seconds instead of minutes. Medium heat steams the patty in its own juices and leaves you with something gray and disappointing.
Cast iron and carbon steel are the right tools because they hold heat. Cold beef hitting the surface drops the temperature hard, and a thin nonstick pan never recovers. Nonstick also isn’t built for this kind of heat, and the coating suffers for it. Preheat a solid five minutes, longer than feels necessary, then test with a drop of water. It should skitter and vanish, not sit there and bubble.
Grilled burgers want a different setup: two zones. Build a hot side and a cooler side. Thick patties get browned over direct heat, then moved to the cooler side to finish cooking through without the outside turning to carbon. That cooler zone is also your escape route when fat drips and a flare-up starts.
Ventilation is the real limit in most kitchens. A proper smash burger makes smoke, and there’s no version of this where it doesn’t. Open a window, run the hood on high, and if the alarm in your hallway is sensitive, take the whole operation outside onto a flat griddle plate over the grill burners.
Hungry before you’ve finished reading? Browse burger spots across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, order the double, and check the edges before the first bite. Dark and ragged means somebody back there knows the rule.
If you run the flat-top people drive across town for, a smash joint, a food truck, a bar griddle that never cools down, every neighbor hunting that sound is a customer you could be feeding. A Gold listing puts your burger in front of more customers for under a dollar a day, or start with your listing here.
### When should you season a burger?
Right at the heat, and on the outside only. Salt mixed into ground beef dissolves proteins and turns the texture springy and sausage-like, so keep it on the surface and apply it seconds before, or just after, the patty hits the pan. Season generously, because most of it never reaches the middle.
Coarse kosher salt and coarse black pepper, more than looks reasonable, on both faces. The patty is thick and the seasoning only sits on the outside, which makes under-salting far more common than over-salting. If you’ve ever wondered why a restaurant burger tastes better than yours with the same beef, this is usually a big part of it.
On a smash burger, salt the top face right after you flatten it, then hit the other side after the flip. Doing it in that order keeps salt from pulling moisture to the surface while you’re trying to build a dry, browned crust.
Save the rest of your ideas for the sauce. Garlic powder, chopped onion, Worcestershire and egg belong in meatloaf, not in a burger patty. Mixing anything into the beef means working the beef, and working the beef is exactly what you were trying to avoid.
### Why is pressing a grilled burger wrong when a smash burger is all about pressing?
Timing is the whole difference. A smash burger gets pressed in the first seconds, while the beef is raw and soft and the rendering fat pools in a hot pan and fries it. A grilled burger gets pressed halfway through, when that same press squeezes cooked juices out and straight into the fire.
Think about where the fat goes. On a flat griddle, rendered fat has nowhere to run, so the patty essentially fries in it, and that is a large part of why smash burgers taste the way they do. On a grill, the fat falls through the grate, and pressing only speeds up the loss. You get flare-ups, a scorched exterior, and a drier burger for your trouble.
So the rule isn’t “never press.” The rule is press once, at the very beginning, or not at all. Once the crust has formed on a smash patty, the pressing job is finished and any more of it just pushes juice out. On a thick grilled burger, the spatula is for flipping and nothing else.
### Does a burger really need to rest?
A thick one does, briefly. Give a grilled patty three to five minutes off the heat and the juices redistribute instead of running onto the plate at first bite. A thin smash patty is a different case: it cooks so fast, and gets eaten so fast, that resting mostly just makes it cold.
Resting also buys time for everything else. Cheese finishes melting on residual heat, buns come off the griddle, and the internal temperature keeps climbing a few degrees after the patty leaves the pan. Plan for that carryover instead of being surprised by it.
Tent loosely with foil if the kitchen is cold, but don’t wrap tightly. Trapped steam softens the crust you just spent all that effort building. And if you salt a thick patty and leave it uncovered in the refrigerator for a while before cooking, the surface dries slightly and browns better. Small thing, real difference.
### How do you know when a burger is done?
Use a thermometer, not the color. The safe internal temperature for ground meats is 160°F, and a burger can turn brown in the middle well before it gets there. Slide an instant-read probe in through the side, into the center.
Color is genuinely unreliable, which is why federal guidance points at temperature instead. Grinding mixes surface bacteria all the way through the patty, unlike a whole steak where the inside stays sealed, and that is the reason the recommendation for burgers is stricter than for a roast.
Insert the probe horizontally through the edge so the tip sits in the middle of the patty and not out the far side. On a thin smash patty a thermometer is close to useless, though it’s also close to unnecessary. Beef that thin, on metal that hot, is cooked through in roughly a minute a side.
If you’re cooking for kids, older adults, anyone pregnant, or anyone with a weakened immune system, treat 160°F as a rule rather than a suggestion. This is general information and not food safety advice for your specific kitchen, so check current USDA guidance when it matters.
A great burger is wasted on a sore tooth. Find a St. Louis dentist.
### Does the bun matter as much as the patty?
Not quite, but it’s the second biggest variable and by far the easiest to fix. A bun’s job is structural: hold everything together for the length of a meal without falling apart. Toast the cut faces in butter or in the beef fat left in the pan, which adds flavor and a moisture barrier at once.
Match the bun to the burger. A soft potato roll compresses around a smash burger and is close to perfect. A big grilled patty carrying a lot of toppings needs something sturdier, like a brioche or a seeded bun with more structure. Anything crusty and chewy fights back when you bite, and the whole build squirts out the far side.
Order matters in the build, too. Sauce on both toasted faces, lettuce on the bottom as a barrier against the juices, then the patty and cheese, then tomato, onion and pickle on top. Salt the tomato slices on a paper towel first if you want them to taste like anything.
Cheese should be a melter above all else. American takes a lot of criticism and still wins on the one thing that counts here, which is melting into the patty instead of sitting on top in a stiff square. Sharp cheddar, Provel, provolone and pepper jack all work; just give them heat and cover the pan for a few seconds.
### Where do you find a great burger near you?
Once you know what to look for, you can spot a good one before the first bite, at Carl’s, at Mac’s, or at the corner bar with a flat-top. Ragged, dark brown edges instead of a perfect circle. Cheese that has run down the sides and pooled a little. A bun with griddle marks on the cut face. Those are all signs that somebody back there is paying attention.
Want to watch the press rule before you try it? Take a stool at Carl’s and watch the spatula, not your phone. The counter now takes credit cards and keeps an ATM on site.
Burgers aren’t the only grill staple with house rules; here’s what to know about hot dogs in St. Louis.
Ask what the grind is if the counter seems friendly. Kitchens that grind chuck in house usually volunteer it, because it costs them more and they know it shows.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are smashburgers better than regular burgers?
A.  They’re different, not better. A smash burger trades thickness for crust: more browned surface, more flavor in every bite, and a much faster cook. A thick grilled patty gives you a juicier center and smoke from the fire. If you want crust, smash it. If you want a pink middle, don’t.
### Q. What is the best type of burger for smash burgers?
A.  Coarse ground chuck at 80/20 is the standard, and some cooks push to 70/30 for extra fat. Skip lean sirloin blends and skip frozen pre-formed patties, which are pressed too tightly to spread properly. Portion loose balls of 2 to 3 ounces and keep them cold until they hit the pan.
### Q. What are common smash burger mistakes?
A.  Pressing too late is the big one, since the patty stops spreading once its surface sets. After that: a pan that isn’t hot enough, balls too large to flatten evenly, a flimsy spatula that bends, lifting instead of scraping so the crust stays behind on the griddle, and crowding the pan until everything steams.
### Q. Is Five Guys a smashburger?
A.  Not in the classic sense. Five Guys describes its burgers as fresh, hand-formed patties hot off the grill. A true smash burger starts as a loose ball and gets flattened hard in its first seconds on a flat-top, the way Carl’s Drive In does it, which is what builds those thin, lacy, browned edges.
### Q. Do I cook burgers on medium or high heat?
A.  High, for almost every burger. Smash burgers want a griddle around 400°F to 450°F so the crust forms in seconds. Thick grilled patties get seared over high direct heat, then moved to a cooler zone to finish. Medium heat the whole way through mostly steams the beef gray.
### Q. What does a 160 degree burger look like?
A.  Usually brown throughout, but appearance is not a reliable test. USDA research shows 1 in 4 hamburgers turn brown before they reach a safe internal temperature, which is why the advice points to a thermometer instead. Probe through the side into the center and read the number.
### Q. Should you let burgers sit after cooking?
A.  Yes for thick patties, for roughly three to five minutes. That pause lets the juices redistribute and lets carryover heat finish the job, so the burger doesn’t empty itself onto the plate. Thin smash patties are the exception, since they cook in about a minute a side and are best eaten immediately.
### Q. Should you put oil in the pan when frying burgers?
A.  A very thin film, on a dry preheated surface. An 80/20 patty renders plenty of its own fat within seconds, so you only need enough high smoke point oil to guarantee full contact with the metal. Too much and the patty floats and browns unevenly. On well seasoned cast iron, wipe the pan and use almost none.

## Voice Still Cracking? Don't Wait Out the Old 90 Days
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-you-should-see-an-ent-not-your-regular-doctor
Your voice cracks on the first word of every sentence, like a radio that won’t quite tune in. By evening it’s a dry rasp, and you clear your throat so often your family has stopped noticing. You’ve told your coworkers and the cashier at Schnucks that it’s just allergies. If it has gone on for four weeks without getting better, the ENT specialists’ own guideline says it’s time to have the voice box examined. That call doesn’t mean something is wrong. It means the waiting has done its job.
Most people think the wait is much longer, and for years it was. The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation updated its hoarseness guideline and shortened the time hoarseness can be managed conservatively from 90 days to four weeks before the larynx should be evaluated.
Three months used to be the rule. Now it’s four weeks. Plenty of people are still waiting out the old clock.
The St. Louis numbers to call are a few paragraphs down. This is general information, not medical advice; a clinician who examines you decides your case.
### What are signs you should see an ENT?
The clearest sign is time. The specialists’ guideline says hoarseness that does not resolve or improve within four weeks should have the voice box looked at, and sinus symptoms lasting longer than 12 weeks meet the definition of chronic sinusitis. Symptoms that keep coming back, or that do not budge after a first round of care, also earn a specialist look.
Recurrence has real numbers behind it. If the dull pressure behind your cheekbones keeps coming back and the tissue box never leaves the nightstand, this part is for you. ENT Health, the academy’s patient site, says recurrent acute sinusitis is four or more sinus infections in one year with no symptoms in between. For a child’s throat infections, the academy’s tonsillectomy guideline recommends watchful waiting when there have been fewer than seven episodes in the past year, fewer than five a year for two years, or fewer than three a year for three years. Writing down the dates makes that count easy to show.
### Which St. Louis door to walk through
Make the call on a weekday morning with your dates open on the phone beside you, so you’re not trying to remember them while on hold. WashU Medicine’s Otolaryngology Appointment Center is 314-362-7509, and the department says new and returning patients can also schedule online. Its main clinic is the Center for Advanced Medicine at 4921 Parkview Place, Suite 11A. If you’re in Florissant or anywhere in North County, the same number books Suite 201 in Medical Office Building 2 at Christian Hospital Northeast, 11125 Dunn Rd. Veterans can be seen by WashU ENT doctors at the John Cochran VA, 915 N Grand Blvd, (314) 289-7600.
On the south side, SLUCare Physician Group’s otolaryngologists are at 1225 S. Grand Blvd. Skip the main entrance and look for the Garden Level, Door 3. Call 314-617-2500, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. SLUCare lists voice disorders, dizziness, hearing loss, ear disease, pediatric ENT, and disorders of the nose and sinuses among its services.
For the four-year-old in O’Fallon on his fourth ear infection, WashU’s pediatric line is 314-454-6162. At St. Louis Children’s Hospital, take the Atrium/Green elevators to Floor 3; exit the elevator bay and the ENT suite is on your left. It helps to know that before you’re carrying a tired, hot-cheeked child through the lobby.
One caution. Booking a slot online does not mean your insurance will pay for it without a referral. Call your insurer first. That’s the call with money attached.
### The voice rule almost nobody knows
A teacher in Webster Groves whose voice is gone by Thursday afternoon, talking over a room of kids in a whisper, is not being dramatic. The academy’s fact sheet says 20 percent of teachers miss work due to hoarseness, and it names teachers, singers, clergy, coaches and healthcare workers among the people at higher risk. ENT Health says vocal professionals who cannot do their job should see an ENT as soon as they can.
There’s a second line in that guideline worth carrying into any exam room. Patients with isolated hoarseness should not be treated with anti-reflux, antibiotic or steroid medications before the larynx has been looked at. So if you’ve been handed a heartburn pill for a scratchy voice and nobody has looked at your vocal cords, it’s fair to ask, calmly, whether it’s time someone did.
And if you smoke, the clock is shorter still. ENT Health says smokers who develop hoarseness should see an ENT specialist right away.
### When is your regular doctor still the right first call?
Most of the time, honestly. A single cold, a mild earache, a short sinus infection that is behaving itself: those are primary care problems, and primary care handles them well. ENT Health says acute laryngitis can usually be managed by your primary care physician with supportive care and voice rest. It also says that if a sore throat lasts more than five to ten days, you should see your doctor.
Your regular doctor sees the whole picture: medications, blood pressure, allergies, the thing you mentioned last spring and forgot. A first round of care is not wasted even when it fails. It’s information, and the specialist who knows what was tried starts several moves ahead.
So the honest framing is sequence. Start where the common explanations live, and move up when the calendar says they’ve run out.
### How to keep the count
Write down dates. Open the notes app on your phone and type the day it started and every day it flared. “It keeps happening” is easy to wave off. “Four sinus infections since January, here are the weeks” is not, and that short list changes the conversation on both sides of the desk.
After a long run of appointments, eat well. Candicci’s in Chesterfield is worth the drive.
### What will an ENT do on your first visit?
Expect conversation, then examination, then a plan. Practices differ and your clinician decides what is appropriate, but the shape is fairly consistent.
### The history
When did it start, what makes it better or worse, what has been tried, what happened? This is where your dated list earns its keep. Bring your medications, including anything over the counter, and any notes from your regular doctor.
### The examination
Ears, nose and throat get looked at directly. For a voice problem, ENT Health says the specialist may pass a very small, lighted flexible tube with a camera, called a fiberoptic scope, through your nose to view your vocal cords, and that most patients tolerate it well. You may feel a cool, odd pressure in the back of your nose for a moment. Then it’s over.
### The plan
Leave knowing three things: what they think is going on, what happens next, and what would make you call sooner. If one is missing, ask before you stand up.
### Can I go straight to an ENT without a referral?
Sometimes. Two things decide it: your insurance plan and the practice. Some plans only cover a specialist visit that came through a primary care referral, and some offices schedule only from referrals. Ask your insurer whether a referral is required for a specialist office visit under your plan, then ask the practice what it needs from you.
There’s a reason to want the referral even when nobody demands it. It usually arrives carrying records: what was tried, what was seen, what was ruled out. And if the specialist’s wait is long, keep the primary care appointment and keep the notes going.
### What conditions do ENTs treat?
The name is the map: ears, nose and throat, plus much of the head and neck around them. Hearing loss, ringing in the ears and balance problems. Ear infections that keep coming back, especially in children. Sinus infections that return and congestion that won’t clear. Hoarseness, trouble swallowing, frequent throat infections, snoring and sleep apnea, and a lump in the neck that doesn’t go away.
Ear tubes are the one many parents meet first. ENT Health says more than half a million ear tube surgeries are performed on children each year, making it the most common childhood surgery performed with anesthesia.
### Which symptoms should not wait?
Some things don’t belong on a watch-and-wait plan. ENT Health lists difficult breathing and pain when speaking among voice symptoms that call for an ENT as soon as you can, and the guideline names a neck mass and breathing distress as reasons to speed up care.
Trouble breathing, an airway that feels like it’s closing, or bleeding you can’t stop is an emergency. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Not a referral request. Not a search.
For the gray zone in between, call your regular doctor’s office and describe the symptom out loud to a person. They triage every day, and they’ll tell you whether this is a next-available appointment or a today problem.
### What should you ask at the appointment?
Write your questions down beforehand, because the room moves faster than you expect. These work for a first visit with almost any specialist:
What do you think is causing this, and what else is on the list?
What would you need to see to be sure?
Is any test or scope done here today, or scheduled separately?
What are the options, including waiting?
What would make you want to hear from me sooner?
Will you send a note back to my regular doctor?
Does anything you’re suggesting need prior authorization from my insurer?
### Where do you find ENT doctors near you?
Start close to home and check two things: whether the practice takes your insurance, and whether it needs a referral before it will book you. Those two answers remove most of the frustration before it starts.
Bring your dates and your medication list to the very first phone call. Browse ear, nose and throat providers across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each office the same two questions about insurance and referrals before you book.
If you run an ENT practice, an audiology office or a hearing aid shop, the patient holding a list of dates is searching tonight. List your practice and get more customers: the new patients already holding the phone, ready to book.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I go straight to an ENT without a referral?
A.  Sometimes. Your insurance plan and the practice decide it. WashU Medicine’s ENT department says new patients can schedule online or through its Appointment Center at 314-362-7509, but booking is not the same as coverage. Call your insurer first, then the office, and ask whether a referral is required.
### Q. What is the most common ENT problem?
A.  There’s no single honest ranking, and this page won’t invent one. Two numbers give a sense of scale: the academy says hoarseness affects nearly one-third of the population at some point in their life, and more than half a million ear tube surgeries are performed on children each year. Your clinician will tell you where your symptom fits.
### Q. What will an ENT do on your first visit?
A.  Take a history, examine your ears, nose and throat, and set out a plan. For a voice complaint, that may include a small lighted flexible scope passed through the nose to view the vocal cords, which ENT Health says most patients tolerate well. Bring your medication list and dated notes.
### Q. What are the most common ENT procedures?
A.  For children, ear tubes lead: ENT Health calls them the most common childhood surgery performed with anesthesia. Tonsil and adenoid surgery and sinus surgery are others patients often hear about. Most first visits involve no procedure beyond an exam and possibly a scope or hearing test.
### Q. How long do ENT appointments usually take?
A.  Ask when you book, because it varies by practice and by what the visit involves. A first appointment generally runs longer than a follow-up, since it includes a full history, an exam, and sometimes a hearing test or scope in the same session.
### Q. What conditions do ENTs treat?
A.  Ears, nose, throat and much of the surrounding head and neck. SLUCare’s otolaryngologists, for example, list head and neck tumors, hearing loss and ear disease, voice disorders, pediatric ENT problems, dizziness, and disorders of the nose and sinuses.
### Q. What are some common questions I should ask an ENT doctor?
A.  ENT Health suggests three for hoarseness: What is the cause of my hoarseness? Are any of my medications drying me out? When should I see a specialist? Add what the options are, including waiting, and whether a note goes back to your regular doctor.
### Q. Does ENT see throat infection?
A.  Yes, especially the ones that keep coming back. The academy’s children’s tonsillectomy guideline says surgery may be recommended after at least seven throat infections in the past year, at least five a year for two years, or at least three a year for three years. A single throat infection is usually a primary care matter.

## How Long Eyelash Extensions Really Last, and Why Day 22 Costs You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-long-eyelash-extensions-really-last
It shows up on the pillowcase first. One short, pale natural lash with a longer, darker one still glued to it, lying on the white cotton like a dropped eyelash in a cartoon. You pick it up between two fingers and feel your stomach drop a little, because you paid for that one. Then you find another on the bathroom counter. By the weekend you’re tilting your head at the car mirror on Manchester Road, trying to decide whether the outer corner of your left eye has gone thin or whether you’re just tired.
You’re not imagining it, and nothing went wrong. The American Academy of Ophthalmology says it’s normal to lose between one and five eyelashes each day, and an extension falls off when the lash it sits on sheds. Your set is leaving on a schedule you can’t stop. The part almost nobody tells you is that the salon has a schedule too, and it is printed on the menu.
Here is the one that stings. LUSH Aesthetics Lash & Hair in Saint Charles prices its classic fills at $70 and up at two weeks and $90 and up at three. Book outside 3 weeks (21 days), and its menu says the touch-up is charged as a new set, which starts at $160. Same chair. Same lashes. Day 21 is a fill. Day 22 is a new set, and the bill roughly doubles.
Say it out loud to the friend who keeps stretching her fills: one day past three weeks can cost you a whole new set.
### How long do lash extensions last before a fill?
Most sets need a fill every two to three weeks. Your natural lashes shed one to five a day, and each one takes its extension with it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology says extensions typically last three to four weeks, falling off as your natural lashes shed.
Those are two different clocks, and mixing them up is where most of the disappointment comes from. Three to four weeks is how long extensions hang on in some form. Two to three weeks is when LUSH’s menu recommends a touch-up to keep the set you photographed in the parking lot looking full. Plan around the shorter one.
And the salon’s clock is shorter than both of them.
### Four St. Louis lash menus, four different cutoffs
Published menus across the metro show no two artists drawing the line in the same place, and that line decides whether you pay fill money or full-set money.
Start on Delmar Boulevard in the Loop, where She Nail Beauty Bar, a Black-owned salon in Suite 108 at 5621 Delmar, sells its fill as a two-week service: an hour and a half in the chair for $85. Call 314-440-8116; it’s open Tuesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Beauty & The Lash comes to you instead. The mobile artist sets up in clients’ homes, needs 40% of lashes remaining and a fill within 3.5 weeks, or it’s a full set. Even the drive is priced by neighborhood: plus $25 for North County and Downtown, plus $40 for the Central West End and Shaw, plus $55 for Kirkwood and Webster Groves.
Head west and the rules tighten. LUSH, the Saint Charles studio above, wants 50% of your extensions still on for fill pricing, on top of its 21-day line. In O’Fallon, Refine Beauty says refills should only be required every 2 to 4 weeks, with classic fills starting at $60 against a $150 classic full set, and a 1 week fill if you want the set at its fullest. At The Lash Society, Loft 14 inside Salon Lofts, 314-374-5799, hybrid fills run $75 to $95.
So before you book anywhere, ask three things and type the answers into your phone next to the appointment. What percentage has to be left for it to count as a fill? How many days until a fill becomes a full set? And what does each cost, side by side? Thirty seconds at the front desk is the difference between a $70 fill and a $160 full set. Menus change, so confirm on the phone.
### Why your lashes leave on their own schedule
Lean into the bathroom mirror in week two, chin up under the vanity light, and you can see it: short new lashes coming in bare between the long ones. Every extension rides on one natural lash, and that lash has its own life. The Academy says lashes go through their natural cycle every six to 10 weeks, the same way the hair on your head does. When a lash reaches the end, it lets go, and it takes its passenger along. That’s the system working, not failing.
You never noticed this before because a short natural lash dropping onto your cheek is invisible. A long black one is not. Same shedding, now with a spotlight on it.
It also explains the lopsided look that makes people think the application was bad. Your lashes are not synchronized. A little cluster at one outer corner can hit the end of its cycle in the same week, so one eye looks thinner than the other by the middle of week two. That’s timing, not a botched set.
### What each week feels like
Week one, you wake up already finished. No mascara wand, no smudge under the eye at 3 p.m., and you catch yourself blinking slowly in elevator doors because you like how it looks.
Week two, you can’t name what changed, but the line looks a little less awake than it did last Tuesday. This is the cheapest moment to book.
Week three, the gaps are real. A few survivors have grown out and stick out at odd angles, and you start noticing them at every stoplight. Book now, before day 22 decides for you.
Week four, you’re down to a scattered handful, and most menus will charge it as a new set anyway.
### What does a realistic fill schedule look like?
A fill is the quiet appointment. Eyes closed, a bright lamp on your face, the faint sharp smell of glue, tweezers ticking at the lash line while you try not to fall asleep. Book it every two to three weeks, for as long as you want to keep them. LUSH’s own menu says touch-ups are recommended every 2-3 weeks and prices them in 14-day and 21-day steps. That’s the honest shape of the commitment: a standing appointment, not a one-time purchase you revisit when things look rough.
Two weeks and three weeks are different appointments. At two weeks it’s a top-up and a shorter visit. At three, there’s more to rebuild, and the price on the menu climbs with it. Stretch past the line and you’re not saving money, you’re paying full-set prices on a longer loop.
The people who stay happy with extensions almost always do one boring thing: they book the next fill before they leave the chair. Put the date in your phone while the lash glue smell is still in the room.
### Booking around a date that will not move
A wedding in Webster Groves, family photos in Kirkwood, a cruise. Work backward from the date, and leave yourself a few days of buffer so you can go back if one corner isn’t sitting right. If the event lands past your next fill date, plan for two appointments instead of hoping one set survives a full month and a camera.
Fresh lashes deserve somewhere to go. The Kaslik Mediterranean menu is a decent excuse.
### What actually shortens your retention?
Mostly force and oil, and both belong to you. The Academy is blunt about the first: rubbing, tugging or pulling can fracture your natural lashes and can even cause permanent damage to the lash follicle. That itch at the corner of your eye at 11 p.m. is the most expensive itch you’ll have all month.
### Friction, and the way you sleep
Sleeping face-down presses and drags your lashes against the pillowcase for hours. So does the towel after a shower, pulling a sweater off over your head, and resting your face in your hand at a desk. None of it feels like rubbing your eyes. All of it counts.
### Oil, and skipped cleaning
Lash techs will tell you to keep oily cleansers and heavy creams away from the lash line, and to keep the lash line clean rather than leaving it alone. Ask your artist exactly what to use for your skin, then actually use it. If your skin runs oily, your realistic interval may be the two-week one, and that’s a better thing to know before you book than after.
### How much should a full set of lash extensions cost?
Here is what real St. Louis-area menus said when I checked them. At LUSH Aesthetics Lash & Hair in Saint Charles, a classic full set starts at $160, hybrid at $185 and volume at $225. At The Lash Society, Loft 14 inside Salon Lofts, a NovaLash hybrid install is $135 and hybrid fills run $75 to $95. Prices change, so call before you book.
The style drives most of the gap. Classic puts one extension on one natural lash. Volume builds a fan of several fine extensions for each lash, which is more work and more time in the chair. Hybrid sits between.
The number nobody quotes you is the year. A fill every two or three weeks adds up to far more than the first set, so ask what a fill costs and where the cutoff sits in the same conversation.
### Are eyelash extensions worth it?
If you wear eye makeup every day, the trade is easy to feel: you roll out of bed already done, and those minutes come back every single morning. If you can’t fit an appointment every two to three weeks, the honest answer is probably no, and there’s nothing wrong with landing there. And if you know you’ll pick at them the moment they start to shed, they’ll frustrate you.
### Do fake lashes damage real lashes?
The Academy lists the risks plainly: trauma to or infection of the eyelid or cornea, allergic reaction to the glue, and permanent or temporary loss of eyelashes. It also notes that eyelash extensions and glue are not currently regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Its advice: ask for the glue’s ingredient list, and request a spot test on the inside of your wrist before the glue goes near your eyes.
If your eyes turn red, itchy or swollen, don’t pull the set off yourself. The Academy says to see an ophthalmologist immediately. This is general information, not medical advice.
### Where do you find a lash tech near you?
Add one more question to the three above: will they fill another artist’s work? Both Beauty & The Lash and LUSH say they won’t fill over another tech’s set, so switching artists usually means paying for a removal and a new set. Ask how long the appointment runs, too. Refine Beauty puts a full set at about 90-120 minutes and a refill at 45-60 minutes.
Then check the license. You can look up a Missouri cosmetology or esthetics license through the state’s MOPRO system, or call the Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners at 573-751-1052.
If you’re already budgeting for fills every few weeks, read what laser hair removal costs in St. Louis before you add another standing appointment.
Book your next fill before the 21-day line finds you. Browse eyelash services across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, ask each one where their fill cutoff sits, and book the next fill before you leave the first appointment.
If you’re the lash artist working out of a salon loft, a spare room or the trunk of your car, the client counting days on her calendar is searching for you right now. List your lash business so more of those customers find your chair first.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do fake lashes damage real lashes?
A.  They can if they’re handled roughly. The American Academy of Ophthalmology says rubbing, tugging or pulling can fracture natural lashes and even damage the lash follicle, and lists permanent or temporary lash loss among the risks. Have sets removed professionally, ask for a wrist spot test of the glue, and see an ophthalmologist if your eyes react. This is general information, not medical advice.
### Q. Are eyelash extensions worth it?
A.  They are if you can live with the schedule. The payoff is daily: no mascara, and you look finished the moment you wake up. The cost is a fill every two to three weeks, a no-rubbing habit, and daily cleaning. Miss the salon’s cutoff and you pay for a full set again.
### Q. What are the downsides to lash extensions?
A.  Upkeep and the cutoff. You shed one to five natural lashes a day, so the set thins steadily, and many menus charge a full set once too few are left or too many days have passed. LUSH Aesthetics in Saint Charles draws that line at 21 days. There are also the aftercare rules and the Academy’s list of risks, including allergic reaction to the glue.
### Q. How much should a full set of lash extensions cost?
A.  On menus checked in the St. Louis area, a classic full set at LUSH Aesthetics Lash & Hair starts at $160 and a hybrid install at The Lash Society in Salon Lofts is $135. Volume costs more because it takes longer. Ask about fill pricing in the same call, since fills are the bigger number over a year.
### Q. Are lash extensions painful?
A.  They shouldn’t be. You lie back with your eyes closed the whole time, and the Academy says the application can take as long as two hours, so many people doze off. Stinging, burning, itching or swelling is not something to sit through. Tell your artist right away, and see an ophthalmologist if it continues.
### Q. Can I use mascara on my lash extensions?
A.  Most artists will say no. Mascara has to come off again, and getting it off usually means rubbing at the lash line, which is exactly the tugging the Academy warns can fracture lashes. If you want mascara three weeks in, that’s usually your sign that you’re due for a fill.
### Q. How long should a full set of lash extensions take?
A.  Plan on a long appointment. The Academy says the procedure can take as long as two hours, and Refine Beauty in O’Fallon puts a full set at about 90-120 minutes. Volume generally takes longest because each natural lash gets a fan instead of a single extension. Ask for the expected time when you book.

## One Word on the Tub Changes Your Missouri Tax and Your EBT Card
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-health-food-store-actually-sells
Turn the tub of protein powder around before you carry it to the register, because one word on the back is about to change your receipt. Crack the seal if you want and smell that chalky vanilla, but read the box above the ingredients first. If it says Supplement Facts instead of Nutrition Facts, your EBT card just stopped working on it, and so did Missouri’s reduced food tax rate.
Federal SNAP rules are blunt about it: “If an item has a Supplement Facts label, it is considered a supplement and is not eligible for SNAP purchase.” And Missouri’s reduced state sales tax on food, 1.225% instead of 4.225%, applies to food items that may be purchased with food stamps. So the bottle with the Supplement Facts panel gets neither. One word on the back costs you three extra cents on every dollar in state tax and takes the purchase off the EBT card entirely.
The same word tells you who checked what’s inside, and for whether it works, the answer is nobody. The FDA says it “does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.” So the real vetting happens at a counter, by a person, and two St. Louis stores show what that looks like when the person has skin in the game.
None of that makes the store a con. Most of it is honest groceries you can see straight through a plastic bin: oats that hiss into a paper bag, the cold breath off the kombucha door. The trick is knowing which aisle is food and which aisle is a promise.
In south St. Louis County, The Healthy Shopper tells its own beginning without any polish. The store “was born from a Mother’s desire to help an infant son with emphysema.” JoAnn opened it in 1981 with the help of her mother, Blanche Earl, and today she works it with her daughter, her granddaughter and a friend. The shelves at 139 Concord Plaza carry over one hundred brands of health foods, vitamins, supplements and cosmetics. Call (314) 849-1050 before you make the drive.
iShop Naturals started even smaller. Its own timeline says that from 2003 to 2010, Nuka “started Selling natural products to friends & family from my small rental apartment.” In 2011 came the first store, at 4511 S. Kingshighway in South City, and later a second at 2715 N. Highway 67 in Florissant. The shelves run to bulk herbs and spices, shea butter, raw black soap and Irish sea moss, plus a whole section of Dr. Sebi’s recommended herbs and foods. It’s open every day, 10am-7pm. Call (314) 335-7995 if you’re after one thing in particular.
Notice what both stores lead with. Not a lab. Not a seal. A mother at a register in 1981, a founder selling to friends out of a rental apartment. That is what you’re really shopping for at a St. Louis counter, and you can test for it in ten seconds. Pick up the bottle you came for, set it on the counter and ask: what would you not take? A store that steers you off a bottle is a store you can believe about the next one.
### Should I buy supplements at health food stores?
Sometimes, but not because the shelf vetted it. The white caps and clinical fonts look like medicine. They aren’t reviewed like medicine: the NIH supplement office says the FDA “does not determine whether dietary supplements are effective before they are marketed.”
What you can check with your own eyes, in the aisle, is a testing seal from U.S. Pharmacopeia, NSF International or ConsumerLab.com. A seal indicates the product was properly manufactured, contains the ingredients listed on the label and does not contain harmful levels of contaminants. The same office adds: “These seals do not guarantee that a product is safe or effective.” It tells you what’s in the bottle, not what it does for you.
If you take prescription medication, carry the list to a pharmacist before adding anything, because some supplements might interact with medicines or other supplements. Everything on this page is general information, not medical advice.
Missouri also has a phone line most people only think to call when a toddler gets into the bleach. The Missouri Poison Center, at SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital, offers “free, fast, and confidential expert help for poisonings and drug information; 24 hours a day, 7 days a week,” with registered nurses and pharmacists on the phones. Its own list of things that can poison you starts with medicines: prescription, over-the-counter, herbal and vitamins. Put 1-800-222-1222 in your phone today, before the bottle of gummy vitamins ends up on a counter a five-year-old can reach.
### What does a health food store actually stock?
Walk past the vitamin wall and the rest of the store is food. Strip away the branding and most of these stores are a small grocery with a different emphasis. Six departments do the heavy lifting: bulk bins, specialty diet and allergen items, refrigerated and frozen, supplements, body care and household goods, and sometimes a small deli or juice counter. The mix shifts with square footage. The categories rarely do.
### Bulk bins
This is the department a supermarket usually can’t match. Gravity bins and scoop bins hold grains, rolled oats, dried beans and lentils, rice, nuts, seeds, dried fruit, granola, flours, pasta, coffee, loose tea, spices, and often a grinder for fresh nut butter. You bring a container or take a bag, fill what you want, and write down the bin number. The point isn’t volume. It’s that you choose the amount.
### Specialty diet and allergen items
Gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, soy-free, egg-free, low FODMAP, keto, vegan, halal and kosher items tend to get real shelf space here instead of a token half-aisle. If you’ve ever hunted for sorghum flour or a certified nut-free granola bar, this is the practical reason to make the trip. Depth of selection, not magic ingredients.
### Refrigerated and frozen
Expect tofu and tempeh, plant milks, cultured dairy and yogurt, kefir, kombucha, a cheese case that leans local or specialty, frozen fruit and vegetables, frozen entrees built around a specific diet, and often a small selection of meat, eggs and fish. This is also where refrigerated probiotics live, which sit with the supplements in some stores and with the dairy in others.
### Body care and household goods
Shampoo, soap, deodorant, toothpaste, lotion, sunscreen, essential oils, cleaning products, laundry detergent, and refill stations in the stores that run them. Worth knowing: personal care products are regulated differently from food, and words like “natural” and “clean” carry no fixed legal meaning on a bottle of shampoo. Read that ingredient list the way you’d read one on a cereal box.
### The deli, juice bar or hot case
Bigger stores add prepared food: a salad bar, a soup and hot case, sandwiches, smoothies, cold-pressed juice, sometimes a coffee counter. It’s convenient, and it’s priced like convenience. A smoothie built from the same frozen fruit sold four aisles over carries a large markup, which is fine when you want it made for you and worth noticing when you don’t.
### Where does a health food store beat a supermarket?
Four places, and they’re specific. Bulk quantities you choose yourself, allergen-free and specialty-diet items a chain won’t stock, staff who genuinely know the inventory, and local or small-batch suppliers who never enter a regional distribution system. Outside those four, a supermarket with a decent natural foods aisle competes just fine.
The bulk bins are the clearest win, and the savings run two directions. Buying a large quantity of a staple you eat constantly usually works out cheaper per unit than the packaged version. Buying one tablespoon of a spice you need for a single recipe means you’re not paying for a whole jar that goes stale in the cabinet. Same bin, two different kinds of savings.
Allergen shopping is the other real advantage, and it has nothing to do with virtue. It’s about a household where somebody reacts to something. Depth of selection means comparing three certified gluten-free breads instead of taking whatever the single option happens to be, and a manager can often special order a case of the thing you buy every week.
Then there’s staff knowledge, which is unevenly distributed and worth testing early. Ask a question you already know the answer to. Somebody who says “I’m not sure, let me read the label with you” is more useful than somebody with a confident answer for everything. In our experience, the second type costs shoppers more money.
Local suppliers round it out. Small bakeries, regional honey, area coffee roasters, a farm’s eggs, somebody making one hot sauce in tiny runs. That’s a perfectly good reason to shop a store like this, and it isn’t a nutrition reason. You’re buying proximity and variety, which is a legitimate thing to buy.
### Where is the premium not buying you more nutrition?
On plenty of shelves, and those deserve naming. A snack food is still a snack food when it’s made with cane sugar instead of corn syrup. Cookies, chips, granola bars, sweetened drinks and dessert products carry the same basic nutrition math in a health food store that they carry anywhere else, wearing better packaging.
Watch the halo effect on ordinary groceries too. Salt is salt. Sugar behaves like sugar in the body whether it arrived as honey, agave, maple or coconut sugar, and paying more for a less refined version buys flavor and trace minerals, not a different metabolic outcome. The same goes for “natural” sodas and juice, which are concentrated sugar in a nicer bottle.
Some price differences are real and defensible. Small production runs cost more per unit than industrial ones. A store with three registers can’t buy the way a chain with three hundred buys. Local delivery in small volume is expensive. None of that is a scam. It’s a supply chain premium rather than a nutrition premium, and marketing blurs those two on purpose.
Here’s the test we’d use. Turn the package over, read the Nutrition Facts panel and the ingredient list, then ask whether you’d still buy this exact food in a plain wrapper at that price. If the front of the box is doing the persuading, the back of the box is where you check its work.
### What does the “health food” label actually promise?
Less than most people assume, because “health food” is a marketing category rather than a regulated one. No agency defines what a health food store is, certifies what may be sold inside one, or screens the shelves before you get there. Certain individual terms do carry legal weight. The store category itself carries no standard at all.
Sort the words into two piles. Terms like “organic” sit behind a certification program with rules and inspections, and “gluten-free” has a defined threshold underneath it. Terms like “natural”, “clean”, “superfood”, “wellness” and “detox” are copy. They’re not lies exactly. They just don’t commit anybody to anything.
Organic deserves its own sentence, since it’s the term people most often mistranslate. It’s a standard about how food is produced, covering permitted inputs and farming practices. It isn’t a nutrition claim, and organic cane sugar is still sugar. Buy it for the production standard if that matters to you, which is a completely legitimate reason to buy it.
### What should you check before you buy?
Price is its own subject, and it is covered in detail in how to shop a health food store without overpaying. What follows here is the shorter question of what to look at on the label before it reaches the register.
Split your list before you leave the house. Staples you eat constantly and allergen-specific items are what these stores are good at. Everything else, the paper towels and the soda and the snack food, is usually a chore best done somewhere else. The shoppers who get burned are the ones doing a full weekly grocery run out of habit.
A short checklist that holds up in practice:
Weigh your own container first and note the tare, then fill the bulk bin only to the amount you’ll finish before it goes stale.
Buy spices, dried herbs and specialty flours from the bins rather than in jars and bags.
Check unit price against a supermarket for anything ordinary: paper goods, canned staples, standard produce.
Read the Nutrition Facts panel on anything marketed as a health product, especially bars and drinks.
Look for a third-party verification mark before you consider any supplement at all.
Ask a staff member what they’d skip. Then ask what sells out, and why.
Check the clearance shelf and the near-date refrigerated case, where local products often land.
If you take medication, ask a pharmacist before adding a supplement, not the person stocking the aisle.
One more habit worth building. Nuts, seeds, whole grain flours and oils go rancid faster than people expect, so bulk only saves money when the quantity matches how fast your household actually eats. A large bag you throw out in April was never a bargain. Buy for six weeks, not for the apocalypse.
Knowing your own neighborhood counts too: here is what the Delmar forensic treatment center does.

Wondering whether the juice counter down the block is worth the walk? Here is what a juice bar actually sells.
Across the metro, and they don’t look alike. Some are a single room with a supplement wall and one cooler. Some are a full grocery with a deli, a juice counter and a bulk aisle you could get lost in. Call ahead when you need something specific, because bin selection and allergen depth vary enormously from store to store.
Check what’s near you before you drive across the county. You can browse health food stores across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call and ask two questions: what’s in the bulk bins right now, and how deep the allergen-free selection actually goes. Those two answers decide whether the trip is worth it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are examples of bulk foods?
A.  Rolled oats, rice, dried beans and lentils, quinoa, pasta, flours, nuts and seeds, dried fruit, granola, coffee beans, loose tea, spices and dried herbs, plus a grinder for fresh nut butter in many stores. Some also run refill stations for oils, honey, syrup and cleaning products. You pick the amount, which is the whole point.
### Q. What are the healthiest foods to buy in bulk?
A.  Whole grain staples hold up best: oats, brown rice, barley, dried beans and lentils. Nuts and seeds are nutritious but turn rancid faster, so buy those in smaller amounts. Spices and dried herbs are the sleeper win, since you can take a spoonful instead of a jar. Store everything airtight, away from heat and light.
### Q. What are the top 5 health supplements?
A.  The categories stocked most heavily are multivitamins, vitamin D, omega-3 fish oil, probiotics and protein powder, with magnesium close behind. Popularity is not evidence that any of them benefits you specifically. Supplements aren’t reviewed for effectiveness before sale, so ask a clinician or pharmacist what, if anything, you actually need. This is general information, not medical advice.
### Q. What is the cheapest but healthiest food?
A.  Dried beans and lentils are hard to beat, alongside oats, brown rice, potatoes, cabbage, carrots, onions, eggs and frozen vegetables. They’re nutrient-dense, they store well, and bulk bins let you buy them in whatever quantity fits your kitchen. Frozen produce belongs on that list too, since it’s picked ripe and keeps for months.
### Q. What is the cheapest food to live on?
A.  Rice, dried beans, lentils, oats and potatoes are the classic answer, because they’re shelf-stable and filling. Living on them alone is a different question, though. A diet built only from cheap staples runs short on several nutrients over time, so add eggs, frozen vegetables and a source of fat wherever the budget allows.
### Q. Which superfoods are worth eating every day?
A.  “Superfood” is a marketing word with no regulatory definition, so treat any list of them as advertising. The foods that hold up daily are unglamorous: vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds. An expensive powder does not outperform a bag of frozen berries or a cup of lentils, and it costs far more per serving.
### Q. Is health food actually healthy?
A.  Sometimes, and the store category won’t tell you which. “Health food” isn’t a regulated term, so a cookie sold in one of these stores is still a cookie. Whole foods like produce, grains and legumes are exactly what they appear to be. For anything in a package, the Nutrition Facts panel and ingredient list are the only honest answer.
### Q. Can a health food store order something it doesn’t stock?
A.  Often yes, and it’s the most underused thing about small stores. Many will special order by the case from their distributor, sometimes at a case discount, particularly for an allergen-specific item you buy repeatedly. Ask a manager rather than a cashier, and expect it to take days rather than the same afternoon.

## St. Louis Hobby Shops: Four Nails, a Pine Block and a Race on Saturday
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-local-hobby-shop-actually-carries
Four wheels, four nails and a block of pine. That is the whole kit, and somehow it eats a week of evenings. Sawdust works its way into the carpet. Graphite turns a kid’s fingertips silver. Somebody holds the car at eye level, squints down the axles, and asks the question every parent hears the night before the race: is it heavy enough?
You can order a weight kit online and pray it lands by Saturday. Or you can drive to Gravois Road, where Schaefer’s Hobby Shop says on its own website that the Pinewood Derby “may only come once a year” but the shop is your year-round source for official Pinewood Derby materials and tools. In March. In August. Whenever the panic hits.
Schaefer’s has been family owned and operated since 1946. Third-generation owners Art and Sherri Schaefer run it now, and their homepage carries a line most stores would be scared to print: “Our specialty is our service.”
Here is the part worth texting to whoever in your house drives radio control cars. The shop’s service department works on Traxxas, Arrma, Axial and Losi, and it says flat out that it does not service other brands. Then it tells you to bring the car in for a quick check anyway, because “if we can’t help, maybe we can point you in the right direction.” A store that tells you up front what it won’t fix is a store you can believe about what it will.
The second thing worth texting costs people real money. If a new plane or drone is headed for the Buder Park Flying Field, the Greater Saint Louis Model Association says you need both a current AMA card and a Buder Park flying permit. The cheap card is the trap: the club says the “Park Flyer” AMA membership does not carry the minimum amount of insurance St. Louis County requires there, and flying without the right paperwork can get you stopped and fined under county park ordinances. Nobody prints that on the box. Somebody behind a hobby counter will tell you before the first flight.
Before you go, do two things. Call first, 314-729-7077, and ask whether they have your part, your gauge or your paint line on the shelf today. Then check the clock: the posted hours are 9am-6pm Monday through Saturday and 11am-5pm on Sunday, and Sunday is the day a servo always picks to die. Bring the broken piece, the empty bottle or the derby car itself. Holding the actual thing over the counter beats describing it every time.
That is what an independent hobby shop sells that a search box never quite does: a person who has already glued the thing you are about to glue. Here is what these places carry, and what the counter is worth.
### What can you buy in a hobby shop?
Push the door open and your nose gets there first: the sharp, sweet bite of model cement and enamel, a little cardboard, a little machine oil. Then the walls. Most independent shops are built around a handful of connected worlds, scale modeling, radio control, model railroading, rocketry, puzzles and tabletop games, and each one brings its own kits, its own consumables, and its own drawer of small parts that wear out and get replaced. Schaefer’s hobby department alone lists cars, planes, boats, military, Gundam and pop culture models, “thousands to choose from.”
For a family, the useful shelves are the ones nobody photographs. Metal Earth kits are cut from steel sheet with no glue or solder required, which is the right answer for the eight-year-old you do not trust with a tube of cement yet. Slot cars, the kind a lot of parents remember buzzing around a basement track, are still on Schaefer’s shelves for ages 6 and up. Its puzzles run from 24 to 1000 pieces, so the toddler and the grandparent both leave with a box.
### Radio control, and the parts that keep it running
You usually hear this aisle before you see it, a motor whining across the shop floor while somebody tests a car on the tile. Cars and trucks, planes and gliders, helicopters, drones and boats, sold both ready to run and as kits you finish yourself. The vehicles are the visible half of the aisle. The other half is the wall of parts behind them.
Batteries and chargers, servos, speed controllers, receivers and transmitters, propellers, tires, shock oil, bearings, spur gears, hinges, control horns, and screws in sizes you would not think existed. Radio control is a hobby where things break during normal use. A shop that stocks the small stuff is the difference between a repair on Sunday afternoon and a package that shows up Thursday.
### Plastic and die-cast model kits
Plastic kits are the backbone, and you can hear it in the aisle: the dry rattle of a box with two hundred parts still on the sprue. Aircraft, armor, cars, ships, figures and a steady supply of oddities nobody expected to want. The box tells you two things worth reading before you pay: the scale, where the bigger the second number the smaller the model, and the skill level, from snap-together to photo-etched brass that will test a grown adult’s patience.
Die-cast sits right beside them and drops into your palm cold and heavier than it looks. It comes built and painted, so it is a display piece rather than a project, and it is often the first model a kid owns before asking for one they get to build.
### Paint, glue and finishing supplies
Twist the cap off a jar of enamel and the whole table smells like it for an hour. This is the part online shopping handles worst, and the part a shop quietly lives on. Expect acrylics, enamels and lacquers, primers, thinners, washes and weathering powders, clear coats in gloss, satin and flat, decal setting solutions, filler, sanding sticks, masking tape, and brushes in the sizes that actually matter.
Adhesives get their own attention because they are not interchangeable. Liquid cement works by softening styrene so two pieces weld together. Cyanoacrylate grabs resin, metal and clear parts, though it will fog a canopy if you use it in the wrong place. White glue handles wood and scenery. Epoxy handles joints that have to take a load. Getting that wrong ruins an afternoon, which is exactly why the question gets asked at the counter every single day.
### Model railroading
Trains are the deepest aisle in a lot of shops, and the quietest, until somebody runs a locomotive on the test track and the whole room turns around. Schaefer’s, for one, stocks gauges N, HO, G and Lionel O. Scales run from tiny N through the common HO up to O and garden-sized G, and each one carries its own track, its own locomotives and rolling stock, and its own accessories that do not cross over.
Beyond the trains sits everything else a layout eats: flex track and turnouts, roadbed, wiring, digital command control decoders and sound chips, then the whole scenery side. Ground foam, static grass, plaster cloth, rock molds, trees, figures, vehicles, and structure kits that turn a plywood board into somewhere. Layout builders are repeat customers by nature, because a layout is never really finished.
### Rockets and other things that leave the ground
Model rocketry usually gets a rack of its own: kits from beginner cardboard-tube designs up through multi-stage builds, plus engines, igniters, recovery wadding, launch pads and controllers. Shops that carry it tend to know the local clubs and the fields people actually use, which matters more than which kit you pick.
Kites, hand-launch gliders and the occasional slot car track share this corner too, depending on what the owner is into. That is worth saying plainly. Independent shops reflect the person running them, and the inventory follows their obsessions.
### Puzzles, board games and trading cards
Jigsaw puzzles in the hundreds and the thousands of pieces, family games, strategy games that take a whole evening, miniatures and the paints for them, dice, card sleeves, deck boxes, playmats, sealed booster product and single cards. Some shops run open tables and a play space. Some keep it to a shelf near the register.
For families this is usually the way in. A puzzle or a game is a low-commitment purchase that gets people through the door, and the door is where all the rest of it is sitting.
### Tools, adhesives and the small hardware
Hobby knives and a lifetime supply of blades, sprue cutters, tweezers, pin vises, needle files, clamps, cutting mats, magnifiers and lamps, airbrushes and compressors, spray booths, paint racks. Then the raw material: styrene sheet and rod, brass tube, piano wire, balsa, plywood, thin aluminum.
Tools are the purchase people regret buying cheap. They are also the purchase where holding the thing in your hand before you pay changes your mind most often.
### What is considered a hobby shop?
A hobby shop is a store built on depth instead of breadth. A big box toy aisle carries what sells to everybody. A hobby shop carries the third paint color you need for one panel and the replacement gear for a model that came out six years ago. The stock is narrow on purpose and deep where it counts.
The category is wide enough to cover several different animals. Some shops are almost entirely trains. Some are game stores with tables in the back and tournaments on weeknights. Some are radio control specialists tied to a club track or a flying field. Plenty are general shops that carry all of it and lean toward whatever the neighborhood keeps buying.
What they share is the combination that defines the format. Kits and finished goods, the consumables those kits need, the spare parts that keep them running, and somebody on staff who has personally built the thing you are holding. Take away that last piece and you just have a shelf.
### What does the counter actually give you?
Judgment, mostly, and it is the one item in the building you cannot order. The person behind the counter has built some version of what you are attempting, watched other people fail at it, and knows which step is where beginners quit. That is a different service from a search result, and it tends to save more than it costs.
Start with the glue question, because it comes up constantly. Which adhesive melts which plastic, which one fogs clear parts, which one grabs metal, which one gives you enough working time to line up a long seam without panicking. Getting that answered in ten seconds at a counter is worth more than the tube itself.
Then there is test fitting. Bring a part in and somebody will check it against the thing it has to mate with, before you pay for it. Bring the broken piece and they can tell you whether the replacement is a straight swap or the beginning of a much larger project. Nobody does that from a listing photo.
The most valuable thing a good shop does is talk you out of purchases. A store that wants you back next month will say the kit is too complicated for a first build, that the cheap airbrush will disappoint you, that you already own something close enough. Ever had a screen tell you not to buy what is in your cart?
And then there is the Sunday afternoon problem. A servo dies, a gear strips, a bottle of thinner runs dry halfway through, and the gap between finishing today and finishing next week is whether somebody nearby has one hanging on a peg. That is the entire argument for local stock, and it never shows up in a price comparison.
### What are the benefits of shopping at a hobby store?
You get the thing today, you get it checked before you leave, and you get a person to go back to if it does not work. Those three are the practical core of it. Almost everything else people list as a benefit turns out to be a version of one of them.
Open box matters more here than in most retail. Plenty of shops will open a kit so you can see the parts, run a radio control car across the floor to prove it works, or show you the difference between two paint finishes on a scrap. Photographs flatten everything. Scale in particular is close to impossible to judge on a screen, and people routinely order a model that arrives half the size they pictured.
Repair and after-sale support is the quieter benefit. When something arrives faulty or fails early, a local shop handles the conversation, and often has the part in a drawer instead of a claim form. Some will do minor repairs outright, or at least diagnose the fault while you stand there. That is not the same experience as photographing a broken piece for a support ticket and waiting.
Buying one of something is underrated too. One screw, one servo horn, one bottle, one length of track. Online you buy the pack of fifty and pay to ship it. There is also a whole category of goods that travels badly: paints, solvents, aerosols and certain batteries often come with shipping restrictions, which is a large part of why the shelf exists at all.
### What happens on club nights and swap meets?
Most shops host something, and newcomers miss it entirely. Build nights, paint nights, open game tables, race days, running sessions on a club layout, occasional contests. The pattern varies from shop to shop, so the only reliable move is to walk in and ask what runs, when it runs, and whether anyone can join.
Swap meets and shop sales are where the used market lives. People sell off collections, downsize a layout, or clear out the kits they are honestly never going to build. For somebody starting out, a swap table is the cheapest way into a hobby that looks expensive from the outside, and it comes bundled with people who know what the thing is actually worth.
The social side is not a bonus feature. Hobbies with a local community survive. Hobbies you do alone in a basement tend to stall at the first genuinely hard step. Sitting at a table beside somebody who already solved your problem is a shortcut nothing online reproduces at the same speed.
Spent all afternoon browsing? Fallon’s Bar and Grill is a decent landing spot afterward.
### Is it cheaper to buy stuff online or in store?
Sometimes, on the sticker, for some items. That is the honest answer and it is also the incomplete one. A marketplace listing is one number. What you actually pay includes shipping, the wait, the friction on returns, the pack of fifty when you needed one piece, and the support you do not get when the thing turns up wrong.
Price-matching a listing at the counter misses what is being sold. The shop price includes somebody who answers the glue question, test fits your part, orders the item nobody else stocks, and is still there in three weeks when the gear strips. Asking a shop to match a marketplace price is asking them to sell you the object without the service, at a store that only exists because of the service.
There is risk inside the listing itself as well. Counterfeit and grey-market goods circulate in hobby categories, particularly batteries, electronics and sealed card product, and a photograph does not tell you which one is coming.
