## Your 2-Year-Old Pulls You to the Fridge Instead of Asking? In Missouri, You Can Make the Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/signs-your-toddler-needs-speech-therapy-in-st-louis
A small warm hand closes around your wrist and pulls, hard, toward the fridge. No word. Just the pull, and a look up at you, and then the whine when you guess wrong. In a St. Louis County kitchen or a South City flat, the next thing you hear is usually a grandparent or a friend across the table: “He’ll talk when he’s ready.” Sometimes that is even true. But you are the one hearing the quiet at bath time, and you are allowed to want an answer instead of a guess.
Here is what most families are never told. On Missouri’s official list of who can refer a child to First Steps, the state’s early intervention program for children under three, the first entry is not a doctor. It is parents. You do not need anyone’s permission to find out. Call 866-583-2392, extension 3, and you are connected to the office for your area, or enter the referral online. Federal rules say the evaluation is one of the steps that cannot be billed to you. At three and older, federal law lets a parent request the evaluation from the public school system directly.
In St. Louis County, which office answers depends on your district. Special School District runs early childhood special education for 14 of the county’s 22 public school districts. The other eight run their own programs, and SSD tells parents in those eight to start with their district’s Parents as Teachers staff. So the first question on the phone is a short one: does SSD serve my district, or do you? Ask it first. It can save you a week of being transferred.
Not sure it is worth a referral yet? There is a gentler door. Parents as Teachers, the home-visiting program whose national office is right here in St. Louis, is voluntary and free for all Missouri families through their local school district, and it offers annual developmental screenings. It is a trained second pair of eyes on your child, on your own living room floor, with no waiting room.
### What are the signs that a toddler needs speech therapy?
The signs most worth raising with your pediatrician are about communication as a whole, not clear pronunciation alone. Very few words compared with other children the same age. Little pointing or gesturing. Losing words your child once used. Real frustration when trying to be understood. Speech that people outside the family cannot follow. None of those is a verdict.
Now picture where those signs actually show up. In the grocery aisle, a two-year-old in the cart seat strains toward the bananas and grunts, and when you hold up the bunch and ask “banana?” she just keeps reaching. At daycare pickup, the other kids run to the door shouting a name; yours runs, grabs your knee and says nothing at all, and the teacher’s smile holds a half-second too long. Those are the moments to write down. What is not on the list matters too. Not being a chatterbox is not a sign. Being shy around strangers is not a sign. Being a second or third child with older siblings who answer every question first is not, by itself, a sign either, though it is the reason a lot of parents wait longer than they meant to. The signs that matter are about whether your child has a way to tell you things, and whether that way is growing month over month.
### Which signs are worth a phone call
At the front door, she hands you a shoe instead of saying the word. Write down moments like that for a week before the appointment, because specifics travel better than worry. How many different words does your child use, not counting the sounds you interpret generously? Does she point at things to show you, or only to get them? Does he bring you objects, take your hand, shake his head, wave? Can a neighbor understand him, or only you? Does she follow a simple instruction when you are not gesturing at the same time? Has anything gone backward, meaning words or skills that were there a few months ago and are not now?
That last one deserves its own sentence. If your child used words and no longer does, raise it promptly rather than saving it for the next well visit. Not because it means any particular thing, since it does not, but because it is the kind of change an evaluator wants to hear about while it is recent. The same goes for anything worrying you enough to search at nine at night. That feeling is information too, and pediatricians are used to hearing it.
### Understanding and talking are two different questions
Speech-language pathologists separate what a child understands from what a child can produce, and parents almost never do. A toddler who follows directions, finds the shoes, points to the dog in the book and clearly gets the joke is showing you a great deal, even with very few words. A toddler who seems to miss instructions is showing you something different. Both are worth describing to your pediatrician, and neither is something you can sort out yourself from a chart. That sorting is exactly what an evaluation is for.
### Who do you call first in Missouri?
It depends on the birthday. Under three, the call goes to Missouri First Steps. From three to five, your local school district’s early childhood special education program is responsible for finding and evaluating children. Tell your pediatrician what you are doing, since the medical side still matters, but the referral itself is yours to make.
### Under three: Missouri First Steps
First Steps is Missouri’s early intervention system for infants and toddlers, and it runs through the state rather than through your school. You contact the program, describe your concerns, and go through an intake and evaluation process that determines whether your child is eligible for services and what those services would look like. For a child without a diagnosed condition, eligibility turns on whether the child is functioning at half the developmental level expected for their age in an area such as communication. That is a high bar, which is why a “not eligible” letter at two is not the last word. Ask for the current criteria in writing when you call.
### Three and older: your school district
At three, responsibility shifts to the public school district where you live, and it does not matter whether your child attends any school yet. Districts across the metro run early childhood special education, and each one has somebody whose job is intake for exactly this. Call the district office and ask who handles early childhood special education evaluations. If your child is already in a preschool, those teachers usually have useful observations to hand over, and how to choose a preschool in St. Louis covers what to look for in that setting.
### Where your pediatrician fits
Your pediatrician is still the front door for everything medical, and a good one will want to check things on their side while an evaluation runs in parallel. If you have felt brushed off more than once, take that seriously as information about the fit. How to choose a pediatrician in St. Louis goes through what to look for and how to switch without drama. Private therapy billed to insurance is a third route, and the questions to ask about that are in the FAQ below.
### What actually happens in an evaluation?
Less testing than parents expect, and a great deal more playing. An evaluation usually combines a long conversation with you about your child’s history and daily communication, direct observation of your child at play, and some structured tasks. The evaluator is watching how your child communicates overall, not only whether the words come out clearly.
You are part of it, not a spectator in the hallway. Expect questions about pregnancy and birth history, ear infections, feeding, family history, which languages are spoken at home, and what a normal hour looks like in your house. Bring the notes you made. “He has about ten words and three of them are for the dog” is far more useful than “he does not talk much,” and it saves everybody a round of guessing.
Then they play. Bubbles, blocks, picture cards, a toy that requires asking for help to work. The evaluator is looking at receptive language, meaning what your child understands, and expressive language, meaning what your child can produce, along with how sounds are formed and how your child uses gestures, eye contact and turn-taking to get things done. A toddler who refuses to perform on cue is completely normal, and a decent evaluator plans for it.
You come out with a report and a recommendation, and the report is worth reading slowly with somebody who can translate it. If services are recommended through the school route, a plan document and a meeting come with it, and you are a member of that team rather than an audience for it. Special education in St. Louis: what parents need to know walks through how those plans and meetings work, which is a genuine relief to read before your first one.
Long therapy weeks need a break. Here is how to get cheap movie tickets.
### What can you do at home while you wait?
Waiting lists are real, and the weeks between a phone call and a first appointment are not wasted time. Most of what helps at home is not a drill or an app. It is a change in how you talk during the hours you already spend together: in the car, at the sink, in the bath, at the bottom of the stairs.
Narrate, then stop talking. Say what you are doing in short, plain phrases, then leave a gap long enough to feel awkward. Adults fill silence quickly, and a toddler who is working hard to produce a word needs more room than we naturally give. Count to five in your head before you jump in. That pause does more than most of what gets sold to parents in this situation.
Offer choices instead of yes-or-no questions. “Milk or water?” invites a word. “Do you want milk?” invites a nod. Repeat back what your child meant with one word added, so “ball” becomes “big ball.” Respond to gestures rather than ignoring them, because pointing and reaching are communication, and shutting them down teaches a child that trying does not work. Read together, and let your child pick the book and skip half the pages.
And one caution, because it comes up constantly in parent groups. Do not withhold a cup or a toy to force a word out. It turns something your child needs into a negotiation. In our experience families who try it end up with more meltdowns and less talking, not more. If a specific prompting technique is right for your child, the person who evaluates them can teach it to you properly, with the reasoning attached.
### How do you choose a speech-language pathologist?
Shortlist two or three and interview them the way you would interview a doctor. Credentials are the floor, not the decision. What separates one speech-language pathologist from another for a two-year-old is experience with this age group, whether they coach parents or only work with the child, and whether the schedule on offer is one your family can actually keep.
Start by saying plainly what you want. Say how old your child is and what you are seeing at home. Say whether you need somebody who can work around a preschool day, a night shift, or a drive in from Troy. Say whether you want to be in the room. Say what you hope will be different in six months, even if you are not sure it is realistic. Then listen carefully to what comes back.
### What to ask
Six questions, asked the same way at each place. How much of your caseload is toddlers this age? Will I be in the session, and will you teach me what to do between sessions? How do you decide what to work on first? How will I know it is working, and when would you tell me it is not? How often would you want to see us, and for roughly how long? And what happens if we turn out not to be the right fit for you?
### What to listen for
The gaps, more than the answers themselves. One person describes how they coach parents and tells you what the first month tends to look like. Another says every child is different and moves on to scheduling. A third promises a specific result on a specific timeline, which is the answer that should worry you most, because nobody can promise that for a toddler. Those are three different years. The distance between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.
Ask about the practical side too. Where the office is, whether teletherapy is offered, what happens when your child is sick, how cancellations are handled, and whether you are billed for missed visits. Families who quit therapy usually quit over logistics rather than over the therapy, and a drive that looked fine in September looks very different in January.
### What if you are told to wait and see?
You are allowed to ask for an evaluation anyway. Wait-and-see is sometimes sound advice and sometimes just a habit, and from the outside the two look identical. A parent can make the referral without a doctor, and a First Steps evaluation cannot be billed to you, so the price of checking is a few phone calls and some paperwork.
Some children who are slow to talk do catch up on their own. That is true, and any honest page has to say it. What nobody can tell you is which children those are, in advance, from the outside, at the age when knowing would actually be useful. That is the entire reason evaluations exist. An evaluation that finds nothing is not a wasted morning. It is an answer, and you get to stop carrying the question around.
If you disagree with a result, ask what your options are and ask in writing. Both routes have processes for questions, re-referral and review, and the people who run intake will tell you what those are if you ask directly. Keep a folder. Dates, names, what was said, what you were told to do next. Parents who keep a folder get better outcomes from systems, and that holds well beyond this one.
People are asking
### What are the common symptoms of developmental language disorder (DLD)?
It can look like stubbornness, and the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) says it isn’t: younger children with DLD may be late to put words together into sentences, struggle to learn new words and make conversation, make frequent grammatical errors, and have trouble following directions “because they do not fully understand the words spoken to them.” DLD often starts as late talking that never fully catches up, it affects about 1 in 14 children in kindergarten, and 50 to 70 percent of children with DLD have at least one family member with the disorder. Speaking more than one language at home does not cause it. If your child hears “go get your shoes” and drifts to the window instead, write that down, add any parent or sibling who was slow to talk, and hand both to the evaluator.
### For speech-language pathologists in the metro
If you are on the provider side of this, notice that every parent described above starts with a fear and a search box, not with your name. They are trying to work out whether this is worth a phone call at all. The pages that answer that plainly, in words a worried parent can absorb at nine at night, are the ones that get the call the next morning.
Publish the specifics. The ages you serve, whether you coach parents inside the session, which insurance you take, where you are and whether teletherapy is an option, and roughly how a first appointment goes. Say what you do not do, as well. A family in Jennings or St. Ann choosing between two options will pick the one that already answered three of their questions before anybody picked up the phone.
Make the First Steps or district call first, then interview two or three therapists. You can browse speech therapists across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then say plainly what you are seeing at home, what schedule your family can keep, and whether you want to be coached in the session.
If you’re the speech-language pathologist a worried parent is searching for at nine at night, make sure they can find you before they find a waiting list. Put your practice on St Louis Near Me Directory and let new customers see your ages, insurance and openings before they ever call.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should a toddler get speech therapy?
A.  There is no single age that switches it on, and any page handing you one is guessing about your child. The practical trigger is concern: yours, your pediatrician’s, or a preschool teacher’s. Because a parent can refer directly to either Missouri route, the threshold for asking is low. Raise it at your next well visit, and call the program yourself if the worry is not going away on its own.
### Q. Is 3 too late for speech therapy?
A.  No. Three is not a cutoff, it is the age where the route changes hands. Before three, Missouri First Steps handles early intervention for the state. At three, your local public school district’s early childhood special education program becomes the place to call, whether or not your child attends school anywhere yet. Plenty of children start therapy at three, four or later. The only thing waiting costs you is time nobody can give back.
### Q. What is done in speech therapy for toddlers?
A.  It looks like play, and that is deliberate. A therapist follows the child’s interest into an activity, then builds language into it: modeling words, waiting for attempts, adding gestures or pictures, shaping sounds, and rewarding any attempt to communicate rather than only perfect words. Good toddler therapy also coaches the adult, because an hour a week matters far less than what happens across the other hundred and sixty-seven. Expect homework for you, not worksheets for your child.
### Q. Can a child outgrow speech delay?
A.  Some children who talk late do catch up without any help, which is why wait-and-see survives as advice. The problem is that nobody can identify those children in advance, and a family living it has no way to tell the difference from the inside. An evaluation is how the question gets answered instead of guessed. If the answer turns out to be that nothing is needed, you have spent a morning and gained back every evening after it.
### Q. What qualifies a kid for speech therapy?
A.  Eligibility is decided by the program or the insurer, not by a checklist online, and the criteria differ between Missouri First Steps, school district early childhood special education, and private therapy billed to insurance. Each one uses its own evaluation and its own standards, and those standards get revised. Ask the specific program for its current criteria when you call. A child can be turned down by one route and be a good fit for another.
### Q. Do insurances cover speech therapy?
A.  Coverage varies a great deal by plan, so the answer has to come from your own policy. Call the number on the card and ask precise questions: is speech therapy covered, is a referral or prior authorization required, is there a visit limit per year, what is the copay, and is this provider in network. Ask the clinic to verify benefits too, then compare the two answers. For MO HealthNet, how to apply for Medicaid in Missouri covers the application itself.
### Q. At what age do late talkers talk?
A.  There is no reliable single age, and the ranges you find online disagree with each other because they come from different sources measuring different things. Some children who are slow to start pick up speed quickly. Others need support to get going at all. That variation is exactly why an average is useless for planning your own child’s year. Use an evaluation to answer it for your child rather than a chart written about other people’s.
### Q. Why is my 2.5 year old not talking but understands?
A.  That gap between understanding and speaking is a familiar pattern to speech-language pathologists, and it is one of the most common reasons families get referred for an evaluation. It can have several different explanations, and sorting between them is precisely the work a qualified evaluator does. It is not something to settle from a search result or a relative’s story. Call Missouri First Steps, or your district if your child has turned three, and describe exactly what you just described here.

## Taxidermy Costs in St. Louis: $600, $700 or $980?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-taxidermy-costs-in-st-louis
$600 in Jefferson County. $700 in Troy. $980 and up in Dorsey, Illinois, about 40 minutes from St. Louis. Those are the prices three working taxidermists print on their own websites for the same job, a whitetail shoulder mount. Same deer, same wall, and at least $380 between the $600 price and the $980 starting price. That gap is worth three phone calls before the head leaves your garage.
Before you call any of them, put your hand on the neck of the deer. Cool hide and hair that stays put when you tug it means you have a cape worth paying for. Hair that lifts out in a tuft between your fingers is slip, and no price list on earth fixes it.
Then there is the clock. Missouri wants every deer Telechecked by 10 p.m. on the day of harvest, and a deer taken in a CWD Management Zone county has to be checked before it leaves the county where it fell. Do it from the tailgate with cold thumbs on the phone and the dome light on, then pencil the confirmation number onto the permit before you forget it. The shop can wait an hour. The deadline cannot. And if your opening-weekend buck ends up at an MDC sampling station, like last season’s St. Louis County stations at Powder Valley, Rockwoods and Bellefontaine, say the words “shoulder mount” before anyone picks up a knife. MDC staff will not cut through the cape of a deer headed to a taxidermist.
Now the money, straight. One trade-press breakdown of a plain whitetail shoulder mount came to $487.50 before tax: $130 in materials, $60 in overhead, $200 for eight hours of labor at $25 an hour, and $97.50 in profit. The writer’s advice was to expect a minimum of $500 for a quality mount. A quote far below that is coming out of the form, the tannery or the hours, and those are the parts you will be looking at for years: the eyes, the seams, the set of the ears.
### What is the average cost to mount a deer head?
Around St. Louis, plan on $600 to $980 and up for a whitetail shoulder mount from a shop that publishes its prices, with about $500 as the honest floor. Head south into Jefferson County and Sitting Fox Taxidermy lists $600 with a $100 deposit. Go north to Troy and Midwest Taxidermy of Missouri lists $700, $775 with an oak or walnut panel, $800 for a wall pedestal and $825 and up for a table or floor pedestal. Cross the Mississippi and Log Home Taxidermy in Dorsey starts at $980, adds fees for alterations, larger deer or special forms, and takes a non-refundable half deposit at drop-off. Same whitetail in the cooler on all three drives.
A skull, or European, mount is the cheap seat: $100 in Jefferson County, plaque not included, and $150 with no panel in Troy. You feel the difference the moment you pick one up. A European mount is bone, light and clean in your hands. A shoulder mount is a tanned cape with weight to it, glass eyes, and a seam you should not be able to find with your fingertips.
### The three numbers to ask for
When the bag hits the counter, ask for three numbers, not one. The price of the mount as you described it. The deposit due at drop-off. And what happens to the price if the cape turns out to be damaged and needs repair or replacement. That third question is the one almost everybody skips, and it is the one that changes bills.
The deposit tells you a lot. One metro shop asks $100 down on a $600 mount. Another wants half, non-refundable, at the counter. Neither is wrong, but you should know which kind of shop you are standing in before you hand over the head. Ask when the balance is due, and what their policy is on a finished mount nobody picks up.
### Telecheck first, cape second: the Missouri rules a St. Louis hunter needs
Notch the permit the moment the deer is down, in the MO Hunting app or by tearing a small notch in the month and day on a paper permit. Then Telecheck it by 10 p.m. on the day of harvest, before you process it, or before you leave the state, whichever comes first. In a CWD Management Zone county, check it before it leaves the county. Use the app, mdc.mo.gov, or call 800-314-6828 between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., and write the confirmation number on the permit.
That confirmation number is what you carry to the shop. Once a deer is checked, anyone can process, store or transport it, as long as it is labeled with your full name, address, the date taken and the Telecheck confirmation number. Write those four things in black marker on a strip of duct tape across the bag, pressed down hard so it does not peel off in the freezer. The taxidermist is going to ask anyway: Missouri requires licensed taxidermists to keep records of every animal they receive, with the full name and address of the person who brought it in, and to hold those records for three years.
Opening weekend has one more step in some counties. A deer taken in a designated county of the CWD Management Zone during opening weekend of the November portion must go, or its head must go, to a CWD sampling station on the day of harvest. In the most recent season, MDC named St. Louis County a designated county, with stations at Bellefontaine Conservation Area, Rockwoods Reservation and Powder Valley Nature Center. The list can change, so check MDC before opening day.
That is where the cape-saving line from the top of this page matters. Tell the staff the buck is going to a taxidermist for a shoulder mount; MDC says its staff will not cut through the cape, and it is fine to remove the cape before you get there.
Shot one across the river in Illinois? A head with the cape attached and no more than six inches of neck may be brought into Missouri only if it is delivered to a licensed taxidermist within 48 hours of entering the state. Call the shop before you cross the bridge, not after. Whatever you do not keep or hand to the taxidermist goes in trash bound for a sanitary landfill, or stays on the property where the deer was harvested.
People are asking
### How much meat do you get off a 100-pound deer?
About 48 pounds of boneless venison, if that 100 pounds is field-dressed weight: a University of Wyoming meat-lab bulletin found that about 48 percent of a field-dressed carcass is boneless meat, and that weight still included the head and hide. A deer that weighs 100 pounds whole gives you noticeably less, because in the bulletin’s own conversion table it takes a 142-pound whole deer to dress out at 100 pounds and yield 48 pounds of boneless lean. Where the bullet landed shows up on the freezer shelf, too, since deer shot once in the hind leg or shoulder had yields 1.9 or 3.1 percentage points lower. The study weighed mule deer, not Missouri whitetails, so treat it as a ballpark, and get the head and cape bagged and labeled for the taxidermist before the processor ever sees the rest.
### What actually moves the price of a mount?
Six things, roughly in order of how much they matter. The species. The mount type. The pose. The form. The condition of the cape. And anything the shop has to do that sits outside its normal run of work. Understand those six and you can read a price list instead of guessing at it.
### Mount type is the biggest lever
This is the largest single choice, and it is entirely yours. A European or skull mount is the simplest thing a shop does: the skull cleaned, whitened and set on a plaque or a stand, with no cape involved at all. A shoulder mount is the classic wall piece, head, neck and shoulders built on a form. A wall pedestal turns the animal outward so it reads more like sculpture. A pedestal mount stands on a base, on a table or on the floor, and gets viewed from every side. A full body or life-size mount is the whole animal, and it is a different order of work entirely.
Those are not small differences in labor. A skull mount and a life-size mount are not the same job with a different sticker on it. They are related crafts sharing a building. If your budget is the real constraint, mount type is where you have the most control, and a good shop will tell you that plainly rather than talk you upward.
### The pose, the form, and the eyes
Within a shoulder mount there are still choices to make. Straight ahead, turned left or right, a sneak pose with the head low, upright and alert. Some poses need a different form and more work at the seam, and the shop will tell you which ones. The form itself matters too, because shops buy forms in different grades, and a better one fits a specific cape with less altering.
Ask what form and what tanning they use, and why. It is a fair question and taxidermists like answering it, because the form is the thing underneath everything and it is exactly where a careless shop cuts corners. The eyes, the ear liners, the nose and the finish work around the eye are where a mount either looks like the animal or just looks like a mount.
### The cape, which is the part you control
The cape is the hide from the head, neck and shoulders, and its condition on arrival is the single biggest variable you personally influence. A cape cut too short cannot be stretched back into existence. A cape that slipped, meaning the hair came loose because it got warm and stayed warm, may not be usable at all. A bullet hole or a fight tear can often be repaired, but repair is labor, and labor gets billed.
If the cape cannot be saved, the shop can usually buy a replacement cape in, and that cost gets passed along to you. Nothing about that is a scam. It is a purchase the shop makes on your behalf so you still get a mount. But it is precisely why the question “what happens to the price if the cape is damaged” belongs in your first phone call, not in a conversation eight months later.
### Rush work, storage and the extras
Two more lines that catch people out. Some shops charge for rush work if you want something moved up the queue, and most have a policy on storage if a finished piece sits past a certain point. Habitat bases, driftwood, custom panels and engraved plates are extras. None of it is hidden, and none of it is in the headline number either.
### Why does a mount take the better part of a year?
Because a hide has to be tanned before it can be mounted, and because a taxidermist takes in most of a year’s work inside a few weeks. Both halves of that sentence matter. The first is chemistry, and it cannot be hurried. The second is arithmetic, and it is the reason a busy November drop-off is not first in line.
Walk the sequence. The cape comes in and is fleshed, turned and prepared. It goes to a tannery, or through the shop’s own tanning process, and that step takes as long as it takes. It comes back and waits for bench time. The mount is built on the form, sewn, set and groomed. Then it dries, which is its own stretch of weeks. Then the finish work: eyes, nose, ear butts, paint. Only after all of that does it get a hanger and a phone call.
Now add the season on top. Missouri deer season fills a shop’s year in a matter of weeks. Everybody drops off inside the same narrow window, and the work comes back out in the order the bench allows. A shop quoting you a long turnaround is usually telling you the truth about its workload. A shop promising something suspiciously fast in December deserves a follow-up question.
Ask for their current turnaround before you leave the counter, and ask how they will contact you when it is ready. Do not carry an old number around in your head because a friend quoted it three seasons ago. Turnarounds move with workload, tannery and staffing. The people who handle the wait best treat it like any other seasonal booking around here, where the good dates go early, which is the same instinct behind how to book a campsite near St. Louis.
### What do you do with the animal before the shop opens?
Keep it cool, keep it out of the sun, and get it to a taxidermist or into a freezer as fast as you reasonably can. Hair slips when a hide gets warm and stays warm, and a slipped cape is the most common avoidable loss in this entire process. Nearly everything else can be worked around. That one frequently cannot.
### Cape it long, or do not cape it at all
If you are not confident caping an animal, do not learn on the one you want mounted. Bring the whole head and cape to the shop, or cape it long, taking far more hide than you think you need from well behind the shoulders. A taxidermist can always trim. Nobody can add. The most common damage a shop sees all season is a cape cut short by somebody trying to be tidy.
Do not cut the throat. Do not split up the front of the neck. If you are field dressing an animal you intend to have mounted, the cuts you make in the first ten minutes decide what is possible eight months later. When in doubt, stop, take a photo, and call somebody.
### Freezing, bagging, and the things not to do
If the shop is closed, or you are two hours from home, the freezer is your friend. Get the cape and skull cool first, then double-bag it, press the air out, and freeze it. Label the bag with your name and the date. A chest freezer beats a kitchen freezer for a whole head, and a frozen cape holds far better than a cool one sitting in a garage.
Do not salt it, and do not treat it with anything, unless your taxidermist has specifically told you to. Salting is a real step in a real process and it is easy to do badly. Do not leave a head in a truck bed in the sun while you finish out the day. And do not seal a warm cape into a plastic bag and walk away, because you have just built an incubator.
Here is the call worth making, and it costs you nothing. Ring a shop before the season opens and ask what they want you to do. Every taxidermist has preferences, and every one of them would rather spend four minutes on the phone in September than open a bag in November and deliver bad news. Getting the rest of your season squared away early is the same instinct that makes a list of outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis worth writing down before opening weekend.
Another long wait worth planning: how to get into nursing school in St. Louis.
### How do you interview a taxidermist before you hand anything over?
Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then go and look at their finished work in person. Photographs flatten everything. Standing in front of a real mount tells you in ten seconds what a gallery page never will: whether the eyes look alive, whether the ear butts sit right, whether the seam disappears, whether the whole thing carries the animal’s posture or just its parts.
Then say plainly what you want. The mount type, the pose, where it is going to hang, what the animal means to you, and roughly what you are able to spend. A taxidermist who hears all of that can tell you what is realistic and what is not, and will often suggest something better than what you walked in asking for. One who cannot get past a number is telling you something too.
### What to ask
Six questions, asked the same way at every shop. What is your current turnaround, and how will you contact me? What is the deposit, and when is the balance due? What form and what tanning do you use? What happens to the price if the cape turns out to be damaged? Can I see finished work in person rather than photos? And what do you want me to do with the animal between the field and your door?
### What to listen for
Listen to the gaps rather than the numbers. One shop answers all six plainly, hands you a price list, and shows you a mount in progress on the bench. Another answers two and goes vague on the rest. A third quotes fast and cheap and does not want to discuss the tannery. Those are not three versions of the same shop. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.
In our experience, the shops people are happiest with a year later are rarely the cheapest ones. They are the ones that were straight about the wait. A long honest turnaround, stated up front, is a far better sign than a short one offered casually. Ask, too, how they handle it if you are not happy with the finished mount. That conversation is much easier before any money changes hands.
### What about a fish, a bird, or a pet?
Different work, different shops, different conversations. Not every taxidermist handles every category, and plenty specialize on purpose. A shop that builds beautiful whitetails may not touch a fish, and a bird specialist may carry a waiting list of their own. Ask before you drive across the county with a cooler in the back.
### Fish
Fish split into two paths. A skin mount uses the actual fish. A reproduction is built from a blank and painted to match your fish, which means the fish itself can go back in the water or into a pan. For a reproduction the shop typically needs good measurements, length and girth, plus clear photographs taken quickly before the color fades. If you fish the water around the metro and think a wall fish is in your future, learn the measurement routine now and keep a tape in the boat alongside your notes on the best fishing spots in St. Louis.
### Birds and small game
Birds are delicate and the handling advice changes again. Smooth the feathers down, tuck the head under a wing, slide the bird into a smooth bag or a stocking so nothing bends or breaks, and freeze it. Do not gut it. Do not cram it into a game pouch for the rest of the afternoon and hope for the best.
### Pets
Pet preservation is a real service, and emotionally it is a very different thing from game work. Shops differ on whether they take it at all, and some decline it for perfectly good reasons of their own. If it is something you are considering, have that conversation directly and in advance, rather than making an assumption during a bad week.
Telecheck it, label it, then call two or three shops. You can compare taxidermists across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then go look at finished work in person and ask each one for a written price, the deposit, the current turnaround, and what changes if the cape is damaged. Bring the bag with your name, address, date taken and confirmation number already on it.
If you’re the taxidermist with a bench full of capes every November, hunters are searching for a shop they can trust with the best animal of their lives. List your shop on St Louis Near Me Directory and put your price list and turnaround where those customers are already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to get a deer shoulder mounted?
A.  Around St. Louis, published prices for a whitetail shoulder mount run $600 in Jefferson County, $700 in Troy and $980 and up in Dorsey, Illinois, and one cost breakdown puts a quality mount at a minimum of $500. Pose, panel or pedestal, and the condition of the cape add to it. Call two or three shops, get the price and the deposit in writing, and ask what changes if the cape needs repair or has to be replaced.
### Q. How long does it take a taxidermist to shoulder mount a deer?
A.  Longer than most first-timers expect, and the shop will give you their own current number at drop-off. The hide has to be tanned before anything can be mounted, the mount has to dry before finish work can start, and shops take in most of a year’s work during the few weeks of deer season. Ask for their current turnaround, ask how they will contact you, and do not rely on a figure a friend quoted three seasons ago.
### Q. Can you freeze a deer head before taxidermy?
A.  Yes, and freezing is usually the right move if you cannot reach a shop quickly. Cool the cape and skull first, double-bag it, press the air out, and freeze it, ideally in a chest freezer rather than a kitchen one. Label the bag. Do not salt it or treat it with anything unless your taxidermist told you to, and call the shop to confirm how long they are comfortable with it sitting frozen.
### Q. How long will a taxidermy animal last?
A.  A well-built mount kept in reasonable conditions can last for decades, which is why inherited mounts turn up in families all the time. What shortens that life is environment rather than age: direct sunlight fading the hair, damp, heat, smoke, and insect damage. Keep it out of a sunny window and out of an unconditioned shed or attic, dust it gently, and have a taxidermist look at anything that is fading, shedding or coming loose.
### Q. Do the ears on a deer mount look better forward or back?
A.  That is taste rather than a rule, and it is worth settling before the shop starts instead of after. Ears forward reads alert and attentive, the way a deer looks when it has caught something. Ears back, or one back, reads tense and aggressive, which suits a rut pose. Ask to see finished examples of both in the shop, decide which matches the animal and the room it is going in, and put your choice in writing.
### Q. What is the most popular pose for a deer mount?
A.  The standard shoulder mount with a slight turn is the one most people picture, because it hangs well on a wall and shows the rack cleanly from the front. Beyond that, sneak poses with the head low, upright alert poses, and wall pedestals that turn the animal outward all have their followings. Popularity should not decide it for you. Look at where the mount will hang, how the light falls, and what you will see from your chair.
### Q. Can you wipe down deer mounts with WD-40?
A.  You will hear this passed around, and it is worth asking your own taxidermist before you try it on a mount you care about. Shops differ on what they recommend for cleaning and conditioning, and the wrong product can attract dust, dull the hair, or affect the finish work around the eyes and nose. For routine care, gentle dusting in the direction of the hair is the safe default. For anything beyond that, ask the person who built it.
### Q. Are taxidermied animals killed?
A.  Not by the taxidermist. A taxidermist works on animals that are brought to them, and for game work that means legally harvested animals brought in by hunters and anglers under state regulations. Shops also work on animals found dead, on livestock and pets, and on legally acquired specimens, with the paperwork rules varying by species. If you are curious about a particular mount, ask where it came from. Reputable shops are used to the question and answer it plainly.

## Missing Every Ball Is Fine: Start Tennis in St. Louis for $35

Pock. A ball comes off the strings, skids on the hard court and rattles into the chain-link fence, and somebody on the next court calls out “sorry!” without looking up. If you have ever sat in your car outside a public court after work, still in your work shoes, watching two strangers rally and wondering whether anyone would mind you out there missing most of the balls, here is the good news. Everybody on those courts missed most of the balls once, and in St. Louis you can find out for free whether the game is for you.
Noon on a weekday at Tower Grove Park, and the free public hours at the Henry Shaw Memorial Tennis Courts have just begun. First come, first served. Across town in Forest Park, the Dwight Davis Tennis Center carries the name of the St. Louisan who donated the Davis Cup. Dwight Davis served as City Parks Commissioner from 1912 to 1915, and he is remembered for pulling up the “Keep Off the Grass” signs that filled the city’s parks. His line: “If we can’t have the grass and the people in our parks, let’s sacrifice the grass.” The center named for him has 18 lighted courts, it is completely open to the public, and all courts need to be reserved online; the pro shop is (314) 361-0177. Under the lights on a summer night you hear the hum of the bulbs, the squeak of shoes and a dozen conversations about whose ball that was. This city decided more than a century ago that tennis belongs to whoever shows up. That includes you, in borrowed shoes, on your first night.
### How much do beginner tennis lessons cost?
Around here, the cheapest honest number is a group clinic. The St. Louis Tennis Collective lists its Adult Beginner clinic at $35 a clinic, available at Dwight Davis in Forest Park and at Ackfeld Park, and takes $50 off when you buy 10 clinics together. Do the math and ten beginner clinics come to $300, or $30 apiece. Add free afternoons at Tower Grove and your whole first summer can cost one racquet, one can of balls and that $300. Each clinic is a coach, a full basket of yellow balls and a handful of other nervous adults who are exactly as new as you are. One warning while it is still warm out: if you want to keep playing past October, the indoor plan gets made in early fall, not in January.
A private hour costs more, because you are buying one coach’s undivided attention. Winter changes the math too. ### Where to play free, and how the courts actually work
Public courts are the whole cheap-start strategy: a hard court still holding the afternoon heat through your soles, a water fountain that runs a little too cold, a bench with somebody’s forgotten ball can on it. Tower Grove’s free hours cover weekday afternoons and every weekend afternoon into the evening, and the City of St. Louis and the county’s municipal parks departments maintain more courts of their own. Each department publishes its current hours, fees and any reservation rules, and a two-minute phone call settles the rest. Do not trust a court count or an hours listing from any blog, including this one, without checking the owner’s page first.
The etiquette is short. Wait behind the fence until a point ends; never walk behind a live rally. If people are waiting, an hour is a fair limit, and you offer the court up. Send stray balls back with an easy bounce, not a rocket. That is close to the whole code. The players who look like they might judge you are usually the ones who end up feeding you a few balls, because everybody on that court remembers their own first night.
### The pickleball question you will run into
Plenty of public courts now carry both sets of lines, and Tower Grove itself added eight pickleball courts beside its tennis courts. A court marked for both is a court you may be sharing, and on a mild Saturday you may hear the hollow clack of paddles before you see a free net. It is not a grievance, just a planning fact: go earlier, go on a weekday, or keep a second court in mind.
### What do you genuinely need to buy on day one?
Four things. A racquet, a can of balls, court shoes and water. That is the entire list. The second racquet, the bag, the dampener, the apparel, the custom stringing and everything else marketed at beginners can wait, possibly forever. You can walk onto a public court for the first time for the price of one racquet and one tube of balls.
### The racquet
Buy it in person if you can, because holding one for ten seconds tells you more than an hour of reading specifications. Beginners are generally better served by a lighter frame with a larger head, which is more forgiving of the off-center contact you will be making constantly for the first month. Buy it pre-strung and do not think about string again until it breaks. If you want to handle a few before you commit, the shops in where to buy sporting goods in St. Louis are the place to start, and some will let you demo a frame before you pay for one.
### The shoes
This is the one place not to improvise. Running shoes are built to push you forward and they are usually built tall and soft to do it. Tennis is a lateral game, and a lateral game in a running shoe is how ankles roll. Court shoes sit lower, sit wider and are reinforced along the sides for exactly that reason. For the reader who came to tennis because running started hurting, this is the single most important purchase on the list, and it is not the one most beginners make first.
### What can wait
Everything else. A bag is a convenience, not equipment. A backup racquet matters when you are breaking strings, which you are not. Ball machines, radar apps, weighted trainers and specialist apparel are all purchases for a person who has already decided they are staying. Give it eight weeks. Buy the shoes, then buy one block of lessons, not a season. ### How do beginners find people to play with?
The hardest part of adult tennis is not technique. It is finding somebody at roughly your level who is free when you are free. Group lessons and clinics solve that almost by accident, because everybody in the session is a beginner and half of them are also quietly looking for a hitting partner. Leagues and ladders solve it formally, and they are organized by level.
That last point is the one that changes people’s minds. Adult league play is graded, not open. The USTA sanctions adult league play nationally and uses a rating system so that players compete against others of similar standard, which means a first-year adult is not being fed to a former college player. Locally, league and ladder play is organized through clubs, parks departments and sanctioned team play, and the specific divisions, seasons and fees vary by organizer. Ask whoever runs the one near you rather than trusting a schedule you found online.
### Say you are new, out loud, on the first call
Beginners tend to hide it, and hiding it is what produces the bad experience. Tell the organizer you have never played competitively and ask which level fits. A good one will tell you honestly, and sometimes the honest answer is that you are three months of clinics away from being ready, which is useful information rather than a rejection.
### Start with a clinic, then collect phone numbers
In our experience the smoothest route into the metro’s tennis population is six or eight weeks of a beginner group, followed by asking three people from that group for their numbers on the last night. That is it. That is the whole social strategy. Drop-in sessions and round robins do the same job faster if you can find one that genuinely welcomes new players, and it is fair to ask directly whether theirs does.
### What happens to tennis in St. Louis between November and March?
It moves indoors, and that is where the budget changes shape. Outdoor public courts are free and weather-dependent. Indoor courts are a paid, booked, limited resource with an entire region’s winter demand pressing on them. Most adults who start in June meet this problem in October, and almost nobody warned them while the weather was still good.
Indoor court time is generally sold by the hour and reserved in advance, and a large share of it gets committed early through season-long bookings and standing groups. The practical consequence is a deadline. If you intend to keep playing through the winter, the decision belongs in September or October, not in January when you finally notice the outdoor courts have gone quiet. You can also buy a smaller block of indoor hours and treat it as maintenance rather than progress. ### How do you interview a coach or a program before you pay for a block?

The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal, not the hourly rate.
### Five questions worth asking every time
Is there a beginner-only group, or would I be joining a mixed one. How many players per coach. What does the full block cost and what is inside that number. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to start tennis as a beginner?
A.  Get a lightweight racquet with a larger head, a can of balls and a pair of court shoes, then find a public court and hit against a wall or a friend for an hour. Do that twice before you spend anything else. Then sign up for a beginner group session, which handles technique and the social problem at the same time. Most adults who quit early quit because they were alone, not because they were bad.
### Q. Can I self teach myself tennis?
A.  Partly, and further than people assume. A wall, a bucket of balls and video will get your forehand, your backhand and your movement to a usable place. The serve is where self-teaching usually stalls, because it is the most technical motion in the sport and the easiest to groove wrong. A handful of early lessons is cheaper than a year spent unlearning a habit. Self-teach the volume, buy instruction for the parts that need eyes on you.
### Q. Can beginners join a tennis league?
A.  Yes, and this is the most common misconception keeping new adults off the court. League play is graded by level rather than open to all comers, so beginners are placed with other beginners rather than dropped in against experienced players. Call the organizer, say honestly that you have never played competitively, and ask which level fits you. If the answer is that you need a season of clinics first, that is useful guidance rather than a refusal.
### Q. What tennis leagues are available in St. Louis?
A.  Adult league and ladder play around this metro is organized through clubs, municipal parks departments and USTA-sanctioned team play, and the USTA rating system is what keeps divisions matched by ability. Specific divisions, seasons, team structures and fees vary by organizer and get rebuilt every year, so any list you find online goes stale quickly. Contact the organizers running play near you directly, and ask which division suits a first-year adult.
### Q. Where can I find tennis camps in St. Louis?
A.  Camps and multi-day clinics run through clubs, academies and parks department recreation programming, with most of the volume landing in summer and school breaks. Adult camps exist too, though they are less advertised than junior ones. When you call, ask two things: whether the camp is genuinely built for beginners, and how many players there are per coach. A camp with a heavy ratio is a fun week rather than a teaching week, which is fine if you know that going in.
### Q. Where can I find tennis lessons in St. Louis, MO?
A.  There are three routes. Municipal parks departments and the City of St. Louis Parks system sometimes carry adult beginner instruction in their seasonal recreation programming, which is often the lowest-cost option. Private clubs and academies run the widest range of formats. Independent coaches teach at both public and private courts. Call two or three across those categories rather than one, because the formats and prices are not comparable until you have heard them side by side.
### Q. Is tennis a cheap hobby?
A.  Cheap to start, variable to continue. A racquet, balls, court shoes and a free public court is close to the least expensive way an adult can take up a sport in this region. The costs arrive later and are optional in different degrees: lessons, restringing, replacing shoes that wear out faster than you expect, league fees, and indoor court time from November through March. Outdoor summer tennis is nearly free. Winter tennis is not.
### Q. What sport is replacing tennis?
A.  Pickleball is the honest answer, at least in terms of court space. It has grown very quickly, it is easier to learn in an afternoon, and in a lot of metros, this one included, it has taken over shared courts that used to be tennis only. For a new tennis player hunting a free public court, that is a real friction rather than a talking point. A court marked with both sets of lines is a court you may be sharing, so plan around evenings and weekends.

## How to Choose Art Classes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-art-classes-in-st-louis
A mother in Brentwood is standing at the kitchen counter on a Sunday night, turning over a cereal box her nine-year-old has covered edge to edge in ballpoint drawings. Dragons, mostly. She has been finding these for a year now, on receipts, on a church bulletin, on the inside cover of a library book she had to apologize for. She has typed “art classes near me” into her phone four times this month and closed the tab every time, because every result looks the same and none of them tell her which one is right for a kid who draws dragons.
The same week, other people around the metro are opening those same results for completely different reasons. A sixteen-year-old in St. Charles who needs a portfolio for a college application eighteen months out and has no idea what a portfolio is supposed to contain. A retired man in Webster Groves who has wanted to paint since he was twelve and has finally run out of excuses. A homeschooling parent in Ellisville trying to find something that counts as art for two kids at once, on a Tuesday, without driving forty minutes each way. A woman in Maplewood who was told by a teacher at nine that she could not draw, believed it for twenty-five years, and would like to find out whether it was true.
They are all asking versions of the same four questions. What kind of class is this. Is my kid, or am I, the right age for it. What will it cost in total and what am I actually buying. And how do I tell a real class from an hour of following instructions. Here is how the formats differ, what age genuinely changes and what it does not, the shape of a typical bill and where it surprises people, what free access looks like around here, and how to interview a studio before you hand over a term of tuition.
### What is the best age to start art classes?
There is no single best age, and anybody who gives you one is describing the class they happen to sell. Almost any age works. What actually changes with age is the format that fits: open-ended messy exploration for the youngest, real skills instruction in the elementary years, technique and critique for teenagers, and a genuine fresh start at any point for adults.
That reframe matters, because the wrong format at the right age is what kills interest. A four-year-old in a class built around copying a demonstration will quietly conclude that she is bad at art. A ten-year-old who wants to learn how shadows work will be bored senseless by another hour of free painting. Both children were, technically, the right age. Neither one was in the right room.
### Before kindergarten, the point is the mess
Two-, three- and four-year-olds are not learning to draw. They are learning what materials do. Paint runs. Clay holds a thumbprint. A fat crayon on rough paper feels nothing like a marker on glossy card. Programs for this age should be short, sensory, tolerant of chaos, and completely uninterested in whether the finished thing resembles anything. If a class for this age sends home twelve identical butterflies, that is a craft session wearing a class label.
Practical filters: is a caregiver expected in the room, how long is the session, and does the studio actually mean it when it says smocks are provided. Thirty to forty-five minutes is plenty. Ask what happens if your child spends the entire first session watching from your lap. A good teacher for this age will tell you that is normal, expected, and not worth worrying about.
### Five to ten, the first real skills window
This is where instruction starts to bite. Children in these years can hold attention for an hour, follow a sequence across several weeks, and genuinely absorb technique: how to see proportion, how to mix a color instead of squeezing it straight from the tube, how to build a drawing up rather than outlining and filling. They are also old enough to get frustrated, which is the part parents tend to underestimate.
The frustration is the work. A child who wants her horse to look like a horse and cannot make it happen is standing exactly where learning lives, and a good teacher sits inside that moment instead of taking the pencil and fixing it. So ask any studio how they handle a kid who wants to quit in week three. The answer tells you nearly everything about the teaching.
### Eleven and up, when they start judging themselves
Somewhere around middle school most young artists develop a critical eye faster than they develop the hands to satisfy it. They can now see that their work does not look the way they wanted it to. An enormous number of kids stop drawing at precisely this point, permanently, and the ones who keep going usually had somebody tell them that the gap is normal and teachable.
Classes for this age should look different. Longer sessions. Specific mediums instead of general art. Actual instruction in perspective, value, anatomy and color theory. Critique, handled kindly but honestly. And if a teenager is aiming at a portfolio for an art school or a scholarship, that is a distinct track. Ask for it by name, because portfolio prep is not the same thing as Saturday morning drawing with a mixed-age group.
### Adults, including the ones who were told they could not draw
You can start at any age, and the adult beginner classes around this metro are full of people who did. The obstacle is almost never ability. It is a leftover verdict from a childhood teacher, plus an understandable reluctance to be visibly bad at something in front of strangers in your forties, or your sixties, or your eighties.
In our experience the adults who stick with it pick a narrow subject rather than a broad one. Beginning watercolor. Introduction to the wheel. Figure drawing fundamentals. A broad general art class leaves a beginner guessing what they are supposed to be doing, while a narrow one hands you a single skill and a visible finish line. If you want the whole household in something at once, the best kids’ music, art and dance classes in St. Louis covers how these programs sit alongside each other.
### What kinds of art classes actually exist around the metro?
More formats than a search result reveals, and the format matters more than the studio name. The main ones are weekly term classes, drop-in sessions, open studio time, week-long camps and intensives, private one-on-one instruction, homeschool day classes, teen portfolio tracks, adult evening classes, and single-session social painting events, which are a night out rather than a course.
### Weekly term classes
The default, and usually the right choice. A group meets at the same time for six, eight, ten or twelve weeks and the material builds. You pay for the block. The advantage is sequence, since week four assumes week three happened. The disadvantage is the same thing: two missed weeks out of eight is a quarter of the course, which is why the make-up policy is worth settling before you enroll rather than after.
### Drop-in and open studio
Drop-in sessions charge per visit and teach something self-contained each time, which suits an unpredictable schedule and a child who is not sure yet. Open studio is a different animal. The space, the equipment and often a monitor are available, but nobody is teaching. Open studio is excellent for a person who already knows what they are doing and close to a waste of money for a true beginner.
### Camps and intensives
School breaks and summer. Half-day or full-day, usually a week at a time, and the total hours can exceed an entire term of weekly classes. A camp is a good way to find out whether a kid actually likes this before committing to a year, and an equally good way to burn a child out on a medium if the week is badly run. Ask what the days look like hour by hour.
### Private instruction
The most expensive per hour and occasionally the cheapest overall, because one hour of undivided attention can move a serious student further than six hours in a busy room. Worth considering for a teenager on a portfolio deadline, for a child whose needs make a group setting hard, and for adults who would rather not be watched. The same trade-off runs through how to choose music lessons in the St. Louis metro, and the reasoning transfers almost exactly.
### The civic option people forget
Public library branches across the city and both counties run programming for children, teens and adults, and a good deal of it involves making things. County and municipal parks and recreation departments run classes out of community centers. Community colleges run continuing education courses open to adults with no intention of earning a degree. Museums with free general admission run family days and studio activities. None of this is permanent, so check the current season on the organization’s own site, and register the day it opens, because seats go fast.
### What separates a real art class from a craft session?
One test does most of the work. In a craft session everybody leaves with the same object. In an art class the outcomes differ, because the students made decisions instead of following steps. Both have their place. A craft session is a fine birthday party and a poor art education, and the price tag rarely tells you which one you are buying.
Look for four things. The teacher demonstrates a technique rather than distributing a template. The instruction includes vocabulary, value, composition, proportion, negative space, so students can talk about their own work. The materials are real rather than the cheapest available. And the sequence across the term goes somewhere, so a parent watching in the last week can see what the first week was for.
There is a blunter test too. Look at the student work on the wall from the previous session. If twenty pieces are nearly identical, an adult made most of the decisions. If twenty pieces are recognizably about the same problem and yet plainly made by twenty different people, you are looking at teaching. That wall is the most honest marketing material any studio has, and most of them do not realize it.
### How does the money work, and where does it go wrong?
Prices vary too much across the metro to quote honestly, and any page handing you a single number is guessing. What you can learn instead is the shape of the bill, because the shape stays consistent even when the numbers do not. Almost every unpleasant surprise comes from the same handful of lines, and every one of them can be settled before you pay.
Start with the billing unit. A term class is quoted as a block, and the per-session cost is usually lower than drop-in. Drop-in is quoted per visit and costs more per hour in exchange for flexibility. Private instruction is quoted per hour and sits well above both. Camps are quoted per week, sometimes with an extra charge for early drop-off and late pickup. Compare like with like, or you will decide one studio is expensive when it is simply selling a different product.
### The lines that catch people
Materials first. “Materials included” can mean everything, or it can mean everything except the good paper. A lower tuition attached to a two-page supply list of specific paints, brushes and a sketchbook can easily cost more overall than a higher tuition with nothing to buy. Ask for the supply list before you enroll, not after, and ask whether anything on it carries over to next term.
Then the add-ons. Some organizations charge a one-time registration fee or an annual membership on top of tuition. Ceramics has its own economics, since clay, glaze and kiln firing are consumed rather than borrowed, and a wheel class may bill those separately by the bag or by the piece. Figure drawing sessions sometimes carry a model fee. None of that is unreasonable. It is only a problem when you discover it in week two.
Now the discounts, which almost nobody advertises loudly. Sibling rates. Member rates, if the organization has a membership. Multi-class or full-year pricing. Early registration pricing. Scholarship or sliding-scale seats, which more places offer than say so publicly, and which usually require nothing more embarrassing than an email asking whether any are available.
### The two policies that decide whether it hurts
Ask about make-ups and refunds in the same breath, and get both answers in writing. What happens if we miss two weeks to a flu: is there a make-up session, a credit, or nothing? And if my child hates it after the second class, is any part of the term refundable, transferable to a sibling, or credited toward a later session? A studio with clear, humane answers here has thought about families. A studio that gets vague is telling you something.
Judging any course uses one test. See how to judge an AI course.
### What if the budget is zero right now?
Then you still have real options, and they are better than most people expect. Free and near-free art access in this metro arrives in five categories: public library programming, family and studio days at museums with free general admission, parks and recreation offerings through community centers, school and community organization programs, and the enormous amount of free instruction available online.
Libraries are the most underused of those. Branches across the city and both counties run children’s, teen and adult programming, and making things is a regular part of it. Some branches lend equipment and supplies as well. None of it is permanent, so the current calendar lives on the library system’s own site, and the popular sessions fill within days of registration opening. Set a reminder rather than checking casually.
Museums with free general admission run family activities and studio programs of their own. Parks and recreation departments run low-cost classes out of community centers, often at a fraction of private studio pricing. Community colleges run continuing education courses that cost less than most private terms and welcome adults with no degree ambitions at all. In every case the same rule applies: check what is actually running this season on the organization’s own site, because a program that existed two years ago may not exist now.
The online tier is genuinely vast. Free structured drawing curricula, thousands of hours of technique instruction, and communities that will critique your work if you ask them to. What free online instruction cannot give you is the thing people quietly need most: a scheduled time, a room, and somebody who notices whether you showed up. That is a large part of what you pay a studio for, and it helps to name it so you know whether you need it.
### How do you interview a studio before you pay for a term?
Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, and treat it as a conversation rather than a price check. Say plainly what you want out of it. Then compare that against what each place is actually prepared to provide. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal, not the tuition.
Being specific is the whole trick. “Do you have classes for eight-year-olds” gets you a schedule. “My eight-year-old draws constantly, gets frustrated when it does not come out right, and I want him taught how to actually see proportion” gets you a real answer, and occasionally an honest one saying their program is not built for that. That is a useful answer too, and it just saved you a term.
### What to ask
Six questions, asked the same way at each place. Who teaches this class, and what is their background? How many students, and is there an assistant? What will my child, or I, be able to do at the end of the term that we cannot do now? What is included and what do I buy? What are the make-up and refund policies? And may I watch a class, or sit in on one, before I enroll?
That last one carries more weight than the other five combined. A studio confident in its teaching will find a way to let you observe, or offer a trial session, or at minimum walk you through student work from the last term. Hesitation is not automatically bad, since some rooms genuinely do not work with a parent in them and any place serving children has policies about visitors. But how they handle the question is data.
### What to listen for
Listen for whether the teacher describes children or describes activities. “This term we do watercolor, then collage, then clay” is a supply list. “Most kids arrive outlining and filling, so the first three weeks are about getting them to build shapes up instead” is teaching. One studio talks about outcomes, another talks about projects, a third talks about how cute the finished pieces look on the fridge. Those are three different years.
And pay attention to what a room sounds like. Working quiet, a teacher moving between tables, questions surfacing here and there. That is a class. The same interviewing habit works for other family decisions, and how to choose a preschool in St. Louis runs the same frame.

They were trying to work out which format fits, what it costs in total, and whether the teaching is real. The pages that answer those three things plainly are the ones that get the phone call.
If the kitchen appeals more than the easel, here is what to expect at a St. Louis cooking class.

Term length, start dates, and what happens when a family misses two weeks. What is included and what sits on the supply list. Sibling, member and sliding-scale options if you have them. And photographs of student work from an ordinary week rather than the single best piece of the year, because parents can read the difference and they trust the ordinary week far more.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to choose art classes for kids?
A.  Start with format rather than studio. Match the class to your child’s age and temperament: messy exploration for preschoolers, skills instruction for elementary kids, specific mediums and critique for teenagers. Then shortlist two or three places worth interviewing, tell them plainly what you want your child to get out of it, and ask to watch a class. Check class size, who teaches, what is included, and the make-up and refund policies before you pay for a term.
### Q. Are art classes expensive?
A.  They range enormously, from free library and parks programming to private instruction costing several times a group rate, so the honest answer is that it depends entirely on format. Term classes are usually the best value per hour. Drop-in costs more per session but risks less. The expensive surprises are rarely the tuition itself. They are supply lists, registration or membership fees, ceramics firing costs, and terms with no make-up policy when life gets in the way.
### Q. How much does an art course cost?
A.  There is no single number worth quoting, since prices shift by format, length and organization. Learn the shape of the bill instead. Ask whether the quote is per term, per session or per hour, how many sessions it covers, whether materials are included or on a supply list, whether a registration or membership fee applies, and whether sibling, member or sliding-scale rates exist. Get every one of those answers in writing before you pay anything.
### Q. Are there free art classes?
A.  Yes, in several categories, though nothing stays on the calendar permanently. Public library branches run programming for children, teens and adults that regularly involves making things. Museums with free general admission run family and studio days. Parks and recreation departments and community centers offer low-cost or free sessions. Schools and community organizations run their own. Because these rotate by season, check the current calendar on the organization’s own site and register early, since seats go fast.
### Q. Where can I learn art for free?
A.  Two places, locally and online. Locally, start with your library system’s event calendar, your municipal or county parks and recreation listings, and the free-admission museums in the metro. Online, there are full structured drawing curricula, thousands of hours of technique instruction, and communities that will critique your work if you ask. What free instruction cannot supply is a scheduled time and somebody who notices you showed up, which is often the real reason people pay.
### Q. What are some basic art lessons for kids?
A.  The foundations are the same everywhere: drawing what you see rather than what you know, breaking objects into simple shapes, understanding light and shadow as value, mixing color instead of using it straight from the tube, and composing a page. Add hands-on work with real materials, clay, watercolor, printmaking, collage, so children learn what each one does. A good beginner class also teaches vocabulary, so a child can talk about their own work.
### Q. Is art school actually worth it?
A.  It depends on the goal, and it deserves the same scrutiny as any degree. Formal art school can be worth it for someone aiming at a field where the portfolio, the critique culture and the network genuinely matter. It is a poor fit for someone who mainly wants to get better at drawing, which classes and steady practice deliver far more cheaply. Weigh the total cost, the debt, and the work it actually leads to before enrolling.
### Q. How to learn art for beginners?
A.  Pick one narrow thing and repeat it. Beginning watercolor, basic drawing, or an introduction to the wheel beats a broad general class, because a narrow subject gives you a single skill and a visible finish line. Draw more often than you take classes. Expect your eye to outrun your hand for a while, which is normal and is exactly what instruction fixes. And choose something close to home, because the class that gets finished is usually the nearest one.
