You can browse vegan food on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three places worth calling, and give each one the same short summary: one vegan in the party, no dairy or eggs, and here is when we want to come in. What comes back, and how confidently, tells you plenty before you spend an evening on it.
If you’re the one doing this for a living, list yours.
### For St. Louis restaurants and food shops
Think about Ruthie in that Southampton dining room, happily eating a risotto she would not have ordered if she had known. She was not looking for a special menu. She was looking for one sentence that nobody had written down.
So write it down. Mark dishes vegan, not just vegetarian, because the two words are doing completely different jobs and only one of them answers the question. Say whether your stock is vegetable or chicken. Say what the fryer is shared with, plainly, even when the answer is “everything.” Note which dishes can be made vegan on request and what actually changes: no butter finish, no cheese, oil instead of cream. That last line is the one diners screenshot and send to their friends.
Then put it on the online menu, not in the server’s head. Menus in a diner’s hand at 6pm are the ones that get read, and a server on a busy Friday cannot be the single point of truth for an ingredient question. Shops can do the same with a short page on which sections carry plant milks, tofu, tempeh, nutritional yeast and vegan baking staples, and whether the deli or bakery counter has anything without dairy or egg. A little of this in writing turns a maybe into a table, and it costs nothing but an afternoon.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can vegans eat fish?
A.  No. Fish and shellfish are animals, so they are not vegan, and neither are fish sauce, oyster sauce or the anchovy in Worcestershire and classic Caesar dressing. People who eat fish but no other meat are usually described as pescatarian, which is a different thing entirely. This matters at a restaurant, because a “seafood only” dish is sometimes offered as the vegetarian substitute when it is neither.
### Q. Do vegans eat potatoes?
A.  Yes. Potatoes are a plant, and they are one of the cheapest and most useful staples in a vegan kitchen: baked, roasted, mashed, in soup, in curry, in tacos. The catch is what happens to them. Mashed potatoes are usually made with butter and milk, restaurant fries often share a fryer with breaded meat, and some potato salads are bound with egg-based mayonnaise.
### Q. Can vegans eat ice cream?
A.  Not dairy ice cream, which is made from milk and cream and often eggs. Vegan versions do exist and are widely sold, usually built on oat, coconut, almond, soy or cashew bases, and plenty of sorbets are dairy-free by nature. Check the label rather than the front of the package, since “non-dairy” is a marketing phrase and some products still contain whey or casein.
### Q. Are bananas vegan?
A.  Yes. Bananas are fruit, so they are vegan, and they double as a useful egg replacement in baking when you mash about half a banana per egg. The question comes up because a few producers have used a coating to slow ripening, and some coatings are not animal-free. For everyday purposes a banana is a banana, and it is not a thing most vegans think twice about.
### Q. What are some cheap vegan meals?
A.  Rice and beans with hot sauce. Lentil soup. Pasta with garlic, olive oil and whatever green is in the crisper. Chickpea curry with frozen spinach. Fried rice with frozen mixed vegetables and tofu. Baked potatoes topped with beans. Oatmeal with peanut butter and banana. Chili made from two cans of beans and one of tomatoes. All of them scale up cheaply and reheat well.
### Q. What is the average cost of a vegan diet?
A.  There is no honest average to hand you, because the range is enormous and prices move constantly. A cart of dried beans, lentils, rice, oats, potatoes and frozen vegetables is among the cheapest ways anyone eats. A cart of meat substitutes, specialty cheeses and frozen entrees costs more than the meat version of the same week. Track your own receipts for a month; that number is the only one that applies to you.
### Q. Is a vegetarian dish automatically vegan?
A.  No, and this is the single most common mix-up. Vegetarian only rules out meat, so a vegetarian dish can still contain butter, cream, cheese, milk, eggs or honey, and it very often does. Menus label things vegetarian far more often than vegan. Treat the vegetarian section as the shortlist to ask about, not as the answer.
### Q. How do you ask whether a dish can be made vegan?
A.  Ask “can this be made vegan?” rather than “is this vegan?” The first sends someone to the kitchen; the second invites a guess. Then name the three usual culprits: butter or cream, including at the finish, chicken or beef stock, and a shared fryer. Ask at ordering rather than afterward, and call ahead in the mid-afternoon lull if the place is new to you.

## The $57.20 Morning: What After-School Care Costs at the Y
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-after-school-programs-cost-in-st-louis
$219.70. That is what five mornings of before-school care cost a month on the Gateway Region YMCA’s Y Club fee table when you buy them by themselves. Buy them together with the afternoons and those same five mornings cost $57.20.
Think about what those mornings are. The kitchen still dark. A travel mug going cold on the counter, one shoe missing, a lunchbox zipper that sticks, and you due at work before the school doors even open. Then the other end of the day: the last bell, a kid on the sidewalk with a backpack slapping the backs of his knees, scanning every car for yours while you are still two hours from clocking out.
Here is the math, straight off the Y Club table for schools like J.L. Mudd Elementary and Hawthorn Elementary. Five afternoons a week cost a Y member $329.55 a month. Five mornings plus five afternoons cost $386.75. Subtract, and the whole morning shift, with care from 6:30 AM until the school day starts, adds $57.20 a month.
If you are paying for afternoons and patching the mornings together with a neighbor’s favor and a lot of hoping, ask about the bundle before you ask about anything else.
And there is a line on that same Y page that people scroll right past. The Y says it accepts state childcare reimbursements. Missouri’s Child Care Subsidy program is open to a family with a child from birth to age 13 who needs care to work, search for work, train or attend school, with income at or below 150% of the federal poverty level. What a family then pays is a sliding fee, which the state says is set by household size and income and can run from $1 per year to $5 per day. The state’s help line for the application is 573-415-8605. You can also click Apply for Assistance on the state’s subsidy page to apply online, and ask the program at the same time whether it takes the subsidy, because the help only works where it is accepted. One phone call, made sitting in the car before you walk in the house, can change what that monthly number means for you.
### How much do after school activities cost?
There is no single price for the whole metro, and anyone who hands you one is guessing. The Y figures above are one program’s published rates for licensed staff, a snack and homework help until 6:00 PM. Use them as a yardstick, not a promise. Programs run out of a school building or a public recreation center are often cheaper because the room is already paid for. Private academies with real instruction built into the afternoon usually cost more.
Membership moves the number too. Non-members pay $390 a month for the same five afternoons and $487.50 for mornings plus afternoons. Registration is $75 per child or $150 per family. The gap on afternoons alone is $60.45 a month, so price a family membership at your branch before you decide the Y card in your wallet is a luxury.
Inside the city limits, start with the recreation centers. The City’s Commissioner of Recreation calls them places for “positive, healthy activities, throughout the year at no charge.” Then call before you drive, because the map has moved. In August 2024 the City was pointing after-school families to computer lab and homework help at the Wohl Recreation Center, soccer training at the Cherokee Recreation Center and Girls Talk at the Gamble Recreation Center. A City notice dated August 20, 2026 says Wohl would close beginning Monday, August 24, for approximately six months, and that Cherokee was closed for repairs with no reopening date. Each is getting a new roof, updated locker rooms and a new gym floor, which will be lovely in spring and is no help this October. The City is steering Wohl regulars to the Tandy Recreation Center and Cherokee regulars to the Marquette Recreation Center. Ask whichever center is nearest your school what runs this season, what it costs and how late the doors stay open.
Activity programs price on a different clock. Dance, martial arts, music and club sports tend to bill by the class, the month or the season, and most last an hour or two. Two lessons a week is not child care, and a patchwork of lessons leaves most of the week uncovered. To see what exists near your school before you start calling, try Blueprint4, a program of the Clark-Fox Family Foundation. It runs a free search site for after-school programs across the St. Louis region, and its help line is 314-899-5248.
### Where the real monthly total comes from
Tuition is one line on the form. The total is everything the school calendar does to it. The Y says its Y Club runs on the school calendar, offering care on school days, early releases and many no-school days. “Many” is the word to circle with a pen. Ask any program, the Y included, which closure days are covered, which cost extra, and which leave you on your own. The snow day is the one that bites. You find out from a text before sunrise, the street outside is quiet and white, and the plan you thought you had is gone.
The hours matter just as much. Five full days is the most expensive version of the arrangement, and sometimes it is the only one that works. But if a grandparent really does have two afternoons, the Y’s own table shows how the price steps down by the day: three afternoons a week is $197.73 for a member. Ask every program what a partial week costs before you assume it does not exist.
Then ask the questions that live on page three. Is there a late-pickup charge, and when does the clock start? What happens to the bill in a week your child is home with a fever? Is there a sibling rate? Most programs bill for the spot, not the attendance, and the rain on the windshield on the highway home does not stop the meter.
### Is paid after-school care worth it, or is a St. Louis rec center enough?
It depends on what you are buying. If you are buying coverage, the value is plain: it is the difference between finishing your shift and leaving early again. A snack, a table where somebody checks whether the math sheet got done, and an hour of running around a gym when it is sleeting outside cover most of what a family in that gap needs.
The weaker case is the one parents talk themselves into: premium rates for enrichment a child does not care about. A kid who sulks through coding club is not going to become a programmer because you paid for coding club, and you will both know it by the third week. Ask your kid which room they would actually walk into before you ask the front desk for a price.
There is a middle road a lot of families land on. Cheap, reliable coverage most afternoons, and one activity the kid picked, once a week. The coverage keeps your job. The one activity is the thing they talk about in the back seat on the drive home, mouth full of goldfish crackers, telling you who fell off the climbing wall. That pairing often costs less than a premium program, and it buys the child something they chose instead of something you chose for them.
One more Missouri detail changes the math for a family sitting just over the line. The state’s subsidy has steps above 150% of poverty, called Transitional Levels. Level 1, for 151 to 185%, sets the parent’s sliding fee at $7.50 for a full day of care, $3.75 for a half day and $2.50 for a part day. Level 2, for 186 to 215%, is $8.75, $4.40 and $2.90. Those fees took effect for eligibility decisions and re-certifications in November 2025. Whether a family that already earns over 150% can start at one of those levels is a question I could not confirm from the state’s page, so put it to the call center at 573-415-8605 before you decide you earn too much.
### Nanny or daycare in Missouri: which costs less, and who checks on them?
For one child, group care is usually cheaper per hour, because one adult’s time is split across a room of kids. A nanny is paid by the household, not by the child, so the comparison shifts as the family grows. Somewhere around two or three kids the two start to meet, and where they cross depends on the rates you are quoted.
The rest of the comparison is not money. A sitter at home means no drive, no rushed curb, a kid already in socks on the couch when you walk in. A program means a room full of other children, and someone else covering when a staff member calls out. Before you hire anyone to work in your home, talk to an accountant about household-employer rules, so the hourly rate is not the only cost you planned for.
Missouri adds one more difference. Under state law, anyone caring for six or fewer children at one address, with no more than three under the age of two, is not required to be licensed and does not have to tell the state he or she is providing child care. A nanny in your kitchen falls under that, so the reference check is yours to do. A licensed center is different: the state’s Show Me Child Care Provider Search lists all licensed, license-exempt and subsidy-contracted providers in Missouri, so you can look a center up before you ever tour it.

### What are kid-friendly activities in St. Louis after school?
Two of the biggest cost nothing to walk into. Admission to the Saint Louis Zoo is free, and at the Saint Louis Science Center entry is always free, with a mix of free and paid attractions inside. For a kid who is tired of the same four walls, that is an afternoon of sea lions or rockets for the price of parking.
### Interview two programs at closing time
Shortlist two or three and talk to each one the way you would talk to a new doctor. Say exactly what you need: these days, these hours, a kid who melts down at transitions, a pickup that sometimes runs late. Then listen to what each program is actually prepared to deliver. The gap between your list and their answer is the signal.
Go see the room in the last hour, not the first. A room right after the bell is easy. A room near closing, when half the kids have gone home and the staff have been on their feet for hours, tells you who these people are. Listen for the noise level. Smell the room, too: old popcorn and wet sneakers are normal, but a room that smells like nobody opened a window since lunch is telling you something about attention. Watch whether the adults are down on the floor with the kids or leaning on the door with their phones.
Driving across the river for pickup? Gas prices differ by state line.
Ask the money questions early. Does the program accept state child care assistance? Is there a scholarship fund or a sliding scale? Is there a sibling discount? Ask for the full fee list in writing, including closure days and late pickup. That is a normal request, and the programs worth your money hand it over without a sigh.
Still doing the curb math at your desk? Browse after-school programs on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two near your school, and ask each one for its full monthly fee sheet before you tour.
If you run the after-school room, the dance studio or the tutoring table down the block, the parents in this article are searching for you right now. A listing that shows your hours and your rates is how they become your customers - put your program in front of them.
### For St. Louis after-school programs and community centers
Think about the parent at the kitchen table with the enrollment packet, the overhead light buzzing, doing subtraction they should not have to do. They are not hunting for a discount. They want one page that tells them the truth about a month.
So publish it. Put your rates online, even as a range. Then put the rest of the total beside them: registration, sibling rates, what a half-day and a closure week cost, when late pickup starts and what it costs. Say which schools you pick up from, whether you are licensed, and whether you accept state child care assistance. A short video of the real room at the end of the day will do more for enrollment than any brochure.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does afterschool childcare cost?
A.  It depends on the program, the days and the hours. One published example: a Gateway Region YMCA branch lists five afternoons a week of Y Club at $329.55 a month for members and $390 for non-members, plus a $75 registration fee per child. School-run and recreation-center options are often cheaper, and private academies usually cost more, so ask each program for its current fee sheet.
### Q. How much does aftercare usually cost?
A.  Aftercare in a school building is often the cheaper end of the market because the room is already there. Before you compare, ask what the monthly price covers: regular school days only, or early releases and closure days too. Add registration, late pickup and any closure-day charges to the tuition, then compare totals instead of headlines.
### Q. Are after school programs worth it?
A.  When supervision is what keeps you at work, it usually pays for itself. Enrichment is worth it when your child actually wants to be in the room. Paying premium rates for an activity a kid is indifferent to is the version that rarely pays off.
### Q. What’s cheaper, a nanny or daycare?
A.  For one child, group care is usually cheaper per hour. A nanny is paid per household, so the gap narrows as you add children. Price both with your real hours, and ask an accountant about household-employer rules before you hire someone to work in your home.
### Q. What questions should I ask before enrolling?
A.  Ask what an afternoon looks like hour by hour, how many adults are in the room, and how they reach you when something goes wrong. Ask for the full fee list in writing, including closure days and late pickup, and whether they accept state child care assistance. Then visit near closing time.

## How to Tell If Amish Furniture Is Real
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-amish-furniture-is-real-st-louis
The tag said “Amish crafted” and that was enough for Marcy. She and Ted had been shopping for a dining table for most of a year, the kind of table their kids would argue over someday, and this one had the heft. Heavy top, thick square legs, a warm brown finish that looked like it had been rubbed in by hand. Ted did the thing his father taught him and pulled the leaf drawer all the way out. The sides were pale, smooth and perfectly uniform, with a thin dark line running along the top edge where the surface stopped and something underneath it started. He did not know what he was looking at. He only knew it did not look like the drawer in his grandmother’s sideboard.
A month later, a couple driving out past Breese on a Saturday stopped at a shop with a gravel lot and a hand-painted sign. Roughly the same money. A completely different half hour. The man behind the counter opened a drawer, tipped it toward the window so they could see the corner joint, then told them who had built the piece and how long he had been building them. He also volunteered which parts of it were solid wood and which were not, before anyone thought to ask. That was the whole difference. Not the price, not the sign out front. He would just tell them.
Here is what this covers. Why the word “Amish” on a tag is a marketing decision rather than a certification, and what you can verify instead. How to tell solid wood from a veneered composite core using the edge, the end grain, the drawer and the underside. The joinery that signals a shop cared: dovetails, mortise and tenon, dust panels, and the little fasteners that let a solid top move with the seasons. Which hardwoods get used and what each one actually does over twenty years. What drives the price and why nobody can hand you a number that stays true. Whether any of it holds value. And at the end, a note to furniture stores and woodshops around the metro about the one sentence most of them are not writing down.
### How to tell if Amish furniture is real?
Check the furniture, not the label. “Amish” is not a legally protected term, and “Amish style” and “Amish-inspired” are marketing phrases that say nothing about who did the work. What is verifiable is the piece itself: the joinery, whether it is solid wood or a veneered core, the finish, and whether the shop will name the builder.
That reframing matters more than it sounds. Once you stop trying to authenticate a word and start inspecting a table, the answers get checkable. A drawer either has dovetails or it does not. A shop either knows who built the piece or it does not.
### What the label can and cannot tell you
A tag reading “Amish made” is a claim, and claims from a good shop are usually accurate. But the phrase carries no legal weight, no inspection behind it, and no shared definition across sellers. Some retailers use it for furniture built by small family woodshops under contract. Others use “Amish style” for a look: heavy legs, simple lines, a mission or shaker silhouette. Both signs can hang in the same lot on the same weekend, and the second one is not lying. It is describing a design, not a maker.
### What a shop is willing to tell you
This is the single most useful test, and it costs you one question. Ask who built this piece. A shop working directly with small woodshops will generally answer with something specific: a family name, a region, how long that shop has supplied them, sometimes a stamp or a signature under the tabletop or inside a drawer. A shop selling a look will answer in categories, and you will hear words like line, collection, and imported. Neither answer is proof of anything. The difference in how the answer arrives tells you plenty.
Follow it with two more. What species is this, and is the whole piece that species, including the drawer sides, the back panel and the interior? What is the finish, and what happens when a joint fails in year eight? A shop with a real relationship with a builder answers all three without hesitating. A shop that cannot answer them is not necessarily selling junk. It is selling something it has not looked at closely, which is a different problem with the same cost to you.
### How do you tell solid wood from veneer?
Look at the edges, the end grain and the parts nobody bothered to finish. Solid wood shows the same grain running over an edge and continuing on the other side, with visible end grain where a board was cut across. Veneer over particleboard or MDF shows a thin applied band, grain that stops at the corner, and a uniform, sandy edge underneath.
### Look at the edge and the end grain
Run a finger along the front edge of a tabletop and follow one visible grain line with your eye. On a solid top, that line rolls over the edge and reappears underneath, because it is one board. On a veneered top, the face grain stops abruptly and a separate strip of edge banding takes over, often with a hairline seam and a grain pattern that does not match the face at all. Then find a cut end, the short end of a tabletop or the top of a leg, and look for open pores and growth rings running through the thickness. That is end grain, and it is hard to fake convincingly.
### Open a drawer, then look underneath
Pull a drawer completely out and turn it over. You are looking for four things. Dovetails at the front corners, either hand-cut with slightly irregular spacing or machine-cut with even spacing, both of which beat a stapled butt joint or a drawer held together with glue and brads. A drawer bottom that sits in a groove instead of being nailed to the bottom edge. Solid drawer sides with visible end grain rather than that pale, uniform composite. And a dust panel: a thin horizontal divider between one drawer and the next, which is a quiet sign the shop was not saving minutes.
Now get under the table itself. Where the top meets the apron, a well-built solid piece uses fasteners that let the top move: figure-eight fasteners, Z-clips sitting in a saw kerf, or wood buttons in a groove, often riding in slots slightly wider than the screw. Solid wood expands and contracts across its width with the seasons, and a Midwest house swings a lot between February and August. A solid top screwed down rigidly through the apron with no room to move is a crack waiting for its second winter. Breadboard ends should be pinned through elongated holes and glued only near the center, for the same reason.
### Weight, sound and the parts nobody finishes
Weight is a weak signal on its own, since particleboard is genuinely heavy, but combined with the rest it helps. Better is the unfinished territory: the underside of a top, the back of a case, the inside of a cabinet. Those surfaces get the least attention and tell the most truth. Look for real grain and mill marks rather than a printed pattern or a smooth gray core. Tap a case back with a knuckle. A thin hardboard back sounds hollow and flexes; a solid or plywood panel set into a groove does not.
One honest caution. Plywood is not a failure. Good shops use quality veneer-core plywood for case backs and drawer bottoms on purpose, because it stays flat and does not split, and that is a considered choice rather than a shortcut. The thing worth spotting is a piece sold as solid hardwood that turns out to be a composite core with a printed or paper-thin surface, because that construction cannot be refinished, does not hold a screw the same way, and swells permanently once water gets in.
### What kind of wood is Amish furniture made of?
Mostly domestic hardwoods. Red oak and white oak, cherry, hard and soft maple, hickory, walnut, and sometimes elm, ash or quartersawn white oak for mission pieces. Softwoods like pine show up on painted or rustic work. Species drives a large share of the price, and it changes how the piece looks and behaves for the rest of its life.
Ask two things about species, not one. What is it, and is the entire piece that species. It is common and not dishonest to build a cherry table with cherry on the visible parts and a different secondary wood for drawer sides or a case back. It is another thing entirely when the top is cherry and the legs are a stained lookalike. Only one of those should surprise you later.
### What the common species do differently
Cherry darkens noticeably with light and age, going from a pinkish tan to a deep reddish brown, which is why a cherry table and its leaf can drift apart in color if the leaf lives in a closet. Red oak has an open, coarse grain and takes stain readily. White oak is denser and more water resistant, and quartersawn white oak shows the ray fleck that mission furniture is known for. Hard maple is pale, tight-grained and very hard, and it can blotch under stain, so it often looks best clear or lightly toned. Hickory is extremely hard with dramatic color variation between the pale sapwood and the darker heartwood. Walnut is the expensive one, naturally rich brown, and sometimes steamed at the mill to even out its color.
Finish matters as much as species for how a table survives a family. Many production woodshops spray a catalyzed conversion varnish, which cures hard and stands up well to water, heat and household cleaners. Oil and wax finishes look and feel warmer and are far easier to touch up at home, but they mark more easily and need occasional attention. Neither is the right answer for everyone. Ask which one you are buying, then ask what the shop recommends when something eventually gets spilled on it.
### How much does Amish furniture typically cost?
More than mass-market furniture, and the gap is wide rather than fixed. A solid hardwood dining table from a small shop generally costs several times what a similar-looking particleboard version costs at a big-box store, with chairs usually priced separately. Ranges move constantly with lumber prices, species and size, so confirm current pricing locally rather than trusting any figure in an article.
That vagueness is deliberate. Anyone quoting a firm number for a category this broad is quoting one table they saw once. What helps is knowing which variables push the number around, so that two different quotes can be read as either a discount or a different piece of furniture.
### What actually moves the number
Species is usually the biggest lever, and walnut and quartersawn white oak sit at the top while red oak and soft maple sit lower. Size is next, then thickness of the top. Leaves add cost, and self-storing leaves with good extension hardware add more than you would guess. Finish adds cost, especially a multi-step glaze or a distressed treatment. Chairs are typically sold individually, and a set of six can rival the table. Then delivery, which is real money for something this heavy, and lead time, because custom work is built after you order it.
Two more that catch people out. Custom dimensions and custom stain colors are often available and often carry an upcharge, and a stain sample on the wrong species will not predict the result, so ask for a sample on the wood you are actually buying. And the quoted lead time is a lumber-and-shop estimate, not a promise from a warehouse. Ask what it has actually been running lately for that shop.
### How to shortlist shops worth interviewing
Pick two or three stores or woodshops and go interview them with the same short summary. Here is the room, here is the size, here is the species we like, here is what we expect this table to survive, and here is when we need it. Then listen. One will tell you who builds their tables and walk you to a drawer to show you why. One will talk about the collection. One will start negotiating before you have finished describing the room. That spread is the signal, and it shows up in about ten minutes.
You are not asking anyone to break out labor costs or produce three written estimates. Nobody selling furniture works that way, and asking for it mostly tells the room you have never done this. What you are comparing is the gap between what you plainly said you wanted and what each shop is actually set up to deliver. In our experience that gap predicts satisfaction better than the price tag does.
Furnishing a first home for someone? A local gift basket beats another gift card.
### Does Amish furniture hold its value?
It holds up better than it resells. Solid hardwood furniture can be repaired, re-glued and refinished for decades, so it keeps its usefulness in a way composite furniture cannot. But used furniture of almost every kind sells for a fraction of new, and there is no reliable public pricing data on secondhand pieces from small woodshops.
So separate two ideas that often get blurred together in sales conversations. Durable value is real and easy to see: a solid top can be sanded and refinished after a decade of hard use, a loose mortise and tenon joint can be knocked apart and re-glued, and a broken chair leg on solid stock can be replaced by any competent shop. A veneered composite top cannot be sanded, because there is not enough material to sand.
Resale value is a different market and a harsher one. Buyers of used furniture are usually shopping on price and delivery convenience, and a heavy solid table is expensive to move, which suppresses what people will pay for it. Documented older pieces with a known maker sometimes do better in the antique market, but that is a specialist market where condition, original hardware and original finish matter enormously. If someone tells you a new table is an investment, they are selling, not appraising.
The practical measure is cost per year of use. A table your kids did homework on, that can be refinished twice and handed down, does something a replaced-every-six-years table never does. That is a fair reason to spend more. It is just not the same claim as appreciation.
Ready to go look at some furniture in person? You can browse Amish furniture stores on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three worth a Saturday, and bring the same four questions to each one: who built this, what species is it all the way through, what is the finish, and what happens if a joint fails in year eight. How readily those answers come back tells you most of what you need.
If you run a business in this space, get on the directory.
### For St. Louis furniture stores and woodshops
Think about Ted holding that drawer up to the light, seeing a thin dark line along the top edge and having no idea whether it meant anything. He was not trying to catch anybody. He was trying to spend a lot of money responsibly, and nobody had given him a way to do it.
So give it to him in writing. Put the species on the tag, and say whether it runs through the whole piece or only the visible surfaces. Say what the drawer boxes are made of and how the corners are joined. Say what the finish is, in plain words, and what a customer should do when a glass of water sits on it overnight. Name the shop or the region that built it, if you are allowed to, or say honestly that you buy through a distributor and cannot. That last sentence loses you nothing and buys you an enormous amount of trust.
Then publish it online, not just on the floor tag, because most of this decision happens on a phone before anyone drives anywhere. A short page on construction, species, finish options, custom sizing, lead times and delivery answers the questions your staff repeat all week. And if you build custom, post the honest current lead time and keep it updated. A family from New Baden planning a holiday table around a delivery date will forgive a long wait far more easily than a missed one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Amish furniture high quality?
A.  Often, but the label is not the reason. The reputation comes from small shops building solid hardwood pieces with traditional joinery, and plenty of them earn it. Quality still varies from shop to shop and piece to piece, so judge the furniture in front of you: dovetailed drawers, mortise and tenon joints, real end grain at the edges, and a finish someone will describe to you specifically.
### Q. How long does Amish furniture last?
A.  Solid hardwood furniture built with sound joinery commonly serves for decades, and the more useful point is that it stays repairable. Joints can be re-glued, tops can be refinished, and broken parts can be replaced in matching stock. Lifespan depends heavily on humidity swings, sunlight and how the piece is treated, which is why care matters as much as construction over the long run.
### Q. Is Amish furniture overpriced?
A.  It depends entirely on the comparison. Against flat-pack or particleboard furniture it looks expensive, because it is a different product with a different service life. Against other solid hardwood furniture built to order, it is often competitive. The fair way to judge is cost per year of expected use plus repairability, and to compare like with like: same species, same construction, same finish.
### Q. Do the Amish make good furniture?
A.  Many shops in that tradition have a long-standing reputation for solid wood construction and careful joinery, and that reputation was earned by the work. What the reputation cannot do is guarantee any individual piece, since the term is not protected and anyone may print it. Treat it as a reason to look closely rather than a reason to stop looking.
### Q. How to tell if old furniture is worth money?
A.  Look for construction clues first: hand-cut dovetails with uneven spacing, solid wood throughout, mortise and tenon joints, and old hardware with irregular screws. Then look for a maker’s mark, stamp or label, usually inside a drawer or on the back. Condition, original finish and original hardware move the number a great deal. For anything that might be significant, get an appraisal locally before refinishing it.
### Q. How do I tell if my furniture is solid wood?
A.  Thirty seconds in a showroom does it. Pick one grain line on the top and follow it over the front edge; on solid wood it keeps going, on veneer it stops at a seam. Find a cut end and look for open pores. Open a drawer, turn it over, then feel under the top. Lift a corner. Tap the back panel.
### Q. Can Amish furniture be custom sized and stained to order?
A.  Usually yes, and it is one of the real advantages of buying from a shop rather than a warehouse. Custom dimensions, species, stain color, edge profile, leaf configuration and hardware are commonly options, often with an upcharge and a longer lead time. Ask for a stain sample on the same species you are ordering, since the same color reads very differently on maple, oak and cherry.
### Q. How should solid wood furniture be cared for in a humid Midwest house?
A.  Keep indoor humidity reasonably steady through the year, since solid wood swells in summer and shrinks in winter and it is the swing that causes cracks and stuck drawers. Store table leaves flat and, ideally, in the table so they age in the same light. Use coasters and felt pads, lift rather than drag, wipe spills promptly, and keep cherry out of direct sun unless you want it to darken unevenly.

## What It Costs to Start Archery in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-it-costs-to-start-archery-in-st-louis
The bow was too much bow. Dale found it on a marketplace listing on a Tuesday night, a compound with a sight still mounted and a hard case, priced like a deal, and he drove most of an hour to pick it up for his twelve-year-old. Nora pulled it back maybe six inches and started shaking. Second try, she got a little further and let it slip, and the string caught her forearm hard enough to leave a welt she showed off at school for a week. She would not touch the thing again for a month. The bow itself was fine. It was a good bow. It was just built for a grown man with a longer reach and forty more pounds of pull, and nobody had measured her for anything.
Priya was running the other version of the same problem. She had wanted to shoot since a week of summer camp in high school, and she spent most of March reading about it instead. One page told her she could get started for about what a nice dinner costs. Another laid out a setup that ran more than her first car. Both were describing something real. Neither one told her which version applied to a woman in her thirties who wanted to put arrows in a target on Saturday mornings and had no idea what her draw length was. So she kept not starting.
Here is what this covers. What a beginner actually has to buy, and the difference between a simple recurve package and a compound that has been fitted and tuned. The costs nobody puts in the first estimate: arrows, a target, range time, a tab and an armguard. Why the smartest first purchase is usually a lesson rather than a bow, and how to figure out which range or pro shop is worth your Saturday. How hard the sport really is, and the one mistake that makes it far harder than it needs to be. What actually governs shooting in your own yard, which is not what most people assume. Whether this stays a cheap hobby or quietly turns into an expensive one. And at the end, a note to ranges and pro shops around the metro about what they ought to be publishing.
### How much does beginner archery equipment cost?
Less than the enthusiast forums imply and more than the boxed kit at the sporting goods store suggests. A simple starter recurve package generally sits in the low hundreds. A compound bow, once it has a sight, a rest and a release on it, runs several times that. Prices move constantly, so confirm with a local shop.
The bigger point is that cost is the wrong first question. Fit is the first question. Two numbers decide whether a bow works for you: draw length, which is a function of your reach, and draw weight, which is how many pounds you have to pull to get to full draw. Get those wrong and the most expensive bow on the wall shoots worse than a borrowed one that fits. Get them right and a modest bow will carry you for years.
### What a first setup actually includes
A recurve beginner is usually buying a riser and limbs, a string, a half dozen arrows cut and spined for that bow, an armguard, a finger tab or glove, and a quiver. That is the whole list. It is refreshingly short. A compound beginner is buying the bow plus a sight, an arrow rest, a peep sight, a release aid, a stabilizer and a case, and most of that has to be installed and tuned rather than clipped on in a parking lot.
Arrow spine is the detail beginners skip and shops never do. Spine is the stiffness of the shaft, and it has to be matched to the draw weight and draw length of the specific bow shooting it. Arrows that are too stiff or too limp will not group no matter how good your form gets. A cheap online bundle of arrows sized for somebody else is one of the most common reasons a new archer decides they have no talent.
### The costs that show up later
Arrows are a consumable. You will break some, you will lose some in the grass, and a bad shot can put one through a fletching on the arrow already in the target. Budget for replacements the way you budget for tennis balls. A target of your own is the other quiet expense, and a bag target that stops a beginner recurve will not necessarily stop a set-up compound, so buy for the bow you own.
Then there is time on a range. Some places charge by the session, some sell a punch card, some run an annual club membership that works out cheaper if you shoot most weekends. Strings stretch and wear and get replaced. Lessons cost money. None of it is dramatic, but the sticker on the bow is maybe half of what year one really costs, and it helps to know that going in.
### What is the best way to learn archery for beginners?
Take a beginner class before you buy anything at all. Most places that teach archery keep loaner equipment for a first lesson, and one hour on borrowed gear will teach you more than three weeks of reading. You also walk out knowing your draw length, which is the number every purchase after that depends on.
Buying first and learning second is the expensive order, and it is the order almost everybody uses. Dale did. The bow he bought was not wasted money in the abstract, it just belonged to a different archer. Had Nora shot a light loaner for an hour first, somebody would have measured her, handed her twenty pounds instead of sixty, and she would still be shooting. Instead she has a bruise and a bad memory, and that is the actual cost of skipping the lesson.
### How to shortlist a range or a pro shop
Pick two or three places worth interviewing and go see them, or call if that is easier. Say plainly what you want. Never shot before, want a first lesson, here is who is coming and here is roughly when. Then listen to what comes back and compare it against what you asked for. The gap between the two is the signal. It tells you more than any price does.
Three questions do most of the sorting. Do you have loaner equipment for a first lesson, or do I need to own a bow to walk in? Do you measure draw length before you sell somebody a bow? Do you run a beginner class, or is it open shooting only? A shop that measures you and has a class is set up for new people. A place that is only open shooting is not worse, it is just built for archers who already know what they are doing, and showing up cold is going to feel like walking into a gym with no idea how the machines work.
### What a good first hour looks like
Safety first, and it is not a formality. You learn the whistle or verbal commands, where the shooting line is, when you may go retrieve arrows and when you absolutely may not. Then stance, nocking the arrow, drawing, finding an anchor point on your face, releasing and following through. The target will be close, closer than feels dignified, and the bow will be light. Both of those are on purpose. Close targets and light bows are how form gets built.
### Is archery difficult to learn?
It is easy to start and slow to master, which is an unusual and pleasant combination. Most people put an arrow into a target within their first hour. Putting five arrows into the same fist-sized spot, on purpose, on a breezy afternoon, is the work of years. The sport gives you a win on day one and then keeps you honest forever.
What makes it hard is repeatability, not strength or eyesight. Every shot has to be the same shot: same stance, same grip pressure, same anchor point against the same spot on your jaw, same release, same follow-through. A change of a quarter inch anywhere in that chain moves the arrow inches downrange. Good archers are not doing something exotic. They are doing one ordinary thing identically, several hundred times a week.
The single mistake that makes it much harder is being over-bowed. Pulling more weight than your back and shoulders can hold comfortably forces you to muscle the shot, and every bad habit follows from that: creeping forward at full draw, punching the release, dropping the bow arm, flinching. Those habits are miserable to unlearn once they set. Almost every experienced coach will start an adult lighter than the adult expects, and the adult almost always resents it for about two weeks and then thanks them.
Draw weight is also not permanent. It goes up as the muscles that hold a bow at full draw get stronger, and on most beginner recurves you can swap limbs later rather than replace the whole bow. Starting light is not settling. It is buying yourself a form that still works when the weight climbs.
### Can I legally practice archery in my backyard?
That is decided by city or county ordinance, not by any single rule you can look up once. It varies enormously across the metro and again across the state line. Plenty of municipalities prohibit discharging a bow inside city limits outright, and others allow it but attach conditions.
Those conditions are usually about space and containment: a minimum lot size, a required setback from property lines or structures, a backstop behind the target, or a rule about how close you may shoot to a road or a neighboring house. Some places treat a bow the same way they treat a firearm in their code, some carve out a specific exception for target archery, and some say nothing at all, which is its own kind of answer. Ordinances also get amended, so a neighbor’s confident recollection from six years ago is not a source.
The only reliable answer is a phone call about the specific address. Call the city clerk for that address, or the police department non-emergency line, and ask directly whether discharging a bow for target practice is permitted at that property and what conditions apply. It takes one call. Then check the layer underneath the ordinance: a homeowners association, a subdivision restriction or a lease can prohibit it even where the city allows it, and those get enforced by the people who live closest to you.
### The safety side, which matters even where it is legal
Build the backstop before you build the range. A target alone is not enough, because beginners miss the target, and a miss at head height goes somewhere. Something solid behind the target, an earth berm, a stacked bale wall or heavy backstop netting rated for archery, is what turns a lawn into a range. Shoot into a hill if you have one.
Then think about the overshoot zone, which is the part people forget. An arrow that skips off the top of a bag target or leaves the bow at a bad angle travels a long, long way, far past any fence line. Look at what is beyond and above your target: houses, a road, a yard where kids play, a trail. Talk to the neighbors before they see a stranger with a bow through a kitchen window and call it in. A dad out toward Gillespie can shoot in the yard all afternoon and never think about it. In much of the metro, the same fifteen yards simply do not exist safely, and the range is the honest answer.
### If hunting is where this is heading
Bowhunting is regulated at the state level, and the rules differ on either side of the river. Missouri handles seasons, permits and hunter education through the Missouri Department of Conservation. Illinois handles the equivalent through the Illinois Department of Natural Resources. Both publish current regulations every year, including equipment requirements, season dates and the education certification you need before you can buy a permit. Get it from them rather than from an article or a forum thread, because those details change and the penalties for guessing are real. Target practice in the yard is a separate question from hunting, and the local ordinance still applies either way.
Backyard range plans? Check how home insurance premiums react before you build it.
### Is archery an expensive hobby?
It can be either, and the equipment is not what decides it. Target archery with a simple recurve is one of the cheaper ongoing hobbies once the bow is paid for: arrows, a target and range time, and none of those move much year to year. What makes archery expensive is ambition, not gear.
The upgrade path is where the money actually goes. Better limbs, a better sight, a stabilizer setup, a bow press, a chronograph, a second bow for a different discipline. Then tournaments, entry fees, three-dimensional courses out in the country, travel on weekends. Every one of those is optional and every one of them is fun, which is exactly why the budget drifts. The archer who shoots the same fitted recurve for ten years and replaces arrows twice a season is spending very little, and there is always a quiet guy up around Mt Olive who has done exactly that since the nineties and outshoots everybody.
Hunting is the other fork in the road, and it is a different budget entirely. Add a compound suited to it, broadheads, camouflage, a stand or a blind, permits, and access to land. People who start in target archery and drift into bowhunting are usually surprised by the second wave of spending, not the first.
Compared with hobbies that need ice time, greens fees, a boat or a case of ammunition every weekend, archery sits comfortably in the middle. The entry cost is real and mostly one time. The ongoing cost is small. Priya, if she had just booked the class in March, would have spent less by June than she spent on the three weeks of reading that talked her out of it.
Not sure where a first lesson would even happen? You can browse archery on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three ranges or pro shops worth calling, and give each one the same short summary: never shot before, want a first lesson, here is who is coming. Then ask whether they have loaner equipment and whether they measure draw length before they sell anybody a bow. What comes back, and how readily, tells you plenty before you spend a dollar.
If you run a business in this line of work, list your business.
### For St. Louis archery ranges and pro shops
Think about Dale on that Tuesday night, driving most of an hour with cash in his pocket for a bow his daughter could not draw. He was not being careless. He was doing what a parent does when nobody has told him there was a question to ask. One paragraph on a website would have sent him to you instead.
So write the paragraph. Say plainly whether you have loaner equipment for a first lesson, because that is the single fact that decides whether a curious person can show up at all. Say whether you run beginner classes and how often, or whether you are open shooting only. Say that you measure draw length before selling a bow, because most beginners do not know that is a thing and it is the strongest argument you have against a marketplace listing. Say what your youngest age is and whether you have youth bows.
Then put the practical details where a stranger can find them at nine on a Saturday morning: session fees or membership structure, what a first lesson includes, whether you cut and spine arrows in house, whether walk-ins work or everything is by appointment. Ranges that publish this get people who arrive prepared and stay for years, including the family from Bunker Hill who will happily make the drive twice a month once they know the Saturday class is real. Ranges that keep it in a staff member’s head get phone calls that end in “we’ll think about it,” and then a bow bought sight unseen from a listing, and a kid with a welt on her forearm who never comes back.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is archery a cheap hobby?
A.  It can be. Once the bow is paid for, target archery with a simple recurve costs about as much per month as arrows, a target and range time, and none of that is much. It stops being cheap the moment upgrades, tournaments, travel or hunting gear enter the picture. The equipment is not the variable. What you decide to do with it is.
### Q. Can I teach myself archery?
A.  You can, and plenty of people have, but you will build habits in the first month that take a year to unlearn. The hardest things to self-correct are anchor point and release, because you cannot see your own form while you shoot it. One or two early lessons cost less in time than fixing a punched release later. Filming yourself helps. Someone standing behind you helps more.
### Q. Is 30 too late to start archery?
A.  No. Archery has one of the widest age ranges of any target sport, and adults who start in their thirties, fifties or seventies shoot and compete for decades afterward. Draw weight can be set to whatever your shoulders currently handle and raised as you get stronger. Nothing about the sport rewards being young. It rewards being consistent, and that is a habit, not an age.
### Q. How far will a 50 lb bow shoot an arrow?
A.  Much farther than anyone should ever aim one. Maximum distance depends on draw weight, draw length, arrow weight and launch angle, so a single number would be misleading. What is true is that a fifty-pound bow at an upward angle can send an arrow well past where you can watch it land. That is precisely why an overshoot zone and a real backstop matter. Accurate shooting happens at a small fraction of that distance.
### Q. Is archery an expensive hobby?
A.  It sits in the middle of the pack. The entry cost is real but largely one time, and the ongoing cost is modest next to sports that require ice time, greens fees or ammunition every weekend. Archers who find it expensive are usually chasing equipment. Archers who find it cheap shoot the same fitted bow for ten years and spend their money on arrows.
### Q. What is the best way to learn archery for beginners?
A.  Borrowed gear, a close target and a coach watching, in that order, before any money changes hands. If no beginner class runs near you, a single private lesson to establish your measurements and basic form is still worth more than the same money spent on accessories. Owning a bow does not teach you to shoot it, and a bow bought before that first hour is a coin flip.
### Q. What is the difference between a recurve, a compound and a traditional longbow?
A.  A recurve has limbs that curve away at the tips, is simple and light, and is the style shot at the Olympics. A compound uses cams and cables so you hold only a fraction of the peak weight at full draw, which makes it easier to aim and far more mechanical to tune. A traditional longbow is one long curve, shot without sights and largely by feel. Same word, three fairly different sports.
### Q. What age can a child start archery lessons?
A.  Programs commonly start somewhere around eight to ten, and some take younger children with very light equipment and close supervision. Birthday is not really the test. The test is whether the child can follow range commands reliably and handle a bow scaled to their body. Ask a range what their youngest class is and whether they keep youth loaner bows, because fit matters even more for kids than it does for adults.

## Auction Buyer’s Premium: Your $1,000 Bid Can Cost $1,300
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/auction-buyers-premium-st-louis-what-you-really-pay
Two hundred fifty dollars. That is what one downtown St. Louis auction house adds to a $1,000 winning bid, and it lands on your invoice after the hammer has already cracked and the room has moved on to the next lot. Your paddle is still in your hand. Your pulse is still up from the last two raises. And the number you just shouted is not the number you owe.
Nobody hid it from you. It is called the buyer’s premium, and Selkirk Auctioneers & Appraisers, at 555 Washington Avenue, prints its rate in plain type on its own How to Bid page: a 25% Buyer’s Premium for all in-person, absentee and phone bids up to and including $1 million. Every house writes its own terms. Selkirk’s happen to sit where anyone in St. Louis can read them, which makes them the cleanest real numbers to do the math with.
Here is the line worth saying out loud to whoever rides with you to the next sale: at Selkirk, the couch costs extra. The same page says buyers bidding online are subject to an additional 5% buyer’s premium. On a $1,000 lot, that is $1,250 if you raise a paddle in the room and $1,300 if you tap a button at home. Fifty dollars for staying in your slippers. Pay by credit card and the house’s payment page lists a 3% surcharge on top, so if that example bill is $1,300, the card adds about $39 more. Not one cent of that is sales tax yet.
So do the math backward, before the lot comes up. If the most you will spend on that dresser is $1,000 all in, your real ceiling at a 25% house is $800, because $800 plus a quarter of it is $1,000, and tax still comes after. Write $800 on the back of the catalog. When the chant climbs past it, sit on your hands, feel the itch, and listen to somebody else win it. That itch is the expensive part.
The rest of this page walks the whole bill one line at a time: who pays the premium, what the seller pays on the other side of the same sale, how tax and pickup work, and the mistakes that cost bidders real money before the first lot ever crosses the block.
### How much is buyer’s premium at auction?
Each house sets its own rate in its own written terms. At Selkirk Auctioneers & Appraisers in downtown St. Louis, it is 25% of the hammer price for in-person, absentee and phone bids up to and including $1 million, and bidding online adds another 5%. So if you win a lot at $1,000, say, it becomes $1,250 in the room or $1,300 online, before sales tax.
The tiers only matter on serious money. Selkirk drops to a 20% Buyer’s Premium in excess of $1.0 million and 15% in excess of $5.0 million. For the box of Depression glass, the oak sideboard and the oil painting that hung in a grandmother’s hallway for as long as anyone remembers, the story is short: 25% when you are standing in the room, 30% when you are not.
Other houses around the metro set their own numbers, and the same company can write different terms for different sales. A weekly consignment night, a whole-house estate sale and a curated catalog sale can each carry their own rate. The terms for the exact sale you are bidding in are the price tag, and reading them takes about as long as a cup of coffee cools: find the percentage, find whether online costs more, find the card surcharge, find the pickup deadline.
### Why the button costs more than the paddle
Selkirk spells it out: all online bidding, whether through the Selkirk website or a third-party, is subject to a higher buyer’s premium. Online, the bid feels weightless. A thumb on glass, a soft chime, a green banner that says you are winning. In the room you feel every raise in your arm and in your stomach, and maybe that is the point. If a sale is close enough to drive to, the in-person rate is real money back in your pocket, and you get to open the drawers yourself.
### Who pays buyer’s premium at auction?
The winning bidder does. In Selkirk’s words, all items purchased at auction are subject to a buyer’s premium in addition to the hammer price. It is added to your invoice, not taken out of the seller’s check, and you owe it whether or not you noticed the line before you raised your hand. You find out for sure at the cashier’s window, with the receipt printer whirring and a line of people behind you holding their own lamps and boxes.
Both sides of an auction pay the house. The buyer pays the premium. The seller pays a commission out of the hammer price, plus whatever their contract lists for photography, cataloging, moving, storage or unsold lots. Two agreements, two people, one auctioneer collecting from both. That is the business model, and there is nothing shady about it as long as both numbers are written where the person paying can read them.
### When a sale says no premium
A few sales advertise no buyer’s premium, and that is genuine when it is in the written terms. It usually means the house is earning its money entirely on the seller’s side. Treat it the way you treat everything else at an auction: a claim you check in the terms, not a promise in an ad.
### The whole bill, line by line
Say, as an example, you win a lot at $1,000 at Selkirk. Here is the bill, built only from the numbers the house publishes:
Hammer price in this example: $1,000
Buyer’s premium at 25%, bidding in the room: $250, for $1,250
Bidding online instead: another 5%, for $1,300
Paying by credit card: a 3% surcharge, about $39 if the example bill is $1,300
Then sales tax, unless you have a resale certificate on file
That last line catches people. Selkirk’s payment page says that in order to be exempt from sales tax, you must hold a current resale certificate and have a copy on file, using a Missouri Form 149. Hand it over before you settle, not after. Asking for tax back on a paid invoice is a much colder conversation.
### The clock starts when the hammer falls
Selkirk says payment must be made within five (5) business days of the auction, and that any purchase greater than or equal to $10,000 must be submitted by wire transfer or ACH. Then the other clock: everything must be picked up or shipped within fifteen (15) days following an auction. Fifteen days sounds like plenty until you are standing next to a walnut armoire with no truck, no helper and a back that already knows how this ends.
Do the backward math before your next sale. Browse auctions on St Louis Near Me Directory, open the terms for the one you want, find the premium, the online rate, the card surcharge and the pickup deadline, and write your real ceiling down before the first lot crosses the block.
If you run the auction house or the estate sale crew, put your terms where bidders can read them and claim your spot to get more customers who show up ready to bid.
### Is it worth selling stuff at auction?
Sometimes. It depends on what you have and what your other option is. Auction is fast, it clears volume, and it puts your things in front of people who came to buy. What it does not do is promise a price. You net the hammer price minus commission minus whatever fees the contract lists, and there is no floor unless you negotiated a reserve.
The strongest case is a house that has to be emptied on a deadline. An estate is being settled, a closing date is coming, a shop is winding down. Auction turns rooms full of a life into one date, one crew and one check. Selling the same things one at a time online might bring more per piece, and it will eat months of your evenings, the garage still full, the boxes still smelling like somebody else’s basement.
### Questions to ask before you consign
Talk to two or three houses and ask each the same things. What is the commission on a lot like mine? Do you charge for photography, cataloging, moving or unsold lots? When do I get paid, and how? What happens to anything that does not sell? Can I set a reserve, and what does it cost if the lot passes? You are not shopping for the lowest commission. You are listening for the house that answers before you finish asking.

### How much is buyer's premium at auction?
Each house prints its own rate. Selkirk Auctioneers & Appraisers downtown charges 25% of the hammer price for in-person, absentee and phone bids, plus another 5% online, so a $1,000 win becomes $1,250 in the room or $1,300 from your couch, before sales tax.
### What not to do at an auction?
Do not treat the hammer price as the price. That one habit costs more than anything else here. Close behind: skipping the terms, skipping the preview, bidding on something you cannot move, and missing the pickup window.
### Do not skip the preview
Most auctions sell as is. Photos flatter and box lots hide things. The preview is where you pull the drawer and hear it scrape, flip the frame and smell the old glue, count what is really in the box. If you cannot go to the preview, bid like somebody who did not go.
The cheapest part of a big lot is the bid. Price the moving truck before you raise your hand.
### Do not bid against yourself
Set the ceiling before the lot comes up, with the premium, any surcharge and the tax already figured in, and let it go when the bidding passes it. There will be another table. The room is built to make you feel there will not be, and that feeling is what you pay the premium on.
### Do not assume you can undo it
A winning bid is a promise to pay, not a reservation. Read what the terms say about disputes, lot descriptions and what happens if you do not pay. Selkirk’s own payment page says that if payment is not made within ten (10) business days, it reserves the right to charge a credit card on file.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a 20% buyer’s premium in an auction?
A.  It means the house adds twenty percent of the hammer price to your invoice. On a $1,000 bid that is $200, for $1,200 before sales tax and any other charges the terms list. Twenty percent is an example, not a standard. Selkirk in downtown St. Louis charges 25% in the room and 30% online on lots up to $1 million.
### Q. What percentage does an auctioneer usually take from an estate sale?
A.  There is no usual number worth quoting. Commission varies by house, by what is being sold, by how much labor the job takes, and by whether the house also charges buyers a premium. Ask each house you interview what the commission is on an estate like yours, and what else gets billed on top.
### Q. What sells most in an auction?
A.  Things with a broad resale market tend to move fastest: tools and shop equipment, outdoor gear, solid-wood furniture in good shape, jewelry, coins, and anything a dealer can resell. Box lots clear quickly because they are cheap to bid on. Bulky furniture in ordinary condition moves slowly.
### Q. What is the 15 minute rule in an auction?
A.  There is no industry-wide fifteen minute rule. People usually mean soft close or extended bidding online: a bid in the closing minutes pushes the end time out so nobody wins by sniping at the last second. How long the extension runs is set by the platform or the house and stated in that sale’s terms.
### Q. What happens to stuff not sold at estate sales?
A.  It depends on the contract. Common outcomes are a marked-down final day, a bulk lot sold cheap to a dealer, donation, return to the family, or a paid cleanout. Some agreements bill the seller for that last step, which is why “what happens to anything that does not sell” belongs in the interview.
### Q. What sells well at estate auctions?
A.  At a whole-house sale, the garage and the basement often outdo the living room. Tools, ladders, yard equipment and hardware draw serious buyers, and so do jewelry, coins, advertising signs and well-kept vintage furniture. Kitchenware, books and linens usually go as bulk lots, which is fine, because the point of the day is to clear the house.
### Q. Is the buyer’s premium taxed?
A.  It can be, so read how the sale’s terms say tax is figured before you set your ceiling. If you buy to resell, get your exemption on file first: Selkirk, for one, asks for a Missouri Form 149 and a current resale certificate before it will remove sales tax. Ask an accountant about anything business-related.
### Q. What is the difference between an absolute auction and a reserve auction?
A.  An absolute auction sells the lot to the highest bidder with no minimum. A reserve auction has a confidential minimum the bidding must reach, and the lot can pass unsold if it does not. The listing should say which one you are in.
