## Candle Making Classes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/candle-making-classes-st-louis-what-to-expect
Rachel had run out of date nights. She and Dev had eaten at everything within ten minutes of their place in Maplewood, and a Friday that starts with “where do you want to go” had stopped being fun sometime last winter. Someone at work mentioned pouring candles. Sit at a bench, smell a hundred little bottles, pick two, make something. She booked it mostly to break the pattern. What she could not find anywhere on the studio’s page was the one thing she actually wanted to know: does the candle come home with you that night, or do you drive back across town later to collect a jar you already paid for? She booked anyway and hoped.
A few weeks earlier, out in St. Charles, Nadia was trying to fill an afternoon. Her sister’s bridal shower needed something between brunch and dinner. Twelve women, two of them in their seventies, one very pregnant, and a mother-in-law who gets a headache from strong perfume. Nadia called two places. The first talked about availability and a deposit. The second asked how many people, what ages, how long she had, and whether anyone was sensitive to scent, then said the room seats fourteen, the fragrance table can sit on the far wall, and they open the back door between pours. Nadia booked the second one before she hung up. Same activity, roughly the same money. One of them had obviously done this for a group before.
Here is what this covers. What a pour-your-own session actually looks like from the minute you sit down, and how much of the hard work the studio has already finished before you walk in. What you personally do: choose a fragrance, weigh it, stir, pour, wait. Why the waiting matters, and the difference between a candle being cool enough to carry out and cured enough to burn well. Why wick sizing is the genuinely difficult part of candle making, and why that is the strongest argument for a class over a first kit. How sessions are priced and what is usually included. How to pick one for a date night, a birthday, a group of twelve, or a serious first run at the hobby. The safety rules worth knowing before you light anything. And at the end, a note to studios and shops around the metro about the handful of details people search for and almost never find.
### Is a candle making class worth it in St. Louis?
It is worth it when you want the session as much as the candle. The studio has already chosen the wax, sized the wick and picked the vessel, so you leave with a jar that burns properly on the first try, plus an evening out that is not another dinner.
The honest comparison is not class versus store candle. If a candle is all you want, buying one is faster and cheaper per jar, because a studio is charging you for a seat, a teacher, a clean bench and a room, not for wax. The comparison that makes sense is class versus a restaurant table, class versus a paint night, class versus a birthday party you have to run yourself in your own kitchen. Judged that way it holds up. You sit with people, you do something with your hands, nobody is on a phone, and at the end there is an object with your name on the bottom of it.
The second kind of value is instructional, and it is easy to underrate. A first candle kit at home usually fails in a specific, predictable way, and the person holding the jar has no way to tell whether the wax, the wick, the fragrance or the pour temperature caused it. In a class every one of those variables is locked down by somebody who has poured a few hundred jars. You get to watch a correct pour before you develop any bad habits, and you find out what melted wax at the right temperature actually looks like, which is surprisingly hard to learn from a photo.
### What actually happens in a candle making class?
Most of the technical work is done before you arrive. The studio has selected the wax, matched a wick to the vessel, and set the melt and pour temperatures. Your part is the enjoyable part: smell your way through a fragrance library, build a blend you like, weigh it, stir it into hot wax, pour, and wait for the jar to set.
### What the studio has already decided for you
Four decisions are made before the door opens. The wax, which might be soy, a coconut blend, a soy and paraffin blend or straight paraffin, each behaving differently in the jar. The vessel, chosen for its diameter as much as its looks, because diameter drives everything downstream. The wick, sized and centered for that wax in that vessel. And the temperatures, meaning how hot the wax gets, at what point the fragrance goes in, and how cool it should be when it hits the jar. None of that is glamorous and all of it is why the candle works.
### What you actually do at the bench
You start at the fragrance table with scent strips, which is where most of the session’s pleasure lives. Sniff broadly, narrow to a few, then usually blend two or three into something that is yours. From there it is measurement, not guesswork. Fragrance is dosed as a percentage of the wax weight, and every wax has a maximum load its manufacturer publishes, so the staff will weigh your oils on a digital scale against the wax going into your jar. Then you stir, and you stir longer than feels necessary, because that is how the fragrance binds into the wax instead of sitting on top of it. Then you pour, straighten the wick, and label the bottom.
### The wait, and then the longer wait
This is the part nobody explains and everybody wants to know. A freshly poured candle is too hot and too liquid to move, so it has to sit before you can carry it out. Some studios build that into the session with a drink, a snack or a label-making break. Others have you come back for it. Ask which, because it changes your evening. Then there is the second wait. A poured candle needs days to cure before it burns and smells its best, and if you light it on the drive home it will underperform and you will blame yourself. Set it somewhere with the lid off, be patient, and let the scent settle in.
### Why is wick sizing the hardest part of candle making?
Because the wick has to match the wax, the jar diameter and the fragrance all at once, and the only way to know you got it right is to burn a test candle and watch. That is the single job a class does for you, and it is the reason a first kit at home so often disappoints.
A wick that runs too small tunnels. It burns a narrow well straight down the middle and leaves a thick ring of unmelted wax stuck to the glass, and once that happens you rarely recover it. A wick that runs too large burns hot, mushrooms a carbon ball on the tip, soots the jar, and can make the glass uncomfortably warm. In between there is a narrow band where the melt pool reaches the edge in a reasonable time and stays there. Change the fragrance and that band moves. Change the jar and it moves again. Serious makers keep test logs for exactly this reason.
So a class hands you a solved problem. If you later want to pour at home, the transferable lesson is not the recipe, it is the method: change one variable at a time, write down what you did, and burn the result before you make twenty of them. In our experience that is the difference between people who keep the hobby and people who put the kit in a closet.
### What does a candle making class cost and what is included?
Sessions are almost always priced per person, and that price usually covers the vessel, the wax, your fragrance selection and the instruction. Bigger vessels and add-ons cost more. Private group bookings are typically quoted per head with a minimum number of guests. Prices move, so confirm the current one when you book rather than trusting a number in an article.
What pushes the number around is worth knowing, because it lets you read two quotes as either a discount or a different experience. Vessel size and style is the biggest lever, followed by how many candles you are making. A walk-in pour bar priced by jar size works differently from a scheduled class with a set start time. Private rooms, weekend evenings, holiday dates and anything involving food or drink all add. So do extras like wax melts, room sprays or a second small jar. None of that is a markup trick, it is just a longer list of things you are taking home.
When you call, ask what is included at the base price, whether there is a minimum for a private booking, and what happens if two people cancel the day before. Those three answers make quotes comparable in a way that the headline number never does.
### How do you pick a session for a date night, a birthday or a first try?
Match the format to the occasion, not the other way round. A walk-in pour bar suits two people with a loose evening. A scheduled class with a teacher suits a birthday or a shower where somebody has to be in charge. A small hands-on workshop suits the person who wants to keep doing this at home afterward.
### For a date night
Flexibility beats structure here. A pour bar or open studio night lets you arrive, take your time at the fragrance table, and talk while you work, which is most of the point. Check two things: whether the studio is next to somewhere you would happily eat afterward, and whether the candle can leave with you. Couples in Webster Groves and Maplewood are often within a short drive of both. Nobody wants a romantic evening that ends with a scheduled return trip.
### For a group, a birthday or a shower
Now you want structure and a person running it. Ask about the minimum and maximum group size, the age policy if kids are coming, whether the room is private, and how long the whole thing takes from arrival to leaving. Say out loud if anyone in the party is pregnant, asthmatic or scent-sensitive, because a room full of open fragrance oils is a lot, and a studio that has thought about it will tell you where to sit and how they ventilate. Groups traveling in from Belleville, Granite City or Cottleville should also ask about parking, which sounds trivial until twelve cars arrive at once.
### For a genuine first try at the hobby
Look for a smaller class where you can actually ask questions. The things you want explained are the wax type and why they chose it, how they matched the wick to that jar, the fragrance percentage and where they found the maximum, and the pour temperature. If the answers come easily, you have found a teacher. If the format is more party than instruction, that is fine, just book it knowing what it is.
### Shortlist two or three, then call them
Pick two or three studios worth an actual phone call and give each one the same short summary. Here is the group size, here is the occasion, here are the ages, here is how long we have, and here is who is sensitive to scent. Then listen. One will ask you three questions back and describe the room. One will send you to a booking page. One will tell you they can do it and get vague when you press. You are not asking anyone to itemize a quote or produce estimates in writing. You are comparing the gap between what you plainly said you wanted and what each place is set up to deliver, and that gap shows up in about four minutes.
Booking a kid’s birthday next? Swim lessons have their own right age.
### What is the 3-hour rule for candles?
Burn a candle no more than about three to four hours at a time, then put it out and let it cool before you relight it. Trim the wick each time, back to a short stub. Long burns overheat the container, let the wick mushroom and soot, and shorten the life of the candle you just made.
The companion rule matters just as much, and it applies the very first time you light it. Let that first burn run until the melted wax reaches the edges of the jar all the way around. Wax has a memory. If you blow it out early, the candle will keep tunneling down that same narrow channel for the rest of its life. So plan the first burn for an evening when you will be home and sitting down.
The rest is ordinary fire sense. Never leave a burning candle unattended. Keep it away from drafts, vents and open windows, since moving air makes the flame flicker, smoke and burn unevenly. Keep it well clear of curtains, paper, bookshelves, kids and pets, and on a stable, heat-safe surface. Stop burning when a small amount of wax is left in the bottom, rather than running it dry against the glass.
### Is candle making a profitable hobby?
It can be, but a class is not a business course, and the gap between the two is wide. Selling candles means buying wax, vessels, wicks, fragrance, labels and packaging at volume, testing every combination until it burns safely, and pricing your own labor into a product that customers compare against mass-produced jars.
Want another hands-on hobby? Here’s how to learn cake decorating.
The part people underestimate is testing. Every new vessel, every new fragrance, every new wax lot potentially changes how a wick performs, and a candle sold to the public needs to burn safely in someone else’s house. That is burn logs, discarded batches and time before a single sale. There are also labeling and safety expectations for anything sold, which are worth researching properly for your state and your sales channel before you list anything. Take the class because it is fun. Treat the business question as a separate project with its own homework.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long do candle making classes take?
A.  It varies a lot by format, so confirm it when you book. A drop-in pour bar can be quick, while a taught class with a set start time runs longer. The question that trips people up is whether the posted length includes the time your jar needs to set before you can carry it out, or whether that is extra.
### Q. Is candle making difficult?
A.  Pouring one is easy. Designing one is not. In a class the hard decisions, wax, wick size, vessel and pour temperature, are already made, so the skill you use is choosing a scent and following instructions. Doing it from scratch at home is harder, because you have to test wicks and pour temperatures yourself and burn the results to find out what worked.
### Q. Where can I make my own candle in St. Louis, Mo?
A.  Look at a few venue types rather than one. Dedicated candle studios and pour bars run open sessions and private bookings. Craft and paint studios often add candle nights to their calendar. Some gift and home goods shops host workshops in a back room, and independent makers take private group bookings. Community centers and event spaces sometimes bring a maker in for a one-off.
### Q. Is it cheaper to make your own candles or buy them?
A.  Buying is cheaper for one candle, every time. Making becomes competitive only at volume, once you have bought wax, wicks, vessels, fragrance and equipment and spread that across many jars, and only if you do not count your own time. A class is priced as an experience, not as a cheaper way to get a candle, and it is fair to judge it that way.
### Q. How many candles does a 10 lb bag of soy wax make?
A.  It depends entirely on your vessel, not on the wax brand. The arithmetic is simple: divide the usable wax weight by the fill weight of one jar. A small tin takes a fraction of what a wide three-wick vessel takes, so the same bag might fill a lot of little containers or far fewer big ones. Weigh one filled jar and do the division.
### Q. What not to do when making candles?
A.  Do not eyeball the fragrance. It is a percentage of wax weight, and every wax has a published maximum you should stay under. Do not pour at a guessed temperature, do not skip stirring after the fragrance goes in, and do not move or chill a jar to speed setting. Never leave melting wax unattended, and never assume an untested wick is safe.
### Q. Where can I find a candlemaking course?
A.  Beyond one-off studio sessions, check community college continuing education catalogs, city and county parks and recreation class listings, and library maker spaces, which run seasonal craft classes. Online, wax and fragrance suppliers publish detailed technical guides and structured courses, and independent makers sell recorded curricula. For safety and testing method, supplier documentation is usually the most reliable reading.
### Q. Can kids do a candle making class?
A.  Often yes, but age policies differ and you must ask first. Some studios set a minimum age for anyone handling hot wax, some let younger children choose the fragrance and decorate while an adult pours, and some run family sessions built around that split. Confirm the policy and the adult-to-child ratio before you promise a birthday party.

## Aerial Silks Classes: How Hard Is It?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/aerial-silks-classes-st-louis-how-hard-is-it
Dana went to the show for somebody else’s birthday. Folding chairs, a low stage, a converted warehouse space with exposed beams, and she spent the whole second act with her head tilted back. Two performers climbed a pair of red silks to the ceiling, wrapped themselves in the fabric, and dropped. She got a ride back to Tower Grove and could not stop thinking about it. The next morning she looked up classes and talked herself out of it before lunch. She had not done a pull-up since middle school. She was thirty-four. Everyone in the videos looked like they had been doing this since they were nine, and none of them looked like her.
The same week, a mom in Kirkwood was working on a different version of the question. Her daughter had spent one week of summer camp on a low trapeze and a fabric hammock and had talked about almost nothing else since. The mom wanted the boring answers. How young is too young. Whether anyone stands underneath the kid. What happens the first time she is eight feet up and gets scared. She had signed this family up for enough activities to know that a five-minute phone call would tell her more than the website did.
Here is what this covers. What a beginner aerial silks class actually asks of your body, and why grip and skin, not upper-body strength, are what stop most people in the first month. What happens in a first class, including the two or three foundation skills nearly every studio teaches first. What to wear and what to leave in the car. How recreational circus programs are structured, and what lyra, aerial sling, static trapeze and floor acrobatics feel like next to silks. The honest answer to the weight question, which is a rigging question rather than a body question. The real risks, and the health conditions a studio will ask about before you climb. How pricing tends to be structured. How to shortlist two or three studios worth visiting. And at the end, a note to studios around the metro about the beginner page most of them have not written yet.
### How hard is it to learn aerial silks in St. Louis?
Hard in an unglamorous way, and easier to start than it looks. A beginner class is mostly conditioning plus two or three foundation skills. Grip strength and skin tolerance limit you first, not upper-body power. Progress arrives in months rather than weeks, and twice-a-week attendance beats occasional long sessions.
That is the part the videos hide. What looks like a strength sport from the audience is, for the first few months, mostly a patience sport. Nobody walks into a beginner class and gets asked to muscle their bodyweight up a rope. They get asked to hold on, to squeeze fabric between their feet, and to stop gripping so hard with their hands that their forearms quit before the drill does.
### Grip and skin, not biceps
Ask anyone in their first month what hurts and you will hear the same two answers. Forearms, and skin. Grip endurance is the true early limiter, because everything on silks starts with holding fabric that wants to slide. Your hands give out well before your back or shoulders do, and that feels like failure when it is really just a very trainable weakness.
Skin tolerance is the second one, and it surprises people more. Fabric under load rubs, and the classic beginner marks show up on the insides of the upper arms, the backs of the knees, and the tops of the feet where a footlock sits. Bruises and raw patches are normal. They fade, and the same spots stop complaining as tolerance builds, which is a real physical adaptation and not just toughness. In our experience the people who quit in week three quit because nobody told them this was expected.
### What progress actually looks like
Measure it in months. A reasonable arc for an adult beginner attending consistently looks something like this: the first few weeks are conditioning and learning to trust the fabric, the next stretch is a climb that finally works without a fight, and somewhere after that come clean inverts and the first wrapped shapes that look like something. Two shorter sessions a week beat one long weekend session almost every time, because grip and skin adapt to frequency rather than duration.
One honest note about plateaus. Almost everybody hits a wall right where the climb should be getting easy, and almost everybody thinks it is a strength problem. Usually it is technique: feet in the wrong place, hands too high, or a body trying to pull when it should be standing up. Good instructors spot that in about four seconds. That is most of what you are paying for.
### What happens in your first aerial silks class?
Less flying than you expect and more floor work. A typical beginner session opens with a warm-up and conditioning, then teaches two or three foundation skills that everything else is built from: a climb, a basic footlock, and an invert. You stay low. You repeat things. You leave sore in places you did not plan for.
The climbs have names, and you will hear them on day one. A French climb uses the fabric wrapped around the body and is often taught first because it is forgiving. A Russian climb, sometimes taught alongside it, uses a foot lock created by the fabric and moves faster once it clicks. A footlock is exactly what it sounds like: a wrap that secures one foot so you can hang and shape without holding your whole weight in your hands. Inverting is turning upside down from a hang, and it is a core skill dressed up as a trick.
### What to wear, and what to leave in the car
Leggings and a fitted top with sleeves. That is the standard answer everywhere, and it is not a dress code, it is friction. Bare skin slips against fabric and then burns when it stops slipping, so covering the backs of the knees and the insides of the arms makes a real difference on day one. Fitted matters too, because loose fabric gets caught in wraps.
Leave the rest in the car. No jewelry, especially rings and dangling earrings, and no watches. No zippers, buttons or hardware that can snag or tear silk. No lotion, oil or heavy moisturizer that day, because slick skin is genuinely dangerous on fabric. Long hair tied back and off the neck. Nails short enough that you can grip without them digging in. Most studios go barefoot, so no socks unless the studio says otherwise.
### Mats, spotting and how crowded the class is
Crash mats under the apparatus and a spotter nearby are standard practice for beginners, and their absence is worth asking about rather than assuming. Beginner classes are usually capped, because one instructor cannot spot six people at once and everyone needs their own fabric. If a beginner class is large, ask how many instructors are on the floor. That single number tells you a lot about how much correction you will actually receive.
### How does circus school work?
Recreational circus runs on levels, not seasons. You start in a beginner or intro class, learn a fixed set of foundation skills, and move up when an instructor says you are ready rather than when a calendar says so. Most adults never audition for anything. They take class the way other people take yoga.
There is usually a split worth understanding. Recreational tracks are open enrollment, ability-mixed and built around fitness and fun. Pre-professional or performance tracks add training hours, technique requirements, sometimes an audition, and a student showcase at the end of a term. A studio may run both under the same roof, and the beginner door is the same door. Youth programs run on their own ladder with age minimums, and if you are also weighing a tumbling class for a kid, the same evaluation habits apply as when you are signing a kid up for gymnastics.
### The rest of the apparatus family
Silks are one member of a family, and trying the others early is smart. Aerial sling, also called hammock, is a loop of the same fabric rather than two tails, and it is often the gentlest entry point because it supports more of you and asks less of your grip. Lyra, the aerial hoop, is a steel ring that gives you something rigid to hold, which many beginners find far less intimidating than fabric that moves.
Static trapeze is a bar and two ropes, and it is deceptively demanding on the shoulders and the hands. It is a different animal from flying trapeze, which needs a rig, a net and a catcher and is far less common as a weekly drop-in. Floor acrobatics, handstands and partner acro round out the family, and they are the least glamorous and most useful thing you can add, because almost every aerial problem is a core and shoulder problem in disguise. Plenty of people end up loving an apparatus they only tried because silks class was full.
### Is there a weight limit for aerial silks?
This is a rigging question, not a body question. Aerial equipment is engineered and rated, and the rated capacity belongs to the rigging point, the hardware and the apparatus, not to a rule of thumb someone repeats online. Some studios publish a policy, many have none, and the only reliable answer comes from asking the studio.
Say it plainly, because people are anxious to ask and often just quietly do not sign up. Properly installed aerial rigging is rated well above what a person weighs, with a substantial safety factor built in, because equipment has to handle dynamic load, which is the force of a drop, not just the static weight of a body hanging still. That engineering margin is why the honest answer is about hardware.
So ask it as a hardware question when you call. What is your rigging rated for, who installed it, and do you have a stated policy? A studio that answers clearly and without weirdness is telling you exactly what kind of room it is. And if a studio has a published limit, that is not a judgment, it is a specification that comes from their building and their gear. Aerial classes around the metro are full of adults of every build who could not do a single climb in January.
### What are the risks of aerial silks?
Real but manageable, and mostly ordinary. The everyday stuff is skin abrasion, bruising, and sore forearms and shoulders. The overuse injuries that show up later cluster in the shoulders, wrists and elbows. The serious risk is a fall, which is exactly why crash mats, spotting and a coached progression from low heights are standard for beginners.
The everyday risks resolve themselves. Fabric burns and bruises are the cost of admission and they fade, though it helps to know that a hot shower over a fresh fabric burn is its own small education. Nobody warns you about that one twice.
Overuse is the one that quietly ends people’s first year, and it comes from doing too much too soon. Shoulders take a lot of load in a hang, and wrists take it in inverts and acro. Adding a third or fourth class a week the moment things start clicking is the classic mistake. Build slowly, rest, and tell an instructor when something aches rather than working around it silently.
### The health conditions a studio will ask about
Studios commonly ask new students to disclose a short list, and inversion is the reason for most of it. Typical categories include recent surgery, pregnancy, uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or other eye conditions affected by being upside down, heart conditions, vertigo, osteoporosis, a recent concussion, and existing shoulder or wrist injuries.
None of that is a list of disqualifications, and none of it is something you should decide from an article. These are conversations to have with the studio and with your physician, in that order or the reverse, and a good instructor will often have a modification ready that keeps you upright while everyone else inverts. What matters is that you say it out loud on the intake form instead of hoping it will not come up.
### How much do aerial silks classes cost?
Pricing follows a predictable shape even though the numbers move. An intro or trial class is usually priced below a regular drop-in. Class packs and monthly memberships cost less per class than drop-ins. Small-group and private lessons cost more. Apparatus rental or open-gym time is often sold separately. Confirm current pricing with the studio.
Anybody quoting you a firm number for this category is quoting one studio they saw once. What is stable is the structure, and once you know the structure you can read any price sheet in about a minute. The intro class exists to get you in the door and is the right first purchase for almost everyone. A pack makes sense only once you know you will use it before it expires, so ask about expiration dates before you buy one.
Two costs people forget. Open-gym or practice time, where you work on your own without instruction, is frequently a separate line and is often the single best value once you have skills worth drilling. And gear is minimal, which is a genuine relief: leggings, a fitted top, maybe grip aids later. There is no equipment purchase standing between you and a first class.
Chasing a stage life, not a hobby? See how St. Louis performers get signed.
### How do you pick a studio worth a first month?
Shortlist two or three worth visiting, then go interview them. Say plainly what you want and where you are starting from: your goal, your current fitness, any injury history, and the nights you can realistically show up. Then compare that against what each studio is actually set up to provide. The gap is the signal.
You are not asking anyone for three written estimates. Nobody in this world works that way and asking for it tells the room you have never taken a class. What you are doing is much simpler. You describe your situation the same way to each place, and you notice which one asks a follow-up question, which one recommends the sling class instead because you mentioned a cranky wrist, and which one just sends you a link to the schedule.
### The four questions worth asking
Ask who rigs and inspects the equipment, and how often. Ask what the instructor’s training and certification path was, since aerial has several recognized instructor pathways and the answer should come easily. Ask how many students per instructor in a beginner class. Ask whether crash mats and spotting are standard for beginners, or only sometimes. Four questions, five minutes, and the difference in how the answers arrive is worth more than any price comparison.
Then go stand in the space. Ceiling height, floor surface, how the mats look, whether the room is hot in August, and whether the class before yours looked like people having a good time. Aerial studios sit in the same category as the metro’s independent gyms and studios in one important way: the room’s culture decides whether you come back in week four.
Ready to find an intro class near you? You can browse circus and acrobatics studios on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three worth a visit, and bring the same four questions to each one: who rigs and inspects the equipment, what training the instructors have, how many students are in a beginner class, and whether mats and spotting are standard. How readily those answers come back tells you most of what you need.
If you run a business in this space, get on the directory.
### For St. Louis aerial and circus studios
Think about Dana at eight in the morning, phone in hand, three tabs open, talking herself out of the thing she wanted to do. She was not shopping on price. She was looking for one page that told her she would not be the only beginner in the room, and nobody had written it.
So write it. Describe an actual beginner class minute by minute: the warm-up, the conditioning, the two or three skills you teach first, how low the fabric stays. Say what to wear in plain words, and say the leave-it-at-home list too, because no jewelry, no zippers and no lotion is exactly the kind of detail that removes anxiety before it starts. Name the path from intro class to level one, and say who decides when someone moves up.
Then publish the operational facts that people are too polite to ask. Which apparatus you offer and which are open to beginners. Age minimums by program, stated as numbers. Who rigs your equipment, who inspects it, and on what schedule. Your beginner class cap and your instructor-to-student ratio. Whether mats and spotting are standard. If you have a rigging capacity policy, publish it as a specification with the reason attached, because how you word that sentence decides whether a whole group of people ever emails you.
And write one honest paragraph about what the first month feels like. Sore forearms. Bruises on the insides of the arms and the tops of the feet. A climb that does not work for three weeks and then suddenly does. Studios worry that honesty scares people off. It does the opposite: it is the paragraph a nervous adult in Maplewood or Florissant screenshots and sends to a friend with the words “ok, doing this.”
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I take trapeze classes in St. Louis?
A.  Look for studios with a rigged ceiling that list trapeze on their schedule, and check which kind they mean. Static trapeze, a fixed bar on two ropes, is the common recreational class and often shares a class slot with lyra or silks. Flying trapeze needs a dedicated rig, a net and a catcher, so it is far rarer and usually offered as a session or a special event rather than a weekly class. Ask before you book.
### Q. Where can I find aerial classes in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the circus and acrobatics category in the directory, then filter by what your week can hold: distance, evening availability, and whether the studio runs a true intro class rather than dropping newcomers into a mixed level. Aerial spaces need high ceilings, so they are often tucked into converted industrial buildings and gyms rather than storefronts, which means map searching alone tends to miss several of them.
### Q. What is the best age to start aerial classes?
A.  There is no single right age, and studios set their own minimums by program, commonly starting somewhere in the elementary years for youth classes and around the teen years for adult-track classes. What matters more than age is whether a child can follow safety instructions reliably and listen when an instructor says stop. Adults start at every age, including in their fifties and sixties. Ask each studio for its stated minimum.
### Q. Is aerial silks a good hobby?
A.  For a lot of people, yes, and for reasons beyond fitness. It builds real strength and body awareness, it has a visible skill ladder that keeps motivation high, and the social side is unusually warm because everyone in the room remembers being terrible at it. The honest counterweights are the time it takes to progress, the bruising, and the fact that you cannot practice at home without proper rigging.
### Q. What are people who do aerial silks called?
A.  An aerialist. That covers anyone working on hanging apparatus, so silks, lyra, sling and trapeze performers are all aerialists, and someone may specify further by naming the apparatus. The silks themselves go by several names: aerial silks, tissu, and simply fabric. You will hear all three in the same class, sometimes in the same sentence, and none of them is more correct than the others.
### Q. Who should not do aerial yoga?
A.  Because aerial yoga involves inversions, studios commonly ask about recent surgery, pregnancy, uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or other eye conditions affected by being upside down, heart conditions, vertigo, osteoporosis, recent concussion, and shoulder or wrist injuries. None of these is automatically disqualifying. They are conversations to have with the studio and your physician, and instructors can often offer an upright modification rather than turning someone away.
### Q. Is aerial silk harder than pole dancing?
A.  They are hard in different places, so most people find one clicks faster than the other. Pole gives you a rigid surface and lets you build from standing, and skin contact and grip strength are still central. Silks give you a moving surface, more height early, and more work in the hands and shoulders before anything looks graceful. Try one class of each if you can before committing to a pack.
### Q. Do I need to be flexible to start aerial silks?
A.  No. Flexibility makes shapes look prettier later, but it stops nobody at the beginning, and beginner classes are built for average range of motion. What helps far more on day one is being willing to hang on when your forearms complain, and being fine with looking clumsy in front of strangers. Flexibility improves as a side effect of showing up, which is the easiest kind of progress to get.

## Your Coffee Should Smell Like Highway 40: Where to Buy Fresh Beans in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-fresh-coffee-beans-in-st-louis
Highway 40 smells like coffee. Crack the window where it runs past the Kaldi’s and Ronnoco roasteries and the car fills with it, warm and toasty. Kaldi’s own marketing director calls that little stretch “roasters row.” Then you get home, slit open the bag you grabbed at the grocery store, lean in, and smell almost nothing. Same city. Same week. Two completely different cups.
Here is the part most of us never learned in school. In 1920, St. Louis was considered the largest inland coffee hub in the United States, with green beans coming up the Mississippi from New Orleans to be roasted here. Ronnoco, still based in town, is the O’Connor brothers’ last name spelled backward, and they started it after watching a gas-powered roaster at the 1904 World’s Fair. A century later this is still a roasting town. You can buy a bag that came out of a roaster a few miles from your kitchen this week. You just have to know which counter to walk up to, and which date to read on the bag.
St. Louis Public Radio spent a morning at Sump Coffee on South Jefferson and described the fruity smell of fresh-brewed coffee filling the room. The pour-over menu tells you where each coffee grew, Sumatra or Colombia or Kenya, and every bean brewed there is roasted a few miles north in an unassuming warehouse in Old North. Owner Scott Carey loads about 20 pounds of beans at a time, and as he told the station, if you listen closely you can hear them cracking as they roast. That is what fresh means. Not a word on a shiny bag. A sound, a smell, a date.
### Where can I buy decent coffee beans in St. Louis?
Buy from the people who roast it. Sump Coffee at 3700 S. Jefferson Ave. sells beans roasted in its own Old North roastery. Goshen Coffee Roasters is at 910 Geyer Ave., La Cosecha Coffee Roasters is at 7360 Manchester Road in Maplewood, and Blueprint Coffee pours on Watson Road. Pick the bag with the most recent roast date, keep it whole, and buy only enough for a week or two.
That last line is the one that saves you money. The National Coffee Association says coffee begins to lose freshness almost immediately after roasting, and that roasted beans keep their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature. Do the math on the big “value” bag. If it takes you six weeks to finish, you spend at least the last three of them paying for flat coffee. The cheapest bag in the aisle per ounce is often the most expensive one per good cup. The association’s own advice is to buy smaller batches, enough for one or two weeks. A roaster’s counter is the one place in town where the bag in your hand might have been roasted days ago, and where the person behind the register can tell you the exact day without looking it up. Ask. A good roaster loves that question.
The map is wider than one neighborhood. Northwest Coffee has a cafe at 8650 Big Bend Blvd. in Webster Groves and another at 4251 Laclede Ave. in the city. Coffeestamp sits at 2511 S. Jefferson Ave., a short drive up the street from Sump. Out in St. Charles, Picasso’s Coffee is at 101 N. Main St. on the old brick street. If Maplewood is your corner of the map, the walkable stretch of Manchester Road gets its own write-up in our local guide to coffee in Maplewood.
### The Saturday market run
Some of the best bean shopping in town happens on a folding table. The Tower Grove Farmers’ Market runs Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in Tower Grove Park during the season. If a roaster has a table that morning, you can taste before you commit, ask how last week’s batch turned out, and carry home a bag that was roasted days earlier. That is also where you meet the smallest roasters, the ones too new to have a storefront.
The habit that pays off here is simple. Ask which roaster your favorite coffee bar pours, then buy a retail bag of that exact coffee to take home. You already know you like it. Now you can drink it in your own kitchen, in your own mug, at six in the morning before anyone else is awake.
### How to read a coffee bag in ten seconds
Flip the bag over and look for a roast date first. A far-off “best by” stamp only tells you when the seller stops vouching for it. The roast date tells you when the clock started. If a bag shows no roast date at all, that silence is your answer, and it belongs back on the shelf.
Then read the rest. A useful bag tells you where the coffee grew, how it was processed, and roughly how dark it was roasted. Process, whether washed, natural or honey, shapes flavor as much as origin does. Lighter roasts lean bright and fruity, darker roasts lean bold and bittersweet, and neither one is better. Buy toward the flavors you already enjoy. Words like “gourmet” and “premium” in a fancy font tell you nothing about the cup. A plain bag from a small roaster with a clear date and a few honest details will almost always beat the glossy one beside it.
Whole bean or ground? Whole bean, nearly every time. The oils and gases that carry coffee’s smell stay locked inside the bean until you break it open, and grinding exposes all of it to the air at once. That is why the same coffee tastes bright at the bar and dull at home: the shop ground it seconds before brewing. If you have no grinder, buy smaller bags more often and ask the roaster to grind for your specific brewer.
Wide awake and looking for a Saturday that isn’t errands? Here’s how hard aerial silks really is in St. Louis.
### Keeping a good bag good at home
Air, moisture, heat and light are what turn a great bag flat. Keep beans in an opaque, airtight container in a cool, dark cupboard, and keep them away from the cabinet over the oven or next to the dishwasher, which the National Coffee Association flags as spots that get too warm. That pretty clear jar on the counter? It lets in light. The association’s own advice is to use jars of beans as decor only.
The freezer is the eternal argument. According to the association, roasted beans keep their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature and three to four months frozen, but only in a truly airtight container, because coffee soaks up moisture and odors from the air around it. If you freeze, pull out no more than a week’s worth at a time and put the rest back before condensation forms. For most people finishing a bag in a week or two, the cupboard is all you need.
### What coffee gear actually improves your cup at home?
A burr grinder does more for your coffee than any brewer you can buy. It crushes beans between two burrs to an even size, so the grounds brew evenly, while a blade grinder just chops them into chunks and dust. If your budget stretches to a single upgrade, make it the grinder and keep your old brewer.
Everything after that is polish. A small kitchen scale lets you use the same coffee-to-water ratio every morning, so a good cup becomes repeatable instead of lucky. A gooseneck kettle gives you control for pour-over. A drip machine, a pour-over cone and a French press all make excellent coffee for very little money. Dial in a pour-over and a good plate and you’ve nearly recreated the city’s best breakfast and brunch at your own counter.
### Why a river town has so many roasters
The modern chapter started small. Howard Lerner and Suzanne Langlois opened the first Kaldi’s Coffee on DeMun Avenue in 1994, one of the first modern coffeehouses in the area, and Kaldi’s now runs 13 cafes around St. Louis. Its marketing director says plenty of people now working at roasters around town got their start in its training program. Scott Carey opened Sump in 2011 and began roasting his own beans in 2012, back when, as he puts it, there was specialty coffee in New York but it didn’t feel like that was happening here.
The door is wider now. Co-roasting spaces like First Crack walk newcomers through the roasting process and give them access to the equipment, which is how a lot of very small roasters get going. Firaol Ahmed used First Crack to sample coffee while he built Moii Coffee from his dorm room at St. Louis University, and Moii now helps local roasters connect with coffee farmers in Ethiopia. So when you pick up a bag at a market table with a hand-written label, it may well have started in a shared roaster like that, run by someone still learning your name. That is a good bag to buy. You are early.
Katie Moon, who curated a coffee exhibit at the Missouri History Museum, put the whole guide in one line: “I don’t know if I’ve ever had bad coffee in St. Louis. So if there’s one by you, just go.”
### Keep the roaster in business
Buy direct and buy often. When you buy beans at the roaster’s counter, a market table or their own website, more of your money stays with the person who stood next to that loud machine. Tag the roaster when you post your pour-over. Leave an honest review. Bring a bag as a host gift instead of a bottle of wine. None of it costs much, and all of it adds up for a small shop on thin margins.
Many roasters also run a coffee bar, which turns a bean run into a good hour. You can taste the whole range in one sitting and grab a bag on the way out. Some of those rooms double as solid places to get work done, which we sorted through in our guide to the best coffee shops to work remotely.
Want a bag roasted this week, not this season? Browse coffee stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the roaster or shop closest to you, and walk in with one question ready: when were these roasted?
If you own a roastery, a coffee bar or a little cafe that smells like this at 7 a.m., this part is for you. The people reading this page are your next regulars, and they are deciding where to buy before they ever leave the house. List your shop, then step up to Gold so your roast days, your bags and your hours sit right where those customers are already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I know which coffee beans to buy?
A.  Start with the roast date, then match the label to your taste. Origin, process and roast level tell you far more than words like “premium.” Lighter roasts lean bright and fruity, darker roasts lean bold and bittersweet. Pick the flavors you already enjoy, and favor the bag roasted most recently.
### Q. How can you tell if coffee beans are high quality?
A.  Quality shows in specifics, not slogans. A good bag names the origin, the process, the roast level and a recent roast date. The beans should look even in size and color and smell fresh when you open the bag. Vague words and glossy packaging are not quality signals.
### Q. Is it okay to store coffee beans in a Ziploc bag?
A.  It works in a pinch, but it isn’t ideal. A zip bag is clear, so it lets in light, and it rarely seals out all the air. If you use one, squeeze out the air, seal it tight and keep it in a dark cupboard. An opaque, airtight container does better.
### Q. How long do coffee beans stay fresh in a sealed bag?
A.  An unopened retail package keeps until its best-by date, according to the National Coffee Association. Once opened and moved to an airtight container, roasted beans hold their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature. That is why buying a week or two at a time beats buying in bulk.
### Q. What is the best way to store coffee beans for long-term storage?
A.  Freeze them in a truly airtight container. Frozen roasted beans keep their freshness for about three to four months. Take out no more than a week’s worth at a time and return the rest quickly, before condensation forms, because coffee soaks up moisture and odors from the air.
### Q. Is it really worth buying an expensive coffee bean?
A.  Often yes, but price isn’t the point, freshness is. A pricey bag that sat for months loses to a cheaper bag roasted last week. Spend a little more for a specific origin, careful processing and a recent roast date, and you’ll taste it. Skip the premium that is really just packaging.

## That 1964 Quarter in Dad's Coffee Can Isn't a Quarter
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-sell-coins-in-st-louis-without-getting-ripped-off
Dad’s coffee can weighs more than loose change should. Cold metal against your palm, and when you tip it on the basement floor of a parent’s house in Florissant, the coins slide against each other with a dull, heavy hiss. Under it sits a blue folder of pennies pressed into little round holes, and nobody left to ask what any of it meant to them.
You do not have to become a coin expert this week, and you do not have to decide anything today. You need three things: the silver math, more than one offer, and one look from someone who is not trying to buy.
That last one matters most. The person who prices your coins at a counter is often the person hoping to buy them. That is a conflict, not a crime, and the fix is not suspicion. It is more offers.
### How do you get coins appraised without getting ripped off?
Get two or more offers, ask each buyer to separate melt value from collector value out loud, and do not clean anything first. For an inherited collection, let someone who is not buying take a look before anyone writes you a check. In St. Louis, a coin club meeting or the big summer coin show in St. Charles gives you both.
Here is what that looks like at the show. The Missouri Numismatic Society says its annual show at the St. Charles Convention Center brings together more than 150 coin dealers, buying and selling. You set the same Morgan dollar on one felt-covered table, then another, then another. Offers stop being a verdict and start being a market. You hear a number, say thank you, walk twenty steps and hear another. The society posts the next dates on its annual coin show page.
You do not have to wait for summer for that second look. The society says it normally meets on the fourth Wednesday of each month at the American Legion Post # 397, with doors at 6:00 p.m. and the meeting at 7:00 p.m. Getting there is the easy part: off Olive and Ballas, just east of Highway 270, turn onto E. Rue de la Banque, the short street that runs between Bristol’s Bar & Grill and a bank on the north side of Olive. The post is at number 934. Its welcome page puts it simply: “You are welcome to attend our next monthly club meeting.” Each meeting centers on a 30 to 40 minute talk by a member. Walk in with a few coins in a sandwich bag, the plastic crinkling in your coat pocket, and your questions written down. These are people who come to learn, not to buy from you.
And one Missouri detail most coin guides never mention: the Missouri Department of Revenue says eligible individuals can subtract 100% of their federally reported capital gains on their Missouri income tax return. More on that below.
### Sort the silver before anyone else does
Spread the coins on an old bath towel under a good lamp, so nothing rolls and nothing scratches. Then sort by date. The Coinage Act of 1965 eliminated silver from the circulating dime and quarter, and cut the half dollar from 90% silver to 40%. Before that, the dime, quarter and half dollar were struck in 90 percent silver. Every dime, quarter and half dated 1964 or earlier goes in your silver pile. Can’t read a worn date? Tilt the coin on its edge under the lamp. Clad coins give themselves away with a thin copper stripe, their copper core showing right there on the rim. Silver stays bright white all the way around.
Now the math nobody at a counter will do for you. A 1964 quarter weighs 6.25 grams, and 90% of that is silver: about 0.18 of an ounce, the same kind of ounce silver is priced in. Search “silver spot price” on the day you sell, multiply it by 0.18, and that is roughly the melt value of one 1964 quarter. Write it on a sticky note and put it in your pocket.
That little yellow square changes the whole conversation. When a buyer quotes you a price on common silver, you know in five seconds whether it is fair, because you did the arithmetic at your own kitchen table first. Everything above melt is collector value, the premium someone pays because a coin is scarce or beautifully kept.
### Do not clean anything. Not even once.
This is the mistake that costs families the most, and it comes from love. You want Dad’s coins to look their best, so you reach for a toothbrush. Stop. Cleaning a collectible coin scratches the surface and can slash its collector value. Collectors prize original surfaces, toning and all. Leave every coin exactly as you found it, dust and all, and handle it by the edges.
### Can you check a coin’s value at home first?
Yes, and you should, as long as you know what home tools can and cannot do. A free coin-identifying app is good at naming a coin. It is weaker at pricing yours, because value depends on condition and a phone photo cannot grade a coin the way a person holding it can.
Use the app to sort the pile fast. Then look the standouts up in a recognized price guide or in completed sales, not asking prices. Anyone can list a coin for a dream number. Sold prices are what buyers actually paid. Match your coin’s honest condition to the price column, not the best-case one.
### Where to sell in St. Louis: dealer, pawn, auction or show
You have a handful of realistic paths in the metro, and each fits a different kind of collection and a different kind of hurry.
### Coin and stamp dealers
A dedicated dealer is usually the best place to start for anything beyond loose silver, because they know the market and can price collector coins on the spot. Good ones explain how they reached a number and separate melt from collector value in front of you. A dealer buys to resell, so the offer sits below retail. That is normal. Get two anyway.
### Pawn shops
A pawn shop is built for speed, not specialist coin knowledge. It can be fine for common silver you want turned into cash today, but a genuine key date can get treated like scrap. Know your melt number before you walk in, and read up on how pawn shops work in St. Louis first.
### Auction houses
For real rarities, an auction lets collectors bid against each other, which can beat a single dealer offer. The cost is time and a commission. Learning how auction houses work in St. Louis tells you whether your coins are worth consigning. The Missouri Numismatic Society’s show even hosts a Friday evening auction by Scotsman Auction Company, and the society says more than 1,000 lots were offered at the last show.
### The summer coin show
If you can wait, this is the protection play. Pack your inventory list, your sticky note and the coins in their original holders, and walk the bourse floor at the St. Charles Convention Center. Show the same coins to several dealers. Write down every number. The highest offer that comes with a clear explanation is usually the one to take.
Line up two or three offers before you sell a single coin. Browse coin & stamp dealers across the St. Louis metro, bring the same coins to each one, and ask every buyer to split melt from collector value out loud. Thinking about a quick loan instead of a sale? See how pawn shops work in St. Louis.
If you’re the coin shop, the estate-sale crew or the appraiser who explains every number out loud, families clearing a parent’s house are searching for exactly you right now. Put your shop in front of those customers.
### Handling an inherited collection
Go slow. Grief and a full house create pressure to just be done, and that pressure is exactly what a lowball offer feeds on. The coins are not going anywhere. A week of patience costs you nothing.
### Make an inventory before anyone sees it
Lay everything out and write a simple list: dates, denominations, mint marks, and anything already sealed in a plastic grading holder. Photograph the standouts. The list tells you what you have, and it protects you, because a written inventory makes it far harder for anyone to quietly set a coin aside or underquote the lot.
### Pay for an appraisal when the collection is big
For a large or clearly valuable collection, a paid written appraisal from someone who is not also trying to buy it gives you a number you can trust. For a jar of worn silver, skip it and use your sticky note.
### The red flags that mean a lowball
Pressure to decide right now. One lump price for a whole mixed pile. A shrug when you ask how the number was reached. A fair buyer expects you to shop around and will happily walk you through the math. If you feel rushed, that is your cue to say thank you and leave.
If a deal goes wrong after the fact, Missouri has a place to take it. The Missouri Attorney General’s office says to call its Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-392-8222 for more information about filing a complaint. Keep your inventory list and any receipt, because the paper trail is what makes a complaint stick.
Need to clear your head after a day of sorting? Here’s where to rent a bike and ride St. Louis.
### One Missouri tax note before you cash out
If you sell coins for more than you paid, that profit is a capital gain. The Missouri Department of Revenue says the state’s capital gains subtraction lets eligible individuals subtract 100% of their federally reported capital gains on their Missouri income tax return, claimed on Form MO-A with the MO-1040. That is the state return only. Your federal return is a separate question, so ask a tax preparer before you assume anything.
### What about the stamps in the same box?
Stamps follow different rules. The thick album of canceled stamps a relative saved for decades is often a labor of love with modest resale value, because common canceled stamps are everywhere. When value exists, it tends to hide in a handful of items: early issues, printing errors, unused stamps with original gum, or whole envelopes. Do not soak them, do not rearrange them, and do not peel anything off an old envelope. Get them in front of someone who actually trades stamps. The habits in our guide to flea market shopping in St. Louis carry over neatly to selling.
Whether it is a shoebox in Affton, a sock of wheat pennies in Belleville or a roll of halves on a counter in St. Charles, the rule is the same. Sort the silver. Never clean anything. Get more than one number. And let somebody who is not buying take a look first.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can I check if my old coins are worth anything?
A.  Sort by date first. Dimes, quarters and half dollars dated 1964 or earlier were struck in 90 percent silver, so they carry melt value. Then check the date and mint mark on the rest, use a free app to name anything unusual, and confirm value against sold prices or a dealer.
### Q. What is the best way to sell your old coins?
A.  Sort melt coins from possible collector coins, check the standouts against sold prices, then show the same coins to two or three buyers. Ask each one to explain the number. If you can wait for summer, the Missouri Numismatic Society’s show in St. Charles puts more than 150 dealers in one place.
### Q. How can I find out if my old coins are worth money?
A.  Identify each coin’s date and mint mark, then check whether that pair is scarce and how worn yours is. For a second opinion from people who are not buying, the Missouri Numismatic Society says you are welcome at its monthly meeting, normally the fourth Wednesday.
### Q. Where can I lookup the value of a coin?
A.  Use a recognized price guide for the exact date and mint mark, then cross-check completed sales rather than asking prices. For common silver, do the melt math: a 1964 quarter holds about 0.18 of an ounce of silver, so multiply that by the day’s spot price.
### Q. What is the best free app to check the value of coins?
A.  Several free coin-identifier apps will name a coin from a photo and give a rough range, which is great for sorting a big pile. Treat the price as a ballpark only, since a photo cannot grade condition. Confirm anything promising with sold listings or a dealer.
### Q. What year of coins are worth money?
A.  For silver, the line is 1964. The Coinage Act of 1965 took silver out of the circulating dime and quarter and cut the half dollar to 40% silver. Beyond silver, specific date-and-mint pairs in strong condition carry collector premiums in many years.

## $5.75 to Laugh, 18% on the Food: St. Louis Comedy Clubs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-comedy-clubs-what-to-expect-and-what-it-costs
The cocktail comes in a souvenir cup, and it is a double. That is printed right on the Funny Bone’s drink menu at Westport Plaza, a few lines above a shot called the Tanquerschäger and the menu’s own verdict on it: “It’s that kinda night!” The house lights drop. Chairs scrape. A spotlight finds a stool and a mic stand, and for the next hour a stranger is going to try to make a room full of St. Louisans laugh at things they would never say out loud.
That is the part everybody pictures. Nobody pictures the check. It slides onto a table the size of a dinner plate, in a room too dark to read it, while the headliner is still mid-bit. You tilt it toward the stage light, squint, and find a line you never budgeted for.
Better to know it now. Every price, minimum and rule below comes straight from the St. Louis clubs’ own pages: the two Funny Bone rooms at Westport Plaza and the Streets of St. Charles, Helium, and The Improv Shop in The Grove, the one that promises in writing not to pick on you.
### How much is it to go to a comedy club in St. Louis?
Cheap on a weeknight, more once a touring name and a minimum stack up. The Funny Bone’s Tuesday open mic at Westport Plaza is listed at $5.75, and its Wednesday open mic at the Streets of St. Charles is listed at $3.45. The Improv Shop says most of its shows are under $12. Helium adds a two-item per person minimum in the showroom on top of the ticket.
The ticket is the cheap part on a Tuesday. At Westport that is a five-dollar bill and three quarters, and you are in. So price the exact show you want, not the club. The good news is that the two Funny Bone rooms post their prices the way you wish everyone did: the club’s own pages say “All in pricing includes taxes and fees,” so the number you see is the number you pay at checkout.
Helium works a little differently. Its FAQ says ticket prices “include all fees (before taxes),” so expect the total to tick up once tax hits. Neither one is a trick. You just want to know which kind of price you are looking at before the group text starts doing math. Questions about a specific show go to the box office: Helium lists 314.727.1260, and the Funny Bone at Westport Plaza lists (314) 469-6692.
### The 18 percent nobody mentions at the door
Here is the line most people only find on the receipt. Helium’s own FAQ says “there will be an 18% administrative fee on all food and beverage purchases.” Same FAQ, same answer: “Food and drinks purchased in our bar and lounge do not count towards the two-item minimum.”
Read those two sentences together and the move is obvious. That cold beer you grabbed at the bar while you waited for the doors, the one sweating a ring onto the counter, does not count. You still owe two items once you sit down in the showroom. So wait. Order your first drink from your seat, and every sip counts toward the minimum instead of sitting on top of it.
That is the tip worth texting the friend who is buying. The two items do not have to be cocktails, either: Helium says the minimum “can be fulfilled with any food or drink items from the menu,” so a basket of something fried and a soda clears it. And if you want a real dinner first, Helium says food and drinks bought with a pre-show dinner reservation for the Thursday, Friday and Saturday early shows count toward the two-item minimum.
### Which room fits the night you want?
Four very different evenings hide under the word comedy, and picking the wrong one is how a good night goes flat. It almost never has anything to do with the club.
### The cheap, loud, hit-or-miss night: open mic
The Funny Bone calls Tuesday “our weekly Open Mic Night” at Westport Plaza, a room the club says has hosted St. Louis talent and nationally touring comedians since 1984. Open mic is where jokes get tested in front of strangers. Some land so hard the table shakes. Some die in a silence so complete you can hear the ice settle in your glass. For a few dollars, that swing is the whole show, and comics who love the craft will tell you it is the most honest hour in the building.
### The night where nobody gets picked on: improv
The Improv Shop sits at 3960 Chouteau in The Grove, and its FAQ answers the question every nervous first-timer is quietly asking: will they pick on me? “No. We may ask for audience suggestions, but that’s about it.” Then the line worth repeating: “we won’t single you out. We think that’s annoying.” Seating is open, parking is free in the club’s own lot east of the building, and after the show there is a fire pit on the patio. The shop rates its shows like an R movie, and says 17 is probably the minimum recommended age.
### The big-name night: touring headliners
This is the polished hour from someone you might have seen in a special or on TV. Helium says its shows usually run between 90 and 105 minutes, and it gives advice more clubs should: research the comedian first, because comedy is subjective and certain comics are not for everybody. Watch one clip before you buy four tickets. If the clip makes you wince, the live set will too.
### The sampler night: showcases
A showcase stacks several comics on one bill. It is the safest bet for a mixed group, because if one voice is not your thing, a different one is up in ten minutes. It is also how you find the local comic you will be telling people about next year.
### Do you need a reservation, and how old do you have to be?
For a weekend headliner, buy ahead. For age, it depends on the room, so check the exact show. Helium says plainly, “We are an 18+ venue.” The Improv Shop leaves kids to your discretion but calls its shows rated R. Wherever you go, bring a valid ID even if nobody has carded you in a decade.
Seats are the other surprise. At Helium, general admission is “first-come, first-sat,” and the club recommends arriving no later than 30 minutes before showtime, adding that late arrivals are not guaranteed seats. Want your whole party at one table? Helium says general admission groups should arrive at least an hour early and walk into the showroom together. It also says all sales are final, so be sure of the date before you click.
Prefer a mellower night out? Try a St. Louis candle-making class instead.
### Where to park
Helium’s FAQ says parking right outside is limited, with more on the east side of the building near Dillard’s and in the parking garage. The Improv Shop has its own free lot. Downtown and Soulard nights are a different story, so give yourself ten extra minutes to circle.
### How do you find comedy shows in St. Louis this week?
Go straight to the club calendars, because lineups change weekly and the clubs post their own prices there. Then follow the two or three comics you like, since touring dates get announced on their feeds first. When you want to compare rooms side by side by neighborhood and night, the unique things to do for adults guide pulls the city’s grown-up nights into one place.
Read the listing before you buy. Look for the words headliner, showcase or open mic, note whether there is an early and a late show, and check the age rule on that show’s own page rather than the venue’s homepage. The show is where the real rules live.
### What the clock looks like on show night
Timing is where first-timers lose the good seats. The clubs publish their own schedules, and they are more specific than most people expect.
At The Improv Shop, the first shows start at 8 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays and at 7 p.m. on Thursdays, with a later 10 p.m. show on Fridays and Saturdays. Doors open at 6 p.m., the box office opens thirty minutes before showtime, and the shop says its shows typically last around 60 to 90 minutes. The kitchen runs until 11 p.m. on Thursdays and until midnight on Fridays and Saturdays, so you can order a burger from your seat while the scene builds.
A night out, priced
### How much is it to go to a comedy club?
Cheap on a weeknight. The Funny Bone’s Tuesday open mic at Westport Plaza is listed at $5.75 and its Wednesday mic at the Streets of St. Charles at $3.45, and the Improv Shop says most of its shows are under $12. Touring headliners cost more, and Helium adds a two-item minimum per person.

The box office closes between shows, so a late show ticket cannot be picked up during the early one. At the Funny Bone at Westport Plaza, the Tuesday open mic lists doors at 7 p.m. and the show at 7:30 p.m.
Put those together and the rule is simple. Get there early, eat or drink from your seat so it counts, and leave your phone in your pocket once the lights go down. The comic can see the glow from the stage, and so can everyone behind you.
Plan the whole night, not just the hour in the dark. Browse comedy clubs across the St. Louis metro, pick the room that fits your crowd, and check that show’s price, minimum and age rule before you leave the house.

A.  At Helium, yes: a two-item per person minimum in the showroom, which any food or drink from the menu can fill. Items bought in the bar and lounge do not count, and an 18% administrative fee applies to all food and beverage. Rules differ by club, so check each show page.

A.  Helium recommends arriving no later than 30 minutes before showtime and says late arrivals are not guaranteed seats. Groups who want to sit together should come at least an hour early. The Improv Shop opens its doors at 6 p.m. and its box office thirty minutes before each show.
### Q. What are some fun adult activities in St. Louis?

### Q. Is St. Louis a party town?

A.  A comedy show is a low-pressure pick, because the room does the talking and you get an easy opener afterward. Improv works especially well if you are nervous about being singled out, since The Improv Shop says it will not do that. Catch an early show, then grab a nightcap.

## The Upload Box Won't Take Your Resume: Free St. Louis Computer Help Before You Pay for a Class
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/computer-classes-in-st-louis-beginner-to-job-ready
Where did the resume go? At a public computer in a St. Louis library, the box on the screen says “Upload your resume,” and you have no idea where the file went. You saved it. You know you saved it. The cursor blinks, the little wheel spins, and somewhere behind you a printer coughs out somebody else’s pages. Your neck is hot. You close the tab and tell yourself you’ll try again tomorrow, which is what you said yesterday. Your bus comes in twelve minutes. The application doesn’t care.
Before you pay anyone to fix that, know this: the City of St. Louis runs a job agency, SLATE, that offers financial assistance for training programs in high-demand, high-growth occupations, help that can cover tuition, books and supplies. Its Missouri Job Center also runs no-cost workshops on resume writing, online job search and succeeding on hiring tests, the timed online test that can stand between you and an interview.
Screenshot that before you pay for any computer course in St. Louis: the city may help cover it. Ask first. Pay second.
### Where can I learn basic computer skills for beginners in St. Louis?
Start at the library. The St. Louis Public Library’s Tech Connect program books in-person or virtual one-on-one appointments for technology help, scheduled for one hour, and its listed topics include searching for jobs online and basic resume writing. The St. Louis County Library has Digital Navigators who take appointments for computer and mobile device learning; fill out the form and they contact you within four weekdays to schedule. Neither one expects you to know anything when you walk in.
One change most guides haven’t caught, at the city library: St. Louis Public Library announced its hotspot checkout would end on February 28. Over $4 million in federal Emergency Connectivity Fund grants paid for it, and that federal funding has ended. If your cousin is about to ride the bus downtown for a library hotspot, text her this first, and tell her to reserve a library computer instead.
One-on-one beats a big class when you’re nervous, because the whole hour is your problem, not the room’s. Bring your own phone or laptop and a written list: the email you can’t open, the password you keep losing, the resume file that vanishes every time you hit save. Sit down, put the list on the table between you, and work it from the top.
Start one rung lower than you think you need to. There’s no shame in sitting through “this is a folder, and this is where your saved file actually goes.” That one lesson ends more of the upload-box panic than any spreadsheet class ever will.
### The free training money most people never ask about
If you are aiming past the basics, at a certificate or a real career change, go to SLATE before you pay anybody. The Missouri Job Center at 1520 Market Street downtown has resource rooms with computers, internet, printers and phones for your job search, plus workforce staff who specialize in career transitions. Register on MoJobs first, which SLATE calls the first step for job seekers, then call (314) 589-8000 and ask one plain question: “Do I qualify for training assistance?” If the answer is no, you’ve spent one phone call.
SLATE says its training programs help St. Louisans who are minorities, women and long-term unemployed get into careers in growing industries. If that’s you, the money is meant for you. Walk in with your ID, a rough resume on a thumb drive, and the one job posting that made you think “I could do that if I knew Excel.” That posting is your syllabus. Fold it in half, set it next to the keyboard in the resource room, and let every question you ask start with a line on that page.
### The handful of skills worth learning first
Every application that ever beat you has one of these five underneath it. The mouse that skates off the edge of the form, so learn mouse and keyboard control until clicking stops eating your attention. The resume that vanished, so learn files and folders. The job site that wanted you to search, filter and scroll, so learn a web browser. The “attach your resume” email that went out naked, so learn email with attachments. And the too-good message from a “recruiter” at 11 p.m., so learn internet safety: real passwords, and which links never to click.
Files and folders comes first for a reason. The afternoon you click Downloads and the resume is just sitting there, where it was the whole time, you’ll laugh out loud in a quiet library and nobody will mind. Tell anyone stuck at that upload box what took you weeks to learn: the upload box was never the test. The folder was.
### How much does a computer course cost in St. Louis?
It ranges from free to a few thousand dollars, and the price tracks the goal. SLATE’s workshops are no-cost. Community-college continuing-education courses usually carry a modest fee. Job-focused certificates cost more, and multi-week bootcamps sit at the top. Confirm current pricing directly with the provider before you commit, and ask SLATE about assistance before you pay a dime toward anything job-focused.
Two costs people forget. First, a device: a class teaches the skill, but you still need somewhere to practice. Second, time. A free class you can actually reach two evenings a week beats an expensive one across town that you’ll quietly stop attending by week three. Match the schedule to the shift you actually work. If you close at the restaurant and open at the store, a Saturday-morning appointment you can keep is worth more than a weeknight class you’ll miss twice and then drop. Look at the bus route too. A class that takes two transfers in January stops being a class by February. Choosing among options works a lot like weighing tutoring and learning centers across the metro: fit and pace matter more than the brochure.

### Where can seniors learn basic computer skills for free?
The same library appointments work beautifully for older beginners, because nobody rushes you and nobody grades you. Bring the grandkid’s text you couldn’t open and the bank login that locked you out. Write each step in a spiral notebook while the helper talks, then do it again yourself before you leave. The second time is when it sticks.
Ask a grandkid or a neighbor to sit with you for the first practice session at home, but keep your hands on the mouse. Helpers mean well and then do it for you, fast, and you’re left watching instead of learning. Say it kindly and out loud: “Tell me, don’t touch.” It feels awkward for about four minutes and then it works. Practice the same small task three days in a row, open the email, open the attachment, save it, find it again, before you move on to anything new.
Learning this later in life isn’t harder, just different, and confidence is usually the real barrier rather than ability. Give yourself permission to book a second appointment for the same question.
