### How do you turn a class into real skill?
Shoot between lessons, on purpose. A class hands you the map; the skill comes from mileage. Give yourself one small project a week: one week on window light, one on portraits of the people at your own dinner table, one on your own street at dusk. Then sit with the results, the bad ones especially. You learn far more from a failed frame you understand than a lucky one you don’t.
Planning a family trip to practice on? If you would rather sleep in a camper than a tent, see what renting an RV in St. Louis actually costs before you reserve a site with hookups.
Find your people, too. A class group chat or a weekend photo walk keeps you shooting when the motivation dips. Some hobbyists turn that momentum into side income, shooting events, portraits or products, and our guide to part-time jobs in St. Louis is a good place to see what’s out there. A few go further and build a real business around the camera, which carries its own startup math, laid out in our look at the cost to start a business.
People are asking
### Do photographers make good money?
Modest money, mostly counted by the hour: in its latest count the Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median photographer at $21.47 an hour, with the lowest 10 percent under $14.82 and the highest 10 percent above $44.14. The niche moves the number, from a median of $30.04 an hour in publishing, broadcasting and content work to $18.84 in photographic services, and 67 percent of photographers are self-employed, which means the advertising, the scheduling and the bill paying are theirs too. Part-time work is common and wedding photographers are busiest in the summer and fall, so the honest test is a few weekend jobs first, on your feet for hours with heavy gear on your shoulder, before you quit anything.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth it to take photography classes?
A.  For most beginners, yes. A class gives you a structure, a deadline and someone who catches the mistakes you can’t see yet. In St. Louis the risk is small: STLCC’s continuing-education photography classes start at $29 for a single online session, so you can test the water before committing to anything longer.
### Q. What is the best photography course for beginners?
A.  A broad fundamentals class that covers exposure, aperture, shutter speed and composition, with hands-on assignments and real feedback. If you only shoot on a phone, a short iPhone class is a gentle start. If you own a camera with interchangeable lenses, begin with an introduction class and build from there.
### Q. What are the 7 basics of photography?
A.  There’s no single official list, but the version beginner classes keep coming back to is exposure, aperture, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, composition and focus. The first four decide how bright and sharp the picture is. White balance handles color, composition arranges the frame, and focus decides what’s crisp.
### Q. How long does it take to learn photography?
A.  The basics take a few weeks; confident shooting takes a few months of regular practice. Many continuing-education classes run four or five sessions, which is enough to get you off automatic mode. After that, how often you shoot matters far more than the calendar.
### Q. What do I need for beginner photography?
A.  Less than you think. A phone or basic camera, a memory card and a spare battery cover most beginner needs. Check each class listing for its camera requirement, since some ask for an interchangeable-lens camera. Skip extra lenses, lights and filters until you know exactly what frustrates you.
### Q. How can I teach myself photography?
A.  Pick one free fundamentals course and finish it, then shoot every day with the camera you own. Give yourself a small project each week, review your pictures honestly, and study photos you admire to work out where the photographer stood and where the light came from. A gallery visit helps more than you’d expect.

## The Sign by the Arena Gate Is Also in Your Lease
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/leasing-a-horse-vs-lessons-in-st-louis-when-to-make-the-jump
The heater is on, the floor mats smell like arena dirt, and a voice from the passenger seat says the word you knew was coming: lease. You’re on the highway home from a barn out past Wentzville or Troy, or coming up the interstate from St. Clair, and in January it is already dark when you pull out of the gravel lot. The instructor, apparently, thinks they’re outgrowing the school horses. You turn the radio down, which is how you know you’re already doing math. Lessons already eat a horse-sized slice of the month. What on earth does a lease add?
One Wentzville barn will actually tell you. Silver Fox Stables in Wentzville publishes its show lease sheet: a $1,500-a-month board and lessons package, plus a yearly lease fee that starts at $1,500 and runs up to $5,000 depending on the horse, with the farrier extra. That buys a full show season, January through November, not a first half lease. But a ceiling you can check beats a guess in the dark.
Start with the sign you’ve walked past a hundred times on lesson nights, coffee in hand, eyes on your kid. Black letters on a white sign, every letter at least an inch tall, screwed to the wall beside the arena gate. It starts with one word in capitals: WARNING. Missouri law makes the stable post it, and the same law puts that warning, word for word, inside the lease your rider is about to beg you to sign.
Here is the part nobody says on the barn aisle: a lease is not a bigger lesson. It is a contract, and in Missouri it is a contract with a legal script baked into it. Under Section 537.325 of the Missouri statutes, every written contract an equine professional or activity sponsor signs for riding, lessons or the use of a horse has to carry that same warning notice in clearly readable print. You will meet it again in the barn office, pen in hand, while somebody’s horse stamps in the crossties outside. The notice tells you, in plain terms, that the barn is generally not liable for injuries that come from the inherent risks of being around horses. Spooks, bucks, a hoof landing where your foot was. Those are on you.
There are exceptions written into the same section, and they are the reason this matters before you sign anything. The barn can still be on the hook if it provided tack it knew or should have known was faulty and that tack caused the injury, or if it provided the horse and failed to make reasonable and prudent efforts to determine whether the rider could safely handle the activity. Read that twice. Under a lease, who provides the saddle and bridle stops being a small detail. It decides whose problem a snapped billet strap becomes.
So the next time you are standing at that gate, hay dust in the air and fly spray on your sleeve, do three things before anyone hands you a pen. Ask to see the barn’s actual lease contract and find the WARNING paragraph in it. Ask who supplies and checks the saddle and bridle, and get that answer written into the lease. And ask who pays the farrier and who pays the vet, routine and emergency, because that split is where most lease budgets quietly go sideways. One caution for families who ride across the river in Highland: the statute above is Missouri’s, so ask that barn which state’s law its contract follows.
One more date belongs on the calendar if your rider is in a youth horse club and dreams of showing at the Missouri State Fair. The rules for the fair’s youth horsemanship show say exhibitors must manage every horse they show beginning no later than May 1, and ownership is not required. Those rules define manage as the horse being under the young rider’s complete care for the project. So a lease that starts in June can still be a great summer of riding, but it starts too late for that year’s fair. Ask the barn, before May, whether the lease you are signing would count.
A lease doesn’t have to be a private deal between two families, either. Silver Fox Stables, on Highway DD in Wentzville, runs a show lease program that its own site pitches as a way to move from its academy lessons to a more competitive outlet without needing to purchase a horse first, and you do not have to be an existing student to join. Ask every barn you visit whether it runs something like that, and whether the program’s rules come in writing.
If you’re still deciding whether riding is even for your family, our guide to horseback riding lessons in St. Louis for beginners is the better first stop. This page is for the rider who is past that point and wants more saddle time than one Tuesday slot can give.
### How does leasing a horse work?
A horse lease is a rental agreement. You pay the horse’s owner a fee, or you cover the horse’s expenses, and in exchange you get scheduled riding days and a say in how that horse is ridden and cared for. Leases come full or partial, and a partial lease is often called a half lease. They also come paid or free, and a free lease usually still leaves you paying for the horse’s care. The written agreement sets your days, who pays the farrier and the vet, and what happens if the horse gets hurt or sold. In Missouri, a written lease from a barn also has to carry the state’s equine WARNING notice. You get much of the feel of ownership without a purchase, and you can walk away when the term ends.
At a riding school, the barn usually sits in the middle. Sometimes the school owns the horse and leases it to a student. Sometimes a private owner boards there and the barn manager pairs that horse with a student who is ready. Either way, the barn keeps doing the feeding, turnout and stall work, so your job is mostly the riding, the grooming and the money. You will feel the difference the first evening you show up on a non-lesson day, lift the halter off its hook yourself, and walk out to the paddock with nobody calling the time.
A full lease makes you the only rider for the term. You ride as many days as the barn allows, often take the horse to shows, and make most of the day-to-day calls on training and tack. In return you usually carry the bulk of the bills: board, shoeing, routine vet care and sometimes insurance. It is the closest thing to owning, and it is usually the second lease a rider signs, not the first.
A half lease, also called a partial or shared lease, splits the horse between you and the owner or another rider. You get set days each week and pay a flat fee or a share of the costs. It is the most common first step out of lessons, because the commitment is smaller and someone else keeps the horse fit on your off days.
A care lease, sometimes sold as a “free” lease, has no lease fee. You pay the horse’s actual expenses instead, usually board, farrier, feed and routine vet work. Owners offer these when the horse needs riding and they can’t do it. Don’t let the word free fool you. Add up board and shoes and a care lease can cost more each month than a half lease with a fee. Who pays for what is the part that changes most from barn to barn, which is exactly why it belongs in writing next to that Missouri warning.
### The night the school horses stop being enough
You can usually hear it before anyone says it. The lesson ends, the instructor calls “walk them out,” and your rider groans because the hour went too fast. They stay at the rail brushing a horse that isn’t theirs. That groan is data.
The practical signs are steady attendance for months, a rider who can tack up, mount, walk, trot and canter without help and handle the horse safely on the ground, and an instructor who has started saying things like “she needs more miles.” Instructors usually see readiness before the rider or the parent does. Ask them straight out.
The money sign is the one that settles it for a lot of families. If you are already booking extra lessons one at a time just to get more rides, a half lease may simply be the cheaper way to buy saddle time you are paying for anyway. That’s the honest version of ready: the lease costs less than the workaround. The not-ready signs are honest too. Lessons skipped for other things, enthusiasm that rises and falls with the season, basics that still need the instructor’s voice every stride. A lease rewards routine. If riding is one of several activities competing for the same weeknights, it helps to see the whole picture in our guide to St. Louis youth sports clubs and what it costs to join.
### Should you lease a lesson horse or a private horse?
For a first lease, a lesson horse at your own barn is usually the safer bet. You already know the horse, your instructor is on site, the barn handles the care, and the exit is simple. The trade-off: the horse still works in the lesson program, so your days are what is left after the schedule fills, and they can shift. Lesson horses are chosen for patience, not spark, so a rider who has plateaued on them may plateau on a lease too. The barn can also reassign the horse. Ask how often that happens and how much notice you would get.
A privately owned horse at the same barn is a different animal, literally. Often it is a boarder’s horse that needs more work than its owner can give, and a half lease on that horse can teach a rider things no school horse will. The catch is that the owner writes the rules: which days, which trainer, whether jumping or shows are allowed. And if the horse isn’t at your barn already, you may end up arranging board yourself, a separate decision covered in our breakdown of what horse boarding costs in St. Louis.
### Where the real cost hides
Think in tiers, not price tags, because fees swing widely by horse and barn and I could not find a reliable St. Louis average to give you. A half lease usually costs more per month than one weekly lesson but less than boarding your own horse. A full or care lease lands near the cost of boarding, since you are paying most of the same bills. And nearly every barn expects leasers to keep taking lessons, so the lease sits on top of the lesson fee, not in place of it.
The fee is rarely what breaks the budget. The extras are. A second weekly lesson because now you can. Show entries and a trailer ride. A saddle that actually fits this horse, new boots for a kid who grew over the summer, a vet call for a lameness nobody can explain. Set a monthly ceiling before you sign, write it on the fridge, and look at it again after ninety days.
Shop the barn before you shop the horse. Browse horse riding schools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, and ask each one to show you its lease contract, warning notice and all, before you ever sit on the horse.
If you’re the riding school, the boarding barn or the one-person lesson program, the families reading this are deciding where to sign their first lease. A listing puts your lease options in front of those customers while they are still comparing. See how to get more customers from St Louis Near Me Directory.
### What belongs in a horse lease agreement?
Start with the basics: the horse, the parties, the term, the fee and your riding days. Then the money: board, farrier, routine vet, dental, deworming, emergency vet, and whether there is a cap on what you owe in an emergency and who decides when to call the vet. Then the use: are shows, trail rides off the property and jumping allowed, and at what height? Are lessons included or separate?
Then the two clauses Missouri law makes worth extra attention. First, tack: who provides it, who checks it, who pays if it breaks. Because the statute keeps a barn liable for tack it knew or should have known was faulty, a lease that says “rider supplies own tack” quietly moves that responsibility onto your side of the table. Second, the warning notice itself. If the contract in your hand doesn’t include it, ask why, because the statute says it should.
Last, the exits. How much notice does either side owe? If the horse goes lame for six weeks, does the fee pause, continue or get prorated? What if the owner sells mid-term, or your rider breaks a wrist and is out for a season? Don’t assume your homeowner’s policy covers any of it. Ask the barn what insurance it carries and what it expects you to carry. Good barns answer without flinching.
Want a hobby that stays on the ground? Photography classes in St. Louis.
### Why the lesson stays on the calendar
A lease adds practice. Lessons still supply the teaching. Ask whether your barn writes a weekly lesson into the lease, and budget for it either way. A common half-lease week is one lesson on the leased horse plus a couple of solo rides, with the instructor handing out homework for those rides and checking it next time.
That rhythm is where things speed up. On a lesson-only schedule, the first ten minutes go to remembering what your body learned last week. Ride the same horse three times a week and the feel carries over, so the lesson can teach something new. Riders often describe the first few months of a lease as the stretch where it finally clicked: the horse’s ear flicking back to listen, the half-halt that works on the first try.
### Ninety days from “can we?” to signed
Most families can go from the car-ride question to a signed lease in two to three months without rushing. Start with the instructor: say what the rider wants, more saddle time, a shot at a schooling show, a horse that asks more, and ask whether they are ready and which horses might be available. Some barns don’t lease lesson horses at all.
If your barn has nothing that fits, visit two or three others, watch a lesson, and ask every barn manager the same questions: lease types, days, what the fee covers, whether lessons are required, how often leased horses are reassigned, what insurance they expect, and whether you can see the contract. A barn that hedges on the schedule or can’t explain its own fees is telling you something. Then ask for a trial, a few extra rides or a month-to-month start. A horse that feels perfect in a lesson can feel very different when you are alone in the arena and the only sound is hooves on sand.
Finally, read the agreement with your instructor, sort out insurance, set the budget ceiling and ride. Book a check-in at day ninety with three questions: is the rider progressing, is the horse happy, is the budget holding? Three yeses means you made the jump at the right time.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the downsides of leasing a horse?
A.  The big ones are commitment, cost creep and the fact that the horse isn’t yours. You owe your days and your fee when life gets busy. Extras like added lessons, shows and tack push the real cost past the fee. The owner can sell the horse or the barn can reassign it, and an injury on either side can pause everything. A clear written agreement softens most of it.
### Q. Is it better to lease or own a horse?
A.  For most riders coming out of lessons, leasing is the better next step. It gives regular saddle time with one horse without a purchase price, open-ended vet bills or the problem of what to do when the rider outgrows the horse. Ownership makes more sense after a lease or two, once you know exactly what horse you want and can budget for board indefinitely.
### Q. What is the average cost to lease a horse per month?
A.  There is no reliable single average, because the fee depends on the lease type, the horse and the barn. As a rule of thumb, a half lease at a riding school costs more per month than one weekly lesson but less than boarding your own horse, and a full or care lease lands near the cost of board. Get each barn’s fee and what it includes in writing.
### Q. Can you lease a lesson horse?
A.  It depends on the barn, so ask the barn manager first. The horse stays in the lesson program and you get set days around that schedule, usually as a half lease. You know the horse, your instructor is on site and the barn handles daily care. The trade-off is that your days can shift and the horse can be reassigned, so ask how much notice you would get.
### Q. What should be included in a horse lease agreement?
A.  The horse and parties, the term and fee, your riding days, and who pays for board, farrier, routine vet care and emergencies. It should also say what the horse may be used for, who provides tack, whether lessons are required, what happens if the horse or rider is hurt or the horse is sold, the notice needed to end it, and what insurance each side carries. In Missouri, a written contract with a barn should also carry the state’s equine warning notice.
### Q. What to do before leasing a horse?
A.  Ask your instructor honestly whether the rider is ready. Visit two or three barns, say plainly what you want, and compare it with what each offers. Ask for a trial or a month-to-month start, ride the horse on your own several times, read the agreement with your instructor, sort out insurance, and set a monthly budget ceiling before you sign.

## Saffron, Not Salsa: Spanish Food in St. Louis and How to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/spanish-food-in-st-louis-tapas-paella-and-how-to-order
Spain gave St. Louis a building, and an Imo’s Pizza lives in it now. Stand at South Broadway and Market, Busch Stadium at your back, and you’re looking at what became of the Spanish Pavilion from the New York World’s Fair, now part of a hotel. It rode west in pieces by truck and rail and opened here on May 29, 1969, while a parade of 1,600 people and the Budweiser Clydesdales clopped from City Hall to the door. Spanish chefs cooked the pavilion’s inaugural St. Louis dinner.
Mayor Alfonso Juan Cervantes had talked the Spanish government into gifting the building and its contents to his city. He wasn’t reaching. St. Louis was a Spanish colony for nearly half a century in the 1700s, and on May 26, 1780, the defenders of the Franco-Spanish village met a British-allied attack in what is also known as the Battle of Fort San Carlos. Spain is in this city’s bones.
Then the turn. The Spanish International Pavilion closed in April 1970, eleven months after opening, and filed for bankruptcy a month later. The shell lives on inside the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark, a Starbucks and that Imo’s in other parts of it. The red tile floors are gone. One account says the statue of Queen Isabella may still be hidden somewhere in the hotel.
The lesson the city paid for: Spain doesn’t land as a spectacle. It lands at a small table, one dish at a time. A clay dish of shrimp arrives still spitting oil, the garlic gone gold at the edges, and you tear bread to drag through it before anyone says a word. A croqueta cracks under your teeth and floods hot and creamy. A glass of dry sherry comes so cold the glass fogs in your hand. And the move that makes the whole night work is simple: order the paella first.
Spain lives on in smaller rooms now. On The Hill, the neighborhood St. Louis knows for Italian food, Modesto Tapas Bar & Restaurant at 5257 Shaw ran for 15 years before it closed. Down the same street, Guido’s at 5046 Shaw Avenue calls itself a “Taste of Spain in the Middle of Little Italy.” Its menu lists a Paella Valenciana with chicken and fresh seafood at $27.99, a vegetable Paella de la Huerta at $20.99, and Gambas al Ajillo at $10.99, shrimp in olive oil, garlic and cayenne that come out still hissing. Under both paellas, the menu prints the warning that matters: “Please allow additional time for preparation.” It’s open Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., closed Mondays, and you can book at (314) 771-4900. Menus and prices change, so check before you go.
Here is the whole order for a table of two, word for word, so you never freeze while the server waits: “Paella for the table, please, and go ahead and start it now. Something cold and quick while we wait, then the gambas and the croquetas. And whatever you pour that’s dry and cold, a fino if you have sherry.” Then sit back, tear the bread, and let the garlic oil do its work. Before you go, settle the question every table asks first.
### Is Spanish and Mexican food the same?
No. Spanish food is the cooking of Spain, in Europe: olive oil, garlic, saffron, smoked paprika, seafood, cured jamón and sherry, served as shared tapas and pan-cooked paella. Mexican food grew out of corn, chiles, beans, lime and cilantro in North America. The two share a language and a handful of colonial-era ingredients, and very little else.
Your tongue tells you first. Spanish cooking is almost never hot; the closest it comes is the smoky, brick-red warmth of pimentón. And the chorizo trap catches everyone once. Mexican chorizo is fresh and loose, crumbled into a skillet of eggs. Spanish chorizo is cured, firm and sliced thin, oily and red at the edges, eaten with bread and wine. Same word. Different sausage. Calling the two cuisines the same is like calling a toasted ravioli and a pierogi the same because both are dough around a filling.
### The menu that reads like a pop quiz
Most Spanish menus sort into four drawers: small plates, rice, cured meats and cheese, and a short run of sweets. Learn the drawers and the strange words stop being strange, because the same classic dishes show up from kitchen to kitchen.
The small plates carry the night. Patatas bravas are crisp fried potatoes under a smoky paprika sauce, often with a stripe of garlic aioli. Croquetas crack open to a molten, creamy center of ham or salt cod. Gambas al ajillo arrive still spitting in a little clay dish of olive oil and sliced garlic, and the oil is the point: you drag bread through it. Pan con tomate is grilled bread rubbed with ripe tomato, olive oil and salt, so simple it feels like a trick. Tortilla española is a thick potato and onion omelet, served in wedges, never folded around anything.
Further down you’ll meet pimientos de padrón, small blistered green peppers under flaky salt, most of them mild and the odd one hot enough to make you grab your water. Boquerones are white anchovies in vinegar, bright and nothing like the salty ones on a pizza. Albondigas are meatballs in tomato sauce. Pulpo is tender octopus dusted with paprika.
The cured meat drawer is where Spain shows off. Jamón serrano is dry-cured ham sliced so thin you can see the plate through it. Jamón ibérico comes from the black Iberian pig and tastes richer and nuttier, with fat that goes soft and glossy at room temperature. It costs more. It’s worth one plate. Manchego, the firm sheep’s-milk cheese, usually comes alongside with a sweet slab of quince paste.
Then the sweet end. Churros con chocolate are ridged sticks of fried dough you dunk into hot chocolate thick enough to coat a spoon. Crema catalana is a custard with a burnt-sugar lid you crack with the back of your spoon. If the churros are fried to order, you’ll smell them before you see them.
### How does ordering tapas actually work?
Everything is shared and you order in rounds. Plates come out when the kitchen finishes them, not in courses, so the table fills up unevenly, one sizzling dish, then a cold one, then a lull. That’s the design. Once you expect it, the meal relaxes.
Open with the fast, cold things: pan con tomate, olives, a plate of jamón, a wedge of tortilla. They land quickly and keep everyone’s hands busy while the hot plates cook. Then pick a few hot ones, gambas, croquetas, bravas, the padrón peppers. When those are wiped clean, look at each other, look at the menu, and decide whether there’s room for another round.
Ask the server what comes out first and say how hungry the table is. It’s a normal question in a tapas room, and a good server will pace the order with you. If paella is on the way, they may tell you to go lighter on small plates.

The rookie mistake is ordering everything at once. A dozen plates hitting a four-top in a rush means cold shrimp, elbows in the aioli and a table that looks like a buffet line. Two rounds, maybe three, keeps every plate hot. It also keeps the bill honest, because you stop when you’re full instead of when the menu runs out.

### Why the best thing on the menu makes you wait
Paella is cooked to order in a wide, shallow pan, usually for the table, and it takes real time. The rice cooks uncovered in a thin layer, drinks up the broth, and then sits on the heat until the bottom turns into socarrat, the crisp, toasty crust that crackles when your spoon hits it. That crust is the prize. A kitchen that rushes paella never gets it.
So order it the moment you sit down, not after the tapas are gone. Ask how long it takes and whether there’s a minimum number of people. Then let the small plates carry you while the pan cooks. If your evening has a hard stop, a Cardinals first pitch or a show at the Fox, say so when you book.
Judge it by the rice, not the shrimp on top. Good paella rice is tender but separate, each grain gold with saffron and broth, never mushy, never swimming. Scrape the bottom and listen. If you hear the crackle, you found a kitchen that knows what it’s doing. Taste a bite plain before you squeeze the lemon.
### Sherry is the insider move
Spanish food was built around Spanish wine. A dry red like Rioja or Ribera del Duero stands up to jamón and chorizo. A crisp Albariño or a Verdejo suits shrimp and paella. Cava, Spain’s sparkling wine, works from the first olive to the last churro. Sangria is the tourist pour.
Sherry is the one that surprises people. Forget the sticky bottle in your grandmother’s cabinet. Fino and Manzanilla are bone-dry, faintly salty and served cold, and next to a plate of olives and fried croquetas they taste like the sea air they came from. Amontillado and Oloroso are darker and nuttier, good with mushrooms and cheese. Pedro Ximénez is the sweet one, poured over vanilla ice cream. If a menu lists sherry by the glass, the kitchen probably takes the rest of the menu seriously too.
On a sticky St. Louis July night, ask for tinto de verano: red wine over ice with lemon soda, lighter and less sweet than sangria. After dinner, a cortado with a plate of churros is the proper way to end it.

### Two at the bar, or eight around one pan
For a date, sit at the bar or a two-top, order small rounds and split one paella. Nobody guards an entrée, nobody watches the other person eat while their plate is still in the kitchen. A couple driving in from Alton can put in for the paella, share the gambas, and let the evening stretch over a glass of Albariño. If you’re building a whole night around it, our guide to the best date night restaurants in St. Louis covers the rest.
For a big table, a birthday crowd from Des Peres or a work crew coming over from Fairview Heights, hand the menu to one person and let them order rounds for everyone, so plates land together and nobody has to defend a single croqueta. Ask ahead whether the kitchen offers a chef’s selection for groups. Order two different paellas so the seafood people and the meat people both go home happy.
### How to spot a kitchen that cooks Spain on purpose
Look at the pantry the menu reveals. Does it name the ham, serrano or ibérico, or just say “ham”? Is the chorizo cured and sliced? Is there at least one dry sherry by the glass? Does the paella come with a stated wait? A menu that puts tacos next to paella and leads with a sangria pitcher is a “Latin” blend, which can be fun, but it isn’t Spain.
Fusion isn’t a crime. Just know what you’re ordering so the meal matches the craving. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most famous Spanish dish?
A.  Paella, the saffron rice cooked in a wide, shallow pan and shared straight from it, is the dish most people name first. Close behind are tortilla española, the thick potato omelet, plus gazpacho, jamón ibérico and churros with thick hot chocolate.
### Q. How to eat tapas for beginners?
A.  Share everything and order in rounds. Start with quick cold plates like pan con tomate, olives or jamón, then add hot ones such as gambas al ajillo, croquetas and patatas bravas. Eat as they arrive and order more only if you’re still hungry. Ask the server what the kitchen is proudest of that night.
### Q. What is a typical tapas menu?
A.  Cold plates like olives, jamón, Manchego, pan con tomate, boquerones and tortilla española, then hot plates like patatas bravas, croquetas, gambas al ajillo, pimientos de padrón, albondigas and pulpo. Paella usually sits in its own rice section, followed by a short dessert list with churros and crema catalana.
### Q. What is the proper etiquette when eating tapas?
A.  Share every plate, take a modest portion, and ask before claiming the last croqueta. Use the serving spoon when there is one. Dragging bread through the garlic oil left in the gambas dish is expected, not rude. Splitting the bill evenly is the usual move for a shared table.
### Q. How many tapas should you order?
A.  Fewer than you think, at first. Order a small first round for the table, see how big the plates run, then add a second round. If paella is coming, go light, because the rice fills you up. The server can tell you how hungry a table usually needs to be for their portions.
### Q. What do Spanish people eat daily?
A.  The Spanish day runs late. Breakfast is light, often coffee with toast rubbed with tomato and olive oil. Lunch is the big meal of the day, eaten in the afternoon. Dinner comes late and lighter, and tapas with a drink often fill the stretch in between.

## $65,000 Down to $1: When You Need a St. Louis Tax Attorney, Not a CPA
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-you-need-a-tax-attorney-in-st-louis-not-a-cpa
Sixty-five thousand dollars, down to one. That is not a late-night radio promise. It is what a tax clinic at the Washington University School of Law reports doing for a St. Louis woman it calls Katie. Medical setbacks pushed her out of a long career. She pulled all of her retirement money to buy a home, didn’t have enough withheld, and ended up owing a large tax bill. Then came a lien against the house she had bought with every retirement dollar she had, and the threat of her Social Security being garnished. Think about what that does to a person: the home that was supposed to be the safe place becomes the thing with a claim on it. The clinic built an offer in compromise, and the debt went from over $65,000 to $1.
That story carries the whole lesson of this page. Katie didn’t need someone to redo her math. The math was done. She owed it. What she needed was someone who could stand between her and the government and argue about what should happen next. That is a different job from preparing a return, and it is the line between a CPA and a tax attorney.
You probably know the feeling that sends people searching for this. The envelope with the IRS eagle sits on the kitchen counter in Bridgeton for two days before you open it. Your thumb tears the flap crooked. The first page is fine. The second has a number on it with a comma in the wrong place, and your chest goes tight, and the coffee goes cold while you read it a third time. You call the CPA who filed the returns. They are good at what they do. But there is a pause on the line before they answer, and that pause is the thing you’re really asking about.
Here is the plain truth, before anything else: most tax trouble does not need a lawyer. Some of it does, and guessing wrong costs you in either direction. Hire an attorney for a routine notice and you pay lawyer rates for a letter an accountant could have answered over lunch. Bring only an accountant into something that turns criminal and you may have handed the government a witness who has to talk.
So here is tonight’s order of operations, with the letter still on the counter. If your household income is at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, your first call is not a firm at all. It is the Low Income Taxpayer Clinic at WashU Law, the same clinic that handled Katie’s case. Its own report says its student attorneys, working with faculty, have represented or consulted with nearly 500 taxpayers and corrected or compromised over $1.5 million in federal tax liabilities, penalties and interest. That is a St. Louis door most people walk past on the way to a radio ad. If you earn more than that and the letter is about numbers, call your CPA or an enrolled agent in the morning. If the letter or the person at your door uses the word criminal, call a lawyer and nobody else. The federal trial court for St. Louis is the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse on South 10th Street downtown, and nobody should walk up those steps with only an accountant beside them.
### Why might you seek the help of a tax attorney rather than a CPA?
You seek a tax attorney when the problem has turned legal rather than arithmetic. A lawyer brings four things a CPA can’t: attorney-client privilege that holds even if the matter turns criminal, the right to argue your case in court, the training to defend anything with a fraud or criminal angle, and legal opinions on how a sale, business or estate should be structured. If your problem touches one of those, the lawyer is not a luxury.
Privilege is the one people don’t see coming. There is a federal rule that gives conversations with a CPA or enrolled agent some of the same protection a lawyer gets, but the statute itself spells out the hole: it can only be raised in a noncriminal tax matter before the IRS or a noncriminal tax case in federal court. The day a matter crosses into criminal territory, your accountant can be made to describe what you said and what you handed over. Your lawyer generally can’t.
That is why a good tax lawyer, once hired, will sometimes ask you to stop calling your accountant. It feels rude. It is protection. If the accountant’s help is needed, the lawyer arranges it so the work is done for the lawyer, and they make that call, not you.
The rest of the line is simpler. A CPA works in numbers: what you owe, why, and how to owe less next year. A tax attorney works in rights and consequences: what the government can prove, what it can take, and what it can do to you. Both read the same code. They ask it different questions. If you’re weighing the accountant route first, our guide to what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis sorts the tiers.
### The quiet audit, and other signs the lawyer’s turn has come
Most audits are paperwork, and they end with a folder closing. Watch for the shift. The agent stops asking what you did and starts asking why you did it. The questions reach into years nobody said were under review. Or a friendly exam goes silent for weeks, the phone just doesn’t ring, and the silence feels heavier than the questions did. Any of those can mean the file is being looked at by someone else. A restaurant owner in Sunset Hills who notices that silence should stop answering questions and call a lawyer before the next contact.
If people with badges who call themselves special agents show up at your door or your business, or a letter mentions a criminal investigation, a grand jury or a summons, you have a legal matter and nothing else. Be polite. Take their cards. Say your attorney will contact them. Don’t explain, and don’t call your CPA first, for the privilege reason above.
Money alone can tip it too. A balance you can pay in a few years with a payment plan is usually an accountant’s job. A balance you can never realistically pay, especially once a lien has landed on your house in Ballwin or a levy has hit your paycheck, turns into a negotiation, and Katie’s story shows how much room a negotiation can have. Several unfiled years need care as well, because the order and the way you file can change what you face. The same goes for a partnership breaking up, payroll taxes the government wants to collect from the owners personally, the sale of a business, or an estate fight over what something was worth. And a serious dispute with the state deserves the same respect as a federal one.
### When a CPA or enrolled agent is plenty
For most notices, routine audits and payment plans, you don’t need a lawyer and you shouldn’t pay for one. The IRS itself says enrolled agents, CPAs and attorneys all have unlimited representation rights before the IRS, which covers audits, payment and collection issues, and appeals. If nobody is questioning your honesty and the fight is about what the numbers should be, an accountant can carry it.
Enrolled agents are the option most people in St. Louis have never heard of. Representing taxpayers is their whole trade, and for a confusing notice or a manageable balance, a good one is often the best value in the room. A retired nurse in Hazelwood holding a notice about a rental she sold most likely needs one of these, not a litigator.
The rule of thumb is short. If your CPA or enrolled agent reads your letter and says it’s routine, believe them. If they read it and go quiet, or say “you might want to talk to an attorney,” take that sentence home and act on it. Good accountants know where their protection ends.
If the pause on the phone has already happened, start your shortlist tonight. Browse tax attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three to call, and put your letters in date order before the first meeting.
If you’re the tax attorney, the enrolled agent or the one-person practice that takes these calls, the people holding those envelopes are your next customers, and a listing for your practice is a quiet way to get more customers who already know they need you.
### How do you tell a real lawyer from a tax relief ad?
A real tax attorney is a named person licensed in Missouri who signs a written engagement letter and never promises a result. A tax relief ad is a phone number. Many of those spots are lead generation: a call center takes your details and passes them along, and the “pennies on the dollar” line that hooked you was never said by anyone who will do the work. Katie’s $1 result is real, but it came from a clinic that looked at her actual facts, not from a jingle.
Three checks before you hand over a dime. Get a name: ask which attorney will handle your matter, then confirm that person’s license with the state’s public lawyer lookup. If the answer is “one of our tax professionals,” hang up. Get the engagement letter before you pay, with the scope and fee in writing. And listen for guarantees, because nobody can promise the IRS will accept an offer.
Treat the first meeting as an interview. Say plainly what you have and what you want: “I have three years of proposed changes and a balance I can’t pay in full, and I want my realistic options.” One lawyer will describe a process. Another will describe an outcome. Hire the process. Then ask the question that tells you the most: “What would you tell me if my case were weak?” A lawyer with a ready answer has said it to other clients.

### What’s the difference between a tax advisor and an accountant?
When the IRS writes back, the difference that counts is the credential, not the title on the business card. Enrolled agents, CPAs and attorneys have unlimited representation rights before the IRS, while a preparer with only a PTIN and no credential can prepare your return but has no authority to represent you. Annual Filing Season Program participants sit in between: they can speak for you only on returns they prepared and signed, and never on appeals or collection issues. So before that envelope with the eagle on it slides across anyone’s desk, ask which credential they hold and look the name up in the IRS directory of preparers with credentials.
### What the bill looks like, and what to carry in
Tax attorneys bill by the hour, by a flat fee for a defined job, or against a retainer you refill as it’s used. Hourly fits open-ended matters like an audit nobody has sized yet. Flat fees fit defined jobs, like an offer in compromise or a set of late returns. Retainers are common for litigation and criminal work. Expect a lawyer’s rate to sit above an accountant’s, and confirm every number with the attorney, because rates vary widely across the metro. The real comparison isn’t rate against rate. It’s the fee against the outcome you’re trying to avoid.
Bring every letter, with its envelope, in date order. Bring the returns for the years in question, or the preparer’s name. Bring notes on who you talked to at the IRS or the state, with dates. For a collection problem, bring a rough picture of what you own, earn and owe, because the options depend on it. Then sit at the Bridgeton kitchen table for ten minutes and write a one-page timeline; it can save an hour of billed time. Retirees should bring pension and Social Security figures too, and our guide to how Missouri taxes retirement income covers the basics before you sit down.
### What if you cannot afford a tax attorney?
Go back to Katie. She didn’t hire a downtown firm. She got help from a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic, and the WashU LITC helps people at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, with student attorneys working alongside faculty on real IRS disputes. If your household fits, call before you call anyone else. The contractor in Ballwin with four unfiled years and thin cash flow is exactly who these clinics were built for.
There is one more door. The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent organization within the IRS that helps taxpayers resolve problems. When a file has gone dead and nobody calls back, that silence is exactly what to bring them. For the filing side, free volunteer programs prepare returns for eligible households, and our guide to free tax preparation in St. Louis explains who qualifies. Getting late returns filed is usually the first thing any representative asks for.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should you use a tax attorney?
A.  Use a tax attorney when the matter is adversarial, criminal, headed to court, or too large to pay. That means an audit that has turned hostile, any contact from IRS special agents, a lien or levy on a balance you can’t realistically pay, several unfiled years, or a business or estate dispute. Routine notices and simple payment plans usually don’t need one.
### Q. Do you need a lawyer to negotiate with the IRS?
A.  No. The IRS says enrolled agents, CPAs and attorneys all have unlimited representation rights before it, covering audits, collection issues and appeals. A lawyer adds the most on large balances, offers in compromise, and anything where privilege or a courtroom could come into play.
### Q. Are tax relief attorneys worth it?
A.  A real tax attorney is worth it for the right problem. A “tax relief” ad promising pennies on the dollar often isn’t a law practice at all. Ask for the named Missouri-licensed attorney who will handle your case, a written engagement letter, and an honest read on your odds. If you get a guarantee instead, walk away.
### Q. What exactly does a tax attorney do?
A.  A tax attorney handles the legal side of tax: disputes with the IRS or the state, negotiations over large balances, offers in compromise, liens and levies, appeals, court cases, defense in criminal investigations, and legal opinions on structuring a business, sale or estate. The federal privilege for a non-lawyer “federally authorized tax practitioner” can only be raised in noncriminal tax matters, so a criminal case is lawyer territory.
### Q. How much does a tax lawyer cost in the US?
A.  Tax lawyers bill hourly, by flat fee for a defined job, or against a retainer. Rates sit above an accountant’s and vary with experience, city and complexity. A single offer in compromise is often quoted flat; litigation and criminal matters usually run on a retainer. Get the structure and the numbers in writing before work starts.
### Q. What if I can’t afford a tax lawyer?
A.  In St. Louis, the Low Income Taxpayer Clinic at the Washington University School of Law helps people at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, and it is where one woman’s debt went from over $65,000 to $1. The Taxpayer Advocate Service, an independent organization within the IRS, helps taxpayers resolve problems. For simpler pieces, an enrolled agent costs a fraction of a lawyer.
