### Why two honest quotes for the same charge can be miles apart
The price tracks the work, and the work depends on more than the charge printed on the paper. Misdemeanor or felony is the first fork. Plea or trial is the second. Then come the court, the facts, the evidence, and how much experience the lawyer brings. A case with hours of body-camera video to watch is not the same job as one with a two-page report.
Where the case is filed matters too. A charge in the city moves on its own calendar, and the same charge filed in an Illinois county near North Venice or Livingston may move differently again. Add an expert witness or a lab question, and the number climbs. That is not padding. It is the case being bigger than its one-line description.
The cheapest quote and the priciest quote are both just numbers until you know what is behind them. The higher one may get you out of a courtroom faster. The lower one may be exactly right for a simple plea. Match the lawyer to the case in front of you, and let the fee be one part of that fit.
People are asking
### Is a $5,000 retainer too much for a criminal defense lawyer?
It depends on the work behind it: The Missouri Bar’s ethics column on flat fees explains that Rule 4-1.5 says all fees must be reasonable and requires weighing at least eight factors, among them the time and labor required, the fee customarily charged in the locality for similar legal services and the experience of the lawyer. One line in that column should steady the hand holding the pen: fee reasonableness is viewed in retrospect, not at the time of fee negotiation. The same column describes a criminal flat fee earned in milestones, a portion after arraignment, after a review of discovery, after pretrial motions and finally after a trial or plea agreement. Ask for those milestones in writing, and the number at the bottom of the agreement turns from a guess into a map of the work.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth it to hire a criminal defense attorney?
A.  For anything past a minor ticket, usually yes. A criminal charge can touch your job, your record, your housing and your freedom, and a lawyer’s value is measured against those stakes, not just the fee. A good defense lawyer knows the local court and the realistic options. On a serious charge, going it alone is often the expensive choice.
### Q. How can I afford a criminal defense attorney?
A.  Ask about the fee structure and a payment plan in the first call, because many lawyers offer one. A flat fee on a misdemeanor is easier to budget than an open-ended hourly case. If money is truly tight, ask whether the work can be scoped narrowly, and check whether you qualify for a public defender. Comparing two or three quotes shows you what is normal.
### Q. What is the hardest criminal case to beat?
A.  Cases built on strong physical evidence, believable witnesses or a recorded statement from the accused are the toughest to defend. Video, forensics or an admission leave less room for reasonable doubt. That does not make a case hopeless. A skilled lawyer may still challenge how evidence was gathered or negotiate a better result, and those odds shape both the strategy and the cost.
### Q. How do I get a lawyer if I cannot afford one?
A.  Ask for a public defender through the court that has your case. In Missouri you file an affidavit about your finances with the court. For a City of St. Louis case, the public defender’s District 22 office is in the Carnahan Courthouse at 1114 Market St. If you land just over the line, ask private lawyers about payment plans.
### Q. Does a lawyer keep a retainer fee?
A.  Only the part they earn. In Missouri, a lawyer must refund the unearned portion of an advance fee if the relationship ends early, and calling a fee “nonrefundable” does not change that, according to Missouri Bar ethics guidance. Ask for a written accounting of what was earned. In Illinois, ask the lawyer to explain the refund rules before you sign.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of a retainer fee?
A.  A retainer ties up money before you know the final cost, and on an hourly case you may be asked to replenish it as the work goes on. It can also feel like the money is gone the second it clears, even when it is not. The fix is not avoiding retainers. It is knowing yours: what it covers, how it is billed and where it sits until earned.
### Q. Is a retainer the same as the total cost of my case?
A.  Not usually. On an hourly case, the retainer is a starting balance the lawyer bills against, and you top it up as the work continues, so the total can end higher. On a flat-fee misdemeanor, the retainer may be the whole price. Ask the lawyer directly which one your quote is.
### Q. Do criminal defense lawyers offer payment plans?
A.  Many do, especially on flat-fee cases, though the terms vary from office to office. Some take part up front and spread the rest across the case. Others want the full retainer on serious matters where the work is hard to predict. It is a fair thing to raise in your first conversation, and a plain answer tells you a lot about the lawyer.

## Low-Cost Dental Care at St. Louis Dental Schools
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/low-cost-dental-care-at-st-louis-dental-schools
A retiree in Vinita Park has been chewing on one side of her mouth for months. A back molar cracked last winter, and the quote from a private dentist sent her credit card straight back into her wallet. She keeps meaning to call around. She keeps not doing it. The tooth keeps aching.
She is far from alone. A young dad in East Alton has put off a filling since spring because payday never quite stretches far enough. A woman in Truesdale is hunting for an affordable extraction for her mother, who lives on a fixed income and hates the idea of being a burden. A community-college student in Smithton has a wisdom tooth that flares up every few weeks. Different lives, one shared piece of math: the care they need on one side, a bill they dread on the other.
Here is the part a lot of people never hear. A dental school runs a teaching clinic, and that clinic can cut the cost of care sharply. Students perform the treatment, and licensed faculty dentists supervise every step. The savings are real, and so are the trade-offs. This guide walks through how teaching-clinic pricing works, who it is right for, the other low-cost routes worth a look, and the questions to ask before you book a single appointment.
### Is it cheaper to get work done at a dental school in St. Louis?
Yes, dental care at a teaching clinic is usually far cheaper than a private practice, often a fraction of the standard fee. The savings come from students doing the work under close faculty supervision. The trade-off is time: expect longer appointments and more visits than you would spend at a regular dentist. For someone weighing a painful tooth against a tight budget, that swap can be well worth it.
### Why the price drops so much
A teaching clinic is not chasing profit the way a private office has to. It exists to train the next class of dentists and hygienists, so the fee mostly covers materials, lab work, and overhead rather than a full professional rate. In our experience, people are surprised by how wide the gap can be, especially on cleanings, fillings, and routine extractions. Ask the clinic for its current fee schedule, because the exact numbers change and vary by procedure.
### Where the money is not saved
Cheaper does not mean free, and it does not mean corners get cut on safety. You still pay for materials, X-rays, and any lab-made pieces like crowns or dentures. Complex work can still add up, just from a lower starting point. And some cases are too involved for a student clinic to take on, which is why the screening visit matters. If your situation is urgent or complicated, the clinic will tell you whether it fits or point you elsewhere.
### How does teaching-clinic pricing actually work?
Teaching-clinic pricing runs on a reduced-fee model: students provide the care as part of their training, and the clinic charges enough to cover its costs rather than a market rate. Because a student is still learning, a licensed faculty dentist checks the work at each stage. That oversight is the reason the low price does not come with a drop in safety, though it does stretch the clock.
### Who does the work, and who is watching?
A supervised dental student or dental-hygiene student does the hands-on work, and a licensed instructor reviews it before, during, and after. Think of it as care with a second set of experienced eyes built into every visit. The student takes their time and double-checks; the faculty dentist signs off. Many patients find that thoroughness reassuring once the longer appointment stops feeling strange.
### Why the appointments run longer
Plan for longer visits, and more of them. A procedure a seasoned dentist finishes in half an hour may take a student two or three times as long, partly because the instructor stops to check each step and turn it into a teaching moment. A crown or denture a private office handles in a couple of visits might stretch across several weeks at a school. If you cannot take time off easily, weigh that before you commit.
### What the screening visit is for
Most teaching clinics start with a screening appointment before they accept you as a patient. Staff review your mouth, your X-rays, and your history to decide whether your case fits what students need to learn and what the clinic can safely handle. Not everyone is accepted, and not every procedure is offered. Bring a list of your concerns, any recent X-rays, and a clear description of what hurts, so the screening moves quickly.
### What other low-cost dental options exist in St. Louis?
A dental school is one route, not the only one. St. Louis and the surrounding metro have community health centers, sliding-scale clinics, and nonprofit programs built for people without dental insurance or with tight budgets. Costs at these sites often shift with your income, so what you pay can look very different from what your neighbor pays. It is worth calling a few before you settle on one.
### Community health centers and FQHCs
Federally qualified health centers, often called FQHCs, provide dental care on a sliding scale tied to household income and family size. Many serve patients whether or not they have insurance, and some accept Medicaid. Bring proof of income when you go, since that is what sets your fee. These centers fill up, so call ahead and ask about wait times and what their dental side actually covers.
### Sliding-scale and nonprofit clinics
Some nonprofit and charitable clinics offer discounted or donation-based dental care, sometimes through occasional free-care events run by dental associations or volunteer dentists. Availability comes and goes, and spots are limited. Keep a short list and check back, because a clinic that is full today may open a slot next month. A quick call saves a wasted trip from as far out as Trenton or Wilbur Park.
### Other ways to stretch a dental dollar
A dental savings plan, which is a membership discount rather than insurance, can lower fees at some private offices for a yearly cost. Payment plans and third-party medical financing spread a bill over months, though watch the interest. And if you are staring at a big-ticket bill, it never hurts to ask the office directly whether they discount for paying in cash up front. The worst answer is no.
Sticker shock is not unique to dentistry. The same habit of calling around before you commit saves real money on medical bills too, which is exactly the approach we lay out in what an MRI costs in St. Louis and how to pay less.
### Is a dental school clinic the right choice for you?
A teaching clinic fits some people beautifully and frustrates others. It is a strong choice if your budget is tight, your schedule is flexible, and your needs run from routine to moderately complex. It is a poor fit if you are in acute pain that cannot wait, if you need everything done in one or two visits, or if your case is unusually complicated. Match the clinic to your situation honestly.
### Who benefits most
People on fixed incomes, students, the uninsured, and anyone rebuilding after a long stretch without care tend to get the most out of a teaching clinic. If you have the patience for longer visits, the savings can free up money for the rest of life. The retiree in Vinita Park and the dad in East Alton from the top of this guide are exactly who these clinics were built to serve.
### When to look elsewhere first
A cracked tooth throbbing at 2 a.m. is an emergency, not a screening-visit situation. Severe swelling, a knocked-out tooth, or signs of infection need same-day help, and an urgent-care or emergency dental option comes first. Once the crisis passes, a teaching clinic can pick up the longer-term work. Never let the promise of a lower price talk you into waiting through real pain.
Guarding your budget everywhere? Compare St. Louis car security systems too.
### What should you ask before you book?
Before you commit, treat the clinic the way you would interview any provider: call, ask plain questions, and compare the answers with what you need. Ask what the screening visit costs, how long the wait is for new patients, and which procedures students actually perform. A few minutes on the phone can save you a wasted drive and set honest expectations about time and money.
Then get specific. How much is a cleaning, an exam, a filling, or an extraction right now? Do they take Medicaid, or offer a payment plan? How many visits should you expect for the work you need? Is there a waiting list, and how long is it? Who supervises the students, and are they licensed faculty? A clinic that answers clearly is telling you it is organized. One that dodges is telling you something too.

Bring your paperwork and your patience. Recent X-rays, a list of medications, proof of income for sliding-scale sites, and a written note of what hurts will all speed things along. Line up two or three options across the metro before you choose, from the city out to Smithton or Trenton, and compare the all-in answer, not just the first fee they quote.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do dental schools offer free dental work?
A.  Not usually free, but far cheaper than a private office. Most teaching clinics charge a reduced fee that covers materials and overhead. Some run occasional free screening days or community events, and dental-hygiene programs sometimes offer very low-cost cleanings. Ask each clinic what is free, what is reduced, and when any events happen.
### Q. How can I go to the dentist if I can’t afford it?
A.  Several routes exist. A dental-school teaching clinic offers supervised care at a reduced fee. Federally qualified health centers charge on a sliding scale tied to your income. Nonprofit and charitable clinics run discounted or occasional free events. Many offices offer payment plans too. Call a few, compare, and start with the one that fits your budget and timeline.
### Q. How to get teeth cleaned for free?
A.  Fully free cleanings are limited, but they exist. Dental-hygiene student programs sometimes offer no-cost or very low-cost cleanings because students need the practice. Community health fairs and occasional free-care events run by dental groups are another option. Availability changes often, so call local teaching clinics and health centers and ask what is scheduled.
### Q. How can I get a tooth removed if I have no money?
A.  A simple extraction is one of the cheaper procedures at a teaching clinic, where students perform it under faculty supervision. Federally qualified health centers offer extractions on a sliding scale, and some charitable events cover them outright. In an emergency with infection, get same-day care first. Call ahead and ask about cost and whether they take Medicaid.
### Q. How can I fix my teeth if I don’t have money?
A.  Start by triaging: handle pain and infection first, then plan the rest. A teaching clinic can spread bigger work like fillings, crowns, or dentures across time at a lower fee. Sliding-scale health centers, payment plans, and dental savings memberships all help. Fixing everything at once is rarely the goal; steady, affordable progress is.
### Q. Why is my root canal $3000?
A.  A root canal price climbs with the tooth. Molars have more canals and are harder to reach, and a specialist called an endodontist often charges more than a general dentist. A crown to protect the tooth afterward adds to the total. A teaching clinic can lower that cost, though very complex cases may be referred out. Ask for an itemized estimate.
### Q. Does a dental school clinic take insurance or Medicaid?
A.  It varies by clinic. Some teaching clinics accept dental insurance or Medicaid; others are cash-based but already priced well below a private office. Because policies change, call and ask directly what they accept and how billing works. Even without coverage, the reduced fee often lands lower than an insured visit somewhere else.
### Q. How long is the wait to become a patient at a teaching clinic?
A.  Waits vary with demand and the school calendar. Because students train on a schedule, popular clinics can carry a waiting list, and slots may open between academic terms. A screening visit usually comes first to decide whether your case fits. Call early, ask about the current wait, and get on the list while you compare other options.

## The Paper on Your Kitchen Table: What a DUI Lawyer Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-dui-lawyer-costs-in-st-louis
It looks like nothing. One sheet of paper, folded in thirds, on a South City kitchen table under your keys, and you keep sliding it out to read it again as if the words might change. They won’t, but you have more time and more say than that knot in your stomach suggests. The sheet is Form 2385, the Notice of Suspension/Revocation, and it’s the paper to find before you price a single lawyer. Look at the date it was issued and count 15 days. That’s how long you have to ask the Missouri Department of Revenue for a hearing on your license, and in money terms it matters more this week than the court date on your ticket.
Here’s why. In Missouri, what most people call a DUI is charged as driving while intoxicated, DWI, and it moves on two tracks that don’t wait for each other. One is the criminal case: a courtroom, a judge, a prosecutor. The other is your license, handled on paper by the state, and it can be decided before your first court appearance. The hearing request goes in writing to the Department of Revenue, ATTN: General Counsel’s Office, PO Box 475, Jefferson City MO 65105-0475, or by fax to (573) 751-7151, and you or your attorney can send it. So when you sit down for a consultation, the most useful question you can ask isn’t “how much?” It’s “does your fee cover the license hearing?” People who skip that question sometimes pay for a good result in court and still lose the license.
### Is a lawyer worth it for a DUI?
For most people in St. Louis, yes. Not because a lawyer works magic in front of a judge, but because there are two cases to work, the criminal charge and the Department of Revenue license case, and one of them has a 15-day fuse. A fee is a bill you can plan around. A lost license, a conviction and years of higher insurance are not.
Where does the criminal side play out? It depends on who wrote the ticket. In the city, the St. Louis City Municipal Division, part of the 22nd Judicial Circuit, handles traffic citations issued by the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department and the Missouri State Highway Patrol. It sits at 1520 Market St., Suite 1120, downtown. The city’s court page even notes the metered parking out front on Market. You feed the meter, come in through the main entrance on the Market Street side, and follow the signs, with the paperwork in a folder so your hands have something to hold. That court matters for your budget, too: the Missouri State Public Defender says that if your case involves a municipal violation or traffic violation, you are not eligible for its services. Some DWI charges are filed as state cases instead, which is one more thing a lawyer reads off your paperwork in about a minute and a stranger online can’t.
About the price itself: we looked for a St. Louis DWI fee range from a source that wasn’t selling something, and couldn’t find one. The one defense fee schedule we did find in writing belongs to the public defender, and it holds the Missouri detail almost nobody prints. The public defender isn’t free. By Missouri state law, the Public Defender must charge a fee, set per case from a schedule, and an unpaid fee can be taken out of your Missouri income tax refund or lottery winnings for 10 years after the case ends. Nobody can be turned away for being unable to pay, and the fee doesn’t change the quality of the defense. But it’s a real bill, so lay it next to a private lawyer’s quote and compare honestly.
When your name is called on that first court date, the charge on the prosecutor’s file for a first DWI is a class B misdemeanor under Missouri law. That carries up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. A prior offense makes it a class A misdemeanor, and so does having a child under 17 in the car. Those are ceilings, not what most first-timers get. But they’re what the other side of the room is holding while you stand there in your good shirt, hands not sure where to go.
Then there’s the license, the plastic card that’s ridden in your wallet for years. If you were arrested with a blood alcohol content of .08 percent or higher, the state processes it administratively as well as criminally. With no alcohol- or drug-related driving offense in the past five years, that means a 90-day suspension. With one, it’s a one-year revocation. Refuse the breath test and the revocation is one year, full stop. Ninety days is a full season of asking a sister, a coworker or a neighbor for a ride to the early shift, and watching the clock on the dashboard of someone else’s car.
### The quote on the table, and what it quietly leaves out
You’ll hear “flat fee” in almost every consultation for a first offense with no crash and no refusal. One number, a defined job: review the stop, show up to court, negotiate with the prosecutor. It sounds simple, and it can be. The detail to pin down, before you sign anything at that conference-room table, is whether the number includes the Department of Revenue hearing? Some lawyers treat the license case as separate work with its own fee. For a lot of drivers, keeping the license is the whole reason they called.
Since nobody publishes a St. Louis range we can stand behind, we won’t print a number. What we can tell you is what moves it. A prior offense. A crash, or anyone hurt. A refusal. A very high reading. A commercial license. A case headed for trial instead of a plea, because trial means days of motions and preparation, not one morning at a podium. Each of those adds hours and risk, and the fee follows. A clean first offense and a felony-track repeat are not the same purchase, and nobody honest will price them alike.
One more thing to listen for in that first conversation: whether the lawyer brings up the 15-day window before you do. If you mention Form 2385 and they reach for a calendar, good. If they wave it off as paperwork for later, you’ve learned how they’ll treat the part of your case that keeps you driving to work next month.
### What skipping the lawyer actually costs
The fee is one bill, and you see it coming. Going it alone is a stack of smaller bills that keep arriving long after the courtroom empties out. Even when the case goes fine, the state still wants its receipts before you drive freely again.
The first receipt is a class. Any alcohol offense on your driving record, even an administrative suspension with no conviction, means Missouri law requires you to complete the Substance Awareness Traffic Offender Program, SATOP, to get your license back. The second is insurance proof. You need to file an SR-22 for two years from the starting date of your suspension or revocation, and that filing tells your insurer exactly what happened. Picture the renewal envelope on the counter, the one you open standing up. That’s the cost people forget when they compare a lawyer’s fee to “just pleading guilty.”
There is some relief built in. On a 90-day suspension you may be eligible for a Restricted Driving Privilege, which can keep you getting to work. And if a hearing is granted, a permit to drive is mailed to you, good until 15 days after the hearing decision is mailed, provided you surrendered your license and are eligible to drive in Missouri. Miss the 15-day request window and you give up that breathing room before anyone has looked at your stop.
Hold a Missouri medical marijuana card? Here is what a cannabis clinic does.
People are asking
### What jobs won’t hire you with a DWI in Missouri?
I could not find a Missouri list of jobs closed to anyone with a DWI, but driving for a living takes the hardest hit. Under RSMo 302.755, a first DWI, even in your own car, disqualifies a driver from commercial motor vehicles for at least one year, and so does a first alcohol-related enforcement contact, which state law defines to include a suspension under sections 302.500 to 302.540, the same administrative track that put Form 2385 on your table. A second violation from a separate incident can mean disqualification for life. If a CDL pays your rent, say so in the first minute of every consultation, before anyone quotes you a fee.
### When the money just isn’t there
This is the part people are ashamed to ask, so we’ll say it first. If you can’t pay a private lawyer, you still have a door. The Missouri State Public Defender’s St. Louis City office is in the Mel Carnahan Courthouse at 1114 Market St., Suite 602, a few blocks east of the city’s municipal court. Call (314) 340-7625, ask how to apply, and ask plainly whether your kind of case is one they take. It’s a short phone call that can change the whole budget.
If you’re hiring privately, ask about payments before you ask about anything else. Many DWI lawyers split a flat fee into installments or bill against a retainer, and plenty offer a free first consultation. Use that meeting. Bring your ticket, Form 2385 and any bond or tow paperwork, and watch who reads the paper before they quote you.
Put two or three attorneys side by side before day 15. Browse DUI attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call the ones you like, and ask each the same question: does your fee cover the license hearing?
If you’re the defense attorney or the small firm that takes DWI cases, the drivers reading this page are your next customers, and most of them are deciding this week. Listing your practice puts you in front of them when they’re ready to call.
### Your first 15 days, in order
Find the issue date on Form 2385 and count 15 days. That’s your real deadline, not the court date.
Get a written hearing request to the Missouri Department of Revenue, ATTN: General Counsel’s Office, PO Box 475, Jefferson City MO 65105-0475, or fax (573) 751-7151. You or your attorney can send it.
Say on the request whether you want the hearing in person or by phone. If you don’t ask for in-person, they schedule a telephone hearing.
Book two or three consultations and ask each lawyer what the fee covers, who shows up in court, and how payment works.
Look up a SATOP provider early. You’ll need it for reinstatement whatever happens in court.
### Sitting across the desk from a lawyer you might hire
Treat the first meeting as a job interview, because you’re the one hiring. Say it straight: “First DWI, the reading was close, and I want to keep my license and my record.” Then listen to the answer. One lawyer will walk you through a process: the license hearing, the likely plea paths, what the prosecutor tends to do. Another will promise an outcome. Nobody honest guarantees a result in a courtroom, and the one who does just told you something.
Ask how many cases like yours they’ve handled, and what they’d tell you if your case were weak. It’s the same instinct that tells you when a problem needs a specialist, the way our guide to when you need a tax attorney, not a CPA sorts one legal problem from another. A lawyer who answers the hard question without flinching has answered it before.
And notice how you feel walking back out to the car. Not thrilled, nobody is. But steadier, with a next step you can name: who files the hearing request, by what date, and what you owe and when. If you leave more confused than you came in, keep looking. You have a few more calls left in those 15 days, and the right one usually sounds calm.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best defense for a DUI?
A.  There’s no single best one; it depends on your facts. Common angles are the reason for the stop, how the field sobriety or breath test was given, whether the machine was maintained, and gaps in the paperwork. A lawyer reads the whole stop looking for the weak point, which is why a real review beats any list of what “usually works.”
### Q. Is it worth fighting a DUI charge?
A.  Often, yes, even if dismissal isn’t likely. Fighting can mean a reduced charge or a better result on the license side. Weigh it against two years of SR-22 filings and what a conviction does on background checks, and the effort usually earns its cost. Get a lawyer’s read on your specific facts first.
### Q. Do DUI lawyers take payments?
A.  Many do. Some split a flat fee into installments; others bill against a retainer as the work gets done. It varies by firm, so ask in the free consultation how payment works, what the fee covers, and what happens if the case gets more complicated halfway through.
### Q. Can a 1st offense DUI be dismissed?
A.  It can happen, but it isn’t the norm, and nobody honest will promise it. Dismissals usually turn on a real problem: a bad stop, a mishandled test, missing evidence. More often a first offense ends in a reduced charge or a resolution that limits the damage. A lawyer’s review tells you which is realistic.
### Q. Can you be 100% honest with your lawyer?
A.  Yes, and you should be. What you tell your lawyer while they’re representing you stays between you. Holding back the embarrassing parts is how good lawyers get blindsided in court. They can only defend the facts they know, so give them all of it.
### Q. What makes you look bad in court?
A.  Showing up late, dressed carelessly, or with an attitude, because a judge notices all of it. So does arguing or interrupting. Silence your phone, dress like the day matters, be respectful, and let your lawyer talk. It won’t save a weak case, but disrespect can sink a close one.
### Q. Do you need a lawyer for a first DWI in Missouri?
A.  An arrest at .08 percent or higher is processed administratively as well as criminally, and the license side has a 15-day deadline. A short consultation tells you whether this is a case you can carry yourself or one worth handing off.

## The Tax Line You Keep Looking Up: Teach Your AI to Leave It Blank
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-a-st-louis-small-business-can-build-its-first-ai-skill
Your thumbs know this quote by heart. Thanks for calling, here’s what we talked about, parts and labor, the warranty line, how long the price holds. Then the line you always stop on: the tax. You look it up again. The water heater is going into a bungalow in Dutchtown, which is the city, but last week’s job was over the line in the county, and the one before sat inside some fire district you couldn’t name. The laptop fan whines. The coffee grows a skin. It is the third quote this week built out of the last one.
That isn’t a flaw in you. It’s a job that never got written down, so it gets rebuilt every time, and the tax line is the part that bites. St. Louis has run the city and the county as separate governments since the 1876 vote often called the Great Divorce. Missouri’s Department of Revenue says cities and counties may add a local sales tax and special taxing districts, fire districts among them, may add more. Local changes take effect on the first day of a calendar quarter, January, April, July or October, and the state keeps an address-by-address lookup because the right number depends on where the job is.
So the smartest thing you can teach an AI about that line is to leave it blank.
That is the whole idea of an AI skill. Not a robot that knows everything. A page of plain English that says how you write the quote, what it must never guess, and what a good one looks like. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, calls it a skill. Who gains when you believe it takes a developer? The people who would charge to “set up your AI.” It doesn’t. Every product fact below comes from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s own help pages, not from a video thumbnail.
### What is an AI skill?
A skill is a folder with one required file inside it, a text file called SKILL.md. At the top of that file sit two labels, a name and a description. Below them, in ordinary sentences, goes whatever you would tell a new hire. Anthropic’s developer docs describe the whole arrangement as organized like an onboarding guide you would create for a new team member. Here is the one for that water-heater job. Nothing in it is code:
name: writing-customer-quotes
description: Drafts customer quotes in the owner’s voice and layout. Use when the owner asks for a quote, estimate or bid on a job.
Open with the customer’s first name. List the work in the order we would do it. Never guess a price or a tax rate. Leave the tax line blank, write “look up by job address,” and ask me which side of the city line the job is on. Close with how long the quote holds and one line about the warranty. Keep it to a page.
Here is what separates that from pasting instructions into a chat. Claude does not haul the whole folder around. When it starts up it loads only each skill’s name and description, about 100 tokens per skill by the docs’ count, a few sentences’ worth, and it opens the rest of the file only when your request matches. The description is the doorbell. Ring it with the right words and the whole page walks in.
The whole method fits in four sentences. Do the job once with Claude the ordinary way, with a real quote of yours pasted in. Fix the draft until it sounds like you. Then type: create a skill that captures this. Zip what it hands you, upload it, and test it on three real jobs.
### Which plan has skills? Anthropic’s two pages give two answers
It is late. The Department of Revenue’s rate lookup is open in one tab, Claude’s settings in the other, and the button you were promised is not where the page says it is. Open Anthropic’s help center and you’ll read that for the Max, Pro and Free plans you can upload your own skills in Customize, then Skills. Open the developer docs, the paragraph about claude.ai, and uploading custom skills is listed for Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise. Free sits on one page and not the other, and nothing on either settles which list your account is on.
So check your own screen. On Free, Pro and Max the help center says to turn on code execution and file creation under Settings, then Capabilities, and then look for Skills under Customize. If the upload option is there, everything below works for you. If it isn’t, you have lost nothing, because the skill you write is a plain text file you can keep for the day your plan catches up. The menu names have moved around between Anthropic’s pages, so hunt for the word Skills rather than a fixed path.
### Is a skill just a Project, a custom GPT or a saved prompt?
Four things look alike and are not. A Claude Project is the binder on the shelf. Anthropic says Projects provide static background knowledge that is always loaded when you start a chat inside one, while skills are task-specific and only load when relevant. The binder holds who you are: the salon on Cherokee Street, the neighborhoods you serve, what you sell. The skill is the laminated card you pull out when the job comes up.
A custom GPT is OpenAI’s version of a saved setup. OpenAI’s help center says it is planning to retire custom GPTs and move creators to plugins, and that under the migration the GPT’s instructions become a skill inside the new plugin. A second OpenAI page says new GPT creation and publishing are not available on personal accounts, Free, Go, Plus or Pro. So here is the line worth repeating at the supply counter: the word skill now shows up in both companies’ products. Learn to write your way of working down once, and you are not betting on one brand.
An artifact is the thing Claude makes, not the instructions for making it. Anthropic defines it as anything Claude makes that you would put in front of someone: a document, a deck, a small tool. The skill is how the quote gets written; the artifact is the quote on your screen. And a command, in Claude Code, the programmer’s version of Claude, is a shortcut you trigger by name. The Claude Code docs say custom commands have been merged into skills, so you can ignore commands unless you ever open that tool.
### How do you build your first skill in one evening?
Which job did you retype the most this month? Start there, and do not start by writing. Do the job once with Claude the ordinary way, which is what Anthropic’s authoring guide recommends: work a real task and notice what you keep explaining. Then:
Pick one job you repeat and dislike. The guide says the best skills solve a specific, repeatable task and stay focused on one workflow. A quote is a good first one. So is the weekly post.
Do it once, out loud, with a real example. Paste a finished quote of yours with the customer’s name taken out, add the notes from the job, and fix the draft until it sounds like you at your best.
Then ask for the skill. Say: create a skill that captures this. The authoring guide says Claude handles the skill format natively and generates the SKILL.md with its frontmatter, the two labels at the top. You do not write any code.
Read the two labels. The name takes lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, and the words claude and anthropic are reserved, so writing-customer-quotes works and claude-quotes does not. The description should say what the skill does and when to use it, written in the third person.
Zip the folder and upload it. The help center says the folder name must match the skill’s name and the ZIP should hold the folder itself, not loose files. Then Customize, Skills, and the plus button.
Test it on three real jobs. Anthropic says to try several prompts that should trigger it, and to rewrite the description if Claude does not use the skill when you expect it to.
The first time Claude hands back a quote with the tax line blank and the warranty line worded your way, read it out loud to check. It will sound like you on a good day. It is not available on Windows or on Free.
### What a skill will not do for you
It will not always open. Claude decides from the description whether to pull the file, which is why the troubleshooting advice is blunt: name the skill in your request if Claude is ignoring it. And it does not know your prices. Anthropic’s authoring guide says to avoid time-sensitive information that will become wrong, and Missouri moves local sales tax rates at the start of a quarter. A rate typed into a skill is a small lie waiting for next quarter. Tell the skill to ask, or to leave a blank.
It stays with you. The help center says custom skills you upload are not visible to colleagues until you share them, and the developer docs say custom skills do not sync across surfaces: one uploaded to claude.ai is not on the API or in Claude Code. They add that on claude.ai each team member uploads separately, though Team and Enterprise admins have a way to provision skills for everyone.
And a stranger’s skill is software you have never read. The developer docs say to use skills only from trusted sources, the ones you made or got from Anthropic, because a malicious one can direct Claude to run code in ways the description never mentions. Treat a free skill pack from a social post like a USB stick from a parking lot.
Ask an AI who to call for your trade in St. Louis. Was it you?

People search for answers, not websites, and a website stays invisible until a friend, Google or an AI points at it. One sentence about this week’s work, a finished porch in Soulard, a cancelled slot, a new product on the shelf, and the skill turns it into the Google post, the Facebook post and the line for your listing, each in your voice, each with your never-say list applied. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I use Claude skills?
A.  Turn on code execution, open Customize, then Skills, and switch on the ones you want. Claude picks a skill by matching your request to its description, so you rarely call one by name. If it ignores a skill, name it in your request or tighten the description.
### Q. Are Claude skills the same as custom GPTs?
A.  No. A custom GPT is a saved setup that lives inside ChatGPT, and OpenAI says it plans to retire them in favor of plugins that carry skills. A Claude skill is a folder of instructions Claude opens only when a task matches. The habit of writing your process down once carries over to both.
### Q. What’s the difference between a Claude Project and a Claude skill?
A.  A Project holds background knowledge that is always loaded when you chat inside it. A skill holds instructions for one kind of task and loads only when that task comes up. Use a Project for who you are, and a skill for how you do a specific job.
### Q. What is the difference between Claude skills and Artifacts?
A.  An artifact is something Claude makes for you, such as a document, a deck or a small tool, that opens beside the chat so you can edit and share it. A skill is the set of instructions that shapes how Claude does a task. One is the output, the other is the recipe.
### Q. How do I use AI in business?
A.  Start with one narrow, repeated job and write down how you do it. Read every draft before it reaches a customer, and keep private customer details out of what you paste. Add a second job only after the first one runs clean for a few weeks. A skill is simply how you keep each job done your way.
### Q. What is the difference between Claude skills and commands in Claude?
A.  The Claude Code docs say custom commands have been merged into skills, so a command file and a skill both create the same shortcut. For a shop owner the practical answer is simpler: you can ignore commands. Build the job as a skill, give it a name you will remember, and test it on one real quote before you trust it with a customer.
### Q. Do I need to know how to code to build a skill?
A.  No. A skill can be a few lines of instructions in plain English. Do the job with Claude first, then ask Claude to create the skill from that conversation. Anthropic’s guide says Claude models handle the skill format and structure natively, so you review the text instead of writing it.
### Q. Is it safe to use a skill someone else wrote?
A.  Only if you trust the source. Anthropic says to use skills you wrote yourself or got from Anthropic, because a skill can include code and can direct Claude to run it. Read every file in a skill from anyone else before you switch it on, the way you would read a contract.

## Scholarships for St. Louis Students: A Verified Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/scholarships-for-st-louis-students
Searching for scholarships is overwhelming — and, unfortunately, crawling with scams. So we did the tedious part for you. Every scholarship below was checked on its official page, every one is free to apply (a real scholarship never charges a fee), and every one is open to St. Louis and Missouri students — from state programs, to hometown foundations, to the biggest national awards.
### Where can St. Louis students find real scholarships?
Start with My Scholarship Central — one application from the St. Louis Community Foundation that matches you to 130+ regional awards and interest-free loans at once. Then file the FAFSA at studentaid.gov, which automatically unlocks Missouri state aid like Bright Flight and Access Missouri, and add the reputable national scholarships below. Two rules first: file the FAFSA (several of the best awards need only that), and always confirm the current deadline and amount on the official page, because both shift every year.
### Missouri state programs
All official, through the Missouri Department of Higher Education & Workforce Development.
Bright Flight Scholarship. Missouri’s merit award, for MO residents scoring in roughly the top 5% of state ACT/SAT test-takers. Up to $3,000 a year (top tier). No application — hit the score and it follows you to a participating Missouri school. Official page →
Access Missouri. The state’s main need-based grant, for full-time MO undergrads with financial need. $500 to $3,500 a year depending on your school. No separate form — just file the FAFSA by the spring priority date. Official page →
A+ Scholarship Program. Can make community college essentially tuition-free. For graduates of an A+ designated Missouri high school (2.5+ GPA, 95% attendance, 50 tutoring hours) attending a participating community or technical college. Official page →
Fast Track Workforce Incentive Grant. Built for adult learners and career-changers — Missourians 25+ (or out of school two-plus years) with no bachelor’s, under the income cap, enrolling in a high-need field like healthcare or the skilled trades. Official page →
Minority & Underrepresented Environmental Literacy Program (MUELP). A niche, low-competition award for Missouri minority students pursuing an environmental, engineering, or natural-science degree (3.0 HS GPA or 2.5 in college). Official page →
### St. Louis & regional
The Scholarship Foundation of St. Louis. A century-old St. Louis institution. For students who’ve lived two-plus years in the STL service area with significant financial need. Renewable interest-free loans up to $11,000 a year, plus possible grants — no interest, no fees. Confirm the current deadline through Scholarship Central. Official page →
New Era Scholarship. One of the largest renewable awards for STL students already in college-access programs (College Bound, KIPP St. Louis, Wyman, UMSL Bridge, Little Bit Foundation, Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern MO, and more). Up to $15,000 a year; deadline is typically mid-April. Official page →
St. Louis Community Foundation Scholarships. The region’s hub: 80+ named programs, one application, matched to you. Amounts vary; the Foundation recently awarded $2.5M+ to 700+ students in a single year. This is your first stop — apply through My Scholarship Central. Official page →
### Major national awards
All open to Missouri students.
Coca-Cola Scholars. Flagship national merit award. Current high-school seniors, 3.0+ GPA, judged on leadership and service. $20,000, 150 awarded a year. Closes in the fall — confirm the date. Official page →
The Gates Scholarship. Among the most generous need-based awards in the country. Pell-eligible seniors, 3.3+ weighted GPA. A last-dollar award covering the full cost of attendance not met by other aid. Official page →
Jack Kent Cooke College Scholarship. Up to $55,000 a year for high-achieving seniors with financial need — one of the largest per-student undergraduate awards nationally. Official page →
QuestBridge National College Match. Matches high-achieving, low-income seniors (typically households under ~$65,000) to full four-year scholarships at top partner colleges — including WashU right here in St. Louis. No parental contribution, no loans. Official page →
Horatio Alger Scholarships. Rewards resilience over grades — for seniors with critical financial need who’ve overcome adversity. National awards around $25,000; Missouri state awards around $10,000. Confirm current amounts and dates on the official site. Official page →
### By field & background
Hispanic Scholarship Fund. The largest Hispanic-serving scholarship provider. Students of Hispanic heritage (any race), 3.0 HS or 2.5 college GPA, must file FAFSA. $500 to $5,000, plus mentorship and career support. Official page →
mikeroweWORKS Work Ethic Scholarship. One of the best-known awards for the skilled trades, and a great fit for St. Louis’s demand for workers. For students enrolling in an approved trade, vocational, or technical program — judged on work ethic, not GPA. Confirm the current amount and deadline on the official page. Official page →

File the FAFSA first. It’s the key that unlocks Missouri’s state aid and most need-based awards, and it’s free at studentaid.gov.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I have to pay to apply for these scholarships?
A.  No. Every scholarship in this guide is free to apply. A real scholarship never charges an application fee, a “processing” fee, or asks for your bank login. If one does, it’s a scam — walk away.
### Q. What is the FAFSA, and why should I file it?
A.  The FAFSA is the free federal financial-aid application at studentaid.gov. Filing it is what automatically unlocks Missouri’s state aid, including Bright Flight and Access Missouri, and it’s required for many need-based awards. File it even if you think you won’t qualify.
### Q. Which scholarship should a St. Louis student apply to first?
A.  Start with My Scholarship Central from the St. Louis Community Foundation. A single application matches you to 130+ regional scholarships and interest-free loans at once, so it’s the highest-leverage first move before you chase individual awards.
### Q. Can adults or career-changers get scholarships too?
A.  Yes. Missouri’s Fast Track Workforce Incentive Grant is built for adults 25 and older (or anyone out of school two-plus years) with no bachelor’s degree, enrolling in a high-need field like healthcare or the skilled trades. Scholarships aren’t only for graduating seniors.
### Q. How do I spot a scholarship scam?
A.  Watch for any request for money, a “guaranteed” award, pressure to act immediately, or a vague sponsor you can’t verify. Legitimate scholarships come from government agencies, established foundations, or schools — and you can always confirm them on an official page before you share a single detail.

## What an Entertainment Attorney Does in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-an-entertainment-attorney-does-in-st-louis
A songwriter in Millstadt just got an email from a small label out of state. There’s a PDF attached, twenty-two pages long, with a line near the bottom that says the label will own her masters “in perpetuity throughout the universe.” She has read it twice. She still isn’t sure what she’d be giving away, whether that phrase is normal, or whether she should just sign before they change their mind.
She’s not the only one around St. Louis staring at paperwork this week. A documentary filmmaker in New Haven needs to clear a song for a festival cut and has no idea who actually owns it. A podcaster in Clifton Heights was offered a network deal that wants exclusive rights to her entire back catalog. A comedian in Mascoutah just found out a clip of his set is running in someone else’s ad. And a two-person game studio in Winchester is being asked to sign a publishing agreement that mentions “all derivative works” without ever saying what that covers.
Every one of them is asking the same quiet question: is this a moment for a lawyer, or am I overthinking it? This guide answers that. It explains what an entertainment attorney actually does, how one differs from the general business lawyer your cousin uses, how they charge, and when a creator in a mid-size market like St. Louis genuinely needs one versus when the smart move is to wait. We won’t quote you a fee, because fees vary and depend on the work. We will tell you how the pricing works so you can ask the right questions.
### Why would you need an entertainment lawyer in St. Louis?
You need an entertainment lawyer when someone hands you a contract that controls your creative work, your name, or your income for years. Recording, publishing, management, sync licensing, and distribution deals all fall in that bucket. A St. Louis entertainment attorney reads the fine print, explains what you’d give up, and negotiates better terms before you sign.
The hard part is that entertainment contracts are written by the side with more money and more experience. They look like boilerplate. They’re not. A single clause about ownership, exclusivity, or term length can decide whether you get paid on a song ten years from now, or whether you can even release work under your own name. The songwriter in Millstadt isn’t overreacting. “In perpetuity” means forever, and forever is a long time to regret a signature.
The other reason is leverage. An offer usually arrives with a friendly deadline and a note that this is the standard deal. A lawyer who has seen a hundred of these knows what’s actually standard, what’s negotiable, and what’s a red flag. That knowledge is the whole product. You’re not paying someone to say no. You’re paying someone to know which yes is safe.
### What is an entertainment attorney?
An entertainment attorney is a lawyer who focuses on the contracts, rights, and disputes that come with creative work. Music, film, podcasts, comedy, publishing, and games all run on agreements about who owns what and who gets paid. The attorney’s job is to protect your side of those agreements, in writing, before the deal and after it.
### Contract review and drafting
Most of the work is contracts. A recording agreement sets who owns the masters and how royalties flow. A publishing deal covers the songs themselves, the composition and lyrics. A management contract decides what share a manager takes and for how long. Sync licenses put your music in a film, a show, a game, or an ad. Distribution deals control how and where your work is sold. An entertainment attorney reads each of these for traps, and drafts them when you’re the one making the offer.
### Rights and ownership
Copyright is the backbone. In the United States, you own the copyright to something you create the moment it’s fixed in a tangible form, unless you signed it away or made it as a work-for-hire. That last phrase matters. If you produce beats for a studio under a work-for-hire clause, the studio may own them outright, not you. An entertainment lawyer explains what you actually hold, what you’re being asked to transfer, and how to keep the pieces that pay over time.
### Negotiation and disputes
Beyond reading, they negotiate. A lawyer can push back on a term, ask for a reversion clause, cap an exclusivity window, or restructure how an advance gets recouped. When a deal breaks down, they handle the dispute: a label that stopped paying, a co-writer who claims a bigger share, an unlicensed use of your work. Sometimes that’s a letter. Sometimes it’s a lawsuit. Usually it’s a phone call that fixes things before either one.
### How they differ from a general business lawyer
A general business attorney can form your LLC, write an operating agreement, and review a commercial lease. Our guide to when a St. Louis small business needs an attorney covers that side well. What a generalist usually lacks is fluency in industry terms: recoupment, controlled composition clauses, mechanical royalties, reversion. An entertainment attorney lives in that vocabulary. For a creative career, that difference is the difference between a contract that works and one that quietly costs you for a decade.
### What kind of lawyer works with musicians?
Musicians work with entertainment attorneys, sometimes called music attorneys or music lawyers. It’s the same job with a narrower focus: recording contracts, publishing, licensing, and the ownership split between masters and compositions. Around St. Louis, most lawyers in this space also handle film, podcast, and game work, since a mid-size metro doesn’t support a specialist for every niche.
### Masters versus publishing
Every recorded song carries two copyrights. The master is the specific recording, the audio file itself. The publishing side is the composition: melody, chords, lyrics. You can own one without the other. A label deal often takes the masters; a publishing deal takes a share of the composition. When the songwriter in Millstadt reads “the label will own the masters,” that’s only half her song. A music attorney makes sure she knows which half she’s keeping and what it’s worth.
### Work-for-hire and session players
If you play on someone else’s record, or produce for a client, the paperwork decides whether you own any of it. A work-for-hire agreement means you don’t. That can be perfectly fair, if the fee reflects it, or it can quietly erase a future royalty stream. Before you book a session, it helps to know what recording studio time costs in St. Louis and what the studio’s standard agreement says about who owns the session files. Ask. It’s a short question that prevents long arguments.
### Sync, distribution, and streaming
Sync licensing, placing a song in a film, game, ad, or show, is where many independent artists earn real money now. Each placement is its own license with its own fee, territory, and term. Distribution deals control how your music reaches streaming platforms and what cut the distributor keeps. Both are contract-heavy, both are negotiable, and both are places where a music attorney can earn the fee back many times over. The filmmaker in New Haven clearing a song for her festival cut is standing on the other side of that same sync deal.
Run a St. Louis small business? See how to build its first AI skill.
### How much does an entertainment lawyer charge?
Entertainment lawyers charge four main ways: hourly, flat fee, a percentage of the deal, or a retainer billed against over time. Which one applies depends on the work. Reviewing a single contract is often a flat fee. Negotiating a long deal is often hourly. Representing a working artist month after month may run on retainer or percentage. Rates vary widely, so confirm with the attorney.
### Hourly billing
Hourly is the default for open-ended work: a negotiation that could take three rounds or ten, a dispute with no clear finish line. You pay for the time actually spent, usually tracked in fractions of an hour. The upside is you only pay for what happens. The downside is uncertainty. Ask for an estimated range up front, and ask to be told when the work is approaching it.
### Flat fees
A flat fee is one price for a defined task, like reviewing a recording contract and sending you a written summary of the risks. It’s common for creators who have one document and one decision to make. Ask what the flat fee covers. Reading the contract and explaining it is one job. Going back to the label with redlines three times is another, and it may be priced separately.
### Percentage of the deal
Some entertainment attorneys take a percentage of the money a deal brings in, rather than billing by the hour. That aligns their interest with yours, since they earn more when you do. It also means they may pass on small deals, and you should understand exactly what income the percentage attaches to and for how long. Get the arrangement in writing before any work starts, and read it the way you’d read any other contract.
### Retainers
A retainer is money paid up front that the attorney bills against as work happens. It’s typical for creators with ongoing needs: a touring act with a new agreement every month, a podcaster fielding sponsorship contracts. Ask whether any unused portion is refundable, how often you’ll see a statement, and what happens when the balance runs low. The comedian in Mascoutah with one clip problem probably doesn’t need a retainer. A studio shipping a game through a publisher might.
### Can you get out of a music contract?
Sometimes, but it depends entirely on what the contract says and what the other side has done. Contracts can end because a term expired, because the other party breached it, because a clause lets you leave, or because both sides agree to walk away. A lawyer reads the exit routes that already exist before anyone talks about a fight.
### Reading the exit clauses
Most contracts have doors built in. A term with a fixed end date. A key-person clause that lets you leave if the executive who signed you departs. An option the label can decline to pick up. A performance clause that releases you if the other side fails to put out your record or pay on time. An entertainment attorney finds those doors first, because walking through one is cheaper than breaking down a wall.
### Breach and renegotiation
If the other side isn’t holding up its end, late payments, missing royalty statements, no promotion when promotion was promised, that may be a breach. A breach can justify termination, but it has to be documented and, usually, the other side gets notice and a chance to fix it. More often the realistic outcome is renegotiation: a shorter term, a better split, or a buyout. Your lawyer’s job is to know which outcome is realistic for your facts, and to say so plainly.
### The 35-year rule
US copyright law gives creators a termination right. Under Section 203 of the Copyright Act, an author who transferred rights on or after January 1, 1978 can, in general, terminate that grant 35 years later, during a five-year window, by serving advance written notice within a specific timeframe. It doesn’t apply to works made for hire, and the mechanics are strict. The rule exists so a bad early deal doesn’t have to last forever. If a contract you signed decades ago still pays someone else, ask a lawyer whether this applies and what the deadlines are.
### When does a St. Louis creator actually need one?
You need one before you sign anything that transfers ownership, grants exclusivity, or lasts more than a year. You can usually wait if you’re gigging locally, releasing independently through a distributor with public non-exclusive terms, and nobody has put a contract in front of you. The moment money, ownership, or a long term shows up, the math changes.
### The wait-and-watch list
Early on, most of what you do is low risk. Playing shows, posting episodes, self-releasing through a distributor whose terms are public and non-exclusive, selling merch at a folding table. These don’t usually need a lawyer. Register your copyrights, keep clean records of who wrote what, and use simple written agreements with collaborators. Those habits are free, and they make any lawyer’s job faster and cheaper later.
### The call-someone list
Call one when a label, publisher, network, manager, or platform sends you a contract. Call one before a co-writer dispute turns into a public fight. Call one when your work shows up somewhere you never licensed it, like the comedian in Mascoutah watching his set run in a stranger’s ad. Call one when a game publisher asks for “all derivative works,” because that phrase can reach sequels, merchandise, and a film option the Winchester studio hasn’t even imagined yet.
### How to interview an entertainment attorney
Treat the first meeting as an interview, because it is one. Shortlist two or three attorneys, sit down with each, and say plainly what you have and what you want: “This is a recording deal. I want to keep my publishing and cap the term at two albums.” Then listen. One lawyer will explain what’s realistic, what’s standard, and where they’d push. Another will nod and promise the moon. The gap between what you asked for and what each one is prepared to deliver is your signal. Our guide on how to find the right lawyer in St. Louis walks through the same approach for other legal needs.
Before you hire anyone, confirm they’re licensed. Missouri lawyers are licensed through the Missouri Bar, and you can look up an attorney’s status there in about a minute. If a lawyer is licensed in another state but not Missouri, ask how that affects representing you in a Missouri dispute. Entertainment deals often cross state lines, but a dispute that lands in a St. Louis courtroom needs someone who can stand in it.
