### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it safe to store a snowmobile outside during the summer?
A.  It is the worst of the common options, though plenty of people do it. Sun destroys the seat, hood, and windshield, a plastic tarp traps humidity against metal and breeds corrosion, and rodents treat a parked sled as free housing. If outside is your only choice, get it off dirt onto pavement or blocks, use a breathable cover rather than a tarp, keep the track off the ground, and check on it monthly. Indoors and shaded beats outdoors every time.
### Q. Should I store my snowmobile with a full tank of gas?
A.  Most owners store a full or nearly full tank with stabilizer added, because empty space collects condensation and ethanol blended fuel pulls water out of humid air. Add the stabilizer first, then run the engine long enough to move treated fuel through the pump, lines, and carburetors or injectors, since untreated fuel sitting in those passages is what actually gums things up. If your owner manual specifies something different for your engine, that instruction wins over general advice.
### Q. How often should you change snowmobile chaincase oil?
A.  Check your owner manual first, because intervals differ by machine, but many riders change it annually or roughly every thousand to fifteen hundred miles, whichever comes sooner. It is a cheap job, and the drained oil is a diagnostic. Dark is normal. Metallic glitter or a gritty feel means the chain and sprockets are shedding material and you should look closer. For a metro-owned sled ridden a few weekends a year, doing it each spring before storage is easy to remember.
### Q. What kind of gas should you put in a snowmobile?
A.  Use the octane printed in your owner manual or on the sticker near the fuel cap. Many trail sleds run fine on regular or midgrade, while turbocharged and high compression engines usually require premium. Just as important, keep the ethanol content low. Most manufacturers allow up to E10 and prohibit anything higher, so avoid E15 and E85 pumps entirely. Ethanol free fuel, where you can find it, is noticeably easier on a machine that sits most of the year.
### Q. What happens if you use 87 octane instead of 93?
A.  If your engine only calls for 87, nothing happens and you saved money. If it requires premium, low octane fuel can detonate under load, and detonation is what melts pistons in a two-stroke. Engines with knock sensors often protect themselves by pulling timing, so the symptom is a sled that feels flat rather than one that fails outright. Do not gamble on it. If you already put in the wrong grade, run the tank low and refill with the correct fuel.
### Q. How many miles can a snowmobile go on a full tank of gas?
A.  It varies more than new owners expect, because tank size, engine type, throttle habits, snow depth, and passenger weight all change it. A four-stroke cruising a groomed trail travels considerably farther than a big two-stroke working through deep powder. Read your spec sheet for tank capacity, then measure your own real range over the first few fill ups and plan around that number. On unfamiliar trail systems, refuel whenever you pass a station rather than testing the reserve.
### Q. Are snowmobiles difficult to drive?
A.  Not difficult to start doing, but harder than it looks to do well. Throttle and brake are simple, and a groomed trail at a moderate pace is manageable within an afternoon. What takes practice is body position, because you steer a sled by shifting your weight as much as by turning the bars, and beginners fight the machine in corners and in deep snow. Take a safety course, start on flat groomed trails, and ride with someone experienced the first few times.
### Q. Do I need a trailer, or can I haul a snowmobile in a pickup bed?
A.  Some short track sleds fit in a full size long bed with the tailgate down and a proper ramp system, but most riders trailer, and for a long haul north a trailer is the safer choice. Loading a sled into a bed alone is where people get hurt. A trailer also gives you room for gas cans, gear, and a second machine. Whatever you use, secure the sled at four points and re-check the straps after your first stop.

## Whose Name Is That? Laser Tattoo Removal in St. Louis, Honestly
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/laser-tattoo-removal-in-st-louis-what-to-expect
“Whose name is that?” Your kid asks it at the pool, finger on your forearm, and the knot lands in your chest before you can answer. Third inning at Busch Stadium in July, you’re the only one in long sleeves, cotton glued to your skin while everyone around you smells like sunscreen and nacho cheese. At a counter it’s the palm you lay flat across your wrist when you sign.
Then comes the consultation chair: goggles pressed tight to your face, a cold-air blower roaring against your skin, the first pulse landing like a hot rubber band snapped hard. Most people ask how many sessions. Around here, the question that matters more is who examines you before that laser fires - and on the Illinois side of the river, the rules answer that for you.
### Can a tattoo be 100% removed?
Some tattoos clear completely and many do not. Black ink on light skin, done by a professional and given enough sessions, often fades to nothing visible. Dense color, layered cover-ups and stubborn greens, reds and yellows often stop at a faint shadow. An honest provider tells you that before the first pulse, as a range.
There’s also gone, and gone-gone. Skin that reads as plain skin across a dinner table on The Hill is a result most people take happily. Chasing the last gray ghost can eat as many sessions as the whole visible fade did, and sometimes the skin is better left alone. And one warning nobody prints on the flyer: white and flesh-tone ink can turn black under the laser, and the FDA says pigment that oxidizes that way is no longer treatable by laser. A good provider tests a speck of it first.
For plenty of people, gone isn’t even the goal. If you want new art over the old, you may only need the old ink quieted - faded enough that an artist has room to work - and that usually takes far fewer sessions than full removal. It also brings a second professional into the job, and that one you can check fast. A tattoo shop in the city needs a City of St. Louis tattoo permit in addition to a state license, and that permit serves as the shop’s business license. Ask to see it before anyone on Cherokee Street lays a needle over your faded piece. If they bristle at that, keep walking.
### The side of the river changes who has to look at you first
Here’s the line worth screenshotting: the snap feels identical on your arm, but the paperwork behind it depends on which end of the Poplar Street Bridge the clinic sits. On the Illinois side, Section 1285.336 of the Illinois medical practice rules says a physician must examine the patient and determine a course of treatment before any procedure utilizing a laser. The physician can hand the actual pulses to a nurse or other trained staff, but only with the physician on site or available by phone to respond to a complication. If you live in Brighton, Bunker Hill, Gillespie or Benld and book close to home, that’s the rulebook your clinic works under.
On the Missouri side, I couldn’t find a rule that spells it out the same way. That doesn’t make a Missouri clinic worse. It means the answer lives with the clinic instead of in a rulebook you can look up, so you have to ask it out loud.
Say it at the front desk, word for word, before you hand over a card: “Before I book, what is the name of the physician who will examine me, when will that exam happen, and who will set the energy on the laser?” Write the name down, and look that doctor up on the state medical board’s website before your first visit. On the Illinois side, the answer should be a doctor who actually looks at your skin before the first pulse. On the Missouri side, follow up with two more: is there a medical director, and is a physician or nurse in the building on treatment days? A clinic with nothing to hide answers in one breath.
### How does a laser break up ink that’s been there for years?
Lie back with the goggles on and you hear it before you feel it: a sharp snap with every pulse, fast and dry. The laser isn’t burning ink out of you. It fires extremely short pulses of light that tattoo pigment absorbs and the surrounding skin mostly ignores. The pigment heats and expands faster than it can shed that energy, and the particle cracks apart. Clinicians call it photoacoustic, or photomechanical, shattering. Think shockwave, not frying pan.
Ask which device they use, because the two common families fire at very different pulse lengths, and the shorter, sharper spike tends to break pigment into smaller pieces. Wavelength matters just as much. As the FDA puts it, different colors of ink absorb different wavelengths of light, so a multi-colored tattoo may need more than one laser, and a clinic with a single wavelength should tell you at the consultation what it can’t treat - not four sessions in, when the black has faded and the green hasn’t moved.
Then comes the slow part. Macrophages, the cleanup cells of your immune system, swallow the shattered fragments and carry them off through the lymphatic system over the following weeks. That’s why removal takes multiple treatments with weeks in between, often longer on delicate areas or skin still pink from the last visit. Treating sooner fires at pigment already on its way out, adding inflammation without progress. Drinking water, not smoking and moving your body all support that cleanup, which is dull advice that happens to be the real work between appointments.
### What decides whether it takes four sessions or fifteen?
A handful of things, mostly: ink color, density and layering, amateur versus professional work, age, placement, skin tone, and whether the piece has already been covered once. They multiply against each other, which is why an honest answer comes as a range and why a test spot beats any chart.
Start with the ink nobody can read. Artists buy from many suppliers, so two black tattoos done a mile apart - one off South Grand, one in Soulard - can behave differently under the same laser. A provider can only watch how yours answers and adjust.
Black and dark blue are the easiest targets. Green, red and yellow are the hardest, and they need specific wavelengths not every clinic owns. White ink and flesh-tone pigments are the trap: they can oxidize and turn black the instant the laser hits them, and the FDA notes that oxidized pigment is no longer treatable by laser. That’s exactly why a careful provider tests a speck first instead of treating blind.
Density is its own problem. A modern piece with heavy saturation and layered shading holds far more pigment per square inch than a thin line drawing, and every particle has to be broken and hauled away. A cover-up is worse: two tattoos stacked in the same skin, and the laser has to work through the top one to reach the one underneath.
The kitchen-table stick-and-poke has a surprising edge. Amateur work usually sits shallower with less pigment, so it often clears in fewer sessions than machine-applied professional ink, though uneven depth can make it fade blotchy for a while in the middle. Age helps too. Your immune system has been nibbling at old pigment since the day it went in, and most providers want a fresh tattoo to settle for several weeks to a few months before treating it at all.
Location matters more than people expect, because clearance rides on blood supply. Chest and upper-back tattoos, close to the heart, tend to move faster. Hands, fingers, ankles and feet are the slowest ground on the body. A nurse with script across two fingers, pulling twelve-hour shifts, should budget more appointments than someone with the same lettering on a shoulder.
Skin tone changes the method more than the outcome. Melanin absorbs laser light too, so on deeper skin the operator has to choose settings that go after ink without going after the surrounding skin, which usually means gentler energy, more sessions and longer gaps. With the right device and an experienced hand it works well. With aggressive settings meant for pale skin it goes badly, so if this is you, ask about it first.
### The snap, the frost and the two weeks after
Short and sharp. Most people describe each pulse as a hot rubber band snapping the skin, or bacon grease spitting off a skillet, over and over. A small tattoo can be done in a few minutes, and big pieces often get split across visits. Many clinics run a cold air blower, some have you apply numbing cream ahead of time, and some inject local anesthetic for sensitive spots like ribs and feet. Ask before you book.
Right after a pass the area usually turns chalk-white for several minutes. That frosting is gas released as the ink shatters, and it fades on its own. Then comes the red, the swelling, the tight heat of a bad sunburn for a day or two. Blistering, scabbing and pinpoint bleeding are common and expected, not automatic signs that something went wrong.
Keep the site under a sterile dressing for as long as your provider says. Wash gently with mild soap and cool water, pat dry, and use whatever ointment they recommend. Don’t pick scabs. Don’t pop blisters. If one opens on its own, keep it clean and covered, and call the clinic if it starts to look infected.
Then stay out of the sun. It’s the rule people break most, and treated skin is far more prone to pigment changes with sun exposure. A St. Louis July doesn’t take days off, so a Saturday in Forest Park or a float trip on the Meramec means covering the site, then high-SPF sunscreen once the skin has closed. Skip pools, hot tubs, saunas and hard workouts for a few days while it’s still open.
### What can go wrong, and on whose skin?
Blistering, swelling, scabbing and temporary pigment shifts are the common ones, and they usually settle. The risks worth real attention are scarring and lasting color change: hypopigmentation, where treated skin ends up lighter than the skin around it, and hyperpigmentation, where it ends up darker. Hypopigmentation is more likely on deeper skin tones and with overly aggressive energy, and it can take many months to recover. Hyperpigmentation is more common and more often temporary, and sun between sessions makes it worse.
Does tattoo removal leave scars? Usually not when the laser is used well. Scarring gets more likely when someone treats too hard, stacks sessions too close together, or when healing skin gets picked at.
Bring your history to the consultation, plainly and early. Eczema or psoriasis, a history of keloid scarring, any photosensitizing medication including certain antibiotics and acne drugs, pregnancy, an active infection over the site, a recent tan, or an old reaction to a tattoo all change the plan. Providers aren’t hunting for reasons to turn you away. They’re avoiding a result nobody wants. Everything on this page is general information, not medical advice, and your own skin history changes the plan. If a specialist already manages your skin, our guide on when to see a dermatologist in St. Louis explains how those visits usually go.
### Peroxide, salt and Vaseline all do the wrong job
None of them work, and several cause real injury. Tattoo pigment sits in the dermis, below the layer of skin that turns over and flakes away. Anything you put on the surface either can’t reach it or has to destroy the skin above it to get there, and that’s precisely how a home method leaves a scar where the tattoo used to be.
Hydrogen peroxide fizzes, stings and bleaches the surface. It can’t reach dermal pigment, and repeated use slows healing. Salt abrasion, sometimes sold as salabrasion, works by scrubbing skin away until it bleeds. People do report lightening, because they’ve injured themselves down to the ink, and what they keep is the scar. Lemon juice belongs in the same bucket: acidic, irritating, useless against ink in the dermis.
Will Vaseline fade a tattoo? No. Petroleum jelly has no bleaching action at all. The myth is a misreading of aftercare, where it can keep healing skin moist, which is a fine job for it. And the creams? The FDA has not approved tattoo removal ointments and creams or do-it-yourself kits, and says they cannot reach tattoo pigment in the deeper dermis.
### Should you remove it, fade it, or let an artist cover it?
Whether it’s better to get a tattoo removed or covered up depends on what you want to see in the mirror afterward. Full removal aims for skin with no visible design and takes the most sessions by a wide margin. Fading aims only to lighten the piece so a new artist has room to work, and typically needs far fewer. A straight cover-up skips the laser, but dark ink can’t hide under light ink, so it nearly always ends up bigger and darker than the original.
Fading is the option most people never hear about, and it’s often the best value on the table. Take a chest piece with reds, a green banner and one patch where an earlier artist already buried something. Its owner, driving in from Brighton, doesn’t need that ink gone. He needs it quiet. A handful of sessions can drop the saturation enough that the next artist gets real design freedom instead of being forced into another dark, heavy block.
Order matters. See the tattoo artist first, then the removal provider, because only the artist can say how much lightening the new design needs. Bring the sketch to the laser consultation and let them plan around it. ### Frequently asked before the first pulse
### Does laser permanently remove tattoos?
It can. The laser shatters the ink into small particles and your immune system clears them over time, which is why it takes multiple treatments. What nobody can guarantee is complete clearance. Some tattoos fade to nothing visible and others stop at a faint shadow, depending on ink, depth, color, placement and skin tone.
### Can a tattoo be removed in 3 sessions?
Rarely, if the goal is full removal. It can happen with small, old, faded amateur black work in a well-supplied spot like the upper arm, but most professional tattoos need more, which is why providers quote ranges. A short run of sessions is a more realistic target for a different goal: fading a piece enough for an artist to cover it.
### Is it better to get a tattoo removed or covered up?
It depends on what you want to see afterward. If you want clear skin, removal is the route, and it takes the most sessions. If you want new art, fading the old piece first usually gives the artist far more freedom than a straight cover-up, which nearly always ends up bigger and darker than the original.
### Do tattoo removal leave scars?
Usually not, when the device suits your skin and the settings stay conservative. Risk climbs with aggressive energy, sessions packed too close together, picked scabs and a history of keloids.
### Will vaseline fade my tattoo?
No. Petroleum jelly has no bleaching action at all. The myth comes from aftercare, where it is sometimes used to keep healing skin moist, which is a perfectly good job for it. Tattoo pigment sits in the dermis, below the layer of skin that sheds, and nothing you smooth on the surface reaches it without damaging the skin above.

## Fighting a Traffic Ticket in Missouri: What to Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/fighting-a-traffic-ticket-in-missouri-what-to-know
The citation has been sitting on the kitchen counter for nine days. A nurse who lives in Freeburg picked it up on her way home from a twelve-hour shift, and there is a web address printed near the bottom that will take her card and close the whole thing out in about four minutes. Four minutes is exactly the problem. Nothing on that screen tells her what she is agreeing to.
A contractor drives in from Breese five days a week with his tools in the bed of the truck. This is his second citation in about a year. He is not lying awake over the fine. He is lying awake over one word he heard from a guy on a job site: suspension. He has no idea whether he is close to it, or how a person would even find out.
A nineteen-year-old in Velda City got his first ticket ever and hasn’t told his parents, because he is still on their policy and he has already done the math on that conversation. He is hoping that if he pays it quietly, it stays quiet. It does not work that way, and nobody has told him.
And a driver with a commercial license who lives out near New Baden is holding a citation that looks identical to everyone else’s. It is not. The rules that apply to his license are federal, they are stricter, and the option most drivers reach for is closed to him.
All four are standing in front of the same decision: pay it, or do something else. This guide walks through what paying actually means, how Missouri’s point system is built, why insurance rather than the fine is usually the real bill, what a traffic attorney typically tries to do and what that does not accomplish, when a ticket is genuinely worth fighting, how a municipal case differs from a state case, and what a court date really looks like. One thing up front: this is general information, not legal advice. Outcomes depend on the court, the charge, and the driver’s record, and the only numbers worth trusting are the ones you get from the Missouri Department of Revenue and the court named on your citation.
### Is it worth fighting a speeding ticket in Missouri?
Often, yes, and the fine is rarely the reason. Paying a Missouri speeding ticket is a guilty plea that puts a conviction and points on your license. The insurance increase that follows can outrun the fine several times over. It depends on the court, the charge, and your record, which is why nobody can answer it for you in one sentence.
The fine is a one-time number you can see. Everything else is a number you cannot see yet. Points sit on your driving record and accumulate toward a threshold. Insurers look back over a multi-year window when they price a policy, so a conviction entered this month can still be shaping a renewal quote a long time from now. The payment screen does not mention any of that.
There is a real case for just paying, and we won’t pretend otherwise. If the charge is a non-moving violation that carries no points, if your record is clean, and if you do not drive for a living, paying may honestly be the cheapest path once you count your own time. The point is that it should be a decision you made, not a button you pressed.
So the question worth asking is not “what does this cost me this month.” It is “what does this cost me over the next three years.” Ask it before you type in a card number, because after that the answer is mostly locked in.
### What happens when you pay the ticket online?
You plead guilty. That is the entire mechanism. When you pay the fine, the court enters a conviction, reports it to the Missouri Department of Revenue, and the department assesses whatever points that violation carries. There is no step in the process where somebody checks whether this was a good idea for you.
Once the conviction is entered, it is on your driving record, and undoing it later is far harder than dealing with it while the case is open. Prosecutors negotiate open cases. They do not reopen closed ones as a courtesy. The window is short and it closes quietly.
Read what you were actually charged with before you decide anything. The citation names a statute or an ordinance number, and those are not interchangeable. Some citations are non-moving from the start, equipment or paperwork matters that carry no points at all. Others are moving violations that do. And a ticket that looks routine can carry a charge more serious than the word speeding suggests.
There is also a date printed on the citation, and it matters more than the dollar figure does. Ignoring it is the one option with no upside at all. Missing a court date or a payment deadline can bring a warrant, added costs, and action against your license, which turns a small problem into an expensive one. If the date is unclear or the paperwork is lost, call the court named on the citation and ask. Clerks answer that question all day long.
### How does Missouri’s point system work?
Missouri assigns points by type of conviction, not by how the stop felt. State law sets the point value attached to each violation, the Department of Revenue keeps the running total for your license, and crossing a threshold inside a set time window triggers a suspension or a revocation. Points then come back off over time if you stay clean.
### Where the points come from
The charging document drives the point count. As a general structure, a moving violation charged under a municipal ordinance carries fewer points than the same conduct charged under state statute, and a non-moving violation generally carries none. That gap is exactly why what the charge is called matters more than what the fine is. Verify current point values with the Missouri Department of Revenue rather than a number from a forum thread, including any number you read here.
### What accumulation actually triggers
Points are counted in rolling windows. Accumulate enough inside an eighteen-month period and Missouri suspends the license. Larger totals measured over twelve, twenty-four, or thirty-six months bring a revocation instead, and repeat suspensions run longer each time. The contractor driving in from Breese is asking the right question, and he does not have to guess at the answer. He can request his own driving record from the Department of Revenue and read the total.
### How points come back off
Missouri steps an accumulated total down over time for a driver who picks up nothing new. The total is reduced after a year without a new conviction, reduced again after two, and reaches zero after three. The conviction itself can stay visible on the driving record longer than the points last, which is one reason your point total and your insurance quote do not always tell the same story.
Missouri does not have a general statewide traffic school that erases points the way some states do. Individual courts sometimes offer their own programs or dispositions, so ask the court named on your citation what it actually offers rather than assuming. The reliable lever is how the charge gets resolved in the first place, which is why an open case is worth more than a closed one.
### Why is insurance the real cost, not the fine?
Because the fine happens once and the insurance happens every renewal for years. Carriers price a policy partly on your driving record, and most of them look back over a multi-year window. A single moving-violation conviction can quietly add to every renewal inside that window, which is how a modest fine turns into a much bigger number.
How much bigger depends on the carrier, the violation, the driver, and everything else already on the record. Anyone who quotes you a percentage is guessing. What you can do is ask your own agent a direct question before you resolve the ticket: how does this company treat a moving-violation conviction, and for how long? Our guide to what car insurance costs in St. Louis covers what moves premiums around the metro generally.
Not every conviction is weighted the same. A conviction for a large amount over the limit reads differently to an underwriter than a minor one, and a conviction tied to a crash reads differently again. A non-moving violation generally does not surface the same way at all. That single fact is the whole reason the amended-charge path exists.
Household policies are where this stings most. The nineteen-year-old in Velda City is already priced as an expensive driver, and a conviction on top of that can move the household’s premium, not just his share of it. Staying quiet does not help him. His parents will meet the number at renewal whether or not he brings it up first.
### What is an amended charge, and what does it not do?
An amended charge is the path most traffic attorneys work toward. The attorney asks the prosecutor to amend the moving violation to a non-moving one, so the conviction that gets reported carries no points against the license. The fine and court costs are usually higher than the original ticket. It is a trade, not a rescue.
The logic is not mysterious. The city or the state still gets a resolved case and a paid fine. You still get a conviction, just one that does not touch your point total. Everyone involved has a reason to say yes, which is why the path exists in the first place.
Here is what it does not do. It is not a dismissal, and nothing about it is guaranteed. Prosecutors have discretion, courts differ from one another, and policies change. A driver with a long recent record is a harder case than a driver with a clean one, and some charges are not eligible at all. No honest attorney will tell you in advance what a prosecutor will agree to, because they genuinely do not know.
It also leaves a record. Something appears on the case file, and in certain situations that matters. It is not the same as never having been charged, and anyone describing it that way is smoothing over the details. Ask an attorney what the realistic outcomes are in the court named on your citation, then listen for whether the answer uses the word “typically” or the word “guaranteed.” Only one of those is a real answer.
### When is a ticket actually worth fighting?
When the conviction would cost you more than the case does. That is the whole test, and it turns on four things: how many points you already carry, whether your job depends on driving, what class of license you hold, and how serious the charge is. Work through those four before you decide anything.
It tilts toward fighting when you already have points on your record, when you hold a commercial license, when you are a new or intermediate license holder, or when the charge is heavier than routine speeding. A large amount over the limit, careless and imprudent driving, driving while suspended, or anything involving a crash is a different animal, and it deserves advice built around your actual situation rather than a general article.
It tilts the other way when the charge is already non-moving and carries no points, when your record is genuinely clean, and when you do not drive for work. Even then, one call to your insurance agent is worth making first. That call costs nothing, takes five minutes, and it sometimes flips the answer entirely.

### Municipal court or state court: what is the difference?
Who wrote the ticket usually determines where the case lives. A citation issued under a city ordinance is handled in the municipal division, and a citation charging a violation of state law goes to the circuit court for the county where it was issued. That one distinction shapes the points, the possible penalties, and the process you are about to sit through.
Municipal ordinance cases are, structurally, the lighter track. The point value attached to an ordinance conviction is generally lower than the state equivalent, the penalty is typically a fine plus costs, and the docket moves quickly. That is a description of how the two systems are built. It is not a comment on any particular city, court, or department.
A state charge can carry a misdemeanor classification, which brings a different set of possible consequences and a different kind of record. Whether a given speeding charge lands as an infraction or a misdemeanor depends on the statute charged and the circumstances of the stop. Read your citation, and if the statute number means nothing to you, ask the clerk or an attorney what you are actually facing before you respond to it.
### What actually happens on a court date?
Less drama than most people expect. Traffic dockets are volume operations: a room full of people, a clerk calling names off a list, and most cases resolved in a few minutes at the front. Arrive early with your citation and a photo ID, silence your phone, and expect to wait while the room works through the list.
In many courts the practical business happens before the judge ever speaks to you. Cases are discussed with the prosecutor, an agreement is reached or it is not, and the judge then takes the plea and enters the disposition. If you need more time, a continuance is often available for the asking. Ask the court for it. Do not simply skip.
If an attorney represents you, they can appear on your behalf in many municipal traffic matters, and you may never see the inside of the courtroom. That is not universal, though. Some courts and some charges require the driver to be present, and a judge can order it. Your attorney should tell you which situation you are in well before the date, not on the morning of.
Not sure when or where your date is? Our guide to how to find your court date and records in Missouri walks through looking it up. If anything is still unclear after that, call the clerk of the court named on your citation, because that is the only source guaranteed to be current.
### Which drivers face higher stakes?
Three groups carry more risk from the same piece of paper: commercial license holders, new and intermediate license holders, and drivers licensed in another state. For all three, the usual advice about routine tickets does not transfer cleanly, and the cost of getting it wrong is measured in a job or a license rather than a fine.
### Commercial drivers
Federal rules bar states from masking a commercial license holder’s conviction, which means the disposition that helps other drivers is generally not available. Serious violations can lead to disqualification of the commercial privilege, and a conviction picked up in a personal vehicle can still count against it. The driver out near New Baden should talk to an attorney who handles commercial license matters specifically, and should do it before the deadline on the citation rather than after.
### New and intermediate license holders
Missouri’s graduated licensing system puts extra conditions on younger drivers, and convictions can affect the path to a full license as well as the point total. Parents usually find out about the ticket at renewal, which is the worst possible order for everyone involved. If the driver in your household is a teenager, treat the citation as a family decision and make it early, while the case is still open and options still exist.
### Out-of-state drivers
States share conviction information with one another, so a Missouri conviction can follow a driver home and be treated under the home state’s rules and its own point system. A driver who lives in Caseyville or Freeburg and picks up a citation on the Missouri side is dealing with two systems at once. Ask an attorney who practices in that court how a conviction there is typically reported, and ask your own licensing agency how it treats an out-of-state conviction.
### How do you interview a traffic attorney?
Shortlist two or three attorneys worth interviewing, then actually interview them. State plainly what you want and what you expect: no points if that is achievable, no appearance if that is possible, a clear fee, and straight answers about your odds. Then compare that against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal.
Ask whether they regularly handle cases in the specific court named on your citation, because familiarity with that court’s process is most of what you are paying for. Ask what dispositions are realistic there for a charge like yours and a record like yours. Ask who will actually appear, the person you are talking to or somebody else from the office you have never met.
Traffic attorneys commonly charge a flat fee for a routine citation rather than billing hourly, and that fee usually covers the negotiation and the appearance. What it may not cover is the fine and court costs you still owe, a second court date, a different charge if new facts turn up, or an appeal. Get the fee and its limits in writing before you hire anyone, as a number rather than a range. Our guide to what a DUI lawyer costs in St. Louis explains how flat fees get structured when the charge is far more serious.
The clearest red flag is a promise. Nobody can tell you in advance that a charge will be dismissed or amended, and an attorney who says otherwise is selling rather than advising. A good answer sounds like a realistic range of outcomes with the reasoning attached to it. Vagueness about money is the second flag. So is anyone who cannot tell you plainly whether you will need to show up.
One more time, plainly: this is general information, not legal advice. A ten-minute conversation with an attorney who practices in the court printed on your citation is worth more than any article about Missouri traffic tickets, including this one.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many points is a speeding ticket in MO?
A.  It depends on what you were charged with. Missouri assigns points by violation type under state law, and a speeding conviction under a municipal ordinance generally carries fewer points than the same conduct charged under a state statute. Non-moving violations generally carry none at all. Because those values are set by statute and can change, check the current figures with the Missouri Department of Revenue and read the ordinance or statute number printed on your citation before assuming anything.
### Q. How long does it take for points to come off your license in MO?
A.  Missouri steps an accumulated point total down over time for drivers who pick up nothing new. The total is reduced after one year without a new conviction, reduced again after two years, and reaches zero after three. The underlying conviction can stay visible on your driving record longer than the points last, and insurers apply their own lookback periods on top of that. Confirm the current schedule and your own totals with the Missouri Department of Revenue.
### Q. How do you remove points off your license in Missouri?
A.  Mostly by not adding any. Missouri reduces an accumulated total on a schedule for drivers who stay conviction-free, and there is no general statewide traffic school that wipes points the way some states offer. A few courts run their own programs or dispositions, so ask the court named on your citation what it actually offers. The bigger lever is how a charge gets resolved while the case is still open, which is why paying quickly closes doors.
### Q. Is 20 mph over the speed limit a felony in Missouri?
A.  No. Speeding by itself is not a felony in Missouri. Depending on how it is charged it can be an infraction or a misdemeanor, and Missouri law treats a large amount over the limit as a more serious misdemeanor class than a small one. Felony exposure comes from other conduct, such as a crash causing injury or an alcohol-related charge with prior history. Read the statute or ordinance number on your citation and ask the court or an attorney what class applies.
### Q. Can I hire a lawyer to go to traffic court for me?
A.  Usually yes, for routine municipal traffic matters. An attorney can enter an appearance and handle the case without you present, which is why plenty of drivers hire one purely for the scheduling relief. It is not universal, though. Some courts and some charges require the driver to appear personally, and a judge can order an appearance. Ask any attorney you interview, before you hire them, whether you will need to be in the room on your date.
### Q. When should you hire a traffic lawyer?
A.  When a conviction would cost you more than the case does. In practice that means you already carry points, you hold a commercial license, you are a new or intermediate license holder, your job depends on driving, or the charge is heavier than routine speeding. Anything involving a crash, a large amount over the limit, or driving while suspended deserves advice specific to your situation. A clean-record driver with a non-moving citation often does not need one.
### Q. Does a 10 mph speeding ticket affect insurance?
A.  It can. Carriers price partly on your driving record, and most look back over a multi-year window, so a moving-violation conviction can shape renewals for years rather than months. How much depends on the insurer, your record, and the violation itself, and anyone quoting you a percentage is guessing. The useful move is calling your own agent and asking how they treat a moving-violation conviction and for how long, before you resolve the ticket.
### Q. Is any of this legal advice?
A.  No. This is general information about how the process is structured in Missouri, and it is not legal advice. Outcomes depend on the specific court, the specific charge, your driving record, and facts no article can know. Point values, thresholds, deadlines and fees change over time, so verify current numbers with the Missouri Department of Revenue and with the court named on your citation, and talk to an attorney about your own case.

## Who Is Liable in a St. Louis Truck Accident?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/who-is-liable-in-a-st-louis-truck-accident
A driver merging onto I-70 near the river gets pushed into the barrier wall when a tractor-trailer changes lanes into her. She feels fine at the scene, signs nothing, and takes a rental home. Two days later she cannot turn her head, and an adjuster she has never spoken to is already asking her to record a statement.
A man headed home to St. Louis County is stopped in backed-up traffic on I-70 when the truck behind him does not slow. He spends four days in a hospital. His wife comes home with a crash report, a tow yard receipt, and a problem she did not expect: the name painted on the cab, the name on the trailer, and the name on the insurance card are three different companies.
A crew leader driving up from Fayetteville on I-64 is hit by a load that shifted and broke its strapping. He was nowhere near that truck when the load was built. Nobody at the scene can tell him who loaded it, or who was supposed to check it before it rolled.
Three crashes, one structural question: when a commercial truck is involved, who is actually on the hook? This guide walks through it in order. Who can be liable and why, what makes a truck case different from a fender bender, the evidence federal rules force into existence, how fast that evidence can vanish, why the carrier’s adjuster calls before your first follow-up appointment, what to do in the first hours and the first week, how Missouri handles shared fault, the filing deadline question, what a lawyer costs, and how to interview one. This is general information and not legal advice. No article can tell you what your situation requires, and this one will not try.
### Who is liable in a truck accident?
Often more than one party. A truck crash can involve the driver, the motor carrier that employs or contracts with them, the trailer or cargo owner, the loading company, a maintenance contractor, a freight broker, a parts manufacturer, and sometimes a public body responsible for the road. Each is a separate question of duty and breach.
That list is not a menu you pick from. It is a set of relationships that existed before the crash and that the crash exposes. A driver on hour fifteen of a long day is one problem. A company that built a delivery window only reachable at hour fifteen is a different problem, and the second one is often the one that matters most.
### The driver and the motor carrier
When a driver is an employee acting within the scope of the job, the employer is generally answerable for what that driver does behind the wheel. Lawyers call it respondeat superior. It does a great deal of quiet work in these cases, because it moves the question from one person’s bad thirty seconds to the business that put him on the road.
Carriers sometimes answer that the driver was an independent contractor and not their responsibility. That defense is more complicated than it sounds. Federal leasing rules attach obligations to the carrier whose operating authority the truck is running under, and courts have spent decades working through where the line sits. Do not accept the label on the paperwork as the end of the discussion.
A carrier can also be liable for its own conduct, separate from the driver’s. Negligent hiring, negligent training, negligent retention, negligent supervision, and negligent entrustment are all claims about what the company knew and what it did about it. They are not about the last three seconds before impact. They live in the personnel file, the training records, and the dispatch history.
### The cargo, the loader, and the equipment
A trailer is often owned by someone other than the carrier pulling it. The freight inside may belong to a third party, and a fourth may have loaded and secured it. Federal cargo securement rules set standards for how a load is restrained, and when a load shifts, spills, or comes off, the question of who built it becomes central rather than incidental.
Maintenance is its own branch. Brakes, tires, lighting, and steering components are subject to inspection and repair requirements, and much of that work is farmed out to shops. If a brake job was done badly, the shop that did it can be a defendant. If a component failed in a way it should not have, the manufacturer can be. Around the terminals and rail yards near Brooklyn and the tank traffic running out of Roxana, that equipment turns over constantly, which is exactly why the records matter.
### Brokers, road conditions, and the parties nobody expects
Freight brokers arrange loads without owning trucks. Whether a broker can be liable for selecting an unsafe carrier is an area courts continue to work through, and the answer is not uniform. It is worth raising rather than assuming. In some cases a public body responsible for a roadway or a work zone can be a defendant too, though claims against public entities carry their own rules and their own, often much shorter, notice deadlines.
Why does the list matter so much? Because a claim built only around the driver can miss the decisions that actually produced the crash. The schedule, the hire, the skipped inspection, the load nobody checked. Those decisions were made somewhere else, by someone who was not in the truck.
### Why is a truck crash different from a car crash?
Because trucking is a federally regulated industry and ordinary driving is not. A two-car collision is governed by state traffic law and whatever the drivers remember. A commercial truck operates under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, which impose duties on the company, require records to be created and kept, and give an investigator something firmer than memory to work with.
### The physics are not comparable
A loaded tractor-trailer can weigh many times what a passenger car weighs, and it needs considerably more distance to stop. That weight difference is why truck crashes produce serious injuries at speeds a car-to-car impact would shrug off, and why underride and jackknife events behave the way they do. St. Louis puts those two vehicle classes side by side constantly: I-70, I-44, I-55, I-64, I-255 and I-270 all carry through freight, and the Poplar Street Bridge stacks it with commuters twice a day.
### The other side is a business, not a neighbor
In a fender bender you exchange information with a person. In a truck crash you are now dealing with a company, a commercial insurance program that is often layered across several policies, and defense counsel who may be involved within days. Nobody on that side is being sinister. They are simply organized, funded, and practiced, and they were practiced before your crash happened.
### What evidence does a trucking case produce that a car crash never does?
A great deal, and most of it belongs to the carrier. Hours-of-service records and electronic logging device data. The driver qualification file. Inspection, repair, and maintenance records. Post-accident drug and alcohol testing. Dashcam footage, telematics, engine control module data, dispatch messages, bills of lading, and weight tickets. None of that exists after a two-car crash.
### Hours of service and the electronic log
Most interstate drivers must record duty status electronically, which means the truck has been quietly keeping a timeline. When the driver went on duty, how long he drove, when he took a break, how fast he was moving, whether the pattern matches what he told the officer. Supporting documents such as fuel receipts and gate logs can corroborate or contradict that timeline, which is why both get requested together.
### The qualification file and the maintenance history
A driver qualification file is the paper trail behind the person in the seat: application, employment history, motor vehicle record, road test, medical certification. Alongside it sits the maintenance side, including annual inspections, daily vehicle inspection reports, and repair invoices. Read together, those two files answer a question nobody can answer from the roadside. Should this driver, in this truck, have been out there at all?
### Testing, cameras, and the black box
Federal rules require post-accident drug and alcohol testing in defined circumstances, and the testing windows are tight, which makes whether it happened a fact of its own. Many fleets run forward-facing and driver-facing cameras plus telematics that report speed, braking, and following distance in near real time. The engine control module can hold data from the seconds before impact. Getting a proper download usually takes a qualified expert and, often, a court’s help.
### Why can that evidence disappear?
Because most of it was never built to last. Retention requirements for several categories of trucking records are measured in months rather than years, camera systems commonly loop and overwrite, telematics feeds age out, and the truck itself gets repaired and put back into service because it is a revenue asset sitting idle. Routine business practice destroys evidence without anyone deciding to.
That is what a preservation letter is for. It is a written demand, sent early to the carrier and its insurer, identifying the specific items that must be preserved: the ELD data, the ECM download, the camera footage, the driver files, the maintenance records, the load paperwork, and the truck and trailer themselves in their post-crash condition. It converts a general duty into a specific one that a court can measure later.
Different kind of road trip? Here’s what renting an RV in St. Louis costs.
### Why does the carrier’s adjuster call so fast?
Because the carrier’s side is already working. Many motor carriers and their insurers keep rapid-response arrangements: investigators, sometimes a reconstruction expert, occasionally counsel, dispatched toward a serious crash scene within hours. By the time an injured person is discharged, the other side may have photographs, measurements, statements, and the driver’s account already locked down.
That is not misconduct. It is competent claims handling, and any well-run company would do the same. It does mean the two sides are not starting from the same place. One has a process that begins at hour two. The other is trying to arrange a ride to a follow-up appointment and figure out who is paying for the emergency room bill.
The early call to you usually asks for three things: a recorded statement, a signed medical authorization, and sometimes a quick settlement in exchange for a release. Each one deserves thought. A recorded statement taken while you are medicated and shaken becomes a permanent document. A broad medical authorization can open years of unrelated history. A release, once signed, generally ends the claim, including the parts of the injury that had not shown up yet.
You are allowed to be polite and still say you are not ready. Report the crash to your own insurer, get the claim number, and tell the other side you will follow up. That is not stonewalling. It is pacing. The same discipline applies later if a claim gets pushed back on, which we cover in our guide to what to do when an insurance claim is denied.
### What should you do in the first hours and the first week?
In the first hours, get medical attention and get the scene documented. In the first week, get organized and get advice. Those two windows do most of the work in a trucking case, because they are when the physical evidence still exists, the memories are fresh, and the decisions that limit your options have not been made yet.
### The first hours
Call 911 and let the responding officer write the report. Accept the evaluation even if you feel fine, because adrenaline hides a lot and a gap in treatment gets used against you later. If you can photograph safely, photograph widely: both vehicles, the whole scene, skid marks, debris, the load and its strapping, the road surface, the weather, and every marking on the truck and trailer.
Photograph the door of the cab specifically. Commercial vehicles carry the carrier name and a USDOT number, and that number identifies the operating company even when the paint says something else. Get the trailer number too. Get names and phone numbers for witnesses before they drive off, because the report may not include them all. Our companion guide to what to do after a car accident in St. Louis covers the scene basics in more depth.
### The first week
Start a single folder and put everything in it: the report number, medical records and bills, the tow yard paperwork, wage information if you are missing work, and a short daily note about pain, sleep, and what you could not do. That note is unglamorous and it is often the most useful document you own months later.
Ask that your vehicle not be repaired or scrapped yet, since it is evidence. Stay off social media about the crash, because a photo of you at a barbecue becomes an exhibit. And talk to an attorney early, even if you are undecided about hiring one, because the preservation letter and the deadline analysis are both time-sensitive and both belong to someone who does this work.
### How does Missouri handle shared fault?
Missouri follows pure comparative fault. If more than one party contributed to a crash, responsibility is apportioned, and an injured person’s recovery is reduced in proportion to their own share rather than eliminated by it. That structure is why the other side works so hard, so early, to establish that you did something wrong.
Illinois applies a different, modified approach, one that bars recovery once a plaintiff’s share of fault passes a threshold. That distinction is not academic in a metro that straddles the river. A crash near Hamel on I-55 and a crash on I-270 in St. Louis County can be governed by different rules, and which state’s law applies is a question for a lawyer with your actual facts, not for a guess.
The practical takeaway is simple. Do not narrate fault at the scene, do not apologize reflexively, and do not speculate about your speed or your attention. Say what you observed. Let the apportionment be argued from evidence rather than from a sentence you said while your hands were shaking.
### How long do you have to file?
Missouri sets a multi-year deadline for personal injury claims, but treating that as your working timeline is a mistake. Shorter deadlines and formal notice requirements can apply in specific situations, including claims involving a public entity. Wrongful death runs on its own clock with its own rules. The only safe move is to confirm the deadline that fits your facts with an attorney, promptly.
There is a second clock that nobody legislates. It is the one running on the camera footage, the log data, and the truck sitting in a yard waiting on a repair order. A claim filed inside every legal deadline can still be a thin claim if the proof stopped existing in month three. That is the real argument for calling early, and it has nothing to do with rushing to sue anyone.
If the crash crossed a state line, if a government vehicle or a road authority may be involved, or if someone died, assume the timeline is shorter and more complicated than you think. Ask the question out loud in the first conversation you have with a lawyer, and get the answer written down.
### What does a truck accident lawyer cost?
Personal injury work is almost always handled on a contingency fee, which means the lawyer is paid a percentage of what is recovered and is paid nothing from your pocket if there is no recovery. Initial consultations are commonly free. That is the structure. The details inside the structure are what you need to see in writing.
Ask for the percentage, and ask whether it changes if the case is filed, if it goes to arbitration, or if it goes to trial. Stepped fees are ordinary and worth understanding before you sign rather than after. Then ask the second question, which people forget: how are case costs handled, and who carries them along the way?
Costs and fees are not the same thing. Filing fees, deposition transcripts, records retrieval, accident reconstruction, an ECM download, and expert testimony are expenses, and trucking cases tend to run heavier on all of them than a typical car case. Find out whether the firm advances costs, whether you owe them if the case does not succeed, and whether costs come out before or after the fee percentage is calculated. That last one changes the math meaningfully. Our broader guide to hiring a personal injury lawyer in St. Louis goes through the agreement line by line.
### How do you interview a truck accident lawyer?
Shortlist two or three attorneys worth interviewing, then actually interview them. State plainly what you want and what you expect: how you want to be communicated with, what outcome you are hoping to work toward, how involved you want to be, and what you are worried about. Then compare that against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal.
Trucking experience is a specific thing, not a general one. A capable car-crash lawyer is not automatically a trucking lawyer. Ask whether they have handled cases under the federal motor carrier regulations, whether they have obtained ECM downloads and ELD data before, who they use for reconstruction, and how quickly they send preservation letters. A firm that has done this will answer in specifics and will not need a run-up.
Ask who will actually work your file. The person in the consultation is not always the person who returns your call in March. Ask how often you will hear from them, whether the firm tries cases or refers them out when they get hard, and what they think the weak points of your situation are. A lawyer willing to tell you an uncomfortable thing in the first meeting is showing you something useful.
One thing not to expect: nobody honest will tell you what your case is worth in a first meeting, and a confident number should make you more cautious, not less. There are too many unknowns that early, starting with how your injuries resolve. A driver from Smithton and a driver from Roxana with the same crash report can end up in very different places for reasons that have nothing to do with the lawyer’s skill.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What happens if a commercial truck hits you?
A.  You enter a process that moves faster and involves more parties than an ordinary collision. The carrier and its insurer may begin investigating within hours, and an adjuster often contacts you within days. Meanwhile federal safety rules mean records exist that a car crash never produces, including duty logs, maintenance history, and sometimes camera footage. Get medical care, document the scene and the markings on the truck, keep everything in one folder, and get advice early. This is general information, not legal advice.
### Q. What is the first thing you should do immediately after an accident?
A.  Check for injuries and call 911. A police response creates an official report, brings medical help, and gets the scene documented by someone other than the two people involved. Accept evaluation even if you feel fine, because serious injuries can announce themselves a day or two later and a treatment gap gets used against you. After that, photograph everything you safely can, including the carrier name and USDOT number on the cab door and the trailer number.
### Q. What should you not do after an accident?
A.  Do not leave before officers arrive, do not skip medical evaluation, and do not argue fault at the roadside. Do not give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurer before you have advice, and do not sign a broad medical authorization or a release without understanding what it closes. Do not let your vehicle be repaired or scrapped while it is still evidence. And stay off social media about the crash, because posts get pulled into the file.
### Q. What should you not say when making an insurance claim?
A.  Avoid guessing. Do not estimate your speed, the distance, or how long you looked away, and do not say you are fine before you have been examined. A reflexive apology can be read as an admission. Do not describe injuries as minor early on, since symptoms evolve. Stick to what you actually observed, give the basic facts, and say you will follow up rather than filling silence. Accurate and brief beats helpful and speculative every time.
### Q. Who determines liability in an accident?
A.  Not the police report, though people assume otherwise. Officers document the scene and may note a citation, but that is evidence rather than a verdict. Insurers make their own liability determinations for claim purposes, and those are negotiating positions. If a case is filed and not resolved, a judge or jury decides. In a trucking case, liability is usually argued from records: logs, maintenance history, load paperwork, telematics, and what the company knew before the trip.
### Q. When should I hire a truck accident lawyer?
A.  Sooner than most people do, because the preservation letter and the deadline analysis are both time-sensitive. Camera footage loops, log data ages out, and the truck gets repaired and returned to service. Consultations are commonly free, so an early conversation costs you the hour and nothing else. If anyone was seriously injured, if fault is disputed, if multiple companies appear on the paperwork, or if an adjuster is already pressing for a statement, do not wait.
### Q. Can I afford a truck accident lawyer?
A.  Most personal injury attorneys work on a contingency fee, meaning they are paid a percentage of any recovery and nothing out of your pocket if there is none. Consultations are usually free. Get the percentage in writing, ask whether it steps up if the case is filed or tried, and ask separately about case costs. Find out who advances expenses, whether you owe them if the case does not succeed, and whether costs come off before or after the fee.
### Q. How long after an accident can you still make a claim?
A.  Missouri sets a multi-year deadline for personal injury claims, but shorter deadlines and formal notice requirements can apply in particular situations, including claims involving a public entity, and wrongful death runs on its own clock. Illinois rules differ, which matters across this metro. Confirm the deadline for your facts with an attorney promptly rather than relying on a general figure. Separately, insurance policies impose their own prompt-notice requirements that arrive long before any court deadline.

## The Furnace Email ChatGPT Gets Wrong
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-make-chatgpt-sound-like-your-st-louis-business
“We appreciate your inquiry and look forward to serving your needs.” That is what comes back when you ask ChatGPT, at nine at night, to answer the woman whose furnace quit. She is reading it on a couch in a south city bungalow a few blocks from Bevo Mill, her coat still on. The sentence is grammatical. It is warm the way a hotel lobby is warm. And she can tell in the first four words that nobody who has ever knelt in front of a pilot light wrote it.
Who taught the machine to talk like that? Nobody. It is the factory default, the same polite stranger for every shop in the country, and it will sign your name to that voice until somebody teaches it better. Most owners across St. Louis try it once, wince, and go back to typing every reply at the kitchen table. Is that really the only choice?
It isn’t, and the tutorials are why it feels that way. They send you to the wrong box. They say paste your writing samples into custom instructions, but OpenAI’s help center says that box holds 1,500 characters on a Free or Go account and 5,000 on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, Business and Education. That is a couple of short paragraphs, not a voice. So where do the samples go? Into a Project, where a Free account can keep five files and where, per OpenAI, the project’s instructions override your global ones. What goes in the small box is rules. Here is a set a heating shop could paste today:
Who I serve: homeowners and landlords in the city of St. Louis and nearby.
What I do: residential heating and cooling repair.
How I sound: plain, direct, a little warm. Short sentences. First names. Never corporate.
Never invent a fact about my business: no years in business, awards, guarantees, prices or availability. If a fact is missing, leave a blank and ask me. Never write “we appreciate your inquiry” or “valued customer.”
Licenses: never write “licensed” or a license number unless I give it. Furnace permits in the city of St. Louis go through my City mechanical license, so leave a blank for it and ask me. Ask whether the job is in the city or the county before promising a permit.
Look at those last two rules, because here they carry the weight. In Missouri, the state’s Merchandising Practices Act makes any deception, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise an unlawful practice, and the statute’s definitions count services as merchandise. In the city, the Building Division says mechanical permits are issued to licensed mechanical contractors certified by the City of Saint Louis, and that the permits are required to install things like boilers and furnaces. So a chatbot that signs “fully licensed and insured, family-owned for three generations” on a shop you opened last spring is not being charming. It is making claims the state and the city both know how to read, and drafting a problem under your name. This is not legal advice, but one sentence of that statute is worth reading for yourself.
### Can ChatGPT talk like a human?
Not by default. Left alone it writes like the average of everyone, which is why it reads like no one. Handed a few things you actually wrote, it picks up the rhythm quickly: how long your sentences run, whether you say “heads up” or “please be advised,” whether you ever use an exclamation point. What it cannot do is hear you. It has the page, not the pilot light. So who does the last step? You do, out loud, cutting whatever you would never say to a customer’s face.
Here is the difference on that furnace email. The default says, “We appreciate your inquiry.” A project trained on your own replies might say: “Dana, that’s a rotten way to find out the igniter is shot. I can be there first thing tomorrow with the part on the truck, so it’s one trip. My City of St. Louis mechanical license number is [ask me], if you’d like to check it. Call me if it gets worse overnight.” Same facts, plus one honest blank: the bracket is the rule working, because the one fact the bot cannot know was left for you to fill in. One of those replies sounds like somebody who is coming.
### Where do the samples go, and where do the rules go?
Open your sent folder. Scroll past the quotes and the “running late” texts until you hit the replies that sound like you at the end of a long day, radio on, talking to a customer you actually like. Those go in a Project. In ChatGPT you select New project in the sidebar, name it, and add material by uploading files or pasting text. OpenAI’s Projects page says Free accounts can keep up to five files in a project, Go and Plus up to 25, and Pro, Business and Enterprise up to 40. There is a catch on the Free plan: OpenAI’s upload page also says Free users are limited to three file uploads a day. Hit that wall, and the Projects page lists pasting text as an allowed way to add material.
Which replies would you want a stranger to judge you by? The one to the regular who texts at seven in the morning. The one where you said no without losing the customer. The one where you apologized and meant it. Anything a marketing person polished for you can stay out, because the model will faithfully learn the polish.
Rules go in the Project’s own instructions: select the more options menu, then Project settings. OpenAI says project instructions apply only within that project and override your global custom instructions. That gives you one voice for customer emails and a different one for social posts, each in its own Project, with your account-wide custom instructions as the floor under both.
### How do the account-wide instructions get in there?
Thirty seconds at the shop counter with your phone in your hand: under Settings, then Personalization, with Enable customization switched on; on the iPhone and Android apps the menu reads Customize ChatGPT. OpenAI says they apply immediately to all chats, including existing ones. So what belongs in a box that small? Rules that never change. Notice what the heating-shop version leaves out: adjectives like “friendly but professional,” because those describe a thousand shops. Notice what it includes: a refusal list. The robot tone hides in what the model reaches for by habit, so the habits you want gone are the ones to name.
### Doesn’t ChatGPT just remember how I write?
It feels like it should, after all the times you have told it about the shop. Sometimes it does, and you cannot count on it. OpenAI’s memory page says Memory does not retain every detail from every conversation, that ChatGPT decides which available information is relevant to a response, and that Memory can change as your context changes. That is fine for remembering you have a shop in the city. It is a shaky place to keep a voice you are trusting with customers. Samples in a Project stay where you put them. A memory is something the model keeps or drops on its own schedule.
The same page warns that sensitive information can appear in Memory if you share it with ChatGPT, and lists custom instructions among the sources Memory can draw on. One more reason to keep the rules short and the customer details out.
Before you paste one customer email into ChatGPT, read this first.
### What stays out of the samples?
A customer’s address on Arsenal Street is not yours to give away. Customer names, phone numbers, addresses and anything with an account number all come out. Take them out before you paste, the way you would black out a check before photocopying it. The reason is on OpenAI’s data page: for individual plans, Free, Plus and Pro, it says it may use your content to train its models unless you turn off Improve the model for everyone under Settings, then Data controls. The same page says it does not use inputs or outputs from ChatGPT Business, Enterprise or Edu to improve its models by default. Even your custom instructions are covered: OpenAI says information from your use of custom instructions will also be used to improve model performance.
So the instructions box is no place for a customer’s street in Tower Grove, and the samples are no place for a last name. If you want to ask something sensitive, OpenAI says a temporary chat is not used to improve its models while it stays temporary, and it does not create memories. Passwords and card numbers never belong in any chat, on any plan.
### How do you read a draft out loud and fix it for good?
Standing up, in the driveway in Affton or in the shop, at your normal speed. The places you stumble are the places the draft is lying. A tidy list of three where you would have named one thing. A phrase like “rest assured.” An exclamation point you have never once used. Cut it, then tell ChatGPT what you cut and why: “I took this out because it sounded like a brochure. Keep it this direct.” Do that a handful of times and the same tells stop coming back, because edits carry more information than adjectives ever do.
If you think faster than you type, talk. OpenAI’s Projects page lists voice among the tools you can use inside a project. Say the reply out loud the way you would in the driveway, then ask ChatGPT to fix the grammar without changing a single word or the order. You keep your real cadence, minus the “um.”
Then comes the unglamorous part. Is every number, date, hour and promise in the draft actually true? The model writes fluently whether or not it is right, and fluent is the dangerous kind of wrong.
### Your first evening, in order
Choose one kind of writing. Customer replies, review responses or the weekly post. Not all three at once.
Collect the samples. Real messages you sent, with names, numbers and addresses taken out. A Free project holds five files, or paste them as text.
Make the Project. New project in the sidebar, then the samples go in as sources.
Write the rules in Project settings. Who you serve, how you sound, and the never-invent line, in a handful of sentences.
Turn off training if you are on an individual plan. Settings, Data controls, Improve the model for everyone.
Ask for the next real reply. Read it out loud, cut what you would never say, and tell ChatGPT what you cut.
Tomorrow morning the first reply will take you a few minutes instead of a half hour of staring, and it will have your pilot-light patience in it. The second will take less. That is the part nobody mentions: the setup is tedious exactly once, and the edits you make after that are the training. Want a person next to you for the first run? The Missouri SBDC’s St. Louis office at 120 S. Central Ave. serves the city and five counties, and 314-241-1697 reaches the office, where you can ask which AI sessions are on its calendar.
### Why does a real voice matter more once an AI is answering for you?
Because your customers now meet you in more doorways than they used to. There is the website you already pay for, the Google listing, the Facebook page, a reply to a review, a text. If each one sounds like a different stranger, people feel it before they can say why. People search for answers, not websites, and a website stays invisible until a neighbor, Google or an AI points at it. When they do arrive, the voice is what tells them they have found a person.
That is the case for doing this once and doing it well. The same voice that answers the furnace email writes the Facebook post and the line for your St Louis Near Me Directory listing. If you can post to Google or Facebook, you can post here too. Same effort, and it adds up.
