### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the characteristics of a good bagel?
A.  A good bagel feels heavy for its size, with a glossy, slightly blistered crust and a springy squeeze. The crust cracks lightly, then gives to a chewy, tight crumb inside. It tastes faintly sweet and malty on its own, before any topping. Same-day freshness ties it all together, since a bagel fades fast once it cools.
### Q. What makes a New York bagel different from a regular bagel?
A.  A New York bagel is boiled, hand-shaped, and baked dense, with a shiny, chewy crust that locals credit partly to the water. A “regular” supermarket bagel is usually steamed or simply baked, so it turns out soft, fluffy, and bread-like. The real difference is the boil and the chew, not the shape.
### Q. What are some common mistakes when making bagels?
A.  The usual slips: skipping the cold overnight rest, over-proofing so the dough goes slack, and boiling in plain water without malt. Too long in the kettle makes the crust leathery, while too short leaves it pale. Underbaking causes a gummy center, and crowding the pan flattens the rings. Rushing is the root of most of them.
### Q. Why do you have to boil bagels before you bake them?
A.  Boiling sets the crust and locks the shape before the oven. Hot water gelatinizes the surface starch, which bakes into that signature glossy, chewy shell. It also keeps the bagel from puffing up like a roll. Malt or baking soda in the water deepens the color. No boil, no real bagel.
### Q. What are different styles of bagels?
A.  The big two are New York, larger and puffy-chewy, and Montreal, smaller, sweeter, wood-fired, and boiled in honey water. Beyond those you’ll see kettle-boiled, steamed, sourdough, mini, and flat “flagel” versions. St. Louis adds its own trick: the bread-sliced bagel, cut vertically like a loaf for sharing.
### Q. What is the most popular type of bagel?
A.  Plain and everything trade the top spot depending on who you ask, with everything winning loyalty for its garlic, onion, sesame, poppy, and salt mix. Sesame and cinnamon-raisin round out most lists. The most popular type of bagel, honestly, is whichever one your neighborhood shop nails, batch after batch.
### Q. How do you store bagels and refresh a stale one?
A.  Eat them the day they’re baked if you can. To keep more, freeze them within hours: slice first, bag them, and pull out only what you need. Skip the fridge, which stales bread faster. To revive a firm one, sprinkle it with water and warm it in the oven for a few minutes.
### Q. Why are some St. Louis bagels sliced like bread?
A.  The bread-sliced, or St. Louis-style, bagel gets run through a bread slicer into vertical strips instead of one horizontal cut. The local story is convenience: it feeds a crowd, suits office and party spreads, and is easy for little kids to hold. It went viral online, and opinions about it stay loud.

## What to Order at a Brazilian Steakhouse in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-a-brazilian-steakhouse-in-st-louis
You sit down and there’s no menu. Just a little disc by your plate, green on one side, red on the other. Someone pours your water. Then a guy in gaucho pants strolls over with a yard of beef speared on a long skewer, shaves a slice onto your plate, and asks if you want more. You do. You have no clue what you just ate. It was some of the best beef of your life.
That’s a churrascaria, a Brazilian steakhouse, and the first visit can rattle you a little. No ordering. No prices on a card. Meat just keeps coming until you say stop. First-timers freeze, pile the salad bar to the ceiling, fill up on cheese bread, and then the picanha finally swings by and there’s no room left. It happens to almost everyone.
Good news: the whole thing runs on one simple system, and once you get it, you relax and eat like you mean it. Below is how a churrascaria works, what to grab first, what to leave alone early, and how to pace a meal that could otherwise flatten you before the best cuts ever reach the table.
### What to eat first at the Brazilian steakhouse?
Eat meat first. Skip the bread, go light on the salad bar, and wave down the picanha, the signature top sirloin, the moment it comes around. Flip your card to green, take the premium beef cuts while you’re hungry, and treat the sides as support, not the main event.
The logic is simple. You’ve got finite room, and the kitchen knows it. Bread, rice, and cheesy fried things are cheap to serve and heavy to eat, so they fill you fast. The picanha, the ribeye, the lamb, that’s what you actually walked in for. Guard the space for it. A little salad early is fine. A giant plate of it is a rookie move.
Show up hungry, too. This isn’t a meal to ease into. Skip the big lunch, drink some water beforehand, and arrive with a real appetite. When you do, those first rounds of beef hit differently, and you get your money’s worth instead of surrendering at round three with a plate of greens you didn’t need. Simple rule: protein before starch. Every time.
### How does a churrascaria actually work?
A churrascaria serves meat rodizio style, meaning continuous rounds carved right at your table until you stop it. You pay one fixed price per person for the whole spread: the salad bar, the hot sides, and unlimited passes of grilled meat. Servers called passadores circle the room with skewers, offering cut after cut.
Here’s the rhythm of a visit. You get seated. You hit the salad bar once if you want. Then you settle in, and the passadores come to you. Each one carries a different cut on a long skewer, names it, and slices it straight onto your plate. You catch the piece with small tongs. No ordering, no waiting on a kitchen ticket. The food finds you.
Good passadores work a loose order, leading with the crowd-pleasers and circling back with the premium cuts as the meal rolls on. You don’t have to wait for your favorite, though. If you want picanha and it hasn’t come by in a while, flag any server and ask. They’ll bring it, or send someone who has it. The parade bends to what the room wants.
The pace is yours to control, which trips people up at first. Nobody’s rushing you, and nobody stops bringing meat on their own. A table from Overland might sit for two hours and never see the parade slow down. That’s the deal you paid for. Your job is to manage the flow, and the restaurant hands you a tool to do exactly that.
### What do the green and red cards mean?
Each diner gets a small two-sided card or coaster, green on one side, red on the other. Green up tells the passadores to keep the meat coming. Red up means pause, you’re full or just catching your breath. Flip it whenever you like. That card is the entire ordering system, no words required.
Use the red side on purpose. When you want to raid the salad bar, sip your caipirinha, or actually taste what’s in front of you, flip to red so a passador doesn’t stack three more cuts on your plate mid-bite. Flip back to green when you’re ready for the next round. The staff read the whole room off those little cards, so keep yours honest.
Green up. Red up. That’s the whole language. A first-timer from Hazelwood can master it in about four seconds, which is part of the charm. You spend zero energy on logistics and all of it on eating.
### Which cuts should you order, and in what order?
Start with picanha, the crown of any churrascaria. It’s the top sirloin cap, ringed by a band of fat that bastes the meat as it grills, and most Brazilians will tell you it’s the best thing on the skewer. Take it first, take it more than once, then branch out into ribeye, filet, pork, and lamb.
### The beef cuts worth chasing
Picanha reaches you a few different ways: a thick crescent, thinner fanned slices, sometimes crusted in rock salt. Say yes every time it passes. Past that, keep an eye out for ribeye, marbled and rich, filet mignon often wrapped in bacon, alcatra, another sirloin, and fraldinha, the deeply flavorful flank. Beef is where a churrascaria makes its name, so lean into the beef and don’t apologize for it.
### Pork, lamb, chicken, and the sausage
Once the beef edge wears off, the rotation opens up. Linguica, the smoky Brazilian pork sausage, wins a lot of fans. So does bacon-wrapped chicken and garlic-rubbed pork loin. Lamb, chops or leg, turns up at the better spots and is worth flagging. Chicken hearts are the traditional deep cut, small and smoky. Try one. You might shock yourself and ask for seconds.
One more thing on ordering: you can request a doneness. If a passador is carving picanha and only the well-done end is left, ask for a rarer slice from the middle. Most will oblige or swing back with a fresh skewer. Same goes for lamb or filet. Speak up. The meat’s better when it’s cut the way you like it.
### What about the salad bar and the hot sides?
The salad bar is a full production, not a token gesture: cured meats, imported cheeses, hearts of palm, marinated mushrooms, and often hot dishes too. The hot sides usually land at your table for free: pao de queijo, crispy polenta, garlic mashed potatoes, caramelized bananas, and rice with black beans. All of it sits inside that one fixed price.
Treat the salad bar like a tasting, not a trough. A few hearts of palm, a slice of cured meat, a spoonful of feijoada, the black bean and pork stew, if it’s out. That’s plenty. The fried bananas and the warm cheese bread are hard to resist, and you shouldn’t skip them cold, but two bites tell the same story as a full plate for a fraction of the stomach room.
One habit worth keeping: taste before you commit. The salad bar rewards a small exploratory plate. If the feijoada is excellent, go back for more. If a marinated vegetable doesn’t grab you, no loss, you only took a spoonful. Grazing wide and shallow beats loading one heavy plate you feel obligated to finish.
St. Louis has a deep food scene well beyond the churrascaria, and it rewards exploring on other nights. Our local’s guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis is a solid starting map. And if a red-sauce tradition is more your speed, the guide to eating on the Hill, the city’s Little Italy points you toward a whole different feast.
### What should you drink with all that meat?
The classic pairing is a caipirinha, Brazil’s national cocktail, made with cachaca, lime, and sugar. It’s bright and sharp, and it cuts through rich beef nicely. Beyond that, a bold red like a malbec or cabernet holds up against the meat. Plenty of diners just stick with water, which keeps room free for more picanha.
Go easy on the sugary sodas and the big beers early. Both bloat you and steal space you want for the skewers. If you’re driving back to Collinsville or Madison after dinner, remember that one caipirinha packs more punch than it tastes like, since cachaca is strong and the lime hides it. Sip slow, keep water on the table, and let the meat be the main show.
For a non-alcoholic option, look for guarana, a sweet Brazilian soda with a berry-ish bite, or a fresh limeade. Both fit the food and won’t knock you out the way a heavy beer can. Coffee at the end, Brazilian and strong, is a fine way to reset before you roll home.
### How do you pace yourself so you don’t tap out early?
Pace it like a long walk, not a sprint. Take one or two slices per round instead of a heaping plate, keep your card red between passes, drink water over soda, and eat the best cuts while your appetite is sharp. The meat keeps coming all night, so there’s no reason to overload any single pass.
The classic mistake is going all-in on rounds one and two. Big salad plate, four cuts stacked, a basket of cheese bread, and by the time the second picanha comes around, you’re waving the white flag. Slow it down. One slice. Taste it. Decide if you want more of that cut or something new. Flip to green. Repeat. That loop keeps you eating well for the long haul.
Save a little room for dessert if that’s your thing. Grilled pineapple dusted with cinnamon is a churrascaria staple, and many places do a papaya cream or a flan. You don’t strictly need it. But after a mountain of beef, something bright and sweet closes the night out right. Small plates, slow rounds, red card when in doubt. That’s the whole strategy.
Making a night of a big celebration? See what a wedding officiant costs.
Once you’ve got the system down, the only thing left is picking a spot. The St. Louis metro has churrascarias worth the drive, from Des Peres out to the Illinois side.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What food is served in a churrascaria?
A.  A churrascaria serves fire-grilled meats as the centerpiece: picanha, ribeye, filet, pork loin, linguica sausage, lamb, and bacon-wrapped chicken, all carved tableside. Alongside comes a loaded salad bar with cured meats and cheeses, plus hot sides like pao de queijo, fried bananas, and rice with black beans.
### Q. How does a churrascaria work?
A.  You pay one fixed price per person, then servers called passadores circle the room with skewers of grilled meat, carving cuts straight onto your plate. A two-sided card controls the flow: green means keep it coming, red means pause. The salad bar and hot sides are included in that single price.
### Q. What is the difference between picanha and churrasco?
A.  Churrasco is the broad term for Brazilian-style barbecue, the whole method of grilling meat over open flame on skewers. Picanha is one specific cut used in churrasco: the top sirloin cap, prized for its fat layer. So churrasco is the style, and picanha is the star cut within it.
### Q. What is the difference between a churrascaria and a rodizio?
A.  A churrascaria is the restaurant itself, a Brazilian steakhouse. Rodizio is the all-you-can-eat service style it uses, where servers bring continuous rounds of meat until you signal enough. Most churrascarias run rodizio style, but the word rodizio also applies to other cuisines, like pizza, served the same rolling way.
### Q. How much does churrascaria usually cost?
A.  Most churrascarias charge a fixed prix-fixe price per person for the full rodizio, and it varies by restaurant, by day, and by lunch versus dinner. Lunch usually runs cheaper. Kids and salad-only options often cost less. Check the spot’s current menu, or browse the directory to compare local options.
### Q. Do you need to dress up for Brazilian steakhouse?
A.  Usually no. Most churrascarias sit in the smart-casual range, so clean jeans and a collared shirt fit right in. Some upscale spots lean dressier for dinner, especially on weekends, but few require a jacket. When unsure, call ahead or check the restaurant’s site. Comfortable clothes help, since you’ll eat a lot.
### Q. Is a Brazilian steakhouse all you can eat?
A.  Yes, the rodizio format is all-you-can-eat for the meat, the salad bar, and the hot sides, all under one fixed price. Servers keep bringing cuts until you flip your card to red. It’s not a buffet you walk to, though. The food comes to your table, round after round, until you say stop.
### Q. How does the card flip system work?
A.  Each place setting gets a small two-sided disc, green on one side, red on the other. Leave it green and passadores keep offering meat. Flip it red to pause between rounds, taste your plate, or visit the salad bar. Flip back to green when you want more. That coaster is your whole order.

## How an All-You-Can-Eat Buffet Works in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-an-all-you-can-eat-buffet-works-in-st-louis
The hostess at a place off the highway in Fenton hands you a plate still warm from the dishwasher, points at forty feet of stainless steel, and walks off. No menu. No specials board. Just steam, a row of chafing dishes, and a guy ahead of you stacking fried rice like he’s being graded on height. You already paid at the register. Now what?
Most people wing it. They fill up on whatever sits closest to the plate stack, eat until it hurts, and leave feeling stuffed and cheated at the same time. That’s not bad luck. It’s how the room was laid out to work, and once you see the layout you can’t unsee it.
This post walks through how the one-price deal actually works, what the restaurant is counting on, the unwritten rules regulars follow without thinking about them, how to pace yourself so the third plate tastes as good as the first, and how to tell whether a buffet in Brentwood, Manchester, or Arnold deserves a second trip. No prices and no names. Just how the machine runs.
### How does an all-you-can-eat buffet work?
You pay one flat price per person at the register, and in exchange you can go back to the serving line as many times as you like during your visit. The restaurant supplies clean plates, keeps the trays stocked, and clears your table. Drinks are often charged separately, kids and seniors sometimes pay a different rate, and busy hours may carry a time limit.
That’s the whole contract. You aren’t renting a table or buying a set number of dishes. You’re buying access to the line for the length of one sitting. Everything else, from how the trays are arranged to what sits nearest the plates, is the restaurant managing the cost of that access. Understanding that one idea explains almost every rule and every layout choice you’ll run into.
It’s a fair trade when both sides play it straight. The kitchen keeps hot food hot and the trays full. You bring a clean plate each trip, eat what you take, and don’t try to feed the table next to you. Simple rules. The strategy is where it gets interesting.
### How do buffets charge, and what counts as one price?
The price is per person, per visit, and it usually changes with the clock. Weekday lunch is the cheap seat. Dinner costs more because the line changes, with carved meat or seafood showing up in the evening. Weekends and holidays often run at the dinner rate all day. Same room, same plates, different number at the register depending on when you walk in.
Drinks are the first thing to check. Water is free almost everywhere. Fountain soda, tea, and coffee are sometimes bundled and sometimes billed per person on top. Anything with alcohol is always extra. Ask before you sit, because a table of five ordering sodas can add a surprising chunk to a bill that felt settled at the door.
Kids and seniors get their own math. Some places price children by age, some by height, and a few let toddlers eat free off a parent’s plate. Senior discounts usually kick in at a stated age and may only apply at lunch. None of this is standard across the metro, so the only way to know is to ask. If you’re bringing the whole crew, our guide to eating out with kids in St. Louis covers what to check before you load the car.
### Why the math works for the restaurant
A buffet is a bet the restaurant makes on averages. A few diners eat far more than they paid for. Most don’t. The kitchen wins by keeping the average plate cheap, and it does that with layout. Rice, noodles, bread, potatoes, and fried anything sit at the front where you pick up your plate. The carved roast and the shrimp sit at the far end, in a smaller tray, often behind a staff member with tongs.
Plate size is part of it too. Big plates invite big first trips, and a big first trip full of starch means you’re done by the time you reach the good stuff. Dessert, cheap and sweet, waits at the end to finish you off. None of this is sneaky. It’s just business, and knowing it is the whole edge you get.
A Brazilian steakhouse runs a cousin of this model, one price with servers bringing skewers to your table, and the same front-loading trick applies with the salad bar. If you’ve wondered how to handle that version, what to order at a Brazilian steakhouse in St. Louis walks the skewer order the same way this post walks the line.
### What are the unwritten rules regulars follow?
Clean plate, every trip. It’s the one rule you’ll get corrected on out loud. A used plate back at the line carries whatever was on your fork to the serving spoon and to everyone behind you. Leave the old one on the table. Staff will clear it, and stacking them neatly at the table edge is a small kindness they notice.
Don’t feed the person who didn’t pay. The friend who “just wants a bite” of your plate is eating for free, and every place watches for it. Same with sneaking a plate to a kid you claimed was too young to count. If someone at your table is going to eat, they pay. That’s the whole deal, and breaking it is the fastest way to a conversation with the manager.
No to-go boxes unless they’re offered. The price covers what you eat in the chair, not lunch for tomorrow. Some places will sell you a box by weight or at a flat rate, and that’s fine, because that’s them offering. Wrapping chicken in napkins and dropping it in a purse is not the same thing, and yes, people try it every single day.
Use the utensil that lives in the dish and put it back where it was. Don’t dig through a tray for the biggest piece with your fingers or with a fork from your plate. Don’t hover over a pan a staff member is swapping out. Step back, let them set it down, then go. Regulars do all this without thinking. New folks stand out fast.
### Tipping the person who clears your plates
Yes, tip. The server at a buffet doesn’t take your order, but they clear three or four plates per person instead of one, refill your drink half a dozen times, and reset your table faster than a full-service restaurant would. A smaller percentage than you’d leave a full-service server is typical. Leaving nothing is not. Cash on the table is cleanest, because tips added at a register don’t always find their way to the right person.
Time limits show up at busy hours, especially Friday and Saturday dinner. A place might post a window, or a host might mention it when you’re seated. Camp past it and you’ll get a polite nudge, then a less polite one. On a slow Tuesday nobody cares. Read the room. If there’s a line at the host stand, the table isn’t yours all night.
### How do you pace a buffet so you don’t tap out early?
Walk the whole line before you touch a plate. All of it. Both sides, the carving station, the dessert case. You’re scouting, not shopping. Most of the regret at a buffet comes from committing to plate one before you knew plate three existed. One lap takes ninety seconds, and it changes everything about what goes on that first trip.
Then go small. Take the salad plate if there is one, or leave half the dinner plate empty on purpose. Two or three items a trip. It feels wrong. It also means you sit down with hot food, eat it while it’s hot, and go back for more of the thing that was actually good instead of finishing something lukewarm because it’s already in front of you.
Protein first, starch last. If the carved meat and the shrimp are what you came for, they go on the first plate. Bread, rice, noodles, and potatoes are the restaurant’s best friends, not yours. Have some at the end if you still want them. You usually won’t.
Drink water. Soda is sugar and carbonation, and both fill you faster than you’d think. It’s also often the one thing on the table that isn’t included. A glass of water with each plate keeps you going and costs nothing. Sit down between trips, put the fork down between bites, and give your stomach a chance to report in. Twenty minutes is the number people throw around for that, and in our experience it’s close enough to use.
### What should you skip, and what should you grab first?
Grab first anything a person is cooking or carving in front of you. Made-to-order eggs, a carving station, a wok line, a grill. That food hasn’t sat under a lamp, and it’s the most expensive thing to produce, which is exactly why it’s at the back. Grab the tray that just came out too. A fresh pan of something plain beats a fancy one that’s been sitting.
Skip, or at least delay, the fillers. Dinner rolls, plain rice, plain noodles, mashed potatoes, mac and cheese, breaded anything that’s gone soft, cream soups, and the salad bar if you didn’t come for salad. Fine foods, all of them. They’re just cheap, heavy, and placed where you’ll grab them out of reflex. If you want value out of one price, don’t fill up on what you could make at home for pennies.
### Food safety on the line
Hot food should be steaming. Cold food should be on ice or in a chilled well, not sitting on a counter. If a tray has a dried crust around the edge, sauce that’s separated, or a skin on top, it’s been out a while. Skip it, or ask for a fresh pan. Staff at a well-run place will thank you for asking, because they’d rather swap it than have you eat it.
Look at the sneeze guard. It should be there, and it should be clean. Look at the serving utensils. Handles resting in the food, or one spoon shared across three trays, tells you something about how the back of the house runs too. And if the place is empty at dinner on a Saturday in Arnold or Fenton, the trays have been sitting a long time between refills. Busy is safer. Busy means turnover.
The cheapest way to eat well in this town isn’t always a buffet, either. Sometimes a counter-service spot with one great dish beats forty trays of average. Our cheap eats guide covers that side of the coin, for the nights when a one-price line isn’t the right call.
### Which buffet is worth your money?
Pick two or three buffets you’d actually drive to, and treat each one like you’re interviewing it. A quick call to the host stand, or two minutes of questions before you sit, tells you more than any review. You’re not being difficult. You’re being the diner who knows what one price is supposed to include.
Ask what’s included at the rate you’ll pay. Ask how drinks and dessert are charged, whether a kids’ or senior rate exists and when it applies, how often trays get rotated during a rush, and whether there’s a time limit at dinner. Then compare the answers to what you walked in expecting. A place that answers plainly and quickly has been asked before. A place that hedges on every question is telling you something.
The gap is the signal. If you expected soda included and it’s not, that’s a small gap. If you expected carved meat at dinner and they only run it on weekends, that’s a big one. Neither makes the place bad. It just means the one-price deal you had in your head isn’t the one they’re selling, and it’s better to learn that on the phone than at the register with four hungry people behind you.
Then do the walk-through on your first visit. Trays labeled, staff visible on the line, hot things hot, a fresh pan landing while you watch. A buffet that passes that test in Manchester or Brentwood is worth a second trip. One that doesn’t isn’t, no matter how long the line looks or how low the number at the door was. You’ll know within one lap.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do all-you-can-eat buffets charge you?
A.  One flat rate per person, paid at the register on the way in or at the table on the way out, with the number usually changing by time of day. Weekday lunch is cheapest, and dinner and weekends cost more. Drinks are often billed separately, and children and seniors may pay a reduced rate. Ask before you sit so the total doesn’t surprise you.
### Q. Can they kick you out of an all-you-can-eat buffet?
A.  Yes. It’s a private business, and management can ask anyone to leave. In practice that happens for a short list of reasons: sharing food with someone who didn’t pay, packing food to take home, wasting large amounts, or staying well past a posted time limit during a rush. Eat what you take and follow the house rules and it won’t come up.
### Q. How long can you stay at an all-you-can-eat buffet?
A.  As long as one normal sitting takes, unless a limit is posted. On a slow weekday afternoon nobody will hurry you. At Friday dinner with a line at the host stand, many places set a window, often somewhere around an hour or two, and staff will let you know. If you plan to linger, ask when you’re seated.
### Q. Are you expected to tip at a buffet?
A.  Yes. Somebody clears three or four plates per person, refills drinks, and resets your table faster than a full-service server would. A smaller percentage than you’d leave for table service is the norm, but leaving nothing isn’t. Cash on the table is the surest way it reaches the person who actually cleared your plates.
### Q. Is it okay to take leftovers from a buffet?
A.  Only if the restaurant offers it. The price covers food eaten at the table, and some places will sell a to-go box at a flat rate or by weight. That’s fine. Filling a box or a purse on your own is not, and staff watch for it. If you want a box, ask. If the answer is no, the answer is no.
### Q. How to not overeat at a buffet?
A.  Walk the full line before picking up a plate, then use a small plate and take two or three items a trip. Put protein and made-to-order food on the first plate, save bread and rice for last if you still want them, drink water instead of soda, and sit down between trips. Stop when you’re satisfied rather than when the plate is empty.
### Q. What are some unwritten rules of buffet etiquette?
A.  Fresh plate every trip. Use the utensil in the dish and put it back. Don’t pick through a tray with your fingers or reach around someone. Step back when staff are swapping a pan. Don’t share with a guest who didn’t pay, don’t pack food to go, and tip the person clearing your table. Keep moving along the line, because nobody wants to wait behind a browser.
### Q. Is buffet food safe to eat?
A.  Usually, if the place is doing its job. Hot food should be steaming, cold food should sit on ice, and a sneeze guard should be in place and clean. Skip any tray with a dried edge, a skin, or separated sauce, and ask for a fresh pan instead. A busy line is a safer line, because the trays turn over before they have time to sit.

## How to Learn Cake Decorating in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-learn-cake-decorating-in-st-louis
The cake is sitting on a counter in Ferguson at 9:40 on a Friday night. It’s for a seven-year-old’s party tomorrow at noon. The layers are baked. The frosting is made. Then the first pass with a butter knife drags a strip of crumb clean across the side, and now the whole thing looks like it lost a fight. Somebody says the word bakery. Somebody else says no.
That’s how most people start. Not with a class or a kit, but with a cake that needs to look decent by a deadline and a growing suspicion that the internet made this look easier than it is. It did. The videos cut the boring part, and the boring part is where the cake gets ruined.
So this post is the boring part, in order. Which way of learning is worth your Saturday, the short list of tools that matter, why buttercream misbehaves and how to make it stop, the techniques that look skilled but aren’t, your first three cakes, and what to ask a class before you hand over money. If you’d rather skip all of it and buy the cake, no judgment. Here’s how to find a good bakery in St. Louis.
### How to learn cake decorating for beginners?
Start with one in-person beginner class where you frost and take home a real cake, then practice the same three moves at home on cheap box-mix layers: a smooth crumb coat, a piped rosette, and a textured side. Watch video for detail after you’ve felt the frosting under a spatula, not before. Buy the six basic tools, not the 40-piece kit.
Why that order? Because decorating is a hand skill, like parallel parking. You can watch a hundred clips and still not know how much pressure a piping bag wants until you squeeze one. A single class gives you the feel in two hours. Home practice makes it stick. Video fills in the details you now have a reason to ask about.
And the box mix isn’t a shortcut you should feel bad about. Nobody at the party is grading the crumb. They’re looking at the outside, and the outside is the part you’re learning.
### Class, video, or just a box mix and a Saturday: which way should you start?
There are four real paths, and they’re not equal. Which one fits depends on how you learn, how much you’ve got to spend, and whether you need a cake by a specific date or just want the skill. Here’s the honest version of each.
### A single in-person beginner class
This is the best first dollar most people spend. You show up, a cake and frosting are usually waiting, and an instructor walks the room fixing hands. Watching someone correct the angle of your spatula does more than any explanation. Two or three hours, one cake, and you leave knowing whether you like this. Bakeries, community centers, and independent studios around Alton and Fairview Heights run these, often on weekends.
### A craft-store class series
These run several weeks, one technique per session, and they’re built around a tool kit you buy up front. Cheap per hour and structured, which helps if you drift without a schedule. The catch: you often bake and bring your own cake each week, and the curriculum is aimed at one style of piped decoration that may not be the look you want. Ask before you sign up.
### Video and the self-taught route
Free, endless, and the way most home decorators actually learned. The problem isn’t quality. It’s that video can’t see your cake. When your frosting breaks, nobody tells you why. Self-teaching works if you’re patient and willing to make three ugly cakes for every good one. Pair it with one class and it works a lot faster. Go it alone first only if the budget says so.
### What tools actually matter for a first cake?
Six things. Not the 40-piece kit with the plastic case. Most of what comes in a starter set is tips you’ll never use and a flimsy turntable you’ll replace within a month. Buy these, buy them decent, and stop.
A turntable. Metal or heavy plastic, and it should spin without wobbling. This is the tool that makes smooth sides possible at all.
An offset spatula. The bent one, medium size. It keeps your knuckles out of the frosting.
A bench scraper. A straight metal edge, taller than your cake. Held still while the turntable spins, it does the smoothing for you.
Two or three piping tips and a handful of bags. One large open star, one large round, one small round. That covers rosettes, borders, dots, and writing.
A serrated knife or a leveler. Domed layers slide and crack. Flat ones stack.
Cake boards. Cardboard rounds the same size as your cake. You’ll frost on the board and move the cake without ever touching it.
Everything else is optional until you know what you like. A tip coupler is handy. A cheap digital scale earns its spot if you bake from scratch. Fondant tools, airbrushes, and flower nails can wait until you’ve done ten cakes and still want more.
### Why does buttercream fight you, and how do you win?
Buttercream fails for two reasons, and almost never for the reason you think. It’s either the wrong temperature or the wrong consistency. Beginners blame the recipe, the humidity, the oven, the mixer. In our experience it’s the butter, and it’s fixable in five minutes.
### Crumb coat first, then chill
The Ferguson cake failed because there was no crumb coat. That’s a thin, ugly first layer of frosting whose whole job is to trap loose crumbs. Spread it, scrape most of it back off, and put the cake in the fridge for twenty or thirty minutes until the surface is firm. Then frost for real. The second coat glides over a cold, sealed cake instead of dragging crumb through it.
Chilling the layers before you even fill them helps too. A cold cake is stiffer, slides less, and stacks straighter. A warm one shifts under the spatula and sheds crumbs like a wool sweater.
### Temperature and consistency
Room temperature butter means cool to the touch and giving under a fingertip, not soft and shiny. Too warm and the frosting slumps, turns greasy, and won’t hold a rosette. Too cold and it tears the cake. If it’s slumping, refrigerate the bowl for ten minutes and re-whip. If it’s stiff and dull, add a spoonful of milk or cream at a time, mixed on low.
Consistency is the other half. Frosting for smooth sides should be a little looser than frosting for piping. Piped flowers want it stiff enough to hold a peak. Many people make one batch, split it, and adjust each half. Small steps. You can always add liquid. You can’t take it out.
### What are the easiest cake decorating techniques that still look good?
Here’s the good news. The techniques that look most confident are also the most forgiving. None of these need a steady hand. They need the frosting to be right, which you now know how to manage.
### Rosettes
A large open star tip, a bag that’s only half full, and a spiral from the center outward. Cover the whole cake in them, sides and top, and every mistake disappears into the pattern. It’s the single highest-payoff move in beginner decorating, and it’s the one to learn first.
### Rustic textured sides
Frost the cake roughly, then drag the tip of the offset spatula in short horizontal strokes, or in one continuous spiral from bottom to top while spinning the turntable. Uneven is the point. Nobody can tell where you messed up because the whole thing looks deliberate.
### A simple drip
Chocolate and cream, melted together, cooled until it’s thick enough to hang. Spoon it around the top edge of a cold cake and let it run. The cold cake is the secret. On a warm cake the drip races straight to the plate. Test one drip on the back first.
### Sprinkles, done well
Press them into the bottom inch of the sides while the frosting is still tacky, or scatter them on half the top and leave the other half clean. All-over sprinkles read as a kid’s cake. Deliberate placement reads as intent. It’s the same instinct that makes a candy buffet look planned instead of dumped out.
### What should your first three cakes be?
Don’t start with the birthday cake. Start three weekends earlier. Each cake below teaches one thing, and each one is edible enough that the neighbors in Bridgeton won’t complain when you hand it over the fence.
### Cake one: a single layer, smooth top, rosette sides
One box mix, one round pan, one batch of buttercream. Level it, crumb coat, chill, frost the top smooth with the bench scraper, then hide the sides in rosettes. You’re learning the crumb coat and the piping bag at the same time, and the rosettes cover whatever the sides end up looking like.
### Cake two: two layers, filled, fully smooth
Same mix, two pans, and now you stack. Pipe a dam of stiff frosting around the edge of the bottom layer before you fill it so the filling doesn’t squeeze out. Then the real test: smooth sides with the scraper, top edge cleaned up with the offset spatula. It won’t be perfect. That’s the point of cake two.
### Cake three: the one with the drip and the writing
Repeat cake two, add a drip, and pipe a short message with the small round tip. Practice the words on parchment first. If the writing goes wrong, scrape it off and put a rosette there. Now you’ve done every move the birthday cake needs, and you did them without an audience.
### Before anyone asks you to sell one
Somebody will. Decorating at home for your own family needs no license anywhere. Selling is different. Missouri and Illinois both have cottage-food rules that decide what you can make in a home kitchen, how it’s labeled, and where you can sell it, and the details differ by state and sometimes by county. Call your county health department before you take a single order. It’s a ten-minute call that keeps a hobby from turning into a problem.
### Which mistakes cost beginners the most cake?
Four, and they’re all about patience rather than skill. Every one of them happened in that Ferguson kitchen on a Friday night, which is why it went the way it did.
Frosting a warm cake. The top offender. Warm cake sheds crumbs, warm cake melts the frosting touching it, and warm layers slide. Bake the day before if you can. Wrap the cooled layers and refrigerate. Cold cake is easy cake.
Thin frosting. Beginners under-make and over-scrape, and the crumb shows through like a shirt that’s been washed too many times. Make more frosting than you think you need. Load the sides thick, then let the scraper take the excess off.
Over-filling the piping bag. A full bag is warm from your hand, hard to control, and squirts out the top. Half full, twisted closed, and refilled often. Your rosettes get better the moment you do this.
Rushing. Every chill step exists for a reason. Skipping twenty minutes in the fridge costs you an hour of repair. Decorating rewards the person who walks away from the cake and comes back later.
### How do you pick a cake decorating class worth paying for?
Same way you’d pick anyone you’re about to pay: shortlist two or three, ask each the same questions, and see whose answers match what you actually want. The gap between what you expect and what they’re set up to deliver is the whole signal. It’s the same approach that works for picking a candle-making class in St. Louis, and the questions are nearly identical.
Ask what a beginner leaves with after session one. A finished cake and two techniques you can repeat is the right answer. A demonstration you watched is not. Ask the class size. Eight people and one instructor means your hands get corrected; twenty means you watch. Ask whether the cake, frosting, and tools are supplied or whether you bake and bring. Ask whether you take the cake home. You should.
Then the question that separates a real instructor from someone reading slides: what do you do when a student’s frosting breaks in the middle of class? A good answer sounds specific. Ten minutes in the fridge, re-whip, here’s why it happened. A vague answer, or a laugh, tells you they haven’t seen it enough times to have a fix ready. And frosting breaks in every class. Someone’s does.
Write down what you told them you wanted. Compare it with what each one said they’d deliver. Pick the one with the smallest gap, not the cheapest or the closest. A class twenty minutes farther out in Fairview Heights that sends you home with a cake beats a nearby one that sends you home with a handout.
Cake vanishes in one night. Want a gift that keeps ticking? Pick a watch instead.
Ready to frost your first real cake? Browse cake decorating classes and suppliers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them with the questions above and see who has a real answer for broken frosting.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is cake decorating hard to learn?
A.  The basics aren’t. A smooth crumb coat, a rosette, and a textured side are all learnable in a single afternoon once the frosting consistency is right. What’s hard is patience: chilling between steps, not rushing, and accepting that the first two cakes are practice. Fine piped flowers and fondant work take months. Nobody needs those for a birthday.
### Q. What equipment do I need to decorate a cake?
A.  Six things: a turntable that doesn’t wobble, an offset spatula, a metal bench scraper, two or three piping tips with disposable bags, a serrated knife or leveler, and cardboard cake boards. That covers smooth sides, rosettes, borders, and writing. Skip the big boxed kit. Most of it is tips you’ll never use and a turntable you’ll replace.
### Q. What common cake decorating mistakes should I avoid?
A.  Frosting a warm cake, which sheds crumbs and melts your buttercream. Skipping the crumb coat and the chill after it. Making too little frosting and scraping it thin. Over-filling the piping bag until it’s warm and uncontrollable. And rushing, which causes all of the above. Every one of these is a patience problem, not a talent problem.
### Q. What is the easiest cake decorating technique?
A.  Rosettes with a large open star tip. Half-fill the bag, hold it straight up, and pipe a tight spiral from the center outward. Cover the whole cake and every imperfection underneath disappears into the pattern. A close second is a rustic textured side made by dragging a spatula through the frosting while the turntable spins. Uneven is the look.
### Q. Do you need a license to be a cake decorator?
A.  Not to decorate at home for yourself, your family, or a friend’s party. Selling is where rules apply. Missouri and Illinois each have cottage-food laws covering what home kitchens may produce, how it must be labeled, and where it can be sold, and counties add their own requirements. Before you take money for a cake, call your county health department and ask.
### Q. How to become a cake decorator with no experience?
A.  Take one hands-on beginner class, then bake three practice cakes at home over three weekends: rosettes, then smooth sides, then a drip with writing. Bring a photo of each to a local bakery and ask about entry-level help. Plenty of decorators started washing pans and filling piping bags. The photos matter more than the resume, and three decent cakes is a portfolio.
### Q. What does a beginner cake decorator need?
A.  A cake that’s cold, frosting that’s the right consistency, the six tools listed above, and about three free Saturdays. That’s honestly the whole list. A class helps because someone corrects your hands in real time. Video helps after that, once you have questions. Expensive gear and a big tip collection can wait until you know you like it.
### Q. How long does it take to decorate a beginner cake?
A.  Plan on an afternoon the first time, chill breaks included: twenty minutes to level and fill, a crumb coat and half an hour in the fridge, then the final coat and rosettes. Bake the layers the day before so they’re cold. By cake three you’ll be closer to an hour of hands-on time, with most of the rest spent waiting on the fridge.

## How to Choose a Halloween Costume in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-halloween-costume-in-st-louis
The bag says medium. Your kid is a medium. Then the thing goes on and the sleeves quit at his elbows while the pant legs puddle over his shoes. It’s the night before Halloween in St. Peters, the aisle is down to one clown and a pair of lonely bananas, and you’re holding a roll of tape wondering how this happened. Again.
It happens to almost everyone. Packaged costumes get sized by people who’ve never met your child, cut from fabric thinner than the bag it ships in, and photographed on a model who had a stylist and a fan blowing her hair. The letter on the front is a suggestion, not a promise. Adults get burned the same way, just with more money on the line and fewer excuses.
So here’s the adjuster’s version of costume shopping. What to measure before you buy. When to rent instead. Why the costume never looks like the photo, and the cheap fixes that close most of that gap. What survives a St. Louis October, which runs warm at 4pm and cold by 8. And which questions to ask a costume shop before you drive across the metro to visit it.
### How to know what size Halloween costume to get?
Ignore the S/M/L letter and read the measurement chart printed on the bag. Measure chest, waist, and height with a soft tape, then match those numbers to the chart for that specific costume. When you land between two sizes, go up. You can pin, belt, or hem a costume down, but you can’t make it bigger.
There’s no industry standard behind those letters. One manufacturer’s medium fits like another’s small, and kids’ costumes are often labeled by age range, which tells you nothing about a tall seven-year-old or a small ten-year-old. The chart on the back of the bag, or on the product page, is the only number that came from the actual pattern. Trust that. Ignore the rest.
Measuring takes two minutes. Chest: wrap a soft tape around the fullest part, over a t-shirt, not squeezing. Waist: the natural line, roughly where a belt sits. Height: barefoot, back against a wall, book flat on the head. Write the three numbers in your phone. You’ll need them again next year, and probably next week when the kid switches from pirate to astronaut.
Then compare, and be honest about it. If the chest number sits at the top edge of the medium range, buy the large. A costume that’s a little roomy gets a belt and a couple of safety pins. A costume that’s too tight gets a split seam halfway down the block and a very short night. If the shop lets you try it on, do that instead of guessing. It beats every chart.
### Should you buy, rent, or build it?
Buy for kids and for anything you’ll wear more than once. Rent when it’s a single night and you want the piece to look real: a period gown, a full-body character suit, anything with structure. Build when you have time, a base garment already in the closet, and a look that’s more about the idea than the fabric.
### When renting makes sense
Rental costumes come from a different world than bagged ones. They’re made to be worn many times, so the seams hold, the fabric has weight, and the fit gets adjusted by someone who does this all day. For an adult party where you actually want to look like the character, a rental usually lands closer to the photo in your head than anything in a plastic bag. The trade-off is you can’t spill on it, and you have to bring it back.
### When buying is the smarter call
Kids wear costumes hard. They eat in them, run in them, and wear them to school, to the grocery store, and to bed if you let them. A rental can’t survive that, and a rental shop won’t want it to. Buy the kid costume. Same rule for anything you’ll pull out again: a decent cape, a good hat, a lab coat. Repeat use turns a purchase into a bargain.
### When building wins
Building doesn’t mean sewing from a pattern. It means starting from clothes you own and adding the parts that sell the idea. Black jeans, a striped shirt, and a knit cap is a burglar. A trench coat and a fedora is a detective. Most homemade costumes that work are one base garment, one strong accessory, and a little makeup. They also fit, because they’re your clothes.
One honest caveat from experience: building takes longer than you think, every single time. If it’s the 28th and you have a full week of work ahead, buy the bag and spend your free evening fixing it instead.
### Why does the costume never look like the bag photo?
Because the photo was staged. The model was picked to fit the sample, a stylist pinned the back, the plastic sword was swapped for a real prop, and a lighting rig hid every wrinkle. What’s in the bag is the garment, the cheapest version of the accessories, and nothing else. The gap isn’t your fault. It’s the business model.
The good news is that most of the gap closes with a few moves that cost less than a second costume. Here’s what actually moves the needle, in rough order of impact.
Fix the fit first. Belt it, pin it, or hem it with iron-on tape. Most of what reads as “this looks cheap” is really “this doesn’t fit.”
Wear real shoes. The photo model wore boots; the bag gave you nothing. Your own boots, sneakers, or dress shoes beat any shoe cover ever made.
Swap the plastic accessories. The included hat, belt, and weapon are the weakest parts. A thrift-store belt or a real hat changes the whole read.
Add makeup. Even simple face paint, a drawn scar, or dark eyes makes a cheap costume look intentional.
Weather it. For pirates, zombies, scarecrows, and anything “old,” soak the fabric in strong cooled tea for a dingy tint, then rough the edges with sandpaper. Test a hidden spot first.
Weathering deserves a warning. Tea stains are permanent, and sandpaper doesn’t un-fray. Do it on a costume you own, never on a rental, and never on the night of. Give it a full day to dry so nobody ends up with brown streaks on a couch in Creve Coeur.
### What makes a costume actually work in a St. Louis October?
Layers, real shoes, and something reflective. A St. Louis Halloween can start warm enough for shorts at the school parade and drop into jacket weather by the time the porch lights go out, so the costume needs to work over a base layer and under a coat without falling apart. If it only works at one temperature, it only works for an hour.
### Dress for the 8pm version of the night
Plan the costume around the cold hour, not the warm one. A thin base layer underneath, thermal or long-sleeve, disappears under almost anything. For small kids, size the costume to fit over a hoodie so nobody has to choose between warm and in character. Adults heading to a party can stash a jacket in the car, but a kid on a sidewalk in Granite City can’t. Build the warmth in.
### Shoes you can walk a mile in
Trick-or-treating is a mile or two of walking, plus stairs, plus one fall on a wet leaf. Costume shoe covers slide, tear, and come off in the first block. Put the kid in sneakers and let the costume be the costume. Adults, same story. If your character needs heels, bring flats for the walk from the car.
### Visibility for kids
Dark costumes on dark streets are the real safety issue, not the fake blood. A strip of reflective tape on the back, a glow stick on a lanyard, or a small clip light on the candy bag fixes most of it. Masks that block side vision are a problem on stairs and at curbs. Face paint sees better than a mask every time, and it doesn’t get ditched in someone’s yard by the fourth house.
Lots of families make a whole night of it, with a trunk-or-treat or a haunted walk before the neighborhood loop. If you’re planning that, the St. Louis Halloween events guide covers what’s worth the drive. Just remember that an outdoor event at 6pm and a sidewalk at 8pm need the same jacket.
### How do you pick a costume for a kid who changes their mind weekly?
Set a decision date and buy pieces that convert. A kid who’s been a dinosaur, a firefighter, and a ghost in the same month isn’t fickle, they’re five. Don’t buy on the first ask. Wait until the pick survives two weekends, then shop, and lean toward costumes where the base works for more than one idea.
Convertible pieces save you. A black sweatsuit is a cat, a ninja, a spider, or a bat depending on what you clip to it. A brown one is a bear, a dog, a monkey, or a gingerbread man. Buy the accessories, not the whole outfit, and the mid-October pivot costs you a pair of ears instead of a second costume.
Do the comfort test at home. Put the whole thing on, shoes and all, and have the kid wear it for twenty minutes while doing normal kid stuff. Scratchy neck? Mask fogging? Cape catching under feet? You want to find that out on a Tuesday, not at the first porch. What they say they want and what they’ll actually keep on are two different costumes.
Give them ownership somewhere. Let them pick the accessory or the face paint color, and the costume becomes theirs, which is the strongest defense against a meltdown on the 31st. And if the plan includes dinner out first, the guide to eating out with kids in St. Louis has the pre-trick-or-treat strategy covered.
### What should you skip entirely?
Skip anything that treats another group’s culture as a costume, anything built on a real tragedy or a recent crime, and anything you physically can’t see or walk in while herding kids. Those are the three hard lines. Everything else is taste, and taste is negotiable.
The overdone list changes a little each year but the shape stays the same: whatever the biggest movie was, whatever the biggest show was, a witch, a vampire, a cat, and a generic zombie. There’s nothing wrong with any of them. You’ll just see six more at the party. If you want to wear one anyway, twist it. A vampire who’s clearly a dentist. A witch on her way to a job interview. A zombie in a full tuxedo, tea-stained. The twist is what people remember, and it usually costs one accessory.
Then there’s the practical list. Full-face masks with kids in tow. Long capes on stairs. Anything with a trailing hem you’ll drag through wet leaves. Inflatable suits, which are hilarious for ten minutes and a sauna after that. And anything that reads as a real uniform from a distance, because at night, on a doorstep, that confusion isn’t funny to the person opening the door.
### How do you choose a costume shop worth the drive?
Shortlist two or three shops, call each one, and tell them exactly what you want and expect. Then compare that against what they’re actually set up to deliver. The gap between the two is the signal. A shop that’s honest about a gap is worth more than one that says yes to everything.
Here’s what to ask, in plain words:
Can we try it on before we buy? Where, and is there a mirror?
What’s the return or exchange window, and does it close before Halloween?
If we rent, does the price include cleaning, and what happens if it comes back with a stain?
What sizes do you actually have in the back, not just on the rack?
Can you adjust the fit, or point us to someone who can?
Listen for specifics. “Sure, we have all sizes” means nothing. “We’ve got that one in medium and large, the small sold out last week” means they looked. A shop that knows its stock will save you a drive from St. Clair for a costume that isn’t there. The same interview frame works for a lot of one-night purchases; our post on what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis uses it for tables and tents.
### Early for selection, late for clearance
Timing is the other half of choosing a shop. Early October has the full range of sizes, and the staff has time to help. The last week has clearance pricing, empty racks, and a line. If you know what you want and it’s a common size, shopping late can pay off. If your kid sits at the edge of a size range or wants something specific, go early and pay for the selection.
Pop-up seasonal stores and year-round costume shops play different games. The pop-up has volume and price. The year-round shop has rentals, fitting help, and someone who’s seen your exact problem before. In our experience the year-round shop earns its keep on adult costumes and anything that has to look right up close, while the pop-up wins on kids’ costumes you’ll retire in November.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Should you size up in costumes?
A.  Yes, when you’re between sizes or at the top of a range. Packaged costumes run inconsistent and often small, and a roomy costume is easy to belt, pin, or hem. A tight one splits. The one exception is a very young child in a long costume, where sizing up creates a tripping hem. Hem it, or pick the smaller size and skip the base layer.
### Q. What to do if your Halloween costume is too big?
A.  Take it in where nobody looks. Safety pins at the back seam, a belt at the waist, and iron-on hem tape at the cuffs and hem fix most of it in fifteen minutes. Layer a hoodie or thermal underneath to fill out the chest. For a kid, roll the sleeves and pin them from the inside so the pins never touch skin.
### Q. How to save money on Halloween costumes?
A.  Build from clothes you already own and spend on one strong accessory. Buy convertible basics like a plain sweatsuit that works for several characters. Shop clearance in the last week if your size is common. Borrow or swap with other families, since kids outgrow costumes after one wear. Skip the shoe covers and use real shoes you already have.
### Q. How to make a Halloween costume look better?
A.  Fix the fit first, since most of what reads as cheap is really a bad fit. Wear real shoes instead of covers. Replace the included plastic belt, hat, or weapon with a thrifted real one. Add face paint or a drawn scar. For pirates, zombies, and scarecrows, tea-stain the fabric and rough the edges with sandpaper.
### Q. What is the most overused Halloween costume?
A.  Whatever the biggest movie or show of the year was, followed by the evergreens: witch, vampire, cat, and generic zombie. You’ll see all of them at any party. If you love one anyway, twist it with a job, a mood, or an era. A vampire dentist or a witch at a job interview gets remembered. A plain vampire doesn’t.
### Q. What not to dress up as for Halloween?
A.  Anything that turns another group’s culture into a costume, anything based on a real tragedy or a recent crime, and anything that reads as a real uniform on a dark doorstep. Practically, skip full-face masks and long capes if you’re walking kids, and skip anything you can’t see, walk, or climb stairs in.
### Q. Why are Halloween costumes so expensive now?
A.  A few things stack up. Licensed characters carry a licensing fee before the fabric is even cut. Costumes are seasonal, so a retailer has a few weeks to sell what it had to ship and store for months. Materials and shipping have gotten pricier across the board. And a packaged costume sells once, with no repeat-customer discount built in. Rentals and homemade builds sidestep most of that.
### Q. When is the best time to buy a Halloween costume?
A.  Early October if you need a specific size, a specific character, or help with fit, because that’s when the shelves and the staff are both full. The last week before Halloween if your size is common and you want clearance pricing. Reserve rentals early either way, since the good pieces go first.

## What to Expect From a CPR Class in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-from-a-cpr-class-in-st-louis
Saturday, 8:55 a.m., a community room in Ballwin. Twelve folding chairs, a coffee urn that has seen things, and a row of plastic torsos lined up on blue mats like they’re waiting for a bus. A woman in scrubs is already kneeling by one of them, stretching her wrists. The dad next to her keeps checking his phone. Then the instructor walks in with a rolling case, pops it open, and pulls out a box with a speaker on it that says AED. Everybody gets a little quieter.
That’s the moment most people realize they have no idea what the next few hours look like. Is there a test? Do you have to put your mouth on the manikin? Will the card actually count at work? Half the room is here because a boss, a licensing board, or a coaching gig said so. The other half is here because someone they love has a heart condition and they don’t want to stand there useless. Both are good reasons.
This post walks you through the whole thing: how long the class runs, what happens in the room, which type of class fits your situation, why some online cards get bounced by employers, what drives the price, and how to pick a class that won’t waste your Saturday. No medical instruction here. That’s what the class is for.
### How long does a CPR training class take?
A basic adult, child, and infant CPR-and-AED class for laypeople typically runs a few hours in one sitting, usually a morning or an afternoon. Healthcare-provider classes, often called BLS, run longer because they cover more skills. Blended courses move the lecture online and cut the in-person part to a shorter skills session. Renewal classes are shorter than first-time classes.
Why the range? Class size, mostly. An instructor with four students and four manikins moves fast. An instructor with sixteen students and six manikins has to rotate people through, and every rotation eats clock. Add a question-heavy group, a slow projector, or a skills check where two people need a second try, and a class that was scheduled for a morning slides into lunch.
Plan for the full block on the schedule, plus a little slack. Don’t book a 1 p.m. commitment in South County if the class is listed to end at noon in University City. Providers usually post the length on the sign-up page. If they don’t, ask. It’s a fair question and a good early read on how organized they are.
### What actually happens in the room?
You’ll spend most of the class on your knees. That surprises people who expected a lecture. There’s some talking, usually with a video, but the bulk of the time is hands-on: pushing on a manikin’s chest, giving breaths, working the AED trainer, then doing it all again while the instructor watches and scores you.
### Compressions on the manikin
The manikins are torsos, sometimes full bodies, usually adult-sized with a smaller infant model passed around later. Many of the newer ones click or light up when you press deep enough and fast enough. Your instructor shows the hand position, the depth, and the rhythm, then you do it. And do it. Your shoulders will feel it by the second round. That’s the point. Real compressions are physical work, and the class wants you to learn that here, not in a parking lot.
### Breaths, the AED, and the skills check
Rescue breaths get practiced with a barrier, either a face shield or a pocket mask, so you’re not putting your mouth on a shared manikin. Then the AED trainer comes out. It talks. It tells you where to put the pads and when to stand clear, and you follow it. Most people find this the least scary part once they see the machine does the thinking.
The skills check is pass/fail. You run through the sequence on your own, compressions, breaths, and the AED, while the instructor checks boxes. If you miss something, most instructors coach you and let you go again. Nobody’s trying to fail you. They’re trying to make sure you can do it without them standing there.
### The written test
The written test is short, multiple choice, and covers what was just taught. Some classes do it on paper, some on a tablet, and blended courses often do it online before you show up. Retakes are normally allowed. A nurse from Wentzville isn’t going to sweat it, and neither should a first-timer who paid attention. Read each question twice. That handles most of the misses.
### Which kind of CPR class do you need?
It depends on who’s asking you to have it. A parent, coach, or office volunteer usually needs a layperson class covering adult, child, and infant CPR plus the AED. Nurses, EMTs, dental staff, and most clinical students need a healthcare-provider class. A blended format works for either group, as long as whoever wants your card accepts that provider’s in-person skills session.
### Layperson: adult, child, and infant with AED
This is the class most people mean when they say CPR. It covers recognizing an emergency, calling for help, compressions, breaths, choking, and the AED, across the three age groups. Youth coaches, daycare staff, babysitters, and new parents fill these seats. If you’ve got a kid starting lessons at one of the St. Louis swim schools this year, this is the one you want. The pool staff will already have it.
### Healthcare provider, usually called BLS
BLS adds two-rescuer technique, bag-mask ventilation, and more decision-making, and it runs longer. Clinical programs typically require it before you set foot in a facility. If you’re working through how to get into nursing school in St. Louis, check the program’s admissions page for exactly which card they want and how recent it has to be. Taking the wrong one costs you a second Saturday.
### Blended: online lecture, in-person skills
Blended courses put the video and the written test online, then you show up for a shorter skills session with a manikin and an instructor. Good option for people who hate sitting in a room for the lecture part. Two catches. You must finish the online portion first and bring the completion certificate, and the skills session still has to happen in person. Skip that, and you don’t have a card most employers will take.
### Why do employers reject some online-only cards?
Because nobody watched you push on a chest. An online-only certification, the kind with no in-person skills check, proves you clicked through slides and passed a quiz. It doesn’t prove you can do compressions at the right depth or work an AED with a little stress on you. Employers, schools, and childcare licensing usually want that hands-on proof, so they list those cards as not accepted.
The frustrating part is that these online-only sites look official. Nice seal, quick turnaround, a card in your inbox within the hour. Then the coach from University City who bought one for a league job finds out three weeks later that the league won’t take it, and now he’s paying twice. It happens more than you’d think.
The fix is boring and reliable: ask whoever requires the card what they accept, in writing, before you book anything. An email from HR or the licensing office that says “we accept a card with a hands-on skills component” is worth more than any promise on a sign-up page. Blended is fine for most. Online-only, almost never.
### What does a CPR class cost, and why does it vary?
No dollar figures here, because they shift by provider and by month, and a stale number would just mislead you. What you’re paying for is instructor time, manikins and AED trainers that need cleaning and replacement, the card itself, and the overhead of a room. Change any one of those, and the price moves.
Class size matters most. A small class costs more per seat because the instructor’s time is split fewer ways. Big classes are cheaper per head but slower. Healthcare-provider classes cost more than layperson classes because they run longer and need more equipment. Renewals cost less than first-time classes. And a workplace class, where an instructor comes to your office in South County and trains twelve people at once, is usually priced per group rather than per person, which can work out well if you’re the one organizing it.
Free classes exist. Fire departments, hospitals, and community groups sometimes run them, often as hands-only sessions with no card, or with a card that’s fine for personal knowledge but not for an employer. Worth going to if you just want to know what to do. Not a substitute if a licensing board is waiting on paperwork. Ask before you attend.
### How do you pick a CPR class worth your Saturday?
Shortlist two or three providers and interview them. Not a long call. Five questions, and you’ll know. Tell each one what you need the card for and by when, then listen to whether the answer matches. The gap between what you expect and what they’re set up to deliver is the signal.
Which certifying body’s card do you issue, and does it include a hands-on skills session?
How big is the class, and how many manikins do you have per student?
Is the AED portion included, or is that a separate class?
When does the card arrive, and is it digital, printed, or both?
Will my employer, school, or licensing office accept this card? Then confirm that yourself.
Listen for hesitation. A provider who says “we’ll figure out the card later” or won’t say how many students they cap at is telling you something. A provider who answers all five without looking anything up has done this many times. That’s who you want on a Saturday morning in Wentzville with your kid’s league deadline on Monday.
One more thing. In our experience, the best instructors have real field time, nurses, medics, firefighters, and they tell short stories that make the sequence stick. If the provider mentions that their instructors work in the field, that’s a plus. If they say the instructor is “certified” and nothing else, fine, but it’s not the same.
### Before you show up
Wear clothes you can kneel in. Pants and sneakers, hair tied back, nothing dangling. Bring a photo ID, and if it’s a blended class, the completion certificate from the online portion, printed or on your phone. Eat something first. Rooms run cold until you start compressions, then you’ll wish you’d worn layers. Get there ten minutes early so the instructor isn’t doing paperwork on your time.
Kids out at 3 and you’re not? See what after-school programs cost.
