### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does an opera usually last?
A.  Most operas run about two to three hours, including one or two intermissions, though grand classics can push past three and a half. The exact time varies by title and production. Check the run time when you buy tickets if you have a babysitter, a train, or an early morning waiting on the other end.
### Q. Is there a dress code for an opera?
A.  There’s rarely a strict, enforced dress code. Smart casual is the safe default: slacks or dark jeans, a nice top, a button-down, or a simple dress. Evening and opening-night performances draw dressier crowds, and some people go formal for fun. You won’t be turned away for skipping a suit, so aim for put-together and comfortable.
### Q. What is a good opera to see for the first time?
A.  Start with a famous, story-driven classic instead of a rarely staged deep cut. The big tragic love stories and the comic favorites carry melodies you’ll half-recognize and plots that are easy to follow. Surtitles above the stage translate every line, so you never feel lost. Read a three-line summary beforehand and just enjoy the ride.
### Q. How long do ballets usually last?
A.  Ballets typically run shorter than operas, roughly ninety minutes to a bit over two hours with intermissions. A mixed-repertory program of shorter pieces and a full-length story ballet feel different, but both usually finish inside a normal evening. The holiday Nutcracker sits on the shorter, family-friendly end. Confirm the exact run time at the box office.
### Q. Is it okay to wear jeans to the ballet?
A.  Yes, dark, clean jeans are completely fine at most ballet performances, especially matinees and family shows. Pair them with a nice top, a sweater, or a blazer and you’ll fit right in. Skip ripped, faded, or gym-adjacent denim if you want to feel put-together. For a gala or opening night, you might reach for something dressier.
### Q. Do people dress up to go to the ballet?
A.  Some do, some don’t, and both look right. You’ll see cocktail dresses and sport coats next to nice jeans and sweaters in the same row. Holiday shows and opening nights tilt fancier, while summer and matinee programs run relaxed. Dressing up is welcome and never out of place, so match the outfit to your own mood.
### Q. What should you avoid wearing to the opera or ballet?
A.  Skip anything you’d wear to the gym, the beach, or a muddy job site: athletic shorts, flip-flops, tank tops, and stained casual wear read as too far down the range. Heavy perfume or cologne bothers close-seated neighbors, so go light. Otherwise the range is wide, and comfortable, put-together clothes cover almost every performance.
### Q. How early should you arrive for a show?
A.  Aim to walk in twenty to thirty minutes before curtain. That buffer covers parking, coat check, finding your seat, and a glance at the program. Latecomers often wait at the door until a scene break, so a late arrival can cost you the opening. Build in extra time if you’re driving in or eating first.

## Persian Food in St. Louis: What to Order, Starting Inside a South Grand Gin Bar
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-persian-food-is-and-what-to-try-in-st-louis
The Persian kitchen that started feeding St. Louis in 1983 is cooking again, and you’ll find it inside a gin bar. Walk into The Gin Room at 3200 South Grand, in a bar the family’s site says houses over 300 different gins, and order the koubideh. The skewer lands over a mound of white rice with its edges charred, and a pat of butter slides down the rice and disappears. The steam smells floral and faintly sweet. That’s saffron.
It started with a layoff. In 1982, Behshid and Hamishe Bahrami had their only child, Natasha, and the same year Behshid lost his job in a sudden downturn. In 1983 they opened The Little Kitchen downtown, cooking on a convection oven and an electric burner, and in their own words, “The lines wrapped around the building.” Café Natasha followed on Delmar in 1993, and a third restaurant opened on South Grand in 2001.
So here’s the contrarian truth about Persian food in this city: the dish matters less than the door. The family’s own site now announces it in capital letters, “MOM IS BACK OPEN,” and points diners to The Gin Room for the Persian menu. If you’ve been waiting for Café Natasha’s food to come back, it already has, in the same space, just through a different door.
The posted dinner menu reads like a first-timer’s map. Koubideh kabobs, $24. Jujeh chicken kabob, $20. Gormeh sabzi, the green herb stew, $24. Fessenjune, the walnut and pomegranate one, $22. Natasha’s Signature Osh, a thick soup, $8. The Gin Room’s own site lists the full menu Wednesday through Sunday, so call (314) 771-3411 before you drive and book through the reservation link.
### What is classic Persian food?
Classic Persian food is built on saffron-scented rice, grilled meats, and slow herb stews, seasoned with dried fruit and citrus rather than chili heat. Think chelo kabab, skewers served over buttered rice; ghormeh sabzi, a deep green herb-and-bean stew; and tahdig, the crackly crust from the bottom of the rice pot. It’s aromatic, tangy, and gentle, and it rewards a slow table.
The word “kabab” here doesn’t mean what a lot of American menus mean by it. Koobideh is ground meat pressed onto a wide skewer and grilled fast. Barg is thin slices of marinated fillet. Joojeh is saffron-and-lime chicken. Each one comes over long-grain rice, usually with a grilled tomato whose skin has split and blistered, and butter you stir in yourself.
Stews are the other half, and they’re where the cooking gets patient. Ghormeh sabzi simmers a mountain of chopped herbs down for hours with kidney beans and dried limes until it turns almost black-green. Fesenjan blends ground walnuts and pomegranate into something dark, sour and rich. Neither gets poured over rice at the last second. They come in a bowl beside it, and you spoon them on.
### Why does Persian food taste different from its neighbors?
Persian cooking uses sourness and floral aromatics where nearby cuisines reach for chili, tomato or heavy spice. Dried lime, sumac, pomegranate, barberries and rosewater show up constantly. The result is bright and layered instead of hot. The first bite of a dried lime from the bottom of a stew is a jolt, bitter and sour at once, and it wakes up everything else on the plate.
Herbs get treated as a main ingredient, not a garnish. A plate of raw herbs, the sabzi, is meant to be eaten in real quantity: mint, basil, tarragon and scallion folded into warm bread with salty cheese, or chewed between bites to reset your mouth. If you’ve eaten around the eastern Mediterranean, some of this rhymes. Our local’s guide to Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis covers the overlap.
Saffron deserves its own sentence. Persian cooks bloom a few threads in warm water and streak it over rice or stir it into a sweet. On its own it tastes like almost nothing. In a dish, it turns rice gold and leaves a perfume you’ll recognize for the rest of your life.
### What should you order the first time?
For a first visit, order koubideh or jujeh chicken, split one herb stew like gormeh sabzi across the table, and start with the osh. That combination shows you the three pillars at once: grilled meat, a slow stew, and rice. At the Bahramis’ table, the menu also lets you swap in jeweled rice or biryani rice for a few dollars more.
Koubideh is the safest, happiest first bite. It’s seasoned ground meat grilled until the edges char, and it lands somewhere familiar even if you’ve never had it. Order it “chelo,” with rice, squeeze the lime, and stir the butter into the hot rice until every grain shines.
If you want the other half of the cuisine, order a stew to share. Ghormeh sabzi is the one to try first, herby and tangy and a little funky in the best way. Fesenjan is bolder, sweet-sour and thick with walnuts, and not everyone loves it on the first spoonful. The menu also carries an apricot chicken and a lamb biryani tachin, a baked saffron-rice dish, if the table wants a third.
Then there’s the rice itself. Persian rice is par-boiled, drained, then steamed with butter and oil so the grains stay separate and long. The bottom of the pot forms tahdig, a golden crust of rice, bread or thin-sliced potato that cracks like glass under a spoon. People genuinely negotiate over it. Ask your server whether the kitchen has it tonight.
Vegetarian, vegan or gluten-free? The menu carries a vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free key, and the appetizers are where meat-free eaters do best: kashke bademjune, a smoky eggplant dip; pomegranate yogurt; a walnut-olive feta spread; and shirazi, the chopped cucumber, tomato and onion salad that tastes like a cold glass of water on a hot day.

### How is a Persian meal actually put together?
A Persian meal spreads out rather than arriving in strict courses. Bread, herbs and cheese come first, then rice and kabab or stew land together, and everyone shares. There’s no rush and no rigid sequence. Tea and something sweet close it out. The rhythm is built around the table more than the clock.
The herb plate, the sabzi khordan, sets the tone before anything hot arrives: fresh herbs, radishes, walnuts and a slab of feta-like cheese with warm flatbread. You build small bites, bread, cheese, a pinch of mint, maybe a walnut. The herbs are cold and sharp, the cheese is salty, the bread is warm, and your hands stay busy while the grill works.
Portions run generous, and sharing is the default. A platter of kabab splits easily. With a group, order a couple of different skewers and one or two stews, pass everything around, and treat the rice as the common thread. This isn’t a one-plate-per-person tradition, and forcing it into one misses the point.
Drinks stay simple at most Persian tables. Doogh is a salty, fizzy yogurt drink that tastes strange for one sip and perfect by the third. Black tea shows up at the end, poured strong. At this particular South Grand address, of course, the drink list runs the other way: The Gin Room was built as a house of gin, so ask the bar what pairs with a stew.
### What drinks and desserts finish the meal?
Persian desserts lean floral and lightly sweet rather than heavy. Bastani, a saffron-and-rosewater ice cream flecked with pistachio, is the crowd favorite. Faloodeh pairs thin rice noodles with rosewater syrup and lime. Sholeh zard is a saffron rice pudding. Alongside strong black tea, these close a meal on a fragrant, cool note.
Bastani is the easy yes: saffron ice cream, a little chewy, studded with pistachios and perfumed with rosewater, sometimes pressed between two thin wafers. Faloodeh is the surprising pick, cold rice-flour noodles in a sweet-tart rosewater and lime slush, and it’s wonderful when you’re too full for anything creamy. Menus change, so ask what’s sweet tonight.
Tea is less a dessert than a closing ceremony. It comes black, strong and unhurried, and it’s the cue to sit a while longer. None of it is fussy. The point is to slow down and stay at the table a little past full.
### How do you find good Persian food around St. Louis?
Good Persian food in St. Louis rewards a little homework. The dishes that mark a serious kitchen are fresh tahdig, properly bloomed saffron and stews that taste cooked all day rather than rushed. Call ahead and ask a few questions, because the best sign is a kitchen happy to talk about its rice and what came off the grill today.
Treat picking a spot like a short interview. Ask whether they make tahdig and whether it’s on tonight. Ask what stews are running, since a rotating pot of ghormeh sabzi or fesenjan usually means someone’s cooking from scratch. Ask if the kabob is marinated in house. A kitchen that’s proud of the answers is the kitchen you want.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Persian food the same as Indian food?
A.  No. Both use rice and aromatic spice, but the flavors go different directions. Indian cooking leans on chili heat, turmeric and rich, often creamy sauces. Persian cooking chases sourness and floral notes, dried lime, saffron, pomegranate and rosewater, with far less chili. Persian rice is served long and separate, not folded into a heavily spiced gravy.
### Q. What is Persian food similar to?
A.  Persian food shares DNA with the cuisines around it: Central Asian pilafs, Caucasian grilled meats, and the herb-and-lemon side of eastern Mediterranean cooking. You’ll notice echoes of Turkish and Levantine kebabs, plus the rice traditions of the Indian subcontinent. Even the Bahramis’ South Grand restaurant began with a menu that reached into Indian, Arabic and Turkish cooking.
### Q. Is Persian and Turkish food the same?
A.  No, though they’re cousins. Both grill skewered meats and love yogurt, bread and eggplant. Turkish cooking uses more tomato, red pepper and olive oil, with a Mediterranean tilt. Persian cooking reaches for saffron, dried lime and fresh herbs, and builds meals around long-grain rice with its prized crust. Same neighborhood, different accent.
### Q. What are the top 5 Persian dishes?
A.  Five that define the table: chelo kabab, skewered grilled meat over buttered rice; ghormeh sabzi, the herb-and-bean stew; fesenjan, a walnut-and-pomegranate stew; zereshk polo, saffron rice with tart barberries and chicken; and tahchin, a baked saffron-rice cake. On South Grand, chelo kabob, gormeh sabzi and fessenjune all sit on one menu.
### Q. What is the Persian national dish?
A.  Chelo kabab is the dish most often named as Iran’s national plate: grilled kabab served over saffron-scented rice with a charred tomato and butter. Many people hand the honor to ghormeh sabzi, the slow herb stew, instead. Both answers are defensible, and Café Natasha’s menu lists both chelo kabob and gormeh sabzi.
### Q. What is the etiquette for eating at a Persian restaurant?
A.  Keep it relaxed. Sharing is normal, so order a few dishes and pass them around. Use bread and herbs to build small bites while you wait. Stir the butter into your rice, squeeze the lime, and grab tahdig when it appears. Tea closes the meal, and there are no strict rules to trip over.
### Q. What is tahdig?
A.  Tahdig is the crisp, golden crust that forms at the bottom of the rice pot, and it’s the most fought-over bite on a Persian table. It can be made from rice, thin flatbread or sliced potato, cooked until it’s deep gold and crackly. Ask whether the kitchen has it tonight, because it isn’t guaranteed every day.
### Q. Can vegetarians eat well at a Persian restaurant?
A.  Yes, and often better than they expect. Herb plates, flatbread, eggplant dips, yogurt sides and chopped salads make a full meal, and several stews and rice dishes turn up without meat. Menus that mark vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free dishes, like the one on South Grand, make it easy. Ask which stews are meat-free tonight.

### What do police supply stores sell in St. Louis?
Most sell the working kit an officer wears on shift: duty belts and holsters, high-output flashlights, boots, uniforms with patches, body armor carriers, handcuffs, and first-aid or trauma gear. Walk the aisles and the theme is obvious. Nearly everything is built to survive being worn hard, every day, by someone who can’t stop to baby it. The belts are stiff and wide. Load-bearing gear means belts, suspenders, holsters, magazine and radio pouches, and cuff cases. Illumination runs from pocket lights to weapon lights to big rechargeable spotlights. Safety and medical fills a wall with tourniquets, trauma dressings, gloves, and small first-aid kits. One more thing worth knowing up front. A police supply store and a gun shop aren’t the same business, even though they overlap. Some supply stores sell firearms and ammunition through a licensed counter; many don’t touch them at all and stick to the belt-and-boots side. If firearms are what you’re after, ask on the phone first, because that answer shapes which door in St. Louis you should be walking through.
### Can a civilian actually buy this gear?

Where does it get specific? Body armor is legal to buy and own for most people in most places, but there are exceptions tied to a person’s record and, sometimes, to how it’s bought or shipped. And gear tied to firearms follows firearm law. None of that is a reason to stay home. It’s a reason to ask a direct question and get a direct answer.

### How do you choose a duty belt and holster that fit?
Fit and retention decide everything here, and both are easier to judge in person than online. A duty belt should sit stiff enough to carry weight without folding over, and a holster should hold your specific model of light, blade, or sidearm with a click you can trust. Bring what you plan to carry, and try before you buy.
Interview the person at the counter the way you’d interview any specialist. Ask what the belt is made of and whether it keeps its shape loaded down. Ask how the holster retains its contents and how you release it in a hurry. Ask whether the pouches you’re eyeing lock or just snap. A good counterperson has fitted hundreds of these and will steer you off the wrong choice before you pay for it. Comfort matters more than it sounds. A belt rides against your hips for a whole shift, and a bad one leaves marks and a sour mood. If you’re layering gear for a specific job — security, dispatch ride-alongs, EMS — describe the job out loud so the recommendation fits the reality. ### What should you look for in tactical boots?
Fit, sole, ankle support, and durability separate a boot worth the money from one you’ll regret by winter. Several established brands compete hard in this space, and no single one wins for every foot. The right boot is the one that fits your foot and your job, which is why trying them on beats chasing a name.
Start with fit, because nothing else matters if the boot rubs. Try them late in the day when your feet have swollen a little, wear the socks you’ll actually work in, and walk the whole store. Then look at the sole. A good outsole grips wet floors and gravel without wearing smooth in a season, and the way it flexes at the ball of the foot tells you how it’ll feel after ten thousand steps. The cue ball rolled the whole length of the table, kissed the far rail, and drifted back to almost exactly where it started. Nobody had touched a single object ball. A kid stood there holding the stick like a push broom, and somebody’s uncle in the corner chair pretended to study his phone so he wouldn’t laugh out loud.
Everybody starts right there. Pool looks simple, which is the trap. The table is flat, the balls are round, the pockets don’t move. Then you lean over, poke the white ball, and send it three feet wide of everything. The good news? The gap between that first ugly miss and a clean, satisfying pot is smaller than it feels.
Picture a rainy Sunday. You’re at a friend’s place out past New Melle, there’s a table in the basement that’s been collecting laundry, and somebody clears it off and hands you a stick. You don’t know the rules. You don’t know how to hold it. Nobody does at first. By the end of that afternoon, though, you want to be the one who sinks a ball on purpose. This is how you get there.
### How do you play pool for beginners in St. Louis?
Rack fifteen balls in the triangle, break from behind the line, and watch what drops. In 8-ball, whoever sinks a striped ball first plays stripes; the other player takes solids. Clear your whole group, then sink the 8-ball last to win. Stand balanced, form a loose bridge with your front hand, and stroke the cue straight through the white ball. Keep it smooth, not hard.
That’s the entire game in five sentences, and you can start playing with nothing more. Everything after this is detail that makes you sharper and keeps arguments from breaking out at the table. Let’s take the pieces one at a time, because each one has a small trick nobody tells you on your first night.
### What are the basic rules of 8-ball?
8-ball is the game on almost every bar table and basement table you’ll meet, so learn it first. Two players or two teams, fifteen numbered balls plus the white cue ball. Solids are one through seven, stripes are nine through fifteen, and the black 8 sits in the middle of everything, literally and strategically. Sink your seven, then the 8, and the table is yours.
### Racking the balls
Set the triangle rack on the foot spot and pack the balls in tight. The 8-ball goes dead center. One back corner should hold a stripe and the other a solid, and the ball on the foot spot is usually a solid or a stripe by house habit. Squeeze them together with no gaps, lift the rack straight up, and you’re ready to break.
### The break
Place the cue ball anywhere behind the head string, the imaginary line across the near quarter of the table. Then hit the front of the pack hard enough to scatter it and, ideally, drop a ball. A legal break usually needs a ball pocketed or several balls driven to the rails; rooms vary, so ask. Aim for the lead ball and stay level. Wild, jumpy breaks lose control of the cue ball.
### Calling your group
The table starts open, meaning stripes and solids aren’t assigned until someone makes a called ball after the break. Sink a stripe cleanly and stripes are yours for the rest of the rack. In friendly games people call the obvious shots out loud; in league or money games you call the ball and the pocket every time. When in doubt, say what you’re shooting at before you shoot.
### Sinking the 8-ball
The 8-ball goes last, always, and it’s where beginners lose games they had already won. Clear all seven of your group first. Then call which pocket the 8 is heading for and send it there. Drop the 8 early, sink it in the wrong pocket, or scratch the cue ball while shooting it, and most house rules hand the win to your opponent. Slow way down for that final shot.
### How do you hold the cue and line up a shot?
Balance first, grip last. Stand so your dominant foot is back and your body opens slightly toward the shot, then bend at the hips until your chin drops near the cue. Your back hand holds the stick lightly, a few inches behind the balance point, like you’re cradling a bird you don’t want to crush. A death grip is the fastest way to steer a shot off line.
### Building a bridge
Your front hand is the bridge, and it’s the part beginners fumble longest. Lay your hand flat on the felt, spread your fingers, then raise the knuckles and loop your index finger over the cue to make a channel. The stick slides through that channel like a train on a rail. Keep the bridge hand still. It aims the cue; it doesn’t push it.
### The stroke
Stroke straight, follow through, and don’t stab at it. Take two or three slow practice slides, eyes moving between the cue ball and your target, then deliver one smooth stroke that finishes with the tip past where the ball sat. Most misses come from jerking the hit or lifting up to watch too early. Stay down. Let the shot finish before your head pops up.
### Where to aim
Aim at the object ball, not the white one. Find the spot on the object ball that points straight at the pocket, then send the cue ball to kiss that exact spot. On your final stroke your eyes should rest on the target ball, the same way you watch the road and not your hands on the wheel. Center-ball contact keeps the whole thing predictable.
### Where can beginners practice pool around St. Louis?
The best table to learn on is the one you can reach without a plan. Bar tables, basement tables, rec-center tables, the coin-op table at the back of a pizza place, all of them teach the same fundamentals. What matters when you’re starting is quiet reps: a table where nobody’s waiting on you, so you can shoot the same shot ten times without feeling watched.
Basement and garage tables are gold for a beginner. A friend with a table out in Jerseyville, or a family setup near New Melle, gives you unlimited time and zero pressure. Neighborhood spots help too. Community rooms and pool halls around St. Louis, Pine Lawn, and Washington Park often have open tables on weeknights when the leagues aren’t running, and weekday afternoons tend to be dead quiet.
Bar and grill tables are the next step, since you learn to play with a little noise and a jukebox going. If you like catching a game while you practice, a spot like game day at Heritage Sports Bar and Grill shows how a good room balances screens, food, and a table you can actually get to. And if you’d rather warm up somewhere loud and bright, the best arcades in St. Louis sometimes keep a pool table or two tucked past the claw machines.
One warning about bar tables: they play differently. Coin-op tables use a slightly bigger or heavier cue ball so the machine can return it, the felt is often faster and more worn, and the rails can run lively. Don’t let that rattle you. Learn the basics on whatever’s in front of you and adjust to each table as you go. Even a slightly warped table in a garage out by Pontoon Beach will teach you a straight stroke.

### What gear do you actually need to start?
Almost nothing, and that’s the honest answer. Every table you’ll play on as a beginner comes with house cues on the wall and a ball set in the tray. Grab a cue that stands roughly as tall as your chin on end, check that the tip isn’t flattened or split, and roll it on the table to make sure it isn’t badly warped. That’s your whole shopping list for month one.
Chalk is the one thing worth understanding early. That little blue cube isn’t decoration; it grips the tip to the cue ball so your stick doesn’t slide off and miscue. Chalk before most shots, brush it on, don’t grind it in. When you’re ready to own a little gear, a local hobby shop is a friendlier first stop than the internet, because you can hold a few cues and feel the weight difference before you buy.
Skip the expensive cue for now. A personal cue in the standard weight range is a nice upgrade once you know you love the game, and a cheap glove can help your bridge hand slide if your skin drags on the felt. None of it makes a beginner better than reps do. Interview the shop staff about weight and tip hardness the way you’d interview any pro, tell them you’re brand new, and let them steer you off the stuff you don’t need yet.
### How do you get better without wasting table time?
Slow down and shoot on purpose. The single biggest jump for a beginner isn’t power or fancy spin; it’s hitting the cue ball dead center and following through straight. Set the white ball a foot from a pocket with nothing in the way and pot it ten times. Then move it back a foot. Boring? Sure. It also builds the straight stroke that everything else sits on.
Learn to think one ball ahead. Beginners chase the easiest ball on the table and ignore where the cue ball ends up. Start asking a simple question before every shot: after this drops, where does the white roll, and does that leave me a shot? You’ll miss position constantly at first. Asking the question anyway is what separates people who improve from people who just keep playing.
Play people better than you and watch what they do between shots. Notice how they leave the cue ball out in the open, how they avoid clusters, how they never look rushed. Copy the pre-shot routine even before you understand it: chalk, line up, two practice strokes, one real one. Habits carry you on the nights your touch isn’t there, and every table hands you those nights.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What’s the easiest pool game to learn?
A.  8-ball, and it isn’t close. The goal is intuitive: sink your group of seven, then the black ball. Almost every bar and basement table gets used for 8-ball, so you’ll always find a game. Straight pool and 9-ball have their fans, but 8-ball teaches position and pattern play in the friendliest package a beginner could ask for.
### Q. What is the best way to learn to play billiards?
A.  Play often, on any table you can reach, and shoot slowly on purpose. Fundamentals first: a balanced stance, a steady bridge, a straight stroke through center ball. Watch better players and copy their pre-shot routine. Cheap reps on a quiet table beat expensive gear every time. A patient friend who explains position beats a video, too.
### Q. What is the two finger rule in pool?
A.  It’s a casual bar rule, not an official one, so it varies by room. When the cue ball sits within about two finger-widths of a rail, some houses say you can’t shoot straight into that same rail; you have to play away from it. Ask the locals before you break, because every table carries its own house customs.
### Q. What are some cool pool tricks for beginners?
A.  Start with the ones that build real skill. The stop shot: hit dead center and the cue ball freezes on contact. The follow shot: strike slightly high and it rolls forward. The draw shot: strike low and it spins back toward you. Those three control the whole table, and they look impressive once they’re clean.
### Q. Where to look when aiming in a pool?
A.  Look at the object ball, not the cue ball, on your final stroke. Pick the exact contact point where the cue ball must strike it to send it toward the pocket. Your eyes should rest on that target as you deliver, the same way you watch the road, not the steering wheel. Center-ball contact keeps everything predictable.
### Q. How to improve your pool game fast?
A.  Drill the boring stuff. Straight-in shots from a foot out, then two feet, then across the table. Groove a dead-center hit and a straight follow-through before touching spin. Then add one habit: before every shot, ask where the cue ball stops. Playing opponents a level above you speeds all of it up, because you learn patterns by losing.
### Q. Do bar pool tables really play differently?
A.  Yes, and it catches everyone off guard. Coin-op tables often use a larger or heavier cue ball so the machine can return it, the felt runs faster and more worn, and the rails can be bouncy. None of that should scare a beginner. Learn your fundamentals anywhere, then adjust to the speed and roll of each new table.
### Q. How long does it take a beginner to get decent at pool?
A.  Faster than you’d think for the basics. A few focused afternoons will get you making straight shots and understanding 8-ball. Reading position and controlling the cue ball takes months of regular play. The people who improve quickly drill the dull straight-in shots instead of only playing games. Consistency beats talent on a pool table nearly every time.

## What to Expect at a Pool Hall in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-at-a-pool-hall-in-st-louis
Tuesday night, a little after nine, and the only sound on table twelve is the click of the 3-ball dropping in the corner. The man who shot it doesn’t celebrate. He chalks, walks the long way around, and studies the next one. Two tables over, a birthday group from Winchester is laughing loud enough to turn heads. Nobody minds. Both things belong here.
Now picture yourself at the door. Maybe you grew up on a bar table and finally want the real thing. Maybe a coworker who lives out in Crystal City talked you into trying league. Maybe you drove past a room with the lights on and thought, why not. You walk in and there’s a counter, a wall of cues, twenty tables under long lights, and no sign telling you what to do next.
That’s the moment this guide is for. A dedicated pool hall runs on a handful of customs nobody prints on the door, and once you know them, the room stops feeling like a club you weren’t invited to. It becomes one of the easiest, cheapest nights out in St. Louis. Here’s how it works.
### How does a pool hall work in St. Louis?
You check in at the counter, get assigned a table, and the clock starts. Most dedicated pool halls rent tables by the hour rather than by the game, hand you a tray of balls and a house cue if you need one, and settle the bill when you turn the balls back in. Coin-op bar tables charge per rack instead.
The counter is the nervous system of the room. The person behind it knows which tables are open, which ones are held for league, whether the 9-footers are taken, and how long the wait runs on a Friday. Talk to them first. Tell them how many people you’ve got and whether you want a big table or a bar-size one, and they’ll point you somewhere and note your start time.
Tables are numbered, usually on the light fixture or a small plate on the rail. Your number is your address for the night. Need a rack, a bridge stick, or a fresh cube of chalk? Ask by table number. Most rooms sell food and drink from that same counter, some run a full bar and kitchen, and a few keep it to soda, chips, and a vending machine. The mood runs from hushed and serious to loud and social, sometimes in the same building on different nights.
One thing before you shoot. If you’ve never played, the room won’t teach you, and that’s fine. Read how to play pool for beginners in St. Louis on the drive over and you’ll know enough to rack, break, and hold your own. This post is about the room, not the game.
### How much do pool halls charge per hour?
It depends on the room, the day, and the hour, and the honest answer is to call and ask. Hourly table rates are the norm in dedicated halls, and most rooms post them at the counter and online. What moves the number is predictable: weekend evenings cost more than weekday afternoons, tournament-size tables sometimes cost more than bar boxes, and a few rooms charge per player instead of per table.
So plan around the pattern rather than a figure. A Tuesday afternoon in a half-empty room is the cheap seat. Saturday at ten p.m. is peak. Some halls run daytime specials, student rates, or flat-fee blocks on slow nights, and the counter will tell you if you ask. Don’t be shy about it. Regulars ask about specials constantly.
### Table time versus coin-op
Here’s the split that confuses first-timers. A coin-op table, the kind in a bar or a pizza place, swallows quarters or a card swipe and gives you one rack of balls. Miss and scratch all you like, the meter doesn’t care, but every new game costs another feed. A timed table charges for the clock, not the games. Play one long rack or fifteen fast ones. Same price.
That’s why serious players prefer table time. Practice drills that would eat a roll of quarters cost nothing extra when the clock is running anyway. It’s also why a pool hall feels different from the bar down the street: nobody’s stacking quarters on the rail to claim the next game, because you don’t share your table with strangers. It’s yours until you close out.
### How you actually pay
Most rooms want a card or an ID at the counter when you open a table. That holds your time and, in some places, works as a deposit on the ball set. When you’re done, you carry the tray back, they stop the clock, and you pay for time plus any food, drink, or cue rental. Splitting a table between four people is normal. Say so up front if you want the bill divided.
A couple of quirks to expect. Some halls round to the quarter hour. Some carry a minimum on busy nights. Rental fees for a nicer house cue or a break cue exist in some rooms and not in others. And tipping the counter staff, the way you’d tip a bartender, is common and appreciated. Play there often and they’ll start saving you the good table.
### What is the etiquette at a pool hall?
Stay out of the shooter’s line, keep drinks off the rails, never sit on a table, and keep your voice down near a live game. That’s the core of it, and it’s the same at a quiet room in Clifton Heights as it is at a loud one across town. The rest is common courtesy dressed up in felt.
Line of sight matters more than most newcomers realize. When someone is down on a shot, don’t walk behind the pocket they’re aiming at, don’t stand in their peripheral vision, and don’t reach across their table for the chalk. Wait the three seconds. If you must pass, go behind the shooter, not in front. A good room is full of people freezing mid-step for each other, and it looks like a dance once you notice it.
Your own table has customs, too. Chalk your tip over the floor, not the cloth. Don’t drop the rack on the felt or slide the tray across it. Don’t lean cues against the table, since they fall and dent the rails. Return the balls to the counter when you leave rather than leaving them scattered. None of this is hard. It’s simply how the room stays nice for the next person.
### What not to do
Don’t coach a stranger. Even a friendly tip, unasked, lands as an insult in most halls. Don’t offer to play for money unless someone brings it up, and don’t accept if you don’t know the room. Don’t shark, meaning no talking, tapping, or moving while an opponent shoots. Don’t masse or jump the cue ball on a table where you haven’t been told it’s allowed, because a bad jump shot tears cloth. And don’t set a wet glass anywhere near the rail. Ever.
What do regulars expect from a first-timer? Less than you’d guess. Nobody cares that you miss. They care that you’re aware of the tables around you, that you don’t hover over their game, and that you handle the equipment like it belongs to someone else, because it does. Tap the butt of your cue on the floor when an opponent makes a great shot. That’s applause here. Do that once and you’re in.
Driving out to play tonight? Check how often your car needs an oil change.
### What are the house rules for a billiard hall?
House rules are the posted policies of the building, separate from the rules of the game, and they cover age limits, hours, damage, food and drink at the table, and which shots are off limits on their cloth. Every room writes its own. Most tape them to the counter or a wall by the cue rack, and the staff will recite them if you ask.
Age is the big one to check before you drive. A hall with a liquor license may allow minors during the day and turn into a 21-and-up room after a certain hour. A dry room may welcome families all night. Neither is standard. Call ahead if you’re bringing a teenager from House Springs on a Friday, and save yourself the U-turn at the door.
Damage rules are the other common surprise. Torn cloth from a jump shot, a cue snapped in frustration, a ball chipped from being slammed into the rack: rooms charge for that, and the amount is theirs to set. Treat the table like a rented car. Most halls also bar outside food and drink, ask you to keep bags off the tables, and reserve the right to shut down a game that’s gotten too loud or too heated.
### House cues versus your own
House cues live on a wall rack and they’re free with your table. Quality varies. Sight down a few, roll each one on the felt to check for warp, and pick one with a tip that’s rounded rather than flat or mushroomed. A decent house cue is plenty for a first night. Nobody looks twice at someone using one.
Bringing your own is welcome everywhere, and it’s the clearest signal you’re a regular in the making. Carry it in a case. Most rooms ask you not to break with a playing cue that isn’t yours, so if you own a break cue, bring it, and if you don’t, use the house cue for the break and switch to your own after. Don’t leave a personal cue on a table unattended. Cases get confused, and so do people.
### Leagues and open tables
League night changes the room. Several tables get reserved for teams, the pace tightens, and there’s a scorekeeper at every match. Leagues around St. Louis typically run through national organizations with weekly handicapped matches, and most rooms will happily put a new player on a roster mid-season if a captain has a slot. Ask the counter which nights are league and which are open before you plan a loud group outing.
Open tables are anything not held for league or a tournament. On a timed table, open simply means available to rent. On the coin-op tables some halls keep near the bar, open follows the old bar custom: quarters on the rail hold your place, winner stays, challenger pays. If you’re not sure which system a table runs, ask whoever’s playing. They’ll tell you, usually with a grin, because everyone got that wrong once.
### What size pool tables do pool halls use?
Dedicated halls lean on 9-foot tables, the tournament standard, with a row of 7-foot bar boxes for players who want the size they know from bars. An 8-foot table shows up in home basements far more often than in halls. The number is the length of the playing surface, and every foot changes how the game feels.
A 9-footer plays long and honest. Shots you’d make blind on a bar box become real shots when there’s another two feet of cloth to cross, and pockets on a serious table are often cut tighter, so a slightly off-center hit rattles out instead of dropping. Beginners find it humbling for about an hour. Then something clicks, and the bar table back home starts to feel like a toy.
Bar boxes in a hall are the friendlier starting point. Same balls, same rules, shorter distances, and the cue ball on a hall’s 7-footer is usually a standard weight rather than the heavy coin-op ball, so it rolls truer. Ask for one if you’re nervous. There’s zero shame in it, and plenty of leagues play on 7-footers anyway.
Some rooms also keep a snooker table or a pocketless three-cushion table in a corner. Those are bigger, slower, and usually rented at their own rate. Leave them alone your first night unless someone at the counter offers to walk you through it. And if you’re weighing a pool hall against the other rooms in town, the guide to types of bars in St. Louis and how to pick one lays out the whole spectrum.
### Where the name pool hall comes from
The word pool has nothing to do with water and everything to do with betting. In the 1800s a poolroom was a betting parlor where people pooled money on horse races, and owners installed billiard tables so customers had something to do between results. The tables outlasted the wagering. The name stuck to the game, and pocket billiards has been called pool ever since.
That history explains a lot about the room you’re walking into. The long lights, the counter, the quiet, the sense that people here take the thing seriously: it all descends from a place built for men waiting on results. Billiards is the broad family, covering snooker and carom games too. Pool is the pocketed branch. And a pool hall, in the St. Louis sense, is a room built around the tables first and everything else second.
It also explains the old reputation. For a long stretch of the last century, pool halls carried a whiff of hustlers and lost afternoons, and some parents still hear the phrase that way. Walk into one now and you’ll find league teams in matching shirts, retirees playing straight pool at two in the afternoon, a couple from Hanley Hills on a date, and a teenager grinding drills on a back table. The room outgrew the reputation a long time ago.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do pool halls charge per hour?

### Q. How much does it usually cost to play a game of pool?
A.  On a coin-op bar table you pay per rack, so a single game costs whatever the machine takes, and a long night of short games adds up. On a timed table in a pool hall, one game costs a slice of your hourly rate, which means a fast game is nearly free and a slow one costs more. Split the table four ways and a casual hour is one of the cheaper nights out around St. Louis. Ask the room for its posted rate.
### Q. What is the etiquette at a pool hall?
A.  Stay out of a shooter’s line of sight, keep drinks and bags off the rails, never sit or lean on a table, and keep your voice down near live games. Chalk over the floor, not the cloth. Don’t coach strangers, don’t distract an opponent while they shoot, and return your balls to the counter when you leave. Tap your cue on the floor to applaud a good shot, and thank the counter on the way out.
### Q. What are the house rules for a billiard hall?
A.  House rules are the building’s own policies, separate from the rules of any game. They usually cover age limits and hours, outside food and drink, damage charges for torn cloth or broken cues, restrictions on jump and masse shots, table reservations for league, and general behavior. Every room posts its own, typically at the counter. Read them or ask the staff before you start your first rack.
### Q. What size pool tables do pool halls use?
A.  Most dedicated pool halls run 9-foot tables, the tournament standard, alongside a set of 7-foot bar boxes for players who prefer the size they know from bars. Eight-foot tables are mostly a home-basement size. The bigger table plays longer and often has tighter pockets, so shots feel harder at first. Ask for a 7-footer if you’re new and want a softer landing on your first night.
### Q. Why is it called a pool hall?
A.  The name comes from betting, not water. In the 1800s a poolroom was a parlor where bettors pooled money on horse races, and owners added billiard tables to keep customers busy between results. The tables outlived the wagering and the name stuck to pocket billiards. Billiards is the wider family of cue games, pool is the pocketed branch, and a pool hall is a room built around those tables.
### Q. Can you bring your own cue to a pool hall?
A.  Yes, and it’s welcome everywhere. Carry it in a case, keep it with you rather than leaving it on a table, and use a dedicated break cue or the house cue for breaks so you don’t flatten the tip on your playing cue. House cues are free with your table if you’d rather not bring one. Roll a house cue on the felt to check for warp before you commit to it.
### Q. Do pool halls in St. Louis allow kids?
A.  It depends on the room and the hour. Halls with a liquor license often allow minors during the day and become 21-and-up in the evening, while dry rooms may welcome families all night. Neither setup is standard, so call before you drive, especially on a weekend. ## Where to Ski Near St. Louis and How to Plan a First Trip

Seven-fifteen on a Saturday morning in January, and a kid in Mascoutah is standing in the driveway in snow pants that still have the tag on them. Her dad is in the garage trying to work out whether goggles go over the helmet or under it. Nobody in this family has ever stood on a ski slope. The car is warm. The thermos is full. They’re going anyway.

### What is the closest ski resort to St. Louis, MO?
The closest ski hill to St. Louis is Hidden Valley Ski Resort in Wildwood, Missouri, on the west side of St. Louis County, close enough for a day trip. For most of the metro that’s a drive measured in minutes, not hours, which is the whole reason a first ski outing here can be an afternoon instead of a vacation. Missouri has one other ski area, Snow Creek, north of Kansas City. That one’s a real haul from here and better saved for a weekend.
One thing to understand about a Midwest hill before you go: it lives on snowmaking. Cold nights, not snowfall, decide whether the runs are open. Hidden Valley posts its own hours, rates, and snowmaking status, and all three change with the weather. Check the hill’s site the morning you plan to drive. Then check it again from the driveway. ### What do I need for a first time ski trip?
For a first ski trip you need warm layers you already own, rented skis, boots, and poles, a lift ticket, and a lesson. That’s the list. Rent everything that touches snow. Buy nothing with a binding on it until you’ve skied a few times and know you like it, because the fastest way to hate a new hobby is to own a closet full of it after one bad afternoon.
### Rent or buy?
Rent. Boots are the strongest argument, since boots are the piece beginners get wrong most often, and a rental counter will size you in two minutes and swap them if your toes go numb after the first run. Skis and poles come with the package. Helmets usually rent too, and you want one. The one item worth owning early is goggles. Rental goggles are hit or miss, and a fogged lens ruins a run faster than a fall does.
### What to wear
Dress like you’re going to be wet, then cold, then sweating, because you’ll be all three before lunch. A base layer that isn’t cotton. A fleece or a sweater. A waterproof shell on top and waterproof pants on the bottom. Ski socks, tall and thin, one pair, never two. Gloves that can get soaked. If you’ve already sorted out what outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis, most of it crosses over; the rain shell you wear to a soggy October ballgame is a perfectly fine ski jacket for a Missouri hill.
Skip the cotton hoodie. Skip jeans. Both soak through on the first fall and stay wet for the rest of the day, and a wet, cold kid is done skiing whether or not the lesson is over. If somebody in the family owns nothing waterproof, a cheap pair of rain pants pulled over sweatpants beats jeans by a mile.
### How much money do I need for a ski trip?
Less than a mountain trip and more than a movie, and the exact number depends on choices you control. Every ski budget is the same four lines: lift ticket, rentals, lesson, and food. The hill’s own rate sheet is the number that counts, so pull it up before you build a budget and treat anything you read elsewhere, this page included, as a description of what moves the price rather than the price itself.
### What drives the price up or down
Timing is the biggest lever. Weekend and holiday sessions cost more than weekday ones almost everywhere, and many hills sell shorter night sessions for less than a full day. Buying online ahead of time often beats walking up to the window. Then there’s the gear you already own. Every layer, glove, and pair of goggles you don’t have to rent is money that stays in your pocket.
Lessons look like the expensive line, and they’re the best one. A beginner group lesson often bundles beginner-area lift access, and sometimes the rental, so compare the package rather than the pieces. A family of four renting everything on a Saturday afternoon will spend more than a couple who owns their outerwear and shows up for a weeknight session. Neither is wrong. Just know which one you’re planning.
Food is the sneaky line. Lodge food is priced like stadium food. Pack a cooler, eat in the car or at a lodge table, and you’ve just paid for somebody’s helmet rental. Bring more water than seems reasonable. Cold air dries you out, and tired, thirsty beginners fall more.
### What is the cheapest month to ski?
At a Midwest hill, the cheapest skiing is usually midweek and at night, in whichever month the hill is fully open and the holiday crowds have gone home. Early-season and late-season windows sometimes carry lower rates too, but the trade is fewer open runs. A quiet Tuesday night in the middle of the season is the beginner’s sweet spot: cheaper, emptier, and forgiving.
Why does the session matter more than the calendar? Because a beginner needs space. A packed Saturday means long lift lines, a crowded beginner area, and faster skiers whipping past a kid who’s still learning to stop. The same session on a weeknight gives that kid room to fall without an audience. Cheaper and better at the same time doesn’t come along often. Take it.
Watch the weather, too. The cold snap that has you looking up what snow removal costs in St. Louis is the same one that lets the hill run its snow guns all night, and the snowmaking status will tell you what’s open. Warm spells thin the runs. Cold, dry stretches build them back. Book a lesson a week or two out, then check conditions the day before and be willing to shift.
Snowed out this weekend? Learn how to play pool for beginners instead.
### Is skiing really hard to learn?
No. Skiing is awkward to learn and easy to get decent at. In our experience most adults and kids can ride the beginner lift and make it down a gentle run with controlled turns after one lesson and an afternoon of practice. The hard part is the first ninety minutes, when your feet are locked into boots that feel like casts and your skis want to go two different directions at once.
### Take the lesson
Take the lesson from the hill, not from a friend. A friend who skis well usually can’t explain how, and a friend who skis badly will teach you every bad habit with total confidence. Instructors teach the wedge, the stop, and how to get up after a fall, in that order, on terrain built for it. One group lesson on day one saves you three days of frustration and, honestly, a few bruises.
Interview the ski school the way you’d interview any provider. Call ahead or ask at the counter: which ages get grouped together, how many students per instructor, does the lesson include the beginner lift and the rental, and what happens if weather closes the hill after you’ve booked? Tell them what you expect, which is a kid who can stop on purpose by the end of the hour, and listen to what they say they can deliver. The gap is the signal.
### How many days for a beginner
One day is a taste. Two or three days is where a beginner turns into a skier, because day two is when the boots stop feeling strange and day three is when you stop thinking about your feet. Four days is fine for adults who are enjoying it and too many for most kids on a first trip. Legs get tired, patience runs thin, and the last day of a long trip is where beginners get hurt. Quit while it’s still fun.
### A first-trip plan, step by step
Here’s the whole thing in order, from picking a date to the drive home. Do it in this sequence and you’ll skip most of the mistakes that turn a first trip into a last one.
### Step one: pick the date
Pick a weekday or a night session if you possibly can. Check the hill’s calendar for hours, then check the forecast for the week before, since that’s the weather that builds the snow you’ll ski on. Give yourself one backup date. A family driving in from Sullivan doesn’t want to make that trip twice for a closed hill.
### Step two: book the lesson and rentals
Book the lesson first, then the rental package, then the lift ticket, in that order, because the lesson slot is the one that sells out and the one that may include the rest. Do it online if the hill offers it. Write down every height, weight, and shoe size the rental form asks for before you start, so you aren’t guessing at a kid’s weight with a checkout timer running.
### Step three: pack the night before
Lay it all out on the floor: base layers, mid layers, shells, ski socks, gloves, goggles, a neck gaiter, sunscreen, and lip balm. Yes, sunscreen. Snow bounces sunlight straight up into your face. Add a change of dry clothes for the drive home, a cooler, water, and a garbage bag for the wet stuff. Charge the phone. Settle the helmet question by planning to rent one.
### Step four: the morning of
Eat a real breakfast. Get to the hill early, well before your lesson, because the rental line takes longer than anyone expects and boots take longer than that. Walk around in the boots for a few minutes before you clip in so they stop feeling like a mistake. Use the bathroom before the boots go on. Everyone learns that one exactly once.
### Step five: on the hill
Do the lesson. Then practice what the lesson taught you on the beginner slope, and only the beginner slope, for the rest of the session. Take a break every hour whether anyone wants one or not. When somebody says they’re cold, they were cold twenty minutes ago; go inside. Stop while everyone still likes each other.
### Step six: after
Return the rentals early rather than in the closing rush. Change into dry clothes in the lodge or the car. On the drive home, ask each person the one thing they’d do differently and write it down, because that list is your packing list for trip two. Then decide, honestly, whether trip two is another local day or a bigger weekend.
### Day trip or weekend?
Your first trip should be a day trip to the local hill, full stop. A weekend at a bigger Midwest ski area or a week in the Rockies makes a fine second or third trip, once you know everyone in the car can stop and turn. Bigger mountains mean longer runs, longer lifts, altitude, and a lot more money on the table if it turns out somebody hates it. Learn close to home. Travel once you’re hooked.

### Q. What do I need for a first time ski trip?

You don’t need to own anything with a binding on it for a first trip; rent what touches snow and wear what you already have.
### Q. What are some tips for a first-time ski trip?
A.  Take a lesson on day one, pick a weekday or night session, and arrive early because rentals take longer than you think. Stay on the beginner slope. Break every hour. ### Q. How much money do I need for a ski trip?

### Q. What is the cheapest month to ski?

Midweek and night sessions after the holiday crowds leave are usually the lowest-priced and least crowded. Early and late season sometimes bring lower rates with fewer open runs. ### Q. Is skiing really hard to learn?

Most beginners can ride the beginner lift and make controlled turns down a gentle run after one group lesson and an afternoon of practice. The trick is learning the wedge and the stop from an instructor rather than a friend, and staying on the beginner slope until stopping feels automatic. Ski boots will feel strange for a day. That passes.
### Q. Is 4 days of skiing too much?
A.  For a beginner, usually yes. Days two and three are where skiing starts to feel natural, and that’s plenty for a first trip. By day four, legs are tired and patience is thin, and that’s when beginners get hurt. Adults who are loving it can push to four with a rest afternoon built in. Kids on a first trip are better off with two or three days and a good memory.
### Q. Should a beginner take a lesson or learn from a friend?
A.  Take the lesson. A friend who skis well usually can’t explain what they’re doing, and a friend who skis badly will pass along every bad habit with confidence. A group lesson teaches the wedge, the stop, and getting up after a fall, in that order, on terrain made for it. ## What First-Time Skydiving Costs and Feels Like in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-first-time-skydiving-costs-and-feels-like-in-st-louis
The alarm goes off at 5:15 on a Saturday and for one blank second neither of you remembers why. Then it lands. Today is the jump. You booked it six weeks ago after a birthday dinner in Glendale, somewhere between the second glass of wine and the check, and now the sun isn’t up and the coffee maker is gurgling in the dark like it knows something you don’t.
The drive out of St. Louis is quiet. Highway, then two-lane, then a gravel lot with a wind sock hanging limp beside a metal hangar. Your brother-in-law out in High Ridge did this last summer and hasn’t stopped talking about it, which is the entire reason you’re here. He said two things you keep replaying. It costs more than you think once you add the video. And it eats the whole morning. Both true.
This is the guide for that morning. What the money buys, why you’ll sit around for hours, what freefall does to your body, and who the drop zone will politely turn away at the counter. None of it is meant to scare you off. It’s meant to get you to the hangar door with the right expectations and the right shoes.
### How much is it to skydive in St. Louis?
A first tandem jump near St. Louis runs a few hundred dollars before add-ons, and every drop zone quotes its own number. What moves the price: the tandem base rate, exit altitude, video and photo packages, weekday versus weekend booking, group discounts, and whether a deposit is refundable or only transferable when weather cancels. Call two or three and compare.
Notice what isn’t in that answer. Nobody quotes you a flat, all-in number on the phone, because the all-in number depends on choices you haven’t made yet. The base rate is the floor. The video package is the thing that turns the floor into something noticeably taller. Most first-timers walk in planning to skip the video and walk out having bought it, because the person at the counter asks one question: do you want to remember this?
So plan your budget in two tiers. The number you’d pay if you jumped with nothing extra, and the number you’d pay if you said yes to everything. The truth for most people lands in between, and you’ll feel better on the drive home if you decided that before the adrenaline did.
### What are you actually paying for on a tandem jump?
Every line on a tandem receipt traces back to the same handful of things: the aircraft, the instructor, the gear, and the time. Understanding which one you’re moving when you say yes to an upgrade makes the counter conversation a lot less fuzzy. Here’s how the pieces break out.
### The tandem base rate
The base rate covers the ride up, the instructor strapped to your back, the parachute system, the ground briefing, and the landing. That’s the whole jump. Drop zones price it against what it costs them to keep an aircraft fueled and an instructor rated and current, which is why the number varies from one place to the next and why a suspiciously cheap quote deserves a second question.
### Altitude
Some drop zones offer a standard exit altitude and a higher one for an extra fee. Higher means longer freefall. The plane has to climb longer to get you there, which burns fuel and time, and that’s what you’re paying for. Ask the drop zone how much longer the freefall runs at the higher altitude; they know their own numbers and will tell you. Don’t trust a blog, including this one, to quote you seconds.
### Video and photo packages
This is the big one. Options usually run from a handheld camera on the instructor’s wrist to a separate camera flyer who exits with you and films the whole thing from outside. The outside camera costs more because it’s another trained jumper on the load, taking a seat. Photos, video, or both, edited or raw, delivered by download or on a drive: each choice moves the price. Decide before you arrive.
### Weekday, weekend, and group rates
Weekends fill up. Weekdays don’t. Many drop zones price accordingly, and a Tuesday morning can be quieter, faster, and cheaper than a Saturday, with fewer loads ahead of you. Groups often get a per-person break once you hit a headcount, which is why bachelor parties and office outings show up in vans. If you’re bringing four friends from Dellwood, ask about the group rate before anyone pays on their own.
### Deposits and weather rebooking
Almost every drop zone takes a deposit to hold your slot. Read the policy before you pay it. The usual pattern is that a deposit is non-refundable if you cancel, but transferable to another date if weather scrubs the jump. Some let you gift it. Some put a clock on it. Ask what happens if the clouds roll in at noon after you’ve waited four hours, because that scenario is common, and you want to know the answer while you’re calm.
### Why does skydiving take 3 hours?
Because the drop zone is running an airfield, not a ticket line, and airfields move on weather, aircraft, and load order. Three hours is a normal first-timer estimate, and plenty of people spend longer. You’re paying for the jump itself, which is minutes, but you’re living through the wait, which is most of the day. Knowing why the wait exists makes it easier to sit through.
Start with the paperwork. You’ll sign a waiver that runs several pages and, at many drop zones, watch a video explaining what you’re agreeing to. That alone can take half an hour. Then comes the ground briefing, where your instructor walks you through the exit position, the arch, where to keep your hands, and what happens at pull time and on landing. Pay attention here. It’s short and it matters.
Then you wait for a load. Aircraft go up in cycles carrying a set number of jumpers, and tandems, camera flyers, and experienced fun jumpers all share those seats. If six tandems are booked ahead of you, you’re several loads back. Add refueling. Add a gear check. Add the instructor from your load finishing with the person before you and repacking.
And then there’s weather, the thing nobody controls. Skydiving needs clear air below the exit altitude and winds inside limits the drop zone sets. Clouds parked at the wrong height ground everyone. So does gusty wind, even on a sunny day. A couple who drove over from Bethalto at dawn might sit on a bench watching a perfectly blue sky and still not jump, because the wind at the landing area is over the number. It happens. Bring a book and a charged phone.
If all that sitting in a hangar gets you curious about the front of the airplane instead of the door, it’s a short hop from here to wondering what flight lessons cost in St. Louis. Same hangars, different addiction.
### Do you feel it in your stomach when you skydive?
No, and that surprises almost everyone. The roller-coaster stomach drop comes from going from still to falling in an instant. In a skydive you’re already moving with the aircraft when you leave it, so there’s no sudden change your gut registers. What you feel instead is wind. A lot of it. Loud enough that your instructor’s voice disappears, strong enough to flap your cheeks, and steady enough that within a few seconds it feels like lying on something solid.
The exit is the strangest second of your life. You’re sitting at the door with your legs in the air, your instructor rocks you forward, and then the ground is everywhere and the plane is gone. Your brain has no file for this. Most first-timers describe a short burst of total overload, then a click, then something close to calm. That’s the arch doing its job and the wind holding you.
Then the parachute opens. You’ll feel a firm pull upward, as if someone grabbed your harness and lifted, and the roar cuts out. Ears ring. Then quiet. Real quiet, the kind you don’t hear anywhere else, with the whole region laid out below you, the river a brown ribbon, the bluffs on the Illinois side catching morning light. Your instructor will check the canopy, loosen your harness a little, and probably hand you the steering toggles.
The canopy ride is long enough to talk, look around, and realize you’re not scared anymore. That’s the part people don’t expect. The freefall is the sales pitch; the canopy ride is the reason they come back. Landing is a slide or a step, depending on wind, with your legs up and your instructor doing the work. Then you’re standing in a field grinning like your brother-in-law.
Landed wrong? Here is what diagnostic imaging costs in St. Louis.
### Who is not allowed to skydive?
Drop zones turn people away for four reasons: age, weight, medical conditions, and alcohol. The legal minimum age to skydive in the US is 18, and United States Parachute Association member drop zones don’t take a parent’s signature as a workaround. Most drop zones set a tandem weight limit somewhere in the low-to-mid 200s, and they weigh you at check-in, so the number on your license doesn’t settle it.
Medical is where it gets individual. Heart conditions, recent surgeries, back and neck problems, uncontrolled blood pressure, pregnancy, and certain medications can all disqualify you or require a doctor’s sign-off. The waiver asks. Answer honestly. The opening shock and the landing both put load on your spine, and the drop zone would rather move your deposit to another day than find out mid-jump that you left something out.
Alcohol is the simplest rule and the most often broken. If you’ve been drinking, you don’t jump. Period. Most drop zones extend that back to the night before, because someone who was closing down a bar at 1 a.m. is not someone they want at the door at 9. Save the celebration for after you land. There’s usually a place nearby that expects you.
On safety numbers, skip the blogs. The United States Parachute Association publishes its own annual safety summaries and the standards its member drop zones follow, and any drop zone worth your deposit will talk about its own record when you ask. Read the source, then ask the operator. Don’t take a figure from a stranger on the internet, including this one.
### Is 40 too old to skydive?
Not even close. Plenty of first-timers are in their forties, fifties, and well beyond, and drop zones see grandparents on tandems every season. Your birth year matters a lot less than your knees, spine, and heart, because those are what take the opening and the landing, and that’s a conversation for your doctor rather than the calendar. Can you climb a few flights of stairs? Can you pull your knees toward your chest while seated? Then you’re in the conversation.
### Can a 300-pound person skydive?
At most drop zones, no, at least not on a tandem, and this one is worth hearing before you drive out. Tandem gear is certified to a combined weight of student, instructor, and equipment, and that certification is why the limit exists. Most drop zones land somewhere in the low-to-mid 200s for the student. Some add a surcharge above a certain weight and stop hard above another. Call ahead, give your honest weight, and let them tell you where their line is.
### Do and don’ts of skydiving?
Most of the do’s come down to arriving rested, fed, sober, and dressed like you’re going hiking, and most of the don’ts come down to not bringing anything that can fall off you at speed. The drop zone will hand you a jumpsuit, goggles, and a harness. Everything else is on you.
### Do
Eat a normal breakfast. An empty stomach and adrenaline are a worse combination than a full one. Wear closed-toe, lace-up shoes with no hooks and clothes you can move in, with a layer for the plane ride because it gets cold on the climb. Tie long hair back. Bring your ID, your confirmation, and patience. In the briefing, ask the dumb question. Everyone else is thinking it.
### Don’t
Don’t drink the night before. Don’t wear sandals, boots with hooks, or anything with drawstrings that can catch. Don’t bring your own camera; drop zones don’t let first-timers carry one, and they’ll ask you to leave phones and keys on the ground. Don’t book anything important afterward, because a weather hold can push your jump to late afternoon. Don’t scuba dive the day before; ask the drop zone how long they want between the two.
### Picking a drop zone the interview way
Treat this like choosing a doctor. Shortlist two or three drop zones within a reasonable drive of St. Louis, on either side of the river, and interview them. Ask if they’re a United States Parachute Association member drop zone and whether their tandem instructors hold current ratings. Ask what the base price includes, what altitude it buys, and what the video options cost. Ask about the deposit policy and what happens on a weather day.
Then compare what you want against what each one is prepared to provide. The gap is the signal. A drop zone that answers every question plainly, quotes its own numbers, and doesn’t flinch at the weight question is showing you how they run the rest of the operation. If someone is vague on the phone, they’ll be vague at the counter.
One more thing. A tandem is a gateway. People who swore they were doing it once end up planning a whole season around the outdoors, and a jump pairs well with the rest of what’s out here, whether that’s a slow trail morning out past Gray Summit or a float on the river. The best outdoor activities in St. Louis for every adventure level covers the ground-level options for the day after, when your legs still work but your nerves are spent.
