### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should you pay a private bartender?
A.  There’s no single metro rate, because the number moves with guest count, total hours including setup and breakdown, travel distance, the date, and how much of the bar the bartender supplies. A person who brings tools, ice, coolers, garnish and glassware prices differently than one who brings only themselves. Get two or three quotes against the same written brief and compare scope, not just the hourly.
### Q. How many bartenders per 100 guests?
A.  Two, as a baseline, using the common one-per-fifty guideline. Go to two plus a bar back if you’re running a full cocktail menu, serving a champagne toast, or working a venue where ice and stock live far from the bar. Beer, wine and a couple of batched cocktails can sometimes stretch further. The moment a line forms and stays, you were short.
### Q. What do you pay a bartender for a wedding?
A.  Weddings usually cost more per hour than a backyard party, and the reasons are structural. Longer service windows, a cocktail hour and a reception, a toast that compresses two hundred pours into minutes, rented glassware, premium dates, venue insurance requirements and a larger crew. Ask specifically about the staffing plan for the toast. That single moment breaks more wedding bars than the whole rest of the night.
### Q. Do you have to have a bartender license in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no statewide bartender license. Alcohol is regulated through state liquor control plus local city and county ordinances, which differ across this metro, and any business selling or serving alcohol needs its own liquor license. What matters for a private host is whether alcohol is being sold, what the venue requires, and whether the bartender carries liquor liability coverage. Confirm specifics with your own city or county.
### Q. What is the 50% rule in bartending?
A.  It isn’t a law or an industry standard. It’s bar-trade shorthand, and more than one version circulates. The reading most event planners use: assume roughly half your guests are actively drinking in any given hour when you size the bar, the ice and the staffing. Useful as a sanity check. Don’t treat it as gospel, and don’t build a shopping list on it alone.
### Q. Is $20 a good tip for a bartender?
A.  For one drink at a bar, that’s generous. For a private event, it’s low, because event tipping runs off the service total rather than per drink. The customary range is about 15 to 20 percent of what you paid for the service. Ask upfront whether gratuity is already built into the quote so you’re not guessing at breakdown.
### Q. Who buys the alcohol, the host or the bartender?
A.  Usually the host. It’s cheaper, and it keeps the bartender clear of licensed-sales territory. Many bartenders will write your shopping list down to bottle counts and sizes, which is worth asking for during the interview. Buy where unopened bottles can be returned, and confirm that policy before you load the cart, since it varies from retailer to retailer.
### Q. Do you need a bar back for a big party?
A.  Past roughly a hundred guests, yes, and sooner if ice and stock are stored far from the bar. A bar back hauls ice, restocks bottles, runs glassware and keeps your bartender behind the bar instead of walking to a garage cooler every ten minutes. Ask whether help is included at your guest count or billed as a separate person.

## What a Backyard Basketball Court Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-backyard-basketball-court-costs-in-st-louis
The hoop is bolted to the garage fascia, slightly crooked, the way they always end up. Ball goes up, rattles the rim, drops, and then keeps rolling, because the driveway falls off toward the street at whatever pitch the builder poured decades ago. Somebody sprints after it. A car slows down. That is the moment a backyard court actually gets decided, with a kid standing in the street holding a ball.
Two phone calls into pricing a real pad out back, most people learn the same thing. The hoop was never the expensive part. You aren’t buying a basketball goal. You’re buying flatwork, and flatwork in eastern Missouri has opinions.
Chalk lines on the grass are a good first move. Mark the footprint, walk it, shoot on the grass for a week and see whether the size feels right. Then start asking about what goes underneath it, because the dirt decides both the price and the lifespan.
### How much does it cost to build a basketball court in your yard in St. Louis?
The slab drives the number, not the hoop. Square footage, how much grading your yard needs, slab thickness, reinforcement, the sub-base under it, and where the water goes matter far more than surfacing or the goal. Prices swing hard by yard and by contractor, so get two or three quotes.
Nobody honest prices this over the phone. Any square-foot figure you found online was quoted in another state, in another year, on a flatter lot, with cheaper trucking. Two yards a mile apart in South County can come back thousands apart and both bids can be correct. One needs a truckload of fill and a drain line. The other needs a skid steer for an afternoon and a broom.
So treat any range you read, including one you hear from a neighbor, as something that varies by yard and by contractor. What you can actually control is knowing which decisions move the number. Court cost is roughly square footage multiplied by site conditions, plus a short list of choices about thickness, steel, joints, drainage and surface. Learn those, then get quotes from people who have stood in your backyard.
### Where does the money actually go on a backyard court?
Into dirt and concrete. On most residential courts, excavation, sub-base, forms, reinforcement and the pour eat the large majority of the budget. The goal, the net and the painted lines are small by comparison. People shop the hoop first because the hoop is the part that photographs well in a catalog.
### Excavation and grading
Your yard isn’t flat. A court has to be. Somebody has to cut into the high side, build up the low side, and either haul the difference off or spread it where it does some good. Cut and fill is the least predictable line on a court budget. A pad area with a two-foot fall across it is a different job from one with an eight-foot fall, and the second may need a retaining wall before anyone talks about concrete at all.
Access changes the math too. If a ready-mix truck can back within a chute length of the forms, great. If it can’t, because the only route to the back of a narrow Tower Grove lot is a four-foot gate, then material moves by buggy, conveyor or pump. That’s labor and equipment, and it shows up in the bid whether or not anybody explains it.
### The sub-base under the slab
Crushed stone, placed in lifts and compacted to a depth your contractor specifies for your soil. This is the layer homeowners cut first, because nobody will ever see it, and it’s the layer doing the most work. It spreads the load across soft spots, and it gives water a path that isn’t the underside of your concrete. Go cheap here and you’ve built an expensive cracker on top of pudding.
### Slab, steel and forms
Thickness is real money. Every extra inch across a pad the size of a three-car garage floor is a meaningful jump in yardage, and the concrete itself is priced by the yard. Reinforcement is a separate decision: welded wire mesh laid flat is cheaper than rebar tied in a grid and held up on chairs, and it doesn’t behave as well over moving soil. Forms, screeding, finishing and curing are labor hours. If that sounds familiar, it should. Our breakdown of what a concrete driveway costs in St. Louis is built on the same handful of variables.
### Everything sitting on top
Surface coating, the goal, its footing, fencing, lighting, lines and nets. Any one of those is modest. Together they can rival a chunk of the slab. One adjustable in-ground hoop with a decent backboard is a manageable purchase. Two goals, black vinyl fence on two sides, and pole-mounted lighting is a second project riding on the back of the first.
### Why does St. Louis clay decide whether your slab survives?
Eastern Missouri sits on expansive clay. Every contractor who pours here knows it, and it’s the quiet reason two identical-looking courts age completely differently. Clay swells when it takes on water and shrinks back when it dries, so the ground under a flat slab rises and settles with the seasons. Now add a St. Louis winter, where a slab can cross the freezing line again and again between December and March. Those two forces, together, are what break flatwork.
Which means the boring items on an estimate are the ones worth your attention. Not the color. Not the net. The dirt, the stone, the steel, the joints and the drain. Every one of those is a fair question to put to your concrete contractor, and the answers tell you a lot about who you’re talking to.
### Ask about the sub-base by name
Say it plainly: what depth of compacted aggregate are you putting under my slab, what material, compacted in what lifts, and why that number for this soil? You’re not quizzing anybody. You’re listening for whether there’s a reason behind the spec or just a habit. Ask what happens if they hit soft clay while they’re digging, because on plenty of lots around here, they will.
### Reinforcement and the joint plan
Concrete cracks. That’s a material property, not a defect, and a court is one big uninterrupted plane of the stuff. Control joints decide where those cracks show up. Tooled or saw-cut, laid out on a grid, at spacing tied to the slab thickness. On a sport surface the joint layout is also a play decision, because a joint running straight through the free-throw line is a spot where a hard dribble skips sideways. Ask where the joints will land relative to the key and the arc, and ask about air-entrained mix for freeze-thaw exposure.
### Where the water goes
You’re about to drop a thousand square feet or more of impervious surface into a yard that used to soak up rain. That water still exists. If nobody decided where it goes, it decides on its own, and its favorite destination is usually a foundation. Occasionally it picks the neighbor’s yard, which turns a fun summer project into a conversation nobody wanted.
Answers vary by lot. A consistent pitch across the pad. A trench drain along the low edge. A swale. A dry well. Pipe daylighted somewhere downhill that isn’t someone else’s problem. The specific solution matters less than the fact that somebody chose one on purpose and can point at it on the ground.
### Is asphalt, concrete, or modular tile the right surface?
Concrete for longevity, asphalt for a lower up-front number, modular tile as a layer that sits on top of either one. They aren’t three competing products, which is where the comparison usually goes wrong online. Two are pavements. One is a covering. A lot of good courts are a combination.
### Concrete
Rigid, long-lived, and the default choice for a residential court in this climate when the budget allows. It costs more going in. It holds a true plane better over clay, it doesn’t soften in August heat, and it accepts tile, coating or paint later. The tradeoff: when concrete does fail, it fails visibly and repairs are patches, not invisible fixes. Get the sub-base and the reinforcement right and that day is decades out.
### Asphalt
Flexible pavement, cheaper to install, faster to put down, and genuinely common on outdoor courts. It moves with the ground instead of fighting it, which sounds ideal on clay until you remember that it also softens in summer, requires periodic sealing, and needs a cure period before anything gets coated over it. Budget for maintenance you’ll actually have to do. An asphalt court that never gets sealed ravels at the edges and starts shedding aggregate.
### Acrylic sport coating
This is the cushioned, colored, textured system you see on tennis and pickleball courts, built up in layers over asphalt or concrete. It plays great, it looks finished, and it turns your pad into something that reads as a court rather than a patio with a hoop. It also needs recoating on a cycle, and it telegraphs any crack that opens up underneath it.
### Modular tile over a slab
Interlocking polypropylene tiles snap together over an existing slab, no adhesive, and the good ones are shock-absorbing and drain through. Nice knees. Nice ball bounce. Easy color and line layout, and you can lift a damaged tile out and replace it. The catch is honest: tile is a surface, not a foundation. Lay it over a slab that heaves and you’ll feel the ridge through your shoes within a season or two.
### How big does the pad need to be, and where can it sit?
A regulation NBA court runs 94 by 50 feet. High school is 84 by 50. Nobody is fitting that behind a house in Ballwin. Actual backyard courts are half courts, narrowed half courts, or a key-and-arc shooting pad, and the useful question isn’t how big it can be. It’s what you want to practice on it.
Here’s the dimensional reality, which is the one part of this post that doesn’t vary by contractor. The free-throw line sits 15 feet from the face of the backboard. The high school three-point arc is 19 feet 9 inches from the center of the rim. The NBA arc is 23 feet 9 inches at the top and 22 feet in the corners. Those distances are fixed, so your pad either contains them or it clips them.
A true half court is 47 by 50 feet. Plenty of families are thrilled with 30 by 50, which keeps the whole arc and gives up the sidelines. A 30 by 30 pad holds the key, the free-throw line and the top of a high school arc with almost nothing to spare, and the corner three disappears entirely. A 20 by 25 pad is a shooting station, and that is a completely legitimate thing to build.
Placement is its own puzzle. Property lines and easements first, then the septic field or lateral lines if you’re on one, then utilities, which must be located before anybody puts a blade in the ground. Watch the trees: roots under a slab are a future crack, and a court under heavy shade stays wet, grows algae and gets slick. Note where your downspouts discharge. Think about which neighbor’s bedroom window faces the spot you want to light. A new-build lot in Wentzville with a flat half acre is a different conversation from a sloped lot with a mature oak in the only open corner.
One more overlap worth catching early. If the flattest part of your lot is also where a future garage or addition would go, price the two together before you pour, because a slab is an awkward thing to demolish. Our look at what it costs to build a garage in St. Louis is a useful comparison if you’re weighing which project takes the good ground.
### What the next owner sees
A court is a taste amenity, and that cuts both ways. A well-built pad with a clean surface, straight joints, a hoop that still adjusts and water that clearly goes somewhere reads as a feature. Some buyers will love it outright. Others see a pad they can turn into a patio, a shop floor or a pickleball setup, which still counts as flexible square footage rather than a liability.
The other version is a cracked, weed-seamed slab with a rusted goal leaning over it and a green stripe where runoff crosses it. That’s not neutral. That’s a removal estimate in the buyer’s head, and demolition and haul-off of reinforced concrete isn’t cheap. Build it well or build it smaller. A modest pad done right ages better than an ambitious one done thin.
### Do you need a permit, and who else gets a say?
Depends entirely on where you live, and this metro is a patchwork of dozens of jurisdictions that don’t agree with each other. Whether a slab, a hoop footing, a fence or a light pole triggers a permit is set by your specific municipality, or by the county if you’re in an unincorporated area. Rules differ on impervious surface coverage, setbacks, fence height and electrical work.
Call your own city or county building department before you spend a dollar. Ask about the slab, the footing, the fence and any wiring as four separate questions, because the answer can be different for each. Ask about impervious coverage limits by name. Get whoever answers to tell you what drawing or site plan they want to see.
Then read your subdivision indentures, because in a lot of St. Louis neighborhoods the trustees are the stricter authority. HOA and subdivision covenants routinely regulate permanent structures, fence type and color, lighting, and sometimes the hoop itself. A project that sails through city review can still get stopped by a covenant from 1978. Better to find that out on a phone call than after the forms are set.
### What do the hoop, the footing, the fence and the lights add?
A real in-ground goal is a small foundation project of its own. The pole sits in a footing, or in an anchor sleeve set in a footing, dug below the local frost depth so seasonal freezing doesn’t heave it out of plumb. That footing usually gets poured before or separately from the slab, with an isolation joint around the pole so slab movement doesn’t torque it.
Ask about extension and backboard while you’re at it. The distance the backboard hangs out past the pole is what keeps a driving player from meeting steel, and the wider, thicker boards behave much better than the budget ones. Height adjustment is worth paying for if you have a seven-year-old, because a rim they can reach is a rim they use.
Fencing is the sleeper cost. Ball containment on the open sides saves you fifty trips into the neighbor’s hostas, and a half-height fence behind the baseline does most of the work of a full one for much less. Rebound netting on posts is a lighter, cheaper option that plenty of families prefer. Lighting means a trench, conduit, a licensed electrician and a real conversation about glare direction and hours. Lines can be painted on, inlaid in a coating system, or laid out in contrasting tile, and that choice is mostly about how permanent you want them.
Feeding the crew after? Try what to order at an Armenian restaurant.
### How do you pick someone to pour it?
Shortlist two or three contractors worth interviewing, then interview them. Not a bid-collecting exercise. An actual conversation in the yard, where you state plainly what you want and expect: this slab thickness, this reinforcement, a joint plan that keeps cuts out of the key, and a drainage solution you can point to on the ground.
Then compare what you asked for against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal. Not the price. One contractor tells you why they want more stone than you expected on your particular soil, walks the low corner with you, and explains what they’ll do if they hit soft clay at eighteen inches. Another says concrete is concrete. You just learned something more useful than a number.
Look at their flatwork, in person, on jobs that have been through at least a couple of winters. Fresh concrete always looks good. Four-year-old concrete tells the truth. Ask who actually runs the crew and who’s finishing the surface. Confirm insurance. Our guide to how to hire a concrete contractor in St. Louis goes deeper on the vetting, and it applies to a court exactly the way it applies to a patio.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a permit to build a basketball court?
A.  Maybe, and only your jurisdiction can tell you. Requirements for a slab, a hoop footing, a fence and any lighting are set municipality by municipality, or by the county in unincorporated areas, and this metro has dozens of them. Call your own building department first, then check your subdivision indentures, because trustees and HOA covenants are often the stricter constraint.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to build a basketball court?
A.  Build less court. A key-and-arc shooting pad on the flattest part of your yard, bare broom-finished concrete or asphalt, painted lines, and one adjustable goal covers most of what a family actually uses. Skip the fence, the lights and the tile at first. Do not economize on excavation, sub-base or reinforcement, since those are the items that decide whether you pay twice.
### Q. Is asphalt or concrete better for a basketball court?
A.  Concrete generally lasts longer and holds a truer plane, which matters on expansive clay and through freeze-thaw winters. Asphalt costs less going in, flexes with ground movement, and needs periodic sealing plus a cure period before coating. Both work outdoors. Concrete is the more common residential choice here when the budget allows it.
### Q. Does a basketball court add value to a home?
A.  It’s a taste amenity, not a guaranteed return. A sound, well-drained pad with a clean surface appeals to some buyers and reads as flexible space to others, since it converts to a patio or pickleball court easily. A cracked slab with a rusting goal works against you, because the buyer is mentally pricing demolition and haul-off.
### Q. How much does it cost to pour a concrete slab for a basketball court?
A.  It varies by yard and by contractor, so treat any figure online as orientation only. The drivers are square footage, how much cut and fill your lot needs, sub-base depth, slab thickness, whether you use mesh or rebar, truck access, and drainage work. Get two or three quotes from people who have walked the actual site.
### Q. Is 30x30 big enough for a basketball court?
A.  Big enough to play on, not a regulation half court. A real half court is 47 by 50 feet. On 30 by 30 you fit the key, the free-throw line 15 feet off the backboard, and the top of a high school arc at 19 feet 9 inches with very little margin. Corner threes and sideline play are gone.
### Q. How thick should a backyard basketball court slab be?
A.  That’s a spec your contractor should set for your soil, your sub-base and your drainage, not a number to copy from a forum. What you can do is ask for the reasoning and ask about reinforcement in the same breath, since thickness, steel type and joint spacing work together. Rebar on chairs outperforms mesh laid flat over moving clay.
### Q. Can you put modular tile over an existing driveway or patio?
A.  Often yes, if the slab is sound, reasonably flat and drains. Tile is a surface layer, so it inherits whatever is beneath it. Check for heaved joints, active cracks and low spots that hold water, and remember that a sloped driveway still plays like a sloped driveway once the tile is down. Fix the base before you cover it.

## What a Gift Basket Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-gift-basket-costs-in-st-louis
The basket lands on a kitchen counter in University City. Cellophane off. Ribbon set aside, because it’s genuinely nice ribbon. Then the digging starts, and it keeps going, because there are a good six inches of crinkled paper shred between the top of the basket and anything a person can actually eat. Three small jars. A sleeve of crackers. One chocolate bar. That’s the haul, and roughly half the volume of the gift is already in the trash bag before anybody has said thank you.
Different room, same arithmetic. Someone in Clayton builds an online cart for her sister two time zones away, picks the medium size, feels good about the choice, and then reaches the shipping step. The box gets weighed. Jars are heavy. Cellophane turns a modest gift into something wide and tall, and wide and tall is exactly what carriers price on. The number she agreed to at the top of the page is not the number at the bottom.
This guide is about the invoice, not the contents. Where your money actually goes, which parts of the bill you can move, and why a good basket feels so expensive relative to what comes out of it. If what you need is help deciding what belongs inside, our companion piece on St. Louis gift baskets and what to put inside covers that end of it. This one is the money question and nothing else.
### What is the average cost of a gift basket?
There isn’t a single useful average, and any one number you see quoted hides more than it tells you. A gift basket isn’t a product with a spec sheet. It’s a container plus whatever somebody decided to put in it, wrapped in whatever they decided to wrap it in.
The price tracks four separate things, and they move independently of each other. The contents. The packaging shell around the contents. The labor to build the thing. And how it gets from the maker’s table to the recipient’s hands. A basket built around one bottle and two small-batch items costs what those items cost, plus the shell. That same basket shipped three states away in the second week of December costs meaningfully more than the identical basket handed across a porch in Maplewood on a slow Tuesday.
Ranges exist, sure. They vary so widely by maker, by contents and by season that quoting one would mislead you more than help you. Local makers buy at different volumes, pay different rent, and source from different suppliers. A basket heavy on food costs differently than one heavy on ceramics. What you want from a maker isn’t an average and it isn’t a line-by-line receipt. It’s tiers. Ask what a small, a middle and a generous version of your idea would each look like at their prices, then compare the three.
### Where does the money in a gift basket actually go?
Into more places than most buyers expect. Peel the bill apart and you get seven lines: the container, the filler, the outer wrap, the ribbon, the card, the assembly time, and finally the contents. Delivery sits outside all of that as its own animal. Here’s what each one is quietly doing to your total.
### The container
Containers span an enormous cost range and the recipient notices every dollar of it. A thin woven basket from a craft-store shelf sheds fibers, flexes when lifted, and reads exactly as cheap as it was. A wood crate, a solid metal tin, a ceramic bowl, a canvas tote, a sturdy shallow tray: all of those cost more, and all of them get kept. That’s the trade. Money spent on a container the recipient reuses isn’t really packaging money at all. It’s a gift they happen to be carrying the rest of the gift in.
### The shred nobody asked for
Filler is the cheapest line per unit and one of the most expensive lines by consequence. Its actual job is honest enough: hold items upright, keep glass from knocking, and fill the empty space so the basket looks full from above. The problem is what it does to everything else. Deep filler requires a bigger container. A bigger container requires more wrap, a longer ribbon, and a bigger shipping box. You pay for the shred once, then you pay for the shred again in every other line it inflates.
### Wrap, ribbon and the card
Cellophane or a shrink bag is cheap material and slow labor, since somebody has to cut it, gather it, tie it and shrink it without scorching anything. A rigid box costs more up front and survives a truck, which matters later. Ribbon is where the math gets interesting. Wide fabric ribbon is the single most visible dollar in the whole build, and thin curling ribbon undoes a basket’s entire impression in about two seconds. A printed card and a tag cost almost nothing and carry a surprising amount of the perceived value.
### The hour you don’t see
Assembly takes far longer than anyone guesses who hasn’t done it. Sourcing, checking dates on food items, wiping the container, cutting wrap to size, staging the items so nothing hides behind anything else, tying a bow that actually reads right, hand-writing the card, then repacking the whole thing for transit. Multiply that by a rush of twelve baskets in one afternoon. A maker who doesn’t charge for that time isn’t giving you a deal, they’re quietly paying for the privilege of working, and they won’t be answering the phone next December.
### Why does so much of the price sit in the packaging?
Because presentation is most of what a basket sells. A pile of the same items in a grocery bag is a favor. The same items staged, wrapped and tied is a gift, and the staging costs real money. This is the central insight of the whole bill: a meaningful share of what you pay is the part that gets thrown away within ten minutes of arrival.
That share is a dial, not a fixed setting. It’s the number you have the most control over, and almost nobody asks about it. People do ask what makes a cheap filler, and the usual answers are shredded kraft paper, tissue, clean butcher paper, or a tea towel folded into the base. Fine. The genuinely cheap filler, though, is less basket. Drop to a shallower container and the shred problem solves itself, because there’s no cavern left to fill.
Want the thing to look more expensive without spending more? Go shorter and wider instead of deep. Pick one tall anchor item so the eye has somewhere to land. Keep the colors talking to each other rather than fighting. Spend on wide fabric ribbon and on a container that gets kept, skip the cellophane entirely, and let the items sit visible and snug. Three items filling a small tray honestly beats six items rattling around in a big one. The second version costs more and looks worse.
The same logic runs the inexpensive end. A budget basket doesn’t mean more small things, it means a smaller, better-fitting shell around fewer good things. And here’s the judgment call underneath all of it, offered as judgment and not as a statistic: the same money spent on fewer, better items beats that money spread thin across filler, every time. Nobody remembers the tenth sachet of cocoa. They remember the one thing they actually used, and they remember who sent it.
Which is also why locally made contents tend to earn their higher per-item cost. A jar with a story attached does work that three anonymous jars can’t, and our rundown of St. Louis gifts that are actually from here is a decent place to see which local items carry that weight. Same principle for a kid’s basket, where one real toy usually outperforms a handful of trinkets. Our guide to where to buy toys in St. Louis besides Target covers the sourcing side of that decision.
### How do delivery and shipping change the total?
This is usually the line that stops people cold, and it’s the one nobody budgets for. Getting a basket into someone’s hands is a separate business from building it, priced separately, and the gap between local delivery and out-of-state shipping is much wider than the gap between a modest basket and a nice one.
### Hand delivery inside the metro
Local delivery is a person, a car, fuel, and a block of time that can’t be spent building anything else. Makers price it as a flat zone fee, a mileage charge, or they fold it in and set a minimum order. One stop in Clayton on a route that already has three other stops is cheap. One stop on the far edge of the metro, at a specific hour, with a signature required, is not. Ask how a maker prices distance before you fall in love with a design.
### Shipping a heavy box out of state
Here’s where the total can jump past anything you predicted. Carriers price on weight and on dimensions, whichever hurts more, and a cellophane-wrapped basket is mostly air inside a large box. Glass and jars pile on weight. Anything perishable needs cold packs and faster service, and both cost. Fragile items want cushioning, sometimes a second box around the first. Then add the box itself, the void fill, the tape and the label. Shipping a big basket a long way can genuinely approach what’s inside it, and in peak December weeks it gets worse.
### How to shrink that line
Four moves, all of them real. Send a rigid, tightly packed box instead of a wrapped basket, because dimensions are what’s killing you. Pull the single heaviest item and replace it with something light and better. Skip perishables for a long shipment entirely. Or have the gift built by a maker near the recipient and skip the freight altogether, which is unglamorous and often the smartest thing on the list. Decide shipping before you design the basket, not after.
Buying for a practical person? See what army navy surplus stores sell.
### What do corporate gifting budgets look like per recipient?
They’re set by policy and by tier, not by any market average. A company decides what a client at one level is worth, what a staff thank-you is worth, and what the total program can absorb. Then the per-recipient number falls out of that arithmetic. Nobody is consulting an industry figure.
A handful of things usually drive the number. Headcount, obviously, since a list of fifteen and a list of four hundred are different problems. The recipient’s own employer matters too, because plenty of organizations cap what their people are allowed to accept, and a gift over that cap creates a small crisis instead of goodwill. Whether shipping comes out of the same budget or a different one changes the contents dramatically. Branding adds cost. And timing does real damage, since everyone wants the same two weeks in December.
If you’re the one buying for a company, the useful approach is to hand a maker three things: the per-recipient number, the headcount, and how the gifts travel. Then let them design to it. Most will build you a good tier, a better tier and a top tier for the handful of relationships that warrant it. That conversation goes far better than asking what a corporate basket costs, which has no answer.
### What a maker has to charge to stay in business
More than buyers assume, and for reasons that have nothing to do with greed. A basket maker’s price has to clear six things before a single dollar is profit, and if any one of them goes uncounted, the business is running on borrowed time and the owner usually finds out in January.
Cost of goods first, at whatever wholesale or retail they can actually get. Packaging second: container, filler, wrap, ribbon, card, tape, box. Then assembly time, paid as real time at a real rate, not treated as a hobby. Then delivery or shipping. Then overhead, which is the invisible one: storage space, insurance, business licensing, payment processing fees, a website, market or booth fees, and the shelf of leftover inventory from a design that didn’t sell. And then waste, which is spoilage, breakage, and the occasional basket that has to be rebuilt.
Margin comes after all six. Not a multiple somebody read on a forum, just the amount that keeps the lights on and allows for a slow month. The reason two quotes for the same idea can land far apart is rarely that one maker is gouging you. It’s that one of them counted their own hours and the other didn’t.
### How should you shortlist a basket maker?
Interview two or three, and lead with your budget instead of asking for a catalog. A catalog tells you what somebody already built for a stranger. A number and a recipient tells them what to build for you, and what comes back is far more informative than any price list.
Say it plainly: here’s my number, here’s who it’s for, here’s where it’s going, here’s when. One maker will ask what the person actually likes, tell you honestly that shipping will eat a third of your budget and suggest a lighter design, then offer you two tiers. Another will send a stock photo. The gap between those two replies is the signal, not the price. Don’t ask anyone for a line-by-line cost breakdown, by the way. No small maker will produce one, and asking mostly tells them you haven’t done this before.
Ask by tier instead. What does a modest version of this look like, what does the middle look like, what does generous look like, and what changes between them? Then watch where each maker spends the extra money as the tier climbs. If it goes into better contents, you’ve found someone thinking about the recipient. If it all goes into a bigger shell and deeper shred, you’ve learned that too.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should you spend on a gift basket?
A.  Set the number by the relationship and the occasion, then protect it from the packaging. A useful habit is deciding your total first, subtracting delivery or shipping, and treating what’s left as the real contents budget. If that remainder looks thin, shrink the container rather than adding small filler items. Fewer good things in a smaller shell lands better than a big basket stretched thin.
### Q. Why are gift baskets so expensive?
A.  Because you’re paying for seven things, not one. Container, filler, outer wrap, ribbon, card, assembly labor and contents, plus delivery on top. A large share of that goes to presentation, which is the part discarded on arrival. Add a maker’s overhead, spoilage and breakage, and the price of a nice basket stops looking unreasonable, even though it still stings.
### Q. How to calculate the cost of a basket?
A.  Add the contents at what you actually paid, then every piece of packaging including tape and the shipping box. Add your assembly time at a rate you’d accept from an employer. Add delivery or freight. Add a slice for overhead and waste. That figure is your cost, not your price, and knowing it is what lets you spot which line is out of proportion.
### Q. What are the shipping fees for gift basket delivery?
A.  They depend on weight, box dimensions, distance, speed and whether anything inside is perishable, so no fixed figure applies. Cellophane-wrapped baskets ship badly because dimensions often cost more than weight. Local hand delivery inside the metro is usually a flat zone or mileage fee. Long-distance shipping of a heavy basket is the line that shocks people most, especially in December.
### Q. How much should you charge for a gift basket?
A.  Enough to cover cost of goods, every packaging component, your assembly time paid as real time, delivery, overhead like insurance and processing fees, expected spoilage and breakage, and then a margin that survives a slow month. Avoid copying someone else’s markup formula. Build your own number from your own costs, then check it against what your market will actually pay.
### Q. How much do companies spend on corporate gifting?
A.  It’s set by internal policy and recipient tier rather than by any market average. The per-recipient number is usually driven by headcount, the relationship’s value, whether the recipient’s employer caps what staff may accept, whether shipping comes from the same budget, and whether branding is required. Give a maker the per-recipient number and the headcount, and ask them to design tiers to it.
### Q. Is it cheaper to make a gift basket yourself?
A.  Usually yes on materials, rarely by as much as expected, and never on time. Retail buying means you pay retail on every item and on the packaging, and you’ll likely overbuy shred and ribbon. Where you genuinely save is labor, because you’re donating it. Where you genuinely lose is shipping, since a home-wrapped basket tends to be bulkier and more fragile than a professionally packed box.
### Q. Does a bigger basket mean a better gift?
A.  No, and size is where most gift budgets go to die. A larger container needs deeper filler, more wrap, longer ribbon and a bigger shipping box, so it converts your money into volume rather than into anything the recipient keeps. A small tray holding three things they’ll actually use reads more generous than a wide basket holding nine things they won’t.

## Where to Find a Beach Near St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-find-a-beach-near-st-louis
The cooler is in the trunk, towels piled on top of it, and nobody in the car has decided where you are going. Two kids in the back. Halfway across a bridge one of them asks why you can see that much water and still not get in it. Fair question. The answer takes longer than the bridge does.
That gap catches families out here every June. St. Louis sits where two enormous rivers meet, and those rivers are the one kind of water in the region that is genuinely off-limits. The places with sand, a buoy line and somebody watching the water are almost never the water you drove past on the way there.
Here is the order that actually works. Decide what kind of water day you want. Set a drive time you can live with on the way home, wet. Check the water and the calendar the morning of. Then pack for the rules you will meet at the gate, because those rules differ park to park, and a chain across an entrance ends a Saturday fast.
### Where is the closest beach to St. Louis, MO?
The closest real swimming beaches to St. Louis are inland lake and park swim areas, mostly state park and county park beaches in Missouri and Illinois within an easy drive. Ocean sand is a day-plus drive away. The big rivers are not swimming water at any distance.
Practically, that means one of a few kinds of place. Missouri and Illinois state parks operate designated swimming beaches on lakes. County park systems on both sides of the river do the same. Campgrounds with a lake, membership lake clubs, and quarry swim parks sell day passes to people who are neither members nor campers.
“Where can I swim in Missouri?” is the search most people run, and the honest answer is a list of designated swim areas rather than a list of lakes. The lake is not the permission. The marked rectangle inside the lake is.
Which one is closest depends entirely on which edge of the metro you start from, and that is not a dodge. A family in Chesterfield and a family in O’Fallon get pointed at different water by simple geography, and both have a shorter drive than somebody leaving from downtown. Put the drive-time filter on a map first. Then start reading what each operator posts about its own swim area.
Ocean sand is a different trip entirely. Every coastline sits a day-plus drive from here in any direction, which makes it a vacation with a hotel night in it rather than a Saturday. Worth knowing before you promise a six-year-old a beach.
### What counts as a beach in a river metro?
A marked swim area. That is the whole definition, and it is more useful than it sounds. At most inland lakes around here, swimming is legal only inside a roped or buoyed rectangle and prohibited everywhere else on the water, including the shoreline twenty feet past the last buoy.
The sand is usually imported. Somebody hauled it in, graded it, and rakes it a few times a season. The bottom slopes off faster than a pool does, and it changes shape across a summer as water levels move. None of that makes it a bad place to swim. It means the water is not a pool and should not be treated like one.
Lifeguards are the variable people get wrong most often. Plenty of designated swim beaches in this region are posted swim at your own risk, with no guard on duty at any hour, and the sign at the entrance is the only notice you get. Larger operations sometimes staff guards during peak weeks only. Ask, or read the operator page, before you decide how closely you need to watch.
### State park and county park lake beaches
These are the backbone of swimming near St. Louis. Missouri state parks are run by the Missouri Department of Natural Resources, Illinois state parks by the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, and county systems in both states run their own sites. Expect day-use parking, a changing house, restrooms, sometimes a concession stand, and a swim area that opens and closes on a posted seasonal schedule.
### Campgrounds, lake clubs and quarry swim parks
Private operators fill in the rest of the map, and a lot of them sell day passes to non-members. A campground lake with a small beach. A membership club that opens to guests on weekdays. A worked-out quarry turned into a swim park with a gate and a fee. Rules here belong to the operator and can be stricter than a state park’s. Call first.
### Pools and water parks, the honest fallback
When an advisory closes a beach, or the season has not opened yet, a pool covers the same afternoon without the water-quality question hanging over it. Municipal outdoor pools, aquatic centers with slides, splash pads. Families who want the option in February look at St. Louis hotels with indoor pools for exactly this reason.
### Why can you see a river and not swim in it?
Because the Mississippi, the Missouri and the Meramec are working rivers, not recreation water, and the hazards in them cannot be judged by looking. Public health and park agencies in both states advise against swimming in them. That advice is not overcaution. It is an accurate reading of the risk. Curious what those tows carry, or what actually swims down there? See barges on the Mississippi and what really lives in the river.
Start with traffic. Barges and towboats move through the main channel constantly, they cannot stop, and the wash and draw behind a loaded tow pulls hard enough to move a swimmer well off from where they expected to be. A tow that looks a mile away is closer than it looks and quieter than you expect.
Then the water itself. Current in a big river runs uneven, faster in some lanes than others, and harder below the surface than on top. Bridge piers, wing dams and rock revetments create eddies and downward pull that will take a strong adult under. Add debris nobody can see: logs, rebar, cable, chunks of concrete, sunken hulls and cars. Visibility is close to zero a foot down.
Bacteria is the quieter problem. After heavy rain, runoff and sewer overflow push contamination into the rivers and their tributaries, and levels stay elevated for a day or more. The same thing happens in small creeks, which is why the shallow-looking stretch behind a park in Webster Groves is not the safe substitute it appears to be.
Wading at a boat ramp. Floating a tube near a sandbar. Letting the dog swim out and going after it. Those are the patterns behind most river drownings in this metro, not deliberate swims. Sandbars shift and drop off vertically, sometimes within one step. There is no shallow edge you can trust on a river like this.
### How far should you plan to drive?
Sort your options into drive-time bands before you sort them by anything else. It keeps the day from collapsing on the way home. Under an hour gets you county park and smaller lake swim areas. One to two hours opens up most of the state park beaches on both sides of the river.
### Under an hour
Good for a half day. Leave after breakfast, swim, eat the sandwiches you packed, and get home before the afternoon falls apart. Expect a smaller swim area and a busier one on a hot weekend. Arrive early. Day-use lots at popular sites fill by late morning, and some operators close the gate outright once parking is gone.
### One to two hours
This band is where most of the real beach days live. Bigger lakes, longer sand, more shade, better restrooms, and enough room that a crowded Saturday still works. Budget honestly for the return leg, though. Driving two hours with three sunburned kids and a trunk full of wet towels is not the same drive as the one out.
### Two to four hours and beyond
Now you are into Ozarks country, spring-fed streams and larger reservoirs, and the trip wants an overnight to make any sense. Same for anything further out. The coast is a day-plus in every direction, so treat it as a vacation and price the hotel before anybody starts packing flip-flops.
### How do you check whether the water is safe before you leave?
Two pages and a phone call. Read the operating park’s own page for closures and hours, read the state beach-monitoring page for current advisories, and call if either one looks stale or contradicts the other. Do it the morning you leave. A page updated Tuesday tells you nothing about Saturday water.
### What an advisory actually means
Beach advisories in Missouri and Illinois are usually tied to E. coli counts in samples taken at the swim area. E. coli is mostly a marker: an indicator that fecal contamination reached the water and that other pathogens may have arrived with it. An advisory means counts came back elevated. A closure means the operator shut the swim area. Either one is a reason to pick a different lake.
### The rain rule
Treat the 48 hours after a hard rain as suspect everywhere, whatever any page says. Runoff carries manure, pet waste, septic seepage and street pollution into lakes, and bacteria counts commonly spike right after a storm. Sampling lags behind the weather. The lab result posted online may predate the rain that changed the water. Poured Friday night? Sunday is the better swim.
### What to look at once you arrive
Look before anybody gets in. Water the color of chocolate milk, a sheen on the surface, a strong smell, foam collecting along the shoreline, mats of bright green or blue-green algae, dead fish on the sand. Any one of those is a turn-around, advisory or not. Harmful algal blooms sicken people and kill dogs, and they can show up between one sample and the next.
### What are the rules and fees like at public swim areas?
They vary more than people expect, park to park and even between areas inside a single park. Missouri state parks publish their regulations through the Missouri Department of Natural Resources, Illinois through the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, and county and private operators post their own. Read the specific one. A blog, this one included, is not the authority on a gate policy.
Fees follow a few patterns. Many Missouri state parks charge nothing for day-use entry and take their money on camping, showers and shelter reservations instead. Illinois state parks and some county systems charge per vehicle or per person at certain sites. Private swim parks, quarry beaches and lake clubs run on day passes, which often cost more on weekends and sometimes sell out. Cash-only gates still exist.
### Rules that catch families out
Glass containers are banned at a lot of swim beaches, which means the drinks and the condiments both need rethinking. Alcohol policy varies by park and by area within a park, and swim beaches in particular often restrict or prohibit it. Pets are commonly barred from the sand even where they are welcome on the trails. Inflatables and rafts are allowed at some swim areas, restricted at others. Swimming outside the marked area is prohibited nearly everywhere.
Off-season project? Here is what it costs to build an app.
### What should a family pack and plan for?
Pack for the two things a lake does that a pool does not: the bottom disappears, and nobody is necessarily watching. So, Coast Guard approved life jackets for weak swimmers, water shoes for rocks and mussel shells, and one adult assigned to watch the water with nothing else to do.
Life jackets, specifically. Water wings, noodles and inflatable rings are toys, and they slip or deflate without warning. A properly fitted life jacket does not. Plenty of lake swim areas keep a free loaner board at the beach, which is worth checking before you buy. If your kid sits between lessons and confidence, the jacket goes on. Our guide to when to start swim lessons in St. Louis covers the timing side of that.
The rest of the bag: drinking water, more than you think, because a hot beach dehydrates fast. Shade, since most lake beaches have almost none past mid-morning. Sunscreen reapplied after every swim. A zip bag for phones and keys. A trash bag, because pack-in pack-out is the standing rule at a lot of day-use areas. Snacks that survive melted ice. And a full change of clothes each, which sounds obvious until the drive home.
Two habits worth building. Walk the swim area yourself first, find where the bottom drops away, then show the kids exactly where that line sits. And count heads out loud on a fixed interval, every few minutes, all day. A busy beach is loud, and a child in trouble in the water is silent. If the suit situation is what is holding the trip up, finding a swimsuit that fits in St. Louis is its own small project.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I swim for free in St. Louis?
A.  Free public swimming in the city and county generally means municipal outdoor pools and spray grounds run by parks departments, not open water. Residency rules, hours and season dates vary by municipality, so a pool that is free for a Webster Groves resident may charge somebody driving in from Chesterfield. Check your own city or county parks department for its current schedule and fees.
### Q. Are Missouri lakes safe to swim in?
A.  Inside a designated swim area, usually yes, with two conditions. Check the operator’s page and the state beach-monitoring page for a current advisory, and stay out for roughly 48 hours after heavy rain, when bacteria counts commonly spike. Outside the marked area, swimming is prohibited at most lakes for real reasons: boat traffic, sudden depth changes and submerged debris.
### Q. Are there any natural springs in Missouri that are safe to swim in?
A.  Missouri has thousands of springs, and some feed streams inside state parks where a designated swimming area exists. Many spring branches themselves are protected and closed to swimming. Spring water also runs cold year-round, cold enough to cause gasping and cold-water shock. Rules differ site to site, so confirm with the Missouri Department of Natural Resources or the managing agency before you get in.
### Q. Is the Missouri River clean to swim in?
A.  No, and cleanliness is not even the main reason. The Missouri is a working navigation river: strong uneven current, undertow around wing dams and structures, barge traffic that cannot stop, submerged debris nobody can see. Bacteria levels also climb sharply after rain. Health and park agencies advise against swimming in it. Use a designated swim area instead.
### Q. Can you drink alcohol in Missouri State Parks?
A.  Policy varies by park and by area within a park, so there is no single yes or no. Swim beaches and some day-use areas commonly restrict or prohibit alcohol, and glass containers are frequently banned regardless. Check that specific park’s regulations with the Missouri Department of Natural Resources before you pack a cooler, because staff at the gate enforce their park’s rule, not a general one.
### Q. How can I tell if water is safe to swim in?
A.  Combine three checks. Read the operating park’s page for closures, read the state beach-monitoring page for advisories tied to E. coli counts, and look hard at the water once you arrive. Turn around for a chocolate-milk color, a surface sheen, strong odor, shoreline foam, bright green algae mats or dead fish. And skip the first 48 hours after a hard rain.
### Q. Do swim beaches near St. Louis have lifeguards?
A.  Many do not. A large share of designated swim areas at state, county and private lakes are posted swim at your own risk with no guard on duty, and that status can change mid-season with staffing. Assume no lifeguard unless the operator says otherwise in writing, then put one adult on water-watch duty with no phone in their hand.
### Q. When does swim beach season start and end around St. Louis?
A.  Most operators run a summer season that opens in late spring and closes in early fall, with exact dates set by the park and often driven by staffing rather than weather. The shoulder weeks are unpredictable. A warm May afternoon in O’Fallon does not mean a gate an hour away is open, so confirm the current schedule on the operator’s page before you load the car.

## What to Expect at a Bed and Breakfast in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-at-a-bed-and-breakfast-in-st-louis
The porch light is on. It’s 11:40 at night, your connecting flight sat on a taxiway for two hours, and the house in front of you has no lobby, no night clerk and no revolving door. What it has is a lockbox, a code somebody texted you at four in the afternoon, and a handwritten note taped inside the storm door with your name on it.
That thirty seconds on a dark sidewalk is the whole difference between a bed and breakfast and a hotel. A B&B is somebody’s building, run by one or two people, usually with a small number of guest rooms. Things a chain absorbs quietly behind a desk, a late arrival, a missed breakfast, a peanut allergy, a second parking space, get arranged with an actual person ahead of time.
Handle that part well and the format is hard to beat. Handle it badly and you’ll spend a weekend feeling like a guest in a stranger’s home, which, technically, you are. Here is what the stay actually involves in St. Louis: what’s in the rate, what the house expects from you, how breakfast runs, what tipping looks like, what moves the price against a hotel, and who should book something else entirely.
### What does bed and breakfast usually include?
A bed and breakfast stay usually includes a private guest room, a cooked breakfast the next morning, and use of shared spaces like a parlor or porch. Wi-Fi, linens and coffee are standard. Parking, a private bathroom and evening snacks vary by house, so confirm them when you book rather than assuming.
The word “included” carries more weight here than it does at a chain. A hotel sells you a room, then sells you breakfast, then sells you the garage, then adds a fee with a name nobody can explain. Small inns tend to bundle instead, because bundling is how two people run a building without maintaining a menu of add-on charges. That bundle is the real product.
### What is nearly always in the rate
The room, the bed made up, towels, soap and the morning meal. Coffee and tea, often available well before breakfast service starts. Wi-Fi. Run of the common rooms, which at an older St. Louis property might mean a front parlor, a dining room with one long table, a back porch and a small yard. Many houses also keep a guest refrigerator, a bowl of fruit or an afternoon plate of something baked.
### What changes from house to house
Bathrooms first. Most rooms in restored city houses have their own bath now, but shared or hall baths still exist and the rate usually reflects it. Parking is the second question, and in older neighborhoods it can mean a small pad behind the building, a permit sticker, or street parking you fight for on event nights. After that: air conditioning that might be window units, a television or deliberately none, stairs with no elevator, pet policies, child policies, and whether a third person can sleep in the room at all.
Ask about all of it in writing. A house that answers plainly is telling you something about how the rest of the stay will go.
### What is a typical breakfast at a bed and breakfast?
A typical B&B breakfast is a cooked, sit-down meal served during a set window, not a buffet that runs all morning. Expect a hot main course, fruit, baked goods, coffee and juice, usually one menu for everybody that day. Dietary needs are commonly accommodated with advance notice, rarely on the spot.
Timing is the part guests underestimate. Service might run from eight to nine thirty, full stop, because one person is cooking, plating and clearing it. Show up at 9:45 and you have missed it. Some innkeepers will leave a plate, a continental spread or a bag to take with you if you say the night before that you have an early start. Say it the night before.
### Communal table or your own?
Both formats are common. A single long table means conversation with strangers over eggs, which some travelers love and others dread. Separate two-tops mean you can read your phone in peace. Neither is better. It is worth asking which one a house runs, especially if you are traveling for work and want thirty quiet minutes before a meeting.
### Allergies, diets and the honest ask
Tell them when you reserve, then again two days out. A small kitchen shops for the guests it has, so a gluten-free or vegan breakfast is usually a yes with lead time and a no at the table. Severe allergies deserve a direct conversation about shared pans and shared surfaces. If you would rather eat out anyway, our local guide to breakfast and brunch in St. Louis covers the rooms worth walking to.
### What are the rules for a bed and breakfast?
House rules at a B&B typically cover check-in windows, quiet hours, smoking, shoes, outside visitors, kitchen access and cancellation terms. They exist because guests share walls, stairs and a dining room with each other and often with the owners. Most are posted at booking and repeated on a card at arrival.
None of this is fussiness. An 1890s house transmits sound through the floor joists like a drum, so a 1 a.m. return that nobody flagged wakes three rooms and the innkeeper. The rules are mostly a translation of that physical reality into sentences.
### Check-in windows and keys
There is no 24-hour desk. Arrival is usually a window, often late afternoon into early evening, because somebody has to be there to hand you a key and show you where things are. Late arrivals are normally fine when arranged, through a lockbox, a keypad or a text when you land. Arrive unannounced at midnight and you may stand on a porch. Keys are frequently real brass keys, one per room, and losing one can mean a rekeying charge.
### Quiet hours, guests and the rest
Quiet hours in the common rooms are close to universal. Smoking indoors is banned almost everywhere, including vapes, and outdoor smoking may be restricted to one spot. Bringing a non-registered visitor upstairs is often prohibited outright. Kitchens are working kitchens, not guest kitchens, unless you are told otherwise. Cancellation terms tend to be stricter than a hotel’s, sometimes a week or more, because one empty room out of six is a real hit to the night.
### What are the shared spaces actually like?
Shared space is the trade at the center of this format. You give up the anonymity of a hallway and get a parlor, a porch, a yard and a dining room that would cost a fortune to rent. Most guests find the exchange worth it. Some do not, and that’s worth knowing about yourself before you book.
Practically, it means you will meet people. The couple on the second floor in town for a wedding. A traveling nurse on a thirteen-week contract. Someone house-hunting in Maplewood Park who needed a month of mornings in a real neighborhood rather than a room off an interstate. Conversation is optional at most houses, but proximity isn’t.
It also means the innkeeper is a resource a front desk can’t match. They know which block is torn up this week, which restaurant stops seating at nine, and how long it really takes to get to a game. Guests planning a ballpark weekend often compare the inn against hotels close to Busch Stadium and end up choosing on walkability rather than price.
Hosting the party instead? Here is how to hire a bartender.
### What moves the price against a hotel?
Compare all-in nightly totals, not headline rates. A B&B rate normally carries breakfast and often parking inside it, while a hotel rate frequently doesn’t, so the two numbers on a search page are not measuring the same thing. Lodging taxes apply to both. The gap narrows or flips once you add what each night actually costs you.
We won’t quote you a nightly number, because any figure printed today is wrong by next season and wrong across the street. What’s stable is the list of things that move it.
### The levers that raise a rate
Room tier, first. A suite with a fireplace, a soaking tub or a private entrance sits well above a small room under the eaves in the same house. Then the calendar: big weekends in St. Louis, home stands, marathons, graduations and holidays, push rates up and frequently trigger a two-night minimum. Weekends cost more than weeknights nearly everywhere. Peak fall color and spring travel behave like holidays.
### Where the savings hide
Breakfast for two, every morning, is real money against a restaurant bill. Parking included is real money downtown. No resort fee, no destination fee, no charge for the coffee. Weeknight and extended-stay rates at small inns can drop sharply, and long-stay guests sometimes negotiate directly in a way no chain allows. Ask about a weekly rate if you need one.
### How does tipping work at a small inn?
Tipping at a B&B is customary but not required, and the deciding factor is who owns the place. Owner-innkeepers frequently decline tips or redirect them to staff, since the business is theirs. Where housekeepers, cooks or servers are employed, a modest tip at the end of a stay is the normal practice.
The clean method: one envelope, left at checkout, marked for the house staff. It covers whoever cleaned the room and whoever cooked, without you having to guess at the org chart of a five-room building. Cash reads better than an added line on a card, because card tips may route through the business rather than to a person.
Extras earn their own thank-you. An airport run, a fixed flat tire, a birthday cake produced on two hours’ notice, a bag stored for six hours after checkout. And when an owner waves off cash entirely, the currency they actually want is a specific, named review. Write it. It does more for a six-room house than twenty dollars ever will.
### How should you interview a B&B before you book?
Shortlist two or three houses, then interview them. Say plainly what you need, a 9 p.m. arrival, a gluten-free breakfast, one covered parking spot, a room away from the stairs, and listen to what the innkeeper is prepared to provide. The gap between your list and their answer is the signal. It tells you more than any photo gallery.
A useful call takes six minutes. Ask when check-in closes and what happens if your flight slips. Ask whether the bathroom is private and whether the shower is a tub. Ask where you park, and whether that changes on event nights. Ask what time breakfast starts and ends, and what happens if you have to leave before it. Ask about stairs, about quiet hours, and about the cancellation window in days.
### Read the answers, not just the words
A confident innkeeper answers fast and specifically, including the noes. “No, we can’t do a 6 a.m. breakfast, but I’ll leave you a thermos and a bag” is a better answer than a vague yes. Hesitation on parking usually means parking is genuinely hard. Vagueness about cancellation means read the policy twice.
### Match the house to the trip
A couple driving in from Lake St. Charles for one anniversary night wants a quiet room with a good tub and a late breakfast. A contractor spending five weeks near St. John wants a desk, reliable Wi-Fi, laundry access and nobody talking to him at 7 a.m. Those are different bookings, and the same house rarely does both well. Travelers extending a stay into a river drive can build a second night around the best stops on the Great River Road.
### Who should skip the B&B format?
This format suits fewer people than its fans admit. Skip it if you need late-night staffing, guaranteed accessibility, a gym, room service, points on a loyalty account, or total flexibility to cancel. Old houses and small teams simply can’t provide those things, and no amount of charm substitutes.
Accessibility deserves the bluntest treatment. Many St. Louis B&Bs occupy historic homes with front steps, narrow doorways, no elevator and bathrooms that were carved out of closets in 1985. Some houses have a ground-floor room built for exactly this. Ask for measurements and photos, not reassurance.
Families get a mixed answer too. Plenty of inns welcome kids; plenty quietly don’t, and a few set a minimum age because of the stairs and the shared quiet. Late-shift workers, light sleepers who need a white-noise machine and total darkness, and anyone who wants to check in at 2 a.m. unannounced are better served elsewhere. Redundancy is the other issue: when something breaks in a six-room house, there may be no other room to move you into.
