### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a bistro vs. a brasserie?
A.  A bistro is small and chef-driven, with a short menu that changes and fixed lunch and dinner services. A brasserie is large, runs one long printed menu all day without closing in between, and treats beer as seriously as wine. The menus overlap heavily. Size and hours are the difference you can actually verify.
### Q. What kind of food is served in a brasserie?
A.  Hearty French classics off a long, stable menu. Oysters and shellfish platters, charcuterie and pâté, onion soup, frisée salad, steak frites, roast chicken, mussels with fries, choucroute and sausages carried over from Alsace, croque monsieur, omelets, a whole fish. Dessert runs to crème brûlée, profiteroles and fruit tarts. Beer belongs with all of it.
### Q. Why are French restaurants called brasserie?
A.  Most aren’t. Brasserie names one specific format, and the word means brewery, from brasser, to brew. Places that brewed beer and served food with it kept the name after the brewing stopped. Alsatian families opened them across Paris in the late 1800s, which is why beer, sausages and choucroute still anchor the menu today.
### Q. What is an American brasserie?
A.  A French brasserie adapted to American operations. Same room signatures, same core classics, usually with a longer local beer list, a serious weekend brunch, regional sourcing and bigger portions. The most common divergence is hours: many US versions split lunch and dinner instead of running the kitchen straight through the afternoon.
### Q. What is a casual French eatery called?
A.  Several words, and they aren’t interchangeable. Bistro means a small, casual, chef-led room with a short menu. Brasserie means a large all-day room with a long menu and beer. Café means coffee first and light food second. Bouchon is the Lyon version, meat-heavy and very much its own thing.
### Q. How is brasserie pronounced?
A.  In French it’s roughly brah-suh-REE, three syllables, weight landing on the last one, with a soft s rather than a z sound. Americans commonly say bra-suh-REE or brass-uh-REE and nobody blinks. The plural, brasseries, sounds identical in French. Saying it confidently matters more than saying it perfectly.
### Q. Can you eat at a brasserie in the middle of the afternoon?
A.  At a true brasserie, yes, and that’s the defining feature. The same full menu runs from late morning until late at night with no gap. Plenty of American versions split lunch and dinner, so check the posted hours or call and ask straight out whether the kitchen serves at 3:30 on a weekday.
### Q. Is a brasserie a good choice for a large group?
A.  Usually one of the best in town. Large rooms, light tables designed to push together, staff accustomed to walk-ins, and a menu wide enough that ten people with ten different appetites all find something. Call ahead when you can. Show up anyway when you can’t, because this format absorbs unplanned groups better than nearly any other.

## What to Order at a British Pub in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-a-british-pub-in-st-louis
A slab of battered fish hanging off both ends of the plate, a heap of chips under it, and a small pot of something green that nobody at the table ordered on purpose. That’s the British pub meal most Americans remember. The rest of the menu is where the interesting food hides.
British pub cooking gets flattened here into fish and chips plus a burger. The actual list is longer and a lot stranger. Pies with the gravy built in. Sausages named for the sound they made in a wartime frying pan. A boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and fried. Cheese on toast with a national name attached. Puddings that are not dessert, and one pudding that is made of blood.
None of it is hard to order once the words stop lying to you. That’s the whole job here. A British menu uses plain English to name things an American reader will guess wrong about, and about ten minutes of translation turns a confusing page into an obvious one.
### What is typical British pub food in St. Louis?
Typical British pub food means fish and chips, bangers and mash, meat pies like steak and ale or shepherd’s pie, a full English breakfast, Scotch eggs, and a ploughman’s plate of cheese, bread and pickle. Sunday roast shows up weekly. Cask ale, cider and tea sit alongside it.
Pub is a format, not a cuisine. A public house sells drink first and food second, and the food grew up around that order of business. Small kitchen. Long hours. Dishes that hold well and go out fast. Braises, pies, fried fish, cold plates, a pot of something with mashed potato baked on top. That constraint explains the menu better than any history lesson does. If the line between a pub and a bar still feels blurry, what makes a pub different from a bar lays out the difference.
Around the St. Louis metro, a British-style pub almost always runs two menus stapled into one. Half is genuinely British. The other half exists because a table of six will want wings, a quesadilla and a burger, and no owner wants that argument at seven on a Friday night. Read past the second half.
The British half is where a room shows its hand. A kitchen making its own pie filling, baking Yorkshire puddings to order, and leaving malt vinegar on the table instead of keeping it behind the bar is a kitchen that means it. All three of those are visible from your seat before you order a thing.
### What is the most popular food at a British pub?
Fish and chips, and it isn’t close. Nearly every British pub in America leads with it, and it anchors the menu at home too. Cod or haddock in a beer batter, thick-cut chips, malt vinegar on the side, tartar sauce, and mushy peas if the kitchen cares enough to make them.
The batter is the tell. Beer batter fried properly comes out pale gold and hollow-sounding, and it cracks when your fork goes in rather than bending. Heavy, dark, dense coating usually means the oil was too cool or the fish sat too long under a heat lamp. Ask for it fried to order if the room is slow. Most kitchens will say yes.
Cod gives you big flakes and a mild, clean flavor. Haddock is slightly sweeter and finer-grained, and a lot of British eaters swear by it. Some places offer plaice or pollock. Either of the first two is a safe first order.
### The chips, and what goes on them
Chips are not fries. They’re cut thick, cooked twice, and built to stay soft inside so they can soak up vinegar without collapsing. Skinny, crisp, salted fries are a fine thing and a different thing. A pub serving matchstick fries with its fish has made a choice, and it usually tells you which half of the menu the kitchen actually loves.
Malt vinegar goes on the chips, generously, which surprises first-timers. Salt after. Curry sauce is a legitimate chip-shop tradition, mild and thick and faintly sweet, and it shows up on some American pub menus as a side. Gravy on chips is also real. Nobody in Britain would blink.
### What else sells out first
Bangers and mash runs a steady second: fresh pork sausages, a mound of mashed potato, and onion gravy poured over everything. Pies come next, usually steak and ale or chicken and mushroom, sometimes a shepherd’s pie that is not a pie at all. And on Sundays, the roast. A good Sunday roast is the single best reason to plan around a pub’s schedule rather than your own.
### What do the confusing words on a British pub menu mean?
Six or seven words do almost all the damage. Pudding, chips, crisps, pie, pickle, rarebit and jacket. Each one means something different from what an American reader assumes, and each mistake sends the wrong plate to the table. Learn these and the menu stops being a puzzle.
### Pudding does not mean dessert
Pudding is a category, not a flavor. Yorkshire pudding is a puffed, hollow popover baked in hot beef drippings and served with roast beef and gravy. Black pudding is a sliced blood sausage, dark and mineral and faintly spiced, usually fried for breakfast. White pudding is its milder cousin, made with oatmeal and fat and no blood. Steak and kidney pudding is a savory filling steamed inside a suet crust.
Then there’s sticky toffee pudding, which is a dessert: a dark date sponge drowned in toffee sauce, usually with cream or vanilla ice cream. Spotted dick is a steamed sponge with dried fruit. Both are desserts. The word just refuses to pick a lane.
### Chips, crisps and jacket potatoes
Chips are thick fries. Crisps are what Americans call chips, and they come in flavors that sound made up until you try them: prawn cocktail, salt and vinegar, cheese and onion. A jacket potato is a baked potato, split and loaded, most often with beans and cheese or tuna and sweetcorn. Order one at lunch. It is more satisfying than it sounds.
### Shepherd’s pie is lamb, cottage pie is beef
This one matters. Shepherd’s pie is minced lamb with vegetables under a layer of mashed potato, browned on top. Cottage pie is the same construction with beef. Neither has pastry. If a menu offers shepherd’s pie and the server says it is made with beef, that is a cottage pie wearing a more familiar name, and plenty of American kitchens do exactly that.
Real pies do have pastry. Steak and ale is the workhorse, slow-braised beef in dark gravy under a lid of shortcrust or puff. A proper pie has a bottom crust too, not just a hat. Chicken and mushroom, steak and kidney, and pork pies round out the family. A Cornish pasty is a hand pie, crimped along one edge, filled with beef, potato, onion and swede, which is what the British call a rutabaga.
### Ploughman’s, Scotch eggs and the cold plates
A ploughman’s lunch is a composed cold plate: a wedge of sharp cheddar, crusty bread, butter, pickled onion, and a spoonful of brown pickle, which is a chunky sweet-sour chutney rather than anything resembling a dill spear. Ham, apple slices and a hard-boiled egg often join in. It is widely described as a mid-twentieth-century marketing invention rather than an old farm tradition, so treat the romance with a little salt and enjoy the cheese.
A Scotch egg is a soft or hard-boiled egg wrapped in seasoned sausage meat, breaded and fried. Pork scratchings are fried pork rind, aggressively salty, meant to be eaten standing up with a pint in your other hand.
### Toad in the hole, bubble and squeak, Welsh rarebit
Three names that sound like jokes and describe real food. Toad in the hole is sausages baked into Yorkshire pudding batter, served with onion gravy, and it is the best cold-night order on most British menus. Bubble and squeak is leftover mashed potato and cabbage fried together into a crisp-edged cake, traditionally a Monday dish built from Sunday’s roast. Welsh rarebit is a thick, savory cheese sauce loosened with ale and sharpened with mustard, broiled on toast until it blisters. Not a sandwich. Not grilled cheese. Better than both.
### What’s the difference between a full Irish breakfast and a full English breakfast?
The puddings and the bread. A full Irish usually puts white pudding on the plate next to the black, and it leans on soda bread or a potato farl. A full English leans on toast or fried bread and gives baked beans more prominence. Everything else largely overlaps.
Here is the standard English plate. Two fried eggs. Back bacon, which is cut from the loin and comes out meaty and round rather than as the thin streaky strips Americans grew up on. Pork sausages. Baked beans in a mild tomato sauce, which are not sweet like American baked beans and are much better for it. A grilled tomato half. Mushrooms cooked down in butter. Black pudding. Buttered toast or a slice of fried bread. Sometimes a hash brown, which is a recent and popular intruder. Tea.
Brown sauce goes on it. That is HP or a store-brand equivalent, tangy and fruity and vinegary, and it belongs on the sausage and the bacon. Ketchup on a full English is a live argument in Britain and nobody will stop you.
The Irish plate swaps in soda bread, sometimes adds a boxty or a potato cake, and treats the two puddings as the centerpiece. Scotland does its own version with a tattie scone and sometimes a square sausage. Wales adds laverbread, a seaweed paste cooked with oatmeal, which is genuinely good and almost never shows up here.
One practical note. A full English is a two-hour breakfast and a ruined lunch plan. Order it when the day after has nothing scheduled. If you are hunting for morning food more broadly, how to find good breakfast and brunch in St. Louis covers the wider field.
Different receipt, same homework: what a bike tune-up costs in St. Louis.
### What should you drink with a plate like that?
Cask ale if the pub pulls it, cider if it doesn’t, tea if it is morning. A British pint is 20 imperial fluid ounces, roughly 568 milliliters, which is a fifth larger than the 16-ounce American pint. That difference catches people out by round three.
### Cask ale, and why it is not warm
Cask ale is unfiltered, unpasteurized beer that finishes fermenting in the container it is served from, pulled by a hand pump instead of pushed by gas. That is why it arrives soft and lightly carbonated rather than fizzy. It is served at cellar temperature, meaning cool, not warm and not ice cold. Cold mutes flavor. A bitter served at cellar temperature tastes of bread crust, orchard fruit and dried leaves, and the same beer served at refrigerator temperature tastes of almost nothing.
Look for the tall, curved handles behind the bar. Those are beer engines, and a pub that installed them is signaling something about how seriously it takes this. A half pint is a completely normal order if you want to try two.
### Cider, shandy and everything else
British cider is dry, still or lightly sparkling, and tastes like apples rather than candy. It cuts through fried fish beautifully. A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, and British lemonade means clear lemon soda, so a shandy lands closer to a beer spritz than to anything sweet. Pimm’s Cup shows up in summer, heavy on cucumber and mint. Black tea with milk is the default non-alcoholic order and the correct partner for a breakfast plate.
### Ordering at the bar, the way it actually goes
In Britain you order at the bar and pay right then. No host stands at the door. No server appears at your table to take a drink order. You find a seat, note the table number, walk up, order food and drink together, pay, and carry your glasses back yourself. That single habit is the biggest adjustment for American visitors.
There is no formal line at the bar, but there is absolutely a queue, and everyone in it knows the order. The bartender tracks who arrived when. Wait to be seen. Do not wave money, do not snap, do not lean over somebody mid-order. Buying in rounds is standard among a group, and when your turn comes you cover everyone. Tipping is not customary for drinks, though offering the bartender one for themselves is an old and appreciated gesture.
American British-style pubs mostly do not run this way. Almost all of them use table service with a check at the end, and normal American tipping applies. Some hybrid rooms take drinks at the bar and food at the table. Watch what other tables are doing for thirty seconds before deciding. It is the fastest read in the room.
One more thing worth knowing. Closing time in a traditional pub is announced, often with a bell and a last call, and the kitchen shuts well before the bar does. If food is the point of the trip, aim early rather than late.
### Where the British plate turns up around St. Louis
The format needs three things: a long bar, a kitchen willing to braise, and a room dark enough to feel like evening at four in the afternoon. Those show up in old corner buildings and converted storefronts all over the metro, not just downtown. Somebody driving in from Caseyville or Bunker Hill passes a dozen buildings shaped exactly right for it.
The British influence here is quieter than the German one, and it shows up in pieces rather than whole rooms. A Scotch egg on a bar menu in Wellston. A steak and ale pie as a winter special. Sunday roast advertised on a chalkboard in Wilbur Park, gone by three. A Black Jack kitchen doing a full English on weekends and calling it a British breakfast so people know what they are getting.
Call before you drive. Sunday roast is the one dish worth confirming by phone, because kitchens run out and they do not restock. Weekend British breakfast service is similarly limited, and if that is the mission, our breakfast and brunch guide is a useful second stop for planning the morning.
Irish kitchens overlap with British ones more than people expect, so here’s what to order when you want Irish food in St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some classic British pub dishes?
A.  Fish and chips, bangers and mash with onion gravy, steak and ale pie, shepherd’s pie, cottage pie, toad in the hole, Sunday roast with Yorkshire pudding, a ploughman’s lunch, Scotch eggs, jacket potatoes, bubble and squeak, Welsh rarebit, Cornish pasties, and sticky toffee pudding for dessert. Most are braised, baked or fried, because that is what a small pub kitchen does well.
### Q. Why do they call it bangers and mash?
A.  Banger is slang for sausage, and the usual explanation traces to wartime rationing, when sausages were padded out with water and rusk filler. Heated in a hot pan, the trapped moisture turned to steam and the casings burst with an audible pop. The nickname stuck long after the recipes improved. Treat the origin story as widely repeated rather than firmly documented.
### Q. What kind of sausage is bangers and mash?
A.  Fresh pork sausage, uncured and unsmoked, with breadcrumb or rusk worked into the mix so the texture stays tender rather than springy. Cumberland is the peppery version, often sold in a long coil. Lincolnshire is seasoned heavily with sage. Both are mild by American standards and both want onion gravy poured over them.
### Q. What is the American equivalent of bangers?
A.  A fresh bratwurst is the closest widely available match, similar in size, pale color and soft texture, though a brat is usually coarser and less bready. Breakfast sausage links share the seasoning but not the scale. Smoked kielbasa and fennel-heavy Italian sausage are both wrong, because bangers are raw when you buy them and mild when you eat them.
### Q. What are the unwritten rules of etiquette in a British pub?
A.  Order at the bar and pay immediately. Respect the invisible queue and wait your turn without waving cash. Buy in rounds and cover everyone when it is your turn. Carry your own glasses, return the empties, and do not block the serving area. Tipping is not expected on drinks. American British-style pubs mostly use table service, so normal tipping applies here.
### Q. What is the American version of a full English breakfast?
A.  The diner platter. Eggs any style, streaky bacon or sausage links, hash browns or home fries, buttered toast, and bottomless coffee. The structure matches: protein, starch, egg, bread, hot drink. What goes missing is black pudding, baked beans, the grilled tomato and the mushrooms, and the bacon switches from meaty back cuts to thin crisp strips.
### Q. Is a Scotch egg served hot or cold?
A.  Traditionally cold, as portable picnic and travel food, with the yolk cooked through. Modern pubs mostly serve them warm from the fryer with a jammy, barely-set yolk, cut in half and plated with mustard or a brown sauce. Both versions are correct. The warm one is harder to make and noticeably better, so order it that way when a kitchen offers it.
### Q. What are mushy peas, and are they worth ordering?
A.  Dried marrowfat peas soaked overnight and cooked down until they collapse into a thick, grassy puree, sometimes with mint or butter stirred through. They are not mashed English peas and they are not sweet. Treat them as a condiment rather than a vegetable side, spooned onto the fish or the chips. Yes, order them once.

## What Commercial Building Maintenance Covers and Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-commercial-building-maintenance-covers-and-costs-in-st-louis
Six-fifteen on a Tuesday, and one corner of the lobby carpet is still damp. Trash gone. Glass clean. Somebody was in the building at eleven the night before and you never saw them, which is exactly the point. Then the invoice shows up with one line on it: MONTHLY SERVICE. That line is where the arguments start.
A maintenance agreement gets sold like a single product. It isn’t one. It’s a stack of separate jobs with separate labor rates bundled into one number, and the bundle shifts from company to company. Two proposals for the same 12,000-square-foot office can land far apart and both be honest, because one carries restroom supplies and quarterly hard-floor work and the other quietly doesn’t.
So the question worth asking isn’t what it costs. It’s what sits inside the number, what drops out the second something breaks, and who eats the 2 a.m. call about water running down a stairwell. Answer those three and the pricing stops feeling like a guess.
### How much does building maintenance cost in St. Louis?
Rates aren’t published, and building maintenance in St. Louis gets quoted four ways: a flat monthly contract for recurring janitorial and preventive work, per square foot for cleaning, per visit for scheduled service, and hourly for reactive repair calls. Square footage, floor type, traffic, restroom count, frequency and after-hours access move the number.
Nobody posts a rate card, and there’s a reason for that. A quote gets built from a walkthrough. How many square feet, how many restrooms, what the floors are made of, how many nights a week, what time a crew can get in the door, and whether you or the vendor buys the paper towels. Move any one of those and the price moves with it. A published number would be wrong for almost every building that read it.
### The flat monthly contract
One number, every month, for a defined list of recurring work. Nightly or three-nights-a-week janitorial, filter changes on a schedule, lamp replacement, a quarterly walk of the roof. Predictable for your budget and predictable for their scheduling, which is why most vendors push it. The risk is vagueness. A flat fee attached to a loose scope is a flat fee attached to nothing.
### Per square foot
Standard for cleaning, usually written as a monthly rate per cleanable square foot. Cleanable is the operative word. Stairwells, mechanical rooms and a warehouse mezzanine are not the same work as open office carpet, and a serious bidder measures what the crew will actually touch instead of copying a number off your lease.
### Per visit
Used for anything scheduled but not constant. Window washing, carpet extraction, strip and wax, gutter clearing, spring and fall HVAC changeovers. Priced per occurrence, so frequency is the lever you control. Four extraction visits a year instead of two is a real budget decision, not a technicality.
### Hourly, for reactive work
The one that surprises people. Repairs outside the scope get billed by the hour, usually with a minimum, and usually at a higher rate nights, weekends and holidays. Parts are separate. If your building is older and things break, this is the line that decides whether the year came in on plan.
Most real agreements mix all four. Flat monthly for the recurring, per visit for the periodic, hourly for the surprises. That’s normal and it’s fine. What matters is knowing which bucket every task lives in before you sign, because the tasks nobody assigned are the ones that turn into an emergency invoice in February.
### What is bundled into a contract, and what gets billed separately?
The bundle is smaller than most owners assume. Recurring, predictable, low-skill-mix work goes inside the monthly fee. Anything that needs a specialty license, a lift, a permit, or a part with a real price tag on it comes out and gets billed on its own. That split is the entire negotiation.
### Usually inside the monthly fee
Trash and recycling pulls. Vacuuming and dust mopping. Restroom cleaning and restocking. Breakroom wipe-down. Glass at entry doors and interior partitions. High and low dusting on a rotation. Lamp and ballast swaps at ordinary ceiling heights. Filter changes. Belt checks. Visual inspection of the roof, the exterior and the mechanical room, with a written note back to you. Salt and shovel work at the entrances, sometimes. Minor plumbing, like a flush valve or a faucet cartridge.
### Usually billed separately
Hard-floor refinishing. Carpet extraction. Window washing above the first floor. Parking lot sweeping, striping and sealcoating. Full snow plowing, which is nearly always its own contract with its own trigger depth. Licensed electrical and licensed plumbing. Refrigerant work. Fire alarm and sprinkler inspection, which are code-driven and go to a licensed specialty firm. Elevator service, always its own agreement. Pest control. Anything behind a locked tenant door. And any part over a stated dollar threshold, which the agreement should name.
Notice how many of those sit under a separate license. That’s not a vendor being cheap with you. Missouri and Illinois both gate real trade work behind licensure, and a good general maintenance company knows where its own edge is. The ones who claim they handle everything in-house are usually subcontracting it anyway, with a markup you never see. Our breakdown of property maintenance services and what they cover maps the same boundary from the property side.
### How much does it cost to clean a 10,000 square foot building?
Square footage alone can’t answer it, and any vendor who quotes off that one number over the phone is guessing. Nobody publishes a local rate. Six variables decide the price of a 10,000-square-foot job, and two buildings of identical size can sit a long way apart on every one of them.
Start with the floors. Ten thousand feet of open carpet is a vacuum and a spot check. Ten thousand feet of VCT is dust mop, damp mop, and a burnisher on a cycle, plus strip and wax somewhere in the year. Polished concrete, sealed terrazzo, ceramic tile in a restroom block, sheet vinyl in a clinic exam room. Each one carries a different labor time and a different chemical. Mixed floors cost more than one floor type does.
Then count restrooms and fixtures. Restrooms are the most labor-dense square feet in any commercial building, and a fixture count tells a bidder more than a floor plan does. Two single-occupancy restrooms in a Pine Lawn storefront and eight stalls across two floors of a Barnhart office are not the same job at the same size.
### The other four levers
Traffic and use type. A dental practice, a machine shop and an insurance office each shed a completely different mess. Frequency, which is the biggest lever you actually control: five nights a week versus three versus one changes the whole structure. Access, meaning what time the crew can get in, whether there’s an alarm code, a dock, an elevator, or a landlord who locks the building at nine. And supplies, because liners, paper, soap and can liners inside the price versus billed at cost is a genuine difference between two bids that look identical.
Want the number to mean something? Make every bidder walk the building, at the hour the work would happen, with your fixture count and your floor types in hand. If you’re comparing cleaning specialists specifically, our guide to top-rated commercial cleaners in St. Louis is the companion read.
Different contract, same math: what a kids birthday party costs
### How long does it take to clean a 10,000 sq ft building?
Nobody can give you an honest hours figure without seeing the building, and the variables that set the time are the same ones that set the price. Floor type, restroom and fixture count, traffic, frequency, crew size and how fast the crew can get through the door. Those six write the schedule.
Frequency does the heaviest lifting. A building serviced five nights a week gets light nightly passes, because nothing has time to build up. The same building serviced once a week needs a longer, harder visit every time, since a week of coffee rings, restroom use and parking lot grit walked across the entry is waiting. Cutting frequency in half rarely halves the total labor hours.
Crew size changes the clock without changing the work. Two people splitting a floor plan finish in roughly half the wall time one person needs, and vendors staff to the window you give them. A tight window costs more because it forces more bodies on site at once. A loose window is cheaper. If a crew can work from seven to midnight, they will price it differently than a building that must be clear by nine.
### What stretches the time out
Hard floors that need machine work. Restrooms, always. Stairwells, because a vacuum and a mop both have to be carried. Glass, which is slow and unforgiving. Buildings with many small private offices instead of one open floor, since every door is a stop, a light switch and a separate trash can. Security procedures, badge-in logs and alarm resets. Elevators that need a key after hours. And a dock or trash enclosure sitting a long walk from the interior.
Here’s the part that gets skipped. Specials aren’t part of the nightly clock at all. Strip and wax, extraction and window washing are separate visits with separate crews and separate hours, and they land on the calendar quarterly or annually. When a vendor tells you the nightly visit takes a certain time, ask what that excludes. The answer is usually everything expensive.
### What actually drives the number up or down?
Building age and mechanical condition drive it harder than anything else, and both show up in the hourly reactive line rather than the monthly fee. A 1970s strip retail building in Freeburg and a five-year-old flex building on the same acreage will produce wildly different annual totals under identical contracts.
### The local factors
St. Louis weather taxes buildings from both directions. Road salt gets tracked across entry floors from December through March and it destroys finish, which means more matting, more frequent scrubs, and sometimes an extra refinish cycle. Summer humidity pushes condensate lines, drain pans and roof drains to the front of the list. Freeze and thaw cycles work on parking lots and on sealant joints. A building with a flat roof and a lot of rooftop equipment carries more scheduled labor than one without, every single year.
### The things you can change
Frequency. Scope. Access window. Whether supplies are your purchase or theirs. Whether you keep the specials in the same agreement or bid them out on their own. Matting at every entrance, which is cheap and directly reduces floor labor. And how fast you approve repair work, because a small leak approved on Tuesday costs a fraction of the same leak on a Saturday after the drywall came down.
### The things you cannot
Square footage. Number of floors and restrooms. Tenant mix. Wage pressure in the local labor market, which nobody controls. Code-driven inspections on fire, sprinkler and elevator systems, which happen on their own schedule whether or not you budgeted for them. Insurance and licensing costs carried by the vendor and passed through in the rate.
One more, and it catches new owners constantly. Read the lease before you shop anything. In a multi-tenant building, a chunk of this work is a common-area expense you recover from tenants, and some of it isn’t recoverable at all. The commercial leasing guide for the St. Louis metro covers how those pass-throughs get written, which determines whether a scope increase is your cost or a shared one.
### How do you tell a real scope from a thin one?
A real scope is countable. It names tasks, frequencies and quantities, and a stranger could audit the building against it without calling anybody. A thin scope uses adjectives. Once you know that single difference, you can sort two proposals in about four minutes.
### Signs the scope is real
Task lists broken out by frequency: nightly, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual. A fixture count for restrooms. Square footage by floor type, not one lump number. Named specials with named frequencies, priced per occurrence. A stated threshold above which a repair needs your approval. Response times for routine and emergency calls, in hours. A named supervisor and a stated inspection cadence. Proof of insurance and a clear statement of which licensed trades get subcontracted.
### Signs it is thin
The phrase general cleaning as a line item. As needed with no definition. A single square footage figure with no floor types attached. No mention of who buys supplies. Specials listed with no frequency, so they exist on paper and never on the calendar. No after-hours rate stated anywhere. A quote produced without a walkthrough. And a scope that never once says what is excluded, which is the biggest tell of all.
A thin scope isn’t always dishonest. Sometimes it’s a small operator who works on handshakes and does genuinely good work. But it means every disagreement for the next three years gets settled by memory, and memory favors whoever talks faster.
### Interview two or three providers, then look at the gap
Shortlist two or three companies worth an hour of your time. Walk each one through the building. Say plainly what you want, in specifics, then listen to what they are actually prepared to deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal. Not the bottom-line number.
Come to the walkthrough with your own list first. Nightly trash and restrooms, five nights, crew in after six. Hard floors burnished monthly, refinished twice a year. Filters quarterly. Roof inspected after every major storm. A named person who answers the phone. Whatever your building actually needs. Now say it out loud and watch.
### What the good ones do
They push back on something. A vendor who agrees to every item without a single question hasn’t thought about your building, and the disagreement usually lands where you were wrong. They’ll tell you monthly burnishing is too much for that traffic level, or that your entry matting is costing you more in floor labor than the matting would cost to replace, or that they won’t touch the rooftop units and here’s the mechanical company they’d call. That’s a partner. The ones who say yes to everything are selling you the signature and solving the details later, at your expense.
Ask three questions at the end of every walkthrough. Who is the actual person in my building at night, and how long have they worked for you? What happens if a pipe fails at 3 a.m. on a Sunday? And what is on this list that you would tell me to drop? The third one sorts the field faster than anything else, because it asks a salesperson to argue against revenue.
### A note on turnover
Janitorial turnover is high across the whole industry, and it’s the reason good service degrades at month seven. A company with a real supervisor structure and a written inspection cadence survives losing a cleaner. A company where one person does everything does not. Ask how they onboard a replacement, and ask who inspects the work when nobody is watching.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What falls under building maintenance?
A.  Four groups. Janitorial and custodial work, meaning trash, floors, restrooms and glass. Preventive mechanical work on HVAC, plumbing and electrical systems. Reactive repairs when something fails. And exterior and grounds work: lot sweeping, landscaping, snow and ice, gutters. Life safety systems like fire alarm, sprinklers and elevators usually sit outside the contract with licensed specialty firms.
### Q. What are the duties of a building maintenance worker?
A.  Daily inspection rounds, minor plumbing and electrical repairs, filter and belt changes, lamp replacement, drywall patching and painting, hardware and lock work, floor care, trash removal, snow and ice clearing, and logging everything for the owner. They triage. A good one knows which problems are theirs and which need a licensed trade, and calls it early rather than late.
### Q. What are the four types of preventive maintenance?
A.  Commonly grouped as time-based, usage-based, predictive and prescriptive. Time-based runs on the calendar, like quarterly filters. Usage-based runs on a meter or runtime hours. Predictive uses condition monitoring, such as vibration or thermal readings, to act before failure. Prescriptive goes further and recommends the specific fix. Most small commercial buildings live almost entirely in the first two.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in maintenance?
A.  A rule of thumb, not a measurement. It gets used two ways: roughly 80 percent of your problems come from about 20 percent of your assets, and a healthy program runs near 80 percent planned work to 20 percent reactive. Neither ratio is precise. Both are useful for deciding where attention goes first in a building with a long list.
### Q. What are the common commercial cleaning services?
A.  Nightly janitorial covering trash, vacuuming, mopping, restrooms and breakrooms. Then the periodics: carpet extraction, hard-floor strip and wax, burnishing, window washing, high dusting, upholstery, and pressure washing at entrances and sidewalks. Disinfection services and post-construction cleanup are common add-ons. The periodics are priced per visit, so frequency is where most of the budget decision actually lives.
### Q. What is another name for building maintenance?
A.  Facilities maintenance, facility management, building services, property maintenance, or plant operations, depending on who is talking. Janitorial and custodial services name the cleaning portion only. In facility management language you will also hear soft services for cleaning and grounds, and hard services for mechanical, electrical and structural work. The terms overlap, so confirm the scope rather than the label.
### Q. Does a maintenance contract cover HVAC repairs, or only filter changes?
A.  Usually filters, belts, coil cleaning and seasonal changeovers, and that is all. Compressor work, refrigerant and control board replacement require licensure and go to a mechanical contractor, billed separately by the hour plus parts. Ask where the line sits and whether they subcontract it or hand you a phone number, because that answer changes how fast a failure gets resolved.
### Q. Should a small office use a contract or pay per visit?
A.  A small single-tenant office with light traffic and simple floors often does fine paying per visit, twice weekly or weekly. Contracts start earning their keep once you have multiple restrooms, hard floors needing machine work, rooftop equipment, or tenants who call you instead of the vendor. Predictable budgeting and guaranteed response times are what you are buying.

## What Cambodian Food Tastes Like and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-cambodian-food-tastes-like-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
A banana leaf cup arrives at the table still steaming, and the fish inside has set soft and almost custardy, the color of turmeric. That’s amok. It smells like lemongrass and coconut. The first bite lands savory and warm rather than hot, and it doesn’t taste like anything else in the neighborhood.
Khmer food, the cooking of Cambodia, sits between two cuisines plenty of people around here already know cold. It shares a long border and a shelf of ingredients with Thailand. It shares a border and a tangled history with Vietnam. And it tastes like neither one.
So if you’ve eaten your way through pad thai and pho and you assume Cambodian food is a variation on one of them, get ready to be wrong in a good way. Less sugar. Less chili. Far more fermented fish, more turmeric, more sour. Here’s what’s actually on the plate, why it tastes the way it does, and what to point at the first time you sit down.
### What is traditional Cambodian food?
Traditional Cambodian, or Khmer, food is built on a pounded lemongrass paste called kroeung, a fermented fish paste called prahok, palm sugar and lime. It reads savory and herbal rather than sweet or fiery. Rice anchors every meal, dishes arrive together, and chili sits on the side.
Start with the table instead of the recipe. A Khmer meal isn’t coursed. Rice goes in the middle and everything else lands at once: a soup, something stir-fried, something grilled, a pickle, a dip, and a plate of raw vegetables and herbs nobody cooked at all. You assemble each bite yourself. A little rice, a piece of fish, a swipe through the sauce, a bite of raw long bean to reset your mouth.
Sour is the dominant note, and it shows up in more forms than most American kitchens bother with. Tamarind. Lime. Green mango. Underripe tomato. Kaffir lime leaf and zest. There’s a whole family of soups called samlor machu, which translates to sour soup, and every region argues about its own version. Sweetness comes from palm sugar, which tastes smoky and caramel-ish rather than clean, and it shows up in small doses.
Then there’s the bottom note. The one doing the heavy lifting that nobody prints in the menu description. Fermented fish runs underneath a huge share of Khmer savory cooking the way anchovy runs under a Caesar dressing. You almost never taste it as fish. You taste depth, and you can’t name it, and the dish falls flat without it.
### What is prahok, and why does it matter?
Prahok is salted freshwater fish, mashed and fermented in crocks for months. It’s the most distinctly Cambodian ingredient there is, and cooks use it the way the rest of us use salt: a spoonful into a pot, never a serving on a plate. Pungent alone. Nearly invisible in the finished dish.
It came out of necessity. Cambodia’s freshwater fishery, centered on the Tonle Sap lake and its seasonal flood, delivers small fish in enormous quantity for a short window each year. Salt them, press them, ferment them, and you have protein that keeps through the dry months. Generations of home kitchens were organized around that crock. Preservation first, flavor second, and then the flavor became the point.
The smell is genuinely strong, and Khmer cooks are the first to tell you so. Cambodians tease each other about it the same way people here tease each other about limburger or fish fries. None of that follows the ingredient into the pot, though. Heat and coconut milk round it out fast.
### Prahok ktis, where it steps forward
One dish puts prahok in the spotlight on purpose. Prahok ktis simmers ground pork with coconut milk, kroeung and prahok into a thick, brick-colored dip, served with a mound of raw cucumber, cabbage, long bean and slivered eggplant. It eats like a rich meat ragu with a savory hum underneath. Order it if it’s on the menu. It’s the single best introduction to how this cuisine thinks.
### How Khmer flavor actually gets built
Three things do most of the work: a wet aromatic paste, an acid, and pepper. Learn those and a menu you’ve never seen before stops looking random. You start predicting what a dish will taste like from the name, which is most of what confidence at a new table really is.
### Kroeung, the paste behind almost everything
Kroeung is lemongrass, galangal, fresh turmeric, kaffir lime leaf, garlic and shallot pounded together in a mortar until the fibers break down. Not a dry spice blend. A wet, fragrant, slightly stringy paste made fresh. Yellow kroeung is the everyday base. Red kroeung adds dried chilies. Green kroeung leans on fresh herbs and green peppercorn.
Cooks pound it rather than blend it, and that isn’t nostalgia. A blender bruises and waters the lemongrass; a pestle crushes oil out of it. You can taste the difference across the room. Kroeung goes into amok, into sour soups, into char kroeung stir-fries, and into marinades for anything headed to a grill.
### Sour where Thai cooking would go sweet
Acid drives the balance here. Tamarind pulp for a soft, dark sourness. Lime for a sharp one. Green mango and unripe fruit shredded raw into salads. Pickled vegetables, called chrouk, alongside grilled meat to cut the char. Palm sugar shows up to round the edges, not to lead. That’s the single biggest reason a Khmer dish and its Thai cousin taste different from the first spoonful.
### Kampot pepper and the plate of raw greens
Before chilies reached Southeast Asia through Portuguese trade, the heat in this region came from pepper, and Cambodia kept that habit. Pepper from Kampot province is the famous one, floral and sharp. Fresh green peppercorns, still on the stem, get tossed straight into fried crab. And tuk meric, a dip of lime juice, salt and cracked black pepper, sits next to grilled beef at tables all over the country.
The raw plate deserves its own mention, because visitors often mistake it for garnish and leave it sitting there. Don’t. Banana blossom, water lily stems, cucumber, Thai basil, mint, whole lettuce leaves. They’re structural. They’re the crunch and the cool against a rich, salty, sour bite of rice and curry.
### Is Cambodian food spicy?
Usually not, by Thai or Lao standards. Heat in Khmer cooking works as a condiment rather than as construction. A dish of sliced bird chilies in fish sauce sits on the table and each person adjusts their own bowl, which means the base dish has to taste complete before any chili touches it.
There are exceptions. Red kroeung dishes carry real dried-chili heat. Cooking from the northern provinces, where Lao influence runs strong, gets hotter and more aggressive with fermented notes. Some salads come dressed hot on purpose. But the default register is aromatic, sour and gently sweet, not burning.
Practically, this makes Khmer food one of the easier Southeast Asian cuisines to bring a mixed table to. A kid who won’t touch chili can eat rice, grilled pork and amok happily. Somebody who wants to sweat can reach for the chili dish. Nobody has to compromise, and nobody has to send a plate back.
### How is a Khmer menu organized?
By cooking method, not by course. Khmer menus group dishes with words like samlor for soup and stew, cha for stir-fried, ang for grilled, chien for fried, nhoam for salad, num for anything made from flour or rice dough, and tuk for dips. Once you know six words, the whole page opens up.
### Samlor, the soup that isn’t a starter
A samlor is not an appetizer. It sits on the table for the length of the meal and gets spooned over rice again and again. Samlor machu is the sour family. Samlor korko is the mixed-vegetable stew thickened with toasted rice powder and seasoned with prahok, often called the most everyday dish in the country. Samlor kari is the mild coconut curry that arrived through centuries of Indian and Malay trade.
### Cha, ang and chien
Cha means it hit a hot wok. Char kroeung sach ko is beef stir-fried with that lemongrass paste until the kitchen smells like a citrus grove. Ang means grilled, so sach ko ang is skewered beef off live coals, usually with tuk meric alongside. Chien means fried, which is how you get kdam chaa, crab cracked and fried with fresh green pepper.
### Num, which covers more than noodles
Num trips people up because it covers noodles, bread and sweets all at once. Num banh chok is the fermented rice noodle dish eaten in the morning. Num pang is the baguette sandwich, a leftover of French colonial rule that Cambodia kept and made its own. Num plae ai are little sticky rice balls with palm sugar inside, rolled in coconut. Same word. Three very different plates.
One small logistical note while we’re here. The standard Khmer utensils are a fork and a spoon, spoon in the dominant hand, fork used to push. Chopsticks show up for noodle soups and for dishes with Chinese roots, not for a rice meal. If a cuisine that organizes itself this way is new to you, our guide to what African food is and what to order in St. Louis walks the same kind of ground for a different set of kitchens.
### What should you order on a first visit?
Order amok, one noodle dish and one grilled plate. That trio covers the three things Khmer cooking does better than anybody: steamed coconut curry, morning noodles with a fish-based sauce, and beef with a lime and pepper dip. Add a raw vegetable plate. Skip the impulse to order five curries.
### Fish amok
Freshwater fish folded into yellow kroeung and coconut milk, then steamed in banana leaf until it sets like a savory custard. Soft, fragrant, barely spicy, faintly sweet from the coconut. Most people call this the national dish and they’re not really arguing about it. If you order one thing, order this.
### Kuy teav
Rice noodles in clear pork bone broth, finished with fried garlic oil and whatever the house tops it with: pork, shrimp, beef balls, offal, a scatter of herbs. It’s Cambodia’s breakfast. Clean broth, garlic on top, a wedge of lime and chili at your elbow. Pho and kuy teav are cousins, and you’ll notice the garlic oil immediately.
### Lok lak
Cubed beef seared hard and quick, piled on lettuce and tomato with rice and a fried egg, and served with tuk meric on the side. French technique, Khmer seasoning, and a dip that makes the whole thing work. This is the easy sell for anybody at the table who claims they don’t like unfamiliar food.
### Num banh chok
Thin fermented rice noodles under a pale green fish gravy built on kroeung and lemongrass, buried in raw vegetables: banana blossom, cucumber, bean sprouts, water lily stem. Cambodians eat it in the morning, sold from baskets and carts. Nothing in Thai or Vietnamese cooking tastes quite like it. Order it if you see it, because you may not see it again soon.
### A nhoam salad
Nhoam trayong chek is shredded banana blossom with chicken, herbs, peanuts and a lime dressing. Crunchy, sour, herbal, cold against everything hot on the table. It does the job a slaw does at a barbecue, and it keeps a heavy order from feeling heavy.
Eating on the water instead? What boating costs near St. Louis
### How Cambodian cooking differs from Thai and Vietnamese
The ingredients overlap heavily and the results don’t. Thai cooking pushes all four tastes hard at once. Vietnamese cooking runs lighter and leans on raw herbs and fish sauce. Khmer cooking sits between them, quieter than Thai, deeper and more fermented than Vietnamese, and more committed to turmeric than either.
### Against Thai food
Thai kitchens build a dish to hit sweet, sour, salty and hot in a single bite, with palm sugar and chili doing the loud work. Khmer kitchens dial both of those back and let lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and fermented fish carry the dish instead. A Thai green curry announces itself. A Khmer sour soup sneaks up. Coconut milk shows up less often on a Khmer table than most visitors expect, and when it does, it’s usually thinner. For where to eat the Thai side of that comparison around the metro, our Thai food guide covers it properly.
### Against Vietnamese food
This one is closer, and the shared French colonial history explains a lot of it. Both cuisines have a baguette sandwich. Both have a garlicky rice noodle soup. Both put a plate of raw herbs next to almost everything. The split is in the seasoning backbone. Vietnamese cooks reach for fish sauce and a light hand; Khmer cooks reach for prahok and a pounded paste, which gives dishes a rounder, earthier body. If you want to taste the contrast in one week, pair a Khmer meal with a bowl from our Vietnamese food and pho guide and the difference stops being abstract.
### Why are Cambodian restaurants rarer than Thai or Vietnamese ones?
Because the arrival pattern was different. Cambodians came to the United States overwhelmingly as refugees after 1975, following the Khmer Rouge period, and resettlement concentrated them in a handful of cities rather than spreading them widely. Smaller diaspora, fewer restaurants, and most metros ended up with none at all.
There’s a second reason, and it’s commercial. Families opening a business in a new country tend to open one Americans already recognize. Cambodian owners often went into doughnut shops, or ran menus labeled Chinese or Thai, because those had established demand and a working supply chain. Good food, different sign on the door. The cooking survived inside homes and at temple gatherings long before anybody printed it on a menu.
Which is why you’ll sometimes find one or two Khmer dishes tucked into a Thai or Vietnamese menu, listed without fanfare. Amok on a Thai menu. Lok lak under the beef section. Those are worth asking about directly.
### How do you find Khmer food around the St. Louis metro?
Look wider than restaurant listings. The St. Louis area has a small Cambodian community, so the cooking turns up at Southeast Asian groceries, at temple gatherings and holiday events, in pop-ups, and as individual dishes on menus that call themselves something else. Ask a question, and ask it specifically.
Start with the groceries. A market carrying prahok, palm sugar, fresh turmeric, galangal and banana leaf is a market serving cooks who want them, and the people behind the counter usually know where those cooks eat. Ask for prahok by name. It’s a short conversation and it tends to be a productive one.
Then the calendar. Khmer New Year falls in mid-April and Pchum Ben lands in the fall, and both bring food out in public in a way a regular Tuesday doesn’t. Temple and community events are frequently where a first Khmer meal actually happens in a city like this one.
Budget the drive honestly. Coming in from Dupo or Caseyville, a Southeast Asian grocery run and a meal fit into one afternoon without much planning. From Fairmont City it’s shorter still. Hamel and Gillespie sit far enough out that this becomes a deliberate trip, so call ahead, confirm hours, and ask whether the Khmer dishes need a day’s notice. Some do, especially amok and anything steamed in leaf.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Cambodia’s most famous dish?
A.  Fish amok, usually written amok trey. Freshwater fish is folded into yellow kroeung and coconut milk, then steamed in a banana leaf cup until it sets like a savory custard. It’s mild, fragrant and slightly sweet. Most people treat it as the national dish, though samlor korko has a fair claim too.
### Q. Is Cambodian food like Thai food?
A.  Related, not the same. They share lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime and fish sauce. Thai cooking leans much harder on chili and palm sugar and builds every taste into a single loud bite. Khmer cooking pulls both back and uses fermented fish, turmeric and sourness instead. Khmer food is generally milder and earthier.
### Q. Is Cambodian food like Vietnamese food?
A.  Closer than Thai, and the shared French colonial history is why. Both have baguette sandwiches, garlicky rice noodle soups and plates of raw herbs at the table. The difference sits in the base. Vietnamese cooks build on fish sauce and a light touch; Khmer cooks build on prahok and a pounded lemongrass paste.
### Q. What do Cambodians eat for breakfast?
A.  Savory food, mostly noodles. Kuy teav, a clear pork broth with rice noodles and fried garlic oil, is the standard. Num banh chok, fermented noodles under green fish gravy, is the other classic. Bai sach chrouk, grilled marinated pork over rice with pickles, is common too, usually with strong coffee and condensed milk.
### Q. What are the top 10 dishes in Cambodian cuisine?
A.  Fish amok, num banh chok, kuy teav, bai sach chrouk, lok lak, samlor korko, samlor machu kroeung, prahok ktis, kdam chaa with green Kampot pepper, and a nhoam salad such as shredded banana blossom. That list covers steamed, stewed, grilled, fried, noodle and raw, which is the point of ordering across it.
### Q. What’s the difference between Thai and Cambodian?
A.  On the plate, chili and sugar versus fermented fish and sour. Thai dishes hit louder and sweeter; Khmer dishes run milder, more herbal and more turmeric-forward, with heat added at the table. Off the plate, the languages differ too: Thai is tonal, Khmer is not, and the two use different scripts.
### Q. What does kroeung taste like?
A.  Bright and resinous, like lemongrass with weight behind it. The paste pounds together lemongrass, galangal, fresh turmeric, kaffir lime, garlic and shallot, so you get citrus oil first, then a warm earthy finish from the turmeric. Yellow kroeung is mild. Red kroeung adds dried chili and real heat.
### Q. Do Cambodians eat with chopsticks or a fork and spoon?
A.  A fork and spoon for rice meals, with the spoon in your dominant hand and the fork used to push food onto it. Chopsticks appear for noodle soups and dishes with Chinese roots. Many dishes also get eaten with your hands, wrapped in lettuce or a raw green from the vegetable plate.

## What Caribbean Food Is and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-caribbean-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
Smoke off a halved steel drum, thyme and allspice riding on it, and six people in line who already know their order. That’s one version of Caribbean food. Here’s another: a steam table behind glass, oxtail in one pan and curry goat in the next, and somebody asking whether you want gravy over the rice.
Both are real. Neither is the whole picture, because Caribbean food isn’t a cuisine at all. It’s a region. Roughly thirty territories, more than a dozen languages, and kitchens shaped by wildly different colonial histories. A Jamaican plate and a Cuban plate share a pantry. They do not taste alike.
That matters the first time you order. Walk into a Haitian kitchen expecting jerk, or a Puerto Rican kitchen braced for fire, and you’ll be confused by a perfectly good meal. So here’s what the region actually shares, why jerk is a technique instead of a bottle, how hot any of it really gets, and what changes the second the sign names a different island.
### What is typical Caribbean food?
Caribbean food isn’t one cuisine. It’s the cooking of dozens of islands built on a shared pantry, rice, beans, root vegetables, plantain, coconut, fish, goat and fresh chile, shaped by African, Indigenous, Indian, Spanish, French and British hands. Jamaican jerk, Trinidadian curry and Cuban roast pork all live under the same label.
Start with the pantry, since that part does travel. Rice. Beans, called peas across most of the English-speaking islands. Root vegetables, yam, cassava, taro, sweet potato, lumped together as provisions. Green and ripe plantain. Coconut, as milk and as oil. Salt fish. Goat, chicken, pork. Scotch bonnet or habanero. Lime or sour orange for acid. Then the seasonings split: allspice, thyme and scallion in one kitchen, cumin, oregano and annatto in another, curry and roasted geera in a third.
Now think about who built the recipes. Enslaved West and Central Africans brought the techniques that still run the region: the one pot, the long stew, the fritter, the pounded starch, the refusal to waste any part of an animal. Indigenous Taíno, Kalinago and Arawak people contributed cassava, the pit-cooked barbacoa and the pepperpot. Indian indentured laborers arrived in Trinidad and Guyana after 1845 with curry, roti and dal. Chinese, Lebanese, Syrian, Spanish, French, British, Dutch and Portuguese hands each left something behind.
The overlap with West African cooking is direct and easy to taste, which is why our guide to what African food is and what to order reads as a companion to this one rather than a detour. Same beans. Same greens. Same logic about time.
And that logic is almost always one-pot logic. Season the meat hard, a day ahead when there’s time. Brown it. Let it go low and slow with aromatics until the sauce becomes the point and the starch underneath soaks it up. Cheap cuts, long hours, nothing thrown out. That thread runs from Haiti to Jamaica to Cuba even when the spice jar changes completely.
### Why isn’t jerk a sauce?
Because jerk is a way of cooking. Jerk means meat worked over with a scotch bonnet and allspice paste, then cooked slowly over a low, smoky wood fire until the outside goes dark and lacquered. The seasoning matters. The fire and the patience matter just as much, which is why bottled jerk sauce brushed on a grilled breast is a different dish wearing a borrowed name.
The technique is Jamaican and it’s old. Maroons, communities of Africans who escaped Spanish and later British enslavement and held ground in the Blue Mountains and the Cockpit Country, cooked seasoned meat slowly in covered pits over pimento wood. The smoke preserved the meat and kept the cooking hidden. Where the word itself came from is genuinely argued over, and honest sources hedge. The most common explanation traces it to the Spanish charqui, from the Quechua ch’arki, dried strips of meat. Same root as jerky.
### What goes into the seasoning
Scotch bonnet for heat. Allspice, which Jamaicans call pimento, for the warm clove-and-pepper backbone. Thyme, scallion, garlic, ginger, black pepper, a little brown sugar or soy, sometimes a whisper of nutmeg or cinnamon. It gets ground wet into a paste or kept dry as a rub, then pushed into the meat and left overnight. Chicken and pork are standard. Fish, goat and sausage all take it well.
### What the fire does
Pimento wood is the traditional fuel, and the allspice tree’s smoke is doing real flavor work rather than just delivering heat. The halved steel drum with a hinged lid came later and became the street-corner standard. Either way the meat sits off to the side of the flame, low and unhurried, anywhere from half an hour to a couple of hours depending on the cut, until the crust turns near-black and the inside stays wet.
### So what is that bottle on the counter?
Usually two bottles, doing two jobs. Jerk marinade is the thick paste, meant to go on raw meat and sit. Jerk sauce is thinner and sweeter, built for dipping or finishing at the end. Neither one converts a pan-seared thigh into jerk chicken, and anybody serious about it will tell you so. Look for the drum, the wood smoke, or a pit. That’s the tell.
### How hot is Caribbean food really?
Less uniformly hot than the reputation suggests. Scotch bonnets are genuinely fierce, but across much of the region the pepper goes into the pot whole and comes back out before serving, lending perfume and a low warmth instead of burn. The Spanish-speaking islands barely use chile heat at all. Heat tends to live in a bottle on the table, by choice.
Jamaican cooking is the one most likely to come at you hot, and even there it swings dish to dish. Jerk can scorch. Curry goat and brown stew usually don’t. Escovitch fish carries pepper and vinegar together, which reads sharper than it is. In Trinidad the curry is warm-spiced rather than fiery, and the heat arrives separately as pepper sauce or kuchela that you add yourself. Haitian plates often run mild until you spoon on pikliz.
Puerto Rican and Cuban food are, as a rule, not spicy. Sofrito, adobo, cumin, oregano, garlic, annatto and sour orange do the work instead. A Puerto Rican table may keep pique, a vinegar-and-pepper hot sauce, off to one side. Plenty of people never reach for it. If somebody told you all island food burns, they were describing one island.
So ask, and ask specifically. “Is this hot?” earns you a shrug. “How hot is the jerk today, and can I get the pepper sauce on the side?” earns you a real answer, because it signals you already know there’s a choice being made. It’s the same move that works in a Thai kitchen, and our local guide to Thai food covers that negotiation from the other direction.
### How does the island on the sign change the plate?
Enormously, and it’s the single most useful thing to clock before you order. The sign tells you which seasoning tradition runs the kitchen, which starch will show up under the gravy, and whether allspice, curry or cumin is in charge. Five kitchens, five different meals, every one of them correctly labeled Caribbean.
### Jamaica
Jerk chicken and jerk pork off the drum. Curry goat, bone in. Oxtail stewed soft with butter beans. Brown stew chicken. Escovitch fish under pickled onion, carrot and pepper. Ackee and saltfish, the national dish, usually a breakfast or weekend thing. Rice and peas alongside, steamed cabbage, fried plantain, festival, hard dough bread. Beef patties in flaky yellow pastry up front. Sorrel, ginger beer and Irish moss to drink.
### Trinidad and Tobago
The most Indian-inflected food in the region, and it eats completely differently. Roti, either dhalpuri stuffed with ground split peas or buss-up-shut torn into soft sheets, wrapped around curried goat, chicken, shrimp, channa and aloo. Doubles for breakfast: two soft fried flatbreads holding curried chickpeas, tamarind, kuchela and pepper sauce. Pelau, rice browned in burnt sugar with pigeon peas and chicken. Callaloo from dasheen leaves with coconut and crab. Bake and shark. Green seasoning heavy on chadon beni instead of Jamaican thyme and scallion.
### Haiti
French and West African, with a vocabulary of its own. Griyo, pork marinated in epis then boiled and fried crisp. Poul nan sos, chicken in tomato and pepper. Legim, a long-cooked vegetable and meat stew mashed nearly to a paste. Diri ak pwa, rice with beans, often under sos pwa, a smooth bean gravy poured over the top. Mayi moulen, cornmeal. Tasso, fried goat or beef. Pikliz beside all of it. Soup joumou, the squash soup eaten every January first, marks Haitian independence and carries real weight; UNESCO added it to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
### Puerto Rico
Sofrito is the engine: garlic, onion, cubanelle and ají dulce peppers, cilantro and culantro blended and frozen in batches. Arroz con gandules, rice with pigeon peas and pork. Pernil, pork shoulder roasted until the skin shatters. Mofongo, green plantain fried then mashed with garlic and cracklings, sometimes stuffed with shrimp or steak. Tostones and maduros. Alcapurrias and pastelillos from a roadside window. Pasteles, a masa of green banana and root vegetables steamed in leaves, mostly at Christmas.
### Cuba
Restrained, garlicky, cumin-forward, almost never hot. Ropa vieja, shredded beef stewed with peppers and tomato. Lechón asado. Masas de puerco fritas. Picadillo with olives and raisins. Congrí, or moros y cristianos, black beans cooked into the rice rather than served beside it. Yuca con mojo, drowned in garlic and sour orange. Sweet plantains. Croquetas. A pressed Cuban sandwich. The seasoning here is mojo and sofrito, not pimento and not curry.
Same instinct, different room: what makes a restaurant a brasserie
### What is rice and peas actually made of?
Rice, coconut milk and beans, because the peas are beans. Jamaican rice and peas uses red kidney beans, or gungo peas, which are pigeon peas, simmered with coconut milk, scallion, thyme, garlic, allspice berries and a whole scotch bonnet dropped in for aroma. The rice cooks in that liquid. That’s why it arrives faintly brown and smelling like coconut.
Every island has a version and none of them are interchangeable. Haiti’s diri ak pwa leans on epis and often comes with a separate bean sauce to pour. Puerto Rico’s arroz con gandules is built on sofrito and pork, tinted with annatto. Cuba’s congrí cooks black beans right into the rice with cumin and garlic. Trinidad turns the whole idea sideways into pelau by caramelizing sugar first and browning the meat in it.
Rice and beans together show up wherever the African diaspora cooked, which is no accident. Red beans and rice in Louisiana. Hoppin’ john in the Carolinas. Jollof and waakye across West Africa. If that lineage interests you, our piece on soul food in St. Louis works the same thread from the American side of the water.
One ordering note. If the peas seem to be missing, you may simply be looking at plain white rice, which some kitchens serve by default. Ask which one comes with the plate. Rice and peas is the one you want under stew gravy.
### What should you order on a first visit?
Order something stewed, eat a beef patty while you wait, and put rice and peas underneath. That combination tells you more about a Jamaican kitchen in one sitting than anything else on the board, because all three are slow and impossible to hide behind. Jerk is the famous order. It’s also the one most often faked.
### Start with a patty
Flaky deep-yellow pastry, ground beef inside with real pepper behind it, eaten out of a paper bag while you make up your mind. A patty is a fast signal, since the pastry gets laminated by hand in most small kitchens and a bad one has nowhere to hide. Chicken, vegetable and ackee versions turn up too.
### Then order something stewed
Oxtail with butter beans is the benchmark. It should slide off the bone with a fork, the gravy thick and faintly sticky from collagen, deep brown rather than merely salty. Curry goat is the other candidate, bone in, the meat barely holding itself together. Neither can be rushed and neither can be rescued, so both of them tell the truth.
### Save jerk for a place with a fire
See a drum grill, smell wood smoke, spot a pit? Order jerk right then. Chicken quarters chopped straight through the bone with a cleaver, handed over in foil with white bread or festival to catch the sauce. No visible fire anywhere? Get the stew instead and chase jerk down somewhere else another day.
### A few practical notes
Bones are normal, in goat, in oxtail, in chopped jerk chicken. Weekend menus differ from weekday menus, and ackee and saltfish, cow foot and soup joumou often live there. Steam table pans run out, so ask what’s left before you plan a whole order around it. Sides usually mean rice and peas, cabbage and plantain, and they are part of the point, not filler. Drinks deserve attention: sorrel is hibiscus and ginger, Irish moss is thick and malty, mauby is bark and frankly bitter until it grows on you.
### Where do you find Caribbean food around the metro?
In small formats, mostly. Caribbean cooking around St. Louis tends to arrive as a food truck, a counter tucked inside a bigger building, a Saturday steam table, or a catering operation selling out of a parking lot on announced dates. Reliable public figures for the size of the metro’s Caribbean population are hard to come by, so treat any number you see with suspicion.
The practical consequence is that hours are harder than the food. A truck posts its location the morning of. A kitchen closes when the oxtail runs out, not at a printed time. A caterer takes Sunday orders by Thursday and then stops answering. Drivers coming in from Wellston, Black Jack, Pontoon Beach, Trenton or New Baden should call before committing to the drive, and should ask what’s cooking today instead of trusting a menu posted two years ago.
A lot of this food also moves through churches, barber shops, groceries and plain word of mouth long before it ever gets a storefront. If a coworker mentions a woman who sells patties on Fridays, that’s a real lead. Follow it.
