### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the top 3 Colombian dishes to try?
A.  Bandeja paisa, ajiaco and arepa con queso. The bandeja gives you beans, rice, chicharrón, chorizo, plantain, avocado and a fried egg on one tray, so it works as a tour of the whole cuisine if you split it with somebody. Ajiaco is the chicken and potato soup from Bogotá, thickened by the potatoes themselves and finished with cream and capers. The arepa is the everyday one: griddled corn, butter, melted cheese, done in minutes.
### Q. What is Colombia’s national dish?
A.  Bandeja paisa is widely treated as the national dish, though it belongs specifically to Antioquia and the coffee-growing region around Medellín. It grew out of farm labor: beans, rice, pork in several forms, plantain, avocado and an egg, loaded onto a tray big enough to fuel a long day outdoors. Colombians from other regions will happily argue for ajiaco or sancocho instead. The argument itself tells you how regional Colombian cooking really is.
### Q. Is Colombian food different from Mexican food?
A.  Very. No tortillas, no tacos, and almost no chile heat in the cooking itself. Colombian kitchens lean on corn in a different form, the arepa, and build meals around beans, rice, potato, yuca and plantain with cumin, scallion, cilantro and achiote. Heat lives in the ají served on the side, which you control. Cheese is fresh and salty rather than melted over everything. If you arrive expecting a Tex-Mex flavor profile, you’ll be surprised, then usually pleased.
### Q. What’s a typical Colombian breakfast?
A.  Savory and warm. Calentado is the everyday one: leftover rice and beans fried back to life with an egg, a small arepa and often chorizo or a slice of steak. Caldo de costilla, beef rib broth with potato and cilantro, has a national reputation as morning repair. Changua is a Bogotá milk broth with a poached egg, scallion and torn bread. Bakery versions are simpler still: pandebono or almojábana with a small black coffee called a tinto.
### Q. Are Colombian and Venezuelan arepas the same?
A.  Same name, two different foods. Colombian arepas are usually thinner and act as a base or a side, griddled and topped with butter and cheese, or set beside the plate as edible flatware. Venezuelan arepas are thicker and split open like a pocket, then stuffed with shredded beef, chicken salad, black beans or cheese until they barely close. Both start from precooked corn flour, and neither copied the other. Order both if you get the chance.
### Q. What drinks are popular in Colombia?
A.  Fruit juices lead, made from lulo, maracuyá, guanábana, mora and tamarindo, served either en agua or en leche depending on whether you want it sharp or creamy. Aguapanela, unrefined cane sugar melted into water with lime, is the everyday drink hot or cold. Refajo mixes beer with red cream soda and pairs beautifully with grilled meat. Coffee comes small and strong as a tinto, sold at every hour, or as café con leche in the morning.
### Q. How much food is a bandeja paisa for one person?
A.  Too much, almost every time. Treat it as a platter for two adults, or three if you already ordered empanadas and patacones to start. It carries two or three proteins, a starch, a legume, a fruit and an egg on a single tray, and it was designed for someone heading back out to physical work afterward. Split it, order one soup or one extra small plate on the side, and you’ll have a properly balanced table.
### Q. Can you eat well at a Colombian restaurant without meat?
A.  Yes, with some care. Arepa con queso, arepa de choclo, pandebono, almojábana, buñuelos, patacones with hogao and plain fried plantain are all meatless and all genuinely satisfying. The catch is the beans, which are frequently cooked with pork, and the soups, which are built on meat broth. Ask before ordering rather than assuming. The bakery half of most Colombian counters is the easiest place to eat well without meat, and it’s usually the cheapest half too.

## How Open Mic Comedy Nights Work in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-open-mic-comedy-nights-work-in-st-louis
A guy in a hoodie is standing near the back wall doing math. Eleven names ahead of him. Five minutes apiece, plus the host talking between each one, which puts him on stage somewhere around an hour from now if nobody runs long, and somebody always runs long. He has a folded index card in his fist with four lines written on it. He has read those four lines maybe sixty times since he parked. He tells himself he is done looking at it. He looks at it again.
That is an open mic from ten feet away, and some version of it happens around this metro most nights of the week. Nobody on that list is famous. A few are three weeks in. One has been at this eleven years and is still trying to make a bit about his mother land the way it lands in his head.
Here is the part nobody says out loud, because everyone already in the room assumes you know it. How the sign-up works. How long you actually get. What the light means, what happens in the ninety seconds after you step off, and what a first-timer should walk in holding. If you came to watch instead of perform, stay anyway. The etiquette from a seat matters more than people think.
### What is open mic at a comedy club?
An open mic is the part of the week where anyone can get stage time. You sign up on a list or drop your name in a bucket, wait your turn, and do three to five minutes in front of whoever showed up. Most performers are working on new material.
Two things separate it from a booked show. Everybody on that list is a peer rather than a headliner somebody paid to fly in, and a good chunk of the material is unfinished on purpose. A comic gets a laugh on a premise Tuesday, then spends Thursday trying three different endings on it. You are watching the workshop, not the finished thing.
Rooms differ wildly. Some are a real club night with a stage, lights and somebody running sound. Plenty more are the corner of a bar: a microphone stand, a folding table, a host mixing the levels off a phone, and four people at the bar who came for a beer and got comedy instead. Both count. The second kind is where most comics learn to hold a room that did not ask for them.
For the audience side of the metro scene, the room-picking and the what-it-costs math, our guide to St. Louis comedy clubs and what to expect handles all of that. This one lives on the other side of the microphone.
### How does the sign-up actually work?
Two systems, and the room usually tells you which one it runs the second you walk in. A list is first come, first served: write your name, go in that order. A bucket draw means every name goes in a hat or a coffee can and the host pulls at random, so showing up forty minutes early buys you a decent seat and nothing else.
List rooms reward the early. Sign-up commonly opens a fixed number of minutes before showtime, though some rooms post a link the morning of and fill up before lunch, and a few still run a clipboard by the door with a pen tied to it. Ask a comic standing outside. They will tell you, and they will be nicer about it than you expect.
### Why rooms use a bucket
Because a list quietly punishes anyone working a shift. Show up at seven or you are going up at eleven to an empty room. A bucket levels that. It also fixes the other problem hosts hate: on a list, the comics who go early do their five minutes and walk out the door, and by the back half of the night the audience is three bartenders and a dog. Random order means nobody can leave, so everybody stays. Rough on your nerves. Great for the room.
Either system carries the same unwritten rules. Sign up under the name you want announced, and print it, because a host reading your handwriting wrong is the worst possible opening line. Do not sign up and then leave before your name is called. If you genuinely cannot stay to the end, tell the host that before the show starts rather than after, and most will work with you once.
### How long do you get on the mic?
Three to five minutes is the common range for newer comics at most rooms. Some give seven. A few cut it to two or three when the list runs long, which it often does. The host sets the time, announces it at the top, and is not opening negotiations about it.
Your clock starts when the host says your name. Not when you reach the stand. The walk up counts, the tapping on the microphone counts, the part where you adjust the stand to your height counts, and the little joke about the stand counts double because it is the joke a hundred people before you made. Grab the mic, say something, go.
Running long is the fastest way to become the guy hosts remember for the wrong reason. It pushes every comic behind you, it eats the show, and it reads as though you think your five minutes matter more than theirs. Time yourself at home, standing up, out loud, at the pace you will actually talk. Everybody speeds up on stage. Write three minutes of material for a five-minute slot and you will land closer to right than you think.
### What does the light at the back of the room mean?
The light is a warning, not a buzzer. It is usually a phone flashlight, a penlight, or the host standing up and waving from the back wall. In most rooms it means you have roughly a minute left, though some light at thirty seconds and some light exactly when your time is up. Ask first.
That one question, asked before the show instead of guessed at from stage, saves the whole set. Where will the light come from? How much time does it mean? Ten seconds of conversation. Hosts love being asked, partly because it signals you intend to respect the clock.
When you see it, finish the joke you are inside of and go straight to your closer. Skip whatever was in the middle. Nobody in that room knows what you planned, which is the great mercy of stand-up. And do not announce the light. Saying “oh, I am getting the light” hands the audience a stopwatch and drains the last thirty seconds of everything.
### What happens before and after your set?
Before: you move toward the front or the back wall about two comics out, so the host is not scanning the room for you. You leave your drink on a table, not on the stage. You take one last look at the card and then put the card away, because reading off a phone on stage is visible from every seat in the house.
Record yourself. Nearly every working comic does it, and at an open mic it is the single highest-value habit available to you. A phone face down on a table near the stage, voice memo running, is enough. Video is better if the room allows it, but ask the host before you set up a tripod, and never point a camera at the audience.
After is stranger than anyone warns you about. Adrenaline eats memory. You will walk off genuinely unsure whether the third bit got a laugh or a cough, and you will spend the drive home constructing a version of events that is wrong in both directions. That is exactly why the recording exists. Listen to it the next day, not that night. That night you are not a reliable witness.
Then stay. Sit down and watch the rest of the list. Comics keep quiet score on this, and the person who does five minutes and bolts for the parking lot gets noticed every single time. Staying is also how you learn, since you will hear eleven people fail and succeed at things you are about to try.
Unrelated, but ordering a Philly cheesesteak in St. Louis has rules.
### How should a first-timer prepare?
Go watch a night before you sign up for one. That is the whole answer and almost nobody does it. One evening in a seat tells you the room’s time limit, its sign-up system, its crowd, and whether the host is warm or dry. You will walk in the second week knowing things the other new comic does not.
### Write three minutes, not five
Pick three ideas you already tell people at work. Not concepts. Things you have said out loud that made somebody laugh without you trying. Build each into a minute with a beginning and an ending, then cut every sentence that is setup you do not need. Most first sets are two good minutes stretched over five, and the stretching is what hurts.
### Say it standing up, out loud, on a timer
Reading it in your head is a different skill than saying it with a microphone near your mouth. Stand in a kitchen, hold a hairbrush if you have to, and run it start to finish without stopping to fix anything. Do that five times. You are not memorizing a script, you are memorizing the order of the ideas, which is the part that vanishes under lights.
### Know your first line and your last line cold
Everything in the middle can wobble. Those two cannot. A locked opener gets you through the first fifteen seconds when your hands are doing something weird, and a locked closer gives you an exit that is not “anyway, that is my time, thanks.” As for clothes: wear what you would wear to meet a friend at a bar. Nobody dresses up, and a costume is a joke you have to justify.
### What kills a set at an open mic?
Apologizing. It outranks every other mistake by a wide margin. The instant you say “sorry, this is my first time” or “that one usually works,” you have told the audience to stop trusting you, and they will happily comply for the rest of your four minutes.
Running past the light is second. After that, in no particular order: reading off a phone, starting with “how is everybody doing tonight,” which is a host’s line and not yours, launching crowd work you have no plan for, and going after the server carrying a tray past the stage. She is at work. She cannot fight back. The room knows that.
Stealing is the one that ends things permanently. Doing somebody else’s joke, even a joke you honestly forgot you heard on a podcast, gets a quiet word the first time and gets you uninvited the second. Comics have long, unforgiving memories for this.
Bombing, though, is not on the list. Bombing is not failure. It is data, and it is the price of the thing you came for. Every comic in that room has eaten a silence so complete they could hear the cooler humming, and most of them can tell you which joke they rewrote because of it. Silence is information. Take the recording home.
### Does anybody get paid at an open mic?
Almost never, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Open mics are practice, run at cost or close to it, and most pay performers nothing at all. Some hand out a drink ticket. A few split a small door when there is a door. Nobody is doing this for the check.
Paid work grows out of the mic instead of at it. Hosts building a showcase pull from people they have watched be reliable for months. Bookers and room-runners stand at the back more often than you would guess, and what they are grading is not only whether you are funny. Do you show up. Do you hit time. Do you stay for the whole list. Are you easy to have around.
That economy looks a lot like the one on the music side of the metro, where the same reliability question decides who gets called back. If you are the one hiring entertainment rather than performing it, our guide to booking live music for an event in St. Louis walks through how those conversations tend to run.
### What does an open mic feel like from a seat?
Uneven, and that is the deal you are making. In a two-hour night you might get four sets that are genuinely sharp, six that are fine, and a couple that go nowhere in front of you in real time. The good ones hit harder than a polished show does, because you can feel the room deciding.
Your job in the seat is simple. Laugh when something is funny. Stay quiet when it is not. Silence is not cruelty, it is honest feedback and the comic needs it more than a pity laugh. Heckling is not participation, and at an open mic it is worse than at a booked show, because the person on stage is four weeks into this and does not yet have the tools to hand it back to you.
Two practical things. Sit closer than feels comfortable, because a front row that is full changes the entire energy of a room. And put the phone away. A lit screen in a dark room is visible from the stage, and every comic reads it as a scoreboard.
### Where do open mics happen around the metro?
Scattered, and rarely where a map would suggest. Some weeks the strongest list in the region is in a back room with eleven chairs. The scene moves: nights start, nights fold, a host takes a job on the road and a Tuesday disappears. Checking a room is still running before you drive out is not paranoia, it is just how this works.
Small-town rooms run on different physics than city rooms. A night in Kimmswick or Marthasville might be a dozen regulars, a bartender who has heard your material three times already, and an audience that knows each other by name, which is forgiving in some ways and brutal in others, since a bit that relies on anonymity has nowhere to hide. Somebody living out in Warrenton is probably driving toward the city for a full list, and probably making that drive on a weeknight, alone, to do four minutes. That drive is the actual entry fee.
So shortlist two or three rooms rather than committing to one. Go sit in each. Say plainly what you want out of it, honest stage time, a room that stays full, a host who gives notes, and then compare that against what the night in front of you is actually delivering. The gap is the signal. A room that shrugs about feedback but packs forty people in is telling you exactly what it is good for, and that is worth knowing before you build a habit around it.
Want a night out that costs you almost nothing? Browse comedians around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then find out whether the room runs an open list or a bucket draw before you show up.
If you’re the comic or the room running the show, list your act.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long is a typical comedy open mic?
A.  The night usually runs one and a half to three hours, depending on how many names are on the list. Individual sets are far shorter: three to five minutes is the common range for newer comics, with some rooms giving seven and some cutting to two or three when twenty people sign up. The host announces the time at the top of the show. Plan for the whole night rather than your slot, since a bucket draw can put you on last.
### Q. What is a bucket draw at an open mic?
A.  Every comic writes a name on a slip, it goes in a bucket or a hat, and the host pulls the order at random instead of running a first-come list. Rooms use it for two reasons. It stops rewarding whoever could get off work earliest, and it keeps the room full, because nobody can do their five minutes and slip out the door when they have no idea when they are up. Nerve-racking. Also fair.
### Q. How to prepare for an open mic night?
A.  Watch a night before you sign up for one. Then write three ideas you have already said out loud to friends, build each into about a minute, and aim for three minutes of material in a five-minute slot because everyone speeds up on stage. Run it standing, out loud, on a timer, five times through. Lock your first line and your last line cold. Everything between those two can wobble without hurting you.
### Q. What should you not do at an open mic?
A.  Do not apologize, do not go past the light, and do not read off your phone. Skip the opener about how everybody is doing tonight, since that is the host’s line. Leave the working staff alone. Never do another comic’s joke, even one you forgot you heard somewhere. And do not perform your five minutes and walk straight out the door, because the rest of the list notices, and the host notices hardest of all.
### Q. Do open mic nights pay?
A.  Rarely, and you should plan on nothing. Most open mics pay performers nothing at all, some offer a drink ticket, and a few split a small door when one exists. The value sits elsewhere. Stage time, reps, recordings you can study, and visibility with the hosts and room-runners who book actual showcases. Paid spots tend to come months later, and they come to comics who hit their time and stay for the whole list.
### Q. Should you record your first open mic set?
A.  Yes, without exception. Adrenaline wrecks memory, and you will step off stage unable to say honestly whether a joke landed or died. A phone face down on a table with a voice memo running is enough. Ask the host before you set up video, and never point a camera at the audience. Listen the next day, not that night, because on the drive home you are not a reliable witness to your own set.
### Q. How should I dress to go to a comedy club?
A.  Wear what you would wear to meet a friend at a bar. Open mic rooms are casual almost across the board, and jeans are the uniform on both sides of the microphone. If you are performing, pick something you have worn before and forget about, since new shoes and a stiff collar are two more things your hands can fidget with. A costume reads as a joke, which means you now have to justify it on stage.
### Q. Where can I find an open mic night in Saint Louis?
A.  Rooms move around, so check a listing close to the date rather than trusting anything months old. Comics themselves are the best source: ask at the back of any mic and somebody will name three more nights that week. Expect a mix of city rooms with real stages and small-town nights out toward places like Kimmswick or Warrenton that run on a dozen regulars. Confirm the night is still happening before you drive, since hosts and schedules change often.

## How to Pitch Your Story to St. Louis Local Media
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-pitch-your-story-to-st-louis-local-media
The folding table was still out on the sidewalk in Wright City at nine at night, hours after the block party had packed itself up. Somebody had left a spiral notebook on top of it. Two columns of names and numbers, and a third column added in pen partway through the afternoon, in different handwriting, with the word RIDES at the top. That third column is the reason the street now has a group text that finds somebody a car by Tuesday morning.
The woman who started the notebook knows that’s a story. She said it out loud in the car on the way home. What she has no idea about is the next part: who you send that to, what you say, and whether anybody at a newsroom is going to care about a spiral notebook on a card table.
This is the part nobody explains. Plenty of people around the St. Louis metro are sitting on something genuinely worth covering — a fundraiser that outgrew the garage it started in, a family shop hitting forty years, a neighbor rebuilding something everyone else wrote off — and they either never send anything, or they send the wrong thing to the wrong address and hear nothing back. Here’s how the other version goes.
### How do I pitch a story to a local newspaper?
Send one short email to a named reporter who covers your subject. Put the news in the first two sentences, say why it matters now, and add three plain facts, a date, a place and a phone number. Offer photos. Then wait a few days and follow up once.
That’s the whole shape of it. Notice what isn’t in there. No letterhead. No press release. No paragraph about how honored and excited your group is. A press release is a document written for nobody in particular, and it reads that way, which is why so many of them get deleted on sight. A pitch is a note written to one human being who has a job to do today.
The difference shows up in the first line. A release opens with your name. A pitch opens with what happened. Reporters are reading email between a meeting, a phone call and a deadline, often on a phone, usually with a hundred other unread messages stacked behind yours. You have about one screen. Use it on the news, not on the introduction.
### What makes a story newsworthy instead of just nice?
Something has to have changed. That’s the test, and it’s a hard one. Nice is a fundraiser happening. News is the fundraiser outgrowing the parking lot, or the person running it doing it for the fortieth straight year, or the thing it raised money for opening its doors next month.
Try this before you write a word. Finish the sentence: last month this wasn’t true, and now it is. If you can’t finish it, you don’t have a pitch yet. You might have a nice thing, and nice things deserve the world, but a newsroom is choosing between yours and eleven others on a Tuesday.
The angles that reliably work are boring to list and powerful to use. A first. A last. A milestone with an actual date attached. A number that moved in a direction nobody expected. One person who did something unreasonable on purpose. Conflict, meaning two sides who both care. And the quiet one that carries most neighborhood coverage: a small thing that turns out to be happening everywhere, which is really what people mean when they talk about why local matters in the first place.
One more filter. Ask who else this affects besides the people already in the room. A church rummage sale affects the church. A church rummage sale that became the only place in Venice where somebody can get a winter coat on a Saturday affects a lot more than that. Same event. Completely different pitch.
### Who should you actually send it to?
A person, with a name, who has already written about something close to your subject. Not a general tips inbox. Not a contact form. Not the main newsroom line. Those exist, they get read eventually, and they are where pitches go to sit for three weeks.
Finding the right name takes maybe twenty minutes. Go to the outlet’s site and read five or six recent stories in the section where yours would live. Neighborhoods, small business, schools, nonprofits, whatever fits. The same two or three bylines keep showing up. That’s your list. Most reporters publish their email at the bottom of a story or on a staff page, and most newsrooms use one predictable email format across the building, so if you have one address you effectively have all of them.
The metro daily, a neighborhood weekly, a public radio newsroom, a TV assignment desk and a volunteer-run newsletter all want different things, and they all want to be approached differently. If you’re not sure which outlets serve your corner of the map or who reads them, our rundown of St. Louis local newspapers and magazines lays out the landscape before you start emailing.
Television runs on a different clock. TV stations use an assignment desk, a shared inbox and phone line staffed early, and the desk decides what gets a crew that day. Pitch the desk, not an anchor. And pitch them something with motion in it, because a story that can’t be photographed is a story they physically cannot air.
### What belongs in the first two sentences?
Everything that matters. A reporter decides whether to keep reading before the scroll bar moves, so the top of your email carries the entire weight. Say what happened, where, and why anyone outside your circle should look up. Then stop and let the details sit underneath.
### The subject line
Write it like a headline, not like a greeting. Eight words, maybe ten. Something concrete: a block party in Wright City turned into a ride network for neighbors who can’t drive. That’s a subject line a person opens. Story idea, Press release, and For your consideration are three ways of saying nothing, and they all get skipped.
### The first sentence
What happened, plus when and where. No wind-up. Compare these two. My name is Dana and I volunteer with a group that, well, we started something. Versus: a summer block party in Wright City left behind a phone list that now gets a dozen neighbors to medical appointments every week. The second one is doing work. The first one is clearing its throat.
### The second sentence
Why now, and who else this reaches. Timing is the hinge. Is there a date coming, an anniversary, a closing, an opening, a season, a decision somebody has to make? If the answer is honestly no, say what’s at stake instead. Then under those two sentences, put three short lines of facts and your phone number. That’s the email. Under two hundred words total, nothing attached.
### When do you send it, and how much lead time do reporters need?
Earlier than feels natural, and in the morning. The single most common mistake people make is sending a pitch about Saturday’s event on Friday afternoon. By then the weekend is assigned, the crew is booked, and there’s no room left even if somebody loves it.
Lead times run roughly like this, and the ranges are general rather than promises. A daily newsroom wants a few days of warning at minimum, more if you want a real story instead of a listing. A weekly publishes on one fixed day, so find that day and work backward a week or two. Monthly magazines are planning seasons ahead, which means a holiday story needs to land in somebody’s inbox while it’s still warm outside. A TV assignment desk can move same-day, but only for something happening, visible, and reachable before the evening shows.
Time of day matters more than people think. Mid-morning, Tuesday through Thursday, is the sweet spot at most outlets. Monday is triage. Friday afternoon is a void. Avoid sending on a day when something enormous is already consuming the region, because your email is competing with weather, an election or a fire, and it will lose.
And if the thing already happened? You need a new reason. An event that wrapped three weeks ago isn’t news anymore, but the result of it might be. The block party is old. The ride network is current. Pitch the part that’s still moving.
Off topic: booking a birthday clown in St. Louis works differently.
### What should you do with photos?
Offer them, don’t attach them. A pitch with four twelve-megabyte files stapled to it can get stuck in a spam filter or simply annoy the person opening it on a phone. Write one line at the bottom: photos available, happy to send whatever’s useful. They’ll ask if they want them.
When they do ask, send the originals off the camera or the phone, not a version that’s been through a text message twice. Horizontal frames get used more often than vertical ones in print and on a web page. Photos of people doing the thing beat photos of people standing in a row, and a shot of somebody handing over an oversized check is the one image every editor in America has already run.
Caption them plainly. Who is in the frame, left to right, spelled correctly, plus where and when it was taken. That saves a reporter a phone call and makes your photo the easy one to use. Get permission from the people in it, and be especially careful with anybody’s kids — a newsroom will ask, and if you can already answer yes, you’ve removed the last obstacle.
Television doesn’t want your photos at all. It wants access. Tell an assignment desk what a camera can point at, exactly when, and where to park. Something happening at ten on Saturday in a church lot, with people moving and talking, is a story they can staff. A finished thing sitting still is not.
### What happens after you hit send?
Usually nothing, for a while, and that silence is normal. Reporters rarely reply to say no. They just move on, because the alternative is spending an hour a day writing rejection notes. Don’t read the quiet as an insult. Read it as a scheduling problem.
Follow up once. One time. For a daily, give it about three business days. For a weekly or a monthly, give it a week. Reply to your own original email so the whole thread is right there, and keep it to two sentences: checking whether this is useful, here’s the date it’s tied to, happy to send more. If that gets nothing, let it go and try a different outlet or a different angle. A third email turns you into a problem.
If somebody bites, move fast. They’ll want a phone call, correct spellings, a time and a place, and probably one more person to talk to. Answer the same day. Have a name and a number ready for whoever else should be interviewed, and warn that person first, because nothing stalls a story like a source who had no idea this was coming.
A no is worth something too. If a reporter says it’s not for them, ask one polite question: is there someone there who covers this? That single line has redirected more stories into print than any clever subject line ever has.
### Why do most pitches die?
Because the news was buried, or there wasn’t any. Those two account for most of it. The rest is logistics: wrong person, wrong week, no date, no phone number, nothing to photograph, or an email so long that the actual story showed up in paragraph five where nobody found it.
Here’s the pattern we see again and again in the way people write these. They start with the organization. Founded in such a year, with a mission to serve. Three paragraphs of background. Then, finally, the thing that happened. Flip it. The background belongs at the bottom, or in a link, or in the phone call. What happened goes on top.
The other killer is tone. A pitch that reads like an advertisement gets treated like one. Words like proud, thrilled, premier and unique do nothing for a reporter and quietly signal that you’re selling rather than telling. Plain, specific, slightly underwritten language works far better. Say the shop has been on the same corner since the owner’s father ran it, and let that land on its own.
Sometimes it’s none of your doing. The day blew up. The reporter got pulled onto breaking news. Your email arrived ninety seconds before something on fire. Send it somewhere else in a week with a fresh subject line, and don’t take it personally. Really. Don’t.
### What about newsletters and the smaller outlets?
Start there, honestly. A neighborhood newsletter, a school bulletin, a library mailing list or a block association email is the easiest yes you will ever get, and it’s frequently where bigger outlets find things in the first place. Reporters read local newsletters. That’s not a rumor, it’s how the pipeline works.
These are usually run by one volunteer with a day job. Which changes your approach completely. Write the item for them, in their voice, ready to paste in: a short headline, three or four sentences, a date, a contact, one photo. You just saved that person forty minutes, and your item goes in the next send. Ask what day they publish and what their cutoff is, and then respect it.
A small newsletter also gives you something to point at later. When you pitch a weekly or the metro daily a month on, you’re no longer describing an idea. You’re describing a thing that already got written up, that people responded to, that grew. That’s a much stronger email.
The same logic runs the other direction in a place like Marine, where the newsletter and the bulletin board outside the post office may reach more households than anything with a masthead. Coverage isn’t a ladder you have to climb in order. Sometimes the small room is the right room, and staying in it is the correct call.
Once an editor answers, the next thing they ask for is the written version — here is how to write a press release in St. Louis.
Sitting on something worth covering? Browse community voices across St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then read how other neighbors framed their own stories before you write the first two sentences of yours. Not sure which outlet fits your story? Start with St. Louis local newspapers and magazines.
If you run the business or organization behind the story, this part is about your next customers. If you run the organization behind the story, list your organization.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I suggest a story to local news?
A.  Email one reporter who already covers that subject, and put the story in the first two sentences. Say what happened, where, and why it matters this week. Add three short facts, a date, a location and your phone number, then offer photos rather than attaching them. Keep the whole thing under two hundred words. Skip the general tips inbox if you can find a byline instead, because a named person answers and a shared inbox often doesn’t.
### Q. How do I get a news channel to cover my story?
A.  Give them something a camera can see, and tell the assignment desk exactly when and where. Television runs on pictures and access, so a scheduled event with people moving beats a finished project sitting still. Email the desk early in the morning, include a precise start time, an address and parking notes, and name one person who will be there and is willing to talk on camera. If nothing is physically happening, build the event first, then pitch it.
### Q. How do I contact a local newspaper with a story?
A.  Read five or six recent stories in the section where yours belongs and write down the bylines that repeat. Those reporters usually list an email at the end of a story or on a staff page, and most newsrooms use one email format across the building. Send one short note to one of them, mid-morning, Tuesday through Thursday. Calling the main line works less well, because whoever answers the phone almost never assigns stories.
### Q. How do I get my story in the newspaper?
A.  Have actual news, then make it effortless to say yes. News means something changed: a first, a last, a milestone with a date, a number that moved, or one person doing something unreasonable. Send it early enough to be scheduled, name the right reporter, keep the email short, and have photos, spellings and a second source ready the moment somebody asks. Most pitches fail on timing and on burying the point, not on the story itself.
### Q. Should you send the same pitch to several outlets at once?
A.  You can, with one rule: never send it as one email with everybody on the line. Write each outlet separately and change the top two sentences to fit what that newsroom covers. A weekly cares about the neighborhood angle, a TV desk cares about what happens at ten on Saturday. If a reporter asks for an exclusive, that usually means they’re serious, and giving them a few days of room is generally worth more than three lukewarm mentions.
### Q. What if a reporter gets a detail wrong?
A.  Email the reporter directly, politely, with the correct detail and nothing else attached to it. Factual errors like a misspelled name, a wrong date or a wrong address usually get fixed quickly online. Framing you simply dislike is a different matter, and arguing about it rarely changes anything except your odds of being covered again. Pick the errors that actually mislead a reader, let the rest go, and keep the relationship.
### Q. What are some ideas for a community newsletter?
A.  Anything a neighbor would tell another neighbor at the mailbox. A calendar of what’s happening in the next two weeks. One short profile of a person most people recognize but nobody knows. Construction, road closures and anything changing on a familiar corner. A before-and-after photo. Lost pets. A thank-you list after a cleanup. Short items about a business hitting a milestone. Keep pieces brief, name real people, and run at least one photo every single issue.
### Q. What makes a really good newsletter?
A.  Showing up on the same day, every time, with specifics instead of announcements. The good ones are short, name actual people, and answer the question a reader already has rather than the one the organizers want to talk about. One clear subject line, a scannable layout, a photo, and a plain way to reply or contribute. Consistency beats polish by a wide margin. A plain newsletter that always arrives on Thursday outperforms a beautiful one that arrives whenever.

## What a Copywriter Does and When to Hire One in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-copywriter-does-and-when-to-hire-one-in-st-louis
The laptop is open on the shop counter at ten past nine, long after the lights out front went off. The homepage is up. It says Welcome to our website, and under that sits a paragraph about passion for quality and a commitment to excellence that a well-meaning nephew wrote three years ago. The owner reads it one more time. Real money went out the door today pushing people onto that page, and the phone never rang.
That gap has a name. Traffic showed up, the words did nothing. New photos will not fix it. Neither will a rounder button or a different font. And that’s usually the exact moment somebody types copywriter into a search bar, hits a wall of strangers promising to double conversions, and starts to suspect the whole trade is a made-up job invented mostly to sell itself.
It isn’t made up. It’s also narrower than most of those pitches suggest, and hiring at the wrong moment burns cash just as efficiently as never hiring at all. So here’s the honest version: what the work is, what it flatly is not, the signals that it’s time, how the money gets structured, what AI moved and what it left alone, and how to tell a good writer from a confident one.
### What exactly does a copywriter do?
A copywriter writes the words that make somebody act. Web pages, emails, ads, menus, signs, scripts, product descriptions. The job is research first and writing second: figuring out who is buying, what they are worried about, and what to say so they stop scrolling and call, book or buy.
Most of the work happens before a single sentence gets typed. A copywriter asks what your customer was doing five minutes before they found you. What nearly stopped them from buying. Which objection comes up on the phone every single week without fail. They read your reviews, all of them, including the bad ones. Then they listen to how your best customers describe you and quietly steal that language, because those customers already wrote the good line for free.
Then structure. What goes at the top, what the button says, what order the proof arrives in, what gets cut. An enormous amount of copywriting is deletion. The page that finally works is often the old page with two thirds removed and the one real reason to buy dragged up above the fold where a tired person can see it in three seconds.
The deliverables run wide. Website pages, landing pages built for one offer, email sequences, ad variations, sales letters, service descriptions, product listings, takeout menus, postcards, video scripts, and the little line under the logo that nobody has touched since the doors opened. Same skill. Different container.
### What a copywriter is not
Not a designer. A copywriter writes words; somebody else decides how those words sit on a screen, a sign or a card. Plenty of writers will hand you a rough wireframe so a developer knows where the headline belongs and how long it can run. That’s a courtesy. It is not the job you are paying for.
Not an SEO agency, either. A capable copywriter works keywords in without wrecking the sentence and understands search intent well enough to answer the question somebody actually typed. Technical audits, link building, page speed, schema markup, redirect maps: separate trade, separate skill set. If that’s where your bottleneck really sits, our guide to digital marketing for small business sorts out which piece fixes which problem.
Not a social media manager. Writing a launch post is copywriting. Posting four times a week, answering messages, watching trends and keeping a calendar alive is a different job with different hours and a different temperament. Some people genuinely do both. Ask straight out instead of assuming, because the assumption is where most sour freelance relationships start.
And not an agency. An agency sells a bundle: strategy, media buying, design, reporting, with the writing folded in somewhere. A freelance copywriter sells you the writing and nothing else. If words are the broken link, the second option is faster and cheaper. If you have no plan at all yet, the bundle may be the better fit, and our piece on content marketing for St. Louis small businesses is a sane place to start before anybody writes anything.
### When is it time to hire a copywriter?
When traffic arrives and nothing happens. That’s the cleanest signal in the whole business. People are landing, opening, clicking, and then leaving without doing the thing. The audience found you. The words lost them. No redesign fixes a message problem, and no budget increase fixes it either — it just buys more people to lose.
### The clicks come and the calls don’t
A detail shop in Berkeley runs ads for a month. The dashboard looks healthy. The bay stays empty. That pattern almost always means the page is describing the service instead of answering the worry, which for most buyers is some version of will this be a hassle and will you actually show up.
### You explain it better out loud than on paper
You close deals over the counter all day. Then you look at your own website and it sounds like a hostage statement. That distance between how you talk and how you write is the single most common reason a business needs a writer. The good sales pitch already exists. It just lives in your mouth instead of on the page.
### You are about to spend real money on traffic
Sending paid clicks to a weak page is the most expensive mistake on this list, and it compounds daily. Fix the destination before you turn on the tap. A writer hired the week before a campaign launches is cheap. A writer hired after three months of wasted spend is also cheap, just far too late to matter.
### Nobody opens the email
You built a list. You send to it. Opens sag, clicks flatline, unsubscribes tick up. Subject lines are a specialty inside a specialty, and the fix is rarely sending more. Usually it’s sending something a human would want to receive, written by somebody who has done it a few hundred times.
### How do copywriters price their work?
Four models, and the one a writer defaults to tells you something real about how they work. Per word, per project, hourly, and monthly retainer. You will not find figures here, because rates swing hard by experience, industry and research load, and a number scraped off an article is worse than no number at all.
### Per word
Common in article and blog work, inherited from publishing. It’s predictable for long pieces and easy to compare. It’s a poor fit for a headline that gets rewritten forty times, or a nine-word tagline that took two days of thinking. Paying by the word quietly rewards length, which is the opposite of what good sales writing does.
### Per project
The most common arrangement for a business owner, and usually the easiest to live with. One defined scope, one number, a set number of revision rounds. The thing worth clarifying up front is what counts as a revision versus a new scope. Changing a headline is a revision. Deciding halfway through that the whole offer is different is not.
### Hourly
Good for messy, undefined work: consulting sessions, editing what you already have, ongoing small fixes, sitting in a meeting. Riskier on big projects for everybody involved, since a fast writer with fifteen years behind them gets penalized for being fast. Many writers keep an hourly rate for odd jobs and quote projects for anything with a shape.
### Monthly retainer
You buy a set volume of work every month: the email program, ongoing ad tests, a rolling set of pages. Retainers reward continuity, because a writer who has known your business for eight months writes faster and closer to the mark. Get the scope written down anyway. Vague retainers quietly rot into resentment on both sides.
What pushes a quote up or down is mostly research and revision. Customer interviews, industry complexity, regulated language, the number of pages, turnaround speed, whether strategy is included or you are handing over a finished brief, and whether a brand voice already exists on paper. A rush job costs more. A job where you can answer every question in one sitting costs less.
One more pricing note, because it trips people. Some writers offer performance or royalty arrangements tied to results. Those work when the offer is proven and the tracking is honest, and they fall apart fast when either half is shaky. For a first project with somebody new, a flat project fee keeps everyone calm.
Completely unrelated, but Chinese herbal medicine in St. Louis surprises people.
### How do you brief a copywriter without wasting three weeks?
Answer six things and you have a brief. Who is this for. What do you want them to do. What stops them from doing it. What proof do you have. What can you absolutely not say for legal or practical reasons. When do you need it. Everything past that is helpful, not required.
Then hand over raw material, not adjectives. Reviews, good and bad. The three questions every customer asks before booking. The sentence you say on the phone that always closes it. Old pages that worked and old pages that flopped. Photos of the actual place. A copywriter can do something with that. Nobody can do much with professional and friendly.
Timelines shift with scope. A single landing page is usually days rather than weeks. A full site rebuild or a whole email sequence runs longer, often a few weeks end to end. And the delay is nearly always on the client side: the interview never got scheduled, the feedback sat in somebody’s inbox for nine days, the owner was busy running the business, which is fair and also fatal to a deadline.
One discipline saves more time than anything else. Gather all feedback into one document from one decision maker, and describe the problem rather than prescribing the fix. Saying this headline doesn’t sound like us is useful. Rewriting the headline yourself and sending it back is how you end up paying a professional to type.
### What did AI actually change about copywriting?
It changed the floor, not the ceiling. Drafts are effectively free now, the blank page is gone, and the low end of the market — filler articles, product blurbs by the hundred, thin listicles — got flattened almost overnight. None of that touched the part that was ever hard.
Here’s the part it cannot do. It cannot call your customer in Bellefontaine Neighbors and hear the hesitation in her voice when she mentions the last contractor. It cannot stand in your storefront and notice the sign contradicts the website. It cannot decide that your real advantage is the Saturday hours nobody mentions anywhere. It cannot be responsible for the outcome, and responsibility is a large share of what you buy.
There’s a second effect, subtler and more damaging. Everybody’s page now reads like everybody else’s page. Same rhythm, same three-item lists, same tidy reassurance. Sameness is invisible. If a buyer reads four sites in a row and they blur together, price becomes the only thing left to compare, and that’s a fight small operators lose.
Practical guidance for an owner. Use the tools to get a rough draft you can react to, because reacting is easier than creating. Then bring in a writer for the pages where money changes hands. And don’t hire somebody purely to polish machine output. You’ll pay professional rates for the least valuable half of the work.
### How do you tell a good copywriter from a confident one?
Listen to the questions, not the pitch. In the first fifteen minutes, a confident writer talks about their process, their frameworks and their results. A good writer asks who your best customer is, what they nearly bought instead, and why the last three people who called decided not to book. Questions beat vocabulary every time.
Read the portfolio differently, too. Anybody can show a pretty page. Ask what the goal was, who it was written for, and what happened afterward. A writer who says we never tracked it properly is being honest, and honest beats a polished claim you cannot verify. Ask for one sample in their own unedited words as well, not a piece a team rewrote.
Red flags, in rough order of seriousness. Guaranteeing a specific result before seeing your business. Asking no questions at all. Refusing to explain their reasoning on a headline. Delivering something that could be pasted onto a competitor’s site with the name swapped. That last one is the quiet killer, and you can usually spot it yourself in ten seconds.
Specialization cuts both ways. A writer who knows your trade ramps up fast and already knows the objections. A writer from outside sometimes sees the obvious thing you stopped seeing years ago. Either can work. What matters is whether they’re willing to do the research when they don’t already know the answer.
### How do you choose between two copywriters?
Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then actually interview them. Say plainly what you want, when you need it, and what a win looks like to you. Then compare that against what each writer is prepared to deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal. Not the number at the bottom.
Do not ask for an itemized quote or a labor breakdown. No working freelancer produces one, the request marks you as difficult before the job starts, and the resulting spreadsheet would be fiction anyway. Writing time is not hours of assembly. Two quotes usually differ because the scope underneath them differs, so make the ask identical and the comparison gets easy.
A small manufacturer in Herculaneum asked two writers for the same four pages. One came back with a flat number and a one-week turnaround. The other came back with a customer interview, a competitor read, two headline directions and three weeks. Different jobs entirely. The owner picked the second one, correctly, because the problem was never the word count.
Distance barely matters here, which surprises people. A writer working with a shop on the far side of the metro may never set foot in the building, and the work can still be excellent, provided they talk to your customers and not only to you. Ask how they plan to do that. If the answer is vague, so is the copy you’re about to buy.
Ready for your words to start earning their keep? Browse copywriters around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then interview two or three and say plainly what you want before anybody quotes you a thing.
If you’re the writer rather than the one hiring, list your services.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a copywriter cost?
A.  It depends on the model and the scope, and anyone quoting a universal figure is guessing. Work gets priced per word, per project, hourly, or on a monthly retainer. The drivers are research depth, customer interviews, page count, revision rounds, turnaround speed and whether strategy is included. To compare two writers fairly, hand both the identical scope and deadline, then judge what each one plans to do with it rather than the number alone.
### Q. Should I hire a copywriter or a marketing agency?
A.  Hire a copywriter when you know what you sell and who buys it, but the words are underperforming. Hire an agency when you need strategy, media buying, design and reporting managed together and you don’t want to coordinate four freelancers yourself. The agency bundle costs more because it includes more. If your only broken link is the message on the page, the bundle is mostly overhead you don’t need yet.
### Q. How long does a copywriting project take?
A.  A single landing page or a short email sequence usually lands in days. A full website or an ongoing campaign runs weeks, sometimes longer, depending on how many interviews and approvals sit in the middle. Delays are almost always on the client side: unscheduled calls, feedback from four people who disagree, silence for a week. Consolidate feedback into one document from one decision maker and the timeline holds.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in copywriting?
A.  It’s an old trade rule of thumb: roughly eighty percent of the impact comes from the headline, so give it eighty percent of your effort. Most people read the first line and nothing else, so the headline decides whether the body copy is ever read at all. Treat the number as a reminder rather than a measurement. The practical takeaway is simple — write thirty headlines, keep one.
### Q. Is AI replacing copywriters?
A.  It replaced the bottom of the market and left the top alone. Bulk articles, filler descriptions and thin blog posts got commoditized fast. Customer research, positioning, deciding what not to say, and being accountable for whether a page converts did not. There’s a side effect worth knowing: the more businesses publish machine-default writing, the more a page that actually sounds like a person stands out.
### Q. What skills do you need as a copywriter?
A.  Research and interviewing come first, ahead of writing talent. You need to pull the truth out of a busy business owner, read reviews for patterns, and hear how customers describe a problem in their own words. Then structure, ruthless editing, and enough understanding of how people buy to know which objection to handle first. Add the unglamorous ones: hitting deadlines, taking blunt feedback, and cutting your favorite sentence without sulking.
### Q. Can I be a copywriter with no experience?
A.  Yes, though not by waiting for permission. Build samples without clients: rewrite a local business page and document why you changed each part, write three versions of an email for a product you actually use, publish your reasoning. Pick one narrow area rather than offering everything. Early clients hire evidence of thinking, not credentials, and a folder of sharp spec work beats an empty portfolio with a certificate attached.
### Q. Do copywriters get paid well?
A.  Income varies more in this field than almost any other writing job, and averages hide that completely. The gap usually comes down to what you sell: writing priced by the word pays like typing, while writing tied to a business outcome pays like consulting. Specialization, repeat retainer clients, and the ability to show what your work did tend to separate a comfortable practice from a grinding one.

## How to Choose a Cosmetic Surgeon in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-cosmetic-surgeon-in-st-louis
She has three tabs open and one page of handwriting in a notebook. Tab one is a practice with a wall of before-and-after photos and a countdown clock on a seasonal special. Tab two is a plain physician page, black text on white, no photos at all, which somehow feels less reassuring. Tab three is a review site full of people describing staff who were lovely. Not one of the three screens tells her the fact she actually needs, which is what training the person holding the scalpel finished, and where.
That gap is the whole problem. Elective cosmetic surgery gets marketed the way kitchen remodels and cars get marketed: financing offers, seasonal pricing, a friendly coordinator who calls back inside the hour. The surgery is not a kitchen remodel. It’s anesthesia, an incision, a body that has to heal, and a result you keep.
So handle it as a medical decision. You’re hiring a surgeon, not buying a package. What follows covers how to read credentials, why the job title on the door means less than you’d guess, where the operation happens and why the room matters, and what a consultation should feel like when it’s being run properly. None of it can tell you whether a particular procedure is right for you. Only your own health history and a real examination do that.
### How do you pick a good plastic surgeon?
Verify board certification with the American Board of Plastic Surgery, an American Board of Medical Specialties member board, then ask where the operation happens and whether that facility is accredited. Shortlist two or three surgeons worth interviewing. State plainly what you want. Compare it against what each one is prepared to deliver.
Everything after this is detail hanging off those four moves. Verify. Look at the room. Interview. Compare. Most people run the order backward, falling for a photo gallery first, booking with whoever answered the phone fastest, and getting around to credentials only once they’re already sitting in a paper gown with a marker in somebody’s hand.
Slow down. There’s no emergency in elective surgery. The procedure will still exist in six weeks and the surgeon who is genuinely good will still have a calendar then, probably a fuller one. Any pressure to sign today tells you something about the practice and nothing about your timeline.
### Does it matter if a plastic surgeon is board-certified?
It matters more than almost anything else you can check from a laptop. Board certification documents that a physician finished a full residency in a specialty and passed the examinations that specialty requires. In the United States, the board recognized for plastic surgery is the American Board of Plastic Surgery, which is a member board of the American Board of Medical Specialties.
Here’s where people get tripped. Many boards exist. Some are member boards of the American Board of Medical Specialties, with defined residency requirements and continuing certification. Others are private organizations with official-sounding names, and joining one can be a matter of dues and a short course. Both kinds issue certificates. Both look identical hanging in a hallway, matted and framed, catching the light.
Check the board, not the frame. The American Board of Medical Specialties runs a public verification tool, and the American Board of Plastic Surgery keeps its own directory of who currently holds certification. Look the name up yourself, at home, before the appointment. Two minutes. And it spares you having to ask a stranger an awkward question across a desk.
Other specialties are built the same way, which is useful context if you’re comparing across fields. Our explainer on what an oral surgeon does and what it costs lays out a parallel structure: separate residency, separate board, separate scope of practice. Same logic, different part of the body.
### Why is “cosmetic surgeon” not a protected title?
Because a state medical license licenses a physician, not a specialty. A licensed physician in Missouri or Illinois may legally offer and advertise services outside the field they trained in, and “cosmetic surgeon” functions as a marketing description rather than a credential. That isn’t fraud. It just isn’t the same sentence as “board-certified in plastic surgery,” and the two get used interchangeably in advertising all the time.
Which means the sign, the headline and the business card carry almost no verified information. You’ll find physicians from unrelated specialties offering body contouring. You’ll find practices where the physician of record is rarely on site and the person doing most of the talking is a patient coordinator. None of that is automatically disqualifying. It simply has to be checked instead of assumed.
Ask one flat question, in a level voice. Which board certified you, and in what specialty? A plastic surgeon answers that in a single sentence and moves on. Somebody whose training sits elsewhere tends to produce a longer answer with more words in it, words about experience and volume and continuing education. The length of the answer is the signal.
Worth separating out: plenty of what people want fixed isn’t surgical at all. Texture, pigment, stubborn acne, a mole that changed, sun damage from thirty summers. Those belong with a board-certified dermatologist first, and our guide to when to see a dermatologist in St. Louis covers where that line sits. Starting in the wrong office costs time you could have spent healing.
### Where will the operation actually happen?
In one of three kinds of room, and the difference is not cosmetic: a hospital operating room, a licensed ambulatory surgery center, or an office-based surgical suite inside the practice. Any of the three can be entirely appropriate for the right procedure. What you want to know is whether the facility holds accreditation from a recognized accrediting body, and who is administering the anesthesia.
Office suites are where the questions get sharper. Not because office surgery is unsafe by nature, but because the oversight varies and accreditation there is voluntary in a way hospital licensure is not. A practice that sought accreditation and kept it chose to be inspected by outsiders. That choice tells you something real about how the place runs when nobody is watching.
Then ask what happens if the day goes sideways. Where does a transfer go, and how fast? Does the surgeon hold admitting privileges at a hospital for the same procedure they’re proposing to perform in their own office? Privileges matter because hospitals credential physicians against their documented training. Somebody who can do a procedure inside a hospital has already been vetted by an institution with no financial stake in your booking.
Geography deserves a line here too, because people underestimate it badly. The first couple of weeks after a procedure usually mean follow-up visits, and you won’t be driving yourself to the early ones. A run into the metro from Ste. Genevieve or Wood River is nothing on a normal Tuesday and genuinely rough when you’re sore, swollen and riding in the passenger seat with a pillow against the seatbelt. Count the round trip before you choose.
### What does a real consultation feel like?
Like an appointment with a doctor who is still deciding whether to operate on you. Not a meeting with a predetermined ending. A proper consult has a medical history, a physical examination of the area in question, a conversation where you describe the problem in your own words, and a plain statement about what surgery can and cannot do given your particular anatomy.
It usually runs the better part of an hour once history, exam, photographs and discussion are all counted, though practices differ and complex cases take longer. Wear something you can get in and out of quickly without help, since standardized photographs are routine. Separates beat a fitted one-piece. Bring a written list of your medications, supplements and past surgeries, because trying to recall them under fluorescent light never goes well.
### The questions that get a straight answer
Which board certified you, and in what specialty? How many of these do you perform in a typical month? Where will this be done, is that facility accredited, and who gives the anesthesia? What are the common complications of this specific procedure, and what does your plan look like if one happens to me? Who covers me at two in the morning on day three? Every one of those has a short, direct answer available to a surgeon who does the work regularly.
### What a good surgeon asks you
Plenty. Full medical history, every medication and supplement, nicotine in any form including the ones people don’t count, prior operations, how your weight has moved over the last year, what you’re expecting afterward and why now. A surgeon who never asks why now is not evaluating you. Be straight in your answers. Hiding a supplement or minimizing the vape does not protect you, it just removes information the surgeon needed to keep you safe.
Different subject entirely: what to ask a leasing agent in St. Louis.
### Which answers should make you walk?
The ones that dodge. A vague reply about which board certified them. A refusal to name the facility, or a shrug about whether it’s accredited. Discomfort at the question of who handles a complication. And a promise that nothing ever goes wrong, which no honest surgeon makes, because every operation carries risk and the honest ones say so out loud early.
Sales pressure is its own category. Pricing that expires at the end of the week. Financing paperwork handed over before the examination. A coordinator who does the talking while the surgeon appears for four minutes near the end. A refusal to give you the consent documents to read at home, slowly, with somebody you trust. None of these are medical decisions. They’re conversion tactics, and they belong to a different industry.
One more. Watch what happens when you describe a result the surgeon thinks is unachievable on your anatomy. The good ones say so, plainly, and sometimes talk you out of the whole thing. That sentence costs them a booking. It’s the single most useful thing you can hear in a consultation, and it’s the reason interviewing more than one surgeon is worth the afternoon.
### What disqualifies you from plastic surgery?
Some of it is temporary and some of it isn’t, and only a surgeon who has examined you and read your chart can make the call. In general terms, the issues that pause or stop an elective procedure include uncontrolled medical conditions, active nicotine use, an active infection, a clotting history, a weight that’s still moving, and expectations that surgery cannot meet.
Nicotine is the one people argue about most. Smoking, vaping, patches, pouches: all of it affects blood flow to healing tissue, and surgeons take it seriously enough that many will postpone rather than proceed. Some test for it. That isn’t moralizing. Elective surgery on tissue that can’t reliably heal is a bad trade, and a surgeon who says no to that is doing the job correctly.
Mental health belongs in this conversation too, without stigma attached. Body dysmorphic disorder is a recognized condition in which surgery rarely delivers the relief a person is hoping for, and careful surgeons screen for it and refer rather than operate. Timing counts as well. Grief, a divorce, a job loss: none of it disqualifies anyone, but a good surgeon will ask why now and listen closely to the answer.
### Should you expect to pay for a consultation?
Often, yes, and it’s a normal practice rather than a warning sign. Some surgeons charge a consultation fee, some credit it toward the procedure if you book, and some waive it entirely. Policies vary from office to office, so ask when you schedule and ask what the fee covers before you drive anywhere.
A fee often buys protected time with the surgeon, which is exactly what you came for. Free consultations aren’t automatically worse, but they do raise a question worth holding: if the visit generates no revenue on its own, what is it designed to generate? Sometimes the answer is a genuine practice-building decision. Sometimes it’s a funnel.
Either way, multiply the fee by the number of surgeons on your shortlist and treat that as the cost of doing this properly. Against a permanent surgical result, consulting two or three people is the cheapest quality control you will ever buy. A family in Weldon Spring who budgets for three consults and picks the third surgeon has spent their money extremely well.
### What does recovery really ask of you?
More than the brochure suggests, and for longer. Recovery details depend entirely on the procedure and on your health, so the only reliable instructions are the ones your surgeon writes for you. What’s broadly true across elective surgery is that you’ll need time off, a ride home, an adult with you the first night, and a stretch of doing considerably less than you think you can.
Swelling is the part that surprises people. Final results often take months to settle, well past the point where you feel fine and look mostly normal in a mirror. That in-between stretch is where regret talks loudest, and it is almost always too early to judge anything. Ask at the consultation what the realistic timeline looks like from week one to month six, and write the answer down.
Plan the logistics before the date, not after. Who drives. Who cooks. Who handles the kids or the dog. Whether you can sleep the way you’ve been told to sleep in the bed you actually own. Whether your job lets you sit still. Recovery goes better when the boring arrangements are already made, and it goes badly when you’re solving them on day two with a tight compression garment on.
### How do you compare your shortlist?
Narrow it to two or three surgeons who clear the credential and facility checks, then interview them the way you’d interview any doctor before agreeing to treatment. Say out loud, in ordinary language, what bothers you and what you want to be true afterward. Then listen to what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal.
That gap shows up fast once you’re comparing. One surgeon proposes a smaller procedure than you asked for and explains why. Another proposes more. A third declines part of it outright. Disagreement between qualified people is normal and it’s informative, and hearing it is the actual reason to book more than one visit. Second opinions aren’t an insult to anybody. Good surgeons expect them and some will suggest one themselves.
What shouldn’t decide this: price. Not the deposit, not the financing offer, not which office quoted lowest. Cosmetic surgery is one of the few purchases where the cheapest version can cost you a revision, a second recovery, and a result you live with either way. Choosing a cheaper surgeon two exits closer to home is not really a budget decision. It’s a health decision wearing a budget costume.
Trust the quiet stuff too. Whether the surgeon looked at you or at a screen. Whether the staff answered a hard question without glancing at each other first. Whether you felt free to say no in that room, and whether anyone made that feel expensive. You’re about to let this person operate on you. Feeling comfortable saying no is not a soft criterion, it’s a structural one.
