### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the five basic rules of disc golf?
A.  Tee off from behind the front of the tee pad. Play your next throw from wherever the disc came to rest, with your supporting foot behind that mark. The player farthest from the basket throws next. Count every throw, penalties included. The hole ends when the disc rests in the basket or its chains. Safety sits above all five: never throw toward a person.
### Q. How much does a round of disc golf cost?
A.  Most public courses are free to play, which is the honest headline. Some charge a small fee, and a few sit inside parks that require a permit or an entrance payment at the gate. Your real expense is the discs themselves, bought once and used for years. Call the park or ask a local shop before you drive out, because policies differ course to course.
### Q. How far should a beginner disc golfer throw?
A.  Shorter than you think, and that’s fine. New players consistently overestimate their distance and underestimate how much straightness is worth. A mid-range thrown flat and clean will finish farther down the fairway than a driver thrown badly, every single time. Chase a repeatable release angle first. Distance arrives on its own once the form stops fighting you.
### Q. What is the golden rule of disc golf?
A.  Never throw when anybody could be hit. That’s the rule that outranks everything else in the rulebook, because a disc is heavy, fast and edged. Some players quote a second one alongside it: leave the course better than you found it, meaning no broken branches, no litter, no new trails. Both come down to respecting the people and the park sharing the space with you.
### Q. Is disc golf basically frisbee?
A.  Same family, different equipment and a different motion. A recreational frisbee is large, light and blunt, built to float gently between two people. Golf discs are smaller, denser and beveled at the rim so they cut through air and carry. The throw is a pull across your body rather than a flick, and the game is scored hole by hole like golf.
### Q. What’s the 2 m rule in disc golf?
A.  A disc stuck in a tree or other object more than two meters above the ground costs you a penalty throw, and you play from the ground directly beneath it. Here’s the catch: that rule is optional and usually switched off, applied only when a tournament director specifically puts it in play. Casual rounds almost never use it. Play from underneath and move on.
### Q. Do you need special shoes or clothes for disc golf?
A.  No. Sneakers or trail shoes you don’t mind soaking will do the job, since fairways cross wet ground and creek beds. Long pants help in wooded layouts where thorns live, and sunscreen matters more on open courses than any gear choice. There’s no dress code at a public course, and nobody is going to look at your outfit twice.
### Q. How many discs should a beginner carry?
A.  Three, plus a small marker disc for your lie. A putter, a mid-range and one slower fairway driver cover everything a new player will face for a full season. Carrying eight discs before your throw repeats itself just adds decisions you aren’t equipped to make yet. Add the fourth disc when you can name the specific shot it’s meant to solve.

## How to Hire a DJ in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-hire-a-dj-in-st-louis
Nine forty on a Saturday in a banquet hall. Cake was cut twenty minutes ago, and the dance floor is holding two nine-year-olds and one cousin. The song playing is fine. People like that song. Forty guests are sitting with half a drink in front of them, coats not on yet, waiting for something, and not one of them could tell you what. Nothing broke. The night just quietly stopped moving.
Catching that was the DJ’s job.
Here’s what almost nobody tells you while you’re shopping. You are not hiring a playlist. Playlists are free and you already have one. You’re hiring the person who watches a room fill and empty, who knows the toasts have to land before the plates clear, who gets your grandmother out there at nine and gets everyone else off the floor at eleven because the venue said eleven.
Same job at a graduation open house, a fiftieth anniversary, a company holiday party, an eighth-grade dance. Different room, identical skill. Running the room and the timeline is the work, and it separates the DJs worth interviewing from the ones who own a speaker.
### What are good questions to ask a DJ?
Ask who runs the timeline, who makes the announcements, and what happens if they wake up sick. Ask about ceremony sound, a wireless mic, overtime, setup time and the cancellation terms. Then hand over your do-not-play list and listen to what they ask you back — the good ones interview you too.
Those questions do something more useful than collecting facts. They show you how a person thinks. A DJ who has worked two hundred receptions hears “what happens if you get sick” and answers in one sentence, because there’s a name and a phone number ready and it has been used before. Someone newer pauses. That pause is information. It isn’t disqualifying, but you want it in February rather than in October.
Watch for the questions coming back at you, too. Good ones start interviewing you about forty seconds in. How many guests? Is the ceremony in the same room? Who’s giving toasts, and does your uncle know he’s giving one? Is there a hard stop on sound? Any songs that would upset somebody in the room? Those are the questions of a person who has been surprised before and has decided not to be surprised again.
Write your own short list on paper before you call. Who runs the timeline on the day, you or my coordinator? Will you announce, and how much? What’s the overtime rate and how is it billed? When do you load in, and how long is setup? Is ceremony sound separate? How many wireless mics come with that? What’s the move if a speaker dies at nine? And who exactly is showing up, you or an associate?
That last one catches people off guard. Some companies book under one name and send whoever is free. Neither answer is wrong. Not knowing is.
### Do I really need a DJ for my wedding?
If you want anyone announced, any moment cued, or a floor that stays busy past ten, yes. A phone and a good speaker will play music. They will not read a room, fade out of a song nobody is dancing to, track down the maid of honor who wandered to the bar, or get a microphone loud enough for four generations at once.
The friend-with-a-laptop wedding fails in a very specific way, and it’s never the music. It’s the silence between the music. Fifteen seconds of nothing while somebody scrolls. A speech that starts before half the room looks up. A first dance that begins twice because the song had an eight-second intro nobody planned for. Small things. They stack fast.
There’s also the favor problem. You just handed a guest a four-hour shift. They’re at the laptop through dinner, at the laptop through toasts, and at the laptop when they should be out on the floor with you. People rarely regret hiring a DJ. They regret the favor they asked pretty often.
A band is a real alternative, not a lesser one, and it solves a different problem in a different way. If a trio or a full group is what you actually picture, our guide to booking live music for an event in St. Louis walks through how that conversation changes.
### What is actually in a DJ contract?
Six things, and you should be able to point at each one: total hours and when the clock starts, the overtime rate, setup and teardown time, what happens if the DJ cannot make it, which sound they’re providing in which room, and the deposit and cancellation terms. Any of those six missing? That’s the conversation to have before money changes hands.
### Hours, and when the clock starts
A contract that says “five hours” isn’t finished. Five hours starting when? Most DJs bill from the first song rather than from load-in, which is what you want, and it still belongs in writing. Ask what overtime costs and whether it bills in half hours or whole ones. At eleven fifteen with a packed floor, you do not want to be doing arithmetic.
Now ask the reverse, which hardly anybody does. If dinner runs long and dancing gets squeezed, does the end time move with it? Usually no, because the venue has its own clock. Knowing that in April keeps you from arguing about it in October.
### Setup and teardown
Setup runs longer than guests imagine. A ceremony rig, a reception rig, lighting and a real sound check is not a fifteen-minute affair, and all of it has to finish before the first guest walks in, which means the DJ needs the room earlier than your invitation says. Teardown is the same story backward, usually with a building manager watching. Confirm that neither one gets billed as event hours.
### A backup plan if they wake up sick
Ask it plainly, because it happens. A working DJ answers with actual humans: a partner, a second DJ on the roster, a circle of people around St. Louis who cover each other on Saturdays. Then ask the follow-up. Would your music notes, your do-not-play list and your timeline travel to that replacement? A backup who shows up without your paperwork is barely a backup at all.
Gear dies too. Two questions handle it. Is there a spare speaker and a spare mic in the vehicle, and does the laptop carry a second copy of the music?
### Who brings the ceremony sound and the wireless mic
This is the gap that turns up most often in signed contracts. A reception package frequently does not include ceremony sound, and a ceremony in another room or out on a lawn is a second setup with its own speaker, its own power and its own microphone. Some venues have house sound. Some venues have a wall jack and a prayer.
Count your microphones out loud. Officiant, readers, toasts, maybe a singer. Then ask how many wireless mics are coming and whether a lapel mic is one of them, because a handheld on a stand between two people saying vows photographs badly and sounds worse.
### Should your DJ also be your MC?
Decide before you book, because not every DJ wants the microphone and not every couple wants theirs holding one. The MC is the voice that moves people: announcing the entrance, calling the toasts, telling two hundred guests which end of the buffet to start at. Done well, you barely register it. Done badly, it’s the thing everyone remembers.
There’s a wide range out there. Some DJs are quiet technicians who’ll make four announcements and otherwise stay invisible, and for plenty of receptions that is exactly right. Others are hosts: they work the mic, run the games, keep the energy up, coax your cousins onto the floor. Neither is better. They’re different hires for different nights.
So say what you want in words, out loud. “Five announcements and no games” is a spec a DJ can hit exactly. “Someone who keeps it moving and talks to people” is also a spec. Vagueness produces the wrong night, because in the absence of instruction a DJ does whatever they usually do.
Names, too. Hand over the phonetic spelling of every name that gets said into a microphone, and confirm who’s announced as a couple, who’s announced with a title, and which relatives absolutely have to be mentioned. Ten minutes of typing. It prevents the one mistake nobody forgives.
### What belongs on the do-not-play list?
Anything that would change the temperature of the room, and it’s usually shorter and far more personal than people expect. Three buckets: songs tied to an ex or a hard family history, songs that empty your particular crowd, and the two or three wedding standards you are sick of. Write them down. A DJ cannot dodge a landmine nobody mentioned.
Keep it tight, though. A do-not-play list running sixty songs deep is really an instruction to play your playlist and nothing else, and that deletes the exact skill you paid for. A DJ’s value on a dance floor is adjusting in real time to the forty people standing on it. Fence the field. Don’t choreograph every step across it.
The other list matters just as much and gets a fraction of the attention. Ten to fifteen must-plays, plus the four songs with actual jobs: entrance, first dance, parent dances, last song. Add a line about the feel you’re after. “Nothing explicit, heavy on nineties, we like it loud after nine” tells a DJ more than forty titles ever will.
One more piece. Decide in advance whether guests can walk up and request songs, then tell your DJ the answer, because the default varies by person and a room full of requests can steer your night somewhere you never chose.
### What does your venue need settled before load-in?
Three things, and a good DJ asks about all three unprompted: where the load-in door is and how far gear has to travel, what power exists near where the booth goes, and when amplified sound has to stop. Every hall answers differently, and every answer changes what the DJ brings and when they show up.
Load-in is a physical problem. A barn outside Augusta with a gravel approach and no elevator is a different evening than a hotel ballroom with a service dock, and it moves setup time, sometimes a second pair of hands, occasionally the size of the rig. Stairs-only back entrance? Say so on the first call. DJs would much rather hear it in March.
Power is boring and it ruins receptions. A DJ rig, uplighting and a caterer’s coffee urn on one circuit is how a breaker trips during the father-daughter dance. Your DJ needs to know how many outlets sit near the booth and whether the kitchen is already on them. Put those two vendors in the same email and let them sort it out.
Then the cutoff. Outdoor spaces and neighborhood halls often carry a noise ordinance or a house rule that kills amplified sound at a specific minute, and that minute rules your whole timeline backward: last song here, so cake there, so toasts there. Get the number from the venue in writing and hand it to your DJ early. It decides more about your evening than the song list does. Still choosing a room? Our roundup of the best event venues in St. Louis for your next celebration is a reasonable starting point.
### How many songs will a DJ play in 3 hours?
Roughly forty-five to sixty, and the range is the interesting part. Most tracks run three to four minutes, but a DJ working a live floor rarely plays anything end to end. They mix out at the point the energy peaks, which fits more songs into an hour and keeps a room from drifting during the last chorus of anything.
Do the arithmetic on what that means for your requests. Fifteen must-plays is under an hour of a three-hour dance block, which leaves a DJ plenty of room to work. Hand over ninety songs and you have written the entire night in advance, including the parts that weren’t landing. That’s the most common way couples accidentally kill their own dance floor.
Song count tells you something about pacing, too. An eight-minute singalong eats two and a half slots. A slow-dance block of four songs is fifteen minutes with your floor sitting down. Neither is a mistake. Both are choices, and a DJ who discusses your night in those terms is thinking about the room instead of the queue.
Running the DJ business yourself? Pitch your story to St. Louis media
### What changes for a graduation party, an anniversary or a school dance?
The gear looks similar and the job is not. Weddings run on a fixed sequence of moments, so a DJ is mostly protecting a timeline. Everything else is looser, which sounds easier and is harder: with no entrance, no toast and no cake cutting, nothing creates momentum except the person standing at the controller.
### Graduation parties
Open-house style, guests arriving across four hours, three generations in a yard in Cottleville. Volume management is most of the job here: background under conversation early, a real floor later once the grandparents have headed home. Ask for a setup that sits at conversation level without sounding thin, and give the DJ one announcement, the toast, so it actually gets heard. A yard party also means tables, a canopy and sometimes a power run, and what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis covers that half of it.
### Anniversaries and milestone birthdays
Music is memory at these. A fiftieth anniversary in Godfrey wants the decade the couple met in, not the current chart, and the guests of honor should be asked directly for a handful of titles. Plan for hearing as well. Older rooms need the volume lower and the vocals clearer, and a DJ who won’t adjust for that empties a room very politely.
### Company holiday parties
You’re serving two audiences, which is why these go sideways. Somebody from the company has to own the do-not-play list, and it should be broad: nothing explicit, nothing that reads as a joke about anyone standing in the room. Schedule the awards or remarks at a specific minute and tell the DJ, or the speeches will land while half the office is in line for food.
### School dances
Clean versions only, verified in advance, and a written school policy the DJ has actually read. Chaperones and an administrator need to know who can stop a song and how that gets signaled. Lighting carries more weight here than at a wedding, because a bright gym with thirty kids in it stays empty until the room starts to feel like somewhere.
### What drives a DJ’s quote, and how should you ask about it?
Hours, rooms, gear and the date, roughly in that order. Five hours with ceremony sound in a second space, uplighting around the walls and an hour of travel each way is a bigger job than four hours in one room with two speakers, and a peak Saturday in wedding season is the most contested day on any DJ’s calendar. Ask what moves the number for your night.
That question is fair and a good DJ answers it happily. What isn’t fair, and what marks you as someone who has never done this, is demanding an itemized breakdown with a price beside every speaker. Nobody quotes that way. Ask what’s included, what’s extra, and what a longer night or a second setup would add. You’ll get a straight answer.
Uplighting, a monogram projection, a photo booth, extra sound for a cocktail hour outside: those are add-ons, priced as add-ons. Decide which ones you genuinely care about before the call, because a DJ who senses indecision will describe all of them, and why wouldn’t they? Much easier to open with “just sound, plus one uplighting color.”
On the band comparison everybody wants: a band costs more, and the reason is structural rather than artistic. You’re paying several musicians instead of one person, plus backline, monitors, a bigger stage footprint and a much longer load-in, and they play sets with breaks that something has to fill. A DJ is one person, one rig, continuous music, with nearly any recording ever made on hand. Different product, different math.
### The deposit and what happens if plans change
A deposit holds your date and it’s normally non-refundable, which is reasonable enough: that DJ turned down other work for your Saturday. What varies enormously is everything after the deposit. When is the balance due, and paid how? Is the deposit transferable if you move the date, and to any date or only inside a window? What if the venue closes, or the date shifts for reasons neither of you controls?
Get those four answers before you send money, not after. Ask them in one email and keep the reply. Anybody who has run this business a few years has answered all four before and won’t be offended that you asked.
### How do you choose between two DJs you both like?
Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then meet or call each one and say plainly what you want: the vibe, the timeline as you picture it, your do-not-play list, who announces what, and your venue’s cutoff time. Compare all of that against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal, not the price.
One DJ hears “six announcements, no games, hard stop at eleven, my grandmother has to dance” and comes back with a rough timeline, a question about whether the ceremony sits in the same room, and a note that the booth will need an outlet off the caterer’s circuit. The other says they’ve done hundreds of weddings and sends a rate. Both might be good. Only one has shown you your night.
Listen for the room inside their answers. Ask what they do when the floor empties at nine thirty. You’ll hear either a story about a specific save in a specific hall or a sentence about reading the crowd. A story means it happened to them. A slogan means you’re the test case.
And book earlier than feels reasonable. Prime spring and fall Saturdays around St. Louis go close to a year out, holiday party season fills from September, and a spring formal in Eureka or Town and Country competes with every other school on the same three weekends. Nobody raises the price on a late caller. The good calendars are simply full, and you end up choosing from whatever is left.
Ready to start calling? Browse DJs around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, and call with your date, your venue and your cutoff time already written down.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How far in advance should I book a DJ?
A.  Nine to twelve months is comfortable for a wedding, and a prime Saturday in May, June, September or October can be gone eighteen months out. Graduation parties and holiday parties want two to three months, and December fills early because every company wants the same three Fridays. Inside six weeks you’re calling several people and taking whoever is free.
### Q. Who usually pays for the DJ at a wedding?
A.  Tradition puts reception music on the bride’s family, and in practice most couples now cover it themselves or split it with whichever parents are contributing. No rule here is worth defending. What matters is deciding early who owns the contract, because that person signs it, gets the emails, and makes the call about overtime at eleven at night.
### Q. Do you normally tip a DJ at a wedding?
A.  It’s customary but not obligatory, and it isn’t a formula. Decide on the service you actually got. Did they hold the timeline, handle a problem quietly, stay past the end without being asked, keep the floor busy? Then a cash tip handed over at the end is a normal, appreciated gesture. Check the contract first in case a gratuity is already built in.
### Q. How long does a DJ usually play at a wedding?
A.  Four to six hours of reception coverage is typical, with five the most common booking, and ceremony or cocktail sound often added as separate blocks. That covers dinner background, toasts, the formal dances and roughly three hours of dancing. Ask how those hours get counted and what overtime costs, because the decision to add thirty minutes always gets made late at night.
### Q. Is a DJ or band cheaper for a wedding?
A.  A DJ, and the reason is structural rather than a judgment on either one. A band is several people to pay instead of one, with more gear, a bigger stage area, a longer load-in and sets that come with breaks. A DJ is one person, one rig, continuous music, any recording available. A band brings something a DJ cannot, at a different price shape.
### Q. What are some common mistakes to avoid when hiring a wedding DJ?
A.  Booking on price alone. Never asking who actually shows up on the day. Skipping the ceremony sound question. Handing over a ninety-song playlist that leaves no room to read the floor. Forgetting to tell anyone the venue’s noise cutoff. The other big one is never discussing the MC role, which leaves the DJ guessing how much talking you wanted.
### Q. Can I give my DJ my whole playlist?
A.  You can, and mostly you shouldn’t. Ten to fifteen must-plays, the four songs with jobs, a short do-not-play list and one sentence about the feel you want gives a DJ everything they need. A fully scripted night removes the thing you hired them for, which is adjusting to the forty people standing on the floor at ten.
### Q. Do I need a DJ for a school dance or a company party?
A.  If anything is being announced or awarded, yes, for the same reason as at a wedding: somebody has to run the room. School dances additionally need clean versions verified in advance and a chaperone who knows how to stop a song. Company parties need one person from the company owning the do-not-play list before the doors open.

## How to Find a Dog Walker in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-a-dog-walker-in-st-louis
At 2:14 on a Tuesday afternoon, a brindle boxer is standing at the front window of a house in Valley Park, watching the street. She has been standing there since about one. Nobody gets home until six-thirty, and by then she has held it for nine hours and chewed the corner off a floor vent out of plain boredom.
Hiring somebody to break up that afternoon sounds like a small errand. It isn’t. Almost every other service you buy for a pet happens on their turf, with you standing right there watching. A dog walker is a different animal. You’re handing a stranger a key to your house, probably an alarm code, and a dog who physically cannot tell you what happened between 1:40 and 2:10.
So the question that matters here isn’t what a walk costs. It’s what you can actually verify.
### What is the best way to find a dog walker?
Ask the people who already handle your dog: your vet, your groomer, the neighbor whose retriever gets walked at noon. Then shortlist two or three worth interviewing, meet them at your kitchen table with the dog present, and hire the one whose answers match what you’d asked for — not the cheapest one.
Referral first, search second. That ordering matters more in this hire than in nearly any other, because the thing you’re screening for — does this person behave the same way when nobody is watching — never shows up in a profile photo or a five-star average. It shows up in the fact that somebody you trust has been letting this person into their kitchen twice a week for two years running.
Then go verify the things a referral can’t tell you. A neighbor’s recommendation proves the walker is kind and shows up on time. It says nothing about whether there’s liability coverage, who covers the route when she has the flu, or what the plan is if your dog starts limping on a sidewalk in Ellisville a mile from your front door. Those are yours to ask, out loud, before anybody gets a key.
The interview is the whole job. Not the quote.
### Where do you actually look for a dog walker in St. Louis?
Five places, roughly in order of how much each one tells you: your vet’s front desk, your groomer, the neighbors on your own street, a local directory of independent walkers, and an app-based platform. The first three come with a real human attached to the recommendation. The last two hand you volume and leave the vetting to you.
Vet staff are the most underused source in this whole process. They see the aftermath of careless pet care, and the same walkers’ names on intake paperwork year after year. Ask a technician rather than the front desk, and ask about people instead of businesses: who brings dogs in here and clearly knows what they’re doing? Groomers are nearly as good, because a groomer gets the same dogs wet and restrained and unhappy every few weeks, and learns fast which local handlers are gentle.
Now walk your own street at two in the afternoon. You’ll meet the walkers who already work your block, which is worth more than it sounds. A walker with three houses on your street barely changes her route to add you, and a route that barely changes is a route that runs on time in sleet. Ask her who she is, then ask the neighbor how it’s gone.
A local directory is the efficient version of that same instinct. You get walkers who genuinely serve your side of the metro, with contact details and a service area you can read before you spend an evening calling people who turn out to cover the other end of the county. Use it to build the shortlist, not to make the decision.
App-based platforms solve one problem beautifully: availability. You can find somebody for tomorrow at nine o’clock tonight, which matters when a work trip lands on your head. The trade-off is real. The platform did the screening instead of you, and the relationship lives inside software rather than with a person you can call at 1:55. Plenty of households run this way for years without trouble. Just be clear-eyed about which part of the vetting you quietly inherited.
### What should you ask at the meet-and-greet?
Have the dog in the room, then say plainly what you want: the arrival window, the route, the length, the report, and what happens if the dog comes up lame. A good walker will ask you more questions than you ask her. The meet-and-greet is normally free, and it’s the single most useful hour in this entire process.
Watch the first ninety seconds. Does the walker crouch sideways, look away, let your dog come to her? Or lean over the dog’s head and reach for the collar? Dogs sort people faster than we do, and somebody who reads a nervous dog correctly in a hallway will read her correctly at a crosswalk.
Questions worth saying out loud: How long has walking dogs been your actual job? How many dogs are on your route during the hour mine would be walked? What’s your arrival window, and what counts as late? Do you text on arrival or on departure? What do you do if my dog won’t come to the door for you? Have you ever had a dog get loose, and what happened next? Who walks my dog when you’re sick? What’s the cancellation policy, and is there a holiday rate?
Then say the awkward thing. “She guards the couch.” “He snapped at a delivery driver in May.” “She pulls hard enough to take a small person off their feet.” Softening a behavior problem to get somebody hired is how walkers get hurt and how arrangements collapse in week three. Anybody who hears the unflattering version and stays interested is the person you want holding the leash.
And if the honest version of your dog is that nobody can hold that leash yet, a walker isn’t the fix. Start with what dog training costs in St. Louis and how to choose a trainer, then hire the walk once the dog can do the walk.
### Is the walker insured and bonded, and what does that actually cover?
Those are two separate things. Liability insurance covers harm: your dog injured, another dog bitten, a neighbor’s gate broken. Bonding covers theft from inside your home. A walker may carry one, both or neither, and plenty of good independents carry only the first. Ask which, then ask to see the certificate.
Seeing it is the step everyone skips. A certificate of insurance is a one-page document, and any walker who genuinely carries coverage can photograph it and send it inside of five minutes. How fast that arrives tells you something real about how the business is run. So does a cheerful “I’ve never needed it,” which is not an answer to the question you asked.
Bonding matters more the more your house key is worth. A walker who isn’t bonded isn’t automatically a no, and in a metro full of solo operators you’d rule out some of the best people that way. It does mean thinking for thirty seconds about what sits within arm’s reach of your kitchen, and whether a rotating lockbox code beats a loose key in a bag. Ask about pet first aid and CPR certification while you’re there. It’s a short course, and a decent proxy for somebody treating this as a profession.
### Solo walker or a company with backup walkers?
Solo walkers give you consistency and one relationship. Companies give you coverage. The honest trade is that one walker who has known your dog for three years is better on nearly every single walk, and worse on the one Tuesday she wakes up with strep throat and nobody else has ever met your dog or knows which hook the harness hangs on.
Put the backup question to a solo walker directly, and listen for specificity. A serious independent has a real answer: a named colleague who has already met your dog and been walked through your house, or a flat admission that there is no backup and you’ll need your own plan for those days. Either of those is workable. A vague one isn’t.
Companies flip the equation. Coverage is built in, somebody always comes, and a phone gets answered at four on a Friday when your flight slips. What you give up is the guarantee of the same hands on the leash, and dogs notice that more than owners expect. Ask how many walkers would rotate through your house in a normal month, and whether you can request a primary. Many will say yes if you ask at the start.
For longer absences the math changes completely, and a midday walk may be the wrong product altogether. Our guide to dog boarding and daycare in St. Louis covers what to do with the week you’re gone rather than the afternoon.
### Should your dog be on a group walk or a solo walk?
That depends on the dog, and for a lot of dogs the honest answer is solo. Group walks cost less per dog and they’re genuinely good for a sociable, well-mannered adult who enjoys company. They’re wrong for reactive dogs, puppies still learning leash manners, arthritic seniors, and anyone who can’t be managed safely beside two or three others.
Ask how many leashes end up in one hand. Three is common. Four is a lot. Past that you’re paying somebody to direct traffic rather than walk your dog, and a tangle at a curb with five dogs is exactly how a handler gets pulled into a street.
Some group setups involve transport, which opens a second category of questions. Is every dog crated or harness-restrained? Is the vehicle air conditioned? How long does any one dog ride? Ask to see the van. People who keep a clean one are proud to show you.
Solo costs more and what it buys is attention. If your dog needs a slow route, time to sniff, and no other animals in the mix, that’s the product. It also means that on the afternoon something goes sideways, one set of eyes is on one dog instead of four.
A leashed walk also isn’t the same thing as off-leash running, and some dogs need both in a week. The best dog parks in St. Louis guide covers where to go on the Saturdays you’re the one holding the leash.
### How should a walker handle your house key?
A lockbox on the spigot beats a key in a stranger’s coat pocket. The question isn’t whether you trust this person. It’s what happens to that key if a bag gets stolen, a walker changes careers, or somebody stops answering texts in March. A code you can change in ten seconds is a better system than trust.
Roughly best to worst for most houses: a smart lock with a code issued only to the walker, a lockbox with a combination you rotate, a physical key carried on a tag with no identifying information, and a key under the mat. That last one isn’t a system. It’s a hope.
Tag rules are worth stating. Whatever a walker carries should never show your address, your last name or your dog’s name, because a lost keyring with all three on it is a house tour. Ask where keys live between walks, whether any key sits in a car overnight, and what happens to yours the week the arrangement ends.
Write that ending down now, while everyone is friendly. Key comes back, or the code gets deleted, and you’re the one who deletes it. Decide too what a walker should do if the door is already unlocked at 1:50, or the alarm is chirping, or the garage sits open. Somebody with a written instruction for that doesn’t stand in your driveway guessing.
### What should the report after every walk tell you?
Five things: arrival and departure times, the route or rough distance, whether your dog went to the bathroom and how it looked, water or treats given, and anything out of the ordinary. A limp, a cough, a refused walk, a new dog barking through a fence. Most walkers send it as a text or an app note with a photo attached. Every walk.
The photo isn’t sentimental. It’s evidence. Time-stamped, outdoors, your dog visible in it. That one image confirms the walk happened, roughly when, and that your dog was upright and moving under her own power. A walker who sends the same shot of a dog on a living room rug every day is sending you a picture, not a report.
The bathroom note reads like a joke right up until it saves you a vet bill. A dog who hasn’t produced anything in two days, or produced something alarming, is the sort of thing an owner catches three days late and a walker catches that same afternoon. Consider it part of what you’re paying for.
### What happens if your dog gets hurt on a walk?
You decide that before it happens, in writing. A vet authorization note on file at your clinic, a spending ceiling the walker can approve without reaching you, your vet’s name plus the after-hours emergency clinic, and a second human who can make the call when your phone is face-down in a meeting. Ten minutes of paperwork, once.
Most clinics will keep a note on file saying a named person may bring your dog in and authorize treatment up to a limit you set. Without it, a walker at an emergency desk at 2:30 with a dog who got into something is just a stranger with no authority and no way to pay.
Ask the walker for her version of the plan as well. What would you do if my dog collapsed on a sidewalk? The answer you’re listening for is a sequence: get the dog somewhere safe, call you, call the clinic, and never drive off with an animal without telling somebody where you’re going. The answer you don’t want is “I’d figure it out.”
Cover the small emergencies too, because those are the ones that actually occur. A torn nail. A bee sting on a lip. A cut pad from broken glass behind a strip of shops in Union. Most of that needs a text and a note rather than a clinic, and a walker who reliably tells you about the little stuff is a walker who will tell you about the big stuff.

### Leash rules, harnesses, and St. Louis heat and ice
No retractable leashes, ever, and no off-leash anything without your written permission. A fixed four to six foot leash clipped to the gear you specify, a backup slip lead in the bag, and a walker who understands that a ninety-degree July afternoon and a salted January sidewalk are both injuries waiting to happen.
Spell the gear out rather than assuming it. Which harness, which clip point, whether tags stay on, where the spare leash lives. Then spell out what isn’t allowed: no prong collar, no e-collar, no swapping to her own leash because yours is in the wash, no handing your dog off to a friend who came along that day. Written once, it never has to be a conversation again.
Pavement in a St. Louis summer does something people badly underestimate. Asphalt in direct sun runs far hotter than the air above it, and a paw pad blisters at temperatures your hand shrugs off for a second or two. The seven-second test settles it: press the back of your hand flat to the surface, and if you can’t hold it for seven seconds, your dog shouldn’t walk on it. Grass routes, shade, earlier or later, water in the bag. Ask what the hot-weather protocol is.
Winter is the quieter hazard, and the one that shows up in February feet. Rock salt and de-icer burn pads, split them open, and make dogs sick when they lick their paws in the doorway afterward. A walker who wipes feet at the door, carries balm or booties for the dogs who tolerate them, and routes around the stretch of sidewalk somebody just treated is doing real work you’ll never see happen.
Then ask the blunt weather question: at what point do you not walk my dog? Lightning, ice storms, a heat advisory, bad air. The answer you want is that the walk becomes a short potty break plus indoor time and you hear about it, not that it gets skipped quietly and billed anyway.
### Is it okay to not walk my dog every day?
For most healthy adult dogs, an occasional missed day does no harm. A pattern of missed days does. Exercise needs swing wildly by breed, age and health, so ask your vet what your specific dog needs, because a thirteen-year-old beagle and a two-year-old cattle dog are not running the same program at all.
What goes wrong on skipped days is rarely fitness. It’s behavior. Chewing, barking at nothing, digging at a door frame, pacing, the six o’clock sprint through the house that ends with a lamp on the floor. A dog who hasn’t been outside since seven in the morning isn’t badly behaved at four in the afternoon. She’s under-stimulated and out of options.
Bathroom timing is the harder ceiling. Adult dogs can hold it considerably longer than is comfortable for them, and puppies, seniors and dogs on certain medications can hold it far less. That’s why plenty of households in Sunset Hills and Oakville book a short midday visit rather than a long walk. The point is the break, not the mileage.
### How do you choose between the two you interviewed?
Line up what you asked for against what each one actually told you, then hire the gap rather than the rate. You asked for a one-to-three window, a solo walk, a photo report, and a same-day text if anything looked off. One walker addressed all four. One addressed two and changed the subject. There’s your decision.
The right person gives herself away by asking things you hadn’t considered. Where does she like to be touched? Is she reactive to bikes? Which door should I use? Does the mail carrier come while I’m here? Is there a room she’s not allowed in? That’s somebody who has walked a hundred dogs in a hundred houses.
Start small anyway. Two weeks at a reduced schedule, a real check-in call at the end of it, and an honest conversation about what to adjust. Ask for the package rate and the cancellation policy in that same conversation, since both get easier to sort out before a routine has calcified. Most trouble in this arrangement is fixable, and nearly all of it is communication.
Watch the dog, in the end. Two weeks in, a dog who has made up her mind about her walker will tell you at 1:45 by parking herself at the back door, ears up, waiting. That’s the only review worth anything.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the red flags in a pet sitter?
A.  No proof of insurance when you ask for it, no written service agreement, no answer to the backup question, and reluctance to do a meet-and-greet with your dog in the room. Add vague arrival windows, reports that arrive late or in batches, and any resistance to giving you a vet clinic plan in writing. One of those is a conversation. Three is a pass.
### Q. Are dog walkers worth it?
A.  For a dog alone eight or nine hours on weekdays, usually yes, and the return shows up in behavior more than fitness. Less chewing, less barking, fewer accidents, a calmer evening. The value isn’t really the exercise, it’s breaking a very long day in half. Households with puppies, seniors or high-energy breeds tend to feel the difference inside two weeks.
### Q. How many hours a week should a dog be walked?
A.  Think in daily habit rather than a weekly hour total. Most healthy adult dogs do well with outdoor time every day, split across one or two outings, and working or sporting breeds generally need noticeably more than that. Seniors, flat-faced breeds and dogs with joint problems often need shorter and more frequent instead. Ask your vet for a number that fits your actual dog.
### Q. How much should you pay to walk a dog?
A.  Rates vary across the metro, so judge the structure instead of hunting for a figure. What moves a price: walk length, solo versus group, number of dogs in your house, whether a key pickup is involved, distance from the walker’s other stops, holidays, and last-minute bookings. Ask for the package rate for your regular schedule and get the cancellation policy in the same sentence.
### Q. How long should a pet sitter stay at your house?
A.  Match the visit to the job. A bathroom break and fresh water fits a short drop-in. A real walk plus a settle-down usually wants a half-hour block. Medication, a puppy, or a dog with separation anxiety often needs a full hour, and dogs who can’t be left overnight need overnight care instead of visits. Decide the task first, then buy the length that covers it.
### Q. Is it okay to walk my dog once a day?
A.  For many adult dogs, one solid daily walk plus yard time works fine. It falls short for puppies who can’t hold it that long, seniors who need frequent short outings, and high-drive breeds who empty a single walk’s worth of stimulation in twenty minutes. Watch for chewing, pacing and evening restlessness. Those are the signs one walk isn’t covering it.
### Q. How do I know the walk actually happened?
A.  Ask for a time-stamped outdoor photo with every report, plus arrival and departure times and the route. Many walkers use apps that log a GPS track automatically, which settles the question entirely. A doorbell camera on your own house closes the loop without anybody feeling watched. Set that expectation at the meet-and-greet, not after a week you’re unsure about.
### Q. Should I give my dog walker a house key or a lockbox code?
A.  A code beats a key for most households, because you can change it yourself in seconds and you never have to chase anything down when the arrangement ends. A smart lock code issued only to your walker is the cleanest version. If you do hand over a physical key, keep the tag free of your name, address and dog’s name, and agree in writing on how it comes back.

## What Dominican Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-dominican-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
A plate lands and the middle of it is a pale mound about the size of a fist, smooth as mashed potato, glossed with oil, wearing a tangle of red onion that has been sitting in vinegar since morning. Around the mound: a slab of white cheese browned on both faces, two thick coins of fried salami, a fried egg with the yolk still loose. Nothing on the plate is spicy. Not one thing.
That mound is mangu. The three things around it are los tres golpes, the three hits: cheese, salami, egg. It’s Dominican breakfast, and plenty of kitchens will hand it to you at two in the afternoon without comment.
Dominican cooking runs on a short ingredient list and a lot of patience with it. Plantains at two different stages of ripeness. Rice cooked so the bottom layer toasts on purpose. Beans simmered soft with a piece of squash that melts into the pot. Chicken or beef browned hard, then left in liquid until a fork slides through. Garlic, oregano, cilantro, bell pepper, vinegar, citrus. Salt and sour do the work that other islands hand to chile heat, and if you want the wider map, our guide to what Caribbean food is and what to order in St. Louis sets the islands next to each other.
So: the pantry, the plate, and what to say at the counter the first time.
### What to order at a Dominican restaurant?
First visit, order la bandera dominicana: white rice, stewed red beans, a stewed meat, and salad. That is the everyday lunch plate, and it tells you how the kitchen cooks. Add tostones on the side. If breakfast is running, get mangu with los tres golpes instead, and ask for concon.
Why that plate instead of something more interesting? Because it’s the thing a Dominican kitchen makes every single day, which makes it the thing you can actually judge. Pollo guisado that was browned before it was stewed tastes nothing like chicken boiled in sauce. Beans cooked down with squash taste nothing like beans from a can with seasoning stirred through. You’ll know within three bites.
Steam-table counters make this simple. Point at the rice, point at the beans, point at the meat, and somebody ladles it over the top. Most places keep three or four stewed meats going at once: chicken, beef, oxtail, sometimes goat on a weekend. Ask which one went into the pot earliest. That’s the one that’s had time.
Ordering for two? Split the job. One person takes la bandera, the other takes mangu with the fried plate, and you trade halfway across the table.
### What is mangu, and why is it breakfast?
Mangu is green plantain, boiled until soft, then mashed with some of its own cooking water and a slick of oil until it turns smooth and heavy. No butter. No cream. On top goes cebolla encurtida, red onion cooked briefly in vinegar until it goes pink and sharp.
The sourness is the entire design. Green plantain by itself is starchy and flat, nearer a boiled potato than a fruit, and it needs acid the way a plain bean needs salt. Those onions supply it. Push them to the side of the plate and you have eaten the dish wrong, which first-timers do constantly.
Los tres golpes are the traditional partners. Queso frito is a firm white frying cheese that squeaks a little and browns rather than melting. Salami frito is thick-cut Dominican salami, fried until the edges curl and darken and go faintly sweet. Huevo frito is the egg, and the yolk is meant to run down into the plantain. Three hits, because the plate is supposed to land.
Texture tells you more than seasoning does. Good mangu is dense and holds the mark of the spoon. Watery means too much cooking liquid went in; lumpy means the plantain came off the heat early. Look at the onions too. Pink, glossy, still with some bite.
### What is la bandera dominicana?
La bandera dominicana means the Dominican flag, and it’s the country’s standard midday meal: white rice, stewed beans, a stewed meat, and a simple salad, all on one plate. Lunch is the big meal of the day there, and in a lot of households this plate turns up close to daily.
### Habichuelas guisadas, the stewed beans
Red beans, usually, simmered with sofrito and a chunk of auyama squash that dissolves and thickens everything around it. Some cooks add a spoon of sugar. Others have opinions about the cooks who do. The result is soupy rather than refried, closer to a sauce than a side, and it gets spooned over the rice until the rice stains at the edges.
### Pollo guisado, the stewed chicken
Chicken browned in caramelized sugar, which is the step that makes it Dominican rather than generally Caribbean. Sugar goes into hot oil until it darkens, the chicken goes in and takes color, then liquid, tomato, sofrito, and time. The sauce comes out mahogany and a shade sweet. Beef pulls the same trick under the name carne guisada.
### The rice and the salad
Long-grain white rice, cooked dry and loose. The salad is usually cabbage and tomato with vinegar and oil, or a potato salad tinted pink with beet. Neither one is trying to be the point. They cut the richness and reset your mouth between bites of stewed meat, and that is a real job.
### Tostones, maduros and the plantain rules
One fruit, two completely different dishes, and ripeness is the whole difference. Green plantain fries up starchy and savory. Black-skinned ripe plantain fries up sweet and soft. Tostones are the green version, smashed and fried twice. Maduros are the ripe version, sliced and fried once.
Tostones begin as thick green rounds fried pale gold, then pulled out, flattened with the bottom of a cup or a wooden press, then sent back into the oil. The second fry is where the crust happens. They arrive craggy and salted and they want something sour with them: lime, a garlic sauce, or the same pickled onions from the mangu plate.
Maduros go the other direction entirely. Ripe plantain cut on the bias, fried until the sugars caramelize at the edges and the middle goes nearly custardy. Sweet against salty stewed meat, which is exactly why they belong on the plate. Cannot decide? Maduros with anything stewed, tostones with anything fried.
Chicharron lives in the same neighborhood. Pork belly or shoulder cut into chunks, seasoned, fried until the skin blisters hard and the meat underneath stays soft. Squeeze lime over it. Eat it with your hands.
### Sancocho, and the reason it takes all day
Sancocho is the pot a family cooks for a birthday, a funeral, a cold rainy Sunday, or any afternoon when everybody is coming over. Several meats in one broth, plus root vegetables added on a schedule: yuca, yautia, name, auyama, green plantain, corn.
The meats are where the pride lives. Sancocho de siete carnes uses seven, some combination of beef, pork, chicken, goat, longaniza sausage and smoked pork, and each one enters the pot when it needs to so nothing shreds while something else is still tough. The roots break down at different speeds as well. By the end, the broth has thickened itself on starch alone, with no flour anywhere near it.
It comes in a bowl with white rice on the side and avocado on top, and the rice is meant to go into the bowl. Do that. Sancocho without rice is a soup; sancocho with rice is dinner. Other countries cook their own version, and the Colombian one runs clearer with different roots, which what to order at a Colombian restaurant in St. Louis covers. Same word, different pot.
If a kitchen only makes it on certain days, believe the sign.
Different country, same bakery case: Czech food and what to order
### What is concon, and should you ask for it?
Concon is the layer of rice that toasts and sticks to the bottom of the pot, scraped up in sheets and eaten on purpose. Regulars ask for it by name. It’s crunchy, deeply toasted, slightly chewy where it met the wet rice above, and in many houses it’s the most fought-over thing on the table.
Every rice culture has a version. Persian tahdig. Korean nurungji. The socarrat at the bottom of a paella pan. Dominican cooks build theirs on purpose, letting the pot sit over low heat after the rice is done, sometimes with a little extra oil underneath. A good one lifts out in a piece rather than in crumbs.
Ask early. There’s only ever one layer per pot, and it disappears long before the rice does. Saying “concon, si hay,” meaning if there is any, is the polite version, and it quietly tells the person serving you that you know what you’re looking at.
### Why isn’t Dominican food spicy-hot?
Because heat was never the seasoning of record. Flavor here is built from garlic, onion, cilantro, oregano, bell pepper, vinegar and citrus, with sofrito under nearly every stew. Chiles show up as a bottle on the table, if at all, rather than in the pot.
That surprises people who hear Caribbean and expect fire. Most of that expectation comes from Jamaica, where scotch bonnet and jerk seasoning run hot by design. The Dominican Republic went a different route. Sour, salty, sweet where sugar gets caramelized for a stew, aromatic from herbs rather than sharp from capsaicin.
Small mild peppers do go into some sofrito, the kind grown for perfume rather than punch. They add smell, not sting. So bring anyone: kids, grandparents, the friend who orders mild at every taco counter. Nothing on a standard Dominican menu is going to ambush them.
### Mangu is not mofongo
Both are mashed plantain, and that’s where the resemblance stops. Mangu is Dominican: boiled, then mashed smooth into a soft flat mound. Mofongo is Puerto Rican: fried, then pounded in a wooden mortar with garlic and pork cracklings, coarse and chunky, usually packed into a dome.
Method changes everything. Boiling keeps the plantain pale and starchy and lets it drink liquid, so mangu ends up creamy and dense. Frying dries the outside and concentrates the sugar, so mofongo ends up savory and studded with crisp bits. One is a breakfast base for eggs and cheese. The other is often a vessel, hollowed and filled with shrimp or stewed meat.
Order the wrong one and you won’t be disappointed, only confused. Anyone lining up the islands’ plantain traditions side by side should know Cuban kitchens have their own entry, fufu de platano, and where to find Cuban food in St. Louis is the next stop for that comparison.
### A first order, and a second visit
Round one is lunch. La bandera with pollo guisado, tostones on the side, concon if any is left. Ask about avocado. Drink a morir sonando, orange juice whipped with milk and sugar over ice, and yes, that combination works despite everything your instincts are telling you right now.
Round two is breakfast, and go earlier than you think you need to. Mangu with los tres golpes, the full plate, no substitutions. Take one bite with all four elements at once: plantain, pickled onion, cheese, running yolk. That single bite is the argument for the whole cuisine.
Round three, if you get one, is sancocho on whatever day they make it. Bring somebody. It arrives in a volume that assumes company. On the way out, look at the sweets: habichuelas con dulce, a sweet cream of beans thickened with coconut milk, cinnamon and raisins and traditionally eaten during Lent, tastes far better than that description suggests. Flan, majarete, small cups, heavy sugar.
### Notes for the person cooking it, or running the kitchen
Two things separate a good home version from a flat one, and neither costs a cent. First is browning. Caramelizing sugar in oil before the meat goes in, then leaving the meat alone long enough to take real color, is where the mahogany sauce comes from. Rush that and you get pale, watery stew that no amount of later seasoning will save.
Second is the cooking water. Mangu gets mashed with the liquid the plantains boiled in, added a splash at a time, because that water carries starch and salt. Tap water thins the texture. Milk turns it into something else. Go slow and stop while it still holds a ridge.
For anybody running a kitchen, labeling matters as much as technique. A menu that spells out mangu, habichuelas guisadas, concon and sancocho, with one plain line of English under each, gets ordered by people who have never eaten the food before. A menu that says “mashed plantain” and stops there gets skipped. Name the dish properly, then explain it in eight words. That’s how a first-timer turns into a regular.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most famous Dominican food?
A.  La bandera dominicana, the everyday lunch plate of white rice, stewed beans, stewed meat and salad, is what most Dominicans would name first, because it’s what they actually eat. Outside the country, mangu with los tres golpes probably carries the bigger reputation. Sancocho is the dish families cook for anything worth gathering over. All three are fair answers, depending on who you ask.
### Q. What are some traditional Dominican dishes for dinner?
A.  Dinner runs lighter than lunch, since lunch is the big meal. Expect pollo guisado or carne guisada with rice and habichuelas guisadas, mangu with fried cheese and salami, or a bowl of sancocho on a cool night. Locrio, rice cooked in one pot together with chicken or pork, is another regular. Asopao is its soupier cousin, somewhere between rice and stew.
### Q. What do Dominican people eat for breakfast?
A.  Mangu, most often: boiled green plantain mashed smooth, topped with red onion pickled in vinegar, with los tres golpes alongside, meaning fried cheese, fried salami and a fried egg. Avocado if there is any in the house. Lighter mornings might be bread with butter and coffee, or the mashed plantain on its own. Nothing about it is sweet, and nothing about it is hot.
### Q. What do people eat mangu with?
A.  Pickled red onions first, always, because the vinegar cuts all that starch. After that, los tres golpes: queso frito, salami frito and a fried egg with a loose yolk. Avocado wedges turn up constantly. Some kitchens serve mangu under stewed chicken or beef instead, which pushes it into dinner territory, and plenty of people eat it plain with a spoonful of the onion liquid.
### Q. What is the English name for mangu?
A.  There isn’t a real one. Menus translate it as mashed green plantains, which is accurate and undersells the dish, since mangu depends on being mashed with its own cooking water and finished with oil rather than butter or milk. If a Dominican menu says “mashed plantain,” that’s mangu. The pickled onions on top are not a garnish, and they’re not optional either.
### Q. What is mofongo vs mangu?
A.  Boiled versus fried. Mangu is Dominican: green plantain boiled, then mashed with its cooking liquid into a smooth dense mound, usually eaten at breakfast. Mofongo is Puerto Rican: green plantain fried, then pounded in a wooden mortar with garlic and pork cracklings, so it lands coarse, chunky and savory. Mangu is a base for eggs and cheese. Mofongo is often a bowl for shrimp or stew.
### Q. Why is la bandera dominicana called the flag?
A.  The colors on the plate echo the national flag, with the white of the rice and the red of the beans doing most of that work. The name is affectionate rather than official, and the plate is so routine that plenty of families simply call it la comida, the food. Order it if you want to know how a kitchen cooks on an ordinary Tuesday.
### Q. How should you order sancocho for the first time?
A.  Ask which day the kitchen makes it, since many cook it only on weekends, and go then. Get white rice on the side and put the rice into the bowl. Avocado on top if it’s offered. Order one bowl between two people on a first try, because the portion assumes company, and taste the broth before you add anything at all to it.

## What Egyptian Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-egyptian-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
The bowl lands heavy enough to rattle the spoon. Rice and brown lentils underneath, short macaroni running through the middle, chickpeas scattered over the top, and across all of it a ladle of tomato sauce gone dark with cumin. Then the onions, fried in thin ribbons until they snap when you press them. Sweet scorched onion and vinegar. That is what an Egyptian lunch counter smells like.
This is koshari. Learn this one plate and you have a handle on the whole cuisine: cheap, filling, meatless almost by accident, assembled fast and eaten standing up. Carts sell it in Cairo. So do storefronts with four stools and a sign painted by hand.
People who have never eaten Egyptian food usually expect it to be hot. It isn’t. Cumin and coriander do most of the talking, garlic and vinegar sharpen the edges, and the chili sits in a squeeze bottle on the table where you decide how much of it you want. Beans carry the protein. Bread does the work of a fork.
So here is the pantry, the plate, and what to point at the first time somebody hands you a menu you can’t read.
### What is a typical Egyptian dish?
Koshari, and there isn’t much argument about it. Rice, brown lentils and short macaroni layered in one bowl, chickpeas over the top, cumin-heavy tomato sauce ladled across, crisp fried onions last. You finish it yourself from the table with daqqa, a thin garlic-vinegar liquid, and shatta, the chili sauce.
Nobody designed this dish. It reads like three kitchens colliding, lentils and rice from one direction, pasta from another, Egyptian tomato and fried onion holding the whole thing together, and by the late nineteenth century it had settled into the bowl you get today. Street food first. Restaurant food second, and some shops still serve nothing else.
The other honest answer is ful medames. Ask a hundred Egyptians which dish is the national one and the room splits. Ful is dried fava beans stewed slow and long, often overnight in a tall narrow pot, then mashed roughly and dressed with olive oil, lemon, cumin, sometimes tahini, sometimes a chopped tomato. Millions of people eat it before work.
Both dishes say the same thing about this food. Legumes sit at the center of the plate rather than off to the side, and that holds across a lot of the continent. Our guide to what African food is and what to order in St. Louis runs into the same principle from Ethiopia and West Africa.
### What goes into koshari, layer by layer?
Six parts, built in order, and the order is the point. The bottom stays relatively dry, the middle gets sauced, the top stays crisp. Then you stir the whole thing together yourself once you have tasted it, which is exactly what Egyptians do.
### The base
Medium-grain rice cooked with brown lentils so the grains take on color, then a layer of small macaroni, elbows or short tubes, boiled separately and kept plain. Chickpeas go on next, cooked soft. Four starches in one bowl, which sounds absurd until you eat it and realize every one of them has a different chew.
### The sauce and the onions
The sauce is tomato reduced with garlic, cumin and a hit of vinegar, thinner than a pasta sauce and much more sour. Onions get sliced fine, salted, patted dry and fried deep until they turn mahogany. A good shop fries them through the day. A tired shop fried them at eight in the morning, and you can tell, because they bend instead of breaking.
### Daqqa and shatta
Daqqa is garlic, vinegar, often lemon and cumin, loose enough to pour, and it goes on generously. Shatta is the chili sauce: red, sharp, built from fresh or dried chilies with garlic and vinegar, and it is the only genuinely hot thing on most Egyptian tables. Start small. Add more. Nobody will judge you either way, and the bottle is right there.
### What do Egyptians eat for breakfast?
Ful medames and ta’meya, with bread, usually before the sun is properly up. Add a boiled egg, some soft white cheese, a plate of raw vegetables, olives, maybe an egg fried in the pan the ful came out of. Tea afterward, always.
### Ful medames
The beans are small dried favas, and the cooking is the entire skill: hours over low heat until the skins go tender and the starch thickens the liquid around them. It arrives in a shallow dish, mashed partway with the back of a spoon, then finished at the table with oil, lemon, cumin, chopped tomato and sometimes tahini.
### Ta’meya, the fava falafel
Here is the thing most Americans get wrong. Egyptian falafel isn’t made from chickpeas. Ta’meya is ground dried fava beans worked hard with parsley, cilantro, dill, scallion, garlic, coriander and cumin, so the inside comes out green rather than beige. Flatter patties, a sesame crust, a softer and moister texture than the Levantine version. Split one open and look at the color.
If chickpea falafel is your reference point, order both side by side sometime. The difference isn’t subtle, and once you have noticed it you will spot a fava patty from across a counter.
### Why is baladi bread the only utensil you need?
Baladi bread is whole wheat, dusted with bran, slapped into a furiously hot oven and puffed into a round with a pocket. You tear off a piece, fold it against your thumb to make a small shovel, and scoop. No fork ever touches the ful.
It is darker and nuttier than the pale pita most Americans know, chewier too, with a faintly sour edge from a long ferment. Fresh baladi is soft as cloth. An hour later it firms up and suits stew better than dips. In Cairo people buy it by the stack, still warm, off the back of a bicycle.
Ask whether the bread is baked in-house. A kitchen that bakes its own baladi is telling you something about the rest of the menu, and you will taste it in the first bite.
### What is molokhia, and will you like it?
Molokhia is a soup of jute mallow leaves, minced to almost nothing and cooked in broth, usually chicken or rabbit. Texture is the whole conversation here. It is slippery and faintly viscous, closer to okra than to spinach, and people either love that or they don’t.
What makes it worth ordering anyway is the taqliya. Garlic gets crushed and fried in ghee with ground coriander until it sits just short of burnt, then the sizzling fat goes into the pot and the pan hisses. That smell carries through a whole building. One of the best smells in any kitchen anywhere.
Eat it over rice with the chicken it was cooked with, a squeeze of lemon, raw onion in vinegar alongside. Try it. If the texture isn’t for you, you will know inside two spoonfuls, and no Egyptian cook will be even mildly surprised.
### Mahshi, hawawshi and the plates that come out for a feast
Mahshi means stuffed, and it covers a family of dishes rather than one. Grape leaves, cabbage leaves, hollowed zucchini, peppers, tomatoes, sometimes eggplant, all packed with short rice mixed with dill, parsley, mint, onion and tomato, then simmered in a tomato broth until the vegetable gives up and goes soft. Cold mahshi the next day is arguably better.
Hawawshi is the sandwich to know. Spiced minced beef or lamb with onion, parsley and chili gets pressed inside a round of baladi bread, then baked until the crust crisps and the fat soaks into it from the inside out. Messy in the correct way.
Fattah appears at celebrations, Eid al-Adha especially. Toasted or fried bread on the bottom, rice over that, a garlic-and-vinegar tomato broth poured through all of it, then chunks of boiled beef or lamb on top. It is a dish built around a big pot of meat and a lot of relatives. See it offered, order it.
Hamam mahshi, pigeon stuffed with cracked wheat or rice and roasted, is a real Egyptian specialty and a harder sell on a first visit. Good to know it exists. Try it on visit four.
### How is Egyptian food different from Turkish or Levantine menus?
Three things separate it. Fava beans instead of chickpeas in the falafel, whole-wheat baladi instead of pale pita, and a cumin-and-coriander spine where a Levantine kitchen reaches for sumac, allspice and za’atar. Egyptian cooking also spends far less time over charcoal than Turkish cooking does.
Turkish menus lean on the grill and on wheat: kebabs over coals, pide and lahmacun out of a wood oven, yogurt on everything. Egyptian menus lean on the pot. Stewed beans, braised greens, layered rice, bread used as an ingredient rather than a wrapper. If kebab is your comfort zone, our piece on what Turkish food is and what to order in St. Louis maps that grill in detail.
Greek and Levantine tables will feel closer, and the overlap is real: tahini, lemon, olive oil, stuffed vine leaves, rice pudding. Where they part company is the spicing and the beans. A local guide to Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis is the useful next stop if mezze is what you actually want.
Shawarma exists in Egypt too, and it isn’t so much a Levantine import as a shared regional dish with an Egyptian accent. Usually beef or veal, sometimes chicken, shaved off a vertical spit, tahini and pickles, wrapped in baladi rather than thin lavash.
Eating well is one night out; choosing a dance studio is a habit
### What should you order the first time?
A bowl of koshari, an order of ta’meya, a plate of ful, and bread. That is the entire beginner order, and it usually costs less than people brace for. Split it across two people so nobody has to commit to a full portion of anything unfamiliar.
Eat the koshari plain for three bites before you add a thing. Then a little daqqa, then a little shatta, then stir. That sequence teaches you what each element is doing, and it keeps you from drowning the bowl before you know what it tastes like underneath.
Second visit, go heavier. Hawawshi, molokhia over rice with the chicken, mahshi if they made it that day, shawarma if the spit is turning. Ask what came out of the kitchen an hour ago instead of reading the menu top to bottom. That answer beats anything printed.
### What to drink, and how the sweets work
Karkade is the one to try. Dried hibiscus steeped into a deep red infusion, hot in winter and ice cold in summer, tart like cranberry with none of the fruit sweetness behind it. Sweetened heavily as a rule. Ask for less sugar and most kitchens will oblige.
Egyptian mint tea is strong black tea with fresh mint pushed down into the glass, not an herbal tisane standing on its own. Sugar goes in before it reaches you. It arrives scalding and you drink it anyway.
Dessert starts with roz bel laban. Rice pudding, thick and milky and barely spiced, sometimes dusted with cinnamon or scattered with pistachio, served cold in a small dish. Om ali is the extravagant one: torn pastry or bread baked in sweetened milk with coconut, nuts and raisins until the top browns and the middle sets into custard. Order the rice pudding if there is only room for one.
### If you cook it at home, or cook it for a living
Stocking an Egyptian pantry is cheap. Cumin and coriander, whole and ground. Dried mint. Brown lentils, short macaroni, medium-grain rice, split dried fava beans, chickpeas. Tomato paste, white vinegar, decent olive oil, ghee, tahini. That is most of it, and a Middle Eastern grocery anywhere around St. Louis will have all of it on one aisle.
For anyone running a kitchen or a bakery: texture words are what sell these dishes to a newcomer. Say slippery about the molokhia, crisp about the onions, green inside about the ta’meya. Describe what a thing is like and not only what it is called. People order the dish they can picture.
Ready to go eat? Browse Egyptian food around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two, and go hungry enough to order the koshari and the ta’meya in the same sitting.
