### At home, for a guest
Cooking for a kosher guest in your own kitchen is harder than it looks, because your pots and oven aren’t kosher even when every ingredient is. The kindest move is to ask. Many observant guests will gladly eat sealed, certified food served on disposable plates, or whole fruit, or something from a certified bakery left in its packaging. Some would rather bring their own. Neither answer is an insult. Those are just the rules.
### Frequently asked questions about kosher food
### Q. What are the three main rules of kosher?
A.  Eat only permitted animals: cud-chewing mammals with split hooves, fish with fins and scales, and traditionally accepted birds, so no pork and no shellfish. Slaughter and prepare meat properly, through shechita and blood removal. Never mix meat with dairy. Certification, separate dishes and agency symbols all grow out of those three rules.
### Q. Which is stricter, kosher or halal?
A.  Neither, really. Each forbids things the other allows. Kosher bans shellfish outright and never mixes meat with dairy, while many halal traditions permit seafood and have no meat-and-dairy rule. Halal forbids alcohol, while kosher allows supervised wine. Both ban pork and blood.
### Q. What is the difference between U and K for kosher?
A.  The circled U is the trademarked symbol of the Orthodox Union, one of the largest kosher agencies, so it means that agency supervised production. A plain K can’t be trademarked. Any company can print it, and it only tells you the maker claims the product is kosher, without saying who supervised or whether anyone did.
### Q. Is there a universal kosher symbol?
A.  No. No single government office or religious authority issues one mark. Hundreds of independent agencies certify kosher food, each with its own logo, from the circled U to stars, triangles and Hebrew letters. In St. Louis, one local certifier is the Vaad Hoeir. Observant shoppers learn which marks they trust, and many communities keep lists.
### Q. What kosher foods can Jews eat?
A.  Plenty. Fruits, vegetables, grains, beans and nuts are kosher in their natural state, though produce gets checked for insects. Eggs from kosher birds, fish with fins and scales, and meat from kosher animals slaughtered by shechita all qualify. Processed foods work too when they carry a trusted certification, and wine needs its own supervision.
### Q. Is kosher certification worth it?
A.  For a bakery, caterer or restaurant, it depends on who you want to feed. Certification opens the door to customers who keep kosher and can’t eat at uncertified places, and some shoppers who don’t keep kosher read the symbols anyway. It also brings fees, inspections and kitchen changes. Talk with two or three agencies before deciding.
### Q. What does pareve mean on a label?
A.  Pareve means the food has no meat or dairy in it and wasn’t made on meat or dairy equipment, so it can be eaten with either kind of meal. Fruits, vegetables, grains, eggs and kosher fish are pareve. Watch the letters by the symbol: P means Passover, not pareve, and DE means dairy equipment.

## Shopping at a Kosher Grocery Store in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/shopping-at-a-kosher-grocery-store-in-st-louis
The cooler goes in the trunk before the kids do. It’s a Sunday morning in High Ridge, and a dad is working through a list his sister-in-law texted him the night before: two whole chickens, ground beef, a brisket if the price doesn’t scare him, a challah, something pareve for dessert, and “the good grape juice, the one with the symbol.” She keeps kosher. She’s staying a week. He has never once set foot in a kosher grocery store and has no real idea what he’ll find when he gets there.
His kids don’t either. They’re mostly worried about snacks.
That trip is what this guide is about. Not the theology of kashrut, not a full symbol decoder, just the practical part: what a kosher supermarket actually is, what sits on its shelves, how to fill a cart at an ordinary store instead, why the meat bill runs higher, and how to plan around holidays when the shelves empty fast. No store names. No prices. The rules and the labels work the same way across St. Louis, and you can learn them in an afternoon.
### What is a kosher supermarket?
A kosher supermarket is a grocery store where the food on the shelves is certified kosher, usually under the supervision of a rabbinical agency. Fresh meat comes from a kosher butcher, the bakery and deli run under a hechsher, and meat and dairy are kept apart. Some stores are fully kosher; others are regular markets with a kosher department.
The difference between those two setups matters more than it sounds. In a fully kosher store, everything inside has passed through a certifying agency, and the store itself usually posts a certificate near the door or the register naming who supervises it. You can grab almost anything without flipping the box over. In a regular supermarket with a kosher department, that section sits beside everything else, and the job of checking shifts right back to you.
Smaller shops often split the work. One might be a kosher butcher with a few shelves of groceries up front. Another is a bakery that also sells soups from a freezer. A few run as full supermarkets with carts and checkout lanes. Same word on the sign. Very different trips.
Timing is its own thing. Stores under Orthodox supervision typically close before sundown Friday for Shabbat, stay closed through Saturday, and shut for major Jewish holidays as well. Friday mornings get crowded, and the days just before a holiday can be worse, because that’s when families stock up. Want a calm aisle and a butcher with time to talk? Go early in the week.
### What will you find inside a kosher grocery store?
Expect a meat counter or butcher, a deli with sliced meats and prepared dishes, a bakery, separate dairy and meat sections, a deep freezer aisle, and, each spring, a Passover section that can swallow a good part of the store. The mix depends on the store’s size, so a quick phone call before a long drive saves time.
### The meat counter
This is the reason most people make the trip. Kosher beef, lamb, chicken and turkey are slaughtered by a trained shochet, inspected, then soaked and salted to draw out the blood before they ever reach the case. The butcher may sell fresh cuts, sealed trays or both. Front-quarter cuts dominate: brisket, chuck, short ribs, shoulder, rib steaks. Hindquarter cuts are rare in American kosher shops, because removing the forbidden sciatic nerve and fats from the back half takes a great deal of skilled labor.
Talk to the butcher. Ask what’s fresh, what’s coming in later in the week, and whether they’ll cut or grind to order. You’ll also see the word glatt on a lot of packages. Strictly, it refers to a stricter lung inspection on beef, though many shoppers read it as shorthand for a higher standard overall.
### The deli and prepared foods
Behind the glass you’ll often find sliced corned beef, pastrami, turkey and salami, plus trays of ready-made food: roast chicken, kugel, stuffed cabbage, latkes, chopped liver, sides by the pound. For a working parent, that case can be the whole Friday dinner. Remember that the deli sits on the meat side. Anything bought there usually counts as meat, even a potato kugel, if it came out of a meat kitchen. Some stores label their pareve dishes separately. Not sure? Ask.
### The bakery
Challah is the headline. Braided, often sold in pairs for Shabbat, and baked round around Rosh Hashanah, sometimes with raisins. After that come rugelach, babka, cookies, sheet cakes and hamantaschen near Purim. Many kosher bakeries keep most of their goods pareve, made without butter or milk, so dessert can follow a meat meal. Not all of them do, though. If a cake is marked dairy, it means dairy.
### Dairy and meat, kept apart
The layout follows the rules. Meat and dairy live in separate cases, often at opposite ends of the store, and a store with its own kitchen may run separate prep areas for each. Cheese deserves a closer look. Kosher cheese needs supervision from start to finish, largely because of how rennet and equipment are handled, so the cheese case in a kosher store tends to look smaller and less familiar than the one at a regular market.
Milk, butter and yogurt are usually easy to find. Some shoppers also look for cholov Yisroel dairy, meaning milk supervised from the milking itself, and many kosher stores give it a shelf of its own.
### The freezer aisle
Freezers carry more of a kosher store than people expect. Chicken parts, ground beef, schnitzel, fish sticks, blintzes, pizza, soups, whole ready-to-heat dinners. For families who live a long way from a kosher butcher, frozen meat is how a couple of weeks of meals get bought in a single trip. It keeps. It also rides home in a cooler far better than fresh meat does.
### The Passover aisle
Every spring, weeks before the holiday, the shelves change over. Matzo in towers, matzo meal, macaroons, gefilte fish, jarred horseradish, kosher-for-Passover wine and grape juice, cake mixes made without flour, even Passover versions of ketchup and soda. Everything in that section should carry a P or the words “Kosher for Passover.” Regular kosher products don’t qualify just because they’re kosher the rest of the year. That’s the whole point of a separate aisle.
### How do you find kosher items in an ordinary supermarket?
Read the package. A huge share of everyday packaged food, from cereal and crackers to canned beans and soda, already carries a kosher agency symbol somewhere on the label. Larger supermarkets may also group kosher specialty items into one aisle or one freezer case, especially in the weeks before Jewish holidays.
Here’s the catch with that one kosher aisle: it’s mostly specialty stuff. Matzo, gefilte fish, borscht, imported snacks. The crackers, peanut butter and pasta your guest would happily eat are probably scattered across the whole store in their normal spots, each with a small symbol printed on the side. Don’t stop at the international foods aisle.
That dad from High Ridge figured this out by accident. He skipped the drive, went to his usual store first, and found half his list in the regular aisles before he ever reached the kosher shelf.
### Reading labels in the aisle
Flip the box. Check near the brand name first, then on the back near the ingredients or the nutrition panel. The symbol is often tiny. It might be a U in a circle, a K in a star, a triangle or Hebrew lettering. Next to it, look for a letter: D for dairy, M for meat, P for Passover, or the word Pareve. A plain K by itself tells you less, since any company can print one. For every symbol and what each letter means, our guide on how to tell if food is kosher in St. Louis goes much deeper.
Speed comes with practice. On the first trip you’ll flip every box in the cart and feel a little silly doing it, but by the third you’ll know which products you trust, which flavors carry a symbol, and exactly where on the package to glance. Snap a photo of labels you like. Next trip goes faster.
### Fresh produce and bulk bins
Raw fruits and vegetables don’t need a symbol, which makes produce the easiest part of the store. Washed, cut and bagged produce can be a different matter, and kosher kitchens check leafy greens for insects at home anyway. Bulk bins are trickier. Scoops get shared and bins get refilled from sources you can’t see, so many kosher shoppers skip them unless the store posts certification for the bins themselves.
### Ask at the counter
Store staff know more than you’d guess. The meat department can tell you whether any certified poultry or beef comes in, fresh or frozen. Customer service may know when holiday stock arrives. A manager can sometimes special-order a product if enough people ask. Plenty of kosher sections started exactly that way.
Waiting for challah to rise? Knit a scarf. Start with good yarn
### Do big-box and national chains carry kosher food?
Yes, though what shows up varies by store. Big-box retailers, warehouse clubs, discount grocers and national supermarket chains all sell packaged products with kosher symbols, because certification belongs to the manufacturer, not the retailer. Certified fresh meat is far less predictable. Some locations stock it, often frozen, and many don’t. Check the symbol and ask the store.
There’s a simple reason for the gap. A box of crackers gets certified at the factory, so it’s just as kosher on a shelf in any state. Fresh meat has to come from a kosher slaughterhouse and stay in its certified packaging, and a chain has to decide a particular store has enough demand to bother. Two locations of the same chain can carry wildly different selections. One has a full kosher freezer. The other, nothing.
Watch out for repackaging. If a store cuts or rewraps kosher meat in its own ordinary meat room, most observant shoppers won’t treat it as kosher anymore. The certification has to stay intact, usually as a sealed package bearing the agency’s mark, and poultry often carries its own tag or clip. Store brands show the per-product rule nicely. Some private-label items are certified. Others on the very same shelf aren’t.
Heading to a warehouse club before a big hosting weekend? Call first, and ask the meat or grocery department what certified products that location has right now. Two minutes on the phone beats a wasted drive.
### Why does kosher meat cost more?
Kosher meat usually costs more than conventional meat because more skilled work goes into every pound. A trained shochet handles the slaughter, inspectors reject animals with certain defects, workers soak and salt each piece, and an agency supervises the whole chain. Kosher plants also run smaller volumes, and much of the hindquarter gets sold off to the regular market.
Each of those steps is real labor. Salting takes time and floor space. Some animals that pass the standard federal inspection still fail kosher inspection, and they leave the kosher supply entirely. Supervision costs get built into the price. And since demand is small next to the conventional market, kosher suppliers don’t get the economies of scale that a giant national packer running around the clock enjoys.
Pantry goods are another story. A certified box of pasta from a national brand often costs about what any comparable box costs, and frequently there isn’t even an uncertified version, because the regular box is the kosher one. Specialty imports and holiday items can run higher. So can kosher cheese.
### How families plan around the cost
A common approach is to split the list. Pantry staples, produce and certified dairy come from wherever is closest. Meat comes from the kosher butcher or a kosher freezer case, bought in bigger batches and frozen at home. Front-quarter cuts like chuck and brisket reward low, slow cooking, so a slow cooker earns its counter space. Chicken stretches further than beef. A second freezer in the garage? For many kosher households outside the city, that’s standard equipment.
### When should you shop ahead for Jewish holidays?
Start weeks ahead for Passover and the fall holidays, and shop early in the week for Shabbat. Kosher stores close for Shabbat and major holidays, popular specialty items sell out, and holiday shipments arrive on the store’s schedule, not yours. Ask the store when holiday stock comes in, and place meat and challah orders early.
The fall stretch opens with Rosh Hashanah, then Yom Kippur, then Sukkot, often packed into a few weeks of September and October. Round challah, honey, apples, brisket, a pre-fast meal and a break-fast spread. Bakeries take challah orders in advance. Butchers take brisket orders in advance. Show up the morning before the holiday without an order and you may be staring at an empty case.
Passover is the big one. Eight days outside Israel, a seder or two with a crowd, and a whole kitchen that has to switch over to Passover food. The aisle usually opens weeks ahead, and the most popular items can vanish well before the first night. Shelf-stable goods like matzo, wine and grape juice can be bought early. Meat can be ordered for pickup a few days out.
Picture a family in Warrenton hosting cousins for a seder. They’re a long drive from any kosher butcher, so the smart version of their month looks like one big trip a few weeks out for shelf-stable goods, a meat order placed early and collected in a single run with a cooler, and a freezer cleared out ahead of time to make room. Hectic? Sure. But it’s hectic on their terms.
Hanukkah is gentler. Oil, potatoes and flour are sold everywhere, and latkes don’t need a specialty store. Purim brings hamantaschen and gift baskets of treats, and some bakeries do sell out, so an early order never hurts.
### Can you buy kosher groceries online?
Yes. Many kosher butchers, bakeries and specialty grocers ship across the country, and frozen meat usually travels in insulated boxes with dry ice or gel packs. Online ordering suits families far from a kosher store, but shipping costs, delivery windows and order minimums vary. Check the certifying agency on every product page before you buy.
Grocery delivery apps that pull from local supermarkets can help with certified pantry goods too. The problem is that you can’t flip the box. Product photos don’t always show the symbol clearly, and a substituted item may not be certified at all. Turn off substitutions for kosher items if the app lets you.
For shipped meat, be home. A box of frozen brisket sitting on a porch in Glendale on a July afternoon is a real problem. Pick a delivery day when somebody can carry it inside right away, check that everything arrived frozen solid, and get it straight into the freezer. Anything show up soft? Contact the seller before you cook it and follow their guidance.
Online works best as a backup. A local kosher butcher can answer questions, cut to order and tell you what’s good this week. A website can’t.
Planning a kosher grocery run? Browse kosher grocery stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call ahead before Friday afternoon, and ask what the meat counter has in stock.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when a family needs brisket, challah and a full Passover order in one stop, so list your kosher market, butcher shop or bakery.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to find kosher items in a grocery store?
A.  Check each package for a hechsher, the symbol of a kosher certifying agency, usually printed near the product name or on the back by the ingredients. Many larger stores also group kosher specialty foods into one aisle or freezer case. Ask customer service or the meat counter what they stock, since layouts and selection differ from store to store.
### Q. Which food brands are kosher?
A.  More than most people guess. Plenty of mainstream national brands certify many of their products, so kosher crackers, cereal, soda and canned goods turn up in almost any store. Certification belongs to each product, not the whole brand, though. One flavor may carry a symbol while the next one doesn’t, and certifications can change, so read every package.
### Q. Does Aldi sell kosher products?
A.  Discount grocers, Aldi included, typically stock some packaged products that carry kosher symbols, but there’s no blanket answer for any chain. Certification is printed product by product, and what a given store carries depends on location and season. Look for the hechsher on each item and ask the staff whether that store brings in extra kosher goods before holidays.
### Q. Is Costco meat kosher?
A.  Not by default. Meat at a warehouse club is conventional unless a package is specifically certified, and certified meat carries an agency symbol on its own sealed label. Some warehouse locations may stock kosher meat or poultry, often frozen, while others don’t. Check the label on the package itself and ask the meat department what that store carries.
### Q. Does whole food sell kosher meat?
A.  Natural-food grocers like Whole Foods sometimes carry certified kosher items, but availability varies a lot by location. Don’t assume the fresh meat case is kosher. Look for an agency symbol on a sealed package, and ask the butcher counter whether that particular store stocks kosher poultry or beef, fresh or frozen, and when it usually arrives.
### Q. What to look for when buying kosher?
A.  Look for a recognized agency symbol first, then the letter beside it: D for dairy, M or Meat, Pareve for neither, and P for Passover. On fresh meat, make sure the certified packaging is sealed and wasn’t rewrapped in a regular meat room. Shopping for a guest who keeps kosher? Ask which agencies they accept.
### Q. Are kosher grocery stores cheaper?
A.  Usually not. Kosher meat tends to cost more because of the supervision, skilled slaughter, inspection and salting behind it, and specialty stores buy in smaller volumes than giant chains. Certified pantry staples from national brands often cost about the same as comparable products, so many families buy those anywhere and save the kosher store for meat.
### Q. Is kosher meat actually healthier?
A.  Not necessarily. Kosher rules are religious, not nutritional. The inspection process rejects some animals with certain defects, and people sometimes read that as a health advantage, but there’s no settled evidence that kosher meat is healthier overall. Salting can add sodium. If you’re watching salt or managing a health condition, ask your doctor or a dietitian.

## Laser Eye Surgery in St. Louis: Who Is a Candidate?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/laser-eye-surgery-in-st-louis-who-is-a-candidate
It’s 6:40 on a weekday morning in Bethalto, and a nurse heading out for a twelve-hour shift is on her knees on the bathroom tile, patting around for a contact lens that just jumped off her fingertip. She finds it. It’s got lint on it. She rinses it, puts it in, blinks hard, and decides, not for the first time, that she’s going to look into LASIK this year.
Then the questions start.
Is she too old at forty-three? Are her eyes too dry? Does it matter that her prescription crept up a couple of years ago? And why do the ads all sound so sure of themselves when her sister-in-law was told flat out she wasn’t a candidate?
This guide walks through how candidacy actually gets decided, what a screening consult checks, the alternatives when laser surgery isn’t the right fit, and what to ask a surgeon before you book anything. No practice names, no prices, no promises. Your eyes are your own, and the only opinion that settles the question is the one from a surgeon who has measured them.
### How do I tell if I’m a candidate for LASIK?
You’re likely a candidate if you’re an adult with a prescription that has held steady for a year or more, healthy corneas that are thick and regular enough to reshape, no significant dry eye or active eye disease, and no health condition that slows healing. A surgeon’s screening exam is the only thing that confirms it.
### Is your prescription stable?
Eyes that are still changing are a moving target. If your glasses or contacts prescription has shifted recently, most surgeons will want to wait, because reshaping the cornea corrects the eye you have today, not the one you’ll have after it drifts again. Dig out your old prescriptions before the consult. They tell a story.
That’s one reason age matters. LASIK in the U.S. is generally limited to adults, and many surgeons prefer patients somewhat past their early twenties, when nearsighted prescriptions often settle down. Is there an upper limit? Not a hard one. Older eyes bring different questions, like early cataracts and presbyopia, and we’ll get to both.
### What about the shape and thickness of your corneas?
The laser removes tissue. That’s the whole trick, and it means your cornea needs enough thickness left over afterward to stay strong. Surgeons also study its shape. A cornea that’s irregular, or shows early signs of keratoconus, a condition where it thins and bulges outward over time, can be a reason to skip LASIK entirely, since removing tissue could make things worse. You can’t judge any of this in a mirror.
Very strong prescriptions run into the same wall. The bigger the correction, the more tissue has to go, and at some point a surgeon may steer you toward a different procedure altogether.
### Do dry eyes rule you out?
Not always, but dry eye is one of the most common reasons a consult slows down. LASIK can make dryness worse for a while because it disrupts corneal nerves that help trigger tears. Someone who already fights gritty, burning eyes by midafternoon might need treatment first, or a different procedure, or a frank talk about whether surgery makes sense at all. Tell the surgeon how your eyes really feel. Downplaying it helps nobody.
### Which health conditions matter?
Healing matters as much as the laser work. Surgeons tend to look closely at autoimmune conditions such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes that isn’t well controlled, anything that weakens the immune system, and eye problems like glaucoma, cataracts or a history of eye infections. Some medications raise flags too. None of that is an automatic no for everyone. It’s a conversation, so bring a full list of what you take.
### What about pregnancy?
Pregnancy and nursing are usually a pause, not a no. Hormonal shifts can temporarily change your prescription and your tear film, so most surgeons prefer to wait until things settle after you’ve finished nursing. Planning a pregnancy soon? Mention it. Timing matters here.
### What does the screening consult actually check?
A good screening consult measures far more than your prescription. Expect corneal thickness readings, a map of the corneal surface, pupil measurements, a tear-film check, eye pressure, a dilated look at the retina and lens, and a long talk about your health history, your job and what you’re hoping surgery will do for you.
Plan on it taking a while. Dilation drops blur your near vision for hours and make daylight feel blinding, so bring sunglasses and, ideally, a driver. Contact lens wearers usually get told to leave the lenses out for a stretch beforehand, because contacts can temporarily change the shape of the cornea and throw off the measurements. How long depends on the lens type. Ask when you book, not the night before.
Sometimes the consult turns up something that needs a medical eye doctor first, like signs of glaucoma or a retina problem. That’s the system working. Our guide on when to see an ophthalmologist in St. Louis covers the difference between routine eye care and a specialist visit.
### What does a no at screening really mean?
A practice that turns you away is telling you something useful. So is one that recommends a different procedure than the one you walked in asking about. Picture a guy from Wellston who’s been saving up for LASIK for two years, only to hear that his corneas are on the thin side and PRK or a lens-based option would be safer for his eyes. Disappointing? Sure. It beats the alternative.
### What if LASIK isn’t the right fit?
LASIK is one option among several. PRK reshapes the cornea without cutting a flap. SMILE removes a small disc of tissue through a tiny incision. Implantable lenses sit inside the eye and remove no corneal tissue at all, and refractive lens exchange replaces your natural lens. Which one fits depends on your measurements, and your surgeon makes that call.
### LASIK
In LASIK, the surgeon creates a thin hinged flap in the front of the cornea, folds it back, reshapes the tissue underneath with an excimer laser, and lays the flap back down. Many people see well quickly, often within a day or so. The flap is also its main tradeoff, since that part of the cornea doesn’t fully regain the strength of untouched tissue.
### PRK
PRK came before LASIK and it’s still widely used. Instead of making a flap, the surgeon removes the thin surface layer of the cornea and reshapes what’s underneath, and that surface grows back over the following days. Recovery is slower. It’s more uncomfortable, too, and vision can take weeks to sharpen fully.
So why pick it? PRK leaves more of the cornea intact, which can make it the better choice for thinner corneas, and there’s no flap to dislodge. People in contact sports, the military or law enforcement sometimes care a lot about that last part.
### SMILE
SMILE uses a femtosecond laser to shape a small lens-shaped piece of tissue inside the cornea, then removes it through a short incision. No flap. It’s newer than LASIK and PRK, it’s approved for a narrower range of prescriptions, and not every practice offers it. Ask whether it applies to your eyes specifically, not just in general.
### Implantable lenses
An implantable collamer lens, or ICL, is a thin lens placed inside the eye in front of your natural lens, a bit like a contact lens that stays put. Nothing gets removed from the cornea. That makes it a common suggestion for very high nearsighted prescriptions or corneas too thin for laser work. It’s surgery inside the eye, though, and it carries its own risks your surgeon should walk you through.
### Refractive lens exchange
Refractive lens exchange removes your natural lens and replaces it with an artificial one. It’s the same basic operation as cataract surgery, just done before a cataract forms. It tends to come up for people in their mid-forties and beyond with high prescriptions, early lens changes or a strong wish to cut back on reading glasses. Bigger step. And unlike a contact lens, you can’t just take it out.
### What happens to your reading vision after 40?
Somewhere in your early to mid-forties, the natural lens inside your eye stiffens and loses its ability to focus up close. It’s called presbyopia, and it catches up with nearly everyone. LASIK reshapes the cornea, not the lens, so it doesn’t stop presbyopia. Plenty of people over 40 still need readers after surgery.
This is the part that surprises people. Say you’re nearsighted at 45 and you’ve been slipping your glasses off to read a menu. That trick works because your nearsightedness happens to offset your aging lens. Correct the distance vision fully and the menu trick disappears, so you may walk out reading highway signs crisply and reaching for drugstore readers at dinner.
### What about monovision?
One workaround is monovision. The surgeon corrects your dominant eye for distance and leaves the other slightly nearsighted for reading, and your brain learns to use each eye for its own job. Some people love it. Others find their depth perception or night driving feels off. Many surgeons suggest trying it with contact lenses first, which makes for a cheap, reversible test drive.
### What changes after 60?
A retiree in Kimmswick asking about LASIK at 62 might hear something different altogether. By the sixties, many people have early cataract changes, and reshaping a cornea that sits in front of a slowly clouding lens may not make much sense. Cataract surgery with a lens chosen to reduce glasses dependence often becomes the better conversation. Age alone isn’t the barrier. The lens is.
### Will insurance pay for any of it?
Most health and vision plans treat LASIK and similar procedures as elective, so they usually don’t cover them. Some vision plans offer member discounts through certain providers. Flexible spending and health savings accounts may help, since refractive surgery is often an eligible expense. Confirm with your plan administrator before you schedule anything at all.
Call the member number on your card and ask three things. Does the plan cover refractive surgery at all? Does it have a discount arrangement, and with whom? What counts as an eligible expense for your FSA or HSA? FSA money often comes with a use-it-or-lose-it deadline, so timing a procedure around your plan year can matter. We’re not tax advisors, though, and your administrator is the one who knows your plan.
The routine eye exams around surgery are a separate question. Plenty of plans cover an annual exam even when they won’t touch the procedure, and our look at eye exam costs with a St. Louis optometrist explains how that usually works. Ask the surgical practice what care comes after the procedure, too, like follow-up visits and what happens if you need a touch-up later.
### What are the real downsides?
Dry eye is the most common downside, and for many people it eases over the following months, though for some it lingers. Glare, halos and starbursts around lights at night are common early on. Serious complications like infection, flap problems or corneal weakening are rare but real, which is exactly why careful screening exists in the first place.
Night vision complaints deserve a straight answer before surgery, not after. People with larger pupils or stronger prescriptions sometimes notice more halos. Drive at night for work? Say so at the consult, and expect the surgeon’s answer to be about your measurements, not a general pat on the shoulder.
Some people also end up slightly under- or over-corrected and need an enhancement, meaning a second, smaller treatment. Vision can drift again over the years as the eye ages. Surgery changes the cornea you have. It doesn’t freeze your eyes in time.
And the stuff nobody prints on the brochure? Recovery-week logistics. You’ll use drops on a schedule, avoid rubbing your eyes, skip swimming and eye makeup for a while, and need a ride home on surgery day. Small things. They pile up fast if you’re a parent or work a physical job.
New eyes, same squint at the grocery label: spotting kosher food
### How should you interview a laser eye surgeon?
Shortlist two or three surgeons and interview them the way you’d interview any doctor you plan to trust with something important. Tell each one plainly what you want and expect from surgery. Then listen for what they’re prepared to deliver for your eyes specifically. The gap between those two things is the signal, not the price.
### Questions worth asking
Am I a good candidate, and for which procedures? A surgeon who explains why you’re better suited to PRK or an ICL, using your own measurements, is showing their work. That’s what you want.
Who performs the surgery, and who handles follow-up? Ask whether the surgeon you meet is the one operating, and who you call if something feels wrong at midnight.
What do you expect my reading vision to look like in five or ten years? That’s the presbyopia question in disguise. A thoughtful, specific answer is a good sign.
What happens if I need an enhancement? Ask how they decide one is needed and how it’s handled.
When would you tell someone like me not to do this? Our favorite. A surgeon who answers without hesitation has probably turned people away before, and that’s reassuring.
### What should make you walk away?
Pressure to book on the spot. A consult that skips the dilated exam or the corneal mapping. Promises of perfect vision or never needing glasses again, because nobody can guarantee that and good surgeons don’t try. The nurse in Bethalto doesn’t need a sales pitch. She needs someone who’ll look at her dry eyes, her forty-three-year-old lenses and her shift schedule, then tell her the truth about all three.
Ready for a screening consult? Browse laser eye surgery across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three surgeons, and bring your old prescriptions to each consult.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when someone tired of fishing contacts off the bathroom floor finally asks whether they qualify, so list your refractive surgery or eye practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth getting LASIK after 40?
A.  It can be, if you go in knowing LASIK won’t fix presbyopia. Many people over 40 get sharp distance vision and still need reading glasses up close. Monovision is one option, and lens-based procedures may make more sense for some eyes. A screening exam and an honest talk about your daily life decide it.
### Q. Does insurance cover LASIK eye surgery?
A.  Usually not. Most health and vision plans treat it as elective. Some vision plans offer discounts through participating providers, and FSA or HSA funds may be usable, since refractive surgery is often an eligible expense. Call your plan administrator to confirm what applies to you before you pick a procedure date.
### Q. What is the downside of laser eye surgery?
A.  Dry eye is the most common, and it often improves over months but can linger. Glare, halos and starbursts at night are common early on. Some people need an enhancement. Serious complications like infection or corneal weakening are rare but possible, which is why screening matters and why some people get turned away.
### Q. Is there an alternative to laser eye surgery?
A.  Yes. Glasses and contacts are the obvious ones. Surgically, an implantable collamer lens corrects vision without removing corneal tissue, and refractive lens exchange replaces your natural lens, much like cataract surgery. For some people, PRK or SMILE is the better laser choice. Your surgeon’s measurements decide which options you actually have.
### Q. Do you still wear glasses after laser eye surgery?
A.  Many people don’t need glasses for distance afterward, but plenty still reach for a pair sometimes. Reading glasses are common after 40 because LASIK doesn’t stop presbyopia. Some people keep a light prescription for night driving, and vision can shift over time. Ask your surgeon what they expect for your eyes specifically.
### Q. Is 60 too old for laser eye surgery?
A.  Not automatically. There’s generally no firm upper age limit. By 60, though, many people have early cataract changes, and LASIK doesn’t address the lens. A surgeon may suggest cataract surgery or refractive lens exchange instead. Healthy eyes and a stable prescription matter more than the number on your birth certificate.
### Q. Can your vision still deteriorate after LASIK?
A.  Yes, it can. LASIK reshapes the cornea but doesn’t stop the eye from aging. Presbyopia still arrives in your forties, cataracts can develop later, and some people notice a small drift that may call for an enhancement. Keep up with routine eye exams after surgery so changes get caught early.
### Q. What disqualifies you from getting LASIK?
A.  Common reasons include an unstable prescription, corneas that are too thin or irregularly shaped, keratoconus, significant dry eye, certain autoimmune or poorly controlled health conditions, some eye diseases, and pregnancy or nursing, which usually means waiting. Very strong prescriptions can also rule it out. A screening exam is the only way to know.

## Sandal Tan Line? It Can Send You Home From Your First Laser Session
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-laser-hair-removal-in-st-louis
That pale stripe across the top of your foot, the one your sandal straps left after a summer of Saturdays in Forest Park, is about to matter more than your razor. Laser light hunts pigment. A tan, even a faint strap-shaped one, hands it a second target besides the hair, and the nurse who spots it under the treatment lamp may turn the settings down or send you home to rebook. So prep for laser hair removal in St. Louis doesn’t start at the bathroom sink. It starts on a porch in September, when you decide your legs are done with the sun for the year.
And here the sun has a long season to work with. The National Weather Service office for St. Louis says that since 1870, the city has hit 90 degrees or higher on about 35-40 days a year. That’s more than a month of shorts, tank tops and car-door-hot seatbelts, every one of them laying down pigment the laser will have to work around.
The other thing the prep email skips is who will be holding the handpiece. Section 334.010 makes it unlawful for anyone who isn’t a registered physician “to practice medicine or surgery in any of its departments.” Meanwhile the esthetician license in section 329.010 covers “removing superfluous hair by means other than electric needle,” wording that reads like it was written for wax pots and tweezers.
Where a laser lands between those two lines is exactly what med-spa compliance guides argue about. One Missouri med-spa guide puts it flatly: laser hair removal “must be done by or under the direct supervision of a physician.” That’s a secondary source, and we could not get a state agency to confirm it for us, so if an answer you get sounds vague, you can put the question to the Missouri Board of Registration for the Healing Arts.
Ask two St. Louis clinics the same question and you can hear the difference. WashU Medicine’s aesthetic services page says “Our dermatologists offer a wide variety of laser services,” with laser hair removal on the list, and books at 314-996-8810. Meanwhile Milan Laser says its clinics “are overseen by highly trained medical professionals specializing exclusively in laser hair removal.” Two different setups, both in writing. Neither one tells you whose hand will be on your shin at 4:30 on a Thursday, so that’s still your question to ask.
Here’s the line worth texting a friend before her first consult: the person with the laser in their hand should be able to name the doctor behind it, without checking. If they hesitate, you’ve learned more than the brochure will tell you.
Ask at the consult, clipboard on your knee and nothing paid yet, not at the front desk with your card already out. Which licensed clinician will treat me, and which physician supervises them? Will that same person be in the room at every session? Then borrow the question on the American Academy of Dermatology’s prep list: “How many of these laser treatments has the doctor performed on people with my skin coloring?” And the money one nobody thinks of until it happens: if I arrive tanned or with a patch unshaved, do I lose that session’s fee?
Now the thing you actually came for. You’re at the sink, warm water running, skin tight and pink from the blade, wondering if Tuesday is too early for a Friday appointment. Still sorting out the money? Start with what laser hair removal costs in St. Louis. Everything here is general information, and your provider’s consult decides what applies to your skin.
### Do I shave before laser hair removal?
Yes. Most providers want the area shaved, usually within a day or so of the appointment, so the laser reaches the root rather than hair on the surface. Don’t wax, pluck or thread, because the root has to stay in place. Your provider’s own instructions win if they differ.
Here’s the twist: the razor you were ready to retire is the tool you pick back up. Waxing, plucking, threading, sugaring and epilators all pull the root, and the root is the target. The laser hunts pigment in the hair and sends heat down the shaft into the follicle. Hair lying on top just soaks up energy it can’t use and can overheat the surface. You’ll smell it, too: the AAD describes the little plumes of smoke from vaporized hair as having “a sulfur-like smell,” and there’s more of it when there’s more hair to burn. A clean shave leaves the root exactly where the light can reach it.
### Shaved Tuesday for a Friday appointment?
Some clinics want a shave the night before or the morning of. Others prefer a day or two ahead so razor irritation settles. Is it okay to shave 2 days before laser hair removal? Often, yes, so long as nothing has grown back enough to sit above the skin. If the prep email doesn’t say, call. It’s a quick question.
### What about a little stubble?
A shadow of regrowth is usually fine. Real bristle isn’t. Run your palm up your shin: a faint rasp is okay, a prickle means shave again.
### The spots everybody misses
The backs of the thighs, the lower back, the hollow behind the knee. Use a hand mirror or a helper. Many providers will shave a small missed patch in the room; some charge, some don’t, and some reschedule if a whole area shows up unshaved, which is why the fee question at the top of this page matters.
Depilatory creams sit in a gray zone. Some clinics allow them between sessions, some don’t, and they can irritate skin right before treatment, so ask first.
### Before you sit down: what to stop, and what to write down
Stop waxing, plucking and threading the area, stay out of strong sun, skip self-tanner, and write down every medication and supplement you take. Exact waiting windows vary by clinic and by device, so follow the one your provider gives you, not a number from a forum.
### The pause on pulling hair
If you’ve waxed for years, this is the adjustment that stings. Clinics commonly ask for several weeks without anything that removes hair from the root before a first session, so the follicles grow a hair the laser can find. Shave in the meantime. It feels like going backward. It isn’t.
### Sun, sandal stripes and self-tanner
Tanned skin carries more pigment, and pigment is what the laser hunts, so a tan puts your skin in competition with your hair. A fresh tan, a sunburn or self-tanner can raise the chance of burns or of lighter and darker patches afterward, and a provider may turn the settings down or send you home to rebook. Spray tans count. So does that sandal-strap stripe from the top of the page. Check your legs in daylight before you book. The AAD’s instructions are blunt: “Do not tan (outdoors and indoors). Do not use sunless tanners.”
### Medications and photosensitivity
Some medications make skin more sensitive to light. Certain antibiotics, some acne treatments (especially ones taken by mouth) and a few supplements tend to show up on clinic lists, though the lists aren’t identical. Retinoid creams on the area can matter too. Never stop something a doctor prescribed on your own. Bring the full list, doses included, and let the provider and your prescribing doctor sort out timing.
Say these out loud too: cold sores if you’re treating the upper lip or chin, a tendency toward keloid scars, a recent skin infection, pregnancy, or a rash that won’t quit. If something on your skin needs a closer look first, a dermatologist is the right stop, and our guide to when to see a dermatologist in St. Louis explains how that usually works.
### Does your skin tone and hair color change the plan?
Yes, a lot. Laser generally works best when the hair is darker than the skin around it, because the light has an obvious target. Deeper skin tones can be treated with the right device and settings. Gray, white, red and light blond hair usually respond poorly, since there’s little pigment to find.
Different lasers use different wavelengths, and those interact with melanin differently, so the machine on the wall matters. So do the settings, the cooling and the person running it. The AAD notes that people with dark skin can now be treated, but that it “must be performed very carefully in these patients.”
With deeper skin, it’s fair to ask straight out: which laser would you use on me, and how often do you treat skin like mine with it? A confident, specific answer is what you’re listening for.
### Who is not a good candidate for laser hair removal?
If the hair holds very little pigment, most lasers just won’t see it, and a good provider says so before taking your money. Electrolysis, the electric-needle method that Missouri’s esthetician law carves out by name, is the usual alternative to ask about. Other reasons to pause, like a fresh tan or an active skin infection, get sorted at the consult.
Unrelated but overdue: a doctor who knows the rest of you. Try internal medicine.
### What do you do the day before and the morning of?
Shave on the schedule your clinic gave you, then keep the skin clean and bare. On the day, skip lotion, oil, deodorant, makeup and perfume on the treatment area, and wear loose clothing over it. If you’ve had sun since the consult, say so before the first pulse.
Bare matters because products sit between the light and the hair, and some leave a residue that heats up. Underarms are the classic trap: you swipe on deodorant out of habit and remember it in the parking lot, the clean-linen smell still on your skin. Many clinics keep wipes for exactly that.
Numbing cream is its own question. Some clinics offer it, some let you use an over-the-counter version, some would rather you skip it. Check before you slather anything on, since the amount and the area covered matter for safety. Then: loose clothes, earrings out if it’s the face, a clean shirt in the bag.
### What the chair actually feels like
How painful is hair laser removal? The AAD says many patients describe the pulses as “warm pinpricks or a rubber band being snapped against the skin.” It’s sharper over bone and in thick, dense hair like the underarm or bikini line, milder on the legs, and pain tolerance varies widely.
The room is quiet and a little clinical. Goggles go on for the whole session (the AAD says everyone in the room wears protective eyewear), and the world shrinks to the inside of the lenses. The provider may draw a white pencil grid so no patch gets skipped or hit twice. Then the cold: a chilled tip, a stream of cold air or a layer of gel, depending on the device. That cooling does a lot of the work of making it bearable.
And the smell: a faint burnt-hair odor drifts up with some pulses. Normal. It’s the hair, not your skin. The first session often stings most, partly nerves, partly more hair soaking up light. Speak up if a spot feels too hot. That isn’t complaining. Settings can be adjusted on the spot.
### When does the hair fall out, and what does your skin do first?
Expect redness and small raised bumps around each follicle, a bit like goose bumps crossed with a mild sunburn, and the AAD says the common side effects usually last 1 to 3 days. Anything that blisters, crusts or keeps getting worse is a call to your provider. As for how long after laser hair falls out, treated hairs usually shed over the following days to weeks.
### Right after
Cool is your friend. A cold compress or a soothing gel the clinic recommends takes the heat out. Many providers suggest skipping hot showers, saunas, hot tubs and hard workouts for a day or so, and fragranced products and scrubs until the redness fades. Sunscreen goes on every day, on anything the sun can reach.
### The shedding stage
In the days and weeks after, treated hairs work loose. At first it looks like stubble coming back, with little dark dots under the skin that people call peppering. Then they slide out in the shower or wipe off with a washcloth. Don’t pluck them.
### How far apart should sessions be?
How often is each laser hair removal session? There’s no single number. Sessions are spaced to match how hair grows in each area, so the face often comes back sooner and the body waits longer. Your provider sets the interval after seeing your hair, and going back early doesn’t speed anything up. For reference, the AAD says most patients can have a treatment “once every 4 to 6 weeks.”
Facial hair tends to cycle faster, legs and backs usually run on a slower clock, and underarms and bikini areas land in between for many people. Treating several areas? Ask whether they can share one calendar.
Will 3 sessions of laser hair removal do anything? Usually you’ll notice something. The AAD puts it at “a 10% to 25% reduction in hair after the first treatment,” and says most patients need 2 to 6 treatments. Hairs resting during those visits haven’t been treated yet, though. Slipping a week past your window isn’t usually a disaster, but letting months drift can mean fewer hairs caught at the right stage. Book the next appointment before you walk out.
### Why so many St. Louisans start when the leaves turn
St. Louis summers are long, bright and spent outdoors, and sun exposure is one of the main things that complicates laser. Starting in fall or early winter means the first several sessions happen while skin is covered and last summer’s tan has faded. By swimsuit season, a good chunk of the work is behind you.
Think of an ordinary summer here: Forest Park afternoons, lake weekends, yard work in humidity so thick the sunscreen is sliding off by noon. Say a guy in House Springs spends every Saturday on a boat. He isn’t walking into a July appointment with pale shins, and his provider knows it. Scheduling around the sun is easier than fighting it.
Summer isn’t off limits. Plenty of people treat year-round, especially areas that stay covered, like underarms or the bikini line. Faces and legs are harder, and in warm months sunscreen, hats and clothing coverage become part of the plan. Say a bride in Millstadt is counting back from a June wedding: she’s doing the same math in reverse, and autumn is where it points. Ask at the consult how far ahead to begin.
### How do you interview a laser provider before the first pulse?
Shortlist two or three providers and interview each the way you would a new doctor. Tell them plainly what you want treated, what your skin and hair are like, what you take, and what your summer looks like. Then listen to what each is prepared to deliver. The gap between those two is the signal, not the price.
Start with the questions from the top of this page. Then add: Which laser would you use on my skin, and why? What do you want me doing the week before and the morning of? What happens if I react badly two days later?
Ask about a test spot too, especially with deeper skin or a history of sensitivity. Many clinics will pulse a small patch and have you wait before the full session. A careful provider asks about medications before you mention them, actually looks at your skin, and tells you plainly if your hair color is a poor match. One who promises everything and asks nothing has told you something as well.
Book the consult before you book the first session. Browse laser hair removal providers across the St. Louis metro, pick two or three, and ask each one the same thing: who holds the laser, and which doctor stands behind them.
If you run the med spa, the laser studio or the one-chair clinic that answers that question without blinking, say so where people are already looking. A Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your clinicians, your devices and your fall openings in front of neighbors planning their first session, and that’s how careful clinics get more customers.
### Frequently asked questions from first-timers
### Q. Is it okay to shave 2 days before laser hair removal?
A.  Often, yes. Many clinics accept a shave a day or two ahead, and some prefer it because razor irritation has time to settle. Others want it the night before or that morning. Hair should be short enough that nothing sits above the skin. If your clinic’s instructions differ, theirs win.
### Q. Is a little stubble ok for laser hair removal?
A.  A trace of very short regrowth is usually tolerated, and some providers like seeing a hint of it to confirm where the hair is. Longer stubble is the problem, because hair above the skin absorbs energy, singes and heats the surface. Unsure? Shave again and let your provider decide.
### Q. How long after laser does hair fall out?
A.  Treated hairs usually shed over the days and weeks after a session. At first it can look like regrowth, with dark dots under the skin. Then the hairs slide out in the shower or wipe off with a washcloth. Don’t pluck them.
### Q. How painful is hair laser removal?
A.  Most people describe a rubber band snapping against the skin, followed by a burst of heat. Dense, coarse hair and bony areas tend to hurt more; legs usually hurt less. Built-in cooling helps, and some clinics offer numbing cream. Tell the provider if a pulse feels too hot, because settings can change.
### Q. Will 3 sessions of laser hair removal do anything?
A.  Usually you’ll notice something. Many people see thinner, patchier regrowth after a few sessions, though hairs that were resting during those appointments haven’t been treated yet. Stopping there tends to leave uneven results. How far three sessions get you depends on your hair, skin and area, so ask your provider what to expect.
### Q. What disqualifies you from laser hair removal?
A.  Usually nothing is permanent, just a reason to wait or change approach. Common pauses include a recent tan or sunburn, an active infection or open wound in the area, pregnancy, and some photosensitizing medications. Very light hair may not respond at all. The consultation, not a checklist online, makes the call.

## The Asterisk Next to Raw Kibbeh Is Missouri Law: Lebanese Food in St. Louis and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lebanese-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
A plate of raw minced meat slides past your elbow at a St. Louis Lebanese table, glossy under a thread of olive oil, mint leaves on top, a heap of raw onion on the side. Nobody at the next table flinches. They ordered it on purpose. Meanwhile your own table is frozen over a menu that runs for pages, and half the words on it have never been said out loud.
That plate is kibbeh nayyeh. Find it on the menu and look just past the name: there should be a small asterisk, and a footnote at the bottom of the page. That little star is the law talking. Section 3-603.11 of the Missouri Food Code says a kitchen serving beef, lamb or any animal food raw has to tell you in writing, and the reminder works by asterisking the dish to a footnote along the lines of “Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness.” No star, no footnote, no table card? Ask before you order.
The rest of the menu is easier than it looks. A Lebanese menu isn’t a list of entrees. It’s a box of parts, and you build the meal in waves. For two people, use the 2-1-1: two cold mezze, one hot, one grill, everything split, pita torn by hand. And if you want to taste those parts made by people who grew up on them, St. Louis has a street literally named Lebanon. At St. Raymond Maronite Cathedral, 931 Lebanon Drive, the parish runs a Wednesday Luncheon of Lebanese and Middle Eastern food; check the parish’s posted kitchen closing dates before you drive, or call the cathedral at 314-621-0056. Over one September weekend, Friday evening through Sunday afternoon, the same cathedral hosts the St. Louis Lebanese Festival, a party nearly six decades old, with kibbe aras, tabbouli, meat pies, spinach pies, cabbage rolls and stuffed grape leaves on the menu, dabke by the cathedral’s youth dancers, and free admission and free parking. The flyer and food pre-order go up on the cathedral’s own site, straymond-mc.org, ahead of the weekend.
### What dishes are typically on a Lebanese menu in St. Louis?
Expect cold mezze like hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh and labneh with warm pita, plus hot mezze like kibbeh and falafel. Then come grills such as shish tawook and kafta with garlic toum, shawarma, and sweets like baklava and knafeh. Order to share: a few cold plates, one or two hot ones, one grill.
Cold plates land first, with a basket of thin pita that doubles as your fork, and they sit happily on the table while everyone talks. Hot plates follow. The grilled meat arrives when the table is already a little too full, and somehow there’s still room. In Lebanon, a traditional mezze table can run to dozens of small dishes and last for hours, with arak, an anise spirit that turns cloudy when water hits it, poured slowly alongside. You don’t need dozens. Five or six plates for four people is a strong start.
### The one line to look for before you order raw kibbeh
Kibbeh nayyeh is minced raw meat worked with fine bulgur and served with olive oil, mint and raw onion. It’s traditional, it’s cold, it tastes clean and green and a little peppery, and it’s exactly what that food-code section has in mind. Under the Missouri Food Code, the written notice can be a menu advisory, a table tent, a placard, a brochure or a label, and the dish itself gets the asterisk. So scan the bottom of the menu and the little card by the napkins. Here’s the part worth knowing: one of the three footnotes the code allows reads “Regarding the safety of these items, written information is available upon request.” See that line? You’re entitled to ask for the written information, so ask. Still can’t find it? Ask the server two things: is it beef or lamb, and when was it ground? A kitchen proud of its nayyeh answers both without a pause. I could not confirm the exact wording any St. Louis restaurant prints, and the city and county write their own food rules on top of the state’s. Curious what St. Louis County’s own Food Code says about raw dishes?
### What a Missouri home kitchen can and can’t sell you
A tin of maamoul from a neighbor’s oven, powdered sugar on your fingers before the lid is all the way off: that one you can legally buy. Under Missouri’s Cottage Law (RSMo 196.298), home kitchens may sell baked goods, canned jams and jellies, and dried herb mixes, per the state health department’s home-based food guidance. Cooked dishes aren’t on the list. So the neighbor who bakes maamoul or baklava for the holidays can legally sell you a box, even online when seller and buyer are both in Missouri. The neighbor whose hummus or kibbeh is the stuff of legend can’t sell it from a home kitchen under that law. Which is why the best baklava of your life might come from a neighbor’s kitchen, while the best kibbeh still comes from a licensed one. Check the state’s current limits before you buy or sell.
### Ordering for two
Call it the 2-1-1: two cold mezze, one hot, one grill, everything split. Hummus and tabbouleh open well, one rich and creamy, the other so sharp with lemon it makes your jaw tingle. Add kibbeh or falafel for crunch, and eat it while it still hisses. Then share shish tawook or a mixed grill, which often comes with rice, grilled tomato and onion, and a cup of garlic sauce. Still hungry afterward? Order dessert, not another dip.
### Ordering for a group
Groups get the best version of this food. With six or eight people you can order a real spread: three or four cold mezze, three hot ones, a mixed grill or two, a stack of extra bread. Plenty of Lebanese kitchens offer a mezze sampler or a family-style feast, and asking the server to “bring us a good spread” is a normal request, not a lazy one. A birthday table that drove in from Sullivan can let the kitchen run the whole show and never open the menu twice. Same logic on Lebanon Drive at festival time: one person in the food line, one holding the picnic table, and nobody eats until the kibbeh lands.
Order in rounds, though. Fried kibbeh sounds different at minute two than at minute twenty: crackle, then nothing. Cold dips hold up fine, so add hot plates as the first ones disappear instead of flooding the table at once.
### Cold mezze: the plates that hit the table first
The pita is warm, the plates are cool, and the first bite is nearly all lemon. These are the typical Lebanese mezze dishes: hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and stuffed grape leaves called warak enab. Most are vegetarian, all lean on lemon, garlic, olive oil, tahini, parsley and mint, and every one gets scooped up with pita. They double as the popular Lebanese appetizers, though at a Lebanese table they’re less a warm-up than the main event.
### Hummus
Forget the grocery-store tub. Lebanese hummus is chickpeas whipped very smooth with tahini, lemon and garlic, spread in a shallow bowl with a well of olive oil in the center and a dusting of paprika or sumac. Some menus list hummus with meat, topped with sizzling ground lamb or beef and toasted pine nuts. See it? Get it.
### Baba ghanoush
Eggplant gets charred over open flame until the skin blackens and the inside collapses, then it’s mashed with tahini, lemon and garlic. The smoke is the point. Names drift from kitchen to kitchen, and some menus call the tahini version mutabbal and save “baba ghanoush” for a chunkier eggplant salad with tomato and pepper. Unsure which is coming? Ask.
### Tabbouleh
First-timers get a surprise: real Lebanese tabbouleh is a parsley salad, not a grain salad. Finely chopped flat-leaf parsley does the work, with mint, tomato, onion, a small handful of fine bulgur, lemon juice and olive oil. It should taste green, bright and a little sour. A bowl that looks mostly like bulgur is somebody else’s version.
### Fattoush
The salad for people who want crunch. Lettuce, cucumber, tomato, radish and herbs get tossed with toasted or fried pita pieces and a dressing sharpened with sumac, a tart deep-red spice, and sometimes pomegranate molasses. It began as a way to use up yesterday’s bread. Now people fight over the last forkful.
### Labneh
Yogurt strained until it spreads, somewhere between Greek yogurt and cream cheese. It comes swirled on a plate under olive oil, often with dried mint or za’atar. Tangy and cool, it’s the plate you keep dragging bread through after the grills arrive, because it calms the garlic down.
### Warak enab
Grape leaves rolled tight around a filling and simmered. The cold vegetarian kind holds rice, tomato, parsley and onion and is cooked with lemon and olive oil, so each roll comes out soft and tart. Hot versions filled with rice and ground meat exist too, and they usually sit on the hot side of the menu or arrive as a main.
### Which hot mezze should you order?
Listen for the crackle: that’s kibbeh or falafel leaving the oil. Hot mezze are the fried, baked and grilled small plates, falafel, kibbeh, fatayer, sambousek and arayes, and they’re the crunchy half of the table. If you order only one, make it kibbeh.
### Falafel
Lebanese falafel is usually made from soaked, uncooked chickpeas, sometimes with fava beans, ground with herbs, onion, garlic and spices and deep-fried. The outside should crackle. The inside should be green-flecked and tender, never dry. It arrives with tahini sauce and pickles, and rolled into pita with tomato and parsley it makes a sandwich worth the trip.
### Kibbeh
More forms than anything else on the page. The fried kind is a football-shaped shell of bulgur and finely ground meat, stuffed with more spiced meat, onion and pine nuts, then fried dark and crisp. It can also be pressed into a tray, scored into diamonds and baked. Then there’s the raw kind, kibbeh nayyeh, which is why the county note near the top matters.
### Fatayer and sambousek
Fatayer are small baked pies folded into triangles. Spinach is the classic, filled with spinach, onion, lemon and sumac so it bites back with a pleasant sourness; cheese and meat versions are common. Sambousek are their crispier cousins, half-moon pastries, usually fried, filled with spiced meat and pine nuts or salty white cheese. Both travel well, which is why trays of them turn up at so many family parties.
### Arayes
Maybe the most underrated plate on the menu. Pita is stuffed with a thin layer of seasoned ground meat, the same mix used for kafta, then grilled or pressed until the bread crisps and the juices soak through. Cut into wedges. Dip in labneh. Repeat until someone stops you.
### What belongs on a grill order?
Char and garlic reach you before the plate does. The grill section is where the skewers live: shish tawook, kafta and lamb. A mixed grill gives you some of each, which makes it the smartest first-visit order, and it usually arrives with some mix of rice, grilled tomato and onion, pickles, pita and garlic sauce, depending on the kitchen.
### Shish tawook
Chicken cubes marinated in yogurt, lemon, garlic and spices, sometimes with a spoonful of tomato paste, then skewered and grilled. The yogurt keeps the meat tender while the edges char. It’s the safe order that doesn’t taste safe, and one swipe through garlic sauce explains why regulars rarely order anything else.
### Kafta and lamb
Kafta is ground beef, lamb or a blend, worked with chopped parsley, onion and warm spices, pressed onto flat skewers and grilled. Juicy and herby, and the same mixture that fills arayes. Some kitchens also bake it in a tray with sliced potatoes and tomato sauce, a homestyle dish worth grabbing off the specials board. Lamb skewers, chops or a slow-cooked special may appear too; lamb is the meat Lebanese cooking has leaned on for generations, often seasoned simply. Cuts and portions vary, so ask how it’s cooked.
### Toum, the garlic sauce
Garlic, oil, lemon juice and salt, whipped until it turns white and fluffy, a bit like mayonnaise with no egg in it. Fierce. Take too big a swipe and your eyes water, yet people ask for extra cups to carry home, and in a humid St. Louis summer the smell rides in the car with them all the way. Don’t plan a first date around it.
### Shawarma, and what a Lebanese platter really is
Shawarma is marinated meat stacked on a vertical spit, roasted slowly as it turns and shaved off in thin slices. Chicken shawarma usually comes with toum and pickles, while beef or lamb tends to get tahini sauce, onion and parsley. Wrapped in pita it’s a sandwich: a tight roll, pickles tucked inside, sometimes pressed on the grill so the outside crisps and the paper goes translucent with grease. That’s lunch. Piled on a plate, it’s dinner.
### What’s actually on the platter?
A Lebanese platter, sometimes called a plate or a combo, is a whole meal on one dish. Most pair a protein, such as shawarma, shish tawook, kafta or falafel, with rice, a salad, hummus or garlic sauce, and pita. The rice is often cooked with toasted vermicelli, a home-kitchen staple that gives it a nutty flavor. What lands on the plate changes from kitchen to kitchen, so read the description or just ask.
Platters make sense when you’re eating alone or the table can’t agree on anything. Everybody gets a little of everything. Nobody has to share.
Hungry now? Pick one kitchen and order the 2-1-1 tonight. Browse Lebanese food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, check the hours before you drive, and open with hummus and fried kibbeh while the pita is still warm.
