### What do Lebanese people eat for breakfast?
Manakish, a lot of the time, still warm and smelling of thyme. It’s a round flatbread baked with a topping, and the classic is za’atar: wild thyme, sumac, toasted sesame and salt stirred into olive oil and spread over the dough. Cheese manakish, often made with a mild white cheese called akkawi, runs a close second.
Many Lebanese families eat it in the morning, folded around tomato, cucumber, fresh mint and olives, with a glass of hot tea. Some bakers make a half-and-half, za’atar on one side and cheese on the other, so nobody has to choose. Kishk, a fermented mix of yogurt and bulgur, makes another topping with a sour, funky edge. Worth trying once.
Foul, warm fava beans with lemon, garlic and olive oil, is another breakfast classic, scooped up with bread beside labneh and olives. Around St. Louis, manakish mostly turns up at Lebanese bakeries and at restaurants that open early. Go in the morning. Fresh bread doesn’t always last until lunch.
### Which Lebanese dishes work for vegetarians?
More than in most cuisines. The cold mezze are nearly all vegetarian, and hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and cold warak enab make a full meal on their own. Add falafel, spinach fatayer, cheese sambousek and mujaddara, lentils cooked with rice or bulgur under a heap of deeply browned onions, and nobody misses the grill.
There’s a reason the meatless side runs so deep. Lebanon has large Christian communities with long lenten fasting traditions, and generations of cooks built a repertoire cooked in olive oil with no meat at all. Batata harra belongs on that list: cubed potatoes fried, then tossed with garlic, cilantro, lemon and chili. Crispy, spicy, gone in minutes.
Vegans do well too, since so many plates skip dairy. Double-check anyway. Labneh is dairy, some pastries use butter, rice may be cooked in chicken stock, and falafel might share a fryer with meat. One quick question settles it, and our guide to how to eat out as a vegetarian in St. Louis covers how to ask without making it awkward.
Craving something that isn’t garlic? Here’s how to order Irish food without guessing.
### Lebanese or Greek: how can you tell on a Mediterranean menu?
They share a sea and some ingredients, but the flavors part ways fast. Greek cooking reaches for oregano, feta, yogurt-and-cucumber tzatziki and lemon potatoes. Lebanese cooking reaches for tahini, sumac, za’atar, parsley, pomegranate molasses and garlic toum. A menu labeled “Mediterranean” often mixes both, so it helps to know which side a dish came from.
The gyro and the shawarma make a handy test. In the U.S., a gyro usually means slices off a cone of seasoned ground meat, tucked into thick, fluffy pita with tzatziki, tomato and onion. Shawarma is stacked slices of marinated whole meat in thinner bread, with toum or tahini where the tzatziki would be. Salads split the same way: Greek salad is chunky tomato, cucumber, olives and a slab of feta, while fattoush brings toasted pita and sumac.
Desserts drift apart too. Baklava lives on both sides, but Lebanese versions tend to favor pistachios and a syrup perfumed with orange blossom or rose water, while Greek versions often use walnuts, cinnamon and honey. For the Greek half of the menu, see our local’s guide to Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis. Notice some overlap with Armenian cooking? You’re not imagining it, and what Armenian food is and what to order in St. Louis shows how neighboring kitchens trade dishes back and forth.
### Sweets worth saving room for
Syrup on the fingers, pistachio crumbs on the napkin. Baklava is paper-thin pastry layered with chopped nuts and soaked in fragrant syrup. Knafeh is warm, stretchy cheese under a crust of shredded pastry or semolina, drenched in syrup. Maamoul are crumbly cookies filled with dates or nuts, often baked for Easter and Eid.
### Knafeh
Order it hot. Soft white cheese goes under shredded pastry or a semolina crust, the pan bakes until golden, and then it’s soaked in syrup and showered with crushed pistachios. Salty, sweet, gooey. In Lebanon it’s eaten at breakfast too, stuffed into a sesame bread roll. Yes, really.
### Maamoul
Maamoul get pressed in carved wooden molds, so each cookie carries a pattern that often hints at the filling, dates in one shape and nuts in another. Buttery, crumbly, not too sweet. Bakeries often sell them by the box around the holidays, and a holiday box from a neighbor’s oven fits the Cottage Law rule covered near the top: baked goods in, cooked dishes out.
Close with Lebanese coffee, thick and strong and often scented with cardamom. Or mint tea, if you’d like to sleep tonight.
### Frequently asked questions about ordering Lebanese food
### Q. What to order at Lebanese restaurant?
A.  Start with hummus and tabbouleh, add kibbeh or falafel, then share one grill with garlic toum on the side. Use the 2-1-1: two cold, one hot, one grill, split. Order in rounds so fried plates stay hot. Order raw kibbeh only after finding the menu’s raw-food note or asking, and save room for knafeh.
### Q. What is the most famous Lebanese food?
A.  Outside Lebanon, hummus is probably the best known, with tabbouleh, falafel and shawarma close behind. Inside the country, many people point to kibbeh, a mix of bulgur and ground meat that’s fried, baked or eaten raw, as the national dish. Tabbouleh gets plenty of votes too, since it appears on nearly every Lebanese table.
### Q. What are some typical Lebanese mezze dishes?
A.  Cold: hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and warak enab, the stuffed grape leaves. Hot: falafel, kibbeh, fatayer, sambousek, arayes and batata harra, the spicy garlic potatoes. Olives, pickled turnips, raw vegetables and warm pita fill the gaps between plates, and the whole spread is meant to be shared and eaten slowly.
### Q. What is a Lebanese platter?
A.  A Lebanese platter is a full meal on one plate: a protein such as shawarma, shish tawook, kafta or falafel, plus rice, a salad, hummus or garlic sauce, and pita. The rice is often cooked with toasted vermicelli. Contents change from kitchen to kitchen, so read the menu description or ask before you order.
### Q. What is traditional Arabic mezze?
A.  Mezze is a spread of small shared dishes served together at the start of a meal, or as the whole meal, across Lebanon and much of the Arab world. It mixes dips, salads, pickles, pastries and fried bites, all eaten slowly with bread. In Lebanon it’s often paired with arak, an anise spirit mixed with water.
### Q. What are some good Lebanese dishes for a dinner party?
A.  Choose dishes that hold up on a buffet. Hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh and fattoush can be made ahead, with the fattoush bread added last so it stays crisp. Baked kibbeh, spinach fatayer and a tray of shish tawook or kafta skewers cover the hot side, and baklava or maamoul make an easy dessert.
### Q. What are the top 5 Lebanese dishes?
A.  Ask five Lebanese cooks and you’ll get five lists, but these come up again and again: kibbeh, tabbouleh, hummus, shish tawook and manakish. Plenty of people would add fattoush, shawarma or knafeh. For a first visit, order the first three as mezze and the tawook as your grill, and you cover a lot of ground.

## She Paid the City $20 to Stand Here. Your Review Is Free.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-support-local-businesses-in-st-louis-for-free
A woman halfway down the long hall at Soulard Market is stacking peaches into a pyramid nobody is watching. She paid the City $20 to stand there today, the Wednesday rate for a half-stand about 8 feet by 4, before selling a single peach. The hall echoes. Your shoes are louder than a radio playing somewhere down the aisle, and the fuzz comes off on your fingers when you pick one up.
Ten percent. That’s the share of vendors the City’s own market page lists for a Wednesday. Come back Saturday and the same page lists 100%. Shoulder to shoulder, onions and kettle corn in the air, and somewhere a stranger leans over a crate and says the most valuable sentence in the building: “Get the peaches from her stand, not that one.”
That sentence costs nothing. It’s also the thing a small shop in this city can’t buy, and you can say it for a shop you love tonight, from the couch, without spending a dollar.
Take Dana, a made-up example with a real problem. Her college roommate just opened a little upholstery shop, all foam dust and staple-gun oil, and its newest post, a reupholstered chair, has eleven likes. Dana can’t buy a sofa. She can do something better, and it’s free.
### How to support a friend’s small business for free?
Write a specific review, add real photos, and recommend them by name whenever someone asks for what they do. Share and save their posts, show up to their free events, and make sure their listings show the right hours and phone number. And if your friend sells at Soulard Market, go on a Wednesday, when the City lists only 10% of vendors open: the ones who showed up need your post more than any Saturday crowd does.
### The review Google actually counts
This is the part most “support local” lists skip. Google’s own help page on local ranking says prominence is based partly on how many reviews a business has, and that “more reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” Your review isn’t a nice gesture. It’s one of the inputs that decides whether the shop shows up when a stranger searches.
Screenshot this. The four-line review: “Came in for ___. Noticed ___. Know before you go: ___. I’ll be back for ___.” Fill in the blanks while the smell of the shop is still on your jacket. On a computer, Google’s steps are short: sign in to Google Maps, search for the place, scroll and click Write a review. About as long as waiting for a light on Grand. Only review what you actually bought - a staged review can hurt more than it helps.
So Dana opens Google Maps: five stars, one sentence typed with both thumbs about a job she actually paid for. “Brought in my grandmother’s 1970s cushion and she matched the fabric so well I can’t tell which side is new.”
A five-star tap with no words is a high-five. One sentence is the stranger at the crate, pointing. The likes are gone by breakfast. Her sentence is still under the shop’s name when somebody off South Grand types “cushion repair” into a phone.
### Go on the quiet day, and say so
She paid the City $20 to stand there. Your review costs you nothing, and on a Wednesday it’s worth more than it is on Saturday. The few who show up on a day the City lists at 10% need you most. The City’s page lists Wednesday hours as 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Buy one thing if you can, or nothing at all. Ask the vendor’s name and what they’re proud of this week, then post it that afternoon, name the stand and tag the market. A Wednesday photo of a nearly empty hall with one good stand in it tells your friends exactly where to go on Saturday.
Sunday is quieter still. The City lists the market as closed, with the exception of Sal’s Produce, and says to call the market at (314) 622-4180 before coming down. That one open stand on a closed day is the easiest shout-out in St. Louis.
### Post the photo from the stand, not the stock shot
On Google Maps you can leave a review and also post photo or video updates about a place, and Google’s help page notes that Local Guides can get points when they add them. So take the picture you’d actually want to see: the finished wingback chair in late-afternoon window light, the storefront from the curb so someone crawling down South Grand knows which door to look for, the peach pyramid before the Saturday crowd knocks it down. Daylight, no heavy filter, and ask before you put a person in the frame.
The same goes off the market floor. If your person farms, bakes or jars sauce, ask whether they’re in Missouri Grown, the Missouri Department of Agriculture program that promotes local products to local consumers. If they are, share their member page. If they aren’t, you just handed them a free tip.
Want a shop to start with tonight? Browse the local business spotlight and pick one worth a detailed review. Our earlier piece on why local matters in St. Louis covers the bigger picture; this one’s the to-do list.
### Why does a share beat a like for a St. Louis shop?
Because most social feeds decide who sees a post partly by how people interact with it, and a like is the weakest signal. Shares, saves and real comments generally tell a platform that a post is worth showing to more people, including folks who don’t follow the business yet. It’s free reach. Takes seconds.
### Share it, and tag it
When your friend posts a new product, a holiday schedule or a job opening, share it to your own feed or story and tag the business account so your followers can tap straight through. Add one line of your own. “My friend made our dining chairs look brand new” beats a silent reshare every time, because it tells people why they should care.
Tagging works in the other direction, too. When you post about something you bought, a meal, a haircut, a finished deck, tag the business and, if the platform allows it, the location. Those tags leave a trail of real customers that anyone sizing up the business can follow.
### Save it, then say something real
Saving a post takes one tap, and on several platforms it’s read as a sign the content is useful enough to come back to. Comments work best when they’re more than an emoji. Ask a question. “Do you do custom sizes?” gets the owner talking, and every reply adds to the conversation the platform sees under that post.
Don’t overdo it, though. Commenting on every single post within thirty seconds of it going up starts to look like a friend doing a favor, which, well, it is. Pick the posts you honestly like. A couple of times a week feels natural.
### How do you recommend a business without sounding like an ad?
Recommend it by name, in answer to a real question, and say why. That’s the whole trick. When somebody in a neighborhood group or family group chat asks “anyone know a good tailor?” a reply with the business name, what they did for you and how to reach them carries more weight than a paid post ever will.
Word of mouth has always powered small businesses. It’s just moved online, into community pages, neighborhood apps, church and school parent groups, and the endless family text thread. People in those spaces ask for recommendations constantly. Plumbers. Bakers. Somebody who’ll hem a prom dress by Friday.
### Use the exact name
Give the full business name, spelled the way they spell it. “That lady by the post office” doesn’t help anyone look them up later. Drop a link to their listing or website if the group allows links. Then add the one detail that fits the question: if someone asked about a rush job and your friend turned yours around fast, say exactly that.
### Be the friend who remembers
The best referrals happen offline, standing in a driveway in Marine or waiting in a school pickup line, when a neighbor mentions they need exactly what your friend does. Have the name ready. Better yet, keep the business saved as a contact in your phone so you can text it on the spot. Tiny habit. Pays off for years.
A quiet warning about groups: read the rules. Some community pages ban business promotion outside a set day, and owners who post ads in the wrong place can get removed. A genuine recommendation from a customer answering a question is usually welcome. A copy-pasted ad isn’t.
### Free moves for a Saturday, not a paycheck
Go to their free events, subscribe to their email newsletter, follow them on the platforms they actually use, and tell the owner directly what you liked. Each of those grows the owner’s audience or confidence, and none of them asks anything of your wallet beyond a little time on a Saturday.
### Show up when it’s free
Open houses, ribbon cuttings, free tastings, craft nights, pop-ups at a church fair: small businesses run these to get people through the door. A full room makes the next passerby more likely to stop in. It also gives the owner photos of a crowd, which look a lot better on social media than an empty shop. Bring someone. Two of you doubles the turnout.
### Join the newsletter
An email list belongs to the business. Social platforms can change what gets shown overnight, but a newsletter lands in an inbox the owner can reach without asking anyone’s permission. Signing up costs you nothing, and opening and clicking the occasional email tells them their list is alive. Forward the good ones to someone who’d care.
### Tell the owner what worked
Owners hear complaints fast. Praise travels slower. When something went right, tell them directly and be specific: the careful wrapping, the follow-up call, the way they explained the warranty without rushing you. That tells them what to keep doing, and on a rough week it might be the thing that keeps them going. Honest notes on what didn’t work help too, as long as you say them privately first.
### Help them get noticed by local media
Some owners have a story bigger than the product. A second career. A grandmother’s recipe. A reopening after a flood. If that sounds like your friend, nudge them toward our guide on how to pitch your story to St. Louis local media, and offer to proofread the email. One good feature can introduce a business to people no social post would ever reach.
All this typing earns you a paddle. Beginner kayaking around St. Louis
### How do reviews and listings shape what AI and search recommend?
When someone asks a search engine or an AI assistant “who does upholstery near me,” the answer is built from what’s published online: business listings, directory pages, reviews, photos and the words people use to describe the work. A business with accurate listings and detailed reviews gives those systems more to go on. Thin profiles get skipped.
This is where review detail pays off twice. Say you wrote that your friend reupholstered two wingback chairs and matched the fabric on a cushion from the 1970s. You’ve just put “wingback,” “reupholster” and “fabric matching” right next to their name, so someone asking for exactly that job has a better shot at finding them. Nobody can promise a business will come up first. Detail just improves the odds.
### Check the listing like a customer would
Pull up your friend’s listings on the map apps, review sites and local directories, then read them as a stranger would. Is the phone number right? Do the hours match the sign on the door? Is the address current, or does it still show the old home-based setup? Does the category actually describe what they do?
Wrong details cost real customers. A family drives out on a Sunday and finds the lights off. Somebody dials a dead number and gives up. If you spot a problem, tell the owner first, since they can fix it directly. Many platforms also let the public suggest an edit, which helps when the owner is buried in work.
### Make sure they’re listed where locals look
Some owners never get around to claiming their listings. If your friend isn’t on the local directories people in their area actually check, point it out and offer to help set things up on a slow evening. A laptop, a few good photos and a short description, and most of the job is done. The goal is the same name, address and phone number everywhere, so neither people nor search tools get confused.

### Can your friend’s LLC get grant money?
Sometimes, just rarely the way the ads promise. The SBA says it does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business; its grants go to nonprofits, Resource Partners and educational organizations that run counseling and training, and a small business doing scientific research and development may qualify for federal grants through SBIR or STTR. So when a text lights up her phone at the register promising free government money for the shop, forward her the FTC’s blunt line instead: offers of free money from government grants are scams, and the only full list of federal grants is free at grants.gov.
### Where a St. Louis dollar goes when you do spend it
Local owners hire people who live here, buy from nearby suppliers, pay local taxes and tend to sponsor the teams and fundraisers down the street. That’s why the free help above matters. Every customer a small business wins through your review or referral feeds that loop, even in a month when you personally didn’t spend a dollar.
### Where does the money go?
Follow a dollar spent at a locally owned shop. Part goes to wages for employees who live nearby and spend their paychecks here. Part goes to local suppliers: the printer, the bookkeeper, the farmer. The owner lives here too, so profits don’t get shipped off to a distant headquarters. Sales and property taxes help pay for roads and schools.
### What about local food?
Food grown or made close to home usually spends less time in transit, so produce can be picked closer to ripe. Buying it keeps nearby farms working. And when a market stand in Venice or a bakery down your street knows its regulars, you can ask how something was grown or made and get a real answer from a real person. Try that in a big-box aisle.
None of this means swearing off chains. Budgets are real, and nobody should feel guilty about a cheaper option in a tight month. That’s exactly why the free stuff counts.
Looking for more local businesses to cheer on? Browse the local business spotlight on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick one that deserves a detailed review, and pass it along to someone who needs what they do.
If you’re the shop, the market stand or the one-person crew people keep recommending, a complete listing with real customer reviews gives neighbors and AI tools something to name when someone asks who to call. List your business and get more customers out of every word-of-mouth tip.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can people support local businesses?
A.  Buy from them when you can, and when you can’t, give them attention. Write detailed reviews, share and save their posts, recommend them by name in group chats and neighborhood groups, attend their free events, join their newsletter, and check that their listings show the right hours and phone number.
### Q. What are the best ways to promote local businesses?
A.  The strongest free promotion is a specific, named recommendation from a real customer. After that come detailed reviews with photos, shares with a personal note, tags on your own posts, and accurate listings on the directories and map apps locals use. Helping an owner pitch a local reporter can reach even further.
### Q. What are the advantages of shopping locally?
A.  You usually get more personal service, owners who can answer questions directly, and products or skills you won’t find at a chain. Your spending also supports local jobs, local suppliers and local tax revenue, and it helps keep storefronts in your area open and occupied.
### Q. Why is it better to buy local products?
A.  Local products often travel shorter distances, can be fresher, and come from makers you can actually talk to. Buying them keeps local craftspeople, farmers and small producers working, and it gives your area a character chains can’t copy. It isn’t always cheaper, so buy local where it counts most to you.
### Q. Why should people be encouraged to buy locally produced food?
A.  Locally produced food generally spends less time in transit, so it can be harvested closer to ripeness. Buying it keeps nearby farms in business and farmland in use. You can also ask the grower how it was raised or produced, which is hard to do with food shipped across the country.
### Q. How much money stays local when you shop local?
A.  There’s no single number, and it varies by business. The mechanism is what matters: local owners live here, pay local employees, buy from nearby suppliers and pay local taxes. Spend there and more of the chain of people who touch that dollar live here.
### Q. What should a good review of a small business say?
A.  Say what you bought or hired them for, one specific detail about how it went, anything practical a newcomer should know like parking or turnaround time, and if you’d go back. Four or five honest sentences with real details help the next customer and give search tools more to match.
### Q. Does sharing a small business post on social media really help?
A.  It can. Most social feeds weigh shares, saves and genuine comments more heavily than a quick like when deciding who else sees a post. Sharing with a personal line about why you recommend the business also puts it in front of your own followers, who trust you more than they trust an ad.

## A Missing Rent Receipt Can Shrink Your SNAP. Here’s the St. Louis Fix
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-do-if-your-snap-food-benefits-get-cut-in-st-louis
The new number on the SNAP renewal letter is smaller, and nothing on the page says why. It came to a south city two-family on a Thursday. You read it under the kitchen light while the fridge hums behind you, then read it again. At the table, a kid is asking what’s for supper, and inside that fridge there are eggs, half a loaf of bread and a jar of peanut butter.
That smaller number may be a missing lease, not a cut. Since October 1, Missouri leaves out your rent, utility and child care costs if you can’t prove them on paper, and those costs help set the size of your benefit. Send the proof and the deduction may come back, no appeal needed. No written lease? A rent receipt with your landlord’s contact information, the amount and the date counts. Upload it at mydssupload.mo.gov, fax it to 573-526-9400, or carry it to a Family Support Division resource center: 3101 Chouteau Ave. in the city, 9900 Page Ave. in the county.
### What to do if your SNAP benefits stop in St. Louis?
Get food moving today, then fix the benefit. Dial 211 any hour, or text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310 to find the nearest pantry. Call Operation Food Search at 314-726-5355. If your SNAP was reduced, you have 90 days to appeal, 10 days to keep benefits during it.
A pantry visit is quieter than most people expect: a sign-in sheet, a short wait, and a volunteer handing over a box or letting you pick from the shelves. Nobody asks you to fix your SNAP case first. Some sites want a photo ID or proof of address, so bring both if you have them and call before you drive.
Then make the SNAP you still have go further at Tower Grove Farmers’ Market. Swipe your EBT card at the market’s information booth, and Double Up Food Bucks matches what you spend, up to $25 a market day, in free tokens for fruits and vegetables. The market says it takes EBT year-round.
Mistakes do happen, and Missouri gives you a real window to challenge one. So get food this week, then read the proof and appeal steps below. Free pop-up giveaways move fast, too, so it helps to watch our running list of free food giveaways happening in St. Louis.
### Where can you find food today across the St. Louis metro?
Two numbers open almost every door. Operation Food Search maps 150-plus food sites and answers a live hunger hotline, and the St. Louis Area Foodbank runs a locator plus the Plentiful app. Add 211 for a real person around the clock, and you can find a pantry near you within minutes, day or night.
Operation Food Search (Hunger Hotline) Phone: (314) 726-5355, press 1. Text your ZIP code to (785) 503-3310. Food-finder map (150+ sites): operationfoodsearch.org/find-food Headquarters: 1644 Lotsie Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63132 (offices only, no food handed out on site).

One habit saves a wasted trip: call before you go. Hours shift, and some pantries ask for a photo ID or proof of address. Community fridges and little free pantries are scattered around the region too, but they move and refill unpredictably, so the Operation Food Search map and 211 are the reliable way to find one that’s stocked today.

### How do you push back on a SNAP cut or denial?
You have more power here than the notice makes it feel. In Missouri you can request a fair hearing within 90 days of the date on your Action Notice, and if you ask within 10 days, your benefits keep flowing while the case is decided. That 10-day window is the one people miss most, so circle it on the calendar right now.
Here’s how to file. Contact the Family Support Division (FSD), say you want a fair hearing on your SNAP case, and put it in writing whenever you can. Any one of the channels below starts the clock.
Missouri Family Support Division: fair hearing Email: IMHearing.FSD@dss.mo.gov Fax: 573-526-4554 Mail: FSD, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102 Phone: 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO); TTY 1-800-735-2966 Deadlines: within 90 days to appeal; within 10 days to keep benefits during the appeal.
You don’t have to do this alone. Free legal aid attorneys in the St. Louis area handle benefit appeals and can represent you at the hearing at no cost; ask FSD for a referral, or dial 211. And if the denial means starting fresh, our step-by-step guide to applying for SNAP in Missouri walks through the whole application.
### What proof do you need for SNAP in Missouri now?
Under Missouri’s new food stamp rules, which started October 1, you need paper proof of your rent or mortgage, utility bills, child or dependent care costs and bank balances when you apply for SNAP, renew it, or add someone to your case. Your word used to be enough. Not anymore. Already on SNAP? Unless you’re adding someone, hold off until your next renewal.
If your amount dropped at a renewal, check this first. A cost you can’t prove doesn’t sink the case. FSD still processes it, just without that deduction, which can shrink your benefit. Send the proof later and the deduction may be added back. You get 10 days to answer any FSD request.
Most of it is already in a kitchen drawer: the lease, the Ameren or Spire bill, the daycare receipt folded into a coat pocket. A clear phone photo works fine.
What to gather Renting: a landlord-signed lease, or a rent receipt with the landlord’s contact info, amount and date Homeowners: latest mortgage or property tax statement Utilities: recent electric, gas, water, sewer, trash or heating fuel bills Care you pay for to work, job hunt or train: the provider’s itemized receipt, a sitter’s signed note of hours and pay, or canceled checks and e-payment receipts Bank accounts: most recent statements No lease, or an informal sitter: a signed note from the person you pay, with their name, phone, address, amount and how often
Where to send it Upload (fastest): mydssupload.mo.gov Fax: 573-526-9400 (your name, DCN or SSN and birth date on each page) Mail copies, never originals: Family Support Division, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102 In person: any FSD Resource Center, like the City office on Chouteau below No phone or internet? ### How do you report a change without a penalty later?
Reporting on time protects your future benefits. Missouri asks you to report certain changes by the 10th of the month after they happen: a jump in income, a gambling or lottery win over $4,750 in a single game (a cutoff adjusted each year), or a working-age adult’s hours dropping below 20 a week. Report late, and you may have to repay benefits you weren’t eligible for.
The easiest route is online at mydss.mo.gov under “Report a Change.” You can also call 855-373-4636 or visit an FSD office in person. In the City, the resource center below takes walk-ins during posted hours.
Missouri Family Support Division (SNAP questions and changes) Phone: 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO); TTY 1-800-735-2966 Online: mydss.mo.gov/manage-benefits City FSD Resource Center: 3101 Chouteau Ave, St. Louis, MO 63103; (314) 933-7035 Hours: Monday and Tuesday 8:00am-4:45pm, Wednesday 9:00am-4:45pm, Thursday and Friday 8:00am-4:45pm.

### Food help for seniors, kids, and new parents
Some of the best help is aimed at a specific household, and it stacks on top of everything above. Adults 60 and older can get meals delivered or served nearby. Kids can eat free in summer with no sign-up. Pregnant parents and young children have WIC. If any of these fit your home, use them alongside the pantries, not instead of them.

### Help for pregnant parents and young children (WIC)
WIC supports pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five in households at or below 185% of the federal poverty level. It covers specific healthy foods, infant formula, and nutrition support, and it stacks with SNAP and pantries.

### What if your benefits run out before the month does?
Stack your sources, and do it without guilt. Most pantries allow one visit per month each, which means you can visit several different pantries in the same month and legitimately rebuild a week or two of groceries. Layer in free kids’ meals, senior meals, and WIC where you qualify, and a short month starts to fill back in.
Here’s the part people rarely get told out loud: the system is built to be combined. One pantry is a single box of groceries. Four different pantries, plus a WIC appointment and a summer meal site, is close to a month of food. Use the Operation Food Search text line (785-503-3310), 211, or the Foodbank locator to line them up by day and by neighborhood. The neighbors who run these pantries want you to walk in. Being found, and finding help, is how a hard month stays just a month. You’ve got this, and the whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.

### Can I still use my EBT card if the government shuts down?
Yes, for whatever is already on the card. During the last federal shutdown, Missouri’s Department of Social Services told families that any benefits left on the EBT card from previous months could still be used, and that people could still apply for SNAP and its other programs. Before you push a full cart to the register, check the balance at ebtedge.com, in the ebtEDGE app or through the number on the back of the card, so the surprise happens at your kitchen table and not in the checkout line.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why would my food stamps get cut off?
A.  Sometimes it’s a simple agency error. Other times income rose, a working-age adult’s hours fell below 20 a week, or a lottery or gambling win topped the yearly cutoff, now $4,750 in a single game. Reporting late can also cut you off, and at renewal any rent, utility or child care cost you can’t prove gets left out. You have 90 days to appeal.
### Q. What are the new food stamp rules for Missouri?
A.  The big one started October 1. Missouri now wants proof of rent or mortgage, utilities, child or dependent care costs and bank balances when you apply, renew, or add someone to your case. Unproven costs are left out, which can lower your benefit, but you can send proof later. Already on SNAP? Nothing is due until renewal, unless you add someone.
### Q. Where can I get food today in St. Louis?
A.  Text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310, or call Operation Food Search at 314-726-5355, press 1, to find the closest pantry. You can also dial 211 any hour of the day. The St. Louis Area Foodbank locator at stlfoodbank.org/find-food and the free Plentiful app show hours and let you reserve a slot.
### Q. How to appeal denied SNAP benefits?
A.  Request a fair hearing with the Missouri Family Support Division within 90 days of your Action Notice date. Ask within 10 days if you want benefits to continue during the appeal. Reach them by email at IMHearing.FSD@dss.mo.gov, fax 573-526-4554, mail FSD, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102, or phone 855-373-4636.
### Q. How do I report changes to my food stamps in Missouri?
A.  Report it online at mydss.mo.gov under “Report a Change,” by phone at 855-373-4636, or at a local Family Support Division office. Do it by the 10th of the month after the change, for things like income shifts or work hours dropping. Reporting on time protects you from repaying benefits later.

## Warming Centers in St. Louis: Reach a Code Blue Rally Point by 7 p.m. and the City Drives You to a Bed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/warming-centers-in-st-louis-where-to-stay-warm-this-winter
Between 5 and 7 p.m. on the City’s coldest nights, a Metro Call-A-Ride shuttle pulls into the Loughborough Commons parking lot, the stretch of asphalt between the Schnucks and the Lowe’s. Breath hangs in the headlights. A driver sits up front, and an outreach worker rides along, because the whole point of that van is to carry people who are out in the cold to a shelter bed. You just have to know the van comes.
Most people don’t. That lot is one of the City of St. Louis’s Code Blue rally points, and on recent Level 3 and Level 4 nights there were three of them: the Urban League Women’s Business Center at 4401 Natural Bridge Ave. in north city, Centenary United Methodist Church at 1610 Olive St. downtown (use the Pine Street entrance), and that Loughborough Commons lot in south city. Each one had a warming bus or an indoor warming room waiting, plus the shuttle. Locations can change from winter to winter, so call 211 before you set out. But keep this in your head: if you can get to a rally point by 7, you don’t have to find the shelter yourself.
### Where can I go to stay warm in St. Louis tonight?
Call 211 or the City Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444; they route you to the nearest open bed. In the City, Biddle Housing Opportunities Center (1212 N. 13th St.) and Peter & Paul’s Jugan and Kingshighway shelters have taken walk-ups during Code Blue. In St. Louis County, Salvation Army Family Haven (10740 Page Ave.) runs a 24-hour overnight shelter.
Screenshot those numbers. Text them to your own phone. Write 211 on the back of your hand in pen if that’s what it takes, because a dead battery at midnight is exactly when you’ll need it.
### How Code Blue decides which doors open
The City runs its cold-weather response on a ladder called Code Blue, and the rungs are set by the thermometer. Code Blue is inactive from March 1 to December 1. Inside that winter window, the baseline is 400 year-round shelter beds. Then the cold climbs the ladder for you.
Level 2 starts when the temperature drops below 32°F or the wind chill falls below 25°F, the kind of cold where your fingers ache inside your pockets. About 150 surge beds open and select warming centers come on, but there’s no transport yet. Level 3 hits at 25°F or below, or a wind chill under 10°F. Up to 450 surge beds open, more warming centers activate, and the rally points and shuttles start running. Level 4 is the dangerous end: 10°F or colder, or a wind chill below minus 10°F. Every warming center opens, 600 surge beds come online, and the full transport fleet goes out. The City counts a level only when the weather is expected to last 2 or more hours, and it can jump a level early for things like ice, a long cold stretch or shelters filling up.
So what does that mean for you at 4 p.m. with the sky going gray? It means the number on the bank sign tells you how much help is out tonight. Below freezing, start calling. In the twenties, aim for a rally point. In the single digits, the City is pulling out everything it has, and nobody should be outside.
### Daytime warmth: the rooms that keep your hands working
A warming center is not a bed. It’s a heated room with a chair, a bathroom, maybe an outlet and a cup of something hot, where you can stop shaking long enough to think. The City lists 22 of them, and many are St. Louis Public Library branches: Central, Barr, Buder, Carpenter, Schlafly and Baden are all on the City’s warming center list. The library main line is (314) 241-2288, and the City says to check the library’s own site for hours and weather closures, since a branch can close in a storm.
Closing time is the trap. A warm afternoon in a reading room feels like a plan until the lights flick off and the doors lock behind you with the temperature still falling. Use the daytime hours to make the evening call, and charge your phone while you’re there.
### Overnight: where the beds are
Biddle Housing Opportunities Center at 1212 N. 13th St. does double duty. It runs drop-in hours every day from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and an overnight shelter for men, reachable at (314) 612-1675. On recent Code Blue nights, the City also listed Peter & Paul’s Jugan shelter at 3225 N. Florissant Ave., which takes single men, single women and families, and its Kingshighway shelter at 3205 S. Kingshighway Blvd. for single men and women, as walk-up options. When a walk-up shelter reaches capacity, the City says it provides transportation to another shelter with room.
Got kids, or a dog you won’t leave behind? Say so on the phone. The City says added space for families and for people with pets is set up by appointment through the United Way 211 Helpline or with a coordinator at a rally point. For women and families, Gateway 180 at 1000 N. 19th St. calls itself Missouri’s largest emergency and transitional living shelter serving women, children and families. Its line is (314) 231-1515.
### City warming centers, with phone numbers
Call before you walk. Hours below are the City’s listed warming hours, and any site may close in bad weather.

### Where can you stay warm in St. Louis County?
Out in the County, start with the phone, because hours vary by site. Family Haven is listed as a 24-hour overnight shelter, and the Salvation Army corps community centers list daytime warming hours.

### Cold before December 1? Here’s what still runs
Code Blue sleeps from March 1 to December 1, and a hard frost in late fall doesn’t wait for the calendar. The first raw night of the season, when the wind off the river bites through a hoodie, can land while the City’s ladder is still switched off. That doesn’t mean nothing is open. Biddle lists drop-in hours Sunday through Saturday, and the Salvation Army lists Family Haven as a 24-hour overnight shelter. The difference is that before December 1, Code Blue’s warming centers and transportation are listed as inactive. So on an early cold snap, skip the waiting and call 211 in the afternoon, while there’s still daylight to get where you need to go.
### West across the Missouri River, and over in Illinois
Across the Missouri River, overnight warmth runs through the Emergency Weather Response (EWR) program. When temperatures are predicted to be 20 degrees or below overnight, it activates a free warming center response with safe sleeping locations for the night. Older flyers still print its hotline as 636-395-0492. A host church’s own page now gives (636) 395-0328, answered after 3 p.m. during an activation, and says transportation may be available. Try the newer number first. The two Salvation Army corps on that side of the river list daytime warming hours too: (636) 946-7966, Monday-Thursday, 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and (636) 240-4969, Monday-Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. The city-run Rec-Plex on Mexico Road is at (636) 939-2386; call before you go to ask whether it’s taking people in from the cold.
On the Illinois side, the Salvation Army Alton Corps Community Center at 525 Alby St. runs warming hours Monday-Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Questions go to 618-465-7764.
Need a bed tonight, not just a warm room? Call United Way 211 (or 1-800-427-4626, which also takes texts), and read our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis for how intake works.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What do warming centers do?
A.  Warming centers give people protection from dangerous cold: a heated room to sit, warm up and make a plan. In the City, more of them switch on as Code Blue climbs from Level 2 to Level 4, and at Level 4 all warming center locations are activated.
### Q. How do warming centers work?
A.  In the City, they follow Code Blue. Select centers open below 32°F or a wind chill under 25°F, additional ones open at or below 25°F, and all locations open at 10°F or below. Hours vary by site, so call 2-1-1 for the most current list.
### Q. What is an overnight warming shelter?
A.  It’s a place with a bed for the night, not just a warm chair. Salvation Army Family Haven in St. Louis County runs a 24-hour overnight shelter, and Biddle in the City runs an overnight shelter for men.
### Q. What to bring to a warming center?
A.  Bring what you can’t afford to lose: your ID, any medications, your phone and its charger. If you have a pet or children with you, tell 211 when you call, because the City sets up space for families and pets by appointment.
### Q. Where can I find temporary shelter?
A.  Dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626, or call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444. During Level 3 and Level 4 Code Blue, City rally points offer pickup between 5 and 7 p.m. with a ride to shelter.
### Q. How to help homeless during cold weather?
A.  Point people to 211 and the rally points, and pass along the Housing Helpline, 314-802-5444. The City also takes a Homeless Services Inquiry form for someone seeking help and a separate form to report an encampment.
### Q. Are there any programs in St. Louis that offer free hotel vouchers for homeless individuals?
A.  I could not confirm a standing hotel-voucher program on any official City page. Ask 211 directly when you call. It is the line that knows what emergency options are open that night.
### Save this before the cold comes
Winter always comes back to this river town, and so does this list. Save three things now, while your hands are warm and your head is clear: 211, the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, and the 5-to-7 rally point window. Pass them to the neighbor who sleeps in his car, the coworker whose furnace just quit, the person you see every morning at the bus stop. Share this page on Facebook so it’s in their feed before the first Code Blue.
And if you’re the one who’s cold tonight, there’s no shame in any of this. Make the call. You deserve a warm room. Run a nonprofit that helps people get there? Add your organization to St Louis Near Me Directory.

## Missouri TANF Tops Out at $292 a Month. Here Is Faster Help in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/emergency-cash-and-tanf-help-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
The bill is on the table under your phone, and you have done the math three times. It comes out the same every time. If someone told you to “just apply for TANF,” here is the honest number first: Missouri’s cash program, called Temporary Assistance, pays a family of three at most $292 a month. That is 13% of the federal poverty level. And once you are approved, the state says the first payment can take up to 45 days to land on your EBT card.
That is not a reason to skip it. It is a reason to make a second call the same day, to an office that can pay the bill itself. Which office depends on which side of the city line your front door sits on.
Save this for yourself or a neighbor: City, call the Urban League at 314-615-3632. County, call CAASTLC at 314-863-0015. Everything else, call 211. Three numbers, and you skip the week of calling offices that already ran out of money.
Being short on cash doesn’t make you a failure, and you don’t have to sort this out alone. Below: what Missouri’s cash program really does, and where St. Louis families and single adults find one-time help with rent and utilities when it isn’t the answer. For the wider map of local aid, keep our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub open in another tab.
### How to get immediate financial help in St. Louis?
Make the first call from wherever you are sitting right now, with the bill in your hand. Dial 211; it is free and it answers at any hour. Read the person the amount, the account number and the date printed on the notice, and ask which fund near you still has money. Then call the utility office for your side of the line.
There isn’t one office in St. Louis that hands out emergency money. Help here is drawn along lines you can find on a map. The city limit decides whether your utility help comes from the Urban League on North Kingshighway or from CAASTLC on Woodson Road in Overland. Knowing whose map you are on saves you a bus ride to the wrong office.
### What Temporary Assistance pays, and why it is slow
The notice on the refrigerator has a date on it, and the date is close. Temporary Assistance runs on a slower clock. The state says it can take up to 10 days just to process your application, then a letter arrives in the mailbox telling you whether you qualify, and once you are approved the first payment can take up to 45 days. You are counting days. The state is counting weeks.
None of that makes it worthless. The Missouri Department of Social Services describes it as “a cash benefit for low-income families to help cover costs for the household’s children, such as clothing, utilities and other services.” Apply online at mydss.mo.gov, or call the Family Support Division information line at 855-FSD-INFO (1-855-373-4636), and do it today so the clock starts.
Just don’t pin this month’s rent on it. The National Center for Children in Poverty’s profile of Missouri has the numbers: Missouri spent 3.5% of its federal TANF block grant on cash assistance, against 21.8% nationally, and only 6 of every 100 families with children living in poverty took part. Families can receive it for no more than 45 months in a lifetime, and once approved, adults must take part in employment and training through the Missouri Work Assistance program. It is one piece of your plan, not the whole plan.
### Where can I get immediate financial assistance?
From a handful of St. Louis nonprofits, each with its own turf and its own bills it will cover. In St. Louis City, energy and LIHEAP help runs through the Urban League; in St. Louis County, through CAASTLC. Add the Salvation Army, St. Vincent de Paul and Guardian Angel Settlement Association, and call 211 to find which one has money now. Every one of these funds is finite, so a quick call beats a long drive.
Bring the bill itself, not just a photo of it. The account number and due date are printed right there, and a crumpled shutoff notice in your bag is worth more than the clearest memory of what it said. Need rent help specifically? Our guide to emergency rent assistance in St. Louis goes deeper.

Volunteers who meet families face to face. You reach the Society by calling the United Way 2-1-1 helpline. Address: 1310 Papin St, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-881-6000 Web: svdpstlouis.org/need-help

Emergency shelter, supportive housing and affordable apartments for people working toward a stable place to live. Address: 4445 Lindell Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63108 Phone: 314-367-5500 Web: ccstl.org

If a place to live is the deeper need, see our guide to finding low-income housing in St. Louis. Address: 800 N. Tucker Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: 314-802-0700 Web: stpatrickcenter.org

### How do I get emergency help with bills in St. Louis?
Call 211 or 1-800-427-4626, any hour, and say which bill and how much. For gas, electric or water, City residents go to the Urban League (314-615-3632) and St. Louis County residents go to CAASTLC (314-863-0015). For rent or a bill the energy programs won’t touch, the Salvation Army takes requests through an online form, and Guardian Angel Settlement Association offers emergency rental and utility assistance.
### What types of low-income assistance programs are available in Missouri?
Think of it as four doors. Cash for families with children is Temporary Assistance. Food is SNAP. Energy bills go to the Urban League’s LIHEAP program in the City and Wellston, or to CAASTLC in the County. One-time rent, deposit and emergency help comes from the nonprofits above. If a health condition keeps you from working, ask about disability benefits too.
Single adults without children hit a wall with Temporary Assistance, because it is built for households with kids. For them, the path runs through SNAP, LIHEAP and the local charities, and 211 is still the fastest way to find which of those has money this week.
People are asking
### What is a hardship grant for single mothers in Missouri?
Most help sold online as a “hardship grant for single mothers” is really a set of public programs and local charities. In Missouri, the cash program for a parent raising children is Temporary Assistance, which pays up to $292 a month for a family of three and you can apply online at mydss.mo.gov. For a one-time bill, call 211 to reach St. Louis nonprofits that help with rent and utilities.
### What to have ready before you apply
Gathering your paperwork first is the single biggest time-saver, because most of these programs stall on missing documents. Have a photo ID, Social Security numbers for your household, proof of income (or proof you have none), a recent copy of the bill you need help with, and any shutoff or eviction notice you’ve received.
Keep it all in one folder or envelope, so you can answer questions in a single call instead of three. If you’re applying for Temporary Assistance, the Family Support Division accepts documents online at mydssupload.mo.gov or by fax at 573-526-9400.
Call 211 first. It’s free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day. Dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626, or search stl.211helps.org. Prefer to browse yourself? Our guide to findhelp.org shows another way to find nearby programs.
If you run a food pantry, clinic, ministry or aid agency in St. Louis, the neighbors who need you should be able to reach you - list it with us.
### Asking is a skill, not a weakness
People most often miss out not because they don’t qualify, but because they never reached the one office that still had funds that week. So make the calls, leave the messages, and call back. Write down who you talked to and when, on the back of the envelope the bill came in; the next caseworker will ask.
Asking well, early, organized and at the right door, is how the lights stay on. Start with one call today, and keep our help and assistance hub handy for whatever comes next.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who is eligible for TANF in Missouri?
A.  A parent or guardian of a child under 18 who lives in Missouri, does not own resources worth more than $1,000 (not counting a home and one vehicle), stays under the income limit, and has or applies for a Social Security number for everyone in the household.
### Q. How much is TANF in Missouri?
A.  The maximum for a family of three is $292 a month, which is 13% of the federal poverty level. The amount your household gets depends on the size of your household and your current expenses.
### Q. How do you get cash from TANF?
A.  Once you are approved, the first benefit is loaded to your EBT card or sent by direct deposit to your bank account within 45 days. After that, it arrives monthly.
### Q. Is TANF different than SNAP?
A.  Yes. TANF, called Temporary Assistance in Missouri, is a cash benefit for low-income families with children. SNAP is a monthly benefit to help people in need buy food. Many families need both.
### Q. What happens if I apply for TANF?
A.  The Family Support Division processes your application, which can take up to 10 days, and sends a letter saying whether you qualify. If you are approved, you must take part in employment and training through Missouri Work Assistance, and the first payment arrives within 45 days.
### Q. How to apply for energy assistance in MO?
A.  Missouri LIHEAP applications go to the contracted agency for your area, by mail, fax or in person. In St. Louis City and Wellston that is the Urban League (314-615-3632); in St. Louis County it is CAASTLC (314-863-0015). You can also call 855-FSD-INFO (855-373-4636) to have an application mailed to you.
### Q. Where can I get immediate financial assistance?
A.  Start with 211 or 1-800-427-4626, which can connect you with local shelters, housing programs and other resources. Then work down the list of local agencies on this page, starting with the one that matches the bill in your hand.
### Q. What can I do if I need money urgently?
A.  Ask for help with the bill itself rather than chasing cash, and keep every shutoff or eviction notice together in one folder. When you call, have the amount, the account number and the due date in front of you, and write down the name of each person you speak with and when you called.

## St. Louis Water and Sewer Bill Help: Your LIHEAP Letter Can Halve the Sewer Rate
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/water-and-sewer-bill-assistance-in-st-louis
Fifty percent. That is how much MSD takes off a qualifying household’s sewer rate, for two full years, and one paper that can prove you qualify may already be folded in your kitchen drawer: a LIHEAP acceptance letter.
Almost nobody connects the two. The letter came for the heat bill, got read once at the counter, and slid under the takeout menus. Meanwhile the sewer bill keeps landing. The water bill keeps landing. If you’re behind, you know the sound by now: the flat slap of another envelope on the table, the little drop in your stomach before you tear it open, the way you set it face down so you don’t have to look at the number while you make dinner. This guide is the short way through. Who bills you, who can help, what to bring, and the City deadline most families hear about too late. For the bigger map of local aid, keep our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub close by.
### How can I get help with my water bill in Missouri?
Match the help to the name printed on your bill. City of St. Louis water customers call the Water Division at (314) 771-2255 about its assistance programs and repayment plans. Missouri American Water customers apply for H2O Help to Others through a Community Action Agency, which in St. Louis County is CAASTLC. MSD sewer bills can drop 50% through its Customer Assistance Program. Not sure where to start? Dial 211.
That’s the whole map in five sentences. Everything below is the detail that decides whether a phone call ends in a yes: the paperwork each office wants, the income lines, and the order to make the calls so one approval opens the next door. Read it with your bills spread out in front of you. Being behind on a utility bill in Missouri is common, fixable and nothing to be ashamed of, and the people answering these phones hear the same story all day long.
### Why does one house get two bills from two different places?
Lay the envelopes side by side under the kitchen light and look at the logos. The sewer bill comes from MSD Project Clear, the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District. It started out serving the City of St. Louis and the part of St. Louis County east of I-270, then annexed most of the rest of the County in 1977. Today MSD says it serves about 1.3 million people over 520 square miles. So if you live almost anywhere around here, your sewer money goes to the same place your neighbor’s does.
Drinking water is different. Inside the City, drinking water comes from the City of St. Louis Water Division. Out in the County, Missouri American Water serves St. Louis County instead. Each of the three bills has its own help program. That is the trap. You can do everything right on the water side and still lose ground on sewer, simply because nobody told you it was a second line to stand in.
### The letter that cuts a sewer bill in half
MSD’s Customer Assistance Program, called CAP, gives eligible customers a 50 percent reduction in wastewater rates. Once you’re approved, the lower rate starts on the first full month after approval and stays for two years, and MSD mails a renewal application 60 days before it runs out. You can be the owner or a tenant, in a single-family home or a building of up to six units.
The income line is 200% of the federal poverty guidelines, which on MSD’s own table works out to $66,000 a year for a family of four. If you’re 62 or older, or disabled, the line rises to 250%, or $82,500 for four. There’s also an asset test: liquid assets and real estate under $10,000, not counting your home or your car, and people 62 and up skip that test entirely.
Now the part almost nobody uses. MSD gives you two ways to prove you qualify. Option A is the full stack: income proof for every person in the house and a statement of your assets. Option B is a single page: an acceptance letter from another energy assistance program, such as LIHEAP. One approval letter. Two bills lighter. If you got LIHEAP help for heat, that letter can do a second job, so dig it out of the drawer and smooth the creases flat on the table before you call MSD billing at (866) 281-5737.
No letter yet? In St. Louis County, CAASTLC takes LIHEAP heating applications on a split schedule. Households with someone 60 or older, or someone disabled, including a child, can apply starting October 1. Everyone else can apply starting November 1. Get the heat application in first, and you may walk out with the paper that unlocks the sewer discount too.
### City water: ask about the tornado-recovery rate before the window shuts
If your water bill says City of St. Louis Water Division, this is the call to make first. After the May 16 tornado, the City opened a Tornado Recovery Water Affordability Program: a 50% discount on eligible water charges through December 2028, plus a 50% credit on delinquent balances that piled up since that storm. The Water Division lists enrollment as open through October 31. You can enroll online or in person at the STLRecovers Outreach Center on Natural Bridge. If you’re reading this after that date, call (314) 771-2255 and ask what replaced it, because the City has more coming.
Here’s what’s coming. The Water Division says an Affordability Rate, established by city ordinance, is launching in the fall to help customers who qualify. That is a standing rate written into local law, not a one-time grant that dries up when a federal check runs out. Ask about it by name.
You may also have heard about the $500 TAP credit. It was paid for with $1 million in federal ARPA money, first come, first served, for City residents at or below 80% of area median income who were more than 90 days behind. The Water Division’s own page now labels it discontinued, so don’t build your plan around it. What the Division still offers is a repayment plan, tailored to your circumstances. Hearing a calm voice on the phone say “let’s set up a plan” is worth more than another week of dread.
People are asking
### What is the St. Louis water bill aid program, and how can I apply?
For City of St. Louis water customers, the current one is the Tornado Recovery Water Affordability Program: a 50% discount on eligible water charges plus a 50% credit on delinquent balances since the May tornado. The Water Division lists enrollment as open through October 31, online or in person at the STLRecovers Outreach Center. The older $500 TAP credit is now marked discontinued. Call (314) 771-2255 to apply or ask about repayment plans.
City of St. Louis Water Division (water, City only) Phone: (314) 771-2255 Ask about: the Tornado Recovery Water Affordability Program, the coming Affordability Rate, and a repayment plan In person for tornado recovery: STLRecovers Outreach Center, Natural Bridge Ave. Online: stlwater.com, then Resources, Assistance Programs
### County water: H2O Help to Others, before the shutoff notice
If the bill says Missouri American Water, your emergency fund is H2O Help to Others. It was created by Missouri American Water and Missouri’s Community Action Agencies, and it is paid for by the company plus customers who check a box on the back of their own bill. Think about that for a second: a neighbor you’ll never meet chipped in a few dollars so your faucet keeps running. Taking that help is exactly what it was built for.
In St. Louis County, CAASTLC handles it. The program can stop a disconnection or restore service to a home, and CAASTLC says plainly that a disconnection is not required to apply. Household income can’t exceed 200% of the federal poverty guidelines, which on CAASTLC’s table is $64,300 a year for a family of four, and a caseworker looks at your basic needs. Don’t wait for the red notice.
Missouri American also offers an installment plan for residential customers in hardship: pay 25% of the past-due balance up front, then the rest over a schedule of up to six months, while keeping up with new bills. The catch is timing. The company says to contact it before your water is shut off to keep your eligibility for that plan. Once the tap coughs and goes dry, that door narrows.
H2O Help to Others (Missouri American Water customers) Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) 2709 Woodson Rd., Overland, MO 63114 Main line: (314) 863-0015 Office hours: Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. LIHEAP energy line on the state’s agency list: (314) 446-4420 Missouri American Water customer service: 1-866-430-0820
### Can your water be shut off in winter in Missouri?
Yes, and this is the myth that bites in January. Missouri’s Cold Weather Rule runs from November 1 to March 31, and the state rule that defines it talks about the discontinuance of gas and electric service. So a cold snap that protects your furnace does nothing for the kitchen faucet, and a family can sit in a warm house with dry pipes.
What actually protects your water is getting into a program or a payment plan before the shutoff date. If heat is also on the line, our guide to the Missouri Cold Weather Rule and how to stop a winter shutoff covers gas and electric step by step.
And the heat application does double duty, as you saw above. Our walkthrough of LIHEAP energy assistance in St. Louis gets you to that acceptance letter, which MSD accepts as proof for the sewer discount.
Rent, groceries and the water bill all due the same week? Emergency cash and TANF help in Missouri is the next page to open.
### Is there statewide help for water, not just heat?
Missouri’s Department of Social Services still keeps a page for LIHWAP, the Low Income Household Water Assistance Program. It describes a one-time payment of up to $750 for a water and/or sewer bill, from November through September, and it can cover disconnection or reconnection fees, a threat of disconnection, and past-due or current bills. You must be responsible for the bill (renters count), have $3,000 or less in the bank, and fall under the income line.
I could not confirm that LIHWAP money is flowing right now, so treat it as a question, not a plan. Call your contracted agency or 855-373-4636 and ask one thing: “Are you taking LIHWAP applications today?” If the answer is yes, apply the same day. Keep the lanes straight, too. LIHEAP itself is for home energy bills: heating and cooling. For the full list of who covers which bill, see our roundup of essential St. Louis utility assistance programs.
### Not sure who to call first? Dial 211
When the envelopes blur together, one number sorts them. United Way 211 connects you to a trained resource specialist 24/7. Have your bills in hand when you call. Read the specialist the name at the top of each one, the amount past due, and any shutoff date. Then write down every name and number they give you on the back of the envelope itself, so the next call is already waiting for you.

### Where can I get utility bill assistance in Missouri?
Start with LIHEAP through the Missouri Department of Social Services: a one-time payment toward heating or cooling from October to May, plus crisis help (ECIP) of up to $800 in winter and $300 in summer when you have a shutoff notice. For water and sewer, the state’s LIHWAP page lists a one-time payment of up to $750. Call 855-373-4636 or dial 211 to reach the agency that serves your area.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What emergency utility assistance programs are available in Missouri?
A.  LIHEAP is the main one: the Missouri Department of Social Services pays a one-time amount toward heating or cooling, and its Energy Crisis Intervention Program helps when you have a disconnect notice, up to $800 in winter and $300 in summer. For water and sewer, the state’s LIHWAP page lists up to $750. Then check MSD’s sewer discount, H2O Help to Others, and the City Water Division’s programs.
### Q. How to get emergency help with bills?
A.  Dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626. United Way 211 connects you to a trained resource specialist 24/7. Have each bill in hand, with the past-due amount and any shutoff date, and call the utility itself too: Missouri American Water says to reach out before a shutoff to stay eligible for its installment plan.
### Q. How long does LIHEAP assistance last?
A.  Regular LIHEAP Energy Assistance is a one-time payment for one fuel type, offered from October through May. The crisis program runs in two seasons, based on funding: winter ECIP from November to May, and summer ECIP from June to September. Your approval letter matters beyond that season, though, because MSD accepts a LIHEAP acceptance letter as proof for its two-year sewer discount.
### Q. How many times can you get energy assistance in Missouri?
A.  The state describes regular Energy Assistance as a one-time payment for one fuel type in the October to May season. Crisis help is separate: winter ECIP can pay up to $800 and summer ECIP up to $300, each based on funding and a shutoff notice or similar emergency. Ask your contracted agency, CAASTLC in St. Louis County, what is still open before you apply.
### Q. What is the $500 direct cash assistance program in Missouri?
A.  That was a City of St. Louis program that sent relief funds to City residents hit by the COVID-19 pandemic, and the City says it has completed. The City Water Division’s separate $500 TAP credit is now marked discontinued too. For current water help in the City, call (314) 771-2255 and ask about the tornado-recovery rate and repayment plans.
### Q. How can I reduce my water bill?
A.  Go after the rate, not just the balance. City water customers can ask about the Tornado Recovery 50% discount and the coming Affordability Rate set by city ordinance. Sewer customers can apply for MSD’s Customer Assistance Program, a 50% cut in wastewater rates for two years. Missouri American Water customers can split a past-due balance into 25% down and up to six months of payments.
