## Your Last Day Does Not Count: Filing for Unemployment in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-file-for-unemployment-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
The badge stops working at the side door. The cardboard box rides home on the passenger seat, a coffee mug rattling against a phone charger, while I-270 traffic does what it always does. At home, someone is going to hear the garage door at the wrong hour. A state website is the last thing on your mind.
Give it ten minutes anyway. Missouri dates an unemployment claim to the Sunday, not your last day. The Division of Employment Security says the effective date of your claim will be the beginning, the Sunday, of the week that you file. Your last shift does not set that date, and neither does your layoff letter. The day you log in does, so every week you wait is a week the claim does not cover. Take the evening if you need it. Then file before the week is out.
Here is the line worth texting to anyone you know who just got walked out of a building: Missouri counts from the Sunday of the week you file, and then gives you 14 days after each week ends to ask to be paid for it. Miss that second window and the state says that week is not paid, even if you did everything else right. Two clocks. Most people only hear about the first.
If the screens make your eyes swim, go in person, and the visit does double duty. Downtown, SLATE runs a Job Center at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor, open weekdays from 8 a.m., except Wednesdays, when the doors open at 9. In the county, the St. Louis County Job Center moved to 6347 Plymouth Ave., Room 206, at (314) 377-0445, so an old map or an old bookmark can send you to the wrong address. Sitting in on a Missouri Job Center workshop at either one counts as one of the three job-search activities the state asks for each week. For claim questions, the St. Louis Regional Claims Center line is 314-340-4950.
### How much does unemployment pay in Missouri?
Missouri pays a weekly benefit of 4 percent of the average of your two highest base-period quarters, up to a maximum of $320 a week, per the Division of Employment Security, and the most you can draw in a benefit year is 20 times that weekly amount. That caps a single claim at $6,400. File at uinteract.labor.mo.gov the week you lose work, because your claim starts the Sunday of the week you file.
Now do the math on the back of the layoff letter. Picture it as pay for a 40-hour week, and $320 comes to $8 an hour. The City of St. Louis sets its own floor for people who work on covered city contracts, and its Living Wage Bulletin, posted by the city’s compliance office at the airport, puts that rate at $17.08 an hour where health benefits are provided. That figure is 130% of the federal poverty guideline for a family of three, and the city resets it when the guideline changes. So the biggest check Missouri writes covers less than half of what St. Louis itself calls a living wage. Knowing the size of that gap on night one, not in week four, is what lets you plan around it.
### The second clock: 14 days, every single week
Sunday night, the kitchen light on, the laptop warm on your knees. That is when this part happens, every week. Filing the claim opens the door. Keeping it open is a weekly chore, and the state is strict about the timing. A claim week runs Sunday through Saturday, and you must wait until the week is over before you ask to be paid for it. Then DES says you must file your weekly request for payment within 14 days from the end of the week, the Saturday, you are claiming. Miss that window and the state is blunt: you will not receive unemployment benefits for any week that was not requested in a timely manner.
Picture how it slips. Week one, you file on Sunday morning with your coffee. Week four, your kid is sick, the car needs a tire and Sunday turns into Thursday turns into the next Sunday. Nothing feels urgent because no check has shown up yet anyway. That is exactly the trap. DES tells people to file a weekly request each week even if you are not yet receiving a benefit payment. Set a phone alarm for every Sunday at the same hour and treat it like a shift you cannot skip.
Each weekly request also carries a job search. For each week you ask to be paid, you are required to complete three work search activities, unless you are in approved training, have a definite recall date from an employer or are part of a shared work plan. The good news is that a lot counts. DES lists accessing and searching for work on MoJobs, responding to a Missouri Job Center work referral, going to a Missouri Job Center workshop, submitting a paper application, visiting employers about job openings and attending job interviews. Keep a notebook on the kitchen counter and write down three things every week: where, who and the date.
And every week, report every dollar. DES says you must report all wages earned during the week, even though you may not be paid until later, and that includes tips, commissions, bonuses, show-up time, military reserve pay, board and lodging. The Saturday shift at a friend’s bar, the two days of DoorDash, the cash from helping a neighbor move: write it down and report it. Hiding it is how a benefit turns into a bill.
### Before you click start: what the state will ask
The online claim is faster when your papers are on the table before you open the laptop. Put your Social Security card, your last few pay stubs and a list of every recent employer, with addresses and the dates you started and left, on the table first. The claim asks about all of it, and hunting for an old manager’s address halfway through is how people give up at 11 p.m. Make a username and password you will remember, because you will log in every week from here on. No computer, or the screens keep freezing? DES lists its Regional Claims Centers for filing a claim or getting claims information: toll free at 1-800-320-2519, St. Louis at 314-340-4950 and Jefferson City at 573-751-9040.
A few days after you file, watch the mailbox. DES says it will mail you a form called the Notice of Initial Determination of Status as an Insured Worker. It shows your weekly and maximum benefit amounts, the beginning date of your claim, your base period and the wages each employer reported by quarter. Read every line of it at the kitchen table with a pay stub next to it. If wages are wrong or missing, or you disagree with the claim date, DES says to contact a Regional Claims Center at 800-320-2519 by the date shown on the bottom of the form.
### The waiting week you still have to file
You check the bank app on the first Monday and the balance has not moved. That is not a mistake. Your first eligible week pays nothing up front, and it confuses almost everyone. DES calls it the waiting week: the first week of your claim for which you are eligible for benefits but not paid them. You must still file a weekly request for it. Skip it and you are not saving time, you are breaking the chain. There is a small reward for doing it right, too. DES says you may receive compensation for the waiting week as the last payment on your regular unemployment claim.
When the money does start, do not wait for a text. DES says it will not notify you when a payment is processed. Payments are made the following business day after the week you requested is processed, not counting weekends or state and federal holidays. If you are paid on the Money Network Visa debit card, the Money Network mobile app can show you nearby surcharge-free ATMs and send balance and deposit alerts.
People are asking
### Why is unemployment taking so long in Missouri?
Usually because there is an “issue” on the claim. DES says benefits can be paid within 22 days after a new claim, unless an issue is being investigated, and that an issue takes on average 4-6 weeks to be completed. An issue is any question about your eligibility, and DES lets you answer it through UInteract, a mailed questionnaire or by phone, so answer fast and keep filing your weekly requests while you wait.
### Am I eligible for Missouri unemployment?
The state’s eligibility page lays out the basics. You must:
Lose your job through no fault of your own, or quit for good cause related to the work or the employer.
Make at least $2,250 from an insured employer during your base period, with at least $1,500 in one calendar quarter and at least $750 in the rest of the base period.
Have total base-period wages of at least 1.5 times your highest quarter, or meet the state’s alternate wage test.
Be able and available for work each week, meaning no illness, injury or personal circumstance keeps you from working full time.
Visit jobs.mo.gov at least once a month.
Your base period is the first four of the last five completed calendar quarters before the quarter your claim begins. If you were fired, or you are not sure your reason for quitting counts, file anyway. DES decides, not you, and guessing yourself out of a claim costs the same as losing it.
Did the job end the week after you got hurt on it? Read when to call a workers’ comp attorney before you sign anything.
### Denied? You have 30 days, and the clock is on the letter
A denial letter feels final. It isn’t. DES says you have 30 days from the date of the determination to file an appeal, and the last day to file is printed on the determination itself. Circle it in pen the day it arrives. You can appeal through UInteract, or by mail to the Division of Employment Security Appeals Tribunal, P.O. Box 59, Jefferson City, MO 65104-0059, or by fax to 573-751-1321. The state is clear that appeals cannot be filed by e-mail or over the telephone.
While you wait, keep filing every weekly request. Remember the 14-day rule: if you win the appeal, the state can only pay the weeks you actually claimed on time. Stopping because you were angry, or because it felt pointless, is how a win still leaves money on the table.
### Where can you get free, in-person help in St. Louis?
Sometimes you need a person across a table, not a portal. In the city, SLATE, the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment, runs a Job Center at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor. The city lists its phone as (314) 589-8000 and says the Job Center is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Wednesdays, when it opens at 9 a.m. It is closed on legal holidays. SLATE suggests registering with MoJobs and updating your profile before you visit, which will save you time at the Job Center.
A Job Center workshop or work referral can count toward your three weekly work search activities, so the visit pulls double duty. Bring the notebook. Bring your Notice of Initial Determination. Ask the counselor to look at your weekly request with you if the screens are confusing. That is what they are there for.
In the county, the St. Louis County Job Center moved to 6347 Plymouth Ave., Room 206, and its number is (314) 377-0445. The state says its hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on Friday. The north county Job Center on Pershall Road keeps the number 314-475-7900, and the Jefferson County Job Center is at (636) 865-6060. The state’s toll-free Job Center line is 1-888-728-5627.
An older version of this page listed (314) 244-8020 for north county, (314) 244-2131 for the city Job Center and (636) 442-7011 for the center across the Missouri River. Dial the numbers the agencies post today instead: 314-475-7900 for north county, (314) 589-8000 for SLATE and 636-255-6060, the number St. Charles County lists for its MO Job Center.
When you are ready to look past the next paycheck, these St. Louis guides can help:
Felon-friendly jobs and re-entry strategies
Fulfilling jobs for seniors over 60
Trade schools and apprenticeships in St. Louis

### Your first move tonight
Open the laptop. Go to uinteract.labor.mo.gov. File the claim this week, set the Sunday alarm, start the notebook and put the mailed notice in a folder when it comes. None of it gives you the job back, and $320 a week is a slice of an old paycheck, not the whole thing. But every week you claim on time is a week of money you keep, and that is something you control tonight.
Rent or groceries running short while you wait for that first deposit? Start with our St. Louis help and assistance resources, then file your weekly request on Sunday like clockwork.
If you run the staffing agency, the job-training program or the small shop that hires neighbors after a layoff, the people reading this page are looking for you this week. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory helps them find you, for under a dollar a day. List your business.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does it take to get approved for unemployment in Missouri?
A.  DES says benefits can be paid within 22 days after a new claim is established, unless an issue is being investigated. If there is an issue, a question about your eligibility, it takes on average 4-6 weeks to be completed. Keep filing weekly requests the whole time.
### Q. How is unemployment calculated in Missouri?
A.  Your weekly benefit amount is 4 percent of the average of your two highest quarters in the base period, up to Missouri’s maximum of $320. The base period is the first four of the last five completed calendar quarters before your claim begins. The most you can draw in a benefit year is 20 times your weekly amount, or one-third of your base-period earnings, whichever is less.
### Q. How much unemployment will I get if I make $40,000 a year?
A.  If you earned it evenly, $40,000 a year is $10,000 a quarter. Four percent of a $10,000 average is $400, which is over Missouri’s $320 maximum, so you would get $320 a week. Uneven quarters can change the math, so check the Notice of Initial Determination DES mails you.
### Q. What disqualifies you from unemployment in Missouri?
A.  Losing your job through your own fault, or quitting without good cause related to the work or the employer, can keep you from qualifying. So can earning less than $2,250 in your base period or not being able and available for full-time work. Refusing an offer of work may result in denial, and any week you do not request on time is not paid.
### Q. What is the phone number to file a weekly unemployment claim in Missouri?
A.  Weekly requests are filed online, 24/7, at uinteract.labor.mo.gov, and DES says you can also use its Virtual Agent Chat Bot to file without logging in. For help with a claim, call a Regional Claims Center: 1-800-320-2519 toll free or 314-340-4950 in St. Louis.
### Q. What is the downside of receiving unemployment?
A.  It replaces only part of a paycheck: the maximum is $320 a week, and no more than 20 times your weekly amount in a benefit year. It also comes with weekly work. You must file a request every week, complete three work search activities, report every dollar you earn and stay available for full-time work.
Did a local group help you through this? Tell them about us. Basic listings are free on St Louis Near Me Directory, so the next neighbor who loses a job can find them too. And if this page helped, share it on Facebook with someone who just got walked out.

## St. Louis Shelters Close in the Morning. Here Is Where to Go by Day
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/daytime-drop-in-and-day-centers-in-st-louis
The lock clicks behind you. The morning air hits your face, the bag strap digs into the same sore spot on your shoulder, and your feet pick a direction before your head does. Shelters in St. Louis typically open around 6 p.m. and close in the morning, the City says, so the whole day stretches out in front of you before anyone will let you back in.
That day does not have to be spent on a bench. Across the city there are rooms with hot water, washers that thump and hum, and a table where someone will sit down across from you and start a plan. What costs people a whole day is the wrong door at the wrong hour. This guide is built so you spend your feet and your battery where they count.
### Where can a homeless person go during the day in St. Louis?
Shelters in St. Louis typically close in the morning and reopen around 6 p.m., so days run through drop-in centers. Walk into St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. on a weekday, ideally at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m.; intake is in person only. Bridge of Hope (4001 Cottage Ave.) offers showers and laundry. Call 211 or the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444.
That is the short version. The longer one matters because the details are where people lose a whole day: the lunch hour when a front desk goes dark, the center that only takes young people, the number that turns out to be a fax machine. If you have nowhere to stay tonight as well, the Housing Helpline is where shelter referrals start, and our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis walks through tonight.
### The front door that will not open over the phone
St. Patrick Center, at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. downtown, does its first conversation with you face to face or not at all. Its own contact page says it does not handle these discovery sessions by phone, email or social media, and that all intakes and assessments happen in person. You can call 314-802-0700 with a question, but the call will not get you into the system. Your feet will.
So go to the side entrance, the Welcome Center. No appointment is needed. The center says the smartest times to arrive are 8 a.m. and 1 p.m., Monday through Friday, and that the Welcome Center closes for lunch from noon to 1. Show up at a quarter past twelve and you spend forty-five minutes on the Tucker sidewalk waiting out the lunch hour. Show up at eight and the whole working day is still in front of you. Your feet get you in faster than your phone does. Tell that to the next person you see waiting outside.
Veterans have a separate door. If you, or anyone in your household, served and is homeless or about to be, St. Patrick Center runs Supportive Services for Veteran Families, and the line for it is 314-356-0657. And if the problem is a bed for a single man, the City’s Biddle Housing Opportunities Center at 1212 N. 13th St. (314-612-1675) provides emergency shelter to single adult men. You get there by referral, through the Housing Helpline, 211, or that same Welcome Center.
### Where can I get a shower and wash my clothes?
The first hot shower after a night in a shelter or a car does something no form can. The water runs gray, then clear, and you can feel your shoulders drop. In the City’s own list of drop-in centers, Bridge of Hope Ministries in the Ville is the adult stop for that: it is described as a drop-in service for the unhoused, with showers, clothing, laundry, and adult classes in GED, reading and computer access. It sits at 4001 Cottage Avenue, and the number is 314-405-0253. Hours are not posted online; call 314-405-0253 before you go.
The St. Louis Empowerment Center at 907 Dock Street (314-652-6100) is the other adult name on the City’s list. The City describes it as a drop-in center for people with mental health needs and co-occurring disorders, built around peer specialists, self-help and classes such as anger management. Self-help there means you start the conversation. Nobody chases you down, which can be exactly what a worn-out person needs.
If you are young, the shower and the washer are easier to find, and the next section is yours.
### Where can young people go during the day?
The City’s drop-in page gives young people a list of their own. Covenant House Missouri, at 2727 North Kingshighway (314-533-2241), runs its youth drop-in Monday through Thursday, 9 a.m. to 11 a.m., with showers, laundry, food, clothing and blankets, and LGBTQ+ youth are welcome. That window is short. Get there at nine with whatever needs washing already in the bag.
The SPOT / Project ARK, 4169 Laclede Street, 314-535-0413 (option 5). By appointment, ages 13 to 24: shower, laundry, computer, food.
Restoration House / The Rock, 2912 Chippewa Street, 314-370-7180. Ages 18 to 24: food, hygiene essentials, a laundry room and a clothing closet.
Epworth Youth Drop-in Center, 7520 Natural Bridge Road, Normandy, 314-222-4877. Ages 11 to 20: hot meals, case management, education, employment and legal help.
Center for Youth on the Rise, 12079 Bellefontaine Road, Spanish Lake, 314-615-0221. Ages 12 to 19: life skills, counseling, school and job support.
### A job, a class, a person who knows the forms
Some days the shower is the goal. Other days the goal is a paycheck. Employment Connection, at 2838 Market Street, works with people who are homeless, veterans, people coming home from jail and others shut out of steady work. Its office is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the main line is 314-333-5627. Its World of Work classes meet at that Market Street headquarters on Monday and Tuesday, 8:45 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and the site tells you to arrive on time on the first morning.
If you are in St. Louis County, the library may be the quietest help in town. St. Louis County Library has social workers at six branches who give free one-on-one help with housing insecurity, food, medical needs and more. Book through 314-994-3300, ext. 4000. The carpet is soft, the outlets work, and nobody asks why you are there.
For mental-health care, Places for People at 1001 Lynch Street says recovery there begins with a conversation. Its own site lists the main line as 314-535-5600 and, in a crisis, says to call or text 988.
People are asking
### Where can I find homeless services in St. Louis?
Start with the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, the City’s listed line for housing help, or dial 211 any hour. For a face-to-face assessment, walk into St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd., Monday through Friday, since it does not do intake by phone. For daytime help, the City’s drop-in list names Bridge of Hope Ministries and the St. Louis Empowerment Center for adults.
### When the cold or the heat turns dangerous
Winter changes the math. The City runs Code Blue when temperatures sit at or below 25 degrees, or the wind chill drops below 10, for two hours or more. Then shelters can stay open longer, sometimes around the clock, and warming centers open. Those warming centers are typically open during daytime hours and are not overnight shelters, so treat them as the place to get feeling back in your fingers, not the place to sleep. Code Blue is inactive from March 1 to December 1.
Summer has its own version. United Way 211 keeps a list of cooling sites that open their doors for air-conditioned relief and cool water during the hottest part of the day, activated when the National Weather Service issues an excessive heat advisory or warning. When the sidewalk is shimmering at two in the afternoon, dial 211 and ask for the nearest one.
If drinking or using is part of what makes the days so long, there is free help for that too: addiction treatment and free help in St. Louis.
### Numbers that will waste your battery
When your phone is the only thing keeping you connected, a dead number costs more than time. A few that still circulate on printed lists will not get you what you need. Sunshine Ministries, whose office is at 1315 Howard Street, lists 314-231-5177 as its fax; the phone is 314-231-8209, and it says it cannot answer requests for services by email. For Peter & Paul Community Services at 2612 Wyoming Street, call 314-588-7111, the number its accreditation listing gives. An old City newsletter sends people to The Bridge at 1610 Olive St. and 314-421-3136; I could not confirm that day program still runs, so call before you walk there.
Older lists still print two numbers that will only get you a fax tone: 314-615-2105 is Places for People’s fax, and 314-621-9875 is Peter & Paul’s. One old number is still worth saving: 800-811-4760 reaches the Behavioral Health Response hotline, the line to call when the crisis is in your head, not just your housing.
Families have a different front door again. Gateway180, at 1000 N. 19th St., works to end family homelessness in St. Louis; its office line is 314-231-1515, and it points families looking for a bed to the housing hotline, 314-802-5444.
Save two numbers before your battery dies. Dial 211 (or 1-800-427-4626) any hour, and call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444 for shelter. When evening comes, our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis covers where to go tonight.

### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  Call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444 or dial 211, which runs 24/7. Single men are referred to the Biddle Housing Opportunities Center, families to programs like Gateway180, and young people can turn to Covenant House Missouri at 314-533-2241. ### Q. What housing assistance programs are available in St. Louis?
A.  Most housing help runs through the St. Louis Continuum of Care’s Coordinated Entry system, which starts with the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444. The Biddle Housing Opportunities Center works on Housing First principles, St. Patrick Center runs Supportive Services for Veteran Families (314-356-0657), and Gateway180 works to end family homelessness.
### Q. How to apply for emergency housing assistance in Missouri?
A.  In St. Louis, start by phone or in person. Call the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, dial 211, or walk into St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center, where every intake is done in person. Elsewhere in Missouri, United Way 211 covers Missouri and Illinois and can point you to the agency that handles your county.
### Q. Where can I get immediate financial assistance?
A.  Start with 211, where a trained resource specialist answers 24/7 and the site points people to utility assistance programs. A St. Patrick Center specialist can also look at your situation in person at the Welcome Center, and St. Louis County Library social workers give free one-on-one help finding resources. I could not confirm any center here that hands out cash at the door.
### Q. What does “overnight shelter” mean?
A.  An overnight shelter gives you a safe place to sleep at night. In St. Louis, the City says shelters generally operate during evening and overnight hours, typically opening around 6 p.m. and closing in the morning. A day center or drop-in fills the hours in between, with showers, laundry, classes and case help.

## 9 to 1, Three Days a Week: When LSEM Takes Phone Applications for Free Legal Aid
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-and-low-cost-legal-aid-in-st-louis
The court date is printed in the corner of the page. A thin envelope, your name in the little window, and a tight feeling under your ribs that makes you want to slide the whole thing under the fruit bowl and deal with it later. Please don’t. You can get a free lawyer in St. Louis, and the first step takes one phone call.
Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, the region’s free civil-law office, takes applications for help by phone from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday only. Call 800-444-0514 or (314) 534-4200 inside that window. Outside it, you can leave a message from 1 to 5 p.m. on those same days, and the office says it tries to return calls within 3-5 business days. You can also apply online at any hour through the “Apply Now” link on its Get Help page.
So if a friend is holding one of these envelopes, tell them this: call in the morning, and have the paper in your hand when you do. That one sentence can save a week.
Below are the main doors to free and low-cost legal help in St. Louis, who each one serves, and what to have on the table. If rent or a shutoff is part of the same mess, our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub covers those.
### Where can I get free legal aid in St. Louis, Mo.?
For most civil problems, start with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, usually called LSEM. Its St. Louis office is at 701 Market Street, Suite 1100. It provides free civil legal help to low-income people and older adults in 21 counties of eastern Missouri, and its own FAQ is plain about cost: “No, you do not have to pay any attorney fees to Legal Services.” If there are court costs, the office says you will be told in advance.
It helps to know what LSEM cannot take, so you don’t lose a morning on the wrong line. Its intake page says it cannot handle personal injury, traffic law, bankruptcy or criminal cases, and it does not handle family law cases unless they are directly related to domestic violence or abuse. If your problem is one of those, skip ahead. There is a different door for you below.
If English is not your first language, or you are deaf or hard of hearing, LSEM offers interpreter services. Ask for an interpreter when you first call the intake line. You don’t have to arrange it yourself.
### How do I apply for legal aid in Missouri? The call, step by step
Clear a corner of the kitchen table. Put down a pen, the papers you received and a phone with some charge in it. That is the whole setup. Then work through it in this order:
1. Call inside the window. LSEM’s phone applications run 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday. Its page says all calls for assistance go to its Advocacy Referral Team, and you may have to wait on hold. Keep the phone on speaker so your hands are free for the papers.
2. Or apply online. The online application is in English. After you finish it, LSEM says you will be contacted for more information.
3. Have your answers ready. LSEM’s FAQ says you will be asked about your household’s income, the property you own, your zip code, family size and composition, age, race, and citizenship or immigration status. Jot the income number on the back of the envelope before you dial. It is one less thing to remember with your heart pounding.
4. If you have a summons, have it in front of you. LSEM asks people who have received a summons to be ready with the specific court, the opposing party and the court date. All three are printed on the paper. Read them out slowly.
5. Write down what happens. Note the date you called and anything they tell you. If you leave a message in the afternoon, mark three to five business days out on a calendar so you know when to try again.
That is the whole process. No retainer. No contract to sign before anyone listens. Before a case is accepted, LSEM says it has to meet guidelines and household income limits set by the federal Legal Services Corporation, which is why the income questions come first.
### Where can I get help with eviction in St. Louis?
If the notice was taped to your door, peel it off slowly so the tape doesn’t tear the date, and keep it flat. You will want it in your hand on the call. If you rent in the City of St. Louis and you have an eviction notice or a court date, there is a program built for exactly this moment. The city’s Housing Eviction Law Program, called HELP STL City, started in August of 2024. The city contracted with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri to run it and offer free legal services to tenants facing eviction.
To be eligible, the city’s request page says you need to be a renter living in the City of St. Louis. To ask for help, call the Department of Human Services at (314) 657-1671 or (314) 657-1654. If you received an eviction notice from your landlord, have it with you when you call. If you have been summoned to appear on the eviction court docket, have that information too. The department’s main line is (314) 612-5900, and its office is at 1520 Market, 4th Floor.
If you and your landlord might still talk it through, the Conflict Resolution Center at 20 S. Sarah Street offers mediation. Its number is (314) 255-7449.
Older lists also send renters to the Equal Housing and Opportunity Council, EHOC, at (314) 534-5800. That is still its number, but its own contact page says right now that EHOC is not currently accepting new inquiries, so don’t spend your one free morning waiting on it.
The worst thing you can do with an eviction summons is let it sit. The court date on that paper is real. A lawyer may see something you can’t, but only if you reach one before the hearing.
### If your landlord changes the locks without going to court
Coming home to a key that won’t turn is its own kind of cold. Know this: in Missouri, a landlord cannot evict a renter without a court order. In the City of St. Louis, Board Bill 87 makes a lockout without a court order a city offense, punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both. The same law bars the landlord from collecting rent for the period you were locked out. The National Low Income Housing Coalition has the backstory on how the law passed. Call the police, then call HELP STL. If a housing voucher is part of your situation, our guide to navigating Section 8 in St. Louis City covers the voucher side.
### Clearing an old record in Missouri
An old charge has a way of showing up at the worst moment: the background-check box on a job application, the apartment you really wanted. Missouri lets people petition to expunge many records under section 610.140 of the Revised Statutes. The waiting period is the part people get wrong. The statute says that when you file, it must have been at least three years for a felony, or at least one year for a misdemeanor, municipal violation or infraction, counted from the date you completed your sentence or other authorized disposition.
Because LSEM does not handle criminal cases, start with ArchCity Defenders, a St. Louis legal advocacy organization that lists expungement among the work it does. Its office is at 5939 Goodfellow Blvd, and its numbers are (314) 361-8834 and (855) 724-2489. If clearing a record is one piece of a bigger fresh start, our guide to starting over after incarceration in St. Louis connects the other pieces.
### Help with an order of protection
If you’re in immediate danger, call 911. Reach out from a safe place, on a phone or device the person hurting you can’t check. For emergency shelter, LSEM points people to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
An order of protection is a court order, and you can get free help starting one. The Crime Victim Center in St. Louis lists a helpline at (314) 652-3623 and a domestic violence legal assistance line at (314) 664-6699, with phone hours of 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. Its office is at 539 North Grand Blvd., Suite 400.
Call the Crime Victim Center helpline (314-652-3623) during those hours. If it is after hours, or you just need a human voice right now, Safe Connections runs a 24-hour crisis helpline at (314) 531-2003. LSEM can take family law cases when they are directly tied to domestic violence or abuse. For hotlines, shelters and a fuller safety plan, see our guide to domestic violence help in St. Louis.
### What if you earn too much for free legal aid?
Maybe the intake worker asked about your income and you heard yourself say a number that was a little too big. That is not the end of the road. Programs funded by the federal Legal Services Corporation set income ceilings that, under federal regulation 45 CFR 1611.3, may not exceed 125% of the current Federal Poverty Guidelines. The guidelines change every year, so ask the intake worker for the current figure for your household size. There are exceptions. Section 1611.5 allows some applicants up to 200% of the guidelines in specific situations, such as people seeking help to get or keep government benefits for persons with disabilities. If you are close to the line, apply anyway and let them decide.
If you are clearly over it, you still have a path. The Bar Association of Metropolitan St. Louis runs St. Louis Lawyer Search, which it describes as a free online lawyer directory of attorneys in the St. Louis metropolitan area. Be clear-eyed about one thing: the page says referred attorneys charge fees for their services, and its referral form asks you to pay a referral fee. BAMSL’s main line is (314) 421-4134, toll free (833) 743-8212.
What this help costs you
Nothing, if Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes your case: its own Get Help page says “Services are Free,” for low-income people and the elderly in 21 counties of eastern Missouri. HELP STL City eviction help for City renters is free legal services too. The price only appears when you go private: St. Louis Lawyer Search attorneys charge fees, and the referral form asks you to pay a referral fee before you are matched.
The Catholic Legal Assistance Ministry is another door, listed by Saint Louis University at 100 North Tucker Blvd. and (314) 977-3993. For older adults, our guide to legal services for seniors walks through options built for people 60 and up.
One problem often travels with another. If rent or the light bill is part of this, start here: St. Louis help for rent, utilities and more.
### What to have on the table before you dial
Lines get busy, and the hold music can loop for a while on speaker. Being ready can be the difference between a full intake and a callback days later. Gather these first:
Your household income for the month, and how many people live with you.
Any court papers, with the court name, the other party and the court date easy to find.
An eviction notice from your landlord, if you have one.
Any denial or termination letter from an agency, with its date circled.
A short, plain description of the problem. Two or three sentences is plenty.
A pen and something to write on, for names, dates and the next step.
None of these offices can help someone they never hear from. The lawyers are there. The programs exist for exactly this work. The move that changes everything is small and a little scary: you pick up the phone while the number is still in front of you.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I apply for legal aid in Missouri?
A.  In the St. Louis area, call Legal Services of Eastern Missouri at 800-444-0514 or 314-534-4200 between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday or Thursday, or apply online through the “Apply Now” link on lsem.org. Have your household income and any court papers ready, including the court, the opposing party and the court date.
### Q. What is the maximum income to get legal aid?
A.  For programs funded by the federal Legal Services Corporation, the income ceiling may not exceed 125% of the current Federal Poverty Guidelines, which change every year. Federal rules allow some applicants up to 200% in specific situations. Ask the intake worker for the current dollar figure for your household size.
### Q. How do I get a lawyer if I have no money?
A.  Start with a legal aid office. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes civil cases such as housing and benefits, and its FAQ says you do not have to pay any attorney fees to Legal Services. For criminal records and expungement, contact ArchCity Defenders at 314-361-8834. The Catholic Legal Assistance Ministry (314-977-3993) is another door to ask about.
### Q. Where can I get help with eviction in St. Louis?
A.  City of St. Louis renters can request free legal help through HELP STL City by calling the Department of Human Services at (314) 657-1671 or (314) 657-1654. The program is run with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri. Have your eviction notice or court date information with you when you call.
### Q. Can a landlord evict you without a court order in Missouri?
A.  No. Under Missouri law, a landlord who removes a renter or changes the locks without a court order is guilty of forcible entry and detainer. In the City of St. Louis, Board Bill 87 makes a lockout without a court order a city offense, with a fine of up to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both. Call the police, then call HELP STL at 314-657-1671.
### Q. What is pro bono legal assistance?
A.  Pro bono comes from a Latin term meaning for the public good. Cornell’s Legal Information Institute defines it as legal service provided voluntarily by law firms, law schools and attorneys without monetary compensation. In practice, it means a lawyer helps you without charging a fee.
### Q. Can I call a lawyer and ask a question for free?
A.  You can call a legal aid intake line for free. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes phone applications at (800) 444-0514 from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday. If you earn too much for legal aid, BAMSL (314-421-4134) runs St. Louis Lawyer Search, which lists private attorneys, but referred attorneys charge fees for their services.

## Addiction and Substance Use Treatment in St. Louis: Detox, Rehab, and Free Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/addiction-and-substance-use-treatment-in-st-louis
If this is an emergency, start here.
Overdose or any life-threatening emergency: call 911 now, then give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it. Missouri’s Good Samaritan law offers limited legal protection to people who call 911 to report an overdose.
Suicidal, mental-health, or substance-use crisis: call or text 988, free and 24/7. In eastern Missouri, 988 is answered by Behavioral Health Response.
St. Louis regional crisis line: 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644, Behavioral Health Response, 24/7.
Free, confidential treatment referrals, 24/7: SAMHSA National Helpline 1-800-662-4357.
It’s a little after 2 a.m. in Affton, and someone is sitting on the edge of the tub with a phone in their hand, typing the same search and deleting it. They already know something has to change. What they don’t know is who to call, whether it costs money they don’t have, or whether the voice on the other end will judge them.
If that’s you, or someone you love, read the box above first. Then take a breath. You’re not too far gone, and you’re not doing this wrong by looking. Reaching out is the hard part, and you’re already doing it.
What follows is a plain, no-shame map of where St. Louis actually offers help: crisis lines, medically supervised detox, residential rehab, outpatient care, medication treatment, and the doors that stay open when you have Medicaid or no insurance at all. It’s part of our larger guide to St. Louis help and assistance resources. Every phone number and address here was checked by hand.
### How do people with no money go to rehab in St. Louis?
Start with BJC Behavioral Health’s Same Day Access walk-in at 314-747-7491, the region’s entry point for people on Medicaid or with no insurance. They assess you and connect you to care on a sliding scale. Federally qualified clinics like Affinia Healthcare (314-814-8700) and CSTAR programs through Preferred Family Healthcare and Queen of Peace Center also offer low or no-cost treatment.
Cost is the wall most people hit first, and it turns them around before they ever start. So let’s clear it now. In Missouri, being broke or uninsured does not mean going without treatment. MO HealthNet, the state’s Medicaid program, now covers the full range of care, from outpatient counseling to medication treatment to residential rehab, for eligible members. You apply at mydss.mo.gov.
No insurance and not sure whether you qualify? That’s exactly what the CSTAR programs and the community clinics below are built for. Many use a sliding fee scale tied to your income, and some draw on state Department of Mental Health funds to cover people who can’t pay. For a wider look at care without coverage, see our guide to free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis.
### Who do I call right now for a substance-use crisis?
Call or text 988 for any mental-health or substance-use crisis, free and around the clock. In the St. Louis region, you can also reach Behavioral Health Response directly at 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644. If someone is overdosing, call 911 first and give naloxone if it’s within reach. Minutes matter more than anything else.
Behavioral Health Response covers St. Louis City and County plus St. Charles, Franklin, Jefferson, Lincoln, Warren, Iron, St. Francois, and Washington counties. Teens can text BHEARD to 31658. For a free, confidential referral to treatment anywhere in the country, the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 runs 24/7 and can filter for Medicaid and sliding-fee options.
### Where can I get free naloxone (Narcan)?
Free, and no strings attached. Missouri mails naloxone to your door through getmonaloxone.com (order form at redcap.link/getsupplies), run by UMSL’s Addiction Science team. Prefer to pick it up? All roughly 20 St. Louis County Library branches, county naloxone vending machines, and county health centers hand it out free, with no ID and no cost. Keeping a dose nearby can buy the time an ambulance needs.
### What’s the difference between detox, residential, outpatient, and MAT?
These four words get used interchangeably, and that confusion costs people time. Here’s the short version. Detox handles the first few days safely. Residential means you live on site. Outpatient means you live at home and come in for treatment. MAT is medication plus counseling. Most people move through more than one of these, in whatever order fits their life.
### Detox
Detox is short-term, medically supervised withdrawal, usually a few days. For alcohol and some other drugs, quitting cold on your own can be dangerous, so this step belongs under medical eyes. Think of it as stabilizing, not curing. It gets your body to a safe baseline so the real work can begin.
### Residential and inpatient
Residential, or inpatient, care means living at a facility around the clock while you focus fully on recovery, often for a few weeks. It pulls you out of the triggers and routines at home. This suits people who need structure, a medically supported setting, or simply distance from a situation that keeps dragging them back.
### Outpatient and IOP
Outpatient means you live at home and come in for scheduled treatment. Intensive outpatient, or IOP, is a heavier version, often several sessions a week for a few hours each. It lets you keep a job, care for your kids, or stay in school while still getting real, structured help.
### MAT (medication-assisted treatment)
MAT pairs FDA-approved medication with counseling. For opioids, that usually means methadone, buprenorphine (Suboxone), or naltrexone; for alcohol, naltrexone and a few others. It isn’t swapping one drug for another, and it’s backed by strong evidence. For many people, MAT is what finally makes recovery hold.
### Where do you find medical detox and residential rehab in St. Louis?
Because detox carries medical risk, start by calling a program directly or dialing SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357 to check current beds and coverage. The nonprofit and hospital programs below offer medically supervised detox and residential care across the metro, and several take Medicaid or will work with you on cost.
Harris House 2706 S. River Rd, St. Charles, MO 63303 (transitional housing at 8315 S. Broadway, St. Louis, MO 63111) Phone: 314-631-4299 Web: harrishousestl.org Nonprofit medical detox, residential, PHP, IOP, and sober living. Accepts Medicaid and Department of Mental Health funding.
CenterPointe Hospital 4801 Weldon Spring Pkwy, St. Charles, MO 63304 Admissions: 800-345-5407 (main line 636-723-9306) Web: centerpointehospital.com Detox (ages 12 and up), residential, IOP, MAT, and dual-diagnosis care. Accepts Medicare and Medicaid.
Queen of Peace Center 325 N. Newstead Ave, St. Louis, MO 63108 Phone: 314-531-0511 Web: qopcstl.org Family-centered residential and outpatient treatment for women, children, and families, with housing and child care. Medicaid and DMH funded.
Preferred Family Healthcare (which absorbed Bridgeway Behavioral Health) 4066 Dunnica Ave, St. Louis, MO 63116 (314-833-6155) and 4928 Delmar Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63108 (314-899-0846) Web: pfh.org CSTAR outpatient, women’s, children’s, and adolescent residential, and MAT. Medicaid and DMH funded, with a sliding scale.
### Where can I get MAT, methadone, or Suboxone?
Medication treatment is more available here than most people realize, and some doors open the same day. The programs below prescribe and manage MAT, from methadone to buprenorphine (Suboxone) to naltrexone. CenterPointe and Preferred Family, listed above, offer MAT too, so ask whichever program you reach which medications they support.
Assisted Recovery Centers of America (ARCA) 1430 Olive St #100, St. Louis, MO 63103, and 10208 W. Florissant Ave, St. Louis, MO 63136 (North County) Phone: 314-645-6840 Web: arcamidwest.com Outpatient care, MAT (naltrexone and buprenorphine), medical detox and stabilization, an on-site pharmacy, and naloxone. Walk in with no appointment for a free, confidential assessment, plus help enrolling in Medicaid.
St. Louis Metro Treatment Center (New Season) Phone: 877-284-7074 Web: newseason.com MAT and methadone maintenance. Call for the current clinic location and intake hours.
Center for Life Solutions Phone: 314-731-0100 (crisis line 314-302-6728) Web: centerfls.org MAT paired with therapy. Call for the current office location and scheduling.
### How do the uninsured and Medicaid members get care?
There is a “no wrong door” way in, and it starts with a walk-in. BJC Behavioral Health runs the region’s Same Day Access, where you can walk in for an assessment of mental-health and substance-use needs without an appointment. They see you whether you have Medicaid, Medicare, private insurance, or nothing at all, using a sliding scale and state funds for people who can’t pay.
BJC Behavioral Health Phone: 314-747-7491 or 877-729-4004 Web: bjcbehavioralhealth.org The DMH point of entry with Same Day Access walk-in assessments. Serves St. Louis City and County plus St. Francois, Iron, and Washington counties. Call for the nearest site.
Affinia Healthcare Phone: 314-814-8700 Web: affiniahealthcare.org A federally qualified health center offering primary care plus behavioral health, substance-use care, and MAT on a sliding fee scale. Serves the uninsured. Call for the nearest location.
Places for People 1001 Lynch St, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: 314-535-5600 (crisis 1-800-811-4760) Web: placesforpeople.org Case management and substance-use counseling with central intake for serious mental-health and co-occurring needs. Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurance.
Prevent+Ed (formerly NCADA) 9355 Olive Blvd, St. Louis (Olivette), MO 63132 Phone: 314-962-3456 Web: prevented.org Not a detox or residential provider. Think of them as navigation: prevention, a confidential helpline, and free assessment and referral to point you toward the right program.
The Salvation Army Midtown also runs men’s inpatient and outpatient programs; call 314-652-3310 for current details. And if your struggle is tangled up with anxiety, depression, or trauma, that’s common, not a personal failing. Our guide to free and low-cost mental-health and substance-use help in St. Louis covers treating both at once.
Here’s the thing nobody says out loud: the help already exists. What’s usually missing is just the one phone number and the nerve to dial it. You now have both.
### Is there help for pregnant women, mothers, and families?
Yes, and this is one area St. Louis does especially well. Queen of Peace Center at 314-531-0511 specializes in family-centered treatment for women, children, and families, combining residential and outpatient care with child care and housing, so a mother doesn’t have to choose between recovery and her kids. Preferred Family Healthcare also offers women’s and children’s residential programs.
The fear of losing custody keeps many mothers from asking for help, which is exactly backward. Getting into treatment is the single strongest step toward keeping or reuniting a family, and these programs are built to protect that bond, not break it. If you’re pregnant, say so when you call, since pregnancy often moves you up the list for a bed.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What number do I call for a substance-use crisis in St. Louis?
A.  Call or text 988 anytime, free and confidential. In the St. Louis region, Behavioral Health Response also answers directly at 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644. If someone is overdosing, call 911 first and give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it. These lines run 24 hours a day, every day.
### Q. Where can I get free Narcan (naloxone)?
A.  Order it free by mail at getmonaloxone.com, using the form at redcap.link/getsupplies, run by UMSL’s Addiction Science team. You can also pick it up free, with no ID and no cost, at all roughly 20 St. Louis County Library branches, county naloxone vending machines, and county health centers.
### Q. Do you have to pay for drug rehabilitation?
A.  Not always. In Missouri, being uninsured doesn’t mean going without care. MO HealthNet covers eligible members, while CSTAR programs and clinics like BJC Behavioral Health (314-747-7491) use sliding fee scales and state Department of Mental Health funds to cover people who can’t pay. Start with a walk-in assessment.
### Q. How much is rehab in Missouri?
A.  Cost varies by program and level of care, and many people pay little or nothing. MO HealthNet (Missouri Medicaid) covers eligible members for outpatient, MAT, and residential rehab. Uninsured? CSTAR programs and clinics use sliding fee scales and state funds. Call a program directly for current pricing and coverage.
### Q. Does insurance pay for addiction rehab?
A.  Usually yes. Most private plans, Medicare, and MO HealthNet (Missouri Medicaid) cover substance-use treatment, from outpatient counseling to MAT to residential rehab. Under Missouri’s substance-use waiver approved in December 2023, MO HealthNet covers the full range for eligible members. Apply at mydss.mo.gov, and ask each program which plans it accepts.
### Q. How do you pay for rehab without insurance?
A.  Several doors stay open. BJC Behavioral Health’s Same Day Access (314-747-7491) sees you with no insurance on a sliding scale. CSTAR programs through Preferred Family Healthcare and Queen of Peace Center draw on state Department of Mental Health funds. ARCA (314-645-6840) also helps you enroll in Medicaid during a free walk-in assessment.
### Q. How to get funding to go to rehab?
A.  Start by applying for MO HealthNet at mydss.mo.gov, since Missouri’s Medicaid now covers the full range of care for eligible members. No coverage? Ask programs about sliding fees and state Department of Mental Health funds. The SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) can filter for Medicaid and sliding-fee options, free and 24/7.
### Q. How long does rehab usually last?
A.  It depends on the level of care and the person. Detox is short-term, usually a few days. Residential or inpatient care often runs a few weeks. Outpatient and IOP let you live at home while attending scheduled sessions, often several a week. Many people move through more than one stage over time.
If you read only one line of this, read this one: the first call is the hardest, and it gets easier from there. You don’t need to have it all figured out before you dial. The person who answers does this every day, and their whole job is to take it from here.
Save a couple of these numbers in your phone right now, while you’re thinking about it: 988, and the SAMHSA helpline at 1-800-662-4357. ## Free and Low-Cost After-School and Summer Programs for St. Louis Kids
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-and-low-cost-after-school-and-summer-programs-for-st-louis-kids
You’re standing at the sign-up table, and the number on the flyer is more than a week of groceries. Your kid is tugging your sleeve, eyes lit up, already picturing the friends, the gym, and the summer field trips. And you’re doing the quiet math every parent in this spot knows too well. Here’s what nobody prints on that flyer: in St. Louis, price is almost never the real gate. Sliding-scale fees, scholarships, and flat-out free programs exist across the metro, and asking for them is ordinary, not shameful.
This is the plain-language map to getting your child through the door, even if you can’t pay full price, or can’t pay a dime. We’ll cover who offers sliding-scale fees, who never turns a child away, which programs are completely free, and the two calls that find a seat near your ZIP code. It sits inside our bigger guide to help and assistance across St. Louis. Let’s get your kid signed up.
### Where can St. Louis families find free or low-cost after-school and summer programs?
Start with three front doors: dial 2-1-1, call ARCHS at (314) 534-0022, or search Blueprint4. Then reach programs directly. Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club turns no child away, LifeWise StL runs a free after-school program, and the Gateway Region YMCA and Boys & Girls Clubs offer sliding-scale fees and scholarships.
Think of ARCHS as the region’s switchboard for free seats. It doesn’t run a clubhouse you drop your kid at; it funds free after-school programming at other agencies and can point you to an open spot. Recent reporting credited its After School for All Partnership with about $2.5 million funding free programs for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at around 29 sites across St. Louis Public Schools and Jennings (KSDK/St. Louis American, 2024).
ARCHS (Area Resources for Community and Human Services) Address: 539 N. Grand Blvd, 6th Floor, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 534-0022 Website: stlarchs.org
Two more catch-alls belong on speed dial. Dial 2-1-1 (United Way) any hour for a free, confidential referral to programs near you. And Blueprint4, at blueprint4.com, is a searchable directory of free and low-cost St. Louis youth programs you can filter by neighborhood. Being found is the whole game here: the seat already exists, and these front doors connect your child to it.
### How do you get help paying if you can’t afford full price?
Four tools carry most families through: sliding-scale fees, scholarships, formal financial-assistance applications, and the state child-care subsidy. The Gateway Region YMCA alone awards about $2.58 million in assistance each year (gwrymca.org), covering memberships, programs, child care, and camp. You qualify on need, not on a perfect record, and applying is routine.
Here’s how the YMCA process works. Download the financial-assistance application, bring proof of income and dependents to any branch Welcome Center, and expect a decision in about ten business days; you renew once a year. For child-care aid specifically, apply for Missouri or Illinois state child-care assistance first, and if you’re denied, bring the denial letter. Our guide to child care assistance in Missouri walks through that state step.
Gateway Region YMCA (YMCA of Greater St. Louis) Financial-assistance details: gwrymca.org/financial-assistance Association office: 2815 Scott Avenue, Suite D, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 436-1177 Find your nearest branch: gwrymca.org/locations
The Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis run on the same sliding-scale idea. Membership listings put the annual fee around $25, with some summer camps near $275, but the clubs don’t publish prices online, so call (314) 335-8000 to confirm and ask about aid. Fees slide with self-reported household income and family size, there’s no registration fee, and scholarships are available for ages 6 to 18.
Its clubs include: Herbert Hoover Club — 2901 N. Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63107 — (314) 335-8100 Mathews-Dickey Club — 4245 N. Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63115 — (314) 382-5952 Adams Park Club — 4317 Vista Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63110 — (314) 335-8203 Teen Center of Excellence — 9200 West Florissant Ave, St. Louis, MO 63136 — (314) 335-8240 Website: bgcstl.org
### Which St. Louis programs never turn a child away?
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club is the clearest answer. Program listings describe a firm policy of “no child turned away” regardless of a family’s ability to pay. Fees slide with self-reported income and household size, there’s no registration fee, and scholarships are available. In 2024 the club served 722 members and 51,276 meals (Blueprint4 listing).
The fee is set once, at registration, so you learn your monthly number up front. It serves ages 6 to 16 for City of St. Louis residents, after school and through the summer. Because that exact policy wording comes from a 211/Blueprint4 listing rather than the club’s own page, confirm it with the membership desk before you count on it.
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis Soulard campus: 2524 S. 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Main phone: (314) 772-5661; membership desk: (314) 655-9767 Website: gsgbcstl.org
### Are there completely free after-school programs in St. Louis?
Yes, several charge families nothing at all. LifeWise StL (Kingdom House) runs a free Young Scholars after-school program, and ARCHS funds free seats for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at about 29 St. Louis sites (KSDK/St. Louis American, 2024). Free doesn’t mean less; these include homework help, meals, and sometimes a ride home.
Listings describe Young Scholars as free for ages about 6 to 13, Monday through Friday from 3:30 to 6:00 p.m. on the SLPS calendar, with homework help, MAP-test enrichment, a healthy dinner, and free transportation from school and home when needed. Because “free” and the eligible ZIP list appear in secondary listings, confirm current cost and eligibility at (314) 421-0400.
LifeWise StL (Kingdom House) Address: 1321 S. 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: (314) 421-0400 (Young Scholars intake also cited at (314) 627-1241) Website: lifewisestl.org
The ARCHS-funded free seats, its After School for All Partnership, are aimed at K-5 kids whose parents work, train for a job, or attend school, and who qualify economically for free meals. That’s the door to a no-cost seat, and ARCHS or 2-1-1 can tell you which nearby school or agency has one open.
### What free mentoring and teen programs support St. Louis kids?
Two standouts cost families nothing. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern Missouri matches kids with mentors at no program fee and no application fee; its 2025 impact report cites 9,228 youth served and more than 1,400 active matches. Wyman Center delivers free teen leadership programs through schools and partners. Both wrap around your child rather than replacing daytime care.
Big Brothers Big Sisters serves kids roughly 5 to 17 across St. Louis City and County, St. Charles County, and Jefferson County. Think of it as a steady, caring adult in your child’s corner, not day-to-day coverage. You can start the match at bbbsemo.org/enroll-child.
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern Missouri Main office: 501 N. Grand Blvd, Suite 100, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 361-5900 Website: bbbsemo.org
Wyman Center focuses on teens from tight-budget households, running the Teen Outreach Program, the Teen Connection Project, and Wyman Leaders. These leadership and college-and-career programs are delivered largely free through schools and community partners, so call to find a participating site near your teen.
Wyman Center Address: 600 Kiwanis Drive, Eureka, MO 63025 Phone: (636) 938-5245 Website: wymancenter.org
### Are there free or low-cost programs in St. Charles County or the Metro-East?
Yes. Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Charles County, a separate nonprofit from the city clubs, runs after-school, summer camp, sports, and ACT prep on sliding-scale fees; membership listings run about $25 to $35 by unit (Blueprint4). Across the river, the Bethalto club serves Metro-East Illinois families. City rec centers and the library add still more free options.

Don’t overlook the free public options either. The City of St. Louis offers free summer camps, outdoor pools, sports, and youth employment; the St. Louis Public Library runs free week-long camps and summer reading; and Beyond Housing’s CDF Freedom Schools hosts a free six-week summer reading program for grades K-5. Check each program’s current-year offerings by phone or website before you plan around them.
Here’s the truth worth holding onto: these programs were built for your family, funded so a child’s afternoon or summer never hinges on a parent’s bank balance. The staff behind these desks want your call. Make the two calls, say the fee question out loud, and let your kid have the chance. If groceries are tight this month too, our guides to WIC food and nutrition help and free food giveaways happening today stack right on top, and the full St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you. LifeWise StL’s Young Scholars, Big Brothers Big Sisters mentoring, and Wyman Center’s teen programs also cost families nothing.

A.  Several places charge nothing. LifeWise StL runs a free Young Scholars after-school program, and ARCHS funds free seats for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at about 29 St. Louis sites. City rec centers, outdoor pools, and the public library add more no-cost options. Call ARCHS at (314) 534-0022 to find one nearby.
### Q. Are there free summer camps?

Beyond Housing’s CDF Freedom Schools hosts a free six-week summer reading program for grades K-5. Check each program’s current-year offerings by phone or website before you plan around them.

A.  It varies, so call first, but most programs ask for a photo ID, proof of income such as recent pay stubs or a tax return, and dependent verification. Some also want your child’s birth certificate, immunization records, or a recent report card. For YMCA child-care aid, add any state denial letter.
### Q. What are some good summer camps for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Several run on sliding-scale fees or scholarships. Both Boys & Girls Clubs networks offer summer camp, sports, and ACT prep, with some camps near $275. The Gateway Region YMCA runs camp with financial assistance, and Gene Slay’s serves ages 6 to 16 through the summer. Call each site to confirm dates and aid.

A.  Four tools carry most families: sliding-scale fees, scholarships, formal financial-assistance applications, and the state child-care subsidy. The Gateway Region YMCA alone awards about $2.58 million in assistance each year, and Gene Slay’s turns no child away. You qualify on need, not a perfect record, so ask about aid when you register.
### Q. What if I can’t afford summer school?
A.  Price is rarely the real gate. Sliding-scale fees, scholarships, and formal financial assistance keep summer programs within reach, and Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club turns no child away regardless of ability to pay. ### Q. Can I still get help if I was denied state child-care assistance?
A.  Yes. The Gateway Region YMCA asks families to apply for Missouri or Illinois state child-care assistance first, then accepts you with the denial letter and applies its own financial aid. A state denial is not the end of the road. Bring that letter to your nearest branch Welcome Center to keep going.

## Locked Out Tonight in St. Louis? Where a Teen Can Go
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/youth-and-teen-emergency-shelter-in-st-louis-runaway-help
“I need Safe Place help.” Five words. Say them to the person behind the counter at a QuikTrip or a Walgreens, under the hum of the coolers and the white light that never shuts off, or to the driver of a Metro bus or train. Youth In Need, the regional Safe Place provider in eastern Missouri, says every site is trained to call a designated help line, and a Safe Place case worker is then sent right away to assess the situation and, if it comes to that, pick the young person up and take them to a shelter. The program is free for any child or teen who needs help.
If you’re the teenager reading this with your hood up and your phone almost dead, breathe. You are not in trouble for needing a bed. If you’re the aunt, the coach, the teacher or the friend whose couch ran out, you’re in the right place too. Everything below is the door, the number and who it is for, so you can stop scrolling and start dialing. If anyone is in danger right now, call 911 first. For rent, food and everything that comes after tonight, we keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis.
### Where can a homeless or runaway teen get emergency shelter in St. Louis tonight?
For a safe place tonight, young people 16 to 24 can walk into Covenant House Missouri at 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, open 24/7; for bed availability call (314) 351-4866. Ages 10 to 19 can call Youth In Need’s 24-Hour Help Line at 636-946-3771, and it accepts collect calls. Anywhere, call 1-800-786-2929. In danger? Call 911.
Two numbers matter at Covenant House, and most lists only give you one. The general line is 314-533-2241. But the shelter’s own Get Help page says that for bed availability, call (314) 351-4866. Dial that one first and you skip a transfer while the battery bar turns red.
Here is what waits on the other side of that call. Covenant House runs the Genesis Shelter Program, a 20-bed emergency shelter where youth can stay for up to 30 days, with longer stays approved case by case. Intake is first-come, first-served, and the shelter describes its approach as open intake and housing first, meaning services are open to all with no prerequisites. Staff start with the basics, food and clean clothes, before anyone asks you to fill out a plan. Then they sit down with each young person and work out the next step together.
Age decides the door. Sixteen and up, Covenant House on North Kingshighway in the city. Ten to nineteen, Youth In Need, the agency based in St. Charles. Sixteen to nineteen and not sure? Call both. Nobody on either line will be annoyed that you asked.
### The five words work on a bus, too
Safe Place is the St. Louis-area option almost nobody mentions, and it is built for the moment you have no plan at all: standing at a bus stop at night, the doors folding open in front of you, nowhere to tell the driver you are going. Youth In Need is the regional provider of Safe Place services in eastern Missouri, and it lists its sites as all QuikTrips, Walgreens, Gateway Region YMCAs, St. Charles City-County Libraries and most fire departments, as well as all Metro buses and trains in Missouri. Look for the yellow and black Safe Place sign. Walk in, find an employee, and say you need Safe Place help. That is the whole script.
Youth In Need is specific about who it is for: a young person who is a runaway, lost, in danger, being abused, locked out of the house, having trouble at home or school, avoiding a bully, on an unsafe date, or in a car with an unsafe or drunk driver. Locked out with the porch light off counts. So does a ride that went wrong. You do not have to prove anything to the person at the register. Safe Place staff also give talks to schools, churches and youth groups about the program and the St. Louis County Youth Connection Helpline. For more information, the number is 636-614-4055.
### Can a 16 year old go to a homeless shelter without a parent’s signature in Missouri?
This is the question that keeps a lot of teenagers curled up in the back seat of a car with the engine off, and Missouri has its own answer, written into state law. A national hotline script will not read it to you. Section 431.056 of the Missouri statutes says a minor is qualified and competent to contract for housing and for admission to a homeless shelter, among other things, when four things are true at once.
In plain words: first, you are 16 or 17. Second, you are homeless, unless you are already under the Children’s Division or the juvenile court. Third, you are self-supporting, meaning you are living without the physical or financial support of a parent or guardian. Fourth, your parent or guardian has consented to you living on your own.
That last condition sounds like a dead end. It is not. The law says consent can be expressed or implied, and implied consent includes a parent barring the minor from the home or otherwise indicating that the minor is not welcome to stay. If you were told to get out, that may already count. The statute also lets a letter stand in as proof: one signed by the director of an agency that serves homeless people, a school’s homeless liaison, a school social worker or counselor, or a lawyer representing the minor.
So a 16 year old does not have to win an argument with a parent at 1 a.m. to get help started, and the school counselor you already know can be part of the answer. This is not legal advice, and every situation is different, but it is the law on the books. Missouri’s juvenile code still calls anyone under eighteen a child, so a shelter may have to bring in family or the Children’s Division. Ask how that works before you decide anything.
### Which St. Louis youth shelters take a young person tonight?
Call first if you can, both to confirm a bed and so someone is watching the door for you. These three keep a door or a crisis line open around the clock.
### Covenant House Missouri
Covenant House says it plainly: for individuals age 16-24, call us, drop in, or use the emergency resources. Beyond the bed, its residential services include individual and group therapy, on-site psychiatry appointments, a health clinic, education and employment support, and case management. Two full-time therapists work on-site, and career staff run job-skills classes every day on campus.
Covenant House Missouri Address: 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63113 Bed availability: (314) 351-4866 Other information: 314-533-2241 Ages: 16-24 Hours: open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week Website: covenanthousemo.org
### Youth In Need Emergency Shelter
Youth In Need’s Emergency Shelter is a 12-bed emergency residential group home for youth ages 10 to 19 who are in crisis. It is voluntary and free. Intakes happen through the 24-Hour Help Line or on a walk-in basis at the shelter, and staff start with the young person’s immediate needs before explaining the program. The top of its website carries one line: if you are in a housing crisis, call 636-946-3771.
Youth In Need Emergency Shelter 24-Hour Help Line: 636-946-3771 (collect calls accepted) Central office: 1815 Boone’s Lick Road, St. Charles, MO 63301, 636-946-5600 Ages: 10-19 Cost: free Website: youthinneed.org

Annie Malone Children & Family Services Address: 2612 Annie Malone Dr, St. Louis, MO 63113 Main phone: 314-531-0120 Crisis line: 844-803-7233 Website: anniemalone.org
Eighteen or older and none of these fit? Our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis covers adult options across the metro tonight.
### What if home is the thing that isn’t safe?
If a young person is being hurt at home, or is scared they will be, Missouri’s Children’s Division runs a toll-free hotline that answers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Anyone can call: the teen, a grandparent, a neighbor who heard it through the wall. You can stay anonymous. The state’s own page puts it bluntly: if you have the thought “Maybe I should call,” do it. Not every call turns into an abuse case, and the Division can often bring in services that help a family in crisis.
Missouri Child Abuse and Neglect Hotline Phone: 1-800-392-3738 (24 hours a day, 7 days a week) Immediate danger: call 911
Already 18, or the one who just got the call from a cousin who is? Adult beds run on different rules - here is where a grown-up in St. Louis can sleep tonight.
### Where can a teen get food, a shower and clean clothes during the day?
Not everyone needs a bed at 2 p.m. Some need a hot plate of food, a shower that runs warm, and a dryer to sit next to. The Epworth Drop-In Center is a safe space for youth ages 11 through 20, with a recreation room, computer lab, full-service kitchen, laundry, shower and a clothes and food pantry. Hot meals are prepared daily. Check the hours below before you go: it closes at 5 p.m., so line up a bed for the night too.
Epworth Drop-In Center Address: 7520 Natural Bridge Road, Normandy, MO 63121 Phone: 314-918-3470 (Director of Older Youth Services) Ages: 11-20 Hours: Monday through Thursday 12:00-5:00 PM, Friday 1:00-5:00 PM (call to confirm) Website: epworth.org
Epworth’s street outreach team also brings goods and resources to young people who won’t or can’t come in. For more places to warm up and wash up in business hours, see our guide to daytime drop-in and day centers in St. Louis.
### Is there help for a teen being trafficked or exploited?
The National Human Trafficking Hotline is confidential and answers 24/7 at 1-888-373-7888, or text 233733. For a bed tonight, pair that call with Covenant House at (314) 351-4866.
Two local organizations do the longer work once the first night is behind you. The Covering House serves sexually exploited and trafficked children and teens through a residential home, community-based services and prevention training, and its new residential home has space for up to ten girls. Referrals go through its website. If you copied 314-962-6450 for The Covering House from an older version of this page, cross it out: the number on The Covering House’s own site is (314) 962-3450.
The Covering House (referrals through its website) Phone: (314) 962-3450 Mail: P.O. Box 431, Arnold, MO 63010 Website: thecoveringhouse.org
Marygrove (therapeutic services for youth) Address: 2705 Mullanphy Lane, Florissant, MO 63031 Phone: 314-830-6201 Website: marygrovechildren.org
### Which hotlines answer for runaways and worried parents?
When you don’t know where to start, a hotline is the fastest first move. The National Runaway Safeline is free, confidential and available 24/7. Call 1-800-786-2929, or text that same number. Its staff can work toward locating an open bed in a shelter in your area, and if home is the problem, they can help you sort out when an abuse report has to be made.
Ready to go back, or to a relative who will take you? The Safeline’s Home Free program gives young people ages 12 to 21 a free Greyhound bus ticket to a parent, a legal guardian or an approved alternative living arrangement. It starts with a phone call and a plan, not a lecture.
For a mental-health or suicide crisis, call or text 988. In St. Louis, the city’s health department lists Behavioral Health Response’s 24/7 Crisis Line, where you can talk with a clinician free of charge at 314-469-6644, and its Youth Connection Helpline at 314-819-8802, or text BHEARD to 31658. Kids Under Twenty One (KUTO) runs a crisis helpline staffed by trained youth volunteers at 1-888-644-5886; its site says it opens every day after 4 p.m.
Parents, this part is for you. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children tells families to immediately call local law enforcement when a child is missing, and to ask that the child’s name go into the FBI’s National Crime Information Center Missing Person File. Then call the center at 1-800-843-5678. Call the Runaway Safeline too. It is there for caregivers as well as youth, and once your teen reaches out, it can set up a conference call so everyone on the line feels heard. For counseling once things settle, see our guide to teen mental health and crisis help in St. Louis.
Write two numbers on your hand or the back of a receipt tonight: (314) 351-4866 and 636-946-3771. Phones die. Ink doesn’t.
