### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can a 16 year old go to a homeless shelter?
A.  Yes. Covenant House Missouri serves ages 16 to 24 and takes drop-ins around the clock; call (314) 351-4866 for bed availability. Youth In Need’s shelter serves ages 10 to 19 through its 24-Hour Help Line, 636-946-3771. Under section 431.056, a 16- or 17-year-old who is homeless and self-supporting may contract for admission to a homeless shelter if a parent has consented, and that consent can be implied.
### Q. Can a 17 year old leave home without parental consent in Missouri?
A.  Missouri treats a 17-year-old as a child under its juvenile code, so leaving home is not the same as being on your own legally. Section 431.056 does let a homeless, self-supporting 16- or 17-year-old contract for housing and shelter, but only when a parent has consented, and consent can be implied, for example when a parent bars the minor from the home. Call the Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929 to talk it through.
### Q. Is a 17-year-old considered a minor in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Missouri’s juvenile code defines a child as any person under eighteen years of age, and the legal age to contract in Missouri is eighteen. The narrow exception for homeless 16- and 17-year-olds in section 431.056 covers things like housing, shelter admission and medical care, not adulthood in general.
### Q. Can my mom call the cops if I leave at 17?
A.  Yes. At 17 you are still a child under Missouri’s juvenile code, which covers any person under eighteen, and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children tells parents to immediately call local law enforcement when a child is missing. If home is not safe, say so: call the Missouri child abuse hotline at 1-800-392-3738 or the Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929, which can also set up a conference call with your parent.
### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  If you are 16 to 24, go to Covenant House Missouri at 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, open 24 hours a day, and call (314) 351-4866 for bed availability. Ages 10 to 19 can call Youth In Need at 636-946-3771. No plan at all? Walk into a QuikTrip or Walgreens with the Safe Place sign, or step onto a Metro bus or train, and tell an employee you need Safe Place help.
### Q. Where can I find emergency housing in St. Louis?
A.  For young people, Covenant House Missouri runs the Genesis Shelter Program, a 20-bed emergency shelter where youth can stay up to 30 days, first-come, first-served. Youth In Need runs a 12-bed emergency shelter for ages 10 to 19. Annie Malone’s 24-hour Crisis Center answers at 844-803-7233. Adults can start with our emergency homeless shelters guide.
### Q. Where can I send my troubled child for free in Missouri?
A.  Youth In Need’s Emergency Shelter is voluntary and free to participants, for ages 10 to 19 in crisis, with counseling and case management; call 636-946-3771. Safe Place is free for any child or teen who needs help. For counseling referrals and emergency help, Annie Malone’s Crisis Center is at 844-803-7233.
### Q. What happens if a child becomes homeless?
A.  In the St. Louis area, the first trained adult they reach can start the help. At a Safe Place site, staff call a designated help line and a case worker is sent to assess the situation and, if necessary, take the young person to a shelter. If abuse or neglect is involved, the Missouri hotline at 1-800-392-3738 answers 24 hours a day, and the Children’s Division can step in with services.
### Q. Can a runaway get a free bus ticket home?
A.  Often, yes. The National Runaway Safeline’s Home Free program gives youth ages 12 to 21 a free Greyhound bus ticket to a parent, legal guardian or approved alternative living arrangement. It starts with a call to 1-800-786-2929 and a conference call with family to plan the trip.

## Foster Care in Missouri and Aging Out Support in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/foster-care-in-missouri-and-aging-out-support-in-st-louis
The question can arrive quietly. A caseworker asks a couple, over coffee, whether they’ve ever thought about fostering. Across the metro, in another kitchen, a seventeen-year-old marks a calendar toward a birthday most teens count down to, and she quietly dreads. Foster care in Missouri holds both of those moments at once: the family thinking about opening a door, and the young person about to walk through one alone.
This guide is written for both of you. If you’re weighing whether to become a foster parent, we lay out the real steps, who to call, and what it costs, which is nothing. If you’re aging out, or you love someone who is, you’ll find the health coverage, housing, and college money Missouri keeps ready for former foster youth, including free MO HealthNet coverage all the way to age 26. For the wider picture, keep our guide to help and assistance across St. Louis nearby. Let’s begin.
### What support is available for youth aging out of foster care in St. Louis?
You don’t lose everything at 18. If you were in Missouri foster care around your 18th birthday, you keep free MO HealthNet coverage to age 26. The Chafee Older Youth Program (ages 14-23) adds housing help, and the ETV pays up to $5,000 a year. Start with your caseworker or the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition at (314) 367-8373.
Here’s what the paperwork rarely says out loud: turning 18 in foster care is not a cliff. Missouri built a bridge, and it runs for years. The catch? Most of it won’t come find you. You have to reach for it, or ask someone to reach alongside you. If you have a Children’s Division worker or an Older Youth Transition Specialist, that person is your fastest door to every benefit below.
### Free health coverage until age 26
This one surprises people, so read it twice. Young adults who were in Missouri foster care around their 18th birthday qualify for free MO HealthNet (Medicaid) until they turn 26, with no income test at all. The Medicaid.gov former-foster-care rule counts youth who were in care any time in the 30 days before turning 18. You don’t have to be broke, employed, or in school to keep it.
Moved here from another state’s foster system? Missouri also covers residents under 26 who spent at least six months in another state’s care and had Medicaid at 18. When you reach 26, reapply through the Family Support Division for a different category so your coverage doesn’t lapse. Ask your caseworker to confirm your enrollment before any birthday sneaks up.
### The Chafee Older Youth Program (ages 14-23)
Missouri’s Older Youth Program is the Chafee “Foster Care Program for Successful Transition to Adulthood.” The state Department of Social Services runs it for youth ages 14 to 23 who are in, or were in, Children’s Division custody. It works across three lanes: Education Services, Help with Independence, and Finance and Life Skills.
An Older Youth Transition Specialist is the person who verifies what you qualify for and connects you to housing help and benefits. If you don’t know who yours is, ask your Children’s Division office, or let the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition’s Navigator find out for you. One conversation can open several doors at once.
### Money for college and job training: ETV and Missouri Reach
Two programs help foster youth pay for what comes after high school, and you can often use both. The Education & Training Voucher (ETV) covers up to $5,000 a year for tuition, books, supplies, and living costs while you study. Funds are limited and first-come, first-served, so the real advice is simple: ask early.
The ETV application route changed recently, so don’t trust an old online form you find floating around. Ask your Older Youth Transition Specialist or Children’s Division worker for the current ETV application and deadline. They’ll point you to the live process rather than a dead link.
Missouri Reach is the other big one. It waives tuition and fees at Missouri’s public colleges and universities for eligible foster youth. To keep it, you complete at least 100 hours of community service or a public internship each year, and you apply for other non-loan aid first. Most students must apply by their 21st birthday, so put this on your list now.
### Where can a young person who aged out find housing in St. Louis?
Start with Covenant House Missouri, the metro’s round-the-clock anchor for young adults ages 16 to 24. It’s open 24/7, free, and offers emergency beds with private bedrooms plus transitional housing for up to two years. Beyond Covenant House, Epworth, Marygrove, and Annie Malone all run transitional and independent-living programs across the region.
Aging out without a plan is more common than anyone admits, and it’s nobody’s fault. If you need a bed this week, call one of these numbers directly. If you’re facing a true crisis tonight, our guide to youth and teen emergency shelter in St. Louis lists faster options, and for longer-term stability see finding transitional housing in St. Louis.
Covenant House Missouri Address: 2727 N. Kingshighway Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-533-2241 Website: covenanthouse.org Ages 16-24, open 24/7 and free. Emergency shelter (60-90 days), transitional housing up to two years, on-site medical and mental health care, plus employment and education support. LGBTQ+ affirming; walk-ins welcome.
Epworth Children & Family Services Main campus: 110 North Elm Avenue, Webster Groves, MO 63119 Main phone: 314-961-5718 Normandy Drop-In Center: 7520 Natural Bridge Road, St. Louis, MO 63121; 314-222-4877 Website: epworth.org Runs the Chafee program, transitional and independent living, a youth drop-in center, and street outreach for at-risk youth.
Marygrove Address: 2705 Mullanphy Lane, Florissant, MO 63031 Phone: (314) 830-6201 Website: marygrovechildren.org Transitional and independent living with scattered-site apartments and houses where young adults (roughly ages 17-20) live on their own with support as they leave care.
Annie Malone Children & Family Services Address: 2612 Annie Malone Dr., St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: (314) 531-0120 Website: anniemalone.com A St. Louis institution since 1888. Transitional and independent living, plus an Economic Mobility Program for youth 16-21 that blends academics, job training, and mental health support.
Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition — Older Youth Readiness Program Phone: (314) 367-8373 Website: foster-adopt.org A Navigator helps youth ages 13-24 secure housing, food, clothing, jobs, medical care, and continued education. Serves St. Louis City and County plus Jefferson, Franklin, and St. Charles counties. Full address in the agencies section below.
### How do you become a foster parent in Missouri?
You need to be at least 21, and it costs you nothing. The Missouri Department of Social Services charges no fee for the foster-parent license or for the background checks it runs. You’ll apply, complete free pre-service training, host a home study, and pass a health physical. Call the Children’s Division at 800-554-2222 to begin, or work with a local licensing agency.
Wondering whether you’re “qualified” enough? Most people who ask that question already have what matters most: steady ground and room to care. The formal requirements are practical, not perfect-family fantasies. Here’s the honest checklist.
### What are the requirements to foster in Missouri?
Be at least 21 years old. Pass background checks, which apply to every household member age 17 and up. Show adequate income to cover your own household, since foster payments support the child, not your bills. Have room in your home, and complete pre-service training, a home study, and a health physical. That’s the core of it.
Notice what’s not on the list. You don’t need to be married, own a home, or have a big income. Singles and renters foster all the time. If you’re raising your own kids, working full-time, or new to the area, a licensing agency can look at your situation and tell you what to expect. Fostering can sit alongside a busy life; if child care is part of your plan, see our guide to child care assistance in Missouri.
### What does it cost, and how long does it take?
The license itself is free, and so are the background checks and the required training. What it asks for instead is time: an application, a training series, a home study visit, and a health check. Timelines vary by agency and by how quickly paperwork moves, so the best move is to call and ask your agency for their current schedule.
A quick tip from families who’ve done it: pick one agency and let them guide you, rather than juggling several. Every licensed agency in the metro can walk you through the exact same state process, so you’re free to choose the one whose people you click with.
### Which St. Louis agencies license and support foster families?
Several trusted agencies handle licensing across the metro, and the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition serves youth and families in five counties: St. Louis City, St. Louis County, Jefferson, Franklin, and St. Charles. The Missouri Children’s Division is the state licensing authority, but you rarely need to drive to Jefferson City. Start with a phone call to any name below.
Missouri Children’s Division (Department of Social Services) Become-a-foster-parent line: 800-554-2222 Child Abuse & Neglect Hotline: 800-392-3738 Website: dss.mo.gov/cd/foster-care The state authority that licenses foster parents and runs the Older Youth/Chafee transition program. Licensing happens through regional and county offices across the St. Louis area, so call the 800 line to be routed locally.
Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition Address: 1220 N. Lindbergh Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63132 Phone: (314) 367-8373 Website: foster-adopt.org Recruitment and licensing support for foster and adoptive parents, plus the Older Youth Readiness Program for young people leaving care. Known for national models like Extreme Recruitment and 30 Days to Family.
KVC Missouri — St. Louis office Address: 330 N. Gore Ave., Webster Groves, MO 63119 Phone: (844) 424-3577 Website: missouri.kvc.org Foster-parent licensing, case management, family strengthening, children’s mental health care, and independent-living support. KVC Missouri took over the former Great Circle operations in Missouri in 2023 and now serves families from the Gore Avenue site.
Lutheran Family and Children’s Services of Missouri (LFCS) Address: 9666 Olive Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63132 (call ahead to confirm the current suite) Phone: (314) 787-5100 (toll-free 866-326-5327) Website: lfcsmo.org Foster care, adoption, counseling, and youth mentoring across Missouri.
Epworth Children & Family Services and Marygrove, both listed with full contact details in the housing section above, also license and support foster families. Don’t rule them out if their location or programs fit your family better.
Whether you’re opening your home or leaving one, the same truth holds: nobody does this alone, and being found is how a hard season stays just a season. Make one call this week, to an agency, a caseworker, or a Navigator, and let a real person carry the next step with you. For everything else a St. Louis neighbor might need, keep our guide to help and assistance across St. Louis close.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the requirements to foster a child in Missouri?
A.  You must be at least 21, pass background checks (every household member 17 and older is screened), show adequate income, and have room in your home. You’ll also finish pre-service training, a home study, and a health physical. Marital status and home ownership are not requirements, per the Missouri Department of Social Services.
### Q. What disqualifies someone from being a foster parent?
A.  Missouri screens every household member age 17 and older with background checks, so a serious criminal or child-abuse history can be a barrier. What doesn’t disqualify you: being single, renting, having a modest income, or not owning a home. Singles and renters foster all the time, so ask your agency about your own situation.
### Q. What age is best to become a foster parent?
A.  There’s no single best age. Missouri’s only age rule is that you must be at least 21, with no upper limit, so people foster in their twenties through their sixties and beyond. What matters more than age is stable income, safe space, and time. If you’re 21 or older, you can start today.
### Q. How much money do foster parents get in Missouri?
A.  The state provides foster payments meant to cover the child’s needs, not your own bills. That’s why Missouri asks you to show adequate income for your household before licensing. The license itself, the required training, and the background checks all cost nothing. Ask your licensing agency for the current payment rates when you apply.
### Q. Can you choose to foster only babies?
A.  You can share the ages you feel ready to parent with your licensing agency, and they’ll weigh it during your home study. Keep in mind the young people in this guide, though: teens and older youth aging out of care are often the ones who most need a stable home. Ask your agency where the need is greatest.
### Q. What is the hardest part of fostering?
A.  Every family’s answer differs, but two hard truths run through this guide. Placements can be uncertain, and you may not know how long a child will stay. And the young people who reach 18 still in care can face adulthood with too little support. That’s exactly why the aging-out help here matters.
### Q. What benefits do youth get when they age out of foster care in Missouri?
A.  Free MO HealthNet (Medicaid) coverage to age 26, Chafee Older Youth services for housing help and life skills, Education & Training Voucher money up to $5,000 a year, and Missouri Reach tuition waivers at public colleges. Your Children’s Division worker or Older Youth Transition Specialist confirms exactly what you qualify for.
### Q. Where can a young person who aged out of foster care get housing in St. Louis?
A.  Covenant House Missouri (2727 N. Kingshighway) houses youth ages 16-24 around the clock, with transitional housing up to two years. Epworth, Marygrove, and Annie Malone run transitional and independent-living programs too. The Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition’s Navigator can line up a bed and benefits. Walk-ins are welcome at Covenant House.

## Teen Mental-Health and Crisis Help in St. Louis: Who to Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/teen-mental-health-and-crisis-help-in-st-louis
Maybe it’s the bedroom door that stays shut now, or a text you weren’t meant to read. Maybe your teenager said the words out loud, and the floor dropped out from under you. Or maybe you’re the teenager, reading this late at night because everything feels like too much and you don’t know who to tell. Wherever you’re standing, take one breath. Help in St. Louis is closer, kinder, and more real than it can feel right now, and you don’t need the perfect words to reach it.
This guide keeps it simple. The exact number to call in a crisis, where a teen can talk to someone free and confidential, and how to find counseling that doesn’t hinge on having insurance or money. It covers the City, the County, St. Charles, and eastern Missouri. We keep a broader guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but if tonight is hard, start with the first number below.
### What number do you call for a teen mental-health crisis in St. Louis?
Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. In St. Louis, local counselors at Behavioral Health Response answer it, free and around the clock. For a counselor who works specifically with young people, call BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline at 314-819-8802. If a teen is in immediate danger, call 911. LGBTQ+ teens can also reach The Trevor Project at 1-866-488-7386.
Here’s the part that matters most: a teen can reach any of these on their own. No parent has to be in the room, and the call or text is confidential. If you’re a parent, you can call too, to talk through what you’re seeing and what to do next. These are the numbers to keep on the fridge and saved in a phone.
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. Free, confidential, 24/7. In the St. Louis region a local BHR counselor answers. Press 1 for Veterans, Press 2 for Spanish.
Behavioral Health Response (BHR) Address: 5501 Delmar Blvd., Suite B300, St. Louis, MO 63112 Local crisis line: 314-819-8811 Youth Connection Helpline: 314-819-8802 (toll-free 844-985-8282) Web chat: bhrstl.org Free, all ages, 24/7, no insurance needed. BHR is Missouri’s largest 988 provider and runs mobile crisis outreach across the region.
The Trevor Project (LGBTQ+ young people under 25) Call 1-866-488-7386, text START to 678-678, or chat at TheTrevorProject.org. Free, confidential, 24/7, with counselors trained on LGBTQ+ experiences.
Call 911 for immediate danger to life: an active suicide attempt, an overdose, or a serious injury.
### What happens when a teen calls or texts 988, and will they send the police?
You reach a trained local counselor, not a dispatcher. The large majority of 988 contacts are handled entirely by phone or text, start to finish. Emergency services are sent only in the smaller number of cases where someone is in imminent danger to life. The call is free, confidential, and a teen can end it whenever they want.
We say this plainly because the fear of police showing up is the single most common reason a teen won’t pick up the phone. The counselor’s whole job is to listen, help the moment settle, and figure out a next step together. Sometimes that’s a plan for the night. Sometimes it’s a follow-up call. Only rarely is it anything more.
### 988 or 911: which one do you use?
Call 911 or head to the nearest emergency room when life is in immediate danger, an active attempt, an overdose, a serious injury. Call or text 988 for an emotional or mental-health crisis, frightening thoughts, or when a teen simply needs someone to talk to. Not sure which fits? 988 counselors can help you decide, and connect you to mobile crisis help when it’s needed.
### Is there a crisis line just for teens in St. Louis?
Yes. BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline (314-819-8802, toll-free 844-985-8282) connects young people to counselors trained for their age, free and 24/7. KUTO, Kids Under Twenty One, runs a helpline answered by trained teen and young-adult volunteers, so a struggling teen can talk to a peer who actually gets it. Both are free and confidential.
KUTO (Kids Under Twenty One) Crisis Helpline: 314-644-5886 (toll-free 888-644-5886) Business office: 314-963-7571 Free, confidential, youth-to-youth peer support for teens, LGBTQ+ youth, and parents across Missouri. Hours vary, so call to confirm when the helpline is staffed. For overnight or immediate help, use 988. Website: kuto.org
Crisis Text Line Text HOME to 741741, or text HOLA to 741741 in Spanish. Free, confidential, 24/7, staffed by trained volunteer counselors. Texting can feel easier than talking out loud, and that’s completely okay.
### Where can your teen get free or low-cost counseling in St. Louis?
More places than you’d expect, and cost should not be the wall it seems. Youth In Need offers counseling at no cost for kids under 19. Compass Health Network, Provident, and Saint Louis Counseling all use sliding-scale fees and accept Medicaid (MO HealthNet). CHADS Coalition offers youth suicide-prevention counseling through partner schools. Our guide to free and low-cost mental-health help in St. Louis goes wider still.

If your family also needs medical care without insurance, our guide to free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis lists clinics that see patients regardless of ability to pay.
### School-based suicide prevention
CHADS Coalition for Mental Health Address: 4121 Union Rd., Suite 224, St. Louis, MO 63129 Office: 314-952-2046 Family Support Warm Line: 314-952-8274 (Mon-Fri 9am-5:30pm) Youth suicide-prevention counseling, mentoring, and Signs of Suicide education through partner schools, plus support for families after a suicide loss. It is not a 24/7 crisis line and directs emergencies to 988. Website: chadscoalition.org
### How do you know when a teen needs help right now?
Trust the shift you can feel. Watch for talk of death, suicide, or being a burden; giving away treasured belongings; pulling away from friends and the things they used to love; big changes in sleep or eating; new drug or alcohol use; self-harm; deep hopelessness; or a sudden, eerie calm after a dark stretch. Any talk of suicide is a reason to call 988 today, not next week.
You will not “plant the idea” by asking directly. Ask the plain question: are you thinking about hurting yourself, or about dying? Naming it out loud, gently and without panic, tells a teen they can finally put the weight down. If drugs or alcohol are part of the picture, our guide to addiction and substance-use treatment in St. Louis can help you find the next door.
### Where to start if it isn’t an emergency
Start with the people who already know your teen. A pediatrician can screen and refer. A school counselor sees them five days a week. NAMI St. Louis can point you toward the right kind of support, and the sliding-scale providers above take new clients without a referral. You don’t have to diagnose anything to make the first call.
NAMI St. Louis Address: 12125 Woodcrest Executive Dr., Ste 205, St. Louis, MO 63141 HelpLine: 314-962-4670 (Mon-Fri 8:30am-5pm) Free peer support groups, family education like Family-to-Family, and “Ending the Silence” presentations for middle and high schoolers. This is information and referral, not a crisis line, so use 988 for emergencies. National NAMI HelpLine: 800-950-6264, or text “NAMI” to 62640. Website: namistl.org
### A last word, for the parent and for the teen
You found this page. That already counts for something. Reaching out isn’t weakness or failure, it’s the bravest, most ordinary thing a person can do on a hard day. Every number here exists because someone believed a young life is worth answering the phone for, at 3 a.m. or 3 p.m., insurance or no insurance.
Being found, and finding help, is how the worst night stays just one night. Save 988 in the phone right now, before you close this tab. Then, when you’re ready, our full St. Louis help and assistance network is here for whatever comes next, from housing to food to counseling. You are not doing this alone.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to help a teenager with mental health issues?
A.  Trust the shift you feel, and ask directly; you won’t plant the idea by asking. Start with people who know them: a pediatrician can screen and refer, a school counselor sees them daily, and NAMI St. Louis can guide you. Any talk of suicide means calling or texting 988 today.
### Q. What to do when your child needs mental help?
A.  For a crisis, call or text 988; local BHR counselors answer, free and around the clock, and a teen can reach them alone. If it isn’t an emergency, a pediatrician or school counselor can refer, and sliding-scale providers take new clients without one. BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline is 314-819-8802.
### Q. What are some signs that a teenager might have mental illness?
A.  Trust the shift you can feel. Common signs include pulling away from friends, big changes in sleep or eating, new drug or alcohol use, giving away belongings, self-harm, deep hopelessness, or talk of death and suicide. A sudden, eerie calm after a dark stretch can also be a warning.
### Q. What are 5 warning signs of depression in teenagers?
A.  Five to watch: pulling away from friends and the things they used to love; big changes in sleep or eating; deep hopelessness; self-harm; and talk of death or being a burden. These overlap with crisis warning signs, so any mention of suicide means calling or texting 988 today, not next week.
### Q. What is the best treatment for teen depression?
A.  There’s no single fix, but professional counseling is the usual starting point. A pediatrician can screen and refer, and sliding-scale providers like Youth In Need, Compass Health Network, Provident, and Saint Louis Counseling offer teen therapy, many accepting Medicaid. For a crisis, call or text 988 before anything else.
### Q. Where can I send my troubled child for free in Missouri?
A.  Youth In Need provides counseling at no cost for young people under 19 across St. Louis, St. Charles, and Lincoln Counties, no referral needed. CHADS Coalition offers free youth suicide-prevention counseling through partner schools. For free, confidential crisis support any time, a teen can call or text 988 or the Youth Connection Helpline.
### Q. What happens when you call or text 988, and will they send the police?
A.  You reach a trained local counselor, in St. Louis that’s BHR. The large majority of contacts are handled entirely by phone or text. Emergency services are sent only when there’s imminent danger to life, a small share of cases. It’s free, confidential, and you can hang up any time.
### Q. Is there a crisis line for LGBTQ+ teens in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Trevor Project is free and 24/7 for LGBTQ+ young people: call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678, with counselors trained on LGBTQ+ experiences. KUTO also serves LGBTQ+ youth. Note that 988’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth “Press 3” option ended in July 2025.

## Stuck on Algebra at 9:40 p.m.? A Free Live Tutor Is Online Until 11
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-tutoring-ged-and-dropout-help-in-st-louis
It’s 9:40 on a school night, the algebra is due at 8 a.m., and the one adult at home who could explain it is on a night shift. The laptop is the only light on at the kitchen table. Sign in to Brainfuse through the library, and a live tutor is there. The City library lists its live tutors every day from 2 p.m. to 11 p.m. The cost is nothing.
Finishing school costs money, though, and the numbers are worth seeing before you plan anything. And the cheaper of the two tests earns the same certificate from the state.
The whole price list: prep classes $0. HiSET at a test center $120. GED at a test center $142. The same tests from home: $172.50 and $181.96.
### Where can I find a free tutor?
Start at the library, either one. The City’s Central Library is at 1301 Olive Street, and the County’s Clark Family Branch, which replaced the old headquarters building, is at 1640 S. Lindbergh Blvd., but the tutoring happens on your own screen. St. Louis Public Library (314-241-2288) and St. Louis County Library (314-994-3300) both offer Brainfuse HelpNow, with live tutors for students in grades K-12 and for adult learners. Through the County, tutoring, homework help and test prep are there around the clock with a valid County library card. Through the City, a live tutor needs no registration, though signing up lets a student track progress. No card yet? The City library has an eCard form that opens its online resources.
### What the clubs cost, and the one program that is free
The afterschool program at the Soulard club runs from 2:30 to 7:30 on weekdays, with daily homework help in it. Not everything here is free, so here are the real prices. Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club in Soulard (314-772-5661) charges $200 for the school year, turns no child away over money, and offers scholarships. Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis (314-335-8000) charges $25 a year, and that covers homework help and tutoring. College Bound is free, but it works by application: it starts in 9th grade and is aimed at first-generation students with financial need.
### Free prep classes: three places to start
Evening classes at Saint Louis Public Schools meet Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the day classes run Monday through Thursday. The district’s Adult Education & Literacy Center is at 955 Arcade (314-367-5000). St. Louis Community College’s Fast Track HiSET/GED class meets at 5600 Oakland Ave in Forest Park, and the admission contact is Susan Ryffel at 314-951-9432. St. Charles Community College’s program is at 4601 Mid Rivers Mall Dr. in Cottleville (636-922-8411). Nobody has to have everything figured out before the first call. Prep classes at these adult education programs are free to eligible Missourians, and who qualifies is in the details below.
### Getting a Missouri high school equivalency, step by step
At the end of this road is a certificate issued by the State of Missouri to the mailing address on your account, and the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE) calls it comparable to a traditional high school diploma that can help you pursue employment, education or training. Missouri recognizes two tests that lead there, the GED and the HiSET, and the Missouri State Board of Education approves both. They earn the same certificate, and DESE doesn’t endorse one over the other.
Here is what each costs, straight from the state’s fee page. All four GED tests at a test center come to $142. The five HiSET tests come to $120. Take either one from home with an online proctor and the totals rise to $181.96 for the GED and $172.50 for the HiSET. Each total includes a $10 annual state fee. At a test center that makes the HiSET $22 cheaper than the GED; from home, it’s $9.46 cheaper.
To test, you set up your own account with the test publisher and schedule there, because a test center can’t book the exam for you. Missouri also requires a Missouri mailing address, and you must be 17 or older.
Under 17? You need an approved age waiver, and by law there are three ways to qualify: being in an approved Missouri Option Program for at-risk youth, having withdrawn from school with 16 units of credit and written confirmation from the superintendent, or being homeschooled with a parent’s written permission. Scores don’t expire in Missouri until the exam is replaced or rewritten, so you can take the tests one at a time. And Missouri lets you combine GED and HiSET subtest scores toward one credential, as long as you pay the fees for both exams. The passing score is 145 on each GED subtest. On the HiSET it’s a minimum of 8 on each subtest and an average of 9.
Years from now, when an employer asks for proof, the place to get it is DiplomaSender.com. DESE says all Missouri equivalency certificates, transcripts and verification letters come only from DiplomaSender, and requests sent to DESE are not processed. The state’s plain-language sites are hse.mo.gov for equivalency and ael.mo.gov to find free classes, and DESE’s main line is 573-751-4212.
### The tutoring options in detail
### St. Louis County Library: Brainfuse HelpNow
A library card is required, and anyone with a valid St. Louis County Library card can use it. Brainfuse connects students in grades K-12 with live tutors for tutoring, homework help and test prep, and it has resources for adult learners, job seekers and veterans too. The Clark Family Branch, which replaced the library’s old headquarters building, sits at 1640 S. Lindbergh Blvd. Questions go to 314-994-3300.
St. Louis County Library (Brainfuse HelpNow) Address: Clark Family Branch, 1640 S. Lindbergh Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63131 Phone: 314-994-3300 Website: slcl.org/resources/brainfuse-helpnow Free with a valid St. Louis County Library card.
### St. Louis Public Library: online homework help
The City’s library runs the same Brainfuse HelpNow service for grades K-12 and adult learners. Live tutors are on every day from 2 p.m. to 11 p.m., and video lessons and other resources are there around the clock.
St. Louis Public Library (Central Library) Address: 1301 Olive Street, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-241-2288 Website: slpl.org/resources/online-learning Free online tutoring; sign-up recommended so a student can track progress.
### Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis
The Soulard club’s afterschool program is for kids from age 6, once they’ve finished kindergarten, up to age 16. It runs weekday afternoons, 2:30 to 7:30 p.m., and daily homework assistance is part of it, with Missouri-certified educators working as learning specialists. The cost is $200 for the school year, $100 at the start and $100 on January 3. No child is turned away because of money, there is no fee to register, and scholarships are available.
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis (Soulard Campus) Address: 2524 S 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: 314-772-5661 Website: gsgbcstl.org $200 a year; scholarships available.
### Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis
Membership is $25 a year and covers after-school homework assistance and tutoring, along with college and career planning and free dental care. Power Hour, a club-wide study period for ages 6 to 18, offers daily after-school homework help, and one-on-one tutoring for ages 6 to 18 runs during the school year, with special attention on reading. Call the main office to find the club nearest you.
Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis (Admin Offices) Address: 2901 N. Grand Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63107 Phone: 314-335-8000 Website: bgcstl.org $25 a year; ask which club serves your neighborhood.
### College Bound
College Bound is free. Its own FAQ says all of its programs are completely free to students and families. It isn’t an open tutoring line, though. Students apply, and the To and Through program starts in 9th grade with an application, an interview and a summer orientation. It gives priority to first-generation students with financial need, and it asks for a 2.5 GPA or higher. Tutoring and ACT prep sit inside a larger program that also covers college counseling, mental health services and career development, and tutoring isn’t required of every student.
College Bound Address: 110 N. Jefferson Ave., St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 557-223-7890 Website: collegeboundstl.org Free; application-based.
### Where the free prep classes are
Free test preparation comes through Adult Education and Literacy (AEL) programs. DESE says the services are free to anyone at least 17, or 16 if the student has met Missouri’s compulsory school attendance requirements, who lacks a diploma or equivalency, has low basic skills, or is learning English. ael.mo.gov leads to a program near you, and three in this area are below.
### Saint Louis Public Schools: Adult Education & Literacy
Saint Louis Public Schools Adult Education & Literacy offers free programs, including HiSET and GED preparation. Day classes run Monday through Thursday and evening classes Tuesday and Thursday, and the office is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. DESE’s program list puts the Adult Education & Literacy Center at 955 Arcade, with its own line at 314-367-5000. The district’s main number is 314-231-3720.

Fast Track is an accelerated class for students who score at the ninth-grade level or above in reading and math on the TABE test. Classes are free. In St. Charles County, St. Charles Community College runs the Adult Education and Literacy program listed in DESE’s directory, with sites in Cottleville and St. Charles. The state’s eligibility rules above apply. If childcare is the hurdle, see our guide to child care assistance in Missouri.
St. Charles Community College Adult Education & Literacy Address: 4601 Mid Rivers Mall Dr., LRC 209, Cottleville, MO 63376 Phone: 636-922-8411 Website: stchas.edu/ael Free adult education classes for eligible Missourians.
Leaving school was one day. Coming back can start with one phone call - and if rent, food or a ride is what’s in the way, St. Louis help for all of it is in one place.
### If a teen has already left school
Leaving school early is not a dead end. Two programs pair education with job training for young people.
### St. Louis Job Corps Center
Job Corps is a free, residential career training and education program for low-income young adults ages 16 through 24. It covers housing, meals, basic medical care and a living allowance. Students with children are asked to arrange childcare before they begin, so ask about that on the first call.
St. Louis Job Corps Center Address: 3860 Lindell Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63108 Phone: 1-800-733-5627 (national number) Website: stlouis.jobcorps.gov Free for eligible low-income youth ages 16-24.
### SLATE Missouri Job Center: youth programs
SLATE, the City’s workforce agency, runs programs for St. Louis City youth ages 17 to 24. The Out-of-School Youth Program serves young people who are at risk of dropping out of school or already have. YouthBuild lets disadvantaged City youth ages 17 to 24 earn pay and help build affordable housing. Summer jobs are open to ages 16 to 24, and a Youth Empowerment Program serves ages 19 to 24. Registering with MoJobs before you visit saves time.
SLATE Missouri Job Center Address: 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 589-8000 Website: stlouis-mo.gov/slate Open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Wednesdays from 9 a.m.
A few honest words for the young adults reading this. If you are also job hunting or between jobs, our guide to filing for unemployment in Missouri can steady the ground while you study. And if you are rebuilding after time away, including incarceration, our guide to starting over after incarceration in St. Louis walks the road with you. A diploma is not the finish line. It is the door.
### Four numbers that may not reach these programs
Older lists, including earlier versions of this guide, carry numbers that don’t lead where they claim. 314-622-4800 shows up as a SLATE number, but the City lists it for City Hall at 1200 Market Street. 314-406-0175 shows up as a youth line, but SLATE’s youth page lists it for the state’s Local Equal Opportunity officer. Charity Navigator still lists 314-361-4441 for College Bound, while the organization’s own contact page prints 557-223-7890. And 314-480-3725 is the number an old local news post gives for UrbanFUTURE, a mentoring and tutoring group that Saint Louis Public Schools lists among its volunteer organizations. I could not confirm that UrbanFUTURE is operating today, so call before you go.
One last thing. Needing free help to learn is not a shortcoming. It is what these programs were built and funded to do. Librarians, tutors and teachers across this region want your student to walk in and log on. The whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some free classes available in St. Louis?
A.  Free GED and HiSET prep classes are offered through Adult Education and Literacy programs, including those run by Saint Louis Public Schools, St. Louis Community College and St. Charles Community College. DESE says free test preparation is offered to eligible Missourians at AEL programs across the state, and ael.mo.gov leads to one near you. For tutoring, Brainfuse HelpNow is free through both the County and City libraries.
### Q. Can I just take the GED test without classes?
A.  DESE’s testing rules ask for a Missouri mailing address and an age of 17 or older, or an approved age waiver. Free prep classes are offered, and you schedule the exam yourself in your GED or HiSET account, because a test center can’t book it for you. Check the current fees at hse.mo.gov before you pay.
### Q. How do I show proof of GED?
A.  Order it through DiplomaSender.com. DESE says all Missouri equivalency certificates, transcripts and verification letters are available only there, and requests sent to DESE are not processed. DiplomaSender keeps all of Missouri’s records, including historical ones, so a certificate earned decades ago can still be found. Create an account and order what you need.
### Q. How hard is it to pass a GED exam?
A.  Missouri’s passing score is a minimum of 145 on each GED subtest. The HiSET asks for a minimum of 8 on each subtest and an average of 9, plus at least a 2 on the Language Arts Writing essay. Subtest scores don’t expire in Missouri until the exam is replaced or rewritten, so you can take them one at a time after free prep.
### Q. How to get GED Missouri?
A.  Create a GED or HiSET account with the test publisher, enter a Missouri mailing address, and schedule your exams there. You must be 17 or older, or approved for an age waiver. At a test center the four GED tests cost $142 and the five HiSET tests cost $120. Free prep classes are listed at ael.mo.gov.
### Q. What is required to graduate high school in Missouri?
A.  The state minimum is 24 units of credit, earned across several subject areas, and each unit requires meeting all course requirements and earning a passing grade. Local school boards can add requirements of their own. Ask your school counselor for your district’s exact list, since it can be longer than the state minimum.
### Q. What are the differences between the GED and the HiSET?
A.  Both are approved by the Missouri State Board of Education and earn the same certificate from DESE, which doesn’t endorse one over the other. At a test center in Missouri the GED has four tests and costs $142, while the HiSET has five tests and costs $120. Both are available in Spanish, and both can be taken at home with an online proctor.
### Q. Can a 16-year-old take the GED in Missouri?
A.  Only with an approved age waiver. The three conditions are being in an approved Missouri Option Program, having withdrawn from school with 16 units of credit and the superintendent’s written confirmation, or being homeschooled with a parent’s written permission. Apply through hse.mo.gov, and if none of the conditions apply, the test waits until age 17.

## LGBTQ+ Support Organizations in St. Louis: Where to Find Community and Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lgbtq-support-organizations-in-st-louis
Maybe you just typed something into your phone that you have never said out loud. Maybe you’re a parent who wants to get this right for your kid and isn’t sure where to begin. Whoever you are, take a breath: you’re welcome here, exactly as you are. St. Louis has a real, rooted network of LGBTQ+ organizations, some of them running for forty years and more, built by neighbors who wanted no one to feel alone.
This is the friendly front door. We’ll point you to a local helpline, trans-specific help, support for families, affirming healthcare, and the groups that advocate and celebrate. Think of it as your map of who does what across the City, the County, and St. Charles, and how to reach each one. For everything beyond this list, we keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis. Being found is the first step. Let’s get you connected.
### Is there an LGBTQ+ helpline in St. Louis?
Yes. Call the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) at 314-380-7774 for free, confidential, identity-affirming peer support, Friday through Monday, 1 to 7 p.m. For LGBTQ+ youth under 25 who need someone any hour, The Trevor Project answers 24/7 at 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678.
SQSH is answered by and for the local LGBTQIA+ community, so the person on the line already understands St. Louis. They offer emotional support and resource referrals, and they keep a community resource guide going. There’s no public drop-in office, and that’s by design. The helpline and online scheduling are the front door.
St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) Phone: 314-380-7774; toll-free 844-785-7774 Hours: Friday through Monday, 1:00 to 7:00 p.m. Central (closed Tuesday to Thursday) Website: thesqsh.org (resource guide at sqshbook.com); phone and online only, no public office
The Trevor Project (24/7, for LGBTQ+ youth under 25) Call: 1-866-488-7386, any hour of the day Text: START to 678-678; TTY 1-866-803-3699 Website: thetrevorproject.org (online chat, plus the TrevorSpace peer community)
What if it’s the middle of the night and you’re nineteen? That’s exactly the gap Trevor fills. The local helpline covers Friday through Monday; Trevor covers every other hour for young people. Keep both numbers in your phone. And you never need a full crisis to call. A hard day is reason enough.
### What LGBTQ+ organizations serve the St. Louis metro?
The metro holds a real mix of front-line help and long-running community groups, spread across the City, the County, and St. Charles. The simplest way to use them is to sort by what you need today: someone to talk to, trans-specific support, help for youth and families, affirming healthcare, or advocacy and celebration.
Here’s the quick map. Talk to someone now: SQSH and The Trevor Project. Trans community and daily essentials: Metro Trans Umbrella Group. Youth and families: The Trevor Project, TransParent, and PFLAG. Affirming healthcare, PrEP, and HIV care: Vivent Health. Advocacy and community: PROMO Missouri and Pride St. Louis. Each section below has the full details and contacts.
### Where can transgender people find help in St. Louis?
Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) is the region’s trans community center, open since 2013 to trans, nonbinary, genderqueer, and intersex people and their allies. It offers far more than a meeting: a food pantry, a clothing closet, free bus passes, peer support groups, and name-change assistance, all under one welcoming roof.
MTUG is an 18-and-over community resource, so families of younger kids should look to PFLAG and TransParent below. For medical care, Vivent Health provides affirming primary and gender-related services. And for the step-by-step of a legal name or gender-marker change, we go deep in our guide to transgender resources in St. Louis.
Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) Address: 3133 Oregon Ave, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: 314-349-1402 Website: stlmetrotrans.org Community hours, food pantry (pickup or delivery), Alix’s Closet clothing, free bus passes, peer support groups, and name-change help
A legal name or gender-marker change runs through the Missouri courts, and it’s more routine than it looks once you have a guide. MTUG helps with the paperwork itself. For the wider process and your rights, see our overview of LGBTQ+ legal help and advocacy in Missouri and the metro’s free and low-cost legal aid.
### Where can LGBTQ+ youth and their families find support?
For a young person in crisis, The Trevor Project is the 24/7 lifeline: call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678, any hour, free and confidential, for ages 13 to 24. Its TrevorSpace platform is a moderated online community where LGBTQ+ teens meet peers who simply get it.
Parents and caregivers have their own places to land. TransParent, founded in St. Louis in 2011 by local parents, runs peer support for families of transgender and gender-expansive kids of any age. PFLAG Saint Louis, one of the country’s oldest chapters, offers family support meetings and a parent-to-parent helpline, so you can talk to a parent who has walked this road.
TransParent For parents and caregivers of transgender and gender-expansive children Contact: through the website form (no public office or posted phone) Website: transparentusa.org
PFLAG Saint Louis Phone: 314-821-3524; parent-to-parent helpline 314-872-0288 Email: pflagstl@gmail.com Monthly support meetings for LGBTQ+ people, parents, families, and allies. Meeting day and location can change, so confirm the current schedule by phone or on the national site at pflag.org before you go.
West County and St. Charles families have a closer option in PFLAG St. Charles, reachable at 636-928-5639 or stcharlespflag@gmail.com. For safe spaces, peer groups, and family-acceptance resources aimed squarely at young people, see our fuller guide to LGBTQ+ youth support in St. Louis.
Is a young person carrying more than a single hard week? Affirming counseling helps, and it doesn’t have to cost a fortune. Our guide to free and low-cost mental health and substance use help in St. Louis lists sliding-scale options across the metro.
### Where can I find LGBTQ-affirming healthcare, PrEP, and HIV care?
Vivent Health, on Locust Street, is the metro’s dedicated home for LGBTQ+ and HIV-related care. Formerly St. Louis Effort for AIDS, it brings primary care, behavioral health, dental, an on-site pharmacy, PrEP, and free HIV, STI, and hepatitis C testing under one roof, along with case management and support services.
You do not need insurance to start, and the staff are used to helping people sort out coverage and cost. Whether you want to begin PrEP, get tested quietly, or simply find a doctor who gets you, this is a solid first call. For clinics, free testing sites, and PrEP access across the region, see our guide to LGBTQ health, free HIV testing, and PrEP in St. Louis.
Vivent Health — St. Louis Address: 2653 Locust St, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-645-6451 Website: viventhealth.org HIV and primary care, behavioral health, dental, pharmacy, PrEP, free HIV/STI/hep-C testing, and case management
### Who advocates for and celebrates the LGBTQ+ community here?
PROMO Missouri is the state’s LGBTQ+ public-policy and advocacy organization, working for more than 35 years on community education and grassroots organizing. Its focus areas span health and wellness, transgender justice, youth and education, and older LGBTQ+ adults. PROMO also keeps a statewide LGBTQ organization directory, which is handy when you need a resource we haven’t named here.
PROMO Missouri Address: 2200 Gravois Ave, Ste 201, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: 314-862-4900 Email: promo@promomissouri.org Website: promomissouri.org
On the celebration side, Pride St. Louis produces the region’s annual PrideFest and Grand Parade downtown each June, plus year-round events. It’s an all-volunteer nonprofit, which means there’s always a way to pitch in. Their motto says it plainly: educate, advocate, celebrate. Joy is part of survival, too.
Pride St. Louis, Inc. Mailing: P.O. Box 15051, St. Louis, MO 63110 (all-volunteer, no public office) Phone: 314-325-9794 Email: info@pridestl.org Website: pridestl.org
### How can you support these organizations?
Nearly every group here runs on volunteers and small donations, so a little goes a long way. Pride St. Louis needs hands for PrideFest. MTUG welcomes food-pantry and clothing-closet donations. SQSH and PROMO take gifts and volunteers year-round. If one of these organizations carried you through a hard stretch, giving back keeps the door open for the next neighbor.
You can also help just by sharing. Tell one friend which door to knock on. Being seen, and being found, is how a person survives a lonely season, and it’s how these small, mighty organizations keep going. Check each org’s website for current volunteer and donation options, and lean on the wider St. Louis help and assistance network whenever you need it. You belong here.

### Q. What are some LGBTQ+ organizations in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis has many. For peer support there’s SQSH and The Trevor Project; for trans community, Metro Trans Umbrella Group; for families, TransParent and PFLAG; for affirming healthcare, Vivent Health; and for advocacy and celebration, PROMO Missouri and Pride St. Louis. Each section above lists full contact details.

## Transgender Resources in St. Louis: Name Change, Healthcare, and Support
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/transgender-resources-in-st-louis-name-change-healthcare-support
Maybe you’ve been putting off a phone call for weeks. Maybe a form asked for a name that no longer fits, and you felt that quiet flinch again. Or maybe you’re a parent holding your kid’s hand, wondering where on earth to begin. Wherever you’re standing right now, take one breath. St. Louis holds far more affirming, practical help than most people ever realize, and none of it asks you to have everything figured out first.
This guide pulls the real organizations into one place: community groups, affirming clinics, free legal aid, and crisis lines, each with contact details you can act on today. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but this page is for you specifically. Let’s find your people, and your care.
### What transgender resources are available in St. Louis?
St. Louis holds a full network. The Metro Trans Umbrella Group offers community, a food pantry, and name-change help. Planned Parenthood Great Rivers and the WashU Transgender Center provide affirming care. SQSH runs a peer helpline at (314) 380-7774, and TransParent supports families. Start with a single call.
Think of these as four kinds of help that stack together. Community groups give you belonging and everyday support. Affirming clinics handle your health without judgment. Legal aid walks you through name and document changes. And peer helplines are there for the hard nights. You don’t have to use all of them, and you don’t have to use them in order. Pick the one that matches what you need this week, and go from there.
One quiet truth runs under all of it: being found is its own kind of survival. When you can reach the right group, and when that group can be found by the next person, a scattered city turns into a net. That’s the whole reason this list exists. Everything below is a real door you can walk through.
### Where do trans and nonbinary people find community in St. Louis?
Community is often the first step, and St. Louis has anchored it around the Metro Trans Umbrella Group since 2013. MTUG runs support groups, a food pantry, a clothing closet, bus passes, and emergency help, all in one place. Alongside it, a peer helpline and a statewide advocacy group round out the network, so you’re never starting from zero.
Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) Address: 3133 Oregon Ave, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: (314) 349-1402 Website: stlmetrotrans.org Support groups, a food pantry, Alix’s Closet for clothing, bus passes, emergency assistance, and name-change help. MTUG replies within one to two business days through its site contact form. Hours are often by appointment for member safety, so confirm before you visit.
St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) Helpline: (314) 380-7774 Toll-free: (844) 785-7774 Hours: Friday through Monday, 1:00 to 7:00 PM Website: thesqsh.org A free, confidential, identity-affirming peer helpline, built by and for the St. Louis LGBTQIA+ community. ### How does the name and gender-marker change process work in Missouri?
Here’s the plain-language overview, and it’s information, not legal advice. In Missouri, any adult can petition the circuit court in the county where they live to change their name for a lawful reason, including gender identity. You don’t need a lawyer. The court reviews the petition and issues an Order of Name Change, the document you use to update your IDs.
A few details vary, so confirm them locally. Some courts have simplified adult name changes and may not require an in-person hearing, while others still do. Missouri law has historically required newspaper publication, though a court may waive it for safety. Filing fees vary by county, commonly around one hundred dollars, and fee waivers may be available if money is tight. Ask the clerk or a legal aid attorney.
Changing a gender marker is a separate step. The durable, standing route for a driver’s license, state ID, or birth certificate is a court order, with a birth certificate then filed through the Missouri Bureau of Vital Records. These government-document requirements have shifted and are contested in Missouri, so don’t assume today’s rule is permanent. Confirm the current process with legal aid or the issuing agency before you go.
This is the short version on purpose. For the full walkthrough of forms, hearings, and your rights, see our guide to LGBTQ+ legal help and advocacy in Missouri, and for free representation if you qualify, our roundup of free and low-cost legal aid in St. Louis.
Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (LSEM) Address: 701 Market Street, Suite 1100, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: (314) 534-4200 Toll-free: (800) 444-0514 Website: lsem.org Free civil legal aid for low-income residents across 21 eastern Missouri counties since 1956, including help with legal name changes. Eligibility is income-based, so think of it as free legal help if you qualify. Interpreter services are available.
ACLU of Missouri, “Show-Me My Rights” trans guide Guide: aclu-mo.org/know-your-rights/your-rights-as-a-trans-person Email: showmemyrights@aclu-mo.org A plain-language rundown of your rights as a trans person in Missouri, including high-level overviews of the name-change and gender-marker processes and anti-discrimination protections. It’s a solid reference to read before you file.

If tonight is hard, you have people to call right now. For local peer support, the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline answers at (314) 380-7774. For around-the-clock help, several national lines are staffed by people who understand. None of them will judge you, and all of them are free.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I legally change my name in St. Louis or Missouri?
A.  File a name-change petition in the circuit court of the county where you live, such as St. Louis City, St. Louis County, or St. Charles. You don’t need a lawyer. The court reviews it and issues an Order of Name Change, which you use to update your IDs. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri and MTUG offer free help.
### Q. Do I need a lawyer to change my name in Missouri, and where can I get free legal help?
A.  No, a lawyer isn’t required to change your name in Missouri, and many people file on their own. If you want support, Legal Services of Eastern Missouri offers free civil legal aid to those who qualify at (314) 534-4200, and the Metro Trans Umbrella Group provides name-change assistance for the community.
### Q. How much does a name change cost in Missouri?
A.  Filing fees vary by county, commonly around one hundred dollars, and courts may add small charges for certified copies or publication. If money is tight, ask the clerk or a legal aid attorney about a fee waiver, which many low-income filers qualify for. Confirm the current amount with your local circuit court before filing.
### Q. Can I still change my gender marker?
A.  In Missouri, the durable route to changing a gender marker on a driver’s license or state ID is a court order presented to the Missouri Department of Revenue. Because these requirements have shifted and remain contested, confirm the current process with legal aid, such as Legal Services of Eastern Missouri or the ACLU of Missouri, before you go.
### Q. How do I correct my gender in my birth certificate?
A.  A Missouri birth certificate is amended through a court order, which you then file with the Missouri Bureau of Vital Records. Because government-document rules have changed and remain contested, treat this as a high-level path and confirm the current steps with legal aid before starting. The ACLU of Missouri’s rights guide is a helpful reference.
### Q. Where can I get gender-affirming hormone therapy in St. Louis?
A.  Planned Parenthood Great Rivers offers hormone therapy for adults at its Central West End Health Center using an informed-consent model, so no mental-health letter is required. Book at (314) 531-7526 and ask about self-pay pricing. Vivent Health provides LGBTQ+-affirming primary care, and the WashU Transgender Center serves youth and young adults.
### Q. Is there a transgender support group in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Metro Trans Umbrella Group runs support groups, a food pantry, and a clothing closet from 3133 Oregon Ave, reachable at (314) 349-1402. For confidential peer support by phone, the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline answers at (314) 380-7774, Friday through Monday, 1 to 7 PM.
### Q. Who do I call if I’m a trans person in crisis in St. Louis?
A.  For local peer support, call the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline at (314) 380-7774. Any time, day or night, dial or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, which has an LGBTQI+ service. Trans Lifeline answers at (877) 565-8860, and The Trevor Project supports youth at 1-866-488-7386.

## LGBTQ+ Youth Support in St. Louis: Safe Spaces, Peer Help, and Family Acceptance
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lgbtq-youth-support-in-st-louis
Maybe it’s late, and you’re reading this on a phone under the covers, wondering if anyone out there really gets it. Maybe you’re a parent whose kid just said a few words that changed the whole room, and you badly want to get this right. Either way, take a breath. You landed somewhere safe. If things feel heavy right now, The Trevor Project answers 24/7 for LGBTQ+ young people: call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678.
St. Louis holds more affirming support than most people realize, spread across the City, the County, St. Charles, and the Metro-East. This is the calm map: who to call in a hard moment, where teens find peers who simply get it, and where parents learn to show up well. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but this page is for LGBTQ+ youth and the people who love them. Let’s find your people.
### Where can LGBTQ+ youth find safe spaces and support in St. Louis?
LGBTQ+ young people in St. Louis have free, affirming options. For local support by phone, the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) answers Friday through Monday, 1 to 7 PM, at 314-380-7774. PFLAG Greater St. Louis (314-328-9432) helps parents affirm their kids. In a crisis, The Trevor Project is free 24/7: call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678.
Think of support as two layers. One layer is for a hard moment right now, a crisis line staffed by people trained to sit with you until the wave passes. The other is the slower, steadier kind: peer groups, an online community, a parent learning to listen. You’re allowed to reach for both in the same week, and no one will ask you to prove you tried everything else first.
### Who can you call right now if you’re in crisis?
If tonight feels like too much, you are not alone, and you don’t have to carry it by yourself. For LGBTQ+ young people, The Trevor Project is the affirming crisis line: free, confidential, and staffed every hour of every day. Trans-specific peer support and the general 988 line round out your options.
The Trevor Project (LGBTQ+ youth, ages 13 to 24) Call: 1-866-488-7386 (TTY for deaf or hard of hearing: 1-866-803-3699) Text: text START to 678-678 Chat: thetrevorproject.org/get-help Hours: 24 hours a day, every day. 100% free and confidential.
Trans Lifeline (peer support, all ages) Call: 1-877-565-8860 Run by and for trans and questioning people. Trans Lifeline does not do nonconsensual active rescue, which means they will not call 911 or the police on you without your consent. Hours are not 24/7; check translifeline.org for current hours.
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (everyone, 24/7) Call or text: 988 Chat: 988lifeline.org A general crisis line for anyone, any age, any hour. For an LGBTQ-affirming counselor specifically, The Trevor Project above is the better fit.
If the harder truth is ongoing anxiety, depression, or thoughts that scare you, affirming care exists well beyond the crisis line. See our guide to teen mental health and crisis help in St. Louis for low-cost counseling and youth crisis options across the metro.
### What happened to the 988 LGBTQ+ option?
You may have heard you could call 988 and “press 3” for LGBTQ+ youth support. That specialized option ended on July 17, 2025, so it is no longer available. Here is the current path, plainly: 988 still serves everyone in crisis 24/7, and for an identity-affirming counselor, LGBTQ+ young people should turn to The Trevor Project at 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678.
### Where can LGBTQ+ teens find local peer support and community?
Crisis lines are for the storm; community is for the long haul. Locally, the St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) offers identity-affirming peer support by phone, answered by neighbors who get it. When in person feels out of reach, TrevorSpace is a moderated online community built for LGBTQ+ young people. Both are free.
St. Louis Queer+ Support Helpline (SQSH) Call: 314-380-7774 (toll-free 844-785-7774) Website: thesqsh.org Resource guide: sqshbook.com Email: general@thesqsh.org Hours: Friday through Monday, 1 to 7 PM Central. Free, confidential peer support and referrals by and for the St. Louis metro LGBTQIA+ community. This is a phone and online helpline, so there’s no walk-in address.
TrevorSpace (online community, ages 13 to 24) Visit: thetrevorproject.org/visit-trevorspace/ A moderated, affirming online space where LGBTQ+ young people connect with peers. A safe way to find community when meeting in person isn’t possible.
Wondering about a club at school? Ask a school counselor or a teacher you trust whether your school has a GSA, a Gender-Sexuality Alliance. If it doesn’t, the GSA Network (gsanetwork.org) and GLSEN (glsen.org) publish free guides for starting one. And if your school is being hostile about LGBTQ+ students, the family section below points you to PROMO.
For the wider regional picture, our overview of LGBTQ+ support organizations in St. Louis maps the affirming groups, centers, and services worth knowing.

Transgender young people and their families have a real lifeline here. The Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) is a trans-community resource hub in St. Louis with practical, all-ages support. ### Where do parents and families find support after a child comes out?
Parents, if your child just came out and you’re scared of saying the wrong thing, that worry is love in disguise. You don’t have to figure it out alone. PFLAG Greater St. Louis, one of the oldest PFLAG chapters in the country, exists to help families learn to show up for an LGBTQ+ loved one.

One more thing worth saying out loud. If home has turned unsafe for a young person, whether after coming out or for any reason, that is an emergency worth acting on. Our guide to youth and teen emergency shelter in St. Louis lays out where a teen can go tonight and who to call.
Here’s the belief we’d leave you with. Being found, by the right person, the right group, a steady voice on a hard night, is not a small thing. For a lot of LGBTQ+ young people, it’s close to everything. The organizations on this page exist because someone decided you were worth finding, and they want you to reach out. So save a number. Send the text. Walk into the meeting. Being seen is how a hard season becomes just a season, and the whole St. Louis help and assistance network is standing behind you.

### Q. What if my child is in crisis right now?
A.  If there’s immediate danger, call 911. For LGBTQ+ mental-health crisis support any time, contact The Trevor Project (1-866-488-7386 / text START to 678-678). You can stay with your child while they reach out.

## LGBTQ+ Health in St. Louis: Free HIV Testing and PrEP
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lgbtq-health-free-hiv-testing-and-prep-in-st-louis
You made the appointment with yourself weeks ago, and today you finally typed the question into your phone. Where do I go, and will they be kind about it? That worry is real, and you are not overthinking it. Plenty of neighbors across St. Louis have sat exactly where you are, wanting a test, a prescription, or simply a doctor who won’t flinch. Here’s the good news: this metro has affirming, low-cost, and free places to get HIV and STI testing, PrEP, and welcoming care, and most of them will see you no matter your insurance or income.
This is the plain-language map. Where to get free testing this week, how the path to PrEP actually works, and which clinics treat LGBTQ+ patients with respect. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but your health comes first here. Everything below is information, not medical advice, so use it to find a provider and let them handle your care.
### Where can I get free HIV testing in St. Louis?
You can get free, confidential HIV and STI testing across the metro. Vivent Health on Locust Street, Project ARK on Laclede Avenue (which also offers a free in-home test), Williams & Associates on North Kingshighway, and the St. Louis County Sexual Health Clinic in Pine Lawn all test at no cost. The county clinic is walk-in, with no appointment or insurance needed.
One habit saves a wasted trip: call before you go. Walk-in windows shift often, and a few sites ask you to book ahead. Every place below serves you regardless of income, and several ask for no ID or paperwork at all. Pick the one closest to you and start there.
Vivent Health (formerly Saint Louis Effort for AIDS) Address: 2653 Locust St, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 645-6451 Website: viventhealth.org Free, confidential HIV, STI, and Hepatitis C testing, plus an on-site pharmacy and dental care.
