### How do I get PrEP in St. Louis?
Getting PrEP is more routine than it sounds. PrEP is medicine that prevents HIV, taken as a daily pill or an every-other-month shot, and several St. Louis clinics prescribe it, some the same day. WashU Medicine’s PrEP Program offers same-day prescriptions with no insurance required. Vivent Health, Planned Parenthood, and the St. Louis County clinic prescribe it too, including for uninsured patients.
Here’s the path most people follow. First, book a visit at any clinic below. Second, you’ll get a quick HIV test and a short lab panel, because PrEP is for people who are HIV-negative. Third, the clinic writes the prescription and a navigator sorts out the cost. That last step is where the worry usually melts.
Is PrEP expensive? Usually not. Most private insurance and Missouri Medicaid cover PrEP at $0 out of pocket. If you’re uninsured, programs like Gilead’s Advancing Access and the federal Ready, Set, PrEP can bring the cost to zero, and the navigators at these clinics fill out that paperwork for you. Ask about it on your very first call.
WashU Medicine Infectious Diseases (PrEP Program) Address: 620 S Taylor Ave, Suite 100, St. Louis, MO 63110 Phone: (314) 362-9098 Website: sites.wustl.edu/prep The metro’s specialist PrEP program, offering same-day PrEP prescribing with no insurance required and patient-assistance help for the uninsured.
Planned Parenthood of the St. Louis Region and Southwest Missouri South Grand Health Center: 3401 S Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63118; (314) 865-1850 Central West End: 4251 Forest Park Ave, St. Louis, MO 63108; (314) 531-7526 North County: 2796 N Hwy 67, Florissant, MO 63033; (314) 921-4445 Website: plannedparenthood.org PrEP navigation and STI testing, with insurance, Medicaid, and sliding-scale fees accepted.
Vivent Health (2653 Locust St, (314) 645-6451) also provides PrEP and PrEP navigation on site, with sliding-scale pricing. The St. Louis County Sexual Health Clinic prescribes PrEP as well, including for uninsured patients. Affinia Healthcare’s centers focus on HIV prevention and care; call (314) 814-8700 to confirm whether PrEP prescribing is available at your nearest site.
### Where can I find affirming, LGBTQ+-friendly care in St. Louis?
Affirming care means a provider who uses your name and pronouns and treats you without judgment. Several St. Louis organizations are built around exactly that. Vivent Health centers LGBTQ+ patients, Planned Parenthood offers gender-affirming hormone care at some Missouri health centers, and the Metro Trans Umbrella Group helps trans and nonbinary neighbors find welcoming clinics. Start with whichever feels safest to call first.
Vivent Health’s Wednesday evening walk-in testing (4:00 to 7:00pm) is set aside for gay, bisexual, transgender, pansexual, and same-gender-loving men, which tells you plenty about the room you’ll walk into. Planned Parenthood provides gender-affirming hormone care at some Missouri locations, so call ahead to confirm the service by site. For a wider circle of community and support, see our guide to LGBTQ+ support organizations in St. Louis.
Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) Website: stlmetrotrans.org MTUG is not a clinic and does not offer HIV testing or PrEP directly. It’s an affirming community group that helps trans, nonbinary, and questioning people find welcoming testing, PrEP, and primary care, alongside support groups, a clothing closet, and name-change help. It’s a good first stop when you want a person, not a website, to guide you.
### Can I get HIV and STI testing without insurance?
Yes, and it’s common. Every free-testing site above serves you with no insurance, and several ask for no ID or documentation at all. The St. Louis County Sexual Health Clinic and Williams & Associates require neither insurance nor proof of residence. Community health centers like Affinia Healthcare charge on a sliding scale, so your bill follows your income.
What should you bring? Not much. A phone number where a clinic can reach you privately helps, and a photo ID speeds some visits, though the free sites above won’t turn you away without one. If cost is your only worry, just say so when you call. For more options, see our guide to free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis.
If a test comes back positive, that isn’t the end of anything. It’s the start of care that keeps people healthy for life. Ongoing HIV treatment, case management, and mental-health support are available through Vivent Health and the SLUCare / SSM Health Saint Louis University Infectious Diseases clinic. Emotional support matters too, so keep our guide to free and low-cost mental health help handy.
SLUCare / SSM Health Saint Louis University Infectious Diseases Center for Specialized Medicine, 1225 S Grand Blvd, 2nd Floor, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: (314) 977-9050 HIV medical care, case management, mental-health support, and peer coaching. Call to confirm the current clinic location, hours, and whether PrEP is offered before your visit.
Here’s the last thing, and we mean it kindly. Wanting a test, a pill, or a doctor who respects you is not a big ask, and needing help to afford it is not a flaw. These clinics exist for exactly this, staffed by people who want you to walk in. Being found, and finding care, is how a scary week becomes just a week. Save one phone number from this page, make the call, and let a navigator carry the rest. The whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does PrEP usually cost?
A.  For most people, PrEP costs little or nothing. Private insurance and Missouri Medicaid typically cover it at $0 out of pocket. If you’re uninsured, Gilead’s Advancing Access program and the federal Ready, Set, PrEP program can bring the cost to zero. Navigators at clinics like WashU’s PrEP Program handle that paperwork for you.
### Q. Where can I get free STD testing in St. Louis County?
A.  In St. Louis County, the St. Louis County Sexual Health Clinic in Pine Lawn (4000 Jennings Station Rd) offers free, walk-in HIV and STI testing with no appointment or insurance needed. Affinia Healthcare’s neighborhood centers, including its Ferguson site, also test on a sliding scale. Call first to confirm current walk-in hours.
### Q. How do I qualify for PrEP?
A.  PrEP is for people who are HIV-negative, so qualifying is straightforward. At your visit, the clinic gives a quick HIV test and a short lab panel to confirm you’re negative and can take it safely. Then a provider writes the prescription and a navigator sorts out the cost, often the same day.
### Q. Can I get PrEP without seeing a doctor?
A.  You’ll need a brief clinical visit, since PrEP requires a quick HIV test and short lab panel before a provider can prescribe it. The good news: it’s routine, and WashU Medicine’s PrEP Program offers same-day prescribing with no insurance required. Call (314) 362-9098 to book, and a navigator handles the cost.
### Q. Can I do an HIV test for free?
A.  Yes. Several St. Louis sites test for free with no insurance needed. The St. Louis County Sexual Health Clinic (walk-in, Pine Lawn) and Williams & Associates ask for no insurance or documentation. Vivent Health and Project ARK also test at no cost, and Project ARK offers a free in-home HIV test.
### Q. Does Planned Parenthood in St. Louis do PrEP and STI testing?
A.  Yes. Planned Parenthood of the St. Louis Region provides PrEP navigation and STI testing at its South Grand, Central West End, and North County health centers. It accepts insurance, Medicaid, and sliding-scale fees. Call the South Grand Health Center at (314) 865-1850 to book or ask about current services.
### Q. How to tell if a doctor is LGBT friendly?
A.  An affirming provider uses your name and pronouns and treats you without judgment, which is the clearest sign. Vivent Health, for example, sets aside Wednesday evening walk-in hours for LGBTQ+ men. Groups like the Metro Trans Umbrella Group (stlmetrotrans.org) can also point you to welcoming clinics before you book.
### Q. Can I get an at-home or in-home HIV test in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Project ARK offers free in-home HIV testing across the metro; call (314) 282-1581 to arrange it. This is a good option if getting to a clinic is hard or you’d simply rather test privately. Project ARK also runs free walk-in HIV testing at 4169 Laclede Ave.

## LGBTQ+ Legal Help and Advocacy in Missouri: Name Change, Discrimination, and Your Rights
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lgbtq-legal-help-and-advocacy-in-missouri
Maybe you’ve just signed your old name for the last time. Maybe a landlord went quiet the moment they read your file, or a manager started finding reasons that never came up before. Whatever brought you to this page, take one breath. You are not asking for a favor, and you are not doing this alone. St. Louis holds real legal help for LGBTQ+ neighbors: free clinics, fair-housing investigators, a statewide advocacy team, and licensed attorneys who will treat you with plain respect.
One honest note before we start. This guide is information and referral, not legal advice, and nobody here can tell you how your own case will turn out. What we can do is walk through how Missouri’s standing processes work and point you to the people who can look at your exact situation. For anything specific, a licensed attorney or a legal-aid intake line is the right call. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, and this page zooms in on legal help.
Need someone right now?
The Trevor Project (LGBTQ+ youth): 1-866-488-7386, or text START to 678-678. Trans Lifeline (peer support): (877) 565-8860. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988.
### How do I legally change my name in Missouri?
In Missouri, an adult changes their name by filing a verified petition in the circuit court of the county where they live. Free official forms, including Form CAFC401, live at selfrepresent.mo.gov. A lawyer isn’t required, though one helps. Free local help is available through Metro Trans Umbrella Group and the Legal Services of Eastern Missouri intake line.
A little more on how it works. Missouri Supreme Court Rule 95.01 sets out what the petition must include, and the statewide adult process does not require fingerprints or a criminal-history report. You file in your home county, and a judge reviews the request.
After the court grants your order, Missouri law generally asks you to publish notice once a week for three consecutive weeks, usually within 20 days, in a local newspaper. Some petitioners ask the court to waive or seal that publication step for safety reasons. Whether a judge grants that is up to the court, so it’s a good question to bring to a clinic or an attorney rather than guess at on your own.
You don’t have to figure this out solo. Metro Trans Umbrella Group runs name-change support through its open hours and clinics, in partnership with STL Name Change Mutual Aid, and it’s the strongest hands-on help in the metro for actually completing the paperwork.
Metro Trans Umbrella Group (MTUG) Address: 3133 Oregon Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: (314) 349-1402 Website: stlmetrotrans.org Drop-in hours: Tuesday and Thursday, noon to 6:00pm, no appointment needed; other times by appointment.
Prefer to start with a lawyer? Call the Legal Services of Eastern Missouri intake line to ask whether they can help with your name change or point you somewhere that can. For the full picture on name and document changes, our guide to transgender resources in St. Louis walks alongside this one.
### Where can you find free LGBTQ-friendly legal help in St. Louis?
Free and low-cost legal help does exist here, and the right door depends on your issue. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri offers free civil aid if you qualify. Start with free civil aid. Their name-change work isn’t listed as a standing clinic, so the honest move is to call intake, describe what you need, and ask whether they can help or refer you.

### Does Missouri law protect LGBTQ+ people from discrimination?
The honest answer is that coverage is layered. The Missouri Human Rights Act lists protected classes such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability, and age, but the state statute itself does not list sexual orientation or gender identity. For LGBTQ+ people, protection often comes instead from federal law and local ordinances.
On the job, federal law reaches further. In Bostock v. Clayton County (2020), the U.S. Supreme Court held that Title VII’s ban on sex discrimination includes discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That standing holding is enforced by the federal EEOC.
In housing, the federal Fair Housing Act applies, enforced by HUD, with free local help available through EHOC. And close to home, several jurisdictions add their own protections. The City of St. Louis and unincorporated St. Louis County, along with municipalities like Clayton, Richmond Heights, Kirkwood, University City, and Creve Coeur, include sexual orientation and gender identity in ordinances covering housing, employment, and public accommodations.
Because what protects you depends on where you live and work and on the details of your situation, this is exactly the kind of question to bring to EHOC, the Missouri Commission on Human Rights, or an attorney. They can look at your facts; a web page can’t.
### Where do you report LGBTQ+ discrimination in Missouri?
Which office you call depends on what happened, and deadlines are real, so it pays to act early. The Missouri Commission on Human Rights investigates discrimination in housing, employment, and public accommodations, and complaints generally must be filed within 180 days of the act. For federal claims, the EEOC covers work and HUD covers housing.
Missouri Commission on Human Rights (MCHR) Phone: (573) 751-3325, or toll-free (877) 781-4236 Email: MCHRIntake@labor.mo.gov Website: labor.mo.gov/mohumanrights Investigates housing, employment, and public-accommodation complaints; file generally within 180 days.
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Phone: (800) 669-4000 Website: eeoc.gov Handles federal employment discrimination claims, including those under the Bostock ruling.
For a home you were denied, rented, financed, or insured unfairly, start local. EHOC is the region’s only private nonprofit fair-housing organization, and its counseling and investigation services are free. You can also file a federal complaint with HUD.

U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Phone: (800) 669-9777 Website: hud.gov
### What about changing your gender marker in Missouri?
Here we’ll be careful on purpose. Changing gender markers on Missouri IDs, birth records, and federal documents runs through separate agency and court processes, and those rules shift over time. Rather than print steps that might be out of date by the time you read them, the honest move is to get current guidance built around your own documents and situation.
Two reliable doors. Metro Trans Umbrella Group offers name and gender-marker support through its open hours and clinics, and a legal-aid intake line or an attorney can advise you on what applies right now. Between them, you can get accurate, up-to-date help without guessing.

## Free Clothes in St. Louis: Bring a Photo ID and Go on the Right Day
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-clothing-closets-in-st-louis
“It won’t zip.” Your kid says it standing by the front door, arms out, last winter’s coat riding up over wrists that grew all summer. The zipper bites halfway and stops. Outside the window the grass is already stiff with frost, and you are doing the math you do every morning, the one where every dollar already has a name on it.
Here is the part most people in that doorway don’t know. On North Kingshighway, the Urban League’s Community Clothes Closet hands out clothing for the whole family, work clothes included, and the rule on its own page is short: you must be 18 or older and have a picture ID. That’s it. No sermon, no form about how you got here. On South Grand, Isaiah 58 Ministries opens its clothing room Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday from 10:00am to 1:00pm, and on Wednesday mornings it runs showers where guests leave with a t-shirt, pants, undergarments and socks. Clean socks, still folded, after a hot shower. If you have ever gone without, you know exactly what that is worth.
So the screenshot line for this page is simple. Free clothes in St. Louis are rarely about who deserves them. They are about which day the door is open and whether you brought your ID. Get those two right and you walk out carrying something.
This guide sorts the free closets by what you need, everyday clothes, work clothes, kids’ clothes or a coat, and by how you get in. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but this one is only about getting you dressed.

One honest note before the addresses. Free and cheap are not the same thing. A free closet costs you nothing. A thrift store sells clothes at low prices to everyone. This page is about free first, and when something on it costs money, we say so.

## Free Furniture and Household Goods Banks in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-furniture-and-household-goods-banks-in-st-louis
The key turns, the door swings open, and you step into an apartment that is finally, truly yours. And it’s empty. Bare floors, a kitchen with no table, a bedroom with no bed. Maybe you just left a shelter. Maybe you got yourself and the kids away from someone. Maybe you stood on the lawn and watched a fire take the rest. Getting the keys felt like the finish line. Then the room echoed when you set down your bag, and you realized it was the starting line instead. Take a breath. This part is survivable, and St. Louis has real furniture help built for exactly this moment.
Here is the one thing almost nobody tells you up front: free furniture in St. Louis runs on referrals, not walk-ins. So this plan starts with the phone call that unlocks everything else, then walks you through every furniture bank, voucher, and free-bed program across the metro. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but right now let’s furnish this home, one room at a time.
### Where can I get free furniture in St. Louis?
The main furniture bank, Home Sweet Home in Maplewood, is free but referral-only, so you cannot walk in. Your real first step is getting a caseworker or calling 2-1-1 any hour. A case manager, shelter, or DV advocate then refers you. St. Vincent de Paul and the Salvation Army offer voucher routes too.
Think of it as two moves, in order. First, you get connected to a person: a case manager who can vouch for your situation. Second, that person refers you to a furniture bank or writes you a voucher. Get the order right and furniture follows. Go hunting for a warehouse to walk into, and you hit a locked door, which is the saddest and most avoidable dead end in this whole process.
So the list below is not really a list of stores. It’s a map of doors, and 2-1-1 is the key to most of them. Keep that number close as you read.
### Why do you need a referral to get free furniture?
Free furniture programs route through caseworkers on purpose. Home Sweet Home, the largest furniture bank in the region, accepts no self-referrals at all. St. Vincent de Paul sends trained volunteers to your home first. This is not a hoop meant to punish you. It is how limited donations reach the neighbors who are genuinely starting over.
There’s a quiet upside to the referral, too. The caseworker who refers you for furniture usually connects you to far more: rent help, utility assistance, a bed for your child, a real plan. One phone call can open several doors at once, so the extra step is worth it even when all you want today is a couch.
And if a small voice is telling you that you don’t deserve to ask? Please let that go. These programs exist for this exact moment, funded by neighbors who wanted you to have a bed. Being found, and letting yourself be helped, is how a hard season turns back into an ordinary life.
### How do you get connected to a caseworker or 2-1-1?
Two paths reach a caseworker fast. Dial 2-1-1, the free United Way line, any hour of any day, and a real person routes you to the right agency. Or work with a case manager you may already have, at your shelter, your domestic violence program, or a housing agency like St. Patrick Center, whose Coordinated Entry intake assigns you one.
United Way 2-1-1 Dial 211, free and confidential, 24 hours a day, every day. Tell them your situation and ZIP code, and they route you to the caseworker, parish conference, or corps nearest you.
St. Patrick Center Address: 800 N Tucker Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: (314) 802-0700 Website: stpatrickcenter.org One of Missouri’s largest housing agencies. Their Coordinated Entry intake assigns you a case manager, the very person who can submit a referral to Home Sweet Home.
Still figuring out where you’ll sleep tonight? Housing comes before furniture, so start with our guides to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis and finding transitional housing across the metro. A shelter or housing caseworker is often your fastest route to a furniture referral anyway.
### Home Sweet Home: the St. Louis furniture bank
Home Sweet Home is the region’s dedicated furniture bank, and it furnishes around 1,000 families every year, entirely free. It serves people leaving domestic violence, homelessness, addiction, or incarceration, plus veterans, refugees, and families moving into housing. The one rule that trips people up: you cannot refer yourself. A partner agency’s case manager has to start it.
Home Sweet Home Address: 10 Sunnen Dr, Ste. 100, Maplewood, MO 63143 Phone: (314) 448-9838 Website: homesweethomestl.org Hours: Monday through Friday, 9am to 2pm Cost: 100% free to clients, referral required.
Here is how it flows. Your case manager submits a referral, the Client Services Coordinator reviews eligibility, and you go on a waiting list. When your turn comes, you’re scheduled for a warehouse shopping appointment where you pick your own items with staff, and delivery usually arrives the next business day. You leave with beds, mattresses, a table, and seating, plus kitchen basics: dishes, towels, and sheets included.
One heads-up: older listings still show a Brentwood warehouse. The current home is the Maplewood address above, so use that one. And if you’re coming from a domestic violence shelter, your advocate can make this referral directly, because Home Sweet Home specifically serves survivors.
### How does St. Vincent de Paul give away furniture?
St. Vincent de Paul helps through your neighborhood parish conference, and yes, the furniture is free. Call 2-1-1 or use the Conference Finder to reach the conference covering your address. Volunteers visit your home, and if you lack beds, a kitchen table, or basics, they issue a voucher you redeem for those goods at their stores.
Society of St. Vincent de Paul, St. Louis Council office: 1310 Papin Street, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 881-6000 Website: svdpstlouis.org How it works: call 2-1-1 or use the Conference Finder to reach your parish conference; volunteers do a home visit and issue vouchers for furniture, beds, and household items.
Across the river, St. Vincent de Paul serves the Metro-East the same way, through a home-visit voucher.
St. Vincent de Paul, East St. Louis Address: 3718 State Street, East St. Louis, IL 62203 Phone: (618) 271-6230
Metro-East neighbors can also try Catholic Urban Programs in East St. Louis at (618) 398-9005, which serves communities like Cahokia, Centreville, and Caseyville with rent, utility, and clothing help. Call first to confirm whether furniture assistance is available, since that piece can change.
### How do you get a Salvation Army furniture voucher?
The Salvation Army offers furniture vouchers through its local corps community centers, and the Midland Division runs 27 of them around the region. Availability and eligibility vary by location, so the move is to contact the corps nearest you, or call 2-1-1. They also provide material help right after a home fire.
The Salvation Army, Midland Division Divisional headquarters: 1130 Hampton Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63139 Phone: (314) 646-3000 Website: centralusa.salvationarmy.org/midland Note: the Hampton address is the division office, not a walk-in voucher desk. Ask for your nearest corps, or dial 2-1-1. Vouchers are redeemed at Salvation Army Family Stores.
### How do you get a free bed for you or your child?
Beds split by age. For adults, a free bed comes from Home Sweet Home or a St. Vincent de Paul voucher, both through a referral. For children ages 3 to 17 sleeping on the floor or a couch, Sleep in Heavenly Peace builds and delivers a brand-new twin bed, mattress, and bedding, completely free.
### Free beds for kids ages 3 to 17
Sleep in Heavenly Peace Apply: shpbeds.org/apply Find your local chapter: shpbeds.org/chapters National phone: 844-432-2337 (844-432-BEDS) Website: shpbeds.org A guardian applies online and enters a ZIP code to reach the nearest chapter. A school or agency referral strengthens the request. Volunteer-built beds are delivered as inventory allows.
Enter your ZIP on the apply page to route to the chapter serving your area, rather than searching for a local street address. That national portal is the correct front door, and it puts your request in front of the right volunteers.
### Free baby items, bedding, and safe sleep
Nurses for Newborns Address: 3 Sunnen Dr, St. Louis, MO 63143 Phone: (314) 544-3433 (24-hour Nurse On Call: 314-448-4004) Website: nursesfornewborns.org For pregnant women and families with a baby age 0 to 2. Registered nurses visit your home with diapers, formula, clothing, and safe-sleep bedding, plus health and parenting support.
One important note for new parents: Nurses for Newborns no longer provides cribs, following a federal rule change. If you need a safe place for your baby to sleep, ask them about safe-sleep alternatives when you call. Families can reach out directly, with no formal referral required.
### What help can you get after a house fire?
After a fire, your first call is the American Red Cross, not a furniture bank. Their Disaster Action Team typically responds within about two hours with emergency lodging and financial help for immediate needs like food, clothing, and medications. The Red Cross responds to 10 to 15 home fires a day across the region.
American Red Cross, Greater St. Louis Phone: 1-800-733-2767 (1-800-RED-CROSS) Website: redcross.org/local/missouri Immediate post-fire help: emergency lodging, financial assistance for essentials, replacing medications and toiletries, and recovery casework.
Furniture comes later. Once you’re rehoused, the caseworker from your Red Cross recovery, or a new one through 2-1-1, can refer you to Home Sweet Home or St. Vincent de Paul to refill the rooms. First safety and essentials, then the couch.
### Where can you find cheap furniture if you don’t qualify?
If you don’t qualify for free help, or you need something today, the Habitat for Humanity ReStore is the low-cost fallback. It is not free, but couches, tables, dressers, and appliances sell at a deep discount off retail. Two metro locations are open Tuesday through Sunday, with a donation pickup line for larger pieces.
Habitat for Humanity ReStore South Side: 3830 South Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63118, (314) 531-4155 Des Peres: 2117 Sams Drive, Des Peres, MO 63131, (314) 678-4596 Website: habitatstl.org/restore Hours: Tuesday through Sunday, 10am to 6pm; closed Monday. Donation pickup: (314) 678-4576.
If it’s cash you need to bridge the gap, our guide to emergency cash and TANF help in Missouri covers programs that can free up money for the pieces no one gives away.
Furnishing a home from nothing feels impossible on day one. It isn’t. It’s a sequence: get a caseworker or dial 2-1-1, collect your referral, and let each program do what it was built to do. A bed this week, a table the next, a real kitchen by the end of the month. You are not behind, and you are not asking for too much. You are doing exactly what these neighbors set this help up for. Being found is how it starts, and the whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where is the best place to get free furniture?
A.  The region’s main furniture bank is Home Sweet Home in Maplewood, which furnishes around 1,000 families a year, entirely free. You cannot walk in, though: it is referral-only. Your best first move is calling 2-1-1 any hour, then a caseworker refers you to Home Sweet Home, St. Vincent de Paul, or the Salvation Army.
### Q. Do I need a caseworker or referral to get free furniture?
A.  Almost always, yes. Home Sweet Home accepts no self-referrals at all; a partner agency’s case manager must refer you. St. Vincent de Paul sends volunteers for a home visit first. The fastest way to reach a caseworker is to call 2-1-1 any hour, or work with your shelter or housing agency.
### Q. How do furniture banks work?
A.  Furniture banks like Home Sweet Home run on referrals, not walk-ins. Your case manager submits a referral, a coordinator reviews your eligibility, and you join a waiting list. When your turn comes, you shop the warehouse with staff and pick your own items, and delivery usually arrives the next business day, beds and kitchen basics included.
### Q. Which charities offer free furniture donations?
A.  Several do, all through a referral or voucher. Home Sweet Home in Maplewood furnishes homes free, St. Vincent de Paul issues vouchers after a home visit, and the Salvation Army offers vouchers through its local corps. For children’s beds, Sleep in Heavenly Peace builds new twin beds free. Call 2-1-1 to start.
### Q. Do churches ever offer free furniture?
A.  Yes, indirectly. St. Vincent de Paul operates through neighborhood parish conferences: call 2-1-1 or use their Conference Finder, and volunteers visit your home before issuing a furniture voucher. The Salvation Army, a faith-based charity, offers vouchers through its local corps community centers too. Both routes are free and start with a referral.
### Q. What kind of furniture can I find for free?
A.  Through Home Sweet Home, you leave with the essentials: beds, mattresses, a table, and seating, plus kitchen basics like dishes, towels, and sheets. St. Vincent de Paul vouchers cover beds, a kitchen table, and household goods. Programs focus on furnishing a whole home, not luxury pieces, so expect solid, practical items.
### Q. Where can I get free baby items, bedding, or a crib in St. Louis?
A.  Nurses for Newborns serves pregnant women and families with a baby age 0 to 2. Call (314) 544-3433 for diapers, formula, clothing, and safe-sleep bedding, delivered through in-home nurse visits. Note they no longer provide cribs, so ask about safe-sleep alternatives instead. Families can self-refer by phone.
### Q. How to get a free sofa?
A.  A free sofa comes through the same referral route as other furniture. Home Sweet Home includes seating when it furnishes your home, and a St. Vincent de Paul voucher can cover a couch after a volunteer home visit. Both need a caseworker referral, so call 2-1-1 first. There are no walk-ins.

## A Free Staircase Up a Cleanup Hill: Scenic Drives Near St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-near-st-louis-beyond-the-arch
Flat, they say. Every recycled top-10 list treats St. Louis like a parking lot with an Arch on it, then tells you the pretty drives start three hours south in the Ozarks. About 30 miles west of downtown, on Route 94, a free staircase climbs a 75-foot hill that didn’t exist until 2001. From the platform on top you can see across two counties.
Here’s the turn the roundups skip: that hill is a lid. Sealed inside one engineered structure is what was left of a World War II explosives plant and a Cold War uranium plant. Then the Department of Energy built a staircase up the side, laid a crushed-gravel walkway along the top and put a viewing platform at the summit, with viewfinders mounted in four directions. Your legs feel the climb first. Then the gravel crunches, the viewfinders swing, and a planted prairie runs out below you to the wooded hills. Plenty of people heading out to the Augusta tasting rooms pass it every weekend without slowing down.
The staircase is free, and the cell is open from dawn to dusk, about 45 to 50 minutes from the Arch. The interpretive center at the bottom closes at 4 on weekends and 5 on weekdays, so aim for about 2 p.m. on a Saturday and you get the exhibits and still have daylight for the platform. The site’s number is (636) 300-2601.
This page is about the roads, not the towns at the end of them. The small towns outside St. Louis have their own town-by-town guide. Here you get the driving: three routes within about 80 minutes of the Arch, the hour to arrive, what closes when, and one afternoon pick for each. Every drive time is an estimate from the Arch, so add a cushion on a fall weekend.
### What are some scenic drives around Saint Louis, Missouri?
Three, plus the Great River Road you already know. What sets them apart from the Ozarks-or-nothing lists is that each hands you something free to stand in front of: a staircase over a sealed cleanup site on Route 94, a 1939 gas station turned interpretive center on old Route 66, and carvings about a thousand years old off Highway 21. The longest of the three is about 80 minutes from the Arch, and Missouri color usually peaks around mid-October.
Past the staircase, Route 94 becomes the bluff road, winding west along the north side of the Missouri River. A few minutes from the stairs, the Busch Memorial Conservation Area holds about 100 old TNT bunkers, and in October the woods around them crunch with leaf litter underfoot. Farther on, Klondike Park sits in a former sand quarry, where a fishing lake has a pale, sandy shoreline that looks wrong for Missouri. Busch is open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., which makes it the easy late-light fallback. Klondike is about 65 to 70 minutes from the Arch and stays open until half an hour after sunset, with Augusta wine country about 70 to 75 minutes out. An afternoon that starts around 1 p.m. covers the stairs, Busch and Klondike.
Cross into Illinois and old Route 66 turns playful. In Mt. Olive, about 55 minutes from the Arch, a gas station a former coal miner opened in 1926 is still standing. In Livingston, about 45 minutes out, the antique mall parks a giant pink elephant out front, and the soft-serve comes out of a building shaped like an ice cream cone. Eat it standing up and it’s cold, sweet and already running down your wrist. Start in Edwardsville, about 30 minutes out, at the West End Service Station, a 1939 gas station. It’s open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday, so be there by about 2:30. Then finish with a cone, because the Livingston antique mall stays open until 7.
The quiet one is south. At Washington State Park on Highway 21, you follow a level paved path, step under a covered shelter onto a wooden deck, and the carvings sit in the stone in front of you: birds, arrows, footprints, all about a thousand years old. Your boots knock on the boards once, and then you stand still. The park is about 80 minutes from the Arch, and the grounds and both petroglyph sites are open from 7 a.m. to sunset, year-round, so arrive with at least two hours of daylight. With only an afternoon, leave by noon and spend it at the main site and on the stone 1,000 Steps Trail.
One honest caveat. None of these are mountain roads. What makes them work is the water. The Missouri and the Mississippi cut limestone bluffs along their banks, and the old roads hug the rivers because that’s where the towns were. Drive one in mid-October and you’ll stop believing the flat line.
No full afternoon? An hour on the grounds at Powder Valley Conservation Nature Center in Kirkwood puts leaf litter underfoot and fall color overhead, about 25 minutes from the Arch. The grounds are open daily from 8 to 6. The building is closed Sundays, Mondays and federal holidays, so don’t count on going inside on a Columbus Day drive.
Then there’s the Great River Road, the drive every St. Louisan already knows. Step out at the first bluff-top pull-off and the river air reaches you before the view does. The road starts in Alton, where the parks in Alton, Illinois give you those pull-offs, and runs under the limestone to Grafton, about 60 minutes from the Arch. We mapped the best stops along the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton separately, so the eagles and the ferry stay there and this page spends its time on the other three.
### Is there a scenic drive along the Missouri River near St. Louis?
Yes, and the best hour is the last one of daylight, when the prairie below the Weldon Spring platform goes gold. Route 94 leaves St. Charles, climbs into the hills around Weldon Spring, then winds west along the bluffs on the north side of the Missouri River toward Augusta and Marthasville. The stop sits about 45 to 50 minutes from the Arch, and the Department of Energy keeps the climb free from dawn to dusk.
The bluffs, the river bottoms and the little wine towns are why people drive it. The stop almost nobody makes comes first.
The Weldon Spring disposal cell. From 1941 to 1945 the Army made TNT here, on 17,232 acres the government acquired in the early 1940s, displacing 576 residents of three small towns. From the late 1950s until 1966, the Atomic Energy Commission refined uranium on part of the same ground. The cleanup took years. When it wrapped up in 2001, the waste went into one engineered structure: 41 acres at the base and about 75 feet tall.
Then the Department of Energy did something you wouldn’t expect from a federal cleanup site: it invited the public up. From the platform you look out over St. Charles and St. Louis counties, the 150-acre native prairie the government planted around the base and a long line of wooded hills.
The site is free and open to the public, and the cell itself is open from dawn to dusk. It’s monitored, groundwater and all, and inspected every year, and in 2020 the EPA gave it a national award for site reuse.
The interpretive center at the bottom, 7295 Highway 94 South, tells the TNT years, the uranium years and the cleanup in a 4,500-square-foot exhibit gallery. It’s open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and weekends from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. It closes on federal holidays, New Year’s, Easter and Christmas, so call (636) 300-2601 if you’re unsure. Leashed pets are fine on the grounds but not inside the buildings. A 6-mile multiuse trail built on an old haul road starts here too and links to the conservation land next door and on to the Katy Trail.
That’s the myth-bust in one stop. St. Louis has no views? Stand on a hill built to hold the cleanup from World War II and the Cold War, and count the counties.
August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area. It has no street address. Find Route D and drive 1.5 miles west of Highway 94, about 50 minutes from the Arch. The Missouri Department of Conservation keeps it open daily from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. with no entry fee, which makes it the easy late-light fallback after the stairs. The area holds about 100 old TNT bunkers from the plant years. The Lake 34 north area is closed for now, so call (636) 441-4554 or check MDC’s page before you go.
Klondike Park. Keep going west on 94. At 4600 Highway 94 South, just east of Augusta, St. Charles County runs a park built in an old silica sand quarry, where for most of the 20th century miners dug sand for glass. What they left behind is a fishing lake and a pale, sandy shoreline that looks wrong for Missouri. Leave the swimsuit home: swimming isn’t allowed, and neither are glass containers.
There are more than 4 miles of paved and natural trails, plus kayaks and paddleboards on the lake. Cabins run $65 a night with a two-night minimum, and tent sites are $10. The shower house closes from November 1 through March 31. The park opens at 7 a.m. and closes half an hour after sunset. Call 636-949-7535 to confirm rates, and expect about 65 to 70 minutes from the Arch.
Augusta. A few minutes on, Augusta holds a title most Missourians have never heard of. On June 20, 1980, it became the first American Viticultural Area in the country, the first wine region the federal government ever recognized. The tasting rooms are the obvious stop, and they fill up fast on fall weekends. I could not confirm their hours, so call ahead. Plan on about 70 to 75 minutes from downtown.
The loop home. Stay on 94 to Marthasville, pick up Highway 47 and cross the Missouri River bridge into Washington. That bridge was rebuilt in 2018, and the town on the other side earns a stop of its own; our guide to things to do in Washington, MO covers the Amtrak run, the walk across the river bridge and Lions Lake. From there, Highway 100 brings you east through Gray Summit on the south side of the river, so you never repeat a mile. Shaw Nature Reserve sits on that stretch, and its last entry is 4:30 p.m., so don’t linger over lunch.
If you only have an afternoon: leave downtown around 1 p.m. and be at the Weldon Spring stairs by about 2, while the interpretive center is still open. Walk up, then drive to Busch, which stays open until 10 p.m. If daylight is left, push on to Klondike Park for the last light.
### Can you still drive old Route 66 near St. Louis?
Yes, and the first thing it hands you is cold and sweet. At the cone-shaped Twistee Treats building in Livingston, about 45 minutes from the Arch, the soft-serve starts running the minute it’s in your hand, and that’s the playful end of old Route 66. The Illinois side is the best-kept stretch near St. Louis, and it runs north out of Edwardsville.
Start in Edwardsville at the West End Service Station, 620 St. Louis St., a 1939 station the city reopened as a free Route 66 interpretive center. It’s open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday, and it’s one of the free things to do in Edwardsville that earns the stop by itself. Spaces beside the station are for Friday, Saturday and Sunday only. Other days, park near West and Schwarz streets. I could not confirm a phone number for the station itself, only city hall’s. Then head north through Hamel toward Livingston.
The Pink Elephant Antique Mall, 908 Veterans Memorial Dr., fills the town’s old high school with dealers’ booths. The mall is open 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily and the diner from 11 to 7, until 8 on Fridays and Saturdays. Holiday hours may vary, so call (618) 637-2366 on a holiday weekend. It’s a photo stop first and a shopping stop second, which is exactly how Route 66 was supposed to work.
Mt. Olive is the payoff. Stand in front of the Soulsby station and you’re looking at what the Illinois Route 66 Scenic Byway calls the oldest, most original station on the Illinois route that hasn’t been completely rebuilt. Henry Soulsby followed his father, an Irish immigrant, into the coal mines until an injury in the mid-1920s forced him aboveground. He put most of his life savings into two lots at the edge of town, and in 1926, the same year Route 66 was designated, he opened a gas station there. It stayed in business for years. It has been on the National Register since 2004 and now works as a visitor center and museum at 710 W. 1st St. I could not confirm its hours or admission, so call ahead through the regional tourism line, (800) 258-6645.
Then drive across town to Union Miners Cemetery. Mother Jones, the labor organizer, is buried there, and in 1936 coal miners raised a monument over her. They paid for it mostly in small donations during the Depression and dug the site themselves. The Mother Jones Museum, in City Hall at 215 E. Main St., calls it the only Union-owned cemetery in the United States. I could not confirm the museum’s hours. City Hall is open 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays, and the museum’s number is (217) 999-4261. A gas station built by a miner, a monument built by miners. That’s the whole drive.
On the Missouri side, the old road’s best-known stop is in Eureka, where the Route 66 State Park visitor center picks up the story. It’s about 35 minutes from the Arch at 97 N Outer Rd, and it’s free. The grounds are open from 7 a.m. to half an hour after sunset. The visitor center runs 9 to 4 daily from March through October and closes November through February, except the second week of December. Call 636-938-7198.
If you only have an afternoon: be at the West End station by about 2:30, before it closes at 4, and give the exhibits half an hour. Then roll on to Livingston, where the mall stays open until 7 and a cone is waiting. Save Mt. Olive for a day when you’ve called ahead and can give the cemetery a quiet half hour.
Every drive ends at a table. Find where St. Louis locals eat.
### Is there a scenic drive south of St. Louis that ends at a thousand-year-old carving?
Yes, and the first sound is your own boots on a wooden deck. A level paved path leads to a covered shelter and that deck, and from it you are looking at figures cut into stone about a thousand years ago, no scrambling required. Washington State Park is about 80 minutes from the Arch, not the hour people guess. Admission is free, and both petroglyph sites are open from 7 a.m. to sunset, year-round.
The road starts as one you only know as a commute. Inside St. Louis County, Highway 21 is Tesson Ferry Road, named for the man who ran a ferry across the Meramec in the 1800s. Keep going past I-270 and it opens up into Jefferson County, past Barnhart and Hillsboro, into the first folds of the Ozarks. For the park itself, the Missouri Department of Conservation’s directions say to travel west on Highway 21 about 8 miles from De Soto. The address is 13041 State Highway 104, De Soto.
Washington State Park protects the largest group of petroglyphs found in Missouri, almost three-quarters of all the ones known in the state. Mississippian people, related to the builders of the great mounds across the Mississippi in Illinois, carved them roughly a thousand years ago. The two sites hold more than 350 symbols: birds, arrows, footprints, turkey tracks, human figures. Guided tours run only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, usually Saturdays at 2 p.m. Call 636-586-5768 to confirm.
The other reason to go is the stone. In the 1930s, Company 1743, an African American unit of the Civilian Conservation Corps, built much of the park by hand. They called their camp Camp Thunderbird after the symbols in the carvings, and they carved a thunderbird into the chimney of the stone dining lodge they built, now Thunderbird Lodge. They laid the stone 1,000 Steps Trail and the octagonal lookout shelter, so when you climb those steps you are standing on stone set by hand in the 1930s. Come for the petroglyphs. Stay for the steps.
People ask which is the most beautiful state park in Missouri. That’s subjective, but this is the strongest case within an easy day of St. Louis. Fall is the time, and from November through March, roads to some areas close to vehicles and you go on foot. There’s camping if you want the morning there too. Check Missouri State Parks’ advisories page for closures before you drive.
The other southern run is I-55 to Ste. Genevieve, about 80 minutes from downtown. Established by 1750, it was the first permanent European settlement in Missouri, and on October 30, 2020 it became the 422nd unit of the National Park Service as Ste. Genevieve National Historical Park. That makes it the closest national park to St. Louis after the Arch. It’s fee-free. Stop at the Welcome Center, 66 S. Main St., (573) 880-7189, to sign up in person for the free house tours: 15 people at most, same-day signup only. Our guide to things to do in Ste. Genevieve covers the town once you park.
If you only have an afternoon: leave the Arch by noon, reach the park around 1:20, and give the main site and the 1,000 Steps Trail two unhurried hours before the sunset closing. Heading to Ste. Genevieve instead? Get to the Welcome Center early, because the house tours depend on same-day sign-up.
### Where can you see fall colors on a drive near St. Louis?
The bluffs along the Missouri turn from solid green to red, yellow and orange, and a Saturday either catches it or misses it. The Missouri Department of Conservation says peak color in Missouri is usually around mid-October, when the maples, ashes, hickories and oaks turn together. Its fall color reports post weekly from the second half of September to about mid-November, usually by Thursday evening. Read the latest one before you spend a Saturday on it.
Illinois peaks later. The Enjoy Illinois fall color tracker typically puts Southwest Illinois, including Alton and Grafton, in the last week of October. If you missed Missouri’s peak, the Great River Road may still be worth the gas.
MDC’s advice on where to look is blunt and useful: pick routes along rivers with views of forested bluffs, or along ridges with long views over wooded hills. For color drives, it names state highways 94 and 21, two of the routes on this page. Statewide lists send you to the Ozarks for the most scenic drive in Missouri, but the state’s own conservation department points you to roads inside 80 minutes of the Arch.
The department also names its own St. Louis-area color spots, and several sit right on these drives:
Busch Memorial Conservation Area, off Route D beside the Weldon Spring site. Open daily 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., no entry fee, a few minutes from the staircase.
LaBarque Creek Conservation Area, in northwestern Jefferson County, about 50 minutes out. Sandstone bluffs, narrow wooded valleys and a trail about three miles long where the creek pools reflect the color. Open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, no fee. Camping is prohibited, and hunting season applies. The lot is in the valley off Doc Sargent Road; from Eureka, take Highway 109, then Route FF, then Route F. Call (636) 441-4554.
Shaw Nature Reserve at Gray Summit, about 60 minutes out, right on your way home if you loop Route 94 back through Washington on Highway 100. Open 8 to 5 with last entry at 4:30. Admission is $5 for ages 13 and up and free for ages 3 to 12. It closes Mondays in January and February. Call (314) 577-9555.
Powder Valley Conservation Nature Center in Kirkwood, about 25 minutes out, for an hour of leaf litter underfoot and color overhead when you can’t take the whole day. The grounds are open daily 8 to 6. The building is open Tuesday through Saturday, 8 to 5, and closed Sundays, Mondays and federal holidays, Columbus Day included. No pets. Call (314) 301-1500.
For a view down onto the color instead of up into it, time your drive around one of these overlooks. The top of the Weldon Spring cell, with a planted 150-acre native prairie below. The octagonal stone lookout the Civilian Conservation Corps built at Washington State Park. Go on a weekday if you can. Route 94 is a two-lane road shared with cyclists, Katy Trail traffic and the wine-country crowd, and October weekends fill it.
### What are some beautiful places to visit near St. Louis?
At Lone Elk Park the windshield is the viewing glass. St. Louis County keeps 546 acres near Valley Park where bison, elk, deer, wild turkey and waterfowl live, and you drive the park road through their range, about 40 minutes from the Arch. The park opens at 8 a.m. and closes at official sunset.
The name is the story. The land was part of a World War II ammunition plant, and the county started elk and bison herds there in 1948. When the federal government took the land back, the herds were destroyed for safety reasons, and county history dates that to 1958. One bull elk survived. The park opened to the public in October 1971. Same arc as Weldon Spring: military ground turned into a wildlife drive anyone can take. Give the bison room, and leave the dog home, because pets aren’t allowed here, even inside a vehicle. I’m working from the county’s own summary, so call 314-615-4386 to check before you go.
Bluff Road in Columbia, Illinois. The Illinois side has a second bluff drive most people never try, about 25 to 30 minutes from the Arch. The official Great River Road listing says Bluff Road runs along the bluffs from Palmer Road in Columbia. It’s a quiet back road, so drive it slowly.
Pere Marquette State Park. The Great River Road ends its run at Grafton, and the park sits there at 13112 Visitor Center Ln, about 60 minutes from the Arch. From November through March its visitor center is open Monday through Saturday, 8 to 3:30, and closed Sundays. Call 618-786-3323 for the rest of the year. Our guide to things to do in Grafton covers the town.
### How do you turn a scenic drive into a cheap weekend getaway near St. Louis?
The cheapest weekend is a campsite and a full tank. Klondike Park sells tent sites at $10, and Washington State Park has a campground, so Saturday can be Route 94 and Sunday can be Highway 21. The Weldon Spring platform and the petroglyph deck charge nothing. What you actually spend is gas and lunch.
Looking for good places to take a road trip from St. Louis? Pick by direction. Which city is an hour away depends on where you point the car: Mt. Olive is about 55 minutes north, Grafton about 60 up the river, Augusta about 70 to 75 west, and Ste. Genevieve about 80 south. Of the prettiest towns in Missouri within that circle, Augusta, Washington and Ste. Genevieve are the three I’d drive to first.
Next time someone tells you St. Louis is flat, you’ll know about the staircase, the miners’ monument and the carvings off Highway 21. Check the MDC report Thursday night, pick a direction Saturday morning and go find the view the lists missed.
Hungry at the end of the drive? Browse where to eat around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory before you’re an hour from home with nothing open.
If you’re the tasting room, the diner or the shop on Route 94, old 66 or Highway 21, claim your spot and turn the people already driving past into customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most scenic drive in Missouri?
A.  Statewide lists send you to the Ozarks, and those drives are lovely. Inside about 80 minutes of St. Louis, though, the Missouri Department of Conservation names state highways 94 and 21 for fall color. Take Route 94 west from Weldon Spring toward Augusta in mid-October, climb the free staircase first, and finish at Klondike Park, which closes half an hour after sunset. MDC posts its color reports weekly, usually by Thursday evening, so check the latest before you pick a Saturday.
### Q. What is the closest national park to St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Gateway Arch National Park, on the downtown riverfront, is the closest. Next is Ste. Genevieve National Historical Park, about 80 minutes south, which became the 422nd unit of the National Park Service on October 30, 2020. It protects the French colonial houses of Missouri’s first permanent European settlement, established by 1750. The park is fee-free. Free house tours take 15 people at most, with same-day sign-up in person at the Welcome Center, 66 S. Main St.
### Q. What are some good places to take a road trip from St. Louis?
A.  Start with the four runs on this page: Route 94 to Augusta, old Route 66 to Mt. Olive, Highway 21 to Washington State Park and the Great River Road to Grafton. Each has a stop worth the gas, and all sit within about 80 minutes. If you’ll drive farther, our roundup of the best day trips from St. Louis within two hours covers the longer runs. Leave early, though: the Weldon Spring interpretive center and the West End station in Edwardsville both close at 4 on weekends.
### Q. What are some cheap weekend getaways near St. Louis?
A.  Build one around a campsite. Klondike Park near Augusta has tent sites at $10 and cabins at $65 a night with a two-night minimum, and Washington State Park has a campground. Missouri state parks charge no admission, and the Weldon Spring platform is free too. Your real cost is gas and lunch. Klondike’s shower house is closed from November 1 through March 31, so plan around that, and confirm rates with the park before you book.
### Q. What city is 1 hour away from St. Louis?
A.  Pick a direction. Mt. Olive is about 55 minutes north on old Route 66, Grafton about 60 minutes up the Great River Road, and Augusta about 70 to 75 minutes west on Route 94. To the south, Washington State Park and Ste. Genevieve each run about 80 minutes. Each sits at the end of a drive on this page, which is the point: make the road the trip. Those times are free-flow estimates from the Arch, so add a cushion on a fall weekend.
### Q. What are some of the prettiest towns in Missouri?
A.  Close to St. Louis, start with three on these drives. Augusta sits in the wine-country hills on Route 94 and was the first federally recognized American Viticultural Area, on June 20, 1980. Washington has a working riverfront across the Highway 47 bridge, and Ste. Genevieve still has French colonial houses from the late 1700s. Drive the bluff road between the first two and judge for yourself. Plan on about 70 to 75 minutes to Augusta, and call ahead for tasting-room hours, which I could not confirm.
### Q. What is the most beautiful state park in Missouri?
A.  It’s subjective, but close to St. Louis the strongest case is Washington State Park near De Soto: the largest group of petroglyphs found in Missouri, Ozark overlooks and stone buildings laid by an African American CCC company in the 1930s. It’s about 80 minutes south on Highway 21, free to enter, and open from 7 a.m. to sunset year-round, with camping if you want to stay over. Guided petroglyph tours run only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, usually Saturdays at 2 p.m.
### Q. Can you walk on top of the Weldon Spring disposal cell?
A.  Yes. A staircase climbs the roughly 75-foot cell to a crushed-gravel walkway and a viewing platform with viewfinders. The Department of Energy says the site is free and open to the public, and the cell is open from dawn to dusk. The interpretive center at the base is open weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and weekends 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Keep dogs leashed, and out of the buildings.

## Hidden Gems in St. Louis: Rare Water Towers, Ruins You Can Legally See, Free Art
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hidden-gems-in-st-louis
We’ll admit it: the first version of this page read like every other St. Louis list. It sent you to the same handful of places every roundup sends you, in roughly the same order. Meanwhile three of the last seven standpipe water towers left in the United States stand in our own city, and the one those lists still tell you to climb has been locked for years.
So we started over. This version is for the person who has done the big weekend more times than they can count and wants the places that never make the roundups: a 154-foot Corinthian column on Grand that hasn’t been used since 1912, two stone towers standing out in the Mississippi like something off the Rhine, the last surviving mound in a city once nicknamed Mound City, and a burned hotel that Henry Shaw turned into fake ancient ruins. Almost all of it is free. Most of it is visible from a car window, which is exactly why people drive right past it.
If you’ve already worked through the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the same idea pointed back at the city and the county. Everything below was checked this month, and where something is closed or gone, we say so.
### What are some underrated places to visit in St. Louis?
Start with what the lists skip: three of the last seven standpipe water towers in the U.S., castle-like intake towers standing in the Mississippi, a burned hotel’s stones arranged into ruins in Tower Grove Park, Ulysses S. Grant’s free White Haven farm, and a walk-in Richard Serra spiral at the free Pulitzer museum.
Here’s the short list, roughly in the order we’d hand it to a friend who swears they’ve seen everything:
The three standpipe towers. Compton Hill on the south side, plus the Bissell Street “Red” tower and the Grand Avenue “Old White” tower a few minutes apart in north city. One morning, one car, three landmarks.
The Chain of Rocks intake towers. Two stone towers in the river off north St. Louis, built to draw water for the city’s Chain of Rocks waterworks and best seen from the old bridge.
The Ruins in Tower Grove Park. Fire-damaged stones from the 1867 Lindell Hotel, arranged by Henry Shaw into three “ancient” clusters.
Richard Serra’s Joe. A torqued steel spiral you can walk into, in the courtyard of a museum that charges nothing.
White Haven. The farm where a young Army officer named Grant met Julia Dent. Entry and house tours are free.
Jefferson Barracks. The 1826 Army post where Grant, Lee and Sherman all served, with three small museums that ask only for a donation.
Bellerive Park. A 1908 overlook in Carondelet where nearly every bench faces the river.
The Mural Mile. A riverfront floodwall that graffiti artists have been painting since 1997.
Notice what’s missing from most of that list: a ticket. That’s the pattern. The places St. Louis overlooks tend to be the ones nobody is selling.
One more belongs on this list even though you can’t walk onto it, and it may matter more than anything else on the page.
The last mound in Mound City. St. Louis got that old nickname from the earthen mounds that once stood here, hundreds of them across the area, built centuries before the city existed. Settlers turned some into house sites and beer gardens, then leveled the rest. By 1875, according to the Osage Nation, nearly all of them were gone. One survived. Sugarloaf Mound, on Ohio Avenue in south city, went up sometime between AD 600 and 1200, and it’s the oldest known human-made structure in St. Louis. In 1928 somebody built a house on top of it.
The Osage Nation, which considers the mound sacred, bought the first third of it in 2008 and spent 17 years getting the rest back. It bought the house on the summit in 2009 and took it down in 2017. On September 22, 2025, the Nation announced that the entire mound was under its control again, with help from Counterpublic, the arts nonprofit behind this fall’s citywide exhibition. The plan now is to remove the remaining structures, stabilize the mound and build an interpretive center.
Until that center exists, this isn’t an outing. It’s sacred land and it isn’t open to visitors. If you want to see it, see it from the public street, briefly and quietly, the way you’d pass a cemetery, and if it moves you, the Osage Nation is raising money for the preservation work. For the region’s even older story, head south of the county line to the Kimmswick Bone Bed, where a stone spear point turned up among mastodon bones. It’s where our list of things to do in Arnold, MO starts.
### Can you legally climb a water tower in St. Louis?
Not right now, and that’s the part the other lists get wrong. The only St. Louis water tower that ever opened for public climbs is Compton Hill, at Grand and Russell, and it has been shut for years. Tours stopped during the pandemic in a pause that was supposed to be temporary. St. Louis Magazine reported in September 2025 that masonry deterioration and falling debris had kept it closed for several years, and Nine PBS’s Living St. Louis dates the closure to 2019. The preservation society’s own website now says the tower is closed for preservation.
Here’s the trap. The city’s park page for Compton Hill Reservoir Park still lists climbing hours: the first Saturday of the month and full-moon evenings, April through November. At least one travel article published this year repeats them. Anyone who trusts those pages is planning a night around a door that stays locked. The other two aren’t open to climbers either, and going up any water tower without permission is trespassing, on top of being a good way to get hurt 179 feet off the ground.
What you can do is see all three from the ground, and that’s better than it sounds once you know what you’re looking at. A standpipe tower is a disguise. Inside each one stood a tall iron pipe that soaked up the surges from the pumps and kept the city’s water pressure even. The brick, stone and terra cotta around it were there to make plumbing look like a monument. Only seven of these towers are left in the country. St. Louis kept three.
Compton Hill (1898). Harvey Ellis designed it: 179 feet of Romanesque brick and terra cotta on a stone base, with 198 steps inside. The city decommissioned it in 1929, when it moved to a more modern water system. A 2025 structural assessment found weathering in the limestone base, spalling on the terra cotta and water getting into the upper shaft, and the Water Tower & Park Preservation Society says a phased restoration plan is being worked out. The park around it is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and it rewards a walk even with the tower locked. The reservoir wall has steps and fountains laid out like an Italian villa garden, and near Grand stands the Naked Truth, a bronze unveiled in 1914 to honor three editors of the German-language Westliche Post, with its inscription in German and English. For a reopening date, watch watertowerfoundation.org and ignore any calendar that doesn’t come from there.
Bissell Street “Red” tower (1885). William S. Eames drew it as a Moorish minaret, red brick under a copper roof gone green, at Bissell Street and Blair Avenue in Hyde Park. During World War II, St. Louis Magazine recounts, city leaders called it useless to anyone but the scrap-metal dealers, and the city came close to losing it. Kids in the neighborhood grew up calling it a castle.
Grand Avenue “Old White” tower (1871). The oldest of the three stands at 20th Street and Grand in College Hill. George I. Barnett designed it as a 154-foot Corinthian column during the postwar waterworks expansion led by Thomas Whitman, the poet Walt Whitman’s brother, and it was once declared the largest free-standing Corinthian column in the world. It was retired in 1912. In the 1920s and ’30s beacons on top helped pilots find the airport. When a 1933 recommendation proposed tearing it down, Mayor Bernard Dickmann said wrecking it would “verge closely on an act of sacrilege.”
Make it a loop. Old White and the Red tower are a few minutes apart, and Compton Hill is a straight run south on Grand. Keep one more name in your pocket for the drive: William Eames, the architect behind the Red tower, also designed the first of the two water intake towers standing in the Mississippi. That’s where the next section starts.
### What are some abandoned places in Saint Louis, Missouri?
Plenty, and most of them are a bad idea. An abandoned building still belongs to someone, whether that’s an owner, a bank or the city, and walking into one is trespassing before you even get to the rotten floors. So this list sticks to places that look abandoned, ruined or salvaged and that you’re allowed to see.
The Ruins in Tower Grove Park. In 1867 the Lindell Hotel, the largest hotel in America at the time, burned to the ground. Henry Shaw was about to deed the land for Tower Grove Park to the city, and he looked at the fire-damaged blocks and saw ancient ruins. He had the stones arranged in three clusters, and they’ve stood in the park ever since: a fake ruin made from a real disaster. Go on a weekday. The park says wedding parties line up there for photos on Saturdays.
The intake towers at Chain of Rocks. Just south of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, close to the Missouri shore, stands Intake Tower No. 1. William Eames designed it in a Richardsonian Romanesque style, it was finished in 1894, and the city’s landmark page compares it to the Mouse Tower on the Rhine near Bingen. When it couldn’t keep up with the city’s thirst, a second intake followed in 1913. You can’t reach either one, and the water around the Chain of Rocks is no place for a boat or a swimmer. You don’t need to. The view from the bridge is the point.
The National Building Arts Center, Sauget. Across the river sits a campus full of buildings that no longer exist, much of it St. Louis: terra cotta, cast iron and carved stone salvaged from demolitions. It isn’t a walk-in museum. You see it on a ticketed campus tour. Its 2026 calendar listed tours on Saturday, October 10, and Saturday, November 14, both at 11 a.m. In 2026 it’s also a Counterpublic exhibition site through December 12, and its Route 66 exhibition, City 66, is listed through October 17. Book through the center’s events page, and check the details there before you cross the bridge.
The Mural Mile. The riverfront floodwall between Victor Street and Chouteau Avenue, south of the Arch, has been painted since 1997, when the Paint Louis gathering began drawing graffiti artists from around the country. More than 250 have left work on it. The city owns the wall, and paint-overs come with the territory, so what you see this year won’t match the photos from five years ago. This fall Counterpublic added a new painted work nearby, Yatika Starr Fields’s Melted Destiny, at 1450 S. Wharf Street. The same flood wall carries the St. Louis Riverfront Trail north of the Arch, and it held through the Great Flood of 1993 with less than three feet to spare.
That’s the honest version of urban exploring in St. Louis. You get the ruin, the salvage and the paint, and nobody has to call a lawyer.
### What to do in St. Louis, MO for free?
The usual free answers are the big museums in the big park. They’re fine, and you’ve done them. These are the free ones the lists leave off.
Walk into a Richard Serra. The Pulitzer Arts Foundation, at 3716 Washington Boulevard in Grand Center, is a Tadao Ando building with free admission and free parking. The museum keeps short hours, Thursday through Sunday from 10 to 5 and until 9 on First Fridays. Joe stands in its outdoor courtyard, a torqued steel spiral Serra made for the building and named for Joseph Pulitzer Jr., and you walk its leaning walls around and around until you reach the center. Plan on museum hours for that one. The rest of the outdoor campus, including Park-Like, a native garden across the street, and the Spring Church, an open-air stone pavilion, is open every day from sunrise to sunset.
See Grant’s St. Louis farm. Most cars on Grant Road are headed somewhere else. Turn in at 7400 Grant Road instead. Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site preserves White Haven, the Dent family farm where Grant, fresh out of West Point, met Julia Dent, the sister of his roommate. Entry is free, the house tours are free, and the visitor center is open daily from 9 to 5 except Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day. Ulysses and Julia picked the house’s Paris Green exterior themselves in 1874, which is why it’s that startling shade of green. The Park Service is direct about the hard part, too: by 1850 Julia’s father enslaved upwards of 30 people on two St. Louis properties, 17 of them at White Haven, and Grant himself freed the one man he is known to have enslaved, William Jones, in 1859.
Then go where he was stationed. Grant reported to Jefferson Barracks in 1843, and it was from that post that he rode out to White Haven. The post opened in 1826 as the country’s first Infantry School of Practice, and Lee, Sherman, Sheridan and Jefferson Davis served there too. Its northern 420 acres became a St. Louis County park in 1950, on the bluffs in south county, open from 7 a.m. until half an hour past sunset. Stone buildings from the old post hold three small museums, the Ordnance Room, the Powder Magazine and the Visitors Center, open Wednesday through Sunday from noon to 4. Admission is free with a suggested donation. County hours can shift, so check before you go.
See a citywide art show for nothing. Counterpublic 2026, titled Coyote Time, is free and on view through December 12. It puts about 50 new commissions in public places across the city: along the riverfront, in The Ville, in Tower Grove Park, in Grand Center and across the river in Sauget. Much of the riverfront work is grouped at 101 Chouteau Avenue. The organizers bill it as one of the largest public art exhibitions in the country, and it only comes around every three years, so fall 2026 is the window.
Sit on a bench that faces the river. Bellerive Park costs nothing and gives you the best quiet river view in south city. More on that below. If you’re working the free list in the inner suburbs too, our guide to free things to do in Webster Groves picks up where this one stops.
Touring the towers? Here’s where to eat in St. Louis.
### Where can you watch the Mississippi without the riverfront crowds?
Skip the crowded steps downtown. Three quieter spots do it better: one south, one north and one across the water.
Bellerive Park, south. The city set this 8.67-acre park aside in 1908, first as Riverside Park, to give the public a scenic viewpoint over the river, then renamed it for an early French governor of St. Louis. It sits at 5570 S. Broadway in Carondelet, and the city’s own description is blunt: nearly every bench faces the Mississippi. A crescent drive off Broadway climbs to a pavilion with an overlook, and the view runs south down the river. Bring coffee and watch the barges work. There are no bike racks, so plan to walk the last bit or lock up elsewhere.
Chain of Rocks Park, north. Great Rivers Greenway’s park at 10840 Riverview Drive is the Missouri-side front door to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, open from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. Walk out onto the bridge and look downstream, and the two intake towers stand in the river just south of you. Two warnings for this fall. The canal bridge on the Illinois side closed for construction on June 22, 2026, cutting off the Illinois approach until it reopens, so plan to come from Missouri and check the greenway’s park page for the current status. And the westbound I-270 exit to Riverview Drive is temporarily closed; the greenway’s posted detour uses the Lilac Avenue exit and Dunn Road. The bridge itself, a mile of old Route 66 with a bend in the middle, gets its full due in our guide to historic sites in St. Louis.
Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, across the river. In East St. Louis, this park has an elevated river overlook that its managers call the best view in the region of the St. Louis skyline. It’s also where the lists are wrong a second time. The Gateway Geyser there, a fountain built to reach 630 feet to match the Arch, was the tallest fountain in the country and went off at noon on summer days. In late 2023 the Metro East Park and Recreation District announced the end of it: nearly 30 years had worn out the pumps, the generators and the pond liner. Some travel pages still tell you to show up at noon. Don’t bother. The park itself is open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., it’s free, and the view hasn’t gone anywhere. If you’re on the Illinois side anyway, our guide to parks in Fairview Heights covers the next stop east.
Want a river from higher up, on foot? The bluff trails around the county do that best. Start with our easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis, or head to Emmenegger Nature Park’s bluff trails in Kirkwood, where a short, steep climb ends at a rocky outcrop over the Meramec.
### Where do the quieter lists lead past the city limits?
Mostly west and south, to places that sit a few minutes off a highway everyone takes for something else.
The Black Madonna Shrine and Grottos, Pacific. About eight miles outside Eureka, at 100 St. Joseph Hill Road, a set of grottos built from Missouri tiff rock sits in the woods, part of a shrine that traces back to six Franciscan brothers from Poland in 1927. The shrine says it’s about a 40-minute drive from west county. The grounds are open from 9 to 5 from April through October and from 9 to 4 from November through March. Admission isn’t posted online, so call the office at 636-938-5361 before you go. It pairs well with the rest of our list of unique things to do in Eureka.
Next time somebody tells you they’ve done St. Louis, ask them which water tower is the oldest, or where Henry Shaw put a burned hotel. You’ll be the one who knows the climb is closed, the geyser is off and the mound is back in Osage hands. Pick one this weekend.
Planning a north-side tower loop or a weekday morning at the Ruins? Check where to eat around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and put lunch near the stop.
If you run a café, gallery or shop within a few blocks of one of these places, the people reading this are deciding where to stop next, so list your business with us.
Want the intake towers from mid-river? Our Chain of Rocks Bridge guide covers parking, the bend and which side is open.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why are secret towers in the Mississippi River?
A.  They’re water intakes, not secrets. The two stone towers off north St. Louis, just south of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, were built to draw river water into the city’s Chain of Rocks waterworks. Intake Tower No. 1 dates to 1894 and was designed by William Eames, who also drew the Bissell Street water tower, and the second followed in 1913. See them from the bridge.
### Q. What was the original purpose of the water tower?
A.  In St. Louis, pressure control. Each of the city’s three historic standpipe towers hides a tall iron pipe that absorbed surges from the pumps and kept the water pressure even. The decorative shells were architecture wrapped around plumbing: the Grand Avenue tower’s 154-foot Corinthian column hides a standpipe about five feet across, and it hasn’t been used since 1912.
### Q. How illegal is it to explore abandoned places?
A.  Illegal enough to skip. In Missouri, knowingly entering or staying unlawfully in a building is trespass in the first degree under RSMo 569.140, generally a class B misdemeanor, and entering someone else’s land unlawfully is second-degree trespass under 569.150, an infraction. This isn’t legal advice. It’s the reason every place on this page is one you can see legally.
### Q. What are some strange and unusual things to do in St. Louis?
A.  The famous-weird circuit, City Museum and the rest, lives in our guide to unique things to do in St. Louis. This page is the quieter list: a 1914 bronze called the Naked Truth, a fake ruin built from a burned hotel, and a Mississippi water intake that looks like a castle on the Rhine.
### Q. What to do in downtown St. Louis today?
A.  Walk the Mural Mile, the painted floodwall that runs along the riverfront south of downtown between Chouteau Avenue and Victor Street, then come back to the Counterpublic works grouped at 101 Chouteau Avenue, part of the free 2026 exhibition (on view through December 12, 2026). Yatika Starr Fields’s new painted work is close by at 1450 S. Wharf Street. Check counterpublic.org for each site’s hours first.
### Q. What are some hidden places to visit in Missouri?
A.  Start with the river towns and small places most people only drive through. Our guide to day trips from St. Louis maps the ones within two hours. Closer in, the Black Madonna Shrine’s rock grottos near Pacific are about 40 minutes from west county.
### Q. Why are there so many abandoned buildings in downtown St. Louis?
