### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is O'Fallon, MO a suburb of St. Louis?
A.  Yes, technically. O’Fallon sits about 30 minutes west of downtown St. Louis, where I-70 and I-64 both cross St. Charles County. Calling it a bedroom suburb undersells it, though. At the 2020 census it was the seventh-most populous city in Missouri and the largest in St. Charles County, with more than 90,000 residents and a full festival calendar of its own.
### Q. What is O'Fallon, MO famous for?
A.  Around St. Louis, mostly the Celebration of Lights, the drive-through holiday display at Fort Zumwalt Park that has run every year since 1991 and draws more than 13,000 vehicles. It’s also known for its 9/11 memorial made from 22 tons of World Trade Center steel, the bronze-boot Veterans Memorial Walk, and summer Hoots baseball at CarShield Field.
### Q. What are some fun things for adults to do in O'Fallon, MO?
A.  Bring a cooler to a free Tuesday Jammin’ concert at Civic Park in summer, catch a $2 Tuesday Hoots game, or get a pint and wood-fired pizza at Interruption Public House on Sonderen Street. In October, book one of the city’s fall hayrides, with a bonfire after. Any Thursday through Sunday, an hour of axe throwing at 18 North Central runs $25 a player.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in O'Fallon this weekend?
A.  It depends on the season, so check the city’s parks and events calendar first. The 2026 calendar: the city’s fall hayrides Thursday through Sunday through October 25, the Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market on Saturday mornings through October 31, and the Celebration of Lights nightly from November 27 to December 30, with a few dates closed to cars.
### Q. Can you fish at Fort Zumwalt Park?
A.  Yes. Lake Whetsel, the 3.5-acre lake in the middle of the park, is open to anglers during park hours, dawn to dusk. You can keep four channel catfish a day, and all other fish are catch and release. It’s pole and line only with a two-pole limit, no boats or wading, and anglers 16 to 64 need a valid Missouri fishing permit.
### Q. Can you swim at Lake St. Louis?
A.  Only if you’re part of the Lake Saint Louis Community Association. The city describes both lakes as private, owned by association members, and the beaches at the Clubhouse, the Main Marina and Jefferson Point are association amenities. If you know a member, ask about guest rules. Otherwise, the Renaud Center’s heated indoor pool in O’Fallon sells day passes year-round.
### Q. What are some free family activities in St. Louis?
A.  Out in O’Fallon, many of the best ones cost nothing: fishing Lake Whetsel and playing the 18-hole disc golf course beside it, O’Day Park’s adventure playground and creek play area, the one-mile loops at Dames Park, and free Tuesday concerts at Civic Park in summer. City and county parks across the region fill in the rest.
### Q. What are some fun things to do at night in St. Louis?
A.  If you’ll drive about 30 minutes west, O’Fallon’s nights are underrated. Drive the Celebration of Lights from late November, catch a summer Hoots game under the lights at CarShield Field, play tactical laser tag or throw axes at 18 North Central, or catch a weekend band at Brewskeez Smokehouse & Music, which stays open until 1:30 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

## Things to Do in Ste. Genevieve, MO: What the Usual Lists Miss
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-ste-genevieve-mo
Three of five. That’s how many of the country’s known surviving poteaux-en-terre houses stand in Ste. Genevieve, according to the National Park Service. The name means posts in the ground: upright logs sunk straight into the dirt, the way French colonists built along the Mississippi in the late 1700s. Nobody put them behind glass. They sit on ordinary streets, a few minutes’ walk from wherever you park.
The usual top-10 list walks right past them. It tells you to tour the national park, taste some wine, maybe hike, and a lot of those lists still point you to wineries that have stopped pouring, like the saltpeter-cave tasting room at Cave Vineyard and the Chaumette estate, which closed in August 2025. Follow one and you’ll drive an hour to a tasting room that isn’t there.
Here’s the part St. Louis never hears about. In May 1780, when British-allied forces attacked the village of St. Louis, reinforcements from Ste. Genevieve helped bring its defenders to roughly 300 men. One of the young militia officers in that fight, François Vallé fils, built a house here in the 1790s. It’s open to visitors now, and the exhibit inside is called Saving St. Louis.
So this guide is for the St. Louisan who has done the Arch, done the usual weekend loop, and wants the Ste. Genevieve that locals use. Which houses earn a ticket. Which wineries are open this fall. Where to eat a liver dumpling, when the town throws its best parties, and how to cross the Mississippi for five bucks.
### What festivals are held in St. Genevieve, Missouri?
Ste. Genevieve’s calendar runs all year: the King’s Ball in February, the French Heritage Festival in June, Jour de Fête in August, the Fly with the Hive honey festival in September, Rural Heritage Day and a lantern cemetery tour in October, Pecanapalooza in November, the Holiday Christmas Festival in December, and La Guignolée on New Year’s Eve.
Here’s the full year in one place, with the dates as they usually fall. Most of these run downtown and cost nothing to walk into.
February: the King’s Ball (Bal du Roi), first full weekend, at the VFW Hall. Colonial dress, the old dances, and whoever finds the figure baked into the king cake reigns for the year. Ticketed.
April and October: the Milice Encampment, usually the second Saturday, when the LeMeilleur House grounds become a working 18th-century militia camp with gun building, spinning, and leatherwork. Free.
April through October: the 4th Friday Art Walk, 6 to 9 p.m., when the downtown galleries stay open late. The season’s last one is the fourth Friday of October (October 23 in 2026).
May: the Master Gardeners’ Garden Walk, the weekend after Mother’s Day, with a rare look behind the gates of historic gardens.
June: the French Heritage Festival, second Saturday, which ends with dancing in the lantern-lit gardens of the historic houses.
July: fireworks over Pere Marquette Park around the Fourth, then the Ste. Genevieve County Fair and its truck pull on the second full weekend.
August: Jour de Fête, the second full weekend, with more than 150 craft vendors filling the historic district. 2026 was its 58th year.
September: Fly with the Hive, a free honey festival on Merchant Street that held its second run on September 12, 2026.
October: Rural Heritage Day at the Felix Vallé House and the Déjà vu Spirit Reunion, a lantern-light cemetery tour, both on the fourth Saturday. In 2026 that’s October 24.
November: Pecanapalooza, a pecan street festival, and the Robin Hood-themed Sherwood Forest Festival on Merchant Street. The 2026 dates: November 7 and November 14.
December: the Holiday Christmas Festival on the first weekend, then La Guignolée on New Year’s Eve.
If you can only do one fall weekend, pick the one that pairs an Art Walk Friday with the Saturday heritage events. In 2026 that’s October 23 and 24. Walk the galleries Friday night, watch apple pressing and soap-making Saturday afternoon, then take the cemetery tour by lantern after dark. Dates drift a little year to year, so check the organizer’s page before you commit a Saturday.
### Which historic houses in Ste. Genevieve are worth touring?
Start at the Welcome Center, 66 S. Main St. It’s free, it’s where rangers hand out same-day tickets for the National Park Service houses, and it holds a 12-by-12-foot diorama of the whole town as it looked in 1832. The park tours cost nothing but cap at 15 people, first come, first served. On a fall Saturday, get your tickets before you get coffee.
Green Tree Tavern, 244 St. Marys Road, is the one to see if you only see one. Built in 1790, it’s the oldest building still standing in town, and over two centuries it has been a home, a tavern, an inn, a tobacco shop, and a Masonic lodge. It’s also one of the few places where you can plainly see the vertical logs that make up the walls. The park lists it as open daily for self-guided visits, with ranger programs on top.
The Bauvais-Amoureux House, built around 1792, is one of the three post-in-ground survivors, and it looks out over le Grand Champ, the Big Field whose rich bottomland drew French farmers here in the first place. Its story runs through Pelagie Amoureux, who inherited the house after her husband died. The Jean Baptiste Vallé House at 99 S. Main shows the other method, poteaux-sur-solle, where the logs stand on a sill instead of in the dirt. Keeping the wood out of wet ground is a big reason more of those houses lasted.
Then walk over to Market Street. The Centre for French Colonial Life, 198 Market St., sells tickets for guided tours of the Louis Bolduc House and the Bolduc-LeMeilleur House at 10:30 a.m., 1:30 p.m., and 3:30 p.m. (no 10:30 tour on Sundays). The Centre bills Bolduc as the only authentically period-furnished French colonial house open to tour in town, and it shows. The same desk sells tickets for the François Vallé fils House, the militia officer’s home, with guide-led visits at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and 12:30 and 2:30 on Sunday.
The Felix Vallé House State Historic Site at 198 Merchant St. is the after picture. Built in 1818 in the American Federal style and furnished the way it would have looked in the 1830s, it shows how fast French Ste. Genevieve changed after the Louisiana Purchase. Missouri State Parks runs tours at set times through the day. Reserve online or walk up.
Short on time? Do Green Tree Tavern for the logs and Bolduc for the furniture. Those two tell the story better than any five-stop checklist. On Saturdays from late March through the first weekend of November, the Linden House across Main from Bolduc adds living history demonstrations from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
### Which Ste. Genevieve wineries are still open?
The Route du Vin changed faster than the lists that describe it. Cave Vineyard’s Facebook page says its winery and cave are permanently closed. Chaumette Vineyards & Winery shut down on August 15, 2025, after 25 years; Life Teen International, a Catholic youth ministry, bought the property for a campground called Camp Cana. Crown Valley on Route WW is shut too, and online winery guides now list it as permanently closed. The little downtown Lewsi Winery closed back in 2022. If a guide still sends you to any of the four, close the tab.
Here’s what’s pouring as of fall 2026, going by the town’s tourism office and the wineries’ own pages:
Brix Urban Winery & Market, 245 Merchant St. Downtown, under a grape arbor. Mead flights, wine slushies, and craft beer, and the Star Lite River Restaurant kitchen inside opens at 6 a.m. with pastries and coffee. Closed Mondays.
Charleville Brewery & Winery, 16937 Boyd Road. High above the Saline Creek valley on the county’s west side. You tap a wristband at a 24-tap self-serve wall of beer, wine, and Charle-Ritas and pay for what you pour. There’s an 1860s log cabin you can rent for the night. Wednesday through Sunday.
Chateau Sainte Genevieve Winery, 8921 Jackson School Road, north of town. Family-run, with every wine made and bottled on-site next to its own vines. Its site lists daily hours of 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. and free tastings and tours.
Weingarten Vineyard, 12323 Rottler Road, west of downtown. Reopened under new owners with a full restaurant, Garten Haus. Late-week and weekend hours.
One more name you’ll see: Watertower Winery on Route M. These days it shows up mostly as a venue for concerts and private events, so call before you count it as a tasting stop. Seasonal hours shift everywhere on the trail. Brix and Weingarten make the easy pairing since both sit close to downtown. Charleville is a drive, and it’s also the one with the view, so save it for a clear day and bring a designated driver.
Skip the closed cave. Plan real pours with our winery day trip guide.
### What’s worth finding in the downtown Ste. Genevieve shops?
The downtown grid is small enough to cover on foot, and the best stops aren’t museums. At ASL Pewter Foundry, 183 S. Third St., Tom and Patricia Hooper have spent close to 40 years making pewter by hand, some of it cast in molds from the 1700s, and you can watch them work. Their pieces turned up in HBO’s John Adams miniseries. The studio lists daily hours, but it’s a two-person shop, so call if you’re making a special trip.
Rust Artisan Shop, 173 N. Main St., turns corrugated tin pulled off old Missouri barns into lamps and luminaries that throw patterned shadows across the ceiling. It’s open Friday through Sunday. On the fourth Friday of each month from April through October, the galleries stay open from 6 to 9 p.m. for the Art Walk, and some pour drinks and put out food while you browse. It’s the closest thing this town has to a date night block.
Two more details most visitors miss. The Old Brick House at 90 S. Third St. is generally cited as the oldest brick building west of the Mississippi, put up around 1780 (some sources say as late as 1785), and it was a courthouse, a school, and a fur trading post before it became a restaurant in 1940. And at the corner of Merchant and Main, the Civil War living history day in late August has staged Federal troops taking money from the town bank, an early-war episode that really happened here, with a camp set up in the Felix Vallé House yard.
### Where can you get liver dumplings in Ste. Genevieve?
Start with the dish nobody in St. Louis has heard of. Liver dumplings came over with German immigrants: minced liver worked into dumpling dough and simmered in broth. They’re on menus all over town, and the tourism office’s app even maps out a liver dumpling tour. Order them once. You’ll either get it or you won’t.
The Old Brick House runs a buffet with fried chicken and liver dumplings Thursday through Monday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Its owners also run the Anvil Saloon & Restaurant at 46 S. Third St., which serves liver dumplings too and has sold them cooked or raw to take home. Between the two, you can eat lunch in a building older than the Constitution and dinner a short walk away.
Audubon’s, at 9 N. Main St., fills the old Palace Bar building with a menu that runs German, Cajun, French, and Italian to match the town’s mix; the pork schnitzel is the dish people talk about. Mornings take more planning, because the coffee spots keep short hours. Common Grounds, 10 S. Third St., is a coffee house that employs people with special needs, serving coffee, quiche, wraps, and pastries on weekdays and Saturdays. Birdies Coffee + Bakery on North Main keeps weekend-morning hours, Friday through Sunday the last time we checked, and the homemade oatmeal cream pie is the order. Up at dawn? The kitchen at Brix starts at 6 a.m. Our full rundown of where to eat in Ste. Genevieve covers the rest of the downtown tables.
### What’s on in Ste. Genevieve for Halloween, Christmas, and New Year’s Eve?
Late October is the sleeper. On the fourth Saturday of the month, the Foundation for Restoration of Ste. Genevieve holds the Déjà vu Spirit Reunion in Memorial Cemetery, which it bills as Missouri’s oldest cemetery. You walk the graves by lantern light while costumed “spirits” tell you who they were. Recent tickets ran $5 to $10. That same Saturday, Rural Heritage Day at the Felix Vallé House shows apple pressing, spinning, lace-making, and soap-making; the state parks calendar lists it for October 24, 2026. Call it Halloween for grown-ups who’d rather hear a good story than stand in line for a haunted house.
The Holiday Christmas Festival takes over the first weekend of December, and the 2025 edition was the 41st. AAA magazine has ranked it among the top two Christmas celebrations in the Midwest. Expect a parade, music from Renaissance sacred pieces to jazz inside the old churches, Santa photos, and craft workshops. Nearly all of it is free. It pairs well with the city lineup in our guide to Christmas events in St. Louis.
New Year’s Eve is the night you can’t get anywhere else around here. La Guignolée is a French begging-song tradition still practiced in only two U.S. towns. In Ste. Genevieve, singers in old-fashioned, sometimes masked costumes traditionally set out from the American Legion Hall, work their way through restaurants, bars, and nursing homes asking for food and drink in song, and finish at midnight at the Knights of Columbus Hall. The lyrics jokingly demand the household’s oldest daughter. Nobody hands her over.
### What can you do in Ste. Genevieve for free, or close to it?
A lot, because the biggest attraction in town doesn’t charge admission. The national historical park is fee-free, so the ranger-led tours of Green Tree Tavern, the Jean Baptiste Vallé House, and the Bauvais-Amoureux House cost nothing; you only need a same-day ticket from the Welcome Center. The 1832 diorama there is free too. So is watching the Hoopers work pewter, the Art Walk, the Milice Encampment, most of the Christmas festival, and the Fourth of July fireworks. Chateau Sainte Genevieve lists free tastings.
Then spend five dollars on the best view of the trip. The river ferry, which locals call the French Connection, has crossing records going back to at least 1798, carried whole rail cars on cradles starting in 1904, and has run as a modern passenger ferry since 1997. Walk on at the Missouri landing, 8205 Little Rock Road, for $5 each way and you’re on the Illinois bank 10 to 15 minutes later. Cars pay $20 one way and $10 for a same-day return; bikes and horses pay $5. It’s one of only a handful of car ferries left on the river near St. Louis; our guide to ferries near St. Louis has the rest, all the way down to the Dorena-Hickman Ferry.
The summer schedule is Wednesday through Saturday, 6 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Sundays from 9 a.m.; it’s closed Monday and Tuesday, and in winter it drops to Friday through Sunday. Be at the landing 30 minutes before closing for the last run. River levels can shut it down, so call the Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 the morning you go. Cyclists know it as the official Great River Road crossing, and it’s the only way over the river along a roughly 60-mile stretch.
### Where else should you stop on the drive back?
The drive home runs up I-55 through a string of Jefferson County towns. Our Arnold guide covers the stretch closest to the city, and the full guide to things to do in St. Louis, town by town, maps the rest. Stacking trips? Our list of day trips from St. Louis has more within two hours.
Next time somebody at work says they did Ste. Genevieve, ask whether they saw logs standing in the dirt, ate a liver dumpling, or rode the ferry just for the view. You’ll be the one who knows the cave tasting room is gone, the Bolduc tour leaves at 1:30, and the best night of the year is December 31. Pick a Saturday. Check the calendar. Go.
Heading south? Use the St Louis Near Me Directory guide to where to eat in Ste. Genevieve to line up lunch between house tours before you leave the city.
If you run a winery, an inn, or a shop on Main Street, the day-trippers driving down I-55 are already asking Google and ChatGPT where to stop, so list your business where they’re looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Ste Genevieve, Missouri known for?
A.  It’s known as Missouri’s oldest town, established by 1750 according to the National Park Service, and for the vertical-log French Creole houses that survived here after they vanished almost everywhere else. Three of the five known post-in-ground houses left in the country stand in town. Locals would add liver dumplings and La Guignolée, the costumed New Year’s Eve singing tradition.
### Q. Where to eat in St. Genevieve, MO?
A.  For the local dish, the Old Brick House at 90 S. Third St. serves a fried chicken buffet with liver dumplings Thursday through Monday, and the Anvil Saloon & Restaurant at 46 S. Third St. serves them too. Audubon’s on North Main handles dinner with schnitzel and Cajun plates. For breakfast, try Common Grounds, Birdies on weekend mornings, or the early kitchen at Brix. Hours change, so call ahead.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Sainte Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Ride the car ferry across the Mississippi just for the view, watch Tom and Patricia Hooper make pewter at ASL Pewter, pour your own tastes from the wristband tap wall at Charleville, and step inside Green Tree Tavern, where the 1790 vertical logs are still visible. In late October, take the lantern-light cemetery tour. On New Year’s Eve, follow the La Guignolée singers from bar to bar.
### Q. What is there to do in Ste Genevieve?
A.  More than a day’s worth, and most of it is walkable from the Welcome Center at 66 S. Main St. Pick up free same-day tickets for the National Park Service houses there, add a guided tour at the Bolduc House or the Felix Vallé House, eat lunch downtown, then choose an afternoon: a winery or two, the river ferry, or the trails at Hawn State Park out in the county.
### Q. How many wineries are in Sainte Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Fewer than older lists claim. As of fall 2026, four are pouring in town or a short drive out: Brix Urban Winery & Market downtown, Charleville Brewery & Winery, Chateau Sainte Genevieve Winery, and Weingarten Vineyard. The tourism office’s Route du Vin list adds a couple of stops farther out. Cave Vineyard, Chaumette, Crown Valley, and Lewsi have all closed.
### Q. Is there a ferry in St. Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Ste. Genevieve ferry, locally called the French Connection, carries cars, bikes, horses, and walk-on passengers across the Mississippi to Illinois from a landing at 8205 Little Rock Road. The crossing takes 10 to 15 minutes, and a standard vehicle pays $20 one way. It doesn’t run Mondays or Tuesdays, and river conditions can close it, so call the Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 first.
### Q. How far is Ste Genevieve from St. Louis?
A.  About 60 to 65 miles south of downtown St. Louis, roughly an hour down I-55 without traffic. That’s an easy day trip. Still, the Friday night Art Walk, the evening lantern tour in October, and the La Guignolée route on New Year’s Eve all make a strong case for booking a room and staying the night.
### Q. What is the oldest town in MO?
A.  Ste. Genevieve. The National Park Service calls it the first permanent European settlement in Missouri, established by 1750. The original village sat on the river bottom about three miles from today’s downtown; after the flood of 1785, residents moved to the higher ground where the historic district stands now. Its oldest standing building, Green Tree Tavern, dates to 1790.

## Buffalo Bill Married Here: Things to Do in Arnold, MO
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-arnold-mo
Buffalo Bill got married in Arnold.
Not in a church out West. On a farm along the road that became Jeffco Boulevard, in the house of a girl named Louisa Frederici. Today that stretch is storefronts and traffic lights, and almost nobody driving past knows it.
Then there’s a street across town you can actually walk. At the end of Hollywood Beach Road the asphalt keeps going, curb and all, and there are no houses. Leaves pile against the old curbs. Trees stand where front porches were. The only sound is your kids’ sneakers and, somewhere close behind the woods, the Meramec. After the 1993 flood, with federal help, Arnold bought out some 500 homes and turned the low-lying land into parks. “Hollywood Beach and Bradley Beach Roads are now walking trails,” as one local report put it. A whole neighborhood, handed back to the river and the birds.
Back to the wedding, since your kids will ask. On March 6, 1866, a 20-year-old Civil War veteran named William F. Cody married Louisa at her parents’ home, the farmhouse where she was born in 1844, near what is now Jeffco Boulevard and Church Road. The city’s own history says that house is known today as “The Old Rock House.” In 1867 he started hunting buffalo to feed workers for the Kansas Pacific Railroad, and that’s where the nickname came from.
A few minutes south, the creek bank tells an even stranger story. In 1839, a St. Louis museum owner named Albert Koch dug bones out of the banks of Rock Creek, decided he had found a brand-new animal, named it the Missouri Leviathan and toured it through the United States and Europe. An anatomist at the British Museum in London finally convinced him it was an American mastodon. Then, in 1979, a dig on the same bone bed turned up a stone Clovis spear point lying with mastodon bones, the first site in eastern North America where people and mastodons were conclusively shown to have been there together. When the interstate was being built in the 1970s and the site looked doomed, local school children were part of the push that helped the state buy the land in 1976. Kids helped save it. That’s the line to repeat in the back seat.
String it into one Saturday from May through October. Start at the Arnold Farmers Market in Arnold City Park, coffee in hand, then walk the old streets while the kids still have legs. Drive south to Mastodon State Historic Site; from March 16 through November 15 the museum is closed Monday and Tuesday, it costs $4 for ages 13 and up and nothing for 12 and under, and the site office answers at 636-464-2976. Swing back for the Arnold Historical Society Museum, open Saturdays from noon to 4 with a $5 donation requested. Its 1906 Victrola still plays records through its horn, a thin, scratchy sound from before your great-grandparents, and the volunteers know the Buffalo Bill story better than anyone.
### What are some fun activities to do in Arnold, Missouri?
For a family, the best things to do in Arnold are to stand where a Clovis spear point turned up among mastodon bones at Mastodon State Historic Site, a few minutes south (kids 12 and under get into the museum free), walk the old flood-buyout streets of Hollywood Beach and Bradley Beach roads at Arnold City Park, fish its 8-acre lake from the bank, and launch onto the Meramec at Flamm City Park.
Most of that costs nothing but gas. The mastodon museum charges $4 for ages 13 and up, and kids 12 and under get in free.
### What to do at Mastodon State Park?
Walk into the museum and look up. The impressive mastodon skeleton replica is what most kids remember, and Missouri State Parks calls it “a sight that is not easily forgotten.” Around it are cases of fossils and artifacts and a 15-minute film that usually plays every hour. The site’s formal name is Mastodon State Historic Site, and it protects the Kimmswick Bone Bed, where bones of mastodons and other extinct animals were first reported in the early 1800s.
Then walk the Wildflower Trail, which starts near the museum and runs about half a mile to the spot where the bones and the spear point were found. There are no excavations now, and the bone bed is safely buried. You’re standing on the place where Ice Age hunters met a mastodon, and for a kid holding your hand, that’s enough. The site has three trails in all, plus picnic sites, a shelter, a playground and a wildflower garden that pulls in birds and butterflies.
Timing trips people up. The grounds are open 8 a.m. to a half hour after sunset, every day. The museum keeps shorter hours: from March 16 through November 15 it’s closed Monday and Tuesday and open 9 to 4:30 Wednesday through Saturday and noon to 4:30 on Sunday. From November 16 through March 15 it opens only Thursday through Saturday, 11 to 4. Show up on the wrong day and you’ll get the trails without the skeleton.
### Where can you fish in Arnold, MO?
A folding chair, a bucket and a bobber riding on flat water: that’s the easy version. Arnold City Park, at #1 Bradley Beach Road off Jeffco Boulevard, is a 68-acre park wrapped around an 8-acre fishing lake, with four pavilions, a playground, restrooms and a paved half-mile trail. Plan to stay on the bank: city rules ban swimming, wading and boating in all park waterways.
The bigger water is the Meramec. Flamm City Park, at Telegraph Road and the river, is 36 acres of public land with a paved lot that has room for boat trailers and a ramp into the river. Right next to it, Teszars Woods Conservation Area is 90 acres of forest and wetland, and the city lists channel catfish, flatheads, carp, paddlefish, drum and white bass in its water. A paddlefish, with that long flat bill, is the kind of thing a kid talks about at school for a week.
On permits: Missouri sells a daily fishing permit to residents and nonresidents, and you can buy it for more than one day. Missouri residents 65 and older are exempt from needing a fishing permit, and on Free Fishing Days anyone can fish without one. For more water around the metro, see our guide to the best free public fishing spots in St. Louis.
Got the kids in the car and the whole afternoon free? Try scenic drives around St. Louis.
### Are there hiking trails in Arnold Park?
Yes, two kinds, and you’ll feel the difference underfoot. The paved half-mile trail is the easy one, smooth enough for strollers and small legs. The better walk is on Hollywood Beach and Bradley Beach roads, now walking trails where homes and clubhouses once were. Our story of the Great Flood of 1993 covers what that summer did across the region. Down at Teszars Woods, the Teszar Woods Trail runs a moderate quarter mile and the Meramec River Trail an easy 0.60 mile.
For the quiet one, drive to Strawberry Creek Nature Area: 118 acres on Upper Tenbrook Road, about half a mile past Highway 231, with a pond, four walking trails and Strawberry Creek winding through the whole property. There’s no electricity or running water, only a portable restroom and a pavilion near the entrance, so pack snacks and water.
Dog families get their own loop. Arnold’s two Paw Parks are fully fenced, split into areas for dogs 25 pounds and under and over 25 pounds, run on donations and free to all. The Ozark Drive Paw Park, at 1839 Ozark Drive, connects to Ferd B. Lang Park by a half-mile walking trail and a bridge. City parks open a half hour before sunrise and close a half hour after sunset.
### Indoor stops for a cold or rainy day
The Arnold Historical Society Museum at 1723 Jeffco Boulevard is small, volunteer-run and wheelchair friendly, and it’s better than its size. There’s an 1873 Bible carried across the Atlantic by a German settler named Max Stengele, a cast iron sewing machine from the 1890s in its original wooden case, and that 1906 Victrola still playing records through its listening horn. Ask about the town’s start, too: Arnold traces itself to a 1776 trading post between St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve, though it wasn’t incorporated as a city until 1972.
The mastodon museum is indoors as well, so a wet Saturday can still be a full one. One warning before you promise anyone a swim: the city says the Arnold Recreation Center’s indoor pool closed for renovations beginning August 31. Call the rec center at 636-282-2380 before you pack towels.
### What’s free in Arnold for families?
More than you’d guess. The Paw Parks are free to all. Jim Edwards Archery Park, at 1136 Telegraph Road, is ADA accessible with year-round targets for bows only, open regular park hours but closed Tuesday from sunrise to noon for maintenance. The Arnold Jaycees Skate Park is for inline skates, roller skates and skateboards.
The Arnold Farmers Market runs Saturday mornings from the first Saturday in May through the last Saturday in October, skipping the Saturday of Arnold Days in September. The city says 80 vendors bring veggies, meats, honey, eggs and baked goods, plus coffee and breakfast. Walking it costs nothing. The smell of coffee and warm bread does most of the selling.
When the lights come out in December, Arnold’s parks still close a half hour after sunset, so check the city’s events calendar for anything special in the park.
Hungry after the bone bed and the lake loop? Check where to eat in Arnold, MO before the kids start asking from the back seat.
If you run a bait shop, a café or a kids’ party spot in Arnold, list your business with us so the families driving down for the mastodon become your customers.
### What’s near Arnold for a longer day?
Arnold works as a base. Head northwest and you’re in Fenton, where our guide to things to do in Fenton picks up the thread. Go south past Imperial and Kimmswick and you’ll eventually reach Ste. Genevieve, the old French town at the far end of the same road Arnold’s trading post served, covered in our Ste. Genevieve guide. Next door in Imperial, the Limestone Hill Trail at Mastodon State Historic Site climbs above the same Ice Age bone bed. For every other town on the map, start with our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
Next time someone says there’s nothing to do south of the Meramec, you’ll be the one who knows where Buffalo Bill said “I do,” and which streets the river took back.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some fun activities for kids in Arnold, MO?
A.  Fish the 8-acre lake at Arnold City Park from the bank, walk the old flood-buyout streets, and save a day for Mastodon State Historic Site a few minutes south, where kids 12 and under get into the museum free and the Wildflower Trail leads to the spot where the bones and spear point were found. Add the 1906 Victrola at the Arnold Historical Society Museum on a Saturday.
### Q. What are the current hours of operation for the Mastodon State Historic Site?
A.  The grounds are open daily from 8 a.m. to a half hour after sunset. From March 16 through November 15 the museum is closed Monday and Tuesday, open 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday and noon to 4:30 on Sunday. From November 16 through March 15 it opens Thursday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 636-464-2976 to check the film.
### Q. Can I get a one-day fishing license in Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Missouri Department of Conservation sells a Daily Fishing Permit to residents and nonresidents, and it can be bought for multiple days if you’re in town for a long weekend. Missouri residents 65 and older don’t need a fishing permit, and on MDC’s Free Fishing Days anyone can fish without one. Check MDC’s permit page for current prices.
### Q. Where is Arnold City Park?
A.  Arnold City Park is off Jeffco Boulevard at #1 Bradley Beach Road. It’s a 68-acre park with an 8-acre fishing lake, four pavilions with electricity and BBQ pits, a playground, restrooms and a paved half-mile walking trail. Like all city parks, it opens a half hour before sunrise and closes a half hour after sunset.
### Q. How do I get to the creek at Mastodon State Park?
A.  The creek is Rock Creek, the same creek whose banks gave up the first mastodon bones in the 1800s. The site’s creek programs meet at the picnic shelter off Seckman Road before heading to Rock Creek, so that shelter is your landmark. Ask the site office at 636-464-2976 which trail gets you closest that day.
### Q. Are there any American mastodon skeletons on display?
A.  Yes. The museum at Mastodon State Historic Site displays an impressive mastodon skeleton replica, alongside fossils, artifacts and a 15-minute film about the Kimmswick Bone Bed. It’s a replica, not the original bones, and Missouri State Parks calls it “a sight that is not easily forgotten.” Check museum days before you drive, since it closes on Mondays and Tuesdays in season.
### Q. Is Kimmswick worth visiting?
A.  For a family already in Arnold, yes. It’s the small river town that gave its name to the Kimmswick Bone Bed, where mastodon bones were first reported in the early 1800s, and it pairs easily with the Mastodon museum. Our full guide to things to do in Kimmswick covers its shops, festivals and the quieter weekends.
### Q. What is the current Meramec River level at Arnold, MO?
A.  It changes daily, so read it live on the Meramec River at Arnold gauge page on NOAA’s water site. Check it the morning you go, and if the river is up or rising after rain, keep the kids on the lake bank instead of the Meramec shore.

## Things to Do in Clayton, MO: Free Art, Bell Concerts and Quiet Parks
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-clayton-mo
What do you picture when someone says Clayton? Glass office towers. The county courthouse. A parking meter ticking down while you sit through jury duty. That’s the Clayton the recycled top-10 lists keep selling, and most of them run out of ideas somewhere around the steakhouses.
Try a harder question. Why is the courthouse in Clayton at all? Because two farmers gave away land for it in the 1870s, and one of their farmhouses is still standing on a quiet residential street. Where’s the free museum on Clayton’s doorstep with a Henry Moore and a Keith Haring on view this fall? Which Clayton tower holds 49 bells, and on what night of the week do they play for anyone who shows up with a blanket? And what happened to the Saturday farmers market the internet still lists?
If you can’t answer those, that’s not on you. The lists never asked. Start with the market, because it shows how stale the usual advice has gotten.
### Does Clayton have a farmers market?
Not one we could confirm for 2026. The downtown Clayton market that used to run Saturday mornings on Forsyth Boulevard is missing from this year’s area market guides and the city’s event calendar. The closest weekly markets are The Boulevard in Richmond Heights on Sundays and the U City Farmers Market in Heman Park on Saturdays.
That surprises people, because a few market directories online still list a Saturday Clayton market, and one even shows 2026 dates. We couldn’t find a single current source to back that up, and St. Louis Magazine’s 2026 farmers market guide doesn’t include Clayton at all. If you remember buying tomatoes on Forsyth on a Saturday morning, you’re not imagining it. It just isn’t running now, as far as anyone can confirm.
The replacements are close. The Boulevard market sets up Sunday mornings from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. through late October, a few minutes south of downtown Clayton. The U City Farmers Market runs Saturday mornings from 8:30 to 12:30 in Heman Park at 7210 Olive, and its season stretches into late November. Dates shift every year, so check both before you go. Once you’re there, our guide to buying fresh produce in St. Louis covers whether market produce really costs more and whether haggling is ever okay.
### What are the best free things to do in Clayton?
Start with the art, because there’s more of it than the business district lets on. The St. Louis Artists’ Guild, around since 1886, runs free galleries behind green doors at the corner of Forsyth and Jackson. They’re open Tuesday through Friday from 10 to 6 and Saturday from 10 to 4. Park in the two-hour retail spots, not the visitor spaces. The Guild spent 20 years inside Oak Knoll Park before moving downtown in 2015.
Then cross to the Wash U edge of town for the Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, on the east end of the Danforth Campus near Skinker and Lindell, directly west of Forest Park. Admission is free. It’s open 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day but Tuesday, and it’s a short walk from the Skinker MetroLink stop. Founded in 1881, the Kemper is one of the oldest teaching museums in the country, and its two big fall 2026 shows, one on Argentine modern art from 1935 to 1950 and one from the artist Carolina Caycedo, are set to stay up through January 4, 2027. The coffee bar sells Sugarwitch ice cream sandwiches. On a warm afternoon that alone justifies the trip.
The rest of the free list is outdoors, and it runs on the calendar. Clayton’s Musical Nights concerts at Oak Knoll Park happen one Sunday evening a month from late June through September, 5 to 7 p.m., no ticket. Concordia Seminary’s carillon concerts are free too, at 7 p.m. every Tuesday in June. And here’s the detail that changes the math on any evening out: street parking across Clayton is free after 5 p.m. on weekdays, all day on weekends, and on city holidays. The meters are for the lunch crowd.
### What are the best parks in Clayton, MO?
Clayton has a dozen city parks, and the biggest one gets nearly all the attention. For a slow hour, Oak Knoll Park is the better pick. It covers 14.5 acres at the northwest corner of Clayton Road and Big Bend Boulevard, became a park in 1958, and takes its name from a native stand of post oaks the city puts at about 150 years old. A half-mile path loops past a rain garden, a sunken garden and the Uchitelle Garden of Reflection, then drops you at a pond with a lighted fountain. Look for the turtles. They sun themselves on an old stump in the water. There’s a large playground by the picnic tables, two early-1900s stone mansions still standing on the grounds, and the park is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
Bring binoculars in spring. Clayton was named a Bird City Missouri community in 2026, only the second city in the state to earn it, and Oak Knoll is where its World Migratory Bird Day event was held this spring.
Want something smaller? Wydown Park is a half-acre square at 7619 Wydown Boulevard, just east of Hanley Road, with cafe tables, vine-covered pergolas, a Little Library and a stone sculpture called “Youth” by Todd Frahm. Get a coffee nearby and sit. Remembrance Park, the city’s smallest, is a pocket park the city pitches for a workday break or a game of chess. And if you’d rather cover miles than minutes, the Centennial Greenway starts at a trailhead in Shaw Park and runs about two and a half paved miles north toward Olive Boulevard, tying Clayton to University City and Ladue.
Tired of the usual list? See offbeat St. Louis for grown-ups.
### What are some unique things to do in Clayton, MO?
The strangest good answer is a seminary. It holds a lot more than most people expect from a campus they’ve only ever driven past. Concordia Seminary has sat on 72 acres in Clayton since 1926, and when it was dedicated it was the largest Protestant seminary in the United States. The stone quad looks like it was lifted from an old East Coast college, and the seminary openly invites visitors to stroll the grounds.
Look up first. Luther Tower rises 156 feet over the east side of the main quad. It was drawn into the original 1922 plans, but it wasn’t finished until the funding came through in 1966, 44 years later. At the top hangs a 49-bell carillon. The biggest bell weighs two and a half tons; the smallest weighs 17 pounds. The seminary’s dean of chapel calls it one of only 175 such instruments in North America. It chimes on weekdays before chapel, and every Tuesday in June at 7 p.m. a visiting carillonneur plays a free concert while people spread blankets on the quad or near the Luther statue with a picnic. If it rains, the crowd shelters under the tower and its covered passages.
Then walk the rest. The bronze Luther statue stands more than nine feet tall on a granite base taller than that. It’s a replica of the famous one in Germany and has been on this campus since 1926. Beside the library sits a log cabin, a 1938 replica of the 1839 cabin school the seminary grew out of. Inside that library, among more than 6,000 rare items, is Johann Sebastian Bach’s personal Bible. It’s part of the rare book collection, not a lobby display, so ask the library before you plan around it. Still. Bach’s own Bible is sitting in a library in Clayton.
Mark one more date. The seminary’s 2026 Advent Lessons and Carols was set for Tuesday, December 1, at 7 p.m., and its fall 2026 music series also lists a choral evening prayer for All Saints’ Day on Sunday, November 1, at 4 p.m., plus a recital dedicating the seminary’s new Steinway on November 15. All of it is free.
### Where should you go for a date night in Clayton?
Skip the downtown dinner rush and go to DeMun. It’s a short, leafy stretch of DeMun Avenue near the seminary, and it’s where the regional coffee chain Kaldi’s got its start: the original coffeehouse opened there in 1994 and still overlooks little Concordia Park. For dinner, Louie at 706 DeMun takes reservations online or by phone, and its patio tables go first come, first served when the weather cooperates.
The other block worth knowing is where Wydown Boulevard meets Hanley Road. Pick up something warm to drink, carry it to the cafe tables in Wydown Park, and you’ve got a better first hour than most rooftop bars can sell you. That’s also the start of a good slow Saturday: coffee on DeMun, a lap around the seminary quad, the Artists’ Guild galleries before they close at 4, then an early dinner back on DeMun or Wydown. Total weekend parking cost? Nothing.
Summer evenings are where the free parking really pays off. Pack a picnic for Musical Nights at Oak Knoll or a June Tuesday under the carillon, then head to dinner after. Downtown, the city throws two free street parties on North Brentwood Boulevard: the Music & Wine Festival in early June and the Clayton Jazz Festival in early October, both from 5 to 10 p.m. This year’s jazz night, the sixth, was October 3. Put next fall’s on the calendar now.
### Why is Clayton the county seat?
Because of a land gift you can still go look at. When St. Louis County split from the city in 1876, the new county needed a seat. Farmer Ralph Clayton donated 100 acres, and his neighbor Martin Franklin Hanley gave four more. The downtown you know grew out of that donated farmland.
Hanley’s 1855 brick farmhouse still stands at 7600 Westmoreland Avenue, the oldest surviving home in Clayton and a National Register property. The city bought it in 1968 and opened it as a museum in 1971. It closed in 2020, went through masonry and waterproofing repairs, and held a ceremonial reopening in May 2026, with public tours expected to resume next year. Until then it’s a walk-by, so check with the city before you plan on going inside. When it does open, look for the original furnishings and the family letters still tucked in a desk. Out back stands something rarer: a detached brick kitchen and the preserved quarters of the three people the Hanleys enslaved, including a woman named Lydia Jackson. It’s an honest piece of county history on a street most people never turn onto.
### What are the best seasonal events in Clayton?
Work backward from the calendar and Clayton gets a lot more interesting than its office hours suggest.
Fall. Party in the Patch, a family Halloween night with a candy hunt, hayrides and inflatables, is held in Shaw Park, hosted by the Clayton and Brentwood parks departments. In 2026 it was set for Friday, October 16, from 6 to 8 p.m. Kids register ahead for the hot dog dinner. The Kemper’s fall 2026 shows are set to stay up into January 2027. Reading this after Halloween? Check with the Clayton parks department for next year’s Party in the Patch date.
Winter. Advent Lessons and Carols at Concordia Seminary (December 1 in 2026) is the quiet, free alternative to a packed light show, and it’s indoors.
Spring. Migration. Oak Knoll’s pond and old oaks are the place to look, and the city has made a point of planting native habitat for birds.
Summer. The busy stretch. Music & Wine on North Brentwood in early June, carillon concerts every Tuesday in June, and Musical Nights at Oak Knoll from late June through September.
September. The Saint Louis Art Fair filled downtown for its 33rd year on September 18 to 20, 2026, with 233 artists. Admission is free. Friday runs 5 to 10 p.m., which makes it an easy after-work stop.
### What’s near Clayton for a longer day out?
Clayton makes a good base. The Kemper puts you on the edge of Wash U’s campus for a longer walk, U City’s Saturday market in Heman Park is about ten minutes north, and The Boulevard’s Sunday market is just south in Richmond Heights. For the shops, services and businesses in between, our Clayton city guide lists what’s open in town. Heading west on I-64? Our Chesterfield guide covers the next town out. For every town we’ve written up, start with our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis, by town.
Next time somebody tells you Clayton is offices and a courthouse, you’ll know which night the bells play. Pick one date from this page and go.
Planning a Clayton afternoon? Settle dinner first with the where to eat in Clayton guide on St Louis Near Me Directory, then park once and walk.
