### Where can you see Christmas lights in O’Fallon, IL?
Downtown, on parade night. The O’Fallon Illuminated Holiday Parade steps off at 6 p.m. on Saturday, November 28, 2026, according to the parade’s official site. The 2026 theme turns it into a Where’s Waldo for Santas: businesses, schools, dance troupes and families build the most obviously fake Santa entries they can, and the real one waits at the very end of the route. Every unit has to be at least half lights. Weather pushed the 2025 parade up a day, and one events listing gave Sunday, November 29, as the 2026 date, so check the parade site that week. Reading this after November 28? Check the same site for the next parade.
When the last Santa passes, everybody walks to Community Park for a free Santa party and the community tree lighting, where the crowd sings Santa into town to light the City Tree. Floats line up on State Street, which leaves more room to park and walk. Come early. That Saturday is also Small Business Saturday in the Downtown District.
In December 2026, the calendar fills in around it. Santa at the Station is free on Tuesday, December 8, and Thursday, December 10, from 6 to 7:30 p.m. at O’Fallon Station. An Evening with Santa, with photos and holiday activities, is Saturday, December 5, from 4 to 7 p.m., at $20 per child with pre-registration. Home for the Holidays takes over downtown on Saturday, December 12.
For lit-up houses, the city runs a Light Up O’Fallon contest, with 2026 judging December 14 through 17. It’s a residents’ contest with no public route, so watch the city’s pages for the winners. We don’t publish home addresses.
One mix-up to clear up. If you searched for drive-through lights at Rock Springs Park, you were probably thinking of Christmas Wonderland, and that’s Rock Spring Park in Alton, a different park in a different county. Our page on drive-through Christmas lights in Alton has the hours and the cash-only donation. It opens the day after Thanksgiving. In 2026 that’s Friday, November 27, the night before O’Fallon’s parade, which makes for a pretty good two-night weekend.
### What can you do in O’Fallon, IL on a rainy day?
Go look at cars. Gateway Classic Cars’ showroom is climate-controlled, has a gift shop on top of the 200-plus cars, and opens Monday through Saturday from 9 to 5. A wet Saturday also lines up with the museum’s 1 to 4 p.m. hours, a short drive away.
The O’Fallon Public Library, 120 Civic Plaza, is the all-day option, with 3D printing, a makerspace and study rooms. It’s open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 9 to 5 Friday, 9 to 4 Saturday and 1 to 5 Sunday. Dogwood Social House opens at 3 p.m. on weekdays and 11 a.m. on weekends, and on Tuesdays and Sundays its family night deal has been $25.99 for a large pizza, wings, soft drinks and two one-hour game cards. Prices move, so check.
Parents of little ones, this one’s for you. Indoor Playdate opens the gym at the Katy Cavins Community Center, 308 E. Fifth St., on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to noon, November 4, 2026, through March 10, 2027. It’s $2 at the door for ages 5 and under, with toys and books provided and no registration. It’s closed November 11 and 25, December 23 and 30, and February 24.
Next time somebody tells you O’Fallon is ballfields and an exit ramp, you’ll be the one who knows about the bank on State Street, the trumpet player who lost three fingers and painted presidents, the six planes outside the gate and the parade where only the last Santa is real. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do you find free local events?
A.  Go to the source, because the big event sites lag. In O’Fallon that means the Parks and Recreation department’s seasonal brochure, which is where free dates like Family Fishing Night, the Fantastic Fall Festival and Santa at the Station show up first, plus the city’s online calendar and the Downtown District’s events page for the market, the pub crawl and Small Business Saturday. The Historical Society posts museum news on its own site.
### Q. Where can I fish in Illinois without a fishing license?
A.  Anywhere in the state during Illinois Free Fishing Days, a four-day weekend every June. In 2026 it ran June 19 to 22. Anglers under 16 never need a license. An Illinois resident on active duty who entered the service from Illinois can fish without one while on leave, which matters around Scott. Everyone else 16 and up needs one, and a 24-hour resident license is $5.50. Check IDNR for current rules.
### Q. Can I leave my dog at the dog park?
A.  Not at O’Fallon’s. The rules at the Rock Springs Rotary Park dog park say dogs must stay under their handler’s control and in view at all times, and handlers are responsible for any injuries their dogs cause. There’s a two-dog limit per handler, kids must be at least 10, and the park closes Fridays from 8 a.m. to noon for mowing.
### Q. Can civilians enter Scott Air Force Base?
A.  Only with a sponsor and a visitor pass. Since February 28, 2026, when the base suspended its Trusted Traveler program, the sponsor starts the process with the Dixon Visitor Center, open daily from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., and for an in-person pass both people must be there. Bring REAL ID-compliant identification, plus vehicle registration to drive on. The Scott Field Heritage Air Park on Seibert Road needs none of that.
### Q. What towns are near Scott Air Force Base?
A.  O’Fallon sits just to the north and grew up alongside it. Mascoutah is on the east side, Lebanon to the northeast and Belleville to the west, with Swansea and Fairview Heights a little farther out on the west side. From O’Fallon, I-64 exit 19A and Route 158 lead to the base, and downtown St. Louis is about 18 miles west.
### Q. Where is the best place to drive through Christmas lights in Illinois?
A.  Close to O’Fallon, it’s Christmas Wonderland at Rock Spring Park in Alton: more than 4 million lights, built by volunteers and opening the day after Thanksgiving, which is Friday, November 27, in 2026. Entry is a suggested cash donation per car. O’Fallon’s own big lights night is the Illuminated Holiday Parade, which you watch on foot. In 2026 it’s the next evening, Saturday, November 28.
### Q. Is it illegal to use Bluegill as bait in Illinois?
A.  No. IDNR says legally caught bluegill or other sunfish can be used as bait, but only in the same body of water they came from. They have to be taken by a licensed angler with legal gear, size and creel limits apply where you caught them and where you use them, and you can’t have cut-up fish on water with a size or bag limit for that species.
### Q. Is the Rock Springs Park with Christmas Wonderland in O’Fallon, IL?
A.  No. Christmas Wonderland is at Rock Spring Park, singular, in Alton. O’Fallon’s park is Rock Springs Rotary Park, with an s, at 1428 E. 3rd St., home of the dog park, the fire pit and the Fantastic Fall Festival. Search engines mix them up all the time. O’Fallon’s December lights are downtown, at the parade and the tree lighting in Community Park.

## St. Louis Bans the Sign. Google Hides the Address.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-st-louis-businesses-get-found-without-a-storefront
No sign by the door. For a business run out of a home in the City of St. Louis, that isn’t a matter of taste. It’s in the home occupation rules of the Zoning Code.
So much of this city’s work happens somewhere else. A kitchen table with a label printer at one end and a stack of flattened boxes at the other. The screech of packing tape late at night, after the other job is done. A notary stamp in a zippered pouch on the passenger seat. A carpet cleaning machine strapped down in the back of a van, still smelling faintly of wet wool. No lobby. No parking lot. No name painted on glass.
The City’s home occupation rules, rewritten by Ordinance 70150, list the conditions a business in a home has to meet. Condition eight is one line long: “The home occupation does not display a sign.” Condition nine says it does not “regularly and routinely accept customers” into the home. Condition ten says it does not advertise, solicit or invite customers, clients or the general public to the home.
Set beside a storefront, that stings. A storefront pulls strangers in with two things: a sign they can see from the street, and a door that says come in. The law that makes the kitchen-table business legal asks it to give up both.
None of that is the owner’s doing. The rulebook was written for a building with a name over the door, and the habit that grew up around it, a website plus a pin on Google’s map, still treats a house like a storefront that forgot to open. The work gets done. The customers who never saw it go somewhere else, and nobody hears the call that didn’t come.
The strange part is how friendly the same ordinance sounds. Its opening lines say it is a priority of the City “to make it as easy as possible” for people to start a new business and to grow an existing business. And the paperwork really is light. The cost of an application for a home occupation is $50.00 on the City’s permit site, and the business-type menu on that form already names the work that happens in spare bedrooms: Notary Public, Personal Chef, Carpet Cleaning, Online Retail Sales.
Then comes a second, smaller fee most people never hear about. The ordinance lets a home occupation operator register with the License Collector and pay a home occupation registration fee of $25.00 in lieu of the graduated business license tax. The catch is the earnings line: gross earnings from the home occupation for the preceding calendar year have to be less than one hundred thousand dollars, shown on the E-234 Business Earnings Tax Form. A brand-new business that had nothing to file yet can register without it for that first year. The certificate that comes back is kept at the home itself, where no customer will ever see it. The Office of the License Collector that issues it sits in City Hall, Room 102-104, at 1200 Market Street, at (314) 622-4528, open 8 AM to 5 PM.
### How does a St. Louis business get more customers without a storefront?
With a page where neighbors and AI assistants already look, naming the work, the areas served and how to reach the owner, because neither a sign nor a map pin will carry it. A home business in the City of St. Louis may not display a sign or invite the public to the home. Google tells a service-area business to hide its address and list up to 20 service areas, and an online-only business isn’t eligible for a Google profile at all.
### Google’s map draws the same line from the other side
Google starts from a different question, and lands in nearly the same spot. Its guidelines say that “to qualify for a Business Profile, a business must make in-person contact with customers during its stated hours.” The notary who drives to a kitchen table qualifies. The carpet cleaner who hauls the machine into a living room qualifies. The online shop that ships every order from a spare bedroom does not: “If your online-only business doesn’t have a physical location that your customers can visit nor do you visit customers in-person, your business isn’t eligible.”
For those who do qualify, the house still comes off the map. Google’s guidelines say “if you’re a service-area business, you should hide your business address from customers,” and the example they give is a plumber running the business from a residential address. The switch lives in the profile under Edit profile, then Location, then Edit next to “Business location,” where the toggle reads “Show business address to customers.” Once it’s off, the profile shows only a service area. Google allows up to 20 service areas, set by city, postal code or other areas served, and says the overall area shouldn’t extend farther than about 2 hours of driving time from where the business is based.
A rented mailing address the business doesn’t operate from, “also known as a virtual office,” isn’t eligible. “P.O. boxes or mailboxes located at remote locations aren’t acceptable.” And stuffing extra words into the business name “could result in the suspension of your Business Profile.”
Side by side, the two rulebooks rhyme. The City says no sign and no invitation to the house. Google says no address on the map, and for the shop that only ships, no map at all. Neither one is wrong, and neither one was written with the kitchen table in mind. So when a neighbor needs a mobile notary or a personal chef by the end of the week, where is the name they are supposed to see? Is the work the problem, or is it a rulebook drawn for a door? And is quiet really the price of working from home?
### The belief that cost the kitchen-table business
The old idea went like this: a website plus a Google listing equals customers. It made sense when the map was the front door to everything. For a business the law asks to keep its front door quiet, it never quite worked. The listing hides the address, or the listing can’t exist, and the website sits silent until something points a stranger to it.
That’s not a failure of the work. The person boxing orders at midnight, the chef hauling a cooler up someone’s back steps, the notary who drove across the county for one signature, are doing exactly what a business does. ### The City paperwork, line by line
The rules are short, and the order matters. Here is what the City’s own pages and Ordinance 70150 ask for.
The waiver. A Home Occupation Waiver application on the City’s permit site costs $50.00. Step 1 of 4 is an address lookup in the Assessor’s database, so the house has to come up there first.
Renters. Unless the owner of the building applies personally, the City will require a notarized letter of authorization from the owner.
The trades that take a longer road. Home cooking for resale, home daycares, recording and film studios, and home offices for general construction, electrical, painting, plumbing or landscaping contractors are treated as a conditional use, not a simple waiver.
The uses that can’t be home occupations at all. The ordinance lists repair shops, doctor and dentist offices, mortuaries, and auto detailing and washing among them.
The $25.00 registration. With the waiver in hand, the License Collector registration in lieu of the graduated business license tax asks for a copy of the waiver, the prior year’s E-234 form, and a written statement of clearance showing no City earnings or personal property taxes are due. It runs for one year and renews each year.
Every one of those lines is about the house: who owns it, what happens inside it, who may come through the door. None of them tells a stranger the business exists. That part has always been left to the owner, and to whatever the owner can afford to keep running on top of the work itself.

## Google Business Profile Categories When You Do Two Things in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/google-business-profile-categories-two-services-st-louis
Imagine you run a contracting business in Webster Groves. Half your calendar is kitchen and bath remodels. The other half is roofing: tear-offs, storm repair, the works. You’re genuinely good at both. So when you set up your Google Business Profile, you hit a wall you didn’t expect. Google wants one primary category, and one only. Remodeler or roofer. Pick.
A few miles west in Mt Olive, a couple runs a corner spot that’s half bakery, half cafe. Morning regulars come for croissants and a loaf to carry home. The lunch crowd comes to sit, sip, and stay. On Google, though, the place reads as one thing. The other half quietly fades into the background.
Same story for a Maplewood salon that’s also a full spa, or an Livingston plumber who’s a licensed electrician too. Two real services, one profile that only wants to lead with one. If that’s your business, you’re not imagining the problem, and you’re not doing it wrong. This is simply how Google Business Profile categories work. Here’s what’s happening, and what to do about it.
### What happens on Google when a St. Louis business offers two different services?
On Google, one of your two services wins and the other under-surfaces. Your Business Profile allows a single primary category, and that primary carries by far the most ranking weight. Google matches a searcher’s query to your primary first, so the second service shows up weaker, if it shows up at all.
Here’s the honest version. Google’s category system gives every Business Profile one primary category and up to nine additional ones. The primary isn’t just a label. It’s the single strongest signal Google uses to decide which searches you deserve to rank for. Everything else is a supporting act.
So the Webster Groves remodeler who roofs has to choose. List “General contractor” or “Roofing contractor” as the lead. Whichever one loses the coin toss gets the weaker treatment: fewer map-pack appearances, lower placement, less of the phone-ringing visibility that made a Google listing worth claiming in the first place. It’s a real, frustrating limit, and it hits plenty of good St. Louis businesses.
### Why does one category get almost all the ranking weight?
Because Google built its local ranking around matching intent to a primary category first. When someone searches “roofer near me,” Google looks hard at who calls roofing their primary business, then weighs relevance, distance, and prominence from there. Local SEO studies consistently rank your primary category among the top handful of ranking factors, well ahead of the additional ones.
Additional categories still matter. They land roughly eighth on most local ranking-factor lists, which is useful but not decisive. Think of your primary as the headline and your additional categories as the fine print. Both are on the page. Only one gets read first.
This is why a single-service business has it easy and a two-service business doesn’t. A dedicated roofer in Livingston points everything at one category and compounds its strength. The remodeler-who-roofs splits the same effort across two, and Google only lets one of them lead. In our experience, that split is the quiet reason so many owners feel invisible for half of what they actually do.
### What the one-primary rule looks like on the ground
Let’s put real businesses back in the picture, because the rule gets concrete fast once you do. Two services, one profile, and a daily cost that shows up as missed calls rather than a line on a report.
### The Webster Groves remodeler who also roofs
Set “General contractor” as primary and the remodeling calls come in fine. But when a storm rolls through and half of Webster Groves needs a roof inspection, this business ranks below the dedicated roofers down the road, even with years of roofing work behind it. The roofing category is there, listed as additional. It just doesn’t carry enough weight to win the search that matters that week.
### The Mt Olive shop that’s part bakery, part cafe
Pick “Bakery” and the morning pastry crowd finds you. Someone searching “cafe near me” for a place to sit with a laptop and a latte may never see you, because “Cafe” is the secondary label. The food, the seating, the easy vibe are all there in real life. On Google, half the story is whispered, and the owners compete for only part of the customers they serve.
### Can extra categories rescue your second service?
Partly, and it’s worth doing, but don’t expect a rescue. Those nine additional category slots genuinely widen the searches you can appear in, so always add the ones that fit. What they won’t do is match the ranking power of your primary. They sit roughly eighth among local ranking factors, which means they broaden your reach without lifting your second service to the top.
So add “Roofing contractor,” add “Cafe,” add “Day spa.” Fill the relevant slots and write about both services in your profile and your posts. You’ll pick up visibility you’d otherwise miss. Just go in clear-eyed: additional categories help you show up, not win. For a two-service business, that gap is exactly where customers slip away to a specialist who only does the one thing.
And please don’t try to game it by stuffing both services into your business name. A keyword-stuffed name is one of the fastest ways to draw a warning or a soft strip from Google, and it doesn’t fix the underlying category math anyway. The one-primary rule still applies, name tricks or not.
### How can one listing show both services equally?
By getting off the one-primary system entirely. A directory listing doesn’t force you to crown a single category, so it can present both of your services with equal prominence. No “one primary wins” penalty, no second service banished to the fine print. The remodeler is a remodeler and a roofer on the same page, equally findable for both.

It’s a findable local presence that needs no storefront, can’t be suspended by Google, and shows everything you do side by side. ## Why St. Louis Businesses Shouldn't Rely on Google Alone
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-st-louis-businesses-shouldnt-rely-on-google-alone
Picture an HVAC company run out of a house in O’Fallon. The first real heat wave of the summer is three days out, the phone normally starts ringing by 7 a.m., and the owner opens Google one morning just to double-check the holiday hours. The listing is gone. Not edited, not hidden. Gone. Where the business used to sit there’s a “suspended” notice and no explanation.
He didn’t change the address. He didn’t stuff the name with keywords. He just disappeared from the map the week before the busiest stretch of his year, and the only way back is an appeal form with no case number, no phone line, and no promised date. Meanwhile the competitor two ZIP codes over is still showing up for every “AC repair near me” search in the county.
Here’s the part nobody warns you about. For a lot of St. Louis businesses, Google isn’t one marketing channel among several. It’s the only front door they have, and they don’t hold the keys. This isn’t a reason to panic or to declare war on Google. It’s a reason to stop betting the whole company on a platform that can switch you off without a conversation.
### Why shouldn’t a St. Louis business rely only on Google to get found?
Because Google can suspend your profile overnight with no clear reason, lock some businesses out entirely, and change its ranking rules whenever it likes. Meanwhile AI assistants are a fast-growing way people find local services, and Google doesn’t control those. One channel you don’t own is a single point of failure.
Think about what that single point of failure actually controls. For most local service businesses, the Google Business Profile feeds the map pack, the knowledge panel, the reviews, the call button, and the directions. When it works, it’s wonderful and it’s free. The problem isn’t that Google is bad at this. The problem is that you’ve handed one company the power to make you visible or invisible, and that company never signed anything promising to keep you around.
None of this means Google doesn’t matter. It matters enormously, and you should absolutely claim and optimize your profile. The argument is narrower and more practical: don’t let it be the only place a customer in St. Louis County or Gray Summit can find you. Resilience isn’t built on one channel. It’s built on a few that fail at different times, for different reasons, so a bad week on one doesn’t take the whole business dark.
### What actually happens when Google suspends your profile?
You usually get no explanation and a slow, opaque wait. According to Sterling Sky, a firm that specializes in Google Business Profile issues, reinstatements commonly take about a week and can stretch to five or six, with no ticket or case ID to track. Google rarely tells you the exact reason, so you’re guessing while your listing sits dark.
Suspensions hit for a long list of reasons, and plenty of them catch honest businesses off guard. Sterling Sky points to causes like excessive or rapid edits to your profile, no genuine physical presence (a PO box, a virtual office, or a rented coworking desk doesn’t count), a keyword-stuffed business name, duplicate listings, and an address that doesn’t match your eligibility. Spam-prone industries such as locksmiths, garage-door repair, and rehab facilities draw extra scrutiny. Even a suspended Google user account can take your listing down with it.
To get reinstated, you typically have to assemble proof: a business license, a tax certificate, a utility bill, and photos or video of your physical location. Then you submit it and wait, often without knowing whether you sent the right thing. If you’re in the middle of that right now, we walk through the whole process in our guide to getting a suspended Google Business Profile reinstated in St. Louis. This article is about something different: making sure a suspension never takes you fully offline in the first place.
One myth worth killing here. Suspensions aren’t purely random or always instant. Keyword-stuffing your business name, for instance, often earns a warning or a quiet strip of the extra words rather than an immediate ban. The system is messier and more human than the horror stories suggest, which is both reassuring and frustrating, because “messy and opaque” is hard to plan around.
### Which St. Louis businesses can’t get a Google profile at all?
Any business without in-person customer contact. Google’s own guidelines for representing your business are blunt: you qualify for a Business Profile only if you either have a physical location customers can visit or you travel to meet customers in person. A purely online operation with no face-to-face contact is simply ineligible. For those owners, Google was never an option.
That rules out more St. Louis businesses than people realize. The online-only consultant, the e-commerce seller working from a spare bedroom, the service that handles everything by phone and email, none of them get a pin on the map. ### What about service-area and home-based businesses?
Service-area businesses can use Google, but with real limits. ## No LLC Needed for Google. Your Shop Name Is Another Story.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/google-business-profile-without-a-registered-business-st-louis
Missouri calls it a misdemeanor. Not skipping the LLC. Doing business under a name that isn’t your own, without filing that name with the state first.
The kitchen table, after the second shift. The label printer whirs. A sheet of stickers peels off its backing, and every one carries the shop name the regulars already say out loud. The laptop is open to Google’s sign-up page, and the cursor blinks in the name field.
That one name is where three offices meet. None of them talks to the others.
### Can you get a Google Business Profile without a registered business in St. Louis?
Yes. Google never asks for an LLC, a tax ID, or a registration certificate to create a Business Profile. What it does require is eligibility: either a physical location customers can visit, or in-person travel to customers. A purely online side hustle stays ineligible no matter how it’s registered, and that catch trips up more St. Louis sellers than the paperwork ever does.
Registration and eligibility are two different locks on two different doors. Google cares whether a customer ever meets you. Missouri cares what you call yourself. And the City of St. Louis cares about both the name and the kitchen.
### The name on the sticker is the part the state reads
If the name on that sticker is anything other than the owner’s own, it is what Missouri calls a fictitious name, a DBA. Section 417.200 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri requires anyone doing business under a name other than their true name to file a fictitious name registration with the Secretary of State’s office. The clock is short: the filing is due within five days after beginning business under the name.
The Secretary of State’s FAQ says online registration of a fictitious name can be accomplished at bsd.sos.mo.gov, and a paper form can go by mail or in person to the main office in Jefferson City or any of the Corporations Division branch offices. A registration is good for five years, and renewals must be made in the six-month period before it expires.
It is not a trademark. The FAQ says there may be an infinite number of businesses using the same name, because there is no name protection under the Fictitious Name Act. A business sold under the owner’s own legal name sits outside all of it.
### St. Louis counts trade names, not just storefronts
Here is the line almost nobody prints. On the City’s Graduated Business License page, the License Collector says a separate Graduated Business License is required for each business location or trade name. Candles under one name and gift baskets under another, both from the same table? To the City, that is two trade names.
The price drops for the kitchen table, too. A license is required for all businesses to operate in the City of St. Louis, and the initial Graduated Business License is $200.00, unless it is a city home-based business, in which case the fee is $25.00. The License Collector’s fiscal year runs June 1st through May 31st.
The City spells out the rest of the ask. Applications go in online or in person at the License Collector’s office in Room 104 of City Hall, 1200 Market Street, reachable at (314) 622-4528, Monday - Friday 8 AM - 5 PM. Alongside the license comes a clearance statement from the Collector of Revenue’s office showing all city taxes are paid, and a business located in the city also needs an Occupancy Permit from the Building Division. Paying by check, the page warns, can hold the application for several working days until the check clears.
So the three offices line up in a natural order. The state’s five-day clock on the name comes first. The City’s license follows, one per trade name. Google comes last, because it wants the business’s real-world name, as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers, and by then the same name is already on file twice.
And the LLC, if it ever makes sense for taxes or liability? The City’s Business Assistance Center page notes that registering a domestic LLC is $55 when done through the online portal at the Missouri Secretary of State site, and warns that many sites will try to charge more for the same transaction.

Then, a few lines away, it says home office use for general construction, electrical, painting, plumbing or landscaping contractors shall require a Conditional Use permit and may be allowed subject to Section 26.80.010 of the Revised Code. Listed, and then sent down a separate road.
Home cooking for resale, home daycares, and recording and film studios go down it too, along with any home occupation that is not specifically prohibited but cannot comply entirely with the requirements.
Then Google writes its own rule about the very same plumber. Its Business Profile guidelines say a service-area business should hide its business address from customers, and the example it picks is this one: “if you’re a plumber and run your business from your residential address, clear the address from your Business Profile.”
So the City wants the house named on the paperwork, and Google wants the house gone from the map. One kitchen table, two rulebooks, pointing opposite ways. Neither one was written for the person who works a day shift and takes the side calls at night.

### What each rulebook asks for, line by line
The City’s side is an online application at stlcitypermits.com, filled out on a laptop wedged between the invoices and the coffee maker. The waiver application costs $50.00. ## Google Won’t Map a Ship-Only Shop. Soulard Rents a $20 Table
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-found-locally-when-you-sell-online-st-louis
$20. That is what the City of St. Louis charges for a stand at Soulard Market, Wednesday through Friday, from October through March. ### The paperwork behind a $20 table
The list is short, and the City prints it on one page. Daily stands start with the market manager, who decides whether there is space for your type of product. If you are approved, Soulard Market asks for a Missouri State Retail Sales Tax License from the Missouri Department of Revenue, (573) 751-5860; a City of St. Louis Business License from City Hall, 1200 Market Street, (314) 622-4528; proof of liability insurance of $1,000,000 that names “The City of St. Louis” as an additional insured; and a description of what you sell.
After that, the market assigns you a vendor ID number, and that number goes on every stand you rent. Sign-in for daily stands begins at 6:30am on Saturdays and 7am Wednesday through Friday. In the dark of a winter morning, that is a cold walk with a folding crate in each hand. Stands are assigned on a first come basis.
Two details catch people off guard. Electric power is not available at the stands, so a string of lights or a card reader runs on batteries; small generators may be allowed with advance permission. And food vendors are not eligible to use daily stands at all. The market office answers at (314) 622-4180 or soulard-market@stlouis-mo.gov, 730 Carroll St., and keeps hours of 8:00am-5:00pm Wednesday through Friday and 7:00am-5:30pm on Saturday.
From April through September, Wednesday and Thursday stay at $20, Friday rises to $30 and Saturday to $40. A long-term stand runs roughly $1,400.00 per year.

## My Website Is Dead: Why Isn’t Anyone Finding It?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-isnt-anyone-finding-my-website-st-louis
You spent three weekends building a website. Maybe you paid someone a few hundred dollars to make it look sharp, and it does. The logo pops, the photos are clean, the booking button actually works. Then nothing happens. A month goes by. The only visitor was you, refreshing the page to see if anyone else showed up.
Here’s the part nobody warned you about. A website is a building, not a megaphone. A building on a street with no signs, no map pin, and no address out front is a building nobody walks into. Whether you bake out of a kitchen in Ellisville, detail cars across Wildwood, or keep books from a spare room in Sunset Hills, the problem is almost never the site. It’s that the site has no way to be found.
Let’s figure out why, and fix it, without rebuilding a single thing.
### Why isn’t anyone finding my website, and how do I fix it in St. Louis?
Nobody’s finding your website because a website is a destination, not a discovery layer. Google has to index it, rank it, and connect it to local signals before a single St. Louis customer sees it. Most small sites clear none of those bars. The fix is getting listed somewhere people and AI already search.
Think about how you actually find a plumber or a cake decorator. You don’t type a web address you’ve never heard of. You search, you check Google Maps, or lately you ask an AI assistant. Your website only wins if it shows up inside one of those moments. A brand-new site with no links, no reviews, and no local footprint shows up in none of them. That’s not a design flaw. It’s a discovery flaw, and it needs a discovery fix.
Here’s the good news. The fix is cheaper and faster than the rebuild you’re dreading, and you don’t need to touch the site at all. You need your business on a page that is already findable, already trusted, and already read by the search tools and assistants your customers use. The rest of this post shows you where the breakdowns happen, and how to route around every one of them.
### Is your website even indexed, or just sitting there?
Start with the most basic failure. Your site might not be in Google’s index at all. If Google hasn’t crawled and stored your pages, they cannot rank for anything, ever. Plenty of brand-new St. Louis sites sit un-indexed for weeks because nothing links to them and nobody told Google they exist. No index, no traffic. Simple as that.
You can check in under a minute. Type “site:yourdomain.com” into Google. If a list of your pages comes back, you’re indexed. If you get nothing, you’re invisible, and all the design work in the world won’t change that. This one check saves people in Waterloo and Wildwood a lot of wasted guessing.
### What keeps a small site out of the index?
Usually isolation. Google finds new pages by following links from pages it already trusts. A fresh site with zero inbound links is an island with no bridge. Leave a “noindex” tag on from a theme, block the robots file, or launch a domain last week, and you get silence. A listing on an established directory hands you an instant bridge: a trusted page that links straight back to yours.
### Why does your site have no discovery layer?
Here’s the idea that reframes everything. Your website is a destination. A discovery layer is the system that sends people to destinations. Google Search, Google Maps, local directories, and AI assistants are discovery layers. Your homepage is not. You built a shop, then forgot the road, the signs, and the map that lead people to the door.
This is why the prettiest site can still be dead. Design doesn’t generate discovery. Signals do. When a customer in Ellisville asks their phone for a mobile groomer, the phone doesn’t browse the whole web. It pulls from indexed, structured, trusted sources it already knows. If your business isn’t sitting inside one of those sources, you don’t exist in that moment, no matter how good your logo looks.
We’ve had this exact conversation with owners who swore the website was broken. It wasn’t. The site worked fine. It just lived in a place no discovery layer could reach. If you’re weighing whether to keep sinking time into the site at all, our take on whether a website or a listing is enough is worth a read.
### Do local signals matter more than a pretty homepage?
For a local business, yes, by a wide margin. Local signals tell search engines and AI who you are, where you serve, and whether real people trust you. These are the category you list under, the areas you cover, your reviews, and consistent contact details. A gorgeous homepage with none of these is a mannequin in a dark window.
Google’s own rules make this concrete. You can hold a Business Profile only if your business either has a location customers can visit or travels to customers in person, so a purely online business is ineligible (Google, “Guidelines for representing your business”). If you do qualify as a service-area business, Google tells home-based owners to hide the street address and set up to 20 service areas by city or region, not a mile radius. Your privacy and your visibility aren’t actually in conflict.
### Why your category choice quietly decides your ranking
Categories carry real weight. You pick one primary category plus up to nine extras, and the primary carries by far the most ranking power. A two-service business, say baking plus cake delivery, has to pick one primary, so the second service under-surfaces. That’s a built-in ceiling on a single profile, and it’s a big reason one channel is rarely enough to carry a whole business.
### Are you betting everything on one channel?
If your whole plan is “I have a website” or “I have a Google profile,” you’re one algorithm change away from zero. Discovery is splintering fast. BrightLocal’s Local Consumer Review Survey 2026 found 45% of consumers used AI tools to find or recommend local businesses this year, up from just 6% in 2025, making AI the third most-used local-discovery channel.
Look at where those searches go. BrightLocal put ChatGPT at 31% and Google AI Mode at 23% among people using AI for local discovery. Traditional search still leads, and this is one survey, so don’t bet the farm on it. But the direction is clear enough. If you only live on one channel, you’re invisible on all the others, and the others are growing.
There’s also the risk nobody mentions. A single Google profile can be suspended for a keyword-stuffed name, a PO box with no real presence, or an address that doesn’t match your eligibility (Sterling Sky). Reinstatement is slow and opaque, often a week and sometimes five or six, with no case number. Leaning on one fragile channel is how a dead website becomes a dead business. ## No Storefront, No Strangers: St. Louis Side-Business Rules
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-customers-for-a-side-business-st-louis
Two leashes hang on the hook by the back door, still damp from the morning walk. Somewhere across the neighborhood, a person who has never heard of the walker who owns them types dog walker into a phone, scrolls a map full of pins, and books a name that was on it.
Nobody turned the walker down. The walker was never on the screen. That is how a lot of first strangers slip away: not to better work, but to a quiet set of rules about what a business is supposed to look like.
In St. Louis there are two of those rulebooks, and both were drawn for a building with a sign over the door. One belongs to the City. The other belongs to Google.
The City’s lives on a web form, the Home Occupation Waiver application on stlcitypermits.com, and the cost of an application for a home occupation is $50.00. Scroll its business-type menu and the side work of half a block is already there, spelled the City’s way. Dog Walking. Pet Sitting/ Pet Care. Making Hand-Crafted Items. Mobile Car Washing.
Then the same form turns hard. It names businesses that are prohibited as home occupations, where an application will not be accepted, and the list opens with animal clinics and boarding facilities, including kenneling and day care. Restaurants are on that prohibited list. So are repair shops, dancing schools, and auto detailing and washing.
So the leashes on the hook have a line on the form. Keeping a neighbor’s dog for the day, at home, is on the list the City won’t accept.
Lay the two lists side by side and the car-wash bucket lands in both. Mobile Car Washing sits on the menu. Auto detailing and washing sits on the list of uses the City says it will not accept. The form doesn’t say where one ends and the other begins.
Food gets a third road. Home Cooking/ Food Production shows up on the menu too, yet the City sends home cooking for resale, along with home daycares, to a Conditional Use permit that may be allowed under Section 26.80.010 of the Revised Code of the City of St. Louis.
A rented home meets one more gate. Unless the owner of the building applies personally, the City will require a notarized letter of authorization from the owner of record, carrying the owner’s name, address and telephone number. The landlord signs off before the first stranger ever calls.
Google’s rulebook is shorter, and colder. Its Business Profile guidelines say a business that rents a physical mailing address but doesn’t operate out of that location, also known as a virtual office, isn’t eligible, and that P.O. boxes or mailboxes located at remote locations aren’t acceptable. The rule never weighs why a home business would want its own front door kept off a public map. A box across town simply reads to Google as a reason to say no.
Neither rulebook asks how clean the car came out, or whether the dog came home tired and happy. One wants a building. The other wants an address a stranger could walk up to. The work never comes up.
### How does a new side business in St. Louis get its first customers?
The fee and the notary are the City’s part. The stranger’s part is smaller and stranger: the minute between typing a service into a phone and tapping a name.
### What the City’s form asks, one screen at a time
The bucket rides in the trunk with a bag of rags and a bottle of tire shine, and the form’s first question is where all of it sleeps at night. Step 1 of 4 is an address search in the Assessor’s database, with 1234 N. Grand Blvd as the example. When an address won’t come up, the page points to the Zoning Dept at 314-622-3666.
The $50.00 is the City’s price. A card adds a 2.55% processing fee, with a minimum of $1.55, and the page notes that the City does not receive any of those funds.
That’s the whole ask. An address the City can find, a business type from its menu, a fee, and for renters a notary’s stamp. None of it sends a customer. It only clears the road for one.
### The map that was drawn around a door
A pet sitter’s key ring gets heavier every season, one brass key for every family that hands over the house for a long weekend. None of those doors carries the sitter’s name. Google’s map was drawn around a different kind of door, one with the business’s own sign on it.
The paid lane runs on the same logic. On Google’s Local Services ads, an advertiser only pays when it gets a lead, and Google’s help page says that when similar local businesses bid on the same lead, those bids determine how much the lead is worth. A side business that runs on evenings and weekends lands in an auction against companies with marketing departments, all for its first phone call.
So the stranger who would have hired the walker, the sitter or the detailer with the bucket meets a map and an auction built before any of them arrived. Nothing about the work put them at the back of the line. The rules did.
### How a review turns a stranger into customer one
A photo lands from a customer’s driveway: the hood beaded with water, the tires black and wet, a thumbs-up emoji under it. That photo is the shortcut from never heard of you to sure, come by this week. A stranger can’t test the work in advance, so the stranger borrows trust from someone who already did.
Most happy customers say yes when asked. They just never think of it on their own.
Here’s the contrarian part. A hundred reviews can wait; the first ten customers can’t. A small cluster of honest, detailed ones beats a pile of vague stars. “She showed up when she said, and the dog slept all afternoon” does more work than fifty taps that say great.
### Word of mouth needs somewhere to land
A row of hand-poured candles cools on wax paper along the counter, wicks still soft, the whole kitchen smelling faintly of cedar. A friend posts one in a neighborhood group, and a dozen strangers ask the same thing underneath: where can I get one?
That’s the moment the old advice was built for, and it still works. A flyer on the board at the laundromat, a mention at a church supper, a tag in a comment. Real first customers start there. What the advice skips is the second step. The stranger who heard the name now searches it, and if the search turns up nothing, the warm lead goes cold on a dead end.
Word of mouth only carries a name so far. A page with the photos, the hours and a number carries it the rest of the way, at the exact minute the stranger is curious enough to look.
A rulebook written for storefronts shouldn’t decide who meets the first stranger. Before leaning everything on one Google profile, read what happens when a profile gets suspended, so one bad day can’t wipe out the reviews that took months to earn.

## A Stranger’s Bid Prices Your Lead. The Library Charges $0
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-it-costs-to-get-a-st-louis-business-found-online
A stranger’s bid. That’s what priced the buzz on the kitchen counter just now, the new lead with a first name and a question about a quote. Somewhere across the county, another business in the same trade typed a number into a box, and Google’s help page for its pay-per-lead Local Services ads says exactly what that number does: “When similar local businesses bid on the same lead, those bids determine how much the lead is worth.”
Nobody standing at that counter got a vote.
Now the other price in this county: $0. That’s what St. Louis County Library charges for a mailing list of real names and addresses near the work, built at a library computer on the 2nd floor of the Clark Family Branch.
And on the free side of Google, the local rankings, money doesn’t move a name at all. Google’s Business Profile help is blunt: “There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.” One corner of the screen is an auction with the meter running. The corner beside it isn’t for sale at any price.
### What does it really cost to get a St. Louis business found online?
It can cost nothing but evenings, a fixed yearly fee, or a weekly ad budget with no end date. On Google’s pay-per-lead ads, rival bids set what each lead is worth, and Google recommends budgeting for at least 10 leads a week. St. Louis County Library’s Reference Solutions database builds mailing lists of potential customers at no charge.
### Upstairs at the Clark Family Branch, nothing is sold by the bid
The Clark Family Branch sits at 1640 S. Lindbergh Blvd., open 9:00 a.m.-8:00 p.m. Monday - Thursday, and its 2nd floor holds the library’s Small Business Center. The research desk answers at 314-994-3300. The center’s page, slcl.org/small-business, lists computers, Wi-Fi, a copy center and private rooms that can be reserved: a closed door, a table, and a list that costs nothing to print out and carry home.
The library’s page lays the database out in the order a new business would use it. First, competitors: the page says you can “learn about your competitors’ locations, executives, sales volume and expenses using Reference Solutions.” Second, the list itself: “Reference Solutions allows you to create free mailing lists containing names and addresses of potential residential and business clients.” Third, the size of the market: Simply Analytics and Reference Solutions, it says, “will help you determine the market demand and size for your product or service.”
That third question is the one a side business lives or dies on, and it usually gets answered the expensive way, one paid click at a time. Here it gets answered before a single dollar moves. The help costs nothing either: the library provides free training on these databases for individuals or groups, and Book A Librarian on the same page is how a session gets requested.
So the zero-dollar lane in St. Louis County isn’t a slogan about hustle. It’s a floor of a library building, a phone number and a list of real names and addresses near the work.
### Why does pay-per-lead feel like a slot machine?
Because it’s fed one pull at a time. Google’s bidding page lays out the mechanics in two short lines: “A bid is the most you’d pay for a lead.” And: “You only pay when you get a lead.” The charge is for the lead, not the job. Then comes the line that explains how the machine grows: “The higher your weekly budget, the more leads you could get.”
The burn is real, and it was built into the design. An auction rewards the deepest pocket in the room, and most St. Louis side businesses are funded out of the same checking account that pays the light bill. That isn’t a marketing failure on the owner’s part. It’s the system doing exactly what it was made to do.
If the price of a lead is set by whoever wants the same customer most, who is the auction really working for?
### The retainer that arrives on the first of the month
An agency sells hours of labor, and the invoice lands in the inbox on schedule whether the phone rang or not. For a company with healthy margins and several locations, that can pay off. For a one-person crew still testing whether people want the product, a monthly retainer is a second rent check, due on the first whether the month was slow or busy, and it never once asks how the month actually went before the payment clears.
Paying monthly for attention is renting it. When the payments stop, the attention fades, and what stays behind is a login to somebody else’s dashboard. That treadmill is what wears small owners down: money out every month, nothing on the shelf at the end of the year that they own.

### What a flat yearly price changes at the kitchen table
The difference shows up on the bank statement first. A yearly fee is one line, once, and then the statement goes quiet. A per-lead bill is a column of small charges that keeps growing down the page, each one a reminder that someone else set the number. One kind of cost can be planned around in one evening with a calculator and a cup of coffee. The other one gets discovered.
The second difference is privacy. Google’s own Business Profile rules say “P.O. boxes or mailboxes located at remote locations aren’t acceptable,” and a service-area business is told to hide its address. For a baker working out of a home kitchen or a detailer who drives to the customer, that leaves little room on Google’s map. A listing that takes a service area instead of a street address keeps the porch light off and the business still public.
The third difference is what stays. Photos of real work, reviews from real jobs, every service named the way a customer would type it, and every part of town the work reaches. A presence like that keeps working while the owner is at the day job, and it’s still there in month twelve, when an ad budget would have needed refilling every single week.
### Five questions any seller of customers should answer
Whoever is selling leads, clicks or a listing, five answers tell the whole story, and they fit on the back of the envelope the light bill came in.
Who sets the price? If the answer is “the market” or “your bid,” the cost climbs every time another business in the trade decides it wants the same neighborhood. What stays if the payments stop tomorrow? A page with real photos and reviews, a mailing list built at the library, those stay. A rented ad spot disappears the minute the card declines.
Is the charge per lead, per click, per month or per year? Each one lands differently in the gut. A yearly fee stings once. A per-lead charge stings every time the phone buzzes, even when the caller wanted somebody else. Does it require a home address on display? For anyone working from a spare bedroom, that answer decides a lot. Is there a look before the charge? A seller who believes in the product lets people see it first.
Run any offer through those five and the slick ones start to look different. Nobody has to sweet-talk anyone into a contract when the numbers make sense on their own, and a seller who dodges even one of the five has already answered it.

### What the city and state actually ask for

The state asks $7 to register a fictitious name. Missouri’s Corporations Division takes it online with a credit card at bsd.sos.mo.gov under Online Business Services, or on a paper form, and the registration runs five years.
The city asks for $50 and four screens. On stlcitypermits.com the waiver runs from Step 1 of 4 to Step 4 of 4. It starts by finding your address in the Assessor’s database, then asks for your business type, and one step takes an upload of a lease agreement or authorization letter.

### The launch script that sells cards before customers

### The St. Louis tax that follows your work, not just your address
Here’s the thing every new commission worker in this city should hear before the first check clears. The moment you take commission work, you’re a business in the eyes of City Hall. The City of St. Louis Collector of Revenue says its 1% tax on a business’s earnings is collected from all businesses located in the City of St. Louis - and from non-resident businesses that perform work, services or business activity in the city.
Read that second part twice. Live outside the city but do work inside it, and the city says non-resident businesses that perform work there owe it too. It follows the work. Most people who try a side hustle never hear that until a letter shows up.
The math is plain: 1% is a penny on every dollar of business earnings. Small, until nobody set it aside. A contract worker or self-employed person files it as an E-2 return on Form E-234, and a calendar-year return is due on or before April 15th. Questions go to the Earnings Tax Department at earningstaxcor@stlouis-mo.gov, or in person at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 410.
The federal side has its own catch. The IRS says sole proprietors generally have to make estimated tax payments if they expect to owe $1,000 or more when they file, and the self-employment tax rate is 15.3%. People find this out in a cold sweat at the kitchen table in spring. You’re finding it out now, while it’s still just a number on a screen.
So set money aside from the first commission, before it feels like yours. A separate savings account works. So does an envelope in a drawer.

### Four moves before the next empty week

Refreshments are allowed, but you can’t prepare food on library property, and alcohol isn’t permitted. Rooms are only scheduled during regular hours. Personal events such as weddings, funerals, parties and reunions aren’t allowed. Library and Foundation programs get priority, and the library can cancel a confirmed reservation with a minimum of 30 days’ notice, rescheduling whenever possible. Anyone using a room follows the policy and the library’s Code of Conduct.

## Your Cake Got the Hearts. Someone Else Got the Call.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-social-media-isnt-enough-to-get-your-st-louis-business-found
5 a.m., south city. The oven ticks as it cools, the kitchen smells like browned butter and burnt sugar, and you’ve got one cup of coffee’s worth of time before you leave for the job that pays the light bill. You post the cake you just finished. By seven the hearts are rolling in. By noon your cousin has shared it to her stories. And the phone that matters, the one with an order on the other end, sits face-down by the sink and stays quiet.

Here’s the part that stings. You did every grown-up thing. The City of St. Louis charges a home-based business $25 for its first business license, while everyone else starts at $200, and you paid it. Missouri’s cottage food law, section 196.298, says a home baker isn’t a food service establishment, and you put the label it requires on every box: your name, your address, a line saying the food isn’t inspected by the health department. Twenty-five dollars bought you the right to be legal. It didn’t buy you a single stranger who can find you. That’s not you failing. That’s a feed built for a different job.
Read that law one more time, because it quietly settles the whole argument. A cottage baker can sell over the internet only when the buyer is in Missouri too. The follower three states away who hearts every cake can’t legally order one from you online. The mom a few blocks over can. Your feed is built to please the first person. Search is where the second one is standing, card in hand.
A heart is not a deposit. Tape that over the stove. The feed was built to keep people scrolling, and it does that brilliantly. It was never built to hand your number to a stranger with a deadline and a debit card. That’s the machine doing its job instead of yours.

### What are four things a small business should never do on social media?
Start with four the FTC’s rule on consumer reviews and testimonials bans: buying fake followers or views generated by bots or hijacked accounts, paying for reviews on the condition they’re positive, posting reviews from your own managers or employees without disclosing the connection, and using threats or intimidation to get a bad review taken down. Courts can impose civil penalties for knowing violations, which turns a follower count that jumps overnight from faceless accounts into a liability, not a shortcut. It leans on structured, citable pages it can trust: clear names, categories, service areas, reviews, facts a machine can pull out and quote. So ask the question the way owners ask it - will ChatGPT find my business from social media? Probably not. A caption with three hashtags and a flame emoji gives it nothing to cite.
A social profile is made for humans skimming on a phone. A machine needs a page it can quote with confidence, and your Reels can’t do that job, however good they look.
It isn’t a knock on your work. Your posts can be wonderful and still be invisible to the tools doing the recommending. The gap isn’t talent. It’s format. Humans and machines read the web differently, and the machines now handle a growing share of the recommending.
So when an assistant names some other St. Louis business instead of yours, it’s usually because that business had a clean, structured presence and you had a feed. The machine went where the clean facts were. The practical move is to give it something to cite. Every image, blog, coupon and video on a Gold listing can be indexed on its own and can be cited by AI.
Nobody ever regretted a second set of house keys. Google alone is one key.
### What are some alternatives to Google My Business, and do you still need it?
Here’s a rule worth knowing. Google lets service-area businesses hide their street address and show only the area they serve. So a baker working out of her own kitchen doesn’t have to publish her front door to claim a Google Business Profile (plenty of people still say Google My Business). But a rented mailing address you don’t actually work out of (Google calls it a virtual office) isn’t eligible, and P.O. boxes aren’t acceptable either, according to Google’s own guidelines. Its address help page explains how a service-area business hides its address. If you deliver, or meet customers at their door, tell Google you’re a service-area business. Flour on your hands, a delivery bag on the passenger seat, and a profile that shows the neighborhoods you cover and not your driveway.
So the alternatives to Google My Business aren’t replacements. They’re the other doors. One listing on one platform is a thin thread, and thin threads are easy to snap, whether by an eligibility rule or by a platform that changes its mind. Local directories add doors Google doesn’t control. St Louis Near Me Directory welcomes home-based and service-area owners with no public address required. A listing works as a standalone web presence.
There’s a longer argument for spreading out, and it’s worth ten minutes of your evening: the case against relying on Google alone. Every invisible day is a cake, a drain, a haircut that paid someone else, and you never see the call you didn’t get.

Own something searchable, structured and yours. You don’t have to abandon social; you need ground under it. And do you need a website if you have social media? A.  No. Good commission programs expect to train beginners, because they only pay when you produce, so coaching you well is in their own interest. What matters is being coachable, consistent and comfortable talking to people.
### Q. How do I build a resume with no work history?
A.  Make experience you can describe truthfully, even if nobody paid you for it yet. A real project for a real local business counts. So do volunteer work, freelance gigs and commission results. List specific results and skills rather than job titles. One finished project with a real business name on it beats a page of soft adjectives every time.
### Q. Are commission-only jobs good for beginners?
A.  They can be, if the role trains you and the product is easy to believe in. The upside is flexible hours, pay tied to your own results and fast skill-building. The downside is lumpy early income and plenty of rejection. If you need steady pay right now, start with a paid program and add commission work on the side.

## You Know Everyone in St. Louis. Here’s the $25 Step to Getting Paid for It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/turn-your-st-louis-network-into-income
“You should be getting paid for this.” Your sister says it every time your phone buzzes on the arm of the couch. Who’s good for a water heater? Who cuts curly hair without wrecking it? That’s the number worth repeating. The City of St. Louis charges $200 for a first Graduated Business License, unless it’s a home-based business in the city. Then it’s $25. Screenshot that and send it to the friend with the candle table and the “someday” business plan.
### How do I turn my connections into income in St. Louis?
Get paid for the introductions you already make. Commission work, like connecting local owners to a directory listing that helps them get more customers, pays when a referral signs up. If you live in the City of St. Louis and work from home, the city says you need a business license, a St. Louis City Tax Clearance and a Home Occupation Waiver, and it calls its Business Assistance Center the first stop.
Notice what that answer doesn’t ask for. No résumé. No interview. No portal that swallows your application and sends back a “we’ll be in touch” that never touches anything. You know everyone, and you still can’t get hired, because a job posting has no box for “half the block runs decisions past me.” The problem was never your value. It was the form trying to measure it.

### The $25 license and the two city steps that come with it
Most side-hustle advice stops at “go make money.” Then April shows up and a city envelope lands on the kitchen table with the bills. So here’s the St. Louis paperwork, straight from the city’s own Business Assistance Center page, which calls the BAC the first stop when you open a business in the city.
The license. The city says a license is required for all businesses to operate in the City of St. Louis. The first Graduated Business License is $200, or $25 for a city home-based business. One quirk: the License Collector’s year runs June 1 through May 31, so renewal comes due June 1, not New Year’s.
The earnings tax account. The city’s earnings tax is 1% of a business’s earnings. Someone who works on a contract basis or is self-employed files an E-2 return on Form E-234, and a calendar-year return is due on or before April 15. If you don’t have a city tax account yet, you open one with Form E9, in person at 1200 Market Street, Room 410, or by email. Miss the deadline and the city adds a penalty of 5% of the tax for each month, up to 25%, plus interest. You can’t file electronically yet, but you can pay online.
The Home Occupation Waiver. If you operate a business in your home, the city says you need one, and you apply at stlcitypermits.com. Some need a zoning hearing, so call the Building Division Zoning Section at (314) 622-3666 if you’re unsure. Not sure which of these fits a part-time commission gig? That’s exactly the question to bring to the BAC before you earn your first check, not after.
And one warning the city puts in plain words: an EIN is free when you use the IRS site, and a Missouri LLC is $55 through the Secretary of State’s online portal. The city adds that many sites will try to scam you by charging more. If a site wants a fee for your EIN, close the tab.

## That Free Lash Fill Counts as Pay. Get Paid for the Rest.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/turn-your-st-louis-online-following-into-income
Three DMs. Zero dollars. The phone buzzes face-down on the couch cushion, then again. You type the answers with one thumb while the other hand holds a cold toasted ravioli. It eats most of the evening. It pays nothing.
St. Louis runs on two questions. Where’d you go to high school? And who do you use for...? Only the second one can pay you.
A like is applause. A recommendation is a paycheck you keep handing to somebody else. Here are the four honest ways to keep it, and the one federal rule most local creators break without knowing it exists.
### How do you make money from a social media following?
Four honest ways, in the order most people can start them: a local shop pays you to post, a link pays you when someone buys, you sell your own thing, or you get paid for local work your audience already proves you can do. Pick by your hours, not your follower count. And whichever you pick, disclose it, because a free product counts as payment under the FTC’s Endorsement Guides.
### That free lash fill already counts as pay
You walk out of the salon with your eyes still stinging a little from the glue. The owner waved off your card - “on the house, just tag us” - and you post the close-up from the car. Feels like a favor between friends.
Federal rules read it differently. The FTC’s Guides Concerning Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising say material connections “can include monetary payment or the provision of free or discounted products (including products unrelated to the endorsed product)”, and when your audience wouldn’t reasonably expect that connection, it must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. That free fill is a material connection. So is the comped brunch.
Screenshot that and send it to the friend who posts every free thing she gets. It isn’t a reason to stop. It’s proof you were already working. Say it in the post itself - “they gave me this free” or “paid partner” - where people see it before they tap away.
### Way one: a St. Louis shop pays you to post
Not a national brand. The taco truck by your office, the barber whose chair sits empty on Wednesday afternoons. You already post about them for free. Get the price, the deadline and who owns the photos in a text before you shoot a frame.
### Way two: links that pay when someone buys
The federal guides use this exact case: a blogger’s link leads to a product, and “whenever a consumer clicks on such a link and buys the product, the blogger receives a portion of the sale.” Legal, common, disclosable. The local version is simpler. Ask the lash tech or the gutter guy you already recommend: do you pay for referrals? You’ll know by Friday.
### Way three: sell your own thing
A printed neighborhood map, a recipe card, a class on shooting food with a phone. It pays the most per sale and eats the most evenings. Two St. Louis moves before you start. If it’s a physical thing, Missouri’s Department of Revenue says a business must obtain a sales tax license by registering with the Department if it’s making sales of tangible personal property. If it’s a video or a voice, skip the studio: the St. Louis Public Library’s Creative Experience lets anyone with a valid library card use a recording room, in two-hour reservations, booked up to one week in advance by calling 314-241-2288. It’s at the Central Library at 1301 Olive Street. Shut the door, hear the room go dead quiet, and record what you’d otherwise film in your kitchen with the dishwasher running.

### The text to send before any deal

### What is a good monthly income in retirement?
Start with the last pay stub you folded into your wallet, not a magic number. The federal Department of Labor says experts estimate you’ll need 70 to 90 percent of your preretirement income to keep your standard of living, and that Social Security replaces about 40 percent of preretirement income on average. The space between those two numbers is what a pension, savings or a few paid hours a week has to fill, so get your own figure from the retirement estimator on the Social Security Administration’s website before you decide how many hours you want.

### What would you actually do as a St Louis Near Me Directory rep?
Mostly, you’d have conversations you already have. A coffee with an old colleague. A chat at the farmers market while the kettle corn pops behind you. A call to the handyman who mentioned that new customers only ever come from his brother-in-law. You notice a hardworking owner nobody can locate online - a mobile dog groomer, a home baker, a fix-it man who works out of his truck - and you tell them about a listing that can help.
You’re not pushing something hollow. A St Louis Near Me Directory listing works as a standalone web presence, with photos, hours, reviews and click-to-call, even if the owner never builds a website. No public address is required, so the home baker keeps her home private. For someone who has tried and failed to bring in new customers, that’s a real relief, and you get to be the neighbor who brought a working answer instead of more jargon.
It matters more now than it did a few years ago. BrightLocal’s Local Consumer Review Survey found that use of ChatGPT and other AI tools for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in a single year, making AI the third most popular source of business recommendations. The handyman with no website feels that shift in a quiet phone. You can explain it to him in plain English over a cup of coffee. Our deeper look at working from home helping St. Louis businesses win customers walks through the rhythm of the work, and our guide to putting a St. Louis side hustle online is a good one to send an owner who wants to understand it first.
### What does “on your terms” really mean here?
It means you set the pace, not a manager. No clock to punch, no mandatory Monday meeting. You work from the kitchen table or the back porch with the screen door creaking, and you take a few weeks off to see the grandkids when they’re in town. Effort and reward stay linked, which is the appeal and the risk in the same sentence.
For a lot of retirees, that trade feels right. You’re not swapping your hours for a wage anymore. You’re trading a handful of good conversations for income you can dial up or down as life allows. If a month gets busy with doctor visits or a new grandbaby, you ease off, and nobody writes you up for it.
This kind of bend-around-your-life earning isn’t only for retirees. It fits busy parents just as well, as our piece on flexible work-from-home income for St. Louis parents explains. The common thread is simple: income that fits your life, instead of a life rearranged around a shift.
Retired from the job, not from being the one people call. See a local role that still needs you.
### Start with one conversation
You don’t have to leap. Pick the door that fits this season of your life and take one step: one phone call to the AARP Foundation, one email asking about pay terms, one coffee with an owner you already know. See how it feels in your chest when you hang up. If it fits, lean in. If it doesn’t, you’ve lost an afternoon and gained a story. Either way, you’ll have used the thing a long career gave you, and that feels better than another quiet Tuesday.
The next time someone at the potluck asks what you’re doing with yourself, you won’t need the bright, practiced answer. You’ll have a real one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the best flexible part-time jobs for retirees?
A.  The best ones let you set your own hours and build on what you already know: consulting, tutoring, bookkeeping, mentoring or community-based referral work. In St. Louis, a commission-only rep role with St Louis Near Me Directory lets you work remotely and decide how many hours you put in each week, while the AARP Foundation’s senior employment program offers paid training for those who qualify.
### Q. What are low-stress jobs after retirement?
A.  Low-stress work usually means no commute and nobody hovering over your shoulder. Roles built on conversation - helping neighbors, giving advice, making introductions, mentoring a new owner - tend to feel light rather than draining. The goal at this stage is purpose and a little income, not the pressure you happily left behind.
### Q. Are there remote jobs for retirees?
A.  Yes. Many pay on commission or per project, so you can work from your kitchen table on your own schedule. St Louis Near Me Directory’s commission-only rep role is remote, and you can help local businesses bring in more customers from anywhere with a phone. Ask for the pay terms in writing before you start.
### Q. What part-time jobs are good for seniors over 65?
A.  Jobs that value judgment and trust over speed or heavy lifting suit this stage best: advising, connecting people, light sales and flexible remote roles. If income is limited, the Senior Community Service Employment Program offers paid training for people 55 and older who meet its income rules, and its participants average 20 hours a week.
### Q. Do you need experience for flexible retiree work?
A.  Usually not. For a commission referral role, you mainly need to be comfortable talking with people and following up, two things most retirees learned long ago. Formal sales experience helps but isn’t required. Your relationships and credibility around St. Louis matter far more than any line on a resume.
### Q. Are commission-only jobs worth it?
A.  They can be, if the product is real and the terms are honest. Commission-only means no base pay, so income follows effort, but it also means no cap and total schedule freedom. Before you start, get the rate, the payout timing and the renewal terms in writing. If an employer won’t put them on paper, that’s your answer.
