## $20 to Drive Across the Mississippi, and 7 More Small Towns Outside St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-st-louis-a-complete-local-guide-by-town
Twenty dollars, cash or check. That’s what it costs to roll your car onto a boat at Ste. Genevieve and cross the Mississippi River, and the ferry says it currently doesn’t take credit cards, so have the bills out before you reach the landing. For 10 to 15 minutes the only road is moving water. The Missouri bank slides away behind you, the Illinois shore comes up ahead, and then you drive off in a different state. Your car never touched a bridge.
It’s the longest drive on this list. By OpenStreetMap routing, the Missouri landing sits about 66 miles and 82 minutes from the Arch, so “about an hour south” is true of the town and generous for the dock. The river decides whether the boat runs, so the Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 is worth a call before you go.
### What are some small towns outside St. Louis?
So what do people in St. Louis do for fun after they’ve done the Arch and the zoo? They drive to the edges. If you’ve been hunting for cute towns to visit around St. Louis, Ste. Genevieve and Kimmswick are the usual answers, and they earn it. Ste. Genevieve, founded by French colonists in the 1700s, is often called Missouri’s oldest town. The other seven stops on this list each begin with something you can see or hear.
In Belleville, you turn the dial to 90.1 FM and a double feature arrives through your car radio. In Wentzville, a green building off Interstate Drive holds 32 horseshoe courts, half of them indoors. In Clayton, turtles sun themselves on an old stump while a lighted fountain plays in the same pond. In O’Fallon, you sit in your car while a whole town’s volunteer-built scenes pass the windshield. Out on the Chesterfield levee, a very flat, sunny trail runs toward the Katy Trail. In Fenton, a flat riverside path trades shade for sun. In Arnold, the river has paddlefish in it.
Staying inside the city limits instead? Our guide to unique things to do in St. Louis for adults covers the quirky things to do in St. Louis proper. Gone all day? The best day trips from St. Louis lays out fifteen escapes within two hours.
### Is there still a drive-in movie theater near St. Louis?
Tune the radio to 90.1 FM and the movie starts talking inside your car. That’s Screen 1 at the Skyview Drive-In in Belleville, and Screen 2 plays on 101.9. Some regulars skip the seat altogether, unfold a lawn chair in front of their own car and watch from there. Skyview allows it.
Yes, and it has been doing this since July 8, 1949. Through the 1960s and ’70s the whole place wore a pink so specific that the paint supplier named it Bloomer Pink. The pink is long gone, but the projection booth and concession stand from that era still stand, and each of the two screens now runs a double feature a night. A 1955 tornado wrecked the wings added to the screen for CinemaScope, and a 1981 windstorm took down more than half of it. The owners added the second screen in 1982.
Skyview sits at 5700 N. Belt West in Belleville, IL 62226, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from downtown. As of this writing it’s open Friday and Saturday only. Have cash in hand at the window when the box office opens at 6:30 p.m.; it takes cash only, though the concession stand takes cards. The first show never starts before 8:00 p.m. The season runs from late March or early April into October, and only rarely into early November. Call (618) 233-4400 or check skyview-drive-in.com, because we couldn’t confirm the current adult ticket price.
Load the back seat with your own food (no grills) and a leashed pet if you have one. Each paid admission lets one child age 12 or under in free, which means one child per paying adult, not every kid in the car. Reserved spots cost $10 each, with a maximum of five per screen, Friday and Saturday only, booked by email.
Want smaller charming towns in Illinois to pair it with? Belleville has a historic downtown. Eat early with where to eat in Belleville so you’re at the box office by 6:30 p.m. The Belleville business directory and city guide lists the rest of the local spots, and our Belleville guide covers the Metro East side beyond the drive-in and the shrine everybody already knows.
### Can you still take a car ferry across the Mississippi near St. Louis?
Walk Ste. Genevieve’s old French colonial houses in the morning. By afternoon, drive onto the boat and watch the bank you started from slide away. Some form of ferry has linked these two banks for well over two centuries, and this is the one south of the city. Most St. Louis lists that mention river ferries point north, toward Grafton.
Yes, it still runs. The Ste. Genevieve-Modoc ferry carries cars, bikes and walk-on passengers between Missouri and Illinois, with a boat every 15 to 20 minutes and a crossing of 10 to 15. A car up to 30 feet pays $20 one way, in cash or check. Buy the return with your outbound ticket and the trip back is $10, so a same-day round trip runs $30. A bike or walk-on is $5, a motorcycle with one rider is $7, and a vehicle from 31 to 55 feet is $40. Anything over 65 feet can’t board.
Summer hours are Wednesday through Saturday, 6 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. It’s closed Monday and Tuesday. Winter hours are Friday and Saturday, 6 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with Monday through Thursday closed. The ferry doesn’t post the dates it switches seasons, so ask. The last ride leaves 30 minutes before closing. It runs year-round, except when river conditions make a crossing unsafe.
The Missouri landing is at 8205 Little Rock Rd, Ste. Genevieve. The Illinois landing is at 3482 Levee Rd, Modoc. Call the Ste. Genevieve Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 to hear whether the boat is running, or check stegenmodocferry.com. The river keeps its own schedule, so make that call before you build a day around it.
Get lunch from our list of where to eat in Ste. Genevieve. Most visitors drive an hour to look at old buildings. You crossed the Mississippi on a boat. Our Ste. Genevieve guide has the historic district and the rest of the day.
### Oak Knoll Park in Clayton: a pond, old post oaks and sunning turtles
Turtles sun themselves on an old stump in the pond. A lighted fountain plays in the same water. Overhead stand post oaks the city puts at about 150 years old, the ones that gave Oak Knoll Park its name. Shaw Park gets the crowds. This is where Clayton goes to be quiet.
Clayton is the closest stop on this list. The 14.5-acre park sits at the northwest corner of Clayton Road and Big Bend Boulevard, at 1 Oak Knoll Park, Clayton, MO 63105. It’s free, and it’s open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Clayton Parks & Recreation answers questions at 314-290-8500, and claytonmo.gov has the details. Walk the half-mile path past the rain garden, the sunken garden and the Uchitelle Garden of Reflection. On summer Sundays from 5 to 7 p.m., the city’s free Musical Nights set up by the pond, and dogs, lawn chairs and picnic baskets are welcome.
The history is the part hardly anyone knows. Clayton bought the land in 1958, and it came with two stone mansions of about 20 rooms each. In 1959 the Academy of Science of St. Louis moved part of its century-old collection into them and ran the St. Louis Museum of Science and Natural History there for decades. Admission was free. The academy paid the city $1 a year in rent. Part of that collection went on to the Science Center. Both mansions still stand, and one now houses the Greater St. Louis Community Foundation.
One caution. Recent parks-commission minutes say the pavilion’s tornado-damaged roof repair was still being finalized and a lighting project was delayed, so call the parks office before you plan an evening there. Then head toward downtown Clayton with our guide to where to eat in Clayton, browse the Clayton business directory and city guide, or read our Clayton guide for the rest of the city.
### From the Chesterfield levee to the Katy Trail by bike, with no interstate lanes
A very flat, sunny trail with benches and shade structures: that’s Great Rivers Greenway’s own description of the Monarch-Chesterfield Levee Trail, and it fits. On the river side you get the Missouri and its timbered banks. On the other, the valley. Same valley as the outlets. Completely different afternoon.
Yes, you can bike from here to the Katy Trail. The paved path runs 11.09 miles along the levee system, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from downtown, and since 2016 a separated bike and pedestrian path on the Daniel Boone Bridge has carried it across the Missouri River. You never share a lane with interstate traffic. The bridge path runs about 0.75 mile and climbs gradually. On the far side, the Katy Trail is crushed rock rather than pavement, open sunrise to sunset. Missouri State Parks calls it the longest developed rail-trail in the country, at 240 miles.
Pick a trailhead: Railroad Park at 17634 Edison Ave, River’s Edge at 17017 N Outer 40 Rd, the Athletic Complex at 17891 N Outer 40 Rd, or Premium Outlets at 18575 Outlet Blvd. Each city sets its own hours, and Great Rivers Greenway is at 314-436-7009.
Two cautions. Great Rivers Greenway has closed the trail under the bridge at high water, and restrooms and water are unavailable at some trailheads from November through March. It’s sunny out there, so go early on a summer morning and carry water. That flat surface also makes it one of the easier good outdoor activities near Saint Louis. Besides Faust Park, the valley has plenty more. Find lunch with our list of where to eat in Chesterfield, look up local shops in the Chesterfield business directory and city guide, and read our Chesterfield guide for the rest.
### Why is there a horseshoe hall of fame in Wentzville?
Pull into Quail Ridge Park off Interstate Drive and the green building you see first is the horseshoe hall of fame. Most people flying past on I-70 have no idea it’s there. Inside the museum are hundreds of steel shoes, photos of the hall of famers, memorabilia going back to the 1800s, and items from President George H.W. Bush’s White House horseshoe games. You can watch footage of top matches and learn how serious pitchers actually throw.
Why here? The national horseshoe pitching hall of fame and museum live at the Quail Ridge Horseshoe Club, a 21,000-square-foot facility with 32 courts, 16 indoors and 16 outdoors. Among the quirky things to do in St. Louis, this one costs nothing. The address is 100 Bluestem Way, inside Quail Ridge Park at 560 Interstate Dr, about 45 minutes from downtown. The hall is open to the public Saturday and Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. A weekday tour only happens if a club member arranges it, so call 636-679-0609 or check nhpf.net first. The park opens at 7 a.m. and closes half an hour after sunset.
Then use the rest of the park. Quail Ridge has more than seven miles of trails through rich bottom land near Peruque Creek, plus fishing lakes and ponds, an 18-hole disc golf course and a fenced dog park. The dog park is free, but your dog needs an updated immunization record. Afterward, here’s where to eat in Wentzville, the Wentzville business directory and city guide has the local shops, and our full Wentzville guide covers the rest of town.
### O’Fallon’s Celebration of Lights: the rules first-timers learn the hard way
Once you’re in line at Fort Zumwalt Park, you stay in your car. No stepping out for photos. No restrooms. On a Friday or Saturday night the wait can run 60 to 90 minutes. Then the loop opens up, and every scene along it was designed and paid for by a local organization, church or business. You’re driving past a whole town’s volunteer work. The Celebration of Lights started in 1991, and the city says it draws more than 13,000 vehicles a year.
It runs nightly from late November to December 30, 6 to 9 p.m., at Fort Zumwalt Park, 1000 Jessup Ln, O’Fallon, MO 63366. Some vehicle nights are closed and Christmas Day is closed entirely, so check this season’s calendar at ofallonmo.gov or call the city at 636-240-2000. Tickets are online only. The city puts it bluntly: no sales are allowed at the gate.
This season it’s $18 a car, $40 a van and $65 a bus, and the city posts each season’s prices on its page. A ticket is good only for the year you buy it, so don’t stock up for next winter. The city’s own words: “Make sure to use the ticket the year you purchase it!”
If you’d rather be warm, there’s the trolley. It’s $18 a person, completely enclosed and heated, it runs Thursday through Sunday, and the city asks you to reserve at least two weeks ahead. A few nights each season the drive becomes the Old-Fashioned Holiday Stroll, on foot only, with fireworks over Lake Whetsel and a visit from Santa. Stroll parking and the shuttle are at Fort Zumwalt West High School, 1251 Turtle Creek Dr, and nowhere else.
Pair it with Wentzville, because Quail Ridge Park is 16 minutes and 10 miles away. The hall of fame is open weekends from noon to 5 and the lights start at 6, so a Sunday in season skips the Friday and Saturday waits.
Ask what city is 30 minutes from St. Louis, Missouri, and O’Fallon is the one that claims it, by its own city count. It has grown past 90,000 residents and still gets treated like an exit sign on the way to somewhere else. Plan dinner first with where to eat in O’Fallon, check the O’Fallon business directory and city guide for local shops, and see our O’Fallon guide for the rest of the year.

### Where does the Meramec Greenway go from Fenton?
Along the river, through the oldest part of town, and across a bridge to a park that used to be a beach. Most people start by the playgrounds and the 9/11 Heroes Memorial in Fenton City Park. The trail runs flat, with both shade and sun and views of the Meramec most of the way, as part of a 5.1-mile paved stretch between two St. Louis County parks, George Winter and Unger.
Fenton City Park is at 1215 Larkin Williams Rd, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from downtown. Check with Great Rivers Greenway at 314-436-7009 before you go. A section near Unger Park is closed for repeated flooding while it waits on a rebuild. Fenton Parks & Recreation is at (636) 349-8155, and the Stoneywood Dr lot is open from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Heading toward George Winter, the paved trail ends in Old Towne Fenton at Water and Mound streets, where traffic is light enough that most people on bikes ride the street for a few blocks. Follow Water Street to Old Gravois and you’ll see the bridge over the Meramec, with its own separated path for walkers and cyclists. On the far side is Minnie Ha Ha Park in Sunset Hills. The city describes it as a resort from the 1930s known as Mini Ha Ha Beach. Now it has walking trails, picnic shelters and a scenic overlook of the water.
Bring a rod. George Winter has a boat ramp onto the Meramec, and Unger has a lake of its own. Arnold is about 23 minutes and 13 miles away, so a greenway morning pairs well with an afternoon at Teszars Woods. Refuel with our list of where to eat in Fenton, and our Fenton guide covers the rest of the city’s parks.
### Where can you fish the Meramec River in Arnold?
At 4 a.m., Teszars Woods is already open, and you can stand at the river’s edge with a rod while the sky is still dark. Somewhere in that water is a paddlefish, the long-billed fish that looks like it swam out of the fossil record. The City of Arnold lists it among what swims in the Meramec here, along with channel catfish, flatheads, carp, drum and white bass.
The conservation area is east of Arnold, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from downtown. Take Telegraph Road off Highway 61/67, then head east on Rockwood Drive. It’s open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, and it’s free. The two trails are short, a quarter-mile woods trail and a 0.6-mile one, so the place works with kids or a leashed dog. No camping. Birders work the shrub-scrub wetland, and the state lists wood ducks among the things to watch for.
Fishing takes a Missouri permit unless you’re exempt. Anyone 15 or younger needs none, and neither do Missouri residents 65 or older, except for trout. Free Fishing Days fall on the Saturday and Sunday after the first Monday in June, on state waters only, so city, county and private areas may still charge. Questions go to Arnold Parks & Recreation at 636-282-6680 or the Missouri Department of Conservation at (636) 441-4554.
Hauling a boat? Stop first. Teszars Woods sits just south of Flamm City Access, but MDC closed that boat ramp after the flood and has posted no reopening. Call MDC at (636) 441-4554 before you plan a launch. When you’re done, here’s where to eat in Arnold. For the rest of town, including the 8-acre fishing lake at Arnold City Park, see our Arnold guide.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What do people in St. Louis do for fun?
A.  More than the usual lists suggest. On a free weekend, locals ride the levee trail in Chesterfield, walk the Meramec Greenway in Fenton, catch a double feature at the Skyview Drive-In in Belleville (Friday and Saturday nights, cash-only box office, (618) 233-4400), fish the Meramec at Teszars Woods in Arnold, or catch a local band at a neighborhood bar. The fun is spread across the whole region, not packed into one downtown block.
### Q. What are some cute towns to visit around St. Louis?
A.  Ste. Genevieve is the classic answer: a French colonial river town about an hour south, with a car ferry across the Mississippi ($20 a car, cash or check; call 573-880-6970 to confirm the boat is running). Kimmswick, in Jefferson County, is a tiny historic town known for its June Strawberry Festival and October Apple Butter Festival. On the Illinois side, Alton and Grafton sit along the Great River Road, and Belleville has a historic downtown.
### Q. What are some smaller charming towns in Illinois?
A.  Within an easy drive of St. Louis, Grafton sits where the Illinois River meets the Mississippi, and Alton has river bluffs and antique shops on the Great River Road. Belleville pairs a historic downtown with its 1949 drive-in, open Friday and Saturday nights at (618) 233-4400, with a cash-only box office. Waterloo and Columbia, two quieter Monroe County towns south of the Metro East, are good for a slow afternoon.
### Q. What are some fun things to do near Saint Louis?
A.  Watch a double feature at the Skyview Drive-In in Belleville, tour the free National Horseshoe Pitchers Hall of Fame in Wentzville (Saturday and Sunday, noon to 5 p.m., 636-679-0609), ride the car ferry across the Mississippi at Ste. Genevieve, or drive through O’Fallon’s Celebration of Lights from late November through December. All sit within about an hour of downtown, though the ferry landing is closer to 80 minutes.
### Q. What city is 30 minutes from St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  O’Fallon, Missouri, which sits about 30 minutes west of downtown by the city’s own count, is a good example. Depending on traffic, Chesterfield, Fenton, Arnold and Belleville are all roughly 20 to 30 minutes out. Clayton is closer, Wentzville runs about 45 minutes, and Ste. Genevieve is about an hour south, with its ferry landing nearer 80 minutes.
### Q. What are some good outdoor activities near Saint Louis?
A.  Ride the 11.09-mile Monarch-Chesterfield Levee Trail across the Daniel Boone Bridge to the Katy Trail, walk the 5.1-mile Meramec Greenway out of Fenton after checking Great Rivers Greenway (314-436-7009) for flood closures, hike the seven-plus miles of trails at Quail Ridge Park in Wentzville, or fish at Teszars Woods in Arnold, open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. All are free to enter. Fishing needs a permit unless you’re exempt.
### Q. What are some quirky things to do in St. Louis?
A.  Inside the city, our guide to unique things to do for adults has the strange stuff. Out in the towns, the quirks are quieter: a free horseshoe pitching hall of fame with items from President George H.W. Bush’s White House games, a drive-in once painted a color called Bloomer Pink, a $20 car ferry that takes cash or check, and turtles sunning on a stump in a Clayton pond.
### Q. What are some cities and towns near St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  On the Missouri side, Clayton, Chesterfield and Fenton are in St. Louis County, Arnold is in Jefferson County, and O’Fallon and Wentzville are in St. Charles County. Across the river in Illinois are Belleville, Alton, Edwardsville and Collinsville. Ste. Genevieve is about an hour south. For O’Fallon lights questions, call the city at 636-240-2000.

## Things to Do in Maryland Heights, MO: Free Blues Practices, Fee Fee Greenway, Bike to the Katy Trail
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-maryland-heights-mo
The lists skipped this. On most weekday mornings during the NHL regular season, the St. Louis Blues practice on a rink off Casino Center Drive in Maryland Heights, and anyone can walk in and watch. No ticket. No charge. Don’t take a group chat’s word for it, either: Centene Community Ice Center’s practice viewing page says so in plain words.
Now look at what the recycled lists for this town still recommend. Search for things to do in Maryland Heights and you’ll get pointed to two zipline parks. RYZE Adventure Park, the four-story tower off Grace Church Road, closed for good in September 2026 after four seasons. Go Ape, the treetop course in Creve Coeur Park, says on its own location page that it’s closed for the 2026 season. Both still float near the top of the results. Neither one will let you in.
That’s how it goes with the small towns outside St. Louis. Most people know Maryland Heights as the place they sit in amphitheater traffic. The people who live here know a shady creek trail that runs all the way to the Katy, a vault of Gold Glove Awards you can walk into, and a national wildlife refuge unit inside city limits. Everything below was checked against city, county, federal and venue pages in October 2026, and anything closed is labeled closed.
### What is there to do in Maryland Heights, MO?
In Maryland Heights, you can watch the St. Louis Blues practice free on most regular-season weekday mornings at Centene Community Ice Center, bike the Fee Fee Greenway through Creve Coeur Park and across the Missouri River to the Katy Trail, try bats in the free Rawlings Experience, and walk a national wildlife refuge unit inside city limits.
Start with the hockey, because it’s the one nobody believes. Centene’s page says the Blues practice most days of the week on the NHL Rink between 9:30 a.m. and noon during the regular season. Admission is free and tickets aren’t required. You walk in, find a seat, and watch an NHL team run drills from a few rows back.
Read the fine print before you burn a vacation morning on it. The team’s schedule is fluid, and day-of cancellations happen. The Blues can close any practice to the public without notice. They won’t be at Centene on travel days or home game days, practices and pregame skates at Enterprise Center downtown are closed, and visiting teams’ practices are closed too. Everyone goes through a security search at the door. Rink staff can’t tell you who’ll skate or whether a given practice is open, so check the practice schedule and the Blues’ game calendar the night before, and bring a backup plan.
The backup plan is in the same building. Public skating runs almost daily, year-round, at $12 general admission, $5 for Maryland Heights residents and $5 for skate rental, and sessions often land around lunchtime, right after practice wraps. Confirm the session on Centene’s calendar first. If you want to compare rinks, our guide to what ice skating costs in St. Louis lines up every public option in the region.
The building itself opened in 2019 and cost $83 million, and the city co-owns it with St. Louis County. Its covered outdoor rink, called The Barn, turns into the 4,500-capacity Saint Louis Music Park every spring. Hockey in winter. Concerts in summer. Same roof.
After the rink, the rest of the answer splits by what you came for. Riders and walkers want the Fee Fee Greenway and its car-free route to the Katy Trail. Anyone on a budget wants the free list, which runs longer than you’d guess. Rainy days, nights out, the dog and December each get a section of their own. One more thing for the trivia crowd: before it was Maryland Heights, this was Mokeville, named for a blacksmith called George Moke. It became Castello in 1900, and the Maryland Heights name, chosen because settlers from Maryland said the rolling hills looked like home, was made official in 1914. The city didn’t incorporate until 1985. Our Maryland Heights city guide covers the neighborhoods and local businesses; this page sticks to what to do.
### Where does the Fee Fee Greenway go?
From the Maryland Heights Community Center to Creve Coeur Lake, and from there, if your legs agree, all the way to the Katy Trail. Great Rivers Greenway’s Fee Fee Greenway page puts it at 2.74 miles: a shady, paved trail that runs through McKelvey Woods along Fee Fee Creek and ends in Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park. The city’s parks page rounds it to three miles and notes it used to be called the McKelvey Woods Trail. It was the first public off-road trail Maryland Heights helped build, paid for partly with federal grants.
Where to start. The north trailhead is on McKelvey Woods Court, beside Aquaport and the Dogport dog park, close to the Community Center at 2300 McKelvey Road. The best place to park and regroup is McKelvey Woods Park, at 2480 McKelvey Woods Ct., which has restrooms, a playground, a pavilion with picnic tables and a spot to grill. Great Rivers Greenway also lists drinking water, shelters and trash cans along the route. The south end drops you into Creve Coeur Park by the Marine Avenue parking lot.
What it’s like. Paved, shaded and quiet, with the creek beside you much of the way. Great Rivers Greenway calls it “perfect for a dog walk,” and it works just as well with a stroller or a kid on training wheels.
Who runs which part. This matters for hours and rules. Maryland Heights Parks manages the stretch from Aquaport to Rule Avenue, and St. Louis County Parks takes it from Rule Avenue to the Marine Avenue lot. City parks are open sunrise to sunset, so plan your walk in daylight. Great Rivers Greenway posted in February 2026 that new wayfinding signs are going in between the Fee Fee, the Creve Coeur Connector, the Centennial Greenway and the lake loops. The trail stays open while crews work, so follow their directions where you see them.
The name. Fee Fee Creek is named for Nicholas Beaugenou Jr., a settler nicknamed Fifi who farmed along its bank in 1795, according to the State Historical Society’s place-names file. That’s why a creek in St. Louis County sounds like it was named after a poodle.
Where it ends. At Creve Coeur Lake. The lake loop, the boat rentals and the old rowing history are the next town’s story, and our guide to fishing at Creve Coeur Lake covers them, along with the Historic Aircraft Restoration Museum nearby. For this page, the park is the hinge. From here, the Creve Coeur Connector picks up the route and heads for the river.
### Can you bike from Creve Coeur Park to the Katy Trail?
Yes, and the last stretch is the best part. The Creve Coeur Park Connector Trail carries you from the park to the Page Avenue (Route 364) bridge, and that bridge has its own walking and biking lane across the Missouri River. On the far side it meets the Katy Trail at mile 42.8, just south of the Family Arena in St. Charles County.
Halfway across, there’s a bump-out in the lane where you can stop and look straight down at the Missouri. Great Rivers Greenway put it on its list of the best river views in the region, and it’s a view nobody in the car lanes beside you gets to enjoy.
How far is the whole trip? Great Rivers Greenway lists the Connector at 3.6 miles on one page and 4.7 on another, so the ride from the Community Center to the Katy runs somewhere between 6.3 and 7.5 miles one way. Check the GRG map before you plan your water. BikeKatyTrail.com puts the bridge span at about 0.6 miles and warns about the quarter-mile switchback ramp that drops you to the trail on the St. Charles side. Save something for climbing it on the way home.
Once you’re on the Katy, you’re on the longest developed rail-trail in the country: 240 miles of the old Missouri-Kansas-Texas railroad bed, open sunrise to sunset, according to Missouri State Parks. That sets your clock. Leave enough daylight to ride back over the bridge and down the greenway.
Check Great Rivers Greenway’s trail alerts before a long ride. On the St. Charles side, part of the Centennial Greenway has been rerouted onto Hemsath Road, and sign crews are still working around Creve Coeur Park.
Back from the Katy and starving? Where to eat in Maryland Heights
### What can you do for free in Maryland Heights?
More than the lists suggest. The Blues practices and the greenway cost nothing. So do these.
The Rawlings Experience. Rawlings moved its world headquarters to Westport Plaza, and the public side of it, at 462 W. Port Plaza Dr., is a roughly 14,000-square-foot space you can walk into. St. Louis County called it a free attraction when it opened in April 2024. Inside is the Glove Vault, with current and historic Rawlings Gold Glove Awards and game-day gloves from past legends and current MLB players. There’s a giant Gold Glove statue to pose with and a Hit Lab where you can demo Rawlings and Easton bats. Designing a custom glove with a master glove craftsman costs money. Looking doesn’t. Hours run 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday, 10 to 8 Monday through Thursday and 10 to 9 Friday and Saturday. Ask the staff about Hit Lab time when you walk in.
A national wildlife refuge unit, inside city limits. In 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service bought about 500 acres of Missouri River bottomland in Maryland Heights for the Howard Bend Unit of the Big Muddy National Fish and Wildlife Refuge. To get in, drive about three-quarters of a mile down John Pellet Court to a gravel lot at the base of the levee, park, and walk over the levee into the unit. It’s foot traffic and hand carts only, no bikes, and the refuge’s own visitor page says there’s no charge to visit. Bring binoculars; eBird tracks it as a birding hotspot. Three cautions. It’s a public hunting area under a city permit, so wear something bright in the fall. The refuge warns that its units can flood from rain far upstream. And cell service is spotty. A few miles upriver, Big Muddy’s Boone’s Crossing Unit has a one-mile loop off the Monarch Levee Trail, one more reason to keep our list of places to walk around Chesterfield handy.
A garden you’re meant to explore with your eyes closed. Vago Park, at 2700 Fee Fee Rd., holds the Judy Barnett Memorial Scented Garden, dedicated in 2011 to the councilwoman often called the Mother of Maryland Heights for her work getting the city incorporated. The city asks you to cover your eyes and identify the plants by touch and smell, to get a small sense of what neighbors with visual disabilities live with every day. The rest of the 20-acre park is free too: a splash pad, a lighted ballfield, five horseshoe pits, a walking track and three playgrounds.
An outdoor gym nobody charges for. Quiet Hollow Park, at 12469 McKelvey Rd., has a Fitness Court, an outdoor bodyweight gym with 30 pieces of equipment and room for 28 people at once, plus a free app that walks you through 4 to 7 minute workouts. The city’s Beautification Commission is choosing a Missouri artist to paint a mural on its training wall, expected late fall to early winter 2026. There are no restrooms, and parking is tight.
A short trail for bird-watching. McKelvey Woods Nature Park, at 2530 McKelvey Rd., is a short walking trail that ends at a quiet spot to sit and watch birds. Pair it with the greenway, which starts nearby.
Musick Baptist Church. The congregation began in 1811 on land Rev. Thomas Musick gave the people he enslaved for a church. They built a log cabin on the spot where the church and its cemetery still stand, and historians note it as the oldest Black church west of the Mississippi. It’s an active church, not a museum, so the respectful way to visit is a Sunday service. Call ahead for service times. The mayor proclaims October 8 as Musick Baptist Church Day every year.
Free fall dates (2026; check current dates). The Fall Family Fair at Vago Park was set for Saturday, Oct. 17, from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., with free pony rides, hayrides, a petting zoo, pumpkin painting and a kids’ costume contest at noon. Westport Plaza’s Halloween Parade, for kids 10 and under, is set to step off at 6 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29, followed by a free outdoor double feature of Hotel Transylvania 1 and 2. In summer, watch for the city’s free concert series at Vago and Parkwood parks, and in spring for WorldFest, a free one-day festival at the Saint Louis Music Park.
### What can you do in Maryland Heights on a rainy day?
Go back to the rink. A rainy weekday is the perfect excuse to catch a Blues practice in the morning and stay for the lunchtime public skate, both under one roof. Same caveat as above: check the practice schedule and the skate calendar first.
Swim under a zip line. The Indoor Aquatic Center at the Community Center, 2300 McKelvey Rd., packs a lot into 9,000 square feet: three lap lanes, a zero-entry leisure pool, a current channel, a 4-foot drop slide, climbing walls and a kids’ area. You don’t need a membership. A Community Center day pass runs $15 for adults and $13 for youth 4 to 13 or seniors 62 and up at the general rate. Two rules worth knowing before you promise anything to a kid: swimmers have to pass a swim test to use the rock wall and the zip line, and the drop slide takes a swim test plus a height of 48 inches. Children 11 and under need an adult with them. Open swim times shift, so check the schedule.
Pumpkins in the pool. In mid-October, the Pumpkin Plunge floats a patch of pumpkins in that same indoor pool and lets kids swim out to pick one. In 2026 it was set for Friday, Oct. 16, with ages 6 and under at 5 p.m. and ages 7 to 12 at 6:30 p.m., for $20 at the general rate. Register ahead.
Climb indoors. Upper Limits, at 1874 Lackland Hill Pkwy., has more than 14,500 square feet of climbing surface and a Top Rope 101 class for first-timers.
See a show in an office tower. The Westport Playhouse is a 240-seat theater on the second floor of Westport’s Gold tower, with free parking. It has operated at the plaza since the 1970s, went dark for two years after the pandemic and reopened in fall 2022 under new management. Use thewestportplayhouse.com for current shows. An older web address for the theater now leads somewhere else entirely.
### What is there to do in Maryland Heights at night?
Westport Plaza after dark, plus a concert stage with a stranger history than most people know.
A $5.75 Tuesday. The Funny Bone, at 614 W. Port Plaza Dr., has booked comics here since 1984. Its Tuesday open mic costs $5.75 all-in, with doors at 7 p.m. and the show at 7:30 on the current calendar. Weekend headliners run roughly $11.50 to $23 on the October 2026 listings, and the club slips in an occasional free show. Prices move, so check the calendar.
Jazz next door. Backstreet Jazz & Blues shares the address and opens Thursday through Saturday from 8 p.m. to 1 a.m. and Sunday from 8 to 11:30 p.m. The city describes local performers, karaoke, open mic and trivia nights there. Confirm the night’s act and any cover before you go.
A drink on the roof. 360 Westport, in Suite 1200 at 111 West Port Plaza, is the rooftop bar. It opens at 4 p.m. daily and stays open until 11 on Sunday and Monday and 1 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday. The plaza pitches it for an intimate date, which is fair.
Bingo in a cowboy hat. Wild West Bingo at the Community Center is 21 and over, with costumes encouraged and outside food and drinks welcome. In 2026 it was set for Friday, Nov. 6, from 7 to 9:30 p.m. The city’s fall guide lists it at about $20 general. Register ahead.
The amphitheater’s other names. Hollywood Casino Amphitheater opened in summer 1991 as Riverport, with Steve Winwood on the first bill. Weeks later, a Guns N’ Roses show there ended in what locals still call the Riverport Riot. It has since been UMB Bank Pavilion and Verizon Wireless Amphitheater, and it took its current name in 2014. The city counts 7,000 seats plus lawn room for 13,000 more.
The stage that came first. In 1940, coal merchant A.J. Bolton opened Bolton’s Oak Grove in what’s now Maryland Heights, a private park where Black St. Louisans could swim, dance and hear music when much of the region was segregated. It booked Count Basie, Chuck Berry, Ike and Tina Turner and B.B. King. It no longer operates, and the city tells its story in its own entertainment history. Think about that the next time you’re stuck in amphitheater traffic.
### Is the Maryland Heights dog park free?
No, and that catches people off guard. Dogport, at 2490 McKelvey Woods Ct., runs on a membership key fob. A yearly membership costs $40 for residents and $70 for non-residents, or $20 and $35 for a partial year after July 1, with extra dogs from the same household at $10 or $15 each. Memberships bought in 2026 are good until Dec. 31, 2026. To join, bring proof of rabies and Bordetella shots, plus spay or neuter confirmation, to the Community Center.
The park has been rebuilt. It opened in 2006, then a historic amount of rain in the summer of 2022 sent Fee Fee Creek over its banks and washed away the old pink granules. The city put down sod that can take heavy traffic, added shade structures and concrete paths, and reopened it with the fob system.
The free option starts right beside it: the Fee Fee Greenway, which runs from Dogport into McKelvey Woods. Leash up and walk it. Westport Bark brings adoptable dogs, training tips, giveaways and a doggie playground to Westport Plaza; in 2026 it was set for Saturday, Oct. 24, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. And Aquaport closes its pool season with Dog Days of Summer, a dogs-only swim with vaccine records required, where the people stay out of the water. The 2027 date wasn’t set as of October 2026.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Maryland Heights?
On a map the city makes for you. Light It Up Maryland Heights is the city’s holiday decorating contest, and every home that enters goes on one public Light It Up map, so you can plan your own route and vote for a favorite. According to the city’s Light It Up announcement, 2026 applications are set to open Nov. 17 and close in mid-December, with judging Dec. 14 to 20 by elected officials and the community. Winners get a yard sign. Drive slowly, stay on public streets and keep it quiet. These are people’s homes.
The season starts with a tree. The Holiday Tree Lighting gathers outside the Community Center; in 2026 it was set for Friday, Dec. 4, at 5:30 p.m. Santa arrives at 6 and lights the tree, and then the building turns into a Winter Wonderland with food, photos and crafts until 8:30. The indoor pool closes at 4 that day, so don’t plan a swim first. Reading this after Dec. 4? Ask the Community Center for next year’s date.
A month earlier in 2026, on Friday, Nov. 6, Westport Plaza is set to show The Polar Express outdoors, with the movie starting at 7 p.m. Bring a blanket. And for the record, Aquaport runs a summer swim with Santa called Jingle Jangle, which tells you how seriously this town takes the holidays.
For the big shows, our guide to drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis lists the region’s best, and the Christmas lights in St. Charles are just across the Page Avenue bridge.
Next time somebody says there’s nothing in Maryland Heights but the casino, you’re the one who knows the Blues skate there on a Tuesday morning, the creek trail runs to the Katy, and the Gold Gloves cost nothing to see. Check the practice schedule. Pump up the tires. Go.
After practice or a ride over the river, our guide to where to eat in Maryland Heights covers the lakeside grill on the Creve Coeur Park trail, a hot-salami walk-up window and the hibachi tables at Westport.
If you run a bike rental, a skate shop or a coffee counter near Centene, where fans kill time between practice and public skate, list it with us so they find you that morning.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where is the best place to start the Katy Trail?
A.  From the St. Louis County side, start at McKelvey Woods Park or the Maryland Heights Community Center, ride the Fee Fee Greenway into Creve Coeur Park, pick up the Creve Coeur Connector and cross the Missouri on the Page Avenue bridge lane. It meets the Katy at mile 42.8, just south of the Family Arena in St. Charles County. No bike rack on the car required.
### Q. Is Katy Trail safe early morning?
A.  Early morning on the Katy officially starts at sunrise. Missouri State Parks lists Katy Trail State Park as open sunrise to sunset, and Maryland Heights city parks keep the same hours. For a first-light ride, run front and rear lights, carry a phone, ride with a friend if you can, and tell someone your route and when you expect to be back.
### Q. What is Katy Trail known for?
A.  Being the longest developed rail-trail in the country. Missouri State Parks says it runs 240 miles on the old Missouri-Kansas-Texas (MKT, or Katy) railroad corridor, with 26 trailheads and four fully restored depots, and most of it follows the Missouri River. It joined the Rails-to-Trails Conservancy Hall of Fame in 2008.
### Q. Where is the best Christmas light trail?
A.  In Maryland Heights, it’s the one you build from the city’s Light It Up map. Every home entered in the contest goes on one public map, so you can tour them in any order and vote for a favorite. In 2026, applications are set to open Nov. 17, with judging Dec. 14 to 20, so plan your tour for mid-December, once entries close.
### Q. What free events are on today near me?
A.  In Maryland Heights, check the city’s events calendar and Westport Plaza’s event page the day you go. Free fall 2026 dates: the Fall Family Fair at Vago Park on Oct. 17, the Westport Halloween Parade and outdoor double feature on Oct. 29, and outdoor movie nights at Westport on Oct. 30 and Nov. 6. On most regular-season mornings, the Blues practice free at Centene too.
### Q. What are unique free attractions in St. Louis?
A.  Three in Maryland Heights that most St. Louis lists skip: Blues practices at Centene Community Ice Center, with no ticket needed; the Rawlings Experience at Westport Plaza, with its Glove Vault and Hit Lab; and the Howard Bend Unit of the Big Muddy National Fish and Wildlife Refuge, which costs nothing to visit. Add Vago Park’s scented garden, built to be explored with your eyes closed.
### Q. Are the zipline parks in Maryland Heights still open?
A.  No. RYZE Adventure Park, the four-story tower off Grace Church Road, closed for good after four seasons, the Post-Dispatch reported in September 2026. Go Ape in Creve Coeur Park lists itself as closed for the 2026 season. If you want height, Upper Limits has more than 14,500 square feet of indoor climbing walls.
### Q. Can you swim at the Maryland Heights Community Center without a membership?
A.  Yes. A day pass covers the 9,000-square-foot Indoor Aquatic Center at 2300 McKelvey Rd. At the general rate it’s $15 for adults, $13 for youth 4 to 13 or seniors 62 and up, and $5 for toddlers. Swimmers must pass a swim test to use the climbing wall and zip line. Open swim times vary, so check the schedule before you go.

## Things to Do in Collinsville, IL: The Catsup Bottle the City Turned Down
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-collinsville-il
Workers swung their baskets around a riveted steel catsup bottle more than 100 feet in the air, scraping off old lead paint, and the painters who followed did the job by hand, hanging from cables. The bottle’s shape wouldn’t take scaffolding, so there was no other way to do it. That was April 1995 in Collinsville, and the people paying for it weren’t the city.
The city had already said no. When the plant’s parent company decided to sell the property in 1993, Brooks was willing to deed the water tower to Collinsville, and the city declined, citing the cost of repairing and repainting it. So volunteers did it the hard way, with bake sales, auctions and more than 6,000 T-shirts and sweatshirts sold across the country. The lowest bid came in at three times the first guess. They raised it anyway.
On the evening of June 3, 1995, after a parade down Main Street, they lit the bottle. Red, white and blue steel, glowing over a town that hadn’t wanted to pay for it. Collinsville’s catsup bottle is the landmark the city turned down, and the neighbors saved it with T-shirt money.
It mattered across the river, too. At one time, in the greater St. Louis area, Brooks catsup outsold all other brands combined, 2 to 1, and old-timers in town still lament the sweet smell of catsup that no longer wafts through the streets. You can’t smell it anymore. You can still stand under it at 800 S. Morrison, just off Route 159, crane your neck at a 70-foot bottle on 100-foot legs, and feel a little proud of people you never met.
That’s the thread through this whole town, and it’s why the usual top-ten lists miss it. The best stops here are things somebody refused to throw away: a water tower, an old-time farm, even the town dump. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the one the lists rush through fastest, and the first stop, Cahokia Mounds, says it is just eight miles from downtown St. Louis.
### What are some fun things to do in Collinsville, Illinois this weekend?
Start free. Climb the stairway up 100-foot Monks Mound at Cahokia Mounds, which charges no admission or parking fee; meet the donkeys and goats at Willoughby Heritage Farm, free and open 9 a.m. to dusk; then fish or throw disc golf at Woodland Park, built on the city’s first landfill. Finish under the 170-foot catsup bottle at 800 S. Morrison.
Do it in that order and the day follows the sun. The mound grounds open at dawn. The farm, at 631 Willoughby Lane, opens at 9. Woodland Park is at 2 Pine Lake Road. Save the bottle for last, while you can still see the top of it against the sky. Pack a leash, a rod and a disc if you own one.
### Climb Monks Mound first, while your legs are fresh
Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site carries a Collinsville address, 30 Ramey Street, and it’s the reason to come early. Visitors may climb a stairway to the top of Monks Mound, which the site lists as 100 feet high and the largest earthwork in North America. Your calves will feel every step. At the top, interpretive signs explain what you’re standing on: the center of a city that, around 1100, stretched over 4,000 acres with about 120 earthen mounds and nearly 20,000 people, larger than London at that time.
There is no admission or parking fee. The grounds and trails are open daily from dawn until dusk, dogs are welcome on a leash, and restrooms and water fountains wait in the Monks Mound parking lot. The Interpretive Center lobby, with its gift shop, site model and canoe exhibit, is open Wednesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., while the site works on its exhibits. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
Leave time for the flat ground, too. The state’s historic sites division points to a reconstructed stockade wall and Woodhenge, a circle of posts around a large central post from which the sunrise can be aligned to determine the season. Stand in that circle and the open sky does the explaining. Of the original 120 mounds, the site preserves 70, so the walk between them is longer than it looks from the parking lot.
### The park that used to be the town dump
Woodchip paths climb and dip through the trees at Woodland Park, 2 Pine Lake Road. Bridges cross the lake and its little streams. Feeding the ducks is right on the tourism bureau’s to-do list for the place. Nothing about it says garbage. But the Metro East Park and Recreation District’s page mentions, almost in passing, that the parkland was at one time the site of a landfill, the city’s first. After it closed, the ground became 47 acres with four playgrounds, several baseball fields, pavilions and public restrooms.
The disc golf course is the draw for grown-ups. The park district calls it highly lauded, and the tourism bureau lists 18 holes over 1,645 yards with concrete tees and DISCatcher targets. That works out to about 91 yards a hole, a friendly length for a first round with one borrowed disc. Leashed dogs are welcome. The tourism bureau lists hours of 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., so check the sign at the entrance before an evening round.
Stand on one of those lake bridges knowing what’s underneath, and the place looks different. Somebody decided the town dump could become a park people drive in for. Then it did.
### Is Willoughby Heritage Farm really free?
Yes. The park district’s page puts it in capital letters: general admission is FREE to the public. Hours run 9 a.m. to dusk. Chickens, goats and donkeys live here, and the farmyard sounds like it.
The tourism bureau describes it as a return to farm life in the 1940s, with barns, tractors, a Craftsman-style farmhouse and 30 acres of wildlife preserve behind it. Hiking trails follow winding paths and cross bridges, and the park district warns that some of them are challenging and hilly, which makes the bench at the end feel earned. Kids get a playground and a gaga ball pit. Bring the dog on a leash.
The farmhouse keeps shorter hours, Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Primitive camping is allowed with a reservation, guided tours are available for groups by appointment, and the farm’s phone is 618-977-0941.
### Where can you fish near Collinsville without a boat?
Start at Woodland Park. The park district lists a fishing dock on the lake, and the playgrounds sit close by for anyone who loses interest after ten minutes. It’s a quiet hour with a bobber, or a kid’s first cast. Read any posted rules at the dock before you keep a fish.
Up Route 159, the same question gets a different answer. See fishing in Edwardsville without a boat.
Want to sleep near the water? How to book a campsite near St. Louis
### A recipe printed on a historical marker
Walk West Main Street and look for the giant horseradish root. Its marker, erected in 2026, says the sculpture is 14 feet wide. The same marker calls Collinsville the Horseradish Capital of the World and prints a recipe for Easy Shrimp Cocktail Sauce: half a cup of chili sauce, half a cup of catsup, a quarter cup of prepared horseradish, and a tablespoon each of lemon juice and Worcestershire sauce. Blend and chill. Few historical markers double as a recipe card, and this one ties both of the town’s condiments together in five lines.
The marker also explains why the root grows here. Collinsville is a bluff community, and the lowlands below are rich in potash, a key nutrient for horseradish. Taste fresh-ground horseradish and you’ll feel it in your sinuses before your tongue catches up.
### The rest of the catsup bottle story
The fundraiser was bigger than it looked from the street. A 14-member preservation group ran it. The first guess for the job was around $28,000, and the restoration came in at $77,440, done by Diversified Coatings of O’Fallon with paint donated by the Tnemec Company of Kansas City. There was enough left over to start a maintenance fund and buy a flood light so the bottle could glow after dark.
The brand had its own drama. It was sold as “Brooks Tabasco Flavor Catsup” until the McIlhenny Tabasco Company threatened a lawsuit, so the Suppigers changed the name to “Brooks Old Original Tangy Catsup.” Catsup bottling moved to Indiana in the early 1960s. The bottle stayed.
### What is there to do in Collinsville for Halloween?
October here is a farm calendar, not a haunted-house industry. Willoughby Farm holds Fall Farm Day, which the tourism bureau lists with 40 vendors, activities for kids and adults, and fall foods and sweets. The farm also runs a barn dance in spring and fall, with dance instruction and three hours of dancing, line dancing included. Dates move every year, so check the farm’s events listing in September and plan around it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is there a ketchup bottle in Collinsville, IL?
A.  Because it was a water tower. The W.E. Caldwell Company built it for the Brooks catsup plant, and it was completed in October 1949 to supply water for plant operations and a new fire sprinkler system. Company president Gerhart S. Suppiger suggested the shape. It’s a 70-foot riveted steel bottle on 100-foot steel legs, 170 feet in all, with a capacity of 100,000 gallons, at 800 S. Morrison just off Route 159. Volunteers finished restoring it in June 1995, and in August 2002 it was named to the National Register of Historic Places.
### Q. Who is the most famous person from Collinsville, Illinois?
A.  You’ll hear a few names around town, but we couldn’t confirm one from a primary source, so we won’t guess. The resident every visitor already knows needs no source: it’s 170 feet tall, made of riveted steel, and the city once turned it down.
### Q. Is there an aqua park in Collinsville, Illinois?
A.  Yes, the Collinsville Aqua Park at 10 Gateway Drive. Its centerpiece is Monsoon Mountain, a 50-foot water castle with five slides and a bucket on top that holds 500 gallons and dumps it on the kids, or unsuspecting parents, every five minutes. The lazy river runs in a figure-eight pattern, the leisure pool has zero-depth entry, and there’s a 12-foot Aqua Climb wall over the deep end of the lap pool. Parking and life jacket rentals are free.
### Q. Where is the horseradish capital of the world located?
A.  Collinsville, Illinois. The city’s horseradish marker says the town produces roughly 60% of the global supply, that German immigrants brought the crop in the 1800s, and that the city has hosted the International Horseradish Festival the first weekend in June since 1987.
### Q. Which state grows the most horseradish?
A.  Illinois. St. Louis Public Radio, citing the U.S. Department of Agriculture, reported that just 16 Illinois growers harvest horseradish from 1,779 acres, about 60 percent of the nation’s horseradish.
### Q. How far is Collinsville, IL from STL?
A.  Close. Cahokia Mounds, which carries a Collinsville address, says it is just eight miles from downtown St. Louis. The rest of town is a short drive on, and the marker on West Main calls Collinsville a bluff community.

## Things to Do in Brentwood, MO: Free Brentwood Park, a Lost Neighborhood, Glow Skating
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-brentwood-mo
Who lived here before the parking lot? Ask that at the Brentwood Promenade and you’ll mostly get a shrug, because every copy-paste list of things to do in Brentwood, MO, sends you there to shop and stops. Walk around to the back of the Micro Center instead, to Rose Avenue. Two brick pillars stand there. Former residents unveiled them in July 2023 to mark Evans Howard Place, a neighborhood that stood on that ground from the early 1900s until 1997.
That’s the Brentwood the lists miss. The whole city covers less than two square miles and about 8,100 people, and most of the region knows it as the traffic around the I-64 and I-170 interchange. Inside those lines sit a free 32-acre park built to flood on purpose, a playground zip line that exists because an 8-year-old booked a meeting with the parks director, glow-skate Friday nights at a city rink, a skating club older than the 1904 World’s Fair, and a dog park on the street that was built over an old brickworks. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, Brentwood may be the one people drive straight through most often.
Everything below was checked against City of Brentwood, Great Rivers Greenway and local news sources in October 2026. It’s all Brentwood, Missouri, in St. Louis County. Search results mix it up with Brentwood, Tennessee, and Brentwood, California, constantly, so if a listing names another state, it isn’t this one.
### Is Brentwood Park free to enter in Brentwood, MO?
Yes. Brentwood Park, at 2924 Brazeau Ave. in Brentwood, MO, charges no admission and is open sunrise to sunset year-round. Its 32 acres hold a 2.7-acre destination playground with a zip line, a splash pad that recycles its water, an amphitheater, a lake with no fishing or swimming, and a Deer Creek Greenway connector.
The only things that cost money are the pavilions you can reserve. The city’s park page lists no entry fee at all, just sunrise to sunset hours, and reservations for the Event Pavilion and the Destination Playground Pavilion go through the Brentwood Community Center at 314-963-8689. Check that page before a summer visit for anything seasonal, such as splash pad hours.
The playground the kids asked for. When Brentwood surveyed residents about the new park land, a destination playground was the No. 1 request, St. Louis Magazine reported. It opened April 6, 2024, cost about $7 million, and two of its pieces came straight from kids. The viking swing was the parks director’s daughter’s idea. The zip line is there because an 8-year-old boy in town set up a meeting with parks director Eric Gruenenfelder to make the case for one. He got it.
The splash pad is a model of the creek. It was designed as a nod to the Deer Creek watershed. Press an activation pillar and the water runs for 10 to 15 minutes, the whole water feature tops out at 6 inches deep, and a reclamation tower recycles all of the playground’s water. Around it you’ll find a three-story net climber, a climbing wall, hopping logs, a roller slide designed with kids who have cochlear implants in mind, and paths that add up to a full 5K. Solar panels sit on the all-seasons pavilion. Parents get benches and the shade of about 250 newly planted trees.
Why build a park that’s meant to flood? Because that’s its other job. Brentwood Park came out of Brentwood Bound, a $79.6 million flood fix along Deer Creek between Brentwood Boulevard and Hanley Road. The city says the lower part of the park, along the creek, is designed to hold water the way a natural floodplain would. A Brentwood Historical Society photo from the 1950s shows Manchester Road underwater at Dorothy Avenue. Now the creek has room to spread out, and the playground sits on the high ground above it.
Where to park. This is the catch. The lot in front of the Event Pavilion fills fast on nice days, so the city points overflow to Russell Avenue, the Brentwood Sports Complex, the Community Center, and two gravel lots off Manchester Road: 23 marked spots reached from Dorothy Avenue and 68 from Bompart Avenue. From those, cross Brentwood Boulevard at the traffic light just south of Russell, by the Metro garage. The lot at 8700 Manchester is private, so skip it. Driving straight in? The city says to enter from Brentwood Boulevard via East Pendleton Avenue and turn right on Brazeau.
Summer nights. The park also hosts free Family Nights. In 2026 they fell on one Friday a month in June, July and August, with food trucks from 5:30 p.m. and live music at 7. The season is over for this year, so watch the city calendar for next summer’s dates.
### What stood where the Brentwood Promenade is now?
A whole neighborhood: Evans Howard Place covered the ground where the Brentwood Promenade shopping center sits today, off Brentwood Boulevard near the I-64 and I-170 interchange in Brentwood, MO. It grew from the early 1900s around a fire-brick works run by the Evens & Howard Fire Brick Co. The company spelled it Evens; the neighborhood is usually written Evans. KMOV traced the first homes to 1907, built for brickworks employees, and the memorial marker counts families living there from 1917 to 1997.
Many of its families were Black families who had come north in the Great Migration, and a small group of Italian immigrants lived on Evans Avenue. The early houses were often called two by twos: two rooms on each side, no basement, and at first no electricity or indoor plumbing. Kids went to L’Ouverture School on Rose Avenue, which opened in 1925 and ran through eighth grade, then on to Brentwood High. Families filled the pews at New Hope Missionary Baptist and Brentwood Temple Church of God in Christ. Allison Reed, who grew up there in the 1960s, told St. Louis Public Radio that everybody knew everybody and the kids were inside before the streetlights came on.
The brickworks burned in 1968, and Hanley Industrial Court was built on its site. Then came the highway plans. In 1977 an interchange redesign would have torn down about 50 homes, and residents and local officials worked to block it. In the late 1980s and early 1990s MoDOT proposed pushing I-170 south to I-44, and that was stopped too.
In 1995 the shopping center was proposed, and how it came about depends on who’s telling it. Ed Holt, who lived there 55 years and led the Evans Place neighborhood association, told KMOV in 2024 that residents saw a highway and eminent domain coming, organized, and chose a commercial buyout on their own terms, and he rejects the idea that anyone took the neighborhood from them. About 90 percent of residents agreed to sell, many for three to four times their homes’ $30,000 to $40,000 value, and only one house went by eminent domain. Not every neighbor saw it that way. One resident, in a Post-Dispatch archive clipping KMOV published with its report, called it “gentrification turned genocide.” Both views come from people who lived there.
The first memorial, in 1998, was a plaque on a small rock near the shopping center’s exit, tucked between a lighting store and a liquor market. Reed told St. Louis Public Radio she didn’t know it existed until a push to replace it began around 2019, and the plaque eventually fell off. Former residents shaped the new one. On July 8, 2023, they gathered to unveil brick pillars built to call back the brick company, with a marker telling the neighborhood’s story, on Rose Avenue behind the Micro Center. Rose Avenue is the same street L’Ouverture School stood on.
How to see it. Park on the Micro Center side of the Promenade and walk around back to Rose Avenue, east of Brentwood Boulevard. It takes five minutes. The marker’s page on the Historical Marker Database has been viewed fewer than 200 times since it went up in December 2024, which tells you how few people know to look. Afterward, Hanley Industrial Court, the street on the old brickworks site, is a short drive away. It’s where the city dog park is today, and where a rum distillery opened in 2020. Both are below.
It isn’t the only name Brentwood lost. Until 1919 the town was Maddenville, after Thomas Madden, who arrived in the 1870s and ran a rock quarry, a tavern, a barbershop, a grocery and a blacksmith shop on the old Manchester Trail. When residents learned Maplewood was weighing annexation, they incorporated as the Village of Brentwood on Dec. 15, 1919. Madden’s quarry, near today’s Ace Hardware on Manchester, shook the St. Mary Magdalen school when it blasted, then spent years as the town dump.
### Where can you walk or bike in Brentwood?
Start at Brentwood Park in Brentwood, MO. It’s the west end of the Deer Creek Greenway, a paved path of about 3.6 miles that runs east through Webster Groves to Deer Creek Park and the Deer Creek shopping center in Maplewood. The newest piece is Brentwood’s own: a quarter mile beside Brentwood Boulevard that opened with a public celebration on May 10, 2025. The mayor called it the last piece of Brentwood Bound.
Two things make the Brentwood end worth knowing. An underpass carries the path beneath Manchester Road, tying the park into Brentwood’s neighborhood trails and toward Manchester and Hanley near the Maplewood MetroLink station, so you can come by train. And the paths around the playground add up to a 5K on their own, so a few laps of the park count as a real walk. For the Webster Groves stretch, see our list of free things to do in Webster Groves.
The small-park loop. This is the part visitors never find. Hanley Park’s asphalt trail links Oak Tree Park at its east end, Broughton Park to the south and Memorial Park at its west end. Memorial Park, at 8600 Strassner Dr., is the wooded one: 15.5 acres with nature hiking trails, paved paths, a toddler playground and a youth playground, and an outdoor inline skating rink. It was called Buder Park until a mid-1970s remodel. Oak Tree Park adds an 8-acre stretch with a paved path along a creek. Broughton Park is tiny, about a third of an acre, and back in the 1960s and 1970s the city used to flood it for public skating.
What’s next. Great Rivers Greenway and the cities of Brentwood, Rock Hill, Webster Groves and Ladue are studying a westward extension from Brentwood Park to Tilles Park in Ladue. At open houses in June 2026 they showed three routes, one along Deer Creek, one along Litzsinger Road and a neighborhood connector, and the public backed studying all three. There’s no construction date yet, so for now the greenway stops at the park.
### Is the Brentwood dog park free?
No, the Brentwood Dog Park in Brentwood, MO, is open to registered members only. It’s the fenced, off-leash area in Hanley Park at 610 W. Hanley Industrial Ct., split into a large-dog side and a side for dogs under 30 pounds. That puts it on the street built over the old brickworks from the Promenade story. Search for it and you’ll get dog parks in Tennessee and California, so here are the local rules.
Memberships run through Dec. 31: $25 per dog for residents and $50 per dog for non-residents, with a limit of three dogs per household. Sign up in person at the Brentwood Community Center with payment, current rabies and Bordetella records, spay or neuter paperwork and a signed release. Residents also bring proof of address. For 2026, renewals opened Dec. 1, 2025, new resident members could join from Jan. 2, and new non-residents from Jan. 15. Expect a similar calendar for 2027, and call 314-963-8689 to confirm.
Is it worth it? For a non-resident who comes every week, $50 a year works out to about a dollar a visit. For a one-time run, our guide to the best free dog parks in St. Louis covers off-leash options across the metro. And if your dog will wear a costume, keep reading.

Glow skate starts at 7. Eat first: where to eat in Brentwood, MO
Rink Recess. Skated as a kid and want your edges back? Rink Recess is a 30-minute lunchtime clinic for people who can already get around the ice: stopping, skating backwards, crossovers, inside and outside edges, turning both ways and falling safely. The fall 2026 dates are Tuesdays, Oct. 20 and 27, Nov. 10 and 17, and Dec. 1 and 8, from 11:45 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. Drop in for $12 as a resident or $15 as a non-resident, or pay $60 or $72 for all six. You’re back at your desk by 12:30 with a hockey stop you didn’t have yesterday.
A club older than the World’s Fair. The rink is home ice for the St. Louis Skating Club, founded Dec. 13, 1894, on Post-Dispatch Lake in Forest Park and headquartered in Brentwood today. Its partner club moved into the city’s brand-new rink in 1975, and the current rink opened with the rec center remodel in September 2015. The St. Louis Rockets youth hockey club skates here too.

Courts after work. Hanley Park has pickleball and sand volleyball courts, and it’s where the city’s sand volleyball leagues play. The distillery, with a caveat.
