## Things to Do in Waterloo, IL: Caving at Illinois Caverns, Kayak Lakes, a Stagecoach Inn
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-waterloo-il
Wait past October and the only cave in Illinois that ever sold admission goes dark until mid-April. The recycled Waterloo lists never mention it. They send you to a golf course and a winery, and the most visible online review of the cave still says it’s closed. That review dates to 2019. The cave reopened in June 2021, and its 2026 season opened April 16.
Some orientation first, because search results blur three different Waterloos together. This one is Waterloo, Illinois, the Monroe County seat, about 20 minutes south of downtown St. Louis by the city’s own count. During the 1904 World’s Fair, a steady stream of sightseers came down here by train, rode horse-drawn wagons the last few miles, and paid to walk a cave lit by kerosene lamps. The lamps are long gone. Now you bring your own light, sign a state permit, and walk the same passages with a creek running past your boots.
That cave is the reason to come, and it’s only the start. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Waterloo is the one where the best afternoon happens underground and the rest of the day still fills up: fishing lakes you can paddle, a stagecoach inn, the lawn where Lincoln talked for two hours straight. Everything below was checked against Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR), park district, city and organizer pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do.
### What are some fun things to do in Waterloo, Illinois?
In Waterloo, Illinois, go caving at Illinois Caverns, the wild cave south of town, open Thursday to Sunday from mid-April to late October. Fish or kayak the three old water-works lakes at Lakeview Park, stand on the courthouse lawn where Lincoln spoke in 1840, and tour the Peterstown House, the only surviving stagecoach stop on the Kaskaskia-Cahokia Trail.
Notice what’s missing. Besides Annbriar Golf Course, which the usual lists lead with, Waterloo has a second layer that only shows up when you plan around its calendar. The cave keeps short hours. The historic houses open on weekend afternoons. The lakes run dawn to dusk at no charge. Get the order right and one Sunday covers all of it.
Morning, underground. Illinois Caverns opens at 9 a.m., Thursday through Sunday in season, and nobody goes in after 3 p.m. Go early. You’ll come out wet to the knees and muddy to the elbows, so pack a full change of clothes and a trash bag for the boots.
Midday, downtown. Drive back to the courthouse square for lunch and read the historical markers while you’re there. The one at 114 N. Main St. explains the town’s name, and it’s better than anything on a menu.
Afternoon, 1800s. The Peterstown House on North Main opens 1 to 4 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. On Sundays from May through December, the Bellefontaine House on the south side keeps the same hours, so a Sunday gets you both ends of the rivalry that named the town.
Evening, on the water. Finish with a lap of the 2.25-mile paved loop at Lakeview Park while the anglers pack up. The park closes at dusk.
### What are some interesting caves to visit around St. Louis?
Ask that question online and you mostly get threads about the old lager caves under South St. Louis streets, the ones you can read about and can’t legally walk into. City Museum’s caves were built, not found. The cave at Cliff Cave Park is gated except on ranger-led summer trips. If you want a real cave, mud and all, with no tour guide, the honest answer sits about 35 miles south of the city in the county with more caves than any other in Illinois.
Illinois Caverns State Natural Area is that cave. IDNR calls it the only cave in Illinois that has ever been operated commercially. A bound register kept at the site shows the first paying sightseers arrived April 23, 1901. During the 1904 World’s Fair, IDNR says, a steady stream of curiosity seekers came out to see it, which makes it a strange underground cousin of the buildings left from the 1904 World’s Fair back in the city. When the fair closed, visitors dropped off, and that first business ended in 1907. A second try after 1947 strung electric lights through the main passages and advertised the “Mammoth Cave of Illinois.” The crowds never came. The state bought the 118-acre tract in 1985. Most of the fair was torn down long ago. The cave those fairgoers rode out to see is still open, and it’s darker now than it was then.
What you walk into today is a wild cave. No paved path, no handrails, no lights. IDNR describes about 6 miles of mapped passage with an underground stream winding through it, plus stalactites, stalagmites, rimstone dams, flowstone and soda straws, many of them still growing. It holds near 58 degrees all year. Little brown bats and tricolored bats live inside, along with cave salamanders and the Illinois cave amphipod, a tiny federally endangered crustacean known from only a handful of caves in this corner of the state.
The rules are part of the adventure. You don’t buy a ticket. You fill out an IDNR cave exploration permit at the site, and the form lists no fee. Then the conditions kick in:
At least four people per group. No solo trips, and groups of 25 or more must register with the site ahead of time.
A hard hat or plastic protective headgear for everyone.
Three light sources per person. A headlamp and two flashlights is the usual kit.
Closed-toe shoes with treaded soles, and clothes you’re willing to ruin. IDNR’s own advice is to expect to get wet and muddy.
Anyone under 18 needs a parent or guardian’s signature on the permit, and youth groups need one adult for every five kids.
No entry after 3 p.m. Don’t drink the cave water or let open cuts touch it; the permit warns about bacteria.
The season is the catch. IDNR lists current hours as 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., Thursday through Sunday, mid-April through late October, and site staff close the cave whenever conditions turn unsafe. After late October the gate stays shut until spring, and the bats get the place to themselves. This cave has lost years to bat trouble before. It closed in early 2010 over white-nose syndrome, the fungal disease that has killed bats across the country, and stayed closed until June 16, 2021. That long closure is why stale reviews still call it shut. Call the site at 618-458-6699 before you drive, especially after a heavy rain.
The bigger cave you can’t enter. Monroe County sits on the Sinkhole Plain, which IDNR calls one of the densest concentrations of sinkholes in the country, and the county has more than 100 recorded caves. The largest cave in Illinois is down here too, and it’s permission-only (more on it in the FAQ below). So Illinois Caverns is the one you get. It’s plenty.
Before you go: the address is 4369 G Road, which IDNR files under Waterloo, roughly 7 miles south of the Monroe County Courthouse as the crow flies. Up top there’s a picnic area and trails across restored prairie, so anyone who’d rather not crawl still gets a walk. It’s one of the very few caves near St. Louis you can explore yourself, so treat it that way. The permit’s rule is simple: take nothing out, leave nothing in.
### Where can you fish or kayak in Waterloo, IL?
At the old city water works. Lakeview Park, on the southwest edge of town off Lakeview Drive, was Waterloo’s water works until the city leased it to the park district in 1998. Its three large lakes, Demint, Schorr and Korte, are now open for fishing, and you can paddle them.
Lakeview Park. All three lakes allow fishing with an Illinois license, and there’s a handicapped-accessible fishing dock. The park district’s rules on the water are short. Small boats, canoes and kayaks are allowed. The only motors permitted are electric trolling motors, and every boat launches from an approved area. No swimming, water-skiing or scuba. That adds up to a calm first paddle with no wakes and no jet skis. Bring your own boat.
A 2.25-mile paved loop runs through the park, and it’s for walkers only. Bikes, scooters and skateboards are banned; strollers and wheelchairs are welcome. You’ll also find a butterfly garden, two pickleball courts, the Monroe County Veterans Memorial near the flagpole and gazebo, and the fenced Lakeview Dog Park, the one spot in the park district where a dog can run off leash. Dogs can’t swim in the lakes, so the retriever watches from the bank.
Konarcik Park. It’s east of town off Konarcik Road (Fourth Street), on land the Pupava family gave the park district in 1956. The lake allows fishing with a valid license. The bigger draw is the 18-hole disc golf course, which the park district calls one of the premier courses in the St. Louis area, and it has hosted events that post scores to the Professional Disc Golf Association. There’s also a short walking trail, two sand volleyball courts and six pavilions.
License math. Illinois requires a fishing license on every public lake, these included. Anglers under 16 don’t need one, and during Illinois Free Fishing Days, a long weekend each June (June 19 to 22 in 2026), nobody does. Both parks are free and open dawn to dusk. For more public water closer to the city, see our picks for the best fishing spots in St. Louis.
### Where is the haunted trail in Waterloo, IL?
Out at the Waterloo Sportsman’s Club, 4903 Sportsman Road. The club is private, but it says all of its events are open to the public, and every October it turns its grounds into a Haunted Trail and Hayride. The 2026 nights are Fridays and Saturdays, Oct. 2, 3, 9, 10, 16 and 17, from 7 to 11 p.m. The club’s page lists all ages at $20, though an older line on the same site still says $15, so check before you go. Younger kids get the Pumpkin Express instead of the full scare, and there are concessions and kids’ games while you wait.
Miss those six nights and October still has a run of smaller things, all on the city’s 2026 calendar:
Night at the Museum, Bellefontaine House: Friday, Oct. 9.
PumpkinFest: Saturday, Oct. 10, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Courthouse Square. Bring an item for the charity drive.
Witches Night Out: Thursday, Oct. 15, at participating downtown merchants and restaurants.
“The Story of Exorcism”: Thursday, Oct. 29, 6:30 p.m., at the History Museum of Monroe County.
Trunk-or-Treat: Saturday, Oct. 31, 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. on Courthouse Square.
Events can change, so confirm the week of. And mind the clock. The haunted trail ends in mid-October, the cave season ends late in the month, and neither one waits.
### Can you tour the Peterstown House and Bellefontaine House in Waterloo, IL?
Yes, both, on weekend afternoons, and together they explain how Waterloo got its name. Bellefontaine grew up on the south side and Peterstown on the north, two rival settlements with a creek between them. The legend, told on a marker at 114 N. Main St. and on the city’s history page, says that in 1818 an Irishman named Charles Carroll built his house on one side and his barn on the other and settled the argument: “It won’t be Bellefontaine, and it won’t be Peterstown, but begorra, I’ll give ye’s both your Waterloo.” The name points back to Napoleon’s defeat three years earlier. Treat the Carroll story as a legend. It’s a good one.
The Peterstown House, 275 N. Main St., is the only remaining stagecoach stop on the 60-mile Kaskaskia-Cahokia Trail, the road that linked the old French villages on the river. Its oldest section dates to somewhere between 1815 and 1830, an estimate based on its nine-over-six windows. Over the years it served as an inn, a general store and a tavern, and it later gained a second-floor ballroom and theater. Out back are two century-old log cabins, a watering trough and a hand pump. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1977. The Peterstown Heritage Society opens it Saturdays and Sundays, 1 to 4 p.m., with no reservation needed; groups and school trips book ahead at 618-939-4222. The society doesn’t post admission, so ask when you call, and call ahead in winter, when hours have thinned in past years. Come December, watch its calendar for the Christmas Ball.
The Bellefontaine House, run by the Monroe County Historical Society at 709 S. Church St., sits where Waterloo began. The society says that by spring 1782, Capt. James Moore, an officer under George Rogers Clark, and a group of Revolutionary War veterans had settled at a spring the French called La Bellefontaine, “the beautiful spring.” The society calls it one of the first American settlements in what is now Illinois, and by 1800 it counted 286 people. The house opens Sundays, 1 to 4 p.m., May through December, and closes on some holiday weekends and the last two Sundays in July for the county fair. Near the house stands the 1877 Bellefontaine Bridge, a stone arch over Moore’s Run restored in 2015. Its marker says it connects the only intact stretch of the original Kaskaskia-Cahokia Trail. Ask at the house about seeing it.
The History Museum of Monroe County, 724 Elaine Dr., is the curveball: a Western collection in an Illinois river county. Built around Col. Edd Kueker’s collection, it fills three galleries with saddles, spurs, wagons and a stagecoach, plus a reconstructed 1860s general store. Its posted hours have been weekends 1 to 4 p.m., closing for the season around Dec. 20, with evening programs that start at 6:30, so confirm before you go. The Kuekers also placed the bronze bison on the courthouse grounds in 2014. It honors the herds whose paths became the Kaskaskia-Cahokia Trail, the same road that runs past both houses.

### What are some free things to do in Waterloo, IL?
Most of the best ones. The park district charges no admission to any of its parks or attractions, and the cave permit lists no fee. Add these.
Stand where Lincoln spoke. On Aug. 25, 1840, Abraham Lincoln gave a political speech at the Monroe County Courthouse as a Whig presidential elector. A marker at 114 N. Main St. fills in the rest. He arrived on Sunday, Aug. 23, a notice went up at the courthouse Monday, and on Tuesday he spoke for two hours. Then Democrat Adam Snyder answered him for two more. The spot is marked today by the Monroe County Bicentennial Bandstand at Main and Third streets.
Walk the markers. The Historical Marker Database lists 97 markers in Waterloo, a lot for a town of about 11,000. Downtown, the city’s Self-Guided Historic Building Tour adds plaques on 25 buildings, written from research that Gibault Catholic High School history students began in 2014. The district has been on the National Register since 1978. Start at the bandstand, find the bison, read the name legend at 114 N. Main, and keep going.
Hear the band where Lincoln stood. Every Tuesday at 8 p.m., from the first Tuesday after Memorial Day through the last Tuesday in August, the Waterloo Municipal Band plays a free concert at Main and Third. More than 50 musicians from both Illinois and Missouri work through marches, show tunes, standards, a little rock and roll and, in a nod to the town’s German roots, an occasional polka. A marker says the band formed in 1931 because the town got tired of paying an out-of-town band that charged too much. Bring a lawn chair. The Chamber of Commerce adds a free Downtown Concert Series on second Sundays, June through September, starting at 4:30 p.m.
The Saturday market. The Monroe County Farmers Market has been run by its own vendors for nearly four decades, with a 10-person board made up entirely of sellers. It runs Saturdays, 7:30 a.m. to noon, from late April through Oct. 31 in 2026, in the Annex building lot at 901 Illinois Ave. facing Route 3. Browsing costs nothing. One rule the market asks everyone to follow: never park on the drive north of the Annex. It’s an ambulance exit.
### What is there to do in Waterloo, IL at night?
More than the drive-through lists suggest, as long as you know the season.
A play at the Capitol Theatre. Monroe Actors Stage Company, the local community theater group, puts on five shows a year in the historic Capitol Theatre at 202 S. Main St., a building whose downtown plaque also lists it as the old Oddfellows Lodge. The company’s November 2026 show is “The Cottage” by Sandy Rustin, a romantic farce, on Nov. 6, 7, 8, 13, 14 and 15. Call 618-939-7469 or check the company’s site for tickets, curtain times and the shows that follow. It’s the easiest date night in town: dinner downtown, then walk to the show.
Breweries and a winery. Downtown has two breweries, Stubborn German Brewing and Hopskeller Brewing, and Schorr Lake Vineyards sits just south of town. All three are in our Waterloo where-to-eat guide. For wine country beyond Waterloo, our St. Louis winery day trip guide covers tasting rooms on both sides of the river.
A movie from the front seat. For a drive-in night, Belleville’s Skyview Drive-In is the classic, and it usually runs into October before closing for winter. By fall it’s often down to weekends, so check the schedule first.
For teenagers. The Optimist Skate Park at Koenigsmark Park stays open until 9 p.m. from April through October and until 8 p.m. the rest of the year.
Summer evenings belong to the Tuesday band concerts. October belongs to the haunted trail. December belongs to Santa.
### When is the Waterloo, IL Christmas Walk and Santa Float?
The Christmas Walk always falls the week and weekend of Thanksgiving, and in 2026 the Santa Float takes the ten nights leading up to Christmas Eve. The city’s 2026 calendar lays the season out like this:
Waterloo Christmas Walk: Nov. 28 and 29 at participating downtown merchants. Get your shopping card stamped at each stop for a gift certificate drawing, and catch free carriage rides and visits with Santa.
GLOW Lighted Holiday Parade: Saturday, Nov. 28, 5:30 p.m., downtown.
Lamppost Decorating Contest judging: Sunday, Nov. 29, noon to 3 p.m. on Courthouse Square.
12th Annual Community Christmas Tree Lighting: Sunday, Nov. 29, 6:30 p.m., at Mill and Main.
Cookie Walk: Saturday, Dec. 5, 9 a.m. to noon, at Immanuel Lutheran Church.
Candle Light Tour with Santa: Saturday, Dec. 12, 6:30 p.m., at the History Museum of Monroe County.
Santa Float: Monday, Dec. 14, through Wednesday, Dec. 23, heading out at 5 p.m. each night and running until about 8:30.
The Santa Float is the one to plan around. Harry Wolf and the Waterloo German Band started it, and the city, the Chamber of Commerce and the town’s sister-city group keep it rolling. Each neighborhood route runs two nights, and the second night runs it in reverse, so the kids who live at the end of the line see Santa before bedtime too. A city vehicle with flashing red and green lights leads the way, and an online Santa Tracker shows where the float is right now. Then there’s the part kids remember for years. Every night, three golden tickets are hidden among the candy bars. Find one, bring it to City Hall at 9 a.m. on Christmas Eve, and Santa has a gift waiting. Only kids 13 and under can win.
Want a second cookie walk the same weekend? The Kimmswick Cookie Walk and Christmas Festival fills that first weekend of December across the river. Waterloo’s takes one Saturday morning. Kimmswick’s runs four days.
So the next time somebody tells you there’s nothing south of the Jefferson Barracks Bridge, you’re the one who knows where the 1904 crowds went, which lakes take a kayak, and why the kids chase the Santa Float for golden tickets. Pick a weekend before the gate closes for the bats. Bring three lights.
After a muddy morning underground, our guide to where to eat in Waterloo, IL covers the two downtown breweries, the German restaurant and the bakery a few minutes from the courthouse.
If you run a downtown shop that stamps Christmas Walk cards, sell bait near Lakeview Park or stock the headlamps first-time cavers forget, list it with us so the people planning a cave weekend find you before they leave St. Louis.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Waterloo, IL known for?
A.  Waterloo, Illinois is known as the Monroe County seat, a role it has held since 1825, and for German roots deep enough that a marker says two-thirds of the county’s citizens traced their heritage to one German town, Porta Westfalica, now Waterloo’s sister city with its own festival every June. It also has Bellefontaine, settled by 1782, a downtown historic district on the National Register since 1978, Lincoln’s 1840 courthouse speech and, a few miles south, the only cave in Illinois ever run commercially.
### Q. What famous people went to Waterloo?
A.  Abraham Lincoln is the big name in Waterloo, Illinois. He arrived on Sunday, Aug. 23, 1840, and spoke for two hours at the courthouse that Tuesday as a Whig presidential elector. Another local marker notes that Barack Obama campaigned at the Waterloo VFW hall during his 2004 U.S. Senate run, and one more says Gov. Thomas Ford, Illinois’ eighth governor, grew up in a log house on Main Street.
### Q. What is the largest cave in Illinois?
A.  Fogelpole Cave, in southern Monroe County, Illinois, not far from Waterloo. More than 15 miles of it have been mapped. It’s a state nature preserve, dedicated in 1989, and access is by permission only. The cave you can actually walk into is Illinois Caverns, with about 6 miles mapped, open on a state permit from mid-April through late October.
### Q. What are some good walks around Waterloo?
A.  In Waterloo, Illinois, start with the 2.25-mile paved loop around the three lakes at Lakeview Park. It’s walkers only, with strollers and wheelchairs welcome and no bikes or scooters. For history, walk the downtown building plaques and markers around the courthouse square, from the Lincoln bandstand to the bison statue. Konarcik Park adds a short trail, and the prairie trails at Illinois Caverns give non-cavers a walk while the rest of the group is underground.
### Q. What are some fun activities for adults in Waterloo?
A.  For adults in Waterloo, Illinois, the strongest picks are a permit caving trip at Illinois Caverns (your group needs four people), a round on Konarcik Park’s 18-hole disc golf course, and a Monroe Actors Stage Company show at the Capitol Theatre. In October there’s Witches Night Out downtown (Oct. 15 in 2026), and the History Museum’s 6:30 p.m. talks and the two downtown breweries cover other evenings.
### Q. What to do in Waterloo, IL today?
A.  In Waterloo, Illinois, it depends on the day. Thursday through Sunday from mid-April to late October, Illinois Caverns is open 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., with no entry after 3. On Saturday mornings in season (through Oct. 31 in 2026), the farmers market runs 7:30 to noon. On Saturday and Sunday afternoons the Peterstown House opens 1 to 4, and on Sundays from May through December, so does the Bellefontaine House. Every park is free and open dawn to dusk.
### Q. What is there to do around Waterloo?
A.  Around Waterloo, Illinois, Columbia is the next Monroe County town north, and our Columbia, IL guide covers it. Belleville sits a short drive northeast, with the Skyview Drive-In and antique shops. Across the Mississippi, Kimmswick and Ste. Genevieve keep the same river-history thread going.
### Q. Do you need a ticket for Illinois Caverns?
A.  No. Illinois Caverns, south of Waterloo, Illinois, doesn’t sell tickets. You fill out an IDNR cave exploration permit at the site, and the form lists no fee. Only groups of 25 or more must register ahead. Bring at least four people, a hard hat for each and three lights apiece, and confirm hours with the site at 618-458-6699 before you drive.

## Things to Do in Union, MO: Winter Trout at City Lake, Free Live Steam Trains, Bourbeuse River Access
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-union-mo
Winter fly anglers, this one’s yours. Every recycled Union, MO list, the city’s own included, sends you back up I-44 to a theme park or out to wine country. The city’s Things to Do page opens with Six Flags. Meanwhile, MDC stocks rainbow trout in a four acre town lake that Union rebuilt for exactly that job, and from Nov. 1 through Jan. 31 it’s catch-and-release, flies and lures only, off a floating dock.
Union is the Franklin County seat, about 50 miles southwest of St. Louis on the Bourbeuse River, and most people know it only as an exit on the way to somewhere else. Stop, and it gets odd in the best way. A club founded in 1968 is still laying track for a ride-on railroad in a city park, and the rides are free. There’s a public boat ramp on the Bourbeuse beside a QuikTrip. The county’s first dog park is here. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Union is the one you’ve probably driven past without stopping.
Everything below was checked against City of Union, MDC, East Central College and organizer pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do. Dates move. Check before you drive.
### What are some fun things to do in Union, MO?
Fun things to do in Union, MO include casting for the rainbow trout MDC stocks in the four acre City Lake each winter, launching a kayak on the Bourbeuse River at Union Access, riding live steam trains free at Grant Station Park, running your dog at Franklin County’s first dog park, and cosmic bowling on weekend nights.
Besides the 1920s courthouse on the square and the county fair in June, Union has a second layer the drive-by lists never reach. By season:
November through January: catch-and-release trout at City Lake. April through October: free live steam train rides one Saturday a month, plus paddling and bass fishing on the Bourbeuse. May through September: free first-Friday concerts and third-Friday movies in City Park. Friday and Saturday nights, all year: cosmic bowling until midnight. December: a parade around the courthouse square, then a free party where every kid 10 and under goes home with a gift.
### Where can you catch trout in Union, MO?
City Lake, 502 Clark Ave., on the corner of Clark Avenue and Memorial Parkway. It’s four acres, with ADA accessible paths, an accessible floating dock, two pavilions you can rent and a lit 0.3 mile loop that runs partly along Clark Avenue. And from November on, it holds rainbow trout.
How it got them is the story. The lake was built in 1955. By 2016 its 61-year-old dam was leaking in several spots and needed major repairs, so the city opened talks with MDC about what the fishery should become once the dam work was finished. Accessibility and a winter trout program were part of those very first conversations. In January 2017 the city and MDC signed a Community Assistance Program agreement, and the grant put $262,000 toward new sidewalks, three jetties, the floating dock, two parking lots, four aerators and a sediment basin to keep silt from filling the lake back in. On Nov. 1, 2018, the two agencies held a celebration to open winter trout fishing. A few months later the Missouri Park and Recreation Association handed MDC a statewide citation award, and the city’s parks director had nominated the department mainly for this lake.
Why that matters to you: MDC runs its winter trout program so St. Louis anglers can drive minutes for trout instead of hours to an Ozark trout park. Last season it stocked nearly 40,000 rainbows from November into February in 11 lakes in St. Louis city and county, five lakes at Busch Conservation Area in St. Charles, and Union City Lake, the only Franklin County water on the list. It’s the same program behind trout fishing at Walker Lake in Kirkwood. Union’s lake has nearly twice the water, plus a dock to fish it from.
The winter rules, in plain English. From Nov. 1 through Jan. 31, every trout goes back. You can fish flies, artificial lures and unscented soft plastics, one pole per person, and no chum. That means no worms, no corn and no dough bait. From Feb. 1 through Oct. 31 the bait rules relax, the city allows up to three poles, and you can keep four trout a day. Once you have four in possession, you stop fishing for everything, trout or otherwise.
Permits. Anglers 16 through 64 need a Missouri fishing permit, and anyone who keeps a trout needs a trout permit on top of it, at any age. At MDC’s 2026 prices that’s $14 for a resident annual fishing permit and $12 for a resident trout permit.
The city’s own limits. Union posts a few extra rules at the lake: largemouth bass are two a day with an 18 inch minimum, catfish are four a day, and it’s pole-and-line fishing only. So the lake earns its keep in July, too.
2026 timing. As of early October, MDC hadn’t announced this winter’s stocking dates. Save the St. Louis fish stocking hotline, 636-300-9651. Its recording says where fish went, when, and how many as soon as each stocking run is done, so call it before you load the car in November.
Bring a disc. Clark-Vitt Memorial Park sits directly across Clark Avenue: 13.8 acres with restrooms, a playground, asphalt and natural trails, and the 11-hole Autumn Hill disc golf course. Park at the upper lot, 310 Autumn Hill Drive. Fish the morning. Throw the afternoon.
Two free fishing days. The parks department runs Operation Catch and/or Release, a free fishing event for veterans at the Veterans Memorial Park lakes. The 2026 event was set for Saturday, Oct. 10, from 10 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., with lunch at noon, and the city planned to stock 50 hybrid bluegill, 200 bluegill and 125 channel catfish of 12 to 16 inches for it, plus a few big ones. In spring the city also holds a free kids’ fishing derby at the Garden Club pavilion beside City Lake. The 2026 derby was May 16, with prizes for the biggest fish and the most caught, so watch for a May date in 2027. For more free public water around the metro, our guide to the best fishing spots in St. Louis covers the city and county trout lakes and where to fish by part of town.
### Where can you put a kayak in the Bourbeuse River in Union, MO?
Union Access, an MDC site right in town. It’s 10.3 acres off Highway 50 near the Highway 47 intersection, next to the QuikTrip, with a boat ramp that suits kayaks, canoes and small boats. The grounds are open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., but MDC allows fishing and launching around the clock. No camping. Dogs are fine on a leash.
Say it BUR-biss or BUR-buss. Bourbeuse is French for muddy, which is a fair description after a hard rain, and it’s one of the two major tributaries of the Meramec. It’s a small, winding river, and it fishes better than its size suggests. MDC lists white bass, sunfish, catfish and black bass at Union Access, and names spotted bass and golden redhorse among the things to look for there.
Reiker Ford Access is the quieter choice, 10.9 acres of MDC land southwest of town. From Union, take Highway 50 west 1 mile, Route UU south 5 miles, Snake Hill Road south half a mile, then Reiker Ford Road east to the area. MDC points anglers there toward smallmouth and spotted bass.
One to skip: Mayers Landing Access. MDC says the river’s main channel has shifted away from its boat ramp, so you could find mud where you expected water.
No boat? Clearview Park, 22.82 acres at Clearview Drive and North Bend Road, has what the city calls great views of the Bourbeuse and a natural walking trail through a secluded patch of forest. It’s the walk to take while someone else fishes.
Before you launch, check the USGS gauge for the Bourbeuse River at Union, site 07016500, because a small river can drop to scraping depth in a dry spell or come up fast after rain. We couldn’t verify published float times for this stretch, so start with short out-and-backs from the ramp. If it’s your first time in a boat, our beginner’s guide to kayaking in St. Louis covers which kayak to pick, what to bring and how to plan the first trip.
### Where can you ride a steam train for free in Union, MO?
Grant Station Park, 200 Grant St., on the seven Saturdays a year when the Missouri Live Steamers open their railroad to the public. Rides run 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., all ages are welcome, and there are no tickets and no reservations. You walk up and climb on.
The club was incorporated in November 1968 and has run trains at several public and private sites around the region; before Union, it operated out of Eureka. In March 2022 it signed a lease with the City of Union to build a railroad in Grant Station Park, and the club says the whole project is paid for by donations and volunteer members, with no city, state or federal money. The trains are 1/8 scale, an inch and a half to the foot, on rails 7.5 inches apart, and one section adds a rail at 4.75 inches for the smaller one-inch-scale engines. You ride on top of the cars, knees up.
The first season explains why this is the runner-up for best thing in town. The club told Union’s aldermen last December that 2,239 different people took 3,679 rides in 2025. Phase one was a 1,268 foot loop that each train circles twice, about half a mile a ride. Over the winter, members were digging and rocking the roadbed for a second line, with a goal of about 4,500 feet of track, close to a mile the way they plan to run it. Most of the steam engines belong to individual members, and the club also runs a donated propane engine, so not every train you board will be steaming.
Two details we liked. Every train carries a conductor on the last car whose whole job is watching riders; if someone starts rocking or sticking their feet out, he blows a whistle and the engineer stops. And the park sits on ground where houses stood until floods led to their demolition. Members digging the new roadbed have turned up windshield wipers and small wheels.
2026 run days: April 11, May 9 (Founder’s Day), June 6, July 11, Aug. 15, Sept. 12 and Saturday, Oct. 10, the last public run of the year. The 2026 schedule was public by late December, so look for 2027 dates on the city’s special events page and the club’s site around then, before you promise a kid a train ride in April.
Off the train and somebody’s hungry? Where to eat in Union, MO
### What parks are in Union, MO?
More than you’d guess from the highway. The city counts 122 acres of municipal parkland across 14 parks and facilities. City Lake, Clark-Vitt and Clearview are covered above, and three more stand out.
K-9 -n- Kiddos Park. Franklin County’s first dog park, built in 2013 at 226 N. Christina Ave. Its 2.23 acres hold two separate fenced yards, one for dogs over 25 pounds and one for small dogs, and each has its own agility equipment, water spigots and drinking buckets. Veterans Memorial Park. The big one, 43.8 acres at 600 Progress Parkway, opened in spring 2017. Everybody in Union already knows this one, so we’ll leave it there.
Summer swimmers: the Ann Schroeder Swimplex, 375 W. Park Ave., charged $7 for ages 3 and up in 2026, $3 for the last two hours. Check the city’s pool page for 2027 dates and rates.

Franklin County Historical Society museum. Down the street at 300 E. Locust St., open noon to 4 p.m. on the first and third Wednesdays and the second and fourth Saturdays from March through November, or by appointment at 636-583-3247. Admission is free. The society, formed in 1969, also holds a history fair each October with 20-plus vendors and antique fire trucks. We couldn’t confirm the 2026 date, so call first.
Longmeadow Rescue Ranch. The Humane Society of Missouri’s ranch for rescued horses and farm animals is at 480 Josephs Road in Union. It’s open to the public Fridays noon to 3 p.m. and Saturdays 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. with no reservation, and the ranch asks you to arrive by 2:30 and leave your own pets at home. There’s a gift shop, and the visit page lists no admission charge.
Stargazing at the college. The Eastern Missouri Dark Sky Observers set up telescopes for the public one Saturday a month, March through October, at East Central College, 1964 Prairie Dell Road, in the parking lot by the sand volleyball courts. The last 2026 night was set for Saturday, Oct. 10, from 7:30 to 10 p.m., and clouds cancel it. That’s the same Saturday as 2026’s last train run, which makes for a very good day. The club also opens its 30 inch telescope, Big Blue, for public nights in New Haven.
### What is there to do in Union, MO at night?
More than the drive-by lists think, and two of the better nights out happen on a college campus.
Cosmic bowling. Oasis Lanes, 120 Dell Centre Way, turns the lights down for cosmic bowling on Friday and Saturday nights from 10 p.m. to midnight. It’s $12 a person with shoes included, or $10 with a student ID. The arcade runs on a reloadable card that stores your prize points, so nobody has to carry a fistful of tickets to the counter.
A movie. Great 8 Cinema, 5 Prairie Dell Plaza, has been showing first-run films in Union since 1996.
The college stage. East Central College’s John Edson Anglin Performing Arts Center, 1964 Prairie Dell Road, is the night out St. Louis visitors miss. For Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, it booked a screening of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” with a live cast performing alongside the film: lobby at 6 p.m., theater at 7 and showtime at 7:30, with tickets through Etix. The college’s theater program set “Goosebumps the Musical: The Phantom of the Auditorium” for Oct. 8 to 11, 2026. The box office number is 636-584-6693.
Halloween for grown-ups. Scare on the Square, from the downtown nonprofit ReDiscover Union, takes over Hansen Park and the courthouse square, and the 2026 edition, set for Saturday, Oct. 24, has a Goosebumps theme: the movie, a haunted maze and a hayride around the square. When organizers pitched the first one to the aldermen in 2025, they described it as geared more toward teens and adults and running later than the kids’ events. Those still happen. Boo Bash, the free family trunk-or-treat, was set for Friday, Oct. 30, in 2026, at the Large Pavilion in City Park. Reading this after Halloween? Check ReDiscover Union for next year’s Scare on the Square.
A February date night. The parks department’s 21-and-over Valentine’s Comedy Show and Dinner was set for Feb. 13, 2027, at the City Auditorium. Tables of six were due to go on sale Dec. 1, 2026, and the price hadn’t been announced when we checked.
### What does Union, MO do for Christmas?
One big night, plus a couple of quiet ones.
Winter Wonderland Parade and Children’s Christmas Party: Friday, Dec. 11, 2026. The Union Area Chamber of Commerce runs the parade, and the parks department throws the party right after it, at 7 p.m. in the City Auditorium, 500 E. Locust St. The party is free: refreshments, face painting, balloon sculptors, pictures with Santa (bring your own camera) and a gift for every child 10 and under. Bring canned food for the pantry. In 2025 the parade started near Union Middle School, rounded the courthouse square and ended near City Hall, and 306 gifts, from sleds to Lego sets, went home with local kids. For the 2026 route and start time, or next year’s date once this one passes, call the chamber at 636-583-8979.
A choir in a church. East Central College’s 2026 Christmas Choir Concert was set for Friday, Dec. 4, at 7 p.m. at Zion United Church of Christ, 115 S. Washington Ave. Ask the ECC box office about seating.
The quiet option. City Lake stays catch-and-release trout water straight through the holidays. A cold morning on the floating dock the day after Christmas, thermos in one hand, is a fine way to work off a week of ham.
### Nearby, up Route 47 and back down I-44
Washington sits seven miles north on Route 47, on the Missouri River. Our guide to things to do in Washington, MO covers its Amtrak depot, the walking path on the river bridge and Lions Lake, so we kept those off this page. Heading home on I-44, Purina Farms and Shaw Nature Reserve are both out by Gray Summit, and a little farther east, the Route 66 State Park visitor center in Eureka makes a good last stop.
So the next time someone says there’s nothing in Union but a courthouse and a stoplight on Highway 50, you’re the one who knows the town lake has a trout dock, the trains are free, and the river ramp is next to the QuikTrip. Pick a Saturday. Bring a rod. Go.
After a cold morning on the City Lake dock, our guide to where to eat in Union, MO points you to the nearly 90-year-old diner a short walk from the courthouse and the small-batch coffee roaster out on Highway 50.
If you run a bait shop, a kayak rental or a store on the square that anglers and train families walk past, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
On the way back toward St. Louis, Jensen’s Point Overlook in Pacific is a 1939 stone lookout on old Route 66.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many rods are you allowed to fish with in Missouri?
A.  Statewide, one person can fish up to three unlabeled poles at a time, with no more than 33 hooks across everything they’re running. On the Mississippi River the limit is two poles. Special waters can set tighter rules, and Union City Lake does: one pole from Nov. 1 through Jan. 31, and up to three the rest of the year.
### Q. How much is fishing without a license in Missouri?
A.  More than the permit. Fishing without a required permit breaks the Wildlife Code, which Missouri law treats as a misdemeanor, and the fine and court costs are set by the county court, so there’s no single statewide number. The permit is the cheap part: MDC lists a resident annual fishing permit at $14, a daily permit at $9 and a resident trout permit at $12 for 2026. Missouri residents 65 and older don’t need a fishing permit.
### Q. Is there a dog park in Union, MO?
A.  Yes. K-9 -n- Kiddos Park, 226 N. Christina Ave., opened in 2013 as Franklin County’s first dog park. It has separate fenced yards for dogs over 25 pounds and for small dogs, each with agility equipment and water, plus a playground and sand volleyball courts for the people.
### Q. Are state parks free in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Missouri State Parks doesn’t charge an entrance or day-use fee; camping, lodging and some guided tours cost extra. Union’s city parks don’t sell admission either, with the Swimplex pool as the exception. Route 66 State Park in Eureka is an easy stop on the drive back to St. Louis.
### Q. What are some free attractions in Missouri?
A.  In Union alone: the live steam train rides at Grant Station Park on run days, the Franklin County Historical Society museum, the first-Friday concerts and third-Friday movies in City Park, and the Liberty Swing at City Park. Add the winter trout at City Lake, where the fishing costs nothing beyond the permit you’d need anywhere in the state.
### Q. What events are happening in Union, MO this weekend?
A.  Union runs on a steady rhythm. From April through October, one Saturday a month brings free live steam train rides at Grant Station Park. From May through September, City Park has a free concert on first Fridays and a lawn chair movie on third Fridays. Music on Main fills Hansen Park on Thursday evenings in season, and East Central College posts plays, films and concerts through the school year. For this weekend, check the city’s special events page and the ECC events calendar.
### Q. What are some fun Christmas events in Missouri?
A.  Close to St. Louis, the 2026 calendar puts Union’s Winter Wonderland Parade and free Children’s Christmas Party downtown on Friday, Dec. 11, and East Central College’s Christmas Choir Concert on Dec. 4 at Zion United Church of Christ. Seven miles north, Washington meets Santa off the train, and in 2026 that’s the same Friday, Dec. 4, so an afternoon there and the 7 p.m. concert in Union make one easy December evening.
### Q. Is the Rock Island Trail open in Union, MO?
A.  Not yet. Missouri State Parks says the developed section of Rock Island Trail State Park is 47.5 miles of trail in west-central Missouri. East of that, a 144 mile stretch of corridor stays closed to the public until it’s developed, and the last 12.6 miles into Union is an active rail line the state lists as available for a future “rail with trail.” For now, Union is the trail’s eastern end on paper only.

## Things to Do in Troy, MO: Free Backcountry Camping, Frenchman's Bluff, Live Wrestling
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-troy-mo
Flat farm country? That’s how the recycled top-10 lists brush off the drive up Highway 61, and it stops being true about three miles outside Troy. Missouri State Parks sells Cuivre River State Park (locals say “quiver”) with a question, “Looking for the Ozarks in northern Missouri?”, and the ground backs it up with limestone bluffs, sinkholes, springs and boulders the glaciers carried in and left behind. Four backcountry campsites sit on the trails that cross its two state-designated wild areas, about an hour from St. Louis. They cost nothing, as long as you register first.
You won’t see them on the pages that fill a search for Cuivre River camping, which are mostly booking widgets, RV rentals and a Facebook thread. The usual Troy lists stop at “visit the state park” and move on. So if you’ve done the Arch and the Zoo enough times to give the tours yourself, start here. The park is a New Deal project that turns 80 in November 2026, and one of its group camps was founded in 1939 by the St. Louis YWCA’s Phyllis Wheatley Branch. Back in town, the wrestling promotion an eight-time world champion founded still runs live Saturday-night shows, with two left on the 2026 calendar.
Of all the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, Troy is the one where you can sleep in a wild area for free and be home for lunch. Everything below was checked against Missouri State Parks, Missouri Department of Conservation, city and organizer pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do.
### What is Troy, MO known for?
Troy, MO is the Lincoln County seat, about an hour northwest of St. Louis, best known as the front door to Cuivre River State Park: more than 6,400 acres of bluffs, prairie and two state-designated wild areas that the state pitches as the Ozarks in northern Missouri. In town, the wrestling promotion Harley Race founded runs live shows.
Ask anyone in Troy and you’ll hear about the park first. Fair enough. But the town has layers of its own. It started out as Woods Fort, and the city still keeps the lot its founders, Joseph Cottle and Zadock Woods, gave it in 1819, with two log cabins standing on it. Downtown, 39 buildings dating from about 1832 to 1966 make up a National Register historic district, anchored by the Lincoln County Courthouse, built in 1869 and 1870. And every July the Lincoln County Fair fills the fairgrounds just north of town with a demolition derby, truck and tractor pulls, horse shows and 4-H and FFA exhibits.
One mix-up to clear up. Troy, Missouri isn’t the Troy in the Metro East. That’s Troy, Illinois, a different town in Madison County. This page is about the Lincoln County one, ZIP 63379, up Highway 61 north of Wentzville.
### How much does it cost to camp at Cuivre River State Park?
Nothing, if you carry your camp in on your back. Campground sites run $14 to $42 a night, depending on the season and the hookup, and the posted rates include tax. Here’s the rate card for Campground 1. The 2026 and 2027 sheets match, but confirm the price when you book.
Booking ahead adds a reservation fee of $6.50 online or $8 by phone at 877-422-6766, and Missouri now opens state park reservations up to 12 months out. Campers 65 and older, people with disabilities, and military members and veterans get $2 off per night if they ask when they pay and show proof. The park also rents three CCC-era group camps to organized groups, sized for 150 to 190 people.
Where the four free sites are. The park limits backcountry camping to four designated sites on three trails: Lone Spring Trail, Big Sugar Creek Trail and the North Loop of the Cuivre River Trail. Lone Spring runs through the Northwoods Wild Area, 1,102 acres of mature oak woodland north of Highway KK. The other two cross the 1,675-acre Big Sugar Creek Wild Area, where bluffs line the creek and sinkhole ponds sit back in the woods. Missouri manages its wild areas “as wilderness for solitude and primitive recreation,” in the state’s own words. No hookups. No showers. No RV idling next door.
How to claim one. Register online before you start. The park’s backcountry page puts it plainly: “Camping is free, but registration is required.” Horses can’t camp on the trail. For site 1, park overnight at the Lone Spring trailhead, where Lincoln Hills Road meets Highway KK. For sites 2, 3 and 4, use the Big Sugar Creek trailhead lot off Lincoln Hills Road, next to Park Road. Rules on that form can change, so read it the week you go, not the month before.
What people forget to pack. Water. Big Sugar Creek is a gravel-bottom stream, and the park describes much of it as intermittent, so don’t count on it running when you get there. Expect stream crossings without bridges on Big Sugar Creek Trail. And give yourself daylight, because Lone Spring alone is 5.1 rugged miles.
The drive-in side. Campground 1 and the equestrian campground stay open all year, with showers from April 15 to Oct. 31. Off-season, drinking water comes from the frost-free spigot at site 69. The campground gate closes at 10 p.m. in season and 8 p.m. off-season, which matters on a late Friday in November. The platform tents come down Nov. 1, so winter campers on those pads bring their own. Eight walk-in tent sites suit people who want a campground without a car parked beside the tent. Dogs are welcome on a leash of 10 feet or less, and the park recommends no more than two per site. For how the state’s booking system works, see our guide on how to book a campsite near St. Louis.
One weekend to skip. In 2026 the whole park, backcountry included, is set to close from 3 p.m. Friday, Oct. 30, to 7:30 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2, for a managed deer hunt. Only registered hunters get in. If that was your weekend, Troy’s Pumpkin Festival lands on that same Saturday downtown. It’s further down this page.
### What are the best trails in Cuivre River State Park?
That depends on what you came for, and there are 12 designated trails to pick from. Watch the ground on any of them. The park says the Lincoln Hills were once covered by glaciers, and glacier-carried boulders and rocks are scattered throughout. The distances below come from the park’s own trail sheets, so trust them over an app.
For the view: Frenchman’s Bluff Trail. A 1.6-mile loop that starts on the west side of the picnic shelter, follows Geode Creek, then climbs onto a 120-foot limestone bluff over the Cuivre River valley and stays up top for about half a mile. Down below, the river runs along the park’s southwest edge for about a mile. The trail sheet rates it moderate, about an hour and 10 minutes, blue blazes, walked counterclockwise. It also warns that loose gravel on top makes footing unsure. Believe it.
For solitude: Lone Spring Trail. 5.1 rugged miles, hiking and backpacking only, named for a spring that flows all year. About three miles of it run through the Northwoods Wild Area, with spurs to Shady 80 Lake and to the backpack camp. It starts from its own trailhead on Highway KK, well away from the lake crowd.
For creek scenery: Big Sugar Creek Trail. 3.7 rugged miles. From a spot the trail sheet calls keyhole bluff, you look down on the gravel-bottom creek that, by the park’s account, shaped the whole place. Some crossings have no bridge. Pick shoes you don’t mind soaking.
For a full day: Cuivre River Trail. A 13.4-mile set of loops that tops 15 miles once you add the white connector trails. Along the way you pass Civilian Conservation Corps stonework and the old quarries the CCC cut its stone from. Horses use it too, so step off the tread and say hello when riders come through.
For wildflowers: Blazing Star and Prairie trails. Blazing Star covers 1.7 miles through the tallgrass of Sherwood Prairie, and it’s best in summer and fall. Prairie Trail is a 0.3-mile easy walk through a remnant of the Sac Prairie, short enough for a toddler or a tired grandparent. Eastern blazing star shows up on the park’s list of rare species.
For big trees and old foundations: Hamilton Hollow and Old Schoolhouse. Hamilton Hollow is only 0.9 miles, starting at the 1930s CCC stone shelter and passing what the sheet calls some of the largest trees in the park. Old Schoolhouse runs 3.8 miles for hikers and mountain bikers, past the foundation of an early-1900s one-room schoolhouse.
For bikes. Besides Old Schoolhouse, the Blackhawk Point Mountain Bike Trail runs from the CCC stone shelter out along Frenchman’s Bluff to Blackhawk Point.
For a quick leg-stretch. Mossy Hill and Turkey Hollow are 0.8 miles each, and Lakeside Trail circles Lake Lincoln in 3.4.
Two hedges. Staff use prescribed burns to keep the prairie and oak woodland healthy, and a trail can close briefly while one is burning. And every trail closes during the managed deer hunt, Oct. 30 to Nov. 2 in 2026.
### Can you swim at Cuivre River State Park?
Yes, in one place. Lake Lincoln, the park’s 55-acre lake, has a public swimming beach with a change house. Swimming is limited to the beach area, it’s at your own risk, and pets aren’t allowed on the beach. The park’s swimming page links a beach status check and the beach hours, so look before you load the cooler.
We cover Lake Lincoln’s fish in our guide to things to do in Wentzville, down Highway 61, so here’s the part that guide skips: what floats.
Gas motors can’t run, and the launch is free. The concrete launch charges no fee. On the water it’s electric trolling motors only, though the park says a gas motor doesn’t have to come off the boat. It just stays quiet. That makes a sunrise paddle here sound like birds and paddle drips, not outboards.
The rental myth. An older outdoors blog that still turns up in Troy searches says you can rent kayaks near the beach. You can’t, unless you’re staying in one of the park’s organized group camps. The park says rentals go only to group-camp guests, and that day visitors and people in the main campground, the equestrian campground or the special-use area must bring their own boat. So strap the kayak to the roof before you leave home.
Fishing, in one line. Anglers 16 and older need a Missouri fishing permit unless they’re state residents 65 or older.
Off the bluff and starving? Where to eat in Troy, MO
### Can you ride horses at Cuivre River State Park?
Yes, on your own horse. The Cuivre River Trail is the horse trail. Its 13.4 miles of loops are open to riders, and with the connectors the park counts more than 15 miles of multi-use trail. The North Loop used to be the horse section of Big Sugar Creek Trail before the park renamed it. Short stretches of Frenchman’s Bluff and Hamilton Hollow share its tread, but the rest of Hamilton Hollow is closed to horses.
Here’s where one horse-trail website gets it wrong. It lists Lone Spring as an 8-mile horse trail. The park’s trail sheet says Lone Spring is for hiking and backpacking only, and so is Big Sugar Creek Trail. Go by the sheet, because a ranger will.
The equestrian campground is open all year with basic, electric, and electric and water sites, and the rule there is short: occupants must camp with a horse. There’s no stable at the park. The park has posted that its equestrian trails close after heavy rain, so call the office at 636-528-7247 before you hitch the trailer. Don’t own a horse? Start with our guide to horseback riding lessons in St. Louis for beginners.
### What free things can you do in Troy, MO?
Start with the park, since Missouri state parks don’t charge admission. Every trail above, the beach and the bluff cost nothing. In town, the list is longer than you’d guess.
The park’s visitor center. Free exhibits on the area’s natural and cultural history, and the naturalists there lead nature hikes and campground evening programs. It’s open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays all year and 10 to 4 on Saturdays from April 15 to Oct. 31, plus Sundays from 11 to 4 between Memorial Day and Labor Day weekends. From Nov. 1 to April 14 it’s closed on weekends, so plan a winter visit for a weekday if you want the exhibits.
Woods Fort. Troy’s founders, Joseph Cottle and Zadock Woods, gave this lot to the city in 1819, back when the settlement itself went by Woods Fort. Two log cabins and a memorial marker stand on it. A natural spring here supplied the area until blasting for Highway 47 stopped it. There are benches and tables across the street at Boone and Main. Give it 10 minutes.
A downtown walk. The Downtown Troy Historic District went on the National Register in 2013 with 39 contributing buildings. Look for the 1832 Sherman Cottle House, the Universalist Church and Masonic Hall (dated 1837 and 1851), the 1906 Farmers & Merchants Bank and the 1929 Lincoln County Motor Co. building. No guide needed.
The Old Jail Museum. At 211 W. Collier St., the Lincoln County Historical Society keeps an 1870s Gothic Revival jail with brick buttresses, limestone arches and iron-barred windows, joined to a two-story Italianate house where the jailer lived. The original cells are inside, along with photos and artifacts donated by residents. It opens by appointment only, at 636-528-7562, so call ahead and ask about any fee.
The Pumpkin Festival. The Troy Historic Business Group runs it on Historic Main Street, and the 2026 date is Saturday, Oct. 31, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Expect live music, vendors, pumpkin painting, face painting and a costume contest open to kids and pets. It’s free to walk in, and in 2026 it lands on the one weekend the park is closed, which makes it the obvious plan B.
A Saturday market and free talks. The Lincoln County Farmers Market runs Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Its 2026 posts put it at 170 Market Place Dr., and the chamber lists a season from March into November, so check the market’s page before late-season trips. Browsing is free. The apple butter isn’t. The Lincoln County Historical Society also hosts free evening talks, with donations welcome, so keep an eye on the chamber calendar.
City parks with a story. Weinand Park, at 1305 Boone St., has an Angel of Hope statue, a replica of the Christmas Box Angel, placed to honor children who have died. Avery Park has a half-mile wooded walking trail. Fairgrounds Park, which locals call the duck pond park, has skate ramps.
Planning ahead? Cuivre River ran a free First Day Hike on New Year’s Day 2026, from 10 a.m. to noon. Watch the park’s events page for a 2027 repeat.
### What is there to do in Troy, MO at night?
Troy’s nightlife is short and specific. Here’s the list.
Live wrestling at the Harley Race Wrestling Arena. Harley Race, an eight-time NWA World Heavyweight Champion, founded World League Wrestling in 1999, and it still runs shows at its home arena at 198 Cherry Blossom Way. The 2026 Troy dates are Saturday, Nov. 7, for the WLW 27th Anniversary show, and Saturday, Dec. 12, for the Christmas Bash. Most Troy shows open the doors at 6 p.m. and ring the bell at 7, and the promotion bills them as family friendly. Recent listings put tickets around $15 to $20, so check the event page for current prices. The Harley Race Wrestling Academy trains here too.
A movie for $9. Troy Movie House, an independent theater at 1436 S. Main St., charges $11 for adults and $9 for kids and seniors, and every show before 6 p.m. is $9. Kids 2 and under get in free. It opens 30 minutes before the first showtime, so check the schedule first.
Campground programs. In season, the park’s naturalists run campground evening programs. If you’re camping, ask at the visitor center what’s on that weekend, and remember the campground gate shuts at 10 p.m.
Grown-up nights at The Barn. The Barn at Woods Fort books ticketed 21-and-over evenings, like a witch-themed night of music, shopping and drinks this October. Watch the chamber calendar for the next one.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Troy, MO?
Downtown, on one night. Night of 1000 Stars is Troy’s luminaria night on Main Street in early December, and the city describes caroling, horse-drawn carriage rides and dance troupes. Luminaries have traditionally lined Main and Cherry streets, set out by the Troy Key Club.
The 2025 edition, on Saturday, Dec. 6, from 5 to 8 p.m., added photos with Santa and Mrs. Claus, food trucks, vendors and shops open late. Zion Church, at 725 Main St., opened its 95-year-old sanctuary for free tours with cookies and hot chocolate, and the Choral Arts Singers sang at 7. For 2026, one event listing showed Saturday, Dec. 5, but nothing official had been posted when we checked, so confirm with the Troy Historic Business Group before you plan the night around it.
What Troy doesn’t have, as far as we could confirm for 2026, is a big public drive-through light show. Home displays come and go from year to year, and we don’t publish house addresses. For a drive-through, the O’Fallon Christmas lights at Fort Zumwalt Park are a short drive south, and our guide to Christmas lights in St. Charles covers the neighborhood displays a little farther on. Then come back up Highway 61 for the Christmas Bash at the wrestling arena (Dec. 12 in 2026).
### What else is near Troy, MO?
Two conservation areas, one southeast of town and one to the north, are worth the extra miles if you own binoculars or a boat.
Cuivre Island Conservation Area, near Old Monroe. 1,461 acres on the Mississippi, most of it the 1,240-acre Cuivre Island, which you reach by boat at normal river levels. The 100-acre mainland tract has a parking lot and a boat launch onto Cuivre Slough. MDC lists white bass, sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass, and the area is open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m.
B.K. Leach Memorial Conservation Area, near Elsberry. 4,307 acres of wetlands managed for migrating waterfowl, and MDC lists bird watching among its uses. Parts of it close from Oct. 15 to March 1 to protect the birds, so check the area map before you go. Same hours, 4 a.m. to 10 p.m.
On the way home you’ll pass Moscow Mills and Wentzville. Next time someone tells you there’s nothing up Highway 61 but corn, you’re the one who knows about the four free campsites, the 120-foot bluff and the 7 o’clock bell. Register for a site. Pack water. Go.
After a night on Lone Spring Trail or a 7 p.m. bell time, our guide to where to eat in Troy, MO picks up where this one stops.
If you run a bait shop, an outfitter or a Main Street business that campers pass on the way to Highway 147, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
Farther north near Elsberry, our guide covers what to do at Ted Shanks Conservation Area, where the Salt River meets the Mississippi.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I rent a kayak on the Cuivre River?
A.  Not at the state park as a day visitor. Cuivre River State Park rents canoes and kayaks only to people staying in its organized group camps. Everyone else brings a boat to Lake Lincoln’s concrete launch, where there’s no launch fee and only electric motors may run. For the river side, MDC’s Cuivre Island Conservation Area near Old Monroe has a boat launch onto Cuivre Slough. We couldn’t confirm a public kayak rental on the river near Troy, MO.
### Q. Where can I go backcountry camping in Missouri?
A.  About an hour from St. Louis, Cuivre River State Park outside Troy, MO has four designated backpack sites on Lone Spring Trail, Big Sugar Creek Trail and the North Loop of the Cuivre River Trail. You register online before the trip, and the camping itself is free. Missouri’s 2026 statewide rate chart lists a nightly backcountry fee at some other parks, so check each park’s page before you assume.
### Q. What is the history of Cuivre River State Park?
A.  It started as a federal project. From 1934 to 1946 it was a Recreational Demonstration Area run by the National Park Service, and Civilian Conservation Corps Company 3771 built much of what’s still in use: the rock bridge on Highway 147 over Little Sugar Creek, the stone picnic shelter and Camp Sherwood Forest, a group camp in use since 1937 with 53 original buildings. On Nov. 8, 1946, President Truman signed the letter transferring it to the state, so the park turns 80 in November 2026. Camp Derricotte, another group camp, was founded in the park in 1939 by the St. Louis YWCA’s Phyllis Wheatley Branch and named for educator Juliette Derricotte.
### Q. Do seniors get into state parks for free?
A.  In Missouri, everyone does. State parks charge no admission, and fees apply to things like camping. Campers 65 and older get $2 off each night, year-round, if they ask at payment and show proof of age. The state asks for something other than the federal Senior Pass as that proof, since the federal pass is issued at 62.
### Q. Do I need a camping permit to camp in Missouri?
A.  At Cuivre River State Park you don’t need anything beyond a reservation or a walk-up registration for the campgrounds. Reserve up to 12 months ahead online or at 877-422-6766, or take an unreserved site by following the posted card or signs. The backcountry is different. The park’s free online registration, titled a backcountry camping permit form, has to be done before you start.
### Q. What are some things to do at Cuivre River State Park?
A.  Hike Frenchman’s Bluff for the river-valley view, swim at the Lake Lincoln beach in summer, paddle your own kayak on a lake where gas motors can’t run, walk the 0.3-mile Prairie Trail, ride Old Schoolhouse or the Blackhawk Point trail on a mountain bike, trailer a horse to the Cuivre River Trail, or backpack to one of four free sites. On a rainy weekday, the visitor center’s exhibits cover the park’s natural and cultural history.
### Q. Is there a dog park in Troy, MO?
A.  Not one we could find. The city’s parks list names Fairgrounds, Avery, Weinand and Woods Fort, and none of them has an off-leash area. Leashed dogs, on 10 feet of leash or less, are allowed at Cuivre River State Park, but not in the beach area or inside buildings. For fenced off-leash space, see our roundup of dog parks around St. Louis.
### Q. Is Cuivre River State Park open in November?
A.  Mostly. Campground 1 and the equestrian campground are open all year, but the showers shut off after Oct. 31, ice isn’t sold, and firewood comes from the campground host or the park office. The visitor center closes on weekends from Nov. 1 to April 14. In 2026 the entire park is also closed from 3 p.m. Oct. 30 to 7:30 a.m. Nov. 2 for a managed deer hunt, backcountry sites included.

## Step Inside Bigfoot's Wheel: Things to Do in Pacific, MO
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-pacific-mo
Black tread curves up past your head on both sides. The tire you’re standing in is a 10-foot Firestone, as tall as a basketball rim, and Bob Chandler came across it in a junkyard near Seattle. Whoever came with you backs up, and keeps backing up, to fit the whole wheel in the shot.
This is Bigfoot 5, parked outside B&H Market at 2244 W. Osage St. in Pacific, the truck Bigfoot 4x4 calls the world’s largest, widest and heaviest pickup. The company’s own visiting note puts it plainly: “step inside one of its huge wheels and have your picture taken.” One honest catch: the truck is on site unless it’s away at an event.
Then walk inside. The BIGFOOT Cafe is in the same market, and you eat surrounded by a Bigfoot display that covers the walls and, in the company’s words, “our entire history.” That history starts close to home. In 1981, on a whim, Chandler drove his truck over a pair of junk cars in an empty cornfield in rural Missouri, with one video camera rolling and a small crowd watching. The company calls the live version of that stunt the catalyst that ignited the whole monster truck industry.
Most St. Louisans who know the name still picture Hazelwood, where the team moved into a custom-built shop in 1984. Today Bigfoot 4x4’s headquarters sits on Rose Lane in Pacific, “where our fleet of BIGFOOT monster trucks is maintained.” Say that at the next tailgate: monster trucks were born in a Missouri cornfield, and the fleet still gets its wrenches turned in Pacific.
The plan that works. On a weekday, start at the Bigfoot shop on Rose Lane when it opens at 8, then the wheel at B&H Market. Next, climb the stone steps at Jensen’s Point, where the 1939 walls look down on Route 66, and run a hand along the chinked log walls of the Red Cedar Inn a few doors down. The shop is closed Friday through Sunday, so on those days start at BIGFOOT Plaza beside City Hall instead, where a Bigfoot is on display 24 hours a day. End the day at the Black Madonna grottos, where concrete rabbits poured in cupcake molds sit among seashells and costume jewelry pressed into the rock. The Black Madonna Shrine’s grounds are open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. from April through October and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. from November through March. The Red Cedar Inn’s visitor desk answers at 636-271-0500, ext. 222, and Bigfoot 4x4 posts holiday hours on its Facebook page.
### What are some attractions in Pacific, Missouri?
Pacific’s best attractions are Bigfoot 5 outside B&H Market, where you can stand inside one of its wheels, the Bigfoot on display around the clock at BIGFOOT Plaza, Bigfoot 4x4’s headquarters on Rose Lane (open Monday through Thursday), the 1939 stone overlook at Jensen’s Point, the Red Cedar Inn museum on Route 66, the Civil War cannon in Blackburn Park, Meramec fishing at Pacific Palisades and the hand-built Black Madonna grottos.
Start with the trucks. Nobody else can copy them.
### The Bigfoot trail, and the days the shop is closed
The headquarters keeps Monday-through-Thursday hours. The Rose Lane shop at 2286 Rose Ln. posts Monday through Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and lists Friday through Sunday as closed. That’s the detail that sinks most weekend plans. Inside there’s a small gift store of official Bigfoot merchandise, and the company says to check its Facebook page or call for holiday hours.
The weekend version still works. BIGFOOT Plaza sits right off the interstate beside Pacific City Hall, 300 N. Hoven Dr., and the company says a Bigfoot is on display there 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Pull in after dark and it’s still standing there. Then drive to B&H Market for Bigfoot 5 and lunch at the BIGFOOT Cafe. Downtown, The BIGFOOT Collection at 142 W. St. Louis St. sells art prints of the truck by artists from around the world. It’s closed Monday and Tuesday and open the rest of the week.
One more stop that only fans know: the Red Cedar Inn museum carries an exclusive Bigfoot t-shirt that, according to Bigfoot 4x4, you can’t get anywhere else.
### How do you get to the top of Jensen’s Point Overlook?
Park in the paved lot at the base of the hill, 1039 E. Osage St., and climb the stone steps. That’s it. The city has repaired the steps, patios and walls, and from the top the point overlooks Route 66, the old highway running below the stone you’re leaning on. The state tourism office lists the site as not wheelchair accessible, so anyone unsteady on stairs should take it slowly.
The overlook exists because of a road beautification plan. Jensen’s Point was part of the Henry Shaw Gardenway, a project of the National Park Service and the Missouri State Highway Commission, and the Civilian Conservation Corps built it in 1939. It’s named for Lars Peter Jensen, the first president of the Henry Shaw Gardenway Association and manager of the Shaw Arboretum. If the old road hooks you, our guide to scenic drives around St. Louis picks up Route 66 from here.
### A log roadhouse, white cliffs and a Civil War cannon on one road
The Red Cedar Inn. Down the road at 1047 E. Osage St., the city’s museum and visitor center fills a 1934 restaurant built from logs off the family farm and chinked to look like pioneer days. It was famous for fried chicken and stayed open until 2005. Now it’s a museum, visitor center, children’s museum and gift shop on Route 66. The city posts hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Saturday and noon to 4 on Sunday. Run a hand along the old log walls and you can almost hear the plates.
The sand caves. Drive W. Osage St. near downtown and the bluffs go bright white, with dark mouths cut into them. Starting in the 1870s, miners carved deep into that St. Peter Sandstone for high-purity silica, and by 1904 Pacific sand was riding railcars to glassmakers as far away as France and Germany. When Route 66 came through, road crews cut straight into the bluffs and exposed the caves you see now. Look from the road. Don’t go in.
Blackburn Park. On October 1, 1864, Confederate cavalry under Gen. William Cabell burned the railroad depot in a town still called Franklin. Union troops rerouted from St. Louis met them just east of town, with artillery up on the sandstone bluffs. A historical marker and a replica Civil War cannon in Blackburn Park tell the story now. Put a hand on the cold iron barrel and look down at the tracks the raid was after.
The railroad named this town. Pacific was platted as Franklin in 1852, the railroad laid tracks in 1853, and by 1859 Franklin had renamed itself Pacific in the railroad’s honor. The city’s own history page keeps the strangest line of all: “The US Air force acquired land in the city to construct its Nike-Hercules Missile base.” The base was turned over to the city in 1969, and in 1970 the Meramec Valley School District opened a school in its old barracks. Kids went to class in rooms built for a missile base. Pacific spreads across three counties, Franklin, Jefferson and St. Louis, and of all the small towns outside St. Louis, it may be the one people drive past fastest.
Climbed the stone steps and stood in the wheel? Now go find lunch. Our guide to where to eat in Pacific, MO is the next tab to open.
If you run the coffee counter, the bait shop or the truck garage along W. Osage St., put your business in front of them so the people driving out for Bigfoot become your customers.
### Where can you fish the Meramec near Pacific?
Pacific Palisades Conservation Area, immediately east of town. It’s a 695-acre Missouri Department of Conservation tract in Jefferson and St. Louis counties with three miles of lower Meramec frontage, and MDC says anglers come for bass, crappie, bluegill and non-game fish. Early on a cool morning, the gravel crunches under your boots and the river slides by green and quiet.
Two old gravel pits connect to the river when the water is high. MDC says they aren’t stocked or managed, so treat them as a gamble. The area is open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., but fishing and launching boats are allowed around the clock where permitted, so a night catfish run is fair game. Pets must stay leashed.
The boat ramp is on the St. Louis County side, and you won’t find it by guessing. MDC’s directions: take Exit 261 south to Business Loop 44, go west to Dozier Crossing, turn south across the railroad tracks, then west on Franklin Road. For more of the same river, we also mapped the Meramec River access points in Fenton, farther downstream.
### Is there a grotto in Missouri?
Yes, and the best-known set near St. Louis carries a Pacific address: the Black Madonna Shrine and Grottos, 100 St. Joseph’s Hill Rd., in the countryside about eight miles outside Eureka. The shrine puts it at about a 40-minute drive from west St. Louis County. Take the interstate to the Eureka exit, go south on Highway 109 to FF, right on FF, left on F, then right on St. Joseph’s Road.
In 1927, six Franciscan brothers came to Missouri from Poland. One of them, Brother Bronislaus Luszcz, started clearing these woods in 1937 and built a cedar chapel. One evening in 1958 an arsonist set the altar on fire and the chapel burned. He kept building. By hand, without power tools, he raised grottos of tiff rock hauled from a mining community 30 miles southwest, pressing in seashells from foreign missions and costume jewelry from visitors.
Look closely and the walls start talking. The rabbits and lambs at the St. Francis grotto were made by pouring concrete into cupcake molds. The flower pots at Our Lady of Perpetual Help are stacked Jell-O molds. Colored jars set into the Gethsemane grotto once filtered sunlight onto the sleeping apostles. And Our Lady of Perpetual Help is where he died: on August 12, 1960, still weak from the flu, he was overcome by the summer sun, left a trail of tools from his unfinished Fatima statue and made it to this grotto. The brothers knew something was wrong when he didn’t come to evening prayers.
Grab the free walking-tour brochure at the gift shop. Grounds are open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. April through October and 9 to 4 November through March, with the gift shop and museum closing at 4 in season. Questions go to the office at 636-938-5361. Through January 10, 2027, it’s also a pilgrimage site for the Jubilee Year of St. Francis.
Our roundup of underrated places to visit in St. Louis gives the shrine a short entry, and our list of unique things to do in Eureka covers the rest of that exit.
Want the river with a paddle in your hands? See what Eureka has on the Meramec
### What events are happening in Pacific, MO this weekend?
It depends on the weekend, and the city keeps its list on its own tourism events page. This year’s ran heavy in late summer: car cruises at the Red Cedar Inn in August, an outdoor Route 66 movie series showing the Disney Cars trilogy, and the Pacific Iron Horse Rodeo at Liberty Field in September, gates at 5:30 p.m. Check that page and the Red Cedar Inn before you go.
No event on your weekend? The plaza truck stays on display around the clock, the shrine grounds open at 9, and the Meramec is there at sunrise.
### Nearby, on the same river and road
Pacific sits at the western edge of the metro, an easy hinge for a longer day. Keep going west to the Missouri River, where our list of things to do in Washington, MO picks up the trail. Downriver, the best trails at Castlewood State Park start in Valley Park, and to the west, the things to do in Union, MO pick up from there.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where is the monster truck Bigfoot located?
A.  Bigfoot 4x4’s headquarters is at 2286 Rose Lane in Pacific, where the fleet is maintained, open Monday through Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Any day, a Bigfoot is on display at BIGFOOT Plaza beside Pacific City Hall, 300 N. Hoven Dr., and Bigfoot 5 sits outside B&H Market, 2244 W. Osage St., unless it’s away at an event.
### Q. Who owns the original Bigfoot monster truck?
A.  BIGFOOT 4x4, Inc., the Pacific company that lists “BIGFOOT” and “THE ORIGINAL MONSTER TRUCK” as its registered trademarks. Its history traces the first truck to the Ford F-250 that Bob and Marilyn Chandler ordered in 1974, a parts-shop errand truck that kept getting bigger until a shop employee nicknamed Bob “Bigfoot” for his heavy right foot.
### Q. How many Bigfoot monster trucks exist?
A.  The numbering runs to #24. According to the company’s history, the newest trucks, #23 and #24, first appeared in 2023 and 2025, the year the team marked the original monster truck’s 50th anniversary. Bigfoot #20, finished in 2012, is the world’s first battery-powered monster truck, and a licensed team in the United Kingdom runs Bigfoot #17.
### Q. Is red cedar native to Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Missouri Department of Conservation calls eastern red cedar a native plant, one so tough it invades prairies, glades and woodlands, and notes Missouri has one other native juniper, Ashe’s juniper. Its small cones carry what MDC describes as an odor of gin.
### Q. What is free this weekend?
A.  In Pacific, a good day costs almost nothing.
