Bigfoot 4x4 says its plaza truck beside City Hall is on display 24 hours a day, every day, and the Black Madonna Shrine hands out its walking-tour brochures free of charge. The Jensen’s Point climb, the Blackburn Park cannon and the sand cave bluffs are all out in the open. The Bigfoot shop itself is closed Friday through Sunday.

## Things to Do in Cottleville, MO: Golf Cart Streets, Legacy Park, a BB Gun Bar
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-cottleville-mo
Nobody tells you Cottleville is a golf cart town. The recycled top 10 lists file it as a dinner stop on Highway N, somewhere between the Mid Rivers Mall Drive traffic and the drive home, and move on. The city’s own 2026 map says otherwise. It calls Cottleville a “golf cart friendly city,” it lists golf cart parking in Old Town, and the Legacy Park lot by the amphitheater reserves its first two aisles for golf carts, handicap parking and the band.
Once you know that, the town makes sense. Carts are legal on Cottleville streets posted 30 mph or less and on the paved Dardenne Greenway that follows the creek behind Old Town. Park once, and the paths carry you to a log cabin trailhead, two lakes, a bark park and a wooded trail named for a War of 1812 fort. Across town, inside a subdivision off Mid Rivers Mall Drive, there’s an 18 acre lake where you rent a kayak from your phone. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Cottleville might be the one people have driven through most often without ever seeing it.
Dates, hours and rules below come from city, county, Great Rivers Greenway and business pages checked in October 2026. Small-town calendars move fast. Check again before you go.
### What are some fun things to do in Cottleville?
Fun things to do in Cottleville include cruising the paved Dardenne Greenway by golf cart, bike or foot to Legacy Park’s log cabin, lakes and bark park, renting a kayak by app on 18 acre Buchheit Lake, shooting at a self-styled BB gun bar, playing heated bocce, and coming back in March for Irish Fest.
The thread through all of it is the golf cart, and the rules fit on one sheet of paper. The Cottleville Police Department posts them as a public safety notice, and they’re worth a minute before you roll out.
Who can drive. Drivers must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver’s license. Walkers and bikes have the right of way, and you can’t carry more people than the cart was built to seat.
Where you can drive. On any street with a speed limit of 30 mph or less, or on a sidewalk wider than 6 feet. The cart speed limit is 25 mph. Before dawn or after sunset, the headlight and taillight go on.
Who enforces it. The same officers who enforce car laws, under Section 340.105 of the city code. Cart drivers get tickets and go through municipal court like anyone else.
Where to park. The city map lists golf cart parking in Old Town, alongside bike racks and street parking. In Legacy Park, the first two aisles of the lot are reserved for golf carts, handicap parking and band loading. Keep carts off the amphitheater hill and the grass. The city asks for that in writing.
Where it stops. Here’s what the brochure doesn’t spell out. Those are Cottleville’s rules. The Dardenne Greenway keeps going into St. Peters, and Great Rivers Greenway says each city along a greenway sets its own rules for use, parking and hours, so the rules can change as you cross a city line. Check before you drive a cart past the Cottleville stretch.
No cart? You lose nothing. The town was walkable long before it was cart friendly. Old Town grew up where the old Boone’s Lick Road crossed Dardenne Creek, and in the early 1800s travelers got stranded here every time the creek flooded the bottoms. Highway N is that road. The creek is still right there, and the trail along it ties the rest of this page together.
### What is there to do at Legacy Park in Cottleville?
A lot more than the playground. Legacy Park runs along Dardenne Creek beside City Hall at 5490 Fifth St., and the city calls it its most used park. Most visitors see the amphitheater and the swings, then leave. Walk ten minutes in any direction and it opens up.
Don Yarber Bark Park. Two fenced sections: one for small dogs and puppies, and a one acre side for big dogs. It’s named for Don Yarber, mayor from 2002 to 2013, who wanted the bark park to stand as part of his legacy of public parks. Know two things before you load the car. It closes when the ground is too muddy, and the full rules are posted at the site. The city lists no fee. For more off-leash space around the metro, see our guide to dog parks around St. Louis.
The log cabin. It belonged to the Sargent family and stood on Eagle Hill, just north of Old Town, until the city bought it and moved it here. Now it’s a Dardenne Greenway trailhead with a self-composting restroom, and it’s where the city brings in live animals. In 2026 the cabin hosted a bald eagle display in May, reptiles in July and owls in September. In December, Mrs. Claus reads stories there.
Koontz Fort Trail. This is the history you can walk. It’s a 0.4 mile, 8 foot wide trail through the woods between the Brittany Place subdivision and Legacy Park. The name comes from Nicholas Koontz, who built a fort on what’s now Highway N during the War of 1812. A mail stop operated inside it. When settlers asked for federal troops and got no answer, they raised their own ranger companies, one of them called the Boone Company. The city built it as a dry weather trail, so skip it after a hard rain.
Harmony Lake and Vantage Lake. Two lakes, two different walks. Harmony Lake is 5 acres, with a fishing dock, Pavilions C and D and the 0.6 mile paved Podhorn Memorial Trail. It’s named for the peace and harmony Mrs. Podhorn, a lifelong resident, said she found on her farm here. You can drive in from Cottleville Parkway near St. Charles Community College. Vantage Lake is 9 acres, with a small gazebo and a 0.7 mile paved loop, and the easy way in is the 10 foot wide pedestrian bridge over Dardenne Creek. The community garden plots sit near Vantage Lake.
The Liberty Swing. Plenty of parents in the county have never heard of this one. The playground has a Liberty Swing, designed so a person in a wheelchair can swing safely, a gift from the Cottleville Firemen’s Outreach. It’s kept locked. Stop by the Police Department, City Hall or the Fire Department for the key. The police non-emergency line, 636-939-9966, is answered 24 hours a day if you want to call ahead.
Free sand volleyball and pickup hoops. The Marie Mannino courts are two Florida sand courts, open for free play day or night, first come, first served, except when the city leagues are playing. You can’t reserve them. Four basketball hoops stand at the tennis courts.
Twilight Tuesdays. In summer, the Cottleville Weldon Spring Rotary Amphitheater hosts the city’s Tuesday night concerts from 6 to 8:30 p.m. The 2026 season ran May 19 to Sept. 1, with cover and tribute bands from Motown to Elvis to the 80s. Bring chairs or a blanket, and shade umbrellas are welcome. Food trucks park across the street at Frankie Martin’s Garden. And this is where those golf cart aisles come in.
### What is there to do in Cottleville at night?
Dinner is the easy part, and our guide to where to eat in Cottleville covers the Old Town kitchens and patios. This section is about what comes after. Cottleville nights run on games more than bar stools, and the four places below sit a short cart ride apart.
Top Shot. It bills itself as “The World’s First BB Gun Bar,” and that’s its own claim. What’s inside is easier to vouch for: low-powered BB guns with a mild simulated recoil (an AR-style rifle, a 1911-style pistol and an airsoft bow) fired at interactive targets, after a safety briefing and with eye protection for everyone. It sits inside Top Notch Axe Throwing at 5055 Highway N, so a group can split between axes and targets. The site lists beer, wine and canned drinks for sale (no more BYOB) and says there’s no age limit. Posted hours are Tuesday through Thursday 5 to 8:30 p.m., Friday 5 to 11:30, Saturday noon to 11:30 and Sunday noon to 8, and reservations are required Monday through Thursday and on Sundays. The price is per person, listed as $35 in one spot and $38 in another, so confirm it when you book. One quirk: its address says St. Charles. It’s in Old Town Cottleville, which shares the 63304 ZIP code.
Aiello’s heated bocce. This is the cold-night move. Aiello’s Cigar Bar, at 5286 Highway N, has covered, heated bocce courts. Leagues take them Monday through Thursday from 6 p.m. to close. Any other time, play is free as long as you buy a cigar or a drink, so the open courts are Friday through Sunday, or a weeknight before 6. It’s a cigar bar. Expect smoke, and it’s 21 and over only. Posted hours run until 10 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 6 p.m. Sunday.
Frankie Martin’s Garden. It’s built on the old property of Frank J. Martin, a longtime Cottleville resident who died in 2020, and his house was brought back as the centerpiece. There are food trucks and a long whiskey list, but it lands in this section for everything else: pickleball courts with leagues and court reservations, a Wednesday disc golf putting league ($10 cash, 6 to 8:30 p.m., five putting stations), free music bingo on some Tuesdays, and live bands most Wednesday through Saturday nights, many of them billed as free, all-ages shows. Leave the cooler in the car, because outside food and drinks aren’t allowed. It’s at 5372 St. Charles St., across the street from Legacy Park.
The Field at Cottle Village. Out at 6470 Highway N, the owners are restoring the old Kurtz Nursery and Farm, and they kept the farmstead buildings. The farmhouse grew from 2,000 square feet to 8,000. The property holds a tavern, a distillery that pours straight from the barrel, and The Field, an outdoor stage with fire and a 15 foot LED screen. Bands are booked on October weekends, and on October Thursdays the screen becomes a free Halloween movie theater. Check its events page for hours.
Dinner before the bocce court? Where to eat in Cottleville
### What Cottleville events are coming up for Halloween and Christmas?
October is Cottleville’s busiest month outside of Irish Fest, and most of it costs little or nothing. Here’s the 2026 run in date order. Check each organizer’s page before you go, because small events shift.
CottleWeen movie Thursdays. Cottle Village shows a classic Halloween movie on The Field’s 15 foot screen every Thursday in October at 6:30 p.m., with popcorn, a candy stand and snacks themed to the film. Admission is free, and no ticket is needed. The 2026 lineup includes Beetlejuice on Oct. 8, The Nightmare Before Christmas on Oct. 15, Hotel Transylvania on Oct. 22 and Halloweentown on Oct. 29.
Halloween Movie in the Park, with hayrides. The city’s own version runs Tuesday, Oct. 20, from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. at the Legacy Park amphitheater, with hayrides along the Dardenne Greenway. The city hadn’t posted a price when we checked, so see its Twilight Tuesdays page. Reading this after Halloween? Watch that page for next year’s dates.
Family campout and stargazing. A community partner runs an overnight campout on the Kochanski Multi Sports Field in Legacy Park, from 4 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 24, to 6 a.m. Sunday. Sign up through the link on the same city page.
Golf Cart Trunk-or-Treat. Of course Cottleville has a golf cart trunk-or-treat. Frankie Martin’s Garden hosts it on Sunday, Oct. 25, from 2 to 5 p.m., with costume contests and a prize for the best decorated cart. Kids come in costume. Cart owners reserve a spot through the garden’s ticket link for a small fee and bring their own candy.
Run Witch Run, and a grown-up night before it. On Friday, Oct. 30, Frankie Martin’s goes 21 and over from 6 p.m. for a Halloween party with a costume contest and a live band. The next morning, Saturday, Oct. 31, runners in costume take the Legacy Park trails at 9 a.m. in a 1 mile, 5K or 10K, with posted prices of $30, $50 and $55 that rise after Oct. 25. The Kids Dash starts at 8:45 with candy at the finish. For haunts and pumpkin patches across the rest of the metro, see our St. Louis Halloween guide.
Then December. Cottleville keeps Christmas small, and that’s the appeal. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, from 6 to 7 p.m., the city lights the tree at the clock tower at City Hall, with the Salvation Army’s Red Kettle kickoff, a choir and Santa. On Tuesday, Dec. 8, from 4:30 to 7:30 p.m., Mrs. Claus reads stories in the log cabin while carriage rides roll along the Dardenne Greenway. For the big drive-through displays a few exits away, see our guides to Christmas lights in St. Charles and O’Fallon Christmas lights.
### Is the Cottleville St. Patrick’s Day parade still happening?
No, and the search results haven’t caught up. The city started its St. Patrick’s celebration in 2008, with a parade, community activities and a 5K, and it grew into one of the largest single-day events in St. Charles County. Rising costs ended the parade in 2022, and since 2025 Old Town’s businesses have run the day as Irish Fest. That first year, the festival wasn’t officially sanctioned by the city, though officials spent months working with owners on safety changes. The police chief put the 2024 crowd at around 30,000 people.
Here’s how the 2026 day ran. The morning opened with the Cottleville Firefighters Outreach 5K at 9 a.m., a race that has run since 2008 as the Shamrock Run, where the top finishers win green fire helmets and the post-race party has donuts and cold beer. Roads through Old Town closed from about 8:30 to 11 a.m. Irish Fest itself went from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Saturday, March 14, with live bands and Irish-themed events hosted by Old Town businesses. Venues checked IDs and handed out 21+ wristbands, and they didn’t allow backpacks or outside coolers inside.
Three practical things. Rideshare pickup is the lot next to the police department entrance at 5490 Fifth St. Parking on grass is banned anywhere in the city, and cars get ticketed and towed. And the 2027 date isn’t posted yet. The festival has landed on the Saturday before St. Patrick’s Day for two years running, so watch the city’s and the firefighters’ pages.
### Where can you kayak and fish in Cottleville?
On a lake most of St. Charles County has never heard of. Scott A. Lewis Park is Cottleville’s newest park, 65 acres inside the Miralago subdivision off Mid Rivers Mall Drive, at 1000 Scott A. Lewis Lane. Its centerpiece is 18 acre Buchheit Lake (the park’s two lakes total 22.5 acres), and the city set it up for paddling. Kayak and stand-up paddleboard rentals run through the Rent.Fun app. The city doesn’t publish prices, so check the app. A boat ramp takes kayaks, canoes and paddle boats. Gas motors aren’t allowed. Electric only.
Fishing follows Missouri regulations, so carry a permit if you need one, and the city adds one rule of its own: no netting fish. An 8 foot paved trail runs along the lake, and in 2019 the city extended it to the trails along Dardenne Creek by Calvary Church. The park is named for Scott A. Lewis, the longtime police chief and city administrator who became St. Charles County sheriff and still serves as the city historian. The lake honors Don Buchheit, a Ward 2 alderman for more than 30 years. In 2026 the city set its Arbor Day tree planting here for Tuesday, Oct. 13, starting at 4 p.m.
Rather fish from a dock? The one on Harmony Lake in Legacy Park is the easy pick, and Great Rivers Greenway notes two fishing lakes at Woodlands Sports Park, down the Dardenne Greenway in St. Peters. If you want moving water, St. Peters is also where you kayak the Dardenne Creek Blueway, the same creek that runs behind Old Town.
### Can you walk, bike or drive a golf cart on the Dardenne Greenway in Cottleville?
Yes, all three on the Cottleville stretch, and that’s the stretch to use right now. Great Rivers Greenway posted on Aug. 24, 2026, that the Dardenne Greenway between Mexico Road and Dardenne Park, plus the underpass beneath Mexico Road, is closed for construction through summer 2027. Mexico Road is in St. Peters. The Cottleville end sits south of the closed section and stays open.
The route. The city says the paved trail connects Old Town to St. Charles Community College, The Woodlands, Rabbit Run Park and on toward the St. Peters Golf Course. Start at the log cabin trailhead in Legacy Park. Along the college campus, Great Rivers Greenway planted “botanical vignettes” of native flowers and grasses. Woodlands Sports Park adds 92 acres with two fishing lakes and a paved 1 mile loop, and Rabbit Run Park has two miles of paved trail of its own. The whole Legacy Park to Dardenne Park segment is 7.32 miles, mostly flat with a few rolling hills, and you’ll pass woods, wetlands and prairie.
The disc golf course on campus. College Meadows Park, St. Charles County’s 11th regional park, covers 80 acres on the St. Charles Community College campus near the west entrance at 4601 Mid Rivers Mall Drive. The city calls its 18 hole disc golf course just the third of its kind in the region, and course listings show it as free to play. In June 2026 the county held its fifth annual Doubles Glow tournament there, with lit baskets on all 18 holes through the woods and open fairways. Bring your own discs.
The short ones. The Jim Hennessey Trail follows the north side of Highway N west of Weiss Road, named in 2021 for a former mayor. The Warren Cottle Trail is a safe routes to school path that winds through the community garden to Warren Elementary. It’s named for the captain whose 1798 Spanish land grant on Dardenne Creek started the town.
### Nearby, along the same creek
Cottleville sits between bigger neighbors, and we cover each of them on its own page. St. Peters owns the blueway and the Rec-Plex, and one tip from that page is worth repeating here: Cottleville residents with a Cottleville Privilege Card pay the Rec-Plex resident rate. Head west, and historic downtown Wentzville makes a good second stop on a county day.
Next time someone calls Cottleville a place to grab dinner on the way home, you’ll know better. You’ll know the carts are street legal under 30 mph, the War of 1812 trail ends in the same park as the bark park, the swing key is at the police desk, and the kayak rents from your phone. Pick a fall evening. Park once. Go.
Before the concert or after the bocce, our guide to where to eat in Cottleville covers the Old Town kitchens a short walk or cart ride from Legacy Park.
If you run a shop on one of the Old Town streets where golf carts can legally pull up, list it with us so the people parking outside find you first.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Cottleville, MO known for?
A.  Its Old Town, first. Cottleville grew up where the old Boone’s Lick Road, now Highway N, crossed Dardenne Creek, on land Captain Warren G. Cottle got through a Spanish land grant in 1798. Before 1839 the village was sometimes called Dardenne or Pin Hook, and in 1846 it even circulated petitions to take the county seat from St. Charles. It lost. Today it’s known for Old Town’s bars and restaurants, the Irish Fest crowds every March and its golf cart friendly streets.
### Q. What events are happening in Cottleville, MO this weekend?
A.  It depends on the week, but a few things are close to constant. Frankie Martin’s Garden books live music most Wednesday through Saturday nights, many of them free, all-ages shows, and Cottle Village books bands on The Field on weekends. In October, Thursday nights bring free CottleWeen movies at Cottle Village. For city events, the Twilight Tuesdays page on the City of Cottleville site lists the year’s concerts, classes, holiday events and community partner events.
### Q. Are dogs allowed in Legacy Park?
A.  Yes. The city lists walking your pet among the uses of the paved Dardenne Greenway through the park, and Legacy Park has its own off-leash area, the Don Yarber Bark Park, with a side for small dogs and puppies and a one acre side for large dogs. It closes when the ground is too muddy, and its rules are posted at the site.
### Q. What time is the St. Patrick’s Day parade?
A.  In Cottleville, there isn’t one anymore. The city ended its parade in 2022 over rising costs, and Old Town businesses now run Irish Fest instead. In 2026 it ran from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Saturday, March 14, after the firefighters’ 5K at 9 a.m., with Old Town roads closed from about 8:30 to 11 a.m. Check the 2027 date with the city.
### Q. What are some good paved bike trails in St. Louis?
A.  On the St. Charles County side, the Dardenne Greenway is an easy one to start with. Great Rivers Greenway lists its Legacy Park to Dardenne Park segment at 7.32 paved miles, mostly flat, past lakes, wetlands and the St. Charles Community College campus. The stretch between Mexico Road and Dardenne Park is closed for construction through summer 2027, so start from the log cabin trailhead in Cottleville’s Legacy Park and ride out and back.
### Q. How many people live in Cottleville, Missouri?
A.  About 6,378, according to the City of Cottleville, which cites the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2024 figure. Some older tourism write-ups still say just over 3,000, so if a guide you’re reading uses that number, the rest of it may be out of date too.
### Q. Where does the Greenway Walk start and end?
A.  For the Dardenne Greenway through Cottleville, the natural start is the old log cabin in Legacy Park, which the city uses as a trailhead, near Highway N and City Hall. From there the paved trail runs past St. Charles Community College and north toward Mexico Road in St. Peters. Great Rivers Greenway has it closed from Mexico Road to Dardenne Park through summer 2027, so plan to turn around before Mexico Road for now.
### Q. Can you drive a golf cart in Cottleville?
A.  Yes, if you’re 16 or older with a valid driver’s license. Cottleville police allow carts on streets with a speed limit of 30 mph or less and on sidewalks wider than 6 feet, at a cart speed limit of 25 mph, with a headlight and taillight on before dawn and after sunset. The city’s trail page even invites you to cruise the Dardenne Greenway in your cart.

## Things to Do in Valley Park, MO: Castlewood Trails Past Resort Ruins, Walking Lone Elk Park
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-valley-park-mo
More than 10,000 visitors every summer weekend. That’s the crowd Missouri State Parks says used to descend on Castlewood, the old resort strip on the Meramec just upriver from Valley Park, at the height of its popularity, and the park superintendent told St. Louis Public Radio they usually came by train. The concrete stairs they climbed from the depot are still on the bluff, crumbling beside a state park boardwalk. The trail next door is named for a Prohibition speakeasy. Meanwhile the recycled top-10 lists treat Valley Park as an exit on I-44 and send you somewhere else.
They have the town backward. Valley Park was built to be the getaway. The city’s own history counts 88 daily trains stopping here at its industrial peak, before a record flood in August 1915 wiped out the factories, and 24 trains a day in the 1920s carrying St. Louisans out to the river resorts. The leftovers sit in plain sight: an 1880s railroad crew hotel that now sells toy trains, a 1935 Frisco caboose, and an 1887 grain elevator that’s still a working hardware store. Even the elk have a backstory: the herd was restocked in 1966 with six Yellowstone elk, with help from Rockwood School District kids.
Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the one where the history is underfoot on the trail. Everything below was checked against Missouri State Parks trail sheets, St. Louis County, the City of Valley Park and the World Bird Sanctuary in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do.
### What is Valley Park, MO known for?
Valley Park, MO is known as the old Meramec River resort and railroad town, and as the doorway to Lone Elk Park’s elk and bison, the World Bird Sanctuary’s raptors and Castlewood State Park’s bluff trails. It also has a paved 3.2-mile levee trail, a city archery range and a toy train store in an 1880s railroad hotel.
Underneath all of that is a river town that spent most of a century losing arguments with the river. Floods kept knocking the old town back, and eventually even the resorts and clubhouses gave in. Then came the Meramec Valley levee, which the city dates to 2006. ProPublica described it as a single levee about 3 miles long that cost $50 million, and it kept Valley Park dry through the record floods of 2015 and 2017. Today you can ride a bike along the top of it.
So here’s the map in one breath. Castlewood’s trails are the deep end, with resort ruins, a speakeasy’s name and the highest point in the park. Lone Elk Park has real walking trails, not only a scenic drive. The levee trail costs nothing, and neither does watching the model planes at Buder Park. The toy train hotel saves a rainy Saturday. And from October on, the owls take over.
### What is the best trail at Castlewood State Park?
River Scene is the one to start with, and the reason isn’t the overlook everyone photographs. It’s a 3.4-mile loop rated moderate, about two and a half hours, that climbs to the bluff edge and follows it for about a mile, with the Meramec valley more than 200 feet below. Then a wooden boardwalk drops off the end of the bluff past what the state’s trail sheet calls “the crumbling remains of the ‘Grand Staircase.’”
Those steps were the front door of a resort. They climbed from the Castlewood railroad depot to the hotel and cabins on the bluff, and on a summer weekend in the resort era, more than 10,000 people came through. The park superintendent described the scene to St. Louis Public Radio in 2019: a couple hundred buildings, from clubhouses and dance halls to a place to get a haircut, ice cream or whiskey. Almost none of it is left. You’ll pass a few old foundations on the bluff. Then the boardwalk ducks through a tunnel under the Union Pacific tracks, right where the depot stood, and the trail runs flat along the river for about two miles. The bluff section is hiking only; bikes are allowed on the bottomland.
Watch for a big open field on that river stretch. That was Lincoln Lodge, a hotel. Across the water sat Lincoln Beach, a sand beach made by dredging the river bottom, and the state calls it the prime gathering spot of the resort era. Floods erased it long ago. One plain fact about that water: Castlewood has no designated swim area, the Highway Patrol says the Meramec runs wider and deeper here, with currents and debris that change every time the river rises and falls, and Post-Dispatch reporting counts more than a dozen deaths along the river inside the park since 2004, with a 19-year-old drowning there in July 2026.
Lone Wolf, for the second story. This 1.7-mile loop is rated rugged, and the state figures about an hour and 40 minutes. It climbs the old Ridge Road to the bluffs alongside River Scene, then splits off and drops through fern-covered hillsides into the Kiefer Creek valley. The name honors what the trail sheet calls Castlewood’s “most notorious roadhouse tavern/speakeasy” of the resort era. St. Louis Public Radio reports it served liquor through Prohibition. Two siblings who grew up in a one-room clubhouse nearby in the late 1940s told the station it stayed members-only long after, and they never even made it into the parking lot. One of them called it the “classiest-looking joint in Castlewood.” The state says all that remains of the club is a stone fireplace and memories, and what survives of the building stands on private property outside the park. The trail is as close as you get.
Cedar Bluff Loop, the hard one to reach. It’s 2.3 rugged miles at the far west end of the park, cut off from every road. You can only reach it from the Al Foster Trail, through two early 20th century tunnels under the Union Pacific. It climbs to the highest point in the entire park. And the state admits, with a straight face, that it doesn’t actually go along Cedar Bluff. In summer, look for two big blackberry brambles in the creek wash at the back of the valley.
Grotpeter, for riders. Missouri State Parks calls Castlewood one of the best mountain biking locations in the St. Louis area, and Grotpeter is where riders log the miles: a 4.4-mile moderate loop over the wooded ridges, plus four white connectors totaling 2.6 miles that let you skip the steepest climbs or stretch the day. Lone Wolf and Cedar Bluff take bikes too.
The Valley Park side. A straight answer on the address: Castlewood’s mailing address is 1401 Kiefer Creek Road in Ballwin, and that’s where you park for River Scene, Lone Wolf and Grotpeter. The park’s south bank is reached from Valley Park. The Chubb Trail starts inside Lone Elk Park and crosses Castlewood on flat, forested bottomland and a couple of restored prairie fields, then climbs to West Tyson County Park at the Eureka end, and our list of unique things to do in Eureka covers what’s out that way. It’s hilly at both ends, and the county puts the whole trail at about 7 miles. Off the Chubb, the 2.8-mile Castlewood Loop skirts the edge of old Lincoln Beach, which the state calls a swimming hole and gathering place from 1915 to 1940. Both trails are open to horses as well as hikers and bikes. Park grounds open at 7 a.m. and close a half hour after sunset.
Hiking with little kids? Our roundup of easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis has gentler picks. These are the trails with a story.
### Can you walk around Lone Elk Park?
Yes, on its trails, and the drive gets all the attention. St. Louis County runs Lone Elk as a 546-acre wildlife management area with bison, elk, deer, wild turkey and waterfowl, and the county’s rule is to stay in your vehicle unless you’re on the walking trails. So park at the visitor center and walk.
The White Bison Trail. This is the long one, an earthen and rocky loop the county lists at 4 miles. Hiking apps clock it closer to 3.1 to 3.4, so plan on 3 to 4. These are wild animals, not props. Keep your distance, and give bulls extra room in fall, when elk mate.
The 30-30 hike. Short on time? The county’s 30-30 route leaves from the visitor center trailhead and goes 0.8 miles to the northwest corner of the lake and back, 1.6 miles total.
The rules that matter. Open 8 a.m. to official sunset, with no admission. No motorcycles. And no pets, even if they never leave the car: the county says domestic animals aren’t allowed “even if confined in a vehicle.” The visitor center keeps a restroom open year round. The county reopened the bison area in June 2026 after storm damage, so check its parks Facebook page for closures before you go.
The herd’s origin story. In 1964 the county paid $60,787 for 405 acres. Six elk arrived from Yellowstone in 1966, through the efforts of Rockwood School District children and the West St. Louis County Lions Club. The park opened on Oct. 17, 1971, and six bison came over from the Saint Louis Zoo in July 1973. Why “Lone” Elk? One bull that survived after the earlier herd on the old ammunition-plant land was destroyed. Our guide to scenic drives around St. Louis tells that story and covers the drive itself.
The World Bird Sanctuary. You reach it through Lone Elk, and it sits on land leased from Castlewood State Park, 305 acres of hardwood forest and aviaries. Entry is $5 a person, daily 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. The sanctuary says it treats more than 750 raptor patients a year in its hospital, and it’s marking 50 years. The seasonal Taking Wing flight show comes with admission. For something you’ll talk about on the drive home, keepers run a $50 “Handle an Exotic Raptor” session daily at 2 p.m. for ages 13 and up.
### What free things can you do in Valley Park?
Start on top of the levee. The city’s Levee Trail is 3.2 paved miles from Marshall Road and the railroad tracks to the tracks behind Leonard Park, open sunrise to sunset. City ordinance requires a helmet on anything with wheels. You’re riding on the thing that keeps the town dry.
The 10-mile flat loop. St. Louis County maps a “relatively flat 10-mile paved ride” from Simpson Park: out the Meramec Greenway to Greentree Park and back, then west to Arnold’s Grove, then the spur that crosses the flood gate at Marshall Road and runs along the top of the levee on the north side of town. Arnold’s Grove is the trailhead to know. It sits on the levee just west of Highway 141, off Meramec Station Road, with parking and a 30-person pavilion, and it was dedicated in October 2009. Greentree Park is the far end of the Greenway, and our list of things to do in Kirkwood picks up from there.
The archery range. Inside the 69-acre Meramec Levee Recreation Park, at 1111 Cal Hedrick Way, the city keeps an archery range with two 10-yard targets for beginners, two each at 20, 30 and 40 yards, and one at 50. It’s open sunrise to sunset, with access to the river trail. The city doesn’t post a fee for walk-up shooting, so call Parks at 636-861-1851 before you bring the bow.
Model planes at Buder Park. Model airplanes have flown at Buder Park, the county park at Highway 141 and I-44, since 1960. Model Aviation magazine reported in 2019 that its fenced control-line speed circle is one of only two permanently enclosed ones in the country. The other is in California. Flying takes club membership. Watching is free from the paved Meramec Trail, a 1.9-mile loop along the river and the model airplane fields.
Railroad leftovers. Frisco Park, at Beckett Memorial Drive and St. Louis Avenue, holds Frisco caboose No. 398, built in 1935. It started in Valley Park, left in 1962, and was donated back to the city in 1998. The planters beside it came from the 1913 Frisco depot and returned in 2013. The Valley Park Elevator at 2 Marshall Road, built in 1887, is the last grain elevator in St. Louis County and a county landmark, and the Grellner family has run it and its hardware store since 1976. The town’s other county landmark is Sacred Heart Church, built in 1907 and 1908, whose spire the city calls one of the most striking in the county.
The lake and the drive. Simpson Park’s 72-acre lake allows electric motors only, and it’s free to fish with a permit. Species and the dock are covered in our guide to free public fishing spots in St. Louis. If you’d rather paddle, Big Muddy Adventures at Simpson Lake rents canoes, kayaks and stand-up paddleboards first come, first served, on weekends in season; check current hours and prices. The Lone Elk drive costs nothing. In summer, the city adds free Movies in the Park and Music in the Park, so watch its events page.
Earned an appetite on the levee? Where to eat in Valley Park, MO
### What can you do in Valley Park on a rainy day?
Frisco Train & Toy Store. Go for the building as much as the toys. The store at 24 Front St. fills the old Frisco Hotel, which the St. Louis & San Francisco Railroad put up in the early 1880s to house the crews building its line from Pacific to St. Louis. By 1917 it had a restaurant, a theater and its own orchestra. Later came bars, a tea room, a barbershop and, from 1999 to 2005, a factory turning out Whittle Shortline wooden trains. Today there’s a 16-foot multi-level train table and a play kitchen where kids can try the stock before anyone buys it. The building sits between the Union Pacific and BNSF lines, so real trains pass in front and in back every day. Check current hours before you go.
The Axe House STL. At 20 Meramec Valley Plaza, this indoor axe-throwing range has been open since 2017, and first-timers can book an “Axe Master” session to get coached through it. When the weather turns, it’s also the town’s easiest date-night answer. Check booking and age rules ahead.
The raptors, rain or shine. Most of the World Bird Sanctuary is outdoors, but a drizzle doesn’t cancel everything. The sanctuary says that in bad weather its seasonal flight shows may be shortened or swapped for a meet and greet. Add the aviary walkway and the gift shop, and a gray morning is covered for $5 a head.
### What’s happening in Valley Park this fall and at Christmas?
Hayrides and bonfires, Oct. 23 and 24, 2026. New on the city’s calendar in 2026: hayrides from Meramec Levee Recreation Park, 998 Cal Hedrick Way, at 6, 7 and 8 p.m. on that Friday and Saturday. Each ride runs about 45 minutes, then your group gets an hour at the bonfire. It’s $100 per hayride for a group of up to 20, by reservation form only, with no walk-ins, so it suits a scout troop, a team or a few families splitting the cost.
Fall Festival. The city holds it every October, with trunk or treat, pumpkins, a petting zoo, hayrides, live music, the Great Bubble Bus and fireworks at dusk. The 2026 date wasn’t posted when we checked, so watch the city’s Fall Festival page.
Owl-O-Ween, Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. The World Bird Sanctuary’s Halloween day brings a costume contest, crafts, games and free-flying bird shows at 11 a.m., 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., all for the usual $5 admission. Confirm the day’s hours on the sanctuary’s site.
Owl Prowls, October through March. On select evenings, a keeper introduces live owls and their calls, then leads an easy night walk across the grounds to try to call in a wild one. Tickets are sold separately, so check the current price. For a date that isn’t dinner and a movie, it’s hard to beat.
Light Up the Holidays, Saturday, Dec. 5, 2026. The Christmas parade steps off at 5 p.m. from Meramec Levee Recreation Park and winds along Marshall Road and St. Louis Avenue to the Old City Hall on Benton Street. Then comes the tree lighting, and Santa sets up inside for photos. For 2026, the city said he’d bring his reindeer. Reading this after Dec. 5? Check the city’s calendar for next year’s parade.
### Nearby, up and down the Meramec
Valley Park sits in the middle of the lower Meramec’s chain of trails and ramps. Meramec Landing Park, at the end of the levee park, has a concrete boat ramp, and the city lists a 1.3-mile off-road bicycle track there with details still marked coming soon. Downstream, our guide to Meramec River access points in Fenton maps the public ramps, including the 11.5-mile float that ends at Meramec Landing. Upstream, Eureka picks up at the far end of the Chubb Trail.
Next time somebody calls Valley Park just another I-44 exit, you’re the one who knows the stairs on the bluff were a resort’s front door, the Lone Wolf was a speakeasy, and the elk got here with help from a bunch of schoolkids. Pick a cool morning. Park on Kiefer Creek Road or at the Lone Elk visitor center. Walk.
After a morning on the Castlewood bluffs, our guide to where to eat in Valley Park, MO runs from a family-owned diner and ice creamery dating to 1954 to a bait shop with a Cajun kitchen inside.
If you run a paddle rental, a bait shop or a store near the levee trail, list it with us so hikers coming back from Lone Elk find you before they hit the highway.
Farther west on I-44, Jensen’s Point Overlook in Pacific is a 1939 stone lookout on old Route 66.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long is the hike at Castlewood State Park?
A.  It depends on the trail. Missouri State Parks’ trail sheets put River Scene at a 3.4-mile loop and about 2.5 hours, Lone Wolf at 1.7 miles and about 1 hour 40 minutes, Cedar Bluff at 2.3 miles and about 2 hours 20 minutes, the Castlewood Loop at 2.8 miles and a little over 2 hours, and Grotpeter at 4.4 miles and over 3 hours, plus 2.6 miles of connectors. Lone Wolf links to both River Scene and Grotpeter, so you can string the three into most of a day.
### Q. Does it cost to drive through Lone Elk Park?
A.  No. Lone Elk is a St. Louis County park with no admission, open 8 a.m. to official sunset. Two rules to know before you go: motorcycles are prohibited, and pets aren’t allowed even inside your car. The World Bird Sanctuary, reached through the park, is separate and charges $5 a person.
### Q. How many elk are at Lone Elk Park?
A.  The county doesn’t publish a head count, and the numbers floating around online don’t agree, so we won’t guess. What the county does say is that the 546 acres hold elk, bison, deer, wild turkey and waterfowl. The herd was rebuilt with six elk from Yellowstone in 1966, and the bison started with six from the Saint Louis Zoo in 1973.
### Q. What is a herd of elk called?
A.  A herd. That’s the standard term. Some collective-noun lists, including Oxford, also allow “a gang of elk,” and the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation has written about the word, but you’ll mostly hear it from trivia fans. During the fall rut, the group of cows a bull gathers is called a harem.
### Q. What are the best swimming holes near Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  Not the river bends. Castlewood had the area’s famous one, Lincoln Beach, which the state calls a swimming hole and gathering place from 1915 to 1940, and floods erased it. Today the better answer is a designated swim area at a state or county park lake. Our guide to where to find a beach near St. Louis walks through the options and how to check the water before you leave home.
### Q. What is the best bait to use when fishing the Meramec River?
A.  Match it to the fish. For channel catfish, the Missouri Department of Conservation suggests nightcrawlers, chicken liver, crayfish or a prepared dip bait fished on the bottom. Flatheads want live bait such as large minnows, green sunfish or crayfish, fished at night around drift piles, fallen trees and big rocks. The park says its stretch also holds bluegill and largemouth bass. Read MDC’s live-bait rules first, and carry a fishing permit if you need one.
### Q. Can you bring a dog to Lone Elk Park?
A.  No. St. Louis County bars domestic animals from Lone Elk even if they stay in the car, and the World Bird Sanctuary next door doesn’t allow dogs on the property or left in vehicles either. Take the dog to Castlewood instead, where Missouri State Parks allows pets on a leash no longer than 10 feet.
### Q. Is the World Bird Sanctuary free?
A.  No, though it’s close. Entry is $5 per person, or $40 per bus, and the sanctuary is open daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. The seasonal Taking Wing flight show is included with admission. Extras such as the $50 exotic raptor handling session and the evening Owl Prowls cost more.

## Things to Do in Godfrey, IL: Free Eagle Watching, a Bluff Waterfall Trail, the Great Godfrey Maze
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-godfrey-il
Recycled lists lose Godfrey somewhere on Route 3, and what falls out is the best story on the road. In August 1926, the federal government leased a level 40-acre field on Airport Road here as an emergency landing strip for the air mail. The pilot who picked that field himself was Charles A. Lindbergh. Less than a year later, he flew the Atlantic.
The strip had floodlights every 200 feet and a 1,250-candlepower beacon on a 60-foot steel tower, so a mail pilot who couldn’t get into Lambert Field in bad weather had somewhere to come down. A historical marker still tells the story beside Village Hall on Godfrey Road, next to a reproduction of the little station building where pilots kept oil, fuel, parts, a cot and the mail. It costs nothing. It’s there every day. It isn’t on the usual lists.
That’s the pattern here. Godfrey keeps its best stuff behind ordinary roadside. A bluff-top trail runs past industrialist John M. Olin’s old skeet range, trap houses still standing. A bronze Sacagawea on Godfrey Road exists because the Olin Corporation in East Alton developed the alloy for the Sacagawea dollar. And every winter, bald eagles work the Mississippi below a 3-acre village park that doubles as a bike-trail rest stop. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Godfrey rewards the person who slows down.
Everything below was checked against village, Nature Institute, tourism bureau, college and historical marker pages in early October 2026. Hours and prices move, so check before you drive.
### What is Godfrey, Illinois known for?
Godfrey, the village just north of Alton, is known for free winter eagle watching at Clifton Terrace Park, the Olin Nature Preserve trails on the bluffs above the Mississippi, the village-run Great Godfrey Maze every fall at Glazebrook Park, and the field Charles Lindbergh picked in 1926 for emergency air-mail landings.
Notice what isn’t on that list. The Piasa Bird and the antique shops belong to Alton, the city next door. Godfrey is the village on the bluffs just north, with its own parks department, a 294-acre nature preserve and a calendar that runs like a relay. The maze wraps up at the start of November. The Olin trails close for winter on December 1. The Snowflake Festival takes the first Friday of December, and by late December the eagles are back on the river, where they stay into March. Fitting, for a town with Lindbergh’s relay station on its main road.
### Where can you watch bald eagles near Alton for free?
At Clifton Terrace Park in Godfrey, just upriver from Alton on the Great River Road (Illinois Route 100). Search both names. The village calls it Captain Jake Ringering Park at Clifton Terrace, while Google’s map listing says Clifton Terrace Park. It’s a 3-acre village park on the Meeting of the Great Rivers Scenic Byway with a playground, a prairie remnant, an information kiosk and restrooms, and it’s a rest stop on the state-owned Sam Vadalabene Bike Trail. The village’s own parks page calls it a great place for eagle watching in the winter months. No ticket, no reservation, no tour bus. Village parks are open sunrise to sunset.
When to go. The regional tourism bureau, Great Rivers & Routes, says the eagles arrive in late December and the best watching runs from January through early March. Cold works in your favor. Regional eagle-watching tips say more birds show up when the rivers freeze, because the eagles fish the open water and ride the ice floes downstream. A clear, cold morning beats a rainy one. In the rain, they mostly sit tight on the roost.
What time. Early. Eagles feed along the river from about sunrise to 11 a.m., and in late afternoon they leave the water for night roosts in sheltered timber. The bureau names dusk as a second active window, but Clifton Terrace closes at sunset, so mornings are your real shot here. Afternoons aren’t wasted, though. That’s when eagles ride the updrafts and circle overhead.
Where to look. Scan the trees along the bluff, then the ice. Adults are the easy ones, with the white head. Juveniles are big, dark birds whose heads haven’t turned white yet, and they’re eagles too. Watch behind a towboat, because the open lane a barge cuts through the ice makes for easy fishing. Bring binoculars. Even a small pair changes the morning. Every one of those tows passes through Melvin Price Locks and Dam just downriver, and our guide to barges on the Mississippi explains what they carry.
Two rules. Don’t pull onto the narrow highway shoulder to look; use a park or a marked parking area. And if you find an eagle feather, photograph it and leave it where it lies. Bald eagles and their feathers are protected by federal law, and keeping one without a permit is illegal.
The bike trail is the other way in. Pick up the Vadalabene path and pedal to Clifton Terrace, then keep going toward Grafton with the bluffs on one side and the Mississippi on the other. Want someone else to find the birds for you? Pere Marquette State Park runs guided eagle programs each winter, and reservations open in mid-November. Our list of things to do in Grafton in winter has the tour details. Make a morning of it with a second stop on the same stretch of Route 100. Great Rivers Park, the village’s newest, sits on Route 100 with river views framed by the rock face of the bluffs. It’s still being built out, with gardens planned in honor of Godfrey’s first mayor, but it keeps the same sunrise-to-sunset hours. One more reason the river road is Godfrey’s winter spot: the Olin Nature Preserve counts bald eagles among its 150-plus bird species, but its trails close December 1, before the big winter arrival. For the whole drive, stop by stop, see our guide to the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton. Past Grafton, the free Brussels Ferry crosses the Illinois River into Calhoun County, and our guide to ferries near St. Louis covers it and the boats across the Mississippi.
### How much is the Great Godfrey Maze, and when is the haunted maze open?
For 2026, the maze is $8 for adults 12 and up, $6 for ages 6 to 11 and free for kids 5 and under. Adding the haunted maze makes it $10 and $8, and the haunted side runs from dark until 10 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. It’s a fall-only maze: it opens in September and closes the first weekend of November (Sunday, Nov. 1, in 2026). That’s the short version. The long one has a better story in it.
The Great Godfrey Maze is run by the village Parks and Recreation Department, not a farm, inside Robert E. Glazebrook Community Park at 1401 Stamper Lane. The pandemic wiped out 2020. In 2021 the corn came up short, about four feet tall, the parks director told FOX 2, and that season was lost too. So in May 2022 the Village Board approved a maze grown from sunn hemp instead. Godfrey grew hemp mazes until corn came back in 2024. This year’s design is built around the characters from the Inside Out movies.
Hours. Weekends only during the season (in 2026, through Sunday, Nov. 1): Fridays 6 to 10 p.m., Saturdays 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. and Sundays noon to 6 p.m. Ticket sales stop half an hour before closing. It’s outdoors, so the village closes it for bad weather and posts closures on its Facebook page.
Prices for 2026.
Maze only: $8 adults (12 and up), $6 ages 6 to 11, free for 5 and under.
Maze plus haunted maze: $10 adults, $8 ages 6 to 11.
Combo with unlimited maze entry for the day and one ride each on the Cow Train, Hay Wagon and Jumping Pillow: $13 adults, $11 ages 6 to 11.
Unlimited one-day wristband: $25.
Single rides: $3 each for the Cow Train, the 12 to 15 minute Hay Wagon, the Jumping Pillow and the new Vortex Tunnel. The Corn Crib is free for young kids.
The haunted maze. An additional maze opened on the first Friday in October and runs from dark until 10 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays through the final weekend. The village says it’s designed to scare and doesn’t recommend it for kids under 10. After dark, every visitor needs a flashlight, and the concession stand sells them for $3. Kids 13 and under need an adult with them, the grounds are alcohol-free, and the uneven paths mean the maze isn’t fully wheelchair accessible.
The 2026 event days. Player Appreciation Day on Saturday, Oct. 10, Teacher Appreciation Day on Oct. 17 and Kid Fest on Oct. 24, each from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The parks department’s first-ever Trunk or Treat at Glazebrook on Sunday, Oct. 11, from 2 to 4 p.m., free, with music and candy and the maze open noon to 6. And Dog Days at the Maze to close the season on Sunday, Nov. 1, from 11 to 5. Event days shift from year to year, so check the village’s maze page before you go.
Reading this after November 1? The maze comes back each September on the same weekend pattern, so watch the village page late in the summer for the new design and prices. For farm mazes and pumpkin patches around the region, see our guide to Halloween events around St. Louis. Godfrey’s is the rare one a parks department runs.
### Which Olin Nature Preserve trail should you hike?
Pick by time and knees. The John M. Olin Nature Preserve covers 294 acres of limestone bluff above the Mississippi, owned by The Nature Institute and dedicated as an Illinois Nature Preserve, so it’s protected for good. It was once Olin’s own land, and his old skeet range is still up top, original trap houses and shooting stations included, about 150 feet above the river valley. Trails start from the Institute at 2213 S. Levis Lane. From easiest to hardest:
Frog Trail (green, 0.5 mile, paved). Flat, past sinkholes, with a Mississippi view from the skeet range. Hayner Library’s StoryWalk lines this loop, which makes it the stroller and grandparent pick.
Fox Trail (orange, 1 mile). Mostly level, with a detour to a site bald eagles once used for nesting.
Rock Trail (red, 1.5 miles, up to 2 hours). Down to the bottoms, past a small stream and exposed bedrock to the Underground Railroad Monument.
Beaver Trail (purple, 2.3 miles, up to 2.5 hours, rated difficult). Straight to Beaver Falls. More on that below.
Deer Trail (black, 3 miles, up to 3 hours). The full tour: hill prairie, savanna, mature forest, restored prairie and plenty of up and down.
On the same trail system, the Institute’s Mississippi Sanctuary adds the Bluff Trail (yellow, 1 mile). It climbs to the highest point, crosses a creek twice and follows the bluff edge over the river, so watch your footing. Owl Trail (0.75 mile) is the spring wildflower walk.
Know the rules before you park. The trails are free, but this is private land the Institute opens to the public, so dogs, bikes and horses aren’t allowed at any time, and everyone stays on the marked trail. Fall hours are 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the trails close for the winter season on December 1, both per the Institute’s site in October 2026. Restrooms are typically open weekdays only.
For a hike you won’t forget, the Institute’s Moonlight Hike runs once a month near the full moon. It’s a moderate to difficult walk by moonlight, and guides discourage flashlights for most of it. Members go free, everyone else pays $5, registration is required, and there’s usually a wait list.
### What are some good waterfall hikes near St. Louis?
Start with an honest warning: Beaver Falls only runs well after rain. The Nature Institute says so on its own trail page, and a dry week leaves you staring at wet rock. Time it right, though, and you get a real waterfall on a preserve that overlooks the Mississippi from limestone bluffs.
Beaver Falls is the largest waterfall on the Olin Nature Preserve, and the purple Beaver Trail goes straight to it and back to the parking lot. It’s 2.3 miles, rated difficult, and can take up to 2.5 hours. The preserve is karst country, full of sinkholes, ravines and bedrock outcrops, and the falls depend on whatever the last storm left behind. Go within a day or two of a soaking rain. Wear boots with grip, because wet limestone is slick.
Want water and a view on the same outing? The Bluff Trail in the Mississippi Sanctuary crosses its creek twice before it reaches the bluff edge, and Owl Trail gives you creek access through the woods. Both are on the same free trail system with the same rules: no dogs, no bikes. Season matters, too. The trails close December 1 for winter, so Godfrey’s waterfall is a fall and spring hike. Spring rain plus wildflowers on Owl Trail is the combination to aim for once the Institute reopens; check its site for the date.
