### Did Charles Lindbergh really pick a landing field in Godfrey?
Yes, and the historical marker spells it out. Charles A. Lindbergh, then an air-mail pilot flying out of St. Louis, personally chose a level 40-acre tract on Airport Road as an emergency landing field. The U.S. government leased it in August 1926 from William L. Waters, who also owned Benjamin Godfrey’s old home on Godfrey Road. The man who owned Captain Godfrey’s house also owned Lindbergh’s airfield.
Pilots put down there when weather, visibility or mechanical trouble kept them out of Lambert Field. Floodlights stood 200 feet apart along the strip, and a 1,250-candlepower beacon sat on top of a 60-foot steel tower. A small frame station with a telephone line held oil, fuel and spare parts, a cot for a pilot stuck overnight, and the mail itself.
What you can see. The marker stands at Homer Adams Park on the Village Hall campus, 6810 Godfrey Road (U.S. 67), beside a reproduction of the station building. It’s free and self-guided, and village parks are open sunrise to sunset. Five minutes is plenty. Then keep going, because the rest of Godfrey’s history is a short drive down the same road.
The Sacagawea bronze. On the Lewis and Clark Community College campus at 5800 Godfrey Road, a full-standing bronze of Sacagawea, her son Jean Baptiste on her back, faces west from the central courtyard. It’s by Glenna Goodacre, the sculptor the U.S. Mint commissioned to design the Sacagawea dollar, and it was dedicated May 14, 2002. Here’s the Olin thread again. The Olin Corporation of East Alton created the bronze alloy for those coins, and the company’s long relationship with the college led to the commission. The Monticello Sculpture Gardens around it are open to stroll, and the college offers free half-mile guided group tours on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. by reservation.
The 1838 seminary and the 1854 chapel. The same campus began as the Monticello Female Seminary, which Captain Benjamin Godfrey founded in 1838 with a curriculum that mirrored the men’s seminaries: sciences, classical languages, math. It became Monticello College and later the Lewis and Clark campus. The Benjamin Godfrey Memorial Chapel, built in 1854 and on the National Register since 1979, is described as one of the six most authentic copies of New England church architecture outside the Northeast. Look for the two aisles and no center aisle. It’s a rental venue with limited dates, so plan to see it from the outside.
### Can you fish at Glazebrook Park?
Yes, and the ponds are a big part of why families come. Glazebrook is Godfrey’s main park, about 120 acres at 1401 Stamper Lane, and the regional tourism bureau lists two large fishing ponds among its features, along with more than 3 miles of walking trails. Watch the banks and you’ll spot red-eared slider turtles, geese and ducks.
Every spring the village holds a free catch-and-release Youth Fishing Derby here for ages 4 to 12, paired with Arbor Day in 2026. There are awards for the biggest catch, the most fish and the strangest catch, and the village’s event page asks whether you’ll land a “wood bass” or a boot. Kids bring their own pole and bait.
In past summers, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources has also run free Urban Fishing clinics at Glazebrook, with rods, reels, bait and tackle supplied for families who’ve never fished. The 2023 clinics ran in July and took sign-ups through Godfrey Parks and Recreation at (618) 466-1483, so call in late spring to ask whether they’re back. Ask about everyday fishing rules on the same call, since the village doesn’t post separate pond rules online. Anglers 16 and older need an Illinois fishing license.
Glazebrook works with or without a line in the water. There are playgrounds, a big gazebo, pickleball courts, a dog play area and, in summer, a splash pad. Leashed dogs are welcome in every village park.
Pair it with disc golf. Across town off Route 3, LaVista Park is 93 acres of bluff land the village keeps for passive use. It holds the Godfrey 18-hole disc golf course, a mile-long trail whose lower half got a face-lift with help from a Scenic Byways grant, and a Discovery Garden where kids learn where food comes from. Players describe the course as rolling, mostly open, with about a third of it in the woods. Like every village park, it’s free and open sunrise to sunset.
### What’s happening in Godfrey for Christmas?
One free night, done right. The Snowflake Festival fills Glazebrook Park on the first Friday of December with photos with Santa in the gazebo, s’mores over an open fire, carriage rides, hot cocoa and cookies. Admission is free, and the village collects toys that night for the Marine Corps’ Toys for Tots campaign in Alton. In 2025 it ran from 6 to 8:30 p.m. on December 5. The first Friday of December 2026 falls on December 4, so that’s the likely 2026 date; confirm it on the village’s events page. Reading this after the festival? The next one should land on the first Friday of December again.
It’s a short night, so make it a double. Next door, Alton’s Christmas Wonderland is a drive-through display of more than 4 million lights in Rock Spring Park, and our guide to drive-through Christmas lights in Alton has the dates. Still around the river in late December? The eagles will be back by then, and Clifton Terrace is a short drive up Route 100.
### Nearby, up and down the river
Godfrey sits in the middle of a good river day. Downriver, Alton has the Piasa Bird painted on the bluff, the Clark Bridge and the riverfront. Upriver on Route 100, Grafton has the ferry, the wineries and Pere Marquette State Park. Godfrey is the stretch in between, the part people tend to drive through on the way to somewhere else.
Next time somebody calls Godfrey a stretch of highway north of Alton, you’re the one who knows where Lindbergh’s beacon stood, which trail reaches the falls, and which village park to stand in on a cold January morning with binoculars. Pick a season. Godfrey has one waiting.
Eagle mornings start early, and our guide to where to eat in Godfrey, IL includes a family diner that serves breakfast from 6 a.m. and a frozen custard window for after the maze.
If you run a bait shop, a bike rental or a kitchen that eagle watchers and maze crowds pass on Route 100 and Godfrey Road, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where to eat in Godfrey, IL?
A.  Our guide to where to eat in Godfrey, IL covers the independents along Godfrey Road, Delmar Avenue and the Montclaire area, from barbecue to a farm-to-table kitchen that grows its own vegetables. In season, Pearson’s Produce & Ice Cream at 6304 Humbert Road is a family farm stand with an ice cream window. It’s seasonal, so check its Facebook page for fall hours.
### Q. Is there a trick to corn mazes?
A.  The classic trick is to keep one hand on the same wall and keep walking. Starting from the entrance, it will eventually lead you out, but it isn’t guaranteed to reach a goal in the middle of a maze with loops, and it can march you right back to where you started. Godfrey’s practical tricks are simpler. Bring a flashlight if you’re staying past dark, because the village requires one ($3 at the concession stand if you forget). Pick a Saturday for the longest window, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. And skip the haunted maze with kids under 10.
### Q. Can I take my dog to a corn maze?
A.  In Godfrey, plan on the day built for it: Dog Days at the Maze, the last day of the season (Sunday, Nov. 1, in 2026, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.). For any other day, call Godfrey Parks and Recreation at (618) 466-1483 before you load the dog. Glazebrook Park itself allows leashed dogs, like every village park. Just leave the dog home for the Olin Nature Preserve, where dogs aren’t allowed on the trails at any time.
### Q. What time of day are bald eagles most active?
A.  Early morning. Eagles along this stretch of river feed from about sunrise to 11 a.m., soar on updrafts in the afternoon, and leave the water in late afternoon for night roosts in sheltered timber. The regional tourism bureau adds dusk as a second active window. Clear, cold mornings once the river starts to freeze are the best bet; on rainy days they mostly stay on the roost.
### Q. What are some beautiful places to visit near St. Louis?
A.  From Godfrey, three views stand out. The old skeet range on the Olin Nature Preserve sits about 150 feet above the Mississippi River valley, and the paved half-mile Frog Trail gets you there. The Bluff Trail in the Mississippi Sanctuary runs along the bluff edge over the river. And in winter, Clifton Terrace on the Great River Road puts bluffs, river ice and eagles in the same frame. All three are free.
### Q. What are some good small towns to visit in Illinois?
A.  Close to St. Louis, start along the river. Godfrey gives you bluff trails, a village corn maze and winter eagles. Grafton, up Route 100, has the ferry and Pere Marquette State Park. Alton, next door, has the riverfront and a drive-through light show every holiday season. And Edwardsville, the Madison County seat, has its own long list of free things to do in Edwardsville.
### Q. Is the Olin Nature Preserve free?
A.  Yes. The Nature Institute owns the land privately and opens its trails to the public at no charge. Trails are typically open dawn to dusk seven days a week, with fall hours of 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. posted for 2026, and they close for the winter season on December 1. No dogs, bikes or horses. Programs such as the monthly Moonlight Hike cost $5 for nonmembers.
### Q. When does the Great Godfrey Maze close for the season?
A.  The first weekend of November. In 2026 the last day is Sunday, Nov. 1, with Dog Days at the Maze from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. A few event listings said the end of October, but the village and the regional tourism bureau both listed Nov. 1. The maze returns each September on the same weekend schedule, so check the village’s maze page for next season’s dates and prices.

## Things to Do in Imperial, MO: Mastodon Bones, the Limestone Hill Trail and Cosmic Bowling
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-imperial-mo
London got there first. A mastodon skeleton stands on the ground floor of Hintze Hall in the Natural History Museum there, and a 2016 history paper traces parts of it to a creek bank in Imperial, where a St. Louis museum owner named Albert Koch dug for bones in 1839. Sixty-five years later, crowds from the 1904 World’s Fair rode the train south to a wooden fossil shack on the same creek. Then that whole collection vanished.
You won’t find any of that in the recycled top-10 lists. Search for things to do in Imperial this fall and the first result is a list of things to do in Arnold. Part of that is structural. Imperial is a census-designated place, not a city, so there’s no city hall, no parks department and no tourism office putting out a list of its own. The aggregators fill the gap with the next exit up.
So this is the other list, for the St. Louisan who has done the Arch and the Zoo enough times to give the tour. The bone bed’s strange backstory. A 2-mile bluff loop the state rates rugged. A free night hike by the light of the full moon. Cosmic bowling with fog machines off the Outer Road. An arcade with upstairs laser tag that lets you bring a crock pot. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Imperial may be the one most people know only as a highway sign.
Everything below was checked against Missouri State Parks, museum and business pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do. Hours and prices move, so confirm before you drive.
### Is there a mastodon bone found in Missouri?
Yes. The best-known is the Kimmswick Bone Bed in Imperial, now Mastodon State Historic Site, first dug in 1839. Parts of a skeleton sold to the British Museum in the 1840s came from here, and a 1979 Clovis point found with the bones was eastern North America’s first solid evidence of people living alongside mastodons.
The spear point gets the headlines. The rest of the story is stranger, and almost nobody tells it. One naming note first: the bone bed carries Kimmswick’s name, but it sits in Imperial, a town that was originally called West Kimmswick.
The leviathan, 1839. According to Missouri State Parks, Albert C. Koch, a private entrepreneur who ran a museum in St. Louis, heard about bones weathering out of the banks of Rock Creek and dug there in 1839. Koch was a showman before he was a scientist. London’s Natural History Museum describes the beast he built from his Missouri finds: a skeleton about twice the size of a real mastodon, padded with extra vertebrae and ribs, with wood wedged between the bones and the tusks set to stick out sideways. He named it the Missouri Leviathan, decided it lived underwater and used those tusks to hook onto branches, and toured it across North America and Europe.
London, the 1840s. The tour ended at an exhibition hall in Piccadilly. Richard Owen, the British anatomist, convinced Koch the animal was an American mastodon, not a new species, and bought the fossils for the British Museum. The Natural History Museum dates the sale to 1844 and puts the terms at $2,000 up front plus $1,000 a year for the rest of Koch’s life. Koch lived another 22 years. The bill came to roughly $24,000. Owen pulled the monster apart and remounted it in an accurate pose, and the museum calls the result “the first accurate mount of a mastodon, anywhere, ever.” It’s the skeleton in Hintze Hall today.
So how much of it is Imperial? A 2016 paper in Earth Sciences History by R. Bruce McMillan says the bone bed won international recognition when Koch sold the British Museum a composite mastodon skeleton, parts of which came from Kimmswick. The paper dates that sale to 1843, a year earlier than the museum does. Koch dug elsewhere in Missouri too, so nobody can point at one bone in London and say it came out of Rock Creek. Part of that skeleton started here, though, which is more than most people driving past Exit 186 will ever know.
The World’s Fair side trip, 1904. Nearly 60 years after Koch, Charles W. Beehler, a St. Louis mechanic, inventor and amateur fossil hunter, spent several months of every year from 1897 to 1904 digging the bone bed. He put up a wooden building on the site to hold his finds, called it a museum, and timed it for the crowds headed to the Louisiana Purchase Exposition in Forest Park. Missouri State Parks says railroad tours from St. Louis brought visitors down to his shack, especially during the fair. Beehler also turned up stone artifacts he believed lay with the extinct animals, but his digs were poorly documented, and the leading scientists of the day didn’t accept it.
After the fair, Beehler went back to St. Louis, and his collection vanished. McMillan found no evidence that any significant part of it ever reached an institution where it was preserved. Nobody knows where it went. For the pieces of that fair still standing in the city, see our guide to the buildings left from the 1904 World’s Fair.
Quarried, then saved, 1976. The bone bed took its worst damage from a quarry that worked the site from the 1870s through the 1930s and destroyed many of the Ice Age remains. Digs sponsored by the Works Progress Administration recovered more fossils from 1940 to 1942. Then Interstate 55 came through in the 1970s. The Mastodon Park Committee organized to save the site, and with local legislators, private citizens, corporations and local schoolchildren behind it, plus a federal grant, the state bought the 418 acres holding the bone bed in 1976. The site turned 50 this year.
The spear point, 1979. Russell W. Graham’s team found a stone Clovis point with mastodon bones that year, making this the first site in eastern North America where people and mastodons were conclusively shown together. It went on the National Register of Historic Places on April 14, 1987.
That’s the backstory. For the visit itself, from the replica skeleton to admission and the three trails at a glance, our Arnold guide covers visiting Mastodon State Historic Site. What follows is what that guide leaves out.
### How hard is the Limestone Hill Trail?
Harder than 2 miles sounds. Missouri State Parks rates the loop rugged, and its trail sheet warns of steep grades over 10 percent, shifting rock, roots, drop-offs beside the path, a road crossing and stream crossings with no bridge. The state’s estimated hiking time is 1 hour and 57 minutes. Its New Year’s hike notes put the climbing at about 300 feet. That’s no mountain. On a humid July afternoon, it’ll feel like more.
The route, as the state describes it, runs along the base of a limestone bluff, climbs through oak, hickory and cedar woods, and crosses the hilltop with views over the Seckman valley. Follow the green blazes. Among the ravines and boulders you can find wild columbine and wild hydrangea, and small yellow and red funnel-shaped mushrooms poking out of the moss on the limestone. Benches and overlooks are spaced along the way. You’ll use them.
Two ways in. The main trailhead is by the museum, at 1050 Charles J. Becker Drive. A second trailhead off Seckman Road, near the picnic area, makes for a shorter 1.75-mile hike. Grounds open at 8 a.m. and close a half-hour after sunset, every day of the year. Walking them costs nothing. Only the museum charges.
The easy alternative. If someone in your group isn’t up for roots and rock, Spring Branch Trail is 0.8 miles of packed gravel that the state calls manageable for wheelchairs and strollers, about 23 minutes at an easy pace. It follows a small stream from Bollefer Spring past the remains of the Bollefer springhouse, built in 1937, where the farm family kept milk, eggs, fruit and vegetables in the spring water. Then it loops back through sycamores and cottonwoods along Rock Creek. The third trail, Wildflower, runs under half a mile and takes stairs down to the spot where the bones were found.
The New Year’s Day tradition. Limestone Hill is the site’s First Day Hike. On Jan. 1, 2026, the site offered a free, guided 2-mile loop from the museum lot at 10 a.m., with a gentler Spring Branch walk at the same hour, both with registration required and leashed dogs welcome. The 2027 listing isn’t posted yet, so check the site’s events page in December.
### What is there to do in Imperial at night?
Two things, and they could hardly be more different: a moonlit hike on a bluff and a bowling alley full of fog.
The Hunter’s Moon Hike. The grounds normally close a half-hour after sunset, and the state bills this as a rare chance to be in the park after hours. The 2026 date: Monday, Oct. 26, for a guided night hike the site leads on Limestone Hill. Check in at the museum parking lot at 6:45 p.m. The hike starts at 7 and is back by 8:15. You’ll cover up to 1.5 miles of natural, rugged surface, and the idea is to rely on your senses and the light of the full moon. Bring a flashlight for emergencies anyway, plus sturdy shoes, water and a snack. Reading this after Oct. 26? Ask the site whether another after-hours hike is on its calendar.
It’s free, but registration is required and the group is capped at 25, so call the site office at 636-464-2976 sooner rather than later. Bad weather can cancel it. The name, Missouri State Parks explains, goes back to Native American hunters using the light of the first full moon after the harvest moon to hunt animals feeding on the last of the harvest.
Cosmic bowling. At Strike & Spare Imperial Bowl, 6045 W. Outer Road, the lights drop for cosmic bowling Friday from 9 p.m. to close and Saturday from 1 to 4 p.m. and again from 9 to close. Expect laser lights, black lights, haze machines pumping fog, loud music and lanes that glow in the dark. Cosmic games run $6.75 a person or $32 an hour for a lane, plus $5 shoes, and the center lists Friday and Saturday hours to midnight. Moonlit bluff one night, fog and black lights the next: that’s two date nights nobody else in your group chat has thought of.
Cosmic isn’t the cheapest way to bowl late, though. That’s the next question.
### How much does bowling cost at Imperial Bowl?
Less than you’d think, if you pick the right hour. The posted open-bowling rates are per person, per game, before tax:
Weekdays, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.: $5 a game, or $24 an hour for a lane
Monday through Thursday after 5 p.m.: $6 a game, or $28 an hour
Weekends: $6.75 a game, or $32 an hour
Shoes: $5, and they’re required to bowl
The specials are where it gets cheap. On Tuesdays, Two for Tuesday makes games $2 from open to 5 p.m. and again from 9 to close. On Monday, Wednesday and Thursday nights, $9 buys all you can bowl from 9 p.m. until the 11 p.m. close. Daytime all-you-can-bowl is $12 from open to 5 p.m. Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, and Sunday after 5 it’s $13.50. Bowling as a group of four? Pizza, Pins, Pop is $69.95 for an hour of bowling, four pairs of shoes, a large one-topping pizza and a pitcher of soda, all day Saturday and Sunday and after 5 p.m. Friday.
One honest caveat: those price pages carry old publish dates, taxes are extra and the center says to call 636-464-2695 for holiday rates. Confirm before you go. Bumper lanes, lightweight balls and small shoes are on hand for kids.
The part the lists miss. This is a serious bowling house. Imperial Bowl hosted the team event of the 2026 Missouri State USBC Women’s Tournament, which ran from March 7 to April 12, with doubles and singles bowled at Crestwood Bowl. Its leagues include 9-pin tap, where nine or more pins on your first ball counts as a strike. And you can start a league of your own with as few as eight bowlers, four teams of two, in sessions of 90 minutes or less. Coworkers, neighbors, the group chat that keeps saying it should do something: that’s a league.
Mastodons ate twigs. You have better options: where to eat in Imperial, MO
### Where can kids play laser tag in Imperial?
Upstairs at Cactus Pete’s Family Fun Center, 1045 Main St. The arena is called Area 51: a black-light maze on the second floor, played with a one-hand phaser light enough for a small kid and no sweaty vest. Rounds cap at 10 players, so nobody spends the game waiting for a phaser to come back on after a hit.
The house legend is the best part, and it’s theirs, not ours. According to the center, a prospector named Randall C. Peterson, better known as Cactus Pete, was panning for gold on the Meramec when a bright light led him to a deserted mine shaft that’s now part of the building, and he made friends with the aliens inside. The green ooze in the laser tag room, the story goes, helps them breathe. Take it up with Pete.
The real origin is plainer. Two Jefferson County dads got sick of driving their kids to South County, Fenton and St. Charles for overpriced arcades and laser tag, so they built their own with a couple of house rules. Bring your own food: pizza delivery, a picnic, even a crock pot is welcome. Outside drinks aren’t, and the center sells soda, water, tea and a few beers. And keep the pricing simple.
How the pricing works. Buy credits, or buy time. Timed Power cards come in 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes and cover every game plus laser tag. The home page lists the Power 60 at $30 for an hour of unlimited play, but the FAQ says to email for current pricing, so check first. Four or more cards get 10 percent off. The cards skip only two things: a charity ring toss and the coin-operated pinball machines, added for old-school players who miss quarters.
When it’s open. Wednesday and Thursday 4 to 8 p.m., Friday 4 to 9, Saturday 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday noon to 7. Monday and Tuesday are kept for private events. It’s recommended for ages 4 and up, and there’s a hockey shop on site that does instant skate sharpening. Once your crew has beaten every machine here, our guide to the best arcades in St. Louis covers the rest of the metro.
For toddlers. Mastodon State Historic Site runs free Toddler Thursdays at 10 a.m., lasting up to an hour: story time and a craft, right outside the museum, or in the auditorium if the weather turns. No registration. Bring a water bottle and a lawn chair or blanket. Its last three 2026 sessions: Oct. 22 (Mother Earth), Nov. 19 (Indigenous Americans) and Dec. 17 (animals in winter). For later dates, check the site’s calendar. On a rainy day, the museum is indoors and free for kids 12 and under, with a $4 ticket for everyone 13 and up.
### What is free to do in Imperial, MO?
Most of the best of it. Missouri doesn’t charge to enter its state parks and historic sites, so at Mastodon the only ticket is the museum’s.
All three trails, from the rugged Limestone Hill loop to the springhouse walk, daily from 8 a.m. to a half-hour after sunset.
The bone bed itself. The Wildflower Trail ends at the spot where the bones and the spear point came out of the ground. There’s no open dig to look into. The state says what remains of the bone bed is safely buried, so you’re standing on top of it.
The wildflower garden, which the state says draws birds and butterflies, plus the picnic shelter and the playground.
The Hunter’s Moon Hike (Oct. 26 in 2026) and Toddler Thursdays, both above.
A Mississippi River walk. Kimmswick Park, on Mississippi Street, carries an Imperial mailing address, and a natural-surface trail heads north along the river from it. Our list of things to do in Kimmswick covers that walk and the 1874 iron bridge on Windsor Harbor Road.
### What’s near Imperial for a longer day?
Kimmswick is the natural pairing, since Imperial wraps around it on the land side. Its Apple Butter Festival fills the village for a weekend (Oct. 24 and 25 in 2026, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.), so expect festival traffic then and check current details before you go. Head south on I-55 and the free light shows at Crites Park in Festus run a Halloween edition in October and a Christmas edition later in the year, per the 2026 schedule. Keep going south for the old French river town in our guide to things to do in Ste. Genevieve.
Next time somebody calls Imperial an exit sign, you’re the one who knows a piece of it may be standing in London, the bluff loop has green blazes and a 300-foot climb, and $9 buys a night of bowling on a Wednesday. Pick one. Go this month, while the moon is still on the calendar.
Breakfast before the bluff loop or pizza on Seckman Road after it, our guide to where to eat in Imperial, MO covers the Italian kitchens, the breakfast spot and the taquerias on Main Street.
If you run a business along the Outer Road or Main Street that hikers and league bowlers drive past, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Did mastodons ever live in Missouri?
A.  Yes. During the last Ice Age, mastodons roamed the Midwest alongside giant ground sloths and peccaries, according to Missouri State Parks. Paleontologists think the Imperial site was once swampy, with mineral springs, and that animals coming to the springs got stuck in the mud, which helped preserve their bones. People had reached what’s now Missouri by at least 12,000 years ago, and for a short stretch at the end of the Ice Age, the two overlapped.
### Q. Which were bigger, mammoths or mastodons?
A.  Mammoths. The Indiana State Museum puts a typical American mastodon at 8 to 10 feet tall at the shoulder and 4 to 6 tons, while mammoths stood 10 to 12 feet and weighed 6 to 8 tons. Mastodons were stockier, with straighter tusks and cone-cusped teeth for browsing shrubs and trees. Koch’s Missouri Leviathan beat them both. London’s Natural History Museum says his version stood about 4.5 meters, close to 15 feet, which was exactly the problem.
### Q. How much is a mastodon tooth worth today?
A.  There’s no single price, and we won’t guess at one. What matters locally is that you can’t take one home from Mastodon State Historic Site. Missouri’s state park rules (10 CSR 90-2.040) bar anyone from digging or removing rock, artifacts or relics from a state park or historic site without the director’s written permission. The museum’s displays of fossils and ancient artifacts are the way to see one up close.
### Q. What are some hidden places to visit in Missouri?
A.  Start with one off I-55 in Jefferson County. In Imperial, the Wildflower Trail drops to the creek bottom where a Clovis spear point turned up among mastodon bones, a 2-mile limestone bluff loop climbs above it, and a 1937 springhouse ruin sits along Spring Branch. Pair it with the river walk at Kimmswick Park next door and you’ve filled a Saturday.
### Q. Is there a bowling tournament in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, several. The Saint Louis USBC runs tournaments through the year, from city championships to youth and senior events, with entry forms on its site. Statewide events come through too: in 2026, Imperial Bowl hosted the team event of the Missouri State USBC Women’s Tournament from March 7 to April 12, with doubles and singles at Crestwood Bowl in St. Louis. Check the association sites for the 2027 schedule.
### Q. Why is 4 strikes a hambone?
A.  Hambone is bowling slang for four strikes in a row, one more than a turkey. Bowling glossaries generally credit PBA television announcer Rob Stone with popularizing it on broadcasts. Before it caught on, some bowlers called four straight a four-bagger. If you want to chase one, a $9 late-night all-you-can-bowl session at Imperial Bowl gives you plenty of frames.
### Q. Can you camp at Mastodon State Historic Site?
A.  Only as a group. There’s no regular campground for individual campers. The special-use area is set aside for group camping, with nonprofits and youth groups getting priority, and it has vault toilets, water, picnic tables and fire rings. The fee is $2 per person, per night. Call the site office at 636-464-2976 to reserve. When no group has it booked, the area is open for general use.
### Q. Is Imperial, MO a city?
A.  No. Imperial is a census-designated place in Jefferson County, not an incorporated city, and the 2020 census counted 4,947 people in it. It was originally known as West Kimmswick, and the State Historical Society of Missouri’s place-names file also lists Liberty as an earlier name. With no city government, nearly everything to do here is run by the state, the county or a private business.

## Things to Do in Granite City, IL: Public Ice Skating, Chouteau Island, a Neon Sign Park
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-granite-city-il
Don’t look up. Every Granite City list puts you on the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge to squint at the Arch on the skyline, waves you toward Horseshoe Lake, then sends you back across the river. Look down instead. The water below the bridge’s Illinois end, along Chouteau Island, is the one natural stretch of the working Mississippi that barges never use. They can’t. A low-water dam crosses the river there, so every tow detours through an 8.4-mile canal dug on the Illinois side and through Lock 27, which the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers says moves more cargo than any other navigation structure on the Mississippi. Our guide to barges on the Mississippi follows those tows past the lock and into the St. Louis harbor.
Here’s the other thing the lists skip. Granite City has no granite. The Niedringhaus brothers incorporated the town in 1896 and named it for graniteware, the speckled enamel pots and pans their company stamped out, and since 2025 a 16-foot graniteware coffee pot has stood downtown on actual bricks from the old enamel plant. The town keeps doing that. There’s a park district ice rink from 1967 that still charges $6 to skate, a sunken garden that began as a swimming pool’s diving tower, and a first-run movie theater owned by the city. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the one the recycled lists get most wrong.
Everything below was checked against park district, city, state and organizer pages in October 2026. It’s sorted by what you came to do, starting with the rink.
### What are some fun things to do in Granite City, Illinois?
Skate public sessions at the park district’s 1967 ice rink in winter, walk Wilson Park’s 1920s gardens and its 18-hole disc golf course, and see It’s Electric Neon Sign Park light up at dusk beside a 16-foot graniteware coffee pot. A mile west, Chouteau Island borders the one natural stretch of the working Mississippi that barges never use.
All of it sits within a few miles, and most of it costs little or nothing. Here’s how a Saturday in skating season can run.
Afternoon in Wilson Park. Walk the formal gardens and find the sunken garden, then play a few holes of the Mick Suess disc golf course. The rink is in the same park, so you’ll be back tonight.
Dusk downtown. Drive to 19th Street and Delmar Avenue as the light goes. The three old signs at It’s Electric Neon Sign Park switch on at dusk, the coffee pot stands beside them, and Rusty the Steel Worker, all 20 feet of him, waits a few minutes away at the entrance to Lincoln Place.
Dinner, then the ice. Eat downtown, then head back to Wilson Park for the 7:45 p.m. Saturday public skate. Friday’s starts at 7:30. Two adults from out of town, with rental skates, spend $16. Check the park district’s current session times first, because the rink sets them season by season.
Sunday morning, the river. Park on the Missouri side at Chain of Rocks Park and walk out to Chouteau Island. It’s the one approach that works whether or not the Illinois road onto the island is open, and that road has been shut for canal-bridge repairs since June 22, 2026. Directions are two sections down.
### Where can you go public ice skating in Granite City?
At the Granite City Ice Rink in Wilson Park, run by the Granite City Park District. It’s the town’s own rink, and it has been since 1967, when the district built it after a campaign to sell $465,000 in bonds. In 1994 the current Wilson Park pool went in right beside it, so summer and winter share a parking lot.
Last season’s public sessions ran from Nov. 7, 2025, to Feb. 16, 2026. The 2026-27 dates weren’t posted when we checked in early October. The season usually opens in early November, so check the park district’s website and Facebook page for current session times before you drive over. Here’s the schedule and price list the district posts on its rink page.
Public sessions. Fridays 7:30 to 9:30 p.m., Saturdays 7:45 to 9:45 p.m., and Sundays 1:30 to 3:30 p.m. Last season a handful of Sunday sessions slid 15 minutes later. Check the date you want.
Prices. If you don’t live in the district, adults pay $6, and kids and seniors pay $5. A Granite City Park ID knocks a dollar off each. Skate rental is $2. A family of four from across the river, two adults and two kids, all renting, spends $30 for the session.
Stick and puck. Three times a week: Tuesdays 4:30 to 5:30 p.m., then Wednesdays and Thursdays 3:15 to 4:15 p.m. The ages allowed change from day to day, so call the rink or check its Facebook schedule before you load the gear.
Adult drop-in hockey. This is the one almost nobody outside the hockey crowd knows about. Thursday nights during the season, 10 to 11:30 p.m., $10 a skater, full pads required. If you played in high school and still miss it, that’s your Thursday.
Bring gloves and a warm layer, for the skaters and for whoever’s watching from the boards. Evening sessions run late, so eat first. And if you’re weighing this against the Missouri rinks, our guide to what ice skating costs in St. Louis walks through how admission, rental and the extras add up.
### How do you get to Chouteau Island from Granite City?
Walk in from Missouri, which works every day the bridge is open. Chouteau Island sits about a mile west of Granite City, between the Chain of Rocks Canal and the Mississippi, and the only road onto it crosses a one-lane bridge over the canal. That bridge closed for repairs on June 22, 2026, which cut off the Illinois-side access to the island and to the Illinois end of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge.
The agencies don’t agree on when it reopens. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources posted that there would be no access to Chouteau Island until approximately Oct. 1, 2026. Madison County Transit’s trail page says reopening is anticipated in October. Great Rivers Greenway lists the closure as running through 2026. When we checked on Oct. 7, 2026, the canal bridge was still closed and none of them had posted a reopening date. Before you drive to the Illinois side, check Great Rivers Greenway’s Chain of Rocks Park page or MCT’s trail closures page. If the closure notice is gone, the road onto the island is open again.
The way in that always works: walk from Missouri. Park at Chain of Rocks Park, 10840 Riverview Drive in St. Louis, open 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. Walk east across the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, and the Illinois end sets you down on the island. Great Rivers Greenway puts the round trip from the lot to the Chouteau Island trailhead at 2.1 miles. Bikes work too, since the bridge is closed to cars. Coming on westbound I-270? The Riverview Drive exit is temporarily closed. Take the Lilac Avenue exit 33, turn right on Lilac, right on Dunn Road for 1.1 miles, then right on Riverview Drive for about 0.3 miles. The park is on your left.
What you’re walking to. HeartLands Conservancy, the land trust that helped assemble the public land here, counts about 5,500 acres across three islands: Chouteau, Gabaret and Mosenthein. Chouteau itself only became an island when the canal was dug between 1946 and 1953. The 10 miles of Mississippi along its west side are the barge-free stretch, with no tows and no wakes, just the river moving past wooded banks. HeartLands also reports Mississippi kites, a small raptor that had nearly vanished from Illinois by the late 1920s, coming back to the island’s forests.
The trails and the fishing. The City of Madison has cut mulch hiking trails into the woods just below the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, open 9 a.m. to dusk. The Chouteau Island Fishing Area sits below the bridge as well, and Illinois fishing rules apply. Lewis and Clark camped on neighboring Gabaret Island on Dec. 11, 1803, before they built Camp Dubois upriver, so the walk covers a very early page of that story.
A fall warning. The islands are an IDNR hunting site, with archery deer, waterfowl, dove and upland game seasons. From fall into winter, wear something bright on the trails.
The walk across the bridge itself, with its bend in the middle, its Route 66 markers and the two stone intake towers in the river, already has a home in our guide to historic sites in St. Louis and our list of underrated places to visit in St. Louis. This page sticks to the Illinois end, the island and how to reach it.
### What is there to do at Wilson Park in Granite City?
More than the rink, and the history is half the fun. Wilson Park, at 2900 Benton Street, is the park district’s founding park. Voters created the Granite City Park District in a special election on Feb. 19, 1921, passed a $135,000 bond issue later that year, and opened Wilson Park to the public on June 1, 1923. It covers 74 acres today.
The sunken garden. Here’s the detail no list carries. The district’s first swimming pool was built in 1922, with a sand bottom. The diving tower of that pool still exists, and it’s what the park now calls the sunken gardens. Most people stroll through without knowing they’re standing in a piece of the park’s first pool. The formal gardens around it date to the mid-1920s, laid out under the district’s first superintendent, Ernest Svieking.
Disc golf with a backstory. The Mick Suess course has 18 holes and a good reason for existing. In 2020, Suess handed the park district a check to thank it for what the parks had meant to him over his life. The district put the gift toward a disc golf course, and the St. Louis Disc Golf Association helped pick the location and layout. Installation began in May 2022. Concrete pads went in during spring 2023, paid for with a county park grant. On April 27, 2024, the finished course was dedicated to him. Bring a disc or two and a friend who keeps score honestly.
The rest of it. Pickleball and tennis courts, ball diamonds, basketball, playgrounds, picnic shelters, a gazebo, walking trails and a prairie the park district keeps as a songbird site, which birders log on eBird. The Wilson Park pool traditionally opens Memorial Day weekend and closes the day before Granite City schools go back. One honest note: a storm on May 16, 2025, brought down some of the park’s century-old trees, so an older write-up about its shade may promise more than you’ll find.
Worthen Park, for next summer. Across town at Maryville Road and Parkview Drive, 45-acre Worthen Park got a splash pad in May 2026, and it’s free. Its first season ran May 23 to Aug. 12, so it’s closed until next May. Worthen also has a dog park, trails, a playground and soccer fields.
Golfers have a park district option too. Legacy Golf Course, 18 holes designed by Hale Irwin, has belonged to the district since October 2009.
### Where is the neon sign park in Granite City?
Downtown, on the southeast corner of 19th Street and Delmar Avenue (1300 19th St.). Its full name is It’s Electric Neon Sign Park. It opened in August 2024, it’s free, and a $500,000 grant from the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau and the Illinois Office of Tourism paid for it, part of the run-up to Route 66 turning 100 in 2026.
The signs. Three restored neon signs from the early 1900s, each from a business the town remembers: Hudson Jewelers, Reese Drug Store and the Washington Theatre. Plaques at their bases tell each story. The signs stay lit from dusk to dawn, so come after sunset. Two large murals cover the town’s Route 66 history, and in the middle of the lawn stands a model of the Chain of Rocks Bridge where couples hang love locks.
The coffee pot. Since 2025 the park has also held the Giant Graniteware Coffee Pot. It’s 16 feet tall, and its marker says it sits on actual bricks from the plant of the National Enameling and Stamping Company, NESCO, whose speckled enamelware gave Granite City its name. A giant Make-It-Toy stands nearby. Both products were once made here.
The giants. Rusty the Steel Worker stands 20 feet tall at 614 Niedringhaus Avenue, at the entrance to Lincoln Place, one of the town’s oldest working-class neighborhoods. Fiberglass artist Mark Cline molded him from a 1960s Muffler Man and gave him a red sledgehammer, a hard hat and a lunchbox at his feet that reads “Made in America.” Cline also built Earl the Mechanic, 14 feet, who has stood since June 2025 outside O’Brien Tire & Auto Care at 3924 Nameoki Road. That shop opened in 1906, which makes it older than Route 66. And at 1901 Cleveland Boulevard there’s a literal fork in the road: a dining fork sized for a giant. None of them charges admission.
Early October. Sizzlin’ on 66 takes over Civic Park, 1301 Niedringhaus Ave., for two days; the 2026 dates are Friday and Saturday, Oct. 9 and 10. Friday from 6 to 10 p.m. brings the free Amateur Backyard Pork Steak Throwdown, and Saturday the Pro Series BBQ competition. It’s also a pickup spot for the Last 100 Miles Festival trading cards. To follow the rest of that stretch of the Mother Road, see our guide to scenic drives around St. Louis.

### Where can adults celebrate Halloween in Granite City?
At a haunted house that pays for a theater. The Cutting Room Haunted House, at 1930 Cleveland Blvd., is the annual fundraiser for Alfresco Productions and its nonprofit arts center, and it dates to 2019. Its 2026 run: Fridays and Saturdays from Oct. 9 through Oct. 31, 7 to 10 p.m., at $15 for adults and $10 for kids 12 and under. Your ticket keeps a community theater on Delmar Avenue running, which beats paying a chain haunt.
Then see a play. Same company, different mood. Alfresco closes its 2026 season with Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike, the Christopher Durang comedy, on Oct. 16 to 18 and Oct. 23 to 25 at the Alfresco Performing Arts Center, 2041 Delmar Ave. Its site still said tickets were coming soon when we checked, so look there for tickets. The 2026 dates split neatly across two October weekends: the play one Friday, the haunted house the next. Reading this after Halloween? Check Alfresco’s site for its next season and next year’s haunted house.
In daylight: Relleke Pumpkin Patch. At 473 Sand Prairie Lane, the farm is open daily from the last weekend of September through Halloween. The full lineup runs Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., priced per person in $1 tickets: a 6-acre corn maze, a hayride, a corn pit and a pumpkin cannon aimed at a target. Weekdays are quieter, with a $7 wristband for kids that covers a set of activities. Adults don’t need tickets to tag along on the farm activities, only for the mechanical rides. Check the farm’s site for this week’s hours.
### When is the Granite City Christmas parade?
The 2026 date: Saturday, Dec. 5, at 3 p.m. That’s the Candy Cane Parade, presented by the Granite City Area Community Foundation, and 2026 is its sixth year. The 2025 lineup started in the Granite City High School lot by the football field. The foundation hadn’t posted the 2026 route when we checked, so watch its Candy Cane Parade Facebook page in late November. Reading this after Dec. 5? Check that page for next year’s date. A 3 p.m. start gets the kids home before dark, and it puts you downtown right about when the neon comes on.
After the parade. The city also lists a Winter Wonderland Festival at Civic Park with an Elf Walk, so check the city’s events page for this year’s date. And the neon sign park glows every night from dusk to dawn. No ticket, no line.
The big drive-throughs. WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway sits next door in Madison, and our roundup of the best Christmas lights in St. Louis covers it. Up the river, the drive-through Christmas lights in Alton put more than 4 million lights in Rock Spring Park starting the day after Thanksgiving.
### What can couples do in Granite City on a rainy night?
Go to the movies at the theater the city owns. Granite City Cinema, at 1243 Niedringhaus Ave., is a three-screen, roughly 500-seat first-run theater that opened on Aug. 20, 2010, built by the city for about $4.6 million. The prices are small-town. Matinees before 6 p.m. are $7 for adults Monday through Thursday and $8 Friday through Sunday, evening shows run $9 and $10, and 3D adds $2.25. Check the cinema’s site for current prices.
A play or a gallery opening. Alfresco Performing Arts Center on Delmar stages four shows a year, and this year’s October show is in the Halloween section. Downtown on State Street, the Granite City Art and Design District, known as G-CADD, is an artist-run group that has turned former industrial buildings into studios and galleries. In May 2026 it opened its 40th exhibition and marked ten years. Openings are evening events, so check its calendar.
A live show. The Mill, at 1311 20th St., is a city-built venue that books tribute bands, Pro Wrestling Epic and improv comedy. Its events page wasn’t loading when we checked, so look up what’s on before you plan around it.
A rainy Sunday afternoon. The Old Six Mile Museum fills the Emmert-Zippel House at 3279 Maryville Road, Granite City’s oldest building. William Emmert built it in 1837, when the area was still called Six Mile for its distance from St. Louis. The Zippel family lived there until 1984, when the Old Six Mile Historical Society bought it, and it went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1996. Listings show Sunday hours of 1 to 4 p.m. Call ahead at 618-975-1863.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Granite City famous for?
A.  Steel and speckled enamel pots. The Niedringhaus brothers built the town around their graniteware works and incorporated it in 1896, naming it for that enamelware rather than for any rock. Their National Enameling and Stamping Company became one of the country’s largest makers of enamel kitchenware. Today the town is also known for its stretch of Route 66’s Last 100 Miles in Illinois, It’s Electric Neon Sign Park and Rusty the Steel Worker.
### Q. What city is close to Granite City, Illinois?
A.  Madison and Pontoon Beach border it, and Collinsville and Edwardsville are short drives east and northeast. Downtown St. Louis is about 6 miles away by the tourism bureau’s count, just across the Mississippi. Chouteau Island, technically in Madison, sits about a mile west of town.
### Q. What is Chouteau Island known for?
A.  The river beside it. The 10 miles of Mississippi along its west side are the only natural stretch of the working river without barge traffic, because tows use the Chain of Rocks Canal and Lock 27 instead. It also holds the Illinois end of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, the Chouteau Island Fishing Area and mulch hiking trails, and Lewis and Clark camped on neighboring Gabaret Island on Dec. 11, 1803.
### Q. Can you camp on Chouteau Island?
A.  Not at a developed campground. The nearest state campground, at Horseshoe Lake State Park, is closed along with its access road until May 2027 for a causeway project, according to IDNR. Chain of Rocks Park on the Missouri side doesn’t allow overnight parking either, so plan Chouteau as a day trip.
### Q. Does anyone live on Chouteau Island?
A.  Essentially no. After the Great Flood of 1993, governments bought out the homes in the island complex. Most of the land now belongs to the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the City of Madison, and HeartLands Conservancy owns 22 acres.
### Q. Who are some famous people from Granite City, Illinois?
A.  The one the city’s own history page singles out is Andy Phillip. He captained the Lincoln Place kids who won Granite City’s only state basketball championship in 1944, went on to the NBA and is in the Basketball Hall of Fame. Rusty the Steel Worker now stands at the entrance to that same neighborhood.
### Q. How much is public ice skating in Granite City?
A.  On the park district’s posted price list, non-residents pay $6 for adults and $5 for kids and seniors, and a Granite City Park ID drops each by a dollar. Skate rental is $2. Public sessions run Friday and Saturday evenings and Sunday afternoons in season, which usually opens in early November. Check the park district’s current session times before you go.
### Q. Is the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge open from the Illinois side?
A.  Not when we checked on Oct. 7, 2026, and our Chain of Rocks Bridge guide tracks the reopening. The canal bridge that leads to the Illinois end closed for repairs on June 22, 2026, and agencies gave different reopening estimates, from October to the end of 2026. The bridge itself stays open from the Missouri side at Chain of Rocks Park, 10840 Riverview Drive. Check MCT’s trail closures page or Great Rivers Greenway before you go.

## Things to Do in University City, MO: A World's Fair Searchlight, Heman Park, the Ruth Park Trail
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-university-city-mo
Loop regulars, look up. The usual lists of things to do in University City, MO, walk you down Delmar to Blueberry Hill and stop at the door. None of them mentions the 80-inch searchlight folded into the roof of City Hall, three blocks west, the beam that was switched on for the opening night of the 1904 World’s Fair to pull fairgoers toward a magazine publisher’s tent city and the town he was building.
That publisher, E.G. Lewis, built University City as a showpiece, and his marketing is still standing on the street: lions on 40-foot pylons at Delmar and Trinity, a bronze fish pedaling a bicycle across a pond in the park named for him, and an eight-sided tower that used to be his magazine’s headquarters. A few minutes north and west sit two places most visitors never get to. Heman Park just reopened with brand-new pickleball and basketball courts. Ruth Park Woods hides a 1-mile trail through old oak and hickory that almost nobody has written up. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, U City may be the one people think they know best from a single street.
Everything below was checked against City of University City, Green Center, Great Rivers Greenway and local news sources in October 2026. It’s all University City, Missouri, the inner-ring suburb in St. Louis County that everyone here calls U City. Search results mix it up with places called University City in Pennsylvania, California and North Carolina, so if a listing names another state, it isn’t this one.
### What is University City, Missouri known for?
Most people know University City, Missouri, for the Delmar Loop. Fewer know the rest of founder E.G. Lewis’s early-1900s model city: City Hall was his octagonal Woman’s Magazine headquarters, an 80-inch searchlight first lit for the 1904 World’s Fair is still folded into its roof, and two lions on 40-foot pylons guard Delmar.
The Loop is the part everyone already has. Its restaurants and Walk of Fame stars live in our guide to where to eat on the Delmar Loop, and they can stay there. This page is about the town around it.
Lewis was a publisher with a gift for spectacle. He bought 85 acres here in 1902, built his Woman’s Magazine headquarters on Delmar, and laid out a planned city around it. University City incorporated in September 1906 with Lewis as its first mayor, and its name was a bet on the neighbor next door: Washington University, whose campus sits just to the south. Today it’s about 35,000 people on under six square miles. The surviving pieces of Lewis’s plan stand within a ten-minute walk of each other on Delmar. The parks, the woods and the Saturday market are a short drive north and west.
### What’s hidden in the roof of University City Hall?
A searchlight from the 1904 World’s Fair. University City Hall, at 6801 Delmar Blvd. in University City, MO, keeps an 80-inch carbon-arc searchlight tucked inside the dome above the council chambers. To use it, crews open two sections of the roof and an elevator raises the light into the open air. Lewis had it installed on his Woman’s Magazine Building and lit it on April 30, 1904, opening night of the fair, to steer fairgoers toward Camp Lewis, his tent city, and toward his magazine.
The building is the other half of the stunt. Lewis started it in 1903 as his publishing headquarters, an octagonal Beaux-Arts tower 135 feet tall, and it became City Hall on Nov. 1, 1930.
Lost, found, lost again. The light was fired up for City Hall’s 1930 dedication and then forgotten. In 1964 assistant city engineer Robert Norvell rediscovered it, refitted it with the insides of World War II searchlights, and had it shining again on May 10, 1965. Bill Kaufman, son of former Mayor Nathan Kaufman, kept it running for decades. Then it went dark. It hasn’t run in about ten years, and the Historical Society of University City says people living a block away have no idea it’s up there.
Why now. In June 2026, City Manager Brooke Sharp put $45,000 for repairs into the fiscal 2027 budget, and the City Council approved it on Monday, June 22. The money goes at the biggest obstacle: the elevator that lifts the light out of the roof is off balance and can hang up partway. The light itself still works. The Historical Society wants it out for special events. Its vice president, Eric Kusnierkiewicz, told St. Louis Magazine, “We could hit the Arch with it.” No date yet. Watch for it.
The lions. The Lion Gates at Delmar and Trinity, also called the Gates of Opportunity, are Lewis’s too: 40-foot limestone pylons he commissioned in 1909, topped by a lion and a lioness from George Julian Zolnay, who also sculpted for the World’s Fair. By the 1970s the pylons leaned so badly that the council nearly cut them down to 14 feet. Instead, in 1991 the city straightened them and swapped the concrete lions for lightweight fiberglass casts. The originals went to the Missouri Historical Society’s collection. The pair in your photos are stand-ins.
The fish. Keep walking west to Lewis Park, 7001 Delmar. In the middle of its pond, a smiling bronze fish appears to pedal a bicycle across the water. Fish on a Bicycle is a 1997 piece by London-based sculptor Steven Gregory, maintained by the Gateway Foundation. It plays on the old feminist line that a woman needs a man like a fish needs a bicycle, and on Lewis, whose magazine empire launched the American Women’s Republic in 1911 to prepare women for the vote.
How to see all three. City Hall is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but the searchlight isn’t on public view, so do it from the sidewalk: the lions, then the University City Public Library at 6701 Delmar, City Hall’s tower, and the fish. The library is open seven days if it rains.
### What is there to do at Heman Park in University City?
Heman Park, at 7200 Olive Blvd. in University City, MO, is the city’s largest park: 85.26 acres bounded by Olive, Midland, Purdue, Pennsylvania and Vernon. This fall that means brand-new pickleball and basketball courts, a Saturday farmers market, an indoor track for bad-weather days, a 1.5-mile jogging course, eight tennis courts with four lit for night play, ball diamonds and soccer fields, a large playground and four picnic pavilions. The pool is closed for the season, and the city’s dog park sits in the corner at Vernon and Pennsylvania.
The new courts. The old basketball courts closed on March 11, 2026, for a full rebuild paid for by a $575,000 St. Louis County Municipal Parks grant. In September the parks department reopened the space with three new pickleball courts, three new basketball courts and a soccer mini-pitch. Come in through the Shaftesbury entrance; the courts keep regular park hours. Search for the park and the March closure story still sits near the top of the results, so don’t let an old headline fool you.
The Saturday market. The U City Farmers Market sets up outdoors in Heman Park near Centennial Commons, 7210 Olive, every Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., through Nov. 21 in 2026. Along with Missouri and Illinois produce, cheese, eggs, grass-fed beef and honey, vendors sell Missouri rainbow trout. Parking is free. The outdoor season wraps with a Holiday Market (Saturday, Dec. 5, in 2026, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.). From January through March 2027 the market moves indoors to the Heman Park Community Center, 975 Pennsylvania Ave., on the second and fourth Saturdays from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The market also lists an October Harvest Fest; check its page for the date.
Market ends at 12:30. Lunch next: where to eat in University City, MO
The rainy-day track. Centennial Commons has a suspended indoor running and walking track. In lane 1, it takes 14.25 laps to make a mile. Daily admission is $5 for resident adults, $4 for resident youth and seniors and $7 for non-residents, on top of the city’s annual ID card, which costs $5 for residents and $7 for everyone else. Check current rates before you go.
Pool, splash pad and summer music. The Heman Park pool ran from May 23 to Sept. 7 in 2026 and is closed until next season. A splash pad was added beside it in 2025 and comes with pool admission. In summer the park also hosts the city’s Starlight Concert Series and Summer Band concerts, which run in June, July and September; watch for next year’s lineup.
The bus stop with fan mail. One more stop, on the park’s Olive Boulevard edge. The final episode of the animated web series The Amazing Digital Circus, released in June 2026, ends at a real St. Louis bus stop, and r/StLouis pinned it down the next day: the southbound Metro stop at Olive and Purdue. Fans have been leaving notes and fan art there ever since. It’s a working stop on the 91 line, and the city has taken down art taped to the glass so riders can see out, so what’s on it changes week to week. Take your photo and let the riders through.
### Where is the Ruth Park nature trail?
The Ruth Park nature trail is in University City, MO, inside Ruth Park Woods on McKnight Road, near Ruth Park Golf Course. It’s a flat 1-mile loop of crushed limestone through what the Green Center, the nonprofit that cares for the woods, calls the last large stand of oak-hickory hardwood forest in the St. Louis area. The city lists the woods at 1160 McKnight Rd., and the Green Center uses 1100 McKnight. Both put you at the same trees.
Look the trail up by name and most of what comes back is trails in other states, which is a fair measure of how few people have written about this one. The woods are open to the public. Along the loop you’ll pass interpretive tree markers built by an Eagle Scout, benches and a picnic shelter, and a branch of the River Des Peres runs through the woods. The Green Center counts them at 26 acres; the city’s page says 23. Either way, it’s short and flat enough for small kids, and the oaks keep most of it in shade.
Bring binoculars. The Green Center ran a yearlong bird study here from May 1997 to April 1998 and has kept logging sightings since, and more than 100 species have now been recorded in the woods. Some are backyard regulars. Others are travelers between tropical rainforests and the Arctic tundra, stopping over in University City on the way. The center points out that habitat loss has thinned many of the 37 warbler species that pass through the St. Louis area every spring and fall, which is the case for keeping woods like these whole. Go early on a migration-season morning and walk slowly.
The Green Center. The nonprofit behind that work was founded in 1997 and is based in a 1932 house at 8025 Blackberry Ave., in a corner of Kaufman Park, whose 7.77 acres include a wooded nature-study area of their own. Its building and gallery are open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. It also throws the town’s fire-dancing fall party, which you’ll find in the next section.
Two more stops nearby. The Mona Trail, at 1100 Groby Rd., is a short 0.24-mile walk. Ruth Park Golf Course, 8211 Groby Rd., has been open since 1931, when it was University Golf Course: nine holes and a driving range laid out by Scottish-born designer Robert Foulis, with rental clubs for $12 if you show up without a bag. Tee times are at 314-727-4800; check current greens fees.
### What’s happening in University City this fall and holiday season?
In University City, MO, the grown-up night to circle is the one around a bonfire in the woods (Saturday, Nov. 7, in 2026). The Green Center’s Fall Fire Fest runs from 5:30 to 8 p.m. on its grounds at 8025 Blackberry Ave., with fire dancing by the Aalim and Chuvani Bellydance troupes and Scheherazade Drums, live music, two art exhibitions and s’mores at the fire. Every ticket includes two adult drinks: beer, wine or spiked hot chocolate. The plain hot chocolate is free for everyone. Adults pay $10 in advance or $15 at the door, kids 12 and under get in free, and a VIP package for four is $75. Bring a blanket or a chair, and buy ahead, because presale ends at noon that day.
The same evening, the free Dia de los Muertos festival fills Delmar from 4 to 10 p.m. with dancers, mariachi and stilt walkers. Leave the fire at 8 and you’ll still catch two hours of it.
A free orchestra. Every University City Symphony Orchestra concert is free. Its October 2026 U City concert: Sunday, Oct. 18, at 3 p.m., with a pre-concert talk at 2:15, at the 560 Music Center, 560 Trinity Ave. The program pairs Beethoven’s Coriolan Overture and Piano Concerto No. 2 with Mozart’s Concerto No. 10 for two pianos, played by Amelia Ly and Dickran Atamian. After that, the orchestra’s November and February concerts are in Kirkwood, and it’s back in U City on May 2, 2027. Check the orchestra’s site for any changes.
December. The farmers market’s Holiday Market takes over Heman Park for a Saturday morning (Dec. 5 in 2026, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.), a good time to knock out local gifts. We couldn’t verify a big public lights display inside U City in 2026, so for lights after dark, head south for the Christmas lights in Webster Groves. For Halloween night itself, our guide to Halloween events around St. Louis covers the rest of the metro.
### Where can you walk or bike in University City?
In University City, MO, start with the east stretch of the Centennial Greenway. It’s roughly a mile and a half of paved path from Skinker Boulevard and Forsyth, at the edge of Forest Park, through Washington University, north on Kingsbury to the Chuck Berry statue plaza on Delmar, then north again on the Ackert Walkway through the Parkview Gardens neighborhood to Vernon Avenue. There are bike racks along the way and a MetroLink station close by, so you can come without a car.
Ackert Park. The Ackert Walkway itself is a 0.34-mile path between Delmar and Vernon. Its park has a playground and a sprayground, improved with help from a $525,000 county grant, so a summer walk can end with wet kids.
The greenway’s other U City piece, from Shaw Park north to Olive along I-170, begins on the Clayton side, and we cover it in our list of things to do in Clayton, MO. Counting everything, the city has about 8 miles of trails.
The small-park loops. These never make a tourist list, and they’re the walks that fill a week. Fogerty Park, 1540 N. 82nd Blvd., has a half-mile jogging trail, a splash pad and a weatherproof shelter with restrooms. Janet Majerus Park, 1300 Partridge, rings a pond and fountain with a one-third-mile trail and fitness stations. Millar Park, 7603 Carleton, has a half-mile trail with its own fitness stations. Add Heman Park’s 1.5-mile jogging course, Ruth Park’s woods loop, Ackert’s walkway and the fish at Lewis Park, and you have a different U City park for every day of the week.
### Is the University City dog park free?
No. The University City Dog Park in University City, MO, is open to members only. It’s a 1-acre fenced park at 6860 Vernon Ave., at Vernon and Pennsylvania in the corner of Heman Park, with separate areas for large and small dogs. Here are the local rules.
For 2026, annual memberships cost $40 for one dog or $60 for two if you live in U City, and $60 or $90 for non-residents, with a limit of two memberships per household. You sign up in person at the Finance Department on the first floor of City Hall, 6801 Delmar, so you’ll be standing in the same building as the searchlight. Bring payment, proof of spay or neuter, and paper vaccination records for rabies, Bordetella, canine hepatitis, distemper and parvo. Residents also need proof of address. The 2026 cycle opened renewals on Dec. 3, 2025, new resident members on Dec. 10 and new non-residents on Jan. 7. Expect a similar December window for 2027, and confirm with the city before you go.
Is it worth it? A non-resident who comes every week pays a little over a dollar a visit. For a one-time run, our guide to the best free dog parks in St. Louis covers off-leash options across the metro.
### Nearby, out Olive and down the greenway
U City sits right against its neighbors. The greenway carries you south toward Clayton, and Olive Boulevard runs west into Creve Coeur. Want a fishing rod in the plan? The ponds at Lewis and Majerus parks are decorative, so head out to Creve Coeur Lake instead; our Creve Coeur list covers fishing at Creve Coeur Lake.
Next time someone says U City is just the Loop, you’re the one who knows there’s a World’s Fair searchlight folded into City Hall’s roof, that the lions on Delmar are fiberglass stand-ins, and where a fish rides a bicycle. Pick a Saturday. Hit the market at Heman Park, walk the Ruth Park loop, and end the day on Delmar, looking up.
After a morning on the Ruth Park loop or the courts at Heman Park, our guide to where to eat in University City, MO covers the dining room built around a working root beer bottling line and the Korean-Mexican tacos that started on a 2011 food truck.
If you run a shop or kitchen on Olive or Delmar that Saturday market regulars pass on the way home, list it with us so they find you before they head back to the highway.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is it called University City, MO?
A.  The name points at its neighbor. Founder E.G. Lewis chose it for the town’s closeness to Washington University, whose campus sits just south of the city, and for his hope that the place would grow into a center of learning and culture. University City incorporated in September 1906, and Lewis served as its first mayor.
### Q. What is the population of University City, Missouri?
A.  University City had 35,065 residents at the 2020 census, on about 5.88 square miles in St. Louis County. It borders the City of St. Louis on the east, and Delmar Boulevard runs through both.
### Q. What universities are in University City?
A.  None is based inside University City, Missouri. The town is named for Washington University, whose main campus sits just to the south, and the university owns buildings in and around the Loop, including the 560 Music Center on Trinity Avenue, where the University City Symphony Orchestra plays its free concerts.
### Q. What famous people went to University City High School?
A.  The best-known graduate is playwright Tennessee Williams, author of The Glass Menagerie and A Streetcar Named Desire, who finished at University City High School in 1929. The school inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 1999, and the district keeps an alumni Hall of Fame list with other graduates.
### Q. How did Delmar get its name?
A.  According to St. Louis historian Norbury L. Wayman, two early landowners on opposite sides of the road, one from Delaware and one from Maryland, combined the names of their home states. The road went by another name before that. Today Delmar Boulevard carries U City’s lions, its library and City Hall.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in University City, Mo?
A.  Walk the 1-mile oak and hickory loop in Ruth Park Woods. Play the new pickleball courts at Heman Park, then shop the Saturday farmers market there, whose 2026 outdoor season runs through Nov. 21. Find Fish on a Bicycle in the pond at Lewis Park, stand under the lions at Delmar and Trinity, and look up at City Hall, where a World’s Fair searchlight hides in the roof. Catch a free U City Symphony concert at the 560 Music Center. Check current dates first.
### Q. Is the Heman Park pool open?
A.  Not right now. The pool at Heman Park in University City ran from May 23 to Sept. 7 in 2026 and is closed for the off-season. A splash pad beside it, added in 2025, is included with pool admission. Expect the next season to open around late May, and check the city’s pool page for 2027 dates and rates.
### Q. What time do University City parks close?
A.  University City parks close at 10:30 p.m. and reopen at 5 a.m. Alcohol is prohibited in every city park, and dogs must be leashed outside the members-only dog park. Some spots keep their own schedules: the Green Center’s building is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and the pool and golf course run on seasonal hours.

## Things to Do in Maplewood, MO: Oldest Bowling Alley in St. Louis, Route 66 Plaques, Tango Night
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-maplewood-mo
Why does every “things to do in St. Louis” list skip the bowling alley that was already ten years old when Route 66 first came through town? Saratoga Lanes has been rolling on the second floor of a building on Sutton Boulevard, just south of Manchester Road, since 1916. Route 66 didn’t reach Manchester until 1926. You still keep score up there with a pencil.
The lists never get that far. They send everyone to the same five places, and even the search results for Maplewood pad themselves out with the Zoo and Forest Park, neither of which is in Maplewood. Meanwhile this inner-ring town runs a 1920s room with a maple floor where a tango night opens with a free lesson, a stretch of sidewalk that reads like a Route 66 history book, a free art market on a brewery parking lot, and a chocolate shop where you can watch the caramel get stirred by hand. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Maplewood is the one you can park once and walk.
Everything below was checked against the City of Maplewood, the Mid County Chamber of Commerce and the venues’ own pages in October 2026. Hours, prices and event dates change, so check before you go.
### What is there to do in Maplewood?
Maplewood packs a lot into a few walkable blocks. Bowl upstairs at Saratoga Lanes, open since 1916 and billed as the oldest alley west of the Mississippi. Walk original Route 66 by its sidewalk plaques on Manchester Road. Catch a folk concert or tango night at The Focal Point, then try barrel-aged beer at The Side Project Cellar.
All of it sits on two streets, Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard, and that’s the real trick of the place. The chamber points visitors to the public Marietta lot behind the 7300 block of Manchester and to street parking on Sutton south of Hazel. From either one, the bowling alley, the plaques, the music room and the beer bar are a few minutes apart on foot.
The fourth-Sunday stack. If you only get one day, make it the fourth Sunday of the month, because that’s when the town’s best things line up. Sundaze at Schlafly, a free art market of about 50 vendors on the Bottleworks lot, runs 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saratoga opens at 2 p.m. on Sundays. At 6, The Focal Point hosts a free beginner tango lesson ahead of its Milonga del Domingo dance. Walk the Route 66 plaques in between. Late-2026 fourth Sundays include Oct. 25 and Nov. 22. Check all three calendars that week.
### What is the oldest bowling alley in St. Louis?
Saratoga Lanes, at 2725 Sutton Blvd. in Maplewood. It opened in 1916, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2008, and both its owners and the City of Maplewood bill it as the oldest bowling alley of its kind west of the Mississippi. Eight lanes, up a flight of stairs. That’s it.
Why it’s upstairs. In 1916, bowling had a bad name. It was a saloon game, played in back rooms and basements by a crowd polite company avoided. Albert Carl Blood, who owned the Maplewood Planing Mill, put the lanes on the second floor of his new office building on purpose, to lift the game into respectable company. Literally. It worked. Factory-sponsored leagues filled the place, and in the 1930s the Maplewood News-Champion ran bowling scores on its front page. By Saratoga’s own account, it was the only alley in St. Louis County to make it through both Prohibition and the Great Depression, and one of the first in the country to host women’s and mixed leagues.
The Stein years. After Blood, the Stein family ran the alley for decades, back when they were the most famous bowlers in St. Louis. Otto Stein Jr. won the national ABC Tournament in 1929. His brother Clarence staged celebrity matches that put Maplewood’s factory bowlers up against champions from across the country. In the 1950s, the alley added automatic pinsetters and ball returns, which is how it outlasted the wave of big standalone bowling centers that came next.
What it’s like now. The owners have kept it old on purpose. There’s no automatic scoring, so somebody in your group keeps the sheet by hand, and the house balls are made to look like billiard balls. An August 2026 First Alert 4 report says Saratoga drew international attention after an American Airlines inflight magazine featured it in a Route 66 story, and travelers from overseas still climb the stairs because of it. Learn how to score a frame before you go. The owner likes to joke that the person holding the pencil has the edge.
How to go. Walk-ins are welcome except when a private party has rented the whole place, so Saratoga asks you to call (314) 645-5308 before you head over. Posted hours are noon to 1 a.m. Monday through Friday, 2 p.m. to 1 a.m. Saturday and 2 p.m. to midnight Sunday. Open bowling is $40 an hour per lane on weekdays and $45 on weekends, plus $5 shoes, and the time is prorated to the minute. Six friends on a weekday lane pay under $7 each for the hour, before shoes. Pool runs $6 per person per hour, capped at $18 a table. Individual lanes can be reserved, but not more than a week out. If smoke bothers you, ask about it when you call. The owners’ own history says they’ve resisted cutting it out, and we couldn’t confirm the current policy.
### Was Route 66 really in Maplewood?
Yes, for its first seven years. From 1926 to 1933, the original Route 66 ran through Maplewood on Manchester Road, and the town grew into a busy retail hub selling travelers food, rooms and gas. Then the route moved. By the late 1950s, malls and newer suburbs had pulled the shoppers away too. The comeback started in the late 1990s, driven by locally owned shops and restaurants, and the city now calls its business district the nation’s first Green Dining District.
The plaques. Walk the 7200 and 7300 blocks of Manchester Road and look down. The sidewalk carries two sets. Seven tribute plaques honor Maplewood businesses from the Route 66 years: Empire Supply, Citizens National Bank, Jay B. Smith Funeral Home, Scheidt Hardware, Saratoga Lanes, Kalb Electric and Sunnen Products Company. Six memorial plaques honor landmarks that made the route famous around St. Louis: the Chain of Rocks Bridge, Fun Fair Park, The Wedge, Katz Drug Store, the 66 Park-In Theatre and Coral Court. It’s free and self-guided, any hour. Scheidt Hardware still sells hardware at 7320 Manchester, so one of the names on the sidewalk is a store you can walk into.
The footnote. The city’s Route 66 page also takes up the Green Book, the guide Black travelers relied on from 1936 to 1964 to find places that would serve them, and explains why Maplewood never appears in it. The route had already moved off Manchester in 1933, before most of those guides were published. It’s an unusually honest note for a city page, and a good read on your phone between plaques.
The centennial. Route 66’s 100th birthday is Nov. 11, 2026, which makes Saratoga ten years older than the road it sits beside. For a longer walk, the city’s free self-guided history tour, “A Stroll Through Time,” was written for Maplewood’s 2008 centennial with Esley Hamilton and Doug Houser, and it covers the late-19th-century neighborhoods and the commercial strips that predate the streetcar. For the later alignments, the giant Amoco sign and the rest of the route across the region, our guide to historic sites in St. Louis picks up where Manchester leaves off.
### What can you do in Maplewood at night?
Dance, if you know which night. The Focal Point, at 2720 Sutton Blvd. on the same block as Saratoga, is best known as a folk and roots listening room, and our roundup of the neighborhood venues locals actually love covers that side of it. It started in 1975 as a coffeehouse in Webster Groves and moved to Maplewood in 2000, into a 1920s building with a maple floor. Yes, a maple floor in Maplewood. On nights without a concert, that floor belongs to the dancers.
Milonga del Domingo. St. Louis Gateway Tango runs an Argentine tango social on the fourth Sunday of each month. A free beginner lesson runs from 6 to 7 p.m., and the milonga goes from 7 to 10:30 p.m. for a small cover at the door. Recent event listings say it’s BYOB, with snacks provided. If you’ve never danced a step, the lesson hour is the whole reason to go.
The rest of the week.
