On scheduled Friday nights from March through November, a volunteer astronomy club opens a 30-inch telescope in a field two miles west of town to anyone who walks down the rock road at dusk. Downtown, an Art Deco movie house that opened in 1940 still projects onto its original screen, and a ticket still costs $5, cash or check.
New Haven sits on the south bank of the Missouri River in Franklin County, 11 miles west of Washington on Highway 100 and about 64 miles from downtown St. Louis. It has 2,414 people, a short downtown on Front Street, a levee you can walk on, and a reputation as a wine-and-gin stop that empties out once the tasting bars close. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, it’s the one most people leave an hour too early.
Everything below was checked against the astronomy club’s, the theater’s, the Missouri Department of Conservation’s, the chamber’s and the organizers’ own pages on Oct. 6, 2026. Small-town schedules move. Check before you drive.
### Is there anything to do in New Haven MO?
Yes, and the best of it happens after the tasting rooms close. New Haven, MO has a 1940 Art Deco movie house where tickets are still $5, a 30-inch telescope a club opens to the public on scheduled Friday nights, a levee river walk past John Colter’s memorial, and a Pumpkin Glow and Christmas by Moonlight downtown.
Besides Röbller Vineyard and Pinckney Bend Distillery, which lead every list and which our guide to where to eat in New Haven, MO already covers, the town runs a second shift. For everything else, here’s New Haven sorted by when you’d go:
Friday nights, March through November: Big Blue, the 30-inch telescope, on the club’s scheduled dates. Friday, Saturday and Sunday, most weeks: a first-run movie at the Walt for $5. Any daylight hour: the levee walk and the cluster of historical markers at John Colter Memorial Park. Rainy afternoons: theater seats facing a glass furnace at Astral Glass, and two free museums in an 1883 schoolhouse. October: the Scarecrow Festival and Pumpkin Glow downtown, plus a U-pick pumpkin patch out on Highway E. December: two free Fridays of Christmas by Moonlight.
A lot of that is free. The movie is five dollars.
### How much is a movie at the Walt Theatre in New Haven?
Five dollars. That’s the ticket price at the Walt Theatre, 111 Front St., and children 2 and under get in free. The box office takes cash or check only, so bring cash. Shows run Friday and Saturday at 7 p.m. and Sunday at 5 p.m., and the box office opens 30 minutes before each one. The Walt plays first-run movies, meaning current releases, plus the occasional special screening.
Here’s why it’s worth the trip. The Walt opened on Nov. 14, 1940, with three showings of the western “Wyoming,” starring Wallace Beery. Kids paid 10 cents. Adults paid 25. More than 85 years later the theater still has the same marquee out front, and it still projects onto the same white screen that first movie played on. The one big change came in the summer of 2014, when it switched from 35mm film to digital; the first digital show was Friday, Aug. 29, 2014. It’s a fully restored Art Deco house, and it’s locally owned and operated.
Do the date-night math. Two tickets cost $10. The Sunday 5 p.m. show has you back in St. Louis at a reasonable hour before the work week starts.
One 2026 date: on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 7 to 9 p.m., the Walt is set to screen “The Trail State,” a documentary about how Missouri turned a flooded rail line into the Katy Trail, America’s longest rail-trail. Gov. Mike Kehoe proclaimed Sept. 22 Trail State Day, the day the film premiered at the Missouri History Museum. Seeing it in a 1940 theater, in a river town that sits across the water from the trail, beats watching it at home. Its 2026 schedule also had the Walt closed Oct. 9 to 11 and on Oct. 18, so check the Now Showing panel on its homepage before you drive.
For cheaper seats closer to home, our guide to cheap movie tickets in St. Louis covers discount days and the independent single screens around the city. The Walt is the long-drive version of the same idea, with a better marquee.
Dinner before the 7 p.m. show? Where to eat in New Haven, MO
### Where can you look through a 30-inch telescope near St. Louis?
At Big Blue Observatory, two miles west of New Haven, on the public nights the Eastern Missouri Dark Sky Observers schedule from March through November. The club dates to 1991, and Big Blue is its 30-inch telescope, housed in an observatory on the grounds of Cedar Creek Conference Center, 1401 Olive Road. Nights start at dusk. The club’s site lists no admission charge, and there’s no ticket to buy. You park, walk down a rock road and wait your turn at the eyepiece.
Why 30 inches matters. What a telescope can show you depends mostly on the width of its main mirror. A 30-inch mirror gathers roughly 12,000 times the light of a fully dark-adapted human eye, and about 14 times what a common 8-inch backyard scope collects. Faint galaxies and nebulas that look like gray smudges in a small scope start to show structure. That’s the difference you drive out for.
2026 public nights. Friday, Oct. 9; Friday, Nov. 6; and Friday, Nov. 13. Those three close out the 2026 season. There are no public nights in December, January or February, and the club warns that November weather often cancels. The 2026 season opened March 13, so look for the 2027 list to start around mid-March; it wasn’t posted as of early October 2026. Clouds or bad weather cancel a night, and the club’s Big Blue page lists a phone number to call if you’re not sure. Check the club’s schedule at emdso.org the day you go.
How to find it in the dark. Take Highway 100 two miles west of New Haven and watch for three blue tourism signs and a covered wagon. Turn right at the covered wagon onto Olive Road. In about half a mile, turn left at the third covered wagon into Cedar Creek’s parking lot, park at the south end, and walk about 300 feet down the rock access road to the observatory. Wear shoes you don’t mind getting dusty.
What to bring, and what to leave home. The club’s list is short: flashlights, bug spray, lawn chairs, a jacket when it’s cool, and an insulated reusable cup, because they provide the water. The site rules are shorter: no alcohol, no dogs, no firearms. The observatory is handicap accessible, and a video eyepiece lets someone observe from a seat. A club post in late August mentioned a second instrument, a 12-inch computerized GoTo scope, so there may be two lines.
Stack it with a movie. In 2026 the Walt is set to close Oct. 9 to 11, meaning no movie after that year’s October sky night. November is the better double. Once the clocks fall back, dusk lands around 5:30 p.m., which leaves time for a turn or two at the eyepiece before the Walt’s 7 p.m. Friday show two miles away. If the sky clouds over, you still have the movie.
Two closer options keep the habit going between Big Blue nights. Every Friday night, weather permitting, another club sets up telescopes at Broemmelsiek Park, and our guide to things to do in Wentzville has the details. The Big Blue club also runs public Saturday nights at East Central College, covered in our guide to things to do in Union, MO. Big Blue is the upgrade: a 30-inch mirror, farther from the city’s glow.
### Where is John Colter buried?
Nobody knows, and the granite marker in New Haven says so. The Daughters of the American Revolution set it in 2006 at the front of John Colter Memorial Park, at Main and Miller streets, and it states plainly that “his gravesite has never been located.” The same stone says he’s believed to lie several miles east of town on a bluff top overlooking the Missouri River. The National Park Service lists his burial place as unknown.
Who he was explains why people keep asking. Colter was a private on the Lewis and Clark Expedition, the only member allowed to leave early, so he could go back to the mountains and trap. The Park Service credits him as the first American to see what became Yellowstone. In 1810 he came home and settled near the mouth of Boeuf Creek, about three miles east of here, where he married and had a son named Hiram. Military records show he died May 7, 1812, while serving with the U.S. Mounted Rangers under Nathan Boone, Daniel Boone’s son.
When we searched for his grave in October, the first memorial listing that came up belonged to a different John Colter, one born in 1833, 21 years after this one died. The local version comes with a legend: in 1926, a railroad cut through a ridge east of town known as Tunnel Hill turned up old coffins, and accounts still disagree on whether Colter was among them. Treat that as a story, not a location.
What you can actually visit. The memorial park is the town’s front porch. A log shelter and visitor center went up in 2003 for the Lewis and Clark bicentennial, with interpretive signs and a monument to Colter. From there a river walk runs about a quarter mile along the top of the flood-control levee, with signs on the expedition and on local history, and the Missouri sliding by below. About eight historical markers stand in or beside the park, out of 18 that marker databases count in New Haven. Three are worth the stop.
Colter’s Escape from the Blackfeet, on the kiosk in the middle of the park, tells the naked footrace that made him famous (the short version is in the FAQ below). Miller’s Landing marks where Philip Miller bought the riverbank on June 23, 1836, to sell firewood to passing steamboats, which is how the town began. The Iron Horse Arrives covers 1855, the year the Pacific Railroad reached the landing.
The whole loop takes about 30 minutes and costs nothing. Then drive up to 225 Selma St. and look at the Anna Bell Chapel from the street. It’s a small white AME church on a hill, on the National Register since 1992, and in February 2025 it was one of 30 historically Black churches in the country picked for a $200,000 grant from the Preserving Black Churches program of the National Trust for Historic Preservation’s African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund. Restoration started in fall 2025, so it’s an outside-only stop for now.
### Can you get on the Missouri River at New Haven?
Yes, at New Haven Access, a public ramp at river mile 82 at the very end of Front Street. Take Miller Street north from Highway 100, cross the railroad tracks and turn right on Front Street. It’s a single-lane concrete boat ramp on a one-acre site, and you can fish from the bank on the riverfront next to it. The Missouri Department of Conservation (MDC) lists catfish for anglers and eBird for birders. MDC doesn’t own the site; it regulates it under a cooperative agreement with the owner, and the info line it lists is (636) 441-4554. Anglers 16 through 64 need a Missouri fishing permit. Before you launch, check the river stage on the USGS gauge at Washington, the one MDC points to for this ramp.
The full-moon float. Paddle Stop, the river outfitter at 204 Front St., built its flagship trip around this riverfront: a 16-mile paddle that shuttles you upstream to the next river town’s ramp and brings you back down to New Haven. You’re fitted for a paddle and life jacket at the shop first. Guides stop on a sandbar and cook dinner while the sun sets and the moon comes up, then you paddle the rest of the way by moonlight. Plan on five to six hours. The listed price is $80. As of early October 2026 the booking page says the trip isn’t available, so treat it as next season’s plan and contact the outfitter for dates.
The ferry that ran on horses. Before there was a bridge anywhere close, there was a ferry, and its marker stands near the Colter memorial. Ferryboats docked below the bank here for nearly a century, starting in 1831 at a spot a mile west. By the late 1800s they made hourly trips across to Warren County, and high school students from the north side rode the ferry to class in New Haven. The strangest of them was the Tilda-Clara, around 1900, whose paddlewheel was turned by a team of horses walking a treadmill. The marker ties the end of ferry service to the opening of the bridge at Washington in 1936.
The Katy Trail question. The trail runs along the north bank, across the water from town, and there’s no bridge at New Haven. The nearest crossing is the Highway 47 bridge at Washington, 11 miles east. Our guide to things to do in Washington, MO covers that bridge’s walking path, the Katy shuttles that leave from Washington, and MDC’s numbers on the river’s blue catfish, so we kept all three off this page.
### What can you do in New Haven on a rainy day?
Watch glass get made from a theater seat. At Astral Glass Studio, 133 Front St., two rows of theater-style seats sit behind a thin sheet of glass, facing a furnace that The Missourian reported in 2024 often burns hotter than 1,500 degrees. On the other side of the glass, the studio’s artists shape molten glass on blowpipes while you watch. Gary and Judy Rice run it with their granddaughter, Katelynn Escobar, and Lance Stroheker, who started with them as an apprentice. The business began in California in 1974 and marked 15 years in New Haven in 2024. Demos usually happen on Saturdays, but the furnace schedule changes, so call (573) 237-5159 before you count on one.
Two museums, free. The New Haven Preservation Society keeps two of them, “Springgate” and “The Journey Begins,” inside the Old Grade School, 810 Maupin Ave., built in 1883. The society bought the building in 1989 and later put back its steeple, which had been gone since about the 1930s. On the lower level, in what used to be the cafeteria and locker rooms, the Steamboat Room has an interactive pilot-house model that lets kids play steamboat pilot, and a 22-foot cityscape lays out the downtown businesses of the 1800s and 1900s. There are Civil War and World War II exhibits and a gallery of photos called “Fires, Floods, and Train Wrecks.” Admission is free and donations are welcome. Tours are by appointment, through the number on the society’s museum page.
A tasting you take standing up. Pinckney Bend’s tasting bar is indoors, standing-only and set right in front of the still, and it runs every half hour, Monday through Saturday, with no reservation. That’s all we’ll say here; the where-to-eat guide has the rest.
End with the Sunday show. The Walt’s Sunday movie starts at 5 p.m. So here’s a wet-weekend plan: book the museum for late morning, catch a glass demo after lunch, and finish in a 1940 theater seat while it rains on Front Street.

It lights up the whole town, and most of it is free.

The lights. The New Haven Lions Club works with the city to put up the Holy Family display at the Highway 100 water tower, plus the Christmas lights that line streets all over town. You’ll pass the water tower display on Highway 100 coming into town.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is New Haven, Missouri known for?
A.  Its riverfront and its history. New Haven began in 1836 as Miller’s Landing, a woodyard where Missouri River steamboats stopped for fuel, and it was platted as a town in 1856. John Colter of the Lewis and Clark Expedition settled about three miles east in 1810. Today it’s known for Röbller Vineyard and Pinckney Bend Distillery, the 1940 Walt Theatre and its $5 tickets, the furnace-side seats at Astral Glass Studio, and the levee walk at John Colter Memorial Park.
### Q. How far is New Haven, MO from St. Louis?
A.  About 64 miles by road from downtown, or roughly an hour and 15 minutes, depending on your route and traffic. Whichever way you come, the last stretch is usually Highway 100 west out of Washington, which is 11 miles east of New Haven.
### Q. How many people live in New Haven, MO?
A.  2,414 at the 2020 Census, up from 2,089 in 2010. Some regional tourism sites still show the older number.
### Q. What’s happening in New Haven this weekend?
A.  Start with the regulars. The Walt Theatre shows a movie Friday and Saturday at 7 p.m. and Sunday at 5 p.m., unless its homepage says it’s closed that weekend. Pinckney Bend’s tasting bar runs Monday through Saturday. On scheduled Friday nights from March through November, the astronomy club opens Big Blue at dusk. For one-off events, check the New Haven Chamber of Commerce site and the Downtown New Haven Inc. Facebook page.
### Q. How did John Colter survive?
A.  He ran. The National Park Service marker in New Haven’s Colter Memorial Park tells it this way: in the fall of 1808, a Blackfeet war party caught Colter and his partner, John Potts, trapping beaver on the Jefferson River. Potts was killed. Colter was stripped naked and made to run for his life across a prairie covered in prickly pear cactus, with the river about six miles ahead. He outran all but one pursuer, turned, took the man’s spear and killed him, then dove into the river and hid in a pile of driftwood until the search gave up after dark. From there he walked about 300 miles, living on roots, back to Manuel Lisa’s fort.
### Q. How accurate are John Colter’s stories?
A.  Hard to say, because Colter left nothing in writing beyond his signature. His stories reach us through other people: the English botanist John Bradbury, who met him in St. Louis and published the escape in 1817, and the trapper Thomas James, whose memoir tells a somewhat different version of the fight. Even the basics drift. The New Haven marker puts the run in the fall of 1808, some histories say 1809, and his death date shows up as both May 7, 1812, and Nov. 22, 1813. His reports of geysers and bubbling mud were laughed off at the time, and the area earned the joking name “Colter’s Hell.” The thermal country he described turned out to be real.
### Q. What is the best month to go stargazing?
A.  Around here, September and October are the sweet spot for Big Blue. Dark comes early enough to make a Friday work, the bugs ease off, and you’re ahead of the November cold that the club warns often cancels its nights. Its public nights run March through November and sit close to the new moon, when the sky is darkest. December through February has no public observing at all. Whatever the month, a clear, moonless night beats everything else, so check the forecast before you leave St. Louis.
### Q. Do you need tickets for the Big Blue telescope nights?
A.  No. Public nights are walk-up: there’s no ticket, and the club’s site lists no admission charge. Show up at dusk on a scheduled Friday, park at the south end of Cedar Creek’s lot and walk the 300 feet to the observatory. Groups that want their own night can send a reservation request through the Eastern Missouri Dark Sky Observers’ website, and the Big Blue page lists a number to call if you think clouds have canceled it.

## Old Chain of Rocks Bridge: Parking, Which Side Is Open, and the Scrap Price That Saved It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/old-chain-of-rocks-bridge
Just a bridge. That’s how the recycled lists treat the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge: a mile of old Route 66, a bend in the middle, a photo of the river, next stop. They leave out the part where it nearly wasn’t here. In the early 1970s, Army demolition teams looked at the closed bridge as something to blow up for practice. Demolition was planned for 1975. Then the price of scrap steel fell, and tearing down a mile of steel truss stopped paying for itself, according to the bridge’s own National Register nomination. You can walk it today because, for about twenty years, it wasn’t worth enough to wreck.
The lists skip the practical part, too. Where do you park? Which end is open this fall? Is the Missouri lot still the one people warned you about? Those questions mostly get answered in old forum threads, and some of those answers stopped being true in 2024. Most of our day-trip pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one keeps you eight miles north of downtown, on a deck more than 60 feet above the Mississippi.
Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against Great Rivers Greenway, the National Park Service, the bridge’s National Register file, Illinois DNR, the City of St. Louis and the Missouri Department of Conservation.
### Can you walk across the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge?
Yes. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge is open only to people walking and biking, daily from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. It runs about 5,350 feet, just over a mile, from Chain of Rocks Park in north St. Louis to Chouteau Island in Illinois, with a sharp bend midway across the Mississippi.
Cars haven’t used it since the late 1960s. You walk on the concrete deck between the steel trusses, behind a 4-foot steel guardrail added when the bridge was converted for people, according to its National Register nomination. Bikes share the deck with walkers. There’s no shade anywhere on it, so bring water in July and a windbreaker in January.
How the walk runs. From the gated lot at Chain of Rocks Park, 10840 Riverview Drive, a path leads straight onto the Missouri end. About halfway across, the bridge turns. That bend is why most people come, and it’s where everybody stops for the same photo. Keep going and you step off onto Chouteau Island, the Illinois end. Great Rivers Greenway, which runs the park, puts the round trip from the lot to the Chouteau Island trailhead and back at 2.1 miles. At an easy pace with a stop at the bend, plan on 45 minutes to an hour.
What to bring, and what to leave. From April through November the park has a drinking fountain with a bottle filler and a pet bowl, plus two portable restrooms. Outside those months, bring your own water. Dogs are welcome on a leash, and you’re expected to pick up after them. Leave the glass bottles, the grill and the fireworks at home, since the park rules ban all three. No motorized vehicles go on the bridge or the greenway unless Great Rivers Greenway authorizes them.
### Is the Chain of Rocks Bridge open right now?
Yes. When we checked Great Rivers Greenway’s Chain of Rocks Park page on Oct. 7, 2026, it said the bridge “is OPEN and accessible from the Missouri side only,” because the canal bridge on the Illinois approach has been closed since June 22, 2026. The park and the bridge keep their usual hours, 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. If that notice is gone from the park page, the Illinois side is open again.
Why the Illinois side is closed. The old bridge isn’t the problem. The only road to its Illinois end crosses the Chain of Rocks Canal on a much smaller bridge, and that canal bridge is closed for construction. No canal bridge means no way to drive to the Illinois lot, and Great Rivers Greenway notes that no detour was provided.
When it reopens, nobody’s saying for sure. The agencies don’t agree. On Oct. 7, 2026, Great Rivers Greenway’s park page gave the closure as “June 22, 2026 through 2026.” Illinois DNR’s Horseshoe Lake page still said there would be no access to Chouteau Island “until approximately October 1, 2026,” a date that came and went with the bridge still closed. Madison County Transit’s trail closures page said “Anticipated reopening in October.” No reopening had been announced. Check Great Rivers Greenway’s Chain of Rocks Park page before you go.
What the closure changes. While the canal bridge is closed, the bridge is an out-and-back. You can still walk or ride the full mile to Chouteau Island and return, but you can’t continue onto the MCT Confluence Trail in Illinois, because that link runs over the closed canal bridge. The loops that come back to Missouri over the McKinley Bridge are off until it reopens.
One more detour. The westbound I-270 exit to Riverview Drive is temporarily closed. Great Rivers Greenway’s posted detour: take the Lilac Avenue exit 33, turn right on Lilac, then right on Dunn Road for 1.1 miles, then right on Riverview Drive for about 0.3 mile. The park is on your left.
### Where do you park for the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge?
At Chain of Rocks Park on the Missouri side, 10840 Riverview Drive, St. Louis, MO 63137. It has 55 spaces, three of them accessible, and right now it’s the only lot that reaches the bridge.
If someone told you the Missouri lot was a bad idea, that advice is out of date. For years the standard tip was to park in Illinois, because cars left at the Missouri end got broken into. Great Rivers Greenway rebuilt that end as a 16-acre park and opened it in May 2024. It came with a fence around the site, a gated entrance, staff on site during peak visiting hours, lot lighting, video cameras and an emergency phone. The gate is automatic. Pull forward to open it, and if it stays shut, put the car in park and push the button.
A few rules catch people. There’s no overnight parking. The park opens at 7 a.m. and closes 30 minutes after sunset, so in winter your window is short. And on big event days the lot fills fast. When the 2024 Bridge Boogie came to the park, Great Rivers Greenway told the crowd to park in Illinois and walk over.
The Illinois lot, once the canal bridge reopens. Great Rivers Greenway counts 80 spaces in the Chouteau Island west lot at the bridge’s east end, and the Park Service lists free parking at the Illinois entrance. Its directions from Missouri: take eastbound I-270 across the river to the first Illinois exit, Exit 3A, go south on Route 3, turn right (west) on West Chain of Rocks Road and follow it onto Chouteau Island to the lot. Until the canal bridge reopens, that road won’t get you there.
The long way in: North Riverfront Park. The City of St. Louis’s northernmost park, 250 acres on the river south of the bridge, has two trail lots, a north lot with 70 spaces and a south lot with 20. Park there and ride the Riverfront Trail north to the bridge. From Chain of Rocks Park to the south end of North Riverfront Park and back is 5.9 miles by the greenway’s count, which turns a short walk into a real morning.
Back from the bend and hungry? Where to eat in North County, MO
### Why does the Chain of Rocks Bridge bend in the middle?
Because the river men won. St. Louis engineer Baxter L. Brown drew the bridge straight, a single line of five continuous trusses forming ten spans. Riverboat pilots protested. The straight line would have set the piers just upstream of the city’s two water intake towers, so a captain coming downriver would have had to thread the piers and then the towers. The War Department ordered the design changed. The straight route also crossed a stretch where the bedrock couldn’t carry the piers. So the bridge turns at about mid-span, which lines its piers up with the intake towers and lets boats clear both in one pass.
Drivers paid for it. The designer told officials the turn wouldn’t be a problem. It became a legendary Route 66 bottleneck anyway, the National Register nomination says, despite special signs and signals meant to keep traffic moving. Picture a 20-foot roadway, a sharp turn 60 feet over the Mississippi, and an ornate toll booth waiting at the Missouri end.
So how sharp is it? Here’s where the copy-and-paste lists fall apart. Most of them say 22 degrees, and so does the Great Rivers Greenway marker standing on the bridge. The National Register nomination says 30, and so does the National Park Service. The nomination even spells out the mess in a footnote: at least two sources say 22, another says 24, and a 1994 engineering inventory documented 30. Stand at the bend and judge it yourself. Just know the number on the sign isn’t the one in the federal file.
### Why didn’t they tear down the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
Money, twice. The first time, money built it. A group of local investors, the Chain-of-Rocks and Kingshighway Bridge Company, got a congressional charter in 1927, and the toll bridge opened on July 20, 1929, about six months late after ice and spring floods slowed the work. It cost $2.5 million, double the estimate. In the 1930s, the City of Madison, Illinois, bought it with $2.3 million in bonds. Madison still owns it. Great Rivers Greenway leases it.
Route 66 moved onto it in 1936, rerouted off the McKinley and MacArthur bridges to skip downtown’s warehouse-district traffic, and it brought drivers into St. Louis past the Chain of Rocks Amusement Park on the Missouri hills. During World War II, the bridge’s red sections were painted green so it would be harder to spot from the air. That’s the dull green you see today. Gas rationing cut traffic, so the tolls went up to 35 cents a car plus a nickel for every passenger besides the driver. As the Park Service points out, that’s a carpool lane in reverse.
The second time, money nearly killed it. The New Chain of Rocks Bridge opened for I-270 about 2,000 feet upstream in 1967. Traffic on the old one dried up, Madison couldn’t afford its upkeep, and the city closed it in 1968. Army demolition teams eyed it for practice. Demolition was planned for 1975, and then scrap steel prices crashed. The bridge sat for about twenty years, too costly to knock down and too narrow for modern traffic.
Hollywood found it in that state. In 1980, director John Carpenter used the rusting bridge for Escape from New York. A local trails group saw something better. Trailnet hatched the idea of a walking and biking bridge in 1989, signed a 20-year lease with Madison after seven years of work, started cleanup in January 1997 and reopened it in 1999 as the Route 66 Bikeway. It went on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006, and Trailnet passed the lease to Great Rivers Greenway in December 2014.
Route 66 turns 100 this year, and this is a stretch of it you can only cross on foot or by bike. For the rest of the old road, start at the Route 66 State Park visitor center in Eureka, or follow it by car with our scenic drives around St. Louis. Our guide to historic sites in St. Louis covers the Route 66 signs still standing in the city.
### What can you see from the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
Two castles in the river. Look downstream from the Missouri half. The smaller stone tower close to the Missouri shore is Intake Tower No. 1, built in 1894 and designed by William Eames in a Richardsonian Romanesque style. The city’s landmark page compares it to the Mouse Tower on the Rhine near Bingen. The bigger one, Intake Tower No. 2, came from the firm of Roth and Study in 1915, in a Roman Renaissance style. It had full-time crews until the late 1920s, and the city says it now serves as a backup to the onshore intakes. Neither is open to visitors, and the bridge is the best seat you’ll get. Eames also drew one of St. Louis’s three historic water towers, the red Bissell Street tower, if you want to see more of his work the same day.
The rocks that aren’t the chain. The Chain of Rocks was a 17-mile run of rock ledges north of St. Louis, bad enough that the Army Corps of Engineers dug an 8.4-mile canal on the Illinois side to get around it, finished in 1953. The churning line of rock just south of the bridge is not that chain. It’s a low-water dam the Corps built in 1964 to raise the river over the ledges upstream. The real ledges stay underwater most of the time and show only in extreme low water. Admire the dam from the deck. That water isn’t for wading, swimming or paddling.
Bald eagles, in winter. The Missouri Department of Conservation lists the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge among the best places in the state for winter eagle viewing. From late December through early February, look for eagles perched in big trees along the water’s edge, and go early, when they’re flying and fishing. MDC set up spotting scopes on the bridge for a free eagle-watching open house on Feb. 28, 2026. Watch Great Rivers Greenway’s events calendar for the next one.
The 1929 road. At the Illinois end, about 1,000 feet of the original concrete roadbed still runs off the bridge toward Chain of Rocks Road, according to the 2006 National Register file. That’s the pavement Route 66 drivers rolled over on their way to the toll booth. Upstream, the I-270 bridge that replaced it carries the traffic now.
### Where can you walk or ride from the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
South on the Riverfront Trail. The bridge anchors the north end of the Mississippi Greenway, also called the Riverfront Trail, a flat, paved route that follows the river toward downtown. Great Rivers Greenway counts 16.19 miles including the Old Chain of Rocks and McKinley bridges, and it puts a ride from Chain of Rocks Park to the Arch grounds and back at 23.2 miles. It’s an industrial ride, along both sides of the floodwall, with very little shade. Two cautions from the greenway. Some stretches double as a levee road, so you may meet authorized vehicles. And at Maline Creek, by the train trestle, the trail squeezes through concrete barriers around flood damage, with repairs set to start this fall and finish by the end of the year. Our guide to the St. Louis Riverfront Trail covers the whole ride south to the Arch.
The Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing. Roughly halfway between the bridge and the trail’s downtown start at Biddle Street sits Missouri’s first nationally designated Underground Railroad historic site, per Great Rivers Greenway. Make it your turnaround and the ride has a point.
North Riverfront Park. On the way you pass the city park where anglers drive and walk right up to the bank. The city’s own park page says they’re mostly after buffalo, usually fried.
Across to Illinois, once the canal bridge reopens. East of the bridge, Chouteau Island has trails and a fishing area below the bridge. We cover the trails, the fishing and how to reach Chouteau Island below the Chain of Rocks Bridge on our Granite City page. Past the canal, the MCT Confluence Trail heads north along the river toward the parks in Alton, Illinois, and Great Rivers Greenway maps a 21.8-mile loop back to Missouri over the McKinley Bridge. Both wait on that canal bridge.
A short drive north, Columbia Bottom Conservation Area is mostly closed for levee work as of October 2026, so for now the land view of where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet is across the Missouri at Confluence Point State Park. For the rest of the river, from the steps below the Arch to the ferries, see our guide to the St. Louis riverfront.
Next time somebody calls it just a bridge, you’re the one who knows it was almost scrap, that the bend reads 22 on the sign and 30 in the federal file, and that the Missouri lot is the one to use now. Pick a clear morning. Check the closure. Walk out to the bend.
Off the bridge and ready to eat, our guide to where to eat in North County, MO includes two Bellefontaine Neighbors kitchens a short drive from Riverview Drive.
If you run a kitchen, a bike shop or a bait shop within a few miles of the gated lot at Chain of Rocks Park, list it with us so the people walking off the bridge find you before they get back on I-270.
For every other crossing, our guide to the bridges in St. Louis covers which ones you can walk, bike or only drive.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it safe to walk across the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  During open hours, it’s a straightforward walk on a concrete deck with a 4-foot steel guardrail. Since 2024 the Missouri end has sat inside a fenced park with a gated entrance, staff on site at peak times, lot lighting, cameras and an emergency phone. The bridge’s rough reputation dates to the decades it sat abandoned. Go between 7 a.m. and 30 minutes after sunset, stay on the deck, and stay out of the river.
### Q. What happened on the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  In April 1991, while the bridge sat closed and abandoned, sisters Julie Kerry, 20, and Robin Kerry, 19, were murdered there by four young men. Their cousin survived, and all four men were convicted. The bridge reopened to walkers and cyclists in 1999, and its Missouri end now sits inside a gated park that closes 30 minutes after sunset.
### Q. What movie was filmed on the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  Escape from New York. Director John Carpenter filmed the closed, rusting bridge in 1980 for the 1981 movie, where it plays the fictional 69th Street Bridge, the way off Manhattan in the final escape. Several other St. Louis locations stood in for New York in the same film.
### Q. When did they close the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  The City of Madison closed it to traffic in 1968, according to the National Register nomination and the National Park Service, a year after the New Chain of Rocks Bridge opened for I-270. The Great Rivers Greenway marker on the bridge says 1970. Either way, it stayed officially closed until it reopened for walking and biking in 1999.
### Q. Can you drive over the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  Not on an ordinary day. Great Rivers Greenway can approve vehicle crossings for special events, and its permit rules have cars enter from the Illinois lot, drive single file down the center at no more than 15 mph with a greenway representative present, and leave through the Missouri gate onto Riverview Drive. Everyday traffic uses the New Chain of Rocks Bridge on I-270, about 2,000 feet upstream.
### Q. How long does it take to walk the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  Most people need 45 minutes to an hour round trip, with a stop at the bend. The bridge is about 5,350 feet long, just over a mile, and Great Rivers Greenway puts the round trip from the Chain of Rocks Park lot to the Chouteau Island trailhead and back at 2.1 miles. In winter, add time for scanning the trees for eagles.
### Q. Does the Chain of Rocks Bridge still exist?
A.  Yes. It came close to demolition in 1975, but it’s still standing, it has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 2006, and it’s open daily to people walking and biking. The City of Madison, Illinois, owns it, and Great Rivers Greenway leases and runs it as the north end of the Mississippi Greenway.
### Q. Can you bring a dog on the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  Yes, on a leash at all times, and you’re expected to pick up after it. From April through November, the drinking fountain at Chain of Rocks Park has a pet bowl. The deck is concrete with no shade, so on hot afternoons, go early in the day.

## Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park: The Best Arch View, Why the Geyser Went Dark, How to Get There
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/malcolm-w-martin-memorial-park
Turned off on purpose. Plenty of travel listings still tell you to be in East St. Louis at noon, when the Gateway Geyser threw a column of water up to 630 feet, the height of the Arch across the river. It was switched off for good in February 2024, and it isn’t coming back. Age and cost played a part. So did the National Park Service. The park’s owners want the Arch’s national park to cross the river and take this land someday, and by the park’s own account the Park Service had major reservations about a fountain the park itself calls “clearly incompatible” with the Arch’s story. So the tallest fountain in the country went dark, and the park district started pulling out its plumbing to leave what its director called “a blank slate.”
The view didn’t go anywhere. Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park still sits straight across the Mississippi from the Arch, it’s still free, and its overlook still puts the Arch and the whole downtown skyline in one frame. Most of our day-trip pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one sends you just over the river, to the platform the park says a lot of St. Louis postcard shots come from.
Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against the park’s own site and posted rules, the Metro East Park and Recreation District, the National Park Service, Great Rivers Greenway, St. Louis Public Radio and the Belleville News-Democrat.
### Where can I find the best views of the St. Louis Arch?
Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park in East St. Louis, Illinois, sits directly across the Mississippi from the Arch, and its owners call it the best view in the region. Climb its Mississippi River Overlook, about 40 feet up, for the Arch and downtown skyline in one frame. It’s free and open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.
Why from here? Because you see the Arch face-on. Its legs stand north and south, so on the Missouri side you’re mostly underneath it, craning up. From Illinois you get the whole curve, the river in front of it and the skyline stacked behind it. Line it up right and the Old Courthouse, where Dred and Harriet Scott filed their freedom suit in 1846, sits inside the Arch’s legs. That’s the frame photographers cross the river for, and our guide to historic sites in St. Louis picks up the Scotts’ story from there.
Keep your expectations simple. The park calls itself a passive park: lawn, paths, benches, a flagpole and the overlook. Bring what you need. The Metro East Park and Recreation District owns and runs it, and the Gateway Center of Metropolitan St. Louis, the nonprofit Malcolm Martin founded, still pays for most of it. The park puts the center’s donations for building and running the place at more than $15 million.
The Missouri side has good angles of its own, and the Arch grounds are free and open from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. But they all show you the Arch from close in. This park was built for the express purpose of looking back at it.
### Why is the Gateway Geyser closed?
Because its owners shut it off for good in February 2024 and chose not to bring it back. Bryan Werner, executive director of the Metro East Park and Recreation District, told reporters in January 2026 that the district turned it off to save money and was removing all of the infrastructure tied to the geyser.
The park’s own explanation, still posted on its geyser page this fall, comes down to three things. First, age. Nearly 30 years had worn out the pond liner, the pumps, the generators and everything around them, and the park compares it to driving a 30-year-old car every day. Second, cost and the environment: what once made sense to run, the park says, no longer outweighed the money and the environmental impact. Third, and least known, the national park. The park district and the Gateway Center want Gateway Arch National Park to expand into Illinois and take over this site, and the Park Service balked at the geyser because, as the park puts it, a giant fountain didn’t fit the Arch’s story as a memorial to westward expansion. Pulling it out also clears room for the new Illinois Route 3, which will run right next to where the geyser stood.
What it was. The geyser first erupted on May 27, 1995, with Martin himself at the switch. His nonprofit raised about $4 million for the pool, the geyser and four smaller fountains, according to St. Louis Public Radio, after an earlier push to buy land for the national park stalled. Three 800-horsepower pumps pushed 7,500 gallons a minute out of the nozzle at roughly 250 feet per second, and on a calm day the column reached 630 feet. The four smaller fountains stood for the four rivers that meet near St. Louis: the Mississippi, the Missouri, the Illinois and the Meramec. In the warm months it went off daily at noon, if the wind allowed. A sensor shut it down whenever the wind topped 13 mph.
What’s there now. The park files the geyser under “The End of an Era” on its website. We couldn’t find a public update on whether the teardown is finished, so don’t expect the pond and nozzle you see in older photos. If a page tells you to show up at noon, it’s out of date. Our list of underrated places to visit in St. Louis flags the same stale advice.
### What’s at the top of the Mississippi River Overlook?
A view, a bronze statue and a webcam. The Mississippi River Overlook is a tiered walkway that climbs in five levels to a platform about 40 feet above the riverbank; the park lists the whole structure at just over 43 feet tall. It opened in June 2009, built with support from the Gateway Center, which Martin left more than $5 million when he died. The ramps are ADA accessible, so a wheelchair or a stroller can make it to the top, and the stainless steel railings light up after dark.
The statue and the line beside it. At the top, a bronze statue of Martin by St. Louis sculptor Harry Weber faces the Arch he spent decades trying to extend across the river. An inscription up there reads “Malcolm Martin represents the need to dream.” His old friend Marshall Hier told St. Louis Public Radio this year that he still thinks about those words.
The ArchCam. A live webcam watches the overlook with the Arch in the background, and the park streams it on its website, along with 24 hours of archived footage. The park’s own suggestion: call a friend or a relative while you’re standing up there, so they can pull up the camera and watch you live, waving in front of the Arch.
Overlook manners. Smoking is banned on the overlook at all times under the park’s posted rules, and the park’s event guidance keeps chairs, blankets and food off the platform too. Picnic on the lawn instead.
### Where is the best place to take pictures of the Gateway Arch?
From the top of the overlook at Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, at the right hour. The park calls itself the best place to photograph the Arch, and height is the reason. Down on the lawn, the riverbank, the rail lines and the utility lines crowd the bottom of your frame; St. Louis Public Radio noted this year that power lines cut across the view. Up top, you have more room to compose around them, with the river as your foreground.
The light decides everything. The park faces west, toward the Arch. That one fact tells you when to come.
Morning puts the sun behind you, so it falls on the side of the Arch you’re facing and the steel lights up. The catch is the gate. The park opens at 7 a.m., and in St. Louis the sun rises after 7 only for most of October, from about December into early February, and for a few weeks after the clocks spring forward in March. October is one of those windows, so a sunrise trip works right now. Look up the sunrise time for your date before you set the alarm.
Sunset drops the sun behind the skyline, so you get silhouettes and glare rather than a lit Arch. Sunset here never comes later than about 8:30 p.m., and the park stays open until 10, so you’ll never get kicked out before it.
After dark is the sleeper. Stay about half an hour past sunset for a deep blue sky behind the buildings and the skyline lights coming on, with the overlook’s lit railings to see you back down.
The Fourth of July. The park opens its lawn for the Celebrate STL fireworks over the riverfront. On July 3 and 4, 2026, it was free, stayed open until the show ended around 10 p.m., and put on a 1,500-drone show over the Mississippi right before the fireworks. The park warned that its lots would fill, banned on-street parking for the event and pointed people to MetroLink. Watch the park’s site next summer for 2027 details.
Leave the drone at home. Drones are banned at the park unless you have a filming permit from the park district plus clearance from the Federal Aviation Administration. Ordinary photos, including engagement, senior and family portraits, need no permit at all. The details are in the FAQ below.
### Why is the park named for Malcolm W. Martin?
Because he spent most of his life trying to finish the Arch. Not the steel part. Eero Saarinen’s late-1940s design for the memorial also imagined a park on the Illinois bank, with playgrounds, sports facilities and a boat basin, St. Louis Public Radio reported this year. The Arch was finished in 1965. The Illinois half never got funded.
Martin, a St. Louis lawyer born in 1912, picked up that unfinished half after World War II, when his father steered him to Luther Ely Smith, the civic leader now remembered as the father of the Arch. In 1968, by the park’s account, Martin founded the Gateway Center of Metropolitan St. Louis to protect land on the East St. Louis riverfront. He and the nonprofit bought old railroad property a piece at a time, much of it with his own money. Congress authorized an Illinois expansion of the memorial in 1984, and President Ronald Reagan signed it. The money never came. In 1987 Martin chaired the executive committee of a federal commission set up to plan the Illinois extension, and the Interior Department gave him its National Conservation Award the next year.
When Congress finally set aside money to start buying land in the early 1990s, some of the riverfront went to casino developers instead. So Martin’s group raised its own money and built the geyser, a 630-foot exclamation point aimed straight at the Arch.
Late in life, Martin was hit by a driver while crossing Fourth Street near the Arch grounds, and he never fully recovered. His board, including Hier, took an offer to the Metro East Park and Recreation District: take the land and look after it, on two conditions. Hand it to the National Park Service when the time comes, and name the park for Martin. Martin asked them not to, Hier told St. Louis Public Radio, then laughed and told them to go ahead. He died in 2004. The district took title in 2005, and the overlook opened four years later.
Two more things you won’t read on a plaque. His brother, William McChesney Martin Jr., became the longest-serving chair of the Federal Reserve. And Martin loved trains. The first time he took the young Hier to lunch, he suggested they drive to a rail crossing afterward to watch one particular locomotive come through. His park sits beside working rail lines, and its own directions page warns that the wrong route can leave you stopped by a train.
### How do you get to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park?
Don’t trust your GPS. That’s the park’s advice, not ours. Its directions page says most mapping apps get the route wrong and can leave you stuck at a rail crossing. Set your phone for the Casino Queen first, then the park. The park’s rule of thumb: if you don’t pass the Casino Queen coming and going, you’re on the wrong route.
The address. 185 W. Trendley Ave., East St. Louis, IL 62201, per the local tourism bureau’s listing. The park sits on the riverfront just south of the casino.
Parking. There’s a free lot on site. On big nights like the Fourth of July, the park warns that the lots fill early and bans on-street parking, so carpool or take the train.
MetroLink. Ride to the East Riverfront station, the first stop in Illinois after the train crosses the Eads Bridge, and walk south about three-tenths of a mile on a paved path from the Casino Queen to the park. The park calls it a flat, easy walk of about five minutes.
On foot from downtown. You can walk it. The Eads Bridge, open since 1874, carries a sidewalk across the river, and a ramp off that sidewalk drops down to the East Riverfront station, where the path south to the park begins. Cyclists on local forums say the ramp is awkward with a bike, and some ride the bridge’s traffic lanes instead.
Hours. The park’s hours page says 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., seven days a week, 365 days a year, and the tourism bureau lists the same. Its geyser page still says dawn to dusk; go by the hours page. The park can close for ice and snow, so in bad weather call 618-581-5811 before you drive over. Your car has to be gone by closing time. The posted rules say any vehicle left after hours gets towed at the owner’s expense.
What to leave at home. The posted rules ban alcohol, grills and any open flame, fireworks and sparklers, skateboards and roller skates, and music you can hear more than 50 feet away. Nothing gets staked into the lawn, because irrigation and electric lines run underneath. Park security works on site, and the park district’s site map marks a security and restroom building. Use the park’s route in, come during posted hours, and it’s an easy, quiet visit.
Stayed for the skyline lights? Where to eat in East St. Louis, IL
### Will Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park become part of Gateway Arch National Park?
Maybe, and it’s closer than it has been in decades. On March 10, 2026, U.S. Reps. Nikki Budzinski and Mike Bost of Illinois and Wesley Bell and Ann Wagner of Missouri filed a bipartisan bill to push the boundary of Gateway Arch National Park across the river. It would put Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park and nearby parcels, roughly 50 acres in all, inside the national park. On July 14, Illinois Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth filed a matching bill in the Senate. As of Oct. 6, 2026, we found no report that either one had passed.
The groundwork started in January, when the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, the nonprofit partner of the national park, announced it was studying what an Illinois expansion would take. East St. Louis had already acquired about 50 acres of riverfront north and south of the park, including more than 20 wooded acres directly south that the House bill covers, and it lined up an Illinois EPA grant to evaluate the cleanup. The park district says it’s ready to donate its 25 acres to the Park Service whenever the time comes. The architecture firm PGAV is working with the foundation on what a national park here would look like, including whether visitors would need a way to cross the river.
Don’t plan around a ribbon cutting yet. St. Louis Public Radio reported in May that no timeline or funding plan had been released, and Ryan McClure, the foundation’s executive director, has said the expansion could take years, if not decades. Until then, it’s a free park run by the Metro East Park and Recreation District, with a 40-foot overlook and the view the Arch’s designer always meant to include. Visit now and you’re seeing the before picture.
### What else is close by on the Illinois side?
Make an afternoon of it. Besides Cahokia Mounds, the towns a few miles east have plenty most St. Louisans never cross the river for. Our guide to parks in Collinsville starts with a park built on the city’s old landfill and a heritage farm. In Fairview Heights, our guide to parks in Fairview Heights also tracks down a lost log cabin. If you stay into the evening, Belleville’s Skyview Drive-In is a short drive south and east; its schedule thins out in the fall, so check it first. For the rest of the city around the park, our East St. Louis city guide covers its history, its music and the riverfront.
Watching the boats from this side? Our St. Louis riverboat cruise guide covers the trip they make and what it costs, and the St. Louis riverfront covers the Missouri bank you are looking at.
Next time someone says they’re going over to see the geyser, you’re the one who knows it was switched off so the Arch’s park could cross the river, that the bronze man on the overlook worked at it from 1968 until he died, and that October is one of the few months when you can catch sunrise from the overlook. Go before it turns into a national park. Bring a camera.
Off the overlook and hungry, our guide to where to eat in East St. Louis, IL covers barbecue and fish spots a few minutes from the park.
If you’re the portrait photographer working the overlook, or you run a kitchen or a tour a short drive from it, list it with us so the people who just took their best Arch photo can find you.
From this bank you can see several of the bridges in St. Louis at once, and our guide covers which ones you can walk or bike.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who was Malcolm W. Martin?
A.  A St. Louis lawyer and civic leader who lived from 1912 to 2004. As an Army planner before D-Day, he studied the tides of the English Channel to help pick the best place, time and method for landing ships on the beaches, and he earned a Bronze Star. He helped found KETC Channel 9, served as president of the St. Louis Board of Education, and spent decades working to extend the Arch’s park into Illinois. The park is named for him.
### Q. Can you see the Gateway Arch for free?
A.  Yes. The national park grounds around the Arch are free and open from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., and the museum under the Arch is free with no ticket. Only the tram ride to the top costs money. Across the river, Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park is free too, open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the full face-on view from its overlook.
### Q. What is the best time of day to visit the St. Louis Arch?
A.  For the tram, go early, because the Park Service warns that summer tickets sell out early and often. For the view from Illinois, go late in the day: Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park stays open until 10 p.m., so you can catch sunset behind the skyline and stay for the lights. For sun on the Arch itself, come in the morning, since the light comes from behind you.
### Q. Is the Gateway Arch shut down?
A.  No. The Park Service lists the Arch visitor center and museum as open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, until 8 p.m. on summer Fridays and Saturdays, with the grounds open 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. It closes only on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day. What shut down was the Gateway Geyser across the river, in February 2024. Check the Park Service’s alerts page before you go.
### Q. Can you still go to the top of the Gateway Arch?
A.  Yes. The tram ride to the top runs daily, and the last tram leaves one hour before the visitor center closes. The Park Service lists tickets at $11 to $19, so check current prices, and recommends buying in advance online, since summer dates sell out. Plan on about an hour for the ride, and leave extra time for the airport-style security check at the entrance.
### Q. How long is the St. Louis Riverfront Trail?
A.  Great Rivers Greenway puts its Riverfront Trail, from Chouteau Riverfront to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, at 16.19 miles, counting that bridge and the McKinley Bridge. It’s flat, paved and on the Missouri side. To add the Illinois view, take MetroLink over the Eads Bridge to the East Riverfront station and walk south to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park. Our St. Louis Riverfront Trail guide has the trailheads and parking.
### Q. Do you need a permit to take photos at Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park?
A.  Not for ordinary photos. The park district says recreational shoots like engagement photos, senior pictures, wedding parties and family portraits need no permit. You do need one for commercial work, actors or props, anything that disrupts other visitors, or a drone. That permit carries a $100 nonrefundable fee and proof of liability insurance, and the district wants applications at least 30 days ahead. Call 618-346-4905 first.
### Q. Can you bring a dog to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park?
A.  Yes, on a leash no longer than six feet, under your control the whole time, per the park’s posted rules. Don’t tie the leash to a tree or a railing, which the rules also forbid. Pets aren’t allowed during the park district’s own events, like the Fourth of July fireworks, though service animals are always welcome.

## St. Louis World's Fair: What's Left of the 1904 World's Fair, the $3,500 Birdcage, Food Myths
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/1904-st-louis-worlds-fair
Folding chairs, January 1905. Less than six weeks after the 1904 World’s Fair closed, a snowstorm hit Forest Park, and fair workers grabbed folding chairs and rode them down Art Hill. Forest Park Forever dates the ride to Jan. 8, 1905, and credits it with starting a St. Louis tradition. So every sled run down that hill traces back to the fair. The recycled top-10 lists about the St. Louis World’s Fair never mention it. They send you to the World’s Fair Pavilion for a photo instead, and the pavilion wasn’t built until 1909.
Here’s the real count. The fair put roughly 1,500 buildings on about 1,200 acres, almost all of them made of staff, a plaster and fiber mix that was never meant to last. Two were built to stay. Both still stand, both are free to walk into, and a third group of fair buildings sits on a college campus that most visitors never connect to 1904. The rest of what survives is a basin, a hill, a bronze king and a museum paid for with the fair’s profit. Most of our day-trip pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one keeps you in Forest Park, with a few side trips at the end.
Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against the Saint Louis Art Museum, the Saint Louis Zoo, the Missouri Historical Society, Forest Park Forever, Washington University, the City of St. Louis and the International Olympic Committee.
### Is there anything left in St. Louis from the 1904 World’s Fair?
Yes. Two structures were built to outlast the fair and still stand in Forest Park: the Palace of Fine Arts, now the Saint Louis Art Museum, and the Flight Cage at the Saint Louis Zoo. Brookings Hall and other Washington University buildings served the fair, the Grand Basin survives, and fair profits built the Missouri History Museum.
In the order we’d walk it, here’s what that looks like on the ground:
Saint Louis Art Museum, One Fine Arts Drive. Cass Gilbert’s center block of the 1904 Palace of Fine Arts, minus its temporary wings. Free, closed Mondays.
The 1904 Flight Cage at the Saint Louis Zoo. The Smithsonian built it, the city bought it, and it now holds the zoo’s Cypress Swamp. Admission is free. Parking in the zoo lots isn’t.
Art Hill and the Emerson Grand Basin. The fair’s central view, restored in 2003, with the bronze statue of St. Louis at the top of the hill.
The Missouri History Museum, on the spot where the fair’s main entrance stood. The fair’s profit paid for its original building, and its free 1904 World’s Fair gallery holds a scale model of the entire fairground.
Washington University’s Danforth Campus. Brookings Hall was the fair’s headquarters, and Francis Olympic Field hosted the 1904 Olympics.
Two famous leftovers don’t belong on that list. The World’s Fair Pavilion was built in 1909 with money the fair made, according to the city and Forest Park Forever, so it’s the fair’s receipt, not one of its buildings. And the Ferris wheel isn’t buried anywhere in the park, whatever your uncle says. Both stories are below.
### What was the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair?
Officially, it was the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, thrown for the 100th anniversary of the 1803 purchase. The centennial year was 1903. The fair opened a year late, on April 30, 1904, and closed on Dec. 1. Forest Park Forever puts attendance at more than 20 million, upward of 100,000 people a day, and the 1904 Olympics ran alongside it.
The fair rebuilt the park to suit itself. The city’s preservation plan says it entirely changed Forest Park’s original look, down to draining a swamp on the western side. At the center, the Cascades poured 45,000 gallons of water a minute down Art Hill into the Grand Basin, according to the Missouri Historical Society. They spilled from in front of Festival Hall, a plaster auditorium the society says held the world’s largest pipe organ. Exhibit palaces fanned out around the basin, and the Palace of Agriculture alone covered 23 acres. The Pike, a mile of rides, shows and restaurants, ran along Lindell Boulevard. Near Skinker and Forsyth turned George Ferris’s original wheel, shipped down from Chicago in pieces.
It was also, in the Missouri Historical Society’s words, “grand and shameful.” The fair’s largest exhibit was the Philippine Reservation, 47 acres where more than 1,100 Filipinos lived as living displays, six years after the United States took the islands in the Spanish-American War. The Saint Louis Art Museum says it was designed to present Filipinos as uncivilized and justify colonial rule. Organizers also brought Native American artists to live on the grounds beside a model federal boarding school, as a before-and-after display of forced assimilation. The history museum’s gallery now tells that side of the fair right next to the palaces.
And it made money. The city’s preservation plan says that was contrary to expectation. The profit went to the city, and you can still walk through what it bought. At midnight on Dec. 1, 1904, fair president David R. Francis pressed a button and the lights went out.
### Which 1904 World’s Fair buildings are still standing?
Three groups, and only two of them were meant to last.
The Palace of Fine Arts, now the Saint Louis Art Museum. The fair needed a fireproof building for borrowed art, and the city’s art museum, then downtown, needed a new home. So the two struck a deal: a permanent palace on the park’s highest hill that the museum would take over after the fair, Forest Park Forever says. Cass Gilbert drew a center block of limestone and brick. During the fair it was flanked by sprawling temporary wings, and the whole palace held about 11,000 works of art from 26 countries, according to the museum. The wings came down. Gilbert’s building stayed.
Two details to look for. On the north facade, the side facing Art Hill, the stone band over the columns reads “Dedicated to Art and Free to All,” followed by the year 1903 in Roman numerals. Inside, Sculpture Hall, the grand entrance hall that runs through the middle of Gilbert’s building, was inspired by the Baths of Caracalla in Rome, and its barrel-vaulted ceiling crests at 78 feet. A contract in the museum’s archives puts the palace’s final cost at $945,000.
The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and until 9 p.m. on Fridays. It’s closed Mondays. Admission is free every day, and the main ticketed exhibitions are free on Fridays. Park free in the two lots across Fine Arts Drive, or use the underground garage, which runs $15 from March through October and $10 the rest of the year.
The 1904 Flight Cage at the Saint Louis Zoo. This is the one with the better story. The Smithsonian commissioned a giant walk-through birdcage for the fair and planned to move it to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., afterward. St. Louisans rallied to keep it. The city bought it for $3,500, the zoo says, though it had cost $17,500 to build. Within a few years that cage pushed the city into building a real zoo around it, and the Saint Louis Zoo calls itself the first municipally supported zoo in the world.
The city’s preservation plan lists the cage at 228 feet long and 50 feet high. The zoo has remodeled the inside three times, most recently for the fair’s 2004 centennial, when it became the Cypress Swamp: a floating boardwalk past cypress snags, with roseate spoonbills, snowy egrets and night herons, birds of the swamps along the Mississippi. Find it in the zoo’s Historic Hill area. Admission is free. For Oct. 8 through Dec. 31, 2026, the zoo set its hours at 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, with shorter hours on Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve and a closure on Christmas Day. Outside that window, check the zoo’s hours before you go. Parking in the zoo’s own lots is $20 a car, and limited free street parking is available in the park.
Washington University’s first buildings. Almost nobody connects this set to the fair. In 1901 the fair company leased the university’s brand-new hilltop campus for $650,000, according to the Missouri Historical Society, and the school held off moving in until the fair was over. University Hall, renamed Brookings Hall in 1928, became the fair’s Administration Building, with Francis and the press office inside. Busch Hall housed the fair’s Division of Works. Cupples I held anthropology exhibits. Cupples II was home base for the Jefferson Guard, the fair’s private police force. And Ridgley Library, now Holmes Lounge, served as the Hall of International Congresses, per the university’s library guide.
Those buildings still stand on the Danforth Campus. So does Francis Field, where the 1904 Olympics ran. They were the first Games held in North America and, the International Olympic Committee says, the first to award gold, silver and bronze medals. Football, soccer and track teams still play there, now on what’s called Francis Olympic Field. Our guide to the oldest buildings in St. Louis covers the field’s stands and the Latin inscription on Brookings Hall. You can stroll the main quad on your own; check the university’s visitor information for parking first.
### Where can you see the 1904 World’s Fair in Forest Park today?
Stand at the bottom of Art Hill and you’re in the middle of the old fairground. The Grand Basin and its plaza were the fair’s central view, Forest Park Forever says, with a dozen temporary palaces of plaster and wood on either side. The palaces are gone. The basin isn’t.
The Emerson Grand Basin and Art Hill. The basin was restored in 2003 under the park’s master plan, with eight lit fountains that run year-round. Festival Hall and the Cascades are gone, but the slope they spilled down is Art Hill, and the folding-chair sledders of January 1905 started a habit this city never dropped. Forest Park Forever calls the basin one of the most popular spots in St. Louis for wedding and prom photos. It’s free, open with the park from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
The bronze king on top. The equestrian statue in front of the museum is the Apotheosis of St. Louis, King Louis IX on horseback with his sword held out. During the fair, a plaster version stood near the main entrance, where the history museum is now. The fair company gave the city a bronze version in 1906, and it stands over 40 feet from the ground to the hilt of the sword, pedestal included, according to the city’s landmark listing. For almost 60 years before the Arch went up in 1965, the Missouri Historical Society says, the king was the city’s symbol.
The Missouri History Museum. The museum’s original home, the Jefferson Memorial Building, stands where the fair’s main entrance did, and the fair’s profit paid for it. It was dedicated in 1913 as the first national monument to Thomas Jefferson, the city says. Inside, on the north side, the free 1904 World’s Fair gallery reopened in April 2024 after a full rebuild. Its centerpiece is a 1:400 scale model of the 1,200-acre fairground, surrounded by more than 200 artifacts, from souvenir ruby glass to the desk of the fair’s president, according to museum historian Adam Kloppe. Find the Art Museum on the model. Then walk outside and find it for real.
The gallery’s back room changes every two years. The current one, A Marvel in Motion, opened April 11, 2026, and it’s all about the Ferris wheel, down to a room built the size of one of its cars, which held 60 people. Staff lead a free 25-minute tour of the gallery every Thursday and Sunday afternoon. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., until 8 p.m. on Thursdays, and closed Mondays. Admission is free. The lots beside the building are small, and 400 more free spaces sit in the Twin Lots next to the Dwight Davis Tennis Center.
The World’s Fair Pavilion, with an asterisk. The open-air pavilion on Government Hill gets called a fair building all the time. It isn’t one. Henry Wright designed it in 1909, with landscaping by George Kessler, who designed the fair’s grounds and then supervised putting the park back together afterward, according to the city’s preservation plan. The fair’s profit paid for it, which makes it a leftover of the money rather than the event. The lit fountain and reflecting pool below it were added in 1930, Forest Park Forever says. Walking up is free during park hours. The pavilion itself is reserved by permit for weddings and events.
### What happened to St. Louis World’s Fair buildings?
Most were torn down within months, and that was the plan from the start. The palaces were built of staff, plaster mixed with fiber over wood frames, so they could go up fast and come down fast. Missouri History Museum curator Sharon Smith told the West End Word in 2011 that most of the buildings were quickly torn down and discarded, many in a landfill near the park’s southwest corner, to return Forest Park to its earlier condition. Forest Park Forever says the next seven years went into putting the park back together.
A few pieces got away. The bronze king stayed. The Flight Cage was bought. Alabama’s 56-foot cast-iron Vulcan, an iron-industry showpiece, went home in pieces by train and still stands there today, according to Atlas Obscura. Other bits scattered around the region, and we track them down in the last section.
The Ferris wheel, and the story that won’t die. George Ferris built his wheel for Chicago’s 1893 fair. It was rebuilt at a Chicago amusement park, then shipped to St. Louis for 1904. After the fair it sat idle. Missouri Historical Society public historian Amanda Clark told Nine PBS this year that the city shopped it to amusement parks, including the Highlands right next to Forest Park, and the cost of moving it killed every deal. So it was scrapped. Ferris Wheel Heritage, citing a Chicago Tribune dispatch, dates the dynamiting to May 11, 1906.
Then the legend took over. Ask anyone raised here and you’ll hear that the wheel, or at least its giant axle, is buried somewhere: under Wydown, under Skinker at Lagoon, under Art Hill. Clark says it isn’t. A reporter covering the demolition wrote that the axle fell, was loaded onto a cart and went to Chicago, and men who worked for the wrecking company later reported seeing it there for years. Not everyone has let go. A 2007 magnetometer survey found a large magnetic anomaly under Skinker Boulevard, consistent with a buried steel cylinder, and nobody has ever dug it up, Ferris Wheel Heritage notes. The Missouri Historical Society’s money is on Chicago.
Done walking the old fairgrounds? Where to eat in University City, MO
### What foods were introduced at the 1904 World’s Fair?
Fewer than the legend claims. The usual list credits the fair with the ice cream cone, iced tea, the hot dog and the hamburger, and the record doesn’t back most of it. Even the Missouri History Museum’s own gallery takes the food myths apart, KSDK reported when it opened. Here’s what holds up.
Iced tea: popularized, maybe. Invented, no. The story goes that Richard Blechynden, a tea commissioner at the India pavilion, poured his hot tea over ice when nobody wanted it on a sweltering day. Food historian Robert Moss found a syndicated newspaper item recommending iced tea with lemon in 1868, more than 30 years earlier, and iced tea turns up in plenty of 19th-century cookbooks.
The ice cream cone: the closest call. The famous version has Ernest Hamwi, a Syrian-born waffle vendor, rolling a waffle into a cone when the ice cream stand next door ran out of dishes. Other vendors claimed it too. The Library of Congress hedges, saying only that by some accounts Charles E. Menches came up with the ice cream cone on July 23, 1904. Washington University put it plainly for the fair’s centennial: cones, iced tea and hot dogs likely existed before the fair, but many visitors saw them for the first time in St. Louis.
The hamburger: older than the fair. “Hamburg steak” was in print before the Civil War, and hamburger sandwiches show up by the 1880s, Moss writes. In 1904, a Kansas City paper was already warning its readers about doctored hamburger meat.
The hot dog: same story. The tale of a sausage vendor whose customers kept walking off with his serving gloves, so he switched to buns, is a good one. Sausages in buns were around before 1904 anyway.
Cotton candy: the real debut. A Tennessee dentist, William Morrison, and confectioner John C. Wharton brought their spinning machine to the fair and sold “fairy floss” for 25 cents a box, half the price of admission, Smithsonian magazine reports. They sold more than 65,000 boxes. Britannica calls 1904 the machine’s first introduction to the public.
Puffed rice, fired from cannons. In the Palace of Agriculture, the Quaker Oats exhibit loaded rice into giant cannons every 50 minutes and blew it out puffed to eight times its size, Moss writes. The process had been invented the year before.
So the fair didn’t invent the American snack. It put a lot of snacks in front of 20 million people at once, which goes a long way toward explaining why St. Louis still gets the credit.
### Where else around St. Louis can you find pieces of the 1904 World’s Fair?
The fair pulled in the whole region, and bits of it are still out there, in towns the fair lists never reach because they never leave Forest Park.
University City. An 80-inch carbon-arc searchlight sits folded inside the dome of University City Hall, 6801 Delmar Blvd. Publisher E.G. Lewis lit it on April 30, 1904, the fair’s opening night, to steer fairgoers toward his tent city and his magazine. The octagonal tower was his Woman’s Magazine headquarters long before it became City Hall. It’s a short drive north of Brookings Hall, and our page on what to do at Heman Park in University City tells the rest of the searchlight’s story.
Creve Coeur Lake. The 1904 Olympic rowing races ran on this lake on July 29 and 30. After the fair, a 255-foot observation tower was moved here from the fairgrounds. The tower is long gone. The water isn’t, and our page on fishing at Creve Coeur Lake covers what you can do on it now.
Glen Carbon, Illinois. SIUE’s Madison Historical encyclopedia says the St. Louis Press Brick Company in Glen Carbon supplied brick for the Palace of Fine Arts, the building that became the Art Museum. A fire in 1906 destroyed most of the brickyard, and nobody rebuilt it. Some of its old rail beds are trails now. Start with things to do at Miner Park in Glen Carbon.
Grafton, Illinois. The Ruebel Hotel’s hand-carved burled walnut bar was shown at the 1904 fair, and the regional tourism bureau says residents have carried it to safety through more than one flood. It’s the best excuse we know for the river drive. Our list of things to do in Grafton in winter covers the rest of the trip.
Kimmswick. At the Anheuser family’s estate on Water’s Point, above the Mississippi at the south end of town, the house tour includes a pair of hand-carved beds from the 1904 World’s Fair. Tour days are limited, so check before you drive down. Our guide to things to do in Kimmswick has the details.
Imperial. Charles W. Beehler, a St. Louis mechanic and fossil hunter, put up a wooden museum on the mastodon bone bed at Rock Creek and timed it for the fair crowds. Missouri State Parks says railroad tours brought visitors down from the city to see it. The shack is gone and the bones are famous, and our page on the story of the Kimmswick Bone Bed explains why.
If this is your kind of outing, our list of underrated places to visit in St. Louis keeps going in the same spirit.
Next time somebody says nothing’s left of the fair, you’re the one who knows the birdcage cost the city $3,500, the pavilion showed up five years late, the axle went to Chicago and the sledding started with folding chairs. Pick a Thursday. Catch the 1904 gallery tour, cross the park to the Flight Cage, and finish on Art Hill.
When the walk is done, our guide to where to eat in University City, MO covers the Delmar Loop, a short drive north of the old fairgrounds.
If you run a café, a bookshop or a walking tour within a mile of Forest Park, list it with us so the people coming down Art Hill find you before they head home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What happened to St. Louis World’s Fair?
A.  It closed on Dec. 1, 1904, after seven months and more than 20 million visits. At midnight, fair president David R. Francis pressed a button that shut off the lights. Over the following months nearly all of the plaster buildings came down, and Forest Park Forever says it took about seven years to put the park back together. The fair turned a profit, and that money built the Jefferson Memorial Building and the World’s Fair Pavilion.
### Q. How long did the 1904 World’s Fair last?
A.  About seven months, from April 30 to Dec. 1, 1904. It was meant to open in 1903 for the centennial of the Louisiana Purchase but ran a year behind.
