The Olympics stretched across most of that run: the International Olympic Committee dates the 1904 Games from July 1 to Nov. 24, spread over four and a half months.
### Q. What popular drink was introduced at the St. Louis World’s Fair in 1904?
A.  Iced tea usually gets the credit, through the story of tea commissioner Richard Blechynden pouring his unsold hot tea over ice. The fair may have helped make it popular, but it wasn’t new: newspaper tips for iced tea with lemon were circulating by 1868. Washington University’s centennial account lists iced tea among the things visitors met for the first time in St. Louis, not things invented there.
### Q. What exhibits were on display at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair?
A.  Nearly everything. Exhibit palaces covered agriculture, electricity, machinery, transportation, mining, education and fine arts, and the Art Museum counts about 11,000 works of art from 26 countries in its palace alone. The Pike offered a mile of rides and shows. The fair also put people on display, most notoriously on the 47-acre Philippine Reservation, which the Missouri History Museum’s gallery now addresses head-on.
### Q. What were some of the inventions introduced at the 1904 World’s Fair?
A.  Mostly inventions shown to the public there, not invented on the spot. Washington University’s centennial list includes the X-ray machine, the telautograph, an early ancestor of the fax machine, wireless telegraph messages sent from a tower on the grounds, electric kitchen appliances and infant incubators, which held premature babies on the Pike while visitors paid to watch the nurses work. Thomas Edison came in to oversee the electrical exhibits.
### Q. What were some interesting facts about the 1904 World’s Fair?
A.  Three favorites. Art Hill sledding started with fair workers riding folding chairs down the hill after a snowstorm on Jan. 8, 1905. The city bought the Smithsonian’s birdcage for $3,500, and it grew into the Saint Louis Zoo. And the Ferris wheel cars were big enough to rent for parties and even weddings, a Missouri History Museum curator once said, with a full ride taking about an hour.
### Q. What unusual event happened at the 1904 Olympics?
A.  The marathon. Fred Lorz crossed the finish line first after riding about 11 miles in a car, and he was disqualified. The winner, Thomas Hicks, was given doses of strychnine mixed with egg whites by his handlers during the race, plus brandy, and his trainers carried him over the line, according to Smithsonian magazine. Cuban runner Félix Carvajal ate some rotten apples along the way and stopped to take a nap.
### Q. What was the controversy surrounding the 1904 Olympics?
A.  Two big ones. The Games got swallowed by the fair, spread over four and a half months, and the International Olympic Committee itself says they repeated the mistakes of 1900. Worse were the fair’s Anthropology Days, when people recruited from its villages of Indigenous and colonized peoples were entered in athletic contests staged for the amusement of white spectators, Smithsonian magazine reports.

## Old Courthouse St. Louis: Free Ranger Tours, Where the Scotts Won, and the Courtroom That Vanished
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/old-courthouse-st-louis
They won here. The quick version on most travel lists files the Old Courthouse as the place where the Dred Scott case “was heard.” Snap the dome, move on. It leaves out the part that should stop you on the steps. On Jan. 12, 1850, in a first-floor courtroom in the west wing, a St. Louis jury decided that Dred Scott and his family should be free. Two years later the Missouri Supreme Court took that away, and in 1857 the U.S. Supreme Court made the loss famous. The win happened in this building, and almost nobody tells you.
You can’t stand in that courtroom, either. It’s gone. A construction flaw threatened its ceiling, so in 1855, while the Scotts’ case was still in the courts, a new east-west hallway was cut through the room, leaving two smaller courtrooms that could hold up the floor above, according to the National Park Service. The building kept the story. It lost the room.
Most of our day-trip pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one stays downtown, at Fourth and Market, in a building you can still walk into for free. Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against the National Park Service, the Missouri State Archives, the Missouri Historical Society and St. Louis Public Radio.
### What is the significance of the Old Courthouse in St. Louis?
The Old Courthouse is where Dred and Harriet Scott sued for their freedom in 1846, and where a jury declared them free in 1850. Higher courts took that away, ending in the 1857 Supreme Court ruling that pushed the country toward civil war. Hundreds more freedom suits were filed here, and Virginia Minor’s fight for women’s votes began here.
The freedom suits. The Scotts were far from alone. Hundreds of enslaved people sued for their freedom in the Old Courthouse, which is why the Park Service lists it in its National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom as a place tied to legal challenges to slavery.
The city. Virginia Minor’s 1873 suit for women’s right to vote was argued here too, and like the Scotts’ case it reached the U.S. Supreme Court. The Missouri Historical Society counts four precedent-setting Supreme Court civil rights cases that began in St. Louis, possibly the most to reach the high court from any one place. When the courthouse opened in 1845, it was one of the largest public spaces in town, and emigrants heading west on the Oregon and California trails met in its rotunda. At 192 feet to the top of the dome, it was Missouri’s tallest habitable building from 1864 to 1894. The city gave it to the federal government in 1940, and today it belongs to Gateway Arch National Park.
### Can you tour the Old Courthouse in St. Louis?
Yes, and it costs nothing. The National Park Service’s Old Courthouse page, last updated July 27, 2026, says the building is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and closed only on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day, with no admission fee and no tickets. Check that page before you go.
The 2:15 ranger tour. Rangers lead a free guided tour every day at 2:15 p.m. It covers the architecture, the building’s history and the court cases tied to it, and it usually runs 20 to 40 minutes, depending on the ranger and how many questions people ask. No reservations. The Park Service says a tour can be canceled now and then when staff aren’t available, and it asks groups of more than 10 to call ahead at 314-655-1731 or 314-655-1636. A school or club that wants a formal ranger program has to book at least 30 days out through the park’s group sales specialist at 314-923-3048.
On your own. Most visitors need about an hour, the Park Service says. The building reopened on May 3, 2025, after a $24.5 million renovation that ran from 2020 to 2025 and added an elevator, new heating and cooling, a new fire suppression system and four new galleries:
See You in Court sits in a recreated 1850s courtroom, and visitors can take part in mock trials there.
Designed for Justice is about the architects, artists and craftsmen, with hands-on pieces that kids tend to love.
Pathways to Freedom traces Black life in St. Louis from slavery onward, including the wealthy Black families of the 1800s known as the Colored Aristocracy.
Dred and Harriet Scott tells the family’s story. The park’s superintendent, Jeremy Sweat, told St. Louis Public Radio the old exhibit centered on the court case, and this one centers on the Scotts as people.
Upstairs, two historic courtrooms are restored and open to wander. Kids can work through the Junior Ranger challenges for a badge.
Getting in and parking. The address is 11 N. Fourth St. You can enter through the east or west wing, and both entrances have ramps. The park doesn’t run its own parking. Its preferred garage is Stadium East, at $10 for five hours if you prepay through the park’s parking program. Skip the prepay on a ballgame or big event day and you’ll pay event rates. It’s also one of the better free rainy-day stops downtown, and our list of indoor things to do in St. Louis has more for when the weather turns.
### When was the Old Courthouse in St. Louis built?
Construction began in 1839 and wrapped up in 1862, 23 years in all. The cornerstone went down on Oct. 21, 1839, with newspapers from several cities, a handful of coins and the names of government officers sealed inside. The doors opened to the public in February 1845, long before the building was done. That unfinished courthouse is the one the Scotts walked into on April 6, 1846, to file their petitions.
The land came with a string attached. In 1816, Auguste Chouteau, one of the city’s founders, and Judge John B.C. Lucas donated the block to St. Louis County on the condition that it be “used forever” as the site of the county courthouse. Before that, official business bounced between a church, a tavern and a fort. The first courthouse on the block was a plain brick building in the Federal style, and the county outgrew it ten years after it opened. Architect Henry Singleton’s cross-shaped design, chosen in an 1838 competition, wrapped a new building around it, with the old courthouse serving as the east wing until it was torn down and replaced starting in 1851.
The dome almost didn’t happen. The first dome was a smaller classical one. In the rebuilding that began in the 1850s, architect William Rumbold designed a far bigger one in wrought and cast iron with a copper skin, modeled on St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome. At the same moment, the federal government was raising a dome modeled on the same church over the U.S. Capitol. Critics in St. Louis were sure Rumbold’s would be too heavy for the building to carry. He built a test model to prove it would stand. He also patented the lightweight iron skeleton he used, and the Park Service calls his dome one of the first of its type, a design that later showed up on the Capitol and other statehouses. It was finished in 1862 and rises 192 feet.
The paintings under it. Carl Wimar painted the oval murals inside the dome, called lunettes, in 1862, showing four turning points in St. Louis history. He was very sick with tuberculosis while he worked and died soon after he finished. Italian artist Ettore Miragoli painted the other murals in 1880. All of it cost about $1.2 million, which the Park Service puts at around $44 million in today’s money.
### What was the most famous court case in St. Louis?
Dred Scott v. Sandford, and it began in this building. Dred and Harriet Scott sued for their freedom here in 1846. Eleven years later, on March 6, 1857, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans, enslaved or free, were not citizens and had no right to sue in federal court, and that the Missouri Compromise’s ban on slavery in the territories was void. The Park Service says the ruling hastened the Civil War.
Who they were. Dred Scott was born into slavery in Virginia around 1800, by the Park Service’s estimate, and came to St. Louis in 1830 with the Blow family, who soon sold him. His buyer, Dr. John Emerson, an Army surgeon at Jefferson Barracks, took him to posts in Illinois and at Fort Snelling, in what is now Minnesota, where slavery was barred. Harriet Robinson, also enslaved, married Dred at Fort Snelling. Their first daughter, Eliza, was born on a steamboat on the Mississippi, and a second, Lizzie, came later. After Emerson died in 1843, his widow, Irene, hired the family out to other households and kept most of their wages. Harriet probably did laundry, cleaned houses and cared for children.
Why they had a case. Missouri courts had long followed a rule known as “once free, always free.” If an enslaver kept a person for a long stretch on free soil, that person could claim freedom back in Missouri. The Scotts had lived on free soil for years. On April 6, 1846, they filed separate petitions, one for Dred and one for Harriet. Under the law of the day, the Park Service notes, the court wasn’t deciding whether people have a right to be free. It was deciding a property question.
The trials here. The first trial, on June 30, 1847, went against them on a technicality. The one witness who could show that Irene Emerson held them in slavery was ruled to be offering hearsay. Judge Alexander Hamilton granted a new trial. Then a citywide fire in May 1849 and a cholera outbreak that summer pushed the retrial to Jan. 12, 1850. With new testimony and Hamilton presiding again, the jury found for the Scotts. They were free.
How it was taken back. Irene Emerson appealed. In 1852 the Missouri Supreme Court reversed the verdict and broke with its own past decisions, declaring that “times now are not as they were” when the earlier cases were decided. In 1854 the Scotts tried federal court, suing Irene Emerson’s brother, John F.A. Sanford. That trial wasn’t held here. It was heard a few blocks away in the Papin Building, and the family lost again. The appeal went to Washington as Dred Scott v. Sandford.
The ending most lists leave out. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney wrote that the framers of the Constitution had believed Black people had “no rights which the white man was bound to respect.” Less than three months later, on May 26, 1857, Dred and Harriet Scott went back before the St. Louis Circuit Court and were freed. By then Irene Emerson had married Calvin Chaffee, an abolitionist who had won a seat in Congress. Ownership of the family passed to Taylor Blow, from the family that had first brought Dred to St. Louis, because Missouri law let only a citizen of the state free someone there. The judge who approved the papers was Alexander Hamilton, the same judge who had first heard their case.
Freedom came late. Dred Scott took a job as a porter at Barnum’s Hotel at Second and Walnut streets, where he became something of a celebrity, and he died of tuberculosis on Sept. 17, 1858. Harriet lived free in St. Louis for 19 more years, working as a laundress, until her death on June 17, 1876.
The other case that went to Washington. On Oct. 15, 1872, Virginia Minor, who had launched the woman suffrage movement in Missouri, tried to register to vote and was refused by registrar Reese Happersett because she was a woman. Married women couldn’t sue on their own in Missouri until 1889, so her husband, lawyer Francis Minor, brought the suit with her. There was no jury and no trial. Both sides argued on paper at a hearing on Feb. 3, 1873, in Circuit Court No. 5, which is now the park’s library, Room 212. The Missouri Supreme Court heard her appeal in its chambers in the courthouse’s south wing. In 1875 a unanimous U.S. Supreme Court ruled against her, holding that the Constitution “does not confer the right of suffrage upon anyone.”
Out of the rotunda and hungry? Where to eat in downtown St. Louis
### Were enslaved people sold at the Old Courthouse?
Yes, sometimes. The Park Service says enslaved people were sold from the steps of the east wing to settle estates and property suits, though it was not a regular business there. The same building heard hundreds of freedom suits. People were sold on its steps and sued for their freedom in its courtrooms, and you can’t understand the place without holding both.
How a freedom suit worked. A Missouri law from 1824, built on an 1807 territorial statute, let anyone held in bondage petition the local court for permission to sue. The petition needed a legal basis, and most fell into three kinds. The person had been taken to live where slavery was illegal. Or they’d been freed by a will or a purchase and were being held anyway. Or they could show their mother had not been legally enslaved. The burden of proof sat on the person suing: papers, witnesses, all of it.
The odds got worse. More than 300 enslaved people in St. Louis sued for their freedom between 1812 and 1865, the Park Service says, and fewer than half won. By the time the Scotts filed, the courts had turned colder. The Missouri State Archives counts 25 freedom suits filed in the St. Louis Circuit Court from 1844 to 1846, and only one ended in freedom. Lucy Delaney was 17 when she sued for her freedom at the Old Courthouse in 1844. Every one of those suits has been scanned and can be searched through the St. Louis Circuit Court Historical Records Project.
Free, but licensed. Winning didn’t end it. Under an 1835 Missouri law, a free Black person had to carry a license proving it at all times or risk jail. Free Black Missourians weren’t considered citizens, and after 1847 their children couldn’t attend school. Original freedom bonds tied to many of those licenses are preserved today at the Missouri Historical Society.
### When did St. Louis stop using the Old Courthouse?
In 1930. That year the courts moved a few blocks west into a new building, and the Old Courthouse’s run as a working courthouse ended after about 85 years. A bond for the new courthouse passed in 1923 and ground was broken in 1926. Since everyone knew the old building was on its way out, maintenance stopped and it began to decay.
The odd decade. For ten years after that, the building held an art school, a workshop where a religious group fixed up toys for children in need, and offices for two justices of the peace and their constables.
The heirs who wanted it back. Remember the 1816 condition, “used forever” as the courthouse site? Descendants of the Chouteau and Lucas families did. Once the courts left, they sued in the Missouri Supreme Court, arguing that the property should revert to them. They lost. In 1940 the City of St. Louis gave the building to the federal government, and it became part of Jefferson National Expansion Memorial, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt had designated in 1935. The Park Service put on a new roof in 1941. The memorial was renamed Gateway Arch National Park in 2018.
The long closure. The building closed in 2020, first for the pandemic and then for the renovation, the final piece of the $380 million CityArchRiver project around the riverfront park. It reopened on May 3, 2025, with a ribbon cutting and a Journey to Justice festival in nearby Kiener Plaza, where Lynne Jackson, the Scotts’ great-great-granddaughter, was among the speakers. If an old listing or forum post tells you the courthouse is closed for renovation, it’s out of date.
### What should you look for at the Old Courthouse?
The floor under your feet. The rotunda floor is original polished limestone, every slab at least 3.5 inches thick. Stand in the middle and look up through three tiers of balconies. Stone pillars hold up the first. The two above it rest on white oak columns.
The two old courtrooms. Both are on the second floor. Circuit Courtroom No. 4 in the west wing is the older of the pair, set to look the way it did in the mid-1800s. No. 13, in the east wing, is restored to about 1910. Neither is the room where the Scotts won, since that one no longer exists, but No. 4 sits in the same wing, one floor up.
The turtles on the fence. Look closely at the iron fence around the lawn. The wrought iron turtles worked into it are a nod to James Quigley, a 19th-century caretaker who put turtles in the courthouse fountain every summer. The fence and the three-tiered green fountain are both reconstructions. The bronze sundial in the southeast courtyard is the only original landscape feature still standing.
The statue. The life-size bronze of Dred and Harriet Scott on the south lawn was dedicated on June 8, 2012, by the Dred Scott Heritage Foundation, the Park Service and St. Louis sculptor Harry Weber. The Regional Arts Commission says it was the first statue of the couple anywhere in the world.
The small stuff outside. A plaque on the east sidewalk, placed in 1947, marks where Joseph Pulitzer bought the St. Louis Dispatch in 1878. The Corinthian and Ionic capitals in the northeast and northwest courtyards were salvaged from a building torn down to make way for the national park.
The view from Illinois. The courthouse and the park were laid out on a single east-west line. Cross the river to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park and you’ll find the Old Courthouse framed between the Arch’s legs, the shot photographers cross the river for.
### Where else in St. Louis can you follow Dred and Harriet Scott?
The Freedom Suits Memorial. On the east plaza of the Civil Courts Building, at Market and Tucker about eight blocks west, Chicago sculptor Preston Jackson’s memorial was unveiled on June 20, 2022, for the hundreds of people who went to court in St. Louis to sue for their freedom. Pair it with the courthouse and you’ve seen both ends of the story in one morning.
Calvary Cemetery. Dred Scott was buried in St. Louis in 1858. His grave was moved to Calvary Cemetery in north St. Louis in the 1860s, and it got a marker in 1957, a century after the decision, thanks to the Rev. Edward Dowling.
Greenwood Cemetery. Harriet Scott is buried at Greenwood, one of the first Black burial grounds in the St. Louis area. Our guide to historic sites in St. Louis has the addresses for both cemeteries and the rest of the region’s Underground Railroad stops.
Next time somebody calls it the place where Dred Scott lost, you’re the one who knows the Scotts won here first, that their courtroom was cut in two before the case was over, and that the judge who heard them in 1847 approved their freedom ten years later. Get there by 2. Catch the 2:15 tour. Then walk west to the memorial. Our list of underrated places to visit in St. Louis has more afternoons like this one.
Done with the galleries and ready to eat? Our guide to where to eat in downtown St. Louis groups 41 spots by walkable pocket, and one of them sits on Fourth Street a block south of the courthouse.
If you run a kitchen, a coffee bar or a walking tour within a few blocks of Fourth and Market, list it with us so the people coming out of the 2:15 ranger tour find you before they head back to the garage.
Up Market Street, St. Louis City Hall hides its own surprise: for about 40 years St. Louisans thought it was built of black stone.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is the Old Courthouse in St. Louis free?
A.  Yes. There’s no entrance fee and no ticket, and the daily 2:15 ranger tour is free too. Your only cost is parking, about $10 for five hours at the park’s preferred garage if you prepay. The Old Courthouse Shop even sells the annual national parks pass.
### Q. Can you go inside the Old Courthouse in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. It reopened on May 3, 2025, after a renovation that kept it closed from 2020, and it’s open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. except Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day. Inside are four galleries, two restored courtrooms and the rotunda, with a new elevator.
### Q. What is the Old Courthouse in St. Louis?
A.  It’s the city’s former courthouse at 11 N. Fourth St., built from 1839 to 1862 and used by the courts until 1930. Today it’s a free museum run by the National Park Service as part of Gateway Arch National Park, best known as the place where Dred and Harriet Scott sued for their freedom.
### Q. Was Dred Scott ever freed?
A.  Yes. On May 26, 1857, less than three months after the Supreme Court ruled against him, Dred Scott, Harriet and their daughters were freed in the St. Louis Circuit Court, with Taylor Blow signing the papers and Judge Alexander Hamilton approving them. Dred died of tuberculosis on Sept. 17, 1858. Harriet lived free until 1876.
### Q. Are there any descendants of Dred Scott?
A.  Yes. Lynne M. Jackson, the great-great-granddaughter of Dred and Harriet Scott, founded the Dred Scott Heritage Foundation, which helped dedicate the couple’s statue at the Old Courthouse in 2012. She spoke at the courthouse’s reopening in May 2025 and told St. Louis Public Radio that a permanent gallery for the Scotts was a huge honor.
### Q. What did Dred Scott v. Sandford do to the Missouri Compromise?
A.  It declared it void. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney ruled that Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories, so the 1820 Missouri Compromise’s ban was unconstitutional, and Dred Scott’s years at Fort Snelling had never made him free. The ruling deepened the national split over slavery in the years before the Civil War.
### Q. What is the oldest building in St. Louis?
A.  Not the Old Courthouse, which wasn’t started until 1839. Inside the city limits, the building usually named is the Old Cathedral, the Basilica of St. Louis, King of France, built from 1831 to 1834 a short walk southeast of the courthouse. Our roundup of the oldest buildings in St. Louis covers older survivors in Florissant and St. Louis County too.
### Q. Is the Old Courthouse the same as the Civil Courts Building?
A.  No. The Civil Courts Building, at 10 N. Tucker Blvd., is the courthouse that replaced it in 1930, the tall one with the stepped pyramid top modeled on the ancient Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. It’s still a working courthouse for the 22nd Judicial Circuit, and in December 2024 the city renamed it the Clyde S. Cahill Courts Building, after one of St. Louis’s first Black judges.

## St. Louis City Hall: The Pink Granite Everyone Thought Was Black, the Lost Tower, Tours
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-city-hall
Black stone. That’s what St. Louis thought its City Hall was made of. For decades the building at Market and Tucker wore so much coal soot that people took the soot for the stone. Then, in 1934, crews sandblasted the walls, and the city finally saw what it had paid for: pink Missouri granite along the bottom, orange-toned brick above it, buff sandstone around the windows. The city’s own 1990 history of the building put it plainly: “Many people were shocked to see the true colors, believing it was made of black stone.”
The pink came up from Graniteville, in Iron County, where a 1904 state survey said the granite had “the deepest red color of any in the State.” And the boulevard City Hall faces is named for Raymond Tucker, who became the city’s first smoke commissioner in 1937, three years after the sandblasting, hired to fight the same coal smoke that had turned the building black.
Search for St. Louis City Hall, as we did this month, and Google hands you ordinances, protest and encampment news, and a MapQuest page for a different city hall. Almost nobody writes about the building. Most of our pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one stays downtown, at a building plenty of St. Louisans have only ever seen through a windshield.
Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against the City of St. Louis’s own pages and its 1990 history brochure, the federal Historic American Buildings Survey file on the building, and small-town newspapers printed while the granite was being cut.
### Is St. Louis City Hall still in use?
Yes. St. Louis City Hall, at 1200 Market St., has housed city government since April 1898, when officials moved in before it was even finished. The mayor, the Board of Aldermen, the Recorder of Deeds and the Collector of Revenue all work there, and it’s open to the public Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
It has never been anything else. The city has worked out of it continuously since moving in, and some room numbers haven’t changed in decades. The mayor’s office is Room 200 and the Board of Aldermen is in Room 230, the same numbers the city’s 1990 brochure gives. The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 128 and the Collector of Revenue is in Room 110, according to the city’s department pages.
What changed is who uses which room. City Hall was designed for a two-house city government, a House of Delegates and a City Council, set up a lot like the Missouri Legislature. The 1914 city charter got rid of the Council and turned the House of Delegates into the Board of Aldermen. The aldermen took over the old House of Delegates chamber, and they still meet there. The Council’s old room became the Board of Public Service chamber, under a half-dome ceiling about 30 feet high.
Getting in is simple. The public doors are on Tucker Boulevard and Clark Avenue, and the accessible entrance is at the tunnel on the west side, near Market.
### What is St. Louis City Hall made of, and why did it look black?
Start at the bottom. The first story is what the city’s brochure calls “Missouri pink granite.” Above it runs pink-orange Roman brick, with buff sandstone trim in an irregular pattern around the windows, and the roof is burgundy-red clay tile. Some newer city documents call the brick yellow. Stand on Tucker and decide for yourself.
Coal smoke did the rest. The brochure describes the walls as “coal-blackened” before they were sandblasted in 1934, and again in 1960. The 1960 job also added anti-pigeon strips along the roof and windows, which came off in 1968. Even now the building looks duller than it should. The city’s history page blames “a poorly executed acid cleaning” on top of years of coal smoke. In 2003 a group led by architects went looking for $2 million in private money to clean the outside and fix the roof, according to an Associated Press report carried by St. Louis Public Radio. We couldn’t find a record that the cleaning ever happened.
Where the pink came from. The federal survey file lists the Schneider Granite Co. as the contractor for the granite of the first story. Its quarries sat at Graniteville, about five miles northwest of Ironton, the Iron County seat, roughly 70 miles south of downtown as the crow flies. The newspaper in Ironton followed the job like a hometown team. In May 1891 it reported that Schneider had won the contract. In September 1892 it said the company’s superintendent had been sent to St. Louis to run the granite work on the new city hall, and in April 1893 it reported that Schneider had just about finished all the stone. A September 1893 story put it simply: the granite came from Iron County.
St. Louis already knew that rock. The same 1904 state survey says Phillip Schneider supplied the first granite paving blocks used in St. Louis, about 1877, and that the quarries around Graniteville went on to produce millions of them for the city’s streets.
One honest gap: a second firm, the St. Louis Granite Co., cut the granite for the basement story, and no record we found says where that stone came from.
Raymond Tucker closes the loop. An engineering professor who went to work as Mayor Dickmann’s secretary, he became the first smoke commissioner in 1937 and later served as mayor himself. Twelfth Street, the street City Hall faces, now carries his name.
### When was St. Louis City Hall built, and why did it take 14 years?
Ground was broken on July 19, 1890, when Mayor Edward Noonan’s daughter Zoe dug the first shovelful. The cornerstone went down on June 6, 1891. Officials moved in on April 11, 1898, with the building still unfinished, as Mayor Henry Ziegenhein led a parade of city officials over from the old building. The rotunda, the Tucker Boulevard vestibule and the grand staircase came last. The city counts the building as officially complete on Nov. 5, 1904, when Mayor Rolla Wells held an open house.
Why so long? Nobody borrowed for it. No bond issue was ever passed. The money came out of general revenue and the sale of city property, and every year or two the city authorized another $110,000 or so to keep the crews working. The city’s own history page says that pay-as-you-go plan explains the 14 years.
The Ironton paper, whose readers were cutting the granite, tracked the stalls. In February 1893 it reported a local worker home because rough weather had shut the job down. That spring another small Missouri paper predicted the building would be finished and turned over to the city that fall. By June 1893 the Ironton paper was reporting that work would stop on July 1 for lack of money, and in October it said there wasn’t enough money in sight to finish and the city council didn’t know how to raise it. The fall finish slipped by five years.
The city wanted it badly, because it had been making do for decades. Its 1827 combination city hall and market on the riverfront survived the 1849 fire and was torn down the next year. A replacement burned in 1856, and the city ended up renting a wing of the Old Courthouse in St. Louis for about $1,000 a year. In 1872 it put up a “temporary” three-story building on the block at 11th and Market that everyone called the Barn. It cost $70,000, and the brochure says it was so shoddily built that newspaper accounts said the floors creaked. City government stayed in the Barn until 1898.
The finish line had a deadline. The federal survey file says the rotunda, vestibule and staircase were completed for the 1904 World’s Fair, and the open house came on Nov. 5, less than four weeks before the fair closed. Our guide to the St. Louis World’s Fair covers what else from that year is still standing.
### Who designed St. Louis City Hall, and why does it look like Paris?
George Richard Mann, of the firm Eckel & Mann in St. Joseph, Missouri, won the national design competition. He titled his entry “St. Louis 1892,” the year he expected it to be done. It took until 1904. Mann, who trained at MIT, went on to design the Arkansas State Capitol and spent his last three decades in Little Rock.
The city’s own records can’t agree on how many designs he beat. The 1990 brochure says six leading architects from around the country submitted plans. The city’s current history page says there were 37 national entries. Neither says where its number came from.
Two other names belong next to Mann’s. Harvey Ellis, a draftsman in his office, is believed to have contributed a great deal to the design, the federal survey file says, though there’s no official record of it. And Albert B. Groves of the St. Louis firm Weber & Groves designed the 1904 finish: the rotunda, the Tucker vestibule and the grand staircase.
The Paris connection is real. The city describes the plan as French-style, “inspired by the Hotel de Ville or City Hall of Paris,” and says the ornamental dormer windows recall the Château de Chambord on the Loire. The federal survey calls the French Renaissance Revival style comparatively rare for American public buildings and reads it as a gesture to the city’s French heritage. You can see it from the sidewalk: corner pavilions, a grand central entry pavilion on Tucker, tall dormers and a red tile roof. The brochure says the exterior has been compared to a “sumptuous French chateau.”
The decorations nobody carved. Every side of the building has ornamental dormers called belvederes, and each one has bare limestone panels that were meant to be carved. They never were, the city says, probably for lack of money. A pay-as-you-go building ran out of pay.
### How much did St. Louis City Hall cost to build?
$1,787,159.16, to the penny, according to the city. The 1889 ordinance capped the cost at $1 million. A September 1893 ordinance raised the cap to $2 million, and the finished building came in $212,840.84 under it.
In 2026 money, that’s roughly $66 million to $72 million. Treat that as an estimate, and here’s how we got it. We used the Minneapolis Fed’s historical consumer price table, which links modern CPI to economist Albert Rees’s cost-of-living index for the years before 1913. On that table, prices in 1904 sit at 27 and the Fed’s 2026 estimate sits at 1004.8, a factor of about 37. Count the whole bill as 1904 dollars and you get about $66.5 million. The money was actually spent from 1890 to 1904, when the index ran between 25 and 27, and counting it all as 1898 to 1900 dollars pushes the total to about $72 million. A cross-check against the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI lands on the same $66.5 million.
Two warnings come with that number. Consumer prices are only one yardstick, and measured against wages or the size of the economy, a public project from the 1890s looks far bigger. Prices from before 1913 are also reconstructions, not the government CPI. By the same method, the $212,840.84 it came in under the cap is worth about $7.9 million today.
For scale, the Barn cost $70,000. Its replacement cost about 25 times as much.
### Who actually built St. Louis City Hall?
The contractors are on record. The federal survey file, compiled from city records in 1981, lists W.F. Hopkins on excavation, John Hill on foundation masonry, the St. Louis Granite Co. on the basement-story granite, the Schneider Granite Co. on the first-story granite, Pickel Marble & Granite Co. on cut stone and marble wainscoting, Ward & Hartley on brickwork, Koken Iron Works on the roof and ornamental iron, Albert McCartney on ornamental plaster and Drey & Kahn on glass.
Some of the men who cut the granite turn up in the Ironton paper by name, coming and going between the quarries and the job in St. Louis. Jas. Sizemore in December 1891. Jno. Lindsay in February 1893. In August 1892 the paper expected every granite worker on the City Hall job at the Graniteville Labor Day picnic. That December it put Schneider’s workforce at about 300 men, but that counted the whole company, not the City Hall crew.
Past that, the record goes quiet: we found nothing documenting how many people built City Hall, who they were or where they came from, whether anyone died or struck on the job, or where the brick, sandstone and iron came from. We’re not going to guess.
Later work is better documented. In 1934 a decorator named Carl Bonfig was paid $1.37 an hour under a federal works program, about $34 an hour today, to paint copies of existing pictures for six murals at the Tucker and Market entrances. He finished three: Lindbergh’s plane, the Spirit of St. Louis; the statue of King Louis IX on horseback; and “Front Street in 1840,” a copy of a lithograph of the riverfront and the city’s first city hall. Then the Municipal Art Commission halted the project, saying the murals didn’t meet the artistic standards required for a public building.
### Why did the 1896 Republican convention meet on City Hall’s lawn?
Because the hall it booked wasn’t ready. The 1896 Republican National Convention was supposed to meet in the St. Louis Exposition and Music Hall, but repairs and upgrades couldn’t be finished in time. So a temporary wooden convention hall went up on the lawn south of City Hall, built in about 60 days for about $60,000. City Hall itself was still a construction site.
The delegates met there June 16 to 18, 1896, and nominated William McKinley of Ohio for president on the first ballot. He won that November. The convention came less than a month after the 1896 tornado tore through the city and killed at least 255 people, and there was speculation the city couldn’t host it. After a big cleanup, it went ahead as planned. When it ended, the temporary hall came down. The federal survey file notes only that the convention met on the grounds next to City Hall, in a building put up for the purpose.
### What happened to St. Louis City Hall’s tower?
It came down in 1936, and it never went back up. A 1911 photo in the city’s brochure shows a lantern-like central tower about 80 feet tall over the Tucker Boulevard entrance, with a spire about 19 feet tall on each side. During a reroofing job, crews found the towers’ structural steel so corroded that the central tower had to be taken down with great care, piece by piece.
People were furious. The local chapter of the American Institute of Architects objected, and Mayor Bernard Dickmann promised a new tower when the city had the money. The replacement was estimated at $10,000, roughly $240,000 today. A campaign to rebuild it started in 1946, a study found it too expensive, and the project was dropped. One city landmark page dates the removal to around 1938, but the brochure and the federal survey both say 1936. If the roofline over the main door looks like it’s missing something, it is.
The clock that shook the tower. A pneumatic clock went in above the Tucker entrance in 1906. By 1912 the tower shook every time the clock struck, so the striking was shut off. In 1971 the clock’s numeral 6 fell off and turned up on a fourth-floor balcony. Ten years later, in 1981, Mayor Vincent C. Schoemehl Jr. put it back himself.
The name that took 45 years. The words City Hall weren’t carved over the Market, Tucker and Clark entrances until 1943, 45 years after the city moved in. That happened only after the City Art Commission refused to let Mayor Dickmann hang a neon City Hall sign, in red, white and blue, over the door.
Craned your neck in the rotunda? Where to eat in downtown St. Louis
### Can you tour St. Louis City Hall?
Not on a scheduled tour. We couldn’t find any recurring public tour of City Hall. The city’s Visiting City Hall page covers hours, entrances and parking and says nothing about tours, and the City Hall “tours” on big booking sites turn out to be general city bundles. The last city-run open house we found was a one-off on Nov. 2, 2013.
You can still see the best parts on your own. It’s a public building, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and you’re welcome to walk in. Remember it’s a working office: people are there to pay bills and pick up records, so keep your voice down and stay out of the way of the lines. Here’s what to look for.
The rotunda. It’s a 45-by-65-foot atrium that rises four stories, ringed by balustraded balconies on the upper three floors. The floors are white Italian marble. The walls mix white marble with light and dark Tennessee marble wainscoting and black Glen Falls marble. Look up: the skylit ceiling is framed in “obscured” gold glass.
The frescoes. In the spandrels between the arches, artist Frederick Lincoln Stoddard painted early scenes of Native Americans and settlers in St. Louis.
The staircase. The grand marble staircase climbs half the height of the lobby, then splits in two directions on its way to the second floor.
The mural that flunked. Bonfig’s “Front Street in 1840” is the one the city’s history page still sends you to inside the Tucker Boulevard entrance, for a look at the 1827 city hall on the riverfront. The art commission didn’t think it was good enough for a public building. It’s still on the wall.
Outside. The bronze Ulysses S. Grant at the corner of Market and Tucker is by Robert P. Bringhurst, moved there in 1914. A bronze Pierre Laclède by George Julian Zolnay stands on the City Hall grounds too. Then walk the block for the carved City Hall over the doors, the blank belvedere panels and the empty spot over the Tucker entrance where the tower used to be. The city announced in 2021 that the Gateway Foundation had donated about 120 LED fixtures, valued at $400,000, to light the outside, so try a slow drive past after dark.
### What was St. Louis City Hall built for, and what’s in it now?
It was built for a city that still tied up its horses out front. The original plans show a modest landscape of sidewalks, grass, trees and flower beds, with no parking except the circular drive on Tucker and hitching posts every 25 feet along Tucker Boulevard. Inside, it was laid out for that two-chamber government: 150 rooms across four floors and a basement, on a footprint 380 feet long and 205 feet deep. It was considered fireproof by the standards of 1904. The city had already lost one city hall to fire.
The block filled in over time. A Municipal Courts building went up on the site in 1909 and the City Jail in 1915. The Marriage License Bureau once had a fountain with a three-foot metal cupid in the middle of the floor; it came out in the 1950s. The open cage elevators were enclosed in shafts in 1957. Mayor A.J. Cervantes redecorated the mayor’s office in 1967 and put down a carpet woven with the city seal, and double-glazed aluminum windows went in in 1981. Ornate five-globe lamp posts and the copper finials over the lower dormers disappeared at dates nobody wrote down.
The mayor’s office stayed in its original second-floor space. As of the 1990 brochure, its walls carried five panels by Stoddard, and the west wall showed early St. Louis with Laclède’s line, “I have chosen a site for a settlement which may become one of the great cities of America.” It’s a working office, so don’t expect a look inside.
Next time you’re stopped at Market and Tucker, you’re the one who knows the black building was pink all along, that the granite came up from Iron County, that the tower came down in 1936 and never went back, and that the name over the door is there because somebody wanted neon. Go on a weekday. Walk in through the Tucker doors. Look up. Then find more underrated places to visit in St. Louis for the rest of the afternoon.
Out of the rotunda and ready for lunch? Our guide to where to eat in downtown St. Louis lists 41 spots, including Asian Arch a few blocks up Tucker from City Hall’s front steps.
If you run a lunch counter, a coffee bar or a walking tour within a few blocks of Market and Tucker, list it with us so the people walking out of City Hall, records in hand or still staring up at the pink granite, find you before they head back to the lot.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who is the architect of St. Louis City Hall?
A.  George Richard Mann of Eckel & Mann, a firm from St. Joseph, Missouri, won the national design competition with an entry titled “St. Louis 1892.” His draftsman Harvey Ellis is believed to have contributed a great deal, though no official record proves it. Albert B. Groves of the St. Louis firm Weber & Groves designed the rotunda, the Tucker vestibule and the grand staircase finished in 1904.
### Q. Is City Hall open today in St. Louis?
A.  On weekdays, yes. The city lists general hours of Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except city holidays, and most cashier windows run 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Some offices keep their own hours, so for marriage licenses, records, parking or anything else you need done, check that office’s page on the city’s Visiting City Hall site before you go. The City Hall lot is reached from Clark, Tucker and Market, and there’s more parking at the Kiel Center Garage.
### Q. What is the history of St. Louis City Hall?
A.  The city bought the site in 1840 for $25,000 and left it a park for about 50 years. Construction started on July 19, 1890, the city moved in unfinished on April 11, 1898, and the building was declared complete on Nov. 5, 1904, at a cost of $1,787,159.16. Since then it has lost its central tower in 1936, gained its carved name in 1943 and served as the seat of city government the whole time.
### Q. What are some of the most famous architecture in St. Louis?
A.  Beyond the Gateway Arch, start with the city’s official landmark list. It opens with Eads Bridge at No. 1, the Old Courthouse at No. 2 and the Old Cathedral at No. 3, and the Wainwright Building is No. 7. City Hall is No. 29, designated in 1971. Our guide to historic sites in St. Louis covers more of them, including older buildings out in the county.
### Q. What is the oldest building in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Not City Hall, which dates to the 1890s. Inside the city limits, the building usually named is the Old Cathedral, the Basilica of St. Louis, King of France, built from 1831 to 1834 downtown near the river. The Lewis Bissell Mansion on Randall Place is older, built around 1823 to 1828, but it’s private property and not open to visitors.
### Q. What are some free tours available in St. Louis?
A.  City Hall is free to walk into on weekdays, though there’s no guided tour. Head east on Market toward the river and the Old Courthouse is free too, and National Park Service rangers have been leading a free tour there every day at 2:15 p.m. Ranger schedules change, so check the Park Service’s Old Courthouse page before you go.
### Q. Is St. Louis City Hall on the National Register of Historic Places?
A.  We couldn’t find it listed on its own. It is City Landmark No. 29, designated by the city in 1971, and the federal Historic American Buildings Survey documented it as HABS MO-265 in a 1981 report, with photographs added in 1986. Those records, held at the Library of Congress, are where much of the detail on this page comes from.
### Q. What is the St. Louis City Hall rotunda used for?
A.  It’s the building’s great hall and the city’s ceremonial room. In recent years it has hosted a mayoral swearing-in, a Mardi Gras ball and Black History Month events. To book it for an event, ask the city how permits work now.

## Bridges in St. Louis: Walk the Eads, Bike the McKinley, and the 1989 Bridge Swap
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/bridges-in-st-louis
Nice skyline backdrop. That’s about all the photo boards and social posts that fill this search will tell you about the bridges in St. Louis. They skip the best story on the riverfront. In 1989, the City of St. Louis traded one Mississippi River bridge for another. It handed the MacArthur Bridge to the Terminal Railroad Association and took the 1874 Eads Bridge in return, so MetroLink could run trains across the Eads’ lower deck. That swap is why MetroLink trains still rumble across a bridge that opened while Ulysses S. Grant was president.
Then it gets better. A $48 million rehab finished in 2016 left the Eads fit to carry trains and cars until at least 2091. Just upriver, the 1951 Martin Luther King Bridge is under weight restrictions, and officials are eyeing a $629 million replacement. And the 1967 Poplar Street Bridge, the one most of us actually drive? In late September, a MoDOT spokesperson said there are no plans yet. The 152-year-old bridge has a longer future on paper than the 75-year-old one next door.
Below: what each crossing carries, which ones you can walk or bike, the names nobody uses and what’s actually planned, all checked Oct. 6, 2026, against both state transportation departments, Metro, Great Rivers Greenway, the National Park Service and dated local reporting. Most of our day-trip pages send you out to the small towns outside St. Louis. This one stays on the river.
### What bridges cross the Mississippi in St. Louis?
Five road bridges link St. Louis to Illinois. North to south: the McKinley, the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial (I-70), the Martin Luther King, the Eads and the Poplar Street (I-55 and I-64). The Merchants and MacArthur bridges carry only trains. At the city’s northern edge, I-270 crosses near the walk-and-bike-only Old Chain of Rocks Bridge.
The five you can drive, north to south. The McKinley Bridge, from 1910, runs from north St. Louis to Venice, Illinois, with a separate lane for walkers and bikes. The Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge, opened in 2014, carries I-70. The Martin Luther King Bridge, from 1951, is a three-lane connector to East St. Louis. The Eads Bridge, from 1874, carries cars and people on foot up top and MetroLink trains below. The Poplar Street Bridge, from 1967, carries I-55, I-64 and U.S. 40 just south of the Arch. None of them charges a toll now, though the McKinley and the MLK were toll bridges for decades.
The two you can’t drive. The Merchants Bridge, from 1889, and the MacArthur Bridge, opened to traffic in 1917, carry only trains, and the Terminal Railroad Association owns both. The MacArthur started life as the city’s Municipal Free Bridge, built to get around the railroad’s grip on crossings at the Eads. It carried Route 66 from 1929 to 1955, and the city closed its road deck in 1981. The Merchants got three new main spans in a $222 million project finished in 2022.
The ones at the edges. I-270 crosses at the city’s north end, about 2,000 feet upriver from the walk-and-bike-only Old Chain of Rocks Bridge. South of the city, I-255 uses the Jefferson Barracks Bridge.
### Why is the Eads Bridge famous?
Because the experts said it couldn’t be built. James B. Eads, a self-taught engineer, had never built a bridge. He made his money salvaging sunken steamboats, after more than 500 trips to the river bottom in a diving bell, and he built ironclad gunboats for the Union. In 1867 he proposed three steel arches of 500 feet or more, when steel had never been used to build a bridge. A convention of engineers recommended no span longer than 350 feet. Jacob Linville, the Keystone Bridge Company engineer who later oversaw erecting the steel, wrote that the design “will not stand up.” It opened on July 4, 1874, and the National Park Service calls it the oldest bridge standing on the Mississippi River.
The firsts. The Park Service also calls it the very first steel bridge. The city’s landmark list, where it’s No. 1, adds that it was the first U.S. bridge built on pneumatic caissons and the first whose superstructure went up entirely by cantilever construction, since nothing could stand in the river to prop up the arches. The footnote nobody prints: the Gateway Arch Park Foundation’s museum exhibit counts nearly 2,400 tons of steel and more than 3,100 tons of wrought iron. Measured by the metal, the famous steel bridge is mostly iron.
The men who paid for it. The piers sit on bedrock about 100 feet below the river’s surface. Workers dug inside pressurized caissons at more than 40 pounds per square inch, before anyone understood decompression sickness. The Missouri Historical Society counts 119 workers who got the bends and 14 who died of it. Eads’ family doctor, Alphonse Jaminet, ran a floating hospital beside the pier site and worked out that coming up slowly was vital, early groundwork for modern diving practice.
The elephant. St. Louisans were nervous about a kind of bridge nobody had tried. In mid-June 1874, a circus elephant was led across, on the popular belief that an elephant won’t set foot on an unsafe structure. On July 2, crews loaded the bridge with 14 locomotives. The dedication two days later brought fireworks and a parade 15 miles long.
The flop. Eads told investors he could build it for $3 million in three years. It took seven years and cost $6,536,729, and the bridge company went bankrupt on April 19, 1875, when the railroads didn’t use it the way its backers had counted on. By the 1880s it was in railroad hands, and it stayed there until the 1989 trade.
The bridge today. MetroLink started crossing the lower deck in 1993, and the road deck, closed to cars in 1991, reopened in 2003. Bi-State Development, Metro’s parent, co-owns the bridge with the city. Metro’s $48 million rehab, finished in October 2016, replaced about 1.2 million pounds of steel and blasted off roughly nine coats of paint, and St. Louis Public Radio reported it left the bridge fit for MetroLink and cars until at least 2091. At the 1874 dedication, Eads said it “will endure as long as it is useful to man.” So far, he’s right.
### How old is the McKinley Bridge in St. Louis?
It opened in November 1910, so it’s 115 years old and turns 116 next month. The Illinois Traction System, an electric interurban railroad, built it to bring its trains into St. Louis, and engineer Ralph Modjeski designed it. The name trips people up. It honors William B. McKinley, an executive of that railroad, not President William McKinley, a point the Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT) stresses in its project newsletter. The whole bridge cost $4 million.
Route 66, then a long slide. In 1926 it became part of the original alignment of U.S. Route 66. Trains quit using it by 1978, upkeep fell behind, and in 2001 it closed as unsafe. Illinois took ownership in 2003, Missouri and Illinois rebuilt it together, and it reopened toll-free at the end of 2007.
The lane that makes it worth a trip. The McKinley Bridge Bikeway is a 14-foot-wide lane, 2,600 feet long, cantilevered off the side of the bridge and separated from traffic. On the Missouri side, the Trestle at Branch Street, a 2,400-foot paved ramp, climbs from street level and ties it into the Riverfront Trail. Great Rivers Greenway put $4 million into the trestle alone, the same $4 million the entire bridge cost in 1910. Stop at midspan and you’re standing on the state line.
Plan around 2028. More than 13,000 vehicles cross the McKinley a day, IDOT says, and the agency is planning a preservation job: deck patching, a new overlay, expansion joints and paint. As of Oct. 6, 2026, IDOT’s project page says construction should run from early spring to fall 2028, and that the bridge is expected to close fully to cars, walkers and bikes during the work. Check before you count on it that year.
### What is the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge?
It’s the cable-stayed bridge that carries I-70 across the river just north of downtown, open to traffic since early on the morning of Feb. 9, 2014. MoDOT puts it at 2,800 feet long and 400 feet tall, about two-thirds the height of the Arch. Its 1,500-foot main span, the stretch between the two towers, was the third-longest cable-stayed span in the country when it opened. The bridge itself cost about $239 million. The full project, approaches and interchanges included, came to nearly $700 million.
Why it’s there. Before 2014, I-55, I-64 and I-70 all crossed on the Poplar Street Bridge, and MoDOT says roughly 140,000 vehicles a day were crossing there between the two states. Getting I-70 its own bridge took nearly 20 years of Missouri-Illinois talks over location and money. The states built four lanes that can be restriped to six.
The name. It honors veterans and Stan Musial, the Cardinals great who served in the Navy during World War II. Locals call it the Stan Span, a nickname that was in print before it opened.
Can you walk it? No. It’s an interstate. The exception was opening weekend, when thousands of people walked, ran or biked across on Feb. 8, 2014, almost 3,000 of them in a 6K run to Illinois and back.
### What year was the Poplar Street Bridge built?
It opened on Nov. 9, 1967. The 2,164-foot bridge carries I-55, I-64 and U.S. 40 from just south of the Arch grounds to East St. Louis. From the riverfront it barely registers, a flat deck with nothing rising above the roadway. By one transportation history’s account, it was the first orthotropic bridge in the U.S., built with a steel-plate deck that works as one unit with the steel beneath it. When it was planned in the late 1950s, its builders asked for 25 acres of the future Arch grounds. After a fight, they got 2.5.
The name nobody uses. It was officially the Bernard F. Dickmann Bridge, for a former mayor. In 2013 the Missouri General Assembly renamed it the Congressman William L. Clay Sr. Bridge, for Missouri’s first Black member of Congress, who joked at the ceremony that it was “payback” for the 1980 bill he sponsored naming the St. Louis post office for Dickmann. Neither name stuck. The Missouri end sits over Poplar Street, and then-Mayor Francis Slay blamed early traffic reporters for the nickname.
The 9-foot slide. On March 31, 2018, MoDOT slid the eastbound side of the bridge 9 feet south to make room for another eastbound lane.
Is the Poplar Street Bridge being replaced? Not on any schedule, as of Oct. 6, 2026. Here’s exactly what exists, with dates:
March 2024: an IDOT engineer told the Belleville News-Democrat the agency had a larger future project planned to repave and repair the bridge, estimated at $288 million. IDOT crews were back doing deck repairs on the eastbound side in December 2025.
December 2025: St. Louis Magazine reported the bridge was on track for major work beginning in 2040, and a MoDOT spokesman said a study of the downtown area was in its very early stages, with investments in the Poplar Street and MLK bridges coming.
Sept. 30, 2026: Ryan McClure of the Gateway Arch Park Foundation told First Alert 4 that the Poplar Street Bridge, the I-64 double-decker and the elevated lanes by Laclede’s Landing will need replacing within 15 years, and that his group is raising private money to study capping, burying or removing the downtown highway. In the same story, a MoDOT spokesperson said “there are no plans,” and that the regional downtown study hasn’t started.
So big work is expected within about 15 years, and nobody has drawn a replacement. Watch MoDOT and the East-West Gateway Council of Governments for word on that downtown study.
### Is the Martin Luther King Bridge being replaced?
Maybe, if somebody finds the money. In June 2026, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that officials are eyeing a replacement estimated at $629 million, because the bridge is in deteriorated condition and has restrictions on how much freight trucks can haul across it. Route 66 News, summarizing that report, added that IDOT has pledged $10 million for engineering, that Missouri and Illinois would split the cost, and that funding is the big hurdle. No construction date has been announced.
How it got here. It opened in January 1951 as the Veterans Memorial Bridge, a toll bridge built by the City of East St. Louis, and it carried Route 66 for about a dozen years. It was renamed for Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968, the year he was assassinated. Once the free Poplar Street Bridge opened in 1967, the toll money dried up and the bridge ran down. It was rebuilt and reopened without a toll in 1989. In 2009, after 38 serious crashes in six years, it went from four narrow lanes to three with a concrete divider. Then it closed from October 2018 to August 2020 for a rehab that replaced its Illinois approach spans.
### Which St. Louis bridges can you walk or bike across?
Three, and each one is a different outing.
The Eads Bridge, for the downtown walk. The upper deck has a sidewalk, and the bridge sits right between Laclede’s Landing and the Arch grounds, so start from either. Out over the water, MetroLink trains run on the deck below you. On the Illinois side, a ramp off the sidewalk drops to the East Riverfront MetroLink station, and a paved path runs about three-tenths of a mile south to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, the Illinois park with the straight-on view of the Arch and the skyline. Walk back, or ride MetroLink one stop back to Missouri. Our guide to the best way to get around St. Louis has current fares.
The McKinley Bridge, for the bike ride. That separated 14-foot lane makes it the easy crossing on two wheels. Get on at the Trestle at Branch Street, at the foot of Branch east of North Broadway, where it meets the Riverfront Trail. In Illinois, the MCT Confluence Trail runs 20.5 miles north from the bridge toward the parks in Alton, Illinois. Keep the planned 2028 closure in mind.
The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge gets its own section below.
Make a day of it. Great Rivers Greenway’s Riverfront Trail runs 16.19 miles, counting the Old Chain of Rocks and McKinley bridges. It’s flat and paved, with very little shade, and its trailhead is at Biddle Street, a few blocks north of the MLK Bridge. Need wheels? Here’s what it costs to rent a bike in St. Louis.
The rest. The Poplar Street and Stan Musial bridges are interstates, and the Merchants and MacArthur are railroad bridges.
Off the Eads and hungry? Where to eat in St. Louis, MO
### What about the Chain of Rocks bridges?
There are two, about 2,000 feet apart at the city’s north end. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge opened in 1929, carried Route 66 starting in 1936, and is famous for the sharp bend in the middle. It’s open only to people walking and biking, daily from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. As of Oct. 7, 2026, Great Rivers Greenway said it was reachable from the Missouri side only, while a smaller canal bridge on the Illinois approach was closed for construction. Our full guide covers parking, the closure and the bend.
The newer one carries I-270, and it’s being replaced. The original went up in 1966, and by IDOT’s count its traffic grew from a projected 19,800 vehicles a day to more than 51,000. IDOT and MoDOT are building twin bridges in its place, and in May 2026 the project reported the last steel girder was in place on the second span, with construction on schedule.
Route 66 turns 100 this year, and it crossed the river here on at least five of these bridges: the McKinley in 1926, the MacArthur from 1929, the Old Chain of Rocks from 1936, the Veterans Bridge that became the MLK, and finally the Poplar Street. To follow the old road west, start at the Route 66 State Park visitor center in Eureka.
### What about the Jefferson Barracks and Clark bridges?
They’re the bookends, and both are bigger than most people realize. The Jefferson Barracks Bridge carries I-255 and U.S. 50 across the river about 11 miles south of the Eads. It’s really two bridges, twin tied arches with three lanes each, and each arch spans roughly 900 feet over the navigation channel, its top about 180 feet above the deck. The twins went up in stages through the 1980s and early 1990s, replacing an old two-lane steel bridge that opened in the 1940s as a toll crossing.
MoDOT put about $50 million into repainting and repairing both spans in 2022 and 2023, and the closures there this fall were single-lane daytime jobs. No walkway or bike lane is listed for it, so treat this one as a drive.
The Clark Bridge sits about 17 miles north of the Eads and carries U.S. 67 between Alton and the Missouri side. It’s a cable-stayed bridge, 4,620 feet long, opened in January 1994 to replace a two-lane bridge from 1928, and it’s named for William Clark of Lewis and Clark. Its design, a double plane of cables hung from single towers, had never been used in the U.S. when it went up. PBS’s NOVA followed the whole job for “Super Bridge,” which aired in 1997 and caught the 1993 flood putting the Missouri approach under water. It has unprotected bike lanes on both sides, though the highway shoulders south of it are no place for a bike.
Cross it for the start of the Great River Road and the free lock tours at Melvin Price Locks and Dam, just downriver on the Illinois side. IDOT has been running off-peak lane closures on the bridge since Sept. 8, 2026, so expect one lane each way outside rush hours.
The water under all of these spans has its own guide: where to see the Mississippi in St. Louis covers the riverfront steps, the overlooks and the ferries, and Laclede’s Landing starts right at the Missouri end of the Eads Bridge.
Next time somebody calls them the bridges you sit in traffic on, you’re the one who knows the city once traded one for another, and that there’s a spot on the McKinley where you can stand in two states at once. Pick a clear evening. Walk out to the middle of the Eads. Wait for a train to pass under your feet.
Back on the Missouri side and ready to eat, our guide to where to eat in St. Louis, MO lists city kitchens from Broadway Oyster Bar to Pappy’s Smokehouse.
If you run a cafe, a bar or a bike shop within a few blocks of the Eads on Laclede’s Landing or the McKinley Bikeway at Branch Street, list it with us so the people walking off the bridge find you before they find their car.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most famous bridge in St. Louis?
A.  The Eads Bridge. It was the city’s symbol long before the Arch, according to the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, and businesses put it on their letterheads as soon as it opened. Walt Whitman called it a structure of “perfection and beauty unsurpassable” in 1882. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, with its mid-river bend and its turn in Escape from New York, runs a close second.
### Q. What are the names of some bridges in St. Louis?
A.  The McKinley, Stan Musial Veterans Memorial, Martin Luther King, Eads and Poplar Street bridges carry traffic, and the Merchants and MacArthur carry trains. Several go by names almost nobody uses. The Poplar Street is officially the Congressman William L. Clay Sr. Bridge. The MLK opened as the Veterans Memorial Bridge, the MacArthur began as the Municipal Free Bridge, and the Eads was the St. Louis Bridge while it was being built. The Musial is the Stan Span.
### Q. What is the oldest bridge in St. Louis?
A.  Among the river crossings, the Eads Bridge, dedicated July 4, 1874. The National Park Service calls it the oldest bridge standing anywhere on the Mississippi. Next comes the Merchants, from 1889, though its main spans are new as of 2022. If old structures are your thing, our list of the oldest buildings in St. Louis picks up where the bridges leave off.
### Q. Is the Eads Bridge still in use?
A.  Yes, every day. MetroLink makes about 300 trips a day across the lower deck, by Bi-State Development’s 2016 count, and cars and people on foot use the upper deck, which was closed to cars from 1991 to 2003. The 2016 rehab is meant to keep it working until at least 2091.
### Q. Did Carnegie build the Eads Bridge?
A.  Not personally. Andrew Carnegie managed the Keystone Bridge Company, which erected the steel superstructure, and he clashed with Eads over the unusually high quality of steel Eads demanded. PBS’s American Experience notes Carnegie got so fed up that he sold his stock in the bridge in 1871. Keystone also built Kimmswick’s 1874 iron bridge, which first carried traffic over the River des Peres in Carondelet before Jefferson County moved it to Rock Creek.
### Q. How long is the Eads Bridge?
A.  About 6,442 feet end to end, roughly 1.2 miles, counting the approaches on both banks. The part over the water is three arches of 502, 520 and 502 feet. When it opened in 1874, St. Louis Magazine notes, it was the longest arch bridge in the world.
### Q. Is the MLK bridge open in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. As of early October 2026, the Martin Luther King Bridge is open, one lane into St. Louis and two into Illinois, with weight restrictions because of its condition. IDOT closes lanes for maintenance now and then, as it did during off-peak hours Sept. 9 to 11. A $629 million replacement is under discussion but isn’t funded.
### Q. What town is across the river from St. Louis?
A.  East St. Louis, Illinois, sits directly across from downtown, and the Eads, MLK and Poplar Street bridges all land there. The McKinley Bridge lands farther north in Venice, Illinois. Our East St. Louis, IL guide covers the city itself.

## Mill Creek Valley, St. Louis: How 20,000 People Lost a Neighborhood, What Stands There Now, Where to Remember It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mill-creek-valley-st-louis
The headlines called it the city’s “No. 1 Eyesore.” About 20,000 people called it home. Mill Creek Valley ran from 20th Street west to Grand Boulevard, and in February 1959 the city started tearing it down on Laclede Avenue, on the spot where Saint Louis University’s Marchetti Towers stand today, according to the Missouri Historical Society. Within a few years the neighborhood was rubble and open ground.
Most of what turns up about Mill Creek is a set of before-and-after photos or a short list of famous names. The people get lost. So this page goes block by block. If you’ve been to a CITY SC match at Energizer Park, a Billikens game at Chaifetz Arena or a class at Harris-Stowe State University, you’ve already stood in Mill Creek Valley. Below: who lived there, how the city decided to clear it, where the families went, what stands there now, and the places you can still go to remember it.
Everything below was checked on Oct. 6, 2026, against the Missouri Historical Society, Saint Louis University’s PRiME Center, St. Louis Public Radio, Great Rivers Greenway, the City of St. Louis, the State Historical Society of Missouri and Harris-Stowe State University.
### What happened to Mill Creek, St. Louis?
The city tore it down. Mill Creek Valley, a mostly Black neighborhood of nearly 20,000 people between 20th Street and Grand Boulevard, was cleared for urban renewal under a 1955 bond issue. Demolition began in February 1959 and was largely done by the mid-1960s. Interstate 64, two universities and a soccer stadium now stand there.
The short version, in dates:
Aug. 7, 1954: Mayor Raymond R. Tucker announces that Mill Creek Valley, stretching west toward Saint Louis University, will be cleared, the Post-Dispatch reported.
1955: City voters pass a $110 million bond issue. The Missouri Historical Society says $10 million of it was set aside to demolish Mill Creek Valley.
March 1958: The Board of Aldermen approves the clearance 27 to 1.
Feb. 16, 1959: The first wrecking ball hits, by Great Rivers Greenway’s count.
1960s: Clearance is finished. The Missouri Historical Society says the district was unrecognizable.
Feb. 16, 2023: Exactly 64 years later, former residents gather on Market Street to unveil Pillars of the Valley, a mile-long memorial.
### Where is Mill Creek Valley located?
Right in the middle of the city’s central corridor, west of downtown. Researchers at Saint Louis University’s PRiME Center put the boundaries at Grand Boulevard on the west, Olive Street on the north, 20th Street on the east and the railroad tracks on the south. Union Station sits at the southeast corner. The Missouri Historical Society counts 454 acres; the 1954 announcement said 465. Today that ground falls mostly inside two city neighborhoods, Midtown and Downtown West, and our Midtown neighborhood guide covers what’s there to do now.
The name comes from the creek, not the people. University of Missouri-St. Louis historians trace it to 1765, when Joseph Taillon built a mill on a creek that ran from present-day Vandeventer Avenue to the Mississippi. The creek became a millpond, the millpond was drained, and the valley filled with rail yards. That’s why the railroad tracks still run along its southern edge.
To find it on today’s map, use the landmarks:
East end: Energizer Park, home of St. Louis CITY SC, on Market Street between 20th and 22nd streets. The club says the stadium district sits in Mill Creek’s footprint.
Middle: Harris-Stowe State University, between Compton Avenue and Ewing Avenue, from Olive down to Market.
West end: Saint Louis University’s buildings south of Olive, out toward Grand. Chaifetz Arena, at Compton and Market, stands where Waring Elementary School did, according to the PRiME Center.
South edge: the rail corridor, with Interstate 64 running beside it.
### What is Mill Creek known for?
Being a city within a city. That’s the Missouri Historical Society’s phrase, and its 2025 exhibit counted the pieces: more than 800 businesses, 43 churches, seven schools and three theaters on ground smaller than Forest Park, with about 95 percent of residents Black. Everything a family needed was a walk away. “Our lawyers were there, our doctors were there,” former resident Bettie Battle-Turner told SLU’s student paper.
Music. The Missouri Historical Society calls Mill Creek the birthplace of ragtime. The Market Street blocks at the valley’s east end were part of the old Chestnut Valley sporting district, where Tom Turpin ran the Rosebud Cafe at 2220-22 Market, and the St. Louis American names Scott Joplin as one of the neighborhood’s own. On the same stretch, at 23rd and Market, stood the Booker T. Washington Theatre, which opened in 1913 and booked Ethel Waters, Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey and Bill Robinson on the Black vaudeville circuit. Jazz trumpeter Clark Terry grew up in Mill Creek, and his horns were part of the history museum’s exhibit.
Josephine Baker. Yes, the connection is real. The Missouri Historical Society says she grew up in Mill Creek Valley and danced on the sidewalk by the Booker T. Washington Theatre. A Nine PBS documentary places her childhood on Eugenia Street, just southwest of Union Station. Her nephew told Nine PBS she danced in the streets for money to help the family. At 15 she joined a traveling troupe, and from there it was New York, then Paris. The theater closed in 1930 and came down for the widening of Market Street, long before urban renewal.
Baseball. At Market and Compton stood Stars Park, home of the Negro National League’s St. Louis Stars from 1922 to 1931. James “Cool Papa” Bell played center field there. The Stars won league titles in 1928 and 1930, and the historical marker on the site calls it the first professional ballpark in the country owned exclusively by African Americans. Its left-field wall was the side of a trolley barn, MLB.com reports, only 270 feet from home plate.
Institutions. City Hospital No. 2 and People’s Hospital. The Pine Street YMCA and the Phillis Wheatley YWCA, where a young Maya Angelou spent time. The original Vashon High School, whose graduates include Rep. Maxine Waters, activist Percy Green and civil rights leader Norman Seay. And at Jefferson and Market, the People’s Finance Building, which held offices for the NAACP, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters and the St. Louis American newspaper. Madam C.J. Walker and NAACP leader Roy Wilkins both lived in the neighborhood at one point, the St. Louis American reports.
### Why was Mill Creek Valley destroyed?
Because the people running the city wanted the land, and the federal government would pay for most of the clearing. The neighborhood’s hard conditions gave them the case. A 1962 city report counted 80 percent of buildings without a private bath and toilet and 67 percent without running water. Mill Creek got that way for a reason, the PRiME Center notes: Black families arriving in the Great Migration were steered into a few neighborhoods hemmed in by racial covenants and industry, absentee landlords let buildings decay, and the city didn’t invest.
The plan behind it was bigger than one neighborhood. The city’s 1947 comprehensive plan marked large parts of the old city for clearance, and the federal Housing Act of 1949 put up the money. Terry Jones, a UMSL political science professor emeritus who covered the clearing as a SLU student editor, told St. Louis Public Radio that Mayors Joseph Darst and Raymond Tucker and the business group Civic Progress built their plans around the central corridor, and the neighborhood sat right in the middle of it. A civic group backing the plan complained that every visitor arriving by train rode past Mill Creek on the way into town.
Not everyone went along. When the Board of Aldermen voted 27 to 1 in March 1958, the one no came from Alderman Archie Blaine, whose ward held nearly all of the site. He objected that the plan had no provision for low-income residents, telling the Post-Dispatch he was not in favor of “moving slums to other parts of the city.” The 1958 redevelopment plan called for demolishing 93 percent of the neighborhood. Saint Louis University was the first redeveloper to express definite interest in the cleared land, the Post-Dispatch reported at the time.
Historian Colin Gordon, whose book Mapping Decline traces how St. Louis emptied out, describes a steady mismatch between how the city defined its problems and the fixes it chose. Gwen Moore, who grew up in Mill Creek and later curated the Missouri Historical Society’s exhibit on it, put it more directly in 2018: Mill Creek became “sort of the poster child of how not to do urban renewal.”
### Where did Mill Creek Valley’s 20,000 residents go?
Mostly north and west, and mostly into neighborhoods that were already crowded. The PRiME Center estimates about 2,400 very low-income households were displaced into public housing, including the new Pruitt-Igoe towers about a mile away, or into neighborhoods northwest of Mill Creek. Moore was one of the children who left. “I remember being traumatized when we were told that we had to move,” she told St. Louis Public Radio.
Schools show the path. Lincoln and Johnson elementary schools in Mill Creek were closed by 1960, and Vashon High School followed its families northwest to the JeffVanderLou neighborhood in 1963. The north side schools filled past capacity.
