### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much should I pay a pet sitter for 3 days?
A.  Count the visits, then multiply. For a cat at one visit a day, three visits come to $84 with House of Paws Pet Care’s 20-minute visit or $102 and up at a $34 starting price. For a dog at three visits a day, that’s nine visits: $252 with House of Paws or $306 and up at $34 a visit. Add holiday and after-hours fees where they apply.
### Q. How much do dog sitters charge for 2 nights?
A.  For a sitter staying in your home, two nights at PetWorks’ Saint Louis range of $75 to $175 a night come to about $150 to $350. If the sitter boards your dog at her own house instead, ask for her license first, because in Missouri a home boarder needs one.
### Q. How much should I pay a friend to watch my dog?
A.  There’s no going rate, so anchor it to the real alternative. A professional 20-minute visit costs $28 at House of Paws Pet Care, so a friend’s visit priced somewhat below that is fair to both of you. Then cover what a pro would bill separately, like gas for a long drive or a holiday. Write out the vet authorization anyway.
### Q. How much should I pay someone to look after my dog?
A.  Price the job, not the day. Decide how many visits or nights your dog needs, then multiply: $28 to $60 a visit at House of Paws Pet Care depending on length, $34 and up at a larger local company, and $75 to $175 a night for an overnight sitter on PetWorks. Shortlist a few local sitters and walkers on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each for a written quote on the identical schedule.
### Q. What’s the average pay for dog sitting per day?
A.  PetWorks puts typical Saint Louis drop-in visits at $25 to $60 per visit, and a dog usually needs two or three of them. At the two local companies above, three visits a day come to $84 to $102.
### Q. Is $100 a day good for dog sitting?
A.  In St. Louis, three visits at a $34 starting price come to $102, and three 20-minute visits at House of Paws Pet Care come to $84, so that daily figure buys roughly full professional coverage. For an overnight sitter, it sits near the low end of PetWorks’ $75 to $175 a night.
### Q. Is $20 a day good for dog sitting?
A.  Only for a quick favor. It’s below the lowest published price on this page, the $28 twenty-minute visit at House of Paws Pet Care, and the $34-a-visit company requires at least two visits a day for a dog on a weekend trip and three on a longer one. For a neighbor letting your dog out once at lunch on a workday, it’s reasonable.
### Q. Do you tip a pet sitter?
A.  You don’t have to, but it’s welcome. The $34-a-visit company says tips are never expected but always appreciated, and that you can leave one separately marked for your Care Team at your home. A tip makes the most sense after a holiday booking, a messy week, or a sitter who handled an emergency well.

## Cat Boarding in St. Louis: Nightly Prices, Cat Hotels With No Dogs, and the State Inspection Check
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cat-boarding-in-st-louis
Four square feet. That’s the floor space Missouri requires a licensed boarding kennel to give a cat over 8.8 pounds, inside an enclosure at least 24 inches tall. Picture a bath mat with a ceiling two feet up. And for stays of three months or less, the state rule doesn’t require a shelf to sit on.
You won’t find that number on a boarding brochure. Brochures lead with the word that sits next to it: licensed. The word means something real, because the state does inspect these places, unannounced, at least once a year. What it doesn’t mean is the thing a cat owner hears, which is that somebody checked whether your cat will be comfortable. A license sets a floor. Plenty of cat rooms in this metro sit far above it, and at least two cats-only hotels now operate here that look nothing like a kennel.
Your job is to find out which kind of room you’re booking before the carrier door opens. Below: what the metro posts per night right now, where the cats-only rooms are, how to pull a cattery’s state inspection record, and when a sitter at home beats all of it.
### Is it stressful for a cat to be boarded?
Usually yes, at first, and then it eases. In a study of 140 cats boarded for two weeks, stress fell sharply over the first few days and about two-thirds adjusted well. A third stayed tense, and 4 percent never settled. What you control is the room: floor space, a place to hide, and no barking dogs within earshot.
That study is the best-known one on the subject. Researchers followed 140 cats through a two-week stay in a boarding cattery and scored stress by watching posture and behavior, publishing in the journal Animal Welfare in 1997. The drop was steepest in the first days. By week two, about a third of the cats still rated above “weakly tense,” and for 4 percent the stay was judged inappropriate because their stress never came down. Housing them alone, in pairs or in groups made no difference. Neither did age.
A follow-up from the same team tested something you can actually shop for: room size. Boarding cats in single cages of about 10.8 square feet were measurably calmer on days one, two and six than cats in cages of about 7.5 square feet. Remember the state minimum from the top of this page. It’s four.
Stress has a physical side, too. Feline herpesvirus, one of the two viruses behind most cat colds, hides in a cat’s nerves for life after the first infection. The feline vaccination advisory panel of the American Association of Feline Practitioners names boarding and shelter facilities as places where stress can wake that virus up and carrier cats can spread it. It’s one reason a cat can come home from a spotless cattery sneezing.
None of this says don’t board. Two-thirds of those cats did fine. It says the outcome rests on two things you control: which cat you have, and which room you book. A bold, food-motivated cat who has boarded before is a different case from a shy 14-year-old who disappears when the doorbell rings, and you already know which one lives at your house.
### How much does cat boarding cost in St. Louis?
Posted rates around the metro ran from $27 to $69 a night for one cat when we checked in October 2026, with most standard rooms between $30 and $45. Rates change, so treat every number below as a starting point and confirm the price for your dates before you book. Listed from the lowest posted rate up:
Williamsburg Pet Hotel, 13998 Manchester Rd in Ballwin: standard cat condos from $27 a night, $30 with a window. Cats stay in quiet areas away from the dogs, and a 30-minute catio playtime is $20.
Petropolis, in Chesterfield and St. Charles: $31 a night for a private cat room and $47 for the larger room, plus $25 for each additional cat. Cats board in dedicated cat areas, and play or cuddle sessions run $22.
Silver Maple Pet Center, 2014 N Ballas Rd in Des Peres: $36 a night for a two-room condo of about 15 square feet, $38.50 for a Purradise suite with climbing tiers, and $30.25 for a second cat sharing the suite. Stays over 30 days get 10 percent off.
Creve Coeur Animal Hospital, 12550 Olive Blvd: $38 a day for a multilevel cat condo and $20 for an adjoining one. Routine medications are included at no added charge.
Elm Point Animal Hospital, 3250 Elm Point Industrial Dr in St. Charles: $45 a day for cat boarding, plus $10 to $25 a day if your cat needs medication.
Cattails Lodge, 16497 Clayton Rd in Wildwood, cats only: $45 a night for a lodge condo and suites from $69, with $25 a day for each extra cat sharing a suite.
Happy Cat Hotel & Spa, 3460 Hampton Ave in south city, cats only: no nightly rate on its rooms page. Reservations run through its online booking system or (314) 888-5222, and a second cat sharing a room adds a per-cat fee.
So a week runs roughly $189 to $483 for one cat before extras. The extras are where bills drift. Medication can be free at one clinic and $25 a day at the next. Arrival day is billed differently everywhere: Elm Point charges a full day the moment your cat checks in, Creve Coeur bills by the quarter day, and Cattails may charge a half day for a late pickup. Holidays cost more, too. Cattails adds $10 a day per suite, $4 per lodge, during its peak periods. Ask for the total, in writing, for your exact dates.
Flying out right after drop-off? Where to park at Lambert
### Are there cat-only boarding rooms in St. Louis?
Yes. Two cat hotels we found in the metro board cats and nothing else: Cattails Lodge in Wildwood and Happy Cat Hotel & Spa on Hampton Avenue. Several mixed facilities also keep cats in separate rooms away from the dogs. That’s a different arrangement, and it’s worth asking exactly how separate.
Cattails Lodge sits in a small commercial center at Clayton and Strecker roads. Every cat gets a private suite or lodge condo, daily play and up to an hour in an enrichment lounge. Suites come with a private camera, and cats from different households are never mixed. It gives insulin ($5 a dose) and subcutaneous fluids ($10), doesn’t accept cats that aren’t spayed or neutered, and requires rabies and FVRCP vaccines. Tours are by appointment on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the office keeps weekday hours, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Happy Cat Hotel & Spa opened at 3460 Hampton Ave in 2026, a franchise location owned by a local couple. Its themed private suites run 280 to 512 cubic feet. Guests get the chance at 15 minutes or more out of their rooms each day, at the staff’s discretion, and cats from different families are never out at the same time. It doesn’t accept diabetic cats. Check-in runs 4 to 5:30 p.m. and checkout 8:30 to 10 a.m., seven days a week, except on seven holidays when nobody checks in or out at all, Thanksgiving and Christmas Day among them.
Among the mixed facilities, Petropolis and Williamsburg both say cats board in their own areas away from dog activity. Creve Coeur Animal Hospital keeps a separate cat room inside a kennel wing that runs on its own heating and cooling, apart from the hospital, and its condos have portals that can connect up to three units for a family of cats.
Here’s the detail the brochures bury. Both cats-only hotels say plainly that nobody is on site overnight; they rely on locked, monitored buildings. Elm Point Animal Hospital in St. Charles says it has staff dedicated to its boarders 24 hours a day. Neither answer is wrong. A healthy cat asleep in a quiet suite doesn’t need a person at 3 a.m. A fragile senior on three medications might.
Some cats-only vet clinics have boarded over the years, so don’t assume. City Cat Clinic in the Central West End, which treats cats exclusively, lists its boarding service as currently not available. Call before you plan around anyone.
### How much space does Missouri require for a boarded cat?
At least 3 square feet of floor for a cat up to 8.8 pounds and 4 square feet for a bigger one, in an enclosure at least 24 inches high, under the state’s animal care facility rule, 2 CSR 30-9.030. Floor under a low shelf doesn’t count toward it. For stays of three months or less at a boarding kennel, an elevated shelf isn’t required.
That number isn’t abstract around here. When Wildwood’s planning commission approved the site plan for Cattails Lodge in June 2025, the city wrote the same floor into its conditions: kenneled cats get a minimum of four square feet. The lodge’s actual suites run 180 to 256 cubic feet. A four-square-foot box two feet tall holds eight.
For a benchmark, look at what shelter veterinarians accept. The Association of Shelter Veterinarians, whose standards shape how shelters across the country house cats, calls individual housing under 8 square feet unacceptable for an adult cat and puts the ideal at 11 square feet or more. They also say every cat must be able to hide, climb, perch and scratch, and must be able to eat and sleep away from its litter. Those are shelter guidelines, not boarding law. A shelter cat and a boarded cat are in the same spot, though: a strange room, strange smells, nowhere they chose to be. Missouri’s legal floor for a boarded cat is half the size shelter vets call unacceptable.
Posted sizes around town give you something to measure against. Silver Maple’s two-room condo is about 15 square feet and puts the litter box in its own compartment. Happy Cat’s suites run 280 to 512 cubic feet, Cattails’ 180 to 256. Most places don’t publish a size at all.
So ask for the room in feet. Not “spacious.” Not “luxury.” Feet. Then ask whether there’s a shelf, whether your cat can get behind or under something to hide, and whether the litter box shares a space with the food bowl. Ask about sight lines, too. Happy Cat says its guests can see one another through windows and doors and learn to ignore each other, and plenty of cats do. If yours spends evenings glaring at the neighbor’s cat through your back door, ask for a room without a direct view of another guest.
### How do you check a cattery’s state inspection?
Ask the cattery for its Missouri Animal Care Facilities Act license number, then call or email the state’s ACFA program and request the facility’s inspection reports. Anyone boarding cats for pay at a place that isn’t the owner’s home needs that license, and the reports are public records under Missouri’s Sunshine Law.
The Missouri Department of Agriculture runs the program with a field staff of 18 for the whole state. Licensed facilities are inspected at least once a year. Routine inspections are unannounced and can happen any weekday from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. A place with multiple, direct or repeat violations gets reinspected, also unannounced, and a complaint brings its own unannounced visit. Licenses renew every year and expire January 31, with a separate license for each physical location.
To get the records, call (573) 751-3076, email acfa@mda.mo.gov, or use the open records webform on the department’s ACFA program page. We couldn’t find a public search tool for licensees or reports on the department’s site, so this is a request, not a lookup. Almost nobody makes it, which is exactly why inspection history never shows up in anyone’s star rating.
Ask one more question while you have the cattery on the phone: who is your attending veterinarian? A licensed boarding business files a written program of veterinary care signed by its vet, and that vet is supposed to visit the premises at least once a year. A cattery that can name its vet on the spot is a cattery that has done the paperwork.
Running a boarding kennel without a license is a class A misdemeanor under the state rule, and the department takes reports of unlicensed facilities through a webform it calls Operation Bark Alert. Complaints are public records, names included. The same license and the same phone number cover dog boarding in St. Louis, so a household sending a dog and a cat out the door can check two places with one call.
### Cat boarding or a sitter at home: which is better?
For a healthy adult cat on a short trip, a sitter at home usually wins, because the cat keeps its own room, its own smells and its own routine. Boarding wins for cats that need medication on a strict schedule, cats that bolt for any open door, and long trips where one visit a day is too little company.
Missouri draws a line here that most owners never hear about. The state license covers anyone boarding cats for pay away from the owner’s home, and the department says that explicitly includes a pet sitter who takes cats into her own house. A sitter who comes to your house isn’t boarding anything, so the boarding license doesn’t cover that arrangement, and references, insurance and a meet-and-greet are your whole check. Our guide to pet sitters in St. Louis covers what those visits cost and what to ask.
If you go with a licensed sitter who boards in her own home, the state rules for that setup are stricter than a kennel’s in one striking way: a cat boarded in someone’s home can’t be caged or crated unless it’s medically necessary. The house has to stay between 60 and 85 degrees. You have the right to meet the caregiver and see the room your cat will stay in. And the head count is capped at one animal per standard room, so a four-room house tops out at four.
Then match the setup to the cat in front of you. A shy cat that vanishes when company comes over often does better with its own sofa and a visiting stranger than with its own blanket in a strange room. A cat on insulin needs somebody there at seven and seven, every day, which points to a vet clinic or a cattery that medicates. A door-dasher is safer in a cattery than with a sitter opening your front door twice a day. For a two-week trip, either can work, but one visit a day is thin company for that long. Book two.
### What should you ask a cattery before you book?
Ask what happens on the worst day, not the best one. Can I hear dogs from the cat room? Stand in it and listen. How big is the room, in feet? Is anyone here overnight? What’s your license number, and when was your last state inspection? Who is your attending vet, and which emergency clinic do you use after hours? If my cat doesn’t eat for a day, what do you do, and when do you call me?
Then the money and calendar questions, because those are the ones that surprise people at pickup. What’s the full bill for my dates, with medication, a second cat and any holiday fee? Which days can’t I check in or out? Happy Cat closes check-in and checkout on seven holidays. Cattails takes drop-offs between 3 and 6 p.m. by appointment, and Elm Point wants boarders out by noon to avoid another day’s charge.
A good cattery answers all of it without flinching, and usually offers a tour before you ask. One that goes vague on the license question, or won’t let you see the actual cat room, has told you what you needed to know.
### How do you get your cat ready for its first boarding stay?
Start two weeks out. Confirm vaccines, book a trial, and get the carrier out of the closet. Every cattery we checked that spells out its cat rules requires rabies plus a distemper shot, usually the FVRCP combination, and Creve Coeur Animal Hospital wants new patients examined by its own vets at least 14 days before boarding.
If your cat’s FVRCP is more than a year old, the AAFP vaccination panel mentioned above says an extra booster 7 to 10 days before a high-risk stay like boarding may be warranted. That’s a call for your vet, and if you don’t have one you trust yet, start with how to choose a vet in St. Louis.
For the trial, Cattails sells a $35 Day Pass, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., with $15 for each extra cat. It’s pitched for days when the house is chaos: roofers, showings, the exterminator. It also works as a dress rehearsal. Anywhere else, ask for a single night before the real trip. Pack your cat’s own food, which both cat hotels ask for, and a small washable item that smells like home. Cattails caps comfort items at two and wants one cat per carrier.
And book the holidays now. Cattails charges peak rates from the Wednesday through the Sunday of Thanksgiving, and again from the Friday a week before Christmas through the Sunday after New Year’s, with a 21-day cancellation window on peak stays. Happy Cat lists November 17 to December 1 and December 15 to January 5 as peak season. If your cat needs a room at Thanksgiving, October isn’t early.
Most people pick a cattery off a photo of a cat in a hammock. You’ll be the one who asked for the square footage, the license number and the overnight answer, then watched your cat stroll out of its carrier on day two like it owned the place. For the rest of pet-friendly St. Louis, from parks to patios, start with our guide.
Ready to compare? Browse pet boarding around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two catteries with your dates and the questions above in hand.
And if you run a cattery whose rooms clear Missouri’s four-square-foot minimum by a mile, put the dimensions where cat owners and AI search tools can find them and list your cattery with us.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long is cat boarding?
A.  As long as you book. Catteries price by the night, so a single overnight works and so does a month. Silver Maple Pet Center takes 10 percent off stays over 30 days, and Happy Cat Hotel & Spa quotes extended stays case by case. Watch the edges: some places bill a full day on arrival, and Cattails Lodge keeps two days of fees if you come home early and credits the rest.
### Q. Is it better to leave a cat at home or board?
A.  For most healthy cats on trips of a week or so, home with a sitter visiting once or twice a day is easier on the cat. Boarding makes more sense for medicated cats, door-dashers and long trips. If you board, choose a cats-only building or a cat room out of earshot of dogs, and ask for the room’s size in feet before you pay a deposit.
### Q. How much does a vet charge to board a cat?
A.  Two area animal hospitals we checked post their cat rates. Creve Coeur Animal Hospital charges $38 a day for a cat condo with routine medications included, and Elm Point Animal Hospital in St. Charles charges $45 a day plus $10 to $25 a day to medicate. Those were the posted prices in October 2026, so call to confirm. Some clinics also require an exam by their own vet first.
### Q. Is 2 weeks too long to board a cat?
A.  Not for most cats. In the 140-cat study, two-thirds had adjusted well by the end of two weeks. About a third were still tense, and for 4 percent the stay never got easier. Book a trial night first, ask for a daily photo, and agree in advance on when the cattery calls you if your cat stops eating.
### Q. Is it traumatic for cats to be boarded?
A.  For a small minority it can be. Most cats show stress for the first few days and then settle. The ones that don’t usually make it obvious: they stop eating, hide around the clock, or quit grooming. A cattery that tracks appetite and litter every day will catch that early, and your vet can tell you whether your cat belongs in the stay-at-home column.
### Q. Do cats get sad being alone all day?
A.  Some do. A 2020 survey of owners of 223 cats, published in PLOS ONE, found about 13 percent showed signs of separation-related problems, most often destructive behavior, excess meowing and peeing outside the box. Cats with no toys and no other animal in the house were more likely to show it. Thinking about a companion? The cat cafes in St. Louis are a low-pressure way to meet adoptable cats.
### Q. What vaccines does a cat need for boarding in St. Louis?
A.  Rabies and a distemper vaccine, usually the FVRCP combination covering rhinotracheitis, calicivirus and panleukopenia. Every cattery we checked that posts its cat rules requires both. Some ask for a feline leukemia test or vaccine without requiring it. Bring paper or digital records to check-in, because most places won’t take a cat without proof, and a few will call your vet for them if you ask ahead.
### Q. Can two cats share a boarding room?
A.  Usually, if they live together and get along. Silver Maple charges $30.25 a night for a second cat in a suite, and Cattails and Petropolis each add $25 per extra cat. Cats from different households never share space at Cattails or Happy Cat. If your two squabble at home, book two rooms side by side. Williamsburg can adjoin two condos for a pair that wants to stay close.

## Pet-Friendly Hotels in St. Louis: Two Big Dogs Pass at Red Roof, Fail at Drury
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-friendly-hotels-in-st-louis
Two 45-pound dogs, two leashes wound around your wrist, nails clicking on a lobby floor, and a long car ride you can still smell on both of them. At a Red Roof, each dog is under the line, because Red Roof caps weight at 80 pounds per pet. At a Drury, the same pair is over it, because Drury counts 80 pounds combined. Same dogs. Same number. Opposite answer at the front desk.
That’s the whole problem with booking a pet-friendly room in St. Louis. The paw-print icon on a booking site says “yes.” It doesn’t say per pet or combined, per night or per stay, or whether your dog can stay in the room while you’re at a wedding reception. From Ballpark Village to the Delmar Loop, those answers live in each hotel’s own fine print, and that’s the only place this page reads them from.
Here’s the one to tell a friend before they book downtown. Magnolia Hotel St. Louis lets four-legged guests stay free, with no deposits or added fees, and the brand takes all sizes and breeds. And the downtown dog park your map app shows a few blocks away may have a locked gate: Lucas Park Dog Park runs on a board-approved membership and a gate code. The free one, Nestle Purina Laclede’s Landing Dog Park, is on the Landing. A hotel is one stop on a bigger map of dog-friendly places in St. Louis. It’s also the stop that can quietly add a line to the bill you didn’t plan for.
### What hotels allow dogs to stay for free in St. Louis?
Magnolia Hotel St. Louis lets pets stay free with no deposits or added fees, and the Magnolia brand welcomes all sizes and breeds. Red Roof’s brand policy lets the first pet stay free, up to 80 pounds per pet, with $15 a night for a second. Free never means rule-free: read the damage terms before you book.
Magnolia’s catch sits a few lines down in its brand policy. Owners pay for damage, soiling or extensive cleaning after checkout, and those fees begin at $400. No more than two pets per room. Housekeeping only comes in if the pet is out of the room, or if you’re there and the pet is caged. So the walk you take after breakfast doubles as your room-cleaning window. Put on the leash, hear the tags jingle, and let housekeeping in behind you.
Red Roof’s rule is simple on paper. Two pets per room, cats or dogs, each up to 80 pounds. The first one is free. A second costs $15 a night, and that fee can’t pass $105 per pet for stays of seven nights or longer. You have to declare every pet at check-in. If a pet damages the room, the manager can charge you for it.
Notice the trade. The hotels that skip the up-front fee lean on the back end: damage minimums, cleaning rules, a desk that has to see the dog. That’s fair. Just read that paragraph before you assume “free” covers a chewed lampshade.
### The two-minute call that ends the argument at the front desk
Call the hotel itself, not the national reservations line, and ask three things in this order. Is the pet fee per night or per stay? Is the weight limit per pet or combined? Can the dog stay in the room alone while we’re out? Then ask them to type the answers into your reservation notes, so the words are in your confirmation email before the tags jingle across the lobby.
The numbers, straight off each hotel’s own site: Magnolia Hotel St. Louis at 421 North 8th Street, 314-436-9000. Live! by Loews at Ballpark Village, 799 Clark Avenue, 314-597-9700. The Royal Sonesta Chase Park Plaza at 212 N. Kingshighway, 314-633-3000. The Moonrise at 6177 Delmar Blvd, 314-721-1111. Four Seasons Hotel St. Louis, 314-881-5800. On a game night at Ballpark Village, that call is the difference between a dog asleep on the bed and a dog barking at every cheer through the wall.
### Per stay or per night: what the St. Louis fees really cost
The fee itself matters less than how it’s counted. A per-stay fee is paid once. A per-night fee keeps running every morning you wake up to a cold nose on your hand. And a per-pet fee doubles the moment the second dog jumps out of the back seat.
At Ballpark Village, Live! by Loews St. Louis welcomes cats and dogs, two per room, for $50 per accommodation, per stay. Pets get their own room-service menu, a welcome letter from the general manager, toys and bedding. In the Central West End, the Royal Sonesta Chase Park Plaza says it has no breed or weight restrictions, allows up to two pets, and charges an $80 fee per stay. Out on the Delmar Loop, the Moonrise Hotel says “big or small, we love them all,” puts every pet on one designated floor, and charges a non-refundable $50 cleaning fee per pet, not per day.
Then there’s Drury. Its pet guidelines apply chain-wide: no more than two pets per room, a total combined weight of 80 pounds, and a daily fee on any room with pets. The guidelines don’t print a dollar figure for that daily fee, so ask the specific hotel before a long weekend. A nightly fee is the one that grows while you sleep. Drury also asks you to take the stairwells with your pet, and not to leave a pet alone in the room at any time.
Four Seasons Hotel St. Louis, on the riverfront downtown, takes cats and dogs up to 40 pounds. Its posted terms list a cleaning fee for damage or stains, plus a possible fee if a pet left alone draws noise complaints, and they ask you not to leave your pet unattended at all. Your room is serviced only when you’re present. There’s an in-room dining menu for both dogs and cats, which tells you somebody there has watched a dog stare at a room-service cart.
### Which St. Louis hotels set weight limits or two-pet caps?
Magnolia, Red Roof, the Loews and the Chase Park Plaza cap you at two pets. So does Drury. Weight is where they split: Four Seasons stops at 40 pounds, Drury at 80 pounds combined, Red Roof at 80 pounds per pet. The Chase Park Plaza says no weight restrictions, and Magnolia takes all sizes.
So if you travel with a big dog, a Newfoundland or a pair of labs, your shortlist is the Chase Park Plaza in the Central West End, Magnolia downtown, the Moonrise on the Delmar Loop, or Red Roof at up to 80 pounds each. Call the front desk at that specific hotel, not the national number, and ask them to type the fee, the weight limit and the pet count into your reservation notes. A sentence in your confirmation email beats any icon on any site.

### Can a St. Louis hotel charge a pet fee for a service dog?
No. The Justice Department’s ADA rules say that if a business charges a deposit or fee to guests with pets, it must waive it for service animals. A hotel can still charge for damage a service animal causes, the same as it would any guest. Staff may ask only two questions: is the dog a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task has it been trained to perform. They can’t require documentation or ask the dog to demonstrate. And per the ADA’s FAQ, you can’t leave a service dog in the hotel room when you go out; the dog must be under your control at all times.
Emotional support animals are different. Under the ADA, dogs whose sole function is comfort or emotional support don’t qualify as service animals, so each company decides. In this one metro the two policies sit side by side. Drury says animals whose sole function is emotional support are pets, so its daily pet fee applies. Red Roof welcomes service animals and emotional support animals at no additional charge. If that difference matters to your budget, it’s worth a phone call.
One Missouri warning. Under RSMo 209.204, knowingly misrepresenting a dog as a service dog is a class C misdemeanor, with civil liability for any actual damages. A vest bought online to dodge a pet fee isn’t a clever hack in this state. It’s a crime.
Your dog’s share of the bill
From the hotels’ own pages: free at Magnolia downtown and for Red Roof’s first pet, $50 per stay at Live! by Loews, $50 per pet at the Moonrise, $80 per stay at the Chase Park Plaza. What moves it most is whether the fee runs per night or per stay, and how many pets you bring.
### Where can you walk a dog near downtown and Central West End hotels?
Downtown, the free off-leash spot is the Nestle Purina Laclede’s Landing Dog Park. Laclede’s Landing calls it a free park pets can enjoy daily, on and off their leash, and the Four Seasons puts it five minutes away. The district also points dog owners to the 12.2-mile Riverfront Trail, with watering stations for you and your pet along the way.
Now the gate most visitors don’t know about. Lucas Park Dog Park downtown runs on membership: an online application, approval by its board, an annual fee of $80 plus $40 for an additional dog, then a gate code and a membership tag. Memberships cover the calendar year and can’t be prorated. A guest in town for two nights isn’t getting through that gate, no matter what the map app says.
The Gateway Arch grounds, a seven-minute walk from the Four Seasons by the hotel’s own count, welcome pets anywhere outdoors on a leash no more than 6 feet long. Only service animals go inside buildings, and dogs may not swim in the reflecting pools. Show a ranger at the visitor center photos or videos of your dog following the B.A.R.K. rules and it earns a keepsake, in person only.
Out west, the Moonrise sits on the Delmar Loop, where patio tables fill on warm nights. Near the Chase Park Plaza, ask the desk for the vet and park information the hotel keeps for pet guests. You want the vet’s number before you need it. ### What should you ask before booking a pet-friendly room?
Six questions, and get every answer in writing:
The fee and how it’s counted. Per night or per stay, per pet or per room. $50 per stay at the Loews and a daily fee at Drury are different animals on a four-night trip.
Weight, per pet or combined. Drury’s 80 is combined; Red Roof’s is per pet.
Species. Some hotels that say “pets” mean dogs. Ask about your cat by name.
Alone in the room. Four Seasons and Drury say never. Red Roof allows it only in an emergency, after you tell the front desk and leave your contact information, and not if the pet is disturbing guests or causing damage. If a wedding or a ballgame is on the schedule, line up one of the pet sitters in St. Louis before you arrive.
Housekeeping. Four Seasons services the room only when you’re present. Red Roof won’t clean with the pet inside. Magnolia cleans only if the pet is out, or caged with you there.
Damage. Magnolia’s damage and cleaning fees begin at $400. Ask for the minimum before your dog meets the curtains.
And if your dog is over every limit here, price a few nights of dog boarding in St. Louis against the hotel fee. Sometimes the kennel is cheaper. Sometimes the dog is happier, too.
Your dog may not be allowed to stay alone in the room. Four Seasons asks you never to leave a pet unattended, and Drury says the same. If your trip includes a dinner or a game she can’t come to, book one of the dog walkers around St. Louis for those hours before you check in.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is the Four Seasons hotel St Louis pet-friendly?
A.  Yes. Both cats and dogs are welcome, as long as the pet weighs no more than 40 pounds and is trained, vaccinated and leashed outside the room. Pets can’t go into the restaurants, pool, spa or fitness center, and the hotel asks you not to leave your pet unattended at any time. The hotel lists a cleaning fee for damage or stains and recommends dog walkers with 24 hours’ notice. Confirm the current terms when you book.
### Q. Can you leave your pet unattended in a hotel room?
A.  Usually not. Four Seasons St. Louis and Drury both say never. Red Roof allows it only in an emergency, after you notify the front desk and leave your contact information, and never for a pet that’s disturbing guests or causing damage. Under ADA guidance, even a service dog can’t be left behind in the room. If you’ll be gone for hours, book a sitter or a dog walker.
### Q. How to avoid pet fees at hotels?
A.  Book a hotel that charges no pet fee. Magnolia Hotel St. Louis lets pets stay free with no deposits or added fees, and Red Roof lets your first pet stay free. On longer trips, look at per-stay fees: $50 per stay at the Loews, $80 per stay at the Chase Park Plaza. Read the damage terms, because that’s where free hotels make it up. And don’t fake a service dog. In Missouri that’s a misdemeanor.
### Q. What hotel chain has the cheapest pet fee?
A.  At Red Roof the first pet stays free, and a second costs $15 a night, capped at $105 per pet for stays of seven nights or longer. Magnolia charges nothing at its downtown St. Louis hotel. Drury charges a daily fee, and the Loews charges $50 per stay. Red Roof says to confirm details with the specific hotel before booking, and that’s good advice everywhere.
### Q. Can I take my pet to a hotel?
A.  In St. Louis, usually yes, if that hotel’s policy allows it and you declare the pet at check-in. Most cap you at two pets, and many set a weight limit, either per pet or combined. Some keep pets to certain rooms or a single floor, like the Moonrise. Ask for a pet-friendly room when you book, not when you arrive.
### Q. Where can I find dog friendly vacations in Missouri?
A.  Start with Missouri State Parks. Its Cabins for Canines program makes approximately 30% of park lodging units available to owners with dogs, including cabins, camper cabins and yurts, with two dogs per unit regardless of size and a per-dog, per-night fee that varies by unit. Outside, dogs stay on a leash no longer than 10 feet, and they go in a crate or kennel if you leave them in the unit.

## Fish and Reptile Stores in St. Louis: Who Sells What, Reptile Show Dates, and the Tap Water Trap
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/fish-and-reptile-stores-in-st-louis
The overnight bucket doesn’t work here. Fill it at the kitchen tap, leave it on the floor until morning, and the chlorine is supposed to drift off so the new tetras can go in safe. That trick was built for plain chlorine. St. Louis City Water and Missouri American Water both disinfect with chloramine, and Missouri American Water’s own fact sheet says chloramine is stable enough to stay in water for weeks.
No store list mentions that. The recycled ones are too busy sending you to a fish shop on Gravois that Google now marks permanently closed, or to a Collinsville aquarium store that has closed too.
So here’s the version a regular would give you. St. Louis has a real web of independent fish and reptile shops, most of them on the south side and out Manchester Road, plus two reptile show circuits, a fish club whose auctions are stocked by local hobbyists, and a few animal rules that change at the city line and again at the river. Know those, and the shop you choose matters less than the questions you ask inside it. This is the scaly, finned corner of pet-friendly St. Louis, and it pays off for the people who do their homework.
### Where can I buy live fish?
In St. Louis, live fish are sold at independent aquarium stores, at chain pet stores with aquatics departments, at the Missouri Aquarium Society’s auctions and swaps, and by aquatics vendors at reptile and exotic shows. Independent shops usually carry the most species, plants and saltwater livestock, and their staff can match fish to your tank.
Each one sells something a little different. The pet superstores keep the longest hours and stock the fish most beginners start with: guppies, mollies, tetras, bettas, goldfish. The independents go deeper. Planted-tank shops carry shrimp, live plants and driftwood. Reef shops sell saltwater fish and coral, and some grow their own. Hobbyist auctions sell fish raised in somebody’s fish room in the metro, in water a lot like yours.
Shows are the wild card. The Show Me Reptile Show’s vendor list for its Bridgeton dates has included an aquatics seller offering freshwater, saltwater and brackish stock alongside the snakes and geckos. Don’t count on any one vendor being there twice.
Online livestock shippers exist too, and plenty of serious keepers use them for rare species. The trade-off is a day or two in a box. For a first tank, buying local lets you watch the fish eat before it goes in the bag. That’s worth more than a discount.
### Where are the independent aquarium stores in St. Louis?
Four of them sit on a short list of south-side roads: Telegraph, Gravois, Watson and South Lindbergh. West County, St. Charles County and the Metro East have the rest. Several of these shops open at noon or later, and a few close early in the week, so check current hours before you drive. They’re listed here by area, not by preference.
STL Aquatics, Telegraph Road in South County. Freshwater and saltwater fish, coral, tanks and supplies, plus pond design, installation and upkeep. If an older list sends you to Gateway Aquatics, this is the same storefront. According to the shop’s own history, an electrical fire hit Gateway Aquatics in 2023, long-time employees became the new owners, and the remodeled space reopened under the new name.
Art of Aquaria, Gravois Road in south St. Louis County. A planted-tank and aquascaping shop whose own social accounts list fish, shrimp, aquatic plants, hardscape, reptiles and arachnids. Reviewers keep mentioning a room where you can lay out rock and driftwood before you buy any of it.
Tropical World Pets, Watson Road in Webster Groves. A fish and reptile shop with what it calls a huge tank showroom, plus freshwater fish, reptiles and dry goods. Its website lists hours into the evening six days a week.
Seascape Studio, South Lindbergh in Sunset Hills. Saltwater only. The shop’s site says it has carried 957 different marine species and keeps a curator in charge of husbandry to limit the parasites and disease that reach customers’ tanks. It tests water, too.
Aqua World, Manchester Road in Ellisville. Freshwater, saltwater and pond stock, and by its own description a large selection of live aquarium plants. Its former South City store on Gravois is the one Google lists as permanently closed, so make sure your map pin lands in Ellisville.
Marine Solutions, Triad South Drive in St. Charles. Open since 1998, per its website, with freshwater and saltwater stock, reef-keeping education and tank maintenance. Most days it doesn’t open until the afternoon.
Aqua-Nook, Troy Road in Edwardsville. Freshwater fish, saltwater fish and coral, with local delivery and tank setup service. Listings have shown it closed Monday and Tuesday.
The Corner Reef, Columbia, Illinois. A saltwater boutique that describes itself as about ten minutes from the South County mall and grows some of its own coral from small cuttings called frags. An older map listing at a different Columbia address shows as closed, so confirm the current location before you go.
Midwest Tropical Fish, State Street in Jerseyville. Freshwater fish, cichlids, plecos, saltwater stock, live reptiles and feeders, according to its site.
The chains have aquatics departments all over the metro, too. Every question in the next few sections works there just as well.
### Where can you buy a reptile in St. Louis?
Three reptile-first shops show how different these places can be.
Exotic A.R.C. (Amphibian Reptile Center), Lemay Ferry Road in south St. Louis County. A reptile breeding facility with a retail store attached, selling live animals, feeders and supplies. Its Facebook page lists it open seven days a week. It’s also on the vendor roster for November’s NARBC show in St. Charles.
The Reptile Room, Manchester Road in Ballwin. Its parent company, Tarantula Cribs, started in 2020 selling tarantula enclosures, and the shop grew out of that. It’s mostly a supply and feeder shop: frozen and live rodents, dubia roaches, crickets, hornworms, enclosures and lighting. Per its own FAQ, it sells animals only now and then, when it breeds them in house or works closely with a trusted breeder. The draw for families is the ticketed Wildlife Discovery Zone, where kids and adults meet the animal ambassadors up close. On a wet Saturday it belongs on the same list as the rainy-day indoor play places for kids in St. Louis.
Show Me Reptile Shop, Triad Center Drive in St. Peters. Run by the team behind the Show Me Reptile Show, it sells live reptiles, feeders, enclosures and supplies, and it offers free UVB bulb testing. That last one matters more than it sounds. The shop points out that older bulbs lose the ability to put out the UVB many reptiles need, and a bulb can keep glowing long after that happens.
Several fish shops keep reptiles too. Tropical World Pets, Art of Aquaria and Midwest Tropical Fish all list them. The chains usually carry the common starter species, bearded dragons, leopard geckos and ball pythons, along with most of the supplies.
### Why does St. Louis tap water kill new fish?
Because it’s designed to kill things, and it keeps working long after it leaves the faucet. St. Louis City Water’s 2025 water quality report lists chloramine in the distribution system at 1.84 to 3.44 parts per million. Missouri American Water, which serves much of St. Louis County, uses chloramine at its St. Louis treatment plants as well.
Chloramine is chlorine bonded to a little ammonia. People drink it with no trouble. Fish take it straight across their gills. And unlike plain chlorine, it doesn’t float out of a bucket overnight. Missouri American Water’s chloramine fact sheet says it can stay in water for weeks and tells fish owners to remove it from any water used in tanks or ponds.
The fix costs a few dollars. Buy a water conditioner that names chloramine on the label. A chlorine-only product isn’t enough. Dose it for the full volume of water you’re adding, every single time. A 20 percent change on a 55-gallon tank is 11 gallons that need treating, not a capful.
Not on City or Missouri American water? Plenty of St. Charles County, Jefferson County and Metro East towns run their own systems or buy water from a neighbor. Your utility’s annual water quality report names its disinfectant, and the City’s is posted as a PDF. Read yours before your first water change.
Then give the tank time. A brand-new tank hasn’t grown the bacteria that break down fish waste, and a crystal-clear tank can still turn lethal in week two. Many shops will test a water sample for you. Bring one in before you bring fish home.
### Big-box or local fish store: where do fish come out healthier?
Neither, automatically. Chains and independents mostly buy from wholesalers and fish farms, and a fish’s odds have more to do with what happened after it arrived than with the sign out front. The difference is how long a shop holds new fish, whether it treats them, and whether the person at the tank can tell you.
Some shops publish their process. The Corner Reef says every fish that arrives is observed for a minimum holding time, most go through a low-salinity, copper-treated system with ultraviolet sterilization, and a fish that doesn’t look right doesn’t get sold. Seascape Studio puts a husbandry curator on the same job. That’s the bar. Ask any shop, chain or local, how close it gets.
Questions that sort it out fast: How long has this fish been here? Has it eaten today, and can I watch it eat? Does this tank share water with the ones around it? Do you quarantine new arrivals? What happens if it dies in the first week?
Then look for yourself. Skip any tank with a dead fish in it, even if the one you want looks fine, because when a row of tanks runs on one shared filter system, those tanks share whatever is going around. Pass on fish with white specks, clamped fins, ragged edges or a hollow belly.
Chains win on hours, and often on return policies. Independents usually win on range, and on staff who keep tanks at home. Pick on the answers you get. The logo tells you nothing.
Wanted fish for dinner instead? St. Louis seafood boils and crawfish
### Which aquarium fish outgrow a St. Louis living room?
The ones sold at three inches that want to be three feet. The Missouri Aquarium Society won’t allow them to be sold at its auctions, its swaps or on its social media at all. Its written policy bars any fish that can’t live comfortably as an adult in a 200-gallon aquarium, which for most species means anything over about 14 inches.
The club names names: redtail catfish, iridescent sharks, pacu, silver arowana, tiger shovelnose and arapaima. Several of those turn up as small juveniles in tanks around town. The club drew that line for itself. Most stores leave it to you.
You don’t need a monster for this to bite. The owner of a shop just south of Arnold put it plainly to the Leader, Jefferson County’s newspaper, in February 2026: an Oscar grows to about 10 inches, that calls for a 55-gallon tank, and a buyer who only wants a 20-gallon tank is headed for trouble. Ask for the adult size of every fish before it goes in the bag. Then size the tank to the adult, not the baby.
Already have one that’s outgrowing its tank? The club’s policy lets those fish be offered free for rehoming or rescue. That’s a better ending than a creek.
### Can you buy fish straight from St. Louis hobbyists?
Yes, and it’s the least-known way to stock a tank in this town. The Missouri Aquarium Society, a nonprofit hobby club, runs auctions three times a year, in winter, spring and fall, at Jost Chemical on Lackland Road. In 2026 the fall auction was set for Saturday, November 7; after that, the winter auction comes next. Doors open at 10 a.m. and bidding starts at 11, per the club’s auction page.
Buyers register free at the door. You don’t have to be a member to buy or to sell. An auctioneer runs a spoken auction through the day with a silent auction alongside it, and everyone settles up in cash or card at the end.
What’s on the table is often bred locally. The club’s Breeders Award Program, running since 1971, gives members points for spawning fish and writing up how they did it, and members donate fry to the monthly meetings. Those platies may well have grown up in a basement fish room twenty minutes from yours.
The club also runs swaps three times a year, free to walk in, where vendors and other clubs sell fish, plants, amphibians, isopods and equipment from tables. The winter 2027 swap date hadn’t been set when this was written. General meetings are the third Thursday of the month at 7:30 p.m., and guests are welcome.
### When are the St. Louis reptile shows, and are they cheaper?
Two organizers run the big recurring shows here, and the rest of 2026 has three shows between them.
Show Me Reptile Show, District 9 Machinists Hall, St. Charles Rock Road in Bridgeton. Its 2026 calendar ran eight show days, the last two on Sunday, October 25, and Sunday, December 6, both listed from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. with a paid VIP hour before that. Event listings put kids 6 and under in free, and adult admission has been listed between $10 and $15, so check the organizer’s site before you go.
NARBC St. Louis, Saint Charles Convention Center. The 2026 dates: Saturday and Sunday, November 14 and 15. Per NARBC’s show page, a one-day ticket is $15 for ages 13 and up and $10 for ages 6 to 12, kids 5 and under get in free with a paid adult, and a $50 VIP pass adds a Friday preview during setup. The show is captive-bred only, checked by inspection. Venomous animals may appear on educational display, never for sale. The roster topped 117 vendors by late July 2026, and local names on it include Exotic A.R.C. and Show Me Reptile Shop. Bring cash, too. NARBC warns that the on-site ATMs aren’t its own and can run dry by Saturday afternoon.
Are they cheaper? For common captive-bred species, often, because you’re buying from the breeder with no storefront in the middle. For rare color morphs, not necessarily. NARBC says plainly that it can’t set or negotiate vendor prices and that any animal you buy is between you and that vendor. Price the same species at a shop the week before, so you know a deal when you see one.
Whatever you buy, get the seller’s name and contact, the hatch date, and what the animal has eaten and when. A breeder who won’t write that down is telling you something.
### What should you check before buying a reptile in Missouri?
Start with the animal, then the law. Plenty of buyers get the first part right and never think about the second.
Is it eating, and what? Ask for the last feeding date, and whether a snake takes frozen-thawed prey or only live. A reptile that hasn’t eaten since it changed hands is a vet bill waiting to happen.
How big, and what will the setup cost? The enclosure, heat and UVB lighting often cost more than the animal. Write the list before the show, the same way you’d plan what to buy for a new puppy, so you aren’t buying a tank on impulse at a folding table.
Who’s the vet? The Show Me Reptile Show’s own advice is to get a new pet established with a vet and have a fecal exam done. Not every clinic sees reptiles, so line one up from our guide to exotic vets in St. Louis before the animal comes home. The questions in how to choose a vet in St. Louis still apply, plus one more: how many reptiles do you see in a month?
Is it legal where you live? This is where the metro gets complicated.
Missouri law, RSMo 578.023, requires anyone keeping a deadly, dangerous or poisonous reptile, or a dangerous reptile over eight feet long, to register it with local law enforcement in the county where it’s kept. Skipping that is a class C misdemeanor.
The City of St. Louis goes further. Its animal laws page lists all venomous snakes and any constrictor snake over eight feet among its prohibited pets, along with alligators, crocodiles and caimans. A big python a County keeper has registered can become a prohibited pet the day it moves across the city line.
Some St. Louis County municipalities add their own layer. One North County city’s code requires a city permit to buy, sell or keep any non-domestic animal, and its list of exempt household pets names dogs, cats, caged birds, small caged animals such as hamsters and rabbits, and aquarium animals. Reptiles aren’t on it. Call your city hall before the bearded dragon comes home.
Across the river, Illinois handles reptiles under its Herptiles-Herps Act. Venomous species and crocodilians count as special use herptiles there, and you need a permit from the Illinois Department of Natural Resources before you acquire one.
Two more rules catch people at shows. Native Missouri reptiles taken from the wild can’t be bought, sold or traded, according to the Missouri Department of Conservation, and while residents may keep a limited number of many native species, that allowance doesn’t cover venomous snakes or rare ones. So a three-toed box turtle, Missouri’s state reptile, offered for sale should raise questions. And under a federal rule dating to 1975, turtles with shells under four inches long can’t be sold as pets because of the salmonella risk to kids, per the FDA. A table of tiny turtles is a table to walk past.
Ordinances change. Check the current rules with your city or county before you buy anything that isn’t a fish.
Ready to shop? Compare aquarium stores around St. Louis and pet stores near you on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call ahead with your tank size and your water utility’s name in hand.
If you run a fish room, a reptile shop or a pond service anywhere in the metro, list it with us so the family walking out of the Bridgeton show with a new ball python finds your feeders on the drive home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are snakes cheaper at Expos?
A.  Often, for common captive-bred species, because you’re buying from the breeder with no store in the middle. Not always, though. Show organizers don’t set prices, and a rare morph can cost more at a table than a normal one does at a shop. Price the same species at a local shop first, then compare at the show.
### Q. Can you bring your own reptile to a reptile expo?
A.  Usually not. NARBC’s St. Louis show admits only service animals as defined by the ADA, with documentation, and asks people not to walk pets through the venue. Outside animals can carry mites or disease onto a floor full of other people’s stock. If you want a breeder’s opinion on your animal, bring photos and ask.
### Q. Where is the best place to buy fish for an aquarium?
A.  The one that can answer three questions: how long has this fish been here, is it eating, and how big will it get? Independent shops around St. Louis usually carry more species and plants. Chains keep longer hours. Hobbyist auctions sell fish bred locally. Ask the same three questions at all of them.
### Q. How much does an aquarium fish cost?
A.  Common freshwater fish are cheap. The owner of a shop south of Arnold told the Leader in February 2026 that some fish cost $1 and some $10, depending on how rare they are, and that tanks ran about $2 a gallon. Saltwater fish and coral cost far more. Prices change with every shipment, so read the tank label.
### Q. What are the easiest aquarium fish to keep?
A.  Hardy community fish such as zebra danios, platies, white cloud mountain minnows and a small group of corydoras catfish. Bettas are easy too, given a heated, filtered tank instead of a cup. The tank matters more than the fish: cycle it first, treat St. Louis tap water for chloramine, and don’t overstock.
### Q. How often should I change tank water?
A.  Most keepers change part of the water, often 10 to 25 percent, every week or two, and heavily stocked tanks need more. In St. Louis, treat every bucket of tap water with a conditioner rated for chloramine, dosed for the volume you’re adding, and match the temperature so the fish don’t get shocked.
### Q. Can I let St. Louis tap water sit overnight to make it safe for fish?
A.  No. St. Louis City Water and Missouri American Water both disinfect with chloramine, which doesn’t gas off the way plain chlorine does. Missouri American Water says it can stay in water for weeks. Use a water conditioner labeled for chloramine every time tap water goes into a tank or a pond.
### Q. Can you sell your own fish in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Missouri Aquarium Society’s auctions take sellers who pre-register with the auction chair, and you don’t need to be a member, though members get priority for seller spots. The club won’t sell fish that outgrow a 200-gallon tank. At its swaps, a seller’s table costs $30.

## $100 More to Come to You: What Mobile Vets in St. Louis Charge
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mobile-vets-in-st-louis
Your cat hears the carrier before you touch it. The click of the closet door, and she’s gone under the bed, and you’re on your knees with a flashlight while the clock runs toward the appointment. This time the carrier stays put. A van idles at the curb, its generator humming, and the vet walks up your front steps with your cat still twenty feet from her own food bowl.
Here’s the part nobody says out loud on the phone. A house call is a normal vet visit with a drive stapled to it, and the drive has a price. One St. Louis practice prints that price in plain dollars. Pets at Rest Hospice & Home Euthanasia, in Creve Coeur, charges $375 for a euthanasia visit at its Comfort Center on Decker Lane and $475 for the same visit in your home. Same visit, $100 apart. The difference is the drive to your door.
Out in Franklin County, Pet Country’s mobile clinic posts its trip fee too: it starts at $56 for the first 10 miles, before a $46 exam.
So do this before you book anyone. Call and ask for two numbers, the visit and the drive, and ask whether the exam is priced per pet. Then ask the neighbor with the beagle if she wants in. Pet Country invites friends, relatives and neighbors at one address to share the house call fee, which turns one trip fee into two or three exams and no car ride for anybody. If you’re new in town and still building your list, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis covers the rest of pet life here.
### Is a mobile vet cheaper than a regular vet?
Usually not, visit for visit. You pay for the exam and the shots much like you would at a clinic, then a trip fee on top, so one pet almost always costs more at home. The math narrows when several pets share one trip fee, and for a pet that panics in the car, you’re paying for calm.
Here are real numbers from each practice’s own website. Pet Country Housecall Veterinary Services works out of a 26-foot mobile clinic based in Sullivan. Its house call fee starts at $56 for the first 10 miles, plus $1 to $4 for each extra mile, up to 20 more. A physical exam is $46 per pet, or $40 per pet when it’s the yearly exam that comes with vaccinations. Vaccines run $22 to $40 apiece. One dog, a yearly exam and two shots, inside those first ten miles: roughly $140 to $176 before any lab work.
Now drive the same dog to Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic on South Jefferson, a not-for-profit that posts its wellness prices. The wellness exam is $25. Rabies is $25. The DHLPP distemper shot is $20. That’s $70 for the same visit. The catch is the sidewalk: walk-in clients line up before wellness hours start, and the clinic tells you to be ready to wait outside. It also doesn’t see sick or injured pets. A full-service clinic usually lands somewhere between the two, and few publish an exam fee, so ask when you call. If price is the whole question, our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis goes deeper.
The math flips in a house with three cats. Pet Country charges the trip fee once per visit and the exam per pet, so three yearly exams come to $56 plus three $40 exams: $176, before the shots. Weigh that against three carriers, three cats who heard the closet door and vanished, one car and one waiting room. Plenty of people would pay $176 to skip that afternoon entirely.
### What a van can do in your driveway, and what still needs a building
Most of a normal year travels well: exams, vaccines, blood draws, hospice care and euthanasia. Overnight stays and after-hours emergencies don’t. How much falls in between depends on which of two very different setups pulls up to your curb.
The first is a clinic on wheels. St. Louis MobileVet, run by Drs. Jaime Plappert-Waltman and Brad Waltman, works from a 2008 Dodge Sprinter with a 6,000-watt generator. The practice says the layout started as a drawing on graph paper, then moved up to sidewalk chalk and cardboard cutouts before it was built in Austin, Texas. In the back are stainless steel cages, one with a clear airtight door for oxygen therapy, and a lab with Doppler blood pressure, ECG and a microscope. In the middle: an exam table with running water and an anesthesia machine. It keeps weekday hours, 8:30 to 5.
Pet Country’s 26-footer goes further. Its in-house chemistry analyzer needs two drops of blood and gives results in about 12 minutes. It takes digital x-rays for $160 and does spays, neuters and other soft-tissue surgery. The practice says plainly that it isn’t staffed or equipped to hospitalize patients or handle after-hours emergencies, and that urgent care during office hours is for current clients only.
People are asking
### Is it cheaper to go to a regular vet or an emergency vet in St. Louis?
A regular vet, for anything that can wait for office hours. Carol House Quick Fix on South Jefferson charges $25 for a wellness exam, while Animal Emergency Clinic on Big Bend Road, open 24/7, requires a deposit for every emergency exam and gives you a good-faith estimate before it treats. For the in-between night, UrgentVet’s St. Louis urgent care is open after hours, weekends and holidays and says it costs up to 40% less than the emergency vet.
The second setup is a vet with a bag. Daniel Randall Veterinary Clinic in Godfrey, on the Illinois side, lists what its house calls cover: physical exams, vaccinations, parasite prevention, urine collection and blood draws, plus in-home euthanasia. Anything that needs an x-ray machine or an operating table means a trip to the building.
Neither one replaces a hospital. A dog that needs IV fluids overnight, a cat straining in the litter box at 2 a.m., a leg that won’t hold weight after a fall off the deck: those belong somewhere with people awake all night. Even if a van handles the rest of your pet’s year, keep our guide to finding an emergency vet in St. Louis where you can reach it fast.
One more limit is species. Home with Dignity, for one, asks owners of rabbits and guinea pigs to call first and says it can’t help with reptiles. For a bearded dragon, a cockatiel or a rabbit with a bad tooth, start with exotic vets in St. Louis instead.
### Which parts of the metro do St. Louis mobile vets cover?
The edges, mostly. The general-practice vans and house-call vets we could verify work St. Charles County, west St. Louis County, Franklin County and the Illinois side. Inside the city limits, the in-home vets who pick up the phone are mostly end-of-life practices. That gap is why so many people in South City decide nobody here makes house calls.
West County and St. Charles County: St. Louis MobileVet’s service-area page says it has limited its area and is accepting new patients in most of St. Charles County and West County. Call, text or email before you plan around it.
Franklin County: Pet Country covers a 30-mile radius around Sullivan for routine visits and stretches to 60 miles for home euthanasia.
End-of-life practices cover the most ground. Compassionate In-Home Euthanasia, Dr. Laura Kee’s practice, lists St. Louis City plus St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson and Franklin counties, and says it has helped over 6,500 families since 2015. Home with Dignity names Ballwin, Chesterfield, Wildwood, Fenton, Florissant, Arnold, St. Peters, Hillsboro, Festus and High Ridge among the towns it serves regularly, and adds $100 outside its area. Pets at Rest adds $50 for its extended area.
Then there’s the river. The Veterinary Medicine Mobility Act, approved August 1, 2014, lets a vet transport and dispense controlled substances outside the clinic, but only at a site in a state where that vet is licensed to practice. If you live on the Illinois side, ask before the van heads over the Poplar Street Bridge. You can check any vet yourself on Missouri’s license lookup or the Illinois license lookup.
### Can a mobile vet put a pet to sleep at home?
Yes, and in St. Louis it’s the easiest house call to find. A licensed vet comes to your home, gives a sedative so your pet slips into a deep sleep, and only when you’re ready gives the final injection. Among the practices that post prices near the city, the home visit runs $370 to $475, with cremation on top.
Home with Dignity says the sedation typically takes 5 to 15 minutes to take full effect, while your pet grows drowsy and relaxed, and that many families use that time for final moments. Hands on the fur. The weight of a head in your lap. It can happen on a favorite bed, on the couch, or in the yard under the tree where the dog always slept. Most of its home visits last 30 to 60 minutes from arrival to departure.
Other pets can be there, and so can kids. Home with Dignity says that letting other pets see or smell their companion after passing helps them understand the loss, and its vets talk with families about the right involvement for children.
Here’s what the practices publish:
Home with Dignity: $370 if you keep your pet at home for burial; with transport included, $415 up to 49 pounds, $440 for 50 to 99 pounds and $450 for 100 and up. Weekends add $30 and after-hours visits add $100. Communal cremation is $160 and private cremation $310. A lock of fur in a memorial pouch is included.
Pets at Rest: $475 at home or $375 at the Comfort Center. Private cremation is $250 to $350 by weight, with the ashes returned in a cherry wooden box; communal starts at $100.
Pet Country, out in Franklin County: $120 to $400, with sedation and a clay or ink pawprint included.
Compassionate In-Home Euthanasia works by appointment only; text Dr. Kee for a price.
Some details matter more than the price. Pets at Rest says that for pets over 75 pounds, cremation has to be arranged directly with the crematory. Home with Dignity settles payment over the phone before the appointment, so nobody is reaching for a card in that room; it takes no cash or checks and adds 2.5% for credit cards. If your pet is suffering tonight and nobody can come, an emergency hospital can help at any hour.
There’s also a middle path most people never hear about. The Pets at Rest Comfort Center exists for families who want the quiet of a living room without the memory of a death in their own. The practice says you’ll feel at home there, and your house is still just your house when you get back.
