Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/columbia-bottom-conservation-area
Stale review pages still describe Columbia Bottom Conservation Area like a park somebody forgot about. One review on a travel site went further and said the place “should be permanently closed.” As of October 9, 2026, it mostly is. Nobody gave up on it, though. The Missouri Department of Conservation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers are building new setback levees so that about 3,500 acres of this river bottom can flood again. On purpose.
That’s the most interesting thing happening on any St. Louis riverfront right now, and the review pages haven’t caught up. They won’t tell you that the Missouri River boat ramp is the only way in this fall, why the gates went up, or that the same ground grows about 14 fields of sunflowers in summer to feed mourning doves. This page will. It also covers the blue catfish, the hunting and shooting rules, the birds, and the odd history of roughly 4,300 acres the city once bought for an airport.
Columbia Bottom is one stop in our guide to the St. Louis riverfront. Every date, rule and number below comes from MDC and its magazines, Missouri’s Wildlife Code, St. Louis Public Radio or other published sources, current as of October 2026. Construction changes things week to week, so call MDC’s St. Louis Regional Office at (636) 441-4554 before you load the truck.
### Where can I find a sunflower field in Missouri?
The Missouri Department of Conservation plants sunflower fields on its conservation areas to feed mourning doves. Near St. Louis, the best known are at Columbia Bottom Conservation Area, where about 14 fields go in around early May and are staggered so blooms run from early July to mid-August. Check MDC for access before you go.
Here’s the catch if you’re planning ahead. As of October 9, 2026, Columbia Bottom is closed to the public except for its Missouri River boat ramp, and MDC hasn’t said when the rest reopens. The 2026 flowers made it through. St. Louis Public Radio reported in April that the sunflower fields would stay open for the summer even after the road to the confluence closed, and MDC announced the bloom on July 6. Whether fields get planted in 2027, with the levee work still finishing, is a question only MDC can answer.
Columbia Bottom isn’t MDC’s only sunflower ground. The department plants dove fields on other conservation areas around the state, and each July it posts a bloom announcement. That release is the one to watch next summer. It’ll tell you which fields are blooming, where to park, and whether this river bottom made the list again.
### Is Columbia Bottom Conservation Area open right now?
Only the boat ramp. MDC’s area page, checked October 9, 2026, says public access is “currently limited to the boat ramp.” The road to the Missouri River ramp reopened on September 30, about three weeks after MDC closed the entire area “until further notice.” Trails, fields, the confluence platform and the Mississippi paddle access remain off-limits, with no reopening date announced.
The closures came in steps, which is why so much of what you’ll find online contradicts itself:
November 2025: the Army Corps awarded the setback-levee project.
January 8, 2026: MDC said work was underway and expected to finish in December 2026.
April 2026: the road and foot trail to the confluence closed until the old river levee is demolished, and the kayak and canoe access to the Mississippi closed with them. The sunflower fields stayed open for the summer.
September 8, 2026: the entire area closed until further notice.
September 30, 2026: the road to the Missouri River boat ramp reopened. Everything else stayed restricted.
Even in a normal year, parts of the area close from October 15 to March 1 for waterfowl. So when MDC does lift the construction closure, don’t be surprised if some roads stay shut through the winter anyway.
When it’s open, Columbia Bottom keeps daylight hours: it closes a half hour after sunset and opens a half hour before sunrise. MDC lists no entry fee. Put 801 Strodtman Road in your phone. That’s north St. Louis County, about 3 miles north of I-270, and the road you take north becomes Columbia Bottom Road at Larimore Road. Don’t count on working restrooms during construction.
Don’t plan around the visitor center, either. The Howard and Joyce Wood Education and Visitor Center stopped serving as a public contact office on January 1, 2020. Staff still work in the building, but most of MDC’s education programs moved to another St. Louis location. Questions go to the regional office.
Say you live in Jennings, own a johnboat and have an open Saturday this month. You can still launch here. You just can’t wander. Drive the reopened ramp road, put in on the Missouri, and treat everything beyond the ramp as a job site until MDC says otherwise.
### Why is MDC letting 3,500 acres flood on purpose?
Because the old levee kept losing. St. Louis Public Radio counts five failures of the river levee here, and MDC says high water closed the area in 2008, 2013, 2015, 2017 and 2019. In 2019, water sat on Columbia Bottom for almost six months. Rather than keep patching a wall the river keeps breaking, MDC and the Corps are moving the line back.
The damage list reads like a weather diary. The 1993 flood overtopped the levee and covered most of the area, and the 1993 and 1995 floods left sand behind. In December 2015 the river breached the levee in eight places, and the boat ramp stayed closed until September 2016. The 2019 flood left up to 4 feet of silt and mud, and the area reopened only in part on August 29 that year. Out at the confluence, floods dumped 2 to 4 feet of sediment.
Here’s what’s being built. New setback levees, about 10 feet tall, go up on the northwest and south sides to protect MDC’s office, the maintenance area and the neighbors. The damaged eastern levees come out so the land floods naturally. When the work is done, about 3,500 acres reconnect to the floodplain. The bill runs about $27 million: $12 million from MDC and $15 million from the American Rescue Plan Act. The Corps is aiming to finish tearing down the old levee by the end of 2026, and MDC has said it wants the area to “function as a wetland.”
Sit with that for a second. Nearly every levee you’ve driven past was built to keep the river off the land. This project tears one out to let it back in. No review page captures that, and neither does a top-ten list that treats the river as a backdrop.
There are trade-offs, and MDC hasn’t hidden them. MDC’s Dan Zarlenga told St. Louis Public Radio that parts of the area may become unreachable in some floods. He also said the reflooded land could raise bird diversity. MDC has already shut off the pumps and no longer maintains the waterfowl blinds. The Columbia Bottom you remember, with its seven managed wetland pools, is turning into something wetter and harder to predict.
The bigger picture explains the bet. MDC says Missouri has lost about 87 percent of its wetlands, and St. Louis Public Radio has called wetlands the most threatened ecosystem in the country. A few thousand acres where the Missouri meets the Mississippi won’t reverse that. It’s still a rare chance, this close to the city, to watch farmed bottomland go back to the river.
### When do the sunflowers bloom, and what are the rules?
Usually from early July to mid-August. MDC says a sunflower takes about 60 days to flower and each planting peaks for about 10 days, so the department plants about 14 fields in early May and staggers them. In 2025 a wet spring delayed planting slightly, and the 14 fields still went in staggered two weeks apart.
The flowers aren’t there for your photos. MDC plants them for mourning doves. The seed feeds the birds, the standing stalks give dove hunters cover, and the fields help other birds and pollinators along the way. That’s the part the photo posts tend to skip: the field you shoot in July can be a hunting field once dove season opens. For the first seven days of the season, doves here are managed hunt only, after 1 p.m.
In 2026 MDC leaned into the crowds. Its July 6 announcement added extra viewing plots near the road and signs pointing to the fields in bloom. The department knows the fields draw people, and it would rather steer them than fight them.
The rules MDC repeats each summer are short:
Don’t pick the flowers.
Park in the lots or on the shoulders, and never block a road or a gate.
Pack out whatever you bring in.
An ordinary photo session needs no permit. You do need one for drones, large props, groups of 10 or more, or shooting in closed areas or after hours.
Keep dogs leashed or confined.
One tip for the camera. Researchers at UC Davis reported in the journal Science in 2016 that mature sunflower heads face east. If that holds in these fields, morning light should land on the faces, and an evening session may leave you staring at the backs of the flowers. That’s our inference from the research, not an MDC rule, so walk the field edge before you set up.
Picture a family from Black Jack heading out on a weekday in mid-July with a toddler and a phone. The good version of that morning is an early start, a field MDC’s signs say is blooming, and a parking spot that doesn’t block a gate. The bad version is rolling in at the end of August, after the last planting has peaked, and deciding the whole place is overrated.
### What can you catch from the bank at Columbia Bottom?
Big catfish, mostly. MDC’s fishing prospects for the lower Missouri River promise “great bank fishing,” with many blue catfish of 25 to 35 inches, flatheads of 20 to 30 inches and a few fish reaching 45 inches. Columbia Bottom has more than 6.5 miles of river frontage, so when it’s fully open, there’s plenty of bank to work.
Then there’s the record. On July 20, 2010, an angler pulled a 130-pound blue catfish out of the Missouri near Columbia Bottom. For a while it was a pending world record, waiting on review by the International Game Fish Association. It still stands as the Missouri state record, and MDC’s Xplor magazine was still listing it in July 2025. Think about that the next time a 30-inch blue feels big.
Statewide fishing rules apply in the rivers and sloughs, with a few local specifics from MDC’s brochure and the Wildlife Code:
No seining or trapping live bait on the area.
Carp, buffalo, suckers and gar may be taken by atlatl, gig, bow or crossbow.
No boats left unattended overnight.
No houseboats, airboats or personal watercraft.
Now the rule that trips people up. Missouri’s statewide rule for conservation areas, 3 CSR 10-11.115, keeps most areas open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. but lets you fish, and launch or land a boat, at any hour where that’s authorized. Columbia Bottom is a named exception. Here you follow the posted daylight hours, closed from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise. Confirm with MDC’s St. Louis office at (636) 441-4554 before you plan anything after dark.
For now, most of that bank has to wait. With access limited to the boat ramp, the long stretch of shoreline along the River’s Edge Trail is off-limits until MDC reopens it, so ask the regional office what’s allowed around the ramp itself. Taking a boat up instead? Our breakdown of what boating costs near St. Louis covers the money and who needs a license. For shore fishing elsewhere while this one’s closed, our list of fishing spots in St. Louis includes the Mississippi.
### Can you hunt or shoot at Columbia Bottom?
Hunt, sometimes. Shoot targets, never. Deer hunting here is by managed hunt only, and MDC’s list shows all four 2026-27 Columbia Bottom managed deer hunts canceled. Target shooting isn’t allowed on the area, and there’s no range. With public access limited to the ramp, check with MDC before you plan any hunt this season.
Here’s how the rules read for when access returns:
Doves: managed hunt only, after 1 p.m., for the first seven days of the season, then normal legal hours.
Waterfowl: self-register with a Daily Waterfowl Hunting Tag, under a rule in effect since August 30, 2026. Don’t expect pumped pools or blinds.
Squirrel, rail and snipe: allowed with a daily tag.
Trapping: special use permit required.
Shot: no lead.
Rifles, handguns and slugs: single-projectile firearms are banned except for deer.
Hoping for archery-only ground instead? MDC keeps a sortable answer. Its “Conservation Areas: Deer Hunting Quick View” lists 559 areas and has a Method filter. Pick “Archery Methods Only” for the strictest list, or widen it with “Muzzleloader and Archery” and “Archery and Firearms.” All three allow bowhunting. If you’re a bowhunter in Berkeley who usually counts on a managed hunt up here, that filter is where this fall starts.
Target shooting follows one statewide rule. The Wildlife Code permits it only on designated public shooting ranges or by special use permit. Columbia Bottom has no range, and MDC says plainly that target shooting is not allowed here. Leave the clay thrower at home.
### What are the trails like, and where can you walk instead?
Flat, easy and closed for now. MDC’s map shows three trails, among them the paved Confluence Trail and the River’s Edge Trail, about 2.5 miles of flat natural surface through bottomland forest along the Missouri, from near the boat ramp to the confluence platform. As of October 2026, every trail on the area is closed.
When they reopen, bikes are allowed on the multi-use trails year-round, and e-bikes can use posted multi-use trails and service roads. Groups of 10 or more need a special use permit. Pack with the other area rules in mind:
Dogs on a leash or confined, except for hunting and training in designated portions.
No camping, no fireworks and no open fires.
No trail cameras, and no remote-control boats or vehicles.
Drones only with a special use permit.
Nuts, berries, fruits, mushrooms and wild greens are fine to gather for personal use.
Vehicles stay on roads and parking lots, at 45 mph unless posted.
Need a walk this weekend? Our roundup of easy, family-friendly hiking trails has flat options for short legs, and the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge puts you on foot over the Mississippi.
### What birds can you see at Columbia Bottom?
Close to 300 species. MDC counted 286 on eBird in 2019, and Audubon lists 285. The rarities include Fulvous Whistling-Duck, White Ibis, Tricolored Heron, White-tailed Kite and Golden Eagle. Bald eagles perch in the cottonwoods along the river, trumpeter swans turn up, and February is a good month for migrating waterfowl.
The habitat explains the variety. The area holds about 800 acres of bottomland forest, a 110-acre island and seven managed wetland pools, where pelicans, gulls and shorebirds gather. Eurasian Tree Sparrows have shown up at the visitor center feeders. And St. Louis Magazine reported in 2023 that snowy egrets, listed as endangered in Missouri, were appearing here too.
The reflooding could reshuffle that list. Zarlenga’s point was that reconnected floodplain could raise bird diversity, and the pumps are already off. Nobody can say yet which species gain and which lose. If you keep eBird checklists for this hotspot, the next few years of them will be the record of what happened.
For now, nearly all of that birding ground sits behind the closure. When it reopens, the first hour after the area opens, a half hour before sunrise, is the one to plan around.
Planning a dawn bird walk? Fill the thermos with fresh coffee beans
### What was this land before it was a conservation area?
An airport that never happened, and before that, a river town that vanished. In the 1940s the City of St. Louis bought this ground planning an airport, then leased it to farmers, who worked about 3,300 acres of crops alongside about 900 acres of forest, according to MDC’s Missouri Conservationist magazine.
Go back further and the maps get stranger. MDC’s brochure says a river town, later called St. Vrain, appeared here on plat maps in the mid-1800s and was gone by 1870. Read the flood list above and you can probably guess why a town on this ground didn’t last.
MDC bought the land from the city in the late 1990s. MDC’s own history says 1997, while the Missouri Conservationist reported in July 1998 that the purchase came in early 1998, for $9.1 million. The state then spent almost $3 million building it out. The developed area opened on May 30, 2003, with about 5 miles of paved road, about 5 miles of limestone bike trail and about 3 miles of hiking trail. Its viewing platform at the east tip was billed as the first on the Missouri side looking directly at the confluence.
The visitor center followed, dedicated on May 27, 2004, and named for Howard and Joyce Wood. MDC built it around the site’s old barn, and the original post-and-beam frame is still visible inside. The farm years are still standing out there, wrapped inside the newer building.
### Where can you see the confluence while the platform is closed?
At Confluence Point State Park, at the end of Riverlands Way on the tip of the peninsula between the rivers. Columbia Bottom’s own Confluence Observation Platform, about 2.5 miles down the River’s Edge Trail from near the boat ramp, has been cut off since April, when the road and trail to it closed. Our guide to where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet covers the vantage points you can still reach.
Most people who search for Columbia Bottom want a sunflower picture or a look at the confluence, and this fall they’ll find a closed area and a review that’s years out of date. You know what’s really going on out there. Call (636) 441-4554 before you drive up, launch at first light if you fish, and watch for MDC’s bloom announcement next July. You’re the one who knows this river bottom is still open for business, even with most of the gates shut.
If the ramp is your way onto the Missouri this fall, find bait, tackle and a river guide among the fishing shops and guides in St. Louis we list.
If you run a bait-and-tackle shop, a kayak outfitter or a north county diner on the drive up to Strodtman Road, list your business with us and put it in front of the anglers already driving past your door to the only open ramp at Columbia Bottom.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Columbia Bottom Conservation Area open?
A.  Only partly. As of October 9, 2026, MDC limits public access to the Missouri River boat ramp, whose road reopened on September 30 after a full closure that began September 8. The trails, sunflower fields, confluence platform and Mississippi paddle access stay closed during the setback-levee project, and MDC hasn’t announced a reopening date. Call (636) 441-4554 before you go.
### Q. Can you fish at night in Missouri?
A.  On most conservation areas, yes. The statewide rule keeps areas open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. but allows fishing, and launching or landing a boat, at any hour where authorized. Some areas are exceptions, and Columbia Bottom is one: it follows posted hours and closes from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise. Check each area’s rules first.
### Q. Which conservation areas in Missouri allow archery only?
A.  MDC’s Conservation Areas: Deer Hunting Quick View answers that. It covers 559 areas and has a Method filter, and choosing “Archery Methods Only” gives you the archery-only list. Columbia Bottom won’t be on your fall shortlist this year: deer hunting there is by managed hunt only, and all four 2026-27 managed deer hunts were canceled.
### Q. Can you shoot on conservation land in Missouri?
A.  Only in specific places. The Wildlife Code allows target shooting on designated public shooting ranges or by special use permit, and hunting follows each area’s own rules. At Columbia Bottom, target shooting isn’t allowed and there’s no range, lead shot is banned, and single-projectile firearms are banned except for deer hunting.
### Q. Which conservation areas in Missouri allow bow hunting?
A.  Many more than allow archery only. In MDC’s Deer Hunting Quick View, which covers 559 conservation areas, three method filters all include bowhunting: “Archery Methods Only,” “Muzzleloader and Archery” and “Archery and Firearms.” Run all three to see every option, then check each area’s page for seasons, managed-hunt rules and temporary closures like this fall’s at Columbia Bottom.
### Q. What is the best time to see sunflower fields?
A.  Near St. Louis, early July to mid-August. At Columbia Bottom, MDC plants about 14 fields in early May and staggers them, and each planting peaks for about 10 days, so something is usually blooming across that window. Watch for MDC’s July bloom announcement. Mature sunflower heads face east, so morning is likely the best light for photos of the faces.
### Q. What ecosystem is the most threatened in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the measure. MDC says Missouri has lost about 87 percent of its wetlands and that less than 1 percent of its original prairie remains, with about 99.6 percent of wet prairies destroyed. St. Louis Public Radio calls wetlands the most threatened ecosystem in the country. MDC’s plan for Columbia Bottom is to let it function as a wetland.
### Q. Where are the most beautiful sunflower fields?
A.  That’s your call, but near St. Louis the best-known fields are at Columbia Bottom, where MDC staggers about 14 plantings so the bloom runs from early July into mid-August. In 2026 MDC added extra viewing plots near the road. Elsewhere in Missouri, MDC plants dove fields on other conservation areas and posts a bloom announcement each July.

## Laclede’s Landing: The Wax Museum, Where to Eat Now, What Happened to the Bars
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lacledes-landing-st-louis
What actually happened to Laclede’s Landing? The recycled top-ten lists act like nothing did. They still send people down these cobblestones to bars that closed years ago, and even the district’s own website, last refreshed around 2022, names venues that went dark long before. Follow one of those lists on a Friday night and you get a locked door, an empty sidewalk and a lot of quiet brick.
The real story is short. For about three decades this was the city’s late-night district. Mississippi Nights, a club that held about 1,000 people, opened here in 1976, and in 1991 Nirvana played its only St. Louis show on that stage, 23 days after Nevermind came out. Then the anchors went, one at a time. The club came down in 2007 for a casino. The interstate moved. Construction on the park grounds next door shut the street along the Landing’s southern edge, and half the bars and restaurants didn’t make it through.
What’s here now is smaller, and stranger in a good way. The Landing is turning into a neighborhood. St. Louis Public Radio reported in 2024 that more than $75 million had gone into rehabbing the old warehouses, and in September 2026 KMOV reported that the apartments upstairs were 94% leased. A wax museum that dates to 1983 has outlasted nearly every bar around it. Below is what we could confirm as of October 2026: what’s open, what it costs, how to get in and what’s a short walk away on the St. Louis riverfront. Hours shift with the seasons, so call ahead.
### What is there to do at Laclede’s Landing?
Walk the cobblestone streets and brick and cast-iron warehouses of a nine-block historic district, tour the wax museum’s 250-plus figures on five levels, eat at The Old Spaghetti Factory, Kimchi Guys or The Cobblestone, then walk to the Eads Bridge and the riverfront. MetroLink stops right under the bridge.
None of that takes a full day. The Landing works best as an afternoon that rolls into dinner, so here’s one way to run it.
Start under the bridge. Ride MetroLink’s Red or Blue line to Laclede’s Landing station and step off beneath the Eads Bridge, at the mouth of a railroad tunnel dug in 1874. It’s the best front door the Landing has.
Walk the grid. The historic district covers nine blocks and 22 acres, according to The Cultural Landscape Foundation. That’s small enough to wander without a plan. Look up as you go. The brick and cast-iron fronts are the show, and a section below explains why the whole place still looks like the 1880s.
Give the wax museum 90 minutes. More than 250 life-size figures on five levels, with the Chamber of Horrors waiting in the basement and sub-basement. It’s at 720 N. Second St. Call first; the museum section below has the hours and what visitors have been paying.
Throw a disc. In 2024, two vacant lots on the Landing became an art park with disc-golf cages, St. Louis Public Radio reported. It’s a small thing, and a clear sign that somebody now plans for the people who live here.
Sit by the river. The Katherine Ward Burg Garden, a half-acre plaza on the Mississippi Greenway, opened at the Landing’s riverfront on April 23, 2023, according to Great Rivers Greenway. Grab a coffee on the way and let the river do the entertaining.
Check the calendar. Counterpublic 2026, an art exhibition with commissions along the riverfront, runs through Dec. 12, 2026, so look at its map for anything near the Landing. One date not to count on: the Big Muddy Blues Festival has filled these streets over Labor Day weekend, but the latest edition we could verify was 2024.
### What happened to Laclede’s Landing?
It lost its anchors. Mississippi Nights, the roughly 1,000-capacity club that ran from 1976, closed on Jan. 19, 2007, and was torn down for a casino, St. Louis Public Radio reported. Then the interstate moved, and the Post-Dispatch reported that 7 of the Landing’s 14 bars and restaurants closed during the Arch-grounds construction.
It began as a rescue. On Feb. 19, 1975, the city’s aldermen approved the Laclede’s Landing Redevelopment Corporation, formed by downtown businessmen led by William Maritz to bring back the old riverfront warehouse blocks. On Aug. 25, 1976, the district went on the National Register of Historic Places. The same year, Mississippi Nights opened.
The club years. Mississippi Nights booked bands on the way up. AC/DC played its ninth U.S. show there in 1977, fourteen years before Nirvana’s night. Around the club, the Landing filled with bars and restaurants: The Big Bang, Fusion Nightclub, Heartbreakers, Jake’s Steaks, Big Daddy’s, Morgan Street Brewery. Every one of them is closed now.
The casino. Eleven months after Mississippi Nights shut, Lumiere Place casino opened next door on Dec. 19, 2007. Caesars renamed it Horseshoe St. Louis in May 2022. Down on the riverfront, the older President Casino aboard the Admiral closed in June 2010.
The highway. On Feb. 9, 2014, I-70 moved off the downtown riverfront and onto the new Stan Musial bridge, according to MoDOT. The highway beside the Landing still runs; it carries I-44 now. Directions telling you to take I-70 to the Landing are a quick way to spot a stale page.
The construction. The $380 million rebuild of the park grounds next door shut Washington Avenue, the Eads Bridge approach along the Landing’s southern edge, and that’s when the closures piled up. Picture someone from Wellston who used to come down for shows and hasn’t been back since. The bridge, the bricks and the river are right where they left them. The crowd isn’t.
What’s happening now. People live here. St. Louis Public Radio reported in August 2024 that 119 apartments on the Landing were about 90% filled. In February 2026, KMOV reported that Advantes Group runs about 150 units, including Peper Lofts, and by September it put the apartments at 94% leased. A 5,300-square-foot rooftop deck is planned at Greeley Lofts. The city has swapped a run-down garage for green space, and in early 2026 a farmers market near the old Admiral casino site was in the planning stage.
The ground floors are the gap. Cushman & Wakefield and the St. Louis Development Corporation are marketing 55,000 square feet of empty retail space here, KMOV reported. So the honest answer to “what happened” goes like this: the party moved out, the neighbors moved in, and the storefronts in between are waiting for someone to open them.
### Is the Laclede’s Landing Wax Museum worth the stop?
Yes, if you like your museums a little odd and you’ve got 90 minutes and about $10. Per its website, the Laclede’s Landing Wax Museum fills five levels and 10,000 square feet of an 1885 cast-iron-front warehouse with more than 250 life-size figures. It opened in 1983 and is still going.
What’s inside. The galleries run by theme: movie stars, presidents and world leaders, sports, super heroes, World War II, movie monsters and the Life of Christ. Where else do a president, a superhero and a movie monster share a warehouse? There’s an ice-cream shop and a gift shop, too. Roadside America, the guide to offbeat stops, rates the place “Major Fun.”
The Chamber of Horrors. It’s downstairs. All the way down, in the basement and a sub-basement of an 1885 warehouse. A family from Vinita Park with a nine-year-old who has seen every monster movie twice will probably call it the best room in the building. With a five-year-old who startles at shadows, send one adult down first and decide from there.
Hours. The museum’s website posts two seasons and says both are subject to change:
March 1 through October 31: Sunday through Wednesday, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and Thursday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.
November 1 through the end of February: Thursday through Sunday only, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.
That winter switch matters if you’re reading this in the fall. Starting Nov. 1, a Tuesday visit won’t work. Thursday through Sunday does, all year.
Price. The website doesn’t list one. Visitors writing in 2024 and 2025 reported paying $10 per person, so plan on about that and confirm when you call. We couldn’t verify kids’ pricing, so ask about that too.
Call before you go. The museum was operating as of 2026, with current hours posted, but a small private museum can change plans quickly. The number is 314-241-1155. Plan on about an hour and a half inside; that’s how long one recent visitor said a full visit took.
Finding it. The address is 720 N. Second St., and the museum’s own directions put it a half block west of The Old Spaghetti Factory. Pair the two, but mind the restaurant’s hours: Monday through Thursday, it doesn’t open until 5 p.m.
The detail most lists skip. The museum books private events for up to 150 guests and rents out figures, starting at $300. If you’ve ever wanted a wax figure standing in the corner of a birthday party, this is the call to make.
### Where can you eat and drink on the Landing right now?
On the cobblestones themselves, three places we could confirm open in 2026, mostly through KMOV’s reporting: The Old Spaghetti Factory at 727 N. First St., Kimchi Guys at 612 N. Second St. and The Cobblestone at 701 N. First St. Next door, the Horseshoe St. Louis complex adds a steakhouse, Ramsay’s Kitchen and pizza.
The Old Spaghetti Factory, 727 N. First St. Its website lists Monday through Thursday, 5 to 9 p.m., and Friday through Sunday, 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. There’s no Monday-through-Thursday lunch on that schedule, which is easy to miss. The address has a second life in the history books, too. The next section explains.
Kimchi Guys, 612 N. Second St. KMOV’s September 2026 story on the Landing listed it among the businesses operating here. We didn’t find posted hours we’d stand behind, so check before you go.
The Cobblestone, 701 N. First St. A deli, bar, cafe and grocery under one roof, KMOV reported in February 2026. For the people who now live on the Landing, groceries on the block are the bigger news. For a visitor, it’s a sandwich and a drink between the museum and the bridge.
Next door at Horseshoe St. Louis, 999 N. Second St. Caesars’ site listed Morton’s The Steakhouse, Ramsay’s Kitchen, Riverfront Grill, a Starbucks and The Slice Pizzeria as open in October 2026. Ramsay’s Kitchen took over from Cinder House in 2024. The Four Seasons Hotel St. Louis is part of the same complex, and its spa reopened on May 18, 2026.
And the bars? That’s where the stale lists fail hardest. Big Daddy’s on the Landing closed in January 2021, and Brew Tulum closed in late 2024. Several other names still circulating on older pages had no 2026 proof of life when we checked, so we’ve left them off. If an old list sends you to a Landing bar, call before you walk over.
Miss the Landing’s bar-crawl days? Here’s what to expect at a pool hall
### Why does the Landing still look like the 1880s?
Because a fire cleared the old riverfront and the city rebuilt it in brick and iron. The Great Fire of May 17, 1849, started on the steamboat White Cloud and destroyed 23 steamboats and about 15 blocks. The warehouses you see now mostly went up between the 1850s and 1900, many in the 1880s, per The Cultural Landscape Foundation.
Read the pavement. The north-south streets keep their original cobbled paving. The east-west streets are concrete. For the photo of stone streets lined with iron storefronts, shoot along First or Second Street, not the cross streets. Wear real shoes. Cobblestones and heels don’t get along.
Read the fronts. Brick walls and cast-iron storefronts, block after block. The wax museum’s building dates to 1885. The oldest dated building on the Landing association’s list is older than the fire: the Schoellhorn-Albrecht Building at 721 and 723 N. Second St., which the association dates to before 1844. It was already standing when the riverfront burned.
Order dinner at the first legislature’s address. Missouri’s first General Assembly met in September 1820 at the Missouri Hotel, at Main and Morgan streets. The Landing’s association places that site at 727 N. First St., which is The Old Spaghetti Factory’s address today. So you can twirl spaghetti at the address tied to the state’s first lawmakers. Try finding that on a recycled top-ten list.
The name. The Landing is named for Pierre Laclede, the New Orleans fur trader who chose the site of St. Louis in 1763. His stepson, Auguste Chouteau, began building the trading post on Feb. 14, 1764, according to the National Park Service. Laclede named the settlement for King Louis IX of France. The city got the king’s name. These cobblestones got the trader’s.
### How do you get to the Landing, and where do you park?
Take MetroLink if you can. Laclede’s Landing station, at 200 Washington Avenue on the Red and Blue lines, drops you at the district’s edge, though it has no parking of its own, per Metro Transit. If you drive, city meters charge Monday through Saturday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. and are free on Sundays and city holidays.
Why the train is the better arrival. The station sits on the lower deck of the Eads Bridge, at the east portal of the 1874 Downtown Tunnel. Trains stopped using that tunnel in 1974. MetroLink reopened it, and the station opened on July 31, 1993. Step off and you’re standing where a 19th-century rail tunnel meets a 19th-century bridge.
If you drive. Here’s what parking costs as of October 2026, from the city’s parking information:
Street meters: $2.00 an hour in high-demand areas and $1.50 an hour elsewhere, Monday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Free at the meters: Sundays and city holidays, plus evenings after 7 p.m. Check the meter or posted sign before you walk away.
Tickets: an expired meter can cost you $20, or two wax museum admissions.
City garages: the Central Downtown Garage at 707 Pine St. was listed at $4 an hour.
Lots on the Landing: private lot rates aren’t published online, so read the posted sign before you pay.
Say you’re coming in from Shrewsbury on a Sunday. The meters are free all day, the wax museum’s posted hours include Sundays in every season, and The Old Spaghetti Factory opens at 11:30 a.m. That’s the cheapest, easiest version of a Landing day, and it’s the one we’d pick for a first visit.
### What can you walk to from the Landing?
Start with the Eads Bridge. The National Park Service calls the 1874 span the oldest bridge standing on the Mississippi, and its upper deck carries people on foot as well as cars. From the Landing you can also walk to the riverfront, downtown and the Old Courthouse, or catch a riverboat. Here’s the order we’d take them.
The Eads Bridge. On June 14, 1874, an elephant was led across it to prove it was safe. MetroLink trains run on the lower deck now, through the station you probably arrived at. Our bridge guide covers how to walk the Eads Bridge, so check it before you set out.
The river itself. Head to the Katherine Ward Burg Garden and follow the Mississippi Greenway along the water. If you’d rather be on the river than beside it, our guide to a St. Louis riverboat cruise covers which boats run, how long the trips last and what a ticket costs.
Downtown. Washington Avenue marks the Landing’s southern edge. Cross it and you’re in downtown St. Louis, where uniformed safety ambassadors work from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. Gateway Arch National Park is next door, and you’ve probably done it already.
The Old Courthouse. If the 1849 fire and the first legislature got you curious, keep walking south through downtown to the Old Courthouse, where the city’s history continues.
So the next time someone pulls up an old list and plans a bar crawl on the Landing, you’re the one who knows what actually happened. The club gave way to a casino, the warehouses hold apartments, and the wax museum is still on Second Street with a Chamber of Horrors under the floor. Call the museum, take the train, and go on a Sunday.
When the wax museum closes and you’re not ready to call it a night, our guide to nightlife in St. Louis takes over where the Landing’s short bar list ends.
If you run a restaurant, bar, studio or shop on or near the Landing, where 55,000 square feet of empty storefront space is on the market right now and the apartments upstairs are 94% leased, list your business with us and turn the visitors and new neighbors already walking these cobblestones into more customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to visit the Laclede’s Landing Wax Museum in Saint Louis?
A.  About $10 per person, based on what visitors reported paying in 2024 and 2025. The museum’s website doesn’t post a price, so confirm it when you call 314-241-1155, and ask about kids’ pricing while you’re at it. Budget a little extra for the ice-cream shop and gift shop. Private events and figure rentals, from $300, are priced separately.
### Q. What restaurants are located on Laclede’s Landing in St. Louis?
A.  As of October 2026 we could confirm The Old Spaghetti Factory at 727 N. First St., Kimchi Guys at 612 N. Second St. and The Cobblestone, a deli, bar, cafe and grocery at 701 N. First St. Next door, Horseshoe St. Louis has Morton’s The Steakhouse, Ramsay’s Kitchen, Riverfront Grill, The Slice Pizzeria and a Starbucks. Older lists name places that have closed, so check hours first.
### Q. What is the landing in St. Louis?
A.  It’s Laclede’s Landing, a nine-block, 22-acre historic district of brick and cast-iron warehouses on the riverfront just north of Gateway Arch National Park. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on Aug. 25, 1976. Once the city’s late-night district, it’s now home to apartments, a few restaurants, the wax museum and cobblestone streets by the Eads Bridge.
### Q. Who is Laclede’s Landing named after?
A.  Pierre Laclede, the New Orleans fur trader who chose the site of St. Louis in 1763. His stepson, Auguste Chouteau, began building the trading post on Feb. 14, 1764, according to the National Park Service. Laclede named the settlement for King Louis IX of France, so the city carries the king’s name and the riverfront district carries the trader’s.
### Q. Is Laclede’s Landing safe?
A.  It’s a mixed residential and entertainment district beside a 24-hour casino-hotel, and its apartments were 94% leased in September 2026, per KMOV. Downtown has uniformed safety ambassadors from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., reachable at 314-978-2233. As of August 2026, every MetroLink platform is gated, and Bi-State reports incidents fell from 17 to 9 per 100,000 riders since 2022, a preliminary figure. Use ordinary city sense after dark.
### Q. How much time for wax museum?
A.  Plan on about an hour and a half, which is how long one recent visitor said a full visit took. Five levels and a two-level Chamber of Horrors fill that time quickly. Arrive at least 90 minutes before closing, which is 6 p.m. on most days and 8 p.m. on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays from March through October. Call ahead, since hours can change.
### Q. How much does it cost to park in downtown St. Louis?
A.  City street meters charge $2.00 an hour in high-demand areas and $1.50 an hour elsewhere, Monday through Saturday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., per the city’s parking site, and an expired meter can cost you a $20 ticket. Garage rates vary; the city’s Central Downtown Garage at 707 Pine St. was listed at $4 an hour. Private lots on the Landing don’t publish rates.
### Q. Where can I find free parking in downtown St. Louis?
A.  At the city’s street meters on Sundays and city holidays, and after 7 p.m. Monday through Saturday, when the meters stop charging. Read the meter or posted sign to be sure. That’s why a Sunday on the Landing is the cheap way to do it. Or skip the car: Laclede’s Landing station has no parking, but MetroLink drops you right at the district’s edge.

## St. Louis Riverboat Cruise: Fares, the Dinner Cruise and What High Water Costs You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-riverboat-cruise
Twenty-six dollars gets an adult the sound first. The engine on the Tom Sawyer starts its deep, rhythmic churn before the boat casts off, the cobblestone levee slides away behind you, and the Gateway Arch stops being a postcard. From the water it’s 630 feet of stainless steel standing over a brown river. If your timing is good, a towboat muscles a string of barges past, loaded with coal or grain.
That hour gets sold three ways, and they aren’t the same deal. The boat’s own box office sells it for $26. The Arch bundles it with the tram ride to the top. And a new pass from an outside company, Let’s Roam, sells it as one pick in a $72.19 bundle. Pair the cruise with the Arch tram on that pass, give its $28.87 app scavenger hunt full credit, and you’ve still paid 32 cents more than the Arch charges for the same two rides at its top price of $43.
On a river that floods, one rule matters more than any fare. If the operator cancels for river conditions or extreme weather, it doesn’t issue cash refunds. You reschedule, or you take a full-value voucher good for one year.
A voucher is fine if you live an hour away. It stings if you flew in for one weekend.
So this guide goes to the source. Every fare, date and rule below comes from the operator’s own ticket page, fact sheet and news releases, the pass prices come from Let’s Roam’s own page, and the history comes from city records and the reporters who covered it. It’s written for the local who has stood on the levee a dozen times without once leaving it, and for the visiting family that wants more than a photo of the water. Our guide to the St. Louis riverfront covers where to see the river and how to cross it. This one is about getting on it.
### How much is a riverboat cruise down the Mississippi River?
The one-hour St. Louis Riverfront Cruise costs $26 for adults 16 to 59, $24 for seniors 60 and up and $16 for kids 3 to 15, and babies 2 and under ride free with a ticket. The two-hour Skyline Dinner Cruise is $64 for anyone 13 and up. Overnight Mississippi cruises from Viking’s St. Louis stop start at $6,499. The riverboats run March through November.
Bi-State Development, which bought the riverboats in 2001, sells these seats itself: online, by phone at 877-982-1410 and at the ticket center at the Gateway Arch. Same-day tickets can go on sale at 9 a.m., but the operator warns they aren’t guaranteed and sell out early and often.
Read the age brackets twice. They shift from cruise to cruise, and that’s where families overpay without noticing. A 14-year-old rides the sightseeing hour as a $16 child and the Skyline Dinner Cruise as a $64 adult. So two parents with kids of 10 and 14 pay $84 for the one-hour cruise and $220 for dinner on the water.
Boarding is quick. Your ticket gets scanned, someone takes a souvenir photo you can buy later, and you choose between the open-air deck and the climate-controlled cabin. Bring the dog if you like: leashed, well-behaved dogs are welcome on the one-hour Riverfront Cruise, though not on the dinner, brunch or other specialty cruises. Making a day of it with the dog? Here are dog-friendly patios and breweries in St. Louis.
### What do you actually see on the one-hour cruise?
A working river, with a captain explaining it. The operator says the narration covers the Mississippi’s role in St. Louis history and its significance as a working river today, and that second half surprises people. Keep watch for towboats working enormous barges, and listen for the Port of St. Louis, which the operator says handles more than 20 million tons of cargo a year. The skyline is the backdrop. The freight is the show.
The bridges get their own stories. The narration covers the Eads and the Poplar Street, you’ll also see the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial and the MacArthur, and from the water the Eads sits low and side-on, an angle nobody walking its deck ever gets. If you’d rather be up there, here’s how to walk the Eads Bridge.
Then the boat turns and the floodwall becomes a gallery. Large murals and graffiti cover the city’s massive concrete floodwalls, and the operator counts that view among the things you simply can’t experience from the shore. About then, people drift to the concession stand for a hot dog, a bucket of popcorn or a cold drink.
The riverfront has a darker story too. On May 17, 1849, at 9 p.m., the steamer White Cloud caught fire at the foot of Cherry Street. Her moorings parted and she drifted downstream, setting 22 other steamers on fire. By 8 the next morning the blaze had taken 23 steamboats, 430 buildings and three lives, and the city’s own history counts 15 blocks of riverfront destroyed. It started on the water you’re about to ride.
The riverboats came much later, and for a reason almost nobody guesses. The operator’s fact sheet says they were originally brought to St. Louis in 1964 for spectators who wanted a closer look at the Gateway Arch going up. The first riverboat crowds came to watch a construction job.
Some sailings add a second voice. National Park Service rangers narrate select cruises through the season, and kids can work through a Mississippi River activity book with a ranger on board and earn a Junior Ranger badge. On the first Wednesday of the month, the narration turns to freight and the “Ag Coast of America.” On select Thursdays, Amanda Clark of the Missouri History Museum takes over the narration to dig into the historic riverfront and the Eads Bridge.
Take a family from Byrnes Mill with a 9-year-old who has announced that boats are boring. A ranger sailing with a badge on the line is a different hour from the one that kid is dreading. Ranger times vary, so ask which departures carry one when you book.
### Every fare on the river this season
Here’s the full fare sheet from the operator’s ticket page, one row per ride. Screenshot it before you’re at the window explaining to a 14-year-old why they’re a kid on one boat and an adult on the next.
Prices change, and the Arch tram’s price varies by date, so check the operator’s ticket page before you pay. Dinner cruises board 30 minutes before cruise time and leave on schedule. In the operator’s words: “We run a tight ship.”
### Is the new St. Louis sights pass cheaper for a cruise day?
Usually not, and you don’t have to take our word for it. Let’s Roam, an outside company whose “city adventures” are self-guided app scavenger hunts and ghost tours, now sells a St. Louis Top Sights Pass that lists the Riverfront Cruise among its seven attraction picks. We have no tie to Let’s Roam and earn nothing either way. Its 3 Sights Pass costs $72.19 plus tax for anyone 12 and up and $67.19 for kids 3 to 11, and it covers two attractions plus one of its app adventures, which Let’s Roam prices at $28.87.
The cruise is one of the pricier picks. Among the seven attractions on Let’s Roam’s own price list, its $26 adult fare trails only the Aquarium’s $29.75. The pass headline promises “Save up to 36%.” Its own worked example pairs the Aquarium with this very cruise, then adds two of its app games at $28.87 each, a scavenger hunt and a ghost tour, to reach a “regular price” of $113.49. Take the app games out and the two real tickets cost $55.75, which is $16.44 less than the $72.19 pass.
Now set the pass beside the bundle the Arch already sells. The Captain’s View combo, the tram to the top plus the one-hour cruise, costs $39 to $43 for adults 16 to 59. Pick those same two attractions on the 3 Sights Pass and you pay $72.19, which is $29.19 more than the combo’s top price of $43. Give the pass full credit for one $28.87 app hunt and the tram and the cruise still cost you $43.32 ($72.19 minus $28.87), which is 32 cents more than the combo’s $43.
Kids widen the gap. The Arch charges child prices through age 15 on the tram and the cruise, and the combo costs $25 to $29 for kids 3 to 15. The pass counts anyone 12 and up as an adult, so a 13-year-old rides the boat for $16 at the dock but needs the $72.19 adult pass. Even the $67.19 child pass for a 3-to-11-year-old costs $38.19 more than the combo’s $29 top price.
Then there’s the calendar. The riverboats operate March through November, and the pass gives you 365 days to start and then 10 consecutive days to use it. Start it on a gray January weekend, or any day from December through February, and your cruise pick, one of the priciest on the list, is off the table, because the daily sightseeing cruises operate from March to November.
So when does the pass win? Only when you’d also pay for one of Let’s Roam’s app games. Add one $28.87 hunt to the $55.75 Aquarium-and-cruise pair and the three come to $84.62, so the $72.19 pass saves you $12.43. Our guide to St. Louis’s must-see attractions runs the same test on the 4 Sights and 5 Sights tiers. Let’s Roam lists its terms on its pass page.
### Which boat will you be on?
The Tom Sawyer. The operator describes her as a replica 19th-century paddlewheel riverboat, and its history page says she was built in 1966 for Streckfus Steamers by the Dubuque Boat & Boiler Company in Dubuque, Iowa, and worked in Tampa before she came to St. Louis. The Tom Sawyer is the boat running the cruises, with open-air decks outside and climate-controlled space inside.
A new, bigger Becky Thatcher reached St. Louis on August 25, 2026, the first new riverboat for St. Louis since 1987, and she hasn’t carried passengers yet. Her page on the operator’s site still says she “will soon be welcoming passengers” and asks you to join a newsletter for cruise news. In August, Bi-State said she first had to complete U.S. Coast Guard certifications and staff safety training. If anyone sells you a seat on her before the operator announces a first cruise, ask for the date in writing.
The numbers: 132 feet from gangway to paddle wheel, three decks, room for up to 400 passengers, and a 2,100-pound paddlewheel pushing her along at about 5 mph. She was built in 1987 as the Capt. JP and cruised the Caloosahatchee River in Fort Myers, Florida. Bi-State paid $549,500 for her, then put $3.2 million into repairs and renovations at a shipyard near Mobile, Alabama, funded from existing riverboat revenue. She’s about 31% larger than the boat she replaces.
Save her route for dinner conversation. She didn’t come straight up the Mississippi. From Mobile Bay she ran up the Mobile and Tombigbee rivers, through the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway and its 10-lock system, across the Tennessee River and Kentucky Lake, into the Ohio near Cairo, Illinois, and only then north on the Mississippi. The nearly 1,000-mile trip took about 10 days.
Count the names and she’s the fourth. The operator calls her the 4th generation of replica paddlewheel riverboats to bear the name Becky Thatcher. The first began life in 1879 as the U.S. Snagboat C. B. Reese, built in Carondelet; she sank in 1965 after listing in low water, and her hull became the landing barge for the next Becky Thatcher. The one before this one, built in 1963, retired on January 1, 2024, and was sold that July to Memphis Riverboats, which renamed her the Belle of Memphis.
### What happens if the river is too high?
When the Mississippi runs high, the brown water climbs the cobblestones toward the levee lot and the boat you booked stays tied to the dock. You get a new date or a voucher instead of your money back. If the operator cancels for river conditions or extreme weather, it doesn’t issue monetary refunds: you can reschedule to a future cruise date or take a full-value voucher valid for one year. Rain alone won’t do it. The boats sail rain or shine, on climate-controlled decks.
High water makes trouble before it stops the boats. Levee parking sits right on the cobblestones, costs a fee (card only), isn’t run by the Arch or the riverboats, and may be unavailable when the river comes up. At high water, the ramps from the levee road might not be accessible either. The riverfront was raised in a renovation led by Great Rivers Greenway, part of a $380 million project around the Arch, to cut down on flooding, but the levee still runs down to the water.
Here’s the trap nobody plans for. When the levee lot is closed, the operator points drivers to the Stadium East garage at 200 S. Broadway, a little over a mile from the boats, and warns the walk can take up to 30 minutes. The riverboat still departs at the scheduled cruise time. Park there just before a sailing and you’ll watch the paddlewheel turn from the wrong end of the park.
The easy way around all of it is the train or your feet. The dock is about a 9-minute walk south through the park from the Laclede’s Landing MetroLink station, and about 6 minutes from the Arch’s south-leg exit. If you drive anyway, take the operator’s own tip: put “The Mural Mile” into your GPS, because GPS directions to the levee aren’t always accurate.
So what does the voucher rule really cost? Depends who you are. A family from Carlyle that loses a July Saturday to the river loses a drive and an afternoon, then rebooks for a cooler weekend in September. A family that flew in for one summer weekend goes home holding a voucher for a city it may not see again within the year.
If you’re in the second group, three habits help. Book the cruise early in your trip, so a cancellation leaves you days to reschedule. If the river has been rising, check the operator’s site the morning you sail. And plan the rest of the day so the boat is the one piece you can lose.
Build the rest of the day around the boat. Browse our listings of activities in St. Louis for the hours before you board and after you dock.
If you’re the riverfront restaurant, the kayak outfitter or the photographer who shoots proposals by the water, the people reading this page are planning a day on the river right now, and plenty of them will ask their phone who to call next. A St Louis Near Me Directory listing gives your photos, your menu or your trip list a place where those planners look. Claim your spot before the next boat docks.
### Is the dinner cruise worth it?
For a date night or a birthday, often yes. For young kids, usually not. The two-hour Skyline Dinner Cruise costs $64 for anyone 13 and up, against $26 for the one-hour sightseeing cruise, and the ticket buys a chef-inspired menu, live music or a DJ, and the skyline after dark. Then take the operator’s own advice and stroll around the top deck to see the city from new angles as it lights up the night sky.
Run it for two adults. At $26 each, two adults pay $52 for the sightseeing hour, and you still have to eat somewhere afterward. At $64 each, the same two pay $128 for the Skyline Dinner Cruise. The dinner cruise costs two adults $76 more than the hour ($128 minus $52), so if dinner downtown for two was going to cost $76 or more anyway, the dinner cruise comes out even or ahead, with a second hour on the river thrown in.
That’s the case for the couple driving in from Wright City for an anniversary. One booking covers dinner and the river, and nobody hunts for a downtown table on a Saturday night. This season’s calendar lists Skyline Dinner Cruises at 7:30 p.m. on November 6, 7, 13, 14, 20 and 21, and every dinner cruise boards 30 minutes before it sails. Groups of 20 to 60 can book it as a group without chartering the whole boat.
Young kids flip the math. Kids 3 to 12 pay $28 on the dinner cruise against $16 for the hour, and two hours is a long sit for a 5-year-old. With little ones, take the sightseeing cruise and eat on land. Closest of all is the Paddlewheel Café on the riverboat dock, which the operator calls St. Louis’s only riverfront restaurant: a cheeseburger with chips and a drink is $13, a pretzel with cheese is $7, and you’re welcome to carry your food aboard a cruise. The fact sheet lists it April through October, so check before a November trip. Our guide to Laclede’s Landing covers the restaurants just north along the riverfront.
Adults-only nights cost a little over half what dinner does. The Blues Cruise and Groove & Spin are $35 each and the Halloween costume cruise is $34, all 21 and over. This season’s calendar has the Halloween cruise at 8:30 p.m. on October 30 and 31, the Blues Cruise on November 12 and Groove & Spin on November 22.
December changes the boat’s job. The daily sightseeing cruises stop after November, and the operator runs holiday-themed cruises instead, including Caroling with Santa at $29 and PJs and Pancakes with Santa at $45, one price for everyone 3 and up. Watch its calendar for dates. The Floating Sleigh, a $10 holiday pop-up bar for ages 21 and up, stays docked all evening, and you come and go as you please.
Planning a proposal on the top deck? The riverboats host weddings, and one of the captains is ordained to marry couples. Here’s what a wedding officiant costs in St. Louis if you’d rather say it on land.
### What happened to the floating McDonald’s and the Admiral?
St. Louis’s floating McDonald’s opened on the riverfront on March 11, 1980, according to The Drive, which calls it the world’s first floating McDonald’s. It closed in November 2000, after McDonald’s told the St. Louis Business Journal the barge was “in need of extensive renovation, which is financially not justifiable at the present.” The Admiral, the giant excursion boat a generation of St. Louisans remembers, was sold for scrap in 2011.
It was never really a boat. It was a cement barge built up to look like an 1880s-style paddleboat, 185 feet long and more than 700 tons, with seats for 134 inside and 200 outside on benches, and a crew of 200. People remember the smell as well as the food. The Riverfront Times recalled summer days when “the scent of fryer grease mingled with boat diesel and washed-up catfish.” Even the christening was a bad omen: breaking the champagne bottle on the bow took two tries.
What happened to the barge after it closed doesn’t seem to have been documented, The Drive reported. So, to the question people still type into search bars: the answer is in the postcards. The Drive says the floating McDonald’s seems to live on only in scans of official postcards. The McBarge in the other headlines is a different vessel, a second floating McDonald’s that opened in Vancouver in 1986 and copied the St. Louis original.
Then the riverboat operator had some fun with it. On April 2, 2025, it announced that the floating McDonald’s was coming back and the Tom Sawyer would become “McBarge 2.0,” complete with a sauce-infused “McRib Current” and a “Supersize Sundae Slide.” The post’s disclaimer: “This is an April Fools’ joke.” If you landed on that post from a search and stopped reading early, now you know.
The Admiral is the bigger loss. Construction began in 1938 on the hull of the Albatross, a vessel built in 1907, and the finished boat could carry 4,400 passengers. She traded steam for diesel in 1973, became a casino in 1993 and was sold for scrap in 2011, according to the operator’s history, whose timeline starts with Streckfus Steamers beginning river excursions in St. Louis in 1910.
One more coincidence for the ride home. Three of this riverfront’s boats came out of the same yard, the Dubuque Boat & Boiler Company in Dubuque, Iowa: the Huck Finn, which began cruising here on October 1, 1964; the 1963 Becky Thatcher; and the Tom Sawyer. The Huck Finn was sold in 1995 and that Becky Thatcher in 2024, so the Tom Sawyer is the one still carrying the cruises.
### Can you paddle the river instead?
Yes, with an outfitter. Big Muddy Adventures, at 3120 Locust St., was established in 2002 and calls itself the first professional outfitter and guiding company on the Middle Mississippi and Lower Missouri rivers. It says you don’t need any paddling experience to join a trip, and its trips run from hour-long paddles to multi-day expeditions to private island dinners. Ask for prices when you book. Think of it as the riverboat cruise turned inside out: you’re at water level, with a paddle in your hands and the current under the hull.
The boats have personalities. The fleet includes 29-foot voyageur canoes named Stan The Man, Rosie and Heron. Don’t read any of this as a dare to launch your own boat off the levee, though. Big Muddy itself advises anyone without advanced paddling skills against a self-guided trip on the Mississippi or Missouri, and its cancellation policy fits in one line: “We go only if it is safe.” To build skills on calmer water first, start with our beginner’s guide to kayaking in St. Louis. Pricing a boat of your own? Here’s what boating costs near St. Louis.
Is it possible to travel the entire Mississippi River by boat? People do it every year. The Mississippi runs 2,350 miles from its source at Lake Itasca, according to the National Park Service, and barges on the upper river move through a system of 29 locks and dams. KWQC reported that 30 to 50 paddlers attempt the full length each year; one kayaker the station followed finished 55 days after launching in 2025.
### Can you take an overnight cruise from St. Louis?
Yes, on the big river-cruise lines. Which cruise lines depart from St. Louis? Viking lists its 8-day Heartland of America between its St. Louis stop and St. Paul from $6,499, and its 15-day The Big Easy to the Gateway City from New Orleans up to that same stop from $8,899. Read the port name closely before anyone plans a send-off at the levee: Viking lists the stop as St. Louis with a second town’s name in parentheses.
American Cruise Lines sells a 9-day, 8-night Upper Mississippi River Cruise between St. Louis and St. Paul, with a reverse itinerary available. Its fares change by sailing date, so price it with the line directly.
One hour or a week aboard
### What do Mississippi River cruises cost?
From the levee under the Arch, $26 buys an adult a narrated hour and $64 buys two hours with dinner. Overnight, Viking’s 8-day Heartland of America from its St. Louis stop starts at $6,499, and its 15-day trip up from New Orleans starts at $8,899. The nights on board are what move the price.
And on the Missouri? We couldn’t find an overnight cruise on it. Big Muddy paddles the Lower Missouri, and if what you’re really after is the two rivers together, here’s where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet.
Put the two ends side by side: $6,499 for eight days, or $26 for one hour from downtown. There’s no shame in starting with the hour.
The river has a box office, a boarding ramp, a refund rule and a new boat still waiting on her first passengers, and now you know all four. Pick a sightseeing hour on the Tom Sawyer before the daily cruises stop after November, bring the dog if you like, check the river the morning you go, and watch the operator’s site for the day the new Becky Thatcher finally carries passengers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is the St. Louis Riverfront cruise worth it?
A.  For most first-timers, yes. It’s one narrated hour on a working river for $26 an adult and $16 for kids 3 to 15, with towboats, four bridges and floodwall murals the operator says you can’t experience from shore. Leashed dogs can come along. Families should skip the dinner cruise, where anyone 13 and up pays the $64 adult fare.
### Q. How long is the St. Louis river cruise?
A.  The daily St. Louis Riverfront Cruise lasts one hour. The Skyline Dinner Cruise and the Sunday Brunch Cruise each run two hours, and dinner cruises board 30 minutes before they sail. Private charters are built on a two-hour rental plus a half hour of boarding. Pick the Captain’s View combo and the Arch tram adds 45 to 60 minutes.
### Q. Is there a dinner river cruise available in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Skyline Dinner Cruise is a two-hour evening sailing with a chef-inspired menu, live music or a DJ and the skyline after dark, at $64 for ages 13 and up and $28 for kids 3 to 12. This season’s calendar lists 7:30 p.m. sailings on November 6, 7, 13, 14, 20 and 21. Reservations are required.
### Q. What happened to the St. Louis McDonald’s riverboat?
A.  It closed in November 2000. The floating McDonald’s opened on March 11, 1980, on a 185-foot cement barge built to look like an 1880s-style paddleboat. McDonald’s told the St. Louis Business Journal it was “in need of extensive renovation, which is financially not justifiable at the present.” What became of the barge afterward doesn’t seem to have been documented.
### Q. Is there still a floating McDonald’s in St. Louis?
A.  No. It closed in November 2000. The confusion comes from an April 2, 2025, post by the riverboat operator announcing that the Tom Sawyer would become “McBarge 2.0.” The same post carried the disclaimer “This is an April Fools’ joke.” The Tom Sawyer still runs the one-hour sightseeing cruises, at $26 for adults, with no burgers on board.
### Q. Which cruise lines depart from St. Louis?
A.  For trips of a week or more, Viking and American Cruise Lines. Viking’s 8-day Heartland of America sails between its St. Louis stop and St. Paul from $6,499; American Cruise Lines sells a 9-day, 8-night Upper Mississippi cruise between St. Louis and St. Paul. For one hour on the water, the Riverboats at the Gateway Arch run the only riverboat tours in downtown St. Louis.
### Q. What are some good restaurants on the river in Saint Louis?
A.  Start on the dock. The Paddlewheel Café sits on the riverboat dock at 50 S. Leonor K. Sullivan Blvd., and the operator calls it St. Louis’s only riverfront restaurant, with a $13 cheeseburger, a $7 pretzel with cheese and a dockside bar. You can carry your food aboard a cruise. For more choices, see our guide to Laclede’s Landing.
### Q. What’s the best time to go on a river cruise?
A.  In St. Louis, any day from March through November, when the daily sightseeing cruises run; December brings holiday-themed cruises instead. For extra narration, pick a weekend ranger-led sailing, the first Wednesday’s freight-focused cruise or a select Thursday with the Missouri History Museum. If the river has been rising, check the operator’s site that morning.
### Q. Is it possible to travel the entire Mississippi River by boat?
A.  Yes, and people do it every year. KWQC reported that 30 to 50 paddlers attempt the full length annually, and a kayaker it followed finished 55 days after launching in 2025. The river runs 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca, the National Park Service says, and the upper river alone has a system of 29 locks and dams.

## Where the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers Meet: Confluence Point State Park and the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-the-missouri-and-mississippi-rivers-meet
The confluence moved. When the Corps of Discovery pushed off from its winter camp on May 14, 1804, and turned up the Missouri, it entered that river about 2 miles upstream of where the two rivers meet today, by the count of the Missouri Department of Natural Resources. And the camp? The National Park Service says the Mississippi’s channel shifted east and the Missouri’s mouth shifted south, so the ground where Clark’s men spent that winter is likely under the river now, or on the Missouri side of it. A camp built in Illinois may have changed sides without moving an inch.
Search the question and the top answers come from a bank’s blog, a pair of Facebook posts and a travel forum. They’ll get you to the water. What they skip is the part that changes your day: there are three classic places to watch the Missouri pour into the Mississippi near St. Louis, and right now only two of them are open.
Here’s the short version. Confluence Point State Park puts you on the tip of the peninsula, on the Missouri side. The Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower and the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, about a mile apart, look across from the Illinois bank. The third, the viewing platform at Columbia Bottom, is closed, and on September 8, 2026, the Missouri Department of Conservation shut the whole area around it.
It’s part of our larger guide to the St. Louis riverfront. Every hour, fee and date below was checked against state, federal and operator pages in October 2026. Any of it can change, so confirm before you drive.
### Where do the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet?
The Missouri River flows into the Mississippi just north of St. Louis, at the tip of the peninsula between them. You can stand at the point itself in Confluence Point State Park on the Missouri side, or look across from the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower and State Historic Site on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3.
That’s the map. The Missouri Department of Conservation puts the meeting point just north of St. Louis and says the Missouri adds nearly half the flow of the Mississippi below it. The viewpoints on each bank work differently, so it helps to know which one fits your day:
Confluence Point State Park, Missouri side: the view at water level, at the end of Riverlands Way. No admission fee.
Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower, Illinois side: the view from above, with a top deck at 150 feet.
Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, Illinois side: the story, with a full-scale keelboat replica and a colonnade facing the confluence.
Columbia Bottom Conservation Area, Missouri side: closed as of October 2026, with no reopening date posted.
Which should you pick? To stand where the water meets, go to the state park. To see the line between the rivers from above, go to the tower. Doing both takes one day, and the last section lays out the drive.
### Can you see the two colors meet?
Often, yes, because the two rivers carry very different loads of silt. The U.S. Geological Survey measured a median of 427 milligrams of suspended sediment per liter in the lower Missouri, against 139 in the Mississippi, roughly three times as much. Side by side, the Missouri reads as the browner river.
The Missouri Department of Conservation calls the upper Mississippi “relatively clear” and describes the Missouri as still “muddy-looking.” Still is the word to notice. Dams upstream have already cut the Missouri’s sediment load to about 20 to 25 million tons a year, by the department’s estimate, and it remains the muddier river anyway. There’s a reason it goes by Big Muddy.
Here’s the detail that surprised us most. The two rivers don’t blend the moment they touch. A 1965 U.S. Geological Survey report found them still unmixed as they passed St. Louis, with water along the west bank carrying up to 2,400 parts per million more sediment than water near the Illinois shore. For miles below the point, two rivers share one bed.
So where do you look? At the state park you’re at the tip, close to the water, with the two currents coming together in front of you. From the tower you look down on the river rather than across it, which should be a better angle for spotting a line on the surface. Nobody we found publishes a forecast for it, though, so treat the line as a bonus rather than a promise.
### What is at Confluence Point State Park?
About 1,100 acres of river bottom and a short walk to the point. The Missouri Department of Natural Resources describes a path of about a quarter mile, part pavement and part compacted gravel, from the parking lot to the confluence overlook. There’s no admission fee, and the park is open daily, year-round, from 7 a.m. to a half-hour after sunset.
The full name is a mouthful: Edward “Ted” and Pat Jones-Confluence Point State Park, at 1000 Riverlands Way. That road runs out across the peninsula from US-67, past the Audubon Center at Riverlands, and ends at the park. Follow it until it stops.
What’s out there is spare. Interpretive displays and a vault toilet sit at the parking area, and a short interpretive trail leads straight to where the rivers merge. No visitor center, no gift shop. The state lists the route on its accessibility page, and a path of pavement and packed gravel should suit most strollers.
The best story about this ground comes from the day it became a park. At the dedication in May 2004, St. Louis Public Radio reported, benefactor Pat Jones touched both rivers at once. That’s the point in one picture: the land narrows until there’s nothing left but water on either side.
There’s a newer piece that older write-ups miss. A half-mile walking and biking trail named for Ted and Pat Jones runs along the Mississippi levee, and the state held its ribbon-cutting on October 5, 2024. That ceremony had first been planned for May. Flooding postponed it.
Which brings up the one real drawback. The park is day-use only because it’s floodplain, and the river doesn’t always stay out. Since 2007, high water had topped the 7-mile Kuhs agricultural levee six times by early 2021, Terrain magazine reported, and the closure after the 2019 flood dragged into 2021. The concrete path came back as crushed rock. The state now describes the route as pavement and compacted gravel.
When we checked on October 9, 2026, we found no closure notice. Still, after any big rise on either river, check the state park page before you drive out.
### Is the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower worth the climb?
Yes on a clear day, and you don’t actually have to climb. The tower has decks at 50, 100 and 150 feet, reached by stairs or an elevator, and its posted admission is $10, with kids 5 and under free. From the top deck at 150 feet, you’re looking down on the confluence instead of across it.
It stands on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3, run by the local village together with the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau. The view runs three ways: the confluence, downtown St. Louis to the south and the Clark Bridge to the north. On very clear days, the National Park Service says, you can pick out the Gateway Arch.
The tower went up for the 200th anniversary of the expedition, and the Park Service dates its completion to May 14, 2010. It later closed for about a year of renovation and reopened on May 14, 2026, with an expanded park, new murals and a children’s playscape, the tourism bureau announced.
Look at those dates again. May 14 is also the day in 1804 that the Corps of Discovery pushed off from Camp River Dubois, so the reopening landed 222 years to the day after the expedition left. We don’t know whether anyone planned that. It makes a good trivia question for the elevator ride.
Now the catch. The tower keeps a season, May through October plus January, and it closes on holidays. Two official pages list different days and hours, so we won’t guess for you. Check current hours: (618) 251-9101. If you’re reading this after October, call before you assume it’s open. Bringing a scout troop or a family reunion? Groups of 12 or more pay $5 a person.
Is it worth $10 a head? For two adults and two kids over 5, that’s $40. Our take: it’s the one paid stop on this trip, and it earns the money. The state park gives you the meeting point at ground level, and the colonnade at the Historic Site gives you a quieter look. Only the tower puts you 150 feet up, where the whole shape makes sense: two rivers coming in, one going out.
### What is at Camp River Dubois today?
A state historic site that re-creates the camp, about a mile from the tower. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources runs the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, where an interpretive center of about 14,000 square feet holds a 55-foot, full-scale replica of the expedition’s keelboat. The state lists no admission fee and points visitors to a donation page.
The keelboat is the reason to go inside. It’s cut away to show how the supplies were packed, and standing next to it does more for a ten-year-old than any map in a textbook. Fifty-five feet sounds like plenty of boat. Then you see what had to fit in it.
Outside stands a replica fort built to the Army’s 1803 regulations for a military post, with a settlers’ cabin nearby. Clark reached the camp site on December 12, 1803, according to the National Park Service, while Lewis spent that winter in St. Louis gathering supplies.
Then walk out to the colonnade. Eleven columns overlook the confluence, one for each state the expedition crossed, according to the Illinois DNR. Count them with the kids, then see who can name all eleven.
And the original camp? The Park Service says the channels moved, the Mississippi east and the Missouri’s mouth south, so the real campground is likely under the river now or on the Missouri side. The fort you walk through is a careful model standing near history rather than on top of it.
Hours follow the season. From September through May the site is open Wednesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. From Memorial Day to Labor Day it’s open daily, same hours. The address is 1 Lewis & Clark Trail, on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3, and the phone number is 618-251-5811.
### Why can’t you get to the Columbia Bottom platform right now?
Because the Missouri Department of Conservation closed all of Columbia Bottom on September 8, 2026, and only its Missouri River boat ramp has reopened, on September 30. The platform was shut even earlier: in April, St. Louis Public Radio was already sending readers to the state park instead. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is targeting the end of 2026 to demolish the old levee, and no reopening date has been posted. That stings. In 2003, the same station billed this spot on the south bank of the Missouri, right at its mouth, as the first Missouri-side platform looking straight at the confluence. Our guide to Columbia Bottom Conservation Area tracks the closure.
### Did Lewis and Clark start at St. Louis?
No, though St. Louis was their supply base and their finish line. According to the National Park Service, the boats left Camp River Dubois, on the Illinois bank, on May 14, 1804, and camped six miles up the Missouri that night. Day one of the expedition began in Illinois.
The full party didn’t come together for another week. The boats worked up the Missouri to a river town, where Lewis joined them from St. Louis on May 20, and the whole Corps left there on May 21, 1804. So where did it start? Take your pick: the Illinois bank, a river town up the Missouri, or St. Louis, where Lewis spent the winter gathering supplies.
