## Business Description Examples: Write the About Section That Makes a Stranger Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-description-examples-st-louis
Here’s what nobody tells you about the About section on your business listing: hardly anyone reads all of it. A stranger reads the first two lines, maybe three, and decides. So does the AI assistant somebody just asked, out loud, from a car on I-70, for a plumber who can come today. Neither one gets as far as the year you opened.
And most About sections spend those two lines on exactly that. Founded in. Family-owned and operated. Committed to quality and customer satisfaction. It reads fine. It also reads like every other business on the page, because it came from the same template every listing form seems to invite. The template is the problem. You’re not.
Picture a plumber working out of a small shop in Hanley Hills. She’s good. Licensed, insured, two decades of clearing drains and swapping water heaters in the old brick houses of north St. Louis County. Her About section says: “Family-owned and operated since 2005. We take pride in quality workmanship and customer satisfaction.” Every word is true. Not one of them tells a stranger with two inches of water in the basement that she’s the one to call.
This guide fixes that with a four-part formula, before-and-after examples for five St. Louis trades, and two quick tests. It’s the companion to our map of where to advertise your business for free, because your About is the one piece of writing you’ll paste onto almost every one of those sites. Write it well once and it gets you more calls everywhere it lands.
### What do I put for a business description?
Put four things in this order: who you help and with what, where you work, why you’re the safe choice, and what to do next. Lead with the first two in plain words, because a stranger and an AI both read your opening lines first, and both skip adjectives they can’t check.
Here’s the formula, one line per part:
Who you help, with what. The job in the customer’s own words. “Clogged drains and water heaters,” not “comprehensive plumbing solutions.” Nobody has ever typed “solutions” into a search bar at 11 p.m. with a wet floor.
Where. The places you actually work, named the way people here say them: north county, south city, the Metro East, both sides of the river. “Serving the greater St. Louis area” covers everyone and promises nobody anything.
Why you’re the safe choice. Proof a stranger can check. Who issued your license. How many years you’ve done this exact work. What you guarantee. Who actually shows up at the door.
What to do next. One action, with a detail that makes it easy. Call before 10 for same-day. Order by Wednesday for Saturday. Text a photo of the problem.
That’s the whole thing. History, mission, how Grandpa started with one truck: keep it if you like, after those four lines. Interested strangers read on. The rest never would have.
St. Louis has a famous shortcut for sizing up someone new: “Where’d you go to high school?” One answer and people can place your neighborhood, maybe your parish, maybe your cousin. Your About section gets read the same way, fast and hunting for a shortcut. Give the stranger theirs in the first line.
### What does a stranger read in the first two lines of your About?
They read for three answers, in about the time it takes a light to change: do you do my job, do you do it near me, and can I trust you with it. Yes to all three and they call. Otherwise the thumb moves on.
On a phone it’s even tighter. Plenty of listing pages show only the opening of your description and tuck the rest behind a “more” link. For most people who see it, your opening sentence is the whole pitch.
Try two tests on your own About.
The swap test. Paste a competitor’s name over yours. If the paragraph still works, it isn’t yours yet. “Quality service at a fair price” survives the swap every time. “Licensed with St. Louis County, same-day if you call before 10” doesn’t, because it belongs to one business.
The city test. Replace “St. Louis” with “Omaha.” If nothing else breaks, a stranger here has no reason to pick you over a business in any other city. Name the places, the housing, the local quirks you know cold.
Most About sections fail both. That isn’t a writing problem. It has a cause.
### Why do most About sections sound exactly alike?
Because the old advice was to list everywhere and let customers find you. So owners did the sensible thing with an impossible job: wrote one blurb fast, pasted it into twenty sign-up forms, and never went back. Every blank box that said “Tell us about your business” got the same polite filler.
Years later, that blurb is still out there. On one profile you close at 5. On another you still list the cousin who left in 2019. On a third, the platform runs a competitor’s ad right beside your paragraph. You didn’t do anything wrong. The list-everywhere-and-hope approach did exactly what it was built to do: it gave you mentions. It never gave you answers.
And answers are what people want now. Not “a plumber exists in north county.” Who can come today. Who’ll tell me the price before starting. An About that answers questions like those, kept current in one place you control, beats a hundred copies of filler.
That’s the shift this whole guide is built on. Your About isn’t a biography. It’s the answer to the question the stranger just typed.
### What do good business description examples look like?
They’re specific, local and a little boring in the best way. Here are five, all made up for this guide, each with a “before” written the way most of us start and an “after” built on the formula. Borrow the structure; swap in your own facts.
1. The plumber in Hanley Hills
Before: “Family-owned and operated since 2005. We take pride in quality workmanship and customer satisfaction. Call today!”
After: “Clogged drains, leaks and water heaters in older brick homes across north St. Louis County and the city. Licensed with St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis, insured, and you get the price before we start. Call before 10 a.m. for a same-day visit.”
Why it works: the stranger’s problem is in the first five words, and so is the kind of house they live in. The license line does real work too. Missouri doesn’t license plumbers statewide; St. Louis County runs its own plumbing license office, and the City of St. Louis runs its own, separately. So “licensed” by itself answers nothing. “Licensed with St. Louis County” answers the exact question a careful homeowner asks.
2. The bakery in Trenton
Before: “Welcome to our bakery! Everything is baked fresh daily with love and the finest ingredients. Stop in and treat yourself!”
After: “Gooey butter cake by the slab or the pan, custom birthday cakes, and coffee from 6 a.m. We’re on Route 50 in Trenton, about 30 miles east of downtown St. Louis. Order cakes by Wednesday for the weekend; call or message us.”
Why it works: gooey butter cake is the St. Louis word people actually type, and “the finest ingredients” is what every bakery types. The location line tells an Illinois commuter you’re on the way, and tells someone in the city it’s a real drive, so they order ahead instead of meeting an empty case.
3. The bookkeeper who works both sides of the river
Before: “We provide comprehensive bookkeeping and accounting services tailored to your unique business needs.”
After: “Monthly bookkeeping and payroll for contractors and restaurants with up to 20 employees, in Missouri and Illinois. If your crew works inside the City of St. Louis, we handle the city earnings tax and payroll expense tax filings so they’re right the first time. Book a 20-minute call to see if we’re a fit.”
Why it works: “tailored to your unique needs” is what a service business says before it has decided who it’s for. The after picks a customer, then names the local headache that customer dreads, and it isn’t going away: city voters renewed the earnings tax again in April 2026. A bookkeeper who names it up front sounds like someone who’s filed it a hundred times.
4. The dog groomer who takes the big dogs
Before: “We love pets! Our caring, professional team treats every pet like family.”
After: “Grooming for big and double-coated dogs: huskies, goldens, shepherds and doodles. One dog at a time, no cage dryers, and a full deshed before the St. Louis summer gets sticky. Text us a photo of your dog’s coat and we’ll tell you the time and the price.”
Why it works: the owner of an 80-pound shedding machine has been turned away before. Naming those breeds in line one says yes, yours too. “Treats every pet like family” sits on nearly every grooming page there is, which is why it can’t help.
5. The portrait photographer
Before: “Capturing life’s precious moments with passion and creativity. Every session is unique!”
After: “Senior portraits and family photos outdoors around St. Louis. Sessions run 45 minutes and your gallery arrives within two weeks. I’ll help you pick a spot and sort out any permit it needs. Message me your date and your school.”
Why it works: it answers the logistics a parent is quietly worried about (how long, how soon, is this allowed here) before they have to ask. And “your school” is a very St. Louis way to open a conversation.
Selling yourself, not a product? Steal the coaches’ playbook.
Notice what none of the five say. No “best.” No “premier.” No “one-stop shop.” Every claim is something a customer could check or hold you to, and that’s why it’s believable.
### How long should a business description be?
Long enough to answer the four questions, short enough that the first two lines work on their own. For most small businesses that’s three to six sentences up top, with any history or extra detail after.
Different sites give you different boxes. Google, for one, caps the description on a Business Profile at 750 characters as of October 2026 (our guide to the Google local business listing covers the rest of that profile). Other sites differ, so keep three versions that share one opening line:
One sentence for bios, social profiles and tight fields.
The short version, about 50 to 80 words, for most listing boxes: the four-part formula, nothing else.
The full version for any About with room to breathe, plus your services, your story and answers to the questions people ask on the phone.
Same first sentence everywhere. The stranger who bumps into you on three sites hears the same answer three times, and that’s how a name turns into trust. You’ll paste this onto Yahoo local business listings, map apps and every directory you join, so make sure the version that spreads is the good one.
### Does AI read your About section, and what does it look for?
It reads what it can find, and it looks for answers. When someone asks an assistant “who grooms huskies near Trenton?” or “a plumber in north county who can come today,” the reply gets built from text it can read about real businesses. A line like “licensed with St. Louis County, same-day if you call before 10” can be lifted straight into that reply. “Committed to excellence” can’t, because it answers nothing anyone asked.
This is the part the list-everywhere advice missed. A mention is not an answer. Twenty profiles that carry your name, phone and “quality service” give an AI twenty ways to know you exist and zero reasons to recommend you. One clear About, specific enough to quote, gives it a reason.
Nobody can promise you an AI will name your business, and anyone who does is guessing. What you control is whether there’s something worth quoting when it looks. Write your first two lines as if they’ll be read aloud to a stranger in a car, because sometimes they are.
### What should your logo, photo and banner say before anyone reads a word?
The same thing your first line says: what you do, and that you’re real. Our free basic listing gives you three images, a logo, a profile photo and a banner, and each one has a different job. The same three jobs apply anywhere you’re listed.
The logo has to read at thumbnail size, on a phone, in a list of other businesses. If it turns to mush at the size of a fingernail, simplify it.
The profile photo works best as a real face: you, your crew, the person who’ll actually show up.
The banner should show the work, somewhere that looks like here. Your van on a street of brick houses. A tray of gooey butter cake on your own counter. Not a stock photo from somewhere sunnier.
Use the same logo and photo on every site you’re on. When the stranger who saw you on a map app lands on your listing and sees the same face, the second look feels like recognition. Small things decide calls.

On a listing you control, with room for the whole story and nothing competing with it. Paste your short version into the free profiles everyone checks, the big search engines and map apps among them. Then give the full version a real home.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I describe my business in one sentence?
A.  Use this shape: what you do, for whom, where, plus one thing a stranger can check. For example: “Licensed plumber fixing drains and water heaters in older brick homes across north St. Louis County, same-day if you call before 10.” If it would still be true with a competitor’s name on it, add the detail only you can claim.
### Q. Can you provide an example of a short business description?
A.  A made-up bakery: “Gooey butter cake by the slab or the pan, custom birthday cakes and coffee from 6 a.m., on Route 50 in Trenton. Order cakes by Wednesday for the weekend.” What, where and what next, and not a word spent on a founding year.
### Q. What to put in a business profile?
A.  Your name, address and phone exactly as they appear everywhere else, your hours, the categories you really work in, a logo, a real photo and an About built on the four-part formula. Our free basic listing holds the name, address, phone, three images and About. More categories, locations and posts come with Gold.
### Q. What is an example of a business description?
A.  A made-up auto shop: “Brakes, suspension and check-engine diagnosis for Hondas, Toyotas and Subarus, in a two-bay shop in north St. Louis County. ASE-certified techs, a written estimate before any work, and a ride to MetroLink while you wait. Call or book online.” It never says “quality.” It shows it.
### Q. What are some good words to describe a business?
A.  Concrete ones a customer can check: licensed, insured, same-day, by appointment, written estimate, plus your exact services and places. Words that praise without proving, like quality, passionate, premier, best and solutions, get skimmed by people and give AI nothing to quote. If a word fits any competitor’s page, it isn’t helping yours.
### Q. Can AI create a company profile?
A.  Yes, as a draft. An AI turns notes into clean sentences in seconds. What it can’t know is your license, your service area, what you guarantee and how people should book. Give it those specifics, check every claim, and cut anything you couldn’t say to a customer’s face. Left to guess, it writes the old template.
### Q. What is a good simple bio?
A.  Name, what you do, who it’s for, one proof and one human detail: “I’m a portrait photographer shooting seniors and families outdoors around St. Louis. Galleries in two weeks. Ask me where I went to high school.” Use first person if you are the business, and keep the human detail true.
### Q. How to write a description for a business?
A.  List the questions customers ask you on the phone. Answer the top four in this order: what you do, where, why you’re the safe choice, what to do next. Read the first two lines alone and rewrite them until they stand up. Run the swap test, then paste the same opening everywhere you’re listed.

## Where to List Commercial Property for Lease and Rentals in St. Louis: What Each Site Gets You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-list-rental-and-commercial-property-st-louis
Every week a space sits empty is rent that never comes back. Not late rent. Not rent you’ll make up in the spring. Gone, the way an empty table is gone once the dinner rush ends. And the usual way of filling a vacancy, post it on a site or two and wait for the phone, is built to burn exactly those weeks.
Say you own a one-bay garage with a small office up front in Eagle Park, a small Metro East village on the Illinois side of the river. You post the bay on a commercial listing site and on Craigslist. A few inquiries come in the first week. By week three the post has slid below newer ones and the calls have stopped. The bay is still empty, and nothing in the listing tells a stranger who you are.
Or say you own a two-family flat in Pine Lawn, the North County city where most of the houses went up in the 1910s and 1920s. The downstairs unit opens on the first. You post it on Zillow Rental Manager, which charges nothing to list, and it shows up on Zillow, Trulia and HotPads. Two weeks in, Zillow emails to ask whether it’s still available. Miss that email and the listing switches itself off on day 21. That’s a sensible rule for a site that wants fresh listings. It’s also a three-week clock running on your vacancy.
Neither owner is doing it wrong. The old way is the problem: list the space where tenants browse, then hope the right one browses past before the post goes stale. Below: where a St. Louis owner can list a commercial space or a rental, what each site gets you as of October 2026, what your ad can say on each side of the river, and the one place a listing sits next to who you are. It’s one stop on our map of where to advertise your business for free in St. Louis.
### Where can I list my commercial property for lease?
In St. Louis, list commercial space where tenants browse: Crexi, which lets property owners post spaces for lease at no charge; LoopNet, which sells listing packages; and Craigslist, which charges a fee per commercial real estate post. Then put the same ad on your own business profile, next to your name and phone number, where it stays up.
Here’s what each one gets a small owner with one storefront, a couple of flex bays or a single office suite. Terms change often, so check current rules before you post.
Crexi. Crexi says listing costs nothing and there’s no cap on how many listings you publish. Owners can list spaces for lease there, though not properties for sale, and Crexi’s help center asks owners to add the Property Manager role to their profile first. You can build the listing by hand, upload a brochure for Crexi to pull the details from, or send the details by email. Tenants and buyers search it at no cost.
LoopNet. LoopNet’s own FAQ answers the question plainly: you can’t list a property there for free. It sells advertising packages at different levels of visibility, and its terms of use define the base-level listing as one with “no or limited exposure” on the site. What you can do at no cost is add the listing to CoStar, the research platform from the same company, though CoStar requires a subscription to view listings. Tenants browse it at no charge.
Craigslist. Most Craigslist posts cost nothing, but commercial real estate is one of the exceptions: Craigslist charges a small fee for every commercial real estate post in the US. You get a text ad with photos in the St. Louis commercial section, competing with everything posted after it.
A sign in the window, and the people you know. Still works. A banner on the storefront reaches every car that passes and nobody else. It also can’t answer what a tenant wants to know before calling: how big, what the zoning allows, what it costs to occupy, who owns it.
Then there’s the ad nobody puts on these lists: a real estate ad posted on your own business profile. More on that below, because it’s the only option here that carries your name, your phone and your track record along with the space. If you’re on the other side of the deal, hunting for space instead of filling it, our guide to leasing commercial space in St. Louis covers the tenant’s view.
### Where can you list a rental property for free in St. Louis?
For houses and apartments, three well-known places charge nothing to post: Zillow Rental Manager, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist. Each has limits worth knowing before you count on it.
Zillow Rental Manager. Since May 2022, listings posted directly to Zillow Rental Manager have been free to publish, and one listing posts to Zillow, Trulia and HotPads. An optional paid premium upgrade runs up to 90 days and places the listing higher in renters’ searches. The fine print to plan around: listings stay active 21 days by default, Zillow asks you to confirm availability after day 14, and a listing you don’t confirm deactivates on its own. Rental Manager covers houses, condos, apartment units and townhouses, and Zillow points communities with 25 or more units to its advertising program instead.
Facebook Marketplace. You can post a home for rent through Marketplace’s property for sale or rent listing type, and renters browse a property rentals category by area. Two rules matter. Meta’s discrimination policy bans Marketplace listings that state a preference about race, religion, sex, disability, marital status or the presence of children, among others. And if you turn the listing into a paid Facebook ad, US advertisers have to choose the Housing special ad category, which restricts how the ad can be targeted.
Craigslist. Posting an apartment or house for rent on Craigslist costs nothing in St. Louis; Craigslist charges for apartment rentals only in the Boston, Chicago and New York areas. It’s the bare-bones option. A post shows what you write and the photos you add, and it doesn’t show a renter much about who’s behind it.
Notice the pattern. Every one of these works best while the post is fresh. And on every one of them, the space is the star and you’re a contact line at the bottom.
### Why does a listed space still sit empty?
Because a portal post answers one question, is it available, and only while it’s live. Tenants arrive with a dozen more. The old way leaves the rest to a phone call, and a stranger scrolling at 11 at night doesn’t call. They keep scrolling.
Think about what a small business tenant wants to know before dialing. Can I run a detailing shop out of the bay, or is it storage only? Is there a restroom? Who handles snow on the lot? Who is this owner, and will they fix the roll-up door when it sticks in January? A renter looking at that Pine Lawn flat has a list too. Is the landlord local? How fast do repairs happen? Does anyone actually pick up? A portal post has room for square feet and a rent. It rarely has room for you.
Then there’s the clock. Zillow’s default is 21 days unless you keep confirming. A classified competes with everything posted after it. Paid boosts end on a date. That’s fine for a unit that rents in a week. For a commercial bay that takes a season to fill, it means re-posting, re-confirming and re-paying over and over, just to stay in front of people.
And here’s the part most listing advice skips. Some tenants no longer scroll a portal at all. They ask an AI assistant. Who has a small shop bay for lease near Route 3? Is there a two-bedroom for rent in Pine Lawn from an owner who lives nearby? The assistant doesn’t hand back a pile of mentions. It tries to hand back an answer, and it builds that answer from pages it can read: an address, a size, the terms, a real business with a working phone number behind it. A listing that switched itself off last Tuesday isn’t one of those pages anymore.
A mention is not an answer. The old way gets your space mentioned for a few weeks at a time. What gets you more calls is an ad that answers the tenant’s questions, sits on a page tied to a business that clearly exists, and is still there when someone, or something, comes looking.
### What can a rental ad say in Missouri and in Illinois?
It can describe the space, the rent, the terms and the screening standard you apply to every applicant. It can’t state a preference for or against people because of who they are. The federal Fair Housing Act, at 42 U.S.C. 3604(c), makes it illegal to publish a housing ad that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Under that section the ad itself can be the violation, even if nobody is ever turned away.
So the familiar shortcuts are out. “Perfect for a single professional.” “No kids.” Describe the unit instead: two bedrooms, second floor, steep stairs, off-street parking for one car, pets considered. Describe the property, never the person you picture living in it.
Now cross the river, because the St. Louis metro sits on two sets of state rules. Missouri’s Human Rights Act covers housing discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability and familial status. Illinois goes much further. The Illinois Department of Human Rights lists about twenty protected characteristics for real estate transactions, including age (40 and over), marital status, military status, arrest record, order of protection status, immigration status and, since January 2023, source of income. Its guidance names ads like “No Section 8” as possible discrimination, and it says a minimum-income rule may count only the tenant’s share of the rent when a voucher covers the rest.
That’s why the two owners up top can’t share a template. Copy the Pine Lawn ad for a flat in Eagle Park, and a line that passed on one side of the river can be a problem on the other. The Illinois act also reaches past housing: the department says it covers the sale or rental of commercial property too, so the Route 3 bay is in scope. Check city and county ordinances on top of state law, and treat this as general information, not legal advice.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to advertise rental property on Facebook?
A.  Post it on Marketplace using the property for sale or rent listing type, with bright photos, the rent, the terms and the general location. Describe the unit, never the tenant you want: Meta’s policy removes listings that state a preference about race, religion, sex, disability, marital status or the presence of children. If you turn it into a paid ad, US advertisers must choose the Housing special ad category, which limits targeting.
### Q. Are Zillow rental listings free?
A.  Yes, for listings posted directly to Zillow Rental Manager, which Zillow has made free to publish since May 2022. One listing reaches Zillow, Trulia and HotPads. An optional premium upgrade costs a flat fee, lasts up to 90 days and places the listing higher in searches. Listings stay up 21 days by default unless you confirm availability, and communities with 25 or more units go through Zillow’s advertising program. Check current terms.
### Q. Where is the best place to list an apartment for rent?
A.  Wherever renters near the unit already look. In St. Louis the common choices are Zillow Rental Manager, where one listing reaches Zillow, Trulia and HotPads, plus Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist’s apartments section, which has no posting fee here. Post the same accurate ad on each and keep it current. Then add it to your business profile as a real estate ad, a Gold feature, so it doesn’t vanish between portal posts.
### Q. What’s the best way to list a house for rent?
A.  Price it against similar rentals nearby, shoot bright daytime photos of every room, and write the facts a renter needs: rent, deposit, lease length, utilities, pets, parking and move-in date. Put your screening standard in writing and apply it to everyone. Post on the major rental sites, answer inquiries the same day, and re-confirm or renew before a listing expires so it doesn’t quietly drop off.
### Q. Can you list a rental on Zillow without a realtor?
A.  Yes. Zillow Rental Manager is built for owners to post directly with a regular Zillow account. You add the address, unit, property type, details, photos and your contact information, then publish, and the listing posts to Zillow, Trulia and HotPads. Its applications, lease signing and rent collection tools work without an agent. It covers houses, condos, apartment units and townhouses.
### Q. What are red flags for tenants?
A.  Facts you can verify, judged the same way for every applicant: an application that doesn’t match the ID or income documents, income you can’t confirm, past landlords who report unpaid rent or damage, and pressure to skip the application or the lease. A protected trait is never a red flag. In Illinois that includes source of income and arrest record, so count voucher income and don’t screen on arrests.
### Q. What are the four types of commercial leases?
A.  Most lists name gross, modified gross, net and percentage leases. In a gross lease the tenant pays one rent and the owner covers taxes, insurance and upkeep. A modified gross lease splits some of those costs. A net lease passes one or more of them to the tenant, and a triple net lease passes all three. A percentage lease adds a share of the tenant’s sales, which shows up most in retail.
### Q. Which website is best for posting rental property?
A.  There isn’t one best site; match the site to the tenant. For houses and apartments, Zillow Rental Manager reaches three rental sites with one listing, and Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist reach local browsers. For commercial space, Crexi lets owners list spaces for lease at no charge, and LoopNet sells listing packages. Whichever you use, put the same ad on a page tied to your business so tenants can see who you are.

## Video Marketing for Small Business: Which Platform Actually Brings St. Louis Customers
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/video-marketing-for-small-business-st-louis
Views don’t ring the phone. Most of the video advice handed to small businesses was written for creators, people who get paid for attention, so it says post every day, ride the trends and feed the algorithm. For a creator that’s sound advice. Their video only has to win this week. Yours has to make somebody call you, and the person about to call usually isn’t scrolling. They’re searching.
Picture a small-engine repair shop in Evansville, on the Illinois side, a short drive from the river. The owner props his phone against a parts bin and films a rebuilt outboard coughing back to life. Forty seconds, no music. He posts it on a Tuesday. His cousin likes it. Two regulars leave a comment. By Friday the feed has buried it under everyone else’s week, and that’s the last anybody sees of it.
The video was fine. The plan around it is what let him down. Every spring around Evansville somebody drags a boat out of the garage, pulls the cord and gets nothing. That person doesn’t follow repair shops. They type “outboard repair near me” into a phone, or ask an AI assistant who can look at a motor this week. So the useful question was never which app has the most users. It’s where your video will still be sitting when that person goes looking.
This guide is the video chapter of our map of where to advertise your business for free and what each place actually gets you. It covers what each platform does with a clip, four videos you can shoot on a phone this week, the FTC lines around customer testimonials, and why the best home for a video sits right next to your phone number.
### Which platform is best for video marketing?
There’s no single best platform, because each does a different job. Feed apps such as Instagram, TikTok and Facebook show a new video while it’s fresh. YouTube is built for search. Your Google Business Profile shows video to people already looking at your business. Post where a video keeps bringing customers after this week.
Here’s what each one does with the same clip, described plainly as of October 2026. Platforms change their rules often, so check each one’s help pages before you plan around a number.
Feed apps (Instagram Reels, TikTok, Facebook). A feed is built around what’s new and what’s catching attention right now, so every post competes with everything published after it. That suits staying in front of people who already know you: regulars, neighbors, the cousin. It’s a short window for anyone who doesn’t.
YouTube. It has its own search box, and its videos can also turn up in Google results, so a clip that answers a real question can keep drawing views long after upload day. A vertical or square video up to three minutes long counts as a Short, a limit YouTube raised for uploads after October 15, 2024.
Your Google Business Profile. Video here lands on your profile in Search and Maps, the panel people see when they look up your business by name or spot you on the map. Google’s help page sets videos at up to 30 seconds, up to 75 MB and 720p or higher. Uploads are reviewed first, can take 24 to 48 hours to appear, and nothing shows until the profile is verified.
A video post on your directory listing. On St Louis Near Me Directory, a video you post (a Gold feature) gets a page of its own, marked up with VideoObject schema, the structured data search engines read to understand a video. It sits on the same profile as your phone number, your hours and your About section.
You don’t have to choose. One 30-second clip, trimmed once, fits all four. The mistake in the old playbook is treating the feed as the finish line, when it’s closer to the starting gun.
### Where does a video keep working after this week?
In search. A video keeps working wherever people go looking for something: on YouTube, on Google and Maps, and on listing pages that carry your name and number. It fades fastest where people only scroll. So before you post, ask one question. Who will see this in March?
Scrolling and searching are different moods. Someone scrolling wasn’t looking for you. You interrupted them, and the next video interrupts them right back. Someone searching asked a question first, which means a video that answers it is exactly what they came for. One crowd is passing by. The other is already standing at the counter.
Run the outboard clip through that test. On the feed it had a decent Tuesday. On YouTube, titled the way a boat owner would actually type it (spring outboard tune-up: what we check before you launch), it can still turn up next April. A 30-second cut on the shop’s Google Business Profile plays for people who already looked the shop up. And on a directory profile it sits right under the phone number, which is the whole reason he made it.
Followers still matter. They’re your regulars, and regulars send referrals. But a town of about 3,000 people mostly knows its repair shop already. Growth comes from the people 20 or 40 miles out who don’t, along the highways into Macoupin County and across the Metro East, and those people find a business by searching for it. A feed that forgets you by Friday can’t reach them twice.
None of this means you’ve been doing video wrong. You were handed a playbook built for people who sell attention. You sell tune-ups, haircuts and brake jobs.
### What can a small business film this week with only a phone?
Four videos cover most of what a new customer wants to see: a 30-second walkthrough, a before and after, a straight answer to the question you hear most, and a customer telling their own story. None of them needs a crew. A phone held steady, decent light and a quiet room will carry all four.
Each one also lines up with a real category on our video board, which makes it easy to file when you post it to a directory profile.
The 30-second walkthrough. Start at the front door with the phone at chest height and show what a first-timer sees: where to park, the counter, the bay, the chair, the waiting area. It answers the question every new customer carries in silently, which is what am I walking into. On the board, this is a Virtual Tour.
The before and after. Same angle, same light, two short clips: the stained deck and the clean one, the overgrown fence line and the cleared one, the cracked screen and the fixed one. Fifteen seconds is plenty. These live under Success Stories.
The question you hear most. Whatever people ask on the phone before they book (Do you do same-day? Do you drive out to Evansville? How long does it take?), answer it to the camera in under a minute. The board has a Frequently Asked Questions category built for exactly this, and it’s the video most likely to match what someone types into a search bar or asks an AI.
The customer testimonial. A real customer, in their own words, saying what the problem was and what changed. Get their permission in writing before you post it. The rules for this one get their own section below.
A few phone habits do most of the heavy lifting. Shoot vertical if the clip is headed for Shorts, Reels or TikTok, and keep one cut at 30 seconds or less so it also fits a Google Business Profile. Put the light in front of you, never a bright window behind. Get the microphone close, because viewers forgive shaky footage long before they forgive bad sound. And say where you work out loud: the town, the side of the river, the area you cover. Captions pick up spoken words, which hands search one more clue about who you serve.
For formats to borrow, browse our video board, which holds hundreds of videos sorted into categories such as Customer Testimonials, Virtual Tours, How-To Tutorials and Behind-the-Scenes. Borrow the format. Never the footage.
### How do you use customer testimonial videos without breaking FTC rules?
Use real customers describing what actually happened to them, disclose anything you gave them for appearing, and never script, invent or AI-generate a customer. The FTC’s Endorsement Guides and its 2024 rule on consumer reviews and testimonials both reach the videos you use in your own marketing, whether they run on your website, your profile or anywhere else.
That last part surprises people. The FTC’s own Q&A says a business that puts testimonials on its own site is disseminating them, not merely hosting them. Your testimonial video is your ad. Here are the lines in plain English, as of October 2026:
Real people, real experience. An endorsement has to reflect the honest opinion of the person giving it, and they have to have actually used what they’re praising. A customer can’t vouch for a service they never bought.
Say what you gave them. If the customer got a discount, a gift, a payment or anything else of value for appearing, disclose it clearly. In a video, the FTC says a text disclosure has to stand out enough that viewers would actually notice it.
No rewards for praise. The FTC’s Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, in effect since October 21, 2024, bans incentives that require a positive opinion. Thanking someone for their time is fine. Paying them to say they loved you is not.
No made-up customers. The same rule bans testimonials that misrepresent who’s giving them, including AI-generated people who don’t exist.
Insiders say so. If your brother-in-law or your lead tech is on camera praising the business, the relationship has to be clear to the viewer.
Typical results, or say what’s typical. If the result in the video isn’t what customers generally get, the ad needs to make the generally expected result clear.
This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice. The FTC’s business guidance pages are short and readable, so check them before you build a campaign on testimonials. Fake praise was always somebody’s shortcut. Now it’s a federal problem, which leaves the honest version, real customers and real work, as the only kind worth filming.
### Why does a video on your own listing reach customers a feed can’t?
Because it sits where people look for answers, right beside the answer they need most, which is how to reach you. On a listing that works like your own website, each video gets an indexed page of its own, so a search engine or an AI assistant can find it and send someone straight to your phone number.

A reel that scrolled past on Tuesday is hard to point anyone to on Thursday. A 40-second video titled for same-day laptop screen repair near UMSL, on a page of its own, attached to a business with an address, hours and a phone number, is easy to point to.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some good video ideas?
A.  Start with what customers ask before they book. A 30-second walkthrough of your space, a before and after of real work, a short answer to your most common question and a customer telling their own story cover most needs. After those, rotate in a behind-the-scenes clip or a quick introduction to the person who answers the phone.
### Q. What are some creative video ideas for companies?
A.  Film the part customers never see: the early-morning prep, the parts order arriving, the test after the repair. Show a whole job start to finish in 20 seconds. Bust one myth in your trade. Introduce your team one person at a time. Creative usually means specific, and a real job on a real St. Louis street beats a clever concept.
### Q. How do I make a marketing video for my business?
A.  Pick one question a customer asks, answer it in under a minute and film it on your phone in good light with the sound close. Trim the dead air, add captions, and put your business name and town in the title. Post a 30-second cut to your Google Business Profile and the full clip to YouTube and your directory profile.
### Q. What kind of videos attract viewers?
A.  Videos that answer something the viewer already wants to know. On a feed, faces, motion and a strong first second hold attention. In search, the title and the opening seconds have to match the question. For a local business the viewer who matters is the one deciding whether to call, so clarity beats polish every time.
### Q. What is a testimonial video?
A.  A short video in which a real customer describes their experience with your business in their own words: the problem, what you did and how it turned out. Under FTC guidance it has to reflect the customer’s honest opinion and real experience, and you have to disclose anything you gave them for appearing.
### Q. What are some examples of customer testimonials?
A.  The common types are a before-and-after story told by the customer, a first-time customer explaining why they finally called, a longtime customer explaining why they keep coming back, and a quick reaction on site when the job is done. Our video board files these under Customer Testimonials, so you can see how the format looks before you film.
### Q. What is a customer testimonial?
A.  A statement from a real customer about their experience with a business, used in that business’s marketing. It can be written, audio or video. The FTC treats a testimonial you publish on your own site or profile as your advertising, so it has to be genuine, show typical results or say what’s typical, and disclose any connection or reward.
### Q. How can I market my business online?
A.  Start with the profiles customers and AI check first, such as your Google Business Profile, Bing and Apple Maps, which cost nothing to claim. Then put answers where people search: videos, posts and offers on a listing that works like your own website. Followers help you keep customers, but most new ones arrive by searching.

## Coupon Advertising for Small Business: 13 Coupon Ideas That Bring St. Louis Customers Back
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/coupon-advertising-for-small-business-st-louis
Deal sites rent you a crowd. You pay for it twice, once in the discount and again in the cut the site keeps, and then the crowd leaves with the deal. It came for the price. It never learned your name, never saved your number, and the next time its car makes a noise it opens the same app and picks whoever is cheapest that week.
Picture a mechanic with a two-bay shop just off I-70 in Truesdale. Say he runs a half-price oil change through one of those sites. The bays fill for a month. Most of the drivers have never heard of him and won’t think of him again, because the voucher in their pocket carried the site’s name, not his. When the deal ends, so do they.
He didn’t do anything wrong. He followed the old playbook: put a deal where the crowd is and hope some of it sticks. The playbook is what’s broken. The coupon worked. It just worked for somebody else’s address.
This guide is the other way to run coupon advertising for a small business: coupon ideas that fit St. Louis owners on both sides of the river, the margin math that tells you what you can afford to give, the rules that keep an offer honest, and where to post it so first-timers come back. It’s one stop on our bigger map of where to advertise your business for free, and what each option actually gets you.
### What are some good coupon ideas?
The best coupon ideas buy a first visit without teaching people to wait for a sale: a first-time customer discount, a no-charge estimate, a complimentary first consultation, a gift with purchase, a referral discount that rewards both people, a loyalty reward, a bundled offer, or a seasonal discount for your slow month. Pick the one your margin can carry.
Those aren’t pulled from thin air. They’re the real offer types on the St Louis Near Me Directory coupon board, where a business tags the kind of deal it’s running so shoppers can browse by it. Here’s what each one does well, and the trade it suits.
First-Time Customer Discount. The cleanest coupon there is, because it says exactly what you want: come try us once. A salon can take a slice off a first cut and color, then win the second visit on the work itself. New clients only, one per household, and say so.
Estimate (no-charge). Built for anyone who quotes a job. A landscaper walks the yard, a mechanic reads the check-engine code. It costs you an hour, not inventory, and it puts you on the property or under the hood, which is where trust starts.
Initial Consultation (complimentary). The service-business version. A tutor’s first session on the house lets a parent see the fit before committing to a semester. A bookkeeper or a personal trainer can do the same with a half-hour sit-down.
Gift with Purchase. Buy a dozen cookies, take home a loaf of the day’s bread. The customer values the loaf at shelf price. You pay what it cost to bake.
Buy One, Get One. Strong where the second item costs you very little: a second coffee, a second car wash, a kid’s meal with an adult entrée. Dangerous almost everywhere else, as the math below shows.
Bundled Offer. Package what people already buy together and price the bundle a little under the parts: brakes plus a tire rotation, a haircut plus a beard trim, a mowing season plus fall cleanup.
Referral Discount. Pay your happiest customers to talk. Reward the referrer and the newcomer both, and you’ve bought a first visit that shows up pre-sold by a neighbor.
Loyalty Rewards. The tenth wash, the sixth lesson, the punch card that ends in a pie. It rewards the exact people you want more of.
Seasonal Discount. Aim it at your dead weeks, not your busy ones. A landscaper’s early-spring booking deal. A tutor’s summer slots. A furnace tune-up in September, before the first cold snap fills the calendar on its own.
Group Discount. Teams, offices, church groups, birthday parties. One yes brings ten people through the door.
Percentage Discount. Simple and familiar, and the one most likely to cost more than you think, because it grows with the ticket.
Instant Savings. Taken off at the counter, no clipping, no codes. Good for impulse buys and for customers who hate paperwork.
Special Discount. The catch-all for a reason that’s yours: teachers, nurses, veterans, a grand reopening.
Look at what the strongest ones share. They ask for something small (a first visit, a referral, a return trip) and hand over something worth more to the customer than it costs you. That gap is where a coupon makes money. Contests, partnerships and community events are a different toolbox, and we cover them in small business promotions that bring customers.
### Do coupons bring in new customers, or just bargain hunters?
Both, and which one you get depends mostly on where the coupon lives. A coupon on a deal site goes to people who browse deal sites. They’re shopping the discount, not the business, and the site is built to keep them shopping discounts, so the next offer they see is a competitor’s. Nobody’s wrong for hunting bargains. The setup just routes their loyalty to the platform instead of to you.
There’s a second cost nobody prints on the coupon. Deal sites usually keep a share of what the customer pays, so the discount and the site’s cut stack on top of each other. Terms vary and change often, so read the current ones and run them against your own numbers before you sign anything.
Now put the same offer where your business already lives. Someone searching for a mechanic finds your first-visit deal, and right beside it sit your phone number, your hours, your About section and what other customers said. They aren’t comparing coupons anymore. They’re deciding whether to trust you, and the coupon tips the yes. That’s the customer who comes back, because they chose you first and the deal second.
### How big should the discount be?
Smaller than your gut says, and you figure it in profit, not price. A discount comes straight out of what you keep, not out of what you charge, and that changes the math fast.
Say a bakery keeps about a third of every sale after flour, butter, wages and rent. Take a quarter off, and it keeps a twelfth. It now has to sell four times as much just to earn what it earned before the coupon. That’s how a big percentage-off deal can pack a shop and still lose the month.
Buy one, get one is harsher. On an item where you keep a third, handing over the second one means you collect for one and pay to make two, so every pair loses money. It only works on things that cost you very little to produce: drip coffee, a fountain drink, a second scoop.
Second coffee on the house? First, know where St. Louis buys fresh beans.
A gift with purchase runs the other way. The customer feels the gift at full value. You pay your cost. The same logic carries over to service businesses: a no-charge estimate or a complimentary first consultation costs an hour of your time, not product off a shelf. If your calendar has open hours on Tuesday afternoons, an offer that fills them is close to pure upside.
Three questions settle the size of any offer. What do I keep on this sale today? How many extra customers would I need just to break even? And how many of them have to come back at full price for this to be worth it? If you can’t answer the third one, you’re running a giveaway, not an ad.
### Where should your offer live so first-time customers come back?
On your own listing, next to your phone number, your About section and your reviews. Scattering profiles across a dozen free sites and hoping is the old way. A listing that works like your own website, with your offers, events, openings and stories in one place that people and AI can read, is what gets you more customers.
Here’s how that works on St Louis Near Me Directory. Our free basic listing holds your name, address, phone, three images and an About section. That’s a fine start, but coupons aren’t part of it. Coupons and offers are a Gold feature. Gold is the foundation everything else is built on: your profile, up to 10 categories, up to 40 location tags, and every coupon, event, job, product, video and story you post. Each coupon sits on your profile and on its own page, and Gold posts “also appear in directory menus & search results,” so a shopper browsing the coupon board finds your offer, then finds you. If you want more from us, Platinum doubles what Gold includes and Diamond triples it. The Gold plan page lays out the whole list.
Then comes the part most owners never see. A mention isn’t an answer. People don’t just type “mechanic” anymore. They ask their phone or an AI assistant something like “who’s running a first-visit deal on brakes near me” or “which salon has a new-client discount this month.” A deal-site voucher answers that for the deal site. An offer on its own indexed page, tied to a real business with a phone number and an About section, is something search engines and AI can read and quote, even to someone who has never heard of us. Nobody can promise an AI will name you. But it can’t name you for an offer it can’t read.
Say you run a diner in Fayetteville, the little Metro East village that sits just west of the Kaskaskia River, where Illinois 4/15 crosses it. The Kaskaskia River State Fish and Wildlife Area stretches downriver from town, so weekend mornings bring anglers who’ve never sat at your counter. A deal-site coupon might catch one of them once. A loyalty offer on your own listing, the sixth breakfast on the house, catches the one who drives in every Saturday in season. That regular is worth more than any crowd a site can rent you.

### How do you turn a coupon customer into a regular?
Treat the coupon as the start of a conversation, not the end of a sale. You paid for the first visit. The second one is where the profit is.
Go back to the Truesdale mechanic. This time his first-visit deal sits on his own listing, so the driver who pulls in has already seen his number, his hours and his reviews. When the job’s done, he does three small things. He writes the next service date on the windshield sticker. He asks whether he can text a reminder. And he mentions, without a speech, that a review helps a two-bay shop more than any ad. None of that costs a discount, and all of it turns a coupon customer into his customer.
Then hand them the next reason to return. A loyalty reward or a referral discount makes the perfect second coupon, because it only pays out when they come back or bring somebody. Post it on your listing so it’s waiting when they look you up again.
Give every place you post a different code, too. FIRSTBRAKE on the listing, FIRSTBRAKEFLYER on the counter card. A month later you’ll know which one pulled, instead of guessing. And retire stale offers on schedule. A coupon that’s been up since last spring tells a visitor nobody’s minding the store. For a full year of promotions beyond coupons, the local promotions playbook lays out the calendar.
### How do you write coupon terms that won’t backfire?
Put every condition right next to the offer, in plain words, and give it an end date. That one habit heads off most of the trouble.
The Federal Trade Commission keeps a guide for offers that hand over something at no charge with a purchase, 16 CFR Part 251, first published in 1971 and still current as of October 2026. A few of its lines read like they were written for a corner shop:
State the terms, conditions and obligations clearly at the outset, close to the offer. An asterisk pointing to fine print at the bottom doesn’t count.
Sell the item the customer has to buy at its regular price, which the guide describes as a price you’ve openly charged for a substantial stretch, about 30 days. Quietly marking it up to cover the gift is exactly what it warns against.
Don’t run the same with-purchase deal on the same item for more than six months out of any twelve in one trade area, and let at least 30 days pass between runs.
Calling it a gift or a bonus doesn’t change any of the above.
Both sides of the river have their own law here too. Missouri’s Merchandising Practices Act and Illinois’s Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act each make deception or a hidden material fact in advertising unlawful, and the Illinois act tells courts to consider the FTC’s interpretations. The safe habit is identical in Truesdale and in Fayetteville: say what the customer gets, what they have to do, and when it ends. This is a starting point, not legal advice, so run anything unusual past a lawyer.
Sales tax is friendlier than most owners expect. Missouri’s rule (12 CSR 10-103.555) says the value of a store coupon you issue and redeem isn’t part of your taxable receipts, and Illinois treats a retailer’s own discount coupon the same way (86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.2125), so you charge tax on what the customer actually pays. The two states split on manufacturer coupons a retailer gets reimbursed for: Illinois taxes the full price, Missouri taxes only what the customer paid. Your accountant gets the final word.
Expiration dates do two jobs. They give the offer urgency, and they protect you from honoring a three-year-old coupon at a price you’ve since changed. Every coupon on our board shows its expiration date, and Google asks for start and end dates when you post an Offer on a Business Profile. One caution: a gift certificate someone paid for isn’t a coupon. Federal rules (12 CFR 1005.20) generally keep its funds from expiring for at least five years, so keep the two separate.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is couponing still a thing in 2026?
A.  Yes, it just moved to phones. In a February 2025 nationally representative Consumer Reports survey of 2,015 U.S. adults, 36 percent of grocery shoppers said they use coupons or member discounts frequently and another 38 percent occasionally. Consumer Reports also notes digital redemptions passed print back in 2020. For a local business, that means your offer has to be somewhere a phone can find it.
### Q. How can I create coupons for my business?
A.  Decide the one thing you want the customer to do: a first visit, a referral, a return trip. Pick the offer type your margin can carry, then write the headline, the terms and an end date in plain words. Add a short code so you can track it. Post it where customers check you out, such as a Gold listing with us, an Offer post on your Google Business Profile, and a card at the counter.
### Q. Can you give me an example of a coupon?
A.  Here’s one a Truesdale tutor could post: “New students: first 45-minute session on the house. Call to book and mention code FIRSTMATH. One per family, grades 3 through 8, expires December 31.” It names who qualifies, what they get, how to redeem it and when it ends, so nobody walks in confused and nobody argues at the door.
### Q. How do discounts attract customers?
A.  They lower the risk of trying someone new. A first-time customer isn’t weighing your price so much as the chance you’ll disappoint them, and a discount or a complimentary first consultation makes that bet cheaper. Discounts also reward habits. Consumer Reports’ February 2025 survey found 80 percent of Americans who shop for groceries belong to at least one store loyalty program. People like being rewarded for coming back.
### Q. What are the downsides of couponing?
A.  Three big ones. A deep discount can wipe out your profit on every sale it touches. Deal-site coupons tend to draw people loyal to the deal, not to you. And an offer that never ends trains customers to wait for it. Loyalty programs can sour too: in that same Consumer Reports survey, the top complaint among dissatisfied members was that the discounts weren’t as good as expected.
### Q. Do stores lose money from coupons?
A.  On the coupon sale itself, often yes, and that’s fine if it’s planned. A coupon is a marketing cost, the price of a first visit. It turns into profit when the customer returns at full price or sends a friend. The shops that lose money for good usually picked a discount too deep for their margin, or ran it somewhere customers had no reason to come back.
### Q. What are some creative coupon code ideas?
A.  Make the code do two jobs: describe the offer and tell you where it came from. A salon might use NEWLOOK on its listing and NEWLOOKCARD at the register. A landscaper could run SPRINGFIRST for early bookings, and a bakery DOZENPLUS for a gift with purchase. A Fayetteville diner might try RIVERMORNING for its anglers. Keep codes short, easy to say aloud, and skip look-alike characters like 0 and O.
### Q. What are the best coupon websites?
A.  For shoppers, the big categories are store apps, coupon-code browser tools and daily-deal sites. For an owner, the best one is the page where your customer meets you, not a middleman. That means your Google Business Profile, which lets you post an Offer with a coupon code and terms, and a listing you control, where coupons and offers are included with Gold and sit beside your phone number and reviews.

## Does Blogging Help SEO for a Small Business? The 2026 Answer for St. Louis Owners
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/does-blogging-help-seo-for-small-business-st-louis
Somebody gets quoted. Tonight a homeowner in Mt Olive will type a question about her house into her phone, and the answer that comes back will borrow its explanation from somebody’s page. Maybe a page written by someone in her own county. More likely a national site that has never once mentioned Macoupin County.
Here’s her question. She just closed on an older house in a town with coal-mining roots, and a line in her insurance paperwork mentions mine subsidence. Does she need that? Can she drop it? Now picture an insurance agent a few minutes from her front door who could answer it half asleep. Macoupin is one of 34 Illinois counties where mine subsidence coverage is automatically included in a property policy, and an owner who doesn’t want it has to reject it in writing, according to the Illinois Mine Subsidence Insurance Fund. That agent has explained it across a desk more times than she can count.
She has never once written it down anywhere a search engine, or an AI assistant, can read it.
That’s the real question hiding inside “does blogging help SEO.” Forget whether blogs are fashionable. What matters is whether the answer you give out loud every week exists anywhere in writing, so the next person who asks a machine gets your answer and not a stranger’s.
You’ve probably heard that blogging is dead. What died is the post that could have been written for any town on earth: “5 Tips for Choosing the Right Insurance Agent,” padded out to whatever length somebody swore Google prefers. Google says flatly that it has no preferred word count. What it does publish is a long list of questions about whether a page shows first-hand expertise and tells readers something beyond the obvious. The filler flunks them. The agent’s answer about mine subsidence passes without trying.
Still sorting out where your business should show up at all? Start with our map of where to advertise your business for free, then come back for the part those sites can’t do for you.
### Are blogs still relevant in 2026?
Yes, for a small business, as long as each post answers a question your customers really ask. Generic “top tips” filler is what died. A page that answers one real question, with details only you know, is the kind of page Google says it wants to reward, and the kind AI answers draw from.
Forget the online-diary picture. For a business, a blog post is a page that answers one question in writing, under your name. People never stopped asking questions. More of them now ask an AI assistant instead of clicking through ten links, and that assistant still has to read somebody’s page to answer.
What changed is the bar. For years a business could publish a thin post on a popular topic and pick up a trickle of traffic. Google’s guidance on helpful, people-first content now reads like a checklist aimed squarely at that habit. Its warning signs include content made mainly to attract search visits, pages that mostly summarize what others already said, and writing to a particular word count. On the other side of the ledger sit original information, first-hand expertise, and a reader who leaves having learned enough to reach their goal.
Read that list as an owner and something flips. You can’t outspend a national publisher. You can out-know one. Nobody writing generic advice for every zip code in the country has sat across from a Mt Olive homeowner holding a mine subsidence form. You have. That first-hand detail is the one thing filler can’t fake, and it’s exactly what Google says it’s looking for.
So yes, relevant. Different, though. Fewer posts, and every one of them carrying something only you could have written.
### Does blogging help SEO for a small business?
Yes, when each post answers a specific question better than anyone else nearby has. No, when it’s filler. SEO is a long name for a simple idea: showing up when someone searches. Every useful post is one more page that can show up, for one more question, in front of one more person who’s about to call somebody.
In plain words: your listing or homepage shows up for a short list of searches, mostly your name, your trade and your town. It can’t answer two hundred different questions. A post can answer one, all the way down. Publish a couple dozen over a few years and you’ve built a couple dozen extra doors into your business, each standing on the exact words somebody typed.
The posts help each other, too. A post on mine subsidence links to one on insuring an older home, and both link back to your profile and your phone number. Search engines follow those links the way readers do. Google’s advice on its AI features lists making content easy to find through internal links as one of the fundamentals that still matter.
What a blog won’t do is fix the basics. If your hours are wrong and your phone number is two numbers ago, a post won’t save you. It won’t pay off in a week, either. Our guide to content marketing for small businesses covers where to start and the honest timeline, so this page won’t repeat it. The short version: think in months, and know that the slow start is where a lot of owners give up.
### How does an AI answer decide whose page to quote?
It needs a page that answers the question, and then it shows the reader where that answer came from. Google says a page has to be indexed and eligible to appear in Search with a snippet to be shown as a supporting link in AI Overviews and AI Mode, and that there are no additional technical requirements. Translation: the same kind of page that can rank can be quoted.
The part most owners haven’t heard is how those answers get assembled. Google describes a “query fan-out” technique, where the AI may run several related searches across subtopics and gather supporting pages from each. So the Mt Olive homeowner might ask something broad, like what to know before insuring an older house in her part of Illinois. Behind the scenes, that can splinter into narrower searches, and one of them lands on mine subsidence. That narrow search is where a small local page can win, because almost nobody else bothered to write the narrow answer.
Other assistants work along similar lines when they search the web. OpenAI, for one, says it runs a crawler called OAI-SearchBot to surface websites in ChatGPT’s search features. None of these companies publishes a formula for who gets cited, so anybody promising you a guaranteed spot in an AI answer is guessing. What they all need is the same raw material: a public page that says the thing clearly.
Which is why a mention is not an answer. A listing that says “insurance agent, Mt Olive” is a mention. It tells a machine you exist. A post explaining how mine subsidence coverage works in Macoupin County, what it means for a buyer and what to ask before turning it down, is an answer. Machines quote answers. And since the post sits on its own page, a stranger can land on it from an AI answer without ever having heard of you, or of us.
### What does a blog post worth quoting look like?
It reads like your best answer across the counter, typed up. Before you publish anything, run one test: could a competitor in another city post it by swapping out the town name? If yes, it’s filler, however polished it sounds.
Take a tax preparer in Washington Park, the small Metro East village with its own MetroLink stop. Lots of people on that side of the river work on the other side of it, and every spring some of them walk in asking the same thing: I live in Illinois and get paid in Missouri, so where do I file?
The filler version is called “Top Tax Tips for the New Year.” Seven bullet points. Keep good records. Don’t miss the deadline. It could run on any website in America.
The version worth quoting is titled with the question itself and answers it in the first two sentences. Then it says the thing a Metro East preparer says every spring. According to the Illinois Department of Revenue, Illinois has reciprocal agreements with four states, Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan and Wisconsin, and Missouri isn’t on that list. For a lot of households that means a Missouri return plus an Illinois return that claims a credit for the Missouri tax, and working from home can change the picture, so the post tells readers to check their own situation. That one paragraph outweighs the seven bullets combined, because nobody finds it on a page written for everywhere.
Posts worth quoting tend to share the same bones:
The title is the question, worded the way customers actually say it.
The first two or three sentences answer it, plainly, before any backstory.
At least one detail only somebody local and in the trade would know.
A real job, with no names and all the details: what the customer asked, what you found, what happened next.
Cost in words, not numbers. What pushes the price up, what keeps it down, what people regret skimping on. Prices change; the reasons don’t.
Your name and your business at the bottom. Google’s guidance encourages accurate bylines, and readers trust a post signed by the person who does the work.
Tempted to let ChatGPT write it? Teach it to sound like you first
About drafting with AI, since everybody asks. Google says generative AI can be useful for researching a topic and adding structure to original content, and that using it to churn out many pages without adding value may violate its spam policy on scaled content abuse. It also says to fact-check everything AI produces before you publish. Treat it like an assistant taking dictation. The local fact, the real job and the opinion still have to come from you, because those are the parts a machine can’t know.
### Where should a small business post its blog if it has no website?
Somewhere you control, next to your phone number, hours and reviews, where search engines and AI tools can read it. A website is one way to get that. It isn’t the only way, and for a lot of owners it’s the slowest.
Here’s how the usual options stack up as of October 2026, so check each platform’s current terms. Medium lets anyone publish with a free account, and posts can reach readers who already browse there. LinkedIn lets members and company page admins publish articles that show up in their connections’ and followers’ feeds, a natural fit for professional services that sell to other businesses. Either way, though, the post lives on that platform’s site, under that platform’s rules, a click or two away from anything that lets a reader hire you.
Your own website keeps every post next to everything else, and if you already have one you keep current, post there. The catch is everything a site asks for once it exists: hosting, updates, security, and a brand-new domain search engines have never heard of. We wrote a whole guide on whether you need a website or a listing. The short version: plenty of owners need the second one first.

### Is a blog worth the time for a one-person business?
Only at a pace you’ll actually keep. A blog has three real costs, and all three land on the owner.
Time. A post worth quoting takes a real evening: thinking it through, writing it, checking the facts, reading it out loud once. Picture the Mt Olive agent after a day of renewals and claims calls. That evening has to come from somewhere.
Consistency. One strong post a month, month after month, beats ten in January and silence until next year. Customers notice the rhythm. So does anyone deciding whether you’re still active.
The abandoned blog. This one stings. A customer clicks your blog and the newest post is three years old. Nobody thinks “busy owner.” They wonder whether you’re still open. An abandoned blog can look worse than none at all, and changing the dates won’t fix it. Google lists updating a page’s date to make it seem fresh, when the content hasn’t substantially changed, among its warning signs.
Here’s the reframe. You’re not behind because you never blogged. The old way told you to list everywhere and wait for the phone. It never mentioned that the answers you give away every single day are the most valuable marketing you own, or that each one disappears the second the customer hangs up. Writing one of them down a month is a smaller job than it sounds.
Start with the question you answered most this week. Write it the way you said it. Then post it somewhere it sits beside your phone number.
