### What is the income limit for the Missouri property tax credit?
On the Missouri Department of Revenue’s credit FAQ, a renter or part-year owner qualifies with total household income of $27,200 or less if single, or $29,200 or less if married filing combined. If you owned and occupied your home the entire year, the limit is $30,000 single or $34,000 married filing combined. For calendar years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, RSMo 135.030 raises the maximum upper limit to $38,200 single, $42,200 single for a full-year owner, $41,000 married filing combined and $48,000 for a married couple who owned and occupied the home all year.
How the math works, in plain words. If your income is $14,300 or less, the formula subtracts nothing, so your credit equals the tax, or the rent share, you paid, up to the cap. Above $14,300 the credit tapers as income rises. Past the ceiling it’s zero. The exact figure comes off a table in the claim instructions, but the shape is simple: the lowest incomes get the most back.
### Can you get the freeze and the credit at the same time?
Yes. Neither program rules out the other, and they work on different things. The freeze keeps the bill from growing; the credit refunds part of whatever tax you actually paid, which RSMo 135.010 defines as tax paid before you file. Here’s how that stacks, on round, made-up numbers.
Take a widow in north county, 67, who owns her brick ranch outright and lives on $13,800 a year in Social Security. Her base-year bill was $2,600. Two years later, a reassessment and a school levy increase would have pushed it to $3,000. With the freeze, she’s billed $2,600, give or take any change in the Blind Pension Fund levy, and the $400 increase never shows up.
Now the circuit breaker. Her income is under $14,300, so the formula subtracts nothing, and she paid more tax than the cap. A claim for 2025 puts her in line for the full $1,100. A claim for 2026 reaches $1,550. Put the two together and a $3,000 bill nets out to about $1,050 out of pocket.
The renter version: a 72-year-old in Dutchtown paying $650 a month, same $13,800 income. That’s $7,800 of rent a year, and 20 percent of it, $1,560, counts as her property tax share. A 2025 claim caps her at $750. A 2026 claim caps her at $1,055. She gets no freeze, because the freeze is for owners. The circuit breaker is hers as long as her landlord pays property tax on the building.
Real claims move with every dollar of income, so treat those as the shape of the math, not a promise.
The freeze can’t follow you to assisted living. Here’s what pays for it.
### How do you apply for each one without paying a middleman?
Directly, through the government office that runs it, and for the circuit breaker, with a counselor who charges nothing. Here’s each path.
The county freeze. You apply in the county’s online portal while a window is open, and in-person help is offered at the county government center at the county seat and at two other county offices. The county ordinance sets the deadline at June 30 of the tax year you’re applying for, and the county posts each window on its freeze page, which currently reads “Applications Are Currently Closed.” Have these ready:
Your parcel (locator) number, from the county’s property tax lookup
Proof of age and identity: a state driver’s license or ID, or a birth certificate
Proof of ownership: your warranty, quit claim, grant or survivorship deed
Proof you live there: license or ID, voter registration card, license renewal card or a utility bill
If the house is in a trust: two pages, the one naming you trustee or beneficiary (or the certificate of trust) and the signature page
The deed is where seniors get squeezed. The county posted a buyer-beware notice about a deed-copy website that enrolled seniors in a $30 monthly membership, sometimes charged them twice, and often never delivered the deed. The county’s own price for a deed recorded after 1974 is $2 for the first page and $1 for each page after, with most deeds landing between $3 and $5 plus a small convenience fee. Bring a credit or debit card; that’s all the county takes for deed copies.
Renewing the county freeze. Through the 2026 window, approved seniors had to renew every year. In August 2026, the County Council passed Substitute Bill No. 1 for Bill No. 133, which says approved taxpayers “shall not be required to renew their status” and keeps everyone found eligible as of January 1, 2026, enrolled. The county hasn’t posted its next window yet, so confirm your status on the freeze page, or with the county Department of Revenue at (314) 615-7100, before you skip a renewal.
The City freeze. March 1 to June 30, every year, through the City Assessor’s Office. Miss it and you wait a year.
The circuit breaker. If you have to file a Missouri income tax return, you claim it on Form MO-PTS attached to your MO-1040. If you don’t have to file, you send Form MO-PTC by itself. Owners attach the paid real estate tax receipt. Renters attach Form MO-CRP plus a Form 5674 rent verification signed by the landlord. Everyone includes the SSA-1099 and other income forms. The claim is due April 15, and the department gives you three years from the original due date to file a missed one, so a first-timer can reach back for more than one year.
For hands-on help, the City’s St. Louis Area Agency on Aging fills out circuit breaker claims at no charge by appointment at (314) 612-5918, according to the City. Volunteer tax sites can file it alongside a return, too; our guide to free tax preparation in St. Louis explains how those work.
### Why doesn’t Missouri have a homestead exemption?
Because the state constitution won’t allow one. Missouri has no general homestead exemption on property taxes. Article X, Section 6 lists exactly which property can be exempt, then declares every law exempting anything else “shall be void.” An ordinary family home isn’t on the list. That’s why Missouri’s senior relief comes as credits. The freeze is legally a homestead property tax credit, and the circuit breaker is a credit too.
The word homestead does show up in Missouri law, which is where the confusion starts. RSMo 513.475 shields a slice of home equity from creditors, the homestead exemption people mean in bankruptcy and debt collection, and a 2026 law sets that protection at $40,000 starting January 1, 2027. It does nothing to your tax bill. And the old Missouri Homestead Preservation Credit for seniors? The City lists it as no longer available.
### What are the property tax benefits for veterans in Missouri?
There are two, and both are narrower than most veterans hope. First, a veteran who is 100 percent disabled from military service qualifies for the circuit breaker at any age, and doesn’t count VA payments as income under RSMo 135.010. For a couple near the line, leaving that check out can decide whether they qualify. Second, the same Article X, Section 6 fully exempts the homestead of a former prisoner of war with a total service-connected disability.
Past those, a veteran 62 or older gets the freeze on the same terms as any other homeowner. If the furnace is the real budget problem, free home repair and weatherization help in St. Louis can help with that side.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can run your circuit breaker numbers, an elder law attorney can sort out a trust or deed question, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Wondering whether you’ve left a freeze, or a few years of circuit breaker refunds, on the table? Bring your last tax bill, your SSA-1099 and your deed to one of the tax preparers around St. Louis and have them check.
If you run a tax practice or an elder law office in St. Louis, the adult kid sitting at that kitchen table is asking a neighbor or an AI who can sort this out, and a listing with us is how you get more customers from that question.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri have property tax freeze for senior citizens?
A.  Not statewide. A 2023 state law, RSMo 137.1050, lets each county adopt a freeze for homeowners 62 and older, either by ordinance or through a voter petition and referendum. St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis both adopted one, with very different coverage. Whether you have a freeze depends on the county your home sits in, so your county collector or assessor is the place to ask.
### Q. Can I renew my St. Louis County Senior property tax Freeze online?
A.  Renewals have run through the same online portal account you apply with. In August 2026 the County Council passed a bill ending renewals for seniors already approved as of January 1, 2026. The county hasn’t posted its next window yet, so confirm your status on its freeze page or at (314) 615-7100 before you skip a year.
### Q. Who is eligible for the property tax credit in Missouri?
A.  Missourians who, by December 31 of the claim year, are 65 or older and lived in the state all year, are 100 percent disabled from military service or otherwise, or are 60 or older and receive Social Security surviving spouse benefits. Household income has to fall under the limit, and renters qualify only if their landlord pays property tax on the building.
### Q. How to qualify for circuit breaker?
A.  Meet one of the age or disability tests, stay under the household income limit, and pay real estate tax or rent on the Missouri home you live in. For 2025 claims, the limit is $30,000 single or $34,000 married for full-year homeowners, and $27,200 or $29,200 for renters. Starting with 2026, the statute raises those ceilings and the maximum credit.
### Q. What is the new property tax law for seniors in Missouri?
A.  Two changes matter most. The freeze law was amended in 2024 to replace a Social Security requirement with a flat age of 62, and in 2025 to cover anyone who turns 62 by December 31. Separately, House Bills 594 and 508 raised the circuit breaker caps to $1,550 for owners and $1,055 for renters, starting with calendar year 2026.
### Q. Is Missouri going to freeze property taxes for seniors?
A.  The state left that choice to counties. RSMo 137.1050 lets a county grant the freeze by ordinance, or lets voters force a referendum with a petition signed by 5 percent of the county’s voters from the last governor’s race. There’s no statewide freeze on the books, so it comes down to your county.
### Q. At what age do you stop paying property taxes in Missouri?
A.  There isn’t one. Missouri never stops taxing a senior’s home, and its constitution blocks a general homestead exemption. What age buys you is relief. At 62, a county freeze can stop most increases, and at 65 the circuit breaker can refund part of what you paid, if your income is low enough.
### Q. Can you still homestead in Missouri?
A.  Not for property taxes. Missouri has no general homestead exemption, and the old Homestead Preservation Credit for seniors is no longer available. The homestead protection in RSMo 513.475 shields some home equity from creditors, not from the tax bill. For tax relief, seniors look to the county freeze and the state circuit breaker instead.

## Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House in Missouri: The State Exemption and the Federal $250,000 Rule
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-on-selling-a-house-in-missouri
Zero state tax. That’s what Missouri now charges on the profit when you sell your house, your stocks or the rental duplex you’ve been nursing along for years. Starting with the 2025 tax year, Missouri became, in the Department of Revenue’s own words, “the first state in the nation to completely exempt such tax for individual filers.” You can read it in the department’s announcement of House Bill 594.
Here’s the catch nobody mentions at the closing table. The IRS never signed on. Federal tax still reaches part of some home sales, and the federal rules are where St. Louis sellers get blindsided: a purchase price from 1994, a shoebox of lost receipts, the house you rented out for three years, the bungalow Mom left you. Missouri’s break isn’t automatic, either. You claim it, on a form most people have never opened.
None of this was taught in school, and the gap between knowing these rules and guessing can run five figures on one sale. So here’s the state rule, the federal rule and the math in round numbers, one piece of our St. Louis money guide.
### Do I have to pay capital gains when I sell my house in Missouri?
Usually not to Missouri, and often not to the IRS. Missouri now lets individuals subtract 100% of their federally reported capital gains. Federally, if you owned and lived in the home at least two of the five years before the sale, up to $250,000 of gain is excluded, or $500,000 for most married couples filing jointly.
Put those two rules side by side and most St. Louis homeowners who’ve lived in their place a while owe nothing on the sale. The federal exclusion removes the gain before it ever lands on your federal return, so there’s nothing left for Missouri to tax in the first place.
That changes how you should read the headline. For the typical owner-occupied house, Missouri’s new exemption doesn’t do much, because the federal exclusion already did the work. Where it pays off is exactly where the federal rules bite: the gain above $250,000 or $500,000, the rental, the second home, the house you inherited and sold, the place you didn’t live in long enough. Those sales used to be taxed twice. Now the IRS is the only one with a hand out.
### What exactly did Missouri stop taxing, and how do you claim it?
Every capital gain an individual reports on a federal return. House Bill 594, signed in 2025, added a subtraction to section 143.121 of Missouri law: for all tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, an individual can subtract 100% of income reported as a capital gain for federal purposes. Short-term or long-term. The department’s release names stocks, real estate and cryptocurrency as examples.
The catch is mechanical. Missouri’s return generally starts from your federal adjusted gross income, and that figure already includes any taxable gain. The state doesn’t strip it out for you. On the 2025 return, you file Form MO-A with your MO-1040 and enter the capital gain figure from your federal Form 1040 (Line 7a on the 2025 form) on MO-A, Part 1, Line 18, according to the MO-1040 instructions. Subtractions total on Line 19 and carry to Line 4 of the MO-1040. Line numbers can move from year to year. The idea doesn’t: no MO-A, no subtraction.
A few details from the department’s capital gains subtraction FAQ:
Losses get no extra Missouri break; they already count in your federal adjusted gross income.
On a joint return where only one spouse has a gain, only that spouse reports it on the MO-A.
Trusts can’t use it. The FAQ says a fiduciary isn’t an individual under the law.
Corporations get a version later, starting the year after Missouri’s top individual rate drops to 4.5% or less. It was 4.7% for 2025.
One wrinkle. An answer on that same FAQ page says 2026, but the page’s opening answer, the statute and the 2025 MO-1040 instructions all say 2025, and the form already carries the line. Sold something in 2025 and filed without it? An amended return, also filed on the MO-1040, is the usual fix.
Two local footnotes. City of St. Louis residents also pay the 1% earnings tax, which the city describes as a tax on earned income such as salaries, wages, commissions, tips and other compensation. And across the river, Illinois has no matching break. Its flat 4.95% income tax starts from federal adjusted gross income, so a Metro East seller owes Illinois on whatever gain the federal exclusion doesn’t cover. For how Missouri taxes everything else you earn, see Missouri’s state income tax rate.
### How much profit can you make on a house before the IRS taxes it?
Up to $250,000 of gain if you’re single, and up to $500,000 for most married couples filing jointly, under the home sale exclusion described in IRS Topic 701. To get the full amount, you have to pass these tests for the five years before the sale:
Ownership: you owned the home for at least 24 months.
Use: you lived in it as your main home for at least 24 months. The months don’t have to be in a row, and the two tests can be met in different stretches.
Look-back: you didn’t exclude gain from another home sale in the two years before this one.
For couples, only one spouse has to meet the ownership test, but each spouse has to meet the use test for the full $500,000, per IRS Publication 523.
Notice what isn’t on that list. No age requirement. No rule that you buy another house. You can sell, rent an apartment downtown, and still take the exclusion. And once two years pass, it’s available again on the next home.
There’s one window almost nobody hears about. A surviving spouse can still use the $500,000 limit when selling within two years of the spouse’s death, as long as they haven’t remarried and the other conditions are met. Miss that window by a month and the limit drops to $250,000.
Didn’t make it two full years? You may still get part of the exclusion if the main reason you sold was a job change (a new work location at least 50 miles farther from the home than your old one), a health reason, or an unforeseeable event such as a death, a divorce, or a home destroyed or condemned. The math is a fraction. Take the shortest of your time living there, your time owning it, or the time since your last exclusion, divide by 24 months, and multiply by $250,000. Live there 12 months before a qualifying job transfer, and a single seller’s limit is $125,000.
### How do you figure the gain on your house?
Gain is the amount you realized minus your adjusted basis. In plain words: what you sold it for, less your selling costs, less what you paid for the house and the improvements you put into it. Basis is the tax word for your total investment in the property.
Selling costs that cut your gain include sales commissions, advertising, legal fees, and loan charges you paid that would normally have been the buyer’s. Our breakdown of what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis shows what usually lands on the settlement statement. Basis starts with the purchase price, adds certain closing costs from when you bought, and adds improvements.
Improvements are where people quietly lose money. An improvement adds value, extends the home’s life or adapts it to a new use: a new roof, a finished basement, central air, an addition. A repair that just keeps the house in shape, like painting, fixing a leak or replacing broken hardware, doesn’t count, unless it was part of a bigger remodeling project.
Here’s a worked example with round numbers. Picture a single homeowner in St. Louis County who bought her house in the mid-1990s for $100,000, spent $60,000 over the years on a roof, a kitchen and a finished basement, and sells now for $450,000 with $30,000 in selling costs.
If her income puts her gains in the 15% bracket, she owes about $1,500 in federal tax on that $10,000. Missouri takes nothing, once she claims the subtraction.
Now lose the receipts. Without proof of the $60,000 in improvements, her basis falls to $100,000, her gain jumps to $320,000, and $70,000 is taxable. At 15%, that’s $10,500. The folder of invoices in the basement was worth $9,000. And if she were a widow selling within two years of her husband’s death, the $500,000 limit would cover the whole gain either way.
Sell Mom’s house or rent it? Ask a real estate consultant first.
### What changes with a rental, a second home or an inherited house?
A rental or a second home. No exclusion, because it isn’t your main home, so every dollar of gain is in play federally. Then there’s depreciation. Each year you own a rental, depreciation lowers your basis, and the IRS counts depreciation you took or were allowed to take, so skipping the deduction doesn’t protect you. When you sell, the part of the gain that came from depreciation, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, is taxed at a maximum 25% rate, per IRS Topic 409. The rest gets the regular capital gains rates.
Round numbers again. Buy a rental for $120,000, take $40,000 of depreciation over the years, and sell for $220,000 after selling costs. Your basis is $80,000 and your gain is $140,000, with $40,000 of it in that up-to-25% bucket. Missouri’s subtraction follows the capital gain figure on your federal return, so whatever lands there comes off your Missouri income.
Investors sometimes push that bill down the road with a like-kind exchange under section 1031, trading one investment or business property for another. It defers the tax. It doesn’t erase it, and cash you pull out along the way is taxable up to your gain. You have 45 days after the sale to identify replacement property and 180 days to receive it, per the Form 8824 instructions, and a home used solely as your personal residence doesn’t qualify.
Lived in a former rental? The exclusion can still apply if you pass the two-of-five-years tests, but gain tied to periods after 2008 when the place wasn’t your main home generally can’t be excluded, with exceptions. Depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 is never covered by the exclusion. That rule catches a depreciated home office, too.
An inherited house. This is the good news nobody explains. Your basis generally isn’t what your parent paid. It’s the fair market value on the date of death, or on an alternate valuation date if the estate’s personal representative picks one, per Publication 523. And inherited property counts as held more than a year no matter how long you actually owned it, according to IRS Publication 544, so any gain gets long-term rates.
Say your mother bought a small frame house in Warrenton decades ago for $60,000, and it’s worth $260,000 the day she passes. You sell eight months later for $280,000 and pay $16,000 to sell. Amount realized: $264,000. Basis: $260,000. Gain: $4,000, taxed at long-term rates by the IRS and not at all by Missouri. Use her $60,000 by mistake and you’d report a $204,000 gain. What proves the higher basis is evidence of the house’s value on that date, such as an appraisal.
One Missouri trap. If the house sells inside a trust rather than in your own name, remember the FAQ line above: a trust can’t claim the capital gains subtraction. Ask whoever prepares the trust’s return how that gain will be handled, and if a deed or trust transfer is part of the picture, read whether you need a real estate attorney in Missouri.
### What federal rate applies to the part that’s taxable?
Long-term gains, on property held more than a year, are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on your total taxable income. For 2026, under Rev. Proc. 2025-32:
0% while taxable income stays at or under $49,450 for single filers, or $98,900 for married couples filing jointly.
15% above that, up to $545,500 single or $613,700 joint.
20% on gains above those amounts.
Those thresholds are adjusted every year. The gain itself counts toward taxable income, so a big sale can push part of it out of the 0% band. Sell property you’ve held a year or less and the taxable gain is short-term, taxed as ordinary income at your regular rates.
Then there’s the net investment income tax, an extra 3.8% that applies when modified adjusted gross income tops $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. Those thresholds aren’t indexed for inflation, according to the IRS questions and answers on the net investment income tax, so they don’t rise with home prices. Excluded home sale gain doesn’t count toward it. Taxable gain does, including the gain on a rental.
Over 65? The home sale rules have no age test, so retirees get the same exclusion everyone else does. What tends to help is income. A retiree with modest taxable income may see part of a taxable gain land in the 0% band. Missouri now exempts the gain at any age. For the rest of the picture, see how Missouri taxes retirement income.
### What paperwork backs up your numbers when you sell?
If the closing agent issues you a Form 1099-S, you report the sale even if every dollar of gain is excluded. You also report it if any part of the gain is taxable. It goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D. If no 1099-S arrives and the whole gain is excluded, Publication 523 doesn’t require you to report it. And a loss on your main home isn’t deductible.
The records that hold all this together are the ones nobody tells you to keep: the settlement statement from when you bought, every invoice for an improvement, and the settlement statement from the sale. The IRS says to keep them until three years after the due date of the return for the year you sell. Own a house for 30 years and that’s 33 years of paper.
One number to ignore: the county’s market value on your property tax notice. That figure is for property tax. It isn’t your basis. If it looks too high, appealing your property assessment in St. Louis County is a separate process with its own deadlines. And the agent who lists your house isn’t the one to run this math; how to choose a real estate agent in St. Louis covers what to ask them instead.
This is general information about how the rules work, not tax advice for your sale. A CPA or enrolled agent can run your actual numbers, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Selling soon with a rental, an inherited house or a gain near the limit? Bring your purchase settlement statement, your improvement invoices and any Form 1099-S to one of the accountants and tax preparers around St. Louis before you file, and ask them to check the Missouri subtraction on Form MO-A.
If you run a tax practice or sell houses around St. Louis, this part is about your next customers. And if you’re a CPA, enrolled agent or real estate agent who explains this math for a living, the neighbor asking an AI about the Missouri exemption tonight will be handed one name first, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long do you need to own property to avoid capital gains?
A.  For the home sale exclusion, you must have owned the home and lived in it as your main home for at least 24 months of the five years before the sale. For lower long-term rates on any property, you need to hold it more than one year. Missouri doesn’t care how long you owned it: individuals subtract both short-term and long-term gains on Form MO-A.
### Q. How much can you make on selling a house without paying capital gains?
A.  Federally, up to $250,000 of gain if you’re single and up to $500,000 for most married couples filing jointly, as long as you pass the two-of-five-years ownership and use tests. That’s gain, not sale price. A $450,000 sale can carry far less than $250,000 of gain once you subtract what you paid, your improvements and your selling costs. Missouri doesn’t tax individuals on the gain.
### Q. Are capital gains taxed in Missouri?
A.  Not for individuals, starting with the 2025 tax year. House Bill 594 lets individual filers subtract 100% of the capital gains reported on their federal return, claimed on Form MO-A with the MO-1040. Trusts can’t use it, and corporations qualify only after Missouri’s top individual rate drops to 4.5% or less. Federal capital gains tax still applies on its own terms.
### Q. What happens if I sell my house and don’t buy another?
A.  Nothing changes for the exclusion. The federal home sale rules don’t require a replacement home; they look at whether you owned and lived in the house two of the last five years and didn’t use the exclusion in the two years before. You can sell, rent an apartment or move in with family and still exclude up to $250,000, or $500,000 for most joint filers.
### Q. How to avoid capital gains tax over 65?
A.  Today’s federal home sale rules have no age-based break, so the $250,000 or $500,000 exclusion is the main tool at any age. Retirees with modest taxable income may see part of a taxable gain fall in the 0% band. Heirs generally receive a basis equal to the home’s value at death. And Missouri exempts individual capital gains regardless of age.
### Q. Who qualifies for 0% capital gains tax?
A.  For 2026, long-term gains are taxed at 0% while your taxable income, counting the gain itself, stays at or below $49,450 for single filers or $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. The IRS adjusts those thresholds every year. Short-term gains, on property held a year or less, don’t get the 0% rate; they’re taxed as ordinary income.
### Q. How to calculate capital gains on sale of rental property?
A.  Start with the sale price, subtract selling costs, then subtract your adjusted basis: what you paid plus improvements, minus all depreciation you took or were allowed to take. The depreciation portion is taxed at up to 25% federally, the rest at 0%, 15% or 20%, and the 3.8% net investment income tax may apply. Rentals get no home sale exclusion. Missouri subtracts the federal capital gain figure.
### Q. How much capital gains tax do I pay on my house?
A.  Often nothing. If your gain fits under the $250,000 or $500,000 exclusion, you owe no federal tax, and Missouri doesn’t tax individuals’ capital gains. Above the limit, the taxable part is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on your taxable income, plus 3.8% if you’re over the net investment income tax threshold. Gains on property held a year or less are taxed as ordinary income.

## Filing a Tax Extension in Missouri: More Time to File, Not More Time to Pay
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-file-a-tax-extension-missouri
Extensions delay paperwork. Not payments. The most expensive misunderstanding of every April is the belief that filing for a tax extension moves your tax bill to October, and the IRS says the opposite on its own extension page: the extension is only for filing your return, and any tax you owe is still due by the April filing date. Nobody taught that in school. A software pop-up offering “more time” doesn’t always lead with it, either.
In St. Louis the trap has extra layers, because you may be juggling three returns. The IRS return, which Form 4868 extends six months. The Missouri return, which rides along on the federal extension automatically but charges a flat 5% the moment your payment misses April. And if you live in the City of St. Louis and your employer doesn’t withhold the 1% earnings tax, the City’s Form E-1, which can’t be extended at all. Three agencies. Three rulebooks. One date that matters more than the others.
Here are all three side by side, with the penalties priced in real dollars from each agency’s own pages. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English series on money rules nobody hands you at graduation. The regular deadline is April 15, or the next business day when the 15th lands on a weekend or legal holiday. The extended one is October 15.
### Does Missouri have an automatic extension?
Yes. If you get a federal extension, Missouri automatically extends your filing deadline to October 15, and you attach a copy of the federal extension to your Missouri return. You file Form MO-60 mainly when you expect to owe Missouri tax or want a state-only extension. Any tax owed is still due by the original April deadline.
That comes straight from the Missouri Department of Revenue’s individual income tax FAQ and the instructions on Form MO-60. The automatic part is real. Get a federal extension, by Form 4868 or by an IRS payment marked as an extension, and Missouri gives you the same six months with no separate application, as long as you don’t expect to owe the state more or you’re due a refund.
The catch is the money. Missouri law fixes the payment date without regard to any extension: section 143.511 of the state statutes says the tax is due on or before the date set for filing the return, determined without regard to any extension of time for filing. So if your Missouri return will show a balance due, the Department wants Form MO-60 and your payment by the original April deadline. It’s one page: estimate your Missouri tax, subtract what’s been withheld or paid, and send the difference to Jefferson City. The Department’s payments page also takes extension payments online, by e-check for a 50-cent fee or by card for 2% plus 25 cents.
MO-60 also covers a Missouri-only extension, or a request for more than the federal six months, which the Department grants only when the need is clearly shown. It contacts you only if it denies the request.
Now the line worth taping to the refrigerator. In Missouri, missing the payment date costs a flat 5% of whatever you didn’t pay. The Department’s FAQ says a 5 percent addition to tax applies when the tax isn’t paid by the original due date, even when the return itself comes in on time under the extension. The IRS charges half a percent a month for the same miss. One month late, Missouri’s charge is ten times the federal one. If you need help estimating that state number, our guide to the Missouri state income tax rate shows how the brackets stack up.
### How do you file a federal extension with Form 4868?
Three ways, and the IRS doesn’t ask why. The Form 4868 instructions say you don’t have to explain the reason, and the IRS contacts you only if the request is denied.
Pay and check the box. Make a payment through IRS Direct Pay, your IRS online account, EFTPS, a debit or credit card, or a digital wallet, and mark it as an extension payment. The IRS processes the extension automatically and gives you a confirmation number. No separate form.
E-file Form 4868. Tax software and tax professionals can send it, and IRS Free File has no income limit for extensions.
Mail a paper Form 4868. Missouri filers send it to the IRS in Kansas City, MO 64999-0045 when no payment is enclosed, or to the payment address in Louisville listed in the instructions when one is.
All three are due on the same day as the return itself, April 15 or the next business day, and the extension gives you until October 15 to file, according to the IRS’s Topic 304. U.S. citizens and residents who live and work outside the country on the due date get an automatic two months, to June 15, without asking.
Here’s the sentence in the instructions almost nobody reads. To qualify, you have to properly estimate your tax with the information you have, and if the IRS later finds the estimate wasn’t reasonable, the extension is null and void. You don’t have to pay the estimate. You do have to make an honest one. Writing zero on line 4 when you know a bill is coming can turn your extension into no extension at all, with the late-filing penalty counted from April.
Then there’s the 90% rule, the most useful paragraph in the whole form. You’re treated as having reasonable cause for paying late during the extension, which means no late-payment penalty for those months, if two things are true: at least 90% of your total tax was paid by the April due date, through withholding, estimated payments or a payment with the extension, and you pay the rest when you file. Interest still runs on that last 10% from April until it’s paid. The penalty doesn’t.
### What does it cost to file late versus pay late?
Per month, filing late costs ten times what paying late does. That one ratio is the whole case for filing an extension even when you can’t pay a dime. At the IRS, the failure-to-file penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%. The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% a month, also capped at 25%. Here’s how the three St. Louis returns compare.
Two federal details change the math. When both penalties hit in the same month, the filing penalty is reduced by the payment penalty, so the combined charge is 5% a month. And once a return is more than 60 days late, a minimum kicks in: currently $525, adjusted for inflation, or 100% of the tax due, whichever is less. Owe $400, skip the extension, file three months late, and the late-filing penalty alone can equal the full $400. Interest on unpaid federal tax is 7% a year right now, compounded daily and reset every quarter.
Run it on a round number. Say you owe the IRS $4,000 at the April deadline and can’t pay until mid-August, four months later.
Extension filed in April: failure-to-pay of 0.5% times four months, or $80, plus roughly $95 of interest. Call it $175.
No extension, filed in August: failure-to-file of 4.5% times four months, or $720, plus the same $80 and the same $95 of interest. Call it $895, before interest on the penalties themselves.
Same tax. Same payment date. A $720 gap created by a form that takes ten minutes. Missouri works the same way with smaller numbers: owe the state $1,000, extend, and pay in mid-August, and you’ll see the flat $50 addition plus about $23 of simple interest at the state’s 7% statutory rate. Pay in May instead and the $50 doesn’t shrink. Only the interest does.
One newer federal wrinkle cuts the other way. Starting with returns for the 2025 tax year, the IRS is replacing first-time penalty abatement with an Automatic Exemption from Penalty: three prior years filed and paid on time, and it won’t assess failure-to-file or failure-to-pay penalties at all. Interest still applies, and it does nothing for a Missouri or City bill.
Extensions don’t pay bills. Legit work-from-home jobs in St. Louis might.
### Do City of St. Louis residents need a separate extension?
They can’t get one. The Collector of Revenue’s individual earnings tax page says in a single sentence that the City of St. Louis does not allow individuals to file extensions on their earnings tax returns. Form E-1 is due April 15, no matter what you filed with the IRS or Missouri.
The 1% earnings tax applies to everyone who lives in the city, wherever they work, and to everyone who works in the city, wherever they live. Plenty of people never see it, because their employer withholds it. If your employer withholds the full amount, the Collector’s filing instructions say you don’t have to file or pay separately. The people who get caught are city residents whose employer doesn’t withhold it. Picture a Bevo Mill resident working remotely for a company in another state that never set up City withholding. Not sure? The Earnings Tax Department checks withholding status at (314) 622-4101; have your W-2 handy.
Miss April and the City charges a penalty of 5% of the tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%, plus interest of 1% a month, which works out to 12% a year. Take a hypothetical city resident earning $60,000 with no City withholding. That’s a $600 E-1. Send it in October alongside an extended federal return, six months late, and the penalty hits the 25% cap, $150, with $36 of interest on top. A $600 bill becomes $786, because the extension everyone else honored never reached City Hall.
The state won’t remind you; Missouri’s Department of Revenue says it doesn’t collect the St. Louis or Kansas City earnings taxes. You can’t e-file the E-1, either. You pay online and mail, fax or email the return, or handle both at City Hall, Room 410. Our St. Louis earnings tax guide covers who owes it and how it’s collected.
Self-employed? Your City business earnings go on Form E-234, which does have an extension. Form E-8 buys up to six months, but only with 100% of the tax you expect to owe attached, and the form says the City can reject it if you’re behind on earnings, payroll expense or personal property taxes.
### What if you can’t pay by the April deadline?
File anyway, pay what you can, and set up a plan, in that order. Filing or extending on time takes the 5% a month failure-to-file penalty off the table. Every dollar you pay by April shrinks the payment penalty and the interest, at the IRS and at the Missouri Department of Revenue alike.
The IRS offers two kinds of payment plans. A short-term plan gives you up to 180 days with no setup fee; you can apply online if you owe less than $100,000 in tax, penalties and interest combined. A long-term installment agreement spreads the balance into monthly payments and can be set up online if you owe $50,000 or less and have filed all required returns. Online setup runs $29 with automatic bank withdrawals or $69 without, versus $107 or $178 by phone, mail or in person. Low-income taxpayers get the direct-debit fee waived.
If you filed on time and you’re on an approved plan, the failure-to-pay penalty drops from 0.5% to 0.25% a month. Ignore a notice of intent to levy for 10 days and it climbs to 1%. Interest keeps running either way. A plan is a ramp, not a pause button.
Missouri runs its own system: an online Internet Installment Agreement Application, reached from the Department’s payments and payment plans page. If a Missouri assessment becomes final and stays unpaid, the state can file a lien in the county where you live or own property. For a City E-1 you can’t cover, call the Earnings Tax Department before April 15, not after.
If the balance is big enough that no payment plan fits, or a levy notice is already on the counter, that’s the point where a tax attorney, not a CPA, may be the right call.
### What mistakes make an extension backfire?
Five come up again and again. Each one hides in fine print, and none of them is about being bad with money.
Guessing low on purpose. Form 4868 asks for a proper estimate of your total tax. An estimate the IRS later finds unreasonable voids the extension, and the late-filing clock runs from April as if you’d never asked.
Forgetting the state. Missouri’s extension is automatic for filing only. A Missouri balance still needs MO-60 and a payment by April, or the flat 5% applies.
Forgetting the City. If you file an E-1, there’s no extension to forget. It’s due April 15, period.
Forgetting this year’s estimated tax. Self-employed and gig workers pay as they go, and the first quarterly payment for the new year is due April 15, the same day as last year’s balance, per the IRS estimated tax guide. Missouri’s first MO-1040ES installment is due April 15 too, and the state requires estimates once your expected Missouri tax reaches $100. An extension moves neither.
Assuming a disaster extension crosses state lines. After a FEMA declaration, the IRS often postpones deadlines automatically for counties listed on its disaster relief page. When it did that after the spring 2025 storms, for a list of Missouri counties that included St. Louis, the Department of Revenue matched the date but said Missouri does not automatically apply extensions. Filers had to send MO-60 with the disaster extension written on it.
And a quiet sixth: forgetting October. Once the extended deadline passes, the 5% a month late-filing penalty starts counting. Put October 15 in your phone the day you file the extension.
### Should you pay a pro to handle the extension?
For the extension itself, usually not. Marking an IRS payment as an extension takes minutes, and Free File handles the form at no cost. A professional earns the fee on the estimate behind it: the number that keeps the extension valid, clears the 90% line, and tells you whether Missouri needs an MO-60. One who also asks about a City E-1 can head off the most expensive surprise on this page.
If cost is the worry, our breakdown of what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis shows the typical ranges, and households that qualify can get free tax preparation in St. Louis through VITA and AARP Tax-Aide. Bring last year’s federal return either way; e-filing Form 4868 asks for information from it to verify who you are.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply these rules to your return, and our St. Louis financial services directory is a place to start.
Want one person to run your federal, Missouri and City numbers before April? Compare tax preparers around St. Louis and ask each one a single question: do you handle the E-1 earnings tax return, too, or only the IRS and state forms?
And if you’re the enrolled agent or preparer, the neighbor who asks an AI who handles all three returns is going to hear one name first, so make it yours and list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does the IRS penalize you for filing an extension?
A.  No. Filing Form 4868, or marking a payment as an extension, carries no penalty, and the IRS doesn’t ask why. Penalties come from what surrounds it: unpaid tax after the April due date draws 0.5% a month plus interest, and a return filed after October 15 draws 5% a month. An on-time extension prevents the bigger one.
### Q. What is the downside to filing a tax extension?
A.  Mostly false comfort. Interest on unpaid tax still runs from April, currently 7% a year at the IRS, compounded daily, and Missouri adds a flat 5% to any state balance you didn’t pay. It doesn’t cover the City of St. Louis E-1. Any refund waits until you file. And a lowball estimate on Form 4868 can void the extension entirely.
### Q. What happens if you don’t file taxes by April 15th?
A.  If you neither file nor extend, the IRS failure-to-file penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%. Past 60 days, the minimum is $525 or 100% of the tax owed, whichever is less. Missouri charges 5% a month up to 25%, too. Due a refund? The penalty is figured on unpaid tax, so there’s nothing to charge it on.
### Q. How do I pay taxes if I file an extension?
A.  Pay your best estimate by the April due date. Federally, Direct Pay, your IRS online account, EFTPS, a card or a digital wallet all work, and marking the payment as an extension files the extension for you. For Missouri, send MO-60 with a check or pay online. For a City E-1, pay the Collector online, by mail or in person.
### Q. What happens if I don’t file state taxes?
A.  In Missouri, a late return draws an addition to tax of 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%, under section 143.741 of state law. That’s on top of the flat 5% for paying late and simple interest, currently 7%. A balance that becomes final and stays unpaid can lead to a lien on property in your county.
### Q. How long of an extension can I get to pay my taxes?
A.  There’s no automatic extension to pay; Form 4868 covers filing only. What you can get is a payment plan: up to 180 days on an IRS short-term plan with no setup fee, or monthly payments on a long-term installment agreement. Missouri takes installment requests online. Interest keeps running either way.
### Q. Who qualifies for a tax filing extension?
A.  Any individual can get the automatic six-month federal extension by requesting it by the April due date, no reason required. The exceptions in the Form 4868 instructions: people who want the IRS to figure their tax, or who are under a court order to file by the due date. Missouri extends automatically with the federal one. City E-1 filers can’t extend at all.
### Q. Does my federal extension cover my St. Louis earnings tax?
A.  No. The City of St. Louis doesn’t allow individuals to file extensions on earnings tax returns, so Form E-1 is due April 15 even when your IRS and Missouri returns are extended. It matters when your employer didn’t withhold the full 1%. A late E-1 draws 5% a month, up to 25%, plus interest of 1% a month.

## Missouri State Income Tax: The Rate, the Brackets, and Whether It's Really Going Away
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-state-income-tax-rate
Why does a tax with eight brackets charge nearly every working Missourian its top rate? Because the staircase is only $9,436 tall. The Missouri Department of Revenue’s 2026 withholding formula, the table employers use to take state tax out of paychecks, puts the 4.7% top rate on every dollar of taxable income above $9,436. Taxable income is what’s left after the standard deduction, and on the 2026 table that deduction is $16,100 for a single filer.
Run that forward. A single person with plain W-2 wages crosses into the top bracket at roughly $25,800 a year. A full-time job at Missouri’s $15 minimum wage pays about $31,200. So the cashier and the surgeon pay the same 4.7% on their next dollar. And the graduated part that looks so generous on the chart, all seven lower steps put together, is worth about $180 a year compared with a flat 4.7%. To anybody. At any income.
Nobody explains that in school, and it isn’t printed on your W-2. You’re not bad at taxes; the chart is built to look gentler than it is. Below is what Missouri actually charges, a line-by-line $70,000 paycheck, what the state leaves untaxed, what really happened to the plan to scrap the income tax, and the St. Louis layer most state guides skip. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the series on the money rules nobody walks you through.
### What is the Missouri state income tax?
Missouri taxes residents’ wages and most other income at graduated rates from 0% to 4.7%. The catch is where 4.7% begins: $9,436 of taxable income on the current table, after the standard deduction, adjusted for inflation each year. So most working people pay the top rate on most of what they earn.
The rules sit in Section 143.011 of the Missouri statutes. That section has indexed the bracket lines to inflation since 2017, which is why they creep up every January. A 2022 rewrite set the top rate at 4.95% starting in 2023 and allowed further cuts only in years when state revenue grows by set amounts. Two of those cuts have happened since. The Department of Revenue’s income tax changes page shows 4.7% on the 2025 return, with the top bracket starting at $9,191, and the 2026 withholding formula keeps 4.7% with the line moved up to $9,436.
Residents pay on all of their income, wherever they earn it. Nonresidents pay only on what they earn in Missouri. Either way, the starting point is your federal adjusted gross income, or AGI, which is your total income minus a short list of federal adjustments, straight off your federal Form 1040. That’s why the federal return always gets done first. From there Missouri adds and subtracts its own adjustments, takes off a standard deduction that simply matches the federal one, lets you deduct a slice of the federal income tax you paid, and runs what’s left through the table.
Three terms make the rest of this page easy. Taxable income is what remains after every deduction, and it’s the only number the rates ever touch. Your marginal rate is what your next dollar pays, which is 4.7% for almost every full-time worker. Your effective rate is your total tax divided by your total income, and it always comes out lower, because the first $9,436 of taxable income gets the cheap seats.
### Why does almost every working household hit the top rate?
Because the brackets stop climbing at $9,436 of taxable income, and the standard deduction that comes off first is bigger than the whole ladder: $16,100 for a single filer on the 2026 tables, and $32,200 for a married couple. Once your income clears the deduction plus about $9,400, every additional dollar is taxed at 4.7%. Here’s the full ladder from DOR’s 2026 withholding formula:
Read the right-hand column. A taxable income of exactly $9,436 owes $263. A flat 4.7% on that same $9,436 would be about $443. The difference, roughly $180, is the entire benefit of the seven lower brackets, and it’s the same $180 whether you make $30,000 or $3 million. Past that line, Missouri runs a flat tax in a graduated costume.
Married couples get a twist that helps a little. Missouri requires spouses on a combined return to split their income between them, then figures each spouse’s tax on his or her own share, as the MO-1040 instructions explain. So each spouse climbs the ladder separately. Picture a couple outside New Offenburg, one on a plant shift and one at a clinic front desk, each earning about $35,000. After the $32,200 deduction and the federal tax deduction, each spouse’s share of taxable income lands near $18,600. Both are deep in 4.7% territory. Two ladders, same roof.
So the honest answer to “what bracket am I in?” is short. If you work full time in Missouri, almost certainly the top one. The lower brackets mostly matter for part-time workers, students and retirees with small taxable incomes, and even then the most they can save is about $180 per person.
### How much will I earn after taxes if I earn $70,000 per year in Missouri?
About $55,770 a year, or roughly $4,650 a month, for a single filer with $70,000 in wages taking the standard deduction on the 2026 tables. Federal income tax takes about $6,570, Social Security and Medicare take $5,355, and Missouri takes about $2,306. Live or work in the City of St. Louis and the city’s 1% earnings tax trims another $700.
Here’s the Missouri piece line by line, using the IRS’s 2026 brackets and standard deduction for the federal tax and the DOR table above for the state. Round numbers, wages only, no 401(k) or pre-tax insurance, which would lower both income tax lines.
Look where the money comes from. Of that $2,306, about $2,043, nearly 89%, is the 4.7% slice. All seven lower brackets together produce $263. Your effective Missouri rate is about 3.3% of gross pay, which is the number for a budget. The 4.7% is the number for a decision, like a raise, a weekend shift or a side job: each extra $1,000 of wages adds roughly $45 of Missouri tax once the federal tax deduction nudges it down.
That federal tax deduction is a Missouri quirk worth knowing by name. Under Section 143.171, you subtract a percentage of your federal income tax: 35% if your Missouri adjusted gross income is $25,000 or less, 25% up to $50,000, 15% up to $100,000, 5% up to $125,000, and nothing above that. It’s capped at $5,000 on a single return and $10,000 on a combined one. Software fills it in. On a paper MO-1040 it lives on Lines 12 and 13, and it’s easy to miss.
Now the whole paycheck. Social Security takes 6.2% of wages and Medicare 1.45%, per the IRS: $4,340 and $1,015 on $70,000. Add $6,570 federal and $2,306 Missouri and the total is $14,231, leaving about $55,770. A City of St. Louis resident, or anyone whose job is inside city limits, pays $700 more in earnings tax and lands near $55,070. Whether that stretches depends more on rent, car insurance and childcare than on any bracket, and our St. Louis cost of living breakdown runs those numbers.
### What income does Missouri leave untaxed?
Social Security for anyone 62 or older or on disability, every dollar of federally reported capital gains, a large slice of public pensions, and part of your federal income tax. One surprise runs the other way: the new federal breaks for tips and overtime don’t carry over to Missouri.
Social Security. DOR’s 2025 income tax reference guide lets you deduct 100% of the taxable amount of Social Security and Social Security disability if you’re 62 or older or receiving disability benefits. Filers age 62 through 64 have to check the box for that age on Form MO-1040, or the deduction gets disallowed.
Public pensions. Pensions from a federal, state or local government can be exempt up to $47,633 per person on the 2025 return. Private pensions get up to $6,000, and only under income limits.
Capital gains. Starting with the 2025 tax year, Missouri lets individuals subtract 100% of the capital gains reported on the federal return, per the DOR changes page linked above. Selling a home? Our guide to capital gains tax on selling a house in Missouri shows how that stacks with the federal home-sale exclusion.
Part of your federal income tax, through the deduction in the $70,000 example above.
Now the surprise. The newer federal deductions for tips, overtime, car loan interest and the enhanced senior deduction can’t be claimed on the Missouri return, the DOR says on that same changes page. Missouri starts from federal AGI, and those breaks come off after AGI on the federal form, so they never reach the state. Picture a server in Soulard who takes a big tip deduction on her federal return. Missouri still taxes every one of those tips.
For the rest of the retirement picture, see our guide to how Missouri taxes retirement income. The short version for most retirees: the Social Security check is out of Missouri’s reach, and the pension exemptions come with caps and income limits worth checking before you plan withdrawals around them.
Missouri skips your Social Security but taxes your retirement side gig.
### Is Missouri eliminating state income tax?
No. Lawmakers asked voters to phase it out, and on August 4, 2026, voters said no, by about 83% to 16%, the Missouri Independent reported. The income tax stays, at 4.7% on the current table. What remains on the books is a slower set of revenue triggers that can trim the top rate a tenth of a point at a time, down to 4.5% at the lowest.
The plan began as House Joint Resolution 173, which the legislature gave final passage on April 21. Per the Senate’s summary, it would have required lawmakers to set revenue-based triggers to keep lowering the individual income tax rate, ended the tax once the top rate fell below 1.4%, and given lawmakers the option to broaden the sales tax base to make up the money. The ballot summary in the governor’s announcement placing it on the August ballot as Amendment 5 added required cuts to property and other local taxes to offset any local sales tax gains, while preserving local funding for public schools.
In a statement on election night, Gov. Mike Kehoe said the amendment did not earn the support it needed and that he remains committed to working with the General Assembly on ways to keep cutting taxes. That’s a statement of intent. It isn’t a bill.
So here’s the scorecard, without the spin. Law: a 4.7% top rate, bracket lines indexed to inflation every year, and triggers in Section 143.011 that allow up to two more cuts of a tenth of a point, to 4.5%, only in years when net general revenue (the money flowing into the state’s general fund, minus refunds) beats earlier years by set amounts. Proposed and rejected: ending the income tax through a constitutional amendment. Not law: any plan to eliminate the tax. If one returns, it starts over in the legislature, and a constitutional change would go back to voters.
### What does living or working in St. Louis add on top?
One more percent. The City of St. Louis collects a 1% earnings tax from residents of the city, wherever their employer is, and from people who work inside the city, wherever they live. Retired and unemployed people don’t pay it. It’s separate from the state tax and usually comes straight out of your paycheck.
That makes the top rate on a city worker’s next dollar 5.7%: 4.7% to Jefferson City and 1% to the city. On $70,000 of wages, the city’s share is $700 a year. That’s more than the $263 the state collects from all seven of its lower brackets combined. Nonresidents who spend whole days working outside the city can ask for a refund of the tax withheld for those days on Form E-1R, with the employer verifying the days. Our St. Louis earnings tax guide covers who qualifies and how to file.
Across the river, the Metro East has its own wrinkle. Missouri taxes all income earned in Missouri, so an Illinois resident with a Missouri job files a Missouri nonresident return with Form MO-NRI. Illinois has reciprocal agreements only with Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan and Wisconsin, so there’s no shortcut with Missouri. Instead, Illinois lets its residents claim a credit for tax paid to another state on Schedule CR. Two returns, one paycheck.
### When is a Missouri return due, and who has to file one?
April 15 for most people, the same day as the federal return; the 2025 return was due April 15, 2026, per the DOR’s individual income tax FAQ. You generally don’t have to file if you aren’t required to file a federal return. Even if you are, Missouri lets you skip it as a resident with less than $1,200 of Missouri adjusted gross income, a nonresident with less than $600 of Missouri income, or anyone whose Missouri adjusted gross income is under the standard deduction.
A W-2 showing Missouri tax withheld changes that math. If you didn’t have to file but money came out of your checks anyway, filing is how you get it back.
More time to file is easy to get. A federal extension automatically extends your Missouri filing deadline to October 15, but the payment is still due in April; if you expect to owe, Form MO-60 goes in with a payment by the original due date. Our guide to filing a tax extension in Missouri walks through what paying late costs.
Gig work, freelancing or a side business with no withholding? The reference guide says Missouri expects quarterly estimated payments on Form MO-1040ES once your Missouri tax is expected to be $100 or more and isn’t withheld. Returns get complicated fast with two states, a mid-year move, a pension or a business, and if you’re pricing help, our breakdown of what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis shows what typical returns run.
This is general information about how Missouri’s income tax works, not advice for your return. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply these rules to your own numbers, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Want a second set of eyes on your next Missouri return? Compare tax preparers around St. Louis and bring last year’s federal and Missouri returns, so they can check the federal tax deduction, the pension and Social Security lines, and any earnings tax refund you might be owed.
