### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the state income tax rates in Missouri?
A.  Eight brackets, from 0% to 4.7%. On DOR’s 2026 table the first $1,348 of taxable income is taxed at 0%, and each $1,348 slice after that steps up through 2%, 2.5%, 3%, 3.5%, 4% and 4.5%. Every dollar over $9,436 is taxed at 4.7%. The dollar lines are indexed to inflation each year; the rates change only by law or by the revenue triggers in Section 143.011.
### Q. How do I calculate my state income tax?
A.  Start with federal adjusted gross income from your 1040. Add or subtract Missouri modifications on Form MO-A, then subtract any pension and Social Security exemption, a percentage of your federal income tax, and the standard deduction. Run the result through the DOR table: $263 on the first $9,436 on the 2026 table, then 4.7% of the rest. DOR’s online income tax calculator is a good way to check your math.
### Q. What is the average tax in Missouri?
A.  There isn’t one official average, because it depends on income and household. As a benchmark, a single filer earning $70,000 in wages pays about $2,306 in Missouri income tax, roughly 3.3% of gross pay, even though the top rate is 4.7%. At the register, the state sales tax rate is 4.225%, and cities and counties can add their own on top.
### Q. Which states have no income taxes at all?
A.  Missouri’s own 2025 income tax reference guide lists nine: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington State, Wyoming and New Hampshire. Rules on narrow items like investment income vary, so check that state’s revenue department before you count on it. Missouri isn’t on the list, and its plan to phase out the income tax failed at the ballot box in August 2026.
### Q. Where can I find Missouri tax forms?
A.  On the Department of Revenue’s forms and manuals page, and DOR also runs an online tax form selector. Most residents file Form MO-1040, or the short MO-1040A if their return is simple. Common add-ons are MO-A for modifications and pensions, MO-NRI for nonresidents and part-year residents, MO-CR for credit on tax paid to another state, MO-60 for an extension payment and MO-1040ES for estimated tax.
### Q. What is the 183 day rule in Missouri?
A.  It’s how Missouri can treat you as a resident even when your legal home is somewhere else. If you keep permanent living quarters in Missouri and spend more than 183 days of the year here, the DOR counts you as a resident and taxes all of your income, not only what you earned in Missouri. The test is spelled out on DOR’s nonresident and other-state income page.
### Q. Can you be a resident of two states?
A.  Yes. You can be domiciled in one state and count as a resident of another under a rule like Missouri’s 183-day test, and both can tax your full income. The relief is a credit: Missouri residents claim tax paid to another state on Form MO-CR, and Illinois residents use Schedule CR. Part-year movers are treated as nonresidents, though Missouri lets them figure the tax as full-year residents.
### Q. Can I claim the federal tips and overtime deductions on my Missouri return?
A.  No. The Department of Revenue says the newer federal deductions for tips, overtime, car loan interest and the enhanced senior deduction can’t be claimed on the Missouri return. Missouri starts from your federal adjusted gross income, and those deductions come off later on the federal form, so tips and overtime pay stay in the income Missouri taxes, at 4.7% on the margin for most workers.

## St. Louis Sales Tax Rate: Why Your Receipt Changes From One Store to the Next
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-sales-tax-rate
Same shampoo. Same shelf price. Buy it at a store on one side of a busy St. Louis road and the tax line on your receipt comes to one number. Drive a mile, buy the identical bottle at another store, and the tax line is bigger. Neither receipt tells you why. Both just print TAX and a total, as if sales tax were one fixed thing that everybody pays the same way.
It isn’t one thing. The rate on a St. Louis receipt is a stack of separate taxes, and the top layer is often a district most shoppers have never heard of: a community improvement district or a transportation development district, drawn around a shopping center, a hotel or a few downtown blocks, and allowed to add up to a full percentage point of its own. In the City of St. Louis, the state’s current rate table lists the base rate and then 78 more rows for these district combinations. For St. Louis County, it lists 393 separate rate rows.
Nobody teaches this in school, and the register isn’t going to explain it. So here it is, one layer at a time: the rate where you shop, why it jumps from one parking lot to the next, how groceries and online orders are handled, and the state’s own lookup that gives you the exact rate for any address. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, which walks through the other bills that arrive with no explanation attached.
### What is the sales tax rate in St. Louis County?
There’s no single rate. Unincorporated St. Louis County starts at 7.738%: Missouri’s 4.225% plus 3.513% in county taxes. A city, fire protection district, community improvement district or transportation development district can add more, and the state’s rate table shows county addresses as high as 13.238%. Look up your exact address with the Department of Revenue.
Those numbers come straight from the Missouri Department of Revenue’s rate table for October through December 2026, and they’re the only kind worth trusting, because local rates move whenever something new is approved and the state reissues its tables every quarter. Treat any figure here, including ours, as a snapshot. The lookup is the live answer.
Here’s what’s inside that 3.513% county share. It isn’t one tax. It’s ten, according to the state’s tax rate breakdown: a 1% general county tax, 1.25% for public transit spread across three separate levies, 0.5% for public safety, 0.25% for children’s services, 0.125% for the zoo, 0.1% for emergency services, and two small regional parks taxes of 0.1% and 0.188%. That last one, tied to the Arch grounds, is the only one of the ten with an end date printed in the table: September 30, 2033.
Then the address takes over. If the store sits inside one of the county’s municipalities, that city’s own taxes go on top. If it sits inside a fire protection district with a sales tax, add another 1%. That fire layer is new. In the October 2026 table, 13 fire protection and ambulance districts in St. Louis County show a 1% sales tax that wasn’t in the July table, and it touches 151 of the county’s 393 rows. The state’s rate change notice lists them one by one. If receipts at your usual county stores crept up when that table took effect, that’s a likely reason.
The City of St. Louis is a separate thing entirely. It’s an independent city, not part of the county, and the same table puts its base rate at 9.679%. The why is a few sections down.
### Why can two stores a mile apart charge different sales tax?
Because one of them can sit inside a special taxing district while the other doesn’t. Missouri lets two kinds of district charge their own sales tax on top of everything else: community improvement districts (CIDs) and transportation development districts (TDDs). The Community Improvement District Act lets a CID add a sales tax in eighth-of-a-percent steps, up to a maximum of 1%. The TDD law carries the same 1% ceiling. Put a CID and a TDD on the same piece of ground and that’s two extra points.
You can see it plainly in the City’s rows of the state table. The base rate is 9.679%. Below it come 78 district rows: 48 at 10.679%, 29 at 11.679% and one at 10.179%. A shop inside the Soulard CID charges 10.679%. A shop inside the Ballpark Village CID and TDD charges 11.679%. Same city taxes underneath, same state tax, different receipt.
Run it on a $1,000 refrigerator. At a City store outside any district, the tax is $96.79. At one inside a CID plus a TDD, it’s $116.79. The county stretches the gap further: $77.38 at an unincorporated address with no districts, $132.38 at the highest-rate row in the county. That’s $55 on one appliance, decided by which side of a line the building sits on.
The money is meant to stay close to the register. Under Missouri’s CID law, a district can pay for sidewalks, parking garages, lighting, landscaping, security staff, cleaning and marketing inside its own boundaries. A TDD pays for transportation work, which the statute defines to include streets, interchanges, signals, parking lots, bus stops and similar projects.
Now the part that surprises people. These taxes need a vote, but when no registered voters live inside a district’s lines, Missouri hands the ballot to the property owners instead. That’s written into the CID definitions and into the TDD law, which gives those owners one vote per acre. A district drawn around a retail center may have nobody living in it at all. The people who’ll pay the tax at the checkout, shoppers from everywhere else, never see a ballot.
There is one protection, and it’s easy to miss. Missouri law says every retailer in a TDD with a sales tax must prominently display the rate at the cash register area. So when a district tax shows up on your receipt, look around the register. The sign is supposed to be there.
Two carve-outs matter for big purchases. CID and TDD sales taxes don’t apply to cars, trailers, boats or outboard motors, and they skip utility sales. Vehicle tax runs on a different system altogether, which our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis dealership walks through before you sign anything.
### How is the St. Louis sales tax rate built?
Think layer cake. Every Missouri receipt starts with the state’s 4.225%, which the Department of Revenue splits four ways: 3% to general revenue, 1% to education, 0.125% to conservation and 0.1% to parks and soils. Then the local layers go on, and that’s where St. Louis gets expensive.
Inside the City of St. Louis, the local share is 5.454%, and it’s 12 taxes, not one. The state’s breakdown lists a 1% general city tax plus a 0.375% add-on, 0.5% for capital improvements, 1% for transit split between a public transportation tax and a MetroLink tax, 0.5% for economic development, 1% for public safety across two levies, 0.125% for storm water and local parks, the same two regional parks taxes the county pays, and 0.666% that the state labels St. Louis City desegregation, which traces to the law that set up the City’s transitional school district. Add those to the state’s 4.225% and you land on 9.679%. Thirteen taxes, before a single district shows up.
None of it happened at once. The City’s layers carry effective dates from 1970 to 2018, each added for its own job. That’s why the rate feels high and arbitrary at the same time: nobody ever voted on 9.679% as a number. It got there a fraction at a time.
Here’s how the two halves of St. Louis compare in the state’s table for October through December 2026:
Two things jump out. The county’s floor is lower than the City’s, but its ceiling is higher, because a county address can pile municipal taxes, a fire district, a CID and two TDDs on top of the county’s ten. And Missouri’s own share is the modest part of the bill. It’s the local stack that does the damage, which is also why living costs on a receipt don’t match the ones on a rent check. Our breakdown of the cost of living in St. Louis puts sales tax next to the bigger monthly numbers. Income tax is its own story, covered in Missouri’s state income tax rate.
### How do I find the exact sales tax rate for an address?
Use the state’s lookup, not a ZIP code chart. The Department of Revenue keeps a sales and use tax rate map that covers city and county taxes plus community improvement, transportation development, fire protection, ambulance and other districts. Enter an address and it shows the boundaries, the combined rate and the jurisdiction code businesses use when they file. District lines can split neighboring buildings, so a ZIP code can’t tell you which side of the line a store sits on.
For something you buy in a store, enter the store’s street address. The state says the combined sales tax rate depends on where the seller is located, not where you live.
For an order shipped to you from out of state, enter your delivery address. Use tax follows the place the item is stored, used or consumed.
Check the quarter. The map shows past rates back to January 2023, which helps when you’re checking an old receipt against the rate that applied that day.
Compare. Divide the tax on your receipt by the taxable subtotal and line it up against what the lookup says.
If you sell taxable goods yourself, even on weekends, the same lookup decides what you collect, and the registration side is covered in our guide to the Missouri sales tax license. Collect too little and you still owe the state the full tax, under section 144.080.
Shopping for a bottle? St. Louis liquor store rules, Missouri and Illinois.
### Are groceries taxed less in Missouri?
Yes, at the state level. Missouri cuts its share on qualifying food from 4.225% to 1.225% under section 144.014. Local taxes still apply, so the full grocery rate stays well above 1.225%. In the state’s table, qualifying groceries come to 6.391% in the City of St. Louis and 4.35% in unincorporated St. Louis County, against 9.679% and 7.738% for everything else.
What counts as food? The reduced rate covers items you could buy with SNAP benefits, the program once called food stamps: food for eating at home, cold or room temperature, plus seeds and plants for growing your own. It doesn’t cover food from a place where meals prepared for immediate eating make up more than 80% of sales, which takes in restaurants, fast food, delis and cafes, whether you eat there or carry out. Warm doesn’t automatically mean full rate, though. The state’s own example is donuts from a grocery store: still the reduced rate, even when they’re warm from the oven.
So a grocery receipt is really two receipts printed on one strip. The bread, eggs and coffee ring up at the food rate. The paper towels and dish soap don’t, because they aren’t food. On a $200 City grocery run that’s all food, the reduced rate means about $12.78 in tax instead of $19.36 at the full rate. Big order? Glance at the tax line. A grocery bill taxed like a hardware bill is worth a question at the service desk.
### Do you owe Missouri tax on online and out-of-state orders?
Usually yes, though the big online sellers now have to collect it for you. Missouri calls it use tax, and the state rate is 4.225%, the same as the sales tax. Remote sellers and online marketplaces with more than $100,000 in taxable Missouri sales over the previous 12 months have to collect it at checkout.
The local part depends on your delivery address, and here the City and the county split hard. The City’s use tax rate in the state’s table is 9.013%. Unincorporated St. Louis County’s is 4.225%, the state’s share alone, because no local use tax applies there. The state’s FAQ says it plainly: where a local government hasn’t passed a use tax, out-of-state sellers collect only the 4.225%. The new fire district taxes don’t reach use tax either, according to the state’s notice.
When a seller doesn’t collect, the tax doesn’t disappear. It becomes yours. Missouri’s individual consumer’s use tax return, Form 4340 or 53-C, is required once your untaxed purchases pass $2,000 in a calendar year, and the state is blunt that the $2,000 is a filing trigger, not an exemption. Cross it and you owe on the whole amount, not just the part above the line. The return is due April 15 of the following year.
Across the river the math changes again. Illinois’ state rate on general merchandise is 6.25% before local taxes, and its 1% state tax on groceries ended January 1, 2026, with cities and counties allowed to add their own. Fuel has its own split between the two states, laid out in St. Louis gas prices, Missouri vs. Illinois.
### What should you do if the tax on a receipt looks wrong?
Check the math before you assume anything. Divide the tax by the taxable subtotal. A $7.74 tax line on an $80 purchase works out to about 9.68%, which is the City’s base rate give or take a penny of rounding. If your number comes out a full point or two higher than the lookup shows, you’ve probably found a district. Or a register set up for the wrong one.
Then look for the TDD sign near the register, and ask the store. If the register is coded to the wrong jurisdiction, the store is the only one that can fix it at the source, and a manager can see the setting you can’t.
If it’s real money and the store won’t make it right, Missouri has a formal route. Under section 144.190, tax collected in error is refunded to the business that sent it to the state. A buyer can file with the Department of Revenue directly only in specific cases: the seller won’t give a written assignment of its refund rights within 60 days of your written request, or it can’t be found or has closed. You’d file with either the seller’s notarized assignment or a notarized statement of what you tried.
Sales tax is the tax you see on the day you pay. The one that ambushes people months later is the bill for the car in the driveway, explained in St. Louis County personal property tax.
This is general information about how Missouri sales and use tax works, not tax advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply it to your purchases or your business, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a good place to start.
Crossed the $2,000 line on untaxed online orders, or starting to sell things yourself? Find accountants around St. Louis and ask one question up front: do you file Missouri consumer’s use tax and sales tax returns for people like me?
And if you’re the bookkeeper who keeps a shop’s district codes straight, the next St. Louis store owner who asks a neighbor, or an AI, who handles this should hear your name first, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the local sales tax rate in Missouri?
A.  It depends on exactly where the sale happens. Local taxes are everything above the state’s 4.225%, and in the Department of Revenue’s table for October through December 2026, combined rates run from 5.225% in parts of three rural counties to 13.238% at the top row in St. Louis County. That puts the local share anywhere from 1% to just over 9%. The state’s address lookup gives the exact figure.
### Q. Why is sales tax so high?
A.  In St. Louis it’s the stacking. Missouri’s state rate of 4.225% is lower than Illinois’ 6.25%. The height comes from local layers added one at a time for transit, public safety, parks, the zoo and schools, then special districts on top. The City of St. Louis carries 12 local taxes before any district. Each looks small alone. Together they’re more than half the rate.
### Q. What is a community improvement district in Missouri?
A.  It’s a separate local taxing district created under Missouri’s Community Improvement District Act to pay for things inside a defined area, such as sidewalks, parking, lighting, security, cleaning and marketing. A CID can charge a sales tax of up to 1%, in eighth-of-a-percent steps, after a vote. If no registered voters live in the district, property owners vote instead. The tax doesn’t apply to cars, boats or utilities.
### Q. What items are exempt from sales tax in Missouri?
A.  The household exemptions are mostly medical: prescription drugs, insulin, durable medical equipment, prosthetic and orthopedic devices, wheelchairs, hearing aids, and over-the-counter drugs sold to people with disabilities, all listed in section 144.030. Qualifying clothing, school supplies and computers are exempt during the back-to-school holiday, from the first Friday in August through Sunday. Groceries aren’t exempt; they get a lower rate.
### Q. Do you have to pay sales tax in Missouri?
A.  Yes, on most retail purchases of goods and on the services the law lists, including restaurant meals, hotel rooms, admissions, utilities and phone service. The seller collects it at the register. If you buy from an out-of-state seller that doesn’t collect, you owe use tax instead, and once those purchases pass $2,000 in a calendar year you have to file a return and pay on all of them.
### Q. Is it illegal to overcharge sales tax?
A.  Sellers are required to collect the tax Missouri sets for their location, and tax collected in error can be refunded. A wrong rate can simply be a register coded to the wrong jurisdiction, so ask the store first. If that fails, section 144.190 lets the seller claim the refund, and lets a buyer file with the Department of Revenue directly when the seller won’t assign its refund rights within 60 days.
### Q. How do I calculate Missouri sales tax?
A.  Find the combined rate for the store’s address with the state’s lookup, turn it into a decimal and multiply by the taxable price. At the City of St. Louis base rate of 9.679%, an $80 purchase carries $7.74 in tax. Qualifying groceries use the lower food rate. To check a receipt, divide the tax by the taxable subtotal and compare the result with the lookup.
### Q. What is not taxed in Missouri?
A.  Most services. Missouri’s sales tax law taxes goods plus a specific list of services, such as meals, lodging, admissions, utilities, phone service and rentals. A service that isn’t on that list, like a haircut or an accountant’s fee, generally isn’t taxed. Internet access is left out of the phone service tax, and special district sales taxes skip cars, boats and utility bills.

## $2,000 Offer, $1,531 Paycheck: Missouri W-4 and Your Pay Stub
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-w-4-and-how-to-read-your-pay-stub
$2,000 is what you expected. $1,531 is what your phone shows, buzzing against your leg as the 70 Grand lurches away from the curb. First real payday from the job on Grand, and this morning, on this same bus, you did the math: the offer letter said $52,000 a year, 26 paydays, $2,000 each.
Your stomach dips the way it does on a missed step. Above that bottom line sits a column of minus signs and abbreviations nobody ever taught you to read.
Nobody stole $469. It went to six places, each with its own rule, and the only map was two forms HR slid across the desk on day one, with a pen and about four minutes to spare. Then a relative told you to “claim zero,” which is advice for a box the federal form dropped in 2020. Missouri’s form doesn’t have it either.
One of those six lines barely exists outside this city. The City of St. Louis takes 1% from everyone who lives in the City, wherever they work, and everyone who works for a business in the City, wherever they live. Here’s the part nobody mentions at orientation: if you live outside the City and work some days from home, the Collector of Revenue’s own earnings tax page says you can file Form E-1R for a refund, and your employer has to verify the days you worked outside the City.
So here it is, line by line: the Missouri form, the City’s 1%, and the one MO W-4 checkbox that can nearly halve the state tax taken from a $52,000 salary. Every pay stub figure below is illustrative, for a single worker, run through the real federal and Missouri withholding formulas. Your own numbers will differ. This page is part of our St. Louis money guide, which covers the rest of what nobody explained.
### How to fill out Missouri W4?
Form MO W-4 has four lines and no allowances. Check one filing status box on line 1, put any extra amount you want withheld each paycheck on line 2, leave line 3 blank unless you want a set dollar amount withheld instead, and write EXEMPT on line 4 only if you qualify. Then sign it, or it isn’t valid.
That’s the whole form. One sheet, the kind you sign on a clipboard in under a minute, and it quietly sets every state tax line on every paycheck after. It’s Missouri’s own form, the MO W-4 Employee’s Withholding Certificate. Missouri doesn’t copy your federal choices, so you fill out both. The current version lives on the Missouri Department of Revenue’s site.
Line 1 is filing status, with three boxes: “Single or Married Spouse Works or Married Filing Separate,” “Married (Spouse does not work)” and “Head of Household.” Most people starting a first job are single, which puts them in the first box. Line 2 is additional withholding, a flat extra dollar amount taken from every check. The form names the usual reasons, like interest, dividends or income from a part-time job, and gives the math: divide the extra tax you expect to owe by your number of paydays.
The reduced withholding line tells your employer to skip the standard calculation and withhold only the amount you write in. Line 4, exempt, covers the situations the form lists: a full Missouri refund last year with no Missouri tax expected this year (renewed with a new form every year), the military spouse residency rules, or active-duty pay that qualifies for Missouri’s military income deduction.
Now the trap. Behind line 1, Missouri’s withholding formula subtracts a standard deduction from your yearly pay before it figures any tax: $16,100 for the first box, $24,150 for head of household, and $32,200 for “Married (Spouse does not work).” The formula even notes that the last one isn’t a separate filing status. It’s just a checkbox. Tick it when your spouse does work and the formula shelters an extra $16,100 of your pay from withholding. On a $52,000 salary that’s about $757 a year less withheld, roughly $29 a check if you’re paid every two weeks, and it tends to come back as a bill when you file. Those deduction amounts are adjusted each year.
Two more things on the form that almost nobody reads. Your employer must send the Department of Revenue a copy within 20 days of hiring you, and the state uses it for income tax withholding and child support enforcement. It also points you to the department’s online withholding calculator. If you’re the one hiring, our guide to hiring your first employee in Missouri covers the employer side of this paperwork.
### How do you read the deductions on a St. Louis pay stub?
Read it top to bottom with your finger on the screen, the way you’d check a long receipt at the register, and watch which number each line is figured on. Gross pay comes first, then pre-tax deductions that shrink your taxable wages, then the taxes, then net pay. Here’s the paycheck from the top of this page. The numbers are illustrative: a single worker, paid every two weeks, at a job inside the City, putting 5% into a 401(k), with each tax run through the current official formula.
The 401(k) line is your money, not a tax. It comes out before income tax, so the federal, Missouri and City lines are all figured on $1,900. The IRS still counts it as wages for Social Security and Medicare, though, so those two are figured on the full $2,000. One stub, two different versions of your wages. The tax on it comes due in retirement, the story of how Missouri taxes retirement income.
Federal income tax, $144, comes out of the IRS’s Publication 15-T tables: payroll annualizes the $1,900, applies the schedule for your filing status, and divides by 26. This is the line your W-4 controls.
Social Security is a flat 6.2% and Medicare a flat 1.45%, according to the IRS, and no form you sign changes either one. Social Security stops once your wages for the year pass a cap that’s adjusted annually; it’s $184,500 for 2026. Medicare has no cap, and once one employer pays you more than $200,000 in a calendar year, it has to withhold an extra 0.9% on the rest. Stubs label these two FICA, OASDI, SS or MED.
Missouri withholding, $53, runs through the state formula: yearly pay minus the $16,100 standard deduction, then rates that climb from 0% to 4.7%. In that formula, every dollar of taxable pay above $9,436 a year is figured at the top 4.7% rate. The state rounds each check’s withholding to the whole dollar. Our guide to the Missouri income tax rate covers how the actual return settles up.
City earnings tax, $19, is the line people from outside St. Louis have never seen. It’s 1% for anyone who works in the City, wherever they live, and for City residents, wherever they work. The City’s own list of taxable and non-taxable items puts deferred compensation under the tax code’s retirement-plan sections, the 401(k) among them, on the non-taxable side, along with cafeteria-plan benefits and health savings accounts. That’s why the 1% here is figured on $1,900, not $2,000. Our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax has the full story.
Add the five taxes and you get $369, about 18.5% of gross. Add the $100 you saved for yourself and there’s your $469. Nothing went missing. Nobody explained it.

### Why is “claim 0” advice for a form that no longer exists?
Because the federal W-4 dropped allowances in 2020, and Missouri’s current form doesn’t use them either. The IRS says it flatly in Publication 15-T: starting with the 2020 form, employees can no longer adjust their withholding with allowances. There’s no box left to put a zero in.
Under the old system, each allowance told payroll to shelter a slice of your pay from withholding. More allowances meant bigger paychecks. Zero meant the most tax taken and, usually, a refund in the spring. That’s where the family advice comes from, and it was decent advice for its day. The IRS still keeps a conversion for people with a pre-2020 form on file: each old allowance becomes $4,300 of deductions in today’s math.
Now you give payroll dollars, not a count. Want more withheld? Federal Step 4(c) takes an extra amount per paycheck, and Missouri line 2 does the same for state tax. Want the default? Fill in your filing status and sign, and payroll uses the standard deduction for that status. If an onboarding portal or a photocopied form asks how many allowances you claim, it’s an old version; Pub 15-T says a new W-4 has to be on the current year’s revision.
And the refund habit deserves a second look. A big April refund is your own money, returned without interest. Some people like it as forced savings. Fair enough. It just shouldn’t be an accident.
### How do you fill out the federal W-4 correctly?
Complete Step 1 and Step 5, and do Steps 2 through 4 only if they apply to you. That instruction is printed on the form, and for a single person with one job and no kids it really is that short. The current form and its instructions are on the IRS Form W-4 page.
Step 1, personal information. Name, address, Social Security number and filing status: single or married filing separately; married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; or head of household. The status sets the standard deduction and rates used on your paycheck.
Step 2, multiple jobs or spouse works. For anyone holding two jobs at once, or married filing jointly with a working spouse. Pick one of three routes: the IRS estimator, which is the most accurate; the Multiple Jobs Worksheet; or a checkbox when there are only two jobs in total, checked on both jobs’ forms.
Step 3, dependents and other credits. If your income will be $200,000 or less ($400,000 married filing jointly), multiply qualifying children under 17 by $2,200 and other dependents by $500. With two jobs, Steps 3 through 4(b) go on one form only, and the IRS says the highest-paying job’s form is most accurate.
Step 4, other adjustments. 4(a) adds income with no withholding, like interest or dividends. 4(b) lowers withholding through a deductions worksheet that now includes the new federal deductions for qualified tips, overtime pay, passenger vehicle loan interest and seniors. 4(c) is extra tax per paycheck.
Step 5, signature. No signature, no valid form.
Two details catch new hires. Pub 15-T says the tip and overtime deductions cover tax years 2025 through 2028, and that tips and overtime generally still owe Social Security and Medicare. So a server in Soulard who expects qualifying tips can use Step 4(b) to have less federal income tax withheld, while her FICA lines stay put. And the exempt checkbox below Step 4(c) is only for someone who owed no federal income tax last year and expects to owe none this year. It expires, too: a new W-4 is due by mid-February of the next year to keep it.
Skip the form entirely and Pub 15-T has your employer withhold as if you checked single and left the rest blank. With two jobs, that’s the start of a problem.
Teen chasing a first paycheck? Here are summer jobs in St. Louis.
### What W-4 mistakes leave St. Louis workers owing in April?
The expensive ones share a blind spot: every employer withholds as if its paycheck is your only income. Neither payroll department knows the other one exists. Here’s what that does to illustrative salaries run through the current federal tables and Missouri’s formula:
The two-job gap is about $2,080 federal and $937 Missouri, and no single paycheck looked wrong all year. Each employer hands you the full standard deduction and the lowest brackets, so you get them twice on paper and once in real life. Check the Step 2(c) box on both federal forms and each job gets half the standard deduction and brackets; here, withholding lands at $4,060 exactly. Missouri’s form has no such box. Its tool is line 2, where about $36 extra per biweekly paycheck on one job would cover the $937.
The married version is the same trap. Two $52,000 salaries look like two modest paychecks to two payroll systems, and each one spends the couple’s whole standard deduction and lowest bracket on its own check. In this example, Step 2(c) checked on both forms brings withholding to the full $8,120. On the Missouri side, the form puts a working couple in the first box, both of them.
Then there’s the side hustle. Weekend delivery runs, a booth at a craft fair, freelance design work: that money shows up with nothing withheld, and the W-4 instructions warn that you’ll generally owe both income tax and self-employment tax on it. The federal form lets your day job cover it through Step 4(c) or the estimator, and Missouri’s line 2 does the same for state tax. Our guide to side hustle taxes in Missouri walks through the quarterly-payment route instead.
### Who owes the City’s 1% earnings tax, and who can get it back?
Two groups owe it: everyone who lives in the City of St. Louis, no matter where their employer is, and everyone who works for a business located or doing work in the City, no matter where they live. The City’s individual earnings tax page spells out both.
The trap runs in both directions. Say you live in Dutchtown and take a warehouse job out in the county. If that employer doesn’t take out the 1%, you still owe it. Form E-1 is the return a resident files to pay City tax that wasn’t withheld. It’s due April 15, the City doesn’t allow extensions on it, and tax paid late picks up a penalty of 5% of the tax for each month. On $40,000 of wages, the tax itself is $400.
Now flip it. Say you live outside the City, work for a downtown employer, and spend two days a week working from home. Your employer may withhold the 1% on all of your pay, but the days you worked outside the City can come back through Form E-1R, the nonresident refund return on the City’s earnings tax forms page. Your employer has to verify how many days you worked outside the City, and the deadline is one year from the date the original return and tax were due. Hybrid schedules make this common, which is good to know before you take one of the legit work-from-home jobs in St. Louis.
### How can you check your withholding before tax season?
Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with your latest pay stub in hand. It works from your pay, what’s been withheld so far and your household, then tells you what to put on a new W-4. It doesn’t ask for your name, Social Security number or bank details, and the IRS says your answers aren’t saved. Filing jointly? Bring your spouse’s latest stub too.
Missouri has its own withholding calculator on the Department of Revenue’s site, and the MO W-4 suggests a fresh form every year and whenever your personal or financial situation changes. A new job. A second job. A wedding, a baby, a side business, a move into or out of the City. Each one changes at least one line on that stub. The IRS adds a timing note in Pub 15-T: a W-4 changed partway through the year can over- or under-withhold once it runs a full calendar year, so January is a good time to look again.
How close is close enough? Under the IRS’s underpayment penalty rules, you generally won’t owe a penalty if you owe less than $1,000 after withholding and refundable credits, or if your withholding and estimated payments covered at least 90% of this year’s tax or 100% of last year’s, whichever is smaller. Higher earners have special rules. Withholding doesn’t have to be perfect. It has to be close, and on purpose.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply these rules to your pay, your household and your side income, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri have a W4?
A.  Yes. Missouri uses its own Form MO W-4, separate from the federal W-4, so a new hire fills out both. It has four lines: filing status, additional withholding, reduced withholding and exempt status. Your employer sends the Department of Revenue a copy within 20 days of hiring you.
### Q. Do you still claim 0 or 1 on W4?
A.  No. The federal W-4 stopped using allowances with the 2020 version, and Missouri’s current form doesn’t use them either. Both work in dollars now: extra withholding in federal Step 4(c) or Missouri line 2, deductions in Step 4(b), credits in Step 3. A form asking for allowances is an outdated version.
### Q. What is a pay stub supposed to look like?
A.  Most show gross pay, each tax and deduction, and net pay, often with a column for this check and one for the year to date. Missouri’s wage law, section 290.080, requires corporations doing business here to give workers at least a monthly statement of total deductions.
### Q. What percentage is usually taken out of your paycheck for taxes?
A.  No single number, but some pieces are fixed. Social Security and Medicare take 7.65% up to the yearly Social Security cap, Missouri withholding runs from 0% to 4.7% after a standard deduction, and the City adds 1% if you live or work there. In this page’s illustrative example, taxes came to about 18.5% of gross.
### Q. How to fill out W4 to not owe taxes?
A.  Start with the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, which turns your pay stub and household details into W-4 entries. Two jobs or a working spouse means completing Step 2. Income with no withholding can go in Step 4(a), or extra withholding in Step 4(c). Owing under $1,000 at filing generally avoids the IRS underpayment penalty.
### Q. Is it better to claim 1 or 0 allowances on state taxes?
A.  In Missouri, neither, because the current MO W-4 has no allowances. State withholding depends on the filing status box you check and any dollar amount on line 2 or line 3. The box matters most: “Married (Spouse does not work)” doubles the formula’s standard deduction to $32,200.
### Q. What is a MO W-4 withholding?
A.  It’s the Missouri income tax your employer takes from each paycheck based on your MO W-4. The state formula annualizes your pay, subtracts a standard deduction tied to your line 1 box, applies rates from 0% to 4.7%, divides by your paydays and rounds to the dollar. It’s a prepayment, not the final bill.
### Q. Why is my first paycheck smaller than my offer letter?
A.  The offer letter quotes gross pay. The stub subtracts pre-tax deductions like a 401(k), then federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, Missouri withholding and, for City jobs and City residents, the 1% earnings tax. In this page’s illustrative example, a $2,000 check became $1,531.

## Side Hustle Taxes in Missouri: 1099s, Estimated Payments and the $100 Line Nobody Mentions
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/side-hustle-taxes-missouri-1099-and-estimated-payments
Paid every week, warned never. The delivery app dropped money into your account all year, for the Soulard dinner rush and the late runs through the Central West End, and not one of those deposits had a cent of tax taken out. No screen said April. No pop-up said Missouri. The money looked like yours, and most of it was.
That silence is how the system is built. When an app or a client pays you as an independent contractor, nobody withholds anything, so the IRS calls what you owe estimated tax: tax on income that isn’t subject to withholding. The federal form for it, Form 1040-ES, lists self-employment earnings, “including gig economy work,” as its very first example. Nobody mails you a reminder, either. The Missouri Department of Revenue says it in five words, printed on its own estimated-tax worksheet: “You will not be billed.”
Then the law made the silence louder. For payments made in 2026, the line that triggers a 1099-NEC from a client jumped from $600 to $2,000, and payment apps are back to sending a 1099-K only after you pass $20,000 and more than 200 transactions. Lots of side hustlers will never see a form. The tax didn’t move an inch.
None of that means you’re bad with money. It means nobody sat you down and explained that a St. Louis side hustle can answer to three tax collectors (the IRS, the Missouri Department of Revenue and, if you live in the city, the Collector of Revenue) and that none of them sends a bill before the due date. This page does the explaining, with the numbers taken straight off the official forms. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English money stuff school skipped.
### How do I calculate my estimated taxes in Missouri?
You estimate the year’s profit, then figure two bills. Federal: self-employment tax of 15.3% on 92.35% of profit, plus income tax at your bracket. Missouri: run taxable income through the MO-1040ES rate chart. Subtract withholding from each. If Missouri’s remainder reaches $100, or the IRS’s $1,000, pay in four installments: April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15.
Here’s the same math as steps, using the 2026 versions of both forms. Rates, brackets and deductions are adjusted each year, so check the current form before you run your own numbers.
Profit first. Add up everything the apps and clients will pay you for the year, form or no form, then subtract business costs. What’s left is net profit, the number everything else runs on.
Self-employment tax. Multiply profit by 92.35%, then by 15.3%. On $10,000 of profit that’s about $1,413. The Form 1040-ES worksheet runs exactly this calculation.
Federal income tax. Add profit, minus half of that self-employment tax, to your other income and apply your bracket. On the 2026 rate schedule, a single filer’s 12% bracket covers taxable income from $12,400 to $50,400, and 22% runs from there to $105,700.
Subtract withholding. Whatever your day job will withhold for the year comes off. If you still expect to owe $1,000 or more, the IRS expects estimated payments.
Missouri. The MO-1040ES worksheet starts from your federal adjusted gross income after Missouri’s own adjustments, including a 20% business income deduction on Schedule C profit, subtracts the Missouri standard deduction ($16,100 for a single filer on the 2026 form) and taxes every dollar of Missouri taxable income over $9,436 at 4.7%. Subtract Missouri withholding. If what’s left is $100 or more, Missouri expects a declaration and payments.
Divide by four, or by however many due dates are left in the year.
Look at that Missouri step again, because it’s the local trap. Missouri’s line is one-tenth of the IRS’s. At 4.7%, it takes only about $2,130 of extra Missouri taxable income to produce $100 of tax. So if your day-job withholding already covers your wages, a side gig netting roughly $2,900 can put you over Missouri’s line, while owing the IRS $1,000 takes roughly $3,300 to $4,300 of profit, depending on your bracket and using the worked example below. It’s easy to stay current with the IRS and miss Missouri entirely.
### Do you owe tax on side hustle income if no 1099 shows up?
Yes, from the first dollar. The IRS’s gig economy tax center says gig income has to be reported even when it isn’t on a 1099-K, 1099-NEC, 1099-MISC or W-2, and even when you’re paid in cash, property or virtual currency. The form is a receipt, not a permission slip.
What changed is who gets a form. Two thresholds moved:
1099-NEC, from clients who pay you for services: $600 for payments made before 2026, $2,000 for payments made in 2026, with an inflation adjustment after that, according to the IRS’s information return filing page.
1099-K, from payment apps and online marketplaces: required only when your payments top $20,000 and more than 200 transactions. The IRS says the One, Big, Beautiful Bill retroactively reinstated that older threshold. Card processors, by contrast, have no threshold at all.
You can still get a form below those lines. And a 1099-K reports only gross payments, before the fees the platform kept or the refunds you gave. Its number is a starting point, not your taxable income.
The line that matters more is $400. Once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400, the IRS’s gig work guidance says you must file a return, with Schedule C for the profit and Schedule SE for the self-employment tax. A summer of weekend dog walking can get there.
### Why is self-employment tax so high?
Because you’re paying both halves. On a regular paycheck, Social Security and Medicare take 7.65% of your wages, and your employer pays a matching 7.65% you never see. Work for yourself and you’re the employer too. The self-employment tax is 12.4% for Social Security plus 2.9% for Medicare: 15.3% in all.
Two things soften it, and both are printed on the IRS forms. First, the tax applies to 92.35% of your net profit, not all of it. Second, you deduct the employer-equivalent half of the tax when you figure adjusted gross income, which lowers your income tax (not the self-employment tax itself). On $10,000 of profit, $9,235 is taxed at 15.3% for about $1,413, and about $706 comes off your adjusted gross income.
The Social Security piece stops at a wage base, $184,500 of combined wages and self-employment earnings for 2026, and day-job wages count toward it first. Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% Medicare tax applies above $200,000 for single filers. If your combined pay is nowhere near those figures, ignore them.
Here’s why it stings. Income tax has a standard deduction standing in front of it. Self-employment tax doesn’t. It starts at $400 of net earnings, so someone who owes zero income tax can still owe the 15.3%. That’s the bill the app never mentioned.
### Which side hustle expenses actually shrink the bill?
Ordinary costs of doing the work, subtracted from what you were paid: business miles, parking and tolls, the business share of your phone, supplies you used up, platform fees. Every real expense comes off profit, and profit is what both the 15.3% and your income tax run on. One deduction, two smaller bills.
Mileage. The IRS standard mileage rate for business was 72.5 cents a mile for January through June 2026, then 76 cents from July 1, a mid-year raise. At 76 cents, every 1,000 business miles takes $760 off your profit. The Schedule C instructions let you add parking fees and tolls on top, but not depreciation, lease payments or gas and repairs when you use the standard rate. The rate is reset each year.
Your phone. Only the business share counts. If the phone is half work and half life, the personal half stays personal, and a preparer will ask how you arrived at the split.
Supplies. Insulated delivery bags, a ring light, packaging, ink for invoices. Schedule C allows supplies to the extent you actually used them in the business.
Platform fees. Since a 1099-K shows gross payments, the fees the platform kept come off through your own records.
The catch is proof. The IRS tells gig workers to collect and keep records and receipts during the year, not rebuild them in March. A mileage log kept as you drive is worth far more than one pieced together from memory. If the shoebox is winning, here’s what a bookkeeper costs and why Missouri doesn’t license them.
One more tax lives next door. If you sell physical products rather than services, check whether you need a Missouri sales tax license. That’s a separate tax on your customers’ purchases, with its own filing schedule.
Paying tax on creator income? Make your following earn more of it.
### How much of every payout should you set aside?
In the worked example below, the honest number lands between 26% and 35% of profit, which is roughly 18% to 23% of every dollar the app deposits. Setting aside about 30% of profit is a workable starting point in the 12% bracket, closer to 35% if a day job already puts you in the 22% bracket or you live in the city. Treat it as a first draft and let a preparer tune it.
Picture a nurse in Bevo Mill who drives deliveries three nights a week. Say the app pays her $15,000 over the year, and her business miles, phone share and supplies come to $5,000. Net profit: $10,000. Her hospital paycheck withholding already covers the tax on her wages, and she files single. Here’s what the side gig adds:
Self-employment tax: $10,000 times 92.35% times 15.3% is about $1,413.
Federal income tax: profit minus the $706 half-of-SE-tax deduction leaves $9,294. The qualified business income deduction, which lets many sole proprietors deduct up to 20% of that business income and which recent legislation made permanent, trims about $1,859 more. Roughly $7,435 is left: about $892 of tax at 12%, about $1,636 at 22%.
Missouri income tax: The federal deduction doesn’t carry over, but Missouri has its own: a 20% business income deduction on Schedule C profit, claimed on Form MO-A. That takes $2,000 off the $9,294, so about $7,294 lands at 4.7%. Call it $343.
City earnings tax, if she lives in the city: 1% of net profit, about $100.
Add it up. Outside the city in the 12% bracket, about $2,648, or 26% of profit. Inside the city at 22%, about $3,492, or 35%. Against the $15,000 the app actually deposited, that’s 18% to 23% of each payout. Not one dollar of it was withheld.
The way to keep that number from ambushing you is boring on purpose: a separate savings account, a transfer the day each deposit lands, four calendar alerts. Come April, the money’s already sitting there.
### When are federal and Missouri estimated payments due?
Both use the same four dates: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the following year, moved to the next business day when one falls on a weekend or holiday. They’re called quarterly, but they aren’t evenly spaced. The gaps run two months, then three, then four. June 15 arrives fast.
Federally, you generally avoid the underpayment penalty if withholding and on-time payments cover the smaller of 90% of this year’s tax or 100% of last year’s, or 110% of last year’s if your adjusted gross income topped $150,000 ($75,000 married filing separately). That prior-year rule is why a first-year side hustler with a well-withheld day job can owe no penalty at all and still owe a four-figure bill in April. The rule protects you from the penalty. It doesn’t make the tax smaller.
There’s a quieter federal option if you also hold a job: more withholding. File a new W-4 at work and ask for an extra amount per paycheck. IRS Publication 505 treats one-fourth of your year’s withholding as paid on each installment date, unless you choose to count it on the actual dates, so extra withholding added in the fall still counts toward April and June. Our guide to the Missouri W-4 and reading your pay stub walks through the form.
Missouri runs on the same dates with its own rules. The MO-1040ES instructions skip the extra charge when each installment is on time and your payments reach either last year’s Missouri tax (from a full 12-month return that showed tax) or 90% of this year’s. Otherwise Missouri adds a charge figured at its current interest rate from the first underpaid installment. If the side gig starts mid-year, Missouri’s first due date moves with it: June 15, September 15 or January 15, depending on when your estimated tax changes.
City residents have one more stop. The Collector of Revenue’s E-234 instructions say a City resident who is self-employed owes the 1% earnings tax on 100% of business net profit, even for work done outside city limits, and that all 1099-NEC and 1099-MISC income goes on that return. It’s due April 15. A federal extension won’t cover it: the city wants its own Form E-8, received before the deadline, because the IRS doesn’t tell the city about federal extensions. Our St. Louis earnings tax guide covers the rest, and our page on filing a tax extension in Missouri covers the state and federal side.
### How do you pay taxes on self-employment income?
In installments during the year, then at filing time on Form 1040, with Schedule C for the profit and Schedule SE for the 15.3%. The IRS takes estimated payments through your online account, IRS Direct Pay from a bank account at no cost, EFTPS, a debit or credit card (the card processor charges a fee) or a check with a 1040-ES voucher. Missouri accepts estimated payments online by e-check or card, or by check with the MO-1040ES voucher mailed to P.O. Box 555 in Jefferson City.
The part nobody explains is that you start the payments yourself. There’s no account to wait on and no bill coming. You figure the number, pick the installment, and send it. That’s the whole system. The second time through, it’s routine.
