And the store-card promo that says no interest if paid in full in 12 months. That’s deferred interest, and if any balance is left when the clock runs out, the CFPB warns you could owe the interest back to the original date of the charge.
One more trap hides in “pay on time.” On time and in full aren’t the same thing. Pay the minimum by the due date and you’re on time, with no late fee. The rest of the balance is still charging interest every day.
### Why am I paying interest on my credit card when I paid it off?
Because interest kept running between the day your statement printed and the day your payment arrived. When you’ve been carrying a balance, the CFPB says most card companies charge interest from your billing date, and once interest starts it generally keeps going until they receive your payment. It’s called residual or trailing interest, and it’s the small charge that shows up the month after you were sure the card was at zero. That sinking feeling when you open the app is the most common credit card surprise there is.
Round numbers. Say you carried about $2,000 on a card charging 24%, then paid the whole $2,000 statement balance on the due date, 25 days after the statement closed. Those 25 days still had a price: $2,000 times 24%, divided by 365, times 25, is about $33. Ignore it and it becomes an unpaid balance, with more interest behind it.
The grace period has a memory, too. Pay in full some months and not others, the CFPB warns, and you may lose your grace period for the month you didn’t pay in full and the month after.
To shut it off, pay the trailing charge when it posts and keep paying the full statement balance after that. To close it out in one shot, ask the card company for a payoff amount good through the day your payment will post. If a charge still looks wrong after you’ve read the interest section of your cardholder agreement, the CFPB takes credit card complaints at (855) 411-2372.
### How does credit card interest actually work?
The rate is quoted as a yearly number, the APR, short for annual percentage rate. Most cards don’t charge it yearly, though. They slice it into a daily periodic rate, generally the APR divided by 360 or 365, and apply it to what you owe each day. Interest on interest, every night, while you sleep.
One month of it: a 24% APR divided by 365 is about 0.0658% per day. Carry $3,000 through a 30-day cycle and that’s roughly $59. Sixty dollars a month, just for carrying it.
What’s a normal rate? In the Federal Reserve’s G.19 consumer credit release, the average rate on bank credit card accounts assessed interest was 22.36% for August 2026. Our own Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis carries the series in its FRED database, where you can watch how far it has climbed.
Credit unions play under a different ceiling. The NCUA board has kept an 18% loan interest rate ceiling in place for federal credit unions, most recently extended to September 10, 2027. Next to a bank average above 22%, a federal credit union card that can’t legally top 18% deserves a look.
### How long does it take to pay off a credit card with minimum payments?
On a few thousand dollars at today’s rates, it can run well past a decade. You don’t have to guess. Your statement has to show it in a box: how long the balance takes to pay off with only minimums, and how much you’d need to pay each month to clear it in three years. Most people have never read that box. It’s the most honest paragraph on the bill.
Here’s the math behind it, with round illustrative numbers. Say you owe $3,000 at 24% APR, and your card sets the minimum at 1% of the balance plus that month’s interest, with a $25 floor. Formulas vary; yours is in your cardholder agreement. Month one, interest is about $60. The minimum is $30 plus that $60, so $90. Only $30 of it touches what you borrowed.
Keep paying only the minimum as it shrinks, add nothing new, and it takes about 15 years, with close to $4,900 in interest. That’s more than you borrowed. A flat payment of about $118 a month clears the same $3,000 in three years with about $1,240 in interest.
Same card. Same rate. About $28 more in month one, and roughly twelve years of your life stay yours. The minimum keeps the account current. It was never built to get you out.
The rate matters as much as the payment. The CFPB’s own card-shopping guide shows how much a lower rate saves on the same balance and the same monthly payment.
### What are the fees associated with credit cards?
Annual fees, late fees, cash advance fees and balance transfer fees, plus a penalty APR that can follow a late payment. Every one is spelled out in the card’s terms.
Late fees are where the headlines got tangled, so here’s what’s in effect. The CFPB finalized a rule that would have cut the typical late fee at big card companies to $8. It never took hold: a federal court vacated it, as the CFPB’s own compliance page notes. What still applies is the Regulation Z rule that a late fee can’t exceed the minimum payment that was due.
Balance transfers deserve a warning label. Most cards charge a fee to move a balance, and some charge a one-time 3 to 5 percent of the amount, so a 0% offer on $3,000 can cost $90 to $150 up front. The promo rate ends on a set date. That’s how a lot of 0% deals quietly turn into interest. If you’re weighing a transfer against a loan, our guide to debt consolidation in St. Louis walks through the choices.
Fees don’t stop at the card. If overdraft charges keep nibbling the account that pays it, here’s how to avoid bank fees in St. Louis. And every tap at the register costs the shop a fee too; here’s what Missouri businesses pay to accept cards.
That monthly car wash club riding on your card every month? Here’s whether it pays off.
### How can you build up your credit fast?
Fast, honestly, means months, not days. Open one account that reports to the credit bureaus, pay on time every single time, keep the balance low, and pay in full. That record builds one statement at a time. There’s no shortcut, and anyone selling one is selling something else.
Starting from zero, or rebuilding? The CFPB points to products built for exactly this:
A secured credit card. Your deposit becomes your limit.
A credit-builder loan, like the Credit Matters Loan above. The lender holds the money while you pay it off, the payments land on your credit report, and then the money is yours. In a CFPB study, people with no existing loans who opened one were 24% more likely to have a credit score.
Rent. On-time rent can help, the CFPB says, if your landlord uses a rental reporting program.
Ask at credit unions especially, since federal credit unions also carry that 18% ceiling. Our guide on how to join a credit union in St. Louis explains why you probably already qualify.
Keep the balance small next to the limit. Experts advise using no more than 30 percent of your total limit, per the CFPB, which on a $500 card is $150. Autopay for at least the minimum is cheap insurance against a late mark, and only as good as the checking account behind it, so if you’re moving accounts, here’s how to switch banks in St. Louis without missing a bill.
Now the trap with a Missouri address. Payday loans don’t build credit: even paid on time, those payments aren’t reported to the nationwide credit reporting companies, the CFPB says. Missouri allows renewals, with total interest and fees capped at 75% of the original loan. On $300, that cap still allows $225. On a card at 24%, $300 carried for a month costs about $6. That’s the real reason to build credit before you need it.
Check the report your score is built from. The three national credit bureaus let you see it once a week for free at AnnualCreditReport.com. See an account you never opened? Here’s how to freeze your credit and handle identity theft in Missouri. And skip the fix-it-fast crowd. The FTC says it’s illegal for credit repair companies to charge you before they help you.
Ready to open a secured card or a credit-builder loan? Compare banks and credit unions around St. Louis and ask each one whether it reports to all three credit bureaus, what the APR is and which fees come with it.
If you’re the credit union, the community bank or the financial coach who helps people build credit from scratch, see who AI names instead of you and get more customers from the St. Louis neighbors asking that question right now.
### Is buying now, pay later a bad idea?
Not by itself, but it’s easy to stack. Buy now, pay later, or BNPL, usually splits a purchase into four or fewer payments, often interest-free, and most lenders charge late fees when you miss one. Your payment history may not be reported to the credit bureaus, so it usually won’t build credit the way a card paid in full does.
The trouble is what nobody can see. In a CFPB study of BNPL borrowers, a large share had more than one of these loans going at once. Say four plans run at the same time, each pulling from the same checking account on its own schedule. That’s sixteen due dates, and not one is on your card statement.
The rules are thinner, too. The CFPB once said BNPL lenders owed shoppers some of the same protections as card companies, then withdrew that rule. Read the lender’s returns and disputes policy before you click.
This is general information about how credit cards and credit scores work, not advice for your situation. A nonprofit credit counselor, a licensed financial advisor or the loan officer at your bank or credit union can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis financial services directory is a place to start.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to pay a credit card in full or monthly?
A.  In full, every month, if you can. Paying the whole statement balance by the due date keeps your grace period, so purchases cost zero interest, and the CFPB says paying in full helps get you the best scores. Paying part of it still counts as on time, but the leftover charges interest daily.
### Q. What is a good APR for a credit card?
A.  Anything below average is a fair start. The Federal Reserve’s G.19 release put the average at 22.36% for bank card accounts assessed interest in August 2026. Federal credit unions are held to 18% under the NCUA’s current ceiling. Pay in full monthly and you never pay it.
### Q. Do I pay APR if I pay on time?
A.  Yes, if on time means only the minimum. No, if it means the full statement balance by the due date, which keeps purchases interest-free. The minimum avoids a late fee, but the rest of the balance keeps charging interest every day.
### Q. How long do you have to pay a credit card off?
A.  There’s no fixed deadline as long as you pay at least the minimum each month. To avoid interest, pay the full statement balance by the due date; card companies have to mail or deliver the bill at least 21 days before it’s due. Minimums alone on $3,000 at 24% take about 15 years in our example.
### Q. What is a balance transfer?
A.  Moving debt from one card to another, usually for a low or 0% promotional rate. Most cards charge a fee to do it, and some charge 3 to 5 percent of the amount moved. The promo rate ends on a set date, so plan to clear the balance before it does.
### Q. Is getting a secured credit card a good idea?
A.  It can be, if you can’t get approved for a regular card. Your deposit becomes your limit, and on-time payments build a record if the card reports to the credit bureaus. Compare a few before you put money down.
### Q. Does paying utilities build credit?
A.  Usually not. Most utility companies don’t report your payment history to the big credit bureaus, but a bill sent to a collection agency will most likely show up on your credit reports. Rent can count if your landlord uses a reporting program.
### Q. Does carrying a balance help your credit score?
A.  No. The CFPB says you don’t need to carry a balance to get a good score, and you don’t need any outstanding debt at all. Using the card and paying the statement balance in full each month builds the same on-time history, keeps your utilization low and costs you zero interest.

## How to Freeze Your Credit for Free: Ten Minutes, Three Bureaus, and a Missouri Identity Theft Plan
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-freeze-your-credit-and-handle-identity-theft-missouri
Thieves are counting on you putting this off. Ten minutes, three websites, zero dollars, and the thing they do most often with a stolen name and Social Security number stops working: they can’t open new credit in your name. Not a card. Not a car loan. The lender pulls your file, hits a wall, and the application dies.
This isn’t a someday problem. Missourians filed 11,535 identity theft reports with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024, per the FTC’s Consumer Sentinel Data Book, and credit card fraud showed up in 32 percent of them, more than loans, bank accounts or phone accounts. Nationally, the biggest subtype the FTC counted was new credit cards opened in somebody else’s name: 406,110 reports. Across the river, Illinois ranked ninth among the states for identity theft reports per person; Missouri ranked 28th. A credit freeze stops that exact crime, and federal law has made it free since September 21, 2018.
Nobody teaches this in school, and the free option sits on the same pages as paid products with similar names. Here’s the freeze, what it leaves open (including a Missouri tax form almost nobody files), your kids’ credit, and the first-hour order if somebody already got in. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide.
### Can I freeze my credit report?
Yes. Anyone can freeze their credit report at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, for free, for any reason, without waiting for a breach. Request it online or by phone and each bureau must place it within one business day; ask to lift it and the bureau must do that within one hour. You contact all three separately.
A freeze, also called a security freeze, shuts the door lenders use to check your file before opening a new account. That includes your own applications. The FTC’s recovery site, IdentityTheft.gov, puts it simply: a freeze limits access to your credit report until you lift or remove it, and it lasts until you do. No renewal date. No monthly charge.
The deadlines make it livable. Per the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a freeze requested online or by phone has to be in place within one business day, and a lift requested the same way has to happen within one hour. Mail is the slow lane: three business days either direction. You can also lift a freeze for a window of dates you pick, at no cost.
The catch nobody mentions until you’re at a car dealership: you have to remember it’s on. The FTC’s list of times to lift it covers applying for credit or a job, renting an apartment, and buying insurance. Lift first, then apply, or the lender sees a wall and treats it like a problem with you.
### What does each credit bureau ask for when you freeze?
A free account and proof that you’re you. Set aside about ten minutes for all three, and do them back to back, because a freeze at one bureau does nothing at the other two. Experian says so directly: its freeze isn’t shared with Equifax or TransUnion.
Equifax: a myEquifax account (you have to be 18). By phone, (888) 298-0045, you verify with a one-time PIN by text or questions drawn from your own Equifax file.
Experian: a free Experian account, no PIN needed anymore, and online changes happen in real time. Phone: 1-888-397-3742. By mail it wants your full name, Social Security number, addresses for the past two years, date of birth, a copy of a government ID, and a utility bill or bank statement.
TransUnion: a TransUnion Service Center account. Phone: 800-916-8800. By mail, your name, address and Social Security number, and it says one proof of identity plus two proofs of address help it find your file.
Two traps. First, the upsell: the bureaus also sell monitoring and lock products, and the freeze costs nothing, so a page asking for a card number is the wrong page. Second, the login. Write down all three the same day and keep them with your car title. The day you need a lift is usually the day you’re sitting across from a loan officer.
### What’s the difference between a credit freeze, a credit lock and a fraud alert?
A freeze blocks most access to your file for new credit, is free by federal law, and stays until you lift it. A lock does a similar job as a product run on the bureau’s terms, often inside a paid membership. A fraud alert blocks nothing. It tells lenders to confirm it’s really you before they open anything.
The law is the difference that matters. A freeze carries the one-day and one-hour deadlines in federal law; a lock’s rules are whatever the product terms say. The CFPB is blunt: credit locks are paid products, often bundled with other paid services, and no more effective than a freeze, which is free and which you have a right to by law.
Alerts and freezes stack. The FTC says you can add an alert on top of a freeze, and an initial alert comes with a free copy of your report from each bureau. Either way, read your reports. All three are free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, a program the bureaus have made permanent.
None of this touches your score. The CFPB says security freezes do not affect your credit scores in any way, and the accounts you already have keep reporting the whole time. Our guide to how credit cards and credit scores work covers that side.
### What can a thief still do after your credit is frozen?
Plenty, just not new credit. A freeze does nothing about cards you already have, checking accounts screened through a separate bank file, tax refunds, medical care billed to your insurance, or a job worked under your Social Security number. Each has its own lock.
Existing accounts. A card number copied at a gas pump is still a working card number. The CFPB notes that your current creditors can still see a frozen file, and a charge on a card you already have never asks the bureaus anything. Your defense is your bank’s transaction alerts and reading statements. Fraudulent debits can also set off overdraft charges, so know how to get bank fees waived before you call.
New bank accounts. The gap most people never hear about. Opening a checking account can run through a different file: ChexSystems, a specialty agency that, in the FTC’s words, compiles information about your checking accounts. The FTC logged 62,982 reports of bank accounts opened in someone else’s name in 2024. ChexSystems runs its own security freeze, which it says is designed to keep checking, savings and other accounts from being approved without your consent. Place it through its consumer portal or at 800-887-7652, keep the PIN it issues, and if you plan to switch banks soon, lift it before you apply.
Medical care. Someone uses your name, insurance number or Medicare number to see a doctor, fill prescriptions or file claims. No lender is involved, so the freeze never fires. The FTC’s warning signs: an Explanation of Benefits for a visit you never made, a collector calling about medical debt you don’t owe, or a notice that you’ve hit a benefit limit. Report errors to the provider in writing; the FTC says it must respond within 30 days.
A job under your number. Someone working on your Social Security number can have wages reported in your name to the IRS and the SSA. E-Verify’s Self Lock, for myE-Verify account holders, makes an employer’s E-Verify check on your locked number come back as a mismatch until you unlock it for a new job. It only reaches employers that use E-Verify, so also scan the earnings history in a my Social Security account for jobs you never held.
### Does a credit freeze protect your tax refund in Missouri?
No. A fake tax return goes to the IRS and the Missouri Department of Revenue, not to a lender, so a freeze never sees it. The federal lock is an IRS Identity Protection PIN. The Missouri lock is a one-page form most people have never heard of, Form 5593, and you don’t have to wait for trouble to send it.
An IP PIN is a six-digit number that stops anyone else from filing a federal return with your Social Security number or ITIN. Anyone with one of those numbers who can verify their identity can get one, and parents can request them for dependents. The fastest route is your IRS online account; anyone under 18 uses one of the other enrollment options. A new PIN comes every calendar year, and the IRS says it will never ask for yours. A call, email or text asking for it is a scam.
Your Missouri return is a separate target, and the IP PIN doesn’t cover it. The Department of Revenue’s Form 5593, the Identity Theft Declaration, asks the department to mark your account so it can spot questionable activity. One box is for people whose Missouri tax records are already affected. The other covers an event that might affect them later, and the form names the examples: a lost or stolen wallet or purse, questionable credit card activity, odd entries on a credit report. Send it with a copy of your driver’s license, passport, military ID or other government ID, plus any police report, to idtheft@dor.mo.gov.
The department says it has stopped more than $157 million in fraudulent refunds since 2021. Two of its screens are worth knowing. You can add your driver’s license information when you e-file, as an extra identifier. And it mails paper checks to some filers who asked for direct deposit, so a refund can’t land in an account a criminal controls. A Missouri refund that shows up as a check you didn’t expect may be that screen doing its job.
If a return was already filed in your name, the federal side runs through IRS Form 14039, the Identity Theft Affidavit, and the IRS Identity Protection Specialized Unit at 1-800-908-4490. The FTC took 54,725 tax fraud reports nationally in 2024.
Thieves hate paperwork. Here’s how to file a St. Louis police report.
### Should you freeze your child’s credit too?
Yes, and it’s free. Parents and guardians can freeze credit for children under 16 at each bureau. If the child has no file, the bureau creates one just to freeze it, and the CFPB says that protected record can’t be used for credit. Kids generally don’t have credit reports unless someone is using their information, the FTC says, so a problem can sit unnoticed until a first car loan or apartment application turns it up.
The catch is paperwork. Equifax uses a Minor Freeze Request form, Experian takes minors’ requests by mail, and TransUnion says it can’t place a protected consumer freeze online or by phone at all. Send copies, never originals, of proof that you can act for the child and proof of identity for both of you. One envelope per bureau. One afternoon.
The freeze stays until someone removes it, and TransUnion lets a minor request removal on their own at 16. ChexSystems also takes a parent’s freeze request for a minor by mail, with the birth certificate and the child’s Social Security card. Worried it already happened? TransUnion’s Child Identity Theft Inquiry Form checks for a file without creating one. If something turns up, tell the company your child is a minor who can’t enter into a legal contract, and ask for a letter confirming your child isn’t liable.
### What is the first thing to do when your identity is stolen?
Call the fraud department at the company where the fraud happened, ask them to close or freeze the account, and change that login, password and PIN. That’s step one on the FTC’s checklist. The rest of the first hour is a free fraud alert, your credit reports, an FTC report, and the freeze.
Call the company, using the number on the back of the card or a statement, never one from a text that just arrived. Close or freeze the account and change your logins.
Place a free fraud alert with any one bureau, which must tell the other two. It lasts a year and can be renewed.
Pull your reports at AnnualCreditReport.com or 1-877-322-8228 and mark every account or inquiry you don’t recognize.
Report it at IdentityTheft.gov or 1-877-438-4338 to get an FTC Identity Theft Report and a recovery plan. Without an account, save both before you leave the page, or they’re gone.
Freeze all three bureaus, plus ChexSystems if a bank account was involved.
File a police report when it helps. The FTC says most victims can use the FTC report instead, but go to police if you know the thief, if the thief used your name in a traffic stop or other police encounter, or if a creditor or collector insists. Our St. Louis police report guide sorts out which department takes it.
Then the cleanup, which runs on paper. Write to each bureau with your FTC report and proof of identity and ask it to block the fraudulent items. With an FTC Identity Theft Report, the bureaus must honor that, and once a debt is blocked, companies can’t try to collect it from you. Ask each business for a letter confirming the fake account isn’t yours, you aren’t liable, and it’s off your report. Upgrade to the seven-year extended alert. Log every call: who, when, what they promised.
If a collector calls about a fake account, write to it within 30 days of getting its collection letter, say the debt came from identity theft, and include your FTC report. Our guide to debt collectors in Missouri covers your rights when the call is about a debt that isn’t yours.
### Who helps identity theft victims in Missouri?
Start with the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection hotline, 800-392-8222. The office says its staff help advise identity theft victims, and its identity theft page carries a complaint form for the AG and an Identity Theft Incident Report you file with local police. It recommends filing with the county, state and federal agencies so a record exists at each level.
The rest of the Missouri map is short. State tax trouble goes to the Department of Revenue through Form 5593. A driver’s license issued to someone else is a DOR matter too: the AG’s office says to get your driving record from the DOR, correct the errors, report the bad record to local police, and apply for a replacement. Social Security number misuse goes to the Social Security Administration at 1-800-269-0271.
None of this means you did something wrong. Breaches, skimmers and phishing texts catch careful people every day. What thieves count on is the gap between the moment your information leaks and the moment you lock the doors. You can close that gap tonight, in about the time it takes to make dinner.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A consumer protection attorney can apply it to a dispute that stalls, a CPA or enrolled agent can handle the tax side, and our St. Louis financial services directory is a place to start.
Starting over with a clean account after fraud? Compare banks and credit unions around St. Louis, and ask each two questions before you open anything: which screening file it checks for new accounts, and whether it can text you on every card transaction.
And if you run a bank, credit union or identity-protection practice, the neighbor reading this at midnight is about to ask somebody, or some AI, who to trust next, and being the name it gives first is the whole game, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Will freezing my credit affect my score?
A.  No. The CFPB says security freezes do not affect your credit scores in any way. Your score is built from the accounts you already have, and those keep reporting while the freeze is on. You can still pull your own reports for free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com to watch for anything new.
### Q. Can someone steal your identity if your credit is frozen?
A.  Yes, just not the most common way. A freeze stops new credit accounts, and new credit cards were the most-reported subtype in the FTC’s 2024 identity theft data. It doesn’t stop charges on cards you already have, tax refund fraud, medical identity theft, someone working under your Social Security number, or bank accounts approved through ChexSystems.
### Q. How do I unfreeze my credit instantly?
A.  Log in to the bureau online or call it. Federal rules give a bureau one hour to lift a freeze requested online or by phone. Experian says online changes happen in real time, and TransUnion says a temporary lift can be immediate and can be scheduled up to 15 days ahead. A mailed request can take three business days.
### Q. Do I need to call all three credit bureaus to unfreeze my credit?
A.  No. The FTC suggests asking the lender which bureau it uses, lifting the freeze at that one, and putting it back once the credit check is done. Each bureau’s freeze is separate, so the other two stay frozen the whole time. If a lender checks more than one bureau, lift each one it names.
### Q. Can I freeze my credit without paying?
A.  Yes. Since September 21, 2018, federal law has made it free to place, lift and remove a freeze at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, including for children under 16. If a sign-up page asks for a card number, you’re looking at a paid product such as a lock or monitoring plan, not the freeze.
### Q. Can someone open a bank account if my credit is frozen?
A.  Possibly. Checking and savings accounts can be approved through ChexSystems, a separate specialty file the three-bureau freeze doesn’t touch. ChexSystems offers its own security freeze through its consumer portal or at 800-887-7652. If you suspect a bank account in your name, the FTC says to order your free ChexSystems report and contact each bank involved.
### Q. How can I find out if my SSN is being used by someone else?
A.  Check four places. Your credit reports, free weekly at AnnualCreditReport.com, for accounts you don’t recognize. The earnings history in a my Social Security account, for wages from jobs you never held. Any IRS notice about a return you didn’t file. And your ChexSystems report, for checking accounts opened in your name.
### Q. Can you get a new Social Security number if someone steals your identity?
A.  Rarely. The Social Security Administration says to start by reporting the number stolen. If you’ve tried to fix the misuse and are still affected, call 800-772-1213 for an appointment and bring proof of the ongoing problems plus proof of identity, age and citizenship or immigration status. The FTC warns a new number won’t fix everything, since records still link you to the old one.

## Why It's Easier to Buy a Car Than a House: Credit Scores, Debt-to-Income and the Down Payment Wall
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-its-easier-to-buy-a-car-than-a-house
Why does $40,000 take one Saturday afternoon, and a house take a month? You sit in a dealership’s finance office, sign a few screens, and drive home on a loan bigger than a lot of people’s yearly pay. Try that with a brick bungalow in Bevo Mill and the lender wants proof of your income, savings, job and debts, usually an appraisal, and then a few more days before you’re even allowed to sign.
It can feel like the mortgage people just don’t trust you. They don’t trust anybody, and federal law tells them not to. Nobody covered this in school: the car and the house run on two different rulebooks. One is built for speed. The other makes a lender show you can pay before you get the keys.
Here’s the part that actually costs St. Louis buyers money. The fast loan makes the slow loan harder. A car payment lands right inside the ratio a mortgage lender uses to decide how much house you get, and around here the price tag usually isn’t the wall. The median listing price in the St. Louis metro was $285,950 in September 2026, against $419,250 nationally, roughly a third less. When the houses cost less, the monthly math becomes the thing that says no.
Below: why the two loans feel so different, how the debt-to-income ratio works with real numbers, what a good credit score means for each, and what FHA and conventional loans ask for, every figure checked against the agency that publishes it. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide.
### Is buying a house easier than buying a car?
No. Buying a car is easier, on purpose. A car loan is backed by a vehicle the lender can repossess and resell, and the dealer can shop it to several lenders while you wait. A mortgage falls under the federal ability-to-repay rule, so the lender has to document your income, assets, job, credit history and monthly expenses first.
Start with what backs each loan. Stop paying on a car and the lender can take it back, and a car is easy to move and resell. That’s why the yes comes so fast. Once you agree to buy, the dealer’s finance office forwards your information, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says most dealers reach out to roughly five lenders, then pick one loan to show you. The rate a lender quotes the dealer is the buy rate. Yours can be higher, and the difference pays the dealer for arranging it.
Missouri adds one speed bump in front of the tow truck. On a dealer installment contract or a consumer car loan, state law generally bars repossession over a missed payment until 20 days after the lender sends written notice of your right to catch up, under RSMo 408.555. Twenty days isn’t long. A lender holding your title can afford to ask fewer questions.
A mortgage plays by a different rulebook. Since January 10, 2014, the federal ability-to-repay rule has barred most lenders from making a home loan without a reasonable, good-faith determination that you can pay it back, and they have to find out, consider and document your income, assets, employment, credit history and monthly expenses. The CFPB’s summary of the rule traces it to the mortgage crisis, when too many loans ignored whether people could repay. It covers credit secured by a home, so car loans sit outside it.
Then there’s the clock. A mortgage lender owes you a Loan Estimate within three business days of your application, and a Closing Disclosure at least three business days before you close. In between: usually an appraisal, title work, and an underwriter reading your pay stubs and bank statements. Nobody’s stalling you. That’s the design.
### What does the fast car loan leave out?
Mostly, the price of speed. The Federal Reserve’s G.19 consumer credit release tracks what new-car loans cost. In August 2026, commercial banks averaged 7.54% on a 60-month new-car loan and 7.17% on a 72-month one. Finance companies averaged 6.3% in the second quarter, on an average of $41,705 financed over 67 months. National averages, not your quote.
Sixty-seven months. That’s five and a half years of a payment sitting on your credit report, which matters more than it sounds once you reach the house math below. The rate is negotiable, too, the CFPB says, and our comparison of credit union and bank auto loans in St. Louis shows what the spread costs in dollars.
Then there’s the Missouri surprise: titling the car and paying the sales tax is on you, at a license office, not at the dealership. The Department of Revenue charges the 4.225% state rate plus your local rate on the price after any trade-in, due within 30 days of purchase, with a $25 penalty on day 31 that grows to as much as $200. Our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis dealership walks through that bill.
And the biggest thing the Saturday deal leaves out? The loan you haven’t applied for yet.
### How can a car payment cost you a house?
By eating the room a mortgage lender would have given the house. Lenders take your gross monthly income, set a ceiling on how much of it can go to debt payments, subtract what you already owe each month, and whatever’s left is the most your house payment can be. Every dollar of car payment comes straight out of that leftover.
Picture a buyer who earns $72,000 a year, or $6,000 a month before taxes, paying $250 on a student loan and a $50 card minimum. Three months before house hunting, they buy a $40,000 car on a 72-month loan at the Fed’s 7.17% bank average. The payment comes to about $685. Here’s the room left for a house payment at two common ceilings, both explained below:
That’s $685 a month of house payment, gone. Freddie Mac’s weekly survey had the average 30-year fixed rate at 7.40% on October 8, 2026, and at that rate $685 a month covers the principal and interest on about $98,900 of mortgage. Taxes and insurance would claim part of that room, so the real drop in price range is smaller. It’s still well past the $40,000 the car cost.
Now look at it the way an underwriter does. Say the house this buyer wants comes with a $2,000 monthly payment, taxes and insurance included. Before the car, their total debt-to-income ratio is 38.3%. After it, 49.8%. That squeaks under the 50% Fannie Mae allows through its automated system, sits well over the 43% FHA uses as its baseline for a manually reviewed loan, and one small surprise, a bigger tax bill or a quarter-point rate move, tips it over.
The car isn’t a bad car. The order is the problem, and nobody in the finance office has a reason to bring it up.
### What is a debt-to-income ratio, and what counts in it?
Your debt-to-income ratio, or DTI, is all your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income, meaning pay before taxes and other deductions. That’s the CFPB’s definition, and its example is clean: $1,500 for a mortgage, $100 for a car loan and $400 for everything else, against $6,000 of monthly income. $2,000 divided by $6,000 is 33%.
Lenders read it two ways. The front-end ratio is just the housing payment divided by income. The back-end ratio, the one that usually decides things, adds every other debt. Fannie Mae’s rules on monthly debts spell out what lands in the back end:
Car, student and personal loans with more than ten monthly payments left. One with fewer can still count if it would seriously strain your budget.
Car leases, no matter how few months remain, because a lease usually ends in another lease or a purchase.
Credit cards and other revolving accounts.
Court-ordered alimony and child support that will run more than ten more months.
A loan you co-signed for someone else, unless the lender can document 12 months of on-time payments by the other person.
Groceries, utilities and your phone bill aren’t in it. That’s why DTI can say yes to a budget that feels tight in real life.
So what’s a good DTI? It depends on the loan, and the limits are published. Fannie Mae’s Selling Guide caps a manually underwritten conventional loan at 36% of stable monthly income, stretchable to 45% with the credit score and reserves its eligibility matrix requires, and allows up to 50% through its automated system, Desktop Underwriter. FHA’s Single Family Housing Policy Handbook starts a manually underwritten loan at 31% for housing and 43% overall, with room to go higher at a 580 score or above plus compensating factors like cash reserves.
The 28/36 rule says keep housing under 28% of gross income and all debt under 36%. It’s a rule of thumb, not a law, though the 36 has a real twin in Fannie Mae’s manual baseline. On $6,000 a month, that’s a house payment around $1,680 and total debts around $2,160. And 43%? That used to be the federal line for a standard qualified mortgage. For applications taken on or after October 1, 2022, the CFPB’s general qualified mortgage test is based on the loan’s price instead, though lenders still have to consider your DTI or residual income.
House on hold another year? Rent smarter in St. Louis meanwhile.
### What is a good credit score for a car loan versus a mortgage?
Most credit scores run from 300 to 850, per the CFPB. On FICO’s base scale, 670 to 739 is rated good, 740 to 799 very good, and 800 or above exceptional. Below 580 is poor, and 580 to 669 is fair. Payment history carries the most weight at 35%, followed by how much you owe at 30%, length of credit history at 15%, and new credit and credit mix at 10% each.
Here’s what almost nobody tells you: the dealer and the mortgage lender may not be looking at the same number. FICO’s guide to its score versions says most auto financing decisions use industry-specific FICO Auto Scores, which run from 250 to 900, while mortgage lenders typically use older FICO versions, one from each of the three credit bureaus. Fannie Mae requires lenders to request a score from all three, and FHA uses the middle score when three are reported and the lower one when there are two. A strong number at the dealership doesn’t promise the same number on a mortgage application. Neither one is wrong.
The car loan moves your mortgage score, too: a new account and a hard inquiry land in the new-credit slice, a big balance in the how-much-you-owe slice. Still building a file? Start with our guide to credit card interest and building credit.
Is 700 good, then? Yes, by FICO’s labels. For a mortgage, a higher score mostly buys you price. Fannie Mae assesses loan-level price adjustments based on credit score, and those show up in your rate or your closing costs.
### What do FHA and conventional loans actually ask for?
Less than most people assume on credit, and more than most people assume in cash. The FHA rule is short. Under HUD’s Handbook 4000.1, a minimum decision credit score of 580 or higher makes you eligible for maximum financing, which on a purchase is 96.5%, so the minimum down payment is 3.5%. A score from 500 to 579 caps the loan at 90%, which means 10% down. FHA also charges an upfront mortgage insurance premium of 1.75% of the base loan, which can be rolled into the mortgage, plus an annual premium paid monthly.
Conventional loans that Fannie Mae buys work differently. Its credit score rules set a 620 minimum for manually underwritten fixed-rate loans and 640 for adjustable-rate ones. For loans run through Desktop Underwriter, Fannie Mae sets no minimum score at all; the system weighs the whole credit report. That doesn’t mean a 560 sails through. It means the score isn’t the only gate.
Run it on a $300,000 house, close to what plenty of St. Louis listings ask. FHA’s 3.5% minimum is $10,500 down. At a score from 500 to 579, the 10% rule makes it $30,000. The upfront insurance on a $289,500 base loan adds about $5,066, usually financed. Then come closing costs, itemized on your Loan Estimate.
That cash is where the help is. Our rundown of down payment assistance programs St. Louis buyers can use covers both sides of the river, and the first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis lays out the whole process. For a neutral look at your numbers, HUD points buyers to approved housing counselors at (800) 569-4287.
### Why can’t so many Americans afford housing anymore?
Nationally, it’s price and rate hitting at once. The national median listing price was $419,250 in September 2026, and Freddie Mac’s average 30-year rate climbed from 6.65% on August 20 to 7.40% by October 8. On a $250,000 loan, that seven-week move adds about $126 a month in principal and interest, from roughly $1,605 to $1,731.
St. Louis gets a different version of the problem. With a median listing of $285,950, about $133,000 below the national figure, plenty of households here can afford the house on paper. What stops them is the stack of monthly payments already on their credit report, and DTI counts every one. A car. A boat. A camper you use twice a summer. Before that last one, read whether an RV or boat is a bad investment, because it lands in the same ratio.
The hopeful part: monthly debt is the one wall you can actually move. Prices and rates aren’t yours to set. Which payments you add, and when, mostly is.
### If you want both, which loan comes first?
For DTI purposes, usually the house, because a mortgage is underwritten on the debts you carry when you apply. A preapproval reflects your debts on the day it was issued, too. Sign for a car after it and you’ve changed the math the lender approved, sometimes days before closing.
Two of the rules above make the order matter even more. A car loan with ten or fewer payments left may drop out of Fannie Mae’s DTI math, while a lease never does. And a longer term lowers the payment DTI sees but stretches the debt for years, on top of a finance-company average that’s already 67 months.
None of this means skipping the car. Sometimes the old one is dying, and that’s that. It means pricing the car with the house in mind. A mortgage lender can run your numbers both ways before you sign at a dealership, and our guide to choosing a mortgage lender in St. Louis covers what to ask.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A loan officer or a HUD-approved housing counselor can apply it to your actual income, debts and credit, and our St. Louis financial services directory is a place to start.
Want to see what a car payment would do to your house budget before a dealer does the math for you? Ask one of the mortgage lenders around St. Louis for a preapproval run both ways, with the car payment and without it.
And if you’re the lender, broker or car dealer who explains it straight, the buyer who just read this needs you, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a good debt-to-income ratio?
A.  Lower is better, and the hard limits depend on the loan. Fannie Mae caps manually underwritten conventional loans at 36%, stretchable to 45% with strong credit and reserves, and allows up to 50% through its automated system. FHA’s manual baseline is 31% for housing and 43% overall. Staying near 36% leaves room for what DTI ignores, like groceries and utilities.
### Q. Is 43 DTI too high?
A.  Not automatically. 43% is FHA’s baseline limit for a manually underwritten loan, and Fannie Mae’s automated system can approve up to 50%. It was also the old federal line for a standard qualified mortgage, replaced by a price-based test for applications from October 1, 2022. At 43%, though, one new payment like a car loan can push you past what some loans allow.
### Q. What is the 28/36 rule?
A.  It’s a budgeting rule of thumb: spend no more than 28% of gross monthly income on housing, and no more than 36% on all debt payments combined, housing included. On $6,000 a month, that’s about $1,680 for the house payment and $2,160 in total. It isn’t a law, but the 36 matches Fannie Mae’s baseline limit for manually underwritten loans.
### Q. Is 700 on your credit score good?
A.  Yes. On FICO’s base 300 to 850 scale, 670 to 739 is rated good, 740 to 799 very good and 800 and up exceptional. A 700 clears FHA’s 580 mark for a 3.5% down payment and Fannie Mae’s 620 floor for manually underwritten fixed-rate loans. Above that, a higher score mainly buys a better price.
### Q. Are mortgages harder to get now than in the past?
A.  Harder to get without paperwork, yes. Since January 10, 2014, the federal ability-to-repay rule has required most lenders to document your income, assets, employment, credit history and monthly expenses and make a good-faith judgment that you can repay. The score floors aren’t sky-high, though. FHA starts at 500 with 10% down, and Fannie Mae sets no minimum score for loans run through its automated system.
### Q. What credit score is needed to buy a $300,000 house?
A.  The price doesn’t set the score; the loan program does. FHA accepts 580 and up with 3.5% down, which is $10,500 on $300,000, and 500 to 579 with 10% down, or $30,000. Fannie Mae requires 620 for a manually underwritten fixed-rate loan and sets no minimum in its automated system. Your income and debts decide whether the payment on $300,000 fits.
### Q. Should I buy a $40,000 car if I make $60,000 a year?
A.  That’s your call, but here’s the math a lender sees. $60,000 is $5,000 a month before taxes. A $40,000 loan at the Fed’s 7.17% average for 72 months runs about $685 a month, nearly 14% of gross income before rent or any other debt. If a house is a few years out, that payment counts in your DTI while more than ten payments remain.
### Q. What is the average car loan interest rate?
A.  On new cars, the Federal Reserve’s G.19 release showed commercial banks averaging 7.54% on 60-month loans and 7.17% on 72-month loans in August 2026. Finance companies averaged 6.3% in the second quarter, on an average $41,705 financed over 67 months. That release doesn’t include a used-car average. Your own rate depends on your credit, the term and the lender.

## Is an RV or Boat a Bad Investment? Why Paid Off Still Costs You in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-an-rv-or-boat-a-bad-investment
Paid off isn’t free. Picture a bass boat on a trailer beside a garage in north county. The loan ended two summers ago, the title sits clean in a kitchen drawer, and the owner figures it’s the one thing in the driveway he’s done paying for. Then a tax bill for it comes due by December 31, same as last year, whether the boat went out twenty times or never left the slab.
That bill is Missouri personal property tax, the part of owning a boat, an RV or a motorcycle that rarely comes up at the dealership. The assessor takes a snapshot of what you own on January 1. Own the boat that morning and you owe for the whole year, even if you sell it on January 2, because Missouri has no provision for prorating it. Then, when the boat’s registration comes up for renewal, the state wants last year’s paid tax receipt in your hand.
None of that makes toys a mistake, and if nobody ever told you about the January 1 rule, that’s on the system, not you. It’s a cost you can plan for once you see the whole bill. Below: good debt versus bad, net worth with a worked example, what a paid-off toy costs here every year, boat insurance, and how people keep their campers and boats without bleeding money. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the stuff school skipped.
### What is the difference between good debt and bad debt?
Good debt buys something that grows in value or raises your income, like a home or training that leads to a better job. Bad debt buys something that shrinks or gets used up, like a new boat, an RV or a vacation. Even good debt turns bad when the loan outlasts the thing it paid for.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is more careful, and it’s right. Its Your Money, Your Goals toolkit notes that people often call borrowing for school, a reliable car or a home a good use of debt, then warns that the payoff isn’t guaranteed and that no type of debt is good or bad for everyone. A degree you never finish is a bad loan. So is a house you can’t keep up with. The label depends on what the money buys and whether you can carry it.
Then the toolkit makes the point that matters most for toys. If a car loan runs longer than the car’s remaining life, you can still owe money on the old one when it’s time to borrow for the next one. Swap the car for a boat and you have the whole problem, because toy loans can run very long. One large bank’s published boat and RV loan terms go up to 240 months. That’s 20 years of payments on something built for weekends.
Meanwhile, the thing shrinks. J.D. Power, which now publishes the old NADA boat values, puts typical used-boat depreciation at 10% to 20% after one year, 20% to 30% after five years and 30% to 40% after ten, in its guide to what a boat is worth. It adds that fishing boats and pontoons tend to lose value faster than leisure boats. Its camper depreciation guide estimates a new RV loses about 20% of its value just by driving off the lot, and puts a fifth-wheel down 45% after five years.
So a toy loan is usually bad debt twice over. You pay interest on the purchase, and the purchase loses value while you pay. A house can lose value too, but a boat almost always will. Lenders treat the two kinds of borrowing very differently, as our guide on why it’s easier to buy a car than a house explains.
### What is net worth, and where does a boat show up in it?
Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. The Federal Reserve uses exactly that definition, the difference between a family’s assets and its debts, in its Survey of Consumer Finances, and it counts motor homes, RVs, motorcycles and boats as assets, right next to the family car. Your boat counts. So does its loan.
Here’s a worked example. Picture a hypothetical household that bought a $40,000 boat, motor and trailer package five years ago and financed all of it over 20 years at a round 8%. Each value below is what the thing would sell for today, and each debt is what it would take to pay it off today.
Their net worth is $359,000 minus $224,000, or $135,000. Now read it one line at a time, because the total hides the story. The house line is positive: worth $240,000, owing $170,000, so $70,000 of equity. The boat line runs backward. It would sell for $30,000 and they owe $35,000, so the boat is subtracting $5,000 from their net worth while it sits in the driveway looking like an asset. Lenders call that being underwater.
And the payments don’t fix it quickly. At 8% over 20 years, a $40,000 loan runs about $335 a month and about $80,300 in total, so roughly $40,300 of that is interest. At year ten they’d still owe about $27,600 on a boat that J.D. Power’s ranges would put somewhere around $24,000 to $28,000. A decade in, still roughly underwater.
For context, the Federal Reserve’s 2025 survey put the median family’s net worth at $215,900, according to its release of the results. Median means half of families had more and half had less. Don’t grade yourself against it; age and income swing it hard. The useful number is your own, measured on the same day every year. January 1 works, since it’s the day Missouri’s assessors take their snapshot of your boat.
### Why does a paid-off boat still send you a tax bill every year?
Because in Missouri, boats, RVs, motorcycles and trailers are taxable personal property, and the tax comes every year you own them, loan or no loan. The State Tax Commission’s property tax FAQ lists vehicles, boats, motors and trailers among what you report, assesses cars and boats at one-third of market value, and fixes value, ownership and taxability on January 1.
Here’s the math, using the City of St. Louis as the example. The assessor values your property, takes one-third of that as the assessed value, then applies the local tax rate. The City’s 2025 rate sheet lists $8.1122 per $100 of assessed value for personal property. So if the assessor values your boat, motor and trailer at $30,000 together:
Assessed value: one-third of $30,000, or $10,000.
Tax: $10,000 at $8.1122 per $100, or $811.22 for the year.
A travel trailer valued at $24,000 comes to about $649 at the same rate. St. Louis County rates depend on the taxing districts where you live, so your own bill is the real number, and our guide to St. Louis County personal property tax walks through how the county figures yours.
Three details turn this from annoying into expensive when nobody tells you:
January 1 decides the whole year. The State Tax Commission says Missouri has no provision for prorating personal property tax, so an RV you own on January 1 and sell in February still costs you the full year.
A boat can be three taxable items. The St. Louis County assessor lists watercraft, boat motors and trailers as taxable personal property, and Missouri titles an outboard motor separately from the hull.
You can’t skip the bill and keep boating. The Department of Revenue requires last year’s paid personal property tax receipt, or a statement of non-assessment, to register or renew a boat, according to its boat and outboard motor page. Plate renewals for motorcycles and motorhomes work the same way under its license plate renewal rules.
The paperwork runs on its own calendar. The City assessor wants your declaration, the list of what you owned on January 1, by April 1, with a 10% penalty for filing late. St. Louis County’s deadline is March 1. The City’s collector mails personal property bills in November, they’re due by December 31, and a balance still open on January 1 picks up penalty and interest.
### What else does a toy cost after the loan is gone?
Plenty, and most of it shows up whether you use the thing or not. The honest list for a paid-off boat, with the Missouri figures we could verify:
Personal property tax: about $811 a year in the City on that $30,000 boat package at the 2025 rate, shrinking slowly as the value falls.
Registration: $55 plus a $9 processing fee for a boat 16 feet to under 26 feet, renewed every three years, per the Department of Revenue’s fee schedule. Under 16 feet it’s $25, and 26 feet to under 40 feet it’s $100.
Insurance: whatever your agent quotes. More on whether Missouri requires it below.
Storage or a slip, winterizing, maintenance and fuel: storage usually leads, as our guide to what boating costs near St. Louis lays out.
Depreciation: no bill arrives for it, but on J.D. Power’s ranges a $40,000 boat loses $12,000 to $16,000 of value over ten years. That comes straight out of your net worth, roughly $1,200 to $1,600 a year on average.
Look at the gap between the two government lines. The state charges $64, processing fee included, to register that boat for three years. The local tax on the same boat can top $800 every single year. People budget for the small one because it comes with a decal. The big one shows up in the fall mail.
So here’s the “but it’s paid off” objection, answered straight. Paying off a toy ends the interest. It doesn’t end the ownership costs, and it doesn’t stop the value from sliding. A paid-off boat still costs money every month; it just bills you in lumps instead of payments. That’s fine if you’re using it. It’s a slow leak if you aren’t.
Motorcycles are the cheapest toys to keep legal: Missouri registration for a two-wheeler is $8.75 a year plus the $9 processing fee. But Missouri law defines a motorcycle as a motor vehicle, and a motorhome counts too, so both need the same liability coverage as your car, at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per accident and $25,000 for property damage, per the Department of Commerce and Insurance. Both land on the tax bill as well. Shopping used? Our guide to what to avoid when buying a used motorcycle in Missouri covers the title traps.
Snowmobiles follow the same math, with a twist: around here they sit in storage most of the year and get trailered hours north to ride, so the trailer and the trip are part of the price, as our snowmobile buying guide explains.
Smallest toy here, biggest safety bill: what motorcycle gear to buy first.
### Does Missouri require boat insurance?
We couldn’t find any Missouri law that requires insurance on a recreational boat. The state’s mandatory insurance law, section 303.025, is written for motor vehicles, which covers your car, your motorcycle and a motorhome, and nothing we found makes the same demand of a boat. That’s where the free pass ends.
Lenders typically require coverage on a boat or RV that secures their loan, because it’s their collateral too. Marinas commonly want proof of liability coverage before they rent you a slip. Ask both before you sign anything.
The bigger reason to carry it is liability: if your boat hurts someone or wrecks their dock, you’re the one they come after. And don’t assume your homeowners policy has you covered. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the group of state insurance regulators, warns that a homeowners policy gives a small boat only limited coverage, with limited liability, and leaves a large boat out entirely. Jet skis and other personal watercraft often need a policy of their own.
Put two questions to an agent in writing. Can coverage pause while the boat is winterized? The NAIC notes some watercraft policies can be suspended in the off months, though some carry minimum or fully earned premiums. And which policy covers the boat while you tow it down the highway? If a claim goes sideways later, the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance takes consumer calls at 800-726-7390.
Missouri does require other things. Motorized boats, sailboats longer than 12 feet and outboard motors other than trolling and electric ones must be titled and registered, and you have 60 days from purchase to title them, per the Department of Revenue. Operators born after January 1, 1984, need a boater safety card on board to run a motorboat or a sailboat over 12 feet on Missouri lakes. Starting January 1, 2027, anyone born on or after January 1, 2006, has to carry it on all waters of the state, not only the lakes, according to the Highway Patrol’s Water Patrol Division. The card costs $15, and a classroom course taught by a marine trooper carries no fee. If you’re buying secondhand, our guide to what to know before buying a used boat in Missouri covers the title side.
### How do you own an RV or boat without wrecking your net worth?
Rent first, buy used, pay cash or borrow short, and budget for December. That’s the short version, and none of it means skipping the fun.
Rent before you own. A week in a rented camper tells you more than any showroom: whether your family likes it, what size you can tow, how many weekends you’ll really use. Our guide to renting an RV in St. Louis covers the cost. If the honest count is a handful of days a year, renting may stay cheaper for good.
Buy a few years old. J.D. Power’s figures show the steepest drop comes early, and that boat depreciation slows after about ten years, when condition and maintenance records start driving the price. Letting the first owner take that hit is the biggest discount going. Get the unit inspected, and lean on our first-time RV buyer’s guide for what to check.
Pay cash, or borrow short. The rule of thumb that keeps people out of trouble: a loan shorter than the time you expect to keep the toy, so you never owe more than it would sell for. That’s the CFPB’s car-loan warning, applied to a boat.
Build a toy fund for the December bill. Add up the yearly tax, insurance, storage and registration, divide by 12, and move that amount every month into its own savings account. Then the tax bill is a transfer, not an ambush.
Mind the January 1 snapshot. Timing matters at both ends. A camper bought on January 2 isn’t on that year’s bill, and one sold on December 30 won’t be on next year’s.
Count the days. Once a year, divide everything the toy cost you by the days you used it. If the number makes you wince, sell before another January 1. If it makes you grin, keep it and drop the guilt. A boat your family uses thirty days a year isn’t a money failure. It’s a choice made with open eyes.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed financial advisor, a CPA or a licensed insurance agent can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Want to see a well-kept used unit before you sign anything long? Start with RV dealers around St. Louis, and ask each one for the out-the-door price, the model year and whether it also rents.
And if you run an RV, boat or bike dealership, the buyers reading this are about to ask you exactly that, so list your dealership.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are examples of bad debt?
A.  Debt that buys something that shrinks or gets used up, especially at a high rate. Credit card balances carried for meals out, gifts or vacations are the classic case; the CFPB notes that borrowing doesn’t build assets. A long loan on a new boat, RV or jet ski fits too, since the value falls while you pay. Even a car loan goes bad when it outlasts the car.
### Q. Are used boats a good investment?
A.  No boat is an investment in the sense of growing in value, but a used one is usually the smarter buy. J.D. Power puts typical boat depreciation at 10% to 20% in the first year and 30% to 40% by year ten, after which condition matters more than age. Buying a few years old lets the first owner absorb the steepest drop. Fishing boats and pontoons tend to lose value faster.
### Q. Do you need to have insurance on a boat in Missouri?
A.  We found no Missouri law requiring insurance on a recreational boat; the state’s mandatory coverage law is written for motor vehicles. Lenders typically require it on a financed boat, and marinas commonly want proof of liability coverage for a slip. The NAIC warns that a homeowners policy gives small boats only limited coverage and excludes large ones, so ask an agent about a separate boat policy.
### Q. How do I figure out my net worth?
A.  List everything you own at what it would sell for today: home, savings, retirement accounts, cars, boats and campers. Then list every debt at its payoff balance. Subtract the debts from the assets, and that’s your net worth. Do it on the same date every year, January 1 works, and watch the direction more than the number.
### Q. Is your net worth all your money?
A.  No. Net worth counts things you can’t spend this week, like home equity, retirement accounts and the resale value of a camper, and it subtracts debts you aren’t paying off today. In the example household above, net worth is $135,000 while checking and savings hold $7,000. The cash you can reach quickly is a separate number, and it’s the one that pays a surprise bill.
### Q. Why is the 10 year RV rule?
A.  It’s a policy some private RV parks and resorts set to limit rigs older than about ten years, usually framed around condition and appearance. It isn’t a Missouri law. If your camper is older, call before you book and ask whether the park will look at photos or make an exception for a well-kept unit.
### Q. Is debt or equity better?
A.  For a household, equity is the goal and debt is a tool. Equity is the part of something you own outright, its value minus what you owe on it. Debt helps when it builds equity, as a mortgage often does; the Federal Reserve put the typical homeowning family’s home equity at $230,000 in 2025. Debt hurts when it buys something whose value falls faster than the balance.
### Q. What is the average lifespan of an RV?
A.  There’s no official average, but J.D. Power’s camper guide says a well-built RV can last up to 20 years and most motorhomes can travel 200,000 miles before needing engine work. The same guide flags water damage and uncovered outdoor storage as big threats, so roof seals and winterizing matter more than mileage. In Missouri, an old RV still draws a tax bill every year you own it.

## What Is a Mortgage Rate? Rate vs APR, Points, and the Number the St. Louis Fed Tracks Every Week
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-is-a-mortgage-rate
Broadway and Locust, downtown St. Louis. That’s the home address of the bank that publishes the mortgage-rate chart economists, reporters and lenders reach for when they want the long view. Freddie Mac collects the number. The long-run chart of it lives on FRED, the public database built and maintained by the research department of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. One wavy line, one point a week, going back to April 1971. It peaked at 18.63% in October 1981. It bottomed at 2.65% in January 2021.
Here’s what nobody says when that line shows up in a news story. It isn’t your rate. It’s an average for one particular kind of borrower, and a lot of ads, teaser quotes and fine print work because most people were never shown who that borrower is or how their own number gets built. That’s not a you problem. Nobody taught mortgage pricing in school.
So here’s the whole thing, built for St. Louis: what the rate measures, what moves it, rate versus APR, points, the payment math to the penny, the federal 3-7-3 rule, and how to check a Missouri loan officer before you hand over a Social Security number. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide.
### What is a mortgage rate?
A mortgage rate is the price of borrowing for a home, stated as a yearly percentage of what you still owe. The market sets the baseline, not the Fed directly. Your lender then prices it to you by your credit, down payment, loan type, term and any points you buy. It isn’t the APR, which adds fees.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau puts it in one line: the interest rate is the cost you pay each year to borrow the money, expressed as a percentage. No fees, no points, no other charges folded in.
Borrow $100,000 at 6% and the first month’s interest is $500, because 6% of $100,000 is $6,000 a year, split twelve ways. On a 30-year fixed loan, your principal-and-interest payment stays the same every month, but the mix inside it shifts. In month one, $500 of a $599.55 payment is interest and only $99.55 chips at the balance. As the balance shrinks, so does the interest, and more of each payment goes toward the house itself. That slow tilt has a name: amortization.
Two layers decide the number on your quote. The first is the market layer, roughly the same for every lender in the country on a given day. The second is you: your file, your loan, your choices. You can’t touch the first one. You have a real say in the second.
### Why isn’t the rate on the news the rate you’ll get?
Because the headline number describes a borrower you may not be. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey, the source behind that FRED line, averages the rates on thousands of loan applications lenders submit to Freddie Mac through its Loan Product Advisor system. Applications from Thursday through Wednesday go into each week’s number, and it comes out Thursday at noon Eastern. That’s 11 a.m. in St. Louis.
And it only counts certain loans. Freddie Mac’s criteria: conventional, conforming home-purchase loans on owner-occupied, one-unit single-family homes, for borrowers with good to excellent credit putting 20% down. Since November 2022 the weekly rate has been built from those applications, a change FRED notes on the series page.
Now picture who’s actually shopping in St. Louis: a first-time buyer with a small down payment on an FHA loan, a veteran on a VA loan, someone whose credit took a hit in a rough year. None of them is the survey’s borrower, and the CFPB says plainly that rates can be significantly different depending on loan type. The FRED line shows you direction. It doesn’t show you your offer.
One local wrinkle. The CFPB also notes that many lenders price slightly differently by state, and sometimes by county. Weighing a house in the Metro East against one on the Missouri side? Ask for quotes on both addresses. Same lender, same week, the numbers can differ.
### What moves mortgage rates up and down?
The bond market, mostly. The St. Louis Fed answered this one itself in a Page One Economics explainer, and the short version is a formula: the mortgage rate is roughly the 10-year Treasury yield plus a mortgage spread. If the 10-year Treasury yields 4% and the spread is 2 percentage points, you’re looking at about 6%.
Why the 10-year note and not a 30-year bond? Most mortgages get paid off or sold long before year 30, so the 10-year is the closer match. The spread on top pays for the cost of making and servicing the loan, the lender’s profit, and the extra risk investors take when they buy mortgage bonds instead of Treasuries.
And the Fed? It doesn’t set mortgage rates. The St. Louis Fed’s own explainer calls the link between Fed policy and mortgage rates “less direct” than it is for short-term rates. The Fed works mostly through what markets expect about inflation and future short-term rates, and through buying or selling Treasury notes and mortgage-backed securities. That’s how a Fed rate cut can lead the news while mortgage quotes barely budge.
Then comes your layer. The CFPB lists seven things that set your rate:
Credit score. Higher scores generally get lower rates.
Location. Pricing can vary by state, even by county.
Loan size. Very small and very large loans can carry higher rates.
Down payment. Bigger usually means lower.
Term. Shorter loans carry lower rates and bigger payments.
Rate type. An adjustable rate may start lower, then rise.
Loan type. Conventional, FHA, USDA and VA loans price differently.
Lenders also weigh your debts against your income. That’s the DTI, or debt-to-income ratio, story we told in why it’s easier to buy a car than a house.
### How do you turn a mortgage rate into a monthly payment?
With one formula that every lender, calculator and spreadsheet uses. Monthly principal and interest = P × r × (1 + r)n ÷ ((1 + r)n - 1). P is the amount you borrow. r is the yearly rate divided by 12. n is the number of monthly payments.
Run the example people search for most: $100,000 at 6% for 30 years. That makes r = 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005, and n = 360. Raise 1.005 to the 360th power and you get about 6.0226. So the payment is $100,000 × 0.005 × 6.0226 ÷ 5.0226, which comes to $599.55 a month in principal and interest.
Stretch that over 360 payments and you hand the lender about $215,838: the $100,000 back, plus roughly $115,838 in interest. More interest than you borrowed.
Now make it local. The median listing price for the St. Louis metro, a number FRED also charts every month, was $285,950 in September 2026. Put 20% down and you’d borrow $228,760. Here’s what one percentage point does to that loan:
One point of rate is about $150 a month on a median-priced St. Louis listing, and more than $54,000 over the full term. Those two rates are round illustrations, not this week’s market. For that, check the FRED line, then get real quotes on your own file.
These are principal and interest only. Property taxes, homeowners insurance and often mortgage insurance ride on top, and that’s its own story in escrow and PMI explained.
### What’s the difference between the interest rate and the APR?
The interest rate is the price of the money. The APR, or annual percentage rate, is the price of the whole loan. The CFPB calls APR a broader measure of the cost of borrowing: it reflects the interest rate plus any points, mortgage broker fees and other charges you pay to get the loan. That’s why the APR almost always runs higher.
On a Loan Estimate, the standard three-page form every lender has to use, the interest rate sits on page 1 under Loan Terms. The APR is on page 3 under Comparisons. Most people read page 1 and stop. Turn the page. If two lenders quote the same rate and one APR is noticeably higher, that gap is fees, and fees are where an attractive rate hides its real cost.
Two cautions from the CFPB. An adjustable-rate loan’s APR doesn’t reflect the highest rate the loan can reach, so don’t stack it against a fixed loan’s APR. And don’t judge by APR alone. Its math spreads up-front costs over the full term, so if you sell or refinance in year five, those closing fees weigh far more than the APR suggests.
Closing costs are the other half of that comparison, broken down line by line in what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis.
### What are mortgage points, and when do they pay for themselves?
Points are an up-front fee you pay the lender at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate. One point equals 1% of the loan amount, so on that $228,760 median-listing loan, one point costs $2,287.60. The flip side is a lender credit, sometimes called negative points: the lender covers part of your closing costs and you take a higher rate. The CFPB walks through both.
The test is simple division. In the CFPB’s own example, on a $180,000 30-year fixed loan, paying 0.375 points to drop the rate from 5.0% to 4.875% costs $675 more at closing and saves about $14 a month. $675 ÷ $14 is about 48 months. Keep the loan four years and you’re even. Keep it ten and the points paid off. Sell or refinance in year two and you bought a discount you never got to use.
A CFPB data study found that 58.7% of home-purchase loans made from January through September 2023 carried discount points. The same report says points are less useful for cash-strapped borrowers and for anyone who expects to move or refinance soon. Here’s the catch nobody mentions at the closing table: if rates fall and you refinance two years in, the money you spent lowering the old rate doesn’t come back.
Locked a great rate on a 1920s brick? Now check its old-house wiring.
### How much time do you get to check the numbers before closing?
More than most buyers use. Federal disclosure rules, known in the industry as TRID, build in a 3-7-3 rhythm. The lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days of your application. Closing can’t happen before the seventh business day after that Loan Estimate is delivered or mailed. And you must receive the Closing Disclosure, the five-page final version, at least three business days before closing.
Business days have their own fine print. For the seven-day wait and the three-day Closing Disclosure window, the regulation counts every calendar day except Sundays and federal legal holidays. Saturdays count. The three-day deadline for sending the Loan Estimate counts days the lender’s offices are open for business.
Some changes restart the clock. An APR that becomes inaccurate beyond the rule’s tolerance, a switch to a different loan product, or an added prepayment penalty means a corrected Closing Disclosure and a fresh three business days. Use the pause. Put page 1 of the Closing Disclosure beside page 1 of your Loan Estimate and check that the loan amount, rate and monthly payment match.
Then there’s the rate lock, the lender’s promise that your rate won’t change between the offer and closing, as long as you close within the lock period and your application doesn’t change. The CFPB lists what can knock it loose: switching loan type or down payment, an appraisal that comes in higher or lower than expected, a credit score change from a new loan or a missed payment, or overtime, bonus or other income the lender can’t document. Extending a lock that runs out can be expensive. Your Loan Estimate shows whether your rate is locked, and for how long.
### At what point is it worth it to refinance?
When the monthly savings pay back the cost of the new loan before you’d move or refinance again. Same division as points: total refinance costs ÷ monthly savings = months to break even.
Say a refinance costs $4,800 all in and trims your principal-and-interest payment by $150 a month. $4,800 ÷ $150 = 32 months. Planning to stay five more years? It pays. Thinking about selling in two? It doesn’t.
Three traps hide inside that easy math. First, the reset. Refinance a loan you’ve paid on for eight years into a fresh 30-year loan and part of your lower payment comes from stretching the debt back out, not from a better rate. Compare total interest left on the old loan against total interest on the new one. Second, “no-cost” offers. The CFPB says no-closing-cost loans cover those costs one of two ways, with a higher interest rate or by adding them to your loan balance. The cost moved. It didn’t vanish. Third, a prepayment penalty on the loan you’re leaving. The CFPB says these usually apply only when you pay off the whole balance, typically within the first three or five years. Which is exactly what a refinance does.
Watch the FRED line to know when the conversation is worth having. Only a Loan Estimate on your own file tells you whether the break-even works.
### How do you check a St. Louis lender before you hand over your Social Security number?
Look them up. It’s quick. Missouri’s Division of Finance enforces the state’s laws on residential mortgage brokers and originators, Sections 443.701 through 443.893 of Missouri law, and since July 31, 2010, every residential mortgage originator has needed a license. The exception is loan officers employed by banks and other deposit-taking institutions, who are exempt from the state license.
