The CFPB points consumers to the free NMLS lookup to see whether a company or loan officer is authorized to do business in your state, and the Division runs its own bank and licensee search. Federal rules also print the lender’s and the loan officer’s NMLS ID numbers on page 3 of the Loan Estimate, under Additional Information About This Loan, so you can match the person across the desk to the record.
While you’re at it, these are the red flags worth stopping for:
A loan officer who won’t give you an NMLS number, or whose name doesn’t match the lookup.
A Loan Estimate that says YES next to Prepayment Penalty or Balloon Payment when nobody told you about either. A balloon means the final payment is a lump sum much larger than the regular ones.
A rate that looks great on page 1 and an APR on page 3 that doesn’t.
Anyone who suggests rounding up your income or leaving a debt off the application. Knowingly making a false statement to a mortgage lender to influence a loan decision is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. 1014, with penalties up to a $1,000,000 fine and 30 years in prison.
An email near closing with new wiring instructions. The CFPB warns that closing scammers pose as your agent or settlement agent by email. Call a number you already had before you send a dollar.
For who to call, see our guide to choosing a mortgage lender in St. Louis. Buying your first place? Add the first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis, the down payment assistance programs for St. Louis buyers, and a HUD-approved housing counselor as one more set of eyes before you sign.
This is general information, not advice for your loan. A licensed loan officer or a HUD-approved housing counselor can apply it to your numbers, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Ready to compare real numbers? Get Loan Estimates from two or three mortgage brokers around St. Louis on the same day, then read page 1 and page 3 side by side.
And if you’re the loan officer across that desk: when a St. Louis neighbor, or the AI they ask, wants a straight answer on rate versus APR, being the name that comes up first is the whole game, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is $100,000 mortgage at 6% for 30 years?
A.  $599.55 a month in principal and interest, using the standard amortization formula: a 0.5% monthly rate over 360 payments. Over the full term you’d pay about $215,838, so roughly $115,838 is interest. Taxes, homeowners insurance and any mortgage insurance come on top of that.
### Q. What happens if I pay an extra $100 a month on my 30 year mortgage?
A.  On a $100,000 loan at 6%, an extra $100 toward principal every month pays the loan off in 21 years instead of 30 and saves about $39,900 in interest. The CFPB says prepayment penalties don’t normally apply to extra principal paid in small chunks, but check your loan terms, and tell your servicer the extra goes to principal.
### Q. What is the 3 7 3 rule for a mortgage?
A.  It’s shorthand for federal disclosure timing. The lender delivers your Loan Estimate within 3 business days of your application, closing can’t happen before the 7th business day after that estimate is delivered or mailed, and you must receive the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. An inaccurate APR, a new loan product or an added prepayment penalty restarts that last wait.
### Q. What not to tell a mortgage lender?
A.  Nothing untrue. Overstating income or leaving out a debt to sway a loan decision is a federal crime. What trips people up is what they do after applying: opening a new credit card, financing furniture or missing a payment. The CFPB lists credit changes, and overtime or bonus income the lender can’t document, among the things that can change even a locked rate.
### Q. When should you not refinance?
A.  When you’ll move or refinance again before the break-even month, when the lower payment mostly comes from restarting a 30-year clock, or when the loan you’d leave carries a prepayment penalty that eats the savings. Be wary of “no-cost” refinances too. The CFPB says those costs get covered by a higher rate or added to your balance, so you still pay them.
### Q. Does refinancing hurt my credit score?
A.  A little. A lender’s credit check is an inquiry, and the CFPB says an inquiry typically has a small negative effect on your scores. Shopping several lenders doesn’t multiply the hit if you keep it tight: credit checks from mortgage lenders within a 45-day window are recorded as a single inquiry.
### Q. How to get the cheapest mortgage?
A.  Work the levers you actually control: a stronger credit score, lower debts, a bigger down payment, a shorter term if the payment fits. Then make lenders compete. Get Loan Estimates from several on the same day, compare the APRs on page 3 instead of just the rates, and judge any points by the break-even math.
### Q. What is a red flag in a mortgage?
A.  A loan officer who can’t or won’t give you an NMLS number. A Loan Estimate showing a prepayment penalty or balloon payment nobody mentioned. An APR far above the rate. Advice to fudge your income. And an email with new wiring instructions right before closing, which the CFPB flags as a possible scam.

## Escrow and PMI Explained: Why Your St. Louis Mortgage Payment Changes and How to Drop PMI
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/escrow-and-pmi-explained-st-louis
Fixed rate, bigger payment. Picture a high school teacher in Bevo Mill who locked a 30-year fixed rate a few years back and has paid the same amount every month since. One evening in February a letter from his mortgage servicer turns up between a pizza coupon and the gas bill. Starting in April, it says, his payment goes up $130 a month. Columns labeled projected, actual and cushion. A number at the bottom he never agreed to. No sentence anywhere that says why.
He calls and says the obvious thing. My rate is fixed. The rep agrees, because it is. What moved was the slice of his payment that was never fixed to begin with, the escrow, and the warning had come nine months earlier in an envelope from the Assessor that he left on the counter.
That’s the St. Louis piece nobody explains at the closing table. Missouri sets new home values every odd-numbered year, the new value lands on a tax bill due December 31, the servicer pays it out of escrow, and the yearly escrow review turns it into a bigger mortgage payment. By the time that letter arrives, the deadline to argue with the value closed back in July. This chapter of our St. Louis money guide covers both meanings of escrow, how to read that letter, and how PMI actually comes off. You’re not bad at this. Nobody ever walked you through it.
### What is escrow for when buying a house?
Escrow means two different things when you buy a house. At closing, a Missouri title or escrow company holds the money, from the lender’s wire to your cash to close, until the sale is done. After closing, your servicer runs an escrow account that collects part of each payment and pays your property taxes and homeowners insurance.
The first escrow is short. Most Missouri home sales close at a title company, the neutral party in the middle. It holds the money for both sides, collects signatures, pays off the seller’s loan, sends out the checks and gets the deed recorded. When the closing ends, so does that escrow. Our guide to choosing a title company in St. Louis covers what it does and why you can usually pick your own.
The second escrow lasts as long as the loan, and it changes your payment. Your servicer, the company you pay each month, keeps an account on your behalf, adds a slice of every payment, and pays the tax bill and insurance premium when they come due. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes that many lenders require escrow, and that because taxes and premiums change, your payment can change with them.
Federal rules cap what goes in. Under Regulation X, the rulebook for the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA), a servicer can collect one-twelfth of the year’s expected bills each month, plus a cushion no bigger than one-sixth of the year’s total. That’s two months’ worth, and it matters the year a bill jumps.
The account gets its starting money at closing, the initial escrow deposit in Section G on page 2 of your Loan Estimate. It surprises people who close late in the year here. The whole year’s property tax is due December 31, and the rules let the servicer collect at closing for taxes built up since they were last paid, plus the cushion. Close in October and the deposit runs bigger. Our breakdown of what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis shows where it sits.
### Why did my mortgage payment go up if my rate is fixed?
Because the escrow part changed, not the loan. On a fixed-rate mortgage the principal-and-interest payment stays the same for the life of the loan, but property taxes and insurance don’t. Once a year the servicer reruns the math in an escrow analysis. In St. Louis the two usual reasons for a jump are the odd-year reassessment and a homeowners insurance renewal.
Here’s the reassessment calendar nobody lays out in one place, for a house in the County or the City:
January 1 of an odd-numbered year. New values are set as of this date, and they carry into the following even-numbered year too, under RSMo 137.115.
May. The County Assessor mails residential Change of Assessment Notices, and the City’s notices go out May 1 to 15. For an escrowed homeowner, this envelope is the real warning.
The second Monday in July. The last day to appeal to the Board of Equalization, set by RSMo 137.275.
November and December. Bills go out and are due December 31. In the City, an escrowed bill is sent to your lender to be paid from the escrow account.
After the bill is paid. The servicer’s yearly analysis catches the bigger number, and the letter follows.
The timing is the trap. The appeal window shuts in July. The bill comes months later, the servicer pays it, and the escrow letter can land after New Year’s, when the value is set for two tax years. The letter is only the receipt. If the tax line jumped, the fix runs through the Assessor. Our guide to appealing a St. Louis County or City assessment covers the evidence and dates for the next round, and older County homeowners should check the senior tax freeze and the Missouri Property Tax Credit.
Insurance is the other half. Escrow pays your homeowners renewal at whatever price the insurer sets, so a premium increase flows straight into your payment, even in a year taxes didn’t move. If that line jumped, call your agent and compare quotes; our look at what drives St. Louis home insurance premiums explains why the number moves.
The servicer has duties too. Federal rules require it to pay your taxes and insurance on time, before any penalty, as long as your own payment isn’t more than 30 days overdue, fronting its own money if the account runs short. That matters in the County, where taxes paid or postmarked after December 31 draw up to 18% interest a year plus a 2% penalty.
### How do you read an escrow analysis letter?
Hunt for three words: shortage, deficiency and surplus. Each means something specific under federal rules. The analysis happens once a year, and the servicer has to send the statement within 30 days of the end of your escrow year, under Regulation X.
Shortage. The balance is below the target the servicer needs. Money’s still in there, just not enough.
Deficiency. The account went negative, and the servicer covered the gap with its own money.
Surplus. The account holds more than the target. At $50 or more, if you’re current, the servicer has to refund it within 30 days. Under $50, it can refund it or credit next year.
Here’s the teacher’s letter, in round illustrative numbers. His servicer expected $3,600 in property tax and $1,800 in insurance, $5,400 in all, so it collected $450 a month and held a $900 cushion. Then the reassessment pushed his tax bill to $4,080, and his insurance renewed at $2,040.
Follow the money and the $130 makes sense. The account started the year at the $900 cushion, took in $5,400 and paid out $6,120, so it bottomed out at $180. Bigger bills mean a bigger allowed cushion, and if the servicer keeps the full one-sixth, the target becomes $1,020. The gap between $180 and $1,020 is an $840 shortage, or $70 a month over 12 months. Add that to the new monthly share of $510 and you get $580. His principal and interest didn’t move a penny.
Two pieces, two futures. The $60 is the new normal while those bills hold. The $70 is a one-year catch-up, so if nothing else changes, the payment drops back to $510 a year later.
Know the rules on the shortage. When it’s at least one month’s escrow payment, as $840 is, the servicer can let it ride or spread it in equal payments over at least 12 months. It can’t demand it all within 30 days; that option exists only for smaller shortages. Would rather pay the $840 at once and hold the payment at $510? Ask whether your servicer will take one check.
### Can you lower an escrow payment or drop escrow altogether?
You lower it by lowering the bills underneath it. Sometimes you can drop it, though in St. Louis that’s more responsibility than it sounds. Escrow is only a pass-through, so the levers are:
Pay the shortage in one check, if your servicer will take it, and the catch-up line goes away.
Challenge the value at the next reassessment, in the odd-year window that closes the second Monday in July.
Shop the insurance at renewal, comparing the same coverage and the same deductible.
Once a lower tax bill or a cheaper policy is in hand, ask the servicer to rerun the analysis so the payment reflects it.
Dropping escrow depends on your loan and your lender. On a higher-priced mortgage loan, one priced well above the going rate, federal rules require escrow and won’t let it be canceled at your request until at least five years after closing, and only once you owe less than 80% of the home’s original value and aren’t behind.
If your lender allows it, think about December. Without escrow, a St. Louis homeowner owes the whole year’s property tax at once, plus the insurance renewal. Some people like holding that money in savings until it’s due. For most first-time owners, the forced monthly saving is the whole point.
Escrow covers taxes and insurance, never the furnace. Free repair help.
### What is PMI, and who does it actually protect?
Private mortgage insurance protects the lender, not you. On a conventional loan with less than 20% down, the lender usually requires it, and it pays the lender if you stop paying. The CFPB is blunt about the rest: you can still lose the home to foreclosure. You pay the premium, most often monthly as part of the mortgage payment, sometimes up front at closing, sometimes both.
Back to the teacher. Say he bought a $250,000 house with 10% down, borrowing $225,000 on a 30-year fixed loan at 6.5%. Those are illustrative numbers, not a quote; our explainer on what a mortgage rate is covers what sets a real one. His principal and interest come to about $1,422 a month, with PMI on top as its own line.
PMI isn’t the villain. It’s why he could buy at 10% down instead of renting for years while he saved 20%. The villain is paying it one month longer than the law requires because nobody mentioned the date.
### When does PMI come off a conventional loan?
The federal Homeowners Protection Act gives you three exits, all measured against original value, generally the lower of the purchase price or the appraisal when you bought. They cover single-family primary homes on loans closed on or after July 29, 1999, per the CFPB’s summary of the cancellation rules.
80%, by request. When your balance is scheduled to reach 80% of original value, or gets there early through extra payments, you can ask in writing to cancel. You need a good payment history, current payments, no second mortgage or other junior lien, and possibly evidence, such as an appraisal, that the value hasn’t dropped. Meet those and the servicer has to say yes.
78%, automatically. On the date your balance is scheduled to hit 78%, the servicer must end PMI on its own, if you’re current.
The midpoint. Failing both, PMI ends the month after the halfway point of the schedule, 15 years into a 30-year loan, again if you’re current.
Run the teacher’s numbers. Eighty percent of $250,000 is $200,000, which his schedule reaches around payment 95, just shy of eight years. Seventy-eight percent, $195,000, comes around payment 109, a little over nine years. Waiting for the automatic date instead of asking costs him about 14 extra months of premiums. The first date he can ask should be on the PMI disclosure form from his closing. Dig it out.
Extra principal moves that date. Add $200 a month from the start and the balance hits $200,000 in about 54 payments, four and a half years. The 80% request looks at your real balance; the automatic 78% date runs off the original schedule, so prepaying won’t pull that one forward.
### Can a higher home value get PMI removed sooner?
Sometimes, but not under the federal law, which measures against original value. That path runs through whoever owns your loan. If it’s Fannie Mae, its servicing guide lets a borrower on a one-unit primary home cancel PMI based on today’s value:
Loan between two and five years old: balance at 75% or less of current value.
Loan more than five years old: 80% or less.
Improvements you made, such as a kitchen or bath renovation or added square footage, raised the value: 80% or less, and the two-year wait can be waived. Upkeep repairs don’t count.
Payment record: current, nothing 30 or more days late in the past 12 months, nothing 60 or more days late in the past 24.
You pay for the valuation up front. Fannie Mae’s guide calls for an interior and exterior broker price opinion on a one-unit home at $190, or $450 when an appraisal is required by law. Two years in, the teacher owes about $219,800, so the house would need to come in around $293,100 or more to pass the 75% test. A little past five years, with roughly $210,300 left, a value near $263,000 clears 80%.
Other loan owners set their own rules, so ask your servicer who owns the loan and what it needs, in writing, before you pay for anything. Refinancing is the other way out, but it brings new closing costs and a new rate.
### How is FHA mortgage insurance different?
It follows HUD’s rules, not the Homeowners Protection Act, and for most FHA buyers it never falls off at 78%. The CFPB notes that FHA and VA loans have different requirements. FHA’s current premium table charges an upfront premium of 1.75% of the base loan amount plus an annual premium billed monthly.
The duration stings. On a loan longer than 15 years, if the loan-to-value starts at 90% or less, roughly 10% or more down, the annual premium runs 11 years. Above 90%, it runs the whole mortgage term.
Put the teacher’s $250,000 house on an FHA loan with 3.5% down. The base loan is $241,250, the upfront premium about $4,222, and at that loan-to-value the annual rate is 0.55%, about $1,327 a year, roughly $110 a month at the start. For the life of the loan. The exit is ending the loan, usually by refinancing into a conventional mortgage once there’s enough equity, or selling.
That doesn’t make FHA a bad choice; for plenty of first-time buyers it’s the way in. Just ask each lender to lay the FHA and conventional payments side by side, mortgage insurance included. Our guide to choosing a mortgage lender in St. Louis has the questions to bring.
This is general information, not advice for your loan. A loan officer or a HUD-approved housing counselor can run it against your own statement, a CPA can handle the tax side, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Holding an escrow letter or a PMI disclosure you can’t decode? Take it to one of the mortgage lenders around St. Louis and ask three things: when does my PMI come off, what is my payment without the shortage line, and would a different loan shed mortgage insurance sooner.
And if you run a lending or title shop, the neighbor asking those questions, or the AI they ask first, calls whoever gets named first, so list your company where they’re looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why did my escrow go up $400 a month?
A.  A jump that size usually means bigger bills plus a shortage being repaid. If your yearly taxes and insurance rise by $2,400 together, that adds $200 a month going forward. Refilling the hole it left, plus a larger cushion, can add about $230 more for a year. The letter shows which line moved; in St. Louis it’s often the odd-year reassessment.
### Q. Do I ever get my escrow money back?
A.  Yes, two ways. A surplus of $50 or more at the yearly analysis must be refunded within 30 days if you’re current. And when the loan is paid off by a sale or refinance, the servicer must return the leftover balance within 20 days, weekends and holidays excluded, unless you agree to roll it into the new loan’s escrow with the same lender or servicer.
### Q. Is it smart to get rid of escrow?
A.  Usually not for a first-time owner. Without it you owe the full St. Louis property tax bill by December 31, and County taxes paid late draw up to 18% interest a year plus a 2% penalty. Higher-priced loans must keep escrow at least five years anyway. If your lender permits it and you’re disciplined, holding the money yourself can work.
### Q. Do I pay escrow every month?
A.  Yes, if your loan has an escrow account. Each payment carries one-twelfth of the year’s expected taxes and insurance, plus enough to keep a cushion of no more than two months’ worth, and the servicer pays the bills when due. Without escrow you pay nothing monthly toward them but owe the full bills yourself, including the December 31 tax bill.
### Q. Does PMI go away at 20%?
A.  It can. Once your balance reaches 80% of original value, meaning 20% equity against the price or appraisal when you bought, you can ask in writing to cancel if your payment history is good, you’re current and there’s no second lien. At 78% it ends automatically. Equity from rising values counts only under your loan owner’s rules, such as Fannie Mae’s.
### Q. What is the fastest way to get rid of PMI?
A.  Usually extra principal, since every extra dollar pulls the 80% request date closer. In our example, $200 a month extra cut the wait from about eight years to four and a half. If your home’s value has jumped and the loan is at least two years old, a current-value cancellation under your loan owner’s rules may be faster still.
### Q. Can I deduct PMI on my taxes?
A.  Not on a 2025 return; Publication 936 said the deduction had expired. For premiums paid in 2026, the IRS’s draft 2026 Publication 936 says it’s reinstated, on Schedule A line 8d if you itemize. It shrinks once adjusted gross income passes $100,000 ($50,000 married filing separately) and disappears above $109,000 ($54,500). FHA, VA and private mortgage insurance qualify.
### Q. Who holds the money in an escrow account?
A.  It depends which escrow. At closing, the title or escrow company holds the funds until the sale is done. After that, your loan servicer holds the escrow account and pays your taxes and insurance from it. Federal rules make it pay on time, even fronting its own money when the account runs short, as long as you’re no more than 30 days behind.

## Mobile Home vs House in Missouri: Land, Title, Taxes, Financing and Why One Loses Value
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mobile-home-vs-house-in-missouri
Mobile homes depreciate. You’ve heard it from a relative, a coworker, maybe a loan officer. It isn’t a law of physics. Missouri will let the very same factory-built house be titled through the motor vehicle system, like a pickup, or recorded at the county as real estate, like a brick ranch, and which one it becomes drives the loan you get, the tax bill you pay and what it’s worth when you sell.
The vinyl siding has nothing to do with it. A form at the Department of Revenue does, and so does whoever owns the dirt under the floor. None of that is printed on the sticker, and the federal consumer bureau has raised concerns that some buyers sign without knowing the downsides, or get steered toward the costlier loan.
This guide is about ownership. If you’d be renting the lot, our guide to lot rent, park rules and what happens when a park sells covers that side, and the St. Louis money guide is the place to start on the bigger picture.
### Is it better to buy a mobile home or a house?
It depends less on the building than on the ground. A manufactured home on land you own, with its Missouri title surrendered and the home recorded as real estate, can get a 30-year mortgage and has gained value about as fast as site-built houses. On rented land it stays personal property, financed like a vehicle, and usually loses value.
Missouri’s titling law, RSMo 700.320, sends every new or used manufactured home through the same process used to title motor vehicles, with the same fees and the same penalties. So a three-bedroom home starts life in the state’s records next to your car. Whether it ever leaves that system is up to you.
The middle column is the trap. Owning the land doesn’t convert the home by itself. Picture a double-wide on its owner’s own acreage, taxes paid, mower in the shed, and a title in a drawer that still says, legally, the house is a vehicle. A lender sees it exactly that way.
### Why are mobile homes so much cheaper than houses?
Mostly because the price you see is a house without land, built on an assembly line. The Census Bureau’s dealer survey put the average new manufactured home sold in the Midwest at $112,100 in May 2026, with dealer setup included under the survey’s rules. The St. Louis Fed, which publishes the series in its FRED database, points out that the price covers only the house. No land.
Add land and the gap shrinks. In the second quarter of 2024, the median manufactured home sold as real property, land included, went for $231,000 among loans bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, against $367,000 for a site-built home, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency. FHFA credits factory efficiencies, economies of scale and one national building code, HUD’s construction and safety standards, known as the HUD Code.
The sticker leaves plenty out: land, a foundation, a well or septic system, utility hookups, permits. Missouri’s Department of Revenue taxes a new manufactured home on 60 percent of its purchase price, while a used one owes no sales or use tax at all. And skip the land entirely and you trade a one-time purchase for lot rent that never ends.
### Which manufactured homes gain value, and which ones lose it?
The ones sold with their land as real estate have gained value; the ones on rented ground mostly haven’t. FHFA built its manufactured home price index only from real-property homes financed through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and it removed personal property loans from the data entirely. From the first quarter of 2000 to the second quarter of 2024, that index rose a cumulative 212 percent. Site-built homes rose 213 percent.
One point apart over 24 years. FHFA calls the index developmental and notes it doesn’t adjust for manufactured homes leaning rural and running smaller. Still, the doomed-to-depreciate rule doesn’t hold for homes that own their dirt.
On rented land there’s no comparable index, and the reasons are structural. Much of a house’s appreciation lives in the land, and a rented lot gives the owner none of it. The next buyer will likely need a chattel loan, one secured by the home alone, since neither Fannie Mae nor Freddie Mac had an active program to buy personal property manufactured home loans, FHFA noted in late 2024. And in the CFPB’s 2019 data, only 27 percent of manufactured home loan applications became loans, against 74 percent for site-built homes. Fewer buyers who can get financing tends to mean a softer price.
So when someone says mobile homes depreciate, ask them back: which paperwork, and whose land?
### How does a manufactured home become real estate in Missouri?
You attach it permanently to land you own, record an affidavit of affixation (a sworn statement that the home is permanently attached to the land) with the county recorder of deeds, and surrender the title to the Department of Revenue within 60 days. After that, Missouri stops treating the home like a vehicle. The rules sit in RSMo 442.015 and RSMo 700.111:
Own the land, or hold it under a lease in recordable form that runs at least 20 years, with the landowner’s consent.
Make the home permanently affixed: anchored to a permanent foundation built to state and local codes and the manufacturer’s specifications under federal installation standards, and connected to residential utilities such as water, electricity and sewer or septic.
Complete Form 5312-5313, the Manufactured Home Affixation or Severance form, and record it with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits.
Within 60 days of recording, mail it to the Department of Revenue’s Motor Vehicle Bureau in Jefferson City, with Form 108-M and the title or manufacturer’s certificate of origin. Fees: $8.50 plus a $9.00 processing fee, no title penalty.
The department cancels the title and issues a Certificate of Affixation. The home now sells and borrows with the land.
Seventeen dollars and fifty cents. That’s the state’s charge to move a home from the vehicle column to the real estate column, before the recorder’s fee and the foundation work. For a landowner, it may be the best $17.50 they ever spend.
Two snags. Any lien on the title must be released before the department accepts the surrender. And a lost title isn’t fatal: Form 108-M has a confirmation-of-conversion section an attorney or title insurance agent completes. Don’t miss the window: the department won’t accept filings made more than 60 days after recording.
The door swings back, but it’s heavier. Once a home is recorded as affixed, the department won’t issue a title or record a lien on it, and moving it off the land takes a recorded affidavit of severance certified by an attorney or licensed title insurance agent.
### How is a mobile home taxed in Missouri, and does the title change it?
Here’s the surprise: the assessment rate doesn’t change. Under RSMo 137.115, Missouri assesses a manufactured home used as a dwelling at the same percentage as residential real estate, 19 percent of its market value, whether it’s titled like a car or recorded like a house. The car parked beside it is assessed at 33 1/3 percent.
What changes is which bill it lands on. A home in a rental park, or on land the owner doesn’t own, is personal property under the statute, and its tax goes on the owner’s personal property statement with the vehicles. Our walk-through of St. Louis County personal property tax shows how that bill is built and when it’s due. Once a home is real estate under the affixation law and assessed as an improvement to the land, its tax moves to the parcel’s real estate statement.
That undercuts one reason the CFPB listed for landowners keeping chattel loans: lower property taxes. Here the assessment percentage is 19 percent either way, though levy rates can differ between the two bills, so have the assessor run your parcel’s numbers first.
Renting while you shop for land? Find affordable apartments in St. Louis.
### Is it difficult to get a mortgage on a mobile home?
It’s hard on rented land and much easier once the home is real estate. FHA’s Title II program and Fannie Mae back mortgages of up to 30 years on manufactured homes, Freddie Mac buys them too, and all three want the home titled as real property on a permanent foundation. A home on a rented lot usually gets a chattel loan.
FHA Title II. HUD’s guidance to lenders requires at least 400 square feet, construction after June 15, 1976, real estate classification, one mortgage covering home and site, a term of no more than 30 years and a permanent foundation. The rule that catches people: the home can’t have been installed or lived in anywhere else before your land.
FHA Title I. This one can finance the home alone. On a leased lot, HUD requires an initial lease term of three years with at least 180 days’ written notice before it ends. The maximum terms are 20 years and 32 days for the home only or a single-section home with its lot, and 25 years and 32 days for a multi-section home with its lot.
Fannie Mae. Its product matrix wants at least 400 square feet and 12 feet of width, the HUD Code, a permanent chassis and foundation, and real estate title, with terms up to 30 years. A standard manufactured home bought as a principal residence can go to 95 percent loan-to-value (the loan as a share of the home’s value), so 5 percent down.
Freddie Mac. Its requirements page says the home must be titled as real property, permanently affixed to a foundation and built on or after June 15, 1976. Single-wides must be a primary residence.
Now the number that should bother you. In the CFPB’s study of 2019 loan data, more than 60 percent of manufactured home borrowers owned the land under the home, which may make them eligible for a mortgage. Seventeen percent of those landowners took a chattel loan anyway. Possible reasons the bureau listed include not wanting to risk the land, not knowing chattel loans’ downsides, and being steered by a lender, dealer or retailer. And only mortgage borrowers get the disclosure protections of the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act.
Run round numbers. Borrow $100,000 at an illustrative 9 percent for 23 years, the median chattel term in the CFPB data, and the payment is about $859 a month, with about $137,000 in interest. At 6.5 percent for 30 years, it’s about $632 a month and roughly $128,000 in interest. Keep the 23-year term at 6.5 percent and you’d pay about $699 a month and $93,000 in interest, so the rate gap alone is worth roughly $44,000. Those rates are assumptions, not quotes; the gap between median chattel and manufactured home mortgage rates in the CFPB’s 2019 data was wider, 3.7 points.
New to this? Read what a mortgage rate actually is and why a car loan is easier to get than a home loan, then use our guide on how to choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis to compare lenders who write both kinds.
### What about older mobile homes built before the HUD Code?
They’re the ones the big federal loan programs won’t touch. June 15, 1976 is the line: HUD says every manufactured home built in the U.S. after that date must be certified by its maker to federal construction and safety standards. FHA Title II and Freddie Mac exclude homes built before it, and the CFPB reserves the older term, mobile home, for exactly that pre-code housing.
To check, look for the metal HUD label on the outside of each section, and the paper data plate inside, often in a kitchen cabinet, at the electrical panel or in a bedroom closet. HUD doesn’t reissue lost labels but can issue a Letter of Label Verification when it finds the records. Missouri still titles older homes; on Form 108-M, a pre-1976 home needing a new serial number requires a Public Service Commission inspection and a $16.50 plate and processing fee.
As for lifespan, no Missouri or federal rule sets an expiration date. Lenders set the age limits that matter, and some have loosened: Fannie Mae dropped its rule that a single-wide be ten years old or newer on December 14, 2022.
### Is a modular home the same as a manufactured home?
No. A modular home is also built in sections in a factory, but to the same state and local codes as a site-built house, while a manufactured home is built to the national HUD Code on a permanent chassis. The CFPB draws the line exactly that way, and HUD’s lender guidance treats modular construction the same as stick-built housing.
In Missouri, the Public Service Commission covers both. It licenses manufacturers, dealers and installers, approves plans for modular units sold in the state, and inspects construction and anchoring. It’s also Missouri’s agency for HUD complaints, with a hotline at 1-800-819-3180. Buying used? Its authority there is mostly limited to manufacturer defects that create safety hazards.
Better? For lending and resale, a modular home usually behaves like a house because, legally, it is one. A manufactured home closes much of that distance once it’s real estate on land you own. On a rented lot, the comparison isn’t close.
### Who is a manufactured home a smart buy for?
Someone who owns the land, or can buy it, and will do the real estate paperwork. That buyer gets a lower entry price, a shot at a 30-year mortgage and a home type that has kept pace with site-built values.
Say you inherited ten acres an hour outside St. Louis. A new double-wide on a proper foundation, affixed and recorded, can put a mortgage-financed home on that land for less than most site-built houses sell for, going by FHFA’s medians. That’s the strongest case there is.
Family land is trickier. The CFPB found 24 percent of chattel borrowers leased their land for free, and industry contacts told the bureau many of those deals are with family. Picture a new home set on a parent’s farm on a handshake. In Missouri, that handshake keeps it personal property. The affixation law also accepts a recordable lease of at least 20 years with the landowner’s consent, but lenders set their own rules on leased land, so line up the lease and the lender before delivery day.
On a rented lot, treat the home as housing rather than wealth-building, and expect it to sell more like a vehicle than a house. Built before mid-1976? Expect few financing options. Weighing all this against a first house in the city or county? Our first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis covers that side.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A real estate attorney, a title company, a loan officer or a HUD-approved housing counselor can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Real Estate directory is a place to start.
Shopping for a home and land together? Start with manufactured home dealers around St. Louis and ask every one the same question before you sign: will this home close as real estate or as personal property, and which loans can it qualify for on my land?

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do manufactured homes depreciate in value?
A.  Not automatically. FHFA’s index of manufactured homes sold as real property, with their land, rose 212 percent from early 2000 to mid-2024, against 213 percent for site-built homes. Homes on rented lots aren’t in that index, and they tend to lose value: no land to appreciate, and the next buyer usually needs a chattel loan.
### Q. What do you need to title a mobile home in Missouri?
A.  Form 108-M, the Application for Manufactured Home, with the manufacturer’s certificate of origin for a new home or the signed-over title for a used one, plus any sales tax. Fees total $17.50. Missouri applies its motor vehicle title penalties: $25 after 30 days, $25 more for each further 30 days, capped at $200.
### Q. Why would you de-title a mobile home?
A.  To make it real estate. Once the title is surrendered and the affixation recorded, the home sells and borrows with its land, can qualify for a mortgage, and is taxed on the land’s real estate bill. Moving it off the land later takes a recorded severance certified by an attorney or title agent.
### Q. Are you a homeowner if you own a mobile home?
A.  Yes, you own the home. On a rented lot you don’t own the ground, though, and Missouri treats the home as personal property, so you’re a homeowner and a tenant at once. Own the land and record the home as real estate, and you hold the same kind of property a house buyer does.
### Q. Do banks give 30 year mortgages on mobile homes?
A.  On homes titled as real estate, yes. Fannie Mae allows terms up to 30 years, and FHA’s Title II program insures mortgages of up to 30 years on homes that meet its rules, including a permanent foundation and construction after June 15, 1976. Homes on rented land usually get chattel loans, which ran a median 23 years in CFPB data.
### Q. How many years will a mobile home last?
A.  No Missouri or federal rule gives it an expiration date; installation, the roof, moisture and maintenance decide it. The age that matters most is the lender’s. Homes built before June 15, 1976, when HUD’s standards began, are shut out of FHA Title II and Freddie Mac loans, while Fannie Mae dropped its ten-year limit for single-wides in December 2022.
### Q. What is the longest you can finance a mobile home?
A.  Thirty years, with a mortgage, once the home is real estate. Without that, FHA’s Title I program caps a home-only loan at 20 years and 32 days, and a multi-section home financed with its lot at 25 years and 32 days. Chattel loans in the CFPB’s 2019 data ran a median of 23 years.
### Q. Is a modular home better than a mobile home?
A.  For lending and resale, usually yes. A modular home is built to the same state and local codes as a site-built house, and FHA treats it like one, while a manufactured home is built to the national HUD Code. Recorded as real estate on land you own, a manufactured home can close much of that gap.

## How Much Rent Can I Afford in St. Louis? The 30% Rule, Real Rents and What Landlords Check
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-rent-can-i-afford-st-louis
Thirty percent of your pay. That’s the line every rent calculator draws, and it didn’t start as budgeting advice. It started as a federal rent formula. A 1969 amendment to the Housing and Urban Development Act capped public-housing rent at 25% of a tenant’s income, and in 1981 the cap rose to 30%. A rule written for subsidized apartments quietly became everybody’s rule of thumb, and nobody explained it to you in school.
Then you walk into a St. Louis leasing office and meet the same rule from the other side of the desk: your gross income has to be at least three times the rent. Same idea, flipped. Here’s what nobody mentions. The two versions don’t measure the same thing. HUD’s 30% counts rent plus utilities. The landlord’s 3x counts rent alone and lets it reach a full third of your pay. Get approved right at the line, pay utilities at the St. Louis average, and about 41% of your gross income goes to housing. The building said yes. Your budget never got a vote.
So this page does the math the leasing office won’t: the 30% line and the 3x screen for real incomes, what HUD says St. Louis rents run by bedroom count and by ZIP code, the cash it takes to get the keys, what gets an application turned down, and when 30% is the wrong number entirely. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide. Already past this step and holding a lease? Our guide to renting an apartment in St. Louis covers the clauses, deposits and repairs, so we won’t repeat them here.
### What is the 30% rule for rent?
The 30% rule says your housing costs, meaning rent plus utilities, shouldn’t top 30% of your gross monthly income. Multiply your monthly pay before taxes by 0.30 to find the ceiling. HUD calls anyone above that line cost-burdened, and above 50% severely cost-burdened. Landlords run the same idea backward with a three-times-rent income screen.
The definition is HUD’s, and the utilities part matters more than most people realize. In the agency’s housing data glossary, cost burden means monthly housing costs, including utilities, above 30% of monthly income, and severe cost burden starts at 50%. HUD’s research office traces the percentage straight back to that 1969 public-housing cap, and its PD&R Edge summary says the measure remains central to how HUD defines affordability.
The math takes ten seconds. Earn $4,000 a month before taxes? Thirty percent is $1,200, and that $1,200 has to cover rent, electric, gas, water and trash. Paid by the hour? Multiply your rate by 2,080, the hours in a full-time year, then divide by 12 to get your monthly gross.
Now flip it. A leasing office that asks for income of three times the rent is saying rent can be one-third of your gross pay. That’s 33.3%, not 30%, and the screen usually looks at base rent only. No Missouri statute sets that multiple; each building picks its own, and some ask for more. Same rule, other side of the desk, a little looser, and silent about the utility bills that will arrive in your name.
### How much rent can you afford on a St. Louis paycheck?
Take your gross monthly pay and multiply by 0.30 for the comfortable ceiling on rent and utilities together. Divide the same number by 3 for the most a typical 3x screen will approve on rent alone. Here’s that math for the incomes people ask about most:
One note before the examples. The 30% column is a total for rent and utilities. In the Census survey data HUD feeds into its St. Louis Fair Market Rent calculation, utilities make up about 18% of gross rent. That’s the local average, not your bill, but it’s a fair way to split a 30% budget: roughly 82 cents of each housing dollar for rent and 18 cents for utilities.
$70,000 a year. That’s $5,833 a month gross. Thirty percent is $1,750 for housing, which at the local utility share works out to about $1,435 in rent and $315 in utilities. A 3x screen would approve rent up to $1,944, so you’ll be shown more apartment than the 30% rule says to take. Live inside the City of St. Louis and the 1% earnings tax also comes out of your wages, $700 a year or about $58 a month; our breakdown of the St. Louis earnings tax explains who owes it.
$60,000 a year and a $1,500 apartment. That salary is $5,000 a month. The 3x screen only needs $4,500, so you’ll probably get approved. But $1,500 is already exactly 30% of gross before a single utility bill. Add utilities at the St. Louis average share and the total lands near $1,830, about 37% of your gross pay. Workable if the rent includes utilities and you carry no car payment. Tight if not.
$3,000 a month. Thirty percent is $900 for rent and utilities. The 3x screen will approve rent up to $1,000, and that’s the trap from the top of this page: $1,000 in rent plus average utilities is roughly $1,220, or 41% of gross. Approved and cost-burdened on the same afternoon.
A $1,200 apartment. To pass a 3x screen you need $3,600 a month, or $43,200 a year, about $20.77 an hour at full time. The 30% rule on rent alone asks for $48,000. Count utilities the way HUD does and the target climbs to about $58,500. For scale, MIT’s living wage estimate for a single adult with no kids in the St. Louis metro is $21.79 an hour.
Missouri’s minimum wage. It’s $15.00 an hour for 2026, which comes to $31,200 a year for a full-time worker, or $2,600 a month. Thirty percent of that is $780. Hold that number up against the rents in the next section.
### What does rent really cost in St. Louis?
HUD’s benchmark for a two-bedroom in the St. Louis metro is $1,349 a month, utilities included. That figure comes from HUD’s Fair Market Rents for fiscal year 2027, which took effect October 1, 2026. HUD resets them every year, and the table below shows how far they moved.
Read those numbers the way HUD builds them. The Federal Register notice for this round describes a Fair Market Rent as HUD’s best estimate of the 40th percentile gross rent, rent plus utilities, paid by recent movers into standard-quality units. In plain terms: of the people who just moved into a decent, non-luxury place, about four in ten paid less and six in ten paid more. It’s a modest benchmark, and it jumped. The two-bedroom figure rose $131 from the year before, roughly 11%.
Here’s the detail that explains why your quote beats your coworker’s lease. HUD’s worksheet for the area starts with the Census five-year figure for a standard two-bedroom, $1,059 with utilities, then checks what recent movers paid in 2024: $1,272. That gap was wide enough that HUD multiplied its estimate by about 1.2 to account for movers alone. Your neighbor who signed four years ago isn’t paying your rent. The market charges the person walking in the door.
Then there’s the ZIP code, and St. Louis is one of the places HUD prices ZIP by ZIP. Every Housing Choice Voucher program in the metro uses Small Area Fair Market Rents, set for each ZIP code. Across the region the two-bedroom figure runs from $960 to $2,020. Inside the city alone:
63111, Carondelet’s ZIP: $880 for a one-bedroom, $1,070 for a two-bedroom
63104, Soulard and Lafayette Square: $1,220 and $1,490
63108, the Central West End: $1,640 and $2,000
Run the $3,000-a-month earner through those. A one-bedroom at the 63111 figure is about 29% of gross, under the line. The same size unit at the 63108 figure is about 55%, severe cost burden by HUD’s own definition. Same city, same paycheck. The ZIP did that. If a voucher is part of your plan, our guide to finding low-income apartments in St. Louis explains how to get on the list. And the minimum-wage worker from the last section? HUD’s metro studio benchmark of $1,064 eats 41% of a $2,600 month.
### When is the 30% rule the wrong rule?
When debt, kids or a thin take-home paycheck already have a claim on your money. The rule compares housing to gross pay and nothing else. It never asks about your car note.
Start with debt. The CFPB defines your debt-to-income ratio, or DTI, as all your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income. Mortgage lenders put the house payment inside that number, and doing the same with rent is a useful gut check. Picture a nurse earning $60,000 with a $520 car payment and $180 a month in student loans. Rent of $1,500 passes the 3x screen and sits right at 30%. Add the loans, and $2,200 of every $5,000 is gone before groceries. That’s 44%.
Then gross versus take-home. The 30% rule runs on pay before taxes. Say that same $5,000 month deposits about $3,800 after taxes, health insurance and a retirement contribution. The $1,500 rent is now almost 40% of the money that actually lands in your account, and a City address shaves off another 1%. If you’ve never built a budget from the deposit side, our guide on how to budget on a St. Louis paycheck starts there.
Kids change the math most. MIT’s figures for the St. Louis metro put child care for one adult with one child at $13,740 a year, and the living wage for that household at $38.52 an hour, against $21.79 for a single adult. A parent who follows the 30% rule to the dollar can still come up short every month.
Researchers have measured that gap. In a study of working-age renter households that HUD’s research office summarized, Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found 62% couldn’t cover basic necessities after rent, while the 30% rule flagged only 48%. The shorthand they borrowed from author Matthew Desmond says it plainly: “rent eats first.” So treat 30% as a ceiling, not a target. With heavy debt or child care, the number that works may sit closer to 25%.
Rent math $200 short of 3x? Your contacts could close that gap.
### How much cash do you need to move into a St. Louis apartment?
Plan on two to three months of rent before the first night, plus fees. The rent figure is only the monthly part. Signing day has its own price.
Say the unit is $1,100 a month. Here’s what can be due before you get keys:
First month’s rent: $1,100.
A security deposit. Missouri caps it at two months’ rent under RSMo 535.300, so anywhere up to $2,200. Plenty of buildings ask for less, and a shaky screening result can push it up. It also can’t double as your last month’s rent, as the Missouri Attorney General’s landlord-tenant guide points out.
A pet deposit, which that same statute leaves outside the two-month cap. Our guide to renting with pets in St. Louis covers pet rent and fees.
Application fees, which are generally nonrefundable.
Utility deposits, maybe. Under Missouri Public Service Commission rules, a utility can require one for new service if you have an unpaid, unchallenged bill from the last five years or can’t meet its credit standard. You can ask to pay it in installments, some companies take a written guarantee from an existing customer with good credit instead, and the money comes back with interest after 12 billing periods of on-time payments.
A renters insurance policy, which many leases require. Here’s what renters insurance in Missouri costs and covers.
With a one-month deposit, that’s $2,200 in rent and deposit alone. At the two-month cap it’s $3,300, before the truck, the mattress and the shower curtain. Our move-in setup checklist for St. Louis walks through turning on each utility. If the cash isn’t there yet, a cheaper unit with a smaller deposit can beat a perfect unit you’d have to put on a credit card.
### What will disqualify you from an apartment?
Usually one of four things: income below the building’s multiple, a past eviction case or unpaid rent, credit trouble like collections, or the building’s criminal-history policy. Most of it shows up in a tenant screening report. The CFPB says those reports can include credit history, rental history with eviction actions and lawsuits, employment verification, criminal history, and a risk score built on criteria the landlord chooses.
A few Missouri specifics. An old utility balance can follow you twice, once on your credit and again as a deposit demand when you open new service. Missouri landlord suits are public court records on Case.net, the state courts’ online search, so look up your own name before a leasing agent does. And roommates planning to beat the 3x screen by stacking four incomes into a two-bedroom should know that Missouri law presumes a limit of two people per bedroom is reasonable, under RSMo 441.060.
A “yes, but” counts too. The CFPB treats requiring a co-signer, a larger deposit or higher rent than other applicants pay as an adverse action, which entitles you to a notice naming the screening company and a free copy of the report if you ask within 60 days. The CFPB also notes that a landlord who refuses to rent to anyone with a criminal history may be violating the Fair Housing Act. How to use that report and dispute errors is covered in our apartment renting guide.
### Is it better to rent or buy?
It depends on how long you’ll stay and what owning really costs each month, not on whether a mortgage payment looks smaller than rent. Renting fixes your housing cost for the lease term and hands repairs to someone else. Buying builds equity, but it adds costs a rent check hides: closing costs up front, then property tax, homeowners insurance, and every repair the furnace or the roof decides you need.
The tax side has a Missouri rhythm. Under RSMo 137.115, homes are assessed at 19% of market value, and assessors set new values as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year. You can lock a mortgage rate for 30 years. Your tax bill doesn’t lock.
The fair comparison runs the same 30% test on the whole monthly cost of owning: principal, interest, taxes and insurance, plus a repair fund. If that lands near your rent and you expect to stay several years, buying starts to make sense. If a job could move you in two years, closing costs can eat the advantage. Our first-time homebuyer’s guide to St. Louis covers down-payment help in the city and county, and how to choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis covers the loan itself. A HUD-approved housing counselor can run both paths with your real numbers before you commit.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A HUD-approved housing counselor, a loan officer or a licensed real estate agent can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Real Estate directory is a place to start.
Know your number? Compare apartment buildings around St. Louis, and before you pay a single application fee, ask the leasing office three things: what income multiple it uses, whether roommates’ incomes combine, and what the unit’s utilities averaged last year.
If you’re the landlord, property manager or leasing agent a renter on a budget should find, see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much rent can you afford making $70,000 a year?
A.  About $1,750 a month for rent and utilities together, using the 30% rule on $5,833 of monthly gross pay. A typical three-times screen would approve rent up to about $1,944, which is more than the 30% rule suggests. If your utilities run at the St. Louis average share, $1,750 covers roughly $1,435 in rent. City of St. Louis residents also lose 1% of wages, about $58 a month, to the earnings tax.
### Q. Can I afford $1500 rent on a 60k salary?
A.  You can likely get approved: $60,000 is $5,000 a month, and a three-times screen only needs $4,500. Affording it is tighter. $1,500 is already 30% of gross pay before a single utility bill, and at the St. Louis average utility share your housing total lands near 37%. Low debt and included utilities make it workable. A car payment makes it a stretch.
### Q. What is a proper income to rent ratio?
A.  Two ratios matter. HUD’s benchmark keeps rent plus utilities at or under 30% of gross income, so income should be about 3.33 times your total housing cost. Many leasing offices require gross income of at least three times the rent, which lets rent reach 33% and ignores utilities. Neither is set by Missouri law. With a car payment or student loans, aim below both.
### Q. How much rent can I afford if I make $3,000 a month?
A.  About $900 for rent and utilities under the 30% rule. A three-times screen would approve rent up to $1,000, but $1,000 plus average utilities puts roughly 41% of your gross pay into housing. Location changes everything: HUD’s ZIP-level estimate for a one-bedroom is $880 with utilities in 63111, Carondelet’s ZIP, and $1,640 in 63108, the Central West End.
### Q. What salary do you need to afford $1200 rent?
A.  $43,200 a year passes a three-times screen, about $20.77 an hour at full time. The 30% rule on rent alone asks for $48,000. Count utilities the way HUD does, at the St. Louis average share, and the target is closer to $58,500. For comparison, MIT’s living wage for a single adult with no kids in the St. Louis metro is $21.79 an hour.
### Q. Is it cheap to live in St. Louis?
A.  Cheaper than most big metros, mostly because of housing, but it’s climbing. HUD’s two-bedroom benchmark for the area is $1,349 a month with utilities, $131 more than the year before. And cheap depends on pay: a full-time worker at Missouri’s $15.00 minimum wage would spend about 41% of gross income on HUD’s $1,064 studio benchmark. Our cost of living in St. Louis guide breaks down the rest.
### Q. How to calculate percentage of rent based on income?
A.  Divide your monthly housing cost by your monthly gross income, then multiply by 100. To match HUD’s definition, use rent plus your average utility bills. Example: $1,100 rent plus $190 in utilities is $1,290, and $1,290 divided by $4,200 is 30.7%, just over the cost-burden line. Rent alone gives 26.2%, which is exactly why the utility line matters.
### Q. What do I need in my first apartment?
A.  On paper: photo ID, recent pay stubs or an offer letter, and contact details for past landlords. In cash: first month’s rent, a security deposit that Missouri caps at two months’ rent, application fees, any utility deposits and a renters insurance policy. Then the things people forget until night one: a shower curtain, a plunger, toilet paper and a working smoke alarm. Photograph every room before you unpack.

## Renters Insurance in Missouri: Is It Required, What It Covers, and What It Never Will
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renters-insurance-missouri
Your landlord’s insurance doesn’t cover a single thing you own. Not the couch. Not the laptop, the bike in the hallway or the winter coats crammed in the closet. It covers the building, because the building is what the landlord owns. And if your bathtub overflows on a Saturday morning and the water comes through the ceiling of the apartment downstairs, the landlord’s policy won’t pay that bill for you either. That one can land on you, with a lawyer attached.
If you believed otherwise, you’re in big company. Missouri’s own insurance regulator says most tenants skip renters insurance because they assume the landlord’s coverage protects them, when landlords typically insure only the building they own. Nobody hands you an insurance briefing with the keys. The fine print just sits in a drawer, waiting for the worst day of your year to explain itself.
So here’s the briefing: what Missouri law requires, who pays when water goes through a floor, and the three disasters a renters policy refuses in writing, all of which have a St. Louis address. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide, plain-English explainers on the money stuff nobody taught us in school.
### Do you have to have renters insurance in Missouri?
No. No Missouri law requires tenants to carry renters insurance, but a lease can, and a signed lease is a binding contract. Either way, your landlord’s policy covers the building. It doesn’t cover your belongings, your hotel bill after a fire, or your liability if you damage someone else’s unit.
Start with the law. No Missouri statute makes a tenant buy renters insurance. The state Department of Commerce and Insurance (DCI) describes it as coverage renters “should consider,” and the Attorney General’s guide to Missouri landlord-tenant law lists a tenant’s legal duties (pay rent on time, use reasonable care, dispose of garbage properly, don’t add occupants or sublease without written permission) without a word about insurance.
The lease is a different story. A landlord can write a renters insurance requirement into it, whether the building is a big complex in the Central West End or a four-family in Dutchtown. Once you sign, the Attorney General’s guide is blunt: a signed lease is a binding legal contract, and a tenant isn’t excused from it for not reading it or not understanding it. Violating a condition of a written lease is one of the reasons the guide lists for a landlord ending one.
Read the insurance clause the way you’d read the deposit clause. Look for the liability amount it asks for, when proof is due, and whether it names a particular insurer or lets you shop. Our walk-through on renting an apartment in St. Louis covers the rest of the lease, line by line.
### Who pays when your bathtub floods the apartment downstairs?
You might, and that’s the exact job of the liability part of a renters policy. The Missouri Attorney General’s guide draws the line plainly: landlords should pay for repairs from ordinary wear and tear and natural forces like weather, and tenants should pay for damage caused by their own negligence or a guest’s.
Picture a second-floor flat in a brick two-family in Bevo Mill. You start a bath, the phone rings, and twenty minutes later water is dripping from the light fixture in your downstairs neighbor’s kitchen. Their ruined rug goes on their renters claim, if they have one. The soaked ceiling goes on the landlord’s. Then either insurer, after paying, can pursue whoever caused it. The industry calls that subrogation, which Missouri DCI’s insurance glossary defines as the insurer’s right to recover what it paid on a loss from a negligent third party who caused it.
The third party is you.
Without a policy, that claim comes out of your own pocket. With one, liability coverage answers it. The Insurance Information Institute (III) describes it as protection against lawsuits for bodily injury or property damage that you or your family cause to other people, and DCI adds that it covers unintentional damage you cause to the landlord’s property, using a kitchen fire as its example. The policy pays for your legal defense and any court award up to the limit, and the III says liability limits generally start around $100,000.
Now flip the floors. If the tenant upstairs leaves the tub running and ruins your things, the III’s renters insurance guide lists that exact scenario as water damage a renters policy covers. The landlord’s policy fixes the ceiling. Yours replaces the couch. Nobody else’s will.
### What does renters insurance actually cover?
Three things: your belongings, your liability to other people, and the extra cost of living somewhere else if a covered disaster forces you out. Everything after that is detail, and the detail is where claims get decided.
Personal property. DCI’s consumer guide to renters insurance lists fire and smoke, windstorm and hail, lightning, vandalism and theft, the weight of ice, snow or sleet, and damage from a car. Coverage follows your things, so a laptop stolen from your car can count, though DCI warns coverage away from home may be limited. The III’s example: on a $25,000 policy, off-premises losses might be capped at $2,500.
Liability. Covered above, plus a small no-fault medical piece, generally $1,000 to $5,000, so a friend who trips on your rug can send the medical bills straight to your insurer without anybody suing anybody.
Additional living expenses, also called loss of use. If a covered fire makes the place unlivable, the policy pays toward hotels, temporary rentals and restaurant meals. The III says most policies pay the difference between those costs and your normal spending, usually with a dollar cap or a time limit.
Then come the sublimits, the caps inside the cap. The III says jewelry and similar valuables are generally covered up to about $1,500. DCI suggests a rider (an add-on that raises the limit for a specific item) for jewelry, antiques and firearms, plus a separate add-on if a side business keeps its gear in your bedroom.
### Which three disasters does a Missouri renters policy refuse to cover?
Floods, earthquakes, and sewer or drain backup. Missouri DCI names those three on its renters page, and its printed guide adds normal wear and tear, the building itself and cars parked on the property. Here’s the uncomfortable part for St. Louis renters. None of the big three is a someday risk here. All three have a local address.
Flood. On July 26, 2022, 8.64 inches of rain fell at Lambert airport, a new all-time daily record that broke the 6.85 inches from August 20, 1915, according to the National Weather Service in St. Louis. The service issued a Flash Flood Emergency, a warning it reserves for high-end flash flooding, for parts of the city and county. Water like that can fill a garden-level apartment nowhere near a river, and a standard renters policy won’t pay for any of it. The fix is a separate policy. The National Flood Insurance Program sells renters contents-only coverage for belongings up to $100,000, and FloodSmart says it takes effect 30 days after purchase, with a few exceptions. A policy bought while the rain is falling is a policy for the next storm. Our guide to flood insurance in St. Louis goes deeper.
Earthquake. Missouri is the third-largest earthquake insurance market among the states, behind only two West Coast states, according to DCI. The department cites a U.S. Geological Survey estimate that the New Madrid zone has a 25 to 40 percent chance of a quake larger than magnitude 6 within 50 years. A standard renters policy leaves that out. The III says earthquake coverage can be a separate policy or an endorsement, meaning an add-on, to your renters policy.
Sewer and drain backup. When heavy rain overfills a public sewer, it can push sewage back into a building, which is how a basement unit gets ruined in an afternoon. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District (MSD) runs its own program for this. If an overcharged public sewer discharges into your building, MSD will reimburse up to $3,000, with a $100 deductible, and if a collapsed or blocked public line caused it, MSD reimburses the adjusted losses. You have to contact MSD within 30 days, and its 24-hour emergency line is (314) 768-6260. Two cautions. MSD’s page is written for homeowners, so a tenant should ask directly whether belongings in the unit qualify. And a backup from the private lateral line, the pipe from the building to the public sewer, isn’t MSD’s to pay. MSD itself says damage can exceed its cap, and DCI’s guide lists a sewer and drain backup endorsement you can add to a renters policy.
Two quieter gaps catch people too. Cars aren’t covered by renters insurance at all; the vehicle needs its own auto policy. And living with someone doesn’t put them on your policy. The III says a domestic partner generally isn’t automatically insured the way a spouse is and has to be specifically named. If a roommate’s things burn, your policy wasn’t written to replace them.
Flood took the furniture and no policy? St. Louis furniture banks can help.
### How much does renters insurance cost in Missouri?
Less than most people guess. The average Missouri renters policy cost $173 for the year in 2022, about $14 a month, according to National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) figures published by the III. That’s next to the national average of $171, and roughly a tenth of the $1,668 the average Missouri homeowner paid that year.
You’ll see other numbers, and they don’t match. DCI’s renters page says premiums average $8 to $21 a month for $20,000 to $30,000 of coverage. Its own printed guide, updated in 2023, puts the average at $32 a month for that same range. They weren’t published at the same time, and neither page says how its figure was measured. Every source agrees on one thing, though: this costs tens of dollars a month, not hundreds.
What moves your quote:
Deductible, the amount you pay on a claim before the policy pays. DCI says a $1,000 deductible costs less than a $500 one, and the III says moving to $1,000 can cut a premium by as much as 25 percent. You pay it on every claim, so the right number is one you could cover tomorrow.
Replacement cost. About 10 percent more than actual cash value, per the III. The next section shows why that’s money well spent.
Limits and add-ons. More property coverage, a higher liability limit, a sewer backup endorsement or a jewelry rider each adds to the price.
Discounts. DCI lists monitored fire or burglar alarms, fire extinguishers, sprinklers, deadbolts on exterior doors, and buying auto insurance from the same company.
DCI’s own advice is to get several quotes, since Missouri’s insurance market is highly competitive, and to compare prices every two years. The levers work the same way they do on a house, and our breakdown of what drives home insurance premiums in St. Louis goes deeper on deductibles. Still deciding where to live? Budget the premium right next to rent with our guide to how much rent you can afford in St. Louis.
### Replacement cost or actual cash value: which one actually rebuys your stuff?
Replacement cost does. Actual cash value pays what your things were worth the moment they were destroyed, after depreciation, which is the drop in value from age and use. Replacement cost pays what it takes to buy a similar item new today.
DCI’s guide runs the numbers on two items:
Now put both in a kitchen fire with a $500 deductible. On actual cash value, you’d collect $1,260, which is $1,760 minus the deductible, toward $3,600 of shopping. On replacement cost, you’d end up with $3,100. DCI explains the sequence: the company pays the actual cash value first, then settles up after you replace the item and send the receipt. Keep the receipts.
At about 10 percent extra, replacement cost on a policy near the Missouri average works out to something like $17 a year. The couch alone makes that look cheap. If a fire does happen, our guide to fire damage restoration in St. Louis covers the first hours and how the insurance side fits into cleanup.
### Does renters insurance cover it if your dog bites someone?
Usually, up to your liability limit, and in Missouri that limit matters more than dog owners tend to think. Under Missouri Revised Statutes section 273.036, the owner or possessor of a dog that bites someone without provocation, on public property or lawfully on private property, including the owner’s own home, is strictly liable for the damages, regardless of the dog’s past behavior or what the owner knew about it.
Translation: under that statute, “he’s never done that before” doesn’t get you off the hook. Damages shrink if the bitten person was partly at fault, and the law adds a fine of up to $1,000.
Then look at the size of these claims. Dog bites and other dog-related injuries averaged $65,450 per liability claim nationally in 2025, according to the III, and that average nearly doubled from 2016. Typical liability limits run $100,000 to $300,000, and anything above the limit is the owner’s to pay.
Two catches. Some insurers won’t cover certain breeds or charge more for them, and after a bite a company may raise the premium, decline to renew or exclude the dog. And DCI’s guide notes that damage your pet does to the rental itself is generally not covered, so chewed trim and clawed floors can come out of the deposit, not the policy. Our guide to renting with pets in St. Louis covers breed lists, pet rent and pet deposits.
### How do you set up a claim to pay before anything goes wrong?
Make a home inventory now, while everything is still where it belongs. DCI publishes a room-by-room home inventory checklist, and its tips are the useful kind:
Record specifics. The checklist warns that without the brand, model and serial number, you might get a lower-priced replacement.
Walk each room with your phone recording, opening closets and drawers as you go.
Group the small stuff, like cookware, linens and toys. Bought all at once, it adds up fast.
List what leaves the apartment with you: phone, laptop, tablet, watch, jewelry.
Keep a copy somewhere else, at a relative’s place or in an email to yourself, and update it every year and after big purchases.
When something does happen, the III’s list is short. Report a theft to the police and get the report. Call your insurer right away, because claims have filing time limits. Photograph the damage and don’t throw damaged items out before the adjuster sees them. If you have to move out during repairs, keep every receipt.
And if a claim stalls? Take the problem to the company first, note the name and date of every call and keep copies of everything in writing, the way DCI asks. Then call the department’s Insurance Consumer Hotline at 800-726-7390, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays, or file a complaint online. DCI forwards complaints to the company, requires a response and reviews it against Missouri insurance law. It can’t act as your lawyer or decide what your claim is worth.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can apply it to your lease, your belongings and your address, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Ready to price it? Get two or three quotes from home and renters insurance agents around St. Louis, and bring this page’s questions: replacement cost or actual cash value, what liability limit, and whether sewer backup, flood and earthquake coverage can be added.
If you’re the independent agent, the St. Louis renter weighing those questions, or asking an AI who can answer them, is really deciding who to call, and being the name that comes up first is the whole game, so list your agency.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are three things that renters insurance typically does not cover?
A.  Missouri DCI names three: floods, earthquakes and sewer or drain backup. Flood coverage for belongings is sold separately through the National Flood Insurance Program, up to $100,000, and DCI and the III say sewer backup and earthquake coverage can be added to a renters policy as endorsements.
### Q. What is a fair price for renters insurance?
A.  In Missouri, the average renters policy cost $173 a year in 2022, about $14 a month, according to NAIC data published by the III. A fair price is one that buys replacement cost, a liability limit that fits your life and a deductible you could pay tomorrow. The only way to know you’ve found it is to compare at least three quotes.
### Q. Is renters insurance tax deductible?
A.  Not for a typical renter. IRS Publication 529 lists home repairs, insurance and rent among nondeductible personal expenses. The exception is someone self-employed who uses part of the home exclusively and regularly for business: Publication 587 allows a business share of rent and insurance. Employees working from home can’t take it. A CPA or enrolled agent can say whether a home office qualifies.
### Q. Is it legal to rent without renters insurance?
A.  Yes, as far as Missouri law goes. No state statute requires tenants to carry it. But if your lease requires a policy, going without breaks a lease term, and the Missouri Attorney General’s landlord-tenant guide lists violating a condition of a written lease among the reasons a landlord can end a lease.
### Q. Who should get renters insurance?
A.  Anyone who couldn’t replace their belongings out of pocket or absorb a lawsuit, which describes most renters. Add up the list the III suggests, furniture, clothing, electronics, appliances, kitchen gear and even bedding, and the total usually dwarfs a year of premiums. Dog owners have extra reason in Missouri, where state law holds owners strictly liable for unprovoked bites. College students living off campus usually need their own policy.
### Q. What are my rights as a renter in Missouri?
A.  The Attorney General’s guide covers the basics. A security deposit can’t exceed two months’ rent, and the landlord has 30 days after the lease ends to return it with an itemized list of deductions. Landlords handle ordinary wear and tear, can’t cut off your water, electricity or gas, and can’t evict without a court order. Tenants pay for damage they or their guests cause.
### Q. How much does $20,000 worth of renters insurance cost?
A.  Missouri DCI has published two averages for $20,000 to $30,000 of coverage: $8 to $21 a month on its website and $32 a month in its 2023 printed guide. NAIC data put Missouri’s overall average at $173 a year in 2022. Your price depends on the deductible, the liability limit, replacement cost and discounts, so quote the exact limit you want.
### Q. Does my roommate’s renters insurance cover me?
A.  Usually not, unless you’re named on it. The III says rules vary by state and company, some insurers let people who live together buy joint coverage, and a partner usually isn’t automatically insured the way a spouse is. With Missouri premiums averaging about $14 a month, your own policy is often the simpler fix.

## Flood Insurance in St. Louis: The 30-Day Wait and the Basement Gap Nobody Mentions
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/flood-insurance-st-louis
Your homeowners policy almost certainly excludes flood. The line sits in the exclusions section, a few pages past the part anyone reads, and Missouri’s insurance regulator doesn’t soften it: a standard homeowners or renters policy typically does not cover flooding damage. Water that rises out of the ground, rolls in off the street or comes over a riverbank belongs to a different policy entirely.
And that policy has fine print of its own. A new policy from the National Flood Insurance Program, the federal program FEMA runs, takes effect 30 days after you buy it. Thirty days. So the evening the river forecast scares you, when the crest prediction on the news keeps climbing, is the evening it’s already too late. The wait is longer than the warning.
