Nobody taught that in school, and it’s why so many St. Louis families find out what their insurance pays for while standing on the bottom basement stair.
Here’s the local number that ought to stop you. FEMA’s count of single-family homes carrying a federal flood policy on August 31, 2023 came to 182 in the entire City of St. Louis and 2,190 in St. Louis County. That’s the whole list. About a year before that count, on July 26, 2022, Lambert airport logged 8.64 inches of rain in one calendar day, its all-time record, in what the National Weather Service called the most prolific rainfall event the St. Louis metro has seen since records began in 1874. No river had to crest for that one.
This page is one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English series on the money rules nobody walked us through.
### Is flood insurance worth the money?
Usually yes, if your home sits near a river or creek, takes on water in heavy rain, or carries a mortgage in a high-risk zone. Homeowners policies exclude flood, a new federal policy waits 30 days to start, and nearly a third of flood claims come from outside high-risk areas. The case is weakest for upper-floor condos.
Run the math the way an adjuster would. FEMA’s own agent materials put roughly $25,000 of damage on one inch of water in a home. Drywall wicks it up. Flooring buckles. Against that, the median single-family flood policy in the City of St. Louis cost $948 a year in FEMA’s 2023 data, so a single inch of water would eat about 26 years of that premium. And floods rarely stop at an inch.
The odds aren’t small where the maps say they’re high. Inside FEMA’s high-risk zones, a home has a 1 in 4 chance of flooding at least once over a 30-year mortgage. Outside those zones the chance drops. It doesn’t disappear.
Where it’s honestly a weaker buy: a condo several floors up, or a house high on a ridge with no basement. Even then, get a quote. The federal program now prices each home on its own risk, so a genuinely low-risk house tends to get a lower price.
### Why can’t you buy flood insurance when the river starts rising?
Because the federal policy’s coverage starts 30 days after the purchase date, and the rule doesn’t bend for a scary forecast. FloodSmart, FEMA’s consumer site, lists only four ways around the wait:
No wait if you buy the policy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage.
No wait when you change your coverage at the policy’s renewal.
A one-day wait if your property was just mapped into a high-risk flood zone and you buy within 12 months of the map update.
A one-day wait for flooding caused or worsened by a wildfire on federal land, a rule that rarely touches St. Louis.
Notice what’s missing. No exception for a wet spring or a flash flood watch on your phone. River floods here usually come with days of warning, and none of those days buys coverage. The moment flood insurance feels urgent is the moment it can’t help with this flood.
Two more pieces of fine print change the plan. Building coverage and contents coverage are bought separately, with separate deductibles, so a policy on the house alone pays nothing for the couch. And the federal policy runs one year at a time, with a 30-day grace period to renew and pay in full. Let it lapse past that and you’re buying a new policy, with a new wait.
There’s a bigger version of the same risk. The program itself has to be reauthorized by Congress, and FEMA says that during a lapse in that authority it would stop selling and renewing policies, though it could still pay valid claims. One more reason the right day to buy is a dry one. Missouri’s Department of Commerce and Insurance takes policy and claim questions at 800-726-7390.
### Does St. Louis flood away from the Mississippi?
Yes, and that’s the part people miss. The Mississippi is the river everyone pictures, and its numbers are real: on August 1, 1993 it crested at St. Louis at 49.58 feet, the highest stage on record, and the 52-foot floodwall held it back with just over two feet to spare. That flood broke records set by the Mississippi in 1973 and the Missouri River in 1951. But the riverfront has a wall. A basement two miles from any river doesn’t.
The Meramec rewrote its own record book in the winter of 2015. On December 30, 2015, U.S. Geological Survey crews recorded 18 preliminary record-high flood measurements along the Meramec. Then it came within a foot of doing it again. At one lower-Meramec gauge the National Weather Service tracks, the two highest crests on record arrived 16 months apart: 44.11 feet on December 31, 2015, and 43.31 feet on May 3, 2017. Major flood stage at that gauge is 27 feet.
Then there’s the water that never touches a river. The July 2022 storm dropped 7.68 inches in six hours, a total the Weather Service puts at a 1-in-1,000 chance in any given year, and it issued a Flash Flood Emergency for parts of the city and county. Interstates went under. Homes took water. Crews ran water rescues. Creeks and storm channels that barely trickle most of the year can rise in an hour, and the federal policy counts that rain-driven water as a flood, as long as it covers two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties.
That’s why FloodSmart keeps repeating that from 2014 to 2024, nearly one-third of the program’s claims came from outside high-risk flood areas. Low risk is a map label, not a promise.
### What is not covered in flood insurance?
The biggest hole is the basement, and in a region where so many homes sit on one, that’s the clause to read first. The federal policy covers a basement’s working parts and almost nothing you’d call finished. FloodSmart’s guidance says these items qualify below grade only if they’re installed and connected to power:
Under building coverage: the furnace, water heater, cooling units, sump pump, and electrical outlets and switches.
Under contents coverage, if you bought it: a washer, dryer, freezer and the food in it, and window air conditioners.
What doesn’t qualify is the part people spent real money on. Finished walls and flooring. The sectional. The TV. The boxes of photographs. FloodSmart lists finished basements and home improvements, couches, televisions and keepsakes as not covered, and the policy defines a basement as any area with its floor below ground level on all sides, which can include the lowest level of some split-level houses.
Then there’s the list that applies on every floor. The federal policy won’t pay for cash, precious metals or valuable papers; cars and most self-propelled vehicles; anything outside the building, like landscaping, decks, patios, fences, septic systems and pools; temporary housing while repairs drag on; or lost business income. Valuables such as original art and furs are capped at $2,500. And the limits top out at $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for contents.
Two practical moves follow. Photograph the basement now, while it’s dry, and write down the make, model and serial number of the furnace, water heater and appliances, the same habit we walk through in what to do in the first days after fire damage. Second, anything you’d grieve losing doesn’t belong below grade.
### What type of water damage is not covered by insurance?
It depends on where the water came from, and that single question decides which policy pays, if any. Water that starts inside, like a burst supply line or a failed water heater, is generally a homeowners claim. Water that comes from outside and spreads, like rain pooling and pouring in or a creek over its banks, is flood. And water that comes up through the floor drain is a sewer or drain backup, which is the one that falls through the cracks.
Missouri’s insurance department says a standard homeowners or renters policy doesn’t protect against floods or sewer and drain backup. Sewer backup coverage is a separate add-on to the homeowners policy, usually called an endorsement, with its own limit and terms that vary by company. It isn’t flood insurance, and flood insurance isn’t it.
Here’s where it gets expensive. A flood policy pays for sewer backup only when a flood caused the backup, meaning a general condition of water covering two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties. A clogged line on an ordinary Tuesday isn’t that. Neither is a sump pump that can’t keep up during a hard rain if the street outside never actually flooded. Without a backup endorsement, that’s the water most likely to land in the gap between the two policies.
The other quiet exclusion is slow water. Groundwater that seeps through basement walls over days generally isn’t a flood claim, and seepage is a common homeowners exclusion too, which is why Missouri’s regulator tells people to check their exclusions for words like “water damage,” “seepage” and “runoff.” To see how an add-on like this moves your bill, our breakdown of what drives a St. Louis home insurance premium covers the homeowners side.
Same storm drop a limb on the garage? Here’s what tree removal costs.
### What does flood insurance cost in St. Louis?
In FEMA’s data for single-family homes insured on August 31, 2023, the median policy in the City of St. Louis cost $948 a year and the median in St. Louis County cost $988. FEMA also calculated what the same policies would cost at their full risk-based price. The gap is wide.
Source: FEMA, single-family policies in force August 31, 2023, yearly premiums. Why two prices? In 2021 the federal program switched to the pricing system known as Risk Rating 2.0, which prices each home on flood frequency, distance to water and the types of flooding that reach it, heavy rainfall included, plus its elevation and cost to rebuild. New policies got the new price on October 1, 2021, and the rest moved over at renewals starting April 1, 2022. For existing policyholders, the law says most rates can’t rise more than 18% a year, so plenty of older policies are still climbing toward their full price.
Here’s what that climb looks like. Picture a city policy priced at the $948 median whose full-risk price matches the $2,077 median. At the 18% maximum it rises to about $1,119 the next year, about $1,320 the year after, and needs five straight years of increases to reach full price. That’s a budget line, not a one-time bill. When an agent quotes an existing policy, ask for both numbers: this year’s premium and the full-risk price it’s heading toward.
Two more things about price. Every company that sells the federal policy offers the same rates, so shopping agents won’t change the federal price; shopping private insurers might. And if you’re buying a house that already carries a federal flood policy, the seller can assign it to you, and FEMA says any discount on it can transfer to the new owner. Ask before closing.
### What is the 50% rule in FEMA?
If repairing a home in a high-risk flood area would cost 50% or more of the building’s market value before the damage, the home is declared substantially damaged, and the whole structure has to be brought up to current floodplain rules before it’s rebuilt. Often that means elevating it. The same 50% test applies to big remodels and additions, which FEMA calls substantial improvement.
Three details catch people. First, all damage counts toward the 50%, whether it came from flooding, straight-line winds or a tornado. Second, FEMA doesn’t make the call and neither does your insurer. Your community’s building official or floodplain administrator does, and a community can set a stricter line, such as 45%. Third, the number that matters is the building’s value. Say the structure is worth $120,000. Repairs of $60,000 cross the line, and suddenly you’re pricing an elevation job instead of new drywall.
The federal policy has a built-in answer for this. Increased Cost of Compliance coverage pays up to $30,000 to elevate, relocate or demolish a home in a high-risk zone that floods have substantially or repeatedly damaged. It’s filed as its own claim, on top of the regular building claim, as long as the policy hasn’t hit its $250,000 limit. It only exists if you had the federal policy before the flood. Without it, the code upgrade comes out of pocket.
### Do you have to buy flood insurance with a mortgage in St. Louis?
Yes, if the home is in a high-risk zone and the mortgage is government-backed. FEMA’s maps mark high-risk areas with zones that start with A or V, and FloodSmart says a home there with a government-backed mortgage must carry flood insurance. Lenders typically collect it through escrow; our guide to how escrow and PMI work in St. Louis explains that account. Zones B, C and X are moderate to lower risk, and coverage isn’t federally required there, though a lender can still ask for it.
Check your own address before anyone tells you. The FEMA Flood Map Service Center lets you search by address and pull up the official flood map panel for it, zone included. Two cautions. A zone line on a map isn’t a wall in a storm, and the July 2022 flash flood didn’t check anyone’s zone first. And maps change; if your home is newly mapped into a high-risk zone, buying within 12 months of the update gets you the one-day wait instead of 30.
### Is private flood insurance an option in Missouri?
Yes. Private insurers write flood policies outside the federal program, and federal banking regulators have required regulated lenders to accept qualifying private flood policies since July 1, 2019. Because the company writes its own contract, the limits, waiting period, price and exclusions are whatever that company’s policy says. Prices, and the basement and sewer backup language, can differ a lot from the federal policy’s.
The federal policy charges the same rate through every seller and carries Increased Cost of Compliance coverage. A private policy is only as good as its own wording. Ask an agent to put a federal quote and a private quote side by side, and to show you in writing how each one handles basements, sewer backup and the start date.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can quote your address and read your actual policy with you, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Before the next wet season, get two numbers on paper: a flood quote for your address and the price of a sewer backup endorsement on the policy you already have. Home insurance agents around St. Louis can price both in a single conversation, and a dry Tuesday is the cheapest day to have it.
And if you’re the independent agent or a flood restoration contractor, the neighbor reading this is about to ask someone, or some AI, who to call, and being the name that comes up first is the whole game, so list your agency.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is flood insurance in Missouri?
A.  In FEMA’s data for single-family homes insured on August 31, 2023, the median Missouri policy cost $827 a year, a little above the $786 national median. The median full risk-based price was $1,422, so many existing policies are still rising toward it, by up to 18% a year. Your own price depends on elevation, distance to water and what it would cost to rebuild.
### Q. Can anybody buy flood insurance?
A.  Almost anybody. Missouri’s insurance department says anyone can buy flood insurance if their community participates in the National Flood Insurance Program, regardless of where the home or business sits. Owners, renters and businesses all qualify, with or without a mortgage, in a high-risk zone or out of one. Private flood policies are another route.
### Q. How can I lower my flood insurance premium?
A.  Raise the deductible; FEMA says moving to $10,000 can cut premiums by up to 40%. Elevate the furnace, water heater and other covered equipment to at least the floor above the first floor, add proper flood openings to a crawlspace, and get an elevation certificate. Communities in FEMA’s Community Rating System earn 5% to 45% off every policy.
### Q. Can I write off flood insurance on my taxes?
A.  Not on the home you live in. IRS Publication 530 lists insurance, including fire and comprehensive coverage, among nondeductible payments. On a rental property, insurance is a deductible rental expense. Uninsured flood losses on a personal home are deductible only if tied to a federally declared disaster, after $100 and 10%-of-AGI reductions, per Publication 547.
### Q. How to estimate flood insurance?
A.  Start with FloodSmart’s online quote tool, which asks a few questions about the property and returns a personalized estimate, then confirm it with an agent. For a local yardstick, FEMA’s 2023 data put the median single-family policy at $948 in the City of St. Louis and $988 in St. Louis County. Elevation, distance to water and rebuild cost drive your real number.
### Q. Why would insurance deny a water damage claim?
A.  Usually because the water came from a source the policy excludes. Homeowners policies exclude flood, and sewer backup without an endorsement. Flood policies need a general flood covering two or more acres or properties; FEMA upheld one denial where owners couldn’t show that and missed the 60-day proof of loss. Here’s when to call a St. Louis attorney.
### Q. Is flood insurance always included?
A.  No. Flood is excluded from standard homeowners and renters policies and is always a separate purchase, from the federal program or a private insurer. Even inside a flood policy, building and contents coverage are separate, with separate deductibles. Lenders require it only for homes in high-risk zones with government-backed mortgages, and FEMA’s 2023 count found only 182 single-family homes in the whole city carrying a federal policy.
### Q. Can renters buy flood insurance in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. A renters policy excludes flood just like a homeowners policy does, but renters can buy a federal contents-only flood policy covering belongings up to $100,000, with the same 30-day wait. A landlord’s flood policy, if there is one, covers the building, not your things. Our guide to renters insurance in Missouri covers the rest of the policy.

## The Dealer Didn't Collect Your Car Sales Tax. You Pay It at a Missouri License Office
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-car-sales-tax-at-the-license-office
You still owe the sales tax. The dealer got your signature, your down payment and a handshake, and none of that paid it. In Missouri that bill rides home with you, unpaid, in the folder on the passenger seat next to the paper tag, and it comes due at a license office, not at the lot.
Here’s the part that stings. On the state’s own Motor Vehicle Sales Tax Rate Chart, twelve St. Louis County areas listed outside city limits, from Pattonville to Mid County, charge 4.513% local tax when a licensed Missouri dealer sold the car and 3.513% when the seller was anyone else. Same address. Same car. On a $16,000 purchase, that one point is $160 more, only because the seller had a dealer license.
Buy the identical car from the neighbor two doors down and the local tax drops a full point.
This is the license-office side of buying a car, the half that starts after you sign, and one chapter of our St. Louis money guide. Still shopping? Our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis dealership covers doc fees and the finance office.
### Do you pay sales tax at the dealership or DMV in Missouri?
At the license office, not the dealership, for now. Missouri gives you 30 days from the date of purchase to title the vehicle and pay sales tax, whether a dealer or a private seller sold it. The rate is 4.225% state plus the local rate at your home address, and on the 31st day a $25 penalty starts.
The Department of Revenue’s buying-a-vehicle page says it in one line: you have 30 days from the date of purchase to title and pay sales tax on your newly purchased vehicle.
State law backs it from both ends. RSMo 144.020 puts the vehicle sales tax on the person titling the car, and RSMo 144.070 has it paid when you apply for title. No tax, no title. No title, no plates.
In Missouri you title at a license office, and you can bring your papers to any Missouri license office. The license office locator shows the ones near you. Walk in with the whole stack the first time: the title signed over to you, Form 108, your inspections, proof of insurance and last year’s personal property tax receipt. A second trip means another afternoon in a plastic chair, folder on your knee, watching the clock you are racing.
### Why does a dealer sale cost more in parts of St. Louis County?
Stand at the license office counter for a second, because this is where it happens. Your folder is open, the title is signed over, the bill of sale sits on top, and the clerk is not asking where the lot was. The tax on the screen comes from two things on your paperwork: the street you live on and who sold you the car. Your street picks the rate. The seller picks which line of the state’s chart that rate comes from.
For most St. Louisans the two lines match. The Motor Vehicle Sales Tax Rate Chart lists the city of St. Louis at 5.454% local on both lines, for 9.679% combined with the state’s 4.225%. Base St. Louis County, for unincorporated addresses, reads 3.513% on both, or 7.738% combined. Cities inside the county stack their own tax on top, so an address in an incorporated town has its own line.
The split shows up in twelve St. Louis County areas, each with a pair of lines, tagged with names like Pattonville, Mid County, Metro North and Northeast Ambulance. Each one lists 4.513% for a Missouri-dealer sale and 3.513% on the non-Missouri dealer line, and the chart marks them New. Run a $16,000 car through it: 4.225% plus 4.513% is 8.738%, or $1,398.08, from a dealer. Take the same $16,000 car from a private seller and it’s 7.738%, or $1,238.08.
A dealer can still win on price, warranty or financing. Just know the tax gap before you compare a lot’s sticker with a neighbor’s asking price, and check the line for your own address. The Department’s motor vehicle tax calculator may help you estimate the taxes and fees you will pay. The rate at a store register is a separate question, answered in our guide to the St. Louis sales tax rate.
The law behind both rules fits in one sentence: RSMo 144.069 imposes the sales tax at the rate in effect at the owner’s address, and under RSMo 32.087, places that failed to put the question on the ballot by the November 2022 general election had to stop applying their local sales tax to vehicles purchased from a source other than a licensed Missouri dealer, which is why the chart prints a second line marked non-Missouri dealer.
### How much tax is due on a $5,000 or $16,000 car in St. Louis?
Do this one at the kitchen table with the phone calculator, before the dealer’s numbers start swimming. Multiply the net price by the state rate plus your local rate. Net price means the purchase price less any trade-in allowance. Here are two common price points at the chart’s rates, no trade-in.
Take a $5,000 car as an example: the state share is $211.25, and the total is $386.90 at a base county address (7.738%), $436.90 on a Missouri-dealer sale in one of the twelve 4.513% county areas (8.738%) and $483.95 in the city (9.679%).
Take a $16,000 car as a second example: the state share is $676.00, and the total is $1,238.08 at a base county address, $1,398.08 on a Missouri-dealer sale in one of the twelve 4.513% areas and $1,548.64 in the city.
Here’s the math once, so you can check any quote. A $16,000 car at a base county address: $16,000 times 4.225% is $676.00 for the state, $16,000 times 3.513% is $562.08 local, and together that’s $1,238.08. In the city, the local share is $16,000 times 5.454%, or $872.64, for $1,548.64 in all.
Then add the $8.50 title fee and the $9 title processing fee, $17.50 together. A nurse in Bevo Mill who buys a $5,000 commuter car from a coworker walks into the license office owing $483.95 in tax and $17.50 for the title, before plates. If she walks in on day 45 instead of day 25, add a $25 penalty.
You can pay by cash, personal check, money order or card. The card vendor’s convenience fee is 2.0% plus $0.25 per transaction, so a $1,000 tax payment on plastic adds $20.25.
### What happens if you miss the 30-day window?
You notice it at a red light: the paper tag in the back window has curled at one corner and the date on it is close. The penalty lands on the 31st day, and it grows. Under RSMo 301.190 and the Department’s titling page, the title penalty is $25 on the 31st day after purchase and another $25 for every 30 days you are late, with a maximum penalty of $200.
The penalty is the small part. The paper tag is the bigger trap. A temporary permit may be issued for a period of 30 days from the purchase date, it costs a $5 permit fee plus a $9 processing fee at a license office, and only one temporary permit may be purchased per vehicle. When it runs out, that cardboard square in the back window is just cardboard.
And the state will know a sale happened. Private sellers report it on a Notice of Sale or Bill of Sale. A seller who fails to report the sale is guilty of an infraction with a fine of up to $200, or a class C misdemeanor with a fine of up to $300 if it was done to help the buyer avoid applying for title.
Most late titles are a lienholder slow to mail a title, or a buyer who assumed somebody else had it handled. If you are unable to obtain the title, the Department’s motor vehicle line is 573-526-3669. Call before day 30, not after.
New plates, first dent? Here’s how to read a body shop estimate.
### What to bring to the license office
The folder should be thick enough to bend. For a car getting new plates, the Department’s list comes down to this:
The Certificate of Title signed over to you, or the Manufacturer’s Statement of Origin on a brand-new car.
A signed Application for Missouri Title and License, Form 108.
A safety inspection not more than 60 days old, unless the vehicle is less than eleven years old and the mileage is less than 150,000 miles.
An emissions inspection not more than 60 days old if you live in St. Louis City or St. Louis County. Our guide to Missouri car inspections in St. Louis covers what fails.
A current insurance identification card.
Last year’s paid personal property tax receipt, or a statement of non-assessment. Here’s how to get the personal property tax receipt or waiver.
Any bill of sale that supports a tax credit, covered next.
### Can selling your old car yourself still lower the tax?
Yes. RSMo 144.025 extends the trade-in treatment to a car you sell yourself, as long as you buy the next one within 180 days before or after the date of the sale and bring the bills of sale showing the paid sale price when you title. The sale price comes off the new car’s price before the tax is figured.
Run it on the $16,000 car. Say you sold your old sedan to a neighbor for $6,000, cash counted out on the hood, two months before buying. Bring that bill of sale and you’re taxed on $10,000, not $16,000. At the base county rate of 7.738%, that’s $773.80 instead of $1,238.08, a $464.28 difference.
The window runs both ways: 180 days before or after the sale of the old vehicle.
It doesn’t have to be car for car. The statute covers motor vehicles, trailers, boats and outboard motors, or any combination of them.
More than one sale can count, as long as all the bills of sale are presented at titling.
Sold the old car after you already titled the new one? The Department’s Form 426 has a 180-Day Credit refund box for that case.
### Do family gifts and private sales get taxed the same way?
No. The Department’s instructions for sellers say the new owner of a gifted vehicle will not pay state or local tax on a gift transaction, as long as the paperwork shows it’s a gift:
The giver writes GIFT in the sale price area of the title. The Department says not to use a sale price of $1.
The giver signs a General Affidavit, Form 768, or a written statement that the vehicle was a gift. It does not have to be notarized.
The gift still gets reported to the Department within 30 days on a Notice of Sale or Bill of Sale.
Picture a grandmother in Carondelet pressing the keys to her old hatchback into a grandson’s palm. Done as a gift, he pays title and plate fees and no sales tax. Done as a $1 sale, it’s neither a clean gift nor an honest sale, and the titling manual says the Department of Revenue has the authority to request additional documentation any time the purchase price of a vehicle is questionable.
A private sale from a neighbor, a coworker or an online listing carries the same 4.225% state rate plus your local rate, paid at the license office. Our checklist for checking a used car before buying covers the car itself, and a vehicle won at a public auto auction runs on the same 30-day clock.
### What if you bought the car outside Missouri?
Keep the other state’s tax receipt with the title, not in a junk drawer. You still pay Missouri tax when you title it here, minus what you already paid. The Department’s titling FAQ says tax paid to another state is credited toward the amount due in Missouri, you must provide proof of the amount, and if the other state’s tax was less, you will be assessed the difference. If the vehicle was titled in your name in another state for more than 90 days, no Missouri sales tax will be assessed.
### How much do title, plates and registration add?
Far less than the tax, which is why the receipt the clerk slides across the counter feels lighter than you braced for. Every title carries the $8.50 title fee and the $9 title processing fee. Plates for a passenger vehicle are priced by the taxable horsepower printed on your title, under the Department’s fee chart: a one-year fee from $18.25 for under 12 horsepower or an electric vehicle up to $51.25 for 72 horsepower and up, plus a $9 processing fee. Two years costs $36.50 to $102.50, with an $18 processing fee.
So a $16,000 car at a base county address, titled on time with one-year plates in the 24-35 horsepower bracket ($24.25 plus $9 processing), comes to $1,238.08 in tax, $17.50 for the title and $33.25 for plates. That’s $1,288.83 at the counter.
Then a second bill arrives at the end of the year. The City of St. Louis Assessor lists an auto as personal property that has to be declared, and our guide to St. Louis County personal property tax covers the county side.
People are asking
### Is there a St. Louis personal property tax calculator for a car?
You can run the math yourself in one line. The City of St. Louis Assessor says vehicle values are based on the average trade-in value published by the National Automobile Dealers Association, and personal property is assessed at one-third of its value; its own example is a $15,000 market value divided by 3 for a $5,000 assessed value. Taxes are imposed on that assessed value at the rates the Assessor posts each year, and the bill is due no later than December 31.
### What is changing about how Missouri collects vehicle sales tax?
One day the tax will be on the same desk where you sign, pen still warm. Dealer sales are moving to point-of-sale collection, just not yet. Senate Bill 28 took effect August 28, and the Department of Revenue said in an August 2025 release that once the second phase of its new FUSION system is operational, buyers purchasing through a dealership will pay sales tax at the point of sale. Private-party buyers will continue to take their bill of sale to a Missouri license office.
That release projected late 2026 or early 2027. The Department’s August 2026 dealer newsletter now headlines FUSION implementation in mid-February 2027. When it lands, money you once had 30 days to gather will be due the day you sign.
This is general information, not tax or legal advice. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply these rules to your purchase, and our St. Louis Automotive directory is a place to start.
Look up your own line on the state chart before you sign anything. Then compare out-the-door prices at car dealerships around St. Louis with your real tax number already in hand.
If you run a dealership, a used-car lot or a title and tag service, the buyer reading this is about to ask who can walk them through the paperwork. When a neighbor, or the AI they ask, names a shop, that shop gets the customers. List your dealership where they’re already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the sales tax rate for cars in St. Louis county?
A.  It depends on your address and the seller. On the state’s vehicle rate chart, base St. Louis County carries 3.513% local plus the state’s 4.225%, or 7.738% combined. Twelve county areas show 4.513% local on Missouri-dealer sales, and cities inside the county add their own taxes. The city of St. Louis is 9.679%.
### Q. How much is tax and title on a car in Missouri?
A.  Tax is 4.225% state plus your local rate, on the price less any trade-in. The title adds an $8.50 fee and a $9 processing fee. Take a $16,000 car at a base St. Louis County address: $1,238.08 in tax at 7.738% plus $17.50 in title fees is $1,255.58 before plates. In the city of St. Louis, $1,548.64 in tax at 9.679% plus $17.50 is $1,566.14.
### Q. How much do plates and registration cost in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the taxable horsepower on your title. A one-year passenger registration runs from $18.25 for under 12 horsepower or an electric vehicle to $51.25 for 72 and up, plus a $9 processing fee. Two years runs $36.50 to $102.50, with an $18 processing fee.
### Q. How to avoid sales tax on a car in Missouri?
A.  You can’t skip it, but legal rules shrink it. A trade-in lowers the taxable price, and so does selling your old vehicle yourself within 180 days before or after buying. The new owner of a gifted vehicle does not pay state or local tax on the gift. In twelve St. Louis County areas, a car bought from a seller who isn’t a licensed Missouri dealer also carries a point less local tax.
### Q. What are the recent changes to the Missouri vehicle sales tax law?
A.  Senate Bill 28, which the Department said in August 2025 would take effect August 28, moves sales tax collection to the dealership for dealer sales once the Department of Revenue’s FUSION system is operational. Its August 2026 dealer newsletter points to mid-February 2027. Private-sale buyers will still pay at a license office.
### Q. Do you pay sales tax on vehicles in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Missouri taxes the person titling a vehicle at 4.225% state plus the local rate at the owner’s address, on the price less any trade-in. Dealer and private sales alike are paid at a license office within 30 days. The new owner of a gifted vehicle does not pay state or local tax on the gift.
### Q. How much sales tax will I pay on a $5,000 car in Missouri?
A.  The state share is $211.25. At a base St. Louis County address, $5,000 times 7.738% (3.513% local plus 4.225% state) is $386.90. In the city of St. Louis, $5,000 times 9.679% is $483.95. Subtract any trade-in or qualifying sale of your old car first, then add $17.50 in title fees.
### Q. What is the sales tax on a $16,000 car?
A.  In Missouri, the state share on $16,000 is $676.00. At a base St. Louis County address, $16,000 times 7.738% is $1,238.08; from a Missouri dealer in one of the twelve 4.513% county areas, $16,000 times 8.738% is $1,398.08; in the city of St. Louis, $16,000 times 9.679% is $1,548.64. Sell your old car for $6,000 within 180 days and only $10,000 is taxed, $773.80 at the base county rate of 7.738%.

## Lease vs Buy a Car: The Real Math, Mileage Traps, and When Gap Insurance Is Worth It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lease-vs-buy-a-car-and-gap-insurance
What is that lower lease payment actually buying you? Not a car. It buys the right to drive through the most expensive stretch of that car’s life, the first few years, when its value usually falls fastest, plus a finance charge written as a tiny decimal that federal rules won’t let the leasing company call an annual percentage rate. And if the car is totaled in month eight, the insurance check and what you still owe turn out to be two different numbers. Somebody covers the difference. Unless you planned for it, that’s you.
None of this is hidden. It’s in the federal lease disclosure the dealer slides across the desk, written in words nobody taught us in school: capitalized cost, residual value, rent charge. The finance office uses them all day. You see them once every few years, after a long test drive. That’s the house edge, and it has nothing to do with being bad at money.
Below: what a lease payment is made of, one lease-versus-buy example with the math shown, the Missouri tax rules that shift it, and the gap decision. Our guide to a credit union versus bank auto loan in St. Louis covers the basics of owing more than a car is worth. This goes further. The St. Louis money guide has the rest of the series.
### What are the disadvantages of a lease car?
You build no ownership. Lease payments cover the car’s steepest years of value loss plus a rent charge, and unless you buy it at the end, you hand it back with no equity. You also accept a mileage cap, charges for wear beyond the lessor’s standard, and an early termination bill that can reach several thousand dollars.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau puts the core trade bluntly: leasing is like renting, and your payments don’t go toward owning the car unless the lease includes an option to buy it.
Mileage. Most leases cap you at 10,000 to 15,000 miles a year, the CFPB says, and charge for every mile over.
Wear. The leasing company usually decides what counts as excessive. Federal rules require its standards to be in the lease and to be reasonable, which isn’t the same as lenient.
Getting out early. You can’t simply return the car and stop paying. Federal Regulation M requires a consumer vehicle lease to warn that ending it early may cost a substantial charge, possibly several thousand dollars.
A payment that never ends. Lease, turn in, lease again.
The early-months hole. For a while, the car is usually worth less than it would cost to end the lease. That’s what gap coverage is for.
In fairness, leases have real upsides: a lower payment for the same car, no selling or trade-in haggling, and in a closed-end lease, if the car ends up worth less than the lessor predicted, that’s the lessor’s loss. You still owe excess wear and mileage charges. The trouble starts when the monthly payment is the only number anyone discusses.
### What are you actually paying for in a lease payment?
Two things: the value the car loses while you drive it, and a rent charge for the money tied up in it. Federal rules require your lease disclosure to show the four terms that set both.
Capitalized cost: the car’s price inside the lease, plus anything rolled in. Negotiate it like a sale price.
Capitalized cost reduction: your down payment, trade-in credit or rebate.
Residual value: the lessor’s forecast of what the car is worth at the end.
Rent charge: the lease version of interest.
Depreciation is plain division: capitalized cost minus residual, spread over the months. The rent charge is where the fine print lives. The Federal Reserve’s leasing guide says it’s usually set with a money factor, a decimal like 0.0025, multiplied by the capitalized cost plus the residual, and that the money factor typically isn’t disclosed to you. Regulation M adds a twist: a lessor that quotes a rate at all may not call it an “annual percentage rate.”
So translate it yourself. Multiply the money factor by 2,400 for a close stand-in for an APR, the yearly interest rate you’d compare on a loan. A money factor of 0.0025 is about 6%. One of 0.0040 is about 9.6%. Why 2,400? The formula adds the starting and ending values, which is twice the average amount financed, so you divide out that 2 and the 12 months, then multiply by 100 for a percentage: 2 x 12 x 100. In the example below, the exact rate behind 0.0025 comes to about 6.03%.
Get the money factor in writing and hold the result next to a bank or credit union loan rate on the same car. A few points higher means you’re paying for that friendly monthly number in interest. These disclosure rules cover consumer leases with a total contractual obligation up to $73,400, a ceiling adjusted each year.
### Is it cheaper to lease or buy the same car?
Over three years, it’s closer than most people expect. Over six, buying pulls far ahead, if you keep the car. Here’s an illustrative example in round numbers, before taxes and fees.
The car has a $40,000 negotiated price. The lease runs 36 months with nothing down, a $24,000 residual and a money factor of 0.0025, about 6%. The loan is $40,000 at 6% APR for 60 months.
The lease math: $16,000 of depreciation ($40,000 minus $24,000) divided by 36 is $444.44. The rent charge is 0.0025 x ($40,000 + $24,000), or $160. Together that’s $604.44 a month, which over the term is $16,000 for the value you used plus $5,760 in rent charges.
The buyer pays $773.31 a month and, after 36 payments, still owes about $17,448. If the car is worth the $24,000 the lessor predicted, the buyer could sell it, clear the loan and keep about $6,552. Take that from $27,839 in payments and three years cost about $21,287. Within $500 of the lease.
That’s what nobody explains at the desk. A fairly priced lease isn’t a trick. It charges the same depreciation and roughly the same interest a loan would, sliced smaller because you pay only for the part you use. The real differences are who carries the risk that the residual guess is wrong, and what happens after month 36.
Stretch it to six years. Two back-to-back leases on the same terms cost $43,520 and leave you with no car. The buyer pays the loan off at month 60, about $46,399 in all. Say the car is then worth $15,000. Net cost: about $31,399, roughly $12,100 less than leasing, and the difference grows every month the paid-off car stays on the road. The buyer does pay for the repairs that come with age.
### What do mileage caps, wear charges and early exits really cost?
More than the payment suggests. Federal rules make the lessor disclose the excess-mileage charge, or how it’s figured, before you sign. A 36-month lease at 12,000 miles a year allows 36,000. A 25-mile commute each way across the metro, five days a week for 50 weeks, is 12,500 miles a year before a single weekend errand. Drive 15,000 a year and you return the car 9,000 miles over. At an illustrative 25 cents a mile, that’s $2,250 on turn-in day.
Buying miles up front can cost less. The Federal Reserve’s leasing guide walks through a case where a higher mileage allowance negotiated at signing beat paying the overage at turn-in, because the extra miles were priced into a lower residual. Guess high on your driving.
Wear works the same way. Regulation M requires the lease to warn that you may be charged for excessive wear based on the lessor’s standards for normal use. Read those standards at signing, not the week before turn-in. Kids, a dog and a tight garage all show up at inspection. Many lessors also charge a disposition fee at return to cover part of the cost of cleaning, inspecting and selling the car, while others build it into the payment. Regulation M requires charges like that to be itemized.
Leaving early costs the most. The Federal Reserve says the early termination charge is typically what you still owe on the lease minus the amount credited for the car, often a wholesale value, plus fees. Early on, the car has usually lost value faster than your payments covered, so the charge is biggest then. A baby, a job in another state, a layoff: none of them stop the meter.
Lease turn-in day is payday for detailers. How St. Louis detailers build a business
### How does Missouri tax a leased car?
Differently from a car you buy. Buy one, and Missouri collects 4.225% state sales tax plus your local sales tax on the purchase price, less any trade-in allowance, when you title the car at a license office within 30 days. On a $40,000 car with no trade-in, the state portion alone is $1,690, all at once. Our guide to Missouri car sales tax at the license office covers that visit.
Leases run on a different track. Missouri law lets an approved leasing company either pay the tax when it registers the car or collect sales tax on each lease payment while the car is based here. On the payment route, a 2024 Department of Revenue letter ruling says each payment is taxed at the rate where the lessee is located when it’s made, and the payments stop being subject to Missouri’s motor vehicle sales tax once the lessee moves out of state. That ruling answered one taxpayer, but it shows how the department reads the law.
On our example lease, $21,760 in payments at the same 4.225% state rate is about $919, paid a little at a time, against $1,690 up front to buy. That’s three years of driving, not a car you keep, but it shows the shape. Local tax stacks on both. If the lessor paid at registration instead, ask how that cost reaches you.
Personal property tax trips up lessees at plate renewal. Cars here are taxed every year as personal property, and on a lease the leasing company holds the title. The Department of Revenue says that to register or renew a leased vehicle, the paid personal property tax receipt must be in the leasing company’s name. Ask at signing how the lessor handles that tax and whether it bills you, then keep its receipt with your renewal notice. Our guide to the St. Louis County personal property tax covers the bill itself.
Buying the car at lease end is a purchase, and titling a purchase is when Missouri collects sales tax. Ask the license office how your buyout will be taxed before you sign.
### What happens if a leased or financed car is totaled in month eight?
Your insurer pays what the car was worth, not what you owe. The CFPB says standard auto insurance only pays up to the value of your vehicle. Any balance above that is still yours, on a car headed for salvage.
Run month eight on our example. The $40,000 loan has about $35,330 left after eight payments. Say the insurer values the car at $32,000 and your deductible is $500. The lender gets $31,500 and you still owe about $3,830. Gap would typically cover the roughly $3,330 between balance and value, but the Federal Reserve notes that in most cases it doesn’t cover your deductible.
The lease is worse. Eight payments into our zero-down lease, ending it costs roughly $36,700, depending on how the lessor figures it, so the same $32,000 valuation leaves a hole of about $4,700. The Federal Reserve’s own illustration shows the pattern: on a $22,000 vehicle in month one, a $2,700 gap on the lease against $1,000 on a loan with more money down.
The good news: the Federal Reserve says many leases include gap coverage as a standard feature at no separate charge. Read yours before paying for gap twice.
Know what gap won’t touch. The same guide lists your down payment or capitalized cost reduction, past-due payments, and amounts like personal property taxes or parking tickets. Rolled-in debt digs the hole deeper, too. Put $5,000 of old balance into our example and month eight shows about $39,750 owed on that same $32,000 car, a gap near $7,750.
### Gap insurance or a gap waiver: which one are you buying, and from whom?
Three places sell it, and the product changes with the seller. From your auto insurer, gap is an add-on that sits on top of your collision and comprehensive coverage. From a dealer or lender, it’s a contract attached to the loan or lease, sometimes called a waiver or an addendum. Missouri’s statute lumps them together as a “deficiency waiver addendum, guaranteed asset protection, or a similar product.”
Your auto insurer. The CFPB says your own insurer may offer GAP, so price it there first. Not every insurer sells it.
Your lender. Some direct lenders offer it too, per the CFPB, so ask the bank or credit union making the loan.
The dealer’s finance office. It’s one of several optional add-ons a dealer will likely offer. Told it’s required for financing? Ask where the contract says so. Our guide to what the finance office is selling you covers the rest of that menu.
Missouri adds protections the national explainers skip. Under section 408.380 of state law, GAP or a deficiency waiver sold as part of a loan with collateral needs your written consent, with a reasonable cost disclosed in the loan contract. You can cancel within 15 days of buying it for a complete refund, a right that must be disclosed in 10-point type. If the product ends before the loan’s scheduled maturity, the refund is figured pro rata, in proportion to the time left. The CFPB lists selling, refinancing and paying off early as times a refund may be owed.
One caution. Dealer-arranged financing is typically a retail installment contract, which Missouri governs under a separate motor vehicle time sales law, so don’t assume section 408.380 applies word for word. Your contract’s cancellation section should spell out the refund math. If a refund never arrives, gap sold by an insurer goes to the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance, which takes complaints about insurers and agents. Gap that came with your loan is a lender matter, and the CFPB takes complaints about auto loans.
### When does a lease make sense, and when is it a trap?
A lease fits when your miles are predictable and under the cap, you want a newer car every few years and accept a payment that never goes away, and you’d rather hand the residual gamble to the lessor. That’s a fair price for predictability. It turns into a trap when:
Your miles are unpredictable, or a new job could double your commute.
You might need out early: a move, a baby, shaky work.
You’re rolling negative equity into the lease. That old balance lands in the capitalized cost and raises the payment.
The monthly payment is the only number on the table.
You keep cars six years or longer.
Either way, a car payment is a monthly obligation lenders see when you apply for a mortgage, and our look at why it’s easier to buy a car than a house explains how it weighs on a home loan. Before you sign anything, get the capitalized cost, the money factor, the per-mile charge and every add-on price in writing. Then sleep on it. Nothing about a lease improves at nine o’clock at night in a finance office.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can price gap against your own policy, a loan officer can quote the financing side, and our St. Louis automotive directory is a place to start.
Shopping your next car payment? Line up a loan quote and a gap quote before you visit a lot, then compare auto lenders around St. Louis against whatever the finance office slides across the desk.
And if you’re the dealer, credit union or insurance agent those families are comparing, being the name a St. Louis neighbor, or the AI they ask, hears first is the whole game, so list your business where they look.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to lease a car for 24 or 36 months?
A.  Neither wins on its face. A 24-month lease squeezes the car’s fastest-falling stretch of value into fewer payments, so the monthly number usually runs higher. A 36-month lease spreads that depreciation out and lowers the payment, but adds a year of mileage and wear exposure. Compare total cost: everything due at signing plus all payments, divided by the months you drive.
### Q. Can you customize a leased car?
A.  Check the lease first, because the leasing company owns the car. Add-ons you can remove before turn-in carry less risk. Permanent changes are the lessor’s call, and anything outside its wear-and-use standards, which Regulation M requires it to disclose, can turn into a charge at inspection. When in doubt, ask in writing first.
### Q. How does gap insurance work if a car is totaled?
A.  Your insurer declares a total loss and pays the car’s value, minus your deductible, toward the loan or lease. Gap then covers the difference between that value and the remaining balance. Per the Federal Reserve’s leasing guide, it typically won’t pay your deductible, past-due payments or your down payment.
### Q. Is gap insurance really worth it?
A.  It earns its price when the hole is big and you couldn’t cover it from savings: little or nothing down, a long loan, rolled-in negative equity, or a lease without gap built in. The hole shrinks each month as you pay down the balance, so gap is worth the most at the start.
### Q. When not to get gap insurance?
A.  It has little to do when you owe less than the car is worth from day one, thanks to a big down payment or a short loan, or when you pay cash. Check your lease, too, since the Federal Reserve says many include gap at no separate charge. Once your balance drops below the car’s value, gap has nothing left to pay.
### Q. Can I purchase just gap insurance by itself?
A.  Not as a replacement for car insurance. Gap only fills the difference between a total-loss payout and your balance, so it rides on top of collision and comprehensive coverage. You can buy it apart from the car deal, though: the CFPB says your own insurer may offer it, some direct lenders sell it, and you can decline the dealer’s version.
### Q. Can I get a gap insurance refund?
A.  In many cases, yes. The CFPB says a refund may be owed if you sell, refinance or pay off the loan early. For GAP sold with a secured loan, Missouri’s section 408.380 requires a complete refund if you cancel within 15 days and a pro rata refund if the product ends before the loan’s scheduled maturity.
### Q. Should I keep gap insurance after I paid off my car?
A.  There’s little reason to. With the loan paid off, there’s no balance for gap to cover. If it’s an add-on to your auto policy, ask your insurer to remove it. If you bought it as a contract with the loan, ask the provider whether any unused portion is refundable. The CFPB says you can cancel optional add-ons at any time.

## How to Budget on a St. Louis Paycheck: The 1% City Tax and Car Tax Your Template Misses
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-budget-on-a-st-louis-paycheck
1%. That’s the City of St. Louis earnings tax, and the City’s own earnings tax page says every City resident owes it, regardless of where their employer is located. It became law in 1954. The free budget template you downloaded has never heard of it.
Here’s where that number lands. The kitchen table in spring, a W-2 flattened under a coffee mug, the calculator app open, and the slow sink in your stomach when you realize your job sits outside City limits and nobody withheld a cent of it all year. The City expects the return and the money by April 15 anyway. Its page says plainly that each taxpayer is responsible, penalty and interest included, whether or not the employer withheld.
On $50,000 of wages, 1% is $500. Money you already spent on groceries and gas, now owed in one lump. Then, a few months later, a second envelope: the yearly personal property tax on your car, mailed in November and due by December 31. Neither bill means you’re bad with money. St. Louis simply taxes your paycheck and your car on its own calendar, and a template built for the whole country can’t know that. So this is the budget built the local way, from take-home pay, with both lines baked in. It’s one stop in our St. Louis money guide.
### How should a beginner budget?
Start with take-home pay, the amount that actually lands in your account, not your salary. List every fixed bill, turn once-a-year bills into monthly set-asides, and give each leftover dollar a job: needs, wants, or savings and debt. Track one full month, then adjust. In St. Louis, add the City earnings tax and the yearly tax on your car.
Why take-home? Because gross pay is a rumor. Federal and Missouri income tax, Social Security and Medicare, health premiums, retirement and, for many people, the City’s 1% leave before the deposit alert ever buzzes your phone. Budget from the offer letter and you’re spending money that was never yours. If the stub reads like a foreign language, our guide to the Missouri W-4 and your pay stub walks it line by line.
The pieces are the same for everybody. Income. Fixed bills. Spending that moves around. Savings and debt payoff. And the irregular stuff that wrecks whatever month it lands in. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Your Money, Your Goals toolkit has tools for this, including a spending tracker and a bill calendar.
The bill calendar is the sleeper. Write each due date next to your paydays and the trouble shows itself. Most budgets don’t fail on the total. They fail on timing, when rent is due on the 1st and the check lands on the 5th, and you spend four days refreshing the bank app.
### Which St. Louis bills does a budget template forget?
Two, mostly: the City earnings tax when your employer isn’t withholding it, and the yearly personal property tax on your car. Both are real money. Both run on a schedule nobody explains. Both turn harmless once they become a monthly line.
The earnings tax first. The City collects the 1% from residents of the City, wherever they work, and from people who work for businesses in the City, wherever they live. If your employer withholds it, it’s already gone from your take-home and you’re done. The trap is the City resident whose job is outside City limits. Form E-1 is due April 15, the City doesn’t allow individuals to file extensions, and late tax draws a penalty of 5% a month, up to 25%, plus 1% a month in interest. Not sure yours is withheld? The City says to call its office at (314) 622-4101 with a copy of your W-2. Our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax covers the rest.
The fix is boring, which is the point. On $60,000 of wages the 1% is $600 a year, so move $50 to savings every month and let it sit there until April.
Now the car. The City’s personal property page lays out the cycle: assessment lists go out in January, declarations are due April 1, tax bills are mailed in November, and payment is due no later than December 31. Vehicles are assessed at one-third of their value, and the City prints the example itself: a $15,000 car is $5,000 of assessed value. Your bill is that assessed value times the rate on the City’s yearly tax rate sheet. Take last year’s bill, divide by 12, and that’s your monthly line.
Skip the set-aside and the bill finds you anyway, usually while you’re buying presents. It has teeth, too: to renew your plates, the Missouri Department of Revenue asks for a paid personal property tax receipt or a statement of non-assessment. New residents qualify for that waiver. The bill shows up later, right when the budget finally felt settled. Live in the County instead? It bills at its own rates, and our guide to personal property tax in the County and the City runs that math.
### What does a realistic St. Louis monthly budget look like?
Something close to this, if you rent a one-bedroom and bring home $3,600 a month. The figures are illustrative, but the rent line isn’t a guess. It’s HUD’s fiscal year 2027 fair market rent for a one-bedroom in the St. Louis metro: $1,104 a month. The year before it was $995, a $109 jump in one update, which is why last year’s budget advice can already be stale.
A one-bedroom budget
### What is a realistic monthly budget?
On $3,600 a month after taxes, the 50/30/20 rule gives $1,800 for needs, $1,080 for wants and $720 for savings and debt. In St. Louis the rent line is real: HUD’s fair market rent for a metro one-bedroom is $1,104 a month, and City residents should set money aside for the 1% earnings tax.
HUD sets that figure at the 40th percentile, the amount below which 40% of standard-quality rentals are rented, drawn from recent movers, per HUD’s own definition. Treat it as a rent-plus-utilities line, and keep phone and internet separate.
Health insurance and retirement aren’t listed because they came out before the deposit. The forgot-it line is real, because every budget misses something the first month: the parking ticket, the birthday you remembered at 9 p.m., the co-pay. If you want to see how your split stacks up against real households, the Bureau of Labor Statistics keeps a St. Louis consumer spending release. Our look at the real cost of living in St. Louis and our guide to how much rent you can afford cover the housing side.
### Does the 50/30/20 rule work on a St. Louis paycheck?
Often, yes, as a starting check. The rule splits after-tax pay three ways: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and debt payments beyond the minimums. On $3,600 that’s $1,800, $1,080 and $720. It breaks in two predictable places.
The first is housing. At $3,600 take-home, the metro’s $1,104 one-bedroom figure is 31% of pay. Workable. At $2,800, the same apartment eats 39%, which leaves about $300 of the needs half for groceries, the car, the phone and every minimum payment combined. That doesn’t fit, and it isn’t a character flaw. The wants bucket shrinks until the math closes.
The second is debt. The average rate on bank credit card accounts that were assessed interest was 22.36% in August 2026, according to the Federal Reserve’s consumer credit report. At that price, the 20% bucket should lean hard toward the card. A budget that dutifully saves 20% while a balance compounds at about 22% balances on paper and loses in real life.
The illustrative budget above lands near 58/22/20, and that’s a healthy budget. Rent wasn’t the problem. The car, the student loan and the car tax were. Treat 50/30/20 like a check-engine light. It tells you where to look. It doesn’t grade you.
### What is zero-based budgeting, and when does it beat 50/30/20?
Zero-based budgeting means income minus every planned dollar equals zero. Not zero in the bank. Zero unassigned. Savings, the car-tax set-aside and the forgot-it line all count as assignments, so the month is spoken for before it starts.
It beats percentage rules in three spots. When money is tight, because a percentage can’t say which bill to pay first and a priority list can. When income moves with tips, commissions or a side gig, because you budget the month you’re actually in. And during debt payoff, because every spare dollar gets aimed at a balance on purpose.
Is the kids’ club soccer line the one that never balances? Here’s what a season really costs.
On payday, write the deposit at the top of a sheet of paper. List what must be paid before the next payday, in order: housing, utilities, food, transportation, minimum payments. Then the set-asides, savings and wants, until the remainder hits zero. Crossing off each line with a pen feels better than any app.
One quirk helps. Paid every two weeks? That’s 26 checks a year, so two months bring a third. Build the budget on two checks a month and give each extra one a job in advance. In the illustration, a third check of about $1,660 would build a $1,000 starter emergency fund by itself.
### How much emergency fund do you need in Missouri?
Start with $500, then $1,000. After that, a common target is three to six months of essential expenses, not total spending. In the illustrative budget, essentials run $2,100 a month, so three months is $6,300 and six months is $12,600.
Why such a small first goal? Because most emergencies aren’t layoffs. They’re the tire that goes flat on the way to work, the furnace that clicks and won’t light, the co-pay. The CFPB’s 2022 report on emergency savings digs into how often those shocks hit. A $1,000 cushion covers most of them and keeps them off a card charging about 22%.
The bigger number is for losing a job, and here’s the Missouri math no template includes. The state’s maximum unemployment benefit is $320 a week, for no more than 20 weeks in a benefit year. Your weekly amount is 4% of the average of your two highest quarters, so plenty of people get less. Even at the full $320, that’s about $1,387 a month. HUD’s fair market rent for a two-bedroom in the metro is $1,349. Do the subtraction. The best-case check covers a family’s rent, leaves about $38 for everything else, and stops after 20 weeks.
So three months of essentials is the floor for a household with one steady paycheck. Six fits a single income with kids, a field where job searches drag, or pay that swings. If most of your income is freelance or gig work, plan as if that $320 won’t come at all.
### Where should you keep an emergency fund?
Somewhere insured, boring and one step away from your debit card. The CFPB’s guide to building an emergency fund points to a bank or credit union account, kept where you won’t be tempted to spend it on things that aren’t emergencies.
Insured is the key word. FDIC deposit insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category. At a federally insured credit union, the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund insures individual accounts up to $250,000 as well.
Then put it on autopilot: an automatic transfer from checking to savings the morning the paycheck lands, before you ever see the money. Watch the fees, because a $5 monthly charge on a $500 fund eats 1% of it every month. Our guide to avoiding bank fees in St. Louis lists every charge to ask about. And keep this money out of the stock market. Its job is to be there on the worst day, not to grow.
### When is a full year of emergency savings worth it?
For most people with one steady paycheck, a year is more than they need, and the honest reason is cost. Every dollar past six months is a dollar that could be paying off a card near 22%, collecting an employer’s retirement match, or working toward the next goal. Insured savings is safe. Safe doesn’t pay much.
A year stops being overkill when income could vanish for a long stretch. That covers the self-employed and gig workers who can’t lean on Missouri unemployment, commission and seasonal earners, single-income families with kids, specialized fields where a search can outlast the 20-week benefit cap, and anyone close to retirement who’d rather not sell investments in a down market.
Say you’re a self-employed photographer with $3,000 a month in essentials. A slow winter plus a dead camera can cost four months of income, and no state check is coming. For you, a year of essentials, $36,000, isn’t paranoia. It’s your sick leave, your severance and your unemployment insurance in one account.
Everyone else can take the middle path. Build three to six months first. Once high-rate debt is gone and you’re getting any match on offer, decide whether the next dollar buys a longer cushion or bigger goals. That’s a good question for a planner, and our guide to what a financial planner costs in St. Louis explains the fee models first.
Holding a W-2 and a knot in your stomach? Financial planners around St. Louis can build the budget and the emergency fund target around your real paycheck. Bring a recent pay stub, last year’s car tax bill and three months of statements.
If you’re the tax preparer, the money coach or the planner who sits at that kitchen table with people, list your practice and get more customers from the newcomers searching for help with a surprise City tax bill right now.
### What are the biggest budgeting mistakes?
Budgeting from gross pay, forgetting the yearly bills, and building a plan so strict it breaks by the second weekend. Most failed budgets trace back to one of those, and none of them is a willpower problem.
Budgeting the offer letter. The salary isn’t the deposit.
Forgetting the once-a-year bills: here, the car tax, plate renewal and, for some City residents, the earnings tax. Divide each by 12.
No room to be human. A budget with $0 for fun lasts about as long as a New Year’s resolution.
Calling everything an emergency. Christmas comes every December. Give it a set-aside.
Saving hard while a card compounds near 22%. Keep the starter fund, then aim the extra at the balance.
Quitting after one bad month. The first month is a rough draft.
And when a month goes sideways for reasons no budget could fix, a layoff, a hospital bill, a shutoff notice, the region has more help than most people hear about. Our list of St. Louis help and assistance resources covers housing, utilities, food and more.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed financial advisor or a CPA can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 50/30/20 rule budget?
A.  It splits take-home pay three ways: 50% for needs like housing, utilities, groceries, transportation and minimum payments, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and extra debt payments. On $3,600 a month that’s $1,800, $1,080 and $720. Treat it as a quick check. The illustrative St. Louis budget on this page lands nearer 58/22/20 once the car is counted.
### Q. Does the 50/30/20 rule actually work?
A.  As a starting point, yes. It works best when housing stays near a third of take-home pay and you aren’t carrying high-rate debt. It strains when rent eats 40% of the check or a card compounds near 22%. Then a zero-based budget, which gives every dollar a job in priority order, usually fits better.
### Q. What are the 5 basics to any budget?
A.  Take-home income, fixed bills, variable spending, savings and debt payoff, and irregular bills turned into monthly set-asides. The fifth is the one people miss. In St. Louis it includes the yearly personal property tax on your car, plate renewal and, for some City residents, the 1% earnings tax.
### Q. What bills do most adults pay monthly?
A.  Rent or a mortgage, utilities, phone and internet, groceries, car costs, health premiums, minimum debt payments and subscriptions. In St. Louis, treat two yearly bills as monthly too: the personal property tax on your car, where the City assesses a $15,000 car at $5,000, and the City earnings tax if your employer doesn’t withhold it.
### Q. Is $10,000 a good enough emergency fund?
A.  It depends on your essential monthly costs, not your income. With $2,100 a month in essentials, like the illustrative budget here, $10,000 covers nearly five months, inside the usual three-to-six-month range. A family with $4,500 a month in essentials gets a little over two months. Divide $10,000 by your own essentials to see where you stand.
### Q. Is a 1 year emergency fund overkill?
A.  For most households with one steady W-2 paycheck, yes. Three to six months of essentials covers the usual risks, and extra cash does more against high-rate debt or toward a retirement match. A year makes sense for the self-employed, commission or seasonal earners, single-income families and people near retirement, especially with Missouri unemployment capped at $320 a week for 20 weeks.
### Q. What is the meaning of emergency fund?
A.  Money set aside only for the things you can’t see coming: a car repair, a medical bill, a furnace that quits in January or a gap between jobs. Holidays and the yearly car tax aren’t emergencies, because you know they’re coming. They get their own set-asides.
### Q. How much should I save if I make $3,000 a month?
A.  If $3,000 is take-home, 50/30/20 says $600. Whether that’s realistic depends on rent. A one-bedroom at HUD’s $1,104 metro figure is 37% of that check, so a realistic start might be $150 to $300 a month, moved automatically on payday, until a $1,000 starter fund is built. Then raise it each time a debt is paid off.

## What Causes Inflation? A Plain Explanation From the City That Hosts the St. Louis Fed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-causes-inflation-st-louis-fed
One of twelve. That’s how many regional Federal Reserve Banks the country has, and one of them sits downtown at Broadway and Locust. St. Louis was among the 12 cities picked in 1914, when the banks opened for business that November. Today the St. Louis Fed’s research department runs FRED, a data site it has kept since the early 1990s that now holds hundreds of thousands of economic data series. The same price charts economists pull up are sitting right there. You can look up how fast prices are rising in St. Louis in about two minutes.
Most of us never got that tour. School covered the water cycle and the Louisiana Purchase, then sent us out into a world where the same cart of groceries costs more every year and nobody explains why. The receipt shows the total. It never shows the reason. So prices start to feel like weather, or like somebody running a con, and the only time we think about it is when a bill lands.
You’re not bad with money. Nobody showed you this part. Here’s the plain version, from the city that hosts one of the twelve, right down to where to click for the St. Louis numbers. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the series on the money stuff school skipped.
### Why are prices increasing?
Prices rise for three main reasons: shoppers and businesses try to buy more than the economy can produce (demand-pull), costs like fuel, materials and wages climb and get passed along (cost-push), and people expect higher prices and act on it. A sudden jump in one item, like gas or eggs, often traces to a supply problem.
Lately, energy is doing most of the shoving. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index report for August 2026, released September 11, showed overall prices up 3.4% from a year earlier. Gasoline alone was up 27.4%. Take food and energy out and everything else rose 2.4%, a much calmer number.
St. Louis is running a little cooler. BLS publishes a separate Consumer Price Index for the St. Louis area, covering the city and the surrounding counties on both sides of the river, and it comes out every two months. For the 12 months ending in August 2026, area prices rose 2.9%. Energy was up 12.9%, food 2.1%, and everything outside food and energy 2.2%.
Those figures go stale within weeks. That’s fine. The point is knowing where the next ones live.
One definition first, because it clears up half the confusion. Inflation isn’t one thing getting expensive. The Federal Reserve describes it as a general increase in the overall price level of goods and services. A spike in egg prices is a price problem. Rent, insurance, haircuts, daycare and car repairs all inching up together, month after month, is inflation.
### What actually pushes prices up: too much spending or higher costs?
Both, and they feel different at the register. Demand-pull is the classic. The St. Louis Fed’s Page One Economics describes it as demand outrunning what producers can supply, or in the old shorthand, too much money chasing too few goods.
Picture a spring when half the households in the county decide to redo a bathroom at once. Contractors book out for months. Tile runs short. Quotes go up, and not because tile got harder to make. Everybody just wants it at the same time. Spread that across the whole economy and you have demand-pull inflation.
Cost-push runs the other way. A business’s own costs climb, for fuel, ingredients, freight, insurance or wages, and some of that gets handed to the customer. Nobody suddenly wanted more of anything. It just cost more to make.
Here’s where living in a Fed city pays off: the St. Louis Fed asks businesses about this directly. In its August survey of firms in the Eighth District, the seven-state region the bank covers, businesses said the prices they charge rose about 3% over the previous 12 months, and they expect about the same pace over the next 12. Almost half said their nonlabor costs were higher than a year earlier. Firms said they pass higher costs along whenever possible, though only about a third said they’d actually managed it.
The fine print is shifting, too. In the same survey, 24% of firms saw suppliers adding temporary fees or surcharges, 27% saw suppliers changing prices more often, and 18% saw price quotes staying valid for less time. If a contractor’s estimate now expires in a week instead of a month, that’s cost-push showing up in the paperwork.
Then there’s the third engine: expectations. A business that expects its costs to keep rising marks prices up ahead of time. A worker who expects groceries to cost 4% more next year hears a 2% raise as a pay cut, the same point a St. Louis Fed economist makes in the bank’s explainer on inflation expectations. So workers push for more, employers pay it and raise prices to cover it, and prices climb partly because everyone braced for them to. Economists call that loop a wage-price spiral.
That’s why the Fed watches what people expect almost as closely as what prices do. When expectations sit near 2%, the same explainer notes, the Fed may not need to move rates as much. When they come loose, getting inflation down tends to cost more jobs.
### Why do gas and eggs jump while rent just creeps?
Because some prices sit on a hair trigger and others move like a barge on the Mississippi. Food and energy swing hard on news unrelated to the rest of the economy, so economists also track core inflation, which leaves those two out. The Fed’s explainer says such items go up and down in price dramatically or often.
Eggs are the textbook case. The USDA’s Food Price Outlook says an avian flu outbreak that began in 2022 pushed egg prices up by shrinking laying flocks and cutting egg production. Fix the supply and the price can fall fast. In its September 2026 update, USDA forecast egg prices to drop 29.4% for 2026.
Gas works the same way on a bigger stage. Gasoline follows crude oil, which trades on a world market no St. Louis station controls. There’s a local layer on top, too, which is why gas usually costs more on the Illinois side.
Rent and services are the barge. Leases reset once a year. Pay at a barbershop or a daycare changes gradually. Insurance gets repriced at renewal. Nationally, the shelter index rose 3.0% over the 12 months ending in August, a quieter number than gasoline’s, but one that lands on nearly every household every month.
So when a headline says inflation ticked up, ask which kind. A gas spike can fade within months. A services climb tends to linger: looking back at past slowdowns, St. Louis Fed economists concluded that goods inflation tends to fall quickly, while the last stretch depends on services, which take longer.
### How can you look up St. Louis inflation yourself?
Here’s the two-minute version, on the St. Louis Fed’s own data site.
Open FRED’s page for the national Consumer Price Index, series CPIAUCSL. That’s the CPI for All Urban Consumers, the headline number BLS releases every month.
Click Edit Graph. Under Units, switch Index to Percent Change from Year Ago. The line on your screen is now the inflation rate, month by month, going back decades.
Still in Edit Graph, add a second line: Personal Consumption Expenditures: Chain-type Price Index, the Fed’s preferred gauge, set to the same units. A FRED blog post notes CPI has generally run above PCE, by about half a percentage point on average since 1960.
Bring it home. Search FRED for St. Louis CPI and open the All Items index for St. Louis, MO-IL. FRED shows it as half-year averages, while the bimonthly St. Louis release lives on the BLS St. Louis CPI page.
Hit the Download button above any graph to save it as an image or a PowerPoint slide, or the numbers as an Excel or CSV file.
While you’re there, look at the raw index before you switch units. Both the national and St. Louis indexes are set to 100 for 1982 to 1984.
