And notice that no script on this page asks for a credit card, where federal law protects you from unauthorized charges.
Crypto from a kiosk is the hardest money to get back. Missouri’s kiosk law makes you acknowledge the purchase is final, irreversible and nonrefundable, and requires a receipt with the operator’s complaint number. Keep it.
### Where do you report a scam in Missouri?
Start with whoever can still stop the money, usually your bank, card issuer or payment company. Then build the record: the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) for anything online, the Missouri AG if a business was involved, and the police for any money lost or identity stolen.
Speed pays off most at IC3. The FBI’s 2025 IC3 annual report says its Recovery Asset Team worked 3,900 fraudulent-transfer incidents that year and froze $679,013,183, a 58% success rate. Its guidance: time is of the essence, so ask your bank to recall the funds, then file with IC3 no matter how small the loss. IC3 says it will never contact you directly for information or money, so hang up on anyone who calls claiming to be IC3 or offering to recover your money for a fee.
For the police report, SLMPD’s non-emergency line in the city is 314-231-1212, and St. Louis County Police are at 636-529-8210, though the county’s many municipalities take their own. Our guide to getting a police report in the St. Louis metro sorts out which department is yours.
If a scammer got your Social Security number, IdentityTheft.gov builds a recovery plan, and a freeze at all three credit bureaus blocks new accounts in your name. Here’s how to freeze your credit and handle identity theft in Missouri. If the person losing money is an aging parent, Missouri’s Adult Abuse and Neglect Hotline takes financial exploitation reports at 1-800-392-0210, 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and a durable power of attorney in Missouri lets a trusted person step in on the accounts before a stranger does.
### What are the most common consumer complaints in Missouri?
Illegal telemarketing calls, by a mile. The Missouri Attorney General’s office took more than 104,000 complaints and inquiries in 2025, and more than 33,600 went to the No-Call Unit. Automotive and financial complaints came next at more than 2,400 each, then retail at more than 1,900 and real estate and construction at more than 1,800.
Identity theft drew 984 complaints on the same top-ten list. For sales calls, Missouri’s No-Call list covers home and personal cell numbers; register online or at 1-866-662-2551. Telemarketers can’t call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m., and must stop when you say so.
The FBI’s numbers show where the money goes. Missourians filed 14,087 complaints with IC3 in 2025 and reported losses of $233,933,401, 22nd among the states on both counts. Missourians 60 and older filed 3,247 of those complaints, just under a quarter, yet reported $91,563,419 in losses, about 39% of the state’s total. Older neighbors aren’t the only targets. They’re the ones who lose the most when a script lands, so five minutes with a parent and the STOP list above may be the most valuable money talk you ever have.
This is general information, not legal or financial advice for your situation. A consumer attorney can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Legal directory is a place to start.
Lost money to a business that won’t answer, or wondering what Missouri’s consumer law lets you recover on your own? Talk it through with one of the general practice attorneys around St. Louis while the paper trail is fresh.
And if you run a credit union, a bank branch or a consumer-law practice, the neighbor who just hung up on a fake fraud department is about to ask someone, or some AI, who to trust next, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can a scammer be traced?
A.  Sometimes the money can, even when the person can’t. Caller ID is easy to fake, so the number usually leads nowhere. Bank transfers leave a trail, though, and the FBI’s IC3 Recovery Asset Team froze about $679 million in 2025 by working fast with banks. Missouri also makes crypto kiosk operators run blockchain analytics to help stop payments to wallets known for fraud. Report within hours, not days.
### Q. What should you never say to a scammer?
A.  Never read back a code that was texted to you. Never confirm your Social Security number, birth date or account numbers, and never give the numbers off a gift card. Don’t press a key to get off a call list either, since the FTC says that might lead to more robocalls. The safest thing to say is goodbye, then call the real company yourself.
### Q. Can a scammer get into my bank account with my phone number?
A.  Not with the number alone. They need your login or the one-time code your bank texts you, which is why fake fraud departments ask you to read it back. The bigger risk is a SIM swap, where a scammer talks your carrier into moving your number to their phone so the codes go to them. The FTC suggests adding a PIN or password to your cell account.
### Q. What happens if I answer a spam call and say hello?
A.  Answering isn’t what costs people money. What you do next is. The FTC’s advice is to hang up and not press any number to reach an operator or get off the list, because that might lead to more robocalls. Scammers can also fake the name and number on caller ID, so a local-looking call proves nothing. Block it and move on.
### Q. Who are the most common victims of scams?
A.  Everyone gets targeted, but older adults lose the most. In the FBI’s 2025 IC3 data, people 60 and over filed 201,266 complaints, more than any other age group, and reported $7.7 billion in losses, an average of $38,500 each against $20,699 for all filers. In Missouri, that age group filed just under a quarter of IC3 complaints but reported about 39% of the losses.
### Q. What is the name of the consumer protection law in Missouri?
A.  The Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, sections 407.010 to 407.130 of Missouri law. Section 407.020 bans deception, fraud, false promises, misrepresentation and unfair practices in a sale or ad, and doing it willfully and knowingly with intent to defraud is a class E felony. Section 407.025 lets a consumer who lost money on a personal or household purchase sue for actual damages, and a court may add punitive damages and attorney’s fees.
### Q. Does the Missouri No-Call list stop scam calls?
A.  No. It stops legitimate telemarketers, who get updated numbers from the Attorney General every three months. Scammers ignore no-call lists entirely, and the FTC says the national registry won’t stop illegal calls either. Register anyway, because the AG can enforce the Missouri No-Call law only for numbers on the list.
### Q. Can I get my money back from a gift card scam?
A.  Sometimes, if you move fast. The FTC says to call the company that issued the card, using the number on the back, tell them a scammer tricked you into sharing the card number and PIN, and ask for a refund. Keep the physical card and the store receipt, because you’ll need both. Then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

## How to Teach Kids About Money: By Age, Allowance Rules, and Missouri's Finance Class
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-teach-kids-about-money
Nobody taught us. That’s the quiet confession behind most St. Louis parents trying to teach kids about money. We learned it the expensive way: a first overdraft fee, a first paycheck that came in smaller than the hourly rate promised, a first credit card balance that kept growing while we paid on it.
That isn’t a character flaw. It’s a gap in the system. Missouri’s State Board of Education didn’t add personal finance to the graduation requirements until 2006, according to the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, and the requirements that include it apply starting with the class of 2010. Finished high school here before that? The state never required anyone to show you how a pay stub or credit card interest works. Today, Missouri public high school students must earn a half credit in personal finance to graduate.
Here’s the catch. That class is a high school credit, and the habits it’s trying to shape start years earlier. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis points to University of Cambridge research finding that children’s financial behaviors often develop as early as age 7. So the school class is the backstop. The kitchen table is the main event, and you don’t have to be a money expert to run it.
Below is the plan by age band, allowance rules of thumb, what Missouri’s class actually covers, and the free resources in town, including a downtown museum where your kid can try to lift a real gold bar. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide.
### At what age should you teach kids about money?
Start around age 3. Preschoolers can learn to wait, choose and count coins long before they understand abstract money. Don’t hold off until high school: a St. Louis Fed article, citing University of Cambridge research, says children’s financial behaviors often develop as early as age 7. Teens then add paychecks, accounts and credit.
The federal framework backs that timeline. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Money as You Grow program sorts kids into three stages: ages 3 to 5, ages 6 to 12, and teens into young adulthood. Preschoolers work on focus, persistence and noticing trade-offs. School-age kids build attitudes about saving and learn to plan ahead. Teens practice doing their own research, comparing options and making the call.
Notice what’s missing early on. Math. A 4-year-old doesn’t need to know what interest is. She needs reps at wanting something and waiting for it, the same muscle an adult uses to close the shopping app at 11 p.m. instead of hitting buy. Habits come first, and they come from watching you.
### What can a 3- to 5-year-old learn about money?
Three things: waiting, choosing and the idea that money comes from work. None of them needs a lecture. They need repetition in ordinary moments.
Waiting. The CFPB calls learning to wait essential to good savings habits and suggests practicing it wherever waiting already happens, like taking turns in a board game or standing in line at a restaurant. When your kid waits well, say so out loud.
Choosing. Give a 4-year-old two options and one firm rule: one, not both. Apples or crackers. It feels tiny. It’s actually a budget in miniature. The CFPB’s page for young children puts it in a line any parent can borrow: every time you spend money, you make a choice.
Where money comes from. To a preschooler, money lives inside a card or a phone. Tap it and the store hands over groceries. Correct that with your own job: tell them what you do all day and that the grocery money comes from that work.
Real coins. Let them count change into a clear jar and watch the pile grow, then pay for one small thing themselves. Cash is the only kind of money a 4-year-old can actually watch leave. For bedtime, the CFPB’s free Money as You Grow Bookshelf builds money talks around stories for kids roughly 4 to 10.
### How do you teach a 6- to 10-year-old to save, spend and give?
Give every dollar a job before it gets spent. At this age that usually means three clear jars labeled Spend, Save and Give, and a house rule that new money gets divided the moment it arrives, even birthday money.
The jars aren’t a craft project. They translate one of six lessons the St. Louis Fed’s economic education staff recommends teaching at home: people spend some of their income, save some and donate some, and kids should practice all three.
A few moves make the jars stick:
Put a picture on the Save jar. Saving for “later” means nothing to a 7-year-old. Saving for the exact toy taped to the glass means everything. Planning ahead and saving up for something wanted is one of the CFPB’s milestones for this stage.
Match what they save. The CFPB suggests adding money to their savings, such as five, ten or 25 cents for every dollar they put away, with a weekly or monthly cap. Call it their first employer match.
Let them buy the junk. If the Spend jar goes to a toy that breaks by Tuesday, don’t replace it. The St. Louis Fed’s advice is to let kids live with the consequences of spending choices, then talk them through. A $6 mistake at 8 is a bargain next to a $600 one at 22.
Let them pick the cause. The Give jar works best when the kid decides where it goes.
This is also when kids watch you hardest. The National Credit Union Administration’s youth savings guide notes that children learn by watching parents and caregivers earn, shop, save and borrow. So narrate. “I’m not buying that today because we’re saving for the trip” beats any worksheet.
### How much allowance should a kid get, and should it be tied to chores?
There’s no official number and no Missouri or federal rule. The most common rule of thumb is $1 a week for each year of age, so $7 a week for a 7-year-old, and plenty of families use half that. The right amount depends less on age than on what the allowance is supposed to cover.
That’s the shift worth making: an allowance is a budget, not a salary. If it covers only treats, a few dollars a week is plenty. If it also covers school snacks, a friend’s birthday gift and the occasional movie, it needs to be bigger, and your kid needs to plan. Write down what it pays for. Then the “can you buy me” conversation has an answer that isn’t you.
Those figures illustrate a rule of thumb. They aren’t survey averages.
On chores, families tend to land in one of three camps:
Allowance with no strings. Everyone pitches in because they live there, and the allowance exists to teach budgeting. The money lesson stays clean, but nothing links work to pay.
Pay per chore. Money arrives only when the job is done. It teaches earning. The catch: a kid who doesn’t need cash this week can skip the dishes.
A hybrid. A small base allowance plus paid extra jobs beyond ordinary chores, like washing the car. Plenty of parents end up here because it teaches both lessons without turning the trash can into a contract negotiation.
When to start? A workable test: your kid can count money, knows it buys things and wants something they can’t have today. For many families that lands in the first couple of years of school, which fits the CFPB’s middle stage. Pay on the same day every week. If you front next week’s money, take it back out of next week. That’s a loan, and it’s the gentlest one your kid will ever get.
Touring schools? Ask when the money class happens: how to choose one.
### What should an 11- to 14-year-old handle on their own?
Real accounts and a real bill. Middle school is the time to move money out of the jar and into a bank or credit union, and to hand over one recurring cost so your kid feels what a monthly charge is like.
A youth savings account. Many banks and credit unions offer accounts for minors, usually with an adult as co-owner. The NCUA’s guide to youth savings says accounts designed for young savers typically have no minimum or starting balance, zero or low monthly fees, free online and mobile banking, and free use of in-network ATMs. Deposits at a federally insured credit union are insured up to $250,000 per individual depositor. Bring your own ID, and be ready for questions about the child’s birth date or Social Security number. Credit unions also have membership rules; our walkthrough on how to join a credit union in St. Louis explains how that works here.
Ask three questions before you sign anything. Is there a monthly fee? Who can withdraw, the kid or only the adult? What happens to the account at 18? Let your kid do the asking. Missouri’s high school standards list this exact skill: comparing the services, fees and requirements of different financial institutions.
Comparison shopping. Hand a 12-year-old the grocery list, a set budget and one rule: come in under, and the difference goes to savings. Point out the unit price on the shelf tag. Missouri’s standards ask high schoolers to weigh substitutes when something costs more than the budget allows. Your kid can master it in the cereal aisle.
The phone bill. If your middle schooler has a phone, show them the actual bill, line by line, and decide together what part they cover. In-game currency, subscriptions and app purchases are recurring costs dressed up as fun, and they’re a gentle first lesson in reading the fine print before a company counts on you not to.
Online safety. Scams find kids where they play, from fake giveaways to a “friend” asking for a login. The FDIC’s free Money Smart for Young People parent and caregiver guides include conversation starters on staying safe online.
### What does a teenager need to know before a first paycheck?
How to get hired legally, why the check is smaller than the hourly rate, how credit works before anyone offers a card, and what a car really costs. Fifteen to 18 is when money stops being practice.
The work certificate. In Missouri, 14- and 15-year-olds must give an employer a completed Work Certificate before they start, issued by or under the direction of the public school superintendent in the district where the child lives, even for private school and home-schooled students. There’s one version for the school term and one for time outside it. Teens 16 and older don’t need one, though federal law can still limit their work, according to the Missouri Department of Labor. Then see our roundup of summer jobs in St. Louis for students.
The paycheck. Gross pay is what you earned. Net pay is what lands in the account after taxes and other deductions come out. Missouri’s standards ask students to compare the two and explain deductions like income tax, Social Security and Medicare. Walk through that first stub together, plus the W-4 form your teen fills out on day one. Our guide to a teen’s first paycheck, the Missouri W-4 and the pay stub goes line by line, and our walkthrough on how to budget on a St. Louis paycheck scales down nicely to a part-time one.
Credit, before the offers arrive. Card companies generally can’t issue a credit card to anyone under 21 unless the applicant shows an independent ability to make the payments or someone over 21 co-signs and agrees to be responsible, the CFPB explains. Use that window. Teach APR (the annual percentage rate, the yearly cost of borrowing) and how minimum payments stretch a balance out. Our explainer on how credit cards work, from interest to building credit covers the rest. Missouri’s class goes further than most parents expect: students compare sources of consumer credit, including rent-to-own, title loans and payday loans.
The first car. Teens price a car by the sticker. The CFPB’s guide to talking with kids about buying a car lists the costs that keep coming: insurance, gas, repairs and parking, plus the cost of any loan as part of the total. Missouri adds one most teens never hear about. To renew license plates, owners need a paid personal property tax receipt, or a statement of non-assessment, from their county or the City of St. Louis, according to the Missouri Department of Revenue. No paid tax bill, no plates. Put that on the spreadsheet before the test drive.
### Does Missouri require a personal finance class to graduate?
Yes. Missouri public high school students must earn a half credit of personal finance as part of the state’s 24-credit graduation minimum, and the requirement has applied since the class of 2010. Local school boards can add requirements on top of the state minimum, so your district’s version may look different from the next district’s.
How a school delivers that half credit varies. According to DESE, it can be a stand-alone course or content embedded in another class. Students who get it through embedded coursework must take the state’s online personal finance assessment, and the district sets the passing score. Students can also test out by scoring 90% or higher on that assessment.
What’s actually in it surprised us. The current standards, approved by the State Board in September 2017 and in classrooms since the 2019-2020 school year, run to 74 learning expectations across seven themes: financial decision making, earning income, buying goods and services, saving, using credit, protecting and insuring, and investing. Students are expected to use the Rule of 72 to figure out how long it takes money to double, evaluate a credit report for accuracy, and describe effective responses to deceptive or fraudulent sales practices. Plenty of adults never got that far.
Ask your teen’s school when students take it, then time your home lessons to back it up. A half credit that lands on ten years of jars and phone bills sticks.
### Where can St. Louis families find free money lessons?
Start downtown. The Economy Museum at the St. Louis Fed, at Broadway and Locust, has free admission, is open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and takes about an hour. Kids can try to lift a 28-pound gold bar and leave with a free shredded-money souvenir from the gift shop. Per the museum’s visit page, everyone goes through X-ray screening and metal detection, visitors over 18 need a valid government-issued photo ID, anyone under 18 must come with an adult, and there’s no visitor parking. A teacher work day or a summer weekday is the move.
At home, these free tools are worth a bookmark:
Federal Reserve Education. The St. Louis Fed’s long-running Econ Lowdown lesson site now forwards to FederalReserveEducation.org, a free teacher library parents can use too, from Kiddynomics for pre-K to a budgeting module called Cash for the Concert.
FDIC Money Smart for Young People. Free curricula for pre-K through 12th grade, plus parent guides.
CFPB Money as You Grow. Activities and conversation starters for each age stage.
NCUA learning games. World of Cents and Hit the Road, where kids earn, save and spend through challenges.
This is general information about teaching kids money skills, not financial advice for your family. A licensed financial advisor, or the staff at your bank or credit union, can apply it to your situation, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Ready for that first youth account? Compare banks and credit unions around St. Louis, ask each one about its accounts for minors, and bring your kid along to hear the answers.
And if you’re the banker, credit union rep or tutor who explains this every week: when a St. Louis parent, or the AI they ask, goes looking for help, being the first name that comes up is the whole game, so list your branch or tutoring practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best way to teach children about money?
A.  Let them handle real money early, and think out loud about your own choices, because kids pick up money habits largely by watching adults. Then match practice to age: waiting and choosing for preschoolers, spend, save and give jars for grade-schoolers, a real account and a bill for middle schoolers, and a paycheck for teens.
### Q. How can I teach my kids the concept of money?
A.  Start with where money comes from. Tell your kids what you do at work and that the grocery money comes from that job. Then let them hold it: count coins and pay for one small item themselves. The CFPB’s preschool talking points are simple: you earn money by working, and sometimes you wait to buy what you want.
### Q. What are some good financial lessons for kids?
A.  The St. Louis Fed’s economic education staff lists six: people work to earn income; people spend some, save some and donate some; saving is a good habit; adults can’t have everything they want, and kids can’t either; spending and saving decisions have consequences; and banks and credit unions are safe places for money that pay interest on savings.
### Q. At what age should a child get an allowance?
A.  There’s no rule. Many families start once a child can count money, understands that it buys things and wants something they can’t have yet, often in the first couple of years of school. That fits the CFPB’s middle stage, ages 6 to 12, when saving up for a goal becomes the core skill. Earlier works too if the amount is small and the rules are clear.
### Q. How much money should a kid get for allowance?
A.  A common rule of thumb is $1 a week per year of age, so $10 a week for a 10-year-old, and many families use half that. Treat it as a starting point, not a standard. The better question is what the allowance has to cover. Fun money alone needs less. Fun money plus snacks, gifts and outings needs more, plus a written list of what it pays for.
### Q. Is $10 a week a good allowance?
A.  It depends on your kid’s age and what the money covers. Under the common dollar-per-year rule of thumb, $10 a week fits a 10-year-old. For a 6-year-old it’s generous unless it pays for real expenses. For a 15-year-old buying their own lunches and outings, it may be thin. Decide what the allowance pays for first, then pick the number.
### Q. What is the 50/30/20 rule for kids?
A.  It’s a kid version of a popular adult budgeting guideline that puts about 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings. Kids don’t pay rent, so families often swap the labels: half to spend, 30% to save for a goal, 20% to give or save long term. The exact split matters less than dividing every dollar the day it arrives.
### Q. How much allowance is appropriate for a 7-year-old child?
A.  Using the common rule of thumb of $1 a week per year of age, about $7 a week, or $3.50 under the half-rate version many families prefer. At 7, keep it simple: split it across spend, save and give jars, tape a picture of the goal to the save jar, and consider matching what they save, as the CFPB suggests, with a weekly or monthly cap.

## Roth vs Traditional IRA and 401(k): Which Saves You More, and How Missouri Taxes Each
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/roth-vs-traditional-ira-and-401k
Tax now or tax later? Strip away the fund menus, the acronyms and the benefits packet somebody handed you on your first day, and that one question is the whole Roth versus traditional decision. A traditional account skips the tax today and bills you when the money comes out. A Roth bills you today and never again, as long as you follow the withdrawal rules.
Nobody lays it out that plainly, so most people check a box at enrollment and never think about it again. That isn’t a money failure. Nobody taught it. And one question comes before Roth or traditional: does your employer match? A match is money your employer adds when you contribute, and skipping it usually costs more than picking the wrong tax treatment ever would.
Then there’s the piece national calculators skip. If you live in the City of St. Louis or work inside its limits, the City’s own tax paperwork treats a traditional 401(k) dollar and a Roth 401(k) dollar differently, by 1%, every year you contribute. Missouri and Illinois part ways too once the money comes back out. It’s all below, with every limit checked against the IRS, as one piece of our St. Louis money guide to the stuff school skipped.
### Is it better to put money in a 401k or an IRA?
If your employer offers a match, the 401(k) usually comes first, up to the full match, because no IRA can hand you that money. Past the match, an IRA often gives you more investment choices and more control over fees, while a 401(k) takes far more money each year. Plenty of savers use both.
Here’s why the match jumps the line. Say your plan matches 50 cents on the dollar on the first 6% of pay, and you earn $50,000. Put in $3,000 and your employer adds $1,500. That’s a 50% return before the money is invested in anything. No fund and no tax strategy reliably beats it. Match formulas differ from one employer to the next, so the summary plan description from HR is where your real numbers live.
One catch. Your own contributions are always 100% yours, but a plan can put the employer’s money on a vesting schedule. The IRS gives examples like a three-year cliff, where you own none of it until year three, and a six-year graded schedule that starts at 20% in year two and climbs 20 points a year (IRS vesting rules). Leave early and part of the match stays behind.
After the match, the two accounts trade strengths. For 2026, the IRS lets you put $24,500 of your own pay into a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457 plan, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 or older, or $11,250 if you’re 60 through 63. An IRA tops out at $7,500, plus $1,100 at 50 or older. Both limits are adjusted each year, and the IRS announcement of the 2026 limits lists the rest.
Where the IRA tends to win is choice. A 401(k) gives you the menu your employer picked, and the SEC points out that the cost of running the plan may be passed along to you on top of each fund’s own expenses. An IRA lets you choose the provider and the investments. Where the 401(k) wins is size, the match and, in plans that offer them, loans. The IRS doesn’t allow loans from an IRA at all.
### Is it smarter to pay the tax now or later?
Later, if your tax rate in retirement will be lower than it is today. Now, if it will be higher. And if the two rates match, Roth and traditional come out exactly even, which surprises almost everyone the first time they see it.
Run it with round numbers. Take $1,000 of pay, a 22% federal bracket and Missouri’s 4.7% top rate, about 26.7% combined. In a traditional account the full $1,000 goes in, grows to, say, $4,000 (an illustration, not a forecast), and you pay 26.7% on the way out. You keep about $2,932. In a Roth you pay the 26.7% first, so $733 goes in. It quadruples to about $2,932 and comes out tax-free. Same money.
So the decision is a known tax rate today against a guess about your rate later. Today’s rate is printed in the IRS tables. For 2026, a single filer pays 12% on taxable income above $12,400 and 22% above $50,400, and a married couple filing jointly reaches 22% above $100,800 (IRS 2026 tax brackets). Taxable income is what’s left after deductions, such as the $16,100 standard deduction for a single filer.
A few patterns hold for a lot of people. A worker in the 10% or 12% bracket, early in a career, faces a cheap tax bill now, and that leans Roth. A household in the 24% bracket or above that expects a smaller income in retirement gets more out of the traditional deduction. Someone who honestly can’t guess can split contributions between the two, where the plan offers both, and hedge the bet.
Retirement doesn’t automatically mean a low bracket, either. Required minimum distributions (RMDs) force withdrawals from traditional accounts starting at age 73 whether you need the money or not, while current IRS rules require none from a Roth IRA or a Roth 401(k) during your lifetime (IRS RMD rules). Those forced withdrawals stack on top of Social Security and any pension. That’s how a careful saver can land in a higher bracket at 75 than at 45.
### How do Missouri, Illinois and the City of St. Louis tax each one?
The surprise is the City’s 1%. The City of St. Louis charges a 1% earnings tax to its residents and to anyone working inside city limits. Its Form E-1 asks for wages from box 1 of each W-2, and its list of taxable and non-taxable items puts deferred compensation under tax code sections 401, 403 and 457 on the non-taxable side. Under the IRS rules for W-2s, traditional 401(k) and 403(b) contributions stay out of box 1, and Roth contributions go in.
Read those together and, on the City’s own paperwork, a traditional dollar skips the 1% going in and a Roth dollar pays it. Coming out, a retirement withdrawal isn’t a wage, and the same City list exempts pensions. It’s small but permanent: $6,000 a year into a Roth 401(k) for 30 years is $1,800 of earnings tax a traditional contribution wouldn’t pay. IRAs aren’t affected, because an IRA contribution never changes box 1. Payroll setups vary, so check your own stub, and the Collector of Revenue’s earnings tax office answers at (314) 622-4101.
Missouri taxes a traditional withdrawal as ordinary income. The top rate is 4.7% on taxable income above $9,436 on the state’s 2026 withholding table, and the main offset is a small private pension exemption that phases out at modest incomes. A qualified Roth withdrawal never lands in federal adjusted gross income, so Missouri has nothing to tax. Our guide to how Missouri taxes retirement income has the exemption math. Because 4.7% kicks in so low, most working households save 4.7% on a traditional contribution and pay about the same coming out, a wash unless the rate moves. Our explainer on Missouri’s state income tax rate covers where it stands.
Across the river, the math tilts. Illinois taxes income at a flat 4.95%, starting from the same federal adjusted gross income a traditional contribution lowers, then lets residents subtract 401(k) and IRA withdrawals, and even a traditional IRA converted to a Roth. For a Metro East household, a traditional dollar skips Illinois tax on the way in and on the way out.
### Is there a downside to Roth 401(k)?
Yes, four of them, and the first is the one you feel every payday. Roth contributions come out after tax, so $200 into a Roth 401(k) trims take-home pay by the full $200, while $200 into a traditional account trims it by about $147 at the 26.7% combined rate from earlier. If that gap is what keeps you from saving at all, our guide to budgeting on a St. Louis paycheck shows where to find it. Inside the City, the Roth $200 also carries the 1% earnings tax.
Second, the clock. A Roth 401(k) withdrawal is tax-free only when it’s qualified, and that takes a five-taxable-year period starting with the first year you made Roth contributions to that plan, plus reaching 59 1/2, a disability or death (IRS Roth 401(k) FAQs). Pull earnings out early and they’re taxable.
Third, the match. That same IRS FAQ says employer matching money goes into a pre-tax account even when your own contributions are Roth, so you end up holding both kinds anyway. The newer W-2 instructions mention plans that let workers designate the match as Roth, which makes it taxable that year. Your plan’s documents say which yours does.
Fourth, for higher earners the choice is shrinking. Starting in 2026, if your prior-year wages from the employer sponsoring the plan topped $150,000, the IRS says your catch-up contributions have to go in as Roth.
Retirement math gets easier with a side paycheck: flexible jobs for seniors.
### Is a Roth safer than a traditional account when markets fall?
No. Roth and traditional describe how an account is taxed, not what’s inside it. Either one can hold stock funds, bond funds or cash-like investments, and either one rises and falls with what you picked. A Roth IRA full of stock funds drops in a crash exactly as hard as a traditional IRA holding the same funds.
The SEC’s investor site is plain about the risk. Large-company stocks as a group have lost money in about one year out of three on average, and selling on a day the price sits below what you paid locks in the loss (SEC stock basics). The same page notes that people who held stocks over long stretches, say 15 years, have generally been rewarded. Generally isn’t always.
What a crash can’t take is the tax treatment. The account stays open, the rules on future growth don’t change, and in a Roth IRA, money you withdraw up to the total of your regular contributions comes out without tax, because the IRS counts those contributions as the first dollars out (IRS Publication 590-B). The real danger is needing the money in a down year, or selling in a panic. That’s why the SEC says people nearing retirement may want to hold more bonds than stocks.
### How much do fees and fund choices change the answer?
Sometimes more than the tax choice does. The SEC’s fee bulletin follows $100,000 growing 4% a year for 20 years. At a 0.25% annual fee it ends near $208,000. At 0.50%, near $198,000. At 1.00%, near $179,000. That gap of roughly $29,000 comes from a number most statements show as a tiny percentage.
In a 401(k) you pay each fund’s expense ratio, the yearly cost of the fund taken as a percentage of what you hold, and possibly plan costs passed through to participants. Each fund’s prospectus lists its annual operating expenses. In an IRA you pick the provider and the funds, so that bill is yours to control. Compare both before deciding where the next dollar goes.
If someone manages the money for you, their fee stacks on top. Our breakdown of what a financial planner costs in St. Louis shows what 1% of assets adds up to over decades.
### What are the disadvantages of rolling over a 401k to an IRA?
You can give up protections that only workplace plans carry. Three matter most.
The age-55 exception. Leave your job during or after the year you turn 55 and you can take money from that employer’s plan without the 10% early-withdrawal tax. The IRS says this exception doesn’t apply to IRAs. Certain public safety employees get it at 50.
Loans. Plans that offer loans let you borrow from your own balance, within IRS limits that top out at $50,000. Once the money sits in an IRA, borrowing from it isn’t an option.
The 60-day trap. If the plan mails you a check instead of moving the money directly, it must withhold 20% for federal tax. You then have 60 days to deposit the full amount, including the 20% you never received, or the part you don’t replace is treated as a taxable distribution (IRS rollover rules). A direct, trustee-to-trustee rollover skips the withholding.
The upside is real, too. An IRA usually opens a far wider menu, and folding three old plans into one account makes them easier to watch. Compare fees before moving anything, though, since an IRA isn’t automatically cheaper. And moving pre-tax 401(k) money into a Roth IRA is a conversion, not a plain rollover: the IRS counts the converted amount as income for that year (IRS Publication 590-A). Missouri starts from that same federal income. Illinois exempts a traditional IRA converted to a Roth.
### Is there a tax credit for saving for retirement?
Yes, the Saver’s Credit. It pays back 50%, 20% or 10% of up to $2,000 you put into an IRA or workplace plan, or $4,000 for a married couple filing jointly, so it tops out at $1,000, or $2,000 jointly. For 2026, it disappears above $40,250 of adjusted gross income for a single filer, $60,375 for a head of household and $80,500 for a married couple filing jointly, and those limits are adjusted each year. You have to be 18 or older, not a full-time student, and not claimed as someone else’s dependent.
It works with Roth or traditional money. A traditional contribution also lowers adjusted gross income, which can drop a household into a richer credit tier, a quiet argument for traditional at modest incomes. Freelancers and side-business owners get plan options a W-2 job doesn’t offer; our guide to side hustle taxes in Missouri covers that side of the ledger.
If you’d rather have a professional run your numbers, our guide to choosing a financial advisor in St. Louis lists the questions to ask before you trust anyone with your money. This is general information about how these accounts and tax rules work, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can model your brackets, a licensed financial advisor can apply it to your accounts, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Bring your benefits summary, last year’s tax return and any old 401(k) statements to one of the investing pros around St. Louis, and ask how they’re paid before you ask anything else.
And if you’re the advisor or planner on the other side of that table: when a St. Louis family, or the AI they ask, wants someone to untangle Roth versus traditional, the name that comes up first gets the call, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Should I be in a traditional or Roth IRA?
A.  It turns on one comparison: your tax rate now versus your likely rate when you withdraw. A lower rate now leans Roth, a higher one leans traditional, and equal rates come out even. Roth contributions phase out at higher incomes, and the traditional deduction can shrink if you have a workplace plan. Many people hedge by holding some of each, and a CPA can run your actual brackets.
### Q. Who shouldn’t use a Roth IRA?
A.  Anyone above the income limit can’t contribute directly. For 2026 the Roth IRA phases out between $153,000 and $168,000 of modified adjusted gross income for single filers, and between $242,000 and $252,000 for married couples filing jointly. A Roth also fits poorly for someone in a high bracket now who expects a much lower one later, or who may need the earnings before 59 1/2.
### Q. Can I lose my Roth IRA if the market crashes?
A.  You can lose value, not the account. A Roth IRA is a tax wrapper, and whatever sits inside it (stock funds, bond funds or cash-like holdings) rises and falls on its own. The SEC notes that large-company stocks have lost money in about one year out of three on average. The account stays open, its tax rules survive the drop, and you decide how much risk goes inside.
### Q. Are traditional IRA contributions tax-deductible?
A.  Yes, fully, if neither you nor your spouse is covered by a workplace retirement plan. If you are covered, the 2026 deduction phases out between $81,000 and $91,000 of modified adjusted gross income for single filers and between $129,000 and $149,000 for married couples filing jointly. If only your spouse is covered, it phases out between $242,000 and $252,000. The ranges are adjusted each year.
### Q. What is the downside of a traditional IRA?
A.  Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, federally and in Missouri, except any part that came from contributions you couldn’t deduct. Required minimum distributions start at 73 whether you need the money or not. Taking money out before 59 1/2 usually adds a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies. And with a workplace plan, your deduction can shrink or vanish as income rises.
### Q. Why would anyone do a traditional IRA?
A.  For the deduction now. Someone in the 22% or 24% bracket today who expects a lower rate in retirement keeps more by deferring the tax. The deduction also lowers adjusted gross income, which can help a household qualify for the Saver’s Credit. And Metro East residents get a double break: Illinois doesn’t tax IRA withdrawals, so the state tax skipped going in is never paid back.
### Q. Which is better, a Roth 401k or a Roth IRA?
A.  They do different jobs. A Roth 401(k) takes up to $24,500 for 2026, has no income limit, sits next to any employer match, and needs no lifetime withdrawals under current IRS rules. A Roth IRA takes far less, $7,500, but offers a wider investment menu, and regular contributions can come back out without tax. Plenty of savers use the Roth 401(k) for the match and a Roth IRA beside it.
### Q. What is a Roth 401(k) plan?
A.  It’s a separate after-tax account inside a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457(b) plan, which the IRS calls a designated Roth account. You pay tax on contributions now, and qualified withdrawals, after a five-year period and at 59 1/2 or later, disability or death, are tax-free. There’s no income limit, and Roth and pre-tax contributions share one annual limit, $24,500 for 2026.

## Melvin Price Locks and Dam: Free Lock Tours and the National Great Rivers Museum
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/melvin-price-locks-and-dam
Eleven hundred feet. That’s how long a full 15-barge tow runs on the upper Mississippi, according to the Illinois Department of Natural Resources. By a National Waterways Foundation count, those 15 barges carry what 216 rail cars or 1,050 large tractor-trailers would. About 21 river miles above downtown St. Louis, you can stand roughly 80 feet over the lock where tows like that come through. It costs nothing.
You’d never know it from the recycled top-ten lists. They send you back to the Arch, maybe onto a riverboat, and treat the Mississippi as the brown stripe behind the photo. Not one of them mentions that museum staff lead walk-in tours up onto Melvin Price Locks and Dam three times a day, every day, at no charge. Or that the National Great Rivers Museum beside it doesn’t charge admission either.
For a family, that’s a field trip with no tickets and a real payoff. Kids can move the water in a model lock, step under the frame of a life-size barge, then ride an elevator to the top of the real thing and look down into the locks. If a towboat shows up while you’re there, they’ll see the river trade at work right below their sneakers.
This page is one stop in our guide to the St. Louis riverfront. Everything below comes from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the museum’s nonprofit partner, the tourism bureau and other published sources, checked in October 2026. Tours get canceled for weather, maintenance or security, so call the museum at (618) 462-6979 before a long drive.
### What’s the point of a lock and dam?
A dam holds the river in a staircase of pools at least 9 feet deep so loaded barges can float. A lock is the step between two pools, an elevator for boats that fills and drains by gravity alone. Neither one controls floods. Below St. Louis, the Mississippi is open river with no locks.
The drop is the whole problem. Between its headwaters in northern Minnesota and St. Louis, the Mississippi falls about 420 feet, a 2023 Journal Sentinel explainer noted. Before the dams, the upper river ran free and was sometimes so shallow that people could wade across it. Try floating a loaded barge over that.
Congress answered with the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1930, which authorized a channel 9 feet deep for multi-barge tows. The channel opened in 1940, and by 1964 every lock and dam on the system was done, per the Corps’ timeline.
The lock itself is simple. A towboat pushes its barges into the chamber, the gates close behind it, and operators raise or lower the water until the boat sits level with the next pool. Then the far gates open and the tow moves on. Gravity does all the lifting. No pumps.
What a lock and dam won’t do is stop a flood, and that surprises people. In high water, Melvin Price can run at what the Corps calls open river stage, with every dam gate lifted completely out of the water. The dam keeps the river deep in a dry season. It doesn’t hold it back in a wet one.
### What happens on a Melvin Price lock tour?
You walk about a half mile, ride an elevator roughly 80 feet up and look down into the locks from the top of the structure. Tours are free, daily at 10 a.m., 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., walk-in only and capped at 25 people, according to the Corps and the tourism bureau. Plan on 45 minutes to an hour.
This is the part the lists miss. The Meeting of the Rivers Foundation, the museum’s partner, says the tour lets you “experience the locks and dam from the view of a lockman.” Museum volunteers lead tours alongside Corps rangers. Down below, the main chamber runs 1,200 feet, long enough for a full tow to go through in one piece.
A few rules shape the visit:
Walk-in only. The Corps doesn’t book public tours ahead, and the foundation warns that the 25 spots “tend to fill up quickly.” Tours start promptly, so get to the museum early.
Wear real shoes. Expect about a half mile on foot plus the elevator. The Corps says the museum and the lock tour are both handicap accessible.
Leave bags in the car. Tour rules tighten when the Corps raises its security level, and at the higher levels purses, packs, phones and cameras can all be barred. The current level wasn’t posted when we checked, so ask when you call.
Watch the thermometer. Tours may be canceled when it’s too hot or too cold, the foundation says, and the Corps adds maintenance, repairs, construction and heightened security to that list.
Coming with 10 or more? Book through the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau at 800-258-6645. The Corps asks for one chaperone per five kids under 13.
We couldn’t find a minimum age for the public tour, so if you’re bringing a preschooler, ask the museum what the walk and the height involve.
Now the honest part. Nobody publishes a barge schedule, so seeing a tow lock through while you’re up there is luck. Empty chamber at 10? The 1 p.m. tour is a second chance.
### What’s inside the National Great Rivers Museum?
About 20 interactive, computer-animated exhibits, a 100-seat theater and a gift shop, in a 12,000-square-foot building the Corps put up as part of the Melvin Price project. It’s open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. with no admission fee, the Corps says, and closes only on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day.
Start with the exhibit kids run themselves. In “A Stairway for Boats,” visitors move the water in a model lock to balance the levels, the same job the operators do on the real one. Nearby, “Life Size Barge” lets you step under the frame of a single barge. Now picture 15 of them lashed together. That’s the tow you’re hoping to see from the top.
The tourism bureau also lists “Steer the Barge,” a simulator where “kids of all ages” can push a barge through the locks and dam. We couldn’t confirm it’s working in 2026, so count it as a bonus if it is. Other galleries cover the river, the bluffs, the confluence and a question worth bringing home: how much water do you use?
Don’t walk past the sturgeon. A 28-by-7-foot lake sturgeon wall, with a life-size fish and a pledge wall, went up in August 2021, and the real fish it honors spawn just below this dam. A 2023 magazine story on the museum also pointed visitors to part of a mastodon skull and an old ship wheel.
The theater has shown “Power of the River,” about 27 minutes, and “The Mississippi River Water Trail,” about 10, though the lineup changes. For the museum plus the tour, the foundation and the tourism bureau suggest at least 90 minutes. The Corps says at least two hours. With small kids, take the two.
It’s a bigger deal than it looks from the parking lot. The Corps calls it a Class-A Regional Visitor’s Center, one of only about a dozen it owns and operates nationwide, and it drew more than a million visitors in its first 20 years after opening in 2003. It’s running normally, too: its Facebook page promoted a Haunted Night on Oct. 2, 2026.
### Why do some barge tows split in two at the locks?
Because a full tow doesn’t fit in the small lock. A 15-barge tow runs about 1,100 feet long and 105 feet wide, per the Illinois Department of Natural Resources. Melvin Price’s main chamber is 110 by 1,200 feet, so the whole tow fits there. The auxiliary chamber is only 600 feet long, and a full tow sent into it has to come apart.
That’s the split, and it’s the best show on the river if you catch one. The Corps lays it out in steps. The first nine barges go into the chamber and get unhooked from the back six, which stay with the towboat. That first cut is pulled out the far end by a cable-and-pulley system or a helper boat. Then the towboat brings the last six through, and the crew lashes the halves back together.
Here’s a trick for the kids: you can hear a split coming. Federal lock rules set a whistle code. A tow asking for a single lockage sounds one long blast and one short. A tow asking for a double lockage, the split, sounds one long and two short. The signal lights have a code, too: red means stand clear, amber means the lock is being made ready, and green means it’s ready. Teach them that in the car, and they’ve got a job on the tour.
When does a full tow end up in the small chamber? Repairs are one reason. On Sept. 17 and 18, 2026, the Corps closed the main lock for 10 hours a day to fix armor on its lower wall, leaving only the auxiliary open. During those hours, a full tow had two choices: wait, or split.
The barges themselves get their own page: our guide to barges on the Mississippi picks up where the locks leave off.
### How big is Melvin Price Locks and Dam?
Big enough that the Corps calls it the largest of the 29 lock facilities it maintains on the Upper Mississippi. The dam runs 1,160 feet with nine Tainter gates, each 42 feet high and 110 feet wide. The main lock measures 110 by 1,200 feet, the auxiliary 110 by 600, and the maximum lift is 24 feet, according to a National Park Service engineering history.
The foundation says the structure “towers 80 feet above the water and spans from shoreline to shoreline.” In that 2023 magazine story, a museum spokesperson went further and said the material in it could build six arches. We can’t check that math. It’s still a great line to try on a 9-year-old.
It sits at river mile 200.8, about 21 river miles above the Eads Bridge gauge downtown. It went into service in late 1989, and the second, 600-foot lock was finished in 1994 and dedicated on June 18 that year. The name honors Rep. Melvin Price, an Illinois congressman elected to 21 terms who championed the project and died in 1988, before it was done.
It replaced Lock and Dam 26, about two miles upstream, built from 1934 to 1938 and razed in 1990. The Park Service says the old dam suffered severe structural deficiencies, and it took 33 gates to hold its pool where the new one uses nine. In June 2026, the Corps’ Andrew Schimpf put the reason for replacing it plainly: “it was a reliability issue.”
One gate exists for winter. The main lock’s upstream vertical lift gate “lowers down under the tows,” Schimpf told the Illinois Business Journal, “and the purpose of that is 100 percent to pass ice.” In January, he said, a 1,200-foot tow can push “another thousand feet of ice” ahead of it, in chunks “the size of a house.”
That gate was swapped out in 2025, the first new main-lock gate since 1989. The two new leaves weighed about 450,000 and 490,000 pounds, and the Waterways Journal reported they came by river from Alabama. How else would you move them?
All that work keeps a lot moving. In 2024, the Waterways Journal reported, Corps staff here supported nearly 4,800 lockages and the movement of more than 45 million tons of cargo.
### When do bald eagles gather below the dam?
In January and February, which the Corps calls especially busy months for eagle watchers here. The World Bird Sanctuary’s Roger Holloway told Explore St. Louis that the region typically hosts 1,000 to 3,000 bald eagles a winter. In harsh winters, he said, “the water around the locks and dam is often the only open water in the area.”
The dam feeds them, too. Fish that come through it are short on oxygen and slow, often gizzard shad, and Holloway calls them “easy pickings.” Open water and stunned fish in one spot. For an eagle in a deep freeze, that’s the best table on the river.
The Corps offers ranger-led eagle programs from its Rivers Project Office during eagle season. This winter’s dates weren’t posted when we checked in October, so call the museum in December.
Make it a loop. On the Missouri bank next to the dam, the Corps owns the 3,700-acre Riverlands Migratory Bird Sanctuary, set aside to offset the dam’s environmental impact, and the Audubon Center there is open Tuesday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., at no charge. Upriver on the Illinois side, museum staff had a scope on an eagle nest along the Great River Road in 2023, and our guide to eagle watching on the bluffs picks up from there.
Already bundled up for eagle season? Here’s where to ski near St. Louis
### Where can you fish near Melvin Price Locks and Dam?
From the Missouri bank, just below the dam. Tailwater anglers use the access off Riverlands Way at the boat-launch lot immediately downstream, and a 2021 Corps report calls the area a favorite with both anglers and birders. Federal rules ban fishing from the lock walls, the guide walls and the dam itself, so plan on the bank.
Boaters get a hard line, too. The Corps posts restricted water immediately above and below the dam, and the federal rule is blunt: “No vessel or other floating craft shall enter any such restricted area at any time.” That’s the churned water the eagles love. It’s no place for a johnboat.
A Missouri or an Illinois license works from either bank of the Mississippi itself. The Missouri Department of Conservation says you follow the rules of the state where you’re fishing, and the stricter of the two when you’re in the other state’s waters. Wander up a tributary, though, and you need that state’s license.
The fish to know here is one you have to put back. In 2015, lake sturgeon were seen spawning in this tailwater along the Missouri bank, the first confirmed sturgeon spawning site in Missouri, a 2021 Corps report says. They can grow to 8 feet, top 200 pounds and live more than 100 years, and both states list them as endangered. Catch one and it goes straight back.
Ellis Bay, also on the Missouri side, is the old river channel itself. When the new pool filled in February 1990, the two miles of channel between the old dam and the new one became an 800-acre backwater. From Oct. 1 to April 30 it’s bank fishing only, with boats kept out so migrating waterfowl have a refuge.
We found no source on bank fishing from the museum grounds on the Illinois side, so don’t plan on it. For more places to cast, our list of fishing spots in St. Louis covers the Mississippi closer to home.
### Why does the lock line end at St. Louis?
Because south of the city, the river doesn’t need it. The Corps counts 29 lock facilities on the Upper Mississippi, and the last of them, Locks 27 at the foot of the Chain of Rocks Canal, is the southernmost lock on the river. Below St. Louis, the Missouri and later the Ohio add enough water that the Corps keeps the channel open without dams.
The line starts in Minnesota, where the uppermost lock, Upper St. Anthony Falls, has been closed to barge traffic since 2015. It ends near St. Louis: Melvin Price sits above the mouth of the Missouri, and Locks 27, opened with its canal in 1953, sits below it. The Waterways Journal says Locks 27 moves more cargo than any other navigation structure on the Mississippi.
Want to see the Missouri arrive? Our guide to where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet covers the spots where you can watch it from land.
Downstream, the Corps keeps the channel with dikes, chevrons and bendway weirs that use the river’s own energy to move sediment out of the way, plus dredging. “Dredging is expensive; there’s no way we could dredge the entire channel all the time,” the Corps’ Eddie Brauer explained in 2011.
Free of locks, the tows grow. Below St. Louis they can top 1,500 feet and move more than 72,500 tons, Ingram’s Angela Grett told the Illinois Business Journal in 2026. A tow that long couldn’t fit through Melvin Price’s 1,200-foot chamber in one piece.
### How did a fight over this dam create the barge fuel tax?
The federal fuel tax barge operators pay was born in the fight over replacing old Lock and Dam 26. In 1977 and 1978, Sen. Pete Domenici tied the $400 million authorization to replace “the rapidly decaying Lock and Dam 26” to user charges on barges, the Eno Center for Transportation recounts.
The law that came out of it passed in October 1978, riding on a House bill that began as a Michigan charity-bingo tax measure. It created the Inland Waterways Trust Fund and a barge fuel tax of 4 cents a gallon. It’s 29 cents now. A Mississippi River dam, carried into law by a bingo bill.
Railroads fought the project first. On Aug. 6, 1974, 21 railroads, the Sierra Club and the Izaak Walton League sued, and a federal judge suspended design work about a month later, according to a 2013 history by the Missouri Coalition for the Environment. Congress then authorized one 1,200-foot lock in 1978 and a second, 600-foot lock in 1986.
Why would railroads sue over a dam? Every full tow carries what 216 rail cars would, and none of it rides a train.
### How do you plan a free family day at the locks?
Get to the museum when it opens at 9 a.m., do the exhibits, and be near the front of the line for the 10 a.m. tour, since public tours cap at 25 people. From downtown, the Corps routes you east over the Poplar Street Bridge, north on Illinois Route 3 to IL 143, then 2 miles to Lock and Dam Way. Figure under an hour.
Turn left onto IL 143, then left again at Lock and Dam Way. From the Missouri side, cross the Clark Bridge, follow IL 143 south 2 miles and turn right. Parking is on site, with room for buses, and we found no parking fee listed.
A day that works:
9 a.m.: Doors open. Start at the lock model so the real one makes sense an hour later.
10 a.m.: The lock tour, 45 minutes to an hour. Bags stay in the car. Listen for whistles.
Lunch: The first-come picnic shelter near the museum, or a restaurant on the Illinois side near the locks.
Afternoon: In winter, cross the river to Riverlands for eagles before the Audubon Center closes at 4, and remember it’s closed Mondays. Missed the morning tour? The 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. tours are still ahead.
Before you leave the house, ask two questions. Is it one of the museum’s five holiday closures? Is it brutally hot or cold? Either one can sink the day, and so can a raised security level, so call (618) 462-6979 the morning you go.
Most St. Louisans have crossed the Mississippi more times than they can count and never once watched it work. You’re the one who knows where to watch: an elevator ride 80 feet up at no charge, a model lock the kids can run themselves, and a whistle code that tells you a split is coming. Pick a Saturday, aim for the 10 a.m. tour, and call the museum before you back out of the driveway.
When the kids ask where to go next, browse more museums in St. Louis worth a family field trip.
If you run a restaurant or a fishing guide service on the Illinois side near the locks, the families walking off the 10 a.m. lock tour hungry and the anglers who come for the tailwater are visitors already headed your way, so list your restaurant or guide service with us and turn more of them into customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many locks are along the Mississippi river?
A.  The Corps counts 29 lock facilities on the Upper Mississippi. The uppermost, Upper St. Anthony Falls in Minnesota, has been closed to barge traffic since 2015. The southernmost, Locks 27 at the foot of the Chain of Rocks Canal, sits below the mouth of the Missouri. South of St. Louis there are none; the Corps calls that stretch the open river.
### Q. Why doesn’t the lower Mississippi have locks and dams?
A.  It has enough water without them. Below St. Louis, the Missouri and then the Ohio add so much flow that the channel is deep and wide enough for shipping on its own, as a 2023 Journal Sentinel explainer put it. The Corps keeps it navigable with dikes, chevrons, bendway weirs and dredging, and tows there can top 1,500 feet.
### Q. What is the largest lock and dam in the US?
A.  We couldn’t find a credible source that names one. The Corps calls Melvin Price the largest of its 29 lock facilities on the Upper Mississippi, but its 1,200-foot main chamber matches Locks 27 rather than beating it. Nationally, the Olmsted Locks and Dam on the Ohio River has twin 1,200-foot locks and a 2,574-foot dam.
### Q. How deep is the Lock and Dam?
A.  Deep enough for loaded barges. The pools behind the upper river’s dams are held at least 9 feet deep, the channel depth Congress set in 1930. At Melvin Price, the maximum lift is 24 feet, and the structure stands about 80 feet above the water, which is exactly where the lock tour takes you.
### Q. Where’s the best place to see the Mississippi River?
A.  To watch the river at work, it’s hard to beat the top of Melvin Price Locks and Dam, about 80 feet up on the free lock tour, looking down on a main chamber 1,200 feet long. For eye-level views downtown, our riverfront guide, linked near the top of this page, covers the levee, the overlooks and the bridges.
### Q. Why can’t you swim near a dam?
A.  Because that water is dangerous and off-limits. The Corps posts restricted zones immediately above and below each dam, and federal rules bar any boat or floating craft from entering them at any time. Water coming through the gates churns hard enough to keep the river open in a deep freeze and leave fish stunned. Stay on the bank.
### Q. Do you need a reservation for a Melvin Price lock tour?
A.  Not for the public tours. The Corps runs them for walk-ins only, daily at 10 a.m., 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., capped at 25 people. Groups of 10 or more book through the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau at 800-258-6645. At a raised security level, the Corps can require a reservation 24 hours ahead, so call (618) 462-6979 first.
### Q. Is the National Great Rivers Museum open every day?
A.  Nearly. The Corps lists it open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. with no admission fee, closed only on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day. The museum promoted events as recently as Oct. 2, 2026, but it’s a federal facility, so call (618) 462-6979 before a long drive.

## St. Louis Riverfront Trail: The Riverwalk With a Bent Bridge, Parking and the Mural Mile
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/riverfront-trail-st-louis
Thirty degrees. Halfway across the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, a mile of old Route 66 hung more than 60 feet above the Mississippi, the deck swings through a 30-degree turn, and your handlebars feel it before your eyes believe it. The river below is brown and wide. There’s nothing up there to block the wind. Nobody who walks that bend forgets it.
The bend wasn’t a flourish. Riverboat men protested the original straight plan because it would have made them dodge the bridge piers and two water intake towers at the same time, the National Park Service says, and the bedrock under that straight line couldn’t carry the piers anyway. So the bridge turned. It opened to traffic in July 1929 and closed in 1968. In the 1970s, Army demolition teams considered blowing it up just for practice. In 1980, John Carpenter used the rusting deck as a set for Escape from New York.
Now the part that will save your Saturday. You can’t ride to that bend from downtown right now. Great Rivers Greenway has the Riverfront Trail fully closed between Humboldt Avenue and Chain of Rocks Drive while crews repair it at Maline Creek. There’s no accessible detour, and the agency estimates it reopens in early January, weather permitting. Across the river, the Chain of Rocks canal bridge in Illinois is closed for construction with no end date, so the old bridge is open from the Missouri side only.
So for now, the riverwalk St. Louis actually has is two trips, not one. Drive to the bridge and walk it. Ride the downtown stretch on its own, north along the floodwall from the Arch. Below: where to park for each, what you’ll pass, the Mural Mile at the south end, and the river levels that start shutting the floodwall gates.
### Does St. Louis have a riverwalk?
Yes, though nobody calls it that. The Riverfront Trail, part of Great Rivers Greenway’s Mississippi Greenway, follows the river for 16.19 miles from the Chouteau riverfront downtown to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, a total that counts that bridge and the McKinley Bridge. It’s paved and flat, with limited shade, and it winds along both sides of the floodwall that protects the city.
How long is the St. Louis Riverfront trail, really? Depends who’s counting. The City of St. Louis calls it the 10.8-mile North Riverfront Trail, running from the old Laclede Power Building at Biddle Street, just north of the Arch, to the Chain of Rocks Bridge. Great Rivers Greenway’s 16.19 starts at Chouteau instead and counts both bridges. Plan around the bigger number.
Don’t picture a boardwalk lined with cafes. The City’s own parks page calls it a “gritty, real, industrial trail.” Some sections are levee road, and Great Rivers Greenway warns that you may meet vehicles from neighboring businesses that are allowed to drive on it, so listen for engines behind you. At North Riverfront Park, the City’s northernmost park, men drive and walk right up to the banks to fish, mostly for buffalo, a local catch the City says is usually eaten fried.
### Is the Riverfront Trail closed right now?
Part of it. Here’s the board as Great Rivers Greenway posts it, with what each item means for your day:
Maline Creek: closed. No trail between Humboldt Avenue and Chain of Rocks Drive and no accessible detour. The estimate is early January, weather permitting. Until then, the downtown stretch and the bridge are separate trips.
The Illinois canal bridge: closed. The Chain of Rocks canal bridge has no detour and no posted end date, which means no way onto the old bridge from Illinois.
The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge: open. Daily, 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset unless otherwise posted, from Missouri only.
The nearest I-270 exit: closed. The westbound ramp to Riverview Drive is temporarily shut for construction. Take the Lilac exit (33) instead, turn right on Lilac Avenue, then right on Dunn Road for 1.1 miles to Riverview Drive. Turn right, and Chain of Rocks Park is on your left.
One more thing about that list: it changes. Look at Great Rivers Greenway’s Riverfront Trail page the morning you go, not the night before.
### Can you walk on the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge?
Yes, and right now it’s the easiest part of the trail to do well. Drive to Chain of Rocks Park at 10840 Riverview Drive, a 16-acre park on the Missouri end of the bridge. It’s open daily from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset unless otherwise posted. The entrance gate is automatic, so pull forward to trip it. The lot holds 55 cars, including 3 accessible spaces, and there’s no overnight parking.
The park has a story under it. Great Rivers Greenway says the ground near the pavilion is a capped landfill, where much of what remained of the Pruitt-Igoe homes was buried after they were demolished in the 1970s. Cottonwoods seeded themselves on top of it, and one still stands by the pavilion; in spring its white, fluffy seeds float on the wind. The 2024 renovation planted 42 new trees and built a shade pavilion that seats 60. So the walk out onto old Route 66 starts on top of what’s left of Pruitt-Igoe.
From the park, you walk straight onto the bridge. Route 66 was rerouted over it in 1936, and during World War II its red sections were painted green so the bridge would be harder to spot from the air. After it closed, Trailnet started cleaning it up in the 1980s, and it reopened in 1999 as part of the Route 66 Bikeway. The payoff is what the National Park Service calls “outstanding views of the wide Mississippi River,” and the bend is the place to take them in.
Two things before you go. The portable restrooms and the drinking fountain, which has a bottle filler and a pet bowl, are on site only from April to November, so outside those months, bring your own water. And because the Illinois end is closed, the bridge is an out-and-back: walk out as far as it’s open, turn around and walk back with the wind in your face one way or the other.
### Riding the downtown stretch
The other trip starts under the Arch. If you don’t have a bike, Big Muddy Adventures rents them from a stand at the bottom of the Grand Staircase near the riverboats, 50 Leonor K. Sullivan Blvd., for $15 an hour with a helmet included. Its posted hours are Saturday and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the last bike out at 4 p.m., and the rental season runs through November. It’s card only, first come, first served, and you’ll need a valid ID.
Ride north. Just past the Arch grounds, the Katherine Ward Burg Garden sits beside the Eads Bridge. Laclede’s Landing starts right there, nine square blocks where the north-south streets still have their original cobbled paving. Walk the bike or rattle your teeth. The City’s official start is at Biddle Street, a few blocks north of the Martin Luther King Bridge, where its trail begins at the old Laclede Power Building.
Then the city thins out. The floodwall rises beside you, the river slides past on the other side, and the pavement runs flat and nearly shadeless into north St. Louis. About halfway between Biddle Street and the old bridge, you reach the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing. On May 21, 1855, eight or nine enslaved people rowed across the Mississippi from a ferry crossing here, headed for freedom. Five were caught. It became the first site in Missouri to qualify for the National Park Service’s Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. Stop the bike. Stand there a minute.
Keep going north and you’ll reach the closure at Humboldt Avenue. That’s your turnaround until Maline Creek is fixed. The ride back is the reward: flat all the way, the river on your left now, and the Arch getting bigger in front of you.
No bike of your own, or need a tune-up before the ride? Compare bike rental shops in St. Louis and pick one near the end of the trail you’re starting from.
If you’re the bike shop, the rental stand or the coffee counter a short ride from the floodwall, those riders are already out there with a helmet on and an empty bottle. When one asks a phone where to stop, does your name come up, or somebody else’s? See who AI names instead of you, then decide whether a listing is worth it.
### Where do you park for the Riverfront Trail?
At the north end, parking is easy. Great Rivers Greenway lists these lots near Chain of Rocks Park:
Chain of Rocks Park: 55 spaces, including 3 accessible, behind the automatic gate.
North Riverfront Park, north lot: 70 spaces.
North Riverfront Park, south lot: 20 spaces.
North Riverfront Park covers 250 acres along the bank, and the National Park Service lists it as parking south of the bridge along the Riverfront Trail. For the bridge itself, Chain of Rocks Park is the lot that puts you at the foot of the deck.
Downtown, we couldn’t find a lot set aside for the trail by the City or by Great Rivers Greenway, so budget a few minutes to find parking near the Arch. Or skip hauling a bike entirely and rent at the Grand Staircase.
### Where is the Mural Mile?
Turn south at Chouteau instead of north and the floodwall turns into a gallery. The Regional Arts Commission puts the Mural Mile on the riverfront between Victor and Chouteau avenues, south of the Gateway Arch. That makes it the trail’s southern neighbor: the Riverfront Trail starts at the Chouteau riverfront and heads north, and the paint runs south. Paint Louis, the festival that keeps repainting the wall, lists its address as 1000 S. Wharf St. and says the wall is in the Guinness Book of World Records as the longest graffiti wall in the world.
Every Labor Day weekend, more than 400 writers show up with their cans, from across the U.S. and, lately, from Canada, Mexico, Germany and Australia. The riverfront smells like spray paint all weekend. Then the wall starts to change. After the festival, the arts commission notes, paint-overs become increasingly common, and each piece takes on new lives as the original slowly disappears. The wall you see this week won’t be the one you see next spring.
Paint Louis says it began in 1997, ran through 2001 and came back in 2013, and that it has hosted legendary writers such as Zephyr, Saber and Lady Pink. The City of St. Louis owns the wall, according to the arts commission.
Here’s the pairing worth stealing: walk the Mural Mile south from Chouteau and back, then ride the trail north. One floodwall, a gallery at one end and a working river path along the rest.
The wind on that bridge is free. The legs to push back against it take work. Hiring a personal trainer in St. Louis
### When does the river close the floodwall gates?
The trail threads through the floodwall, and when the Mississippi rises, the city starts sealing the openings. The federal flood-impact list for the Mississippi River at St. Louis gauge reads like a countdown:
32 feet: flood panels go in at Carr Street and Poplar Street.
35 feet: the floodgates at Gratiot Road railroad and Chouteau Street close.
37 feet: a double gate closes at East Grand in north St. Louis.
38 feet: the Mullanphy Street gate closes.
39 feet: North Market Street’s gate closes.
41 feet: the City installs a double floodgate at Branch Street.
54 feet: the floodwall itself is overtopped.
For scale, the 1993 flood crested at 49.58 feet on that same gauge. Stand at the base of the wall on a dry fall afternoon, look up, and try to hold that number in your head. Our guide to the Great Flood of 1993 tells the rest.
The practical rule: the Weather Service’s minor flood category at St. Louis starts at 30 feet. When the gauge is climbing toward that, check Great Rivers Greenway’s alerts before you load the bike.
### Is the Riverfront Trail safe?
It’s quiet and industrial, so treat it that way. Great Rivers Greenway asks riders to use caution because some sections are levee road with authorized business traffic, and its trail notes say shade is limited. In an emergency, call 911. For anything else, the agency takes reports at (314) 436-7009.
Chain of Rocks Park was built with visitors in mind. When it opened in 2024, Great Rivers Greenway listed a fence around the site and a gated entrance, lighting in the parking lot, video surveillance cameras and an emergency phone. Its rules also make parents and caregivers responsible for supervising their children, and they ban glass containers and fireworks. Along the long middle of the trail, plan as if no one is coming: ride in daylight, bring a friend if you can, and tell someone where you’ll turn around.
What to bring, in order of how much you’ll miss it: water, because the north trailhead’s fountain runs only April to November; a layer for the wind on the bridge; a charged phone; and a card, not cash, if you’re renting at the Arch.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How long is the St. Louis Riverfront trail?
A.  Great Rivers Greenway puts it at 16.19 miles, from the Chouteau riverfront downtown to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, counting that bridge and the McKinley Bridge. The City of St. Louis calls its core stretch the 10.8-mile North Riverfront Trail, starting at Biddle Street. A Maline Creek closure blocks end-to-end rides until the repair is done.
### Q. Is the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge closed?
A.  No. It’s open daily to walkers and cyclists from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset unless otherwise posted, but only from the Missouri side, because the Chain of Rocks canal bridge in Illinois is closed for construction. Park at Chain of Rocks Park, 10840 Riverview Drive, and walk it as an out-and-back.
### Q. Why is the Chain of Rocks Bridge bent?
A.  Because the river demanded it. The National Park Service says riverboat men protested the planned straight bridge, which would have made boats dodge its piers and two water intake towers at once, and the bedrock under that straight line couldn’t support the piers. The result is the 30-degree turn midway across.
### Q. Can you drive across Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  No. The old bridge closed in 1968, a year after the new I-270 bridge opened 2,000 feet upstream. Great Rivers Greenway’s rules bar unauthorized motorized vehicles from the bridge and the greenway. You can drive to Chain of Rocks Park on the Missouri end, then walk or bike out onto the deck.
### Q. Is it safe to walk the Chain of Rocks Bridge?
A.  It’s car-free and open only from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. The park at its Missouri end opened with a fenced, gated entrance, parking-lot lighting, video cameras and an emergency phone.
