Go with someone if you can, keep children close, since park rules make caregivers responsible for them, and call 911 in an emergency.
### Q. What are the best bike paths in St. Louis?
A.  For river views, start with the Riverfront Trail: 16.19 flat, paved miles from downtown to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge. It connects to Madison County Transit’s Illinois trails over the McKinley and Old Chain of Rocks bridges, and the National Park Service says the old bridge links to more than 300 miles of trails.
### Q. What are some famous cobblestone streets in St. Louis?
A.  Head to Laclede’s Landing, the nine-block district just north of the Gateway Arch. Its north-south streets keep their original cobbled paving, while the east-west streets were repaved in concrete. It’s the only part of the old riverfront with most of its 19th-century buildings still standing, just north of the Arch, where the downtown ride begins.

## Ferries Near St. Louis: Golden Eagle Hours and Fares, Two Free Boats, One to Kentucky
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ferries-near-st-louis
Somebody usually has to tell you. That’s how most people find out that cars still cross the Mississippi on boats north of St. Louis: a coworker mentions the ferry over lunch, or a relative in Calhoun County asks why on earth you drove the long way around. Go looking on your own and you’ll see why word of mouth wins.
The web is the problem. The Golden Eagle Ferry has no website of its own anymore. The address MoDOT still lists for it forwards to a tourism bureau’s page, and the bureau’s listing for the ferry still prints the old $9 and $17 fares in its text, right above a price block showing $10 and $19. MoDOT’s own ferry list still calls one year-round boat “Seasonal.” When ice stops a crossing, the news shows up as a Facebook post from the operator or the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office. Even IDOT, the Illinois Department of Transportation, heard riders ask for better status information and better signs in its 2024 ferry study.
That’s a shame, because the people who do find these boats save real miles and real time. Calhoun County says the Golden Eagle crossing saves about 30 miles on a one-way trip. In congressional testimony quoted in IDOT’s study, county engineer Kyle Godar said the ferry’s commuters skip nearly 8,000,000 miles of driving a year. Eight million miles, on one family-run crossing.
This page is the ferry stop in our guide to the St. Louis riverfront. It covers the car ferries within a day trip of the city, plus one far to the south worth knowing before you need it. Everything below was checked against operator pages, IDOT, MoDOT, Kentucky’s transportation cabinet and local news on October 10, 2026. Rivers change their minds, so call before you drive.
### Is the Golden Eagle Ferry still running?
Yes. As of October 2026, the Calhoun Ferry Company says the Golden Eagle Ferry is open year-round, seven days a week, crossing the Mississippi between the Missouri side north of St. Louis and Calhoun County, Illinois. Ice or flooding can shut it, as ice did from January 22 to February 10, 2026, so call (618) 535-5759 first.
The operator’s page put it plainly on October 10: “The Golden Eagle Ferry is Open!” That page, hosted by a tourism bureau, is the closest thing the ferry has to a website. The family-owned Calhoun Ferry Company has run this crossing since 1997, and IDOT’s study says about 95 percent of its money comes from tickets, with no public funding.
Last winter showed how a shutdown plays out. Ice stopped the boat at 9 p.m. on January 22, 2026, and it didn’t reopen until 5 a.m. on February 10. A backup crossing covered the gap, and it comes up again below.
A new owner is coming, just not yet. Calhoun County has agreed in principle to buy the Golden Eagle boats so it can draw federal Ferry Boat Program money. Godar told River County News on September 29, 2026, that “we’ve lost 10 years’ worth of ferry boat money because we haven’t owned a boat.” With appraisals, an ordinance and bridge loans still ahead, he said, “we’re not looking at actually signing off on buying a boat until after the first of the year.”
For riders, the sale changes nothing yet. The family company still runs the boat, and a county-owned Golden Eagle is a 2027 story at the earliest.
### What does the Golden Eagle Ferry cost, and when does it run?
A car costs $10 one way or $19 round trip, according to the operator’s page on October 10, 2026. The boat runs 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 5 a.m. to 2 a.m. on Friday and Saturday, and 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Sunday. There’s no timetable. It just shuttles back and forth while it’s open.
The full fare card from that page:
Car or small truck: $10 one way, $19 round trip
Motorcycle: $7 one way, $13 round trip
Bicycle: $6 one way
Walk-on passenger: $5 one way
Dual over 1 ton: $11; tandem: $12; semi: $15
Trailers: $2 per axle, one way
Those prices went up about a dollar in late September 2026, after Calhoun County commissioners approved the increase. River County News reported that fuel prices and the need for reserves to get through the slow winter season drove it. Weekly commuter passes stayed put. The old fare, $9 one way and $17 round trip, is the one the stale listings still show.
Bring cash. The operator’s page says cash, checks and credit cards are all accepted, but two tourism listings for the same boat still say cash only, and a riverbank at dusk is a poor place to find out which one is right.
Holidays aren’t a problem: the operator lists 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year’s Day, and 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Christmas Eve. And that 2 a.m. weekend closing? It makes this the crossing for a Saturday dinner on the Illinois side that runs long.
### How do you find the landings on each side?
On the Missouri side, take Highway 370 to Route 94 north, then Route B to Golden Eagle Ferry Road, and turn right to the landing. The boat drops you in the village of Golden Eagle, in Calhoun County, Illinois. For a commuter, Calhoun County says, the crossing turns an average 80-mile trip into a 30-mile one.
The last stretch is stranger than the map makes it look. IDOT’s study says Golden Eagle Ferry Road is privately maintained from the Route B and Hayford Road intersection down to the water, and it crosses an active BNSF track on an Army Corps of Engineers levee. The study also recommended new signs “at each decision point” on the Missouri side, which tells you something about the drive in.
On the Illinois side, the listed address is 2 Story Hill Road, Golden Eagle. Coming from the free Brussels Ferry, the tourism listing’s route runs Ridge Road to Mississippi River Road into Golden Eagle, then Ferry Road down to the landing.
People have made this crossing for more than a century. IDOT’s study says William Kamp bought a wooden-hull paddle-wheel ferry in 1922, floated it downriver and set up at today’s Golden Eagle site, cutting a 75-mile trip to St. Louis. It got a steel hull in 1935 and kept working until its last crossing in October 1998. A paddle wheel, on a working car ferry, until 1998.
### Which ferries near St. Louis are free?
Two, both run by IDOT: the Brussels Ferry and the Kampsville Ferry. IDOT says both operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, at no charge. Both cross the Illinois River, not the Mississippi, so neither one takes you to Missouri. Think of them as the free doors into Calhoun County, which sits between the two rivers.
The Brussels Ferry. Drive up the Great River Road on Illinois Route 100, and the landing sits just past the spot where the Illinois River comes into the Mississippi. The boat carries you across to Calhoun County near the village of Brussels. It’s busy. IDOT counted 292,000 vehicles on it in 2023, about 801 a day, against 583 a day on the Golden Eagle. The free boat outworks the paid one. On busy days, such as fall weekends, a second boat runs to cut the wait.
Ice is the usual enemy. IDOT closed the Brussels boat at 6 p.m. on January 23, 2026, for “hazardous ice floes” and sent drivers to the Joe Page Bridge at Hardin. It reopened on February 13. The landing’s phone is (618) 786-3636.
The Kampsville Ferry. This one is a state highway that floats. IDOT says it “carries Illinois Route 108 across the Illinois River” to meet Illinois Route 100 near Kampsville. The Federal Highway Administration says it links Calhoun County on the west bank with Greene County on the east and runs every day, around the clock, with no fee, “unless the river is frozen or the water is unusually high.” IDOT counted 215,810 vehicles on it in 2023.
Why do two free boats matter so much? Because Calhoun County runs short on ways out. During the 2019 flood, IDOT’s study says, the Brussels and Kampsville ferries were the main way in and out of the county, because the approach roads to the Joe Page Bridge at Hardin were under water. When that same bridge closed for inspection on September 29 and 30, 2026, IDOT put an extra ferry on at both crossings.
### How do you turn two ferries into one loop?
Use one free boat and one paid boat, and you never retrace a mile. Cross the Illinois River on the free Brussels Ferry, follow Ridge Road and Mississippi River Road to Golden Eagle, then pay $10 to ride the Golden Eagle Ferry back across the Mississippi to the Missouri side north of the city.
Direction only matters at night. The Brussels boat never closes, but the Golden Eagle stops at 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday. If your day might run late, cross on the Golden Eagle first, heading out from the Missouri side, and save the 24-hour Brussels boat for the trip home. On a Friday or Saturday, with the Golden Eagle running until 2 a.m., either order works.
What fills the hours in between is up to you. Our guide to the small towns outside St. Louis is a good place to start, and if the day is really about wine, plan a winery day trip and let the ferries handle the scenery.
Say you live in Carondelet and have a free Saturday in October. Drive up the Illinois side, roll onto the free boat, wander Calhoun County, and come home on the Golden Eagle without seeing the same mile twice. No recycled top-ten list will hand you that route.
Too much fall fruit in the trunk? Try a St. Louis cooking class
### What happens when ice shuts the Golden Eagle Ferry?
The same company opens its backup, the Winfield Ferry. It runs only when ice or flooding closes the Golden Eagle crossing, and on October 10, 2026, the operator’s page listed it as closed. It sits just below Lock and Dam 25, where, IDOT’s study explains, moving water keeps the river freer of ice.
That’s the whole trick: below the dam the water keeps moving, so the backup can run while the Golden Eagle sits iced in. The greatriverroad.com guide notes that it runs beside the lock and the Sandy Island bald eagle sanctuary. Its Missouri landing connects with Route 79, and the Illinois side lands near Batchtown.
MoDOT calls it seasonal, which is fair if ice counts as a season. It shares the Golden Eagle’s phone, (618) 535-5759, and the company’s Facebook page announces each switch. On February 9, 2026, it posted that the Golden Eagle would reopen at 5 the next morning and the Winfield Ferry would close that night at 9.
The backup also has the best origin story on the river. IDOT’s study says the Baalman brothers bought the Batchtown crossing around 1973 to bring diners from the Missouri side to their restaurant and dance hall in Batchtown. By 1986 the ferries paid better than the restaurant did. They built a bigger ferry themselves on the riverbank at Batchtown in 1996, and in 1998 they moved their main operation to Golden Eagle.
Up near the lock with daylight to spare? Our guide to the refuges up the Missouri side picks up where the ferries leave off.
### Which of these ferries actually cross the Mississippi?
MoDOT lists five ferry crossings in Missouri, and all five are on the Mississippi: the Winfield Ferry, the Golden Eagle Ferry, the Grafton Ferry, the Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry and the Dorena-Hickman Ferry. The two free IDOT boats cross the Illinois River instead. None of them lands at St. Louis itself, IDOT’s ferry list shows.
The Grafton Ferry reopened under city ownership on April 10, 2026, and now runs year-round with a $10 car fare, though MoDOT’s list still tags it “Seasonal.” Our Grafton ferry guide has the hours, the fares and the town around the landing.
The city did have its own ferry once: IDOT’s study credits James Piggott with starting the first ferry to St. Louis in 1797.
Here’s the short version as of October 10, 2026. Call before you lean on it.
### Is there a car ferry south of St. Louis?
Yes. The Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry crosses the Mississippi between the Missouri shore and Modoc, Illinois. As of October 10, 2026, its operator lists Wednesday through Saturday, 6 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. A standard car pays $20 one way, and the return is $10 with a same-day ticket.
Walk-ons and bicycles pay $5. Riders must be at the landing 30 minutes before closing for the last ride, and if you miss it, you’re driving the long way to a bridge. In winter the ferry switches to a weekend schedule, Friday through Sunday, and the start date isn’t posted, so check before a late-fall trip. Call (573) 880-6970, and carry cash, since payment methods aren’t posted either.
The operator calls it the only Mississippi crossing between Chester and the St. Louis metro. Without it, the next way over is at Chester or back in town.
The crossing is old even by river standards. The operator’s history page cites written records of a ferry here as early as 1798. From 1904 to 1961, the Missouri-Illinois Railroad floated whole freight cars across on a cradle-rail ferry. The modern car ferry began in 1997. A regional port authority owns it, and Missouri and Illinois help pay to keep it running.
For a full day on the Missouri side, start with our guide to the old river town at the Missouri landing.
Are you traveling south? You might need the Dorena-Hickman Ferry, far outside the metro, but a relief to find when you need it most.
### How far south is the Dorena-Hickman Ferry?
About 195 road miles from St. Louis, by the ferry’s own mileage chart. It crosses the Mississippi between Dorena, Missouri, and Hickman, Kentucky, on demand during daylight. A car pays $20, cash only. The last run from Missouri moves from 6:30 to 5:30 p.m. on October 15, and to 4:30 p.m. on December 1.
Here’s why it matters. Kentucky’s transportation cabinet says Missouri and Kentucky are the only neighboring states with no direct road or bridge between them, which makes this boat the only direct route. WorldAtlas counts about 115 river miles between the Cairo bridge and the Caruthersville bridge with no bridge at all, and the ferry runs inside that gap.
The landings connect Kentucky Route 1354 at Hickman with Missouri Route A and Route 77 near Dorena. Kentucky Tourism says the boat holds 12 cars and 149 passengers, and the Mississippi County Port Authority runs it. Boat on the far bank when you pull up? The ferry’s Facebook page says to press the button on the pole.
IDOT’s study quotes first boats at 7 a.m. from Kentucky and 7:30 a.m. from Missouri, and last runs from Kentucky leave 15 minutes before the Missouri ones. A return trip is half price with your original ticket, and the toll sheet adds, “This offer does not expire.” Motorcycles pay $10, and bicycles and walk-ons pay $5.
Now the honest part. This ferry closes for low water, and it did for several days in September 2026. IDOT’s study found it runs “about 70 percent of the time when it is intended to operate,” with status information limited “except on Facebook.” We couldn’t confirm whether it was running on October 10, so call (731) 693-0210 or check its Facebook page before you commit to the drive.
When the U.S. 51 bridge over the Ohio at Cairo closed in July 2026, the little boat suddenly mattered to a lot more people. “Honestly, normally, it’s two to three cars a trip,” first mate Travis McKay told KFVS. “We’ve had a full barge just about every day since the bridge went down.”
### How do you check a ferry before you drive?
Call the landing or check Facebook, because that’s where status really lives. IDOT’s 2024 study found Golden Eagle riders asking for “improved information on status of ferry” and “better signage.” On October 10, 2026, we found no current closure for the Brussels, Kampsville or Golden Eagle boats.
Golden Eagle and the Winfield Ferry: the Calhoun Ferry Company’s Facebook page, or (618) 535-5759.
Brussels and Kampsville: IDOT’s GettingAroundIllinois.com traveler map, @IDOTDistrict8 on X, or the landings at (618) 786-3636 and (618) 653-4518.
All the Calhoun County boats: the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office Facebook page, which reported the Brussels, Kampsville and Golden Eagle ferries open again on February 13, 2026.
Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry: (573) 880-6970.
Dorena-Hickman Ferry: (731) 693-0210 or its Facebook page.
And read the date on whatever you find. A February post says nothing about today.
So how early should you arrive? None of these ferries takes reservations, so the clock matters most at closing time. The Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry wants you there 30 minutes before closing for the last ride, and the Dorena-Hickman runs fixed last trips. The Golden Eagle shuttles continuously during its hours. At Brussels, expect a line on fall weekends; that’s when IDOT adds a second boat.
Most people who drive up the river turn around where the road runs out and go home the way they came. You’re the one who knows it doesn’t run out: a free boat crosses the Illinois all night, a family company shuttles cars to Golden Eagle until 2 a.m. on weekends, and a cash-only ferry still ties Missouri to Kentucky. Pick a dry Saturday this fall, save (618) 535-5759 in your phone, and take the long way that turns out to be the short one.
Between boats, pick an afternoon tasting room from the wineries near St. Louis in our directory.
If you run an orchard, a winery or a B&B along the ferry loop, list it with us and turn more of the drivers headed your way into customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is it to ride the Golden Eagle Ferry?
A.  As of October 10, 2026, the operator’s page lists $10 one way or $19 round trip for a car or small truck, $7 or $13 for a motorcycle, $6 one way for a bicycle and $5 for a walk-on. Fares rose about a dollar in late September. Bring cash, though the page also lists checks and cards.
### Q. What time does the Golden Eagle Ferry open?
A.  At 5 a.m. Monday through Saturday and 8 a.m. on Sunday, per the operator’s page in October 2026. It closes at 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and runs until 2 a.m. on Friday and Saturday nights. Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year’s Day hours are 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Call (618) 535-5759 when ice or flooding threatens.
### Q. Where does the Golden Eagle Ferry take you?
A.  Across the Mississippi, from the Missouri side north of St. Louis to the village of Golden Eagle in Calhoun County, Illinois. In Missouri, take Highway 370 to Route 94 north, then Route B to Golden Eagle Ferry Road. Calhoun County says the crossing saves about 30 miles on a one-way trip, and the free Brussels Ferry turns it into a loop.
### Q. Is the Brussels Ferry in Illinois open?
A.  We found no closure as of October 10, 2026. IDOT runs it free, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, across the Illinois River from Illinois Route 100 to Calhoun County. Ice closed it from January 23 to February 13, 2026, so in a cold snap call (618) 786-3636 or check GettingAroundIllinois.com first.
### Q. Is the Kampsville ferry running today?
A.  We found no closure as of October 10, 2026, and IDOT added an extra boat there while the Joe Page Bridge was closed for inspection on September 29 and 30. It’s free and runs around the clock unless the river is frozen or unusually high. For today’s status, call (618) 653-4518 or check GettingAroundIllinois.com.
### Q. How early should I arrive for a ferry?
A.  None of these ferries takes reservations, so timing matters most near closing. The Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry wants riders at the landing 30 minutes before closing for the last ride, and the Dorena-Hickman Ferry runs fixed last trips. The Golden Eagle shuttles continuously during its hours, and on busy fall weekends IDOT runs a second Brussels boat to cut the wait.
### Q. Is there a ferry across the Mississippi River?
A.  Yes, though none at St. Louis itself. MoDOT lists five ferry crossings in Missouri, all on the Mississippi, from the Winfield Ferry backup north of the city to the Dorena-Hickman Ferry on the Kentucky line. The Golden Eagle Ferry and the Ste. Genevieve-Modoc Ferry are the easiest day trips. The free Brussels and Kampsville boats cross the Illinois River instead.
### Q. What is the toll ferry to Kentucky?
A.  The Dorena-Hickman Ferry, about 195 road miles from St. Louis, between Dorena, Missouri, and Hickman, Kentucky. A car pays $20, cash only, and a return trip is half price with your ticket. It runs on demand in daylight, with the last trip from Missouri at 5:30 p.m. starting October 15. It closes for low water, so call (731) 693-0210 first.

## 1993 Flood in St. Louis: The Floodwall Scare, Floating Propane Tanks and a Record Crest
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/1993-flood-st-louis
The floodwall leaned. On Friday, July 23, 1993, the Mississippi scoured a hole about 60 feet wide under the north end of the St. Louis floodwall, and a section of the wall tipped forward an inch, UPI reported the next day. Crews dumped 6,000 tons of rock at the spot.
City workers told St. Louis Magazine in 2008 that water jetted 10 to 20 feet into the air there, and that the repair was “done while the city was asleep.” Their memories of the hole and the lean differ from UPI’s, so we use the figures reported that week. Either way, the wall held.
Most anniversary recaps skip that night. They jump to the August crest, show the Arch above brown water and file the whole summer under “big flood, wall held.” That version leaves out how many times the region came close: the Missouri River jumping its levees north of the city, a sandbag levee collapsing in Carondelet, 51 propane tanks floating loose off South Broadway, and pilots still taking off as the river poured across an airport at night.
This page tells it in order, drawing on records from the National Weather Service (NWS), USGS, the Army Corps of Engineers and Missouri’s State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), plus reporting from that summer. When sources disagree on a number, we say whose it is. It’s one chapter of our guide to the St. Louis riverfront, and it’s told plainly, because thousands of families lost homes that year.
### What was the worst flood in St. Louis history?
The Great Flood of 1993. On Aug. 1, 1993, the Mississippi crested at 49.58 feet on the Eads Bridge gauge in St. Louis, nearly 20 feet above flood stage and still the record. USGS put the flow at about 1.08 million cubic feet per second. The National Weather Service counts about 146 days above flood stage that year.
Nothing else on the gauge comes close. The old record, 43.23 feet, dated from 1973, and the NWS says the river stayed above that mark for more than three weeks in 1993. The second-highest crest on record, 46.02 feet in June 2019, fell about 3.5 feet short. Our guide to bridges in St. Louis covers the Eads Bridge itself, where the gauge sits.
What about the floods in the history books? USGS calls Aug. 1, 1993, the largest peak flow at St. Louis since 1844, and the 1844 figure is only an estimate, since the gauge wasn’t installed until 1861. The Post-Dispatch has reported that hydrologists now put 1844’s peak flow below 1993’s. The 1785 “year of the great water” is pegged at about 42 feet, a number the paper called “just a guess.”
The climb took weeks. The river stood near 43 feet on July 12, by USGS figures. It reached 46.9 feet on July 18, a record at the time, the Riverfront Times recounted in 2023, and SEMA has it just over 47 feet on July 22. Then it kept rising. At the crest, a 1995 USGS fact sheet figured, the river carried enough water past downtown to fill Busch Stadium in about 65 seconds.
### How close did the St. Louis floodwall come to failing?
Closer than the record suggests. Most recaps stop at the 2.5 feet of wall left above the crest (USGS). The real scares came from below: a 60-foot-wide hole under the north end on July 23 (UPI), then sand boils behind the wall on Aug. 2 that a Corps engineer called “very, very serious” (Los Angeles Times).
The wall runs 11 miles, from Maline Creek near the Chain of Rocks Bridge to the foot of Cherokee Street, SEMA’s flood history says. To go over it, the river would have had to reach 52 feet on the gauge. It never did. The trouble came from underneath, at the north end.
The repair, pieced together from UPI and SEMA accounts, went like this. The 6,000 tons of rock went in first, and crews built a 7-foot ring dike around the weak spot. On July 26, engineers pumped 111 cubic yards of concrete under the wall. Much of it happened at night.
The danger didn’t end with the crest, either. On Aug. 2, with the river finally falling, water seeping under the wall bubbled up behind it as sand boils and patches of quicksand. Up at Maline Creek, where the wall begins, backwater broke a levee on Aug. 1, and 151 homes there had flooded by Aug. 3, SEMA says.
Why didn’t the river go higher? Upstream federal reservoirs held back more than 17 million acre-feet of water and cut the St. Louis crest by about 3 feet, by the Army Corps’ estimate. Levee breaks downstream in Illinois on Aug. 1 lowered the water here too, and the Christian Science Monitor wrote that they “spared St. Louis a crest of about 50 feet.” The Corps says no urban levee or floodwall was overtopped in 1993.
You can see long stretches of that wall today. Our guide to the St. Louis Riverfront Trail covers where to walk and ride beside it.
### What happened when the Missouri River broke through?
It moved the confluence. Around 5 a.m. on July 16, two half-mile-wide levee breaks let the Missouri River pour across the peninsula north of the city, and news reports that week put its new meeting point with the Mississippi about 20 miles above the usual one. Two weeks later, it flooded a valley in west St. Louis County.
Almost the entire peninsula went under. Estimates of how much of the county across the Missouri was flooded run from about 40 percent (St. Louis Public Radio) to about 47 percent (the NWS). The weather service says nearly all of the roughly 700 private farm levees there were overtopped or destroyed. Our guide to where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet shows where the two normally join and where to watch it now.
The Monarch levee, guarding the Missouri River valley in west St. Louis County, held until Friday, July 30. It broke at 10:17 p.m., by the time on a Great Rivers Greenway historical marker, though local officials remembered it as closer to 10:20 or 10:30. The river poured into the valley around Spirit of St. Louis Airport and covered almost 15 square miles (NWS), more than 8 feet deep by the marker’s count.
The airport had 720 aircraft on the field that day. All but about 15 got out, aviation director Dick Hrabko told St. Louis Magazine, and some were still taking off after the levee broke. Highway 40 went under with the valley, and I-64 didn’t reopen until Aug. 16.
Damage estimates grew with time: $150 million that week by St. Louis County Executive Buzz Westfall’s count, and more than $200 million in a 2021 Army Corps paper. By July 30, only one bridge across the Missouri River was still open between Kansas City and St. Louis. The state was “effectively split in two,” in the NWS’s words.
The valley had one more scare. In September, a second rise brought the river back up, and crews piled as much as 12 feet of rock on Eatherton Road while the Corps built a temporary rock dike. This time the water stayed out.
### What happened in Carondelet when the sandbags gave way?
A sandbag levee failed. The Mississippi pushed back up the tributary that meets it near South Broadway, and on July 18 a 15-foot section of the sandbag levee along it collapsed, flooding part of Carondelet around Alabama Avenue. SEMA counts about 264 houses that flooded or took sewer backups. Another section east of Alabama Avenue gave way on July 20.
Look closely at that SEMA count, because it mixes two different problems. River water coming over a levee and sewer water backing up into a house don’t have the same fix. Our guide to basement waterproofing in St. Louis covers the basement side. Flood coverage is a separate policy from homeowners insurance, and our guide to flood insurance in St. Louis walks through it.
The sandbagging had started on July 16. A park along that tributary became a sandbag factory, the Riverfront Times recalled in 2023, and Fire Chief Neil Svetanics credited thousands of volunteers. The city went through about 1 million sandbags, the Christian Science Monitor reported. Even so, nearly 700 homes in St. Louis city and county had serious damage by Aug. 3, SEMA says.
In a flood, neighbors save neighbors. Here’s what to expect from a CPR class
### Why were about 12,000 people evacuated in south St. Louis?
Because 51 propane tanks were floating. Floodwater from that same tributary reached a Phillips Pipe Line Co. tank farm on South Broadway, and on July 31 nine of the 30,000-gallon tanks broke completely free, UPI reported. About 12,000 people were evacuated at the peak, by the Christian Science Monitor’s count. SEMA’s figure is 11,800. Nothing exploded.
The other 42 tanks were partly afloat. Together they held more than 1.5 million gallons, and officials warned that a vapor fireball could blow out brick walls a mile away, the Los Angeles Times reported. Two vapor clouds flamed briefly, and the AP described a flash fire on the night of Aug. 1 that burned out in under a minute.
The evacuation grew in steps. It began on July 31 with about 600 families in a 40-square-block area (UPI), then widened after the vapor fires. Within days it had reached 9,000 people on the Missouri side, the Los Angeles Times reported, with precautionary moves across the river in Illinois. At its widest, it covered a half-mile radius around the tanks.
Some residents were allowed home on Aug. 6, SEMA says. Others were out for about 19 days, waiting on a tank farm and a river.
### Why did a whole Illinois town move up the bluff?
Because the river took the old one. Levee breaks in Monroe County on Aug. 1 and 2 sent the Mississippi across about 47,000 acres, the NWS says, and roughly 90 percent of Valmeyer’s buildings were damaged or destroyed. The town rebuilt on the bluff, about 400 feet above the floodplain, St. Louis Public Radio reported.
The first break came on the morning of Aug. 1, when the river took the Gummersheimer family’s farmstead live on television. Valmeyer, a town of about 900, saw its first water at about 4:30 a.m. on Aug. 2. A second flood in September finished off many of the buildings still standing. Nobody in Valmeyer died, former mayor Dennis Knobloch told St. Louis Public Radio.
Rebuilding moved fast. The town bought a 500-acre farm tract on the bluff for $3 million and broke ground four months after the flood. By 1996 a new school was open and residents were moving in. About 1,200 people lived there by 2018.
### Why did the rivers rise so high in 1993?
Months of rain fell on ground that was already full. A wet fall in 1992 left soils near saturation, and from June into early August a stalled jet stream parked storms over the upper basin, the NWS says. In July, many Midwest locations had rain on 20 or more days, against a normal 8 or 9, USGS reported.
The pattern stuck. Warm, humid Gulf air rode up over cooler air along a front that wouldn’t budge, building thunderstorms over the same ground. USGS pinned it on “an abnormally stationary jet stream.” Parts of northern and central Missouri got more than 24 inches of rain from June through August, and east-central Iowa got up to 38.4 inches.
St. Louis got its share. From January through September 1993, the city logged more than 41 inches of precipitation, against a 37.5-inch average for an entire year (USGS). The Army Corps called April through June the wettest in the upper basin in 99 years. El Nino “probably contributed,” in the weather service’s words.
Then came the timing that hit St. Louis hardest. The record crests on the Missouri and the Mississippi reached the confluence “within days of each other,” the NWS says. Two rivers peaked together, just above the city.
### What did the 1993 flood cost?
About 50 lives and roughly $15 billion at the time across nine states, by National Weather Service counts, though federal death tallies range from 47 to 50. NOAA’s later figures put the damage near $20 billion. Adjusted for inflation, NOAA’s total is $46.3 billion, the costliest non-tropical inland flood on record.
The levee numbers explain a lot of that. USGS tables list 40 of 226 federal levees and 1,043 of 1,345 non-federal levees as failed or overtopped, about 1,083 in all. At least 10,000 homes were destroyed, the NWS says, and USGS puts the number damaged or destroyed above 50,000.
Missouri took the biggest share of the nine states, about $3 billion, including $1.8 billion in farm losses, by New York Times figures that SEMA reprinted. About 37,000 people in Missouri were displaced, and SEMA says the state’s flooding lasted eight months, longer than any other in its history. Barge traffic stopped for nearly two months, at a navigation loss of about $2 million a day (NWS).
One loss close to home came from local storms rather than the river: on July 23, a flash flood killed six people from a boys’ home group inside Cliff Cave.
Was it Missouri’s biggest flood ever? By size, SEMA says, researchers rank 1993 anywhere from second to fourth largest in state history, but none did more damage. It set records at St. Louis and at Kansas City, where the Missouri River reached 48.87 feet. On the lower Meramec, though, its 45.3-foot crest now ranks third, behind December 2015 and May 2017 (NWS).
### What really happened with James Scott and the West Quincy levee?
Nobody caused the Great Flood. James Scott was convicted of breaking one levee, at West Quincy, Missouri, on the night of July 16, 1993, one of about 1,083 levee failures that summer, by USGS figures. He’s the only person ever convicted under Missouri’s “causing a catastrophe” law, and he still says he’s innocent.
The break came at about 8:20 p.m., after the river there had crested a foot or two below the levee top and started to fall, the appeals court later wrote. A barge swept through the gap and a gas station exploded. Roughly 14,000 to 15,000 acres flooded (the New York Times and the court differ), and the Bayview Bridge to Quincy, Illinois, closed for 71 days. No one was killed.
That night, Scott gave a live TV interview at the bridge, saying he’d seen the levee failing and his warnings were ignored. The Adams County, Illinois, sheriff and a deputy watched and grew suspicious, because they knew his arson record, the court opinion says. Quincy police Sgt. Neal Baker, who had arrested him for arsons, told KOMU in 2018 that he “looked like a deer caught in headlights,” too clean for a levee worker, with no life vest.
Under questioning, Scott admitted pulling four or five sandbags off the top of the levee. He said he did it to draw attention to a leak. Witnesses testified that before the break he had talked about breaking the levee to strand his wife, who worked on the Missouri side, and others said he admitted it afterward.
The trial was moved to Adair County. A jury convicted him in November 1994, and Judge Bruce Normile sentenced him to life in prison. “I did not commit that crime,” Scott told the judge, the AP reported. In February 1997, the Missouri Court of Appeals reversed the conviction because the prosecutor hadn’t disclosed Scott’s oral admissions to two witnesses.
A second jury convicted him in 1998, and he was sentenced to life again on July 6 that year, ABC17 reported. He had his first parole hearing on July 22, 2026, after 33 years in prison. In August 2026, Missouri Department of Corrections spokesperson Karen Pojmann confirmed he’s scheduled for release in July 2028, a date the department calls “subject to change.”
The argument hasn’t ended. Scott still says he’s innocent, and the experts from his trials still disagree, Muddy River News reported in July 2026. Defense soil scientist David Hammer says failure was inevitable: it was the 12th levee failure in 11 days, the levee had been in the water about 100 days, and bulldozed sand had weakened it. Prosecution engineer Mike Klingner says it was built to a 500-year level, was in the best shape of any, and failed because of the sandbags Scott pulled.
A 2007 book by Adam Pitluk, “Damned to Eternity,” and a 2022 Vice documentary argue Scott was a scapegoat. Two juries saw it the other way. Whatever you conclude about that night, his case is about one levee, not the Great Flood.
### What changed after the 1993 flood?
Missouri started buying people out of the floodplain. FEMA counts 4,045 flood-prone properties bought in 99 Missouri communities after 1993 and calls the program a model for the nation. SEMA’s tally is 4,044 parcels for $56.8 million, an average of $14,045 each.
The buyouts held up. Of 3,146 properties bought in 13 Mississippi River communities, 1,623 sites would have flooded again in 2008, FEMA found. St. Louis County had bought 425 properties by May 1995. In one hard-hit community along that south-side tributary, SEMA says, disaster-aid applicants fell from 492 in 1993 to 16 in 1995.
The Missouri River valley in west St. Louis County went the other way. Work began on raising its levee to 500-year protection, in 1994 by the Great Rivers Greenway marker’s account or 1996 by St. Louis Public Radio’s, and the valley filled in behind it. It grew from 240 businesses in 1993 to more than 800 by 2013 (St. Louis Public Radio), and the Army Corps put its assessed value at $1.8 billion in 2021.
Not everyone calls that progress. WashU geologist Robert Criss called the valley a poster child for “an absurd response to flooding,” St. Louis Public Radio reported in 2013. Local officials point to the 500-year levee and wetland mitigation. A chamber of commerce billboard after the flood put the other side plainly: “If you build it they will come.”
### How did the 2019 flood compare?
It ran longer but crested lower. The Mississippi peaked at 46.02 feet in June 2019, the second-highest crest on record, and stayed above flood stage for 127 straight days, from March 16 to July 20, the News-Democrat reported, citing the NWS. That broke 1993’s record for consecutive days above flood stage.
How long was 1993’s run? The NWS says the river finally dropped below flood stage on Oct. 7, 1993, 103 days after the summer rise began, while the Corps’ Don Duncan and the News-Democrat used 104. Counting the spring flooding, the NWS tallies about 146 days above flood stage that year. USGS counted 144 between April and September, and the Post-Dispatch has used 147.
The damage was another story. “We’re not seeing anywhere near that same damage,” Duncan told St. Louis Magazine in 2019, “because the floodplains are being managed better.”
High water is coming more often, too. When the river crested in June 2019, NWS St. Louis noted it was the sixth major crest since 2013, and that of the 12 major crests on record, “half have occurred in the past six years.”
### Where can you still see the 1993 flood in St. Louis?
On the riverfront. The Post-Dispatch wrote in 2015 that the 1993 crest reached exactly halfway up the Grand Staircase, where bronze plaques mark the level. The official reading still comes from the gauge at the Eads Bridge, where the 49.58-foot record was set and where records go back to 1861 (USGS).
That report is from 2015, so look for the plaques before you promise the kids. Then pull up the National Weather Service page for the St. Louis gauge (its ID is EADM7) and compare today’s reading with flood stage at 30 feet and the 1993 line nearly 20 feet above that.
Out west, a Great Rivers Greenway historical marker tells the story of the Monarch levee break; it was photographed for an online marker database in February 2024. More than 800 businesses filled that valley by 2013, on ground that once sat under more than 8 feet of water.
Most people remember 1993 as one number on one day. You’re the one who knows it was a summer of near-misses: a floodwall that leaned, a sandbag levee that broke, 51 propane tanks afloat off South Broadway and a valley that went under at night. Next time you’re downtown, walk the Grand Staircase, find the halfway mark and check the gauge on your phone while you stand there.
If this history has you rereading your own policy, remember that flood coverage is sold separately from homeowners insurance, and compare your options among the home insurance providers in St. Louis we list.
If you run a waterproofing, restoration or sump-pump company, or you write flood insurance, the people reading about the 264 Carondelet houses that flooded or took sewer backups include homeowners already thinking about their own basements, so list your business with us and turn more of them into customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When did the flood of 1993 happen?
A.  From spring into fall. At St. Louis, the Mississippi first topped flood stage in April 1993, rose above it again on June 27, crested at a record 49.58 feet on Aug. 1 and finally fell below flood stage on Oct. 7, the NWS says. The worst of it in the metro came from mid-July to early August.
### Q. How long was the flood of 1993?
A.  At St. Louis, about 146 days above flood stage in 1993 by the National Weather Service’s count, including a summer run of 103 days that ended Oct. 7. USGS counted 144 days between April and September, and the Post-Dispatch has used 147. Statewide, SEMA says Missouri’s flooding lasted eight months, longer than any other in state history.
### Q. What caused the Great Flood of 1993?
A.  Too much rain on ground that was already soaked. A wet fall in 1992 left soils near saturation, then a stalled jet stream kept parking storms over the upper basin from June into early August, the NWS says. In July many Midwest locations had rain on 20 or more days, and El Nino “probably contributed.”
### Q. How many people died in the Great Flood of 1993?
A.  About 50, according to the National Weather Service, across the nine states that got federal disaster declarations. Other federal tallies run slightly lower: a 1995 USGS fact sheet counted 47 deaths as a direct result of the flood, and NOAA’s billion-dollar disaster list shows 48. St. Louis Public Radio has used 50 in its anniversary coverage.
### Q. Who was the guy who caused the flood of 1993?
A.  Nobody caused the Great Flood. The man people usually mean is James Scott, convicted of breaking one levee, at West Quincy, Missouri, on July 16, 1993, one of about 1,083 levee failures that summer. His 1994 conviction was reversed on appeal, a second jury convicted him in 1998, and he still says he’s innocent.
### Q. How did James Scott get caught?
A.  He went on live TV. The night of the break, Scott gave an interview at the bridge saying he’d seen the levee failing. Officers who knew his arson record grew suspicious. Under questioning he admitted pulling four or five sandbags off the levee top, saying he wanted to draw attention to a leak, and witnesses testified he’d talked beforehand about breaking it.
### Q. What was the biggest flood in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the yardstick. SEMA says researchers rank 1993 anywhere from second to fourth largest in state history by size, but no Missouri flood did more damage. It set records at St. Louis (49.58 feet) and on the Missouri River at Kansas City (48.87 feet). Older contenders such as 1844 and 1785 rest on estimates.
### Q. What was the Great Flood of 2019?
A.  A long, slow flood. At St. Louis the Mississippi crested at 46.02 feet in June 2019, second only to 1993, and stayed above flood stage for 127 straight days, from March 16 to July 20, the News-Democrat reported, citing the NWS. The Corps’ Don Duncan said the damage was far below 1993’s because floodplains are managed better.

## Barges on the Mississippi at St. Louis: Where the Locks End, the Port and Deckhand Pay
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/barges-on-the-mississippi-at-st-louis
Why does a tow on the river downtown look so different from one at the locks? The stock photos never ask. They drop a barge into the corner for scale, frame the Arch and treat the Mississippi as a pretty backdrop, as if those long rafts of steel sliding past were set dressing.
They aren’t. Above St. Louis, lock chambers cap tows at 15 barges. Below it, with no lock between here and New Orleans, the big boats push 30 to 40 loaded barges at a time, according to American Commercial Barge Line. The harbor in between can park up to 1,750 barges, says the Missouri Port Authorities website.
That’s the river trade the postcard view leaves out. This page, one stop in our guide to the St. Louis riverfront, makes the barges the subject instead of the scenery. The numbers come from the Army Corps of Engineers, the National Weather Service, USDA, the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the barge lines themselves, checked in October 2026. Rivers change by the week, so check before you go.
### How far north can a barge go on the Mississippi river?
Commercial tows go as far north as St. Paul, Minnesota, which the Army Corps of Engineers calls the head of navigation, and up the lower Minnesota River. Since June 10, 2015, when Congress closed the Upper St. Anthony Falls lock in Minneapolis to block invasive carp, no commercial traffic has passed the falls.
The last working lock up there, Lower St. Anthony Falls, is tiny by river standards: 56 feet wide and 400 feet long, room for a towboat and two barges, per the Corps’ water control manual. The same manual rates the navigation benefit of both St. Anthony Falls locks at “next to nothing.” On the Mississippi itself, barge traffic ends where the Minnesota River comes in, Waterways Journal reported in 2022. From there, tows turn up the Minnesota to reach terminals along its lower stretch.
Measured from here, that’s a long climb. From Lock 27, the southernmost lock on the Mississippi, to Lower St. Anthony Falls is about 668 river miles of what the Corps calls locking river, by our subtraction of the Corps’ river-mile markers. The Corps counts 29 lock facilities on the upper river. The largest, Melvin Price, sits just above St. Louis.
The north end keeps a calendar, too. Ice on Lake Pepin traditionally holds tows back until March, the Corps’ St. Paul District says, and the last tow of 2025 left St. Paul on Nov. 25. In 2026, the first tows arrived on March 23. St. Louis, as you’ll see below, doesn’t wait on the ice.
### Why does a tow downtown look so different from one at the locks?
Because St. Louis sits on the seam between two kinds of river. The Army Corps of Engineers calls the Mississippi above the city a “locking river” and the stretch below it the “open river,” with St. Louis as “the critical transition point.” Upstream, lock chambers decide how big a tow can be. Downstream, the channel and the horsepower do.
On the locking river, tows top out at 15 barges, three wide and five long: about 1,000 feet of barges and 105 feet across, which leaves roughly 200 feet of a 1,200-foot chamber for the towboat. That’s how American Commercial Barge Line’s Marty Hettel laid it out in a 2020 Federal Highway Administration webinar. Below St. Louis, he said, ACBL’s boats of 7,200 to 11,200 horsepower handle 30 to 40 loaded barges southbound and anywhere from 28 to 56 coming back north.
Fifty-six barges sounds like a typo. It isn’t. A Waterways Journal feature, reprinted by the Waterways Council in 2024, showed the MV Ray A Eckstein pushing 56 empties northbound: seven across, about 245 feet wide, and eight long, about 1,600 feet. That’s more than a quarter mile of steel in front of one boat.
St. Louis is where the 15-barge tows from the locks meet the 30-to-40-barge tows of the open river, and the harbor has room to match. Between Lock 27 and the Jefferson Barracks Bridge, its fleets can hold 1,400 to 1,750 barges depending on river stage, according to the Missouri Port Authorities website. Barge lines run fleeting areas, in Hettel’s words, to “build and break down tows for specific destinations.” Deckhands do that by hand, with “lines, wires, ratchets and stationary winches,” as one barge line’s hiring page puts it.
Put those numbers side by side and the harbor starts to look like a rail yard for the river, where strings of barges get parked, sorted and sent on. That picture is ours, not the Corps’. The numbers under it aren’t.
The locks are why upstream tows stay small. A 15-barge tow clears a 1,200-foot chamber in one piece in about 45 to 60 minutes. A 600-foot chamber forces the crew to split it nine and six, lock through twice and rebuild it, which takes about 2.5 hours, ACBL says. For the chamber up close, see our guide to Melvin Price Locks and Dam.
Heading south, the last lock a tow meets is Lock 27, at the foot of the Chain of Rocks Canal on the Illinois side. The 8.4-mile canal lets tows skip what the Corps calls “a 17 mile series of rock ledges” in the main channel, the stretch you look down on from the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge. By the Corps’ count, Lock 27 moves more cargo than any other navigation structure on the Mississippi.
### Where can you watch barges in St. Louis?
Start on the downtown levee below the Arch. It’s free, the park grounds above it are open from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., per the National Park Service, and it sits on the open river, below the last lock. To watch a tow work through a lock, go to Melvin Price Locks and Dam, where free public tours start at 10 a.m., 1 p.m. and 3 p.m.
The downtown levee. You stand on the old cobblestones a few steps from the channel, with the riverboats tied up beside you. No lock chamber limits the tows on this stretch.
The trail north. The St. Louis Riverfront Trail follows the working river toward the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, with stretches on levee roads and along the floodwall. It’s paved, flat and short on shade, so carry water.
Jefferson Barracks Park. South of downtown, a 1.7-mile paved trail runs to the north side of the River City Casino property, with views of the river, the barges and the Illinois bluffs. The Jefferson Barracks Bridge marks the downstream end of the harbor’s fleeting stretch.
Melvin Price Locks and Dam. On the Illinois bank, roughly 20 river miles above downtown. The National Great Rivers Museum there opens daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Lock tours run about 45 minutes for up to 25 people, with some walking and heights of about 80 feet. Sign up at the museum desk 15 minutes early, and know that extreme heat or cold can cancel a tour.
A bridge deck. Looking straight down on a moving tow is a different show. Our guide to bridges in St. Louis covers each downtown crossing and which ones you can walk.
Tows don’t keep timetables, so budget an hour at the water, not ten minutes. Heading up to the locks in winter? Add eagle watching on the bluffs to the same drive.
### How much does one barge carry?
About 1,750 tons, according to the Iowa Department of Transportation’s state freight plan. That’s as much as 16 rail cars or 70 large semis. A full 15-barge tow carries 26,250 tons, the same as 216 rail cars behind six locomotives, or 1,050 semis.
Now picture the lengths. The tow runs about a quarter mile. Line up the 1,050 trucks it replaces, bumper to bumper, and they’d stretch 13.9 miles, by Iowa DOT’s figures. No backdrop photo shows you that.
Depth sets the real load. Barges normally run at about 11.5 feet of draft where the river allows, and every six inches of draft adds roughly 100 tons to a barge, ACBL’s Hettel said. By our arithmetic from his figure, cutting the draft a foot in a dry year leaves a 15-barge tow carrying about 3,000 tons less.
What’s actually in them? Through St. Louis, it’s grain and coal, steel and petroleum, scrap metal, aggregates and chemicals, according to the Missouri Port Authorities website and the Illinois Business Journal. In January 2025, the farm cooperative CHS won exclusive rights to move fertilizer through the city’s Municipal River Terminal.
Grain is the cargo to watch this fall. For the week ending Oct. 3, 2026, grain barge movements at Lock 27 ran 60 percent below the same week last year and 42 percent under the three-year average, USDA’s Grain Transportation Report found. Freight went the other way. USDA put the St. Louis barge rate at $28.85 a ton on Oct. 6, 53 percent above a year earlier.
### Where is the port of St. Louis, and who runs it?
Along the city’s riverfront. The St. Louis Port District covers 19.3 miles of riverbank, from river mile 171.9 to 191.2, and the wider Port of Metropolitan St. Louis covers 70 miles of both banks, according to the Missouri Port Authorities website. The St. Louis Port Authority, part of the St. Louis Development Corporation, is the landlord.
The public dock most people mean is the Municipal River Terminal, about 1.5 miles north of downtown. SCF Lewis and Clark Terminals, an Ingram company, runs it under a 25-year lease signed in 2015, on a 2,000-foot dock with direct rail. About 18 million tons of freight move through it each year, the Illinois Business Journal reported in 2025.
The city calls the terminal “the northern-most lock- and ice-free port on the Mississippi River.” Read that next to the St. Paul dates above and it clicks. North of here, every barge waits its turn at a lock, and the top of the river waits out the ice. St. Louis does neither. As we read it, that goes a long way toward explaining the size of the harbor.
How big is the port? Depends who’s counting, and which year. The newest ranking we found comes from the St. Louis Regional Freightway in March 2025, using 2022 Corps data: the region is the most efficient inland port district in the U.S., moving 369,309 tons per river mile against an average of 92,863 for the other eight districts. Its five metro ports along 70 river miles handled nearly 26 million tons that year. Older pages still quote rankings built on older data, so check the date on whatever you read.
### Can you take your own boat through the locks?
Yes, and it costs nothing. Pull the signal cord on the approach wall or call the lock on VHF channel 14, the Minnesota DNR’s Mississippi River boating guide says, and hold your lines by hand instead of tying off. Federal rules give commercial tows precedence, but if pleasure boats can’t lock through within the time of three other lockages, they get one of their own.
Going all the way? The National Park Service puts the Mississippi at about 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca, and you can’t float every mile. Up around Minneapolis, the Coon Rapids Dam and the Upper St. Anthony Falls Dam have no working locks, so every boater portages around them. The St. Anthony Falls carry alone runs 1.54 miles.
Near St. Louis, the advice for small boats is firm: stay out of the Chain of Rocks Canal. The Mississippi River Water Trail calls it narrow, with “no safe place to pull aside if barge traffic is heavy.” Its route keeps to the main river and, when the St. Louis gauge reads below 16 feet, makes a 200-foot portage on river left, the Illinois side, at Chouteau Island, near river mile 190.3.
Add barge tows and floating debris to the current and the river downtown is water for experienced paddlers with a plan. New to paddling? Start with our guide to kayaking in St. Louis. Pricing a boat first? Our breakdown of what boating costs near St. Louis covers the money and who needs a license. And if you’d rather spend the day beside the water than on it, find a beach near St. Louis instead.
### When does the river close to barge traffic?
Only at the extremes, and it wasn’t closed as of Oct. 10, 2026. That day the St. Louis gauge read about 16.3 feet, and we found no Coast Guard restriction on the harbor. USDA’s Oct. 8 grain report called river levels supportive of “generally reliable navigation.” Floods and droughts are what shut it.
High water first. Above 38 feet on the St. Louis gauge, the National Weather Service says, the Coast Guard will consider closing the harbor to navigation. Above 45 feet, it will consider closing the river to all vessel traffic from downtown St. Louis to Chester, Illinois. The harbor closure isn’t hypothetical. On May 3, 2019, and again on May 23, the Coast Guard closed the harbor between river miles 179 and 184 for “extremely high water levels and fast-moving currents.”
Low water shuts the river a different way. In dry years the Coast Guard caps how deep barges can load and how wide tows can run, and sometimes it closes stretches outright. In early October 2022, it closed the river near Stack Island, Mississippi, and the Associated Press reported more than 2,000 barges waiting there. At St. Louis, the Corps kept its 9-foot channel open, but loads had to be lighter, a Corps spokesman told St. Louis Public Radio.
This year has swung both ways. Last winter the St. Louis gauge bottomed out at minus 4.49 feet on Jan. 21, 2026, its lowest reading since 2013, NWS records show. The gauge’s zero is a reference mark, not the riverbed. Then came this fall. The gauge read minus 0.9 feet on Sept. 11 and 23.9 feet on Oct. 6, a rise of nearly 25 feet in 26 days by our count from National Weather Service data. The forecast issued Oct. 10 had it sliding back to about 2 feet by Oct. 24.
Planning a lock tour or a paddle for late October? Check the NWS gauge for St. Louis, ID EADM7, the morning you go.
### How deep does the water need to be, and how fast do tows move?
The Corps’ St. Louis District maintains a channel 9 feet deep and 300 feet wide on 300 miles of the Mississippi, from Saverton, Missouri, to Cairo, Illinois, plus the lower 80 miles of the Illinois River and the lower 36 of the Kaskaskia. When the St. Louis gauge falls below 1 foot, the NWS says, barges may need to lighten loads, and dredging may be needed to hold that depth. Locks add a margin of their own: under federal rules, a vessel’s draft must be at least 3 inches less than the depth over the sills.
Speed is fuzzier than you’d expect. No agency we checked publishes a current official tow speed, so treat these as rough: about 3 to 6 mph pushing upstream and about 10 to 12 mph downstream, depending on current, load and tow size. Those ranges lean on river guides, Corps averages from the 1970s and a 2024 NTSB report that clocked one southbound tow at 12.9 mph over the ground.
Why the gap? Going south, ACBL’s Hettel said, a towboat has to move faster than the water to keep steering; going north, it burns much more fuel. The river itself runs under 3 mph at St. Louis at low flow and reached an estimated 7.6 mph at the 1993 crest, according to USGS. Near lock gates, a Corps navigation notice holds tows to 2 mph, the “rate of a slow walk.”
### What do barge crews earn, and how do the schedules work?
Solid money, on a hard schedule. Federal 2025 wage data on the Labor Department’s O*NET site puts the median for sailors and marine oilers, the job group that includes deckhands, at $57,450 in the St. Louis metro, against $51,520 nationally. Captains, mates and pilots earn a metro median of $94,990, and $92,460 nationwide.
Ship engineers do better still, with a national median of $109,530, though O*NET lists no Missouri figure for them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects water transportation jobs to grow 4 percent from 2025 to 2035, with about 8,600 openings a year.
The schedule is the real adjustment. At Golding Barge Line, the standard for deckhands is 28 days on the boat and 14 days off, and the whole crew lives, eats and works aboard. ACBL told the federal webinar that its lower Mississippi towboats run 28 days on and 28 off, while harbor boats work 14 on and 7 off. BLS puts it plainly: crews on barges “may spend weeks or months away from home and work on board for long periods 7 days a week.”
So do deckhands get days off? Yes, in blocks of weeks at home rather than weekends. The ladder can be short, too. Golding says a deckhand who moves up to tankerman in about 12 to 18 months more than doubles the starting deckhand wage. One line on its hiring page is worth knowing before anything else: applicants have to be able to swim.
Not ready for 28 days on a towboat? Start earning with no experience
### What sank in the river around St. Louis?
Plenty, and low water keeps bringing it back. The best-known wreck is the USS Inaugural, a World War II minesweeper that served as a museum ship here from 1968. During the August 1993 flood it broke loose from its moorings, took on water through a breach in its hull and rolled onto its side, the National Park Service says.
The ship had cleared 82 mines and earned two battle stars, and it was a National Historic Landmark from 1986 until 2001. It still lies partly submerged south of the Poplar Street Bridge, and low water exposed it in 2012, 2015, 2021 and 2022. For the flood that put it there, see our story on the Great Flood of 1993.
The Missouri River has its own. The 250-foot steamboat Montana, built in 1879 for the Missouri River trade, struck a pier of the Wabash Railroad Bridge on June 22, 1884, and sank with no lives lost, Waterways Journal recounts. Low water uncovered the wreck again in 2012 and 2022.
Fire did worse. On May 17, 1849, the Great Fire began aboard the steamboat White Cloud and burned 23 steamboats, 15 square blocks and more than 400 buildings, St. Louis Magazine reported. Three deaths were confirmed, among them fire captain Thomas Targee.
The deadliest happened downriver. On April 27, 1865, the steamer Sultana exploded near Memphis. Licensed for 376 passengers, it was carrying more than 2,400, most of them soldiers just freed from Confederate prison camps, with one lifeboat aboard. The Coast Guard calls it “the worst marine disaster in American history.” Estimates of the dead conflict, but the toll was well over 1,000.
Most people in this city know the barges as slow gray shapes in the corner of somebody’s skyline photo. You’re the one who knows why a tow downtown can run twice the size of one at the locks, where the harbor parks up to 1,750 barges and what the crew on that towboat takes home. Next clear afternoon, walk the levee and count the barges in the first tow that passes. Then drive up to the locks for the 3 p.m. tour and count again.
If an afternoon of counting barges has you wanting a hull of your own, start with the boat dealers and boating businesses in St. Louis we list.
If you run a towing company, a fleeting operation or a marine repair shop that hires deckhands, list your business with us and put your company in front of the readers who just learned what a 28-day hitch pays and want to know who’s hiring on this harbor.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do barge workers make on the Mississippi river?
A.  Federal 2025 wage data on O*NET puts the median for sailors and marine oilers, the group that includes deckhands, at $57,450 in the St. Louis metro and $51,520 nationally. Captains, mates and pilots earn a metro median of $94,990. Golding Barge Line says moving up to tankerman can more than double starting deckhand pay.
### Q. Do deckhands get days off?
A.  Yes, in blocks rather than weekends. Golding Barge Line’s standard deckhand schedule is 28 days on the boat and 14 off, with the crew living aboard. ACBL has said its lower Mississippi towboats run 28 days on and 28 off. While aboard, BLS notes, crews may work seven days a week for long stretches.
### Q. Is the Mississippi river closed to barge traffic?
A.  Not as of Oct. 10, 2026. The St. Louis gauge read about 16.3 feet, we found no Coast Guard restriction on the harbor, and USDA called levels supportive of “generally reliable navigation.” Closures come at the extremes: above about 38 feet the Coast Guard considers shutting the harbor, and in drought it caps drafts and tow widths.
### Q. How fast does a barge go on the Mississippi river?
A.  There’s no official figure, so treat these as approximate: roughly 3 to 6 mph pushing upstream and about 10 to 12 mph downstream, depending on current, load and tow size. The ranges come from river guides, 1970s Corps averages and a 2024 NTSB report. Near lock gates, tows slow to about 2 mph.
### Q. How deep does a river have to be for a barge?
A.  On the Mississippi from Saverton, Missouri, to Cairo, Illinois, the Army Corps of Engineers maintains a channel 9 feet deep and 300 feet wide. Barges load to about 11.5 feet of draft where the river allows, ACBL says. Below 1 foot on the St. Louis gauge, the NWS warns, barges may need to lighten loads.
### Q. Where is the port of St. Louis?
A.  Along the city’s Mississippi riverfront. The St. Louis Port District covers 19.3 miles of riverbank, river miles 171.9 to 191.2, and the wider Port of Metropolitan St. Louis spans 70 miles of both banks. Its main public dock, the Municipal River Terminal, sits about 1.5 miles north of downtown, run by an Ingram company.
### Q. What are some examples of sunken ships in the Mississippi river?
A.  At St. Louis, the USS Inaugural, a World War II minesweeper turned museum ship, broke loose in the 1993 flood and still lies on its side south of the Poplar Street Bridge. The Great Fire of 1849, which began on the steamboat White Cloud, burned 23 steamboats. Near Memphis, the Sultana exploded in 1865 carrying more than 2,400 people.
### Q. Can you take a boat the entire Mississippi River?
A.  Not without carrying it. The National Park Service puts the river at about 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca, and around Minneapolis the Coon Rapids and Upper St. Anthony Falls dams have no working locks, so boaters portage. Locking through elsewhere is free. Near St. Louis, paddlers skip the Chain of Rocks Canal and portage on Chouteau Island when the gauge is below 16 feet.

## Sharks in the Mississippi at St. Louis: The One Real Bull Shark, Stray Gators and Giant Catfish
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/sharks-in-the-mississippi-river-st-louis
Forget the headlines. In July 2021, a wave of stories announced that two bull sharks had swum up the Mississippi all the way to St. Louis. TV station websites ran it. Science blogs ran it. It was a terrific summer story, and that same year a Missouri Department of Conservation biologist took a closer look at one of the two fish. It wasn’t a bull shark.
So here’s the honest count. One bull shark. It came out of the river on the Illinois side in 1937, and it’s still the only accepted bull shark record anywhere in the upper Mississippi. The second “St. Louis shark” was a different species entirely, probably a hoax or a dumped fish, and the researchers who had counted it published a correction in 2023. Plenty of the 2021 stories are still online, still saying two.
The true version is a better story anyway, and it opens onto a bigger one. This stretch of river holds a 124-pound catfish record, a fish whose paddle-shaped snout senses electricity, and a World War II minesweeper lying on its side on the riverbed. This page sorts the real from the viral using biologists’ papers, state wildlife agencies and USGS surveys, checked in October 2026. It’s one chapter of our guide to the St. Louis riverfront, written for the kid who asked “are there sharks in there?” and the grown-up who wasn’t sure what to say.
### Has there ever been a bull shark found in the Mississippi river?
Yes, once. In late summer 1937, two commercial fishermen caught a 5-foot, 84-pound bull shark on the Illinois side of the Mississippi, about 20 river miles above downtown St. Louis. Biologists confirmed it from photographs and published it in the journal Copeia in 1977. It remains the only accepted bull shark record in the upper Mississippi.
Every version of the story agrees on the size and argues about the rest. Herbert Cope and Dudge Collins fished commercially on that stretch of the river. In one account, credited to the old Illinois Department of Conservation, something kept wrecking their wood-and-mesh fish traps, so they built a heavy wire trap, baited it with chicken guts and found the shark inside the next morning. Another account says it got tangled in a seine. Either way, two working fishermen ended up with a fish nobody expected.
They put it on display at a fish market, and it drew crowds for days. Some people smelled a hoax even then. Forty years later, three researchers, J.E. Thomerson, T.B. Thorson and R.L. Hempel, concluded from the photographs that it was a bull shark and wrote it up for Copeia.
What the record lacks matters, too. There’s no preserved specimen in a museum jar. Nobody pinned down the exact date or the exact spot, and “late summer 1937” is as close as it gets. A descendant’s family legend says Collins bought the shark at a St. Louis fish market and showed it around as his own catch. Scientists who revisited the case in 2023 didn’t buy it. They wrote that the record “has never been satisfactorily falsified,” and that no first-hand evidence against it has surfaced in 85 years.
How far had it come? By the river-mile charts that USGS and the Army Corps keep, the catch site sits more than 1,100 river miles from the Gulf. That’s a long haul upstream for an animal most of us picture in the ocean. The bank where it happened makes a full day on the Illinois river road, and the shark is a good story for the drive.
### What happened to the second shark in the 2021 headlines?
It wasn’t a bull shark. The second fish, about 3 feet 2 inches long and taken off a power-plant intake screen at Rush Island in Jefferson County in 1995, was re-examined in 2021 by Missouri Department of Conservation (MDC) fisheries biologist Robert Hrabik. He identified it as an Atlantic sharpnose shark, a species never reported from rivers.
His conclusion was blunt. The fish was most likely “an improperly dumped individual if not an outright hoax.” Translation: somebody probably put it there.
The mix-up had a paper trail. A 2004 USDA Forest Service report listed the Rush Island fish as a bull shark that did “not appear to be the product of a hoax.” In spring 2021, researchers R. Shell and N. Gardner leaned on that listing in a study of bull shark movement in the upper Mississippi, counting just two upper-river specimens in the entire 20th century. That’s where the July 2021 “two bull sharks” stories came from.
To their credit, Shell and Gardner went back. Their 2023 follow-up, written with Hrabik, printed the 1995 photo and formally retracted the earlier acceptance. The 1937 fish was left standing alone as the only known record in the upper basin. That’s how science is supposed to work. The headlines never got a second edition.
Missouri has seen sillier shark scares. In October 2019, a prank site’s story about a bull shark pulled from the Osage River spread across social media, and MDC’s response was “BULL SHARK? BALONEY!” The department said no bull sharks had been caught in Missouri waters. Federal fish biologists added that decades of sampling on the Mississippi along eastern Missouri had never netted a shark of any kind.
So when the next shark clip makes the rounds, ask two things. Where, exactly? And which biologist looked at it? The 1937 fish had photographs and three scientists behind it. Most viral sharks have a caption and a lot of exclamation points.
### How can a saltwater shark survive in a river?
By making its kidneys work overtime. In fresh water, a bull shark has to hold onto salt and shed extra water, so it lowers the urea in its body and puts out about 20 times more urine, with much less salt in it, than it does in the sea, according to the University of Texas program Science and the Sea.
Yes, kids, that means a shark in fresh water spends a lot of its day peeing. It burns plenty of energy doing it, too. The Save Our Seas Foundation describes a whole-body job, with the gills, rectal glands, blood, hormones and kidneys all taking part.
The Florida Museum of Natural History says bull sharks “readily move into freshwater” and can stay there for long periods. That’s why a bull shark is everyone’s first guess when a shark turns up somewhere it shouldn’t. Some travel astonishingly far. The University of Texas program reports bull sharks more than 2,000 miles up the Amazon. Next to that, 1,100 miles up the Mississippi sounds almost modest.
### Why is a bull shark this far upriver so rare?
Partly because the trip is rare to begin with, and partly because of the dams. A 2023 paper by Shell, Gardner and Hrabik found nothing verified upriver since the locks and dams went in, which “strongly suggests” those structures limited the bull shark’s upriver range for much of the 20th century.
The dates line up. The Army Corps built the original Lock and Dam 26, about 2 miles upstream of today’s structure, between 1934 and 1938. The 1937 shark came through while that dam was still going up. Its replacement, Melvin Price Locks and Dam, went into operation on October 10, 1989, and the old dam came down in 1990. Those locks now lift and lower the tows pushing barges on the Mississippi, and no shark has been verified following them through.
Cold water is the answer most people guess. It isn’t the whole story. Shell and Gardner noted in 2021 that the river near the 1937 catch site reaches or beats the bull shark’s average preferred temperature for a large part of the year. Summer water here is warm enough for a shark.
The plainest answer is that these long trips are, in the 2023 paper’s words, “exceptional and rare events.” Most young bull sharks presumably stay in the lower reaches of rivers. A 1938 report put bull sharks about 300 kilometers up the Mississippi in Louisiana. There are records from the Red River, and an 1829 “white shark” caught at Natchez, Mississippi, was probably a bull shark, judging by its size and the fresh water it came from. Beyond the 1937 fish, though, nothing north of Louisiana has been confirmed anywhere in the Mississippi basin.
How far north is that on a map? The 1937 catch site sits at about 38.9 degrees north, the farthest upstream accepted record in the Mississippi system. Bull sharks have been farther north, just not by river. Summer migrations along the Atlantic coast carry them to Chesapeake Bay and off New England.
So if a kid won’t wade in at a beach near St. Louis because of sharks, you can honestly say the only confirmed one around here was caught in 1937. Save your respect for the Mississippi’s current. At the 1993 flood crest, USGS estimated it downtown at up to 7.6 mph, and that, not a fin, is the river’s real hazard.
### What really lives in the Mississippi at St. Louis?
Bigger fish than the shark, for a start. Tim Pruitt’s blue catfish, caught just below Melvin Price Locks and Dam in May 2005, weighed 124 pounds, 40 more than the 1937 bull shark. It was a world record then and is still the Illinois record, says the Illinois Department of Natural Resources.
Pruitt’s fish measured 58 inches with a 44-inch girth, and the Associated Press reported that it dragged his boat during a fight of more than half an hour. It died on the way to an aquarium afterward. One correction for the internet, since a bad number keeps circulating: the 143-pound blue catfish behind today’s world record came from Kerr Lake, Virginia, in 2011. A 130-pound blue caught on the Missouri River north of the city in 2010 set a Missouri record. Neither came out of the Mississippi.
Giant blues aren’t new. MDC says fish over 100 pounds were common in Missouri before 1900, and reports from the 1800s run as high as 315 pounds. The twist is that blue catfish have nearly disappeared from the Mississippi above the mouth of the Missouri River, partly because dams hamper their seasonal runs upstream. Sound familiar? The same structures may have stopped the sharks.
The rest of the cast, from MDC’s field guides:
Flathead catfish. Commonly 1 to 45 pounds, up to about 100. It hunts live fish and crayfish at night and isn’t a scavenger.
Paddlefish. Missouri’s official state aquatic animal, up to about 7 feet and 160-plus pounds. The paddle is an electrosensory organ that finds plankton, and since the Chinese paddlefish was declared extinct in 2022, it’s the last living member of a family about 120 million years old.
Pallid sturgeon. Endangered under federal and Missouri law. It lives at least 40 years, and if you hook one, it goes back unharmed.
Lake sturgeon. Up to 8 feet and 300 pounds, and it can live 150 years. MDC started stocking them in 1984, and the first confirmed spawning in Missouri came in 2015, below Melvin Price.
Silver carp. An invasive fish whose adults leap out of the water at any disturbance and can injure boaters. One female can produce 500,000 eggs.
Freshwater drum. It grunts, using muscles on its swim bladder, and its ear bones get collected as “lucky stones.”
Freshwater mussels. Called “the livers of the rivers” because they filter water. Missouri has about 69 native species, and nearly 42 percent are species of conservation concern.
The strangest visitor in the record books wasn’t a shark at all. In fall 2006, a West Indian manatee about 10 feet long swam more than 1,200 kilometers up the Mississippi to near Memphis. It was first spotted on October 23, slipped past federal, state and SeaWorld search teams using sonar and infrared, and was found dead 49 days later. It’s a sad ending to a remarkable swim.
Want to try for a big blue yourself? Our list of fishing spots in St. Louis includes places on the Mississippi. Pack a heavy rod and a kid who doesn’t mind waiting.
### Should you eat the fish you catch here?
Yes, in moderation. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services advisory, last updated March 2024, tells everyone to eat flathead, channel and blue catfish over 17 inches and common carp over 21 inches from the Mississippi no more than once a week, because of PCBs, chlordane and mercury. Shovelnose sturgeon and buffalo: once a month.
Never eat sturgeon eggs, the advisory says. Stricter limits apply to pregnant women, women of childbearing age, nursing mothers and children under 13, including one meal a month of those catfish once they pass 30 inches. A meal, by Missouri’s count, is 8 ounces of uncooked fish for a 150-pound adult and 3 ounces for a 40-pound child.
Cross the river and the same water gets different rules. Illinois’s advisory, updated April 2026, sets common carp at one meal a week and shovelnose sturgeon at one a month for everyone. It has carried no catfish advisory on the Mississippi since 2023. Its statewide mercury rule asks pregnant or nursing women, women who may become pregnant and kids under 15 to stick to one meal a week of predatory fish, gar and flatheads included.
Both states agree on the easy wins. Fillet the fish, take the skin off and trim the fat. That cuts your exposure, though trimming does nothing for mercury.
