### Frequently asked questions about race tracks near St. Louis
### Q. Does St. Louis have a NASCAR track?
A.  Yes. World Wide Technology Raceway in Illinois ran the NASCAR Cup Series’ Enjoy Illinois 300 on September 13, before a fifth consecutive sellout crowd, so buy tickets early.
### Q. Is there dirt racing at the Dome in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. FloRacing says the Gateway Dirt Nationals are held on a temporary fifth-mile oval inside The Dome at America’s Center in downtown St. Louis, at 901 N. Broadway. This year’s dates are December 3-5, and tickets go on sale October 20 at 10 a.m. Central.
### Q. What is Fairmount Park called now?
A.  Fairmount Park Casino & Racing. The track went by FanDuel Sportsbook and Horse Racing during its partnership with FanDuel, and FanDuel later announced it was closing its retail sportsbook there.
### Q. How much do tickets cost to attend Fairmount Park racetrack?
A.  For its centennial celebration, Fairmount listed general admission as free. If you want a better seat, the track says you can book a private box or table in the grandstand. Check the track’s site before you go, since event pricing can change.
### Q. Should I bet win place or show?
A.  Win cashes if your horse comes in first, place if it comes in first or second, and show if it comes in first, second or third. For a first visit, show keeps you in the race longest, while win carries the most upside.
### Q. What is the lowest amount you can bet on a horse?
A.  On Fairmount’s September 1 card, the superfecta was a 10-cent bet and the trifecta a 50-cent bet with a $1.00 minimum wager. For win, place and show, Churchill Downs lists a $2 minimum. Minimums vary by track, so ask the Fairmount teller.
### Q. What is the cheapest dirt track racing to get into?
A.  A regular night at Tri-City Speedway, about 8 miles from downtown St. Louis, skips the ticket packages: you pay at the front gate, cash or card, and races generally start at 7:15 p.m. I couldn’t find a posted gate price, so check the track’s social pages before you drive over.

## Your Rug Didn’t Shrink: How to Choose an Area Rug for a St. Louis Room
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-an-area-rug-in-st-louis
Why is your sofa still standing on bare wood? You got the new rug home, heard it slap down on the boards, dragged the coffee table onto it, and stood back. The sofa sat there with all four feet on bare wood like it was waiting for a bus. Your stomach dropped a little. On the showroom floor that rug looked enormous, a whole field of wool under those bright lights. It didn’t change size in the car. Your room just did the math the store never asked you to do.
Here’s the fix, and it costs a roll of blue painter’s tape. Before you set foot in a shop, tape an 8-by-10 rectangle on your living room floor, 8 feet deep and 10 feet across the front of the sofa. Slide the sofa so its front legs sit just inside the line. Then live with it for a day. Carry the laundry through it, put your coffee on the table in the middle, and watch where your feet land when you stand up. If the tape looks like a postage stamp, run a second line out to 9 by 12 and live with that one too. By the next evening you’ll know your size in your gut, and you won’t have spent a cent finding out.
Now the old rug, the flat, faded one the dog has slept on for years. If you live in the city, the fee for its ride out is already on your water bill. The City of St. Louis Refuse Division picks up bulky items once a month, and the service is included in the $14-a-month-per-unit solid waste fee that rides on your water bill. Here’s the catch nobody mentions until the truck rolls past your alley: no container or bundle can be over 6 feet long, over 2 feet across or over 100 pounds. Roll an 8x10 the way everybody does and you’ve built an 8-foot log, two feet too long.
So fold it in half first, then roll it. It comes out about 4 feet long, dust in your nose and grit on your forearms, and you tie it off and drag it out back by 6 a.m. on the Monday of your collection week, up to three items a pickup. Not sure it qualifies? The Refuse Division’s number is (314) 622-4800.
Your old rug’s funeral is already on your water bill. It just can’t be longer than 6 feet.
Most people buy a rug in the opposite order. You fall for a rug first. The color hits you, or the softness under your palm, or the way it makes you picture a winter evening with your feet tucked under you. The logic comes after, and it’s there to protect the feeling: tape the room, flip the corner before you pay, read the little sewn-in tag, and interview the shop before you hand over a card.
If you live in an older brick house, a Soulard rowhouse, a South Grand four-family, one of the big places in the Central West End, you may already know the sound problem. Footsteps ring off the walls. A sock foot finds the one board that creaks. A rug in a house like that earns its keep. It softens the echo. It protects the floor. And it pulls a room of mismatched furniture into one place where people want to sit. Get the size wrong and it fails at every one of those.
There’s a reason so many of those houses are brick, and it starts with a mattress. On the night of May 17, 1849, an ember smoldering in a mattress on the steamboat White Cloud set its cabins burning at the riverfront. According to St. Louis Magazine, the fire claimed 15 square blocks, more than 400 buildings and 23 steamers, and a newly instituted building code called for fire-resistant materials, including plenty of brick. So the ring in your front room has a pedigree. Hard brick, hard plaster, hard boards, and every sound bounces until something soft catches it. In a lot of St. Louis houses, the rug is the softest thing in the room. Your echo started on a burning boat. Your rug is how you finish the story.
### Should I get a 5x7 or 8x10 rug?
For most living rooms, get the 8x10. A 5x7 works when you want every furniture leg off the rug in a small room or a reading corner, while an 8x10 is sized so the front legs of your sofa and chairs can rest on its edge, and that one move is what makes a seating area look like it belongs together.
Start with the sofa, not the room. Lift the front of the couch, slide the rug under, and set it down: the front feet thump onto the wool edge, the coffee table and the chairs suddenly line up around it, and the room pulls together like somebody finally sat down in it. A rug narrower than your couch does the opposite and leaves the couch floating, cut loose from everything in front of it. One sizing guide puts it in plain numbers: under a standard 84-inch sofa, an 8-foot-wide rug, which means an 8x10, is the minimum, and a 9x12 is ideal. So the question people type into their phones at midnight, whether a rug should be bigger or smaller than the couch, has a short answer. Bigger. Almost always bigger.
Then look at the edges. The same guide suggests leaving 18 to 24 inches of exposed floor around the rug. That strip of wood is the frame around the picture. Run the rug nearly wall to wall and it starts to look like carpet somebody forgot to finish. Leave a wide moat of floor all the way around and the rug looks like a bathmat that wandered down from upstairs.
If you’re torn between two sizes, go up. The guide says a too-small rug can make a sweeping space feel cramped, while a larger rug will give even tiny rooms a spacious, coordinated look. You’ll feel the difference the first time you get up from the sofa barefoot on a January morning and your heel lands on wool instead of the cold edge of a board.
The 5x7 still has a job. Tuck it under a coffee table between two armchairs, slide it in front of a fireplace, or put it in a narrow front room where a bigger rug would curl up against the radiator. Just choose it on purpose, with the legs deliberately off, rather than because it was the one on sale.
### Why does every rug look bigger in the store?
Because the store is a warehouse, and your living room isn’t. A showroom has high ceilings, wide open floor and rugs hanging on racks or stacked in piles with no sofa next to them. Your eye has nothing to measure against. At home it has everything: the sofa, the radiator, the doorway to the dining room, the spot by the window where the dog sleeps in the sun.
That’s why the tape test works. It puts the ruler back in the room. And if you can’t decide between the two outlines after a day, go with the one your feet liked. The kids and the dog will have crossed it twenty times by then, and the tape peels up with a little tearing sound when you’re done.
Then stand in the doorway and take a photo of the taped room, the way a guest first sees it. Carry that photo into the shop. It’s worth more than a page of measurements, because it shows the person helping you the room you actually live in: the light from the bay window, the color of the floor, the fireplace that eats one whole wall, the sofa your aunt gave you that isn’t going anywhere.
### What does the back of a rug tell you that the front won’t?
Almost everything. Flip the corner. That’s the whole trick, and hardly anyone does it in a store because it feels a little rude, like checking a stranger’s teeth. Do it anyway. Fold the corner back, put your fingers on the underside, and look.
On a hand-knotted rug, the pattern shows clearly through on the back and you can see the individual knots, like stitches you could count. One rug dealer’s guide to spotting hand-knotted work describes the other case: on a hand-tufted rug, the back is covered entirely by a canvas cloth that hides the construction, and if you can’t see the pattern on the reverse at all, it isn’t hand-knotted.
Now fold it over your arm. The same guide says a hand-knotted rug folds softly and unevenly, while a stiff, board-like fold usually means there’s a backing. Your hands will know the difference before your head does. One drapes like a heavy wool coat. The other bends like a cereal box.
Check the fringe last. On a hand-knotted rug the fringe isn’t decoration. It’s the warp, the foundation threads the whole rug is built on, coming out at each end. On many machine-made rugs the fringe is sewn or glued on afterward as a finishing touch. Look where the fringe meets the pile. If you see a seam or a band of stitching, you know which kind of rug you’re holding.
None of this makes a tufted or machine-made rug a bad buy. It makes it a different thing at a different price, and you deserve to know which one you’re paying for. That’s what high quality really means once you’re standing in the shop: a rug that is exactly what the person selling it says it is. And don’t panic over a rough-looking back. Knot density varies enormously between regions and periods, so a coarser back does not mean a lesser rug. Honest beats perfect.
### What is that little fiber tag really telling you?
Somewhere on the back, usually near a corner, there’s a small sewn-in label. Most people never read it. It should.
Under the Federal Trade Commission’s textile rule, that label has to list the generic names and percentages by weight of the fibers in the product, for every fiber present at 5 percent or more. So “100% wool” isn’t a mood or a marketing word. It’s a statement somebody is on the hook for.
Here’s the part almost nobody knows. For a floor covering with a backing, the rule says the fiber disclosure has to make clear that it relates only to the face, pile or outer surface, and not to the backing, filling or padding. The rule’s own example label reads: “100% Nylon Pile, 100% Cotton Back.” In plain English, the soft part you run your hand across can be one thing, and the layer holding it together can be something else entirely. A tag that says wool is talking about what you touch, not what’s touching your floor. Which is one more reason to fold that corner.
Want to train your eye before you shop? Go look at rugs nobody will ever try to sell you. According to St. Louis Magazine, local lore says a St. Louisan named James F. Ballard fell for rugs one day in 1905, captivated by an oriental rug in a shop window, and the Saint Louis Art Museum ended up with the larger share of his collection: 110 carpets. Admission to the Saint Louis Art Museum is free every day. One fragment of a Mughal court carpet Ballard donated is labeled simply “wool and silk,” which is the museum version of the tag sewn on your rug. I couldn’t confirm which of his carpets are on view on a given day, so check with the museum before you go. Even an hour in the galleries teaches your eyes what a centuries-old knot looks like up close.
That’s also the honest way to think about the blend question people ask most, whether all-wool beats a wool blend. Read the small print first. Under the same rule, a fiber present at less than 5 percent of the total fiber weight can’t be listed by its generic name. It has to be designated as “other fiber.” So the tag tells you the big players in the pile, not every guest at the party. Wool does earn its place in a muggy St. Louis summer, though. The Woolmark Company says wool fibers can absorb large quantities of moisture vapor and allow it to evaporate, which is the cool, dry, never-clammy feel you get when you sink your toes into a good wool pile in July. It doesn’t tell you how that rug will wear in your front room with a dog, two kids and a radiator. So don’t argue percentages with yourself in the aisle. Ask the shop why the blend is there, which room they’d put it in, and how it has held up in homes like yours. A good shop answers that without blinking.
### Will a rug hurt the old wood floor underneath?
It can, and the damage hides until you move the rug. You roll it up a few years later to repaint, and there it is: a pale rectangle, or a cloudy, slightly tacky patch the exact shape of the rug, like a shadow that stayed behind after the rug left.
The usual suspect is the backing, not the wool. Flip the rug one more time. If the underside is a solid sheet of rubber, a slick plastic grid, or a stiff coating that smells like a new tire, ask the shop plainly what it will do to a finished wood floor over a long, sticky St. Louis summer. Ask what pad they’d put under it and what that pad is made of. If the answer is a shrug, keep shopping.
In an older house this one is personal. If your floor has been refinished before, there’s only so much wood left to sand, and a rug that marks the finish costs you a lot more than a rug. So the answer to what rugs to avoid on hardwood floors comes down to three habits: read the back, ask about the pad, and lift the rug now and then to let the boards air out and see what’s going on underneath. If you’re still deciding what goes on the floor itself, our guide to hardwood vs. laminate in St. Louis is a good place to start.
### Lighter or darker than the floor is really a question about light
People ask whether a rug should be lighter or darker than the floor. What you’re really choosing is contrast. A light rug on a dark-stained floor reads crisp and bright. A darker rug on pale oak anchors a room that otherwise feels like it’s drifting. Match the two too closely and the rug disappears, which is a lot of money to spend on something nobody notices.
Then think about the light you actually get. A north-facing front room in a brick house goes gray by mid-afternoon in January, and a dark rug in there turns into a hole in the floor. A sunny back room off the kitchen can carry a deep red or a navy that would sulk anywhere else. And if you want a small room to feel bigger, a lighter rug with a quiet pattern helps, but size helps more. A big, calm rug opens a room in a way a small loud one never will.
Last, think about what walks across it. A golden retriever who sheds like it’s his job. A toddler with a grape popsicle. Boots in from a slushy January sidewalk on Cherokee Street. The prettiest cream rug in the store is a different rug in that house. A soft pattern, a mid-tone color and a little visual noise forgive a lot of life.
### Fall for it first, then interview the shop
Price follows construction, which is why two 8x10 rugs that look the same from across the room can be far apart on the tag. A hand-knotted pile rug can take months on a loom. A hand-tufted rug is made with a tool that punches yarn through a canvas backing in a fraction of the time. Neither is a rip-off at the right price. Either one is at the wrong price.
So don’t walk in asking for the cheapest 8x10. Shortlist two or three local rug shops and go in with your taped-room photo and your measurements, ready to interview them. Tell each one what you want: the room, who walks on it, the floor underneath, and how you want it to feel under bare feet on a cold morning. If you live in an old brick house, say so. Tell them the boards are old, the walls aren’t square, the radiator sits where it sits, and the house rings when the kids run. Then ask whether they’ve laid rugs in houses like yours, and what they put underneath. Ballard fell in love through a shop window. You get to do the falling and the asking.
Then listen. Ask what the rug is made of, front and back, and ask them to flip the corner for you. Ask what pad they’d pair with your floor, whether you can see the rug in your own room before you commit, and how they clean and repair what they sell. Then compare what each shop says it will deliver, the rug, the pad, the advice and the care after the sale, against what you told them you wanted. A good price for an 8x10 is the one where those two lists match.
Your taped-up floor and that doorway photo are the best shopping list you’ll ever carry. Bring them to two or three local shops you find under Rugs on St Louis Near Me Directory, and let them show you what fits the room you actually live in.
If you’re the rug shop, the rug cleaner or the one-person repair crew who flips corners for a living, St. Louis homeowners are already looking for you. More customers are searching this page for exactly what you know, so list your business where they can call you.
And before you say yes, put your hand flat on the rug and close your eyes for a second. It feels silly in a store full of people. It isn’t. You’re going to touch this thing every day for years, and your palm knows more than the price tag does.
### When it finally comes home
It’ll arrive rolled tight and maybe curled at the ends, and the old one goes out to the alley folded in half. Give it a few days flat. Roll a stubborn corner backward against the curl. Put the pad down first, then square the rug to the sofa rather than the walls if your walls aren’t quite straight, which in an older house they often aren’t.
Brain full of rug math? Go eat something red and Malaysian.
Then sit on the sofa and look at it from where you’ll see it most. If the front legs rest on the rug, the edges have their strip of bare wood, and your feet land on something soft when you stand up, you chose well. If the rug still looks small, now you know exactly why, and exactly what to ask for next time.

### Frequently asked questions about choosing an area rug
### Q. Should area rug be bigger or smaller than couch?
A.  Bigger. A rug narrower than the sofa makes the sofa look like it’s floating. One sizing guide says that under a standard 84-inch sofa, an 8-foot-wide rug, an 8x10, is the minimum and a 9x12 is ideal, with at least the front legs of the sofa resting on the rug.
### Q. How can you tell if a rug is high quality?
A.  Fold the corner back. A hand-knotted rug shows its pattern and knots on the back and folds softly, while a tufted rug hides its construction under a canvas cloth and folds stiffly. Neither is automatically better. Quality means the rug is what the shop says it is, so ask them to flip it for you and explain what you’re looking at.
### Q. What rugs to avoid on hardwood floors?
A.  Be wary of rugs and pads with a solid rubber or plastic backing, especially on an older floor with a finish you want to keep. Ask the shop what the backing is made of, what pad they recommend for your floor and why, and lift the rug now and then to check the wood underneath.
### Q. Should a rug be lighter or darker than the floor?
A.  Either works if there’s contrast. A light rug brightens a dark floor, and a darker rug anchors a pale one. A rug that matches the floor too closely tends to disappear. Let your room’s light and who walks across it, kids, dogs, winter boots, decide how light you can go.
### Q. Is 100% wool carpet better than 80%/20?
A.  The tag can’t settle that by itself. The federal textile rule requires the label to list each fiber at 5 percent or more by weight, and on a backed floor covering that disclosure covers only the face or pile. So read the label, then ask the shop why the blend is there and how it has held up in rooms like yours.

## Ukrainian on Paper, Russian on the Menu: Russian Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/russian-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Borscht lands the color of a church window with the sun behind it, deep magenta, a thin shine of fat on top and a little hill of chopped dill. Steam comes off it smelling of beets and broth and something sour underneath. You drop in a spoon of sour cream and drag it once. The white goes pink in a long, lazy ribbon. Bread waits on the side, dark and heavy, and the first spoonful is sweet, then sharp, then warm all the way down to your belt.
Now the part most St. Louisans have backwards. Ask around and that bowl is Russian. Ask UNESCO and it’s Ukrainian: the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking went onto the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in 2022, filed as a case of extreme urgency, because the war displaced the families who carry the recipe and cut communities off from the vegetables that go into it. The soup on your spoon is a soup somebody is trying to save.
In St. Louis, that borderland showed up in a church on Gravois long before it showed up on a menu. Its Russian Orthodox church, named for the Archangel, was founded in October 1909, and its parish was made up of immigrants from “Austria-Hungary, Galicia and Russia” who had come looking for work in the mining areas of Illinois and Missouri. They couldn’t afford a church at first, so they rented stores for services. Then they bought a house at 1125 Hickory Street for $7,000 and stacked a whole parish inside it: services on the first floor, the priest living on the second, a meeting hall on the third. Outside, Gravois was a cobblestone street, and the Bellefontaine streetcar rattled down it.
Visitors are welcome anytime. The parish stands at 1901 Ann Avenue, on the corner of Ann and Gravois. Divine Liturgy is at 10:00 a.m. on Sundays, the services are in English, and the parish holds a coffee hour right after. Parking is on the street only, the church line is 314-884-0394, and its website says it plainly: “Visitors are welcome anytime!”
So where do you go tonight? Start at Astoria Bistro, also known as Astoria Kabob House. One diner called it “a lovely jewel box of a restaurant” and wrote down exactly what landed on the table: the currant compote, the borsch, the Olivier salad, the bliny with meat and the cherry dumplings. Order it in that sequence and you can feel the meal turn. A cold, sweet-tart sip of compote first. Then beet steam on your face. Then the cool crunch of potato salad, a warm pancake folded around meat, and last a dumpling that splits under your fork and bleeds dark cherry into the sour cream. Ask for the sour cream on the side, and say yes to the bread.
The receipt: 12949 Olive Arcade Plaza. Its MapQuest listing shows it closed Sundays and Mondays and opening at 4 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday, so this is a dinner plan. Its menu runs to homemade comfort food: borscht, pelmeni, beef stroganoff, chicken Kiev and stuffed cabbage rolls. Small family kitchens change hours without warning, so call 314-878-7711 before you drive.
Here’s the one idea that changes how you order. Russian food in St. Louis has always been a borderland table. The same hands rolled the dumplings whether the grandmother called herself Russian, Ukrainian or something the census never had a box for. Don’t walk in asking whether a dish is “really” Russian. Ask who made it, how, and what goes on top. That last answer is almost always sour cream.
### Is borscht Ukrainian or Russian?
In 2022, UNESCO inscribed the Culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking. The same record says there are many versions. Each kitchen swears its version is the real one. Each grandmother is right.
One detail from the UNESCO record will stay with you. In the Podillia region, the third day of a wedding has kept its ritual name do nevistky - na borshch, which means “visit daughter-in-law to eat borscht.” The new bride’s soup is how the family takes her measure. Think about the nerves on that stove.
### What goes into a real bowl of borscht?
UNESCO’s record says borscht is cooked with broth combined with beetroot, sugar beet or fermented beet juice, and that last one is where a sour edge can come from. Most kitchens build from there with cabbage, potato, carrot and onion, cut small enough to fit on a spoon. Many add beef and let the bones do the work. Some go meatless. A good cook adds something sour near the end so the red stays bright instead of fading to brown, and you can tell when they didn’t: the soup looks like weak tea and tastes like boiled vegetables.
So what is traditional borscht made of, if you have to say it in one breath? Beets, broth, cabbage and a little sour, finished with dill and sour cream. Everything else is family argument.
What is usually eaten with borscht? UNESCO says borscht is typically served with bread or garlic buns. In a Russian or Ukrainian home that often means dark rye, torn rather than sliced, and the garlic buns are soft little rolls brushed with garlic and oil that you pull apart and drag through the bowl. Sour cream goes on top, a pinch of fresh dill, and maybe a clove of raw garlic rubbed on the crust if the cook trusts you. At a St. Louis restaurant, ask for the bread before the soup comes. Nobody will think you’re greedy. They’ll think you’ve done this before.
### Why is there sour cream on everything?
Because almost everything on a Russian table is either rich, sour or both, and sour cream settles the argument. It cools a hot soup. It softens the vinegar in a pickle. It turns a plate of plain boiled dumplings into something you’d fight your brother for. Our own Russian Food category page says it plainly: sour cream and dill show up throughout by design. St. Louis should get this faster than anyone. Sour cream is Russia’s Provel, minus the argument.
The sour cream at a Russian table is heavier than the tub at the grocery store. It sits on the spoon in a slow curl and doesn’t run. It tastes of cream first and tang second. When it melts into borscht the soup goes from sharp to silky in one stir, and that change in your mouth is half the reason people order the soup at all.
Dill is the other constant. Fresh, feathery, chopped fine and scattered without much ceremony on soup, dumplings, potatoes and salads. If you think you don’t like dill, it’s probably because you’ve had the dried kind. Fresh dill on hot buttered dumplings smells like a summer garden somebody carried indoors.
Unrelated, but have you ever eaten a stew that cooked all night?
### Pelmeni are small on purpose
Pelmeni are the dumpling that tells the kitchen you know what you’re doing. They’re little, about the size of the end of your thumb, made of thin dough pinched around a raw meat filling. The raw meat cooks inside the tightly fastened dumpling, so it fills with its own juices. Bite carelessly and it runs down your chin.
Small is the point. They come glossy with melted butter, and you eat them fast and hot, three to a forkful if nobody’s watching. They freeze beautifully, too, so a bag in the freezer is the plan for the night nobody wants to cook.
What do Russians eat pelmeni with? Butter and sour cream, mostly, often both at once. Some people splash on a little vinegar to cut the richness. Some like a smear of hot mustard. Some eat them floating in the broth they boiled in, with dill on top, which is the Russian answer to chicken noodle soup on a sick day.
Pelmeni vs pierogi is the question every St. Louisan with a Polish grandmother asks first. Pierogi are larger half-moons with fillings like potato, cheese or fruit, and they’re commonly fried in butter. Pelmeni are smaller and rounder, with a thinner dough and a raw meat filling. If that’s the dumpling you’re craving, look on the menu for vareniki: dough folded over the filling into a half-moon, filled with potato and onions, cheese or cherries. If you grew up on church-basement pierogi in South City, vareniki will taste like home with a different accent.
Even the parish on Gravois ran on dumplings. The parish’s own history thanks the “Piroghi workers whose work is really a labor of love” and says they “keep our freezers filled with this popular food item for many people to enjoy.” That’s the borderland table, rolled by hand on Gravois.
### What do you order first at a Russian table?
Not the main course. Russian hospitality starts with zakuski, the little bites often described as Russia’s answer to tapas. Traditionally they meet guests coming in from the cold: pickles of all sorts, salted herring, Salat Olivier, blini and caviar. Order two or three to share, and listen for the pickle that cracks when somebody bites it.
Look for seledka, salt herring, usually laid out with raw onion and boiled potato. It’s oily and briny and much milder than you’re afraid it will be. Look for the Olivier salad, a cold potato salad with peas, pickles, carrots and mayonnaise, a holiday-table favorite that tastes like somebody’s childhood. If red caviar is on the menu, it comes on buttered bread or rolled in blini, and the little orange beads pop against your teeth like warm sea salt.
Then the soup. Borscht if it’s your first time. If the server mentions solyanka, say yes: it’s a sour, salty soup of pickles and several kinds of meat, often with a slice of lemon and an olive floating on top, and it tastes like the best thing that ever happened to a pickle.
Then one hot plate for the table. Pelmeni. Beef stroganoff over noodles or potatoes. Stuffed cabbage rolls. Chicken Kiev, which arrives looking innocent and squirts hot herb butter across the plate the second your knife goes in, so cut it pointing away from your shirt.
Here’s the ordering script that gets you the good stuff. Ask, “Are the pelmeni made here?” Handmade pelmeni have slightly uneven edges and a thinner skin, and a kitchen that makes them by hand is proud to say so. Ask for sour cream on the side so you can use as much as you want. Ask what the cook would order. Then say yes to the bread.
Craving a bowl of buttered pelmeni before the weekend is out? Start your shortlist with Russian Food on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three kitchens and ask which dumplings they roll by hand.
If you’re the cook behind a Russian, Ukrainian or Eastern European kitchen, the people craving your borscht are already searching. Put your menu where they look and list your business so more of those hungry neighbors end up at your door.
### Where can you eat Russian food in St. Louis?
Fewer places than you’d hope, which is why the good ones are worth the drive. For a sit-down dinner, start with Astoria. Bring the friend who isn’t sure about any of this; the kabobs on the same menu are the safe harbor while they steal a spoon of your borscht.
For the night you cook at home, go to Global Foods Market, an international grocery you can reach at 314-835-1112. The store says it carries deli meats and sausages from Turkey, Poland, Russia and Ukraine. Stand at the counter long enough and the cold smell of smoked sausage follows you to the car. Ask what came in this week, then build your own zakuski board with dark bread, a jar of pickles and a tub of sour cream.
The same rule works anywhere: shortlist two or three spots, call and tell them what you want, a first-timer’s borscht and dumpling dinner, then compare what each kitchen says it will put on the table. The one that gets excited on the phone is usually the one to visit.
If you’d rather meet the community than a menu, go back to that parish on Gravois. Its history also remembers the Bazaar, begun in October 1975, as the one event that brought many visitors and friends into its hall. Call the church line from the top of this page and ask when the next one is. Go for the welcome, not to shop for dumplings, and you’ll still leave knowing more about this food than a menu could teach you.

Polish food in St. Louis and what to order

### Save room for blini, tea and something sweet
Blini are crepe-like pancakes, and they swing both ways on a menu. Savory, they’re folded around ground meat or rolled with red caviar and sour cream. Sweet, they come with jam, honey or farmer’s cheese. A plate of them with a glass of hot tea is the Russian version of coffee and a doughnut, only slower.
Look for syrniki, small golden pancakes made from farmer’s cheese, crisp outside and tender in the middle, served with sour cream and jam. And if the menu has cherry vareniki, order them: purple juice seeps out of the dough when you cut one, and with a spoon of sour cream they taste like a cherry pie that wandered into a dumpling.
Drink the compote. It’s a cold drink made by simmering fruit, often currants or cherries, and it tastes like the end of summer in a glass. Then finish with tea, strong and hot. Nobody at a Russian table rushes this part of the meal, and neither should you.
### Frequently asked questions about Russian food
### Q. What is Russia’s national dish?
A.  There’s no single winner, and Russians will happily argue it over dinner. The answers you’ll hear most are pelmeni, the small meat dumplings, and the soups: shchi, the old cabbage soup of the countryside, and borscht, which UNESCO lists as Ukrainian heritage. If you want one plate that tastes like Russia, order pelmeni with butter and sour cream.
### Q. What is Russian comfort food?
A.  Hot, heavy and cheap to make: pelmeni in butter, borscht or cabbage soup with dark bread, buckwheat kasha, mashed potatoes with dill, cabbage rolls baked in tomato sauce, and blini with sour cream. It’s food built for cold kitchens and long winters, and almost all of it gets a spoon of sour cream before it reaches the table.
### Q. What is traditional borscht made of?
A.  Broth and beets are the heart of it. UNESCO’s record describes borscht as cooked with broth combined with beetroot, sugar beet or fermented beet juice. Most cooks add cabbage, potato, carrot and onion, often beef, and a little sour to keep the color bright, then finish the bowl with dill and sour cream.
### Q. What is usually eaten with borscht?
A.  UNESCO notes borscht is typically served with bread or garlic buns. Dark rye is common, and soft garlic rolls are a treat worth asking for. On top: a spoon of sour cream and fresh dill. Some families also put out raw garlic or a plate of pickles.
### Q. What is Russian pelmeni made of?
A.  Thin unleavened dough made from flour, water and often egg, wrapped around raw ground meat, usually beef or a beef and pork mix, seasoned with onion, salt and black pepper. The meat cooks inside the dough as the pelmeni boil, which is why every bite comes with its own little spoonful of broth.
### Q. What is pelmeni vs pierogi?
A.  Pelmeni are small, round, meat-filled dumplings that are boiled and served with butter or sour cream. Pierogi are larger half-moons with fillings like potato, cheese or fruit, and they are commonly fried in butter. If you want something closer to pierogi, look for vareniki: half-moon dumplings filled with potato and onions, cheese or cherries.
### Q. What do Russians eat pelmeni with?
A.  Melted butter and sour cream, often both. Some add a splash of vinegar to cut the richness, a smear of hot mustard, black pepper or fresh dill. Others eat pelmeni in the hot broth they cooked in, like a dumpling soup. Ask your server which way the kitchen likes them and try that first.
### Q. What are some popular Russian desserts?
A.  Syrniki, little farmer’s cheese pancakes with jam and sour cream; sweet blini with honey or jam; cherry vareniki; and pryaniki, spiced honey cookies served with tea. To drink, look for compote, a cold drink of simmered fruit such as currants or cherries.
### Q. What is a typical Russian breakfast?
A.  Often kasha, a warm porridge, with buckwheat the classic, topped with butter or milk. Syrniki and blini are weekend favorites. Many people eat farmer’s cheese with jam or sour cream, or an open-faced sandwich of bread, butter and cheese or sausage, all with a strong cup of black tea.

## Four Seconds of Silence: What a Wedding Singer Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-wedding-singer-costs-in-st-louis
The organ stops. Somewhere near the back, a cough drop wrapper crinkles, and every head in the church hears it. Your mother is holding her breath. The person you’re marrying is staring at the doors. And a singer you have met exactly twice is standing near the front, a folded setlist taped to a music stand, about to open their mouth in front of everyone you love.
That moment is what you are paying for. Not the song. You can stream the song for nothing in your car on Hampton Avenue. You are paying for the four seconds before the first note, when a room full of people goes so still you can hear the air handler kick on, and somebody has to fill that silence without a crack, a wobble or a shriek of feedback.
So here is what a wedding singer costs in St. Louis, where the real numbers are actually published (not where you’d guess), and what the fee buys. And here is the one question to ask before you sign anything, word for word: “Would you sing me the first line, right now, with no microphone?” The rest of this page explains why that question works.
### What is the average price for a wedding singer in St. Louis?
Start with the number a St. Louis church actually prints: St. Ambrose on The Hill lists its parish vocalist at $150-$250 on its own wedding page. The Cathedral Basilica folds a cantor into its wedding fee, so treat $150-$250 as the floor for one singer at one ceremony. Past that floor, an independent singer sets their own price, and it climbs with everything that happens away from the microphone: learning your songs, the rehearsal, the sound gear, the drive and the hours.
Read the St. Ambrose page slowly and it tells you more than one number. The parish offering alone is $750 for active parishioners and $1,500 for visitors. The parish organist is $300. A violin, cello or trumpet runs $150-$200. And every musician fee, organist and vocalist included, is due 15 days before the wedding. Think of the stack of envelopes on the kitchen table two weeks out, each with a name on the front, and the singer’s is one of them. Budget for it then, not on the day.
Bring in a singer from outside the parish and the rule shifts. St. Ambrose says an outside cantor’s fees “are to be determined and paid directly to them,” and the parish music director approves who sings. In plain words: the church does not set a price for your cousin’s voice teacher. You do, in a conversation. And the music director still has a say in whether that voice is the one your guests hear.
At the Cathedral Basilica, the singer hides inside a bigger number. A couple who is not registered there makes a minimum donation of $3,000, and the Cathedral’s own wedding page says the fee includes the services of a Cathedral Basilica cantor who sings the Mass parts and can serve as a soloist. Want the professional chamber choir instead? The Schola Cantorum is $1,200. And here is the line couples skim past: the cathedral cantors have right of first refusal for all weddings there. Your singer is already in the fee. Read the contract before you pay a second voice to stand where the first one is already standing. At the Cathedral, the cheapest singer is the one you already paid for.
### You are paying for four seconds of silence
A ceremony song lasts a few minutes. The fee covers far more than that, and once you see the list, the number stops feeling like a lot of money for very little singing.
The learning happens after dinner. Ask for something outside a singer’s regular book and somebody sits at a piano with a cold cup of coffee, slows the track down, pencils a breath mark over the third line, and runs the key change until it stops being scary. For a while, your song lives in someone else’s house.
The rehearsal costs them a weeknight. At St. Ambrose, rehearsals are usually held on the Thursday before the wedding at 6 p.m. and are scheduled for 45 minutes. A singer who shows up to that is sitting in a pew with your giggling wedding party while their own dinner goes cold at home.
The gear rides in their trunk. Outdoors or in a hall, the singer may be the one hauling the speaker, the mic stand and a coil of cable up your venue’s front steps in July heat, shirt stuck to their back before a single note.
The drive is where St. Louis couples get surprised. Say the vows are in a church in Soulard and the party is out at Keyesport, which its own town website calls the premier northwestern gateway to the lake. Your singer is going to spend part of that afternoon on the highway with a speaker sliding around the back seat. Ask how travel is priced. Some singers fold it into the fee and some list it on its own line. Either is fair, as long as you know before the deposit, not after.
Then there is the part no invoice lists. A good ceremony singer is reading the room the whole time. They see the flower girl freeze halfway down the aisle and stretch the verse. They see the officiant flip back a page and hold a soft note underneath. They hear the shuffle of a hundred people standing up and wait for it to settle. That is the skill, and it is the real product. A recording cannot wait for a four-year-old.
### Why does a church care who sings at your wedding?
Because in a Catholic church the wedding is a sacrament first and a party second, and the music answers to someone. The Cathedral Basilica is blunt about it: all music before, during and after the wedding liturgy must be taken from the treasury of sacred repertoire, and your favorite popular music should be reserved for your reception.
That rule settles one of the questions couples type into their phones at midnight: what songs to play before a wedding ceremony. At the Cathedral, the prelude and the walk-in follow the same sacred rule as everything else. On the Cathedral’s own wedding music form, the choices listed under Bridal Party Procession are Bach’s “May the Grace of Christ” and Pachelbel’s Canon in D, and the list under Bridal Procession opens with Purcell’s Trumpet Voluntary. Save the song from your first date for the reception, when the room is loud again and nobody is kneeling.
The Cathedral also sets the bar for outside singers, and it is worth reading twice. The use of outside musicians or vocalists must be approved by the Director of Sacred Music. References and an audition may be requested. Singers should be professionally trained and experienced singing in large spaces and liturgical settings. Then the kicker, in the Cathedral’s own words: “Amateur musicians may better perform at your wedding reception.”
Ouch. Also, fair. A big stone church hands a voice back to the room a beat late. A voice that sounds warm in a living room can blur into mush somewhere around the middle pews, and the person who finds that out first is the bride walking straight into it. That is why the Cathedral asks for an audition. Steal the idea. Ask every singer where they have sung before, and whether any of those rooms were big.
### What changes when the ceremony moves outdoors?
Outside, the problem flips. In a stone church, a voice has too much room to ring. In a park, it has nothing to bounce off at all. The sound drifts off over the grass, a car door slams in the lot, the cicadas start up in the trees, and the singer is suddenly fighting the whole sky with one small speaker on a stand.
Here is the St. Louis fact that should shape your budget if you are eyeing Tower Grove Park. The Music Stand there was built in 1872 to host concerts on Sunday afternoons, and it is ringed with busts of Henry Shaw’s favorite composers: Beethoven, Gounod, Mozart, Rossini, Verdi and Wagner. The wedding ceremony fee is $400, which includes bench seating for about 200 guests and electricity during your time slot. Then comes the line in the notes that changes who you hire: amplified sound cannot be heard beyond fifty feet of the source.
Fifty feet is not far. It means the big speaker your uncle offered to bring is out, and the singer who only sounds good loud is out with it. You need a voice that carries on its own with a little help, and a singer who knows how to set a small speaker low and close so the back bench catches every word and the dog walkers on the path barely notice.
Now the detail your guests will repeat. One of those busts is Gounod, and his name is on the Bach/Gounod “Ave Maria” that sits on the Cathedral Basilica’s own list of wedding solos. Ask your singer to learn it, and someone gets to sing Gounod under Gounod’s bust, at a bandstand where Henry Shaw put the composers he loved. Tell that story at cocktail hour. Watch your uncle tell it again ten minutes later.
One more thing the park says plainly: there is no backup location in the case of bad weather, and Tower Grove Park does not offer weather-related refunds. If a storm rolls in, the singer’s gear is the first thing that has to move, fast and wet. Ask your singer what happens to the fee if the ceremony is cut short or squeezed under a pavilion.
Off topic: your echoey living room is begging for a decent rug.
### Where does the singer come in during the ceremony?
Couples usually ask this as “what is the lineup for a wedding ceremony,” and the answer decides how many songs you are paying for. The Cathedral Basilica’s music form gives each place music goes its own heading: the bridal party procession, the bridal procession, a responsorial psalm, two vocal pieces for the offertory and communion (Mass only), an optional Ave Maria for flowers to the Blessed Mother, and the recessionals.
Count the spots where a voice is front and center and you have the honest size of the job. A ceremony outside of Mass has fewer of them. A full Mass has more, and at the Cathedral the cantor also sings the Mass parts in between. A civil ceremony in a hall might want one song for the walk in, one during a quiet moment in the middle, and one for the walk out. Three songs is a very different week of practice than seven.
So write your lineup on one sheet of paper before you call anyone. Put a song title next to each spot, or a question mark if you don’t know yet. That sheet is the most useful thing you can bring to a call with a singer, because it turns “how much do you charge” into “how much for this,” and the second question gets a real answer.
### The one question that tells you a singer can hold a quiet room
Shortlist two or three singers. Not ten. Listen to whatever they have posted, then get each one on the phone. Tell them the venue, the date, your lineup sheet and the feeling you want in the room, and listen to what they say back. The good ones start asking about the room before they ask about the money.
Then ask the question that sorts them fast: “Would you sing me the first line, right now, with no microphone?”
A singer who can hold a quiet room will usually laugh and do it, on the phone, in a parking lot, wherever they are standing. You will hear it in the first breath. The pitch lands. The words are clear. There is no hunting for the note. A singer who leans on the speaker will stall, send you a link instead, or tell you it won’t sound right over the phone. Sometimes that’s true. But the Cathedral asks for the same proof in its own language when it says an audition may be requested, and the Cathedral has far more pews than your phone has speakers.
If a phone call feels awkward, send this text to each singer on your shortlist, as is: “Hi, we’re getting married at [venue] on [date]. Here are the songs we’re thinking about: [paste your lineup sheet]. What would you charge for this, does that include the rehearsal, your own sound and travel, and could you send us a phone recording of you singing the first line with no mic?” The replies sort themselves. Some come back within the hour with a voice memo. Some never mention the voice memo at all.
After that, let each singer tell you what they deliver. How many songs? Will they come to the rehearsal? Do they bring their own sound? How is travel handled? When is the balance due, and what happens if the ceremony runs long? Then lay the answers side by side against what you actually need. You are not trying to beat anyone down on price. You are trying to find the voice your grandmother will still be humming in the car on the way home.
Start early, too. The Cathedral wants your music planning meeting about three months before the wedding, and St. Ambrose wants every musician paid 15 days out. Have your singer booked well before either date, so the only things left to worry about are the dress, the weather and whether the flower girl makes it to the front.
If the wedding photos are already booked, here’s what to know before a spray tan.
If you want the vows on film as well as in the air, here’s what a wedding videographer costs.

If you’re the singer who can hush a church with one breath, this is your crowd. St. Louis couples are already searching for a voice like yours, so list your business where they look and get more customers from the weddings you were made for.
### Frequently asked questions about wedding singers
### Q. How much should a wedding singer charge?
A.  In St. Louis, the published church rate is the floor: St. Ambrose on The Hill lists its parish vocalist at $150-$250. An independent singer charges for the whole job, not the minutes on stage, so the price should rise with each song they learn, the rehearsal, the sound gear and the drive. Ask what the fee includes before you compare two quotes.
### Q. How much does a singer cost for 2 hours?
A.  I could not find a published St. Louis rate for that, so ask each singer directly whether they price by the hour, by the song or by the event, and whether setup time counts. Tower Grove Park lists the Music Stand’s available times as 11 a.m.-1 p.m., 2-4 p.m. and 5-7 p.m., every day of the week, and decorating and cleanup have to fit inside your time slot.
### Q. What should a wedding singer wear?
A.  Dressed like a well-turned-out guest, a shade quieter than the wedding party, so nobody mistakes the singer for a bridesmaid. Dark, simple colors photograph cleanly from the side of the altar. Soft-soled shoes matter more than people think on stone church floors, where every heel click carries. Ask the couple about their colors and dress to blend in, not to stand out.
### Q. What is the lineup for a wedding ceremony?
A.  The Cathedral Basilica’s wedding music form includes the bridal party procession, the bridal procession, a responsorial psalm, two vocal pieces for the offertory and communion (Mass only), an optional Ave Maria for flowers to the Blessed Mother, and the recessionals. A civil ceremony is usually simpler: a walk in, one moment in the middle, and a walk out.
### Q. What songs to play before a wedding ceremony?
A.  In a Catholic church, sacred music only. The Cathedral Basilica says all music before, during and after the liturgy must come from sacred repertoire, and popular songs belong at the reception. At a park or hall ceremony you have more room, so pick soft, familiar pieces that let guests talk quietly while they find their seats, and save the loud favorites for later.
### Q. What is the most common wedding aisle song?
A.  I could not find a reliable count of which aisle song is used most. The classics are easy to spot, though: the Cathedral Basilica’s music form lists Pachelbel’s Canon in D under Bridal Party Procession and Purcell’s Trumpet Voluntary under Bridal Procession. A singer can also carry the walk in with a slow solo if you want a voice instead of the organ.
### Q. What song is played when people get married?
A.  It depends on the moment. On the Cathedral Basilica’s music form, the offertory and communion choices include Schubert’s “Ave Maria” and Franck’s “Panis Angelicus,” and the pieces listed under Recessionals include Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy” and Mouret’s “Rondeau.” Outside a church, the couple picks the song that sounds like the two of them.

## It Smelled Fine at the Counter: How to Buy Fresh Seafood in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-fresh-seafood-in-st-louis
A whole snapper lies on a mound of crushed ice, eye still clear, skin wet and silver under the case lights. The man in the rubber apron is already tearing off a sheet of butcher paper. Ask him where that fish came from and he’ll probably tell you. Here’s the rule underneath that: a fish market is exempt from the federal origin label.
It smelled fine at the counter. Then you slide open the crisper drawer at home, peel back the butcher paper, and the smell reaches you before the kitchen light does. Sweet first. Then sour. Then that thin, sharp edge of ammonia that tells you dinner is over and the money you spent on Saturday is going out with the coffee grounds.
The grocery case down the street would have warned you where that fish came from, with a little placard standing in the crushed ice. Under the federal Country of Origin Labeling law, the USDA says, most grocery stores and supermarkets must tell you the country of origin of fish and shellfish, while fish markets and butcher shops are exempt. At a fish market, the origin label isn’t in the ice. It’s in the answer to a question, so ask it, word for word: “What country or water is this from, and when did it come in?” One breath. A good fishmonger answers both halves without looking away from you.
That question earns its keep here. St. Louis sits on two rivers, in a state whose official state fish since 1997 is the channel catfish, a long way from any salt water, so the clock on a fillet started well before you saw it. NOAA Fisheries estimates that 80 percent of the seafood Americans ate in a recent year came from foreign imports. “Fresh” at a St. Louis fish counter almost always means “traveled carefully,” not “caught this morning.” That’s fine, as long as you can tell careful from tired.
This city knows what it feels like to lose a fish counter. Bob’s Seafood started as a fish stand in the Delmar Loop, then grew into a wholesale business at I-170 and Olive that restaurants and home cooks both leaned on. In 2022, according to the company that carried it forward, development plans closed Bob’s doors. Its former VP, Mike Vujević, partnered with Brad Burns to create City Seafood, and the reviews on that page read like a city exhaling: “I missed Bob’s so much. Welcome back guys.” Another came from a transplant: “Since moving to St. Louis from Boston, I’ve been looking for fresh seafood. I finally found it.”
Then read the shop’s front page, because one line there cuts against the fresh-is-always-better story: “There are a few products where freezing is fresher.” That is a St. Louis fish seller saying it in writing. Their delivery orders go out packaged, insulated and on ice, dropped at the door between 3 and 6 p.m., Monday-Friday. Hold every counter in town to that standard: cold the whole way, and honest about what was frozen.
If you’d rather stand at a stall and compare, the city’s own page for Soulard Market at 730 Carroll St. tells you when to go: 10% vendor participation on Wednesday and Thursday, 35% on Friday, 100% on Saturday. Show up on a Thursday and you’re walking past empty stands. Show up Saturday and every seller is there, side by side, for you to press, sniff and question. Walk in with your tools: a nose, a thumb, and that one sentence.
### What to look for when buying fresh fish?
Look for fish that smells fresh and mild, never fishy, sour or like ammonia, with clear, shiny eyes, red gills and firm flesh that springs back when you press it. It should be in a refrigerated case or sitting on a thick bed of fresh ice, not on a bare tray gone dry around the edges.
On a Saturday at Soulard, with every stand open, you can run these checks at stall after stall with the cold coming up off the ice into your face. (FDA: Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely.) Run them in this order.
The nose goes first. Lean in. A good fish counter smells like cold water and wet ice, almost like nothing at all. If the air over the case smells like low tide, keep your wallet in your pocket.
The thumb goes second. Ask if you can press the fish, or ask them to. Fresh flesh pushes back like a ripe peach that hasn’t gone soft yet; the dent fills in and disappears. Tired fish holds your fingerprint. A counter that is proud of what it sells won’t blink when you ask for it.
The eyes go third, and they are a warning, not a verdict. Clear and shiny is what you want. But don’t trust color by itself. The FDA says color can be affected by diet, environment and even treatment with a color fixative such as carbon monoxide, so a slab of tuna glowing cherry red under the lights is not proof of anything. Your nose and your thumb are much harder to fool than your eyes.
### What is the best way to buy fish in St. Louis?
Treat it like hiring someone. Pick two or three counters you can actually reach on a weeknight, a fish market and one or two grocery cases, and go talk to the people behind them before you need a fish for a dinner party. Tell them what you like to cook and how often. Listen to what they say they can do for you, then compare it with what’s lying in the case.
Open with the country-or-water question from the top of this page, then keep going, short and plain. Which mornings does your delivery land? Was this previously frozen? Wild or farmed? What would you take home tonight? At the fish market, that “what country or water” question is doing the job the missing placard would have done. A fishmonger who knows the product answers fast and specific, with a day, a place and a pick for tonight. One who shrugs, or whose answer changes when you point at a different fillet, has told you something too.
That delivery question is also the honest answer to something people search for constantly: what day of the week is best to buy fresh fish? Ask which morning the truck comes in, and shop that morning or the next, when the ice is still mounded and squeaks under the scoop. At Soulard Market, the city’s own schedule tilts the answer toward Saturday, the one day it lists 100% vendor participation.
Before you become anybody’s regular, sit in the parking lot, engine ticking as it cools, and look the store up. The City of St. Louis Department of Health inspects all operations that provide food to the general public, and its list names grocery stores right alongside restaurants, taverns and carry-outs. Inspection reports issued after May 10, 2012 sit in the city’s Healthspace system, linked from that same page; older ones are in the archives. You’re reading what an inspector saw behind the glass you’re about to trust with dinner. The city itself says the lookup tool sometimes has errors, and recommends loading it again in a few minutes. Do. A counter that smells like cold water and has clean reports is the one to learn by name.
And if you get home, open the paper and the smell hits you like a wet dock, you are not stuck just being angry about it. The city says problems with a food establishment, and requests for an inspection, go through the Citizens’ Service Bureau, and the Food and Beverage Control program’s phone number is (314) 657-1539. Take a photo of the fish and keep the receipt before anything goes in the trash.
Watch the case while you talk. Is the ice clean and piled high, or melted into gray slush? Is cooked shrimp touching raw salmon? The FDA says unpackaged cooked seafood should be physically separated from raw, in its own case or behind dividers. A counter that keeps those apart is paying attention to small things, and with fish, the small things are the whole job.
### How fresh is fish at the supermarket, really?
It depends on the case, and the sign tells you more than most people read. Some fish in a grocery case was frozen somewhere on its trip to Missouri and thawed before it hit the ice. When it was, look for the words “Previously Frozen” on the sign.
That is not a scam. The FDA notes that previously frozen fish may not have every sign of fresh fish, the bright eyes, the firm flesh, the red gills, but it should still smell fresh and mild, not fishy, sour or rancid. So the nose still rules. What you shouldn’t do is pay a fresh-fish price for a thawed fillet and then let it sit in your refrigerator for days. It has already spent part of its life on the clock.
The smarter move: buy the same fish still frozen from the freezer aisle and thaw it yourself overnight in the refrigerator. You control the clock. Walk away from any package that is open, torn or crushed on the edges, and from any with frost or ice crystals inside, which can mean the fish was stored a long time or thawed and refrozen. Then squeeze it. Frozen fish should be hard as a brick against your palm, cold enough to sting. If it bends, put it back.
Frozen has one more quiet advantage. If you’re making sushi, poke or ceviche at home, the FDA says one rule of thumb is to eat fish that has been previously frozen, because freezing will kill any parasites that may be present. It doesn’t kill all harmful germs, which is why cooking is still the safest route. But in a city this far from the docks, the freezer is not the enemy. Bad handling is.
Totally unrelated: tattooed eyebrows deserve the same hard questions you ask a fishmonger.
### How do you get it home without cooking it in the car?
A St. Louis parking lot in July is an oven with cupholders. You feel it on the backs of your legs the second you sit down. That is exactly where good seafood goes to die.
The FDA’s rule is that seafood should never sit out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour when it’s above 90 degrees. Here’s the local catch. The National Weather Service office for St. Louis says that since 1870, temperatures of 90 degrees or higher occur on about 35-40 days per year here. That is more than a month of afternoons when your fish gets one hour, not two, and a stop for gas plus a run into the pharmacy can eat that hour before you notice.
So make the fish counter your last stop, not your first. Keep a cooler or an insulated bag in the trunk and ask the counter to pack your fish on ice; the FDA says to put seafood on ice or in the refrigerator or freezer soon after buying it. The bag should feel cold and a little heavy when they hand it over.
At home, the fish goes in the refrigerator before the rest of the groceries, at the back, away from the door that swings open every time someone wants a drink. The FDA says seafood you will use within 2 days should be stored in a clean refrigerator at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below, and it tells you to use a refrigerator thermometer to check, because the dial is a setting, not a reading. If dinner plans slide past that window, wrap the fish tightly in plastic, foil or moisture-proof paper and freeze it. Don’t wait for the smell to make the decision for you.
### Which fish should you stay away from?
For most people, the answer is shorter than the internet makes it sound. The FDA and EPA list seven fish as the choices to avoid because they carry the highest mercury levels: king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico, and bigeye tuna. That advice is aimed most at people who are or might become pregnant, those who are breastfeeding, and young children. These are large, long-lived fish.
The St. Louis answer is different, and it isn’t in the grocery case. It’s the oversized river catfish a neighbor hands you in a cooler, still smelling of mud and outboard fuel. Every year the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services checks sport-caught fish for contaminants, and its advice sits in one table under “Is My Fish Safe to Eat?” Under the listing for the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, the advice for all consumers is no more than one meal a week of flathead, channel or blue catfish longer than 17 inches. Yes, that includes the channel catfish, the state fish itself. Sturgeon eggs, in that same listing, get three words: do not eat. That is the rule for the cooler from the riverfront, not the one for the farmed catfish on the ice.
The good news is the long list. The FDA’s Advice about Eating Fish names “Best Choices” fish that are even lower in mercury, including catfish, clams, crab, crawfish, oysters, pollock, salmon, sardines, scallops, shrimp, tilapia and trout. That FDA page also quotes the Dietary Guidelines for Americans: at least 8 ounces of seafood a week, less for children, based on a 2,000-calorie diet. For sizing a serving, the FDA’s guide is the palm of your hand.
### Shellfish play by their own rules
Live clams, oysters and mussels get different checks. Look for the tag on the sack or container; the FDA says those tags carry the processor’s certification number, which means the shellfish were harvested and processed under national shellfish safety controls. If a counter can’t show you the tag, that is your answer.
Then the tap test. Live clams, oysters and mussels close when you tap the shell. Pick one up, give it a sharp little knock, and watch it clamp shut. Cracked or broken shells go in the trash. Live crabs and lobsters should still show some leg movement, because they spoil rapidly after death, so a good lobster tank is all slow, clicking motion. For shrimp, scallops and lobster meat, look for flesh that is clear with a pearl-like color and little or no odor.
If a crawfish boil is the plan, our guide to seafood boils and crawfish in St. Louis picks up where this one stops.
### From butcher paper to a hot pan
You did the hard part at the counter. Don’t lose it at the stove. Most seafood should be cooked to an internal temperature of 145 degrees, and an instant-read thermometer is the surest way to land it. Without one, the FDA’s sign for fish is flesh that separates easily with a fork. Shrimp, scallops, crab and lobster turn firm, pearly and opaque. For clams, mussels and oysters, the shells open during cooking; throw out the ones that don’t.
There is also an old kitchen shortcut called the 10-minute rule. Here is how it works: you measure the fish at its thickest point, then bake at 450 degrees for 10 minutes per inch of thickness, turning it halfway through. A 1-inch steak gets 5 minutes a side. Add 5 minutes if it’s wrapped in foil or cooked in a sauce, and double the time for fish that goes in still frozen. Don’t use the rule for microwaving or deep frying.
The last check happens with the pan sizzling and the window fogging up. The FDA says spoiled seafood can smell sour, rancid, fishy or like ammonia, and that those odors get stronger once it’s cooked. If you catch either a fleeting or a lasting whiff of ammonia in cooked seafood, don’t eat it. It hurts to scrape a dinner into the trash. It hurts less than the alternative.
