### Frequently asked questions about buying seafood in St. Louis
### Q. How long does seafood stay fresh in the fridge?
A.  Seafood you will use within 2 days of buying it should be stored in a clean refrigerator at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below. If you won’t cook it in that window, wrap it tightly in plastic, foil or moisture-proof paper and freeze it. A refrigerator thermometer tells you whether your fridge is really that cold.
### Q. What is the 10 minute rule for fish?
A.  It is an old kitchen timing guide: measure the fish at its thickest point and cook it 10 minutes per inch, turning it halfway. For baking, the oven goes to 450 degrees. The rule also covers broiling, grilling, steaming and poaching. Add 5 minutes for foil or sauce, and double the time for fish cooked from frozen. It is not meant for microwaving or deep frying, and 145 degrees inside is still the real finish line.
### Q. What day of the week is best to buy fresh fish?
A.  The morning your counter’s delivery lands, or the morning after, so ask the fishmonger which mornings the truck comes in. At Soulard Market, the city lists 100% vendor participation only on Saturday, against 35% on Friday and 10% on Wednesday and Thursday.
### Q. How fresh is fish at the supermarket?
A.  It varies by store and by fish, and some of it was frozen along the way, so look for “Previously Frozen” on the sign. The FDA says previously frozen fish may not have bright eyes or firm flesh, but it should still smell fresh and mild. Supermarkets also have to name the country of origin, so look for it before you point.
### Q. Which fish to stay away from?
A.  The FDA and EPA list seven fish with the highest mercury levels as choices to avoid: king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico and bigeye tuna. That advice is aimed at people who are or might become pregnant, those who are breastfeeding, and young children. For fish from the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, Missouri’s advisory says no more than one meal a week of catfish over 17 inches, and do not eat sturgeon eggs.
### Q. What is the healthiest fish I can buy at the grocery store?
A.  Start with the FDA’s “Best Choices” fish that are even lower in mercury, such as salmon, sardines, trout, pollock, shrimp, catfish and tilapia. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend at least 8 ounces of seafood a week, less for children, based on a 2,000-calorie diet.

## The Galleria Lets Mall Walkers In at 8AM, Before Stores Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-mall-walking-good-exercise-in-st-louis
8AM. That’s when the Saint Louis Galleria opens its north parking garage entrance to mall walkers, and the stores don’t open until 10AM Monday through Saturday. Sneakers squeak down a wide tile hallway past metal store gates still pulled down to the floor. Nobody in here is shopping. They’re walking, warm and dry, while the rest of the city scrapes windshields.
Now think about the St. Louis morning when walking is actually hard. Sleet ticking on the windshield. The driveway wearing that gray shine that means one wrong step. Your knees already filing a complaint, and your brain doing quiet math on what a fall would cost you this winter. You skip the walk. Then you skip it again.
Now the other version of that same morning. A wide, dry, level floor under bright lights. Warm air the second the door sighs shut behind you. Nobody is selling you anything yet. You just walk.
That door isn’t a rumor. The Galleria’s own visitor page says it supports mall walkers, who can enter the north parking garage entrance at 8AM. Shoppers don’t get in until 10AM Monday through Saturday, and the parking is free. The number is 314.571.7000, and the address is 1155 Saint Louis Galleria, St. Louis, MO 63117, off Interstate 64 or Interstate 170.
And here’s what surprises most people. It isn’t the cold that keeps St. Louis walkers inside. The National Weather Service’s climatology of the St. Louis area calls our winters “brisk and stimulating,” which is a lovely phrase to read from a dry chair. It also says prolonged periods of extremely cold weather are rare here, and temperatures drop to zero or below on an average of 2 or 3 days a year. Our winters are mostly just cold enough to turn a wet sidewalk into a trap. It’s the ice.
So here’s the St. Louis secret worth saying out loud to the friend who quits walking every November: it’s not the cold, it’s the ice, and the Galleria’s north garage door opens to walkers at 8AM with free parking.
Then there’s the number on your wrist. The oft-repeated 10,000-steps-a-day mantra grew out of a decades-old marketing campaign for a Japanese pedometer, with no science to back up the impact on health, according to this write-up of a Lancet Public Health step study. That number has guilted a lot of people off the couch and a lot more back onto it.
That’s why plenty of St. Louisans mall walk all winter. The question people type into their phones is whether it really counts or whether it’s exercise for people who gave up on exercise. It counts. Here’s the proof, the step numbers that matter at your age, why pace matters less than you’ve been told, and how to start this week without paying for a gym.
### Is walking at the mall good for you?
Yes, walking at the mall is good for you, as long as you walk briskly enough to breathe a little harder. The CDC gives brisk walking as an example of moderate-intensity activity and says adults need 150 minutes of it a week, which it breaks down as 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week. Your body doesn’t know whether the floor under it is a sidewalk in Dutchtown or polished tile under a skylight. It knows you moved.
What the mall adds is fewer excuses. The CDC’s own page on walking in the mall says malls are protected from the weather, are well-lit, and have flat, wide, and level walking surfaces, plus convenient restrooms and benches if you need to rest. Read that list again with a bad hip or a new baby in a stroller and it stops sounding like a brochure. It sounds like the difference between going and not going.
There’s even a federal playbook for it. Its title is Mall Walking: A Program Resource Guide, which the CDC sponsored and co-authored, and it makes the case plainly: level surfaces can reduce the risk of slips and falls, and the other walkers give you social support. That last part sounds soft until you’ve had someone say “Missed you yesterday” and realized you’re now a person who shows up.
The CDC’s mall page boils the payoff down. For older adults, physical activity helps reduce the risk of falling and of cognitive decline, including dementia. That last line is the one a lot of grown kids quietly read twice.
One honest catch. Walking is the aerobic part of the job, not the whole job. The CDC also wants 2 days a week of muscle-strengthening activity, and for people 65 and older it adds balance work such as walking heel-to-toe. The mall can handle that piece too. Find a straight tile seam on an empty stretch, put one heel against the other toe, and walk the line like a sobriety test you’re trying to pass, one hand near a railing.
### Why do people do mall walking?
Because St. Louis winters are sneaky rather than brutal. The weather service says snowfall has averaged a little over 18 inches per winter season, and the snow is honestly the easy part. It’s the freeze-thaw mornings that get you, the sidewalk that looked wet and was ice, the salt crust ground into the hall rug.
That fear is not paranoia. The National Institute on Aging lists falls on wintry surfaces first among the hazards of cold weather, ahead of frostbite and hypothermia. If you live alone off South Grand and your balance isn’t what it was, a slip on the front steps isn’t a funny story. It’s the beginning of a very long spring.
That mall walking resource guide is blunt about the barriers that keep people from moving at all: many neighborhoods lack sidewalks, have busy traffic, and sometimes have a high level of crime. A mall sidesteps the first two outright. The lighting is the same at 8 a.m. in January as it is at noon in June. The only traffic is a stroller and a guy with a coffee.
Then there’s the reason nobody puts in a brochure. Loneliness. A lot of mall walkers are retired, widowed or working from a kitchen table, and the loop is the one place they’re expected every morning. You start out counting laps. Not long after, you’re the one who notices that the woman in the purple fleece hasn’t been around all week.
### How many steps does your body actually want?
Fewer than your phone says, if you’re past 60. That same UNC report covers a meta-analysis of 15 studies and nearly 50,000 people, published in the Lancet Public Health and led by Amanda Paluch of the University of Massachusetts Amherst. For adults 60 and older, the risk of premature death leveled off at about 6,000-8,000 steps per day. For adults younger than 60, it stabilized at about 8,000-10,000.
Read that slowly if you’ve been beating yourself up for never hitting 10,000. More steps than that range provided no additional benefit for longevity in older adults. Paluch put the bigger message simply: “More steps per day are better for your health.” The key word is more. Moving from very little to a little more is where the gains start.
So how far should a 70 year old walk every day? On that evidence, aim for somewhere around 6,000 to 8,000 steps across the whole day, not all at once and not all at the mall. Your trip from the parking garage, the loop, the walk back to the car and the grocery aisles later all count. For people 65 and older, the CDC says to be as physically active as your abilities and conditions allow, and reminds you that some physical activity is better than none at all.
And does 30 minutes of walking count as exercise? Yes. The CDC’s own example is brisk walking for 150 minutes every week, such as 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week. It also says you don’t have to do it all at once. A few short laps between errands is a real plan, not a cheat.
Off topic, but if the kiosk’s ear-piercing gun tempts you, read this first.
### Does pace matter more than the miles?
Not the way the fitness posters suggest. In a study announced by the National Institutes of Health, about 4,800 U.S. adults aged 40 and over wore activity trackers for up to seven days, and researchers followed them for years afterward. Compared with 4,000 steps a day, taking 8,000 steps was associated with a 51% lower risk of death from all causes, and 12,000 steps with a 65% lower risk.
Here’s the turn. The authors saw no association between step intensity and risk of death after accounting for the total number of steps taken per day. The researchers said they were surprised. The UNC meta-analysis landed in the same place: no definitive association with walking speed beyond the total number of steps.
So, is it better to walk faster or longer? For most people coming off the couch, longer wins, because more total steps is what tracked with living longer. Brisk still matters for the CDC’s 150 minutes of moderate activity, so pick it up when you feel good. But if the only way you’ll keep going is an easy pace and a long loop past the food court, take the long loop. The NIH is also honest that the study was observational and can’t prove cause and effect, which is worth knowing before anyone sells you a speed program.
A practical test: walk at a pace where you could talk but wouldn’t want to sing. If you’re gasping, back off. If you could read the whole food-court menu aloud without a breath, you’ve got more in you.
People are asking
### What are good St. Louis winter activities for adults?
Start indoors, where the ice can’t reach you. The Saint Louis Galleria lets mall walkers in through its north parking garage entrance at 8AM, and parking is free. The city’s Tandy Recreation Center at 4206 W Kennerly Ave runs Water Aerobics Mornings from Sep 9 to Dec 30, 10AM to noon, and the city says recreation programs are free, with nothing to pay. On a mild day, Forest Park’s 6-mile Dual Recreational Pathway has a soft gravel surface meant for walkers and joggers.
### The 8 a.m. door at the Galleria
If you’ve never done it, the first morning feels a little like sneaking into school early. You park in the north garage, where the cold sits low and smells like concrete and exhaust. Then the door, then the warm, then that wide hallway with nothing in it but light and a few people already moving.
The Galleria’s visitor page says pets aren’t allowed, but service animals are. Restrooms are spread out: four on the north end, two on the south end and two at the food court, which matters a great deal halfway through a first walk. There are seating areas throughout the building for the moment your calves start talking.
If walking the whole loop isn’t realistic yet, the mall says wheelchairs are available to rent from the 1st floor Guest Services, and electric scooters are available there too. That means a spouse with a bad knee can come along and still be part of the morning instead of waiting in the car. Policies change, so call before your first trip and ask what walker access looks like that week, Sundays included.
Your first-morning card, straight from the mall’s own page:
Door: north parking garage entrance, 8AM
Mall hours: Monday-Saturday 10AM-7PM, Sunday 11AM-6PM
Call: 314.571.7000
Address: 1155 Saint Louis Galleria, St. Louis, MO 63117
Getting there: off Interstate 64 or Interstate 170
Parking: free
Before you pick a home loop, call ahead and ask any mall about walker hours. Our guide to which St. Louis malls are still open is the place to check before you pick a home loop.
Your best winter walking floor might be closer than you think. Browse Shopping Malls on St Louis Near Me Directory to find the closest one, then call and ask the one question that matters: what time do you let walkers in?
If you’re the shoe fitter, the physical therapist or the coffee counter near the mall doors, those 8 a.m. walkers are already your neighbors, so put a Gold listing in front of them or list your business and get more customers from that crowd.
### A four-week start that survives a St. Louis January
None of this works if you quit in week two, so start embarrassingly small. Week one, walk a short, easy loop on a few mornings and notice where the benches and restrooms are. Week two, add a morning and a few minutes each time. Week three, try one lap at your brisk, can-talk-can’t-sing pace. Week four, aim for close to 30 minutes on most days, which is the CDC’s example week. If anything hurts in a sharp way rather than a tired way, stop and call your doctor.
What to bring is short: shoes you’ve already broken in, a water bottle, your phone for the step count and a layer you can tie around your waist once the building warms you up. Leave the heavy coat in the car if the walk from the garage door is short. You’ll be glad not to carry it lap after lap.
If your feet or knees start complaining, don’t just buy whatever’s on the end cap. Shortlist two or three shoe fitters or physical therapists, tell each one you walk hard tile floors most mornings, say what you want (fewer aches, longer loops) and compare what each says they’d actually do for you. The one who asks how you walk before they talk about price is usually the one worth going back to.
On the mild days, take it outside. Forest Park Forever says a 6-mile Dual Recreational Pathway encircles the park, and its soft gravel surface is meant for walkers and joggers. Closer to the south side, Tower Grove Park has seven miles of running and walking trails. Then come back indoors the morning the sleet returns, without guilt. The habit is the point, not the scenery.

### Frequently asked questions about mall walking
### Q. Does walking in a mall count as exercise?
A.  Yes. The CDC counts brisk walking as moderate-intensity activity, and adults need 150 minutes of it a week. A mall loop at a pace that makes you breathe a little harder counts the same as a sidewalk, and the flat, dry floor makes it easier to keep the habit through a St. Louis winter.
### Q. Does 30 minutes of walking count as exercise?
A.  Yes. Thirty minutes a day, five days a week is the CDC’s own example of reaching 150 minutes of moderate activity, as long as the pace is brisk. You can also split it into shorter chunks, like a few short walks, and it still counts.
### Q. Is it better to walk faster or longer?
A.  For most people, longer. In an NIH-announced study of about 4,800 adults, more daily steps was linked to a lower risk of death, but step intensity showed no link once total steps were counted. Walk briskly when you can, but don’t skip a long, easy walk because you feel slow.
### Q. How far should a 70 year old walk every day?
A.  Researchers found the risk of premature death for adults 60 and older leveled off at about 6,000-8,000 steps a day, spread across the whole day. For people 65 and older, the CDC adds balance activities such as walking heel-to-toe, and says to be as physically active as your abilities and conditions allow.
### Q. How to walk 10,000 steps in winter?
A.  Take it indoors and break it up. A morning mall loop, a second lap after lunch and the steps you already take running errands add up fast. Remember too that 10,000 came from a pedometer marketing campaign, not a study, and older adults saw the benefit level off well below it.
### Q. Where to walk around in St. Louis?
A.  On mild days, Forest Park’s 6-mile Dual Recreational Pathway has a soft gravel surface meant for walkers, and Tower Grove Park has seven miles of running and walking trails. When it’s icy, the Saint Louis Galleria lets walkers in at its north parking garage entrance at 8AM, while its posted hours start at 10AM Monday through Saturday.

## The $300 Violinist: Hiring a Solo Musician in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-solo-musician-in-st-louis-what-it-costs
Is $300 too much for one violin, for one hour, in a St. Louis parish hall that never quite stops smelling like fish-fry Friday? The bow touches the string at six. The player’s night started in your parking lot as early as half past four. In between, the room fills up and gets loud before anyone plays a note: ice knocking around in plastic cups, somebody’s uncle laughing at his own story, folding chairs scraping a parish-hall floor. Then one bow touches one string. Forty conversations drop half a step in volume, and nobody decided to do it. Nobody stops talking. They just start talking like the night matters.
That gap between half past four and six is the price. One St. Louis outfit says its players arrive 30 to 90 minutes before the booking time, depending on what has to be set up, and a St. Louis string ensemble says its musicians arrive at least one hour prior to start time. Nobody bills that time on its own line. It hides inside the first hour, which makes the first hour the most expensive hour you will ever buy from a musician, and the second hour, very often, the cheapest music of the night.
So before you say yes to anyone, ask three things, in this order. What time will you arrive, and is setup inside the hours I’m paying for? What is your minimum, and how short can a set get before I’m paying for a full hour anyway? And if the toasts run long, what does every extra 15 minutes cost? Three answers, one short phone call, and the number on your screen turns into a night you can actually picture: who is standing where at five, what it costs if your uncle grabs the mic at eight, and what you owe the morning after.
### How much does a musician charge per hour in St. Louis?
Published St. Louis rates put one musician at roughly $200 to $300 for the first hour. One local outfit lists solo saxophone at $250 an hour and solo violin at $300, with a $200 minimum, and a solo piano wedding ceremony from one St. Louis pianist starts at $425. Later hours often cost less than the first, which is the single most useful thing to know before you sign.
The top of the market is higher, and it’s upfront about why. One St. Louis string ensemble says pricing begins at $750 for solo instrument, and it notes that many of its musicians are members of the St. Louis Symphony, the Fabulous Fox Theater and The Muny. At the other end, a St. Louis orchestra says its rates begin at just $150. From $150 to $750 is a fivefold spread for what looks, from the folding chairs, like the same job.
### Where will your one player actually stand in St. Louis?
Start with the most St. Louis stage there is. The Music Stand in Tower Grove Park was built in 1872 to host concerts on Sunday afternoons, a red-topped bandstand well-known throughout St. Louis, watched over by busts of Beethoven, Gounod, Mozart, Rossini, Verdi and Wagner. The park rents it for a wedding ceremony at $400, with bench seating for about 200 guests and electricity during your time slot. Then comes the line in the park’s own notes that does your budgeting for you: amplified sound cannot be heard beyond fifty feet of the source.
Read that rule the way a musician would. A band’s whole rig, the speakers on stands and the sound check that squeals once, exists to throw sound across a crowd. A violin under Mozart’s stone face doesn’t need a single cable. On that bandstand, one acoustic player isn’t the budget choice. It’s the one built for the rules.
The clock there is tighter, too. Ceremonies run in two-hour slots, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., 2 to 4 or 5 to 7, and decorating and cleanup must happen inside your slot. Remember the 30 to 90 minutes a player may want before the first note? Ask each player whether that fits inside your slot. So ask every player one extra question: how fast can you be ready from the car? A guitarist with one case on a shoulder beats a keyboard and a PA in that race. And the park says plainly there is no backup location in bad weather and no weather-related refunds, so the rain plan is yours.
Downtown runs on its own clock. The city’s parks policies say music, sound checks or other amplification are not allowed on weekdays at downtown parks and plazas except from 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. and after 5 p.m., and nothing amplified before 8 a.m. The fountains can’t be turned off for events, and at Kiener Plaza they run 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Stand a solo violinist next to falling water and half the notes disappear into the splash. Put the player on the far side of the spray, or ask whether they bring a small amp. If your party needs a city special-event permit, the same page asks for a certificate of insurance with $1,000,000 in property damage coverage, with the City named as additional insured. That’s the host’s paperwork, not the player’s, and it’s why the insurance question further down this page matters.
Forest Park runs through one phone number. Forest Park Forever says permits for weddings, picnic pavilions, the Jewel Box, the World’s Fair Pavilion and Cabanne House rentals go through the Parks Department at 314.289.5300, and the park closes from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Call the park before you call a single musician. The room sets the rules, the rules set the gear, and the gear sets a bigger share of the price than most hosts ever guess.
### Why does the first hour cost the most?
Because the clock starts long before the first note. The arrival window is only part of it. Add the drive, the hunt for parking on a Benton Park side street, the load-in through a kitchen door past the dish pit, and a one-hour booking eats half an evening of the player’s life.
That’s why a short set costs nearly as much as a long one. The same outfit charges a $200 minimum for 45 minutes or less, then prorates in 15-minute increments after the first hour, with cheaper rates for the hours that follow. The first hour pays for the setup. The second hour is mostly music.
So here’s the move most hosts miss. If you’re stuck between a short set from a better player and a long set from a cheaper one, call the better player and ask what more time costs before you decide. The jump is often smaller than you’d guess, and that player is already tuned, already warm, already reading your room. One St. Louis pianist says his most popular combination is a piano and cello duo for the ceremony, followed by solo piano for cocktails and dinner. Same hands, start to finish. Guests feel that kind of continuity even when they couldn’t name it.
The clock bites the other way too. A St. Louis string ensemble’s package terms say any music played past the agreed time is charged $50 per 15 minutes, per musician, invoiced the day after the event. If your family’s toasts run long, and you already know whether they do, buy the extra half hour up front, when it’s a line on a contract instead of a surprise in your email the next morning.
### Send this before you sign anything
Here is the whole first conversation, written for you. Copy it, fill in the brackets and send it to two or three players tonight. The last line is the three questions, so every answer comes back in the same shape and you can lay them side by side:
“Hi, I’m hosting [a 60th birthday dinner] for about [40] people at [the parish hall on our street] on [date], from [6 to 8]. It’s indoors, carpet, no piano on site. I’d love solo [violin] for the cocktail hour, mostly jazz and pop instrumentals, plus three songs that matter to our family. What would you suggest for a night like this, and what would the evening cost all in? Also: what time would you arrive, what is your minimum, and what does each 15 minutes past the end cost?”
Then put the rest on a calendar so nothing lands on you the week of the party, when the cooler still needs ice and the folding chairs are still in somebody’s garage:
Six weeks out: shortlist two or three players, listen to their recordings, send the message above.
Five weeks out: pick one, sign, pay the deposit, and add the extra half hour if your family runs long.
One month out: send your three must-plays, your one do-not-play and, if you like, one Joplin rag (more on that below).
The week of: text the player the load-in door, where to park and the name of the person holding the check.
The night of: a chair without arms, a glass of water within reach, shade if you’re outside, and a plate saved for the break.
### When does one player beat a whole band?
At cocktail hour, nearly every time. A band is built to be heard over people. A solo player is built to be heard under them. The guest by the bar can still follow the story his cousin is telling, and the music sits behind it the way a lamp warms a room without anybody looking at the bulb.
The price gap is wide, too. A St. Louis orchestra’s price-comparison page quotes one booking agency listing four-hour trios starting at $2,000 to $5,000 and 7-12 piece bands at $6,000 to $10,000. That’s roughly what a band for 4 hours looks like when you start shopping. Another agency listing on the same page puts an acoustic jazz combo at $750-$1,500 for four hours. Set that next to a single player at $250 an hour and the math does its own talking.
Part of that gap is gear, and the same page says so plainly: a small acoustic group is lower priced partly because no amplification is required, and amplification can easily add hours to a job on and off site. Think speakers on stands, a snake of cables taped to the floor, a sound check that squeals once, a power strip hunting for an outlet behind the cake table. One violin needs none of that in a living room in the Central West End. One guitar needs none of it on a patio on The Hill.
If you only want a band for a short set, ask each band you talk to whether it has a minimum and what a shorter set saves, because so much of a band’s cost is setup, not playing time. And be honest about the night you’re throwing. A band wins when you want people dancing at ten. One player wins when you want people talking at six. Some hosts book both: a solo player for the cocktail hour, then a band or a DJ once the plates are cleared.
### What should one player actually play at your cocktail hour?
The type of music typically played during cocktail hour is soft, familiar and mostly instrumental: jazz standards, pop songs played without the words, classical pieces people half recognize. One St. Louis pianist describes his cocktail set as solo piano sprinkled into the conversation at your cocktail hour, a mix of jazz and pop, and his vocal and piano duo leans on classic standards from the American Songbook. The rule underneath all of it: music people can talk over without having to raise their voices.
Now the St. Louis card almost nobody plays. Ragtime. Missouri State Parks says Joplin “was ‘The King of Ragtime Writers,’” and that Scott Joplin moved to St. Louis in the spring of 1901, into a room of a flat at 2658A Morgan Street, now Delmar Boulevard. In about a year and a half there he produced “The Entertainer,” “Elite Syncopations” and “Ragtime Dance,” and his audiences were largely patrons of saloons, brothels and restaurants. Ask your pianist to slip one into the set and watch what happens. Someone taps the table. Someone says, “Wait, I know this one.” Then you get to tell them it was written here, on what is now Delmar, by a man who played for people holding drinks, same as tonight.
### The fees that never make the first quote
The quote shows up as one clean number. The night shows up with a loading door behind the dish pit, a dead outlet behind the cake table and a patio with no shade at four in the afternoon. The hourly rate is the headline. These are the footnotes, all pulled from what St. Louis players publish themselves, and every one of them is a question worth asking before you sign:
Sound and a piano. One St. Louis pianist lists a digital piano and PA as a $100 add-on, and a second keyboard and PA for cocktail hour in a separate space at $225. No piano at your venue means that line is yours.
Holidays. One local outfit says its rates increase 1.5x on a major holiday, which may include the day before or after. A New Year’s Eve party pays for the date.
Outdoors. The same outfit generally adds $60 per person per hour for outdoor events and requires full shade out of direct sunlight for performers and equipment.
Distance. A St. Louis string ensemble charges a $50 travel fee per musician when the venue is 30-75 minutes away. A farm party down near Pocahontas means asking about mileage before you sign anything.
The deposit. One outfit asks for $250 or 33% of the total fee, whichever is more, with the signed contract.
The breaks that go your way. One outfit mentions possible cheaper rates for daytime and weekday events, and a St. Louis string ensemble offers a 5% discount to active military, veterans and first responders.
The outdoor line is the one people skip, and it’s the one that ruins afternoons. July sun on a patio in Soulard is hard on a wooden instrument and harder on the person in black holding it. If your party is outside, have a tent or a shady corner picked out before you call anyone, and have a rain plan you can say out loud in one sentence.
### How do you book the right player without regret?
Shortlist two or three players. Listen to a recording from each, the longer and less polished the better, then get each one on the phone for ten minutes. Tell them exactly what you want: the room, the hours, the crowd, the one song your mother will cry at. Then compare what each one says they’ll deliver. You’ll hear the difference in how they answer before you hear a note. These are the questions that sort them fast:
Can I hear a long, unedited set, not just a highlight clip?
Do you bring your own sound, or do I need a piano, an outlet or a table?
How long are your breaks, and what plays while you take them?
Do you carry liability insurance, and can you send my venue a certificate?
What does your contract say if one of us has to cancel?
The insurance question isn’t fussy. The St. Louis musicians’ union, Local 2-197, has been serving the St. Louis area musicians since 1862, and it notes that many states and venues now require musicians to carry business liability insurance, so call your venue first and ask what it wants to see. If your player is a union member, the union also offers a standard AFM contract that, properly filled out and filed with the local, lets a local officer help collect payment if a booking goes bad. A player who works on paper like that is a player who shows up.
Line up two or three players before you fall for one. Browse Solo Musicians on St Louis Near Me Directory, play a clip from each over your morning coffee, then call them with the five questions above.
If you’re the guitarist, the pianist or the violinist with a case in the back seat, this reader is already looking for you. St. Louis hosts come here hunting for one player for one night, so list your business where they search and get more customers from the parties you’d love to play.
### Forty-five minutes nobody planned for
Here’s the review that explains the whole price. A St. Louis couple wrote on their pianist’s site that their wedding started 45 minutes late due to traffic, and he played for their guests the entire time. Forty-five minutes. A church full of people in good shoes, checking their phones, fanning themselves with programs, glancing at the back doors. And one man at the keys making it sound like the plan all along.
Nobody at that wedding remembers the traffic. They remember that it was lovely. That’s the thing a solo musician sells, and it’s why the cheapest quote and the right quote are so often two different numbers. You aren’t paying for an hour of songs. You’re paying for the person who keeps the room together when the hour goes sideways.
Brows that outlast the whole playlist? Read this before you book them.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should a solo musician charge per hour?
A.  In St. Louis, what players publish mostly lands between $200 and $300 for the first hour: one local outfit lists solo saxophone at $250 an hour and solo violin at $300 an hour, with a $200 minimum for 45 minutes or less. A seasoned ceremony player can start higher, and later hours are often cheaper than the first because the setup is already paid for.
### Q. How much is a band for 4 hours?
A.  A St. Louis orchestra’s price-comparison page quotes one agency listing four-hour trios starting at $2,000 to $5,000 and 7-12 piece bands at $6,000 to $10,000. Another agency listing on that page puts an acoustic jazz combo at $750-$1,500 for four hours, and the page notes a small acoustic group is lower priced partly because no amplification is required.
### Q. What type of music is typically played during cocktail hour?
A.  Soft, familiar, mostly instrumental music that guests can talk over: jazz standards, pop songs played without vocals and light classical. One St. Louis pianist describes his cocktail set as a mix of jazz and pop sprinkled into the conversation.
### Q. What are good songs for cocktail hour?
A.  Pick a handful of standards your crowd half knows, a few instrumental versions of songs from your own story, and in St. Louis, at least one Joplin rag. Missouri State Parks says he produced “The Entertainer” in about a year and a half living in a flat on what is now Delmar Boulevard. Give your player three must-plays and one song to skip, and let them fill the rest by reading the room.
### Q. How much do you tip a musician at a restaurant?
A.  There’s no set rate. If you request a song, a bill in the tip jar is the polite thanks, and a little more is kind when the player takes a request they clearly had to work out on the spot. If you hired a player for a private party, a tip is a gift, not a rule; a meal, a glass of water during the break and a written review often mean as much.

## Cornbread Off a Griddle, Closed Saturdays: Southern Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/southern-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Southern cornbread is supposed to come out of cast iron. On South Compton Avenue it comes off a griddle. At Diner’s Delight the batter is poured onto the flat-top, and when St. Louis Magazine critics Joe and Ann Pollack reviewed Diner’s Delight in 2011, they wrote that it looks for all the world like pancakes awaiting syrup. Edges brown, middle soft, the kind of cornbread you tear with your fingers because a fork feels like too much ceremony. At lunch the Pollacks watched city workers and public utility crews carry fried chicken and cornbread out the door to go, the kind of order that turns a paper sack see-through at the corners before you reach the car.
Write this on your hand before you drive: Diner’s Delight, 1504 S Compton Ave., is closed Saturday and Monday. Tuesday through Thursday 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., Friday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., Sunday noon to 6 p.m. Carryout and catering: 314-776-9570.
The kitchen has been serving the city of St. Louis since 1969, in the same location ever since. Jo Alma Lee started it with her late husband, Herman Houston, and at the family’s 50th anniversary former Mayor Francis Slay proclaimed March 5th Diners Delight Day. The Pollacks found large windows over a brightly lighted, spic-and-span room, a short cafeteria line and a couple of high tables at the entrance, and the dining room a few steps up.
Bread there, they wrote, also means biscuits, “big, layered, soft fellers.” A biscuit is the first test anywhere in this city that serves Southern food. Split a hot one with your thumbs and the layers peel apart in soft sheets, the steam hits your knuckles first, and a pat of butter dropped in the seam is gone before you can spread it.
Order a sweet tea with your plate, and somebody at the table will tell you St. Louis invented the stuff. Forget the Forest Park legend. Iced tea was not born at the 1904 World’s Fair, and the story every St. Louisan has heard, the one about a tea man sweating in the heat until he dumped his hot tea over ice, is mostly a tall tale. The man was real: Richard Blechynden, the Tea Commissioner in the India Pavilion. But food historian Robert Moss points out that iced tea had been fashionable for decades by the time the fair opened. In 1868, more than 30 years before the fair, a syndicated newspaper piece was already calling iced tea with lemon juice a popular and healthy drink.
So the South did not need St. Louis to invent its favorite glass. What St. Louis did instead is quieter and a lot more interesting. It became a place where Southern cooking landed, unpacked and stayed, carried up the river by families who brought their skillets, their grandmothers’ ratios and their opinions about cornbread with them. A griddle cornbread on South Compton is one of those opinions, still being served.
### What are typical Southern dishes in St. Louis?
Typical Southern dishes are buttermilk biscuits, fried chicken, smothered pork chops, collard greens, mac and cheese and cornbread. St. Louis Magazine found smothered pork chops, biscuits and peach cobbler at Diner’s Delight on South Compton Avenue, in the same spot since 1969. For a meat-free plate, SweetArt on Lindell is 100% vegan.
The Pollacks’ table at Diner’s Delight is the best map of a Southern menu you will find in this city, so use it. Chicken and dumplings, the juices lightly thickened, the dumplings the tender flat kind many of us grew up with. A smothered pork chop, its meat almost falling off the bone in an onion-laced gravy. Oxtails, four large pieces braised in a brown gravy, hard to manage with a knife and fork and worth the mess. They noted that 59-cent-a-pound oxtails were once a mainstay in that part of town. Not anymore. If they are on the board, order them before somebody else does.
Then the sides, served in generous portions. Mac and cheese properly cheesy and not oversalted. Sweet potatoes lightly sweet, with a note of clove. Cabbage flecked with a few dots of red pepper for a little zing. Green beans from the long, slow school of vegetable cooking, plus black-eyed peas, pinto beans and butter beans. For dessert there was always peach cobbler, and the pound cake with caramel icing, laid on with a gentle hand, was the one they singled out.
Chef Kenny Gilbert of Gilbert’s Social put it plainly: Southern food is “rural, country, comfort food and it is all about the sides.” If you remember one thing when you walk into a Southern spot in St. Louis, remember that. The chicken gets you in the door. The greens tell you whether to come back.
### Order like a regular, not a tourist
The first visit to any Southern kitchen is an audition, and you are the judge. You do not need to order everything. You need three things that tell you the truth: a biscuit, the greens or the slow-cooked vegetables, and the fried thing.
A biscuit cannot hide. Made that morning, it stands tall and pulls apart in soft layers. Out of a freezer bag, it is squat, even and tastes faintly of the box. Then the vegetables. Collards and green beans take hours, and there is no shortcut that tastes right. Good greens are dark, tender and swimming in pot liquor that tastes of smoke and a little vinegar; if they are bright green and squeaky, someone was in a hurry. Third, the fried thing. Fried chicken should crackle loud enough to hear across the table, and the Pollacks gave you permission: eat it with your fingers, and Miss Manners will look the other way while you nibble the best bits off the bone.
Ask one question before you order: “What’s the special today?” Diner’s Delight posted a schedule of daily specials when the Pollacks visited, and they went on a Thursday because Thursday was meat loaf day, individual loaves draped in tomato sauce with a bit of green pepper in the mix. Schedules change, so call 314-776-9570 the morning you go and ask what is on the line. The person who answers knows, and almost everyone loves being asked.
Feeding a crowd? Tell them how many people, what you want on the table and when you will pick up, and let them tell you what holds up best in the car. Diner’s Delight asks catering customers to call the restaurant directly or stop in. And a few words for the menu board: “meat and three” means one main and three sides, and you pick all four. “Smothered” means cooked in gravy, usually onion. “Pot liquor” is the broth left from the greens, and regulars drag cornbread through it until the bowl is clean.
Totally off the menu: where St. Louisans lay a good dog to rest.
### Where else should you order Southern food in St. Louis?
Cross to Lindell for the same tradition with no meat at all. SweetArt has been a St. Louis plant-based kitchen since 2008, and after 16-plus years in Shaw, Chef Reine Keis moved it to its new home on Lindell in 2025. It sits on the lower level of the historic Coronado building at 3701 Lindell Blvd., and it calls itself 100% vegan. One regular quoted on SweetArt’s own site ordered the Maya Angelou with chik’n strips, chickpea curry, kale salad and “their sweet and moist cornbread,” then a raspberry crumble on top of it. Bring the friend who says they cannot do Southern food.
SweetArt is open on Saturday, the day Diner’s Delight is closed. Its posted hours run Saturday 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., with Sunday brunch 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., and it is closed on Tuesday. The phone is 314.571.9009. So the weekend splits itself neatly: SweetArt on Saturday, Diner’s Delight when it opens at noon on Sunday.
Now the hard part. One building in the Grove has now said goodbye to two kitchens. Robbie Montgomery founded Sweetie Pie’s at the Mangrove there and closed it in 2016. Grace Meat + Three opened in the same building in 2017, and chef-owner Rick Lewis served its last day on Sept. 13, exactly nine years after it opened. “It is hard out there,” Lewis told St. Louis Public Radio, and he named his prime customers as “working-class everyday families and young people.” His food truck keeps rolling. The lesson is simple: if a Southern kitchen in this city has your heart, order from it this week, not someday.
That is why the 1969 date on South Compton matters. The family’s own site calls Diner’s Delight a proud small business that has continuously supported the St. Louis community for over 50 years. Rooms like that do not stay open on nostalgia. They stay open on Tuesday lunch orders.
Hungry for a biscuit worth the drive? Browse the kitchens, caterers and brunch spots under Southern Food on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, call each one and ask what they make from scratch today.
If you’re the kitchen, the food truck or the caterer behind that biscuit, the people reading this guide are already hungry and already looking for you, so list your business where they search.
### How did soul food originate, and is it the same as Southern food?
Soul food is African American heritage cooking with Southern roots, and the name is younger than the food. According to Edible Communities, the term soul food originated during the Black Power movement in the late 1960s, while the cooking itself goes back to enslaved cooks who turned scraps, cornmeal and garden greens into meals that could carry a family through a day in the field. The same piece describes soul food as Southern food eaten and prepared by Black people, and that is the simplest way to hold the difference. St. Louis Magazine called Diner’s Delight a stalwart server of soul food, and it sits squarely where the two circles overlap.
Fried chicken, greens, cornbread and mac and cheese sit in the middle of both. Toward the soul food side you find oxtails braised until the meat slips off the bone, smothered turkey wings, chitterlings on holidays, neck bones and ham hocks working quietly inside a pot of beans. Toward the broader Southern side you get pimento cheese, country ham and the coastal seafood cooking of the Carolinas and the Gulf.
Here is the St. Louis part most people never learn. After Reconstruction ended, fear and the Klan pushed Black Southerners north to cities such as St. Louis, and the most famous wave was the Exodusters of 1879. In early March of that year, James Milton Turner, Moses Dickson, John Wheeler and John Turner led the creation of the Committee of Twenty-Five to organize transportation and temporary housing for the 10,000 or so travelers coming through the city. Most moved on to the plains of Kansas, Colorado and Utah; others stopped in St. Louis. More came in the 1910s for factory jobs, and during World War II, according to the city’s own preservation history, the Black population increased 41 percent, drawn by wartime work like the local small arms plant.
Every one of those families arrived with recipes. That is why a plate of greens in North City can taste exactly like one from Mississippi or Arkansas: it is the same pot, carried north and kept going for generations. When you order Southern food in St. Louis, you are often eating a family history that came up the river.
### Are shrimp and grits considered soul food?
Shrimp and grits are Southern first, and whether they count as soul food depends on who is cooking. The dish comes out of coastal Southern cooking, where shrimp and stone-ground corn were both close at hand. In a Black family’s kitchen it often is soul food, and plenty of St. Louis soul food spots serve it with real pride, usually on the brunch menu.
What matters to you, the person holding the spoon, is the bowl. Good grits are cooked slow with butter, loose enough to spread when the bowl hits the table. The shrimp should snap, not squeak, and the sauce on top, often bacon, peppers and onion, should pool into the grits so every spoonful carries some of both. If the grits hold their shape like a scoop of mashed potatoes, they sat too long.
### What is a healthy Southern dish you can still order happily?
The healthiest Southern plates are already on the line; you just order them on purpose. Cabbage with red pepper, slow green beans, black-eyed peas, butter beans and sweet potatoes are the backbone of this cooking, and many of the original African ingredients behind soul food were plant-based. A plate of three vegetable sides and a piece of griddle cornbread is a real Southern meal, not a compromise.
Cooks have been lightening the classics for years. A USC Dornsife piece on soul food’s history notes that chefs and food activists are developing healthier versions, such as substituting smoked turkey for pork in pots of greens and beans. When you call ahead, ask what the vegetables are cooked with; it is a normal question, and the answer tells you whether that pot of beans is vegetarian. Get gravy on the side, split the cobbler, and if you want the whole plate without meat, SweetArt on Lindell calls itself 100% vegan.
### What should you bring to a Southern potluck in St. Louis?
Bring something that travels in a covered dish and tastes good warm or at room temperature: mac and cheese, baked beans, potato salad, deviled eggs, a pan of cornbread, a pound cake or a banana pudding. At a Southern potluck the sides and desserts get judged harder than the mains, so pick one you can make well and make plenty of it.
Think of the long table in a church basement, the foil peeled back on twenty dishes, steam fogging the plastic wrap, folding chairs scraping the floor and somebody’s uncle already going back for seconds. That table has rules nobody writes down. Mac and cheese is baked, not stirred from a box. Potato salad is a personal matter, so if you are new, bring something else. Deviled eggs vanish first. Put your name on a strip of tape under the dish, because you want it back.
If you cannot cook, buy. Shortlist two or three Southern kitchens or caterers, call each one, tell them how many people you are feeding and what you want on the table, and compare what each will deliver and when it will be ready. A good caterer will tell you honestly whether a tray of greens will still taste right after an hour in the car.

### Frequently asked questions about Southern food in St. Louis
### Q. What are some classic Southern dinners?
A.  Fried chicken with mashed potatoes and greens, smothered pork chops in onion gravy, chicken and dumplings, oxtails over rice, and fried catfish with coleslaw are all classic Southern dinners. Almost every one comes with cornbread or a biscuit and a sweet finish like peach cobbler or pound cake.
### Q. What is the best Southern comfort food?
A.  For most people it is fried chicken with mac and cheese and greens, because it hits salt, crunch, cream and smoke on one plate. A smothered pork chop falling off the bone into onion gravy is a close second on a cold St. Louis night.
### Q. What state has the best southern food?
A.  Every Southern state will argue for itself, and none of them will lose the argument politely. The more useful move for a St. Louis diner is to ask the cook where their family is from. The answer usually tells you how the greens will taste before they reach the table.
### Q. What is a healthy southern dish?
A.  A plate of vegetable sides, such as cabbage, green beans, black-eyed peas, butter beans and sweet potatoes, is a healthy Southern meal. Greens cooked with smoked turkey instead of pork, and gravy on the side, keep the flavor and cut the heaviness.
### Q. What to bring to a southern potluck?
A.  Bring a covered dish that holds up warm or at room temperature: baked mac and cheese, baked beans, deviled eggs, cornbread, pound cake or banana pudding. Make plenty, label the bottom of your dish, and skip the potato salad unless yours is famous.
### Q. What is considered Southern soul food?
A.  Soul food is African American heritage cooking from the South: fried chicken, collard greens, cornbread, black-eyed peas, mac and cheese, candied yams, oxtails, smothered turkey wings and chitterlings. It shares much with Southern food but carries its own history of survival and family.
### Q. Are shrimp and grits considered soul food?
A.  Shrimp and grits is Southern coastal cooking first. Whether it counts as soul food depends on the kitchen and the cook, and many Black-owned soul food spots serve it as their own, often on the brunch menu.
### Q. How did soul food originate?
A.  Soul food grew out of plantation life. Enslaved people were given the least desirable cuts of meat alongside rationed staples such as cornmeal, and they transformed them with slow cooking, spicing and garden-grown greens like collards, mustard and turnip greens. The name came much later, during the Black Power movement of the late 1960s, and Southern migrants carried the cooking to cities like St. Louis.
### Q. Is Diner’s Delight open on Saturday?
A.  No. Diner’s Delight on South Compton Avenue is closed Monday and Saturday. It is open Tuesday through Thursday 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., Friday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday noon to 6 p.m., and carryout orders go through 314-776-9570.

## $2,500 Bought a Newspaper: What a Sponsored Article Is and When It Pays
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-sponsored-article-is-and-when-it-pays-for-a-st-louis-business
$2,500. That is what Joseph Pulitzer paid at a public auction in 1878 for the whole St. Louis Dispatch, according to the State Historical Society of Missouri. One bid, a whole newspaper. Today a stranger’s email wants your money for one article in somebody else’s, and it will not say who owns the photos when the week is over.
The subject line says sponsored article opportunity. Your stomach does the thing it always does when a stranger says the word “exposure.” So skip the pitch for a minute and read what one St. Louis outlet actually sells, in writing, on its own help pages.
The enemy here is not you. It is the pay-to-play pitch: a “feature” with no label, auto-renew in the fine print, and a quiet phone afterward that lets you blame your own business. You do good work.
St. Louis Magazine labels its own. Its branded features run under the byline SLM Partner Studio with a Branded Content tag, and its editorial policy says “We clearly label promotional content to avoid confusion.” Its advertiser help page lists what one article buys: “One week on homepage,” a “75K impression campaign,” and “4X placement in relevant newsletters per article.” One week up top. Then the story slides down the page like yesterday’s paper.
Now the line worth a screenshot. The magazine’s Faces of St. Louis package, which it calls “an editorialized, photo-driven advertorial feature,” is “distinguished by artistic black-and-white photography.” You, in crisp black and white, finally looking like the business you built. Then, in the fine print: “Photo usage for Faces of St. Louis only.” Nothing shady about it. It is written down, which is what honest looks like. But it is the question every St. Louis owner should ask before signing anything: when the week is over, who owns the photos?
So here is the shift worth making before you reply. A sponsored article is not a scam and it is not a miracle. It is an ad - an honest one when the label is clean - and it pays you back only when the story keeps working in places you control after its week is up. Whether it earns its price comes down to one small word printed above the headline.
### What does it mean when an article is sponsored?
When an article is sponsored, a business paid for it to run, and the outlet labels it so readers know that before they decide to trust it. It reads like a feature story, but the money, and usually the final say, came from the business instead of the newsroom.
So tonight, before you answer that email, send back two lines and nothing else: How will this be labeled on the page? Can I reuse the story and photos on my own site afterward? An outlet worth paying answers both in one reply. A pay-to-play pitch changes the subject.
That label is the whole deal. The pitch has a sample attached: a glossy feature about some other shop, a smiling owner, a headline that reads like news, and your thumb has to hunt for the word that says somebody paid. The FTC’s own enforcement policy statement on deceptively formatted ads calls this kind of advertising “often indistinguishable from news, feature articles, product reviews.” If you have to squint, the customer on the bus never sees it.
Then morning comes. You are behind the counter of a shop on South Grand, the first tray still ticking as it cools, the contract printed out beside the register because some things you only trust on paper. Your thumb stops on the auto-renew line, the one nobody mentioned on the phone. Run your finger down to the part about photos. Is there one? If not, you just learned something before the pen touched paper.
What a sponsored article buys you that a banner cannot is room. A whole story instead of a slogan. Room to tell how a family recipe ended up on a South Grand menu and why the lights come on before the sun does. A banner shouts across the room. A sponsored article pulls up a chair, slides the first warm tray across the counter, and lets the reader breathe it in before you ever say a price.
### Why did the FTC tell a restaurant column to print one word?
Here is the part almost nobody selling sponsored articles will mention. According to that same policy statement, the Federal Trade Commission “first addressed the issue of print advertisements appearing in a news format in a 1967 press release and subsequent 1968 advisory opinion.” The example it walks through is not a miracle diet pill or a get-rich scheme. It is “a newspaper column, advertising the cuisine of local restaurants.”
Each write-up, the statement says, covered “how a meal was prepared, the name of the chef and/or head waiter, cocktail service offered,” and went on to “whether dancing was permitted, hours, and the price range of the meal.” Read that list slowly. The clink of ice in a glass. The chef’s name said like you already know him. Whether you could dance. The hours painted on the door. It sounds like every warm restaurant feature ever printed, including the ones you have clipped and stuck on the fridge.
The writing was never the problem. The problem was that it was paid for and dressed up as news.
The Commission concluded that “a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the column was an advertisement was necessary,” and the fix it suggested was almost boring: put “ADVERTISEMENT” in “clear type, sufficiently large to be readily noticed, in close proximity to the ad.” One word. It also left a warning that still stings today: a paid piece can copy a news or feature article so exactly that the ADVERTISEMENT caption on top stops meaning anything at all.
So a lesson from a 1968 advisory opinion is the one you need on the day you sign. Your story can be warm. The photos can be gorgeous. The copy can make a reader taste the toasted ravioli through the screen. It just cannot pretend nobody paid for it.
### Is an advertorial just an ad in a nicer suit?
Mostly, yes, and that is not an insult. A plain ad is short and openly selling: a logo, a line, a phone number, maybe a coupon. An advertorial, the older print word for a sponsored article, borrows the shape of editorial - the headline, the photos, the quotes, the story with a beginning and an end - but a business paid for it and usually signed off on it. Editorial is the outlet’s own work. Nobody bought it, and the business in the story may not love how it came out.
That is the real difference between editorial and advertorial: control. With editorial, you do not get it. A writer can walk into your shop on Cherokee Street on the one morning the floor is still sticky from Saturday and put that in print. With an advertorial you get the story you wanted told, and in exchange the reader gets a label telling them you wanted it told.
The advertorials worth paying for answer a question your customers already ask out loud. A roofer explaining what hail does to the shingles on a South City bungalow. A florist walking a nervous couple through what a wedding order looks like a month out. A Dutchtown taqueria explaining why the tortillas taste different when they are pressed by hand. Clearly labeled. Actually useful. The phone number sits at the bottom like a handshake instead of a shove.
Off topic: what does one guitarist on a Soulard patio actually charge?
### Do you have to label a sponsored article by law?
The FTC says the principle “that advertising and promotional messages should be identifiable as advertising” runs through its guidance and its cases. Its test is blunt: “The Commission will find an advertisement deceptive if the ad misleads reasonable consumers as to its nature or source.” An article you paid for, laid out like news, with no label, is the textbook case of misleading people about its source.
Missouri brings its own teeth, and they bite the business, not the paper. The state’s consumer protection statute, section 407.020, says the “concealment, suppression, or omission of any material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise” in Missouri “is declared to be an unlawful practice.” Then comes the line almost nobody reads. The same section carves out the newspaper, magazine or station that ran the ad when it “has no knowledge of the intent, design or purpose of the advertiser.” That carve-out is written for the publisher. It is not written for the business whose name is on the ad.
Read that twice. If an unlabeled piece goes sideways in Missouri, the paper may be able to say it did not know. You will not. Under section 407.100, a court “may award to the state a civil penalty of not more than one thousand dollars per violation.” And people here do complain: the Missouri Attorney General’s office says its Consumer Complaint Unit “received more than 70,400 complaints and inquiries.” The same page gives the Consumer Protection Hotline, 800-392-8222, which is also the number to call if an outlet ever pressures you to run paid copy as news.
None of this is legal advice. For an ordinary sponsored article, the rule fits on a sticky note: the reader should know it was paid for before they finish the first paragraph.
### When does a sponsored article actually pay off for a St. Louis business?
It pays when three things line up, and the price is the least important of the three.
The readers have to be your customers. Not “a big audience.” Your people. Whether your shop is on Cherokee Street or out in Greenfield, a sponsored piece read mostly by people who will never drive to you is a postcard mailed to strangers. Ask the outlet who reads it and where those readers live, and listen for whether the answer is specific or a fog of big numbers.
The label has to be clean. A clear label is not a tax on trust. It is the thing that lets a reader trust everything under it.
The article has to keep working after its week is up. This is the one owners miss. Most paid placements are rented. The story runs, a few calls come in, and a month later the piece is buried under newer posts, tucked behind a paywall, or the link quietly breaks. You paid for a week of attention and you got a week. Then the phone goes back to the silence you know too well: the van idling in the driveway, the schedule with too much white space on it.
The fix is to treat the article as raw material, not the finish line. Get the right, in writing, to reuse your own story and photos. Then put that story where you control the page and where it can keep earning: your website, your Google Business Profile, your directory listing.
This is where a lot of St. Louis owners feel they are already covered. You have a website. You have a Google listing. Maybe a Facebook page a nephew set up three summers ago. But a website is one thin thread, and nobody wakes up searching for websites. They search for answers. Who fixes a furnace in Benton Park on a Sunday. Which bakery on The Hill takes a wedding order. More of them now ask ChatGPT and call the first name it gives back. The sponsored article that pays is the one that gets your story into more of the places those answers come from, not the one that rents you a single Tuesday.

### How much should a sponsored article cost you?
There is no single St. Louis price, and anyone who quotes you an “average” without knowing the outlet is guessing. St. Louis Magazine’s help page, for one, lists what a single article comes bundled with: a week on the homepage and a 75K impression campaign. The glossy media kit that shows up in your inbox will happily lead with the biggest number it has.
Price is the wrong first question anyway. The right one is: what will this outlet actually deliver, and what happens to the article when its run is over? Shortlist two or three outlets your customers really read. Interview each one, on the phone if you can, so you hear how they answer and not just what they type. Tell them plainly what you want: new customers from the neighborhoods you serve, a story you can reuse, a label nobody can miss. Then compare what each one says it will deliver against what you asked for. The outlet that answers with specifics is worth more than the one with the prettier slides.
### Is this offer worth it? A ten-minute check, worked through
Pull the pitch email up next to a scrap of paper. Four checks, in order. Picture the math for a small South Grand bakery, then put your own numbers in.
The break-even count. Divide the price by what one new regular spends with you in a year. If the article costs what six regulars spend in a year, you need six new regulars from this one story just to get your money back.
The gut check on that number. Ask the outlet how many of its readers live in the neighborhoods you serve. If six new regulars out of that crowd sounds like a stretch when you say it out loud, it is.
The label test. Open one sponsored piece the outlet already ran, on your phone, standing up. If you cannot see the label before your thumb scrolls past the first paragraph, stop here. If you had to hunt for it, so will every customer.
The reuse test. Will they put in writing that you can reuse the text and photos? If yes, the story keeps working on your site and listing for years, and six regulars gets easier. If no, you are renting one week, so judge the price as one week.
Clears all four? Sign, and calendar the day it runs. Fails the label test? Walk, politely, today. Fails only the reuse test? Go back and ask once more for the rights, because that answer changes the math more than any discount will.

Ask these on the call, with a pen in your hand. Notice which ones make the other person pause.

If an outlet gets cagey on the first question, you already have your answer. If it gets cagey on the fourth, you are about to rent something you should own.
