### Frequently asked questions about sponsored articles
### Q. What is the difference between editorial and advertorial?
A.  Editorial is written by an outlet’s own staff, nobody pays for it, and the business in the story has no say over how it turns out. An advertorial is paid for and usually approved by the business, and because it borrows the look of a story, the FTC says advertising and promotional messages should be identifiable as advertising.
### Q. Do you legally have to say you are sponsored?
A.  The FTC says advertising and promotional messages should be identifiable as advertising, and it will find an ad deceptive if it misleads reasonable consumers as to its nature or source. Any qualifying information needed to prevent that must be disclosed prominently and unambiguously. In Missouri, section 407.020 declares the concealment, suppression, or omission of any material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise to be an unlawful practice, and under section 407.100 a court may award the state a civil penalty of not more than one thousand dollars per violation.
### Q. How much do native ads cost?
A.  There is no standard price. Each outlet sets its own rates, and online placements can be sold by the piece, by the view or by the click. Shortlist two or three outlets your customers actually read, interview them, tell them what you want, and compare what each will deliver, including how long the piece stays live and whether you can reuse it. For comparison, a Gold listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is $29.75 a month, paid annually, and keeps your own story live year-round.
### Q. Can you trust sponsored websites?
A.  You can trust a sponsored piece about as far as its label. A clearly marked sponsored article is honest about who paid for it, so read it like any ad: useful details, one point of view. Be wary of any page that looks like independent news or reviews but never tells you a business paid for it.
### Q. What is an example of an advertorial?
A.  The one the FTC itself walks through is a newspaper column, advertising the cuisine of local restaurants, written in narrative form so it read like a regular feature. The Commission concluded it needed a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the column was an advertisement. A modern, honest version would be a labeled feature where a roofer explains hail damage or a bakery explains a wedding order, paid for and marked that way.
### Q. How much should you charge for sponsored content?
A.  Charge for what you can actually deliver to the sponsor’s customers, not for the size of your follower count. Put the label, the run length and the reuse rights in writing, and label every paid piece every time, because your readers’ trust is the only thing you are really selling. If you would not stand behind a story without the money, do not run it with the money.

## The FBI Doubts That Signed Ball: What Your Sports Memorabilia Is Worth in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-your-sports-memorabilia-is-worth-in-st-louis
Crack. The rubber band around the shoebox doesn’t stretch anymore. It snaps, leaves a brown stripe across the top card, and drops onto the basement carpet in two dry pieces. The top card is a Cardinal, the two red birds on the bat faded to pink. You’re on your knees with the lid off. Underneath sits a stack of Cardinals with corners gone soft as felt, still giving off that faint sweet smell of old cardboard and attic heat. Further down the box, inside a sandwich bag gone cloudy, is a baseball with blue ink across the sweet spot. Somebody’s name. Maybe a great one.
So which thing in that box is the gamble?
Not the cardboard. After years of undercover work, the FBI’s Operation Bullpen overview says most industry experts concede that over half of the most sought-after athletes’ and celebrities’ autographed memorabilia is forged. The same report calls the card side of the hobby “relatively unencumbered by fraud.” Read that again with the box open in front of you. The soft-cornered cardboard that looks like nothing is the honest part. The ball that looks like the treasure is the gamble.
Then somebody calls down the basement stairs. One cousin swears the ball alone is worth a car. A neighbor offers cash for the whole box, today, before anyone has flipped a single card over. Both of them are betting on the one thing in the box that has to prove itself.
That flips the usual order. Most people start with the autograph, because it feels like the treasure and it’s the thing their dad talked about. Start with the cards instead, tonight, at the kitchen table. Sort them into three piles: stars and rookies, older cards with yellowed borders, and everything else. Turn over each card in the first two piles and copy the back word for word: the year, the maker, the set and the card number. Then type that exact description into a big online marketplace, switch the filter to sold listings, and write down the middle price of the last five or six real sales. Leave the ball alone in its bag, on a shelf out of the sun. It has waited this long. It can wait for an expert.
When you do start taking offers inside the city limits, here’s the leverage the neighbor with the cash doesn’t have. City Ordinance 63461 caps pawn shops at one license per each 30,000 inhabitants, and the city’s license page says the pawn shop quota has been filled and no new licenses are being issued. The pawn counters in the city are the ones already licensed, so work that list. Take your best two or three cards and a photo of the ball to more than one counter, and get each offer in writing before you decide. Ask to see the shop’s city license before anything slides across the glass. Bring a photo ID, too: Missouri law says a pawnbroker shall require a current picture ID issued by the state or federal government from every person it buys from. A counter that waves that off is one to walk away from.
This city has a particular reason to care about getting the story straight. The Sporting News, the paper nicknamed “The Bible of Baseball,” was founded in 1886 and based in St. Louis for more than a century. After years in storage, the bulk of its research library and archives returned to the St. Louis region in 2020 and became part of the Mary Ambler Archives at Lindenwood University, including approximately 20,000 clippings files on players. If the family legend says Grandpa got that ball signed at the ballpark, a collection like that is a real place to check whether the player in the story was where the story says he was. Tomorrow morning, call the University Archivist, Paul Huffman, at (636) 949-4823. The archives are open to the public by appointment, and the university says the Sporting News collection is still being processed, so ask what’s ready to pull before you drive. Have the player’s name and the year of the story on the notepad next to the phone. Buyers pay for stories that check out. They shrug at the ones that don’t.
### How do I find out what my sports memorabilia is worth?
Look up what the exact same item actually sold for recently, not what sellers are asking, and match the condition honestly against yours. For anything that looks valuable, a third-party grader or authenticator turns your guess into a number buyers trust, and only then should you start collecting offers.
“Exact same” is doing heavy lifting in that sentence. A card is identified by its year, its maker, its set and its card number, and almost all of that is printed on the back, usually in type small enough to make you squint under a basement bulb. Write the back of the card down word for word before you search anything. Guessing costs money.
Search only sold or completed listings. Asking prices are wishes. Sold prices are what a stranger with a credit card actually paid. Look at five or six sales, not one, and throw out the highest unless your card is as clean as the one in that photo. The number you write down should be the middle of the pack, not the top.
Condition is where hearts break. Tilt the card under a desk lamp. A crease you can’t see head-on shows up as a thin silver line the moment the light rakes across it. Run a fingertip along the edges; a worn corner feels round and fuzzy, like the end of an old shoelace. Check whether the picture sits centered. Compare only against sold listings with the same flaws, or you’re pricing your card against a better one.
### Which cards in the box are actually worth money?
Most of them aren’t. A tall stack is not a valuable stack. In most family boxes, the value hides in a handful of cards: the stars, the rookie cards, the older cards that survived in sharp shape, and anything the maker numbered, autographed or built with a piece of game-used material.
Sort on the dining room table in three piles. Stars and rookies on the left. Older cards in the middle, the ones with yellowed borders and gum-dusted backs that smell like a drugstore aisle that isn’t there anymore. Everything else on the right, which will almost always be the tallest pile. Price the left and middle piles card by card. Price the right pile as one lot and don’t let anyone make you feel foolish about what it brings. Its job was to be ripped open by a kid on a summer afternoon. It did its job.
That’s the honest answer to whether a baseball card collection is worth anything: usually a few cards carry the whole box, and finding those few is the work. The work is free. It takes an evening, a notepad and card numbers typed in one at a time while the coffee goes cold.
People are asking
### Are sports cards from the 80s and 90s worth anything?
Mostly pocket change, and PSA itself explains why: one of its articles calls the late 80s and early 90s the overproduction years, when dealers had cases of sets gathering dust in their back rooms. The same article shows how fast that can turn, describing sets once dismissed as junk becoming the hobby’s treasure chests after Mark McGwire and Sammy Sosa started hitting home runs. So give the rubber-banded brick from those years the same evening as the older piles: pull the star rookies and the sharp corners, look each one up by card number, and sell the rest as one lot.
### The cardboard is honest. The ink is the gamble.
The same Operation Bullpen overview says industry experts estimate the autographed memorabilia market in the United States at approximately $1 billion per year, and that cooperating subjects and memorabilia experts estimate forged memorabilia makes up over $100 million of it each year. On the undercover tapes, one forger liked to joke that Mickey Mantle “still has one arm out of the grave signing autographs.”
None of that means your ball is fake. It means the signature has to prove itself. A buyer who knows the hobby will discount an unverified autograph hard, or pass on it entirely.
There is one bright spot, and you can check for it right now. The FBI report notes that Major League Baseball unveiled its own memorabilia authentication program, where each piece is witnessed by a person who places a uniquely numbered hologram on it, tracked in a database, and it says those methods “have never been pierced by the forgers.” Turn the ball slowly in your palm, seam by seam, and look for a small shiny sticker that catches the light. If it’s there, write the number down before you do anything else. That little sticker can carry more weight with a buyer than any story about who caught it.
Unrelated, but ask your fishmonger which water that fillet swam in.
### How do I get sports autographs authenticated?
Send the item to a third-party authenticator, an independent company whose whole business is saying yes or no about a signature. PSA, one of the best-known names in the hobby, describes its process plainly: its authenticators conduct ink analysis, autograph structure analysis, object evaluation and side-by-side comparisons, and a certified autograph can be verified publicly through the company’s online certification lookup. That public lookup matters. It’s what lets a buyer three states away trust your ball without ever holding it.
Before you ship, hold the ball by the seams, never the signature, and set it in a clear cube out of the sun. A ball rolling loose in a box rubs its own ink against the cardboard at every pothole. Faded ink doesn’t come back.
A certificate that came tucked in the box with the ball is not the same thing as authentication. Ask who issued it, and whether a serious buyer would recognize that name. Remember who the FBI was chasing: people who forged, fraudulently authenticated and distributed memorabilia. The fake paperwork was part of the scheme, not a guard against it.
If you want a local opinion before you mail anything off, from a dealer or an appraiser here in town, interview them the way you’d interview anyone you’re trusting with a family piece. Shortlist two or three. Ask each one how they judge a signature and whether they also buy what they look at, say what you want, and compare what each will deliver. Somebody who looks at the ball and then offers to buy it is wearing two hats, and you want to see both of them before you hand it over.
### Is a plastic slab worth months of waiting?
Grading is the step that turns “looks pretty clean to me” into a number on a label. PSA’s graders look for doctoring like trimming or re-coloring. Then they grade the condition on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being best. Then the card is sealed in its own sonically sealed, tamper-evident case with the grade and certification number on the label. It’s the clear brick people tilt under a lamp at a show, cool in the hand and heavier than cardboard has a right to be.
Now the part that stings. As of this writing, PSA’s Standard tier costs $59.99 per card, with an estimated turnaround of 90-100 business days and a maximum insured value of $1,000. The company’s Value tiers remain paused, and in its own announcement PSA reported an active global backlog of approximately 9.9 million units. PSA also says it may adjust pricing, services and processing time, so check its page the day you budget, not the day you read this.
So do the math before you fall in love with a card. If it sells raw for less than the grading fee, grading it buys you a nicer box and a loss. Grading earns its keep only when the gap between a raw copy and a high-grade slab is wide and your card truly looks sharp under raking light. Pull up sold prices for the graded version and the raw version side by side. If the difference doesn’t clearly beat the fee and the months of waiting, sell it raw and keep your $59.99.
### Who will actually make you an offer in St. Louis?
It doesn’t matter much whether the box came out of a closet in Dutchtown or a basement out in St. Libory. You have more doors to knock on than the neighbor with the cash: a card shop, an auction house, a pawn counter, a collector at a show. Each pays differently because each carries a different risk.
A shop owner has to resell what they buy, pay rent and keep the lights on, so a cash offer on the spot will land below the sold prices on your notepad. That’s the price of walking out with money today instead of waiting weeks for strangers to bid. Some families want exactly that, especially when the box came out of a house that has to be emptied by the end of the month. Inside the city, watch what happens at the counter. City rules say all secondhand dealers are required to record their purchases from sellers on a Secondhand Dealer Purchase Form, and a dealer’s license application goes to the St. Louis Police Department for approval every year it renews. A buyer who slides that form across the glass and asks for your ID is playing by the city’s rules. One who wants to skip the paper and peel bills off a roll is telling you something too.
An auction house can put a genuinely strong piece in front of more bidders. It also takes a commission from your side, and its buyers often pay a premium on theirs, which quietly shapes how high they’ll go. Ask about both numbers before you sign anything, and ask what happens if a lot doesn’t sell. Then ask one more question nobody thinks to ask: if the house keeps an office in the City of St. Louis, the city says it must still hold an Auctioneer License from the City of St. Louis, even if it’s licensed in a Missouri county. Those licenses are sold at the License Collector’s office in Room 104 of City Hall, and the office answers at (314) 622-4528.
At a pawn counter, expect the paperwork to be real. State law requires a pawnbroker to get proof of identification from every person who sells or pawns property, including a current picture ID issued by the state or federal government. Bring your license. A pawn offer is built for speed and for a shop that has to resell to whoever walks in, so treat it as a floor, not a verdict, and hold it up against your sold-price research before you shake on it. Inside the city limits, the pawn shop quota has been filled and no new licenses are being issued. No new counters are opening to bid against each other for your box, which is one more reason to walk in with your own numbers already written down.
Whoever you talk to, run the same interview. Shortlist two or three. Tell each one exactly what you want: sell everything this week, keep the best few, or get a number for insurance. Ask what they’d do with the box and what they’d pay or charge. Then compare what each one will actually deliver against the numbers you found yourself. The one who explains an offer without getting irritated is usually the one worth trusting.
### Some boxes belong behind glass
Not everything has to be sold. If the box holds something tied to the team itself, a piece of an old ballpark, a game-used item with a paper trail, a document with a story, and you’d like the Cardinals Hall of Fame and Museum to consider it for the collection, the museum’s page says to fill out and submit its Museum Acquisition Study and Consideration Form. Its galleries hold one of the largest team-specific collections of artifacts and memorabilia in the world, and visitors can hold an authentic bat used by a Cardinals great. I could not confirm from that page whether the museum buys items, accepts them as gifts or both, so ask when you submit. Still, there’s a quiet kind of payoff in picturing your grandfather’s piece behind glass while some kid in a red cap presses a nose against it.
Paper has a second home. Lindenwood’s Mary E. Ambler Archives lists archival materials that supplement the Sporting News Collection and sports history among the holdings it has made a priority to expand. Read the fine print first: its donation guidelines say donors must sign a release form that gives Lindenwood free use and ownership of the material. That’s a gift, not a sale. For a stack of old scorecards or letters nobody in the family will ever read again, it may be the right one.
Two money notes before you decide anything. If you sell at a gain, know this before you spend it: net capital gains from selling collectibles are taxed at a maximum 28% rate, and an asset held one year or less produces a short-term gain. And if the box came out of a parent’s estate, settle who legally owns it before anyone sells a single card. Families have fallen out over less than a shoebox.

### Frequently asked questions about sports memorabilia value
### Q. What sports memorabilia is worth money?
A.  Usually the items that are scarce, wanted and provable: cards of star players, rookie cards, older cards in sharp condition, cards a grader has already slabbed, and autographs or game-used pieces backed by an authentication a serious buyer recognizes. Unverified signatures and common cards from big print runs tend to bring little.
### Q. Are baseball card collections worth anything?
A.  Often yes, but rarely evenly. In most family collections a handful of cards carry most of the value and the rest sells as a single lot. Sort out the stars, rookies and older cards in clean shape, look each one up by year, maker, set and card number in sold listings, and price the remainder together.
### Q. Where to sell sports memorabilia in St. Louis?
A.  Your main options are card and collectibles shops, auction houses, pawn shops and private collectors online or at shows. Shops and pawn counters pay fastest; auctions can reach more bidders for strong pieces but charge fees. Shortlist two or three from Sports Collectibles on St Louis Near Me Directory, tell each one what you want, and compare what they’ll deliver against your own sold-price research.
### Q. Can you sell sports cards to a pawn shop?
A.  Yes. In Missouri a pawnbroker must get proof of identification from anyone selling property, including a current government-issued picture ID. If a seller doesn’t provide ID, the law requires the shop to hold the property for thirty days before selling it, provided the seller signs a statement of ownership. Expect a quick offer that sits below collector prices.
### Q. Is PSA grading worth the cost?
A.  Only when the price gap between a raw card and a high-grade slab of that same card clearly beats the fee and the wait. As of this writing, PSA’s Standard tier is $59.99 per card with an estimated 90-100 business day turnaround, so a card that sells raw for less than the fee is almost never worth sending.
### Q. How much does it cost to get sports memorabilia authenticated?
A.  It depends on the item and the service. For cards, PSA’s Standard grading tier is $59.99 per card as of this writing, and faster tiers cost more. I could not confirm a single flat public fee for signed balls and other autographed items, so ask the authenticator what your specific piece will cost before you ship it.
### Q. Is buying sports memorabilia a good investment?
A.  Treat it as something you love first and an investment second. Prices move with demand, forgeries are a real risk on autographs, grading and selling fees eat into gains, and the IRS taxes net capital gains on collectibles at a maximum 28% rate. Buy what you’d be happy to keep if the market cools.

## Learning to Swim as an Adult in St. Louis Can Cost $0
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/learning-to-swim-as-an-adult-in-st-louis
“I can’t swim.” Maybe you have never said those three words out loud, not once, not even to the people you love. Not “I don’t do freestyle.” The real version: you can’t get yourself out of the deep end without the ladder. At birthday parties you stand in the shallow end with the water at your waist and a can sweating in your hand, laughing on cue, one heel parked where the floor starts to tip away. Nobody knows. You have gotten very, very good at nobody knowing.
If your throat just went tight, here is the part nobody puts on the flyer. The City of St. Louis runs a Learn to Swim class at Tandy Recreation Center that its own page says is designed for children and adults of all skill levels, from beginners getting comfortable in the water on up. The price is zero. The registration page says it flatly: “Recreation programs are free. There is nothing to pay.” At the Y, you contact your local branch just to learn the private lesson price. Forward that to the cousin who still sits on the pool steps.
The Tandy class runs Sep 8 to Dec 31, from 4:15 to 7 p.m., at 4206 W Kennerly Ave. Across town, 12th & Park Recreation Center at 1410 S Tucker Blvd runs its own Learn to Swim from Aug 24 to Feb 1, also 4:15 to 7 p.m., also free. Spots are first come, first served, and if a class fills you go on a waitlist and get moved up automatically.
So do one thing before you close this tab. Sign in at parksandrec.stl.gov and register yourself, or call Tandy at (314) 652-5131 and ask, word for word: “I’m an adult beginner. Can I start in Learn to Swim in water I can stand in?” If those evenings don’t fit, call the South City Family YMCA at 314-644-3100 and ask for its adult Stage 1, Water Acclimation class. The Y’s posted session runs October 26 to December 20, with open registration through November 1.
That secret did not start with you. In St. Louis, it has a long history. In 1912, Fairground Park got the city’s first municipal swimming pool, then said to be the world’s largest. A Washington University history of the park calls it the first in a northern state to be formally restricted to Whites, and when the city opened the pool to Black swimmers in 1949, it ended in the riot caused by White people. Hold that next to the shallow end at the birthday party. Some of the fear in this city was handed down.
The way back starts smaller than you think. Both hands on the wall, the tile slick and gritty under your fingers. The water slaps the gutter in a slow, hollow rhythm, and somebody’s whistle echoes off the ceiling. You lower your chin, then your mouth, then your nose, and the whole loud room goes soft and far away. You come up blinking. Nothing bad happened. That is lesson one, and it counts.
### How long should it take for an adult to learn to swim in St. Louis?
Plan on a full session, not one lesson: at the Gateway Region YMCA, each swim session usually consists of multiple weekly lessons over four to eight weeks, and a lesson typically runs 30 to 40 minutes. That first session is about getting comfortable underwater and getting yourself out of a pool, and nobody honest will promise you an exact number of lessons beyond that.
The clock that matters isn’t the calendar. It’s the moment your body stops bracing. Most adults walk in already knowing roughly what freestyle looks like, because they have watched it a thousand times. The arms are not the problem. The problem is the half-second when your ears slip under, the whole room goes muffled and hollow, and every muscle you own votes to stand up.
That half-second is exactly what the Y’s first stage is built around. Stage 1 is Water Acclimation: comfort with underwater exploration, and learning to safely exit a body of water if you fall in. Front crawl and back crawl are the work of Stage 4, Stroke Introduction.
Sit with that for a second, because it is the one thing most frustrated adult beginners never hear. If you spent a few evenings watching freestyle videos, flailed across a hotel pool and decided you’re “just not a swimmer,” you weren’t failing. You were starting on step four. Nobody learns to read by opening a novel.
So how many swimming lessons do you need as an adult? Count it in sessions, not lessons. One session to stop fighting the water: face in, bubbles out, a back float you didn’t think you could do. Often a second session to stitch a breath and a stroke together across the width of the pool. After that, the real teacher is practice, the boring kind, the kind where you go back on some random weeknight when nobody is watching and do it again.
Some adults move through the first stage quickly. Some spend weeks standing in chest-deep water before they will let both feet leave the floor. Both are on schedule. The body learns safety at its own speed, and pushing it past fear tends to buy you a panicked gulp of water and two more weeks of starting over.
You don’t have to wait for summer to start. The free city class at Tandy runs through Dec 31, and the Y’s October 26 to December 20 session is the paid alternative. If South City is a long drive, the Y’s Carondelet Park Rec Complex branch sits at 930 Holly Hills Ave.; call 314-768-9622 and ask it the same Stage 1 question.
### Should I take swim lessons as an adult?
Yes, and you have far more company than it feels like from the edge of the pool. In a national survey conducted for the Red Cross, 80 percent of Americans said they could swim, yet only 56 percent of those self-described swimmers could perform all five of the basic skills that could save their life in the water. Overall, the survey found that 54 percent of Americans either can’t swim or don’t have all of the basic swimming skills.
Read that again from the shallow end. The uncle cannonballing off the diving board, soaking everybody’s towels, may not be able to tread water for a full minute. You are not the one person at the party who can’t swim. You may just be the one person honest about it.
The same survey found that nearly half of Americans, 46 percent, had been in the water at some point and afraid they might drown. Only 2 percent of adults said they planned to take swimming lessons that summer. That gap, between the fear and the fix, is where a lot of grown-ups quietly live for decades. They smile on the pool deck. They skip the float trip. They tell the kids to go ahead without them.
It also found a gap that St. Louis history helps explain: about one in three African Americans said they could perform all five basic swimming skills, compared with 51 percent of whites.
Numbers like that don’t come from nowhere. They come from parents who never learned and couldn’t teach, from summers spent watching the pool through a fence. If that is your family’s story, you are not starting late. You are picking up something that was taken off the table before you were born.
And here is the turn. The park that once kept people out still has a pool, though not the same one; the city replaced the 1912 pool in 1958. Today Fairground Park Pool, at 4011 Natural Bridge, is one of the city’s three outdoor pools, and in season the city says there is no entry fee or charge to swim. Same ground. Different water.
Can you learn swimming at 30? At 45? At 62? Yes. Adults have one advantage kids never do: you can tell the instructor exactly what scares you, and why. Nine-year-olds just cry. You get to say, “I got held under at a cookout when I was eight, and I still feel it in my throat.” A good instructor builds the whole first lesson around that one sentence.
### What does the first lesson actually feel like?
It starts before the water. The door to the pool swings open and the air hits you, warm and wet and thick with chlorine, and every sound in the room bounces twice off the tile: a whistle, a kickboard slapping the deck, somebody laughing at the far end. Your shoulders climb toward your ears. That’s normal. Let them.
Dress for it ahead of time. The Y’s advice is plain: come to class dressed in your swimsuit and don’t forget to bring a towel. Goggles are optional, though plenty of nervous adults find a cheap pair turns the underwater world from a stinging blur into something they can actually look at. The Y also recommends not eating a large meal before swimming, and your stomach will thank you the first time you bob.
Then the steps. The water is cooler than the air, and it climbs your shins, your knees, the soft skin at your waist that makes you suck in a breath. Most first lessons stay right here, in water you can stand in, with the wall a hand’s reach away.
Expect to blow bubbles. It feels ridiculous for about four seconds and then it becomes the most important thing you learn all week, because a slow, steady exhale through the nose is what keeps water from rushing up it. That sharp, sinus-deep burn you remember from childhood? It mostly comes from holding your breath and then gasping. Exhale and it fades.
Then, maybe, the back float. You lie back with an instructor’s palm flat under your shoulder blades. Your ears go under and the room drops away into a low hum. You see the ceiling lights, white and buzzing. Chin up. Hips up. Breathe. At some point you realize the hand has eased to just a fingertip, and then to nothing, and the water is holding you by itself. People cry at that moment. Grown men cry at that moment. Nobody on the deck thinks less of them.
Tell your instructor your story before you get wet. Not the polished version; the true one. Whether you panic when your face goes under, whether you have never once put your head in, whether you can only relax with a foot touching the bottom. Every one of those changes how the first half hour should go.
### What are the five skills that make you actually safe?
This is where most adult swimmers, even confident ones, get a surprise. Being able to splash across the shallow end is not the bar. The Red Cross defines water competency as five specific skills, and these are the 5 basic swimming skills worth aiming every lesson at:
Step or jump into the water over your head.
Return to the surface and float or tread water for one minute.
Turn around in a full circle and find an exit.
Swim 25 yards to the exit.
Exit from the water. In a pool, that means getting out without using the ladder.
Look at what is missing from that list. No butterfly. No flip turns. No pretty freestyle. Every one of the five is about the moment something goes wrong: you slip off a dock at a lake rental, a float tube flips, a kid needs you to get in. The skills are survival first, style a distant second.
That makes a great checklist to bring to any instructor. Ask them which of the five you can expect to do by the end of the session, and how they will test it. A teacher who can answer that in plain words has a plan. One who answers with a pitch for a bigger package probably doesn’t.
Notice too that number two is the hard one for most adults. Treading or floating for a full minute, over your head, with nobody holding you. A minute feels like nothing on land. In deep water, the first time, it feels like a long held note. Practice it in the shallow end first, standing up the second you need to, and stretch it out ten seconds at a time.
### The city pools with no entry fee
Lessons teach you. Practice is what makes it stick, and the City of St. Louis runs outdoor pools you can practice in all summer. Its outdoor pool season runs from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day weekend, and the city says there is no entry fee or charge to swim. The three outdoor pools:
Chambers Pool, 3115 Franklin Ave, 314-534-7953.
Fairground Park Pool, 4011 Natural Bridge, 314-534-9219.
Marquette Park Pool, 4025 Minnesota, 314-353-1250. Pre-registration for a pool pass is required for everyone, kids included, and you can register any time.
The posted outdoor hours were noon to 6 p.m., with the pool closed for a shift change from 2:30 to 3:30. Learn that before you show up at 2:45 with a towel over your shoulder and the lifeguards climbing down.
Marquette’s outdoor pool is the largest in the city, according to the city’s own page for the Marquette Recreation Center. Think of a summer weekday afternoon there: the concrete hot under your feet, kids shrieking in the shallow end, and you, three weeks into lessons, doing a slow back float near the wall while nobody pays you the slightest bit of attention. That anonymity is a gift.
The outdoor pools close for the season after Labor Day, so for the cold months, the city’s pool page also lists indoor pools. 12th and Park, at 1410 South Tucker (314-589-6142), posted lap swim on Monday, Wednesday and Friday mornings from 10 to 11:30 and water aerobics on Monday and Wednesday evenings from 5 to 7. Tandy Recreation Center, built in 1938 at Kennerly and Annie Malone Dr., has an indoor pool too; its posted schedule showed weekday open aerobics and lap swim from 9 a.m. to noon and 4:30 to 7:30 p.m., plus a Friday swim lesson block. Those were the posted summer schedules, so call before you go: Tandy is (314) 652-5131.
Two cautions. The city posted that Cherokee and Wohl recreation centers are temporarily closed for repairs and upgrades, so don’t plan your first practice there without checking. And the affiliated pools, such as the Carondelet Park Rec Complex at 930 Holly Hills Avenue, are not free for city residents and may require a fee.
### How do you pick a teacher who won’t rush you?
Shortlist two or three options and talk to each one before you pay anyone. The free city class, a YMCA branch, a private instructor. Then interview them like you would anyone you’re trusting with something that scares you.
Start with format. The Y’s adult lessons are for ages 16 and up, in group classes or private lessons. Its private lessons are designed for 1:1 instruction, run 30 to 60 minutes, and the Y asks you to contact your local branch for pricing. Group classes are cheaper company; private lessons suit adults whose fear needs a whole instructor.
Inside city limits, the Y’s branch list includes the Bayer YMCA at 5555 Page Blvd (314-367-4646), the South City Family YMCA at 3150 Sublette Ave (314-644-3100) and the Carondelet Park Rec Complex at 930 Holly Hills Ave (314-768-9622). Call the one nearest you and ask whether it runs an adult class, and on which nights.
Then ask the questions that actually tell you something:
What happens in the first lesson if I can’t put my face in?
Do you get in the water with adult beginners, or teach from the deck?
Will I be in a class with teenagers, other adults, or on my own?
Which of the five water competency skills should I have by the end of the session?
What do you do when a student panics?
Tell them plainly what you want. “By the end of this session, I want to float on my back without a hand under me and get myself out of the deep end.” Then compare what each one says they will deliver against that sentence. The right teacher hears it and builds a plan around it. The wrong one hears a sale.
One adult learner put the payoff simply in a testimonial on the Gateway Region YMCA’s lesson page: “When I joined the Y, I did not know how to swim. Adult swim lessons were offered and I am currently enrolled in them. Now I can swim!” The testimonial calls it a feeling of great accomplishment. Read it once more. That’s a grown-up writing an exclamation point about a swimming pool.
The shallow end is not where you have to stay. Shortlist two or three patient teachers this week, starting with Swimming Lessons on St Louis Near Me Directory, and book the one who answers your fears in plain words.
If you’re the swim instructor, the aquatics coach or the one-person private-lesson crew, the grown-ups reading this are looking for someone exactly as patient as you, so put a Gold listing where they search or list your business and get more customers from it.
### Your first lap will be ugly. Swim it anyway.
Somewhere in your second or third session, it happens. You push off the wall, face in, bubbles streaming out of your nose, arms windmilling with no grace whatsoever. You turn your head, gulp half air and half water, and keep going. Your fingers hit tile on the far side. You stand up coughing and grinning, chlorine in your eyes, heart slamming.
It will not look like the Olympics. It will look like a grown-up crossing a pool for the first time. Nobody on the deck cares how it looked.
Somebody’s grandpa is lapping a mall food court right now. Does that count?
What changes afterward is quieter than the lap. You stop scanning for the ladder the second you walk into a hotel pool. You say yes to the float trip. At the next birthday party you stand in water up to your chest, then your shoulders, and you don’t keep one heel on the slope anymore. Your kids, or your nieces and nephews, see a grown-up who learned. That is how a family story changes. One ugly lap at a time.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is 70 too old to learn how to swim?
A.  No. The Gateway Region YMCA’s adult classes are for ages 16 and up, and Stage 1, Water Acclimation, is about comfort with underwater exploration and getting safely out of the water, not strokes. At that age, a private lesson and water you can stand in are a smart start; tell the instructor about any joint or heart concerns first, and talk to your doctor if you have them.
### Q. Can I learn swimming at 30?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis says its Learn to Swim program at Tandy Recreation Center is designed for children and adults of all skill levels, and city recreation programs are free. The Gateway Region YMCA’s adult classes start at age 16 and begin with Stage 1, Water Acclimation.
### Q. How to learn how to swim for adults?
A.  Start with comfort, not strokes: face in, bubbles out, a back float, and getting yourself out of the pool. Sign up for a class that starts there, like the free city Learn to Swim at Tandy or the Y’s Stage 1, then practice between lessons and aim for the Red Cross’s five water competency skills.
### Q. Can swimming help with anxiety?
A.  For many people the water becomes calming once the fear of it fades, because slow exhaling and floating force your breathing to slow down. The catch is that the pool itself is the anxiety for a new adult swimmer, so start where your feet touch, go slow and choose an instructor who will let you set the pace.
### Q. What are the 5 basic swimming skills?
A.  The Red Cross lists five water competency skills: step or jump into water over your head, return to the surface and float or tread water for one minute, turn around in a full circle and find an exit, swim 25 yards to the exit, and get out of the water, which in a pool means without the ladder.
### Q. Does the YMCA offer swim lessons in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Gateway Region YMCA offers group and private adult swim lessons for ages 16 and up, in stages that run from Stage 1, Water Acclimation, to Stage 6, Stroke Mechanics, with 21 indoor and outdoor pools across the region. Private lessons run 30 to 60 minutes; ask your local branch for pricing and session dates.
### Q. What is a good price for swimming lessons?
A.  A good price is the one that buys you a full session with a patient teacher, not the cheapest single lesson. In the city, the best price is nothing: St. Louis recreation programs, including Learn to Swim at Tandy and 12th & Park, are free. For a private teacher, ask what a whole session costs and what you will be able to do at the end.

## St. Louis City Seniors Get Free Tai Chi With One Phone Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-start-tai-chi-in-st-louis
Miss one Sunday in September and the door stays shut until February. That’s the beginner calendar at the St. Louis T’ai Chi Ch’uan Association, around since 1979: new beginners come in only for the fall and spring sessions, fall starts the first Sunday of September, and spring starts the first Sunday of February. If you’re reading this in October or November, the fall window has already closed.
There’s a side door, and it’s the call to make this week. If you’re a senior living in the City of St. Louis, the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging runs tai chi that meets twice a week, an hour each time, and the Fees line on its page reads, in full, “The classes are free.” No studio counter. No membership card. You call the Health Care Coordinator at (314) 657-1670, and a staff member tells you where the class meets and how long the program runs, and helps you sign up.
Free tai chi in this city doesn’t start with a website. It starts with a phone number you can tape inside a kitchen cabinet, or text to your mother tonight.
Then comes the part nobody warns you about: slower is harder. Shift your weight from your left foot to your right over a slow count of eight, knees soft, and your front thigh starts to hum like an old refrigerator. The room goes so quiet you can hear the heating vent tick and somebody’s knee pop. You expected gentle. You got the hardest hour your legs have had all month, and you never once got out of breath.
### How do I begin tai chi in St. Louis?
Two doors, then. City seniors: make that call and ask what’s starting near you. Everyone else: the next beginner door at the Association is the first Sunday of February. The beginners’ hour is Sunday mornings from 10 to 11, and each session lasts five months.
That first February Sunday will probably be gray: road salt crusted on the car door, your breath showing on the walk in, the cold coming up through thin shoe soles. Then a warm room, and a row of strangers in sweatpants who are exactly as new as you are. That’s what the wait buys you. Walk in fresh in the middle of November instead and you’d be joining people who started on the first Sunday in September and have been learning the sequence one posture at a time ever since. Tai chi is taught like a song. You learn the first verse before the second one makes sense.
Whichever door you use, the real first step isn’t buying anything. It’s a phone call or an email with one question: “When does your next beginner session start, and can I try a class before I commit?” Then put the start date on the refrigerator where you’ll see it every morning.
For the class itself, wear clothes you can bend your knees in and flat shoes with thin soles, the kind that let you feel the floor. Eat something light. Get there ten minutes early, because the teacher will want to know about the bad knee, the replaced hip or the shoulder that won’t lift past your ear. Say it out loud. Good teachers change the move for you without making a show of it.
### What does a first class actually feel like?
The federal National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health describes tai chi as a series of slow gentle movements and physical postures, a meditative state of mind, and controlled breathing, and notes it began as an ancient martial art in China. That’s accurate. It’s also about as close to the experience as a recipe is to the smell of the kitchen.
Here’s the experience. The first fifteen minutes are a warm-up: wrists rolling, shoulders circling, ankles drawing small loops on the floor. Then you stand with your feet about hip width apart and the teacher tells you to sink, just a little, as if you were about to sit on a stool that isn’t there. Your breathing gets loud in your own ears. Your hands feel strangely heavy when you raise them slowly, much heavier than when you reach for a coffee cup at normal speed, because speed has been hiding how much work your shoulders do.
Somewhere in the middle of the hour you’ll wobble. Everyone does. You’ll step out of a posture, catch yourself, and feel your face get hot. Look around and you’ll see the person next to you doing the same thing. That wobble is the point. Each slow weight shift is practice for the moment you step off a curb on Grand and the ground is two inches lower than you thought.
By the last ten minutes the room has changed. People breathe out longer. Nobody checks a phone. You walk to the car afterward and notice the asphalt under your shoes in a way you haven’t in years. The next morning your thighs will tell you they worked, a dull ache on the stairs, which is a fair trade for an hour that never once made you breathless.
Your shoulders just dropped an inch. Reward them with Portuguese food.
### How much do tai chi classes cost for beginners in St. Louis?
How much are tai chi classes for beginners? In St. Louis, anywhere from nothing to about $50 a month for a weekly community class. The free end is real: for the city’s senior classes, the Fees line reads “The classes are free.” The paid end is modest by fitness standards.
The Association’s own page lays out the paid version in plain numbers. The Sunday beginners’ class is $50 a month. You register for a five-month session that’s paid monthly, with each month’s payment due no later than the first class of the month. The page says you may pay when you come to class, but asks you to come early so class can start on time, so picture yourself at the door with the month’s $50 folded in your coat pocket, five minutes before ten. If you’re asking how much it costs to join tai chi, that’s a useful local yardstick: about the price of two takeout dinners a month for an hour of instruction every week.
Rec centers and nonprofit programs for older adults often price by the term instead, so you pay once for a block of weeks. St. Louis Oasis, a nonprofit for older adults, lists tai chi among its health and wellness classes, describing gentle, mindful movements to improve balance and reduce fall risk. Prices change by term, so check the current catalog rather than trusting a number someone quoted you last year.
What you shouldn’t pay for: special shoes, a uniform, a sword or a stack of DVDs before your first class. A beginner needs comfortable clothes and a willingness to look a little silly. Everything else can wait until you know you’re staying.
### Where can seniors learn tai chi for free in the city?
Start with that phone number again, because it’s the one most people skip. The St. Louis Area Agency on Aging offers a number of disease prevention and health promotion programs for seniors living in the City, tai chi among them, and the classes are free. The same page lists Matter of Balance, which meets once a week for two hours, if your worry is less about stiff joints and more about the fear of falling itself. Call (314) 657-1670 and ask which programs are starting near you. The agency’s main office is at 1520 Market, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
There’s also tai chi under the trees. A certified teacher of T’ai Chi Chih, a gentler cousin of the classic forms, lists a Tuesday 9:30 drop-in class at Tower Grove Park near Magnolia and Thurman, and calls it a very relaxed class. Picture the cicadas in August, the wet grass soaking the toes of your sneakers, a dozen people moving in slow unison while dog walkers pass on the path. Call before you go and ask what it costs and whether the class still meets in cold weather.
Can’t get out of the house? Free lessons exist online, too. Dr. Paul Lam’s Tai Chi for Health Institute posts a list of free lessons, starting with Tai Chi for Beginners, which it calls “a great start with the Six Easy Steps, almost anyone can learn this.” It comes with one blunt warning from Lam himself attached: “Watching my lesson from your couch will not do much for your health.” Stand up. Clear the coffee table. Follow along as though you were in the room.
### Walking gets you there. Tai chi keeps you upright.
What is better for you, walking or tai chi? The honest answer is that they train different things, and you probably want both. Walking builds your heart and lungs and costs nothing but shoe leather. Tai chi trains the thing walking quietly assumes you already have: balance when your weight is on one foot.
The research backs that up. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health summarizes a 2019 review of exercise for preventing falls in community-dwelling older people, and it found high-certainty evidence that tai chi may reduce the number of people who experience falls by 20 percent. A separate 2020 review of 28 studies found tai chi was better at lowering blood pressure than other exercises, though the authors said the studies were of poor quality and that more research is needed to confirm the conclusions. So treat that one as a promising hint, not a promise.
Think about where falls happen in this city. The icy front steps of a brick two-family in January. The uneven sidewalk slabs heaved up by old sycamore roots. The curb on a dark corner where the streetlight is out. Walking won’t teach your ankles what to do on any of those. Tai chi, practiced slowly enough to feel every shift, might. Walk on the days you don’t have class, and let class teach you how to land.
Your first class is one phone call away, and the hardest part is the doorway. Browse Tai Chi on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three teachers, and call this week to ask when their next beginner session starts.
If you’re the tai chi teacher with a clipboard of sign-up sheets and a Sunday room to fill, the beginners you’re waiting for are already searching this page, so list your business and get more customers through your door by February.
### Nobody licenses tai chi teachers, so interview yours
Here’s a fact that surprises people: tai chi instructors don’t need a license. According to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the practice isn’t regulated by the federal government or the states, and there’s no national standard for tai chi certification. Anyone can rent a room and call it a class. Most St. Louis teachers are careful, patient people who have practiced for decades. You just can’t assume it.
So shortlist two or three and interview them, by phone or for five minutes after a class. Ask how long they’ve practiced and taught, and which style they teach. Ask how they adapt a posture for someone with arthritis in the knees or a fused spine. Ask whether beginners start together or get dropped into an ongoing group. Then tell them what you want, whether that’s steadier balance, a calmer head or a way to move with sore joints, and compare their answers with what each one will actually deliver. You’ll hear the difference fast. A good teacher gets curious about your body. A weak one tells you the form will fix everything.
One program name worth knowing: Tai Chi for Arthritis and Fall Prevention, which the National Council on Aging lists as an evidence-based program. It runs twice a week for 8 weeks, or once a week for 16, with home practice, and NCOA calls it appropriate for people with mild, moderate and severe joint involvement and back pain. If a teacher says they’re certified in it, you know roughly what the course looks like.
### What are the real downsides nobody puts on the flyer?
Tai chi is about as safe as exercise gets. NCCIH reports that a 2019 review of 24 studies with 1,794 participants found adverse events about as often in tai chi groups as in groups doing other activity or nothing at all, and the problems tied to tai chi were minor, such as musculoskeletal aches and pain. In plain words: sore thighs and a cranky knee if you sink too low too soon.
The bigger downsides are human. It’s slow to pay off, so people quit in week three, right before it starts to feel good. Many community classes run on seasons, so a missed start date costs you months. Instructors don’t have to be licensed, so the person at the front of the room is the whole variable. And it’s not medicine. NCCIH is direct about this: don’t use tai chi to postpone seeing a health care provider about a medical problem, and ask about the training and experience of the instructor you’re considering.
None of that is a reason to skip it. It’s a reason to start on purpose: a real beginner session, a teacher you’ve talked to, a doctor who knows, and two evenings a week that are yours.

### Can you really lose weight doing tai chi seven minutes a day?
Not on seven minutes alone, but tai chi done like a real class can move the tape measure. In a Hong Kong trial of 543 adults 50 and older carrying extra weight around the middle, the group that did three one-hour tai chi sessions a week for 12 weeks ended up about 1.8 centimeters slimmer at the waist than a group that didn’t exercise, with no diet plan attached. The CDC adds the part the seven-minute pitch skips: most weight loss comes from eating fewer calories, so keep the short daily practice for balance and let the dinner plate carry the heavy lifting.

### Q. How much does it cost to join tai chi?

### Q. What are the downsides of practicing tai chi?
A.  Physically, very few: a 2019 review of 24 studies found the problems linked to tai chi were minor, such as musculoskeletal aches and pain. The practical downsides are slow results, seasonal start dates that make you wait, uneven teacher quality because instructors don’t have to be licensed, and the temptation to use it instead of seeing a doctor.
### Q. What is better for you, walking or tai chi?
A.  They do different jobs, so most people benefit from both. Walking builds endurance. Tai chi trains balance on one foot, and a 2019 review of falls in community-dwelling older people found high-certainty evidence that tai chi may reduce the number of people who experience falls by 20 percent. Walk on your off days and let tai chi teach your ankles how to land.
### Q. Can I get free tai chi classes online?

If you can get out, an in-person teacher can correct your posture in ways a video can’t.
### Q. Do I need to be flexible or fit to start tai chi?
A.  No. Beginner classes start where you are, and teachers adapt postures for stiff joints. The National Council on Aging describes Tai Chi for Arthritis and Fall Prevention as appropriate for people with mild, moderate and severe joint involvement and back pain. Tell your teacher about any injury before the first class starts.
### Q. Do tai chi teachers need a license?
A.  No. According to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the practice isn’t regulated by the federal government or the states, and there’s no national standard for certification. Shortlist two or three teachers, ask about their training, experience and how they adapt moves, then compare what each one will deliver.

## Eight Hours Dry: What a $55 Spray Tan in St. Louis Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/getting-a-spray-tan-in-st-louis-what-to-know-first
Eight hours without a drop of water on your skin. That is what a $55 spray tan at one St. Louis studio asks of you, and nobody mentions it when a friend says “just go get sprayed before the wedding.”
It’s printed in one blunt sentence on the menu page at Sol Sunless Tan, a studio that has been spraying St. Louis since 2012, tucked between a Dry Bar and a Commerce Bank on South Lindbergh in Ladue: you will not be able to shower or wash your face for 8 hours after your tan.
Now put that rule inside a St. Louis summer. Say the wedding is Saturday, on The Hill, and it’s Thursday. You stand on a little mat in a curtained room in your oldest dark underwear, arms out like you’re waiting for a hug. The gun hisses. The mist lands cold on your shoulder blades first, a fine wet chill that makes you flinch, and then the fan blows warm air across your back and dries it on your skin. You leave in a baggy black hoodie and loose sweatpants, holding your arms slightly away from your sides, and step out into July air so heavy it sits on the back of your neck like a damp towel. Every drop of drizzle on the walk to the car feels like a threat. So does every bead of sweat.
Then you get home, and the shower is right there.
That moment, more than the price, decides whether the money was well spent. One St. Louis-area studio, goGLOW, spells it out on its own FAQ: if you rinse 2 hours later, the end result will be significantly lighter than if you waited 5+ hours. It suggests 3-4 hours for most clients, and at least 12 hours with its regular solution. So the real cost of a spray tan is a dollar figure plus a block of time you agree not to get wet, sweat hard, or scrub.
Hold out, and the payoff comes in two parts. By bedtime the color looks a shade too dark and a little muddy, which is the bronzer sitting on top doing its job. Then Friday morning, a day before the toasts on The Hill, the first rinse: cool water only, tea-brown water circling the drain, a towel patted on instead of rubbed. You wipe the fog off the mirror and the color is still there.
If you have a Saturday wedding circled, work backward from it. goGLOW in Rock Hill suggests booking 2-3 days before a main event like a gala or wedding. Shower and shave the day before. Walk in with bare skin: no fresh lotion, deodorant or makeup. Bring dark underwear you don’t love and the loosest dark clothes you own, and keep the evening clear of rain, sweat and dish water. When you call to book, say it’s your first tan and name the event, so the artist can pick the shade and the formula for you.
If you hold Muny tickets for Thursday night, give them to a friend: a summer night in Forest Park, the backs of your thighs pressed to a warm seat at the nation’s oldest and largest outdoor musical theatre, is exactly the sweat a fresh tan can’t take.
Cross the Missouri River into the next county over and its health department permits and inspects tanning salons, right down to goggles that must be cleaned and sanitized after each use. Then read how the county code defines tanning equipment: any device intended to induce skin tanning of any part of the body through ultraviolet radiation. The bed is on the inspector’s list. The spray gun is not. Statewide, Missouri has no spray-tan-specific license, and the state regulates UV tanning facilities separately.
So the hand holding that hissing gun a few inches from your face answers to the studio that hired it, and that is about it. Ask two things when you book: who trained you, and what do you give me for my eyes, nose and lips before you start? A good artist answers both without a pause.
### How much is an average spray tan in St. Louis?
In St. Louis, a single spray tan runs about $33 to $65 on posted menus. A custom airbrush tan is about $55, a rapid-rinse version near $65 and an automated booth tan about $35, while one tanning salon lists an airbrush spray at $33. Packages and memberships cut the per-tan price.
The $55 and $65 prices come from two spray studios that post their full menus.
At Sol Sunless Tan, a single custom tan by a spray artist is $55 and a single booth tan in its Mystic or VersaSpa booth is $35, with no upcharge for the rapid solution, which develops in 3-4 hours. At goGLOW, a single airbrush session is $55 and the rapid version is $65, which the studio describes as a $10 add-on for a stronger solution that lets you rinse sooner.
Where the price really drops is in bulk. Sol lists 5 custom tans for $200, which works out to $40 each, and a Bronze membership of 2 tans for $75 a month. It also runs half-price Monday mornings, 9-11am, at $27.50 for a custom tan. Students get the same $27.50 price any day from 2-4pm. If your schedule bends, that is half the regular price for the same artist and the same hiss of the gun: a Monday morning on South Lindbergh, the coffee still hot in the cup holder, and $27.50 left over for toasted ravioli later in the week.
The hand-sprayed tan costs more because a person is reading your body as they go. They catch the dry patch on your elbow, feather the line at your ankle, and spray lighter on your hands. A booth is a fixed pattern of mist from fixed nozzles. For a wedding, a photo shoot or the first tan you’ve ever had, most people are happier with the human.
### Before you walk in: the clothes, the skin, the timing
Skin prep is one line: clean, shaved a day ahead, and bare of lotion, deodorant and makeup when you walk in.
So, do you wear undies for a spray tan? Mostly that’s your call. goGLOW recommends dark undergarments or swimwear, reminds you that what you wear during your session will be your tan line, and says undergarments are required for male clients. Sol is even more relaxed: yes, you can be sprayed nude, men need to bring bottoms of some sort, and if you’re sprayed without a bra, plan to leave without one. Bring dark, cheap underwear you don’t love.
What you wear out the door matters just as much. Both studios say the same thing in different words: loose, dark, soft. Sol warns that anything tight can leave lines from bra straps, jeans and flip-flops, and tells you not to wear white after your appointment. goGLOW suggests long, loose cotton sleeves and pants and no denim or tight workout gear for the first few hours. On a sticky July evening in Soulard, that hoodie will feel ridiculous. Wear it anyway. A bra strap line looks like nothing in the booth mirror. It looks like everything in the Forest Park wedding photos, when the late sun comes low across the Grand Basin and every bare shoulder in the bridal party glows except for the pale stripe across yours.
Book your nails first. Sol says not to schedule nail, waxing or hair appointments after your tan, and goGLOW explains why: a full manicure and pedicure afterward means soaking and scrubbing, which strips color from your hands and feet. A day or two before is the move.
And watch your calendar against the sun. goGLOW’s FAQ says you will not be able to spray tan over recently sunburnt skin, within 4 weeks of a sunburn, and that spray tanning on top of sunburned skin is at risk for peeling. If you got cooked at a Cardinals day game last weekend, push the appointment.
### What happens to your face, eyes and lips in the booth?
Yes, a full spray tan usually includes your face. That’s why Sol’s rule is no shower and no face washing for 8 hours, and why it says you can put on dry makeup afterward. You close your eyes, hold your breath for a few seconds while the gun passes, and feel a cool wet puff across your cheeks and forehead. Then the fan, and you breathe again.
Here’s the piece most first-timers never hear. DHA, the active ingredient in spray tans, is approved for external application to the human body. But the FDA says its use in tanning booths as an all-over spray has not been approved, because safety data to support that use has not been submitted. DHA is not permitted for use in the area of the eye, and the agency says the lips and other mucous membranes are not approved exposure routes either.
The FDA’s advice is to ask three questions before you get sprayed: are you protected from exposure around your entire eye area, on your lips and other mucous membranes, and from inhaling or swallowing the product? If the answer to any of those is no, the agency says you should ask for those protections. In practice that means something over your eyes, something on your lips and nose, and a technician who tells you when to hold your breath.
This is also the honest answer to the question people type at midnight before a Central West End wedding, when the dress is hanging on the closet door. The face is the part of a spray tan that fades fastest, too. goGLOW notes that facial skin sheds faster than the rest of your body, so your face loses its color a little sooner.
### When can you shower after a spray tan without wasting it?
Wait for the time your technician gives you, and treat it like a bill you already paid. Sol also says its rapid version develops in 3-4 hours.
Do the math on a 4pm appointment and that 8 hours runs to midnight. On a St. Louis August night, with the window unit rattling and the sheets sticking to the backs of your calves, you sleep in the loose dark clothes on an old towel and leave the shower for morning.
So what if I shower 2 hours after spray tan? You won’t erase it, but you’ll get less than you paid for. goGLOW’s own words: if you rinse 2 hours later, the end result will be significantly lighter than if you waited 5+ hours. That’s money circling the drain because you got impatient.
When it’s finally time, keep the first shower boring. goGLOW says the first rinse is cool water only, no body wash, soap or shampoo, and then you pat dry instead of rubbing. You’ll watch brownish water swirl toward the drain and feel your stomach drop. Breathe. That’s the cosmetic bronzer, the guide color the artist used to see where they sprayed, and it’s supposed to come off. The real tan is underneath it and still developing.
Between the booth and that shower, stay dry. Sol’s list is half instructions, half comedy: no rain, no swimming, no getting wet in any way, and be careful switching laundry loads, unloading dishes or refilling the dog’s water bowl, because water spots show. In a St. Louis August, that also means skipping the walk on South Grand in the heat. goGLOW tells clients to avoid heavy sweating, and a sweaty afternoon is exactly how you end up with stripes behind your knees.
Eight hours of not showering is plenty of time to plan a career move.
### Why does a spray tan look so dark the first night?
Do spray tans look bad at first? They can look a shade too dark and a little muddy for the first several hours, and that’s normal. What you’re seeing is the bronzer sitting on top of your skin, not the finished tan. goGLOW says that after your first rinse, the cosmetic bronzer in the formula washes away. Another area salon puts it simply: the bronzer develops darker as the day goes by, and your first shower is when it rinses off.
The real color is a slower chemistry. DHA reacts with the outermost layer of your skin, and Cleveland Clinic says that reaction takes around two to four hours to begin and can keep going for 24 to 72 hours. So the version of you in the mirror at 10pm is not the version that walks into the reception tomorrow.
That’s also why the studios push you to book ahead. goGLOW suggests getting sprayed 2-3 days before a main event like a wedding, and 1 day before you leave for vacation. For a wedding, it recommends a trial tan 2-6 weeks before the day. Do the trial. It’s the one time you can find out your skin turns a little orange, or your palms streak, without 150 guests and a photographer finding out with you.
If you do end up orange, goGLOW points first at the bottle: low grade DHA and low quality (cheap) products have a tendency to react with skin poorly, and it adds that over-darkening or expired product can do the same. Use a gentle, sulfate-free wash for the week and the fade will look like a tan wearing off, not a map.
### What happened to all the tanning beds?
In St. Louis, part of the answer came out of a study led by dermatologists at Washington University School of Medicine. Its researchers called 375 tanning salons across Missouri, posing as prospective clients. Of the 243 salons that finished both interviews, 80 percent of facility operators said indoor tanning would prevent future sunburns, a claim the study calls false. Read that again as a parent with a sixth-grader begging to look tan for the spring dance.
Missouri moved, a little. A parental consent form became required for teens under 17, according to WashU dermatologist Lynn Cornelius, who also wrote that Missouri has no minimum age restrictions banning tanning bed use. She put the bed itself bluntly: the ultraviolet exposure from tanning beds can be 5-15 times greater than summer mid-day sun, and tanning beds are a completely avoidable cancer risk. Think of the worst noon you ever spent in the left-field bleachers at Busch, then multiply it.
The rest of the country was already walking away. Between 2010 and 2013, indoor tanning among all adults fell from 5.5 percent to 4.2 percent, and the biggest drop came among women ages 18 to 29, from 11.3 percent to 8.6 percent. In raw terms, about 1.6 million fewer women and 400,000 fewer men used indoor tanning devices over those three years. Add a 10 percent excise tax on indoor tanning services, and you can see where the customers went.
A spray tan involves no exposure to UV radiation, and most dermatologists agree that if you simply must have a tan, spray tanning is the safer alternative. Safer is not the same as protected, though. Only sunless tanners that contain sunscreen ingredients and are labeled with SPF numbers may provide protection. Your bronze shoulders on Art Hill on a July afternoon are exactly as burnable as they were before the tan. “It is not a base tan,” states Dr. Lucas, a Cleveland Clinic dermatologist, who says you still need to apply at least a 30 SPF broad-spectrum sunscreen, 15 minutes before you go outdoors.
There’s one more wrinkle worth knowing. Graham Colditz, a cancer prevention expert at Washington University, recommends sunless tanning lotions instead of tanning booths, since they pose no risk of inhalation, as might spray tans. If you’re pregnant, have asthma, or just hate the idea of breathing the mist, a lotion at home gets you most of the way there.
### How to choose a spray tan artist in St. Louis
Don’t pick on price alone, and don’t pick from a single photo. Shortlist two or three studios or mobile artists, then talk to each one, by phone or in a quick visit. Tell them what you want: the event, the date, how dark, whether you’ve ever been orange before. Then listen to what they say they’ll actually do for you and compare.
A few questions sort the pros from the rest fast. Do you hand-spray or use a booth, and which would you suggest for me? What protection do you give for my eyes, lips and nose, and do you tell me when to hold my breath? Do you mix the solution to my skin tone? What rinse time will you give me, and what if I need to sweat tomorrow? Do you offer a trial before a wedding?
Pay attention to how the room feels, too. Clean mats, a fan that actually runs, a technician who explains what’s happening before the gun starts hissing. If it feels rushed or nobody mentions your eyes, walk. There’s another studio across town.
Teens are a separate conversation. goGLOW says clients under 18 can book, but only after a parent or guardian signs a waiver. For a homecoming or prom tan in the city, call ahead and ask what the studio requires, so nobody is turned away at the curtain with a dress bag over one arm.
