### Frequently asked questions about spray tans in St. Louis
### Q. How often can you get a spray tan?
A.  Most people get one about once a week, because the color fades as your skin sheds. goGLOW says its tan lasts 5-7 days on average, and Cleveland Clinic puts a typical spray tan at five to 10 days. Studios price memberships around that rhythm, like Sol’s 2 tans for $75 a month or 4 tans for $150 a month.
### Q. What are the downsides of a spray tan?
A.  The use of DHA in tanning booths as an all-over spray has not been approved by the FDA, and the FDA has received reports of coughing, dizziness and fainting, primarily in the case of spray tanning booths. Fragrances can irritate sensitive skin, a spray tan gives no sun protection, and it fades in about a week, so the cost repeats. Rinse too early and you lose color.
### Q. Do they do your face in a spray tan?
A.  Yes, the face is usually included. You close your eyes and hold your breath as the gun passes. The FDA says DHA is not permitted in the eye area and is not approved for lips or mucous membranes, so ask for eye, lip and nose protection before you start.
### Q. Do you wear undies for a spray tan?
A.  That’s up to you if you’re a woman, and men are asked to wear bottoms. goGLOW recommends dark undergarments or swimwear, and what you wear during your session will be your tan line. Sol says you can be sprayed nude. Pick dark, cheap underwear you don’t mind staining.
### Q. What if I shower 2 hours after spray tan?
A.  Your tan will come out lighter than you paid for. goGLOW says rinsing at 2 hours leaves a result significantly lighter than waiting 5+ hours, and it suggests 3-4 hours for most clients. Sol Sunless Tan asks for 8 hours, and goGLOW asks for at least 12 with its regular solution.
### Q. How expensive is tanning?
A.  A spray tan in St. Louis runs about $33 to $65 a session on posted menus. Tanning bed memberships at one area salon run $32.95 to $65.95 a month with a 3-month minimum, and many businesses offering indoor tanning services must collect a 10 percent excise tax.

## Four Tapas Plates in St. Louis: $59 or $153?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/reading-a-tapas-bar-menu-in-st-louis
“Let’s just get a bunch of stuff and share.” Somebody says it at every tapas table in St. Louis, usually while the server is still setting down two glasses of something cold and red and the room smells like garlic hitting hot olive oil. Five fingers point at five lines on the menu. Nobody reads the small word printed above them.
That word is the price. At Idol Wolf, the restaurant inside 21c Museum Hotel downtown, four tapas (the bravas, the jamón croquetas, the meatballs and the garlic shrimp) add up to $59. Four raciones (the hanger steak, the half chicken, the whole branzino and the duck) add up to $153. Same four plates. Same two people. Nobody at the table did anything except point.
Forty minutes later the table is crowded with platters, half a chicken is going cold beside a pile of crispy potatoes, and the check lands with a number that feels like it belongs to a fancier night. Nobody ordered wrong on purpose. They read the dishes instead of the headings. Learn three of those headings and you can read any tapas menu in St. Louis in about ten seconds, and order a night that tastes like a feast and bills like a weeknight.
### What are the three types of tapas in St. Louis?
The three are the pintxo, the tapa and the ración: a bite on a stick, a small plate that goes with a drink, and a full plate built for the whole table. On Idol Wolf’s downtown dinner menu the tapas run $12 to $28, while the raciones, the full plates, start at $35 and climb to that $65 paella.
Start with the smallest. A pintxo (say it PEEN-cho) belongs to the Basque north of Spain, and the name is the instruction: pintxos got their name from the Spanish pincho, a cocktail stick. One bite, maybe two, and the little wooden stick left on your plate is the only proof it was ever there.
The tapa is the one everybody knows by name and nobody can define. Spain’s own dictionary, the Real Academia Española, calls it a small portion of some food served to go with a drink. One hand carries it to the table. Two or three forks finish it.
The ración is the full portion. At Idol Wolf, the raciones are a coffee-rubbed hanger steak at $35, a spice-rubbed half chicken at $38, a whole branzino at $40, a duck breast at $40, a 12-ounce USDA Prime strip at $50 and the paella at $65. Those are entrees by any other name. Put one in the middle of the table and the table is fed. Put four in the middle and you have ordered four dinners for two people.
So here is the rule for two, and it fits on a napkin: one ración, two or three tapas, then stop and look at each other. On Idol Wolf’s menu that could be the $40 whole branzino with its fried garlic chips, the $12 bravas and the $18 gambas al ajillo, the shrimp still spitting in garlic oil when it lands. Before anyone points, ask the server one question: which of these come out as a full plate? And for the cheapest first round in the building, get to 1528 Locust Street between 3 and 5 p.m., when the daily Pintxos Hour menu cuts the $12 Spanish olives to $6, and order off that card before the dinner menu ever opens (314.325.0360 if you want to check first).
Here is the part that surprises people who think Spanish food arrived in St. Louis with the small-plates craze. A St. Louis mayor once asked Spain’s government for permission to move its World’s Fair pavilion here. Life Magazine called Spain’s pavilion the “jewel” of the 1964 New York World’s Fair. Built on a parking lot at Broadway and Market, it officially opened in May 1969 with a 10-day celebration. A study had projected 2.5 million visitors a year. It drew about 450,000 in the second half of 1969, its restaurants lost money, and within a year of opening it sat shuttered. The building ended up as the lobby of a hotel, and the site is now the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark. Walk past it on the way to a Cardinals game and you are passing the spot where St. Louis once tried to build its monument to Spanish culture.
More than half a century later, the Spanish menu finally stuck, just in smaller rooms. And the vocabulary on those menus still trips people up the same way the pavilion’s backers misjudged St. Louis: by assuming one size fits everybody.
### The heading above the dish is the price tag
Read Idol Wolf’s dinner menu top to bottom and it sorts itself into tiers, even if you never notice the words. First come the bocaditos, little mouthfuls: Spanish olives with roasted garlic, citrus and piquillo pepper at $12, pan con tomate on grilled Union Loafers toast at $12, Serrano ham aged 18 months with chorizo-spiced chips at $24, and a chef’s charcuterie board at $28. These are the nibbles you order the second you sit down, before anybody has opened the wine list properly.
Then the tapas, split into garden, butcher and sea. Patatas bravas at $12. Jamón croquetas with béchamel at $14. Albondigas, the pork and beef meatballs, at $15. Gambas al ajillo, Argentinian red shrimp in garlic, olive oil, chili and brandy, at $18. Octopus with mojo picón and crispy potatoes at the top of the section, $28.
Then the raciones, $35 to $65. The jump between the priciest tapa and the cheapest ración is the whole lesson. You can see it before you taste anything: a tapa arrives in a dish one hand can hold, still sputtering; a ración is a whole fish or half a bird, the kind of plate that makes everyone at the table shift their glasses to clear a spot.
That is the $59-or-$153 table from the top of this page, and now you can see where it comes from. Four tapas sit between $12 and $18 each. Four raciones sit between $35 and $40 each. Every plate in the second order costs more than the priciest plate in the first, before a single drink, tax or tip. The plate count never changed. The heading did.
None of this means raciones are a trap. They are often the best thing on the menu, and a whole branzino with fried garlic chips is meant to be pulled apart by a table full of people with oily fingers. The trap is ordering them at tapas speed. Four raciones is a banquet you’ll be carrying home in boxes.
And don’t assume every kitchen draws the lines in the same place. Over in The Grove, at Aperi on Manchester Avenue, the seafood paella (shrimp, chorizo, mussels and saffron bomba rice) sits on the menu right beside the charred octopus. Same dish name, different portion philosophy. The heading is your best clue, but the only final answer is the person carrying the plates.
Totally unrelated: nobody tells you what to wear into a spray tan booth.
### What’s the difference between appetizers and tapas?
An appetizer has a job: it opens a meal and then gets out of the way for the entree. Tapas are a whole way of eating. You order a few, you drink, you talk, you order a few more, and at some point you realize the small plates were dinner all along. Nobody is waiting for the main course because there isn’t one.
That difference changes how you should order. With appetizers, you order everything at once and the kitchen paces it. With tapas, you order in rounds. Two or three plates, a drink, then look at each other and decide. The rhythm is the point: the crackle of a croqueta when you break it open and the béchamel steams out, then a pause, then the next round. When people ask what the correct way to eat tapas is, that’s the honest answer. Small rounds, shared forks, and nobody claiming a plate as their own.
There’s also the drink. Remember the dictionary line: a tapa is food served to go with a drink. American appetizers rarely assume you’re holding a glass. Tapas almost always do, which is why the happy hours at St. Louis tapas bars are built around the plates instead of just the pours.
### Why does the same bowl of olives cost half at 3 p.m.?
Because at Idol Wolf, the word pintxo isn’t on the plate. It’s on the clock. The restaurant runs a Pintxos Hour daily from 3 to 5 p.m., and the prices on that short menu are a different world from the dinner menu.
The Spanish olives with roasted garlic, citrus and piquillo pepper are $12 at dinner and $6 during Pintxos Hour. Exactly half. The albondigas drop from $15 to $10. The Spanish Caesar goes from $14 to $10. There’s a 16-ounce Broadway Flor Blanca Mexican lager from St. Louis for $5, and a vodka highball for $5. A cheese and charcuterie plate with 18-month jamón Serrano, raisin chutney and sunflower seed brittle is $24.
So when somebody asks what time of day you eat tapas, the St. Louis answer is more practical than romantic. Eat them early. Walk in at 4:15 on a gray afternoon, take a stool, order the $6 olives, the $10 meatballs and a $5 cold lager, and you’ve eaten well before the dinner prices ever kick in.
Aperi in The Grove does its own version: a Wine’d Down Hour from 4 to 5 p.m. daily, in a candle-lit room the bar describes as warm and unhurried. Its menu is driven by the seasons and changes often, so check what’s on before you go rather than counting on a dish you saw last month.
### How do you order for two without doubling the bill?
Treat the server like the expert on the room, because they are. Before anyone points at anything, ask three questions. Which of these are small and which are full plates? How many plates do most couples order here? And which one dish would you be sad if we skipped? You’ll learn more in thirty seconds than you will from reading the menu twice, and you’ll hear things the menu can’t tell you, like whether tonight’s octopus is the size of your palm or your forearm.
Then say plainly what you want. “We’re hungry, but we don’t want a $150 dinner.” “We want to try a lot of little things.” “We came for the paella, so build around it.” A good server would much rather pace your night than watch you leave half a branzino on the table.
A shape that works almost anywhere: one bocadito or a bowl of olives the minute you sit down, two tapas for the first round, then decide. If you’re still hungry and still happy, add a third tapa or split one ración. That’s it.
A few habits keep it honest. Order hot plates when you want them, not all at once, so the shrimp still hisses in its garlic oil when it hits the table. Leave the sticks from any skewered bites on your plate in case the bar counts them. Ask about portion size on anything listed as a board, a whole fish or a paella, since those are the dishes most likely to be bigger than they sound. And if the table is four or more, raciones stop being a splurge and start being the smart buy, because a $65 paella split four ways feeds everybody for less than four separate entrees.

### Where St. Louis reads like a Spanish menu
Idol Wolf sits inside 21c Museum Hotel at 1528 Locust Street downtown, in a historic building that was once a YMCA. The hotel’s rotating contemporary art spills over into the restaurant, so you can drift past an installation on your way back to the table with your mouth still warm from the bravas. Dinner runs 5 to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 5 to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Aperi is the other mood: a small, candle-lit, Spanish-influenced tapas and wine bar at 4317 Manchester Avenue in The Grove, right next to Good Company. It serves à la carte tapas alongside a weekly rotating chef’s tasting with a beverage pairing, and the wine program focuses on naturally produced bottles, including a Spanish Albariño, a Verdejo, a Tempranillo and a Basque txakoli. Walk-ins are welcome, with reservations encouraged. It’s open 4 to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 4 to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Two rooms, two ways to draw the line between small and full. That’s exactly why the three words matter more than any one restaurant’s menu. Once you can read pintxo, tapa and ración, every new tapas bar in the city hands you a menu you already understand.

### Frequently asked questions about tapas bar menus
### Q. What is a Spanish tapas bar?
A.  A Spanish tapas bar is a place built around small plates and drinks, where you order a few dishes at a time and share them instead of each ordering an entree. In St. Louis, Idol Wolf downtown and Aperi in The Grove both serve Spanish-style tapas menus, with plates meant to pass around the table between sips.
### Q. What food is served at a tapas bar?
A.  Expect olives, cured ham, croquetas, meatballs, garlic shrimp, fried potatoes with aioli, octopus and paella, plus cheese and charcuterie boards. Idol Wolf’s dinner menu runs from $12 Spanish olives to a $65 seafood paella.
### Q. How big is a tapas?
A.  A tapa is a small portion meant to go with a drink, usually two or three bites per person when shared. Sizes vary by kitchen, so ask. At Idol Wolf, patatas bravas are $12 and Galician octopus is $28, while a spice-rubbed half chicken is $38 and the seafood paella is $65.
### Q. What time of day do you eat tapas?
A.  In St. Louis, late afternoon is the sweet spot. Idol Wolf’s Pintxos Hour runs daily from 3 to 5 p.m. with olives at $6 instead of $12, and Aperi’s Wine’d Down Hour runs 4 to 5 p.m. daily. Tapas work at dinner too; they just cost more after 5.
### Q. What is the correct way to eat tapas?
A.  Order in small rounds, share everything, and keep a drink nearby. Start with two or three plates, eat them while they’re hot, then decide on the next round. Pluck skewered bites off the stick, and leave the sticks on your plate in case the bar counts them.
### Q. What is the most popular tapas dish?
A.  Patatas bravas, crisp potatoes under aioli, is about as close to universal as it gets. Idol Wolf lists patatas bravas with aioli at $12, Aperi lists papas bravas with Spanish aioli, and it’s a smart, low-cost first order anywhere.

## Macarons for Strangers: Ukrainian Food in St. Louis and What to Order First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ukrainian-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order-first
Blue and yellow macarons, boxed and handed across South City porches by a pastry chef who had outrun a war.
That box came with a story most St. Louisans have never heard. According to St. Louis Magazine’s report on Patisserie Svoi, the couple behind it packed up their car and drove out of Ukraine just hours before the Russian invasion. Ukrainian baker Taisiia Hrynchyshyn and her husband, Dmytro, arrived in St. Louis in 2022 with few resources. What reassured them was the Ukrainian flags they saw on houses in their new South City neighborhood, so Taisiia baked macarons in blue and yellow and they carried the cookies door to door, to every house flying a flag. A neighbor tipped off a TV station. That’s how a lot of the city first tasted her baking.
The name means something too. The magazine explains that the Ukrainian word “svoi” refers to a feeling of unity and connection with your own family and friends. Keep that word in your pocket. It explains the food better than any menu does.
The welcome ran both ways. “I love America because the people are so friendly,” Dmytro told the magazine, and while he and Taisiia’s mother, Hanna, were painting the bakery’s walls in lighter shades of cream and green, a steady stream of strangers on the sidewalk waved hello through the large picture windows. Wet paint inside, St. Louis waving through the glass.
You can taste it this week. Patisserie Svoi describes itself as a family-owned artisan bakery at 8 S Euclid Avenue in the Central West End, just steps from Forest Park. The bakery’s site posts its hours as 9 AM-7 PM on Monday, 7 AM-7 PM Tuesday through Thursday, 7 AM-8 PM on Friday and 10 AM-5 PM on Saturday and Sunday.
The bakery’s FAQ says walk-ins are always welcome and the display case is stocked fresh daily with a rotating selection, so the case changes. If your heart is set on syrniki or a loaf of the rye, message first. The FAQ lists WhatsApp at 314-800-9595. Send it the night before, ask what tomorrow’s case will hold, and walk in at 7 AM on a Tuesday, when the doors open.
If you have a friend who gave up gluten, send them this one: St. Louis Magazine says Hanna’s syrniki are made with rice flour, a high-protein, gluten-free breakfast fried fresh in a Ukrainian bakery on Euclid.
Most people walk into Ukrainian food expecting heavy, bland and brown, and they walk out talking about sour cream, garlic and dill. The first thing worth ordering is the soup you think you already know.
### What is the most famous Ukrainian dish?
Borshch. Ukraine’s own official site names it first among the country’s most famous traditional dishes and calls it a sour soup with a distinctive red color. It’s usually built from meat, beets, cabbage, carrots, onions, potatoes and tomatoes, then served with smetana (sour cream), pampushky (tiny garlic buns), garlic, onion and salo.
The soup is only half the bowl. The garlic bun gets torn and dragged through the broth. The raw onion and garlic are there for the people at the table who want more bite. The salo, salted pork fat eaten cold, sits on the side like a dare.
So when a friend asks what to order first, the answer is borshch, and the reason is not that it’s famous. It’s that it resets your expectations for everything else on the table.
### Where can you eat Ukrainian food in St. Louis right now?
Start with the parish. St. Mary’s Assumption Ukrainian Catholic Church sits at 11363 Oak Branch Dr. in south St. Louis County, and the Archdiocese lists its phone as (314) 303-2893. St. Louis Magazine reported that Rock Church and St. Mary’s Assumption Ukrainian Catholic Church sponsored a fundraiser for Ukraine. The event included homemade Ukrainian dishes and desserts, and a live band sang songs in Ukrainian. The Rev. Oleh Zatvarsky came to St. Louis from California, and St. Louis Public Radio reported that he moved with his family to St. Louis in August to become the first permanent priest at St. Mary’s Assumption Ukrainian Catholic Church in south St. Louis County in at least 20 years. A parish with its own priest is a parish with feast days, and feast days come with food.
And once a year, the whole world sets up in one park. The Festival of Nations is the International Institute of St. Louis’s annual multicultural festival in Tower Grove Park, with 80+ countries represented across more than 100 vendors. St. Louis Public Radio wrote that the parish’s new priest had his first interaction with the community at the Festival of Nations in August, and that he and his family enjoyed food and music from countries around the world, including Ukraine. Go hungry. Follow the smell of dill.
Back on Euclid, St. Louis Magazine’s opening report is where the Ukrainian part of the menu lives. It says the bakery would feature artisan breads such as the Ukrainian staple rye with caraway, baked by Taisiia’s mother, Hanna Burym, and that Hanna’s signature item is syrniki, made from her homemade farmer’s cheese combined with rice flour, egg yolks and vanilla, formed into discs and fried. Dmytro also promised the coffee menu would use the metric system. In his words: “Everything will be listed in kilograms, not pounds.”
### The beet soup on the table is sour on purpose
The beet soup in front of you is not the one you’re picturing. The picture most of us carry is a sweet, pink, cold soup out of a jar. Ukraine’s version can be served hot or cold, and the official guide says it can also be white or green depending on the ingredients. Same name, different bowl, and nobody at the table thinks that’s strange.
The sourness is the point, and it comes from history, not from a chile. Cold Ukrainian winters, the ukraine.ua guide explains, pushed cooks toward drying, curing, pickling, salting and smoking. That’s a pantry built to last until spring, and it tastes like it: tangy, salty, smoky, sharp. Which is also the real answer when someone asks whether Ukrainian food is spicy. It’s not hot in the chile sense. The bite comes from fermentation, raw garlic and onion, and the cold wallop of a pickle.
There’s a holiday bowl, too. On the Christmas Eve table, according to ukraine.ua, the borshch, as a rule, was made with prunes and mushrooms and fermented with beet kvass. Dark, earthy, a little sweet from the dried fruit, sour underneath. If you only ever eat one borshch in your life, that’s the one that surprises you most.
If you want to compare bowls, our Russian food guide walks through where borscht shows up on a St. Louis menu and settles the old argument about whose soup it is. This page stays on the Ukrainian side of the table.
### What should you order first?
Order in the order a Ukrainian day runs. Morning first.
Syrnyky are, according to ukraine.ua, typical food for breakfast in Ukraine, served with sour cream, jam, honey or condensed milk. A good one is crisp and golden on the outside and soft and faintly tangy inside, the cheese still warm enough to steam when you break it with a fork. If the Svoi case has them, that’s your first bite of Ukraine in St. Louis. If it doesn’t, you’ve learned why you message ahead.
Second, bread. Rye with caraway is the loaf you take home. Caraway smells like the inside of a deli counter and tastes faintly of anise. Tear it, don’t slice it, and if you’re making borshch at home this week, that’s the bread it wants.
Third, the cake you’ll be telling people about. The bakery’s honey cake listing describes it as lots of thin honey cakes soaked in a cream base of heavy whipping cream, sour cream and cream cheese. Taisiia’s blog says the bakery’s traditional Ukrainian medovik (honey cake) has been published on the Immigrant Women Chefs platform. Every layer goes soft and damp overnight, and the honey turns almost caramel. A fork goes through it without a fight.
There’s also the Napoleon, which the bakery calls buttery puff pastry and rich vanilla cream, a timeless Eastern European classic. The listing says it serves 10-14 and needs 5-7 days’ advance notice for custom orders. That’s a birthday cake that shatters when you cut it and leaves flakes on everyone’s shirt.
One rule before you order a whole cake: the FAQ asks for at least 48 hours’ notice on cakes and large orders, and the listings ask you to flag any allergies when you order. If you’re weighing two or three bakeries for a big celebration, treat it like hiring anyone else. Shortlist them, talk to each one, tell them what the day is and what you want it to taste like, and compare what each says they’ll actually deliver.
Shoulders creeping up by your ears again? Try ten slow minutes of tai chi.
### Why do varenyky matter so much?
Because they’re the dish your hands remember. Flour on the board, a circle of dough in your palm, a spoon of filling, then the pinch along the edge, over and over, until the tray is full of little half-moons. Ukraine’s official guide says varenyky are made of dough and different fillings, such as meat, potatoes, mushrooms, vegetables, fruits, cheese, or berries. Their fillings can be salty or sweet, lean or meaty.
That last line is the menu decoder. Potato varenyky with fried onion and a spoon of sour cream are dinner. Cherry or berry varenyky are dessert, and the juice runs purple onto the plate. If you’re asking what Ukrainian comfort food tastes like, it’s that plate: soft dough, hot filling, cold sour cream, the onions gone sweet and brown in butter.
They carry luck, too. On the Christmas table, ukraine.ua says, varenyky symbolize prosperity and well-being, and one custom is to stick a coin inside one dumpling. Whoever finds it is believed to be rich for a year. Chew carefully.
The surest plate of varenyky is the one you pinch yourself, though parish events and the festival are worth watching. The Polish cousin, pierogi, is easier to find, and our Polish food guide covers where. Make a batch with a friend once and you’ll understand why nobody ever makes just a dozen.
### Christmas Eve is twelve dishes and not one of them is meat
If you ever get invited to a Ukrainian Christmas Eve, say yes. Ukraine’s official guide to the Christmas dinner says there should be 12 fasting meals on the table, prepared without butter, milk, eggs, sour cream and meat. One explanation is the 12 apostles. The room smells like dill, mushrooms and fried onion, and dinner goes on for hours.
Here is the table:
Kutia, boiled wheat with honey, poppy seeds, nuts and dried fruit, the most important dish of the night
Holubtsi, cabbage rolls, here with rice and mushrooms
Varenyky, with the lucky coin
Lean borshch with prunes and mushrooms
Sichenyky, patties with peas
Fish, fried, baked or jellied
Deruny, potato pancakes with onion
Boiled potatoes with crushed garlic and oil
Stewed cabbage with mushrooms
Pancakes
Uzvar, a drink of dried pears, apples, plums and apricots
Bread
Kutia comes first, and the guide says Ukrainians believe the spirits of ancestors come to the dinner that evening. Uzvar tastes like a warm orchard in a cup. You don’t need a Ukrainian grandmother to taste this in St. Louis. Watch the parish around the holidays, and order a loaf of rye and a honey cake for your own table.

### Frequently asked questions about Ukrainian food
### Q. Is Ukrainian food spicy?
A.  Not in the chile-pepper sense. The bite comes from sourness and garlic. Cold winters, according to Ukraine’s official food guide, pushed cooks toward drying, curing, pickling, salting and smoking, and borshch is served with raw garlic, onion and little garlic buns called pampushky. Expect tang and punch, not burn.
### Q. What are the 12 dishes of Ukrainian Christmas?
A.  Ukraine’s official Christmas guide says there should be 12 fasting meals on the table, prepared without butter, milk, eggs, sour cream and meat. First, Ukrainians eat kutia, boiled wheat seasoned with honey, poppy seeds, nuts and dried fruits. The last, twelfth dish is bread. In between come cabbage rolls, varenyky, a lean borshch, potato pancakes and a warm drink of stewed dried fruit, all listed in the Christmas section above.
### Q. What are some traditional Ukrainian dishes?
A.  The ukraine.ua food guide names borshch, varenyky, holubtsi, Chicken Kyiv, banosh and syrnyky as the most famous, and says the list is not exhaustive. Add salo, uzvar and kutia and you have a full table.
### Q. What is the Ukraine’s national dish?
A.  Borshch. UNESCO inscribed the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking in 2022 on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. Ukraine’s official guide describes it as a sour red soup of meat, beets, cabbage, carrots, onions, potatoes and tomatoes, served with sour cream and garlic buns.
### Q. What is a typical Ukrainian breakfast?
A.  Syrnyky. Ukraine’s official food guide calls these fried curd cheese pancakes typical breakfast food, served with sour cream, jam, honey or condensed milk. In St. Louis, St. Louis Magazine reported that syrniki are the signature menu item of Hanna Burym, Taisiia’s mother, at Patisserie Svoi, and that the dish starts with Hanna’s homemade farmer’s cheese. Message ahead to make sure they’re in the case.
### Q. What is a popular Ukrainian snack?
A.  Salo, salted pork fat. Al Jazeera reports it is eaten raw, smoked, peppered, brine-fermented or fried, and mostly eaten cold. Pickled cucumbers are another favorite appetizer. Both taste like a Ukrainian winter pantry: salty, sharp and built to last.
### Q. What is Ukrainian comfort food?
A.  Varenyky with sour cream and fried onion, or a hot bowl of borshch with a garlic bun torn into it. Ukraine’s food guide says varenyky fillings can be salty or sweet, lean or meaty, so comfort can be dinner or dessert.

## Dad’s Shaking Toast, Kept: What a Wedding Videographer Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-wedding-videographer-costs-in-st-louis
Your dad’s voice goes on your name. Say the vows happened that morning under the Cathedral Basilica’s 41.5 million mosaic tesserae. Now it is the reception, and he stands at the head table, unfolds the paper he has rewritten for a month, clears his throat, and the room goes quiet enough to hear ice settle in the glasses. Whether that moment still exists in ten years comes down to one thing: was a camera rolling?
And at the Basilica, the camera may not be where you pictured it. The Cathedral’s own wedding guidelines say photographers and videographers are never allowed to enter the sanctuary, the balcony or the pulpit, and a professional without the special pass the Cathedral issues for your date and time will not be allowed to film.
Here is the trade. Tony Mellinger, a St. Louis photographer and filmmaker, puts eight hours of your day into the camera in one package, and the highlight film that comes back runs 3-5 minutes. JD Imagery, a St. Louis studio that offers four, six or eight hours, with posted prices from $1,200 to $2,000, puts that same 3-5 minute highlight film in every one of them. Four hours or eight, the film is the same 3-5 minutes. You are buying the hours, not the movie. You are paying for which hours of their day end up on a hard drive at all, and for the late nights an editor spends turning those hours into four minutes that will make your mother reach for a tissue at the kitchen table a year from now.
That changes how you read every quote. The question is not “how long is the film?” It is “will the camera still be rolling when Dad clears his throat?” If the coverage ended before the toasts, the honest answer is nothing. A photo will show his hand shaking. It will not keep his voice cracking on your name.
### How much should I expect to pay for a wedding videographer in St. Louis?
JD Imagery posts four-, six- and eight-hour wedding videography packages priced from $1,200 to $2,000, and Tony Mellinger, who shoots both photo and video, says most of his couples spend around $4,000. That money mostly buys hours on the day and the editing after it, not a longer film.
Want the number lower? Ask about a bundle. Tony Mellinger’s own page says to package both photo and video for a discount, and Complete Weddings + Events, which says it has been creating and capturing memories since 1984, puts “Bundle + Save!” at the top of its videography page. Before you sign two contracts, ask each studio on your list whether one crew can shoot both. And if the Basilica is your church, make one call tonight: the Cathedral says couples should meet with a priest at least six months before the wedding, and the rectory number is 314-373-8202.
Here is what the posted menus actually show. JD Imagery lists four-, six- and eight-hour tiers with posted prices of $1,200, $1,700 and $2,000, and every tier includes the 3-5 minute highlight film plus an unedited recording of the ceremony and an unedited recording of the speeches. So even the smallest tier keeps the vows and the toast; the bigger ones buy the hours on either side, the buttons going up the back of the dress and the last slow song. Tony Mellinger starts his video packages at $2,000. His full-day package puts two videographers on the day for eight hours, so one camera can stay on your face while the other finds his, and delivers a documentary-style ceremony video, a 3-5 minute highlight and the recorded reception speeches. His top package runs ten hours, long enough to still be rolling when the shoes come off on the dance floor, and stretches the highlight to 8-10 minutes.
Complete Weddings + Events, a third St. Louis company, shows “Request Pricing” on its packages page instead of a posted price. One videographer for four hours gets you a 2-4 minute highlight film plus your full vows and toasts with audio. Eight hours brings a 4-7 minute film, a short vertical reel for social media and the raw footage, uncut. Lay those three menus side by side on the coffee table and a pattern jumps out. Hours are the dial. Almost everything else hangs off them.
So when you build the budget, start from the clock, not from a number a cousin threw out at Thanksgiving. Write down the moment you want the camera to walk in, maybe while the curling iron is still hissing in the getting-ready room, and the moment you can live with it walking out. Then price that window. Tonight, send that window to the two or three St. Louis videographers on your shortlist, and in each interview ask one plain question: what will your camera catch inside it, and what time does it leave? Everything that follows on this page is about making that window smaller, smarter or easier to film.
### Where will the camera be allowed to stand?
Here is the part almost no price list mentions, and it matters most if you are marrying in a St. Louis church. At the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis in the Central West End, photographers and videographers are never allowed to enter the sanctuary, the balcony or the pulpit. Flashes and camera lights are not to be used during the ceremony, and videographers are asked to remain stationary while it happens. The Cathedral’s own wedding guidelines add one more line that surprises people: every wedding photographer and videographer is issued a special pass for the date and time, and a professional without one will not be allowed to film. So the first call to make today is not to a videographer: it is to the Cathedral’s Event Coordinator at 314-373-8208, and the guidelines ask that your videographer work directly with the wedding coordinator, who can point out the spots in the church best for filming. Even the room has a price there: the Cathedral asks a $2,000 donation from parishioners active for at least six months and a $3,000 minimum from everyone else before the date is confirmed.
Think about what that does to a quote. Your videographer cannot drift up the aisle for the ring close-up or climb to the balcony for the wide shot of the whole nave. Whatever angle the camera holds when the organ swells is the angle you get, so a second camera stops being a luxury and becomes the only way to see both of your faces during the vows. And this is a building worth seeing. By the Cathedral’s own count, its interior holds 41.5 million mosaic tesserae, the largest collection of mosaics in the world outside Russia. You want that ceiling glittering behind you, and you want it from a spot somebody planned on purpose, not one they got stuck with.
The same guidelines leave a narrow window for the posed shots. With permission, posed photographs may be taken for up to thirty minutes after the ceremony, in the All Saints Chapel only, plus the grounds outside if the weather cooperates. The calendar is tight on the front end too: weddings there run Friday evening, Saturday morning or until 1:30 pm on Saturday, with an hour and a half between ceremonies on days when more than one is booked. That is a lot of rules for one hour of your life, and every one of them shapes what your videographer can promise.
Your church or venue may be looser or stricter. Either way, ask for its photo and video rules in writing before you sign with anyone, and hand that page to every videographer you talk to. A couple coming into the city from Pevely or New Athens for the ceremony does not want to learn about a camera pass in the vestibule, with the processional already lining up and the flower girl tugging at her hem.
Off topic: cake tastings are overrated. Puerto Rican food in St. Louis is not.
### What do the extra hours actually buy?
Go back to the studio that puts the same 3-5 minute film in every package. Moving from four hours to eight does not add a single second to the highlight. What it buys is raw material. It buys the getting-ready hour: the zipper that will not catch, the nervous laugh, your grandmother pinning something borrowed inside your sleeve. It buys the last song of the night, when the dance floor is sticky, the uplights have gone purple and your college friends are shouting every word of a song they swore they had outgrown.
An editor can only cut from what exists. The ten-hour package from one St. Louis filmmaker adds recorded first dances and a 30-60 second social teaser. At the studio with one film for every tier, the extra hours do not make the movie longer. They make it fuller.
Coverage is also where the extras live. The studio with the same film in every tier sells a highlight reel for social media for $175 and a save-the-date video for another $175. At the company that says “Request Pricing,” the vertical social reel and the uncut raw footage are listed in its eight-hour package, not its four-hour one. If your reception is out in Okawville or Maeystown and the toasts land after dinner, the difference between those two tiers may be your best man’s speech.
The cheapest honest move is not cutting hours at random. It is arranging the day so the moments you care about sit inside fewer of them. Do a first look before the ceremony instead of after. Ask your DJ or planner to run the toasts right after dinner, while everyone is still seated and the room is quiet enough to hear a glass clink. Put the first dance and the parent dances back to back. A day built like that can fit nearly everything that matters into a shorter window, and the camera goes home before the bar line gets long.
### Why does a short film take weeks to edit?
Because someone has to watch all of it first. One national wedding film company describes this stage of the edit without any polish: “Someone watches everything. All of it.” It calls that the single largest block of time in the whole process, and the one couples never picture. Before that, two or three camera angles and the separate audio from lapel mics and the sound board have to be lined up to the frame, and on a full ceremony, the same company says, that is hours before a single creative decision is made.
That is the editor at a desk late at night, headphones on, scrubbing back a few seconds of footage to catch your nephew whispering under the organ, then doing it again. That is the part of the price you never see.
So how long does the editing itself take? A common rule of thumb, as one video post-production studio puts it, is one hour of editing per minute of finished video, and if there are a lot of effects and transitions, that number doubles at a minimum. A wedding highlight sits on top of all the watching and syncing above, which is why a short wedding highlight eats far more hours than the rule of thumb alone suggests.
Revisions add time too. The same national company does the math out loud: a four-week edit plus two three-week revision rounds is a ten-week delivery. If you already know the night you want to watch it for the first time, an anniversary dinner or a holiday at your parents’ house, count backward from that date and ask every videographer whether they can meet it.
### The four minutes nobody thinks to film
Photos keep faces. They cannot keep a voice. Ask anyone who has lost a parent since their wedding what they would give for thirty seconds of that parent laughing at the head table, and you will understand the real product here. It is not the drone shot or the slow-motion veil. It is sound: the vows you were too nervous to hear, your grandmother’s toast, the room going quiet and then roaring.
Is it worth hiring a videographer for a wedding? For the toasts alone, a lot of couples decide yes. One St. Louis studio puts an unedited ceremony recording and an unedited speech recording into every package it sells. Another local company puts video of your full vows and toasts with audio into its smallest package. That is the floor of the market, and it is also the part people are most glad to have years later, when the dress is in a box in the basement and the flowers are long gone.
One St. Louis filmmaker who was raised here writes that he loves it all, “from the Soulard cobblestone” on out, and that “filming the people that make St. Louis great is my passion.” That is the right instinct for the film you want: your city, your people, the sound of your own day. A highlight set to a licensed song is lovely. The raw speech file is what you will play for your kids.
### How do you choose between two good videographers?
A good budget for a wedding videographer is the price of the hours you actually need, filmed by someone whose past work makes your throat tighten. Start there. Watch three or four full films from each filmmaker, not just the trailers, with the sound up. If you catch yourself smiling at strangers’ toasts, that is your shortlist.
Then narrow it to two or three and talk to each one. Tell them what you want in plain words: the toasts, your grandmother, the moment your brother walks you down the aisle, the church rules you already have in writing. Let them tell you how they would cover it. Then compare what each one will actually deliver, side by side. Good questions for that conversation:
Who will be behind the camera on the day, and will we meet that person first?
How many cameras will run during the ceremony, and where will they stand under our venue’s rules?
How do you capture the officiant’s audio and the vows, and what is your backup if a mic fails?
What is delivered: highlight length, full ceremony, full speeches, raw footage?
When will it arrive, and how many revision rounds are included?
You do not need a line-by-line breakdown of their costs. You need to hear how they think about your day, and you need what they promise written into the contract. The right person usually makes the conversation feel easy, the way a good friend does at a crowded rehearsal dinner.
Your vows deserve a camera in the right spot, not the last open date on someone’s calendar. Start your shortlist with Videographers on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three whose films move you, and book the conversations this week.
If you’re the videographer, editor or one-camera crew filming St. Louis weddings, couples are already looking for you here. Engaged couples are comparing filmmakers right now, so list your business where they can watch your reel, and get more customers.

Plenty, as long as you protect the audio. The trims that hurt least:
Coverage, not quality. One St. Louis filmmaker offers a ceremony package of up to 2.5 hours with multiple cameras. If the vows are what you want, that is the cleanest cut.
The smallest full tier. The four-hour package at the studio quoted above still includes the highlight film and the unedited ceremony and speech recordings.
The extras. A $175 social reel and a $175 save-the-date are easy to drop, and easy to make yourself from the raw files later.
A camcorder kit. One national film company ships one or two 4K camcorders to your door starting at $729, your friends and family film the day, and its editors cut the footage into a 3-7 minute film delivered with all the raw footage.
What not to cut: the ceremony audio and the toasts. A cousin with a phone in the third pew will catch the kiss and miss every word before it, buried under a sneeze and a crinkling program. If money is tight, fewer hours with a professional on the vows beats a full day of shaky footage with no sound.

### Q. Is it worth hiring a videographer for a wedding?
A.  It is worth it when your venue rules, your timeline and your must-have moments line up with what the filmmaker can deliver. Ask how they will cover the vows under your church’s camera rules before you decide.
### Q. How many hours to edit a 2 minute video?
A.  A common rule of thumb is one hour of editing per minute of finished video, doubling at a minimum with heavy effects and transitions. A wedding highlight takes far longer, because someone first has to sync every camera and watch all the footage.
### Q. How much should a videographer charge per video?
A.  Wedding filmmakers price by package, not by clip. Add-on pieces are the closest thing to per-video pricing: one St. Louis studio charges $175 for a social media highlight reel and $175 for a save-the-date video.
### Q. Can a videographer film from the balcony at the Cathedral Basilica?
A.  No. Its guidelines say photographers and videographers are never allowed in the sanctuary, balcony or pulpit, must stay stationary during the ceremony and need a Cathedral-issued pass to film.
### Q. Do we need both a photographer and a videographer?
A.  They do different jobs: one keeps faces, the other keeps sound and motion. One St. Louis filmmaker who does both offers a discount when you package photo and video together, so ask about a bundle before you book two people.

## Paid by Invoice, Taxed Like Staff: Hiring a Virtual Assistant in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-virtual-assistant-for-a-st-louis-small-business
The envelope sits under the electric bill, thin and official. You slide a thumb under the flap at the kitchen table after the other job, the lamp catching the cracked corner of the laptop, and the first word you understand is payroll. Payroll? You don’t have payroll. You have one assistant, ten hours a week, who sends you an invoice.
That envelope hasn’t come. Here’s how it could.
The IRS says a remote worker is your employee “if you can control what will be done and how it will be done.” An invoice doesn’t decide it. Control does. And once the assistant is staff, the city has its own rule waiting: every employer with employees working in the City of St. Louis withholds the 1% earnings tax and owes a 0.5% payroll expense tax, filed every quarter on Forms W-10 and P-10.
Then the number. Late payroll taxes draw a penalty of 5% a month, up to 25%, plus 1% a month in interest until they’re paid.
You’re not careless. You’re up against a rulebook written for desks down the hall, and VA pitches that quote the hourly rate and stay quiet about which side of that rulebook you land on. So before the first payment, call the Collector of Revenue’s earnings tax department at (314) 622-4101. Say where your business is and where your assistant will sit, ask whether you’d owe the quarterly W-10/P-10 filing, and write the answer on the same pad as the hire date.
### How much does it cost to hire a virtual assistant in St. Louis?
The first quote lands in your inbox on a weeknight, and you squint at the hourly number the way you’d squint at a transmission estimate. Hold it up against what St. Louis already pays an in-house administrative assistant: a typical $22.21 an hour, with the middle half of workers earning $18.36 to $25.75. A contractor virtual assistant pays their own 15.3% self-employment tax, so expect quotes above that wage, while an assistant you hire as an employee costs the wage plus 7.65% in employer payroll tax.
Run it out on the back of the envelope. A $22.21 employee really costs you about $23.91 an hour once your 7.65% share of Social Security and Medicare goes on top, and that’s before you buy the laptop. A contractor quoting more than that is carrying their own taxes, their own computer and their own slow weeks. So the number to hold a quote against is never the bare $22.21 wage. It’s that wage plus 7.65%, plus everything you’d have to buy.
And the real price is never on the invoice anyway. It’s the hour you get back: the phone answered on the second ring while you’re up on the job, the quote out the same afternoon instead of three days later, the customer who didn’t give up and call somebody else. If that hour earns you more than the assistant costs, the math is already done.
### Does the City of St. Louis earnings tax follow your assistant home?
Sometimes. St. Louis collects a one percent earnings tax from residents of the city “regardless of the location of their employer,” and from people working in the city regardless of where they live. It isn’t small change to the city, either. The Collector of Revenue says the earnings tax makes up 36% of the city’s general revenue.
Say your business is out in the county and the assistant you like lives in a second-floor apartment inside the city limits, working from a desk by a window that rattles when the trucks go by. Hire her as a contractor and the city looks at her as a business. It requires businesses located in the City of St. Louis to pay the earnings tax of 1% of their earnings, and a one-person assistant business run from that apartment is one of them.
Hire her as an employee and it can become your problem. The city’s employer withholding page says every employer with employees working in the City of St. Louis has to withhold the 1% earnings tax, and employers also owe a 0.5% payroll expense tax on wages earned in the city. Both get filed together every quarter on Forms W-10 and P-10, due January 31, April 30, July 31 and October 31. Four squares on the kitchen calendar, circled in pen, every year. Miss one and the city adds a penalty of 5% a month to late payroll taxes, up to 25%, plus 1% a month in interest until they’re paid.
Whether a remote employee’s desk in a city apartment makes you a city employer is exactly the kind of question to ask before payroll starts, not after the first notice. Call the Collector of Revenue’s earnings tax department at (314) 622-4101, give them the facts, and write down what they tell you.
If your assistant lives across the river in Illinois and works for your shop inside the city, the same question runs the other way: the city taxes work done in the city, so ask where the work actually happens. The rule of thumb is simple. Know where your assistant sits, and know whether they’re your employee, before the first paycheck.
### Why does the same assistant cost two different prices?
Because there are two ways to pay a person, and each one moves the tax bill to a different side of the table.
Hire the assistant as an employee and you run payroll. You pay the wage, and on top of it you owe your half of Social Security and Medicare: 6.2% for the employer for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare, according to the IRS. That’s the 7.65%. You also withhold the employee’s matching half out of their check and send it in. Most assistants worth hiring clear that easily, but it’s the line you can never go under.
Hire the assistant as an independent contractor and the tax moves to them. They pay the full self-employment tax rate of 15.3%, which the IRS breaks into 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Both halves, the part an employer would have covered and the part a worker always covers. They also buy their own laptop, pay for their own software, cover their own health insurance and eat their own slow months.
So when a contractor quotes you a rate well above $22.21, they’re not padding it. They’re paying for everything an employer would normally carry. Compare a contractor’s hourly rate to an employee’s wage and the contractor always looks expensive. Compare it to the wage plus payroll tax, plus your time running payroll, plus the equipment, plus the hours you pay for when there isn’t enough work to fill them, and the gap shrinks fast.
That’s why most small shops start with a contractor. You buy ten hours a week, you get an invoice, you pay it. The catch is that calling someone a contractor doesn’t make them one.
Back to the local wage for a second. The bottom tenth of St. Louis administrative assistants earns $15.42 an hour or less.
That spread is your map. An assistant who sorts email and books appointments sits near the bottom of it. One who talks to your customers, keeps your quotes moving and knows your pricing well enough to answer a question on a Saturday sits near the top, and is worth it. The wage tells you the floor of the market you’re shopping in. It does not tell you what you’ll pay, because the same person can cost you two different prices depending on one decision you make before day one.

### The IRS rule that turns a remote assistant into an employee
The old assumption says a virtual assistant is a contractor because they work from home. The IRS disagrees: a person working remotely is your employee under the common-law rules “if you can control what will be done and how it will be done. This is so even if the worker can choose to work remotely.”
Read that twice. The laptop in someone else’s spare bedroom doesn’t settle anything. Control does.
The IRS sorts the evidence into three buckets. Behavioral: do you control what the worker does and how they do the job? Financial: do you control the business side, like how they’re paid, whether expenses are reimbursed and who provides the tools? And the type of relationship: is there a written contract, are there employee-type benefits, will it go on, and is the work a key part of your business? No single answer decides it. The IRS says to look at the whole relationship and document how you reached your call.
Here’s how it looks in a real week. You text your assistant at 7:15 a.m. with the exact order to answer emails in, the hours she has to be online and the script she has to read on calls. You bought her laptop. She works only for you, with no end date. That’s starting to look like an employee, whatever the paperwork says.
Now flip it. You send a list of outcomes, the invoices out by Friday and every lead answered within a day. She picks her own hours, uses her own computer and software, sends you an invoice, and has three other clients. That looks like a business serving your business.
If you honestly can’t tell, Form SS-8 asks the IRS to decide, though it may take at least six months. Most owners never need it. Shape the arrangement around outcomes from the start and the question mostly answers itself.

### How do you choose a virtual assistant without getting burned?
A lot of owners have been burned before by someone who promised to take work off their plate and handed back more of it. Pitches that promise help for pennies and never mention who handles the taxes are part of the problem. You don’t fix that with a longer contract. You fix it with a better interview.
Shortlist two or three assistants. Interview each one, on video if you can, so you can hear how they talk when they’re not reading an email. Tell them plainly what you want: the hours a week, the tasks from your sticky-note list, the tools you already use and what “done” looks like on a Friday. Then compare what each one says they’ll deliver and how they’ll bill it, hourly, a monthly retainer or a block of prepaid hours.
Ask a few questions that quietly answer the contractor question at the same time. Do you work with other clients? Do you use your own computer and software? Will you send me an invoice? Do you set your own hours? Yes on those points toward a business serving your business, which is what you want if you’re paying by invoice.
Start small. Two weeks, a short list of tasks, a check-in on Friday. You’ll know by the second Friday whether the inbox feels lighter or you’re just managing one more person.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a virtual assistant worth it?
A.  It’s worth it when the hours you get back earn more than the hours you pay for. If an assistant clears your invoices, answers leads within a day and keeps your St Louis Near Me Directory, Google and Facebook listings current, those hours usually pay for themselves in collected money and customers you would have missed. Start with a short trial and a short task list so you can measure it.
### Q. What are the duties of a virtual assistant?
A.  Whatever repeats and has a clear finish line: email and voicemail, scheduling, invoicing and payment reminders, collecting details for quote requests, data entry, and updating your listings and social posts. Keep pricing decisions, hard customer conversations and anything you sign for yourself.
### Q. Is it legal to hire a virtual assistant?
A.  The legal question is how you classify them. The IRS says a remote worker is your employee if you control what will be done and how it will be done, even if they choose to work remotely. Treat a true contractor as a contractor, run payroll for an employee, and if you can’t tell, Form SS-8 asks the IRS to decide.
### Q. How does a virtual assistant get paid?
A.  A contractor sends you an invoice, usually hourly, as a monthly retainer or as a prepaid block of hours, and you collect a W-9 so you can report the payments on Form 1099-NEC, which the IRS uses for nonemployee compensation. If the assistant is a foreign person, the IRS has them give the payer Form W-8 BEN instead. An employee gets a regular paycheck with taxes withheld.
### Q. What is a good hourly rate for a virtual assistant?
A.  Anchor it to the local wage. St. Louis administrative assistants earn a typical $22.21 an hour, with the middle half between $18.36 and $25.75. A contractor who pays their own 15.3% self-employment tax and their own equipment will reasonably quote above that. Pay for skill: someone who talks to your customers is worth more than someone sorting email.
### Q. Is there a free virtual assistant?
A.  Not a human one. AI chat tools can draft emails and summaries, but someone still has to check them and press send. What does keep working while you sleep is a listing that answers for you. A current St Louis Near Me Directory listing, with your hours, photos of finished work and the questions customers ask, helps you get more customers on the nights nobody is answering email.

### Is a makeup trial worth $100 to $250?

Here’s a Missouri rule that saves trial time. Under section 329.035 of the state’s cosmetology statute, a person working a retail cosmetics counter can help you try on product without a cosmetology license, but may not accept any remuneration from you for it, and can’t make that help conditional on a sale. The same section says there shall be no skin-to-skin contact between the salesperson and the customer, so the work is done with single-use applicators.
That makes a cosmetics counter the place to settle your foundation shade before you pay for a trial. Walk in with a bare face. Feel the cool swipe of a disposable wand along your jawline, two or three shades side by side. Then step outside, under real daylight, and look again. Snap a photo, write the shade names in your phone, and bring them to your trial. Your artist will still match you properly, but your paid trial time goes to the look, not to hunting for a color.
A few habits make the trial pay for itself. Wear a top with a neckline close to your dress. Bring your counter shade notes and two or three photos of looks you love, plus one you hate. ### Who is legally allowed to charge for painting your face in Missouri?
Section 329.030 makes it unlawful for anyone in the state to engage in the occupation of cosmetology without a license. And section 329.010 defines that occupation to include, for compensation, beautifying work on the face using cosmetic preparations, lotions or creams.
Read plainly, a stranger who charges you to do your face is working inside that definition. There’s one carve-out worth knowing: section 329.032 says the chapter doesn’t apply to hairdressing, manicuring or facial treatments given in the home to family or friends when no charge is made. An aunt doing your face for free at the kitchen table is the kind of thing that carve-out describes. A paid artist is a different conversation.
We’re a directory, not lawyers, and we couldn’t find a Missouri ruling that settles exactly how the definition applies to every kind of makeup job, from a film set to a prom. So run the lookup, and let the state’s own record settle it.

## Your Right Thumb, Please: Where to Buy and Sell Music DVDs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-and-sell-music-dvds-in-st-louis
The cases clack against each other as you set the box on the glass, and the clerk asks for your ID, then slides a form over for your right thumb. Your fingers still ache where the cardboard bit into the joints on the walk in from the car, and somewhere in the stack is the one with the cracked hinge you kept meaning to replace. You figured this would be the most anonymous sale in town: a few dollars, no names, out the door. Now your license is lying on the glass, and you’re pressing your thumb onto a form you didn’t know existed.
Inside St. Louis city limits, the City’s secondhand-dealer ordinance says no dealer shall “purchase any article or property” without a photograph of the person selling it, attached to a transaction form. A used concert DVD fits that the same as a used lamp. The transaction form asks for your legal name, date of birth, a copy of your driver’s license and the right thumbprint of the seller. The dealer keeps the photo and the form for one year, and it has to post a notice in a prominent place telling customers it’s required to photograph and fingerprint every person selling to it. Look for that sign. The safe move costs nothing: put your license in your pocket before you lift the box.
There’s a quiet exception in the same section. The photo-and-thumbprint requirement doesn’t apply to a purchase that happens at an auction or in the private house or office of the person selling. If the buyer comes to you, that part of the form stays blank. That matters most when your music DVDs sit next to a wall of LPs, because the record buyers are the ones who make house calls. Dead Wax Records on Cherokee Street says on its own buy page that it “will travel any distance for the right collection.”
The paperwork only matters if the box is worth carrying, so sit down on the floor beside it and pop one case open. The hinge creaks, the booklet is still tucked under the clips, and the disc lets go of the spindle with a small click. Slide it into the tray and there’s a second sound right behind the whir: a crowd, thousands of people standing up at the same second. That’s what you’re really holding.
The disc nobody wants is the one everybody bought, and the disc everybody wants is the one nobody bought. Standard DVDs of mainstream movies are worth $1-$3 at best, because millions of copies were printed. Out-of-print titles can sell for $20, $50, or occasionally over $100. Same plastic case, same shelf. Your thumb can’t feel the difference. A collector can.
You can price your own stack tonight, before you load a single box. Turn each case over and find the barcode. Search that exact edition on an online auction site and filter by sold items, which shows what people actually paid, not what sellers wish they’d get. Anything that comes back above $15-$20 gets a closer look; the rest is a lot sale or a donation. Then make one call: Vintage Vinyl on Delmar, open every day of the week, buys used CDs and DVDs, so read your short list to (314) 721-4096 and ask what it’s paying.
### Where can I find live concert DVDs for sale in St. Louis?
Live concert DVDs in St. Louis turn up mostly secondhand: at the Record Exchange on Hampton, which carries CDs and movies beside its vinyl, at Vintage Vinyl on Delmar, which sells DVDs and Blu-rays, and in pawn shops, thrift stores and estate sales. Best Buy said it would stop selling discs, so the hunt moved to used bins.
Start on Hampton at the Record Exchange, and call 314-832-2249 before you drive over. The collection lives in an old library building in south St. Louis at 5320 Hampton Ave., on the corner of Hampton and Eichelberger. A building made for whispering now holds bins you flip with a dry, papery slap. When you call, ask what’s in the music DVD section this week, because stock in a used shop turns over one trade-in at a time. The Record Exchange was founded in 1977 by Jean Haffner, there’s over 10,000 square feet of music and memorabilia inside, and the shop describes itself as a place to buy, sell and trade, with CDs and movies alongside the vinyl.
Then Delmar. Vintage Vinyl at 6610 Delmar sells DVDs and Blu-rays next to its records, and its paper fliers section just inside the front door tells you which local band is playing where before you’ve touched a single crate.
Cherokee Street is the stop people skip, and it shouldn’t be. Dead Wax Records is a vinyl shop first, but read its buy page before you haul anything to a donation bin. That’s the line worth repeating to whoever is helping you clean out the basement: pull the VHS tapes and the cassettes out of the giveaway box first. VHS movies and cassette tapes are on the Cherokee Street shop’s own list of what it’s interested in buying.
Beyond the shops, the hunt is a route, not a store. The glass counter at a pawn shop, where a box set might be priced by someone who has never heard of the band. A thrift rack in South City the week after a basement cleanout. A laundry basket of discs by the garage door at an estate sale. Bring a phone with a full battery, because you’ll want to look up what you’re holding before you pay for it.
Before you buy anything, borrow it. A St. Louis Public Library card lets you check out up to 100 items at a time, and cardholders in good standing can request DVDs and CDs from other library systems, which usually takes two to three weeks. Watch the show first, volume up, lights off. If you still want to own it after the encore, go hunting. You’ll know exactly which edition you want, and you won’t pay collector money for a concert you only liked once.
Different errand, same city: what’s actually on a St. Louis kosher grocery shelf?
### Why would anyone still buy a concert on a disc?
Because the shows you love most are the ones that slip away. On October 16, 1986, Chuck Berry played his 60th birthday concerts at the Fox Theatre in his native St. Louis, with Eric Clapton and Etta James on the bill. Taylor Hackford directed Hail! Hail! Rock ’n’ Roll, the 1987 film about those nights, and it wasn’t released on Blu-ray for the first time until 2019. A whole theater stood up for a hometown man, and for years the best way to own it was to find someone else’s copy.
That’s the case for music on disc in one story. Streaming libraries change month to month, and a show you watched last spring can be gone by fall with no notice. If the disc is on your shelf, nobody can take it back. You can slide it in on a gray Sunday in February and hear the room breathe before the first chord.
It’s also why the market isn’t dead. Americans spent $870 million on DVDs, Blu-rays and 4K discs in 2025, according to the annual report from the Digital Entertainment Group. That was down 9.3% from the year before, which sounds bad until you see that disc sales fell 23.4% from 2023 to 2024. The slide is slowing. The buyers who are left are the ones who care, and people who care pay for the right edition.

### How much longer will a DVD on your shelf keep playing?
Decades, probably, if it lives somewhere dry: the disc-care guide a NIST staff member wrote for librarians puts expectations for pressed CDs and DVDs, audio and video included, anywhere from 20 to 100 years, while admitting few if any independent labs have published life tests for them. What ends a pressed disc is moisture and oxygen reaching its aluminum layer, until the normally shiny metal turns oxide-dull, the color of a typical aluminum ladder, and high humidity plus heat speeds that up. So keep the concert discs upright in their cases somewhere dry and cool, not in a damp basement or a hot garage, because the same guide warns the plastic can flex if stored a long time out of vertical.
### What is your old stack actually worth?
Tip the stack over on the rug and the cases slide apart with a plastic rattle. Here’s the blunt answer to whether old DVDs are worth selling: most movies aren’t, and a surprising number of music DVDs are. The blockbuster everybody bought is sitting in millions of households, so the used market is flooded with it. A live set from a band with a loyal following, pressed once and never reissued, is a different animal. Those are the discs collectors chase, and they’re often hiding in the same box as the throwaways.
So sort before you sell. Spread the stack out on the living room rug and make three piles. Pile one: big-studio movies and anything you could still buy new. Pile two: concert DVDs, music documentaries and box sets. Pile three: anything imported, out of print, signed or still sealed in its plastic. Pile one is usually donation material. Piles two and three are where your money is. And if a fourth pile of VHS tapes and cassettes shows up from the back of the closet, that one goes to the phone, not the curb.
To find out how much a DVD is worth, do what dealers do. Look up the exact edition by the barcode on the back, then look at what copies have actually sold for, not what sellers are asking. Asking prices are wishes. Sold prices are the market. Check condition while you’re at it: tilt the disc under a lamp and look for the hairline scratches that catch the light, then open the case and make sure the booklet and any posters are still inside. For a collectible set, the paper bits matter more than people expect.
### Your license, your photo, your right thumb
Walk in ready and the whole sale takes minutes. Under the City ordinance, the dealer’s transaction form covers the date and place of the sale, your legal name, date of birth and city of residence, a copy of your driver’s license (or a military ID, passport or state ID if you don’t have one), the amount paid, a photo of you, your phone number, the employee who handled it and your right thumbprint. If the right one can’t be taken, the left one gets used and the form says why. None of that is a sign the shop thinks you stole anything. It’s the same form for everybody.
Bringing the old DVD player along? Check the bottom of it first. The ordinance says no secondhand dealer shall purchase a DVD player, record player or game console, among a long list of items made with a serial number, unless the manufacturer’s serial number is plainly visible on it. A sticker that peeled off in the cabinet years ago can turn a sale into a carry-it-back-to-the-car moment.
Here’s what goes in the car before you leave:
Your driver’s license, or a passport or state ID.
The discs, cased and sorted, rare ones on top and movies at the bottom.
A photo of the spines on your phone, so you can text it to a second shop if the first one passes.
Your written list of the sold prices you looked up for the good pile.
Any player you plan to sell, with its serial number label still on it.
Then shortlist two or three buyers and talk to each one the way you’d talk to anyone you’re handing something you care about. Tell them what you have: roughly how many discs, how many are concert titles, which ones are imports or sealed. Ask how they price, whether they offer more in store credit than in cash, whether they make one offer on the whole lot or pick through it, and what happens to the ones they pass on. Then compare what each will actually do for you. One might pay well for five rare sets and nothing else; another takes everything, and you walk out with an empty box. Choose the one that fits what you want.
Pawn shops are a different deal from a straight sale, because you can borrow against an item instead of selling it. If that’s on your mind, read how pawn shops work in St. Louis before you walk in, so you know which question to ask at the counter.
Got a box by the door and a license in your pocket? Find the shops that buy and sell in Music & DVDs on St Louis Near Me Directory and call two or three to ask what they’re buying this week.
If you’re the record shop or the used-media counter that does the buying, say what you take in plain words. The sellers reading this are sorting piles tonight, and a listing that names your buy hours and formats helps you get more customers: list your business where they’re already looking.
### Is Blu-ray dying, or just getting picky?
Hold a Blu-ray beside a DVD and they feel like twins in your palm, the same cool plastic edge under your thumb. Blu-ray isn’t being phased out as a format for movies and concerts, but it’s shrinking and getting choosier. The headline that scared people was Sony announcing it would end production of all models of Blu-ray Disc media as of February 2025. That was consumer-grade recordable discs, the blank kind people burned at home, not the concert you buy in a case. Meanwhile 4K UHD Blu-ray sales rose 12% even as DVD and regular Blu-ray kept sliding. The people still buying discs are buying the best-looking, best-sounding version they can get.
If you’re thinking about a player, here’s the part that matters: all Blu-ray Disc players can play DVDs. A 4K UHD player goes one step further and plays standard Blu-rays, DVDs and CDs too. So if your old DVD player has started skipping, the tray grinding before it gives up, a Blu-ray player replaces it without stranding a single disc on your shelf.
### The region-code trap that sinks imported concert discs
The worst sound in this hobby is no sound at all: the tray closes, the player thinks, and the crowd never comes. Concert DVDs travel. Plenty of the best live releases were pressed in the UK, Europe or Japan, and they turn up in St. Louis used bins mixed in with domestic copies. Here’s the catch: a standard DVD player sold in the United States is normally set for Region 1 discs, and a Region 2 DVD from the United Kingdom generally won’t play unless the player supports that region.
Flip the case over before you pay. The region mark usually sits on the back near the running time, often as a number inside a small globe. That import isn’t junk. It’s a disc for a different player, and for the right collector with a region-free machine it can be the prize of the bin. If you’re selling one, say the region plainly to the shop. One shortcut collectors love: Ultra HD Blu-ray discs are region-free, so when the same show comes in three versions, the 4K one is the safest import to bring home.
### Where the leftovers go
The box is lighter now, and pile one is still sitting on the rug. It still has a home. The Greater St. Louis Book Fair has been selling books since 1950 to support literacy and local nonprofits, and its donation list includes records, CDs and DVDs alongside books and comics; check its site for the next sale dates. It turns away moldy, dirty or damaged items, so give the cases a once-over with a dry cloth first. There’s a small satisfaction in setting that box down and knowing a college kid might find their first concert film in it.
And keep a short shelf for yourself. Pull the two or three discs tied to a night you actually remember before the sorting starts. Some boxes are for selling. Some are for the gray Sunday in February.
