### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need ID to sell used discs in St. Louis?
A.  Plan on it. The City’s secondhand-dealer ordinance requires a dealer to photograph the seller and complete a transaction form with a copy of the seller’s driver’s license and right thumbprint, kept for one year. The photo and thumbprint rule doesn’t apply when the purchase happens at an auction or in the seller’s own house or office.
### Q. Do places still sell DVDs?
A.  Yes, though fewer than before. Best Buy stopped selling DVDs and Blu-rays at its more than 900 stores, so in St. Louis most disc buying has moved to used record and media shops, pawn shops, thrift stores, estate sales and charity sales. Americans still spent $870 million on DVD, Blu-ray and 4K discs in 2025.
### Q. Are old DVDs worth selling?
A.  Some are. Mass-market movies rarely bring much because so many copies exist. Concert DVDs, music documentaries, out-of-print box sets, imports and sealed copies are the ones worth pricing one by one. Sort the stack first, check sold prices on the good pile, and donate the rest.
### Q. Is it worth selling DVDs for cash?
A.  For a rare concert set or a stack of out-of-print titles, usually yes. For common movies, the cash is often a dollar or two a disc. Ask each shop whether it pays more in store credit than in cash, and if you’re selling to a dealer inside the city, bring your driver’s license, since the ordinance requires a copy on the transaction form.
### Q. Is there a market for old CDs and DVDs?
A.  Yes. US buyers still bought 29.5 million CDs in 2025, according to RIAA figures, even as vinyl outsold them, and disc video spending reached $870 million. The demand leans toward collectible, out-of-print and live titles rather than common releases.
### Q. How do I find out how much a DVD is worth?
A.  Look up the exact edition by its barcode, then check what copies have actually sold for rather than what sellers are asking. Condition matters: scratches, a cracked case or a missing booklet all lower the price. For a rare concert set, ask two or three local shops what they would offer before you decide.
### Q. Is Blu-ray being phased out?
A.  Not as a format for movies and concerts. Sony stopped making blank recordable Blu-ray discs in February 2025, but that was home-recording media. 4K UHD Blu-ray sales grew 12% in 2025, so the format is shrinking toward collectors who want the best picture and sound.
### Q. Can regular DVDs be played on a Blu-ray DVD player?
A.  Yes. All Blu-ray Disc players can play DVDs, and 4K UHD players handle standard Blu-rays, DVDs and CDs too. The catch is region: a standard US DVD player is normally set for Region 1 DVDs, so a Region 2 DVD from the United Kingdom generally won’t play unless the player supports that region.
### Q. Is it worth buying a Blu-ray player?
A.  If you own more than a shelf of discs or care how a live show sounds, yes, because all Blu-ray Disc players can play DVDs, so nothing on your shelf gets stranded. If you watch a handful of DVDs once a year, your old player is probably enough.

## Hire a Personal Chef in St. Louis and You May Become an Employer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-personal-chef-costs-in-st-louis
The glass is cold against your fingers, and the person who filled it may have just made you somebody’s employer. You came home at 6:15 on a Tuesday after crawling up Kingshighway, still in the clothes that smell like the office, opened the fridge, and there they are: stacked glass boxes, lids snapped down, a strip of tape on each one with a date in marker. The kitchen smells like somebody roasted garlic in it hours ago. The counters are wiped. The sink is empty. Dinner is already made, and somebody you pay made it.
Here is the catch nobody mentions at the first tasting, with the kitchen warm and the chef plating a sample of short ribs. Pay a household worker $1,000 in cash wages in a calendar quarter, and Missouri’s Division of Employment Security says you become liable for Missouri unemployment tax. The IRS lists cooks among household workers. Hire a chef who cooks only for you, your way, every week, and you can be past that line before the season changes.
That fridge is real, and in St. Louis it has published prices. They do not agree with each other, which is the useful part. MyChef STL estimates a family of four’s week at around $300 with the groceries included. The Sage charges $325 for four meals of four servings each, and its groceries are extra. They are not the same scope: one is a week of meals with the shopping paid, the other is four entrées with two sides before anyone buys an onion. Even so, the lower number is the one that includes the food.
Not every chef makes you an employer. It turns on whether the chef works for you or runs their own business, and the IRS test in Publication 926 comes down to control: if only the worker can control how the work is done, the worker isn’t your employee but is self-employed. Cross that line and you have 30 days to tell the Division; its employer line is 573-751-1995. If your kitchen sits inside the city limits, there is one more line on top: the city’s Earnings Tax Department says every employer who has employees working in the City of St. Louis is required to withhold St. Louis City earnings tax, a 1% tax imposed on the wages of employees living or working in the City of St. Louis.
So before you call anyone, do one thing tonight. Grab an envelope and a pen, sit where you eat, and write down how many dinners, how many plates and how many sides your family really goes through in a week. Then write one more line under it: will this chef run their own business and cook for other families too, or will they cook only for us? Every number on this page plugs into that envelope, and the last line decides whether a tax form does.
### How much is a personal chef per hour in St. Louis?
St. Louis personal chefs who post their rates charge about $55 an hour for weekly meal prep, plus groceries. MyChef STL says “$55 an hour” gets you “a personal chef who spends around four to five hours weekly crafting your meals”; multiply it out and the labor alone runs about $220 to $275 a week before the food.
The second posted rate is almost the same number. Friend That Cooks’ St. Louis page charges $55.69 an hour with a three-hour minimum, and you hand over the grocery money separately. Its own estimate for a week of meals for a family of four is $215 to $275, plus groceries. Two services, two websites, nearly the same hourly rate. That is about as close to a going rate as this trade gets, and for that money the kitchen should smell like dinner when the chef leaves and look like nobody was there.
The grocery money is the other half, and in St. Louis it pays to ask which day your chef shops. Soulard Farmers Market, which traces its roots to 1779, is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday, but the hours the city posts show only 10% of vendors set up on Wednesday and Thursday, 35% on Friday and 100% on Saturday. A chef who shops on a Wednesday walks past mostly empty stalls and takes what the few open sellers have. A chef who shops on Saturday has every vendor in the market to compare before your groceries land on the bill, so ask for a Saturday shop and a receipt with each week’s groceries. Then open the fridge on Tuesday and read the tape on the lids against that receipt.
### Missouri’s $1,000 line, and the day your kitchen becomes a workplace
April, the dining room table, your thumb aching from scrolling a year of phone payments, while you add up what you paid a cook you thought of as help. This is the cost that shows up on no rate card, and the one that can sting the most.
The Division of Employment Security spells it out for employers of domestic or household workers: liability starts when you pay $1,000 in cash wages in a calendar quarter. In a brick two-family in Tower Grove South, that line gets crossed without a sound: week five, the chef is scraping the roasting pan, steam is fogging the back window over the alley, and you tap $220 into a payment app for four hours at $55, which puts the quarter at $1,100. From that moment you have 30 days to tell the Division: call its employer line, 573-751-1995, or use the Online Business Registration portal, UInteract or an Unemployment Tax Registration form. And it doesn’t end with the quarter: you are liable for all employment during the entire year in which liability was incurred, and for following years until it is terminated.
All of it hangs on one question to settle before the first cook day: is the chef running a business, or working for you?
Start with the title, because it settles nothing. A personal chef is typically a self-employed culinary professional who serves select clients on a rotating or scheduled basis. A private chef works exclusively for one client or household, usually as a full-time salaried position. People swap the two words all the time. The tax test ignores both. In its Household Employer’s Tax Guide, the IRS says the worker is your employee if you can control not only what work is done, but how it is done, and it doesn’t matter whether the work is full time or part time. The same guide lists cooks right alongside nannies, housekeepers and drivers as workers who do household work.
The same guide draws the other side plainly: a self-employed worker usually provides their own tools and offers services to the general public in an independent business. So the chef who rolls in with a bin of pans, cooks for other families on other days and bills you as a company is running a business. The chef who cooks only in your kitchen, on your schedule, with your skillet, starts to look like your employee. A weekly meal-prep service that bills you as a company sits on the business side. A neighbor’s friend you pay by phone app every Friday to cook only for you may not.
The federal lines stack on top. The IRS says that if you pay cash wages of $3,000 or more in a year to any one household employee, a threshold the IRS adjusts each year, you withhold and pay Social Security and Medicare taxes, and each side pays 7.65% of wages. Pay $1,000 or more in cash wages to household employees in any calendar quarter and federal unemployment tax applies too. You give the chef copies of Form W-2 by February 1, and you file Schedule H with your own federal return by April 15.
You don’t need to become a tax expert to dodge that April night. You need to ask one question before you hire anyone who will cook only for you: do you work for other clients, and do you invoice me as a business? If the answer is no, sit down with a tax preparer before the first payday, not in the spring with a shoebox on the table.
### How much is a private chef once a week, by the chefs’ own price lists?
None of these posted prices is a quote for your house, and any of them can change, so treat the table as the honest range and confirm with the chef before you book.
Read the last column twice. MyChef STL says a family of four might expect to spend around $300 total for the week, including groceries, and its FAQ puts the same family at around $300 to $350 total. The Sage lists $325 for four meals of four servings, and that price does not include groceries. The package is not worse; it is built differently. Each meal is an entree with two side dishes, the chef brings all of their own cooking equipment, and the price list includes complete kitchen cleanup. You are buying a fixed number you can plan around, and paying for groceries on top.
Packages grow at the edges, and the edges are written down. The Sage charges an additional $5 per serving if you want more than two sides. Disposable containers are an extra charge on every cooking day; glass is a one-time fee, usually $75 to $150. Glass is the one you want. It doesn’t stain orange from chili, it goes from fridge to oven, and the stack of it on the shelf is the whole picture you were paying for.
Hourly services have their own edges. MyChef STL charges a $50 holding fee for taking a week off and a travel charge for clients outside its normal service area. That $50 is the one families forget in July, when everyone is at the lake and the fridge is empty anyway. Ask every chef the same question: what does it cost me to skip a week?
The minimum matters more than the rate if your household is small. For two people who want three dinners, three hours may be more time than the food needs, and you pay for all of it anyway. Ask how long a week like yours usually runs, and listen for a number, not a shrug.
What fills the hour? Not just a flame under a pan. You are paying for the thinking that happened before the doorbell rang: the menu you approved, the allergy list, the shopping done while you sat in a meeting, the labels, and the sink left empty.
### Why does the day your chef cooks change your grocery bill?
The Sage buys groceries on the scheduled cook day for reimbursement only, which is the clean way to do it: you pay what the receipt says. Ask every chef the same plain question, at cost or with a markup, and will I see the receipts? A chef who answers without blinking has nothing to hide in the bag.
Put a Wednesday cook day against that. Your chef walks under the 1929 hall and finds a tenth of the stalls, the aisles half empty, the echo louder than the voices. Come back Saturday morning and it is a different building: shoulder to shoulder, onions and cut herbs, vendors calling prices over each other. Same market, different week of dinners. Ask where a chef shops and which day. The answer tells you how they think about your money when you’re not watching.
Once you have employees, a claim notice can land in your mailbox too, so here is how the Missouri unemployment protest period works for employers.
One small line rides the receipt too. Missouri taxes food at a reduced state rate of 1.225%, down from 4.225%. It won’t sink you on one grocery run. It is one more reason the receipt never quite matches the number in your head, and why a weekly budget should leave a little air in it.
Ask the business question first, and the fridge full of dinners never turns into a tax form. Shortlist two or three local chefs on Personal Chefs on St Louis Near Me Directory, talk to each one, and bring your written week with you.
If you’re the personal chef with a knife roll and a cooler in the trunk, this one is for you. Families pricing a week of dinners are already reading pages like this, so list your business where they look and get more customers from it.
### Can your household actually afford a personal chef?
Most families asking whether they can afford a personal chef compare the chef to zero. Nobody’s food costs zero. The fair comparison is the chef against what already leaves your account every week.
So try this tonight. Open your banking app and scroll back four weeks. Count the delivery orders, the fees, the tips, the drive-through on Gravois on the way home from practice, the Friday fish fry at the parish hall because nobody had the energy to cook. Then open the crisper drawer and look at the bag of spinach gone to slime, the half onion in plastic, the chicken thighs you bought with good intentions and froze in a panic, the frost-burned bag of toasted ravioli in the back of the freezer. That is your real food budget. It just never shows up as one number.
Now hold it against a posted week: around $300 with groceries at one service, $215 to $275 plus groceries at another, $325 plus groceries for a package. For some households that is closer than they ever expected. Two parents in Dutchtown working opposite shifts, passing each other in the doorway. A family managing a celiac diagnosis, where every takeout order is a gamble. A parent home from surgery who can’t stand at a stove. For them a chef is not a luxury. It is the thing that keeps the week from falling apart at 5:45 every evening.
For others it won’t pencil out, and that is fine. If you love cooking on Sunday afternoons, keep the knife. If the full week is too much, cook for two instead of four and the posted totals come down, or bring a chef in once for a birthday. Friend That Cooks posts a dinner-party rate of $78.80 an hour with a three-hour minimum, using your kitchen, your equipment and your dishes, and estimates a dinner party for eight at $450 to $600, plus groceries.

### What should you ask a chef before you say yes?
Hiring a chef is letting a stranger into the most personal room in your house, the one where the kids leave cereal on the counter and the junk drawer won’t close. Treat the first conversation like an interview, because it is one. Shortlist two or three chefs, talk to each, tell them exactly what you want, and compare what each one says they will deliver for it. Bring the envelope.
Before you meet, write down your week: how many dinners, how many people, which allergies, which nights the kids have practice, and the three meals your family will never eat again. Let each chef walk you through what they would do with that. Then ask the same questions of every one:
How many hours does a week like mine usually take, and what is your minimum?
Do you bill groceries at cost, and will I see the receipts?
What does it cost to skip a week?
Do you bring your own equipment, or cook with mine?
What do containers cost, and do you offer glass?
What does cleanup include when you leave?
Do you have food safety training, such as ServSafe certification?
Do you cook for other clients, and do you invoice me as a business?

### Frequently asked questions about personal chef costs
### Q. Is there a difference between a private chef and a personal chef?
A.  Yes. A personal chef is usually self-employed and cooks for several clients on a schedule, often one cook day a week that fills your fridge. A private chef works for one household only, usually full time and on salary. The difference can matter at tax time: the IRS lists cooks among household workers, and a worker whose work you control, not only what gets done but how, counts as your employee.
### Q. How much is a private chef once a week?
A.  One St. Louis service charges $55 an hour and does not cover the cost of ingredients; another charges $55.69 an hour with a 3-hour minimum, and you provide shopping money for groceries. One service estimates a family of four’s week at around $300 including groceries; another puts it at $215 to $275 plus groceries. A package from a third runs $325 for four dinners of four servings, groceries extra.
### Q. Can I afford a personal chef?
A.  Compare a chef’s full week, labor plus groceries plus extras, against what you already spend on delivery, drive-throughs and food that spoils in the fridge. For two-income homes or families managing a strict diet, the gap is often smaller than expected. If the full week is too much, cook for fewer people, or book a chef only for a special dinner.
### Q. Should you tip your private chef?
A.  On weekly service a tip is a thank-you, not an obligation, because the chef sets their own rate. To a one-person business, a referral to a friend can be worth more than cash. If someone has cooked for your family all year, a holiday bonus or a handwritten note goes a long way. For a full-time private chef who works as your employee, a raise says it best.
### Q. Do private chefs do their own dishes?
A.  Most do. One St. Louis chef’s price list includes complete kitchen cleanup, and another service’s hourly rate for an in-home party covers the chef’s time to plan, shop, cook and clean up. Ask what cleanup covers before you hire, and clear the sink before they arrive so the time you pay for goes to cooking.
### Q. How much do you tip a private chef for a dinner?
A.  For a one-night dinner party, tip on the service, not the groceries, and think of it the way you would a server and kitchen crew at a good restaurant. If the chef brought helpers, make sure the tip covers them too. Ask up front whether a service charge is already on the bill so you don’t pay twice.

## The $50 That Comes Back as Clothes: Hiring a Personal Shopper in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-personal-shopper-in-st-louis
Door shut, street noise gone, the only sound a fitting room curtain sliding on its rod: that kind of quiet feels like a luxury you pay for once and never see again, and it’s the part most people get backwards. At Rushmore Boutique in the Central West End, the $50 reservation for a private styling appointment comes back to you, and its own styling page spells out how: it “becomes a one time use shopping credit applied toward your purchase during your visit.”
What the fifty buys first is quiet. The shop calls it the store to yourself, with uninterrupted time, and compares it to stepping into your stylish friend’s closet with her trusted opinion at the ready. Now look at the closet you’d be paying someone to fix. The door that sticks a little, then gives. The sweater still wearing its cardboard tag, the plastic barb scratching your wrist as you push it down the rail, past the navy blazer from one interview and the jeans that fit two winters ago. The hangers clack against each other. Every one of them is money you already spent, and every morning you stand there, coffee going cold on the dresser, and reach for the same three things anyway.
Rushmore isn’t the only place in St. Louis where the first money counts. Prop the laptop on the kitchen counter for a 55-minute Zoom mini-session with Dacy, a St. Louis stylist who runs a styling business called mindful closet, and you pay $347; the fine print on her services page says the cost of that session is applicable toward her 8-week program if you decide to keep going. Sawyier, another St. Louis stylist, says on her own styling page that if her first closet session takes less than two hours, the leftover time goes to future sessions in 15-minute increments. Your first hour of help doesn’t have to be a sunk cost.
So here’s the line to text a friend who’s standing in a fitting room right now: the free stylist is paid in what you buy, the paid stylist is paid in hours, and at the St. Louis shops and stylists that post their terms, the first money counts toward what comes next. The same independent stylist has a line that belongs taped inside that sticky closet door: “The clothes that never get worn are the expensive part. Not the appointment.”
Tonight, drag a laundry basket to the closet. Fill it with everything you haven’t worn since last winter, hear the empty hangers swing and knock on the rail, and set the basket by the bedroom door. Look at it in the morning light. The women’s pieces in good shape can go back to that same resale shop, which buys gently used clothing for cash on the spot. Hand a stylist a closet that’s already been sorted and the paid hours go to the part you can’t do alone: putting outfits together. Then, on every free first call, ask the same thing word for word: “What does the first visit cost, how long does it run, what do I walk away with, and do you earn anything from where I shop?” If you’re paying hourly, also ask what happens when the closet takes longer than planned.
St. Louis has fixed bad fit before. From the late 19th century until the end of WWII, St. Louis was second only to New York in garment manufacturing, and its big fix was a fit fix: in 1929 Kline’s couldn’t find youthful styles, so the store wrote its own measurements, the bust higher and the waist shorter and smaller. Change the clothes, not the person in the mirror. Walk Washington Avenue past the old redbrick garment buildings, now lofts and bars, and remember that before you buy anything new, a stylist worth hiring should send some of your closet to a tailor.
### How much does it cost to hire a personal shopper in St. Louis?
It can cost nothing: Nordstrom’s personal styling is free, and so is the personal shopper at Clothes Mentor’s St. Louis resale shop. Independent St. Louis stylists who post their prices charge $347 for a 55-minute Zoom session and $1,275 for two hours in your closet, with extra hours billed at $425, while Rushmore Boutique in the Central West End takes a $50 reservation that becomes shopping credit. ### The St. Louis price sheet, from a resale rack to your closet
These are the options I could confirm from each stylist’s or store’s own posted details. Prices are what each one lists today; ask before you book, because menus change.

Dacy says it straight on her own page: “This isn’t about me being your personal shopper.” If what you want is a person who carries the bags, pick the line on the menu that says so.
Here is the honest math most people skip. The free appointment can end up costing more than the paid one. You walk into a store fitting room with one sentence, “I have nothing to wear,” and the only answer a store can give you is something off its own racks. A paid stylist who has no inventory to move can do the thing a store never will: stand in your bedroom, pull out the gray suit, and tell you it just needs new buttons.
### What does a personal shopper actually do once the curtain closes?
At a department store, the visit starts before you arrive. You book online, and a style expert pulls pieces in your size and budget so you try things on in a room instead of dragging armfuls around the floor, the way one stylist describes the free service. The fitting room smells like steamer and new denim. Someone knocks with a second size before you ask. If you have a wedding in three weeks or a work trip and no coat, that is a gift.
An independent stylist works the other direction. The first visit is usually in your home, not a store. They open the closet and start sliding hangers, and you hear them click down the rail one by one. They ask questions that feel strange at first. What do you want people to think when you walk into a room? What did someone talk you out of wearing? Which three things do you reach for every single week?
Then the sorting starts. A keep pile on the bed. A tailor pile. A donate bag by the door that slowly fills with shirts you were saving for a version of your life you’re not living anymore. Only after that do they make a shopping list, and it is short and specific: one belt that fits, dark jeans with a real hem, a jacket that works over both. Then they shop it, sometimes with you, sometimes alone with photos sent to your phone.
The big difference is the closet. A store stylist has never seen yours. An independent stylist has had their hands in it.
### How do store stylists and independent stylists get paid?
Follow the money and you’ll know exactly what advice to expect. At Nordstrom the appointment costs you nothing, and the stylist who wrote about it puts the catch in two sentences: “A store stylist’s incentives are not evil, they’re just structural. Their success is measured in sales.” Nothing sinister about it. It just means the conversation will almost always end in a fitting room, because the store’s racks are the only tool on the table.
Independent stylists are paid by you, and the St. Louis menus above show the two usual shapes: a fixed block of time, like Sawyier’s two hours in your closet, or a set of sessions, like Dacy’s three-session starter package. Because you’re the one paying, their best move is often to talk you out of buying something. A good one will tell you to return the shirt. Out loud. In the parking lot.
That is also the honest answer to a question people whisper: can a normal person hire a stylist? Yes. You don’t need a red carpet or a corner office. Plenty of clients are nurses who need two looks that survive a long shift and dinner after, or a dad rebuilding a closet after a divorce, or someone who lost weight and stands in front of the mirror in clothes that hang like a tent. Ordinary people hire stylists for ordinary reasons. The only requirement is wanting to stop wasting money on clothes that sit.
### Is it worth getting a personal stylist?
It’s worth it when the problem is bigger than one outfit. Here is the test. Open your closet tonight and count the things you have not worn since last winter. If that pile is taller than your forearm, you have a decision problem, not a shopping problem, and that is exactly what a paid stylist is built to fix.
It’s probably not worth it if you need one dress for one event, you already like one store, and you know your size. Book the free appointment, enjoy the dressing room with a stranger who hands you the right size through the curtain, and go home. You don’t need a strategy for a single Saturday.
The in-between case is the one that hurts: the closet is full, you still feel like you have nothing to wear, and every morning starts with the same three shirts. That stuck feeling follows you out the door and into every meeting. A stylist can’t fix your life. They can take that one daily irritation off your plate, and people tend to underrate how much lighter a morning gets when getting dressed takes five minutes and you stop thinking about it. One client, Dave, put the win in plain words on that stylist’s site: she “broke my long-standing addiction to plain old khakis.”

## Just 3% Chicken? How to Choose Pet Food in St. Louis, Where Purina Began
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-pet-food-in-st-louis
Just 3% chicken? Under the pet food naming rules, that’s all a bag called “Dog Food With Chicken” has to hold, because “with” allows an ingredient in the product name at an inclusion rate of at least 3%. Most of us read “with chicken” as a promise. It’s a minimum, and a small one.
You know the moment in the aisle: the bag braced on your hip, the plastic slick and cool under your fingers, a glossy roasted drumstick across the front and a price that made you wince. The drumstick fills most of the photo. The chicken can be a sprinkle of the recipe. Back home a nose is waiting to press into your knee the second the scoop scrapes the bin, and that dog will trust whatever you pour.
You’re not the first St. Louisan to stand in that aisle feeling short-changed. Treats Unleashed started in the summer of 2002 with a batch of Apple Cinnamon Heart treats at a kiosk in the mall, after its founders moved back to St. Louis and, in the owner’s words, “had a difficult time finding healthy and nutritious pet food and treat options for our dachshunds, Max and Mickey.” Warm apple and cinnamon drifting down a mall corridor, two small dogs waiting at home, and a family that decided the bag on the shelf wasn’t good enough. The lesson for the rest of us is smaller and cheaper: the trick was never the brand. It’s the grammar on the front.
Here’s the cheat sheet, short enough to say out loud in the aisle. “Chicken Dog Food” must be at least 95% chicken, not counting added water. “Chicken Dinner” only has to reach 25%, not counting added water. “Dog Food With Chicken” should contain at least 3% chicken. And “Chicken Flavor” only promises that a listed ingredient provides the flavor. Screenshot that and send it to whoever does the shopping in your house. One little word takes the chicken from nearly the whole recipe down to a sprinkle.
Tilt the bag toward the store lights and squint at the tiny box of numbers on the back. Missouri does check those numbers. In this state, all commercial pet food must be appropriately labeled and is subject to random sampling and analysis by the Feed and Seed Program, and the collected samples are tested for adherence to the guarantees listed on the label. The AAFCO name in the fine print, the one that sounds like a seal of approval, is not that check: AAFCO does not regulate, test, approve or certify pet foods in any way.
And if the scoop hits bare plastic before payday, nobody in this city has to stretch the last of the kibble with table scraps. The City of St. Louis’s own pet resources page lists the Bi-State Pet Food Pantry, Stray Rescue of St. Louis and the Carol House Pet Food Pantry under Pet Food & Supplies Assistance. Call before you drive over; a pantry shelf empties faster than a bag of kibble.
And when a bag seems wrong, you have someone to tell. A fresh bag that smells sour or chemical instead of dusty and toasted, a dog who suddenly won’t touch a food they’ve eaten for years and then throws up on the rug: the state says to always contact your veterinarian first. Then, if you suspect the food was adulterated or misbranded, or it hurt your pet, you may file a complaint to the Feed and Seed Program. The program lists its phone as (573) 751-4310 and a pet food email, petfood@mda.mo.gov. Put that number in your phone tonight, right under your vet’s.
One St. Louis catch the bag never mentions: the FDA says to store dry pet food in a cool and dry place at less than 80 F, and a detached garage off a South City alley in July, the air thick enough to taste, is neither. Keep the food in its original bag with the top tightly folded down, and keep that bag indoors, on the basement shelf next to the paint cans.
### How do I figure out what dog food is best for my dog?
Turn the bag over and find the nutritional adequacy statement, the line that says the food is complete and balanced for your dog’s life stage. Then let your own dog be the judge over the next several weeks: firm stools, steady weight, real energy on the walk and a coat that feels clean and soft under your palm, and bring the bag to your vet if anything looks off.
That back-of-the-bag line is the most important sentence on the whole package, and it’s usually printed in the smallest type. The AAFCO label guide says “Complete” means the product contains all the nutrients required, and “Balanced” means the nutrients are present in the correct ratios. The recognized life stages are gestation and lactation, growth, maintenance, and all life stages. A puppy needs a growth or all-life-stages food. A couch-loving senior lab usually doesn’t.
Watch for one phrase in particular: “intermittent or supplemental.” That label means the food isn’t built to be the only thing your pet eats. It shows up on some therapeutic diets your vet may prescribe, and it’s fine in that setting. It is not what you want in the everyday bowl by accident.
Cornell’s Riney Canine Health Center gives a short rule: feed a commercial diet that is certified as providing complete and balanced nutrition for your dog’s life stage, or work with a board-certified veterinary nutritionist. Everything after that, grain or no grain, kibble or canned, is a conversation between you, your vet and the dog who has to eat it every single day.
And the dog does get a vote. You know the sound of a dog who loves dinner: the bowl skating across the floor, tags clinking against steel, the long lick around the empty rim. You also know the dog who sniffs, sighs and walks away. Both tell you something no label can.
### The name on the front of the bag is a math problem
Now the fine print behind that cheat sheet. The product name isn’t just marketing. AAFCO lays out what it calls the 100%, 95%, 25%, “with” and “flavor” rules, and every one of them hangs on a single word in the name.
The 95% rule in dog food covers names like “Beef Dog Food” or “Chicken Cat Food,” where the meat sits right next to the word food. The named ingredients must make up at least 95% of the product by weight, not counting added water, and at least 70% even when you count it. If two ingredients are named, like chicken and rice, the first one listed has to be the bigger share.
Add a softer word and the floor drops. So “Lamb Dinner” can be mostly something other than lamb, and that’s perfectly legal.
Then comes “with.” Under the “with” rule, “with” allows an ingredient in the product name at an inclusion rate of at least 3% of each named ingredient. That drumstick photo? At least three percent chicken, and that’s the floor. And the flavor rule goes further still: a flavor designation can be used as long as a listed ingredient provides that flavor. It doesn’t need to be a big amount of anything.
The bag isn’t lying to you. It’s speaking a language most of us were never taught.
Two more lines on the label do quiet, honest work. The ingredient statement must list everything in descending order of predominance by weight, so whatever is listed first is what there’s the most of. And the calorie statement, under a heading titled “Calorie Content,” has to show kilocalories per kilogram and per familiar unit, like per cup or per can. Hold on to that cup number. It’s the key to the next section.
### Where does the price per meal really land?
The shelf tag shows the price per pound. Your dog doesn’t eat pounds. Your dog eats calories, and two bags that look alike on the shelf can feed very differently once they’re in the scoop.
So what is the cheapest way to buy pet food? Price it per day, not per bag. Flip the bag to the Calorie Content line and find the kilocalories per cup, then multiply by the cups your dog really eats in a day. That’s your dog’s daily calories. Next, multiply the kilocalories per kilogram by the kilograms in the bag, and divide that by the daily number: that’s how many days the bag lasts. Divide the price by the days and you have the only number that matters. Do it on your phone right there in the aisle for two or three bags, the cart wheel rattling, the register beeping up front. A pricier bag packed with more calories per cup can cost less per day, because you scoop less of it. A cheap bag that needs a heaping scoop can quietly cost more.
Then stop paying full price for every bag. Think of the little card in your wallet getting one more punch each month, until the thirteenth bag goes out the door with the register showing nothing but sales tax. That card is real in this city. At Treats Unleashed, the frequent buyer program reads “Buy 12 bags, get 13th bag FREE!” The fine print matters: purchases must be within the same brand, the card is valid for in-store purchases only, customers have 12 months to complete it, and the sales tax on the free bag is yours to pay. Pick the food first, by the label rules above, and only then ask every shop on your shortlist whether that brand has a card. A punch card never makes the wrong food a bargain.
Then feed to your dog, not to the bag. The feeding directions are a starting point, and the real test is your hand on your dog’s side. You should feel ribs under a thin layer, not a washboard and not a cushion. Overfeeding is the most expensive habit in pet food, and you pay for it twice: once at the register and again at the vet.
Treats count too, and this is where budgets leak. VCA’s vets put it plainly: 90% of your dog’s daily calories should come from complete and balanced food, and the remaining 10% can come from treats and snacks. The biscuit after the walk, the cheese at the counter, the crust somebody slips under the table on pizza night on The Hill: all of it lives inside that 10%.
And if money is tight this month, you’re far from alone, and there’s no shame in a bag of help. Our neighbors run food programs for pets as well as people, and we keep a list in our guide to pet food pantries in St. Louis. A full bowl matters more than a fancy one.
### What happens if you skip the slow switch?
You find out in the dark. It’s the wet, rhythmic heave from the hallway that sits you straight up in bed before you’re fully awake, then the hunt for paper towels with the lights still off, then the smell. Can you abruptly switch dog food? Plenty of people do it once. Very few do it twice.
The American Kennel Club warns that switching your dog’s food abruptly can cause gastrointestinal upset, such as vomiting, diarrhea and a decreased appetite, and recommends the change happen gradually over 5-7 days, mixing in more of the new food as you go. Their schedule for most dogs is simple enough to tape inside the pantry door:
Day 1: 25% new diet and 75% old diet
Day 3: 50% new diet and 50% old diet
Day 5: 75% new diet and 25% old diet
Day 7: 100% new diet
The AKC adds that some dogs with sensitive stomachs, food allergies or other gastrointestinal conditions may need a longer transition. If your dog’s stool goes soft partway through, don’t push forward. Stay at the mix that worked for a few more days, then step up again. Slow is cheaper than carpet cleaning.
A practical tip that saves the whole plan: buy the new bag before the old one runs out. Keep a few days of the old food in reserve and the schedule takes care of itself. Two bowls side by side on the kitchen floor, a small scoop moving from one to the other each morning. That’s the entire trick.
### How will you know the new food is working?
Give it real time, longer than feels natural. Stomach changes show up first: firmer, smaller stools and a dog who stops gulping grass in the yard. Skin and coat take longer. You’ll notice it one evening on the couch when your fingers run down your dog’s back and the coat feels less greasy, less flaky, a little softer than you remember.
For dogs with suspected food allergies, VCA’s guidance on diet trials says the elimination diet should be fed for at least eight weeks, although signs of improvement are often seen sooner. Dogs with gastrointestinal signs like diarrhea usually improve sooner than dogs with skin signs, and many dogs see remission of signs by the fifth week. That’s a medical trial run with your vet, not a casual swap, but it tells you something useful about patience: judging a food after three days is judging a book by the cover.
Keep a short note on the fridge. The date you started, what the stools looked like, any scratching, any vomiting, your dog’s weight at the vet. Two months from now you won’t remember, and that scrap of paper will be the most useful thing you bring to the next appointment.
### Shop for pet food in St. Louis the way you’d hire help
The best pet food advice in St. Louis usually isn’t on a website. It’s behind a counter, from someone who has watched a hundred dogs try a hundred foods. Treat choosing a food like hiring someone: shortlist two or three local pet shops or feed stores, whether you live in Dutchtown, Benton Park or the Central West End, and walk in with a photo of your current label.
Tell them what you’re working with. Your dog’s age and weight, what they eat now, what you’re trying to fix, whether that’s itchy paws or a dog who leaves half the bowl, and what you can comfortably spend each month. Then listen. Ask which life stage the food they suggest is labeled for, what the calories per cup are, and whether they’ll help if your dog won’t touch it. Compare what each shop recommends against the label rules above. The one who asks you more questions than you ask them is usually the keeper.
You’ll feel the difference the moment you walk in: the bell over the door, the smell of rawhide and cedar bedding, a shop dog padding over to sniff your shoes. That’s a place that will remember your dog’s name next month.
Your dog can’t read the bag, so you’re the one who has to. Take a photo of your label and find a St. Louis shop that will talk it through with you, starting with Pet Food on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you’re the pet shop, the feed store or the one-person treat kitchen, this reader is already holding a bag and looking for you. Owners like this are searching here right now, so put your shop where they look and get more customers when you list your business.
### What should you do if a bag seems wrong?
Sometimes it isn’t the switch. You open a fresh bag and the smell is off, sour or chemical instead of that dusty, toasted kibble smell you know. Or your dog gets sick on a food they’ve eaten for years. Trust that knot in your stomach.
First, the Missouri Department of Agriculture says you should always contact your veterinarian. Next, check FDA’s recall website for any recalls on the specific food. After that, if you think the issue is the animal food, contact the Missouri Department of Agriculture: you can submit a complaint to the Feed and Seed Program online, and each complaint received will be reviewed to determine if an investigation is warranted. Have the bag in your hand when you do.
Your dog gets a yearly checkup. When did you last book yours?
Keep the bag. Don’t pour the rest into a bin and toss the packaging, because the label and the printing on it are what anyone investigating will need. Snap a photo of the front, the back and the receipt, and fold the top closed with a clip. It takes a moment and turns a bad night into a report someone can act on.

### Frequently asked questions about choosing pet food
### Q. What is the 95% rule in dog food?
A.  The named ingredients must be at least 95% of the product by weight not counting added water, and at least 70% counting it.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to buy pet food?
A.  Compare cost per day, not price per bag: use the kilocalories per cup on the Calorie Content line to work out how many days a bag lasts, then divide the price by those days. After that, ask about a frequent buyer card for the brand you chose. At Treats Unleashed in St. Louis, the program is buy 12 bags and get the 13th free, within the same brand and for in-store purchases only.
### Q. What happens if you don’t slowly transition dog food?
A.  Your dog may pay for it that night. The American Kennel Club says switching your dog’s food abruptly can cause gastrointestinal upset, such as vomiting, diarrhea and a decreased appetite, which is why it recommends a gradual change over 5-7 days.
### Q. Can you abruptly switch dog food?
A.  You can, but it often backfires. The American Kennel Club says switching abruptly can cause gastrointestinal upset, such as vomiting, diarrhea and a decreased appetite, and recommends moving to the new food gradually over 5-7 days. Dogs with sensitive stomachs or food allergies may need even longer.
### Q. What is a good chart for switching dog food?
A.  For most dogs, the AKC says a good transition looks like this: on day 1, 25% new food and 75% old; on day 3, half and half; on day 5, 75% new and 25% old; and on day 7, all new food. If stools go soft, hold at the last mix that worked for a few days before stepping up.
### Q. How long does it take to notice a difference switching dog food?
A.  Digestion usually settles before skin and coat improve. In a formal food-allergy diet trial, VCA says to feed the new diet for at least eight weeks, though many dogs see their signs ease by the fifth week.
### Q. Can I just feed my dog chicken and rice every day?
A.  Not as a long-term diet. Cornell’s canine health center warns against leaning too heavily on chicken and rice, which it says is supposed to be a temporary diet for upset digestive tracts. For everyday feeding, use a commercial food labeled complete and balanced for your dog’s life stage, or work with a board-certified veterinary nutritionist on a home-cooked plan.

## Old Car Taxes Can Block Your $25-a-Day St. Louis Pop-Up Shop License
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-run-a-pop-up-shop-in-st-louis
“It’s just one weekend.” City Hall doesn’t care how short it is. The City of St. Louis won’t issue your $25-a-day pop-up license until every current and past tax under your name is paid, car taxes included.
You know who this is written for. The person who works a full shift and then pours candles at the kitchen table until the wax smell is in the curtains. The one with a trunk full of prints, a card reader still in its box and a friend on Cherokee Street who said, “Use the front room Saturday, I don’t mind.” You don’t have a free weekday to waste. Every morning you spend downtown is a morning you took off from the job that pays the rent. So the whole point of this guide is one trip that works instead of three that don’t.
That tax rule is the step that blindsides people, because it has nothing to do with pop-ups. The License Collector cannot issue any business license or license renewal until all current and past taxes are paid, and the first item on that list is personal property taxes. In the city, that’s the tax the Collector of Revenue charges on motorized vehicles. So a car you sold years ago, at an address you left two moves back, can still be sitting under your name.
Read that twice. In St. Louis, a pop-up license runs through your car tax.
Maybe the bill went to the old apartment. Maybe nobody told the Assessor’s Office the car was gone, and the city says only the Assessor’s Office can change the vehicles or addresses on a personal property tax bill. Either way, you meet it at a window, while somebody reads a screen you can’t see and the people behind you shift their weight. Your thumb finds the crease in the envelope with your money order in it. That’s not carelessness. That’s a person who moved, sold a car and kept working. The thing to be mad at is the relay, not you: a string of counters that only makes sense after you’ve run it once.
Is one old bill a reason to skip the weekend? No. It’s a reason to make one phone call first. The Personal Property Tax Department, in Room 109 at 1200 Market, answers at (314) 622-4101, Monday through Friday, 8:00am to 5:00pm, and it can print tax bills and tax receipts. Ask whether anything is open under your name. A paid receipt tucked in your folder costs you a lunch break now instead of a canceled Saturday later.
Then the license itself. The City of St. Louis charges $25 a day for the Itinerant Vendor license, the one that lets you sell inside somebody else’s storefront, gallery or back room, and it can only be issued for 3 consecutive days at a time. And the $200 street or sidewalk vendor license is not accepted for this setup, so the license a friend uses on the sidewalk won’t cover your table inside a gallery. What catches people is the order. The city’s instructions run seven steps, and the last one sends you back to the counter where you started: after receiving all of the other required permits, you return to the License Collector’s Office for your license to be issued.
The license feels like step one. In St. Louis it’s the receipt at the end of a relay. Plan backward from that last counter and your weekend is safe. Plan forward from a good idea and a borrowed room, and you find out what you’re missing with your shoes squeaking on a City Hall floor and a folder going soft in your hands.
The other step with a long fuse belongs to the state. The city wants your Missouri sales tax number before you visit City Hall, and the Missouri Department of Revenue tells unregistered vendors to contact the Department 3 to 4 weeks before the event to get a sales tax license. Read that as a calendar. The true start of your pop-up is about a month out, before you’ve booked the room, lettered a sign or bought one roll of tissue paper.
### Do I need a license for a pop-up shop in St. Louis?
Yes. If you sell products at an indoor pop-up in the city, St. Louis wants your Missouri state sales tax number before you visit City Hall, and then an Itinerant Vendor license, which costs $25 a day and can only be issued for 3 consecutive days at a time. The space has to be private property inside a building or enclosed structure, not the sidewalk, street or park out front.
Payment for that license is cash, money order or cashier’s check only.
Then there’s the letter. Step 2 on the city’s list is written permission from the owner of the property, on company letterhead or as a notarized letter, and it should include the dates of the sale. “Sure, use the front room” said over coffee is a kindness. It is not a letter. Ask for it in writing the same day they say yes, while the coffee’s still warm and the offer is fresh in both your minds.
### The seven steps, in the order the city wrote them
Here is the whole relay, so you can see where the walking happens. Step 1 is the state sales tax number. Step 2 is the owner’s letter. Step 3 is applying and paying for the Itinerant Vendor license, and the city is plain that your license will be issued only after all the necessary requirements are met. Paying is not the same as having it.
Step 4 is a Statement of Clearance from the Collector of Revenue, in City Hall Room 410. That’s the office that checks the old taxes. Call (314) 622-3291 if you want to ask what they’ll need from you. Step 5 applies only if you sell food. Step 6 applies only if you use propane: a $20 fire permit, and you’ll need proof of a current insurance policy. Step 7 is the return trip to the License Collector’s Office, Rooms 102-104, for the license itself.
Rooms 102-104 and Room 410 are both at 1200 Market. That’s the good news. One building, one morning, if your folder is in order. Put the pages in step order before you leave the house, the owner’s letter on top, the paid tax receipt under it. Wear shoes you can stand in. The License Collector’s office keeps Monday through Friday hours, 8 AM to 5 PM, and its number is (314) 622-4528.
Go on a quiet weekday weeks ahead, not the Thursday before you open. An old bill found in September is a nuisance. The same bill found the day before your sale is a canceled weekend and a friend you have to text with bad news.
People are asking
### What kind of business can you start in St. Louis without a license?
Unless your work is on the City’s exempt list, none: any person who engages in any business inside the City limits is required to have a business license. That list names physicians, lawyers, priests, dentists, CPAs, teachers, ministers and a few others such as credit unions, and the License Collector says plainly that if your business is not on that list, it is not exempt. That LLC certificate you printed and slid into the folder doesn’t count either: registering an LLC with the Secretary of State does not qualify as a business license in the City of St. Louis.
### What does a weekend pop-up really cost in St. Louis?
Less than you fear, more than zero. The cost to do a pop-up shop starts with the city’s part: $25 for every day you’re open. Sell food and the health permit on the itinerant route is $50 per day. Run propane and add the $20 fire permit. That’s the floor, and it’s the only part anybody can price for you.
Everything else is yours to count. The room, if your friend wants a cut. Insurance. Stock. The card reader’s fee on every swipe. Gas. Folding tables if you don’t own them. And the Saturday itself, the one you could have picked up at the other job. Write it all on the back of the owner’s letter before you sign anything.
Then divide. Take the total and divide it by what one sale really leaves you after materials and card fees. That’s how many sales the weekend needs just to break even. If the number makes your stomach drop, good. Better now, at the kitchen table with a pencil, than Sunday at dusk with a cash box that feels too light.
### Email the Soulard manager before you gather a single document
No room yet? Rent half a stand. Soulard Market rents daily space in half-stand sections, approximately 8’x4’. From April through September a Saturday is $40. From October through March, Saturday is $30. Soulard takes the stand fee by check or money order, payable to the City of St. Louis.
Here’s the line on the city’s page that saves people a month of paperwork. It tells vendors to contact the Market manager about stand availability for their type of product BEFORE beginning to assemble the documents. The capital letters are theirs. Parks staff is committed to maintaining the diversity of wares available each day, so if the floor already has enough soap, a perfect folder won’t get you a stand. Email soulard-market@stlouis-mo.gov first, tell them what you make, and wait for a yes.
If you’re approved, the city asks for a Missouri State Retail Sales Tax License, a City of St. Louis Business License, and liability insurance in the amount of $1,000,000 naming the City of St. Louis as an additional insured. Price that insurance before you fall in love with the idea. The city says it may be obtained through the Soulard Market Merchant’s Association or a private insurance company. Ask the License Collector which city license fits a daily stand before you pay for one.
Then the morning itself. Sign-in for daily stands begins at 6:30am Saturdays, when your breath can show in the cold and the pen skips on the clipboard. Stands are assigned on a first come basis. Electric power is not available, so a card reader that dies at noon stays dead. Charge it the night before. Booth fees must be paid before 1:00pm, and if you can’t pay at assignment, you can leave a valid photo ID with the manager until you do. One more rule that matters: food vendors are not eligible to use daily stands.
Why bother with a 6:30 sign-in? Because the market’s hours show you where the shoppers are. Wednesday and Thursday run at 10% vendor participation, Friday at 35% and Saturday at 100%. The people who sell there for a living have already voted with their alarm clocks. Half a stand on a Saturday tells you more about your prices than a month of asking friends.
### How long should your first pop-up run?
The city answers half of this for you: not more than three consecutive days per license period. Your feet answer the other half. A first pop-up should be short on purpose. Three days is a long weekend, and a long weekend is plenty for a test.
Stretch it longer and the last days feel like the end of a party. The same three neighbors drift back in. You rearrange the table for the fourth time. The coffee you brought at 9 is cold by 11 and you drink it anyway. Short is part of the pitch, too. “This weekend only” is honest when the license says so, and it gives a browser a reason to buy now instead of next time.
Then go dark. Count the box, read your notes, and come back a month later. Now you can see who returns, and that’s the number that tells you whether you have a business or a hobby with a nice table.
Nobody at a folding table needs an investment bank. Here’s who does.
### Selling food flips the order
Sell anything people eat and the Health Department joins the relay, with a rule that changes the sequence. The city says the health dept will require a copy of your paid receipt for an Itinerant Vendor License before a health application can be taken. So you pay the License Collector first, carry that receipt to the Health Department at 1520 Market Street, and only then does the food side open. The city lists the health permit for food at $50 per day, which must be paid with a business check or money order.
Timing is tight on that side. Temporary food permit applications and payments must be received no later than two business days before your event. And the rule that stops home cooks cold is short: foods prepared in a home or other facility not under inspection are prohibited. That’s the person holding a cooler of potato salad made the night before, lid sweating, finding out at the door.
Bakers get a break. The city says waivers are no longer required for cottage food, the kind made at home that doesn’t need temperature control, such as breads, cookies and fruit pies. The city points you to the state’s package and label rules instead. Read them before you print a single sticker.
### Do pop-up shops make money, or do they just feel busy?
Some make money. Plenty just feel busy, and busy is convincing. The door swings open all day. Strangers pick things up, turn them over in the light, say “these are so cute” and set them back down. You drive home buzzing, the heater blowing on your sore hands. Then you open the sales log and the buzz turns into arithmetic.
That’s why the break-even count matters before the weekend, not after. If the number of sales you need is more than you’ve ever sold in a month, the pop-up is marketing, not income. That’s fine. Just budget it that way and collect what marketing is supposed to collect: names, emails, and people who know where to find you next.
Because the money isn’t only in the tin. It’s every person who asks, “Where can I find you after this?” If your answer doesn’t work on a Tuesday in February, they buy from whoever turns up first when they search. The weekend seller’s real enemy isn’t a slow Saturday. It’s being invisible the other five days. A website alone doesn’t fix that, because people search for answers, not websites, and a site nobody points to sits in the dark. Hand out a card that points somewhere a neighbor, a search engine or an AI assistant can actually land when your table is folded in the trunk.
### Your pop-up checklist, taped inside the supply bin
Each step unlocks the next one, so the order matters more than the speed.
About a month out: if you aren’t registered, contact the Missouri Department of Revenue 3 to 4 weeks before the event for a sales tax license.
Call the Personal Property Tax Department at (314) 622-4101 and clear anything open under your name.
Get the property owner’s letter, on letterhead or notarized, with your sale dates on it.
At 1200 Market: apply and pay at the License Collector, Rooms 102-104, then get your Statement of Clearance in Room 410.
Selling food? Take your paid itinerant receipt to the Health Department, at least two business days before the event.
Using propane? Get the $20 fire permit and bring proof of insurance.
Go back to the License Collector’s Office for the license itself.
The night before: count change into the cash box, charge the card reader, letter a sign you can read from the door, and pack a clipboard for emails.

### Frequently asked questions about running a pop-up shop
### Q. How much does it cost to do a pop-up shop?
A.  In the City of St. Louis, the floor for an indoor pop-up is the Itinerant Vendor license at $25 a day, issued for up to 3 consecutive days at a time. ### Q. How long should a pop-up shop last?
A.  For an indoor pop-up in the city, the itinerant license sets the limit: not more than three consecutive days per license period. That’s a good length for a first test anyway. Short keeps your costs down and gives shoppers a reason to buy now.
### Q. Do pop-up shops make money?
A.  They can, if you know your break-even before you open: your fixed costs divided by what one sale leaves you after materials and card fees. If that count is out of reach, treat the weekend as marketing and collect every email you can.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of having a pop-up store?
A.  Short windows, paperwork with real lead time, and a crowd that disappears when you do. ## The Cardboard Pays More: What Your Old Video Games Are Worth in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-your-old-video-games-are-worth-in-st-louis
South County basement, damp cardboard, a shoebox of gray cartridges: and the most valuable part already went out years ago, ripped, crumpled and stuffed in a trash bag with the wrapping paper.
You know the box. It came up the basement stairs, and it smells like damp cardboard and old carpet. The lid has gone soft at the corners, and when you tip it, a pile of gray cartridges slides to one end with that dull plastic clatter. One of them has a name written across the label in ballpoint, the letters pressed so hard they dented the sticker. Your kid is hovering at your elbow asking if you’re rich. Somebody upstairs wants the shelf back.
Most of that box is worth a few dollars a game. A few pieces might be worth real money. And the thing that decides which is which usually is not the cartridge in your hand.
It is the cardboard you threw away.
### What are old video games worth in St. Louis?
Most old video games are worth somewhere between a few dollars and a few hundred, and the real number is what the same game, in the same condition, actually sold for recently. At Retro Game Rescue on Bayless, there are no set amounts: condition and completeness are weighed in every offer.
Do this tonight, before you look up a single price: pull the three games you would miss most, and next to each title write cart only, cart and box, or cart, box and manual. That one line moves the price more than anything else on this page.
Tomorrow the shoebox rides shotgun down I-55, rattling every time you hit a seam in the pavement, to Retro Game Rescue, an independent game store at 4217 Bayless Avenue in South St. Louis County, right off Interstate 55. Its own site lists 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, temporarily closed Wednesdays, so call (314) 696-2144 before you load the car. Its motto is “No Game Left Behind!” and the shop says flat out, “We take it all,” working or not.
Here is the line almost nobody reads before they walk in. The shop’s own sell page says, “We don’t have set amounts we give for the items we buy.” Every offer is worked out one deal at a time, and the list of what it weighs starts with “condition, completeness, rarity.” Completeness is the box. The manual. The cardboard you tore open on Christmas morning. Take store credit instead of cash and the shop says you get an even higher amount, and that credit never expires.
Pack your driver’s license with the games. PayMore Maplewood at 3212 Laclede Station Road, (314) 499-8722, buys Nintendo, Sega, PlayStation and Xbox consoles for a fast, fair cash offer or store credit, and says every console and game is fully tested. Its trade-in terms say you sign its seller’s book, a valid photo ID is required as local law calls for, and once you sign the book, the deal is final.
Cross into the City of St. Louis and the counter asks for more than a signature. A city ordinance on secondhand dealers says a dealer can’t buy a thing from you without taking your photograph and your right thumb print, on a transaction form from the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department that records your name, address, date of birth and driver’s license number. The dealer keeps that form for a year, and has to post a notice telling every seller it will photograph and fingerprint them. So you stand at the glass, thumb pressed flat, a cartridge you blew into a hundred times about to change hands. Decide in the driveway which ones you can let go of, not at the counter.
Wherever you sell, set the shoebox on the glass, hear the carts clack against each other one last time, pull out the three games on your list first, and ask for two numbers on each, cash and store credit. Write them next to your condition line before you sign anything.
Now set an empty box on that same glass, soft corners, no game inside. For the right game, the box alone is the bigger number. EarthBound is a Super Nintendo game with a release date of June 5, 1995, and it is one of the famous expensive ones. The price guide PriceCharting lists a loose EarthBound cartridge, just the cart by itself, at under $400. A complete copy, with the original box and the original instruction manual, sits around $2,500. The empty box alone, no game inside, lists at about $700.
The cardboard is worth more than the game.
Most boxes in most basements do not hold an EarthBound. St. Louis County Library has over 2,000 video games in its collection, for consoles including the PlayStation 3, the Wii and the Xbox 360, and it lends them out for 21 days at a time. If the disc you are holding is that kind of game, it is probably not the one that pays for the furnace. Keep it, play it, or let it go for a few dollars without losing sleep.
The money, when there is money, hides in three places: the game is the real thing and not a copy, it still works the way it did when you were nine, and the paper and cardboard it came in survived. Miss one and the number drops fast.
And if the kid at your elbow has never held one of these controllers, let them before the box goes anywhere. ### The box is the detail that changes the price most
Most of us were loose kids. You tore the box open on Christmas morning, the cardboard tab ripped in your fingers, the plastic tray rattled across the floor, and by New Year’s the box was in the trash with the wrapping paper. That is exactly why the boxes that survived are scarce, and scarce is what buyers pay for.
So before you price anything, go looking. Check the closet shelf where the board games live. Check the bin of manuals somebody saved “just in case.” Check the top of the furnace room, where flattened boxes sometimes end up stacked behind holiday lights. A box that smells a little like the basement and has a soft corner is still a box. A manual with a coffee ring is still a manual.
Then leave it alone. Do not tape a torn flap, do not wipe a paper label with anything wet, and do not peel off an old price sticker that has been there for decades, because you can tear the print right off with it. Write down what you have, in plain words, for each game: cart only, cart and box, cart and manual, or all three. That one line is the most important thing you will write all week.
The big-ticket copies show you why. On the EarthBound page, the higher sales are listed with their paper extras spelled out, down to the player’s guide and its Scratch N Sniff Cards. Somebody kept those cards in a drawer for decades without scratching them. That restraint is now worth real money.
### How do you tell what your games really sold for?
Use sold prices, never asking prices. Anyone can list a common sports game for $200, and it can sit there for a year. What matters is what a buyer actually paid. eBay’s advanced search has a “Sold items” option, and checking it is the cheapest education you will get on this whole project.
Here is the kitchen-table routine. Spread the games out on a towel. Under the overhead light, write each title, the system and your condition line. Search sold results for the exact title and system, then look only at copies that match what you have. A loose cart with a worn label is not the same item as a complete copy in a crisp box, and averaging the two will fool you. Take the middle of the matching sales, not the highest one.
Price guides do some of that sorting for you. PriceCharting says it tracks video games sold on eBay and its own marketplace, and that reproductions, imports, video game lots and similar sales are not included in its price data. That last part matters for your shoebox. A lot is a pile sold together, and lot prices get thrown out of the guide because they say nothing about any single game in the pile.
Which leads to the most common mistake in every basement in Labadie and Grover and everywhere else: selling the whole box as one lot to the first person who offers cash. If two games in that box are worth more than the other twenty combined, pull them out first. Sell those on their own. Then let the rest go as a lot if you like.
While each cart is in your hand, check that it is the real thing. Nintendo’s own advice on spotting counterfeits is to look closely at the print on cartridges and packaging, to look for the Original Nintendo Seal of Quality or the Original Nintendo Licensee Seal of Quality, and to confirm the region and language are correct. Tilt the label under the light. Real labels are sharp. Blurry art, odd colors and spelling slips are the tells. Nintendo also notes that a product offered well below the average retail price could be counterfeit, which is worth remembering if you ever buy one back.
### How much can you sell old games for at a St. Louis counter?
Less than the sold price, almost always, and that is not a scam. A shop has rent, has to test the game, and has to wait for the right buyer to walk in. What you are trading for the lower number is speed: cash today, nothing to ship, no strangers in your driveway. Whether that trade is worth it depends on the game. For a stack of common titles, a fair counter offer can be the best deal you will get. For the one complete copy in the box, it probably is not.
Can you trade in games for cash? Yes. GameStop’s trade page offers both cash and trade credit. Read the fine print, though. Its terms say products must be in good condition and have all necessary components to receive the highest trade value, that condition and value are determined by the store, and that all trades are final. Ask for both numbers, the cash offer and the credit offer, before you decide.
If you take the box to a pawn shop, know this before you go. Under RSMo 367.044, a pawnbroker shall require of every person from whom the pawnbroker receives sold or pledged property proof of identification, which includes a current address and a current picture identification issued by state or federal government. If any seller fails to provide that proof of identification, the pawnbroker shall hold the property for a period of thirty days prior to selling it. And under RSMo 367.040, a pawnbroker shall not accept a pledge from a person who is under eighteen years of age, and has to keep a signed document from the seller saying the seller has the right to sell the property.
That last part is the family conversation. If it is your teenager’s collection, plan on going together, with your ID in your wallet and the kid doing the talking. It is their stuff and their first negotiation. Let them hear what the person behind the counter says about each game.
However you sell, the way to get a fair number is the same. Shortlist two or three places that buy games. Call or walk in and ask them to walk you through how they price a game like yours. Tell them what you want, whether that is cash today, the best price on one rare cart, or getting the whole box out of the house. Then compare what each one says they will actually pay against the sold prices you wrote down. You will learn more in those three conversations than in a week of scrolling.
