### Will GameStop take old retro games, or only new ones?
Retro games are on GameStop’s trade list, but not at every store. Its trade page lists Retro Gaming right beside consoles and video games among the things it takes for cash or trade credit, and its fine print says trade-in runs only on select products and in select GameStop stores. So type each title into the page’s “What’s your stuff worth?” search at the kitchen table first, then call the nearest store before the shoebox rattles across the parking lot.
### What if the game will not save anymore?
You slide the cart in and it seats with that stiff, satisfying click. The power light blinks red. The title music comes up, tinny and perfect, and for a second you are cross-legged on shag carpet again. Then you hit Continue and there is nothing there. The file you spent a whole summer on is gone.
That is usually the cartridge, not the console. As one iFixit repair answer explains, certain Game Boy games, especially Game Boy Color games, keep their save files on a soldered-in battery inside the cartridge, and when that battery dies, the board loses its ability to retain a save. The game still plays. It just forgets you every time you turn it off.
Buyers care about this, and they will ask. So test before you list. Start a game, save it, turn the power off, give it a minute and turn it back on. If the save holds, say so plainly in your listing or at the counter. If it does not, say that too. A dead save battery can be replaced by someone who solders, and an honest description keeps a sale from turning into a return.
One more thing, and it is not about money. If the old save is still there, the team you named after your dog or the high score with your initials, take a photo of the screen before the game leaves your hands. The cart can go. The proof that you were there can stay.
Before that shoebox leaves the house, price your three best games against real sales. Then talk to two or three buyers who will explain their offer, starting with the Video Games page on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If you’re the retro game shop or the one-person repair bench, the families holding these boxes need you. More customers are already looking here for someone who will price a game straight, so list your business and be the counter they call first.
### Should the box go to a buyer, a donation bin or the kids?
Not every game needs to be sold. Once the two or three valuable ones are pulled out and priced, the rest of the box is usually worth more to someone as a gift than to you as cash.
Can you donate old video games? In St. Louis, yes. MERS Goodwill lists games, toys and sports equipment among the donations it accepts. Two catches from its own list of accepted items: it is not able to provide home pickups, so check its locations for a donation center near you, and store managers may decline a donation if it is not in clean and sellable condition. Wipe the dust off the carts with a dry cloth, rubber-band each game to its manual if it has one, and the person who picks it off the shelf gets the whole thing.
And then there is the third option, the one that does not show up in any price guide. Hand a few to the kid at your elbow. The games that are worth five dollars at a counter can be worth a whole rainy Saturday in Lonedell or Litchfield, two controllers, the cord stretched across the living room, somebody yelling that it is not fair. You will hear yourself explaining a trick you have not thought about since the fourth grade.
### Where can you play them one more time before they go?
If the console is long gone, you still have options. The Saint Louis Science Center’s GameXPloration exhibit is a 7,500-square-foot gallery with free tickets, located on the main floor of the 5050 Oakland building. It includes a Classic Consoles area where you can play classic console games and see how those early machines were built, plus a free arcade with a couple of classic arcade games and some local creations.
Somewhere in St. Louis, a grown-up is finally learning to swim this month.
For newer games, the library is the quiet answer. St. Louis County Library lends video games for 21 days, and its own page says borrowing games is a great way to try them before you decide to buy. You can even return County Library items to any St. Louis Public Library location. It works in reverse, too. Before you sell a game you have not touched in years, borrow its sequel and see whether the old itch is still there. Some boxes go back under the stairs. That is allowed.
Where you play is less important than who is next to you on the couch when you do. Thumbs on the plastic. The music you could hum before you could read. Somebody laughing at how bad you have gotten. That part of the box was never for sale.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best way to sell old video games?
A.  Pull out the few games worth real money first, write down exactly what comes with each one (cart, box, manual), and price them against sold listings that match their condition. Sell those individually. Then let the rest go together to a local shop, a buyer or a donation center, whichever gets the box out of the house on your terms.
### Q. Can I trade-in games for cash?
A.  Yes. Chains such as GameStop offer both cash and trade credit, and its terms say games need all necessary components to get the highest trade value and that all trades are final. At a Missouri pawn shop, the pawnbroker shall require proof of identification, including a current address and a current picture identification issued by state or federal government, and shall not accept a pledge from a person who is under eighteen years of age.
### Q. Can I donate old video games?
A.  Yes. MERS Goodwill lists games, toys and sports equipment among the donations it accepts. It is not able to provide home pickups, so check its locations for a donation center near you, and a store manager can decline items that are not clean and sellable, so dust them off and keep each game with its manual.
### Q. Are old computer games worth money?
A.  Some are, most are not, and the same rule applies as with console games: completeness drives the price. A disc in a paper sleeve is usually worth little, while a complete copy with its original box and manual can bring much more. Check sold listings for the exact title and edition before you decide.
### Q. Where can I play old retro games?
A.  The Saint Louis Science Center’s GameXPloration exhibit has free tickets and includes a Classic Consoles area and a free arcade with classic arcade games. For newer console titles, St. Louis County Library lends video games for 21 days.

## Your Wet Basement Has a 48-Hour Clock: Water Damage Restoration in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/water-damage-restoration-in-st-louis-the-first-48-hours
$3,000. That is what the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District will reimburse, with a $100 deductible, when excessive rain falls in a short timeframe and an overcharged sewer line discharges into your building. To be eligible, you have to contact MSD within 30 days of the backup. Most water damage starts smaller than that, though. A soft tick from the kitchen ceiling at 2 a.m. The cold squish of carpet under a bare foot at the bottom of the basement stairs. A closet that suddenly smells like a creek bank in August.
Here is the part nobody tells you while you’re standing there in your socks with a flashlight. The water does not decide what this costs you. The next 48 hours do. So do two things before anything else: shut the water off at the main, and photograph the damage before you move a single box. After that, what you pull up off the floor and what you leave sitting wet decide whether this ends with a few fans and a new carpet pad, or with the bottom of every wall in the room cut out and hauled to the curb.
You know the scene, or you will. The cardboard boxes of Christmas ornaments have gone dark and soft at the bottom corners. The paint on the basement wall of a brick two-family in Dutchtown has a wet shine it didn’t have yesterday. The furnace kicks on and the whole floor smells like old pennies and wet dog. Your chest does the quiet math: the deductible, the days off work, the guy you’ll have to call and whether he’ll answer. Nobody thinks clearly at that hour. That’s why it helps to know the clock before you need it.
And St. Louis has a recent lesson in how fast water outruns a plan. On July 26th, 2022, St. Louis-Lambert International Airport set a new all-time record for daily precipitation: 8.64 inches of rain fell since midnight, breaking the previous record of 6.85 inches from August 20th, 1915. The detail that stings is the speed. Plenty of people went to bed with a dry basement that night and woke up to water on the stairs.
That rain had nowhere good to go. The City of St. Louis is served by a combined sewer system, where wastewater and stormwater share the same pipe, so a hard storm can fill the line until it can’t hold any more and push it back into a basement. You smell it before you see it. If that happens to you, call MSD at 314-768-6260, and an MSD representative will inspect your building to see if your situation qualifies.
### Is water damage repairable in St. Louis?
Usually, yes, if the wet materials dry within 24 to 48 hours, which is the window the EPA gives for keeping mold from growing. Past that window, “repairable” slowly turns into “replaceable,” one sheet of drywall and one roll of insulation at a time.
The EPA’s own words are blunt: if wet or damp materials are dried 24 to 48 hours after a leak or spill, in most cases mold will not grow. That is the whole game. Concrete, tile, metal and solid wood forgive you. Paper, fabric and anything with a cardboard face do not. Drywall, the EPA says in its mold cleanup course, may be dried in place if there is no obvious swelling and the seams are intact. Otherwise, removal is necessary.
Press your thumb into the wall a few inches above the floor. Dry drywall pushes back like a closed door. Soaked drywall gives a little, the way a wet cereal box does, and the paint over the tape seams bubbles or splits. That feel tells you more than any app on your phone.
So the honest answer is that the house is almost always repairable. Whether the stuff touching the water is repairable depends on the clock, and the clock started the minute the water did.
### What should you do in the first hour?
Stop the water first. If it’s a pipe or a fixture, find the main shutoff, often a valve near where the water line comes through the basement wall by the meter. In an older house that valve may be stiff with years of sitting still, and you’ll feel it fight you before it gives a quarter turn. If water is near outlets, cords or the electrical panel, don’t walk into it. Stay out and call an electrician or the power company before you go wading.
Then, before you move a single box, take pictures. The Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance tells homeowners to take photographs or video of any damage before beginning cleanup or making repairs, because detailed documentation supports the claim. Shoot wide, then close. The waterline on the wall. The soaked carpet. The burst hose itself, still attached. The serial plate on the water heater. Thirty seconds of video walking the room says more than an hour of explaining later.
Now protect the house from getting worse. DCI notes that most insurance policies require policyholders to take reasonable steps to prevent additional damage after a loss. That means mopping, a wet vac, moving furniture off wet carpet and onto blocks, getting photos and family papers up high. Keep every receipt for materials you buy, because those costs may be reimbursable. What you should not do is the permanent fix. DCI is direct about it: do not make permanent repairs until your insurance company has inspected the damage, or the company may not reimburse you.
Call your insurer the same day. You usually must report water damage that was hidden from view within days after you first see it. Check your own policy for its exact language, but don’t sit on it over a weekend hoping it dries out on its own.
### The drying race runs from hour two to hour 48
Once the water stops, the job flips. Now it’s about getting moisture out of things faster than mold can move in. For carpet, that means you remove water with a wet vacuum, pull the carpet and pad off the floor and dry them using a fan to blow air over them, with a dehumidifier pulling humidity out of the room. It also says something people find out the hard way. Wet vacuums alone will not dry carpets. The pad underneath holds water like a sponge, and it has to be dried too.
You’ll know this phase by its sound. A basement full of drying equipment roars, a steady jet-engine hum that runs all night, and the dehumidifier bucket fills faster than seems possible. The air smells warm and a little stale. It is not pleasant. It is working.
Concrete and cinder block can be cleared with a water-extraction vacuum, and the EPA notes drying can be sped up with dehumidifiers, fans and heaters. Upholstered furniture is harder; the same guidance warns that completely drying it within 48 hours may be difficult. A soaked couch in a finished basement is often the first real loss of the week.
One warning almost nobody hears in time. If the water came up through a floor drain, a toilet or anything connected to the sewer, stop and don’t turn on fans. The EPA says not to use fans until you have determined that the water is clean or sanitary, because blowing air across contaminated water spreads what’s in it through the whole house.
Completely unrelated: someone in St. Louis will shop for your whole fall wardrobe.
### Does the drywall have to come out?
Not always. You don’t have to replace drywall after water damage if it dried fast, isn’t swollen and its seams held. The trouble is what you can’t see. The EPA calls the wall cavity the most difficult area to dry and says it should be ventilated if drywall is left to dry in place. Behind that clean-looking paint is a bay of insulation that can stay wet long after the face of the wall feels dry.
That’s why crews so often make what the trade calls a flood cut: a straight, level line sliced across the wall above the wet zone, with everything below it pulled out. It looks brutal the first time you see it. A neat row of bare studs where your wall used to be, the room suddenly smelling of raw pine and old dust. But it opens the cavity to air, lets them pull wet insulation, and lets them see whether water ran down inside the wall farther than the floor suggested.
How long does it take for drywall to dry after water damage? There’s no honest single number, and anybody who gives you one over the phone is guessing. It depends on how long the water sat, how humid the room is, whether the cavity is open and how much equipment is running. The real answer is a reading. A good crew puts a moisture meter on the wall, writes the number down, and comes back to read it again until it matches a dry wall in an unaffected room. Ask to see those numbers. They’re your proof the wall was dry before anyone hung new board over it.
If your walls are old plaster rather than drywall, which you’ll find in plenty of houses around Soulard and Benton Park, say so on the first call and ask how they plan to dry it. Plaster behaves differently from paper-faced board, and the plan should too.
### What does a restoration crew actually do when it walks in?
The difference between water damage remediation and restoration is the difference between getting the problem out and putting the house back. Remediation is the dirty first half: finding the source, pulling out water, tearing out wet material that can’t be saved, and dealing with any mold or contamination. Restoration is the second half: new drywall, new pad and carpet, paint, trim, the room looking like a room again. Some companies do both. Some only do the first and hand you off to a contractor for the rest. Ask which one you’re getting.
A good first visit sounds like questions before it sounds like equipment. Where did it start? How long was it running? What’s under this floor? Then the meters come out, and someone walks the room pressing a probe into walls and floor, marking where the moisture stops. You’ll see blue tape and pencil numbers on your walls. That map tells them what to cut and what to dry.
Then comes the work you saw in the drying section, done at scale: extraction, wet material out, air movers angled across floors and up walls, dehumidifiers running, and a return visit to take readings again. Expect the house to be loud and a little warm for several days. Expect the crew to want the doors and windows kept shut so the dehumidifiers aren’t fighting the outdoors.
Sewage changes all of it. When water is or may be contaminated with sewage, or with chemical or biological pollutants, the EPA says protective gear and containment are required by OSHA, and that an experienced professional should be consulted if you don’t have that expertise. That is not a weekend job with a shop vac. If the water backed up out of a floor drain, the city and sewer side of that story, including what to ask about backflow and your sewer lateral, is laid out in our St. Louis basement waterproofing guide.
The fans need to be running tonight, not after three days of phone tag. Start a shortlist of local crews who can be at your door fast through Water Damage Restoration on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three of them before the drywall starts to swell.
If you’re the restoration crew who answers at 2 a.m., say so where St. Louis is looking. Homeowners with wet carpet are searching for you right now, and a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory helps you get more customers from that search, so list your business before the next storm.
### Where St. Louis water claims fall apart
Most water claims don’t die on the big question of whether the water was bad. They die on how it got in, and when you said so. Most homeowner and renters policies cover sudden and accidental water damage, such as a burst pipe, toilet overflow or broken washer hose, but most home policies don’t cover water damage from gradual leaks or seepage. The slow drip under the sink that rotted the cabinet floor over a year reads very differently to an adjuster than a hose that split on a Tuesday.
Why would insurance deny a water damage claim? Here are the reasons that come up again and again. The water was a flood, and the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance is clear that homeowners insurance generally does not offer protection against flood losses; flood insurance is available through the federal government’s National Flood Insurance Program, and there’s typically a 30-day waiting period before a new policy goes into effect. The leak was long-term. The policy has exclusions DCI tells people to look for by name: “water damage,” “seepage or leakage,” or “runoff or overflow.” Or the homeowner made the permanent repair before the inspection, or let the room sit wet so the damage grew. That last one is the one you control.
Will my homeowners insurance go up if I file a water damage claim? Nobody can promise you either way, because it depends on your company and your history. But know how the record works. The Washington insurance commissioner’s office explains that if your insurance company starts, denies or pays out a claim, they’ll submit a CLUE report, and that the report generally holds up to seven years of property claims history. Read that twice. A claim that pays nothing can still follow the house. The same office says companies use claims history to decide whether to offer coverage and how much you’ll pay, and that the Fair Credit Reporting Act entitles you to a free copy of your own report.
Under Missouri rules summarized by the nonprofit United Policyholders, insurers must acknowledge a claim within 10 working days, complete an investigation within 30 days unless it can’t reasonably be done in that time, and tell you whether the claim is accepted or denied within 15 working days after receiving proper proof of loss. A denial must be in writing and point to a specific policy provision. If it doesn’t, or the calls stop coming back, DCI’s consumer hotline is 800-726-7390.
### How do you choose who to call while the water is still in the house?
You will want to call the first number that answers. Resist that for about fifteen minutes. Shortlist two or three crews, and interview them on the phone the way you’d interview anyone you were about to hand your house keys to. You can hear the difference fast: one sounds like a person standing in a truck with the engine running, ready to come, and one sounds like a call center reading a script.
Tell each one exactly what you want. Something like: “I need the water out and the room dried and documented for my insurer, with moisture readings every visit, and I don’t want anything cut that doesn’t have to be.” Then listen. How soon can they be there? How will they decide what’s dry? Will they photograph the damage and their readings and give you copies? Do they handle the rebuild, or only the drying? If you’re out past the city, in Bloomsdale or Aviston, ask how long the drive really is and whether they come out at night.
Then compare what each one says they will actually deliver, not just who sounded most confident. Read anything they hand you before you sign it, especially anything about your insurance payment. The right crew won’t mind you taking two minutes to read. The wrong one will be in a hurry for your signature, and that hurry tells you something.
When the fans finally shut off, the silence is strange. The basement smells like concrete again instead of wet cardboard. The new pad goes down, and you stop checking the corner by the water heater every time you walk past. That quiet is what the first 48 hours buy you.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the difference between water damage remediation and restoration?
A.  Remediation gets the problem out: stopping the source, extracting water, removing wet material that can’t be saved and handling any mold or contamination. Restoration puts the house back with new drywall, flooring, paint and trim. Some crews do both and some do only the first, so ask which you’re hiring before they start.
### Q. How much does it cost to fix a house with water damage?
A.  It swings widely with how much got wet and for how long, so treat any phone quote as a guess.
### Q. Does insurance pay for water restoration?
A.  Often, when the water was sudden and accidental, like a burst pipe, toilet overflow or broken washer hose. Policies usually exclude gradual leaks, seepage and flood, and Missouri DCI says homeowners insurance generally does not cover flood losses. Read your policy’s water exclusions and call your insurer the same day you find the damage.
### Q. How quickly does mold grow in wet drywall?
A.  The EPA says that if wet or damp materials are dried within 24 to 48 hours after a leak or spill, in most cases mold will not grow. Treat 48 hours as the outside edge. Swollen drywall, split seams and soaked insulation behind the wall are signs the material may need to come out rather than dry in place.
### Q. Why would insurance deny a water damage claim?
A.  The usual reasons are that the damage came from a flood, from a slow leak over time, or from seepage, or that it falls under a policy exclusion such as “water damage” or “runoff or overflow.” Claims also suffer when permanent repairs happen before inspection. In Missouri, a denial must be in writing and cite a specific policy provision.
### Q. Will my homeowners insurance go up if I file a water damage claim?
A.  It may, depending on your insurer and your claims history. Claims go into a CLUE report that generally covers up to seven years, and Washington’s insurance commissioner notes insurers report claims they start, deny or pay. Insurers use that history in pricing, and you’re entitled to a free copy of your report.

## The Saint Louis Zoo Is Free. Parking Is $20 a Car.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/visiting-the-saint-louis-zoo-what-to-know-before-you-go
Whirr. Click. A parking ticket slides out of the machine off Government Drive, the arm swings up, and you have just spent the only $20 the Saint Louis Zoo was ever going to charge you to get in. The gate a short walk ahead will not charge you a cent. Somebody in the back seat has already unbuckled, and the car smells like sunscreen and the apple slices nobody finished.
Do one thing before you shut the door: keep that ticket where you can reach it. It carries a QR code, and you can scan it to pay any time before you leave, so the exit lane at four o’clock is a wave of the phone, not a hunt under the car seats. Then the walk. Whether you drove in from Innsbrook, South Roxana or Dutchtown on the south side of the city, the gate is free and the day is not, unless you plan it. You file through the security scanners at the entrance, a free paper map goes soft in a sweaty hand, and a small voice is pulling you toward the first animal it can hear.
### Is the St. Louis Zoo still free to get in?
Yes. Walking into the Saint Louis Zoo still costs nothing, and the zoo’s hours and prices page says it plainly: “The Zoo is always free.” Its FAQ adds that you need no tickets and no reservations, so you can decide at breakfast and be looking at a rhino before lunch.
What costs money is everything around the animals: the parking lot, the train, the carousel, the stingray pool and the sea lion show. None of that is a trick. It is just never on the sign at the front, and it is the part that turns a free morning into a pricey afternoon if nobody is watching.
The reason the gate is free is a St. Louis story most people who grew up here have never heard. According to the zoo’s own history of the Zoo-Museum District, St. Louis voters approved a mill tax to build the zoo back in 1916. Fifty-some years later, as city residents moved out to the suburbs and the city’s tax base shrank, civic leaders proposed letting St. Louis County share the load. City and County voters approved the Metropolitan Zoological Park and Museum District in 1971, and it is still funded by property tax from both.
Now the part that changes how you look at the parking ticket on your dashboard. The same page says that today, approximately one-quarter of the zoo’s annual operating budget is met by that tax. A quarter. The other three-quarters has to come from somewhere else, and the places you will personally touch are the lot, the rides and the snack windows. Free admission is real. It is also a deal: the region pays your way in, and the zoo counts on you spending a little once you are through.
So here is the math almost nobody does in the lot. The zoo’s entry-level membership is $80 and drops parking to $5 a visit for a year. Against the $20 a car everyone else pays, that is $15 back every time you pull a ticket. Come four times, and $60 of the $80 has come back in parking alone, before anyone rides the train on the 20 member tickets that come with it. Screenshot that before the next birthday-party trip.
Hours shift with the season, so check before you go. Right now the zoo lists 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, except holidays, with last entry 15 minutes before closing, shorter hours on a few holidays, and the whole place closed on Jan. 1 and Dec. 25. Fall at four o’clock comes fast. The light goes gold over Big Cat Country, the stroller wheels start squeaking toward the exits, and if you arrived at two you are already walking out.
### What quietly costs money once you’re inside?
Start with the car. You pull a ticket on the way in, the ticket carries a QR code, and you scan it to pay any time before you leave. Lose the ticket and there is a “lost ticket” button at the exit. Vehicles over 24 feet are not allowed in the zoo lots at all, so if you came in the camper, plan on a Forest Park permit instead.
There is limited street parking for personal vehicles in Forest Park, and the zoo itself points you there. Limited is the key word. On a warm weekend you can loop past the same full curb three times while the baby wakes up hungry, and the zoo also warns that park roads and entrances sometimes close for events. If the curb is your plan, have the $20 lot as your backup, not your argument.
Cash will not help you once you are inside, either. The FAQ says flatly that the zoo does not accept cash anywhere on campus. If cash is all you have, there are cash-to-card kiosks on site at no additional fee that turn it into a prepaid card. Good to know before a nine-year-old with birthday money in an envelope spots the ice cream.
Then the rides. Each one is small on its own, which is exactly how they add up. The Emerson Zooline Railroad is $8.95 a ticket, children under 2 ride free, and the ticket is good all day with on-off privileges. The Conservation Carousel, with its 64 hand-carved wooden animals, is $3 a person. The 4D Theater is $4.95. Stingrays at Caribbean Cove is $4.95 a person for ages 2 and up, plus $2 for a cup of stingray food. The Sea Lion Show is $4 a person.
The fix the zoo itself pushes is the Adventure Pass: one price, unlimited access to the operating attractions for a single day, and the page says you save by buying it online instead of in person. Stingrays and the Sea Lion Show close from late fall through early spring, which means a winter pass covers less.
Back to that membership. The entry-level tier on the zoo’s membership page is $80 and includes $5 parking per visit for a year plus 20 member tickets for the Zooline Railroad, Dinoroarus and the Sea Lion Show. If the train and the sea lions are on your list anyway, those tickets are where the rest of the $80 comes back.
### Which entrance is best for the St. Louis Zoo?
The best entrance is the one that matches how you are arriving, because the two are not identical. The zoo has a North Entrance and a South Entrance. Both have a Welcome Desk, both have rentals, both hand out free paper maps, and both run the same security screening. The differences are smaller and more practical than that.
Coming by bus or train? Use the North Entrance. MetroBus route #90 Hampton stops within a short walking distance of the North Entrance, at the intersection of Fine Arts Drive and Government Drive, and you can ride MetroLink to the Forest Park/DeBaliviere station, then take the same Hampton bus south. The North Entrance also sits at The Living World, home to Treetop Shop, which the zoo calls its largest store. Which means the biggest gift shop is the last door your kids pass on the way out. Have that conversation in the car, not at the register.
Driving an electric car? The South Parking Lot has two EV charging stations, and the zoo says they are free for guests. The South Entrance is also where Lost and Found lives, inside Security, in case a stuffed giraffe goes missing somewhere between the hippos and the parking lot.
Hauling a lot of stuff? Jumbo lockers, the ones big enough for a real cooler bag, are at North Rentals for $10. Tall lockers are $9 and standard lockers are $8, both at South Rentals. Every price includes a $5 deposit you get back when you return the key the same day.
The real feet-saver is not an entrance at all. It is the train. The Zooline Railroad runs a 20-minute narrated loop of about a mile and a half, rattling through tunnels and past animal habitats, and your $8.95 ticket lets you get off, see an exhibit and climb back on all day. Here is the catch nobody tells you until you are standing on the platform: personal fold-up strollers and zoo-rented strollers may not be taken on the train. If your youngest still rides in one, the train is a loop for the big kids, not a shuttle for the whole family.
### What can you carry through the gate?
More than most families expect. The zoo’s visitor FAQ says guests may bring strollers, small wagons, picnic baskets, coolers, foods and drinks. So yes, you can bring snacks, and yes, you can bring your own water. Fill the bottles at the kitchen sink, slice the apples the night before, and let the cooler ride in the wagon. Glass bottles and alcohol are the two big exceptions.
Both entrances use a screening system called Evolv, and the zoo’s rules and policies say all guests’ bags are subject to search, including backpacks, purses, strollers, wagons and soft-sided coolers. Pack the backpack so the sunscreen and the wipes are on top. You will open it at the gate, and on busy days the FAQ warns there may be some delay at entry. A ten-minute line moves faster when you are not digging for a juice box under a sweatshirt.
There are picnic areas in central parts of the zoo, which is the whole reason the sliced apples are worth it. The grass is cool, the sea lions bark somewhere behind you, and lunch for four costs whatever it cost you at the grocery store. If you would rather buy one treat and refill it, the zoo says you may bring your Zoovenir sipper cups, which are refillable from year to year.
Now the list of what stays in the car. These come straight from the zoo’s prohibited items list:
Dogs or other pets. Service animals are welcome, except in the Cypress Swamp (the 1904 Flight Cage) and the Bird House. Emotional support animals are not allowed inside.
Glass bottles and alcohol. Guests of legal drinking age can purchase alcoholic beverages inside the zoo.
Balloons.
Bicycles. There are bike racks at the entrances.
Skates, skateboards, roller blades and scooters, plus Segways and hoverboards.
Drones, lasers and loud radios.
Costumes and costume masks for anyone 14 and older, except at zoo-sponsored events like Boo at the Zoo.
One more rule that matters for big-family days and cousin trips: children under 14 must be with an adult at all times. And the zoo is tobacco- and smoke-free, e-cigarettes included, so grandpa’s vape stays in the glove box.
### Seven stops worth the walk, bears included
The zoo is too big to see everything with a toddler and a nap clock, so pick a short list and treat anything else as a bonus. These are the stops the zoo’s own pages make the strongest case for, and every one of them is free once you are in.
Grizzly Ridge. Home to Huckleberry and Finley, orphaned grizzly bear siblings from Montana. You watch them through 22 glass-panel windows, and the Cub Crawl is a crawl-through cave where kids may see a bear nose-to-nose.
McDonnell Polar Bear Point. The zoo’s polar bear page names Kallu, a male polar bear, as its resident.
Sea Lion Sound. A 35-foot underwater viewing tunnel through the sea lions’ habitat, so they swim over and around you. No ticket needed to stand in it.
Historic Hill. One of the oldest parts of the zoo, from the 1904 World’s Fair Flight Cage to the Spanish architectural flavor of the 1920s in the Bird House, Primate House and Herpetarium.
River’s Edge. The zoo’s first immersion exhibit, with Asian elephants, Nile hippos and cheetahs.
Red Rocks. Tigers, zebras and giraffes, and Big Cat Country, three open yards that are each almost one-third of an acre.
The Wild. Penguins and puffins at Penguin & Puffin Coast.
Bears are the question half the back seat is asking, so here is the straight answer. Yes, the St. Louis Zoo has bears: the grizzly siblings at Grizzly Ridge and a polar bear at McDonnell Polar Bear Point. Grizzly Ridge sits on the site of the zoo’s historic bear grottos, and the zoo kept three-fifths of the original rockwork, cast from Missouri limestone palisades. Put a hand on the cool glass, watch a bear slide into the pool on the other side, and you are standing where St. Louis kids have watched bears for generations.
Hungry between stops? Get a little St. Louis in the middle of the zoo. East Refreshments, located at the top of Historic Hill, lists toasted ravioli among its zoo favorites, and Hippo Hideaway in River’s Edge offers fresh popcorn you will smell before you see. If the plan was the packed lunch, a single bag of popcorn shared four ways is the cheapest happy moment of the day.
### What does a smart zoo day look like, from first train to last call?
Get there early. The FAQ says keepers work to have animals in their outdoor habitats by 9 a.m., and that some animals are more active in the cooler hours of early morning and early evening. Translation: the first hour is when the big cats pace, the bears move and the paths are still quiet enough to hear the train coming. By late morning you are sharing the glass with three field trips.
Build it around what you want to catch. The Sea Lion Show sells tickets 45 minutes before each show at the booth by Sea Lion Sound, and seating is first-come, first-served in an 811-seat arena. Stingrays at Caribbean Cove and the Sea Lion Show are not open from late fall through early spring, so check both pages before you promise anyone a stingray.
A simple shape that works for most families: park, pay by QR before you forget, walk to the habitat your kids care about most while it is still quiet, ride the train once to rest everyone’s legs, picnic at noon, then do the one paid thing you promised. Leave before the last-entry rush. Nobody remembers the last exhibit they dragged a crying four-year-old through. They remember the bear.
If a grandparent is coming, the rentals page is worth a look before you leave home. Wheelchairs rent for $11 a day and single strollers for $12, first-come, first-served at both entrances, and the zoo says it cannot reserve them in advance. On a busy day, the early family gets the chair.
Already counting down to zoo day? Find the next stop before the kids ask. Browse Zoos on St Louis Near Me Directory to line up the next animal outing for your crew.
If you’re the face painter, the party-rental crew or the family photographer, these are your customers. The same parents planning a zoo day are searching for the birthday party after it, so list your business where they are already looking and get more customers from the families who plan ahead.
### Before you leave the driveway
Three things to do the night before, because the morning will not give you time. Check the hours page for the day’s hours. Charge the phone, since parking is paid by QR and the zoo does not accept cash. And pack the bag in the order the gate will see it: water bottles and snacks on top, sunscreen in the side pocket, no glass bottles.
If you are coming from far enough that an overnight makes sense, we already did the hotel homework, so it is not repeated here. The guide below covers places near the zoo with indoor pools, which is exactly what tired kids want after a day of walking.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does it take to see the whole St. Louis Zoo?
A.  With small kids you will not see all of it in one visit. Current fall hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, except holidays. Pick three or four must-sees, and use the Zooline Railroad, a 20-minute narrated loop with all-day on-off privileges, to rest everyone’s legs.
### Q. Can you bring your own water into the St. Louis Zoo?
A.  Yes. The zoo’s FAQ says guests may bring foods and drinks, along with coolers and picnic baskets. Glass bottles and outside alcohol are prohibited, so bring water in plastic or metal bottles. The zoo also lets you bring refillable Zoovenir sipper cups.
### Q. Does the St. Louis Zoo have bears?
A.  Yes. Grizzly Ridge is home to Huckleberry and Finley, orphaned grizzly siblings from Montana, viewed through 22 glass-panel windows. The zoo’s polar bear page names Kallu, a male polar bear, at McDonnell Polar Bear Point.
### Q. Are there any discounts available for tickets to the Saint Louis Zoo?
A.  Admission is already free, so discounts apply to attractions. The Adventure Pass costs less bought online than in person. Groups of 15 or more can get discounted attraction tickets and Adventure Passes with advance payment. Members of reciprocal AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums may receive a 50% discount on up to four full-price Adventure Passes, bought in person at the Welcome Desks.
### Q. What is the best day to go to the St. Louis Zoo?
A.  The zoo’s FAQ says some of the animals are more active in the cooler hours of early morning and early evening, and on busy days there may be some delay upon entry. Go early, on a day without a field-trip crowd if you can, and remember that Stingrays at Caribbean Cove and the Sea Lion Show are not open from late fall through early spring.

## You Already Paid: Visiting the Missouri Botanical Garden on Free Mornings
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/visiting-the-missouri-botanical-garden-what-to-know
You already paid for your ticket, if your address is in St. Louis City or County. Walk in at 7 a.m. and see what it bought. Gravel crunches under your shoes on a path with nobody else on it. Low sun turns the glass of the Climatron gold, and the air smells like wet mulch. You’re back in the car before lunch with dirt on your shoes and a head that feels rinsed out.
Here is why the gate waves residents through. Since 1971, residents of St. Louis City and County have funded the garden through a property tax district, and the garden says it plainly on its own Zoo-Museum District page: the free admission on Wednesdays and Saturdays before noon is a thank-you for that support. It isn’t a gift from a charity on Shaw Boulevard. You are collecting on something you’ve been paying into for years.
Coming from farther out, say Villa Ridge or Staunton? The same morning is yours too, at the garden’s posted price: $16 general admission for anyone 13 and older, and free for kids 12 and under. City and County residents who miss the free window pay a $6 resident rate instead. Same gravel, same gold glass, a different line on the receipt.
That gap matters the first time a sightseeing pass shows up in your feed. Let’s Roam’s new Top Sights Pass lists the Garden among its picks at $16, and its smallest adult pass, the 3 Sights, costs $72.19 plus tax. If you live in Affton or Florissant, a pass slot spent here buys a gate you could walk through for $6, or for nothing on a Wednesday before noon. Your kids walk through it free through age 12. We ran the numbers further down, at the pass seller’s own prices.
### What day is the Missouri Botanical Garden free?
Wednesday and Saturday, from 7 a.m. to noon, if you live in St. Louis City or St. Louis County and can prove it.
The exact wording on the garden’s homepage is worth reading slowly, because every clause matters. The first two hours, 7 to 9 a.m., are early morning walking hours. Regular opening is 9 a.m. The free resident window runs the whole stretch from 7 a.m. until noon. On Saturdays only, that free admission includes the Doris I. Schnuck Children’s Garden, which itself opens at 9 a.m. On Wednesdays the Children’s Garden is not included. It’s seasonal, too: its final operating day this season is Sunday, November 1, and some of its areas have been off-limits for planned maintenance since Tuesday, October 13.
Then come the four rules that catch people:
You cannot book it online. The garden says the free resident tickets are available onsite for walk-ups only and cannot be reserved online in advance. If you sit at the kitchen table trying to reserve a free Saturday slot, you will not find one. You find it at the counter.
It is subject to availability. The garden’s own words. On a perfect spring Saturday, that is not a technicality.
Bring proof. This is the rule that ends free mornings. You reach the walk-up counter at 7 a.m., the cashier asks for proof of St. Louis City or County residency, and the license in your wallet still shows the apartment you moved out of two years ago. The garden says proof is required, but I could not find a page on its site that lists which documents count. So settle it from the kitchen table the night before: call the garden at (314) 577-5100, the number posted on its homepage, and ask what the counter will take. Then carry a photo ID with your current address, or a second document that shows where you live now.
Bring a card, not cash. The garden accepts cashless payments only, credit or debit. That matters the moment someone in your group turns out to live in Worden or St. Jacob and needs a paid ticket.
And noon is a hard line. The free window closes at noon. If your Saturday starts slow, the free morning is gone before you’ve finished your coffee.
### How much does it cost to visit the Missouri botanical gardens?
Sixteen dollars if you’re 13 or older and your address is outside the City and County. Nothing if you’re 12 or under. Residents pay $6, or $4 at 65 and older, and nothing on those Wednesday and Saturday mornings. So two parents and two kids under 13 from outside the City and County pay $32 at the gate, $16 for each adult, while the same family with a City or County address pays $12, or nothing if they walk up before noon on a Wednesday or Saturday. The extras show up later, usually the moment a kid spots the limestone cave in the Children’s Garden.
Here is every charge a Garden day can run into, from the front gate to the tram, as the Garden lists them:
Festivals and special events carry their own ticket prices, so this table covers a regular Garden day only. Prices change, so check the Garden’s ticket listing before you go.
Coming in from St. Charles or the Metro East more than twice a year? Run the membership math. On its Garden Glow page, the Garden says memberships start at $55 for one adult or $85 for two adults, and always include children 12 and under. Two adults at $16 each pay $32 a visit at the gate, so three visits come to $96, more than the $85 membership, before you count the $5 members get off each adult Garden Glow ticket.
One warning the price list doesn’t carry: skip the private lots nearby. The Garden says vehicles parked on private lots are subject to towing at the vehicle owners’ expense.
### The $72.19 pass and the $6 gate
Let’s Roam now sells a Top Sights Pass for St. Louis. You pick your attractions after you buy, from a list that includes the Gateway Arch tram ride, City Museum, the Garden, the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station, the St. Louis Riverfront Cruise, the St. Louis Cardinals Museum and the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House. Each pass adds one “city adventure”: a self-guided Let’s Roam app scavenger hunt or ghost tour, which its own savings example prices at $28.87. Adults are 12 and up on the pass, children 3 to 11. The 3 Sights pass (two attractions plus the app adventure) is $72.19 for an adult and $67.19 for a child, the 4 Sights is $101.19 and $86.19, and the 5 Sights is $123.19 and $104.19, all plus tax. Here’s how that lands for a Garden morning, at the regular prices Let’s Roam lists itself.
Live in the City or County? Leave the Garden off it. Your gate price is $6, or $4 at 65, and nothing before noon on a Wednesday or Saturday. Put the Garden and the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station on a 3 Sights pass and you pay $72.19 for two tickets that cost $6 plus $29.75, or $35.75, at the door: $36.44 more. Add the $28.87 app hunt as if you’d have bought it anyway, and your $6 Garden ticket, the $29.75 Aquarium and the hunt still come to $64.62, $7.57 less than the $72.19 pass. At $6, your Garden ticket costs less than any attraction on Let’s Roam’s own price list, which makes it the worst possible use of a pass slot.
Bringing kids? A Garden slot buys them nothing. Children 12 and under already walk through the Garden gate free. The ages don’t line up, either: the pass counts anyone 12 and up as an adult, and the Garden lets children 12 and under in free, so a 12-year-old costs you an adult pass for a gate that charges them nothing.
Visiting from out of town? The Garden is one of the cheaper picks. At $16 it’s the third-cheapest attraction on Let’s Roam’s price list, after the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House at $8 and the St. Louis Cardinals Museum at $12. Pair it with the Aquarium and the two tickets cost $16 plus $29.75, or $45.75, against $72.19 for the 3 Sights pass. Even the priciest picks cost less at the door than the pass, tier by tier: the Aquarium and the St. Louis Riverfront Cruise, $29.75 plus $26, come to $55.75 against the $72.19 3 Sights; add City Museum at $20 and it’s $75.75 against the $101.19 4 Sights; add the Gateway Arch tram at $19 and it’s $94.75 against the $123.19 5 Sights. The pass only pulls ahead if you’d also pay $28.87 for one of the company’s app hunts, and then barely: $16 plus $29.75 plus $28.87 is $74.62, just $2.43 more than the $72.19 3 Sights pass.
Let’s Roam’s headline says you can save up to 36%. Its own example gets there by putting two of its app games, a scavenger hunt and a ghost tour at $28.87 each, inside a regular price of $113.49. And for winter visitors, one more catch: the riverboats at the Gateway Arch run March through November only, so a December pass loses the cruise, the second-priciest pick on the list.
We take the pass apart attraction by attraction, kids’ ages and all, in our guide to the must-see attractions in St. Louis.
### How long does a real visit actually take?
The garden doesn’t post a single answer, but its own tours give you the yardstick: the private guided walking tours it offers groups run approximately two hours, and the narrated tram tour covers the grounds in approximately 25 to 30 minutes.
The tram is the sampler, a half hour on a bench seat with a narrator pointing at buildings you’ll want to come back to. The walk is the meal. The classic first-visit mistake is trying to see everything and seeing nothing.
The free window from 7 a.m. to noon is more than enough. The trick is the order. Spend the early walking hours outdoors while the light is low: the loop around the lake in the Japanese Garden, the beds near the Kemper Center. Save the Climatron for later, when you want to be inside anyway.
Want a docent without booking anything? From November through March, the walking tour that comes with admission runs once a day, at 11 a.m., and the garden caps each group at 10 to 12 visitors, so get to the start a few minutes early with your gloves already on.
One more clock to know: the garden is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, and last entry is 4:30 p.m. An afternoon visit that starts an hour before closing is a walk, not a visit. The garden is closed on Thanksgiving and Christmas Day.
### The weekends the free morning quietly disappears
This is the rule that sends people home annoyed. The homepage says free and early morning hours do not apply on holiday or event weekends. Read the festival pages and you see what that means in practice.
On Japanese Festival weekend, Labor Day weekend, festival admission is required for garden entry, and the garden says Saturday morning walking hours and tram tours will not take place. The taiko drums are pounding, and the free Saturday is off.
During the Best of Missouri Market in October, market admission is required for garden entry, and the garden spells it out: St. Louis City and County resident discounts do not apply, and tram service and Saturday walking hours do not take place.
The pattern is simple. The garden’s big festival weekends are exactly the weekends your resident perk is switched off. So if your whole reason for going on a Saturday is that it’s free, check the signature events schedule the night before. If a festival is on, either buy the festival ticket and enjoy it, or come Wednesday instead. Wednesday mornings are the other half of the deal, and the easiest one to forget.
Priced by age, address and hour
### What is the entry fee for the Missouri Botanical Garden?
Anywhere from $0 to $16 a person at the gate. Three things move it: your age (12 and under free, $16 from 13 up), your address (St. Louis City and County residents pay $6, or $4 at 65 and older, with proof of residency) and the clock (residents walk in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon).
### What is the best month to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden?
April is the month worth the drive, with early May a close second. The garden’s own bloom calendar stacks up in those weeks: azaleas and rhododendrons, flowering dogwoods, peonies and viburnums all peak in April and May, magnolias in March and April, and the flowering cherries from March through April. Iris peaks in early May.
Here’s the part that’s easy to miss: spring is planted in the fall. On its seasonal operations page, the garden says 70,000 to 75,000 bulbs are planted for the next spring display. The tulip bed you photograph in April went into cold ground the fall before.
But April is not the only right answer. It depends on what you want to feel:
If you want heat and color, go in late summer. The water lilies peak in August and September, and the garden says their platter-like leaves can grow up to 75 inches wide. Stand at the edge of the pool on a humid afternoon and the air smells like warm water and cut grass.
If you want quiet, go in fall. Ornamental grasses go showy, roses and water lilies hang on into early autumn, and the annual beds are swapped for mums and pansies. The witch hazel starts blooming in October and keeps going through April.
If you want to escape winter, go during the Orchid Show. It runs from the end of January into March, is included with garden admission and puts hundreds of blooming orchids on display from a collection of well over 5,000 plants. Walk in out of a gray winter afternoon and the warm, damp air hits your face first.
If it’s the holiday lights you want, Garden Glow fills the grounds with millions of lights on select nights from November 14 to January 2 this season, and it sells its own ticket: $22 to $25 for nonmember adults depending on the night, $6 to $12 for kids 12 and under, and $2 more for adult tickets bought for the same night at or after 4:30 p.m. Wood smoke drifts from the s’more fire pits at the Central Axis and Linnean Plaza. Our guide to the best Christmas lights in St. Louis sets it next to the rest of the city’s displays.
Your property tax already bought this morning. Spend it before noon.
### What should you see first if you only have one morning?
Our pick for a first morning: the Japanese Garden, then the Climatron, then the Linnean House. Add the Children’s Garden if you have kids and it’s a Saturday between April and October.
It helps to know what you’re walking through. The garden was founded in 1859, it is one of the nation’s oldest botanical gardens in continuous operation, and it is a National Historic Landmark. The 79 acres under your sneakers are the public face of a center for botanical research, which is why a slow stroll here teaches you more about your own backyard than a season of trial and error.
The Japanese Garden, Seiwa-en. The garden’s page calls it a 14-acre Japanese Garden, one of the largest in North America, dedicated in 1977. Its heart is a four-acre lake, and the garden calls the place a “garden of pure, clear harmony and peace.” Raked gravel stands in for waves. Waterfalls stand in for mountain streams. On a Wednesday or Saturday walking morning, do the whole loop before the 9 a.m. regular opening.
The Climatron. This is the glass dome. According to the garden’s history of the building, it was the first geodesic dome used as a conservatory, opened on October 1, 1960, rises 70 feet at the center and spans 175 feet across, with no columns inside. More than 2,800 plants grow under it, including banana, cacao and coffee. The temperature runs from 64 degrees at night to 85 during the day, with average humidity of 85 percent. On a cold morning your glasses fog the second the door closes behind you, and the air tastes like wet soil.
The Linnean House. Built in 1882, it is the only greenhouse left at the garden from Henry Shaw’s own day, says the garden. Its camellia collection dates to the 1920s, and marble busts of Linnaeus and fellow scientists Thomas Nuttall and Asa Gray have looked out from its south-facing front since 1883. Inside the old brick walls, it feels like the garden’s attic in the best way.
If you have more time: Tower Grove House, Shaw’s 1849 country home, is open April through October, Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and is included with garden admission in season. The Children’s Garden covers nearly two acres west of the Climatron, with a limestone cave, Spelunker’s Slide, a steamboat and a tree house. Kids under 14 must be with an adult the whole time.
### Bring a question home: the plants that actually grow here
The most useful room at the garden is an easy one to walk past. The William T. Kemper Center for Home Gardening sits among 23 demonstration gardens spread over 8.5 acres, and inside, at the walk-in Plant Doctor Desk, expert garden staff and Master Gardener volunteers are available in person to answer your gardening questions. This walk-in service is available free with admission. From April through October it’s open seven days a week, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. From November through March it’s Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and closed weekends.
Bring a photo of the sad shrub by your front steps, or a leaf in a sandwich bag.
For the best plants to grow in Missouri, start with the garden’s Plants of Merit, plants it selects for outstanding quality and dependable performance in the lower Midwest, which grow consistently well in Missouri. To be chosen, a plant has to be easy to grow, not known to be invasive here, resistant or tolerant to diseases and insects, good-looking and reasonably easy to buy. The Plants of Merit page lists little bluestem ‘Standing Ovation,’ Carolina silverbell, the ‘Queen of Night’ tulip and the BOBO panicle hydrangea among its selections.
Can’t make it in? The Kemper Center page lists a phone line, 314-577-5143, with hours Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to noon. If the job is bigger than one shrub, our guide to what a gardener costs and does in St. Louis walks through it: shortlist two or three local pros, interview them, tell them what you want the yard to do, and compare what each one says they’ll actually deliver.
Turn the free morning into a two-stop day. Find another garden or green space for the drive home through Botanical Gardens on St Louis Near Me Directory, and pick the one on your side of town.
If you run the garden center, the nursery or the two-person landscaping crew people call after a morning like this, these are your customers. They leave the Kemper beds with a plant name on their phone and a yard that suddenly looks bare, and a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory helps you get more customers from that drive home, so see what the Gold plan includes before the spring rush.
### A free Saturday morning, start to finish
If you live in the City or County and want to try it this week, here is the whole plan.
The night before, check the signature events schedule. If a festival is on, the free Saturday is off.
Put your license, or a document with your current City or County address, in your pocket. Add a debit or credit card for anyone who isn’t a resident.
Arrive a little before 7 a.m. Park in the main lot, or the free overflow lots at Shaw and South Vandeventer.
Walk the Japanese Garden loop first, while the light is low.
From April through October, take the kids to the Children’s Garden when it opens at 9 a.m.; residents get it free on Saturdays until noon.
Duck into the Climatron mid-morning, then the Linnean House.
Be out, or be ready to pay, by noon.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to visit the Missouri botanical gardens?
A.  General admission is $16 for ages 13 and up, and children 12 and under are free. St. Louis City and County residents pay $6, or $4 at 65 and older, with proof of residency, and get in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon. Parking is free. Garden Glow and festivals are priced separately.
### Q. Do you have to pay to park at the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  No. The Garden says there is no charge for parking, and when the main lot is full, the overflow lots at the corner of Shaw Boulevard and South Vandeventer Avenue are free too. Stay out of the private lots nearby, because the Garden warns that cars parked there can be towed at the owner’s expense.
### Q. How long does it take to tour the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  Plan on a morning. The Garden’s private guided walking tours run approximately two hours, and the narrated tram tour takes approximately 25 to 30 minutes in the months it runs. A full morning lets you see the Japanese Garden, the Climatron and the Linnean House without rushing, and it fits inside the resident free window.
### Q. What is the best month to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  April, with early May close behind. Azaleas, dogwoods, peonies and viburnums peak in April and May, and the cherries bloom from March through April. For water lilies, go in August or September. For orchids in winter, go during the Orchid Show, which runs from the end of January into March.
### Q. What are the must-see attractions at the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  Start with the 14-acre Japanese Garden, then the Climatron, the first geodesic dome used as a conservatory, then the Linnean House, built in 1882. With kids, add the Doris I. Schnuck Children’s Garden between April and October. Tower Grove House, Henry Shaw’s 1849 home, is open in season and included with admission.
### Q. What’s going on at the botanical gardens in St. Louis?
A.  This season it’s Garden Glow, on select nights from November 14 to January 2, with its own ticket. The Orchid Show follows from the end of January into March, included with admission, and the Whitaker Music Festival brings free Wednesday evening concerts every summer. The full list is on the signature events page.
### Q. Can you bring outside food into the Missouri Botanical Garden?
A.  No. The Garden doesn’t allow outside food, picnics or coolers anywhere on its property, except during the Whitaker Music Festival. Refillable water bottles are welcome, so fill one at the kitchen sink before you leave. If the kids want a picnic, the Garden points visitors to Tower Grove Park, just south of the Garden.
### Q. What are the best plants to grow in Missouri?
A.  The garden’s Plants of Merit, chosen for dependable performance in the lower Midwest, must be easy to grow, not known to be invasive and resistant or tolerant to diseases and insects. Its selections include little bluestem ‘Standing Ovation,’ Carolina silverbell and the BOBO panicle hydrangea. At the Kemper Center’s Plant Doctor Desk, Master Gardener volunteers answer questions, free with admission.

## You Paid for the Sewer Anyway: RV Parks Near St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/rv-parks-near-st-louis-hookups-costs-and-rules
$35 a night, sewer included, whether you use it or not. Missouri State Parks puts it in one flat sentence on its camping rates page: rates are charged on the basis of available utilities, whether used or not. Back a weekend trailer onto that gravel pad with full fresh tanks and an empty black tank, run nothing but a box fan, and you still bought the sewer.
And you can only buy so many nights of it. Missouri State Parks limits camping to any 15 days within a 30-consecutive-day period, and Illinois will enforce a 14-day maximum stay within a 30-day window. So do one thing today: open the Cuivre River camping page, pick your dates, and choose the post color by the hookups you will actually use, not by the size of the rig. Pick the right post and a state park night within reach of the city runs $15 to $35. Pick the wrong one and you pay for pipes you never touch.
Or you pick a post too small. A July afternoon five minutes from the Gateway Arch, the dinette cushions hot enough to stick to the backs of your legs, gravel dust tracked across the floor. The roof air is grinding away when somebody punches popcorn into the microwave. Then a flat click from the pedestal, and the rig goes quiet: no fan, no hum, just cicadas and the smell of half-popped kernels. You walk out on hot gravel to flip the breaker back, and you do it again at supper. That click is what a 30-amp site sounds like when you ask it for too much.
### What does an RV park cost per month in St. Louis?
At a public park near St. Louis, you cannot buy a month at all: Missouri State Parks limits camping to any 15 days within a 30-consecutive-day period, and Illinois will enforce a 14-day maximum stay within a 30-day window. A real monthly rate comes from a private RV park that sets its own price, while the public option tops out at 15 days.
Illinois is blunter about it in the rule-change FAQ it published at the end of August: its campgrounds are designed for recreational purposes, not as a place of residence, and private campgrounds are a better fit for people using an RV as a residence. The one public crack in that wall within an easy drive is Eldon Hazlet State Recreation Area in Illinois, which the state lists with 56 long-term campsites. A designated long-term site allows 30 days within a 45-day period, not a full year.
For a true month, you are calling private parks. Cahokia RV Parque, just across the river from St. Louis, lists $860 a month for a 50-amp site and $810 for 30 amp, with water, sewer, electric and trash included, and it books monthly stays by phone at (618) 332-7700. Safari RV Park says it is 10 minutes from downtown and lists $650 a month for 50 amp, but its rate page adds that the monthly rate includes electric up to $200.00 per month. The cheaper sticker is not always the cheaper month, not in a July when the roof air never shuts off. Call both today, Safari at 877-271-0954, and tell each one exactly what you are bringing: the rig’s length, the amp service it needs, how many nights, how many dogs, and whether you work from the rig. Ask what you owe past the electric cap, whether there is a minimum stay, and what is at the pedestal. Then hold their answers up against the public ceiling of 15 nights in 30 in Missouri, or 30 in 45 on an Illinois long-term site.
Timing changes the math too. Cuivre River’s on-season runs April 15 through Oct. 31, and from Nov. 1 the same sewer/electric/water site drops from $35 to $29 and a 30-amp electric site from $27 to $23, according to the park’s rate sheet. The trade is comfort. In the off-season the showerhouse is closed, and drinking water at that park comes from one frost-free spigot at Campsite 69. You will fill jugs there in November with your knuckles going red, and you will remember exactly what the on-season rate was buying.
### You pay for the post, not the plug
Walk a Missouri state park loop at dusk and look at the short posts with the numbers on them. Each one carries a color bar, and the state’s campsite guide decodes it: green is a basic site, yellow is electric, blue is electric/water, red is sewer/electric/water. That stripe is the price tag. At Cuivre River this season, basic runs $15, 30-amp electric $27, electric/water $32 and sewer/electric/water $35.
So the cheapest smart move is to match the stripe to the trip, not to the rig. A family on a three-night weekend that rolls in with full fresh tanks and dumps on the way out does not need the red post. A retiree staying all 15 nights, showering in the rig and running the washer, wants red and should not feel bad about it.
Missouri charges $6.50 to reserve on the web and $8 through the call center, $5.25 to change a reservation and $10 to cancel, on top of losing the original fee. You can book up to 12 months ahead now, up from six months, which matters if you want one particular 50-amp site on one particular weekend. Anyone 65 or older, people with disabilities, and current and former military get $2 a night off, but they have to ask for it at the time of payment and show ID. Ask; do not wait to be offered.
One rule catches more Friday-night arrivals than any fee. At Cuivre River, the campground gate closes at 10 p.m. in the on-season and at 8 p.m. in the off-season. Leave work late, hit traffic on the way out, and you can meet a closed gate in the dark with a trailer behind you and nowhere to turn it. Check the gate time for the exact park you booked, and if you were eyeing Halloween weekend there, camping is unavailable Oct. 30 through Nov. 1 this fall for a managed deer hunt.
### What does 30 versus 50 amp mean at the pedestal?
Pull the shore cord out of its bay and look at the end of it. Three prongs means 30 amp: one hot, one neutral, one ground, and up to 3,600 watts. Four prongs means 50 amp: two hots, one neutral, one ground, and up to 12,000 watts split across two legs, according to this plain explainer on RV connections. The extra hot leg is the whole difference. On 30 amp, running an air conditioner, a microwave and a hair dryer at once can trip the breaker. On 50, you can run them together and keep talking.
At a Missouri state park, a 50-amp electric site gives you both a 30-amp and a 50-amp supply at the same post, and the state counts more than 1,200 campsites with 50-amp service. That means a 30-amp trailer can still use a 50-amp site’s 30-amp receptacle. It does not mean you should pay for the bigger site when a 30-amp one is open and you only have three prongs. Before you plug in anywhere, flip the pedestal breaker off, seat the plug all the way, then flip it on. You will hear the hum come up and feel the rig wake around you.
One more pedestal fact that costs people a weekend: at Missouri state parks, water at electric/water and full-hookup sites is only available during the park’s on-season. A blue or red post in December can still have a dry spigot. Fill your fresh tank before you leave home.
### What changes at Illinois state parks on January 1?
If your weekend spot is across the river in Illinois, the prices you know are about to move. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources is rewriting its camping rules and fees effective January 1, and its own FAQ says the last fee increase came in 2008, with a target of roughly 40 percent this time. Under the new fee schedule, an electric site runs $28 a night ($14 camping plus $14 utility), a premium electric site runs $35, and every online or call-center reservation carries a $10 processing fee that you do not get back.
Two smaller changes will hit you on a Sunday more than the price will. The dump station fee goes to $10. And the 14-day maximum within 30 days gets enforced year-round, with only designated long-term sites allowed 30 days within 45. Think about the dump station line just before checkout, the hose already uncoiled in your gloved hand, the trailer behind you idling, a ranger walking the loop for the turnover. Plan to be pulling out early.
The part that does not change is the best part. The Illinois DNR does not charge an entrance fee to any state owned or operated land, and its FAQ says Illinois is one of seven states with no park entry fee. Whether you are rolling in from Pocahontas or Germantown or a driveway off Cherokee Street, the gate is open and the site fee is the whole bill.
### Where can you park an RV for free near St. Louis?
Missouri’s conservation areas cost nothing to camp on. MDC says more than 300 of its conservation areas offer camping, all camping on conservation areas is free, and most of it is first come, first served. The catch is right there on the same page: no RV hookups are provided at any department area, and you should expect to bring your own water. Some areas have fire rings, picnic tables and latrines. Many have nothing but gravel, trees and a sky full of stars you cannot see from the Central West End.
Free comes with its own clock. Campers can stay up to 14 consecutive days in any 30-day period and are limited to 30 total camping days in a calendar year on all department lands. Some areas also change their camping rules during firearm hunting seasons, so read the specific area’s page before you go. Bring a full fresh tank, an empty black tank and a backup spot, because the pad you wanted may already have someone’s camp chairs on it.
Store parking lots are a different thing entirely. Overnight parking at big-box stores is decided store by store, and I could not find a written, chain-wide policy from any retailer that I could quote to you. The only answer that counts is the one from the store you are standing in front of. Walk in, ask for the manager on duty, ask whether one night in the far corner of the lot is OK, and get a name. Then act like a guest: one night, no awning, no chairs, no generator, gone in the morning.
Fried catfish tastes better after backing a trailer in on the first try.
### Is it cheaper to live in an RV park or an apartment?
Sometimes, and the only way to know is to price the whole month, not the site. An RV park’s monthly quote is one line. Electric may be billed on top. Propane, the dump runs, insurance on the rig, the loan payment on the rig and the truck that pulls it all sit outside that quote, and an apartment lease usually rolls more of the basics into the rent. Write both columns out on paper at the kitchen table before you decide. The public parks will not be your loophole, either: as covered above, Missouri caps a stay at 15 days in 30 and Illinois at 14 in 30, with long-term sites at 30 in 45.
The hotel question is easier. If you already own the rig, a $27 to $35 state park site near St. Louis is very hard for a hotel room to beat on price, and you sleep in your own sheets with the windows open to the cicadas. If you are renting the rig for the trip, the rental is the real cost, and the site is the cheap part. We broke that math down separately, along with the other first-trip questions:
