### What is the longest RV allowed in state parks?
The limit is the pad, per the Missouri State Parks campsite capacity rules. All wheeled equipment and vehicles must fit on the parking pad unless that park’s own rules allow parking on the road or the grass, so a long fifth wheel fits where the pad fits it and nowhere else. Look up the length listed for the specific site in the reservation system, then add the truck.
The rule that surprises bigger families is the unit count. A typical site allows two sleeping units, only one of which can be wheeled, plus two non-sleeping vehicles and six people. So a motor home and a camping trailer cannot share one site, however short they are. A family campsite doubles that capacity, and it is often a cleaner fix than booking two separate sites and paying two reservation fees.
### The rules that get you a knock on the door at 10 p.m.
Campground etiquette near St. Louis is mostly written down, which helps, because the people next to you are close enough to hear you open a bag of chips. Missouri’s camping rules set quiet hours from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and every noise-making device has to be powered off then. Generators are generally not allowed during quiet hours, and some parks do not allow them at all. Non-camping visitors have to be out of the campground by 10 p.m., so the friends who drove out from Soulard for burgers need to know that before the second round.
The rest are the ones that get campers a quiet word from a host. Do not drain sewage or gray water on the ground, even the dishwater. Do not tie lanterns, clotheslines, leashes or bungee cords to trees; a hammock is allowed only with a 1-inch nylon strap. Do not leave personal property unattended longer than 24 hours. Keep the trailer and every vehicle on the road or the pad. Check-in begins at 3 p.m., checkout is at 2 p.m. in Missouri, and all the trash leaves with you. Wave at the people across the loop. You will be borrowing a sewer hose fitting from one of them someday.
Ready to stop guessing what a month on a full hookup really costs? Browse RV Parks on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, and call them with your length, your amps and your dates in hand.
If you’re the RV park owner or the mobile RV tech who fixes the dead pedestal, the campers reading this are already looking for you. Put your sites and your service where they search and get more customers: list your business for $29.75 a month, paid annually.
### Frequently asked questions about RV parks near St. Louis
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for RV travel?
A.  It is an informal rule of thumb, not a park regulation: drive no more than 300 miles a day, arrive at your site by 3 p.m. and stay three nights at each campground. Arriving by 3 p.m. lines up neatly with the 3 p.m. check-in at Missouri state parks, and it keeps you well ahead of a 10 p.m. campground gate.
### Q. What is the 10-year rule at RV parks?
A.  It is an informal policy some private RV parks use to turn away RVs older than 10 years, and some use 15 years instead. A poll of 94 RV parks reported by RV Lifestyle found only 3% enforce a strict 10-year rule, while 78% judge older RVs at their discretion. If your rig is older, ask the park whether it is enforced and offer to send recent photos.
### Q. What does FF mean at a campground?
A.  FF is informal shorthand for first come, first served: the site cannot be reserved and goes to whoever arrives and claims it that day. At Missouri state parks, read the post itself; a site without the reservable symbol is first come, first served only, and a vacant card on a reservable post means it is open for walk-up registration.
### Q. Can you park your RV in a Walmart parking lot for the night?
A.  Ask the store you are standing in front of. Go inside, ask the manager on duty, and get a name. If the answer is yes, keep it to one night with no chairs, no awning and no generator, and be gone in the morning.
### Q. Where is the best place to park an RV for free?
A.  All camping on MDC conservation areas is free and mostly first come, first served, but there are no RV hookups at any department area and you bring your own water. Stays are capped at 14 consecutive days in any 30-day period.
### Q. What is the longest RV allowed in state parks?
A.  Every wheeled vehicle must fit on the site’s parking pad, so check the length listed for the exact site in the reservation system and count the tow vehicle too.

## Your Size 7 Started Here: Shopping for Women’s Clothes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/shopping-for-womens-clothes-in-st-louis-fit-fabric-and-quality
The zipper stalls at your ribs. You hold your breath, tug once more, and hear the little metal teeth grind. Out past the curtain the hangers scrape along the rail, someone laughs at the register, and you are standing under that flat white fitting-room light in a size you have worn for years, feeling like your own body has changed the rules overnight.
It hasn’t. Twenty minutes earlier, on a different rack in the same store, the same number slid on with room to spare. The tag isn’t measuring you, and it never was. Here’s the twist most people in this city have never heard: that odd little number started here. Washington University’s newsroom, citing the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, reports that in 1934 St. Louis manufacturers became the first to market juniors’ sizes, such as 5, 7 and 9. They were cut to sell dresses to a young customer, not to measure anybody.
You can still walk on the proof. Down the center of Washington Avenue, the old garment district where sidewalks once filled with window-shoppers and buyers, the American Planning Association describes a zipper-and-stitch-like paving pattern lit at night by LED buttons. A zipper, sewn into the street. So when the one at your ribs sticks, remember who wrote the number on that tag. The fastest way out of the knot in your chest is to stop asking the tag anything and start asking your hands.
### Where can I buy clothes that are actually good quality in St. Louis?
Buy good-quality clothes from shops that let you touch the cloth, turn a piece inside out and try it on without a rush, because quality lives in the seams, not the price tag. In St. Louis, two shops to start with: Assassin Vintage at 3156 Cherokee Street and Rushmore Boutique at 4742 McPherson Ave. in the Central West End.
Before you pay for anything, give it ninety seconds in the fitting room. Squeeze a fistful of the fabric and let go: good cloth springs back, cheap cloth stays crumpled like a paper bag. Turn it inside out and tug gently across the side seam: if you see light between the stitches, it will split. Then flip to the fiber tag: federal labeling rules make it list each fiber by percentage of weight, and a tag that says 40 percent cotton can legally hold anywhere from 37 percent to 43 percent. Three checks, a minute and a half, and the price tag stops doing your thinking for you.
On Cherokee Street, Assassin Vintage at 3156 Cherokee sells men’s and women’s clothing from the early 1900s through the 1980s, and every piece is washed, mended and steamed before it hits the floor. So the dress you lift off the rail is already soft and clean in your hands. Turn it inside out. A seam that has held for decades tells you more about quality than any tag ever will. Then check the pockets. Co-owner Kay Miller says she gets excited when she finds a piece of history in one: ticket stubs, matchbooks.
Over in the Central West End, Rushmore Boutique sits at 4742 McPherson, next door to Pass The Past Coffee & Vintage. It sells nothing online, so every blouse has to win you over in your hands, and the shop says so out loud: “We were wearing cotton before it was cool” and “Better construction means we can love it for longer.” Fist, seam, tag, right there at the rail. Time your visit: a new collection lands on Wednesday of the first full week of each month, with a smaller drop around the 15th. Sizes mostly run Small to Large, so call ahead if you need bigger, and on Sunday the paid parking out front is free.
A high price buys you a nicer bag at the register and, sometimes, better fabric. It does not promise straight seams. A cheap blouse can be beautifully made, and an expensive one can have a hem that waves like a flag after the second wash. The only way to know is to look, and you are allowed to look. Nobody at a good shop in the Central West End or on South Grand will blink if you flip a jacket over and run your thumb along the inside of the seam. Most of them will respect it.
So here is what to do this afternoon. Drop a soft tape measure in your purse, walk into one of those two shops, and in the first fitting room turn a blouse inside out. Pinch the side seam with both hands and pull gently across it. If you see light between the stitches, hang it back up. If the seam stays tight and flat, and the cloth springs back after you squeeze it in your fist, you are holding something worth the money. For the wider map of shops, tailors and return policies, see our guide to shopping for clothes in St. Louis.
### Why does your size 7 fit on one rack and not the next?
Because there is no number you can trust from one label to the next, and there never really has been. Each brand writes its own size chart, cuts to its own idea of a customer, and then prints whatever number it likes on the tag. Two size 8s can differ at the waist by more than you would ever guess from the outside.
Those juniors’ sizes from the top of this page came out of a hunch, not a ruler. According to Washington University’s history of the juniors’ dress, it started with a 1929 student fashion show, after the merchandise manager of a St. Louis department store was struck by how little clothing was designed for high-school and college-age women. Eight student dresses went into production, the sales blew past every expectation, and the juniors’ dress was born. By 1949, the same Washington University history says, more than 250 manufacturers employed 20,000 workers in the city’s garment trade.
Hold that in your head the next time you squint at a tag under a buzzing fitting-room bulb. The sizes St. Louis sent out into the world were a marketing idea from the start: a way to speak to a young customer, not a ruler.
The federal government did try to pin women’s sizes down. The old National Bureau of Standards published PS 42-70, a Voluntary Product Standard called “Body Measurements for the Sizing of Women’s Patterns and Apparel,” in September 1971. Notice the word voluntary. Today its successor, NIST, says plainly that it “is no longer involved in any activities related to apparel-size standards.” Nobody is checking whether one company’s 8 matches another’s. That gap is where vanity sizing lives: a label is free to flatter you with a smaller number if it thinks you will buy more.
So the next time the zipper sticks, say it out loud if it helps: the number was invented to sell a dress. It was never a verdict on you. Bring a soft tape measure in your purse, know your bust, waist and hip in inches, and compare them to the brand’s own chart. Then let the mirror and the fabric decide.
### Turn it inside out: the fitting-room test that tells you more than the price tag
There is a guide for the people who judge 4-H clothing projects at the fair, New Mexico State University’s “Judging Clothing Projects,” and it reads like a secret shopping list. Among the things they score are “No loose threads or fraying seam edges,” “Correct grain lines,” and “Attractive matching and placement of plaids or stripes.” You can run the same test on a store-bought blouse in about the time it takes to read this section.
Start with the fabric, before you even look at the mirror. Close your fist around a handful of it for a few seconds, then let go. Good cloth springs back with soft creases that relax. Cheap cloth holds the crumple like a paper bag. Hold a single layer up to the fitting-room light: if you can read the shape of your fingers through a blouse that is not meant to be sheer, it will be see-through in daylight and thin by spring.
Then turn it inside out. This is where a garment tells the truth.
Seams. Look along the side seams and under the arms. The stitching should be straight and even, with no puckering and no fraying edges. Tug gently across a seam with both hands. If you see light between the stitches, it will split.
Seam allowance. A little extra fabric folded inside the seam means a tailor can let it out later. A seam trimmed right down to the stitching cannot grow with you.
Stripes and plaids. Where two pieces meet, at the side seam or the center front, the pattern should line up. When it doesn’t, someone cut fast to save cloth, and they probably rushed everything else too.
Grain. The fabric’s threads should run straight up and down the body. If the side seam twists toward the front while the garment hangs on the hanger, it was cut off grain, and it will twist more every time you wash it.
Buttons and buttonholes. The judges’ checklist looks for buttons “sewn on with a shank, if required”: a little stem of thread that lifts the button so the fabric can lie flat behind it. Buttonholes should be dense and tidy, with no threads sprouting. Check for a spare button sewn inside. It is a small sign someone cared.
Lining. In a jacket, skirt or dress, the lining should lie smooth and not pull. Put your arms forward like you are reaching for the steering wheel. If the lining tugs at your shoulders, the whole garment will.
Hems. From the outside, the hem stitching should be close to invisible. A deep hem gives you room to lengthen later; a skimpy one does not.
Last, move in it. Sit on the little fitting-room bench. Lift your arms. Bend like you are picking up a grandchild or a bag of groceries. Good clothes move with you and settle back when you stand. Bad ones ride up, gape at the buttons or leave a red line at your waist. The mirror shows you how it looks standing still. Your body tells you how it will feel at four in the afternoon.
Somewhere a shop owner is answering email at midnight. She could hire help.
### What do the fabric and care labels legally have to tell you?
That little white tag scratching the back of your neck? Under the FTC’s textile rules, the label has to list “The generic names and percentages by weight of the constituent fibers” for any fiber making up 5 percent or more of the garment, in order from most to least.
Here is the detail almost nobody knows. Those percentages are allowed to be off. The same rule lets the real fiber content vary by up to 3 percent of the total fiber weight from what the label says. Its own example: where the label says a fiber is present at 40 percent, the real amount may run from 37 percent to 43 percent. So when two sweaters both claim a little cashmere, a few points either way is within the law, and your fingertips are the better judge of which one feels richer.
The care label has rules too. Under the FTC’s Care Labeling Rule, a care label is a permanent tag with regular care instructions, attached so it will not separate from the garment. And the maker has to warn you before you buy if a piece cannot be cleaned by any method without being harmed. Read that tag in the fitting room, not at home. If a silky work blouse says dry clean only, add that cost to the price in your head before you fall for it.
On a humid St. Louis July afternoon, waiting for a bus with the air hanging like a wet towel, you will feel the fiber named on that label on your back long before you think about it.
### How can you find your own style when every rack shouts something different?
Start with your own closet, not a store. Pull out the three pieces you reach for every week and lay them on the bed. Then pull out the one thing that still has its tags on. The favorites are your style. The one with tags is the trap you fall into. Look for what the favorites share: a color, a neckline, a fabric that feels a certain way against your skin, a length that lets you walk to the car without tugging.
Then shop for more of that, on purpose. Take a photo of your favorite outfit and keep it on your phone. When something on a rack catches your eye, hold it up next to the photo. Would it live happily with the clothes you already love? If the answer is no, it is somebody else’s style, however good it looks on the hanger.
One stylist school describes the 3-3-3 rule as 3 tops, 3 bottoms and 3 layers, like jackets or cardigans, which it says can make up to 27 different outfits. A shirtmaker’s version swaps the layers for shoes: three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes, and it suggests starting with clothes you already own rather than buying nine new things. Whichever one you use, the point is the same: nine pieces that all get along will teach you more about your style in a week than a full rack will in a year.
If you would rather have a second set of eyes, a personal stylist can help, and our guide to hiring a personal shopper in St. Louis covers how to choose one. Shortlist two or three, talk to each about how you dress now and how you want to feel, tell them what you want to spend, and compare what each one says they will actually do for you.
### Where should an older woman shop for clothes in St. Louis?
At any age, shop where you can try things on slowly and where alterations are close by. That matters more after 60 than at 25, not because there are rules about what older women can wear, but because bodies shift in ways that sizing never planned for. A waist thickens while the hips stay put. Shoulders round a little. Upper arms want a sleeve. None of that means you have to give up color, prints or a great pair of earrings. It means fit comes first.
The fitting-room test above matters even more here. Look for soft, substantial fabrics that skim instead of cling, a little stretch that springs back when you pull it, pull-on waists with a flat front, and necklines you do not have to keep adjusting. Buy for the shoulders, because shoulders are hard to alter, and let a tailor take in the rest. If a dress fits everywhere except the length, that is an easy fix. If it pulls across the back, walk away.
Small independent shops are often the best fit for this, because the owner will pull three things in your size and stand outside the curtain while you try them. Whether you live in the city or drive in from Breckenridge Hills or Pierron for the afternoon, plan a day on one street, like the Central West End or South Grand, so you can walk, rest over coffee and come back for the piece you keep thinking about.

How to buy shoes that actually fit in St. Louis
Your next favorite blouse is already hanging in a shop with a quiet fitting room. Browse Women’s Clothing on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick a shop or two, and go turn something inside out.
If you’re the boutique owner who stocks well-made pieces and knows every hem on the floor, say so where shoppers are looking. Women hunting for quality are searching right now, and a free audit shows you who they find instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for clothing?
A.  It depends on who you ask. One common version picks 3 tops, 3 bottoms and 3 layers such as jackets or cardigans, which a stylist school says can make up to 27 outfits; another uses three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes. Either way, it is a short challenge to show how far a few pieces that work together can stretch.
### Q. How can I find out what my clothing style is?
A.  Look at what you already wear. Lay out the pieces you reach for every week and find what they share, a color, a neckline, a fabric or a length, then shop for more of that. The clothes in your closet with the tags still on show you what to stop buying.
### Q. What’s my size in women’s clothing?
A.  It changes by brand. NIST says it “is no longer involved in any activities related to apparel-size standards,” so no one checks one label against another. Measure your bust, waist and hips in inches with a soft tape, compare them to each brand’s own size chart, and trust the fit in the fitting room over the number on the tag.
### Q. Where do most boutiques buy their clothes?
A.  Many don’t make anything; they curate. Rushmore Boutique in the Central West End says plainly that it does not make its clothes and instead looks for “the sweet spot of specialness + quality + value” in every piece it chooses. Ask the owner where a piece came from, then turn it inside out and let the seams back up the answer.
### Q. What’s better, 100% cotton or 100% polyester?
A.  Neither wins everywhere. Read the fiber label in the fitting room, then hold the fabric against the inside of your wrist and squeeze a handful in your fist. On a muggy St. Louis summer day, choose the one that feels cool on your skin and springs back after the squeeze.
### Q. Where should a 60 year old woman shop for clothes?
A.  Wherever she can try things on without hurry and get alterations nearby. Small independent shops are often a good fit, because the owner can pull pieces in your size and talk you through fabric and cut. Buy for the shoulders, choose fabrics that skim rather than cling, and let a tailor handle the rest.
### Q. What to wear as a 70 year old woman?
A.  Whatever makes you feel like yourself, cut to fit the body you have now. Soft, substantial fabrics, sleeves you like, waists that do not pinch and shoes you can walk in all day are a good base.

## Locked Pantry Door? Food Pantries Open Today in St. Louis, Day by Day
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/food-pantries-open-today-in-st-louis
8:15 a.m. on a Wednesday, and the door on Michigan Avenue is locked. The list you trusted says the Carondelet food pantry opens then. The Carondelet pantry’s own page lists its Wednesday hours as 1:30 p.m. to 3:45 p.m. So you stand there with an empty bag folded in your coat pocket and a bus fare already spent, more than five hours early.
### Which food pantries are open today in St. Louis?
It depends on the day. Monday through Thursday, Isaiah 58 Ministries at 2149 South Grand Boulevard runs pantry shopping from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. for its zip codes. Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, Our Lady of Perpetual Help at 4335 Warne Avenue opens 9 a.m. to noon. Sunday is the thin one. And whatever the day, call before you leave, because printed hours are exactly where people get burned.
So if your cupboard is down to a sleeve of crackers and a can of beans on a Saturday night, that is the night to make calls, not Sunday morning. Thin is not empty, though. The City’s Food Help page lists Focus Gateway City at 1901 Ann Avenue serving supper from 4:30 to 5:30 p.m. every Sunday from the 2nd through the 21st of the month, with its pantry and clothing closet available every time it is open, and Trinity Episcopal on North Euclid serving a hot lunch Sundays from 2 to 2:30 p.m. The full week, pantry by pantry, is further down.
One more thing before you dial. The St. Louis Area Foodbank, which works with nearly 600 partners in 26 counties, states on its Find Food page that “for most food pantries, an appointment is required.” Most. So “open today” and “will hand me groceries today” are two different promises. A pantry list is a rumor until somebody picks up the phone.
And when the bag comes home, do not throw out the can with last month’s date on the lid. The Foodbank says Best By, Sell By and Expiration dates do not mean food is unsafe to eat after the date listed on the package. The one exception it names is infant formula, which must be used before the date.
### Why does the list say open when the door is locked?
Because the lists are copies, and copies drift. The Carondelet pantry’s own page lists Monday 8:30 a.m. to 11:45 a.m., Wednesday 1:30 p.m. to 3:45 p.m. and Friday 8:30 a.m. to 11:45 a.m. A volunteer-run online resource list prints Monday, Wednesday and Friday at 8:15 a.m. for all three. Show up on a Wednesday morning by the second list and you are standing on Michigan Avenue with the cold coming up through your shoes, hours early.
It happens downtown, too. The City of St. Louis Food Help page lists the St. Nicholas Food Pantry at 701 North 18th Street as Mondays only, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., for zip codes 63101, 63102, 63103 and 63106. That volunteer-run list shows the same pantry at 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and adds 63104 and 63107 to the zip codes it serves. Half an hour apart on each end, and two zip codes in or out depending on which page you trust.
Nobody is lying. A church changes its volunteer shift, a pantry loses a driver, a list gets updated in spring and not again. The city’s own page says its pantry information comes from that volunteer-run list and tells you to “check there for the most up to date information.” Every list is a starting point. The phone call is the answer.
### What do you ask when you call?
Three questions, in this order, and the whole call takes about a minute. First: are you open today, and until what time? Second: do I need an appointment, and can I get one today? Third: do you serve my zip code, and what do I bring? Write the answers on the back of an envelope. When you are tired and the bus is late, you will not remember them.
What to bring is usually the same short stack. The Carondelet pantry asks first-time visitors for a Missouri driver’s license or state ID and proof of city residency, such as a utility bill. Fold it into your wallet the night before, next to the ID. The Foodbank says you do not need to bring any money, and that a reusable bag is a good idea, although bags are usually provided.
If the phone rings out to a full voicemail box, do not give up on the day. Dial 2-1-1 from a cell phone, or 1-800-427-4626 from a landline, to reach United Way 2-1-1, a 24/7 line to agencies near you. Or call the Operation Food Search hunger hotline at 314-726-5355, extension 1, which gives an automated list of pantries by zip code.
### The early week, pantry by pantry
Carondelet opens at 8:30 a.m. on Michigan Avenue. The city list puts St. Wenceslaus at 3014 Oregon Avenue on Monday only, 9:30 to 11:30 a.m., and the Salvation Army at 2740 Arsenal Street from 10 a.m. to noon. On South Grand, Isaiah 58 Ministries at 2149 South Grand Boulevard runs pantry shopping Monday through Thursday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., for zip codes 63104, 63110, 63116 and 63118. The volunteer list notes no appointment there, but you must have a photo ID.
Tuesday belongs to Our Lady of Perpetual Help on Warne Avenue, 9 a.m. to noon. The volunteer list says to arrive early if possible to register and get a ticket to shop, so expect a paper number in your hand and a wait in a chair. In the Central West End, Trinity Episcopal at 600 North Euclid runs its pantry and take-out hot meal Tuesday from 1:30 to 3 p.m.; enter through the Washington Avenue entrance, not the main one, and bring ID. St. Pius V on South Grand opens Tuesday 2 to 3:30 p.m., with its entrance at 3540 Utah Street.
Carondelet moves to the afternoon, 1:30 to 3:45 p.m. And if you work a day shift, St. Anthony of Padua at 3140 Meramec Street hands out food and clothing Wednesday from 4 to 6 p.m., a rare evening window. It serves zip codes 63118, 63111 and 63116; bring a photo ID and a bill or legal document with your current address.

Thursday brings back Our Lady of Perpetual Help, 9 a.m. to noon. Estell Ministries at 3803 Page Boulevard runs its pantry every Thursday, 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The Salvation Army on Arsenal opens 3 to 5 p.m., and Trinity Episcopal opens 4 to 5 p.m., two afternoon slots for people who cannot leave work in the morning.

Saturday is the last real chance. Our Lady of Perpetual Help, 9 a.m. to noon. St. Pius V, 10 to 11:30 a.m. And the Foodbank’s Food on the Move truck parks at Metro transit centers: the first Saturday of the month at the Rock Road Transit Center and the third Saturday at the North Hanley Transit Center, both 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., free of charge. The truck carries three refrigerators, so there is a real chance of something cold and fresh to carry home on the Red Line.
Sunday is close to empty. The volunteer list shows Focus Gateway City at 1901 Ann Avenue, inside St. Michael’s Orthodox Church, with a food pantry on Sundays from the 2nd through the 21st of each month.
### Can you just show up, or do you need an appointment?
At some pantries you can just show up. Isaiah 58 needs no appointment, only a photo ID, and the volunteer list marks St. Nicholas as “no appointment needed.” Others are the opposite: Guardian Angel Settlement on South Jefferson is listed as membership only and appointment only. The Foodbank’s rule of thumb holds: most pantries want an appointment, while food distribution events usually run first-come, first-served and usually do not ask for ID.
No appointment open today? The Foodbank’s food distribution events are the other door. They usually run first-come, first-served, an ID is usually not required, and you do not need to bring any money. Bring a reusable bag if you have one, though bags are usually provided, and something to read for the line. Carry the full bag from the bottom: a few cans, a bag of potatoes and a jug of milk will cut a thin plastic handle into your fingers before you reach the bus stop.
That is why the second question on your call matters most. A pantry that is open but booked solid will still turn you away gently at the door, and gentle does not fill a fridge.
### How often can you go, and to how many?
Each pantry keeps its own count. The Community Action Agency of St. Louis County says a household can receive food assistance every 30 days. Isaiah 58’s emergency pre-packed bags are one per year. Ask on the call how often you can come back. You want to know before you spend the visit, not after.
Going to multiple food pantries in a day is less about permission and more about zip codes. Say you live in 63118. On a Monday, Isaiah 58 serves your zip from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., and St. Anthony of Padua serves it from 10 a.m. to noon. Two pantries, one morning, and a full bag cutting into your fingers on the walk between them. Live in Cahokia Heights or West Alton and none of these city zip codes apply; put your own address into the Foodbank’s locator instead.
If you have never used a pantry before, our guide to how St. Louis food pantries work covers the basics, and the Better Family Life resource page covers the wider safety net. This page answers a narrower, more urgent question: which door opens today, and how do you know before you walk up to it?

A.  Sometimes. Isaiah 58 on South Grand needs no appointment, just a photo ID, but the St. Louis Area Foodbank says most pantries require one. Its food distribution events usually run first-come, first-served without an ID, so if you cannot get an appointment today, check its event calendar.

A.  It is set pantry by pantry. The Community Action Agency of St. Louis County allows a household food assistance every 30 days, and Isaiah 58’s emergency bags are one per year. Ask the limit when you call, before you use the visit.

A.  Yes, and each pantry sets its own. The St. Louis Area Foodbank works with nearly 600 partners in 26 counties, and the rules change from door to door. Ask the limit on the phone, before you spend the visit.

## Missouri Pays Back Half of a Pantry Gift, and Nothing for a Food Bank Gift
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-food-pantry-tax-credit-who-is-eligible
Two envelopes sit on the kitchen counter, the same check inside each, and a paper sack of canned corn and peanut butter leans against the toaster, heavier than it looks. Mail the first envelope to a food bank and the gift does not qualify for Missouri’s credit. Carry the second, and the sack, through the door of a St. Louis pantry and the state returns half at tax time.
Now stand at that pantry table with the sack in your arms and a staff member’s pen over the form. Section 135.647 puts the clock in print: the program “shall expire on December 31, 2026, unless reauthorized by the general assembly,” and the revisor’s page still shows that date. Harvesters, a food bank that monitored the bills, wrote in May that the proposals to extend it “did not make meaningful progress this session.” A sack that crosses this table after that day may earn you nothing, though credits already earned can still be redeemed.
So before the last check of the year leaves your kitchen, do three things. Ask whether the place is a local 501(c)(3) pantry, shelter or soup kitchen and not a food bank. Get a staff member to sign Form MO-FPT for the gift. Clip the receipt to it and drop both in the folder you will open when you file by April 15.
### Who is eligible to receive the food pantry tax credit in Missouri?
Whoever is holding the sack can claim it, as long as they owe Missouri state income tax: an individual, a corporation or a trust that gives cash or unexpired food to a local 501(c)(3) food pantry, soup kitchen or homeless shelter. The credit is 50 percent of what you give, capped at $2,500 per taxpayer per year, and a married couple filing a combined return can each claim up to $2,500.
The family carrying groceries out of the pantry does not receive this credit. The person who stocked the shelf does. Looking for food instead? Start with the St. Louis food pantry guide, which walks through what to bring.
Here is the part that should stop you. Those two groups are often the same people.
When a state lawmaker pushed to soften the penalties tied to this credit, she told the Missouri Independent that many donors to food pantries “are people who have used the free groceries to feed their families.”
The bag is the same weight from either side of the table. Someone who once waited in that line now sets two bags on the same folding table. She qualifies. So would a retired neighbor in Dutchtown who gives twenty dollars a month, and so would a corner restaurant on Cherokee Street that sends over trays.
### Why does a check to a food bank earn nothing back?
This is the mistake that costs St. Louis givers the most, and it is printed in plain words on Form MO-FPT: “Donations to a food bank, out-of-state food pantry, out-of-state homeless shelter or out-of-state soup kitchen do not qualify for the credit.” Can I claim food bank donations on taxes in Missouri, then? Not for this credit. A food bank is the warehouse. The pantry is the folding table at the end of the line.
The region’s big warehouse says so itself. The St. Louis Area Foodbank describes a food pantry as “Supplied by a food bank,” and says it works with nearly 600 partners in 26 counties. Those partners are where the credit lives: the church basement on a Saturday morning that smells of cardboard and coffee, the shelter kitchen, the pantry closet behind a school gym. Your bag belongs on the table, not the loading dock. Pick the door with a staff member who can sign your form. Food Outreach, founded in St. Louis in 1988, lists the credit among its ways to give.
One more St. Louis wrinkle, for owners. The Foodbank’s own giving page says that if you have business income in Missouri, you may receive a reduction in your Missouri state taxes equal to 50 percent of your donation through the Missouri Neighborhood Assistance Program. The Department of Revenue lists a Neighborhood Assistance Credit of its own, separate from the Food Pantry Tax Credit.
Homeless shelters count too. Before you give anywhere, ask the director two plain questions. Are you a 501(c)(3)? Will you sign my Form MO-FPT when I bring it in? Today, before the next bag leaves your kitchen, print a blank Form MO-FPT and fold it into the sack on top of the cans, so a staff member can sign it while you are still standing at the folding table. Then circle April 15 on next year’s fridge calendar, because a gift made this year is claimed on the return you file next spring: returns claiming the credit “must be filed July 1 through April 15 of each fiscal year,” the Department of Revenue says.
### The cap nobody mentions until July
Every pantry flyer says “up to $2,500.” Almost none say what happens next. The whole state gets $1,750,000 in credits per fiscal year, and that pot is shared. The Department of Revenue holds every claim until the April 15 returns are processed, and if Missourians claimed more than the pot, it will “apportion credits in an equal ratio among all valid returns filed.”
That is not a someday risk. The Missouri Independent reported that in one recent year about $2 million was claimed, so every taxpayer got only 87.8% of the credit they asked for, and in each of the two years before that, less than 75% of each claim was allowed. Unless they had paid extra, the disallowance notice said they had to cover the difference, plus interest and penalties on the unused portion. The law gives no way to waive the interest and penalties on the gap. On a full $2,500 claim, the paper worked the math: $2,195 allowed, a $305 remainder, and $21.35 in interest and penalties right away if that remainder was not paid.
The fix costs you nothing extra in the end. If your return would show tax due before the credit, the Department recommends paying the tax the credit would cover by the due date. Whatever turns out not to be owed gets refunded once the credit is apportioned. If your return would show a refund anyway, the Department says it “will issue a partial refund for the amount overpaid in excess of the food pantry tax credit,” and anything else overpaid comes “in a separate check at a later date.” The trimmed slice is not lost, either. You can carry it forward to next year’s return.
### How much do you actually get back?
How much tax credit can you get for donations to a pantry? Half of what you give, up to $2,500. Give $400 in cash and groceries over a year and you claim $200 off your Missouri tax. Give $5,000 and you hit the $2,500 ceiling. Donated food is valued at fair market value, so keep the grocery receipt in the kitchen drawer, crumpled or not. Grocery stores, food brokers, wholesalers and restaurants value their donated food at wholesale instead.
Two limits trip people up. The credit cannot be larger than the Missouri tax you owe that year, and it is nonrefundable, so a household with no state tax bill gets nothing back in cash. Whatever you cannot use carries forward to any of your three following tax years. And if you also deducted the same gift on your federal Schedule A, Missouri wants it added back on Form MO-A. One bag of groceries does not get counted twice.
People are asking
### Who qualifies for the Missouri food pantry tax credit?
Any taxpayer, whether an individual, a corporation or a trust, that donates cash or food to a local food pantry, homeless shelter or soup kitchen qualifies, as long as that pantry is a 501(c)(3). Gifts to a food bank or to an out-of-state pantry, shelter or soup kitchen do not qualify, and food donated after its expiration date does not count. Because the credit is nonrefundable, it only helps a donor who owes Missouri income tax.
Under Section 135.647, food donated after its expiration date does not count, a taxpayer who employs people not authorized to work in the United States cannot claim it, and no one can claim the credit twice for a single donation. It only ever offsets your own Missouri tax.
Unrelated: some Sunday afternoons are better spent smelling roses than reading tax forms.
### How do you claim it on Form MO-FPT and MO-TC?
Start at the pantry, not at the kitchen table in April. Form MO-FPT has lines for the date and amount of every donation, and “An eligible staff member of the food pantry, homeless shelter, or soup kitchen must certify that each contribution reported was received.” That signature is far easier to get in December, when the volunteer who took your bags still remembers your face, than in a rushed spring week with a pen that will not start.
Instead of the form, the pantry can give you a letter that names the pantry, the dates and amounts of your donations and your name. Give to three places and you need three forms or three letters, one for each. Then attach that paperwork, plus a completed Form MO-TC, to your Missouri return. Returns claiming this credit are accepted July 1 through April 15. Questions go to the Department’s Taxation Division at 573-751-3220 or taxcredit@dor.mo.gov.
Print a blank Form MO-FPT tonight and tuck it into the next grocery bag you carry in. Need a pantry to give to? Our St. Louis food pantry guide lists where the folding tables are.
If you’re the tax preparer who fills out MO-TC for St. Louis families every spring, this is your season. More customers are already looking here for someone who knows these forms, so list your business where they are searching.
### Will the credit still be there next year?
Check before you count on it. The statute carries its own sunset line: the program “shall expire on December 31, 2026, unless reauthorized by the general assembly,” and the Department of Revenue says the credit fully terminates September 1, 2027. Credits already earned can still be redeemed after the program expires. I could not find a reauthorization on the revisor’s page as of this writing, so read Section 135.647 before a big year-end gift. If it shows a new date, lawmakers renewed it. If not, the bags you set down before the sunset may be the last ones that pay you back.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What tax credits are available for charitable donations in Missouri?
A.  The food pantry credit is one of about a dozen Missouri credits that reward gifts to causes lawmakers want to support, including groups that promote adoptions, help victims of domestic violence and provide diapers and food for people in poverty, according to the Missouri Independent. Each has its own rules and its own cap.
### Q. Is food donation tax-deductible?
A.  Federally, yes, if you itemize. The IRS lets you deduct gifts of money or property to qualified organizations when you itemize, and donated property is generally deducted at its fair market value.
### Q. Can I claim food bank donations on taxes?
A.  On a federal return you can deduct a gift to a qualified food bank if you itemize. For the Missouri food pantry credit, no: Form MO-FPT says donations to a food bank do not qualify. Give to a local pantry, soup kitchen or shelter instead if you want the state credit.
### Q. How much tax credit can you get for donations?
A.  For the Missouri food pantry credit, 50 percent of the value of your cash or food gifts, up to $2,500 per taxpayer per year. It cannot exceed your Missouri tax for the year, and any unused amount can be carried forward three years.
### Q. How much of a tax credit do you get for charitable donations?
A.  Missouri’s charitable credits are generally 50% or more of a donation, the Missouri Independent reports, and only the donor can use them against their own state taxes. The food pantry credit is shared out of a fixed $1,750,000 yearly pot, so the final amount can come in lower.
### Q. What are the tax credits available in Missouri?
A.  The Department of Revenue says Missouri’s miscellaneous tax credits “are administered by several government agencies including the Missouri Department of Revenue,” and lists them on its tax credits page. The Food Pantry Tax Credit (FPT) is on that list.
### Q. What are the instructions for completing Form MO-TC?
A.  If you are eligible for a tax credit, the Department of Revenue says Form MO-TC must be completed and attached to your tax return, along with the supporting forms each credit requires. For the food pantry credit, that means one signed Form MO-FPT or pantry letter for every pantry you gave to.
### Q. Do you have to prove income for food pantry?
A.  It depends on the pantry. The St. Louis Area Foodbank says “This may include a photo ID and proof of income,” and that “For most food pantries, a photo ID is required.” Call ahead or check the pantry’s website.
### Q. Can I take the Missouri credit and a federal deduction for the same gift?
A.  You can, but Missouri takes part of it back. If you listed the donation as a charitable contribution on your federal Schedule A, the Department of Revenue says you must add that amount back on Form MO-A.

## One Pencil Line: Can You Draw Your Own House Plans Without an Architect?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/can-you-draw-your-own-house-plans-without-an-architect
“Not a licensed architect.” Four words in pencil, in the corner of a plan you drew at your own kitchen table, copied five times and rolled tight under one arm.
### Can you draw your own house plans without an architect?
Yes, for a dwelling house or a flat containing not more than two families. Those four words are the price of admission: Missouri’s exemption holds only when your drawings indicate that you are not a licensed architect.
Unroll the plan on the table and run a finger past the kitchen, past the new closet, to the spot where the old wall comes out. That is where the knot in your stomach lives. The header over the new opening. The joist under the new tub. The beam that has to carry what the wall used to carry. Missouri hands you that pencil too: one law covers the architecture and its twin covers the engineering (Section 327.101 and Section 327.191). What neither one hands over is the title.
In St. Louis, moving one interior wall takes a building permit. Drawing the whole house it stands in takes no architect’s license.
This page starts where our guide to when Missouri law requires an architect leaves off: five rolled sets going across a counter at City Hall, and a stranger reading your pencil lines for the first time.
### The pencil line, and its twin for the engineer
Put them in the title block of every sheet, the small box where the project name and date go. Plain words work: “Prepared by the owner. Not a licensed architect. Not a licensed professional engineer.” Section 327.101 asks for its note on any drawings, specifications, estimates, reports or other documents, so it belongs on your materials list and your written scope too. Leave it off and the exemption has nothing to stand on.
Then the city adds a line most homeowners never hear about until a reviewer asks. Under Ordinance 71063, the City of St. Louis requires new residential construction to be “solar-ready,” and plans for one- and two-family homes have to illustrate the feasibility of a future solar energy system installation. Nobody is making you buy panels; the drawing just has to show the house could take them. If you are drawing a brand-new house on a vacant lot in Dutchtown or off South Grand, that is a sheet, or at least a note, the city expects to see.
### What does the St. Louis permit counter actually ask for?
To make a building permit application in St. Louis City, at a minimum, you will need four things, according to the Building Division’s permit page: the address of the project, a $25 application fee, a letter of authorization from the property owner if you are not the owner of record, and project plans. Online, the portal takes .pdf, .jpg, .png and Word files, so a clean scan of a pencil drawing will upload. In person, bring five copies of the plans to the Permit office in City Hall during business hours, and know that only check or cash payment is accepted. That is five rolled sets on the counter, with a checkbook or folded bills beside them. Not sure your sheets are enough? Call the Permit Section at (314) 622-3313 before you print all five.
The fee comes in two bites. You pay the $25 application fee when you file. The permit fee waits until every reviewer has signed off, and on a job over $3,000 it runs $10 per thousand of estimated construction cost. A small job, up to $1,000 of estimated cost, totals $44. Every dollar paid is non-refundable, so write down an honest estimate, not a hopeful one.
Or skip the counter and the paper. The city now runs applications, plan uploads, fees and status tracking through its STL City Permits portal, and the contractors who pull permits every week noticed. “I’ve submitted permits online and had them back in three days, whereas before it would take weeks,” John Meller of City Carport said in the city’s announcement. “If something’s missing, they just email me.” That email is what a returned plan feels like now. Not a clerk sliding your pages back across a desk, but a buzz in your pocket while you are standing in the lumber aisle.
### What makes the permit office send your plans back?
I could not find a city list of reasons homeowner plans get bounced, and I won’t invent one. After you file, feedback starts arriving from the various city staff assigned to your project, and which agencies review it depends on the job. The city says the portal integrates review workflows across zoning, planning and inspections, so expect questions from more than one desk, and fix each answer on the drawing itself.
The bigger surprise is how much work needs a drawing at all. In a Soulard rowhouse or a Benton Park two-family, the urge is to call it “just a wall.” The city’s residential permit criteria say otherwise: a permit is required for the removal or installation of any partition in a habitable space, for any cutting or removal of structural beams or joists, for decks, porches and retaining walls, and for turning a basement or attic into living quarters. Separate permits for plumbing, mechanical and electrical work are also required when applicable.
And there is one hard stop. The city’s rebuilding guidance puts it plainly: if your property is structurally condemned, you need an architect to make your construction drawings to get a building permit. Not sure where your house stands? The same page lists a line to speak with a Plan Examiner, 314-622-3332. Make that call before you draw a single line on a condemned house, because no title-block note fixes it.
Smallest floor plan you’ll ever love: an RV parked near St. Louis.
### Does an addition change the answer?
Not on a dwelling house. Missouri’s exemption covers architectural services “in connection with the construction, remodeling or repairing” of a privately owned dwelling house. The city still lists “room additions and/or extensions or enlargement of existing rooms” under work that requires a building permit, so the drawing has to answer every reviewer who opens it.
The building is what changes the answer. On a three- or four-family flat, the state’s break shrinks: it covers remodeling and repairing only, and only where the work does not affect the building’s architectural or engineering safety features. The word construction isn’t in that clause, so read it twice before you sketch an addition onto a four-family.
Then there is the brick front your neighbors walk past every morning. If your property sits in a City historic district or is a City landmark, exterior work goes through the Cultural Resources Office, which keeps design standards for the city’s 14 historic districts and 112 landmarks. Call (314) 657-3865 before you draw the street side of anything.
People are asking
### Is there a free program for drawing house plans on a computer?
Yes, and it can start from the pencil sheet already on your table. Sweet Home 3D is a free, open-source program that draws walls to precise dimensions, adds dimension lines and room areas, and imports a home blueprint so you can draw walls right on top of your scan, whether you install it or run it in a web browser. When the plan looks right, export it as a PDF, one of the file types the city’s online permit system accepts, and keep the “not a licensed architect” line in the title block before you upload.
### When should you put the pencil down and call someone?
When the building isn’t a house or a two-family. When the city has called it structurally condemned. When you are guessing at a beam size and the guess is the only thing holding up the second floor. The law lets you sign that beam as the owner; it does not make the math right.
Help does not have to mean handing over the whole job. Shortlist two or three architects or drafters, interview each one, and tell them exactly what you have drawn and what you want from them: a review of your set, the structural sheet only, or the full drawings. Then compare what each says they will actually deliver.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you draw your own plans for a building permit?
A.  Yes, in Missouri, for a privately owned dwelling house or a flat containing not more than two families. State law lets a person who is not licensed render architectural services for those buildings, as long as the drawings indicate the person is not a licensed architect, and, for engineering services, not a licensed professional engineer.
### Q. Can I design my own house without an architect?
A.  Yes. Missouri’s exemption covers the construction of a dwelling house, not just repairs, so a new single-family home can be drawn by its owner with the required “not a licensed architect” note. In the city, plans for a new one- or two-family home also have to show the feasibility of a future solar energy system under Ordinance 71063.
### Q. What are the minimum requirements to apply for a building permit in St. Louis City?
A.  The project address, a $25 application fee, a letter of authorization if you are not the owner of record, and project plans. Apply online through STL City Permits, or bring five copies of the plans to the Permit office in City Hall during business hours, where only check or cash is accepted.
### Q. What documents are needed for a building permit?
A.  In the city, the application, your project plans, and an owner’s letter of authorization if someone else is applying. Separate permits for plumbing, mechanical and electrical work are also required when applicable. If the property is in a FEMA flood area, a Floodway Development Permit is required even when the building code does not require a building permit.
### Q. What if I build without a permit?
A.  A city building permit is the formal and legal authorization to start construction; work done without one has none. The city also keeps a public search where anyone can enter a city address and see past permits issued for that property. If work already happened, call the Permit Section at (314) 622-3313 and ask how to get it permitted.
### Q. How much is a building permit in St. Louis County?
A.  I couldn’t verify St. Louis County’s current fee schedule against its own site, so I won’t quote one here. Call the building department for your address. For comparison, the City of St. Louis charges a $25 application fee plus a permit fee of $10 per thousand of estimated cost on jobs over $3,000.
### Q. Do you need an architect to build an extension?
A.  Missouri’s owner exemption covers architectural services in connection with the construction, remodeling or repairing of a privately owned dwelling house, as long as the drawings carry the “not a licensed architect” note. In the city, room additions and extensions of existing rooms still need a building permit. A three- or four-family building is different: its exemption covers only remodeling and repair that does not affect the building’s safety features.

## Come Alone, Not Late: Single at 40? Where to Go on a Friday Night in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-40-year-old-singles-go-on-a-friday-night-in-st-louis
Showing up alone isn’t the mistake. Showing up late is: you’re on a dark sidewalk in Grand Center in your good shoes, music faint somewhere above you, knuckles stinging on a door nobody answers. The academy that runs the dance even warns you that “the Grandel is generally locked” and the dancers upstairs “will likely not hear you knocking.”
### Where do 40 year old singles go on a Friday night in St. Louis?
They go to rooms that hand them something to do besides stand at a rail and shout: a dance social with a short lesson up front, a trivia table, a late night at the art museum, a quiet bar where you can hear the person on the next stool. In St. Louis that Friday map runs through Forest Park, Grand Center, Cherokee Street and the west edge of downtown, and two of the best stops cost nothing and $12 to walk into. The free one has a twist most locals miss: at the Saint Louis Art Museum, “Admission to main exhibitions is free on Friday,” so the big ticketed show costs you nothing that night. That’s the line to text a friend. (Still sorting out which bar is which? Our guide to the types of bars in St. Louis and how to pick one covers the room types.)
And the thing most people get backwards, straight from the academy’s own site: “Singles and Couples are welcome in all classes; no partner needed.” Coming alone is the normal way in.
### Before you knock on the Grandel’s door
Get it right and the moment is worth it: the door gives, the music drops down the stairwell all at once, and somebody upstairs is already counting out loud. Here’s how to be on the right side of it. The socials happen in the Grand Hall at The Grandel, 3610 Grandel Square, and the Grandel has a large parking lot across the street on the north-west side. Bring $12 cash or Venmo. Wear leather soles if you own them; the academy says “Dance shoes are preferred, but not required. Leather soled shoes are a great alternative, but no sneakers or flip flops, please.” Social dates are subject to change, so check the Monthly Dance Social page the week of, or call the academy at (314) 367-1001. Tell your friend the whole trick in six words: come alone, come early, leather soles.
### The answer sheet does the talking
You’re at a two-top with a pint going warm and a pencil worn flat on one side. The host leans into the mic and reads round three, question four, and you know it. You actually know it. At the next table, a woman is whispering the wrong answer to her friend, so you lean over: “It’s the second one.” She looks at you, looks at the sheet, writes it down. That’s the whole introduction. Nobody had to invent a line.
The good rooms all work that way. Something starts at a set time, so you have a reason to walk in. Something sits in front of you to talk about: the sheet, the dance step, the painting. And there’s a natural break, the last chord or the host reading the answers, so you can drift back to your own table without it feeling like a rejection. A packed bar with a DJ gives you none of that. Save it for later, once you’ve met someone worth shouting over.
The tell is your own shoulders. If they’re up near your ears in the first ten minutes, the room is wrong, not you.
### What is a Friday ballroom social actually like?
A line of strangers, an instructor counting out loud, leather soles scuffing the floor on the turn, everyone half a beat behind. The last posted social ran an American Tango lesson from 7:30 to 8 p.m., general dancing from 8 to 10 p.m., and light refreshments.
That half-hour lesson is the trick. Everyone in it is learning the same steps at the same time, so your first words to a stranger can be about the steps. You don’t need to be good. The lesson starts at 7:30, so be on the right side of that door before it does.
For a bigger, louder version, head south. The Casa Loma Ballroom on Iowa Avenue, in the Cherokee Street Antique Row district, was built in 1927 and has a 5,000-square-foot “floating” dance floor. The ballroom’s own site says it runs a 16- to 24-piece orchestra on Friday nights and oldies on Saturdays, but its event calendar is the thing to trust, so check it or call 314-282-2258 before you put on the good shoes. A full band, a wood floor that gives a little under your heels, and a room old enough that your grandparents could have danced there: that is a Friday you’ll talk about on Monday.
### Is the art museum really a Friday night spot?
By early evening the galleries go hushed. Shoes tap on stone floors. People drift alone, in pairs, in little clusters of friends, and nobody is in a hurry. It’s the easiest room in St. Louis to stand next to a stranger, because you’re both looking at the same thing. Walk a gallery, then walk out to dinner or a drink with the conversation already started.
The Saint Louis Art Museum is open 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Fridays, admission is free every day, and the main exhibitions that charge the rest of the week are free on Friday.
### What happens at City Museum after dark?
On select Fridays, City Museum closes early to the public and reopens for City Nights, which run 7 to 11 p.m. and are “21+ only with valid ID.” The ticket includes general admission for the whole day, food, beer and cocktails are sold throughout the building, and the slides, climbers and ramps stay open to grown-ups.
Here’s why it works when you’re single: it is impossible to look cool while crawling through a steel tunnel with your knees on the grate, so nobody tries. You end up laughing with whoever is stuck behind you. Wear jeans and closed-toe shoes. Leave the bag in the car.
Off topic, but when did you last say hello to a giraffe? Start here.
### Where can you meet singles in St. Louis without an app?
The best places to meet singles in St. Louis are the ones with a repeat crowd: a weekly trivia night, a dance class series, a bar rail with the same bartender every week. One great night is luck. The third week in a row is when the regulars start saving you a seat.
Trivia is the easiest door in. Call the bar a day ahead and ask three things: which night the trivia runs, how big a team can be, and will the host match a solo player with a table. If they say “just show up,” show up early and sit at the bar, not a booth.
For a quieter night, a wine bar or a piano bar beats a club: the scrape of a stool, ice rattling in a shaker, a voice you don’t have to lean in to hear. You can sit at the counter, ask the bartender what they’d drink, and actually hear the answer. The person two stools over heard it too.
### One night, neighborhood by neighborhood
If you want one plan for fun adult things to do in St. Louis on a single Friday, string it together by neighborhood so the next stop is always a short drive away.
Start in Forest Park with an hour in the art museum. Head east to Grand Center if the academy has a social that week and catch the 7:30 lesson. On a City Nights Friday, swap in City Museum downtown instead. On a band night, Cherokee Street is the swing and big-band choice, and you can eat on the street before the music starts. End wherever the conversation is still going. That’s the only rule that matters.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What’s going on in St. Louis on Friday night?
A.  Friday is the late night at the Saint Louis Art Museum, open until 9 p.m. with free admission and free main exhibitions. On select Fridays City Museum runs its 21+ City Nights from 7 to 11 p.m., and dance socials and band nights fill Grand Center and Cherokee Street. Check each venue’s calendar the week of.
### Q. Where to meet singles in St. Louis?
A.  Go where there’s a repeat crowd and a built-in reason to talk: a weekly trivia night, a ballroom or swing class, a dance social with a lesson first, or the same bar rail every Friday. Going back a second and third week is what turns faces into friends.
### Q. Where to go in St. Louis at night?
A.  Pair a calm first stop with a livelier second one: the art museum in Forest Park until 9 p.m. on Fridays, then a dance social in Grand Center, a band night on Cherokee Street or a City Nights Friday downtown. Finish at a quiet bar where you can hear each other.
### Q. What are some fun adult things to do in St. Louis?
A.  City Museum’s City Nights are 21+ only with valid ID and keep the slides and climbers open for grown-ups. Ballroom socials, trivia nights, piano bars and Friday nights at the art museum are all adult-friendly ways to spend an evening without a club’s volume.
### Q. Where is the best place to meet single men over 40?
A.  Rooms with an activity are easier for anyone who came alone, because there’s something to do: trivia teams, dance lessons, and the bar rail at a neighborhood tavern. Show up at the start time, join in, and let the break between rounds or songs do the introductions.
### Q. Do you need a partner for a ballroom social in St. Louis?
A.  No. The Ballroom Dance Academy of St. Louis says singles and couples are welcome in all its classes with no partner needed, and its socials open with a short lesson before general dancing. Arrive a few minutes early, since the Grandel is generally locked.

## Men's Shelters in St. Louis Take Referrals: How to Get a Bed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/homeless-shelters-for-men-in-st-louis
One hundred beds for men, every night of the year, at Peter & Paul Community Services. Not one of them goes to a man who walks up and knocks. “You must have a referral,” the shelter’s own page says. “This shelter does not accept walk-ins and is not open to the public.” So if you are standing outside with the light going, the cold coming through your jacket, tomorrow’s work shirt folded in the bag on your shoulder and your phone battery gone red, the door is not your first move. A phone call is. And that shirt does not make you the odd one out: at Peter & Paul, more than 50% of residents are employed.
### Where are the homeless shelters for men in St Louis?
Two shelters built for a man on his own are the city’s Biddle Housing Opportunities Center at 1212 N. 13th St., just north of downtown, and Peter & Paul Community Services’ year-round, 24-hour Emergency Shelter in the St. Louis Place neighborhood. For shelter referral, call United Way 2-1-1 or the St. Louis Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444, or visit the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd., Monday through Friday.
So with that red battery in your pocket, do three things, in this order. Charge your phone wherever you can find an outlet; a dead phone at the moment someone calls you back is a bed you never hear about. Call 2-1-1 and ask for access to shelter, or call the Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444. Then, on a weekday, be on Tucker at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m., the two times St. Patrick Center calls the most strategic to arrive at its Welcome Center. If you do not get a bed the first night, Peter & Paul’s advice is to keep trying every day, early in the morning, until a bed is available.
Charge the phone. Call 2-1-1. Be on Tucker at 8. That fits in one text to a friend who needs it tonight.
### What time should you show up to get a bed?
Eight in the morning. Or one in the afternoon. In winter, eight o’clock downtown means breath you can see and both hands jammed in your pockets on the walk to the side door. Those are the two times St. Patrick Center itself calls “the most strategic times to arrive” at its Welcome Center, the side entrance of 800 North Tucker Blvd. downtown, Monday through Friday. No appointment is necessary. St. Patrick Center also says all intakes and assessments are conducted in person, and it does not handle discovery sessions by phone, email or social media. So the bus fare to Tucker matters more than the email you were thinking of sending.
If it is a weekend or you cannot get downtown, call 2-1-1 and ask for access to shelter.
### Why can’t a man just walk up to the door?
Because St. Louis stopped working that way. Biddle participates in the St. Louis Continuum of Care Coordinated Entry System, and Peter & Paul says it in plain words on its own page: “You must have a referral. This shelter does not accept walk-ins and is not open to the public.” Biddle’s city page sends men the same direction, to the Housing Helpline, 2-1-1 or the Welcome Center.
Daylight is a different story at Biddle. The city’s own warming-center list gives its drop-in hours as 8:00am to 4:30pm, Sunday through Saturday, with a phone number of (314) 612-1675. That is a seat and a roof out of the weather, with your bag at your feet, while you work the phone for a bed tonight.
Standing on a sidewalk with your bag at your feet, a referral sounds like one more form. It works more like a handoff. The referral is how a caseworker learns your name and whether a discharge paper or a benefit letter could open a door you did not know about. A bed through the system comes with someone working on the next step.
Peter & Paul runs beds for 100 men per night, three meals a day seven days a week, plus showers, laundry and lockers. It is a year-round, 24-hour shelter. Biddle is the city’s own building, operated for the city by the Magdala Foundation, and it is strictly for single adult men. The city lists it as an overnight shelter with 98 beds for single men.
Peter & Paul’s shelter has been housing people since 1981, when concerned community members started it after a man froze to death nearby. It ran out of the basement of the Sts. Peter & Paul Catholic Church in Soulard, serving 60 men a night and turning others away for lack of beds. In July 2024 it moved to a new Community Campus in St. Louis Place, with beds for 100.
### What should a man carry into a shelter?
Less than you think, and the right few things. Peter & Paul’s own page lists what the shelter provides: beds, meals, showers, laundry and lockers. Ask at intake about anything else you want to bring. What it does tell you is that you do not need to haul a week of clothes across town in a trash bag that splits at the corner.
What you cannot replace in a hurry goes in one clear bag you can hold on your lap. Ask at intake about everything else, but carry the papers that open doors: any ID you still have, a benefit letter, your discharge papers, your Social Security card or birth certificate if you have them, every pill bottle in its original labeled container, a phone charger, and any court papers. The scrap of paper with a caseworker’s number on it is worth more than a second pair of shoes.
No ID at all? That is fixable, and it is one of the best-kept secrets in the city. The College Church ID and Birth Certificate Program at 289 N. Grand Blvd. in Midtown helps with Missouri State ID cards and birth certificates from any state, and its program volunteers meet with community members each week to overcome these barriers and provide payment for the needed documents. It opens its doors on Tuesday mornings at 9am; without an appointment, arrive by 8:30am and pull a ticket, or call (314) 266-9557 to book. In one year the program got 2,295 Missouri photo IDs into people’s hands. A man with an ID is a man who can sign a lease.
Somewhere tonight a retiree is losing an argument with an RV sewer hose.
### Winter changes the rules, but not until December
On the coldest nights the city activates emergency shelters. On one such night last December, with temperatures expected to hit 25°F, the city announced 304 emergency shelter beds on top of 400 year-round shelter beds, and listed the Biddle Housing Opportunities Center (single men only) among the shelters. Walk-ups were welcome from 6 p.m. until 9 p.m.; after 9 p.m., the instruction was to dial 211. Shuttles, each staffed with a driver and an outreach worker, picked people up between 5 and 7 p.m. at rally points such as Centenary United Methodist Church, 1610 Olive St.
Here is the catch nobody says out loud: the city’s own page states that Code Blue is inactive from March 1 to December 1. A raw October night with rain on the bus shelter glass is still not a Code Blue night. If you are reading this before December, plan on the referral route.
And when December does come, know the number. Freezing is not the trigger. Code Blue waits for 25. The degrees in between are the stretch where your fingers stop working on a phone screen and frost creeps across the bus shelter glass. Under the city’s Code Blue activation levels, the cold-weather response steps up when temperatures are at or below 25°F, or the wind chill is below 10°F, with those conditions expected for 2 or more hours. Standard winter operations hold 400 baseline beds with 60 or more surge beds on standby. At full activation, 600 surge beds open, every rally point is activated and warming buses park at priority sites. A night that is merely miserable, a few degrees warmer and no wind, can fall short of that line. On those nights the regular system and its referrals are what you have, so make the 2-1-1 call before dark, not after.
The rally points are worth knowing because they worked. In the city’s own review of its first Code Blue winter, rally points and pickup points placed in targeted areas were instrumental in assisting over 500 unique persons into shelters. If you see a shuttle with a driver and an outreach worker on a bitter night, that is the system coming to you.
Write 2-1-1 and (314) 802-5444 on paper tonight, because phones die and paper does not. And if a friend of yours runs a shop that hires or helps men starting over, send them to join on St Louis Near Me Directory so the next man can find them.
If you’re the barber, the laundromat or the work-boot store a man walks into with his first paycheck, this is your neighbor. Men rebuilding their lives are already searching for places like yours, and you can get more customers when you list your business where they look.
### What if you’re a veteran, or a regular shelter will not work for you?
Say the word veteran out loud at intake. At Peter & Paul, 15% of residents are veterans. St. Patrick Center’s Supportive Services for Veteran Families program takes calls at 314-356-0657 for veterans who are homeless or at risk. The VA Hope Recovery Center, which the city lists as a warming center at 515 North Jefferson Avenue, is open Monday through Friday, 8:00am to 4:30pm.
Some men have been in a big shelter before and know it does not work for them: the noise, the rules, the line for the showers before dawn. That is what Grace House is for. St. Patrick Center opened it as the city’s first comprehensive, low-barrier, 24-hour Safe Haven, for 25-40 people who may struggle in a traditional shelter, with 3 meals a day plus snacks. Referrals come through GetHelp, 211, outreach workers or the Welcome Center. Ask for it by name.
If you have nowhere to stay tonight and that battery is still red, call 2-1-1 now, before it dies, then be on Tucker at 8 a.m. Those two moves are the whole system.
