### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do homeless shelters allow men?
A.  Yes. In St. Louis, the Biddle Housing Opportunities Center at 1212 N. 13th St. and Peter & Paul Community Services’ Emergency Shelter in St. Louis Place both serve single adult men. For shelter referral, call United Way 2-1-1 or the Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444, or visit the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center Monday through Friday.
### Q. Is there a men’s homeless shelter in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  Yes. Peter & Paul’s year-round, 24-hour Emergency Shelter has beds for 100 men per night, three meals a day and case management. It does not accept walk-ins, so call 2-1-1 and ask for access to shelter, or go to the Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m. on a weekday.
### Q. What am I allowed to bring to a homeless shelter?
A.  Ask at intake. Carry what you cannot replace: ID, a benefit letter, discharge papers, your Social Security card, medications in labeled bottles and a phone charger. Peter & Paul provides lockers, laundry and showers, so you can leave the heavy bags behind.
### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  Call 2-1-1 or the St. Louis Housing Helpline at (314) 802-5444 and ask for shelter. On a weekday, go in person to the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. St. Patrick Center calls 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. the most strategic times to arrive.
### Q. What to do if you’re homeless with no money?
A.  Start with a call to 2-1-1 and ask for access to shelter. If you need an ID, the College Church ID and Birth Certificate Program in Midtown, whose volunteers provide payment for the needed documents, opens on Tuesday mornings.
### Q. Who is eligible for emergency housing?
A.  Biddle and Peter & Paul serve single adult men experiencing homelessness. Grace House serves people who may struggle in a traditional shelter. Veterans who are homeless or at risk can call St. Patrick Center’s SSVF line at 314-356-0657.

## Same Stamp, Crooked Board: Do Lumber Yards Have Better Lumber Than Home Depot?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/do-lumber-yards-have-better-lumber-than-home-depot
Whose truck got the straight studs? The last two-by-four in the bin curls up off the concrete like a ski tip, your flat cart drags left on one bad wheel, and the lights hum over a bunk somebody else already picked clean.
### Do lumber yards have better lumber than Home Depot?
Usually not better trees, but better odds. What a good yard really sells you is selection, drier stock, more grades and species, and a person who pulls your order straight so you are not the one culling the pile.
Back in the aisle, you are the one culling it. A knot the size of a quarter sits right on the edge of one stud. The next rocks under your palm when you lay it flat. Twenty minutes in, you have six keepers, sawdust in your cuffs and a sore shoulder. Before the seventh goes on the cart, set its end on the floor, lift the other end to your cheek and sight down the edge.
For anything you will sand, oil and run your hand across for years, there is a North City business you should know about. “Most mills won’t buy things from the city,” Joe Wilp of Lumber Logs told St. Louis Magazine, and his yard at 5103 Farlin Avenue sells “Domestic hardwood lumber from the St. Louis forest only.” Walk in on the first or third Saturday of the month, 9am to 11am. All other sales are by appointment only. To book one, email LumberLogsLLC@gmail.com, the address listed on its site. And if a tree comes down in your yard, the same outfit offers curbside log pickup: “Free local log recycling of any species.” Your old oak can skip the chipper and the hauling bill.
### What does the grade stamp promise, and what doesn’t it?
Flip a stud over and rub your thumb across the smudged block of ink: the mill, the species, the grade. Our guide to buying building supplies in St. Louis decodes the whole stamp; the line that matters in the aisle is the grade. Under the Southern Pine Inspection Bureau grading rules, No. 2 “Allows well-spaced knots of any quality.”
So which is better, lumber #1 or #2? Neither, until you name the job. No. 1 is for construction where high strength, stiffness and good appearance are desired; No. 2 is for most general construction uses. Paying for the pretty grade under a deck where nobody will ever look is how a friendly upsell happens at any counter.
What the stamp cannot tell you is where the board has been since, and wet wood keeps moving. Culpeper Wood Preservers writes that “KDAT lumber is far less likely to warp, twist, or cup on the job site.” Read that backward and you know what the soggy board at the bottom of the bunk does on a deck in a St. Louis summer. Same ink, same grade. One is a joist and one is a propeller.
A deck behind a Soulard row house needs paperwork before it needs lumber, too. The City of St. Louis Building Division puts “porches, decks, and retaining walls” under “Work That Requires a Building Permit,” and notes “different rules for properties in historic districts or flood zones.” Call the permit section at (314) 622-3313 before you call the yard.
That is the real gap between stores. Not the wood. The handling.
### The heavy board nobody warns you about
Grab a standard pressure-treated two-by-ten and it is cold and wet through your gloves, heavier than it has any right to be, with a green sheen on the grain and water beading where you squeezed. That weight is preservative and water, and it has to leave. It leaves on your deck, in the sun, and the board shrinks as it goes. By the next summer the deck boards you screwed down flat can cup like shallow gutters and hold a skin of rain.
The fix has a clumsy name: KDAT, kiln-dried after treatment. Culpeper Wood Preservers explains that the kiln “essentially pre-shrinks the wood and locks in its shape.” The boards are lighter, too, which your back will notice by the fortieth one.
Whether any store carries it is a phone question, not a parking-lot discovery. Ask three things before you drive: do you stock KDAT, in what sizes and lengths, and is it kept under a roof?
### What should you leave on the pile?
Buying lumber is hand work in any store, and knowing what to avoid saves the return trip. Set one end of the board on the floor, lift the other to your cheek and look down the narrow edge the way you would check a pool cue. A gentle hump along the edge, called crown, is normal; on a joist it goes up. A curve along the wide face is bow. A board whose two ends point in different directions has twist, and twist is the one you cannot fix with nails. Lay it flat on the concrete and press one corner: if the opposite corner lifts, leave it. Then run your eyes along both edges for wane, the rounded corner where bark used to be, for splits creeping in from the ends, and for knots sitting on the edge of a joist, where the board takes its load. A treated board that feels far heavier than its neighbors is still soaking wet.
At a good yard, the person pulling your order has done this a few thousand times. One south St. Louis County yard, Norrenberns Lumber & Hardware, has been open since 1946 and says plainly that “most of our staff has been in the industry for much of their lives.” That is the thing you are paying for at a yard. Not a different tree. A trained eye on the stack before you ever see it.
### Where does St. Louis keep the lumber no big box sells?
In a warehouse at 5103 Farlin Avenue in North City.
Lumber Logs calls itself an “urban log recycler.” According to St. Louis Magazine, all of its wood comes from “the St. Louis forest”: new subdivisions, cemeteries, parks, anyplace trees have to come down. Ordinary mills steer clear of that wood for a reason you would never guess. City trees swallow bullets, nails and staples, and a hidden spike can wreck a saw. “We metal-detect everything we pick up,” operations manager Joe Wilp told the magazine.
The magazine’s headline put it plainly: Lumber Logs keeps tornado-damaged trees out of the chipper. Wilp harvested 2,000 board feet worth of lumber on Westmoreland Place. The good stuff, walnut, cherry and white oak, goes to woodworkers and furniture makers. Ask him what the saw smells like and you get a menu: “Sawing maple’ll make you want pancakes, hickory makes you want bacon.”
This is not where you buy deck joists. It is where you buy the walnut for a mantel, the cherry for a kid’s bed, the white oak shelf from a tree you may have driven under for years.
### How do you pick the right yard without burning a Saturday?
Treat it like hiring help. Shortlist two or three yards. Call each one and tell them exactly what you are building: a deck off the back of a brick two-family in Dutchtown, a new floor system in a Soulard rehab, a set of shelves in a Benton Park basement. Then ask what they would put on it. What grades and species do they stock in your sizes? Is the treated lumber KDAT? Can you walk the stack and pick your own, or will they pull it for you? Do they deliver to your street, and on what day?
Say what you want, then compare what each yard says it will deliver against what you asked for. The yard that asks you a question back, about your span or your exposure or how soon you need it, is usually the one worth the drive.

Your next straight board is one phone call away. Start your shortlist with Building Supplies on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three yards and ask what they stock before you hitch the trailer.
If you’re the lumber yard or supply house that still pulls orders by hand, say so where people are looking. Homeowners reading this page are already searching for a yard like yours, so list your business and get more customers before they settle for the picked-over bunk.
### When the big box is the right call
Sometimes it is. It is 8:40 on a Sunday night, the yard closed hours ago, you need three studs and a box of screws, and the orange sign is ten minutes away. Long hours, small quantities and simple returns are real strengths. Use them.
Just shop the box the way a yard hand would. Read the stamp. Sight every board. Lay the treated ones flat and feel the weight. Put the bad ones back where the next person can see them.
Put the tape measure down: when did you last walk the Botanical Garden?
Then come back to the board. The straight one is out there, in a box store bin, on a yard’s cart or in a North City warehouse that smells like cherry. The difference is who did the looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy lumber from a lumber yard or Home Depot?
A.  Not automatically. For three studs the big box is the easy answer; for a whole deck, a yard can come out even or ahead once you count delivery and the boards you don’t throw away. Hand two or three stores the identical list, with species, grade, size, length and count, and compare the delivered totals, not the shelf tags.
### Q. Is Home Depot lumber good quality?
A.  It can be. What varies is the pile. How long it sat and how many people picked through it decide what you get, so sight down every board.
### Q. What to avoid when buying lumber?
A.  Leave behind boards with twist, heavy bow or crook, cupping across the face, wane on the edges, splits running in from the ends, and knots sitting on the edge of a joist. Skip treated boards that feel soaking wet and much heavier than their neighbors, because they will shrink and move on your deck.
### Q. What is better, lumber #1 or #2?
A.  No. 1 is recommended for construction where high strength, stiffness and good appearance are desired. No. 2 is recommended for most general construction uses where moderately high design values are required, and it allows well-spaced knots of any quality. Pick by the job and the look, not by the number.
### Q. Is it better to buy wood from a lumber yard?
A.  For a big order, outdoor treated stock or hardwood you plan to finish, usually yes, because a good yard carries more choices and has someone who knows the stack. For a few boards late on a weekend, the big box is fine if you do the sorting yourself.

## The Mailbox Is Full: A St. Louis Contractor Took Your Money and Disappeared
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/contractor-took-your-money-and-disappeared-what-to-do
Third call today, same robot voice: the mailbox is full. Behind you, the dishwasher hookup is still capped off. The cabinets sit stacked in the dining room of a Dutchtown two-family under a drop cloth that still smells like his truck.
### What do you do when a contractor takes your money and disappears?
Send a dated written demand today, and keep the contract, receipts, texts and photos in one folder. What gets money back is paper, and the order you build it in is also what turns “he just didn’t finish” into a report a detective will actually read.
Here is the turn. Under RSMo 570.010, deception “shall not be inferred from the fact alone that he did not subsequently perform the promise.” Not finishing proves nothing. Your paper is what shows he never meant to start.
This page is for the colder version. Not a slow crew. A vanished one. The deposit cleared, the number goes straight to voicemail, and the dumpster he promised never came down the alley.
Most people do this backwards. They call the police first, hear “that’s civil,” and give up on the criminal side for good. The officer isn’t wrong that day. He just isn’t looking at any evidence yet, because nobody has built it. A letter with a date on it is where that evidence starts. You’re not the only one at that table, either: in a single recent year the Missouri Attorney General’s office received more than 1,800 complaints about home repair, construction and real estate, fifth on its list of the state’s top consumer complaints. Filing is not just venting, either. The same office says its Consumer Protection Section recovered more than $14.9 million in restitution for Missouri citizens that year.
Paper first. Police second. The card company inside 60 days. That is the whole order, short enough to text to a neighbor whose contractor just went quiet.
So write it tonight, at the kitchen table, with the contract and the bank statement side by side. One page. What you agreed to, what you paid and on what date, what was never done, and a deadline for him to either start work or return the money. Mail it certified with a return receipt, and text a photo of it to the number he used. Keep the green card when it comes back. That little card, signed or unclaimed, is worth more than every voicemail you’ve left.
Inside the city, that folder has a destination if this ends in court: the Clyde S. Cahill Courts Building at 10 North Tucker, where people representing themselves can file cases in person, or by email. The 22nd Judicial Circuit’s court forms page posts the Petition Small Claims Court form you would start with.
### Why do the police say it’s a civil matter?
The officer listens, clicks his pen shut, and says the word: civil. Stealing in Missouri includes taking someone’s money “by means of deceit or coercion,” but that 570.010 line is the hard catch: a broken promise, alone, is not deceit.
A contractor who got sick, went broke or simply got buried has broken a contract, not a criminal law. What moves a report off the civil pile is evidence that he never meant to do the work at all, and that evidence is usually sitting in your phone.
Scroll it the way a detective would, thumb cold on the glass. Did he change his number the week the check cleared? Did the supply house he named tell you no order was ever placed? Is the name on his truck different from the name on your contract? Did a neighbor in Dutchtown or Benton Park hand him a deposit the same month and get the same silence? Two victims and one story is a pattern, and patterns are what get a case opened.
Inside the city limits, the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department’s non-emergency line is 314-231-1212. In the county, call the department that patrols your address, the way you would for a brick bungalow in Normandy. Bring copies, not originals: the contract, the canceled check or card statement, the screenshots, the certified mail receipt. Ask for the report number before you hang up. Your bank and the Attorney General may both want it.
### Across the river in Madison or St. Clair County
Living on the Illinois side, in Moro or Carlyle, doesn’t change the first move: same certified letter, same folder riding on the passenger seat. What changes is the office you write to. The Illinois Attorney General’s consumer protection page says it takes consumer complaints and can engage in informal dispute resolution for people having problems with home repair and construction services. The hotline number it lists for Carbondale is 1-800-243-0607.
The Illinois court is roomier, too. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 281, a small claim is one for money not in excess of $10,000, exclusive of interest and costs, against Missouri’s $5,000. In Madison County, the circuit clerk charges a $94 filing fee on cases up to $2,500. In St. Clair County, the Small Claims Division answers at (618) 825-2712.
### Did the deposit go on a credit card?
Tear open last month’s card statement and find the charge with his name on it. If your contractor ghosted you after you paid a deposit by card, this is the fastest money on the page, and it has a deadline. Federal billing rules protect a written dispute that reaches your card company no later than 60 days after it sent the first statement showing the charge. Count from the statement, not from the day he stopped answering.
Flip the card over, thumb on the raised numbers, and call the number on the back. Then follow up in writing to the billing-inquiries address, not the payment address. If you’re past that window, California’s Attorney General advises telling the card company you are asserting “claims and defenses,” especially when disputing the charge more than 60 days after it first shows up, because some reps don’t know the phrase and wrongly deny it. A check or cash gives you nothing like this. That’s the quiet reason the worst operators ask for both.
While the bank works, use the Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Complaint Form, available for online submission. The office’s consumer complaints page says it mediates complaints between businesses and consumers, and it asks for copies of contracts, invoices and canceled checks, never originals. Questions go to the Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-392-8222. By law, it can’t give you legal advice. It will put your name on a file that grows if the same guy tries it in Soulard next spring.
Nothing here about drywall: an afternoon at the Saint Louis Zoo, phone in pocket.
### Is suing worth it over a few thousand dollars?
Spread the folder open on the table one more time and add up what you are owed. How difficult is it to sue a contractor? Less than people fear, as long as the number fits the court. Missouri’s small claims judges hear cases where the amount in controversy does not exceed five thousand dollars. Illinois runs higher: Madison County’s circuit clerk defines a small claim as a sum up to $10,000, and its filing fee rises to $264 above $2,500.
The hard part isn’t winning. It’s finding him to serve the papers, and then collecting, long after the drop cloth has come off the cabinets. That’s why the certified letter, the report number and the Attorney General file all come first. They hand the judge a clean story told in dates, and sometimes they convince a contractor who wants to keep working that your refund is cheaper than a judgment with his name on it.
The next contractor you call should be one who picks up on the second ring. When you’re ready to hire someone to finish the job, start with local pros who put their name where neighbors can see it, and join St Louis Near Me Directory to keep that list close.
If you’re the contractor who shows up when you said you would, say so where it counts. Homeowners burned once are already looking for the crew that answers the phone, so list your business where they search.
### How much down is too much?
The sting of a vanished deposit lives in its size. California writes a ceiling into law: a home improvement down payment cannot exceed 10 percent of the project price or $1,000, whichever is less, and the same page warns against letting payments get ahead of the work. Use that as your own rule here, by choice. If a crew needs a big check to buy materials, offer to pay the supply house directly, or pay when the lumber is stacked in your driveway and you can smell the fresh-cut pine.
Before you hire the next one, shortlist two or three, interview them, tell each one plainly what you want done and how you’d like to pay, and compare what each says they will deliver and when.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What to do if you pay a contractor and they don’t finish the job?
A.  Put a written demand in the mail, certified, with a deadline to finish or refund. If any of the money went on a card, dispute it in writing within 60 days of the first statement showing the charge. Then submit a complaint to the Missouri Attorney General, whose office mediates complaints between businesses and consumers. Missouri small claims court hears cases up to $5,000.
### Q. How difficult is it to sue a contractor?
A.  Filing is the easy part. Missouri small claims covers cases up to $5,000, and Madison County, Illinois, takes small claims up to $10,000. The harder parts are serving a contractor who has moved and collecting once you win, which is why the paper trail comes first.
### Q. My contractor ghosted me after I paid a deposit. What should I do?
A.  Stop sending texts and send one certified letter instead, stating what you paid, on what date, and a deadline to start work or return it. Then call your card company if you paid by card, file a police report if you have signs he never meant to do the job, and submit a complaint to the Attorney General.
### Q. What to do when a contractor disappears?
A.  Gather the contract, payment records, texts and photos into one folder, then send a certified demand.
### Q. How much do contractors usually ask for a deposit?
A.  It varies by trade and job, and a large deposit is a request, not a rule. California’s contractor board says that by law, a down payment cannot exceed 10 percent of the project price or $1,000, whichever is less, which makes a useful yardstick when someone asks for far more.
### Q. Is it normal to pay a contractor 50% upfront?
A.  Half down is a lot of money to hand over before any work exists. California’s contractor board says that by law, a down payment cannot exceed 10 percent of the project price or $1,000, whichever is less. If materials are the reason, offer to pay the supplier directly or pay on delivery.
### Q. How much should I pay a contractor upfront?
A.  As little as the job allows, and never so much that payments run ahead of the work. Tie the rest to stages you can see, like materials delivered or a section finished, and pay by credit card when you can so a dispute right stays with you.
### Q. What complaints can be filed under consumer protection?
A.  The Missouri Attorney General’s office mediates complaints between businesses and consumers, and it lists home repair contractors who ask for money up front and provide little to no work among its top complaints. Attach copies of contracts, invoices and canceled checks, never originals, and call 1-800-392-8222 with questions.
### Q. Will the police take a report on a contractor who vanished?
A.  Ask, even if the first answer is that it sounds civil. Missouri law says failing to perform alone doesn’t prove intent to deceive, so bring the evidence that does: a changed number, materials never ordered, a different business name, or other homeowners with the same story.

## That Attic Tap Is a Screw. And Going Metal Needs a Permit
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/biggest-problem-with-metal-roofs-st-louis
Tap. A pause. Tap again, on the same patch of attic insulation, every time a long rain settles over the house. Outside, the roof looks perfect from the sidewalk. No hail mark, no rust. Up in the dark, one screw has loosened its grip a little more each season, and the rubber washer under its head has gone hard and cracked like an old rubber band.
That sound usually traces back to a choice made at the kitchen table, and in the City of St. Louis that choice runs straight into a permit rule most people never hear about. The city requires a building permit for an entire new roof when roof work is not replacement of like material, or when more than 25% of the roof sheathing is removed and replaced. Asphalt shingles and steel panels are not the same material, so ask the Permit Section about your job before the first bid comes in.
### What is the biggest problem with metal roofs?
The biggest problem with metal roofs is leaking at the fasteners: on an exposed-fastener roof, every screw is a hole through the panel, sealed only by a small rubber gasket. Sunlight wears that gasket out faster than the steel, and the panel’s own expansion and contraction can back the screws out until water finds the gap.
Sheffield Metals puts it plainly: exposed fastener systems put the integrity of your roofing structure in the hands of the fastener and the gasket, and springing a leak is one of the most common problems those roofs have. The steel itself can outlast you. The rubber cannot. And St. Louis gives that rubber no rest: the National Weather Service counts about 35-40 days per year at 90 degrees or higher, and 2 or 3 days per year at zero or below, all on the same screw.
That is the real fork in the road. Concealed-fastener panels, usually called standing seam, attach with hidden clips, so no fastener goes through the surface that takes the weather. They cost more and fewer crews install them well. Exposed-fastener panels cost less and go on faster, and they hand you a maintenance chore for as long as you own the house. Our guide to hiring a St. Louis roofer and the deductible law that protects you covers who to call. This page covers what to ask them about the metal.
### Swapping shingles for steel crosses a St. Louis permit line
Read that roof rule twice and tape it to the fridge, because a skipped permit never shows up at the lumber yard. It shows up when a crew is already up top.
Before anyone climbs a ladder, ask every bidder three things, in writing. Whose name goes on the permit? Will they fasten through the face of the panel or use hidden clips? And in a historic district, has this panel profile and color been through the city review before? The clips question decides how often somebody has to climb back up and check screws for as long as you own the house.
Then make one call yourself. The Permit Section sits in Room 425 of City Hall at 1200 Market, phone (314) 622-3313. A roofer who has stood at that counter answers the permit question in one breath.
Live in one of the city’s historic districts and the bar rises again. The bad version looks like this on a red-brick two-family in Benton Park: a trailer of bright panels at the curb, half the old roof torn off, and a crew sitting in their truck with the engine running. The Cultural Resources Office says that if your property is in a City Historic District, you will need a permit for ALL exterior work, except painting wood trim, and every district has its own standards. The city lists 14 historic districts and 112 landmarks. Most of those permits are approved within 5 working days, but a project that cannot comply with the Standards is scheduled for a hearing before the Preservation Board, which meets the fourth Monday of each month. Skip that step and the city’s answer is blunt: you may be stopped by an inspector, and all work must cease immediately until a permit is obtained.
### Why does a metal roof loosen its own screws?
Because steel moves. Lay your palm on a dark panel at 4 p.m. in July and you will pull it back fast. Walk out on a January morning and the same panel is cold enough to sting through a glove. Every swing between those two days stretches the sheet a little and shrinks it back. A panel screwed straight down through its face has nowhere to go, so the screws take the strain.
Sheffield Metals lists what happens when that movement is restricted: oil canning, fastener withdrawal and increased noise. Fastener withdrawal is the leak described above. Oil canning is the one that bothers your eyes instead of your ceiling. The Metal Construction Association defines it as visible waviness in the flat areas of metal roofing, and says no panel manufacturer, fabricator or installer can assure the total prevention of oil canning on any given project. You notice it at sunset, when low light rakes across a flat panel and it ripples like a pond. It rarely leaks. It can be reduced with thicker metal, panels with ribs or striations that break up the flat space, and a low-gloss finish.
This is also the honest answer to how long a metal roof lasts. McElroy Metal, citing Metal Construction Association research, says a residential metal roof routinely delivers 50 to 60 years of service life, while asphalt shingles typically need replacement every 12 to 20 years. That figure comes from a study of Galvalume standing seam systems. On an exposed-fastener roof, the panels can run for decades while the screws need watching, and Sheffield tells exposed-fastener owners to be ready for fastener maintenance as often as two times a year.
Somebody paid to put words in front of you today. Here’s how to tell.
### Does hail ruin a metal roof in St. Louis?
Usually it dents it, and the dent is where the money argument starts. The top hail rating is UL 2218 Class 4, tested with a 2.00 inch diameter steel ball. McElroy Metal is blunt about the limits: a Class 4 rating does not mean a roofing product is hail-proof. When the sky turns green over the Mississippi and hail hammers the roof like gravel thrown at a garage door, a steel roof will most likely keep the water out and may still come through pocked. Afterward you can stand in the driveway with the low sun behind you and count the dimples like a golf ball.
One stone-coated steel maker spells out how the industry treats those pocks. If a steel panel takes an indent, DECRA says this is considered aesthetic and not a functional damage warranty claim. Your insurance policy may draw a similar line, so ask your agent in writing how it treats a dent that does not leak. While you have them, check the declarations page. Missouri’s Department of Commerce and Insurance warns that an ACV policy may pay as little as 20% of the cost to replace the roof on an older roof, where a replacement cost policy pays the full cost.
### What should you ask a St. Louis roofer before you sign?
Shortlist two or three crews who install metal often, not a shingle crew that takes the odd metal job. Sit with each one on the porch and ask the same questions, then tell them what you want: a roof that stays dry for decades, a permit on file and no surprises. Compare what each one says they will deliver.
Ask whether they recommend exposed or concealed fasteners for your house, and why. Ask how the panels are allowed to move with the heat. Ask what goes underneath: McElroy says it does not recommend asphalt-based products under metal panels, and peel-and-stick layers paired with metal need to be high-temperature products. Ask whether the panel carries a UL 2218 label, because McElroy notes UL does not recognize a metal panel as classified unless the label is attached. Ask how many metal roofs they put on last year and whether you can see a local one that is at least five years old. Then ask who checks the screws, and when.
Listen for the pause. A crew that has fixed a fastener leak in Soulard or Dutchtown will tell you about it without being asked, and the ones who wave it off are telling you something too.
Your best protection is a roofer who brings up the screws before you do. Find metal-savvy crews to interview on the roofing map on St Louis Near Me Directory, and take the questions above with you.
If you’re the roofer who actually knows standing seam from screw-down, a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory puts that know-how in front of the St. Louis homeowners asking this exact question, so you get more customers who already want your answer.

### Frequently asked questions about metal roofs
### Q. What is the problem with installing a metal roof over shingles?
A.  You cannot see or fix the deck underneath, and the old shingles can scratch the back of the panels. Sheffield Metals recommends removing the existing shingles so the roof deck can be inspected, repaired and leveled, and warns that installing right over a shingle roof can scratch the protective backside coating. McElroy Metal says a metal roof can be installed directly over one layer of existing shingles, and that local code and the condition of the existing roof determine eligibility.
### Q. What is the typical lifespan of a metal roof?
A.  McElroy Metal, citing Metal Construction Association research on Galvalume standing seam roofs, puts it at 50 to 60 years of service life, compared with 12 to 20 years for asphalt shingles. Exposed-fastener roofs need their screws and gaskets checked along the way to get there.
### Q. How do I stop my metal roof from leaking?
A.  Find the source first. On exposed-fastener roofs, check for screws that are backing out, loose or rusting and replace them. On standing seam roofs, Sheffield Metals says a leak is commonly at some type of flashing area. Sheffield also advises against trying to fix it yourself without professional help, so have a metal roofer walk it.
### Q. Why are metal roofs not more popular?
A.  Price and labor. Standing seam costs more than exposed-fastener metal, and Sheffield Metals notes there are far fewer contractors with a proven track record installing it, because the work is more complex and labor-intensive.
### Q. Do insurance companies prefer metal or shingle roofs?
A.  Many insurers favor impact-resistant roofs of either kind. McElroy Metal says many insurance companies offer reduced insurance premiums for those using Class Four products. Ask your agent which rating earns a credit on your policy, and whether a cosmetic dent that does not leak would be covered.
### Q. Does homeowners insurance go down with a metal roof?
A.  It can. McElroy Metal says discounts vary by carrier and state, so ask your agent specifically about impact-resistant and metal roofing credits before you sign a roofing contract.
### Q. Does a metal roof need underlayment?
A.  Yes. McElroy Metal says underlayment helps shed water that may find its way into the roofing system after construction. It recommends against asphalt-based felt under metal panels and calls high-temperature products essential when peel-and-stick is paired with metal.
### Q. Do I need a permit to put a metal roof on a house in St. Louis?
A.  Usually, yes. The City of St. Louis requires a building permit for a new roof when the work is not replacement of like material, and in a City Historic District the Cultural Resources Office requires a permit for all exterior work except painting wood trim.
### Q. Is a metal roof loud when it rains?
A.  Not on a house built right. McElroy Metal says residential metal roofs go over solid decking and underlayment, and with attic insulation and a ceiling below, rain sounds about the same as on any other roof. The loud reputation comes from barns and carports with nothing under the panels.

## Santa Rides the Amtrak to Hermann, and You Can Leave the Car Home
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/most-christmassy-town-in-missouri
Santa skips the sleigh in Hermann. He rides the Amtrak in on December 5-6, the doors slide open, cold river air hits your face, and your kid grabs your sleeve at the first flash of a red suit on the platform.
### What is the most Christmassy town in Missouri?
Hermann. It’s the river town at the end of that platform: Santa is riding the Missouri River Runner this holiday season and making a stop in Downtown Hermann, and you can ride the same line out of St. Louis Gateway Station. The car rocks, the heater hums, and a gray winter river slides past the window while your kid presses a mitten to the glass. Then you step off a few blocks from everything, into a town whose own calendar promises 8 weeks of Christmas fun, with German Christmas markets and a Children’s Lantern Parade.
Text this one to the other parents: you can leave the car home. Westbound Train 311 departs St. Louis Gateway Station daily at 8:10 a.m., on the same Missouri River Runner line Santa rides into Downtown Hermann on December 5-6. Coming home, MoDOT lists the evening train that leaves Kansas City at 4:05 p.m. arriving in St. Louis at 9:45 p.m., so the kids can fall asleep on the ride back. Here’s the part worth forwarding: Santa’s train weekend is also Weihnachtsfest weekend at the Deutschheim State Historic Site, where the 1840 Pommer House is open for free self-guided tours and staff hand out traditional springerle cookies. Our guide to Christmas events in St. Louis covers what’s lit inside the city. This page is for the family that wants one day out of town and a ride home with sticky fingers and a paper bag of cookies on somebody’s lap.
Hermann’s Christmas runs on St. Louis. When the town throws its Holiday Kick-Off on Saturday, November 14, 102.5 KEZK, which Hermann calls St. Louis’ official Christmas station, broadcasts live from it. On Sunday, December 13, the Showboat Community Theatre hosts a Christmas concert featuring FReSH RAIN, a gospel group from St. Louis. And when a full-length Christmas movie was shot in Hermann in the winter of 2022, the only scenes filmed anywhere else were at Lambert International Airport in St. Louis, according to Visit Hermann’s account of the production. Your home airport made it into Missouri’s Christmas movie. Hermann did the rest.
So the real question isn’t which town. It’s which weekend.
### Which December weekend in Hermann is worth the drive?
Pick by weekend, because the events in Hermann in December stack up on Saturdays and Sundays, and each weekend tastes different. This season’s full list lives on the Visit Hermann Christmas page, and it changes, so read it the week you go.
Mulled wine in your hands and carolers singing between the vendor booths: that’s December 5-6, the German weekend, when Stone Hill Winery holds its Kristkindl Markt, a traditional Christmas market. Across town, the Deutschheim State Historic Site holds Weihnachtsfest, its re-creation of a 19th century German Christmas. The 1840 Pommer House is decorated in the German Christmas style and open for free self-guided tours, and staff hand out traditional springerle cookies while they explain how German immigrant customs became American Christmas habits.
Beeswax candles and ornaments crowd the stalls the second weekend, December 12-13, when the riverfront Festhalle at Hermannhof turns into a European-style Christmas market for the Christkindl Markt. If the stalls look familiar, they should.
On Friday, December 11, Jingle In Your Jammies invites families to stroll downtown through five special stops, and the name tells your kids exactly what to wear: flannel pajamas under puffy coats. Hermann Trolley runs its Christmas tours Fridays at 6pm on December 4, 11 and 18. Then the Hermann Cookie Walk on December 18-19 sends you shop to shop downtown collecting Christmas cookies, powdered sugar on every glove, and it needs advance tickets. One to skip with the kids: Santa Rampage on December 12 is a pub crawl, and you must be 21+ to go.
Can’t decide? The Twinkle Tour is the easy yes. It runs November 25 through December 31 as a self-guided driving tour of lights at businesses and homes all over Hermann. Heater on, cocoa in the cup holder, kids counting houses from the back seat. No ticket line, no schedule to keep.
### Which Christmas movie was filmed in Hermann?
People search for the Hallmark movie made in Hermann, MO. The film they mean is A Christmas Vintage, released in 2023 by Nicely Entertainment. Two heirs to rival Hermann wineries, a wine competition, and a town that pulls them together. Know the studio’s name and you can settle that argument at the dinner table.
When it came out, Visit Hermann listed it on streaming channels including Tubi, Roku and Peacock. Services shuffle their catalogs, so search the title before movie night rather than trusting an old list. The crew shot it over 15 days, using the cellars at Hermannhof, Adam Puchta Winery as the rival “Reserve Cellars,” and a tree-lighting scene filmed on what the town calls a cold night.
Here’s the family move: watch it on the couch the night before, blanket over three sets of knees. The next afternoon, stand at the same Festhalle market with a hot cup warming your gloves while your kid whispers, “That’s the place.” Turning a movie into a scavenger hunt costs nothing and buys you an hour of quiet in the car.
### Can you skip the drive and take the train?
Yes, and it may be the best December move most St. Louis families never make. The Amtrak Missouri River Runner makes 4 daily stops in Hermann, and MoDOT lists westbound Train 311 leaving St. Louis Gateway Station daily at 8:10 a.m. Hermann’s Visitor Information Center sits at the Amtrak stop, open every day from 8am to 8pm, with restrooms inside and free luggage lockers right outside.
From there, Visit Hermann says you can walk, bike or stroll to nearly every restaurant, shop and tasting room in town. No circling for parking. Nobody drawing the short straw to stay sober. Just the rocking car and a gray winter river sliding past the window. Santa rides it too: All Aboard With Santa brings him in on the Missouri River Runner on December 5-6, and Santa Rides The Rails on Thursday, December 17 promises pictures with Santa and a scenic river view into Hermann. Tickets for that one go on sale in December. Train times change, so confirm the schedule with Amtrak the week you book.
### Is Branson worth the longer drive?
If your family measures Christmas in bulbs, Silver Dollar City in Branson is the other honest answer. An Old Time Christmas runs November 7 through January 2 this season with more than 6.5 million lights, including an eight-story animated Christmas tree on Town Square and 1.5 million more in Christmas in Midtown, according to Explore Branson.
Here’s my take. Silver Dollar City is a theme park, built to dazzle, and it earns a weekend. Hermann is a real town where people live. For a day trip from St. Louis with small kids, Hermann wins. Save Branson for the year you want a hotel pool and two days of lights.
### How do you plan a Hermann day without a meltdown?
Book anything marked “advance tickets required” first. That includes the Holiday House Tour on Saturday, December 5, when you walk through decorated Hermann homes, and the Cookie Walk. Then call before you go: the Deutschheim site office is at 573-486-2200, and the state parks page points to capacity and winter weather advisories. If your plan lands on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day, Visit Hermann posts separate restaurant and shop hours for those days, so check them before you promise anybody lunch.
Want the bakers, wreath-makers and gift shops closer to home, too? St. Louis is full of them, and you can find them, follow them and join St Louis Near Me Directory to keep your December list in one place.
If you’re the bakery, the B&B or the one-person craft booth, December is your loudest month. More families are already searching here for exactly what you make, so list your business before the cookie rush.
Pack for standing still in the cold, not for walking in it. Market stalls and a lantern parade mean long minutes in one spot, and that’s when little toes go numb. Hats, a spare pair of gloves, and cash in a pocket for the cookie table.

## The 3:11 Out of Downtown: Places to Travel Within 4 Hours of St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/places-to-travel-within-4-hours-of-st-louis
A soft lurch, and the platform at the Gateway Transportation Center downtown starts sliding backward past your window: 3:11 p.m. Friday, and the weekend has already begun. That’s Amtrak Train 319, and at 8:51 p.m. it pulls into Kansas City.
### What are some good places to travel within 4 hours of St. Louis?
Kansas City and Branson are the big overnight trips at the edge of that radius: Visit KC puts Kansas City 4 hours from St. Louis, and Explore Branson clocks Branson at 3 hours 45 minutes. Both are far enough that you pack a bag instead of a cooler.
The shorter runs live on our list of the best day trips from St. Louis. You leave after coffee, you eat lunch somewhere with a screen door, you’re back on your own couch by dark. Four hours buys a different weekend, and the best one costs almost nothing once you step off the train: ride the 3:11 out of downtown after work with the Missouri River sliding past the window, walk into the Nelson-Atkins for free on Saturday, and catch the 4:05 p.m. train out of Kansas City on Sunday, home in St. Louis by 9:45.
The mistake people make is treating a Kansas City weekend like a day trip. They cram it into one day, see more of I-70 than of Kansas City, and come home with a stiff neck swearing they’ll never do it again.
### Which of these trips really needs a hotel night?
Hour three on I-70 is where it turns: the bag of Gus’ pretzels you grabbed on Arsenal Street is down to salt and crumbs, every field looks like the last one, and somebody in the back seat asks how much longer. That’s why the trips at the edge need a bed. Drive either one there and back in one day and you spend more of the day counting highway mile markers than standing anywhere worth the gas.
So run this test tonight, before you book anything: look up the drive time for the place you’re eyeing, double it, and ask whether you’d sit in a parked car that long for what you’ll get on arrival. If the answer is no, the trip needs a bed at the other end.
### Can you make the Kansas City trip without driving at all?
Yes, and most St. Louisans have never tried it. Amtrak’s Missouri River Runner runs twice a day on a 283-mile route between St. Louis and Kansas City. Here’s the part almost nobody in St. Louis knows: the 3:11 isn’t a St. Louis train at all. Train 319 originates in Chicago, so the seat you drop into downtown has already rolled the length of Illinois before you sit down. Leave work a little early and you’re there in time for a late dinner, without ever white-knuckling past a semi on the interstate in the rain. You step down onto the Kansas City platform at 8:51 with nearly six hours of sitting in your legs, and the first thing you want is barbecue. Tickets book through the Missouri River Runner’s own site, and it says you can bring your bicycle along for the ride.
If you’d rather have the whole day, Train 311 departs St. Louis at 8:10 a.m. and arrives at 1:50 p.m. You sit. You read. You watch the fields slide past with a paper cup of coffee going cold in your hand, and the only thing you’re steering is your own attention.
Once you’re there, Kansas City’s best move costs nothing. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art opens more than 5,000 years of art for free, and its Donald J. Hall Sculpture Park is free to visit and open from sunrise to sundown. One warning that saves a wasted morning: the museum is closed Tuesday and Wednesday. Saturday at 10 a.m. the doors open onto cool, hushed galleries. The art is free; the museum’s Oak Street parking garage is not, at $20 for your visit. Train out the first evening, free art the next day, and your car never leaves the curb, because the KC Streetcar is free to ride from UMKC to the River Market. Plan the art for Thursday through Monday, and spend the rest of the weekend with smoke in your jacket, eating your way across a barbecue town that will happily argue with St. Louis about who does it better.
### Is Lake of the Ozarks worth it for one night?
The drive is about two and a half hours on Interstate 70 and US Route 54: west on I-70 to Kingdom City, then Highway 54 West through Jefferson City.
You get there with light left in the sky. The dock boards are warm under bare feet, an outboard coughs to life somewhere down the cove, and the whole week drains out of your shoulders before the cooler is even unpacked.
What it’s for: water, sun, doing nothing on purpose. If your crew needs to come home actually rested, not just entertained, this is the one. Pick up toasted ravioli on The Hill on the way out of town and the first dinner is handled.
Pack for the dock, not the dresser. Towels, sunscreen, a dry bag for the phones, and one long-sleeve shirt for the night the breeze comes off the water and the deck chairs go cold. Leave the laptop in the car. The lake only works if you let it.
### Where do you go when you want quiet instead of a crowd?
Southern Illinois. The Garden of the Gods Recreation Area in the Shawnee National Forest is, in the Forest Service’s own words, one of the most photographed locations in the state, and plenty of people from the city still haven’t stood on it.
The Observation Trail is only a quarter mile, made of natural sandstone, and the Forest Service says it takes about an hour to walk. That hour is the point. You stop every few steps. The rock is gritty and sun-warm under your palm, the wind comes up over the bluff, and the formations carry names that tell you somebody stood here grinning: Camel Rock, Table Rock, Devil’s Smokestack. The Forest Service warns of high cliffs, so hold small hands.
Here’s why it belongs on any cheap weekend getaway list: Pharaoh Campground, right there, is open year round with 12 campsites, tables, fire grills, toilets and drinking water. Coming home, you cross the river and watch the Arch climb into the windshield, and the city looks better for having left it.
Off topic, but true: a jacket that fits the shoulders forgives nearly everything else.
### Memphis is the weekend that stays with you
Not every good trip is a rest. I-55 is the straight line from St. Louis to Memphis, and at the end of it is the National Civil Rights Museum, located at the former Lorraine Motel, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated on April 4, 1968.
Give it a full morning, not a stop on the way to lunch. People go quiet in there. Strangers stand shoulder to shoulder and nobody checks a phone. You walk back out into the Memphis heat a little slower than you walked in, and you talk about it the whole drive home.
What it’s for: the trip your teenagers will remember long after they forget the hotel pool. Then let the evening be music and food, because you’ll need both.
Eat a real breakfast before you go in. The exhibits ask a lot of you, and an empty stomach makes a heavy morning heavier. When you come out, don’t rush to the car. Sit for a minute in the sun and let everybody find their words. Some of the best talks you’ll ever have with a teenager start on a curb like that one.
### Branson, and the honest case for the longest drive
Branson sits at the outer edge of the radius. Branson is 255 miles from St. Louis Lambert, about the same as Kansas City, but the last stretch winds through the Ozark hills and it feels longer. By the time you pull in, the back seat has gone silent, the kids asleep against the window with seat-belt creases printed on their cheeks.
Arrive the first evening, spend the next day at the shows and on the water, drive home after breakfast.
The trick with Branson is the last hour, not the first three. Fill the tank and the snack bag before you leave the city, because the winding end of the drive is where everyone in the car gets restless at once. Put on music the whole car can agree on. Crack a window when the hills start to roll. Nobody remembers the drive a week later. They remember the first morning: coffee steaming in a paper cup, the hills still soft and blue in the early light.
The trip goes right or wrong in the week before you leave. The oil change, the dog sitter, the bag with the busted zipper: find the local people who handle all of it on St Louis Near Me Directory and keep your short list in one place.
If you’re the mechanic, the pet sitter or the travel agent, the families packing for these weekends are looking for you this week, so list your business where they already search and get more customers before the trip starts.
### How do you pick the right one for your weekend?
Ask what you want to feel the night you get home, then work backward. Want to come home rested? The lake. Want to come home changed? Memphis. Want a weekend that costs almost nothing once you arrive? The Garden of the Gods and a campsite, or Kansas City and a free museum. Want the kids to talk about it at school on Monday? Branson.
Then do the gas math honestly, with real miles and not hope. If the round trip eats a whole day, the trip deserves a bed at the other end. And if you’d rather hand the planning to a pro, shortlist two or three local travel agents, interview them, tell them exactly what kind of weekend you want, and compare what each one says they’ll actually deliver.
Then put a date on the calendar before the week talks you out of it. The weekends people regret are rarely the ones that went sideways. They’re the ones that stayed a browser tab.

## Barnes Has Four Bed Counts, and None Pick Your ER: The Largest Hospital in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/largest-hospital-in-missouri
1,278 beds, and not one of them helps you at 2 a.m. in the driver’s seat, hazards ticking, someone you love breathing wrong beside you. That is the size of the place most St. Louisans just call Barnes. And it still may not be where your ambulance should go.
### What is the largest hospital in Missouri?
Barnes-Jewish Hospital, on the Washington University Medical Campus in St. Louis, is the largest hospital in Missouri. WashU’s emergency medicine department puts it plainly: “At 1,278 beds, BJH is the largest in Missouri.” Barnes-Jewish’s own About page calls it “the largest hospital in Missouri.” For scale, Mercy Hospital St. Louis on New Ballas Road reports 715 staffed beds, and St. Luke’s Hospital out on Woods Mill Road calls itself a 493-bed hospital.
If you have ever walked it, you already know the number in your feet before you know it on paper. The parking garage elevator opens onto a skybridge. The skybridge opens onto a corridor that smells like floor wax and hand sanitizer. The corridor forks, and the sign you need is the one you just passed. People get lost in there on their way to visit a parent, carrying a phone charger and a bag of clothes, and they are not doing anything wrong. It is just that big. Before a planned visit, call Barnes-Jewish guest services at 314-362-5196 and ask for a Greeter escort, so a person walks beside you instead of you squinting at one more sign with that bag cutting into your shoulder.
This page is about size and fit: which of the big St. Louis hospitals is built for which emergency, and what to do before the night you need one. The money side, networks, estimates and charity care, lives on our guide to how hospital billing works in St. Louis, and this page will not repeat it.
### One hospital, four official bed counts
Here is the thing nobody tells you when you search the question. The largest hospital in Missouri does not have one bed count. It has several, and they all come from the hospital’s own side of the street.
One Barnes-Jewish article calls it a 1,315 bed teaching hospital. Another, about the Women & Infants Center, says 1,386 beds. A third, announcing the new neuro intensive care unit, says 1,638 beds. Read those last two again. Same four digits, shuffled. And the WashU page that sends residents to work there says 1,278.
I could not confirm which figure is current, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. Hospitals count beds in different ways, a bed on a license is not always a bed with a nurse beside it, and a boilerplate paragraph at the bottom of a press release does not always get updated when a tower opens or a unit closes. Mercy is one of the few that spells out which kind it means: 715 staffed beds.
Every version agrees on the ranking, though. Barnes-Jewish is the biggest. What matters more is this: when someone you love is gray in the face on the kitchen floor, nobody on the phone with 911 is going to ask you how many beds you would prefer. Call 911, and let the crew pick the door. Then take five minutes tonight: save Mercy Hospital St. Louis’s main line, (314) 251-6000, and the Barnes-Jewish Greeter line, 314-362-5196, in your phone, and tape BJC’s after-care rule to the fridge: call your primary care provider within 24 hours of going to the ER, or have someone call for you if you can’t make the call yourself.
### What are the big hospitals in St. Louis?
Size has more than one measure, and the most honest one for you is how many people walk through the emergency doors. By that yardstick the picture shifts.
Barnes-Jewish sees over 80,000 emergency visits a year, according to WashU. Mercy Hospital St. Louis reported 101,387 emergency department visits and 8,178 births in its last fiscal year, and it says one of every three babies born in St. Louis is born there. So the hospital with roughly half the beds runs the busier front door and the busiest maternity floor. That is the kind of thing you only find out by reading the fine print on two different websites.
Then come the mid-size hospitals that carry a huge share of everyday care. Missouri Baptist Medical Center on North Ballas Road has 489 beds. St. Luke’s has 493 and describes itself as the area’s only independent healthcare provider. St. Louis Children’s Hospital has 465 licensed beds. Christian Hospital on Dunn Road has 240 staffed beds and still logged 86,471 emergency visits. Small building, packed waiting room. If you have sat in one of those plastic chairs at midnight, listening to the doors hiss open every few minutes, you know what that number feels like.
Behind several of these sits one parent organization. BJC comprises 24 hospitals and hundreds of clinics and service organizations. That is why people mix up “Barnes” and “BJC.” One is a hospital. The other is the company that owns it and many more.
### Why doesn’t the bed count decide where the ambulance goes?
Because emergencies are sorted by capability, not square footage. A crushed leg, a burned hand and a newborn struggling to breathe each need a specific kind of team, and those teams are not spread evenly across town.
BJC’s own emergency guidance puts it plainly: call 911 for something like a heart attack or stroke, because having an ambulance transport you is the best option and the crew can start treatment as soon as they arrive. That matters here more than anywhere. The crew knows which doors on this list lead to which teams. You, at 2 a.m., with your keys shaking in your hand, do not need to.
Hospital hallways squeak. Metal roofs crack somewhere else: the rubber, first.
### Which St. Louis hospital is built for what?
This is the part worth reading once now, with coffee, instead of for the first time in a hallway.
Major trauma. Barnes-Jewish is a Level I trauma center, treats more than 16,000 trauma patients a year and calls itself one of nine in Missouri with that national verification. Mercy Hospital St. Louis runs St. Louis County’s only Level 1 trauma center, so a bad crash out west on the highway has a top-level option without crossing into the city.
Burns. Mercy says its burn center is the only verified center in Missouri for both adult and pediatric burn care. A grease fire at the stove does not care which hospital is bigger.
Children. In the county, Mercy lists St. Louis County’s only pediatric intensive care unit, plus a Level IV NICU for the tiniest newborns.
Cancer and transplants. Siteman Cancer Center at Barnes-Jewish and WashU is the only National Cancer Institute designated Comprehensive Cancer Center in Missouri and within a 240-mile radius of St. Louis. Barnes-Jewish also says it has the region’s only comprehensive transplant center, covering heart, lung, kidney, liver and more. These are the planned trips, the ones where size and depth genuinely help.
Save the hospital numbers before you need them, not in the parking lot. Browse Hospitals on St Louis Near Me Directory and put the two or three closest to your home, and to your parents’ home, in your phone tonight.
If you’re the medical transport driver, the home health agency or the urgent care clinic, the families on this page are already looking for you. Help them get to you and get more customers with a listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.
### Do this before the night you need it
Most of the stress in a hospital night is not medical. It is the drive, the parking, the wrong entrance, the cold vending-machine coffee while you wait for someone to come find you. You can take a lot of that off the table in ten quiet minutes.
Ask your own doctor which of these hospitals they actually admit patients to, and which one they would send you to for a heart scare. Shortlist two or three, tell your doctor what matters to you, whether that is distance, your insurance or a specialist you already trust, and compare that with what each hospital says it delivers. And after any ER visit, BJC tells patients to call their primary care provider within 24 hours of going to the ER.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many beds does Barnes-Jewish Hospital in St. Louis have?
A.  WashU Medicine lists Barnes-Jewish Hospital at 1,278 beds, while the hospital’s own news releases have printed 1,315, 1,386 and 1,638 at different times. Whichever figure you use, it is the largest hospital in Missouri.
### Q. Is BJC the largest hospital in Missouri?
A.  BJC is not a single hospital. It is the health system that owns Barnes-Jewish, and it calls itself the largest nonprofit health care organization in Missouri, with 24 hospitals. The largest single hospital is Barnes-Jewish.
### Q. How big is Mercy hospital in St. Louis?
A.  Mercy Hospital St. Louis reports 715 staffed beds, 101,387 emergency department visits and 8,178 births in its last fiscal year. It runs St. Louis County’s only Level 1 trauma center. The main number is (314) 251-6000.
### Q. How big is St. Luke’s hospital in St. Louis?
A.  St. Luke’s describes itself as a 493-bed hospital with more than 30 outpatient locations and services in over 60 specialty areas.
### Q. What is the oldest hospital in St. Louis?
A.  According to the Archdiocese of St. Louis, the Daughters of Charity, who arrived in 1828, established the first hospital west of the Mississippi River, known today as DePaul Hospital. Mercy traces its roots to a 25-bed hospital the Sisters of Mercy opened in 1871.
### Q. Is it better to go to a walk-in clinic or emergency room?
A.  It depends on the danger. BJC lists a hard time breathing, severe chest pain or pressure, choking and severe bleeding among the emergencies that need care right away. For problems that are not emergencies, call your primary care provider first, or use a walk-in clinic if you do not have one.

## A $250 House and a 700-Ton Fireplace: Day Trips for Two
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/day-trips-from-st-louis-for-couples
A $250 house, five rooms, out of a Sears catalog: that is what you are walking past in Carlinville, Illinois, with your shoes the only sound on the block. Families bought these run-down homes for $250 in the mid-1930s, after the coal mines closed and the miners left. Turn toward the river instead and the day ends at a table beside a 700-ton stone fireplace at Pere Marquette Lodge, the wind off the parking lot gone the second the door shuts behind you.
### What are good day trips from St. Louis for couples?
Start after lunch and let the clock run slow. Drive the river bluffs to Pere Marquette Lodge for a glass in its wine room and dinner beside that 700-ton stone fireplace, or spend the afternoon in Carlinville, Illinois, walking blocks of mail-order Sears houses with a hand in each other’s coat pocket. What makes either one work for two is the clock, not the map. Before you back out of the driveway, make one call: the lodge front desk at 618-786-2331, because the lodge says hours of operation may vary, or 217-204-1446 to ask about Carlinville’s free courthouse tour. Then let the drive home be part of the date.
The well-known stops are all in our guide to the best day trips from St. Louis. This is the slow version, for two people who leave the city after lunch instead of at dawn.
### Go in eagle season, and book it by phone
The best weeks for this trip are the cold ones. Pere Marquette Lodge sells an Eagle Package built around the bald eagles’ peak winter population in January and February, and it bundles your Lodge room with dinner and breakfast from a select menu. The lodge lists it at $159 plus tax. Ask for the current price when you call, because that is the step most couples miss: the lodge says package reservations cannot be made online.
So you pick up the phone and dial (618) 786-2331. It feels old-fashioned, and it is the best part of the plan. Nobody has to drive home in the dark after the wine, the room is a short walk from the fireplace, and the next morning starts with breakfast instead of a commute. Pack gloves thin enough to hold a coffee cup and a scarf you can pull over your nose. Winter by the water bites, and a warm room waiting at the end of it changes how the whole cold day feels.
### The neighborhood a mail-order catalog built
Leave the square on foot in the late-afternoon light and the street goes so quiet you can hear your own shoes on the sidewalk and a screen door clap somewhere down the block. These are mail-order homes from the Sears catalog. Walk slowly, and play the game of guessing which house is which model, because Sears named one of its models the “Carlin” after the town.
The story turns sad before it turns sweet. In 1917 Standard Oil of Indiana opened two new coal mines here. Young miners poured in, and the town’s population swelled from 4,000 to 6,000 almost overnight, so short of beds that the company placed an order for $1 million for homes, the largest in Sears history. By the end of 1918, 156 mail-order homes stood in a nine-block neighborhood called Standard Addition. In 1926 the mines closed, the miners left, and the houses sat largely vacant until the mid-1930s. Then the turn worth repeating on the drive home: models that had sold for $3,000 to $4,000 went to families for $250, five rooms and all. Today 152 of them still stand, the largest single collection of Sears kit homes in the United States.
### What should you book before you leave?
Less than you think, and that is the good news for two. The lodge restaurant says reservations are recommended for parties of 6 or more, so a table for two is normally a walk-in. The thing worth booking is the part of the day that is easy to miss: a guided look inside the building you came to see.
The city’s tourism committee offers free tours of the famous Million Dollar Courthouse and 1869 Cannonball Jail, and tour questions go to 217-204-1446. Call a few days ahead and ask what time works. Then plan the rest of the day around it, lunch on the square before and a long walk after, so you are never checking the time on the courthouse steps.
### The courthouse that took forty years to pay off
Stand on the lawn and tip your head back until the cold gets down your collar. The dome is 191 feet from its apex to the ground, and the main courtroom inside covers 4,500 square feet. When it was finished in 1870, the building had cost $1,380,500, which the city’s own history puts at nineteen percent of the assessed value of all property in the county. An independent audit said it should have cost $643,867.
Families went bankrupt paying for it. The final bond was not burned until July 1910, forty years after the building was done, and some 20,000 people came to watch it go up in smoke. That is a story to tell each other on the steps, the kind that makes a pretty building feel like a real place where real people were furious and then, slowly, proud.
There is a quieter connection on the way there, too. Carlinville is named for Thomas Carlin, a state senator from nearby Carrollton, who went on to be elected governor of Illinois in 1838. Pick a back road and drive through the town the man came from. Nobody will be in a hurry, least of all you.
### Why does the hour you arrive matter more than the town?
Because the places that feel romantic at 4 p.m. feel like a parking lot at noon. Two people who leave at noon instead of nine get the second half of the day, and the second half is the good one.
The lodge’s own posted hours make the case. Dinner runs from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m., and the lodge’s wine room opens at 3 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, running to 10 p.m., and from 3 p.m. to dusk on Sundays. That is a built-in schedule for a slow date. Wine in the late afternoon, dinner at 5, and the drive home along the river in the last light, windows cracked, the cold coming off the water.
One honest warning. The lodge says that due to staffing shortages, hours of operation may vary, and asks guests to call the front desk at 618-786-2331. Make that call the morning of. A locked tasting room is a bad surprise at the end of a long drive, and a two-minute call is the cheapest insurance you will buy all day.
Say this one out loud over dinner: the lodge’s own history says Illinois inmates constructed the furniture in the Lodge, so the chair you are sitting in has a past of its own. The Civilian Conservation Corps built the lodge from 1933 to 1939 and did all of its metal work, the chandeliers, the door handles and the window locks. It opened for business in 1940 at a cost of $352,912.
Hold that number up against Carlinville’s courthouse, $1,380,500, and you have the whole day in two buildings: one the county went broke paying for, one a Depression work crew raised out of local stone for a fraction of it. Run your hand along the fireplace on the way out. The fireplace and the lodge floor are both limestone.
### Can you leave the car at home?
Yes, for one of these, and it changes the whole day. Carlinville has its own Amtrak station, a stop on the Lincoln Service. Board downtown at Gateway Station, and nobody has to be the one who stops at a single glass. You get the rattle of the rails, a window seat, farm fields sliding past and time to actually talk with no GPS voice cutting in.
Check the timetable before you plan around it, because the trains only run at set times and you want a return that leaves after dinner, not before lunch. If the schedule does not line up, drive and trade the wheel: one of you takes the bluffs out, the other takes the dark road home.
Unrelated, but do you know which Missouri hospital is the biggest?
### How do you plan a one-day trip for two without rushing it?
Pick one anchor, not four. The fastest way to ruin a day trip for two is a list. Choose the one thing the day is built around, the lodge dinner or the courthouse tour, and give everything else permission to fall off. Then work backward: the call that confirms hours, the time you need to leave the city, and one loose hour you do not fill on purpose.
That loose hour is where the day actually happens. It is the gravel pull-off where you stop because the river looks like hammered tin, the second cup of coffee under the stone wall, the porch you both point at in Standard Addition. Bring a paper map in case the signal drops, a jacket for the bluffs and some cash for a small-town shop, and leave the itinerary in the glove box.
Pick the dinner first and the rest of the day falls into place. If you would rather stay close to home this time, our date-night restaurant guide has the tables worth dressing up for.
If you run the inn, the tasting room or the cafe on the square, couples planning slow afternoons like this one are customers looking for you, so put your business where they search.
### Coming home to the city
End the day back in St. Louis, not on the highway shoulder. Plan the last stop inside the city, a late dessert or one more drink close to home, so the trip lands softly instead of dumping you in the garage with nothing left to say. The drive back is the last chapter. Give it an ending.
