### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How does claiming unemployment affect my employer?
A.  Benefits paid are charged to the employer’s account in ratio to the wages used to set up the claim, which can raise the employer’s experience rate, and reimbursable employers are charged directly. A worker can draw up to twenty weeks of benefits in a benefit year. That’s why a timely, accurate protest matters when a separation was a quit or a misconduct firing, and why it doesn’t when it was a layoff. When the empty shift is the bigger problem, St Louis Near Me Directory is where St. Louis job-seekers can find your job post.
### Q. Does unemployment contact your previous employer?
A.  It reaches out on paper: Missouri mails a notice of the initial claim to each base-period employer and to the last employing unit the worker names, except a contributing base-period employer that paid the worker four hundred dollars or less. That notice is what starts the employer’s ten-day protest period.
### Q. What does issue on file mean with unemployment?
A.  In Missouri’s terms, an issue is the circumstance causing a dispute over whether a claimant may receive benefits, and a pending issue means benefits are on hold because of it. An employer protest about a quit or a firing is one common way an issue gets raised. The claimant is contacted if more information is needed.
### Q. What disqualifies you for unemployment in Missouri?
A.  Quitting without good cause attributable to the employer or the work, being discharged for misconduct connected with work, or refusing suitable work can all lead to disqualification. Misconduct includes things like violating a no-call, no-show policy or two or more unapproved absences after a written warning.
### Q. What happens if I lose an unemployment appeal?
A.  The losing side at the Appeals Tribunal has 30 days to ask the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission to review the referee’s decision, and the Commission generally decides on the existing hearing record. After the Commission, the next step is the Missouri Court of Appeals, and an employer other than a sole proprietor needs a Missouri-licensed attorney to file it.

## Your Zoo Card Can Halve Kansas City Tickets: St. Louis Zoo vs Kansas City Zoo
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-zoo-vs-kansas-city-zoo
“Free one or far one?” The question comes from the back seat before the seat belts have finished clicking.
Your thumb finds the zoo membership card, tucked behind the Schnucks card, its corners gone soft. That soft-cornered card is worth something in Kansas City. The national reciprocity chart lists the Kansas City Zoo & Aquarium at 50%.
### Which zoo is better, KC or STL?
For most St. Louis families, the Saint Louis Zoo is the better zoo day: the gate is always free, and your one real cost is the $20 parking lot. Kansas City gives you free parking, but general admission is $22 to $24 a person online, with ages 2 and under always free.
The question comes through a juice box straw that squeaks on every word. The free one is the Saint Louis Zoo. The far one is Kansas City, the long drive west and a ticket window at the end of it. You run the old math, lot against gate, gas against nap time, and your thumb finds the card in your wallet.
The honest answer depends on which bill stings you more. In Forest Park you pay once, at the lot, and the kids are through the gate and running before the receipt is back in your pocket. In Swope Park the lot costs nothing, and the money changes hands at the ticket window with every kid tugging at your sleeve.
If you have not done the St. Louis side yet, our guide to visiting the Saint Louis Zoo without the parking ambush covers the lot, the rides, the entrances and what you can carry through the gate.
### The free gate and the free lot are the same deal, flipped
The long drive west is behind you, the back seat is a drift of cracker crumbs, and the Swope Park ticket window is finally in view with your wallet already out. Here is the turn. According to the Kansas City Zoo’s Zoological District page, Jackson and Clay counties support the zoo through a 1/8-cent sales tax, paid by anyone, residents and visitors alike, who makes purchases in Jackson or Clay County.
Read that line again with a St. Louis license plate. Grab juice boxes at a store near the zoo, buy the burnt-end sandwich afterward, and you have chipped in to the Kansas City Zoo. Then you pay full price at the gate anyway.
The locals get the break. The zoo’s tickets page lists general admission at $22 to $24 online and $25 to $28 at the gate, with ages 2 and under always free. Jackson and Clay County residents pay $11 to $12 online with ZIP code validation, and the district page adds four free admission days a year through the Postcard to Adventure program. The neighbors who fund it walk in cheap.
Buy online the night before. The gate price is $25 to $28, and that difference for four is a round of drinks at lunch.
### Can a St. Louis Zoo membership cut your Kansas City tickets in half?
Very likely, and plenty of families heading west across the state never think to ask. The Saint Louis Zoo’s own FAQ says it has a reciprocal agreement with many other accredited zoos, and that your membership card entitles you to discounted or free admission at the participating ones. The national AZA reciprocity chart, which the Kansas City Zoo links from its own reciprocity page, lists the Kansas City Zoo & Aquarium at 50%.
Before you load the car, call Kansas City’s Guest Relations at 816-595-1137, card in one hand and phone in the other, and ask two things: how many people does my membership level admit at the discount, and is parking included? The chart flags both. It says the number of visitors admitted with a family membership may vary, that parking may not be included, and that everyone should call ahead. Five minutes on the phone beats a surprise at the window with a toddler on your hip and a line forming behind you.
Now run it. The $80 membership on the Saint Louis Zoo membership page drops your Forest Park parking to $5 a visit for a year. Take the card to Kansas City, and a $25 to $28 window ticket becomes roughly half that. The Kansas City Zoo says reciprocal members do not need to make a reservation: bring the card on the day of your visit and buy the discounted ticket on-site.
### How many animals does the Kansas City zoo have?
Small hands slap the glass at the first big cat, and somebody starts counting out loud. The Kansas City Zoo & Aquarium says it is home to more than 10,000 animals, representing more than 200 species. St. Louis counts 12,000 animals from nearly 450 species. So St. Louis packs in more kinds of animals, and Kansas City gives the ones it has a lot more ground.
You feel that ground in your calves. The zoo’s guest services page puts it at 202 acres and warns that you will be on your feet most of the day. Kansas City is closer to a hike with animals in it.
Then there is the African Sky Safari. The zoo’s rides page says your toes dangle just above zebras, ostriches, giraffes and rhinos, about 40 feet off the ground, on a ride of about seven minutes that lands near the chimpanzees. A round trip is $7. For a nine-year-old, that one ride can be the whole reason to drive.
Somebody in your family is getting married soon. Who’s doing their face?
### Do you have to pay to park at the Kansas City Zoo?
No. The Kansas City Zoo’s hours and parking page says parking is always free, with a drop-off zone right in front of the admission area and handicapped spaces in every lot. Nobody hands you a ticket with a QR code on it.
In St. Louis, the zoo’s parking page sets the non-member fee at $20 per car. In Kansas City, the free lot sits next to a $22 to $24 online ticket for everyone over 2, so it is a nice touch, not a bargain.
In Forest Park, a packed-lunch day costs the lot and nothing at the gate. In Swope Park it costs the tickets, the gas and a long drive home with everyone asleep but you.
### What does the day cost once you are past the gate?
The Gold wristband is $9 for unlimited rides on the railroad, the African Tram and the Endangered Species Carousel. The Platinum is $12 and adds the Sky Safari and the Kenyan Cruise boat ride, which runs weekends only. If the Sky Safari is on your list, the Platinum costs less than the chairlift plus the Gold bought separately.
In St. Louis, the zoo says paid attractions are included in the Adventure Pass; the parent guide prices each one.
Snacks are easy at both. The Saint Louis Zoo’s FAQ says guests may bring strollers, small wagons, picnic baskets, coolers, foods and drinks, with glass bottles and alcohol prohibited. Kansas City’s policies page permits small coolers and ice chests and asks you to leave glass, disposable straws and lids, and balloons at home. Slice the apples the night before, freeze the water bottles so they sweat cold in the cooler by lunch, and either zoo turns into a cheap picnic with a view.
Watch the clock, too. Kansas City opens at 9:30 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m. on weekdays, 5 p.m. on weekends from March through October, and 4 p.m. daily from November through February. It also closes on Martin Luther King Jr. Day and Thanksgiving, two days plenty of families pick for a zoo trip. St. Louis opens at 9 a.m. and, right now, closes at 4 p.m.
### Which trip fits which family
Pick St. Louis if your youngest still naps. The free gate means you can leave at 11:30 with a meltdown brewing and lose nothing but the $20 lot. Pick it, too, if you want the most species in the fewest steps.
Pick Kansas City when the kids are old enough to walk all day and want a ride they will talk about at school. Make it a weekend, buy tickets online or bring your St. Louis membership card, and budget for the Platinum wristband.
Winter tips the scale a little. Kansas City’s guest services page steers cold-weather visitors to its indoor exhibits, including the Sobela Ocean Aquarium, Helzberg Penguin Plaza, Tropics and Polar Bear Passage, and notes that sea lions, river otters, tigers and red pandas enjoy the cooler weather. St. Louis stays open daily year-round, so a cold Tuesday with a thermos of cocoa and almost nobody at the glass is always a free option.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which zoo is better, St. Louis or Kansas City?
A.  For a cheap, flexible day, St. Louis: free admission, 12,000 animals from nearly 450 species, and a $20 parking fee for non-members. Kansas City is better for older kids who want space and rides, with 202 acres and the African Sky Safari, but general admission runs $22 to $24 online.
### Q. How many animals does the Kansas City zoo have?
A.  The Kansas City Zoo & Aquarium says it is home to more than 10,000 animals representing more than 200 species, spread across 202 acres in Swope Park.
### Q. Do you have to pay to park at the Kansas City Zoo?
A.  No. The zoo says parking is always free, with a drop-off zone in front of the admission area and handicapped parking in all lots. You pay for admission instead.
### Q. How much does it cost to go to the Zoo in St. Louis?
A.  Admission to the Saint Louis Zoo is free; the zoo says the Zoo is always free. The main cost is parking, $20 per car for non-members, plus any paid rides. Members at the entry level pay $5 per visit to park.
### Q. Can I bring snacks into St. Louis Zoo?
A.  Yes. The zoo’s FAQ says guests may bring picnic baskets, coolers, foods and drinks. Glass bottles and alcohol are prohibited, so pack drinks in plastic or metal.
### Q. Can you see Zoo animals in the winter?
A.  Yes. The Saint Louis Zoo is open daily year-round, closing only Jan. 1 and Dec. 25. Kansas City is open daily from November through February, and points winter visitors to indoor exhibits like Sobela Ocean Aquarium and Polar Bear Passage.
### Q. What are the top free zoos in the US?
A.  The AZA reciprocity chart marks a handful of accredited zoos free to the public, including the Saint Louis Zoo, the Smithsonian National Zoological Park, Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago, Como Park Zoo and Henry Vilas Zoo.

## Your Pork Steak Sauce Burns at 265 Degrees: Brush It On Last, St. Louis Style
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-bbq-sauce-recipe
Sauce a St. Louis pork steak too early and you will smell it before you see it: sweet going bitter, black creeping along the edges of the meat.
St. Louis knows that smell. A grocer here, Louis Maull, debuted Maull’s Barbecue Sauce in 1926, 22 years before H.J. Heinz would bottle his first barbecue sauce. The city never stopped pouring. St. Louisans, per capita, buy nearly twice as much sauce in a year as average Americans, St. Louis Magazine reports. Not Memphis. Not Kansas City. We are well ahead of both.
“The pork steak is the basis of what makes St. Louis the No. 1 barbecue sauce market,” says Louis Maull V. So the sauce in this recipe is built for that one cut, and it goes on last.
### What is a good St. Louis BBQ sauce recipe?
A good St. Louis BBQ sauce recipe is mostly one ratio: six parts ketchup to one part cider vinegar to one part brown sugar, thinned with water and simmered low for 20 minutes until it runs off the spoon. Yellow mustard, onion powder, garlic powder, cayenne and salt finish it, and nothing in the pot is thick or smoky.
That burnt smell? Blame the sugar. Most barbecue sauces contain it, and by The Spruce Eats’ count sugar burns at about 265 degrees and a grate over hot coals blows right past that. So this thin sauce goes on last, brushed on only over low heat or at the end of cooking. Then comes the good part. The brush crosses the pork steak, the grate hisses, fat pops on the coals, and smoke rolls up past your knuckles.
Turn a burner to low and set a medium saucepan on it. Two cups of ketchup go in, then half a cup of water, a third of a cup of apple cider vinegar and a third of a cup of brown sugar. Add two tablespoons of yellow mustard, a tablespoon each of onion powder and garlic powder, half a teaspoon of cayenne and a quarter teaspoon of salt. Stir now and then for 20 minutes. The kitchen fills with the sharp, sweet steam of hot vinegar and tomato, strong enough to sting your eyes if you lean over the pot.
It should come out thin but not watery: a ribbon off the spoon, not a dollop. The batch makes about 3 1/2 cups. Two cups of ketchup against a third of a cup of vinegar is six to one, the one number worth memorizing. Write it on the inside of a cabinet door and you will never need the card again. (The ratio comes from this St. Louis barbecue sauce recipe.)
Let the pot cool for 20 to 30 minutes and taste it cooled, not straight off the burner: cider vinegar first, sharp at the back of your tongue, brown sugar right behind it. Make it the day before the cookout, because the recipe says it is better after a day in the refrigerator. A squeeze bottle is the handy way to keep it, and it holds up to a week in the fridge or three to four months in the freezer.
### The Pork Steak Gets Sauced Last
Now the meat. Ask the butcher for pork steaks, which are crosscut slabs of Boston butt. Cook the steak until it is nearly done, then slide it to the cooler side of the grill, or wait for the very end, and start brushing. Ribs follow the same rule: ask for St. Louis-style ribs, a squared-off rib slab codified by the USDA, and slather the sauce on three to four times toward the end of cook time. Brush a coat, let it go tacky, brush again, and each layer darkens a shade until the last one shines.
### When the Pot Goes Wrong
Too thick? That happens when the burner creeps past low and the pot reduces faster than you meant. Stir in a splash of water, a spoonful at a time, until it ribbons off the spoon again. Too sharp? Let it cool before you judge it, the way the recipe has you taste it anyway. If it still bites after a night in the fridge, warm it and stir in a little more brown sugar. Too sweet? A splash of cider vinegar pulls it back.
Scorched on the bottom? You will smell it, the same bitter note the grill gave you, and no amount of stirring hides it. Pour the good sauce off the top into a clean pot and leave the black layer behind. When it is right, the squeeze bottle gives a wet little wheeze and lays down a thin red line that settles flat instead of sitting in a bead. One change per batch, written on the tape on the bottle. That is how a recipe turns into a house sauce.
### Why does St. Louis buy so much barbecue sauce?
Start with a grocer and a horse. Louis Maull started out selling groceries from a horse-drawn wagon in 1897, decades before his sauce ever met a bottle. Then look at how the city eats. In Kansas City, people say “let’s go get some” barbecue. In St. Louis, they say “let’s have a barbecue,” and they mean in the yard.
Before a summer weekend, St. Louis Magazine wrote, the shopping list is charcoal, pork steaks and barbecue sauce. Maull put the rest of it in one line: “The best barbecue you can find in St. Louis is not in a restaurant - it’s in your back yard.”
Maull’s formula has 20 ingredients. The pot above keeps the number far lower, and that is the quiet pleasure of making your own: one pot, one ratio, and a bottle in the fridge door with your handwriting on the tape.
### A Second Pot, Modeled on Maull’s
Once the six-to-one pot feels easy, there is a busier version worth a slow afternoon. Steven Raichlen, author of The Barbecue! Bible, wrote that he created a barbecue sauce modeled on Maull’s, and his list empties half the pantry. It starts from 1 1/2 cups of tomato puree and 1/3 cup of distilled white vinegar instead of ketchup and cider. Then come dark corn syrup, brown sugar, Worcestershire sauce and molasses, half a teaspoon of grated lemon zest, 3 tablespoons of fresh lemon juice, a tablespoon of thawed orange juice concentrate and a quarter teaspoon of ground cloves.
Zest a lemon over that pot and the citrus oil reaches your nose before anything else does. The cloves are the part that surprises people. A quarter teaspoon is barely a pinch in your palm, yet it lays a warm, spiced edge under the tomato. Either way, the smoke on your plate still comes off your own coals.
Which pot should you make? The six-to-one batch if you want the taste of a St. Louis backyard. Raichlen’s if you want to know what a long ingredient list feels like on the tongue. Make both once, side by side, and pass the spoons around.
People are asking
### Where can you get St. Louis BBQ downtown?
Sugarfire Smoke House runs a Downtown STL location on Washington Avenue, right next door to the National Blues Museum, with dine-in, carry-out and delivery. Its own page describes glass fire mosaics climbing the columns and a huge neon sign that casts a red glow over the room, with the blues greats pictured in the murals. It is built for office workers, conference-goers and anyone walking out of the museum hungry.
### Why is St. Louis sauce thinner than the Kansas City kind?
Kansas City sauce is the thick one. One barbecue restaurant’s guide to the regional styles describes Kansas City sauce as thick, sweet and tomato-based with a generous hit of molasses, the kind you spoon onto a rib. St. Louis sauce is tangier, thinner and less sweet, and it pours. Whatever smoke reaches your plate comes off your coals, because the St. Louis style has none of the liquid smoke you find in many Kansas City-style sauces. Standing in the sauce aisle? Flip the bottle over and read the label.
The difference comes from the cooking, not just the taste. St. Louis barbecue is usually done by grilling and saucing rather than low and slow, so the brush meets a pork steak that is already sizzling. A thick, sugary sauce would scorch before it soaked in. A thin one slides into the grain, hisses against the grate and sets into a sticky, tangy lacquer.
Sauce on the wedding shirt? The videographer catches it. Here is that price.
### Whose Batch Wins When the Family Argues Over the Sauce?
Maull told St. Louis Magazine that for some people, their barbecue sauce recipe is a very central part of their lives. Anyone who has watched an uncle hover over the grill, tasting off a plastic spoon and refusing to say what is in the jar, knows that is not a joke. So make the base batch this weekend and write the ratio down. Next time, change one thing: more brown sugar for a sweeter house sauce, a splash more vinegar for a sharper one, a pinch more cayenne if your brother-in-law keeps asking where the heat went. Then let the table vote.
Cook first. Brush last. Keep it six to one.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Saint Louis style barbecue?
A.  It is pork, usually ribs or pork steaks, grilled and then sauced rather than cooked low and slow, with a thin, sweet and tangy tomato sauce brushed on near the end. The ribs are a squared-off St. Louis-style slab, and the pork steak is a crosscut slab of Boston butt.
### Q. What is the difference between Kansas City and St. Louis BBQ?
A.  Kansas City sauce is thick, sweet and heavy on molasses, and many Kansas City-style sauces use liquid smoke. St. Louis sauce is thinner, tangier and less sweet, with no liquid smoke. Even the language differs: Kansas City says “let’s go get some” barbecue, while St. Louis says “let’s have a barbecue” at home.
### Q. Will barbecue sauce burn at 225 degrees?
A.  Not usually. Sugar burns at about 265 degrees, so a smoker held below that point lets a late coat of sauce set into a glaze. A hot grill is the real danger, which is why St. Louis cooks brush sauce on over low heat or at the end.
### Q. How do I make my own sauce at home?
A.  Simmer 2 cups of ketchup, 1/2 cup of water, 1/3 cup of cider vinegar and 1/3 cup of brown sugar with mustard, onion powder, garlic powder, cayenne and salt over low heat for 20 minutes. Let it cool, then rest it in the refrigerator for a day. It keeps up to a week chilled.
### Q. What are the four styles of BBQ?
A.  One barbecue restaurant’s guide names Texas, Carolina, Kansas City and Memphis as four of the most iconic regional styles. St. Louis is the backyard style those lists tend to skip: grilled pork, a thin tangy sauce, and a city that buys nearly twice as much sauce per person as the average American.
### Q. Is barbecue sauce good for diabetics?
A.  It depends on how much you use. The homemade recipe on this page has about 6 grams of sugar and 7 grams of carbohydrate in each of its 28 servings. If you manage diabetes, measure the sauce instead of pouring it, and ask your doctor or dietitian how it fits your plan.

## Her ZIP Code, Not Yours: Help for Aging Parents in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/help-for-aging-parents-in-st-louis
The casserole you left in Mom’s fridge on Sunday is still there on Thursday, foil crimped tight, and the pill organizer on her counter still says Tuesday.
You noticed it the way you notice a smell in a house: all at once, and then you can’t stop noticing. The mail stacked unopened by the toaster. The burner knob she swears she turned off. The way she said “I’m fine, honey” a beat too fast. That night you open a laptop at your own kitchen table and type some version of the question every grown child types, and the internet hands you a pile of agencies, acronyms and forms, each one asking for a ZIP code before it will tell you anything.
Here’s the piece nobody puts at the top. In Missouri, one toll-free line, 1-800-235-5503, asks for a ZIP code and connects the caller straight to the Area Agency on Aging for that area. Give it her ZIP, not yours. The help was never really scattered. It’s filed by county lines you never had a reason to learn.
### What to do with elderly parents who can’t take care of themselves?
Call the Area Agency on Aging that covers the place your parent lives. Missouri’s ten agencies work in every county, plus the City of St. Louis, and they are the front door for home-delivered meals, light housekeeping and personal care, rides to the doctor, caregiver support and help sorting out benefits. Have her address, a pen and twenty quiet minutes.
Inside the city limits, that’s the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging at (314) 612-5918. It serves older adults, and adults 18 to 59 with disabilities, who live within the boundaries of the City of St. Louis. Its own list of services reads like a week of worry crossed off: rides for errands to the grocery store and the bank, meals delivered to the home or served at senior centers, help with Medicare, and volunteers who make minor home repairs for city homeowners 60 and older.
Out in St. Louis County the agency is Aging Ahead, and its map runs well past the county line. It covers St. Louis County and three neighboring Missouri counties, Jefferson and Franklin among them, so a mother in Catawissa, a Franklin County village, calls the same Community Options line as a mother anywhere in St. Louis County: (636) 207-0847. Its specialists answer questions about Meals on Wheels, transportation, caregiver support, in-home services, Medicare and Medicaid, long-term care applications, elder abuse and legal services.
Across the river it’s a different state and a different front door. AgeSmart Community Resources is the Area Agency on Aging for seven Illinois counties, among them Madison County, Monroe County and Randolph County, at 618-222-2561. A father in Alhambra, a Madison County village, starts there.
### Why a dad in Dutzow gets his help from Kirksville
This is the part that trips families up, and the real reason the help feels scattered. The agencies are drawn by county, and the places St. Louis families call home spill across more counties than most of us ever count.
Dutzow is a Warren County village, and Warren County belongs to the Northeast Missouri Area Agency on Aging, based in Kirksville, which serves 16 counties in Northeast Missouri. Richwoods sits in a county served by Aging Best, the same agency that covers Boone and Cole counties. New Offenburg is in a county served by Aging Matters, based in Cape Girardeau. Same worry, same casserole in the fridge, three different agencies, and none of them is the one your neighbor in the city told you to call.
You don’t have to memorize any of it. The Missouri Senior Resource Line does the sorting: call 1-800-235-5503, enter the ZIP code, and it connects you to the agency that covers it. That’s the shortcut for the son who lives in Chicago and the daughter who lives ten minutes away, and it works the same for both because it follows her address, not yours.
If your parent lives outside Missouri, the national Eldercare Locator, a public service of the U.S. Administration on Aging, does the same job at 1-800-677-1116. On the Illinois side, the state’s Senior HelpLine is 1-800-252-8966. And if you’re the one living in the city with a parent somewhere else, the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging refers city residents with out-of-state older relatives to the agency on aging where those relatives live.
### What does area agency on aging mean?
It’s a generic term the federal government uses for a nationwide network of nonprofits and public organizations that help seniors, according to the Missouri Association of Area Agencies on Aging. There are more than 620 of them across the country, set up under the Older Americans Act, and Missouri has ten. Each one writes its own area plan from local input, which is why the menu changes a little from one region to the next, and why the honest answer to “does Mom qualify for that?” is usually “ask yours.”
What sits behind that front door is the reason to call. The agencies partner with local providers on home-delivered meals and meals at senior centers, light housekeeping and chores, minor home repairs like grab bars and ramps, rides to doctor visits and grocery shopping, caregiver training and respite, Medicare plan comparisons and Medicaid applications. One item on the statewide list is easy to skip past: telephone reassurance, friendly phone calls to check in with seniors. That’s the phone on Mom’s end table ringing, with somebody kind on the other end who expects her to pick up.
### Before you dial, put these on the table
Make the call from your own kitchen table, coffee going cold, a pen that works and the phone plugged in so it doesn’t die on hold. Missouri’s in-home care assessors use questions like these to decide whether someone is eligible, and the state tells families to be prepared to answer them. Answer them on paper before any call:
Her ZIP code, and the county she lives in.
The specific help she needs now: bathing, dressing, meals, chores or getting to appointments.
How often she needs that help, and how much time each task takes.
Whether anyone holds guardianship or a durable power of attorney for her, with a copy within reach.
Her Medicaid (MO HealthNet) number, date of birth and Social Security number, which the assessor will ask to verify, plus her Medicare card.
Then say the plain thing out loud: “My mother can’t manage alone anymore, and I don’t know what she qualifies for.” That sentence is enough to start the conversation.
### The knock at the door that doubles as a check-in
The sound you’re really asking for is a knock on her storm door, a warm tray in someone’s hands, and a stranger who will notice if she doesn’t answer. In Aging Ahead’s four counties, Meals on Wheels goes to homebound seniors 60 or older who can’t prepare a balanced meal for themselves and can’t get to a congregate meal site. At every visit the volunteer does a well-being check, and family members or emergency personnel are notified if there’s a concern. For many of the seniors on those routes, Aging Ahead says, the volunteer is the only person they’ll come in contact with all day.
Aging Ahead provides its meals without charge, and donations are welcome; request them at 1-800-243-6060. In the city, the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging runs its own Senior Nutrition Program at (314) 612-5918. On the Illinois side, AgeSmart takes Meals on Wheels calls at 618-222-2561.
### What in-home support services are available in Missouri?
For a parent who needs hands-on help, Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services runs Home and Community-Based Services, programs that help older adults live at home rather than moving to a nursing home. Depending on need, the state lists personal care such as bathing, dressing and preparing meals, home-delivered meals, respite care that gives a family caregiver a break, home modifications, transportation for errands, adult day care, and medical supplies like incontinence supplies, lift chairs and walkers. Read that list as a person, not a program: it’s the difference between Mom gripping a towel bar to climb out of the tub alone and a steady hand at her elbow.
The bar is real. Every program requires Medicaid enrollment and a nursing facility level of care, which measures how much help a person needs with everyday tasks like bathing, dressing and getting around. You can start it for her, though. Anyone can make the referral, including a family member, online or by phone at 1-866-835-3505, and an assessor then schedules a face-to-face visit at the house. Watch the phone after that. The assessor tries to reach her once; if nobody answers, a message or letter follows, and there are 10 days to call back before the referral is closed. Make sure her phone can take messages, and that the voicemail isn’t full.
Here’s the detail that changes the math for a lot of families. Under the state’s Consumer Directed Services option, the participant selects, hires and supervises the caregiver, and can hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian. A grown son or daughter can be that hire.
Don’t count on Medicare for the day-to-day. Medicare’s home health benefit doesn’t pay for 24-hour care at home, home meal delivery, homemaker services like shopping and cleaning that aren’t part of a care plan, or personal care such as bathing and dressing when that’s the only care she needs. Our guide to home health care costs in St. Louis walks through what it does pay for.
### If you’re the one doing the lifting
Somewhere in all this there’s you: the drive over after a full shift, the phone pinned to your shoulder on your lunch break, the 2 a.m. arithmetic about whether she took her pills. The agencies serve caregivers too. Aging Ahead’s Family Caregiver Support Program can help unpaid caregivers with in-home respite, adult day services, durable medical equipment, minor home safety changes and incontinence or nutritional supplies, as funding permits; its case managers are at (636) 207-0847. On the Illinois side, AgeSmart’s caregiver specialists offer one-on-one help at 618-222-2561.
If she lives with you, there may be money on the table. Missouri’s Shared Care Tax Credit can be worth up to $500 against your state income tax for the tax year. It’s for the caregiver of someone 60 or older who lives in your home more than six months of the year, whom a physician certifies can’t live alone, and who doesn’t get services paid for by Medicaid. You can’t be paid for the care, and you register with the state each year you claim it. The registration packet comes from the Department of Health and Senior Services at (573) 751-4842.
Found the volunteer, the respite worker or the handyman who made Mom’s house safer? Pass the name on. The next family up the street is typing the same question tonight, and you can join St Louis Near Me Directory to point them to the people who came through for you.
If you’re the home care agency, the handyman who installs grab bars or the adult day program families lean on, they’re already searching for you. Grown children across St. Louis look here for help they can trust, so list your business where more of those customers will see it.
### When you live too far to knock
Distance turns every worry into a phone call you can’t make fast enough. If your parent is here and you aren’t, the Senior Resource Line still sorts by the ZIP code you enter, so enter hers. Ask her agency about telephone reassurance calls and about Meals on Wheels. Between a friendly voice and a knock at the door, she gets two sets of eyes and ears you can’t provide from three states away.
The paperwork travels, too. The first time a Medicare letter confuses either of you, call Missouri SHIP at 1-800-390-3330. It’s the state’s free Medicare help line, formerly called CLAIM, and it doesn’t sell plans. A counselor calls you back within days to set up an appointment or answer the question.
For the nights the phone calls run late: coffee shops open late in St. Louis.
### If she isn’t safe tonight
Some calls can’t wait for an intake appointment. If you believe a parent in Missouri is being abused, neglected or exploited, or is neglecting herself to the point of danger, call the state’s Adult Abuse and Neglect Hotline at 1-800-392-0210. It answers 7 days a week, from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., and you can stay anonymous. Missouri’s Adult Protective Services covers adults 60 and over, and adults 18 to 59 with a disability, who can’t protect their own interests or meet their essential needs.
In Illinois, the statewide Adult Protective Services hotline answers 24 hours a day at 1-866-800-1409. Write both numbers on the inside of a kitchen cabinet door, hers or yours, where the next panicked version of you will find them.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What does the Missouri Department of Health and Senior services do?
A.  Among its jobs, it runs the state’s senior and disability programs. Its Division of Senior and Disability Services is in charge of Home and Community-Based Services, the in-home care programs that help older adults stay at home instead of moving to a nursing home, and its Adult Protective Services program helps adults facing abuse, neglect or exploitation. The abuse hotline is 1-800-392-0210.
### Q. At what age is someone considered a senior citizen in Missouri?
A.  For most of the help on this page, the line is 60. Home-delivered meals through Missouri’s Area Agencies on Aging are for people 60 and older, and the state’s Adult Protective Services covers adults 60 and over, plus adults 18 to 59 with a disability. Other programs set their own ages, so ask the agency about the specific benefit.
### Q. Is Meals on Wheels covered by Medicare?
A.  Not through Medicare’s home health benefit, which lists home meal delivery among the things it doesn’t pay for. Around St. Louis, Meals on Wheels runs through the Area Agencies on Aging instead, and Aging Ahead provides its meals without charge while welcoming donations. Call 1-800-243-6060 in its counties, (314) 612-5918 in the city or 618-222-2561 in Illinois.
### Q. Will Medicare pay for elderly home care?
A.  Only in a narrow case: your parent must need part-time or intermittent skilled services and be homebound. Medicare’s home health benefit doesn’t pay for 24-hour care at home, homemaker services unrelated to a care plan, or personal care like bathing and dressing when that’s the only care someone needs. For that daily help, call the Area Agency on Aging.
### Q. What should I do if my elderly parents refuse help?
A.  Start with respect, because Missouri’s own programs do: they stress a competent adult’s right to make decisions about care, including the right to refuse services. You can still call the Area Agency on Aging as a caregiver and learn the options. If refusing help puts a parent in real danger, report it at 1-800-392-0210, and you can stay anonymous.
### Q. What happens if an elderly person has no one to care for them?
A.  In Missouri, Adult Protective Services can step in when an adult 60 or older can’t protect their own interests or meet their essential needs. The program offers intervention, education and prevention services along with supportive resources. Anyone who suspects someone is being neglected can make a report to 1-800-392-0210, seven days a week.
### Q. What are three signs of caregiver stress?
A.  Three from Aging Ahead’s list: feeling exhausted, overwhelmed or anxious; becoming easily angered or impatient; and having trouble sleeping. The list also includes skipping showers or other personal care, and losing interest in activities you used to enjoy. If you see yourself there, ask its case managers about respite at (636) 207-0847.
### Q. What elderly assistance programs are available in Missouri?
A.  Start with the ten Area Agencies on Aging, reached through 1-800-235-5503, for meals, chores, rides and caregiver support. The state adds Medicaid-funded in-home care through Home and Community-Based Services. Missouri SHIP gives free Medicare help at 1-800-390-3330, and the Shared Care Tax Credit is worth up to $500 for family caregivers.
